## Volume Front Matter

### Series Title Page

# Patrologia Latina, Volume 150

## Complete Course of Patrology, or Universal Library

Complete, uniform, convenient, economical library of all the holy Fathers, Doctors, and ecclesiastical writers who flourished from the apostolic age to the time of Innocent III; a chronological reprinting of all surviving monuments of Catholic tradition from the first twelve centuries of the Church, prepared with the greatest care from the most accurate editions and collated with one another and with several manuscript codices; continually illustrated by dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged with all works discovered after the ample editions produced during the last three centuries; furnished with separate analytical indexes following each volume and each author of importance; adorned with chapters properly arranged within the text itself, as well as with titles distinguishing the upper margin of every page and indicating its subject matter; expanded by works both doubtful and apocryphal, and by works possessing some authority in relation to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with two general indexes: one of subjects, by consulting which whatever each Father has written on any topic may be seen at a glance; the other of Sacred Scripture, from which it is readily apparent to the reader which Fathers, and in what places in their works, have commented on the text of each individual book of Scripture.

A most accurate edition, and one easily preferable to all others if the clarity of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the perfection of the correction, the variety and number of the reprinted works, the highly convenient format of the volumes, consistently similar throughout the whole work, and the low price are taken into consideration—above all, this collection, single, methodical, and chronological, of six hundred fragments and minor works hitherto scattered here and there, but now brought together for the first time in our library from works belonging to every age, place, language, and form.

## Second Series

In which appear the Fathers, Doctors, and ecclesiastical writers of the Latin Church from Gregory the Great to Innocent III. Edited by J.-P. Migne, publisher of the Universal Library of the Clergy, or of complete courses in each branch of ecclesiastical learning.

Patrology has been printed in two editions, one Latin and the other Greek-Latin. The two hundred volumes of the Latin edition are sold for one thousand francs; the eight hundred volumes of the Greek-Latin edition for one thousand three hundred francs. The purely Latin edition embraces all authors, both Western and Eastern; the Eastern authors, however, are presented in it only in Latin translation.

# In the Year of Our Lord 1089

## Blessed Lanfranc, Archbishop of Canterbury and Primate of England

# Prolegomena

[Col. 0009]

## To the Most Serene Prince of Conti, Armand de Bourbon

[Col. 0009A]

The sharpest grief was piercing my heart, most serene prince, when I saw the great Lanfranc, that most splendid eye of the world, lying foul beneath decay and squalor, covered with the thickest darkness and suffering a perpetual eclipse—he who once shone among the other lights of the world with the torches both of learning and of holiness:

> Like Lucifer dispersing the fleeing stars,  
> when with his rosy face he brings forth the bright day.  
> [Note: [Col. 0009C] William of Malmesbury, book III of *The Deeds of the Kings of the English*, speaking of Lanfranc.]

But now, through the divine breath, an end is being put to my complaints, while night is driven out and the darkness of shadows dispelled, and a most brilliant star rises in our West and revisits France, so that by the light of his wisdom he may scatter the mists of error.

Indeed, that supreme Governor of his Church [Col. 0009B] acted at the proper time when, in this age, he raised Lanfranc, as though restored from the tomb of oblivion, so that in this age he might strike down with the weapon of his teaching the revived hydra of heresy—not rising from the Lernaean marsh, but emerging from Lake Geneva—as he once pierced the faithless Berengar.

Therefore, about to fight once more with the most hostile enemies of the faith, he descends again into the arena and seeks as his protector a prince in whose bosom and under whose guardianship he may fight bravely, win gloriously, and rest with confidence. Accordingly, he withdraws himself to you, in whom alone he will find abundantly everything he could desire for the security of the struggle, the hope of victory, and the celebration of triumph.

The splendor of royal birth will give him adornment, piety refuge, [Col. 0009C] humanity favor, learning defense, justice support, and virtue strength.

Nor can anyone be troubled that I have chosen you as the defender of this divine work, if only he understands that I observed the virtues of our Lanfranc shining in you as in a most polished mirror. Thus I ceased grieving that France had been deprived of Lanfranc when I perceived that all of him survives in you, and recognized in you those qualities which the whole world once admired and honored in him, and which deserve to be revered in you with equal honor.

These qualities, expressed not in my own features but in your colors [Col. 0010A] and transmitted to all posterity, the memory of the ages will contemplate with exceptional admiration.

Blessed Lanfranc, phoenix of genius and wonder of his age, attained such learning and erudition as earlier centuries had scarcely seen in anyone and later centuries could admire more readily than imitate. To him, as to another Solomon, not only from the farthest regions of France but also from the most distant provinces of Europe, the most celebrated men flocked in great numbers, to gaze upon that vast theater of divine wisdom. [Note: [Col. 0010C] Milo Crispin, in the *Life of Blessed Lanfranc*; Malmesbury, book I of the *Lives of the Bishops of England*; the Chronicle of Bec.]

He transferred Athens to the monastery of Bec and summoned the glory of Roman eloquence into France. His school was a workshop of wisdom for all Europe, or a Trojan horse from which the most distinguished [Col. 0010B] leaders of learning emerged for the benefit and adornment of the Christian commonwealth. When he thundered, Greece trembled, Italy groaned, and France triumphed.

In the same way, your singular learning, most serene prince, has presented you as a spectacle to the whole world and turned everyone’s minds and eyes toward you. For who has not admired, even to astonishment, your mind—winged by a kind of fire, which no difficulty can hold back; the keenness of your spirit, for which nothing is inaccessible; and the fertility of your intellect, overflowing like a torrent?

From childhood happily nourished on the substance of the liberal arts, you became a most splendid sanctuary of Minerva. While your brother, greater than Caesar, the most invincible prince, the thunderbolt of arms, the terror of Germany and Belgium, the pillar of France, followed the camps of Mars [Col. 0010C]—indeed, being another Mars, he cut down the military laurels with his sword—you, pursuing the gentler camp of Minerva, gathered the laurels and palms of the arts in the studies of the contemplative life.

Those first achievements appeared like torches of your rising intellect, with which you shone forth as a prelude to greater things. In the vigor of your intellect, your youth flew through the celebrated encyclopedia of the ancients, and within a short time you reached the highest summit of the sciences. Supported by the wings of your heavenly intellect, you penetrated into the more hidden mysteries of theology.

Although you adorn your mind greatly with the noblest arts and [Col. 0011A] sciences, what they have contributed to you is nevertheless less than the adornment they have received from you. By a kind of participation in your royal blood, you have made them royal and raised them to such a height of dignity that, just as you surpass every honor and dignity, so nothing of honor or excellence can be added to them through you.

The singular learning of Blessed Lanfranc detracted nothing from his virtue and piety. Rather, by a mutual bond of friendship and an exchange of shared fellowship, he joined piety to learning. His life was an image of the most brilliant virtues, a standard of conduct, and a condemnation of vices. He labored continually to tame the monsters of error, crush the portents of heresies, and eradicate vices.

He restored in his order the original vigor of Benedictine observance [Col. 0011B] and, as his biographer Milo Crispin says, “reformed the monastic order, which had fallen into lay dissolution, according to the most approved discipline of monasteries.” Thus he supported the order when it was collapsing, roused it when it was sluggish, nurtured it when it was being reborn, and strengthened it when it had matured.

In this matter, most serene prince, you have undertaken no dissimilar labor. There is no need to prove at length what has had the sun itself as witness. We ourselves are the clearest monument of your virtue, and in our own experience have learned how devotedly you labored to restore the Benedictine order, with what goodwill you embraced our congregation, with what generosity you adorned it, and with what care you extended it.

That it was recently increased by the addition of three monasteries [Col. 0011C] it owes to you. That it flourishes is your doing. That it remains unshaken it owes to you. If we do not recognize the grace of so great a benefaction, we are blind; if we do not confess it, we are ungrateful.

Nor is your piety confined within these narrower boundaries. It spreads more widely and overflows for the common good of the whole Church, which will find in you a more powerful protection in proportion as the splendor of royal blood has raised you higher.

I would enumerate the other qualities by which you resemble Blessed Lanfranc, were I not restrained by that modesty of spirit which you share with Lanfranc. [Col. 0012A] They are the qualities that display Lanfranc alive in you before our eyes and compelled me to present him as belonging uniquely to you: a most distinguished theologian to the leader of the theologians of this age; a restorer of the order to its most devoted propagator; a prince of royal stock to a prince.

I certainly did not call Lanfranc a prince rashly:

> “When the king was absent, he was prince and guardian of England, with all the princes subject to him and assisting him in matters concerning the defense, administration, or peace of the kingdom according to the laws of the country.”  
> [Note: [Col. 0011C] The same Milo and Malmesbury, in the passages cited above.]

Therefore, I hope that you will admit this most illustrious prince—as I hope—with the same humanity with which you receive even the lowliest. Pope Alexander so greatly revered his learning [Col. 0012B] that, as a mark of singular goodwill, he honored him with a double pallium and scarcely allowed himself to be separated from his tender embrace. [Note: [Col. 0011C] The same authors, in the passages cited.]

You will grant your favor to one whom princes received magnificently, kings held among their favorites, prelates honored with the greatest respect, and whom England—indeed, the whole world—sought with anxious prayers.

Behold that tree, tall in stature, excellent in appearance, luxuriant in the abundance of its fruits, shown from heaven to Blessed Herluin [Note: [Col. 0012C] Gilbert Crispin, in the *Life of Blessed Herluin*]. King William, excessively jealous of our glory, uprooted it from the rich soil of our France and planted it in the garden of the English kingdom. But today, restored by you to its native soil, it recovers its former fruitfulness and, reviving for the honor and benefit of our people, more firmly rooted in its own ground, grows more happily, matures more nobly, [Col. 0012C] and spreads more abundantly.

Therefore, whenever posterity names Lanfranc, it will remember your generosity. Meanwhile, we shall inscribe this immortal gift of grace deeply upon our hearts, so that the memory of your benefactions may live immortally among us. I, in the name of the entire congregation of Saint Maur, promise and profess this.

Your most devoted and most dutiful petitioner,

**F. Lucas d’Achery**, Benedictine monk of the same congregation.

# To the Reader

[Col. 0011D]

It is so, reader: I would never have undertaken to publish the works of the great Lanfranc, much less to illuminate them with notes, had not my superiors, on whose command I wholly depend, and several other learned men, earnestly urged me to do so, both orally and in writing.

Indeed, knowing my own ignorance, necessarily interrupted by monastic exercises and therefore able to devote myself only to studies pursued intermittently, who could bring so noble a work to light worthily and in proportion to the importance of its subject, adorning it with notes and observations?

This is the reason, kind reader, why I have delayed so long to publish the works of that most blessed archbishop [Col. 0012D], and why I have perhaps not responded as quickly or successfully as some desired. However it may be, I ask you to judge favorably and generously what I have contributed in good faith.

It will not be out of place briefly to explain what we have accomplished in this edition. We placed at the beginning of Lanfranc’s works the Life of Blessed Lanfranc which we had previously published. Yet the author seems to have omitted much that is most worthy of notice and pleasing in its variety, and that makes the man’s knowledge, learning, piety, and wisdom more impressive. Because of our singular devotion to this most holy teacher, we were especially pleased to collect such material from various contemporary or nearly contemporary writers [Col. 0013A] and insert it in notes and observations.

To these we added the foundations and privileges of the monasteries of Saint Stephen and of the Most Holy Trinity at Caen; Lanfranc was their author and, so to speak, their founder. They were in the greatest danger, as we have indicated in their proper places, and many learned men had expressly desired these materials. Finally, we adorned the notes with monuments of no little worth, struggling in dust and decay.

The labors on the Epistles of Blessed Paul occupy the first place because of the dignity of the work. Our author regularly brings forward and prefers to his own opinion Saints Ambrose and Augustine, while citing Saint Jerome and Gregory the Great only twice or three times.

We cited the passages of Blessed Augustine, with very few exceptions. As for Saint Ambrose, we were unable to cite him at all. Although we labored long and hard to find them, not a single word of the passages cited by Blessed Lanfranc could be found among the works attributed to Ambrose. This applies chiefly from the Epistle to the Romans through the Epistle to the Galatians.

For in the Epistles to the Romans and Corinthians, some words produced under the name of Saint Ambrose occur in a Commentary wrongly attributed to him. They do not appear consecutively; rather, one or another line seems to have been taken at intervals from within half a page, and sometimes only two or three words.

Hence I strongly suspect that in the age of Blessed Lanfranc there existed Commentaries of Saint Ambrose which have not survived to our time, or which are hidden somewhere. Antonius Possevinus, in the *Sacred Apparatus*, does not reject this conjecture when speaking of these Commentaries:

> “It is now generally believed by learned men,” he says, “that the Commentaries on the Epistles of Paul which have been printed are not Ambrose’s, and that the genuine ones have perished.”

You will also recognize in this same Commentary of Lanfranc certain sentences which bear the name of Ambrose but are in fact Augustine’s. For example, on page 128, in the Epistle to the Galatians, at the words of chapter 3, “But the Mediator,” and “If the Son of God by nature,” and likewise on page 129: “But the Conclusion concluded.” Also, in chapter 4 of the same Epistle, page 131: “The elements,” that is, “the times of servitude,” and so forth.

These passages occur in Augustine’s *Book of Exposition of the Epistle to the Galatians*, before the middle of the work. I thought these matters should be pointed out so that, if you encounter anything of this kind, reader, you may understand that such passages were indiscriminately and carelessly assigned by a copyist to Blessed Ambrose.

To go through everything, restore it precisely, and compare the passages borrowed by Lanfranc from both Doctors would require immense labor—indeed, labor perhaps exceeding human strength—and might well prove fruitless.

The writing was so faded and minute, though written in a contemporary and not inelegant hand, that it sometimes escaped the eye. Moreover, the Commentary was in many places defaced by erasures, was not free from errors, and its margins were burdened with obscure asterisks and obeli. Much material was written obliquely and transversely, so that the order of the Epistles’ text was not preserved. Instead, the material drawn from a single author on each page—for example, from Saint Augustine—was arranged continuously in reverse order.

Nevertheless, since no other exemplar could be supplied, although I had written to learned men and antiquarians in various regions, especially Englishmen, Normans, and Belgians, and had inspected many libraries in Paris, I applied every care, labor, study, and finally every resource of ingenuity so that this Commentary might be published as accurately as possible, with its sentences repeatedly brought back to the file and anvil.

Even so, this effort could not prevent errors from creeping in, both here and in the Appendix, because the typesetters did not always conduct themselves with sufficient care and diligence.

An interlinear gloss existed in the autograph. Since it seemed likely to create obscurity—it sometimes explains a letter grammatically—we decided to publish it in an inserted form, unfolding the words more explicitly. Yet I have not departed by so much as a fingernail, as the saying goes, from the author’s thought or the meaning of his words.

As far as I was permitted and able to determine, I transcribed Lanfranc’s genuine words. Where I could not explain the letters or the meaning, I inserted dots in place of words; and whenever I added anything more obscure, I placed conjectures in the margin.

We collated the passages of divine Scripture with the commonly used Bibles, and the sentences of Blessed Augustine with the Antwerp edition, the most carefully corrected of all. As for Saint Ambrose, we were able to make no collation, for the reasons given above.

Because Blessed Lanfranc almost continuously corrects the text with his gloss, we suppressed the gloss where it offered merely a simple correction and followed the Vulgate itself in our edition, except for a few readings which entered inadvertently—for example, *holocaustomata* instead of *holocautomata*, although the two words have the same sound.

In that Commentary, the author pursued brevity chiefly for two reasons, in my opinion. The first is that at that time, and for a long period before it, commentators on divine matters interpreted Sacred Scripture **λακωνικῶς**—laconicly, concisely. The second is that this man, thoroughly skilled in the knowledge of divine contemplation, knew from experience that understanding the divine Scriptures requires little study but very much meditation.

The passages copied from Peter Lombard’s labors on Paul and added by us at the beginning of the Commentaries seem to indicate that Lanfranc published another work on the Apostle’s Epistles, since, apart from the final two passages, they do not appear in these Commentaries.

Perhaps that work remains buried under dust, gnawed away by cockroaches and moths. Since no one anywhere appears to support my doubt, the Commentary that we are publishing will meanwhile be a consolation to us.

The treatise *On the Sacrament of the Eucharist*—which has been published many times in revised editions—was first brought to light by Francis Carreus, or Quadratus, a monk of Bec, as he himself demonstrates in the dedicatory letter prefixed to his edition, which we have also prefixed to the treatise.

But when I noticed in Carreus’s edition the profession of Berengar made before Pope Gregory VII, together with certain words preceding and following it—from “After these things concerning Gregory VII” to “But when under Nicholas”—I was moved by the conjecture that these passages had been added by the publisher.

For I was aware that Blessed Lanfranc had stated, in his third letter to Pope Alexander, that he had composed his treatise *On the Body and Blood of the Lord against Berengar* while serving as abbot at Caen. It was also established that Gregory was not created pope at the same time, but more than three [Col. 0015B] years later, when Lanfranc was already seated in the see of Canterbury. Therefore, it seemed that Lanfranc could not have inserted that profession into his booklet.

Then, after comparing the Treatise with three manuscripts belonging to the Royal, Bec, and Petau libraries, as well as with all the editions that came to hand, and finding not even the smallest syllable of such a profession, my suspicion increased.

Nevertheless, there is no reason for us to assert that the passages we have printed are additions. It is entirely plausible that Blessed Lanfranc himself added them and worked to make the booklet fuller and more correct, since most authors frequently revise works they have already published.

I shall not linger here in praising this golden work. Writers have already said more than enough about it, and we too have recorded many things about it in our observations. We purged it of the errors with which it abounded, divided the booklet into chapters, and adorned its margins with citations, first comparing them with manuscript or printed codices.

Next follow the decrees for the Order of Saint Benedict. We discussed the short notes on Cassian in the observations on the Life, pages 41 and 252. These decrees had been printed only once, by Clement Reyner, an English Benedictine who was equally learned and devout, but the edition was everywhere filled with obliterated characters and errors caused by scribal carelessness.

We corrected them as far as possible, since no manuscript codex was found. We distinguished most of the material by colons, commas, and periods, and divided several chapters—those made unwieldy by their length—into various sections.

Indeed, to say what I think, they do not everywhere reflect the gravity and majesty of the archbishop’s style. I know that elegant expressions should not be expected in this kind of writing. For that reason I suspect that many decrees were assembled there by a compiler. The passages in chapter 2, section 2, page 257, marked “D.,” seem to demonstrate this, where Lanfranc himself is cited:

> “Let them sing the morning praises”—the Decrees of Lanfranc.

Likewise, chapter 8, section 1, prescribes that on the day when the cellarer renders the account of the reckoning, he should provide the brothers with a festive dinner. This would plainly be unbecoming to a holy man devoted to the strictest abstinence, and to monks observing the holy Rule who were devoting all their efforts to repairing monastic discipline.

Moreover, Selden, in his preface to Eadmer’s History, confirms that the restoration of the solitary life preserved in the Benedictine college at Cambridge is not different from the Decrees, or, as they are called, the Ceremonies.

As for the letters, we used the very exemplar mentioned by Cardinal Baronius in volume II of the *Ecclesiastical Annals*, under the year 1070. He inserted several of them, since they concerned sacred history, into those same Annals. After reporting Lanfranc’s letter addressed to Alexander II, he says:

> “Thus far the letter to Pope Alexander, which I received, together with others, from my very close friend in Christian charity, Nicholas Faber of Paris,” and so forth.

The same Selden, in the passage cited above, testifies that Faber received his copy from the famous Cotton Library in England.

The most learned Sirmond most generously shared that copy with us, and it is chiefly this one that we used in our edition. Assistance was also provided by a copy of the same letters—if I am not mistaken, from the monastery of Saint Stephen at Caen—sent by the highly learned Rouen canon John le Prévôt.

I excerpted one or two letters from the Life of Blessed Lanfranc and from Eadmer’s History. The thirty-seventh letter, of which both copies contained only the opening, was sent in full by the same le Prévôt [Col. 0016C], as we have noted in its proper place.

It is obvious that Lanfranc wrote many other letters, since his learning, virtue, prudence, and holiness had resounded throughout almost all Europe, and he was consulted by supreme pontiffs, bishops, princes, and people of every condition.

Yet we were unable to find even one letter written by him before he assumed the mitre. These were undoubtedly buried beneath the ruins when, around the year 1624, that exceedingly rich and wholly venerable library of Bec collapsed—a disaster to learned men of immense magnitude—for there the manuscripts composed and corrected with care and diligence by both Blessed Lanfranc and Saint Anselm had been carefully preserved.

[Col. 0016D]

We added notes and observations and, insofar as it was permitted us and circumstances required, inserted ancient monuments that had hitherto been disfigured by decay and squalor and treated with contempt. I hope that these will not be unwelcome to investigators curious about ancient matters.

Nevertheless, I greatly wish that some of them might be erased by a kindly hand, especially the passage on page 338, where I stated that I had produced from very ancient parchments a formula for announcing the death of a deceased monk. For I have learned that this very formula had long before been committed to the press and prefixed to the works of Marbod, Bishop of Rennes.

Nor, I ask, should you be angry with me because I may perhaps seem to have gathered monastic matters together rather frequently whenever an opportunity arose. Two causes especially impelled me to do so.

The first required it—as is self-evident—that I should generally treat these matters. The second was that learned men of no ordinary attainments had repeatedly approached me, both in person and in writing, and had instituted various discussions calling into question certain matters concerning the antiquity and splendor of the Benedictine order: for example, the ancient and universal observance of the Rule in Gaul, and the eminent men in holiness and learning who are usually counted among the members of that order.

To satisfy them, since a very rich harvest of material presented itself, I thought it necessary to extend my discussion further.

Certainly, before undertaking to arrange this work with notes and observations, I repeatedly reflected that I would undoubtedly be beaten by the claws and erasures of certain critical readers [Col. 0017B]. For I had always been sufficiently aware that men of the highest renown in speaking and outstanding in learning have long endured the erasing sponges of their critics.

What wonder, then, if this should happen to me as I air the first fruits of my labor? Indeed, even Christ himself did not succeed in satisfying everyone.

> I am greatly mistaken if I seek to please everyone.  
> He who was able to do everything lacked this one gift.

But in truth, if a prudent and learned reader should notice anything worthy of attention, I earnestly ask him to inform me by word or letter. I shall accept his admonitions with a submissive and willing mind, and, in a revised edition—if God grants me life and leisure [Col. 0017C]—I shall not hesitate to correct and reconsider whatever he points out as requiring amendment. For I know that it is written: “Whoever hates correction hates wisdom.” I would not wish to belong to that class of men who, whatever comes into their mouths or whatever work they have cobbled together rather than fashioned, immediately exalt it and consider it worthy of no one’s criticism; indeed, so that everyone may approve and read them, they put themselves on display.

There follows, after the letters, the passage of the speech delivered by blessed Lanfranc at the Council of London. I think Malmesbury borrowed it from Lanfranc’s Ecclesiastical History. The later place is occupied by the little work On Concealing Confession. I must confess that, when it first came into my hands, I was not persuaded that this was truly the offspring of our illustrious archbishop: the meaning of the words seemed rather obscure, the sentences involved, and the opinions unfamiliar in our age. My mind therefore recoiled from numbering such a work among the writings of so great a man, who expresses himself so richly, elegantly, and clearly in his other writings. But when I examined the words more closely, observed the sense, and weighed the opinions with an impartial balance, I found that these opinions were neither singular nor alien to those of the other theologians; indeed, I observed that all the authors whom I had consulted, both those of equal standing and those of middling rank, followed the same path, as has been demonstrated in its proper place. I do not deny, however, that in some passages the meaning is abstruse and cannot be explained without difficulty. I think that anyone who reads through the other writings of Blessed Lanfranc will recognize that this must be attributed to the fault and ignorance of the copyists [Col. 0018A].

Nor, I think, will it seem strange to you, reader, that the great Lanfranc, celebrated by almost all writers as rich in such varied learning and in the highest erudition, left posterity very few monuments of his ability and expertise. Before he was invested with the office of archbishop, he devoted his time, labor, and study to educating the young, lecturing on various authors, teaching theology, and refuting, both publicly and in writing, the Berengarian heresy. Afterwards, when he assumed the weighty burden of the primacy, he gave himself entirely to it; and in settling the controversies of the Church and promoting peace, in correcting and polishing to the utmost both sacred books [Col. 0018B] and the writings of the holy Fathers, which the ignorance of ecclesiastics and the incompetence of scribes had corrupted, he expended immense labor and toil. These matters are treated at length in his Life, letters, and observations on both works. In a similar way, many men of distinguished learning from the Benedictine family, occupied with various ecclesiastical duties, were unable to compose many writings. You, candid reader, favor our efforts and comply with our wishes; and if you should discover that the Commentary on the Psalms and the Ecclesiastical History—or, as others prefer to call it, the Life of William the Conqueror—of that great archbishop is hidden somewhere, I ask and implore you to inform me by letter.

We have appended an appendix chiefly to adorn the works of blessed Lanfranc. At its beginning you will encounter the Chronicle of Bec, which I thought should be included for the sake of the completeness of the work, because this blessed archbishop was, together with Blessed Herluin, the founder of that monastery; and in it he laid the finest foundations of monastic discipline. There he first opened schools and imbued his pupils with such exceptional knowledge and learning that, raised to the highest dignities of the Church, they might illuminate the entire ecclesiastical world by their brilliance. This continued for many centuries afterward. Witnesses are those who devoted themselves to piety and learning in the academy of Bec: Pope Alexander II; the archbishops Anselm and Theobald of Canterbury; Guimundus of Aversa and William of Rouen; the bishops Ivo of Chartres; Hernostus and Gundulf of Rochester; Fulk of Beauvais; Richard and Geoffrey of Évreux; and Turold of Bayeux; and, among the many abbots, Gilbert Crispin of Westminster; Paul of St Albans; Lanfranc, nephew of St Wandrille; Michael and Vincent of Prato; Roger and Geoffrey of Jumièges; John of Bouleia and John Ribaldus of Cerisy; Bernard and Robert, surnamed “of the Mount,” of St Michael in Peril of the Sea, or of the Tomb; and Robert le Tellier of Saint-Evroult, otherwise called of Ouche. Hence, whatever virtue, whatever glory, whatever is worthy of praise and usefulness was found in them, and whatever benefit accrued through them to the Catholic Church, all writers assert must be referred to Lanfranc as their father and teacher. Blessed Herluin sufficiently indicates this when, with outpourings of prayer and tears, he obtained that holy man from God and acquired him for his monastery, so that the monks might be instructed by him in monastic observances and adhere to them perpetually [Col. 0019A]. This is also revealed by the Lives of both men and by the Chronicle of Bec, as well as by the fact that Lanfranc presided as teacher in the schools of this monastery, and that pupils flocked to him from almost all Gaul, England, Italy, and Germany as to a restorer of learning. From these examples one may infer how successfully matters ordinarily proceed for a religious community that cultivates piety as equally as knowledge and applies its mind with keen dedication to acquiring both; for wisdom dwells there, and with it all good things.

This Chronicle was excerpted from a papyrus codex [Col. 0019B], written so corruptly that it could scarcely be read and transcribed except with labor and tedium almost beyond description [vix, E. P.]. It was teeming with errors; contractions of words were extremely frequent and obscure, and many words had been inverted. Consequently, we were often compelled to use conjectures. The author does not maintain a consistent or uniform manner of writing, but repeatedly changes his style, especially up to his own time—as will be clear to anyone who examines it. For he has plundered many passages word for word from the deeds of Blessed Herluin and Lanfranc and of the abbots of Bec, occasionally cutting out or adding a few words. His intention was to refashion this Chronicle, patched together, as they say, with crude skill and stained by the barbarism of its age, in a more elegant style. But friends—very learned men and lovers of antiquity—dissuaded him from this plan, since historical truth and unknown facts in such monuments require neither embellishment nor verbal allurements. Moreover, since that author compiled most of his account from the Bec archives, this is the reason why we have altered absolutely nothing. We have added a brief appendix to the Chronicle, so that the entire succession of the abbots of Bec might be displayed to the reader.

At the urging of those same friends, we have added [Col. 0020A] the Lives of the first four abbots of Bec (I deliberately omitted the Life of Blessed Anselm, since it has been printed many times), together with a Commentary on that Chronicle. For I preferred to publish them whole rather than stitch various fragments into our observations, as John Picard, a regular canon of Saint-Quentin at Beauvais, who deserved exceptionally well of learned men both during his life and after his death, formerly did in his annotations on the letters of Blessed Anselm.

We publish the Life of Saint Augustine, apostle of the English, first archbishop of Canterbury and primate of all Britain, rescued from the ruins and dust of the aforesaid library, since it would very often have to be produced as evidence for the primacy of the Church of Canterbury over that of York [Col. 0020B]. The characters indicate that it was written by a copyist contemporary with Blessed Lanfranc.

Finally, we thought it appropriate to append to the appendix two treatises, On the Sacrament of the Eucharist against Berengar, not unworthy of publication and not unrelated to the subject. Their authors are Hugh, bishop of Langres, and Durand, abbot of Troarn, both contemporaries of blessed Lanfranc. These two most valiant soldiers of the Catholic Church fought under the same banner; they entered the same contest, attacked the same enemy, and conquered him. We have prefixed testimonies concerning Hugh and Durand to the beginning of each work; consult them if you wish. It will be worthwhile merely to know that the passage which begins on page 102, section D, “One bread, one body,” and so forth [Col. 0020C], is found in Saint Bede, in his commentary on 1 Corinthians 10, and not at all in Saint Augustine; although the words that follow immediately afterward, namely, “If anyone eats of this bread,” and so forth, may be read in Augustine’s Treatise 26 on John. Enjoy this modest labor of ours, Christian reader, and farewell in the Lord, to whom alone be honor and glory forever. Amen.

[Col. 0019]

# LIFE OF BLESSED LANFRANC, ARCHBISHOP OF CANTERBURY

By Milo Crispin, monk and cantor of Bec, his contemporary.

(Mabillon, *Acts of the Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict*, sixth century, part II.)

[Note: [Col. 0057D] The list prefixed to the beginning of the manuscript codex—from which I took that Life—taught me that the author of the Life of Blessed Lanfranc was Milo Crispin. That he was a contemporary of Saint Anselm he himself makes sufficiently clear at the end of the same Life. After recounting how a deacon had been freed from demonic servitude through the merits of Blessed Lanfranc, he adds: “I heard this, together with others, from the archbishop Saint Anselm, who related it.” It is also established from the same catalogue that this very author wrote the Lives of the abbots of Bec who immediately followed Saint Anselm. Its words are these [Col. 0058D]: “Gilbert Crispin, monk of Bec and abbot of Westminster, published the Life of Saint Herluin. Edmer, a monk of Canterbury, published the Life of Saint Anselm. Milo Crispin, cantor of Bec, composed the Lives of the others, namely Lanfranc, William, Boso, Theobald, and Letard.” Hence it is clear that Milo prolonged his life to an advanced old age, since, being a contemporary of Blessed Anselm, he described the deeds of Abbot Letard, whom the Chronicle of Bec records as having departed this life in the year 1149.]

## PRELIMINARY OBSERVATIONS

[Col. 0019D] 1. Milo, a monk and cantor of the monastery of Bec, born of the noble family of the Crispins, concerning which we have spoken in the observations on the Life of Blessed Herluin, committed the Life of blessed Lanfranc to writing. We infer his period from this very Life, where, in chapter 14, speaking of blessed Lanfranc’s deacon, who had been seized by a demon, he says: “I heard this, together with many others, from Blessed Anselm, the archbishop” [Col. 0020D]. Although we do not doubt that he was alive before Lanfranc’s death, it is nevertheless probable that he never saw Lanfranc, as is clear from his prologue, where he says that he excerpted what he is about to relate from the Life of Herluin, or at least from what he “had heard from venerable and truthful men.” A little farther on [Col. 0021A] he adds: “Of these matters, indeed, I was not able to hear everything that ought to be told.” There is no doubt that, if he had ever been granted the opportunity to hear or see Lanfranc himself, he would not have concealed that fact, since it would have lent authority to his narrative.

2. There are many things that greatly commend Lanfranc’s merits, both in monastic affairs, in learning, and in the universal Church. To begin with monastic matters, the distinguished monastery of Bec owes him, if not its foundation, at least its growth and stability. No other witness need be summoned for this matter apart from Herluin himself, who asserted that he had asked God with many tears and obtained Lanfranc, so that his monastery—whose proper establishment the holy man considered himself unequal to—might be strengthened by Lanfranc’s counsel and work. “Many times,” he said, addressing Lanfranc himself, “with great groaning I asked God, and with abundant tears I implored divine mercy, that he might grant me such a man, by whose counsel and assistance I might reform this place and restore for the use of the monks those things that were pleasing to God. And when God brought you here, Brother Lanfranc, I believed that the prayers of my humility had been heard.” In fact, the outcome did not disappoint Herluin’s hope; through Lanfranc’s work the monastery of Bec rose from the smallest number of monks to become famous for its monks, distinguished in piety and learning, and also for its abundance of temporal goods, as will become clearer from the continuation of the Life.

What shall we say of the two monasteries at Caen? Lanfranc arranged for one of them, dedicated to Saint Stephen, for monks, and the other, dedicated to the Holy Trinity, for nuns, to be built and endowed by Duke William. Since Lanfranc had refused to approve the prince’s unlawful marriage, he obtained that the matter be referred to the Roman pontiff for the purpose of securing a dispensation. The pope granted it, through Lanfranc’s agency as William’s own representative, on the condition that two monasteries be founded in expiation of the offense. Both still remain under our order. Acherius of our congregation, in his notes on the Life of Lanfranc, and Arthur du Monstier, in *Neustria Pia*, discuss them at length. Of these monasteries, Saint Stephen’s for men had for some years been attached to our congregation of Saint Maur [Col. 0021D].

Concerning the foundation of this monastery, and Lanfranc, whom William, its founder, appointed its first abbot, Peter of Poitiers, a contemporary author, speaks as follows in his *Deeds of William*: “William cherished Lanfranc, a certain man about whom it was disputed whether he deserved greater reverence and glory for his singular mastery of secular and divine letters or for his singular observance of the monastic order, with profound intimacy: he revered him as a father, feared him as a teacher, and loved him as a brother or child. To him he entrusted the care of his soul; to him he entrusted a kind of watchtower from which the ecclesiastical orders throughout Normandy might be overseen. For the vigilant care of such a man, possessing the greatest authority together with the distinction of wisdom and holiness, could promise no small security to the finest solicitude. By a pious kind of force he appointed him abbot of the monastery at Caen, though Lanfranc resisted no less from love of submission than from fear of the higher rank. Afterwards he enriched that same monastery with many possessions, as well as silver, gold, and various ornaments,” and so forth.

3. After Lanfranc had been promoted to the archbishopric of Canterbury, he gave still greater proofs of his inclination toward monastic affairs. At that time the clergy envied the monks, who occupied the principal cathedral churches of the English kingdom, and omitted nothing, whenever an opportunity arose, to expel them from those churches [Col. 0022B]. They had forgotten that this had been the original discipline of the English Church, instituted by Saint Augustine himself, who had brought the English people to the faith together with his companions, monks of our order. The great change in circumstances seemed to offer the clergy a suitable opportunity to persuade the new king to substitute clerics for monks in the cathedral churches. Their expectation would indeed not have deceived them if Lanfranc had not resisted their efforts with all his strength.

For King William had chosen almost all the bishops whom he newly established in England from the clerical order. They therefore favored the efforts of the clergy, or at least did not strongly oppose them. Consequently, the matter seemed so certain to them that, as Eadmer says in Book I, “Bishop Walkelin of Winchester already had nearly forty clerics assembled, tonsured and clothed in the manner of canons, whom he would soon introduce into the Winchester church over which he presided, after expelling the monks.” Only Lanfranc’s consent remained to be obtained, and the bishop assumed that he would secure it without difficulty. But matters turned out quite otherwise, as Eadmer continues: “For when what the bishop was planning reached his ears, he immediately recoiled from the deed and declared that, while he lived, he would never consent that such a wish should be fulfilled in any way.”

The storm against the monks was much more serious when the matter concerned the primatial Church of Canterbury, and Lanfranc therefore needed greater steadfastness to calm it. Yet neither the king’s authority nor the agreement of the other princes could ever induce him to consent to the expulsion of the monks from that Church. Rather, says Eadmer, “lest it should happen after his death—a thing which, while he lived, he knew could by God’s help in no way be accomplished—without knowing the day or hour of his death, he acted with the sagacity and industry in which he excelled, so that by the authority of the Roman and apostolic see the monks’ residence in that same church might be confirmed and established unshaken forever, for as long as the world should last.”

A decree of Pope Alexander II on this matter exists among the other letters of that pontiff; Eadmer and other authors inserted it in full into their writings. From that time the Benedictine order continued in the cathedral churches of Canterbury and many other churches of the kingdom of England until the Catholic faith was renounced in the time of Henry VIII.

What else Lanfranc did for the monks may be gathered from Eadmer and other authors; here it will suffice to touch on a few matters from among many. After the monks’ church of Saint Saviour had been destroyed, he “built another, greatly superior in beauty and size,” says Eadmer. The abbey of Saint Albans, “which had almost fallen into ruin inside and out, he rebuilt from the foundations as his own, appointing Paul, of blessed memory, as its abbot; within he enlarged it with great religious devotion, and outside he increased, beautified, and enriched it by donations of many things.” Through the monk Gundulf, whom he appointed bishop of Rochester, “he overturned the old episcopal church together with the adjoining structure and built everything anew. . . . He established the episcopal see with the adornment of the monastic order and, by assigning lands and other things suitable for the support of those serving God there, made it rich from poor, exalted from humble, as it is seen at present.” So say Eadmer and William of Malmesbury.

That Lanfranc was no less concerned with the careful observance of regular discipline than with the splendor or size of buildings is proved by those celebrated statutes that he issued for the monks and that Acherius of our order published. Finally, his sincere love for the monastic life is attested by the letter he wrote to Pope Alexander, asking to be released from the government of the Church of Canterbury. “I ask,” he says, “for the sake of God and your soul, that just as you bound me by your authority—which it was not lawful to resist—so also you may release me, once I have been bound, by breaking through that same authority the bond of this necessity, and grant me permission to return to the cenobitic life, which I love above all else.” All these things prove that the title “Father of the Monks” was rightly and deservedly granted to Lanfranc.

4. After affairs in England had changed, there was need of a man who could govern the affairs of the Church in such a way that ecclesiastical discipline would suffer no loss amid these disturbances and the rights of the Churches would not be violated by the victors. Lanfranc provided admirably for both matters, prudently using in this cause the authority he possessed with the king, whose adviser he was. For, as Adam of Bremen notes in Book IV, chapter XIV of his *Ecclesiastical History*: “William the Bastard, having removed scandals, appointed him teacher of the Church, through whose efforts many were inspired to divine service.”

Accordingly, when the pious bishop noticed that the practice of councils had lapsed in England for many years, he took care that they should thereafter be held frequently. This was done, and many regulations were established in them for the proper preservation of discipline. He also arranged for the restoration of the temporal goods that had been seized from his Church during the wars. By his wisdom he brought King William, says Eadmer, “to restore, for the redemption of his soul, very many lands of the Church of Canterbury that had been taken away through various causes and human acts of violence” [Col. 0024A]. Rodulfus of Diceto and Matthew Paris enumerate twenty-five manors among them, under the year 1039.

How firmly he resisted Odo, bishop of Bayeux and the king’s uterine brother, when Odo violated the rights of the Church of Canterbury, is related by Eadmer in Book I of the *New History* and by the author of the Life in chapter 9. All these things also won Lanfranc such authority even with the king himself that, when William was in Normandy, “Lanfranc was prince and guardian of England, with the princes subject to him,” as the author of the Life says in chapter 15. Eadmer asserts exactly the same thing in other words, saying that “the sight of the whole kingdom looked to Lanfranc’s command.”

This became especially evident after his death. For William Rufus, who had already succeeded his father, “immediately,” says Eadmer, “brought out into the open what he had kept concealed while Lanfranc was alive. And so he made the Church of Christ venal,” and so forth. Hence, with the same Eadmer, one may rightly say of Lanfranc in a few words: “I say briefly that he was truly a great and unconquerable defender of the Church of Christ, a pious prince of all England, and, insofar as it was permitted him, a good shepherd to all who lived there, while he was alive.”

Pope Alexander II, the supreme pontiff, knew this. In the same author he calls Lanfranc “the Father of the English fatherland,” and had in fact entrusted him with pastoral staffs to be distributed as he saw fit. Our Saxon chronicler, although hostile to the Normans, praises Lanfranc as “a teacher in the Church, through whose efforts many, first in Gaul and afterward in England, were inspired to divine service.”

5. Lanfranc also illuminated the Catholic Church not only by his deeds but by his writings, which earned him a place among ecclesiastical authors. Our own Lucas Acherius first collected and published in one volume all his works that could be found. Their catalogue is as follows: “Commentary on the Epistles of Blessed Paul; A Little Book on the Body and Blood of the Lord against Berengar; Brief Annotations on Some of the Conferences of John Cassian with the Fathers; Decrees for the Order of Saint Benedict; A Book of Letters; The Passage of the Speech He Delivered at the English Council; and the Little Book On Concealing Confession.”

Of these works, the commentary on Paul’s epistles published by Acherius is not genuinely Lanfranc’s; we have in our hands the work that was actually written by him, which we shall bring to light if a suitable opportunity ever arises. Besides these works, he is also said to have published a Commentary on the Psalms of David and an Ecclesiastical History, but neither has so far been found.

Certainly, it seems beyond doubt that Lanfranc wrote a history of his own time. Eadmer bears witness to this in Book I of the *New History*, where he says of Lanfranc: “He himself wrote, with a most truthful and concise pen, about the ecclesiastical matters that took place in his own time.” As I think, William of Malmesbury praises this work in Book I [Col. 0025A] of *The Deeds of the Bishops of the English*, where, treating the controversy that arose between Lanfranc himself and Thomas, archbishop of York, he advises that the matter should be drawn from Lanfranc’s writings in these words: “He himself will better indicate in his own writing what he wrote about his ordination and the controversy that arose and was settled between him and Thomas of York: ‘In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1070 he entered,’” and so forth.

Among his other works, the book that he published while he was still prior of Bec, *On the Body and Blood of the Lord*, against the heresiarch Berengar, easily holds the chief place. He had already refuted Berengar once and again in speeches: first at a Roman synod in the presence of Pope Leo, and again at another synod of 113 bishops before Nicholas II. There Berengar had abjured his heresy, publicly read the formula of the Catholic faith, and professed that he adhered to it sincerely and even under oath, while his books were cast into the fire before the entire synod.

Soon afterward, however, he returned to his vomit. “He attempted,” says Lanfranc, “to defend his depravity in secret disputations before the unlearned.” But he did not escape punishment. For Lanfranc, as Baronius testifies under the year 1059, by publishing a book against him and his errors, “broke the boldness of the arrogant heresiarch, refuted his errors, dissolved his fallacies, and rebuked his blasphemies, turning them back upon his own head,” and so forth.

John Bromton, abbot of Jervaulx, calls this book in his *Chronicle* “The Thunderous Book”; he writes that Lanfranc himself entitled it *Of Sparks*.

6. The fame of Lanfranc’s learning traveled throughout Europe and won him very many disciples. Consequently, the monastery of Bec, which had previously been small and scarcely known, quickly became famous for its extensive possessions and its number of monks. Indeed, Normandy, which until then had been considered devoid of learning, advanced so greatly under Lanfranc as teacher that afterward it abounded in men outstanding in erudition and knowledge.

On this subject Orderic Vitalis must be heard, in Book IV of his *Ecclesiastical History*, where he says of Lanfranc: “He chose the little monastery of Bec in Normandy, distinguished by the remoteness and poverty of its site; by his most watchful prudence and care he enriched it and raised it to the condition of a most beautiful order [Col. 0025D] . . . . . Drawn from the quiet of the cloister by the compulsion of obedience, the master came forth, and under his teaching the library of philosophical and divine letters shone forth. In both fields he was exceedingly powerful at solving the knots of questions. Under this teacher the Normans first investigated the art of letters, and from the school of Bec there emerged sophists eloquent in divine and secular matters. For previously, during the time of the six dukes of Neustria, scarcely any Norman had devoted himself to liberal studies, nor could a teacher be found, until God, the provider of all things, brought Lanfranc to the shores of Normandy. The fame of his expertise became widely known throughout all Europe, and many came to his teaching from France, Gascony, Brittany, and Flanders.”

William of Malmesbury explained all these same matters more briefly in Book I of *The Deeds of the Bishops of the English*, where he says of Lanfranc: “With his remarkable learning he summoned from Latium to Gaul the liberal arts, which had long been held in disrepute, and polished them by his keen intellect . . . . His fame spread to the most distant regions of the Latin world, and Bec became a great and renowned gymnasium of learning.”

Among Lanfranc’s more distinguished disciples are counted Alexander II, the supreme pontiff; Guimundus of Aversa, later archbishop; William of Rouen; Hernostus and Gundulf, bishops of Rochester; Fulk of Beauvais; and Ivo of Chartres, as Robert of Mont-Saint-Michel testifies, along with many others who were raised to the miters of various Churches.

Saint Anselm held Lanfranc’s learning in such high regard that he sent him the *Monologion*, which he had composed, to be submitted to his judgment. Indeed, Anselm asked Lanfranc to give the book whatever title he considered better. “I shall not cease,” says Anselm in Book I, Letter 63, “to demand this insistently from your authority, so that your authority may decide what ought to be done concerning this little work . . . . I have prefixed no title to it, since I did not consider it worthy of being honored by giving it such a name. If, therefore, it should be your judgment that what I have written should be written, let it receive its firmness from the one from whom it receives its name.”

The man whom he had esteemed so highly while alive he defended splendidly after his death against a heretical slanderer. For Roscelin, who asserted that the three persons of the most holy Trinity were three things in the same way that three angels are three things, though with one will or power in those three persons, had reached such shamelessness that he falsely claimed Lanfranc and Anselm as supporters of his doctrine.

Anselm vigorously refuted the heretic’s slanders, as is clear from his letter to Fulk, bishop of Beauvais, which is Letter XLI of Book II. In it he urges Fulk to undertake the defense of Lanfranc and himself at the council that Rainald, archbishop of Reims, was soon to convene on that matter. He speaks of Lanfranc’s learning as follows: “The archbishop Lanfranc, whose life is known to many religious and wise men, because nothing of this kind was ever heard from him, is sufficiently acquitted of this charge,” and so forth [Col. 0026D].

Nor is it surprising that, after Lanfranc’s death, he was charged with what had been done to him while he was still alive. For certain men, led—I do not know by what spirit—had accused him before the Roman pontiff as though he favored Berengar’s errors. He soon entirely removed this slander from himself, not only in writing but also orally, before two pontiffs and the universal synods, as we have already said. Thus, as he himself says in the little book against Berengar mentioned above, he “wiped away from himself the stain of evil rumor,” set forth “his faith,” and “what he said pleased everyone and displeased no one.”

Finally, a great proof of Lanfranc’s learning is that, after his death, the English bishops, assembled together in synod, called him their “Teacher.”

[Col. 0027A] 7. It remains for us to inquire in what year, month, and finally on what day Lanfranc departed this life, for all these matters are disputed. If, however, we follow the testimony of the ancient writers, there will be no difficulty concerning the year. They consistently affirm that Lanfranc died in the year 1089. Thus say Symeon of Durham, John Bromton in his *Chronicle*, Orderic Vitalis in Book VIII of his *History*, the Chronicle of Bec published by Acherius, the Chronicle of Melrose, and many other authors of English history. They were preceded by Ingulf, who was bound to Lanfranc by friendship during his lifetime, as he himself testifies in the new complete edition of his *History*.

There is greater difficulty concerning the month, since nearly all the more recent historians disagree among themselves on this matter. Matthew of Westminster records that he died on the ninth day before the Kalends of April; Matthew Parker on 4 June; Peter of Equilinum on the fifth day before the Nones of July; Bale on the fifth day before the Kalends of July; Arnold Wion, Hugh Menard, and most other recent writers on 3 July. Nevertheless, we prefer the authority of the older writers of England, who unanimously affirm that Lanfranc died in the month of May.

But on what day of that month this occurred is the entire knot of the difficulty; to speak truthfully, no one will easily resolve it because of the excessive disagreement of opinions. Thus Symeon of Durham writes on this matter: “In the year 1089, on Thursday, the ninth day before the Kalends of June, Lanfranc died.” Roger Hoveden, in the first part of his *Annals*, and Florence of Worcester, in his *Chronicle*, make the same assertion in exactly the same words.

Indeed, these chronological indications fit together very well. For in the year 1089 Sunday fell on 20 May, with the Dominical Letter G; consequently, the fifth feria, or Thursday, fell on the 24th of that month, which these authors assign.

But Gervase of Canterbury, in the *Acts of the Archbishops of Canterbury*, assigns Lanfranc’s death to another day in these words: “He died in the nineteenth year of his patriarchate, on the fifth day before the Kalends of June, on the Monday after the octave of Pentecost, at the first hour of the day.” Milo, the author of the following Life, John Bromton in his *Chronicle*, and the tables of the Church of Canterbury agree with him.

Other chronological indications also agree with this calculation, since in that year Easter fell on 1 April and therefore the feast of Pentecost was celebrated on 20 May; its octave was on 27 May, and consequently the following Monday, which Gervase assigns, was 28 May. John Capgrave, who composed the Lives of the Saints of England, adopted this opinion, and after him Edward Maihew in the *Anglo-Benedictine Trophies*. We too shall adhere to this calculation until stronger arguments are produced in favor of the earlier one. What chiefly moves us to do so is that the authors of this latter opinion wrote the Life of Saint Lanfranc expressly for that purpose, whereas the others speak of the matter only incidentally.

8. Moreover, although the memory of blessed Lanfranc is not honored by any public cult, his name has nevertheless been entered with the title “saint” in widely circulated martyrologies, such as the Benedictine Martyrology of Arnold Wion and the General Catalogue of the Saints of Filippo Ferrari. Hugo Menard, Edward Maihew, and others commonly call him “blessed,” and speak of his “highest holiness and learning.” Trithemius, Leland, and Capgrave had previously bestowed the same titles upon him, as earlier writers had long done.

Thus William of Poitiers speaks of him in his book *On the Deeds of Duke William*: “Duke William entrusted to him the counsels concerning his soul; he entrusted to him a kind of watchtower from which he might care for the ecclesiastical orders throughout Normandy. For the vigilant care of such a man, since the prerogative of holiness had gained him the highest authority in wisdom as well, could indeed promise no small security to his solicitude.” Osbern the monk likewise writes in his letter to Saint Anselm: “Let us recover in you what we lost in the most holy Father Lanfranc when he died.” This letter has been published among Saint Anselm’s letters, Book III, no. 5.

William of Malmesbury asserts in Book I of *On the Bishops of the English* that Saint Dunstan was always present to Lanfranc whenever the rights of his Church had to be defended; Osbern also relates this in the *Life of Saint Dunstan*, published in the previous century. “Moreover,” as the same William observes, Lanfranc “rescued a certain sick man, weary of his lingering life, from danger, in a vision in which the man seemed to have engaged in a struggle with him, and restored him to good health.” This may have given some people, especially Wion, occasion to proclaim Lanfranc as exceedingly distinguished for miracles.

Finally, various authors commonly call him “a man of good” or “pious memory.” All these things certainly confirm what William brought forward in Book III of *The Deeds of the Kings of the English* in Lanfranc’s honor: that he was “a man comparable to the ancients in learning and religion, of whom it may seriously be said: ‘A third Cato fell from heaven’” [Note: [Col. 0027D] Juvenal, *Satires* 2.40], so deeply had a heavenly savor permeated his breast and palate.

More concerning his praises is found in the book of obituaries of the Church of Canterbury, where the solemnity with which his anniversary ought to be celebrated is prescribed. If you wish, consult *Sacred England*, vol. I, where it is found on page 55. Finally, scarcely any historian has failed to adorn Lanfranc with many praises.

But now his *Life* must be brought forward. We have restored it to its integrity after it had been edited by our Acherius from a Bec manuscript, with many passages here and there omitted.

# 1. HERE BEGINS THE PROLOGUE TO THE LIFE OF THE GREAT AND GLORIOUS LANFRANC, ARCHBISHOP OF CANTERBURY

[Col. 0029]

Since many people seek the *Life* of the venerable Lanfranc, archbishop of Canterbury, and it cannot be found, I wished to write something about him, according to the smallness of my ability, lest the memory of so great a man be altogether erased by silence. The work, as it seems to me, has hitherto been neglected; for scarcely anyone is found to have written anything about him.

For this reason, in the *Life of our blessed Father Herluin*, the venerable Gilbert, abbot of Westminster, inserted, as though incidentally, as much as seemed pertinent to the history. Borrowing thence and transferring it into this narrative, I added whatever I could find, or had heard from venerable and truthful men.

[Note: [Col. 0058D] Gilbert, venerable abbot of Westminster. [Col. 0059A] Surname: Crispin. You will find the noble genealogy of the Crispins compiled from the manuscript Bec chronicle, after the *Lives of the Abbots* of that same monastery. We are now publishing these works—the *Chronicle* and the *Lives*—for the first time. The chronicle deals at length with Abbot Gilbert. I shall add only what the exceptionally learned John Pits recorded concerning his singular learning in *On the Illustrious Writers of England*: “A man,” he says, “who may rightly be compared in talent, piety, and learning with the chief teachers of his age. For in his monastery—more accurately, at Bec—he carefully learned humane letters, indeed all the liberal arts and philosophical sciences. Then, in theological studies, he had Saint Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury, as his master and teacher; under Anselm’s guidance he penetrated the innermost recesses of Sacred Scripture. Afterwards he visited the schools of Gaul, and, having finally traveled through Italy, he came to Rome and from there returned through Germany to his homeland. His mind, eager for learning, ardently thirsted for whatever knowledge existed anywhere among the nations; indeed, he carefully drank it in.”]

He then appends a catalogue of Gilbert’s works in this form:

*On the Faith of the Church against the Jews*, one book.

*Homilies on the Song of Songs*, one book.

*On the Prophet Isaiah, addressed to Blessed Anselm*, one book.

*On the Prophet Jeremiah*, one book.

*On the Prologues of Saint Jerome to the Bible*.

*On the Fall of the Devil*, one book.

*On the Soul*, one book, in homilies.

*Letters to Anselm on the State of the Church*.

*Against the Sins of Thought, Speech, and Deed*, one book.

Other short works by Gilbert himself also exist, namely:

A commentary on the *Lamentations*, in the monastery of Saint Albins at Angers.

On the Epistles of Saint Paul, in the monastery of Saint Remigius at Reims.

*Disputation against the Jews*—the same work as the one above, *On the Faith*—is found in various libraries. It has sometimes been attributed to Saint Anselm, but incorrectly, for its author dedicates it to Anselm.

The Lord Anselm writes to Abbot Gilbert in Book II, Letter 16.

William Calculus, surnamed of Jumièges, greatly praises Gilbert in Book VII, chapter 22 of his history. Florentius of Worcester bears witness in his *Chronicle*, under the year 1117, that Gilbert died in that year. Westminster is a most celebrated monastery, distinguished as the burial place of the kings of England, situated in the suburb of London. Nearly a thousand years ago Saint Augustine, the apostle of England—as is evident in his *Life*, Appendix, page 67, chapter c—arranged for its construction.]

Drawing upon that material and transferring it into this narrative, I added everything I could find, whether things I had learned from venerable and truthful men or otherwise. I undertook this work so that, insofar as it lay within me, the man who ought to be proposed to others for imitation would not remain unknown, but would become known to all for the honor of God and the benefit of readers; and so that those who wish to know might learn who he was and from where he came, what manner of life he had, how he came to religion, then to the abbacy, and afterwards to the archbishopric, and finally how he departed from this light.

In these matters I was not able to hear everything that ought to be said. Nor should anyone be angry with me because, inexperienced in speech and learning, I dared to undertake so worthy a subject; for I preferred to speak somehow rather than not at all. If anyone dislikes the rusticity of my style and uncultivated speech, and wishes to express the same things more elegantly, I beg him not, by changing the words, to remove the meaning of what happened, unless perhaps he finds that something in it is false.

# HERE BEGINS THE LIFE OF BLESSED LANFRANC

[Col. 0029]

## CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 0029B]

### 1

There was a certain great man, born in Italy, by whom the whole Latin world, restored through him to the ancient condition of learning, acknowledges its supreme teacher with fitting love and honor. His name was Lanfrancus. Greece herself, the teacher of nations in the liberal arts, willingly listened to and admired his students.

[Note: [Col. 0059C] Thus says William of Poitiers, *On the Deeds of Duke William*, among the writers of Norman history edited by André Duchesne, fol. 194; William of Malmesbury, Book III of *The Deeds of the English*, fol. 61, no. 2, London edition, and *The Deeds of the Bishops*, fol. 116; William of Jumièges, in the book cited, chapter 26; Orderic Vitalis, Book IV of the *History*, fol. 519; and Robert of Monte in his manuscript *Chronicle* under the year 1042. It is worthwhile to cite at least Guitmund, archbishop of Aversa, as Lanfranc’s pupil: “Since through the Lord Lanfranc, a man equally most learned, God had caused the liberal arts to grow warm again and flourish excellently,” and so forth. This is from the beginning of *On the Body and Blood of Christ against Berengar*.]

He was a native of the city of Pavia.

[Note: [Col. 0059D] His parents were considered great and honorable. Robert, in the passage cited above, explains more clearly what distinction they possessed: “Lanfrancus, born of the noble senatorial family of Pavia, wonderfully educated in the seven liberal disciplines,” and so forth.]

His parents, citizens of that same city, were regarded as great and honorable among their fellow citizens. For, as is reported, his father belonged to the order of those who preserved the rights and laws of the city.

[Note: [Col. 0029C] Robert of Monte writes the following in his manuscript *Chronicle* under the year 1042: “Lanfrancus, born of the noble senatorial family of Pavia, wonderfully educated in the seven liberal disciplines.”]

Lanfrancus was deprived of his father at an early age. Although he ought to have succeeded him in honor and dignity, he left the city, and, out of love of learning, went to the study of letters. After remaining there for a long time and being perfectly imbued with all secular learning, he returned.

Then he left his homeland, crossed the Alps, and came to Gaul in the time of Henry, king of the Franks, and William, the glorious duke of the Normans, who conquered England by force of arms. Passing through France, he arrived in Normandy with several scholars of great renown and stayed for some time in the city of Avranches, where he taught.

But the most learned man considered that seeking the applause of mortals is vanity, and that all things tend toward nonbeing except him who made everything, who always is, and those who turn toward him. He therefore directed his mind and study toward gaining God’s love.

Having found in letters the more perfect counsel of salvation and of pleasing God, he decided to take it up, so that, after abandoning everything and renouncing even his own rights, he might follow him who said: “If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me” (Matthew 16:24).

And because, the greater he had been, the more he desired to become humble, he did not wish to go to a place where learned men were accustomed to gather and would hold him in honor and reverence.

### 2

Meanwhile, as he wished to go to Rouen, he was traveling, with the day already declining, through a forest beyond the River Risle.

[Note: [Col. 0029C] The Risle is a river of Normandy that rises near the monastery of Saint Ebrulf. From this it may be conjectured that Lanfranc was robbed by bandits in the forest of Ouche, commonly called *la forêt d’Ouche*, which gave its name to the monastery of Ouche. Anyone traveling from Avranches to Rouen had to pass through it.]

He fell in with robbers.

[Note: [Col. 0059D] “He fell in with robbers.” The Bec chronicle relates this story more fully under the year 1041; see the appendix to the works of Blessed Lanfranc, page 2, before the middle.]

[Note: [Col. 0029C] The Bec chronicler relates the matter somewhat differently under the year 1041. He reports that the robbers took everything from Lanfranc except an old cloak. When he himself wished to surrender the cloak to them as well, following the example of Libertinus, whom Gregory the Great recounts in Book I of the *Dialogues*, chapter 2, so that everything might be miraculously restored to him as it had been to Libertinus, his intention was not right, and the opposite happened: the robbers tied him naked to one tree and his student to another. Thus abandoned, he promised God that he would renounce all worldly things if he escaped. As soon as his bonds had been divinely loosed, he freed his companion and fulfilled his vow at Bec.]

The robbers took away everything he had, bound his hands behind his back, drew the hood of his cloak over his eyes, led him off the road, and abandoned him among the dense bushes of the wood.

Caught in such distress, not knowing what to do, he lamented his misfortune. At last, during the silence of night, coming to himself, he wished to offer the Lord the praises due to him, but could not, because he had not previously made time for this.

Turning to the Lord, he said:

“Lord God, I have spent so much time in learning and have worn down body and mind in the study of letters, yet I have not learned how I ought to pray to you or offer you the duties of praise. Deliver me from this tribulation; and, with your help, I will strive to correct and order my life in such a way that I may both be able and know how to serve you.”

At dawn, in the very twilight, he heard travelers taking the road and began to call out loudly for help. At first they were frightened when they heard him; then, recognizing the voice of a man, they went toward the sound. He told them who he was and what had happened.

They then untied him and brought him back to the road. He asked them to show him some poorer and more wretched monastery in that region. They replied:

“We know of no poorer or more despised monastery than this one being built nearby by a certain man of God.”

They pointed out the way and departed. Lanfrancus turned his steps there and came to Bec, which at that time was considered nowhere to have a poorer or more despised monastery.

Perhaps at that time the abbot was occupied in building a furnace and was himself working with his hands. Lanfrancus approached him and said:

“May God keep you safe.”

The abbot replied:

“May God bless you.”

“Are you a Lombard?” the abbot asked.

“I am,” he replied.

“What do you want?” asked the abbot.

“I wish to become a monk,” he said.

The abbot then instructed a certain monk named Roger, who was working on his own task nearby, to show him the book of the Rule.

[Note: [Col. 0059D] This means the Benedictine Rule. [Col. 0060A] Saint Herluin the abbot required that it be observed, since it is prescribed by the holy Rule in chapter 58, “On the Discipline for Receiving Brothers.” That custom was religiously preserved down to our own times, as is clearly shown by various ancient documents of this kind. Among many such documents, one written in an ancient hand during the time of Hincmar, archbishop of Reims and abbot of Saint Remigius, and issued in his presence, will provide evidence.

**FORM OF THE PETITION**  
By which a novice asks that he be permitted to make profession.

“I, Rotfridus, carefully attending to the beginning of my conversion, consider that entrance was not first granted easily to my petitions, but that, after I had knocked for a long time, a place in the guesthouse was scarcely bestowed upon me in mercy. After staying there for a few days, I entered the house of the novices. There the elder first set before me hard and difficult things, my promise of stability was arranged, and the Rule was read and delivered to me three times a year, with the admonition: ‘Behold the law under which you wish to serve as a soldier. If you can observe it, enter; but if you cannot, depart freely.’

“Seeing, therefore, that this carefully ordered yet strict period had been assigned to me, I set aside the entrance of doubt and humbly beg that you deign now to join me to your body. With the Lord’s help I promise to observe the institutions of this Rule, and for the sake of the reward of eternal life I humbly submit myself to serve before God and his angels. From this day onward I may not shake my neck free from beneath the yoke of the Rule, since under the annual option I had been permitted either to make excuse or to accept it. And so that this petition of my profession may be held firmly by you, I deliver it written for the name of Saint Remigius, or of those whose relics are contained here, and of the present lord abbot, namely Hincmar the archbishop.”

Thus far extends the written form, or petition of monastic profession, from the celebrated Benedictine monastery of Saint Remigius at Reims.]

After he had read it, he replied that, with God’s help, he would willingly observe everything. Hearing this and learning who he was and from where he came, the abbot granted what he requested.

Lanfrancus then fell face-first before the mouth of the furnace and kissed the abbot’s feet. He greatly revered and loved the humility of spirit and gravity of speech he perceived in the abbot.

[Note: [Col. 0060C] “There he becomes a monk.” In my opinion this means that he was admitted to the novitiate. For it is known that formerly novices remained in secular clothing throughout the year of probation, both from the Benedictine Rule, chapter 58 cited above, and from councils, various statutes of the Fathers, and the acts of the saints. Our Menardus proves this clearly and learnedly in chapter 6 of his *Concordance of the Rules*, commenting on the words: “Immediately, therefore, let him be stripped of his own possessions in the oratory.”

This is also plainly taught by the ancient form for clothing a monk—or, what is the same thing, receiving him into profession—which the venerable regular canons of Saint Victor at Paris willingly lent me. Since it can scarcely be found, I have made this very form publicly available.
