Perhaps, however, in the period when the Lord Lanfrancus professed himself a monk, this custom had already been abolished; he himself seems later to have established as much in chapter 18 of his decrees.

[Col. 0060D] HERE BEGINS THE BLESSING OF MONKS

After the convert has been led into the church, everyone says, “Have mercy on me, O God.” When this has been said, let him make the profession he has long desired:

“I, Brother N., priest or deacon, and so forth, promise my stability and the conversion of my morals to obedience according to the Rule of Saint Benedict, before God and his saints, in this monastery which has been built in honor of Saint N., in the presence of Lord N., the abbot.”

Afterwards he says three times: “Receive me, O Lord,” and so forth. Let everyone repeat this three times, adding “Glory be to the Father,” and so forth; “Kyrie, eleison, Our Father,” and so forth; “Out of the depths,” and so forth; “Save your servant. Send him, O Lord, help from the sanctuary. Let the enemy have no success against him. Be to him, O Lord, a tower of strength. O Lord, hear my prayer,” and so forth. “The Lord be with you.” Prayer: “God of forgiveness,” and so forth. Another: “God, who through the co-eternal,” and so forth. “Lord Jesus Christ,” and so forth.

Here let the hymn “Come, Creator” be sung, and so forth: “Holy Spirit, who are God,” and so forth.

For blessing the habit: “Lord Jesus Christ, who are the ruler,” and so forth.

For removing the secular habit: “May the Lord strip you of the old man,” and so forth.

For clothing him in the monastic habit: “May the Lord clothe you with the new man,” and so forth. Let the following prayer follow; then, after the kiss of peace has been given to everyone, let him remain in complete silence until the third day.

“Prayer.—Merciful God, gracious God, God to whom all good things are pleasing, without whom nothing holy is begun and nothing good is completed: let the ears of your kindness attend to our most humble prayers. Protect this servant of yours, N., to whom, in your holy name, you have given the habit of sacred religion, from the impediment of the world and from secular desire; and grant him that he may remain devoted in this holy purpose and, having received remission of sins, may be worthy to reach the fellowship of your elect. Through him.”

We have not transcribed these prayers, which are found in the form for clothing a novice and making profession, as well as in the Roman *Pontifical*. This form was certainly solemn in ancient times, as may be inferred with reasonable clarity from the celebrated assembly of the year 817, in the fourth year of the empire of Louis the Pious, chapter 34, “On the Novice Brother,” and so forth:

“Let him entrust the possessions he has to his parents; once the year of probation has been completed, however, let him act according to what the Rule—namely, the Benedictine Rule—prescribes. Let him neither be tonsured nor change his former clothing before he promises obedience.”

Here I should like to insert another, shorter rite for making a monk—that is, for admitting one to the habit or to profession—from an old collection of canons, written by hand in Ireland about the year 800; for, so far as I know, no one has yet brought such rites to light. It reads as follows:

“In the ordinations of monks, the abbot ought to celebrate Mass and complete three prayers over his head; and for four days let him cover his head with his cowl; and on the seventh day let the abbot remove the veil from his head [lacuna]. Just as in baptism the priest removes the infants’ veil on the seventh day, so too the abbot ought to do for the monk, for whom this is a second baptism according to the judgment of the Fathers, and all sins are forgiven, as in baptism.”

But lest anyone should take offense because monastic profession is equated with baptism, and because that Irish canon calls it a second baptism, let him consult the most learned Haeftenus, *Monastic Investigations*, Book IV, Investigations 2 and 3. I shall produce only one or two passages: from Saint Jerome, Letter 25, in which he consoles Paula over the death of her daughter Blaesilla:

“But now, since, through Christ’s favor, about four months ago she washed herself in a certain manner in a second baptism of her religious purpose, and thereafter lived so that, having trampled the world underfoot, she always thought upon the monastery, do you not fear lest the Savior say to you: ‘Are you angry, Paula, because your daughter has become my daughter?’”

And so forth. From Peter Damian, *Opuscule* 16, chapter 8: “In the sayings of the Fathers it is found that the profession of the monastic life is a second baptism.” Saint Bernard should also be read, throughout Book *On Precept and Dispensation*, chapter 23; as should Geoffrey of Vendôme, Book IV, Letter 12, and at the beginning of his sermon on Saint Benedict.]

There he became a monk.

### 3

When this had happened, the venerable Father Herluin was filled with no small joy, because he believed that God had heard his prayers.

[Note: [Col. 0061D] The venerable Father Herluin. His *Life* may be seen after the works of Blessed Lanfranc, in the appendix, page 32.]

For the necessity of procuring supplies compelled him to remain outside the cloister, and there was no one to preside within and preserve the religious observance. After he had repeatedly entreated God, divine mercy supplied him with assistance sufficient for everything that had to be done.

You might therefore have seen a pious contest between them. The abbot, an old layman recently promoted to the clergy, feared the greatness of so great a teacher placed under his authority. Lanfrancus, for his part, showing no arrogance because of his eminent learning, obeyed everything with the greatest humility. He observed, admired, and praised the grace God had granted the abbot in understanding the Scriptures, and said:

“When I consider this layman, I do not know what to say except that ‘the Spirit breathes where he wills’” (John 3:8).

The abbot showed him the reverence due to him, while Lanfrancus strove to show the abbot complete submission. Each became an example of life to the flock: one of the active life, the other of the contemplative.

The abbot was humble, possessed the greatest patience, extremely restrained in caring for his body, and unconcerned with secular pomp. He was highly knowledgeable about the laws of his homeland and served as a defense for his people against unjust exactors. He was most skilled in handling secular lawsuits and arranging external affairs. In constructing or procuring necessities, no one could have been more prudent or effective, without compromising religious observance.

But that great teacher devoted all his labor in the cloister to quiet and silence, cultivating the fallow fields of his heart through constant reading of the sacred word and watering them with the sweet compunction of tears, which he often obtained.

## CHAPTER TWO

### 4

Nor did he forget what he had promised God during his nocturnal captivity. After becoming a monk, he wished to devote the greatest care to learning the offices of day and night, so that he might know how to offer God a sacrifice of praise, just as he had learned other things.

He lived in this way for three years, rejoicing that he was unknown: except for the few to whom he occasionally spoke, he was a stranger to everyone.

When rumor revealed what had happened, it spread the news far and wide, and within a short time the exceedingly distinguished reputation of the man raised Bec and Abbot Herluin throughout the world.

[Note: [Col. 0061D] Clerics hasten there. See more on this matter in Letter I.]

Clerics came, sons of dukes, the most renowned masters of the schools of Latin learning, powerful laymen, and many noble men. Out of love for him, they bestowed many gifts upon that church.

This Lanfrancus, who for God’s sake had renounced himself, content with every humiliation and extremity, took care to submit himself in complete obedience to his superior. It is said, finally, that he would not read a lesson in church unless the cantor had first heard it.

One day, while he was reading at table, he pronounced something in the course of the reading as it ought to be pronounced. This did not please the person presiding, who ordered him to say it differently—as if Lanfrancus had said *docēre*, with the middle syllable lengthened, as is correct, and the other had corrected it to *dŏcēre*, with the middle syllable shortened, which is incorrect. The presiding man was not learned.

But the wise man, knowing that obedience was owed to Christ more than to Donatus, abandoned what he had pronounced correctly and said what he was ordered, incorrectly, to say. He knew that lengthening a short syllable or shortening a long one was not a capital crime; but he knew that failing to obey a command given on God’s behalf was no small fault.

### 5

A certain secular man gave the church of Bec a piece of land.

[Note: [Col. 0031D] I think this land was the monastery of Saint Ebrulf, which William son of Geroy gave to the monastery of Bec, where he received the monastic habit. Lanfrancus lived there for some time with several monks and restored, as best he could, that once-famous monastery, which had been completely ruined. Later, when the village of Russerie was given to the monks of Bec by Blessed Theodoric, as we related in his *Life*, the monastery of Saint Ebrulf recovered its former splendor.]

Lanfrancus was sent there to preserve and restore it. One day, while returning from the monastery to that place, he carried a cat wrapped in a cloth and tied behind him to the saddle.

As he traveled, someone joined him. While they were walking together, the fellow traveler heard the cat’s voice and began to wonder and look around for the cat whose voice he heard. At last he noticed that Master Lanfrancus was carrying it tied behind him, and said:

“Lord, what are you carrying?”

He replied:

“Mice and rats are greatly troubling us, and therefore I am now bringing a cat to suppress their fury.”

Behold the degree of humility to which so great a man was willing to submit himself for God’s sake. And because he humbled himself greatly, God did not delay exalting him in the present life.

### 6

But the brothers who had already gathered in that place were considered neither very learned nor particularly instructed in religious observance.

Lanfrancus saw the brothers’ sluggishness, the depravity of their morals, and their transgression of the order. He also observed that some envied him and feared that he might be placed over them. He did not know what to do or where to go. He was wearied by their dishonorable way of life and ardently longed for the sweetness of solitary existence.

He therefore pretended to suffer from a stomach ailment and asked Fulcrannus the gardener to bring him every day the roots of certain thistles, which he claimed were a remedy for constipation. He did this so that he might accustom his body to the kind of food on which he intended to live in the wilderness.

[Note: [Col. 0061D] Since he was already preparing both mind and body for flight, he seems to have conceived the plan by following the example of Saint Benedict, the legislator. When the monks who had forced him to undertake the burden of the abbacy grew exceedingly impatient with his strict and religious discipline and offered him a poisoned drink to extinguish the holiest Father, the man of God returned to the solitude he loved. He did the same a second time, after enduring for a long while the harassment of the wicked priest Florentius; at last he yielded the place and took flight. Gregory the Great, Book II of the *Dialogues*, chapters 3 and 8.]

As he was now preparing mind and body for flight by escaping during the night, the abbot Lord Herluin, suspecting nothing of this, was resting in bed. Then Hugh, a boy of excellent character who had recently died—the son of Baldric of Sauvarville and nephew of that same abbot—appeared to him in a white garment.

The abbot was not at all disturbed by the sight. He addressed him affectionately:

“What is it, my son? How are you?”

The boy replied cheerfully:

“I am well, good Father, because through God’s mercy and your intercession I have been freed from every torment. But God sent me to you to tell you that, if you do not look to yourself, you will soon no longer have Master Lanfrancus.”

The abbot, astonished, asked:

“How so, my son?”

The boy replied:

“Because he desires a solitary life and has decided to leave the monastery, since the conduct and life of the brothers do not please him. See, therefore, what you must do, for it is not to your advantage that he should abandon you.”

After saying this, the boy disappeared. The abbot, stunned by what he had heard, spent the remainder of the night sleepless in vigils and prayers.

At dawn,

[Note: [Col. 0062A] “As soon as the time for speaking was given”—that is, after the hour of Prime, the hour of daytime prayers, had been completed. The Rule of Saint Benedict, chapter 42, commands: “After Compline no one is to speak.” That is, after the final evening office has been completed, a Benedictine monk may not utter a word until the hour mentioned above. Paul the Deacon explains how this is to be understood in his manuscript commentary on the Rule of Saint Benedict, in the cited chapter: “It must be noted,” he says, “that if during the night someone should see such damage, or there should be a necessity that cannot wait until a suitable time for speaking, the Rule does not forbid speech. For three things must be considered at night: damage, necessity—whether spiritual or bodily—and a prior’s question.” Thus far the Deacon. “By this law,” as Menardus says in chapter 15 of the *Concordance of the Rules*, “Saint Benedict countered many evils that are perpetrated with the assistance of darkness.”]

as soon as the time for speaking was given,

[Note: [Col. 0033D] Namely, after Prime and the prayers recited in the chapter house. Before that time it was forbidden to break the silence, which is more strictly prescribed in chapter 42 of the Rule, except in a grave necessity.]

he summoned Lanfrancus and had him sit privately with him. The abbot’s heart was shaken by profound grief; his voice was choked in his throat, and the tears that burst forth revealed the sorrow of his heart.

Seeing this, Lanfrancus prostrated himself on the ground and humbly begged that the abbot disclose why he was weeping so.

At last the abbot burst out with these words:

“Alas for me, whom God threatens with such a loss! Woe to me, who have lost my counsel and forfeited my help! Many times, with great groaning, I have asked God, and with abundant tears I have begged divine mercy to grant me such a man that by his counsel and help I might reform this place and restore to the use of the monks whatever was pleasing to God.

“When God brought you here, Brother Lanfrancus, I believed that the prayers of my humility had been heard. I was thinking of transferring my burden to you; I hoped that you would carry the whole weight of my burden.

“But now, I do not know for what reason, you are planning to leave this place, abandoning me, and desire to go into the wilderness.”

Lanfrancus realized that his intention had been discovered and that the purpose of his heart, which he had thought hidden, had been clearly exposed. He immediately threw himself at the abbot’s feet and humbly asked how these things had become known to him.

The abbot then revealed the vision to him in a gentle voice and explained in order what had been divinely disclosed to him through the boy, as we related above.

Lanfrancus was struck with amazement beyond words and greatly marveled at God’s grace in the abbot. Prostrate on the ground, he immediately confessed to the Father everything he had intended in his heart. After receiving a penance and obtaining absolution, he promised that he would never leave him and would obey all his commands in every respect.

The abbot gave immense thanks to almighty God and, as soon as he could, appointed Lanfrancus prior. He entrusted to his care everything subject to the monastery’s authority, both within and outside.

Divine protection made them so united in mind that no occasion for disagreement ever arose between them.

Lanfrancus, wishing neither to disclose the vision nor to conceal it entirely,

[Note: [Col. 0062B] He disclosed it to a monk named William. More about him below, in connection with Letter 49.]

reported it to a certain monk named William, whom he had raised and taught from childhood and loved greatly. He ordered him not to tell anyone as long as Lanfrancus himself lived.

William kept this command until extreme old age. After Lanfrancus’s death, when he was no longer bound by the prohibition, he wrote down the matter as he had heard it and sent the written account to the abbot and monks of Bec, as we have set it out above.

[Note: [Col. 0033D] John Picard and our Gabriel Gerberon published this letter from a Bec manuscript in their notes on Letter 41 of Book II of Blessed Anselm. Lanfrancus wrote to William the letter that is numbered 48 in Acher’s edition. According to Orderic Vitalis, Book II, William died around the year 1109. Orderic lists him among the men distinguished in holiness and learning, saying: “At that time several teachers of the Churches, especially distinguished in holiness and wisdom, departed: Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury; William, archbishop of Rouen; and the venerable rulers of monasteries, Hugh, abbot of Cluny; Gervasius of Rennes; and William of the monastery of Cormeilles.”]

That same William was abbot of the monastery of Cormeilles.

## CHAPTER THREE

[Col. 0034D]

7. He was also appointed chief counsellor for administering the affairs of the whole country by William, duke of the Normans. [Note: [Col. 0062B] He was appointed chief counsellor by William himself, the Norman duke. Thus the eyewitness William of Poitiers testifies, *On the Deeds of Duke William*, p. 198; William of Poitiers himself was also Duke William’s chaplain:

“William cultivated a certain Lanfranc, concerning whom the question has arisen whether he deserved greater reverence and glory for his singular mastery of secular and divine letters, or for his singular observance of the monastic order. He honored him with intimate familiarity, venerating him as a father, revering him as a teacher, and loving him as a brother or son. To him he entrusted the counsels of his soul and a kind of watchtower from which the ecclesiastical orders throughout Normandy might be surveyed. Indeed, the vigilant care of such a man, when he had acquired the greatest authority together with the distinction of wisdom and holiness, could promise no small security to the most excellent diligence.” [Col. 0062C]

This is what Poitiers says.

Matthew Paris, describing the Life of Abbot Fretheric XIII in his *Lives of the Abbots of Saint Albans*, inserts the following after the middle:

“The king summoned Lanfranc—a most learned man and extraordinarily energetic in both exceptional undertakings and difficult ecclesiastical affairs—in order to raise him to the archiepiscopate. For the king himself conducted all his affairs, both before and after the Conquest, according to his counsel. The king had him as his foremost counsellor and spiritual confessor in all things.”

The Malmesbury librarian, *On the Bishops of the English*, fol. 121, 2, no. 10:

“Moreover, King William rose before him [Lanfranc] in all things and rejoiced with him and with others whom he heard to be held in good favor.”

And *On the Deeds of the English*, book III, fol. 62:

“By his counsel the king had made himself ready to refuse nothing that Lanfranc said ought to be done,” and so forth.]

His favor, however, was struck by an excessive disturbance which suddenly arose, but God unexpectedly brightened it with serenity. For, provoked against him by the accusations of certain informers, the duke ordered that Lanfranc be driven from the monastery and leave the country. [Col. 0035A] Unable to calm the agitation of his spirit after issuing this command, he ordered the monastery’s estate called Parc to be destroyed by fire. The savage order was carried out. When he departed—he who had been every joy and consolation to the brothers—deep grief remained.

Since no better mount was available, a three-legged horse whose fourth leg was useless was given to him, together with a single servant. The brothers therefore devoted themselves to prayer, in accordance with Jeremiah: “Waiting in silence for the salvation of the Lord” (Lamentations 3:26).

As he was departing, he approached the duke, who was coming to meet him, and saluted his lord, while the horse lowered its head to the ground at every step. Conscious of his innocence, he did not despair of his case if an opportunity to speak were granted. At first the duke turned his face away; but, by divine [Col. 0035B] mercy, he soon looked back compassionately and, with a kindly gesture, granted him an opportunity to speak.

Then Lanfranc said with becoming humor: “By your command I am leaving your province on foot, burdened with this useless quadruped. Or, so that I may obey your command, give me a better horse.”

The duke replied with a smile: “Who asks gifts from an offended judge before the matter of the alleged crime has been concluded?”

At last the most eloquent advocate requested a hearing. With God supplying him assistance, he began his case and brought it to the desired conclusion in a short time. He was immediately restored to the duke’s fullest favor and received a promise that thereafter he would not be subjected to the disadvantage of having to clear himself of any accusation. The most welcome embraces and kisses immediately followed. The duke also promised that everything he had recently ordered to be destroyed would be restored, and with considerable increase.

One of the brothers, [Col. 0035C] running ahead, eagerly announced to the others that Lanfranc was returning. Tears were changed into joy, and not once only but throughout the entire day all hearts and voices resounded everywhere with the devout hymn *Te Deum laudamus*. The abbot could not believe the unexpected news because of the ferocity he knew in his lord, until the longed-for man arrived. Their joy increased because the burned property was fully restored; he also obtained from the same lord confirmation of the lands granted to that church.

8. [Note: [Col. 0062C] They say that the cause of this very rash order was the following, and so forth. Malmesbury adds another cause in the same work, *On the Deeds of the Bishops*, in the section on the eastern English bishops, fol. 136. Speaking of Herfast, bishop of Elmham, he says:

“While Lanfranc was a monk at Bec and scholars everywhere were belching dialectic with puffed-out cheeks, Herfast—then chaplain to Count William, later king—arrived at the famous school with a great retinue of companions and horses. Lanfranc, perceiving from their first conversation how nearly he knew nothing, set before him an elementary primer, mocking the man’s arrogance with Italian wit. Angered by this, Herfast induced the count to have Lanfranc removed from Bec and from all Normandy. But, through God’s intervention, William’s anger was calmed and the other was retained, chiefly through the efforts of William son of Osbern,” and so forth.]

They say that the cause of this very rash order [Note: [Col. 0035D] William of Malmesbury relates another cause of this affair, which it is useful to present in his own words:

“While Lanfranc was a monk at Bec, when scholars everywhere were belching dialectic with puffed-out cheeks, Herfast—then chaplain to Count William, later king—arrived at the famous school with a great retinue of companions and horses. Then Lanfranc, perceiving from their first conversation how nearly he knew nothing, set before him an elementary primer, mocking the man’s arrogance with Italian wit. Angered by this, he induced the count—literally, ‘through the count he caused it’—to have Lanfranc removed from Bec and from all Normandy. But,” and so forth.]

was, they say, that Lanfranc opposed the marriage of the count of Flanders’ daughter, whom the duke had taken as his wife, because she was related to him by close blood relationship. Therefore, by authority of the Roman pope, all Neustria had been suspended from and placed under interdict with respect to the exercise of Christian worship.

For this reason Lanfranc again went to the Roman [Col. 0035D] pope; he had already gone to Rome [Col. 0036A] [Note: [Col. 0062D] On account of a certain cleric named Berengar. This Berengar, the leader and standard-bearer of the Sacramentarians, was born at Tours and became archdeacon of the Church of Angers. He was a man endowed indeed with inflated learning, but poisonous in doctrine, perverse, and heretical. Nevertheless, Hildebert of Le Mans, not yet a bishop, in celebrating his praises and gifts of mind, exceeded the bounds of true praise—because he had once been, I think, his pupil and follower.

The history of this Berengar’s heresy is painted in vivid colors by Blessed Lanfranc in his little book *On the Body and Blood of Christ* and in Letter 50. If you please, read the notes on the same, as well as the accounts by very many modern writers, especially Caesar Baronius, vol. II of the *Ecclesiastical Annals*. I therefore thought it best to refrain from describing these matters again, lest I seem to be doing what has already been done.

Moreover, anyone wishing to know the upbringing of that heresiarch, the beginnings and spread of his heresy, its condemnation in several councils, its principal opponents, what Saint Fulbert, his teacher, thought of him as he was dying, and finally his end, should consult William of Malmesbury, book III of *On the Deeds of the English*, fols. [Col. 0063B] 63–64; Guitmund, archbishop of Aversa, *On the Sacrament of the Body and Blood of the Lord*; Abbot Durandus, on the same matter, in the Appendix to the Works of Blessed Lanfranc near the end; Adelmann, bishop of Brescia, Letter to Berengar; chapter “I, Berengar,” *On Consecration*, distinction 2; Orderic Vitalis, book IV of the *History*, under the year 1065, p. 519; Pope Innocent III, chapter 10, *On the Mystery of the Sacred Altar*; and Nicholas Harpsfield, *History of England*, century II.] on account of a certain cleric named Berengar, who taught concerning the sacrament of the altar otherwise than the Church holds.

5 [Note: [Col. 0063B] For he said that the bread and wine after consecration were only a sacrament, and not the true body and blood of Christ. It would be useful to publish a most elegant and highly readable monument of antiquity, *On the Truth of the Body and Blood of Christ the Lord in the Sacrament of the Venerable Eucharist*: I mean the letter of a certain Anastasius, a monk (if conjecture may be indulged) of the monastery of Saints Sergius and Bacchus at Angers, in which he professes his faith.

“Lord Gerald,” etc. (*Patrologia* CXLIX, cols. 433–436), down to “in heaven. Farewell.”]

For he said that the bread and wine after consecration were only a sacrament, and not the true body and blood of Christ. This cleric, who was almost his intimate associate, had sent Lanfranc letters tainted with the error itself. [Note: [Col. 0063C] He had sent letters, etc. Here are the same letters of Berengar, as I judge, transmitted to Blessed Lanfranc, then prior at Bec, drawn from a handwritten manuscript in the royal library.

“BERENGAR TO BROTHER LANFRANC.

“Word has reached me, Brother Lanfranc, from Ingelran of Chartres which I ought not to have passed over without warning your affection. It is this: that the opinions of John Scotus concerning the sacrament of the altar, in which he dissents from your adopted Paschasius, displease you—indeed, that you have considered them heretical. If this is so, brother, in this matter you have done an injustice to the intellect which God has granted you and which is not to be despised, by pronouncing a hasty judgment. For you have not yet labored sufficiently in divine Scripture along with your more diligent companions.

“And now, brother, however unlearned I may be in that Scripture, I should like at least to hear as much from him, if an opportunity were afforded me, with whatever suitable judges or hearers you wished present. Until that happens, do not look contemptuously upon what I say. If you consider John a heretic, whose opinions concerning the Eucharist we approve, you must consider Ambrose, Jerome, and Augustine heretics as well, to say nothing of the rest.”] Those who read them thought that Lanfranc held such opinions and denounced him as a partner in the error.

At that time, however, Lanfranc had perhaps gone to Rome, while Leo the Eighth [Note: [Col. 0036D] This is Saint Leo IX, called the Eighth by Milo, because some have judged that Leo, who was created pope by the emperor Otto against John XII, ought to be removed from the catalogue of the popes.] [Note: [Col. 0063D] Leo the Eighth: more correctly, the Ninth.] was occupying the chair of blessed Peter. His friends, having heard of the disgrace fabricated against him, sent the letters themselves after him to Rome; there they aroused suspicion of Lanfranc in certain quarters.

The pope summoned Berengar to appear on a fixed day. But, fearing to come, he delayed and sent two clerics to answer for him. When they appeared before the pope and failed in their case, they were rejected and taken into custody.

Lanfranc was ordered to rise. He wiped away the stain of the evil report against him, explained his faith, and established what he had explained more by sacred authorities than by arguments. What he said and proved pleased everyone and displeased no one.

[Note: [Col. 0063D] The same matters were repeated at the Council of Vercelli, and so forth. Concerning Vercelli, see the treatise of Blessed Lanfranc *On the Sacrament of the Eucharist*, placed below, as well as the treatise on the same subject by Guitmund of Aversa, book III.]

These same matters were repeated at the Council of Vercelli. Berengar’s opinion was heard and rejected, while the faith of the Church, which Lanfranc held and defended, was explained and confirmed by the unanimous consent of all. This opinion did not escape the notice of Pope Leo’s successor, Victor.

Finally, at the Council of Tours [Note: [Col. 0036D] Orderic Vitalis testifies that Lanfranc was present at this Council of Tours, book IV of the *History*.] [Note: [Col. 0063D] Finally, at the Council of Tours, and so forth. As the authors cited immediately above testify. Blessed Lanfranc was present at this council, as Orderic Vitalis confirms among others, book IV of his *History*, fol. 519.] whose proceedings were attended and presided over by legates of Victor himself, Berengar was given the option of defending his position. Since he did not dare undertake its defense, he confessed before everyone the common faith of the Church and swore that from that hour onward he would believe as the Church holds.

After violating this oath, however, he nevertheless did not cease spreading his former doctrine among the people. [Note: [Col. 0063D] When Pope Nicholas II heard this, and so forth. These matters are described by Blessed Lanfranc, as shown above, in the treatise *On the Sacrament of the Eucharist*, and Berengar’s confession is reported in chapter 1.

It is hardly surprising that so fatal a monster emerged at that time, since integrity had gone into exile, good morals had fallen into ruin, and nearly everyone—especially ecclesiastics—was wallowing in the mire of pleasures like beasts. “There must be heresies,” says the Apostle, “so that those who are approved may become manifest”; for the holy Fathers unanimously assert that heresy is the punishment of sin.

To confront such evils, Nicholas, the supreme pastor of the Church, wished a council to be held, with Cardinal Stephen acting on his behalf in Gaul. We shall not delay to weave into these notes—even though they perhaps do not fit the subject particularly well—a copy of its text, written in a contemporary hand on a parchment leaf torn from a certain codex and struggling against mold and worms, so that it may not perish.

## Council of Angers

From the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ in the year 1060, indiction XIII, on the Kalends of March, on the thirteenth day of the moon, Wednesday [f. x], with Stephen, cardinal priest of the holy Roman Church and vicar of the Apostolic See, presiding in the basilica of Saint Maurice and his companions, the holy synod—which, at the command of our lord, the most blessed supreme pontiff and universal pope Nicholas, had assembled at Tours, the metropolis of Gaul—after the holy Gospels had been set forth and fervent prayers to God offered, carefully reconsidered those matters in which the condition of the churches throughout almost the entire world, and especially in Gaul, seemed to be wavering and falling into ruin. It decided, with appropriate concern, to establish briefly below the following provisions.

### Chapter I

By the authority of the Holy Spirit, as we believe, the judgment pronounced at the Council of Chalcedon concerning the Simoniacs shall be observed by all in such a way that whoever thereafter attempts, by money, by any unsuitable secular agreement, or by any method contrary to canonical judgment, to give or receive a bishopric, an abbey, an archdeaconry, an archpresbyterate, or any ecclesiastical dignity, or any rank, ministry, or benefice which the authority of the holy Fathers has decreed may be held only by clerics, shall be deprived of his own rank and dignity if he is the giver, while the recipient shall lose the ministry or benefice wrongly usurped, never to recover it.

### Chapter II

If any bishop or other prelate wishes, contrary to the rule established above, to ordain or grant any ecclesiastical ministry, or even the prebend called canonical, clerics shall be freely permitted to object and to appeal to the judgment of neighboring bishops or, if necessary, even to the Apostolic See itself.

### Chapter III

Likewise, no bishop or prelate shall thereafter presume, contrary to the canons, to sell or grant to anyone any new benefice from property belonging to the rights of the Church. Whoever has previously presumed to alienate from the Church anything belonging to its rights, under the name of a benefice or in any other way, shall, if he still survives, either restore to the Church what he wrongly removed or be punished by canonical sentence.

### Chapter IV

No one shall henceforth presume to receive, in any manner, a large or small church from laypeople without the consent of the bishop in whose parish it is. Nor may he receive it from a cleric, monk, or layperson as a sale for any price. If he does so, both seller and buyer shall be deprived of it.

### Chapter V

We also confirm that henceforth no one may receive any clerical office except in the churches of a single city. Whoever violates this shall be struck with canonical punishment.

[Col. 0065A]

### Chapter VI

Furthermore, if any bishop, priest, deacon, or subdeacon, after learning of the prohibition of our lord Pope Nicholas, has continued in the ministry and benefice of the altar while held in carnal union with any woman, or, after learning of the aforesaid prohibition of the Apostolic See, does not immediately abandon either the woman or the ministry of the Church together with its benefice, let him know that no pardon of restoration to his former rank has been reserved for him.

### Chapter VII

Whoever thereafter among the clerics serves as a soldier in arms shall lose both his benefice and his fellowship with the clergy.

### Chapter VIII

Whoever among the laity thereafter presumes to possess, sell, or give to anyone under the name of a benefice anything belonging to the Church’s offerings or almsgiving, whether burial rights or even a third part of the tithes, shall be struck by the sword of anathema.

### Chapter IX

Whoever takes in marriage or thereafter takes a woman related to him by blood, or one whom his blood-relative had previously known carnally, or one whose blood-relative he has taken carnally in marriage; or whoever, after discovering such a relationship, does not immediately dismiss her, or, knowing the matter, does not dismiss her; or whoever has seized another man’s wife, or shall seize her; or whoever, dismissing his own wife without episcopal judgment, has taken or shall take another—until he gives himself to fruitful repentance, let him recognize that he is excluded and alienated from the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ and from the thresholds of the Church, and that he is cut off in every respect like a rotten limb from a healthy body by the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God.

### Chapter X

Whoever is found to be a deserter from monastic religion shall be excluded from the kingdom of God and from the fellowship of Christians as an apostate and shall remain alienated until, coming to his senses, he performs worthy penance. Likewise, whoever refuses to receive persons who have duly repented in such a condition, after being admonished three times, shall, if he does not comply, be suspended from communion with the brothers—whether he is an abbot or an abbess—until he complies.

I, Stephen, called cardinal priest of the holy Roman Church, presiding over the synod in place of my lord Pope Nicholas, have subscribed these constitutions canonically promulgated by us, giving them the assent of my lowliness. Then ten archbishops and bishops subscribed.

[Note: [Col. 0065C] Thus far the council, from the library of the monastery of Saints Sergius and Bacchus at Angers.]

When Nicholas II heard this, he summoned Berengar. He came to Rome, but, distrustful of his case and placing little confidence in the support of those whom he had won over through expenditures and benefits, he did not dare defend his opinion. He therefore asked Nicholas II and his council to explain to him in words the faith they wished him to hold and to confirm it in writing.

Accordingly, at the pope’s command, the faith was explained in words, written down, and confirmed by the assent of all, and was handed to Berengar [Col. 0036D] to read. He accepted it, read it, [Note: [Col. 0065C] and swore that he held it. Berengar’s public confession or oath is found in chapter “I, Berengar,” *On Consecration*, distinction 2, and at the end of the Roman Council under Pope Nicholas II in 1059, held both in Berengar’s case and especially against the Simoniacs.

Berengar made another confession before the supreme pontiff Gregory VII—or rather, in my judgment, before the legate acting in Gaul at Alexander’s command and presiding over the Council of Tours. Blessed Lanfranc confronts him with both confessions in his book *On the Sacrament of the Eucharist*, near the beginning.] and swore that he held it, subscribing it with his own hand.

When this had been done, the pope and many others rejoiced at his return and conversion, whereas previously they had grieved over his turning away. But this sacrilegious violator of the oath later composed a written work against the aforesaid council, against Catholic truth, and against the faith of all ecclesiastical teachers. [Note: [Col. 0065D] He later composed a written work. But, with God’s merciful favor, we shall show in Letter 51 that he eventually returned to sound fruit.]

Lanfranc replied to it in the form of a letter. [Note: [Col. 0065D] He composed an elegant treatise. All writers who have written about Blessed Lanfranc report this. Concerning this treatise, see Letter 4.

Moreover, as was shown above, not only were those general councils convened, but assemblies of very learned men were also privately summoned so that Berengar’s heresy might be refuted and he himself brought back to Catholic truth. Two letters extracted from ancient parchment in the abbey of Casal Benedicto, belonging to our congregation—one from Berengar to Ascelin and one from Ascelin to Berengar—show this. So that they may not perish, we have thought it worthwhile to insert them in these notes.]

### Letter of Berengar to Ascelin

“BERENGAR to Brother ASCELIN.

“It would have been necessary to write to you quite differently if divine will had made that possible for me. Since it has not, I thought I ought to write to you as best I could.

“While passing through your presence, I had resolved to do absolutely nothing with anyone concerning the Eucharist until I had satisfied, in accordance with evangelical and apostolic Scripture, the bishops whom I was going to meet. It therefore happened that I opposed almost nothing to you and agreed with nothing in that conversation. If you consider how unworthily you had then come together, to say nothing of the others, this will not escape you.

“For the same reason I remained silent about that condemnable and sacrilegious opinion of William’s, which he pronounced: that every person ought to approach the Lord’s table at Easter.

“To come to the matter, I have now heard William boast that I could not deny John Scotus to be a heretic. You are my witness that this is false, if you remember my words sufficiently, although you too regard John Scotus as a heretic. May he who promised the faithful, ‘But if you think otherwise, God will reveal this also to you,’ not permit you, in your rashness, impiety, and unworthiness of your priesthood, to remain ignorant of this any longer.

“For you think against all the principles of nature and against evangelical and apostolic teaching if you agree with Paschasius in claiming that, in the sacrament of the Lord’s body, the substance of bread entirely ceases to exist—a notion which he alone has invented for himself.

“My words about John were these: that I had not examined everything he wrote. Even now this remains true. What I had seen that concerned this matter, I said I could recite from the writings of those whom I had named in my letter to Lanfranc as men who would have to be regarded as heretics if that John were considered a heretic.

“Moreover, if I saw anything in him insufficiently defined, I would readily disapprove it. I was speaking truthfully in this matter and maintained that, because I was merely passing through, I was not entering into any discussion, for the reason given above.

“He produced only two statements, as you know, excellent man, which had reached him from what he had heard from me: that the words instituted for the consecration of bread prove that the material of bread does not cease to exist in the sacrament, and that the episcopal staff is not the care of souls.

“The first of these, as you may remember, I affirmed; and it is so clear that even a little boy in school, who does not skillfully understand the force of the joining of words, would be sufficient to hold and prove it.

“As for the second, I both said and affirmed—and affirm now—that the staff is the care of souls, so that anyone who wished could easily perceive what I thought.

“Even now I wish, if it could safely be done, to conduct before you, in the hearing of anyone you wished, what I had undertaken to do before the bishops. But so long as I cannot, I beg you by the name of the Lord: do not make yourself a false witness by claiming that I condemned that John. I warn you to beware of the evangelical woe: ‘You who hold the key of knowledge do not enter yourselves, and you prevent those who are entering from entering.’

“Remember also that prophetic denunciation of the people, where it says: ‘For the people is provoking to anger, and lying children who say to those who see, “Do not see,” and to those who look, “Do not look upon for us the things that are right.”’ This is what your Arnulf said to me in your hearing: that I should allow you to think as you had been instructed.

“Yet I am wholly intent that no one transgress the boundaries set by the Fathers—the Evangelist, the Apostle, Ambrose, Augustine, and Jerome.

“If I am granted the opportunity to deal with you, you will see this to be as clear as daylight, so confident am I in your vigilance.

“I have written these things to you as best I could, meanwhile awaiting from the Lord an opportunity to speak with you. Farewell.”

### Letter of Ascelin to Berengar

“ASCELIN to Lord BERENGAR, his brother.

“I recently received your letter with joy, hoping that it would announce to us the joy of your speedy correction. But after reading it, my joy was turned into sorrow, since you have still not ceased to affirm your former error.

“O God! Where is that liveliness, that subtlety, that prudence in which you used to abound? You have apparently forgotten even what was said in our conversation, to say nothing of greater matters.

“I mean that opinion of William’s which you say he pronounced—that everyone ought to approach the Lord’s table at Easter. If he had stated it in that form, it would rightly have been judged sacrilegious. But those who were present testify that it was expressed differently.

“What was said then, and what we now testify, was that every Christian ought at Easter to communicate from the Lord’s table, unless, on account of some crime committed by that person, he is kept away from so salutary a banquet; and that this should not occur except by the sole command of his confessor. Otherwise the keys of the Church are nullified.

“But to return to myself: after considering everything, I do not believe that I came unworthily to that conversation. For I brought with me something which, as long as I live, with the help of divine power, I shall retain in the shrine of my heart as certain, indubitable, and inviolable by any assaults: namely, that bread and wine on the altar, through the power of the Holy Spirit and the ministry of the priest, become the true body and true blood of Christ. This is sufficiently and clearly proved by the testimony of Scripture, provided it is not corrupted by a perverse interpretation.

“As for John Scotus, I hold him neither rashly, nor impiously, nor unworthily of my priesthood. I see him striving with all his strength and intention for this one purpose: to persuade me that what is consecrated on the altar is neither truly the body nor truly the blood of Christ. He tries to establish this from the works of the holy Fathers, which he interprets perversely.

“It is enough here to note that prayer of Saint Gregory: ‘May your sacraments, O Lord, we ask, accomplish in us what they contain, so that what we now perform under a form, we may receive in the reality of the things themselves.’

“Explaining this, the aforesaid John says, among other statements contrary to our faith: ‘These things are performed under a form, not in reality.’ If I know your vigilance well, you do not fail to recognize that this was not spoken in a Catholic manner—especially since, in the conversation so often mentioned, you did not deny it when I recited that same prayer together with its explanation from John’s book. Yet you then objected, as you do now, that you had not read his treatise through to the end.

“We therefore cannot sufficiently wonder that you, a man of such prudence, praise so greatly what you do not know; for if you knew it, I would not believe that you had praised it. Your prudence knows that the words of heretics must be avoided like the cups of poisoners: they first charm sweetly, and afterward kill lethally.

“Moreover, with Paschasius and the other Catholics I not only agree but also venerate and embrace the true body and true blood of Christ, received by the faithful on the altar under the form of bread and wine. Nor do I act, as you say, against the principles of nature. For I would call nothing the nature of things except the will of God.

“What sane person would call the cause of things ‘nature,’ rather than confess that the will of God is the cause of all natures and of all things born from their own nature? The will of God, moreover, is so effective and omnipotent that his willing alone is doing. Hence, when he willed something, he made it: ‘For the Lord has done whatever he willed.’

“He willed that the bread and wine which are made on the altar through the consecration of the Holy Spirit and the ministry of the priest should truly be created as his flesh and blood in potency, and, by being created, should be mystically sacrificed each day.

“He himself clearly suggests this at the beginning of this sacrament to his disciples, saying: ‘Take and eat; this is my body.’ And lest they receive it lightly or think it to be some ordinary body—for all the faithful are called members of Christ, and thus are called his body—he added a clarification and said: ‘which will be given for you.’ Likewise concerning the cup: ‘which will be poured out for you.’

“See how our Redeemer instructs us; see how he opens and expresses what body and what blood he commends to us. The disciples looked upon bread and wine with bodily eyes, and they heard from the Truth: ‘This is my body, which will be given for you’; and, ‘This is my blood, which will be poured out for many.’

“What could be more open? What clearer? What sweeter? How sound it is to affirm, and how dangerous to strive to refute, what the Truth declares! The Evangelists testify to this, the apostles proclaim it, and the holy teachers discuss it, provided their words are understood rightly. Whoever interprets their good statements perversely must see for himself what he deserves.

“Nor should we wonder or doubt that God can bring it about that what is consecrated on the altar by the power of the Holy Spirit and the ministry of the priest is united to that body which our Redeemer assumed from the Virgin Mary. Both are corporeal in substance; both are visible, if we remember that we ourselves are composed of corporeal and incorporeal, mortal and immortal substance, and if we firmly believe that the divine and human natures were united in one person.

“Let ash and dust explain to me the reason for the second or third matter, and then let it think itself capable of explaining the first: ‘For who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has been his counselor?’

“These brief words are my answer to you, showing that with Paschasius I think neither against the principles of nature nor against evangelical and apostolic teaching.

“Finally, you beg me by the name of the Lord not to make myself a false witness by saying that I condemned John together with us. I shall gladly observe this. But I am a true witness that, compelled by the truth itself, you rejected with us the interpretation he gave above of Gregory’s prayer.

“Finally, I fear that the evangelical woe from which you warn me may, God forbid, be turned back upon your own head. For, while turning over the key of knowledge, you yourself appear not to enter, since you dissent from the universal Church; and by persuading others of what you think, you plainly close the entrance to those who would enter.

“As for what Lord Arnulf the cantor added—namely, that you should allow us to think as we had been instructed—he spoke well and wisely and, if you wished, gave concise counsel for your salvation. He would have deterred you, if he could, from trying, alone or through whatever companions you may have, to change the way which our teachers, so holy, so wise, and so Catholic, have shown us to be so straight, so well-defined, and so well-trodden that no one who keeps to it goes astray, while no one who does not keep to it can avoid going astray.

“But enough of this. For now I ask you as a friend to desist from this perverse intention. Do not impose on us unheard-of and empty cruelties, and do not be so self-confident that you refuse humbly to submit yourself to be nourished beneath the wings of that evangelical hen. Otherwise the splendid intellect God has granted you may become foolish and therefore be cast outside and trampled by everyone.

“Be ashamed to defend a book which we have heard was condemned at Vercelli in a plenary synod, and that you too were marked with the stain of heresy because of it. Return, then, I beg you, to Catholic and apostolic tradition, so that the apostolic saying which you directed to me may also be fulfilled in you: ‘But if you think otherwise, God will reveal this also to you.’”

The Ascelin referred to here seems to be Ascelin of Utica, or a monk of the monastery of Saint Évroul in Normandy, the nephew of the elder Ascelin and a contemporary of Berengar. Our Orderic Vitalis appears to indicate this in book VI of his *History*, p. 623. After describing the destruction of that monastery, he adds:

“The elder Ascelin, however, inhabited the wilderness of Utica with a few poor settlers, and nourished his nephew Ascelin, Guitbert of Gacé, Haimon of Telleia, and other boys; and he taught them the common letters, so that in that place they might render daily service to God.”

Yet Berengar’s letter to a certain monk named Richard is mentioned, where, among other things, he speaks of Ascelin as follows:

“I say this because of Ascelin, who did not fear to twist the words of Blessed Augustine toward the perversity of his own error, like a certain countryman of his who, at Poitiers, while discussing Blessed Augustine’s opinion, etc.”

These words, I think, indicate with little ambiguity an Ascelin of Poitiers.

As for William, I have nothing I would dare assert. But, if conjecture may be permitted, I shall say that he is the same William who later became abbot of Cormeilles, whom Blessed Lanfranc mentions above and to whom he writes Letter 57.

[He] composed an elegant little book, supported by Catholic truth and strengthened everywhere by the authorities of the holy Fathers, in which the things we have mentioned are found. Lanfranc was present at these proceedings, for he had come to Rome on account of this dispute and in order to act before the pope on behalf of the duke of the Normans and his wife, for which reason, as we have said, he had journeyed there. Accordingly, after speaking with Pope Nicholas, he showed that the pope’s decision weighed only upon those who had neither joined nor could separate the couple, since the duke was unwilling by any means to dismiss the girl whom he had taken as his wife. Hearing this and recognizing that it was true, the supreme pontiff, having made a dispensation, permitted the marriage—yet on the condition that the duke and his wife build two monasteries, in which they would gather separate communities of men and women, who would serve God there day and night under the rule of holy religion and pray for their salvation. [Note: [Col. 0037D] We have discussed these two monasteries, erected at Caen, in the observations preceding this.]

The duke obeyed the apostolic dispensation, and they built two monasteries on the estate [Note: [Col. 0069A]

Which antiquity called Caen. Caen—*Cadomum* in Latin—is a large city, famous for its academy of letters, situated in Lower Normandy. That it should more correctly and expressively be called *Campidomum Cenalis* is demonstrated by Cenalis, book II, *On Gallic Affairs*, epitome 4. Nevertheless, the authority of writers and popular usage prevailed, so that it is called more briefly *Cadomum*.

Moreover, we shall set forth the elegance of this most noble city from the very learned Papirius Masson, in his description of the rivers of Gaul:

“Seeking the city of Argentan, five leagues distant, which, though situated on high ground, slopes down toward the place where one descends to the Orne, he encounters the river which, continuing its course, flows through Caen, that splendid city of the diocese of Bayeux, and is joined to it by a bridge composed of three arches. Concerning it Armoricus writes in book eight of the *Philippid*:

> A powerful, wealthy town, spacious and fair in situation,  
> Rich in rivers, meadows, and the fertility of its fields,  
> Its harbor receiving ships laden with merchandise,  
> And adorning itself with so many churches, houses, and citizens  
> That Paris scarcely admits it to be inferior to itself.

“Anyone who has carefully examined the site of Caen will judge it both beautiful and pleasant because of the river Orne, which twice each day is filled by the ebb and flow of the Ocean. Another river, called the Odon, also flows into this city and empties into the Orne.” See, if you please, the notes to letter 2 of the *Beck Chronicle*, before the year 1063, p. 3.]

which antiquity called Caen. [Note: [Col. 0069C]

**The duke’s one monastery.** Nothing at all of the antiquity of that celebrated monastery of Saint Stephen remains. Alas! The fury of the most wanton and criminal Calvinists utterly overturned all its buildings and tore apart or consumed by fire nearly all its charters. Nevertheless, through the study and diligence of the highly religious and by no means unlearned D. de Renchi, cellarer of that same monastery and doctor of sacred theology, the foundation charter, the privileges of Popes Alexander II, Honorius III, and Clement III, as well as those of Rotrod, archbishop of Rouen, and Henry, bishop of Bayeux, were eventually discovered. So that they may not be lost, we shall transcribe them intact. These are copies.

[Col. 0069D] **FOUNDATION CHARTER OF THE ABBEY OF SAINT STEPHEN OF CAEN, MADE BY WILLIAM THE CONQUEROR**

Whoever gives something to God, or for God’s sake, does not alienate it from himself; rather, he preserves it to be multiplied in the future with the hope of eternal life. The pious generosity of the Creator does this, as does his abundant compassion toward created things. Although he has no need of our goods—for the earth and its fullness are his—he nevertheless desires to be honored from our substance and to receive from us the sacrifice of praise for our salvation. He urges us to serve him and grants us something with which to repay him for his benefits; yet the merciful Father receives this as though it were another’s and repays it as though it were ours, forgiving sins in this world and promising himself and the heavenly kingdom a hundredfold to those who receive it in the future.

Led by this hope, I, William, king of the English and prince of the Normans and Cenomans, have resolved to build within the borough commonly called Caen a monastery in honor of God and of the most blessed protomartyr Stephen, for the salvation of my soul, [Col. 0070A] that of my wife, my children, and my parents. To ensure that the worship of divine Religion may not at some time fail in that place through poverty, I have provided for it in the future in the following manner.

Therefore I give to the aforesaid monastery the following villages belonging to my jurisdiction and paying rent: Roz, Alemannia, Pont-de-Dives, and Cabourg, with their colonists and people subject to tenure, or free men, together with their mills, waters, meadows, pastures, woods, and all revenues and customary dues belonging to them, as I and my predecessors have hitherto held them in my domain. I also grant the men of the two villages mentioned above—namely, [Censu?] and Roz—who do not hold free land, to the service of the church and the monks so freely and entirely exempt that they shall never interrupt that service on account of any summons to an expedition or any other matter, unless I myself, personally or by my writ, summon the abbot to send them to me by name; and this only within the boundaries of Normandy and only by name, for the necessity [Col. 0070B] of war threatened by an external people.

I also give the part of the borough in which the aforesaid monastery has been built, from the wall westward in a straight line, as far as the road extends by which one goes from the old monastery of Saint Stephen to the city of Bayeux; and likewise the road by which one goes to the village of Brithwilla of Saint Michael, together with the lands and all the customary dues belonging to me in that same borough, except that foreign merchants shall pay, for everything they buy and sell there on Monday, for as long as the toll-collector sits at his station and the merchants are present in the common market, a toll to the officials who govern the greater borough: from every cart and from the asses carrying firewood for sale, one piece of wood. I give Villiers with all its territory, and the service of the men belonging to it, so that the men who live there may serve me [variant: serve], and so that my service may not be lacking. In the greater borough, I give the house of Turstin Legrin; and the mill-house of Darnestel with the mill itself, and the mill that belonged to Ramard.

All these things are free from every customary due. From the meadows belonging to my jurisdiction, three *jugera* at the Elm Meadow of Brendac, in addition to those belonging to the aforesaid villages; the bed of the Old Odon, from the village of Venintro to the river Orne, with three mills built upon it. The land of William Pavolh, which he holds from me at Caen and Cluilla. In the territory of Brithwilla, the allod held there by Roger the Bald. In the territory of Bracium, the land of William Deslanda; also the allod held by Lupus at Beneto and Walmereto, with the portion of the church belonging to him. In the territory of Curlei, the land of William the chamberlain. In the territory of Balduent, the vineyard, with the vintner’s house, which Hubert the steward held from me. At Barbefloth, two measures of land. In the territory of Boseval, the allod of Radulf son of Ansered; in the villages and in the marsh, the land held there by William the Fat. Also the land formerly held by Hugh of Rozel. In [Col. 0070D] Graymulla, the forest of Malo Pertuoso, and those of Tortavalle, Folonia, and Caisneto, with their waters and lands and everything belonging to them, on the condition that the monks of that monastery shall never destroy or order the destruction of those forests for the purpose of cultivating or inhabiting the land, while the deer, roebucks, and wild boars remain in my domain.

The tithe of Fredetuacum. The service owed from the land held by Boselin of Dives in the villages and at Guarinvilla. I also grant that a market be established for the use of the aforesaid monastery in the village called Balte. In the territory of Caen, a fair lasting three days, so that whenever anyone buys [variant: comes] on any of these three days, the entire market of the greater borough belongs to Saint Stephen.

In the city of Rouen, I grant that a warehouse be established on the Seine, free from every customary due, and that those dwelling in it be free from such dues, both on land and on water, throughout all my territory. I also grant the house with its garden which Bernard son of Ospac gave to the same monastery in that city; and the six *jugera* of meadow which he likewise gave at Batpalmas; and the house given by William the canon, son of Suevi.

In the territory of Liret, one tenant with his land, four and a half *arpents* of vineyard, and one acre of land within that same territory. On the river Audura, I grant that two mills be built, provided that enough water remains free so that, whatever the condition of the water, both ships and fish may conveniently pass through that space upstream and downstream. I also grant the entire allod held by Osmund Aculeus, Richard, and Roger. In the territory of Calvimont over the Dives, and likewise all that is held by any allodial proprietors within the long bridge of Dives.

In the land of the English, in the county of Devon, the manor called Northam. In the county of Dorset, two manors, one called Francona and the other Biencona. In the county of Somerset, in the territory of Cruera, ten hides of land and a church with the entire tithe of that territory. In the county of Wiltshire, the church of Cosham with all the land and the tithe belonging to it. I also grant in the county of Norfolk the manor called Welles, which William of Scotland gave to the aforesaid monastery, together with the church of Morthona and the land with the tithe belonging to that church in Essex.

Likewise, in the county of Essex, I grant the little manor called Panfield; and in London, a certain parcel of land that belonged to Leureth, situated near the church of Saint Peter, free from *geld*, *scot*, and every other customary due, which Waleran son of Ramnulf gave, together with the tithe of all his land in England, both for the sake of his own soul and for mine.
