[Col. 0071D] **PRIVILEGE OF HONORIUS III, OR OF ALEXANDER II, ETC.** (See *Patrologia*, vol. CXLVI, under Honorius III.) A letter of the same Honorius, by which he confirms the immunities of the monastery of Saint Stephen of Caen.

**Honorius, bishop, servant of the servants of God.**

“It is fitting that apostolic protection be present for those who choose a religious life, lest an attack of any sort of rashness either recall them from their purpose or—God forbid—weaken the strength of sacred Religion. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we mercifully assent to your just petitions and receive the monastery of Saint Stephen of Caen, in which you have been devoted to divine service, under the authority and protection of blessed Peter and of ourselves, following the example of our predecessor Pope Alexander III of happy memory, whose privilege we have seen recorded in his register; and we fortify it with the privilege of this present document.

“We decree that whatever possessions and goods that same monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may in the future, by the grant of pontiffs, the generosity of kings or princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, through the Lord’s favor, obtain, shall remain secure, intact, and firm for you and your successors.

“Furthermore, following in the footsteps of our aforesaid predecessor, we decree that no one possessing ecclesiastical or secular rank shall have any authority over the property or administration of the aforesaid monastery, except the Roman pontiff; rather, we determine that every right of that monastery belongs to the care of ourselves and our successors. If you are oppressed by the harassment of any bishop and appeal to the holy apostolic see, then, until your case has been referred to the Roman pontiff and has been settled by him or by his mandate, no bishop thereafter shall be permitted to bring a suit against you.

“We also prohibit the bishop of Bayeux from presuming to excommunicate you for any fault of the abbot or monks, or to prohibit divine worship in the monastery. When you, the abbot of that place, or any of your successors dies, no one shall be placed there through any stratagem of secret seizure or malice, except one whom the brothers, by common agreement or the sounder judgment of the brethren, shall have provided to be elected according to the fear of God and the rule of blessed Benedict.

“Moreover, you may receive for conversion to your way of life persons who flee from the world, provided they are free and released from worldly obligations, and retain them in your community without anyone’s opposition. You shall receive from the bishop of Bayeux the chrism, holy oil, dedications of churches, consecrations of altars, ordinations of your monks and clerics who are to be promoted to sacred orders, and also the counsels and imposition of penances upon laymen who have committed grave sins, provided that he is a Catholic, enjoys the grace and communion of the apostolic see, and is willing to provide these things to you freely and without any corruption. Otherwise, you may approach whichever Catholic bishop you prefer, [Col. 0072C] who, supported by our authority, shall grant what is requested; especially if the bishop of Bayeux delays the ordinations of your monks and clerics for more than one month, as was established by the same predecessor of ours.

“We therefore decree that no human being whatsoever shall be permitted rashly to disturb the aforesaid monastery, or to take away its possessions, or to retain, diminish, or burden its abbey with any vexations; rather, everything shall remain intact and whole, so that it may serve in every way the uses of those for whose governance and support it was granted, without prejudice to the authority of the apostolic see.

“If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowingly attempting rashly to violate this page of our constitution, after being warned once, twice, or three times, does not correct his presumption by a fitting satisfaction, let him lose the dignity of his power and honor, recognize himself as guilty before the divine judgment of the iniquity committed, [Col. 0072D] and be separated from the most sacred body and blood of God and our Lord and Redeemer Jesus Christ, and at the final judgment let him undergo strict punishment.

“But let there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ for all who preserve the rights of that place, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and, before the strict Judge, find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

“I, Honorius, bishop of the Catholic Church.

“+ I, Guido, bishop of Praeneste.

“+ I, Octavianus, cardinal deacon of Saints Sergius and Bacchus.

“+ I, Stephen, priest of the Basilica of the Twelve Apostles.

“+ I, Gregory, [lacuna] priest.

“Given at the Lateran by the hand of William, vice-chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the third Ides of June, in the ninth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1221, in the fifth year of the pontificate of our lord Pope Honorius.”

[Col. 0073A] **PRIVILEGE OF POPE CLEMENT VI**, by which he permits the abbots of Saint Stephen of Caen to use pontifical insignia.

“Clement, servant of the servants of God, for perpetual remembrance of the matter.

“Although unworthy, presiding over the governance of the Holy Roman Church, mother and teacher of all churches, we willingly advance their condition through expenditures of honor and, by clarifying matters as far as is possible for us, remove whatever might at a given time introduce into them material for disputes through the twists of uncertainty.

“Some time ago, having learned through the report of our beloved sons Robert, abbot, and the convent of the monastery of Saint Stephen of Caen, of the Order of Saint Benedict in the diocese of Bayeux, that the aforesaid monastery was among the monasteries of those regions noble and distinguished, and that it possessed a large part of the head of the glorious protomartyr Saint Stephen, as well as the head of Saint Margaret the martyr, as the common opinion of the faithful in those regions asserted, and that many relics of other saints were honorably preserved there, on account of which a large multitude of the faithful frequently gathered from every direction at that monastery with great devotion; and that the body of William, king of England, the principal founder of that monastery, was also honorably buried there—William, who, when he was duke of Normandy, formerly seized the kingdom of England by force of arms; and since the aforesaid abbot and convent in that monastery, together with its thirteen parish churches and their sites, and the chapels adjoining them, lawfully held and possessed, and had hitherto continuously held and possessed, freely, peacefully, and quietly, for so long a time that no memory of its beginning remained, spiritual and ecclesiastical jurisdiction and correction over delinquent clerics and ecclesiastical persons there; and since, from that jurisdiction and from their official, appeal had customarily and regularly been made, not to the episcopal see but to their metropolitan of Rouen, or to the apostolic see, from that time until now; and since the collation of those churches, together with the entrusting, visitation, and provision of their care, belonged to the abbot and convent—

“Desiring to adorn the aforesaid Robert, abbot, both because of the merit of his many virtues and because of the ardent affection of sincere devotion which he bore and bears toward us and the Roman Church, as well as the monastery, with special privileges and marks of honor in consideration of the matters stated above, and inclining to the petitions of the same Robert, abbot, and convent in this regard, we have decided, by apostolic authority and by special grace, to grant to the same Robert, abbot, and to his successors, the abbots of that monastery who shall exist in their time, that Robert and they may freely use golden or gilded mitres bearing plates and gems, decorated with goldwork, as well as plain mitres, rings, sandals, and other pontifical insignia, at appropriate times, wherever they may be, during the solemn celebrations of Mass and the other Hours, except in provincial councils and episcopal synods; and that in such councils and synods they may perpetually use plain mitres; and likewise that in the monastery, its churches, and the aforesaid church sites they may freely give and impart the solemn blessing at Mass, Vespers, Matins, and at table, provided that no bishop or legate of the apostolic see is present, notwithstanding any constitution issued to the contrary.

“And as a token of the privilege obtained from the aforesaid see, we wish the said abbot and convent to pay us and our successors one ounce of gold every two years.

“Since, however, as the petition submitted to us by the same Robert, abbot, stated, some people have called into doubt whether the clause ‘provided that no bishop or legate of the apostolic see is present’ [Col. 0074A] refers to all the preceding clauses, the same abbot humbly petitioned us to clarify this doubt and, if and insofar as necessary, to extend this grant by apostolic benevolence with regard to the white pontificals to be worn by Abbot Robert and his aforesaid successors in the same councils and synods.

“Therefore, to remove every scruple of doubt, by the tenor of this document we declare that it was and is our intention that the aforesaid abbot and his successors may use golden or gilded mitres bearing plates and gems, decorated with goldwork, as well as plain mitres, rings, sandals, and other pontifical insignia, at suitable times and wherever they may be, even in the presence of the diocesan bishop or any other bishop, except in provincial councils and episcopal synods; and that in those councils and synods they may use plain mitres; and that the said clause, ‘provided that no bishop or legate of the apostolic see is present,’ refers only to the immediately preceding clause, namely, that concerning the solemn blessing, and in no way to the other preceding clauses.

“Nevertheless, by the tenor of this document and by apostolic authority, as a more ample grace, we grant to the same Robert, abbot, and his aforesaid successors that they may also perpetually use these white pontificals in the same provincial councils and synods, notwithstanding any contrary constitution.

“Let no one whatsoever be permitted to violate this page of our declaration and grant, or rashly to oppose it. If anyone should presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of his blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

“Given at Villeneuve-lès-Avignon, on the tenth day before the Kalends of July, in the fifth year of our pontificate.”

**Confirmation of the immunities of the monastery of Saint Stephen of Caen, granted by the archbishop of Rouen in the year 1170.**

“Rotrod, by the grace of God archbishop of Rouen, to those present and to those who shall come, greeting.

“It contributes greatly to the welfare of churches and monasteries, and also of ecclesiastical and secular persons, that the things conferred upon them by Catholic men be recorded in writing for the preservation of memory, lest, when oblivion effaces what has been done, what was stable and confirmed be called into question.

“For this reason, granting a favorable assent to the pious petitions of our sons William, abbot, and the convent of Saint Stephen of Caen, we commit to writing and strengthen with the protection of our seal the things that we know to belong in the bishopric of Bayeux to the possession, right, and alms of Saint Stephen of Caen, both in churches and in tithes, meadows, waters, woods, pastures, mills, houses, lands, and their inhabitants. These things were also confirmed to the same monastery by the most illustrious William, king of the English and prince of the Normans and Cenomans, and by other noble men, especially by the venerable Odo and Henry, bishops of Bayeux.

“These, therefore, are the possessions which we recognize as held by the aforesaid monastery and which we grant and confirm to it to be held forever, freely, peacefully, and absolutely, free from synodal dues, circuit-visitation, and the other customary obligations belonging to episcopal jurisdiction: namely, the church of Saint Nicholas in the borough of the monastery; the church of Villiers; two parts of all the tithes belonging to the fief of that monastery throughout the territory of Caen and Villiers; the church of Breteville-l’Orgueilleuse, with the chapel of Putot, its tithes, and all its appurtenances; the church of Aunay, with the entire tithe of the parish and its appurtenances; the two churches of Alemannia, with all the tithes of those parishes and their appurtenances; the church of Ifs, with the chapel of Bracium and the entire tithe [Col. 0075A] of the parish and its appurtenances; also the church of Cabourg, the old chapel of the Borough of Dives, and the church of Saint Mary of Buisson near Mèreville.

“Furthermore, we confirm to the same monastery the episcopal rights in the church of Censio, namely synodal dues, circuit-visitation, and the other customary obligations which that monastery possesses in the aforesaid churches.”

**The bishop of Bayeux confirms the privileges, possessions, and other rights of the monastery of Saint Stephen of Caen.**

“Henry, by the grace of God bishop of Bayeux, perpetual salvation in the Lord to all worshipers of the Christian religion to whom this charter shall come.

“Lest the things that are done fall into oblivion, established practice and common regard for usefulness require that they be recorded in the sequence of writing. Accordingly, we have thought fit to commit to writing, and to strengthen by the protection of our seal, those things which we know in our diocese to belong to the possession, right, and alms of the monastery of Blessed Stephen of Caen, in churches, tithes, meadows, waters, woods, pastures, mills, houses, lands, and their inhabitants; things also confirmed by the most illustrious William, king of the English and prince of the Normans and Cenomans, by other noblemen, and especially by our venerable predecessor Odo, bishop of Bayeux.

“These, therefore, are the things which we know to be possessed by the aforesaid monastery, and which we grant and confirm for its perpetual possession: namely, the church of St Nicholas in the borough of the monastery; the church of Villers; two-thirds of all the tithes arising from the fee of that monastery throughout the whole territory of Caen and Villers; the church of Tortavalle with the whole tithe of the parish and its appurtenances; the church of Folonia with the whole tithe of the parish and its appurtenances; the church of Alneto with the whole tithe of the parish and its appurtenances; the church of Bretteville-l’Orgueilleuse with the chapel of Putot, its tithes, and all its appurtenances; the two churches of Allemagne and all the tithes of those parishes with their appurtenances; the church of Icy with the chapel of Brachy and the whole tithe of the parish with its appurtenances; the church of Cabourg; the ancient chapel in the borough of Dives; and the church of St Mary du Buisson near Maîtreville.

“We grant and confirm that these churches shall remain for ever free and exempt for the aforesaid monastery from synodal dues, circata, and all other customs pertaining to episcopal right. Moreover, we confirm to that monastery the episcopal rights in the church of Cintheaux—namely synod, circata, and the other customs—which that monastery possesses in the aforesaid churches. With our confirmation, the aforesaid monastery also holds this privilege together with those already stated: it is to distribute to the priests of the aforesaid churches, on Holy Saturday of Easter, the holy chrism and oil which it receives from us. The clerics of the specified churches are to come to synod freely and peacefully, so that no money may be demanded from them on any pretext.

“Likewise, we confirm to the aforesaid monastery the processions at Cintheaux on holy Pentecost, and the processions of Allemagne and of Icy, with the dependent places and appurtenances of those villages. We also confirm two-thirds of the tithes of its fee at Ruscavilla, Curley, Amblie, Pierrepont, Bavent, Billy, Vaumeret, Géonville, throughout all the land of Roger the Bald, and at Bretteville-sur-Laize.

“Furthermore, in accordance with the enactments of our predecessors, we grant and confirm to the aforesaid monastery these liberties of pontifical right in respect of all men of the monastery dwelling in the borough of the monks, at Villers, elsewhere in the territory of Caen, at Venuntio, and at Francaville: namely, when any of the aforesaid men has been convicted or has confessed concerning criminal or non-criminal sins, or any offences, if money is to be exacted therefor, it shall be paid to the abbot or monks of the aforesaid monastery. The imposition of penance for non-criminal offences, however, shall lie at the monks’ discretion. When anyone is deemed guilty of a criminal offence, he shall not be summoned or brought to court by the archdeacon of Bayeux; rather, that archdeacon shall notify the abbot or prior of the monastery. The man against whom the charge is made, having been admonished on the abbot’s behalf, shall appear on a fittingly appointed day before the abbot, or someone acting for the abbot, and before the archdeacon, in the parish where he lives; and, in their presence, the truth of the matter shall be investigated. If a judgment must then be rendered, or guilt is established, the Church of Bayeux shall, as is proper, be resorted to, either for examination of the cause or for obtaining reconciliation.

“We confirm the same liberties of episcopal right to the aforesaid monastery in respect of all the men of Rots; all the men of Cintheaux and Allemagne and its members, namely Stavelles; likewise all the men of Icy, Brachy, Fulberfolia, Burgesbu, and Hogue; all Cabourg and the borough of Dives as far as the little bridge dividing the bishopric of Bayeux from that of Lisieux; all those of the parish of Tortavalle and Folonia; those whom the aforesaid monastery has at Hovetot; all inhabitants in the monks’ woods and their appurtenances; the whole tenure of Tortavalle; and also the men whom the monastery has at Ruscavilla, Curley, Siccavilla, Granville, and Bavent; throughout all the land of Roger the Bald of Bretteville-sur-Laize; throughout the land of Louet of Billy; at Vaumeret with the portion of the church belonging to him; and in the village of Buisson.

“We also confirm these liberties of pontifical right to the aforesaid monastery in respect of all men throughout the land which Viscount Ranulf and Robert Bertrand held at Bretteville-l’Orgueilleuse with its appurtenances. We confirm the aforesaid liberties of pontifical right to the monastery in the following possessions—villages, meadows, waters, mills, woods, pastures, lands, and all persons—if an offence occurs: throughout all the land which Milo gave to his daughter Beatrice in marriage at Venuntio; the twelve acres of land bought by Abbot Lanfranc at Venuntio; the meadows sold by William of Corcelle from our fee to that abbot; throughout the land of all Rots except the church; throughout the land of all Cintheaux with its church; the land held by Grimald at Allemagne and its members, namely Stavelles, Icy, Fulberfolia, Burgesbu, and Roger’s house; half an acre at Hogue; the land held by William de Landa at Brachy; throughout the land of all Cabourg and the borough of Dives as far as the aforesaid little bridge; the woods of Malo Pertuso, Tortavalle, Folonia, and Cuinet, with the lands and waters belonging to those woods; two mills in the greater borough of Caen; the vineyard with the vintner’s house at Bavent; all the land given to the aforesaid monastery at Bavent by Filines Herfredi; one ploughland sold there by Ralph son of Constantine; twenty acres given by Ascelin of Abovunilla; five acres given there by Serlo the Marshal; the land held by Richard Goiz at Ruscavilla; that held by William the Chamberlain at Curley; twelve acres sold to the monks by Serlo at Curley; all the land held by Viscount Ranulf and Robert Bertrand at Bretteville-l’Orgueilleuse with its appurtenances; Anschitil Waragnon’s house and land at Honetot; one mill on the Laize, with half an acre of land and the small island adjacent to it; all Roger the Bald’s land of Bretteville-sur-Laize; the half-acre given by Roger son of Bersad; Louet’s land, sold to Lanfranc at Billy and Vaumeret; Hugh’s ploughland at Maîtreville; twelve acres given at Siccavilla by the wife of Robert Balistarius; the land held by Hugh de Rosel at Granville; and at Groceio.

“Moreover, we confirm to the aforesaid monastery the customary due from carts which carry timber for sale from Bissacia to Caen after they have entered within the league of the aforesaid borough; also the rent and every customary due from all houses in the borough of the monastery that pertain to the right of the church of Bayeux. Whoever from the greater borough, whose burial belongs to the right of the bishop of St Mary of Bayeux, asks to be buried in the cemetery of the aforesaid monastery shall, by the grant of our predecessors and of ourselves, have the fullest power to do so without any contradiction. If anyone wishes to transfer there a dead person who did not request this while living, we grant that this may be done with the permission of our official.

“With the foregoing we confirm to the oft-mentioned monastery ten sextaries of grain—four of wheat, three of barley, and three of oats—which it receives yearly in the tithe of St Wandrille at Cenet, from the gift of Odelina, a noble lady and servant of William, king of the English. We also confirm to it the tithe of Roger the Bald’s fee at Bretteville-sur-Laize, with the portion of the church belonging to it.

“In order that the aforesaid liberties and customs in the churches, among the men, and in all the other matters aforesaid might be preserved for ever by our predecessors, by us, and by our successors wholly unimpaired, unshaken, and undiminished, William, king of the English and prince of the Normans and Cenomans, at the dedication of the church of St Mary of Bayeux, gave to that church, to Bishop Odo, and to his successors, for perpetual possession, the wood called Ela.

“We therefore fortify all the foregoing for the aforesaid monastery in this confirmation of our charter and, strengthening them by the authority of our seal, confirm them, following our predecessors, Odo of blessed memory and the others, who endowed the aforesaid monastery with a like privilege. These things were done in the year of the Incarnation of the Lord 1172, when William, a man to be remembered for honourable life and proved witness, presided as abbot over the monastery of Blessed Stephen of Caen; witnesses: Thomas, archdeacon of Bayeux; Walter, archdeacon of Bayeux; Stephen, archdeacon of Bayeux; Master Humphrey Bone; Master Ranulf; Master Ace; Henry de Sar, canons; Richard, archdeacon of Caen; John, priest; and Robert, sacristan of Caen.

“If I set forth the list of abbots of the most celebrated St Stephen of Caen, communicated by the most learned Jean le Prévost, no one, I think, will disapprove.

Series of Abbots of St Stephen of Caen.

1. Lanfranc, an Italian, formerly a monk of Bec, afterwards archbishop of Canterbury. 2. William I, Bona anima, son of Rutbod, bishop of Sées; formerly a canon and archdeacon of Rouen, then a monk of Bec, afterwards archbishop of Rouen. 3. Gilbert, at the funeral of King William in 1087; St Anselm mentions him, book II, letter 44. 4. Robert: died at Falaise in 1107, at an assembly of magnates in the presence of King Henry I. 5. * Tustin. 6. Eudo: died 1140. 7. Adam I, or Alan: died 1151. 8. Peter I: died 1156. 9. William II: died 1179. 10. Peter II: died 1193. 11. Robert: died 1196; on him see William of Newburgh, History of English Affairs, book V, ch. 19. 12. Samson: died 1214, 7 March. 13. Odo governed for 24 years: died 1238, 30 March. 14. Adam II, who governed for 16 years; according to others, Alan: died 1240. 15. Nicholas governed five years: died 1265, 11 June. 16. William III, 1288. 17. Geoffrey: died 1294. 18. Richard: died 1305. 19. Simon de Trévières: died 1344. 20. Thomas: died 1345. 21. William IV: died 1367 or 1368. 22. Robert III de Chambry: died 1393; obtained the right to wear the mitre. 23. John Seneschal: died 1401. 24. Nicholas Millon, elected 1401. 25. William V Cave: died 1428; attended the Council of Pisa in 1409. 26. Hugh de Juvigny, 1439. 27. William VI Toustain: died 1454. 28. Peter de Vierville, son of Philip, baron of Creully, resigned to Charles de Martigny and died in 1483 or 1485. 29. Charles de Martigny, bishop of Castres: died 8 July 1512. 30. Peter de Martigny, his nephew, monk and bishop of Bayeux: died 13 September 1531. 31. Francis, cardinal of Tournon, 1532. 32. Julian, cardinal de’ Medici, 1533. 33. Alexander, cardinal Farnese, bishop of Tusculum: flourished 1569; governed until 1577; had entered into possession in 1543. 34. George Pericard, son of John, procurator-general in the Parlement of Normandy, by resignation of his predecessor; he resigned in favour of the next and obtained the bishopric of Avranches, 1583. 35. Charles d’O, lord of La Férière, abbot of St Julian of Tours, son of John, Baron d’O: entered into possession in 1583; died at Paris in 1627. 36. Anthony de Bourbon began to preside in 1624: died 1630. 37. Alphonse-Louis du Plessis, cardinal and archbishop of Lyons.

“Furthermore, to complete in every respect, so far as my resources and purpose permit, matters relating to this monastery, it will undoubtedly be helpful to report what the ascetics of Caen did when William the Conqueror’s shinbone was found. To show themselves grateful to their pious and most noble founder, they caused a new monument of black marble to be built at great cost. On one side may be seen the old lament concerning the Conqueror, frequently repeated by writers, which begins: ‘He who ruled the stern Normans, etc.’ On the other is the following recent epitaph, composed by one of the monks of the same monastery.

“‘This tomb of William, the most invincible and likewise most clement conqueror, in his lifetime king of the English and prince of the Normans and Cenomans, the most devout founder of this distinguished abbey, having been plundered in the mad fury of the heretics in 1562, was at length restored, through the pious sentiment of gratitude of the religious of the same abbey toward so beneficent a benefactor, in the year of the Lord 1642, when Dom Jean de Bailhache was prior of the Asceterium.’

P. D. C[I] DD.”

] The duke, one of the monks, in the name of Saint Stephen the Protomartyr; and his wife [Note: [Col. 0078D]

(one of the nuns, in the name and honor of the Holy Trinity). Thus reads the foundation charter; it may perhaps be useful at some time to append these notes to it, as well as the foundation and privileges of Saint Stephen set out above.

[Col. 0079A] Foundation Charter of the Abbey of the Most Holy Trinity of Caen

“By divine grace and through the merciful providence of our Lord Jesus Christ, I, William, king of the English and prince of the Normans and Cenomans, and likewise Mathilda, queen, my wife, daughter of Baldwin, glorious duke of the Flemings, aspiring with pious and wise desire to the glory of blessedness and the reward of blessed recompense, in the territory anciently called Caen, have jointly built a church in honor of the Holy Trinity for the salvation of our souls. There we have permanently established holy and religious women who, according to the rule of Saint Benedict, are to serve the Lord under an abbess. To ensure that in the future they may have an adequate supply of the necessities of life, we have provided for them by royal munificence and suitable provision.

“We have therefore delivered to the aforesaid holy church of God the estate called Caluz, with all its appurtenances, except the tithe belonging to the church of Saint Mary of Bayeux. We have also given Oistrehan with all its appurtenances, except what Robert holds there from William, count of Mortain, who is called Charitas, and from his nephew Richard, with the agreement of Gilbert Crispin, in return for the money that we gave them.

“Furthermore, we have given the estate called Calfur, with its appurtenances, which I, Queen Mathilda, purchased from Richard son of Ranulf, with the king’s permission, with Aitord of Nonant consenting, since it was held of his fief. We also approved the donation by which Ralph Taxo gave Villambargae with all its appurtenances. Since there were also one hundred and ten acres of land in the estate of Amblida and one mill in the same Amblida for his sister, who had become a nun in the aforesaid church, I, Queen Mathilda, redeemed Villambargae from a claim made by the daughter of Conan, and redeemed the land and mill at Amblida from a claim made by Waleran son of Ragnulf, from whose inheritance they had come.

“From the same Waleran, with the king’s permission, I, Queen Mathilda, purchased fifty acres of land in the territory of Caen, and this was added to the aforesaid church, Ralph the chamberlain consenting, since it was held of his fief. In addition to these things, we gave Eschonel to the aforesaid church, which I, Queen Mathilda, purchased with the king’s permission from the sons of Wimund Cufel, William and Robert. From this same Robert I, the queen, purchased the land that he had at Hetrufivilla, and, with my lord the king’s permission, it was added to the church.

“Likewise, with my lord the king consenting, I purchased from Richard son of Herlewin the lands that he held at Taxilli and at Mount Boani, on the condition that Richard himself should hold them from the church during his lifetime and that after his death the church should possess them as its own property. I also acquired from Ralph himself the land that Ralph son of Alan held at Willon. From Richard son of Rainfrand I acquired one peasant at the estate called Charon and two sheaves of the tithe that he had in the same estate. Likewise, from Ragnulf of Barberiis, two sheaves of the tithe that he had at Charon; and these things, with the king’s permission, were added to the church.

“In addition, from Milo the marshal and Alethselina his wife, I, Queen Mathilda, purchased the land that they had at Valcellis, together with what they possessed in the church and in one mill of the same estate, except what they had granted in marriage to their daughter Beatrix; with my lord the king’s permission, this was entered below as belonging to the church.

“Over and above what has been stated, I, King William, and my wife, Queen Mathilda, gave to the aforesaid church the Borough of Hulmo with its revenues, my aunt Adelisa kindly consenting, since it was her inheritance. Countess A. of Albemarle also consented, on the specific condition that she should hold it during her lifetime, but that after her death the holy church should possess it for the support of the nuns.

“In the territory of Caen we gave those lands which Godefrid the Younger, Roger the constable, and William Patrich held from me, King William. [Col. 0080A] Within the borough of Caen, we gave the tithe of one of my mills and the tithe of the ovens belonging to me; also the tithe of Diva, consisting of fish and money; likewise the tithe of Divula and of Batvent, consisting of salt and money. In the same way, the tithe of Wachei and of Scocei, consisting of money, fish, and mills.

“On the island of Jersey, one mill and the land of two free men, as well as half the tithe of five parishes; and the sixth sheaf from one and a half parishes. We also granted to the aforesaid church the land and tithes that Rainold, our chaplain, held from me on that same island, at Rainold’s own request, after he had become a monk.

“At the estate called Maintrud, sixty acres of land. At the estate of Belli, the land that Hernost the cleric held there, and the land of Ralph of Billey, in exchange for which William’s daughter was received into the church of Ralph the chamberlain, with the consent of William son of Theodoric and his wife, since it was their inheritance.

[Col. 0080B] “To these things we added to the aforementioned church twenty arpents of vineyard, of which three are at Liriacum together with six acres of land. At Alba Via, seven which I, the queen, purchased from William of Aillio, with the consent of his son Roger, Richard count of Évreux, and Anschitil of Altuillio, since it was their inheritance; at Argentias, seven; at Vernum, three. Of these three arpents, Godelef gave two and a half, together with one house, because she had become a nun in the aforesaid church, and her sister gave the remaining half.

“We also gave half the estate called Carpikech, which I, the queen, purchased with my lord the king’s permission from Eudo son of Thurstan Haldup and from Ragnulf the viscount. Adelais, daughter of Thurstan Haldup, gave to the same church of the Holy Trinity, in which she had become a nun with our permission, with the consent of Ragnulf the viscount and Eudo, Adelais’s brother, the other half of the estate of Carpikech, [Col. 0080C] together with half of its church and tithe.

“We also gave two parts of the estate called Puteus; and between Filcherolas and Hersterville, one hundred and eighty acres of land; likewise the land that Oismelin son of Theodoric and Herbert Folenfant held from her at Goisbertivilla, Dumoldivilla, and Culvertivilla.

“At Coisneriis, half a mill and the land of one plowland in the same place. At Ruscavilla, the land of one plowland. At Ingulfivilla, the land that Anschitil held from her. At Calvavilla, the land of one plowland.

“This same Adelais also gave Fraxinivilla and Maisnille Urcelli, which I, Queen Mathilda, exchanged with the church of Saint Mary of Bayeux through Odo, bishop of that church, with my lord the king’s permission, in return for the churches and tithes of Saint Stephen and Saint Martin of Caen, as Anschitil son of Urf had held them, and in return for the church of Saint George of the castle of Caen.

“Stigand also gave the churches of Falaise with their tithes, and the church of Wibreei with its tithe, and one mill in the same place, to the aforementioned church for his daughter, who had become a nun there, with William of Brajosa consenting, since it was under his jurisdiction; and, to induce him to consent, I, Queen Mathilda, with the king’s permission, gave him money from my own funds.

“Alvered of Moion likewise granted to the same church the land that his sister Ala had received in marriage at Ranvilla, for his daughter, who had become a nun in the same church, except that Saint Leodegarius of Pratellis holds there. I, the queen, redeemed the service due from this land for the use of the church from Hubert of Ria, since it was held of his fief.

“Fredesendis, aunt of Ragnulf the viscount, gave Osbernivilla to the same church, with that Ragnulf consenting, since it was held of his fief; and for his consent I, Queen Mathilda, gave Ragnulf money from my own funds.

“Ragnulf himself gave to the aforesaid church one mill situated within the borough of Caen; and at [Col. 0081A] Goisbertivilla, the land of two free men, for his daughter, who had become a nun in the church.

“Baldwin son of Count Gislebert and his wife Emina gave to the same church, for the salvation of their souls, the churches of La Forêt with their tithes and two hundred acres of land in the same place; for their consent I, Queen Mathilda, gave them money from my revenue.

“Murier of Guitot, for the salvation of his soul, gave the aforesaid church Osbernivilla situated by the sea, on the condition that he should hold it during his lifetime and that after his death the mother church should possess it as its property, with William of Brethoil consenting. I, Queen Mathilda, gave William money for his consent, since it was held of his fief.

“Alberada, sister of Fulco, gave to the same church the land that her father had given her in the estate called Guillon, with that Fulco consenting. Since she was a nun of that place, she lies buried there in the churchyard.

“Billetheldis, daughter of Roger, gave to the aforesaid church what her father had given her at Vernun as her marriage portion, with her nephew William consenting, since it was held of his honor. For his consent I, Queen Mathilda, gave him money from my revenue.

“Roger of Molbray gave to the aforesaid church the land that he possessed at Granivilla for his daughter, who had become a nun there. Roger of Monasteries likewise, for his mother, who had been consecrated to the Lord there, gave Salam with all its appurtenances, half the forest of Mount Alboldus, the monastery of Vals with its tithe, the land of one plowland in the same estate, and one mill—namely, what he possessed in his own domain—and the land that Richard holds in the estate called Lu.

“Fulco of Alno gave to the same church the estate of Fulebech, with its mills and all its appurtenances, both in the open country and in the forests, because his wife Haduissa had become a nun in the same monastery, with their son Fulcholin consenting.

“Athselinoc, daughter of Alvered the Giant, gave to the aforesaid church the land that she possessed at Grandicampus and at Goi, with the consent of William son of Alvered, because of which consent his niece, the daughter of William of Millei, became a nun there.

“William Bacco gave two parts of the tithe of Bleer and one peasant in the same estate for his sister, who had become a nun in that place. Godefrid Lunez gave two parts of the tithe from eighteen peasants and six acres of land at Colevilla for his daughter, who had become a nun in the church.

“Bremarus gave forty acres of land at Anglicavilla, twenty at Charon, and two sheaves from half the tithe of Charon; and at Willon, the tithe that he himself had purchased from Murier, sister of Richard the prince. He gave these for his daughter, who had become a nun in the same monastery.

“Peter gave what he possessed at Monasteries for his daughter, who had become a nun there. Odo the cleric gave forty acres of land at Cambis for his soul, with the consent of William son of Osbern, since it was held of his fief; he gave the church of Burnolfivilla with its tithe, except that Roger son of Hunfred holds there. The men of the same estate gave this for the salvation of their souls, with Odo, bishop of Bayeux, giving his consent.

“Alberada, wife of Ralph Taxo, granted the service due from the land that Fulcher Malaherba held from her at Bleduilla. Gisla, daughter of Thurstan, gave to the same church, for her soul, the land that she possessed at Gray and at Dumvilla, with the consent of Thurstan her nephew, since it was held of his fief.

“I, King William, granted to the aforesaid church the service that Godefrid son of Salomon and Heltho the steward rendered to me from Gray. Ralph son of [or: for the salvation of his soul] gave the land that he possessed at Adevilla.

“Alberada, mother of Hugh and Roger, gave, with their consent, what she possessed in the church and in the tithe of Hainolvilla, and one acre of land in the same estate, for her soul.

“Hugh, the aforesaid church’s cupbearer, gave the land of Fago, on the condition that he should hold it during his lifetime and that after his death the said church should possess it, with Ralph of Thodenio consenting, since it was held of his honor; for that consent I, Queen Mathilda, gave Ralph money.

“Gumnor, mother of William of Brajosa, a nun of the Holy Trinity, gave the same monastery the land that she possessed at Batvent, with Hugh the cupbearer and Roger of Cuilli consenting, since it was held of their honor; to Roger I, Queen Mathilda, gave money for his consent.

“The same Gumnor also gave the lands that she possessed at Roures, Cirreni, Craiscentevilla, and at the estate called Four Wells, with Maurice and Alberada his wife granting their consent, since the land had been their inheritance.

“Robert son of Ansfrid the steward gave the land that he possessed at Condet and half the meadows that he possessed at Wiholmi, for Avicia his wife, who had become a nun in the same church, with his sons consenting.

“Ralph of Aneriis gave to the same church, for his soul, thirty-six acres of land that he held in the same estate of Aneriis, which he had purchased from William of Simillei, with William of Colombariis consenting to the gift, since the land was held of his fief.

“Ursellus gave, for his soul, the land that he possessed in the estate of Saint Anianus. Robert the chamberlain gave the land that Hadebrand held at Lovenium, for his soul and for love of his sister, who was a nun in the church.

“William the chamberlain gave one mill near Chetaoil and the land that he held there from Queen Mathilda.

[Col. 0082A] “In addition, Odo, bishop of Bayeux, through our favor and affection, grants that the aforesaid church of the Holy Trinity, together with its churchyard, the abbess and the nuns, all the clergy serving in that place, and the entire household of the same church supported by food, shall be free from every exaction of episcopal revenues.

“He likewise permits the church of Saint Giles, together with its churchyard, to be free and quiet in the manner stated above, and permits the clerics serving there to be free in the same way.

“Furthermore, in that part of the borough situated outside the walls of Caen, toward the church of the Holy Trinity—which part of the borough I, King William, gave to the aforesaid church—he permits the parish of that part of the borough to come to the church of Saint Giles, and permits the clergy serving there to possess the offerings, the tithe of livestock, and the right of burial in peace.

“He also assigns to the church of the Holy Trinity the toll and the customary payment for quilts that he possessed in that same part of the borough.

“Moreover, whoever commits an offense in these two churches or in their churchyards shall give to the abbess of that place, with the bishop’s consent, the monetary compensation that episcopal custom ordinarily exacts for an offense.

“Whoever among the men of Caen, during his lifetime, chooses burial for himself in the churchyard of the Holy Trinity may, by permission of the same bishop, have it freely and without seeking a burial license from the bishop’s priest.

“And because the bishop of Bayeux granted the aforesaid churches the peaceful liberty that has been described, we offered a gift of worthy recompense to that bishop [Col. 0082D] and to the church of Bayeux.

“But if anyone, through rash presumption, should at any time become a violator of any of all these things shown to have been given to the aforesaid church of the Holy Trinity—and may this never happen—and should persist in his shameless obstinacy, let him know that he has been made accursed by the Lord, deprived of the holy and blessed communion of all the faithful, and destined to be punished perpetually by divine judgment.

“Therefore, so that all these things may endure forever with unshaken firmness, according to the manner in which they are known to have been established by us, I, King William, opposing the privilege of royal majesty to the enemies of the Church of God, have confirmed them by the incontrovertible testimony of the bishops and magnates whose names are written below, and have strengthened them by the protection of my image and by this present lawful enactment, in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1082, in the fifth indiction, while Pope Gregory VII occupied the chair of the Apostolic See, in the sixteenth year of my reign, while Philip reigned in France and Henry ruled the Roman territories by imperial right.

Sign of Gislebert Crispin. Sign of Robert Bertrand. Sign of Henry of Ferrières. Sign of Roger of Beaumont. Sign of Hugh, count of Chester. Sign of Richard son of Herluin. [Col. 0083B] Sign of Roger, cupbearer of Ivry. Sign of Count Robert of Beaumont. Sign of William, count of Évreux. Sign of Hugh the cupbearer. Sign of Fulco of Alnou. Sign of Rannulf, the viscount. Sign of William who is called Charitas. Sign of [a person] of Gournay. Sign of Ralph of Todenio. Sign of William of Bretoil. Sign of Girard of Gournay. Sign of William the chamberlain, son of Ralph. Sign of Eudo the viscount. Sign of Eudo the viscount. Sign of Richard of . . . . . .

“It seemed fitting to add to the foundation charter of the Abbey of the Holy Trinity of Caen a catalogue of abbesses, while the complete history of that monastery and of its abbesses is being prepared, so that meanwhile we may sustain our hope by it.

List of the Abbesses of the Most Holy Trinity of Caen”

1. Matilda I. Died in the year 1113. [Col. 0083C]

2. Cecilia, daughter of William I, king of the English and duke of the Normans. Died in 1127.

3. Izabeth, or Isabella I of Blois, held the prelacy for scarcely one year. Died around 1128.

4. Beatrice I de Huqueville. Died around 1141.

5. Dionysia d’Eschauffou. Died around 1160.

6. Joanna de Coulonces. Died in 1181.

7. Matilda II d’Évreux. Died around 1198.

8. Isabella II d’Ivetot. Died around 1202.

9. Adela I de Thibouville. Died around 1215.

10. Juliana de Saint-Celerin. Died in 1256.

11. Beatrice II de Cambernon. Died in 1289.

12. Amicia de Gournay. Died in 1293.

13. Matilda III of England. Died around 1298. In place of an epitaph, these words are read upon her tombstone: “Matilda, daughter of a king, surnamed the Strong.”

14. Adela II of England. Died around 1305. [Col. 0083D]

15. Nicolaa I de Goullevaz. Died in 1336.

16. Matilda IV de Querville. Died around 1340.

17. Georgia du Molley. Died in 1376.

18. Maria I de l’Orme. Died in 1401.

19. Maria II de Warinières. Died in 1407.

20. Margaret de Warinières. Died in 1417.

21. Agnes de Thieville. Died in 1422.

22. Nicolaa II de Rupalley. Died in 1426.

23. Maria III de Survie. Died in 1434.

24. Margaret II de Thieville. Died in 1441.

25. Blanche d’Auberville. Died in 1470.

26. Catherine I le Viconte. Died in 1492.

27. Renata de Bourbon. Died in 1534.

31. Louise de Mailly. First abbess of Lille near Melun; afterward she also assumed charge of this monastery, while retaining the former office by dispensation. She died in 1554, distinguished for humility and observance.

34. Laurence de Budos.”]

…a second community of nuns in the name and honor of the Holy Trinity, to whom they gave so much of their possessions and revenues as would suffice for those living there, both for food and clothing. [Col. 0037C]

## CHAPTER IV

9. At that same time, as the congregation at Bec was increasing, what the Lord had said through the prophet Isaiah came to pass in that place: “The place is too narrow for me; make room for me to dwell” (Isaiah 49:20). For the limited size of the buildings could no longer contain the assembled multitude of brothers, while the site itself proved unfavorable to the health of its inhabitants. Accordingly, the venerable Lanfranc began urging the holy Father Herluin to undertake the construction of a larger monastery.

Herluin was alarmed at the mere thought of so great an undertaking, having very little confidence in the strength of his already failing age. Lanfranc, who had begun to encourage and exhort him and to press the same point upon him repeatedly, did not desist, saying that the watery site was unsuitable for monks’ habitation. When the abbot refused in every way to agree, Lanfranc is said to have spoken as follows to certain noblemen with whom he was conversing:

“Dom Abbot is wasting his time and labor on this watery site, and he will not believe me when I tell him to cease from this work and begin another in a healthier place. May almighty God give him such an impediment that he may listen to me and cease expending his efforts in so unsuitable a place.” [Col. 0038A]

Not long afterward, the right-hand part of the presbytery collapsed, where the oratory and the altar of Saint Benedict were located. The abbot was distressed and greatly troubled by this; then his comforter came to him in all his desolation, beseeching him now at least to agree and begin larger buildings.

At last, overcome, placing the firmest hope in God and relying greatly upon the assistance of his counselor, through whose efforts all good things came to him, he began a new monastery and its workshops in a much healthier and more suitable place. It was a very great undertaking, which he accumulated not through his own resources—for these were still very small—but through firm faith in God and certain hope, bringing everything together.

Lanfranc also, with the permission of his abbot, [Note: [Col. 0084A]

He again conducted a school. Indeed, I think no one who has turned over histories for even a few months will deny that this custom was exceedingly common in the Benedictine order: namely, to establish schools and to instruct boys both in piety and in letters. The Rule of Saint Benedict, chapters 30, 37, 45, 63, and 70, teaches what care ought to be devoted to boys in monasteries.

For that most holy man clearly understood—“filled with the spirit of all the righteous,” to use Gregory the Great’s words—how much usefulness and advantage would come to the Christian commonwealth from the religious education of boys [Col. 0084B] in monasteries. Many were entrusted to be educated in this discipline from noble senatorial families; among them Saints Maurus and Placidus hold the first place, according to Saint Gregory, *Dialogues*, book II, chapter 3.

Hence the emperor Charlemagne ordered schools to be restored in all the monasteries of his empire and commanded monks to serve as teachers. Thus in the *Councils of Gaul*, volume II, folio 121; he also commands this in the *Capitulary of Aachen*, chapter 72, ibid., folio 152.

On this subject Trithemius, in the *Hirsau Chronicle*, in the section concerning Herard, the fourth abbot of that monastery, writes:

“At that time”—the year 890—“there was a most celebrated custom in the monasteries of our order: that schools of monks should exist in nearly every monastery, headed not by secular men but by monks renowned for their character and learning, who were not only learned in the divine Scriptures but also extremely well educated in mathematics, astronomy, arithmetic, geometry, music, rhetoric, poetry, and all the other secular sciences of literature. [Col. 0084C] Many of these men were learned not only in the Roman language but also highly skilled in Hebrew, Greek, and Arabic, as can easily be recognized from their little works.”

But lest that abbot Trithemius seem to assert without evidence that schools of letters were an established institution in monasteries, I should like to produce testimonies from ancient and medieval writers.

From the *Life of Saint Agilus*, the first abbot of Rebais:

“The boy Agilus was entrusted to Eustasius, a man of approved religion, to be instructed in the sacred letters, together with the sons of other noblemen who afterward became prelates of Churches: namely, Agnoaldus and Walbert, the sons of Hagnaricus [or Agnericus], Agilus’s paternal uncle. They became distinguished in the monastery that their sister Fara built on their father’s estate between the rivers Alba and Mucra, in a place called Eboracus, as masters of building and regular instruction. One of them was ordained bishop of Lauduno Clavato; the other, bishop of Meaux. There was Acharius, who was bishop of the Viromandui, Noviomum, and Nomacum [Col. 0084D]; and Ragnacharius, who shone forth as an outstanding pontiff of the Church of Autun; and Audemar, who flourished as the praiseworthy shepherd of Boulogne and the town of Thérouanne.

“Finally, just as he had received the aforementioned Agilus, entrusted to him more dearly than all the others, so in Agilus, above all, the brilliance of learning and religion shone forth.” For, more thoroughly instructed in the liberal disciplines, he educated many by his eloquence and enlightened very many through the purity of the Catholic faith. He also made some suitable, through splendid instruction, for the profession of sacred religion, after they had laid aside the pomp of worldly elevation.”

Thus the manuscript codex of the monastery of Bec. Saint Agilus flourished around the year of Our Lord 660.

Theodorus of Kempten, on Saint Magnus, chapter 11, in Canisius’s *Ancient Readings*, volume IV:

“Saint Gall and Magnoaldus built monasteries of marvelous size, and stirred up the brothers gathered there, by teaching and example, to desire eternal life. They carefully nourished the boy Othmar and instructed him in the teaching of grammar and the divine books, appointing him master of the school.” [Col. 0085A]

In the *Life of Saint Leufred*, abbot of Saint Taurinus at Évreux, who as a boy frequently attended the monastery school in the suburb:

“But when he found a teacher”—these are the words of the manuscript codex of Bec—“who would devote himself to his education in letters, he began to surpass his companions in instruction in language and in uprightness of character,” and so forth.

The venerable Saint Bede made the monastery of Saint Peter at Wearmouth in England a most famous center of learning. Concerning it, several writers of English history speak, especially William of Malmesbury, *English Bishops*, book III, folio 154, 2, no. 30:

“At Wearmouth,” he says, “Bede’s monastery was a noble center of learning, and [a center] for many men of letters.”

And in book I of *The Deeds of the Kings of England*, folio 11. Concerning Bede’s teacher as well, Saint Benedict Biscop, distinguished for his learning, one should read the account of his life written by the venerable Bede himself. See Malmesbury, at the place cited; and *English Congregation of Triumphs*, volume I, page 640 and following. [Col. 0085B]

Yet long before Bede’s time, schools of letters were common in England, as can be seen in the Floriac manuscript library, folio 431, *Life of Saint Gildas*, chapter 3.

And since the subject of England has arisen, I think the notable passage in the appendix to Ingulf should not be passed over. There it is said that four monks—Gilbert, Odo, Terricus, and William—went to a place called Cottenham near Cambridge:

“Having separated from one another in different places,” says the author, “and following the model of the school at Orléans, early in the morning Brother Odo, at that time an outstanding grammarian and satirist, read grammar to the boys and younger men according to the teaching of Priscian and of Remigius upon Priscian. At the first hour, Brother Terricus, a most acute sophist, taught Aristotelian logic to the younger students according to the introductions and commentaries of Porphyry and Averroes. At the third hour, Brother William expounded the flowers of the rhetoric of Cicero and Quintilian.

“Master Gilbert, however, on every Sunday [Col. 0085C] and feast of the saints, preached the word of God to the people in various churches—unskilled in the English language, but fluent in his Latin and French—and disputed especially against Jewish error. On weekdays, when literate men and priests gathered more particularly to hear him, he explained the text of sacred Scripture before the sixth hour,” and so forth.

The Orléans, or Aurelian, school mentioned above was, unless I am mistaken, that celebrated school of the monastery of Fleury, since that monastery is situated in the territory of Orléans.

From the *Life of Saint Frodobert*, abbot and contemporary of Clovis II, king of the Franks:

“At that time the aforesaid monastery of Luxeuil was almost unique in the regions of Gaul, both in the height of its religious life and in the perfection of its learning. For this reason, many in whom there was an eager desire to advance in either direction came together from all sides to that same place in zealous competition.”

This is found in the *Repository of the Antiquities of Troyes* by the most learned Camuzat. Again, in the same work, one may read, in the *History of Saint Bercharius* [Col. 0085D], abbot, book II, folio 94, about that same intellectual center of Luxeuil. Camuzat likewise produces, in his notes on the *History of the Finding of the Body of Saint Maurus*, folio 56, an ancient fragment concerning the venerable Aderald, bishop of Troyes:

“He”—Aderald—“as a little boy of good character, released from the hiding places of the cradle, was entrusted to the studies of letters for instruction. Nor was he committed to secular schoolmasters, but to monks devotedly serving God,” and so forth.

These were undoubtedly Benedictines, since at that time they alone were leading the monastic life.

I certainly must not remain silent about those ancient and very famous schools of Fleury, commonly called the monastery of Saint Benedict, above the Loire. Aimoinus, in chapter 1 of the *Life of Saint Abbo*, abbot and martyr, in the Floriac manuscript library, page 301, says:

“Abbo, therefore, born of such parents, was entrusted in the monastery of Fleury to the school of the clerics”—that is, the external or canonical school, as we shall observe below—“serving the Church of Saint Peter, to be instructed in letters,” and so forth. [Col. 0086A]

John a Bosco notes in his commentary on this chapter that more than five thousand were enrolled and that each of the students was accustomed to offer his teacher two manuscript books every year. But since he does not at all indicate where he obtained this information, let the responsibility for it rest with the author.

And in chapter 2: “Saint Abbo is placed in charge of instructing the students.” In chapter 5, having been sent to England, he teaches at the monastery of Ramsey.

The ancient customs of that same monastery also speak of the academy of Fleury, folio 404 of the aforementioned library, in these words:

“The community goes to wash its hands and afterward sits in the choir until the school comes.”

And below, where processions are discussed:

“The school, with its teachers, shall follow them”—the deacon and subdeacon—and so forth.

It is not my purpose to prolong this discussion further. I omit the academies once frequented: in Gaul, those of Saint-Denis, Corbie, Cluny, and Saint-Germain at Auxerre; in Germany [Col. 0086B], those of Fulda, Salzburg, Saint Gall, and very many others; in England, those of Oxford and York; in Italy, those of Monte Cassino and Vivarium; in Belgium, those of Douai and Gerardimont.

For anyone wishing to read more about the schools of monasteries—and I have wished merely to excerpt something from manuscripts and from works that are by no means readily available—let him consult the *Antiquities of Fulda*, chapter 9 and following; the *Chronicle of the Order of Saint Benedict*, volume II, under the years 661 and 662, and volume III, under the year 791, at length; the first table of the *Triumphs of the English Congregation*, pages 549–550, and the preface to the third table, page 5 and following; Claudius Espencaeus, *Digressions*, book III, chapter 12, page 344; Jacob Middendorp, *Book of Academies and History of Monasteries*, chapter 6; Goldast, *Alemannic Antiquities*, volume I, chapter 1; Ekkehard, *On the Misfortunes of the Monastery of Saint Gall*; and chapter 7 of the *Life of Blessed Notker* by the same author. This very life is also found in Canisius’s *Ancient Readings*, volume VI.

In the *Assembly of Abbots held at Aachen under Louis the Pious*, chapter 45, someone may perhaps observe the following prohibition: [Col. 0086C]

“That there be no school in a monastery except for those who have been offered”—that is, dedicated to the service of God.

The monks, however, easily dealt with this difficulty, since within the bounds of the monastery they established two schools according to the condition and variety of their pupils. One was the cloister school, in which boys devoted to the ascetic life were trained; the other was the canonical, or clerical, school, in which secular boys were educated. The former was in a more secluded part of the monastery; the latter was outside the monastery in an adjoining building, although the monks themselves were in charge of it.

This division of schools was certainly an established practice at the monastery of Fleury—as we saw above, where we spoke of Saint Abbo being entrusted by his parents to the school of the clerics—and at Cluny, as one of our learned men testified to me that he had seen in the ancient records of that monastery; but especially at Fulda, as Ekkehard testifies in the places cited:

“After a short time,” he says, “let them entrust the cloister school to Marcellus, together with Blessed Notker the Stammerer and the other boys in the monastic habit; but the external school, that is, the canonical school, to Iso with Solomon and his companions.”] [Col. 0086D]

He again conducted the school, and handed over to the abbot what he received from the students; the abbot gave it to the workmen. [Col. 0038B]

10. After three years had been completed, with only the basilica still unfinished, the venerable Lanfranc, the initiator of the undertaking, was appointed abbot of the monastery of Caen at the request both of the duke of Normandy and of the leading men. The duke had built this monastery at the urging of Pope Nicholas.

When Lanfranc departed from the monastery of Bec for this work, he took with him one man who had recently received the habit but had not yet made his profession, named Ralph. Ralph later made his profession there; in due course he became prior of that church of Caen and finally died as abbot of Battle. [Note: [Col. 0037D]

William the Conqueror built the monastery of Battle, commonly called Bataille, in the district of Sussex in England, in the year 1067, at the very place where, after engaging Harold, the invader of the kingdom, in battle, he defeated him. For this reason he called it Battle. Its history is found in volume I of the *Monasticon Anglicanum*, page 310.] [Col. 0038D]

At Lanfranc’s arrival, noblemen and excellent clerics soon began coming to that place to embrace the religious life. Among them was the outstanding and venerable William, son of Rabodo, who governed the Church of Caen after Lanfranc and afterward became archbishop of Rouen. [Note: [Col. 0038D]

William succeeded John in 1079 as archbishop of Rouen, a see which he held until the year 1110. Orderic Vitalis continues his praises in book V, under the year 1079, and other authors agree with him. His father, Ratbod, was bishop of Sées.]

When this William had received the religious habit at Caen, he was sent to Bec to learn the order there, because that place, being a new plantation, was not yet able to instruct others perfectly. This man, born of noble parentage, was simple, adorned with good morals, and religious. After spending some time there, first [perhaps: as] cloister-prior and afterward as abbot, he was taken from there [Note: [Col. 0086D]

He was consecrated archbishop of Rouen. Concerning William’s election, the manuscript codex of the monastery of Saint-Ouen at Rouen says the following, speaking of the archbishop John:

“He withdrew from here—or rather, he advanced; for two years before his death, Dom William, abbot of the monastery of Caen, was enthroned, through apostolic authority, royal appointment, and finally common election. He was truly a man distinguished by the nobility of his lineage and preeminent in the excellence of his character.”

Orderic Vitalis praises William in book V of his *History*, under the year 1079:

“He was good, cheerful, and gentle, and he guarded the flock divinely entrusted to him for thirty-two years. He enriched the mother church with every ornament necessary for divine worship; he elegantly rebuilt from the foundations the episcopal cloister and suitable houses.” [Col. 0087A]

And below:

“He benefited monks and clerics and all subject to him by treating them with the affection of a gentle father. He devoted himself unceasingly to psalms, hymns, spiritual songs, and sacred mysteries. He was most learnedly instructed in ecclesiastical practice and was able to preach the word of God to the unlearned in clear and suitable language. By patience and kindness he softened all who lived with him, and without envy he distributed a large part of his burden among the deans and priests; nevertheless, he eagerly admitted good men to share in the honor,” and so forth.

See more in the same Orderic, at the place cited, and folio 568, under the year 1080; William of Jumièges, *History*, book VII, chapter 28, and book VIII, chapter 3.] [Col. 0087B]

He was consecrated archbishop of Rouen. In that position he lived for a very long time and closed his final day in a good old age.

In that monastery of Caen, during the time of Lanfranc and of those who, leaving the world, undertook the monastic life under him, a great religious observance began, and it continues to this day. [Col. 0038D]

Meanwhile, William, duke of the Normans, invaded the hereditary kingdom of England and arranged its laws as he wished. Then he turned his attention to improving the condition of the Church. Therefore, at the advice and request of Alexander, supreme pontiff of the universal Church, a man outstanding in life and learning, and with the most willing consent of all the leading men of the English and Norman realms, King William—who accepted this counsel as the most important and indeed the only one—selected the teacher mentioned above, namely Lanfranc, to undertake this task.

## CHAPTER V

11. Let us now, as though beginning from another point, direct the course of our narrative and insert certain matters omitted earlier [Note: Up to this point, almost everything has been taken from the *Life of Blessed Herluin*.], and thus pursue everything concerning the same Lanfranc as far as we can.

This man, memorable in every age for religion and wisdom, born of noble parentage, was educated from childhood, according to the custom of his homeland, in the schools of the liberal arts and secular laws. As a young man, he frequently defeated experienced advocates who opposed him in legal cases, speaking with precision in a torrent of eloquence. [Note: [Col. 0087A]

“At that very age he knew how to produce opinions which jurists, and so forth, gladly welcomed.” Indeed, Robert of Torigni testifies in his as yet unpublished *Chronicle* that Blessed Lanfranc discovered Roman laws at that time:

“Lanfranc of Pavia,” he says, “and his companion Garnerius, having discovered at Bologna the Roman laws which the emperor Justinian had abridged and corrected fifty years after the Incarnation of the Lord, devoted themselves to reading them and explaining them to others. But Garnerius persevered in this work, whereas Lanfranc, teaching many in Gaul the liberal disciplines and divine letters, eventually came to Bec and there became a monk.”

Thus far Robert, under the year 1032.] [Col. 0039B]

At that very age he knew how to put forward opinions which jurists, judges, and civic magistrates readily accepted. Papia records these matters.

But while he was philosophizing in exile, a divine fire kindled his spirit, and the love of true wisdom shone into his heart. For he perceived that the prosperity and glory of this world are vanity. Therefore, by a sudden movement of his spirit, denying himself and renouncing the world, he received the religious habit at Bec and began to live according to the Rule.

This same monk was diligent in destroying with the sword of the word any sects he noticed to be injuring the Catholic faith. He was likewise supremely good in the fullness of charity and strove, through the soundness of faith, to restore those who were dead in heresy.

Wise and religious metropolitan bishops, as well as abbots, trembled before Lanfranc’s wisdom, religiousness, and authority, and rejoiced to submit themselves to his correction. Many also asked for him, with an extraordinary desire, as their bishop or abbot. [Note: [Col. 0087B]

Rome, the head of the world, solicited him by letters—especially Leo IX and Gregory VII, as can be seen among their letters.]

Rome, the head of the world, solicited him by letters, striving by entreaty and force to retain him. [Note: [Col. 0039D]

See on this matter Lanfranc’s letter to Pope Alexander, no. 14, below, and Alexander’s letter to William the Conqueror, king of England, which is the tenth letter of that pontiff in Labbe, volume IX of the *Councils*, column 1123.]

For they had recognized him as highly skilled at distinguishing everything honorable from its opposite; most diligent in assigning to each person what was his, according to the measure of reason; and most ready to undertake and endure difficult and arduous things for the sake of the true good.

They had also recognized that his life could rightly be called a very direct and very safe road to the harbor of eternal life. Yet he considered it too lofty for himself to preside over others, never abandoning the lowest place in heart and affection.

The glorious duke of the Normans, William, cherished him with intimate affection; and for this reason he placed him, unwillingly, in charge of the monastery of Caen. [Col. 0040A]

At that time the city of Rouen had been deprived of its holy and venerable archbishop Maurilius. [Note: [Col. 0039D]

We gave an account of Maurilius under the year 1067.]

Then all the clergy and people assembled and wanted to choose Lanfranc as his successor. [Note: [Col. 0039D]

Orderic Vitalis reports the same in book IV of his *Ecclesiastical History*.]

But with all his strength Lanfranc avoided undertaking such a burden, humbly preferring to be subject rather than to preside. For he would gladly have relinquished the abbey of Caen, which he had accepted unwillingly, if he could have done so without grave injury to his soul.

When the king perceived this, [Note: [Col. 0087B]

He arranged to substitute John, to whom Blessed Lanfranc, after becoming archbishop of Canterbury, sent several letters. More concerning John below, in letters 14 and 15.

As for this substitution, Orderic Vitalis gives somewhat more detail in book IV of his *Ecclesiastical History*, page 506, in these words:

“That man devoted to God and intent upon humility, Lanfranc, refused the burden of so great a primacy; and with all his strength he endeavored to place before himself at this height John, bishop of Avranches. Then, so that this appointment might be made canonically, he went to Rome and obtained from Pope Alexander permission for the aforesaid arrangement.”

You will find Alexander’s letter—by which he granted Lanfranc’s request—sent to John, bishop of Avranches, among the testimonies of ancient writers prefixed to the book *On Ecclesiastical Offices* by that same bishop.

At nearly the same time, a similar event concerning Alinard, abbot of the monastery of Dijon, is found in the manuscript chronicle of that monastery:

“He was loved by Kings Robert and Henry,” the chronicle says, “and Emperor Conrad and his son Henry Caesar also venerated him with extraordinary affection. Therefore Emperor Henry offered him the vacant see of Lyons. But Alinard humbly refused it and recommended that Odalric, a cleric of Langres, be sought instead; the father himself escorted him all the way to the see.”

But after Odalric had died, “they ask the emperor,” says the same chronicle, “to give them Alinard; but Alinard did not consent until Pope John commanded him. He led an angelic life in that office,” and so forth.] [Col. 0086D]

He arranged to substitute John, whom he had appointed bishop of Avranches. But, so that this might be done canonically, he sent that same abbot of Caen, Lanfranc, to Rome to request permission. Lanfranc gladly undertook the burden of this embassy, and, since he desired the Churches’ welfare, obtained from Pope Alexander the required authorization. He also brought back the sacred pallium together with permission for this promotion; and hence all Neustria rejoiced.

## CHAPTER VI

12. After this, three legates came together to the king in England: Erminfred, bishop of Sion, and two cardinal clerics, sent at the king’s request by Pope Alexander. At Easter they placed the crown of the kingdom upon his head and confirmed him as king of the English. [Note: [Col. 0087D]

A synod was therefore convened. Florentius of Worcester places this synod under the year 1070, as does Orderic Vitalis at the place cited, folio 516. Concerning this same synod, see the librarian of Malmesbury, *English Bishops*, book I; Roger of Howden, folio 259, 2, no. 30, London edition.]

A great synod was therefore convened at Windsor [or Windreford]. [Note: [Col. 0040D]

The synod at which Stigand of Canterbury was deposed and Lanfranc substituted for him was held at Winchester in the year 1070, during the octave of Easter, and shortly afterward—namely, on the Monday after Pentecost—at Windleshorum. William conferred the archbishopric of York upon Thomas. Our author recounts all these events as though they had occurred together at the synod of Windsor; but Roger Hoveden, in the earlier part of his *Annals*, distinguishes these two synods.

Although English authors do not entirely excuse Stigand, they nevertheless write that he and other bishops and abbots were expelled by King William chiefly so that the Normans, in whom he placed greater trust, might occupy their sees. Norman writers, however, maintain that William acted with upright intention.]

At this synod, with the king presiding, the legates themselves deposed certain bishops unworthy of the episcopate because of their criminal lives and ignorance of pastoral responsibility.

Among them [Note: [Col. 0087D]

They deposed Stigand, condemned with anathema. So report the authors cited, who portray Stigand as burdened with many crimes and give the reasons for his removal. Among them is Florentius of Worcester, his contemporary, at the place cited:

“In the council,” he says, “Stigand, archbishop of Canterbury, was degraded for three reasons: namely, because he unjustly held the bishopric of Winchester together with the archbishopric; because, while Archbishop Robert was alive, he not only assumed the archbishopric but also used Robert’s pallium for some time in celebrating Mass after Robert had been unjustly driven from England by force; and because he afterward received the pallium from Benedict, whom the holy Roman Church had excommunicated.” [Col. 0088A]

Robert of Torigni, in the aforementioned *Chronicle* under the year 1070, records that Stigand had possessed three bishoprics—namely, Elmham or Norwich, Worcester—or rather Winchester—and Canterbury—and that he was deposed.

Eadmer, also called Edmer or Ediner, discusses Stigand in book I of his *History of Recent Events*; William of Poitiers, in his work on William I, pages 205, 206, and 208; Orderic Vitalis, at the place cited; and Malmesbury, *The Deeds of the Kings of England*, book II.]

They deposed Stigand, condemned with anathema and stained by many crimes. He had invaded the archbishopric of Canterbury with unspeakable ambition while holding two bishoprics.

When suitable rulers had been substituted in place of those who had been deposed, the see of Canterbury remained vacant. In it the precious confessor of Christ, Augustine, had presided over all the bishops of Britain.

As the king considered this matter and consulted the nobles of the kingdom, with a most fitting outcome their choice rested upon Lanfranc, so that an abundant light might be raised in this citadel to disperse everywhere the clouds and darkness of depravity and to adorn all things with health-giving radiance. Therefore he sent the aforementioned legates to Normandy to accomplish this task.

When the bishop of Sion invited Lanfranc to undertake episcopal government, announcing in the council of the bishops and abbots of Normandy the king’s request, as well as his own will and that of the other legates of the Apostolic See, and almost their commands concerning this promotion, they found him so disturbed by holy anger and holy sorrow that they thought he would resist entirely and ask for time to deliberate.

For he clearly and unquestionably held that the office of archbishop and the leisure of a monk could not coexist. As was his custom, he despised his own advancement and feared this most burdensome governance.

The queen with her son pleaded with him; Abbot Herluin, whom he was accustomed to obey as Christ, though unwillingly, commanded him; and the leading men, deliberately assembled for this purpose, also urged him. For the king’s command had prescribed this pressure being brought to bear from every side, since he knew the obstinacy of his most beloved Father whenever he was invited to higher things.

Lanfranc did not reject the matter by a hasty decision, just as his every action and word was directed by the rule of discretion. He was careful not to offend obedience, nor those many people who asked, favored, and encouraged him.

Thus he went sorrowfully across the sea to offer his excuses, hoping for joy upon his return. For this exceptional man, the embodiment of perfect humility, could not imagine that he was being dragged unwillingly to the archbishopric.

Yet by what reasoning can one resist the divine disposition? The king received with joy and fitting reverence the helper of the Christian religion; he overcame the reluctant man, beautifully contending against his excuses with humility and majesty.

At his cheerful and festive command, the leading men of the Church of Canterbury were summoned, together with the numerous ecclesiastical and secular dignitaries of the kingdom.

### 13

King William always cultivated Lanfranc’s intimate friendship, both because of his outstanding knowledge of secular and divine letters and because of his exceptional observance of the monastic order, showing him reverence and honor: venerating him as a father, fearing him as a teacher, and loving him as a son or brother. To him he entrusted the counsels of his soul, and a kind of watchtower from which the rule of life for the ecclesiastical orders throughout Normandy and England might be surveyed.

But if anyone, astonished, asks why so great a man was so determined to avoid episcopal office, or why the abbot unwillingly imposed it upon him, let him first understand this about the abbot: he did not do so at all from envy of Lanfranc’s promotion, since he desired his honor and exaltation above all else. He therefore commanded him because he did not dare resist the will of God and the election of the holy Church, which was calling him. Yet he commanded him unwillingly, because he deeply regretted being deprived of the companionship of so great and so dear a friend. Lanfranc had chosen the monastery of Bec, recently founded and terrifying in its situation and poverty; he enriched it through his prudence and most vigilant care and advanced it to the condition of a splendid order, while governing the brotherly community [variant: community of brothers] with strict yet gentle discipline and assisting the holy abbot with humble and useful counsel.

Indeed, while Lanfranc desired only the obscure labor of his own mortification, God, the examiner of thoughts, detected and disclosed him, so that the lamp gathering itself together might spread through the heights into the valley.
