Under that teacher, compelled by obedience, the library of philosophical and divine letters shone forth, and he was most powerful at solving the knots of questions in both fields. I would deserve no credence for what I write unless the breadth of Europe itself bore witness to it. Nor do I think that his fame should be silenced in Africa or Asia.

Lanfranc himself was eager to evade the pontifical burden because, filled with wisdom, he foresaw that the leisure of the monastic order could not be preserved whole amid the most frequent tumult of episcopal occupations.

[Note: Let this example terrify us, and so forth. I cannot restrain myself from bringing forward here two examples, which I once read and found especially worthy of note, of men who vigorously refused the priesthood or episcopate. The first is found in Saint Jerome, volume II, letter 60: Epiphanius, bishop of Salamis in Cyprus, writing to John, bishop of Jerusalem, concerning a certain monk who avoided the priesthood by every possible means, but was eventually brought by force to the bishop and made a priest:

“While, therefore,” Epiphanius says, “the assembly was being celebrated in the church of a village near our monastery, we ordered him, who was unaware and had no suspicion whatsoever, to be seized by several deacons and his mouth held shut, lest, wishing to free himself, he should adjure us by the name of Christ. First we ordained him deacon, setting before him the fear of the Lord and compelling him to minister; for he resisted with great force, declaring that he was unworthy. And while he was ministering at the holy sacrifices, with his mouth held, we ordained him priest with immense difficulty,” and so forth.

The second example is related by Palladius in the twelfth book of the *Lausiac History*. Bishop Timothy had ordered Ammonius, a disciple of the great Pambo, eminent in religion and learning, to be brought so that he might be consecrated bishop. But he consistently refused, and when he was being compelled, he seized a pair of scissors and cut off his left ear. When this was reported to the bishop, he said: “Bring him to me even mutilated in the nose, if he is of good character, and I will ordain him.” They therefore went and asked him again; when he did not comply, they attempted to bring him by force. But he swore to them, saying: “If you compel me, I shall cut out my tongue as well.” So they left him and withdrew.

Almost innumerable examples of this kind may be found everywhere among authors. Thus Saints Ambrose, Augustine, Paulinus, and Anselm were made priests or bishops by the force of an inflamed populace.

Would that men were sought and chosen for the clergy in this way—men who approached when called, rather than aspiring to office for the sake of profit or honor! In that case the Christian commonwealth would indeed be splendidly served.]

Let this example terrify those condemned, together with Simon Magus, by the zeal of the Prince of the Apostles. From it let the most depraved understand their madness: the utterly foolish purchase with gifts what a man who has been offered according to God trembles to accept. They offer money and promise greater things, now in person, now through friends, to whom they promise the heights of dignities if they can attain such an honor.

### 14

Thus Lanfranc, abbot of Caen, overcome both by the will of God, which he understood to be directed toward himself, and by apostolic authority, the command of Lord Herluin, and the agreement of the nobles of Normandy, was brought to England for these many reasons and assumed the archiepiscopate of Canterbury, which holds primacy among the churches across the sea.

Raised to so great an honor, enriched by extensive lands and furnished with gold and silver, he did not forget that divine command: “Honor your father and mother” (Exodus 20:12). He was in every respect kind and generous toward his spiritual father, Herluin the abbot, and toward his mother, the Church of Bec. His migration to those regions was shown in this manner to the venerable Abbot Herluin in a vision, a few days before the summons came from there.

He saw that in his own plantation he had an apple tree whose branches spread widely and whose fruit was abundant and plentiful; the apples themselves were pleasing in appearance and excellent in taste. The king mentioned above asked the abbot for this tree, wishing to transplant it to a certain plantation of his own. The abbot resisted and objected that he himself was sustained by that tree alone. But because the king was lord, he prevailed and carried the tree away. Its roots, however, could not be torn out entirely; shoots sprang from them and immediately grew into large trees.

After a short interval within the same vision, the king mentioned above rejoiced before him over the tree’s abundant fruitfulness, and Herluin answered joyfully that he too had from it exceedingly joyful offshoots. The king invited him to go and see the growth of the transplanted tree, but some cause—I do not know what—prevented him from going.

All these things, as the vision arranged them, were explained by the outcome of events, except that Herluin truly went and saw what he had heard. The abbot’s plantation was the Church of Bec, and its greatest tree was that teacher who, by his example and teaching, sustained not only that church but all the churches throughout the land. Since the aforesaid king requested that he be sent across the sea to teach the English the institutions of sacred religion, through his abbot, whom alone he obeyed as God, Lanfranc—very unwillingly, yet preserving obedience and commanded by an unwilling abbot—obeyed.

Writing to Pope Alexander, after the salutation he says: “When concerning the congregation of Bec …” The rest is contained in Letter 2 of Blessed Lanfranc.

### 15

From these words it can be understood how unwillingly he undertook pastoral care, and how gladly he would have relinquished it if the pope had been willing to permit it. For he feared his own inadequacy and did not yet see the progress of those entrusted to him according to his desire.

[Note: But how great a harvest later came forth there, and so forth. Concerning this, Ediner, in Book I of his history, folio 7, gives a clear account in praise of Blessed Lanfranc:

“He always devoted great effort both to making the king devoted to God and to renewing the religion of good morals among all classes of people throughout the entire kingdom. Nor was his desire frustrated; for through his great persistence and teaching, religion was increased throughout that whole land.”

Therefore Orderic Vitalis rightly writes the following about him in Book IV of his *History*, page 20:

“In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1070, Lanfranc, first abbot of Caen, was divinely given to the English as their teacher.”]

But how great a harvest later came forth from him there is most broadly attested by the condition of ecclesiastical discipline, renewed everywhere.

[Note: The monastic order, which had fallen altogether into lay dissolution, and so forth. The great Lanfranc restored monastic discipline not only in England but also in the Norman monasteries, while he was still serving as prior of Bec, especially in the monastery of Utica, or Saint-Ebrulf’s. Orderic Vitalis, a monk of that place, testifies to this in Book III of his *History*, folio 461:

“Abbot Herluin sent Lanfranc the monk to Utica with three monks; and through them he caused the service of God, which had declined there, to be restored.” This took place around the year of the Lord 1050.

But since the subject is England, let us excerpt something from the eyewitness Eadmer mentioned above. “Who could ever fully declare,” he says, “with what prudence and in what spirit of fatherly care he raised the monks residing in that Church [of Canterbury] from the secular life, in which he found them living excessively, and imbued them with every path of holy conduct, and, after multiplying their number, with what kindness he cherished them throughout his life?”

Matthew of Westminster, *Flores Historiarum*, under the year 1077, where he writes of Paul, abbot of Saint Albans:

“Through him the whole monastic order flourished anew in England, with Lanfranc’s assistance.”

William of Malmesbury, Book I of *The Deeds of the Bishops*, folio 122, no. 3, supports this and finally concludes:

“Today”—that is, the monks of Canterbury—“they are more numerous, as is fitting, than anywhere else in England, and in religion they are not inferior to the Cluniacs.”

See more of this kind in the latest London and Paris editions of Matthew Paris’s *History*, in the *Lives of the Abbots of Saint Albans*, and in the Life of Paul, the fourteenth abbot.

The holy Lanfranc, guided by the divine Spirit, rightly and deservedly devoted all his strength to establishing the vigor of monastic discipline. For as soon as monks deviate from the right path, ignorance, every kind of vice, and heresy begin to spring up; conversely, while monks care for the religious state, as Cardinal Baronius proves most excellently and clearly in his discussion under the year 703 of the most holy abbot Benedict, surnamed Biscop:

“From such a founder,” he says, “monasticism spread wonderfully in England, so that that island, watered as it were by the rains of the divine Spirit, became truly a paradise of God. While complete monastic discipline flourished there and remained unharmed, no heresy could gain access to it; but when that discipline was relaxed and dissolved, the fruitful land was turned into salt by the wickedness of those who inhabited it” (Psalm 106).

Thus Baronius, certainly no monk. Let those haters of the monastic state consider these things—those who continually vomit the poison of slander against men who strive to please God in life and conduct, labor with all their strength to repair regular discipline, and seek to attract those devoted to the world to the imitation and love of Christ the Lord by word and example.

Let them hear even the Lateran Council under Alexander III, part XIII, chapter 3:

“If perhaps we do not possess religion within ourselves, we are nevertheless bound to love and foster it in others.”]

The monastic order, which had fallen altogether into lay dissolution, was restored according to the discipline of the most approved monasteries. The clergy were restrained under the canonical rule. The people, the empty vanity of barbarous rites having been forbidden, were instructed in the right form of belief and life.

## CHAPTER VII

### 16

The fragrance of these fruits, most sweet to God, whose scent had filled the house of God throughout the world, had already been perceived most joyfully by the absent abbot himself; later, when present, he perceived it all the more joyfully the nearer he came, having traveled to England to visit him.

When he had reached the archbishop, what a pious contest then arose between them to humble themselves before one another! The supreme prelate, acting as apostolic representative in the churches across the sea, humbled himself before his former abbot as any other monk would have done. Everywhere he ranked second to him: when he sat for the solemn celebration of Mass, and whenever he received anything from him, he kissed his hand unless the abbot quickly withdrew it. The abbot was given the more eminent seat and all authority to command; he pardoned the faults of offending servants and did everything else in the household according to his will. One bore the name of lord; the other exercised the authority.

The more frequently his court was attended, and the more numerous became the gatherings of distinguished persons from both orders throughout the kingdom, the greater the archbishop’s public deference toward him. Everyone marveled, especially the English, that the archbishop of Canterbury should humble himself in this way before any mortal.

The abbot, for his part, tried to render the submission owed to so great a dignity, but he was in no way permitted to do so.

Behold what the most abundant hand of God repays to those who serve him in this life. He who, embracing Christ’s poverty, was once despised and mocked by everyone, now has the primate of the entire kingdom of England, with all those entrusted to him, obeying his wishes as their bishop.

The same exchange of God’s kindness had also come to the one who, denying himself and having once surrendered his own freedom to God, now saw many consular men—and indeed an entire kingdom, the greatest of them all—bowing at his feet.

### 17

Of the roots of that great tree which, as he had seen in his dream, remained in his garden, the celebrated man Herluin later saw certain shoots springing forth and growing into large trees: that is, many people came, through Lanfranc’s instruction, to great growth in good works.

A tree rich in fruits was the venerable Anselm, a cleric of the Church of Aosta. He followed Lanfranc into the monastic life; afterward he became prior, then, after Abbot Herluin, abbot of Bec, and finally, after that same Lanfranc, archbishop of Canterbury. Concerning him, all that can be said is greater than our speech can relate.

Trees delightful in the pleasantness of their good fruits were Gilbert Crispin, abbot of Westminster,

[Note: Gilbert Crispin, abbot of Westminster. Because of his exceptional and varied knowledge of the sciences, some call him “the Universal.” We praised Gilbert at the beginning, page 1.]

William, abbot of Cormery,

[Note: William, abbot of Cormery. He was the third abbot of that monastery. Milo discusses him above; we shall append a few remarks concerning him to Letter 57.]

Henry, dean of the Church of Canterbury,

[Note: Henry, dean of the Church of Canterbury. I find this same man called prior of that church by Saint Anselm in Book I, Letter 54, to which this letter is addressed, and likewise in Book II, Letter 44. He was a man instructed in every ecclesiastical discipline.]

Ernostus, bishop of the Church of Rochester,

[Note: Ernostus, bishop of the Church of Rochester. Concerning him, see Letter 57.]

and the greatly revered Gundulf, who succeeded him in the same office there.

[Note: Gundulf, a man highly revered for the holiness of his conduct. See the notes to Letter 47.]

[Note: These men, with the help of God’s grace, were taught in the Church of Bec by Master Lanfranc and instructed in holy religion by Saint Father Herluin. Not only those whom Milo Crispin mentions here, but also very many other men of uncommon learning and piety, are attested by numerous writers to have been hearers of the great Lanfranc.

Among his more distinguished disciples were Pope Alexander II and his nephews, as we shall note in Letter 2; William II, abbot of Caen and later archbishop of Rouen, of whom we have already spoken at greater length; and the monk Guitmund, later archbishop of Aversa. According to our Orderic, *History*, Book IV, page 524, Guitmund was a cardinal, “most learned in literary knowledge”—as is evident from his books published against Berengar—and a vigorous defender of ecclesiastical liberty. The same Orderic records his deeds with much praise in the place cited.

He himself acknowledges that he was a disciple of Blessed Lanfranc in Book II of *On the Sacrament of the Altar*, near the middle, in these words:

“I should nevertheless be very pleased if, whenever some negligence or certainly some new miracle occurred concerning such great mysteries, there should happen from it what my teacher, the outstanding and unquestionably trustworthy Lord Lanfranc, told me had happened to him as a boy in Italy,” and so forth.

The great Ivo, bishop of Chartres, must not be counted among the lesser disciples. To prevent any doubt from arising in some minds, I am pleased to publish here for the first time the very words of Robert of Torigni:

“This year,” he says, “died the religious and highly learned man Ivo, bishop of Chartres. While he was still young, he heard Master Lanfranc, prior of Bec, treating of secular and divine letters in that famous school which Lanfranc maintained at Bec. Many men gathered there, distinguished both by secular nobility and by honorable conduct, and afterward attained the highest summit of ecclesiastical dignity and religion.

“Later the same Ivo presided over and benefited the community of regular canons of Saint-Quentin at Beauvais. Finally, having become bishop, he governed the Church of Chartres vigorously and religiously for nearly twenty-three years,” and so forth.

Thus far Robert in his manuscript *Chronicle*, under the year 1117.]

These men, taught by Master Lanfranc in the Church of Bec with the help of God’s grace and instructed in holy religion by Saint Father Herluin, were afterward established as honorable fathers in other churches.

## CHAPTER VIII

### 18

The new church at Bec had not yet been consecrated. It awaited consecration by the very man on whose advice it had been begun and with whose assistance it had been completed; Herluin persistently asked this of God. God, who had shown himself kind to him in other matters, granted his request the desired outcome, fulfilling his wish in every respect.

Meanwhile, after everything necessary for the use of the inhabitants had been prepared, on the vigil of All Saints, after the meal, the brothers left their old dwelling. In ordered procession, singing the responsory “O blessed Trinity,” they came to the new church. Entering the new buildings in which they would henceforth live, they celebrated the feast of All Saints there with everyone’s joy and eagerness.

The following day, while Mass was being sung, the holy Father ordered a gathered crowd of poor people to be brought into the new buildings and refreshed most abundantly with food and drink.

In the fourth year the church was dedicated with great glory, and by the man whom the Father desired. For the oft-mentioned supreme pontiff Lanfranc, archbishop of the peoples across the sea, came to the court of the most illustrious king of the English, William, who was then staying in Normandy, on certain secular and ecclesiastical affairs. He first approached the monastery itself and was received by the brothers with the greatest possible dignity. He himself behaved among them with the greatest possible humility, according to what is written: “The greater you are, humble yourself in all things” (Ecclesiasticus 3:20).

The monastery of Bec lies between two mountains, above a stream called Bec, from which it also takes its name. When Lanfranc had come to the descent of the mountain overlooking the monastery,

[Note: He is said to have removed a ring from his finger. By laying aside this ring, he seems, in my opinion, to have indicated rather clearly how highly he regarded the monks of Bec and that he should conceal none of his wisdom from them, but should provide them, as suitable sons, with the instruction and secrets of his teaching. The words that follow seem to indicate this.

Among the other mysteries signified by the episcopal ring, Isidore teaches that it is a sign of pontifical honor and a seal of secrecy, in chapter 48 on Exodus:

“Thus teachers conceal certain things from those less able to understand,” he says, “and place them, as it were, under a seal, lest the mysteries of God be entrusted to the unworthy.”

Rabanus Maurus, Book I, *On the Instruction of the Clergy*, chapter 4:

“The ring is also given as a sign of pontifical honor, or as a sign of secrets,” and so forth.]

he is said to have removed the ring from his finger and not to have put it on again during the entire time he remained at Bec, except for the solemn celebration of Mass.

This great prelate approached the kiss of the abbot, now bent with age, and tried to throw himself at his feet. The abbot, however, attempted the same in return; after a long struggle [variant: certainly], while each supported the other, neither accomplished what he was trying to do.

After many long-desired embraces,

[Note: The archbishop sat with the brothers in the cloister. This custom was very common among the monks of old: they devoted themselves to the study of letters and to ecclesiastical matters in the cloister. It is certain from the consistent testimony of writers that this practice continued for more than eight centuries, and the very ancient monasteries bear witness to it.

Menardus, in our *Concordance of the Rules*, chapter 55, folio 808, proves that secular persons were formerly barred from entering the cloister:

“And so that the brothers might not be disturbed,” he says, “outsiders were not permitted to enter the cloister except for definite reasons, as can be seen in Statute 23. Peter the Venerable established that no cleric or layman should enter the cloister or any other regular house except either for the sake of some work or to view the buildings, as honorable guests customarily do.”

Menardus discusses the cloister and its antiquity at greater length in the same place.]

the archbishop sat with the brothers in the cloister like any other of them. He addressed each one individually—young men, old men, and children—and encouraged each according to his condition with the appropriate consolation.

Who could adequately describe the humility and kindness he displayed by adapting himself to everyone? At table, the brothers were compelled to sit with the archbishop on his right and left and to take food with him from a common cup and a single dish.

Nor did he offer the brothers comfort only through edification; with generosity worthy of so great a guest, he provided such hospitality that the remains of the feast could have doubled the celebration of the octave.

He refused to have an episcopal chair prepared for himself in the church, but entered the prior’s seat, saying that he was still prior and had not yet laid aside the priorate.

When everyone questioned him about the consecration of the church, he was ready to comply with their wishes. But, intending to go to the court, he asked for a delay until he could learn the king’s will.

Then, commended to the prayers of the brothers, he reached the king, spoke with him concerning the matter for which he had been asked to depart [variant: from which he had departed], received the day of the dedication, and immediately sent back not only someone to announce it but also instructions concerning how it should be carried out.

### 19

Thus, on the tenth day before the Kalends of November, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1077, Lanfranc—the man to be revered by the whole holy Church, primate of the peoples across the sea and supreme pontiff—

[Note: This is how the archbishops of the principal sees were commonly called in this period. Thus Wido, archbishop of Reims, is called “supreme pontiff,” and elsewhere “supreme prelate,” in the *History of the Discovery of Saint Bertinus*.]

arrived to complete through consecration the church which, inspired by God, he had begun and in whose foundations he himself had laid the second stone with his own hand.

All the bishops of Normandy, the abbots, and the other religious men assembled; the nobles of the kingdom were also present. The king and queen, occupied with other affairs, did not attend, but sent gifts from their bounty.

The dedication was celebrated with the greatest joy and with the solemn eagerness of everyone. The air itself, perfectly clear, and the brightest day smiled upon the eagerness of the people.

The illness that had confined the Father of the monastery for the previous eight days then left him, and, by God’s mercy, he recovered fully by the day itself. The celebration ended with greater joy than that with which it had begun.

On the third day, the often-mentioned archbishop of Canterbury, destined to be remembered by the ages, asked all the brothers for permission to depart. Who could look upon a man of such kindness toward them as he departed without tears? Everyone burst into tears; the little ones could not be consoled.

He deliberately hastened his departure so that they might restrain themselves from weeping, either before or after he left. The venerable Herluin, who loved him above all mortals and was loved by him, followed his departing friend for two miles, seeing him as one who would never again return to his own in this life.

For before the anniversary of that very day of the dedication, Herluin ended his final day. What bitterness of heart! What weeping at that last farewell and final separation from one another!

## CHAPTER IX

### 20

Having anticipated these matters in this way, let us now return to the order of events.

After Lanfranc’s translation to England, he did not forget why he had come. He turned all his attention to correcting the morals of the people and putting the Church in order. First he took pains to renew the mother church of the kingdom itself, the Church of Canterbury.

Because it had been burned by fire a few years earlier, he undertook to rebuild it from its foundations—a great and spacious work. He also constructed the buildings necessary for the monks’ use.

What is especially remarkable is that from Caen, where he had been abbot, he had squared stones transported by sea in sailing ships for the rebuilding.

He also built houses for his own residence near the church. He enclosed all these buildings with a great and high wall.

After adequately arranging what was necessary for regular food and clothing, he enriched the church itself with many costly ornaments.

The dignities of the Church of Canterbury, which had declined or been diminished through age or negligence, he restored and reformed. He brought many lands that had been taken away back under the church’s jurisdiction and restored twenty-five manors to the church.

[Note: Hospitals or houses for the poor. Since Milo mentions these almost in passing, I think they add something to the ornament and illumination of the Life of the great Lanfranc if I append here the words of Eadmer’s *History*, Book I, folio 9:

“He divided this palace into two parts, assigning to one those oppressed by various kinds of illness, and establishing women who were unwell in the other. He also arranged for them, from his own resources, clothing and daily food, as well as attendants and guardians who would ensure in every way that they lacked nothing; nor did he permit men to approach women, or women men.

“On the other side of the road he arranged a church in honor of Blessed Pope Gregory, in which he placed canons who would live according to a rule and provide the aforesaid sick people with whatever was suitable for the salvation of their souls, together with burial. He endowed them with so much land, tithes, and other revenues that these seemed sufficient for their support.

“Farther away, on the western side of the city rather than the northern, he built wooden houses on the slope of the mountain and assigned them for the use of lepers, keeping the men there, as in the other houses, separate from the company of women. He likewise ordered that, according to the nature of their disease, everything they needed should be supplied from his resources, appointing for this work such men that, as it seemed to him, no one could doubt their diligence, kindness, and patience,” and so forth.]

He built two hospitals, or houses for the poor, outside the city: one to the north and the other to the west. He supplied them with everything necessary and assigned them annual revenues from his own resources, as much as seemed sufficient.

In his manors he established annual provisions to be given to the poor. In many of those manors he constructed stone houses for his own residence.

### 21

At the time when Lanfranc came to the archiepiscopate, Odo, bishop of Bayeux and brother of King William, was earl of Kent.

[Note: Orderic wrote more extensively about his administration in Books III, IV, and VII of his *History*. As for the dispute with Lanfranc, Eadmer must be read, since he describes it at length in Book I of the *History of Recent Events*, as he does the subsequent dispute with the bishop of Chichester. Eadmer also notes there that Dunstan was present with Lanfranc to defend the rights of his church.]

Odo oppressed the people of that province with many burdens, as well as the people of the Church of Canterbury. Lanfranc resisted him openly and, before everyone, with the testimony of the ancient English who were skilled in the laws of their country,

[Note: “He proved by litigation.” Among the ancients this word appears in various forms: *dirationare*, *disrationare*, *desrationare*, and *disratiocinare*. At times it means to prove a matter; at times to plead a case; at times to refute an opposing assertion; at times to undergo a legal examination; and at times, more frequently, to win a lawsuit and establish or recover the disputed property. It is used here in the last sense. See more in Henry Spelman’s *Archaeologus* and in the glossary appended to Matthew Paris’s *History*.]

proved by litigation the freedom of his land and freed his people from the evil customs that Odo wished to impose upon them.

There are still others who know both the place where the suit was held

[Note: “Who also know the place of the hearing.” We shall explain what a hearing means in connection with Letter 40.]

and the name of the place,

[Note: The matter was disputed twice, as the same Eadmer testifies. The first time was at Pinnenden, where Geoffrey, bishop of Coutances, acting in the king’s place, was vigorously ordered to render justice to Lanfranc concerning his complaints, and did so.

The second time, those who defended the rights of the Church had been defeated, but Lanfranc was absent. Therefore, on the following day, at the urging of Blessed Dunstan, he himself came to the hearing. Taking up the case again, he showed that what had been said the previous day was worthless, so convincingly that, as long as he lived, no one arose to open his mouth against him on that matter.]

and recount the manner and outcome of the lawsuit by which the dispute was concluded.

[Note: And the manner and outcome of the lawsuit by which the dispute was concluded, and so forth. See Eadmer, Book I of the *History of Recent Events*, page 9; and William of Malmesbury, Book I of *The Deeds of the Bishops*, page 122, where he discusses the aforesaid lawsuit and indicates that Saint Dunstan was always present to assist Blessed Lanfranc in difficult matters. He consoles him in these words:

“Lanfranc possessed great vitality of soul, but also the abundant favor of the most blessed Dunstan. Whenever Lanfranc hesitated in such matters and, fearing that things might turn out badly, postponed a suspended judgment, Dunstan was present, exposing the subtleties of his opponents to the drowsy man and showing him paths of escape. Moreover, once, when Lanfranc was ill and weary of his faltering life, Dunstan rescued him from danger in a vision in which he seemed to have wrestled with him and restored him to good health.”]

We have thought it worthwhile to append below what he wrote to the bishop of Chichester concerning the clerics of his villages.

Lanfranc,

[Note: See Letter 40 of Lanfranc.]

by the grace of God … [lacuna]

(This is Letter 40 of Lanfranc.)

## CHAPTER X
[Col. 0047B] **22.** When he was going to the archbishopric, many followed him, and he retained a number of them, enriching them with honors and lands, as their descendants, who remain to the present day, testify. But, to return to an earlier point: on his first arrival in England, by the authority of the supreme pontiff Alexander and of the glorious king William, he summoned the bishops and nobles of the land, clergy and people, to renew the decrees and institutions of the holy Fathers concerning the celebration of synods and ecclesiastical customs. At this assembly it was shown against Thomas [Note: [Col. 0048D] Thomas, a canon of Bayeux, was promoted by King William to the archbishopric of York.]—who opposed the matter—that the archbishop of York ought to be subject to the bishop of Canterbury. Whoever wishes to know more fully how this was handled will be able to learn from what follows. [Note: [Col. 0091B] “In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord,” etc. William of Malmesbury attests that these are the very words committed to memory by Blessed Lanfranc, in the place cited, fol. 117, where he discusses his elevation to the archbishopric: “He himself,” he says, “will explain this better in his own writing; for concerning his ordination and the controversy that arose and was settled between himself and Thomas of York, he wrote as follows: ‘In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation,’” etc. These passages are doubtless excerpts from the Ecclesiastical History that he wrote. That he wrote such a History is confirmed for me by Eadmer, the copyist of Blessed Anselm, in the work cited above, p. 7, where he praises Lanfranc in exceptional terms: “But concerning these and countless other good works,” he says, “by which he completed his life in labor, I need not write—for his works themselves so plainly testify to them, and he himself wrote with a most truthful and concise pen about ecclesiastical affairs that took place in his time,” etc.] In the year [Note: [Col. 0048D] You will find this in the very words used by William of Malmesbury, book I of *The Deeds of the Bishops of the English*, where there is an extensive treatment of the controversy between the sees of Canterbury and York concerning primacy, in volume I of *Anglia Sacra*, p. 653.] from the Incarnation [Col. 0047C] of the Lord 1070, Lanfranc, abbot of the monastery of Caen, entered English territory, at the instigation and command of William, the glorious king of the English, and of Alexander, of blessed memory, supreme pontiff of the whole holy Church. A few days after his arrival, he undertook the governance of the Church of Canterbury. He was consecrated on the fourth day before the Kalends of September, in the metropolitan see, by the suffragans of that see: William, bishop of London; Walchelin of Winchester; Remigius of Dorchester, or Lincoln; Siward of Rochester; Herfast of Elmham, or Thetford; Stigand of Selsey [or, in another reading, Selsey]; Herman of Sherborne [or, in another reading, Schireburne]; and Giso of Wells. The others who were absent explained the reasons for their absence [Col. 0047D] both to the legates and by letters.

**23.** In that same year Thomas, elected bishop of the Church of York, came to Canterbury to be consecrated by him, according to ancient custom. When Lanfranc therefore demanded from him a written profession of obedience, with the addition of an oath, in accordance with the preserved custom of his predecessors [Col. 0048A], Thomas replied that he would never do so unless he first read written authorities on the matter, unless he saw witnesses who affirmed its antiquity, and finally unless he heard suitable reasons why he ought to do this justly and reasonably, without prejudice to his own church. He acted thus more from ignorance than from the obstinacy of an arrogant spirit. For, being a newcomer and entirely unfamiliar with English custom, he gave more credence than was fair and right to the words of flatterers.

Lanfranc nevertheless demonstrated what he was requesting in the presence of the few bishops who had come to him for this consecration. But Thomas, scorning everything, departed unconsecrated. When the king heard this, he took it badly, supposing that Lanfranc was making unjust demands and relying more upon learning than upon reason and truth, although Thomas himself was not lacking in knowledge of Scripture, acquired through great intelligence and great study.

After a few days had passed, Lanfranc came to court and requested a hearing from the king. Having set forth his reasons, he softened the king’s mind and convinced the overseas men who were present that justice lay on his side. For the English who knew the matter bore the strongest possible witness to his claims in every respect. Accordingly, by royal edict and the common decree of all, it was presently determined that Thomas should return to the mother Church of the whole kingdom; write out his profession; read what he had written; and, after it had been read, present it to Lanfranc during an examination conducted in the presence of the bishops according to ecclesiastical custom. In it he was to promise unconditionally, without inserting any qualification, that he would obey all his commands concerning the worship of the Christian [Col. 0048C] religion. With respect to Lanfranc’s successors, however, he was not to make the same promise unless a proper explanation were first given to him, either face to face or in an episcopal council, clearly demonstrating that his predecessors had done this to the primates of the Church of Canterbury and ought to have done so.

Thus Thomas returned, fulfilled what had been ordered, and departed consecrated. Not many days later Lanfranc requested and received professions from all the bishops of the English kingdom who had been consecrated at various times and in various places by other archbishops or by the pope during the time of Stigand.

# CHAPTER XI

[Col. 0048D] **24.** In the following year he went to Rome with the aforementioned archbishop and was honorably received by the Apostolic See. It is said that the pope rose to greet him when he arrived, both because of his great religious devotion and outstanding learning, and because, when he was in Normandy, he honorably received the ministers who came from the Roman Church and carefully instructed certain relatives of the pope. The pope is also said to have remarked: [Note: [Col. 0049D] Eadmer records this in book I of *The New History*.]

> “I did not rise for him because he is archbishop of Canterbury, but because I was a student at Bec in his school and sat with the other students at his feet.”

Accordingly, he gave him two pallia: one which he took from the altar according to Roman custom; the other [Note: [Col. 0049D] This had already been granted to Hincmar of Rheims in the ninth century and to Bruno of Cologne in the tenth. No other examples of this are known.] as a sign, evidently, of his affection, with which he used to celebrate Mass, Pope Alexander himself handed to him. In the presence of this pope Thomas raised a complaint concerning the primacy of the Church of Canterbury and the subjection of three bishops—of Dorchester or Lincoln, Worcester, and Lichfield, now Chester—saying that the Churches of Canterbury and York held equal honor in relation to one another, and that neither ought in any way to be subject to the other, according to the constitution of Blessed Gregory, except that the archbishop of either church ought to be prior and more worthy than the one who was known to have been ordained later; but that the three bishops mentioned had existed subject to his see and to his predecessors from ancient times.

When Lanfranc heard this, although he was displeased, he nevertheless replied with measured discernment that Thomas’s words were entirely devoid of truth, asserting that the Gregorian constitution [Note: [Col. 0049D] Gregory the Blessed had established this concerning the archbishop of Canterbury in relation to the bishop of London. William of Malmesbury discusses the matter at length in book I of *The History of the Bishops of the English*; see that work.] had not been promulgated concerning Canterbury and York. After many arguments had been advanced on both sides concerning this matter and the three bishops, Pope Alexander decreed that the case ought to be heard in England and there settled by the testimony and judgment of all the bishops and abbots of the kingdom.

[Col. 0049C] **25.** Although Lanfranc held Thomas bound, in his own time, by the profession he had made, he nevertheless preferred to labor on behalf of his successors rather than leave this great, unexamined complaint for them to investigate in the future. Both men therefore came to the king during the solemnity of Easter. There, after the arguments of the parties had been brought forward, the royal court gave judgment on the matter. It was then ordered that a written document be made containing the conclusion of the entire case.

Lanfranc sent a letter to Pope Alexander in which he briefly and truthfully recounted the whole course of the affair. Both documents are appended below, preceded by the profession that Thomas presented to Lanfranc, hand to hand, before the king and his court:

> “It is fitting that every Christian submit to Christian laws and not oppose by any arguments what the holy Fathers have beneficially instituted. For from this arise anger, dissensions, envies, contentions, and other such things, which plunge their devotees into eternal punishments. And the higher a person’s rank, the more earnestly he ought to obey the divine commands.
>
> “Therefore I, Thomas, now ordained metropolitan bishop of the Church of York, having heard and understood the arguments, make to you, Lanfranc, archbishop of Canterbury, and to your successors, an unconditional profession of canonical obedience; and whatever shall be justly and canonically enjoined upon me by you or by them, I promise that I shall observe. But because, before I was to be ordained by you, I was uncertain about this matter, I promised that I would obey you without condition, but your successors conditionally.”

## DECREE OF THE COUNCIL

[Note: [Col. 0050D] Spelman reports that this council was held at Windsor, in volume II of *The Councils of England*. William of Malmesbury, however, from whom all this material is taken, specifies no place; hence Labbe, in his edition of the councils, preferred simply to call it English.]

**26.**

> “In the year from the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ 1072, in the eleventh year of the pontificate of our lord Pope Alexander, and in the sixth year of the reign of William, the glorious king of the English and duke of the Normans, by command of the same Pope Alexander and with the king’s approval, in his presence and in that of the bishops and abbots, the case was discussed concerning the primacy which Lanfranc, archbishop of Canterbury, claimed by right of his Church over the Church of York, and concerning the ordinations of certain bishops, regarding whom it was by no means certain to whom they specifically belonged.
>
> “Finally, by the various authorities of various written documents, it was proved and demonstrated that the Church of York ought to be subject to the Church of Canterbury and, as to the archbishop of Canterbury, its primate of all Britain, obey his dispositions in all matters pertaining to the Christian religion.
>
> “The metropolitan of Canterbury granted to the archbishop of York and his successors perpetual possession of the subjection of the bishop of Durham—that is, the bishop of Lindisfarne—and of all the regions from the boundaries of the bishopric of Lichfield and the great river Humber to the furthest limits of Scotland, as well as whatever on this side of the aforesaid river rightfully belongs to the parish of the Church of York. This was arranged so that, if the archbishop of Canterbury should wish to summon a council, wherever he might deem appropriate, the archbishop of York, with all the bishops subject to him, should present himself at his command and remain obedient to his canonical dispositions.
>
> “Lanfranc, archbishop of Canterbury, demonstrated from the ancient custom of his predecessors that the archbishop of York ought to make a profession to the archbishop of Canterbury, even with an oath. But, out of regard for the king, he released Thomas, archbishop of York, from the oath and accepted only a written profession, without prejudicing his successors, should they wish to demand both an oath and a profession from Thomas’s successors.
>
> “If the archbishop of Canterbury should die, the archbishop of York shall come to Canterbury and, with the other bishops of that Church, lawfully consecrate as their own primate the man who has been elected. But if the archbishop of York should die, the man elected to succeed him, after receiving the gift of the archbishopric from the king, shall go to Canterbury, or wherever the archbishop of Canterbury may direct, and receive ordination from him according to canonical custom.”

The aforesaid king and the archbishops—Lanfranc of Canterbury [13] and Thomas of York—as well as Hubert, subdeacon of the holy Roman Church and legate of the aforesaid Pope Alexander, and the other bishops and abbots who were present, consented to this constitution.

**27.** Lanfranc informed Alexander of these proceedings by the following letter:

> “To Alexander, pope and supreme watchman of the whole Christian religion, Lanfrancus . . .”

(Vide Letter 4 of Lanfranc.)

[Col. 0051B] **28.** He wrote about the same matter to Hildebrand, archdeacon of the Roman Church, as follows:

> “The complaint which the bishop of the Church of York has raised against me . . .”

(This letter, like the following one, is found among the letters; they are Letters 6 and 7.)

**29.** To this Hildebrand replied to Lanfranc:

> “The words of your legates,” etc.

# CHAPTER XII

**30.** [Note: [Col. 0091C] In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1075. This council is found in Malmesbury, in the frequently cited place, p. 122.]

In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1075, while the glorious King William was reigning, in the ninth year of his reign, a council of the bishops and abbots of the whole region of England, as well as of many persons belonging to the religious orders, was assembled at London in the church of the blessed apostle Paul. Lanfranc, archbishop of the holy [Col. 0051C] Church of Canterbury and primate of all Britain, ordered the council and presided over it. Seated with him were the venerable men Thomas, archbishop of York [Note: [Col. 0091D] Thomas, archbishop of York. See the extensive discussion in the notes to Letter 10.], William, bishop of London [Note: [Col. 0091D] William, bishop of London. He is mentioned by Malmesbury, book II of *The English Bishops*; Nicholas Harpsfield, *The Second Century*, chapter 15; and Godwin, *On the Bishops of England*, under the bishops of London, at the year 1050. From him I have this epitaph, which he says he transcribed from ancient monuments:

> “To William, a wise man and renowned for the holiness of his life, who was first a familiar of the blessed King Edward the Confessor, then recently raised to the bishopric of London, and not long afterward summoned to the council of the unconquered prince William, first king of that name of England, because of his exceptional prudence and loyalty, and who obtained for this most famous city the most extensive privileges. The Senate and People of London erected this to one who deserved well. He was bishop for twenty years and died in the year 1070 after Christ was born.”]

Godfrey, bishop of Coutances [Note: [Col. 0092A] Godfrey of Coutances. If you wish, consult the note on Letter 33.] [who [Note: [Col. 0051D] He alone, together with Odo of Bayeux among the bishops of Normandy, crossed into England with William the Conqueror.] although he was a bishop from overseas and possessed many estates in England, sat in the council with the others], Walchelin, bishop of Winchester [Note: [Col. 0092A] Walchelin of Winchester. We shall summarize his deeds in the notes to Letters 5 and 16.], Herman of Sherborne [or, in another reading, Schireburne] [Note: [Col. 0092A] Herman of Sherborne. Much concerning Herman is given in the notes to Letter 3.], Wulfstan, bishop of Worcester [Note: [Col. 0092A] Wulfstan of Worcester. This bishop was endowed with remarkable holiness and singular learning. Read Letter 13 and the note attached to it.], Walter of Hereford [Note: [Col. 0092A] Walter of Hereford. Malmesbury, in the place cited, book IV, records that this aged man, entangled in obscene desires, had his groin stabbed with the tongs held by a little woman whom he had attempted to assault.], Giso of Wells [Note: [Col. 0092A] Giso of Wells. Florence of Worcester, under the year 1060, writes: “Duduc, bishop of Wells, died, and Giso, the king’s chaplain, succeeded him; both were born in Lorraine.” This is the man who consecrated Blessed Lanfranc, together with Walter of Hereford, as archbishop, according to the same Florence under the year 1070. [Col. 0092B] “Through the industry of Giso,” says Harpsfield, *The Second Century*, chapter 20, “the number of canons was increased; he built for them a cloister, a place where they could sleep together, and another where they could take their meals; and afterward, after twenty-eight years, he died,” etc.] that is, of Bath, Remigius of Dorchester or Lincoln [Note: [Col. 0092B] Remigius of Dorchester. We shall discuss this prelate below in connection with Letters 4 and 12.], Herfast of Elmham or Norwich [Note: [Col. 0092B] Herfast of Elmham. Letters 20, 22, and 23 are addressed to him. He is treated briefly in the notes to Letter 20.], Stigand of Selsey [Note: [Col. 0092B] Stigand of Selsey. See Letter 28, to which this and Letter 29 are addressed.], Osbern of Exeter [Note: [Col. 0092B] Osbern of Exeter. We shall add a little concerning this prelate in Letter 19.] and Peter of Lichfield. [Note: [Col. 0092B] Or of Chester, as will be clear below in the Life. We shall mention him in the note to Letter 30.]

The Church of Rochester at that time lacked a pastor. The bishop of Lindisfarne, also called the bishop of Durham [Col. 0051D], could not attend the council because he had a canonical excuse. And because the use of councils had fallen into disuse in the English kingdom for many years, several matters were renewed that are also known to have been defined by ancient canons.

Accordingly, from the councils of Toledo IV, Milevis, and Braga, it was decreed that each person should sit according to the time of his ordination, except those who possessed more distinguished seats by ancient custom or by the privileges of their Churches. On this matter, the old men and those advanced in age were questioned about what they themselves had seen or had truthfully and plausibly received from their ancestors and elders. A delay was requested and granted until the following day. On the next day they unanimously testified that the archbishop of York ought to sit at the right hand of the archbishop of Canterbury, the bishop of London at his left, and the bishop of Winchester beside the archbishop of York. If the archbishop of York were absent, the bishop of London should sit at the right and the bishop of Winchester at the left.

From the Rule of Blessed Benedict, from Gregory’s *Dialogues*, and from the ancient custom of regular houses, it was decreed that monks should maintain the proper order; especially children and young men, in all places, were to be placed under the supervision of appointed masters. At night they were to carry lights, and in general all were to be without personal property unless property had been granted by their superiors [Col. 0052B] (*Rule*, chapters 63, 22, 33). If anyone were found at death to possess something of his own without the aforementioned permission, and had not returned it before death while confessing his sin with repentance and sorrow, no bells were to be rung for him, no saving host was to be offered for his absolution, and he was not to be buried in the cemetery (Gregory, *Dialogues*, book IV, chapter 55).

From the decrees of the supreme pontiffs, namely Damasus and Leo, and also from the councils of Sardica (canon 6) and Laodicea (canon 57), which prohibit episcopal sees from existing in villages, it was granted by royal munificence and by the authority of the synod that the aforementioned three bishops should transfer from villages to cities: Herman from Sherborne to Salisbury, Stigand from Selsey [Col. 0052C] to Chichester, and Peter from Lichfield to Chester. The matter of certain others who still lived in villages or hamlets was deferred until the king’s hearing, since at that time he was waging war in lands across the sea.

From many decrees of the Roman prelates and various authorities of the sacred canons: no one should retain or ordain another’s cleric or monk [Note: [Col. 0092B] Without letters of recommendation. On such letters, see Letter 25.] without letters of recommendation.

To restrain the insolence of certain indiscreet persons, it was decreed by common agreement that no one should speak in the council without permission obtained from the metropolitan, except bishops and abbots.

From the decrees of Gregory the Greater [Note: [Col. 0092B] That is, Gregory the Great or Gregory I, and Gregory II, as has already been noted elsewhere.] and also of Gregory the Lesser [Note: [Col. 0092C] That no one should take a wife from his own kindred, etc. Gregory the Great prescribes this in his responses to the questions of Augustine, apostle of the English, question 6, and in book XII, Letter 32, to Felix, bishop of Messana; Gregory the Lesser did so in the First Roman Council, chapter 4 and following.]—that no one should take as wife a woman of his own kindred, or one related to his deceased wife, or a woman whom a kinsman had had as wife, until the relationship on either side had reached the seventh degree.

[Note: [Col. 0092C] That no one should buy or sell holy orders, etc. Thus the Council of Chalcedon, canon 2; and the Second Council of Nicaea, session 8, canon 19, question 3, chapter 2, “If anyone is a giver,” and following.]

No one should buy or sell holy orders or an ecclesiastical office involving the care of souls. This crime was first condemned in the apostle Peter’s case of Simon Magus; afterward it was forbidden and excommunicated by the holy Fathers. [14]

The bones of dead animals must not be hung up anywhere as though to ward off a plague among animals.

No one should practice lots, auspices, divinations, or any works of this kind belonging to the devil.

[Note: [Col. 0092C] All these things the sacred canons prohibited, etc. Namely, canon 12 of the First Roman Council under Gregory II; the Council of Laodicea, canon 36; the Fourth Council of Carthage, canon 89; and the Council of Chalcedon, canon 2.]

For the sacred canons prohibited all these things and, after judgment had been pronounced, excommunicated those who practiced them.

From the councils of Elvira and Toledo XI: no bishop or abbot, or anyone else belonging to the clergy, should sentence a person to death or to mutilation of the limbs, nor lend the support of his authority to those who pass such judgments.

I, Lanfranc, archbishop of Canterbury, have subscribed.

I, Thomas, archbishop of York, have subscribed.

The other bishops and abbots who were present also subscribed [Col. 0053B] [Note: [Col. 0053D] Their names are listed in Labbe’s edition, where three copies of this council are preserved, as also in Spelman.]

# CHAPTER XIII

**31.** After this, Thomas of York humbly [Note: [Col. 0092C] He asked Lanfranc by letter. It is found among the letters of Blessed Lanfranc and is Letter 12.] asked Lanfranc by letter [Note: [Col. 0053D] It is Letter 11 among the edition of Lanfranc’s letters by Achéry; the letter Lanfranc wrote to the same bishops is Letter 12.] to send him two bishops, the bishop of Dorchester and the bishop of Worcester [Note: [Col. 0092C] To consecrate a certain cleric—namely Ralph, as we shall show in the note to Letter 12.], to consecrate a certain cleric whom Paul, earl of the Orkneys [Note: [Col. 0092D] Paul, earl of the Orkneys. We shall indicate what kind of earl he was in annotating the letter cited next.] [Note: [Col. 0053D] The Orkney Islands number approximately thirty and lie near Scotland. The principal one is Pomona, where the see of the bishop of those regions is located.] had sent him, in order to ordain a bishop for those parts. Thomas assured him that henceforth he would not seek the subjection of these bishops for this reason. Lanfranc granted his request and wrote to Wulfstan, bishop of Worcester, and Peter, bishop of Chester, asking them to meet Thomas, as he requested, for the consecration of the aforesaid cleric, on the day he himself should name.

[Col. 0053C] **32.** In the suburb of the city of Canterbury there is a certain church of Saint Martin, in which, as is said, there was formerly an episcopal see [Note: [Col. 0053D] Gervase of Canterbury asserts in his *Acts of the Archbishops of Canterbury*, in the chapter on Saint Elphege, that only a chorepiscopus had sat there. He writes:

> “Formerly the archbishop of Canterbury had a certain chorepiscopus who lived in the church of Saint Martin outside Canterbury. When Lanfranc arrived, this office was abolished, just as we have heard was done throughout the world.”

From this it appears that chorepiscopi continued until the eleventh century.]

They also say that it had a bishop before Lanfranc came to those parts. But since the authority of the canons establishes a prohibition against having two bishops simultaneously in one city, Lanfranc decreed that no bishop should henceforth be ordained for that place.

**33.** On one of the three great festivals on which the king customarily held court, when the king, adorned with his diadem and royal garments, was seated at table on the feast day, with Lanfranc beside him, a certain jester, seeing the king shining with gold and jewels, cried out in the hall in a loud voice of flattery and said: “Behold, I see God! Behold, I see God!”

[Col. 0053D] Lanfranc turned to the king and said: “Do not allow such things to be said to you. These things belong not to a man but to God. Order him to be severely beaten, so that he may never again dare to repeat such things.” The king ordered this to be done exactly as he had said.

[Col. 0054A] The most prudent man knew that the third Herod perished after being struck by an angel because he did not reject the words of flatterers who acclaimed him as though he were God, but accepted them (Acts 12:22–23).

**34.** [Note: [Col. 0092D] He himself restored the Church of Rochester. Numerous authors testify to this, among them Eadmer, *History of Recent Events*, p. 8; Malmesbury, *The English Bishops*, book I, fols. 122 and 132; and Robert of Monte in his manuscript *Chronicle*, under the year 1089.]

He himself restored the Church of Rochester and ordained as its bishop a monk of Bec named Hernost [Note: [Col. 0092D] A monk of Bec named Hernost. He is mentioned briefly in the note to Letter 49.]. At his consecration a verse from the Gospel was found: “Quickly bring out the first robe” (Luke 15:22), etc. When Lanfranc heard this, he foretold that Hernost would soon die, and so it happened. For before he had completed a year in the episcopate, [Note: [Col. 0092D] Gundulf succeeded him at his death. The character and importance of Gundulf as bishop are described by an ancient anonymous author of his manuscript Life in these terms:

> “While Lanfranc held and wisely administered the highest dignity of the Church in England, the Church of Rochester was deprived of its pastor when Bishop Ernost died. He had succeeded the monk Seuvard and that monk in the episcopate, but had lived in it only a year and a half. [Col. 0093A] Wishing the pontiff, according to the custom of the ancients, that a monk should succeed a monk, he began to consider which monk he could choose above all others, one capable of bearing the burden imposed upon him. As he considered, however, the holiness of Gundulf came quickly to mind, for it had already been sufficiently approved by certain proofs. After consulting with the wise, he therefore chose him for the episcopate; and, so that the king might give his assent to the election, he sent him across the sea to the king.
>
> “The king was filled with no small joy, since he had found an opportunity to exalt a man of God, whose holiness had already become well known to him. He willingly assented to the pontiff’s just requests and judged the man of God most worthy of episcopal honor. Lanfranc, having received royal authority, summoned the prelates and sent word to the leading men of Rochester; he declared the will of the king and of himself, and all gave their assent with rejoicing. He appointed him a faithful steward of the house of God. [Col. 0093B] There was no possibility of resistance, since the authority of so great a king and so great a prelate pressed upon them. The voice of one crying out that he was unworthy was silenced; the more unworthy he proclaimed himself, the more worthy he was acclaimed.
>
> “Thus the truly worthy man Gundulf was ordained bishop in the Church of Canterbury on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April, in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1077, the eleventh year after the coming of the Normans into England, under Count William, afterward the most noble king of England. After being consecrated, he set out according to custom to visit his own see. The crowds rejoiced as he entered the city of Rochester, and he was led to the episcopal seat and enthroned. From then onward the prelate was held in all reverence.
>
> “Certain possessions of the Church of Rochester, which Lanfranc had held under his own authority while his predecessors were bishops, were finally restored to him. They were restored on the condition that, as both prelates had already determined, monks should be placed in the Church of Rochester. For they had heard that monks had once been there; returning therefore to the ancient practices, they decreed that an order of monks should be established there. [Col. 0093C] After a short time had passed, a new church was begun after the old one had been demolished. The surrounding buildings were suitably arranged, and the entire work was completed within a few days, since Lanfranc supplied abundant funds.
>
> “When everything had been completed, some of the only five clerics found there came together for the religious habit. Joined by many others, they soon increased to a number exceeding sixty monks under the instruction of Father Gundulf. To these Gundulf became a mirror of life; to these he became an example of the whole religious life.”

Thus far the anonymous author. I have described this at greater length because Selden published it only once, in his notes to Eadmer’s *History of Recent Events*. Since the History itself, furnished with the same notes, is scarcely available, and since these materials contribute considerably to an illustration of the life of the great Lanfranc, I judged that the reader would not be displeased if I inserted them here.]

At his death Gundulf succeeded him, himself also a monk of Bec, a man beloved by God and religious, who continued until the time of Saint Anselm and King Henry.

He also restored the abbey of Saint Albans [Col. 0054B] to its former state. [Note: [Col. 0093D] He appointed Paul as abbot there. There is no need to labor over the character of Paul’s life from various writers, since Matthew Paris, a monk of Saint Albans, has described his deeds at length:

> “King William,” he says, “having been informed of the death of Abbot Frederick, took the vacant monastery of Saint Albans into his own hands; after uprooting the forests and impoverishing the people, he oppressed it. And unless he had been restrained by Lanfranc’s corrections, he would have utterly destroyed the whole monastery beyond repair.
>
> “Lanfranc therefore effectively arranged that Paul, his relative, whom he had brought with him to England, should be appointed abbot. This abbot was a native of Normandy, related by blood to Archbishop Lanfranc, and a monk of the Church of Caen. He undertook the governance of the Church of Saint Albans through the efforts of the aforesaid bishop Lanfranc, who loved the same Paul with filial affection. He was promoted to the abbacy in the year of grace 1077, on the fourth day before the Kalends of July; he was the first abbot of this church after England had been completely subdued by the Normans. [Col. 0094A]
>
> “He rebuilt this church and the other buildings, except the bakery and the mill, from the stones and tiles of the ancient city of Verulamium and from the timber that he found collected and stored by his predecessors. For Archbishop Lanfranc had enriched him and, when he was elected, had made him abundant in many treasures.
>
> “This Abbot Paul was a religious and elegantly learned man, strict and prudent in observing the regular order. He carefully and gradually reformed the whole rule of monastic religion—which the seductive pleasure of the more lax life of both superiors and subjects had long since banished—so that a sudden change would not produce disorder. The Church of Saint Albans thus became, throughout the kingdom of England, almost a school of religion and disciplined observance.
>
> “For he had brought with him Lanfranc’s customs and written monastic statutes, duly approved by the lord pope. Hence the good reputation of this Church spread through the Roman court and distant kingdoms, illuminating them, and happily inclined to it the hearts of many prelates and nobles.”]

Thus Matthew writes in the *Life of Abbot Paul*, at the end of the latest London and Paris edition of his history, 1644, among the *Lives of the Twenty-Three Abbots of Saint Albans*, Life 14.]

He appointed as abbot there Paul, a monk of Caen [Note: [Col. 0054D] Eadmer, book I of the *History of Recent Events*, gives a fuller account of the restoration of the monastery of Saint Albans, which Lanfranc completed after appointing Paul abbot there. Saint Anselm later wrote to this Paul to congratulate him on his election; that letter is Letter 78 in the new edition of book I.], who established there the regular order and the use of ecclesiastical office, as may be seen to the present day.

# CHAPTER XIV
35. One day, while he was celebrating Mass, and the moment had come when he took the Lord’s body into his hands, the deacon who was assisting him at Mass, seized by a demon, grabbed the archbishop by the shoulders. The venerable bishop was not at all disturbed; reaching his right hand backward, he grasped the man by the hair and dragged him before his feet. When the Mass had been completed, he ordered him to be taken to the infirmary, where he remained in the same insanity for several days.

The demon did not torment the possessed man greatly, except that he kept him in a state of madness. He laughed at those present with loud guffaws and answered whatever was said to him. They saw a certain swelling darting from place to place through his limbs; and whenever someone tried to lay a hand upon it, it immediately appeared in another place. It happened that the venerable Gundulf, bishop of Rochester, was present. When he tried to place his hand upon the swelling, it leapt elsewhere, and the bishop said, “Indeed, it jumps like a cat.” The demon replied, “Not like a cat, but like a kitten.”

He also said certain shameful things about some of the brothers of that place. Then they named one of them, saying that the demon would have nothing to say about him. But the demon began to insist that the man they had named would never dare to come into his presence. When the brother heard this, he feared that perhaps the demon would reproach him for some wrongdoing. The wise brothers therefore advised him that, when speaking with the archbishop, he should make a full confession, revealing his entire life to him; and that then, with confidence in the archbishop’s absolution and blessing, he should go to the demoniac.

Without delay, he did what had been advised and immediately entered and stood before him. Those present then said to the demoniac, “Look, here is the man you threatened. Say whether you know anything about him.” Looking at him with a savage eye, the demon laughed and said, “For a bad man, how have you now been reboiled and made white? Who has reboiled and whitened you in this way?” When the others pressed him to say what he had earlier threatened to reveal, he said nothing more.

From this it is understood that the power of confession and absolution either takes away from the devil the memory of the sin that has been confessed sincerely, or at least removes his power to accuse the person. Hence blessed Augustine says: “If you are your own accuser, and the Lord your liberator, what will he be except an accuser?”

After several days, by God’s mercy and with the assistance of the great bishop Lanfranc, together with the prayers of the brothers of the holy see, he was freed from that affliction and restored to his former health. I heard this, along with many other things, from the blessed archbishop Anselm’s account.

## CHAPTER XV

36. [Note: “When the glorious king …” Lanfranc was a leading statesman. Thus Eadmer, book I of the *History*, p. 12, explaining by what means and through what measures William Rufus was raised to the kingdom after his father’s death, says: “Without his [Lanfranc’s] consent he could in no way ascend the throne.” A little later he adds: “He began, both personally and through everyone he could, to promise Lanfranc by oath and pledge that, if he became king, he would observe justice, equity, and mercy in every matter throughout the kingdom,” etc. And below, p. 14: “Lanfranc was a man most learned in both divine and human law; and the gaze of the entire kingdom was directed according to his will.”

For this reason William the Conqueror, approaching death and having drawn up his will, “fearing,” as a fragment of St. Stephen of Caen relates, “that sudden disorder might arise in so extensive a kingdom, wrote a letter concerning the appointment of a king to Lanfranc, the archbishop, and gave it, sealed with his own seal, to his son William Rufus,” etc.]

When the glorious King William was staying in Normandy, Lanfranc was the chief authority and custodian of England, with all the princes subject to him and assisting him in matters relating to the defense, administration, and peace of the kingdom, according to the laws of the country.

[Note: He was assiduous in reading. St. Lanfranc left very few monuments of his intellect. Among authors we have been able to find only the following:

A Commentary on the Psalms, until now buried in darkness.

A Commentary on the Epistles of St. Paul, which we are now publishing for the first time.

A short work on the sacrament of the body and blood of Christ against Berengar, already many times committed to the press.

Statutes, or decrees, for the Order of St. Benedict, printed only once.

A few notes on several of Cassian’s *Collations*, which we are also bringing to light.

Decretal letters, several of which we are making publicly available.

An ecclesiastical history, still in places struggling with worms.

A Life of William the Conqueror, cited by Sixtus of Siena and Gesner, which many people particularly desire.

Concerning the writings of the great Lanfranc, consult Sixtus of Siena in his *Bibliotheca*; Gesner in the abridgment of his *Bibliotheca*; Bale, century 13, author 12; Selden’s notes on Eadmer’s *History*; and Edward Matthew, table 3 of the *Trophies*, under the year 1090, p. 209.]

He was assiduous in reading, both before and during his episcopate, as far as he was able. And because the books of Scripture had been excessively corrupted through the fault of their copyists, he took pains to correct all the books of both the Old and New Testaments, as well as the writings of the holy Fathers, according to orthodox faith. [Note: He devoted himself to correcting them according to orthodox faith. Robert of Torigni reports this word for word in his manuscript *Chronicle* under the year 1089. The *Florilegus* says for that year: “Lanfranc carefully corrected from the beginning the books that English rustic simplicity had corrupted; and the Church rejoices that, through the confirmation of these books, she is strengthened.” The sole surviving proof of this assertion, carefully preserved in the monastery of Saint-Martin at Sées, belonging to our congregation, is this: the first ten *Collations* of Cassian—seventeen in printed editions—corrected with the greatest precision by the hand of that great pontiff, with this marginal note at the end of the tenth *Collation*: “Thus far I, Lanfranc, have corrected.”]

[Note: In the library of our monastery of Saint-Martin at Sées there is a manuscript codex of Cassian’s *Collations*, corrected by blessed Lanfranc, as is evident from a marginal note written in his own hand: “Thus far I, Lanfranc, have corrected.” On the same subject there is a remarkable testimony by Matthew Paris in his *History of the English* under the year 1089, where he says: “In that same year Lanfranc died … He was constantly devoted to reading and undertook to correct the books of the Old and New Testaments that had been corrupted through the fault of their copyists; and by the light of this correction both the English Church and the French rejoice that they have been enlightened.”]

He also corrected with the greatest care many of the texts that we use night and day in the service of the Church; and he did this not only personally but also through his disciples. For this reason, as has already been said at the beginning, Latinity rightly venerates him as a master with honor and affection. [Note: Latinity rightly venerates him as a master with honor and affection. William of Malmesbury, book III of the *Kings of the English*, under William I, fol. 62: “In Kent Lanfranc, of whom I spoke above, shone forth as such a gift to England:

As Lucifer, dispersing the fleeing stars,  
Brings forth the bright day with his rosy face.”

Likewise, book I of the *Bishops of England*, fol. 122: “He was a man whose industry Kent will proclaim, whose teaching Latinity will marvel at in his disciples, for as long as all the years endure.” Many authors inferior to Malmesbury, out of affection, echo the same testimony.]

The entire Church of the western world, both French and English, rejoices that it has been illumined by the splendor of this praise. He was so generous that it was said that no more lavish Lombard had ever come from Italy. [Note: “Driving avarice, a vice familiar to the Lombards, away from his own person and shaking it off,” says the same Malmesbury in the passage cited later.]

At that time the region overseas was full and abundant in all the good things that God created for human use; the archbishop himself was also wealthy, enriched by many possessions. Yet how little he valued these things was shown by the fact that, as far as he could, he retained poverty in the plainness of his clothing, maintaining frugality amid countless luxuries. Many great gifts were also offered to him, and he cheerfully distributed them to those who asked him or were in need.

[Note: He was also so generous to the poor, etc. Writers exalt the almsgiving of this most holy bishop with many encomia, especially St. Anselm, book I, letters 12 and, above all, 13. He advises a certain Gerard, weighed down by debts, to go to England to the excellent Lanfranc in order to relieve his misery: “For,” he says, “that same most merciful and most reverend archbishop is especially concerned for the salvation of souls, and he is very devoted to almsgiving,” etc.

Anselm’s secretary, book I of the *History*, p. 8, says: “What poor man ever cried out to him and was despised? What pilgrim of any order of people ever asked his help and did not obtain it? What congregation of monks or clerics ever sent to him asking assistance and did not experience his generosity beyond what it had hoped? Italy, Gaul, and Britain bear witness to what we say; even to this day they mourn Lanfranc’s death with a sorrowful sigh.”

William of Malmesbury, in the passage cited above, vividly portrays in his customary manner the measure he observed in distributing alms: “He was not an inconsiderate giver, nor did his generosity waste away; discretion and cheerfulness of spirit seasoned it. The brightness of his face did not fall toward the ground, but was most pleasing to the recipient, like the new-rising sun which, dispersing the clouds, stills the winds and clears the air. Bread, shoes, and everything necessary for food and clothing were therefore distributed to the poor. Coins were not given, after more mature consideration and deeper deliberation, so that the common people of this age, even with a stuffed purse, might digest hunger with a dry mouth. To needy clerics and monasteries he amassed an immense quantity of money, often inviting those who were more reluctant to ask. Nor was the archbishop ashamed, with his robes gathered up, to serve food to the poor and to send scholars of reduced fortune into the contest of disputation; afterward both would depart, the victor receiving the prize of knowledge and the defeated the consolation of modesty.”]

He was also so generous to the poor that he is said to have distributed five hundred pounds annually in alms—and deservedly so; for at his consecration there was found above his head the evangelical saying: “Give alms, and behold, all things are clean for you” (Luke 11:41), which he strove to fulfill with complete devotion. [Note: “Above his head the Gospel saying,” etc. The monk of Malmesbury, in the passage repeatedly cited above, recounts this prophecy as follows: “When he received this prophecy from those who acclaimed him, he turned toward the Lord with a cheerful face: ‘Let us therefore compete in mutual exchange: you by giving, I by distributing.’ The heavenly goodness answered the prayer of the praiseworthy man; and such abundance flowed to him that it could satisfy and surpass any degree of desire.”]

He bestowed benefits upon the needy relatives of his monks with great kindness and generosity. He could truly say: “From my youth compassion grew up with me” (Job 31:18).

37. Meanwhile it happened that the holy Anselm, abbot of Bec, who had succeeded blessed Herluin, crossed over into England, both for the interests of his church and in order to speak with the archbishop, whose conversation and counsel he greatly loved. [Note: How highly he valued his teacher Lanfranc, St. Anselm sufficiently demonstrates in the letters addressed to him, especially book I, letter 63. He does so also more than once in book I of his *Life*, particularly near the beginning, where Eadmer records, among other things: “Such a force of devotion then possessed Anselm’s heart, and he believed such a wealth of sound counsel to reside in Lanfranc, that when they were traveling toward Rouen through the great forest above Bec, if Lanfranc had said to him, ‘Remain in this forest, and take care that you do not leave it as long as you live,’ he would unquestionably, as he admitted, have carried out the command.”]

When he reached him, he was received with great affection and due honor. [Note: “And while they were speaking together.” Eadmer inserted this conversation at greater length near the end of book I of the *Life of Blessed Anselm*.]

As they conversed and discussed many matters with one another, the archbishop of Canterbury intimated to the abbot, almost in complaint, that the people of his country venerated certain saints whom he did not favor. In particular, he said, they venerated a certain Ælfheah, the archbishop of that see, whom they insisted on counting not only among the saints but also among the martyrs, although it was clear that he had been killed not for the faith of Christ but because he refused to ransom himself from the enemies who held him captive.
