[Note: “A certain Ælfheah, archbishop of this see,” etc. Osbert, or Osbern, committed his Life to writing at the command of St. Lanfranc; it is preserved in Surius, volume II, under 19 April. Eadmer gives this account in the passage cited above: “He ordered the history of his life and passion [of blessed Ælfheah] to be composed with diligent care. That history, written not only in plain prose for reading but also in musical form for singing by Osbern, a monk of the Canterbury Church of happy memory, was nobly produced at his command. Out of love for that martyr, Lanfranc, in his wisdom, raised it to greater distinction, authorized what he had distinguished, and instituted that it should be read and sung in the Church of God.”

William of Malmesbury discusses St. Ælfheah in book II of *The Deeds of the Bishops of England*, fol. 139, and in book II of *The Kings of England*, chapter 11; Baronius discusses him in the *Annals*, volume II, under the year 1006 and following.]

[Note: We discussed him under the year 1012.]

Anselm then gave this reply: “It is certain,” he said, “that whoever does not hesitate to die rather than offend God by committing even a slight sin would much less hesitate to die before aggravating God by some grave sin. But it is truly graver to deny Christ than to burden one’s own people for a short time by taking their money in order to secure one’s ransom; and Ælfheah refused to do the lesser thing. Therefore he would much less have denied Christ if a mad mob had forced him to do so by threatening him with death.

“From this it is clear how great was the force of justice that possessed his heart, since he preferred to give his own life rather than, by disregarding charity, scandalize his neighbors. Nor, I think, is he without reason counted among the martyrs, since he is said voluntarily to have accepted death for justice. Blessed John the Baptist too, whom the whole Church of God believes and venerates as a preeminent martyr, was beheaded at the request of a dancing girl—not because he refused to deny Christ, but because he refused to remain silent about the truth in defense of divine law.

“And what difference is there between dying for justice and dying for truth? Sacred Scripture testifies that truth and justice are Christ. For he himself says, ‘I am the truth’ (John 14:6). And the Apostle says, ‘Christ was made for us by God wisdom and justice’ (1 Corinthians 1:30). Therefore whoever dies for truth and justice dies for Christ; and whoever dies for Christ is regarded as a martyr by the testimony of the Church.

“Blessed Ælfheah suffered equally for justice, just as St. John did for truth. Why then should anyone doubt more about the true and holy martyrdom of one than of the other, when both endured death for the same cause?”

When Lanfranc heard this, he gladly accepted the argument, praising the man’s wisdom and the penetrating subtlety of his intellect, supported by firm truth. From then on he devoutly venerated the holy Ælfheah as truly a great and glorious martyr.

38. Meanwhile it was reported to Lanfranc that the aforementioned abbot Anselm, coming to his bed one night after Matins, found a gold ring upon it. First signing it with the cross of Christ, lest it perhaps be a demonic illusion, he took the ring as genuine and showed it to everyone through whose hands the monastery’s property passed; no one admitted that he had lost it. The ring was then sold, and the proceeds were spent for the use of the brothers.

When the archbishop heard this, he replied to the person who reported it: “Know with complete certainty that he will be archbishop after me.” We know that it happened as he foretold.

39. Let these few things about so great a man be related in an unpolished style. Yet we believe that what we have said about him is true, and we do not doubt that, by the grace of God, he accomplished more than this. From the time of his conversion he devoted himself wholeheartedly to religion, and, always striving toward better things, sought to advance from virtue to virtue.

Who could adequately recount the splendor of his wisdom, the subtlety of his intellect, the kindness of his heart, the integrity of his diligence, or the purity of his spirit? He was cheerful in liveliness, submissive in humility; generous in almsgiving, catholic in faith, a restorer of the Christian religion, a supporter of the poor, a protector of orphans, and a comforter of widows. Adorned with these and many other virtues, he preserved the faith by living rightly and completed his course by dying well. For one who has lived well cannot die badly. Nor, as blessed Augustine testifies, should a death be considered bad when a good life has preceded it.

As the end of his life approached, he fell ill. [Note: “He fell into illness.” William of Malmesbury, often cited above, more explicitly indicates what kind of illness afflicted him before he breathed his last. In book I of *The Bishops of England*, fol. 122, speaking of the calamities and troubles by which the people were oppressed while William II held the kingdom, he says: “Wearied by these things, he did not prolong his days in the light; but after nineteen years of episcopate he contracted a fever. When the physicians consulted had declared that a necessary potion should be given, he first fortified himself with confession and viaticum. Then, after taking the draught, but when it had turned to the opposite effect, he breathed his last, obtaining the kind of end he had always desired. For he confessed to his household that he prayed the Lord to let him die either from dysentery or from fever, since these illnesses disturb neither the memory nor the power of speech.”

To that holy man, suffering from a fatal illness, St. Anselm wrote in his own name and that of the community of Bec, book II, letter 53, as follows: “We are deeply grieved by the illness of your paternal holiness and do not cease to pray to God for your health, because we believe that your illness is our tribulation and your health our well-being. We understand that your life is necessary not only to us but also to Mother Church, insofar as your name extends,” etc.]

As the illness grew worse day by day, in the nineteenth year of his archiepiscopate, on the fifth day before the Kalends of June, he died, during the reign of William, son of King William. [Note: “The fifth day before the Kalends of June.” Or the ninth day before the Kalends of the same month, according to Florence of Worcester, a contemporary writer, under the year 1089: “Lanfranc, archbishop of Canterbury, died on the ninth day before the Kalends of June, on a Thursday, in that same year; and on the third day before the Ides of August, on a Saturday around the third hour of the day, a very great earthquake occurred throughout England.”

Henry of Huntingdon agrees with Florence concerning the earthquake in book VII of his *History*: “Lanfranc, archbishop,” he says, “a brilliant teacher of clerics and a most loving father of monks, passed from transitory affairs in the following year [1089]; in that year there was a terrible earthquake.” Hoveden does not disagree with them in the earlier part of his *Annals*, under William the Younger; there one finds the same words as in Florence, in his customary manner, as we have already noted once.

Robert of Torigni gives the cause of the earthquake in his manuscript *Chronicle* under that year: “In this year a terrible earthquake occurred, perhaps foreshadowing the evils that, because of the sins of wicked men, we have seen fulfilled in our own times.”

But especially after blessed Lanfranc had been taken from the living, when King William Rufus had loosened the reins for every kind of crime, everything most wicked began to rage throughout all England. More will be said about these matters below in connection with letter 2, letter p.]

The evidence makes it clear, both from the foregoing and from Lanfranc’s own deeds and the testimony of other writers, that he held the archiepiscopal office of Canterbury for nineteen years and ended his life in the year 1089 from the Incarnation of the Lord, in the second year of the reign of William II Rufus. I am therefore readily persuaded that he reached an advanced old age, chiefly for the following reasons.

When he assumed the monastic habit at Bec, he was already advanced in age—that is, approximately forty-five years old—as he himself seems clearly to imply in the prayer he uttered one night when robbers had bound his hands to a tree: “Lord God, I have spent so much time in learning, and have worn out body and soul in the study of letters,” etc.

For even before he had traveled through part of Gaul, when he was already distinguished at Pavia as a source of knowledge to everyone, especially through his expertise in law, he was consulted by highly learned men from every quarter, as was shown above. It is also quite likely that he taught for several years at Avranches in Normandy. Finally, it is reasonable to believe that he possessed the dignity and age appropriate to a man whom William, then duke of Normandy, had chosen as an adviser.

Add, therefore, forty-five years to the forty-seven that elapsed from the year 1042, when he assumed the monastic habit, to the year of his death, 1089, and you will undoubtedly arrive at ninety-two. But enough of this.

I do not think it out of place to append an epitaph of the great Lanfranc by Philip, abbot of Bonne-Espérance, as a conclusion to these annotations.

### Epitaph of Master Lanfranc

You lived, venerable Father, wisely and justly;  
You lived while living, and death too was life to you.

Amid riches you were poor, Lanfranc;  
Though overflowing with riches, you were a lover of the poor.

Through you the flourishing Latin arts prevailed;  
Behold, grace triumphs joyfully through you.

The grief was incomparable to all, and the mourning of his own people inconsolable. He was buried in Christ Church, which he himself had built. [Note: Thus the manuscript records preserved by Gerberon state, in his notes on letter 41 of book II of St. Anselm’s letters: “Lanfranc, archbishop of the metropolitan church of Canterbury, having died, was buried in the basilica of the Holy Trinity, which he himself had constructed with magnificent workmanship.”]

Because that church seemed to have a small eastern end—commonly called the *chevet*—blessed Anselm, his successor, undertook before his own death to enlarge the head of the same church. What he began was built for several years after his death and was finally completed as a great and beautiful work. It was dedicated by William, who became archbishop after Anselm’s successor Ralph, with great glory and an abundance of all things, as the clergy and people of the kingdom who attended bear witness.

When the day of its dedication approached, all the bodies were removed from the church, as is customary. Then a certain brother, either out of curiosity or, as is more credible, in order to keep it as a relic, cut a piece from the vestment of the glorious Lanfranc. From it there came forth a sweetness of marvelous fragrance. He showed it to others, who also perceived the fragrant odor.

From this it may be understood that his soul rests in great sweetness, since the garments of his body emit such a fragrance. This grace is granted especially to those who, while they lived in the body, strove to preserve purity of heart and incorruptibility of flesh until the end of life. May Christ the Lord, our merciful God, who is blessed forever, deign to grant his soul the rest of eternal blessedness. Amen.

## TESTIMONIES OF CERTAIN AUTHORS CONCERNING THE HOLINESS OF BLESSED LANFRANC

Although the holiness of blessed Lanfranc has been sufficiently and more than sufficiently revealed in his Life and in the notes upon it, nevertheless, since some may perhaps still doubt, I thought it would not be inappropriate, in order to remove all scruples more thoroughly, to append here, as though a seal, the testimonies supplied by contemporary, near-contemporary, and more recent writers, as well as by the Martyrologies.

### Pope Alexander II

In the privilege granted to the Abbey of Saint Stephen of Caen, above, column 71:

“Since we know, dearest son Lanfranc, abbot, that you have grown to such a degree of religious excellence that you are zealous not only for your own salvation but also build a monastery for those choosing the common life and provide a pattern of religious observance, etc.”

### William of Poitiers

*On the Deeds of Duke William*, p. 198:

“William entrusted to him [Lanfranc], with his soul’s welfare in mind, a kind of watchtower from which he might provide counsel concerning ecclesiastical orders throughout Normandy. For the vigilant care of such a man, joined with the greatest authority and the distinction of wisdom as well as holiness, could promise no small security to solicitude.”

### Eadmer

Book I of the *Life of St. Anselm*, near the beginning:

“Anselm went to Normandy, wishing to see, speak with, and live alongside a certain Lanfranc, a very good man, truly noble in distinguished religious devotion and wisdom. His exceptionally great reputation had spread everywhere, and it drew to him the most noble of the clergy from every region of the world,” etc.

### Osbern, monk of Bec

Writing to blessed Anselm to hasten his inauguration, book III, letter 5 of Anselm’s letters:

“Let us recover in you what, when the most holy Father Lanfranc died, we lost together with the whole world. We shall always mourn his death until we see him in you.”

### William of Malmesbury

Book III of *The Deeds of the Kings of the English*, under William I, about the middle:

“He built two monasteries, one in England and the other in Normandy. The first was at Caen, where he appointed Lanfranc abbot and later archbishop of Canterbury, a man comparable to the ancients in knowledge and religious devotion. Of him it may seriously be said: ‘A third Cato has fallen from heaven’; so thoroughly had a heavenly savor imbued his breast and palate,” etc.

### Orderic Vitalis

Book IV of the *Ecclesiastical History*:

“In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1070, Lanfranc, first abbot of Caen, was divinely given to the English as their instructor; and by a most honorable election and most faithful consecration he was enthroned as the fourth archbishop of the Church of Canterbury on the fourth day before the Kalends of September, etc. The inhabitants of all Albion, present and absent, would have rejoiced and given great thanks to God if they had recognized how much good was then bestowed upon them from heaven.”

### Peter de Natalibus

In the *Catalogue of the Saints*, book VI, chapter 47:

“Lanfranc, having abandoned the world and secular studies, assumed the monastic habit in the monastery mentioned above and began to lead a humble and despised life. Although he was the teacher of all, he humbly concealed his wisdom,” etc. “He rested in Christ on the fifth day before the Nones of July.”

### Johannes Trithemius, abbot

*On Illustrious Men of the Order of St. Benedict*, book III, chapter 325:

“Lanfranc, archbishop of Canterbury after having been abbot of the monastery of Caen, was a most learned and deeply religious man. He was held in a reputation of great holiness, as is found in the written accounts of his deeds. He flourished in the year of the Lord 1060.”

### Cardinal Caesar Baronius

*Ecclesiastical Annals*, volume II, under the year 1070:

“These things concern the ordination of Lanfranc, that celebrated light of this age, raised in the Catholic Church upon so great a lampstand, a man outstanding in knowledge and in the holiness of his life.”

### Arnoldus Wion

*The Tree of Life*, book III, in the *Martyrology*:

“On the fifth day before the Nones of July, at Canterbury in England, the holy Lanfranc, archbishop, illustrious for the highest learning and the glory of miracles.”

### Appendix to the Roman Martyrology

Or, *General Catalogue of the Saints*, dedicated to Urban VIII, by Philip Ferrarius:

“On the fifth day before the Nones of July, at Canterbury in England, Saint Lanfranc, bishop.”

And below, in the notes:

“From the monastic Martyrologies of Maurolycus and Felicius. He was made the thirty-third bishop of Canterbury after having been abbot of Caen in Normandy, on account of the holiness of his life and his learning. He departed this life in the year 1089.”

### Martyrology of the Saints of the Order of St. Benedict

Compiled by Hugh Menard:

“On the fifth day before the Nones of July, at Canterbury in England, blessed Lanfranc, bishop, a man of the highest learning and holiness.”

## THE ANNIVERSARY OF LANFRANC’S DEATH

(*Anglia Sacra*, part I, p. 55)

[Col. 0099B] On the fifth day before the Kalends of June, Lanfranc, archbishop, of blessed memory, died: the most faithful observer and strongest defender of the Catholic faith. With the cooperation of God’s grace, he founded and completed this church from its foundations, and adorned it with many fine and honorable ornaments: some made of the purest gold, others furnished with gold and gems, and others, although without gold or gems, nevertheless deserving great praise. He enriched it with many devout and religious monastic persons, and beautified it with much and highly venerable religious observance. He also built, with remarkable and admirable workmanship, the cloisters, storerooms, refectories, dormitories, and all the other necessary offices, as well as all the buildings standing within the circuit of the court, together with the circuit itself. Moreover, he greatly ennobled this Church with the precious adornment of books, of which he himself corrected a very great number.

[Note: [Col. 0099C] The learned Edward Brown recently brought a grave accusation against Lanfranc in his preface to his recent edition of the *Fasciculus Rerum Expetendarum*, p. 33, as though the Holy Scriptures and the writings of the holy Fathers had been corrupted by him. He took the basis of the accusation from a brief note by Matthew Parker in the margin of the *Textus Roffensis*: “Lanfranc … because the writings of the Scriptures were excessively corrupted through the fault of copyists, undertook to correct all the books of both the Old and the New Testament, and also the writings of the holy Fathers, according to orthodox faith.” From this the aforementioned writer suspects that monuments of ancient writings were corrupted, falsified, or erased by Lanfranc, and he directed the gravest censure against him, asserting that Parker had undoubtedly drawn this statement from some sound and authentic testimony.

I would readily grant that point: for that most learned primate never annotated anything rashly or needlessly. Yet he did not intend to fasten any such crime upon Lanfranc. He noted only what today stands ready for all to read in the most widely circulated historical records of our nation. Thus Matthew Paris writes (*History*, p. 15, under the year 1089): “Lanfranc devoted himself continually to reading. He diligently sought to correct the books of the Old and New Testaments, corrupted through the fault of copyists; by the light of this emendation both the English and the Gallican Church rejoice that they are enlightened.”

Add to this what Matthew of Westminster and a manuscript chronicle of excellent quality in the Lambeth Library say under the year 1089: “Archbishop Lanfranc carefully corrected the books which English simplicity, in its ignorance, had long ago corrupted; by their strengthening”—the manuscript codex of the *Florilegium* reads “correction”—“the Church rejoices that she is fortified.”

This was certainly a praiseworthy undertaking, and, if one has perceived the profound ignorance of the Latin language formerly prevailing among the English clergy, an especially necessary one. Nevertheless, I believe that it concerned only ecclesiastical books, namely, missals, lectionaries, and other such works. In saying this, I do not at all wish to detract from my learned friend, to whom the republic of letters owes much on account of his excellent edition of a most useful work.]

He also recalled the archbishop of York and the other bishops of this kingdom who were withdrawing from subjection to this Church to true and due subjection. Through this, and by his own action, this Church also recovered all those lands that had long been lost and that are commemorated on the anniversary of King William. Outside the city he established spacious dwellings, which he filled with the poor and the sick; he ordered that food and clothing be given to them from his own resources. Likewise, outside the city he arranged the church of blessed Gregory, in which he installed clerics who would receive without payment those who were dying and had no means of preparing a burial place for themselves; those received there would be carried to that church and honorably buried.

In the manors belonging to the archbishop he built many fine churches and prepared many highly honorable houses, so that they might be a delight and an honor to the archbishops and might relieve the poor people who very often had to prepare houses for the archbishops from so great a labor. He also began the church at Rochester and honorably completed what he had begun, adorning it with many fine and honorable ornaments. Moreover, he established there a venerable religious community of monks. He acquired lands that had long been taken away from the Church and allowed the monks to possess them for food and clothing. He also founded and nearly completed the church of Saint Alban, which he enlarged with many precious ornaments.

The death of Lanfranc is always to be read in its proper order, even though it occurred during the week of Pentecost. When the anniversary of Lord Lanfranc, archbishop, has been announced in chapter, all the brothers are to proceed together into the church, singing “My words,” while all the bells are ringing. After supper, when the signal has been sounded for vigils, all are to assemble in the usual manner; they are to celebrate the vigils festively. Two are to sing the third responsory, three the sixth, and four the ninth. On the following day every priest must celebrate one Mass for him; and those who do not sing Mass are to sing fifty psalms [read: “are to sing,” plural]. The conventual Mass is to be celebrated festively in white vestments; the cantor and two other brothers with him are to attend it wearing copes. Three are to wear copes for the responsory and four for the tract, likewise in copes. On that day the treasurers are to give forty shillings for feeding the poor. The refectory service is to be performed festively, as on the feast of one apostle. The church is to remain prepared, as on the feast of Saint Augustine, until the service has been completed.

[Col. 0101]

## COMMENTARIES OF BLESSED LANFRANC, PRIOR OF BEC, THEN FIRST ABBOT OF SAINT STEPHEN OF CAEN, AND FINALLY ARCHBISHOP OF CANTERBURY, ON ALL THE EPISTLES OF PAUL, WITH AN INTERJECTED GLOSS

Now published for the first time from an ancient manuscript written in the monastery of Saint Melanius of Redon, of the congregation of Saint Maur.

### 3. BEGINNING OF THE PREFACE TO ALL THE EPISTLES OF SAINT PAUL

[Note: [Col. 0101] This preface and the following one are attributed to D. Jerome in the manuscript codex.]

[Col. 0101B] It is first asked why, after the Gospels—which are the supplement of the Law, and in which examples and precepts for living have been set out for us most fully—the Apostle wished to send these Epistles to the individual Churches. The reason seems to have been that he might anticipate the beginnings of the nascent Church when new circumstances arose, cut away present and emerging vices, and forestall future questions, following the example of the prophets. After the Law of Moses had been issued, in which all the commandments of God were read, the prophets nevertheless continually restrained the people’s sins by their renewed teaching, and, as an example for living, transmitted books even for our remembrance.

Next it is asked why he wrote no more than ten Epistles to the Churches. There are ten, including the one called the Epistle to the Hebrews; for the remaining four were addressed specifically to disciples. He wished to show that the New Testament does not differ from the Old, and that he was not acting against the Law of Moses. He therefore arranged his Epistles according to the number of the first commandments of the Decalogue [or: “assigned” them according to that number]. Just as Moses instituted as many commandments for those whom he liberated from Pharaoh, so here he teaches that as many peoples have been won from slavery to the devil and idolatry through these Epistles. The most learned men have also handed down that the two stone tablets represented the two Testaments.

Some indeed maintain that the Epistle written to the Hebrews is not Paul’s, because it is not titled with his name and because of the difference in its language and style. They attribute it either to Barnabas, according to Tertullian, or to Luke, according to some, or certainly to Clement, a disciple of the apostles and bishop of the Roman Church, appointed after the apostles. (Tertullian, *On Modesty*, book 20; Eusebius, *History*, book IV, chapter 8: “that the Epistle to the Hebrews is Paul’s.”)

They must be answered as follows: If it is not Paul’s because it does not bear his name, then it will belong to no one, since it bears no one’s name. But if that is inconvenient and absurd, it should rather be believed to be his, since it shines with such eloquence of doctrine. Since, however, he was regarded among the Churches of the Hebrews under the false suspicion of being a destroyer of the Law, he wished, under an unspoken name, to give an account of the figures of the Law and of the truth of Christ, lest hostility toward the name displayed in the title should exclude the benefit of reading.

It is certainly not surprising if he appears more eloquent in his own language—that is, Hebrew—than in a foreign language, namely Greek, in which the other Epistles were written.

Some are also troubled by the question why the Epistle to the Romans is placed first, since reason shows that it was not written first. He testifies that he wrote it while setting out for Jerusalem, after he had already encouraged the Corinthians and others by letter to collect the ministry—or contribution—that he was going to carry with him. Some therefore understand that all the Epistles were arranged in such a way that the one placed first, although sent later, would lead through the individual Epistles by stages toward more perfect things.

Most of the Romans were so unformed that they did not understand that they had been saved by God’s grace and not by their own merits; for this reason the two peoples were in conflict with one another. He therefore asserts that they needed correction, first recalling the vices of paganism. To the Corinthians, however, he already says that the grace of knowledge has been granted, and he does not so much rebuke everyone as blame them for failing to rebuke those who were sinning, as he says: “Fornication is heard of among you” (1 Cor. 5:2). And again: “When you are gathered together with my spirit, to deliver such a one to Satan” (ibid.). In the second Epistle they are praised and urged to advance more and more.

The Galatians are accused of no crime except this one: that they believed the most cunning pseudo-apostles. The Ephesians deserve no reproach but much praise, because they preserved the apostolic faith. The Philippians are praised even more highly, since they were unwilling even to listen to false apostles. In two Epistles he follows the Thessalonians with every praise, because they not only preserved an unshaken faith in the truth but were also found steadfast amid the persecution of their fellow citizens (2 Thess. 2).

The Colossians were such that, although they had not been seen bodily by the Apostle, they were considered worthy of this praise: “Although I am absent in body,” he says, “yet I am with you in spirit, rejoicing and seeing your order” (Col. 2:5).

What, then, should be said about the Hebrews? The Thessalonians, who were praised so greatly, are said to have become imitators of them. Thus he himself says: “You, brethren, became imitators of the Churches of God that are in Judea. For you suffered the same things from your own countrymen as they did from the Jews” (1 Thess. 2:14). Among the Hebrews themselves he recalls the same thing, saying: “For you had compassion on those who were imprisoned, and you joyfully accepted the seizure of your possessions, knowing that you have a better and lasting substance” (Heb. 10:34).

## BEGINNING OF THE SPECIAL PROLOGUE TO THE EPISTLE TO THE ROMANS

[Col. 0103]

[Col. 0103C] The Romans are those who believed from among Jews and Gentiles. In arrogant contention they wished to place themselves above one another. The Jews said:

“We are the people of God, whom he loved and cherished from the beginning. We are circumcised, descended from Abraham; we come from a holy lineage, and formerly God was known only in Judea (Ps. 75:2). We were delivered from Egypt by God’s signs and mighty acts; we crossed the sea on dry feet while the heaviest waves overwhelmed our enemies (Exod. 14:22). In the desert the Lord rained manna upon us and provided heavenly food for us as for his own sons. Day and night he went before us in a pillar of cloud and fire, to show us the way through a trackless land (Exod. 13).

“To say nothing of his other immeasurable benefits toward us, we alone were deemed worthy to receive God’s Law, to hear the voice of God speaking (Rom. 3), and to know his will. In that Law Christ was promised to us; indeed, he himself testified that he had come to us, saying: ‘I was not sent except to the sheep that have perished of the house of Israel’ (Matt. 15), while he called you dogs rather than human beings. Is it therefore fair that, abandoning today the idols whom you have served from the beginning, you should be compared with us, rather than be assigned, by the authority and custom of the Law, the place of proselytes? And you did not even deserve this, except because God’s abundant clemency has always wished to admit you to imitate us.”

The Gentiles, on the other hand, replied:

“The greater the benefits of God toward you that you recount, the greater the crime of which you show yourselves guilty. For you have always proved ungrateful for all these things. With the very feet with which you crossed the dry sea, you were playing before the idols you had made; with the very mouth with which shortly before you had sung to the Lord over the destruction of your enemies, you asked that images be made for you; with the eyes with which you were accustomed to behold God in the cloud or in the fire, you looked upon images (Exod. 32).

“Manna also became repugnant to you (ibid.), and you were always murmuring against the Lord in the desert, desiring to return to Egypt, from which he had brought you out by a mighty hand. Why say more? Your fathers provoked the Lord so repeatedly that they all died in the wilderness, and no more than two men of the older generation entered the promised land (Num. 14).

“But why rehearse ancient events, when, even if you had not done those things at all, no one would judge you worthy of pardon for this one fact: that you not only refused to receive the Lord Christ, who had always been promised to you by the voices of the prophets, but also killed him by the most wretched death? As soon as we came to know him, we believed in him, although he had not previously been preached to us. Hence it is proved that, if we served idols, this must be attributed not to obstinacy of mind but to ignorance. For whoever follows one whom he has immediately come to know would certainly have followed him long ago, if he had known him earlier.

“You boast of the nobility of your lineage as though imitation of character, rather than carnal birth, made you sons of the saints. In the end, Esau and Ishmael, although they are of Abraham’s stock, are nevertheless not counted among his sons.”

While they were arguing in this way, the Apostle placed himself between them and settled the questions of both parties. He confirmed that neither had earned salvation by his own righteousness, but that both peoples had sinned knowingly and gravely. The Jews had dishonored God through transgression of the Law; the Gentiles, although they ought to have recognized the Creator from the creation and revered him as God, had exchanged his glory for manufactured images. He demonstrates by the truest reasoning that both peoples have likewise obtained pardon and are equal, especially since it was foretold in the same Law that both Jews and Gentiles were to be called to faith in Christ. Accordingly, by humbling them in turn, he exhorts them to peace and harmony.

## 6. LANFRANC’S COMMENTARIES ON THE EPISTLES OF THE LORD PAUL

Saint Anselm mentions them in book I, letter 57, near the end, writing to Lanfranc:

[Col. 0105B]

“We gladly send you the Epistles of blessed Paul, obedient to your command. But since we do not possess elsewhere what is in the same codex concerning your work, you may know well what we would at some time wish to have done.”

## PETER LOMBARD ON THE EPISTLE TO THE HEBREWS, CHAPTER VIII

He cites blessed Lanfranc:

“Regarding these words, ‘If therefore he were on earth, he would not be a priest,’ and so forth: It is as though he were saying: Since every priest offers, then if there were someone upon earth—that is, if there were an earthly priest who could cleanse the human race—and there were no priest according to the order of Melchizedek, there would be enough priests to offer a gift according to the Law, that is, to offer legal offerings. But because they were mortal and sinful, and therefore unable to cleanse the human race, Christ came, who would suffice.

“Or in this way: ‘If therefore,’ and so forth. It is as though he were saying: Since Christ is appointed to offer, he is therefore either an earthly or a heavenly priest. But he is not earthly; for if he were upon earth—that is, if he were an earthly pontiff like Aaron—he would certainly not be a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek, nor would there be any need. Since he is …’ and so forth. Christ is a priest forever, not Aaron; for Aaron, because he died, is not a priest, whereas Christ, who lives, is an everlasting priest, not like those who bear a shadowy priesthood.

“Or in this way: ‘If therefore,’ and so forth. Here the reason is shown why Christ offered himself. It is as though he were saying: Christ must offer something; therefore he must offer himself. And it is truly necessary that he offer, because even if there were upon earth something that could worthily be offered for the sin of the whole world, there would nevertheless be no priest worthy to offer it.”

Likewise, a little later in the same chapter:

“‘Since there are those who offer gifts according to the Law.’ It remains, therefore, that he himself offer himself and so enter into the inner regions of heaven. ‘Who …’ and so forth. When I say that there are those who offer gifts, what do such men serve? That is, they serve fully as a pattern, that is, as a figure, and ‘as’—that is, as a shadow—‘of heavenly mysteries.’ By ‘heavenly things’ he means the Church, one part of which reigns in heaven while the other, which will follow, journeys on earth. By ‘pattern’ and ‘shadows’ he means figures, which are a pattern and an example in relation to different things.”

“Paul, servant of Christ Jesus.” Saul was a very wicked king, the persecutor of the holy servant of God, David; and he too, if you remember, was from the tribe of Benjamin. From this Saul came the man who brought with him a course of savage behavior, though he was not destined to remain in savagery. But if Saul came from Saul, where did Paul come from? Saul came from a savage king: proud, raging, and panting for slaughter. But where did Paul come from? Paul, because he was little; Paul is a name of humility. After Paul had been brought to the Teacher who says, “Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble in heart,” when Paul the proconsul, through Christ’s service, had subdued pride and had been sent under Christ’s gentle yoke, becoming a provincial official of the great King, he too, from his former name Saul, loved to be called Paul because of so great a mark of victory.”

“Paul, servant of Jesus Christ.”

## COMMENTARY

[Col. 0105D]

### CHAPTER I

**1. AUGUSTINE**, from the sermon *On the Conversion of Saint Paul*, chapter 4, volume X:

“Paul, servant of Christ Jesus.” Saul was a very wicked king, the persecutor of the holy servant of God, David; and he too, if you remember, was from the tribe of Benjamin. From this Saul came the man who brought with him a course of savage behavior, though he was not destined to remain in savagery. But if Saul came from Saul, where did Paul come from? Saul came from a savage king: proud, raging, and panting for slaughter. But where did Paul come from? Paul, because he was little; Paul is a name of humility. After Paul had been brought to the Teacher who says, “Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble in heart,” when Paul the proconsul, through Christ’s service, had subdued pride and had been sent under Christ’s gentle yoke, becoming a provincial official of the great King, he too, from his former name Saul, loved to be called Paul because of so great a mark of victory.

**2. LANFRANC.** “Called”—either by human beings or by God.

**3.** “Set apart”—from the other apostles, as the Holy Spirit says in the Acts of the Apostles: “Set apart for me Paul and Barnabas for the work to which I have called them.” The prophet Jeremiah also says: “Behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, and I will complete over the house of Israel and over the house of Judah a new covenant.” Joel likewise says: “Rejoice, daughters of Zion, and be glad in the Lord your God, because he has given you a teacher of righteousness.”

**4.** “Predestined.” Other human beings were predestined to be sons of God by grace. But Christ was predestined to be the Son of God in the power of the divinity of God by which he was assumed; and this power is the Son of God, that is, the Word of the Father.

**5. AUGUSTINE**, *On the Predestination of the Saints*, chapter 15, volume VII:

“Who was predestined.” Christ was predestined so that he who was to be the Son of David according to the flesh might then—or, alternatively, “nevertheless”—be the Son of God in power, according to the Spirit of sanctification, because he was born of the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary.

**6. LANFRANC.** “According to the Spirit of sanctification”: according to what pleased the Spirit, who sanctifies all things.

**7.** “Through the resurrection.” By this it was demonstrated most clearly that Christ Jesus is true God and truly the Son of God, because many bodies rose at his resurrection. For unless he were true God, he could not perform so great and unheard-of a miracle.

**8.** “Called.” That is, called for this purpose, so that you might be holy. The same meaning should be understood in the other expressions of this kind.

**9.** “Grace”: remission of sins.

**10.** “And peace”: by which we are reconciled to the Creator; or observance of good works, through which there is peace between God and humanity.

[Col. 0107C] **11. AUGUSTINE**, book I of the *Retractions*, chapter 24:

“Grace to you and peace.” The grace of God is that by which sins are forgiven us, so that we may be reconciled to God; the peace of God is that by which we are reconciled to God. Nevertheless, let us understand that both belong to the general grace of God.

[Col. 0108A] **12.** “Through Jesus Christ.” Through him, indeed, the offerings of our works are pleasing to God.

**13.** “Impart spiritual grace.” This is the spiritual grace that he desired to impart: that they might possess the same faith in Christ that the Apostle possessed, which they had not yet believed perfectly.

**14.** “To strengthen.” For they had already heard part of the teaching of the Gospel from other apostles.

**15.** “Your faith and mine”: that is, through the teaching of the faith that we commonly possess.

**16. LANFRANC.** “And I have been prevented.” It is as though someone were saying: If you ask God to come; if you desire continually to come, why do you not come? “I have been prevented,” he says, “until now.”

**17.** “For it is the power.” The reason why he is not ashamed of the Gospel is that it is the power of God for everyone who believes the Gospel; through it sins are forgiven, and, when circumstances require, miracles are performed.

**18.** “To the Jew.” By “Jew and Greek” he wished all nations to be understood, taking the whole from a part.

19. AUGUSTINE (*Questions on the Gospels*, book II, question 39). “The righteousness of God is revealed in it from faith to faith”: from faith in words to faith in realities; from faith in which God is served to that in which God is enjoyed (*On the Spirit and the Letter*, chapter 11, volume III); from the faith of those administering [another reading: proclaiming] to the faith of those obeying.

20. LANFRANC. “Righteousness.” This is another reason why he does not blush at the Gospel: because in it is revealed how God makes believers righteous—from the faith of the Old Testament, by which one God was believed in, advancing to the faith of the New Testament, by which the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are believed to be one God, both one and three; thus, from the faith of the one proclaiming, advancing to the faith of the believer, or from faith in words to faith in realities.

[Col. 0109A] 21. “But the righteous.” This is found in Habakkuk, chapter II: “But the righteous lives by his faith.” This testimony, and many others that the Apostle places in the context of his Epistles, seem to differ from the translation of the Hebrew truth that we now use because sometimes they are taken from the translation of the Seventy Interpreters; at other times, without being concerned with the words, he merely unfolds the meanings.

22. “Is revealed.” Righteousness is revealed in the believer, for wrath is revealed in the unbeliever. There is also another reason: the preachers of the Gospel reveal the wrath of God that is to come upon all the ungodly—that is, unbelievers—and upon the unrighteous—that is, those who believe but do not do what they believe.

23. “What is known of God”: that is, what can be known about God.

24. “For the invisible things.” He explains the manner in which he made them manifest to them, namely, by giving them a very keen understanding.

25. “The eternal things also.” Here he shows what the invisible things are, and *quoque* (“also”) is a completive conjunction.

26. “But they became futile”: that is, they thought that they possessed a true thought from themselves; hence it happened that they lost the thought of God.

27. “For, while claiming.” He shows how he previously understood “they became futile in their thoughts.”

28. “Corruptible.” From ancient times it was the custom of the Romans to worship images of human beings, such as Romulus, Jupiter, and almost innumerable others, especially from the time of Aeneas’s arrival in Italy; but images of birds, serpents, and four-footed animals were worshiped from the time when Alexandria was conquered by Augustus and subjected to Rome.

29. “Who exchanged.” That is, at first they formed an understanding about God; afterward they began to believe false things about him.

30. “The truth of God”: that is, the truth they possessed about God, falsely attributing to idols what truly belongs to God alone.

31. “They did not understand”: that is, they not only formed false opinions about God, but also lost the knowledge of good and evil things.

32. AMBROSE. “Not only those who do them, but also those who approve of those who do them.” There are some who do not think themselves guilty if they do not perform evil deeds, but nevertheless approve of those who do them. To approve is to remain silent when one could rebuke, or, while hearing such things, to flatter the perpetrators.

It is no more than the uncircumcision of the Gentiles. Therefore, if the uncircumcision keeps the righteous requirements of the law, will not his uncircumcision be reckoned as circumcision? You will be condemned by comparison with him, and the uncircumcision which is by nature will judge you by fulfilling the law—you who, through the letter and circumcision not observed, are a transgressor of the law. Response. For he is not a Jew who is one outwardly, nor is circumcision that which is outwardly, in the flesh; rather, he is a Jew who is one inwardly and is to be praised, and he is one who has this circumcision: circumcision of the heart, the cutting away of vices in the spirit, not in the letter. His praise comes not from human beings but from God, because human beings sometimes also reproach him.

[COMMENTARY]

[Col. 0110B]

CHAPTER II.—1. LANFRANC. “Therefore you are inexcusable, O every human being who judges.” An attack upon rulers. For he says: Since all who do these things and approve them are destined to perish, so too are those who judge others if they themselves are entangled in the same sin.

2. AMBROSE. “Therefore you are inexcusable.” Lest one who does such things, or approves those who do them, suppose that he could excuse himself, he teaches that such a person will be inexcusable.

[Col. 0111A] 3. LANFRANC. “We know that the judgment of God is.” By his authority he confirms that the sinners guilty of the crimes mentioned above are generally to be condemned.

4. “According to truth”: that is, according to righteousness, without respect of persons.

5. “Do you suppose this, O every human being who judges?” An ignorant person might suppose that one was permitted to sin all the more freely the more diligently one restrained others from sin.

6. AMBROSE. “Or do you despise the riches of his goodness, patience, and forbearance?” He says this so that no one may now think that he has escaped merely because God tolerates him while he sins for a long time.

7. “And of the revelation of the righteous judgment of God.” What is now denied as future will be revealed. When he shows what is believed not to exist, it is revealed. By these things it is shown that those who deny them [another reading: who deny] are thereby exposed, since they are manifest to believers.

8. “To those, indeed, according to perseverance in good work.” To those to whom God gave the confidence of faith, so that, while they remain here for a long time, they may not suffer the loss of the promised life.

9. “Glory and honor.” In the present life glory or honor is frequently lost, because it is corruptible.

10. LANFRANC. “And seek incorruption”: that is, if they seek eternal life as their aim. For many do good works for the sake of human approval.

11. AMBROSE. “But to those who are contentious”: that is, to those who despise God’s patience and strive to nullify God’s judgment.

[Col. 0111C] 12. LANFRANC. “In contention.” From a contentious group that argues that the Christian religion is useless.

13. AMBROSE. “But believe iniquity.” Iniquity is to deny what God promised [another reading: foretold] would happen.

14. “Wrath and indignation,” so that you may understand a spiritual, not a bodily, punishment.

15. “To the Jew first and to the Greek.” He always places the Jew first, so that he may either be crowned first or condemned first, because one who disbelieves must be treated more severely, since he rejected what was promised to the fathers [another reading: the gift].

16. LANFRANC. “The Jews.” By “Jews” he means unbelievers, who will be punished most severely if they do not observe God’s commands; by “Greeks,” the nations, that is, unbelievers: the whole is named from a part.

17. AMBROSE. “But glory, honor, and peace,” so that they may possess a double honor, as children of God. Glory comes through transformation; peace, because those who live well will be at rest in the future, disturbed by no agitation.

18. LANFRANC. “To the Jew.” The Jews first performed good works, and afterward the Greeks.

19. “For there is no respect of persons,” and so forth. This refers back to the preceding passage, where he says: “Wrath,” and “to every soul that works evil.” A little later: “Glory,” and so forth, “to everyone who works good.”

20. AMBROSE. “For whoever sinned without the law will perish without the law,” that is, without judgment. Whoever does not believe has already been judged; he will not stand before the tribunal of Christ, but, rising, will be led to Gehenna.

21. “They will be judged through the law.” The sin of transgressing the law will be added to their sins.

22. AMBROSE. “But the doers of the law will be justified.” To believe in Christ, whom the law promised, is to fulfill the law; and the work of the law written in your hearts is faith.

23. AUGUSTINE (*On the Spirit and the Letter*, chapter 26, volume III). “For when the Gentiles who do not have the law.” The Gentiles who naturally do what belongs to the law clearly belong to the Gospel, since the law has been written in their hearts. Nor should it trouble anyone that he said they naturally do what belongs to the law—not by the Spirit of God, not by grace; for the Spirit of grace acts to restore in us the image of God, in whose likeness we were naturally made. The fault, indeed, is contrary to nature, and grace certainly heals it; therefore human beings naturally do what belongs to the law.

[Col. 0113A] 24. AMBROSE. “Their conscience bearing witness.” On the day of judgment, a person’s conscience alone will suffice as testimony, because then no one will judge except what is true.

25. AMBROSE. “With their thoughts accusing one another.” The Gentile conscience will be accused because it did not persuade itself that what it had seen confirmed both by the testimony of virtues and by the example of many was true. It will excuse that same person because he did not think he was obliged to believe, yet he will not be without punishment. Alternatively, the good thought will accuse the heretic when he understood that the truth was genuine and catholic; the evil thought, however, will accuse him because, in his pride, he contradicted the truth lest he appear corrected.

26. “One another.” He does not say that the same thoughts both accuse and defend, but that some accuse in turn and others defend, against the accusation of evil spirits. Observe also the ablatives used for genitives according to the practice of the Greeks, who lack ablatives. This may be understood in the following way: “and the conscience of the thoughts.”

27. “But you are called a Jew.” He does not want it to seem a very great thing if a Jew believes, since he has been instructed through the law. But it is extremely dangerous if he does not believe, for he has the law as his guide.

28. LANFRANC. “But you are called a Jew.” He endeavors to humble the Jews, who, because they had received the law, grew proud and despised the nations as sinners.

29. AMBROSE. “Through the law you trust yourself to be a guide of the blind.” The instruction of the law is to educate the ignorant, subject the profane to God, and recall them from idolatry to faith.

[Col. 0113C] 30. “The hidden things of human beings.” The hidden things will be judged. Public matters will not be judged when they have been disclosed through humble confession.

31. LANFRANC. “The form of knowledge.” If someone wishes to possess knowledge and truth, let him be able to see in you their form and example.

32. AMBROSE. “You who teach another do not teach yourself”: that is, you who accuse the Gentiles of being without law and without God do not accuse yourself, because you distrust Christ promised in the law.

33. “You who preach that one must not steal, steal.” You do what you preach must not be done, when through an evil interpretation you steal the faith of Christ from the law; you adulterate the law when, having removed the truth, you put falsehood in its place; and you are sacrilegious when you deny Christ, whom prophetic speech signifies.

34. LANFRANC. “Sacrilege.” Sacrilege is to take away the worship of God and give it to demons.

35. “For the name of God is blasphemed because of you.” We must believe that some Jews were Christians of this sort, but not all, lest he contradict himself in the preceding passage, where he says: “Your faith is proclaimed throughout the whole world.” For faith without works is not to be praised. In what follows also, he says that they were full of love together with the others. It is written in Ezekiel: “They entered among the nations to which they came, and they profaned my holy name, which you profaned among the nations.”

36. “For circumcision”: that is, it profits the Gentile as much as if he were a Jew. “And it will judge”: that is, it will make him judgeable and condemnable by comparison with itself.

LANFRANC. “Whatever the law says.” Here he calls the Psalms “the law,” just as in the Gospel: “Is it not written in your law, ‘I said, You are gods’?” The meaning is: The preceding verses of the Psalm also apply to you, O Jews!] whatever the law says, it speaks to those who are under the law [Note: [Col. 0116B] 18. “So that every mouth may be stopped.” This is joined to the preceding sentence, in which he says: “We have charged that all are under sin.”], so that every mouth may be stopped and the whole world may become subject to God, because no flesh will be justified before him by works of the law.
