But now the righteousness of God has been manifested apart from the law, testified to by the law and the prophets. The righteousness of God is through faith in Jesus Christ for all and upon all who believe in him; for there is no distinction. For all have sinned and lack the glory of God, being justified freely by his grace, through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus, [Note: [Col. 0116B] 20. “Whom God set forth.” That is, God ordained in Christ that he would be propitious toward the human race if it believed, and this through his blood, because we have been freed by his death [Col. 0116C].] whom God set forth as a propitiation, through faith in his blood, [Note: [Col. 0116C] 21. “For the demonstration”: that is, so that he might make public the promise by which he would free us from sins, as he had promised previously. He bore with us for a very long time, so that in our time he might show what he had determined long ago, and so that he might be righteous, giving what he promised, and justify those who believe in Christ.] [Note: [Col. 0116C] 22. LANFRANC. “For the demonstration.” For this purpose God caused his Son to be proclaimed to the world: to show that sinners are justified through faith in him.] for the demonstration of his righteousness [Col. 0117], because of the remission of previous sins, in the forbearance of God, for the demonstration of his righteousness in this present time, so that he himself may be righteous [Note: [Col. 0117A] 23. “Righteous and justifying”: that is, truthful, fulfilling what he promised.] and justifying the one who is of the faith of Jesus Christ. Where, then, is your boasting? It has been excluded. Through what law? [Note: [Col. 0117A] 24. “Of works”: that is, has another law been brought forward, having other observances by which your observances are annulled?] Of works? No, but [Note: [Col. 0117A] 25. “Through the law of faith.” He calls the law of Christ the law of faith, in which it is maintained that a person is saved by faith alone, when it is said: “Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved.”] through the law of faith. [Note: [Col. 0117B] 27. AUGUSTINE (*On Faith and Works*, chapter 14, volume IV). “For we reckon.” Therefore, when the Apostle says that he reckons a person to be justified by faith without works of the law, he does not say this so that works of righteousness may be despised after faith has been professed and commanded; rather, each person should know that he can be justified through faith even if works of the law have not preceded.] For we reckon that a person is justified by faith without works of the law. Is God the God of Jews only? Is he not also the God of the Gentiles? Indeed, of the Gentiles also, since there is one God, [Note: [Col. 0117B] 28. “Who justifies circumcision” (*On the Spirit and the Letter*, chapter 29, volume III). This is not said to indicate any difference, as though one thing were “from faith” and another “through faith,” but to vary the expression. Elsewhere, speaking of the Gentiles—that is, of the uncircumcision—Scripture says: “Foreseeing that God would justify all the nations from faith.” Likewise, when speaking of circumcision, from which he came, he says: “We are Jews by nature, and not sinners from the Gentiles, knowing that a person is not justified by works of the law except through faith in Jesus Christ; and we have believed in Christ Jesus.” Thus he says both that the uncircumcision is justified from faith and that circumcision is justified through faith.] who justifies [Note: [Col. 0117C] 29. LANFRANC. “Circumcision from faith”: that is, from faith and through faith.] circumcision from faith, [Note: [Col. 0117C] 30. “And uncircumcision.” From this it is proved that the God of the Jews is also the God of the Gentiles [Col. 0118A]. For he himself justifies the Gentiles. To justify belongs to God alone.] and uncircumcision through faith. [Note: [Col. 0118A] 31. “Do we then destroy the law?” Since we destroy the law’s carnal observances, should it be thought that we, the preachers of the Gospel, also destroy its moral commandments? What, then, is the order? “What according to the flesh,” that is, what of the carnal observances? He proves that a person can be justified through faith without the carnal observance of the law. Abraham, for example, was justified without carnal observances, as Scripture testifies: “Abraham believed God,” and so forth.] Do we then destroy the law through faith? By no means! Rather, we establish the law.

[COMMENTARY]

[Col. 0114B]

CHAPTER III.—1. AMBROSE. “What advantage, then, is there?” Since he showed that the testimony of lineage profited nothing for unbelieving Jews, lest he seem to have treated believers harshly, he teaches that it is greatly useful for believers because they are children of Abraham. For the oracles of God were entrusted to them.

2. LANFRANC. “First, indeed”: that is, some Jews believed the Gospel of Christ, instructed by the preachers of the New Testament in the word of the law and the prophets. This happened more easily among them than among those who were entirely without the Old Testament.

[Col. 0115A] 3. AMBROSE. “Will their unbelief,” and so forth. Will their faithlessness deny the other believers the eternal life that God promised would come through faith in Christ?

4. LANFRANC. “Will it nullify the faithfulness of God?” That is, will it make it so that God ought not to be believed, when we foretold that the Jews would believe? He uses the whole for a part. The prophet Jeremiah says: “In those days Judah will be saved.” And elsewhere: “I will be your God, and they will be my people.” And many other passages.

5. “That you may be justified.” David sinned in the matter of Uriah, knowing that a promise does not benefit sinners. He prays that God may prevail over the judgment by which it is judged that sinners receive nothing, and that he may sanctify him as a penitent, so that, by giving him what he promised to give the righteous, God may be justified [Col. 0115B] in his words.

6. LANFRANC. “That you may be justified.” This proves that God is truthful, for the righteousness of words is truth.

7. “And may prevail.” This is added by way of abundance and has no bearing on the preceding argument. Christ, the man who is God, prevailed when he was judged, because, on account of that very humility, God gave him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bend, and so forth.

8. If unrighteousness. He adds this because, by saying, “that you may be justified in your words,” he seemed to have given the reason why every human being should be a liar. And he calls unrighteousness “falsehood.”

9. AMBROSE. Otherwise, how will he judge? Since it would not have been just for him to judge the world if its sins benefited it.

10. LANFRANC. For if the truth. Again he adds this in the person of those who misunderstand.

11. And not as. The order is: “and as we are slandered, and as some say that we teach: Why should we not do evil, so that good may come?”

12. AMBROSE. Let us do evil. Perverse people said that the apostles taught this: that one ought to sin so that good things might come, that is, so that God might appear good by forgiving.

13. LANFRANC. Are we superior to them? That is: Are we Jews more excellent and more worthy than the Gentiles?

14. For we have already charged. As if he were saying: Since we are equal, we cannot be more excellent. Nor did he say this earlier in this Epistle; but we must believe that he said it in the discourse he delivered to the people.

15. AMBROSE. For we have already charged, that is, we have shown, having given the reasons above, that Jews and Greeks are under accusation.

16. But we know. This is said because, with the Jews convicted, the whole world is subject to God. For no one doubts that the pagans are overwhelmed by impieties.

17. LANFRANC. Whatever the law says. Here he calls the Psalms “the law,” as in the Gospel: “Is it not written in your law: I said, You are gods?” The sense is: The preceding verses of the Psalms also apply to you, O Jews!

18. So that every mouth may be stopped. This is joined to the preceding statement, where he says: “For we have already charged that all are under sin.”

19. AMBROSE. For through the law. We see that the ancients were not ignorant of sin, since Pharaoh’s cupbearer and baker were sent to prison because of sin. But the law shows that, in God’s sight, sin is counted and judgment is to come—something that had previously been unknown.

20. Whom God set forth, that is, that in Christ he had determined to be propitious toward the human race, if it believes, and this in his blood, because by his death we have been freed.

21. To demonstrate. That is, so that he might make public the promise by which he would free us from sins, just as he had promised beforehand. He endured for a very long time so that in our age he might reveal what he had formerly decreed, and might be just, giving what he promised and justifying those who believe in Christ.

22. LANFRANC. To demonstrate. For this purpose God caused his Son to be proclaimed to the world: to show that sinners are justified through faith in him.

23. Because of the remission of the preceding sins. The order is: “of the preceding sins in God’s forbearance.” For God patiently endured the world’s preceding sins, so that he might show what true justification is in the present time, that is, in faith in Jesus Christ. For if he had punished all sinners, there would have been no one who could be justified in the present time.

24. Just and justifying, that is, truthful, fulfilling what he promised.

25. Of works, that is: Has another law been brought forward, having other observances by which your observances are annulled?

26. Through the law of faith. He calls the law of Christ “the law of faith,” in which it is asserted that a person is saved by faith alone, when it is said: “Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved.”

27. AUGUSTINE (*On Faith and Works*, chapter 14, volume IV). For we conclude. Therefore, when the Apostle says that he considers a person to be justified by faith without the works of the law, he does not say this so that the works of righteousness may be despised once faith has been commanded and professed; rather, he says it so that each person may know that he can be justified by faith even if the works of the law have not preceded it.

28. Who justifies the circumcision (*On the Spirit and the Letter*, chapter 29, volume III). This was not said to indicate any difference, as though “from faith” were one thing and “through faith” another, but to indicate a variation of expression. In another passage, when he was speaking of the Gentiles—that is, of the uncircumcision—he says: “The Scripture, foreseeing that God justifies the nations from faith.” Likewise, when he was speaking of the circumcision, from which he himself came, he says: “We are Jews by nature, and not sinners from among the Gentiles, knowing that a person is not justified by works of the law except through faith in Jesus Christ; and we have believed in Christ Jesus.” Here he said that the uncircumcision is justified from faith, and the circumcision through faith.

29. LANFRANC. The circumcision from faith, that is, from faith and through faith.

30. And the uncircumcision. From this it is proved that the God of the Jews is the God of the Gentiles. For he himself justifies the Gentiles. But it belongs to God alone to justify.

31. Do we then overthrow the law? Since we overthrow the law’s carnal observances, should it be thought that we, preachers of the Gospel, also overthrow its moral commandments? What, then? The order is: “What according to the flesh?”—that is, what of the carnal observances? He proves that a person can be justified through faith without the law’s carnal observance. For Abraham was justified without carnal observances, as Scripture testifies: “Abraham believed God,” and so forth.

32. AMBROSE. But we uphold the law. The law is certainly not made void through faith; rather, it is fulfilled, when faith testifies that what it said would come has now arrived.

# CHAPTER IV

[Col. 0117]

[Note: [Col. 0118A] CHAP. IV.—1. AMBROSE. What then shall we say that he found? He calls circumcision “flesh,” by which Abraham neither found nor sought righteousness.]

What then shall we say that Abraham our father found according to the flesh?

[Note: [Col. 0118B] 2. LANFRANC. For if. If, he says, Abraham is believed to have been justified without faith, solely through carnal observance, that justification exists only in human opinion, not before God.]

For if Abraham was justified by works,

[Note: [Col. 0118B] 3. He has glory, because whoever performs the law will live in it, that is, he will not die as one guilty. Yet by this he does not have merit before God.]

he has glory, but not before God.

[Note: [Col. 0118B] 4. For what does Scripture say? As if he were saying: Let us hear what Scripture testifies concerning this.]

For what does Scripture say?

[Note: [Col. 0118B] 5. AMBROSE. Abraham believed God. He believed that he would have offspring in whom the nations would be blessed.]

“Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness.”

[Note: [Col. 0118B] 6. But to the one who works. To one who performs the works of the law, merit is not reckoned as a reward. For he is under obligation to perform the law.]

But to the one who works, the reward is not reckoned according to grace but according to obligation.

[Note: [Col. 0118C] 7. AUGUSTINE. To the one who works, that is, to one who presumes upon works and rightly says that the grace of faith was given to him. To such a person he does not reckon the reward according to grace but according to obligation.]

[Note: [Col. 0118C] 8. LANFRANC. But to the one who does not work. This is to be understood of one who dies immediately after receiving faith.]

But to the one who does not work, yet believes in him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is reckoned as righteousness according to the purpose of God’s grace.

Just as David also speaks of the blessedness of the person to whom God reckons righteousness without works:

“Blessed are those whose iniquities have been forgiven, and whose sins have been covered; blessed is the man to whom the Lord has not reckoned sin.”

Does this blessedness, then, remain only in the circumcision, or also in the uncircumcision? For we say that faith was reckoned to Abraham as righteousness. How, then, was it reckoned? In circumcision or in uncircumcision? Not in circumcision, but in uncircumcision.

[Note: [Col. 0118C] 9. And he received the sign. As if he were saying: Why, then, if he had been justified, did he receive circumcision? He received circumcision, he says, not so that he might be made righteous by it, but so that the righteousness which faith alone had conferred on him might be demonstrated.]

[Col. 0119] And he received the sign of circumcision, the seal of the righteousness of the faith that he had in uncircumcision,

[Note: [Col. 0119A] 10. AMBROSE. So that he might be the father of circumcision. He says this so that he might be the father of circumcision of the heart—not only of those who derive from his lineage, but also of those from the Gentiles who believe in the same way.]

so that he might be the father of all who believe through uncircumcision, so that righteousness might be reckoned to them also; and the father of circumcision, not only to those who are of the circumcision but also to those who follow

[Note: [Col. 0119A] 11. LANFRANC. The footsteps of faith. The order is: “the footsteps of the faith of our father Abraham, which he had in uncircumcision.”]

the footsteps of the faith that our father Abraham had in uncircumcision.

[Note: [Col. 0119A] 12. For not through the law. As if someone were saying: Why did you say “the footsteps of faith,” and not “the footsteps of the law”? For if the opposing position leads to an absurdity, then the observance of the law alone and faith cannot simultaneously be the cause of inheritance; nor can Jews alone and the Gentiles be heirs.]

For the promise to Abraham or to his offspring—that he would be heir of the world—did not come through the law but through the righteousness of faith. For if those who are of the law are heirs, faith has been emptied and the promise abolished.

[Note: [Col. 0119A] 13. AMBROSE. The promise to Abraham. Christ, who is heir of the Gentiles, as David sings: “And I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and your possession to the ends of the earth.” For we die and live with him. Therefore it is from faith. The promise cannot be given under the law, but from faith, through which all are purified and become worthy to be called sons.]

For the law produces wrath.

[Note: [Col. 0119B] 14. LANFRANC. For the law produces wrath. The reason why the promise of inheritance does not come through the law: it produces God’s wrath through the transgression of those who do not fulfill it.]

For where there is no law, neither is there transgression.

[Note: [Col. 0119B] 15. For where there is no law. This too, he says, can show that the law produces wrath: where there is no law, there is no transgression, which is the cause of wrath.]

Therefore it is from faith, so that the promise may be firm according to grace, for all offspring—not only for the one who is of the law, but also for the one who is of the faith of Abraham, who is the father of us all (as it is written: “I have appointed you the father of many nations”)—before God, in whom he believed, who gives life to the dead and calls into existence things that do not exist as though they did.

Against hope, he believed in hope, so that he might become the father of many nations, according to what had been said to him: “So shall your offspring be.” And he did not grow weak in faith, nor did he consider his own body, already dead—for he was almost a hundred years old—or the deadness of Sarah’s womb. He did not waver in disbelief at God’s promise, but was strengthened in faith, giving glory to God, fully convinced that whatever he had promised, he was also able to do.

Therefore it was reckoned to him as righteousness.

But it was not written only for his sake that it was reckoned to him as righteousness, but also for our sake, to whom it will be reckoned if we believe in him who raised Jesus Christ our Lord from the dead, who was handed over because of our offenses,

[Note: [Col. 0120A] 17. AMBROSE. And rose because of. For after the resurrection the Spirit, having been received, contributes to the fullness of our justification.]

and rose

[Note: [Col. 0120A] 18. LANFRANC. Because of our justification, that is, so that those who believe that he rose might be justified. And the whole of faith is designated by reference to one part.]

because of our justification.

[COMMENTARY]

[Col. 0118A]

CAP. IV.—1. AMBROSE. What then shall we say that he found? He calls circumcision “flesh,” by which Abraham neither found nor sought righteousness.

2. LANFRANC. For if. If, he says, Abraham is believed to have been justified without faith, solely through carnal observance, that justification exists only in human opinion, not before God.

3. He has glory, because whoever performs the law will live in it, that is, he will not die as one guilty. Yet by this he does not have merit before God.

4. For what does Scripture say? As if he were saying: Let us hear what Scripture testifies concerning this.

5. AMBROSE. Abraham believed God. He believed that he would have offspring in whom the nations would be blessed.

6. To the one who works. To one who performs the works of the law, merit is not reckoned as a reward. For he is under obligation to perform the law.

7. AUGUSTINE. To the one who works, that is, to one who presumes upon works and rightly says that the grace of faith was given to him. To such a person he does not reckon the reward according to grace but according to obligation.

8. LANFRANC. But to the one who does not work. This is to be understood of one who dies immediately after receiving faith.

9. And he received the sign. As if he were saying: Why, then, if he had been justified, did he receive circumcision? He received circumcision, he says, not so that he might be made righteous by it, but so that the righteousness which faith alone had conferred on him might be demonstrated.

10. AMBROSE. So that he might be the father of circumcision. He says this so that he might be the father of circumcision of the heart—not only of those who derive from his lineage, but also of those from the Gentiles who believe in the same way.

11. LANFRANC. The footsteps of faith. The order is: “the footsteps of the faith of our father Abraham, which he had in uncircumcision.”

12. For not through the law. As if someone were saying: Why did you say “the footsteps of faith,” and not “the footsteps of the law”? For if the opposing position leads to an absurdity, then the observance of the law alone and faith cannot simultaneously be the cause of inheritance; nor can Jews alone and the Gentiles be heirs.

13. AMBROSE. The promise to Abraham. Christ, who is heir of the Gentiles, as David sings: “And I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and your possession to the ends of the earth.” For we die and live with him. Therefore it is from faith. The promise cannot be given under the law, but from faith, through which all are purified and become worthy to be called sons.

14. LANFRANC. For the law produces wrath. The reason why the promise of inheritance does not come through the law: it produces God’s wrath through the transgression of those who do not fulfill it.

15. For where there is no law. This too, he says, can show that the law produces wrath: where there is no law, there is no transgression, which is the cause of wrath.

16. For all offspring, that is, for every imitator of faith, whether Jew or Gentile. For all can easily believe, but not all can fulfill the law.

17. AMBROSE. And rose because of. For after the resurrection the Spirit, having been received, contributes to the fullness of our justification.

18. LANFRANC. Because of our justification, that is, so that those who believe that he rose might be justified. And the whole of faith is designated by reference to one part.

# CHAPTER V

[Col. 0119]

17

[Note: [Col. 0120A] CHAP. V.—1. AMBROSE. Therefore, having been justified. Faith, not the law, enables us to have peace with God. For faith reconciled us to God.]

Therefore, having been justified by faith, let us have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom we also have access by faith

[Note: [Col. 0120A] 2. Into this grace. Previously we lay prostrate; but when we believed, we were raised up.]

into this grace in which we stand and glory in the hope of the glory of the children of God.

And not only this, but we also glory in tribulations, knowing that tribulation produces endurance, endurance produces testing, and testing produces hope;

[Note: [Col. 0120A] 3. But hope does not disappoint. Hope does not disappoint while the foolish and dull-minded are judged by the faithless, because they believe things that lack worldly reason. For we have within us the pledge of love through the Holy Spirit given to us.]

and hope does not disappoint, because the love of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us.

For why did Christ die for the ungodly at the appointed time, while we were still weak? For scarcely does anyone die for a righteous person; perhaps someone might dare to die for a good person.

But God commends his love toward us, because while we were still sinners,

[Note: [Col. 0120B] 4. At the appointed time. He died at the appointed time because he rose on the third day. Or he died for this time, in which the sun rises and sets. For he passed from the body to the underworld, where there is neither time nor age, for the salvation of souls.]

at the appointed time Christ

[Note: [Col. 0120B] 5. LANFRANC. He died. While we still loved temporal things, unless he gave us a good hope which would confound us [lacuna].]

died for us. Therefore, having now been justified in his blood, we shall be saved from wrath through him.

For if, while we were enemies, we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son, much more, having been reconciled, shall we be saved by his life.

And not only this,

[Note: [Col. 0120B] 6. But we also glory, that is, hoping that we shall possess the glory which the children of God possess.]

but we also glory in God through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom we have now received reconciliation.

[Note: [Col. 0120B] 7. Therefore, just as. The sentence continues until [lacuna]. It reads: “just as through one offense,” and so forth.]

Therefore, just as through one man sin entered this world, and through sin death, and so death passed into all human beings, in whom all sinned.

[Note: [Col. 0121A] 8. For until the law. Sin was indeed present even in those who had received the law, but not as much as before; for many were saved through the observances of the law.]

For until the law sin was in the world.

[Note: [Col. 0121A] 9. For sin. Here he understands “sin” differently from above. In this passage sin signifies transgression of the law, which was not reckoned when there was no law.]

But sin was not reckoned when there was no law.

Yet death reigned from Adam to Moses, even over those who did not sin

[Note: [Col. 0121A] 10. AUGUSTINE (*On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins and on the Baptism of Infants*, book I, chapter 11, volume VII). Over those who did not sin, that is, those who had not yet sinned by their own individual will, as he did, but had drawn sin from him by origin.]

in the likeness of Adam’s transgression,

[Note: [Col. 0121A] 11. LANFRANC. In the likeness, that is, those who transgressed God’s commandments, as Adam did.]

who is a type of the one to come.

[Note: [Col. 0121B] 11. Who is a type of the one to come. Adam was a type of Christ. For just as Adam was the father of all according to the flesh, so Christ is the father of the faithful according to faith. And just as Eve was formed from Adam’s side, so from Christ’s side flowed the sacraments through which the Church is saved.]

[Note: [Col. 0121B] 12. AUGUSTINE (ibid.). Who is a type. Because in him was established the pattern of condemnation for future descendants who would be created from his line.]

[Note: [Col. 0121B] 13. AMBROSE. Who is a type of the one to come. For God determined through one person, Christ, to correct what had been sinned through one person, Adam, just as John says in the Apocalypse: “The Lamb who was slain from the foundation of the world.”]

But the gift is not like the transgression.

[Note: [Col. 0121B] 14. But not as the offense. He said this because he had called the one Adam a type of the one Christ.]

[Note: [Col. 0121C] 15. LANFRANC. But not as the transgression. The order is: As if he were saying, Although Adam was a type of Christ, Christ’s gift nevertheless has greater power. For it is greater to give life than to kill.]

For if by the transgression of the one many died,

[Note: [Col. 0121C] 16. AUGUSTINE (ibid.). Much more grace. It does not mean “more many,” or “many more people.” For more are not justified than are condemned. Adam generated the guilty from his own transgression. But Christ, in addition to the original sin in which human beings sinned [alternative reading: “were born”], also forgives and removes the sins they added by their own will.]

much more did the grace of God and the gift

[Note: [Col. 0121C] 17. LANFRANC. In the grace of one man. “In grace,” that is, “because of grace.” Here he calls grace the perfection of virtues that the man assumed by the Word of the Father possessed through God’s grace.]

in the grace of the one man Jesus Christ abound for the many.

[Note: [Col. 0122A] 18. For the many. He says “the many” not with reference to number, but because they are more numerous in vices. For Adam brought death through original sin, whereas Christ freed people from actual and original sins.]

[Note: [Col. 0122A] 19. AUGUSTINE (ibid., chapter 15). And not as through one. From Adam, in whom all sinned, we derived not all our sins but only original sin. From Christ, in whom all are justified, we receive remission not only of that original sin but also of the others that we ourselves added. Therefore it is not “as through the one who sinned, so also the gift.” For judgment arising from one offense—if it is not forgiven, that is, original sin—can already lead to condemnation. But grace arising from many sins that have been forgiven leads to justification: not only from original sin, but also from all the others.]

And the gift is not like what came through one sin.

[Note: [Col. 0122B] 20. LANFRANC. And not as. Alternatively: “Even if the gift is as the sin,” that is, the two are not equal.]

For judgment indeed came from one offense to condemnation,

[Note: [Col. 0122B] 21. Grace, however, from many. The order is: “But grace, for justification, comes from many offenses.”]

but grace came from many offenses to justification.

For if death reigned through the one man because of the offense of the one, much more,

[Note: [Col. 0122B] 22. AUGUSTINE (ibid.). The abundance of grace. What else does it mean that they receive an abundance of grace, justification, and righteousness, except that the grace of remission is given to them not only for the sin in which all sinned, but also for what they added?]

having received the abundance of grace and of the gift and righteousness, they will reign in life through the one Jesus Christ.

[Note: [Col. 0122B] 23. They will reign in life. What does “they will reign much more in life” mean, when the reign of death draws many more into eternal punishment? Unless we understand the same people to be meant in both cases, namely those who pass from Adam to Christ, that is, from death to life, because they will reign endlessly in eternal life, more than death will reign over them temporally and with an end [alternative reading: “reigned”].]

Therefore, just as through one offense condemnation came upon all human beings, so also

[Note: [Col. 0122C] 24. LANFRANC. Through the righteousness of one. Through Christ’s righteousness and obedience the life of all believers has been justified. For through this he became an acceptable sacrifice to God for the sins of all, because he was righteous, immaculate, without sin, and obedient even unto death.]

through one act of righteousness justification of life came upon all human beings.

[Note: [Col. 0122C] 25. Just as. Confirmation and exposition of the preceding verse: every disobedience, if it is entirely evil, is an offense; and every obedience, if it is entirely good, is righteousness.]

For just as through the disobedience of one man many were made sinners,

[Col. 0123]

so also

[Note: [Col. 0123A] 26. Through the obedience of one. Through Christ’s obedience many are righteous; or because obedience commended the sacrifice; or because obedience led Christ to death. Faith in his death, however, justified.]

through the obedience of one many will be made righteous.

[Note: [Col. 0123A] 27. But the law entered in. It is customary in the divine writings, when there are several causes, to enumerate only one, as in this passage: the law was given so that those predestined to life might be saved through legal observances; but those predestined to death might be punished more severely through transgression of the law. Here, however, he mentions only that cause by which he can humble the Jews who grew proud because they had received the law.]

But the law entered in so that the offense might abound.

[Note: [Col. 0123A] 28. AMBROSE. But the law entered in. The Apostle shows what resulted from the giving of the law, not what the law itself did.]

But where the offense abounded,

[Note: [Col. 0123B] 29. LANFRANC. Grace will abound exceedingly. As if he were saying: O Jews! You think that Christ forgave more to the Gentiles, but he forgave more to some of you, whom he found to be transgressors of the law.]

grace abounded exceedingly,

[Note: [Col. 0123B] 30. So that just as it reigned, that is, prevailed.]

so that, just as sin reigned in death, so also

[Note: [Col. 0123B] 31. So also let grace reign, that is, let it prevail.]

grace might reign

[Note: [Col. 0123B] 33. Through righteousness, namely, Christ’s.]

[Note: [Col. 0123B] 32. AMBROSE. Let grace reign. Grace reigns through righteousness if, having received remission, we pursue righteousness.]

through righteousness unto eternal life, through Jesus Christ our Lord.

[COMMENTARY]

[Col. 0120A]

CAP. V.—1. AMBROSE. Therefore, having been justified. Faith, not the law, enables us to have peace with God. For faith reconciled us to God.

2. Into this grace. Previously we lay prostrate; but when we believed, we were raised up.

3. But hope does not disappoint. Hope does not disappoint while the foolish and dull-minded are judged by the faithless, because they believe things that lack worldly reason. For we have within us the pledge of love through the Holy Spirit given to us.

4. At the appointed time. He died at the appointed time because he rose on the third day. Or he died for this time, in which the sun rises and sets. For he passed from the body to the underworld, where there is neither time nor age, for the salvation of souls.

5. LANFRANC. He died. While we still loved temporal things, unless he gave us a good hope which would confound us [lacuna].

6. But we also glory, that is, hoping that we shall possess the glory which the children of God possess.

7. Therefore, just as. The sentence continues until [lacuna]. It reads: “just as through one offense,” and so forth.

[Col. 0121A] 8. For until the law. Sin was indeed present even in those who had received the law, but not as much as before; for many were saved through the observances of the law.

9. For sin. Here he understands “sin” differently from above. In this passage sin signifies transgression of the law, which was not reckoned when there was no law.

10. AUGUSTINE (*On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins and on the Baptism of Infants*, book I, chapter 11, volume VII). Over those who did not sin, that is, those who had not yet sinned by their own individual will, as he did, but had drawn sin from him by origin.

11. LANFRANC. In the likeness, that is, those who transgressed God’s commandments, as Adam did.

[Col. 0121B] 11. Who is a type of the one to come. Adam was a type of Christ. For just as Adam was the father of all according to the flesh, so Christ is the father of the faithful according to faith. And just as Eve was formed from Adam’s side, so from Christ’s side flowed the sacraments through which the Church is saved.

12. AUGUSTINE (ibid.). Who is a type. Because in him was established the pattern of condemnation for future descendants who would be created from his line.

13. AMBROSE. Who is a type of the one to come. For God determined through one person, Christ, to correct what had been sinned through one person, Adam, just as John says in the Apocalypse: “The Lamb who was slain from the foundation of the world.”

14. But the gift is not like the transgression. He said this because he had called the one Adam a type of the one Christ.

15. LANFRANC. But the gift is not like the transgression. The order is: As if he were saying, Although Adam was a type of Christ, Christ’s gift nevertheless has greater power. For it is greater to give life than to kill.

16. AUGUSTINE (ibid.). Much more grace. It does not mean “more many,” or “many more people.” For more are not justified than are condemned. Adam generated the guilty from his own transgression. But Christ, in addition to the original sin in which human beings sinned [alternative reading: “were born”], also forgives and removes the sins they added by their own will.

17. LANFRANC. In the grace of one man. “In grace,” that is, “because of grace.” Here he calls grace the perfection of virtues that the man assumed by the Word of the Father possessed through God’s grace.

[Col. 0122A] 18. For the many. He says “the many” not with reference to number, but because they are more numerous in vices. For Adam brought death through original sin, whereas Christ freed people from actual and original sins.

19. AUGUSTINE (ibid., chapter 15). And not as through one. From Adam, in whom all sinned, we derived not all our sins but only original sin. From Christ, in whom all are justified, we receive remission not only of that original sin but also of the others that we ourselves added. Therefore it is not “as through the one who sinned, so also the gift.” For judgment arising from one offense—if it is not forgiven, that is, original sin—can already lead to condemnation. But grace arising from many sins that have been forgiven leads to justification: not only from original sin, but also from all the others.

20. LANFRANC. And the gift is not like. Alternatively: “Even if the gift is as the sin,” that is, the two are not equal.

21. But grace from many. The order is: “But grace, for justification, comes from many offenses.”

22. AUGUSTINE (ibid.). The abundance of grace. What else does it mean that they receive an abundance of grace, justification, and righteousness, except that the grace of remission is given to them not only for the sin in which all sinned, but also for what they added?

23. They will reign in life. What does “they will reign much more in life” mean, when the reign of death draws many more into eternal punishment? Unless we understand the same people to be meant in both cases, namely those who pass from Adam to Christ, that is, from death to life, because they will reign endlessly in eternal life, more than death will reign over them temporally and with an end [alternative reading: “reigned”].

24. LANFRANC. Through the righteousness of one. Through Christ’s righteousness and obedience the life of all believers has been justified. For through this he became an acceptable sacrifice to God for the sins of all, because he was righteous, immaculate, without sin, and obedient even unto death.

25. For just as. Confirmation and exposition of the preceding verse: every disobedience, if it is entirely evil, is an offense; and every obedience, if it is entirely good, is righteousness.

[Col. 0123A] 26. Through the obedience of one. Through Christ’s obedience many are righteous; or because obedience commended the sacrifice; or because obedience led Christ to death. Faith in his death, however, justified.

27. But the law entered in. It is customary in the divine writings, when there are several causes, to enumerate only one, as in this passage: the law was given so that those predestined to life might be saved through legal observances; but those predestined to death might be punished more severely through transgression of the law. Here, however, he mentions only that cause by which he can humble the Jews who grew proud because they had received the law.

28. AMBROSE. But the law entered in. The Apostle shows what resulted from the giving of the law, not what the law itself did.

29. LANFRANC. Grace will abound exceedingly. As if he were saying: O Jews! You think that Christ forgave more to the Gentiles, but he forgave more to some of you, whom he found to be transgressors of the law.

30. So that just as it reigned, that is, prevailed.

31. So also let grace reign, that is, let it prevail.

32. AMBROSE. Let grace reign. Grace reigns through righteousness if, having received remission, we pursue righteousness.

33. Through righteousness, namely, Christ’s.

# CHAPTER VI

[Col. 0123]

What then shall we say? Shall we remain in sin so that grace may abound? By no means! For we who have died to sin—namely, in baptism—how shall we still live in it? Or do you not know that all of us who were baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death? That is, just as he died once and lives forever, so we too should die to sin once and live forever in good works. When we are baptized, we die with Christ; this is to be baptized into his death, for there sins die. Therefore we were buried with him through baptism into death, so that, just as Christ was raised from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we too might walk in newness of life—that is, rise from vices.

For if we have been planted together in the likeness of his death—that is, if we die to sin once—we shall also share in his resurrection. He says that we can rise blessedly if we have been planted together in the likeness of his death: that is, if in baptism we lay aside all vices, are transferred into a new life, and thereafter do not sin. This is another reason why we are baptized into his death: “planted together” means fastened to or adhering to it. We shall also share in the likeness of his resurrection.

Knowing this, that our old man was crucified together with him—that is, we ourselves insofar as we sin in the manner of the old man—in order that the body of sin might be destroyed, that is, our body insofar as it sins, and that we might no longer serve sin. By “the body of sin” he designates all sins together.

For whoever has died has been justified from sin. This is the reason why sin must not be served: justification is lost through sin. But if we have died with Christ, we believe that we shall also live with Christ, knowing that Christ, having risen from the dead, no longer dies; death shall no longer rule over him. For the death he died, he died to sin once—understand: by removing it from the human race—but the life he lives, he lives to God.

So also you must consider yourselves dead to sin but living to God, in Christ Jesus our Lord. Therefore let sin not reign in your mortal body—that is, the desire of sin—so that you obey its desires. Nor should you present your members as weapons of unrighteousness to sin—that is, its desires—but present yourselves to God as those living from the dead, and your members as weapons of righteousness to God. He does not say “your bodies” but “your members,” for service is rendered by the members, not by the whole body.

For sin shall not rule over you; for you are not under the law but under grace. He clearly shows that sinful desires had greater force among the Jews than among Christians. You are not under the law—not because the law is evil, but because those who are under it are made guilty by its commands without being helped by it.

What then? Shall we sin because we are not under the law but under grace? By no means! Do you not know that to whomever you present yourselves as slaves for obedience, you are slaves of the one whom you obey—whether of sin, leading to death, or of obedience, leading to righteousness?

But thanks be to God that you were slaves of sin, yet obeyed from the heart the form of teaching to which you were delivered—that is, in which you gave yourselves to God on the day of your conversion. Having been freed from sin, you became slaves of righteousness.

I speak in human terms, because of the weakness of your flesh. That is, I prescribe something humble to you, something that does not exceed the capacity of our humanity. In recalling the weakness of the flesh, he indicates that he demands less from man than is worthy in the worship of God. He says this in human terms because something more would have had to be said if they had already been able to do or bear it. For a greater servitude is owed to righteousness than to sin. Bodily punishments withdraw us from the work of sin; righteousness, however, must be loved so greatly that even bodily punishments should not restrain us from its works.

For just as you presented your members to serve uncleanness and iniquity for the accomplishment of iniquity, so now present your members to serve righteousness for sanctification—that is, so that you may be sanctified. For when you were slaves of sin, you were free, that is, without righteousness. What fruit did you then have in those things of which you are now ashamed? For their end is death.

But now, having been freed from sin and made slaves of God, you have your fruit leading to sanctification—that is, the fruit of your work is sanctification—and your end is eternal life. For the wages of sin are death. This explains why they have been freed from sin and why they have become slaves of God. The meaning is that sin gives this wage, that is, this recompense—namely, death.

But the grace of God—that is, the power given through God’s grace—is eternal life; that is, it gives eternal life. Ambrose says that the Apostle appears to demonstrate this by these arguments: one is either in Christ or in the law. For the law has been put to death through the body of Christ, so that you may belong to him who rose from the dead. The same principle appears in other laws. A man dies to one law so that he may now live under another; as long as he lives under the former, he cannot live under the other, for the former still rules. A woman living under the marital law of her husband cannot live under the law of another husband, for she is bound to her husband. But if she dies to the law of her former husband, she can live under the law of another. Therefore, while she lives under the marital law—namely, while her husband is alive—she cannot live under the law of another husband [f.: *vivere*, “to live”]. If she is then with another man, she will be called an adulteress.

But the grace of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord.

## Commentary

### [Col. 0123B]

**Chapter VI, 1. LANFRANC.** “For we who have died to sin”: namely, in baptism. “In Christ Jesus”: that is, in faith in Christ Jesus.

### [Col. 0123C]

**2.** “Into his death”: that is, just as he died once and lives forever, so we too should die to sin once and live forever in good works.

**3. AMBROSE.** “Into his death.” When we are baptized, we die with Christ; this is to be baptized into his death. For there sins die.

**4. LANFRANC.** “For we were buried together.” An indication of when and why we are baptized into Christ’s death.

**5.** “In newness”: that is, let us rise from vices.

### [Col. 0124A]

**6. AMBROSE.** “For if we have been planted together.” He says that we can then rise blessedly if we have been planted together in the likeness of his death; that is, if in baptism we lay aside all vices, are transferred into a new life, and thereafter do not sin.

**7. LANFRANC.** “For if we have been planted together.” Another reason why we are baptized into his death: “planted together” means fastened to or adhering to it.

**8.** “In the likeness”: that is, if we die to sin once, we shall have a similar resurrection.

**9.** “Also of the resurrection”: understand, “in the likeness of his resurrection.”

**10.** “Because our old man”: that is, ourselves insofar as we sin in the manner of the old man.

**11.** “In order that the body of sin might be destroyed”: that is, our body insofar as it sins.

### [Col. 0124B]

**12.** “The body of sin.” He calls all sins together “the body of sin.”

**13.** “For whoever has died.” The reason why sin must not be served: justification is lost through sin.

**14.** “But if we have died”: that is, if Christ truly died according to the flesh, we believe that we have died to all sins, and so forth.

**15. LANFRANC.** “For the death he died to sin”: understand, by removing it from the human race.

**16.** “So also you”: instead of “therefore you also.”

**17.** “Therefore let sin not reign”: that is, the desire of sin.

### [Col. 0124C]

**18. AMBROSE.** “Therefore let sin not reign.” By saying “mortal body,” he signifies the whole man, because those who obey sin are called mortal. For the soul that sins shall itself die—that is, the whole man.

**19.** “Nor should you present.” He does not say “bodies” but “members,” for service is rendered by the members, not by the whole body.

**20. LANFRANC.** “Weapons of unrighteousness”: that is, the desires of sin.

### [Col. 0125A]

**21.** “For you are not under the law.” He clearly shows that sinful desires had greater force among the Jews than among Christians.

**22. AUGUSTINE** (*On Grace and Free Will*, book, chapter 12, volume VII). “For you are not under the law.” Not because the law is evil, but because those who are under it are made guilty by its commands without being helped by it.

**23. LANFRANC.** “To which you were delivered”: that is, in which you gave yourselves to God on the day of your conversion.

**24.** “I speak in human terms”: that is, I prescribe something humble to you, something that does not exceed the capacity of our humanity.

**25. AMBROSE.** “I speak in human terms.” In recalling the weakness of the flesh, he indicates that he demands less from man than is worthy in the worship of God.

### [Col. 0125B]

**25. AUGUSTINE** (from *Letter to Anastasius* 144, volume II). “I speak in human terms,” because something more would have had to be said if they had already been able to do or bear it. For a greater servitude is owed to righteousness than to sin. Bodily punishments withdraw us from the work of sin; righteousness, however, must be loved so greatly that even bodily punishments should not restrain us from its works.

**26.** “For just as you presented.” What does “just as” mean here, followed by “so also this,” except: just as no fear compelled you to sin, but rather the lust and pleasure of sin itself, so, in order to live righteously, let not fear of punishment urge you, but let the delight of righteousness urge you.

**27. LANFRANC.** “For when you were slaves.” The reason why they ought to serve righteousness. It is necessary either to serve righteousness or to serve sin. But when sin is served, righteousness is absent. A fruit is acquired that causes shame, which is inappropriate. Therefore righteousness must be served.

**28.** “Wages.” The reason why they have been freed from sin and why they have become slaves of God. The meaning is that sin gives this wage, that is, this recompense—namely, death.

**29.** “But the grace of God”: that is, the power given through God’s grace, is eternal life; that is, it gives eternal life.

### [Col. 0126A]

**30. AMBROSE.** “But the grace of God.” The Apostle appears to demonstrate this by these arguments: one is either in Christ or in the law. For the law has been put to death through the body of Christ, so that you may belong to him who rose from the dead. The same principle appears in other laws. A man dies to one law so that he may now live under another. As long as he lives under the former, he cannot live under the other, for the former still rules. A woman living under the marital law of her husband cannot live under the law of another husband, for she is bound to her husband. But if she dies to the law of her former husband, she can live under the law of another. Therefore, while she lives under the marital law—that is, while her husband is alive—she cannot live under the law of another husband [f.: *vivere*, “to live”]. If she is then with another man, she will be called an adulteress.

## Chapter VII

### [Col. 0125]

**1. LANFRANC.** “Or do you not know, brothers?” He appears to prove that the law of the Jews is not to be observed by the faithful. For it was given only until the coming of Christ. This is the response, as though someone were to say: Why did you say “in Christ Jesus,” and not “in observance of the law”?

Or do you not know, brothers—for I speak to those who know the law—that the law rules over a person for as long as he lives? For a woman who is under a husband is bound by the law while her husband lives; but if her husband dies, she is released from the law of her husband. Therefore, while her husband lives, she will be called an adulteress if she is with another man; but if her husband dies, she is freed from her husband’s law, so that she is not an adulteress if she is with another man.

Therefore, my brothers, you too have been put to death with respect to the law—understand: you owe nothing to the law, for the law was given until the coming of Christ—through the body of Christ. The Savior permitted his body to be crucified by the devil; therefore he says that we have been saved through the body of Christ. Thus you may belong to another, to him who rose from the dead, so that we may bear fruit for God.

For when we were in the flesh—that is, in carnal observance—the passions of sins, which were through the law, were at work in our members so as to bear fruit for death. Someone might ask why he said “so that we may bear fruit for God,” as though we did not bear fruit when we observed the law carnally. He replies: when we were in the flesh, that is, in carnal observance, and so forth.

But now we have been released from the law of death in which we were held—that is, from the law which commanded sinners to be killed without any mercy; or from the law which increased, through prohibition, the passions of sins, which are the death of the soul—so that we may serve in newness of spirit, renewing the spirit through faith and good works, and not in the oldness of the letter, that is, through carnal observance.

What then shall we say? Is the law sin? This might be asked because he previously spoke of the law of death, or of the passions of sins that were through the law. By no means! But I did not know sin except through the law; for I did not know, or had not experienced, covetous desire to be sin unless the law said, “You shall not covet.”

But when sin—that is, the tinder of sin—had seized an opportunity, sin worked in me every covetous desire through the commandment. Ambrose says: “It worked in me … which also surpassed the law,” though the text here is incomplete.

For without the law sin was dead. Augustine says that “dead” should be understood as though sin did not exist: it lay hidden, did not appear, and was entirely unknown, as though buried in certain unfathomable darknesses of ignorance.

I once lived without the law. Ambrose explains: “I lived without fear, secure in the belief that God would not judge.”

But when the commandment came, sin revived. Augustine asks what “sin revived” means: it began to appear and began to rebel against me.

And I died—that is, I became a transgressor—and the commandment that was for life, if observed, was found by me to be for death, if not observed.

For sin—that is, the tinder of sin, or the devil—having seized an opportunity through the commandment, deceived me and through it killed me. Ambrose says that “sin” here means the devil, who, envious of man—whom he saw as provided for through the law—burned with desire to pervert the law for him who before the law was, as it were, dead because the devil had ceased from deception.

Therefore the law is indeed holy, and the commandment holy and just and good. Did what is good, then, become death to me? By no means! But sin—whether sin as it appears in the act, or because the devil is called sin—worked death in me through what is good, so that sin might become exceedingly sinful through the commandment, through the transgression of sin.

Augustine, or Bede, explains “exceedingly sinful”: this is also because of transgression. When he sinned without the commandment, it was less; when he sinned through the commandment, he exceeded the measure.

Lanfranc explains “exceedingly” as “very greatly.” The order is: so that sin, increased through sin, might become exceedingly sinful through the commandment. “Sinful” is used in the manner by which a quality is called “such,” because it makes something such.

For we know that the law is spiritual—that is, nourishing the spirit—but I am carnal, sold under sin. Augustine explains “sold” as “sinning for the price of temporal pleasures.”

For what I do, I do not understand. “I do not understand” means “I do not approve of it,” as in the Psalm: “Understand my cry.”

For I do not do—an explanation of the preceding verse—the good that I want, but I do the evil that I hate. If I do what I do not want, I agree with the law that it is good.

But now it is no longer I who do it, but sin that dwells in me—that is, the desire of sin, which adheres inseparably.

For I know that good does not dwell in me, that is, in my flesh. “For the good that is in man is either good willing or good action. But,” he says, “the willing of good is not in my flesh. It is near through the soul’s proximity—that is, vice is adjacent to it. But I do not find the accomplishment of good, that is, good action, dwelling in it. Therefore good is not in me, that is, in my flesh; for I do not do the good that I want …” The text is incomplete here; the meaning is: I do not find good dwelling in me, but rather the evil that I do.

For willing is present to me, but I do not find the accomplishment of good. For I do not do the good that I want, but I do the evil that I do not want.

But if I do what I do not want, it is no longer I who do it, but sin that dwells in me. Augustine explains that he consents to the law because the law does not want this.

I find, therefore, a law for me who desire to do good, because evil is present to me. Lanfranc says that this concludes what was previously sought and proved: that the law is good, provided that one desires the good.

The order is: “I find the law good for me who desire to do good.” The meaning is: if I do good, the law is good for me; but if I do evil, the law is death to me.

For I delight in the law of God according to the inner man. Here he clearly explains what he had previously said obscurely in many ways, especially the preceding verse.

But I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind and taking me captive in the law of sin that is in my members. By “another law” he means the inducements of covetous desire, which, as it were, commands a man to sin. “The law of my mind” means that the mind commands one to depart from evils and do good, and this is its law.

Wretched man that I am! Who will free me from this body of death? Augustine explains: Thus, thus you will be freed from the body of this death when this mortal body puts on immortality and this corruptible body puts on incorruption.

The grace of God, through Jesus Christ our Lord. Therefore I myself, with my mind, serve the law of God, but with the flesh I serve the law of sin.

## Commentary

### [Col. 0126B]

**Chapter VII, 1. LANFRANC.** “Or do you not know, brothers?” He appears to prove that the law of the Jews is not to be observed by the faithful. For it was given only until the coming of Christ. This is the response, as though someone were to say: Why did you say “in Christ Jesus,” and not “in observance of the law”?

**2.** “You have been put to death with respect to the law.” As though he were saying: You owe nothing to the law. For the law was given until the coming of Christ.

**3. AMBROSE.** “You have been put to death with respect to the law.” Because the Savior permitted his body to be crucified by the devil. Therefore he says that we have been saved through the body of Christ.

**4. LANFRANC.** “For when we were in the flesh.” As though someone were to say: Why did you say “so that we may bear fruit for God,” as though we did not bear fruit when we observed the law carnally? He replies: when we were in the flesh, that is, in carnal observance, and so forth.

**5.** “From the law of death”: that is, from the law which commanded sinners to be killed without any mercy; or from the law which increased, through prohibition, the passions of sins, which are the death of the soul. [*according to edition P.*]

### [Col. 0127A]

**6.** “I did not know sin”: that is, I had not previously experienced such force of covetous desire as I experienced afterward, when I learned that it was forbidden. Or: I did not know that covetous desire was sin.

**7. AMBROSE.** “It worked in me … which also surpassed the law.” The text is fragmentary.

**8. AUGUSTINE** (*Against Two Letters of the Pelagians*, to Boniface, book I, chapter 9, volume VII). “For without the law.” “Sin was dead” should be understood as though it did not exist: it lay hidden, did not appear, and was entirely unknown, as though buried in certain unfathomable darknesses of ignorance.

**9. AMBROSE.** “But I lived.” I lived without fear, secure in the belief that God would not judge.

**10. AUGUSTINE** (*On the Words of the Apostle*, sermon 5, chapter VII, volume X). “But when the commandment came.” What does “sin revived” mean? It began to appear and began to rebel against me.

### [Col. 0127B]

**11.** “But I died”: that is, I became a transgressor.

**12.** (*Eighty-Three Questions*, question 66, volume IV). “For sin.” When he says, “Sin deceived me, having seized an opportunity through the commandment,” this may mean either that the persuasion of pleasure toward sin is stronger when prohibition is present, or that even if a man does something according to the commands of the law, if he still lacks complete faith, he wishes to attribute the reward to himself rather than to God, and by growing proud he sins more.

**13. AMBROSE.** “Having seized an opportunity.” He calls the devil “sin.” Envious of man, whom he saw as provided for through the law, the devil burned with desire to pervert the law for him who before the law was, as it were, dead because the devil had ceased from deception.

### [Col. 0128A]

**14. AUGUSTINE** (Bede, on chapter 8 of Romans). “Exceedingly sinful.” This is also because of transgression. When he sinned without the commandment, it was less; when he sinned through the commandment, he exceeded the measure.

**15. LANFRANC.** “Exceedingly”: that is, very greatly. The order is: so that sin, increased through sin, might become exceedingly sinful. “Sinful” is used in the manner by which a quality is called “such,” because it makes something such.

**16.** “For we know.” A proof that the law is good. Everything spiritual—that is, nourishing the spirit—is good.

**17. AUGUSTINE** (*Eighty-Three Questions*, question 66, volume IV). “Sold”: that is, sinning for the price of temporal pleasures.

**18. LANFRANC.** “For what I do.” A proof that he is sold under sin. Sin rules to such an extent that it makes him do what he does not want.

**19.** “I do not understand.” I do not accept it as mine, as in the Psalm: “Understand my cry.”

### [Col. 0128B]

**20. AUGUSTINE** (*Sermons on Various Matters*, sermon 45, chapter 6). “For not what I want”: that is, I do not want to covet, yet I covet.

**21. LANFRANC.** “What I do not want.” This must be understood of covetous desire. As though he were saying: I would like to avoid covetous desire, but I cannot.

**22.** “For I know.” By removing one contrary, he customarily proves the other. In the Christian religion, good and evil are immediate opposites. According to the Christian religion, every person is either good or evil.

**23.** “For willing is present.” A proof that good does not dwell in his flesh. Every good that is in a man is either good will or good action. But, he says, the willing of good is not in his flesh. It is near through the soul’s proximity—that is, vice is adjacent to it. But I do not find the accomplishment of good, that is, good action, dwelling in it. Therefore good is not in me, that is, in my flesh; for I do not do the good that I want … The text is incomplete. The meaning is: I do not find good dwelling in me, but rather the evil that I do.

### [Col. 0129A]

**24. AUGUSTINE** (*Against Certain Letters of the Pelagians*, to Boniface, question 1, chapter 10, volume VII). “But if I do what I do not want.” For this reason I consent to the law: it does not want this.

**25. AMBROSE.** “But sin that dwells.” The corruption of sin itself remains in the body through the condition of offense.

**26. LANFRANC.** “I find, therefore.” He concludes what was previously sought and proved: that the law is good, provided that one desires the good.

**27.** “The law.” The order is: “I find the law good for me who desire to do good.” As though he were saying: if I do good, the law is good for me; but if I do evil, the law is death to me.

**28.** “For me who desire.” This is the will of the soul, which desires to do good in God so as to drive out the evil that is adjacent to it through the proximity of the flesh.

### [Col. 0129B]

**29.** “I delight.” Here he clearly explains what he had previously said obscurely in many ways, especially the preceding verse.

**30.** “Another law.” By “another law” he means the inducements of covetous desire, which, as it were, commands a man to sin.

**31.** “The law of my mind.” The mind commands one to depart from evils and do good, and this is its law.

**32. AUGUSTINE** (*On the Words of the Apostle*, sermon 6, chapter 12, volume X). “Wretched man that I am!” You will indeed be freed from the body of this death when this mortal body puts on immortality and this corruptible body puts on incorruption.

## CHAPTER VIII

**1. AMBROSE. “For the law of the Spirit.”** Because the former law imbued one with evil error. But since this law says that one ought not even to sin in the heart, let it be called the law of the Spirit, [Col. 0129C] so that it may make the whole person spiritual.

**2. LANFRANC. “The law of the Spirit.”** The reason why they do not walk according to the flesh. For remembrance of the law of God, [Col. 0130A] which is the Spirit of life, will free them through the grace of Jesus Christ and through remembrance of him from the law of sin and death—that is, so that they may not walk according to the flesh.

**3. “For what was impossible.”** The reason why he said “in Christ Jesus.” It is as though he said: it was impossible for the law, through carnal observances, to free anyone from the persuasion of sin and death; but God sent his Son in the likeness of human flesh, which is often afflicted by the desires of sin, so that remembrance of his incarnation might drive the persuasions of sin away from the flesh of the faithful.

**4. “He condemned sin concerning sin.”** Here he calls the body of Christ “sin,” because it was a sacrifice for sin, just as elsewhere he says that he who knew no sin was made sin for us.

**5. AMBROSE. “Concerning sin.”** When Christ is crucified by sin, which is Satan, Satan sins in the flesh of the Savior; by that sin he is condemned, having lost his dominion over the souls he had held captive.

**6. AUGUSTINE** (*On the Words of the Apostle*, sermon 7, chapter 9). “For those who are according to the flesh.” To walk according to the flesh is to consent to carnal desires.

**7.** (The same work.) “According to the Spirit.” To walk according to the Spirit is to be assisted in the mind by the Spirit and not to obey the desires of the flesh.

**8.** (The same work, chapter 10.) “For it is not subject to the law of God.” This cannot be said of nature, but of the wisdom of the flesh: the vice cannot, not the nature. It is as though one said: lameness is not subject to straight walking. For the foot can, but lameness cannot.

**9. AUGUSTINE** (from *Tractates on the Psalms*, on Psalm 85, near the middle, vol. VIII). “The body, indeed.” Our body, when compared with what it will be, is found to be dead, although it still has a soul.

[Col. 0131A] **10. LANFRANC. “For as many as.”** Proof that those who put the deeds of the flesh to death live. For they are sons of God, and there is no doubt that they live.

**11. “For you did not receive.”** He proves that those who are led by the Spirit of God are sons. “For,” he says, “the Spirit whom you received did not make you slaves.” All worshipers of God, in whatever age, were either slaves, as the Jews, or sons, as Christians. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “I will no longer call you slaves, but friends,” and so forth.

**12. AUGUSTINE** (*On the Words of the Apostle*, sermon 13, chapter 14). “In whom we cry: Abba, Father.” The Spirit of God bears witness to this voice and to the disposition with which we cry, “Abba, Father,” while it remains clinging within us.

**13. AUGUSTINE. “In whom we cry: Abba, Father.”** The Apostle intended to say both, because he saw the cornerstone, which those who rejected it cast aside, receiving both walls, even those coming from different directions [alternative reading: “the one coming from a different direction”]. On one side circumcision, on the other uncircumcision; from one side “Abba,” from the other “Father.”

**14.** (*Eighty-Three Questions*, question 75, vol. IV.) “Heirs indeed of God.” If it is asked how we are heirs of God, since an inheritance is secured by the death of its predecessor, the answer is: when what is perfect has come, what is partial will be taken away. Thus, in a certain sense, the Father dies for us in a mystery, and that same one becomes the inheritance when he is possessed face to face [alternative reading: “seen face to face”].

**15. LANFRANC. “For the expectation.”** He proves from the authority of the whole Church that the glory of the sons is to be revealed; here he calls the Church “creation,” as elsewhere: “If [there is] any new creation in Christ.” And James says: “That we may be some beginning of his creation.” It is as though he said: the Church of Christ awaits the revelation to it of the glory of the sons of God, that is, fellowship with the angels of God.

**16. “For creation was subjected to futility.”** It is as though someone said: Why does the Church, which has so great an expectation, think vain thoughts? Why does it sometimes desire vain things? He answers: it suffers this unwillingly. But it pleased God to subject it to futility, giving it hope that one day it will be freed from the slavery of futility and corruption, when it has been given the freedom of the glory possessed by the sons of God.

[Col. 0132A] **17. AUGUSTINE** (*Eighty-Three Questions*, question 67). “For creation was subjected to futility.” A human being sinned willingly, but was condemned unwillingly. Sin, therefore, was voluntary; in contrast, carrying out the command was an act of truth. But the punishment of sin subjects one to deceit. For creation was not willingly subjected to futility [alternative reading: “therefore, it was not willingly subjected to futility”].

**18.** (The same work.) “But because of him.” Because of him who subjected it in hope—that is, because of his justice and mercy, since he neither leaves sin unpunished [alternative reading: “left it unpunished”] nor wished the sinner to be beyond healing.

**19. AUGUSTINE** (*Against Priscillian and Origen*, *To Orosius in Answer to His Consultation*, chapter 8, vol. VI). “All creation.” In every human being all creation can be understood, because there is in him the rational element, which angels are believed to possess; the sensory element, shared with beasts; and the vital element devoid of sensation, shared with trees. For in us the growth of the body takes place without our awareness.

**20. LANFRANC. “The redemption of the body.”** We truly await the redemption of the body because we hope for what exists. When he says, “we await with patience,” he says “we hope,” because we have been saved in hope; and he proves this because we hope for what we do not see, namely, what has been promised by God, while the redemption of the body has been promised. He proves that we hope for what we do not see because we do not hope for what we see. He proves this because our vision is not hope. He proves this because hope that is seen is not hope, since no vision is hope. He proves this because, if someone sees something, why does he hope for it? For no one who sees hopes. Or it may be understood this way: Do we await redemption? The answer is: truly, because we hope that we have been saved in hope. Thus he explains it: if we hope, we await what exists; but if we hope for what we do not see, we await it with patience (the assumption); yet we hope for what we do not see. He proves this because what is seen is not hoped for as something that exists; but hope that is seen is not hope. He proves this, for no one who sees hopes for what exists; for, if someone sees it, why does he hope for it?

**21. “For in hope we were saved.”** It is as though someone said: Are not those who serve God also freed from futility and corruption in this life? The Apostle answers this objection, saying: We have hope that we shall be freed in eternal life, but we have not yet been freed in this life.

**22. “Likewise.”** It is as though he said: just as hope strengthens our faintheartedness, so also the Spirit helps our weakness, showing us what we ought to do.

**23. AUGUSTINE** (*Against Maximinus*, book I, near the beginning, vol. VI). “But the Spirit himself pleads.” It is said that he “intercedes with groanings” so that we may understand that he makes us intercede with groanings. For he is present with us [alternative reading: “with you”], and by pouring charity into us he makes us intercede with groanings.

**24. LANFRANC. “All things work together.”** It is as though he said: the Holy Spirit is not only a fellow-worker in prayer among those who love God, but also a fellow-worker in the good things that are done by them.

[Col. 0133B] **25. “For those whom.”** The answer to the question why he said “purpose.” The order is: those whom he foreknew would be conformed to the image of his Son—that is, would become imitators of the footsteps of Jesus Christ—and predestined, so that he himself might be the firstborn among many brothers, that is, holding primacy in the company of the saints.

**26. AUGUSTINE** (*On the Gift of Perseverance*, chapter 14). “Predestined.” This is the predestination of the saints, namely, presence [alternative reading: “foreknowledge”] and preparation of God’s benefits.

**27. AUGUSTINE** (*The City of God*, book XXII, chapter 15). “To be conformed.” This can be understood with reference to the inner person. Hence he says to us elsewhere: “Be transformed in the renewal of your mind.” It can also be understood in the sense that we are made like him in immortality. This pertains to the resurrection itself, since he is certainly the firstborn from the dead.

[Col. 0134A] **28. AUGUSTINE** (*On the Words of the Apostle*, sermon 16, chapters 1 and 10). “Predestined.” God predestined us before we existed; he called us when we had turned away; he justified us when we were sinners; he glorified us when we were mortal.

**29. LANFRANC. “Glorified.”** This has not yet happened, but it will happen in the future life.

**30. “What then shall we say?”** That is, what worthy thanks shall we render to God for such great benefits?

**31. “What also concerning the Son.”** It is as though he said: God not only grants us freedom from fear of our adversaries, but also gives us everything, just as he gave us that one.

**32. “Or the sword?”** The implied meaning is: none of these things.

**33. “As it is written.”** This too he proves.

**34. “Because of him,”** that is, because of his love.

**35. “Death,”** that is, the threat of death.

**36. “Life,”** that is, the promise of life.

**37. “Angels,”** namely, evil ones.

**38. AMBROSE. “Nor any other creature.”** Not even if, by the skill and sublimity of its cunning, it should fabricate another creature for a time, as Jannes and Jambres fabricated things before Pharaoh.

## CHAPTER IX
[Note: [Col. 0134B] CHAPTER IX.—1. LANFRANC. “The truth.” As though someone might say: “You once persecuted the Church of God; how is it that you now speak in this way?” He replies: “I grieve incessantly over what I did.”]

I speak the truth in Christ—I do not lie, my conscience bearing witness to me in the Holy Spirit [Note: [Col. 0134B] 2. “In the Holy Spirit,” that is, through the Holy Spirit whom he possesses within himself, from whom truth is inspired in him]—that I have great sorrow and continual anguish in my heart. [Note: [Col. 0134B] 3. “For I could wish.” He explains why he grieves: namely, while he was persecuting the Church of Christ, he wished to be separated from Christ. He indicates that he did this out of a good zeal for his brothers, whose law he seemed to be destroying by preaching the Gospel.] For I could wish that I myself were accursed and separated from Christ for the sake of my brothers, who [Col. 0135] are my kinsmen according to the flesh, who are Israelites, to whom belongs the adoption as sons—that is, who have been adopted as sons—and the glory, and the covenants, and the legislation, and the worship, and the promises; [Note: [Col. 0135A] 4. AUGUSTINE (from book XII, Against Faustus the Manichaean, chapter 3, midway). “And the glory.” And what is their glory, unless especially this: that the utterances of God were entrusted to them? Why, moreover, did he speak of “the covenants” as belonging to the Israelites [addition: “especially,”] unless because the Old Covenant was given to them and the New was prefigured in the Old?] whose fathers are theirs, and from whom Christ is according to the flesh, who is God over all, blessed forever. Amen.

But it is not the case [Note: [Col. 0135A] 5. LANFRANC. “But not that the word of God has failed.” Above he said that the promises of an eternal inheritance had been made to the Jews. But because the Jews, for the most part, did not believe in Christ, the word of God seemed not to have been fulfilled. He answers this: “The word of God has not failed.” For the word of God to fail, or to pass away, means not to fulfill the promises.] that the word of God has failed. For not all who are from Israel—that is, according to the flesh—are Israelites, [Note: [Col. 0135B] 7. LANFRANC. “Israelites.” Not all who were under the worship of God and observance of the law were Israelites. Some passed over to the rites of the Gentiles and the worship of idols, as happened in the time of Jeroboam to the greater part of them. By this God signified that at Christ’s coming some would believe and the greater part would remain in unbelief.] nor are all who are Abraham’s offspring children—that is, children according to the flesh. [Note: [Col. 0135C] 8. “All children.” He calls those born from a lawful marriage children, as in Hebrews: “Therefore you are illegitimate and not children.” They alone are heirs of the Father.]

But “in Isaac shall your offspring be named,” that is, the offspring of the inheritance; in other words, it is not the children of the flesh who are children of God, but the children of the promise are counted as offspring—that is, spiritual offspring, namely, those who are righteous, as you promised. For the word of the promise is this: “At this time next year I will come, and Sarah shall have a son.” [Note: [Col. 0135C] 9. AUGUSTINE (The City of God, book XVI, chapter 32). “But in Isaac.” Explaining what it means that “in Isaac shall your offspring be named,” the Apostle says: “The children of the flesh are not the children of God; but the children of the promise are counted as offspring.” Accordingly, the children of the promise, so that they may be Abraham’s offspring in Isaac, are gathered together by grace, which calls them to Christ.]

And not only this [Note: [Col. 0135C] 10. LANFRANC. “And not only this.” Either: not only are some elected and others rejected; for this was not on account of the works of the father or mother, since they came from one act of intercourse; nor on account of their own works, since they had not yet done anything, because they had not yet been born.], but Rebecca also, when she had conceived children by one act of intercourse with Isaac our father [Note: [Col. 0136A] 11. AUGUSTINE (Letter 105 to the presbyter Sixtus, near the end, vol.
