II). “But Rebecca also.” Why did he add, “from one act of intercourse,” unless so that Jacob could not boast—not only on the basis of his own merits, nor those of his parents, nor even on the basis of the changed and perhaps improved will of his one father—that he had been loved by the Creator because his father, when he begot him, possessed better and more praiseworthy character? “From one act of intercourse,” he says: there was then one merit of the father in begetting them and one merit of the mother in conceiving them; so that, with the same father, the same mother, and one act of intercourse, before they had done anything good or evil, God chose one and hated the other. Let Jacob understand that, from that mass of original iniquity in which he sees that his brother—who shared the whole same cause with him—deserved condemnation by justice, he himself could have been distinguished only by grace.], when they had not yet been born and had done nothing good or evil, so that God’s purpose according to election—that is, according to grace—might remain, it was said to her: “The elder shall serve the younger.” [Note: [Col. 0136B] 12. LANFRANC. “But Rebecca also.” The order is: “Rebecca, having children by one act of intercourse with Isaac.”] As it is written: “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated.” This testimony is found in the prophet Malachi, chapter I.

What then shall we say? [Note: [Col. 0136B] 13. “Is there injustice?” It seemed unjust to reject Esau, who had not yet sinned. Yet he does not solve this great and difficult question.] Is there injustice with God? By no means! [Note: [Col. 0136C] 14. AUGUSTINE (in the same work, shortly before). “Is there injustice?” After he had said, “God forbid that there should be injustice with God,” we might, as it were, say to him: “How do you demonstrate this, when you assert that it was said not on account of works but because of him who calls, ‘The elder shall serve the younger’?” For Moses, he says, declares:] For he says to Moses: [Note: [Col. 0136C] 15. LANFRANC. “For he says to Moses.” He does not answer the question, but the preceding statement in which it was said, “Jacob I loved,” and so forth.]

“I will have mercy on whom I have mercy, and I will show compassion to whom I show compassion.” [Note: [Col. 0136C] 16. “Of him who has mercy.” This can be seen in Jacob, he says, because neither human will nor human life saves a person, but the mercy of God, by which good will and good works are inspired.] Therefore it depends not on one who wills or one who runs—that is, in order to be saved—but on God who shows mercy. [Note: [Col. 0136C] 16. “I will have mercy,” and so forth. He proves that God loved Jacob because he loves all according to his purpose, that is, according to grace; for he says: “I will have mercy,” and so forth.]

For Scripture says to Pharaoh: “For this very purpose I raised you up, to show my power in you and to proclaim my name throughout all the earth.” [Note: [Col. 0137A] 17. “Scripture.” He shows that some benefit arises from the hardening of unbelievers, but he does not thereby prove that it was not unjust to reject Esau.]

Thus, he concludes both questions: Therefore he has mercy on whom he wills, and he hardens whom he wills.

You will say to me, then: [Note: [Col. 0137A] 18. AUGUSTINE (in the same work). “Why does he still find fault?” This amounts to saying: “Why is complaint made against us because we offend God by living badly, when no one can resist his will—he who hardened us by withholding mercy?”] Why does he still find fault? For who can resist his will? [Note: [Col. 0137A] 19. LANFRANC. “Why does he still find fault?” Having heard the statement “whom he wills he hardens,” the worldly person, living amid pleasures, could question it and murmur against God, not attributing to his own fault the fact that he is such a person: “Why is the matter still disputed? I understand what follows. My labor is useless against my vices; my effort is futile. I shall be whatever God wills me to be. For who can resist his will?”]

O man, who are you to answer back to God? [Note: [Col. 0137B] 20. AUGUSTINE (in the same work). “O man, who are you?” For the time being, let it be enough, on the basis of Christian faith [variant: “from Christian faith”], for one who is still living and does not yet behold what is perfect but knows in part, to know or believe this: that God frees no one except by gratuitous mercy through our Lord Jesus Christ, and condemns no one except by the most equitable truth through that same Lord Jesus Christ. But why he frees one person rather than another, let the one who can search out the great depth of his judgments; nevertheless, let him beware of falling.] Does the thing formed say to the one who formed it, “Why did you make me like this?” Or does the potter not have power over the clay, from the same lump to make one vessel for honor and another for dishonor?

But if God, wishing to show his wrath and make known his power, endured with great patience the vessels of wrath prepared for destruction, in order to show the riches of his glory upon the vessels of mercy, which he prepared for glory—whom he also called, not only from the Jews but also from the Gentiles.

As he says in Hosea: [Note: [Col. 0137C] 22. “I will call those who were not my people.” This proves that God called the vessels of mercy from the Gentiles. Before faith, the Gentiles were not the people of God.] “I will call those who were not my people, ‘my people,’ and her who was not beloved, ‘beloved,’ and her who had not obtained mercy, ‘one who has obtained mercy.’”

And it shall be in the place where it was said to them, “You are not my people,” that they shall be called sons of the living God. [Note: [Col. 0138A] 23. “And it shall be in the place.” The Jews had been scattered among many nations even before Christ’s coming; from these nations it was often said that they were not the people of God.]

But Isaiah cries out concerning Israel, concerning the conversion of Israel: [Note: [Col. 0138A] 24. “If it should be.” This proves that the vessels of mercy were called by God from the Jews. The text is found in an unusual translation in this form: “If your people Israel should be like the sand of the sea, the remnant shall be converted from it; a concise consummation has appointed righteousness.” For the Lord, the God of hosts, will accomplish the consummation and concision in the midst of the whole earth.] “If the number of the children of Israel should be like the sand of the sea, the remnant shall be saved.” [Note: [Col. 0138A] 25. “The remnant,” that is, the lowly few who will reign from among the number of unbelieving sinners.] [Note: [Col. 0138A] 26. AMBROSE. “The remnant shall be saved.” When the Jews withdrew from the merit and promise of the fathers, these are the remnant who persist in faith.]

For, having completed and shortened the word—that is, the commandments of the law—in righteousness, the Lord will execute it upon the earth, as Isaiah foretold: [Note: [Col. 0138B] 27. “For the word.” Since, after all the carnal observances of the law have been removed, faith alone has been established for salvation.] [Note: [Col. 0138B] 28. LANFRANC. “For the word.” He calls the love of God and neighbor “the word that completes,” through which many were saved without legal observances.] “Unless the Lord of hosts had left us offspring, we would have become like Sodom and would have been made like Gomorrah.” [Note: [Col. 0138B] 29. AMBROSE. “Unless the Lord of hosts.” He says that the Savior was left to us as an aid to life; from the beginning the Lord had decreed that he should be born. He calls him “offspring” because through him the human race was restored.] [Note: [Col. 0138B] 30. LANFRANC. “Offspring for us.” He calls the apostles and the primitive Church “offspring.”]

What then shall we say? This is the conclusion: The Gentiles, who were not pursuing righteousness, attained righteousness, namely, the righteousness that comes from faith. But Israel, pursuing the law of righteousness—that is, carnal observances, which are justified through faith—did not attain the law of righteousness. Why? Because they sought it not from faith—that is, they did not think that a person is justified by faith—but as though from works. [Note: [Col. 0138B] 31. “They stumbled.” This is the reason why they did not attain the law of righteousness and why they do not believe that a person is justified by faith.] For they stumbled over the stone of stumbling, as it is written: [Note: [Col. 0138C] 32. “As it is written,” with the implied phrase “in which there is faithful emulation.” They imitate us with a good zeal, if they do not know what they are doing: the righteousness of God, which is through faith in Christ.] “Behold, I place in Zion a stone of stumbling and a rock of offense, and everyone who believes in him will not be put to shame.”

## Commentary

[Col. 0134B]

### CHAPTER IX

1. LANFRANC. “The truth.” As though someone might say: “You once persecuted the Church of God; how is it that you now speak in this way?” He replies: “I grieve incessantly over what I did.”

2. “In the Holy Spirit,” that is, through the Holy Spirit whom he possesses within himself, from whom truth is inspired in him.

3. “For I could wish.” He explains why he grieves: namely, while he was persecuting the Church of Christ, he wished to be separated from Christ. He indicates that he did this out of a good zeal for his brothers, whose law he seemed to be destroying by preaching the Gospel.

4. AUGUSTINE (from book XII, *Against Faustus the Manichaean*, chapter 3, midway). “And the glory.” And what is their glory, unless especially this: that the utterances of God were entrusted to them? Why, moreover, did he speak of “the covenants” as belonging to the Israelites [addition: “especially,”] unless because the Old Covenant was given to them and the New was prefigured in the Old?

5. LANFRANC. “But not that the word of God has failed.” Above he said that the promises of an eternal inheritance had been made to the Jews. But because the Jews, for the most part, did not believe in Christ, the word of God seemed not to have been fulfilled. He answers this: “The word of God has not failed.” For the word of God to fail, or to pass away, means not to fulfill the promises.

6. AUGUSTINE. “Whether the word of God has failed.” Since he had said that he possessed continual sorrow of heart because of their unbelief, he now consoled himself by finding in the Law [lacuna] that not all who are from Israel or Abraham would believe. Thus, discovering that this had been foretold long ago, he diminished his sorrow. Their adoption is spoken of in Galatians: “When the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son, so that we might receive adoption as sons.”

7. LANFRANC. “Israelites.” Not all who were under the worship of God and observance of the law were Israelites. Some passed over to the rites of the Gentiles and the worship of idols, as happened in the time of Jeroboam to the greater part of them. By this God signified that at Christ’s coming some would believe and the greater part would remain in unbelief.

8. “All children.” He calls those born from a lawful marriage children, as in Hebrews: “Therefore you are illegitimate and not children.” They alone are heirs of the Father.

9. AUGUSTINE (*The City of God*, book XVI, chapter 32). “But in Isaac.” Explaining what it means that “in Isaac shall your offspring be named,” the Apostle says: “The children of the flesh are not the children of God; but the children of the promise are counted as offspring.” Accordingly, the children of the promise, so that they may be Abraham’s offspring in Isaac, are gathered together by grace, which calls them to Christ.

10. LANFRANC. “And not only this.” Either: not only are some elected and others rejected; for this was not on account of the works of the father or mother, since they came from one act of intercourse; nor on account of their own works, since they had not yet done anything, because they had not yet been born.

11. AUGUSTINE (Letter 105 to the presbyter Sixtus, near the end, vol. II). “But Rebecca also.” Why did he add, “from one act of intercourse,” unless so that Jacob could not boast—not only on the basis of his own merits, nor those of his parents, nor even on the basis of the changed and perhaps improved will of his one father—that he had been loved by the Creator because his father, when he begot him, possessed better and more praiseworthy character? “From one act of intercourse,” he says: there was then one merit of the father in begetting them and one merit of the mother in conceiving them; so that, with the same father, the same mother, and one act of intercourse, before they had done anything good or evil, God chose one and hated the other. Let Jacob understand that, from that mass of original iniquity in which he sees that his brother—who shared the whole same cause with him—deserved condemnation by justice, he himself could have been distinguished only by grace.

12. LANFRANC. “But Rebecca also.” The order is: “Rebecca, having children by one act of intercourse with Isaac.”

13. “Is there injustice?” It seemed unjust to reject Esau, who had not yet sinned. Yet he does not solve this great and difficult question.

14. AUGUSTINE (in the same work, shortly before). “Is there injustice?” After he had said, “God forbid that there should be injustice with God,” we might, as it were, say to him: “How do you demonstrate this, when you assert that it was said not on account of works but because of him who calls, ‘The elder shall serve the younger’?” For Moses, he says, declares.

15. LANFRANC. “For he says to Moses.” He does not answer the question, but the preceding statement in which it was said, “Jacob I loved,” and so forth.

16. “Of him who has mercy.” This can be seen in Jacob, he says, because neither human will nor human life saves a person, but the mercy of God, by which good will and good works are inspired.

16. “I will have mercy,” and so forth. He proves that God loved Jacob because he loves all according to his purpose, that is, according to grace; for he says: “I will have mercy,” and so forth.

[Col. 0137A] 17. “Scripture.” He shows that some benefit arises from the hardening of unbelievers, but he does not thereby prove that it was not unjust to reject Esau.

18. AUGUSTINE (in the same work). “Why does he still find fault?” This amounts to saying: “Why is complaint made against us because we offend God by living badly, when no one can resist his will—he who hardened us by withholding mercy?”

19. LANFRANC. “Why does he still find fault?” Having heard the statement “whom he wills he hardens,” the worldly person, living amid pleasures, could question it and murmur against God, not attributing to his own fault the fact that he is such a person: “Why is the matter still disputed? I understand what follows. My labor is useless against my vices; my effort is futile. I shall be whatever God wills me to be. For who can resist his will?”

20. AUGUSTINE (in the same work). “O man, who are you?” For the time being, let it be enough, on the basis of Christian faith [variant: “from Christian faith”], for one who is still living and does not yet behold what is perfect but knows in part, to know or believe this: that God frees no one except by gratuitous mercy through our Lord Jesus Christ, and condemns no one except by the most equitable truth through that same Lord Jesus Christ. But why he frees one person rather than another, let the one who can search out the great depth of his judgments; nevertheless, let him beware of falling.

21. LANFRANC. “But if God, wishing.” He gives the reason why unbelievers are hardened: namely, so that, through patient endurance of the tribulation inflicted by them, the faithful may be crowned, when God repays them in the future.

22. “I will call those who were not my people.” This proves that God called the vessels of mercy from the Gentiles. Before faith, the Gentiles were not the people of God.

[Col. 0138A] 23. “And it shall be in the place.” The Jews had been scattered among many nations even before Christ’s coming; from these nations it was often said that they were not the people of God.

24. “If it should be.” This proves that the vessels of mercy were called by God from the Jews. The text is found in an unusual translation in this form: “If your people Israel should be like the sand of the sea, the remnant shall be converted from it; a concise consummation has appointed righteousness.” For the Lord, the God of hosts, will accomplish the consummation and concision in the midst of the whole earth.

25. “The remnant,” that is, the lowly few who will reign from among the number of unbelieving sinners.

26. AMBROSE. “The remnant shall be saved.” When the Jews withdrew from the merit and promise of the fathers, these are the remnant who persist in faith.

27. “For the word.” Since, after all the carnal observances of the law have been removed, faith alone has been established for salvation.

28. LANFRANC. “For the word.” He calls the love of God and neighbor “the word that completes,” through which many were saved without legal observances.

29. AMBROSE. “Unless the Lord of hosts.” He says that the Savior was left to us as an aid to life; from the beginning the Lord had decreed that he should be born. He calls him “offspring” because through him the human race was restored.

30. LANFRANC. “Offspring for us.” He calls the apostles and the primitive Church “offspring.”

31. “They stumbled.” This is the reason why they did not attain the law of righteousness and why they do not believe that a person is justified by faith.

32. “As it is written,” with the implied phrase “in which there is faithful emulation.” They imitate us with a good zeal, if they do not know what they are doing: the righteousness of God, which is through faith in Christ.

## CHAPTER X

[Col. 0139]

Brothers, my desire—and I speak not out of hatred for the Jews—is that they may be saved. For my heart’s desire and supplication to God is on their behalf. For I bear them witness that they have zeal for God, and this is why I make supplication for them, but not according to knowledge. For, being ignorant of the righteousness of God, which comes through faith in Jesus Christ, and seeking to establish their own righteousness [Note: [Col. 0139A] 1. “And seeking their own.” The righteousness which they suppose to come through carnal observances], they have not submitted themselves to the righteousness of God; he proves this because they have not submitted themselves to Christ. Why not to the law? Because Christ is the fulfillment of the law. [Note: [Col. 0139A] 2. “For Christ is the end of the law.” He explains what the righteousness of God is, namely, believing in Christ. Even the legal observances, understood spiritually, urged belief in him. The sense is: the purpose of the law, by which a person is to possess righteousness, is the faith of Christ.] For Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes. [Note: [Col. 0139A] 3. AMBROSE. “The end of the law.” Whoever believes in Christ possesses the perfection of the law.] For Moses writes concerning the righteousness that comes from the law: “The person who does these things shall live by them.” [Note: [Col. 0139A] 4. LANFRANC. “For Moses.” He explains the righteousness of the law, by which the Jews thought themselves righteous without faith in Christ.]

But the righteousness that comes from faith speaks in this way: [Note: [Col. 0139A] 5. “But the righteousness that comes from faith.” The order is: Moses thus spoke of the righteousness, which is righteousness from faith.] “Do not say in your heart: Who will ascend into heaven?” [Note: [Col. 0139A] 6. “Do not say.” When you hear Christ preached as having ascended into heaven after his resurrection, he says, do not say in your heart: “It is a lie; for who ascended into heaven?” For this unbelief of yours, insofar as it depends on you, brings Christ down from heaven to earth—that is, Christ is brought down.] That is, to bring Christ down; [Note: [Col. 0139B] 7. “Or who will descend.” Likewise, when you hear him preached as having descended into hell, do not say in your heart: “It is a lie; for who will descend into the abyss?” For this unbelief of yours, insofar as it depends on you, brings Christ back from the dead.] or, “Who will descend into the abyss?” That is, to bring Christ back from the dead.

But what does Scripture say—that is, Moses? “The word is near you,” that is, Moses says that it ought to be near: “in your mouth and in your heart,” that is, the word of faith which we preach. The reason why the word of God ought to be in the mouth and not only in the heart is this: If you confess with your mouth the Lord Jesus and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved, because everyone who believes also confesses. For with the heart one believes for righteousness—that is, in order to preserve it—and with the mouth confession is made for salvation—that is, in order to attain it. For Scripture says: “Everyone who believes in him will not be put to shame.”

For there is no distinction between Jew and Greek, for the same Lord is Lord of all, rich toward all [Note: [Col. 0139B] 8. AMBROSE. “Rich toward all.” He did not say “toward those who believe,” but “toward those who call upon him.” By faith alone forgiveness is given; through prayers what God has promised is given to those who watch with their whole heart] who call upon him. [Note: [Col. 0139B] 9. LANFRANC. “Who call upon him.” Faith must be joined to this calling, because if he is not believed in, he will not be called upon.] For everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord will be saved.

How then will they call upon him in whom they have not believed? Or how will they believe in him whom they have not heard? [Note: [Col. 0140A] 10. “Whom they have not heard.” Hearing is necessary for faith, preaching for hearing, and sending for preaching.] And how will they hear without a preacher? [Note: [Col. 0140A] 11. AMBROSE. “How, then, will they preach?” Unless they are sent by Christ, no signs of power bear witness to them.] And how will they preach unless they are sent? [Note: [Col. 0140A] 12. LANFRANC. “How, then, will they preach?” Here he commends his own authority and that of the others who preach the Gospel, because the prophets had foretold concerning them just as they had foretold concerning Christ.]

As it is written: [Note: [Col. 0140A] 13. “As it is written.” The whole of this is a commendation of the Gospel, so that it may be believed.] “How beautiful are the feet of those who proclaim peace, who proclaim good things!” [Note: [Col. 0140A] 14. AMBROSE. “How beautiful are the feet.” By calling them “feet,” he signifies the arrival of the apostles, who traveled throughout the world.]

But not all obey the Gospel. For Isaiah says: “Lord, who has believed our report?” Therefore faith comes from hearing, [Note: [Col. 0140B] 15. LANFRANC. “But hearing.” It is as though he said: saving faith does not arise from every kind of hearing, but only from that in which the word of Christ is heard] and hearing through the word of Christ.

But I ask: Have they not heard? This concludes the preceding verses, in which he says: “How will they believe in him whom they have not heard, and how will they hear without a preacher?” Indeed, “their sound has gone out through the whole earth, and their words to the ends of the world.”

But I ask: Has Israel not understood? [Note: [Col. 0140B] 16. AMBROSE. “Has Israel not understood?” That is, “Has it not understood me?” Because he had accused them of unbelief, he might seem to be complaining about everyone. He does not deny that Israel attained what had been promised to it in the law, but means the Israel that is Israel in spirit.] It did understand, because Moses and Isaiah spoke. Moses is the first to say: [Note: [Col. 0140B] 17. “I will provoke you to jealousy.” Jealousy was given to them as envy, while they see a nation that formerly lived without God calling the God who had belonged to the Jews its own.] “I will provoke you to jealousy by what is not a nation; by a foolish nation I will provoke you to anger.” [Note: [Col. 0140B] 18. LANFRANC. “I will provoke you to jealousy.” The Jews are said to be provoked to jealousy when they see the glory and exaltation of the holy Church, which before faith was not the people of God.]

But Isaiah is bold and says: “I was found by those who were not seeking me; I became manifest to those who did not ask for me.” But to Israel he says: “All day long I stretched out my hands toward a people who did not believe and contradicted me.” [Note: [Col. 0141A] 19. “Isaiah is bold.” Isaiah, he says, did not refrain, for the sake of the Jews, from foretelling the good that was destined for the Gentiles and the evil that was destined for the Jews.] [Note: [Col. 0141A] 20. “I stretched out my hands.” He may mean the hands extended on the cross, or rather the works that the Lord performed among the Jews.]

## Commentary

[Col. 0139A]

### CHAPTER X

1. “And seeking their own.” The righteousness which they suppose to come through carnal observances.

2. “For Christ is the end of the law.” He explains what the righteousness of God is, namely, believing in Christ. Even the legal observances, understood spiritually, urged belief in him. The sense is: the purpose of the law, by which a person is to possess righteousness, is the faith of Christ.

3. AMBROSE. “The end of the law.” Whoever believes in Christ possesses the perfection of the law.

4. LANFRANC. “For Moses.” He explains the righteousness of the law, by which the Jews thought themselves righteous without faith in Christ.

5. “But the righteousness that comes from faith.” The order is: Moses thus spoke of the righteousness, which is righteousness from faith.

6. “Do not say.” When you hear Christ preached as having ascended into heaven after his resurrection, he says, do not say in your heart: “It is a lie; for who ascended into heaven?” For this unbelief of yours, insofar as it depends on you, brings Christ down from heaven to earth.

7. “Or who will descend.” Likewise, when you hear him preached as having descended into hell, do not say in your heart: “It is a lie; for who will descend into the abyss?” For this unbelief of yours, insofar as it depends on you, brings Christ back from the dead.

8. AMBROSE. “Rich toward all.” He did not say “toward those who believe,” but “toward those who call upon him.” By faith alone forgiveness is given; through prayers what God has promised is given to those who watch with their whole heart.

9. LANFRANC. “Who call upon him.” Faith must be joined to this calling, because if he is not believed in, he will not be called upon.

[Col. 0140A] 10. “Whom they have not heard.” Hearing is necessary for faith, preaching for hearing, and sending for preaching.

11. AMBROSE. “How, then, will they preach?” Unless they are sent by Christ, no signs of power bear witness to them.

12. LANFRANC. “How, then, will they preach?” Here he commends his own authority and that of the others who preach the Gospel, because the prophets had foretold concerning them just as they had foretold concerning Christ.

13. “As it is written.” The whole of this is a commendation of the Gospel, so that it may be believed.

14. AMBROSE. “How beautiful are the feet.” By calling them “feet,” he signifies the arrival of the apostles, who traveled throughout the world.

[Col. 0140B] 15. LANFRANC. “But hearing.” It is as though he said: saving faith does not arise from every kind of hearing, but only from that in which the word of Christ is heard.

16. AMBROSE. “Has Israel not understood?” That is, “Has it not understood me?” Because he had accused them of unbelief, he might seem to be complaining about everyone. He does not deny that Israel attained what had been promised to it in the law, but means the Israel that is Israel in spirit.

17. “I will provoke you to jealousy.” Jealousy was given to them as envy, while they see a nation that formerly lived without God calling the God who had belonged to the Jews its own.

18. LANFRANC. “I will provoke you to jealousy.” The Jews are said to be provoked to jealousy when they see the glory and exaltation of the holy Church, which before faith was not the people of God.

[Col. 0141A] 19. “Isaiah is bold.” Isaiah, he says, did not refrain, for the sake of the Jews, from foretelling the good that was destined for the Gentiles and the evil that was destined for the Jews.

20. “I stretched out my hands.” He may mean the hands extended on the cross, or rather the works that the Lord performed among the Jews.

## CHAPTER XI

[Col. 0141]

I say, then: Has God rejected his people—that is, completely? Certainly not! For I myself am an Israelite, from the seed of Abraham, of the tribe of Benjamin. God has not rejected his people, namely, the creature whom he foreknew.

Or do you not know what Scripture says in the passage concerning Elijah—that is, how he appeals to God against Israel? “Lord, they have killed your prophets, they have dug up your altars, and I alone have been left, and they seek my life.” This is written in the Third Book of Kings. But what does the divine response say to him? “I have kept for myself seven thousand men who have not bent the knee before Baal.”

Thus, then, at the present time also, a remnant has been saved according to the election of grace. But if by grace, then it is no longer by works; otherwise grace is no longer grace.

What then? What Israel was seeking, it did not obtain; but the elect obtained it. The rest, however, were blinded, as it is written: God gave them a spirit of compunction, eyes so that they would not see, and ears so that they would not hear, to this very day.

And David says: “Let their table become a snare, and a trap, and a stumbling-block, and a recompense for them. Let their eyes be darkened, so that they may not see, and always bend their back.”

I say, then: Did they stumble so as to fall? Certainly not! But through their trespass there is salvation for the Gentiles, so that they might provoke them to emulation.

And if their trespass is the wealth of the world, and their diminution the wealth of the Gentiles, how much more their fullness?

For I say to you Gentiles: Since I am indeed the apostle of the Gentiles, I will honor my ministry, if somehow I may provoke my flesh to emulation and save some of them.

For if their loss is the reconciliation of the world, what will their acceptance be but life from the dead?

And if the first portion is holy, so is the whole lump; and if the root is holy, so are the branches.

But if some of the branches have been broken off, while you, though you were a wild olive, have been grafted in among them and have become a participant in the root and richness of the olive tree, do not boast against the branches.

But if you boast, remember: You do not bear the root; the root bears you.

You will say, then: “The branches were broken off so that I might be grafted in.” Well said: They were broken off because of unbelief. But you stand by faith. Do not be high-minded, but fear.

For if God did not spare the natural branches, perhaps he will not spare you either.

See, therefore, the goodness and severity of God: severity toward those who fell, but God’s goodness toward you, if you remain in his goodness; otherwise you too will be cut off.

And they also, if they do not remain in unbelief, will be grafted in; for God is able to graft them in again.

For if you were cut from a wild olive tree by nature and, contrary to nature, were grafted into a good olive tree, how much more will those who are natural branches be grafted into their own olive tree?

For I do not want you, brothers, to be ignorant of this mystery—so that you may not be wise in your own estimation. They would be wise in their own eyes if they thought that the Jews could no longer [the verb is absent in the source]—that blindness has occurred in part in Israel, until the fullness of the Gentiles enters, and thus all Israel will be saved, as it is written:

“He will come from Zion, the one who delivers, and he will turn ungodliness away from Jacob. And this covenant will be fulfilled for them by me, when I take away their sins.”

According to the Gospel, they are enemies for your sake; but according to the election, they are beloved for the sake of the fathers. For the gifts and calling of God are irrevocable.

For just as you once did not believe God, but now have obtained mercy because of their unbelief, so they too have now not believed because of the mercy shown to you, so that they themselves also may obtain mercy.

For God has confined all things in unbelief, so that he may have mercy on all.

O depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How inscrutable are his judgments and unsearchable his ways!

For who has known the mind of the Lord? Or who has been his counselor? Or who first gave to him, so that he should be repaid?

For from him, and through him, and in him are all things. To him be glory forever. Amen.

## Commentary

### Chapter XI

1. **LANFRANC, “But the election.”** Not according to merits.

2. **“A spirit of compunction.”** Here he signifies an evil compunction, by which it often happens that even what is good becomes burdensome to a person.

2. **“Let their table become a snare.”** Their own Scripture became for the Jews a snare, and the other things that follow, because they misunderstood it. Scripture calls it a table because, for those who understand, it is bread for the soul.

3. **“Did they stumble in such a way?”** He asks whether their sin brought about merely the fall of their soul.

4. **“So that they might provoke them to emulation.”** This often happened, and it will happen more fully at the end of the age, when the Jews persecute Christians on account of faith in Christ. It may also be understood to mean that the Gentiles emulate the Jews—that is, that they believe as the Jews themselves believed. Or it may mean that they are moved by emulation of God against their evil deeds.

5. **“And if their trespass.”** The trespass of the Jews enriched the world, because unless they had crucified the Lord, Christ’s cross, resurrection, and ascension would not have been preached and believed throughout the world.

6. **AMBROSE, “Their diminution.”** Their diminution, or loss, is the loss of the promise, through which the Gentiles gained eternal life.

7. **LANFRANC, “Their diminution.”** He calls the apostles the diminution of the Jews, because, when they departed from their unbelief, that people, persisting in its unbelief, remained diminished in part.

8. **“How much more their fullness.”** The fullness of the Jews who will believe at the end of the world will greatly enrich the Gentiles, because, provoked by their example, they will be converted to Christ.

9. **AMBROSE, “My ministry.”** He honors the ministry by which he is the apostle of the Gentiles, if he also wins for life those to whom he was not sent.

10. **LANFRANC, “If somehow I may provoke to emulation.”** It is as though he said: “The Jews whom I cannot convert to Christ by preaching, I shall at least try to invite to believe in Christ by the honor with which I honor you.”

11. **“I will save some of them.”** What concern is it of yours to ask about the Jews, since you are the apostle of the Gentiles? I want to honor my ministry; and it would indeed be honored if the Jews believed, since they were wise in the Law. The Gentiles, however, were regarded as foolish and unstable because they believed so quickly; this reproach would not be made against them if the Jews believed, since the Jews were thought to be stable and wise.

12. **“For if their loss.”** A repetition of the preceding statement. What he previously called “diminution,” he here calls “loss.”

13. **“What will their acceptance be?”** The acceptance of the Jews, when they are received into faith in Christ at the end of the world, will be life from the dead. Or it will be so because he finds many dead in sins, who are provoked by their example and brought to faith in Christ; for shortly afterward there will certainly be the resurrection of the dead, that is, the end of the world.

14. **“The first portion is holy.”** He warns the Gentiles not to grow proud or despise the Jews, saying: If the apostles are holy, it is certain that many in that people are also holy—if not yet in reality, nevertheless in hope and through the divine presence. A first portion is an initial taking from something, such as from fruit, food, or drink.

15. **“Of the olive tree.”** He calls the Jewish people the olive tree, faith the root, and good works its richness.

16. **“But if you boast.”** Hear what I say to you: You do not bear the root, but the root bears you. That is, the Jewish people did not receive faith from you; rather, you received it from them.

17. **AMBROSE, “Into a good olive tree.”** Let us understand the olive tree as faith, through which Abraham was justified. The wild olive, because it is uncultivated and naturally fruitless, signifies unfaithfulness.

18. **LANFRANC, “This mystery.”** That is, the mystery by which the Jews have been blinded in part.

19. **“So that you may not be wise in your own estimation.”** That is, so that you may not appear wise to yourselves.

20. **“He will come from Zion.”** He confirms the subsequent statement by prophetic authority, namely, that all Israel will be saved.

21. **“The one who delivers.”** This deliverance will not be according to the body. Rather, this covenant—that is, the testimony that they will be delivered—will consist in taking away their sins. Or, because he had said this should not be thought to be accomplished by someone else, he says that what he testifies will be accomplished by him.

22. **“According to the Gospel.”** On account of the Gospel that I preach for your salvation, he says, the Jews are enemies to me. Yet the elect among them are beloved by me for the sake of the fathers—that is, the patriarchs and prophets, whose faith they imitate.

23. **“According to the Gospel they are enemies, and so forth.”** Lest anyone should say that he hated the Jews in his heart but outwardly pleased them with his words and thus flattered them, he says: “According to the Gospel,” which is contrary to such conduct.

24. **AUGUSTINE, *On the Predestination of the Saints*, Book I, chapter 16, volume VII, “According to the Gospel.”** What does “according to the Gospel they are enemies for your sake” mean, except that the hostility by which they killed Christ unquestionably benefited the Gospel, as we see? He shows that this came about through God’s arrangement, which he knows how to use well even with evil people—not so that the vessels of wrath might benefit them, but so that, by using them well, he might benefit the vessels of mercy.

25. **AMBROSE, “According to the Gospel.”** Because of their unbelief they are enemies of the Gospel, so that their error and trespass might open the way for the Gentiles to enter into faith.

26. **“For the gifts and calling are irrevocable.”** Grace in baptism does not seek lamentation or weeping.

27. **LANFRANC, “For the gifts and calling are irrevocable.”** This is the reason he said “according to the election.” For those to whom God inspires his faith, he inspires it without their preceding repentance; or, those whom he has chosen for eternal life, he chose without changing his purpose.

28. **“For just as you once.”** He again explains the mystery of why the Jews have been blinded in part.

29. **AMBROSE, “For God has confined.”** This means that he confined all things in unbelief so that the decreed gift might come from God when all were suffering from distrust, so that the grace of the gift might be all the more welcome.

30. **LANFRANC, “O depth.”** Lest anyone inquire into still deeper matters concerning what was said above, he anticipates the question by saying: “O depth!” and so forth.

31. **AMBROSE, “For from him.”** Because God is the creator of all things. All things are from him—the Father—and because he himself works through the Son, all things are through him. And because what is from God is through God, after being reborn in the Holy Spirit all things are in him, since the Holy Spirit is from God the Father.

## Chapter XII

[Col. 0143]

I beseech you therefore, brothers, by the mercy of God, to present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy, pleasing to God—your rational service. And do not be conformed to this age, becoming like those who are wise in worldly matters, but be transformed in the newness of your mind, that you may prove what the good, well-pleasing, and perfect will of God is. He says this because above he had stated certain insoluble questions.

For I say, through the grace given to me, to all who are among you: do not be wise beyond what it is fitting to be wise, but be wise unto sobriety, and to each according as God has apportioned the measure of faith.

For just as we have many members in one body, but all the members do not have the same function, so we, though many, are one body in Christ, and individually members of one another. But having gifts according to the grace given to us, differing according to the proportion of faith—that is, we have them as differing gifts, and likewise in the following matters—whether prophecy according to the proportion of faith; or ministry, in ministering; or he who teaches, in teaching; he who exhorts, in exhorting; he who distributes, in simplicity; he who presides, in diligence; he who shows mercy, in cheerfulness.

Let love be without pretence. Hate evil—namely, be so; or there was a digression from his saying, “For I say, through grace”—and cleave to good. Love one another with brotherly love; outdo one another in showing honour; not slothful in diligence; fervent in spirit; serving the Lord; rejoicing in hope; patient in tribulation; persevering in prayer; sharing in the necessities of the saints, that is, giving them something; pursuing hospitality.

Bless those who persecute you; bless, and do not curse. Rejoice—the same thing, that is, in the same matter—with those who rejoice; weep with those who weep; having the same disposition toward one another, that is, willing the same thing; do not be high-minded in pride, but associate with the lowly. Do not be wise in your own eyes. Repaying to no one evil for evil—evil, namely the vice of taking vengeance upon oneself—provide what is good not only before God but also before all people. If possible, so far as it depends on you, be at peace with all people; not—understand, “be”—defending yourselves, beloved, but give place to wrath. For it is written: “Vengeance is mine”—understand, “reserve vengeance for me”—“I will repay,” says the Lord.

But if your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he is thirsty, give him drink. For in doing this you will heap coals of fire upon his head, that is, upon his mind. Do not be overcome by evil, that is, by vice, but overcome evil by good, that is, by virtue.

### Commentary on Chapter XII

[Col. 0144B]

1. **AMBROSE, “I beseech you therefore.”** After the discussion of the Law and faith, he exhorts the Jewish people and the Gentiles to lead a good life.

2. **“That you present your bodies.”** Bodies subject to sins are not reckoned living, but dead.

3. **LANFRANC, “What is the good will of God.”** That is, the will that makes people good, beneficent, and perfect.

4. **“For I say.”** “Through the grace,” he says, “by which God made me your apostle, I command all not to investigate God’s works beyond what is fitting.”

5. **“But be wise.”** You ought to be wise—that is, to understand—according to the differences among God’s gifts, because every gift of the Holy Spirit differs. This is the meaning of “having gifts,” and so forth below.

6. **“And to each.”** The order is: thus God apportioned to each the measure of his gifts, which the faith of believers merits.

7. **“For just as.”** He explains how God’s gifts are apportioned among the faithful: just as the different offices are distributed among the different parts of one body, so that humility may be preserved in all.

8. **“Differing.”** Either the gifts differ, or we differ.

9. **AMBROSE, “Whether prophecy.”** Prophecy is given according to the measure of faith. The minister is strengthened, insofar as he believes, for rendering service to the brethren.

10. **LANFRANC, “The proportion of faith.”** Faith makes believers possess both prophecy and the things that follow. For unless they believed, they would not possess them. In the other cases too, “according to the proportion of faith” must be understood. The sense is: possessing prophecy, each of us ought to be a member; or, possessing ministry, we ought by ministering to be members of one another; and likewise in the other cases.

11. **AMBROSE, “He who teaches.”** He is aided by faith to hand on heavenly instruction.

12. **“He who exhorts.”** Likewise, he who exhorts to good. Likewise, he who distributes simply, and he who presides, receives vigilance according to faith; in the same way, he who cheerfully performs mercy is strengthened according to faith.

13. **“Not slothful in diligence.”** This is what Jeremiah says: “Cursed is he who does the work of the Lord negligently.” Therefore he added:

14. **“Fervent in spirit.”** That is, they should not be lukewarm in the practice of the divine work or Law.

15. **LANFRANC, “Do not be wise.”** “Do not,” he says, “make your prudence exceed only among yourselves, but rather among your neighbours.”

16. **“To no one evil.”** Evil is the vice, namely, by which a person avenges himself.

17. **AMBROSE, “Providing what is good.”** To provide what is good is to hold future things before one’s eyes, so that deeds may be done that are praiseworthy either before God or before people.

18. **“If possible.”** Even if another person is not a lover of peace, you should nevertheless wish to be peaceable, so far as depends on you. But if someone is irreverent and blasphemous and you cannot have peace with him, this certainly is not to be imputed to you.

19. **LANFRANC, “Give place to wrath.”** He gives place to wrath who permits his adversary to do what he wishes.

20. **“Coals of fire.”** That is, the fervour of love or of the Holy Spirit, so that, provoked by your example, he too may do good.

## Chapter XIII

[Col. 0147]

Let every person be subject to the higher authorities (he said this lest they should rise up, because he had said that the children of God are free); for there is no authority except from God. But those that exist have been ordained by God. Therefore whoever resists authority resists God’s ordinance. But those who resist acquire condemnation for themselves; for rulers are not a terror to good work, but to evil. Do you wish not to fear authority? Do good, and you will have praise from it; for it is God’s minister to you for good. But if you do evil, be afraid; for it does not bear the sword without cause. For it is God’s minister, an avenger for wrath against one who does evil. Therefore be subject by necessity, not only because of wrath—to be avoided—but also because of conscience—your conscience, to be preserved in good or freed from evil.

For this reason you also pay tributes; for they are ministers of God, serving this very purpose. Render therefore to all what is due: tribute to whom tribute is due (they called it *tributum* because subjects paid at home what those same subjects carried to the houses of their lords); tax to whom tax; fear to whom fear; honour to whom honour.

Owe no one anything, except to love one another; understand that, whoever you love, you owe it to love more. For whoever loves his neighbour has fulfilled the Law. For: “You shall not commit adultery; you shall not kill; you shall not steal; you shall not bear false witness; you shall not covet”; and if there is any other commandment, it is summed up in this saying: “You shall love your neighbour as yourself.” Love of neighbour—that is, one who loves his neighbour—does no evil. Therefore love is the fulfilment of the Law.

And knowing this time: it is now the hour for us to rise from sleep. For now our salvation is nearer (and the nearer anyone is to death, the nearer he is to salvation) than when we believed. The night has passed on, but the day has drawn near. Let us therefore cast off the works of darkness—that is, the vices of the flesh, which are hidden and worthy of darkness—and put on the armour of light. Let us walk honourably as in the day: not in revelry and drunkenness, not in beds and shameless acts, not in strife and emulation; but put on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make no provision for the flesh in its desires.

### Commentary on Chapter XIII

[Col. 0147A]

1. **LANFRANC, “Let [every person] be subject.”** One ought to be subject because one ought not resist. For if one resists, one resists God’s ordinance; authority is God’s ordinance, because everything that is from God is God’s ordinance, and authority is from God, for there is no authority except from God.

2. **“Therefore whoever resists authority.”** Namely, in matters belonging to authority: tributes, taxes, and other such things.

3. **“You will have praise.”** Praise comes from authority, whatever kind it is. For either it is good and praises good, or it is evil and persecutes good; and thus, by patiently enduring the tribulation inflicted, God’s servant is praised.

4. **“Be afraid; for it does not bear the sword without cause.”** He proves this because it bears it with cause, and proves it because it is God’s minister.

5. **“For it is God’s [minister].”** The reason why it ought to be feared.

6. **“For it is God’s minister.”** Another reason why those who resist acquire condemnation for themselves.

7. **“An avenger for wrath.”** Supply: against the one who does evil. For this reason they are ordained by God, or because of wrath and conscience.

8. **AMBROSE, “Not only because of wrath.”** That is, because of present punishment, but also because of the future judgment, where, with conscience accusing them, they will be punished.

9. **LANFRANC, “Serving this very purpose.”** That the good may be praised and the evil punished. “They are ministers of God” can also be understood of parents, so that the sense continues: “you pay [tributes], serving this very purpose,” namely, pleasing God.

10. **AUGUSTINE, *Letter 135 to Abbot Severus*, volume II, “Owe no one anything.”** We owe love all the more in proportion as we have apprehended it [variant: “in proportion as we have bestowed it more abundantly”]; the Apostle shows us to be its perpetual debtors when he says: “Owe no one anything, except to love one another.”

11. **AMBROSE, “The night has passed on.”** He means by “night” the old man, and says that it has passed; but that the day has drawn near, that is, Christ, by whose light truth has appeared to us.

12. **“Let us therefore cast off.”** That is, the vices of the flesh, which are hidden and worthy of darkness.

13. **“Let us put on.”** Good actions are the armour of light, assailing the works of darkness.

## Chapter XIV

[Col. 0147]

[Note: [Col. 0148A] CHAPTER XIV.—1. AMBROSE. “But the weak.” There were some Jews who had received the Romans into the faith. It seemed to them that prohibited meat ought not to be eaten; for this reason he calls them “weak.” Others thought otherwise; the Apostle recalls those disputing here, seeking concord.]

[Note: [Col. 0148B] 2. LANFRANC. “But the weak.” It belongs to the perfect faith of Christians to regard no food as unclean, because “all things are clean to the clean.” Yet some who were weak in this faith thought that they ought to abstain from certain foods. The Apostle commands that such a person should not be despised but received with charity, so that he should not be judged guilty even in his thoughts.]

“But the weak”—because some lived by eating pork and others did not, the Apostle moderates their differences. He calls weak the one who did not believe that he ought to eat meat [perhaps: “who did not believe that he ought to eat the meat”]—“receive in faith, not for disputes about opinions.” For one person—that is, this person—has perfect faith and believes that he may eat everything; but the one who is weak, namely, in this faith, should eat vegetables—that is, he should be permitted to abstain.

Let the one who eats, namely, all foods, not despise the one who does not eat; [Note: [Col. 0148B] 3. AUGUSTINE (*On Christian Combat*, ch. 27, vol. III). “The one who does not eat.” “Judgment” is spoken of in the sense of condemnation. The Apostle says: “Let the one who does not eat not judge the one who eats,” that is, let him not think evil of him. And the Lord says: “Do not judge, so that you may not be judged.”] and let the one who does not eat, that is, the abstainer, not judge the one who eats, that is, let him not think evil of him; for God has received him, that is, both the one who eats and the one who abstains.

Who are you to judge another’s servant? [Note: [Col. 0149A] 4. LANFRANC. “He stands or falls before his own master,” that is, for the praise of his own Lord; whether he has perfect faith or is weak in faith, he acts with a good intention.] Before his own master he stands or falls; but he will stand, for God is able to make him stand.

For one person [Note: [Col. 0149A] 5. “He distinguishes one day from another,” that is, some think that one ought to abstain on certain days, while others think that one ought to abstain every day.] distinguishes one day from another, while another distinguishes every day. [Note: [Col. 0149A] 6. “Let each abound in his own understanding.” As though he were saying: Let the one who thinks that everything may be used do so with thanksgiving; and let the one who thinks that he ought to abstain abstain for God’s sake.] Let each person abound in his own understanding.

[Note: [Col. 0149A] 7. “The one who observes the day,” that is, understands that a day is to be kept through abstinence.] The one who observes the day observes it for the Lord, that is, for the Lord’s honor; and the one who eats, that is, all foods, eats for the Lord, that is, for the Lord’s honor. He eats for the Lord because he does not eat for himself—for he does not drink wine for himself, nor does he die for himself—and he gives thanks to God for the abstinence granted to him. And the one who does not eat does not eat for the Lord, and he gives thanks to God. For none of us lives for himself, and none of us dies for himself.

[Note: [Col. 0149A] 8. AUGUSTINE (*Exposition on Psalm 144*). “Whether we live.” Just as the Lord’s greatness has no end, so your praise will have no end. For when you have died in this flesh, you will not cease to praise God. How did it come about that you belong to him even when dead? Because he redeemed you, dead, by the price of his blood. How does he lose a dead servant whose death is your price? Therefore, after saying, “whether we live or die, we are the Lord’s,” he showed that he himself is the price. “For to this end,” he says, “Christ died.” 9. LANFRANC. “For we shall all stand.” Do not despise him, but be concerned for yourself; for each person will render an account for himself, because we shall all stand before Christ’s tribunal.] For whether we live, we live for the Lord; and whether we die, we die for the Lord. Therefore, whether we live or die, we are the Lord’s. For Christ died and rose again for this purpose: that he might be Lord both of the dead and of the living.

But you, namely, the abstainer, why do you judge your brother, namely, the one who eats? Or you, why do you despise your brother? [Note: The supplied text numbers this sentence “9.”] For we shall all stand before Christ’s tribunal. For it is written:

> “As I live, says the Lord, every knee shall bow to me, and every tongue shall confess to God.”

Therefore each of us shall render an account to God for himself. Let us no longer judge one another; but judge this rather: [Note: [Col. 0149B] 10. “Do not place a stumbling-block.” Do not place a stumbling-block before your brother, that is, do not grieve him; for if you grieve him, you are not walking according to charity.] do not place a stumbling-block before your brother, or an occasion of offense.

[Note: [Col. 0149C] 11. AMBROSE. “I know and am confident.” It is clear, by the Savior’s benefit, that all things are clean. By freeing human beings from the yoke of the law, he restored their original condition of freedom.]

[Note: [Col. 0149C] 12. LANFRANC. “I know and am confident.” He gives his judgment between the two preceding positions, saying that no creature made through Christ is common, that is, unclean. For the Jews called what was unclean “common.”]

I know and am confident in the Lord Jesus that nothing is common through him, [Note: [Col. 0150A] 13. AMBROSE. “Except for the one who considers it so,” that is, it is unclean for the one who thinks that it ought not to be eaten. And since he does not do this out of superstition but out of personal fear, it is to be reserved for judgment.] except for the one who considers something to be common; for that person it is common.

[Note: [Col. 0150A] 14. LANFRANC. “For him it is common.” As though he were saying: In reality nothing is unclean; but for the one who thinks something unclean, it is unclean only in his opinion.]

For if your brother is grieved because of food, namely, food that you eat or from which you abstain, you are no longer walking according to charity. [Note: [Col. 0150A] 15. “For if because of food.” Do not grieve him; for if you grieve him because of food, you destroy him by your food. But you ought not to destroy him, since Christ died for him. Therefore do not grieve him; that is, “then our good must not be blasphemed.” He states the consequence of grieving, because from grief it follows that Christianity is blasphemed.] Do not destroy by your food the one for whom Christ died. Therefore let our good not be blasphemed.

[Note: [Col. 0150B] 16. “The kingdom of God is not food.” Food, drink, or consumption does not make a person possess the kingdom of God, but righteousness and the rest.]

For the kingdom of God is not food and drink, but righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit. For the one who serves Christ in this is pleasing to God and approved by human beings. Therefore let us pursue what makes for peace and what makes for edification among one another let us preserve.

[Note: [Col. 0150B] 17. AMBROSE. “Do not destroy God’s work because of food.” The human being is God’s work; and again, he is God’s work when he is renewed through rebirth.]

Do not destroy God’s work, that is, charity, because of food.

[Note: [Col. 0150B] 18. “All things indeed.” Although animals are clean by nature, they become unclean for those who doubt; and it will be an offense to the one who eats while doubting.] All things indeed are clean; but it is evil for the person who eats through an occasion of offense.

[Note: [Col. 0150B] 19. LANFRANC. “Through an occasion of offense,” that is, the one who scandalizes the person who does not eat by his own eating.]

It is good [Note: [Col. 0150B] 20. “Not to eat.” This is what he says: if the one who abstains is present at this moment and is so weak that he cannot patiently watch one who uses God’s creatures, then it is better for the one who has faith that everything may be used to abstain from them than, by his own eating, to inflict distress upon the abstainer.] not to eat meat, nor to drink wine, nor to do anything by which your brother is offended, scandalized, or weakened.

Do you have faith—namely, faith that everything may be used? Keep it to yourself before God.

[Note: [Col. 0151A] 21. AMBROSE. “Blessed is the one who does not judge.” He calls blessed the person who does nothing other than what he approves as useful for himself.] Blessed is the one who does not judge himself, that is, make himself guilty, in the matter that he approves.

[Note: [Col. 0151A] 22. LANFRANC. “The one who does not eat.” Do not eat in the presence of your brothers, because if you do not eat, you are blessed. He proves this as follows: everyone is blessed who does not judge himself, that is, make himself guilty, which happens when he does not eat so as not to offend.] But the one who makes a distinction, [Note: [Col. 0151A] 23. “But the one who makes a distinction.” The one who distinguishes foods, that is, who thinks that some are clean and others unclean, is condemned because his action is not from faith. For our faith requires a person to do what he understands ought rightly to be done.] if he eats, is condemned, because it is not from faith.

[Note: [Col. 0151A] 24. “If he eats, and so forth.” He proves that the person who does not judge himself, that is, does not eat, is blessed, since every eater is condemned. He says it in this way: “The one who makes a distinction, if he eats,” and so forth. There are several oppositions: “does not judge” and “eats”; he proves that the one who makes a distinction—that is, who does not approve eating—is blessed if he does not eat, and condemned if he eats.]

But whatever is not from faith is sin.

[COMMENTARY.]

[Col. 0148A]

CHAPTER XIV.—1. AMBROSE. “But the weak.” Among those whom the Apostle had brought to faith there were some from the Jews. It seemed to them that prohibited meat ought not to be eaten; for this reason he calls them “weak.” Others thought otherwise; the Apostle recalls those disputing here, seeking concord.

2. LANFRANC. “But the weak.” It belongs to the perfect faith of Christians to regard no food as unclean, because “all things are clean to the clean.” Yet some who were weak in this faith thought that they ought to abstain from certain foods. The Apostle commands that such a person should not be despised but received with charity, so that he should not be judged guilty even in his thoughts.

3. AUGUSTINE (*On Christian Combat*, ch. 27, vol. III). “The one who does not eat.” “Judgment” is spoken of in the sense of condemnation. [Col. 0149A] The Apostle says: “Let the one who does not eat not judge the one who eats,” that is, let him not think evil of him. And the Lord says: “Do not judge, so that you may not be judged.”

4. LANFRANC. “Before his own master he stands,” that is, for the praise of his own Lord; whether he has perfect faith or is weak in faith, he acts with a good intention.

5. “He distinguishes one day from another,” that is, some think that one ought to abstain on certain days, while others think that one ought to abstain every day.

6. “Let each abound.” As though he were saying: Let the one who thinks that everything may be used do so with thanksgiving; and let the one who thinks that he ought to abstain abstain for God’s sake.

7. “The one who observes,” that is, understands that a day is to be kept through abstinence.

8. AUGUSTINE (*Exposition on Psalm 144*). “Whether we live.” [Col. 0149B] Just as the Lord’s greatness has no end, so your praise will have no end. For when you have died in this flesh, you will not cease to praise God. How did it come about that you belong to him even when dead? Because he redeemed you, dead, by the price of his blood. How does he lose a dead servant whose death is your price? Therefore, after saying, “whether we live or die, we are the Lord’s,” he showed that he himself is the price. “For to this end,” he says, “Christ died.”

9. LANFRANC. “For we shall all stand.” Do not despise him, but be concerned for yourself; for each person will render an account for himself, because we shall all stand before Christ’s tribunal.

10. “Do not place a stumbling-block.” Do not place a stumbling-block before your brother, that is, do not grieve him; for if you grieve him, you are not walking according to charity.

[Col. 0149C] 11. AMBROSE. “I know and am confident.” It is clear, by the Savior’s benefit, that all things are clean. By freeing human beings from the yoke of the law, he restored their original condition of freedom.

12. LANFRANC. “I know and am confident.” He gives his judgment between the two preceding positions, saying that no creature made through Christ is common, that is, unclean. For the Jews called what was unclean “common.”

13. AMBROSE. “Except for the one who considers it so,” that is, it is unclean for the one who thinks that it ought not to be eaten. And since he does not do this out of superstition but out of personal fear, it is to be reserved for judgment.

14. LANFRANC. “For him it is common.” As though he were saying: In reality nothing is unclean; but for the one who thinks something unclean, it is unclean only in his opinion.

15. “For if because of food.” Do not grieve him; for if you grieve him because of food, you destroy him by your food. But you ought not to destroy him, since Christ died for him. Therefore do not grieve him; that is, “then our good must not be blasphemed.” He states the consequence of grieving, because from grief it follows that Christianity is blasphemed.

16. “The kingdom of God is not food.” Food, drink, or consumption does not make a person possess the kingdom of God, but righteousness and the rest.

17. AMBROSE. “Do not destroy God’s work because of food.” The human being is God’s work; and again, he is God’s work when he is renewed through rebirth.

18. “All things indeed.” Although animals are clean by nature, they become unclean for those who doubt; and it will be an offense to the one who eats while doubting.

19. LANFRANC. “Through an occasion of offense,” that is, the one who scandalizes the person who does not eat by his own eating.

20. “Not to eat.” This is what he says: if the one who abstains is present at this moment and is so weak that he cannot patiently watch one who uses God’s creatures, then it is better for the one who has faith that everything may be used to abstain from them than, by his own eating, to inflict distress upon the abstainer.

[Col. 0151A] 21. AMBROSE. “Blessed is the one who does not judge.” He calls blessed the person who does nothing other than what he approves as useful for himself.

22. LANFRANC. “The one who does not eat.” Do not eat in the presence of your brothers, because if you do not eat, you are blessed. He proves this as follows: everyone is blessed who does not judge himself, that is, make himself guilty, which happens when he does not eat so as not to offend.

23. “But the one who makes a distinction.” The one who distinguishes foods, that is, who thinks that some are clean and others unclean, is condemned because his action is not from faith. For our faith requires a person to do what he understands ought rightly to be done.

24. “If he eats, and so forth.” He proves that the person who does not judge himself, that is, does not eat, is blessed, since every eater is condemned. He says it in this way: “The one who makes a distinction, if he eats,” and so forth. There are several oppositions: “does not judge” and “eats”; he proves that the one who makes a distinction—that is, who does not approve eating—is blessed if he does not eat, and condemned if he eats.

25. “But whatever is not from faith.” He is condemned because what he does is sin; and he proves this as follows: “Whatever is not from faith is sin.” But this is not from faith; this premise has already been stated where he says, “because it is not from faith.”

## CHAPTER XV.

[Col. 0151]

But we who are stronger ought to bear the weaknesses of the weak and not to please ourselves.

[Note: [Col. 0151B] CHAPTER XV.—1. AMBROSE. “Let each of you.” He admonishes them that, devoted to charity, they should please their neighbors for what is useful. For this is edification.]

Let each of you please his neighbor for the good, for edification. For Christ did not please himself, but, as it is written:

> “The reproaches of those who reproached you fell upon me.”

[Note: [Col. 0151B] 2. LANFRANC. “Whatever was written.” As though someone were saying: What does Christ’s having had circumcision performed for himself have to do with life? What does prophecy concerning God have to do with it? What does it have to do with the formation of our morals? He answers: “Whatever was written,” and so forth.]

For whatever was written was written for our instruction, so that through the patience and consolation of the Scriptures we might have hope. Now may the God of patience and consolation grant you to think the same thing toward one another, according to Jesus Christ, so that with one mind and one mouth you may glorify God and the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ.

Therefore receive one another, [Note: [Col. 0151C] 3. “Just as Christ also,” and so forth. He received you, both Jews and gentiles, by approving you; but he shows how Christ accommodated himself to us, because he was circumcised, and that we should accommodate ourselves to the weak.] just as Christ also received you, to the honor of God.

[Note: [Col. 0151C] 4. “For I say.” Praise of the Jews. He says that Christ made himself a minister of circumcision in order to fulfill the truth of God and the promises made to the fathers. For it had been promised that one would arise from the seed of the Jews, in whom all would be blessed. Alternatively: “The ministry of circumcision,” that is, toward the Jewish people, so that the truth of God and his promises made to the fathers might be fulfilled. Such promises include: “I will give you a shoot [or: ornament] of righteousness,” and: “God will raise up a prophet for you,” and so forth.]

For I say that Christ Jesus became a minister of circumcision on behalf of the truth of God, to confirm the promises made to the fathers.

[Note: [Col. 0152A] 5. “But the gentiles.” He proves that he received the gentiles, or that the gentiles should honor God, on the authority of the Jews.] But the gentiles, [Note: [Col. 0152A] 6. AMBROSE. “But the gentiles.” Since no promise had been made to them, as though they were unworthy, they were received into salvation solely through God’s mercy.] on account of mercy—I say that they ought to honor God—as it is written:

[Note: [Col. 0152B] 7. LANFRANC. “But the gentiles.” Praise of the gentiles. He says that God cared so greatly for them that he foretold through his prophets that they would be saved. Through these praises he shows them to be equal to one another, so that neither should presume to put himself before the other.]

> “Therefore I will confess to you among the gentiles, O Lord, and I will sing to your name.”

And again he says:

[Note: [Col. 0152B] 8. “Therefore I will confess.” The voice of Christ, who among the gentiles confesses the Father because through his conversion [or: preaching] they have been converted to the worship of the one God.]

> “Therefore I will confess to you among the gentiles, O Lord, and I will sing to your name.”

And again he says:

[Note: [Col. 0152B] 9. “Rejoice, gentiles.” In Isaiah it is written: “Rejoice with Jerusalem, and exult in her, all you who love her.”]

> “Rejoice, gentiles, with his people.”

And again:

> “Praise the Lord, all you gentiles, and magnify him, all peoples.”

And Isaiah again says:

[Note: [Col. 0152B] 10. “There shall be a root of Jesse.” The order is: “Jesse shall be the root,” and so forth. Understand that from this root there shall arise one who will rise to rule the gentiles.]

> “There shall be a root of Jesse, and the one who rises to rule the gentiles; in him the gentiles shall hope.”

Now may the God of hope fill you with all joy and peace in believing, so that you may abound in hope and in the power of the Holy Spirit.

[Note: [Col. 0152C] 11. “I am confident,” and so forth. He makes them well disposed, as though saying: I corrected you, not because I do not know that you love one another; nor did I admonish you because I do not know that you are wise; rather, it is my duty to admonish you.]

But I myself also am confident concerning you, my brothers, that you too are full of love, [Note: [Col. 0152C] 12. “Filled with all knowledge.” The Apostle’s humility. He says that he wrote to them not because they themselves were in need. For, as he himself admits, they were filled with all knowledge; but he was compelled by the necessity of his office, since he had been appointed by God as the Apostle of the gentiles.] filled with all knowledge, so that you are able to admonish one another.

[Note: [Col. 0153A] 13. “More boldly.” It seemed bold to write to those who were filled with all knowledge.]

But I have written to you somewhat more boldly, brothers, as reminding you again, because of the grace given to me by God, that I should be a minister of Christ Jesus among the gentiles, sanctifying the Gospel of God, so that the offering of the gentiles might be acceptable and sanctified in the Holy Spirit.

[Note: [Col. 0153A] 14. AMBROSE. “Therefore I have glory.” He says that he has glory before God through Christ. By believing [alternate reading: “by believing”] in Christ, he acquired merit before the people, to such an extent that he says there is nothing in himself that Christ did not work through him, so that the power of Christ might commend his exhortation.] [Note: [Col. 0153A] 15. LANFRANC. “Therefore I have glory.” Whatever they may think me to be as a human being [perhaps: “as human beings”], nevertheless I know that I have glory before God in the preaching of Jesus Christ, because I do what I do for God’s honor and the salvation of the gentiles.]

Therefore I have my glory in Christ Jesus before God.

[Note: [Col. 0153A] 16. “For I do not dare.” Another reason why he has glory before God: whatever he speaks, whatever Christ works in him and through him, Christ speaks and works, so that the gentiles may obey the Gospel.]

For I will not dare to speak of anything except what Christ accomplishes through me for the obedience of the gentiles, by word and deed, through the power of signs and wonders, through the power of the Holy Spirit. Thus, from Jerusalem and round about as far as Illyricum, I have filled the region—that is, I have fully preached—the Gospel of Christ.

In this way I have made it my aim to preach the Gospel where Christ has not been named, so that I might not build on another’s foundation, but as it is written in Isaiah, chapter 52:

> “Those to whom he was not announced shall see, and those who have not heard of him shall understand.”

For this reason also I was greatly hindered from coming to you, and I have been prevented until now. But now, since I have no further place in these regions, and since I have desired for many years to come to you, when I begin to travel to Spain I hope to see you as I pass through, and to be sent on there by you, after I have first enjoyed your company in part.

But now I shall travel to Jerusalem to minister, that is, to bring bodily necessities to the saints. For Macedonia and Achaia have approved making some contribution for the poor among the saints who are in Jerusalem. They were pleased to do so, and they are their debtors. They are debtors in material things; and he proves this from the greater, because they received spiritual things from them, which is greater.

For if the gentiles have become partakers of their spiritual things—that is, if the teaching of faith and right living was brought from Jerusalem to the gentiles through the apostles—they ought also to minister to them in material things.

Therefore, when I have completed this and delivered this fruit to them, I shall travel to Spain by way of you. I know that when I come to you, I shall come in the abundance of the blessing of Christ’s Gospel.

I appeal to you, brothers, through our Lord Jesus Christ and through the love of the Holy Spirit, to assist me in your prayers to God on my behalf: that I may be delivered from the unbelievers who are in Judea; that my service may be acceptable to the saints in Jerusalem; and that I may come to you with joy, by the will of God, and be refreshed with you.

May the God of peace be with all of you. Amen.

[COMMENTARY.]

[Col. 0151B]

CHAPTER XV.—1. AMBROSE. “Let each of you.” He admonishes them that, devoted to charity, they should please their neighbors for what is useful. For this is edification.

2. LANFRANC. “Whatever was written.” As though someone were saying: What does Christ’s having had circumcision performed for himself have to do with life, [Col. 0151C] for the sake of the truth? What does prophecy concerning God have to do with it? What does it have to do with the formation of our morals? He answers: “Whatever was written,” and so forth.

3. “Just as Christ also,” and so forth. He received you, both Jews and gentiles, by approving you; but he shows how Christ accommodated himself to us, because he was circumcised, and that we should accommodate ourselves to the weak.

4. “For I say.” Praise of the Jews. He says that Christ made himself a minister of circumcision in order to fulfill the truth of God and the promises made to the fathers. For it had been promised that one would arise from the seed of the Jews, in whom all would be blessed. Alternatively: “The ministry of circumcision,” that is, toward the Jewish people, so that the truth of God and his promises made to the fathers might be fulfilled. Such promises include: “I will give you a shoot [or: ornament] of righteousness,” and: “God will raise up a prophet for you,” and so forth.

5. “But the gentiles.” He proves that he received the gentiles, or that the gentiles should honor God, on the authority of the Jews.

6. AMBROSE. “But the gentiles.” Since no promise had been made to them, as though they were unworthy, they were received into salvation solely through God’s mercy.

[Col. 0152B] 7. LANFRANC. “But the gentiles.” Praise of the gentiles. He says that God cared so greatly for them that he foretold through his prophets that they would be saved. Through these praises he shows them to be equal to one another, so that neither should presume to put himself before the other.

8. “Therefore I will confess.” The voice of Christ, who among the gentiles confesses the Father because through his conversion [or: preaching] they have been converted to the worship of the one God.

9. “Rejoice, gentiles.” In Isaiah it is written: “Rejoice with Jerusalem, and exult in her, all you who love her.”

10. “There shall be a root of Jesse.” The order is: “Jesse shall be the root,” and so forth. Understand that from this root there shall arise one who will rise to rule the gentiles.

[Col. 0152C] 11. “But I am confident,” and so forth. He makes them well disposed, as though saying: I corrected you, not because I do not know that you love one another; nor did I admonish you because I do not know that you are wise; rather, it is my duty to admonish you.

12. “Filled with all knowledge.” The Apostle’s humility. He says that he wrote to them not because they themselves were in need. For, as he himself admits, they were filled with all knowledge; but he was compelled by the necessity of his office, since he had been appointed by God as the Apostle of the gentiles.

13. “More boldly.” It seemed bold to write to those who were filled with all knowledge.

14. AMBROSE. “Therefore I have glory.” He says that he has glory before God through Christ. By believing [alternate reading: “by believing”] in Christ, he acquired merit before the people, to such an extent that he says there is nothing in himself that Christ did not work through him, so that the power of Christ might commend his exhortation.
