15. LANFRANC. “Therefore I have glory.” Whatever they may think me to be as a human being [perhaps: “as human beings”], nevertheless I know that I have glory before God in the preaching of Jesus Christ, because I do what I do for God’s honor and the salvation of the gentiles.

16. “For I do not dare.” Another reason why he has glory before God: whatever he speaks, whatever Christ works in him and through him, Christ speaks and works, so that the gentiles may obey the Gospel.

## CHAPTER XVI.

[Col. 0153]

[Note: [Col. 0154A] CHAPTER XVI.—1. LANFRANC. “I commend to you Phoebe.” She was a very wealthy and noble woman who supported with her resources the church of God that was at a place called Cenchreae. At that time she had gone to Rome on some business. Perhaps he sent this letter through her.]

I commend to you Phoebe, our sister, who is in the ministry of the church at Cenchreae, so that you may receive her in the Lord in a manner worthy of the saints, and assist her in whatever matter she may need you; for she herself also assisted many, and me personally.

Greet Prisca and Aquila, my fellow workers in Christ Jesus, who risked their own necks for my life; to whom not I alone give thanks, but also all the churches of the gentiles. Greet also their household church.

Greet Epaenetus, beloved by me, who is also the first convert of Asia in Christ.

Greet Mary, who labored greatly among you.

Greet Andronicus and Junia, my relatives and fellow prisoners, who are notable among the apostles and who were in Christ before me.

Greet Ampliatus, my beloved in the Lord.

Greet Urbanus, our fellow worker in Christ Jesus, and Stachys, my beloved.

Greet Apelles, approved in Christ.

Greet those who are of Aristobulus’s household.

Greet Herodion, my relative.

Greet those who are of Narcissus’s household who are in the Lord.

Greet Tryphaena and Tryphosa, who labor in the Lord.

Greet Persis, the beloved woman who labored greatly in the Lord.

Greet Rufus, chosen in the Lord, [Note: [Col. 0154A] 2. “And his mother and mine.” Either he commands that his own mother be greeted together with Rufus’s mother; or he calls one and the same woman both his mother and Rufus’s: Rufus’s according to the flesh, and his own through her kindness.] and his mother and mine.

Greet Asyncritus, Phlegon, Hermes, Patrobas, Hermas, and the brothers who are with them.

Greet Philologus and Julia, Nereus and his sister, and Olympias, and all the saints who are with them.

Greet one another with a holy kiss. All the churches of Christ greet you.

I appeal to you, brothers, to watch out for those who create dissensions and occasions of offense contrary to the doctrine that you have learned, and to avoid them. For such people do not serve Christ our Lord but their own belly; and through smooth speech and blessings they deceive the hearts of the innocent.

[Col. 0155] [Note: [Col. 0154A] 3. “For your obedience.” The reason why he appeals to them: the obedient are to be entreated, whereas the disobedient are to be rebuked.]

For your obedience has become known everywhere. Therefore I rejoice in you. But I want you to be wise in what is good and innocent in what is evil.

[Note: [Col. 0155A] 4. “May he crush Satan.” The Lord crushed Satan under the feet of the Church, because he converted to the faith and subjected to the Church the members through whom Satan had persecuted it.]

Now may the God of peace crush Satan under your feet swiftly. The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you.

Timothy, my fellow worker, and Lucius, Jason, and Sosipater, my relatives, greet you.

[Note: [Col. 0155A] 5. “I greet you.” The order is: “I greet you in the Lord.” This Tertius was the Apostle’s third secretary, who wrote this Epistle.]

I, Tertius, who wrote the Epistle, greet you in the Lord.

Gaius, my host and that of the whole church, greets you.

Erastus, the city treasurer, greets you, and Quartus, the brother.

The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with all of you. Amen.

[Note: [Col. 0155A] 6. AMBROSE. “Now to him.” “To him who is able to strengthen you, to the only wise God, be glory forever and ever.”] [Note: [Col. 0155A] 7. LANFRANC. “Now to him,” that is, to the one who can lead you to as much perfection as I proclaim and as Christ proclaimed and established to be proclaimed.]

Now to him who is able to strengthen you according to my Gospel and the preaching of Jesus Christ, [Note: [Col. 0155A] 8. “According to the revelation,” that is, so that you may believe in the way in which God’s mystery has been revealed; and he uses the singular for the plural.] according to the revelation [Note: [Col. 0155B] 9. “Of the mystery.” He calls the incarnation of Jesus Christ a mystery, along with the other things that had been silent through eternal times. Although they were known in part to the ancient Fathers, they were fully known by no one until they were revealed through Jesus Christ in their own time.] of the mystery kept silent through eternal times—which has now been revealed [Note: [Col. 0156A] 10. “Through the Scriptures of the prophets.” Christ revealed the Scriptures of the prophets to his apostles, as it is read in the Gospel: “Then he opened their understanding, so that they might understand the Scriptures,” and so forth.] through the Scriptures of the prophets, according to the command of the eternal God, for the obedience of faith, made known among all the gentiles—to the only wise God [Note: [Col. 0156A] 11. AMBROSE. “Through Jesus,” that is, through Jesus Christ; for, to say nothing of other matters, he himself commanded the gentiles to be baptized in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, where the glory of this undivided Trinity is especially commended.] through Jesus Christ, [Note: [Col. 0156A] 12. “To whom be honor.” The addition of “to whom,” so that he says “to whom,” although it would have been sufficient to say “to him be glory,” indicates an unfamiliar expression in our language; it does not suggest a different meaning that we must seek or about which we should be uncertain.] to whom be honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.

[COMMENTARY.]

[Col. 0154A]

CHAPTER XVI.—1. LANFRANC. “I commend to you Phoebe.” She was a very wealthy and noble woman who supported with her resources the church of God that was at a place called Cenchreae. At that time she had gone to Rome on some business. Perhaps he sent this letter through her.

2. “And his mother and mine.” Either he commands that his own mother be greeted together with Rufus’s mother; or he calls one and the same woman both his mother and Rufus’s: Rufus’s according to the flesh, and his own through her kindness.

3. “For your obedience.” The reason why he appeals to them: the obedient are to be entreated, whereas the disobedient are to be rebuked.

[Col. 0155A] 4. “May he crush Satan.” The Lord crushed Satan under the feet of the Church, because he converted to the faith and subjected to the Church the members through whom Satan had persecuted it.

5. “I greet you.” The order is: “I greet you in the Lord.” This Tertius was the Apostle’s third secretary, who wrote this Epistle.

6. AMBROSE. “Now to him.” “To him who is able to strengthen you, to the only wise God, be glory forever and ever.”

7. LANFRANC. “Now to him,” that is, to the one who can lead you to as much perfection as I proclaim and as Christ proclaimed and established to be proclaimed.

8. “According to the revelation,” that is, so that you may believe in the way in which God’s mystery has been revealed; and he uses the singular for the plural.

9. “Of the mystery.” He calls the incarnation of Jesus Christ a mystery, along with the other things that had been silent through eternal times. Although they were known in part to the ancient Fathers, they were fully known by no one until they were revealed through Jesus Christ in their own time.

10. “Through the Scriptures of the prophets.” Christ revealed the Scriptures of the prophets to his apostles, as it is read in the Gospel: “Then he opened their understanding, so that they might understand the Scriptures,” and so forth.

11. AMBROSE. “Through Jesus,” that is, through Jesus Christ; for, to say nothing of other matters, he himself commanded the gentiles to be baptized in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, where the glory of this undivided Trinity is especially commended.

12. “To whom be honor.” The addition of “to whom,” so that he says “to whom,” although it would have been sufficient to say “to him be glory,” indicates an unfamiliar expression in our language; it does not suggest a different meaning that we must seek or about which we should be uncertain.

# THE FIRST EPISTLE OF BLESSED PAUL THE APOSTLE TO THE CORINTHIANS, WITH THE INTERPOSED GLOSS OF BLESSED LANFRANC.

[Col. 0155]

[Col. 0155C] ARGUMENT.—The Corinthians are Achaeans, and they likewise heard the word of truth from the Apostle. They were led astray in many ways by false apostles: some by the verbose eloquence of philosophy, others having been drawn in by the sect of the Jewish law. The Apostle recalls them to the true faith and evangelical wisdom, writing to them from Ephesus through his disciple Timothy.

## CHAPTER ONE.

Paul, called an apostle of Jesus Christ by the will of God, and Sosthenes, a brother, to the Church of God that is at Corinth,

[Note: [Col. 0155D] **CHAPTER I.—1. AMBROSE. “Sanctified.”** Because, having been regenerated in Christ, they have been sanctified.]

sanctified, dwelling in Christ Jesus, called to be holy, so that they may be holy,

[Note: [Col. 0155D] **2. AUGUSTINE** (*in Exposition of Psalm LI*, vol. VIII). “With all who call upon.” Those who call upon the Lord [elsewhere, “God”] for worldly advantages, earthly goods, the present life, and earthly happiness do not call upon God.]

with all who call upon the name of our Lord Jesus Christ in every place belonging to them and to us—that is, in the Church, in which all things are common. Grace—the remission of sins, or the observance of good works—to you, and peace—that is, reconciliation with God—from God our Father and our Lord Jesus Christ, and from our Lord Jesus Christ.

[Note: [Col. 0156D] **4. AMBROSE. “I give thanks to my God.”** Although he writes to everyone in the Church, he expresses himself in such a way—sometimes reproving, sometimes praising—that each person, when reading, understands what is said for him and what against him.]

I give thanks to my God always for you, for the grace of God that was given to you in Christ Jesus, in the faith of Christ,

[Note: [Col. 0157A] **5. LANFRANC. “That in everything you have been enriched.”** He puts the whole for a part. For they were not all rich in every virtue. Some of them he rebukes later.]

because in everything you have been enriched in him, in every word, so that you may be able to preach, and in all knowledge, so that you may know what must be preached; just as the testimony of Christ—what we testified to you concerning Christ—was confirmed in you, so that nothing is lacking to you—you have been enriched—in any grace, in any gift of the Holy Spirit, while you await

[Note: [Col. 0157A] **6. “Revelation,”** that is, the vision which occurs after death or on the day of judgment.]

the revelation—that is, the vision which occurs after death or on the day of judgment—of our Lord Jesus Christ. He will also confirm you to the end of your life, or to the end of the age, blameless on the day of the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ—that is, at each person’s death or on the day of judgment. God is faithful: he will confirm you, for there must be no doubt concerning his promises. Through him, through whose grace, you were called into the fellowship of his Son Jesus Christ our Lord, so that you might be co-heirs with Christ, his children.

I beseech you, brothers, by the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that you all say the same thing and that there be no schisms among you; but that you be perfected in the same understanding, the same will, and the same judgment—I ask that there be no schisms among you. For it has been reported to me concerning you, my brothers, by those who belong to Chloe, that there are contentions among you.

[Note: [Col. 0157A] **7. “Each one of you.”** Not every individual was saying all four of these things; one must understand: “One says, ‘I indeed belong to Paul,’ while another says, ‘I belong to Apollos,’” and so forth. For he himself explained it in what follows, saying: “When someone says, ‘I indeed belong to Paul,’ while another says, ‘I belong to Apollos,’” and so forth.]

“of Cephas”—that is, Peter. “Cephas” means “head,” whence *acephali*, that is, “without a head”—“but I belong to Christ.”

not

in wisdom of speech, so that the cross of Christ might not be emptied.

it is the power of God—that is, it gives power from God to the believer, through which miracles occur when circumstances require them.

I will destroy the wisdom of the wise—this is the reason why he did not preach in wisdom of speech—and I will reject the understanding of the intelligent.

He declares that they have been brought to nothing—not because he entirely rejects their teachings, since in many matters they agree with the sacred Scriptures, but because they thought and wrote certain things contrary to the Christian religion, especially concerning the worship of the one God.]

[Note: [Col. 0159A] **18. AUGUSTINE** (from *On Pastoral Care*, chapter 12, vol. IX). “Did he not make foolish?” In Scripture, “wisdom” is sometimes used for cunning, through an abuse of the word rather than according to its proper meaning.]

Did God not make the wisdom of this world foolish? For because the world did not know God through the wisdom of God—that is, through divine counsel—it was not pleasing that the world should know God through worldly wisdom;

LANFRANC. “It pleased God through the foolishness,” etc.** “I do not preach in wisdom of speech”—which he proves by saying that it pleased God to save believers through the foolishness of preaching. He proves this because the wisdom of the world was not pleasing: although it exists within God’s wisdom, the world did not know God through wisdom.]

it pleased God, through the foolishness of preaching—that is, through preachers ignorant of worldly letters—to save believers.

For

a stumbling-block indeed to the Jews, because they are said to have crucified their king,

but foolishness to the Gentiles. Yet to those who are called, predestined to life, both Jews and Greeks, Christ is the power of God

and the wisdom of God.

Therefore the Apostle calls Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God. For what is foolish of God is wiser than human beings,

For what is foolish—incarnation and passion—to unbelievers is wiser than human beings;

This foolishness and weakness—the incarnation and passion of Christ—possess such wisdom and power that the devil is defeated and the human race redeemed.]

and what is weak of God is stronger than human beings.

[Note: [Col. 0160B] **30. AMBROSE. “What is weak of God.”** The weakness of Christ is a great victory: he conquered when he appeared to have been conquered.]

For see your calling—that is, through whom you were called—brothers: not many who were wise according to the flesh preached the kingdom of God to you,

not many powerful—that is, not many preached the word of God—not many noble. ## Commentary

[Col. 0155D]

### Chapter I

1. **AMBROSE. “Sanctified.”** Because, having been regenerated in Christ, they have been sanctified.

2. **AUGUSTINE** (*in Exposition of Psalm LI*, vol. VIII). “With all who call upon.” Those who call upon the Lord [elsewhere, “God”] for worldly advantages, earthly goods, the present life, and earthly happiness do not call upon God.

3. **LANFRANC. “In every place.”** He says: “You possess both word and knowledge, just as the testimony of Christ—that is, of his incarnation, passion, and the rest—was confirmed, and by various authorities of the Old Testament among you and between you.”

4. **AMBROSE. “I give thanks to my God.”** Although he writes to everyone in the Church, he expresses himself in such a way—sometimes reproving, sometimes praising—that each person, when reading, understands what is said for him and what against him.

[Col. 0157A]

5. **LANFRANC. “That in everything you have been enriched.”** He puts the whole for a part. For they were not all rich in every virtue. Some of them he rebukes later.

6. **“Revelation,”** that is, the vision which occurs after death or on the day of judgment.

7. **“Each one of you.”** Not every individual was saying all four of these things; one must understand: “One says, ‘I indeed belong to Paul,’ while another says, ‘I belong to Apollos,’” and so forth. For he himself explained it in what follows, saying: “When someone says, ‘I indeed belong to Paul,’ while another says, ‘I belong to Apollos,’” and so forth.

8. **AUGUSTINE. “I belong to Cephas.”** These people divide the Church among themselves and try to make parties out of unity.

9. **AMBROSE. “Christ has been divided.”** He says that Christ has been divided because they have apportioned his glory among human beings.

10. **“Not in wisdom.”** The unlearned were chosen so that the truth of the teaching might commend itself by the testimony of power, lest it appear acceptable through the cleverness of human wisdom rather than through truth.

11. **LANFRANC. “Not in wisdom.”** By “wisdom” he means dialectic, through which the cross—that is, the death of Christ—appears to be nullified to those who understand it simply: God is immortal, but Christ is God; therefore Christ is immortal. If he is immortal, he could not die. The same applies to the Virgin’s childbirth and certain other mysteries. Yet, for those who examine them intelligently, dialectic does not attack God’s mysteries; when the matter requires it, if held entirely correctly, it supports and confirms them.

12. **“In wisdom of speech.”** He does not prove it syllogistically, because in that way it could rather be disproved. Or, even if they were convicted and believed by syllogistic argument, it would not benefit them.

13. **AUGUSTINE** (from *On Nature and Grace against Pelagius*, chapter 7, vol. VII). “So that it may not be emptied.” It is emptied if it is said that one can somehow attain righteousness and eternal life apart from its mystery.

14. **LANFRANC. “For the word.”** This is the reason why he does not preach in wisdom of speech. Those devoted to that art, although strangers to the Christian religion—whom he calls “those who are perishing,” either because their teaching perishes in certain respects or because they are destined to perish eternally—consider the death of Christ foolishness.

15. **“It is the power of God,”** that is, it gives God’s power to the believer, through which miracles occur when circumstances require them.

[Col. 0158B]

16. **“I will destroy the wisdom.”** Another reason why he does not preach in wisdom of speech: the prophecy has rejected it by its authority. It may also be an answer, as though someone had asked, “Why do you say ‘to those who are perishing’?” This is read in Obadiah: “Will I not, on that day, says the Lord, destroy the wise men from Edom and the understanding from Mount Esau?”

17. **“Where is the scribe?”** These are the Apostle’s words. Scribes are the authors of moral and natural books and writers of worldly actions—that is, those who give precepts concerning these arts. Investigators are reasoners who approve something on the basis of the precepts of those arts. “Wise” is the general term for both. He declares that they have been brought to nothing—not because he entirely rejects their teachings, since in many matters they agree with the sacred Scriptures, but because they thought and wrote certain things contrary to the Christian religion, especially concerning the worship of the one God.

[Col. 0159A]

18. **AUGUSTINE** (from *On Pastoral Care*, chapter 12, vol. IX). “Did he not make foolish?” In Scripture, “wisdom” is sometimes used for cunning, through an abuse of the word rather than according to its proper meaning.

19. **LANFRANC. “It pleased God through the foolishness,” etc.** “I do not preach in wisdom of speech”—which he proves by saying that it pleased God to save believers through the foolishness of preaching. He proves this because the wisdom of the world was not pleasing: although it exists within God’s wisdom, the world did not know God through wisdom.

20. **“Jews.”** The Jews were scandalized because they were said to have crucified their king.

21. **AMBROSE. “The Jews ask for signs.”** Hence they say: “We know that God spoke to Moses,” although it is a greater thing that Lazarus came alive out of the tomb.

[Col. 0159B]

22. **“And the Greeks seek wisdom.”** Because they do not wish to hear anything except what is possible according to the reasoning of the world.

23. **“A stumbling-block indeed to the Jews.”** It is a stumbling-block to the Jews when they hear Christ professing himself to be the Son of God and abolishing the Sabbath.

24. **“But foolishness to the Gentiles.”** They hear preached those things which, because they do not accord with human reason, appear senseless, such as the Virgin’s childbirth and the resurrection of the dead.

25. **“The power and wisdom of God.”** He is the power of God because through him God the Father made all things; wisdom, because through him God has been known.

26. **AUGUSTINE** (from book I of *Questions on the Gospels*, question 14, vol. IV). “The power of God and the wisdom.” The Jews said concerning our Lord: “Where did this man get this wisdom and these powers?” Wisdom was shown in what he said; powers in what he did. Therefore the Apostle calls Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God. He referred “power” to signs, because of the Jews; “wisdom,” or teaching, to the Greeks—that is, the Gentiles [elsewhere: “wisdom” refers to teaching because of the Greeks].

27. **AUGUSTINE** (*Expositions on Psalm LXVIII*, sermon 1, vol. VIII). “For what is foolish.” What is more like imprudence than this: although he had the power, with a single word, to overthrow his persecutors, he allowed himself to be seized, scourged, spat upon, struck on the face, crowned with thorns, and fastened to wood? It resembles imprudence and appears foolish.

[Col. 0160A]

28. **LANFRANC. “What is foolish.”** The incarnation and passion of God and man, Jesus Christ, which appeared foolish to such wise people, contain greater wisdom than human beings can seek out and possess greater strength than human beings could have. Through faith in them sins are forgiven, demons are expelled, and other miracles occur when he rises again.

29. **“What is foolish.”** He proves Christ to be wisdom because there is wisdom even in what appears foolish concerning him, and such wisdom that it cannot be comprehended by everyone, since it is wiser than human beings. Then he proves Christ to be power because in what appears weak concerning him there is power, and such power that it is stronger than human beings—that is, cannot be comprehended by them. This foolishness and weakness—the incarnation and passion of Christ—possess such wisdom and power that the devil is defeated and the human race redeemed.

30. **AMBROSE. “What is weak of God.”** The weakness of Christ is a great victory: he conquered when he appeared to have been conquered.

31. **AUGUSTINE** (from *Tractate 15 on John*, vol. IX). “And what is weak.” Why, then, was woman made from the rib as though she were strong, while Adam was made in flesh as though he were weak? Christ and the Church are signified: his weakness is our strength.

32. **LANFRANC. “Not many wise.”** Perhaps he says this with reference to himself, because among the other apostles he alone was skilled in scholarly letters, rich in earthly possessions, and distinguished by kinship with Roman dignity, as he himself testifies in the Acts of the Apostles: “I am indeed a Jewish man, a citizen of Tarsus in Cilicia, a city of no mean repute.” Elsewhere, when the tribune asked whether he was a Roman, he answered, “Yes.” And the tribune said, “I acquired this citizenship for a great sum.” Paul replied, “But I was born a Roman.” Elsewhere, when he was giving an account, Festus exclaimed: “You are mad, Paul; your many letters are driving you mad.”

33. **AUGUSTINE** (*Sermon 9, On the Three Rods*, among the fragments, vol. X). “Contemptible.” Things that are not counted.

[Col. 0161A]

34. **“Who was made for us.”** God chose things that are not—that is, things that are not counted.

35. **AUGUSTINE** (letter 222 to Consentius, vol. II). “He was made righteousness for us by God.” Just as, although life exists in him, he also becomes life for us when we become participants in him, so, although righteousness exists in him, he also becomes righteousness for us when, cleaving to him, we live well.

36. **AUGUSTINE** (from *The Literal Meaning of Genesis*, book XI, chapter 8, vol. III). “He who glories.” Thus let the one who glories glory only in the Lord, when he recognizes that it is not his own but the Lord’s—not only that he exists, but also that it is well with him only through the one from whom he has received existence.

37. **LANFRANC. “He who glories, let him glory in the Lord.”** This testimony is read in Jeremiah as follows: “Let the one who glories glory in this: that he understands and knows me, that I am the Lord.”

## Chapter II

[Col. 0161]

And I, when I came to you, brothers, came not

[Note: [Col. 0161B] **Chapter II.—1. LANFRANC. “Not in sublimity.”** He calls “sublimity of speech” logic, because it is entirely concerned with artificial discourse. He calls the quadrivium wisdom, especially the Platonic books, using the name of a genus to designate a species.]

in sublimity of speech, with syllogistic proofs, or of wisdom, announcing to you the testimony of Christ.

[Note: [Col. 0161B] **2. AUGUSTINE** (*On the Trinity*, book I, chapter 12, vol. III). “For I judged myself not to know.” He was speaking to people who could not grasp higher things concerning Christ’s divinity. He said that he knew only what they needed to know through him. Among them he did not know what they could not know through him.]

For this does not prove that he chose the foolish; rather, he says of himself—this is what follows: “And I, when I came,” etc.—“I did not judge myself to know anything among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified.”

And I—he likewise proves that he chose the weaker, because of what follows: “And I in weakness,” etc.—was among you in weakness and fear of soul, and with much trembling of body. And my speech and my preaching were not in

[Note: [Col. 0161B] **3. LANFRANC. “Persuasive.”** He touches upon rhetoric, in which rules are given for speaking suitably to persuade.]

persuasive words of human wisdom, dialectical proofs, but in the demonstration of the Spirit—“I said only what the Spirit showed me”—and of power, of miracles, so that your faith might not be in the wisdom of human beings but in the power of God.

And lest they should say that he did not know, he adds: We speak wisdom among the perfect; yet not the wisdom of this age,

[Note: [Col. 0161C] **4. “Nor of the rulers.”** Here he calls “rulers” the outstanding philosophers, from whom and through whom philosophy was invented. They are designated by this name even in secular literature, as Cicero says in the *Topics*: “Aristotle, as it seems to me, was the chief of both.”]

nor of the rulers—or demons—of this age, who are being destroyed;

[Note: [Col. 0161C] **5. AUGUSTINE** (from a sermon on the reading in the Gospel of John, preserved by Bede). “But we speak.” This Christian grace—because all things have been handed over to Christ by the Father—was hidden from all the wise of this world. Moses saw it; the prophets saw it. Those great wise men, those clever disputants, were entirely ignorant of it. This is the mystery that was hidden from the ages in God.]

[Note: [Col. 0162A] **6. AMBROSE. “But we speak the wisdom of God.”** The wisdom of God, therefore, was hidden, since it exists not in words but in power; it is not attainable by human reasoning but is believed through the efficacy of the Spirit.]

but we speak the wisdom of God in a mystery,

[Note: [Col. 0162A] **7. LANFRANC. “In a mystery.”** By expounding the mysteries of the Old Testament, in which we assert that Christ was prefigured.]

which was hidden, which God predestined before the ages to come for our glory—that is, so that through it we might be glorified;

[Note: [Col. 0162A] **8. AMBROSE. “Which none of the rulers.”** The rulers of this age are to be understood not only as human beings but also as those against whom we struggle, who knew that Christ had been promised in the Law but did not know his mystery, namely, that he is the Son of God.]

which

[Note: [Col. 0162B] **9. LANFRANC. “None of the rulers,” etc.** He proves that none of the rulers knew it because it is written. He also proves that they did not understand it because those who love him alone know it. Then, in “But God revealed it to us,” he proves that it was revealed: “through the Spirit,” etc. He proves this because “we received the Spirit,” etc.—that is, “the Spirit who is from God,” etc. He proves that they received the Spirit of God because “we did not receive the spirit of this world.”]

none of the rulers of this age knew. For if they had known,

[Note: [Col. 0162B] **10. AUGUSTINE** (from book I of *On the Trinity*, chapter 13). “They would never have crucified the Lord of glory.” He was crucified according to the form of a servant; such was the assumption by which God became human and the human became God. What is said, however, why it is said, and according to what aspect, the prudent, diligent, and devout reader will understand with the Lord’s assistance.]

they would never have crucified the Lord of glory or incited his crucifixion.

But, as it is written—namely, this:

[Note: [Col. 0162C] **11. LANFRANC. “What eye has not seen.”** He proves what he said above: “None of the rulers of this age knew.” The wisdom of God—that is, the Lord Christ—prepared as a reward for those who love him, neither eye has seen, etc. It is written in Isaiah as follows: “Eye has not seen, O God, apart from you, what you have prepared for those who love you.”]

What the bodily eye has not seen, nor the bodily ear heard, nor the bodily heart of a human being conceived—what God prepared for those who love him—God has revealed to us through his Spirit.

[Note: [Col. 0163A] **12. AUGUSTINE** (from a tractate on Psalm LII, vol. VIII). “For the Spirit searches all things.” It is said of the Spirit of God that he searches all things, even the depths of God—not because he searches as one who does not know everything, but because the Spirit has been given to you and makes you search. What you do by his gift is said to be done by him.]

For the Spirit—can this be said of the Spirit of God? He answers—searches all things, that is, knows and causes them to be known, even the depths of God. For who among human beings knows the things of a human being, since no one else does except the spirit of the human being that is in him? So also no one has known the things of God except the Spirit of God.

[Note: [Col. 0163A] **13. AUGUSTINE** (from *On the Nature of Martyrdom of the Massylites*; sermon 42, *On Various Matters*, chapter 3, vol. X). “But we did not receive the spirit.” The spirit of this world is a spirit of arrogance; those who have it are proud and ungrateful toward God.]

[Note: [Col. 0163A] **14. AMBROSE. “But we did not receive the spirit.”** The spirit of the world is the spirit by which fanatics, who are without God, are seized; they call it Python. This is the spirit that spoke through the Sibyl.]

But we did not receive the spirit of this world, but the Spirit who is from God, so that we might know the things given to us by God.

These things we also speak,

[Note: [Col. 0163B] **15. LANFRANC. “Not in learned words.”** He denies that he speaks in words of human wisdom. Yet in his Scriptures there is such subtlety in the treatment of passages and arguments, and such a great and subtle effort to gain goodwill when circumstances require it, that nothing comparable or greater is found in any other kind of Scripture. Therefore, without doubt, we must believe that he did not consider the rules of secular arts in writing or speaking. Rather, through the teaching of the Holy Spirit, from whom and through whom comes every useful skill, he said such things and in such a way. I would expound them individually if I did not fear the complaints of those inexperienced in such teachings.]

not in learned words of human wisdom, but in the teaching of the Spirit, which the Spirit supplies,

[Note: [Col. 0163B] **16. “Comparing spiritual things,”** that is, adapting spiritual teaching according to the capacity of the spiritual hearer; what is heard spiritually is proved to spiritual persons.]

comparing spiritual things with spiritual things according to the measure of what they can receive.

IV). “The animal person.” One who lives according to the body is called a carnal or animal person. “Carnal” because he pursues carnal things; “animal” because he is carried along by the uncontrolled wantonness of his soul, which he does not govern by the spirit and which does not remain within the limits of the natural order. One who governs his soul by the spirit is called spiritual.]

But the animal person

[Col. 0164A]

does not perceive the things that are of the Spirit of God;

[Note: [Col. 0164A] **19. LANFRANC. “The animal person.”** He is called animal because he rejects spiritual things themselves, and therefore cannot labor to understand them.]

for they are foolishness to him, and therefore he cannot understand them, because they are examined—that is, condemned—spiritually, according to the inner person.

[Note: [Col. 0164A] **20. AUGUSTINE** (from *On True Religion*, chapter 31, vol. II). “But the spiritual person.” Such a person judges all things because, when with God, he is above all things. [Note: [Col. 0164A] **21. LANFRANC. “But the spiritual person.”** The spiritual person, he says, understands and reproves everything that ought to be understood and reproved; and he himself is neither reproved nor understood by any of the carnal. The verb is found with both meanings.]

But the spiritual person judges, understands, and reproves all things,

and he himself is judged and reproved by no one.

## Commentary

[Col. 0161B]

### Chapter II

1. **LANFRANC. “Not in sublimity.”** He calls “sublimity of speech” logic, because it is entirely concerned with artificial discourse. He calls the quadrivium wisdom, especially the Platonic books, using the name of a genus to designate a species.

2. **AUGUSTINE** (*On the Trinity*, book I, chapter 12, vol. III). “For I judged myself not to know.” He was speaking to people who could not grasp higher things concerning Christ’s divinity. He said that he knew only what they needed to know through him. Among them he did not know what they could not know through him.

3. **LANFRANC. “Persuasive.”** He touches upon rhetoric, in which rules are given for speaking suitably to persuade.

[Col. 0161C] 4. **NEITHER OF THE RULERS.** Here he calls rulers eminent philosophers, by whom and through whom philosophy was discovered. They are designated by this name even in secular literature, as Cicero does in the *Topics*: “Aristotle, as it seems to me, was the chief of both.”

5. **AUGUSTINE** (from a sermon on the reading in the Gospel of John, cited by Bede). **But we speak.** This Christian grace—for everything has been handed over to Christ by the Father—was unknown to all the wise men of this world. Moses saw it; the prophets saw it. Those great wise men, the clever disputants, were altogether ignorant of it. This is the mystery that had been hidden from the ages in God.

6. **AMBROSE. But we speak God’s wisdom.** God’s wisdom is therefore hidden, since it is not in words but in power; it is not attainable by human reasoning, but is believed through the efficacy of the Spirit.

7. **LANFRANC. In a mystery.** By explaining the mysteries of the Old Testament, in which we assert that Christ was prefigured.

8. **AMBROSE. Which none of the rulers.** The rulers of this age are to be understood not only as human beings, but also as those against whom our struggle is, who knew that Christ had been promised in the Law; yet they did not know his mystery, namely, that he is the Son of God.

[Col. 0162B] 9. **LANFRANC. None of the rulers, etc.** He proves that none of the rulers knew it because it is written. Likewise, he proves that they did not know it because only those who love him know it. “But to us”—that is, “he revealed it.” He proves that it was revealed because it was “through the Spirit,” etc. He also proves that we received the Spirit, etc.—that is, “the Spirit who is from God,” etc. And he proves that he received the Spirit of God because “we did not receive the spirit of this world.”

10. **AUGUSTINE** (from Book I of *On the Trinity*, chapter 13). **They never crucified the Lord of glory.** He was crucified in the form of a servant, for such was that taking-on which made God man and man God. What is said, however, and on account of what, and according to what, the prudent, diligent, and devout reader will understand with the Lord’s help.

[Col. 0162C] 11. **LANFRANC. What eye has not seen.** He proves what he said above: “None of the rulers of this age knew.” For the wisdom of God—that is, the Lord Christ—which has been prepared as a reward for those who love him, “eye has not seen,” etc. It is written in Isaiah as follows: “No eye has seen, O God, apart from you, what you have prepared for those who love you.”

[Col. 0163A] 12. **AUGUSTINE** (from a treatise on Psalm 52, vol. VIII). **For the Spirit searches all things.** It is said of the Spirit of God that he searches all things, even the depths of God—not because he searches as one who does not know, since he knows everything, but because the Spirit has been given to you and has made you search; and what you do by his gift is said to be done by him.

13. **AUGUSTINE** (from the treatise *On the Nature of the Massylite Martyrs*; Sermon 42, *On Various Subjects*, chapter 3, vol. X). **But we did not receive the spirit.** The spirit of this world is a spirit of arrogance; those who possess it are proud and ungrateful to God.

14. **AMBROSE. But we did not receive the spirit.** The spirit of the world is the spirit by which fanatics, who are without God, are seized; they call it the Python. This is the spirit that spoke through the Sibyl.

[Col. 0163B] 15. **LANFRANC. Not in learned words.** He denies that he speaks in the words of human learning. And yet in his writings there is found, whenever the matter requires it, such subtlety in the discussion of subjects and such subtle skill in winning goodwill that nothing equal to it, or greater, is found in any other genre of writing. Hence it must undoubtedly be believed that, in writing or speaking, he did not deliberately employ the rules of secular arts, but that through the teaching of the Holy Spirit—from whom and through whom all useful knowledge comes—he spoke such words and in such a manner. I would explain these one by one, were it not that I feared the complaints of those ignorant of such disciplines.

16. **Comparing spiritual things**, that is, adapting spiritual teaching according to the capacity of the spiritual hearer; things heard spiritually are approved by spiritual people.

17. **AMBROSE. The natural person.** For, being like cattle, he presses his understanding down toward the earth.

18. **AUGUSTINE** (from Book 83 of the *Questions*, question 67, vol. IV). **The natural person.** One who lives according to the body is called a carnal or natural person. He is carnal because he pursues carnal things; he is natural because he is carried along by the unrestrained wantonness of his soul, which the spirit does not govern and which does not remain within the bounds of the natural order. But one who governs his soul by the spirit is called spiritual.

19. **LANFRANC. The natural person.** He is called natural because he rejects spiritual things themselves, and therefore cannot labor to understand them.

20. **AUGUSTINE** (from *On True Religion*, chapter 31, vol. II). **But the spiritual person.** He judges all things, therefore, because he is above all things when he is with God. He is with him when he understands with perfect purity and loves with complete charity what he understands.

21. **LANFRANC. But the spiritual person.** The spiritual person, he says, understands and reproves everything that ought to be understood and reproved; and he himself is neither reproved nor understood by any of the carnal. This word is found in both senses.

22. **And he himself is judged by no one.** The spiritual person is understood by no one, because no one understands; for no one has known the mind of the Lord. He proves this again from the cause: he is reproved by no one because no one reproves him; and he proves this because no one instructs him.

23. **Who has known.** This refers to the preceding meaning of the word.

24. **Who may instruct him.** This refers to the subsequent meaning. For whoever reproves must possess the knowledge required to instruct.

# CHAPTER III

[Col. 0163]

And I, brothers, could not speak to you as spiritual people, but as carnal people (the reason why he did not speak spiritual things to them). As infants in Christ, I gave you milk—that is, lesser commandments—as drink, not solid food, not higher teachings; for you were not yet able to receive them. Indeed, even now you cannot, for you are still carnal. Since there is jealousy and strife among you, are you not carnal, and do you not walk according to human beings rather than according to the Spirit of God? You live in a merely human manner. He explains how they walk according to human beings.

[Note: [Col. 0164B] CHAPTER III.—1. LANFRANC. When someone says. An explanation of jealousy and strife.]

For when someone says, “I am a disciple of Paul,” while another says—

[Note: [Col. 0164B] 2. AMBROSE. I planted. To plant is to evangelize and draw someone to the faith. To water, however, is to baptize with solemn words.]

“I am of Apollos,” are you not human beings? Are you not acting in a merely human way?

[Note: [Col. 0164C] 3. What, then, is Apollos? You ought not to say, “I belong to Paul” or “to Apollos,” but to God; for Apollos and Paul are nothing in comparison with God. They are his ministers, just as the Lord gave to each one. He enumerates the functions of the ministry, namely preaching and baptizing.]

What, then, is Apollos? And what is Paul? Ministers of him in whom you believed, and each of us according to what the Lord gave. [Col. 0165] (To some more, to others less.) I planted through preaching in the faith; Apollos watered through baptizing; but God gave the growth. (He says that Paul and Apollos are nothing because only God gives the growth.) Therefore, since only God matters, neither the one who plants nor the one who waters is anything, but God, who gives the growth. The one who plants and the one who waters are one in the faith. Each, however, will receive his own reward, though their rewards will be different according to their labor and in proportion to the quality of their merits.

[Note: [Col. 0165A] 4. LANFRANC. For we are God’s. The reason why he said “reward”: the laborers, whom he here calls assistants, customarily receive a reward.]

For we are God’s assistants—preachers. You are God’s field; you are God’s building, and so am I. According to God’s apostolic grace, which was given to me, I laid the foundation—the faith of Christ—as a wise architect; another builds upon it. Let each one see how he builds upon it and carry out his works.

[Note: [Col. 0165A] 5. AUGUSTINE (from *On Faith and Works*, chapter 16, vol. IV). Foundation. The faith of Christian grace—that is, the faith that works through love—when laid in the foundation, does not allow anyone to perish. Upon this foundation one person builds gold, silver, and precious stones: namely, the person who considers the things of God and how to please God. Another builds wood, hay, and straw upon the same foundation: namely, the person who considers the things of the world and how to please his wife. (In the same work, from the *Enchiridion to Laurentius*, chapter 68, vol. III.) The work of the one who did not love those things whose loss would cause him anguish is not burned up. The work of the other is burned up, because things possessed with love do not perish without pain. But since, when the choice was presented, he would rather be without those things than without Christ, and because of fear of losing them did not abandon Christ—although he grieves when he loses them—he is indeed saved, yet as through fire. (In the same work, shortly before.) This fire is the trial of tribulation, of which it is written: “The furnace tests the potter’s vessel, and the trial of tribulation tests righteous people.”]

[Note: [Col. 0165B] 6. LANFRANC. For no other foundation. Someone might say: Why did you say, “Let him merely build upon it,” and not say, “Let him lay the foundation”? By no means, he says; for no one can lay another foundation, etc.]

For no one can lay any other foundation apart from that which I laid, which is Jesus Christ—the faith of Christ.

[Note: [Col. 0165B] 7. AMBROSE. But if anyone builds upon it, etc. The first three signify good works; the following three signify empty doctrine.]

But if anyone builds upon this foundation of faith—through these three good works, gold, silver, and precious stones, and through those lesser sins, wood, hay, and straw—each person’s work will become manifest. For the day of the Lord, the day of judgment, will disclose it, because the quality of each person’s work will be revealed in fire and through fire; purifying fire will test it in this way: if someone’s work remains—the work he built upon the faith—he will receive a reward; if someone’s work is burned, he will suffer loss, though he himself will be saved, yet as through fire.

[Note: [Col. 0165C] 8. As through fire. The fire of the final judgment will last until those who are to be saved have been purified.]

[Note: [Col. 0165C] 9. AUGUSTINE (from a treatise on Psalm 122). Do you not know that you are God’s temple? All who are still weak and walk according to faith are, according to faith, God’s temple; and at some time we shall be God’s temple, and already so according to hope [variant: appearance]. How long are they a temple according to faith? As long as Christ dwells in them through faith.]

[Note: [Col. 0166A] 10. AMBROSE. Do you not know that you are God’s temple? He said this beforehand in order to pierce them with remorse, because by living shamefully and violating their bodies they had corrupted themselves.]

Do you not know (so that there may be no schisms among you) that you are God’s temple and that the Spirit of God dwells in you?

[Note: [Col. 0166A] 11. LANFRANC. You are God’s temple. Therefore, so that you do not destroy God’s temple by sinning, you must not violate it; for if you do this, the Lord will destroy you: “For whoever violates God’s temple, God will destroy.” You violate it by sinning, and he proves this as follows. You are God’s temple because the Spirit of God dwells in you; that is to say, you are God’s dwelling place. Moreover, everything holy is God’s temple; but you are holy; therefore you are God’s temple. Yet while you sin, you violate yourselves; therefore you violate God’s temple.]

If anyone violates God’s temple, God will destroy him. For God’s temple is holy, and that is what you are.

[Note: [Col. 0166B] 12. Let no one deceive himself, that is, let no one think that he benefits himself by his own or by human counsel. He returns to what came before.]

Let no one deceive himself (thinking that God disregards this or does not heed these words). If anyone among you seems to be wise in this age—

[Note: [Col. 0166B] 13. To be wise in this age, that is, in the cunning of this age; let him become foolish, that is, recognize himself as foolish and count his wisdom as foolishness.]

—let him become foolish, so that he may be wise. For the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God; that is, let him lay down his own wisdom. He must lay it down, for all foolishness must be laid down. For it is written in Job, chapter 5:

[Note: [Col. 0166B] 14. I will seize the wise. It is written thus in Job: “He who catches the wise in their cunning.” Everything that ensnares must be laid aside; but cunning ensnares—for it is written, “I will seize,” etc.—therefore, and so forth.]

“I will seize the wise in their cunning.” And again:

[Note: [Col. 0166B] 15. The thoughts of the wise. In an unusual translation it reads, “the thoughts of human beings.”]

“The Lord knows the thoughts of the wise, that they are futile.”

Therefore let no one boast in human beings—in preachers or baptizers—because Paul and Apollos are nothing.

[Note: [Col. 0166B] 16. AMBROSE. For all things are yours. The present life has been granted to us so that we may spend it for the glory of God; death, so that we may wish to die for Christ in the hope of the future promise. Present things have been given so that we may use them in such a way as not to offend against future things, and future things so that, believing them, we may entrust ourselves to them.]

[Note: [Col. 0166C] 17. LANFRANC. For all things. It is as though he said: each person ought to glory in himself, in greater and more excellent things, not in those things that belong to him.]

For all things are yours (the reason why they ought not to glory in teachers, namely, because teachers are ministers), whether Paul or Cephas—

[Note: [Col. 0167A] 18. Whether the world. The world was made for the benefit of human beings.]

—or this world,

[Note: [Col. 0167A] 19. Whether life. The life and death of teachers ought to serve for the edification of their subjects. We may also understand by “life” holy human beings and angels; by “death,” the devil and his members, who, while they advise or persecute, serve the benefit of God’s servants.]

—or life, of teachers, which ought to be for the edification of their subjects—or death, or things present, or things future. For all things are yours; but you are Christ’s.

[Note: [Col. 0167A] 20. AUGUSTINE (from Book 83 of the *Questions*, question 57, vol. IV). But Christ is God’s. Not as though he were unlike or of another nature, but as the Son of the Father.]

But Christ is God’s according to his humanity.

[Col. 0164B]

# CHAPTER III

1. **LANFRANC. When someone says.** An explanation of jealousy and strife.

2. **AMBROSE. I planted.** To plant is to evangelize and draw someone to the faith. To water, however, is to baptize with solemn words.

3. **What, then, is Apollos?** You ought not to say, “I belong to Paul” or “to Apollos,” but to God; for Apollos and Paul are nothing in comparison with God. They are his ministers, just as the Lord gave to each one. He enumerates the functions of the ministry, namely preaching and baptizing.

[Col. 0165A] 4. **LANFRANC. For we are God’s.** The reason why he said “reward”: the laborers, whom he here calls assistants, customarily receive a reward.

5. **AUGUSTINE** (from *On Faith and Works*, chapter 16, vol. IV). **Foundation.** The faith of Christian grace—that is, the faith that works through love—when laid in the foundation, does not allow anyone to perish. Upon this foundation one person builds gold, silver, and precious stones: namely, the person who considers the things of God and how to please God. Another builds wood, hay, and straw upon the same foundation: namely, the person who considers the things of the world and how to please his wife. (In the same work, from the *Enchiridion to Laurentius*, chapter 68, vol. III.) The work of the one who did not love those things whose loss would cause him anguish is not burned up. The work of the other is burned up, because things possessed with love do not perish without pain. But since, when the choice was presented, he would rather be without those things than without Christ, and because of fear of losing them did not abandon Christ—although he grieves when he loses them—he is indeed saved, yet as through fire. (In the same work, shortly before.) This fire is the trial of tribulation, of which it is written: “The furnace tests the potter’s vessel, and the trial of tribulation tests righteous people.”

6. **LANFRANC. For no other foundation.** Someone might say: Why did you say, “Let him merely build upon it,” and not say, “Let him lay the foundation”? By no means, he says; for no one can lay another foundation, etc.

7. **AMBROSE. But if anyone builds upon it, etc.** The first three signify good works; the following three signify empty doctrine.

[Col. 0165C] 8. **As through fire.** The fire of the final judgment will last until those who are to be saved have been purified.

9. **AUGUSTINE** (from a treatise on Psalm 122). **Do you not know that you are God’s temple?** All who are still weak and walk according to faith are, according to faith, God’s temple; and at some time we shall be God’s temple, and already so according to hope [variant: appearance]. How long are they a temple according to faith? As long as Christ dwells in them through faith.

10. **AMBROSE. Do you not know that you are God’s temple?** He said this beforehand in order to pierce them with remorse, because by living shamefully and violating their bodies they had corrupted themselves.

11. **LANFRANC. You are God’s temple.** Therefore, so that you do not destroy God’s temple by sinning, you must not violate it; for if you do this, the Lord will destroy you: “For whoever violates God’s temple, God will destroy.” You violate it by sinning, and he proves this as follows. You are God’s temple because the Spirit of God dwells in you; that is to say, you are God’s dwelling place. Moreover, everything holy is God’s temple; but you are holy; therefore you are God’s temple. Yet while you sin, you violate yourselves; therefore you violate God’s temple.

12. **Let no one deceive himself**, that is, let no one think that he benefits himself by his own or by human counsel. He returns to what came before.

13. **LANFRANC. To be wise in this age**, that is, in the cunning of this age; let him become foolish, that is, recognize himself as foolish and count his wisdom as foolishness.

14. **I will seize the wise.** It is written thus in Job: “He who catches the wise in their cunning.” Everything that ensnares must be laid aside; but cunning ensnares—for it is written, “I will seize,” etc.—therefore, and so forth.

15. **The thoughts of the wise.** In an unusual translation it reads, “the thoughts of human beings.”

16. **AMBROSE. For all things are yours.** The present life has been granted to us so that we may spend it for the glory of God; death, so that we may wish to die for Christ in the hope of the future promise. Present things have been given so that we may use them in such a way as not to offend against future things, and future things so that, believing them, we may entrust ourselves to them.

17. **LANFRANC. For all things.** It is as though he said: each person ought to glory in himself, in greater and more excellent things, not in those things that belong to him.

18. **Whether the world.** The world was made for the benefit of human beings.

19. **Whether life.** The life and death of teachers ought to serve for the edification of their subjects. We may also understand by “life” holy human beings and angels; by “death,” the devil and his members, who, while they advise or persecute, serve the benefit of God’s servants.

20. **AUGUSTINE** (from Book 83 of the *Questions*, question 57, vol. IV). **But Christ is God’s.** Not as though he were unlike or of another nature, but as the Son of the Father.

[Note: [Col. 0168C] [[Col. 0167] This note appears at the foot of column 168, but the callout number (14) was not printed in the text.] 14. **LANFRANC. But what do you have?** He is trying to remove another kind of arrogance: namely, that a person should not become proud because of some grace bestowed upon him, thinking that he possesses it from himself. Therefore he says, “But what do you have,” etc., as if he were saying: If you have been separated from sins, you ought not therefore to boast; you ought not to boast in anything that you received from elsewhere. You received separation from sins from elsewhere; for what do you have that you did not receive from another? Nothing, certainly. Therefore, and so forth.]

# CHAPTER IV

[Col. 0167]

[Note: [Col. 0167A] CHAPTER IV.—1. AMBROSE. Let a person regard us in this way. This signifies that some of the Corinthians thought less well of him.]

Thus let a person regard us apostles—not as anything in ourselves, but as ministers of Christ, not as lords, and as stewards of the mysteries of God, of preaching or priesthood and of the other sacred orders.

[Note: [Col. 0167A] 2. LANFRANC. Stewards. The apostles administered the mysteries of God, appointing some as bishops, others as presbyters, and others in similar ways.]

Here, taking occasion from these words to rebuke them, it is sought among stewards that someone be found faithful.

[Note: [Col. 0167B] 4. Faithful. “As” is used in the sense of “truly,” as in: “And being found in appearance as a human being.”]

[Note: [Col. 0167B] 5. But for me. It is as though he said: I do not know what the other stewards think about this. But I attach no value to your criticisms, knowing that, through us—whether worthy or unworthy—God carries out his work.]

But it is a very small matter to me that I should be judged by you or reproved in administering the ministries,

[Note: [Col. 0167B] 6. AMBROSE. Or by a human day. By saying “human day,” he signifies the divine day, on which Christ will judge.]

or by a human day, in my understanding. I do not even judge myself in matters belonging to my office, nor do I reprove myself for something I would do if it ought to be done. For I am conscious of nothing against myself in administering the mysteries,

[Note: [Col. 0167C] 7. But I am not thereby justified. He now humbles himself and speaks as a human being who may incur guilt without knowing it.]

but I am not thereby justified;

[Note: [Col. 0167C] 8. But the one who judges me. He rightly ascribes the greatest authority to the Lord Christ, because, when he judges hidden things, he can make manifest what is concealed from human beings.]

the one who judges me is the Lord. Therefore do not judge before the appointed time, because judgment belongs to the Lord, until the Lord comes,

[Note: [Col. 0167C] 9. AUGUSTINE (*Enchiridion to Laurentius*, chapter 120, vol. III). Who will also bring to light. Then each person will receive praise from God, because what will be praised and loved by one’s neighbor in one’s neighbor is what God himself will illuminate so that it may not remain hidden.]

who will also bring to light the hidden things of darkness—the concealed crimes of the wicked and darkened—and will reveal the counsels of hearts. Then each person will receive praise from God.

[Note: [Col. 0168A] 10. LANFRANC. Now, brothers, these things. That is, the preceding words of humility, in which I said that I planted and Apollos watered. But I also said that neither the one who planted nor the one who watered was anything. Therefore, setting aside the others, I applied these things to myself and Apollos, so that you may learn humility in us.]

Now, brothers, I have applied these things figuratively to myself and Apollos for your sake, so that you may be humbled; namely, so that in us you may learn not to be puffed up on behalf of one person against another beyond what has been written concerning us.

[Note: [Col. 0168A] 11. Beyond what. It was written above that one must in no way become proud on behalf of teachers, because teachers are merely ministers and are considered nothing in comparison with the one from whom and through whom growth is given.]

[Note: [Col. 0168B] 12. For who makes you different? It is as though he said: If your teacher had separated you from the mass of the lost, it might perhaps be tolerable for you to become proud on his behalf. But now, not at all; God separates you through him.]

For who makes you different from sins except God? What do you have—what grace do you have—that you did not receive? [The wording “What do you have, what grace do you have, which you did not receive?” is evidently uncertain in the supplied text.] But if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?

[Note: [Col. 0169A] 15. You are already filled. This is to be understood of certain Corinthians who, after the Apostle’s departure, began to abound in luxuries, to become rich in earthly possessions, and even to turn the gifts of the Holy Spirit toward earthly profit. Of them he says, “You are already filled,” etc.]

You are already filled, already you have become rich in earthly things; you reign without us, you possess earthly power. And would that you did reign—

[Note: [Col. 0169A] 16. Would that you did reign! Namely, with heavenly rule, or so that you might govern yourselves well.]

—that is, that you might reign with heavenly rule, so that we might reign with you.

[Note: [Col. 0169A] 17. The last. Christ wished his apostles to be last, that is, most despised, in the minds of unbelievers, so that they might be crowned with a greater reward in heavenly glory.]

For I think that God has displayed us apostles as the last, the most despised, in the minds of unbelievers,

[Note: [Col. 0169A] 18. As though condemned to death. At that time it was the custom of conquerors to condemn some of those captured in an expedition to death. A very great multitude of people gathered for this spectacle.]

as though condemned to death.

[Note: [Col. 0169B] 19. AUGUSTINE (from a treatise on Psalm 38, vol. VIII). Because we have become a spectacle: angels praise us, human beings revile us—or rather, angels both praise and revile us.]

For we have become a spectacle to this world, to evil angels, and to human beings. This is a rebuke expressed with irony.

[Note: [Col. 0169B] 20. LANFRANC. We are fools. A rebuke or irony; for the apostles are not fools while the Corinthians are wise. Rather, the Corinthians are fools and the apostles are wise.]

We seem to be fools for the sake of Christ, but you are wise in this age in Christ;

[Note: [Col. 0169B] 21. AMBROSE. But you are wise. Whoever is judged wise in Christ by the faithless does not rightly assert Christ. For Marcion, who denies that the Lord became incarnate, is wise to the world, that is, strong and noble.]

we are weak, but you are strong; you are noble, but we are despised. For even to this hour we are hungry and thirsty, naked and beaten, unsettled, changing from place to place because of extreme persecution; and we labor, not seeking payment from you, but working with our own hands. We are cursed, and we bless; we suffer persecution, and we endure it; we are slandered, and we plead—

[Note: [Col. 0170A] 22. LANFRANC. And we plead either with them, that they may not blaspheme, or with God, that he may forgive them.]

—we plead either that they may not blaspheme, or with God that he may forgive them. We have become like the refuse of this world, the scum of all things, unto this very hour.

[Note: [Col. 0170A] 23. AUGUSTINE (from a treatise on Psalm 76). Not to shame you. He says: I am not writing these things to shame you, but to admonish you as dearly beloved children, since he certainly knew that the Lord had said: “Do not call anyone your father on earth, for one is your Father, God.” This was said not so that the title of human honor might be removed from ordinary speech, but so that the grace of God, by which we are reborn into eternal life, might not be attributed to the nature, power, or even holiness of any human being. Therefore, when he had said, “I fathered you,” he later said, “in Christ” [variant: “he had previously said] and “through the Gospel,” so that what belongs to God might not be thought to belong to him.]

I do not write these things to shame you or bring embarrassment upon you, but to admonish you as my dearly beloved children. (Why he called them children.) For even if you have ten thousand tutors and admonishers in Christ, in the teaching of Christ, you do not have many fathers, but only one—me. For in Christ Jesus, through the Gospel, I fathered you; I am your father in the faith of Christ. Therefore I entreat you, since I am your father: be imitators of me, as I also am of Christ. For this reason, so that you may imitate me, I sent Timothy to you, who is my dearly beloved and faithful son in the Lord. He will remind you of my ways and my teaching, which are in Christ Jesus and in the faith of Christ, just as I teach everywhere in every church.

As though I were not going to come to you, some have become puffed up. (He shows that they need admonition because they are puffed up.) But I will come to you soon, if the Lord wills, and I will learn not the speech of those who are puffed up, but their power.

[Note: [Col. 0170A] 24. LANFRANC. For the kingdom of God is not in speech, that is, the kingdom of God is not acquired by words alone, but in power and good works.]

For the kingdom of God is not in speech: the kingdom of God is not acquired by words alone, but in power. What do you want? Shall I come to you with a rod, with correction, or in love and a spirit of gentleness?

[COMMENTARY]

[Col. 0167A]

# CHAPTER IV

1. **AMBROSE. Let a person regard us in this way.** This signifies that some of the Corinthians thought less well of him.

2. **LANFRANC. Stewards.** The apostles administered the mysteries of God, appointing some as bishops, others as presbyters, and others in similar ways.

3. **Here a question is now raised**, that is, on the occasion of these words of mine, in which I said that apostles ought to be regarded as stewards, someone asks who among us is truly found to be a faithful steward, wishing to judge our arrangements according to our merits.

4. **Faithful.** “As” is used in the sense of “truly,” as in: “And being found in appearance as a human being.”

5. **But for me.** It is as though he said: I do not know what the other stewards think about this. But I attach no value to your criticisms, knowing that, through us—whether worthy or unworthy—God carries out his work.

6. **AMBROSE. Or by a human day.** By saying “human day,” he signifies the divine day, on which Christ will judge.

7. **But I am not thereby justified.** He now humbles himself and speaks as a human being who may incur guilt without knowing it.

8. **But the one who judges me.** He rightly ascribes the greatest authority to the Lord Christ, because, when he judges hidden things, he can make manifest what is concealed from human beings.

9. **AUGUSTINE** (*Enchiridion to Laurentius*, chapter 120, vol. III). **Who will also bring to light.** As mortals, we do not know the hearts of mortals; but then the Lord will bring to light the hidden things of darkness and will reveal the counsels of hearts. Then each person will receive praise from God, because what will be praised and loved by one’s neighbor in one’s neighbor is what God himself will illuminate so that it may not remain hidden.

10. **LANFRANC. Now, brothers, these things.** That is, the preceding words of humility, in which I said that I planted and Apollos watered. But I also said that neither the one who planted nor the one who watered was anything. Therefore, setting aside the others, I applied these things to myself and Apollos, so that you may learn humility in us.

11. **Beyond what.** It was written above that one must in no way become proud on behalf of teachers, because teachers are merely ministers and are considered nothing in comparison with the one from whom and through whom growth is given.

[Col. 0168B] 12. **For who makes you different?** It is as though he said: If your teacher had separated you from the mass of the lost, it might perhaps be tolerable for you to become proud on his behalf. But now, not at all; God separates you through him.

13. **AUGUSTINE** (Letter 46, to Valentinus, vol. II). **For who makes you different?** He says this because, from that mass of perdition which arose from Adam, no one but God separates a human being in order to make him a vessel for honor rather than dishonor. But since a carnal and vainly puffed-up person, upon hearing “For who makes you different?” might answer either aloud or in thought and say, “My faith makes me different; my prayer makes me different; my righteousness makes me different,” the Apostle immediately confronts his thoughts and says: “What do you have that you did not receive?”

[Col. 0168C] 14. **LANFRANC. But what do you have?** He is trying to remove another kind of arrogance: namely, that a person should not become proud because of some grace bestowed upon him, thinking that he possesses it from himself. Therefore he says, “But what do you have,” etc., as if he were saying: If you have been separated from sins, you ought not therefore to boast; you ought not to boast in anything that you received from elsewhere. You received separation from sins from elsewhere; for what do you have that you did not receive from another? Nothing, certainly. Therefore, and so forth.

[Col. 0169A] 15. **You are already filled.** This is to be understood of certain Corinthians who, after the Apostle’s departure, began to abound in luxuries, to become rich in earthly possessions, and even to turn the gifts of the Holy Spirit toward earthly profit. Of them he says, “You are already filled,” etc.

16. **Would that you did reign!** Namely, with heavenly rule, or so that you might govern yourselves well.

17. **The last.** Christ wished his apostles to be last, that is, most despised, in the minds of unbelievers, so that they might be crowned with a greater reward in heavenly glory.

18. **As though condemned to death.** At that time it was the custom of conquerors to condemn some of those captured in an expedition to death. A very great multitude of people gathered for this spectacle.

[Col. 0169B] 19. **AUGUSTINE** (from a treatise on Psalm 38, vol. VIII). **Because we have become a spectacle.** Angels praise us, human beings revile us—or rather, angels both praise and revile us.

20. **LANFRANC. We are fools.** A rebuke or irony; for the apostles are not fools while the Corinthians are wise. Rather, the Corinthians are fools and the apostles are wise.

21. **AMBROSE. But you are wise.** Whoever is judged wise in Christ by the faithless does not rightly assert Christ. For Marcion, who denies that the Lord became incarnate, is wise to the world, that is, strong and noble.

[Col. 0170A] 22. **LANFRANC. And we plead**, either with them, that they may not blaspheme, or with God, that he may forgive them.

23. AUGUSTINE (from the Treatise on Psalm 76). “Not that I may put you to shame.” He says, “I am writing these things not to put you to shame, but to admonish you as my dearest ones,” although he certainly knew that the Lord had said: “Do not call anyone your father on earth, for one is your Father, God.” This was said not so that this title of human honor might be removed from ordinary speech, but so that the grace of God, by which we are regenerated for eternal life, might not be attributed to the nature, power, or even holiness of any human being. Therefore, after saying, “I begot you,” he added: “In Christ,” and “through the Gospel,” so that what belongs to God might not be thought to belong to him.

24. LANFRANC. “For not in speech”—that is, not in words [Col. 0170B] alone—is the kingdom of God acquired, but in power and good works.

[Col. 0169]

There is altogether heard among you fornication—and this is the reason why he said “with the rod”—and such fornication as is not even found among the Gentiles, so that someone has his father’s wife. And you are puffed up, rather than having mourned, so that the one who has committed this abominable deed might be removed from your midst through the common life of the community. I, for my part, although absent in body—you ought to have excommunicated him, because, though absent, I have already judged him worthy of excommunication—yet present in spirit, have already judged, as though present, the one who has acted in this way: in the name and to the praise of our Lord Jesus Christ, when you are assembled, and my spirit is assembled with you, with the power of our Lord Jesus [Note: [Col. 0170B] CHAPTER V.—1. AUGUSTINE (from the Sermon on the Mount, book I, chapter 20, volume IV). “To hand over such a one.” And if they do not wish to understand “death” here, perhaps—since it is uncertain—they nevertheless admit that some punishment was inflicted by the Apostle through Satan. That he did this not out of hatred but out of love is made clear by what is added: “so that his soul may be saved.”], I have judged that such a one should be handed over—that is, excommunicated—to Satan, namely to the evil spirit, to be tormented [Col. 0171] for the destruction of the flesh, that is, of carnal pleasure, so that his spirit may be saved, if perhaps that very rejection by the Church may move him and bring him back to repentance on the day of the judgment of our Lord Jesus Christ. Since you retain such a man among you, your boasting is not good, by analogy. Do you not know, he says, that he must be expelled? For if he remained among the others, he would corrupt those who were undefiled, because a little leaven corrupts the whole lump. [COMMENTARY]

[Col. 0170B]

CHAPTER V.—1. AUGUSTINE (from the Sermon on the Mount, book I, chapter 20, volume IV). “To hand over such a one.” And if they do not wish to understand “death” here, perhaps—since it is uncertain—they nevertheless admit that some punishment was inflicted by the Apostle through Satan. That he did this not out of hatred but out of love is made clear by what is added: “so that his soul may be saved.”

2. LANFRANC. “Such a one to Satan.” He had this power, so that whenever he could not remove from a person the foolishness that had taken possession of him, he could hand him over to the devil to be tormented until, professing repentance, he abandoned his evil purpose.

3. “Lump.” A lump is flour and water mixed together without leaven; likewise, unleavened bread. He therefore urges them to be clean from sins in their manner of life, just as they were washed clean in baptism.

4. “For Christ our Passover.” The reason why we ought to live free from sin is that Christ has been sacrificed, and we ought to feast upon him. The order is: “For Christ, who is our Passover, has been sacrificed.”

5. AUGUSTINE (Exposition of the Gospel of John, treatise 55, volume IX). “For Christ our Passover.” When our doorposts have been smeared with his blood—that is, when our foreheads have been marked with the sign of the cross—we are freed from the destruction of this age as from captivity or the Egyptian slaughter, and we make a most salutary passage, when we pass from the devil to Christ and from this unstable age to his most firmly established kingdom. For this reason we pass over to the everlasting God, so that we may not pass away with the passing world.

6. (The same work, from book XXXII Against Faustus, chapter 11, volume VI). “But in unleavened bread.” Those who are Christians of the true faith keep the unleavened bread not in the old leaven [some editions: “of life”—probably an error], that is, in malice, but in the truth and sincerity of that very faith. Not for seven days, but every day—what was signified by the number seven.

7. AMBROSE. “But in unleavened bread.” Let sincerity produce a clean life; let truth exclude every kind of deceit.

[Col. 0171C] 8. LANFRANC. “Of sincerity,” that is, in place of that custom by which the Jews used to eat unleavened loaves; we possess sincerity and truth.

[Col. 0172A] 9. “I wrote to you.” He sent them a certain letter, which is not now extant, in which he commanded them not to associate with fornicators and others whom he mentions. But because he did not distinguish whether he meant Christian or Gentile fornicators, the Corinthians thought that he had spoken of Gentile fornicators. The Apostle corrects their perverse understanding here.

10. “Otherwise,” that is, if I had commanded you to avoid association with the Gentiles, you would have had to leave human society and go out into a deserted place; for such fornicators, greedy people, and so forth, are everywhere.

11. AMBROSE. “Otherwise,” that is, if you associate with them, it would be better for you to die.

[Col. 0172B] 12. LANFRANC. “Not to associate.” The order is: not to associate with such a person, nor to take food with him. “If the one who is called a brother,” and so forth.

13. AUGUSTINE (from book II of the Retractions, chapter 17, volume VII). “Remove the evil.” When the Apostle says, “Remove the evil from among yourselves,” this should not be understood as though each person were to remove evil from himself; rather, the evil person is to be removed from among good people. This is done through ecclesiastical discipline, as the Greek language clearly indicates, where it is written without ambiguity so that “this evil person,” not “this evil,” is understood.
