12. AMBROSE. “The one who clings.” He means that the one who joins himself to contamination becomes one with the person to whom he joins himself. Fornication makes the two one, so that, just as they are one in nature, they are also one in defilement.

13. AUGUSTINE (book XIV On the Trinity, chapter 14, volume III). “The one who clings.” This person approaches participation in that nature, truth, and blessedness, but does not thereby increase in his own nature, truth, or blessedness.

14. “But the one who fornicates.” Nowhere is the whole person so given over to the pleasure of the body itself, and so ineffably or unavoidably affected, that, in comparison with this great evil, the other sins seem to be outside the body—even if they are carried out through the body.

15. AMBROSE. “But the one who fornicates.” The whole body is man and woman, because the woman is a portion of the man; and the man, by sinning against that which is his portion, sins against his own body. Or because fornication is a bodily offense; for it does not occur without the desire of the flesh. For the flesh has its own movement there.

[Col. 0175A] 16. LANFRANC. “For you were bought.” This proves that they are not their own. No one who has been bought belongs to himself; but these have been bought; therefore, and so forth.

17. “Glorify and bear.” This is an inference, as though he said: Since you were bought, glorify God in your hearts, whose servants you have become.

18. AMBROSE. “Bear God in your body.” To bear God is to display the image of God in well-performed deeds.

## CHAPTER VII

[Col. 0175]

Concerning the matters about which you wrote to me—whether wives should be taken or not—I answer as follows: It is good for a man not to touch a woman; but because of fornication, let each man have his own wife [Note: [Col. 0175A] CHAPTER VII.—1. LANFRANC. “Let him have a wife.” He says “wife,” not “concubine,” so that those whom divine authorities do not permit to have wives are excluded from this statement.], and let each woman have her own husband [Note: [Col. 0175A] 2. “Her own husband.” Here he understands “husband” to mean a lawful husband. As in the Gospel: “And the one whom you have is not your husband” [Col. 0175B].].

Let the husband render the due to his wife; likewise also let the wife render the due to her husband. And this is fitting, for a woman does not have authority over her own body, whether to release or restrain her sexuality, but the man does. Likewise, the man does not have authority over his own body, but the woman does. Do not deprive one another of the due, except perhaps by mutual consent for a time, so that you may devote yourselves to prayer; and return again to the same relationship, lest Satan tempt you to worse things because of your lack of self-control, if you are unable to abstain. But I say this by way of concession, not by command. For I wish all of you to be as I am myself, insofar as lies within me; but each person has his own gift from God, one in this way and another in that.

But to the unmarried and widows I say: It is good for them if they remain as I am. But if they cannot abstain, let them marry. [Note: [Col. 0175B] 3. AMBROSE. “It is better to marry.” To be burned is to be driven and conquered by desires: when the will consents to the heat of the flesh, it is burned; for to endure desires and not be conquered by them belongs to an eminent man.] For it is better to marry than to burn—to restrain oneself unwillingly. To burn is to desire the work of lust immoderately in the mind and thereafter to burn in the flesh.

But to those who are joined in marriage I give this command—not I, but the Lord—that a wife should not leave her husband; [Note: [Col. 0175B] 4. LANFRANC. “But if she does leave.” She cannot leave, except for the cause of fornication, [probably “unless”] provided that they live continently by mutual consent.] but if she does leave, that is, if a legitimate cause intervenes—for otherwise it is not permitted—let her remain unmarried or be reconciled to her husband. And let the husband not dismiss his wife.

But to the rest I say—I, not the Lord: If any brother has an unbelieving wife, and she consents to dwell with him, let him not dismiss her. And if any faithful woman has an unbelieving husband, and he consents to dwell with her, let her not dismiss her husband; [Note: [Col. 0175B] 5. “The husband has been sanctified,” that is, made clean, and the woman suffers no impurity from her union with him.] for the unbelieving husband has been sanctified through the faithful wife; or it has sometimes happened that an unbelieving husband was sanctified through a faithful wife, and conversely; and the unbelieving wife has been sanctified, and the woman suffers no impurity from her union with him: through the faithful husband, that is, in the faithful husband. [Note: [Col. 0175B] 6. AUGUSTINE (from *The Sermon on the Mount*, book I, chapter 16, vol. IV). “The husband has been sanctified.” For, he says, “the unbelieving husband has been sanctified in the faithful wife, and the unbelieving wife has been sanctified in the faithful brother.” I believe that it had already come about that some women came to the faith through faithful husbands, and men through faithful wives. (The same work; from *On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins*, book 3, addressed to Marcellinus, chapter 12, vol. VII.) Nevertheless, this must be held without hesitation: whatever that sanctification may be, it is not sufficient for making them Christians and for remitting sins unless they are made faithful through Christian or ecclesiastical instruction and the sacraments. For unbelieving spouses are not cleansed from the iniquity that compels those separated from the kingdom of God to come into condemnation, however closely they may cling to holy and righteous spouses.]

Otherwise your children would be unclean—that is, degenerate and illegitimate—but now they are holy, not degenerate, that is, legitimate. [Note: [Col. 0176A] 7. AMBROSE. “The husband has been sanctified.” That unbelievers possess this benefit shows good will, because they do not shrink from the honor of Christ’s name. The sign of the holy cross belongs to the protection and sanctification of the household.] [Note: [Col. 0176B] 8. “Otherwise your children.” Their children would be unclean if they dismissed those who wished to dwell with them and joined themselves to others; for they would be adulterers, and their children illegitimate.] [Note: [Col. 0176B] 9. LANFRANC. “But now they are holy,” that is, clean. He returns to the reason why a faithful man should not seek divorce from an unbelieving woman, nor a faithful woman from an unbelieving man.] [Note: [Col. 0176B] 10. AUGUSTINE (*Letter 89 to Hilary*, on question 4, vol. II). “But if the unbeliever,” that is, if the unbeliever wishes to remain with the faithful spouse. Here the faithful person should recognize his or her freedom, lest he or she think that subjection to slavery requires abandoning the faith itself, or the unbelieving spouse—]

But if the unbeliever, whether man or woman, departs, let him or her depart; for the brother or sister is not enslaved in such circumstances—that is, he or she is not compelled to follow the unbeliever. But God has called us to peace. We are, as it were, debtors to peace, and therefore we must not be the cause of discord. This is another reason why divorce should not be sought. For how do you know, woman, whether you will save your husband? Or how do you know, man, whether you will save your wife?

Except that each person should walk as the Lord has apportioned to him, each as God has called him, and as I teach in all the churches, by analogy. Was someone called while circumcised? Let him not draw on the foreskin; let him not wish to become uncircumcised. Was someone called while uncircumcised? Let him not be circumcised. Circumcision is nothing, and uncircumcision is nothing, but only the keeping of God’s commandments. [Note: [Col. 0177A] 12. AMBROSE. “And as I teach in all the churches.” He says this so that, while they hear that the others are being taught this, they may attain it [another reading: “follow it”].] [Note: [Col. 0177A] 13. AUGUSTINE (in the exposition of the Epistle to the Galatians, vol. IV). “Each one in the condition.” For he referred this to those customs or conditions [another reading: “to the manner of life”] that do not harm faith and good morals. For if someone was even a robber when he was called, he ought not to remain in robbery.]

Therefore, let each person remain in the calling in which he was called; if circumcised or not, he ought to remain in that calling.

Were you called as a slave? Do not let it concern you; but even if you can become free by flight or otherwise dishonorably, make use rather of that very servitude. [Note: [Col. 0177B] 14. LANFRANC. “Each one in the condition,” etc. “Each person,” he says, “should walk in the calling by which he was called to the faith”; for one who was circumcised and called to the faith in circumcision should not wish that he had not been circumcised. So also with the uncircumcised, because neither circumcision nor uncircumcision contributes anything to attaining blessedness. [Col. 0177B] Only the observance of God’s commandments has value.] [Note: [Col. 0177B] 15. “Were you called as a slave?” That is, if someone was called to the faith as a slave in one respect, let him not wish to become free; for he is free—and of God. If someone free was called to the faith, let him not wish to become a slave; for he is a slave, because he belongs to Christ, since he has been bought by him.] [Note: [Col. 0177B] 16. “Make use rather.” He commands that servitude be used, because the more contemptible someone is in this world for God’s sake, the more he will be exalted in the future.]

For the one who was called in the Lord as a slave, to the faith of Christ, is the Lord’s freedman; likewise, the one who was called as a free person is Christ’s slave. [Note: [Col. 0177B] 17. “For the one who was called in the Lord.” The reason why it should not concern him if he was called as a slave.] [Note: [Col. 0177B] 18. “He is the Lord’s freedman,” that is, the Lord’s freedman and Christ’s slave; but he assigns the more honorable designation to the slave, because the designation “slave” is less honorable.]

You were bought at a price; do not become slaves of human beings, [Note: [Col. 0177C] 19. AMBROSE. “You were bought at a price.” They are human slaves who subject themselves to human superstitions. He says this because at the beginning of the Epistle he rebuked them for saying, “I belong to Paul,” and so forth.] that is, in such a way that you put the service of God second. [Note: [Col. 0177C] 20. “Slaves of human beings.” Namely, so that you subordinate the service of God.]

Therefore, brothers, let each person—whether slave or free—remain before God in the condition in which he was called; he ought to remain in it.

“Concerning married people,” he says, “I have given a command. But concerning virgins, whether men or women, I have no command of the Lord; I give advice. I offer counsel mercifully,” [Note: [Col. 0178A] 21. LANFRANC. “As having obtained mercy.” “I offer counsel mercifully,” he says, because I have obtained this mercy from God, namely, that I believe in him.] as one who has obtained this mercy from the Lord, so that I am faithful and believe in him.

I therefore judge this—that virginity is good—because of the present necessity, since it is good for a person to be a virgin in this way. [Note: [Col. 0178A] 22. “Because of the present necessity.” He calls the present necessity the poverty of this age, which married people frequently suffer because of raising sons and daughters and supporting one another. To avoid this, he says that it is good for a person to live without marriage. Chastity certainly must be preserved for the sake of eternal life; but for weaker teachers he puts forward a weak argument.]

Are you bound to a wife? [Note: [Col. 0178A] 23. “Are you bound to a wife?” Lest, because chastity has been praised, someone wish to dismiss his wife, he adds this.] Do not seek release. Are you released from a wife? Do not seek a wife. [Note: [Col. 0178A] 24. “Do not seek a wife.” One who does not have a wife should not seek to have one. For those who have wives ought to be as though they did not have them. (By analogy:) Those who weep ought to be as though they did not weep. He could conclude the same about the rest: Therefore, since one who has something ought to be as though he did not have it, one who does not have it ought not to seek it. This is equivalent to saying: Therefore I want you to be without a wife, for I want you to be without worldly anxiety. He proves this as follows: If someone is without a wife, he is without anxiety; since I want you to be without a wife, I want you to be without worldly anxiety. But the one who is without a wife is without anxiety, for he is concerned only with the things of the Lord; he is concerned with how to please God.]

But if you take a wife, you have not sinned. And if a virgin marries, she has not sinned. [Note: [Col. 0178B] 25. AMBROSE. “The tribulation of the flesh.” Tribulations are the groans of the womb, the raising of children, and similar things.] Nevertheless, such people will have temporal tribulation in the flesh.

But I spare you—that is, I mercifully order your life. [Note: [Col. 0178C] 26. “But I spare you.” He spares them because he urges them toward those things that exclude the mentioned tribulations of the flesh and anxieties. It may also be understood that he spares them when he permits and does not oppose those who wish to do what he shows to be burdensome.]

But this I say, brothers: [Note: [Col. 0178C] 27. “The time is short.” Because the end is near, he says that they should not be anxious about having children; those who weep should be as though they did not weep, knowing that their consolation will soon come; and those who rejoice in the present should know that mourning will soon follow.] the time is short; [Col. 0179] it remains, therefore, that those who have wives should be as though they did not have them; [Note: [Col. 0179A] 28. LANFRANC. “It remains.” Since, he says, the time is short, it follows that whatever appears to be prosperous or adverse in this world should, because of the brevity of time, rather be regarded as nothing.] those who weep as though they did not weep; those who rejoice as though they did not rejoice; those who buy as though they did not possess; and those who use this world as though they did not use it. [Note: [Col. 0179B] 29. AUGUSTINE (in the exposition of Psalm 147, vol. VIII). “Those who weep.” Whoever eats or drinks or does anything else does everything for the glory of God. 59 If there is any sadness concerning worldly matters, let him weep in such a way that inwardly he rejoices in hope. And if there is any joy in worldly matters, let him rejoice in such a way that inwardly he fears spiritually; let him neither give himself to be corrupted by prosperity nor surrender himself to be broken by adversity. For this is to weep as though not weeping and to rejoice as though not rejoicing.]

For the form of this world is passing away—the reason why the things said above are to be regarded as though they did not exist. [Note: [Col. 0179B] 30. AUGUSTINE (*City of God*, book XX, chapter 14). “For the form is passing away.” The form passes away, not nature (the same work, chapter 16). For when those who are not written in the book of life have been judged and sent into eternal fire, then the form of this world will pass away through the conflagration of worldly fires. So too the flood occurred through the inundation of worldly waters. In that conflagration, as I have said, the qualities of the world’s corruptible elements, which corresponded to our corruptible bodies, will utterly perish by burning.] [Note: [Col. 0179B] 31. LANFRANC. “For the form is passing away.” The reason why the things said above should be considered as though they did not exist [Col. 0179C]. Everything that passes away, however long its duration, is nothing when compared with eternity.]

Now I want you to be without worldly anxiety. The unmarried man is concerned with the things of the Lord, how he may please the Lord. But the married man is concerned with the things of the world, how he may please his wife, and he is divided.

The reason why women ought to be without a husband: the unmarried woman and the virgin think about the things of the Lord, so that she may be holy in body and spirit. But the married woman thinks about the things of the world, how she may please her husband.

I say this for your benefit, [Note: [Col. 0179C] 32. “Not to cast a snare,” that is, I do not urge you to love chastity for the purpose of wanting you, on this occasion, because of lack of self-control, to fall into the snare of lust.] not to cast a snare upon you, not to make you slip into worse things while discouraging marriage, but I urge you toward what is honorable and what gives opportunity to entreat the Lord without impediment—that is, to serve him. [Note: [Col. 0180A] 33. AUGUSTINE (*On the Good of Widowhood*, chapter 5). “[But toward what is honorable.]” When he says, “But toward what is honorable,” he does not show that marriage is disgraceful; rather, he commends what was more honorable than what was honorable under the general name of honor.]

But if anyone thinks that he is behaving disgracefully or dishonorably concerning his virgin daughter, because she is past marriageable age and it is necessary that this happen, since the virgin does not wish to preserve chastity, let him do what he wishes; therefore neither the father nor the daughter sins if she marries. [Note: [Col. 0180A] 34. LANFRANC. “But if anyone,” etc. Since he had previously urged virginity, lest anyone perhaps think it a sin to give a daughter who did not wish to remain continent to a husband, he says that if she does not wish to remain continent, she does not sin if she marries. But if someone has a daughter whom he wishes to keep continent, and he has authority over whether she marries or not, if the father wishes to preserve his daughter as a virgin, he does well.] [Note: [Col. 0180A] 35. LANFRANC. “Thinks that he is behaving disgracefully,” that is, if someone has an adult virgin who does not wish to preserve chastity, and her guardian thinks that he will incur the disgrace of dishonor [Col. 0180B] if he compels her to preserve chastity, neither he nor the virgin sins if the virgin marries.] [Note: [Col. 0180B] 36. AUGUSTINE (*On the Good of Widowhood*, chapter 9, vol. IV). “She does not sin if she marries.” She who does not contain herself should marry; she who has not begun should deliberate; she who has undertaken it should persevere. Let no opportunity be given to the adversary; let no forgetfulness be taken away from Christ.]

But the one who stands firm in his heart, not having this necessity—that his daughter should marry—and who has power over his own will, whether his virgin should marry or not, and has judged in his heart to preserve his virgin daughter, does well. Therefore both he who joins his virgin daughter in marriage does well, and he who does not join her in marriage does well; for the latter does better.

A discouragement from marriage: A woman is bound to the law—that is, the marital law—as long as her husband lives. But if her husband dies, she is released; she is free to marry whom she wishes, only in the Lord, lawfully. But she will be happier, according to my counsel, if she remains in this condition, without a husband. [Note: [Col. 0180B] 37. AUGUSTINE (*Exposition 37 on the Gospel of John*). “But I think that I.” Human beings sometimes express doubt reproachfully concerning matters they hold as certain; that is, they use a word of doubt [singular reading: *ponit*, “he uses”; alternative: *ponunt*, “they use”], although they do not doubt in their heart [addition: *in*, “in”]. It is like becoming angry with your servant and saying, “Do you despise me? Consider that perhaps I am your master.” Thus also the Apostle, speaking to some who despised his own people, says: “But I think that I too have the Spirit of God” [Col. 0180C]. The one who says “I think” appears to doubt. But he was reproaching, not doubting. And our Lord himself, elsewhere reproving the future unbelief of the human race, says: “When the Son of Man comes, do you think he will find faith on earth?”]

But I think that I too have the Spirit of God, so that his counsel may be accepted.

[COMMENTARY.]

[Col. 0175A]

CHAPTER VII.—1. LANFRANC. “Let him have a wife.” He says “wife,” not “concubine,” so that those whom divine authorities do not permit to have wives are excluded from this statement.

2. “Her own husband.” Here “husband” means a lawful husband. As in the Gospel: “And the one whom you have is not your husband” [Col. 0175B].

3. AMBROSE. “It is better to marry.” To be burned is to be driven and conquered by desires: when the will consents to the heat of the flesh, it is burned; for to endure desires and not be conquered by them belongs to an eminent man.

4. LANFRANC. “But if she does leave.” She cannot leave, except for the cause of fornication, [probably “unless”] provided that they live continently by mutual consent.

5. “The husband has been sanctified,” that is, made clean, and the woman suffers no impurity from her union with him.

6. AUGUSTINE (from *The Sermon on the Mount*, book I, chapter 16, vol. IV). “The husband has been sanctified.” For, he says, “the unbelieving husband has been sanctified in the faithful wife, and the unbelieving wife has been sanctified in the faithful brother.” I believe that it had already come about that some women came to the faith through faithful husbands, and men through faithful wives. (The same work; from *On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins*, book 3, addressed to Marcellinus, chapter 12, vol. VII.) Nevertheless, this must be held without hesitation: whatever that sanctification may be, it is not sufficient for making them Christians and for remitting sins unless they are made faithful through Christian or ecclesiastical instruction and the sacraments. For unbelieving spouses are not cleansed from the iniquity that compels those separated from the kingdom of God to come into condemnation, however closely they may cling to holy and righteous spouses.

7. AMBROSE. “The husband has been sanctified.” That unbelievers possess this benefit shows good will, because they do not shrink from the honor of Christ’s name. The sign of the holy cross belongs to the protection and sanctification of the household.

[Col. 0176B] 8. “Otherwise your children.” Their children would be unclean if they dismissed those who wished to dwell with them and joined themselves to others; for they would be adulterers, and their children illegitimate.

9. LANFRANC. “But now they are holy,” that is, clean. He returns to the reason why a faithful man should not seek divorce from an unbelieving woman, nor a faithful woman from an unbelieving man.

10. AUGUSTINE (*Letter 89 to Hilary*, on question 4, vol. II). “But if the unbeliever,” that is, if the unbeliever wishes to remain with the faithful spouse. Here the faithful person should recognize his or her freedom, lest he or she think that subjection to slavery requires abandoning the faith itself, or the unbelieving spouse—

11. “If the unbeliever departs, let him depart.” It is not permitted to take another wife, even after dismissing the unbelieving one; but whether there is a difference between dismissing and departing.

[Col. 0177A] 12. AMBROSE. “And as I teach in all the churches.” He says this so that, while they hear that the others are being taught this, they may attain it [another reading: “follow it”].

13. AUGUSTINE (in the exposition of the Epistle to the Galatians, vol. IV). “Each one in the condition.” For he referred this to those customs or conditions [another reading: “to the manner of life”] that do not harm faith and good morals. For if someone was even a robber when he was called, he ought not to remain in robbery.

14. LANFRANC. “Each one in the condition,” etc. “Each person,” he says, “should walk in the calling by which he was called to the faith”; for one who was circumcised and called to the faith in circumcision should not wish that he had not been circumcised. So also with the uncircumcised, because neither circumcision nor uncircumcision contributes anything to attaining blessedness. [Col. 0177B] Only the observance of God’s commandments has value.

15. “Were you called as a slave?” That is, if someone was called to the faith as a slave in one respect, let him not wish to become free; for he is free—and of God. If someone free was called to the faith, let him not wish to become a slave; for he is a slave, because he belongs to Christ, since he has been bought by him.

16. “Make use rather.” He commands that servitude be used, because the more contemptible someone is in this world for God’s sake, the more he will be exalted in the future.

17. “For the one who was called in the Lord.” The reason why it should not concern him if he was called as a slave.

18. “He is the Lord’s freedman,” that is, the Lord’s freedman and Christ’s slave; but he assigns the more honorable designation to the slave, because the designation “slave” is less honorable.

[Col. 0177C] 19. AMBROSE. “You were bought at a price.” They are human slaves who subject themselves to human superstitions. He says this because at the beginning of the Epistle he rebuked them for saying, “I belong to Paul,” and so forth.

20. “Slaves of human beings.” Namely, so that you subordinate the service of God.

[Col. 0178A] 21. LANFRANC. “As having obtained mercy.” “I offer counsel mercifully,” he says, because I have obtained this mercy from God, namely, that I believe in him.

22. “Because of the present necessity.” He calls the present necessity the poverty of this age, which married people frequently suffer because of raising sons and daughters and supporting one another. To avoid this, he says that it is good for a person to live without marriage. Chastity certainly must be preserved for the sake of eternal life; but for weaker teachers he puts forward a weak argument.

23. “Are you bound to a wife?” Lest, because chastity has been praised, someone wish to dismiss his wife, he adds this.

24. “Do not seek a wife.” One who does not have a wife should not seek to have one. For those who have wives ought to be as though they did not have them. [Col. 0178B] (By analogy:) Those who weep ought to be as though they did not weep. He could conclude the same about the rest: Therefore, since one who has something ought to be as though he did not have it, one who does not have it ought not to seek it. This is equivalent to saying: Therefore I want you to be without a wife, for I want you to be without worldly anxiety. He proves this as follows: If someone is without a wife, he is without anxiety; since I want you to be without a wife, I want you to be without worldly anxiety. But the one who is without a wife is without anxiety, for he is concerned only with the things of the Lord; he is concerned with how to please God.

25. AMBROSE. “The tribulation of the flesh.” Tribulations are the groans of the womb, the raising of children, and similar things.

[Col. 0178C] 26. “But I spare you.” He spares them because he urges them toward those things that exclude the mentioned tribulations of the flesh and anxieties. It may also be understood that he spares them when he permits and does not oppose those who wish to do what he shows to be burdensome.

27. “The time is short.” Because the end is near, he says that they should not be anxious about having children; those who weep should be as though they did not weep, knowing that their consolation will soon come; and those who rejoice in the present should know that mourning will soon follow.

28. LANFRANC. “It remains.” Since, he says, the time is short, it follows that whatever appears to be prosperous or adverse in this world should, because of the brevity of time, rather be regarded as nothing.

29. AUGUSTINE (in the exposition of Psalm 147, vol. VIII). “Those who weep.” Whoever eats or drinks or does anything else does everything for the glory of God. 59 If there is any sadness concerning worldly matters, let him weep in such a way that inwardly he rejoices in hope. And if there is any joy in worldly matters, let him rejoice in such a way that inwardly he fears spiritually; let him neither give himself to be corrupted by prosperity nor surrender himself to be broken by adversity. For this is to weep as though not weeping and to rejoice as though not rejoicing.

30. AUGUSTINE (*City of God*, book XX, chapter 14). “For the form is passing away.” The form passes away, not nature (the same work, chapter 16). For when those who are not written in the book of life have been judged and sent into eternal fire, then the form of this world will pass away through the conflagration of worldly fires. So too the flood occurred through the inundation of worldly waters. In that conflagration, as I have said, the qualities of the world’s corruptible elements, which corresponded to our corruptible bodies, will utterly perish by burning.

31. LANFRANC. “For the form is passing away.” The reason why the things said above should be considered as though they did not exist [Col. 0179C]. Everything that passes away, however long its duration, is nothing when compared with eternity.

32. “Not to cast a snare,” that is, I do not urge you to love chastity for the purpose of wanting you, on this occasion, because of lack of self-control, to fall into the snare of lust.

33. AUGUSTINE (*On the Good of Widowhood*, chapter 5). “[But toward what is honorable.]” When he says, “But toward what is honorable,” he does not show that marriage is disgraceful; rather, he commends what was more honorable than what was honorable under the general name of honor.

34. LANFRANC. “But if anyone,” etc. Since he had previously urged virginity, lest anyone perhaps think it a sin to give a daughter who did not wish to remain continent to a husband, he says that if she does not wish to remain continent, she does not sin if she marries. But if someone has a daughter whom he wishes to keep continent, and he has authority over whether she marries or not, if the father wishes to preserve his daughter as a virgin, he does well.

35. LANFRANC. “Thinks that he is behaving disgracefully,” that is, if someone has an adult virgin who does not wish to preserve chastity, and her guardian thinks that he will incur the disgrace of dishonor [Col. 0180B] if he compels her to preserve chastity, neither he nor the virgin sins if the virgin marries.

36. AUGUSTINE (*On the Good of Widowhood*, chapter 9, vol. IV). “She does not sin if she marries.” She who does not contain herself should marry; she who has not begun should deliberate; she who has undertaken it should persevere. Let no opportunity be given to the adversary; let no forgetfulness be taken away from Christ.

37. AUGUSTINE (*Exposition 37 on the Gospel of John*). “But I think that I.” Human beings sometimes express doubt reproachfully concerning matters they hold as certain; that is, they use a word of doubt [singular reading: *ponit*, “he uses”; alternative: *ponunt*, “they use”], although they do not doubt in their heart [addition: *in*, “in”]. It is like becoming angry with your servant and saying, “Do you despise me? Consider that perhaps I am your master.” Thus also the Apostle, speaking to some who despised his own people, says: “But I think that I too have the Spirit of God” [Col. 0180C]. The one who says “I think” appears to doubt. But he was reproaching, not doubting. And our Lord himself, elsewhere reproving the future unbelief of the human race, says: “When the Son of Man comes, do you think he will find faith on earth?”

[Col. 0181A]

CHAPTER VIII.—1. AMBROSE. “Concerning these matters.” Now he is about to speak of knowledge, but he does not immediately say what kind of knowledge it is; rather, he shows this below when he says: “Because an idol is nothing.”

2. LANFRANC. “Concerning these matters,” that is, we all know what ought to be done with things sacrificed to idols; but knowledge alone is not sufficient for observing what is right. Rather, it puffs up if charity is absent, which—[source ends]
builds up.

3. AUGUSTINE (Exposition on the Gospel of John, tractate 27). “Knowledge puffs up.” Indeed, knowledge alone, without charity, puffs up; therefore he added: “Charity builds up.” Add charity, then, to knowledge, and knowledge will be useful—not in itself, but through charity.

4. LANFRANC. “But if anyone thinks he knows something.” He shows what knowledge without charity is: namely, what a person thinks he possesses from himself.

5. “As one ought to know.” A person ought to know that whatever good he has, he has from God.

6. AUGUSTINE (on Psalm 94, tome VIII). “For even if there are some who are called…” If not to us, then to whom? Hear from another psalm: “For all the gods of the nations are demons.”

7. AMBROSE. “From whom are all things.” He distinguished us from the others who are from him; yet they are not in him, since they still do not believe.

8. “Through whom are all things.” All things were indeed created from the Father, but through the Son. When he says, “and we through him,” he signifies that we have been restored through the one through whom we had been created, to the knowledge of God.

[Col. 0181C] 9. LANFRANC. “But not in everyone.” “Not everyone,” he says, “has knowledge of this God”; therefore they think that idols govern things.

10. “But some.” “Some,” he says, “both know that an idol is nothing and yet knowingly eat what has been sacrificed to an idol.”

11. AMBROSE. “But some.” For some of the common people, still reverencing the image, ate from the sacrifices, as though some divinity were present there.

12. AUGUSTINE (Book X of the *Confessions*, chapter 31, tome I). “For neither, if we eat, will we have more…” This means: neither will that thing make me prosperous, nor will that thing make me wretched.

13. LANFRANC. “Nor, if we do not eat…” It is as though someone were saying: “Hunger compels me to eat such food.” Far from it! For so small a portion is distributed to each person that neither what is taken in satisfies, nor does what is taken away compel one to hunger. One may understand the omitted sense as: “We shall fail in good works,” or, “We shall abound in good works.”

14. “We shall abound,” etc. You ought not to eat sacrificial food; for you will gain no advantage by doing so—for, if we eat, we shall not abound—nor will a greater loss result. He proves this in the book by the contrary argument, as follows: “For if we do not eat, we shall have no danger,” which he expresses equivalently by saying, “we shall fail.”

15. AMBROSE. “But see to it.” This means: Do not, because you say that it is permitted for you to eat meat from a sacrifice, cause offense to brothers who do not yet know that an idol is nothing, simply because you know that an idol is nothing.

16. “Lest it become a stumbling block to the weak.” He proves that it will cause a stumbling block because the person has been built up to eat; but the brother will perish—which you ought not to do, namely, cause him to perish. For if you do this, you sin against the brothers. Likewise, you are striking their conscience, which you ought not to do; for in this way you sin against Christ. Therefore you ought not to eat. This is the meaning of: “Therefore, if food causes scandal,” etc. He puts himself in their place, saying: “I will not eat,” so that they may imitate him as their apostle.

17. LANFRANC. “Therefore, if food causes scandal.” “Although,” he says, “it is permitted to eat sacrificial food, you ought not to do so, because you would prepare a stumbling block for weak brothers. You would build them up toward eating it, and thus they would perish, since they thought that the idol was something.”

18. LANFRANC. “I will never eat meat.” That is: I would abstain not only from other foods, in order to avoid giving scandal to a brother, but also from meat, which is the most pleasant of all foods, forever.

Do we not have the right to take along a woman, a sister, a Christian, as do the other apostles—namely, Judas and James, Prisca, and the brothers of the Lord, and Cephas? Or are Barnabas and I alone without the right to do this work?

to those who are under the Law—he means the Samaritans, who obey the Law of Moses but not the Prophets—as though I were under the Law, although I myself was not under the Jewish Law, so that I might win those who were under the Law; to those who were without the Law,

to the Gentiles, as though I were without the Law, although I was not without the Law of God but was in the Law of Christ, so that I might win those who were without the Law.

Run in such a way that you may seize it—the prize of preaching.
