19. AUGUSTINE (Book *On the Work of Monks*, chapter 11). “And I became as a Jew,” that is, so that he might help a carnal Jew or pagan in the way he would have wished to be helped himself if he were in that condition. He bore their weakness in the likeness of compassion, not deceiving them through a fiction of falsehood.

20. AMBROSE. “And I became a Jew.” Because, on account of their scandal, he circumcised Timothy, went up to the temple after being purified, and agreed that the Law and the Prophets were from God. From them he showed that Christ was the one who had been promised, so that his agreement might have its intended effect.

21. “To those who are under the Law.” These are known as Samaritans. For they accept the Law alone—that is, the books of Moses—and are descended from the Persians whom the king of the Assyrians, after removing the children of Israel, placed in captivity to inhabit the regions of Samaria.

22. “To those who are without the Law.” For he asserts to them—that is, to the Gentiles—in accordance with physical reasoning, that the world was made by God and that we derive our origin from him. Thus he says in the Acts of the Apostles: “As some of your own people have said: ‘For we are indeed his offspring.’”

23. “I became weak,” that is, I became weak for the sake of the weak, while abstaining from things permitted for the sake of the brothers, so that I might not cause them scandal.

24. AUGUSTINE. “I became weak.” He became weak precisely by choosing to exercise his authority, moved by such a compassionate disposition that he considered how he would wish to be treated if he himself became so weak that, on seeing those through whom the Gospel was preached to him accept payment, he might suspect a market of commercial wares.

[Col. 0187A] 25. LANFRANC. “Do you not know that those who…” He warns them that they ought not to run in the same way as those who run in a racecourse. For all run, but one receives the prize. The faithful, however, if they run well, will all be crowned.

26. “Those who run in a racecourse.” “I,” he says, “having become all things to all people, run by preaching in such a way that I may seize the prize of the Gospel; and you should run in such a way that you may seize it. For you know that all who run in this way receive it.”

27. “But I discipline my body.” He gives this example so that Christians may not trust that they will be saved through faith alone unless they also act well and abstain from sins.

# CHAPTER X

[Col. 0187]

[Note: [Col. 0187A] CHAPTER X.—1. LANFRANC. “For I do not want you,” etc. Objection: No baptized person will be rejected. He proves this by the fathers baptized in the Red Sea, who, because they did not act well, perished in the desert.]

“I do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, [Note: [Col. 0187B] 2. “For our fathers,” etc. He presents this example so that Christians may not trust that they will be saved by faith alone, baptism, and the other sacraments unless they act well, even if they abstain from sins.] that our fathers [Note: [Col. 0187B] 3. AUGUSTINE (Book XII Against Faustus, chapter 29). “All under the cloud.” The column, because it was straight and firm and supported our weakness, shone by night; by day it did not shine, so that those who do not see might see, and those who see might become blind. The sea is also called the Red Sea: baptism, certainly, consecrated by Christ’s blood; the enemies following from behind perish, and past sins die. The people are led through the desert. The baptized have not yet all come into possession of the promised homeland, but they await in hope what they do not see, and in patience, as though they were in the desert.] were all under the cloud, and all passed through the sea, and all were baptized into Moses, 65 in Moses’ leadership, in the cloud and in the sea, [Note: [Col. 0188A] 4. LANFRANC. “All the same food,” that is, just as the leaders had, so also did those who were governed have—namely, manna,] and all ate the same [Note: [Col. 0188A] 5. “Spiritual food,” that is, food possessing a spiritual meaning, namely, Christ’s body.] food—their food was the same as ours, not in appearance but in meaning: they ate manna, which signified something spiritual, and all drank the same spiritual drink; [Note: [Col. 0188A] 6. AUGUSTINE, Questions on the Old Testament, on Numbers, Book IV, question 35, volume IV. “They were drinking.” The spiritual grace flowing from Christ was therefore signified, because their inward thirst was refreshed. But the striking of the rock with the staff [additional reading: “the rock”] represents Christ’s cross. For when wood came into contact with the rock, this grace flowed forth. And the fact that it was struck twice signifies the cross still more clearly. For there are two pieces of wood in the cross.] (for they were drinking from water flowing from the rock, which followed them—from the spiritual rock that followed and accompanied them; and the rock was Christ, signifying Christ). [Note: [Col. 0188B] 7. “Following them.” The rock did not truly follow the army; rather, the water flowing from the rock did. He calls it spiritual because it contained within itself a spiritual understanding of Christ.] [Note: [Col. 0188B] 8. “But not in most of them.” It is as though he were saying: the sacraments were the same, but their lives were different; therefore some pleased God and others did not.] But God was not well pleased with most of them, for they were struck down in the desert. These things happened as examples for us, so that we might not be desirous of evil things, as they desired them. For we too would perish as they did.

Nor become idolaters, as some of them did, just as it is written in Exodus 32: “The people sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to play,” namely, before the idol. Nor let us commit fornication by departing from divine worship, as some of them fornicated with the daughters of Moab; and twenty-three thousand fell in one day—and we likewise would fall. Nor let us put Christ to the test—for we too would perish as they did—as some of them tested him, saying: “Can he also give bread, or prepare a table, for his people?” And they perished from the serpents. Nor murmur, as some of them murmured on account of the water, and perished by the destroying angel.

All these things I said because they happened to them as figures; but they were written, therefore, for our correction, upon whom the ends of the ages have come—the last age, or Christ. Therefore, let the one who thinks that he is standing—because those who sinned fell, even though we are baptized—take care lest he fall.

[Note: [Col. 0188B] 9. AUGUSTINE (Book II, On Baptism, against the Donatists, chapter 5, volume VII). “Temptation seize you.” For we are human beings. To think otherwise than the matter actually is constitutes human temptation. But to love one’s own opinion excessively, or to envy those who are better, to the point of undertaking the sacrilege of presuming to take communion [variant: “of cutting off communion”], or of creating a schism or heresy, is diabolical presumption.]

Let no temptation seize you except a human one, so that you do not obey as they did—temptation concerning food, drink, and other such things. [Note: [Col. 0188B] 10. LANFRANC. “Temptation seize you.” Human temptation concerns food, drink, sleep, and the other things of which human weakness cannot be deprived.] But God is faithful—[Note: [Col. 0188C] 11. “Faithful,” that is, he will do what he promised. [Col. 0189A] For in many places of his Scriptures he promised that he would not abandon his faithful ones.] he will not allow you to be tempted beyond what you can bear; rather, with the temptation he will also provide [Note: [Col. 0189A] 12. “A way out,” that is, when temptation comes, he will also cause a means of escape to arise.] a way out, a means of support, so that you may be able to endure it.

[Note: [Col. 0189A] 13. “Therefore, my beloved,” that is, because the sacraments alone could not save them. And the one who stands must take care lest he fall.]

Therefore, my beloved, because twenty-three thousand of them fell, flee from the worship of idols. I speak as to prudent people; judge for yourselves what I say.

[Note: [Col. 0189A] 14. “The cup of blessing.” The whole point of the passage is this: one who eats the Lord’s body and drinks his blood ought not to touch or eat what has been sacrificed to idols, for he would become a participant in idols. He proves this as follows: whoever drinks the Lord’s cup and eats the bread—that is, his body—is a participant in him.]

The cup of blessing, over which we priests pronounce a blessing—is it not communion in the Blood of Christ? Does it not make us participants in Christ’s blood? And the bread that we break—is it not participation in the body of the Lord? [Note: [Col. 0189A] 15. “Because there is one bread.” He explains the manner and reason by which and through which the cup of blessing and the broken bread become flesh and blood for the recipient. By the unity of the bread and the unity of the body, charity must be understood; if it is absent, those who receive them receive judgment for themselves. Figuratively, when the Church is called Christ’s one bread and one body, this is said for your sake: just as one bread is composed of many grains and one body of limbs, so Christ’s Church is composed of many believers, joined together by charity.] Because there is one bread, we, though many, are one body, all who share in the one bread.

[Note: [Col. 0189B] 16. “Observe Israel according to the flesh.” This is an analogy for understanding what was said above: “flesh,” that is, one who observes the precepts of the carnal law.]

Observe Israel according to the flesh. [He proves by another analogy what was said above: those who eat food sacrificed to idols become participants in demons.] Are not those who eat the sacrifices participants in the altar? [Note: [Col. 0189B] 17. “Participants in the altar.” Likewise, those who eat Christ’s flesh and drink his blood are participants in him.] What then? By this I mean that such people become participants in demons. Do I mean that what is sacrificed to idols is something, or that an idol is something? No. But I say that what the Gentiles sacrifice, they sacrifice to demons and not to God. I do not want you, by eating what has been sacrificed to idols, to become associates of demons.

(The reason why they ought not to eat food sacrificed to idols.) You cannot drink the Lord’s cup and the cup of demons. You cannot share in the Lord’s table and the table of demons.

[Note: [Col. 0189B] 18. “Do we provoke the Lord to jealousy?” By eating food sacrificed to idols, we provoke him to anger; this is not fitting, because he would punish us. He is stronger than we are, and we are neither stronger nor equal to him.]

Do we provoke the Lord to jealousy? Are we stronger than he is?

Everything is permitted to me, by the power of free choice, but not everything is beneficial or profitable. Everything is permitted to me, but not everything builds up or benefits others. Let no one seek what is his own, but what belongs to another. We ought to seek not only our own advantage but also that of our brothers.

[Note: [Col. 0190A] 19. “Without asking questions.” It is as though someone were to say: if you ask and are told that it was sacrificed to idols, the listener’s conscience will be strengthened to believe that an idol is something.]

Everything that is sold in the marketplace, eat, asking no questions on account of conscience—whether it is food sacrificed to idols or not—so that those who later see you eating it will not suppose that you regard it as holy. “The earth is the Lord’s,” he says, and everything in it belongs to him, as the Psalmist says:

[Note: [Col. 0190A] 20. “The earth is the Lord’s.” He gives the reason for what he said above: “Eat everything that is sold in the marketplace.”]

“The earth is the Lord’s, and the fullness thereof.”

If one of the unbelievers—of those who do not believe—invites you to dinner and you wish to go, eat everything set before you, asking no questions. For if you were to ask and then knowingly eat it, you would incur the blasphemy of those watching. Do this for the sake of the conscience of the one who provides the dinner. But if someone says, “This was sacrificed to idols,” do not eat it, for the sake of the one who indicated this and for the sake of conscience. By “conscience” I mean not your own, but that of the other person who is watching.

[Note: [Col. 0190A] 21. AMBROSE. “Why, then, is there freedom?” He says this because, when one’s conscience is free from devotion to an idol, why should anyone suppose that he eats what was sacrificed to idols as an act of veneration?]

[Note: [Col. 0190A] 22. LANFRANC. “Why, then, is there freedom?” The freedom of Christians is the ability to use all foods with thanksgiving. But this freedom is shown to be reprehensible and condemnable when it is judged by another person’s conscience—when, by taking advantage of that freedom, we do something that forces those who see us to suspect us of something impious and sacrilegious.]

Why, then—although, he says, your freedom permits you to eat food sacrificed to idols—should my freedom be judged by another person’s conscience? If I [Note: [Col. 0190B] 23. “If I partake with thanksgiving.” It is as though he were saying: Even if, by the freedom of Christian religion, I can partake with thanksgiving of food sacrificed to idols, knowing that an idol is nothing and that no evil comes to God’s good creatures from the sacrifice, and that sin belongs only to those who eat what has been sacrificed to an idol out of reverence for the idol—still, it is foolish, for the sake of that very thanksgiving, to fall into blasphemy and the reproach of ignorant people who think that I regard an idol as something great because they see me eating sacrificial food with thanksgiving.]

partake with thanksgiving, why am I blasphemed for giving thanks?

[Note: [Col. 0190B] 24. AMBROSE. “If I partake with thanksgiving.” If I share in God’s grace because I eat in his name, why should anyone suppose that I am devoted to an idol, since I do not recoil from what has been offered to an idol?]

Therefore, whether you eat, [because you ought not to eat with blasphemy,] or drink, or do anything else, [Note: [Col. 0191A] 25. “Everything to the glory of God.” Something is done to God’s glory when God is praised in a Christian’s actions and conduct.] do everything for the glory of God; you ought to do it for God’s praise.

[Note: [Col. 0191A] 26. “Without offense.” Offense is caused to the Jews when they see Christians—who accept the Law and the Prophets—not recoil from idols, which the Jews abominate.]

Be without offense—that is, be pleasing—to the Jews; [Note: [Col. 0191A] 27. “And to the Gentiles.” For the Greeks, that is, the Gentiles, offense arises if, while remaining in their former condition, they are not only not reproved but become more willing to persist because they do not avoid the vows made to idols.] and to the Gentiles; [Note: [Col. 0191A] 28. “To the churches of God.” An obstacle is created for the Church of God when it sees some of its own number clinging to things hostile to God.] and to the churches of God, just as I also please everyone in every way, seeking not what is advantageous to me alone but what is advantageous to many, so that they may be saved.

[COMMENTARY.]

[Col. 0187A]

CHAPTER X.—1. LANFRANC. “For I do not want you,” etc. Objection: No baptized person will be rejected. He proves this by the fathers baptized in the Red Sea, who, because they did not act well, perished in the desert.

2. “For our fathers,” etc. He presents this example so that Christians may not trust that they will be saved by faith alone, baptism, and the other sacraments unless they act well, even if they abstain from sins.

3. AUGUSTINE (Book XII Against Faustus, chapter 29). “All under the cloud.” The column, because it was straight and firm and supported our weakness, shone by night; by day it did not shine, so that those who do not see might see, and those who see might become blind. The sea is also called the Red Sea: baptism, certainly, consecrated by Christ’s blood; the enemies following from behind perish, and past sins die. The people are led through the desert. The baptized have not yet all come into possession of the promised homeland, but they await in hope what they do not see, and in patience, as though they were in the desert.

[Col. 0188A] 4. LANFRANC. “All the same food,” that is, just as the leaders had, so also did those who were governed have—namely, manna.

5. “Spiritual food,” that is, food possessing a spiritual meaning, namely, Christ’s body.

6. AUGUSTINE, Questions on the Old Testament, on Numbers, Book IV, question 35, volume IV. “They were drinking.” The spiritual grace flowing from Christ was therefore signified, because their inward thirst was refreshed. But the striking of the rock with the staff [additional reading: “the rock”] represents Christ’s cross. For when wood came into contact with the rock, this grace flowed forth. And the fact that it was struck twice signifies the cross still more clearly. For there are two pieces of wood in the cross.

7. LANFRANC. “Following them.” The rock did not truly follow the army; rather, the water flowing from the rock did. He calls it spiritual because it contained within itself a spiritual understanding of Christ.

8. “But not in most of them.” It is as though he were saying: the sacraments were the same, but their lives were different; therefore some pleased God and others did not.

9. AUGUSTINE (Book II, On Baptism, against the Donatists, chapter 5, volume VII). “Temptation seize you.” For we are human beings. To think otherwise than the matter actually is constitutes human temptation. But to love one’s own opinion excessively, or to envy those who are better, to the point of undertaking the sacrilege of presuming to take communion [variant: “of cutting off communion”], or of creating a schism or heresy, is diabolical presumption.

10. LANFRANC. “Temptation seize you.” Human temptation concerns food, drink, sleep, and the other things of which human weakness cannot be deprived.

11. “But God is faithful,” that is, he will do what he promised. For in many places of his Scriptures he promised that he would not abandon his faithful ones.

12. “A way out,” that is, when temptation comes, he will also cause a means of escape to arise.

13. “Therefore, my beloved,” that is, because the sacraments alone could not save them. And the one who stands must take care lest he fall.

14. “The cup of blessing.” The whole point of the passage is this: one who eats the Lord’s body and drinks his blood ought not to touch or eat what has been sacrificed to idols, for he would become a participant in idols. He proves this as follows: whoever drinks the Lord’s cup and eats the bread—that is, his body—is a participant in him.

15. “Because there is one bread.” He explains the manner and reason by which and through which the cup of blessing and the broken bread become flesh and blood for the recipient. By the unity of the bread and the unity of the body, charity must be understood; if it is absent, those who receive them receive judgment for themselves. Figuratively, when the Church is called Christ’s one bread and one body, this is said for your sake: just as one bread is composed of many grains and one body of limbs, so Christ’s Church is composed of many believers, joined together by charity.

16. “Observe Israel according to the flesh.” This is an analogy for understanding what was said above: “flesh,” that is, one who observes the precepts of the carnal law.

17. “Participants in the altar.” Likewise, those who eat Christ’s flesh and drink his blood are participants in him.

18. AMBROSE. “Do we provoke the Lord to jealousy?” By eating food sacrificed to idols, we provoke him to anger; this is not fitting, because he would punish us. He is stronger than we are, and we are neither stronger nor equal to him.

19. “Without asking questions.” It is as though someone were to say: if you ask and are told that it was sacrificed to idols, the listener’s conscience will be strengthened to believe that an idol is something.

20. “The earth is the Lord’s.” He gives the reason for what he said above: “Eat everything that is sold in the marketplace.”

21. AMBROSE. “Why, then, is there freedom?” He says this because, when one’s conscience is free from devotion to an idol, why should anyone suppose that he eats what was sacrificed to idols as an act of veneration?

22. LANFRANC. “Why, then, is there freedom?” The freedom of Christians is the ability to use all foods with thanksgiving. But this freedom is shown to be reprehensible and condemnable when it is judged by another person’s conscience—when, by taking advantage of that freedom, we do something that forces those who see us to suspect us of something impious and sacrilegious.

23. “If I partake with thanksgiving.” It is as though he were saying: Even if, by the freedom of Christian religion, I can partake with thanksgiving of food sacrificed to idols, knowing that an idol is nothing and that no evil comes to God’s good creatures from the sacrifice, and that sin belongs only to those who eat what has been sacrificed to an idol out of reverence for the idol—still, it is foolish, for the sake of that very thanksgiving, to fall into blasphemy and the reproach of ignorant people who think that I regard an idol as something great because they see me eating sacrificial food with thanksgiving.

24. AMBROSE. “If I partake with thanksgiving.” If I share in God’s grace because I eat in his name, why should anyone suppose that I am devoted to an idol, since I do not recoil from what has been offered to an idol?

25. “Everything to the glory of God.” Something is done to God’s glory when God is praised in a Christian’s actions and conduct.

26. “Without offense.” Offense is caused to the Jews when they see Christians—who accept the Law and the Prophets—not recoil from idols, which the Jews abominate.

27. “And to the Gentiles.” For the Greeks, that is, the Gentiles, offense arises if, while remaining in their former condition, they are not only not reproved but become more willing to persist because they do not avoid the vows made to idols.

28. “To the churches of God.” An obstacle is created for the Church of God when it sees some of its own number clinging to things hostile to God.

CHAPTER XI.

[Col. 0191]

“Therefore, because I seek what is useful for you and for many, be imitators of me, just as I also am of Christ.”

[Note: [Col. 0191B] CHAPTER XI.—1. AMBROSE. “I praise you.” He does not affirm this but rebukes them, because, although he was their apostle, they had forgotten his traditions.]

But I praise you, brothers—whether ironically or seriously, at least in part—because you remember me in everything and keep my instructions as I delivered them to you.

But I want you to know that the head of every man [Note: [Col. 0191B] 2. “But the head of Christ.” Christ is the head of man in one way; the man is the head of the woman in another; and God is the head of Christ in another. God is the head of Christ because Christ was begotten by him. The man is the head of the woman because she was formed from his rib by God’s power. Christ is the head of man because man was created through him.] is Christ; the head of the woman is the man; and the head of Christ is God.

[Note: [Col. 0191B] 3. “Every man praying.” He uses “to pray” to mean to make supplication, to prophesy, and to declare in the language of the Creed after the prayer that the Lord’s coming will take place.]

[Note: [Col. 0191B] 4. LANFRANC. “Every man praying,” etc. He turns to remove the practice among the Corinthians by which men prayed in church with covered heads and women with uncovered heads, as though women ought not to be subject to men. Since women ought to be subject, men should pray with uncovered heads and women with covered heads.]

Every man who prays or prophesies about the future with his head covered [Note: [Col. 0191C] 5. “Dishonors his head.” The woman, he says, ought to pray with her head covered; otherwise she dishonors her head, for she does the same thing as if she were shaven.] dishonors his head. But every woman who prays or prophesies with her head uncovered dishonors her head; for it is one and the same thing as praying with her head uncovered and being shaven. (When she has her head uncovered, she parts the hair from the front of her head.)

For if a woman does not cover herself, let her also be shorn. Or, he says, she ought either to be veiled or shorn; but not the latter—therefore the former. But if it is disgraceful for a woman to be shorn or shaved, let her cover her head.

A man, indeed, ought not to cover his head, because [Note: [Col. 0191C] 6. AUGUSTINE (Book XII, On the Trinity, chapter 7). “The image and glory of God.” I believe that, in the nature of the human mind, a woman together with her husband is the image of God, [additional reading: “so that the whole substance may be one image”]. But when what belongs to her alone is distributed for the sake of assistance, she is not the image of God. What belongs to the man alone, however, is the image of God, so full and complete that it is [variant: “as”] joined with the woman into one.] he is the image and glory of God; but woman is the glory of man.

He removes the alternative. For it was not man—that is, Adam—from woman—that is, Eve; rather, woman was from man, considered as a whole. This is another reason why woman is the glory of man. For man was not created for woman’s sake—he removes this—but [Note: [Col. 0192A] 8. “Woman.” Woman too is the glory of God, by whom and for whose glorification she was created, but in the second place; for man is primary.] woman for man’s sake. Therefore [Note: [Col. 0192A] 9. AMBROSE. “The woman ought to have authority,” etc. In the church, out of reverence for the bishop, a woman should not have her head uncovered but covered with a veil; nor should she have authority to speak, because the bishop bears the person of Christ. Thus, as before a judge, so before the bishop, who is God’s representative, she ought to be seen as subject on account of the origin of guilt.] the woman ought to have authority over her head.

[Note: [Col. 0192B] 10. LANFRANC. “Because of the angels.” He calls the preachers angels, who stood in a higher place when they preached. He says that women should cover their heads because, with their hair spread out, they would more easily provoke those looking at them to lust.]

Because of the angels—the preachers—or because of the presence of angels.

[Note: [Col. 0192B] 11. “Nevertheless.” Although the first man was not from woman but woman from him, this is not so in subsequent procreation. Every man thereafter was born from woman, and woman from man. [Col. 0192C] “Created in the Lord,” that is, in the Lord’s creation, in which one is not created without the other.]

Nevertheless, neither is woman without man nor man without woman, in the Lord—that is, in the Lord’s working. For just as woman is from man, so also today man is through woman; [Note: [Col. 0192C] 12. AMBROSE. “But everything is from God.” Thus neither should woman be saddened on account of her subjection, nor should man, being exalted, become proud.] but everything—both man and woman—is from God.

Judge for yourselves: is it fitting for a woman to pray to God with her head uncovered? Does not nature itself—natural reason—teach you that it is disgraceful for a man to nourish his hair, whereas it is a glory for a woman to nourish hers, [Col. 0193] because her hair has been given to her as a covering?

But if anyone seems to be contentious—we are responding to this or to some other statement of mine, namely, that we do not have the custom of women leaving their heads uncovered—we have no such custom, nor does the Church of God.

[Note: [Col. 0193A] 13. AUGUSTINE (Book On the Work of Monks, chapter 31, volume III). “But this I command.” This is what I command: that the authority of the one receiving the command be heeded, rather than requiring the ingenuity of one who argues.]

But this I command—so that no one may be contentious, or so that no one may cover his head—not praising the fact that you meet together not for the better, that is, for good, but for the worse, that is, for evil, in remembrance of the Lord’s supper.

For, first, I say that when you assemble in the church, I hear that there are divisions among you—the disciples of Paul dining separately and the disciples of Peter separately, scorning one another—and to some extent I believe that there are divisions. For Scripture says: “There must also be heresies, so that those who are approved may be made manifest among you.” 69

[Note: [Col. 0193A] 14. AMBROSE. “When you assemble.” He censures those who assembled in the church in such a way that, when the presbyters arrived after they had offered their gifts, each person who had offered claimed the whole of it for himself. For the false apostles had sown disagreements among them, so that they were jealous over their offerings, even though the offerings of all were blessed with one and the same prayer; consequently, those who had not offered, or had nothing with which to offer, were put to shame and confused, as usually happens, and did not take their share.]

[Note: [Col. 0193B] 15. LANFRANC. “When you assemble.” Formerly they had the custom of assembling in the church at appointed times, bringing there whatever food and drink each person could provide, and all sharing together, poor and rich alike. They called this the Lord’s supper because it was done in remembrance of the Lord’s supper. But this custom had become corrupted: the rich, anticipating their own meals, ate, while the poor, having little, were ashamed to eat in their presence. The Apostle rebukes this and says that it would be better for them to eat and drink in their own homes than to assemble in contempt of the church and to the humiliation of the poor.]

Therefore, when you assemble together, it is no longer [Note: [Col. 0193B] 16. AUGUSTINE (Letter 118 to Januarius, chapter 5, volume II). “The Lord’s supper.” He calls the very reception of the Eucharist the Lord’s supper.] to eat the Lord’s supper; for it is not a common meal, as the Lord’s supper was.

[Note: [Col. 0193B] 17. (ibid., chapter 6.) “Each one.” For it is not because the Lord gave it after food that brothers who have breakfasted or dined ought to assemble to receive that sacrament; nor ought they, as those whom the Apostle reproves and commends [variant: “corrects”] for mixing these things with their own tables did, to do so.]

For each person takes his own supper in advance, anticipating the others, in order to eat. One person is hungry, while another is drunk with wine. Do you not have houses in which to eat and drink? Or do you despise the church of God and put to shame those who have nothing? [For it would be better to eat at home than in church before the hour of supper.] What shall I say to you?

[Note: [Col. 0194A] 18. LANFRANC. “I praise you.” I do not praise you in this respect, that you do not partake together. For you are guilty of the Lord’s body and blood, since you receive them unworthily. If the bread and cup that you receive are Christ’s blood and body, then you receive Christ’s body and blood unworthily; and indeed they are. For the Lord said when he was being handed over: “For I received from the Lord, and I delivered to you.”]

Shall I praise you? In this I do not praise you, because you do not observe what I received from the Lord concerning the institution of the supper. For I received from the Lord what I also delivered to you: namely, that the supper should be distributed equally among you. For the Lord Jesus, on the night when he was handed over, took bread, and giving thanks, broke it and said: “Take and eat; this is my body, which will be handed over for you. Do this”—that is, consecrate this body—“in remembrance of me.”

Likewise also the cup, after he had supped, saying:

[Note: [Col. 0194A] 19. “This cup is the new,” etc. The order is: This cup, through the new blood, is the new testament; that is, the new testament is confirmed through my blood, because a testament is confirmed in the dead. Or: through this you have a new promise, that is, full remission of sins.]

“This cup is the new testament in my blood; do this, as often as you drink it, in remembrance of me.”

He explains what kind of remembrance of Christ he means.

[Note: [Col. 0194B] 20. “As often as.” He explains, I say, the Lord’s remembrance—namely, remembrance of his death.]

For as often as you eat this bread and drink this cup, [Note: [Col. 0194B] 21. “You will proclaim the Lord’s death.” In the sacrament of Christ’s body, his death is proclaimed, because the faithful celebrate it daily in remembrance of his death.] you will proclaim the Lord’s death, which has already occurred, [Note: [Col. 0194B] 22. “Until he comes.” Until he comes for judgment. He says this because this sacrifice will not be changed until the end of the age, just as the sacraments of the Jews were changed.] until the Lord comes for judgment.

[Note: [Col. 0194B] 23. “Therefore, whoever.” This is inferred from the Redeemer’s words quoted above: “This is my body,” and “In my blood.”]

Therefore, whoever eats this bread 70 or drinks the Lord’s cup unworthily [Note: [Col. 0194B] 24. AMBROSE. “Will be guilty of the body.” What does it mean to be guilty, except to suffer the penalties of the Lord’s death?] will be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord.

But let a person examine himself—make himself approved—and then let him eat of that bread and drink from the cup. For the one who eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment, condemnation, for himself, [Note: [Col. 0195A] 25. LANFRANC. “Not discerning the Lord’s body,” that is, not understanding that the Lord’s body is received to the condemnation of the unworthy.] not discerning the Lord’s body—not distinguishing the Lord’s body from other foods by a unique act of reverence.

For this reason, because it is received unworthily, many among you are weak and sick, and many sleep—that is, die.

[Note: [Col. 0195A] 26. AMBROSE. “But if we judged ourselves.” He says that if we ourselves corrected our errors, we would not be judged by the Lord; and because we are corrected, this is nevertheless for our benefit, so that we may be reformed by that very fear.]

But if we judged ourselves, we would understand and repent, and certainly would not be judged or condemned. Yet while we are judged, we are corrected by the Lord; we are punished in this age so that we may not be condemned with the world.

Therefore, my brothers, since it is wrong for each person to take his own supper in advance, when you assemble to eat, wait for one another.

[Note: [Col. 0195A] 27. LANFRANC. “If anyone is hungry.” If, he says, anyone cannot wait at home for the appointed time for eating, compelled by hunger, let him eat at home; let him anticipate the hour of supper. [ [Col. 0195B] A word seems to be missing: “the time.”]]

If anyone is hungry, let him eat at home, so that you may not assemble for condemnation. I will arrange the other matters when I come.

[COMMENTARY.]

[Col. 0191B]

CHAPTER XI.—1. AMBROSE. “I praise you.” He does not affirm this but rebukes them, because, although he was their apostle, they had forgotten his traditions.

2. “But the head of Christ.” Christ is the head of man in one way; the man is the head of the woman in another; and God is the head of Christ in another. God is the head of Christ because Christ was begotten by him. The man is the head of the woman because she was formed from his rib by God’s power. Christ is the head of man because man was created through him.

3. “Every man praying.” He uses “to pray” to mean to make supplication, to prophesy, and to declare in the language of the Creed after the prayer that the Lord’s coming will take place.

4. LANFRANC. “Every man praying,” etc. He turns to remove the practice among the Corinthians by which men prayed in church with covered heads and women with uncovered heads, as though women ought not to be subject to men. Since women ought to be subject, men should pray with uncovered heads and women with covered heads.

5. “Dishonors his head.” The woman, he says, ought to pray with her head covered; otherwise she dishonors her head, for she does the same thing as if she were shaven.

6. AUGUSTINE (Book XII, On the Trinity, chapter 7). “The image and glory of God.” I believe that, in the nature of the human mind, a woman together with her husband is the image of God, [additional reading: “so that the whole substance may be one image”]. But when what belongs to her alone is distributed for the sake of assistance, she is not the image of God. What belongs to the man alone, however, is the image of God, so full and complete that it is [variant: “as”] joined with the woman into one.

7. LANFRANC. “The image of God,” etc. Man was created primarily according to the image of God. Woman was afterward formed from man’s rib; therefore the man ought to have his head uncovered.

8. “Woman.” Woman too is the glory of God, by whom and for whose glorification she was created, but in the second place; for man is primary.

9. AMBROSE. “The woman ought to have authority,” etc. In the church, out of reverence for the bishop, a woman should not have her head uncovered but covered with a veil; nor should she have authority to speak, because the bishop bears the person of Christ. Thus, as before a judge, so before the bishop, who is God’s representative, she ought to be seen as subject on account of the origin of guilt.

10. LANFRANC. “Because of the angels.” He calls the preachers angels, who stood in a higher place when they preached. He says that women should cover their heads because, with their hair spread out, they would more easily provoke those looking at them to lust.

11. “Nevertheless.” Although the first man was not from woman but woman from him, this is not so in subsequent procreation. Every man thereafter was born from woman, and woman from man. [Col. 0192C] “Created in the Lord,” that is, in the Lord’s creation, in which one is not created without the other.

12. AMBROSE. “But everything is from God.” Thus neither should woman be saddened on account of her subjection, nor should man, being exalted, become proud.

[Col. 0193A] 13. AUGUSTINE (Book On the Work of Monks, chapter 31, volume III). “But this I command.” This is what I command: that the authority of the one receiving the command be heeded, rather than requiring the ingenuity of one who argues.

14. AMBROS. “When you come together.” He censures those who came together in the church in such a way that, after offering their gifts, each person claimed entirely for himself what he had offered when the presbyters arrived. For the pseudo-apostles had sown dissensions among them, so that they begrudged one another their offerings, even though the offerings of all were blessed with one and the same prayer; consequently, those who had not offered, or had nothing with which to offer, were corrected and put to shame out of embarrassment, and did not receive a share.

15. LANFR. “When you come together.” Previously they had the custom of gathering at the church at appointed times, bringing there food and drink according to each person’s means, and all participating together, both poor and rich. [Col. 0193B] They called this the Lord’s Supper because it was done in memory of the Lord’s Supper. But this custom had become corrupted: the rich, anticipating their own suppers, ate beforehand. The poor, having little, were ashamed to eat in their presence. The Apostle rebukes this and says that it is better for them to eat and drink at home than to assemble in contempt of the church and to the confusion of the poor.

16. AUGUST. (*Letter 118 to Januarius*, chapter 5, volume II). “The Lord’s Supper.” He calls the very reception of the Eucharist the Lord’s Supper.

17. (Ibid., chapter 6.) “Let each person.” For it does not follow that, because the Lord gave it after meals, [Col. 0193C] the brothers should therefore assemble after lunch or dinner [Col. 0194A] to receive that sacrament, or—as those whom the Apostle rebukes did—mix this with their own meals. [The printed text has *commendat*; *emendat* is also reported.]

18. LANFR. “I praise you.” I do not praise you in this, that you do not receive it communally. For you are guilty with respect to the body and blood of the Lord, since you receive them unworthily. If the bread itself and the cup that you receive are the blood and body of Christ, then you receive the body and blood of Christ unworthily; and indeed that is what they are. For the Lord said, when he was being handed over: “For I received from the Lord, and what I received I delivered to you.”

19. “This cup is the new [covenant],” etc. ORDO. This cup, in the new blood, is the new testament—that is, the new testament is confirmed through my blood, because [Col. 0194B] a testament is confirmed in the dead. Or: through this you have a new promise, that is, the full remission of sins.

20. “Whenever.” He explains, I say, the commemoration of the Lord—namely, of his death.

21. “You shall proclaim the Lord’s death.” In the sacrament of Christ’s body, his death is proclaimed, because it is celebrated daily by the faithful in memory of his death.

22. “Until he comes.” Let him come for judgment. He says this because this sacrifice will not be changed until the end of the world, just as the sacraments of the Jews were changed.

23. “Therefore, whoever.” This is gathered from the Redeemer’s words stated above: “This is my body,” and: “In my blood.”

24. AMBROS. “He will be guilty of the body.” What does it mean to be guilty, [Col. 0194C] except to suffer the penalty of the Lord’s death?

[Col. 0195A]

25. LANFR. “Not discerning the Lord’s body,” that is, not understanding that the Lord’s body is received to condemnation by the unworthy.

26. AMBROS. “But if we judged ourselves.” He says this because, if we corrected our own errors, we would not be judged by the Lord; and because we are chastised, this is nevertheless for our benefit, so that we may be corrected by that very fear.

27. LANFR. “If anyone is hungry.” “If anyone,” he says, “cannot wait at home for the appointed time for eating, compelled by hunger, let him rather eat at home; let him anticipate the hour of dinner.” [Note: [Col. 0195B] “Time” seems to be missing.]

# CHAPTER XII

[Col. 0195]

[Note: CAP. XII.—1. LANFR. “Now concerning spiritual matters.” “I made you acquainted with carnal matters,” he says—that is, not eating food sacrificed to idols and not praying with uncovered heads. “I also wish to make you acquainted with spiritual matters,” which you, now that you have become Christians, will obey; for when you lived as pagans, you obediently served idols at the priests’ command, as you know.]

Now concerning the spiritual matters of which I spoke above—or rather, of which I shall speak in what follows—I do not want you to be ignorant, brothers. You know that when you were Gentiles, when you lived as Gentiles, you went, or were going, to mute idols, being led along as you were directed, according to the priests’ pleasure.

[Note: 2. “Therefore I make known to you.” As though he were saying: Since, even in your pagan condition, you were obedient also toward evil, I believe that in the faith of Christ you will be much more obedient toward good.]

Therefore, because you obeyed paganism, I make known to you—so to speak: since, even in your pagan condition, you were obedient toward evil, I believe that in the faith of Christ you will be more obedient toward good—that no one speaking in the Spirit, through the Spirit of God, says “Anathema to Jesus.” To say “Anathema to Jesus,” separating Christ from the Father, is either to think that he is not God or that he is not from God.

[Note: 3. AUGUST. (*Exposition of the Gospel of John*, tractate 74, volume IX). “No one can say.” This is an apostolic utterance: “No one says, ‘Lord Jesus,’ except in the Holy Spirit.” And who says “Lord Jesus” except one who loves him, if he says it in the sense in which the Apostle intended it to be understood? For many say it with their voice, but deny it in their heart and by their actions.]

And no one can say—and believe—“Lord Jesus,” that is, that Jesus is Lord, except in the Holy Spirit, except through the Holy Spirit.

But there are divisions of graces, yet the Spirit is the same. The gifts of the Holy Spirit are indeed diverse, but the Spirit is the same. He shows, in the several parts, that the charisms are indeed diverse, but the Spirit is the same. And there are divisions of ministries, yet the Lord is the same. And there are divisions of operations, yet it is the same God, the Father, who works all things in all.

[Note: 5. “Divisions of ministries.” Grace is not divided among the persons of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit; rather, the undivided nature of the unity is meant, and the one work of the three is understood.]

To each person, however, manifestation is given—and yet manifestation is given to each person—the manifest grace of the Spirit for his own benefit or that of his neighbors.

To one, through the same Spirit, is given a word of wisdom concerning divine matters; to another, a word of knowledge concerning the humility of Christ, according to the same Spirit; to another, faith, so that he may confidently believe, without hesitation, that what he asks for will come to pass, in the same Spirit; to another, gifts of healing, the curing of the sick, in the one Spirit; to another, the working of powers, the raising of the dead; to another, prophecy.

[Note: 6. AUGUST. (*On the Trinity*, book XII, chapter 14, volume III). “A word of wisdom.” I find it written in the Book of Job, spoken by that same holy man: “Behold, piety is wisdom; but to abstain from evil is knowledge.” In this distinction, wisdom is to be understood as pertaining to contemplation, and knowledge to action. For in this passage he called piety the worship of God, which in Greek is called *theosebeia* (θεοσέβεια). This word occurs in this sentence in the Greek manuscripts.]

To another, discernment of spirits, so that he may know how to distinguish which thoughts are from God and which are sent by the devil; to another, kinds of tongues.

[Note: 7. AUGUST. (*On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, book XII, chapter 13, volume III). “To another, discernment.” Discernment is indeed most difficult when the evil spirit acts as though tranquil and, without causing any bodily disturbance, speaks after taking on a human spirit. This is also the case when he speaks truths and proclaims useful things, transforming himself into an angel, as it is written, “as an angel of light.”]

To another, interpretation of tongues.

[Note: 8. LANFR. “To another, interpretation of utterances.” He calls “utterances” allegorical expressions, whether in words or in speeches, such as are frequently found in the Prophets and the Gospels; those who know how to interpret them possess that knowledge through the grace of the Holy Spirit. By “utterances” we can also understand mystical visions, such as appeared to Pharaoh and Nebuchadnezzar. Hence Joseph says: “Because the word of God comes to pass.” And in Daniel it is read: “Tell the dream, and we shall make its interpretation known.” And the king says: “The utterance has departed from me.” The interpretation of these things was granted to both men by divine gift. For Joseph says: “Apart from me, God will answer favorably for Pharaoh.” And Daniel says: “You have shown me what we asked of you, because you have disclosed the king’s utterance to us.”]

But one and the same Spirit works all these things, distributing them individually as he wishes—this to one, that to another, more to one and less to another.

[Note: 9. AMBROS. “But all these things.” What he previously attributed to the three persons, he now declares to be directed [alternatively, done] by the one Holy Spirit. Since they are of one nature, what one works, the three work.]

For just as the body is one and has many members, and all the members of the body, though many, are nevertheless one body, so also is Christ—that is, the head and the body, which is the Church. “We,” he says, “are members of the Church, and we are one.”

For in one Spirit we were all baptized into one body, whether Jews or Gentiles, whether slaves or free; and we were all given to drink of one Spirit. For the body is not one member but many. Although, he says, we are one body, we are nevertheless not all one member, just as in the body.

[Note: 10. LANFR. “For just as the body is one.” By comparison he shows that the Spirit is one and that his gifts are many, just as the body is one while having many members. He places Christ—that is, the head—and not the body, which is the Church, in place of the Spirit by which those members are joined together.]

If the foot should say, “Because I am not a hand, I am not of the body,” is it therefore not of the body? Even if some in the Church are not preachers, are they for that reason not of the Church? Just as the foot, although it is not the hand, is not for that reason outside the body?

And if the ear should say, “Because I am not an eye, I am not of the body,” is it therefore not of the body?

[Note: 11. AUGUST. (*Expositions on the Psalms*, Psalm XXX). “But all the members.” Speaking of Christ’s members—that is, the faithful—he does not say, “So also are the members of Christ.” Rather, he called the whole of what he said “Christ.” Many members, one body: Christ. Therefore, all of us together with our head are Christ.]

[Note: 12. AMBROS. “If the foot should say.” This means that one who appears weak among the brothers cannot deny—or, according to another reading, cannot be denied to be—of the body on the ground that he is not powerful.]

If the whole body were an eye, where would hearing be? If the whole were hearing, where would the sense of smell be? The same applies by analogy. But now God has placed the members in the body, each one of them, just as he wished.

[Note: 13. “If the whole body were an eye.” That is, if everyone were engaged in one kind of work, how would the body’s remaining needs be fulfilled, since it is evident that many functions are necessary for governing the body?]

[Note: 14. LANFR. “If the whole body were an eye.” Nor, he says, should everyone in the Church be a preacher, because it is not fitting for the whole body to be an eye. If this were so, it would no longer be the body itself, since it would lack hearing and the body’s other parts.]

But if all were one member, where would the body be? Therefore, all the members of the body are not one member but many, so that the body may exist as such; but if all were one member, the body would not subsist.

Now there are many members, but one body. He is speaking of the human body, which cannot exist unless it consists of many members.

[Note: 15. AMBROS. “But if they were all one.” It is clear that, if all had possessed the same dignity, they would not be called members, nor would they constitute a body. Therefore—or, according to another reading, “and therefore”—the body is governed by the various functions of its members.]

It is not possible—by this comparison he shows that the members of the Church are necessary to one another, although perhaps not unequal—for the eye to say to the hand, “I have no need of you,” nor again for the head to say to the feet, “You are not necessary to me.”

[Note: 16. “The eye cannot say to the hand.” That is, the superior cannot say to the inferior: “I have no need of you.”]

Rather, those members of the body that appear to be weaker are much more necessary; and those members of the body that we think less honorable—that is, he calls the shameful parts of the body—we surround with more abundant honor, with the honor of clothing.

[Note: 17. “And those that we think.” The despised or humble require exhortation, through which honor may be added to them so that they may become useful.]

[Note: 18. “And those that are dishonorable.” For those wearing a short, dark garment commonly walk with bare feet. Although they appear contemptible, they are in greater honor, because they commonly lead a purer life.]

But our honorable members, such as the eyes, nostrils, and ears, require no clothing of honor. Rather, God has arranged the body, giving more abundant honor in the form of clothing to the part that lacked it, so that there might be no schism in the body, but that the members might have the same concern for one another.

And if one member suffers, all the members suffer with it; if one member is glorified, all the members rejoice with it.

[Note: 19. “But our honorable members.” He is speaking of brothers in whom zeal for learning and conduct flourishes, and to whom there is nothing of honorable character that we can add.]

[Note: 20. LANFR. “But you are.” He fits the comparisons that he made above concerning the body to what he said: “The body is one, and has many members.” What he says—“But you are the body of Christ, and members from a member”—corresponds to this. What he said—“Now God has placed the members, each one, just as he wished”—corresponds to what he says: “And some he placed in the Church: first apostles, second prophets, such as Agabus and the two daughters of Philip, third teachers,” and so forth. What he said—“If the whole body were an eye, where would hearing be?”—corresponds to what he says: “Are all apostles? Are all prophets?” This should be pursued through charity, so that at the end of the Epistle, where he speaks of tongues and so forth, the conclusion may agree with this: “Therefore pursue charity.” We ought to pursue whatever is better and more excellent than the others. Charity, however, is more excellent than the other gifts of the Holy Spirit; this is “a still more excellent way,” and so forth. Therefore, and so forth. Moreover, charity alone is sufficient for blessedness; the others are not sufficient without it. Neither speaking in tongues, nor prophecy, nor knowledge, nor faith, nor almsgiving, nor martyrdom is sufficient for blessedness without charity. Charity alone is sufficient, and this is what he says: “Charity is patient,” and so forth, up to “never falls away.” For both knowledge and prophecy will be abolished: everything imperfect is abolished when the perfect arrives. Now prophecy and knowledge are imperfect; therefore they will be abolished. And what he says—“When I was a child”—proves that everything imperfect is abolished when the perfect arrives.]

But you are the body of Christ and members from a member.

[Note: 21. “Members from a member.” He calls himself the member from whom—that is, from whose preaching—the Corinthians, who were members of Christ, proceeded; or he means Christ, who is the head of the Church.]

And God has appointed some in the Church: first apostles, second prophets,

[Note: 22. AMBROS. “Second, prophets.” We understand prophets as those who speak of future things and reveal the Scriptures.]

third teachers,

[Note: 23. “Third, teachers.” He calls teachers those who instructed children in letters and reading.]

then powers, those who perform miracles; afterward gifts of healings, those who cure the sick; helps, which are discerned in various arts, offices, and skills; governments,

[Note: 24. “Governments.” There are also governors who serve as examples through spiritual direction.]

that is, the leadership of lesser persons; kinds of tongues, those who speak in various languages; interpretations of utterances.

Are all apostles? “Some,” he says, “he appointed as apostles”; for since he appointed some, not all, as apostles, the same applies to the rest. Are all prophets? Are all teachers? Are all powers? Do all have gifts of healings? Do all speak in tongues? Do all interpret?

[Note: 25. LANFR. “Be zealous for the better gifts.” The Corinthians greatly desired the gift of tongues, but the Apostle exhorts them to desire the better gifts, and especially the gift of prophecy.]

But be zealous for the better gifts. And I will show you an even more excellent way to blessedness than those I have mentioned above.

[COMMENTARY.]

[Col. 0195A]

# CHAPTER XII

1. LANFR. “Now concerning spiritual matters.” “I made you acquainted with carnal matters,” he says—that is, not eating food sacrificed to idols and not praying with uncovered heads. “I also wish to make you acquainted with spiritual matters,” which you, now that you have become Christians, will obey; for when you lived as Gentiles, you obediently served idols at the priests’ command, as you know.

2. “Therefore I make known to you.” As though he were saying: Since, even in your pagan condition, you were obedient also toward evil, I believe that in the faith of Christ you will be much more obedient toward good.

3. AUGUST. (*Exposition of the Gospel of John*, tractate 74, volume IX). “No one can say.” This is an apostolic utterance: “No one says, ‘Lord Jesus,’ except in the Holy Spirit.” And who says “Lord Jesus” except one who loves him, if he says it in the sense in which the Apostle intended it to be understood? For many say it with their voice, but deny it in their heart and by their actions.

4. AMBROS. “No one can say.” So that they would not think that human approval belonged within the Christian rule, and for that reason refuse to be reproved, as they did in the matter of idols, he shows that, when “Lord Jesus” is said, no human benefit is involved, but rather the gift of God, who deigned to reveal his mystery to human beings.

5. “Divisions of ministries.” Grace is not divided among the persons of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit; rather, the undivided nature of the unity is meant, and the one work of the three is understood.

6. AUGUST. (*On the Trinity*, book XII, chapter 14, volume III). “A word of wisdom.” I find it written in the Book of Job, spoken by that same holy man: “Behold, piety is wisdom; but to abstain from evil is knowledge.” In this distinction, wisdom is to be understood as pertaining to contemplation, and knowledge to action. For in this passage he called piety the worship of God, which in Greek is called *theosebeia* (θεοσέβεια). This word occurs in this sentence in the Greek manuscripts.

7. AUGUST. (*On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, book XII, chapter 13, volume III). “To another, discernment.” Discernment is indeed most difficult when the evil spirit acts as though tranquil and, without causing any bodily disturbance, speaks after taking on a human spirit. This is also the case when he speaks truths and proclaims useful things, transforming himself into an angel, as it is written, “as an angel of light.”

8. LANFR. “To another, interpretation of utterances.” He calls “utterances” allegorical expressions, whether in words or in speeches, such as are frequently found in the Prophets and the Gospels; those who know how to interpret them possess that knowledge through the grace of the Holy Spirit. By “utterances” we can also understand mystical visions, such as appeared to Pharaoh and Nebuchadnezzar. Hence Joseph says: “Because the word of God comes to pass.” And in Daniel it is read: “Tell the dream, and we shall make its interpretation known.” And the king says: “The utterance has departed from me.” The interpretation of these things was granted to both men by divine gift. For Joseph says: “Apart from me, God will answer favorably for Pharaoh.” And Daniel says: “You have shown me what we asked of you, because you have disclosed the king’s utterance to us.”

9. AMBROS. “But all these things.” What he previously attributed to the three persons, he now declares to be directed [alternatively, done] by the one Holy Spirit. Since they are of one nature, what one works, the three work.

10. LANFR. “For just as the body is one.” By comparison he shows that the Spirit is one and that his gifts are many, just as the body is one while having many members. He places Christ—that is, the head—and not the body, which is the Church, in place of the Spirit by which those members are joined together.

11. AUGUST. (*Expositions on the Psalms*, Psalm XXX). “But all the members.” Speaking of Christ’s members—that is, the faithful—he does not say, “So also are the members of Christ.” Rather, he called the whole of what he said “Christ.” Many members, one body: Christ. Therefore, all of us together with our head are Christ.

12. AMBROS. “If the foot should say.” This means that one who appears weak among the brothers cannot deny—or, according to another reading, cannot be denied to be—of the body on the ground that he is not powerful.

13. “If the whole body were an eye.” That is, if everyone were engaged in one kind of work, how would the body’s remaining needs be fulfilled, since it is evident that many functions are necessary for governing the body?

14. LANFR. “If the whole body were an eye.” Nor, he says, should everyone in the Church be a preacher, because it is not fitting for the whole body to be an eye. If this were so, it would no longer be the body itself, since it would lack hearing and the body’s other parts.

15. AMBROS. “But if they were all one.” It is clear that, if all had possessed the same dignity, they would not be called members, nor would they constitute a body. Therefore—or, according to another reading, “and therefore”—the body is governed by the various functions of its members.

16. “The eye cannot say to the hand.” That is, the superior cannot say to the inferior: “I have no need of you.”

17. “And those that we think.” The despised or humble require exhortation, through which honor may be added to them so that they may become useful.

18. “And those that are dishonorable.” For those wearing a short, dark garment commonly walk with bare feet. Although they appear contemptible, they are in greater honor, because they commonly lead a purer life.

19. “But our honorable members.” He is speaking of brothers in whom zeal for learning and conduct flourishes, and to whom there is nothing of honorable character that we can add.

20. LANFR. “But you are.” He fits the comparisons that he made above concerning the body to what he said: “The body is one, and has many members.” What he says—“But you are the body of Christ, and members from a member”—corresponds to this. What he said—“Now God has placed the members, each one, just as he wished”—corresponds to what he says: “And some he placed in the Church: first apostles, second prophets, such as Agabus and the two daughters of Philip, third teachers,” and so forth. What he said—“If the whole body were an eye, where would hearing be?”—corresponds to what he says: “Are all apostles? Are all prophets?” This should be pursued through charity, so that at the end of the Epistle, where he speaks of tongues and so forth, the conclusion may agree with this: “Therefore pursue charity.” We ought to pursue whatever is better and more excellent than the others. Charity, however, is more excellent than the other gifts of the Holy Spirit; this is “a still more excellent way,” and so forth. Therefore, and so forth. Moreover, charity alone is sufficient for blessedness; the others are not sufficient without it. Neither speaking in tongues, nor prophecy, nor knowledge, nor faith, nor almsgiving, nor martyrdom is sufficient for blessedness without charity. Charity alone is sufficient, and this is what he says: “Charity is patient,” and so forth, up to “never falls away.” For both knowledge and prophecy will be abolished: everything imperfect is abolished when the perfect arrives. Now prophecy and knowledge are imperfect; therefore they will be abolished. And what he says—“When I was a child”—proves that everything imperfect is abolished when the perfect arrives.

21. “Members from a member.” He calls himself the member from whom—that is, from whose preaching—the Corinthians, who were members of Christ, proceeded; or he means Christ, who is the head of the Church.

22. AMBROS. “Second, prophets.” We understand prophets as those who speak of future things and reveal the Scriptures.

23. “Third, teachers.” He calls teachers those who instructed children in letters and reading.

24. “Governments.” There are also governors who serve as examples through spiritual direction.

25. LANFR. “Be zealous for the better gifts.” The Corinthians greatly desired the gift of tongues, but the Apostle exhorts them to desire the better gifts, and especially the gift of prophecy.

# CHAPTER XIII

[Col. 0199]

If I speak in the tongues of human beings, and even of angels—an exaggeration—but do not have charity, I have become like resounding bronze or a clanging cymbal, producing no benefit for myself.

And if I have prophecy and know all mysteries and all knowledge; and if I have all faith, so that I transfer mountains from one place to another, but do not have charity, I am nothing.

And if I distribute all my possessions as food for the poor, and if I hand over my body so that I may burn, but do not have charity, it profits me nothing.

Charity is patient; it is kind. Charity is not jealous; it is not saddened by another’s happiness; it does not act improperly; it is not inflated, because its own happiness does not exalt it; it is not ambitious for honor or for what belongs to others; it does not seek even what is its own; it is not provoked; it does not think about evil; it does not rejoice over iniquity, but rejoices with truth and justice.

It endures all things that must be endured; it believes all things that must be believed; it hopes for all things that must be hoped for; it bears all things that must be borne.

[Note: CAP. XIII.—1. AUGUST. (*On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, book XI, chapter 5, near the end). “It is not inflated,” that is, it does not rejoice in private excellence. Therefore it is rightly not inflated.]

Charity never falls away—that is, it never collapses—because it exists in this world and will exist in the future; faith and hope, and so forth, exist only in this world.

[Note: 2. AUGUST. (*On the Spirit and the Letter*, chapter 32, volume III). “It believes all things.” Charity itself, which believes all things, does not believe every spirit. Accordingly, it believes all things, but believes them with respect to God, since it was not said that it believes everyone.]

[Note: 3. “It hopes all things.” For this reason it endures everything in the present life: because it believes all things concerning the future life. And it bears everything that is imposed here, because it hopes for everything that is promised there. Therefore it rightly never falls.]

[Note: 4. AUGUST. (*On John*, book IV, chapter 16; *Expositions on the First Epistle of John*, tractate 9, volume IX). “Charity never.” “God is love”; and, he says, “whoever remains in love remains in God, and God remains in him.” If God’s house is a house for you, be a house of God. Remain in God, and let God remain in you. God remains in you in order to hold you; you remain in God so that you may not fall. For the Apostle says this about charity itself: “Charity never falls.” How does one whom God holds fall?]

[Note: 5. LANFR. “Charity never falls away,” that is, it does not fall, because it exists both in this world and in the future. Faith and hope will exist only in this world.]

Whether prophecies will be abolished, whether tongues will cease, or whether knowledge will be destroyed.

[Note: 6. “Prophecies will be abolished.” On the day of judgment prophecy will also be abolished, the variety of tongues will cease, and knowledge—whether of worldly matters or of the order to which one arrives—will be destroyed.]

For we know in part and we prophesy in part.

[Note: 7. “For in part.” As though he were saying: Prophecy will therefore be abolished and knowledge destroyed because they are partial; but everything that is partial is imperfect, and everything imperfect will be abolished.]

But when the perfect has come, what is partial will be abolished.

[Col. 0201]

This is a transference from a lesser matter, though it is used by way of comparison.

When I was a child, I spoke as a child, I understood as a child, I thought as a child. But when I became a man, I abolished—cast away from myself—the things that belonged to the child.

Now we see through a mirror, in an enigma; but then, face to face.

[Note: 8. AUGUST. (*On the Perfection of Human Righteousness*, chapter 8, volume VII). “When the perfect has come.” When the perfect has come, what is partial will be destroyed—that is, it will no longer be partial but complete, because reality itself will succeed faith and hope: not something believed and hoped for, but something seen and possessed. Charity, which is greater than these three [alternative reading: “among these”], will not be taken away but increased and fulfilled, having obtained what it believed and hoped for through contemplation. [Alternative reading: “it will be increased and fulfilled.”]]

Now I know in part; then I shall know, just as I have been known—then I shall know God perfectly, just as I have been perfectly known by God.

[Note: 9. LANFR. “Then I shall know.” Then I shall know God perfectly, just as I have been known by God—that is, perfectly.]

Now, in this life alone, these three remain: faith, hope, and charity. But the greatest of these—and the more enduring, since it will also exist in the future—is charity.

[Note: 10. “But the greatest of these is charity.” He again shows that charity is better than all the other gifts. For it is better than faith, hope, and the rest, since it is more enduring. Thus, from what preceded, he concludes the principal question by saying: Therefore, because it is better than all, pursue charity.]
