# CHAPTER XIV

[Col. 0201]

Therefore pursue love; strive to possess love. Be zealous for spiritual gifts: desire the spiritual gifts of the Holy Spirit, but especially that you may prophesy rather than speak in tongues. For whoever speaks in a tongue—that is, in a language unknown to his hearers—does not speak to human beings (a simple benefit, for he alone understands), but to God; for no one hears, that is, understands.

> **[Note: [Col. 0201A] CAP. XIV.—1.** “The Spirit speaks,” that is, understands, as in the Gospel: “Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear,” that is, understand. And in the Apocalypse: “Whoever has an ear, let him hear.]

But the Spirit speaks mysteries; for whoever prophesies speaks both to himself and to human beings for edification (a twofold benefit), and for exhortation and consolation. Whoever speaks in a tongue unknown to others edifies himself—provided that he understands it; but whoever prophesies edifies the Church of God.

Now I want all of you to speak in tongues (he says, “I do not say this because I do not want you to speak in tongues, but because I prefer that you prophesy, since that is beneficial in two ways”); but I especially want you to prophesy.

> **[Note: [Col. 0201B] 3. “But especially to prophesy.”** You ought to desire prophesying more than speaking in tongues. For they did not desire the first kind of speaking in tongues—speaking in a tongue unknown both to themselves and to others—nor the second kind, speaking in a tongue known only to themselves, nor the third kind, speaking in tongues so as to teach others. A twofold benefit ought to be desired more than a simple one. Prophesying, however, is a twofold benefit; whereas speaking in a tongue unknown both to oneself and to others is a simple benefit. Thus, whoever speaks in a tongue has a simple benefit, because he speaks to God—to God alone, and not to human beings—for he is not understood. But whoever prophesies produces a twofold benefit, for he speaks both to God and to human beings. The same arguments apply to the other kind, namely, speaking in a tongue known only to oneself.]

For the one who prophesies is greater, that is, of greater dignity, than the one who speaks in tongues, unless he interprets—that is, explains what he has said—so that the Church may receive edification.

Now, brothers, if I should come to you speaking in tongues unknown to you, what benefit will I bring you unless I speak to you either in revelation, or in knowledge, or in prophecy, or in teaching?

> **[Note: [Col. 0202A] 4. “In revelation.”** Revelation is that by which something is suddenly disclosed through the Holy Spirit at whatever time.]

> **5. “In knowledge.”** Knowledge is understanding acquired through study and diligence.

> **6. “In prophecy.”** Prophecy concerns only future things; teaching is a category encompassing everything.

Still—this is an explanatory addition, or perhaps I shall offer an analogy—things without life that produce a sound, whether a flute (a transference to something similar) or a lyre, are useless unless they give distinctions among their sounds. How will what is being played on the flute or lyre be recognized? Not at all.

For if the trumpet gives an uncertain sound, who will prepare himself for battle? It is of no use, for no one is prepared for battle by it. So also with you: unless through the tongue you give an intelligible utterance by interpreting, how will what is being said be recognized? You will be speaking into the air, speaking in vain.

> **[Note: [Col. 0202B] 7. “So many, for example.”** It is as though he were saying: It is not surprising if an unintelligible utterance is conveyed through a tongue, since there are evidently many kinds, and there is none of them that does not have its own voice, distinct from the others.]

There are, for example, so many kinds of languages in the world, and no kind of language is without a voice, without the particular character of its voice. Therefore, if I do not know the force—that is, the meaning—of the voice, I shall be a barbarian to the person to whom I speak, and I shall be of no benefit to him; and the one who speaks will be a barbarian to me.

So also you, since you are zealous for spirits—that is, for spiritual gifts—seek to abound in spiritual gifts for the edification of the Church. And therefore, because the gifts that are beneficial must be sought, let the one who speaks in a tongue pray that he may interpret.

> **[Note: [Col. 0202B] 8. “Let him pray that he may interpret,”** that is, understand the tongue itself and then explain it. For often the Spirit spoke through a person’s mouth in a foreign language, yet the person himself did not understand either the language or the mysteries uttered in it.]

For if I pray in a tongue, my spirit—that is, my voice—prays, that is, I myself benefit no one; but my mind is without fruit, that is, without compunction, because I do not understand the language in which I speak.

> **[Note: [Col. 0203A] 9. “What then?”** It should be understood as follows, if the passage is sound. If a voice speaking in an unknown tongue blesses God, or food, or something of that kind, the unlearned hearer—that is, one who hears but does not understand—does not know when he ought to respond “Amen,” or “Thanks be to God.” Nor is there anyone to take the place of his response, that is, to respond on his behalf, since everyone is ignorant of the speaker’s words.]

What then is to be done? Since I do not benefit anyone by speaking in a tongue without interpreting, what follows must be this: I shall pray with the spirit—that is, with my voice—and I shall pray also with the mind, so that I may know how to interpret; I shall sing with the spirit—that is, with my voice—and I shall sing also with the mind, so that I may interpret.

Otherwise, if you bless—if you pronounce a blessing—with the spirit, that is, with the voice alone and not with understanding, who will take the place of the unlearned person by saying “Amen” at the end of your prayer? No one. How will he say “Amen” to your blessing, or in response to your blessing, when he does not know what you are saying? For you indeed give thanks well in an unknown tongue, giving thanks; but the other person is not edified, and you are of no benefit to him.

I give thanks to my God that I speak in the tongue of all of you. I do not say this, he says, because I begrudge you; for I give thanks to God in the tongues of all of you. Yet in the Church I prefer to speak five words with my understanding, so that I may be able to interpret and instruct others as well, rather than ten thousand words in an unknown tongue.

> **[Note: [Col. 0203A] 10. “Do not become children,”** that is, do not have childish desires, failing to consider what usefulness the things you desire possess.]

Brothers, do not become children in your understanding, desiring tongues more than prophecy—something that is of little benefit rather than something of great benefit. Be children in malice, however; but be mature in understanding, not desiring kinds of tongues.

> **[Note: [Col. 0203A] 11. “In the Law.”** By the name “Law” he signifies prophecy. This testimony occurs in Isaiah in these words: “For with the speech of the lip and with another tongue he will speak to this people.” To whom he said this is rendered in one version, “Give rest to the weary”; in another: “This is my rest: refresh the weary; and this is my refreshment”; but they were unwilling to hear.]

It is written in the Law:

> **[Note: [Col. 0203B] 12. “Because with other tongues.”** He again proves that prophecy ought to be desired more than speaking in tongues. Prophecy is a twofold benefit, whereas speaking in a tongue is a simple one. For the latter is only a sign for unbelievers that they should believe, while for believers it is also a sign that they should act rightly; and he confirms this with the authority of the Law already cited.]

“For with other tongues and with other lips I shall speak to this people, and even so they will not hear me, says the Lord.”

> **[Note: [Col. 0203B] 13. AMBROSE.** Thus, “tongues”—that is, under the covering of an unknown tongue—the words of God were obscured so that they would not be seen by the faithless. When unknown tongues are heard, it is a sign that this has happened because of their faithlessness, so that those who hear do not understand. Hence in Isaiah: “Go and say to this people: You will hear with your ears, and you will not understand.” [Col. 0204A]]

Thus tongues are for a sign, not to believers but to unbelievers; whereas prophecy is not for unbelievers but for believers. He compares prophesying and speaking in tongues, and by comparing the two he gives prophecy precedence over tongues.

Therefore, if the whole Church should assemble in one place and all speak in unknown tongues, while unlearned people or unbelievers enter:

> **[Note: [Col. 0204A] 14. “Will they not say that.”** It is clear that if everyone spoke in different languages, a kind of tumult would arise in the gathering of the people—perhaps “disorderly” [as another reading has it]—as though they were suffering from madness [another reading: “as though he were suffering from madness.”]

would they not say that you were insane, speaking in unknown tongues? Certainly they would.

But if all prophesy, and an unbeliever or an unlearned person enters, if he wishes to deny what is being said by them, he is convicted by all and judged—that is, his life is recognized by all through the prophecy. For the secrets of his heart are made manifest through prophecy; and so, falling down and humbling himself, he will worship God on his face, declaring that God truly is among you.

What then, brothers? Since prophecy is of such great usefulness, it ought to be desired. He urges them toward brotherly edification.

When you assemble in the church, if each of you has something—one a psalm, another a teaching,

> **[Note: [Col. 0204A] 15. LANFRANC. “Each of you.”** This is how it should be read and understood: Each of you has something—one a psalm, another a teaching, and so on—and all these things were given to them through the grace of the Holy Spirit.]

another a revelation, an unveiling, another a tongue, another an interpretation—let everything be done for the edification of your neighbors.

> **[Note: [Col. 0204A] 16. AMBROSE. “Whether a tongue.”** That is, let two or three speak in tongues, no more, and let them speak individually, not all at once, lest they appear insane. The reason for limiting the number to three is that the interpreters of their tongues would not occupy the whole day, leaving the prophets no time to expound. [Col. 0204B]]

If anyone speaks in an unknown tongue, let it be limited to two, or at most three; let him speak with two or three, not with everyone, and in separate portions, one after another; and let one interpret what the other speaks in an unknown tongue.

> **[Note: [Col. 0204B] 17. LANFRANC. “Whether a tongue.”** If one of you speaks in an unknown tongue, let him not speak before the hearing of everyone, but let him speak with two or three, and in separate portions—that is, intermittently—so that it may more easily be understood when it is explained.]

But if there is no interpreter, let him remain silent in the church before the others.

> **[Note: [Col. 0204B] 18. “But if you are not an interpreter.”** Here he clearly shows that someone often spoke in an unknown tongue in which mysteries had been uttered, yet he himself did not understand the tongue.]

> **19. “But let him speak to himself,”** that is, let him speak in his heart, praising or entreating God.]

Let him speak to himself and to God.

Let two or three prophets speak, and let the others judge; let them be heard.

> **[Note: [Col. 0205A] 20. “But if something is revealed to another.”** If, while two or three prophets are speaking, something is revealed to one of those who are sitting and listening, let the prophet who was speaking first be silent, and let this other person be permitted to speak.]

But if something is revealed to another person who is sitting, let the first be silent. For you can all prophesy one by one, so that all may learn to prophesy, and all may be exhorted and admonished.

> **[Note: [Col. 0205A] 21. “The spirits of the prophets.”** He says “spirit” in the plural because of the multitude of prophets, although there is one Spirit who fills them. This Spirit is said to be subject to the prophets because he does not compel them, against their will, either to speak or to remain silent. It is an answer to someone who might say: Can the first prophet be silent when he wishes—that is, can individuals prophesy whenever something is revealed to them?]

And the spirits of the prophets are subject to the prophets—or, according to another reading, the Spirit is subject to the prophets.

> **[Note: [Col. 0205A] 22. “For God is not a God of dissension.”** They would be spirits of dissension if he compelled all whom he filled to speak at the same time.]

For God is not a God of dissension but of peace, as I also teach in all the churches of the saints.

Let the men prophesy, as has been said. Let the women remain silent in the churches; for they are not permitted to speak, but are to be subordinate to the men. This would not be the case if they were to preach, just as the Law also says:

> **[Note: [Col. 0205B] 23. “The Law says.”** In Genesis God says to the woman: “You shall be under the authority of the man, and he shall rule over you.”]

If they wish to learn anything, let them ask their own husbands at home, not in the church. For it is shameful for a woman to speak in the church.

> **[Note: [Col. 0205B] 24. “Did the word of God come forth from you?”** This indicates that he is referring to certain things which he had earlier rebuked the Corinthians for doing. Thus he reproves them, saying that they ought not to undertake anything novel, but rather to live according to the examples of the other churches, because the word of God did not proceed from them. If it had proceeded from them, it would have been tolerable for them to have done something new.]

Did the word of God come forth from you? Or did it reach you alone? If anyone thinks that he is a prophet or spiritual,

> **[Note: [Col. 0205B] 25. AMBROSE. “Let the spiritual person recognize.”** Here he touches upon the false apostles, who taught not divine things but earthly ones.]

let him recognize the things I am writing to you, because they are the Lord’s commandments.

> **[Note: [Col. 0205B] 26. “If anyone is ignorant, he will be ignored.”** Rightly so, because whoever does not know that the things the Apostle speaks are from God will be ignored by the Lord.]

> **[Note: [Col. 0205C] 26. AUGUSTINE (*Letter 102 to Evodius*, vol. II). “But if anyone is ignorant.”** Not at all, as you write: “Whoever is ignorant will be ignored.” The Apostle says this as though that punishment should be inflicted on the person who is unable, by understanding, to distinguish the ineffable unity of the Trinity in the way that memory, understanding, and will are distinguished in our mind. Elsewhere the Apostle said this: Read, and you will see that the things he spoke were things that could edify the faith or conduct of many, not things that could scarcely reach the understanding of a few—and even then only a small, slight understanding, however little of such a great matter can be attained in this life—that is, so that prophecy might be set forth in tongues.]

But if anyone is ignorant of these and other commandments of God, or neglects them, he will be ignored.

> **[Note: [Col. 0206A] 27. (*Ibid.*) “He will be ignored.”** Many who glory in the cross of Christ and do not depart from that way—even those who are ignorant of the things discussed here with the greatest subtlety—reach the same eternity, truth, and love, that is, stable, certain, and complete happiness. For none of the little ones for whom Christ died is lost. [Another reading: “one of them is not lost.”] [Col. 0206B] There, for those who remain, see, and love, all things are everlasting.]

Therefore, brothers, be zealous to prophesy, because it is a twofold benefit; and do not forbid speaking in tongues. But let all things be done decently: let the men speak, let the women remain silent, and let them be done in order, one first and another afterward, not all speaking at once, among you and by you.

## Commentary

### [Col. 0201A]

**CAP. XIV.—1. “But the Spirit speaks,”** that is, understands, as in the Gospel: “Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear,” that is, understand. And in the Apocalypse: “Whoever has an ear, let him hear.”

**2. “He speaks.”** In that very unknown tongue the Holy Spirit spoke mysteries, that is, allegorical words, which no one understood except the person who had the gift of interpretation.

**3. “But especially to prophesy.”** You ought to desire prophesying more than speaking in tongues. For they did not desire the first kind of speaking in tongues—speaking in a tongue unknown both to themselves and to others—nor the second kind, speaking in a tongue known only to themselves, nor the third kind, speaking in tongues so as to teach others. A twofold benefit ought to be desired more than a simple one. Prophesying, however, is a twofold benefit; whereas speaking in a tongue unknown both to oneself and to others is a simple benefit. Thus, whoever speaks in a tongue has a simple benefit, because he speaks to God—to God alone, and not to human beings—for he is not understood. But whoever prophesies produces a twofold benefit, for he speaks both to God and to human beings. The same arguments apply to the other kind, namely, speaking in a tongue known only to oneself.

### [Col. 0202A]

**4. “In revelation.”** Revelation is that by which something is suddenly disclosed through the Holy Spirit at whatever time.

**5. “In knowledge.”** Knowledge is understanding acquired through study and diligence.

**6. “In prophecy.”** Prophecy concerns only future things; teaching is a category encompassing everything.

### [Col. 0202B]

**7. “So many, for example.”** It is as though he were saying: It is not surprising if an unintelligible utterance is conveyed through a tongue, since there are evidently many kinds, and there is none of them that does not have its own voice, distinct from the others.

**8. “Let him pray that he may interpret,”** that is, understand the tongue itself and then explain it. For often the Spirit spoke through a person’s mouth in a foreign language, yet the person himself did not understand either the language or the mysteries uttered in it.

### [Col. 0203A]

**9. “What then?”** It should be understood as follows, if the passage is sound. If a voice speaking in an unknown tongue blesses God, or food, or something of that kind, the unlearned hearer—that is, one who hears but does not understand—does not know when he ought to respond “Amen,” or “Thanks be to God.” Nor is there anyone to take the place of his response, that is, to respond on his behalf, since everyone is ignorant of the speaker’s words.

**10. “Do not become children,”** that is, do not have childish desires, failing to consider what usefulness the things you desire possess.

**11. “In the Law.”** By the name “Law” he signifies prophecy. This testimony occurs in Isaiah in these words: “For with the speech of the lip and with another tongue he will speak to this people.” To whom he said this is rendered in one version, “Give rest to the weary”; in another: “This is my rest: refresh the weary”; and “this is my refreshment”; but they were unwilling to hear.

### [Col. 0203B]

**12. “Because with other tongues.”** He again proves that prophecy ought to be desired more than speaking in tongues. Prophecy is a twofold benefit, whereas speaking in a tongue is a simple one. For the latter is only a sign for unbelievers that they should believe, while for believers it is also a sign that they should act rightly; and he confirms this with the authority of the Law already cited.

**13. AMBROSE.** Thus tongues—that is, under the covering of an unknown tongue—the words of God were obscured so that they would not be seen by the faithless. When unknown tongues are heard, it is a sign that this has happened because of their faithlessness, so that those who hear do not understand. Hence in Isaiah: “Go and say to this people: You will hear with your ears, and you will not understand.”

### [Col. 0204A]

**14. “Will they not say that.”** It is clear that if everyone spoke in different languages, a kind of tumult would arise in the gathering of the people—perhaps “disorderly,” according to another reading—as though they were suffering from madness [another reading: “as though he were suffering from madness.”]

**15. LANFRANC. “Each of you.”** This is how it should be read and understood: Each of you has something—one a psalm, another a teaching, and so on—and all these things were given to them through the grace of the Holy Spirit.

**16. AMBROSE. “Whether a tongue.”** That is, let two or three speak in tongues, no more, and let them speak individually, not all at once, lest they appear insane. The reason for limiting the number to three is that the interpreters of their tongues would not occupy the whole day, leaving the prophets no time to expound.

### [Col. 0204B]

**17. LANFRANC. “Whether a tongue.”** If one of you speaks in an unknown tongue, let him not speak before the hearing of everyone, but let him speak with two or three, and in separate portions—that is, intermittently—so that it may more easily be understood when it is explained.

**18. “But if you are not an interpreter.”** Here he clearly shows that someone often spoke in an unknown tongue in which mysteries had been uttered, yet he himself did not understand the tongue.

**19. “But let him speak to himself,”** that is, let him speak in his heart, praising or entreating God.

### [Col. 0205A]

**20. “But if something is revealed to another.”** If, while two or three prophets are speaking, something is revealed to one of those who are sitting and listening, let the prophet who was speaking first be silent, and let this other person be permitted to speak.

**21. “The spirits of the prophets.”** He says “spirit” in the plural because of the multitude of prophets, although there is one Spirit who fills them. This Spirit is said to be subject to the prophets because he does not compel them, against their will, either to speak or to remain silent. It is an answer to someone who might say: Can the first prophet be silent when he wishes—that is, can individuals prophesy whenever something is revealed to them?

**22. “For God is not a God of dissension.”** They would be spirits of dissension if he compelled all whom he filled to speak at the same time.

### [Col. 0205B]

**23. “The Law says.”** In Genesis God says to the woman: “You shall be under the authority of the man, and he shall rule over you.”

**24. “Did the word of God come forth from you?”** This indicates that he is referring to certain things which he had earlier rebuked the Corinthians for doing. Thus he reproves them, saying that they ought not to undertake anything novel, but rather to live according to the examples of the other churches, because the word of God did not proceed from them. If it had proceeded from them, it would have been tolerable for them to have done something new.

**25. AMBROSE. “Let the spiritual person recognize.”** Here he touches upon the false apostles, who taught not divine things but earthly ones.

**26. “If anyone is ignorant, he will be ignored.”** Rightly so, because whoever does not know that the things the Apostle speaks are from God will be ignored by the Lord.

### [Col. 0205C]

**26. AUGUSTINE (*Letter 102 to Evodius*, vol. II). “But if anyone is ignorant.”** Not at all, as you write: “Whoever is ignorant will be ignored.” The Apostle says this as though that punishment should be inflicted on the person who is unable, by understanding, to distinguish the ineffable unity of the Trinity in the way that memory, understanding, and will are distinguished in our mind. Elsewhere the Apostle said this: Read, and you will see that the things he spoke were things that could edify the faith or conduct of many, not things that could scarcely reach the understanding of a few—and even then only a small, slight understanding, however little of such a great matter can be attained in this life—that is, so that prophecy might be set forth in tongues.

**27. (*Ibid.*) “He will be ignored.”** Many who glory in the cross of Christ and do not depart from that way—even those who are ignorant of the things discussed here with the greatest subtlety—reach the same eternity, truth, and love, that is, stable, certain, and complete happiness. For none of the little ones for whom Christ died is lost [another reading: “one of them is not lost”]. There, for those who remain, see, and love, all things are everlasting.

## CHAPTER XV

### [Col. 0205]

> **[Note: [Col. 0206B] CHAPTER XV.—1. LANFRANC. “Now I make known to you,” etc.** Since the Corinthians were doubting the resurrection of the dead, the Apostle proves by many arguments that it will truly take place, recalling what he had preached to them; from this it is clearly apparent that there should be no doubt about the resurrection.]

Now I make known to you, brothers, the Gospel that I preached to you, which you also received, in which you also stand, and through which you are also being saved—if you hold firmly to the manner in which I preached it to you, unless you believed in vain, unless you were predestined for destruction.

For I delivered to you first of all the Gospel that I made known, which I also received: that Christ died for our sins, not for his own, according to the Scriptures; and that he was buried; and that he rose on the third day, according to the Scriptures; and that he appeared to Cephas, and afterward to the eleven disciples.

Then he appeared to more than five hundred brothers at once. Nothing is said by the evangelists about this appearance or the one that followed. Of these, many remain until the present, but some have fallen asleep.

Then he appeared to James, then to all the apostles; and last of all,

Someone might argue: “There is no resurrection of the dead.” The Apostle replies: “If there is no resurrection of the dead,” that is, if no dead person has risen at all, then neither has Christ risen, whom you believed to have risen.

From the same premise it follows that the Apostle’s preaching is vain and their faith is vain. And if Christ has not risen, we are false witnesses of God. He proves this from Scripture as follows: “We have given false testimony against God,” for we have said that he raised Christ, whom he did not raise, if the dead are not raised.

Why do you say this? For this is how the matter stands, he says: If the dead are not raised, neither has Christ risen. Our faith is vain, that is, your sins have not been forgiven; for you are still in your sins.

And if you are in your sins, then those who came before you also died in their sins; and if they died in their sins, they certainly perished.

**The principal premise.** But now Christ has risen; therefore our preaching is not vain, nor is your faith. The same conclusion must be drawn concerning everything.

[Col. 0206B]

## CHAPTER XV

1. LANFRANC. “Now I make known to you,” etc. Since the Corinthians were doubting the resurrection of the dead, the Apostle proves through many arguments that it will truly occur, recalling what he had preached to them; from this it is clearly evident that there ought to be no doubt concerning the resurrection.

2. AUGUSTINE (Against Faustus). “Last of all.” But here he appeared already from heaven, after a considerable interval following his ascension.

3. AMBROSE. “As to one untimely born.” He appeared to him first from heaven, afterward to him as he prayed in the temple. He calls himself “untimely born” because, born outside the proper time in Christ, he received the apostleship; the Lord having been received into heaven in the flesh.

[Col. 0207A]

4. “For I am.” He humbles himself and attributes the cause to himself because of the time.

5. “Therefore it is in vain.” He asserts that it works to their detriment if they believe something that will not occur. It is shameful for someone to profess belief in what is false; he brings shame upon them and calls their labors fruitless. No one willingly hears this said about himself, so that, seeing it to be against them, they may return to their former faith.

6. AUGUSTINE (On Christian Doctrine, book II, chapter 31, vol. III). “If the dead.” These are genuine chains of reasoning containing false propositions, which follow from the error of the person with whom one is arguing. Yet a good and learned person introduces them for this purpose: that the one whose error they follow may be ashamed and abandon that same error; for if he wishes to remain in it, he must also be compelled to hold what he condemns.

7. LANFRANC. “Vain is your faith.” He means the faith by which they believed that their sins had been forgiven through faith in Christ’s resurrection. This is not so if Christ has not risen.

8. AMBROSE. “We are more pitiable.” For unbelievers at least enjoy this life.

9. LANFRANC. “Christ has risen.” The Apostle proves that the dead will rise. “If,” he says, “Christ has risen, the dead will rise.” But Christ has risen, for the Scriptures say so. Again, he has risen because, after rising, he was seen by Cephas and others. Likewise, he has risen because you believed that he had risen. As though they were saying: “We believed, but not because you preached it.” “What concern is that?” he says. “Whether I or they preached it, you believed that he had risen.” This is what he says: “Whether I or they, so we preach, and so you believed.” Likewise: If Christ is truly preached as having risen, then he truly rose; and if he rose—by analogy—there is a resurrection of the dead. If that is so, how can some say, etc.? Thus you ought not to say that there will be no resurrection of the dead.

[Col. 0208A]

Someone might argue: “There is no resurrection of the dead.” And the Apostle replies: “If there is no resurrection of the dead”—that is, if no dead person has risen at all—“neither has Christ,” whom you believed to have risen. From this it likewise follows that the Apostle’s preaching is vain and their faith is vain. And if Christ has not risen, “we are false witnesses of God”; he proves this from Scripture as follows: “For,” he says, “we have borne false witness against God,” since we have said that he raised Christ, whom he did not raise, if the dead do not rise.

Why do you say this? “For,” he says, “that is how the matter stands: if the dead do not rise, neither has Christ risen; our faith is vain,” that is, your sins have not been forgiven, for you are still in your sins. And if you are in your sins, then those who came before you [Col. 0208B] died in their sins; and if they died in their sins, they have certainly perished.

This is the principal assumption. But now Christ has risen; therefore our preaching is not vain, nor is your faith. And the same conclusion must be drawn concerning all the points.

10. AUGUSTINE (Exposition on the Gospel of John, Tractate 3, vol. IX). “In Christ all.” All who have been reborn through Christ.

11. LANFRANC. “Each in his own order.” He says “in his own order,” either because Christ rose first and the others will rise afterward, or because a martyr will rise as a martyr, pastors as pastors, and the others in the same way. Thus it is understood as “in his own order” and “in his own dignity.” These will rise afterward, and others as well, but he mentions only these on account of their Christian dignity.

[Col. 0208C]

12. “Those who believe at his coming.” Those who believe that he came to redeem sinners and that he will come to judge unbelievers and reward the faithful.

13. AUGUSTINE (Eighty-Three Questions, question 69, vol. IV). “Then the end.” He himself is the end, namely, that God himself may be all in all. For “end” is used in one way of that which pertains to completion and in another of that which pertains to consumption. A tunic, for example, is finished by weaving, whereas food is finished by eating. God is said to be all in all so that none of those who cling to him may love his own will against God, and so that it may be evident to all what the same Apostle says elsewhere: “What do you have that you did not receive?”

14. AUGUSTINE (On the Trinity, book I, chapters 9–10, vol. III). “When he has handed over.” This is said as though one were to say: “The Lord Jesus Christ will hand over the kingdom to the Father,” without thereby separating himself, or the Father, or the Holy Spirit from it. For to lead believers to the contemplation of God—those deemed worthy to be led through faith and hope, that is, to that very vision by which the one who leads is led—is to hand over the kingdom to God and the Father.

15. AMBROSE. “When he has handed over.” Let no one doubt that the Son will reign forever with the Father. For to hand over the kingdom to God and the Father means to show that he is the one from whom every fatherhood in heaven and on earth is named.

16. LANFRANC. “When he has handed over.” Christ will hand over the kingdom—that is, those over whom he has reigned—to God at the end of the age, when he has shown the Church converted to God through the preaching of himself and of his servants.

17. AUGUSTINE (same work, chapter 8). “When he has abolished,” that is, so that the administration of likenesses through angelic principalities may be unnecessary [variant: “not”].

18. LANFRANC. “When he has abolished.” Or Christ will abolish at the end of the age every principality and power of demons, because thereafter they will have no power to tempt or to lead God’s servants into temptation.

[Col. 0209C]

19. “Until he places all.” Christ will place all his enemies under his feet before the day of judgment, because he will convert some to the faith and hand others over to the prison of hell, where they will no longer oppose either him or his servants. He will also reign afterward, but there could have been uncertainty concerning that period.

20. “But the last enemy.” On the last day death will be destroyed, because human beings will no longer sin and no bodies will thereafter die.

21. AUGUSTINE (Eighty-Three Questions, question 69). “Then the Son himself.” It is therefore clear that this is said according to the assumption of humanity (a little below in the same work). “But when all things have been subjected to him, then the Son himself will also be subject to the one who subjected all things to him,” not as though this were not already so, but because it will then be manifest.

22. AUGUSTINE (City of God, book XXII, chapter 30, vol. V). “That God may be all in all.” What else did he say through the prophet: “I will be their God, and they shall be my people,” than “I will be that from which they are satisfied”? I will be whatever human beings rightly desire: life, salvation, food, abundance, glory, honor, peace, and every good thing.

23. AMBROSE. “Otherwise, what will they do?” By this example he does not prove what they did, but shows their steadfast faith in the resurrection.

24. LANFRANC. “For the dead.” By “the dead” he means those dead in sins, who are performing dead works, as in Hebrews: “the foundation of repentance from dead works.” He therefore says: If there is no resurrection of the dead, what will those do who are baptized for the remission of their sins in remembrance of the death and resurrection of Christ, thinking that they too will rise? For they will deny baptism and change their faith, which is sacrilegious. Some say, and it is found written, that certain uneducated people were baptized on behalf of those who departed this life without baptism, thinking that such baptism could benefit those who died without baptism; and that this is why it was said, “What will those do who are baptized for the dead?” But one should not believe that the Apostle wished to prove from the authority of fools something that so many people regarded as uncertain.

25. “For the dead.” “For the dead,” that is, as though dead. Baptism is a figure of death. The figure of death and resurrection in baptism is of no value unless a true resurrection of bodies after death were to occur. Yet such an institution in the Church is not empty.

26. “Why are they also baptized?” He proves the same point again. “If,” he says, “the dead do not rise, what will those do who are baptized for the dead?” That is, baptism is of no benefit—equivalent to what he later says: “If the dead do not rise at all, why are they baptized for them?” Or it may be understood as follows: If no dead rise, neither do baptized dead; and if baptized dead do not rise, why are they baptized? Again, if the dead do not rise, why do we also endanger ourselves every hour? That is, we suffer daily dangers in vain in the hope of resurrection. Again, if the dead do not rise, what benefit is it to me that I fought with beasts at Ephesus as far as humanly possible? None.

27. AMBROSE. “Why do we also?” By saying “we also,” he distinguished the persons, showing that those who were baptized for the dead were not Catholics.

[Col. 0211A]

28. “If according to human judgment,” that is, according to the human sense which does not at all believe that flesh already dissolved can be restored to life.

29. LANFRANC. “If according to human judgment,” that is, insofar as a human being can endure. “With beasts,” that is, against bestial people; this at Ephesus is to be understood as referring to … disputes and words.

30. “Do not be deceived.” Do not listen to the evil conversations of those persuading you that the resurrection will not occur; for those evil conversations themselves will corrupt good morals, as is proved there by the general principle.

31. “For some have ignorance.” As though he were saying: I urge you to be vigilant and not to sin, lest you imitate those who do not know God.

32. “For reverence.” “For this reason,” he says, “I speak to you, so that you may feel shame and correct your life for the better.”

33. AMBROSE. “And to each of the seeds.” An example of a resurrection improved, not of a substance lost.

34. “Not all flesh.” Just as from one material there are different kinds of the flesh of living creatures, so human beings, though of one flesh, will differ in dignity at the resurrection.

35. AUGUSTINE (Letter 146 to Consentius). “Not all flesh.” The meaning throughout is this: If kinds of flesh, although all are mortal, nevertheless differ among themselves according to the varieties of living creatures; and if bodies, although all visible, nevertheless differ according to the varieties of places—hence one is the glory of heavenly things and another of earthly things—and if in the lofty regions, although they are set against the heavenly bodies, the very brightnesses of the lights also differ, it is not surprising that at the resurrection of the dead the glory of merits will differ.

36. LANFRANC. “It is sown,” etc. No corruptible thing will possess incorruption; but flesh and blood—that is, those living carnally—are corruptible, while the kingdom of God is incorruption. Therefore such people will not possess it.

37. AMBROSE. “It is sown a natural body.” A body is natural while it is sustained by food in order to live; it is spiritual when, transformed into life, it needs none of these things.

38. LANFRANC. “It is sown a natural body.” That essence by which the human body is enlivened, insofar as it gives life and desires earthly things, is called the soul. But insofar as it uses reason and loves God, it is called rational. Hence it is said: “It is sown in the earth a natural body,” that is, corruptible, which desired earthly things; “it will rise a spiritual body,” that is, one doing the will of the spirit in all things and not resisting the spirit.

[Col. 0212B]

39. AUGUSTINE (same work). “If there is a natural body.” A natural body is therefore understood to be called such because it resembles the other animals, on account of death’s dissolution and corruption; it is daily replenished by food, and afterward, when separated, the creature’s bodily frame is dissolved.

40. LANFRANC. “If there is a natural body.” When he says “body,” “natural” would be added in vain unless there were another, spiritual body, in contrast to which it is called natural.

41. “As it is written.” The premise is missing: “If there is a natural body”; and he proves this premise.

42. “The first man was made.” The first man had a vital and spiritual soul, that is, a rational one, according to which Adam and those descended from him were to live.

[Col. 0212C]

43. “The last Adam.” The last Adam, namely Christ, had a vital and spiritual soul, but he mentions only that aspect according to which Christ himself and his imitators were to live more fully. This too is not found written in Genesis, but is added by the Apostle to the preceding statement.

44. “But not first the spiritual,” that is, first came the body of those desiring earthly things, and afterward the body of those living spiritually.

45. AUGUSTINE (Letter 146 to Consentius). “What the earthly is like.” What does “as is the earthly, such are the earthly” mean, except “mortals from a mortal”? And what does “as is the heavenly, such are the heavenly” mean, except “immortals through immortality”? [Variant: “immortal.”]

46. LANFRANC. “Therefore, just as we have borne.” That is, just as by Adam’s example we loved earthly things, so by Christ’s example let us love heavenly things.

47. “Flesh and blood.” Flesh and blood are the human and corruptible body. The meaning is that whoever has lived according to the desire of his body cannot possess the kingdom of God.

48. AUGUSTINE (same work). “Flesh and blood.” And lest anyone think that the Apostle defined this according to the substance of the flesh, he made clear what he meant by adding: “Nor will corruption possess incorruption.”

49. (Same work.) “But we shall not all be changed.” Whether he wished this change to be understood as for the better or for the worse is shown by what follows.

50. AMBROSE. “At the last trumpet.” Because he did not fight with him only once, since he was defeated in the Antichrist; and at this point he will finally fight against him, so that he may then be cast into Gehenna.

51. AUGUSTINE (same work). “And the dead will rise.” What, then, does the distinction mean—“the dead will rise incorruptible, and we shall be changed”—except that all will rise incorruptible? Yet among them the righteous will also be changed into that incorruption which no corruption whatsoever can harm. Therefore those who will not be changed into it will indeed rise incorruptible in the integrity of their limbs, but will nevertheless be subject to corruption through the pain of punishments.

52. LANFRANC. “Death has been swallowed up.” At the end of the age death, both of soul and of body, will be swallowed up in victory, because once all the desires in the flesh of God’s servants have been conquered, neither they nor anything else will die thereafter. In the customary translation of Hosea this testimony is written as follows: “I will be your death, O death!” It signifies the same thing; for the one conquers who grants his faithful the ability to conquer.

53. AMBROSE. “Where is your victory, O death?” These are words of taunting.

54. **AUGUSTINE** (*On the Merit and Forgiveness of Sins*, Book III, chapter 11, volume VII). “The sting of death.” By it death was made, not that which death made. For we die through sin; we do not sin through death. Thus it is said: “The sting of death”—how is it “the tree of life”? Not because it made human life [or: life], but because through it human life was made. And likewise, how is it “the tree of knowledge,” through which human knowledge was made, and not one through whose knowledge humanity was made?

[Col. 0214B]

55. **LANFRANC.** “The sting of death.” He proves that the sting of death has been destroyed. “The sting,” he says, “of death is sin”; but this has been destroyed. He proves it, for it was destroyed through the victory that God gave us through our Lord Jesus Christ—first by comparison, afterward by reference to a part. Was sin not destroyed through the Law? No [possibly: for the Law was an increase of sin, not its destruction].

56. **AUGUSTINE** (*On the Perfection of the Righteous Person*, chapter 6, volume VII). “The power of sin is the Law.” For by forbidding, the Law increases the desire for sin, unless it pours out the love of the Spirit.

## CHAPTER XVI

[Col. 0213]

[Note: [Col. 0214B] **CHAPTER XVI.—1. AUGUSTINE** (*On the Sermon on the Mount*, Book II, chapter 17, volume IV). “Now concerning the collections.” The Apostle Paul may seem to be thinking about the morrow when he says: “Now concerning the collections for the saints: as I directed the churches of Galatia, so also do you. On the first day of the week, let each of you put aside and store up whatever he has been pleased to give, so that collections may not be made when I come.” From these and similar passages of Scripture it is sufficiently clear that our Lord does not disapprove if someone makes such arrangements in the human manner, but if someone serves God for the sake of such things.]

“Now concerning the collections that are made for the saints, as I directed the churches of Galatia, so also do you. On the first [Note: [Col. 0215A] **2. LANFRANC.** “On the first day of the week,” that is, on one day of the week he commands that what was being sent to the saints in Jerusalem be collected.] [Col. 0215] day of the week, then, let each of you set something aside privately, storing up whatever he has judged appropriate and, according to his means, whatever he has been pleased to give, so that collections may not be made—or rather, may already have been made—when I come. When I am present, I shall send those whom you approve by letters, together with the letters, to carry your gift—the gift freely given by you—to the saints who are in Jerusalem. And if it is worthwhile, let the collection be so large that they may go with me as well. They will come to you when I have passed through Macedonia; for I shall pass through Macedonia. I may remain with you, or even spend the winter, so that you may send me on wherever I go. For I do not want to see you now merely in passing, as I pass through; for I hope to remain with you for some time, if the Lord permits. I shall remain in Ephesus until Pentecost. [Note: [Col. 0215A] **3.** “For a great door.” The reason why he intends to remain in Ephesus for so long. He says that a great and evident door of his preaching has been opened, through which, by preaching, he may enter the hearts of his hearers and persuade them of the Christian faith.] For a great and evident door has been opened to me—the reason why he intends to remain in Ephesus for so long [possibly: for such a long time]—and there are many adversaries who, unwilling to believe, attempt to hinder me. If Timothy comes, see that he is with you without fear of the false brothers; for he is doing the Lord’s work—he is a preacher, as I am. Therefore let no one despise him, since he is a preacher. Send him on his way in peace, so that he may come to me; for I am expecting him with the brothers.

Now concerning the brother Apollos, I inform you that I strongly urged him to come to you with the brothers; and certainly it was not his will to come now. But he will come when he has an opportunity. Keep watch, stand firm in the faith, act manfully, and be strengthened; let everything you do be done in love. [Note: [Col. 0215A] **4.** “I urge you.” I urge you also to be subject to the brothers.]

I urge you, brothers, [Note: [Col. 0215A] **5.** “You know the household of Stephanas.” These men had been with the Apostle and with certain Corinthians who were with the Apostle; they themselves had often supplied the Apostle’s necessities.] you know the household of Stephanas, and of Fortunatus and Achaicus, because they are the firstfruits of Achaia: they were the first to believe, and they devoted themselves to the service of the saints. Be subject also to people of this kind and to everyone who works and labors with them.

I rejoice in their presence—that is, because they are with you—in the presence of Stephanas, Fortunatus, and Achaicus, because they have supplied what was lacking in you. For they have refreshed both my spirit and yours: they ministered to me previously, and now they encourage you. Therefore acknowledge and imitate those who are such.

The churches of Asia greet you. Aquila, the husband, and Priscilla, his wife, greet you warmly in the Lord, together with their household church—that is, their family—with whom I am staying. All the brothers greet you. Greet one another with a holy kiss.

The greeting is in my own hand—Paul’s. If anyone does not love our Lord Jesus Christ, [Note: [Col. 0215A] **6. AMBROSE.** “Let him be accursed.” This means: if anyone does not love the Lord Jesus Christ, let him be cut off.] let him be accursed; let him be separated from the Church at the coming of the Lord. [Note: [Col. 0216A] **7. AUGUSTINE** (*Letter 178 to Pascentius*, volume II). “Let him be accursed: Maranatha.” He uses a word that is at once Greek and Syriac. “If anyone,” he says, “does not love the Lord, let him be accursed: Maranatha.” He expressed “anathema” in Greek, meaning “condemned.” He explained “Maranatha” as “until the Lord comes,” or “returns.”] Maranatha. [Note: [Col. 0216A] **8. HERON.** “Maranatha.” It is more Syriac than Hebrew, although, because the two languages border on one another, it may sound somewhat Hebrew as well. It means, “Our Lord has come.” The sense would therefore be: “If anyone does not love the Lord Jesus, let him be accursed”; and, that having been completed, let this be added afterward: “Our Lord has come.” It is pointless to wish to contend with stubborn hatred against one whose coming is already known.] The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you. My love—that is, so that I may love you and you may love one another—with all of you in Christ Jesus, not with the love of the world. Amen.

## COMMENTARY

[Col. 0214]

[Col. 0214B] **CHAPTER XVI.—1. AUGUSTINE** (*On the Sermon on the Mount*, Book II, chapter 17, volume IV). “Now concerning the collections.” The Apostle Paul may seem to be thinking about the morrow when he says: “Now concerning the collections for the saints: as I directed the churches of Galatia, so also do you. On the first day of the week, let each of you put aside and store up whatever he has been pleased to give, so that collections may not be made when I come.” From these and similar passages of Scripture it is sufficiently clear that our Lord does not disapprove if someone makes such arrangements in the human manner, but if someone serves God for the sake of such things.

[Col. 0215A] **2. LANFRANC.** “On the first day of the week,” that is, on one day of the week he commands that what was being sent to the saints in Jerusalem be collected.

**3.** “For a great door.” The reason why he intends to remain in Ephesus for so long. He says that a great door of his preaching has been opened, through which, by preaching, he may enter the hearts of his hearers and persuade them of the Christian faith.

**4.** “I urge you.” I urge you also to be subject to the brothers.

**5.** “You know the household of Stephanas.” These men had been with the Apostle and with certain Corinthians who were with the Apostle; they themselves had often supplied the Apostle’s necessities.

**6. AMBROSE.** “Let him be accursed.” This means: if [Col. 0215B] anyone does not love the Lord Jesus Christ, let him be cut off.

[Col. 0216A] **7. AUGUSTINE** (*Letter 178 to Pascentius*, volume II). “Let him be accursed: Maranatha.” He uses a word that is at once Greek and Syriac. “If anyone,” he says, “does not love the Lord, let him be accursed: Maranatha.” He expressed “anathema” in Greek, meaning “condemned.” He explained “Maranatha” as “until the Lord comes,” or “returns.”

**8. HERON.** “Maranatha.” It is more Syriac than Hebrew, although, because the two languages border on one another, it may sound somewhat Hebrew as well. It means, “Our Lord has come.” The sense would therefore be: “If anyone does not love the Lord Jesus, let him be accursed”; and, that having been completed, let this be added afterward: “Our Lord has come.” It is pointless to wish to contend with stubborn hatred against one whose coming is already known.

# THE SECOND LETTER OF THE APOSTLE PAUL TO THE CORINTHIANS, WITH THE INTERPOLATED BRIEF GLOSSES OF LANFRANC

[Col. 0215]

## ARGUMENT

After the Corinthians had performed penance, the Apostle writes to them a letter of consolation from Troas, through Titus. Commending them, he urges them toward better things, showing that they had indeed been saddened, but had been corrected.

## CHAPTER I

Paul, an Apostle of Jesus Christ through the will of God—not of man, nor by human merits—and Timothy, a brother, to the Church of God that is at Corinth, together with all the saints who are throughout Achaia: grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.

Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies—not of one mercy only, but of many, according to those who participate in them—and [Note: [Col. 0215B] **CHAPTER I.—1. AMBROSE.** “The God of all consolation.” He began with consolation, by which he gives refreshment to those who had been saddened for the sake of correction, and he calls him the Father of mercies because of the various sins, so that it might be recognized that through mercy he restores penitents.] the God of all consolation, [Col. 0217] [Note: [Col. 0217A] **2. LANFRANC.** “Who consoles us.” By this he already shows that the letter is one of consolation. For he wishes all to be consoled: both those who had been saddened and that rejected man who had taken his father’s wife. For this reason he said, “the Father of mercies and God of all,” and so forth.] who consoles us in all our tribulation, so that we too may be able to console by words or example those who are in every kind of distress, through the encouragement by which we ourselves are also encouraged by God inwardly through the Spirit.

**Response.** For just as the sufferings of Christ abound in us—the sufferings that we endure for Christ—so also through Christ our consolation, or encouragement, abounds. Whether, then, we are troubled for the sake of your encouragement, by our example or by a word, and for your eternal salvation; or whether we are consoled for the sake of your consolation; or whether we are inwardly encouraged by the Holy Spirit for the sake of your encouragement, so that we may encourage you, and for your salvation, [Note: [Col. 0217A] **3.** “For your encouragement.” He supplies a certain reason for his tribulation, namely, so that the Corinthians, stirred by his example, might be encouraged to endure tribulations and thus attain everlasting salvation.] that salvation—or consolation, or encouragement—which produces endurance in you, namely, of the same sufferings that we also endure, [Note: [Col. 0217A] **4.** “Which produces endurance.” The hope of eternal salvation produces endurance, that is, patience, in God’s servants, because on account of it adversities are endured.] so that in this way—or from this, or for this purpose—our hope for you may be firm: the hope that we have that you will be saved, knowing that just as you are companions in suffering, so you will also be companions in eternal consolation, or eternal reward. [Note: [Col. 0217B] **5.** “So that our hope.” Since eternal salvation has been stated to be the principal cause of their endurance, he adds another cause, namely, that the hope he held for them might appear firm.] [Note: [Col. 0217B] **6. AMBROSE.** “For we do not want.” He mentions the sufferings of afflictions in order to show what evils he was suffering for the sake of their salvation, so that they would not bear it more heavily if they were corrected by one who endured such hardships for them.] [Note: [Col. 0217B] **7. LANFRANC.** “For we do not want.” He explains what he said above, “Whether we are troubled,” and what he says afterward, “As companions in sufferings,” and so forth.]

For we do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, of our tribulation [**Response:** For we suffered a vehement affliction, and we do not want you to be ignorant of this], [Note: [Col. 0217B] **8.** “Which happened in Asia.” Here he is not speaking of that Asia which is the third part of the whole world, but of a certain province that is part of the greater Asia, although it is called by the same name.] which happened in Asia. For we were burdened beyond measure, beyond human strength, so that we were weary even of living and had no hope of remaining alive, but expected to die.

Indeed, we ourselves had within ourselves the sentence of death [our conscience itself pronounced death for us]; I hoped not to escape the blows of death, so that we would not place our confidence in ourselves but in God. I was so certain of death that, because I did not die, I ought no longer to trust in myself but in God, who rescued me as though already dead. God permitted me to be troubled beyond human strength and wished me to be helped by his assistance, so that we would not be confident in ourselves—God, who raises the dead, which is an emphasis, that is, an intensification.

He rescued and delivered us from such great dangers; in him we hope that he will still rescue us, with your assistance [a captatio benevolentiae, and an act of humility] through the prayer made for us, so that from the [Note: [Col. 0218A] **9.** “From the persons of many.” The reason why he will still rescue him is so that, from the persons of many faces converted to God on account of their preaching, thanks may be given to God through their preaching, by many who possess that gift of faith which is in them. By “persons of many faces” he means infants, children, and the remaining ages of human beings of both sexes.] persons of many—meaning the same as “through many,” of male and female sex—thanks may be given to God for us, for the gift of my confession or deliverance, which is in us, that is, for Christianity.

[Note: [Col. 0218A] **10. LANFRANC.** “For our glory.” The reason why they ought to assist him, namely, in their prayers, is that their conscience bears witness that they conducted themselves sincerely among them.] [Note: [Col. 0218A] **11. AMBROSE.** “For our glory.” The reason why he did not distrust God was that he conducted himself with simplicity. This is the glory of conscience: simplicity and sincerity.]

You ought to pray for us. For this is our glory: the testimony of our conscience, namely, that [for this reason it is right that thanks be given for me, since I conducted myself with simplicity and sincerity among you] we lived in simplicity, not with a divided heart, and in the sincerity that comes from God, and not [Note: [Col. 0218B] **12. LANFRANC.** “In wisdom.” Carnal wisdom is to love pleasures and avoid labors.] in carnal wisdom, as the pseudo-apostles do. [Note: [Col. 0218B] **13.** “But in grace,” that is, in the observance of good works, which is given through the grace of God.] But in the grace of God we conducted ourselves in this world, and more abundantly toward and among you. [Note: [Col. 0218B] **14. AMBROSE.** “More abundantly.” Although he had received from others, he did not wish to receive from these people, lest he lose the authority to rebuke them.] [Note: [Col. 0218B] **15. LANFRANC.** “For we do not write other things.” Or it may be understood thus: You say, “In simplicity: in another letter you promised to come to us, and you did not come.” “I am not,” he says, “fickle, because you recognize that what I wrote, and what you read in my letters, is truly so.]

For we do not write anything to you other than what you have read and recognized to have been in me. [Col. 0219] [Note: [Col. 0219A] **16.** “I hope.” As though he were saying: You recognized us as good at the beginning, and you will recognize us as good to the end.] I hope that to the end of my life you will recognize us, just as you have recognized us—not fully, for a human being sees what is in the face, whereas God sees what is in the heart—but partially, whether of my life or not of all of you. For this reason you will recognize us. [Note: [Col. 0219A] **17. AMBROSE.** “Because we are your glory.” He hopes that they will progress because they gloried in him as in a most beloved father. Hence he also testifies that his glory is seen in obedient children, and that it is seen when he benefits them, namely, on the day of judgment.] For we are your glory, just as you are ours, [Note: [Col. 0219A] **18. LANFRANC.** “On the day of the Lord,” and so forth. For in the present the saints glory in their good conscience, as in the Psalm: “All the glory of the king’s daughter is within.”] on the day of our Lord Jesus Christ.

And in this confidence—that is, on account of this confidence by which we hope to be glorified through one another—I first intended, recently, to come to you, so that you might receive grace, and to pass through you into Macedonia, and again to come to you from Macedonia, and from you to be sent on to Judea.

**Objection:** You wished to come but did not come; therefore you acted fickly. And because you did not come, you did so according to the flesh, that is, for some gain.

**He removes this objection. Response:** When I had intended this, and did not come, did I then act fickly? [Note: [Col. 0219A] **20. AMBROSE.** “Or the things I plan.” One who thinks according to the flesh fulfills [or: does not fulfill] what he plans when he is either influenced by more important persons, or overcome by letters [possibly: lights], or defeated by displays. A spiritual person, however, fails to carry out what he has planned when he considers something more prudently for the salvation of the soul.] Or do the things I plan, [Note: [Col. 0219B] **21. LANFRANC.** “According to the flesh,” that is, in the manner of those who live according to the flesh; they readily change their will for earthly advantage.] do I plan according to the flesh, in the manner of those who live according to the flesh, who for earthly advantage promise or deny, so that with them it is both “yes” and “no”?

But God is faithful, and knows that our word to you is not “yes and no”—changeability and falsehood—but that in it there is “yes.” For the Son of God, Jesus Christ, who was preached among you through us, through me and Silvanus and Timothy, [Note: [Col. 0219B] **22.** “In him is yes and no,” that is, our preaching did not teach you to lie and lightly change your judgment.] was not “yes and no,” but in him there was “yes,” that is, truth. [Note: [Col. 0219B] **23.** “It was not ‘yes and no.’” As though he were saying: Our preaching did not teach people to lie, because our Teacher, whom we preach to you, did not teach us to say of the same matter both “yes” and “no,” that is, to utter a lie. Rather, “yes” only concerning what is, and “no” likewise concerning what is not.] 88

For however many promises of God there are, in him they are truly completed. [Note: [Col. 0219C] **24.** “For however many,” that is, Christ rightly taught the truth because God the Father truly fulfilled his promises in him.] [Note: [Col. 0219C] **25. ## COMMENTARY

[Col. 0215]

**CHAPTER I.—1. AMBROSE.** “The God of all consolation.” He began with consolation, by which he gives refreshment to those who had been saddened for the sake of correction, and he calls him the Father of mercies because of the various sins, so that it might be recognized that through mercy he restores penitents.

**2. LANFRANC.** “Who consoles us.” By this he already shows that the letter is one of consolation. For he wishes all to be consoled: both those who had been saddened and that rejected man who had taken his father’s wife. For this reason he said, “the Father of mercies and God of all,” and so forth.

**3.** “For your encouragement.” He supplies a certain reason for his tribulation, namely, so that the Corinthians, stirred by his example, might be encouraged to endure tribulations and thus attain everlasting salvation.

**4.** “Which produces endurance.” The hope of eternal salvation produces endurance, that is, patience, in God’s servants, because on account of it adversities are endured.

**5.** “So that our hope.” Since eternal salvation has been stated to be the principal cause of their endurance, he adds another cause, namely, that the hope he held for them might appear firm.

**6. AMBROSE.** “For we do not want.” He mentions the sufferings of afflictions in order to show what evils he was suffering for the sake of their salvation, so that they would not bear it more heavily if they were corrected by one who endured such hardships for them.

**7. LANFRANC.** “For we do not want.” He explains what he said above, “Whether we are troubled,” and what he says afterward, “As companions in sufferings,” and so forth.

**8.** “Which happened in Asia.” Here he is not speaking of that Asia [Col. 0218A] which is the third part of the whole world, but of a certain province that is part of the greater Asia, although it is called by the same name.

**9.** “From the persons of many.” The reason why he will still rescue him is so that, from the persons of many faces converted to God on account of their preaching, thanks may be given to God through their preaching, by many who possess that gift of faith which is in them. By “persons of many faces” he means infants, children, and the remaining ages of human beings of both sexes.

**10.** “For our glory.” The reason why they ought to assist him, namely, in their prayers, is that their conscience bears witness that they conducted themselves sincerely among them.

**11. AMBROSE.** “For our glory.” The reason why he did not distrust God was that he conducted himself with simplicity. This is the glory of conscience: simplicity and sincerity.

**12. LANFRANC.** “In wisdom.” Carnal wisdom is to love pleasures and avoid labors.

**13.** “But in grace,” that is, in the observance of good works, which is given through the grace of God.

**14. AMBROSE.** “More abundantly.” Although he had received from others, he did not wish to receive from these people, lest he lose the authority to rebuke them.

**15. LANFRANC.** “For we do not write other things.” Or it may be understood thus: You say, “In simplicity: in another letter you promised to come to us, and you did not come.” “I am not,” he says, “fickle, because you recognize that what I wrote, and what you read in my letters, is truly so.”

[Col. 0219A] **16.** “I hope.” As though he were saying: You recognized us as good at the beginning, and you will recognize us as good to the end.

**17. AMBROSE.** “Because we are your glory.” He hopes that they will progress because they gloried in him as in a most beloved father. Hence he also testifies that his glory is seen in obedient children, and that it is seen when he benefits them, namely, on the day of judgment.

**18. LANFRANC.** “On the day of the Lord,” and so forth. For in the present the saints glory in their good conscience, as in the Psalm: “All the glory of the king’s daughter is within.”

**19.** “And in this confidence,” that is, on account of this confidence by which we hope to be glorified through one another.

**20. AMBROSE.** “Or the things I plan.” One who thinks according to the flesh fulfills [or: does not fulfill] what he plans when he is either influenced by more important persons, or overcome by letters [possibly: lights], or defeated by displays. A spiritual person, however, fails to carry out what he has planned when he considers something more prudently for the salvation of the soul.

**21. LANFRANC.** “According to the flesh,” that is, in the manner of those who live according to the flesh; they readily change their will for earthly advantage.

**22.** “In him is yes and no,” that is, our preaching did not teach you to lie and lightly change your judgment.

**23.** “It was not ‘yes and no.’” As though he were saying: Our preaching did not teach people to lie, because our Teacher, whom we preach to you, did not teach us to say of the same matter both “yes” and “no,” that is, to utter a lie. Rather, “yes” only concerning what is, and “no” likewise concerning what is not.

[Col. 0219C] **24.** “For however many,” that is, Christ rightly taught the truth because God the Father truly fulfilled his promises in him.

**25. AUGUSTINE** (*Exposition of Psalm 71*, volume VIII). “For however many.” All the promises of God have also been confirmed in him—that is, in him—for in him everything that was prophesied for our salvation has been fulfilled.

**26. AMBROSE.** “Therefore also through him.” It is clear that truth is in God; this is “Amen,” made manifest through Christ.

**27. LANFRANC.** “Through him, Amen, to God.” “Amen” is said through Christ because God the Father fulfilled in him whatever he promised concerning him.

**28.** “For our glory.” The glory of the apostles was to preach the true Teacher, in whom the promises of God were completed.

**29.** “Now the one who confirms.” As though he were saying: You ought not to attribute your belief in Christ to our preaching, because it is God by whose grace we are confirmed in faith and made glad in mind to serve him. For he also separated us from unbelievers by the sign of baptism [Col. 0220B] and gave the Holy Spirit, the pledge of the eternal inheritance, in our hearts.

**30. AMBROSE.** “The one who anointed us,” that is, the one who gave us royal honor, as Peter says: “We are,” he says, “a royal race,” through spiritual anointing.

**31.** “He gave the pledge.” If he has given his Spirit even now to mortal people, there is no doubt that he will add glory to those who are already immortal.

**32.** “Not that we lord it over your faith.” Faith is a matter not of compulsion but of will. Therefore he says, “not that we lord it over your faith.” Domination involves compulsion.

**33. LANFRANC.** “We lord it over,” and so forth. Someone might say: “By sparing us, then, you wish to compel us to faith.” “It is not so,” he says; “we do not lord it over your faith; we do not compel you to faith.” Or he said “sparing” with reference to certain people who were not standing firm in the faith. And lest those who were standing firm in faith think that this had been said about them, he says, “we do not lord it over your faith,” that is, we do not wish to exercise dominion over those who stand in faith, but to help you in correcting those who must be reformed.

**34. AMBROSE.** “Helpers of your joy.” Just as there is sadness in evil conduct, so there is joy in correction. He was a helper of this joy by offering admonitions to those who wished to amend their conduct.

[Col. 0221]

I resolved, however, to make this very decision within myself: not to come again to you in sorrow. [Note: [Col. 0221A] CHAPTER II.—1. [Note: [Col. 0221A] 2. “And this very thing.” What causes you sorrow should not make me glad unless you yourselves are made sorrowful unto repentance.] [Note: [Col. 0221A] 3. AMBROSE. “And this very thing.” He says that he wrote for this reason: so that, when he came afterward, there would be nothing over which he might be sorrowful, once the vices had been removed.] And I wrote this very thing—that I did not come, so as not to cause you sorrow—for this reason: so that, when I come, I may not have the sorrow of your impenitence added to the sorrow of your sin; for I ought to rejoice over those—that is, over you—yet I am confident about you all, because my joy is the joy of all of you, since I shall rejoice over your amendment.

For out of much tribulation, sorrow, and anguish of heart I wrote to you with many tears—not in order to cause you sorrow, as though I meant to say “with many” for that purpose, but so that you might know how abundantly I love you. It may also be understood in this way: he did not cause me sorrow completely, but in part.] But if anyone, as an adulterer, caused sorrow, he did not cause sorrow to me altogether, or only to me, but in part—that is, to some degree—or to you also (that is why I say, “if anyone,” or “in part”; I say that I was made sorrowful so that I might not burden all of you with sin); or else, he did not cause me sorrow completely, but in part, so that I might not burden—that is, so that I might not weigh you down—with so great a sorrow.

Sufficient for such a person—the one who took his father’s wife, whom you ought now to receive—is this rebuke, administered by the many, by me and by you: he caused sorrow both to me and to you. Yet, on the contrary, you ought rather to forgive him, to forgive the sin, and to comfort him rather than cause him sorrow. [Note: [Col. 0221B] 5. “You should rather forgive,” etc. It is sufficiently clear that the apostle is not sorrowful on account of the fornicator who had taken his father’s wife, from what he now adds: that he should be received and comforted.] [Note: [Col. 0221B] 6. AMBROSE. “Lest perhaps with excessive sorrow”—that is, lest, despairing of himself, he should turn his mind to enjoying the world, as though he no longer had a place with God. For this reason I also wrote, so that I might learn by experience what you are like: whether I might test you, or your eagerness, to see whether in everything you are obedient to me—just as you were previously obedient in expelling him, so now in receiving the guilty man. Therefore you ought to obey.

But to whomever you have forgiven anything, I also have forgiven it; and in this you should act toward me as well. [Note: [Col. 0222A] 8. “So that we may not be outwitted.” He says that consolation must follow, lest the devil suggest to him that he should enjoy present things, since he has been cast down from hope of the future reward.] [Note: [Col. 0222A] 9. [COMMENTARY.]

[Col. 0221]

[Col. 0221A] CHAPTER II.—1. LANFRANC. “For if I cause you sorrow.” If a teacher causes a disciple sorrow by correcting him, his joy consists in the disciple’s being grieved unto repentance.

2. “And this very thing.” What causes you sorrow should not make me glad unless you yourselves are made sorrowful unto repentance.

3. AMBROSE. “And this very thing.” He says that he wrote for this reason: so that, when he came afterward, there would be nothing over which he might be sorrowful, once the vices had been removed.

4. LANFRANC. “But if anyone.” “If anyone,” he says, “by his preaching caused me sorrow, he did not cause sorrow to me alone, but in part to you”—that is, to some of you—“so that I should not burden you all.” Therefore he says that you were made sorrowful in part, so that he might not impose the burden of sorrow on everyone; for not all of you sincerely love righteousness. It may also be understood in this way: he did not cause me sorrow completely, but in part.

5. “You should rather forgive,” etc. It is sufficiently clear that the apostle is not sorrowful on account of the fornicator who had taken his father’s wife, from what he now adds: that he should be received and comforted.

6. AMBROSE. “Lest perhaps with excessive sorrow”—that is, lest, despairing of himself, he should turn his mind to enjoying the world, as though he no longer had a place with God.

7. “Whether in everything.” So far as can be understood, he approves that these people have become obedient in the other matters as well.

8. “So that we may not be outwitted.” He says that consolation must follow, lest the devil suggest to him that he should enjoy present things, since he has been cast down from hope of the future reward.

9. LANFRANC. “So that we may not be outwitted,” that is, so that there may not be discord among you.

10. “When I came, however,” etc. Having excused himself for not coming, he recounts what he did, commending himself in the same work: “I did not come so as to cause you sorrow. When I came to Troas,” etc.

11. “Titus my brother.” This Titus was the Apostle’s interpreter, and he spoke their language more fluently than the Apostle did.

12. “Taking leave of them,” etc. To support what he said—“I did not come to Corinth, sparing you, but I came to Troas,” where they listened to me willingly—this is what “a door was opened for me” means. Thus he encourages them also to receive him willingly, after hearing this about those others.

13. AMBROSE. “The fragrance of knowledge.” The preaching of Christ. He calls it a fragrance because, just as certain things, although they are not seen, are recognized by their smell, so the invisible God wished to make himself known through the preaching of Christ.

[Col. 0223A] 14. “A good fragrance.” In the Law, one who offered sacrifices with a good intention was a good and acceptable fragrance to God. Likewise, the man [variant: “virtue”] of pious preaching offers God a fragrant scent of teaching.

15. AUGUSTINE (Book of Sentences of Prosper, chapter 35, volume III). “Christ’s good fragrance.” Christ’s good fragrance is the preaching of truth. The person who serves and conforms to the gospel through good morals receives that fragrance unto life. The person whose life disagrees with what he speaks well incurs death. This condition also binds hearers: when sound preaching is heard by some through unbelief, it is unto death; when received by others through faith, it is unto salvation.

16. LANFRANC. “A good fragrance.” The preaching is indeed good in both cases, but to those who are disobedient let the preaching be a fragrance of death—that is, of sin—unto eternal death.

17. AMBROSE. “To some a fragrance of death.” To unbelievers the preaching of Christ is a fragrance of death. For when they hear the word of God, they receive it as though it were a plague from which death arises.

18. “Adulterating”—that is, he is referring to the pseudo-apostles, who adulterated the words of God through bad interpretation. For, removing the divine meaning, they substituted a human one.

19. LANFRANC. “Adulterating.” An adulterer does not seek offspring but to satisfy the desire of the body. Such are those who preach the word of God for earthly advantage, not seeking to beget spiritual children.

[Col. 0223C] 20. “From God.” “We speak from God,” he says, because we receive from God what we preach.

AMBROSE. “From God,” that is, in the manner in which God gave it.

21. LANFRANC. “Before God.” Because we strive to please him.

[Col. 0223]
