[Note: [Col. 0224B] 7. “But the Spirit gives life”—that is, when understood spiritually, it gives life to the soul of the person observing it.]

[Note: [Col. 0224C] 8. “But if the ministry.” A commendation and praise of the New Testament. He says that if the ministry of the old law, formed by letters on tablets of stone, was given to Moses in such glory that the children of Israel could not look upon his face because of the brightness of his countenance, although that glory was transitory, how much more will the ministry of the new law be given to the apostles for eternal glory. The old law is called a ministry of death either because it punished sinners without mercy or because, after Christ’s coming, when observed according to the letter, it ministers death to the soul. The New Testament, however, is called a ministry of the Spirit either because through it the Holy Spirit is given to the person who observes it, or because in it the old law is understood and observed spiritually. [Col. 0225A]] But if the ministry of death—the Old Testament that brings death—formed and written in letters on stones and tablets was in glory, [Col. 0225] in Moses, [Note: [Col. 0225A] 9. AUGUSTINE (Book II Against the Adversary of the Law and the Prophets, chapter 7, volume VI). “So that the children of Israel could not.” The fact that the children of Israel could not look attentively upon his face because of the glory of his countenance was a sign that they would not understand Christ in the Law. [Response, or an argument from comparison.]

For if the ministry of condemnation—the law that condemns—is in glory for Moses, the ministry of righteousness abounds much more in glory for the apostles. [Note: [Col. 0225A] 10. LANFRANC. “For what was glorified.” The order is: “what became bright was not glorified in this respect,” because of the surpassing glory. He explains the glory of the preachers of the New Testament. For if what is being abolished [Note: [Col. 0225B] 11. “What is being abolished.” The veil of the old law is now removed, because whatever the legal observances signified is now explained.] came through glory—for if the ministry of condemnation, etc.—then what remains is much more in glory. Therefore we shall have glory; and since we have hope of glory, we preach with confidence. This is the point:

Since, therefore, we have such hope of the glory to be received from the gospel, we use great confidence in the gospel. We do not act like Moses, who put a veil over his face; we do not put a veil over our face—that is, we do not have veiled words, as Moses did. This was signified by the veil, so that the children of Israel would not look attentively upon his face. The veil of what is being abolished is removed among Christians.

Yet their understanding remains dull—that is, the understanding of the Jews, who still cannot understand. For to this very day the same veil remains, when the Old Testament is read, among the Jews, unrevealed to unbelievers, because it is revealed only to believers; for it is abolished in those who believe through faith in Christ. But to this very day, whenever Moses is read, a veil lies over their heart—the heart of the Jews. But whenever it turns to the Lord, the veil of understanding will be removed from their hearts. [Note: [Col. 0225B] 12. “The Lord is the Spirit.” The order is: The Holy Spirit is the Lord, and he can do whatever he wishes. [COMMENTARY.]

[Col. 0223]

[Col. 0223C] CHAPTER III.—1. LANFRANC. “Are we beginning again,” etc. “We are not commending ourselves,” he says; we need no commendation, neither the commendation made by you nor that made in letters, because it is through a letter (by comparison). [Col. 0224A] “For we do not need a letter sent to you by others.” We do not wish to be commended by a letter, because you are our letter, which commends us—that is, your faith.

2. “Our letter.” “You are our letter,” he says—that is, our faith is praised through it, because by our preaching we converted you to the faith.

3. “In our hearts.” We have not handed you and your faith over to oblivion, but you are always in our memory.

4. AUGUSTINE (Book On the Spirit and the Letter, chapter 17, volume III). “On the tablets of the heart.” He called the tablets of the heart “fleshly,” not in the sense of fleshly wisdom, but as being living and possessing perception, in comparison with stone, which is without perception.

[Col. 0224B] 5. (The same work, chapter 14). “For the letter kills.” Pay attention and observe that, when he says something on account of circumcision, or the Sabbath, or some other shadowy sacrament, he does not say that everything is on account of this; for the letter, which forbids sin, does not give life to [or: justify] a person, but rather kills him by increasing desire and piling up iniquity through transgression, unless grace frees him through the law of faith that is in Christ Jesus.

6. LANFRANC. “The letter kills.” This can be understood in two ways: either because it commands sinners to be killed without mercy, saying, “If anyone does this or that, let him die the death”; or because, when observed carnally, it kills the soul of the person observing it.

7. “But the Spirit gives life”—that is, when understood spiritually, it gives life to the soul of the person observing it.

[Col. 0224C] 8. “But if the ministry.” A commendation and praise of the New Testament. He says that if the ministry of the old law, formed by letters on tablets of stone, was given to Moses in such glory that the children of Israel could not look upon his face because of the brightness of his countenance, although that glory was transitory, how much more will the ministry of the new law be given to the apostles for eternal glory. The old law is called a ministry of death either because it punished sinners without mercy or because, after Christ’s coming, when observed according to the letter, it ministers death to the soul. The New Testament, however, is called a ministry of the Spirit either because through it the Holy Spirit is given to the person who observes it, or because in it the old law is understood and observed spiritually.

9. AUGUSTINE (Book II Against the Adversary of the Law and the Prophets, chapter 7, volume VI). “So that the children of Israel could not.” The fact that the children of Israel could not look attentively upon his face because of the glory of his countenance was a sign that they would not understand Christ in the Law. Therefore a veil was placed between Moses’ face and them so that they would not look attentively, as it is written: “The children of Israel to the end,” etc.

10. LANFRANC. “For what was glorified.” The order is: “what became bright was not glorified in this respect,” because of the surpassing glory. He explains the glory of the preachers of the New Testament. For he says that Moses’ face, which shone in the giving of the old law, cannot be called glorified when this aspect is considered—that is, if it is compared with the glory of the apostles—because of the surpassing glory that they have and will have.

11. “What is being abolished.” The veil of the old law is now removed, because whatever the legal observances signified is now explained.

12. “The Lord is the Spirit.” The order is: The Holy Spirit is the Lord, and he can do whatever he wishes. Consequently, he illuminates those whom he wishes and leaves those whom he wishes in the darkness of ignorance.

13. “Where the Spirit of the Lord is.” He explains why the Jews cannot understand the Old Testament freely and why the preachers of the New Testament understand it freely: namely, because the former do not have the Spirit of God, whereas the latter do.

14. “There is freedom?” The veil will be removed from the Israelite who turns back; for God’s freedom will be in him, because the Spirit will be there and will give it. He proves this as follows: the Spirit is the Lord; but wherever the Lord is, there is freedom. Therefore wherever the Spirit is, there is freedom (from the general principle, through assumption and conclusion). But it will be in the Israelite who turns back; therefore there will be freedom in him.

15. “But we all, with unveiled.” “We all,” he says, all the apostles, with unveiled and uncovered faces, unlike Moses, contemplating heavenly glory. For our intention is directed toward that very glory, since now we see through a mirror and in a riddle the same glory, which does not yet appear as it truly is, but is seen by faith as a kind of image; and we are transformed through good works. For this is our endeavor: that we may be made conformed to it, passing from the brightness of faith into the brightness of hope.

16. AMBROSE. “But we all, with unveiled.” By contemplating through faith, we hope to be transformed into the same image—that is, so that, when this life has passed, we may be found like the image of Christ’s glory. Hence John says: “We know that when he appears, we shall be like him.”

17. AUGUSTINE (Book XV On the Trinity, chapter 8, volume III). “Contemplating the glory of the Lord.” If we seek this mirror, surely the thought occurs that in a mirror nothing but an image is seen [added reading: “not”]. Therefore we have attempted to do this: through this image, to see, however imperfectly, what we are and by whom we were made, as through a mirror. Thus he said “contemplating,” meaning seeing through a mirror, not looking out from a mirror [variant: a watchtower]. When he says “we are transformed into the same image,” he certainly means the image of God, calling it “the same”—that is, this very image, the one we contemplate—because that same image is the image and glory of God, as he says elsewhere: “A man ought not to veil his head, since he is the image and glory of God.” Therefore “we are transformed” means that we are changed and pass from one form into another.

[Col. 0227A] 18. (The same work). “From brightness to brightness.” The most excellent nature among created things, when it is justified from ungodliness by its Creator, is transformed from a deformed form into a beautiful form. Even in ungodliness itself, the more damnable the vice, the more clearly praiseworthy is the nature; and for this reason he added, “from glory to glory”—from the glory of creation into the glory of justification. Yet “from glory to glory” can also be understood in other ways: from the glory of faith into the glory of hope; from the glory by which we are children of God into the glory by which we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is.

19. (The same work). “As from the Spirit of the Lord.” By adding “as from the Spirit of the Lord,” he shows that grace [gratiam; variant: gratia] is conferred upon us as (tanquam; variant: tam, “so”) the good of a desirable confirmation [variant: transformation].

CHAPTER IV

[Col. 0227]

Therefore, because we are transformed through hope, or because with unveiled face we contemplate the glory promised to us, having this ministry of preaching, according to the mercy we have received, we do not falter—not through our own merits—but, in preaching, renounce the hidden things of shame—that is, hidden sins which bring shame—not walking, like false apostles, in craftiness, nor adulterating the word of God, depriving it of its proper meaning, or preaching for earthly gain; but by manifesting the truth we commend ourselves to every human conscience. The very manifestation of the truth commends us to those people themselves before God—not only before human beings, but also before God.

This is an answer to what he said, “with unveiled face.” But if even our Gospel is veiled—not only the ancient Law—it is veiled among those who are perishing;

[Note: **CAP. IV.—1. LANFRANC. “Among those in whom the god of this age…”** As though he were saying: He who rules not only invisible creatures but also this invisible age can also construct things in such a way that the god of this age has blinded the minds of the unbelievers. For if the phrase “the god of this age” is said of the devil, it is understood in the Gospel as “the prince of this world.”]

among whom the god of this age—the author of all things—or the devil, the prince of this age, has blinded the minds of unbelievers, so that the illumination of the Gospel of the glory of Christ may not shine upon them. Through this Gospel Christ is glorified; he is the image of God, like the Father.

**Answer.**

[Note: **2. “For we do not preach ourselves.”** He shows that they are not walking in craftiness or adulterating the word of God, and explains why he said “of the glory of Christ” rather than “of the Gospel of our glory.”]

For we do not preach ourselves, but Jesus Christ our Lord, namely, that he is Lord; and ourselves as your servants—not only his servants, but also yours, through Jesus. For God

[Note: **3. “He who said, ‘Out of darkness…’”** The reason why he preached is that God gave them knowledge through preaching.]

who said, “Let light shine out of darkness”—for he said, “Let there be light”—or who makes the heavens shine with light,

[Note: **4. AUGUSTINE. “He himself shone forth.”** He did so in order to illuminate us, so that through the Son, who is the radiance of the Father by which we are illuminated, we might have knowledge of his glory.]

he himself shone in our hearts,

[Note: **5. AMBROSE. “He shone in our hearts.”** They are illuminated so that through Christ they may have knowledge of the glory of God.]

which were obscure, that is, he made himself known to us so that, by preaching, we might give an illuminated knowledge of the glory of God—that human beings might have knowledge of Christ;

[Note: **6. AUGUSTINE (in Bede, on this chapter). “For the illumination.”** This is the knowledge of God: that we know him to be the light by which our darkness is illuminated. Observe how he repeatedly insists on this.]

for the illumination—that is, the giving—of the knowledge of the glory of God, so that it may be known how great the Father’s glory is through knowledge of the Son whom we preach, since knowledge of the Father comes through knowledge of the Son—in the face, that is, in the knowledge, of Jesus Christ.

Although we are afflicted,

[Note: **7. LANFRANC. “We have this treasure.”** He says that the apostles possess the treasure of the knowledge of God’s glory in earthly bodies, so that whenever they accomplish anything profound, they may attribute it to God’s power and not to themselves.]

we have this treasure—that is, this glory—in earthen vessels, so that the surpassing greatness may belong to the power of God. If this treasure had been given to angels, their dignity would have been said to be sufficient for it; but now only the greatness of God is considered. If we do anything good, it should be ascribed to God, and we should not take glory from ourselves.

[Note: **8. AMBROSE. “In everything afflicted.”** He now shows that they were suitable preachers: although they suffered affliction, they were not distressed—that is, they were not so oppressed that they gave way. “We are perplexed” means that they suffered want, while God the shepherd was present. “We are struck down” means that they were beaten and thrown to the ground, yet were not put to death.]

Therefore, in everything we suffer affliction, but are not distressed in spirit; we are perplexed, we suffer want, or we are oppressed. *Poros* is Greek for “rich,” while *aporos* means “poor”; hence *we are perplexed*—*aporiamur*. But we are not abandoned in our purpose. We suffer persecution through hunger, but are not forsaken by God; we are struck down in body, but do not perish in spirit. We are always carrying in our body the dying of Jesus, so that the eternal life of Jesus may also be manifested in our bodies—when, in the future, our mortal flesh has been made immortal.

For we who live are always being handed over to death because of Jesus, so that the life of Jesus may also be manifested in our mortal flesh. Compressed on every side by affliction, we are ready for death for the name of Christ, so that we may be able to live with him. And this is what he means by “always,” and so forth.

[Col. 0229]

This follows either from authority or by contrast. Therefore,

[Note: **9. “Death is at work in us.”** There is no doubt that Christ is killed in the martyrs. Accordingly, the life by which Christ rose from the dead will be granted to their mortal flesh.]

death is at work in us,

[Note: **10. “But life…”** He says this because he was subjected to death for their salvation, possessing the same Spirit—that is, the Spirit common to them—through whom faith is strengthened, as it is written: “I believed, and therefore I spoke.” Because he believed, he dares to preach this.]

but life—which is the cause of our life, or spoken ironically—is at work in you.

But having

**Answer.** Although death is at work in us, we will not be silent; rather, having the same spirit of faith, we speak about God,

[Note: **12. LANFRANC. “The same spirit of faith.”** Someone might ask: “Why do you suffer?” He answers: “Because we speak about God.” “Why, then, do you speak?” “Because we believe in him.” For all who faithfully believe in him speak about him. It is written of David that he spoke for this reason: because he believed. What follows from this? “We,” he says, “have the spirit of faith that David had.”]

the same spirit of faith, as it is written: “I believed, and therefore I spoke.” We also believe, and therefore we speak about God; and he added another reason: knowing that he who raised Jesus will also raise us with Jesus and establish us in heaven with you. He adds “with you” as an expression of goodwill.

[Note: **13. “Everything is for your sake.”** He explains how they will be established in heaven: everything is for your sake, so that grace—that is, your faith—may abound through your example with thanksgiving, and so you may be established in heaven.]

[Note: **14. AMBROSE. “For everything is for your sake.”** The apostle was not afraid to suffer persecutions and dangers so that more people might believe, and so that God’s abundant gift would not be diminished by the thanksgiving of only a few, to God’s dishonor, but would benefit many and overflow through the thanksgiving of many, to the glory of God.]

For everything is for your sake, so that grace, abounding in faith through the many who believe, may abound in thanksgiving to the glory of God, not so as to incur disgrace.

[Note: **15. LANFRANC. “Everything is for your sake.”** We suffer everything for your instruction, so that grace—that is, thanksgiving—may abound through thanksgiving offered by many and may abound to the glory of God. Therefore—because he will raise us and establish us alive, or because we have the spirit of faith—we do not falter. Although our outward person, which is strong, is corrupted and afflicted, the person within is nevertheless renewed from day to day. He explains why he does not falter: for this present, momentary thing

[Col. 0229]

—each phrase corresponding to its proper referent: “in the present” to “surpassing greatness,” “momentary” to “eternal,” and “light affliction” to “weight of glory”—our momentary and light affliction, our transitory and light affliction, produces for us beyond all measure, beyond human estimation, an eternal weight of glory in surpassing greatness, which will be in the future. It does so for us who do not contemplate or concern ourselves with the things that are seen, but with the things that are not seen.

He gives the reason: for the things that are seen are temporary, but the things that are not seen are eternal.

# Commentary

[Col. 0227]

[Col. 0227B] **CHAPTER IV.—1. LANFRANC. “Among those in whom the god of this age…”** As though he were saying: He who rules not only invisible creatures but also this invisible age can construct things in such a way that the god of this age has blinded the minds of the unbelievers. For if “the god of this age” is said of the devil, it is understood in the Gospel as “the prince of this world.”

**2. “For we do not preach ourselves.”** He shows that they are not walking in craftiness or adulterating the word of God, and explains why he said “of the glory of Christ” rather than “of the Gospel of our glory.”

**3. “He who said, ‘Out of darkness…’”** The reason why he preached is that God gave them knowledge through preaching.

**4. AUGUSTINE. “He himself shone forth.”** He did so in order to illuminate us, so that through the Son, who is the radiance of the Father by which we are illuminated, we might have knowledge of his glory.

**5. AMBROSE. “He shone in our hearts.”** They are illuminated so that through Christ they may have knowledge of the glory of God.

**6. AUGUSTINE (in Bede, on this chapter). “For the illumination.”** This is the knowledge of God: that we know him to be the light by which our darkness is illuminated. Observe how he repeatedly insists on this.

**7. LANFRANC. “We have this treasure.”** He says that the apostles possess the treasure of the knowledge of God’s glory in earthly bodies, so that whenever they accomplish anything profound, they may attribute it to God’s power and not to themselves.

**8. AMBROSE. “In everything afflicted.”** He now shows that they were suitable preachers: though they suffered affliction, they were not distressed—that is, not so oppressed that they gave way. They were perplexed, that is, they suffered want, and God the shepherd was present. They were struck down, that is, thrown to the ground by blows, yet were not put to death.

[Col. 0229A] **9. “Death is at work in us.”** There is no doubt that Christ is killed in the martyrs. Accordingly, the life by which Christ rose from the dead will be granted to their mortal flesh.

**10. “But life…”** He says this because he was subjected to death for their salvation, possessing the same Spirit—that is, the Spirit common to them—through whom faith is strengthened, as it is written: “I believed, and therefore I spoke.” Because he believed, he dares to preach this.

**11. AUGUSTINE (*Against Two Letters of the Pelagians*, ch. 21, vol. VII). “Having the same Spirit.”** What is “the same Spirit” except the Spirit also possessed by the righteous who spoke these words?

**12. LANFRANC. “The same spirit of faith.”** Someone might ask: “Why do you suffer?” He answers: “Because we speak about God.” “Why, then, do you speak?” “Because we believe in him.” For all who faithfully believe in him speak about him. It is written of David that he spoke for this reason: because he believed. What follows from this? “We,” he says, “have the spirit of faith that David had.”

[Col. 0229B] **13. “Everything is for your sake.”** He explains how they will be established in heaven: everything is for your sake, so that grace—that is, your faith—may abound through your example with thanksgiving, and so you may be established in heaven.

**14. AMBROSE. “For everything is for your sake.”** The apostle was not afraid to suffer persecutions and dangers so that more people might believe, and so that God’s abundant gift would not be diminished by the thanksgiving of only a few, to God’s dishonor, but would benefit many and overflow through the thanksgiving of many, to the glory of God.

[Col. 0229C] **15. LANFRANC. “Everything is for your sake.”** We suffer everything for your instruction, so that grace—that is, thanksgiving—may abound through thanksgiving offered by many and may abound to the glory of God. It is as though he were saying: We suffer for this purpose, so that you may learn from us an example of patience, give thanks to God, and be joined by many others in doing so.

# CHAPTER V

[Col. 0229]

An exposition of the preceding verse, or a proof, as follows: For we know—we groan, namely—that if our earthly house of this dwelling, that is, the body in which we dwell, is dissolved, we have

[Note: **CHAPTER V.—1. AUGUSTINE (*Expositions of Psalm 68*, in the first sermon, vol. VIII). “A building from God.”** That is, the immortality prepared for us, with which we shall be clothed at the end, when we have risen from the dead. He says: “In which we do not wish to be stripped, but to be clothed over, so that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life,” if this is possible. We would wish to become immortal in such a way that immortality itself might already come, and that, as we are now, it might invite [variant: change] us so that this mortal nature of ours might be swallowed up, rather than the body be punished through death and received again at the end. Although, therefore, we pass from evils to good things, the passage itself is nevertheless somewhat bitter.]

[Note: **2. AMBROSE. “A building.”** He signifies an immortal body, whose form already exists in heaven, revealed in the Lord’s body.]

a building from God, an immortal body, a house not made by human hands, not temporal but eternal in the heavens.

For in this dwelling also we groan—that is, desiring no other house, we groan because we wish to be there—and we long to put on our dwelling that is from heaven. We shall have the same flesh that we now have in the resurrection, but over it we shall be clothed with immortality and incorruption.

[Note: **3. “If indeed we are clothed.”** That is, if, when we depart from the body, we have put on Christ. For, having been baptized into Christ, we have put on Christ; or, if we are found worthy of the promised heavenly grace through the Holy Spirit [variant: when, having put him on, or having received the Holy Spirit given to us, we shall see him, we shall be worthy to be clothed with the promised heavenly glory].]

If indeed we are clothed with what will be put over us, and are not found naked of good works.

[Note: **4. “For we who are in the tabernacle.”** He says that we, weighed down by the sufferings of the body, direct our petitions to God, so that we may not be naked of the Holy Spirit. Then we shall be able to be clothed with glory, if, when stripped of the body, we have not been stripped of the Holy Spirit. Thus what is mortal will be swallowed up by life, so that it can no longer die or become entangled in sufferings. For it should not be said that it is swallowed up by life because it rises for the purpose of being subjected to punishment [variant: being acted upon].]

He repeats, or gives a proof by comparison: For we who are in this tabernacle, the body, groan because we are weighed down,

[Col. 0231]

since we do not wish to be stripped but to be clothed over, together with Adam, so that what is mortal may be swallowed up—that is, made immortal—by life.

Someone might say: “Who can grant this?” He answers: The one who prepares us for this very thing, so that we may be clothed with immortality, is God, who has given us the pledge of the Spirit—that is, a guarantee—because he will accomplish it.

Therefore we are confident, always confident, and always knowing that while we are in the body,

[Note: **5. “We are absent from God.”** God is everywhere, but because God’s dwelling is in heaven and he is always seen there, we who are placed here, where he is not seen, are therefore said to be absent from him.]

we are absent from the Lord—for we walk by faith and not by sight, that is, not by open vision. But we are confident, and we have the good will—that this confidence and this desire may not be objected to as impossible; he removes that objection by saying this—

[Note: **6. LANFRANC. “To be absent from the body.”** Since, he says, it cannot happen that we go to God in the body, we choose rather to be separated from the body and to be present with God.]

to be absent from the body and to be present with the Lord.

[Note: **7. AMBROSE. “And therefore we strive.”** That is, whether we are placed in this life or present before the tribunal of Christ, we may please him.]

And therefore we strive to be present with him, whether absent from the sight of human beings, or from God insofar as this is possible in this world, or present to the sight of human beings, or before God.

**Answer.**

For we must all be manifested before the tribunal of Christ,

[Note: **8. AUGUSTINE (*Letter 107, to Vitalis of Carthage, on praying for unbelievers*, vol. II). “So that each may receive.”** We shall all stand before the tribunal of Christ, so that each may receive according to what he has done through the body, not according to what he would have done had he lived longer, whether good or evil. We also know that infants will receive good or evil according to what they have done through the body. They did these things not by themselves, but through those who, acting as their sponsors, are said to renounce the devil and believe in God. Hence they too are counted among the faithful, according to the Lord’s statement: “Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved” (Mark 16).]

so that each may give an account, or first receive judgment, for what he himself has done in the body, according to his deeds, whether good or evil.

Knowing this, therefore, we persuade human beings to fear the Lord; but we are manifest before God, because we have not acted for earthly gain. I hope, however, that we are not manifest in your consciences, because we do not preach for earthly gain.

**An excuse.**

We are not commending ourselves to you again so that you may be able to boast against the false apostles on account of our ministry; rather, we give you an opportunity to boast on our behalf, so that you may have something with which to answer those who boast in appearance. Their joy is only in the presence of human beings, or their glory consists entirely in outward behavior and not in acting rightly in the heart.

[Note: **9. AUGUSTINE (*Tractate 7 on the Gospel of John*, vol. IX). “Whether we are beside ourselves.”** What does “we are beside ourselves” mean? It means that we see those things which it is not permitted for a human being to speak. What does “we are sober for you” mean? “I judged,” he says, “that I knew nothing among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified.”]

[Note: **10. LANFRANC. “We are beside ourselves.”** To be beside oneself means to be engaged in divine contemplation. He says that he does this for God, not for human praise.]

For whether we are beside ourselves—that is, whether we go beyond ourselves for the honor of God, or preach the divine mysteries—it is for God, for the praise of God;

[Note: **11. “Whether we are sober.”** The apostles were sober when they descended from the height of heavenly contemplation in order to order the life of those subject to them. He says that he does this for the benefit of those subject to him, not for human glory.]

whether we are sober,

[Note: **12. “We are sober.”** “We do it for you,” he says, because we speak about you as though commending ourselves. We do everything for your sake: whether we are beside ourselves—that is, whether we preach the deep things of divinity—and do so for the praise of God; or whether we are sober—that is, whether, interrupting divine contemplation, we order the life of those subject to us by adapting human matters to it.]

we are sober for you, adapting ourselves to you by instructing you in your ways.

For the love of Christ urges us,

[Note: **13. “Considering this.”** We judge, he says, that if Christ died for all, then all human beings ought to die for his honor.]

# Commentary

[Col. 0229]

[Col. 0229A] **CHAPTER V.—1. AUGUSTINE (*Expositions of Psalm 68*, in the first sermon, vol. VIII). “A building from God.”** That is, the immortality prepared for us, with which we shall be clothed at the end, when we have risen from the dead. He says: “In which we do not wish to be stripped, but to be clothed over, so that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life,” if this is possible. We would wish to become immortal in such a way that immortality itself might already come, and that, as we are now, it might invite [variant: change] us so that this mortal nature of ours might be swallowed up, rather than the body be punished through death and received again at the end. Although, therefore, we pass from evils to good things, the passage itself is nevertheless somewhat bitter.

[Col. 0230B] **2. AMBROSE. “A building.”** He signifies an immortal body, whose form already exists in heaven, revealed in the Lord’s body.

**3. “If indeed we are clothed.”** That is, if, when we depart from the body, we have put on Christ. For, having been baptized into Christ, we have put on Christ; or, if we are found worthy of the promised heavenly grace through the Holy Spirit [variant: when, having put him on, or having received the Holy Spirit given to us, we shall see him, we shall be worthy to be clothed with the promised heavenly glory].

**4. “For we who are in the tabernacle.”** He says that we, weighed down by the sufferings of the body, direct our petitions to God, so that we may not be naked of the Holy Spirit. Then we shall be able to be clothed with glory, if, when stripped of the body, we have not been stripped of the Holy Spirit. Thus what is mortal will be swallowed up by life, so that it can no longer die or become entangled in sufferings; for it should not be said that it is swallowed up by life because it rises for the purpose of being subjected to punishment [variant: being acted upon].

[Col. 0231A] **5. “We are absent from God.”** God is everywhere, but because God’s dwelling is in heaven and he is always seen there, we who are placed here, where he is not seen, are therefore said to be absent from him.

**6. LANFRANC. “To be absent from the body.”** Since, he says, it cannot happen that we go to God in the body, we choose rather to be separated from the body and to be present with God.

**7. AMBROSE. “And therefore we strive.”** That is, whether we are placed in this life or present before the tribunal of Christ, we may please him.

**8. AUGUSTINE (*Letter 107, to Vitalis of Carthage, on praying for unbelievers*, vol. II). “So that each may receive.”** We shall all stand before the tribunal of Christ, so that each may receive according to what he has done through the body, not according to what he would have done had he lived longer, whether good or evil. We also know that infants will receive good or evil according to what they have done through the body. They did these things not by themselves, but through those who, acting as their sponsors, are said to renounce the devil and believe in God. Hence they too are counted among the faithful, according to the Lord’s statement: “Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved” (Mark 16).

**9. AUGUSTINE (*Tractate 7 on the Gospel of John*, vol. IX). “Whether we are beside ourselves.”** What does “we are beside ourselves” mean? It means that we see those things which it is not permitted for a human being to speak. What does “we are sober for you” mean? “I judged,” he says, “that I knew nothing among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified.”

[Col. 0231C] **10. LANFRANC. “We are beside ourselves.”** To be beside oneself means to be engaged in divine contemplation. He says that he does this for God, not for human praise.

**11. “Whether we are sober.”** The apostles were sober when they descended from the height of heavenly contemplation in order to order the life of those subject to them. He says that he does this for the benefit of those subject to him, not for human glory.

[Col. 0232A] **12. “We are sober.”** “We do it for you,” he says, because we speak about you as though commending ourselves. We do everything for your sake: whether we are beside ourselves—that is, whether we preach the deep things of divinity—and do so for the praise of God; or whether we are sober—that is, whether, interrupting divine contemplation, we order the life of those subject to us by adapting human matters to it.

**13. “Considering this.”** We judge, he says, that if Christ died for all, then all human beings ought to die for his honor.

**14. “And Christ died for all.”** Since Christ died for all, we approve no one who lives according to the flesh. And if the apostle knew Christ according to the flesh before he believed in Christ, he knew him according to the flesh because he regarded him as merely human.

[Col. 0232B] **15. “Therefore you.”** That is, because Christ died for all, so that all might die for his honor. From this consideration we know—that is, approve—no one who lives according to the flesh, seeking his own interests and not the things of Jesus Christ.

**16. AUGUSTINE (*Book II against Faustus*, ch. 7, vol. VI). “From now on, no one.”** “Therefore from now on we know no one according to the flesh.” He says this because he considers their future life with him as though it were already present, since those who rise will be transformed. “From now on,” he says, “we know no one according to the flesh,” that is, we hold so firm a hope of our future incorporation and immortality that we already rejoice in that knowledge.

[Col. 0233A] **17. LANFRANC. “And if we have known.”** Before the apostle believed in Christ, he had known him according to the flesh, because he regarded him merely as a human being.

**18. AUGUSTINE (the preceding passage). “According to the flesh.”** In this passage he does not mean the very substance of our body, which the Lord calls flesh after his resurrection, saying: “Touch me and see, because a spirit does not have flesh and bones as you see that I have.” Rather, he wishes the corruption and mortality of the flesh to be understood—something that will not then exist in us, just as it no longer exists in Christ.

**19. (The same work, ch. 8). “If anyone is therefore.”** Every new creation—that is, the people—is renewed through faith, so that for the present it may possess in hope what will later be perfected in reality. In Christ it already possesses what it hopes for in itself. Thus the old things have passed away according to hope, because now it is no longer the time of the Old Testament, in which a temporal and carnal kingdom is expected from God. All things have become new according to the same hope, so that we may hold the promise of the kingdom of heaven, where there will be neither death nor corruption.

[Col. 0233B] **20. AMBROSE. “But all things are from God.”** Although Christ redeemed us, nevertheless all things are from God.

**21. AUGUSTINE (*Expositions of Psalm 68*, sermon 1, vol. VIII). “For indeed God was.”** “God,” he says, “was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself,” because the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, so that not only was God in him, but he himself was also God.

**22. AUGUSTINE (*Tractate 41 on John*, before the middle, vol. IX). “We beseech you on behalf of Christ.”** “We beseech,” he says, “on behalf of Christ,” that is, as though Christ himself were beseeching you. What does he beseech? “Be reconciled to God.”

**23. AMBROSE. “We beseech.”** He beseeches for this reason: so that through some negligence the grace of the remedy may not be deprived of its effect, since the time is present when medicine can be infused into mortal diseases.

**24. AUGUSTINE (*Book I against the Adversary of the Law and the Prophets*, ch. 14, vol. VI). “The one who did not know sin.”** He knew it through wisdom, but did not know it through experience.

**25. AUGUSTINE (*Enchiridion to Laurentius*, ch. 41, vol. III). “He made him sin for us.”** This means a sacrifice for sins, through which we might be reconciled. He is therefore sin, just as we are righteousness—not our own righteousness, but God’s; not in ourselves, but in God. In the same way, he was sin—not his own, but ours—not constituted in himself, but in us. He indicated the likeness of sinful flesh in which he was crucified. This is that righteousness of God—not the righteousness by which he himself is righteous, but the righteousness by which we are made righteous by him.

**26. LANFRANC. “He made him sin.”** The order is: God the Father made Christ “sin,” that is, a sacrifice for sin, so that we might be made the righteousness of God in him—that is, in the faith of Jesus Christ.

Do not enter into an unequal yoke with unbelievers—that is, do not become like unbelievers. For what partnership does righteousness have with iniquity? Or what fellowship does light have with darkness? And what agreement does Christ have with Belial? Or what share does a believer have with an unbeliever? And what agreement does the temple of God have with idols?

[Col. 0234]

[Col. 0234B] CHAPTER VI.—1. LANFRANC. “The grace of God.” He calls the remission of sins “the grace of God”; whoever afterward does not exercise himself in good works receives it in vain.

2. “For he says.” In Isaiah he speaks thus: “At an acceptable time I heard you, and on the day of salvation I helped you.”

3. “At an acceptable time,” etc. Someone might say: “Is the grace of God then something?” It is, because the Lord’s hearing and helping at an acceptable time is grace. He proves this by its effect, because God hears and helps. He also proves it by authority: for God himself said, “At an acceptable time,” etc.

[Col. 0234C] 4. AMBROSE. “Giving no one any cause for offense.” By his vigilance he removes every occasion of offense, so that his ministry may not be blamed; for it would be blamed if he did not complete in his works what he taught.

[Col. 0235A] 5. “In riots.” He was so devoted to God that not even a riot diminished the confidence he had in God.

6. “In labors.” For he worked with his hands, so that he would not be burdensome to anyone.

7. AMBROSE. “In long-suffering.” He was great-hearted in bearing the weaknesses of the brethren.

8. “In the power of God.” There was in him a power which, through signs and wonders, proved him to be an able minister.

9. “Through the weapons of righteousness.” He indicates that he remained free among believers and unbelievers: to those who considered the Gospel a glory and to those who considered it disgrace, to those who gave the faith a good reputation and to those who gave it a bad one, he showed himself upright and steadfast.

10. AUGUSTINE (*Exposition on Psalm 93*, vol. VIII). “Through weapons.” The malice of the wicked is the left-hand weapon of the righteous, just as he says elsewhere: “Through the weapons of righteousness, on the right and on the left,” that is, through glory and disgrace; and so he proceeds to explain everything that follows. He shows the right-hand weapons as glory, good reputation, and truth: that they were known [variant *qua*, “by which,” for *quod*, “that”], that they saw, that they were not put to death, that they rejoiced, that they enriched many, and that they possessed all things. The left-hand weapons were that they were regarded as obscure and of bad reputation, that they were thought to be deceivers, that they were unknown, killed, restrained, saddened, in need, and apparently possessing nothing.

11. LANFRANC. “Through the weapons.” Through the weapons of righteousness, if we are armed in prosperity and adversity, and whether we are regarded as glorious or worthless, infamous or of good reputation.

[Col. 0235C] 12. “On the right and on the left.” Let us present ourselves—that is, as those who are to be regarded as God’s ministers—having righteousness as though it were a balance, so that we do not incline to this side or that: that is, so that we are not broken by adversity or lifted up by prosperity.

13. “Disgrace.” Through glory let us present ourselves as God’s ministers, so that we are not exalted; and through disgrace, [Col. 0236A] that is, lowliness, if we are regarded as worthless, so that we are not broken.

14. “As deceivers.” As though he were saying: “It is not surprising if we are blamed and praised, because some think us deceivers and others truthful; some recognize us and others do not,” and so forth in what follows.

15. “Our mouth is open to you.” He rebukes their avarice and says that they did not receive from him an example of greed, because his heart was broad and enlarged in giving.

16. AMBROSE. “Our mouth is open to you.” He says this on account of freedom and a clear conscience. A mind conscious of evil fears to speak, loses its meaning, and errs in its words.

17. “You are not restricted.” He says that this was not to be attributed to the teachers if the disciples made bad use of things, because he had not kept silent about what concerned the teachers.

18. LANFRANC. “You are not restricted.” That is, in us you do not see an example of narrowness and greed; rather, the fuel of this vice is in your own inward parts.

19. “I speak as to children.” The order is: “I speak as to children, having the same recompense,” namely, the recompense that we have.

20. “For you are the temple.” He proves that entering into a yoke with unbelievers is equivalent to this. No temple of God ought to have agreement with idols; but you are the temple, because God himself dwells in you. For he said: “I will dwell in you.” Therefore, “come out from their midst,” that is, do not enter into a yoke with unbelievers. He uses the prophet’s words [Col. 0236C] as his own.

21. “For I will dwell.” Joel also says: “I will set my tabernacle among them, and I will be their God, and they will be my people” (Joel 2:27).

22. “Therefore come out.” In Isaiah it is read thus: “Depart, depart, come out from there; do not touch what is unclean” (Isa. 52:11).

CHAPTER VII.

[Col. 0237]

Since we have these promises—that he will receive us if we do not touch what is unclean—beloved, let us cleanse ourselves from every defilement of flesh and spirit, that is, from carnal vice and spiritual wickedness, perfecting our sanctification in the fear of God, that is, perfecting those things by which we may be made holy. Make room for us through our admonition.

[Note: [Col. 0237A] CHAPTER VII.—1. AMBROSE. “We have wronged no one.” For the false apostles were harming them by corrupting their minds through cunning deception.]

We have wronged no one, as the false apostles did, by devouring the goods of those subject to us; we have corrupted no one by our evil example; we have deceived no one by flattery.

[Note: [Col. 0237A] 2. LANFRANC. “Not for condemnation,” that is, I do not mention this in order craftily to say that you did what I deny having done.]

I do not say this for your condemnation; I do not say this as though you had done harm in any of these ways, so that I might condemn you.

[Note: [Col. 0237A] 4. AMBROSE. “In our hearts,” that is, he wishes them to share both in present sufferings for Christ [Col. 0237B] and in future life.]

[Note: [Col. 0237B] 5. “I have great confidence.” This confidence arises from the correction in the First Epistle; because they did not receive it harshly, they gave him confidence to admonish them.]

I have great confidence in you; I have much reason to boast about you before others; I am filled with consolation because of you; I abound exceedingly in joy amid all our tribulation.

For when we came into Macedonia, our flesh had no rest, but we suffered every tribulation, [Note: [Col. 0237B] 6. “Battles outside.” The battles were against the body, while it was being beaten; the fears were against the mind. For fear exists where there is understanding. But this fear concerned the believers, lest they should be scandalized by his suffering.] battles outside from unbelievers, or in my own body, [Note: [Col. 0237B] 7. LANFRANC. “Fears within.” From false brothers; or, lest my suffering terrify the brethren—that is, fearing lest those newly converted, seeing our affliction, should turn to their former way: the Jew to Judaism, and the Gentile to paganism.] fears within.

But God, who comforts the humble, comforted us by the arrival of Titus. And not only by his arrival, but also by the consolation with which he was comforted among you, [Note: [Col. 0237B] 8. AMBROSE. “Reporting to us.” Titus announced that they desired to reform themselves, were weeping because they had sinned, and were showing zeal for the Apostle, because, having learned his love for them, they had begun to defend him against his adversaries [Col. 0238A].] when he reported to us your longing to see me, your weeping in repentance, and your zeal for me, [Note: [Col. 0238A] 9. LANFRANC. “Your zeal,” that is, how one emulates another’s desire, so that you may see me.] as you learned either love for me or imitation of me, so that, from the sending of the Epistle or from the things mentioned above, I rejoiced all the more.

For even if I saddened you by the earlier Epistle, I do not now regret it; and although I had previously regretted it, when I saw that the earlier Epistle saddened you (although only for a time), now I rejoice—not because you were saddened, but because you were saddened unto repentance.

[Note: [Col. 0238A] 10. “That Epistle.” The order is: “That Epistle saddened you, although only for a time.”]

[Note: [Col. 0238A] 11. “For you were saddened.” This indicates which repentance he is speaking about; for there is also a bad repentance.]

For you were saddened according to God, so that in nothing you might suffer loss [Note: [Col. 0238A] 12. “Loss.” The hearer suffers loss from the teacher’s preaching when he is disobedient to the teacher’s commands and adds the sin of disobedience to his earlier sin], from us—that is, so that you would suffer no loss of soul in the future because of our commands not being fulfilled.

[Note: [Col. 0238A] 13. AMBROSE. “Loss,” that is, so that all our efforts may have their effect in you, including the fact that we saddened you [Col. 0238B].]

For sorrow according to God produces repentance leading to steadfast, eternal salvation; [Note: [Col. 0238B] 14. LANFRANC. “For the sorrow according to God.” This is another reason why they were saddened according to God.] but worldly sorrow, by contrast, produces death.

[Note: [Col. 0238B] 15. “But worldly sorrow.” Worldly sorrow is to grieve that one gives away what is one’s own and does not seize what belongs to another, and other things of this kind.]

For behold, this very thing—that you were saddened according to God— [Note: [Col. 0238B] 16. “For behold.” This is another argument concerning the same matter.] produces in you great diligence in doing good, that is, salvation.

[Note: [Col. 0238B] 17. AMBROSE. “What diligence in you.” They are anxious lest they sin again and defend themselves against the assaults of demons; they grow indignant at themselves or fear others who sin, because they have sinned; they desire to reform themselves and begin to feel zeal for completing good works; and what they did wrong, they punish in themselves.]

For it produces diligence—which is the cause of salvation—and not only this, but also defense against God; and not only this, but indignation at sins; [Col. 0239] and not only this, but fear of God; and not only this, but also desire for reform; and not only this, but also zeal for what is good; and not only this, but also vengeance, the affliction of sins.

Therefore, because you have done both this and that, you have shown yourselves in every other good work to be undefiled in the matter, [Note: [Col. 0239A] 18. LANFRANC. “To be undefiled in the matter.” In this matter he commanded vengeance against the man who had taken his father’s wife.] since you excluded the fornicator.

[Note: [Col. 0239A] 19. AMBROSE. “Therefore, although I wrote to you.” He shows that he wrote chiefly for the sake of the Church: when one acts wickedly, many are put to shame; and when one suffers insult, many grow indignant. By correcting the unjust, sanctifying the defiled, and reconciling the churches, he demonstrates that he bears upon himself concern for the entire people.]

Therefore, although I wrote to you, it was not merely for the sake of the one who did the wrong—that is, the one who took his father’s wife—nor for the sake of the one who suffered the wrong—that is, the father whose wife was taken away; rather, I wrote to make manifest our concern for you, which we have before God because of your corruption, so that it might please God.

[Note: [Col. 0239A] 20. LANFRANC. “Therefore we were comforted.” Both because of the arrival of Titus and because of your good zeal.]

Therefore, because you were undefiled, we were comforted. And in our consolation we rejoiced even more abundantly over the joy of Titus, because his spirit was refreshed by all of you through your spiritual conversion for the good.

And if I have boasted about you to him, speaking boastfully about you, I was not put to shame—that is, I did not lie; but just as we spoke everything truthfully to you, so also our boasting before Titus proved true, and his affections became more abundant toward you as he remembered the obedience of you all—namely, how you received him with fear of mind and trembling of body.

[Note: [Col. 0239A] 21. “Before him, about you.” The Apostle boasted before Titus about the Corinthians, saying that they were kind.]

I rejoice that I have confidence in you in everything.

[COMMENTARY.]

[Col. 0237]

[Col. 0237A] CHAPTER VII.—1. AMBROSE. “We have wronged no one.” For the false apostles were harming them by corrupting their minds through cunning deception.

2. LANFRANC. “Not for condemnation,” that is, I do not mention this in order craftily to say that you did what I deny having done.

3. “We said before.” Above he said: “You are our letter, written in our hearts.”

4. AMBROSE. “In our hearts,” that is, he wishes them to share both in present sufferings for Christ [Col. 0237B] and in future life.

5. “I have great confidence.” This confidence arises from the correction in the First Epistle; because they did not receive it harshly, they gave him confidence to admonish them.

6. “Battles outside.” The battles were against the body, while it was being beaten; the fears were against the mind. For fear exists where there is understanding. But this fear concerned the believers, lest they should be scandalized by his suffering.

7. LANFRANC. “Fears within.” From false brothers; or, lest my suffering terrify the brethren—that is, fearing lest those newly converted, seeing our affliction, should turn to their former way: the Jew to Judaism, and the Gentile to paganism.

8. AMBROSE. “Reporting to us.” Titus announced that they desired to reform themselves, were weeping because they had sinned, and were showing zeal for the Apostle, because, having learned his love for them, they had begun to defend him against his adversaries [Col. 0238A].

9. LANFRANC. “Your zeal,” that is, how one emulates another’s desire, so that you may see me.

10. “That Epistle.” The order is: “That Epistle saddened you, although only for a time.”

11. “For you were saddened.” This indicates which repentance he is speaking about; for there is also a bad repentance.

12. “Loss.” The hearer suffers loss from the teacher’s preaching when he is disobedient to the teacher’s commands and adds the sin of disobedience to his earlier sin.

13. AMBROSE. “Loss,” that is, so that all our efforts may have their effect in you, including the fact that we saddened you [Col. 0238B].

14. LANFRANC. “For the sorrow according to God.” This is another reason why they were saddened according to God.

15. “But worldly sorrow.” Worldly sorrow is to grieve that one gives away what is one’s own and does not seize what belongs to another, and other things of this kind.

16. “For behold.” This is another argument concerning the same matter.

17. AMBROSE. “What diligence in you.” They are anxious lest they sin again and defend themselves against the assaults of demons; they grow indignant at themselves or fear others who sin, because they have sinned; they desire to reform themselves and begin to feel zeal for completing good works; and what they did wrong, they punish in themselves.

[Col. 0239A] 18. LANFRANC. “To be undefiled in the matter.” In this matter he commanded vengeance against the man who had taken his father’s wife.

19. AMBROSE. “Therefore, although I wrote to you.” He shows that he wrote chiefly for the sake of the Church: when one acts wickedly, many are put to shame; and when one suffers insult, many grow indignant. By correcting the unjust, sanctifying the defiled, and reconciling the churches, he demonstrates that he bears upon himself concern for the entire people.

20. LANFRANC. “Therefore we were comforted.” Both because of the arrival of Titus and because of your good zeal.

21. “Before him, about you.” The Apostle boasted before Titus about the Corinthians, saying that they were kind.

[Col. 0239B] 22. “Everything about you,” that is, just as we spoke truthfully to you about others, so we spoke truthfully to Titus about you.

CHAPTER VIII.

[Col. 0239]

He exhorts them to generosity by the example of the Macedonians. “We make known to you, brothers, the grace of God that has been bestowed in the churches of Macedonia” (he is speaking of the collection that the Macedonians had given to the saints in Jerusalem), “that amid much testing, in an abundance of affliction, their joy was abundant”—that is, while they were suffering greatly for Christ, they rejoiced in this very thing—“and their deepest, greatest, or exalting poverty abounded into the riches of their simplicity,” that is, of their generosity; or, “abounded into a rich simplicity”: the poor man gave as willingly as if he were rich. “For,” that is, I testify concerning them, “according to their ability,” that is, according to the truth of the matter, “I bear them witness, and beyond their ability they were willing, with much exhortation, begging us” for the grace—namely, the grace they would give to the saints in Jerusalem—“and participation in the ministry” or administration “that is performed for the saints.” And they did not give merely as we had hoped, but gave themselves by faith, first to the Lord, then to us, to do whatever we wished, according to the will of God. Thus they urged us to ask Titus that, just as he had begun, so also by his preaching he might complete among you this grace—that is, this generosity—so that you might be like the Macedonians and, as on other occasions, give this grace as well.

But just as in all things I did not ask him alone, so I also ask you: abound in this grace, just as you abound in all things—in faith, in speech, in knowledge of the Gospel, in every diligence, and, moreover, in your love for us—so that you may abound in this grace also.

[Note: [Col. 0240A] 1. AMBROSE. “Their deepest poverty.” Although their material resources were meager, their spirit was found to be rich, so that they offered with tears and thus compelled others to accept from them what did not seem to be acceptable, because it was more than their means could provide.]

I do not speak as one commanding, but—by the diligence of others, that is, of the Macedonians or of other saints—I commend and prove the character, zeal, and goodness of your love. You ought to do this, and he gives the reason:

[Note: [Col. 0240A] 2. LANFRANC. “Their poverty.” They were poor in earthly possessions, but rich in simplicity and kindness.]

“For you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ: although he was rich, for your sake he became poor, so that through his poverty you might become rich.”

[Note: [Col. 0240A] 3. “Testimony.” The order is: “I bear witness to them before others, because it was according to their ability.”]

And I give advice in this matter so that you may act, for this is useful for you. You began last year not only to do what good you could, but also to desire what good you could not do. Now complete that desire by your deed, so that just as the readiness of your will is present, so also the readiness to carry it out may be present according to what you have.

[Note: [Col. 0240A] 4. “Begging us.” That is, they begged me to permit them to make a contribution and share from their possessions in this almsgiving, which is made for the saints who are in Jerusalem.]

See why it is acceptable to God if it is done willingly:

[Note: [Col. 0240A] 5. “So that we might ask Titus.” “We were so moved,” he says, “by their generosity that we asked Titus, so that, just as he began by his preaching and exhortation, he might complete this grace—that is, this generosity—among you.”]

“For if the will is ready to act according to what one has, it is acceptable to God, not according to what one does not have.”

[Note: [Col. 0240A] 6. AMBROSE. “But through that of others.” He exhorts them to send resources to those suffering want and, through the diligence that they reveal, to show their good disposition.]

For I do not command that there be relief for others from our resources and refreshment, while you are brought to exhaustion and tribulation; rather, I say that it should be according to equality.

[Note: [Col. 0240B] 7. LANFRANC. “For you know the grace.” As if he were saying: “For the love of Christ you ought willingly to give, because he who was rich became poor for your sake.”]

At the present time, let your abundance supply their need, so that in turn the abundance of their merits may be a provision for your need in the future.

[Note: [Col. 0240B] 8. AMBROSE. “For if the will.” Since the Corinthians are urged toward this work, they are instructed not to give more than they can, lest, by offering more than they can afford, they appear compelled rather than willing and thus remain without reward; for one who does something under compulsion has no reward.]

Thus let there now and then be equality, sufficiency for you and for them, as it is written in Exodus 16:

[Note: [Col. 0241A] 9. LANFRANC. “According to what he has,” and so forth. Or one gives according to what he does not have who gives four solidi out of five; this is what should be done by one who has ten pounds or something similar. Someone might say: “It is not enough if they give according to what they have; for those Macedonians gave more than their means could bear.” He answers this with: “For if …” The meaning is: Whoever wishes to give according to what he has is acceptable to God, not merely the one who wishes to do more than he has. Or it may be understood this way: The ready will to do more than one can, according to what one wishes, is acceptable, not merely according to what one can.]

“He who gathered much did not have more, and he who gathered little did not have less.”

[Note: [Col. 0241B] 10. AMBROSE. “But according to equality.” More is not required than they ought to retain for themselves, because, as he says, “You shall love your neighbor as yourself.”]

[Note: [Col. 0241B] 11. “Your abundance.” That is, those who have resources should minister to the needs of the saints, so that later the saints, where they are rich while these are needy, may share with them, as if returning the service they received.]

[Note: [Col. 0241B] 12. “So that there may be equality.” This is equality: since these people minister to the saints in the present time, they will repay them in the future [variant: “will be repaid”].]

[Note: [Col. 0241B] 13. “He who gathered much did not.” The saints have more in hope of the future age than those who appear rich in the present age; nevertheless, there the two will be made equal, so that just as the need of the saints is sustained by the benefit of these people, so by the benefit of the saints those who appear poor in this age may become rich in the future age.]

“He who gathered much”—namely, from the manna—“did not have more,” and he who gathered little “did not have less.” Thus, whoever has gathered much money in the present, as the Corinthians have, should not keep it for himself alone, but should distribute it to others.

[Note: [Col. 0240A] 14. LANFRANC. “He who gathered much.” The one who had often gathered much—that is, more than a gomor—did not have an excess; that is, he had no more than a gomor. Likewise, the one who gathered little had less than a gomor. In Exodus, however, it is written thus: “Nor did the one who had gathered more have anything extra; nor did the one who had prepared less find anything lacking.”]

As for what he said, “We asked Titus”: I give thanks to God, who placed in Titus’s heart the same concern that I have for you. For when he first heard my exhortation, he received it willingly, and not only did he hear it, but, being even more concerned, he went to you of his own accord.

We also sent with him our brother Barnabas, whose praise in the Gospel is throughout all the churches. And not only does he have praise in the Gospel—that is, he is not only distinguished in preaching—but he was also appointed by the churches, by the faithful of the Church—that is, by the apostles—as our companion in travel, so that he might carry with me this grace of the collection, which is administered by us for the glory of the Lord.

[Note: [Col. 0242A] 15. “By us for the glory of the Lord.” The order is: “The grace destined by us for the glory of the Lord and according to our will.”]

I speak of a grace destined according to our will.

[Note: [Col. 0242A] 16. “Avoiding this.” As if he were saying: “For this reason we sent a brother of good reputation with Titus, so that no one might reproach us concerning this alms, saying that we retain some of it for our own work.” The word “Epistle” is redundant, or it may properly be understood as enclosed in parentheses.]

We are “avoiding this,” so that no one may reproach us concerning this abundance that is administered and carried to the saints by us, for the glory of the Lord, so that they may devote themselves to God. For this reason we send them.

[Note: [Col. 0242B] 17. AMBROSE. “Avoiding this.” He added this so that he would not be judged negligent in caring for the saints if he carried out this work too sluggishly.]

[Note: [Col. 0242B] 18. “We provide what is good.” He provides what is good before God when he teaches that what God commands concerning the ministries of the saints should be done before human beings, because he sends men of such character to exhort them to this work that, by their integrity, they do not cause scandal.]

[Note: [Col. 0242B] 19. LANFRANC. “We provide what is good.” “For this reason,” he says, “we sent them, lest our ministry be reproached, with people thinking us thieves when they see so many good men to whom the money is entrusted. Or we send so many for this reason, lest we be accused of neglecting the matter by sending only one and lest that one be thought a thief or negligent. It is good for us to avoid being the cause of their bad opinion. This is what he says: ‘We provide what is good …’”]

For we provide what is good not only before God—which would be the case if the Apostle alone carried the money, for perhaps they would not trust him, even though he defrauded nothing—but also before human beings.

We also sent with them our brother Timothy, whom we have often proved to be concerned in many matters, but now much more concerned, having great confidence in you.

[Note: [Col. 0242C] 20. “On behalf of Titus.” He says that the brother whom he was sending had great confidence in them because they had treated Titus and the other apostles well.]

Or he is concerned on behalf of Titus, who is my companion and your helper; or he is concerned on behalf of our brothers, the apostles of the churches—perhaps certain apostles were commending them by reporting their good qualities—the glory of Christ, by whom Christ is glorified in the churches.

For they are such men. Therefore, among those whom we are sending to you, show the proof of your love and of our glory concerning you. Their love is the Apostle’s glory. Show your love toward those whom we are sending; receive them with affection before the churches, so that you may be an example.

[COMMENTARY]

[Col. 0239]

[Col. 0239B] CHAPTER VIII.—1. AMBROSE. “Their deepest poverty.” Although their material resources were meager, their spirit was found to be rich, so that they offered with tears and thus compelled others to accept from them what did not seem to be acceptable, because it was more than their means could provide.

2. LANFRANC. “Their poverty.” They were poor in earthly possessions, but rich in simplicity and kindness.

3. “Testimony.” The order is: “I bear witness to them before others, because it was according to their ability.”

4. “Begging us.” That is, they begged me to permit them to make a contribution and share from their possessions in this almsgiving, which is made for the saints who are in Jerusalem.
