[Col. 0243A] 21. “The proof.” “In those whom we are sending to you,” he says, “show what love you have and how good your glorying on our behalf is.”

107 CHAPTER IX.

[Col. 0243]

Response. I wrote to you about receiving them, not about the collection; for concerning the ministry that is performed for the saints, it is superfluous for me to write to you at length. Here is why.

I know your readiness, for which I boast of you among the Macedonians. By mentioning the Macedonians, the Apostle says that Achaia is prepared, so that the Corinthians may be found prepared there as well.

[Note: [Col. 0243A] CHAPTER IX.—1. AMBROSE. “Because Achaia is prepared.” After mentioning the Macedonians, he says that Achaia is prepared; then he says that the Corinthians should become prepared.]

For Achaia has been ready since last year, and your emulation has stirred up very many. But I sent the brothers mentioned above so that our boasting about you—that is, our boasting of you among the Macedonians—might not be emptied in this matter, in the matter of reporting the contribution; in other words, as I said, so that you might be ready. Otherwise, when the Macedonians come with me and find you unprepared,

[Note: [Col. 0243A] 2. LANFRANC. “That we may be ashamed of you.” “If you are unprepared,” he says, “we shall have shame in this matter,” that is, in this almsgiving; you perhaps will not.]

we would be ashamed of this confidence in which we have boasted about you, not to say that you would be ashamed in this matter, this contribution—which would be the case if you had not prepared it.

And so that we may not be ashamed with you, I considered it necessary to ask the brothers to go to you beforehand

[Note: [Col. 0243A] 3. “And prepare.” The order is: “So that they may prepare this promised blessing to be ready”—that is, so that it may be given willingly as a blessing, not unwillingly as greed. For they had promised the Apostle that they would prepare the alms in this way: as a blessing, not as greed. The reading may perhaps be “with blessing, not with greed.”]

and prepare it—have you prepare this promised blessing, this monetary gift, so that it may be ready, given willingly as a blessing and not as greed, that is, not given unwillingly.

I say this because you ought not to give greedily. For “he who sows sparingly gives greedily,” sparingly, almost nothing, “and he will reap” sparingly; but he who sows gives joyfully “with blessings,” with generosity, and will reap from blessings.

[Note: [Col. 0243B] 4. AMBROSE. “He who sows with blessings.” He sows with blessings who does this with good will in the hope of future recompense.]

Therefore, let each person give according to what he has determined in his heart, whether much or little, not from sadness or necessity—that is, compulsion—but with joy; for God loves a cheerful giver.

And do not fear that you will be exhausted. For God is able to make every grace, spiritual and bodily, abound in you. Someone might say: “If I give what I have, afterward I shall be in need.” He therefore adds: “God is able to make every grace abound,” that is, to grant justification and an abundance of resources, so that, always having every bodily and spiritual sufficiency in all things, you may abound in every good work, as it is written in Psalm 3: “He scattered; he gave to the poor;”

[Note: [Col. 0243B] 5. “His righteousness remains.” The righteous person is one who does not keep for himself alone what has been given to everyone.]

“his righteousness remains forever and ever.” The description is used in place of the thing described.

[Note: [Col. 0244A] 6. LANFRANC. “He who supplies seed.” That is, the one who gives you the means by which you may perform almsgiving will give you the means by which, after the alms have been given, you may sustain yourselves. Nevertheless, because he multiplies the seed and causes the crops to grow, it will not be diminished on this account.]

“He who supplies seed to the sower and bread”—an abundance of resources for eating—“will supply and multiply your seed,” once it has been given, “and increase the fruits of your righteousness,” that is, good works by which you may be justified,

[Note: [Col. 0244A] 7. AMBROSE. “And he will multiply.” He adds “to the giver,” so that he may have still more from which to give.]

so that in all things, richly supplied, you may abound in every simplicity, which produces thanksgiving to God through us. That is, our ministry, through the operation of your simplicity, produces thanksgiving to God.

For the ministry—that is, the administration of giving—of this service of your simplicity

[Note: [Col. 0244A] 8. LANFRANC. “It not only supplies what is lacking.” He says that four things are accomplished through the administration of this service, that is, this benefit. The necessities of the saints who are in Jerusalem are supplied from it; many others, approving this ministry, give thanks to God; and many, stirred by the example of the Corinthians, give abundant gifts both to those saints who are in Jerusalem and to many others. When they see the Corinthians also, because of the surpassing grace they possess, they earnestly pray for them.]

not only supplies what the saints lack—it is a provision for the saints’ need—but also abounds through many thanksgivings to the Lord. That is, because you supply the saints’ need, many give thanks to God through the commendation of this ministry, that is, of our work and your generosity. I say that they glorify God through many people in obedience, because of the obedience that you have in the Gospel through our preaching,

[Col. 0245] of your confession, whether for confessing Christ, or for the praise of God, or for confessing your sins, in the Gospel of Christ. Your simplicity—that is, your generosity—in sharing with them and with everyone also abounds, as does their prayer for you, for they desire and love you because of the surpassing grace of God that is in you.

Therefore, “I give thanks”—or “we give thanks”—to God for his unspeakable gift, that is, a gift that ought to be proclaimed, or a gift worthy of proclamation.

[COMMENTARY]

[Col. 0243]

[Col. 0243A] CHAPTER IX.—1. AMBROSE. “Because Achaia is prepared.” After mentioning the Macedonians, he says that Achaia is prepared; then he says that the Corinthians should become prepared.

2. LANFRANC. “That we may be ashamed of you.” “If you are unprepared,” he says, “we shall have shame in this matter,” that is, in this almsgiving; you perhaps will not.

3. “And prepare.” The order is: “So that they may prepare this promised blessing to be ready”—that is, so that it may be given willingly as a blessing, not unwillingly as greed. For they had promised the Apostle that they would prepare the alms in this way: as a blessing, not as greed. The reading may perhaps be “with blessing, not with greed.”

4. AMBROSE. “He who sows with blessings.” He sows with blessings who does this with good will in the hope of future recompense.

5. “His righteousness remains.” The righteous person is one who does not keep for himself alone what has been given to everyone.

6. LANFRANC. “He who supplies seed.” That is, the one who gives you the means by which you may perform almsgiving will give you the means by which, after the alms have been given, you may sustain yourselves. Nevertheless, because he multiplies the seed and causes the crops to grow, it will not be diminished on this account.

7. AMBROSE. “And he will multiply.” He adds “to the giver,” so that he may have still more from which to give.

8. LANFRANC. “It not only supplies what is lacking.” He says that four things are accomplished through the administration of this service, that is, this benefit. The necessities of the saints who are in Jerusalem are supplied from it; many others, approving this ministry, give thanks to God; and many, stirred by the example of the Corinthians, give abundant gifts both to those saints who are in Jerusalem and to many others. When they see the Corinthians also, because of the surpassing grace they possess, they earnestly pray for them.

9. “Into obedience,” that is, because, while he was preaching the Gospel of Christ to you, you immediately became obedient to confessing Christ.

CHAPTER X.

[Col. 0245]

But I myself, Paul, appeal to you by the gentleness and modesty of Christ. He is responding to those who said that, when present, he spoke humbly, but when absent, he threatened; he appeals by that virtue which he wishes to possess among them.

I, who am humble in appearance when present among you—this is irony—but when absent I am confident toward you, confidently accusing you. I ask you, then, to live in such a way that, when present, I may not dare

[Note: [Col. 0245A] CHAPTER X.—1. LANFRANC. “May I dare.” The order is: “May I dare against certain persons,” that is, “may I inflict some trouble upon certain of you.”]

to act with that confidence

[Note: [Col. 0245A] 2. AMBROSE. “By that confidence.” Confidence signifies the assurance of severity, which he was thought to possess only in the Epistle. Therefore he warns them not to expect him to use the same severity when present, as they had not expected.]

that is, with that boldness—which is thought to characterize me when absent—against certain people who suppose that we walk according to the flesh, that is, that we love carnal things.

For although we walk in the flesh—that is, although we exist in the flesh; this is not meant negatively—we do not wage war according to the flesh, that is, we do not love carnal things.

[Note: [Col. 0245A] 3. “For the weapons of warfare.” He calls them weapons because they resist vices.]

For the weapons of our warfare—he calls them weapons because they resist vices—are not carnal, but powerful through God, by God (he is speaking metaphorically), against fortifications, that is, against the opinions of wicked philosophers.

[Note: [Col. 0245A] 4. LANFRANC. “The weapons of warfare.” The weapons of Christian warfare are the virtues, which are powerful through God’s aid, so that they may destroy the fortified schemes of adversaries, whether human beings or demons, with their various deceits.]

[Note: [Col. 0245A] 5. AMBROSE. “For the destruction.” The spiritual weapons are the faith of incorrupt preaching, by which it conquers the fortifications—that is, the rulers and powers of wickedness—which exalt themselves and arm themselves in the minds of the faithful to oppose Christ.]

For the destruction of fortifications—we wage war against the aerial powers—destroying arguments against God

[Note: [Col. 0245B] 6. LANFRANC. “Destroying arguments.” This is joined to the preceding sentence: “We do not wage war according to the flesh.”]

and every height, every pride, that exalts itself against the knowledge of God, and bringing into captivity

[Note: [Col. 0245B] 7. AMBROSE. “Into captivity.” He takes the intellect captive when he conquers reasoning that contradicts and leads it into the humble and gentle faith of Christ.]

that is, we withdraw from the devil the entire intellect of the predestined—every understanding that understands—into the obedience of Christ,

[Note: [Col. 0246A] 8. LANFRANC. “Into obedience.” “Into” may be understood as “against,” so that the meaning is either “captivating the intellect into the obedience of Christ,” or “captivating the intellect that is against the obedience of Christ.” That is, carefully consider the works of those who act well only in your presence, lest they perhaps lead you astray.]

bringing it into the obedience of Christ. We are also ready, immediately, to punish every disobedience, whenever your obedience has been fulfilled—that is, when the obedient portion of our people has obeyed, or when your contribution to the saints in Jerusalem has been delivered. Your obedience means that you ought to obey me more than the pseudo-apostles and beware of others.

[Note: [Col. 0246A] 9. AMBROSE. “The things that are according to appearance.” Now he wants them to judge what is open and visible, that is, what he is about to say, because it is clear.]

Look at the things that are according to appearance; avoid those who glory in appearance, that is, the pseudo-apostles.

If someone has confidence in himself that he is Christ’s apostle—this is directed against those who placed themselves above the Apostle because they said that they belonged to Christ—the Apostle says: “Let him consider this again within himself: that just as he is Christ’s, so also are we; and they are not greater for that reason.”

[Note: [Col. 0246A] 10. LANFRANC. “For even if I should boast more.” As if he were saying: “I could say, ‘We are apostles, and you ought to obey us more.’”]

For even if I should boast somewhat more than that I am Christ’s, namely, concerning our authority and our apostleship—which the Lord gave us for your edification and not for your destruction—

[Note: [Col. 0246A] 11. “I shall not be ashamed.” He would rightly be ashamed if he called himself an apostle and were not one.]

I shall not be ashamed—an effect is put for the cause—that is, I shall speak the truth.

[Note: [Col. 0246A] 12. AMBROSE. “That I may not seem.” He may appear to frighten them through the Epistle because he has neither any authority nor, when present, the confidence to rebuke them. The variant reads “who” for “because.”]

But I do not want to seem to frighten you through the letters; I do not want to appear to you as though I wished merely to terrify you by threatening you through letters.

[Note: [Col. 0246B] 13. LANFRANC. “That I may not seem.” He says this because of the statement he made above, “ready to punish every disobedience”: “I do not want,” he says, “to seem to you merely to frighten you, when I am less capable of carrying it out. Know that what I shall fulfill less in words, I shall fulfill in deeds.”]

For they say: “His letters are weighty and strong”—weighty to understand and strong to carry out—“but his bodily presence is weak and his speech contemptible.” Let the person who says this consider that, whatever we are in word through letters when absent and threatening, such we shall also be when present in deed. That is, just as we threaten in the letters that we shall act if, when we come to you, you have not been corrected, so we shall carry it out in the deed itself.

[Col. 0247] 110

[Note: [Col. 0247A] 14. “For we do not dare.” He inserts this and compares himself with certain people who imitate their works. “We do not,” he says, “wish to imitate those who commend themselves and flatter you; rather, we praise what is good in you and punish what is bad. As we are in word, so also in deed.”]

For we do not dare to class ourselves among or compare ourselves with certain pseudo-apostles who commend themselves, not measuring themselves but boasting beyond what they are.

[Note: [Col. 0247A] 15. “But measuring ourselves by ourselves.” “We measure ourselves,” that is, we compare ourselves with our own consciences, with ourselves—that is, with our works and abilities—so that we neither say nor attempt more, or something other, than we can or ought to do.]

But we ourselves measure ourselves by ourselves and compare ourselves with ourselves.

[Note: [Col. 0247A] 16. “But not beyond measure.” “We shall boast,” he says, “only to the extent that we call ourselves your apostles. This is the measure of our glory, which God has measured out for us.”]

But we shall not boast beyond measure—that is, not beyond our strength. We boast only of this: that we converted you by our preaching, but according to the measure of the rule

[Note: [Col. 0247A] 17. “According to the measure of the rule.” He explains how the earlier statement, “we shall not boast beyond measure,” is to be understood.]

of governance that God has measured out for us. We boast according to the measure, I say, of reaching you by preaching.

[Note: [Col. 0247B] 18. “Of reaching as far as you.” The measure of our preaching reaches as far as you; that is, we preach within our measure because we do not invade another’s territory. This is what he says: “For we do not …”]

For we do not stretch ourselves beyond you as though we had not reached you; indeed, we reached you in the Gospel, in the preaching of Christ.

We do not boast beyond measure by saying that we preached where we did not preach, in the labors of others, in another’s preaching. But we have hope that, as your faith grows, we shall be magnified in you,

[Note: [Col. 0247B] 19. “As though not reaching.” If others had labored in preaching to the Corinthians before this Apostle, and he had called himself their apostle, he would appear to boast beyond measure, that is, beyond what was proper.]

so that your faith may grow.

[Note: [Col. 0247B] 20. AMBROSE. “To be magnified in you.” He believes that he is magnified before God if his hearers increase in faith.]

That is, so that I may be magnified in you,

[Note: [Col. 0247B] 21. LANFRANC. “According to the rule.” Here he calls governance a rule. “According to this,” he says, “by which we govern you, we are magnified by you”—that is, through you we are magnified by God.]

according to our rule,

[Note: [Col. 0247C] 22. “Into abundance.” He says “into abundance” either because this preaching abounded beyond the preaching of the apostles, or because it contained an abundance of God’s gifts.]

into abundance, having hope of abundance; that is, we hope that we shall preach to others besides you,

[Note: [Col. 0247C] 23. “Even in those regions that lie beyond.” “We have this hope,” he says, “of proclaiming the faith of Christ in those regions that lie beyond us.”]

even in those regions that lie beyond you, to evangelize.

[Note: [Col. 0248A] 24. “Not according to another’s rule.” “We do not,” he says, “hope to boast according to another’s rule,” namely, in regions that have been prepared—that is, evangelized—by the apostles themselves.]

[Note: [Col. 0248A] 25. AMBROSE. “Not according to another’s rule.” He does not dare to boast over those who believed while others preached, nor does he appear to glory in another’s labors. We do not boast according to another’s rule, in another’s preaching, in matters prepared and preached by others. This is because, “Let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord”—or it may be understood as: boast in such a way that the one who boasts boasts in the Lord—not in himself or in another.

[Note: [Col. 0248A] 26. “For it is not the one who commends himself.” The meaning is true because the Lord commends that person. He is approved whom the Lord considers worthy and sends to preach his gift. But the one whom he does not send is not commended by him.]

For it is not the one who commends himself who is approved, but the one whom God commends—those who glory [are approved].

[COMMENTARY]

[Col. 0245A]

CHAPTER X.—1. LANFRANC. “May I dare.” The order is: “May I dare against certain persons,” that is, “may I inflict some trouble upon certain of you.”

2. AMBROSE. “By that confidence.” Confidence signifies the assurance of severity, which he was thought to possess only in the Epistle. Therefore he warns them not to expect him to use the same severity when present, as they had not expected.

3. “For the weapons of warfare.” He calls them weapons because they resist vices.

4. LANFRANC. “The weapons of warfare.” The weapons of Christian warfare are the virtues, which are powerful through God’s aid, so that they may destroy the fortified schemes of adversaries, whether human beings or demons, with their various deceits.

5. AMBROSE. “For the destruction.” The spiritual weapons are the faith of incorrupt preaching, by which it conquers the fortifications—that is, the rulers and powers of wickedness—which exalt themselves and arm themselves in the minds of the faithful to oppose Christ.

6. LANFRANC. “Destroying arguments.” This is joined to the preceding sentence: “We do not wage war according to the flesh.”

7. AMBROSE. “Into captivity.” He takes the intellect captive when he conquers reasoning that contradicts and leads it into the humble and gentle faith of Christ.

[Col. 0246A] 8. LANFRANCUS. “Into obedience.” “Into” can be understood as “against,” so that the sense is: “Captivating the intellect into the obedience of Christ,” or “the intellect that is against the obedience of Christ”; that is, carefully consider the works of those who act well only in your presence, lest they perhaps lead you astray.

9. AMBROS. “Which are according to appearance.” Now he wishes them to consider what is manifest, that is, what he is about to say, because these things are open to judgment.

10. LANFR. “For even if I should boast more.” As if he were saying: “I could say: ‘We are apostles, and you ought to obey us more.’”

11. “I shall not be put to shame.” He would rightly be ashamed if he called himself an apostle and were not one.

12. AMBROS. “That I may not seem.” He himself may appear [Col. 0246B] to terrify them through the Epistle, because [variant: who] he possesses neither any authority nor, when present, confidence to rebuke.

13. LANFR. “That I may not seem.” He says this with reference to the statement he made above, “ready to avenge every disobedience,” so that, he says, “I may not seem to you to be terrifying you by threatening what I am less able to accomplish; know that what I am lesser in words I shall fulfill in deeds.”

[Col. 0247A] 14. “For we do not dare.” He inserts this and compares himself with certain people who imitate their works. “We do not wish,” he says, “to imitate those who commend themselves and flatter you; rather, we praise your good qualities and punish your faults. What they are in word, they are also in deed.”

15. “But they themselves, measuring themselves by themselves.” We measure ourselves, that is, we compare ourselves by our consciences with ourselves, that is, with our works and abilities, so that we do not say or attempt more—or something else—than we can or ought to do.

16. “But we will not boast beyond measure.” “We shall boast,” he says, “only to the extent that we call ourselves your apostles; for this is the measure of our boasting which God has measured out for us.”

17. “According to the measure of the rule.” He explains how [Col. 0247B] what he said above—“we will not boast beyond measure”—is to be understood.

18. “Reaching even as far as you.” The measure of our preaching reaches as far as you; that is, we preach according to the measure, because we do not invade another’s field. This is what he says: “For we do not,” and so forth.

19. “As though we had not reached you.” If others had labored in preaching among the Corinthians before this Apostle, and he had called himself their apostle, he would seem to boast beyond measure, that is, excessively.

20. AMBROS. “To be magnified among you.” He believes that he is magnified before God if his hearers increase in faith.

21. LANFR. “According to the rule.” Here he calls the rule governance. “According to this,” he says, “that we govern you, we are magnified by you, that is, through you we are magnified by God.”

[Col. 0247C] 22. “Into abundance.” He says “into abundance” either because this preaching abounded beyond the preaching of the apostles, or because it contained an abundance of God’s gifts.

23. “Even in those regions that lie beyond.” “We have this hope,” he says, “of evangelizing the faith of Christ in those places that lie beyond us.”

[Col. 0248A] 24. “Not according to another’s rule.” “We do not hope,” he says, “to boast according to another’s rule,” namely, in those places that had been prepared—that is, evangelized—by the apostles themselves.

25. AMBROS. “Not according to another’s rule.” He does not dare to boast among those who believed when others were preaching, nor does he appear to boast in another’s labors. Rather, he strives to preach to those to whom the Gospel had not been announced, so that he may acquire glory through his own labor. He indicates that the glory is to be given to the Lord when he says: “Let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord.”

26. “For it is not the one who commends himself.” It is true that the Lord commends that person; and the one whom he considers worthy and sends to preach his gift is approved. But the one whom he does not send is not commended by him. [Col. 0248B] He commends himself because [variant: who], though not sent, he preaches.

111. 27. LANFR. “That one is approved.” We do not wish to boast in what belongs to others, but in the Lord, because everyone who boasts ought to boast in the Lord—not in himself or in another. He must not boast in himself or in another, because the one who acts in this way is not approved by God.

LANFR. “Would that you would bear with me!” “Would that,” he says, “you were willing to bear with me,” that is, to hear how I commend myself, which appears foolishness! [Note: [Col. 0248C] 3. “For I am jealous over you.” What he has said shows that he intends to speak out of love for them, so that it may contribute not so much to his own praise as to their progress, so that they may learn how to favor their father in the Gospel.]

[Note: [Col. 0248C] 4. LANFR. “For I am jealous over you.” Jealousy is a movement of the mind on account of another’s condition. “For I am jealous over you with the jealousy of God,” [Col. 0249] because I love you; or, if I trouble you, I do so with good intent, so that you may present yourselves as chaste—that is, undefiled—to Christ, to whom I betrothed you.

IV). “For I betrothed you.” Now the Church is betrothed and is a virgin, to be led to the wedding—that is, when she keeps herself from worldly corruption. [Note: [Col. 0249A] 6. LANFR. “For I betrothed you.” The reason why he is jealous over them is that he betrothed them by the ring of faith to one man, namely Christ, so that they might present themselves as a chaste virgin to him.]

“For I betrothed you to one man, as a chaste virgin”—he wishes them to be virgins in faith—“to present you to Christ.”

But nevertheless—

[Note: [Col. 0249A] 7. AMBROS. “But I fear.” He shows why he is compelled to testify truthfully about himself: not to praise himself, but to expose those who, under the name of Christ, preach against Christ. “But I fear lest, just as the serpent deceived Eve by his cunning, so your false senses may be corrupted and fall away from the simplicity and goodness that are in Christ,” or in the things that belong to Christ. You ought not to suffer this.

[Note: [Col. 0249B] 8. “For if the one who comes.” Here he speaks about true preachers, because the Corinthian people were wavering amid various errors. [Note: [Col. 0250B] 17. LANFR. “In what they boast.” “Therefore,” he says, “I do not accept anything, so that in what they boast—that is, in receiving—they may be found to be like us, since we too accept nothing. “so that in what they boast they may be found to be like us.”

Response.

LANFR. “Again I say.” Above he said: “Would that you would bear with a little of my foolishness!”—namely, his self-commendation, which, when done indiscreetly, is called foolishness. “if someone devours you, taking what is yours,

if someone takes you in by deceitful flattery—“to take” means to capture by trickery—if someone exalts himself by boasting,

[Note: [Col. 0252B] 33. LANFR. “If someone strikes you in the face.” To strike someone in the face is to recall past evils to memory.]

“if someone strikes you in the face”—the face is struck when an insult is inflicted upon it—or physically.

[Note: [Col. 0252B] 34. “According to dishonor.” “I speak manfully,” he says, “as though we had been powerless (or more intent), that is, to do such things; for I could speak more grandly: as though we had not been more powerful to do the things they do.”]

“According to dishonor I speak”—if someone exalts himself, and so forth—“as though we had been weak, having nothing in which to boast,” although we are more powerful to do the things they do, in this matter of boasting.

He shows that he has grounds for boasting. In whatever a pseudo-apostle dares to boast—in foolishness, I say—I too dare: They are Hebrews, so am I; they are Israelites, so am I; they are the seed of Abraham, so am I; they are ministers of Christ”—I speak as one less wise—“I more so.” And I am even more a minister of Christ; and he proves this by what follows: “in far greater labors, in more abundant imprisonments, in beatings beyond measure, in frequent dangers of death.”

[Note: [Col. 0252B] 35. “Five times from the Jews.” He was beaten five times, and at each beating he endured forty strokes less one, on each occasion, with a knotted strap. Or “forty” refers to the whip itself, made of forty straps, with which he says he was struck five times, one strap being retained on each occasion; for the Law mercifully prescribed that this be done in this manner.]

“Five times I received from the Jews forty strokes less one. Three times I was beaten with rods; once I was stoned; I suffered three shipwrecks” [Col. 0252C]—the Jews wishing to drown him—“and endured them;

[Note: [Col. 0252C] 36. AMBROS. “By night and by day.” This happened when he was sent to Rome because he had appealed to Caesar. Thus it is written elsewhere: “So that we despaired even of living” [variant: “were weary even of living”] (2 Cor. 1).]

by night and by day, while I was being taken to Rome, I was in the depths of the sea, having appealed to Caesar; often on journeys I suffered much; I was exposed to dangers from rivers, dangers from robbers, dangers from my own race—the Jews; dangers from the Gentiles—the pagans; I was exposed to dangers in the city, dangers in the wilderness, dangers at sea, dangers among false brothers who wished to betray me; in labor and hardship of body, in many vigils, in hunger and thirst, in many fasts, in cold and nakedness—besides those things that are external, besides the other things I suffered in the flesh—my daily preoccupation”—my zeal, or the movement of my mind—“was concern for all the churches.”

“Who is weak, and I am not weak?”—by sharing his suffering. “Who is scandalized, and I am not burning?”

“If it is necessary to boast: if you compel me to boast further, I shall speak the true things that belong to my weakness, the things that my weakness has suffered; I shall boast without inventing anything.”

“The God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who is blessed forever, knows that I do not lie” in the things that follow.

[Col. 0248B]

# CHAPTER XI

1. LANFR. “Would that you would bear with me!” “Would that,” he says, “you were willing to bear with me,” that is, to hear how I commend myself, which appears foolishness! And if I recount these things, you ought to listen; and he adds: “For I am jealous over you,” and so forth.

2. AMBROS. “Would that you would bear with me!” As he begins to praise himself, he calls himself foolish, because it is written: “Let your lips not praise you, but your neighbor’s” (Prov. 27).

[Col. 0248C] 3. “For I am jealous over you.” What he has said shows that he intends to speak out of love for them, so that it may contribute not so much to his own praise as to their progress, so that they may learn how to favor their father in the Gospel.

4. LANFR. “For I am jealous over you.” Jealousy is a movement of the mind on account of another’s condition. He therefore asks them to endure his rebuke patiently, because he is moved concerning their works by a movement that is according to God. There is also a movement in others that is called envy.

5. AUGUST. (Book 83 Questions, question 59, vol. IV). “For I betrothed you.” Now the Church is betrothed and is a virgin, to be led to the wedding—that is, when she keeps herself from worldly corruption. But she will marry at the time when all mortality has passed away [variant: perished in it] and she enjoys immortal union.

6. LANFR. “For I betrothed you.” The reason why he is jealous over them is that he betrothed them by the ring of faith to one man, namely Christ, so that they might present themselves as a chaste virgin to him.

7. AMBROS. “But I fear.” He shows why he is compelled to testify truthfully about himself: not to praise himself, but to expose those who, under the name of Christ, preach against Christ. He does this so that the deceivers may not be heard; he compares them with the devil because of their cunning.

8. “For if the one who comes.” Here he speaks about true preachers, because the Corinthian people were wavering amid various errors. Some favored the pseudo-apostles, while others favored the apostles who had been with the Lord. Concerning these the Apostle says: “If a greater Christ had been preached to you by these men, or a greater Spirit had been given, you would rightly place them before us.”

9. LANFR. “For if the one who comes.” “If,” he says, “the preacher who comes, though not sent by God, were to preach another faith to you, and through that faith you were to receive another Spirit, it would be somewhat tolerable if you endured his condemnation; for you could say: ‘His preaching is better than Paul’s.’ But now, since they preach the same faith and add many things of their own that ought to be rejected, you must not endure them. Here he begins to explain that ‘little foolishness’ of which he spoke above.”

10. “From the great apostles.” From the great ones—how much more from those who are nothing? He says “unskilled,” either because of humility or, as some say, because he had an impediment of speech. For he says that knowledge was the reason why he accomplished so much.

11. AMBROS. “For even if unskilled.” This does not refer to the apostles, but touches those whom the Corinthians preferred because of their polished speech, although in religion the force of the message is necessary, not a pleasant sound.

12. LANFR. “In everything,” and so forth. “I have made myself manifest to all of you: in everything, although unskilled in speech, I have conducted myself knowingly, because I did not sin by humbling myself or by preaching without charge,” that is, by taking no expenses from you while I was preaching. He proves this: “For,” he says, “while preaching to you, I received support from other churches.”

13. AMBROS. “Have I committed a sin?” He humbles himself when he did not demand what was owed to him.

14. LANFR. “For what was lacking to me.” As if someone were saying: “From where, then, did you live?”

15. AMBROS. “This boasting will not be diminished.” Glory consists in abstaining from what is permitted, especially for the salvation of others.

16. “In what they boast.” The glory of the pseudo-apostles consisted in receiving money. Therefore the Apostle rejected this, lest he appear like them; for unless the Apostle had avoided this, a greater opportunity for them to receive would have been provided.

17. LANFR. “In what they boast.” “Therefore,” he says, “I do not accept anything, so that in what they boast—that is, in receiving—they may be found to be like us, since we too accept nothing. Or I do not accept anything because some preachers preached falsehood without support, so that they might appear religious and be able to place themselves before us.”

18. “For such men are pseudo-apostles.” He gives the reason why some of them preached without support. “By this,” he says, “they transform themselves into apostles of light, or of Christ.”

[Col. 0251A] 19. AMBROS. “Again I say.” He continually proposes what he will later develop at length.

20. LANFR. “Again I say.” Above he said: “Would that you would bear with a little of my foolishness!”—namely, his self-commendation, which, when done indiscreetly, is called foolishness. He says it again lest anyone think him foolish, since he does this not for himself but for their edification; otherwise, if they wish, let them think him foolish while he boasts, nevertheless doing so for their edification.

21. “Again I say.” “Again,” he says, “and often I recount their faults, lest anyone who hears me rebuking them think me foolish.”

22. “Otherwise, as foolish.” This is a concession to the opposing party, which is appropriately made when it will not harm the one who concedes.

[Col. 0251B] 23. AMBROS. “So that I may boast a little.” He calls it “a little” because the littleness is in the words, not in the meaning.

24. “What I say.” He does not speak according to God, because these things pertain to the swelling of the flesh; nor does glory arise before God from self-inflation, because humility is glorious before God.

25. LANFR. “In foolishness.” It would be foolishness if he boasted willingly; but because he is compelled, he speaks as though in foolishness.

26. “In this substance,” that is, in this kind of boasting, which occurs according to foolishness.

27. “For you gladly bear with.” The reason why he wishes to boast against the glorying of deceitful preachers is that the Corinthians gladly endured their foolishness, although some of them were wise in the word of God.

[Col. 0251C] 28. AMBROS. “If someone devours.” They were content to have their possessions devoured by false teachers.

[Col. 0252A] 29. LANFR. “If someone brings you into slavery,” that is, into the carnal observances of the Law, which it compelled people to fulfill through servile fear, saying: “If anyone does this or that, let him die the death.”

30. AMBROS. “If someone brings you into slavery.” They were reduced to slavery through foolishness, so that they might serve the pseudo-apostles.

31. “If someone strikes you in the face.” The person struck in the face is the one to whose face an insult is inflicted. Here he signifies those who, because they were descended from Abraham, reproached them for being uncircumcised. Hence what follows: “According to dishonor I speak.”

32. AUGUST. (Book I, On the Sermon on the Mount, chap. 19, vol. IV). “If someone strikes you in the face.” What does it mean to be struck in the face? It means to be despised and scorned. The Apostle does not say this so that they would not endure such people, but so that they might endure him all the more, since he loved them so greatly that he wished to be expended for them as he would for himself.

33. LANFR. “If someone strikes you in the face.” To strike someone in the face is to recall past evils to memory.

34. “According to dishonor.” “I speak manfully,” he says, “as though we had been powerless (or more intent), that is, to do such things; for I could speak more grandly: as though we had not been more powerful to do the things they do.”

35. “Five times from the Jews.” He was beaten five times, and at each beating he endured forty strokes less one, on each occasion, with a knotted strap. Or “forty” refers to the whip itself, made of forty straps, with which he says he was struck five times, one strap being retained on each occasion; for the Law mercifully prescribed that this be done in this manner.

36. AMBROS. “By night and by day.” This happened when he was sent to Rome because he had appealed to Caesar. Thus it is written elsewhere: “So that we despaired even of living” [variant: “were weary even of living”] (2 Cor. 1).

37. LANFR. “Who is weak?” This and what follows are to be reckoned among the things that are external, because [possibly: which] are placed externally.

except in my infirmities. Can you boast in infirmities? Response:

although I am nothing—those men much, I nothing, as some think. Yet the signs of my apostleship, the indications pertaining to an apostle, were performed among you, by which I ought to have been commended: in all patience, in signs in the present, and wonders in the future, and powers—miracles.

and I mourn for many of those who sinned previously

and did not do penance for the uncleanness, fornication, and shamelessness that they committed.

[COMMENTARY.]

[Col. 0253A]

CHAP. XII.—1. LANFRANC. “To visions and revelations.” If these things are not sufficient for boasting, I shall add greater things—which is not [proper], that is, which is foolish. Therefore he conceals his own name and simply says that he knows a man to whom these things happened, and thus voluntarily removes the occasion for boasting. If he boasts on account of such a man—that is, insofar as this man has these visions from God and not from himself—he boasts on his own behalf according to the things he suffers.

2. AMBROSE. “Caught up in such a manner.” He signifies that he was caught up above the firmament, into the third heaven, reckoned among the spiritual heavens.

3. “On behalf of such a man.” On behalf of such a man—that is, he says that this man was so worthy of God that he experienced this—and he does not wish to say openly that he is speaking about himself, lest he appear to praise himself.

4. AMBROSE. “Except in my infirmities.” “I will boast,” he says, “in my infirmities.” For to explain the pressures of sufferings and the weaknesses of distress does not seem glorious but mournful. For this reason he says that he boasts in these things.

5. LANFRANC. “For even if I should wish to boast.” I will boast only on account of those things which God has granted me the ability to do, and only on account of deeds. This is what he says: “For even if I should wish to boast, I will not be foolish.” One person boasts of his own things, another of invented things. But I will not boast of invented things; for I shall speak the truth.

[Col. 0254A] 6. AMBROSE. “Lest anyone should think me.” “Lest anyone should think me,” he says, “to extend my boasting beyond what the boundary of my merits allows.”

7. “And lest the greatness.” This remedy was given to the Apostle so that, pressed by insults, he could not be lifted up in spirit by the greatness of the revelations, lest his heart, having nothing else to occupy it, should be lifted up by the things he had seen.

8. AUGUSTINE, *Exposition of Psalm CXXX*. “An angel of Satan.” Lest he be lifted up like a young man, he is struck on the cheek like a child; and by whom? By an angel of Satan. What does this mean? He is dragged along and violently tormented by some bodily pain. Bodily pains, moreover, are often inflicted by angels of Satan; but they cannot do this unless permitted. Thus also holy Job was tested.

[Col. 0254B] 9. AMBROSE. “My grace is sufficient for you.” He says that he was answered that God’s grace should be sufficient for him, because strength for endurance was added. Hence he goes on to say that he should boast when he is humbled by insults, while Christ supplies the power to endure.

9. LANFRANC. “My grace is sufficient for you.” That is, my grace ought to be sufficient for you; that is, this infirmity, which I give you for the purpose of testing your virtue, so that you may thus be crowned. For every virtue is tested through infirmity.

10. “For virtue is perfected in infirmity.” He says that virtue is perfect when it has an opposing infirmity with which it legitimately struggles, so that it may afterward be crowned.

11. AMBROSE. “For when I am weak.” He speaks truly, because the Christian conquers when he is thought to be losing, whereas faithlessness loses when it rejoices that it has conquered.

12. “For I was inferior in nothing.” He says “beyond measure,” as some thought. For they were also what the Apostle Paul was.

13. LANFRANC. “Although I am nothing.” Although, according to the opinion of certain foolish people, I am nothing, I nevertheless did among you the things that ordinarily identify an apostle. I showed every kind of patience among you; when necessary, I performed signs, wonders, and other works of power. There is, however, a distinction among sign, wonder, and power. A sign is a kind of wonder; power is a kind of both. Any miracle may be called a power; a sign is only that which signifies something at whatever time; a wonder is that which signifies something only in the future.

14. “For what is there?” He confirms the preceding statement: “I did nothing less,” and so forth. As if he were saying: “By this it is clear that I did nothing less than the other apostles, because you possess nothing less than the other Churches instructed by them. For the disciples prove what sort of teachers they have, just as all things prove those without whom they cannot exist.”

15. AMBROSE. “For what is there?” He shows that he was not less than they but greater, because he preached the Gospel to them without charge, whereas this was granted to certain Churches, as the Lord says: “The laborer is worthy of his wages.”

16. “Forgive me this.” Every fool is an accuser of the good. Thus, in order to show them to be ignorant, he asks forgiveness from them for an act on account of which he deserves praise.

[Col. 0256A] 17. LANFRANC. “Behold, for the third time I am ready.” He had come to them once, and on another occasion he had been ready but did not come; this is why he says that he is ready to come to them for the third time.

18. “I will not be burdensome to you.” Lest it be said that he was now coming in order to seize whatever he had previously spared them, he says: “I will not be burdensome to you,” because I do not seek what belongs to you; that is, I will not burden you.

19. AMBROSE. “For children ought not.” He indicates that he is their father. Carnal fathers, however, are those who store up treasures for their children. Spiritual fathers ought rightly to receive expenses from their children. Here he proves that he does not wish to receive anything to such an extent that he transfers the principle concerning a carnal father to a spiritual one.

20. “But I will most gladly.” He says that he is prepared not only to expend his possessions for their salvation but also to die.

21. LANFRANC. “Did I deceive you through any one?” Lest anyone say, “You did not burden us personally, but craftily did so through your associates,” he removes this objection.

22. “Those whom I sent to you.” He says: “I did not deceive you through any one whom I sent to you, because I deceived you neither through Titus nor through Barnabas nor through anyone else, for I was always the same.” This is what he says: “Did we not walk in the same spirit?” and so forth.

23. “For I fear lest perhaps.” They came to the faith more readily because he accepted nothing from them; and if he did accept anything, they would sin more securely. Therefore he says: “For I fear,” and so forth.

24. AMBROSE. “Lest again, when I come.” When they sin, he says that he is humbled, because, like a loving father, he grieves over their sin.

[Col. 0257A] 25. “And I mourn for many.” When he says “that I may mourn for many,” he proves to them that some of these people had done penance and some had not. This is contrary to Novatian, who says that fornicators cannot complete penance.

26. LANFRANC. “And did not do penance.” From this it is proved false that those who misunderstand and carelessly assert it claim that the Apostle wrote in his Epistle to the Hebrews that those who have fallen cannot be renewed to penance.

CHAPTER XIII.

[Col. 0257]

[Note: [Col. 0257A] CHAP. XIII.—1. LANFRANC. “Behold, for the third time this.” He does not say that he came twice and will come a third time, but that he prepared himself twice and could not come, whereas now he will come with this third preparation.]

Behold, for the third time, with this preparation, I am coming to you: “Every matter shall stand on the testimony of two or three witnesses.” In this I will not believe anyone making an excuse unless he is excused by two or three witnesses. I foretold it, and I foretell it,

[Note: [Col. 0257A] 2. “That I am present with you.” At his first coming, in the presence of them all, he twice foretold what follows.]

as when present with you, and now absent, I say beforehand to those who sinned previously and to all the rest that, if I come again, I will not spare you if you remain uncorrected. You know this: I will not spare you.

[Note: [Col. 0257B] 3. AMBROSE. “Or do you seek proof?” They seek to test Christ speaking in the Apostle, while they do not obey his commands, wishing to discover whether he dares to exact punishment.]

[Note: [Col. 0257C] 4. LANFRANC. “Or do you seek proof?” That is, do you wish to test my severity by my taking vengeance on you? Christ is speaking; he says this by way of amplification.]

Or do you seek proof of Christ, who speaks in me and is not weak in you,

[Note: [Col. 0257B] 5. AMBROSE. “But he is powerful.” Christ is powerful in these matters, because they saw the dead raised in his name and demons driven out. All these things belong to power, not weakness.]

but is powerful either to take vengeance or to perform miracles among you?

[Note: [Col. 0257B] 6. LANFRANC. “For even if he was crucified.” As if someone were saying: “How can you say that he is not weak but powerful, when it is evident that he was crucified?”]

For even if he was crucified through the weakness of the flesh,

[Note: [Col. 0257B] 7. “But he lives through the power of God.” He lives—that is, he is full of vigor and strength. As in Hebrews: “For the word of God is living and effective,” through the power of God, from the word of the Father, from which he was assumed.]

yet he lives through the power of God, from the Word of the Father, from whom he was assumed. For—and this proves the point by similarity or from the lesser—we

[Note: [Col. 0257C] 8. “We are weak.” It is no wonder, he says, if Christ is powerful through the power of divinity, since we, though weak, are strong through the same power. “In him,” that is, in the matter in which he himself is weak—that is, in the flesh. It may also be understood as “in him,” that is, in preaching.]

are weak in preaching him—that is, in that aspect in which he himself was weak—but we shall live with him through the power of God toward you, because we are effective in performing miracles or in punishing you, as he is. “Toward you,” that is, in your consciences.

Examine yourselves, one another—or let each examine himself—to see whether you are in the faith; test yourselves: Christ dwells in you for this very purpose. Or do you not recognize yourselves, namely, that Jesus Christ is in you? Unless perhaps you are reprobate.

Similarly, lest they should call him reprobate, he says:

But I hope that you will recognize that we are not reprobate. We do not want you to be reprobate, but we pray to God that you do nothing evil—not in order that we may appear approved, that is, that we may have something to correct in you, but that

[Note: [Col. 0258A] 9. AMBROSE. “You may do what is good.” He prays that, when they do what is good and he does not dare to correct them, he may appear humbled or reprobate; whereas they appear approved by God when they judge sinners by the authority granted to them. Therefore, if there are no sinners for them to judge, their authority ceases in these matters, and they appear almost reprobate.]

you may do what is good, so that we have nothing in you to correct,

[Note: [Col. 0258A] 10. LANFRANC. “But that we may be reprobate.” As if he were saying: “We patiently endure being reprobate in your consciences, provided only that you do what is good.”]

and that we may be reprobate, as though worthless and deprived of our office as teachers.

[Note: [Col. 0258A] 11. AMBROSE. “For we can do nothing.” He says this because authority was not given against the truth, so that they might accuse those living well, but for the truth, so that they might take vengeance on one who is an enemy of the law.]

[Note: [Col. 0258B] 12. LANFRANC. “For we can do nothing.” We wish to be reprobate while you do what is good; for we do not wish to be approved as powerful against the truth—that is, against those who do what is good. Or it may be understood thus: “We can do nothing against the truth,” that is, we neither rebuke nor condemn anything in those who are truthful—that is, those who act well, even if they are liable to criticism.]

For we can do nothing against the truth to instruct it, but only for the truth.

[Note: [Col. 0258B] 13. “Against the truth.” Against justice—that is, truth. I say [perhaps: “when”] he could, if, while they were doing good, he might advance through prayers so as to appear approved in their consciences. It is neither just nor pleasing to God that a holy man should seek to appear approved except for this sole reason: that those who see him may receive a good example.]

[Note: [Col. 0258C] 14. “For we rejoice.” This is another reason why he does not wish to appear approved.]

[Note: [Col. 0258C] 15. AMBROSE. “For we rejoice.” This is what it means to be weak: not to exercise authority. He wishes them, however, to be strong, so that by living well they may conquer vices and keep punishment or correction away from themselves.]

For we rejoice that we are weak, finding nothing in you to punish, while you are powerful by doing good. We also pray for this: your completion, your perfection.

For this reason I write these things while absent, so that when present I may not act too harshly, according to the authority of apostleship that the Lord gave me for building up and not for destruction.

Finally, brothers, rejoice; be perfected; be encouraged; think alike; have peace; and the God of peace and love will be with you. Greet one another with a holy kiss. All the saints greet you.

[Note: [Col. 0259A] 16. “The grace of our Lord.” The love of God sent us the Savior Jesus, by whose grace we have been saved; and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit makes us possess this grace. For it protects those loved by God and saved by the grace of Christ, so that the perfection of the Three may be the completion of the human being unto salvation.]

The grace—the redemption—of our Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, the love of God the Father who sent us the Savior, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with you all.

[COMMENTARY.]

[Col. 0257A]

CHAP. XIII.—1. LANFRANC. “Behold, for the third time this.” He does not say that he came twice and will come a third time, but that he prepared himself twice and could not come, whereas now he will come with this third preparation.

2. “That I am present with you.” At his first coming, in the presence of them all, he twice foretold what follows.

3. AMBROSE. “Or do you seek proof?” They seek to test Christ speaking in the Apostle, while they do not obey his commands, wishing to discover whether he dares to exact punishment.

4. LANFRANC. “Or do you seek proof?” That is, do you wish to test my severity by my taking vengeance on you? Christ is speaking; he says this by way of amplification.

5. AMBROSE. “But he is powerful.” Christ is powerful in these matters, because they saw the dead raised in his name and demons driven out. All these things belong to power, not weakness.

6. LANFRANC. “For even if he was crucified.” As if someone were saying: “How can you say that he is not weak but powerful, when it is evident that he was crucified?”

7. “But he lives through the power of God.” He lives—that is, he is full of vigor and strength. As in Hebrews: “For the word of God is living and effective,” through the power of God, from the word of the Father, from which he was assumed.

8. “We are weak.” It is no wonder, he says, if Christ is powerful through the power of divinity, since we, though weak, are strong through the same power. “In him,” that is, in the matter in which he himself is weak—that is, in the flesh. It may also be understood as “in him,” that is, in preaching.

9. AMBROSE. “You may do what is good.” He prays that, when they do what is good and he does not dare to correct them, he may appear humbled or reprobate; whereas they appear approved by God when they judge sinners by the authority granted to them. Therefore, if there are no sinners for them to judge, their authority ceases in these matters, and they appear almost reprobate.

10. LANFRANC. “But that we may be reprobate.” As if he were saying: “We patiently endure being reprobate in your consciences, provided only that you do what is good.”

11. AMBROSE. “For we can do nothing.” He says this because authority was not given against the truth, so that they might accuse those living well, but for the truth, so that they might take vengeance on one who is an enemy of the law.

12. LANFRANC. “For we can do nothing.” We wish to be reprobate while you do what is good; for we do not wish to be approved as powerful against the truth—that is, against those who do what is good. Or it may be understood thus: “We can do nothing against the truth,” that is, we neither rebuke nor condemn anything in those who are truthful—that is, those who act well, even if they are liable to criticism.

13. “Against the truth.” Against justice—that is, truth. I say [perhaps: “when”] he could, if, while they were doing good, he might advance through prayers so as to appear approved in their consciences. It is neither just nor pleasing to God that a holy man should seek to appear approved except for this sole reason: that those who see him may receive a good example.

[Col. 0258C] 14. “For we rejoice.” This is another reason why he does not wish to appear approved.

15. AMBROSE. “For we rejoice.” This is what it means to be weak: not to exercise authority. He wishes them, however, to be strong, so that by living well they may conquer vices and keep punishment or correction away from themselves.

[Col. 0259A] 16. “The grace of our Lord.” The love of God sent us the Savior Jesus, by whose grace we have been saved; and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit makes us possess this grace. For it protects those loved by God and saved by the grace of Christ, so that the perfection of the Three may be the completion of the human being unto salvation.

THE EPISTLE OF THE BLESSED APOSTLE PAUL TO THE GALATIANS, WITH THE INTERSPERSED BRIEF GLOSSES OF THE BLESSED LANFRANC.

[Col. 0259]

119. ARGUMENT. The Galatians are Greeks. They first received the word of truth from the Apostle, but after his departure they were led astray by false apostles into turning to the Law and circumcision. The Apostle calls them back to faith in the truth, writing to them from Ephesus.

CHAPTER ONE.

[Col. 0259]

[Note: [Col. 0259B] Chapter I.—1. LANFRANC. “Paul, an apostle not from men,” etc. In the other Epistles, after offering a greeting, he immediately begins with thanksgiving; here he does not, for they were not such as to provide him with grounds for giving thanks.]

Paul the Apostle, [Note: [Col. 0259B] 2. AUGUSTINE (Exposition of the First Chapter of the Epistle to the Galatians, vol. IV). “Not from men.” He who is sent by men is a liar; he who is sent through a man can be truthful, because the truthful God can send someone through a man. Thus the earlier apostles were sent by God through a man—namely, through Jesus while he was still mortal. The last Apostle was sent through Christ, who was already wholly God, that is, immortal in every respect. Let his authority, therefore, be equal to theirs, in whose honor the glorification of the Lord is fulfilled; if the order of time entails anything, it is not for that reason lesser, since, after he had said “and God,” he added, “who raised him” [Col. 0259C].] not from men, chosen by other apostles, nor sent through a man—through them, or through Ananias, or through Christ merely as a man—but through Jesus Christ and God the Father, who raised him from the dead; and all the brothers who are with me, to the churches of Galatia.

[Note: [Col. 0259C] 3. AMBROSE. “Not from men.” By saying the same thing, he divides the phrase, to show by the very multiplicity of his account that they in no way speak the truth.]

[Note: [Col. 0259C] 4. LANFRANC. “Not from men.” Some thought that he had not been sent as an apostle by Christ, but by other apostles or by Ananias. He denies this so that he may possess greater authority among those to whom he preached the word of God.]

[Note: [Col. 0259C] 5. AUGUSTINE (ibid.). “Grace to you and peace.” The grace of God is that by which our sins are forgiven, so that we may be reconciled to God. Peace, moreover, is that by which we are reconciled to God [Col. 0260B].]

Grace to you and peace from God the Father and our Lord Jesus Christ, who gave himself [he commends Christ] for our sins,

[Note: [Col. 0260B] 6. AMBROSE. “That he might rescue.” Christ freed us from the life of the present age, in which many things were done that ought not to have been done. He established us in hope of the future life, something the Law was in no way able to provide for us.]

that he might rescue us

[Note: [Col. 0260B] 7. AUGUSTINE (ibid.). “From the present age.” He calls the present age evil because of the evil people who are in it. Just as we call a house evil because evil people inhabit it.]

from the present evil age, from the wickedness of the age, according to the will of our God and Father, to whom be glory for ever and ever. Amen.

[Note: [Col. 0260B] 8. AMBROSE. “I am astonished that so.” A fitting opening in view of the novelty of what has happened. For he says “I am astonished” as though something had occurred that was thought never to be capable of happening.]

I am astonished 120 that you are being transferred so quickly

[Note: [Col. 0260C] 9. LANFRANC. “You are being transferred.” These Galatians, partly Jews and partly Gentiles, had been converted by the Apostle to faith in Christ. But after his departure, false preachers came, compelling those who had been converted from Judaism to practice Judaism, while those who had come from the Gentiles to the faith were compelled to worship the elements of the world and observe days and years.]

[Note: [Col. 0260C] 10. AMBROSE. “You are being transferred.” He does not say “you are being led over” but “you are being transferred,” as though they were lifeless people without any movement of the mind.]

[Note: [Col. 0260C] 11. “From him who called you.” So that they would not seem to be departing from Christ alone, he added “from God.”]

away from him who called you into the grace of Christ, into

[Note: [Col. 0261A] 12. LANFRANC. “Into another gospel.” The gospel is good proclamation; their preaching, therefore, was not the Gospel, because it was not good proclamation. “Another gospel” may also be understood as the observance of the Jewish Law, which does not conflict with the Gospel of Christ if it is understood spiritually. This is what he means when he says, “There are some,” that is, there are indeed those who understand it carnally and perversely.]

[Note: [Col. 0261A] 13. “Another gospel.” The Gospel is different only to those who do not wish to understand it spiritually. Or that is not the Gospel except to those who deceive you—and such people would be accursed. He does not say this directly, but adds it in order to intensify the point.]

another gospel, which is not another, except that there are some who say that there is another gospel, who trouble you and wish to pervert the Gospel of Christ.

[Note: [Col. 0261B] 14. AUGUSTINE (ibid.). “Into another gospel.” If the Gospel is something other than what the Lord gave, either directly or through others, it can no longer rightly be called the Gospel.]

[Note: [Col. 0261B] 15. AUGUSTINE (ibid.). “Those who trouble you.” Having said “who trouble you,” he did not say “and convert you,” but “wish to convert the Gospel”; yet it remains completely firm and unaltered.]

But even if we,

[Note: [Col. 0261B] 16. AMBROSE. “But even if we.” He shows that he is not setting himself above them, but that he is defending the truth.]

or an angel from heaven should preach to you a gospel apart from the one we preached to you, let him be accursed. As we have said before, so now I say again: If anyone preaches to you a gospel apart from what you received, let him be accursed. He places the curse first, so that he may more easily be believed.

[Note: [Col. 0261B] 17. “Or an angel.” He added this to show that neither the dignity of a place nor that of a person could be made equal to the truth.]

[Note: [Col. 0261B] 18. “Now then.” He says this to show that, although he uttered such words on behalf of the truth, he considered those who disparaged him to be of no importance.]

Now then,

[Note: [Col. 0261B] 19. AUGUSTINE (ibid.). “Now then, am I persuading human beings?” The meaning is: “I am persuading human beings and not God.” [Col. 0261C] For we have been manifested to God; and because I am persuading human beings, am I seeking to please human beings? If I were pleasing human beings—that is, if I were seeking to please them—I would not be a servant of Christ.]

am I persuading human beings, or God? Am I seeking to please human beings?

[Note: [Col. 0261C] 20. LANFRANC. “Now then, am I persuading human beings?” It is as though he said: “I am not speaking flatteringly in order to please you, but reproving your fickleness in order to please God.”]

If I were still pleasing human beings, I would not be a servant of Christ.

[Note: [Col. 0262A] 21. “Am I persuading human beings or God?” Someone might say: “Why do you pronounce such a curse?” He replies: “So that I may show that I am neither a participant in nor a persuader of circumcision, as the false apostles are.” Or: “I pronounce the curse because I am not persuading people in order to wish to please them,” with the question understood in this way: “Am I seeking to please human beings?”]

For I make known to you, brothers, concerning the Gospel that was preached by me [in answer to what he said above, “not from men”], that it is not according to man, that is, according to human teaching.

[Note: [Col. 0262A] 22. “For I make known to you.” He is responding to what he said above: “Not from men, nor through a man.”]

For I did not receive it from a human being as something written down, nor did I learn it, but through a revelation of Jesus Christ.

[Note: [Col. 0262A] 23. “For neither did I.” It is as though he said: “No human being taught me, because I did not learn it from a human being.”]

[Note: [Col. 0262A] 24. “For you have heard.” He explains how he received the Gospel through the revelation of Jesus Christ.]

For you have heard of my former way of life 121 in Judaism,

[Note: [Col. 0262A] 25. AMBROSE. “For you have heard.” By explaining how zealously he had labored concerning the Law, he shows that he did not despise the Law, but recognized and chose what was better.]

how excessively I persecuted the Church of God and ravaged it, and progressed in Judaism

[Note: [Col. 0262A] 26. “Above many.” Properly, “my contemporaries.” This is all the more significant if he appeared more impetuous than young men.]

beyond many of my contemporaries, of the same age, in my nation, among the Jews, being more abundantly zealous

[Note: [Col. 0262B] 27. AUGUSTINE (ibid.). “Being zealous,” that is, an imitator of traditions that were opposed to the Church. For the Law is spiritual, but they had handed down many things that dissolved God’s commandments on account of their own traditions.]

for the traditions of my fathers.

[Note: [Col. 0262B] 28. LANFRANC. “But when it pleased him.” He proves that he did not receive the Gospel from a human being, neither after his conversion nor before it. Before his conversion he did not receive it from a human being, because he was attacking what you heard. After his conversion he did not receive it, because he did not submit immediately, nor after three years, nor after fourteen; it is clear that this occurred at another time. He removes the possibilities about which suspicion had arisen.]

[Note: [Col. 0262B] 29. AUGUSTINE (ibid.). “But when it pleased him.” Anyone who is separated from the blind custom of carnal parents is, in a certain sense, set apart from his mother’s womb. Whoever assents to the carnal persuasion of carnal relatives, however, submits to flesh and blood.]

But when it pleased him who set me apart from my mother’s womb—from the unbelief of the synagogue, or from carnal kinship—and called me through his grace, to reveal his Son in me so that I might preach him among the Gentiles, immediately

[Note: [Col. 0262C] 30. AMBROSE. “I did not submit.” The Apostle does not say, “but not to human beings,” but “to flesh and blood.” And he says, “I did not immediately explain it”; for he explained it to them later.]

I did not submit to flesh and blood, or to my relatives, nor did I go up to Jerusalem to those who were apostles before me; instead I went away to Arabia and returned again to Damascus.

Then, after three years, I went up to Jerusalem to visit Peter, [Col. 0263] not in order to learn, but merely to see him, and I stayed with him for only fifteen days, during which I do not seem to have been able to learn anything. But I saw none of the other apostles at that time, except James, the brother of the Lord. Whatever I am writing to you,

[Note: [Col. 0263A] 31. AUGUSTINE (ibid.). “Behold, before God.” Thus he swears an oath. The oath that arises from evil is not the fault of the one who swears, but of the unbelief that compels him to swear. For the Lord’s prohibition against swearing is understood in this way: insofar as it depends on each person, no one should swear. Many do this, keeping an oath on their lips as though it were something important or pleasant.]

behold, before God, with God as my witness, I am not lying. Then I went into the regions of Syria and Cilicia.

[Note: [Col. 0263A] 32. LANFRANC. “But I was unknown by face.” I did not receive it from them, because, although it is established that I was already preaching, I was unknown to them by sight, since I was known only by report.]

But I was personally unknown to the churches of Judaea that are in Christ. They had only heard that the one who once persecuted us—namely, I, Paul—now preached the faith of Christ that he had once tried to destroy; and they glorified God because of me.

[COMMENTARY.]

[Col. 0259B]

Chapter I.—1. LANFRANC. “Paul, an apostle not from men,” etc. In the other Epistles, after offering a greeting, he immediately begins with thanksgiving; here he does not, for they were not such as to provide him with grounds for giving thanks.

2. AUGUSTINE (Exposition of the First Chapter of the Epistle to the Galatians, vol. IV). “Not from men.” He who is sent by men is a liar; he who is sent through a man can be truthful, because the truthful God can send someone through a man. Thus the earlier apostles were sent by God through a man—namely, through Jesus while he was still mortal. The last Apostle was sent through Christ, who was already wholly God, that is, immortal in every respect. Let his authority, therefore, be equal to theirs, in whose honor the glorification of the Lord is fulfilled; if the order of time entails anything, it is not for that reason lesser, since, after he had said “and God,” he added, “who raised him” [Col. 0259C].

3. AMBROSE. “Not from men.” By saying the same thing, he divides the phrase, to show by the very multiplicity of his account that they in no way speak the truth.

4. LANFRANC. “Not from men.” Some thought that he had not been sent as an apostle by Christ, but by other apostles or by Ananias. He denies this so that he may possess greater authority among those to whom he preached the word of God.

5. AUGUSTINE (ibid.). “Grace to you and peace.” The grace of God is that by which our sins are forgiven, so that we may be reconciled to God. Peace, moreover, is that by which we are reconciled to God [Col. 0260B].

7. AUGUSTINE (ibid.). “From the present age.” He calls the present age evil because of the evil people who are in it. Just as we call a house evil because evil people inhabit it.

8. AMBROSE. “I am astonished that so.” A fitting opening in view of the novelty of what has happened. For he says “I am astonished” as though something had occurred that was thought never to be capable of happening.

9. LANFRANC. “You are being transferred.” These Galatians, partly Jews and partly Gentiles, had been converted by the Apostle to faith in Christ. But after his departure, false preachers came, compelling those who had been converted from Judaism to practice Judaism, while those who had come from the Gentiles to the faith were compelled to worship the elements of the world and observe days and years [Col. 0260C].

10. AMBROSE. “You are being transferred.” He does not say “you are being led over” but “you are being transferred,” as though they were lifeless people without any movement of the mind.

11. “From him who called you.” So that they would not seem to be departing from Christ alone, he added “from God.”

[Col. 0261A] 12. LANFRANC. “Into another gospel.” The gospel is good proclamation; their preaching, therefore, was not the Gospel, because it was not good proclamation. “Another gospel” may also be understood as the observance of the Jewish Law, which does not conflict with the Gospel of Christ if it is understood spiritually. This is what he means when he says, “There are some,” that is, there are indeed those who understand it carnally and perversely.

13. “Another gospel.” The Gospel is different only to those who do not wish to understand it spiritually. Or that is not the Gospel except to those who deceive you—and such people would be accursed. He does not say this directly, but adds it in order to intensify the point.

14. AUGUSTINE (ibid.). “Into another gospel.” If the Gospel is something other than what the Lord gave, either directly or through others, it can no longer rightly be called the Gospel [Col. 0261B].

15. AUGUSTINE (ibid.). “Those who trouble you.” Having said “who trouble you,” he did not say “and convert you,” but “wish to convert the Gospel”; yet it remains completely firm and unaltered.

16. AMBROSE. “But even if we.” He shows that he is not setting himself above them, but that he is defending the truth.

17. “Or an angel.” He added this to show that neither the dignity of a place nor that of a person could be made equal to the truth.

18. “Now then.” He says this to show that, although he uttered such words on behalf of the truth, he considered those who disparaged him to be of no importance.

19. AUGUSTINE (ibid.). “Now then, am I persuading human beings?” The meaning is: “I am persuading human beings and not God.” [Col. 0261C] For we have been manifested to God; and because I am persuading human beings, am I seeking to please human beings? If I were pleasing human beings—that is, if I were seeking to please them—I would not be a servant of Christ.

20. LANFRANC. “Now then, am I persuading human beings?” It is as though he said: “I am not speaking flatteringly in order to please you, but reproving your fickleness in order to please God.”

21. “Am I persuading human beings or God?” Someone might say: “Why do you pronounce such a curse?” He replies: “So that I may show that I am neither a participant in nor a persuader of circumcision, as the false apostles are.” Or: “I pronounce the curse because I am not persuading people in order to wish to please them,” with the question understood in this way: “Am I seeking to please human beings?” [Col. 0262A]

22. “For I make known to you.” He is responding to what he said above: “Not from men, nor through a man.”

23. “For neither did I.” It is as though he said: “No human being taught me, because I did not learn it from a human being.”

24. “For you have heard.” He explains how he received the Gospel through the revelation of Jesus Christ.

25. AMBROSE. “For you have heard.” By explaining how zealously he had labored concerning the Law, he shows that he did not despise the Law, but recognized and chose what was better.

26. “Above many.” Properly, “my contemporaries.” This is all the more significant if he appeared more impetuous than young men [Col. 0262B].

27. AUGUSTINE (ibid.). “Being zealous,” that is, an imitator of traditions that were opposed to the Church. For the Law is spiritual, but they had handed down many things that dissolved God’s commandments on account of their own traditions.

28. LANFRANC. “But when it pleased him.” He proves that he did not receive the Gospel from a human being, neither after his conversion nor before it. Before his conversion he did not receive it from a human being, because he was attacking what you heard. After his conversion he did not receive it, because he did not submit immediately, nor after three years, nor after fourteen; it is clear that this occurred at another time. He removes the possibilities about which suspicion had arisen.

29. AUGUSTINE (ibid.). “But when it pleased him.” Anyone who is separated from the blind custom of carnal parents is, in a certain sense, set apart from his mother’s womb. Whoever assents to the carnal persuasion of carnal relatives, however, submits to flesh and blood [Col. 0262C].

30. AMBROSE. “I did not submit.” The Apostle does not say, “but not to human beings,” but “to flesh and blood.” And he says, “I did not immediately explain it”; for he explained it to them later.

[Col. 0263A] 31. AUGUSTINE (ibid.). “Behold, before God.” Thus he swears an oath. The oath that arises from evil is not the fault of the one who swears, but of the unbelief that compels him to swear. CHAPTER II.

[Col. 0263]

Then after fourteen years I went up again [Note: [Col. 0263A] CHAP. II.—1. LANFRANC. “I went up to Jerusalem.” He went up, indeed, not in order to learn; rather, because it was thought that his Gospel differed from that of the apostles, since he had not been chosen along with the others and had not heard it from Christ. Therefore he says that he came by divine revelation in order to compare his Gospel with theirs, so that it could no longer rightly be rejected.] to Jerusalem with Barnabas (but I did not receive it even then), taking Titus with me. AUGUSTINE (Exposition on Galatians, chap. 2). “Privately.” This was not done because he had said something false and therefore told the truth privately to fewer people; rather, he had kept silent about certain things that the immature could not bear. But, on the contrary, when they saw that I had been entrusted with the Gospel of the uncircumcised, of the Gentiles, just as Peter had been entrusted with that of the circumcised—for he who worked in Peter for the apostleship of the circumcised, of the Jews, worked also in me among the Gentiles—and when they recognized the grace that had been given to me, James, Cephas, and John, who seemed to be pillars, [Note: [Col. 0265B] 16. [Note: [Col. 0265C] 18. LANFRANC. “Of fellowship with Barnabas.” By this he shows that he had not been a disciple of Christ’s disciples; otherwise he would not call himself their companion.]

[Note: “Another commendation.”]

[Note: [Col. 0265C] 19. AUGUSTINE (Letter 10 to Jerome, vol. II). “When Cephas came.” We do not deny that Peter was already in the same position in this matter as Paul. AUGUSTINE (Exposition on the Epistle to the Galatians, chap. II). “And not from the Gentiles.” The Jews gave the Gentiles the name “sinners,” out of an ancient arrogance, as though they themselves were righteous—seeing the speck in another’s eye and not the beam in their own. [Note: [Col. 0266C] 25. LANFRANC. “Sinners.” He calls idolaters “sinners” by a general term.]

yet, knowing that a person is not justified by works of the law but only through faith in Jesus Christ, we too have believed in Christ Jesus, so that we might be justified by faith in Christ and not by works of the law; therefore, because justification is by faith in Christ alone, by works of the law no flesh will be justified. Thus far is an interpolation, and these are the Apostle’s words to Peter. [Note: [Col. 0267A] 27. AMBROSE. “But if, while seeking.” The meaning is wrapped in obscurity.
