But if, while believing in him with this hope, we are found to be sinners because we do not keep the law, he seems, by his coming, to have become an agent of sin.]

But if, while seeking to be justified in Christ alone, we ourselves are found to be sinners, is Christ therefore a minister of sin? Certainly not! [Note: [Col. 0267B] 28. AUGUSTINE (Exposition on the Epistle to the Galatians, chap. II). “But if, while seeking.” Did they perhaps sin because they wished to be justified in Christ? For if they were righteous, then by seeking something else they certainly sinned. But if that is so, Christ is therefore a minister of sin.]

Far be it from him! [Note: [Col. 0267B] 29. LANFRANC. “Is Christ therefore?” He says this on behalf of the weak. Earlier he said that the Jews were not sinners, and afterward added that they too are justified by faith in Jesus Christ; but everyone who is justified was in sin. Therefore it seemed, to someone who understood the matter badly—or perhaps “was understood” badly—that Christ first supplied sins and afterward gave life through his faith and grace.]

For if I rebuild the very things that I destroyed, I prove myself a transgressor. [Note: [Col. 0267C] 30. “For if I rebuild what I destroyed.” It is as though he were saying: “I destroyed this question, which has often been brought against me; if I build it again, I make myself a liar and a transgressor.”]

[Note: [Col. 0267C] 31. AUGUSTINE (the same). “For if I rebuild what I destroyed.” He destroyed the pride that boasted in works of the law—pride that both ought to be and could be destroyed, lest the grace of faith appear unnecessary. Therefore he is a transgressor if he builds it up again by saying that even the works of the law justify without grace, so that Christ would be found to be a minister of sin.]

For through the law I died to the law, so that I might live for God; [Note: [Col. 0267C] 32. AMBROSE. “For through the law.” In the law itself I found Christ preached; by believing in him, I died to the law.]

[Note: [Col. 0268A] 33. AUGUSTINE (the same). “For through the law.” Because [125] he had been a Jew and had received the law as a tutor. What is accomplished through a tutor is that there is no longer need of a tutor—just as an infant is nourished by the breast so that he eventually no longer needs the breast.]

[Note: [Col. 0268A] 34. LANFRANC. “For through the law.” He returns to prove what was said above. For he would die to his law in order to live for God in vain if he could be justified by it, since to live for God is nothing other than to be righteous in the sight of God.]

I have been crucified with Christ; [Note: [Col. 0268A] 35. “Crucified with Christ”—that is, I have been crucified with Christ: just as he was crucified in the flesh, so I have been crucified to vices and desires.] yet I live—no longer I, as before, or the person I once was: [Note: [Col. 0268B] 36. AMBROSE. “But I live.” In baptism the form of Christ’s death and resurrection is fulfilled. He calls things that are to occur in reality already accomplished, because he possesses hope of them.]

[Note: [Col. 0268B] 37. “But Christ lives in me,” because by hope he lives the mortal life of Christ.]

but Christ lives in me, because he hopes for his immortal life. He explains: [Note: [Col. 0268B] 38. AUGUSTINE (the same). “But Christ lives in me.” “Christ lives in me”—what follows? Deny yourself; do not live in yourself. What does “do not live in yourself” mean except not to do your own will, but the will of him who dwells in you?]

And the life I now live in the flesh I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me [he commends this] and gave himself for me. Therefore [Note: [Col. 0268B] 39. (The same.) “I do not reject.” If Christ loved me and gave himself for me, I do not nullify the grace of God by saying that righteousness comes through the law.] I do not reject the grace of God. [Note: [Col. 0268C] 40. LANFRANC. “I do not reject.” “Although,” he says, “I am a Jew and may appear righteous through observance of the law, I nevertheless do not reject the grace of God—that is, the forgiveness of sins through faith in Christ.”]

For if righteousness comes through the law, it does not come through Christ’s death; therefore Christ died for nothing. [Note: [Col. 0268C] 41. “For if through the law.” He again returns to prove what was said above: that no flesh is justified by works of the law, and so forth. He leads the contrary position to an absurd consequence.]

[Note: [Col. 0268C] 42. “For if righteousness comes through the law,” and so forth. He continues to prove that righteousness does not come through the law; for if it did, it would not come through Christ. And if it did not come through Christ, Christ’s death was in vain—that is, fruitless, since it produced no benefit. This is a distinction between the definition and the thing defined.]

[Note: [Col. 0268C] 43. “Christ died for nothing.” Christ died for this purpose: to make those who believe in him righteous. Therefore he died for nothing if legal observance could make people righteous.]

[COMMENTARY.]

[Col. 0263A]

CHAPTER II.—1. LANFRANC. “I went up to Jerusalem.” He went up, indeed, not in order to learn; rather, because it was thought that his Gospel differed from that of the apostles, since he had not been chosen along with the others and had not heard it from Christ. Therefore he says that he came by divine revelation in order to compare his Gospel with theirs, so that it could no longer rightly be rejected.

2. AUGUSTINE (Exposition on Galatians, chap. 2). “Privately.” This was not done because he had said something false and therefore told the truth privately to fewer people; rather, he had kept silent about certain things that the immature could not bear. It was therefore necessary that the other apostles should know his perfection.

3. (The same.) “Those who seemed.” They seem to be something to carnal people, for they themselves are not something; although they are good ministers of God, Christ is something in them.

4. (The same.) “Lest perhaps in vain.” “Lest perhaps I run, or have run, in vain?” This should be understood as spoken in the form of a question, so that it might become clear from it that he was not running, or had not run, in vain, since, by the testimony of the others, he was already shown to disagree in nothing from the truth of the Gospel.

5. AMBROSE. “Lest perhaps in vain”—that is, lest at some time I be thought to be pursuing a course of my own, one unsuitable for the other apostles.

6. LANFRANC. “But not even Titus.” The other apostles wanted Titus to be circumcised in order to avoid giving offense to certain faithful people who had believed through circumcision. But the Apostle did not permit him to be circumcised because of certain false Christians who moved secretly among the faithful in order to test their freedom—by which they disregarded circumcision and the other carnal observances. They tested it in order, with some cunning, to destroy that freedom and persuade them to observe the law.

7. “Titus, who was with me.” “But not even then did he receive it.” This is what he means: “I was not subject to them, since not even Titus was.” (An argument from the lesser.) Yet this was not out of arrogance, but because of the false brothers. He calls it “freedom” because he preached freely, neglecting carnal observances. Certain false men came, however, to see whether he himself at Jerusalem would consent to the observances of the law.

8. AUGUSTINE (the same). “That they might bring us into slavery”—that is, so that, now with Paul’s testimony as well, they might preach circumcision itself as necessary for salvation.

9. AMBROSE. “The truth of the Gospel”—that is, so that it might be evident proof that our Gospel had been preached, since we did not fear our opponents, not even when we were among them.

10. LANFRANC. “The truth of the Gospel.” The truth of the Gospel is to observe God’s moral commandments with faith, without circumcision and the other legal observances.

11. “But from those.” He says this so that he might not appear vainly to exalt himself against his superiors. It is an interpolation extending from the place where it says, “But not even Titus,” to the place, “But those who seemed to be something to me.”

12. “But from those.” The order is: “But those who seemed to be something”—this signifies Peter, John, and James, because they were of greater dignity among the other apostles, whom he shortly afterward calls “pillars.” He therefore says that it is irrelevant to him to show what they had been, whether in status or in knowledge, before their calling. He does not detract from the other apostles; rather, because the Galatians were excessively magnifying the other apostles, preferring them to this one and therefore holding his authority in lower regard, he shows that he was their equal and had not received the doctrine of the Gospel from them.

13. “Those who seemed to be something.” Lest anyone should say that he ought to agree with them because they had been better than he, since they had not persecuted the Church as he had, he answers this—not out of envy, but in order to commend himself, that is, his preaching—and says: “But from those who seemed to be something”; that is, those who seemed to be something, although I could say what sort of people they were, namely, contemptible and sinners like myself, contributed nothing to me.

14. “God does not accept a person’s status.” He says this because he was reproached for having formerly persecuted the Church, as though those who are now just, holy, and great in everyone’s estimation had not once been sinners like him. This is because God is not a respecter of persons. Likewise, although I was a persecutor, I should not be despised by you.

15. AUGUSTINE (Exposition on Galatians). “Those who seemed.” Peter, James, and John were more honored than the others because the Lord showed himself to them on the mountain as a sign of his kingdom, after saying six days earlier: “There are some standing here who will not taste death until they see the Son of Man in his Father’s kingdom” (Matthew 16).

16. (The same.) “But, on the contrary, when they saw.” That is, conversely, they became approvers of his perfection instead of reprovers. The order may also be understood in this way: “But conversely, so that we should go to the Gentiles,” who are opposed to circumcision.

17. (In Bede.) “They gave me the right hands.” He says that he came to Jerusalem and compared the Gospel with the apostles, and that they gave him their right hands—that is, a sign of agreement and harmony—because what he had learned from them differed in no respect.

[Col. 0265C] 18. LANFRANC. “Of fellowship with Barnabas.” By this he shows that he had not been a disciple of Christ’s disciples; otherwise he would not call himself their companion.

19. AUGUSTINE (Letter 10 to Jerome, vol. II). “When Cephas came.” We do not deny that Peter was already in the same position in this matter as Paul. Paul was therefore not teaching him then what was true in that matter, but was reproving his dissimulation, by which the Gentiles were being compelled to Judaize. He did so for no other reason than that everything was being done hypocritically, as though what those people were saying were true—namely, that believers could not be saved without circumcision of the foreskin and the other observances that were shadows of things to come.

20. LANFRANC. “When he came, and so forth.” He proves again that he did not receive the Gospel from Peter even at Antioch, because he opposed him; for Peter was blameworthy.

21. “I opposed him to his face.” What was openly harmful should not have been corrected secretly; indeed, one had to presume upon the strength [perhaps: weakness] of so great an apostle’s charity. Or this was because certain men who had been introduced as spies were waiting to report that Paul had not dared to rebuke Peter—and they would have been circumcised.

22. “If you, though a Jew.” He lived like a Gentile because he ate indiscriminately with everyone and considered no one unclean. He proves that, since he was a Jew and nevertheless lived like a Gentile, he ought not to compel Gentiles to Judaize. The whole syllogism is present in the book, except for its conclusion.

23. “You compel them to Judaize.” By his example Peter compelled the Gentiles to Judaize and follow the Jewish rite, when, in the presence of those who had come from the Jews, he withdrew from the company of the Gentiles in the Jewish manner.

24. AUGUSTINE (Exposition on the Epistle to the Galatians, chap. II). “And not from the Gentiles.” The Jews gave the Gentiles the name “sinners,” out of an ancient arrogance, as though they themselves were righteous—seeing the speck in another’s eye and not the beam in their own. Just as there is a difference between those who mock and those who are mockers, between those who murmur and habitual murmurers, between those who write and writers, and in similar cases, so Scripture has become accustomed to call “sinners” those who are exceedingly wicked and burdened with the loads of sins.

25. LANFRANC. “Sinners.” He calls idolaters “sinners” by a general term.

[Col. 0267A] 26. “By works of the law.” “Not by works of the law”; for if this were so, justification would not be in Christ alone, whereas it is in Christ alone. If justification were not in Christ alone, we would sin by abandoning the law and seeking to be justified in Christ alone. But this is not so; for if it were, if we sinned by seeking justification through Christ alone, Christ would be a minister of sin. But far be it from Christ to be a minister of sin! Therefore we do not sin by seeking to be justified in Christ alone. If this is true, then no flesh will be justified by works of the law; for if I say this, I make myself a transgressor, since I have abandoned the law while admitting that it justifies.

27. AMBROSE. “But if, while seeking.” The meaning is wrapped in obscurity. He wishes to say that we are not justified according to the law; we came to Christ as though we were to be justified through him. But if, while believing in him with this hope, we are found to be sinners because we do not keep the law, he seems, by his coming, to have become an agent of sin.

28. AUGUSTINE (Exposition on the Epistle to the Galatians, chap. II). “But if, while seeking.” Did they perhaps sin because they wished to be justified in Christ? For if they were righteous, then by seeking something else they certainly sinned. But if that is so, Christ is therefore a minister of sin.

29. LANFRANC. “Is Christ therefore?” He says this on behalf of the weak. Earlier he said that the Jews were not sinners, and afterward added that they too are justified by faith in Jesus Christ; but everyone who is justified was in sin. Therefore it seemed, to someone who understood the matter badly—or perhaps “was understood” badly—that Christ first supplied sins and afterward gave life through his faith and grace.

30. “For if I rebuild what I destroyed.” It is as though he were saying: “I destroyed this question, which has often been brought against me; if I build it again, I make myself a liar and a transgressor.”

31. AUGUSTINE (the same). “For if I rebuild what I destroyed.” He destroyed the pride that boasted in works of the law—pride that both ought to be and could be destroyed, lest the grace of faith appear unnecessary. Therefore he is a transgressor if he builds it up again by saying that even the works of the law justify without grace, so that Christ would be found to be a minister of sin.

32. AMBROSE. “For through the law.” In the law itself I found Christ preached; by believing in him, I died to the law.

33. AUGUSTINE (the same). “For through the law.” Because he had been a Jew and had received the law as a tutor. What is accomplished through a tutor is that there is no longer need of a tutor—just as an infant is nourished by the breast so that he eventually no longer needs the breast.

34. LANFRANC. “For through the law.” He returns to prove what was said above. He said earlier that no flesh is justified by works, and proves it by saying that through the law of Christ he died to his own law so that he might live for God. For he would die to his law in order to live for God in vain if he could be justified by it, since to live for God is nothing other than to be righteous in the sight of God.

35. “Crucified with Christ”—that is, I have been crucified with Christ: just as he was crucified in the flesh, so I have been crucified to vices and desires.

36. AMBROSE. “But I live.” In baptism the form of Christ’s death and resurrection is fulfilled. He calls things that are to occur in reality already accomplished, because he possesses hope of them.

37. “But Christ lives in me,” because by hope he lives the mortal life of Christ.

38. AUGUSTINE (the same). “But Christ lives in me.” “Christ lives in me”—what follows? Deny yourself; do not live in yourself. What does “do not live in yourself” mean except not to do your own will, but the will of him who dwells in you?

39. (The same.) “I do not reject.” If Christ loved me and gave himself for me, I do not nullify the grace of God by saying that righteousness comes through the law.

40. LANFRANC. “I do not reject.” “Although,” he says, “I am a Jew and may appear righteous through observance of the law, I nevertheless do not reject the grace of God—that is, the forgiveness of sins through faith in Christ.”

41. “For if through the law.” He again returns to prove what was said above: that no flesh is justified by works of the law, and so forth. He leads the contrary position to an absurd consequence.

42. “For if righteousness comes through the law,” and so forth. He continues to prove that righteousness does not come through the law; for if it did, it would not come through Christ. And if it did not come through Christ, Christ’s death was in vain—that is, fruitless, since it produced no benefit. This is a distinction between the definition and the thing defined.

43. “Christ died for nothing.” Christ died for this purpose: to make those who believe in him righteous. Therefore he died for nothing if legal observance could make people righteous.

# CHAPTER III.

[Col. 0269]

[Note: [Col. 0269A] Chapter III.—1. AMBROSE. “O foolish Galatians!” This is inserted from that place up to this point: “I wish to learn only this from you,” etc. For he could have said: “This alone I wish to learn from you.”]

“O foolish Galatians, who has bewitched you”—weak and tender things are said to be bewitched—“so that you do not obey the truth,” [Note: [Col. 0269A] 2. “Before whose eyes.” He was set forth and crucified among you. He means that, when you heard the words of the cross with such deep emotion that you painted the cross itself before our eyes, and almost also the things that occurred at that time, by what enchantment have you cast away so great an affection as you seemed to have for Christ?] [Note: [Col. 0269B] 3. AUGUSTINE (Commentary on the Epistle to the Galatians, chapter III, [Col. 0269B] vol. IV). “Before whose”—that is, while they were looking on, Christ Jesus lost his inheritance and possession, because they took it away from him, expelled the Lord from it, recalled those who had believed to the works of the Law, and deprived him of his possession—that is, of those in whom grace and faith dwell.] [Note: [Col. 0269B] 4. LANFRANC. “Before whose eyes.” Before the eyes of their mind Jesus Christ was publicly proclaimed—that is, he was condemned and crucified; that is, he was held in contempt, since they thought that a person was not justified through faith in him but through observance of the Law.] before whose eyes [Note: [Col. 0269B] 5. AUGUSTINE (ibid.). “Jesus Christ was publicly portrayed.” In another way, Jesus Christ was publicly portrayed as crucified. He added “crucified” so that, when they considered at what price he had purchased the possession that he was losing among them, he might chiefly admonish—or, according to another reading, move—them by this.]

Jesus Christ was publicly portrayed, was condemned, while you are being taken away from him as his inheritance, crucified among you? And he himself is disinherited, crucified for you—or, you who retain in memory that he suffered for you. [Note: [Col. 0269C] 6. (ibid.). “This alone from you.” From this point he begins to demonstrate grace, showing how the grace of faith is sufficient for justification without the works of the Law.] This alone I wish to learn from you. [Note: [Col. 0269C] 7. LANFRANC. “You received the Spirit from the works of the Law.” If you have the Spirit from faith, as he has already proved, and therefore says, “Do you consequently possess miraculous powers from faith,” which are the cause of justification—that is, you possess justification itself from faith—then the one follows from the other. They possess miraculous powers from faith because Abraham’s justification was from faith; for it is written, etc. He treats miraculous powers and justification as equivalents, since one is the cause of the other.]

Did you receive the Spirit from the works of the Law [Note: [Col. 0270A] 8. “You received the Spirit.” Those who believed received spiritual graces; they did not perform the works of the Law.] or from hearing with faith? From this, certainly.

Are you so foolish [Note: [Col. 0270A] 9. “Having begun with the Spirit.” You began with the Spirit, either as living spiritually [the reading may be “to live”], or as understanding the Law spiritually; now you are being brought to an end by the flesh—that is, by a carnal life or by the Law understood carnally. “Are you being consumed” is the subjunctive of *consumor, consumeris*, meaning “may you perish.” “You are being completed” is the indicative of *consummor, consummaris*, meaning “you are ending your life.” Both readings are found in Scripture at this place.] that, having begun with the Spirit, you are now being brought to an end by the flesh? You began to live spiritually; are you returning to carnal observances?

Therefore, because you do not have faith, did you suffer so many things [Note: [Col. 0270B] 10. “In vain.” In vain—that is, uselessly—suffers the person who does not have faith in Christ.] in vain? If indeed it was in vain”—he repeats what he said: that they received the Spirit not from the works of the Law but from faith, because Abraham did so, etc.—“Does he who supplies the Spirit to you and works miracles among you do this from the works of the Law, on account of the works of the Law, or from hearing, on account of hearing, with faith?”

As it is written—he proves that Abraham was justified by faith—“Abraham believed God,” that is, he had faith, and from it justification; “and it was reckoned to him as righteousness.”

[Note: [Col. 0270B] 11. “Know therefore.” Because Abraham was justified by faith, and all are justified by faith alone, which is equivalent to saying: “These are the sons of Abraham.”]

Know therefore that those who are of faith are sons of Abraham. But Scripture, foreseeing that God justifies the nations by faith—for Scripture says so in Genesis XII—announced beforehand to Abraham: [Note: [Col. 0270B] 12. AMBROSE. “They will be blessed in you.” That is, with you, and they will share your blessing.] “In you”—in imitation of your faith, or in him who will be born from you, that is, Christ—“all the nations will be blessed.”

Therefore, since Scripture testifies that those who are of faith will be blessed—that is, justified—together with faithful Abraham, as the faithful are, [Note: [Col. 0270B] 13. LANFRANC. “For whoever.” As though he were saying: Blessing is either from faith or from works; but it is not from works (for blessing comes from faith); therefore it is from faith.] all who are of the works of the Law are under a curse. For it is written in Deuteronomy XXVII—the preceding proposition is established by authoritative testimony— [Note: [Col. 0270B] 14. AMBROSE. “Cursed is everyone.” The Law considers everyone who hangs upon a tree accursed, because this kind of punishment was appointed for those found guilty of many offenses.]

“Cursed is everyone who does not remain in all the things”—this is the assumption and conclusion—“that are written in the book of the Law, to do them.” 126–127

Therefore—and he repeats the point from the contrary—since no one is justified before God by the Law, it is evident that the righteous person lives by faith. [Note: [Col. 0270C] 15. LANFRANC. “Lives by faith.” If righteousness is not from the Law, it is from faith alone.]

Someone might say: “The Law is faith,” and thus righteousness is from the Law. [Note: [Col. 0270C] 16. “But the Law is not.” That is, the faith of Christ does not permit the Jewish Law to be observed, or the Law and faith do not agree. But the Law says, “The one who does”; it does not say, “The one who believes.”]

But the Law is not from faith [Col. 0271]—that is, the Law does not command belief but action. Rather, “the one who does these things that are in the Law will live by them.” [Note: [Col. 0271A] 17. “Christ redeemed us from the curse.” You say that everyone who does not remain in the things written in the book of the Law is accursed; so too are you who remain. To this he replies: “Christ redeemed us,” etc.]

Christ redeemed us from the curse of the Law, [Note: [Col. 0271A] 18. AUGUSTINE (Commentary on the Epistle to the Galatians, chapter III). “Having become a curse for us.” He hung upon the tree in his mortal aspect. Believers know the origin of mortality. It arises from the punishment and curse of the first man’s sin; the Lord assumed this mortality and bore our sins in his body upon the tree.] having become a curse for us—that is, accursed by the Jews, or having become mortal; here he puts the cause for the effect.

For it is written—and he proves that Christ was accursed; for “everyone who hangs upon a tree” is accursed, though this precise statement is not written—“Cursed is everyone who hangs upon a tree.” Christ became a curse for this purpose: so that among the Gentiles [Note: [Col. 0271A] 19. LANFRANC. “The blessing of Abraham might come.” He proves that faith, not the Law, gives justification. For if the Law gave justification, it would destroy the testament of Abraham’s faith made to us. But the Law cannot destroy it; no later testament destroys the first. The testament of faith is earlier, while the Law is later. This assumption is found in the book as follows: “Now I say that a testament confirmed by God,” etc. He proves by analogy that no later testament destroys the first, because human custom establishes that a later testament does not destroy the first after the death of the person who made it; hence the phrase, “I speak in human terms.” When he adds, “The promises were spoken to Abraham,” he answers the question whether any testament had been confirmed by God to someone, saying that it had been made to Abraham and to his seed, who is Christ.] the blessing—the justification—of Abraham might come through faith in Christ Jesus, so that [Note: [Col. 0271B] 20. “The promise of the Spirit.” That is, the promise of the Spirit, whom he promised that he would give to believers; or the justification that the Holy Spirit promised to believers, saying: “In your seed,” etc.] we might receive the promise of the Spirit—that is, the justification promised by the Spirit—through faith.

“Brothers, I speak in human terms.” Yet, by analogy, no one rejects, destroys, or alters a confirmed human testament. Is there, then, some testament confirmed by God to someone? There is, he says: to Abraham and to his seed. “The promises were spoken to Abraham and to his seed.” [Note: [Col. 0271C] 21. “A confirmed testament.” He says: No one rejects a human testament concerning his property; therefore, much less should God’s testament be rejected, by which he testified that all nations would be blessed in Abraham’s seed.]

He does not say “and to seeds,” as though referring to many; [Note: [Col. 0271C] 22. “He does not say ‘and to seeds.’” In making the promise God does not say, “In your seeds all the nations will be blessed,” but “in your seed.”] in saying “to your seed,” and not “to seeds,” he indicates the unity of the Church to which the promise was made. He says this because of those who were creating schisms, but as though referring to one person, [Note: [Col. 0271C] 23. AUGUSTINE. “And to your seed.” From the people of Israel the Virgin was born and gave birth to Christ; and behold, in Christ all the nations are blessed. What is truer? What is more certain? What is clearer?] namely, to your seed, who is Christ.

[Note: [Col. 0272A] 24. AUGUSTINE (from *Treatises on the Gospel according to John*, 39). “In your seed.” Since we too belong to what is Christ, being incorporated with him and joined to that head, there is one Christ. And because he says also to us, “Therefore you are Abraham’s seed, heirs according to the promise,” if Abraham has one seed, and that one seed is understood to be none other than Christ, then we are this seed of Abraham. The whole—that is, the head and the body—is therefore one Christ.]

And, specifically, “to your seed,” who is Christ, [Note: [Col. 0272A] 25. LANFRANC. “Now I say this.” The order is: “I say that the Law, which was made after four hundred and thirty years, does not invalidate this testament.” If only those who observe the Jewish Law were blessed in Abraham’s seed, God’s testament would in some respect have been invalidated, and his promise emptied, by which he promised that all nations would be blessed in Abraham’s seed.] this I say: the faith, or the promise itself, [p. 128], is a testament confirmed by God through God’s own unchangeability. The Law, which was made four hundred and thirty years afterward, after God had made the promise that the earlier testament declares, does not invalidate it so as to abolish the promise, thereby annulling the testament of faith—which would happen if the inheritance of glory were not in charity. [Note: [Col. 0272B] 26. “For if the inheritance is from the Law.” Blessing or inheritance is received through faith alone, not through the Law, because the Law does not destroy the testament of faith previously confirmed by God to Abraham. Therefore, if the Law does not destroy the testament of faith, it does not give blessing or inheritance. The analogy is that a later human testament does not destroy a confirmed earlier testament. This analogy is introduced to prove the proposition that the Law does not destroy the testament, as the book states: “Now I say that a testament [Col. 0272C] confirmed by God,” etc.]

For if the inheritance is from the Law, [Note: [Col. 0272C] 27. “Then it is no longer from the promise.” That is, if only those who observe the Jewish Law are heirs, then the inheritance is no longer given according to God’s promise, which speaks of everyone.] then it is no longer from the promise”—this is the assumption—“but God granted the inheritance to Abraham through the promise,” that is, through faith.

Objection.

[Note: [Col. 0272C] 28. AUGUSTINE (from Sermon 13, *On the Words of the Apostle*, chapter 4, vol. X). “Why, then, the Law? Why, then, the Law?” That is, what was the usefulness of the Law? It was established on account of transgression. This is what is said elsewhere: “The Law entered in so that transgression might abound”; it was established on account of transgression. Thus the necks of the proud, who attributed much to themselves, might be humbled, since they thought that free choice could suffice for them unto righteousness.]

Why [Col. 0273]—for what purpose, then—was the Law established?

Response.

[Note: [Col. 0273A] 29. AMBROSE. “On account of transgressions.” The Law was established for a proud people so that, since they could not receive the grace of charity unless humbled, they might be humbled through transgression and seek grace.]

It was established on account of transgression—that no one might do more than ought to be done—namely, the Law, [Note: [Col. 0273A] 30. LANFRANC. “Until the seed should come to whom.” God the Father had promised Christ the inheritance of the whole world, as in the Psalm: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations,” etc.] until the seed should come to whom he had made the promise.

God—[gives] righteousness, or blessing; the Law was ordained through angels, by the hand and authority of the Mediator, Christ, [Note: [Col. 0273A] 31. AUGUSTINE (Commentary on the Epistle to the Galatians, chapter III, vol. IV). “The seed to whom he made the promise.” The seed to whom the promise was made signifies the people of believers.]

But the mediator—lest two be understood—adds: “A mediator is not of one”; [Note: [Col. 0273B] 32. AMBROSE. “But the mediator.” If the Son of God had wished to remain in natural equality, without emptying himself by taking the form of a servant, he would not have been the Mediator of God and human beings, because the Trinity itself is one God. Thus the only Son of God became the Mediator of God and human beings: the Word of God, God with God, lowered his majesty even to the human condition and raised human lowliness even to the divine, so that he might be the Mediator between God and human beings as a human being.] but God is one. [Note: [Col. 0273B] 33. LANFRANC. “But God is one.” Since he called Christ the Mediator of God—that is, of God and human beings—and Christ is one, they might seem to be two gods; but far from it! For God is one: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.]

Is the Law, then, against the promises of God? [Note: [Col. 0273B] 34. “Is the Law, then, against the promises of God?” He again proves that the Law does not give inheritance, promise, or blessing. For if the Law gave these, the promise—that is, faith—would not give them. But the promise alone gave Abraham the inheritance. Therefore the Law does not give the inheritance, which is the meaning of the question: “Is the Law, then, against the promises of God?”] Certainly not! [Note: [Col. 0273C] 35. AUGUSTINE. “Is the Law, then, against the promises?” He repeats the question itself.]

For if a law had been given that could give life, [p. 129] [Note: [Col. 0273C] 36. LANFRANC. “For if a law had been given.” He proves the point again. The Law does not give inheritance because it does not give life; for if the Law gave life, it would also give righteousness, by parity of reasoning. But it does not give righteousness, because among the Jews everything is under sin, as Scripture says. Therefore the Law does not give righteousness, by relation; consequently it does not give life, by parity of reasoning; consequently the Law does not give inheritance. Therefore inheritance, promise, blessing, and life are given by faith alone, for he uses all these as equivalents.] then righteousness would truly be from the Law.

[Note: [Col. 0274A] 37. AMBROSE. “But Scripture concluded.” Their conclusion was fear of the one God.] But Scripture concluded everything under sin, so that the promise might be given to those who believe through the faith of Jesus Christ. [Note: [Col. 0274A] 38. LANFRANC. “But Scripture concluded.” The Law concluded everything under sin, either because it perfectly freed no evil person from sin, or because it was nevertheless given in such difficulty that, since it could not be fulfilled, it made everyone transgressors.]

Objection: Was the Law therefore given to someone? Before faith came, before Christ’s birth, we were guarded under the Law, [Note: [Col. 0274A] 39. “Shut up into that faith.” “Concluded” means that we were confined by fear, as slaves, in expectation of that faith which was to be revealed at Christ’s coming.] shut up”—so that we might do no more than was fitting—into that faith which was to be revealed.

Therefore the Law was our pedagogue—because we were guarded within it, which is the function of a pedagogue—until Christ, so that we might be justified by faith. But when faith came with Christ’s birth, we are no longer confined under a pedagogue as slaves.

[Note: [Col. 0274A] 40. “For you are all sons of God.” He proves that we are not slaves under the pedagogue of the Law: for you are free, that is, sons, because you have put on Christ, meaning that you perform his works. All baptized persons put on Christ; but you have been baptized. Therefore you have put on Christ. Likewise, since all baptized persons put on Christ, no one is excluded: neither Jew—who might otherwise seem to be excepted—nor Greek, etc. Therefore, since you have been baptized, you have put on Christ; that is, all of you are one.]

For you are all sons of God through faith in Christ Jesus. He shows why believers are sons of God: for all of you who were baptized in Christ have put on Christ. [Note: [Col. 0274B] 41. AUGUSTINE (ibid.). “For you are all sons.” His statement that they are sons of God through faith, because all who have been baptized in Christ have put on Christ, serves to prevent the Gentiles, who were not guarded under a pedagogue, from despairing about themselves.]

There is neither Jew nor Greek—the distinction of nation does not exist; neither slave nor free—the distinction of condition does not exist; neither male nor female—the distinction of sex does not exist. [Note: [Col. 0274B] 42. AMBROSE. “There is neither Jew.” This distinction—whether of nations, condition, or sex—has now been removed from the unity of faith, though it remains in moral conduct.]

For you are all one in Christ Jesus. [Note: [Col. 0274C] 43. AUGUSTINE (ibid.). “For you are all.” Insofar as all are believers, they are one in Christ Jesus. Although faith brings this about, by which one walks justly in this life, how much more perfectly and completely will hope itself bring it about when we see face to face.]

But if you belong to Christ—if, he says, you believe in Christ—you are Abraham’s spiritual seed, by imitating him, by parity of reasoning. [Note: [Col. 0274C] 44. (ibid.). “But if you belong to Christ.” The passage should be divided here, with “you are one in Christ Jesus” understood; then the conclusion follows: “Therefore you are Abraham’s seed.”]

[Note: [Col. 0274C] 45. (ibid.). “Therefore Abraham’s seed.” Here he shows that the one seed is Christ. We must understand not only the Mediator himself, but also the Church, whose body he is the head.]

Therefore you are Abraham’s seed, [Note: [Col. 0274C] 46. AMBROSE. “Therefore the seed.” If Abraham has one seed, and that seed is understood to be only in Christ, then we are this seed of Abraham. The whole—that is, the head and the body—is one Christ.] and therefore heirs according to the promise.

[COMMENTARY.]

[Col. 0269A]

1. AMBROSE. “O foolish Galatians!” This is inserted from that place up to this point: “I wish to learn only this from you,” etc. For he could have said: “This alone I wish to learn from you.”

2. “Before whose eyes.” He was set forth and crucified among you. He means that, when you heard the words of the cross with such deep emotion that you painted the cross itself before our eyes, and almost also the things that occurred at that time, by what enchantment have you cast away so great an affection as you seemed to have for Christ?

3. AUGUSTINE (Commentary on the Epistle to the Galatians, chapter III, [Col. 0269B] vol. IV). “Before whose”—that is, while they were looking on, Christ Jesus lost his inheritance and possession, because they took it away from him, expelled the Lord from it, recalled those who had believed to the works of the Law, and deprived him of his possession—that is, of those in whom grace and faith dwell.

4. LANFRANC. “Before whose eyes.” Before the eyes of their mind Jesus Christ was publicly proclaimed—that is, he was condemned and crucified; that is, he was held in contempt, since they thought that a person was not justified through faith in him but through observance of the Law.

5. AUGUSTINE (ibid.). “Jesus Christ was publicly portrayed.” In another way, Jesus Christ was publicly portrayed as crucified. He added “crucified” so that, when they considered at what price he had purchased the possession that he was losing among them, he might chiefly admonish—or, according to another reading, move—them by this.

6. (ibid.). “This alone from you.” From this point he begins to demonstrate grace, showing how the grace of faith is sufficient for justification without the works of the Law.

7. LANFRANC. “You received the Spirit from the works of the Law.” If you have the Spirit from faith, as he has already proved, and therefore says, “Do you consequently possess miraculous powers from faith,” which are the cause of justification—that is, you possess justification itself from faith—then the one follows from the other. They possess miraculous powers from faith because Abraham’s justification was from faith: for it is written, etc. He treats miraculous powers and justification as equivalents, since one is the cause of the other.

8. “You received the Spirit.” Those who believed received spiritual graces; they did not perform the works of the Law.

9. “Having begun with the Spirit.” You began with the Spirit, either as living spiritually [the reading may be “to live”], or as understanding the Law spiritually; now you are being brought to an end by the flesh—that is, by a carnal life or by the Law understood carnally. “Are you being consumed” is the subjunctive of *consumor, consumeris*, meaning “may you perish.” “You are being completed” is the indicative of *consummor, consummaris*, meaning “you are ending your life.” Both readings are found in Scripture at this place.

10. “In vain.” In vain—that is, uselessly—suffers the person who does not have faith in Christ.

11. “Know therefore.” Because Abraham was justified by faith, and all are justified by faith alone, which is equivalent to saying: “These are the sons of Abraham.”

12. AMBROSE. “They will be blessed in you.” That is, with you, and they will share your blessing.

13. LANFRANC. “For whoever.” As though he were saying: Blessing is either from faith or from works; but it is not from works (for blessing comes from faith); therefore it is from faith.

14. AMBROSE. “Cursed is everyone.” The Law considers everyone who hangs upon a tree accursed, because this kind of punishment was appointed for those found guilty of many offenses.

[Col. 0270C] 15. LANFRANC. “Lives by faith.” If righteousness is not from the Law, it is from faith alone.

16. “But the Law is not.” That is, the faith of Christ does not permit the Jewish Law to be observed, or the Law and faith do not agree. But the Law says, “The one who does”; it does not say, “The one who believes.”

[Col. 0271A] 17. “Christ redeemed us from the curse.” You say that everyone who does not remain in the things written in the book of the Law is accursed; so too are you who remain. To this he replies: “Christ redeemed us,” etc.

18. AUGUSTINE (Commentary on the Epistle to the Galatians, chapter III). “Having become a curse for us.” He hung upon the tree in his mortal aspect. Believers know the origin of mortality. It arises from the punishment and curse of the first man’s sin; the Lord assumed this mortality and bore our sins in his body upon the tree.

19. LANFRANC. “The blessing of Abraham might come.” He proves that faith, not the Law, gives justification. For if the Law gave justification, it would destroy the testament of Abraham’s faith made to us. But the Law cannot destroy it; no later testament destroys the first. The testament of faith is earlier, while the Law is later. This assumption is found in the book as follows: “Now I say that a testament confirmed by God,” etc. He proves by analogy that no later testament destroys the first, because human custom establishes that a later testament does not destroy the first after the death of the person who made it; hence the phrase, “I speak in human terms.” When he adds, “The promises were spoken to Abraham,” he answers the question whether any testament had been confirmed by God to someone, saying that it had been made to Abraham and to his seed, who is Christ.

20. “The promise of the Spirit.” That is, the promise of the Spirit, whom he promised that he would give to believers; or the justification that the Holy Spirit promised to believers, saying: “In your seed,” etc.

[Col. 0271C] 21. “A confirmed testament.” He says: No one rejects a human testament concerning his property; therefore, much less should God’s testament be rejected, by which he testified that all nations would be blessed in Abraham’s seed.

22. “He does not say ‘and to seeds.’” In making the promise God does not say, “In your seeds all the nations will be blessed,” but “in your seed.”

23. AUGUSTINE. “And to your seed.” From the people of Israel the Virgin was born and gave birth to Christ; and behold, in Christ all the nations are blessed. What is truer? What is more certain? What is clearer?

24. AUGUSTINE (from *Treatises on the Gospel according to John*, 39). “In your seed.” Since we too belong to what is Christ, being incorporated with him and joined to that head, there is one Christ. And because he says also to us, “Therefore you are Abraham’s seed, heirs according to the promise,” if Abraham has one seed, and that one seed is understood to be none other than Christ, then we are this seed of Abraham. The whole—that is, the head and the body—is therefore one Christ.

25. LANFRANC. “Now I say this.” The order is: “I say that the Law, which was made after four hundred and thirty years, does not invalidate this testament.” If only those who observe the Jewish Law were blessed in Abraham’s seed, [Col. 0272B] God’s testament would in some respect have been invalidated, and his promise emptied, by which he promised that all nations would be blessed in Abraham’s seed.

26. “For if the inheritance is from the Law.” Blessing or inheritance is received through faith alone, not through the Law, because the Law does not destroy the testament of faith previously confirmed by God to Abraham. Therefore, if the Law does not destroy the testament of faith, it does not give blessing or inheritance. The analogy is that a later human testament does not destroy a confirmed earlier testament. This analogy is introduced to prove the proposition that the Law does not destroy the testament, as the book states: “Now I say that a testament [Col. 0272C] confirmed by God,” etc.

27. “Then it is no longer from the promise.” That is, if only those who observe the Jewish Law are heirs, then the inheritance is no longer given according to God’s promise, which speaks of everyone.

28. AUGUSTINE (from Sermon 13, *On the Words of the Apostle*, chapter 4, vol. X). “Why, then, the Law? Why, then, the Law?” That is, what was the usefulness of the Law? It was established on account of transgression. This is what is said elsewhere: “The Law entered in so that transgression might abound”; it was established on account of transgression. Thus the necks of the proud, who attributed much to themselves, might be humbled, since they thought that free choice could suffice for them unto righteousness.

29. AMBROSE. “On account of transgressions.” The Law was established for a proud people so that, since they could not receive the grace of charity unless humbled, they might be humbled through transgression and seek grace.

30. LANFRANC. “Until the seed should come to whom.” God the Father had promised Christ the inheritance of the whole world, as in the Psalm: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations,” etc.

31. AUGUSTINE (Commentary on the Epistle to the Galatians, chapter III, vol. IV). “The seed to whom he made the promise.” The seed to whom the promise was made signifies the people of believers.

32. AMBROSE. “But the mediator.” If the Son of God had wished to remain in natural equality, without emptying himself by taking the form of a servant, he would not have been the Mediator of God and human beings, because the Trinity itself is one God. Thus the only Son of God became the Mediator of God and human beings: the Word of God, God with God, lowered his majesty even to the human condition and raised human lowliness even to the divine, so that he might be the Mediator between God and human beings as a human being.

33. LANFRANC. “But God is one.” Since he called Christ the Mediator of God—that is, of God and human beings—and Christ is one, they might seem to be two gods; but far from it! For God is one: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

34. “Is the Law, then, against the promises of God?” He again proves that the Law does not give inheritance, promise, or blessing. For if the Law gave these, the promise—that is, faith—would not give them. But the promise alone gave Abraham the inheritance. Therefore the Law does not give the inheritance, which is the meaning of the question: “Is the Law, then, against the promises of God?”

35. AUGUSTINE. “Is the Law, then, against the promises?” He repeats the question itself.

36. LANFRANC. “For if a law had been given.” He proves the point again. The Law does not give inheritance because it does not give life; for if the Law gave life, it would also give righteousness, by parity of reasoning. But it does not give righteousness, because among the Jews everything is under sin, as Scripture says. Therefore the Law does not give righteousness, by relation; consequently it does not give life, by parity of reasoning; consequently the Law does not give inheritance. Therefore inheritance, promise, blessing, and life are given by faith alone, for he uses all these as equivalents.

[Col. 0274A] 37. AMBROSE. “But Scripture concluded.” Their conclusion was fear of the one God.

38. LANFRANC. “But Scripture concluded.” The Law concluded everything under sin, either because it perfectly freed no evil person from sin, or because it was nevertheless given in such difficulty that, since it could not be fulfilled, it made everyone transgressors.

39. “Shut up into that faith.” “Concluded” means that we were confined by fear, as slaves, in expectation of that faith which was to be revealed at Christ’s coming.

40. “For you are all sons of God.” He proves that we are not slaves under the pedagogue of the Law: for you are free, that is, sons, because you have put on Christ, meaning that you perform his works. All baptized persons put on Christ; but you have been baptized. Therefore you have put on Christ. Likewise, since all baptized persons put on Christ, no one is excluded: neither Jew—who might otherwise seem to be excepted—nor Greek, etc. Therefore, since you have been baptized, you have put on Christ; that is, all of you are one.

41. AUGUSTINE (ibid.). “For you are all sons.” His statement that they are sons of God through faith, because all who have been baptized in Christ have put on Christ, serves to prevent the Gentiles, who were not guarded under a pedagogue, from despairing about themselves.

42. AMBROSE. “There is neither Jew.” This distinction—whether of nations, condition, or sex—has now been removed from the unity of faith, though it remains in moral conduct.

43. AUGUSTINE (ibid.). “For you are all.” Insofar as all are believers, they are one in Christ Jesus. Although faith brings this about, by which one walks justly in this life, how much more perfectly and completely will hope itself bring it about when we see face to face.

44. (ibid.). “But if you belong to Christ.” The passage should be divided here, with “you are one in Christ Jesus” understood; then the conclusion follows: “Therefore you are Abraham’s seed.”

45. (ibid.). “Therefore Abraham’s seed.” Here he shows that the one seed is Christ. We must understand not only the Mediator himself, but also the Church, whose body he is the head.

46. AMBROSE. “Therefore the seed.” If Abraham has one seed, and that seed is understood to be only in Christ, then we are this seed of Abraham. The whole—that is, the head and the body—is one Christ.

[COMMENTARY.]

[Col. 0275A]

**CHAPTER IV.—1. LANFRANC. “But I say.”** Someone might say: “We were slaves, as you say, and now you say: ‘We shall be heirs’; that cannot be.” He proves this by the preceding comparison concerning those who are under guardianship.

**2. AUGUSTINE (*Exposition of the Epistle to the Galatians*, chapter IV). “For as long as.”** Since above he made the law a pedagogue under whom the Jewish people were placed, he now calls the elements stewards, under whom the Gentiles served, so that the faithful people were, during the time of their childhood, partly under the law as pedagogue and partly under the elements. To what he had said—that, at the coming of faith, the people were kept as under a pedagogue until the appropriate age, [Col. 0275B] when they were to be called into freedom—he added: “But I say: For as long as the heir is a child.”

**3. LANFRANC. “For as long as.”** This comparison applies only to those who believed from among the Gentiles. “Heir,” “child,” and “slave” are understood in relation to the multitude of human beings, some of whom will believe and others not.

**4. “Under guardians.”** That is, there are guardians and administrators [or agents], but they receive different names according to the diversity of cases. They are called guardians because they protect the person and property of the ward against accusations. Administrators are those who act when injuries are inflicted upon the ward or his property.

**5. “So also we.”** He puts the whole for the part, just as he often puts the part for the whole. For they were never under the gods of the Gentiles, whom he here calls “the elements”—for they worshiped the sun, moon, [Col. 0275C] air, and waters. Some understand “the elements” as carnal observances, but the following sentence does not permit this: “But then indeed,” etc.

**6. AUGUSTINE (ibid.). “Made of a woman.”** Made because of the assumption of created nature.

**7. (ibid.). “Made under the law.”** He said that he was made under the law because he was circumcised and a lawful sacrifice was offered for him. Nor is it surprising that he endured the works of the law, from which he was to liberate those who were held by them in servitude; for he also endured death in order to liberate from it those who were held by mortality.

**8. LANFRANC. “Those who were under the law.”** He also redeemed those who were not [Col. 0276A] under the law; but there could be doubt concerning them, and they were not abandoned without cause [perhaps: “not to be abandoned”].

**9. AMBROSE. [Note: [Col. 0275C] This is Augustine, on chapter III of the Epistle to the Galatians, volume IV.] “So that we might receive adoption.”** He says “adoption” so that we may clearly understand the one and only Son of God. We are sons of God through his benefit and the gracious regard of his mercy. He did not say “let us receive,” in order to signify that we had lost this in Adam, from whom we are mortal.

**10. AUGUSTINE (*On the Epistle to the Galatians*). “Crying, ‘Abba, Father.’”** It is aptly understood that he did not place words from two languages signifying the same thing without reason, on account of the whole people called from Jews and Gentiles into the unity of faith: the Hebrew word for the Hebrews [or Jews], and the Greek word for the Greeks [or Gentiles]. Nevertheless, the identical meaning of both words pertains to the unity of the same faith and Spirit.

**11. (ibid.). “Therefore he is no longer.”** This follows from what he had said: “He differs in nothing from a slave.”

**12. AMBROSE. “Rather, are known.”** For it was not through your knowing or seeing that divine knowledge somehow shone upon you.

**13. AUGUSTINE. “How are you turning again,” etc.** They did not, however, wish to return to paganism itself, but to circumcision. Yet he counts it as the same thing; therefore he says “again” and “anew,” because it is the same in kind, namely, in servitude.

**14. AMBROSE. “Turning again.”** What benefit is it that you escaped the slavery in which you were held when you served the elements of the world, if you return again to other things [perhaps “to those things” or “to other things”]?

[Col. 0276C]

**15. AUGUSTINE (ibid.). “To the weak.”** Because they vary in a weak and unstable form.

**16. (ibid.). “Needy.”** Because they lack the stable form of created things.

**17. AMBROSE. “The elements,” that is, elements belonging to the times of servitude.** For it is clear that the cycles of time are administered through the elements of the world—that is, heaven and earth—and through the movements and order of the stars.

**18. LANFRANC. “You observe days.”** “Days” is a kind of persuasion; for they did not observe days except by giving thanks, as we do.

[Col. 0277A]

**19. AMBROSE. “Become as I am.”** “I too,” he says, “was once under the law; but afterward I chose to live outside the law, just as you were living through the faith that is in Christ. Therefore imitate me also, through the faith that is in Christ, making yourselves strangers to a law-bound way of life.”

**20. LANFRANC. “Become as I am,” that is, conform yourselves to my conduct, because I conform myself to yours.** Or: “Be faithful, as I am,” because I was unfaithful as you were; therefore imitate me, because I did not abandon my former faith without reason.

**21. “Because I too was as you are.”** Someone might say: “How can we be as you are?” He replies: “You can, because just as we are the same in substantial essence, we can be the same in what is accidental—that is, in holiness.”

[Col. 0277B]

**22. “You have done me no wrong.”** So that no one might say that the Apostle reproved them out of envy, he removes this suspicion in the following way: “You have not wronged me, so that I ought to envy you; rather, you did every good thing for me, because you became my friends.” I say this to you because I am your friend, and because it is true.

**23. “Because of an infirmity.”** That is, “in an infirmity,” just as “because of that time” means “in that time.”

**24. “Temptation.”** The Apostle’s bodily weakness was so great that his hearers could be tempted and think that he was not Christ’s Apostle, since Christ permitted him to suffer such illness.

**25. AUGUSTINE (*On the Epistle to the Galatians*). “Temptation.”** They were tempted when the Apostle suffered persecution, as to whether they would abandon him through fear or embrace him through love.

[Col. 0277C]

**26. LANFRANC. “You did not despise,” etc.** When they saw the Apostle afflicted, they could have despised his preaching and thought that God did not care for one who was so afflicted; but they did not despise it.

**27. “Where, then, is your blessedness?”** Their blessedness consisted in loving the Apostle and obeying all his commands; but some of them had lost this blessedness, wishing to return to the worship of demons and serve them.

**28. AUGUSTINE (ibid., B). “By telling the truth.”** But what truth was he preaching except that they should not be circumcised?

[Col. 0278A]

**29. (ibid.). “They are zealous for you,” that is, they envy you, those who wish to make you fleshly instead of spiritual; this is zeal that is not good.**

**30. (ibid.). “My little children.”** Let us understand this childbirth as referring to the anguish of cares.

**31. LANFRANC. “I am in labor.”** They had been born and brought forth in the faith of Christ; but because some of them had abandoned the faith, they had to be brought forth again by the Apostle, until Christ should be formed in them.

**32. AUGUSTINE (ibid.). “Until Christ is formed.”** Christ is formed in a person when he receives the form of Christ.

**33. (ibid.). “To change my voice.”** What else can this mean except that, because he had called them his sons, he spared them in writing, lest, stirred up by harsher rebuke, they should easily be turned against him? “I wish,” he says, “to be present with you now and to change my voice”—that is, to deny that you are my sons, because I am ashamed of you.

[Col. 0278B]

**34. LANFRANC. “Tell me, you who wish to be under the law.”** You ought not to wish to be under the law, but under ecclesial grace; for the law produces slaves, whereas the Church produces free persons. He proves this by the authority of Scripture, saying that the slave woman Hagar bore a slave to Abraham, while the free woman Sarah brought forth a free son. And lest you say that Sarah and Hagar pertain to the law and the Church [supplied: “belong”], and that their sons pertain to both peoples, the Apostle replies that what was said about the two mothers and their sons must be understood allegorically of the law and grace. You will find this explained more fully there: “But he who was of the slave woman,” etc.

**35. “Because Abraham.”** He wishes to show that it is more honorable to be under the grace of the New Testament than under the law of the Jews. Abraham is understood as God the Father; the two sons as the Jewish people and the Gentile people; the slave woman as the law, which produced slaves and compelled them through fear, saying, “If anyone does this or that, let him die”; the free woman as the preaching of the New Testament, which produces free persons and exhorts them with paternal love, saying, “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will give you rest; for my yoke is easy and my burden is light” (Matthew 11).

**36. “According to the flesh.”** That is, according to carnal custom, [Col. 0279A] because a young woman ordinarily conceives from an old man.

**37. AUGUSTINE (*On the Epistle to the Galatians*). “One indeed.”** Hagar signifies the people of the Old Testament because of the yoke of observances; Isaac, born from the free woman through the promise, signifies the people of the New Testament. The old age of Isaac’s parents has the same significance, since although the people of the New Testament are new, their predestination with God—and heavenly Jerusalem itself—is ancient.

**38. AMBROSE. “Which is Hagar.”** Hagar, the slave woman, giving birth according to the course of nature, signifies the law, which those who are born in this life according to the succession of nature must observe; they too lived under the law in the order of slaves. Sarah, however, who gave birth through grace, [Col. 0279B] signifies those who appear to have risen in Christ through grace, who also, beyond the hope of nature, await a second birth, for whom circumcision and the offering of sacrifices are now unnecessary.

**39. “For Sinai is a mountain.”** In ancient times Arabia was not only the region now called by that name, but also included the desert and a considerable part of Egypt, where Mount Sinai is located, on which the law was given. Hence Hagar, who signifies the Old Testament, which produces slavery, is also joined symbolically to the Jerusalem that exists in this age, in which the ordinances of the covenant are fulfilled.

**40. LANFRANC. “Which is joined to it,” that is, it belongs to it by reason of its honor.** Or: “Hagar is joined to it,” that is, the Old Testament is joined to the New and serves, [Col. 0279C] because in this present life the Church serves. Or: it serves, being joined to the Jerusalem that now exists, that is, to the Jerusalem that holds the carnal aspects of the law. Or: it is now joined to the Church, whereas previously it served under the law.

**41. “It serves with its sons.”** He says that earthly Jerusalem serves either under the carnal law, which compelled through fear of death, or under the yoke of Roman rule.

**42. “But the Jerusalem above is free.”** That is, Sarah signifies the heavenly Jerusalem, which is our mother in a certain respect—that is, according to the present Church, which gives birth to God’s sons for us. He proves that it is free because it rejoices; and he proves that it is a mother because it bears sons. For it is written, etc.

**43. “She is free.”** She is free because she has free daughters—that is, the grace of the New Testament and the preaching of Christ. She is our mother because preachers are there, and through the Gospel they have given birth to us.

**44. “For it is written.”** This proves that she is free; for it belongs to free persons to rejoice, whereas it belongs to slaves to fear.

**45. AUGUSTINE (ibid.). “Rejoice, barren woman.”** Scripture calls heavenly Jerusalem barren so long as she has not borne sons on earth; she is also called deserted, because people have abandoned heavenly righteousness and pursued earthly things.

**46. AMBROSE. “Many sons.”** This was said concerning the resurrection. For we are those who, having attained the resurrection, come from every nation; whereas those who are under the law are one nation.

**47. AUGUSTINE (ibid.). “The woman who has a husband,” that is, earthly Jerusalem, which had received the law.** Therefore Sarah signifies heavenly Jerusalem, which for a long time was deserted by the intercourse of a husband because of her acknowledged barrenness.

**48. LANFRANC. “With the freedom by which Christ freed us.”** Lest we suppose that we are free by nature, he defines that freedom itself: “with the freedom,” etc.

AUGUSTINE (On Galatians, chapter V). “Do not again.” How are we to understand what he says—“so that you may not again be held under the yoke of slavery”—when he is writing to people who had never been Jews? he deceives himself.

through whom the world has been crucified to me and made worthless, so that it may not hold me, and I to the world, so that I may not hold it.

Henceforth let no one be disobedient to me, thinking that I am not an apostle of Christ, and so trouble me.

in my body.

[Col. 0284A] CHAP. VI.—1. LANFRANC. “If a person should be overtaken.” Instruct him in such a way that you do not become proud because of your instruction and fall into vice. Or instruct him gently, because you too may perhaps fall into vice.

But those who have charity bear themselves. Someone has injured you and asks forgiveness; if you do not forgive, you do not bear your brother’s burden. If you forgive, you bear the infirm person. And if you too should perhaps fall into some weakness, as a human being, it is right that the other should bear you in the same way as you do.

4. LANFRANC. “The law of Christ,” that is, love. For he himself said: “I give you a new commandment, that you love one another as I have loved you.”

5. AUGUSTINE (Exposition of the Epistle to the Galatians). “He deceives himself.” His flatterers do not deceive him; rather, he himself does, because, since he is more present to himself than they are, he prefers to seek himself in them rather than in himself.

6. LANFRANC. “He deceives himself.” The reason why one’s work must be tested.

7. “Let each person test his own work.” The pseudo-apostles were praising them; therefore he says: “Let each person test his own work,” so that he may not seek glory in another—that is, in what another says—but in himself.

8. “Let him share.” He says: The one who is instructed in the word of God should share all his goods with the one who instructs him. He rebukes their stinginess toward their preachers.

[Col. 0285A] 9. “Do not be deceived.” It is as though he said: “If you say that you have nothing to share with the preacher, you can deceive a human being, but you cannot mock—that is, deceive—God, who knows what is hidden.”

10. “God is not mocked.” He would then be mocked, as it were, if those who do not labor in the vineyard were to receive the denarius.

11. “For whatever a person sows.” You ought, he says, to share your goods with preachers and with your neighbors, for what you sow you will reap. Every person will reap what he has sown: both the one who sows in the flesh by acting carnally, and the one who sows in the Spirit by acting spiritually. The latter will receive eternal life, but the former correction.

12. “For the one who sows.” Everything that is sown is sown either in the flesh or in the Spirit, and all these things will be reaped.

[Col. 0285B] 13. “In the flesh,” that is, the one who performs those carnal works will have Gehenna, which is everlasting corruption.

14. AUGUSTINE (On the Epistle to the Galatians). “To those who belong to the household of faith.” Whom else should we believe he means except Christians?

15. LANFRANC. “For whoever wishes to please,” and so forth. Rhetoric teaches that when someone wishes to persuade another of something, he should mention it at the beginning and at the end. The Apostle does this by saying: “Do not do what the pseudo-apostles persuade you to do,” namely, be circumcised, because they do this only to please the Jews in your mutilated flesh and to avoid suffering persecution from them [Col. 0285C] in preaching the cross. The proposition should therefore be reversed in this way: Whoever wishes you to be circumcised does so only so that he may not suffer the persecution of Christ’s cross; for they do not do it to keep the law or for any other reason.

16. “But far be it from me to boast except in the cross,” and so forth. [Col. 0286A] I will boast only in the cross of Christ, because this alone is effective for obtaining Christ’s salvation; nothing else is, since neither circumcision nor uncircumcision has such force.

17. AUGUSTINE (Exposition of Galatians). “Through whom the world has been crucified to me,” that is, so that it may not hold me; “and I to the world,” so that I may not hold it. That is, neither can the world harm me, nor do I desire anything from the world.

18. (ibid.) “But a new creation.” He calls a new creation the new life that comes through faith in Jesus Christ.

19. (ibid.) “Upon Israel,” that is, upon those who are prepared to live for the vision of God—not upon those who are called by this name but, through carnal blindness, do not wish to see God.

20. LANFRANC. “Henceforth.” “Henceforth,” he says, “let none of you be burdensome and disobedient to me, thinking that I am not an apostle of Christ.”

[Col. 0286B] 21. AUGUSTINE (ibid.). “Henceforth.” He does not wish to be wearied by turbulent disputes over a matter that has been explained sufficiently.

22. (ibid.) “For I bear the marks,” that is, I have other conflicts and struggles with my flesh, which fight alongside me in the persecutions that I endure. The marks of Jesus are called certain signs of servile punishments. For he knew that these had been repaid to him on account of the guilt of the persecution by which he had persecuted the Church of God.

23. LANFRANC. “The marks.” Properly, a *stigma* is a mark impressed upon a fugitive slave; the Apostle says that he bears it because he had previously fled from the Lord.

[Col. 0286C] 24. “In my body.” In his body he carried scars from wounds and blows, chains around his neck and on his hands; all these were signs that he belonged to our Lord Jesus Christ. Marks were also certain signs made on the hands of soldiers, by which they were recognized as belonging to the emperor’s army.

# THE EPISTLE OF THE BLESSED APOSTLE PAUL TO THE EPHESIANS, WITH THE INTERSPERSED GLOSSULES OF THE BLESSED LANFRANC

[Col. 0287]

## ARGUMENT

The Ephesians are Asians. After receiving the word of truth, they persevered in the faith. The Apostle praises them, writing to them from Rome, from prison, through Tychicus the deacon.

[Col. 0288]

## CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 0287]

[Note: [Col. 0287A] CHAPTER I.—1. AMBROSE. He teaches, with thanksgiving, those benefits that Christ bestowed on us by his coming. Afterwards he passes to ethical exhortation, beginning thus: “I beseech you, I, a prisoner in the Lord” (below, IV).]

Paul, an Apostle of Jesus Christ—not of Ananias—through the will of God, not through his own merits or those of human beings, to all the saints, the baptized, who are at Ephesus, and to the faithful, the catechumens, in Christ Jesus, in faith. Grace, the remission of sins, to you, and peace, by which we are reconciled to God the Father, or the observance of good works, which is peace between God and human beings, from God our Father and the Lord 139 Jesus Christ.

[Note: [Col. 0287A] 2. “Blessed be God.” The blessing that is made in relation to God is only a confession of the good things bestowed by him. The blessing that is made by God is fulfilled in us when we are filled with his benefits.]

[Note: [Col. 0287B] 4. AUGUSTINE. “In the heavenly places.” “In the heavenly places,” as though it meant “from heavenly things.” For every good gift and every perfect gift is from above.]

in the heavenly places—that is, the blessing that we shall share in heaven—in Christ. Just as he chose us, so he blessed us, as he predestined us.

[Note: [Col. 0287C] 7. AMBROSE. “In love.” By this the greatness of his generosity is shown.]

in his love. Behold what he said: “he chose.”

[Note: [Col. 0287C] 8. “Who predestined.” What he says about the adoption of sons is greater than what he had said about being holy and blameless. [Col. 0288A]]

He predestined us for adoption as sons, so that we might be holy, through Jesus Christ,

to himself—the same as “in him,” namely, to believe—

in all wisdom and prudence, so that he might make known to us the mystery of his will: that he willed to save the human race, according to his good pleasure, not according to human merits,

[Note: [Col. 0288B] 13. “Which he purposed.” God the Father purposed his good pleasure in Christ, that is, he openly manifested it to the world, saying: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.”]

which mystery he purposed in him, in the Son,

in the dispensation

of the fullness of times. Behold what he purposed: to restore all things in Christ, both those that are in heaven—the diminished order of angels—and those that are on earth—the corrupted human race—in him, in Christ.

In whom—or by whom—we too have been called by lot, not by merit, predestined according to the purpose of him who works all things according to the counsel of his will, so that we might be for the praise of his glory—that we might praise his glory—we who previously hoped in Christ.

In him you too were called, from the time when

you heard the word of truth, namely, the Gospel of your salvation, in which Christ, and believing,

you were sealed

[Note: [Col. 0289B] 20. AMBROSE. “The Spirit of promise.” He rightly called it the Spirit of promise, since the holy ones await participation in the Holy Spirit among the good things they expect in the future.]

with the Holy Spirit of promise, who is

[Note: [Col. 0289B] 21. “The pledge of the inheritance.” He calls that redemption, that enjoyment which will then exist, the pledge that will be given as the form of that future reality.]

[Note: [Col. 0289C] 22. “For redemption.” He calls redemption the immortality that will come through the resurrection; but he calls possession the intimacy with him that will exist in relation to God.]

for the redemption of the possession, so that, redeemed, you may be acquired for God, for the praise of his glory.

For this reason—that is, because you have believed, have been sealed, and have been called—I too, hearing of your faith, which is in the Lord Jesus, and of your love toward all the saints, do not cease giving thanks for you, making mention of you in my prayers,

[Note: [Col. 0289C] 23. “That the God of our Lord.” By saying “of Christ,” he indicates the humanity assumed; “Father of glory” refers to the glorious divine nature.]

that the God of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of glory,

He explains this through the memorable things accomplished in Christ. may give you the spirit of wisdom and revelation in the recognition of him, and may give you enlightened eyes of your heart, so that you may know what is the hope of his calling—that is, what and how great is the thing for which you who are called hope—and what are the riches of the glory of his inheritance among the saints, and

what is the surpassing greatness of his power toward us,

which he will give us as incorruption,

above every principality, authority, power, and dominion,

which is his body, and
