## COMMENTARY

[Col. 0287]

[Col. 0287A] CHAPTER I.—1. AMBROSE. He teaches, with thanksgiving, those benefits that Christ bestowed on us by his coming. Afterwards he passes to ethical exhortation, beginning thus: “I beseech you, I, a prisoner in the Lord” (below, IV).

2. “Blessed be God.” The blessing that is made in relation to God is only a confession of the good things bestowed by him. The blessing that is made by God is fulfilled in us when we are filled with his benefits.

3. “In the heavenly places.” That is, the blessing that we shall share in heaven. For he speaks of the resurrection that will come to us through the Spirit; and, lest this novelty itself disturb the mind, since he had not previously bestowed such great things or stated openly what those spiritual blessings were, he answers both points by saying: “He chose us in him [Col. 0287B] before the foundation of the world to be holy before him.”

4. AUGUSTINE. “In the heavenly places.” “In the heavenly places,” as though it meant “from heavenly things.” For every good gift and every perfect gift is from above.

5. LANFRANC. “In the heavenly places.” He calls the virtues “heavenly things”; through their observance one goes to heaven, and in them, he says, he possesses every spiritual abundance in the faith of Christ.

6. “In him.” “In him” should be understood to mean that we would remain in him; [Col. 0287C] or, “he chose in him,” because he made all things in Wisdom, which is Christ.

7. AMBROSE. “In love.” By this the greatness of his generosity is shown.

8. “Who predestined.” What he says about the adoption of sons is greater than what he had said about being holy and blameless. [Col. 0288A]

9. “To himself.” Since he said, “he predestined for adoption as sons,” it was uncertain whose sons he meant them to be by adoption. He added, “to himself,” that is, to his own self, so that we might be called his sons.

10. “According to the purpose.” Wishing in every respect to exalt these things, since they are worthy of much thanksgiving, he frequently speaks of ordination, good pleasure, and will.

11. LANFRANC. “The riches of his grace.” Through this grace there are not only remission and redemption, but also wisdom—by which one is said to have understanding—and prudence in conduct.

12. “In all wisdom,” that is, giving us every wisdom in the recognition of him, and prudence in our conduct. [Col. 0288B]

13. “Which he purposed.” God the Father purposed his good pleasure in Christ, that is, he openly manifested it to the world, saying: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.”

14. “In the dispensation of the fullness.” Either when he was ordering all times, or in the very period in which Christ was born, which was the fullness because the promises were completed in it; or because other times were empty of salvation.

[Col. 0288C] 15. “Of the fullness.” “In the dispensation,” that is, in the consummation. He explains what that good pleasure of God is: namely, when the time of his ordering had been fulfilled, to restore to the faith of Christ those things that are in heaven—that is, the number of angels that had been diminished—and those things [Col. 0289A] [perhaps: “those who are on earth”] that are on earth, namely, human beings, who had perished to a great extent.

16. AUGUSTINE (*Treatise on Psalm XXX, Sermon 2, volume VIII*). “In whom we also by lot.” He called grace, by which we have been saved, a lot. Why does he call grace by the name of a lot? Because in a lot there is no selection, but the will of God. For where it is said, “This one does, that one does not,” merits are considered; and where merits are considered, there is no election by lot. But when he finds no merits of ours, he saves us by the lot of his will, because he willed it, not because we were worthy. This is the lot.

17. LANFRANC. “In whom we also.” This is a change of case, as though he were saying: “into whom,” that is, “into whose faith”; or “in whom,” that is, “through whom.”

18. AMBROSE. “When you heard.” In him you too heard the words of the Gospel, approached the faith, and received confirmation through participation in the Spirit; for this is what he says: “You were sealed.” [Col. 0289B]

19. LANFRANC. “You were sealed.” The order is: “You were sealed for the redemption of the possession.” For the Spirit seals believers, that is, distinguishes and separates them from other human beings, because he purifies them from sins and adorns them with spiritual graces.

20. AMBROSE. “The Spirit of promise.” He rightly called it the Spirit of promise, since the holy ones await participation in the Holy Spirit among the good things they expect in the future.

21. “The pledge of the inheritance.” He calls that redemption, that enjoyment which will then exist, the pledge that will be given as the form of that future reality.

[Col. 0289C] 22. “For redemption.” He calls redemption the immortality that will come through the resurrection; but he calls possession the intimacy with him that will exist in relation to God.

23. “That the God of our Lord.” By saying “of Christ,” he indicates the humanity assumed; “Father of glory” refers to the glorious divine nature.

24. “What is the surpassing greatness,” that is, what kind of greatness, and how great a greatness, he will bring about from himself toward us who believe in him. He explains this through the memorable things accomplished in Christ. And consider that he does not say “the glory of an undifferentiated inheritance,” but “the riches of glory”; nor “his power,” or even “the greatness of his power,” but more forcefully: “what is the surpassing greatness of his power.” [Col. 0290A]

25. LANFRANC. “Who believe,” and so forth: that is, we believe that everything he accomplished in Christ he can accomplish in us, namely, the resurrection.

26. AMBROSE. “Establishing.” That is, he received him as a participant in honor; he says this concerning the humanity assumed, because of the nature of the Word of God dwelling with me [perhaps: “with him”].

27. LANFRANC. “Above every principality,” and so forth: that is, above the names of angels and archangels that are now known, and above everything presently unknown; or above every heavenly and earthly name. [Col. 0290B]

28. “And every name.” That is, whether something is named in the present life and recognized as great, or whether there is something that we will be able to recognize in the future but perhaps do not know now, he made him superior to all of them.

29. “Which is his body.” We are his body, receiving a likeness of his nature and sharing in the Spirit; and we shall all be one body, because we have received a common resurrection and immortality. In the order of things, Christ will be our head, from whom every cause of the second regeneration appears to have flowed down to us.

[Col. 0290C] 30. LANFRANC. “His fullness.” The Church is the fullness of Christ because in it and through it members are added to Christ, that is, the faithful.

31. AMBROSE. “Is fulfilled in all.” That is, he is full in all things. He necessarily added “all things,” showing that the whole exists in everything, according to what one may wish to understand, whether in essence, in operation, or in power.

# CHAPTER II

[Col. 0289]

And you, when you were previously dead through actual offenses and your original sins, in which you once walked

[Note: [Col. 0291A] CHAPTER II.—1. AMBROSE. “According to the age.” By “age” he does not mean creation, but the temporal conduct of this present age.]

according to the age, worldly, of this world,

[Note: [Col. 0291A] 2. LANFRANC. “According to the prince,” that is, according to what the prince who has power in this air persuaded you to do, whether in tempting the faithful or in stirring up the air itself.]

according to the prince of the devil,

[Note: [Col. 0291A] 3. AMBROSE. “Of the power of the air.” The devil received the command to rule the air and to have power to stir it up.]

of the power of this air—the spirit who, in this order, now works

[Note: [Col. 0291A] 4. LANFRANC. “In the sons of distrust.” They are called sons of distrust either because they distrust the promises of God, or because the faithful have no hope for their conversion.]

in the sons of distrust, who distrust the promises—

[Note: [Col. 0291A] 5. AMBROSE. “Among whom we too.” Since he had said “you,” lest he be thought to withdraw himself from those who seemed to require grace, he added, “among whom we too.”]

among whom we too all once lived in the desires of our flesh—behold how he says “in the desires,” doing the will of the flesh and of thoughts—and we were by nature, through original sin, sons of wrath, just as the others. This is an insertion.

[Note: [Col. 0291A] 6. “But God, who is rich.” He had begun, “And you, when you were dead”; he inserted the intervening material until he resumed that statement, no longer saying “you,” but “we.”]

But God, who is rich in mercy, because of his great love with which he loved us, even when we were dead in sins, made us alive together with Christ—by whose grace you have been saved—and raised us up together,

[Note: [Col. 0291A] 7. “And made us sit together.” He says that he made us share in those things he spoke of concerning Christ, through that union which exists with him.]

and made us sit together in the heavenly places in Christ Jesus,

[Note: [Col. 0291A] 8. “So that he might show.” He rightly said “in the ages to come,” when God will manifest toward us the goodness of those very things, and that grace which he deigned to perfect through the things belonging to Christ.]

so that he might show

[Note: [Col. 0291A] 9. LANFRANC. “In the coming ages.” In us, he says, who have obtained such great mercy from God, God showed how much human beings may hope for in future times. [Col. 0291B]]

in the ages to come—that is, to future human beings—his surpassing riches of grace, so that they might likewise hope for the same concerning themselves, or in the eternal age, because he saved us, in goodness, not through our merits, the goodness he showed toward us in Christ Jesus, in the faith of Christ. This is the manifestation of goodness.

For by grace you have been saved through faith, and this salvation is not from yourselves—it is the gift of God—not from works, so that no one may glory in himself, which would happen if he were saved from works.

[Note: [Col. 0292A] 10. “For we are his workmanship.” The reason why no one should glory in his own works. It is as though he were saying: “He himself made and created us in the faith of Jesus Christ and in the good works that he prepared for us by his grace.” The ablative *factura* may also mean “by workmanship,” so that the sense is: “It is his operation that we were created in the faith of Jesus Christ,” and so forth.]

For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus in good works; even in the fact that we do good works, we have been made by God for the works which God prepared, and this also is not from us, so that we might walk in them.

[Note: [Col. 0292A] 11. “Therefore, remember.” Since, he says, God gave you faith and good works, remember the words of God and the evils in which you once lived, so that in return for the benefits bestowed you may render greater thanks to God.]

Therefore, because you have been saved by grace, remember that you were once Gentiles in the flesh,

[Note: [Col. 0292A] 12. AMBROSE. “Who were called.” What he says, “in the flesh,” should be attached to “who are called,” not to that statement in which he said “Gentiles,” so that the sense is that those uncircumcised in the flesh should be called by that name.]

who are called “the uncircumcision” by what is called “the circumcision” in the flesh, made by hand. And remember that at that time you were without Christ, alienated from the society of Israel, the Jews,

[Note: [Col. 0292A] 13. LANFRANC. “Strangers to the covenants.” The Gentiles were strangers in relation to those who possessed the covenants, either because they came and departed for a time, like guests; or because, if some of them converted to the Jewish rite, they were called newcomers and proselytes.]

and strangers to the covenants, outsiders to the law, without hope of the promise, as the Jews had, and without God in this world.

But now in Christ Jesus, in the faith of Christ, you who once were far from God through sins have been brought near in the blood of Christ. For he himself is our peace, who made both one—either the angelic and human creation, or Jews and Gentiles—

[Note: [Col. 0292A] 14. AMBROSE. “The middle wall.” He caused the hostility and separation produced by circumcision, together with the whole law, to cease. For after the resurrection, granting us immortality, he destroyed these things. In an immortal nature circumcision can in no way be practiced.]

and, by destroying the middle wall—as though dismantling a strong stone barrier—hostility (behold the wall)

[Note: [Col. 0292A] 15. LANFRANC. “In his flesh.” In his flesh, whether assumed or crucified, Christ dissolved the legal observances, which he calls a wall and an enemy [perhaps: “hostility”] between Jews and Gentiles; for the law was not given except until the coming of Christ. [Col. 0292C]]

in his flesh—the Jewish law, or the wall—by emptying the decrees of the commandments through evangelical decrees, so that he might create the two peoples in himself as one new human being, the law having been emptied, in himself, or so that they might be one new human being, making peace. This repeats what came before.

[Note: [Col. 0292B] 16. “That he might reconcile both,” and so forth. He restrains the Jews by saying that they too, like the Gentiles, needed reconciliation. [Col. 0293A]]

And he might reconcile both, so that they may be in one body, in himself, to God through the cross, killing the hostility in himself.

And when he came, he proclaimed peace to you Gentiles, who were far away, and peace to those who were near, because through him we both have access, in one Spirit, who effects this, to the Father.

Therefore, since the hostility has been destroyed, you are no longer strangers and newcomers, but you are fellow citizens of the saints and members of God’s household. He explains how they are citizens: built upon

[Col. 0293]

[Note: [Col. 0293A] 17. “Upon the foundation.” He calls faith the foundation—the same faith, he says, that the prophets also had.]

the foundation—intransitively, or upon the faith—of the apostles and prophets,

[Note: [Col. 0293A] 18. “The chief cornerstone itself.” The order is: “with Christ Jesus existing as the chief cornerstone.”]

with Christ Jesus himself as the chief cornerstone. In him every structure, joined together, grows into a holy temple in the Lord; in him you too are built together into a dwelling place, so that you may be a dwelling place of God in the Spirit.

## COMMENTARY

[Col. 0291]

[Col. 0291A] CHAPTER II.—1. AMBROSE. “According to the age.” By “age” he does not mean creation, but the temporal conduct of this present age.

2. LANFRANC. “According to the prince,” that is, according to what the prince who has power in this air persuaded you to do, whether in tempting the faithful or in stirring up the air itself.

3. AMBROSE. “Of the power of the air.” The devil received the command to rule the air and to have power to stir it up.

4. LANFRANC. “In the sons of distrust.” They are called sons of distrust either because they distrust the promises of God, or because the faithful have no hope for their conversion.

5. AMBROSE. “Among whom we too.” Since he had said “you,” lest he be thought to withdraw himself from those who seemed to require grace, he added, “among whom we too.”

6. “But God, who is rich.” He had begun, “And you, when you were dead”; he inserted the intervening material until he resumed that statement, no longer saying “you,” but “we.”

7. “And made us sit together.” He says that he made us share in those things he spoke of concerning Christ, through that union which exists with him.

8. “So that he might show.” He rightly said “in the ages to come,” when God will manifest toward us the goodness of those very things, and that grace which he deigned to perfect through the things belonging to Christ.

9. LANFRANC. “In the coming ages.” In us, he says, who have obtained such great mercy from God, God showed how much human beings may hope for in future times. [Col. 0291B]

[Col. 0292A] 10. “For we are his workmanship.” The reason why no one should glory in his own works. It is as though he were saying: “He himself made and created us in the faith of Jesus Christ and in the good works that he prepared for us by his grace.” The ablative *factura* may also mean “by workmanship,” so that the sense is: “It is his operation that we were created in the faith of Jesus Christ,” and so forth.

11. “Therefore, remember.” Since, he says, God gave you faith and good works, remember the words of God and the evils in which you once lived, so that in return for the benefits bestowed you may render greater thanks to God.

12. AMBROSE. “Who were called.” What he says, “in the flesh,” should be attached to “who are called,” not to that statement in which he said “Gentiles,” so that the sense is that those uncircumcised in the flesh should be called by that name.

13. LANFRANC. “Strangers to the covenants.” The Gentiles were strangers in relation to those who possessed the covenants, either because they came and departed for a time, like guests; or because, if some of them converted to the Jewish rite, they were called newcomers and proselytes.

14. AMBROSE. “The middle wall.” He caused the hostility and separation produced by circumcision, together with the whole law, to cease. For after the resurrection, granting us immortality, he destroyed these things. In an immortal nature circumcision can in no way be practiced.

15. LANFRANC. “In his flesh.” In his flesh, whether assumed or crucified, Christ dissolved the legal observances, which he calls a wall and an enemy [perhaps: “hostility”] between Jews and Gentiles; for the law was not given except until the coming of Christ. [Col. 0292B]

16. “That he might reconcile both,” and so forth. He restrains the Jews by saying that they too, like the Gentiles, needed reconciliation. [Col. 0293A]

17. “Upon the foundation.” He calls faith the foundation—the same faith, he says, that the prophets also had.

18. “The chief cornerstone itself.” The order is: “with Christ Jesus existing as the chief cornerstone.”

# CHAPTER III

[Col. 0293]

For this reason—that you may be God’s dwelling place—I, Paul, a prisoner of Christ Jesus, imprisoned for preaching to you Gentiles—if indeed you have heard of the stewardship of God’s grace that was given to me for you, because, according to God’s revelation, not through a human being, the mystery was made known to me,

> **[Col. 0293A] CAP. III.—1. LANFR. “If indeed you have heard.”** This is an interruption in the sentence, continuing until another sentence, which begins: “For this reason I bend my knees,” etc.

as I briefly wrote above, as you can understand when you read, according to my understanding of the mystery of Christ, which was not made known to other generations—namely, to the sons of men—as it has now been revealed to his holy apostles and prophets of the New Testament, such as Agabus, in the Spirit. (Behold the mystery of Christ:) that the Gentiles are fellow-heirs with the Jews—or with the angels—members of the same body, and fellow-partakers of his promise in Christ Jesus through the Gospel, through faith, of which I became a minister according to the gift of God’s grace, which was given to me according to the operation of his power.

> **[Col. 0293A] 2. “The mystery was made known.”** This mystery concerns the equality of the Gentiles with the Jewish people; above he wrote briefly about it, saying: “For he himself is our peace, who made both one,” etc., up to: “You are no longer strangers and foreigners.”

> **[Col. 0293B] 3. “I wrote above briefly.”** Briefly: the foregoing passage was written to make known the mystery of his will, namely, to restore all things in heaven and on earth.

> **[Col. 0293B] 4. “Generations.”** It was indeed revealed to the prophets of the Old Testament, through God’s grace, that the Gentiles would be saved. But that they would come to equality with the Jews, so that they would become co-heirs and members of the same body with them, possessing with them one equal inheritance, forming one spiritual body—that is, one Church—with the Jewish people, and becoming equally participants in God’s promise: this was revealed to no one except in the New Testament.

To me, the least of all the saints, this grace was given: to preach among the Gentiles the unsearchable riches of Christ, and to enlighten everyone concerning the administration of the mystery hidden from the ages, from the foundation of the world—or from worldly generations—in God, who created all things,

> **[Col. 0293B] 5. “So that it might be made known.”** It was hidden for this purpose: that afterward the manifold wisdom—shown in the patriarchs, prophets, and apostles whom he sent before—might be made known to the heavenly beings through the Church, that is, through what takes place in the Church.

> **[Col. 0293C] 6. AMBROS. “So that it might be made known.”** This had been so hidden that even the invisible powers could not have known it. Now, however, it has been made manifest through what has been done concerning the Church.

> **[Col. 0294A] 7. LANFR. “So that it might be made known.”** The heavenly spirits also advanced toward knowledge of God’s wisdom through the Church, because, while Christ instructed it either personally or through his apostles, they learned many secrets that they had previously not known.

so that God’s manifold wisdom might be made known to the principalities and powers dwelling in the heavenly places, through the Church,

> **[Col. 0294A] 8. “Manifold.”** The order is: “the manifold wisdom of God,” according to the wisdom of God, which in its own nature is simple but, according to the ordering of the ages, is called manifold, since the ages themselves vary in manifold ways within God’s ordering.

according to the eternal purpose that he established in Christ Jesus our Lord. In him we have boldness and access with confidence through faith in him. [pp. 143–144]

> **[Col. 0294A] 9. “For this reason I ask.”** He asks that they not despair of God’s mercy toward them when they see him suffer so much.

Therefore, because we have confidence,

> **[Col. 0294A] 10. AMBROS. “For this reason I ask.”** Paul, the prisoner, inserted everything from “Paul, the prisoner,” up to this phrase: “For this reason I ask.”

I ask that you not lose heart because of my tribulations for you, which are your glory.

> **[Col. 0294B] 11. LANFR. “I ask that you not lose heart.”** He knew that each of the two depended upon the other: glory upon free will, when he asks that they not lose heart; and free will upon the gift of grace, when he asks God to give them strength.

For this reason—that you may not lose heart; or he repeats what he said above, since he inserted much material—I bend my knees before the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, from whom every fatherhood in heaven and on earth is named,

> **[Col. 0294B] 12. AUGUST. (*Sermon 7 on the Words of the Apostle*, vol. X), “For this reason.”** For what reason, if not the one he stated above: “I ask that you not grow weak in my tribulations for you, which are your glory”? Since, then, you possess the exercise of the will, I ask. But since the exercise of the will is not sufficient for you to accomplish what I ask, “For this reason I bend my knees before the Father.”

> **[Col. 0294B] 13. LANFR. “Fatherhood in heaven.”** He calls spiritual people “heaven”; carnal people, “earth.” “Before the Father,” he says, “I bend my knees.” “From whom,” that is, through whom, all other fathers—whether spiritual or carnal—are named. For he who caused things to be what they are is himself the cause that they are named according to what they are.

> Alternatively: “from whom,” that is, according to whose likeness spiritual or carnal fathers are named. Almighty God is called Father either because he generated the Son from himself or because he governs and rules created things by his own direction. According to this likeness and for the same reason, fathers are so called either because they beget children from themselves or because they govern and rule those subject to them with devoted care.

> If by “heaven” he intended angels, we must believe that lesser angels call greater ones fathers. However the sentence is understood, “good fatherhood” must be understood; for that fatherhood was not from God of which he says in the Gospel: “You are from your father the devil.” And elsewhere: “He was a liar from the beginning,” calling him “the father of lies,” namely, the devil.

so that he may grant you, according to the riches of his glory, to be strengthened with power through his Spirit in the inner person, and that Christ may dwell through faith in your hearts, rooted and grounded in love,

> **[Col. 0295A] 14. AUGUST. (*Letter 120, On the Grace of the New Testament*, chap. 26, vol. II), “Rooted and grounded.”** “Rooted” with reference to agriculture; “grounded” with reference to building. For elsewhere he says: “You are God’s field, God’s building.”

so that, with all the saints, you may comprehend what is the breadth, the true love, and the length, the expectation of God’s gifts, and the height, the true height—that is, seeing God—and the depth, knowledge of God’s secrets;

> **[Col. 0295B] 15. AMBROS. “So that you may be able.”** That is, so that you may remain in the enjoyment of life, as he shows by saying “with the saints.” By “breadth, length, depth, and height” he means the greatness of grace, using terms that seem great to us. “I pray,” he says, “that, with the saints, you may comprehend that great gift of God which Christ’s love has bestowed upon us.”

> **[Col. 0295B] 16. AUGUST. (The same work), “What is the breadth.”** Breadth consists in good works, through which goodwill is extended even to the love of enemies; length means that, with long-suffering, hardships are endured for the sake of this breadth; height means that for these things one hopes for the eternal reward above, rather than for some vain temporal benefit; and depth signifies the depth of gratuitous grace, in which the understanding of many is crushed as they try to investigate it, until finally it is said to them: “O man, who are you to answer back to God?”

> **[Col. 0295C] 17. LANFR. “Breadth.”** The breadth of Christians is largeness of heart, for giving and helping on God’s behalf insofar as one is able. Hence it is said elsewhere: “Enlarge yourselves also.”

> **[Col. 0295C] 18. “Length.”** Length, also called long-suffering elsewhere, is the expectation of God’s promises with joyful readiness of mind.

> **[Col. 0295C] 19. “Height.”** Height is the heavenly life. Hence it is said elsewhere: “An eternal weight of glory beyond all measure in height.”

> **[Col. 0296A] 20. “Depth.”** He calls depth the underworld. The Apostle therefore prays that they may be able to understand these four things and, once they understand them, desire three and avoid one.

and to know the love of Christ, which surpasses knowledge,

> **[Col. 0296A] 21. AGUST. (*Letter 112 to Paulina, On Seeing God*, chap. 23, vol. II), “That you may be filled.”** They will be filled unto all the fullness of God, not when they themselves become fully God, but when they have been perfectly filled with God.

> **[Col. 0296A] 22. AMBROS. “That you may be filled.”** That is, so that you may yourselves be seen in the proportion of the common body in which God dwells.

so that you may be filled with virtues unto all the fullness of God.

> **[Col. 0296A] 23. “Now to him who is able.”** After recounting grace, he prays for them and, concluding under the appearance [reading uncertain: “form”] of thanksgiving, begins the ethical discourse after the doctrinal discourse.

Now to him who is able to do exceedingly more than we ask or understand, according to the power that works in us—which we may know from his giving us the power of miracles—to him be glory in the Church, in the body and in Christ Jesus, and in the head, throughout all the generations of this age, consisting from the beginning of many ages [reading uncertain: “consisting”]—of the ages. Amen.

> **[Col. 0296B] 24. LANFR. “Of the ages of ages.”** The age of ages is eternity, whose parts are times and all the ages. “Ages of ages” may also be understood as this present age, considered as a whole from the beginning of the world to its end, divided into many ages.

**[Col. 0295]**

Therefore I beseech you—I, a prisoner, imprisoned in and for the Lord—to walk worthily of the calling with which you were called, with all humility in words and deeds, and gentleness, with patience, bearing with one another in love, eager to preserve the unity and harmony of the Spirit in the bond of peace (by analogy).

> **[Col. 0296B] CAP. IV.—1. AMBROS. “I, a prisoner.”** He changes the form out of reverence, since he added: “I, a prisoner in the Lord”; for he appears to bear these bonds because of his preaching.

There is one body and one Spirit,

just as you were also called in one hope of your calling. Just as you have one Lord and one faith, one baptism, so you ought to have one Spirit. One God and Father of all,

who is over all, as Lord; through all, as governing; and in us all, as dwelling within us.

First he proves this from authority, then from its parts.

Therefore he says in Psalm 67: “Christ ascending on high led captivity captive”—in himself as a reality, in us as a hope—captivity, whether death or human beings, previously taken captive by the devil; he gave gifts to human beings.

> **[Col. 0297B] 9. LANFR. “But that he ascended.”** He proves that the preceding verse was spoken about Christ; for he ascended into heaven and descended from heaven.

> **[Col. 0297B] 10. AMBROS. “He descended.”** He calls the lower regions the earth itself in comparison with heaven. He means that he would not have ascended unless the divine nature had first existed in him, choosing to dwell in him who was upon the earth.

> **11. “He who descended.”** He means that the one into whom the divine nature descended was exalted above the heavens. He inserted this to show how Christ, as man, could bestow spiritual gifts upon others; afterward he returns to his own point.

He who descended is himself also the one who ascended above all the heavens,

> **[Col. 0297C] 12. LANFR. “That he might fill all things.”** That is, all the Gentiles with divine worship, or all the things that had been foretold about him.

so that he might fill all things. He proves that the gifts are diverse. And he himself gave some as apostles, some as prophets—such as Agabus and his daughters—others as evangelists,

for the perfecting of the saints (from this Spirit other charisms are given to them, that they may bring sanctity to completion in them), for the work of ministry, so that they may build up the saints who belong to the body of Christ, that is, the Church, for the building of the body of Christ, which is to be built up,

This is what he says: “unto the measure of the age of the fullness of Christ,” that is, the age in which Christ possessed the fullness of years and bodily maturity. It may also be understood that we will arrive at one perfect man so that we may all be one perfect man—that is, one Church lacking nothing and to which nothing later needs to be added.

until we all arrive, on the day of judgment, before God, at the unity of faith and the knowledge of the Son of God, remaining in this age, at a perfect man, that we may rise perfected without the loss of any limbs,

unto the measure of the age of the fullness of Christ;

because of the ignorance that is in them, because of the blindness of their heart. They worship idols, and, having become desperate, they handed themselves over to indecency, to the practice of every impurity, to insatiable greed.

# COMMENTARY

**[Col. 0296] CAP. IV**

**1. AMBROS. “I, a prisoner.”** He changes the form out of reverence, since he added: “I, a prisoner in the Lord”; for he appears to bear these bonds because of his preaching.

**2. “One body.”** That is, preserve this unity inviolate through peace and love. He attempts to show in many ways that this is necessary through what follows.

**[Col. 0296C] 3. LANFR. “One body and one Spirit.”** You have one Spirit, just as you are one body, so that you may not be schismatics.

**4. AMBROS. “And one Spirit.”** The Spirit who regenerated us. “You appear,” he says, “to constitute one body through regeneration.”

**5. “Who is over all.”** He who surpasses everyone. This is what he means by “over all”: he also displays his providence through all things and in all things, although he deigns both to exist among us and to dwell in us.

**[Col. 0297A] 6. “To each one of you.”** He means that, although concord is necessary in every respect, there nevertheless appears to be a difference among them because of the variety of gifts.

**7. LANFR. “Grace was given according to measure,” etc.** Although there is one Spirit, his gifts are diverse. This is what he says: “Grace was given according to measure,” that is, in diverse ways: to one this, to another that; to one more, to another less. First he proves this from authority, then from its parts.

**8. AUGUST. (*Exposition on Psalm 67*, vol. VIII), “He led captivity captive.”** Was this because he conquered death, which held captive those over whom it reigned, or because he called the human beings themselves “captivity,” since they were held captive under the devil?

**9. LANFR. “But that he ascended.”** He proves that the preceding verse was spoken about Christ; for he ascended into heaven and descended from heaven.

**10. AMBROS. “He descended.”** He calls the lower regions the earth itself in comparison with heaven. He means that he would not have ascended unless the divine nature had first existed in him, choosing to dwell in him who was upon the earth.

**11. “He who descended.”** He means that the one into whom the divine nature descended was exalted above the heavens. He inserted this to show how Christ, as man, could bestow spiritual gifts upon others; afterward he returns to his own point.

**[Col. 0297C] 12. LANFR. “That he might fill all things.”** That is, all the Gentiles with divine worship, or all the things that had been foretold about him.

**13. AUGUST. (*Letter 59 to Paulinus*, question 4, vol. II), “Others as pastors.”** I think that the pastors and teachers whom you especially wanted us to distinguish are the same, as it also seemed to you, so that we should not understand some as pastors and others as teachers. Rather, after mentioning pastors, he added “teachers” so that pastors might understand that teaching belongs to their office.

**14. LANFR. “Others as pastors.”** For this reason Christ gave different gifts to different people, so that each might be perfectly exercised in the work of the ministry he had received. For if one person had received everything, he could not devote himself perfectly to each task. He then explains what the work of the ministry is for the saints, to whom spiritual graces have been given by Christ, saying: “For the building up of the body of Christ.” Spiritual gifts are given to them for this purpose: to build up the body of Christ, or the Church.

**[Col. 0298A] 15. “Until we all arrive.”** The order is: “until we all, who remain in this age, arrive at the unity of faith and the knowledge of the Son of God in a perfect man.” This signifies the day of judgment: all who now possess one faith and one knowledge of the Son of God will come together from the different regions of the world, so that each may be a perfect man, possessing the age at which Christ passed from this world and rose again. This is what he says: “unto the measure of the age of the fullness of Christ,” that is, the age in which Christ possessed the fullness of years and bodily maturity. It may also be understood that we will arrive at one perfect man so that we may all be one perfect man—that is, one Church lacking nothing and to which nothing later needs to be added.

16. AUGUSTINE (Book XXII of *The City of God*, chapter 15). “Into a perfect man.” Let us understand this statement to mean that the bodies of the dead will rise neither below nor beyond the youthful form, but at the age and strength which we know Christ attained.

17. [The same, cited above.] “Into the measure.” Concerning “the measure of the fullness of Christ’s age,” let us understand it either in this way: that in Christian peoples the measure of his age may be completed in that Head, with the perfection of all the members preceding it; or that this was said concerning the resurrection of bodies.

18. LANFRANC. “Into the measure of the fullness of Christ’s age,” that is, at the age when Christ, possessing the fullness of years and bodily maturity, passed from this world.

19. AMBROSE. “From whom the whole.” The body of the Church is joined to Christ as to its Head, according to which [Col. 0299A] spiritual activity is brought about in each one of us.

20. LANFRANC. “Of the supply.” The supply of a sinner is his conversion to God, by which he is joined to the Church as a member to a body.

21. “According to the operation.” According to what the great [perhaps: one] member does, the growth of the body will take place.

22. AMBROSE. “For the building up of itself.” By “itself” he speaks of Christ, as though he said: Since Christ builds up his own body, on account of that love which he appears to have toward us.

23. LANFRANC. “In love.” He explains the manner of this building up: it occurs only through love. If a member refuses to work, it is not a member.

[Col. 0299B] 24. AMBROSE. “From the life of God,” that is, from that resurrection which is expected to take place.

25. AUGUSTINE (Book XIV of *On the Trinity*, chapter 16, vol. III). “Be renewed.” When he says, “in the spirit of your mind,” he did not intend us to understand two things there, as though the mind were one thing and the spirit of the mind another.

26. AUGUSTINE (Book III of *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, chapter 20, vol. III). “Who is according to God.” Just as, after the fall into sin, man is renewed in the knowledge of God according to the image of him who created him, so he was created in that very knowledge before he grew old through transgression; hence he would be renewed again in the same knowledge [variant: “in the same understanding”].

27. AUGUSTINE (*Expositions on the Psalms*, Psalm XXV, vol. VIII). “Let not the sun go down.” What this means is understood also according to the time. As though from the very condition and weakness of mortality which we bear, anger creeps upon a Christian; it ought not to be held for a long time and become yesterday’s anger. Cast it out of your heart before this visible light sets, lest that invisible light abandon you. But it is better understood another way, because Christ is our sun of justice and truth, by whose truth the human soul is illumined.

28. AUGUSTINE (Sermon on Psalm XI, among fragment 24). “Let it not go down.” Thus the true light of justice and wisdom is what the mind ceases to see when it has been overwhelmed, as by a cloud, through the disturbance of anger; and then it is as though the sun goes down [variant: “and then the sun goes down”] over a man’s anger.

AMBROSE. “To give grace,” that is, in which it is fitting that those who hear should rejoice.

29. AUGUSTINE (Book IV of *The Literal Meaning of Genesis*, chapter 9). “Do not grieve.” For the substance of the Holy Spirit—which is whatever he himself is—cannot itself be grieved, since it possesses eternal and unchangeable blessedness, and is itself rather eternal and unchangeable blessedness. But because he dwells in the saints so as to fill them with love, and because it is necessary that human beings rejoice in due course over the progress of the faithful and their good works, it is therefore also necessary that they grieve over the falls or sins of those whose faith and piety had caused them to rejoice.

30. [The same work.] “The Holy Spirit of God.” The Spirit is said to be grieved by those who act in such a way that the saints are grieved by their deeds, for no other reason than that they possess the Holy Spirit; and by that gift they are so good that evil things trouble them [variant: “make them sorrowful”].

31. LANFRANC. “The day of redemption.” He calls the day of redemption the day of baptism, in which the Holy Spirit, through faith, sacraments, and spiritual graces, marks the faithful [Col. 0300C], that is, separates them from unbelief.

AUGUSTINE (from *Against Lying*, chapter 19, vol. IV). “Blasphemy.” Blasphemy is speech by which false things are said about God himself.

[Col. 0301A] 32. AMBROSE. “As God also.” Since it seemed burdensome that someone should forgive one who had injured him, he added: “Just as God gave you forgiveness in Christ.”

[Col. 0301]

“Therefore be imitators of God, as beloved children, and walk in love, just as Christ also loved us and gave himself for us as an offering and sacrifice to God, for a fragrant odor, so that you may please him. He gives the reason why these things must not be committed. “For know this with understanding: no fornicator, or impure person, or greedy person, which is the service of idols” [Note: [Col. 0301A] CHAPTER V.—1. AMBROSE. “Which is of idols.” He showed the weight of greed by a similar comparison, calling it the service of idols, because it turns a person away from God in the same way], “has any inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and of God.”

[Note: [Col. 0301A] 2. LANFRANC. “Let no one deceive you.” Certain people were deceiving their hearers, persuading them that because of the sins mentioned above a person would not lose eternal life.]

“Let no one deceive us by persuading you with empty words that, because of these things”—for truly because of the sins mentioned above—“the wrath of God comes upon the sons of distrust,” those who distrust God. Because the wrath of God comes on account of this, do not therefore become their companions.

“For you were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord. Therefore, since you are light, walk as children of light.” Here he shows how they ought to walk: namely, in every goodness, that is, truly.

[Note: [Col. 0301A] 3. “For the fruit of light.” He says that the fruit of an enlightened person is every goodness, justice, and truth. Having first stated the genus, he joined the species to it, including justice; some wish “truth” to be understood in deeds, and others in thoughts and words.]

“For the fruit of light is in every goodness, justice, and truth, proving and experiencing what is pleasing to God. And do not share in the unfruitful works of darkness, but rather rebuke those works. For the things they do in secret are shameful even to mention.”

Rebuke them.

[Note: [Col. 0301A] 4. “But all things that are done.” He gives the reason why he said, “but rather rebuke them.” For all the sins of people predestined to eternal life, which are committed in the light—that is, by a just spiritual person—are revealed by confession; and everything that is revealed in confession is light, that is, it makes the one who is revealed into light. And rightly is it said: just as the commission of a crime makes darkness, so its confession makes light.]

“For everything that is done”—namely, the sins of those predestined to life—“and rebuked by the light, by the spiritual person, is revealed through confession.”

[Note: [Col. 0302A] 5. AMBROSE. “But all things that are done.” This was said by the Apostle incompletely. For when he said, “because they are revealed,” he entrusted to silence what followed—namely, that the very revelation might be helpful. For anyone whose offense is revealed suffers shame.]

[Note: [Col. 0302A] 6. “Everything that is revealed.” He referred to another matter when he said, “Do not share in the works of darkness.” That is: do not imitate their works, but do such things as will cause you no sadness if they are revealed. Those works are of the light which are done openly; those works are of darkness which are concealed.]

“For everything that is revealed by confession is light,” that is, it makes the one who reveals it light.

He proves this by authoritative testimony, saying:

[Note: [Col. 0302A] 7. “Rise, you who sleep.” This testimony has no continuity with what precedes; although he was discussing the light, he referred it here to the works of darkness. Some, however, said that at that time, among the other graces, the grace of making psalms was given; hence the Apostle appears to have misused this testimony.]

[Note: [Col. 0302B] 8. AUGUSTINE (*Expositions on the Psalms*, Psalm LXII). “The sleep of the soul” is to forget its God; whatever soul has forgotten its God has slept [variant: “is sleeping”].]

“Rise, you who sleep in vices, and rise from the dead”—that is, from sins—“by confessing your sins, and Christ will illumine you.” This shows what the light is.

“Therefore, brothers, see carefully how you walk, since you are children of light: not as foolish people, but as wise,”

[Note: [Col. 0302B] 9. AUGUSTINE (*Sermon 16, On Various Matters*, in the appendix, vol. X). “Redeeming the time.” To redeem time means this: when someone brings a lawsuit against you, sacrifice something so that you may devote yourself to God rather than to lawsuits. Thus, from what you give up, the price is time.]

“redeeming the time, because the days are evil”—the days of this age, in which the Evil One is permitted to rage. Therefore, since the days are evil, do not become foolish, but understand what the will of God is.

“And do not become drunk with wine, in which there is debauchery, but be filled with the Holy Spirit, speaking to yourselves in psalms”—those of David—“and hymns”—such as those of Prudentius—“and spiritual songs,” with other prayers, singing and making melody in your hearts, not merely with your mouths, to the Lord; always giving thanks for everything, whether prosperous or adverse, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ to God and the Father.

“Be subject to one another in the fear of Christ.” Here he shows how he asks them to be subject.

[Note: [Col. 0302B] 10. AMBROSE. “Wives to husbands.” Three effects are mentioned; among them he placed two natural ones first, and in each he began with those who are lower.]

“Let wives be subject to their husbands,” not hypocritically, but as to the Lord, or to God.

Here is why:

[Note: [Col. 0302B] 11. “For the husband is the head.” Christ has this order in relation to the Church because the Church appears to have the cause of its second life from him. “For the husband is the head of the woman, just as Christ is the head of the Church. The husband did not save the woman, but Christ himself is the Savior of his body. But just as the Church is subject to Christ, so also let wives be subject to their husbands in everything.

“Husbands, love your wives, just as Christ also loved the Church”—in its effect—“and gave himself for her, in order to sanctify her,”

“cleansing her with the washing of water in the word of life,”

“in baptism—that is, in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit—for this purpose,”

VII). “That he might present her to himself.” This will be the case when she is glorious; for it cannot now be said that she is glorious amid so many evils, so many scandals, so great a mixture of the worst people, and so many insults from the ungodly.]

“that he might present the Church to himself as glorious,”

[Note: [Col. 0303B] 15. AUGUSTINE (*Sermon 2 on the Mount*, chapter 22). “Not having a spot.” Not having a spot or wrinkle, that is, being clean and simple.]

“not having a spot of sin, or a wrinkle of hypocrisy, or anything of this kind, but so that she may be holy and immaculate, like Christ.

“Thus husbands also ought to love their wives as their own bodies. He who loves his wife loves himself, his own flesh.”

[Note: [Col. 0303B] 16. LANFRANC. “He who loves his wife.” They ought to love their wives because they love themselves as a whole—that is, their own flesh. For they ought not to have [this is argued] from the contrary. “No one,” and so forth, is from the general category.]

“For no one has ever hated his own flesh, but nourishes and cherishes it, just as Christ does the Church,”

“because we—that is, the Church—are members of his body, of his flesh and of his bones,”

“existing from his weak and strong members,” or possessing the same flesh and the same bones that Christ possessed.
