He proves this by authoritative testimony, saying:

[Note: [Col. 0302A] 7. “Rise, you who sleep.” This testimony has no continuity with what precedes; although he was discussing the light, he referred it here to the works of darkness. Some, however, said that at that time, among the other graces, the grace of making psalms was given; hence the Apostle appears to have misused this testimony.]

[Note: [Col. 0302B] 8. AUGUSTINE (*Expositions on the Psalms*, Psalm LXII). “The sleep of the soul” is to forget its God; whatever soul has forgotten its God has slept [variant: “is sleeping”].]

“Rise, you who sleep in vices, and rise from the dead”—that is, from sins—“by confessing your sins, and Christ will illumine you.” This shows what the light is.

“Therefore, brothers, see carefully how you walk, since you are children of light: not as foolish people, but as wise,”

[Note: [Col. 0302B] 9. AUGUSTINE (*Sermon 16, On Various Matters*, in the appendix, vol. X). “Redeeming the time.” To redeem time means this: when someone brings a lawsuit against you, sacrifice something so that you may devote yourself to God rather than to lawsuits. Thus, from what you give up, the price is time.]

“redeeming the time, because the days are evil”—the days of this age, in which the Evil One is permitted to rage. Therefore, since the days are evil, do not become foolish, but understand what the will of God is.

“And do not become drunk with wine, in which there is debauchery, but be filled with the Holy Spirit, speaking to yourselves in psalms”—those of David—“and hymns”—such as those of Prudentius—“and spiritual songs,” with other prayers, singing and making melody in your hearts, not merely with your mouths, to the Lord; always giving thanks for everything, whether prosperous or adverse, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ to God and the Father.

“Be subject to one another in the fear of Christ.” Here he shows how he asks them to be subject.

[Note: [Col. 0302B] 10. AMBROSE. “Wives to husbands.” Three effects are mentioned; among them he placed two natural ones first, and in each he began with those who are lower.]

“Let wives be subject to their husbands,” not hypocritically, but as to the Lord, or to God.

Here is why:

[Note: [Col. 0302B] 11. “For the husband is the head.” Christ has this order in relation to the Church because the Church appears to have the cause of its second life from him. Here in this passage, he himself, the Savior of the body, says that the husband has this order in relation to the woman, because, in order that she may exist, she receives the man.]

“For the husband is the head of the woman, just as Christ is the head of the Church. The husband did not save the woman, but Christ himself is the Savior of his body. But just as the Church is subject to Christ, so also let wives be subject to their husbands in everything.

“Husbands, love your wives, just as Christ also loved the Church”—in its effect—“and gave himself for her, in order to sanctify her,”

[Note: [Col. 0303A] 12. AUGUSTINE (*Tractate 15 on the Gospel of John*, vol. IX). “Cleansing with the washing.” What is baptism? A washing of water in the word. Take away the water: it is not baptism. Take away the word: it is not baptism.]

“cleansing her with the washing of water in the word of life,”

[Note: [Col. 0303A] 13. LANFRANC. “The washing of water in the word.” He calls “word” the utterance of the divine name which is spoken by those baptizing over the water.]

“in baptism—that is, in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit—for this purpose,”

[Note: [Col. 0303A] 14. AUGUSTINE. 14. (Book *On the Perfection of Justice*, chapter 15, vol. VII). “That he might present her to himself.” This will be the case when she is glorious; for it cannot now be said that she is glorious amid so many evils, so many scandals, so great a mixture of the worst people, and so many insults from the ungodly.]

“that he might present the Church to himself as glorious,”

[Note: [Col. 0303B] 15. AUGUSTINE (*Sermon 2 on the Mount*, chapter 22). “Not having a spot.” Not having a spot or wrinkle, that is, being clean and simple.]

“not having a spot of sin, or a wrinkle of hypocrisy, or anything of this kind, but so that she may be holy and immaculate, like Christ.

“Thus husbands also ought to love their wives as their own bodies. He who loves his wife loves himself, his own flesh.”

[Note: [Col. 0303B] 16. LANFRANC. “He who loves his wife.” They ought to love their wives because they love themselves as a whole—that is, their own flesh. For they ought not to have [this is argued] from the contrary. “No one,” and so forth, is from the general category.]

“For no one has ever hated his own flesh, but nourishes and cherishes it, just as Christ does the Church,”

[Note: [Col. 0303B] 17. “For no one ever.” He proves that husbands love their own bodies.]

“because we—that is, the Church—are members of his body, of his flesh and of his bones,”

[Note: [Col. 0303B] 18. “Because we are members of his body.” This may be read as referring to his body consisting of his flesh and bones—that is, of weak and strong members—or as meaning that we are members of his flesh and bones, possessing the same flesh and the same bones [Col. 0303C] that he himself possessed.]

“existing from his weak and strong members,” or possessing the same flesh and the same bones that Christ possessed.

[Note: [Col. 0303C] 19. “For this reason a man will leave.” Since, he says, we are from his flesh and bones, therefore, as it is written in Genesis, “he will leave”—the Word of the Father who was to become man will leave—the Father, that is, appearing not as the same essence, because he remains with the Father; and his mother, that is, the Synagogue; and he will cling to his wife, that is, the Church. Thus this is called a sacrament. Nevertheless, although it is said concerning Christ, it can also be understood literally, so that many men who love their wives leave father and mother. And this is what follows: “Nevertheless, you also,” and so on.]

“For this reason a man will leave his father and [Col. 0304A] his mother and cling to his wife, and the two will become one flesh.”

[Note: [Col. 0304A] 20. AUGUSTINE (Book XII of *Against Faustus the Manichaean*, chapter 9, vol. VI). “A man will leave.” Who would not recognize that Christ left the Father in this manner? Although he was in the form of God, he did not regard equality with God as something to be seized, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant. He also left his mother, the Synagogue of the Jews, which clung carnally to the Old Testament, and clung to his wife, the Church [variant: “the holy Church,”] so that in the peace of the New Testament the two might be one flesh. For although he is God with the Father, through whom we were made, he became our companion, so that we might be the body of that Head.]

[Col. 0304B] 21. THE SAME (Commentary on the Gospel of John 10, vol. IX). “And his mother.” How did he leave his mother? By leaving the Synagogue of the Jews, from which Christ was born according to the flesh.

22. LANFRANC. “The sacrament.” What he says about man and wife is to be understood literally according to the custom of the world, and spiritually of Christ and the Church. Christ appeared to leave the Father when he emptied himself and took the form of a servant. He left the Synagogue, his mother, from whom he was born, when, while she persisted in her unbelief, he sent apostles to preach to the Gentiles; and when the Church was gathered from their conversion, he clung to it as a bridegroom to his bride, with whom the Only-Begotten became one flesh, because the flesh which he took from the Virgin the Church receives daily in the Mass and in its celebrations.

[Col. 0304C] 23. “Nevertheless.” It is as though he said: Although, therefore, I understand this sacrament spiritually of Christ and the Church, nevertheless do not depart from the moral understanding of the historical sense.

# CHAPTER VI

[Col. 0303]

“Children, obey your parents in the Lord, for this is just”—and he proves this by authoritative testimony—“Honor your father and your mother,”

[Note: [Col. 0304C] CHAPTER VI.—1. LANFRANC. “Which is the first commandment.” On the first tablet there were indeed three commandments pertaining to God: “You shall not worship foreign gods”; “You shall not take the name of your God in vain”; “You shall observe the Sabbaths.” The remaining seven, on the second tablet, pertained to one’s neighbor; the first among them was: “Honor your father and mother.” Hence he says, “which is the first commandment.”]

“which is the first commandment with a promise,” in the Law, which promises to those who fulfill it a land flowing with milk and honey, “so that it may be well with you and you may be long-lived upon the land of the living.”

[Col. 0305] “And you fathers, do not provoke your children to anger, but bring them up in the discipline and instruction of the Lord.

“Servants, obey your fleshly masters with fear of soul and trembling of body,”

[Note: [Col. 0305A] 2. AMBROSE. “In simplicity.” He expands the manner in which he had said this by adding: “Not serving merely to be seen.”]

“in the simplicity of your hearts, as you would obey Christ.” Here is why he said “in simplicity”: “not serving merely to be seen, openly and only externally, as those who please men, but as servants of Christ, doing the will of God from the heart, serving with goodwill, as to the Lord and not to men, knowing that whatever good each person does, he will receive that from the Lord, whether he is a servant or free.”

[Note: [Col. 0305A] 3. LANFRANC. “And you masters, the same,” that is, similar things in simplicity of heart and goodwill, as servants of Christ doing the will of God toward them.]

“And you masters, do the same to them,” that is, in simplicity and goodwill,

[Note: [Col. 0305A] 4. AMBROSE. “Remitting.” He did not say “removing,” but “remitting.” For he does not prohibit correcting servants if they sin stubbornly.]

“remitting threats, knowing that both their Lord and yours is in heaven, and that there is no partiality with him. A free person is not dearer to him than a servant who obeys him.

“Finally, brothers, be strengthened in the Lord and in the power of his strength, not in your own. Put on the armor of God, so that you may be able to stand against the snares of the devil—the armor of God, I say, because”

[Note: [Col. 0305A] 5. “Our struggle is not.” He used the term “struggle” loosely, putting it in place of “war.”]

“our struggle is not only against flesh and blood, but against rulers and authorities, against the rulers of the darkness of this world,”

[Note: [Col. 0305B] 6. AUGUSTINE (*Expositions on the Psalms*, Psalm CXVII, vol. VIII). “Rulers.” “The rulers of this darkness,” that is, the rulers of the wicked who love this world.]

“the rulers of this darkness,” namely,

[Note: [Col. 0305B] 7. “Against spiritual wickedness.” Therefore the spiritual forces of wickedness are in the heavenly places—not where the stars shine in their ordered array and the holy angels dwell, but in the dark dwelling-place of this lower air, where mist also gathers.

AMBROSE. “In the heavenly places.” That is, in place of “heavenly places”: our struggle against them is for the heavenly kingdom.]

“against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places,”

[Note: [Col. 0305B] 8. LANFRANC. “In the heavenly places.” He calls “heavenly” the powers directed toward heavenly things, in whose exercise we suffer opposition from the wicked spirit.]

dwelling in the air, [152] or against the powers that demons attempt to take away from us.

[Note: [Col. 0305B] 9. “Therefore take up.” It is as though he said: Since you are fighting against spiritual enemies, you must take up spiritual armor.]

“Therefore take up the armor of God,”

[Note: [Col. 0305C] 10. AUGUSTINE (likewise, on Psalm XXXIV). “Take up the armor.” [Col. 0306A] Nevertheless, beloved, do not think that these weapons are arranged so that what is a shield is always a shield, or what is a helmet is always a helmet, or what is a breastplate is always a breastplate. In bodily weapons this is indeed so, although even things made of iron can be changed, as a sword can become an ax. Yet we see the Apostle himself say in one place “the breastplate of faith,” and in another “the shield of faith.” It is therefore a shield because it receives and repels the missiles of enemies. It is a breastplate because it does not allow your inner parts to be pierced.]

“the powers, so that you may be able to resist”

[Note: [Col. 0306A] 11. AMBROSE. “On the evil day.” He calls the present life the evil day, because evils [perhaps: evil people] act in the present age.]

“on the evil day, in the present age, where evils are done, and to stand perfect in all circumstances, whether prosperous or adverse.

“Stand, therefore; do not lie fallen in filth. Gird your loins”—that is, restrain the looseness of carnal pleasure—“with truth, and put on the breastplate of justice in action, and”

[Note: [Col. 0306A] 12. LANFRANC. “With feet shod.” He commands our feet to be shod because our thoughts, by which the mind in a certain sense walks, ought to be fortified against the snares of evil spirits, so that we may prepare within ourselves what the Gospel of peace—that is, of Christ—commands.]

“having your feet shod and your minds fortified against the snares of the devil, in preparation for the Gospel, so that you may prepare them by receiving the Gospel of peace, the Gospel that makes peace.

“In all things take up”—used intransitively—“the shield of faith, with which you will be able to extinguish all the fiery darts of the most wicked one, the vices of the devil, and”

[Note: [Col. 0306B] 13. “The helmet of salvation.” Eternal salvation ought to be our helmet, because it should often envelop in our memory our mind, which is signified by the name “head.”]

“take the helmet of salvation, hope, or salvation itself.

[Note: [Col. 0306B] 14. AUGUSTINE (likewise, on Psalm CXLIX). “And the sword.” The word of God is therefore a two-edged sword; hence, when he says “two-edged,” he speaks both of temporal things and of eternal things. The two-edged sword of which the Apostle speaks is the sword with which, striking from both Testaments, they slaughtered those of whom it was said to Peter: “Kill and eat.”]

“And take the sword of the Spirit—which is the word of God—through every prayer and through the cross, or supplication, praying at all times in the Spirit and keeping watch in it with all perseverance, not laxly, and with supplication for all the saints; and for me, so that speech may be given to me in the opening of my mouth”—that is, with confidence and not with fear—“to make known”

[Note: [Col. 0306B] 15. LANFRANC. “The mystery of the Gospel.” By “the mystery of the Gospel”—that is, what the Gospel proclaims—he wishes to be understood the incarnation and passion of Christ and the other sacraments.]

“the mystery of the Gospel, for which I am an ambassador in chains and in prison, so that in it I may dare to speak as I ought.

“But so that you also may know what concerns me and what I am doing, Tychicus, the beloved brother and faithful minister in the Lord, will make everything known to you. I have sent him to you for this very purpose, so that you may know what concerns us, and so that he may console your hearts and you may not lose heart on my account.

“Peace to the brothers, and love with faith, from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. Grace be with all who love our Lord Jesus Christ in incorruption and sincerity. Amen.”

[COMMENTARY]

[Col. 0304]

[Col. 0304C] CHAPTER VI.—1. LANFRANC. “Which is the first commandment.” On the first tablet there were indeed three commandments pertaining to God: “You shall not worship foreign gods”; “You shall not take the name of your God in vain”; “You shall observe the Sabbaths.” The remaining seven, on the second tablet, pertained to one’s neighbor; the first among them was: “Honor your father and mother.” Hence he says, “which is the first commandment.”

2. AMBROSE. “In simplicity.” He expands the manner in which he had said this by adding: “Not serving merely to be seen.”

3. LANFRANC. “And you masters, the same,” that is, similar things in simplicity of heart and goodwill, as servants of Christ doing the will of God toward them.

4. AMBROSE. “Remitting.” He did not say “removing,” but “remitting.” For he does not prohibit correcting servants if they sin stubbornly.

5. “Our struggle is not.” He used the term “struggle” loosely, putting it in place of “war.”

[Col. 0305B] 6. AUGUSTINE (*Expositions on the Psalms*, Psalm CXVII, vol. VIII). “Rulers.” “The rulers of this darkness,” that is, the rulers of the wicked who love this world.

7. “Against spiritual wickedness.” Therefore the spiritual forces of wickedness are in the heavenly places—not where the stars shine in their ordered array and the holy angels dwell, but in the dark dwelling-place of this lower air, where mist also gathers.

AMBROSE. “In the heavenly places.” That is, in place of “heavenly places”: our struggle against them is for the heavenly kingdom.

8. LANFRANC. “In the heavenly places.” He calls “heavenly” the powers directed toward heavenly things, in whose exercise we suffer opposition from the wicked spirit.

9. “Therefore take up.” It is as though he said: Since you are fighting against spiritual enemies, you must take up spiritual armor.

10. AUGUSTINE (likewise, on Psalm XXXIV). “Take up the armor.” [Col. 0306A] Nevertheless, beloved, do not think that these weapons are arranged so that what is a shield is always a shield, or what is a helmet is always a helmet, or what is a breastplate is always a breastplate. In bodily weapons this is indeed so, although even things made of iron can be changed, as a sword can become an ax. Yet we see the Apostle himself say in one place “the breastplate of faith,” and in another “the shield of faith.” It is therefore a shield because it receives and repels the missiles of enemies. It is a breastplate because it does not allow your inner parts to be pierced.

11. AMBROSE. “On the evil day.” He calls the present life the evil day, because evils [perhaps: evil people] act in the present age.

12. LANFRANC. “With feet shod.” He commands our feet to be shod because our thoughts, by which the mind in a certain sense walks, ought to be fortified against the snares of evil spirits, so that we may prepare within ourselves what the Gospel of peace—that is, of Christ—commands.

13. “The helmet of salvation.” Eternal salvation ought to be our helmet, because it should often envelop in our memory our mind, which is signified by the name “head.”

14. AUGUSTINE (likewise, on Psalm CXLIX). “And the sword.” The word of God is therefore a two-edged sword; hence, when he says “two-edged,” he speaks both of temporal things and of eternal things. The two-edged sword of which the Apostle speaks is the sword with which, striking from both Testaments, they slaughtered those of whom it was said to Peter: “Kill and eat.”

15. LANFRANC. “The mystery of the Gospel.” By “the mystery of the Gospel”—that is, what the Gospel proclaims—he wishes to be understood the incarnation and passion of Christ and the other sacraments.

# THE LETTER OF THE BLESSED APOSTLE PAUL TO THE PHILIPPIANS, WITH THE INTERPOSED BRIEF GLOSSES OF BLESSED LANFRANC

[Col. 0307]

153. ARGUMENT.—The Philippians are Macedonians. After receiving the word of truth, they persevered in the faith and did not accept false apostles. The Apostle praises them highly, writing to them from Rome, from prison, through Epaphroditus.

# CHAPTER I

[Col. 0307]

[Note: [Col. 0307A] CHAPTER I.—1. AMBROS. “To the Philippians.” The Philippians were refined men, but there was contention among some of them concerning primacy, and this occurred among those who appeared to be adorned with virtues. He therefore writes to them about safeguarding humility, and so that they would not heed the words of those who urged them to observe the Law.]

Paul and Timothy, servants of Jesus Christ, to all the saints in Christ Jesus who are established in the faith of Christ Jesus and are at Philippi, [Note: [Col. 0307A] 2. “With bishops.” He called them bishops who are now called presbyters; for it was not lawful for there to be many of this order in one city.] with bishops and deacons. Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.

I give thanks to my God at every remembrance of you, always, whenever I remember you—that is, with remembrance of you in all my prayers made for all of you with joy—or I have this remembrance concerning the fact that you share in the Gospel, making supplication for your [Note: [Col. 0307A] 3. LANFR. “Your sharing,” that is, the communion which you have in the Gospel of Christ, or so that you may have a greater share in it; for the expression refers to either interpretation.] participation in the Gospel of Christ, so that God may multiply it, enduring from the first day of your conversion until now; [Note: [Col. 0307A] 4. “Confident of this very thing.” He added this because it seemed imprudent to rejoice over those whose outcome was uncertain.] being confident of this very thing, that he who began a good work in you will bring it to completion until the day of Christ Jesus: [Note: [Col. 0307B] 5. “Until the day of Christ.” He calls the day of Christ Jesus either the final day of each person, when he departs from the body and is brought to the judgment of Christ, or the final day of the age, when the Lord will come to judge.] the day of judgment or of each person’s death; [Note: [Col. 0307B] 6. “As it is right for me also.” As though he were saying: I give thanks to God for you; I pray to God. I have good confidence concerning you, and it is right for me to think this about you—that is, to will this. He explains the reason: “Because,” he says, “I have you in my heart,” whether I am imprisoned, defending the Gospel, or confirming it, so that you may all be sharers in my joy, that is, in the heavenly kingdom.] just as it is right for me to think this about all of you, because you are in my heart—that is, I love you—both in my bonds and in the defense and confirmation of the Gospel, indeed so that I wish you all to be sharers in my joy, that is, in the kingdom of heaven.

154 For God is my witness, and God is my witness as to how [Note: [Col. 0308A] 7. AMBROS. “I long for you.” By saying “in the bowels of Christ,” he meant to speak of that love which is according to Christ.] I long for you all in the bowels of Jesus Christ, that is, to be in the love which is according to Christ.

And this I pray: that your love may abound more and more in knowledge and in every kind of discernment in action; so that you may prove by the very act what is more excellent, and may be sincere and without offense until the day of Christ—the day of judgment or of death—filled with the fruit of righteousness, eternal life, through Jesus Christ, to the glory and praise of God.

I want you to know, brothers, lest they themselves should rage because of the Apostle’s imprisonment, that what concerns me—namely, my bonds—has turned out more for the advancement than for the harm of the Gospel. [Note: [Col. 0308A] 8. “So that my bonds.” For, being imprisoned, he became known to everyone, and the faithful taught with confidence from the things that had happened to him, gaining confidence. Some proclaim Christ out of envy; both matters he indicates more fully by adding: “Some from rivalry, but some from love.”] Thus my bonds became manifest in Christ, because I was imprisoned for Christ, throughout the whole praetorium and in all other places; and many of the brothers in the Lord, taking confidence from my bonds because of my bonds, dared all the more than usual [Note: [Col. 0308A] 9. LANFR. “Without fear.” Seeing the Apostle in chains and not afraid to speak the word of God, others gained greater boldness to speak the word of God without fear, although they themselves were not imprisoned.] to speak the word of God without fear.

[Note: [Col. 0308B] 10. AUGUST. (*Against Lying*, addressed to Consent., ch. 6, vol. IV.) “Some indeed.” Even in the times of the apostles there were those who preached the truth not in truth—that is, not with a truthful mind. The Apostle says that they proclaimed Christ not purely, but out of envy and rivalry; thus even then some were tolerated who proclaimed the truth without a pure intention. Yet they were not praised as though they were proclaiming falsehood with a pure intention. Afterwards he says of them: “Whether by pretext or in truth, Christ is proclaimed.”]

Some indeed preach Christ even [Note: [Col. 0309A] 11. LANFR. “Out of envy,” either so that the Apostle alone would not appear to be a preacher, or because, contending with him, they sought to stir up affliction against the Apostle.] out of envy, to stir up persecution against me, and rivalry; but others preach Christ out of good will. Again: some preach out of love, knowing and seeing that I have been placed in prison for the defense of the Gospel. Again: some preach Christ out of rivalry, not sincerely, [Note: [Col. 0309A] 12. “They proclaim Christ out of rivalry.” Nor did they remind people of the reason for which the Apostle had been imprisoned, so that they might be punished more severely for it.] thinking that they are stirring up affliction against my bonds. [Note: [Col. 0309A] 13. “Thinking.” They disparaged Christ so that the Apostle, who had allowed himself to be bound for such a Lord, might be punished more severely.]

But these things have all turned out rather for the advancement. For what does it matter? It does matter: provided that in every way—whether by pretext, that is, in order to stir up persecution against me, or in truth, with holy desire—Christ is proclaimed; and in this I rejoice now, and I shall also rejoice in the fact that they stir up affliction against me. This is why: [Note: [Col. 0309B] 14. “For I know.” He says that even the disparagement directed by his adversaries against Christ comes to him as salvation, because the more he is punished on account of Christ, the greater his crown.] I know that this, that affliction, will result in my salvation through your prayer [Note: [Col. 0309B] 15. AMBROS. “And the supply.” He signifies a great reward, as much as it is fitting for the Spirit to bestow.] and the supply of the Spirit of Jesus Christ—that is, a generous reward, such as it is fitting for the Spirit to bestow—according to my expectation; and this I expect and hope: that in nothing [Note: [Col. 0309B] 16. LANFR. “In nothing shall I be put to shame.” This would happen if I abandoned what I had begun, or if I did not obtain what I hope for.] shall I be put to shame, 155 but with all confidence, as always, so now also, even in my bonds, Christ shall be magnified in my body, whether through life, by giving others an example of good conduct, [Note: [Col. 0309B] 17. AMBROS. “Whether through death.” For he hoped that, by Christ’s granting it, his death would not be absolute or in vain.] or through death.

[Note: [Col. 0310A] 18. “For me.” Since he had said that Christ would be magnified through life, and did not yet possess this proof, he added: “For me to live is Christ”; for, he says, if I live, I have concern for nothing else.] For me to live is Christ, the cause of my life, and to die is gain, because then I shall rest from my labors. [Note: [Col. 0310A] 19. LANFR. “But if living in the flesh.” As long as I can accomplish something in the flesh, I do not know what to choose, whether to die or to live; for if I could accomplish nothing in the flesh, there is no doubt that I would choose death.]

But if living in the flesh is also a fruit of work for me, as is dying, I do not know what I should choose, since both are beneficial—I do not know whether to live or to die. [Note: [Col. 0310A] 20. AUGUST. (*On Christian Doctrine*, book III, ch. 2, vol. III.) “And what I should choose.” The passage should therefore be punctuated as follows: “And I do not know what I should choose.” “But I am compelled by the two”; this distinction is followed by “having the desire to depart and to be with Christ.” And as though one might ask why he has the desire for this rather than for the other, he says, “For it is much more excellent.”] But I am constrained by the two: having the desire to depart from the body and to be with Christ—which is much better, of course. Yet to remain in the flesh is necessary and useful for you, so that I may give you an example. And, confident of this—that it is necessary for you—I know that I shall remain and continue with all of you, for your advancement and the joy of faith, which faith earns or requires, so that your rejoicing may abound in Christ Jesus through me, that is, through my coming to you again.

Only live in a manner worthy of the Gospel of Christ, so that, whether I come and see you or remain absent, I may hear about you that you stand firm in one spirit, united, laboring together for the faith of the Gospel, and that in nothing you are terrified by your adversaries. Their attempt to terrify you is a cause of destruction for them, but of salvation for you; and this also—that they seek to terrify you—has been given by God, because it has been granted to you for Christ not only to believe in him but also to suffer for him. [Note: [Col. 0310B] 21. AMBROS. “The same struggle.” By his own example he encourages them more effectively.] You are engaged in the same struggle as you saw in me and now hear concerning me.

[COMMENTARY.]

[Col. 0307]

[Col. 0307A] CHAPTER I.—1. AMBROS. “To the Philippians.” The Philippians were refined men, but there was contention among some of them concerning primacy, and this occurred among those who appeared to be adorned with virtues. He therefore writes to them about safeguarding humility, and so that they would not heed the words of those who urged them to observe the Law.

2. “With bishops.” He called them bishops who are now called presbyters; for it was not lawful for there to be many of this order in one city.

3. LANFR. “Your sharing,” that is, the communion which you have in the Gospel of Christ, or so that you may have a greater share in it; for the expression refers to either interpretation.

4. “Confident of this very thing.” He added this because it seemed imprudent to rejoice over those whose outcome [Col. 0307B] was uncertain.

5. “Until the day of Christ.” He calls the day of Christ Jesus either the final day of each person, when he departs from the body and is brought to the judgment of Christ, or the final day of the age, when the Lord will come to judge.

6. “As it is right for me also.” As though he were saying: I give thanks to God for you; I pray to God. I have good confidence concerning you, and it is right for me to think this about you—that is, to will this. He explains the reason: “Because,” he says, “I have you in my heart,” whether I am imprisoned, defending the Gospel, or confirming it, so that you may all be sharers in my joy, that is, in the heavenly kingdom.

7. AMBROS. “I long for you.” By saying “in the bowels of Christ,” he meant to speak of that love which is according to Christ.

8. “So that my bonds.” For, being imprisoned, he became known to everyone, and the faithful taught with confidence from the things that had happened to him, gaining confidence. Some proclaim Christ out of envy; both matters he indicates more fully by adding: “Some from rivalry, but some from love.”

9. LANFR. “Without fear.” Seeing the Apostle in chains and not afraid to speak the word of God, others gained greater boldness to speak the word of God without fear, although they themselves were not imprisoned.

10. AUGUST. (*Against Lying*, addressed to Consent., ch. 6, vol. IV.) “Some indeed.” Even in the times of the apostles there were those who preached the truth not in truth—that is, not with a truthful mind. The Apostle says that they proclaimed Christ not purely, but out of envy and rivalry; thus even then some were tolerated who proclaimed the truth without a pure intention. Yet they were not praised as though they were proclaiming falsehood with a pure intention. Afterwards he says of them: “Whether by pretext or in truth, Christ is proclaimed.”

11. LANFR. “Out of envy,” either so that the Apostle alone would not appear to be a preacher, or because, contending with him, they sought to stir up affliction against the Apostle.

12. “They proclaim Christ out of rivalry.” Nor did they remind people of the reason for which the Apostle had been imprisoned, so that they might be punished more severely for it.

13. “Thinking.” They disparaged Christ so that the Apostle, who had allowed himself to be bound for such a Lord, might be punished more severely.

[Col. 0309B] 14. “For I know.” He says that even the disparagement directed by his adversaries against Christ comes to him as salvation, because the more he is punished on account of Christ, the greater his crown.

15. AMBROS. “And the supply.” He signifies a great reward, as much as it is fitting for the Spirit to bestow.

16. LANFR. “In nothing shall I be put to shame.” This would happen if I abandoned what I had begun, or if I did not obtain what I hope for.

17. AMBROS. “Whether through death.” For he hoped that, by Christ’s granting it, his death would not be absolute or in vain.

[Col. 0310A] 18. “For me.” Since he had said that Christ would be magnified through life, and did not yet possess this proof, he added: “For me to live is Christ”; for, he says, if I live, I have concern for nothing else.

19. LANFR. “But if living in the flesh.” As long as I can accomplish something in the flesh, I do not know what to choose, whether to die or to live; for if I could accomplish nothing in the flesh, there is no doubt that I would choose death.

20. AUGUST. (*On Christian Doctrine*, book III, ch. 2, vol. III.) “And what I should choose.” The passage should therefore be punctuated as follows: “And I do not know what I should choose.” “But I am compelled by the two”; this distinction is followed by “having the desire to depart and to be with Christ.” And as though one might ask why he has the desire for this rather than for the other, he says, “For it is much more excellent,” he says.

21. AMBROS. “The same struggle.” By his own example he encourages them more effectively.

22. LANFR. “Engaged in the same struggle.” When he then said that the Pythoness was proclaiming future events to the Philippians [the printed syntax is uncertain].

[Col. 0309]

If there is therefore any consolation which you expect in Christ, if there is any comfort of love for me among you, [Note: [Col. 0310B] CHAPTER II.—1. AUGUST. X.) “If there is any fellowship.” For that fellowship belongs to him by which we are made one body of the one Son of God.] if there is any fellowship of the Spirit, [Note: [Col. 0310B] 2. AMBROS. “If there is any affection,” that is, if, while loving us, you suffer with us as we endure such things.] if there is any affection and compassion, complete my joy: namely, that you think the same thing, having the same love, united in soul, thinking the same thing, doing nothing through rivalry or empty glory; but in humility considering one another superior to yourselves, not each considering his own interests, [Col. 0311] but those of others. For think this in yourselves which was also in Christ Jesus. AMBROS. “But he emptied himself,” that is, he concealed his dignity; for this alone was thought by those who heard him to be his nature which could also be seen.] Taking the form of a servant, he was made in the likeness of human beings, of sinful flesh, [Note: [Col. 0311B] 8. “The form of a servant.” By saying “taking the form of a servant,” he explained it by adding “being made in the likeness of human beings.” “Made” is used for “dwelling”; “in the likeness of human beings” means “in a human being.”]

and, being found in appearance as a human being, he thirsted, hungered, and so forth. [Note: [Col. 0311B] 9. AUGUST. (*Eighty-Three Questions*, question 73, vol. IV.) “Being found in appearance,” that is, by having a human being, he was found to be [probably “homo,” a human being]. [Note: [Col. 0311C] 10. “Because of which.” Through the words which concerned his divinity he urged us toward humility; through those which were accomplished according to his humanity, he showed that humility itself is a profitable thing.] Therefore, because he humbled himself, God also exalted him, [Note: [Col. 0311C] 11. “And gave him.” It is evident that he acquired not merely a name but some reality, because he was assumed by the Word, so that they might also understand that saying: “The Lord is your name.”] and gave him the name which is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee might bend, whether by force or willingly, [Note: [Col. 0312A] 12. “Of the heavenly.” By “heavenly” he means invisible powers; by “earthly,” living human beings; and by “those under the earth,” those who have died, who themselves also, through the resurrection, will confess God as the author of their resurrection.] of the heavenly, the earthly, and those under the earth, and so that every tongue might confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father.

Therefore, just as Christ humbled himself in all things, my beloved, [Note: [Col. 0312A] 13. “As always.” By recalling the past, he very effectively persuaded them not to think anything unworthy thereafter.] just as you have always obeyed—not only in my presence but much more now in my absence— [Note: [Col. 0312A] 14. Among them you shine like lights in the world, holding fast the word of life, to my glory—hence I shall glory on the day of Christ—because I did not run in vain, nor labor in vain.

[Note: [Col. 0312B] 16. “But even if I am sacrificed.” The Apostle was sacrificed, that is, killed, because he converted these and others to God, offering their faith to God as a sacrifice and service. The meaning is: Although I offer the sacrifice of my body, I add the sacrifice and service of your faith, and so forth.] But even if I myself am sacrificed for you, over and above the sacrifice which I made to God from your faith, and the service of your faith, [Note: [Col. 0312C] 17. “I rejoice, and so forth.” “I rejoice,” he says, “in the service of your faith,” that is, in the fact that I sacrificed your faith to God; and not only in this, but also if it should happen to me for your sake—that is, if I am sacrificed.] I rejoice, [Note: [Col. 0312C] 18. “And I rejoice with you,” that is, I give thanks, because your obedience has brought this about for me.] and I rejoice with all of you, either because you are such people. [Note: [Col. 0312C] 19. “But I hope, and so forth.” Sending this letter through Epaphroditus, the Apostle promises that he will also send Timothy to them not long afterward; for he does not send both at the same time.] But I hope in the Lord Jesus to send Timothy to you shortly, so that I may be encouraged when I learn what concerns you. But you know the proof of his devotion—of Timothy’s devotion—because, as a son with his father, he served with me in the Gospel.

Therefore, because he is such a person, I hope to send him to you as soon as I see what concerns me. But I trust in the Lord that I myself shall also come to you shortly.

I considered it necessary to send Epaphroditus, my brother and fellow worker and fellow soldier, but your apostle and minister of my need—that is, the one who ministers to my necessities—to you, because he was longing to see you all, and he was distressed because you had heard that he was ill; and indeed he was. For Epaphroditus was ill almost to the point of death, but God had mercy on him—not only on him, but also on me, so that I would not have sorrow upon sorrow because of his death, in addition to the sorrow of his illness or of my imprisonment.

Therefore I sent him more eagerly, because you had been distressed about him, so that when you saw him you might rejoice again, as previously when he was present, and so that I might be [Note: [Col. 0313A] 20. “Without sorrow.” The sorrow which I have because you were saddened when you heard of his illness.] without sorrow.

[Note: [Col. 0313A] 21. “Receive him.” The Apostle was in prison, and this man approached him to serve him at great personal risk.] Receive him therefore with all joy in the Lord, and hold such a man in honor, because for the work of Christ he came near to death, exposing his life (not leaving it to his enemies without serving the Apostle in prison), in order to complete what was lacking from your service toward me, which you were unable to provide for me.

[COMMENTARY.]

[Col. 0310]

[Col. 0310B] CHAPTER II.—1. AUGUST. (*Sermon* 11, *On the Words of the Lord*, ch. 17, vol. X.) “If there is any fellowship.” For that fellowship belongs to him by which we are made one body of the one Son of God.

2. AMBROS. “If there is any affection,” that is, if, while loving us, you suffer with us as we endure such things.

[Col. 0311A] 3. LANFR. “For think this in yourselves,” that is, have humility and love in yourselves—seeking what belongs to others—which you know to have been in Christ and which you know Christ practiced. This is: “Think this in yourselves,” and so forth.

4. “Not robbery.” Whoever thinks himself to be what he is not, in a certain sense robs for himself from elsewhere, within that very opinion of his, what he is not.

5. AUGUST. (*Against Maximinus*, book II, ch. 5, vol. VI.) “Not robbery.” Understand, therefore, that the Apostle said “not robbery did he regard himself as equal to God” because he did not regard himself as being what he was by birth as something belonging to others. Yet although he did not regard equality with God as something alien, but as his own, he emptied himself, seeking not what was his but what was ours.

6. GREG. “He emptied himself.” To empty himself means to show himself visible from the greatness of his invisibility, so that he might conceal the form of a servant, while, in an unbounded manner, he penetrated all things through his divinity.

7. AMBROS. “But he emptied himself,” that is, he concealed his dignity; for this alone was thought by those who heard him to be his nature which could also be seen.

8. “The form of a servant.” By saying “taking the form of a servant,” he explained it by adding “being made in the likeness of human beings.” “Made” is used for “dwelling”; “in the likeness of human beings” means “in a human being.”

9. AUGUST. (*Eighty-Three Questions*, question 73, vol. IV.) “Being found in appearance,” that is, by having a human being, he was found to be [probably “homo,” a human being].

AMBROS. “He humbled himself.” Up to this point he appears to have spoken of those things which belong to the divine nature. Now he passes to those which can be applied to human nature.

10. “Because of which.” Through the words which concerned his divinity he urged us toward humility; through those which were accomplished according to his humanity, he showed that humility itself is a profitable thing.

11. “And gave him.” It is evident that he acquired not merely a name but some reality, because he was assumed by the Word, so that they might also understand that saying: “The Lord is your name.”

12. “Of the heavenly.” By “heavenly” he means invisible powers; by “earthly,” living human beings; and by “those under the earth,” those who have died, who themselves also, through the resurrection, will confess God as the author of their resurrection.

13. “As always.” By recalling the past, he very effectively persuaded them not to think anything unworthy thereafter.

14. AUGUST. (*On Grace and Free Will*, ch. 9, vol. VII.) “With fear and trembling.” As though the Apostle were questioned and told: “Why did you say ‘with fear and trembling’?” he gave the reason for these words, saying: “For it is God who works in you.” If you fear and tremble, do not exalt yourselves as though on account of your own good works, because it is God who works in you.

15. LANFR. “For it is God.” This is the reason why he said “with fear and trembling”: that thing must be done with the greatest reverence of both mind and body, of which God is the co-worker.

16. “But even if I am sacrificed.” The Apostle was sacrificed, that is, killed, because he converted these and others to God, offering their faith to God as a sacrifice and service. The meaning is: Although I offer the sacrifice of my body, I add the sacrifice and service of your faith, and so forth.

[Col. 0312C] 17. “I rejoice, and so forth.” “I rejoice,” he says, “in the service of your faith,” that is, in the fact that I sacrificed your faith to God; and not only in this, but also if it should happen to me for your sake—that is, if I am sacrificed.

18. “And I rejoice with you,” that is, I give thanks, because your obedience has brought this about for me.

19. “But I hope, and so forth.” Sending this letter through Epaphroditus, the Apostle promises that he will also send Timothy to them not long afterward; for he does not send both at the same time.

20. “Without sorrow.” The sorrow which I have because you were saddened when you heard of his illness.

21. “Receive him.” The Apostle was in prison, and this man approached him to serve him at great personal risk.

158 CHAPTER III.

[Col. 0313]

Therefore, my brothers, rejoice in the Lord. [Note: [Col. 0313A] CHAPTER III.—1. AMBROSE. “The same things to you.” He says “the same,” because he had taught them these things when he had been among them; and this [perhaps: “this”] is to be referred to what follows.] The same things that I have just said in your presence, I am writing to you now. For me, indeed, this is not burdensome, but for you it is necessary and useful.

Behold those who—[Note: [Col. 0313A] 2. AUGUSTINE (*Letter 120 to Honoratus*, chapter 16). “Beware of the dogs.” He called them dogs not because of their nature, but because of their habit of barking against unfamiliar truth. For this is the nature of dogs: they do not bark at those with whom they are accustomed to associate, whether those people are good or bad; but when they see unfamiliar persons, they become irritated even against the innocent.] [Note: [Col. 0313B] 3. LANFRANC. “Beware of the dogs.” He calls dogs and evil workers those who preached carnal circumcision, and whom he commands them to avoid. He calls them “the concision,” either meaning circumcision—that is, the Jews—or separation—that is, those who separated them from the assembly of the faithful into another doctrine.] [Note: [Col. 0313B] 4. AMBROSE. “Beware of the dogs.” He called them dogs because they have no sense of shame; although frequently reproved, they appear to persist in their empty doctrine.] Beware of the dogs; beware of evil workers.

[Note: [Col. 0313B] 5. “Beware of the concision.” He rightly said “concision,” because as long as circumcision pleased God, it was circumcision; but since it no longer pleases God, it is merely concision.] [Note: [Col. 0314A] 6. LANFRANC. “Beware of the circumcision.” Some, although they were not Jews, were circumcised and afterward boasted that they belonged to Abraham’s lineage.] Beware of the concision, as though addressing those who are uncircumcised and separated.

[Note: [Col. 0314A] 7. “For we are.” The reason why those people must be avoided and the apostles heard is that they preached carnal circumcision, whereas the apostles preached spiritual circumcision.] [Note: [Col. 0314A] 8. AUGUSTINE (*On the True Apostle*, sermon XV, chapter 1, volume X). “For we are the circumcision.” But we are the circumcision. Understand the Apostle to have meant this: “We are righteousness.” For circumcision is righteousness. What he says is commended more strongly when he says that we are righteousness than when he says that we are righteous; yet, when he says that we are righteousness, we are to understand that we are righteous.] For we Christians alone are the circumcision (a quality for “quati” [the printed reading is uncertain]); we who serve God in spirit, not in carnal observances, and glory in Christ Jesus, in the faith of Christ Jesus, and place no confidence in the flesh, that is, in the carnal law. Although I may have, or may be able to have, confidence in the flesh, if anyone else seems able to trust in the flesh, I can boast more: circumcised on the eighth day, possessing the circumcision of the eighth day, not a proselyte—

[Note: [Col. 0314A] 9. (*Ibid.*, chapter 3.) “Of the lineage of Israel”: that is, not a proselyte, [Col. 0314B] not an outsider newly attached to God’s people, not one circumcised later, but a Jew born of Jewish parents; I possess the circumcision of the eighth day.]

—of the lineage of Israel, descended from the tribe of Benjamin, a Hebrew born of Hebrews; according to the law—

[Note: [Col. 0314B] 10. (*Ibid.*) “According to the law, a Pharisee.” Certain men were prominent and, as it were, set apart for Jewish nobility, not mixed with the despised common people; they were called Pharisees. For this word is said to be interpreted as “separation,” just as in Latin *egregius* means, as it were, “separated from the flock.”]

—a Pharisee (the Pharisees hold only the law, not the prophets); in good zeal, formerly persecuting the Church of God; according to the righteousness that is in the law, conducting myself blamelessly, not complaining about the severity of the law.

[Note: [Col. 0314B] 11. LANFRANC. “But what things were.” The carnal observances that before Christ’s coming were gains for souls, when retained after his coming became losses; for the faith of Christ does not permit them to be observed. Since those things signified Christ’s coming alone, if they are now observed, they deny that he has come.]

But whatever things—the law, or the foolish persecution arising from that opinion—had formerly been gains for me, these I have reckoned, for Christ, for the faith of Christ, as losses. Yet even now I consider everything to be loss—

[Note: [Col. 0315A] 12. “The surpassing knowledge.” No one can possess the knowledge of Christ if he observes, or thinks that one ought to observe, the carnal commandments of the law.]

—for the sake of attaining the surpassing knowledge, the knowledge that exceeds all things, of Jesus Christ my Lord. For his sake I have suffered the loss of all things, and I regard them as refuse, because, when observed, they defile the soul, that I may gain Christ and be found in him, not having my own righteousness, which comes from the law, but that which comes through the faith of Christ Jesus: the righteousness that comes from God through faith in Christ—

[Note: [Col. 0315A] 13. “To know him.” As though he were saying: Whoever thinks that he is justified by the law does not know Christ; but I, having rejected legal righteousness, wish to be justified through faith in him, so that I may know him—that is, know that, or how, he became incarnate and died.]

—to know him, and what is pleasing to God, [Note: [Col. 0315A] 14. AMBROSE. “The power of his resurrection.” The power of his resurrection is that all may attain a resurrection like his.] [Note: [Col. 0315A] 15. AUGUSTINE (*Ibid.*, chapter 10). “The power of his resurrection.” When he has mentioned the power of Christ’s resurrection, recognize there your justification. For we are justified by his resurrection.] [Note: [Col. 0315B] 16. LANFRANC. “The power of his resurrection.” The power of Christ’s resurrection is to justify believers; hence he says elsewhere: “He rose for our justification.”] and the power of his resurrection, by which the inner man is raised, [Note: [Col. 0315B] 17. “And fellowship.” He has fellowship in the passion of Jesus Christ who suffers in this world as Christ himself suffered. This fellowship is properly understood when it is believed that through it one reaches heavenly joys.] [Note: [Col. 0315B] 18. AUGUSTINE (*Ibid.*, chapter 12). “And fellowship in his passion.” For if the love of God is in you, you will share in Christ’s sufferings and will be a true martyr. He in whom love is crowned will be [add: “himself”] a true martyr.] and fellowship in his sufferings, [Note: [Col. 0315C] 19. (*Ibid.*, chapter 13.) “Conformed to his death.” For, he says, “we were buried with Christ through baptism into death, so that, just as Christ rose from the dead, so we too might walk in newness of life.”] [Note: [Col. 0315C] 20. LANFRANC. “Conformed to his death.” In baptism: for just as Christ lay three days in the tomb, so there is a threefold immersion in baptism.] being conformed to his death, if somehow in the future I may attain to the resurrection that is from the dead, or from sins.

I do not say this because I have already received the resurrection of the flesh in the knowledge of Christ, or because I am already perfect in the knowledge of Christ; [Note: [Col. 0315C] 21. “I follow.” “I imitate Christ,” he says, “by good works, striving, if in any way, at some time, I may grasp him with perfect understanding, in which he himself began me in this life.” So he says elsewhere: “Then I shall know, just as I also have been known.”] but I follow, if somehow I may comprehend, may know Christ completely, [Note: [Col. 0316A] 22. AMBROSE. “In whom I was grasped.” Christ appeared to him from heaven and showed him his glory. He said this: “I do everything to attain those things in which I perceived Christ to be, when by his revelation he turned me, though persecuting him, toward knowledge of him.”] in whom I have also been completely grasped by Christ Jesus.

Brothers, I do not consider myself to have comprehended it—that is, the knowledge of Christ—in its entirety. [Note: [Col. 0316A] 23. AUGUSTINE (*Ibid.*). “But one thing.” I do not consider myself to have apprehended this.] [Note: [Col. 0316A] 24. (*Ibid.*) “One thing.” I have many things, but I have not yet apprehended the one thing. “One thing I have asked of the Lord; this I shall seek.” What did you ask? “That I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life.”] But one thing I hold: forgetting the things that are behind—that is, the carnal observances—and reaching forward to the things that are before, the better things, I press on toward the goal—

[Note: [Col. 0316A] 25. LANFRANC. “But one thing.” “One thing,” he says, “I can confidently assert about myself: completely forgetting the earthly possessions that I abandoned for God, and extending myself with my whole attention toward eternal things, which are better than temporal things, I hasten toward the appointed goal—that is, toward what I have resolved in my mind to pursue—namely, toward the prize, that is, the reward of the heavenly calling, that is, eternal life, to which God calls us.”]

—toward the prize, the reward of God’s heavenly calling, which calling is in Christ Jesus.

[Note: [Col. 0316B] 26. AUGUSTINE (*Ibid.*, chapter 15). “Therefore, whoever are perfect.” He had said, “I am not perfect,” and he says, “Let as many as are perfect think this way.” “I do not consider myself to have apprehended it,” not because I have already received it or am already perfect; and he says, “Let as many as are perfect think this way”—perfect and not perfect. Perfect travelers, but not yet perfect possessors.]

Therefore, as many as are perfect—that is, because I hold this view while wishing to be perfect—let us have this attitude: that we have not yet comprehended it. [Note: [Col. 0316B] 27. LANFRANC. “And if you think anything otherwise”: that is, if you think that you possess a perfect knowledge of Christ, God will reveal to you, through his mercy, that this is to think wrongly.] And if you think otherwise about what ought to be thought, God will reveal this also to you, so that you may understand that this is how it must be thought.

[Note: [Col. 0316C] 28. AUGUSTINE (*Ibid.*). “Nevertheless.” Whether we have reached wherever we have reached, let us walk in that same way, as the Apostle says—not only in what we do not know but ought to know, but also if we think anything otherwise, he will reveal that to us as well.] Nevertheless, we do not comprehend fully that to which we have attained; in so far as we have advanced, let us think alike and remain in the same rule.

[Note: [Col. 0316C] 29. LANFRANC. “We have reached.” As though he were saying: Let us hold firmly what we understand about Christ and complete it in practice.]

Be imitators of me, brothers, [Note: [Col. 0317A] 30. AMBROSE. “Be imitators,” that is, do not live under the law, just as I do not live under the law.] and observe—imitate—those who walk in the same way as we do, as you have our example: just as you have been baptized, so walk.

For many walk—are all of them not walking in this way?—of whom I often told you, and now say even with tears, that they are enemies of the cross of Christ. Their end is destruction; [Note: [Col. 0317A] 31. “Their god is their belly.” As though certain people, intent upon their belly as upon a god, considered it piety that some should strive to offer one thing and others another, while others offered nothing [perhaps: “that some should strive to offer certain things, others other things, and others nothing at all”].] their god is their belly, and their glory is temporal, ending in their everlasting shame; they set their minds on earthly things.

But our citizenship is in heaven, or it is from heaven, because we live as citizens in heaven. From there also we await the Savior, our Lord Jesus Christ, [Note: [Col. 0317A] 32. “Who will transform.” He will transfer the body that is now humbled under death to immortality, making it like his own body.] [Note: [Col. 0317A] 33. LANFRANC. “Who will transform.” On the day of resurrection Christ will transform our body so that it has the same form of glory as his body has.] who will transform the body of our humiliation, our humble body, making it conformed to the body of his glory. He can do this according to the working of the power of his divinity, by which he is also able to subject all things to himself.

## Commentary

[Col. 0313]

### Chapter III

1. AMBROSE. “The same things to you.” He says “the same,” because he had taught them these things when he had been among them; and this [perhaps: “this”] is to be referred to what follows.

2. AUGUSTINE (*Letter 120 to Honoratus*, chapter 16). “Beware of the dogs.” He called them dogs not because of their nature, but because of their habit of barking against unfamiliar truth. For this is the nature of dogs: they do not bark at those with whom they are accustomed to associate, whether those people are good or bad; but when they see unfamiliar persons, they become irritated even against the innocent.

3. LANFRANC. “Beware of the dogs.” He calls dogs and evil workers those who preached carnal circumcision, and whom he commands them to avoid. He calls them “the concision,” either meaning circumcision—that is, the Jews—or separation—that is, those who separated them from the assembly of the faithful into another doctrine.

4. AMBROSE. “Beware of the dogs.” He called them dogs because they have no sense of shame; although frequently reproved, they appear to persist in their empty doctrine.

5. “Beware of the concision.” He rightly said “concision,” because as long as circumcision pleased God, it was circumcision; but since it no longer pleases God, it is merely concision.

6. LANFRANC. “Beware of the circumcision.” Some, although they were not Jews, were circumcised and afterward boasted that they belonged to Abraham’s lineage.

7. “For we are.” The reason why those people must be avoided and the apostles heard is that they preached carnal circumcision, whereas the apostles preached spiritual circumcision.

8. AUGUSTINE (*On the True Apostle*, sermon XV, chapter 1, volume X). “For we are the circumcision.” But we are the circumcision. Understand the Apostle to have meant this: “We are righteousness.” For circumcision is righteousness. What he says is commended more strongly when he says that we are righteousness than when he says that we are righteous; yet, when he says that we are righteousness, we are to understand that we are righteous.

9. (*Ibid.*, chapter 3.) “Of the lineage of Israel”: that is, not a proselyte, not an outsider newly attached to God’s people, not one circumcised later, but a Jew born of Jewish parents; I possess the circumcision of the eighth day.

10. (*Ibid.*) “According to the law, a Pharisee.” Certain men were prominent and, as it were, set apart for Jewish nobility, not mixed with the despised common people; they were called Pharisees. For this word is said to be interpreted as “separation,” just as in Latin *egregius* means, as it were, “separated from the flock.”

11. LANFRANC. “But what things were.” The carnal observances that before Christ’s coming were gains for souls, when retained after his coming became losses; for the faith of Christ does not permit them to be observed. Since those things signified Christ’s coming alone, if they are now observed, they deny that he has come.

12. “The surpassing knowledge.” No one can possess the knowledge of Christ if he observes, or thinks that one ought to observe, the carnal commandments of the law.

13. “To know him.” As though he were saying: Whoever thinks that he is justified by the law does not know Christ; but I, having rejected legal righteousness, wish to be justified through faith in him, so that I may know him—that is, know that, or how, he became incarnate and died.

14. AMBROSE. “The power of his resurrection.” The power of his resurrection is that all may attain a resurrection like his.

15. AUGUSTINE (*Ibid.*, chapter 10). “The power of his resurrection.” When he has mentioned the power of Christ’s resurrection, recognize there your justification. For we are justified by his resurrection.

16. LANFRANC. “The power of his resurrection.” The power of Christ’s resurrection is to justify believers; hence he says elsewhere: “He rose for our justification.”

17. “And fellowship.” He has fellowship in the passion of Jesus Christ who suffers in this world as Christ himself suffered. This fellowship is properly understood when it is believed that through it one reaches heavenly joys.

18. AUGUSTINE (*Ibid.*, chapter 12). “And fellowship in his passion.” For if the love of God is in you, you will share in Christ’s sufferings and will be a true martyr. He in whom love is crowned will be [add: “himself”] a true martyr.

19. (*Ibid.*, chapter 13.) “Conformed to his death.” For, he says, “we were buried with Christ through baptism into death, so that, just as Christ rose from the dead, so we too might walk in newness of life.”

20. LANFRANC. “Conformed to his death.” In baptism: for just as Christ lay three days in the tomb, so there is a threefold immersion in baptism.

21. “I follow.” “I imitate Christ,” he says, “by good works, striving, if in any way, at some time, I may grasp him with perfect understanding, in which he himself began me in this life.” So he says elsewhere: “Then I shall know, just as I also have been known.”

22. AMBROSE. “In whom I was grasped.” Christ appeared to him from heaven and showed him his glory. He said this: “I do everything to attain those things in which I perceived Christ to be, when by his revelation he turned me, though persecuting him, toward knowledge of him.”

23. AUGUSTINE (*Ibid.*). “But one thing.” I do not consider myself to have apprehended this.

24. (*Ibid.*) “One thing.” I have many things, but I have not yet apprehended the one thing. “One thing I have asked of the Lord; this I shall seek.” What did you ask? “That I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life.”

25. LANFRANC. “But one thing.” “One thing,” he says, “I can confidently assert about myself: completely forgetting the earthly possessions that I abandoned for God, and extending myself with my whole attention toward eternal things, which are better than temporal things, I hasten toward the appointed goal—that is, toward what I have resolved in my mind to pursue—namely, toward the prize, that is, the reward of the heavenly calling, that is, eternal life, to which God calls us.”

26. AUGUSTINE (*Ibid.*, chapter 15). “Therefore, whoever are perfect.” He had said, “I am not perfect,” and he says, “Let as many as are perfect think this way.” “I do not consider myself to have apprehended it,” not because I have already received it or am already perfect; and he says, “Let as many as are perfect think this way”—perfect and not perfect. Perfect travelers, but not yet perfect possessors.

27. LANFRANC. “And if you think anything otherwise”: that is, if you think that you possess a perfect knowledge of Christ, God will reveal to you, through his mercy, that this is to think wrongly.

28. AUGUSTINE (*Ibid.*). “Nevertheless.” Whether we have reached wherever we have reached, let us walk in that same way, as the Apostle says—not only in what we do not know but ought to know, but also if we think anything otherwise, he will reveal that to us as well.

29. LANFRANC. “We have reached.” As though he were saying: Let us hold firmly what we understand about Christ and complete it in practice.

[Col. 0317A] 30. AMBROSE. “Be imitators,” that is, do not live under the law, just as I do not live under the law.

31. “Their god is their belly.” As though certain people, intent upon their belly as upon a god, considered it piety that some should strive to offer one thing and others another, while others offered nothing [perhaps: “that some should strive to offer certain things, others other things, and others nothing at all”].

32. “Who will transform.” He will transfer the body that is now humbled under death to immortality, making it like his own body.

33. LANFRANC. “Who will transform.” On the day of resurrection Christ will transform our body so that it has the same form of glory as his body has.

## CHAPTER IV

Therefore—because God will transform us by giving us immortality—my dearly beloved and greatly longed-for brothers, my joy and my crown, in which I shall rejoice and with which I shall be crowned, stand firm in this way, so that you may live as members of the churches, beloved in the Lord.

I urge Euodia [a proper name] and I entreat Syntyche [a proper name] to be of the same mind in the Lord. I also ask you, Germane [a proper name], my companion, to help these two women who labored with me, supplying what was necessary in the Gospel, together with Clement and my other fellow workers, whose names are in the book of life.

[Note: [Col. 0317A] CHAPTER IV.—1. (*Sermon 37, On the Words of the Lord*, chapter 5, volume X.) “Rejoice in the Lord.” Rejoice in the Lord, not in the world; that is, rejoice in truth, not in wickedness.] Rejoice in the Lord always; again I say, rejoice.

[Note: [Col. 0317B] 2. AUGUSTINE (*Letter 159, in the middle, volume II). “Let your moderation.” They love all good works to be brought into the light, not for human glory, but so that people may see, as the Lord says, your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven.] Let your moderation be known to all people; be moderate toward everyone.

[Note: [Col. 0317B] 3. (*Ibid.*) “The Lord is near.” For he who ascended into heaven, so that he might be taken from our eyes, promised us, saying: “Behold, I am with you all the days, even to the consummation of the age.” Rightly the Apostle addressed us in this way: “The Lord is near; do not be anxious about anything.” Christ sits above the heavens, and the heavens are far away; yet he who sits there is near.] For the Lord is near. (“Behold, I am with you all the days, even to the consummation of the age.”) Do not be anxious about anything, but [Note: [Col. 0317C] 4. LANFRANC. “In every prayer,” and so forth. The prayer that comes before the Gospel; the supplication, the secret prayer; the thanksgiving, after communion. He uses this expression for every prayer.] in every prayer and supplication, with thanksgiving, [Note: [Col. 0318A] 5. “Prayer”: that is, whenever you pray or give thanks, then ask if you wish to ask anything of God.] let your requests be made known to God, [Note: [Col. 0318A] 6. AUGUSTINE (*Letter 121 to Proba, On Praying to God*, chapter 9, volume II). “Your requests.” This should not be understood as though they become known to God, who knew them even before they existed. Rather, they should become known to us before God through endurance, not before human beings through boasting. Or perhaps they become known even to the angels who are with God, so that in some manner they may offer them to God and consult him concerning them, and may bring back to us, either openly or secretly, what they have learned God commands to be fulfilled. For the angel said: “When you were praying, I offered your prayer in the presence of the glory of God.”] not for human ostentation.

[Note: [Col. 0318B] 7. AUGUSTINE (*The City of God*, book XXII, chapter 29, volume V). “And the peace of God.” The peace by which God himself is appeased, as God knows it: neither we nor any angel can know it in this way; therefore it surpasses every understanding.] And the peace of God, which surpasses every understanding—whether meaning the peace by which Christ reconciled us to the Father, or, taken intransitively, the peace which no understanding except God’s can perceive—will guard your hearts and your understandings in Christ Jesus.

Finally—then, or concerning others who need correction—brothers, whatever things are true, whatever things are chaste, whatever things are just, whatever things are holy, whatever things are lovable, [Note: [Col. 0318B] 9. AUGUSTINE (*On the Good of Widowhood*, chapter 22, volume IV). “Whatever things are of good report.” He did not neglect to include “of good report,” and he summed everything up in two expressions when he said: “If there is any virtue, if there is any praise.” The things he mentioned earlier belong to virtue; good reputation belongs to praise.] whatever things are of good report—if there is any virtue and if there is any praise of discipline—think about these things.

What you have learned, received, heard, and seen in me, do these things; and the God of peace will be with you.

[Note: [Col. 0318B] 10. AMBROSE. “I rejoiced.” He says “in the Lord,” so that he would not appear to rejoice because money had been sent to him, but because of the good intention of those who sent it.] I rejoiced greatly in the Lord because at last you have revived your concern for me—

[Note: [Col. 0318C] 11. LANFRANC. “You revived,” that is, you have recovered the former flower of your generosity, so that you might give me something, as you used to give me.] [Col. 0319] —as indeed you were concerned before. But you were occupied. (He removes this objection.) I do not say this because of want; for I have learned to be sufficient in whatever circumstances I am, in whatever I possess. I know how to be brought low, and I know how to abound; if there is abundance, I am not lifted up; if there is lack, I am not cast down. [“Everywhere and in all things I have been instructed.”] [Note: [Col. 0319A] 12. AUGUSTINE (*Book II of Questions on the Gospels*, question [number uncertain], volume IV). “And to be filled.” The issue is not what or how much food someone takes, in accordance with his circumstances, person, and bodily needs, but with how much ease and serenity of spirit he can do without these things when he ought to do so, or when it is even necessary to do so, so that what the Apostle says may be fulfilled in the Christian soul [another reading: “of the Christian”]: “I know how to have less, and I know how to abound in everything; I have been instructed in everything, both to be filled and to hunger, both to abound and to suffer want.”] both to be filled and to hunger—not broken by hunger—and to abound—not elated—and to suffer want, and this not through myself; but I can do all things in him who strengthens me. I am sufficient in everything.

[Note: [Col. 0319A] 13. AMBROSE. “Nevertheless, you did well.” He added this so that, although he had such a disposition, he would not be thought to despise what had been sent by them.] Nevertheless, you did well by sharing in my tribulation, giving something to me in my distress; and even earlier you gave to me. You yourselves also know, Philippians, that at the beginning of the Gospel, when I departed from Macedonia, no church shared with me—

[Note: [Col. 0320A] 14. LANFRANC. “In the matter of giving and receiving.” “No church,” he says, “gave me anything while considering what it would give and what it would receive from me.” For there is an accounting of giving and receiving whenever what is received is weighed and something is repaid accordingly.]

—in the matter of giving and receiving, voluntarily giving earthly things in exchange for heavenly things, except you alone; for even when I was in Thessalonica, you sent for my needs once and twice.

[Note: [Col. 0320A] 15. AUGUSTINE (*Confessions*, book XIII, chapter 25, volume I). “Not because I seek the gift.” The gift is the thing itself that the person who distributes necessities gives, such as money, food, drink, clothing, shelter, or assistance. The fruit, however, is the giver’s good works and right intention.] Not because I seek the gift, but I seek the abundant fruit that increases to your account—that is, the fruit of your righteousness increased when you rendered an account to God for your deeds.

I have everything and abound; I have been filled, having received from Epaphroditus what you sent, a fragrant offering, an acceptable sacrifice, pleasing to God. And my God will fulfill every desire of yours according to his riches in glory in Christ Jesus.

Now to our God and Father be glory forever and ever. Amen.

Greet every saint in Christ Jesus. The brothers who are with me greet you. All the saints greet you, especially those who belong to Caesar’s household.

The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit. Amen.

## Commentary

[Col. 0317A]

### Chapter IV

1. (*Sermon 37, On the Words of the Lord*, chapter 5, volume X.) “Rejoice in the Lord.” Rejoice in the Lord, not in the world; that is, rejoice in truth, not in wickedness.

2. AUGUSTINE (*Letter 159, in the middle, volume II). “Let your moderation.” They love all good works to be brought into the light, not for human glory, but so that people may see, as the Lord says, your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven.

3. (*Ibid.*) “The Lord is near.” For he who ascended into heaven, so that he might be taken from our eyes, promised us, saying: “Behold, I am with you all the days, even to the consummation of the age.” Rightly the Apostle addressed us in this way: “The Lord is near; do not be anxious about anything.” Christ sits above the heavens, and the heavens are far away; yet he who sits there is near.

[Col. 0317C] 4. LANFRANC. “In every prayer,” and so forth. The prayer that comes before the Gospel; the supplication, the secret prayer; the thanksgiving, after communion. He uses this expression for every prayer.

5. “Prayer”: that is, whenever you pray or give thanks, then ask if you wish to ask anything of God.

6. AUGUSTINE (*Letter 121 to Proba, On Praying to God*, chapter 9, volume II). “Your requests.” This should not be understood as though they become known to God, who knew them even before they existed. Rather, they should become known to us before God through endurance, not before human beings through boasting. Or perhaps they become known even to the angels who are with God, so that in some manner they may offer them to God and consult him concerning them, and may bring back to us, either openly or secretly, what they have learned God commands to be fulfilled. For the angel said: “When you were praying, I offered your prayer in the presence of the glory of God.”

7. AUGUSTINE (*The City of God*, book XXII, chapter 29, volume V). “And the peace of God.” The peace by which God himself is appeased, as God knows it: neither we nor any angel can know it in this way; therefore it surpasses every understanding.

8. LANFRANC. “The peace of God”: that is, the peace by which he is reconciled in himself, or by which he reconciled the human race to himself.

9. AUGUSTINE (*On the Good of Widowhood*, chapter 22, volume IV). “Whatever things are of good report.” He did not neglect to include “of good report,” and he summed everything up in two expressions when he said: “If there is any virtue, if there is any praise.” The things he mentioned earlier belong to virtue; good reputation belongs to praise.

10. AMBROSE. “I rejoiced.” He says “in the Lord,” so that he would not appear to rejoice because money had been sent to him, but because of the good intention of those who sent it.

11. LANFRANC. “You revived,” that is, you have recovered the former flower of your generosity, so that you might give me something, as you used to give me.

12. AUGUSTINE (*Book II of Questions on the Gospels*, question [number uncertain], volume IV). “And to be filled.” The issue is not what or how much food someone takes, in accordance with his circumstances, person, and bodily needs, but with how much ease and serenity of spirit he can do without these things when he ought to do so, or when it is even necessary to do so, so that what the Apostle says may be fulfilled in the Christian soul [another reading: “of the Christian”]: “I know how to have less, and I know how to abound in everything; I have been instructed in everything, both to be filled and to hunger, both to abound and to suffer want.”

13. AMBROSE. “Nevertheless, you did well.” He added this so that, although he had such a disposition, he would not be thought to despise what had been sent by them.

14. LANFRANC. “In the matter of giving and receiving.” “No church,” he says, “gave me anything while considering what it would give and what it would receive from me.” For there is an accounting of giving and receiving whenever what is received is weighed and something is repaid accordingly.

15. AUGUSTINE (*Confessions*, book XIII, chapter 25, volume I). “Not because I seek the gift.” The gift is the thing itself that the person who distributes necessities gives, such as money, food, drink, clothing, shelter, or assistance. The fruit, however, is the giver’s good works and right intention; [the printed Latin ends here.]

# THE LETTER OF THE BLESSED APOSTLE PAUL TO THE COLOSSIANS, WITH THE INTERPOLATED BRIEF GLOSSES OF THE BLESSED LANFRANC

[Col. 0319]

[Col. 0319B] **ARGUMENT.** The Colossians, like the Laodiceans, are Asians, and they too had been forestalled by pseudo-apostles. The Apostle himself did not visit them; nevertheless, he corrects them by letter. For they had heard the word from Archippus, who had also received ministry among them. Therefore the Apostle, already bound, writes to them from Ephesus through Tychicus the deacon and Onesimus the acolyte.

## CHAPTER I

[Col. 0319]

[Note: [Col. 0319C] CHAPTER I.—1. AMBROSE. In this Epistle he demonstrates the eminence of those who are in Christ and the superfluous observance of the Law; thereafter, turning to exhortation, he speaks to them about many important and necessary matters.]

The apostle Paul of Jesus Christ, not of Ananias, through the will of God, not through the merits of a man, and Timothy the brother, to those who are at Colossae, holy, baptized, and faithful brothers, catechumens in Christ Jesus, in the faith of Christ. Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.
