We give thanks to God, the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, [Note: [Col. 0319C] 2. “Always praying for you.” The order is: “praying for you because of the hope that has been laid up for you in heaven,” that is, so that you may attain the heavenly goods.] always praying for you, hearing of your faith in Christ Jesus and of the love that you have for all the saints, because of the hope that has been laid up for you in heaven; this hope you heard of in the word, the preaching of the truth of the Gospel, which has come to you, [Note: [Col. 0320C] 3. LANFRANC. “As also in the whole world.” So that they should not think themselves to be the only Christians and thereby be deceived; or so that they should not take pride in having believed alone.] just as it is also in the whole world, and bears fruit and grows, as it does among you, [Note: [Col. 0320C] 4. “From the day on which you heard.” Many hear but do not understand, that is, approve.] from the day on which you heard and understood the grace of God in truth, the forgiveness of sins through the faith of Christ, just as you learned [Note: [Col. 0321A] 5. “Our fellow-servant.” He commends him, knowing that it is useful for the teacher to be held in honor by his disciples.] from Epaphras, our most beloved fellow-servant [Note: [Col. 0321A] 6. “In the portion of the lot of the saints.” The lot is called the eternal inheritance because, just as what is obtained by lot is not acquired by merit, so this is bestowed not by merits but by God’s grace.], who instructed them, and who is a faithful minister of Christ Jesus on your behalf. He also made known to us your love in the Spirit.

Therefore, because you possess the faith of Christ and love, from the day on which we heard this from Epaphras we have not ceased praying and petitioning for you, that you may be filled with the knowledge of his will, so that you may recognize and fulfill God’s will in all wisdom and spiritual understanding; that you may walk worthily of God, pleasing him in every respect; bearing fruit and growing in every good work and in the knowledge of God; strengthened with all power according to the might of his glory—that is, according to the measure by which the power of his glory can strengthen you—with all patience and long-suffering (here is what he meant by “with all power”), with joy, giving thanks to God the Father, who by enlightening us made us worthy to be [Note: [Col. 0321A] 6. “In the portion of the lot of the saints.” The lot is called the eternal inheritance because, just as what is obtained by lot is not acquired by merit, so this is bestowed not by merits but by God’s grace.] a portion, that is, participants, in the lot of the saints, an inheritance freely given, [Note: [Col. 0321A] 7. AMBROSE. “In the light,” that is, through his knowledge.] existing in the light of Christ, [Note: [Col. 0321A] 8. AUGUSTINE (Letter 107 to Vitalis, vol. II). “Who rescued us.” For what is the power of darkness except the power of the devil and his angels? Although they had been angels of light, because they did not remain in the truth through free choice, they fell from it and became darkness.] who rescued us from the power of darkness, whether of demons or of those who are dark, [Note: [Col. 0321A] 9. AUGUSTINE (Book XV, On the Trinity, chap. 19, vol. III). “And transferred us.” What is said, “of the Son of his love,” should be understood as nothing other than “of his chosen [or beloved] Son.”] and transferred us into the kingdom of the Son of his love, his beloved Son. In him, in whose faith, we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of sins; [Note: [Col. 0321B] 10. AMBROSE. “Who is the image.” In the man Christ, as in an image, we see that invisible nature; for when he appears in the future, he will retain for us the order of an image, since in him, as in an image, we in some way contain a divine nature.] he is the image (the Son is being commended) of the invisible God, equal to the Father according to divinity; [Note: [Col. 0321B] 11. LANFRANC. “Firstborn.” By this he proves that he was begotten by the Father before every creature.] [Note: [Col. 0321B] 12. “Firstborn of all creation.” He is prior to everything, he says; everything is later than he, for everything was created by him.]

the firstborn of all creation, before the ages, because in him and through him all things were established in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible (the invisible things being their orders), whether thrones, dominions, principalities, or powers. Therefore, by parity of reasoning, all things were made through him, created in him, and exist in him; therefore, by relation, he himself is before all, and all things hold together in him.

And he himself is the head of his body, that is, of the Church; he is the beginning of the Church, [Note: [Col. 0322A] 13. “Firstborn from the dead,” that is, the first to rise, because resurrection itself is a kind of generation, as in the Gospel: “When he sits in the regeneration,” etc.] the firstborn from the dead—that is, he rose first. [Note: [Col. 0322A] 14. AMBROSE. “So that he might hold first place in everything.” He does not state a cause, but what followed from it.]

So that he himself might hold first place in everything, whether according to divinity or humanity; [Note: [Col. 0322A] 15. “Because in him.” He calls the Church the fullness of God and says that it pleased God that all fullness should dwell in Christ, meaning that he approved joining to himself every creature that had been filled by him; he develops this at greater length.] because (here is the reason) in him the Father [Note: [Col. 0322A] 16. LANFRANC. “It pleased him in himself.” The Father was pleased that in Christ should dwell every fullness, both of divinity and of all virtues.] was pleased—that is, he determined—that all the fullness of divinity, or the mass of the members, should dwell or truly reside in him; and through him, Christ, the Father was pleased to reconcile all things to himself, making peace [Note: [Col. 0322A] 17. “Through the blood of the cross.” At the hour when the blood of redemption flowed from the side of the Lord hanging on the cross, Adam’s sin was forgiven the human race, and the heavenly and earthly things were reconciled, because then the entrance into the kingdom of heaven was opened to human beings.] through the blood of his cross, whether the things on earth or those in heaven.

And he reconciled you, when you had once been [Note: [Col. 0322B] 18. “Alienated,” that is, having an alienated and hostile consent.] alienated from God and hostile in disposition (he explains how), in evil works. But now God the Father has reconciled you to himself in the body of the flesh of his Son, through death, in order to present—or so that he himself might present—you holy, immaculate, and irreproachable before him, not merely before human beings. This will happen if indeed you remain grounded and steadfast in the faith, and immovable from the hope of the Gospel, from what the Gospel promises, which you heard, [Note: [Col. 0322B] 19. AMBROSE. “Which was preached.” It would have been very serious for them to depart from that matter which was proclaimed publicly by everyone.] which has been preached in all creation under heaven, that is, to human beings (he persuades them to hear willingly), of which Gospel I, Paul, became a minister.

[Note: [Col. 0322B] 20. LANFRANC. “Who now rejoice.” He commends himself for two reasons: because he suffers, and because he rejoices in the sufferings inflicted for their sake.] I now rejoice in my sufferings for you, [Col. 0323] and I complete [Note: [Col. 0323A] 21. “What is lacking.” Christ’s sufferings were bonds, spitting, blows, scourging, and finally death itself. He acknowledges that he has already suffered part of these and will suffer another part. Perhaps he calls “what is lacking” the anguish of death, which he had not yet endured. The order is: “I will complete those sufferings in my flesh.”] what is lacking in the sufferings of Christ in my flesh, for the sake of his body, which is the Church. Of this Church I became a minister according to the dispensation of the Gospel of God, not of man, which was given to me for you, so that I might fulfill the word of God—the mystery of the Incarnation—which was hidden from ages and from past generations but has now been revealed, in the time of fulfillment, to his saints, to whom God wished to make known the riches of the glory—the glorious riches, or the riches of this glorious sacrament—of its proclamation among the nations, which is Christ (here is the sacrament), among you Gentiles, the hope of glory, through whom you hope to be glorified.

We proclaim him, first reproving every person who lives badly, so that he may repent, and afterward teaching the faith of Christ in all wisdom, whether concerning divine or human matters, teaching for this purpose, [Note: [Col. 0323A] 22. AMBROSE. “That we may present every person perfect.” He calls perfection a future state in which nothing good will be lacking.] that we may present every person perfect in Christ Jesus. In him I also labor, contending not by my own strength—that is, by merits—but according to his operation, which he performs in me by his power, not mine.

[COMMENTARY.]

[Col. 0319C]

CHAPTER I.—1. AMBROSE. In this Epistle he demonstrates the eminence of those who are in Christ and the superfluous observance of the Law; thereafter, turning to exhortation, he speaks to them about many important and necessary matters.

2. “Always praying for you.” The order is: “praying for you because of the hope that has been laid up for you in heaven,” that is, so that you may attain the heavenly goods. [Col. 0320C]

3. LANFRANC. “As also in the whole world.” So that they should not think themselves to be the only Christians and thereby be deceived; or so that they should not take pride in having believed alone.

4. “From the day on which you heard.” Many hear but do not understand, that is, approve.

[Col. 0321A] 5. “Our fellow-servant.” He commends him, knowing that it is useful for the teacher to be held in honor by his disciples.

6. “In the portion of the lot of the saints.” The lot is called the eternal inheritance because, just as what is obtained by lot is not acquired by merit, so this is bestowed not by merits but by God’s grace.

7. AMBROSE. “In the light,” that is, through his knowledge.

8. AUGUSTINE (Letter 107 to Vitalis, vol. II). “Who rescued us.” For what is the power of darkness except the power of the devil and his angels? Although they had been angels of light, because they did not remain in the truth through free choice, they fell from it and became darkness.

9. AUGUSTINE (Book XV, On the Trinity, chap. 19, vol. III). “And transferred us.” What is said, “of the Son of his love,” should be understood as nothing other than “of his chosen [or beloved] Son.” [Col. 0321B]

10. AMBROSE. “Who is the image.” In the man Christ, as in an image, we see that invisible nature; for when he appears in the future, he will retain for us the order of an image, since in him, as in an image, we in some way contain a divine nature.

11. LANFRANC. “Firstborn.” By this he proves that he was begotten by the Father before every creature.

12. “Firstborn of all creation.” He is prior to everything, he says; everything is later than he, for everything was created by him.

[Col. 0322A] 13. “Firstborn from the dead,” that is, the first to rise, because resurrection itself is a kind of generation, as in the Gospel: “When he sits in the regeneration,” etc.

14. AMBROSE. “So that he might hold first place in everything.” He does not state a cause, but what followed from it.

15. “Because in him.” He calls the Church the fullness of God and says that it pleased God that all fullness should dwell in Christ, meaning that he approved joining to himself every creature that had been filled by him; he develops this at greater length.

16. LANFRANC. “It pleased him in himself.” The Father was pleased that in Christ should dwell every fullness, both of divinity and of all virtues.

17. “Through the blood of the cross.” At the hour when the blood of redemption flowed from the side of the Lord hanging on the cross, Adam’s sin was forgiven the human race, and the heavenly and earthly things were reconciled, because then the entrance into the kingdom of heaven was opened to human beings. [Col. 0322B]

18. “Alienated,” that is, having an alienated and hostile consent.

19. AMBROSE. “Which was preached.” It would have been very serious for them to depart from that matter which was proclaimed publicly by everyone.

20. LANFRANC. “Who now rejoice.” He commends himself for two reasons: because he suffers, and because he rejoices in the sufferings inflicted for their sake.

21. “What is lacking.” Christ’s sufferings were bonds, spitting, blows, scourging, and finally death itself. He acknowledges that he has already suffered part of these and will suffer another part. Perhaps he calls “what is lacking” the anguish of death, which he had not yet endured. The order is: “I will complete those sufferings in my flesh.”

22. AMBROSE. “That we may present every person perfect.” He calls perfection a future state in which nothing good will be lacking.

CHAPTER II.

[Col. 0323]

[Note: [Col. 0323A] CHAPTER II.—1. LANFRANC. “For I want you to know,” etc. The reason why he said that he was laboring was so that it would not be said that he had spoken “I labor” out of boastfulness.]

For I want you to know what concern I have for you, and for those who are in Laodicea, and for all who have not seen my face in the flesh, so that their hearts may be comforted, being instructed in love, [Note: [Col. 0323A] 2. “Into all the riches of the fullness of understanding.” So that they may possess a rich and full understanding, knowing the mystery of God the Father, which is Christ Jesus. [Col. 0323B] For whoever knows Christ perfectly knows what must be thought about God, and how and in what matters one must live.] and into all the riches of the fullness of understanding, into the knowledge of the mystery of God the Father and of Christ Jesus, in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom concerning divine things and of knowledge concerning conduct.

I say this so that you may be instructed and so that no one may deceive you [Note: [Col. 0323B] 3. “In sublimity,” that is, in the loftiness of words, syllogisms, and other kinds of disputation; he does not condemn the art of disputation but the perverse use made of it by disputants.] by lofty speech, speaking dialectically or rhetorically in the loftiness of arguments and syllogisms. [Note: [Col. 0323B] 4. “For although I am absent in body.” If someone should say, “Does someone wish to deceive us?”—yes; but, he says, you are strengthened in faith against them. I know this well, although I am absent.]

For although I am absent in body, I am nevertheless with you in spirit, rejoicing and seeing your order and the firmness of your faith, which is in Christ. Therefore, as you received Jesus Christ our Lord, walk in him, rooted and built up in him and confirmed in faith, just as you were taught, abounding in him in thanksgiving.

See that no one deceives you through philosophy, dialectic, and empty deceit, speaking [Note: [Col. 0323B] 5. “According to tradition.” The philosophers—whom he calls “men”—taught that the Creator of all things could not become a creature; that a human being could not be born of a virgin; and that a dead human being could not rise again. They considered the elements of the world, these visible creatures, in which animals that are born are generated through the union of the two sexes, and in which whatever dies cannot live again.] according to human tradition, such as Aristotle, [Note: [Col. 0324A] 6. AMBROSE. “According to the elements,” that is, according to the observance of days and seasons. By the elements of the world he means the sun and moon, from which the course of days and seasons appears to be produced.] according to the elements of the world, and not according to Christ, [Note: [Col. 0324A] 7. AUGUSTINE (Book XII, On the Literal Meaning of Genesis, chap. 7, vol. III). “Because in him dwells.” Because all the fullness of divinity dwells bodily in him. Divinity is not a body, but since he calls the sacraments of the Old Testament shadows of things to come, he said that the fullness of divinity dwells bodily in Christ by comparison with those shadows: all the things figured in those shadows are fulfilled in him, as though he himself were, in a certain sense, the body of those shadows—that is, the truth of those figures and meanings.] because in him all the fullness of divinity dwells bodily, truly and not shadowily, and you have been filled in him, through him, with spiritual gifts. He is the head and beginning of every principality and power. [Note: [Col. 0324B] 8. AUGUSTINE (Book XVI, Against Faustus, chap. 29, vol. VI). “In whom you were circumcised.” What does circumcision of the flesh signify except the stripping away of mortality, which we carry from carnal generation? This is our faith.]

In him, in whose faith, you were also circumcised [Note: [Col. 0324B] 9. “With a circumcision not made by hands.” Christ’s resurrection—which took place on the third day after his Passion, but on the eighth day in the weekly cycle—circumcises us. Hear of those circumcised by the true rock, as the Apostle admonishes: “If, then, you have risen with Christ, seek the things above, where Christ is seated at the right hand of God; think on the things above, not on those on earth.” Christ rose and removed carnal desires from us; he removed evil lusts; he removed the excess with which you had been born, and, much worse, what you had added by living badly. Circumcised by the rock, why do you still set your minds on earthly things?] with a circumcision not made by hands [Col. 0325]—this is the circumcision of Christ, namely, the mortification of vices—in the stripping away of the body of the flesh, but in the spiritual circumcision of Christ, namely, having been buried with him (he explains how) in baptism. In baptism you also rose from vices through faith in the operation of God, which he performed in Christ (here is the operation), who raised him from the dead.

And you [he determines how he understood “in which you also rose”], when you were dead in trespasses [Note: [Col. 0325A] 10. AUGUSTINE (Letter 59 to Paul, in Question 7, vol. II). “And in the uncircumcision of your flesh.” He calls “uncircumcision” what is signified by uncircumcision, namely, carnal sins, from which we must be stripped.] and in the uncircumcision of your flesh, and when you were in paganism, he made you alive together with him, forgiving and pardoning you all trespasses, [Note: [Col. 0325A] 11. AMBROSE. “Erasing what was against us.” He calls the law a written bond against us because it was opposed to us—that is, because through its scrupulousness it did not permit us to attain the goal. He erased it through resurrection and immortality.] erasing the written bond of the decree that was against us—against our advantage—, [Note: [Col. 0325A] 12. LANFRANC. “Of the decree.” God’s decree was: “You shall not eat from the tree that is in the middle of paradise.” God erased the written bond—the record—of the violation of this decree when, through faith in the blood of Christ, he forgave the human race the sin of the first parent and consigned the sin of that transgression to oblivion.] which was contrary to us, the same as “against us,” or contrary to our advantage. He removed it from between us and God—for it was a wall between us and God—affixing and abolishing it by the cross, and [Note: [Col. 0325B] 13. “Stripping.” While hanging on the cross or descending to the underworld, Christ stripped the infernal powers of the souls they possessed or were going to possess, and led those same powers in triumph—that is, expelled them from his Church—as he said in the Gospel: “Now the prince of this world will be cast out.” Or he led his faithful from the underworld with him confidently, like the sinless God-man.] stripping the principalities, whether of the Jews or of demons, and leading them forth in triumph, [Note: [Col. 0325B] 14. “Openly,” that is, on the cross, or descending to the underworld with angelic legions, triumphing over them—that is, conquering them—in himself, that is, in the Passion of his body, in the presence of his majesty.] openly triumphing over them, or conquering them, or restoring them, in himself, not in another army.

In Christ you were circumcised, with a circumcision not made by hand. [Note: [Col. 0325B] 15. “Therefore let no one.” Since you have been circumcised in Christ with a spiritual circumcision, let no one judge you, who are indebted to nothing under the law—that is, let no one make you liable to condemnation—by persuading you to abstain from food or drink, or to use them according to Jewish practice.] [Note: [Col. 0325C] 16. AMBROSE. “Therefore let no one judge you,” that is, let no one deceive you or take away your prize.] 167 [Note: [Col. 0325C] 17. JEROME. “Let no one judge you.” Let no one overcome you; let no one seize the prize intended for you, as someone in a contest loses the prize through the unfairness of an opponent or through the tricks of trainers.] [Note: [Col. 0325C] 18. “Let no one judge you.” Let no one judge you concerning those who boast that they are teachers of the Law—concerning food and drink, on the ground that some things are clean and others unclean, or concerning a portion of a feast day, so that they think some days are feast days and others are not [Col. 0326A]—things that were shadows of the happiness to come; but in spiritual [perhaps: spiritually] understanding, the truth and the body.]

Therefore let no one judge you in food or drink, or in respect of a feast day, so as to make you participate in Jewish feasts, or in the new moon, [Note: [Col. 0326A] 19. AUGUSTINE (Sermon against the Jews, chap. 1, vol. VI). “Or of Sabbaths.” When we find rest in him, we truly keep the Sabbath; and the observance of the new moon is the sanctification of new life; Christ has been sacrificed as our Passover; our unleavened bread is the sincerity of truth, the leaven of truth [or: not having oldness]. And if there are any other matters in which it is unnecessary to linger now, which were prefigured for them by those ancient signs, they find their end in this one, whose kingdom will have no end.] or of Sabbaths, [Note: [Col. 0326B] 20. LANFRANC. “Or of Sabbaths.” The feast days, new moons, and Sabbaths signified things to come, he says, and in that very signification they were the body of Christ—that is, they signified the body of Christ, whether assumed from the Virgin, or the Church as it now is, or the Church that will exist in another age.] which are a shadow of things to come; but the body—the reality—is Christ. [Note: [Col. 0326B] 21. AMBROSE. “Which are a shadow.” In comparison with future things all these are shadows; therefore, to express the significance of a shadow, he added “body,” saying this because Christ is the truth.]

Let no one deceive you, [Note: [Col. 0326B] 22. LANFRANC. “Let no one deceive you.” Let no one deceive you, he says, wishing to persuade you of things he has never understood, displaying to you in himself humility and devotion toward angels so that you will believe them more readily. By “angels” he means either heavenly spirits or holy preachers.] [Note: [Col. 0326B] 23. JEROME. “Wishing in humility.” For they worshiped the host of heaven. Hence Amos: “He delivered them to serve [Col. 0326C] the host of heaven.”] [Note: [Col. 0326C] 24. AMBROSE. “Wishing in humility.” Do not, he says, attend to those who say that angels become indignant if the Law is not observed, since the Law is said to have been given through angels; pretending to display a certain humility, they hasten to show themselves as though they feared to despise the Law.] wishing, in humility and religion made toward himself, or devotion owed to angels, to say things he has not seen, and walking vainly puffed up by the disposition of his flesh, if he hopes to be saved by a carnal law and is thereby puffed up, and not holding fast to the head, that is, Christ, from whom the whole body—the Church—supplied and constructed through the connections and joints of the faithful grows with growth, to the honor of God.

[Note: [Col. 0326C] 25. “If you have died.” If you have been established as those who have already died together with Christ and have risen with him. He says this concerning the elements of this world.] [Note: [Col. 0326C] 26. JEROME. “If you have died.” The elements of the world from which we have died are to be understood as the law of Moses. Through these elements, as through the beginnings of religious instruction, holy men learn about the Lord. Just as letters are called elements, through which we join syllables and words and proceed to weave speech, so the infancy of holy men is educated through the elements of the Old Testament until it comes to evangelical fullness.]

If, then, you have died with Christ (referring to what he said, “buried in baptism”) [Col. 0327] to the elements [Note: [Col. 0327A] 27. LANFRANC. “From the elements.” He calls these visible creatures, which in the total universe are parts of the world, “elements.” If, he says, after receiving the faith of Christ, you have died—that is, been separated—from abstinence from the world’s creatures, and if you abstained from them according to Jewish practice, why do you still, as though living in the world, decide according to the world—that is, carnally—saying, “Do not touch,” “Do not taste,” and so forth? It can also be understood as “with Christ” [perhaps: “from Christ”], as though he said: if you have died [Col. 0327B] as Christ also died, that is, as the Church of Christ did.] of this world, from carnal observances, from creatures that are to be observed—such as swine’s flesh and other things—why, as though living in the world, according to the world, that is, carnally, do you make decrees? Saying: “Do not touch”—things prohibited in the Law—“nor taste, nor handle,” which all lead to the destruction of the soul merely by their use; I mean things prescribed according to the commands and teachings of human beings. These have indeed an appearance of wisdom in superstition, appearing to be practiced wisely according to their superstition and with feigned humility, [Note: [Col. 0327B] 28. “And not sparing the body.” These regulations—namely, that swine’s flesh must not be eaten—were established not to spare the body, so that the body might be afflicted; for when food is withheld, the body is afflicted. Or they were not established to spare the body, that is, to provide for our body; for when we abstain from deadly foods, we provide for our body. But the Jews do not abstain from such meats for this reason, nor because one could be honorably satisfied more fully with other meats than with the forbidden ones.] and not for the sparing of the body, not with any honor, for the satisfaction of the flesh.

[COMMENTARY.]

[Col. 0323A]

CHAPTER II.—1. LANFRANC. “For I want you to know,” etc. The reason why he said that he was laboring was so that it would not be said that he had spoken “I labor” out of boastfulness.

2. “Into all the riches of the fullness of understanding.” So that they may possess a rich and full understanding, knowing the mystery of God the Father, which is Christ Jesus. [Col. 0323B] For whoever knows Christ perfectly knows what must be thought about God, and how and in what matters one must live.

3. “In sublimity,” that is, in the loftiness of words, syllogisms, and other kinds of disputation; he does not condemn the art of disputation but the perverse use made of it by disputants.

4. “For although I am absent in body.” If someone should say, “Does someone wish to deceive us?”—yes; but, he says, you are strengthened in faith against them. I know this well, although I am absent.

5. “According to tradition.” The philosophers—whom he calls “men”—taught that the Creator of all things could not become a creature; that a human being could not be born of a virgin; and that a dead human being could not rise again. They considered the elements of the world, these visible creatures, [Col. 0323C] in which animals that are born are generated through the union of the two sexes, and in which whatever dies cannot live again.

[Col. 0324A] 6. AMBROSE. “According to the elements,” that is, according to the observance of days and seasons. By the elements of the world he means the sun and moon, from which the course of days and seasons appears to be produced.

7. AUGUSTINE (Book XII, On the Literal Meaning of Genesis, chap. 7, vol. III). “Because in him dwells.” Because all the fullness of divinity dwells bodily in him. Divinity is not a body, but since he calls the sacraments of the Old Testament shadows of things to come, he said that the fullness of divinity dwells bodily in Christ by comparison with those shadows: all the things figured in those shadows are fulfilled in him, as though he himself were, in a certain sense, the body of those shadows—that is, the truth of those figures and meanings.

[Col. 0324B] 8. AUGUSTINE (Book XVI, Against Faustus, chap. 29, vol. VI). “In whom you were circumcised.” What does circumcision of the flesh signify except the stripping away of mortality, which we carry from carnal generation? This is our faith.

9. “With a circumcision not made by hands.” Christ’s resurrection—which took place on the third day after his Passion, but on the eighth day in the weekly cycle—circumcises us. Hear of those circumcised by the true rock, as the Apostle admonishes: “If, then, you have risen with Christ, seek the things above, where Christ is seated at the right hand of God; think on the things above, not on those on earth.” Christ rose and removed carnal desires from us; he removed evil lusts; he removed the excess [Col. 0324C] with which you had been born, and, much worse, what you had added by living badly. Circumcised by the rock, why do you still set your minds on earthly things?

[Col. 0325A] 10. AUGUSTINE (Letter 59 to Paul, in Question 7, vol. II). “And in the uncircumcision of your flesh.” He calls “uncircumcision” what is signified by uncircumcision, namely, carnal sins, from which we must be stripped.

11. AMBROSE. “Erasing what was against us.” He calls the law a written bond against us because it was opposed to us—that is, because through its scrupulousness it did not permit us to attain the goal. He erased it through resurrection and immortality.

12. LANFRANC. “Of the decree.” God’s decree was: “You shall not eat from the tree that is in the middle of paradise.” God erased the written bond—the record—of the violation of this decree when, through faith in the blood of Christ, he forgave the human race the sin of the first parent and consigned the sin of that transgression to oblivion.

[Col. 0325B] 13. “Stripping.” While hanging on the cross or descending to the underworld, Christ stripped the infernal powers of the souls they possessed or were going to possess, and led those same powers in triumph—that is, expelled them from his Church—as he said in the Gospel: “Now the prince of this world will be cast out.” Or he led his faithful from the underworld with him confidently, like the sinless God-man.

14. “Openly,” that is, on the cross, or descending to the underworld with angelic legions, triumphing over them—that is, conquering them—in himself, that is, in the Passion of his body, in the presence of his majesty.

15. “Therefore let no one.” Since you have been circumcised in Christ with a spiritual circumcision, let no one judge you, who are indebted to nothing under the law—that is, let no one make you liable to condemnation—by persuading you [Col. 0325C] to abstain from food or drink, or to use them according to Jewish practice.

16. AMBROSE. “Therefore let no one judge you,” that is, let no one deceive you or take away your prize.

17. JEROME. “Let no one judge you.” Let no one overcome you; let no one seize the prize intended for you, as someone in a contest loses the prize through the unfairness of an opponent or through the tricks of trainers.

18. “Let no one judge you.” Let no one judge you concerning those who boast that they are teachers of the Law—concerning food and drink, on the ground that some things are clean and others unclean, or concerning a portion of a feast day, so that they think some days are feast days and others are not [Col. 0326A]—things that were shadows of the happiness to come; but in spiritual [perhaps: spiritually] understanding, the truth and the body.

19. AUGUSTINE (Sermon against the Jews, chap. 1, vol. VI). “Or of Sabbaths.” When we find rest in him, we truly keep the Sabbath; and the observance of the new moon is the sanctification of new life; Christ has been sacrificed as our Passover; our unleavened bread is the sincerity of truth, the leaven of truth [or: not having oldness]. And if there are any other matters in which it is unnecessary to linger now, which were prefigured for them by those ancient signs, they find their end in this one, whose kingdom will have no end.

20. LANFRANC. “Or of Sabbaths.” The feast days, new moons, and Sabbaths signified things to come, he says, and in that very signification they were the body of Christ—that is, they signified [Col. 0326B] the body of Christ, whether assumed from the Virgin, or the Church as it now is, or the Church that will exist in another age.

21. AMBROSE. “Which are a shadow.” In comparison with future things all these are shadows; therefore, to express the significance of a shadow, he added “body,” saying this because Christ is the truth.

22. LANFRANC. “Let no one deceive you.” Let no one deceive you, he says, wishing to persuade you of things he has never understood, displaying to you in himself humility and devotion toward angels so that you will believe them more readily. By “angels” he means either heavenly spirits or holy preachers.

23. JEROME. “Wishing in humility.” They worshiped the host of heaven. Hence Amos says: “He delivered them to serve the host of heaven.” [Col. 0326C]

24. AMBROSE. “Wishing in humility.” Do not, he says, attend to those who say that the angels become indignant if the Law is not observed, since the Law is said to have been given through angels, and who, pretending to display a certain humility, hasten to show themselves as though they feared to despise the Law.

25. “If you have died.” If you have been established as those who have already died together with Christ and have risen with him. He says this concerning the elements of this world.

26. JEROME. “If you have died.” The elements of the world from which we have died are to be understood as the law of Moses. Through these elements, as through the beginnings of religious instruction, holy men learn about the Lord. Just as letters are called elements, through which we join syllables and words and proceed to weave speech, so the infancy of holy men is educated through the elements of the Old Testament until it comes to evangelical fullness.

27. LANFRANC. “From the elements.” He calls these visible creatures, which in the total universe are parts of the world, “elements.” If, he says, after receiving the faith of Christ, you have died—that is, been separated—from abstinence from the world’s creatures, and if you abstained from them according to Jewish practice, why do you still, as though living in the world, decide according to the world—that is, carnally—saying, “Do not touch,” “Do not taste,” and so forth? It can also be understood as “with Christ” [perhaps: “from Christ”], as though he said: if you have died [Col. 0327B] as Christ also died, that is, as the Church of Christ did.

28. And for not sparing the body. These ordinances—namely, that swine’s flesh should not be eaten—were established for the purpose of not sparing the body, so that the body might be afflicted; for when food is withdrawn, the body is afflicted. Or they were not established for sparing the body, that is, for providing for our body; for when we abstain from deadly foods, we provide for our body. But the Jews do not abstain from such meats for this reason, nor because the body could be more honorably satisfied with other than forbidden meats.

## CHAPTER III

[Col. 0327]

[Note: [Col. 0327B] CHAP. III.—1. AUGUSTINE (*Against Faustus*, book XI, chapter 7, near the end). “Therefore, if you have risen with him.” We have not, to be sure, risen as Christ did; nevertheless, according to the hope that is in him [variant: “in us through him”], he testified that we have already risen with him.]

Therefore—referring to what he said, “in whom you also rose”—if you have risen with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is, sitting at the right hand of God, equal to the Father. Set your minds on the things that are above, not on those that are upon the earth. Each phrase corresponds to the other.

[Note: [Col. 0328A] 2. AUGUSTINE (*On the Resurrection of the Dead*, among fragment 31, vol. X). “Put to death.” He calls the members of wickedness spiritual, and says that they are “upon the earth.” For he continues and explains: greed, uncleanness, and so forth, which he then elaborates—“putting off,” and so on.]

For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ, hidden in God. But when Christ appears, your life also will appear—for when Christ appears, your life will appear—then you too will appear with him in glory.

Up to this point he has spoken about faith; now he speaks about conduct. Therefore put to death, so that you may live with Christ,

[Note: [Col. 0328A] 3. LANFRANC. “Your members,” that is, the parts of the old man, which is understood as the totality of sin; or the desires of our members.]

your members—that is, your evil actions—which are upon the earth. Here are the members: fornication, by departing from God; uncleanness toward one’s kindred; lust contrary to nature; evil desire for things not possessed; and greed for things possessed, which is the service of idols,

[Note: [Col. 0328A] 4. “Service.” He says this because images of emperors are found engraved on coins; hence those who serve coins appear to serve them as idols and images.]

on account of which the wrath of God comes upon the sons of unbelief. In these vices you too once walked, when you lived in them.

But now put away all these things: anger, indignation, malice, robbery, blasphemy against God, disgraceful speech, and jesting, from your mouth. Do not lie to one another,

[Note: [Col. 0328A] 5. AUGUSTINE (book XXIV of *Against Faustus*, vol. VI). “Putting off the old man.” The Apostle calls the old man nothing other than the old life, which is in sin, in which one lives according to Adam.]

putting off the old man with his actions—the mass of vices—

[Note: [Col. 0328B] 6. LANFRANC. “Putting on the new.” That is, clothing yourselves with newness; make yourselves a new man.]

and putting on the new man,

[Note: [Col. 0328B] 7. AUGUSTINE (book XIV of *On the Trinity*, chapter 16, vol. III). “Who is renewed.” This renewal is the reformation of the mind according to God, or according to the image of God. It is said to be “according to God” so that it may not be thought to occur according to some other creature. It is said to be “according to the image of God” so that it may be understood that this renewal takes place where the image of God is, namely, in the mind. Thus we should not understand “according to the image of him who created him” as though there were another image according to which he is renewed, rather than the very image that is renewed.]

who is being renewed in the knowledge of God, in order to know God,

[Note: [Col. 0328B] 8. LANFRANC. “In knowledge.” In the knowledge of God, the human being is renewed according to the image of God. For this is the image of God according to which he created the human being: namely, that he should be rational and should always love heavenly things.]

according to the image of him who created him. Here—in this renewal—no one is excluded, and no one is accepted because of his status: there is neither Gentile nor Jew, circumcision nor uncircumcision, barbarian nor Scythian, slave nor free; but Christ is all things and in all, and Christ receives people from every group.

Therefore put on—putting to death the evil actions in yourselves, but putting on the inward parts of mercy—as the elect of God, holy and beloved: inward parts, that is, parts, of mercy. Here they are: kindness, humility, modesty, and patience, bearing with one another and forgiving one another. If anyone has a complaint against another, just as the Lord forgave you, so also should you.

Above all these things, have charity; let yourselves possess it, for charity is the bond of perfection, the mass of virtues—or of the perfect—and let the peace of Christ, by which he reconciled human beings to God, rejoice in your hearts; let it make your hearts rejoice. In this peace, and through it, you were called to be one body, the Church. And be grateful; give thanks.

Let the word—the preaching—of Christ dwell in you abundantly, in all wisdom. Be teachers and admonishers of yourselves,

[Note: [Col. 0329A] 9. AMBROSE. “Which is the bond.” In the age to come, he says, when we have taken our stand there, we shall remain joined to one another in charity, enduring no further separation.]

[and do so] in all wisdom: with psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs, singing in your hearts in grace, that is, in thanksgiving, not merely with the mouth, to God and not to human beings.

To state it briefly and more fully: whatever you do in word or deed, do everything in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, giving thanks to God the Father through him, Jesus the mediator.

Wives, be subject to your husbands, as is fitting in the Lord. Husbands, love your wives, and do not be bitter toward them. Children, obey your parents in all things; for this is pleasing in the Lord. Fathers, do not provoke your children to indignation, so that they may not become fainthearted, whether in enduring or in fleeing.

Slaves, obey your earthly masters in all things, serving not merely before their eyes, as those who please human beings, but in sincerity of heart, fearing God the Father. Whatever you do, work from the heart, as for the Lord and not for human beings, without considering what human beings are, knowing that from the Lord you will receive the reward of the inheritance.

[Note: [Col. 0329A] 10. LANFRANC. “Serve the Lord Christ.” He might have said: Although I command some of you to be subject to others, some to love, and others to obey others, and so forth in what follows, nevertheless in all these things serve the Lord Christ.]

Serve the Lord Christ.

For the one who does wrong will receive what he has done wrongfully; and there is no partiality with God.

[COMMENTARY]

[Col. 0327B]

CHAP. III.—1. AUGUSTINE (*Against Faustus*, book XI, chapter 7, near the end). “Therefore, if you have risen with him.” We have not, to be sure, risen as Christ did; nevertheless, according to the hope that is in him [variant: “in us through him”], he testified that we have already risen with him.

[Col. 0328A] 2. AUGUSTINE (*On the Resurrection of the Dead*, among fragment 31, vol. X). “Put to death.” He calls the members of wickedness spiritual, and says that they are “upon the earth.” For he continues and explains greed, uncleanness, and so forth, which he then elaborates: “putting off,” and so on.

3. LANFRANC. “Your members,” that is, the parts of the old man, which is understood as the totality of sin; or the desires of our members.

4. “Service.” He says this because images of emperors are found engraved on coins; hence those who serve coins appear to serve them as idols and images.

5. AUGUSTINE (book XXIV of *Against Faustus*, vol. VI). “Putting off the old man.” The Apostle calls the old man nothing other than the old life, which is in sin, in which one lives according to Adam.

[Col. 0328B] 6. LANFRANC. “Putting on the new,” that is, clothing yourselves with newness; make yourselves a new man.

7. AUGUSTINE (book XIV of *On the Trinity*, chapter 16, vol. III). “Who is renewed.” This renewal is the reformation of the mind according to God, or according to the image of God; but it is called “according to God” so that it may not be thought to occur according to some other creature. It is called “according to the image of God” so that it may be understood that this renewal takes place where the image of God is, namely, in the mind. Thus we should not understand “according to the image of him who created him” as though there were another image according to which he is renewed, rather than the very image that is renewed.

8. LANFRANC. “In knowledge.” In the knowledge of God, the human being is renewed according to the image of God. For this is the image of God according to which he created the human being: namely, that he should be rational and should always love heavenly things.

9. AMBROSE. “Which is the bond.” In the age to come, he says, when we have taken our stand there, we shall remain joined to one another in charity, enduring no further separation.

10. LANFRANC. “Serve the Lord Christ.” He might have said: Although I command some of you to be subject to others, some to love, and others to obey others, and so forth in what follows, nevertheless in all these things serve the Lord Christ.

11. “For the one who does wrong.” The reason proving what was said above, beginning at the passage where he says, “Wives,” and so forth.

## CHAPTER IV

[Col. 0329]

Masters, provide your slaves with what is just and equitable, knowing that you too have a Master in heaven.

Devote yourselves to prayer, remaining watchful in it with thanksgiving, praying at the same time for us also, that God may open for us a door of speech, so that we may speak the mystery of Christ; that he may open a mouth for preaching—or the mouth of the hearers, that is, their heart—because of which, since I make it manifest, I am also imprisoned. Let him open the door in such a way that I may make it manifest, speaking as I ought.

Walk in wisdom toward those who are outside—the unbelievers, so that they may not blaspheme Christianity—

[Note: [Col. 0329A] CHAP. IV.—1. AMBROSE. “Redeeming the time.” Making the present time serve our advantage.]

redeeming the time, because you have lived badly, by living well.

[Note: [Col. 0329B] 2. GREGORY. “Redeeming the time.” We redeem time when, by weeping, we restore the former life that we lost through wanton living.]

Let your speech always be seasoned with the grace of salt, tempered, so that you may know how you ought to answer each person.

[Note: [Col. 0329B] 3. LANFRANC. “Let your speech be in grace.” Here he calls “grace” good conduct, which is given through the grace of God, as in the Letter to the Ephesians: “That he may give grace to those who hear.”]

Tychicus, the most beloved brother and faithful minister and fellow servant in the Lord, will make known to you everything concerning me. I have sent him to you for this very purpose: that he may learn how things are with you and comfort your hearts, together with Onesimus, the most beloved and faithful brother, who is one of you—he was a Colossian. They will make known to you everything that is being done here.

Aristarchus, my fellow prisoner, greets you,

[Note: [Col. 0330A] 4. “And Mark.” Because of this Mark there was a disagreement between Paul and Barnabas, as is read in the Acts of the Apostles (Acts 15:39). When the Colossians heard this, they might have dared [variant: “might not have dared”] to receive neither Mark nor Barnabas unless the Apostle had commanded them; for the statement may refer to either of them, concerning whom … [lacuna].]

and Mark, the cousin of Barnabas, concerning whom you received instructions from me not to receive him; but now, if Mark comes to you, receive him. And Jesus, who is called Justus—the proper name—also greets you. These are the only ones of the circumcision who are my fellow workers for the kingdom of God; they have been a consolation to me.

Epaphras, who is one of you, a servant of Christ Jesus, greets you. He is always anxious for you in his prayers,

[Note: [Col. 0330A] 5. AUGUSTINE (book *On Rebuke and Grace*, chapter 7, vol. VII). “That you may stand perfect.” We pray for nothing else concerning one who stands, except that he may persevere. Likewise the Apostle Jude says: “To him who is able to preserve them [variant: “you”] without stumbling and to set them immaculate in joy before the presence of his glory.” Does he not show most clearly that persevering in good to the end is God’s gift?]

that you may stand perfect and complete in every will of God.

For I bear him witness that he has much labor on your behalf and on behalf of those who are in Laodicea and those who are in Hierapolis. Luke, the beloved physician, greets you, and Demas.

Greet the brothers who are in Laodicea, and Nympha, and the Church that is in her house. When this letter has been read among you, arrange that it also be read in the Church of the Laodiceans,

[Note: [Col. 0330B] 6. LANFRANC. “And the one from Laodicea.” The Laodiceans wrote a letter to the Apostle about their questions, which the Apostle commands to be read at Colossae, so that, now that they have seen the questions of those Laodiceans, they may know how to answer them; and they should have the letter that he writes to them [Col. 0331A] read to the Laodiceans themselves. If this had been the Apostle’s letter to the Laodiceans, he would have said “the letter to the Laodiceans,” not “the one from the Laodiceans,” and Paul would have had more than thirteen—[variant: fourteen]—letters. [Col. 0331] Lanfranc denies that the Letter to the Laodiceans is by blessed Paul.]

and that you read the one from Laodicea,

[Note: [Col. 0331A] 7. AMBROSE. “And the one from Laodicea.” The Apostle does not say “the letter to the Laodiceans,” but “the one from Laodicea,” which they wrote to the Apostle, in which certain matters deserving criticism were brought forward. [Col. 0332A]]

And say to Archippus: See to the ministry that you have received in the Lord, so that you may fulfill it.

This greeting is in my own hand—Paul’s.

[Note: [Col. 0332A] 8. “Remember.” That is: Do not shrink from the truth; imitate me.]

Remember my chains. Grace be with you. Amen.

[COMMENTARY]

[Col. 0329A]

CHAP. IV.—1. AMBROSE. “Redeeming the time.” Making the present time serve our advantage.

2. GREGORY. “Redeeming the time.” We redeem time when, by weeping, we restore the former life that we lost through wanton living.

3. LANFRANC. “Let your speech be in grace.” Here he calls “grace” good conduct, which is given through the grace of God, as in the Letter to the Ephesians: “That he may give grace to those who hear.”

[Col. 0330A] 4. “And Mark.” Because of this Mark there was a disagreement between Paul and Barnabas, as is read in the Acts of the Apostles (Acts 15:39). When the Colossians heard this, they might have dared [variant: “might not have dared”] to receive neither Mark nor Barnabas unless the Apostle had commanded them; for the statement may refer to either of them, concerning whom … [lacuna].

5. AUGUSTINE (book *On Rebuke and Grace*, chapter 7, vol. VII). “That you may stand perfect.” We pray for nothing else concerning one who stands, except that he may persevere. Likewise the Apostle Jude says: “To him who is able to preserve them [variant: “you”] without stumbling and to set them immaculate in joy before the presence of his glory.” Does he not show most clearly that persevering in good to the end is God’s gift?

[Col. 0330B] 6. LANFRANC. “And the one from Laodicea.” The Laodiceans wrote a letter to the Apostle about their questions, which the Apostle commands to be read at Colossae, so that, now that they have seen the questions of those Laodiceans, they may know how to answer them; and they should have the letter that he writes to them [Col. 0331A] read to the Laodiceans themselves. [Note: [Col. 0331] Lanfranc denies that the Letter to the Laodiceans is by blessed Paul.] If this had been the Apostle’s letter to the Laodiceans, he would have said “the letter to the Laodiceans,” not “the one from the Laodiceans,” and Paul would have had more than thirteen—[variant: fourteen]—letters.

7. AMBROSE. “And the one from Laodicea.” The Apostle does not say “the letter to the Laodiceans,” but “the one from Laodicea,” which they wrote to the Apostle, in which certain matters deserving criticism were brought forward.

8. “Remember.” That is: Do not shrink from the truth; imitate me.

9. LANFRANC. “Remember my chains.” He asks them to remember his chains, either so that they may pray for him while he is imprisoned or so that they may provide what he needs.

## THE FIRST LETTER OF THE BLESSED APOSTLE PAUL TO THE THESSALONIANS, WITH THE INTERPOSED BRIEF GLOSSES OF BLESSED LANFRANC

[Col. 0331]

[Col. 0331A] 171 **ARGUMENT.**—The Thessalonians are Macedonians who, after receiving the word of truth, persevered in faith even amid the persecution of their fellow citizens. Moreover, they did not accept false apostles or the things that were said by false apostles. The Apostle praises them highly in this letter, writing to them from Athens through Tychicus the deacon and Onesimus the acolyte.

## CHAPTER I

[Col. 0331]

[Note: [Col. 0331B] CHAP. I.—1. AMBROSE. The Apostle wrote this First Letter to the Thessalonians, praising them because they faithfully endured, contending for the faith amid adversity. He also instructs them concerning those matters that he had learned were being improperly conducted among them.]

[Note: [Col. 0331B] 2. LANFRANC. “Paul.” Unlike in the other Letters, he does not add the title of his office, “Apostle,” thereby showing that these people are good and perfect.]

Paul, Silvanus, and Timothy, to the Church of the Thessalonians, established in God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. Grace to you and peace.

We give thanks to God always for all of you, remembering you in our prayers without ceasing, mindful of the work of your faith—which your faith demands, or which you, as faithful people, accomplish—and of your labor and charity, by giving what is yours to others, and of your endurance, the perseverance of your hope in our Lord Jesus Christ,

[Note: [Col. 0331B] 3. AMBROSE. “Before God.” He means: You do these things because they are pleasing to God.]

before God and our Father, not for the eyes of human beings,

[Note: [Col. 0331B] 4. LANFRANC. “Knowing, beloved brothers.” We give thanks either because we know your election, or because you, brothers, are also imitators of us.]

knowing, beloved brothers, that you are chosen by God—here is why we know that you are chosen by God—because our Gospel did not come to you in word only, but also in the power of miracles,

[Note: [Col. 0331B] 5. “And in the Holy Spirit,” that is, in the manifestation of the Holy Spirit, through whom you who believed received spiritual gifts. [Col. 0331C]]

and in the Holy Spirit given to you, and in great fullness, fully,

[Note: [Col. 0331C] 6. AMBROSE. “As you know.” He says this on your account, in order to invite them to reverence. [Col. 0332B]]

as you know—and you know that this is so—what sort of people we were among you, or among ourselves, for your sake.

And you became imitators of us and of the Lord, receiving the word amid great tribulation, which you endured for Christ,

[Note: [Col. 0332B] 7. “With joy.” For otherwise they would not have rejoiced over things that had not yet been seen.]

with the joy of the Holy Spirit, which the Holy Spirit gave. Thus you became an example to all believers in Macedonia and Achaia.

[Note: [Col. 0332B] 8. LANFRANC. “For the word of the Lord has been reported from you.” Someone might say: How did the Macedonians and Achaeans then know that they had received the word of the Lord? He answers: “For the word of the Lord has been reported from you”; the report of your faith is current among them.]

For the word of the Lord has been spread abroad from you, not only in Macedonia and Achaia, but in every place your faith toward God has gone forth, so that we have no need to say anything about your faith. For they themselves report concerning us—or concerning you—what kind of entrance we had among you: namely, that you willingly heard us and our preaching, and how you were converted to God from idols,

[Note: [Col. 0332B] 10. AMBROSE. “To serve the living God.” It should be noted that, in renouncing idols, he affirmed that God is both living and true.]

to serve—to be of service to—the living and true God, and to await—to be waiting for—his Son from heaven,

[Note: [Col. 0332B] 11. AUGUSTINE (book XV of *The City of God*, chapter 25, vol. V). “Whom he raised.” The wrath of God is not disturbance but the judgment by which punishment is inflicted for sin. [Col. 0332C]]

whom he raised from the dead: Jesus, who rescued us from the coming wrath.

[COMMENTARY]

[Col. 0331B]

CHAP. I.—1. AMBROSE. The Apostle wrote this First Letter to the Thessalonians, praising them because they faithfully endured, contending for the faith amid adversity. He also instructs them concerning those matters that he had learned were being improperly conducted among them.

2. LANFRANC. “Paul.” Unlike in the other Letters, he does not add the title of his office, “Apostle,” thereby showing that these people are good and perfect.

3. AMBROSE. “Before God.” He means: You do these things because they are pleasing to God.

4. LANFRANC. “Knowing, beloved brothers.” We give thanks either because we know your election, or because you, brothers, are also imitators of us.

5. “And in the Holy Spirit,” that is, in the manifestation of the Holy Spirit, through whom you who believed received spiritual gifts.

6. AMBROSE. “As you know.” He says this on your account, in order to invite them to reverence.

7. “And you became imitators.” By making mention of the Lord, he seems to have offered an excellent exhortation.

8. “With joy.” For otherwise they would not have rejoiced over things that had not yet been seen.

9. LANFRANC. “For the word of the Lord has been reported from you.” Someone might say: How did the Macedonians and Achaeans then know that they had received the word of the Lord? He answers: “For the word of the Lord has been reported from you”; the report of your faith is current among them.

10. AMBROSE. “To serve the living God.” It should be noted that, in renouncing idols, he affirmed that God is both living and true.

11. AUGUSTINE (book XV of *The City of God*, chapter 25, vol. V). “Whom he raised.” The wrath of God is not disturbance but the judgment by which punishment is inflicted for sin.

## CHAPTER II

[Col. 0333]

[Note: [Col. 0333A] CHAP. II.—1. LANFRANC. “For you yourselves know.” They report what is true; for you know what kind of entrance we had. Or this is another reason why it is not necessary for him to speak. Or: “He rescued us from the coming wrath,” for you yourselves know our entrance, and how much we suffered in it.]

For you yourselves know, brothers, our entrance among you,

[Note: [Col. 0333A] 2. AMBROSE. “Because it was not empty.” He says: You know that we did not come to you in an unqualified or accidental way, but after suffering many things.]

because it was not empty, vacant, or frivolous; rather, after having first suffered many things and having been treated with insults—as you know—in Philippi, we gained confidence in our God to speak the Gospel of God to you amid great anxiety.

For this reason we gained confidence. For our exhortation was not from error, nor from uncleanness, nor in an idol; but just as we were approved by God, so that the Gospel might be entrusted to us, so that we might be shown by God to be worthy of having his Gospel entrusted to us, so we speak,

[Note: [Col. 0333A] 3. LANFRANC. “Not as pleasing human beings.” “To please” may be found in both good and evil; but he adds what kind of pleasing he means here: “in flattering speech.” For flattery is always found in evil.]

not as pleasing human beings, but God, who tests and praises our hearts. For we were never pleasing—or rather, approved—in flattering speech, as you know; nor in an occasion for greed, preaching for profit. God is witness.

[Note: [Col. 0333A] 4. AMBROSE. “Nor seeking.” He very carefully says “not seeking”; that is, not undertaking this and not having this as the intention of our action. [Col. 0333B]]

Nor did we seek glory from human beings by preaching, neither from you—that is, from your side—nor from others. Although we could have been a burden to you, boasting or accepting what was yours, as other apostles of Christ do, we became little ones, humble and unencumbered, in the midst of you,

[Note: [Col. 0334A] 5. AUGUSTINE (*Expositions on the Psalms*, Psalm 49, near the end, vol. VIII). “As a nurse.” Not a nurse of other people’s children, but a nurse cherishing her own children.]

as a nurse, who is a mother, cherishes her children, not those of others.

Thus, desiring you, we eagerly wished to hand over to you not only the Gospel of God but also our own lives, so that we might merit this on your behalf—for this is the reason—because you had become most dear to us, as you know; or, we were not a burden to you by taking what was yours.

[Note: [Col. 0334A] 6. LANFRANC. “For you remember.” He shows how he handed over his soul, that is, his life, to them.]

For you remember, brothers, our labor and toil—here is the labor—working night and day so that we would not burden any of you—here is the toil—we preached the Gospel of God among you.

You are witnesses, and God also, how devoutly—not flattering—and justly—not preaching for profit—and blamelessly we behaved among you who believed, as you know. We exhorted and comforted each one of you, as a father does his children, bearing witness that you should walk worthily of God, who called you into his own kingdom and glory, because God called you, and because we desired only you.

Therefore we too give thanks to God without ceasing,

[Note: [Col. 0334A] 7. AMBROSE. “Because, when you received.” He recalls their praise in order to stir their eagerness. He recalls what concerns himself in order to lead them to reverence.]

because, when you received from us the word of the hearing of God—the word through which God is heard, as in “the one who hears you hears me”—you received it not as the word of human beings, not as something insignificant, but, as it truly is, as the word of God, which works in you—whether miracles or the fact that you believe—who have believed. This is another reason why he gives thanks, or an indication that it is working in them.

[Note: [Col. 0334A] 8. “For you became imitators.” He rightly exhorted them, recalling them so that they too might endure.]

For you became imitators, brothers, of the Churches of God that are in Judaea, in Christ Jesus, in the faith of Christ. You became imitators in this respect, because you too suffered the same things from your fellow citizens, Gentiles, as they did from the Jews, who killed both the Lord Jesus

—and the prophets—and persecuted us. They do not please God and are hostile to all human beings, to the welfare of all human beings, forbidding us, out of envy, to speak and preach to the Gentiles so that they may be saved, thereby filling up their sins always, so that the one who is in filth may become still filthier. For the wrath of God has come upon them—in their higher part, or from above [reading uncertain]—since they have already been judged,

[Note: [Col. 0334A] 9. LANFRANC. “To the end.” Some Jews will remain unbelieving to the end; for then all Israel will be saved.]

to last until the end, lasting until the end of the age.

But we, brothers, having been bereaved because we are absent from you for a time—for an hour—in word and in appearance, though not in heart, hastened all the more eagerly to see your face with great desire. For we wished to come to you—I, Paul, certainly, lest it seem that he was speaking about others and not himself—and once and again, twice; but Satan hindered us, whether through certain tribulations or through his members.

The reason why he desires to come is this: What is our hope, or joy, or crown of glory? Are you not our hope and joy before our Lord Jesus Christ at his coming? Therefore we wish [to come]; or this is merely an anticipation of the objection: for you are our glory and joy.

[COMMENTARY]

[Col. 0333A]

CHAP. II.—1. LANFRANC. “For you yourselves know.” They report what is true; for you know what kind of entrance we had. Or this is another reason why it is not necessary for him to speak. Or: “He rescued us from the coming wrath,” for you yourselves know our entrance, and how much we suffered in it.

2. AMBROSE. “Because it was not empty.” He says: You know that we did not come to you in an unqualified or accidental way, but after suffering many things.

3. LANFRANC. “Not as pleasing human beings.” “To please” may be found in both good and evil, but he adds what kind of pleasing he means here: “in flattering speech.” For flattery is always found in evil.

4. AMBROSE. “Nor seeking.” He very carefully says “not seeking”; that is, not undertaking this and not having this as the intention of our action.

[Col. 0334A] 5. AUGUSTINE (*Expositions on the Psalms*, Psalm 49, near the end, vol. VIII). “As a nurse.” Not a nurse of other people’s children, but a nurse cherishing her own children.

6. LANFRANC. “For you remember.” He shows how he handed over his soul, that is, his life, to them.

7. AMBROSE. “Because, when you received.” He recalls their praise in order to stir their eagerness. He recalls what concerns himself in order to lead them to reverence.

8. “For you became imitators.” He rightly exhorted them, recalling them so that they too might endure.

9. LANFRANC. “To the end.” Some Jews will remain unbelieving to the end; for then all Israel will be saved.

## CHAPTER III

[Col. 0333]

174 Because you are our hope, and because we could no longer endure it, we decided that I alone should remain in Athens, alone, and we recently sent Timothy our brother and minister of God in the Gospel of Christ,

[Note: [Col. 0334B] CHAP. III.—1. LANFRANC. “Timothy.” He did not send him on this occasion together with this Letter, but before he sent this Letter. Otherwise he would not have greeted them together with him in the preface. [Col. 0335A]]

to strengthen you in faith and to exhort you in conduct for the sake of your faith, so that no one may be shaken by these tribulations that you endure. Nor ought you to be shaken;

[Note: [Col. 0335A] 2. “For you yourselves know.” He removes the reason why they ought not to be shaken and confirms their authority [variant: “their conviction”].]

for you yourselves know that we have been appointed for this: to suffer.

[Note: [Col. 0335A] 3. “For even when we were among you.” He confirms the same reason by his own authority.]

For even when we were among you, we foretold you that we would suffer tribulations, just as it happened, and you know it.

Therefore, because you were suffering tribulation, and because I could no longer endure it, I sent to learn about your faith, lest perhaps the tempter—the devil—had tempted you and our labor had become fruitless.

But now that Timothy has come to us from you and has announced to us your faith and charity, and that you always have a good remembrance of us, desiring to see us just as we also desire to see you, therefore we have been comforted, brothers, in you, although we are in all our need and tribulation, because of your faith. For now we live, if you stand in the Lord, and we rejoice.

What worthy thanksgiving can we render to God for you, amid all the joy with which we rejoice because of you before our God, praying night and day all the more abundantly that we may see your face and complete what is lacking in your faith? None, certainly.

But may God himself, our Father, and our Lord Jesus Christ direct our way to you.

And may the Lord multiply you and make your charity abound toward one another and toward all, just as ours does toward you—namely, in a more abundant charity—in order to strengthen your hearts without reproach, so that God may not be reproached because of you, so that you may be, and may remain, holy before God and our Father at the coming, on the day of judgment, of our Lord Jesus Christ, with all his saints. Amen.

[COMMENTARY]

[Col. 0334B]

CHAP. III.—1. LANFRANC. “Timothy.” He did not send him on this occasion together with this Letter, but before he sent this Letter. Otherwise he would not have greeted them together with him in the preface.

2. “For you yourselves know.” He removes the reason why they ought not to be shaken and confirms their authority [variant: “their conviction”].

3. “For even when we were among you.” He confirms the same reason by his own authority.

## CHAPTER IV

[Col. 0335]

[Note: [Col. 0335A] CHAPTER IV.—1. AMBROSE. “Finally, brothers.” After completing the praises he had spoken concerning the weakness [editorial correction: firmness] of their faith, he urges them henceforth to apply diligence to their way of life.]

Finally, concerning the other commandments, then, brothers, we ask and exhort you in the Lord Jesus: just as you received from us how you ought to walk and please God, so also walk, that you may abound still more. For you know what commandments we gave you through the Lord Jesus, and how holy they were. For this is the will of God: your sanctification, [Note: [Col. 0335A] 2. LANFRANC. “That you abstain,” etc. I commanded you to abstain from fornication, etc., up to this point: that you be holy, which is what the Lord wills; and this is it: “For this is the will of God.”] that you abstain from fornication; that each of you know how to possess his own vessel in sanctification and honor, [Note: [Col. 0335B] 3. “Not in the passion.” The passion of desire occurs when sin is desired but not carried out.] not in the passion of desire, which desire brings to completion, as do the Gentiles who do not know God; and that no one overreach or defraud his brother in business, or, through arrogance, oppress him, nor deceive him by making promises and giving nothing, in business or in any matter, because the Lord is the avenger of all these things, as we told you beforehand (so that you would not be fornicators, but holy), and testified. [Note: [Col. 0335B] 4. “For God did not call.” He destroys the contrary in order to establish the opposite contrary, namely, that we should be pure.] For God did not call us to uncleanness, so that you should be unclean, but to sanctification. [Note: [Col. 0335B] 5. “Therefore, whoever rejects these things.” This is inferred from the preceding statement, where he said: “For this is the will of God.”] Therefore, since this is the will of God, do not reject it. Whoever rejects these commandments of God rejects not man but God, who not only gave the foregoing commands but also [Note: [Col. 0336A] 6. “He gave his Spirit.” That is, because he not only imposed upon us the preceding commands for preaching, but, so that we might possess greater authority in preaching, he gave us his Holy Spirit.] gave his Holy Spirit among us.

Concerning brotherly love, we have no need to write to you, [Note: [Col. 0336A] 7. “You yourselves have learned,” through divine inspiration or through the evangelical commandment, where Christ gives instruction concerning love.] for you yourselves have been taught by God to love one another. [Note: [Col. 0336A] 8. “For you do this.” Another reason why it is unnecessary for him to write to them about love.] Indeed, you do this toward all the brothers throughout the whole of Macedonia. [Note: [Col. 0336A] 9. “We ask you,” etc. Against those who, being idle and doing no work, investigated everything.] But we ask you, brothers, to abound still more, to make it your aim to live quietly, to attend to your own affairs, to work with your hands, as we commanded you, to walk honorably before those who are outside, and to desire nothing belonging to anyone.

[Note: [Col. 0336A] 10. “We do not want you,” addressed to those who grieved over their friends as though they would not rise again.]

[Note: [Col. 0336A] 11. AUGUSTINE (*Sermon* 31, *On the Words of the Apostle*, ch. 7, vol. X). “We do not want you.” For this reason he also calls them “those who sleep.” It is the most truthful custom of Scripture that, when we hear of people sleeping, we should by no means despair of their awakening.]

[Note: [Col. 0336B] 12. AMBROSE. “We do not want you.” He rightly did not remove grief, but declared it immeasurable by comparison with the opponents, calling them to shame because the latter have no hope.]

We do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, concerning those who sleep, that is, the dead, so that you may not grieve like the others who have no hope of resurrection. For if we believe that Jesus died and rose again (they will rise, since Christ rose, which we believe), in the same way God will also bring with Jesus those who have fallen asleep through Jesus (on the basis of his and God’s authority). [Note: [Col. 0337A] 13. “This we say to you,” that is, according to revelation.]

For we say this to you by the word of the Lord: we who live, who remain until the coming of the Lord, will not precede those who have fallen asleep, but we shall be caught up together. [Note: [Col. 0337A] 14. “For the Lord himself.” He calls the archangel’s voice, which will say “Arise,” the command or trumpet.] For the Lord himself will descend from heaven with the Father’s command—or commanding as God—with the voice of an archangel and with the trumpet of God; and the dead who are in Christ, the good, will rise first.

[Note: [Col. 0337A] 15. AUGUSTINE (*The City of God*, book XX, ch. 20, vol. V). “Then we.” If, therefore, we believe that the saints who are found alive when Christ comes and are caught up to meet him will, in that same rapture, depart from mortal bodies and immediately return to the same bodies made immortal, they will suffer no difficulty in the Apostle’s words, whether where he says, “What you sow will not be made alive unless it dies,” or where he says, “We shall all rise,” or “We shall all sleep.”]

Then we who live, who are left, shall be caught up together with them in the clouds, carrying us to meet Christ in the air, and thus we shall always be with the Lord. Therefore, since this will surely happen, console one another with these words.

[COMMENTARY.]

[Col. 0335A]

CHAPTER IV.—1. AMBROSE. “Finally, brothers.” After completing the praises he had spoken concerning the weakness [editorial correction: firmness] of their faith, he urges them henceforth to apply diligence to their way of life.

2. LANFRANC. “That you abstain,” etc. I commanded you to abstain from fornication, etc., up to this point: that you be holy, which is what the Lord wills; and this is it: “For this is the will of God.”

[Col. 0335B] 3. “Not in the passion.” The passion of desire occurs when sin is desired but not carried out.

4. “For God did not call.” He destroys the contrary in order to establish the opposite contrary, namely, that we should be pure.

5. “Therefore, whoever rejects these things.” This is inferred from the preceding statement, where he said: “For this is the will of God.”

[Col. 0336A] 6. “He gave his Spirit.” That is, because he not only imposed upon us the preceding commands for preaching, but, so that we might possess greater authority in preaching, he gave us his Holy Spirit.

7. “You yourselves have learned,” through divine inspiration or through the evangelical commandment, where Christ gives instruction concerning love.

8. “For you do this.” Another reason why it is unnecessary for him to write to them about love.

9. “We ask you,” etc. Against those who, being idle and doing no work, investigated everything.

10. “We do not want you,” addressed to those who grieved over their friends as though they would not rise again.

11. AUGUSTINE (*Sermon* 31, *On the Words of the Apostle*, ch. 7, vol. X). “We do not want you.” For this reason he also calls them “those who sleep.” It is the most truthful custom of Scripture that, when we hear of people sleeping, we should by no means despair of their awakening.

12. AMBROSE. “We do not want you.” He rightly did not remove grief, but declared it immeasurable by comparison with the opponents, calling them to shame because the latter have no hope.

[Col. 0337A] 13. “This we say to you,” that is, according to revelation.

14. “For the Lord himself.” He calls the archangel’s voice, which will say “Arise,” the command or trumpet.

15. AUGUSTINE (*The City of God*, book XX, ch. 20, vol. V). “Then we.” If, therefore, we believe that the saints who are found alive when Christ comes and are caught up to meet him will, in that same rapture, depart from mortal bodies and immediately return to the same bodies made immortal, they will suffer no difficulty in the Apostle’s words, whether where he says, “What you sow will not be made alive unless it dies,” or where he says, “We shall all rise,” or “We shall all sleep.”

CHAPTER V.

[Col. 0337]

Someone might ask: When will this happen? [Note: [Col. 0337A] CHAPTER V.—1. LANFRANC. “Concerning the times.” Concerning the times—whether Christ will come to judgment in summer or winter, by day or by night.]

Concerning the times, [Note: [Col. 0337B] 2. “Concerning the moments,” that is, at what hour of the day or night.] and the moments, brothers, you have no need for us to write to you. [Note: [Col. 0337B] 3. “You yourselves know carefully.” As though he were saying: You have no need, because I would write nothing other than what you know: namely, that the day of the Lord will come secretly, and that no one knows either the times or the moments.]

For you yourselves know carefully that the day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night, unexpectedly, while some are at rest. [Note: [Col. 0337B] 4. “When they say, ‘Peace.’” The foolish thought that, after the death of Antichrist, they would be safer; but then destruction will quickly come, and then it will be well with us who escape, as with a woman in childbirth.]

For when worldly people say, “There is peace and security,” then sudden destruction will come upon them, like pain upon a woman with child, and they will not escape; all will die. [Note: [Col. 0337B] 5. AUGUSTINE (*Letter* 80 to Hesychius, vol. II). “When they say, ‘Peace.’” What does the Apostle mean when he says, “When they say, ‘Peace and security’”? After the Gospel had said, “People will wither from fear and expectation,” it immediately added: “For the powers of heaven will be shaken”; and then “they will see the Son of Man coming with great power and majesty.” Let us therefore consider whether it may be better understood that not only will the things foretold in those words be fulfilled, but that they will rather come to pass at the time when there will be such tribulation throughout the whole world that it concerns the Church, which will be afflicted throughout the whole world, and not those who afflict it. They themselves will say, “Peace and security,” so that sudden destruction will overtake them and the coming of the Lord will seize them like a thief in the night.]
