It will come upon them without their knowing, because they are in darkness. But you, brothers, are not in the darkness of sins, so that that day should seize you unexpectedly like a thief. You are not in darkness, for you are all sons of light and therefore sons of day; [by parallel] we are not of night or of darkness. Therefore let us not sleep as the others do, because we are not of night. Let us not rest in sins, but let us keep watch in good works, and let us be sober, not drunk. Those who sleep [Note: [Col. 0338A] 6. AUGUSTINE (*Exposition of Psalm* CXXXI, vol. VIII). “They sleep at night.” By “night” he means iniquity, in which they fell asleep by desiring earthly things; and all those worldly felicities that appear to exist are the dreams of sleepers. For how is the person who sees treasures in dreams rich while sleeping? But he will awaken and be poor. So it is with all these vain things of this world in which they rejoice while asleep. They will awaken when they do not wish to, if they do not awaken now, when it is useful, and discover that those things were dreams.] sleep at night and belong to night; and those who are drunk are drunk at night and belong to night.

But since we belong to the day, let us be sober [intransitive], clothed with the breastplate of faith and love, and with the helmet of the hope of salvation, so that we may hope for salvation, because God did not appoint us to wrath but to the acquisition of salvation through our Lord Jesus Christ, who died for us, [Note: [Col. 0338B] 7. AMBROSE. “Whether we keep watch,” that is, whether during the present life we possess this condition at the Lord’s coming, or whether we have departed from this life, we shall all acquire incorruptible life.] so that, whether we keep watch or sleep in action, or die, we may live together with him. Therefore, because you belong to the day and God will not seize you unexpectedly, console one another and build one another up, just as you are doing.

But we ask you, brothers, [Note: [Col. 0338B] 8. LANFRANC. “That you know them.” This is a kind of expression used when we wish to give someone nothing: “I do not know you; I do not know you.”] to recognize those who labor among you, who preside over you in the Lord and admonish you, [Note: [Col. 0338B] 9. AMBROSE. “That you hold them,” that is, consider them worthy of the greatest honor, not resisting when they wish to correct you; and he appears to have indicated their obstinacy.] and to esteem them very highly in love because of the work of their preaching, and to be at peace with them.

[Note: [Col. 0339A] 10. “We ask you.” He turns his speech to the teachers, for it was necessary to exhort them also, so that they would not withdraw from their work because of the obstinacy of some.]

But we ask you, brothers, teachers, [Note: [Col. 0339A] 11. AUGUSTINE (*On Rebuke and Grace*, ch. 16, vol. VII). “Reprove the disorderly.” Here it must be understood that one returns evil for evil especially if the person who ought to be reproved is not reproved but, through wicked concealment, is neglected.] reprove the disorderly, console the fainthearted, whether in faith or in suffering, support the weak, and be patient toward everyone.

[Note: [Col. 0339A] 12. LANFRANC. “See that no one returns evil.” He returns evil for evil who leaves unpunished someone whom he is able to correct.]

See that no one returns evil for evil to anyone, but always pursue what is good toward one another and toward all.

[Note: [Col. 0339A] 13. AMBROSE. “Always rejoice,” that is, because of all the sorrows that befall you.]

Always rejoice. [Note: [Col. 0339B] 14. AUGUSTINE (*On Heresies*, addressed to Quodvultdeus, heresy 57, vol. VI). “Without ceasing.” The Lord says, “One ought always to pray and not lose heart.” And the Apostle says, “Pray without ceasing.” This is most soundly understood in such a way that set times for prayer are omitted on no day.]

Pray without ceasing. In all circumstances, prosperous or adverse, in words and in deeds, [Note: [Col. 0339B] 15. AUGUSTINE (*Sentences of Prosper*, sentence 3, vol. III). “Give thanks.” The true humility of the faithful is to be proud in nothing, to grumble in nothing, to be neither ungrateful nor querulous, but in all judgments to give thanks to God and praise the Lord, whose works are all either just or benevolent.] give thanks, for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus, in those things that are in the faith of Christ Jesus, in all things concerning you.

[Note: [Col. 0339B] 16. AMBROSE. “Do not extinguish the Spirit.” Among the Thessalonians there were some who did not accept the things they professed in spiritual activity, because, pretending that they were avoiding them for the sake of deceivers and out of caution, they did so. These things were done by the undisciplined because they were rebuked by the prophets. Therefore he said: “Do not prohibit spiritual activity”; but if, he says, you fear deceivers, accept what is said, testing it.]

[Note: [Col. 0340A] 17. AUGUSTINE. “Do not extinguish the Spirit.” If anyone speaks through the Spirit, do not hinder him; for they were unwilling to hear certain persons because the Apostle had said that they should not receive false apostles. Or: do not extinguish either the knowledge bestowed on them through the Spirit or the Spirit in others.]

Do not extinguish the Spirit. Do not despise prophecies. Test everything; hold fast to what is good. Abstain from every appearance of evil, from whatever will seem evil to you. May the God of peace himself sanctify you completely, as he promised, [Note: [Col. 0340A] 18. AMBROSE. “The spirit whole.” He prays that the grace of the Spirit granted to them may be preserved whole, suffering no diminution.] so that your spirit—your power of reasoning—[Note: [Col. 0340B] 19. AUGUSTINE (*On the Soul and Its Origin*, book IV, against Vincentius Victor, ch. 2, vol. VII). “Your spirit and soul.” Although “spirit” properly denotes not the whole soul but something belonging to it, as the Apostle says, “And may your spirit, soul, and body be preserved whole,” or, much more explicitly, in the Book of Job, “You have released my soul from my spirit,” nevertheless the whole soul is also called by this name. Since it is established that there is something in the soul that is properly called spirit, I also say that the part by which we reason and understand is properly called spirit, when these terms are thus distinguished.] and soul—your sensory faculty—and body may be preserved blameless at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ. This he will do, because [Note: [Col. 0340B] 20. AMBROSE. “He is faithful.” He added this so that they might have no doubts about the prayer.] he who called you is faithful, and he will also do it.

Brothers, pray for us. Greet all the brothers with a holy kiss. I adjure you by the Lord that this Epistle be read to all the holy brothers. The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you. Amen.

[COMMENTARY.]

[Col. 0337A]

CHAPTER V.—1. LANFRANC. “Concerning the times.” Concerning the times—whether Christ will come to judgment in summer or winter, by day or by night.

2. “Concerning the moments,” that is, at what hour of the day or night.

3. “You yourselves know carefully.” As though he were saying: You have no need, because I would write nothing other than what you know: namely, that the day of the Lord will come secretly, and that no one knows either the times or the moments.

4. “When they say, ‘Peace.’” The foolish thought that, after the death of Antichrist, they would be safer; but then destruction will quickly come, and then it will be well with us who escape, as with a woman in childbirth.

5. AUGUSTINE (*Letter* 80 to Hesychius, vol. II). “When they say, ‘Peace.’” What does the Apostle mean when he says, “When they say, ‘Peace and security’”? After the Gospel had said, “People will wither from fear and expectation,” it immediately added: “For the powers of heaven will be shaken”; and then “they will see the Son of Man coming with great power and majesty.” Let us therefore consider whether it may be better understood that not only will the things foretold in those words be fulfilled, but that they will rather come to pass at the time when there will be such tribulation throughout the whole world that it concerns the Church, which will be afflicted throughout the whole world, and not those who afflict it. They themselves will say, “Peace and security,” so that sudden destruction will overtake them and the coming of the Lord will seize them like a thief in the night.

6. AUGUSTINE (*Exposition of Psalm* CXXXI, vol. VIII). “They sleep at night.” By “night” he means iniquity, in which they fell asleep by desiring earthly things; and all those worldly felicities that appear to exist are the dreams of sleepers. For how is the person who sees treasures in dreams rich while sleeping? But he will awaken and be poor. So it is with all these vain things of this world in which they rejoice while asleep. They will awaken when they do not wish to, if they do not awaken now, when it is useful, and discover that those things were dreams.

7. AMBROSE. “Whether we keep watch,” that is, whether during the present life we possess this condition at the Lord’s coming, or whether we have departed from this life, we shall all acquire incorruptible life.

8. LANFRANC. “That you know them.” This is a kind of expression used when we wish to give someone nothing: “I do not know you; I do not know you.”

9. AMBROSE. “That you hold them,” that is, consider them worthy of the greatest honor, not resisting when they wish to correct you; and he appears to have indicated their obstinacy.

10. “We ask you.” He turns his speech to the teachers, for it was necessary to exhort them also, so that they would not withdraw from their work because of the obstinacy of some.

11. AUGUSTINE (*On Rebuke and Grace*, ch. 16, vol. VII). “Reprove the disorderly.” Here it must be understood that one returns evil for evil especially if the person who ought to be reproved is not reproved but, through wicked concealment, is neglected.

12. LANFRANC. “See that no one returns evil.” He returns evil for evil who leaves unpunished someone whom he is able to correct.

13. AMBROSE. “Always rejoice,” that is, because of all the sorrows that befall you.

[Col. 0339B] 14. AUGUSTINE (*On Heresies*, addressed to Quodvultdeus, heresy 57, vol. VI). “Without ceasing.” The Lord says, “One ought always to pray and not lose heart.” And the Apostle says, “Pray without ceasing.” This is most soundly understood in such a way that set times for prayer are omitted on no day.

15. AUGUSTINE (*Sentences of Prosper*, sentence 3, vol. III). “Give thanks.” The true humility of the faithful is to be proud in nothing, to grumble in nothing, to be neither ungrateful nor querulous, but in all judgments to give thanks to God and praise the Lord, whose works are all either just or benevolent.

16. AMBROSE. “Do not extinguish the Spirit.” Among the Thessalonians there were some who did not accept the things they professed in spiritual activity, because, pretending that they were avoiding them for the sake of deceivers and out of caution, they did so. These things were done by the undisciplined because they were rebuked by the prophets. Therefore he said: “Do not prohibit spiritual activity”; but if, he says, you fear deceivers, accept what is said, testing it.

17. AUGUSTINE. “Do not extinguish the Spirit.” If someone speaks through the Spirit, do not hinder him. For they did not wish to listen to certain people because the Apostle had said that they should not receive false apostles. Or: do not extinguish either the knowledge bestowed upon them through the Spirit or the Spirit in others.

18. AMBROSE. “The spirit whole.” He prays that the grace of the Spirit granted to them may be preserved whole, suffering no diminution.

19. AUGUSTINE (*On the Soul and Its Origin*, book IV, against Vincentius Victor, ch. 2, vol. VII). “Your spirit and soul.” Although “spirit” properly denotes not the whole soul but something belonging to it, as the Apostle says, “And may your spirit, soul, and body be preserved whole,” or, much more explicitly, in the Book of Job, “You have released my soul from my spirit,” nevertheless the whole soul is also called by this name. Since it is established that there is something in the soul that is properly called spirit, I also say that the part by which we reason and understand is properly called spirit, when these terms are thus distinguished.

20. AMBROSE. “He is faithful.” He added this so that they might have no doubts about the prayer.

## The Second Epistle of the Holy Apostle Paul to the Thessalonians, with the Brief Glosses of Blessed Lanfranc Interspersed

[Col. 0339]

[Col. 0339B] **Argument.**—The Apostle writes the Second Epistle to the Thessalonians and makes known to them the events of the last times and the overthrow of the adversary. He writes this Epistle from Athens through Titus the deacon and Onesimus the acolyte.

# CHAPTER I

[Col. 0339]

[Note: [Col. 0339C] CHAPTER I.—1. AMBROSE. He writes this Epistle first praising them highly; then he instructs them not to think that the consummation of the ages is upon them, and he speaks about Antichrist.]

[Note: [Col. 0340C] 2. LANFRANC. “Paul,” etc. In the preceding Epistle he spoke about the day of judgment: “We who remain will not precede those who have fallen asleep.” Now, so that they would not think that this would happen in their own time, he determines [Col. 0341A] when it will happen; if he had not done this, he would either be thought to be false or the day of judgment would no longer be awaited by later generations.]

Paul, and Silvanus, and Timothy, to the church of the Thessalonians, which exists in God our Father and [Col. 0341] the Lord Jesus Christ. Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.

[Note: [Col. 0341A] 3. AUGUSTINE (*On Grace and Free Will*, ch. 18, vol. VII). “To give thanks.” He said this so that they would not perhaps be exalted as though they possessed such a great good from themselves, rather than from God. “Therefore,” he says, “because your faith grows exceedingly and the love of each of you abounds toward one another, we ought to give thanks to God,” and not praise you as though you possessed this from yourselves.]

We ought always to give thanks to God for you, brothers, as is fitting, because your faith grows exceedingly and the love of each one of you abounds toward one another, so that we ourselves glory in you among the churches of God because of your patience and persevering faith in all your persecutions and [Note: [Col. 0341A] 4. AUGUSTINE (*Against Faustus*, book XXII, ch. 20, near the end). “The tribulations that you endure.” From this it is understood how the wicked are not spared, as though they had been cut off for burning, when the righteous are not spared either, for the sake of completing their purification.]

[Note: [Col. 0341B] 5. LANFRANC. “The tribulations that you endure.” The tribulations that the saints tolerate in this life are an example of God’s just judgment, by which he will judge the reprobate at the end of the world. For he who judges those who sin so terribly and yet justly, and who first lament their sins, will judge even more justly those who never lament and nevertheless do not cease to sin.]

the tribulations that you endure, as an example of the just judgment of God, for which you also suffer. [Note: [Col. 0341B] 6. “As an example of the just judgment of God.” Alternatively, human deeds are an example—that is, a demonstration—that God is just in giving good things to the good and evil things to the evil.] For it is just with God to repay tribulation to those who trouble you, and to you who are troubled, rest with us at the revelation of the Lord Jesus, who will come from heaven with the angels of his power, with whom he will exercise his power, in a flame of fire—Christ, I mean, or the fire—giving vengeance to those who do not know God and who do not obey the Gospel of our Lord Jesus Christ. They will themselves pay the penalties of eternal destruction, away from the face of the Lord and from the glory of his power, when he comes to be glorified in his saints, giving them immortality, [Note: [Col. 0341B] 7. AMBROSE. “Wonderful.” The order is: “to become wonderful on that day.” He means that he will appear wonderful on that day in those who believed, and that you received our teaching [editorial correction: received].] and to be wonderful in all who believed. He will give you rest, [Note: [Col. 0341B] 8. LANFRANC. “Because it was believed.” He gives the reason why he grants them rest: namely, because the testimony he gave concerning the day of judgment, speaking as though from a higher place, was believed by them.] because our testimony concerning you was believed, [Note: [Col. 0341C] 9. “On that day in which.” The order is: “on that day of judgment, so that God may deem you worthy”—that is, judge you worthy—“of his calling; we always pray for you.” Or, “in which,” that is, “for the sake of avoiding which danger, we must always pray.”] on that day, on the day in which we not only give thanks but also always pray for you, so that our God may deem you worthy—may make you worthy—of his calling (“Come, blessed of my Father”), and may fulfill every intention of goodness, now or then, when he will fully repay the reward, and the work of faith, which Christian faith demands, in the power of his divinity, so that the name of our Lord Jesus Christ may be glorified in you (“so that, seeing your good works, they may glorify”—or in the future: “Those who dwell in your house, Lord,” etc.), and you may be glorified in him (“The righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of my Father”), according to the grace of our God and the Lord Jesus Christ, not according to merits.

[COMMENTARY.]

[Col. 0339C]

CHAPTER I.—1. AMBROSE. He writes this Epistle first praising them highly; then he instructs them not to think that the consummation of the ages is upon them, and he speaks about Antichrist.

[Col. 0340C] 2. LANFRANC. “Paul,” etc. In the preceding Epistle he spoke about the day of judgment: “We who remain will not precede those who have fallen asleep.” Now, so that they would not think that this would happen in their own time, he determines [Col. 0341A] when it will happen; if he had not done this, he would either be thought to be false or the day of judgment would no longer be awaited by later generations.

3. AUGUSTINE (*On Grace and Free Will*, ch. 18, vol. VII). “To give thanks.” He said this so that they would not perhaps be exalted as though they possessed such a great good from themselves, rather than from God. “Therefore,” he says, “because your faith grows exceedingly and the love of each of you abounds toward one another, we ought to give thanks to God,” and not praise you as though you possessed this from yourselves.

4. AUGUSTINE (*Against Faustus*, book XXII, ch. 20, near the end). “The tribulations that you endure.” From this it is understood how the wicked are not spared, as though they had been cut off for burning, when the righteous are not spared either, for the sake of completing their purification.

[Col. 0341B] 5. LANFRANC. “The tribulations that you endure.” The tribulations that the saints tolerate in this life are an example of God’s just judgment, by which he will judge the reprobate at the end of the world. For he who judges those who sin so terribly and yet justly, and who first lament their sins, will judge even more justly those who never lament and nevertheless do not cease to sin.

6. “As an example of the just judgment of God.” Alternatively, human deeds are an example—that is, a demonstration—that God is just in giving good things to the good and evil things to the evil.

7. AMBROSE. “Wonderful.” The order is: “to become wonderful on that day.” He means that he will appear wonderful on that day in those who believed, and that you received our teaching [editorial correction: received].

8. LANFRANC. “Because it was believed.” He gives the reason why he grants them rest [Col. 0341C]: namely, because the testimony he gave concerning the day of judgment, speaking as though from a higher place, was believed by them.

9. “On that day in which.” The order is: “on that day of judgment, so that God may deem you worthy”—that is, judge you worthy—“of his calling; we always pray for you” [Col. 0342A]. Or, “in which,” that is, “for the sake of avoiding which danger, we must always pray.”

# CHAPTER II

[Col. 0341]

We ask you, brothers, by the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, [Note: [Col. 0342A] CHAP. II.—1. AMBROSE. “And our assembling.” For he says that at Christ’s coming there will then be an assembling to him.] and by our assembling to him (here in the Church, or in the future in heaven), into Christ, or into unity, that you not be quickly shaken from your understanding, nor [Note: [Col. 0342A] 2. “Be terrified,” that is, whether someone allows himself to say this through a spiritual working, or whether he has been instructed by a word and by our Epistle.] be terrified, neither by a spirit—if someone should say that it has been revealed to him by the Spirit—nor by a word, nor by a letter allegedly sent by us, from us, [Note: [Col. 0342A] 3. AUGUSTINE (Epistle 80 to Hesychius, vol. II). “As though it were imminent.” A Christian ought to keep watch lest the Lord’s coming find him unprepared. That day will find him unprepared whom the last day of his present life will find unprepared.] as though the day of the Lord, that is, of judgment, were imminent. We ask [Note: [Col. 0342A] 4. AUGUSTINE (The City of God, book XX, chapter 19, vol. V). “So that no one deceive you.” Let no one deceive you in any way: [Col. 0342B] “For unless the apostate comes first,” etc. There is no doubt that he said this about the Antichrist and the day of judgment. For he says that the day of the Lord will not come unless the one whom he calls the apostate comes first—namely, the one who has apostatized from the Lord God.] so that no one deceive you in any way, [Note: [Col. 0342B] 5. “For unless he comes.” It is impossible for departure to occur where accession has not first taken place. Therefore, he says, the accession must be fulfilled, concerning which it was said: “In your seed all the nations shall be blessed”; and, “All the nations shall come to him.” When this has been fulfilled, the departure will begin, concerning which it is said: “Because of the abundance of iniquity, love will grow cold.” When the departure has been completed, as though the beast were already prepared, it will be opportune for the rider to appear—that is, the son of perdition, once revealed. He says that, when he was with them, he told them these same things, and that they ought to understand that the Antichrist will not be revealed except at his appointed time, that is, opportunely. For what place would he have found in the time of the apostles, martyrs, and confessors, or while love had not grown cold? But that iniquity will one day abound to such an extent, he says, can be inferred from the fact that, at the very beginnings of the accession, certain first-fruits of the departure appear: some pretend to be disciples of Christ, and [say] that one ought not to concern oneself about the future, since it is enough for each person to hold in religion what he holds, and to remain in it until that man is removed from the midst—that is, until the man who will openly be revealed, destined to assume the role of iniquity, becomes known. Let those who will then exist see what this means; but for me, who am dying in spirit, what use is it to know after how many years the accession must first occur, then the departure, and only afterward the day of the Lord arrive?] for the day of the Lord will not come unless the departure first occurs—the apostasy of the Roman Empire or of the faith—and the man of sin, the Antichrist, the son of his own perdition and of that of others, is revealed, who opposes and will oppose, and is exalted and will be exalted above everything that is called God, or that is worshiped by Christians, [Note: [Col. 0343B] 7. LANFRANC. What is called “God,” that is, above all the saints, who are called gods, and above God [or, according to the variant, “him”], who is worshiped as God.] so that he sits in the temple of God, Jerusalem or the Church, showing himself as though he were God. I told you this, and do you not remember that, when I was still with you, I was saying these things to you? [Note: [Col. 0343B] 9. AMBROSE. “And now what restrains him,” that is, God meanwhile restrains him.] And now you know what restrains the Antichrist, or the day of the Lord—behold what restrains it—so that he may be revealed at his fitting time. He will be revealed, [Note: [Col. 0343B] 10. “For the mystery,” that is, he does not openly carry out apostasy, but through his agents he attempts to tear people away from piety by means of his activity.] for the mystery of iniquity is already at work—that is, it works secretly through its members, [Note: [Col. 0343C] 11. LANFRANC. “For the mystery.” The Antichrist was then working the mystery of his iniquity in Nero and his other members, because through the solidarity and magnitude of the iniquity that he exercised through them, he showed how great the iniquity was that he exercised [or, according to the variant, “will exercise”] through himself. And this is proof that he is to be revealed.] only this much remains, [Note: [Col. 0344A] 12. AMBROSE. “Only that the one who restrains.” That is, when God’s decree, which prevents his coming, ceases, then he will appear.] so that the one who restrains may now continue to restrain—the Roman Empire, or the faith, or, as far as we are concerned, nothing except that he who holds the faith should hold it until he is removed from the midst—until the Roman Empire is destroyed, or until the Antichrist is born; or, he who holds the faith should hold it until he dies. And then that lawless one will be revealed, [Note: [Col. 0344B] 15. AMBROSE. “Whom the Lord Jesus.” Christ, suddenly appearing from heaven, and merely crying out, will make that whole being cease from its work, consuming it entirely. This is what he says: “By the breath of his mouth.”] whom the Lord Jesus will kill with the breath of his mouth, by the power of the Holy Spirit proceeding from him, and will destroy him, the Antichrist, by the manifestation—that is, by the brightness, which will be so great that he will die when he sees it—of his coming, whose coming is according to the working of Satan, [Note: [Col. 0344B] 16. LANFRANC. “By the manifestation,” that is, by the brightness, which will be so great that he will die when he sees it.] whether Satan will work in him, with every power of resurrection, and with signs of miracles and [Note: [Col. 0344B] 17. “Lying wonders.” He calls the Antichrist’s wonders lies, either because what appears will not truly exist, or because these lies will persuade those destined to perish.] lying wonders, for salvation—or because he will appear to act without actually doing so—and with every deceit of iniquity for those who are perishing, because they did not receive the love of the truth so that they might be saved, because he preached it in place of love or redemption. Therefore God will send them a working of error, the worker of it being the Antichrist, so that they may believe the lie, so that all who did not believe the truth but consented to iniquity, to the devil, may be judged and condemned.

But we—or rather, you believed the truth. Therefore we ought always to give thanks to God for you, [Note: [Col. 0344B] 18. “For you, brothers.” “For you” means, implicitly, for your instruction, so that you too may return thanks in the same way for the benefits bestowed; or because you too have been called, as is said shortly afterward.] beloved brothers of the Lord, because God chose you as first-fruits, as the primitive Church, for salvation, granted to you in the sanctification of the Holy Spirit first, and in faith in the truth of Christ. In this he also called you through our Gospel, [Note: [Col. 0344C] 19. “For the acquisition,” that is, so that you might be his acquisition, in which the Lord Jesus Christ is glorified, and so that you too might acquire the glory that the Lord Jesus Christ possesses.] for the acquisition of glory, so that you might acquire the glory of God, or so that you might be acquired by God for the glory of the Lord Jesus Christ. Therefore, because you are acquiring glory, stand firm, brothers, and hold fast to the traditions of the Gospel that you learned, whether through the word spoken by me while present, or through our letter while I was absent.

May our Lord Jesus Christ himself, and God our Father, [Col. 0345] who loved us and gave us eternal consolation by sending Christ or the Holy Spirit, and a good hope through grace, not through merits, encourage your hearts and strengthen you in every good work and word.

## Commentary

[Col. 0342A]

### Chapter II

1. AMBROSE. “And our assembling.” For he says that at Christ’s coming there will then be an assembling to him.

2. “Be terrified,” that is, whether someone allows himself to say this through a spiritual working, or whether he has been instructed by a word and by our Epistle.

3. AUGUSTINE (Epistle 80 to Hesychius, vol. II). “As though it were imminent.” A Christian ought to keep watch lest the Lord’s coming find him unprepared. That day will find him unprepared whom the last day of his present life will find unprepared.

4. AUGUSTINE (The City of God, book XX, chapter 19, vol. V). “So that no one deceive you.” Let no one deceive you in any way: [Col. 0342B] “For unless the apostate comes first,” etc. There is no doubt that he said this about the Antichrist and the day of judgment. For he says that the day of the Lord will not come unless the one whom he calls the apostate comes first—namely, the one who has apostatized from the Lord God.

5. “For unless he comes.” It is impossible for departure to occur where accession has not first taken place. Therefore, he says, the accession must be fulfilled, concerning which it was said: “In your seed all the nations shall be blessed”; and, “All the nations shall come to him.” When this has been fulfilled, the departure will begin, concerning which it is said: “Because of the abundance of iniquity, love will grow cold.” When the departure has been completed, as though the beast were already prepared, it will be opportune for the rider to appear—that is, the son of perdition, once revealed. He says that, when he was with them, he told them these same things, and that they ought to understand that the Antichrist will not be revealed except at his appointed time, that is, opportunely. For what place would he have found in the time of the apostles, martyrs, and confessors, or while love had not grown cold? But that iniquity will one day abound to such an extent, he says, can be inferred from the fact that, at the very beginnings of the accession, certain first-fruits of the departure appear: some pretend to be disciples of Christ, and [say] that one ought not to concern oneself about the future, since it is enough for each person to hold in religion what he holds, and to remain in it until that man is removed from the midst—that is, until the man who will openly be revealed, destined to assume the role of iniquity, becomes known. Let those who will then exist see what this means; but for me, who am dying in spirit, what use is it to know after how many years the accession must first occur, then the departure, and only afterward the day of the Lord arrive?

6. AMBROSE. “Unless he comes.” He calls that time the departure, because then almost everyone will depart from piety; and he called him the man of sin because he will administer sin; and the son of perdition because he will be subjected to perdition.

7. LANFRANC. What is called “God,” that is, above all the saints, who are called gods, and above God [or, according to the variant, “him”], who is worshiped as God.

8. AUGUSTINE (The City of God, book XX, chapter 19). “So that he sits in the temple.” Here they wish the Antichrist to be understood, and they more correctly think that Latin too should say, as the Greek does, not “in the temple of God,” but “into the temple of God he sits,” as though he himself were the temple of God, which is the Church, just as we say “he sits into a friend,” that is, “as a friend.”

9. AMBROSE. “And now what restrains him,” that is, God meanwhile restrains him.

10. “For the mystery,” that is, he does not openly carry out apostasy, but through his agents he attempts to tear people away from piety by means of his activity.

11. LANFRANC. “For the mystery.” The Antichrist was then working the mystery of his iniquity in Nero and his other members, because through the solidarity and magnitude of the iniquity that he exercised through them, he showed how great the iniquity was that he exercised [or, according to the variant, “will exercise”] through himself. And this is proof that he is to be revealed.

12. AMBROSE. “Only that the one who restrains.” That is, when God’s decree, which prevents his coming, ceases, then he will appear.

13. LANFRANC. “So that the one who restrains.” He designates the Roman Empire, upon whose destruction the Antichrist will come. For this is what he says: only this remains, that the Roman emperor, who holds this world, should continue to hold it until he is removed from the midst—that is, entirely taken away. For to be removed from the midst means to be taken away from the common sight of human beings.

14. AUGUSTINE (same work). “So that the one who restrains.” Yet consider what the Apostle says: “Only that he who restrains should continue to restrain until he is removed from the midst,” that is, taken away from the midst; and then the lawless one will be revealed. No one doubts that the Antichrist is signified by him.

15. AMBROSE. “Whom the Lord Jesus.” Christ, suddenly appearing from heaven, and merely crying out, will make that whole being cease from its work, consuming it entirely. This is what he says: “By the breath of his mouth.”

16. LANFRANC. “By the manifestation,” that is, by the brightness, which will be so great that he will die when he sees it.

17. “Lying wonders.” He calls the Antichrist’s wonders lies, either because what appears will not truly exist, or because these lies will persuade those destined to perish.

18. “For you, brothers.” “For you” means, implicitly, for your instruction, so that you too may return thanks in the same way for the benefits bestowed; or because you too have been called, as is said shortly afterward.

19. “For the acquisition,” that is, so that you might be his acquisition, in which the Lord Jesus Christ is glorified, and so that you too might acquire the glory that the Lord Jesus Christ possesses.

## Chapter III

[Col. 0345]

Finally, brothers, pray for us, so that the word of God, which we preach, may run its course, not be rejected, and be glorified, just as it is elsewhere, namely, among you; and pray that we may be delivered from unreasonable and evil people who lie in wait for us (a mere antithesis)—for faith does not belong to everyone. [Note: [Col. 0345A] CHAP. III.—1. LANFRANC. “But the Lord is faithful,” that is, truthful, since he promised that he would be present with his faithful ones until the end of the age.] But the Lord is faithful; he will strengthen you and guard you from evil, the devil. We are confident about you in the Lord that you both do and will do the things that we command. [Note: [Col. 0345A] 3. “But may the Lord direct,” that is, may it be granted to you to remain in that love which is directed toward him, enduring even if it should be necessary to suffer something for him. And what he said, “of God and of Christ,” seems to have been placed jointly.] But may the Lord direct your hearts into the love of God, so that you may love God, and into the endurance of Christ, so that you may suffer for him.

We command you, brothers, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, to withdraw yourselves from every brother who walks disorderly, outside the way of right faith, and not according to the tradition that they received from us. [Note: [Col. 0345A] 4. LANFRANC. “For you yourselves know.” It is as though he were saying: I do not need to explain this tradition of which I am speaking, [Col. 0346A] because you know it.] For you yourselves know how you ought to imitate us, because we were not disorderly among you, wandering here and there, nor did we eat bread from anyone without payment; rather, in the labor of the work of our hands and in the weariness of preaching, working with our hands by night and preaching by day, we were at work so that we might not burden any of you. Lest someone object: “You could not.” It was not because we did not have the authority, but so that we might make ourselves an example for you to imitate us. [Note: [Col. 0346A] 5. “For even when we were.” This is another reason why he worked among them continually in labor and weariness: while he was with them, he was thus urging them to act.]

For even when we were with you, we were commanding you this: that if anyone does not wish to work, neither should he eat. The reason why he mentioned his own labor is this: For we hear that some among you are walking disorderly, idle, doing nothing, but acting inquisitively and spreading rumors. To those who are such we command and exhort in the Lord Jesus Christ that, working quietly, they should not be inquisitive, but should eat their own bread, not another’s.

But you, brothers, do not grow weary in doing good. You who do good, do not grow weary; or, if they do not know how to work, bear with them. [Note: [Col. 0346A] 6. AMBROSE. “But if anyone,” that is, we are speaking through the Epistle.] But if anyone does not obey our word, which we speak through the Epistle, take note of him through the Epistle; rebuke him by separating him from you, and do not associate with him, so that he may be put to shame. Yet do not regard him as an enemy, but correct him as a brother.

May the God of peace himself give you everlasting peace in every place. The Lord be with all of you. [Note: [Col. 0346A] 7. “My greeting.” He added this because those who were saying that the end of the age was near were persuading people of this as though it came from the Apostle’s Epistle. This is added so that they may accept nothing contrary to what is written here.] The greeting is written with my own hand, that of Paul, which is the sign in every Epistle; this is how I write. The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with all of you. Amen.

## Commentary

[Col. 0345A]

### Chapter III

1. LANFRANC. “But the Lord is faithful,” that is, truthful, since he promised that he would be present with his faithful ones until the end of the age.

2. AMBROSE. “But the Lord is faithful.” He applied this to the words of the prayer that he had made.

3. “But may the Lord direct,” that is, may it be granted to you to remain in that love which is directed toward him, enduring even if it should be necessary to suffer something for him. And what he said, “of God and of Christ,” seems to have been placed jointly.

4. LANFRANC. “For you yourselves know.” It is as though he were saying: I do not need to explain this tradition of which I am speaking, [Col. 0346A] because you know it.

5. “For even when we were.” This is another reason why he worked among them continually in labor and weariness: while he was with them, he was thus urging them to act.

6. AMBROSE. “But if anyone,” that is, we are speaking through the Epistle.

7. “My greeting.” He added this because those who were saying that the end of the age was near were persuading people of this as though it came from the Apostle’s Epistle. This is added so that they may accept nothing contrary to what is written here.

# The First Epistle of the Blessed Apostle Paul to Timothy, with the Glosses of the Blessed Lanfranc Interspersed

[Col. 0345]

[Col. 0345A] 183 **Argument.** He instructs and teaches Timothy concerning the ordering of the episcopate and the diaconate, and concerning ecclesiastical discipline, writing to him from Laodicea through Tychicus the deacon.

## Chapter I

[Col. 0345]

Paul, an Apostle of Jesus Christ according to the command of God our Savior and of Christ Jesus our hope, who is our hope, to Timothy, his beloved son in faith, whom I begot in faith. Grace, mercy—[the cause is placed among its effects]—and peace from God the Father and Christ Jesus our Lord.

Just as I urged you to remain at Ephesus while I was going to Macedonia, I urged you to command certain people not to teach otherwise than we do, [Note: [Col. 0345A] CHAP. I.—1. AMBROSE. “Nor to devote themselves.” Because the Jews at that time were taking great pains to show that Christ descended not from Abraham but from David.] nor to devote themselves to myths and [Note: [Col. 0345A] 2. LANFRANC. “Genealogies.” Generations—namely, how many years Methuselah and the others lived. Or the generations of Christ, how they agree or disagree; for Luke there seems to disagree with Matthew.] endless genealogies—without end, indefinite, or forbidden by me—which are investigated. These provide more [questioning]—as though there were much benefit, indeed rather harm—than the edification of God, which is in faith. [Note: [Col. 0347A] 3. AMBROSE. “But the end of the commandment.” Dividing those matters that it was fitting to command them and those from which they ought to restrain themselves, he says: “The end of the commandment is love.”] [Note: [Col. 0347A] 4. AUGUSTINE (Sermon 39, On Time, vol. X). “But the end.” What is the end of the commandment except the fulfillment of the commandment? And what is the fulfillment of the commandment except the fullness of the law? Therefore, what he said there—“Love is the fullness of the law”—he also says here: “The end of the commandment is love.”] [Note: [Col. 0347A] 5. LANFRANC. “But the end of the commandment.” “Of the commandment,” that is, of the commandments, whose end is love—that is, love of God and neighbor. As in the Gospel: “On these two commandments depend the whole law and the prophets.”] But the end of the commandment is [Note: [Col. 0347A] 6. AUGUSTINE (On Christian Doctrine, book I, chapter 40, vol. III). [Col. 0347B] “Love from a pure heart.” When he said “love,” he added “from a pure heart,” so that nothing other than what ought to be loved might be loved. He then adds “a good conscience” because of hope. For the person who has a scruple of bad conscience despairs of reaching what he believes and loves. Third, he says, “and from sincere faith”; for if our faith is free of falsehood, then we neither love what ought not to be loved nor, by living rightly, hope in such a way that our faith is deceived in any manner.] love, so that they may not devote themselves to the things mentioned above, but to love, because love is the end—that is, the fulfillment—of the law, proceeding from a pure heart and a good conscience and sincere faith.

From these things—genealogies, or conscience and faith—some, having wandered, have turned aside to vain talk, wishing to be teachers of the law, although they do not understand either the questions about which they speak, or what they say, or the authority of the Scriptures, or the very questions about which they make assertions.

Lest he seem to accuse the law, he says this. [Note: [Col. 0347B] 7. AMBROSE. “But we know that the law is good.” He said this lest he seem to accuse the law.] We know, however, that the law of the Jews is good if someone uses it lawfully, understanding it spiritually; [Note: [Col. 0347B] 8. “Knowing this.” He added this lest he seem to reintroduce observance of the law.] knowing this—he added it lest he seem to reintroduce observance of the law—that [Note: [Col. 0347B] 9. AUGUSTINE (Exposition of the Epistle to the Galatians, chapter II, vol. IV). “The law is not laid down.” The person who is under God lives for God; the person who is under the law lives for the law. But someone lives under the law insofar as he is a sinner, that is, insofar as he has not been changed from the old person. For he lives by his own life, and therefore the law is above him, because the person who does not fulfill it is beneath it. For the law is not laid down for the righteous—that is, imposed so that it may be above him. Rather, he is in the law than under the law, because he does not live by his own life; the law is imposed on the person who clings to it. Indeed, so to speak, the person who lives righteously with love of righteousness in some way lives the law itself.] the law, as a carnal observance, is not laid down for the righteous, but for restraining the unrighteous and those who are not subject to it: the impious, those who deny God, and sinners who confess God and pray; the wicked and defiled; parricides and matricides; murderers; fornicators; those who have intercourse with males; [Note: [Col. 0348A] 10. LANFRANC. “Kidnappers.” Kidnappers are those who secretly transfer people from one homeland to another and sell them.] kidnappers, or assassins; liars and perjurers; and whatever else is contrary to sound doctrine, which is according to the glorious Gospel of the blessed God, [Note: [Col. 0348A] 11. AMBROSE. “According to the Gospel.” This is bestowed upon us by him, and calls him blessed because blessedness possesses immutability by nature [variant: “in mutability”].] which was entrusted to me.

I give thanks to him who strengthened me, Christ Jesus our Lord, so that I might dare to preach, because he considered me faithful, appointing me to the ministry of the Gospel. I was formerly a blasphemer against God, a persecutor of the Church, and abusive; but I obtained God’s mercy because I acted ignorantly in unbelief.

The grace of our Lord abounded exceedingly with faith and love—which, because he forgave sins, he also added faith and love—in Christ Jesus, who came in order that grace might abound. And this is what he says: The saying is trustworthy, etc.

The saying is trustworthy and worthy of all acceptance: here is the saying—Christ Jesus came into this world to save sinners, [Note: [Col. 0348B] 12. AUGUSTINE (Sermon 9, On the Words of the Apostle, chapter 6, vol. X). “Of whom I am first.” The last Apostle, the first sinner. And in what sense am I the first sinner? “Of whom I am first.” Since I am before all, he wished “first” to be understood as “worse.”] of whom I am the first, the worse. But for this reason I obtained mercy through faith and had my sins forgiven: so that in me, the first and worse sinner, Christ Jesus might show all the patience that he has toward sinners, [Note: [Col. 0348B] 13. LANFRANC. “For an example,” that is, so that those who will believe in Christ may not despair of God’s mercy because of great sins, having been instructed by this example.] as an example for those who are going to believe in him for eternal life, so that they may possess it.

Therefore, to the King of the ages, immortal, invisible, the only God, be honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.

This command I entrust to you, son Timothy, [Note: [Col. 0348B] 14. “According to the preceding prophecies.” The Holy Spirit always foretold to the Apostle whatever he ought to command Timothy. The meaning is: I remind you according to what the inspiration of the Holy Spirit suggests to me.] according to the prophecies previously made concerning you, [Note: [Col. 0348B] 15. AMBROSE. “According to the preceding prophecies.” This was according to divine revelation; having made your election, I entrusted the work of teaching to you.] so that, through them, you may wage the good warfare, having faith and not doubting concerning grace and recompense through faith, etc. [Note: [Col. 0349A] 16. LANFRANC. “A good conscience.” He calls the thoughts a conscience; in these humility must be observed with the greatest care. When it is despised, some have fallen into great errors, as is read in the Epistle to the Romans.]

Have a good conscience, which some, rejecting, have suffered shipwreck with regard to the faith. Among them are Hymenaeus and Alexander, [Note: [Col. 0349A] 17. AMBROSE. “Whom I handed over.” He calls alienation from the Church “handing over to Satan,” showing through this how great an evil it is to be excluded from the Church.] whom I handed over to Satan for punishment, or for excommunication, so that they may learn not to blaspheme.

## Commentary

[Col. 0345A]

### Chapter I

1. AMBROSE. “Nor to devote themselves.” Because the Jews at that time were taking great pains to show that Christ descended not from Abraham but from David.

2. LANFRANC. “Genealogies.” Generations—namely, how many years Methuselah and the others lived. Or the generations of Christ, how they agree or disagree; for Luke there seems to disagree with Matthew.

[Col. 0347A] 3. AMBROSE. “But the end of the commandment.” Dividing those matters that it was fitting to command them and those from which they ought to restrain themselves, he says: “The end of the commandment is love.”

4. AUGUSTINE (Sermon 39, On Time, vol. X). “But the end.” What is the end of the commandment except the fulfillment of the commandment? And what is the fulfillment of the commandment except the fullness of the law? Therefore, what he said there—“Love is the fullness of the law”—he also says here: “The end of the commandment is love.”

5. LANFRANC. “But the end of the commandment.” “Of the commandment,” that is, of the commandments, whose end is love—that is, love of God and neighbor. As in the Gospel: “On these two commandments depend the whole law and the prophets.”

6. AUGUSTINE (On Christian Doctrine, book I, chapter 40, vol. III). [Col. 0347B] “Love from a pure heart.” When he said “love,” he added “from a pure heart,” so that nothing other than what ought to be loved might be loved. He then adds “a good conscience” because of hope. For the person who has a scruple of bad conscience despairs of reaching what he believes and loves. Third, he says, “and from sincere faith”; for if our faith is free of falsehood, then we neither love what ought not to be loved nor, by living rightly, hope in such a way that our faith is deceived in any manner.

7. AMBROSE. “But we know that the law is good.” He said this lest he seem to accuse the law.

8. “Knowing this.” He added this lest he seem to reintroduce observance of the law.

9. AUGUSTINE (Exposition of the Epistle to the Galatians, chapter II, vol. IV). “The law is not laid down.” The person who is under God lives for God; the person who is under the law lives for the law. But someone lives under the law insofar as he is a sinner, that is, insofar as he has not been changed from the old person. For he lives by his own life, and therefore the law is above him, because the person who does not fulfill it is beneath it. For the law is not laid down for the righteous—that is, imposed so that it may be above him. Rather, he is in the law than under the law, because he does not live by his own life; the law is imposed on the person who clings to it. Indeed, so to speak, the person who lives righteously with love of righteousness in some way lives the law itself.

10. LANFRANC. “Kidnappers.” Kidnappers are those who secretly transfer people from one homeland to another and sell them.

11. AMBROSE. “According to the Gospel.” This is bestowed upon us by him, and calls him blessed because blessedness possesses immutability by nature [variant: “in mutability”].

[Col. 0348B] 12. AUGUSTINE (Sermon 9, On the Words of the Apostle, chapter 6, vol. X). “Of whom I am first.” The last Apostle, the first sinner. And in what sense am I the first sinner? “Of whom I am first.” Since I am before all, he wished “first” to be understood as “worse.”

13. LANFRANC. “For an example,” that is, so that those who will believe in Christ may not despair of God’s mercy because of great sins, having been instructed by this example.

14. “According to the preceding prophecies.” The Holy Spirit always foretold to the Apostle whatever he ought to command Timothy. The meaning is: I remind you according to what the inspiration of the Holy Spirit suggests to me.

15. AMBROSE. “According to the preceding prophecies.” This was according to divine revelation; having made your election, I entrusted the work of teaching to you.

[Col. 0349A] 16. LANFRANC. “A good conscience.” He calls the thoughts a conscience; in these humility must be observed with the greatest care. When it is despised, some have fallen into great errors, as is read in the Epistle to the Romans.

17. AMBROSE. “Whom I handed over.” He calls alienation from the Church “handing over to Satan,” showing through this how great an evil it is to be excluded from the Church.

## Chapter II
Therefore I beseech you—since you have been chosen through prophecy—that, first of all, there be made [Note: [Col. 0349A] CHAP. II.—1. AUGUSTINE (Letter 59 to Paulinus, question 5, solution). “Supplications.” Let us understand “supplications” as those which we make in the celebration of the sacraments, before that which is on the Lord’s table begins to be blessed; “prayers,” when it is blessed and sanctified and broken for distribution—a blessing which almost the entire Church concludes with the Lord’s Prayer; “intercessions,” or, as your books have it, “petitions,” are made when the people are blessed. When these have been completed and so great a sacrament has been received, thanksgiving brings everything to a close; the Apostle also commended this as the final part in these words. This was the principal reason why, after these matters had been briefly set out and indicated, what follows should not be thought negligible.] supplications, in the secret prayer; prayers, before the secret prayer; petitions, when the bishop blesses; thanksgivings, after the sacrament has been received—the whole office of the Mass is referred to—for all human beings; for kings and for all who are established in high position, in any authority, [Note: [Col. 0349B] 2. LANFRANC. “That we may lead a quiet life.” In the peace of rulers, the tranquility and governance of the Churches are preserved; for in their wars and dissensions that tranquility is scattered, devotion grows cold, order is dissolved, and, once order has been dissolved, chastity of conduct is violated.] so that we may lead a quiet and tranquil life in all devotion and chastity. [Note: [Col. 0349B] 3. AMBROSE. “For this is good.” He proves this by adding: “who desires all human beings to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth.” He shows this when he adds, “For there is one God”—that is, because he is Lord of all. There is also one Mediator, who strives to unite us human beings to God; he too is one, and he is human. In every respect he shows how necessary it is that concern should be shown for all, since God cares for everyone and is Lord of all, and since Christ himself likewise appears to draw near to everyone by the particularity of his nature; he bestowed a benefit upon all, accepting suffering on behalf of all.] For this is good and acceptable before God our Savior, who desires all human beings to be saved—whether [“saved”] through works—and to come to the knowledge of the truth. [Note: [Col. 0350A] 4. LANFRANC. “For there is one God.” This answers what he had said in the singular, “our Savior God”: he desires all to be saved because there is one God of all, and one Mediator is the cause. Or he proves it from the effect: he desires all to be saved because he gave himself as a redemption for all.] For there is one God, and one mediator between God and human beings, the human being Christ Jesus, who gave himself as a redemption for all, [Note: [Col. 0350A] 5. “Testimony.” He calls “testimony” what the prophets foretold about Christ, or what Christ declared about himself—namely, what was confirmed at the appropriate times in reality and by its fulfillment, when he was to suffer, to rise again, and so forth.] the testimony at its proper times, namely, of the Incarnation, in which I was appointed a preacher, 186 and an apostle—I speak the truth in these matters; I do not lie—as a teacher of the Gentiles in faith and truth. Therefore I wish men to pray, either by command or because I am a teacher, [Note: [Col. 0350A] 6. AMBROSE. “In every place.” The order is: “in every place lifting up holy hands,” in which they pray.] in every place, lifting up pure hands, either toward heaven or through good works, rightly reproving, [Note: [Col. 0350B] 7. “Without anger.” When he says “without anger,” he means hating no one. When he says “without dispute,” he means that they should not doubt in faithful minds that they will receive what they ask; by the one expression he commends love toward one’s neighbor, and by the other, love toward God.] without anger and dispute, without despair of recompense. [COMMENTARY]

[Col. 0349A]

CHAP. II.—1. AUGUSTINE (Letter 59 to Paulinus, question 5, solution). “Supplications.” Let us understand “supplications” as those which we make in the celebration of the sacraments, before that which is on the Lord’s table begins to be blessed; “prayers,” when it is blessed and sanctified and broken for distribution—a blessing which almost the entire Church concludes with the Lord’s Prayer; “intercessions,” or, as your books have it, “petitions,” are made when the people are blessed. When these have been completed and so great a sacrament has been received, thanksgiving brings everything to a close; the Apostle also commended this as the final part in these words. This was the principal reason why, after these matters had been briefly set out and indicated, what follows should not be thought negligible.

2. LANFRANC. “That we may lead a quiet life.” In the peace of rulers, the tranquility and governance of the Churches are preserved; for in their wars and dissensions that tranquility is scattered, devotion grows cold, order is dissolved, and, once order has been dissolved, chastity of conduct is violated.

3. AMBROSE. “For this is good.” He proves this by adding: “who desires all human beings to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth.” He shows this when he adds, “For there is one God”—that is, because he is Lord of all. There is also one Mediator, who strives to unite us human beings to God; he too is one, and he is human. In every respect he shows how necessary it is that concern should be shown for all, since God cares for everyone and is Lord of all, and since Christ himself likewise appears to draw near to everyone by the particularity of his nature; he bestowed a benefit upon all, accepting suffering on behalf of all.

4. LANFRANC. “For there is one God.” This answers what he had said in the singular, “our Savior God”: he desires all to be saved because there is one God of all, and one Mediator is the cause. Or he proves it from the effect: he desires all to be saved because he gave himself as a redemption for all.

5. “Testimony.” He calls “testimony” what the prophets foretold about Christ, or what Christ declared about himself—namely, what was confirmed at the appropriate times in reality and by its fulfillment, when he was to suffer, to rise again, and so forth.

6. AMBROSE. “In every place.” The order is: “in every place lifting up holy hands,” in which they pray.

7. “Without anger.” When he says “without anger,” he means hating no one. When he says “without dispute,” he means that they should not doubt in faithful minds that they will receive what they ask; by the one expression he commends love toward one’s neighbor, and by the other, love toward God.

8. LANFRANC. “Let a woman learn in silence.” A woman is commanded to learn in silence because, when she speaks, she more strongly incites and is incited toward sexual indulgence.

9. AMBROSE. “But to teach.” This command was necessary at that time, when there were prophetesses.

10. LANFRANC. “Nor to exercise authority over a man.” A woman ought not to exercise authority, for she is inferior to a man, as Eve was; she was formed later than Adam, since he was formed first. She is also inferior because she was deceived—condemned in one respect, but in another to be saved. Adam is said not to have been deceived primarily, but out of love for the woman, as were Solomon and many others.

11. AUGUSTINE (The City of God, book XIV, chapter 11, vol. V). “Adam was not deceived.” For just as Aaron did not consent to one gone astray in making an idol, but yielded under constraint, and it is not credible that Solomon thought in error that an idol ought to be worshiped, but that he was compelled to those sacrileges by feminine blandishments, so it must be believed that that man, to his one woman—one human being to a human being, husband to wife—did not, in transgressing God’s law, believe her as though she spoke the truth, being deceived, but complied because of their social bond.

12. LANFRANC. “Adam was not deceived.” He was not deceived in the matter in which Eve was deceived; for he did not believe either that he would become God or like God by eating the fruit. He knew with absolute certainty that he was doing wrong and that what the woman was urging upon him was a lie. But he thought that both things could happen: that he could comply with his wife and, after repenting of the crime committed, obtain forgiveness from God. Therefore the one who intended to repent sinned less than she who, in her transgression, thought nothing either of repentance or of forgiveness, but rather imagined that through disobedience she would become God and like God.

13. AMBROSE. “Adam was not deceived,” since the woman appears to have been the cause of that deception.

14. “But she will be saved.” He shows that offspring appears worthy of salvation through those women who look toward devotion. He did not say this about Eve, but speaks of the race.

15. AUGUSTINE (Exposition on Psalm 85). “But she is saved.” The woman, therefore, who is understood figuratively as the flesh, will be saved through the bearing of children—that is, if she does good works, though not just anywhere: in true faith, in Catholic faith, and in the fellowship of the one Church, let her bring forth her works. Therefore, when the Apostle was questioned about her, he added: “But she will be saved through the bearing of children, if she remains in faith, love, and holiness.”

[COMMENTARY]

[Col. 0351C]

CHAP. III.—1. AUGUSTINE (The City of God, book X, chapter 19). “If anyone desires the episcopate.” The Apostle says: “If anyone desires the episcopate, he desires a good work.” He wished to explain what the episcopate is, since it is the name of a work, not of an honor. The term is Greek and derived from the fact that the one appointed oversees—namely, caring for those entrusted to him. For *skopos* means attention; therefore, if we wish to render ἐπισκοπεῖν in Latin, we may say “to oversee,” so that one may understand that he is not a bishop who loves to preside but does not care to benefit others.

2. LANFRANC. “The episcopate.” The episcopate is attentiveness directed toward one’s own life and that of others; whoever desires this desires a good work.

3. “Of one wife”—that is, one who has had only one wife, whether as a layman or in permitted orders.

4. AMBROSE. “Temperate,” so that he carefully oversees what is fitting.

5. “Well-arranged,” in conduct, movement, and appearance.

6. “Chaste,” because he is appointed as a teacher jointly to men and women.

7. LANFRANC. “If anyone does not know how to govern his own household,” and so forth. Such a person must be chosen who knows how to preside over his own household; for one ignorant of lesser matters is ignorant of greater ones.

8. AMBROSE. “Being puffed up with pride.” Thus, exalting himself because of his teaching office, he differs in nothing from the devil, who was created as a minister of God but strove to claim for himself God’s name and honor.

9. “Into the snare of the devil.” Another reason: lest he rush back into former sins because he appears to have only recently withdrawn from outsiders.

10. LANFRANC. “Into the snare of the devil.” It commonly happens to those who are despised by others that they in turn despise those who despise them, and thus fall into anger and hatred and the devil’s other snares.

[Col. 0352C] 11. AMBROSE. “Holding the mystery.” He calls “mystery” the doctrine concerning Christ.

12. “Not slanderers.” This is because it is customary, and necessary, for other women to report confidently to them the matters in which they are lacking.

13. “A good standing.” He does not mean in the present world.

[Col. 0353A] 14. LANFRANC. “The Church of the living God, the pillar,” and so forth. The Church—that is, the faithful—are the pillar of truth: they directly uphold truth itself, that is, Christ, so that the perverse do not overthrow him.

15. AMBROSE. “Of the living God.” He very appropriately added “of the living God,” to show thereby the dignity of the Church.

16. LANFRANC. “Pillar.” The Church of God is a pillar in great men, who support others; in them we are also strengthened with the firmament of truth, because they confirm the truth of the Gospel by words and miracles.

17. AMBROSE. “Manifestly.” Because he called the Church the pillar of truth, he showed what that truth itself is.

18. LANFRANC. “Great is the mystery of devotion.” The truth and mystery found here—that is, Christ, who is truth and mystery—is manifestly great.

19. AMBROSE. “Justified.” This is applied to human nature, because the spirit received its dwelling in baptism.

20. “Appeared.” That is, he became visible to the angels.

But avoid irreverent and old-womanish tales; [Note: [Col. 0354A] 8. “Train yourself.” He called the exercise of devotion diligence in teaching.] train yourself for devotion; feed the flock entrusted to you with spiritual and bodily nourishment, so that you may be devout. For bodily exercise is useful for a little while, [Note: [Col. 0354B] 9. LANFRANC. “Bodily exercise.” It is understood that he exercised himself in vigils, fasts, manual labor, and other bodily works, but was not equally devoted to works of mercy.] but devotion is useful for all things, [Note: [Col. 0354B] 10. AUGUSTINE (Exposition on Psalm 143, vol. Do not neglect the grace of the episcopate that is in you, which was given to you [Note: [Col. 0354C] 12. “Through prophecy.” He calls “prophecy” the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, through which he foreknew what he and the others would undertake concerning this matter.] through prophecy, with the laying on of the hands [Note: [Col. 0355A] 13. “Of the presbyterate.” “Of the presbyterate” stands for “of the presbyters”; for there cannot be fewer than three, and he calls the bishop a presbyter.] of the presbyterate, or when you received the presbyterate itself. [COMMENTARY]

[Col. 0353B]

CHAP. IV.—1. LANFRANC. “Now the Spirit expressly,” and so forth. Or: the pillar of Christ will strengthen the Church against those who attack it by departing from the faith; and the Spirit expressly says that they would depart.

2. “And seared.” A cautery is an iron instrument by which the surface of a thing is burned.

3. AMBROSE. “Having their own.” For those who pretend to discuss chastity are found to perpetrate every kind of impurity within themselves.

4. LANFRANC. “Forbidding marriage,” and so forth. He commands him to prohibit them from rejecting foods, from marrying, and from preaching by the Spirit, because this is forbidden to them by the false apostles.

[Col. 0354A] 5. AUGUSTINE (Exposition on Psalm 143, vol. VIII, and Against Faustus, book VI, chapter 7, beginning). “For every creature.” He said that certain animals were unclean not by nature but by signification. Thus [variant: “so that”], for example, if one asks about a pig and a lamb, both are clean by nature, because every creature of God is good; but by signification the lamb is clean and the pig unclean.

6. LANFRANC. “Setting these things before the brethren.” He promises himself a double benefit: that he will be a good minister and that through practice itself he will attain the doctrine.

7. AMBROSE. “Nourished.” “This,” he says, “will also benefit you; for while you teach others with due diligence, you are nourished by constant meditation.”

8. “Train yourself.” He called the exercise of devotion diligence in teaching.

9. LANFRANC. “Bodily exercise.” It is understood that he exercised himself in vigils, fasts, manual labor, and other bodily works, but was not equally devoted to works of mercy.

10. AUGUSTINE (Exposition on Psalm 143, vol. VIII). “Having the promise.” “His left hand is under my head.” He does not abandon me even in temporal necessities, but nevertheless that left hand will be under the head; it will not be placed before the head but will remain beneath it. “And his right hand embraces me,” promising eternal life. Thus, with the left hand under the head and the right hand above the head, what is said is fulfilled: “having the promise of the present life and of the future”; what belongs to the present, the left hand is under the head; what belongs to the future, his right hand will embrace me.

11. LANFRANC. “Having the promise of life.” For through works a person possesses it more fully both in this age and in the future.

12. “Through prophecy.” He calls “prophecy” the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, through which he foreknew what he and the others would undertake concerning this matter.

13. “Of the presbyterate.” “Of the presbyterate” stands for “of the presbyters”; for there cannot be fewer than three, and he calls the bishop a presbyter.

14. “Attend,” that is, consider how you live and how you teach.

[COMMENTARY]

[Col. 0355A]

Chapter V—1. AMBROSE. “Do not rebuke an elder.” He means: Do not attack anyone, nor be harsh or bitter.

2. LANFRANC. “An elder.” Here “elder” should be understood not so much in age as in conduct. Of this kind of old age Solomon says: “Gray hairs are a human being’s understanding, and an unblemished life is old age.”

3. “Chastity.” In addressing young women, the young man is most rightly admonished concerning complete chastity, so that he may not be stirred even by the slightest titillation.

4. AMBROSE. “Honor widows,” that is, support them from ecclesiastical resources.

5. “Let her learn.” He speaks of sons and grandsons, not of widows.

6. LANFRANC. “Parents.” He calls “parents” those whom above he called sons and grandsons. The whole lineage is called a family; hence, even in secular law, those to whom succession is already ordered from a parent and by a parent are commanded to repay them in kind and to render assistance and support in their service [variant: “in their old age,” or “in their services”].

7. “Who is truly a widow.” She is truly a widow who is adorned in character and has no one who [variant: “to whom”] may care for her.

[Col. 0356A] 8. “But if anyone does not care for his own.” It is better to be ignorant of the truth than to neglect it once known; this is what the person does who does not care for his own.

9. AUGUSTINE (*The City of God*, book XIX, chapter 14, volume V). “But if anyone.” He has a more suitable and easier opportunity to provide counsel to them, whether by the order of nature or by the fellowship of human society.

10. AMBROSE. “But if anyone.” This refers to the statement: “If any widow has children and grandchildren, let them learn.”

11. “Let a widow be chosen.” He returns to the earlier statement: “Honor widows.”

12. “For when they have become wanton,” that is, when they have been received among two [reading uncertain] and have obtained ecclesiastical support.

13. LANFRANC. “For when they have become wanton.” The reason they are to be avoided is that it often happens that, abandoning their resolve to remain chaste, they become wanton with many lovers and, after much wantonness, wish to marry in Christ, that is, to unite themselves [variant: “be united”] to legitimate husbands.

14. AUGUSTINE (*On the Good of Widowhood*, chapter 9). “Having condemnation.” So that the will—which yields [variant: “has yielded”] to its resolve—may appear to have been condemned, whether marriage follows or not.

15. AMBROSE. “At the same time.” Since, having no concern for temporal matters, they securely obtain what is necessary for their use, they learn by that very generosity to devote themselves to idleness.

16. “Therefore I wish.” So that they may restrain the impulse of youth, which is occupied with excessive concern.

17. “Any occasion.” For those who hasten to disparage us.

[Col. 0357A] 18. “Against a presbyter.” The Apostle therefore foresaw how easily accusations could arise against presbyters, since they sometimes rebuke those subject to them for lost pleasures.

19. LANFRANC. “Three witnesses,” that is, unless the accuser has two or three witnesses to the crime he alleges.

20. AUGUSTINE (*On the Words of the Lord*, sermon 16, chapter 7). “Those who sin.” Therefore those sins should be corrected publicly which are committed publicly; those should be corrected more privately which are committed more privately.

21. LANFRANC. “Share.” Whoever ordains an unworthy man also shares in the sins of the one ordained.

22. “Keep yourself chaste.” As if he were saying: Since you are ordered to reject the unworthy, you must preserve yourself in purity of life.

23. “Do not continue drinking water.” Since he had commanded that chastity be preserved, he adds this so that Timothy would not increase or maintain excessive abstinence. Or because he had been ill and had not yet fully recovered. Or he says this because, while he is still young, he should wait until he is older.

24. AMBROSE. “Do not continue drinking water.” Out of regard for continence he was still drinking water; and because we often do such things for the sake of others, lest we seem indifferent toward their way of life, he added this appropriately.

25. “The sins of some people.” He means that, just as the sins of delinquent people who do not look rightly are made manifest—sins that will bring them punishments in the future age—even though they may do certain things that could have remained hidden from many, so also with those who have resolved to live rightly: very many of their deeds are made manifest to people. There are also many things hidden from many; this is what he signifies by saying, “and those which are otherwise situated cannot be hidden.” Use wine, however, for the sake of the illness itself, knowing that even those things which people conjecture about us, although we live rightly, are good when they are perceived for the most part; we shall suffer no harm from these, even though many of our deeds may appear unknown to many.

26. AUGUSTINE (*On the Sermon on the Mount*, book II, chapter 18). “The sins of some people.” He calls those things manifest concerning which it is clear with what intention they are done; these precede judgment—that is, when judgment follows them, it is not rash. Those things that are hidden follow, and these too will not remain hidden in their own time. The same should be understood concerning good deeds, for he adds: “Likewise good works are manifest; and those which are otherwise situated cannot be hidden.” Therefore let us judge concerning manifest things. As for hidden things, let us leave judgment to God, since they too—whether good or evil—cannot remain hidden when the time comes for them to be revealed.

27. LANFRANC. “The sins of some people.” He gives the reason why hands should not be laid quickly on anyone. By “judgment” he means a council, a synod, or some place in which persons are examined: “The sins of some people,” he says, “are so manifest that their reputation or notoriety reaches the tribunal before the infamous men themselves who come to be ordained. But the sins of others follow them to the tribunal, because they are first revealed when those to be ordained are examined.”

28. “Are otherwise situated.” This must be understood of sins, for not everything is disclosed in the examination itself; many things sometimes remain hidden.

## Chapter VI

[Col. 0357]

All who are under the yoke of a master, being faithful Christian slaves, should consider their masters worthy of every honor, [Note: [Col. 0358C] Chapter VI—1. LANFRANC. “So that the name of the Lord,” etc. The name of God and the teaching would be blasphemed if, on account of what should make them humble, they became proud and despised their masters.] so that the name of the Lord and the teaching may not be blasphemed. Those who have believing masters must not despise them, [Note: [Col. 0358C] 2. “Because they are brothers.” In this way slaves and masters seemed to be equals, because both were Christians; and consequently the slaves despised their masters.] because they are brothers, but should serve them all the more, because they are believers and beloved of God, since they are participants in the benefit of the Christian religion, or because they are more humane. Teach and exhort these things.

If anyone teaches otherwise (avoid him) and does not assent to the sound words of our Lord Jesus Christ, let him be accursed, and to the teaching that is according to piety—that is, religion—he is proud, knowing nothing, [Note: [Col. 0359A] 3. AMBROSE. “But being sick.” He calls their thoughts “sickness,” because, abandoning piety, they turned to disputes.] but being sick (because he does not know how to resolve the questions he proposes) with disputes and quarrels about words. From these arise envy, contention, blasphemies, as one maliciously opposes another, evil suspicions, and conflicts among people corrupted in mind and deprived of the truth, [Note: [Col. 0359A] 4. LANFRANC. “Supposing.” They supposed that Christ should be worshiped only for the profits of this life.] supposing [Note: [Col. 0359A] 5. “That piety is a means of gain.” They present themselves as pious in order to obtain earthly things, since their own resources are not sufficient.] that piety, religion, and preaching are a means of temporal gain. [Note: [Col. 0359A] 6. “But piety is a great gain.” As if he were saying: Christian religion is indeed a gain, but not the kind they think; rather, it is a great gain, that is, eternal.] But piety with contentment is a great gain (he uses “gain” equivocally): faith, for which what is given by God is sufficient. The reason why what exists in the present should suffice is this: We brought nothing into this world; without doubt, neither can we take anything away, nor are these things ours, for we shall not carry them away with us. But having food and clothing, let us be content with these. Let us not seek to become rich. For those who wish to become rich fall into temptation and into the devil’s snare, and into many foolish and harmful desires that plunge people into ruin and destruction. [Note: [Col. 0359A] 7. “The root of all evils,” etc. Greed, that is, desire for riches, produces these evils; and this is not surprising, since desire is the root of all evils.] For the root of all evils is desire; [Note: [Col. 0359A] 8. AMBROSE. “Some, desiring.” In view of the things that happened to them. [Col. 0359B]] some, desiring it, have gone astray from the faith, 193 and have pierced themselves with many sorrows.

[Note: [Col. 0359B] 9. “But you, O man of God.” He plainly appears to have exhorted him, calling him “the man of God.”] But you, O man of God, flee these things; pursue righteousness, piety, faith, charity, patience, and gentleness.
