By fighting in this way, seize eternal life, to which, and for which, you were called, having confessed the good confession, the Catholic faith, before many witnesses, on the day of baptism or at the reception of the presbyterate.

I charge you before God, who gives life to all things, and Christ Jesus, who gave testimony [Note: [Col. 0359B] 10. LANFRANC. “Under Pontius.” When he said, “Everyone who is of the truth hears my voice,” etc.] under Pontius Pilate, not being ashamed of the good confession—namely, of the Father—that you keep [Note: [Col. 0359B] 11. “The commandment,” that is, the evangelical precept, concerning which the Psalm says: “The law of the Lord is blameless.”] the commandment without stain (do not be ashamed before kings of the evangelical precept, concerning which the Psalm says: “The law of the Lord is blameless”), irreproachable, until the coming [Note: [Col. 0359B] 12. AUGUSTINE (*Against Maximinus the Arian*, book III, chapter 12). “At the coming.” Namely, the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, which he will reveal. [Col. 0360A]] of our Lord Jesus Christ, which God, blessed and alone powerful, will reveal at his proper times. [Note: [Col. 0360A] 13. AMBROSE. “The blessed one will reveal.” He called him blessed to confirm the future unchangeability of the nature that will be in us, which in him exists by nature and power. He called him king and lord because he is powerful enough both to subjugate demons and to take away death. He dwells in light because he will illuminate the bodies of the saints.] He is the King of kings and Lord of lords, who alone possesses [Note: [Col. 0360A] 14. AUGUSTINE (*ibid.*). “Immortality.” Immortality is said to belong to God alone. In every mutable nature, change itself is a kind of death, because it causes something that existed in it no longer to exist.] [Note: [Col. 0360A] 15. LANFRANC. “Immortality,” that is, immutability; for every creature is mutable.] immortality and dwells in inaccessible light; whom no human being, remaining in this corruption, has seen, nor can see. [Note: [Col. 0360A] 16. “Can see.” This is to be understood of the present life: human beings cannot see God in this life. For concerning another life it is written: “We shall see him as he is.” [Col. 0360B]] To him be honor and eternal dominion. Amen.

Command the rich of this age not to be high-minded, nor to glory in riches, nor to hope in the uncertainty of riches, but in the living God, who provides us abundantly with all things for enjoyment, not for hoarding. In this regard, either command them to do good, to become rich in good works, to give readily, and to share with needy neighbors, storing up for themselves a good foundation for the future, so that they may seize true life.

O Timothy, [Note: [Col. 0360B] 17. “The deposit,” that is, the spiritual gifts that God entrusted to you, that is, commended to you.] guard the deposit—the faith and the grace of the episcopate—avoiding profane novelties of words, deceptive propositions, and oppositions of falsely named knowledge (he means sophistical technique), which some, [Note: [Col. 0360B] 18. “Penitents.” Construction: he calls the knowledge falsely so named—or sophistical art—something called “knowledge” under a false name, whereas it would more correctly be called error and deceit.] promising and professing, have gone astray concerning the faith, into heresies. Chapter VI—1. LANFRANC. “So that the name of the Lord,” etc. [Col. 0358C] The name of God and the teaching would be blasphemed if, on account of what should make them humble, they became proud and despised their masters.

[Col. 0359A] 3. AMBROSE. “But being sick.” He calls their thoughts “sickness,” because, abandoning piety, they turned to disputes.

7. “The root of all evils,” etc. Greed, that is, desire for riches, produces these evils; and this is not surprising, since desire is the root of all evils.

8. AMBROSE. “Some, desiring.” In view of the things that happened to them.

9. “But you, O man of God.” He plainly appears to have exhorted him, calling him “the man of God.”

10. LANFRANC. “Under Pontius.” When he said, “Everyone who is of the truth hears my voice,” etc.

13. AMBROSE. “The blessed one will reveal.” He called him blessed to confirm the future unchangeability of the nature that will be in us, which in him exists by nature and power. He called him king and lord because he is powerful enough both to subjugate demons and to take away death. He dwells in light because he will illuminate the bodies of the saints.

14. AUGUSTINE (*ibid.*). “Immortality.” Immortality is said to belong to God alone. In every mutable nature, change itself is a kind of death, because it causes something that existed in it no longer to exist.

18. “Penitents.” Construction: he calls the knowledge falsely so named—or sophistical art—something called “knowledge” under a false name, whereas it would more correctly be called error and deceit.

## The Second Epistle of the Apostle Paul to Timothy, with the Interspersed Glosses of Lanfranc

[Col. 0361]

194 **Argument.** Again he writes to Timothy concerning the exhortation to martyrdom, every rule of truth, what will happen [Col. 0362] in the last times, and his own suffering, writing to him from the city of Rome.

## Chapter I

[Col. 0361]

Paul, an Apostle of Jesus Christ through the will of God, according to [Note: [Col. 0361A] Chapter I—1. AUGUSTINE. “The promise of life,” that is: I was made an Apostle so that I might preach the life promised through Christ.] the promise of life (an Apostle preaching the promise of eternal life, according to what God promised), which is in Christ Jesus, in the faith of Christ, not through merits, to Timothy, my beloved son: grace, mercy (the cause being placed among its effects, namely grace and peace), peace from God the Father, from whom I was begotten in the Church, or in the company of the holy fathers from whom I derive my origin, and from Christ Jesus our Lord.

[Note: [Col. 0361A] 2. “I give thanks.” “I give thanks to God, whom I serve”; hence the sentence should be understood in this way: “because I have you continually in remembrance in my prayers.” The order is: “I give thanks, remembering your tears, so that I may be filled with joy,” so that it signifies not the cause but what follows.] I give thanks to God, whom I serve from my ancestors Ananias and others, with a pure conscience, not in hypocrisy, because without ceasing (this is the reason for his thanksgiving) I remember you in my prayers, night and day desiring to see you, remembering your tears, poured out from longing for me, so that I may be filled with joy, receiving the recollection of the faith that is in you, an unfalsified faith, which first dwelt (a good offspring from good ancestors) in your grandmother Lois and your mother Eunice (he makes no mention of your father, who remained in gentile error). I am certain that it also dwells in you.

For this reason I remind you (here he indicates that Timothy was sluggish in preaching) to rekindle (for he was growing dull because of fear) [Note: [Col. 0361A] 3. “The grace of God.” The divine gift granted in ordination.], [Note: [Col. 0361A] 4. LANFRANC. “The grace of God.” He urges him to rekindle the grace of the episcopate, so that he may preach the word of God more confidently, fearing neither earthly powers nor being ashamed to call himself a disciple of the crucified and imprisoned one; for he had been somewhat timid and negligent,] the grace of God, the episcopate, which is in you through the laying on of my hands.

We must not fear. For God did not give us a spirit of fear, but of power, love, and self-control. Therefore do not be ashamed or afraid of the testimony and preaching of our Lord, nor of me, his prisoner, bound on his account. 195 [Note: [Col. 0361B] 5. AUGUSTINE. “But collaborate.” So that you may preach the power of God, who saved us.] But collaborate with the Gospel according to the power of God, insofar as God’s power will assist you—he who saved us and [Note: [Col. 0361B] 6. LANFRANC. “Called us with a calling,” that is, invited us, saying: [Col. 0362A] “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will give you rest.”] called us with his holy calling, not according to our works but according to his own purpose and according to the grace that was given to us in Christ Jesus before worldly times, in predestination.

But it has now been manifested in the time of fulfillment through the illumination of our Savior Jesus Christ, who [Note: [Col. 0362A] 7. “Destroyed,” that is, clearly showed where life and corruption were.] indeed destroyed death, but brought life to light—by illuminating, he gave life—and incorruption, this incorruptible life, through the Gospel. For this Gospel I have been appointed preacher, Apostle, and teacher of the Gentiles.

For this reason I also suffer these bonds; but [Note: [Col. 0362A] 8. AMBROSE. “I am not ashamed.” He rightly said “I am not ashamed,” because he had said, “Do not be ashamed.”] I am not ashamed; I am not embarrassed. For I know whom I have believed and for whom I suffer (taken by analogy from a creditor), and I am certain that I shall not be exempt, [Note: [Col. 0362A] 9. “He is able to guard the deposit,” that is, the perfect grace of the Spirit, in which, in hope, we have at present obtained this grace of the Spirit as a pledge or down payment.] because he is able to guard my deposit, which I deposited with him—that is, the good work that I have done—and to repay it on that day.

Hold to the pattern of sound words; collaborate with the Gospel, or be one who has a pattern of words that bring healing, [Note: [Col. 0362A] 10. LANFRANC. “Which you heard from me,” that is, when I was explaining the faith and love that ought to be held in the faith of Christ Jesus.] which you heard from me in the faith and love that are in Christ Jesus.

Guard the good deposit—the teaching entrusted to you by me—through the Holy Spirit, through the help of the Holy Spirit who dwells in us. To indicate that he should guard this firmly, he says: [Note: [Col. 0362A] 11. “For you know that.” He recalls these men to him so that Timothy himself may also be cautious and not turn away in the same manner.] You know this: that all who are in Asia have turned away from me, among whom are Phygelus and Hermogenes.

But when he came to Rome, he diligently sought me and found me.

May the Lord grant him to find mercy from the Lord on that day before Christ—for the Father has given all judgment to the Son. And how many services he rendered to me in Ephesus, you know better than others, for you were present.

[Col. 0361A]

Chapter I—1. AUGUSTINE. “The promise of life,” that is: I was made an Apostle so that I might preach the life promised through Christ.

2. “I give thanks.” “I give thanks to God, whom I serve”; hence the sentence should be understood in this way: “because I have you continually in remembrance in my prayers.” The order is: “I give thanks, remembering your tears, so that I may be filled with joy,” so that it signifies not the cause but what follows.

LANFRANC. “The grace of God.” He urges him to rekindle the grace of the episcopate, so that he may preach the word of God more confidently, fearing neither earthly powers nor being ashamed to call himself a disciple of the crucified and imprisoned one; for he had been somewhat timid and negligent.

[Col. 0361B] 5. AUGUSTINE. “But collaborate.” So that you may preach the power of God, who saved us.

8. AMBROSE. “I am not ashamed.” He rightly said “I am not ashamed,” because he had said, “Do not be ashamed.”

9. “He is able to guard the deposit,” that is, the perfect grace of the Spirit, in which, in hope, we have at present obtained this grace of the Spirit as a pledge or down payment.

10. LANFRANC. “Which you heard from me,” that is, when I was explaining the faith and love that ought to be held in the faith of Christ Jesus.

11. “For you know that.” He recalls these men to him so that Timothy himself may also be cautious and not turn away in the same manner.

[Col. 0362B] 12. “My chain.” He added this appropriately, because, in exhorting Timothy, he had said: “Do not be ashamed of the testimony of the Lord.”

## Chapter II

[Col. 0363]

Therefore, my son, since they have departed, be strong in the grace that is in Christ Jesus, in the faith of Christ Jesus:

> **[Col. 0363A] CHAPTER II.—1. AMBROSE. “What you heard from me.”** What you heard me frequently teaching others; he says this “through many witnesses.”

And what you heard from me:

But take diligent care to present yourself to God as approved, an unashamed worker, one who is not ashamed to preach and who handles the word of truth rightly. Avoid profane words and empty talk, for they advance greatly toward impiety; and their speech spreads like a cancer.

## Commentary

**[Col. 0363A]**

**CHAPTER II.—1. AMBROSE. “What you heard from me.”** What you heard me frequently teaching others; he says this “through many witnesses.”

**2. LANFRANC. “Through many witnesses.”** “Through many” means “among many.” As Virgil says, *Via secta per ambas*, that is, “a road cut between both.” Or thus: what you heard from me was confirmed by many witnesses, that is, by many testimonies of Scripture.

**3. LANFR. “For whoever competes in the contest.”** “Compete lawfully so that you may be crowned”—by contrast: otherwise you will not be crowned; by analogy: “For whoever competes in the contest,” and so forth.

Hence he suffered great want, because he was weak and could not devote himself to manual labor. He therefore admonishes him, under the figure of a farmer, not to disdain receiving from the field he cultivates the fruit by which he may sustain himself.

Therefore, he says, if we do not believe, he nevertheless remains truthful; he cannot deny himself—that is, the words spoken by him—since he will find others through whom and in whom he may be praised.

**10. AMBROSE. “A firm foundation.”** The Apostle seems to have said this for his consolation, lest God ever give them—that is, so that they might be able to perceive the truth.

**11. LANFR. “A firm foundation.”** Whatever the heretics may chatter, the foundation of God—that is, the human being in whom the faith of God is strengthened and founded—does not tremble or waver. It bears this seal, that is, this memory impressed upon the mind: “The Lord knows those who are his,” and so it stands. Through this he avoids heresies and everything opposed to salvation, because he knows that everyone who invokes the name of the Lord must depart from all iniquity.

**12. “In a great house.”** Lest he wonder that some should depart from the faith, he gives this comparison. Some stand, others fall away, and they are not all alike, just as in a great house.

**[Col. 0365A] 13. “From these.”** That is, from association with those vessels that have been made for dishonor.

**14. “Lest at some time he grant.”** “Lest” is used in place of “if” or “whether”; this preposition is also found with this meaning.

proud because of what they appear to possess,

> **[Col. 0366A] CHAPTER IV.—1. AUGUSTINE (in his exposition of the Epistle to the Galatians, near the end, vol. IV). “Be urgent in season.”** This may be read with two different divisions. “Be urgent in season, out of season; reprove,” so that you may be considered timely when you persist in building up, and when you destroy by reproving; do not care if you appear untimely. Thus the two clauses that follow are assigned to the preceding ones: “Entreat” when, in season, you persist in building up; “rebuke” when, out of season, you appear to destroy in reproving. Then the next two clauses are related to the preceding ones in reverse order: “With all patience,” for enduring the indignation of those whom you reprove; and “with instruction,” for educating the understanding of those whom you build up. Another division is possible: “Be urgent in season”; and if you make no progress in this way, “be urgent out of season”—that is, even if you seem untimely to them, nevertheless, knowing that what you are doing is timely, keep concern for their healing in a gentle spirit. No medicine heals if it is not applied at the proper time.

Be urgent in season and out of season; reprove, entreat, rebuke,

with all patience, outwardly displayed and inwardly possessed, and with instruction in words and deeds.

AUGUSTINE** (same work). **“To the defiled.”** The Apostle calls them unclean because they think carnally, and unbelieving because they do not distinguish the time of grace from the time of the law. He says that nothing is clean for them because they used neither the things they rejected [variant: “rejected”] nor the things they consumed in a holy or righteous manner.

**[Col. 0370B]**

**CHAPTER II.—1. LANFR. “So that they may adorn the teaching.”** This refers to all the preceding material, beginning at the point where he says, “the older men are to be sober.”

# THE EPISTLE OF THE APOSTLE PAUL TO THE HEBREWS, WITH THE INTERPOLATED BRIEF GLOSSES OF B. LANFRANC

[Col. 0375]

[Col. 0375A] ## ARGUMENT

First of all, it must be explained why the Apostle Paul, in writing this Epistle, did not observe his customary practice of stating either his name or the dignity of his office. The reason is that, when writing to those who had believed from circumcision, he did not wish to put forward the merit of his office: he was, as it were, the Apostle of the Gentiles and not of the Hebrews, and, knowing their pride while demonstrating his own humility, he did not wish to place his office first. [Col. 0376A] In the same way, the Apostle John also, out of humility, did not put forward his name in his Epistle for the same reason. This Epistle, therefore, is said to have been sent by the Apostle to the Hebrews, written in the Hebrew language. Luke the Evangelist, retaining its meaning and order, composed it in Greek after the death of the blessed Apostle Paul.

By the same reasoning it is proved to belong to no one.]

in the beginning, Lord”—so that he might not appear to be later; or, “you, Father, in the Son, who is the beginning”—founded the earth, and the heavens are the works of your hands, O Son, who is the hand of the Father—or, literally, they are the heavens.

[Note: [Col. 0377C] 26. “They will perish.” They perish with respect to what they are, while they are changed for the better.]

They will perish, they will be changed; but you will remain, and they will all grow old like a garment. You will change them like a cloak, and they will be changed; but you are the same, and your years will not fail.

This again proves that he is more excellent, as above.

But to which of the angels did he ever say:

“Sit at my right hand,

[Note: [Col. 0377C] 27. “Until I place your enemies.” [Col. 0378A] By the feet of the Lord eternal stability is signified: as though placed beneath his footprints, he stands by the power of omnipotence. Those who, having abandoned their vices, bow before his preaching are evidently to be placed beneath these feet. “Until” does not here indicate the end of time, but eternity.]

until I place your enemies as a footstool for your feet”?

[Note: [Col. 0378A] 28. “Are they not all?” The Son alone saves; these serve the salvation of those predestined. For we read that an angel was sent to Mary; angels also appeared to the shepherds and to the women at the resurrection.]

Are they not all ministering spirits, sent for service on behalf of those who are to inherit salvation?

[Note: [Col. 0378A] 29. LANFRANC, “Ministering spirits.” Having proved that the Son is more excellent, he also proves that the angels are inferior; for they minister both to him and to human beings.]

[COMMENTARY.]

[Col. 0375A]

## CHAPTER I

1. LANFRANC, “In many ways,” and so forth. Conscious of their indignation and envy when they heard the name of the Apostle Paul, he abandons the customary greeting, although the Epistle is rejected for this reason: because it is not titled with his name. By the same reasoning it is proved to belong to no one.

2. “In many ways.” For example, in the case of the prophet to whom he commanded that he take a prostitute as wife (Hosea I); and of the one to whom he commanded that he place a loincloth beneath a stone and inspect it after forty days, when he found upon inspecting it that it had rotted (Jeremiah XIII); and of the one to whom he commanded that he cover his bread with human dung, but, because it could not be eaten, afterward commanded that it be covered with cattle dung (Ezekiel IV).

3. “In many ways,” that is, at one time predicting prosperity and at another adversity, at one time showing future things through the words of the prophets and at another through their actions.

[Col. 0375B] 4. AMBROSE, “And in many modes.” The whole purpose of the blessed Apostle in this Epistle is to call the Hebrews to faith in Christ and to distinguish the excellence of the grace given through the Son from the words of the law.

5. LANFRANC, “He spoke to us in the Son,” and so forth. Having commended the Son, he commends the New Testament given through him; and, having humbled the angels, he shows that through them the Old Testament was humbled.

6. AMBROSE, “In the Son.” As if he were saying: “Through the Son,” just as in many places in the Epistles he is found to use prepositions interchangeably.

7. “Heir,” that is, Lord of the whole world. Jacob is no longer merely the Lord’s portion and Israel his allotted share, but, as it is written of him in the Psalm: “Ask of me, and [Col. 0376A] I will give you the nations,” and so forth.

8. “Who, being the radiance.” Everywhere we need religious understanding, but especially when we speak or hear about God. Where speech or thought fails, we ought to glorify God because we have such a God as transcends both understanding and the vision of thought. He rightly calls him the radiance who is the light of the world, light from light, making the Father known to us. Through “radiance” he declared the unity of essence and disclosed two persons in glory and radiance.

9. “The figure of his substance.” This figure gives evidence of equality, and he calls it “figure” where elsewhere he says “form”: “Who, although he was in the form of God.”

10. LANFRANC, “Purification.” He plainly [possibly: he opens, or: before the Father] presents the humanity that he assumed for us.

11. AMBROSE, “Purification.” He descended to the lowliness of the Incarnation, saying: “Making purification of sins through suffering.”

12. “He sits.” He instructs us concerning his resurrection and ascension. By “the right hand” he demonstrated the greatness of honor.

13. LANFRANC, “I today,” that is, in this eternity; nor could the eternity that continues have been expressed better.

14. “I have begotten you today,” and so forth. He is proved to be the Son, for he is the Father himself, because he says what he is: “I will be a Father to him, and he will be a son to me,” and so forth.

[Col. 0377A] 15. “And when he again.” The order is: “and when he introduces,” and so forth. He says “again.”

16. “Introduces the Firstborn,” and so forth. It is again proved that he is more excellent than the angels, for he is worshiped by them; and whoever is worshiped is more excellent than the one who worships. It is also proved that they themselves are inferior, since they minister to him; this is established by the authority of the words: “And to the angels,” and: “Who makes his angels,” and so forth.

17. “And let them worship.” The angels were to be instructed to worship the incarnate Word; they did not need instruction concerning him in his divinity.

18. “Concerning the angels.” The order is: “Who makes his spirits angels, and his ministers a flame of fire.”

19. “Your throne, O God.” He is again proved to be more excellent; for his throne, that is, his seat, and his scepter remain forever, which is not the case with the angels.

[Col. 0377B] 20. AMBROSE, “Your throne.” God’s throne pertains to the future judgment; he says “unto the age of the age” because the final judgment will stand with eternal discernment.

21. “The scepter of the kingdom.” This scepter is unconquered strength, the most upright equity, and inflexible discipline.

22. “You have loved.” The straight scepter consists in loving equity and hating iniquity.

23. “Therefore.” “Christ,” when anointed, signifies both king and priest; but he is said to have been anointed in that nature in which he was born and suffered. In calling him “God,” he displays a proclamation of great love. The oil of gladness is freedom from the stain of sin; hence the conscience rejoices when it is not gnawed by the recollection of any harshness.

[Col. 0377C] 24. “Companions.” He means the sons of human beings.

25. “In the beginning, Lord.” After the excellence of his humanity, he again turns to the eternity of the Son.

26. “They will perish.” They perish with respect to what they are, while they are changed for the better.

27. “Until I place your enemies” [variant: “until”]. [Col. 0378A] By the feet of the Lord eternal stability is signified: as though placed beneath his footprints, he stands by the power of omnipotence. Those who, having abandoned their vices, bow before his preaching are evidently to be placed beneath these feet. “Until” does not here indicate the end of time, but eternity.

28. “Are they not all?” The Son alone saves; these serve the salvation of those predestined. For we read that an angel was sent to Mary; angels also appeared to the shepherds and to the women at the resurrection.

29. LANFRANC, “Ministering spirits.” Having proved that the Son is more excellent, he also proves that the angels are inferior; for they minister both to him and to human beings.

## [COMMENTARY]

[Col. 0378A]

### CHAP. II

1. LANFRANC. “Therefore.” Because God had and has such great concern that he caused his Son to become incarnate for us and daily summons his angels into our service.

2. AMBROSE. “More abundantly.” That is, more than we were accustomed to hear under the Law.

3. LANFRANC. “Lest we drift away.” Lest we be punished more severely because, having set aside what we had recognized, we neglected it. Or, because we have already fallen away in part, lest we fall away completely.

4. “The word spoken.” He means the Law of the Old Testament, which was given to Moses through angels. For God was not speaking through his own substance, but angels spoke in God’s person.

5. “The word spoken was firm.” We ought to keep his word, for it is firm; indeed, the word given through angels was made firm. We ought to keep it, and, if we do not keep it, we shall be punished; for those who did not keep the Law given through angels were punished.

6. AMBROSE. “If we neglect.” By this he indicates that there was not so great a salvation in the Old Testament: that one was temporal, whereas this one is everlasting.

[Col. 0379A]

7. LANFRANC. “Which, having received its beginning.” Someone might ask: Who announced that salvation to us? He answers: “Which, having received its beginning,” and so forth.

8. “To angels.” He continues in the same line of argument, wishing to prove that Christ has a name more excellent than the angels.

9. “The world.” Here he understands “the world” as the totality of every creature in the age to come. Elsewhere Scripture says of this earth: “My portion is in the land of the living.”

10. AMBROSE. “He testified.” Why did he not give the prophet’s name? I think it was not from a desire to conceal it, but to show that they possessed extensive knowledge of the Scriptures.

11. “The son of man.” He visited him when the Word became flesh and dwelt among us (John 1). For one is said to visit when a physician enters among the sick.

12. “Than the angels.” He rightly said “a little lower than the angels,” because although he assumed a mortal body, he nevertheless had no sin.

13. LANFRANC. “But him.” The order is: “But we see Jesus, who was made a little lower than the angels because of the suffering of death, so that by the grace of God he might taste death for all, crowned with glory and honor”; and this is a hyperbaton, that is, an inverted order, a figure he uses frequently in this Epistle.

14. “Of death.” As though someone were to say: Did God the Father hand his Son over to death? “Yes,” he says: “For he who sanctifies,” and so forth.

15. “Of death, glory”—that is, death assumed in such a way that he might taste death for the salvation of human beings. This is joined to the words: “So that by the grace of God he might taste death for all”; otherwise, unless he tasted death for the salvation of all, it would have been empty and ineffective.

16. AMBROSE. “So that by the grace of God.” He calls him “grace” who tasted death for the salvation of all; he truly “tasted” it because he remained in it for a short time. He was crowned with glory in the resurrection, and with honor in the acknowledgment of the Father’s majesty.

17. LANFRANC. “He might taste death for all.” He tasted it because it was fitting. It was fitting for God, and he was able through Christ to complete—that is, to save—us, because Christ and we come from him. This is what follows: “For he who,” and so forth.

18. “It was fitting.” “It was fitting,” he says, for God the Father to perfect Christ, the author of human salvation, through death. Why it was fitting, leaving aside many reasons, he states shortly afterward: “In order through death to destroy the one who held the power of death,” that is, the devil, “and to free,” and so forth.

19. “All from one”—that is, they depend upon the disposition of one Father.

[Col. 0380B]

20. AMBROSE. “All from one.” There is one God from whom all things come; but he is related to us in one way and Christ in another: Christ as the proper Son, and we as adopted children.

21. “His brothers.” In saying “he is not ashamed to call them brothers,” he shows that our brotherhood is not a matter of nature, but of his mercy and great humility.

22. “I will be.” This was said of the man he assumed.

23. “And my children.” He called them children because of their innocence. Of them the Lord says in the Gospel: “Let the little children come to me” (Mark 10).

24. LANFRANC. “Children.” He calls the faithful children, as in the Gospel: “Children, do you have anything to eat?” (John 21). And elsewhere: “Unless you become like this child” (Luke 18). And the Apostle says: “In malice be infants” (1 Corinthians 14).

25. “Since, therefore, the children shared,” and so forth. Since the Father had destined human beings to be honored by him, and since they, destined to be his, were joined together by flesh and blood, it pleased Christ to become human.

26. AMBROSE. “Since, therefore, the children.” So that he might have something from which to taste death for the children’s salvation.

[Col. 0381A]

27. LANFRANC. “And free them.” He freed human beings, as he proves by contrast: not angels. For if he had freed angels, he would have assumed an angelic nature; but nowhere did he assume the nature of angels. Therefore, and so forth.

28. “Through fear of death.” He means the faithful who, through fear of death—whether of body or of soul—observed the Law throughout their whole life. Christ freed them either from hell or from the unbearable yoke of the Law.

29. AMBROSE. “They were subject.” Indeed, all had been slaves of death because they feared death.

30. LANFRANC. “For nowhere.” He proves the preceding point: God became human so that he might be able to die. If he had not determined to die for human salvation, wishing to appear among human beings, he would have assumed not a human being but an angel, in whom he would speak.

[Col. 0381B]

31. AMBROSE. “For nowhere does he take hold of angels.” Since he had said: “Because the children shared in flesh and blood, he himself likewise shared in the same,” therefore, he says, “he nowhere takes hold of angels, but takes hold of the offspring of Abraham.” Why did he say “takes hold”? Because he pursued and took hold of us as though we were withdrawing from him and fleeing far away, and he joined the nature of our weakness to himself in one person.

32. “Therefore he had to.” The only reason he was made like his brothers in every respect was that, as a faithful high priest, he might be merciful toward us and make satisfaction for our sins.

33. LANFRANC. “Merciful.” In truth, no one is called merciful except a human being; “merciful” comes from “a sorrowful heart.” So also blessed Gregory in the Moralia.

[Col. 0381C]

34. “In order to make atonement.” He proves that he can forgive sins, that is, give assistance—through divinity and through the flesh? Through divinity, because he can do so also through the flesh.

35. AMBROSE. “In that in which he suffered.” In that is, in the human being in whom he suffered, he is able to help those who are tempted so that they are not overcome, because, as a human being, he learned our temptations through experience in himself.

[Col. 0382A]

36. LANFRANC. “In that in which he suffered.” He suffered in the flesh and was tempted in the flesh, and in the flesh he is able to assist those who are tempted.

## CHAP. III

[Col. 0381]

[Note: [Col. 0382A] CHAP. III.—1. LANFRANC. “Therefore, holy brothers,” and so forth. Above he showed that Christ is more excellent than the angels; now he shows that he is more excellent also than Moses, so that he may prefer the New Testament to the Old.]

Therefore—because he is powerful to assist— [Note: [Col. 0382A] 2. AMBROSE. “Holy brothers.” He wishes to raise their spirits toward the greatness of God’s promises by calling them beloved brothers, summoned to heavenly things.] holy brothers, sharers in a heavenly calling, consider, recognize, and honor Jesus, the apostle and high priest of our confession of faith, [Note: [Col. 0382A] 3. “Consider the Apostle”—that is, recognize who Jesus is: a priest and perhaps [probably, “faithful”], needing no other consolation.] [Note: [Col. 0382A] 4. “Who is faithful.” He asserts that he is faithful, that is, devoted, defending what belongs to him and not permitting it to be corrupted.] who is faithful to the one who made him, just as Moses was faithful in all his house, that is, among the Jewish people.

[Note: [Col. 0382B] 5. LANFRANC. “For he has been considered worthy of greater glory,” and so forth. He is more worthy, for he possesses greater glory, since he is the Creator, whereas Moses is a creature. Every creator has greater glory than a creature; for the builder of a house is more honored than the house.] For he has been considered worthy of greater glory than Moses, [Note: [Col. 0382B] 6. “The one who built it has greater honor,” and so forth. He proves that they ought to consider, that is, honor, Christ, because he has greater dignity than Moses; and he proves this by analogy and comparison.] to the extent that the builder of a house has greater honor than the one serving in it. For every house is built by someone, but the one who created all things is God. [Note: [Col. 0382B] 7. “And Moses indeed.” He proves that Christ is more worthy than Moses: every son in his father’s house—and in his own house—is more worthy than a servant.]

And Moses indeed was faithful in all his house as a servant, for a testimony to the things that were to be spoken; but Christ was faithful as a Son over his own house. We are that house, [Note: [Col. 0382B] 8. “If we hold fast,” that is, faith and good works, through which we possess hope.] if we hold fast [Note: [Col. 0382B] 9. “If we hold fast our confidence and the glory,” and so forth. Therefore, in order to be his house, we must have faith; consequently, we must not be unbelieving. This is the meaning of “Take care, brothers”; for the sentence may extend that far.] our confidence and the glory of hope firm to the end.

[Note: [Col. 0382C] 10. “Therefore, as the Holy Spirit says,” and so forth. It is as though he were saying: Since the bearer of the New Testament has such great dignity, let us not harden our hearts, but let us submit to his commands.]

Therefore, as the Holy Spirit says:

“Today, if you hear his voice,
do not harden your hearts,
as your fathers hardened theirs in the provocation,
on the day, at the time of testing in the wilderness,
where your fathers tested me,
put me to the proof,
and saw my works as God for forty years.

Therefore, because they tested me, I was angered with that generation, and I said: ‘They are always—that is, continually—wandering in their hearts.’ But they did not know my ways, my commandments. Thus I swore in my anger: ‘If they shall enter’”—an aposiopesis, an interrupted statement—“no one shall enter into my rest.”

Take care, brothers, lest there be in any of you an evil heart of unbelief, leading you to depart from the living God. Rather, exhort one another every day, while it is called “today,” that is, in the present time while opportunity remains, so that none of you may be hardened by the deceit of sin. [Note: [Col. 0383A] 11. “The deceit of sin.” He calls the devil, or unbelief, “sin,” by which—or by whom—unbelievers are deceived so that they do not believe what ought to be believed.]

For we have become sharers in Christ, as members of the head, [Note: [Col. 0383A] 12. AMBROSE. “For we have become sharers in Christ.” That is, we have become one with him, since he is the head and we are the members.] if only we hold firmly to the beginning of his substance—that is, faith— [Note: [Col. 0383A] 13. “If only we hold the beginning.” What is “the beginning of substance”? It signifies faith, through which we subsist and are born from God as children.] [Note: [Col. 0383A] 14. LANFRANC. “The beginning of substance.” He calls faith “substance” because, like a foundation, it supports good works; that is, it lies beneath them.] firm to the end.

When it is said, “Today, in the present time, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts,” just as your fathers hardened theirs in that provocation, the answer is this: Some who heard provoked him, but not all who came out of Egypt through Moses.

With whom was he angry for forty years? Was it not with those who sinned, whose corpses fell in the wilderness? To whom did he swear that they would not enter his rest, or the promised land, except to those who were unbelieving? And we see that they could not enter because of unbelief.

## [COMMENTARY]

[Col. 0382A]

### CHAP. III

1. LANFRANC. “Therefore, holy brothers,” and so forth. Above he showed that Christ is more excellent than the angels; now he shows that he is more excellent also than Moses, so that he may prefer the New Testament to the Old.

2. AMBROSE. “Holy brothers.” He wishes to raise their spirits toward the greatness of God’s promises by calling them beloved brothers, summoned to heavenly things.

3. “Consider the Apostle”—that is, recognize who Jesus is: a priest and perhaps [probably, “faithful”], needing no other consolation.

4. “Who is faithful.” He asserts that he is faithful, that is, devoted, defending what belongs to him and not permitting it to be corrupted.

[Col. 0382B]

5. LANFRANC. “For he has been considered worthy of greater glory,” and so forth. He is more worthy, for he possesses greater glory, since he is the Creator, whereas Moses is a creature. Every creator has greater glory than a creature; for the builder of a house is more honored than the house.

6. “The one who built it has greater honor,” and so forth. He proves that they ought to consider, that is, honor, Christ, because he has greater dignity than Moses; and he proves this by analogy and comparison.

7. “And Moses indeed.” He proves that Christ is more worthy than Moses: every son in his father’s house—and in his own house—is more worthy than a servant.

8. “If we hold fast”—that is, faith and good works, through which we possess hope.

9. “If we hold fast our confidence and the glory,” and so forth. Therefore, in order to be his house, we must have faith; consequently, we must not be unbelieving. This is the meaning of “Take care, brothers”; for the sentence may extend that far.

10. “Therefore, as the Holy Spirit says,” and so forth. It is as though he were saying: Since the bearer of the New Testament has such great dignity, let us not harden our hearts, but let us submit to his commands.

[Col. 0383A]

11. “The deceit of sin.” He calls the devil, or unbelief, “sin,” by which—or by whom—unbelievers are deceived so that they do not believe what ought to be believed.

12. AMBROSE. “For we have become sharers in Christ.” That is, we have become one with him, since he is the head and we are the members.

13. “If only we hold the beginning.” What is “the beginning of substance”? It signifies faith, through which we subsist and are born from God as children.

14. LANFRANC. “The beginning of substance.” He calls faith “substance” because, like a foundation, it supports good works; that is, it lies beneath them.

## [COMMENTARY]

[Col. 0383A]

### CHAP. IV

1. LANFRANC. “And indeed, from the works.” He proves that there are two rests: one earthly, promised to the Jews; the other heavenly, promised to us. This is an answer, as though someone were to say: Why did you say that we enter into rest, when it would not be especially beneficial for us to enter any promised land? “There are two rests,” he says.

2. “And he rested.” This is the rest promised to the saints, namely, the heavenly and ineffable sweetness of God.

3. “Since, therefore, it remains.” Since some, he says, are going to enter the heavenly rest of God, while those to whom it was announced in the wilderness did not enter because they did not believe the word, the faithful of the present time are warned not to harden their hearts against the word of God, as those earlier unbelievers hardened theirs. He calls them unbelievers when he says: “Do not harden your hearts.”

4. “A particular day.” The order is: “After so long a time he fixes a particular day, ‘Today,’ saying through David,” as was said above: “Today, if,” and so forth.

5. LANFRANC. “For if Jesus had given them rest.” This is not Jesus the Savior of the world, but Jesus, also called Joshua, by whom the Jewish people were led into the promised land. If he had given them the true rest, David would never afterward, on this day—that is, today, at the present time—have spoken of another rest.

6. “If he had given them rest.” They entered, that is, he did not give them that rest; for if he had given it to them, he would never have spoken of another. Or the answer is: Jesus son of Nave did not give them the whole rest—“never of another”—the whole rest, that is, both the temporal and the heavenly.

7. “Therefore it remains.” He concludes what was proved above. It is as though he were saying: Therefore we enter into rest.

8. AMBROS. “He himself rested.” God’s rest is to be understood as the perfection of his works; through that rest which is eternal, however, he summons us to the eternal rest which he called “sabbatism,” not “rest,” because he was speaking to Jews. Nor does he wish such a Sabbath in the kingdom of God that someone should afterward return from it to laborious works, as they did on the carnal Sabbath. Whoever enters this Sabbath of God rests perpetually from his works, just as God rested from his.

9. “Let us hasten to enter.” Since faith is not sufficient, but a life worthy of faith must be added—for if those who murmured deserved the land, how shall we, living indifferently like the Gentiles, deserve heaven?

10. LANFR. “Let us therefore hasten to enter,” that is: since that rest is eternal, let us therefore hasten to enter it by faith. Or: since they did not enter it through unbelief, let us therefore enter it through faith.

11. AMBROS. “Into the same unbelief,” that is, lest we fall into similar things, lest we suffer the same things that they suffered.

12. LANFR. “An example.” He calls God’s vengeance an example of unbelief, because it was inflicted so severely that it could serve as an example to others, lest they presume to be unbelieving.

13. AMBROS. “For the word is living.” Here he shows that we have the same judge who condemned them because of their unbelief.

14. LANFR. “For the word is living,” that is, active, acting with vitality and vigor, as though he were answering unbelievers: “Does God know whether I believe or do not believe?” “It is living,” he says—the word of God, that is, Christ, the Word of the Father made man, and so forth.

15. AMBROS. “Of soul and spirit.” By the soul we live; by the spirit we understand. God’s judgment is so effective that it distinguishes between carnal and spiritual things.

16. LANFR. “Of soul and spirit.” The Son distinguishes between soul and spirit, because he himself knows what a person thinks or does for earthly advantages and what he thinks or does for heavenly ones.

17. “Of joints.” He calls “joints” the connections of thoughts, and “marrow” their intentions; then he repeats the same point more clearly by speaking of thoughts and intentions. The order is: “discerner of joints,” and so forth. For if one thought is joined to another, he knows which is according to God and which according to the world; he also knows toward what the thinker’s intention is directed, whether what he does appears good or evil.

18. “To whom we must give an account.” Our account will be given to Christ, because on the day of judgment we shall render him an account of our deeds.

19. AMBROS. “For the likeness.” He therefore possessed the likeness of sin, although his flesh was entirely without sin.

20. LANFR. “For the likeness of sin.” “For the likeness,” that is, according to the likeness—namely, according to the flesh—because he was made in the likeness of human beings. Or “for the likeness,” that is, for the purpose of providing an example to believers, so that they too might be tempted without consenting to sin, while taking care not to be led into temptation. Or it may be understood thus: “for the likeness,” that is, because of the likeness—namely, because of the flesh he bore. For unless he had been like other human beings, the devil would not have dared to tempt him. The order is: “tempted in every respect without sin.”

21. “In help.” God’s help is always timely, because it comes to our aid in necessities, as in the Psalm: “A helper in timely afflictions” (Psalm 9).

[COMMENTARY.]

[Col. 0386B]

CAP. V.—1. LANFR. “For every high priest.” As though he were saying: We must not doubt that through this high priest we shall obtain mercy and grace, because other high priests also, who are mere human beings, were appointed for human beings to obtain these things.

2. AMBROS. “For every high priest.” Here the Apostle sets forth certain things Christ shares with the priests and certain things that are higher. This is shared by them: he is appointed for all, in order to offer for sins.

3. “You are a priest.” Christ is called a priest, because he offered himself once to be sacrificed, just as Sacred Scripture speaks once of Melchisedech.

4. LANFR. “Melchisedech.” Melchisedech instituted the sacrifice of bread and wine to God; the Lord Jesus Christ observed this rite and commanded that it be observed in his Church.

5. AMBROS. “Supplications.” He says that Christ poured out prayers and supplications not from fear, but for the sake of our salvation. Hence elsewhere he says that Christ’s blood cried out for us more effectively than Abel’s blood: Abel’s blood cried from the earth to accuse his brother’s crime, whereas Christ’s blood cries from the earth to the Father to intercede for us.

6. LANFR. “To save him from death.” Not so that he might not die, but so that, having risen, he might not be held by death.

7. “And indeed, although he was.” He explains that reverence. For it was a great act of devotion for one who was equal to the Father to undergo the harsh obedience of death in his passion [probably: “to undergo death through obedience”].

8. AMBROS. “He learned from these things.” That the Son of God learned obedience means that he willingly undertook it.

9. “And he was made perfect,” that is, perfect and sufficient for the eternal salvation of all believers.

10. LANFR. “And he was made perfect.” Although to others he appeared a deceiver, to those who obeyed him for the sake of eternal salvation he appeared perfect—that is, complete. It can also be punctuated so that “cause” is nominative, as follows: “And, having been made perfect”—that is, complete, or having died to this world—“he became the cause of eternal salvation for all who obey him.” Believers are saved through faith in his passion and resurrection.

11. “According to the order.” According to the rite of offering bread and wine, which Melchisedech is said to have performed first; these are nevertheless changed into Christ’s flesh and blood.

12. “Concerning whom the word is great.” If, he says, we wished to explain to you why Christ was made high priest according to the order of Melchisedech, our discourse would be great, necessary [probably: “necessitating explanation”], and interpretable—that is, containing many explanations of mysteries and allegories.

13. “You have become weak in hearing,” that is, in understanding, as in the Letter to the Corinthians: “No one hears,” that is, understands.

14. “Of the beginnings of the words of God.” He calls the beginning of God’s words the Symbol of the Christian faith. They not only did not understand it, but did not even know by heart the very writing in which it was set forth [probably: “was uttered”].

15. “Need milk.” Milk is a brief exposition and easy observance of moral conduct. Solid food is the reasoning of faith itself and the perfect formation of life. He intends to prove that they need milk, for everyone who is inexperienced in the word of righteousness partakes of milk. This proof is developed in the book. “But you are inexperienced in the word,” [Col. 0388A] that is, after establishing the first proposition, he adds the proof either from the cause or from the class, when he says: “For he is a little one.” But when he says: “Solid food belongs to the mature,” this proves that they do not need customary food.

For God is not unjust, so as to forget your work and the love that you showed in his name, when you ministered to the saints and continue to minister. But we desire each of you to display the same diligence for the fulfillment of hope to the end, so that you may not become sluggish, but imitators of those who through faith and patience will inherit the promises.

For when God made a promise to Abraham, since he had no one greater by whom he could swear, he swore by himself, saying: “Surely, blessing I will bless you, and multiplying I will multiply you.” And thus, after patiently enduring, he obtained the promise.

For human beings swear by one greater than themselves;

[Note: [Col. 0389B] 13. “And the end of every dispute.” If the oath of human beings is to be believed, how much more the oath of God, who can neither be deceived nor lie?]

and the end of every dispute among them, for confirmation, is an oath.

In this matter, wishing to show more abundantly to the heirs of the promise the unchangeability of his purpose, God interposed an oath,

[Note: [Col. 0389B] 14. LANFR. “By two unchangeable things.” The oath and his own person, through which what is said may be unchangeable.]

so that through two unchangeable things, in which it is impossible for God to lie, we might have the strongest consolation—we who have fled for refuge to hold fast the hope set before us.

[Note: [Col. 0389B] 15. AMBROS. “We have as an anchor.” Just as an anchor [Col. 0389C] does not allow a ship to be carried about, even though winds stir it, so hope strengthened by faith brings us into the reality of the things that we hold by faith and hope. Therefore he added: “Reaching as far as the inner part of the veil.” For hope penetrates the inner part of the veil when it believes heavenly things without hesitation.]

We have this hope as a sure and firm anchor of the soul, reaching

[Note: [Col. 0390A] 16. LANFR. “As far as the inner part.” Our hope reaches to the presence of God, which the inner part of the veil signified.]

as far as the inner part of the veil,

[Note: [Col. 0390A] 17. AMBROS. “Where the forerunner entered for us.” He did not simply say “entered,” but “where the forerunner entered for us”; we ought to follow our forerunner. For it is fitting that the forerunner and those who follow should be in the same place.]

where Jesus, our forerunner, entered for us, having become high priest forever according to the order of Melchisedech.

[COMMENTARY.]

[Col. 0388A]

CAP. VI.—1. AMBROS. “Therefore, leaving off.” Since you ought to have faculties trained in the Lord’s law, let us leave off the discourse of Christ’s beginning. The discourse of Christ’s beginning is the beginning of faith. Just as someone being introduced into literary instruction must first hear the elementary principles, so a Christian must first of all be instructed in the Catholic faith. But if he still needs to be taught about faith [probably: “to be instructed”], he does not yet possess the foundation. For if he needs to hear again that he must believe in the resurrection and the future age, he does not yet possess the foundation.

[Col. 0388B] 2. “Toward perfection.” We call someone perfect who possesses a morally upright life together with faith. If either of these is lacking, he will not be perfect; if both are present, he is rightly called perfect [printed: “a little one”].

3. LANFR. “Foundation.” Whenever a teacher converts unbelievers to the faith, he first lays a foundation in their minds, saying that they must repent of their sins, believe in God, be baptized for the remission of sins, be completed through the laying on of the bishop’s hands for the reception of the gifts of the Holy Spirit, and await the day of resurrection and judgment.

4. AMBROS. “Of baptisms.” Just as there is one faith, so there is one baptism; but because of the variety of those receiving baptism, he used the plural “baptisms.” And lest anyone should in any way think that a second baptism could take place after sin, he adds: “It is impossible for those who were once enlightened through the grace of the Holy Spirit, who also tasted the heavenly gift” (that is, the remission of sins), “and became sharers in the Holy Spirit” (in the distribution of gifts), “and tasted the good word of God” (this is evangelical teaching), “and experienced the powers of the age to come” (that is, the resurrection and the blessed life promised to the saints), if they fall into sins, to be renewed again. The power of this baptism rests on Christ’s cross and burial; therefore he adds: “For just as Christ died once in the flesh on the cross, so we die once in baptism—not in the flesh, but to sin.”

5. LANFR. “And of judgment,” because whatever sort of people they emerge from judgment, such they will remain without end.

[Col. 0389A] “Impossible.” He gives the reason why it is not expedient to abandon the first faith and fall into sins: those who return cannot thereafter be baptized again for the remission of sins, as before.

6. “The word of God,” that is, the Father’s Word, who is tasted in the reception of his body and blood.

7. “Crucifying.” They crucify the Son of God within themselves, and hold him up to public disgrace—that is, to insult—those who, despising his grace, lie in sins.

8. AMBROS. “For earth often.” Here he declares that those to whom his discourse was addressed received and absorbed the word of heavenly teaching.

9. “And producing grass.” Nothing is so seasonable as faith in the Son of God and an excellent life.

10. “But producing.” Concerning these thorns the Lord says that the cares of this age and the deceitfulness of riches choke the word, and it becomes fruitless.

11. “Near to a curse.” What consolation this statement contains: it is near a curse, not yet cursed. For what has not yet fallen under the curse is near to it, but can be taken far away from it.

12. “Whose end is for burning.” This burning will not occur unless someone remains in sins to the end.

13. “And the end of every dispute.” If the oath of human beings is to be believed, how much more the oath of God, who can neither be deceived nor lie?

14. LANFR. “By two unchangeable things.” The oath and his own person, through which what is said may be unchangeable.

15. AMBROS. “We have as an anchor.” Just as an anchor [Col. 0389C] does not allow a ship to be carried about, even though winds stir it, so hope strengthened by faith brings us [Col. 0390A] into the reality of the things that we hold by faith and hope. Therefore he added: “Reaching as far as the inner part of the veil.” For hope penetrates the inner part of the veil when it believes heavenly things without hesitation.

16. LANFR. “As far as the inner part.” Our hope reaches to the presence of God, which the inner part of the veil signified.

17. AMBROS. “Where the forerunner entered for us.” He did not simply say “entered,” but “where the forerunner entered for us”; we ought to follow our forerunner. For it is fitting that the forerunner and those who follow should be in the same place.

CHAPTER VII.

[Col. 0389]

[Note: [Col. 0390A] CAP. VII.—1. LANFR. “For this Melchisedech.” The reason why Christ was made high priest according to the order of Melchisedech and not according to the Levitical order is that Melchisedech is of greater dignity. [ [Col. 0389] This does not seem to cohere with what precedes.] “For if we are rejected, we shall be near a curse”; and he proves this by similarity: if what produces thistles is near a curse, he also proves this by contrast, for what produces grass is near a blessing.]

For this Melchisedech, king of Salem, priest of the Most High God, who met Abraham returning from the slaughter of the kings and blessed him, to whom Abraham also apportioned a tenth of everything—first, by interpretation, “king of righteousness,” and then also “king of Salem,” which means “king of peace,”

[Note: [Col. 0390B] 2. “Without father.” He was not truly without father and mother, nor did he truly lack a beginning and end of days; rather, Scripture does not mention where or when he was born, or at what time he died. without father, without mother, without genealogy, having neither beginning of days nor end of life, but made like the Son of God,

[Note: [Col. 0390B] 3. “He remains a priest.” Melchisedech did not remain forever [Col. 0390C], but his priestly institution remains forever.]

he remains a priest forever.

[Col. 0391] Consider how great this man is, to whom even Abraham the patriarch gave a tenth from the chief spoils.

And indeed,

[Note: [Col. 0391A] 4. “From the sons of Levi.” This is raised as an objection to the preceding statement. those who receive the priesthood from the sons of Levi have a commandment, according to the law, to take tithes from the people—that is, from their brothers—although they too have come forth from the loins of Abraham. But the one whose genealogy is not reckoned among them took tithes from Abraham and blessed him who possessed the promises.

[Note: [Col. 0391A] 5. “But without any contradiction.” The answer is: I know that this is so. But Melchisedech not only received tithes; he also blessed Abraham. Therefore, without any contradiction, he is greater than Abraham, because the lesser is always blessed by the better.]

But without any contradiction, the lesser is blessed by the better.

And here, indeed,

[Note: [Col. 0391A] 6. “Receiving tithes from mortal men.” As though he were saying: By this we cannot prove that Melchisedech was immortal—that is, that he signified the immortal one—because Abraham received tithes from him; for here too, that is, in the law and Levitical priesthood, mortal men receive tithes. But there, namely where Scripture mentions him without father and mother and without beginning and end of days, Scripture itself openly testifies that he lives—that is, that he signifies one who lives and is immortal.]

mortal men receive tithes; but there he is testified to be living.

And, so to speak, through Abraham even Levi, who received tithes, was tithed; for he was still in the loins of his father when Melchisedech met him.

[Note: [Col. 0391B] 7. “If therefore perfection.” If, he says, the law was perfected—that is, complete, not to be changed, and destined to remain until the end of the age—when the Levitical priesthood was established, why does he substitute another priesthood? Since both were given at the same time, by the same giver, and under the same promise, what is said of one must necessarily be understood of the other. The whole argument proceeds as follows: If the law was to remain, and the priesthood also, but the priesthood is transferred, the law too must necessarily be transferred.]

If therefore perfection had been through the Levitical priesthood—for under it the people received the law—what further need was there for another priest to arise according to the order of Melchisedech, and not to be called according to the order of Aaron?

[Note: [Col. 0391C] 8. AMBROS. “If therefore perfection.” If the Levitical priesthood was perfection—that is, a perfect priesthood—what need was there for another priest to arise? Therefore, if there must be a transfer of the priesthood, there must also be a transfer of the law; nor can a priest exist without a covenant.]

For when the priesthood is transferred, a transfer of the law must also take place. For the one concerning whom these things are said belonged to another tribe, from which no one served at the altar. For it is evident that our Lord arose from Judah, a tribe concerning which Moses said nothing about priests.

And it is even more evident if another priest arises according to the likeness of Melchisedech, who was not

[Note: [Col. 0391C] 9. LANFR. “According to the law.” Christ was not made priest according to the law of the Jews, which commanded carnal observances, because he is not from the tribe of Levi, from which the law itself commanded priests to be chosen, but according to what pleased the power of his divinity, in which and from which there is indissoluble life—that is, eternal life—which is not dissolved by the intervention of death. Alternatively: he was not made priest in order to observe, or command the observance of, the carnal precepts of the law in sacrifices, but of the spiritual understanding, which is the power through which indissoluble life is given; for “the letter kills, but the spirit gives life.”]

made according to the law of a carnal commandment, but

[Note: [Col. 0392A] 10. AMBROS. “According to the power,” that is, possessing indissoluble life in himself. Although he died in the flesh for a time, he nevertheless lives eternally in his divinity.]

according to the power of indissoluble life.

[Note: [Col. 0392B] 11. LANFR. “He testifies.” He proves by divine authority that another priest has arisen according to the likeness of Melchisedech.]

For he testifies: “You are a priest forever

[Note: [Col. 0392B] 12. AMBROS. “According to the order of Melchisedech.” He interprets his order in many ways: he alone was both king and priest, and he exercised the priesthood before circumcision, so that it was not a nation from the Jews that received the priesthood, but the Jews from the nations.]

according to the order of Melchisedech.”

There is indeed a setting aside of the preceding commandment because of

[Note: [Col. 0392B] 13. LANFR. “Weakness.” The old law was weak because it could not give its practitioners perfect righteousness. For if its practitioners had been perfectly righteous, after death they would have immediately ascended to heaven to possess rest. Through its observance there was some justification and some remission of sins, but not complete remission.]

its weakness and

[Note: [Col. 0392C] 14. “Uselessness.” After Christ’s coming, it was useless to observe those things that were performed in order to foretell that the things now occurring would come to pass.]

uselessness, for the law brought nothing to perfection;

[Note: [Col. 0392C] 15. AMBROS. “Introduction.” It did possess a kind of hope, but not such a hope. Those who pleased God and kept his law hoped to possess the land and to suffer nothing grievous; those who keep the evangelical commandments, however, hope to possess not the land but heaven.]

but there is the introduction of a better hope, through which we draw near to God.

And inasmuch as this was not without an oath—for others indeed became priests without an oath, but he with an oath, through the one who said to him, “The Lord has sworn and will not repent: You are

[Col. 0393]

a priest forever”—

[Note: [Col. 0393A] 16. “To that extent better.” In accordance with what was sworn concerning him, that he would always remain.]

[Note: [Col. 0393A] 17. LANFR. “To that extent.” To the extent that I said above that eternal life is promised, and that this was not without an oath.]

to that extent

[Note: [Col. 0393A] 18. “Better,” that is, of the New Testament, through whose observance we have hope of going to God.]

[Note: [Col. 0393A] 19. “Guarantor.” The ancient priests promised the practitioners of the law an abundance of crops, long life, victory over enemies, and other things of this kind. Jesus, however, guarantees the hope through which we draw near to God—that is, eternal life, in which we shall see God face to face. Alternatively, he is the guarantor of the New Testament according to his divinity, because everything the Father does, he also does.]

he has become the guarantor of a better covenant—Jesus.

And the others indeed became priests in greater number because death prevented them from continuing; but he, because he remains forever, possesses an eternal priesthood.

[Note: [Col. 0393B] 20. AMBROS. “Hence also to save.” Who is the one who intercedes, except the union of human nature with divinity, which he brought to the Father’s throne, always … [lacuna] … capable of saving? Because the other high priests did not exist forever, they did not intercede forever; but he not only saves in this life through the intercession of his humanity, he also glorifies in the future, when he will hand over the kingdom to God and the Father and lead the saints to the vision of the Father’s majesty.]

Hence he is also able to save forever those who approach God through him,

[Note: [Col. 0393B] 21. LANFR. “Through himself.” The Savior himself says in the Gospel: “No one comes to the Father except through me” (John 14). And elsewhere: “I am the door; if anyone enters through me, he will be saved” (John 10).]

since he always lives to intercede for us.

For such a high priest was fitting for us: holy, innocent, undefiled, separated from sinners, and

[Note: [Col. 0393B] 22. AMBROS. “Made higher.” Because all the angels of God worship him.]

made higher than the heavens.

He has no need, like the priests, to offer sacrifices daily, first for his own sins and then for those of the people; for he did this once for all when he offered himself.

[Note: [Col. 0393C] 23. LANFR. “For the law.” The reason why priests need to sacrifice daily for their sins, whereas Christ does not.]

For the law appoints as priests human beings who possess weakness, but the word of the oath, which came after the law, appoints the Son, perfected forever.

[COMMENTARY.]

[Col. 0390A]

CAP. VII.—1. LANFR. “For this Melchisedech.” The reason why Christ was made high priest according to the order of Melchisedech and not according to the Levitical order is that Melchisedech is of greater dignity. [Note: [Col. 0389] This does not seem to cohere with what precedes.] “For if we are rejected, we shall be near a curse”; and he proves this by similarity: if what produces thistles is near a curse, he also proves this by contrast, for what produces grass is near a blessing.

### 2. Without father

He was not truly without father and mother; nor did he truly lack a beginning and an end of days. Rather, Scripture does not mention from whom or when he arose, or at what time he died. For he signified the one who truly would have neither father according to his humanity, nor mother, nor beginning or end according to his divinity.

### 3. He remains a priest

Melchizedek did not remain forever, but his priestly appointment remains forever.

[Col. 0391A]

### 4. From the sons of Levi

This is raised as an objection to the preceding statement. As though someone were saying: “You cannot prove from the fact that Melchizedek received tithes from Abraham that he was superior to Abraham, because priests from the tribe of Levi receive tithes from the other tribes according to the Law—namely, brothers from brothers, and equals from equals.”

### 5. But without any contradiction

The response is: “I know that this is so. But Melchizedek not only received tithes; he also blessed Abraham. Therefore, without any contradiction, he is greater than Abraham, because the lesser is always blessed by the better.”

### 6. Those who die pay tithes

As though he were saying: “By this we cannot prove that Melchizedek was immortal—that is, that he signified the immortal one—because he received tithes from Abraham; for here too, that is, under the Law and the Levitical priesthood, mortal men receive tithes. But there, that is, where Scripture records him without father and mother, without beginning and end of days, Scripture itself openly bears witness that he lives—that is, that he signifies the living and immortal one.”

### 7. If therefore perfection

“If,” he says, “the Law was perfect—that is, complete—not to be changed but destined to remain until the end of the age, and it was given during the period when the Levitical priesthood was established, why does it introduce another priesthood? Since both were given at the same time, by the same person, and under the same promise, what is said of one must necessarily be understood of the other. The whole argument proceeds as follows: if the Law was destined to remain, so was the priesthood; but if the priesthood is transferred, the Law must necessarily also be transferred.”

### 8. AMBROSE. If therefore perfection

“If the Levitical priesthood was perfection—that is, perfect—what need was there for another priest to arise? If, therefore, the priesthood must be transferred, the Law must also be transferred; nor can a priest exist without a testament.”

### 9. According to the Law

Christ was not made priest according to the law of the Jews, which prescribed carnal observances, because he was not of the tribe of Levi, from which the Law itself commanded that priests be chosen. Rather, he was made priest according to what pleased the power of his divinity, in which and from which there is indissoluble life—that is, eternal life, which is not dissolved when death intervenes.

Alternatively: he was not made priest so that he might observe, or command others to observe, the carnal precepts of the Law in sacrifices, but its spiritual meaning, which is the power through which indissoluble life is given. For “the letter kills, but the spirit gives life.”

### 10. AMBROSE. According to the power

That is, having within himself indissoluble life. Although for a time he died in the flesh, nevertheless he lives eternally in his divinity.

[Col. 0392B]

### 11. He bears witness

He proves by divine authority that, according to the likeness of Melchizedek, another priest has arisen.

### 12. According to the order of Melchizedek

He interprets his order in many ways: namely, that he alone was both king and priest, and that he exercised the priesthood before circumcision, so that it was not a nation from the Jews, but Jews from the nations, who received the priesthood.

### 13. Weakness

The old Law was weak because it could not give its worshipers perfect righteousness. For if its worshipers had been perfectly righteous, they would have ascended to heaven immediately after death and obtained rest. Yet through its observance there was some justification and some remission of sins, though not complete.

[Col. 0392C]

### 14. Useless

After Christ’s coming, it was useless to observe those things that were performed in order to predict that the things now taking place would come.

### 15. AMBROSE. Introduction

It did indeed possess hope, but not such hope. Those who pleased God and kept his Law hoped to possess the land and to suffer nothing burdensome. But those who keep the evangelical commandments hope to possess not the land, but heaven.

[Col. 0393A]

### 16. So much better

According to what was sworn concerning him: that he would remain forever.

### 17. LANFRANC. So much

To the extent that I said above that eternal life is promised, and not without an oath.

### 18. Better

That is, of the New Testament, through whose observance we have the hope of going to God.

### 19. Guarantor

The ancient priests promised those who worshiped according to the Law an abundance of crops, long life, victory over enemies, and other things of this kind. Jesus, however, guarantees the hope by which we draw near to God—that is, eternal life, in which we shall see God face to face.

Or he is the guarantor of the New Testament according to his divinity, because everything that the Father does, he also does.

[Col. 0393B]

### 20. AMBROSE. Hence also to save

Who is it that intercedes, except the union of human nature with divinity, which he has brought to the Father’s throne, always … [lacuna] … able to save? Other high priests, because they did not exist forever, did not intercede forever. He, however, not only saves in this life through the intercession of his humanity, but also glorifies in the future, when he will hand over the kingdom to God and the Father and lead the saints to the vision of the Father’s majesty.

### 21. LANFRANC. Through himself

The Savior himself says in the Gospel: “No one comes to the Father except through me” (John 14). And elsewhere: “I am the door; if anyone enters through me, he will be saved” (John 10).

### 22. AMBROSE. Made higher

Because all the angels of God worship him.

[Col. 0393C]

### 23. LANFRANC. For the Law

The reason why priests must sacrifice daily for their own sins, whereas Christ does not.

## CHAPTER VIII

[Col. 0393]

[Note: 1. AMBROSE. Now the summary. A recapitulation of the preceding arrangement, bringing the listener to the subject itself.]

[Note: 2. LANFRANC. Now the summary. A summary is a brief statement, so named because it briefly contains the substance of the whole argument. This summary begins with what follows: “We have such a one,” and ends where it says: “not man.”]

Now the summary of what is being said is this: “We have such a high priest, who has taken his seat at the right hand of the throne of Majesty in the heavens, a minister of the holy places and of the true tabernacle which the Lord established, and not man.” For every high priest is appointed to offer gifts and sacrifices.

[Note: 3. High priest. He returns to the preceding statement: “For he did this once, offering himself.” As though he were saying: It was reasonable that he offered himself, because every high priest is appointed to offer, and so forth.]

Therefore it is necessary that this one too should have something to offer.

[Note: 4. If therefore he were on earth. The reason why Christ offered himself: “If,” he says, “there were on earth something that could worthily be offered for the sins of the whole world, he would not be a priest worthy to offer; and therefore the pure one offered himself well for the world.”]

If therefore he were on earth, he would not be a priest, since there are those who offer gifts according to the Law, who serve a copy and shadow of the heavenly things.

[Note: 5. Heavenly things. He calls the present Church of Christ “heavenly,” because part of it is in heaven while another part, still journeying, remains on earth. Everything that took place in the sacraments of the Old Testament prefigured this. As it is said elsewhere: “All these things happened to them in a figure.”]

As Moses was divinely instructed when he was completing the tabernacle: “See,” he says, “that you make everything according to the pattern shown to you on the mountain.”

[Note: 6. Pattern. A pattern is called both the thing that is made and that according to whose likeness something is made, such as a form, image, figure, or likeness.]

But now he has obtained a more excellent ministry, just as he is also the mediator of a better testament, which was established upon better promises.

[Note: 7. Better. He calls the evangelical commandments a “better testament,” through whose observance true righteousness and eternal life are promised. This is what follows: “which was established upon better promises,” and so forth.]

For if that first testament had been faultless, no place would have been sought for a second.

[Note: 8. For finding fault. He proves by prophetic authority that a place is being sought for a second testament. How full these epistles are of subtle arguments and carefully arranged discussions, although the Apostle himself did not attend to this in writing—for elsewhere he declares that he does not speak in the wisdom of words and subtlety of discourse—a perceptive reader will be able to discover. The substance of the argument is this: If the first testament had been faultless, no place would have been sought for a second; but “finding fault,” and so forth. Therefore the first testament was not faultless, that is, it could not completely free a person from guilt, just as, conversely, the New Testament is called “the commandment without blemish” and “the Law of the Lord, without fault.”]

For finding fault with them, he says: “Behold, days are coming, says the Lord, and I will complete a new testament over the house of Israel and over the house of Judah—not according to the testament that I made with their fathers on the day when I took them by the hand to lead them out of the land of Egypt; because they did not remain in my testament, and I disregarded them, says the Lord. For this is the testament that I will establish with the house of Israel after those days, says the Lord: giving my laws into their mind, and I will write them upon their heart; and I will be their God, and they shall be my people. And no one shall teach his neighbor, nor each one his brother, saying, ‘Know the Lord,’ because all shall know me, from the least to the greatest of them; for I will be merciful toward their iniquities, and I will remember their sins no more.”

[Note: 9. By saying “new.” The New and the Old stand to one another as the great and the small. Whenever two things are compared with one another, if one is called new, the other is old, and conversely.]

By saying “new,” he made the first old. And what becomes old and grows aged is near destruction.

[COMMENTARY.]

[Col. 0393C]

## CHAPTER IX

[Col. 0395]

The first covenant did indeed have ordinances of worship and an earthly sanctuary.

[Note: 1. LANFRANC. Earthly. He calls the sacrifice of the Jews earthly either because it was transitory, like everything belonging to this age, or because the same things were repeated each year according to the cycle of time.]

For a tabernacle was prepared first, in which were the lampstands, the table, and the presentation of the loaves, which is called the Holy Place. Behind the second veil was the tabernacle called the Holy of Holies, having a golden censer and the ark of the covenant covered on every side with gold.
