In it was a golden urn containing manna, and Aaron’s staff that had blossomed, and the tablets of the covenant. Above it were the cherubim of glory overshadowing the mercy seat. Concerning these things we cannot now speak in detail.

When these things had been arranged in this way, the priests were continually entering the first tabernacle, completing the services of the sacrifices; but into the second tabernacle the high priest entered alone once a year, not without blood, which he offered for his own ignorance and that of the people. By this the Holy Spirit signified that the way into the Holy Places had not yet been disclosed, while the first tabernacle still had its standing.

[Note: 2. The way of the Holy Places. The way of the Holy Places is either Christ himself or the spiritual understanding of the Law.]

[Note: 3. First. The first tabernacle is the carnal understanding and observance of the Law; the second is the spiritual understanding.]

This is an allegory of the present time.

[Note: 4. It is an allegory. It signifies the allegory of the Old Testament, namely, the present time in which the Church of Christ is founded and the grace of the New Testament is proclaimed.]

Accordingly, gifts and sacrifices are offered that cannot perfect the worshiper according to his conscience, serving only in foods and drinks and various baptisms and carnal ordinances imposed until the time of correction.

[Note: 5. Conscience. He says “according to conscience” either because the legal sacrifices did not cleanse sins of thought, or because they could not completely wipe from the soul the consciousness of committed wrongdoing.]

But Christ, appearing as high priest of the good things to come, entered through the greater and more perfect tabernacle, not made by hands—that is, not of this creation—and not through the blood of goats or calves, but through his own blood, once for all into the Holy Places, having obtained eternal redemption.

[Note: 6. Tabernacle. He calls the tabernacle into which Christ entered heaven, which is much greater and more perfect than the Jewish tabernacle that they called the Holy of Holies.]

[Note: 7. Into the Holy Places. He explains what he earlier called the tabernacle “not made by hands,” namely, the heavenly Holy of Holies.]

For if the blood of goats and bulls and the ashes of a heifer, sprinkled upon the defiled, sanctify for the purification of the flesh, how much more will the blood of Christ, who through the Holy Spirit offered himself unblemished to God, cleanse our conscience from dead works to serve the living God?

[Note: 8. AMBROSE. From dead works. If someone touched a dead body, he was polluted; likewise, if someone touches a dead work, he is defiled in his conscience.]

And therefore he is the mediator of the New Testament.

[Note: 9. LANFRANC. He is the mediator. Insofar as he is human, he was the mediator of the New Testament, because he brought God’s Law to human beings.]

So that, with death having intervened, those who have been called may receive the promise of the eternal inheritance through the redemption of the transgressions committed under the first covenant.

[Note: 10. With death having intervened. Christ died not only to redeem the Gentiles but also the Jews—both the living and the dead—who had been predestined to eternal life, from the transgressions they had committed under the old Law.]

For where there is a testament, the death of the testator must necessarily intervene. For a testament is confirmed over the dead; otherwise it is not yet valid while the one who made the testament is alive.

[Note: 11. For where there is a testament. He explains why Christ died: namely, because he was going to establish a testament. A testament, however, is not established except by one who is dying.]

Therefore not even the first covenant was inaugurated without blood. For when every commandment of the Law had been read by Moses to all the people, he took the blood of calves and goats with water, scarlet wool, and hyssop, and sprinkled both the book itself and all the people, saying: “This is the blood of the testament that God has commanded for you.” Likewise he sprinkled the tabernacle and all the vessels of the ministry with blood. And nearly everything, according to the Law, is cleansed with blood; and without the shedding of blood there is no remission.

It is therefore necessary that the copies of the heavenly things be cleansed by these means, but that the heavenly things themselves be cleansed by better sacrifices than these.

[Col. 0397]

[Note: 13. For not. He explains the better sacrifices themselves, of which there is one, namely, the body of Christ.

The proper order of the expression would be: “in the holy things made by hands, copies of the true things,” or “in the holy thing made by hands, the copies of the true things.” The reading is uncertain: *visus* [perhaps *usus*].]

For Christ did not enter into holy places made by hands, copies of the true things, but into heaven itself, now to appear before the face of God on our behalf; nor did he enter in order to offer himself often, as the high priest enters the Holy Places every year with another’s blood. Otherwise he would have had to suffer often from the foundation of the world.

But now, once at the consummation of the ages, he has appeared for the destruction of sin through his sacrifice.

[Note: 14. Of sin. He says “of sin” in place of “of sins.” For he destroyed all sins in those who were destined to believe.]

And just as it is appointed for human beings to die once, and after this comes judgment, so Christ also was offered once to exhaust the sins of many.

[Note: 15. AMBROSE. He will appear a second time. For then he was not a sacrifice for sin.]

He will appear a second time without sin to those who await him for salvation.

[Note: 16. LANFRANC. Without sin. He says “without sin,” meaning without the likeness of sinful flesh. At his first coming the Lord bore such flesh as the other human beings, who were sinners, also bore; but at his second coming his flesh will appear in such glory as no mortal can either conceive or explain. It may also be understood as “without sin,” that is, without a sacrifice for sin; for then he will not appear to cleanse sins, but to condemn them.]

[COMMENTARY.]

[Col. 0395A]

## CHAPTER IX

#### 1. LANFRANC. Earthly

He calls the sacrifice of the Jews earthly either because it was transitory, like everything belonging to this age, or because the same things were repeated each year according to the cycle of time.

#### 2. The way of the Holy Places

The way of the Holy Places is either Christ himself or the spiritual understanding of the Law.

#### 3. First

The first tabernacle is the carnal understanding and observance of the Law; the second is the spiritual understanding.

#### 4. It is an allegory

It signifies the allegory of the Old Testament, namely, the present time in which the Church of Christ is founded and the grace of the New Testament is proclaimed.

[Col. 0395B]

#### 5. Conscience

He says “according to conscience” either because the legal sacrifices did not cleanse sins of thought, or because they could not completely wipe from the soul the consciousness of committed wrongdoing.

#### 6. Tabernacle

He calls the tabernacle into which Christ entered heaven, which is much greater and more perfect than the Jewish tabernacle that they called the Holy of Holies.

[Col. 0396A]

#### 7. Into the Holy Places

He explains what he earlier called the tabernacle “not made by hands,” namely, the heavenly Holy of Holies.

#### 8. AMBROSE. From dead works

If someone touched a dead body, he was polluted; likewise, if someone touches a dead work, he is defiled in his conscience.

#### 9. LANFRANC. He is the mediator

Insofar as he is human, he was the mediator of the New Testament, because he brought God’s Law to human beings.

#### 10. With death having intervened

Christ died not only to redeem the Gentiles but also the Jews—both the living and the dead—who had been predestined to eternal life, from the transgressions they had committed under the old Law.

[Col. 0396B]

#### 11. For where there is a testament

He explains why Christ died: namely, because he was going to establish a testament. A testament, however, is not established except by one who is dying.

#### 12. Over the dead

He speaks according to the legal customs of the age, in which it is prescribed that, while the testator is alive, a testament is not valid. A testament—the term being transferred by analogy to the divine testaments—is an ordinance of a person prescribing what is to be done with his possessions after his death.

[Col. 0397A]

#### 13. For not

He explains the better sacrifices themselves, of which there is one, namely, the body of Christ.

The proper order of the expression would be: “in the holy things made by hands, copies of the true things,” or “in the holy thing made by hands, the copies of the true things.” The reading is uncertain: *visus* [perhaps *usus*].

#### 14. Of sin

He says “of sin” in place of “of sins.” For he destroyed all sins in those who were destined to believe.

#### 15. AMBROSE. He will appear a second time

For then he was not a sacrifice for sin.

#### 16. LANFRANC. Without sin

He says “without sin,” meaning without the likeness of sinful flesh. At his first coming the Lord bore such flesh as the other human beings, who were sinners, also bore; but at his second coming his flesh will appear in such glory as no mortal can either conceive or explain. It may also be understood as “without sin,” that is, without a sacrifice for sin; for then he will not appear to cleanse sins, but to condemn them.

## CHAPTER X

[Col. 0397]

[Note: 1. LANFRANC. For the Law, having a shadow. He returns to the preceding argument, where he said that the legal sacrifices could not perfect the worshiper according to his conscience. The response is as though he were saying: Why did you say that sins were to be exhausted through Christ and not through the Law?]

For the Law, possessing a shadow of the good things to come, not the very image of the things,

[Note: 2. AMBROSE. Not the very image. That is, not the very truth.]

with the same sacrifices offered continually year after year, can never perfect those who draw near.

[Note: 3. With the same sacrifices. What, then, of us? Do we not offer every day? We do offer, but for the reconciliation wrought by his death; and this is one sacrifice, not many. What we do is a copy of that sacrifice; it is performed in remembrance of what was done: “Do this,” he says, “in remembrance of me” (Luke 22).]

Otherwise, would they not have ceased to be offered, because those who had once been cleansed would no longer have any consciousness of sin? But in those sacrifices there is a commemoration of sins every year. For it is impossible for the blood of bulls and goats to take away sins.

Therefore, when he came into the world, he said: “You did not desire sacrifice and offering, but you prepared a body for me. You took no pleasure in burnt offerings for sin. Then I said: ‘Behold, I come.’”

[Note: 4. At the beginning of the book. Certainly in the Psalter, where it says: “Blessed is the man.” Some call this psalm the summary of the entire book.]

“In the beginning of the book it is written concerning me: ‘To do your will, O God.’” Above, when he says: “You did not desire sacrifices and offerings and burnt offerings for sin, nor were they pleasing to you, which are offered according to the Law,” then he says: “Behold, I come, to do your will, O God.” He takes away the first in order to establish the second.

By this will we have been sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all.

[Note: 5. And every priest indeed. To minister is the task of servants; but to sit belongs to masters.]

And every priest indeed stands daily ministering and repeatedly offering the same sacrifices, which can never take away sins; but this man, after offering one sacrifice for sins, sits forever at the right hand of God, from then on awaiting

[Note: 6. Until his enemies are placed. Not only the enemies who are unbelievers, but also those who live impurely. For the mind of the flesh is hostile to God.]

until his enemies are placed as a footstool for his feet.

[Note: 7. LANFRANC. Footstool. On the day of judgment, all who are now his enemies will be beneath Christ’s feet, because at his command they will either be converted and go into eternal life, or, if obstinate, suffer everlasting Gehenna.]

For by one offering he has perfected forever those who are sanctified.

The Holy Spirit also bears witness to us.

[Note: 8. He bears witness. That is, he confirms our words, in which we assert that sins have been completely forgiven through the one offering of Christ’s body.]

For after saying: “This is the testament that I will establish with them after those days, says the Lord,”

[Note: 9. AMBROSE. Giving my laws. This law is love: that we should not do to another what we do not want done to us; and, as it is said in the Gospel: “Whatever you wish people to do to you, do the same to them” (Matthew 7:12).]

“giving my laws in their hearts, and I will write them upon their minds, and I will remember their sins and iniquities no more,” he says: “Where there is forgiveness of these, there is no longer an offering for sin.”

Therefore, brothers, since we have confidence to enter the Holy Places through the blood of Christ,

[Note: 10. LANFRANC. At the entrance. He calls heaven the entrance into which the saints, redeemed by Christ’s blood, are to enter.]

the way that he inaugurated for us, a new and living way, through the veil—that is, through his flesh—

[Note: 11. Which he inaugurated. The order is: “the new way,” because no human being ascended into heaven before him, “and living,” that is, not failing but enduring, because his members will ascend until the end of the age. Christ inaugurated this way for us, that is, he began or dedicated it.]

and since we have a great priest over the house of God, let us draw near with a true heart in the fullness of faith, our hearts sprinkled clean from an evil conscience and our bodies washed with pure water. Let us hold fast the confession of our hope without wavering—for he who promised is faithful—and let us consider one another for the provocation of love and good works,

[Note: 12. One another. Let one person consider what good another is doing, not in order to envy him, but to take a good example from him.]

not abandoning our assembly, as is the custom of some, but encouraging one another, and all the more as you see the day approaching.

[Note: 13. As you see. He means either the final day of judgment or a time of temporal affliction.]

For if we sin willingly after receiving the knowledge of the truth, there no longer remains a sacrifice for sins, but a certain fearful expectation of judgment and a fury of fire that will consume the adversaries.

If someone rejects the Law of Moses, he dies without mercy on the testimony of two or three witnesses. How much worse punishment, do you suppose, will be deserved by one who

[Note: 15. The Son of God. He tramples the grace of the Son of God underfoot in himself, and considers the blood of redemption polluted—that is, unable to cleanse sins. He insults the Holy Spirit, through whom sins are forgiven to the one who confesses them, when he willingly lies in sins.]

has trampled underfoot the Son of God, considered the blood of the testament by which he was sanctified polluted, and insulted the Spirit of grace?

For we know who said: “Vengeance is mine, and I will repay.” And again: “The Lord will judge his people.” It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God.

But remember the former days, in which, after being enlightened, you endured a great struggle of sufferings,

[Note: 17. Of sufferings. Sufferings contended against them in order that they might lose their patience and deny the faith.]

sometimes being made a spectacle through reproaches and afflictions, and at other times becoming companions of those who were treated in this way. For you sympathized with prisoners and accepted with joy the plundering of your possessions, knowing that you had a better and lasting possession.

Therefore do not throw away your confidence,

[Note: 18. To throw away. The person who abandons the good and does evil throws away confidence in divine recompense.]

which has a great reward. For you need patience, so that, after doing the will of God, you may receive the promise.

For yet “a little while, and the one who is to come will come, and will not delay. But my righteous one shall live by faith; and if he withdraws, my soul will not be pleased with him.”

But we are not children of withdrawal, unto destruction, but of faith, unto the acquisition of the soul.

[COMMENTARY.]

[Col. 0397B]

## CHAPTER X

#### 1. LANFRANC. For the Law, having a shadow

He returns to the preceding argument, where he said that the legal sacrifices could not perfect the worshiper according to his conscience. The response is as though he were saying: Why did you say that sins were to be exhausted through Christ and not through the Law?

#### 2. AMBROSE. Not the very image

That is, not the very truth.

#### 3. With the same sacrifices

What, then, of us? Do we not offer every day? We do offer, but for the reconciliation wrought by his death; and this is one sacrifice, not many. What we do is a copy of that sacrifice; it is performed in remembrance of what was done: “Do this,” he says, “in remembrance of me” (Luke 22).

#### 4. At the beginning of the book

Certainly in the Psalter, where it says: “Blessed is the man.” Some call this psalm the summary of the entire book.

#### 5. And every priest indeed

To minister is the task of servants; but to sit belongs to masters.

#### 6. Until his enemies are placed

Not only the enemies who are unbelievers, but also those who live impurely. For the mind of the flesh is hostile to God.

#### 7. LANFRANC. Footstool

On the day of judgment, all who are now his enemies will be beneath Christ’s feet, because at his command they will either be converted and go into eternal life, or, if obstinate, suffer everlasting Gehenna.

[Col. 0398B]

#### 8. He bears witness

That is, he confirms our words, in which we assert that sins have been completely forgiven through the one offering of Christ’s body.

#### 9. AMBROSE. Giving my laws

This law is love: that we should not do to another what we do not want done to us; and, as it is said in the Gospel: “Whatever you wish people to do to you, do the same to them” (Matthew 7:12).

#### 10. LANFRANC. At the entrance

He calls heaven the entrance into which the saints, redeemed by Christ’s blood, are to enter.

#### 11. Which he inaugurated

The order is: “the new way,” because no human being ascended into heaven before him, “and living,” that is, not failing but enduring, because his members will ascend until the end of the age. Christ inaugurated this way for us, that is, he began or dedicated it.

[Col. 0399A]

#### 12. One another

Let one person consider what good another is doing, not in order to envy him, but to take a good example from him.

#### 13. As you see

He means either the final day of judgment or a time of temporal affliction.

#### 14. Willingly

He gives the reason why love must be maintained and evil abandoned: while the will to sin remains in us, the sacrifice offered for our sins is of no benefit.

#### 15. The Son of God

He tramples the grace of the Son of God underfoot in himself, and considers the blood of redemption polluted—that is, unable to cleanse sins. He insults the Holy Spirit, through whom sins are forgiven to the one who confesses them, when he willingly lies in sins.

[Col. 0399B]

#### 16. For we know

He proves the preceding statement: “a certain fearful expectation,” and so forth.

#### 17. Of sufferings

Sufferings contended against them in order that they might lose their patience and deny the faith.

#### 18. To throw away

The person who abandons the good and does evil throws away confidence in divine recompense.

[Col. 0400A]

#### 19. Patience

He shows how confidence is not lost: “For in patience,” he says, “you will possess your souls.”

## CHAPTER XI

[Col. 0399]

[Note: [Col. 0400A] CHAPTER XI.—1. LANFRANC. “Now faith is…” Faith ought to be such that it makes the things hoped for subsist in the heart of the believer, even if another doubts that they can exist without proof. Many interpreters of divine speech have done this, proving the resurrection of bodies, eternal life, and many other things to exist or to have existed from the fact that the patriarchs, prophets, apostles, and martyrs are known to have believed them.]

Now faith is the substance of things hoped for, the proof of things not seen. For by this the elders obtained testimony. By faith we understand that the ages were fashioned by the word of God, so that visible things might be made from invisible things.

[Note: [Col. 0400A] 2. Invisible. The elements were invisible before the creation of the world.]

By faith Abel offered to God a greater sacrifice than Cain, through which he received testimony that he was righteous, God bearing witness to his gifts; and through it, though dead, he still speaks. By faith Enoch was translated so that he would not see death, and he was not found, because God translated him; for before his translation he received testimony that he pleased God. Without faith, however, it is impossible to please God. For whoever approaches God must believe that he exists and that he is a rewarder of those who seek him.

By faith Noah, having received an answer concerning things that were not yet seen, in fear prepared an ark for the salvation of his household, through which he condemned the world—

[Note: [Col. 0400A] 3. He condemned the world. Noah condemned the world through the ark, because people incurred a much greater sin in proportion as they saw his greater diligence in building the ark and did not believe.]

—and was appointed heir of the righteousness that comes through faith.

By faith Abraham, when he was called, obeyed by going out to a place that he was to receive as an inheritance; and he went out, not knowing where he was going. By faith he dwelt in the land of promise as in a foreign land, living in huts with Isaac and Jacob, co-heirs of the same promise. For he was awaiting a city having foundations, whose architect and founder is God.

By faith Sarah herself, though barren, received power for the conception of offspring, even beyond the time of her age, because she believed that he who had promised was faithful. Therefore, from one man—and one as good as dead—were born descendants like the stars of heaven in multitude and like the innumerable sand on the seashore.

[Note: [Col. 0400B] 4. “From one they were born.” The order is: “From one, and from one who was as good as dead, they were born like,” and so forth.]

All these died according to faith, without receiving the promises, but seeing and greeting them from afar and confessing that they were strangers and sojourners on the earth. For those who say such things show that they are seeking a homeland. And if they had remembered the one from which they had departed, they would certainly have had time to return; but now they desire a better one, that is, a heavenly one. Therefore God is not ashamed to be called their God, for he has prepared a city for them.

By faith Abraham offered Isaac when he was tested, and he was offering his only-begotten son, he who had received the promises, to whom it had been said: “In Isaac shall your offspring be called,”

[Note: [Col. 0401A] 5. “Considering that…” Abraham believed both that he would have descendants in Isaac and that he would please God if he sacrificed Isaac to him; for he believed that God could raise him from the dead.]

considering that God was able even to raise him from the dead. Hence he also received him back as a figure.

[Note: [Col. 0401A] 6. “As a figure.” The ram found caught by its horns among the bushes, and Isaac, signify the one Christ, both human and divine. Thus, by the fact that the ram was sacrificed but Isaac was spared death, it was signified that Christ would suffer according to the flesh, but according to his divinity would not experience the danger of death. And by saying “as a figure,” he understood him allegorically. He first gave him over to death, but after the test of faith, when the ram had been found, he received him back to be seen. This honor was granted to him on account of his faith and obedience, so that through the son’s life the withdrawal of divinity from death might be signified.]

By faith Isaac also blessed Jacob and Esau concerning things to come. By faith Jacob, when dying, blessed each of the sons of Joseph and worshiped the top of his staff.

[Note: [Col. 0401B] 7. “The top of his staff.” Either Joseph carried a scepter, as was customary for one second to the king; or by “the top of his staff” he means the height of his rule, which Jacob worshiped, that is, held in the highest veneration. He did this by faith, because he believed that it had been established by God.]

By faith Joseph, when dying, remembered the departure of the children of Israel and gave instructions concerning his bones.

By faith Moses, when he was born, was hidden for three months by his parents, because they saw that the child was beautiful and did not fear the king’s command. By faith Moses, when he had grown up, refused to be called the son of Pharaoh’s daughter, choosing rather to suffer affliction with the people of God than to have the enjoyment of sin for a time, considering the reproach of Christ greater riches than the treasures of Egypt; for he was looking toward the reward.

By faith he left Egypt, not fearing the king’s anger; for he endured as though seeing the invisible one. By faith he celebrated the Passover and the shedding of blood, so that the destroyer of the firstborn might not touch them. By faith they crossed the Red Sea as though by dry land; when the Egyptians attempted this, they were swallowed up. By faith the walls of Jericho fell after they had been encircled for seven days. By faith Rahab the prostitute did not perish with the unbelieving, having received the spies in peace.

And what more shall I say? For time will fail me if I tell of Gideon, Barak, Samson, Jephthah, David, Samuel, and the prophets—

[Note: [Col. 0401B] 8. “Jephthah, David.” Jephthah is not brought forward as a witness because he killed his daughter, but because, through faith and with God assisting him, he overcame his enemies.]

—who through faith conquered kingdoms, practiced righteousness, obtained promises, stopped the mouths of lions, quenched the violence of fire, escaped the edge of the sword, recovered from weakness, became strong in battle, and put foreign armies to flight. Women received their dead back through resurrection.

[Note: [Col. 0401B] 9. “Women received.” The order is: “Women received,” namely, from God’s saints, their dead restored through resurrection, that is, rising again—as the widow of Zarephath received her only son from Elijah, and the Shunammite woman received hers from Elisha.]

Others were stretched upon the rack, refusing to accept release, in order to obtain a better resurrection.

[Note: [Col. 0402A] 10. “To obtain a better.” He calls the resurrection “better” because of the more excellent glory in the resurrection: the more one suffers, the more one will be crowned.]

Others experienced mockeries and scourging, and moreover chains and prisons. They were stoned, sawn apart, tested, killed by the sword. They went about in garments of hair and in goatskins,

[Note: [Col. 0402A] 11. “In garments of hair, in skins.” It is a garment made, as they say, from camel hair; Scripture does not expressly say whether anyone in the ancient Jewish people used goatskins. John the Baptist, however, did use such a garment.]

needy, afflicted, and tormented—people of whom the world was not worthy—wandering in deserts, mountains, caves, and caverns of the earth.

And all these, approved by the testimony of faith, did not receive the promise,

[Note: [Col. 0402A] 12. “The promise.” After receiving the blessedness of souls, the resurrection of bodies, which God promised to his saints, is still delayed so that we may all rise together, in order that, in the common joy of all, the joy of each individual may be greater.]

since God had provided something better for us, so that they would not be made perfect without us.

[COMMENTARY.]

[Col. 0400A]

CHAPTER XI.—1. LANFRANC. “Now faith is…” Faith ought to be such that it makes the things hoped for subsist in the heart of the believer, even if another doubts that they can exist without proof. Many interpreters of divine speech have done this, proving the resurrection of bodies, eternal life, and many other things to exist or to have existed from the fact that the patriarchs, prophets, apostles, and martyrs are known to have believed them.

2. “Invisible.” The elements were invisible before the creation of the world.

3. “He condemned the world.” Noah condemned the world through the ark, because people incurred a much greater sin in proportion as they saw his greater diligence in building the ark and did not believe.

4. “From one they were born.” The order is: “From one, and from one who was as good as dead, they were born like,” and so forth.

[Col. 0401A] 5. “Considering that…” Abraham believed both that he would have descendants in Isaac and that he would please God if he sacrificed Isaac to him; for he believed that God could raise him from the dead.

6. “As a figure.” The ram found caught by its horns among the bushes, and Isaac, signify the one Christ, both human and divine. Thus, by the fact that the ram was sacrificed but Isaac was spared death, it was signified that Christ would suffer according to the flesh, but according to his divinity would not experience the danger of death. And by saying “as a figure,” he understood him allegorically. He first gave him over to death, but after the test of faith, when the ram had been found, he received him back to be seen. This honor was granted to him on account of his faith and obedience, so that through the son’s life the withdrawal of divinity from death might be signified.

7. “The top of his staff.” Either Joseph carried a scepter, as was customary for one second to the king; or by “the top of his staff” he means the height of his rule, which Jacob worshiped, that is, held in the highest veneration. He did this by faith, because he believed that it had been established by God.

8. “Jephthah, David.” Jephthah is not brought forward as a witness because he killed his daughter, but because, through faith and with God assisting him, he overcame his enemies.

9. “Women received.” The order is: “Women received,” namely, from God’s saints, their dead restored through resurrection, that is, rising again—as the widow of Zarephath received her only son from Elijah, and the Shunammite woman received hers from Elisha.

10. “To obtain a better.” He calls the resurrection “better” because of the more excellent glory in the resurrection: the more one suffers, the more one will be crowned.

11. “In garments of hair, in skins.” It is a garment made, as they say, from camel hair; Scripture does not expressly say whether anyone in the ancient Jewish people used goatskins. John the Baptist, however, did use such a garment.

12. “The promise.” After receiving the blessedness of souls, the resurrection of bodies, which God promised to his saints, is still delayed so that we may all rise together, in order that, in the common joy of all, the joy of each individual may be greater.

CHAPTER XII.

[Col. 0401]

Therefore, since we too have so great a cloud of witnesses set over us,

[Note: [Col. 0402B] CHAPTER XII.—1. LANFRANC. “The cloud set over us.” He calls the multitude of the saints a cloud because they rain down words and flash with miracles.]

let us lay aside every weight and the sin that surrounds us,

[Note: [Col. 0402B] 2. “Every weight.” He calls sin a weight, as in the Psalm: “For my iniquities have gone over my head; like a heavy burden they have weighed me down” (Psalm XXXVII).]

and let us run with perseverance the contest set before us, looking to Jesus, the author and finisher of faith,

[Note: [Col. 0402B] 3. “Finisher,” that is, he who will perfect us, that is, will give the perfect blessedness of soul and body.]

who, for the joy set before him,

[Note: [Col. 0402B] 4. “Joy.” Either the heavenly kingdom or the earthly kingdom that was offered to him.]

endured the cross, disregarding its shame, and sits at the right hand of the throne of God.

Consider him who endured such contradiction from sinners against himself, so that you may not grow weary and fail in your souls. You have not yet resisted to the point of blood while struggling against sin, and you have forgotten the consolation that speaks to you as sons, saying:

[Note: [Col. 0403A] 5. “My son, do not…” In Proverbs it is written as follows: “My son, do not reject the discipline of the Lord, and do not grow faint when you are reproved by him; for the Lord reproves the one he loves, and, like a father with a son, he takes pleasure in him.”]

“My son, do not neglect the discipline of the Lord, and do not grow weary when you are reproved by him.” For whom the Lord loves, he chastises; and he scourges every son whom he receives. Persevere in discipline. God offers himself to you as sons; for what son is there whom a father does not correct? But if you are without discipline, of which all have become participants, then you are illegitimate children and not sons.

Moreover, we had the fathers of our flesh as instructors, and we revered them. Shall we not much more obey the Father of spirits and live? They indeed instructed us for a few days according to their own will; but he does so for what is useful, in order that we may receive his sanctification.

Now every discipline, at the time, seems not to be a matter of joy but of sorrow; afterward, however, it yields to those exercised by it the peaceful fruit of righteousness.

[Note: [Col. 0403A] 6. “The most peaceful fruit.” The order is: “The most peaceful fruit of righteousness,” that is, the fruit that righteousness earns.]

Therefore raise up the slack hands and the weakened knees, and make straight paths for your feet,

[Note: [Col. 0403A] 7. “For your feet.” He calls thoughts “feet”; they walk rightly when they believe correctly, and they limp when they err.]

so that what is lame may not go astray but rather be healed. Pursue peace with everyone, and holiness, without which no one will see God. See to it that no one falls short of the grace of God, and that no root of bitterness, springing up above, does not hinder you, and that through it many are not defiled.

Let there be no fornicator or profane person like Esau, who for one meal sold his birthright.

[Note: [Col. 0403A] 8. “Know.” This shows how profane Esau was, that is, alienated from the assembly of the faithful.]

For you know that afterward, when he desired to inherit the blessing, he was rejected; for he found no place for repentance, although he sought it with tears.

[Note: [Col. 0403A] 9. “For you have not approached.” When the law was given to the Jews, a tangible fire—that is, one that could be touched—and an approachable one appeared, in which God spoke, along with the other terrifying things that follow. “It was not so,” he says, “when the new law was given”; for everything is announced to you gently and sweetly.]

For you have not approached a tangible mountain and a blazing fire, and a whirlwind, and darkness, and a storm, and the sound of a trumpet, and the voice of words—which those who heard excused themselves from hearing further. For they could not bear what was being said: “Even if a beast touches the mountain, it shall be stoned.” And so terrifying was what appeared that Moses said: “I am terrified and trembling.”

[Note: [Col. 0403B] 10. “But you have approached,” that is, to the height at which or from which God is seen. For “Zion” is interpreted as “watchtower” or “vision.”]

But you have approached Mount Zion and the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, and the assembly of many thousands of angels, and the church of the firstborn who are enrolled in heaven, and God the judge of all, and the spirits of the perfected righteous, and Jesus the mediator of the new covenant, and the sprinkling of blood that speaks better than Abel.

[Note: [Col. 0404A] 11. “That speaks better.” The sprinkling of Abel’s blood cries out for vengeance; the sprinkling of Christ’s blood cries out for mercy.]

See that you do not refuse him who speaks. For if they did not escape when they refused him who spoke on earth, much more shall we not escape if we turn away from him who speaks to us from heaven—him whose voice then shook the earth, but now promises, saying:

[Note: [Col. 0404A] 12. “Yet once more I…” In the prophet Haggai it is written thus: “Yet a little while, and I will shake heaven and earth” (Haggai II).]

“Yet once more I will move not only the earth but also heaven.”

[Note: [Col. 0404A] 13. “He declares.” By saying “I will move,” the transference of heaven and earth is declared, that is, their transformation into another state. He proves this by the fact that the word “once” indicates that afterward they will be immovable. What is said, “the things that are,” should be understood as though it said, “that which they are.” Whatever will exist, whether in the principal essences or in things taken externally, will be immovable according to what it is.]

Now the phrase “yet once more” indicates the removal of things that can be moved, as things made, so that the things that are immovable may remain. Therefore, since we are receiving an unshakable kingdom, let us have grace, through which we may serve God acceptably, with fear and reverence. For our God is a consuming fire.

[COMMENTARY.]

[Col. 0402B]

CHAPTER XII.—1. LANFRANC. “The cloud set over us.” He calls the multitude of the saints a cloud because they rain down words and flash with miracles.

2. “Every weight.” He calls sin a weight, as in the Psalm: “For my iniquities have gone over my head; like a heavy burden they have weighed me down” (Psalm XXXVII).

3. “Finisher,” that is, he who will perfect us, that is, will give the perfect blessedness of soul and body.

4. “Joy.” Either the heavenly kingdom or the earthly kingdom that was offered to him.

[Col. 0403A] 5. “My son, do not…” In Proverbs it is written as follows: “My son, do not reject the discipline of the Lord, and do not grow faint when you are reproved by him; for the Lord reproves the one he loves, and, like a father with a son, he takes pleasure in him.”

6. “The most peaceful fruit.” The order is: “The most peaceful fruit of righteousness,” that is, the fruit that righteousness earns.

7. “For your feet.” He calls thoughts “feet”; they walk rightly when they believe correctly, and they limp when they err.

8. “Know.” This shows how profane Esau was, that is, alienated from the assembly of the faithful.

9. “For you have not approached.” When the law was given to the Jews, a tangible fire—that is, one that could be touched—and an approachable one appeared, in which God spoke, along with the other terrifying things that follow. “It was not so,” he says, “when the new law was given”; for everything is announced to you gently and sweetly.

10. “But you have approached,” that is, to the height at which or from which God is seen. For “Zion” is interpreted as “watchtower” or “vision.”

[Col. 0404A] 11. “That speaks better.” The sprinkling of Abel’s blood cries out for vengeance; the sprinkling of Christ’s blood cries out for mercy.

12. “Yet once more I…” In the prophet Haggai it is written thus: “Yet a little while, and I will shake heaven and earth” (Haggai II).

13. “He declares.” By saying “I will move,” the transference of heaven and earth is declared, that is, their transformation into another state. He proves this by the fact that the word “once” indicates that afterward they will be immovable. What is said, “the things that are,” should be understood as though it said, “that which they are.” Whatever will exist, whether in the principal essences or in things taken externally, will be immovable according to what it is.

CHAPTER XIII.

[Col. 0403]

Let brotherly love remain among you. Do not forget hospitality, for through it some, having received angels as guests, have entertained them unknowingly. Remember those in chains as though chained with them, and those who suffer hardship as though you yourselves were still in the body.

Let marriage be honorable in all, and the marriage bed undefiled. For God will judge fornicators and adulterers.

Let your conduct be without greed; be content with what you have. For he himself said: “I will not abandon you, nor forsake you,” so that we may confidently say: “The Lord is my helper; I will not fear what a human being can do to me.”

Remember your leaders, who spoke the word of God to you. Looking to the outcome of their way of life, imitate their faith.

[Note: [Col. 0404B] CHAPTER XIII.—1. “Jesus Christ yesterday and today.” It is as though he said: “Jesus Christ, who was with them, is with you and will be with his Church until the consummation of the age.”]

Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today, and forever.

Do not be led away by various and foreign doctrines. For it is best to establish the heart by grace, not by foods,

[Note: [Col. 0405A] 2. “Not by foods.” It is understood that there were some who taught that sin did not consist in foods and that one might abound in pleasures.]

which have not benefited those who walked in them.

[Note: [Col. 0405A] 3. “We have an altar.” This explains why one must not indulge immoderately in foods. The body of Christ must be eaten with sobriety; it is also called an altar in other passages of the divine Scriptures, because in it—that is, in faith in him—our prayers and works, offered as though upon an altar, become acceptable to God.]

We have an altar from which those who serve the tabernacle have no authority to eat. For the bodies of those animals whose blood is brought into the holy place by the high priest for sin are burned outside the camp.

[Note: [Col. 0405A] 4. “For the bodies of which animals…” Through a twofold allegory, one from the Old Testament and the other from the New, he proves that the body of Christ is not to be eaten by those who serve the tabernacle. For this reason the bodies of these animals were burned outside the camp; and therefore Christ suffered outside the gate of the city of Jerusalem, so that we, who desire to be cleansed from sins by his body and blood, and who are to suffer reproaches and hardships, might leave behind the delights of the tabernacle.]

Therefore Jesus also suffered outside the gate, in order to sanctify the people through his own blood. Let us therefore go out to him outside the camp, bearing his reproach. For we do not have here a lasting city, but we seek the one that is to come.

Through him, then, let us continually offer a sacrifice of praise to God, that is, the fruit of lips confessing his name. Do not forget kindness and fellowship, for God is pleased by such sacrifices.

Obey your leaders and submit to them. For they keep watch as those who will give an account for your souls, so that they may do this with joy and not with groaning; for this would not benefit you.

Pray for us,

[Note: [Col. 0406A] 5. “For we are confident.” The reason why they should pray for him is that he has a good conscience and desires to conduct himself well both toward them and toward everyone [supplied: “may have”].]

for we are confident that we have a good conscience, desiring to conduct ourselves well in all things. I appeal to you all the more earnestly to do this, so that I may be restored to you more quickly.

Now may the God of peace, who brought back from the dead the great Shepherd of the sheep,

[Note: [Col. 0406A] 6. “In the blood.” In his usual manner, he calls the death through which Christ rose from the dead “blood.” For unless he had died, he would neither have descended to the underworld nor risen from the underworld.]

through the blood of the eternal covenant,

[Note: [Col. 0406A] 7. “Eternal.” “Eternal” is used in two ways: of what has neither beginning nor end, and of what endures only until the end of the age. It is in this latter sense that “eternal” is used here, as it is said through Moses: “The Lord shall reign forever and beyond” (Exodus XV).]

our Lord Jesus Christ, equip you with every good thing so that you may do his will, working in you what is pleasing in his sight, through Jesus Christ, to whom be glory forever and ever. Amen.

Now I ask you, brothers, to bear with this word of consolation. For I have written to you in very few words. Know that our brother Timothy has been released; if he comes soon, I shall see you with him.

Greet all your leaders and all the saints. The brothers from Italy greet you. Grace be with you all. Amen.

[COMMENTARY.]

[Col. 0404B]

CHAPTER XIII.—1. “Jesus Christ yesterday and today.” It is as though he said: “Jesus Christ, who was with them, is with you and will be with his Church until the consummation of the age.”

[Col. 0405A] 2. “Not by foods.” It is understood that there were some who taught that sin did not consist in foods and that one might abound in pleasures.

3. “We have an altar.” This explains why one must not indulge immoderately in foods. The body of Christ must be eaten with sobriety; it is also called an altar in other passages of the divine Scriptures, because in it—that is, in faith in him—our prayers and works, offered as though upon an altar, become acceptable to God.

4. “For the bodies of which animals…” Through a twofold allegory, one from the Old Testament and the other from the New, he proves that the body of Christ is not to be eaten by those who serve the tabernacle. For this reason the bodies of these animals were burned outside the camp; and therefore Christ suffered outside the gate of the city of Jerusalem, so that we, who desire to be cleansed from sins by his body and blood, and who are to suffer reproaches and hardships, might leave behind the delights of the tabernacle.

5. “For we are confident.” The reason why they should pray for him is that he has a good conscience and desires to conduct himself well both toward them and toward everyone [supplied: “may have”].

6. “In the blood.” In his usual manner, he calls the death through which Christ rose from the dead “blood.” For unless he had died, he would neither have descended to the underworld nor risen from the underworld.

7. “Eternal.” “Eternal” is used in two ways: of what has neither beginning nor end, and of what endures only until the end of the age. It is in this latter sense that “eternal” is used here, as it is said through Moses: “The Lord shall reign forever and beyond” (Exodus XV).

[Col. 0405] The Commentary of Blessed Lanfranc of Canterbury on the Epistles of the Blessed Paul ends.

[ON THE BODY AND BLOOD OF THE LORD.]

[Col. 0405]

FRANCIS QUADRATUS, MONK OF BEC, GREETS THE MOST ILLUSTRIOUS G. RATUM, PROFESSOR OF SACRED THEOLOGY, VICAR AND PENITENTIARY OF THE MOST REVEREND FATHER IN CHRIST AND LORD, LORD GEORGE AMBASIANUS, ARCHBISHOP OF ROUEN.

230 It often happens that, when we attempt difficult things or do not test the strength of our intellect, we seek with the greatest zeal to win over those whom we judge likely to be useful to our undertaking. Therefore our letter proceeds more freely to you, most discerning of theologians, so that what we cannot obtain by our own right we may obtain through your favor.

To bring you to the purpose of our undertaking, I shall explain it briefly. A few days ago, while turning over our library in order to collect my thoughts and seeking something concerning the praises of the Virgin taken up into heaven, an old codex came into my hands: *On the Body and Blood of Christ*, written by Lanfranc against a certain heretic named Berengar.

At that moment I persuaded myself that something timely and most necessary had occurred, in an age in which both the faith of the scattered flock of the Lord is weakened by false apostles and the controversy among those within the household has become so great that scarcely any trace or image of the desired city—that is, of Christian peace—appears anywhere.

Therefore, lest I, accursed, hide from the faithful people the grain of salvation, I silently considered to which vigorous commander of the Christian army I should send this experienced soldier of Christ, hitherto neglected and nearly consumed by a long imprisonment as well as by neglect.

Since I could not bear so great a crime, your name came to mind—you who tirelessly offer the richest nourishment of evangelical milk to less advanced beginners, so that, through the moisture of the sacred liquid springing from you, you may renew the excessive sterility of an adulterating and arid age and bring it forth to fruit worthy of God; and you who, carefully refuting and purifying the proud doctrines of fools by reference to that cornerstone—

[Col. 0407]

What was I thinking while considering these things? O happy city of Rouen, which has deserved such a ruler together with its archbishop! Does an excess of grief weigh upon your heart? Approach with confidence, and, as I confidently believe, a wise physician will offer you a sweet remedy.

For in you—or nowhere—is there a means of recovering health, provided that you bring a simple mind. Once again I must call you happy, since, instructed by the worthy and polished discourses of this man, you retain a truly Christian and genuine purity of innocence.

For that power of praying and preaching, if he had not been appointed to those exercises—not so much by royal favor as because his merits themselves demanded it—would, speaking with respect for everyone’s rights, have almost dried up.

Indeed, if you retain him in body, the Church spread throughout the world feels the faith of the absent disciple as though he were present, marvels at his teaching, and rejoices that it has found in him a most powerful bulwark.

As I turn these matters over in my mind, to return to you, most distinguished man, I burn with an incredible desire—one that I do not think blameworthy—that you should undertake this work, whatever its quality may be. For I judged that you alone would be the one whose health-giving advice and weighty authority would move the other professors of sacred theology to fulfill my expectation, and would lead them either willingly to accept the little work or to commend it to the press.

It will truly not be unworthy of your dignity—since it is also most honorable for kings—if you strive to defend this work against the domestic enemies of Christian truth. It will also be glorious for me, if I may say so without vanity, should you, moved by my foolish efforts, undertake to publish it for the benefit of many.

Yet, while I was attempting this bold and excellent undertaking—trying through these same foolish efforts to entice you, the one unique exemplar of Christian purity and of all learning—a certain rustic modesty has so far deterred me. But I rejoice that fortune has brought about this opportunity: as a new petitioner, I may commend this new defender, born for our time, of Christian truth to so great a man, even by means of this brief preface.

I called him “new” on account of those who either claim that this work has already been published through the efforts of Desiderius Erasmus or of someone unknown to me. Certainly it is not extant.

But, so that I may not cause weariness by saying too much, I knowingly pass over the author’s life. I shall do something most pleasing both to God and to human beings if, through your authority, work, advice, and even favor, I bring this little book into the light once and for all in defense of Christian truth.

The desire for this presses upon me all the more ardently because, while the witness Barbatus gives assurance to those suffering violence against the false doctrines of an ancient heresy, this steadfast soldier may also, as a support to those who have fought until now, hurl the weapons of the enemy back upon their authors.

Although I pursue this undertaking, moved by zeal for the faith, I am not so ignorant as not to know that some will call me rash because, being unskilled and lacking in the liberal arts, I have undertaken to commend this little work to so great a man, one whose very elementary letters ought to be objects of worship for me.

Whether they will say this falsely or justly will be for you to judge. For my part, I shall gladly bear everything with complete indifference, if you approve the labor. But if it should seem unworthy of you, at least consider that it was undertaken sincerely and cheerfully by one who is devoted to you in the highest degree.

Farewell.

From our house at Bec, in the year of the Lord 1540, on the day before the Kalends of February.

[Col. 0407]

THE BOOK OF BLESSED LANFRANC, ARCHBISHOP OF CANTERBURY, ON THE BODY AND BLOOD OF THE LORD, AGAINST BERENGAR OF TOURS.

231 CHAPTER ONE.

[Col. 0407A]

LANFRANC, by the mercy of God a Catholic, to BERENGAR, adversary of the Catholic Church.

If divine piety should deign to inspire your heart so that, out of regard for God and your own soul, you might wish to speak with me, and with prudent deliberation choose a suitable place where this could appropriately be done, you would perhaps do much for yourself, but certainly you would benefit those whom you deceive and, once deceived and overtaken by death, send into eternal punishments. For, with the Spirit cooperating—who breathes where he wills—one of two things would come to pass: either you yourself, laying aside the arrogance with which you are filled and with which you have begun to think against the whole world, would submit to the authority of the entire holy Church and to the sound interpretations of the holy Scriptures, [Col. 0407B] and thus rescue yourself and your followers from the darkness of error and the depths of iniquity; or, if you persisted in your obstinacy, those others, hearing the arguments and moved by God’s mercy, would come to their senses and return by better counsel [Col. 0408A] to the true faith, which the holy Church never ceases to preach.

But because you have chosen to defend in secret disputations before the unlearned the perversity that you once imbibed, while publicly, and in the hearing of the holy council, you confess orthodox faith not from love of truth but from fear of death, you therefore flee me and flee religious persons who might pass judgment on your words and mine. In their presence I would most willingly hear you and confer with you on nothing so much as the opinions that, with punishable temerity, you fabricate to suit your own opinions, and that you attribute to the holy doctors—whether from a desire to do harm or from ignorance of the truth—saying: “Augustine, Gregory, Jerome, or any one of those whom the Church of Christ venerates with exceptional honor as placed in the citadel of authority, testifies to this or that in such-and-such a work.”

There all your crafty evasiveness would come to rest, when the sacred books were read in your hearing or placed in your hands for reading, and when, more brightly than by any heavenly lamp, it would be shown that certain things which you sometimes claim to take from the holy Scriptures are either entirely false [Col. 0409A] or corrupted in part, according as the logic of your cause requires. By this diabolical deception you assault, deceive, and overthrow minds ignorant of the divine mystery and trusting in you—so much the more wicked because, in your evil purpose, you are more obstinate in the subversion and scandal of those who are your brothers in Christ. You make little of the words of the Lord, who threatens the one who scandalizes any of his little ones (Matt. 18:6), nor do you sufficiently tremble at the Apostle’s rebuke, when he writes to the proud people of Corinth: “By sinning in this way against the brothers and wounding their weak conscience, you sin against Christ” (1 Cor. 8:12).

You are held fast by this sin to a very great degree, subverting those who, unable to resist you, contemplate the things that are seen and not the things that are unseen. But God’s firm foundation stands unmoved, bearing this seal: “Let everyone who invokes the name of the Lord depart from iniquity,” and it by no means endures without grave scandal that you are not content to speak perversely as a perverse man unless you also send wicked writings, through your wicked disciples, into various regions. The other matters were heard, examined, and condemned by Nicholas of blessed memory, supreme pontiff of the whole Christian name, and by one hundred and thirteen bishops at Rome.

You too, having bowed your body but not humbled your heart, kindled a fire and threw books containing your perverse doctrine into it in the midst of the holy council, swearing by that which is incomparably greater than all things that you would inviolably preserve the faith handed down by the Fathers who were present, and that from that day onward you would not preach your former doctrine [Col. 0409C] concerning the body and blood of the Lord to others. A sacrilegious violator of this undertaking, you later composed a writing against the aforesaid synod, against catholic truth, and against the opinion of all the Churches. Trusting in Christ’s mercy, I have decided to answer it in this little work.

And so that it may appear more clearly what you say and what I answer, I shall distinguish the respective statements by the alternating placement of our names. I shall not answer everything, because you interweave roses with thorns and paint your phantom in white and black colors; you also say certain things that have no bearing on the question at issue. I shall nevertheless strive to proceed concisely, as far as I can. For I would not wish to wear out my life in such dirges, if you would allow the people of God to enjoy their ancient [Col. 0409D] peace.

## CHAPTER II

**BERENGARIUS:** “The writing of Humbert of Burgundy, whom they had made a cardinal-bishop at Rome, which he wrote against catholic truth—as will be shown below—so that Berengarius might be compelled to recite it and, as it were, profess the error of that most foolish Burgundian.”

**LANFRANC:** All who knew Humbert from personal experience, or acquired knowledge of him from others who had experienced him, testify that he was a religious man, steadfastly adorned with Christian faith and most holy works, and exceptionally learned in divine and secular letters. Saint [Col. 0410A] Leo brought him to Rome not from Burgundy but from Lotharingia, ordained him archbishop to preach the word of God to the Sicilians, and afterward the holy Roman Church made him its cardinal-bishop. In that position he lived and taught in such a way that no rumor even of a sinister suspicion ever arose concerning his faith or doctrine.

Almost the whole of Latin Christendom bears witness to this: because of the excellence of the apostolic see, whose councils he always attended and over which he presided, it could not have failed to know him. Even if he had been Burgundian, you would nevertheless foolishly and arrogantly assign the name of his nation to him as a disgrace, since the Spirit of the Lord breathes where he wills (John 3:8), inspires whom he wills, and “the earth is the Lord’s and all who dwell in it” (Ps. 23:1). The prince of the apostles also says: “In truth I perceive that God is not a respecter of persons, but in every nation anyone who fears him and does what is right is acceptable to him” (Acts 10:34–35). Likewise the teacher of the nations says to the Galatians: “God accepts no person according to human standing” (Gal. 2:6).

When you assert that Humbert wrote against catholic truth, you rebuke not him alone but also the Roman pontiffs, the Roman Church, and many holy Fathers. You fall into what the blessed doctors, even if not in the same words, have nevertheless consistently established in many places with the same meaning: that every person who differs from the Roman and universal Church in the doctrine of faith is a heretic. By God’s just judgment, it has therefore happened to you that, while attempting to establish that others are heretics, you yourself have fallen into heresy and are proved to be a heretic.

[Col. 0410C] **BERENGARIUS:** “I anathematize every heresy, especially that which attempts to assert that the bread and wine placed on the altar are, after consecration, merely sacraments and not the true body and blood of Christ.”

**LANFRANC:** You have not inserted the beginning of this oath here, as I suppose, so that your readers might think these words were not yours but those of the venerable Bishop Humbert. Nor is this without reason. For since you obstinately strive to prove them heretical, if you openly declared them to be yours, you would openly prove yourself a heretic. But so that no one ignorant of the Roman council may deliver an indiscriminate judgment on the matter, I shall set down here its beginning, middle, and end together.

“I, Berengarius, an unworthy deacon of the Church of [Col. 0410D] Saint Maurice of Angers, recognizing the true catholic and apostolic faith, anathematize every heresy, especially that concerning which I have hitherto been infamous, which attempts to assert that the bread and wine placed on the altar are, after consecration, merely the sacrament and not the true body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, and that they cannot be handled sensibly by the hands of the priests in the sacrament alone, nor broken, nor crushed by the teeth of the faithful.

“But I consent to the holy Roman and apostolic see, and with mouth and heart I profess that, concerning the sacraments of the Lord’s table, I hold the faith which the lord and venerable Pope Nicholas and this holy synod, by evangelical and apostolic authority, handed down as to be held and confirmed for me: namely, that the bread and wine placed on the altar are, after consecration, not merely the sacrament but also the true body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, and that they are handled and broken by the hands of the priests, and crushed by the teeth of the faithful, sensibly not merely in the sacrament but in truth. I swear this by the holy and consubstantial Trinity, and by these most holy Gospels of Christ. I declare that those who come against this faith, together with their doctrines and followers, are worthy of eternal anathema. If I myself should ever presume to think or preach anything contrary to these things, may I be subject to the severity of the canons. Having read and reread it, I subscribed voluntarily.”

[Col. 0411B] Later, in the time of Gregory VII, when a discussion was being held about these matters in the Church of the Savior, you persisted as a teacher of error, surrounded by a troop of men like yourself. Then, returning when the Spirit of the heavenly Father breathed into your mind, you obtained the pardon you hoped for through apostolic mercy, swearing also the following:

“I, Berengarius, believe in my heart and confess with my mouth that the bread and wine placed on the altar are, through the mystery of the sacred prayer and the words of our Redeemer, substantially changed into the true, proper, and life-giving flesh and blood of Jesus Christ our Lord; and that after consecration they are the true body of Christ, which was born of the Virgin, which was offered for the salvation of the world and hung upon the [Col. 0411C] cross, and which sits at the right hand of the Father; and the true blood of Christ, which was poured from his side—not merely through the sign and power of the sacrament, but in the proper character of nature and the truth of substance, as this brief statement contains, and as I have read and you have understood.

“Thus I believe, and against this faith I shall teach no further: so may God and these holy Gospels help me.”

Afterward the same pontiff ordered you, Berengarius, by the authority of God and of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, not to presume to dispute further with anyone concerning the body and blood of the Lord, except for the purpose of bringing back to this faith those who had departed from it through your teaching.

When you came to Rome under Nicholas, relying on those who had promised you aid because of the benefits you had bestowed on them more than because of any argument they had heard from you, you did not dare defend what you had previously believed. Instead, you asked Pope Nicholas and his council to provide you in words with the faith that ought to be held and to confirm it by writing. The responsibility for this was assigned to Bishop Humbert.

Accordingly, he wrote the words of the faith set out above and, with everyone’s consent, handed them to you to read and confess. You accepted them in submission, read them, confirmed under oath that you believed in this way, and finally subscribed with your own hand.

Pope Nicholas, rejoicing in your conversion, sent your written oath throughout the cities of Italy, [Col. 0412A] Gaul, and Germany, and to every place to which the reputation of your perversity had previously reached, so that just as the Churches had earlier grieved over your turning away from the truth, afterward they might rejoice and give thanks to God for your return and conversion.

Why, then, is this writing attributed more to Bishop Humbert than to you, than to Pope Nicholas, than to his council, or finally than to all the Churches that received it with due reverence and gave thanks to God for your conversion? Why, I ask, unless it is easier for you to persuade the unlearned that one man could have erred than that so many persons and so many Churches could have done so? If you had attributed it to yourself, since you are trying to destroy it, you would appear to be asserting that you are a perjurer. But let us now see how you refute it.

## CHAPTER III

[Col. 0412B]

**BERENGARIUS:** “The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it.”

**LANFRANC:** This can most rightly be turned back against you. The light of faith shines in the darkness of this world, insofar as, with God revealing it, we can behold it through a mirror and in an enigma; but your darkened mind cannot comprehend this light. You despise the rest, thinking yourself alone wise, becoming futile in your thoughts and being made foolish before God.

**BERENGARIUS:** “Because, whether he wishes it or not, the enemy of truth asserts the truth.”

**LANFRANC:** You seem to pay little attention to what you are saying, so intent are you on bringing a servant of God into contempt through the insults you heap upon him.

You make Truth’s defender, whether willing or unwilling, equally an enemy of truth. But whoever asserts the truth does so either willingly or unwillingly. There can be no middle position. Therefore, on your authority, every defender of truth is an enemy of truth. But far be that from us. Truth itself calls its defenders by a very different name in the Gospel, saying: “I shall no longer call you servants, but my friends” (John 15:15); and elsewhere: “You shall be my friends” (ibid., 14). It is therefore false to make the defender of truth, whether willing or unwilling, an enemy of truth.

**BERENGARIUS:** “Because, like Goliath, the Burgundian perishes by his own sword.”

**LANFRANC:** It is your custom to abase others, exalt yourself, boast, and think great things of yourself. You call yourself David and Humbert Goliath. Yet you would more rightly have called yourself Goliath, because you are an exceedingly arrogant man, and you think, write, and say things by which you yourself are, as it were, slaughtered by your own sword. You should have called him David: he lived humbly, taught humbly, was a member of the Church, fought for the Church, and took up the shield of faith and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God (Eph. 6:17).

## CHAPTER IV

**BERENGARIUS:** “But the Burgundian was of the opinion—or rather the madness—of the common people, Paschasius, and Lanfranc: that after consecration the substance of the bread and wine by no means remains on the altar.”

[Col. 0413A] **LANFRANC:** In the time of Pope Saint Leo your heresy was brought before the apostolic see. While he presided over the synod, and a considerable multitude of bishops, abbots, and religious persons of various orders from different regions sat with him, it was ordered that, in the hearing of all, the letter concerning the body and blood of the Lord that you had sent me should be read. For its bearer, your envoy, not finding me in Normandy, delivered it to certain clerics. When they had read it and noticed that it was contrary to the Church’s most customary faith, inflamed by zeal for God they presented it to others for reading and explained its meaning at length to many.

Thus it came about that no less damaging a suspicion arose concerning you than concerning me—to whom, indeed, you had sent such a letter—since many thought that I supported and favored what you were saying, either out of affection for you or because of a faith by which I truly and without hesitation believed it to be so.

Therefore, when a reader recited it at Rome after it had been brought by a cleric from Reims, and it became clear that you exalted John Scotus, condemned Paschasius, and held opinions opposed to the common faith concerning the Eucharist, a sentence of condemnation was pronounced against you, depriving you of communion with the holy Church, which you were striving to deprive of its holy communion. After this the pope ordered me to rise, wipe away the stain of the evil rumor concerning me, explain my faith, and prove what I had explained by sacred authorities more than by arguments.

So I rose, said what I believed, proved what I had said, and what I proved pleased everyone and displeased no one. [Col. 0413C] Then the synod of Vercelli was announced; it was held at Vercelli the following September under the presidency of the same pontiff. You were summoned to it but did not come; I, however, at the command and entreaty of the aforesaid pontiff, remained with him until the synod itself.

At that synod, in the hearing of all who had assembled there from different parts of the world, John Scotus’s book *On the Eucharist* was read and condemned; your statement of doctrine was set forth and condemned; and the faith of the holy Church, which I hold and assert must be held, was heard and confirmed by the unanimous assent of all. Two clerics who claimed to be your envoys, wishing to defend you, failed at the very first entrance and were captured.

Saint Leo never departed from this judgment in any of his councils, whether those at which he himself was present or those which he ordered to be convened through his legates in different provinces. This judgment also did not escape his successor, Pope Victor of blessed memory. Whatever he himself decided or ordered to be decided concerning this or other matters, Victor likewise confirmed by his own authority and that of all his councils.

Finally, at the Council of Tours, whose proceedings were attended and presided over by his legates, you were given the opportunity to defend your position. Since you did not dare undertake its defense, you confessed before everyone and swore that you would believe from that hour as you had sworn at the Roman council, as set out above.

What was done in this matter in the time of Nicholas I, I briefly explained above. I have digressed to say these things because you said: “The Burgundian was of the opinion of the common people, Paschasius, and Lanfranc.” Since the catholic Church is divided into the clerical and lay orders, and the clerical order consists of bishops and the other priests of Christ, as well as ecclesiastical persons of various dignities, and since it is most evident that all these, except for a very few schismatics, hold this faith, you should more rightly have said:

“The Burgundian was of the opinion of the catholic Church, but not of me and my followers, who preferred arrogantly to separate ourselves from it and make schism to our own destruction rather than humbly be its members and healthfully retain the faith we share with it.”

This is what you would have said if you had been a lover of truth, a keeper of justice, and, casting aside the desire for empty glory, had preferred to confess your sins rather than defend them.

But because you call madness the opinion by which we believe that the bread is changed into the true flesh of Christ and the wine into the true blood of Christ, I shall answer you more suitably concerning this when, with God’s help, I have shown by divine authorities and manifest arguments that this faith is true.

Moreover, when you say, “The Burgundian was of the opinion of the common people, Paschasius, and Lanfranc,” you count me among the common people. Be absolutely certain—and let my friends and the Church of Christ believe it without doubt—that, even if I lacked authority and reason with which to defend my faith, I would nevertheless rather be, with the common people, an uncultivated and ignorant Catholic than, with you, a polished and clever heretic. But if the Lord God should deign to bring you and me together in the hearing of the holy council, I trust in his mercy that you would change your words and change your opinion.

**BERENGARIUS:** “He himself overthrew that opinion by his earlier words, and did not pay attention.”

**LANFRANC:** While you pursue him with insatiable hatred, you are not at all ashamed to disgrace yourself. For whoever swears contradictory things must necessarily incur the charge of perjury in one of them. Therefore, since you assert that the words handed to you for swearing are contradictory to one another, you shamelessly proclaim in a clear voice that you are a perjurer.

O unhappy man! O most wretched soul! Why did you swear that you believed what you understood to be so greatly at variance with itself? [Col. 0414D] Would it not have been better, if you thought you possessed the true faith, to end your life by an honorable death than to commit perjury, swear faithlessness, and renounce the faith?

But far be it from us to think that the writing of the holy council is divided by any opposition of contradiction, if a careful reader applies himself to understanding it after removing the desire to slander. This will become clear later.

## CHAPTER V

**BERENGARIUS:** “For whoever says, ‘The bread and wine of the altar are merely sacraments,’ or, ‘The bread and wine of the altar are merely the true body and blood of Christ,’ establishes in every way that the bread and wine remain.”

**LANFRANC:** The Roman synod decreed that none of these things should be believed, nor did Bishop Humbert hand you any of them to confess or swear. The first statement—“The bread and wine of the altar are merely sacraments”—is yours and that of your followers. The second, which declares, “The bread and wine of the altar are merely the true body and blood of Christ,” belongs to no one.

For you deny the reality of the flesh and blood, while the Church of Christ believes that the bread is changed into flesh and the wine into blood in such a way that it nevertheless healthfully believes and truly recognizes it to be the sacrament of the Lord’s passion, divine propitiation, concord, and unity, and finally of the flesh and blood assumed from the Virgin, each in its own distinct manner. These matters will be discussed more clearly in their proper place and time.

For the present I have undertaken only to show that the words of the Roman council, which you confirmed under oath that you would preserve, differ from one another by no contradiction. For when your friends and associates accuse you that you ought either not to have sworn what you were not going to preserve or to preserve what you had sworn, you are accustomed to defame Pope Nicholas and the other Fathers of the Roman council, alleging that, while teaching and knowing contradictory things, they were the cause of your perjury. You strive to accomplish this almost everywhere in the work that I have undertaken to destroy; therefore your words must be compared with theirs.

Pope Nicholas, discovering that you taught that the bread and wine of the altar remained after consecration in their former essences without material change, granted you permission to respond, as stated above. When you did not dare answer anything in defense of your position, moved by compassion toward your requests he ordered that the writing I set out above be handed to you. Its beginning was this:

“ I, Berengarius, anathematize that heresy concerning which I have hitherto been infamous, which attempts to assert that the bread and wine placed on the altar are, after consecration, merely the sacrament and not the true body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ.”

This was entirely right: he ordered it, the synod assented, and you carried it out—if you had not spoken with deceitful lips and a deceitful heart, and if, in your misery and perjury, you had not afterward returned to your former vomit and the mire in which you had wallowed. For we are instructed by the authority of the sacred canons that no one returning from heresy is permitted to share in ecclesiastical communion until he is compelled to condemn the perverse doctrine by the bond of anathema.

Yet in these words no one will be able to find either the words you set out above or their meaning. Hence it is clear that you are a perverter and subverter of the divine writings, scattering clouds of error among the unlearned from corrupted and fabricated statements, and that whatever has proceeded from a false premise is itself false.

## CHAPTER VI

**BERENGARIUS:** “For just as one who says, ‘Christ is the supreme cornerstone,’ does not remove Christ but altogether establishes that Christ exists, so one who says, ‘The bread of the altar is merely the sacrament,’ or, ‘The bread of the altar is merely the true body of Christ,’ does not deny that bread is on the altar but confirms that bread and wine exist on the Lord’s table.”

[Col. 0416A] **LANFRANC:** You would speak truly if anyone, ignorant of the truth, established the first part of the proposition—unless perhaps he uttered that expression in a figurative manner. For we are accustomed to call things by the names of the things from which they are made, even though, after being transferred into another nature, they can no longer be what the things from which they are shown to have been made are.

Thus blessed Augustine, at the end of his exposition of the Psalms, calls “crystal” “snow hardened by many years of time and the succession of ages” (on Ps. 147), although snow is liquid [Col. 0416B] and moist, whereas the nature of crystal is hard and dry. Since the two therefore have such different natures, no one could rightly call crystal snow except in that manner of speech by which a thing produced is customarily called by the material name.

Likewise the Creator says to the first man created from earth in Genesis: “You are earth, and to earth you shall go” (Gen. 3:19), as if he were saying: “Because you were made from earth, you will at some time become earth and return to earth.”
