Nevertheless, as I said, no Catholic accepts these statements; the Christian religion does not admit them. No one who has any doubt can fail to recognize that the first is yours alone and belongs to your sect. But you do not accept the second either, since you deny the flesh and blood; nor do we, who confess both in such a way that we do not deny that they are also the figure and sacrament of many lofty things.

Moreover, the comparison you have made between the Lord Jesus Christ and the cornerstone hinders you but helps us. For just as one who says, “Christ is the cornerstone,” does not actually establish that Christ is a stone but gives him that name because of some similarity between them, so, when the divine page calls the Lord’s body “bread,” it does so in sacred and mystical language—either because it is made from bread and retains certain of its qualities; or because, by feeding the soul incomprehensibly, it satisfies it and supplies it with the substance of eternal life; or because it is the body of the Son of God, who is the bread of angels and upon whom, as the prince of the apostles says, the angels desire to look (1 Pet. 1:12); or for some other reason that the more learned can understand but we cannot.

## CHAPTER VII

**BERENGARIUS:** “For every affirmation cannot stand when one part has been undermined; and this, as blessed Augustine says in his book *On Christian Doctrine*, ‘stands indissolubly in the very truth of eternity, which is God.’”

**LANFRANC:** Having abandoned the sacred authorities, you flee to dialectic. Indeed, when I am about to hear and answer matters that ought to pertain to the mystery of faith, I would rather hear and answer sacred authorities than dialectical arguments. Nevertheless, it will also be my task to answer these things, lest you think that I am deficient here through lack of skill in the discipline—though to some this may seem boastful and more a matter of display than necessity.

But God is my witness, and my conscience, that in treating the divine writings I would neither wish to propose nor answer dialectical questions or their solutions. Yet when the matter under discussion is such that it can be explained more precisely by the rules of this discipline, I conceal the art, as far as I can, through equivalent propositions, lest I appear to trust in technique more than in truth and the authority of the holy Fathers. Blessed Augustine, however, in some of his writings, and especially in *On Christian Doctrine*, praises this discipline very fully and confirms that it is of great value for everything investigated in the sacred writings.

Finally, when contending against the Arian heretic Felicianus, he so hemmed him in by this art (ch. 4) that the heretic himself, unable to endure the intricate and entangling connections of the logical topics and syllogisms, cried out publicly: “You contend with me with Aristotelian subtlety, and you hurl down everything I say like a torrent.”

Thus, when you sought above to establish that the bread and wine of the altar are not essentially changed during consecration, you adopted two propositions as argumentative premises. I proved by clear arguments that one of them was yours alone and that the other belonged to no human being. In this matter you committed a serious error.

For what was yours was a matter for investigation. We are trying to crush and overthrow it with the whole weight and force of our arguments. But no matter under investigation can be a premise of an argument. A premise of an argument must either be certain in itself or be established by certain reasons. What was yours alone therefore ought not to have been assumed to prove a doubtful matter.

Nor was it appropriate by any reasoning to use the remaining proposition, which belongs to no human being, to establish a doubtful matter. For who would think that something all deny and no one confesses is certain or can be made certain? It was therefore not rational to take that as an argument either. You placed both propositions badly.

By repeatedly restating these two most defective premises, you weave your entire argument together all the way to its conclusion. [Col. 0417D] Consequently, whatever has been derived from defective and ungranted premises must necessarily be defective and inadmissible.

You also try to prove by another argument that the bread and wine remain in their principal essences after consecration, saying: “Every affirmation cannot stand when one part has been undermined.” To prove this, you ought not to have introduced a particular negation, from which nothing can be inferred concerning the present question, but rather a universal one, by which it would be stated that no affirmation can stand when one part has been undermined.

Let your negation be particular: “Not every affirmation can stand when one part has been undermined.” Your further assumption is: “The bread and wine of the altar are merely the sacrament,” or, “The bread and wine of the altar are merely the true body and blood of Christ.” Both are affirmations. From these two particular premises, can you regularly conclude that, when one part has been undermined, they cannot stand? Certainly not! In no figure of the syllogism is any conclusion validly inferred from two particular premises. You therefore placed it badly.

Nor should we pass over perfunctorily the fact that you claimed the truth of the aforesaid proposition to stand indissolubly in the very truth of eternity, which is God, and confirmed it by the authority of blessed Augustine’s *On Christian Doctrine*. The proposition itself is indeed true, and, placed in its proper position, it would possess the force of a true proposition; but you placed it badly and ineffectively.

Nor is its truth any more than that of all other propositions, whether concerning things or otherwise, eternally established in the truth of God, who knows and foreknows all things, who established the things themselves in their primary and secondary essences, and appointed them to be the causes of propositions both true and false.

Nevertheless, in the work *On Christian Doctrine*, blessed Augustine nowhere mentions either this proposition or any similar one. Anyone can easily know this if he takes care to read the book, if he has never read it, or to reread it, if he has perhaps already read it. In this matter I am greatly astonished either at your error or at your stupidity: error, if you do not know that the testimonies you have brought forward are otherwise in the sacred books or are entirely absent; stupidity, if you suppose the rest of us so foolish that they will immediately believe your statements against the ancient faith of the Church and pass them by as though they were sacred and unquestionable.

## CHAPTER VIII

**BERENGARIUS:** “There is an affirmation, constant in its most well-known parts, predicate and subject, which states: ‘The bread and wine placed on the altar are merely sacraments’; and likewise one which states: ‘The bread and wine placed on the altar are, after consecration, merely the true body and blood of Christ.’”

**LANFRANC:** You are not ashamed to repeat the same things; therefore I too must repeat what I set out shortly before. I said above that the first statement is yours alone, while the second belongs to no human being, and I established this with clearer evidence. For you deny the flesh and blood, establishing the whole matter in the sacrament alone; whereas we confess the sacrament and nevertheless faithfully and truly confess the reality of both.

As for your effort to insert dialectical terms—“affirmation,” “predicate,” “subject,” and the rest—into the treatment of so great a matter, you seem to do this for no other reason than that, by this opportunity, you may persuade the unlearned that you are skilled in disputation. For even without these names you could assert what you are attempting no less effectively, and we could refute your statements solely by sacred testimonies.

**BERENGARIUS:** “The Burgundian had undertaken to deny that bread and wine remain on the Lord’s table. He does not deny this at all; rather, he entirely confirms that they are bread and wine.”

[Col. 0419A] **LANFRANC:** A member of the Church ought not to disagree with the Church. For the Church, spread throughout the whole world, confesses that bread and wine are placed on the altar for consecration, but that during consecration they are incomprehensibly and ineffably changed into the substance of flesh and blood. With the help, in its proper place, of him whose most sacred body we are discussing, this will be shown to be so and unable to be otherwise by the varied testimonies of different Fathers.

He does not, however, deny bread; rather, he confirms it—but the bread that came down from heaven and gives life to the world, the bread that Ambrose and Augustine, in the same words, call *epiousion*, that is, “supersubstantial,” because Christ’s flesh is greater than all created substances [Col. 0419B] and surpasses all creatures in the most excellent dignity.

Nor is the wine just any wine, but the wine that gladdens the hearts of human beings—not indeed all human beings, but the servants of God—which intoxicates souls and cleanses them from sins.

**BERENGARIUS:** “When he thus states: ‘The bread and wine placed on the altar are, after consecration, [Col. 0419B] merely the true body and blood of Christ.’”

**LANFRANC:** Someone filled with the Spirit of God said: “The mouth that lies kills the soul” (Wis. 1:2). If you feared this fearful sentence, you would not bring a false accusation against a servant of God. For he said all the rest, but he did not at all use the adverb “merely.” Whatever is gathered from a lie that you falsely assert, whatever is inferred from it, necessarily falls apart, is weakened, and is nullified in its entirety. Since I have dealt sufficiently with this in the preceding sections, I shall refrain from saying more here and pass on to other matters.

## CHAPTER IX
BERENGAR. “Through the consecration of the altar, bread and wine become the sacrament of religion—not so that they cease to be what they were, but so that they are what they were and are changed into something else, as blessed Ambrose says in the book *On the Sacraments*.”

LANFRANC. O deranged mind! O shamelessly lying man! O temerity deserving punishment! You presume to summon Ambrose as a witness to the claim that the bread and wine of the altar, through consecration, do not cease to be what they were, but are changed into something else that they were not. [Col. 0419D] Yet if you were to examine all the books written by Ambrose on the sacraments or on other subjects, all those which the Church now uses, you would nowhere be able to find anything said by Ambrose and explained in this way. If he had said such a thing, he would have greatly diminished his illustrious reputation, contradicted himself, and established that an incredible matter ought to be believed. For who in his right mind would believe that something is changed into another thing and yet does not, in that respect, cease to be what it was? But may the truth itself, which is God, always keep far away the possibility that a witness of truth should stand as a witness against the truth.

Rather, hear what he says in the book *On the Mysteries*, or *On Initiation*. Wishing to show the difference between the manna of the Jews and the sacrifice of Christians—namely, that the former was shadow and figure, [Col. 0420A] whereas the latter is light and truth; the former came from heaven, while the latter is the body of the Lord of heaven—lest the mind should refuse to believe that such great elements could be changed into such great realities, he added these words, saying (chapter 9):

> “By how many examples, then, shall we prove that this is not what nature formed, but what blessing consecrated; and that the power of blessing is greater than that of nature, because by blessing nature itself is also changed?”

No one can doubt, and no one is ignorant, that bread and wine are formed by nature. He shows by clear examples that one ought not to doubt their conversion into the true body of the Lord, and he confirms the matter by suitable arguments through parallels: first, recounting Moses’ rod changed into a serpent, then the serpent changed back into a rod; afterward, the waters changed into blood, and then [Col. 0420B] the blood returned to water. He gives many other examples of this kind.

Finally, after first mentioning that great and singular miracle, the Virgin’s childbirth, he says:

> “And this body which we make is from the Virgin.”

And lest you should place nature above divine power, as though God could not change the nature of anything, he responds:

> “Why do you seek the order of nature in Christ’s body, when the Lord Jesus himself was born from a Virgin contrary to nature?”

The sixth book *On the Sacraments*, in which work you falsely asserted that he had uttered the falsehood mentioned above, begins as follows:

> “Just as our Lord Jesus Christ is truly the Son of God—not by grace, as are other human beings, but by nature—so his flesh is truly the flesh which we receive, and his blood is truly the blood which we drink.”

Let these very few statements from among many suffice, so that readers may clearly recognize the fraud with which you fabricate what you have not found; the cunning with which you corrupt what you have found; the obstinacy with which you attempt to twist into something else whatever you leave untouched. Scarcely any heretical depravity since the time of Lucian and Hesychius has been comparable to this wickedness. Both of them distorted the prophetic, evangelical, and apostolic Scriptures for the advantage of their own cause. Every heresy has indeed misunderstood the sacred writings, but nevertheless allowed them to remain in their own state without overturning them entirely.

In the fourth discourse *On the Sacraments*, when the aforementioned teacher was striving to show that it is not surprising if things which exist, by divine power, pass into something else—because, at God’s command, all things made from nothing likewise subsist—he added:

> “If, then, there is such power in the word of the Lord Jesus that things which were not began to exist, how much more operative is it that things which were should exist and be changed into something else?”

He testifies that they are what they were according to visible appearance, but that they are changed according to their inner essence into the nature of those things which previously did not exist. In this way he himself explains the “before” and “after,” using different words but not expressing different opinions. I therefore think that you took from this the statement which you previously introduced, and which, though tolerably said, you have explained intolerably.

In some manuscripts, however, the aforementioned sentence is found in different words, as follows:

> “If, then, there is such power in the word of the Lord Jesus that things which were not began to exist, how much more operative is it that things which were should be changed into something else?”

This reading agrees very closely in meaning with the passage found in the book *On the Mysteries*, or *On Initiation*, published by the same author (chapter 9), in these words:

> “Therefore, can the word of Christ, which was able to make from nothing what did not exist, not change the things which exist into what they were not?”

## CHAPTER X

BERENGAR. “The sacrifice of the Church consists of and is accomplished by two things: the visible and the invisible, the sacrament and the reality of the sacrament. Yet if that reality—that is, Christ’s body—were before our eyes, it would be visible. But, raised into heaven and seated at the right hand of the Father until the times of the restoration of all things, of which the apostle Peter writes, it cannot be summoned down from heaven, just as Christ’s person consists of God and man.”

LANFRANC. Caiaphas, when he was high priest that year, prophesied the truth about the Savior without knowing it, saying that it was more expedient for one man to die for the world than for every man of the whole world to perish (John 11:49–51). He spoke the truth, although he did not know where his words tended. So you too, wishing to speak against our cause, plainly assert the very position which we have undertaken to defend. For this is what we say; this is what we strive by every means to prove against you and your followers: namely, that the sacrifice of the Church is accomplished by two things and consists of two things—the visible appearance of the elements and the invisible flesh and blood of the Lord Jesus, the sacrament and the reality of the sacrament. This reality, to use your own words, is Christ’s body, just as Christ’s person, by your own testimony, consists and is constituted of God and man, since Christ himself is true God and true man, because every reality contains within itself the nature and truth of the things from which it is constituted.

The sacrifice of the Church is constituted, as you too testify, by the sacrament and the reality of the sacrament, that is, by Christ’s body. It is therefore the sacrament and the reality of the sacrament—that is, Christ’s body.

Yet Christ, rising from the dead, dies no more; death shall no longer rule over him (Romans 6:9). But, as the apostle Andrew says, although his flesh was truly eaten on earth and his blood truly drunk, he nevertheless remains whole and alive in heaven at the right hand of the Father until the times of the restoration of all things. If you ask how this can happen, I answer briefly for the present: the mystery of faith may rightly be believed, but cannot profitably be investigated.

## CHAPTER XI

BERENGAR. “Therefore blessed Augustine says in the Gospel: ‘When Christ is eaten, life is eaten. Nor, when we eat, do we make parts of him.’”

LANFRANC. Blessed Augustine said nothing in the Gospel, since no one is ever read to have spoken something in the Gospel except the Lord, the evangelists, and those persons whom the writers of the Gospel report as speaking there according to the nature of the events and the circumstances of the times. He did, however, write an extensive work expounding the Lord’s Gospel according to John historically. In that work the statement quoted above is found, and we devoutly accept and honor it with due reverence, because it supports us and agrees with the truth. He says:

> “Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him” (John 6:55).

“Nor, when we eat, do we make parts of him.”

Far be it from us to understand Christ as eaten in the manner imagined by those who, when they heard the Lord say, “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you shall not have life in yourselves” (ibid., 54), immediately replied, “This is a hard saying; who can hear it?” (ibid., 61). For, as the author mentioned above says in many places, they thought that they would tear the Lord, while he lived on earth, into pieces, and that they would eat his flesh either boiled in cauldrons or roasted on spits; or, if they were unwilling to do this, they could not be his disciples. Therefore they chose to depart and no longer go with him.

May God keep such an opinion far from his Church! We eat and drink Christ, sacrificed on earth, in such a way that he nevertheless always remains whole and alive in heaven at the right hand of the Father.

## CHAPTER XII

BERENGAR. “Therefore blessed Augustine, in the book *The City of God*: ‘A sacrament is a sacred sign.’ In the book *On Christian Doctrine* he defines a sign: ‘A sign is a thing which, beyond the appearance that it presents to the senses, causes something else to come into thought.’”

LANFRANC. We too believe, and urge others to believe, that the sacrament of which we are speaking is a sacred sign. Through this sign, beyond the appearance which presents itself to the eyes of those who look upon it, something far different and very other comes beneficially into the mind of those who understand.

What that is—or rather, what those things are—I briefly mentioned above, and shall explain more fully a little later. Nevertheless, blessed Augustine, in *The City of God* (book X, chapter 5, volume V), did not define a sacrament as a sacred sign as abruptly as you claim. In that passage he was not speaking of the body and blood of the Lord, but was treating the rite of Jewish sacrifices. Since invisible realities—through which human society is directed toward loving God and one’s neighbor—were signified by visible sacrifices, he concluded the approved view in a few words, saying:

> “A visible sacrifice, therefore, is the sacrament of an invisible sacrifice, that is, a sacred sign.”

He explains later in these words what he called the visible and invisible sacrifice:

> “God does not desire the sacrifice of a slaughtered animal, but he desires the sacrifice of a contrite heart.”

And shortly afterward:

> “Moreover, mercy is the true sacrifice.”

## CHAPTER XIII

BERENGAR. “Augustine, in his letter to Bishop Boniface: ‘If sacraments did not bear a likeness to the realities whose sacraments they are, they would not be sacraments at all.’ Likewise, in *On Catechizing the Uninstructed*: ‘The signs of divine realities are indeed visible, but invisible realities are honored in them; nor should the appearance sanctified by blessing be regarded in the same way as it is regarded in ordinary use.’”

LANFRANC. Anyone who has devoted even slight attention to the sacred writings cannot fail to know this. Sacraments always bear a likeness to the realities whose sacraments they are. Thus, in the sacrament about which this dispute is being conducted, when the host is broken and blood is poured from the chalice into the mouths of the faithful, what else is signified than the sacrifice of the Lord’s body on the cross and the outpouring of his blood from his side?

Otherwise it would not be a sacrament, if the name “sacrament” is understood in the way in which we now understand it and in which we believe readers or hearers understand it. For *sacramentum* also means an oath—not because it bears a likeness to some reality, but because the confirmation or denial of something takes place with reference to sacred matters.

Thus blessed Gregory, in his letter to Justin (letter 23), says:

> “With regard to the most sacred body of blessed Peter, we compelled him, in addition, to provide strict oaths.”

A sacrament is also called the consecration of something, just as an argument is the confirmation of a doubtful matter and a support is the sustaining of a thing that is about to fall.

But the passage which you took from the book *On Catechizing the Uninstructed*, asserting that invisible realities are to be honored in visible things and that an appearance sanctified by blessing is not to be regarded in the same way as one that has not been sanctified—I plainly do not see how it benefits your side. Indeed, it seems rather to attack your position and support ours.

For in the appearance of bread and wine which we see, we honor invisible realities, that is, Christ’s flesh and blood. Nor do we esteem these two appearances, from which the Lord’s body is consecrated, in the same way as we esteemed them before consecration, while faithfully confessing that before consecration they are bread and wine—that is, the things which nature formed. During the consecration, however, they are changed into Christ’s flesh and blood, both realities having been consecrated by blessing.

Although blessed Augustine, in that book, was speaking no more about this sacrament than about the other practices which Christian custom commands and solemnly performs, he was instructing a certain deacon of the Church of Carthage how he ought to instruct the uneducated concerning these matters and the others.

## CHAPTER XIV

BERENGAR. “Therefore blessed Augustine, in his letter to Boniface: ‘As the sacrament of Christ’s body is Christ’s body in a certain manner, and the sacrament of Christ’s blood is Christ’s blood in a certain manner, so the sacrament of faith is faith.’”

LANFRANC. The sacrament of Christ’s body, insofar as it concerns the fact that the Lord Christ himself was sacrificed on the cross, is his flesh, which we receive in the sacrament covered by the form of bread; and it is his blood, which we drink under the appearance and taste of wine. Flesh is the sacrament of flesh, and blood the sacrament of blood.

By flesh and blood, both invisible, intelligible, and spiritual, the visible, tangible body of the Redeemer is signified, plainly full of the grace of every virtue and of divine majesty. When the one is broken and distributed for the salvation of the people, while the other is poured from the chalice and taken by the mouths of the faithful, his death on the cross and the outflow of his blood from his side are represented.

Blessed Gregory carefully attends to both matters and explains them clearly in the fourth book of the *Dialogues*, saying (book IV, chapter 58):

> “For his flesh is received there, and his blood is poured—not now into the hands of unbelievers, but into the mouths of the faithful. We must therefore consider what kind of sacrifice this is which continually imitates the death of the Only-Begotten Son for our absolution.”

He said “imitates,” not “effects,” because Christ, rising from the dead, dies no more; death shall no longer rule over him (Romans 6:9).

The flesh and blood by which we are daily nourished in order to obtain God’s mercy for our sins are called Christ’s body and blood, not only because they are essentially the same, though differing greatly in qualities, but also because of that mode of expression by which the signifying reality is accustomed to be called by the name of the reality signified.

No one will rightly be troubled if the same flesh and the same blood are the sacraments of themselves, understood in one way and another, since the Lord Jesus himself, after his resurrection, served as the type and figure of himself according to different circumstances of time.

When he appeared to two disciples and spoke with them, judging that this was sufficient, while he pretended to be going farther (Luke 24:13–28), he signified, as blessed Augustine says, that after a few days he would ascend into heaven. That journey is far removed from ordinary human life, which was very clearly represented by the two disciples. Christ, therefore, is the sacrament of Christ: pretending to go farther, he represented Christ who in due time would ascend farther into heaven. The same and yet not entirely the same. For he was true God and true man both when pretending and when ascending. Nevertheless, the fiction of an earthly journey is one thing, and the truth of the one ascending into heaven another. No one would be so foolish as to presume to deny that the one pretending to go farther was the true Christ, because by that fiction of a longer journey he signified that the true Christ would ascend into heaven.

Moreover, in the same letter to Boniface, blessed Augustine calls baptism the sacrament of faith. True baptism, however, consists not so much in the washing of the body as in the faith of the heart, as apostolic teaching declares:

> “Cleansing their hearts by faith” (Acts 15:9);

and elsewhere:

> “So also baptism now saves you—not the removal of dirt from the flesh, but the appeal of a good conscience toward God” (1 Peter 3:21).

One thing, however, is signified by the other. For through the washing applied externally to the body, the purification of the soul is expressed, which inner faith effects. Baptism is called faith according to that form of expression by which the mystery of the thing whose mystery it is is customarily designated by its name.

The reason for this is the likeness which must always be found both in the sacrament and in the reality of the sacrament, as in baptism and faith. Both wash, cleanse, and purify: the former the flesh, the latter the mind.

Therefore, just as the heavenly bread, which is Christ’s true flesh, is in its own manner called Christ’s body—namely, the body which was visible, tangible, and mortal, and was hung upon the cross—and just as the sacrifice of that very flesh, performed by the priest’s hands, is called Christ’s passion, death, and crucifixion, not by the truth of the event but by the signifying mystery, so the sacrament of faith, which means baptism, is faith.

## CHAPTER XV

BERENGAR. “Blessed Augustine, in his letter to Boniface: ‘Christ was sacrificed once in himself.’ Yet in the sacrament he is sacrificed for the people not only throughout all the solemnities of Easter but every day.”

LANFRANC. Christ was sacrificed once in himself because, in the manifestation of his body and in the distinction of all his members, he hung upon the cross only once as true God and true man, offering himself to the Father as a living, suffering, mortal sacrifice, effective for the redemption of the living and the dead—namely, of those whom the height of the divine counsel judged, foreknew, predestined, and called to be redeemed, in the ways and at the times at which this was fitting.

In the sacrament which the Church continually celebrates in memory of this event, however, the Lord’s flesh is sacrificed, [Col. 0425C] divided, and eaten every day, and his blood is drunk from the chalice by the mouths of the faithful. Both are true; both were taken from the Virgin. The flesh is received by itself and the blood by itself, not without a definite sacramental meaning.

Although, in another mode of expression, the whole Christ is said and believed to be eaten when eternal life—which is Christ himself—is desired with spiritual longing; when remembrance of his commandments, sweeter than honey and the honeycomb, is kept in the mind; when fraternal charity, whose sign this sacrament bears, is cherished for Christ’s sake; and when it is sweetly and beneficially stored in memory that, for the salvation of human beings, he was subjected to insults, hung upon the cross, fastened with nails, and pierced by a lance.

Both forms of eating are necessary, and both are fruitful. Each requires the other in order to accomplish something good. For if the former is absent, the latter not only does not cleanse sins but increases them and condemns those who presume. “Whoever eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself” (1 Corinthians 11:29).

The latter, moreover, cannot or ought not to exist without the former. For this reason the Lord’s prayer speaks of daily bread, as blessed Ambrose (*On the Sacraments*, chapter 4) and holy Cyprian explain, and as the Gospel says:

> “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you shall not have life in yourselves” (John 6:54).

The sacred canons also command that those who do not communicate in the sacrament of Christ’s body are not to be counted among Catholics, unless perhaps they abstain, in the manner of penitents and by episcopal judgment, on account of capital sins.

It is therefore useless for you to infer and say:

> “If Christ suffered once in himself, he also suffered once in his body, because his body can in no way be separated from him.”

This does not follow. For there are many things in realities which cannot be predicated of the parts of those realities. Although the Lord Jesus himself is true God and true man, and every human being consists of a rational soul and a body, neither the soul itself nor the body itself can properly be called a human being or God.

## CHAPTER XVI

BERENGAR. “I agree, says Burgundus, with the holy Roman Church. In truth, Truth itself did not encounter a holy Church, but the Church of the Malignant, a council of vanity—not an apostolic see, but the seat of Satan.”

LANFRANC. You should not say, “I agree, says Burgundus,” but “I, Berengar, agree.” These were your words; by these you deceived the holy council into believing that this was your faith; by oath you affirmed that you would preserve it.

The venerable Humbert, whom you name reproachfully as “Burgundus,” as though God could not have servants of his own in Burgundy, did nothing other than hand you the very document, as the synod had commanded, placing his hand in yours.

But, unhappy soul, you first passed from heresy to perjury, and now you have returned again from perjury to heresy. For this reason, having been handed over to a reprobate mind, you call the holy Roman Church the Church of the Malignant, the council of vanity, and the seat of Satan.

With your impious mouth you babbled what no one is read to have babbled—not a heretic, not a schismatic, not any false Christian. For all who, from the beginning of the Christian Church, gloried in the dignity of the Christian name—even if some, abandoning the path of truth, preferred to walk through the byways of error—nevertheless greatly honored the see of blessed Peter the apostle, and never presumed either to utter or to write such blasphemy against it.

Anyone who reads their writings knows this beyond doubt: writings which the apostolic see received from them, sent or delivered at different times and for different reasons.

Finally, the Lord himself addresses it honorably in the Gospel, saying:

> “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church. And the gates of hell shall not prevail against it. And I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven. And whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven” (Matthew 16:18–19).

Although these words are believed to have been spoken about the pastors of the holy Church and are explained in this way by certain Catholics, the sacred canons and decrees of the pontiffs testify that they are to be understood especially of the Roman Church.

## CHAPTER XVII

BERENGAR. “Who could either conceive by reason or concede that it could happen by a miracle that bread is broken in Christ’s body, which after the resurrection lives in complete incorruptibility and remains in heaven, incapable of being summoned down, until the times of the restoration of all things?”

[Col. 0427A] LANFRANC. The just person, who lives by faith, does not seek to investigate by arguments or conceive by reason how bread becomes flesh and wine is changed into blood, with the nature of each essentially changed. He prefers to place faith in heavenly mysteries, so that he may eventually be able to attain the rewards of faith, rather than, abandoning faith, labor uselessly to comprehend things that cannot be comprehended. He knows that it is written:

> “Do not seek what is too high for you, and do not search into things too strong for you; but always think upon what God has commanded you, and do not be curious about many of his works” (Ecclesiasticus 3:22).

For it is not necessary for you to see with your eyes the things that are hidden.

He nevertheless concedes that this can happen through the miraculous operation of divine power. Nor have there been lacking, for certain doubters, miracles worthy of belief, in which, once the coverings of visible and corruptible things had been removed, the flesh and blood of Christ appeared to bodily eyes just as they truly are. In these events almighty God mercifully healed the weakness of the infirm and terribly condemned and overturned the detestable depravity of all heretics.

It is the business of such people to mock the simple faith of infants and sucklings, from whose mouths Christ perfected praise (Psalm 8:3; Matthew 21:16), and to wish to comprehend everything by reason, although they themselves are devoid of reason. Through arrogance and barrenness they have become like horse and mule, in which there is no understanding (Psalm 31:9).

But when you oppose the incorruption of the Lord’s body, and the fact that it cannot be summoned down from heaven until the day of judgment, as though this were an argument against our faith—by which we believe that it is truly eaten by the faithful—you either do not understand our faith at all, or, by explaining what you have understood perversely, strive to corrupt it to your own destruction.

For we believe that the Lord Jesus is truly and beneficially eaten on earth by those who receive him worthily, while we hold with complete certainty that he exists in heaven undefiled, incorrupt, and unharmed.

You would be foolish if you said that the widow of Zarephath could not have eaten the oil with which her jar was filled because, as sacred history testifies, the jar of oil was not diminished, when the same Scripture says:

> “She went and did according to the word of Elijah; and she ate, and he and her household for many days” (1 Kings 17:15).

You are burdened by no less a folly if you attempt to assert that the Church cannot be nourished by the flesh and blood of her Redeemer because the Apostle says:

> “Christ, rising from the dead, dies no more; death shall no longer rule over him” (Romans 6:9),

while the Lord himself, speaking to his disciples, testifies:

> “Take and eat; this is my body which shall be delivered for you” (Matthew 26:26; Mark 14:22);

and:

> “This is the cup of my blood, the mystery of faith, which shall be poured out for you and for many” (Luke 22:20);

and:

> “The bread which I shall give is my flesh for the life of the world” (John 6:52);

and:

> “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you shall not have life in yourselves” (ibid., 54).

From these words of the Lord two heresies arose in ancient times. In this respect they all agreed: bread and wine were converted into the true flesh of the Son of Man and his true blood. But they did not all hold the same opinion concerning who this Son of Man was.

Some thought that this should be understood as any human being whatsoever, whether just or sinful, into whose flesh and blood the earthly substance would be converted and then received for the remission of sins.

Others thought that this was not just any human being from the crowd, but a just and sanctified man, separated from ordinary human life by the height of his way of life; one who was the temple of God and truly possessed divine indwelling within himself. In the flesh and blood of such a man, they madly asserted with heretical obstinacy, bread and wine of the altar could be changed.

This occurred a few years after the death of blessed Augustine, in the time of Pope Celestine and Cyril, bishop of Alexandria. At their command and through their efforts, the Council of Ephesus was summoned and celebrated—one of the four councils which blessed Gregory, in his letter to the patriarchs (book I, letter 34), confesses that he receives, embraces, and venerates just as he does the four holy Gospels of our Lord Jesus Christ.

At that council both of the deadly plagues described above were condemned, and the faith was strengthened by which we believe that bread is converted into the flesh which hung upon the cross, and wine into the blood which flowed from the side of the one hanging upon the cross.

[Note: [Col. 0427] In the *Symbol*, approximately midway, volume V, in the first part of the Letter of Cyril and the synod to Nestorius.]

Finally, the two hundred bishops who attended that council wrote as follows, among other things, concerning this sacrament, and sent it to Bishop Nestorius as though to the head of the heretics:

> “We approach the mystical blessings and are sanctified, becoming participants in the holy body and precious blood of Christ, the Redeemer of us all—not as receiving common flesh, God forbid! Nor as receiving the flesh of a sanctified man united to the Word according to a unity of dignity, or as receiving one who possesses divine indwelling; but as receiving flesh truly life-giving and made the proper flesh of the Word himself. For since he exists naturally as Life, being God, and has been united to his own flesh, he has declared it to be life-giving.
>
> “Therefore, although he says to us, ‘Amen, amen, I say to you, unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood’ (John 6:54), we must not regard that flesh as belonging to an ordinary man, one of us. For how could the flesh of a man, according to its nature, be life-giving? Rather, we must regard it as truly made his own—the flesh of the one who, for us, both became and was called the Son of Man.”

And near the end of the council (chapter, or anathema, 11):

> “If anyone does not confess that the flesh of the Lord is life-giving and is the proper flesh of the Word of God the Father, but regards it as belonging to another person joined to him according to dignity, or as belonging to one who merely possesses divine indwelling, and does not rather confess that it is life-giving because it has become the proper flesh of the Word who wills to give life, let him be anathema.”

What could you desire to hear more clearly, if you would abandon your mind’s pursuit of new controversy for the pursuit of ancient peace?

As the holy synod defines, this flesh is not [the flesh] of any man from the common people, nor of a just and sanctified man, but rather [the flesh] of him to whom he himself was united—that is, became incarnate—as God and man [the transmitted wording is uncertain].

When the council says “mystical blessings,” understand this as though it had said “secret blessings.” For, as blessed Augustine says in the book *On Catechizing the Uninstructed*, the word *mystery* derives its name from secrecy.

What is more secret than to see the appearance of bread and wine, taste their flavor, feel them by touch, and yet, through God’s marvelous operation, believe, eat, and drink true flesh and true blood?

If you would read these and similar passages, scattered throughout almost the whole body of the divine writings, humbly and with a view to eternal life, having put aside the desire for empty boasting; if, while reading, you understood them through divine grace obtained by pouring out prayers to the Lord; if, with Christian caution, you distinguished what ought to be taken literally from what ought to be understood spiritually, without doubt you would believe what the universal Church believes and proclaim what apostolic teaching established should be proclaimed throughout the entire world: namely, that the flesh and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ are eaten and drunk both by the mouth of the body and by the mouth of the heart—that is, bodily and spiritually.

With the bodily mouth, we eat and drink bodily whenever we receive the Lord’s own body from the Lord’s altar through the hand of the priest. With the spiritual mouth of the heart, however, it is eaten and drunk spiritually when what the Only-Begotten Son of God did for the salvation of the world—taking flesh, hanging upon the cross, rising, appearing, ascending, and coming on the day of judgment to repay each person according to his works—is sweetly and beneficially stored in memory.

This eating is beneficial to Christ’s poor when, seated at so great a table of so rich a man, they eat in such a way that they are filled and remember in such a way that they imitate: always prepared to die for Christ, continually putting to death their members that are upon the earth (Colossians 3:5), and crucifying their flesh with its vices and desires (Galatians 5:24), as it is written:

> “You have sat at a great table; know that you must prepare such things” (Ecclesiasticus 31:12).

Concerning bodily eating, the Lord says to his disciples:

> “Take, eat, and drink; this is my body which shall be delivered for you” (Matthew 26:26);

and:

> “This is the cup of my blood, which shall be poured out for you” (Luke 22:20).

The Apostle says to the Corinthians:

> “Whoever eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself, not discerning the body of the Lord” (1 Corinthians 11:29).

Blessed Augustine sought to demonstrate spiritual eating in his twenty-sixth homily on John, when he said:

> “Eat the heavenly bread spiritually; bring innocence to the altar.”

And shortly afterward:

> “This, then, is the bread descending from heaven, so that if anyone eats of it, he will not die. But this concerns the power of the sacrament, not what concerns the visible sacrament. The one who eats inwardly, not outwardly; the one who eats in the heart, not the one who presses with the tooth.”

A little later he explains what the power of this sacrament is:

> “The faithful know the body of Christ, if they do not neglect to be the body of Christ. Let them become the body of Christ, if they wish to live by the Spirit of Christ.”

And after some further remarks:

> “Hence it is that the apostle Paul, explaining this bread to us, says: ‘Because there is one bread, we, though many, are one body’” (1 Corinthians 10:17). “O sacrament of piety, O sign of unity, O bond of charity!”

## CHAPTER XVIII

Having driven away, as much as seemed sufficient, the calumnies which you rashly brought forward, wrote, and published as an insult to Bishop Humbert and to the holy Roman Church, it remains for us briefly to set forth the faith of the holy Church and the opinion of your sect: by a few authorities and brief arguments, to prove the one and disprove the other.

For the brevity of a letter does not permit the insertion of very many and lengthy testimonies of Scripture or supports for arguments, nor does any reason or necessity demand it. Those who are faithful, or [variant: “but”] depraved, do not stubbornly persist in defending their depravity. Rather, once they understand the authorities and hear the arguments, they desire humbly to return to the way of truth. A few things, and things from a few sources, can be sufficient for them.

But those who have resolved to devote themselves to disputes and persist in their unbelief, even if more material were supplied, would not be satisfied with more.

We therefore believe that the earthly substances which, upon the Lord’s table, are divinely [Col. 0430C] sanctified through the priestly mystery are changed—through the ineffable, incomprehensible, marvelous working of heavenly power—into the essence of the Lord’s body, while the appearances of those things themselves, together with certain other qualities, are retained, lest those who receive them should recoil at consuming what was raw and bloody, and so that believers might receive greater rewards of faith. Yet the Lord’s body itself remains in heaven at the right hand of the Father: immortal, inviolate, whole, undefiled, unharmed. Thus it can truly be said both that we receive the very body which was taken from the Virgin, and yet that we do not receive that very body: we do receive it with respect to its essence, and to the property and power of its true nature; but we do not receive it with respect to the appearance of bread and wine and the other matters mentioned above. [Col. 0430D] This is the faith which the Church, spread throughout the whole world and called catholic, has held from ancient times and still holds.

Accordingly, as was said above, the Lord says in the Gospel: “Take and eat; this is my body, which will be given for you”; and: “This is the cup of my blood, the mystery of faith, which will be poured out for you and for many for the remission of sins.”

Blessed Ambrose, distinguishing the sacrament of Christians from the sacrament of the Jews, says in his sermon *On the Mysteries* addressed to the newly baptized (ch. 9):

“Consider now whether the bread of angels is more excellent, or the flesh of Christ, which is certainly the body of life. The manna was from heaven; this is above heaven. The one was of heaven; the other is of the Lord of heaven. The one was subject to corruption if it was kept until the next day; this is free from all corruption. Whoever tastes it devoutly cannot experience corruption. Water flowed for them from the rock; for you, blood flows from Christ. The water satisfied them for an hour; the blood washes you for eternity. The Jew drank so that he might thirst; you, when you have drunk, cannot thirst. The one was in shadow; this is in truth. If that which you marvel at was a shadow, how great must this be, whose shadow also you marvel at?”

And shortly afterward:

“You have learned what is more excellent. Light is more powerful than shadow; truth than figure; the body of the Author than manna from heaven. Perhaps you say: ‘I see something else; how do you assure me that I receive Christ’s body?’ We still have to prove this to you. How many examples, then, do we use to prove that this is not what nature formed, but what blessing consecrated, and that the power of blessing is greater than that of nature, because by blessing nature itself is also changed! Moses held a staff; he threw it down, and it became a serpent. Again he seized the serpent by the tail, and it returned to the nature of a staff. You see, therefore, that through prophetic grace the nature both of the serpent and of the staff was changed. The rivers of Egypt were flowing in a pure stream of waters. Suddenly blood began to gush forth from the veins of the springs. There was no drink in the rivers. Again, at the prophet’s words, the gore ceased in the rivers, and the nature of the waters returned.”

After recounting these and other miracles of the same kind, which are wrought through the ineffable operation of the divinity, he adds:

“We perceive, therefore, that grace is greater than nature; and yet we continue to enumerate the grace of prophetic blessing. But if human blessing had such power as to change nature, what shall we say of the divine consecration itself, in which the very words of the Lord and Savior operate? For this sacrament which you receive is accomplished by Christ’s word. If Elijah’s word had such power as to bring down fire from heaven, will Christ’s word not have power to change the appearances of the elements? You have read of the works of the whole world: ‘He spoke, and they came to be; he commanded, and they were created’ (Ps. XXXII, 9). Therefore, the word of Christ, which could make from nothing what did not exist, cannot change what exists into that which it was not? For it is no less to create new things than to change natures. But since we use arguments, let us use his own examples and establish the truth of the mystery of the incarnation. Did the ordinary course of nature precede when the Lord Jesus was born from Mary? If we seek the natural order, a woman accustomed to be joined to a man gives birth.

“It is therefore clear that the Virgin gave birth beyond the order of nature, and that the body which we accomplish is from the Virgin. Why, then, do you seek the order of nature in Christ’s body, when the Lord Jesus himself was born from the Virgin beyond nature?”

Likewise, in the fourth book *On the Sacraments* (ch. 4):

“Perhaps you say: ‘My bread is ordinary.’ But this bread is bread before the words of the sacraments. When consecration has been added, from bread it becomes Christ’s body.”

And shortly afterward:

“Heaven did not exist, the sea did not exist, the earth did not exist; but hear David saying: ‘He spoke, and they came to be; he commanded, and they were created.’ Therefore, to answer you, Christ’s body did not exist before the consecration; but after the consecration I tell you that it already is Christ’s body. He spoke, and it came to be; he commanded, and it was created.”

And afterward (ch. 5):

“Before it is consecrated, it is bread. But when the words of Christ have been added, it is Christ’s body. Finally, hear him saying: ‘Take and eat from this, all of you; for this is my body.’ And before Christ’s words, the cup is full of wine and water; when Christ’s words have operated, it becomes blood, which redeemed the people. Therefore, see in how many ways the word of Christ is powerful to change all things. Then the Lord Jesus himself bears witness to us that we receive his body and blood. Surely we ought not to doubt his faithfulness and testimony?”

Likewise, in the sixth book *On the Sacraments* (ch. 1):

“What was said above also applies here. Just as our Lord Jesus Christ is truly the Son of God—not as men are sons by grace, but as a Son from the substance of the Father—so his flesh is true, as he himself said, and this is what we receive; and his blood is true, and this is what we drink. But perhaps you will say what Christ’s disciples also said at that time, when they heard him saying: ‘Unless someone has eaten my flesh and drunk my blood, he will not remain in me and will not have eternal life’ (John VI, 54). Perhaps you will say: ‘How can it be true? I see a likeness, but I do not see the reality of the blood.’ First of all, I told you about Christ’s word, which operates so that it can change and transform the kinds established by nature. Then, when his disciples could not bear Christ’s word, hearing that he was giving his flesh to be eaten and his blood to be drunk, they were withdrawing. Peter alone said: ‘You have the words of eternal life, and where should I go from you?’ (ibid., 69).

“Therefore, lest more people should say this—as though there were some horror of bloodshed—but so that the grace of redemption might remain, you receive the sacrament in a likeness, but you obtain the grace and power of the true nature. ‘I am,’ he says, ‘the living bread which came down from heaven’ (ibid., 44). But the flesh did not come down from heaven; that is, he took flesh on earth from the Virgin. How, then, did the bread come down from heaven, and how is it living bread? Because the same Lord Jesus Christ is a sharer both in divinity and in body. And you who receive his flesh participate in his divine substance through that food.”

Likewise, in the letter to Hireneus (book VIII, letter 62, near the beginning):

“You ask me why the Lord God rained manna upon the people of the fathers, and does not now rain it. If you understand, he does rain it, and every day he rains manna from heaven upon those who serve him. That bodily manna is even now found in many places, but it is no longer such a great miracle, because that which is perfect has come. The perfect thing, however, is the bread from heaven, the body from the Virgin, of which the Gospel teaches you sufficiently. How much more excellent these things are than the former!”

Augustine, in the second homily on Psalm XXXIII:

“The Jews approached Christ in order to crucify him; let us approach him in order to receive his body and blood. They were darkened by the crucified one; we are enlightened by eating and drinking him.” [Col. 0433A]

And afterward:

“Truly great is the Lord, and great is his mercy—truly the one who gave us his body to eat, in which he endured so much, and his blood to drink.”

Likewise, in the homily on Psalm XLV, speaking to the Jews:

“You are baptized in the name of the one whom you killed, and your sins are forgiven you. Did you recognize the physician afterward? Now drink with confidence the blood which you shed.”

Likewise, in the homily on Psalm LXV:

“Now it has been given to murderers—the blood of the innocent has been poured out—and the very blood which in their madness they shed, by grace they drank.”

Likewise, in the homily on Psalm XCVIII:

“I ask what his footstool is, and Scripture tells me: ‘The earth is my footstool’ (Isa. LXVI, 1). In my uncertainty I turn to Christ, because I seek him here and find how the earth may be worshiped without impiety, how his footstool may be worshiped without impiety. For he took earth from the earth, because the flesh is from the earth; and from Mary’s flesh he took flesh; and because he walked here in that very flesh, he gave us that flesh to eat for our salvation. But no one eats that flesh unless he has first worshiped it. The manner has been discovered in which such a footstool of the Lord may be worshiped; and not only do we not sin by worshiping it, but we sin by not worshiping it.”

And shortly afterward:

“When the Lord commended this, he was speaking of his flesh and had said: ‘Unless someone has eaten my flesh, he will not have eternal life in himself’ (John VI, 54). Some of his disciples—nearly seventy—were scandalized and said: ‘This is a hard saying; who can understand it?’ And they withdrew from him and no longer walked with him (ibid., 61, 67). It seemed hard to them that he said: ‘Unless someone has eaten my flesh, he will not have eternal life.’ They received it foolishly. They thought of it carnally, and supposed that the Lord was going to cut off certain pieces from his body and give them to them, and they said: ‘This is a hard saying.’ They themselves were hard, not the saying.”

And after a brief interval:

“Understand spiritually what I have spoken. You are not going to eat this body which you see, nor drink that blood which those who will crucify me are going to pour out.””

You rejoice in these final words of blessed Augustine. [Col. 0433D] You boast that you have conquered in them and are superior; you congratulate yourself on having found here the foundation of your defense. “How,” you ask, “do you attempt to persuade us that we receive true flesh and true blood in this sacrament, when you clearly hear that the disciples were not going to eat the body which they saw, nor drink the blood which those crucifying him were going to pour out?”

This is indeed a slanderous objection. For the one who earlier testified that he gave us, for our salvation, the flesh which he took from the Virgin Mother and in which he walked on earth—how could any statement contrary to this most splendid pronouncement have confronted it? Let such a perverse understanding be far from a sober reader and catholic interpreter concerning the pillar of the Church, [Col. 0434A] the firmament of truth, of whom Pope Celestine asserts in his decrees (*Letter 1 to the Bishops of Gaul*, ch. 20) that, while he lived, not even a rumor of sinister suspicion ever touched him.

Rather, he truly said what the catholic Church faithfully confesses and believes in all its members, and what I too briefly set down and summarized in my profession of faith: namely, that it is the very body, and yet not the very body. For we do not believe that we eat Christ’s visible body in the manner they imagined, or drink the blood which his persecutors were going to pour out and behold with their own eyes. Instead, we believe what we do not see, so that faith may have its place; and faith cannot exist if the things believed are demonstrably subject to bodily senses.

Thus, explaining what he had stated obscurely, he says: “Even if it is necessary for that to be celebrated visibly, it must nevertheless be understood invisibly.” For they supposed that the Lord was commanding them either, like beasts, or in the human manner, to eat the body which they saw or to drink the blood which their persecutors were going to pour out—that is, either raw, or boiled in water, or roasted on spits after the coals had been removed. Rebuking this carnal understanding of theirs, the Lord says in the Gospel according to John: “It is the Spirit who gives life; the flesh profits nothing” (John VI, 64).

Explaining this, blessed Augustine says in the twenty-seventh homily on the same Gospel:

“What, then, does ‘the flesh profits nothing’ mean? It profits nothing—but how did they understand it? They understood flesh in this way: as flesh is torn apart in a corpse or sold in a butcher shop, not as it is enlivened by the Spirit.”

Enough on these matters; let us return to the subject.

## CHAPTER XIX

Augustine, in the eleventh homily on John:

“For the people of the Jews was represented in figure by the Christian people. There was figure; here is truth. There was shadow; here is the body.”

Likewise, in the thirty-first homily:

“But they saw Christ dying through their crime, and believed in Christ forgiving their crimes. Until they drank the blood which they had shed, they had despaired of their salvation.”

Likewise, in the fortieth:

“Those who killed him in their rage, by believing became imitators; and the blood which they had poured out in their rage, by believing they drank.”

Likewise, in the sermon addressed to the newly baptized:

“Receive in the bread that which hung upon the cross. Receive in the chalice that which was poured from Christ’s side. For death, not life, will belong to the one who thinks life a lie.”

Likewise, in the fourth book *On the Trinity* (ch. 13):

“Very few remained with him, when the nations acknowledged him and, with devout humility, drank their price, and in confidence in him abandoned their enemy.”

And in the following chapter (ch. 14), after some intervening material: [247]

“What could be offered and received for cleansing the vices of mortals that would be as pure as flesh born in a womb without any contamination of carnal desire and from a virginal womb? And what could be offered and received with greater gratitude than the flesh of our sacrifice, made the body of our priest?”

Pope Leo, in the sermon on the fast of the seventh month (sermon 6):

“Proclaiming this confession with your whole heart, beloved, reject the impious inventions of heretics, so that your fasts and almsgiving may not be polluted by any contagion of error. For the offering of sacrifice is clean and the gift of mercy holy when those who make these offerings understand what they are doing. Since the Lord says: ‘Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in yourselves’ (John VI, 54), you ought to share in the sacred table in such a way that you have absolutely no doubt concerning the reality of Christ’s body and blood. For what is believed by faith is received by the mouth; and their ‘Amen’ is spoken in vain by those who argue against what they receive.”

Likewise, in the letter sent to Bishop Anatolius:

“For otherwise, in the Church of God, which is Christ’s body, neither priesthoods are valid nor sacrifices true, unless the true High Priest reconciles us in the reality of our nature, and the true blood of the immaculate Lamb cleanses us. Although he is established at the right hand of the Father, he nevertheless performs the sacrament of propitiation in the same flesh which he took from the Virgin.”

Likewise, in the sermon on the Lord’s Passion (sermon 11):

“His wickedness therefore deceived him: he inflicted punishment upon the Son of God, which was to be turned into a remedy for all the sons of men. He poured out righteous blood, which would be both a reward and a cup in reconciling the world.”

Saint Gregory, in his Paschal homily (homily 22 on the Gospel):

“You have learned what the blood of the Lamb is, no longer by hearing but by drinking. That blood is placed upon both doorposts when it is received not only by the mouth of the body but also by the mouth of the heart.”

From these testimonies of the divine utterances, of which I have selected a few from many for the sake of brevity, it is, as I think, clearly evident that Christ’s true flesh and his true blood are offered, eaten, and drunk at the Lord’s table—bodily, spiritually, incomprehensibly.

And lest anyone perverse and intent on perverting things should understand or explain them otherwise than the spiritual children of the universal Church understand and explain them, miracles congruent with this faith have taken place, both in ancient and in modern times, in different churches, whenever, wherever, and to whomever eternal Wisdom wished to reveal so great a secret—eternal Wisdom for whom nothing is impossible, who reaches from end to end and orders all things powerfully and gently (Wis. VIII, 1).

No one who has devoted even a little attention to ecclesiastical histories or to the deeds of the holy Fathers is unaware that these miracles have occurred. Although the writings that record them do not possess that highest summit of authority with which those writings are endowed that we call prophetic or apostolic, they nevertheless suffice to prove that all the faithful who preceded us from ancient times held the faith that we now hold. Otherwise, since apocryphal writings are expressly condemned in the decrees of the Roman pontiffs and in the sacred canons, these writings too would have been specifically condemned, and they would not be solemnly read by Catholics in the catholic Church.

## CHAPTER XX

[Col. 0436A]

You do not cease to oppose the darkness of your question to the light of so many divine authorities, saying:

“What you assert to be Christ’s true body is called in the sacred writings an appearance, likeness, figure, sign, mystery, or sacrament. But these terms are relative. Yet nothing that is referred to something else can be that to which it is referred. Therefore it is not Christ’s body.”

I found this argument in one of your writings, expressed in various and more elaborate words but with the same meaning. This is what your disciples and followers chatter—men who overthrow others, and who themselves have been overthrown by you with your gold, silver, and other money; wandering and leading others into error, not understanding, as the Apostle says, either what they say or what they affirm (1 Tim. I, 7).

Yet these terms in no way prejudice the faith we believe or the truth we defend. For “appearance” and “likeness” are terms for those things which existed previously and from which Christ’s body and blood are made. I mean bread and wine, concerning which, at the end of a certain Mass, the priest prays and says:

“May your sacraments, Lord, we ask, accomplish in us what they contain, so that what we now enact under an appearance we may one day receive in the reality of the things.”

The priest is asking that Christ’s body, which is enacted under the appearance of bread and wine, may one day be received in manifest vision, just as it truly is. For “truth” is often found in the sacred writings in the sense of manifestation.

Concerning this manifest vision, the Lord says to the disciples in the Gospel according to John:

“He who loves me will be loved by my Father; and I will love him, and I will manifest myself to him” (John XIV, 21).

And David, speaking in the person of God the Father:

“I will fill him with length of days, and I will show him my salvation” (Ps. XC, 16).

Although some not implausibly explain “the truth of the flesh and blood” in this passage as their efficacy itself—that is, the remission of sins—Christ’s true flesh and blood exist for all those who worthily receive them in all these ways, since through receiving them they obtain forgiveness of sins.

Thus, in the canon of the Mass, the priest says:

“So that it may become for us the body and blood of your beloved Son, our Lord Jesus Christ”—for us, I say, that is, for believers who worthily receive them through your mercy.

“For he who eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself” (1 Cor. XI, 29).

Hence Saint Gregory, in the fourth book of the *Dialogues* (ch. 59):

“Then it will truly be a sacrifice offered to God for us, when we have made ourselves a sacrifice.”

Christ’s true flesh and true blood are indeed present also for sinners and for those who receive them unworthily, but in essence, not in saving efficacy. Blessed Augustine bears witness to this in the fifth book *On Baptism* (ch. 8), saying:

“For just as Judas, to whom the Lord handed the morsel, provided a place in himself for the devil—not by receiving something evil, but by receiving it evilly—so whoever receives the Lord’s sacrament unworthily does not make it evil because he himself is evil, nor does he receive nothing because he does not receive it for salvation. For the Lord’s body and the Lord’s blood were nevertheless present even for those concerning whom the Apostle said: ‘He who eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself.’”

Ambrose, in the sixth book *On the Sacraments* (ch. 1):

“How can it be true? I see a likeness, but I do not see the reality of the blood.”

And shortly afterward:

“Therefore, in a likeness you receive the sacrament, but you obtain the grace and power of the true nature.”

Here “likeness,” without anyone doubting it, means the appearance of bread and wine, under which the nature of Christ’s body is concealed and is received for salvation by those who partake worthily, without the horror of bloodshed.

“Appearance,” “likeness,” and “figure” are also found in the sense of truth. Thus the Lord says in the Gospel according to John:

“You have never heard his voice, nor have you seen his appearance” (John V, 37).

The Apostle says to the Corinthians:

“For we walk by faith, and not by appearance” (2 Cor. V, 7).

Ambrose, in the book *On the Mysteries* (ch. 4, at the end):

“We read that ‘appearance’ is also to be understood in the sense of truth, both concerning Christ: ‘And being found in appearance as a man’ (Phil. II, 7), and concerning God the Father: ‘You have not seen his appearance.’”

Likewise, in the fourth book *On the Faith to Gratian* (ch. 5):

“For my flesh is truly food, and my blood is truly drink (John VI, 56). You hear ‘flesh’; you hear ‘blood’; you recognize the sacraments of the Lord’s death.”

And shortly afterward:

“But whenever we receive the sacraments which, through the mystery of sacred prayer, are transformed into flesh and blood, we proclaim the Lord’s death.”

Augustine, in the book *On Catechizing the Uninstructed*:

“For we shall become, as we hope and expect from him, equal to the angels of God, and together with them we shall enjoy that Trinity by sight, in which we now walk by faith.”

The Apostle to the Philippians:

“Made in the likeness of human beings and found in appearance as a man” (Phil. II, 7).

Likewise, to the Hebrews:

“Who, being the radiance of glory and the figure of his substance” (Heb. I, 3).

Moreover, “sign,” “mystery,” “sacrament,” and any similar term are designations of the Lord’s Passion, provided that “sacrament” is understood in the sense in which blessed Augustine defines it in the book *On the City of God*: as a sacred sign.

Hence blessed Gregory, in the fourth book of the *Dialogues* (ch. 58):

“For this singular victim saves the soul from eternal destruction; through the mystery it restores to us the death of the Only-Begotten.”

And shortly afterward:

“From this, therefore, let us consider what this sacrifice is for us: it always imitates, for our absolution, the Passion of the Only-Begotten Son.”

And afterward (ch. 59):

“Because we celebrate the mysteries of the Lord’s Passion, we must imitate what we worship.”

Likewise, in the Paschal homily (homily 22 on the Gospel):

“For the blood of the Lamb is placed upon both doorposts when the sacrament of his Passion is received by the mouth for redemption and contemplated with attentive mind for imitation.”

“Sacrament,” moreover, is not found in the divine books with only one meaning. Thus Saint Ambrose, in his book addressed to Gratian, says that the Only-Begotten of the Father appeared to human beings through the sacrament of the assumed man. This means exactly the same as if he had said that he appeared through the man whom he assumed and whom he consecrated as a worthy dwelling for his divinity. The word also has other meanings, about which enough has been said above.

As for the fact that it is called bread, this follows the customary manner of the sacred books, which often call things by the names of those things from which they are made, or which they are thought to be although they are not, or to which they are similar in some way.

Hence blessed Jerome, in the second book of his *Commentaries on Hosea* (at the end of the preface):

“After the earth has returned to its own earth, and pale death has taken away both us who write and those who pass judgment on us.”

And to a proud man it is said by a wise man:

“Why do you boast, earth and ashes?” (Eccl. X, 10.)

And Abraham is read to have seen three men (Gen. XVIII, 2), although they were angels. Concerning this, blessed Augustine says in the second book *On the Trinity* (ch. 10, near the end):

“Under the oak of Mamre Abraham saw three men; and after inviting them, receiving them as guests, and preparing a meal, he ministered to them.”

And in the book of Judges, the barren woman says to her husband concerning the angel:

“A man of God came to me” (Jud. XIII, 6).

And shortly afterward:

“Behold, a man appeared to me whom I had seen before” (ibid., 10).

And after some intervening material:

“Manoah did not know that he was an angel of God” (ibid., 16).

And blessed Jerome, in the same book of *Commentaries* on the prophet Hosea, says concerning God:

“He becomes, as it were, a moth and rottenness—not because God is a moth or rottenness, but because these things appear so to those who endure punishments.”

And in the Gospel according to John:

“They cursed him and said: ‘You are a disciple of that man’” (John IX, 28), although being a disciple of Christ is not a curse but a blessing.

Hence blessed Augustine says in his exposition of the same Gospel (Tractate 44):

“Such a curse upon us and upon our children. It is a curse if you examine the heart, not if you weigh the words.”

And in the Gospel according to Matthew, and similarly according to Luke:

“If therefore you, although you are evil, know how to give good gifts to your children” (Matt. VII, 11; Luke XI, 13).

Concerning this statement, blessed Augustine argues in the second book *On the Sermon on the Lord on the Mount* (ch. 21):

“How do the evil give good things? He called those who love this world and sinners evil. But the good things they give must be called good according to their understanding, because they regard them as good.”

And the Lord Jesus Christ, because of certain likenesses, is called in the same writings a lion, a lamb, a worm, a tree, a rock, a stone, the cornerstone, and many things of this kind.

Thus Christ’s body is also called bread, either because it is made from bread, or because, although it is flesh, it appears as bread to the eyes of those who look upon it, or because it is joined by a certain likeness to bodily and visible bread. For just as this material bread, when taken in appropriate portions, nourishes and sustains human flesh, so Christ’s spiritual and invisible body nourishes and strengthens the soul of the worthy recipient.

You further object and attempt, by the authority of Ambrose, to weaken Ambrose himself, saying:

“Ambrose says in the fourth book *On the Sacraments* (IV, 4): ‘Just as you have received a likeness of death, so you also drink a likeness of the precious blood.’”

Explaining these words, you ask: “What could be more comparable? What could be more similar?”

It cannot be denied that blessed Ambrose compared the sacraments of baptism with the sacraments of the altar. But Christ’s true death is not present in baptism. Therefore neither is his true blood present in this sacrament.

With your permission, you are greatly mistaken in understanding these words. For the adverbs of likeness do not everywhere signify identity or equality. In the Gospel, the Savior says:

“Be merciful, just as your Father is merciful” (Luke VI, 36).

Yet the same or equal mercy cannot exist in God and in human beings. And in the Gospel according to John:

“I have given them the glory which you gave me, so that they may be one, just as we are one” (John XVII, 22).

And elsewhere:

“You loved them, just as you loved me” (ibid., 23).

Hence blessed Augustine says in his exposition of the same Gospel (Tractate 10):

“For the one who says, ‘As this is, so also is that,’ does not always signify equality; sometimes he means only that because this exists, that also exists, or that this exists so that that may also exist.”

## CHAPTER XXI

There is another matter which you bring forward, shouting it in many places whenever the opportunity for speaking is granted, and saying:

“If bread is converted into Christ’s true flesh, then either the bread is lifted up into heaven so that there it may be transferred into Christ’s flesh, or Christ’s flesh is brought down to earth so that here the bread may be changed into it. Yet neither is the bread lifted up, nor is the flesh brought down. Therefore there is no true flesh into which the bread is converted.”

You draw this conclusion according to human wisdom, not according to divine wisdom. But the Apostle forbids the investigation of divine works by human wisdom, saying to the Romans:

“Do not be wiser than it is necessary to be wise, but be wise unto sobriety” (Rom. XII, 3);

and to the Corinthians:

“My speech and my preaching were not in persuasive words of human wisdom, but in a demonstration of the Spirit and of power, so that your faith might not be in human wisdom but in the power of God” (1 Cor. II, 4);

and to the Colossians:

“See that no one deceive you through philosophy and empty deceit, according to human tradition and according to the elements of the world” (Col. II, 8).

And blessed Gregory, in his Paschal homily (26 on the Gospel), says:

“We must know that if a divine work is comprehended by reason, it is not marvelous. Nor does faith have merit when human reason provides the proof.”

Therefore, amid such profound matters, you ought rather to have prayed to God either to understand what can be understood according to human capacity, or patiently and humbly to endure—and nevertheless believe—those things which in so great a mystery surpass the powers of human understanding and cannot at all be understood in this life, rather than to stir up a dispute, dissent from the universal Church, and introduce a new schism by words and writings against the precepts of the holy Fathers.

Indeed, in this way you would be doing what the Lawgiver commands ought to be done:

“Do not move the boundaries of the fathers” [Col. 0440A] (Prov. XXII, 28).

And blessed Augustine, in the first book *On the Sermon on the Lord on the Mount*:

“What sounds obscure or absurd to him, let him not thereby stir up battles of contradiction; rather, let him pray that he may understand.”

And in the third book *On the Trinity* (ch. 10):

“For me, it is useful to remember my own powers, and to admonish my brothers to remember theirs, lest human weakness advance farther than is safe.”

And in the book *Against the Heretic Felicianus* (ch. 2):

“Content with the authority of the Scriptures, I strive rather to obey simplicity than arrogance.”

And shortly afterward:

“What argument can he offer if you proclaim the Virgin’s childbirth, if you do not deny that eyes were restored to the blind, if you show that buried people returned from the dead? If the explanation of these things is incomprehensible, while their truth is manifest, then in matters of faith it is easier to believe the testimonies than to investigate the explanation” [al., “to inquire into it”].

## CHAPTER XXII

Now that we have proved what needed to be proved and excluded what reason urged us to exclude, let us finally see what you believe and what follows from your belief.

You believe that the bread and wine of the Lord’s table remain immovable in substance during consecration—that is, that they existed as bread and wine before consecration and continue to exist as bread and wine after consecration—and that they are therefore called Christ’s flesh and blood because, in memory of the flesh that was crucified and the blood poured from his side, they are celebrated in the Church, so that, reminded by this, we may always recall the Lord’s Passion and, recalling it, continually crucify our own flesh with its vices and desires (Gal. V, 24).
