If this is true, then the sacraments of the Jews were more excellent and more divine than the sacraments of Christians. For who does not know that the manna which the Lord rained from heaven, or the living and sentient creatures which that people was accustomed to sacrifice, were more excellent than a small morsel of bread and a little wine?

Again, who does not understand that it was more divine to foretell future things than to recount past things, since the former cannot be done except by one filled with the Spirit of God, whereas the latter is often done even by an ignorant or wholly uneducated person?

But may this be far from the heart of the faithful and from Christian understanding! For Ambrose, the soldier of Christ, confirms in the book *On the Mysteries* that those things are inferior, while these are more excellent and more worthy, saying (ch. 8):

“We wish to prove with the greatest care that the sacraments of the Church are both more ancient than those of the Synagogue and more excellent than manna.”

And shortly afterward (ch. 9):

“It has been proved that the sacraments of the Church are more ancient; now learn that they are more excellent.”

And after some intervening material:

“You have learned what is more excellent: light is more powerful than shadow, truth than figure.”

Likewise, in the fourth book *On the Sacraments* (ch. 3):

“Receive what I say: the sacraments of Christians are more divine than those of the Jews.”

Therefore what you propose is false.

Moreover, if what you believe and assert concerning the body of Christ is true, then what the Church everywhere throughout the nations believes and asserts about the same matter is false. For all who rejoice to be and to be called Christians glory in receiving, in this sacrament, the true flesh of Christ and his true blood, both taken from the Virgin. Ask everyone who has acquired knowledge of the Latin language or of our letters. Ask the Greeks, Armenians, or any Christians whatsoever of whatever nation: with one voice they testify that they hold this faith. Furthermore, if the faith of the universal Church is false, then either the Catholic Church never existed or it has perished. For nothing is more effective in bringing souls to destruction than pernicious error. But no Catholic will agree that the Church did not exist or has perished. Otherwise what Truth promised to Abraham would not be true: “In your offspring all the nations shall be blessed” (Gen. 22:18). Likewise in the Psalm: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance and your possession to the ends of the earth” (Ps. 2:8). Likewise: “All the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the Lord” (Ps. 21:28). And elsewhere: “Those whom he redeemed from the hand of the enemy, he gathered from the regions, from the rising and setting of the sun, from the north and from the sea” (Ps. 106:2–3).

Likewise, blessed Augustine, in the first part of his exposition of the Psalms (on Ps. 21, Tractate 2): “What is the great Church, brothers? Is a small part of the earth’s circuit the great Church? The great Church is the whole world.” Likewise, in the same work (Exposition of Ps. 39): “‘I have proclaimed your righteousness in the great Church.’ How great? Throughout the whole world. How great? Among all nations. Why among all nations? Because ‘their sound has gone out into all the earth.’” Likewise, in the third part of the same work: “The body of Christ consists of many believers throughout the whole world.” Likewise, in the same work: “The Lord’s tabernacle is this holy Church spread throughout the whole world.” And elsewhere: “The chorus of Christ is now the whole world. The chorus of Christ resounds in harmony from east to west.”

Likewise, in the book *On Christian Combat* (ch. 29, vol. III): “Nor should we listen to those who deny that the holy Church, which is one and Catholic, is spread throughout the world.” And after some omissions (in the same place): “But when his people,” he says, “do not listen to the prophets and the Gospel, in which it is most openly written that the Church of Christ is spread among all nations, and listen to schismatics who seek not God’s glory but their own, they clearly show themselves to be servants, not free.”

And the Lord says in the Gospel: “This field is the world” (Matt. 13:38). And shortly afterward: “The kingdom of heaven is like a net cast into the sea and gathering fish of every kind” (ibid., 47). And to the disciples: “Go into all the world and preach the Gospel to every creature” (Mark 16:15).

## CHAPTER XXIII

Against such clear testimonies of the Lord himself and of his holy Spirit concerning the Church and the condition of the Church, you object, and so do those who, deceived by you, attempt to deceive others. Thus you say:

“The Gospel was preached among all nations; the world believed; the Church was established, grew, and bore fruit; but afterward, through the ignorance of those who understood badly, it fell into error and perished. The holy Church on earth has remained only among us and among those who follow us.”

Evangelical truth and the authority of the prophets and holy Fathers, which must not be violated, overturn this sacrilegious folly. Therefore, in his Gospel, the Lord promises this to his holy Church, saying: “Behold, I am with you all the days, until the consummation of the age” (Matt. 28:20). He would certainly not have said this if he had foreseen that his Church would perish before the consummation of the age. And elsewhere: “Then if anyone says to you, ‘Behold, here is Christ,’ or ‘There,’ do not believe it” (Matt. 24:23).

Augustine, in the second part of his exposition of the Psalms (Exposition of Ps. 56): “The Church is a body—not this one or that one, but spread throughout the whole world.” Likewise, in the same work (on Ps. 64): “‘The hope of all the ends of the earth.’ Not the hope of one corner, not the hope of one Judea, not the hope of Africa alone, not the hope of Pannonia, not the hope of East or West, but the hope of all the ends of the earth, and of the distant sea.”

In the same work (on Ps. 71): “This prophecy was set forth beforehand for those who think that the religion of the Christian name will live in this world only until a certain time and afterward will no longer exist. But it will remain with the sun for as long as the sun rises and sets. That is, for as long as these times revolve, the Church—that is, the body of Christ—will not be lacking on earth.”

Likewise, in the same work (on Ps. 92): “‘Holiness befits your house, Lord’ (Ps. 92:5)—your house, your whole house. Not here, or here, or there, but your entire house throughout the whole world. Why throughout the whole world? Because he who will not be moved has made firm the inhabited world (Ps. 95:10). The Lord’s house will be strong; it will exist throughout the whole world.”

Likewise, in the final part of the same work (on Ps. 101): “What is this that you say, heretic—that the Church has already perished from all the nations, when the Gospel is still being preached so that it may be among all the nations? Therefore, until the end of the age, the Church will be among all the nations.” In the same work: “Where are those who say that the Church has perished from the world, when it cannot even be shaken?”

Likewise, in the same work (on Ps. 105): “Whoever thinks that the Church exists in one part, and does not recognize it as spread throughout the whole world, and believes those who say, ‘Behold, here is Christ,’ and ‘Behold, there’ (Matt. 24:23), as you have just heard when the Gospel was read—although he purchased the whole world because he paid so great a price—such a person, as though Christ were nearby, is scandalized and burned by the moon.” [The final phrase, “a luna uritur,” is obscure and may reflect an uncertain textual reading.]

It is false, therefore, that what you believe and assert concerning the body of Christ is true. Therefore his flesh, which we receive, is true, and his blood, which we drink, is true.

[Col. 0441] Here ends the book of blessed Lanfranc, archbishop of Canterbury, *On the Body and Blood of the Lord against Berengar*.

[Col. 0443]

# NOTES OF BLESSED LANFRANC, ARCHBISHOP OF CANTERBURY, ON SOME OF THE CONFERENCES OF JOHN CASSIAN WITH THE FATHERS

252 From an old manuscript codex of the monastery of Saint-Martin of Sées.

## ON CONFERENCE VII, CHAPTER XIII

[Col. 0443A]

Although we declare that some natures are spiritual, such as angels, archangels, and so forth, they must nevertheless in no way be considered incorporeal. For they have, in themselves, a body by which they subsist, although much subtler than our bodies, according to the Apostle’s statement: “There are celestial bodies and terrestrial bodies” (1 Cor. 15:40).

### NOTE I

Angels and the other spirits, as blessed Augustine says, are corporeal in comparison with that utterly pure incorporeality which is God; yet, when compared with the bodies that we are and that we see, they are incorporeal.

## ON CONFERENCE X, CHAPTER II

[Col. 0443B]

“After a very few days, when, etc., the solemn letters of Theophilus, bishop of the aforesaid city, arrived; in them, together with the Paschal proclamation, he argued at length even against the foolish heresy of the Anthropomorphites.”

### NOTE II

They are called Anthropomorphites because, with rustic simplicity, they suppose that God has the human limbs that are described in the divine books. For *anthropos* (ἄνθρωπος) is Greek and is translated into Latin as *homo*, “man.” They do not understand the Lord’s statement: “God is spirit” (John 4:24). For he is incorporeal, is not distinguished by limbs, and is not measured by bodily mass.

## ON CONFERENCE XIII, CHAPTER XIV

“I have not found such faith in Israel” (Matt. 8:10). For it would have been no praise or merit if Christ had endured in him that which he himself had bestowed. Otherwise he would have said: “Amen, I say to you: I have not given such faith in Israel,” and so forth.

### NOTE III

In this treatise, *On the Faith of Man*, this author is opposed to the other teachers of sacred Scripture, who assert, on the authority of the Gospels and the Apostles, that faith, like works, is given to human beings by God’s grace.

## ON CONFERENCE XVIII, AFTER CHAPTER XVI

[Col. 0444B]

“We have already spoken of the alteration of the unwary definition, etc.”

[Note: “[Col. 0443B] ‘We have spoken of the alteration of the unwary definition,’ etc. These words are found neither in the manuscript codices of the library of Corbie that are older than blessed Lanfranc, nor in the printed editions, except in the translation or paraphrase of Denis the Carthusian. It is reasonable to conjecture either that he used a copy like this one, corrected by Lanfranc himself, or that he grasped Lanfranc’s intention in his own translation.”]

### NOTE IV

From this point to the end of this conference, several opinions of heretics are found inserted in certain codices, teaching that a lie is not at some times a sin.

[Note: “[Col. 0443B] ‘Several opinions of heretics,’ etc. Blessed Lanfranc appears deliberately to have omitted these in the revision of the ten Conferences, since they might perhaps have been more harmful than beneficial to readers. Consult the commentary of our very learned Gazaeus on these same opinions—that is, on chapters 16 and 17 of the seventeenth Conference of John Cassian. Moreover, the codex of Saint Lanfranc contains only ten Conferences, with no division into chapters, as is also the case in the Dionysian translation. In the commonly circulated editions, however, and in the very ancient manuscripts, the same Conferences are divided into sixteen and distributed into chapters.”]

[Col. 0443]

# DECREES OF BLESSED LANFRANC, ARCHBISHOP OF CANTERBURY, FOR THE ORDER OF SAINT BENEDICT, THAT IS, REGULATIONS WHICH THE MONKS OUGHT TO OBSERVE BOTH IN MONASTERIES AND IN CATHEDRAL CHURCHES

253 From an ancient manuscript of the Church of Canterbury, preserved in the episcopal palace at Durham in London.

## PREFACE

[Col. 0443C]

Lanfranc, unworthy bishop of the holy Church of Canterbury, sends greetings and blessing to his most beloved brothers, Henry the prior and the others.

[Col. 0444C]

We are sending you the customs of our order in writing, which we have excerpted from the customs of those monasteries that in our time possess the greatest authority within the order of monks. We have also added a very few things and altered some, especially in the celebration of certain feasts, judging that, on account of the primatial see, these ought to be carried out with greater distinction in our Church.

In these matters we prejudice neither ourselves, who are present, nor those who will come after us, so that we may not be able to add, remove, or alter anything in them if we understand—either by sounder reasoning or by the authority of more learned men—that they can be carried out more suitably in another way. For however much someone may advance, it is his greatest defect to think that he can advance no further. The increased or diminished number of brothers, the resources of places, the variety of circumstances that often arise, and differences of understanding—for some understand matters in one way and others in another—as well as many practices long maintained, frequently compel things to be ordered differently. This is why scarcely any Church can imitate another in every respect.

Nevertheless, this must be observed with the greatest care: those things without which the soul cannot be saved must be preserved inviolable in every way. I mean faith, contempt of the world, charity, chastity, humility, patience, obedience, repentance for sins committed and humble confession of them, frequent prayers, suitable silence, and many things of this kind. Where these are observed, it can rightly be said that the rule of blessed Benedict and the order of monks are being maintained, however much the other practices instituted at the discretion of different people in different monasteries may vary.

Such practices include the following: on the principal solemnities, in some places the singers sing the responsory at Vespers wearing only tunics, which they call frocks, while elsewhere they do so in albs and copes; on the same feasts, in some places they process wearing only albs, and in others wearing copes as well; in certain monasteries twenty or thirty men, or more or fewer, wash their feet together in tubs, while in others each washes his feet separately in his own basin in the cloister before the Maundy; many monasteries begin to say the Office of the Dead after Vespers in February, once the feast of blessed Mary has passed, while many others wait until Septuagesima. There are many other practices of this kind which, because of their length, cannot be briefly listed.

Yet once these very practices have been ordered by the pastors for observance by their subjects, they are in no way violated without fault by those whose entire life is founded upon obedience. Let no one be disturbed, therefore, that in the discussion of these customs only the name of the abbot, and not that of the bishop or archbishop, is given. For the order of monks is being described, and their life is more frequently regulated through abbots than through bishops. Nevertheless, bishops themselves, if they provide paternal care for their subjects in Christ’s place, may not improperly be called abbots—that is, “Fathers”—a title fitting to their actions.

May the God of peace and love remain with you, fill you with his peace and love, and mercifully absolve you from all sins. Amen. Amen.

# CHAPTER ONE. THE ORDER OF THE WHOLE YEAR

[Col. 0446A]

## SECTION I. From October to the Advent of the Lord

On the Kalends of October, let the midday rest which the monks customarily take in summer continue. From the first Sunday of this month, let readings and chant be taken from the Books of the Maccabees until the feast of All Saints. Let hymns be sung on Sundays until the Advent of the Lord: at Nocturns, *Primo dierum omnium* (“First of all the days”); at Lauds, *Aeterne rerum Conditor* (“Eternal Maker of all things”).

On weekdays, after Matins until the feast of All Saints, let them return to their beds. At daybreak, let the church custodian strike the small bell softly. The brothers, rising in their night garments, and the children and young men with their lamps, shall come into the church. After prayer has been made, let them sing Prime, the customary psalms with their collects, the seven penitential psalms, and the litany. Then, leaving, let them sit in the cloister.

The boys are first to read aloud and afterward, if necessary, to sing. At all times, before the boys take the lead, no one in the cloister is to read or sing except in silence, nor is anyone to go to confession. Before the signal for preparing for Terce is sounded, no one is to put on his daytime shoes, except those who have been assigned an obedience outside the cloister. These men must first sit for a while in the cloister and wait until the boys have read in their stoles.

When the time for Terce approaches, let the secretary softly strike the smallest bell, called the *skilla*.

[Note: “[Col. 0445D] Others call it *scilla* or *squilla*, that is, a little bell.”]

Immediately let them go to the dormitory, put on their daytime shoes, and take their knives. Then let them go to the washroom, wash themselves first, and afterward comb their hair. Next let them come to the church, take holy water, go into the choir, and, prostrating themselves on the ground, await the boys.

When the boys have washed and begun to comb their hair, let the larger bell be struck for the hour. The others also shall approach the holy water, come into the choir, and, once the bell has ceased, let all make the three customary prayers together. When these have been completed, let the smaller bell be struck and Terce be sung.

After the psalm *Miserere mei, Deus* (“Have mercy on me, O God”) has begun, let them rise and celebrate the morning Mass; let them make the customary entrance and return, and proceed to vest themselves. After Mass has been celebrated, let everyone remain seated in the choir except certain lay brothers, who must assist the priest and those who served at Mass. When they have completed this service, let they too return to the choir.

Then, at the abbot’s command, let the prior strike the smallest bell. Next let everyone go two by two into the chapter house, in order of precedence: the senior first, then the boys. When chapter is finished and the board has been struck, after the abbot or prior has said *Benedicite* (“Bless”), they may speak in the cloister.

The boys are to hold their own chapter and afterward go to the refectory. After Sext, no one is to speak in the cloister until the boys leave the monastery and the youngest of them says *Benedicite* in a loud voice. After an interval, let the *skilla* be struck for the preparation of Mass; once the bell for Mass has been struck and prayer has been made, let the boy recite the litany. Those who will celebrate Mass and those who will serve at Mass shall vest.

On Wednesday and Friday, if they are to process through the cloister after Sext and before Mass, the *skilla* for the preparation of Mass is not to be struck. Rather, when the secretary sees that the time for the procession is approaching, let him sound one of the medium-sized bells. When it is heard, silence must immediately be observed in the cloister. Let them remove their shoes, wash their hands, and go into the church. After prayer has been made and two bells have been struck, let them make the procession, saying the customary prayers, as on those same days in Lent and in summer, which will be described later.

After Mass, when the bell has been struck, let prayer be made. After prayer, let them go to the refectory to receive the *mistum* from the kitchen-week officer and the table reader. If there are others who, for the benefit of the church, cannot attend the principal Mass, it shall be within the power of the abbot or prior to decide whether they too are to receive the *mistum* and whether they should be given the quantity of bread and drink assigned to the weekly servers.

Meanwhile, let the other brothers remain seated in the choir, and let those who wish read. When the servers return to the choir, let the bell be struck and let None be sung. After None has been sung, let the prior go out to strike the cymbal, together with the kitchen-week officers and the others who will serve in the duties assigned to them.

If the Kalends of November fall on a Sunday, let the feast of All Saints be celebrated solemnly. On the following weekdays, let the responsories *Vidi Dominum* (“I saw the Lord”) be sung, with long lessons from the prophets.

If the day of the Kalends falls on Monday, Tuesday, or Wednesday, let the story *Vidi Dominum* begin on the preceding Sunday, but let the intervals begin only after the Kalends. If the Kalends fall on Thursday, Friday, or Saturday, let the story and the lessons from the prophets begin on the following Sunday; but let the great lessons and the intervals begin immediately after the feast.

From this feast until the Thursday before Easter, except where there are twelve lessons or an octave, let thirty psalms be sung on weekdays, after the prayers and before the nocturnal offices, beginning with *Ad Dominum cum tribularer* (“To the Lord, when I was in distress”) and ending with *Omnis spiritus laudet Dominum* (“Let every spirit praise the Lord”).

The first ten are for the dead, without the *Gloria*. The next ten are for the congregation, in pairs with one *Gloria*. The final ten are for relatives and benefactors; these too are sung in pairs with one *Gloria*, each accompanied by its prayers and collects.

After the Nocturns and the customary psalms, let the Office of the Dead be said, followed by Matins and Lauds for all the Saints and *Verba mea* (“Give ear to my words”), if they observe the *tricenarium*.

After this, coming down from the dormitory, let them sit in the choir. The boys, with lamps, are to be carefully supervised by their teachers in the chapter house. They are to sing whatever is necessary; or, if they have risen too deep in the night, let them rest lying at their seats.

During this interval the prior should go through the choir with a lit lantern (a “blind lantern”) and see whether they are sitting properly. He should then go around the altars and the parts of the monastery, lest someone be sleeping there. If he finds someone praying, let him pass by silently. But if he finds someone sleeping, let him wake him, have the bell struck, and order him to return to the choir.

Then he should go through the cloister and into the chapter house and see how the teachers and boys are conducting themselves, and visit the other places wherever he sees that it is necessary.

When the time comes, let the bell be struck. When the boys arrive and prayer has been made, let Matins and Lauds be sung, with a commemoration of the Saints. Then let Prime be sung with the customary psalms, prayers, and collects, together with the seven penitential psalms and the litany.

After this, let everything be done as was stated above for the month of October. The secretary must carefully ensure that he begins Lauds at such an hour that everything is completed in full daylight.

If there is some uncertainty and any part of the night remains after the litany, let the brothers conduct themselves as above during the first interval: no one, except those bled for medical reasons, is to return to bed. When day has grown light, let them go out and sit in the cloister.

At Compline, the hymn is *Christe qui lux es et dies* (“Christ, who are light and day”).

## SECTION II. From Advent to Septuagesima

On the Sunday before the Advent of the Lord, let the story of the Holy Trinity be sung; the hymn *Primo dierum*; and the psalms *Domine, in virtute* (“Lord, in your strength”) and the others. In the third Nocturn, let the Gospel *Cum sublevasset* (“When he had lifted up”) be recited, and let the same Gospel be read by a vested priest, with the collect *Excita, Domine* (“Stir up, Lord”).

At Lauds, let the psalms *Dominus regnavit* (“The Lord reigns”) and the other psalms be sung. Let the antiphons be from the Trinity, and likewise at the Hours until Vespers, with the chapters, verses, and collects. At the *Benedictus*, let there be an antiphon and collect of the Trinity.

After the collect, let the Gospel antiphon *Cum sublevasset* be said with the *Gloria Patri*, followed by the verse *Dominus regnavit*, the collect *Excita, Domine*, a sermon in chapter, and the morning Mass of Sunday, the principal Mass being of the Holy Trinity. If a feast with twelve lessons occurs, let that feast of twelve lessons itself not be changed.

On the Saturday preceding the Sunday of the Advent of the Lord, let the prayer of the Cross be omitted at Vespers until the octave of Epiphany. If the feast of Saint Andrew falls on that day, let Vespers of the Apostle be celebrated in full.

When Vespers are finished, let the antiphon *Ecce nomen Domini* (“Behold the name of the Lord”) be begun with the *Gloria Patri*. After the antiphon has been said, let the verse and collect of the Advent of the Lord follow.

On the following day, at the invitatory, let two brothers be in albs; in the bishop’s seat, let them be in copes. Whenever the order of monks described here is directed to be in albs at the invitatory, at the *Benedictus*, or at the *Magnificat*, this means that they are to be in albs. In the bishop’s seat they are appointed to be in copes.

Let the lessons be from the prophet Isaiah until the Nativity of the Lord. At Matins and Lauds, let the psalms *Miserere mei, Deus* and the others be sung. At the *Benedictus*, let the priest in an alb incense the altars.

At Prime, let the chapter be *Domine, miserere nostri* (“Lord, have mercy on us”), on all Sundays and feast days until the Nativity of the Lord. Let the *Gloria in excelsis Deo* not be said. At the principal Mass, let the deacon and subdeacon be vested in chasubles. On Sundays and other feasts at which twelve lessons are read, let them eat fat.

If the feast of Saint Andrew falls on this day, let them fast on the preceding Saturday as on a vigil, and let the Mass of the Vigil be said: a commemoration at Vespers, and on the following day at Lauds and at the morning Mass, let the Office of the Apostle be celebrated. The feast itself is to be deferred until the following day.

At Vespers on that day, let the chapter and the other items that follow be said from the Apostle; afterward, a commemoration of Advent. On weekdays, let the prayers be *Oremus pro omni gradu Ecclesiae* (“Let us pray for every order of the Church”).

On the Wednesday, Friday, and Saturday of the Ember Days, let the Gospels proper to those days be recited.

On the vigil of the Apostle Thomas, if it is not a Sunday, let the brothers be shaved. Those who wish to bathe shall do so, so that everyone has bathed two days before the Sunday of the Nativity. If necessary, they may bathe on the very day of the apostolic feast.

The baths themselves are to be arranged in this manner. On the preceding day, the abbot, or the one who holds the office, should appoint a religious and prudent senior and instruct him to take charge of the matter. He is to tell the brothers at what hour they should go and see that they conduct themselves there in an orderly fashion.

When the senior goes there, let him see how the baths have been prepared and what sort of servants have been assigned there—namely, not boys or young men, but men more advanced in age. If he sees anything unsuitable, let him report it to the chamberlain, who must immediately correct it.

When the senior has returned to the cloister, let him remind the brothers of whatever he has determined to be necessary. But he must take care that adolescents and novices do not go together, but go with seniors.

The brothers whom he has summoned, after being shaved, are to take the clothing they must change and go to the place where the baths have been prepared. There they are to remove their clothes in an orderly manner, as they are accustomed to do in the dormitory, and each is to enter the place shown to him. After lowering the veil hanging before him, let him sit in silence.

If he needs anything, let him request it modestly by some sign. The servant, raising the veil, is to bring quickly what he has requested and immediately withdraw. After he has washed sufficiently, let him not take pleasure in remaining there longer. Rising, shod and clothed as he is accustomed to be in the dormitory, and having washed his hands, let him return to the cloister.

The adolescents who are under supervision are to go and return with their guardians. From Prime until Compline, the brothers may go to the baths at all the Hours, but no one may presume to go without the permission of the brother entrusted with this responsibility.

If the vigil of the Lord’s Nativity falls on a Sunday, let two brothers say the Sunday invitatory in albs. Let the first and second Nocturns be of that Sunday, and the third Nocturn and Lauds of the Vigil. After the first collect, let there be a commemoration of Sunday; the morning Mass is to be of Sunday, and the principal Mass of the Vigil.

Otherwise, let the bells be struck and the thirty psalms be said as on weekdays. Let two sing the invitatory, but not in albs. Let the Gospel be recited. The chapter at Nocturn, the prayer, and the verse are to be of the Vigil. The rest is to be as on the preceding days: the Office of the Dead, Matins and Lauds for all the Saints, the boys going to the dormitory and returning to the chapter house.

At Lauds, as on the other days, let one bell be struck. After prayer has been made, let all the bells be struck over the choir stalls. When they have ceased, let Matins and Lauds begin. The psalms are *Dominus regnavit* and the others. Let the weekly server begin the first antiphon.

The chapter is *Paulus servus Christi Jesu* (“Paul, servant of Christ Jesus”). A priest vested in an alb is to incense the altars. The prayers are *Ego dixi, Domine* (“I said, Lord”). Let one psalm, *Miserere mei, Deus*, be sung. Then the commemoration of the Saints, Prime, the psalms, and the litany.

After Terce and the morning Mass have been said, the chapter bell must be struck longer than usual, so that, all other occupations being set aside, everyone may gather at the beginning of chapter. When the Nativity of Christ our Lord is announced, all are to prostrate themselves on the ground, including the reader before the lectern, and pray together until the one in charge of the order, after making the prayer, raises himself.

Let the Gospel be recited and a sermon preached from it. After Sext, following an interval, let the bell be struck. Let the brothers gather in the church and pray together; the litany is not to be said. Those who will celebrate Mass are to vest: the priest honorably; the deacon in a dalmatic; two subdeacons in tunics, one for the prophecy and the other for the Epistle; two in albs for the responsory; the weekly cantor in a cope for the choir; and three lay brothers, one for the censer and two for the candlesticks. Let the signal for the canon be sounded over the choir stalls, and let the covered refectory tables be laid out.

On the night of the Lord’s Nativity, let all the bells first be struck. At the invitatory, let four brothers be in copes. At the third lesson of each Nocturn, let two priests vested in copes carry two censers around: first to the two altars, the principal and the morning altar, and then to the brothers seated in the choir.

In the third Nocturn, let these Gospels be recited: *Liber generationis* (“The book of the generation”), *Exiit edictum* (“A decree went out”), *Pastores* (“The shepherds”), and *In principio* (“In the beginning”). When these have been completed, with their responsories, let the abbot begin *Te Deum laudamus* (“We praise you, God”). When this has been said, let him read the Gospel *Liber generationis*. After the prayer has been said, let the cantor begin the antiphon *O beata infantia* (“O blessed infancy”).

While singing it, let them go to the altar of Saint Mary. There, after the Matins for all the Saints have been said, let them go to the dormitory. Then let one of the larger bells be struck, as the *skilla* is customarily struck in a twelve-lesson service after chapter and before the morning Mass.

At that point the brothers who are to vest for Mass are to go to the appointed place, where an excellent fire has been prepared by the chamberlain’s servants, together with basins, towels, and warm water for washing the hands.

[Note: “[Col. 0449D] *Baccilium* perhaps means a basin, in the vernacular *bassin* or *baquet*.”]

On this one occasion, before washing, they comb their heads; at other times they wash first and comb afterward. After this, let them go into the church, make prayer, and vest themselves for the celebration of Mass.

The priest is to be vested honorably, the deacon in a dalmatic, two subdeacons in tunics—one for the prophecy and the other for the Epistle—and, for the responsory and Alleluia, as many as the cantor directs, these being in copes. There are to be three lay brothers, three singers in the choir, two candlesticks with lighted candles before the choir, and all the boys. Let the *classicum* be sounded, and afterward let Mass begin.

[Note: “[Col. 0450D] Here *classicum* means either the final signal or the larger bell placed in the church tower.”]

Let the *Gloria in excelsis Deo* and the sequence be sung. After Mass has been celebrated, let the priest, those who served at Mass, and those in the choir who were wearing albs or copes leave. When they have removed these vestments and all the bells have been struck, let them sing the Lauds of Matins (as prescribed by Lanfranc).

[Note: “[Col. 0451D] F.; these two words appear to have been added.”]

After this has been completed, and a commemoration of Saint Anastasia has been made and the customary psalms have been said, let them return to their beds. When daylight appears, let one of the larger bells be struck as above. On hearing it, let everyone rise promptly, wash hands and faces, and let those who are to vest for Mass come to the oratory. After prayer has been made, let them vest as for the earlier Mass.

Before this Mass begins, let the *classicum* be sounded. When the Mass has been completed, let them go to the dormitory to put on their shoes. Then, having washed and combed themselves in the customary manner, let them make the three customary prayers in the oratory. After Terce has been said, let everyone wearing copes make a procession.

At this Terce, let the antiphon *Hodie intacta virgo* (“Today the untouched Virgin”) be said. When they come to the place where *ipsum adoremus* (“let us adore him”) is said, let everyone bend both knees to the ground and make supplication. This is to be observed whenever the aforesaid antiphon is sung in the monastery.

The following three feasts—that is, of blessed Stephen, the Apostle John, and the Holy Innocents—are to be celebrated in one and the same manner. On these three days, let the church remain decorated as on the day of the Lord’s Nativity. Let the bells be struck, the lights kindled, and everything else carried out as on the other double feasts and feasts of the second rank, which will be described later.

At Vespers, let antiphons from the respective feasts be placed over the psalms, according to the instructions of the cantor. Once the first days have passed, let no commemoration of those feasts be made except on the final days of the feasts; then only three lessons are to be read.

Throughout the week, the morning Mass is *Puer natus* (“A child is born”); on the fifth day, the principal Mass is *Dominus dixit* (“The Lord said”); on the following day, the introit is *Puer natus*, followed by what belongs to *Lux fulgebit* (“A light will shine”). These two days are to be celebrated as on ordinary twelve-lesson feasts, except that there are to be three lessons. The Gospels of the Lord’s Nativity are to be recited alternately at these services.

Let the feast of Saint Sylvester be celebrated as an ordinary twelve-lesson feast. The third Nocturn and Lauds are to be of the Lord’s Nativity. Before Epiphany, let the Office *Dum medium silentium* (“While deep silence”) be said.

Let the Circumcision of the Lord be celebrated as one of the three preceding feasts, except that the hall of the monastery is not to be decorated; it must be dismantled on the fifth day after the Lord’s Nativity.

On the day after the Circumcision of the Lord, let them begin reading the Epistles of Saint Paul. After the Nocturns, let them celebrate the Office of the Dead. Then let the bell be struck, and let them sing Matins and Lauds for all the Saints. Afterward let them return to their beds. Let this be done until the octave of Epiphany, unless there is a feast with twelve lessons.

On the vigil of Epiphany, let there be no fast. The Office at Mass is *Lux fulgebit*. At Vespers, let there be one antiphon over the psalms: *Stella ista* (“This star”).

On the following day, at the invitatory, let three be in copes. Let there be no procession on that day unless it is a Sunday. If it is a Sunday, however, let there be a procession in albs through the cloister before Terce, with the priest proceeding through the workrooms, as is customary on Sundays.

At Vespers, let the antiphons and psalms be said up to the chapter as on the day of the Nativity. On the final day of the octave, let the entire night service be celebrated from the octave itself, with only a commemoration of Saint Hilary. Let Vespers up to the chapter, and the morning Mass, be as on the day of Epiphany.

After the eighth day of Epiphany, let the responsories from the psalms be begun. Let the psalmody and everything else be carried out by night and by day, as before the Nativity.

At Vespers on the eve of the Purification of Saint Mary [Col. 0452B], let the antiphons *O admirable* and the others be sung; the psalms are those of the weekday, and the chapter reading is *Behold, I am sending an angel*. On the following day, the canticle *The people who walked*. At Terce let all be clothed entirely in white. After Terce has been said, let a carpet be placed before the altar, and candles set upon it; the priest, wearing an alb and stole, shall bless them, sprinkle them with holy water, and incense them. Then let the sacristan distribute them, giving one to each person. When they have begun to be lit, let the cantor begin the antiphon *A light for revelation!* After this has been said, and after the verses of the canticle *Now you dismiss* have been sung and repeated as long as the cantor judges sufficient, let them go out in procession, the cantor beginning the antiphon *Hail, grace*, and others if necessary. They shall enter through the monastery’s greater doors and make a station before the Crucifix. When the singing they had begun has ended [Col. 0452C], let the cantor immediately begin the antiphon *When they brought in*; singing it, let them enter the choir, let the bells be rung, and let them celebrate Mass.

After the meal, let them sit in the cloister until the servants leave the refectory. When they have gone out and entered the monastery, let the two greater bells be rung and let None be sung. When it has been sung, let the prior go out and sound the cymbal; afterward let them go to the refectory. Let them observe this custom until Palm Sunday, except on fast days.

On this day the psalm *To the Lord, when I was in distress* is to be begun; it is to be said for the Vigil of the Dead until the Kalends of November. At Vespers: the antiphon *With you is dominion*, the psalm *The Lord said*; the antiphon *Redemption* [Col. 0452D], the psalm *I will confess*; the antiphon *The light has risen*, the psalm *Blessed is the man*; the antiphon *From the fruit*, the psalm *Remember*.

On ordinary days, after Vespers, let them perform the Vigil of the Dead, unless the following day is a feast of twelve lessons. After the nocturns, on ordinary days until the Thursday before Easter, let them say the customary two psalms, with prayers and a collect; afterward, *They shall exult in the Lord*. Then let them sing Matins of All Saints; let everything else be done as before the Nativity of the Lord.

## SECTION III.—From Septuagesima to Passion Sunday

On the first Sunday of Septuagesima, let the alleluia be entirely discontinued; in place of the alleluia, at each Hour let *Praise to you, Lord, King of eternal glory* be said [Col. 0453A] until Vespers on the Paschal Vigil. Let the Historia *In the beginning God made* be sung. Let the five books of Moses, and Joshua, Judges, and Ruth, be assigned for reading on Sundays and on the other occasions of twelve lessons until Easter. At Prime, let the chapter reading be *Lord, have mercy on us*. Let *Glory to God in the highest* and *The Mass is ended* not be said until Holy Saturday; let neither dalmatic nor tunicle be worn at Mass until the Lord’s Supper; instead, let the ministers be clothed in chasubles. On that day let them eat fat; thereafter let them abstain from it until Easter.

On Wednesday at the beginning of the fast, let the chapter readings be *Turn back to me* and the following passages. After Sext, let them return to the cloister to speak; when the proper time comes, let one of the medium-sized bells be rung [Col. 0453B]. When it has been rung, let silence immediately be observed in the cloister. Let them remove their shoes, go to wash their hands, and then proceed without delay to the church, where they shall make one common prayer. When this has been done, let two bells be rung, the boy beginning *Rise up, Lord*; the psalm *God, with our ears*. When these have been completed, let the priest say *Show us, Lord*. Let *Kyrie eleison* follow; *Our Father*, and *do not lead us*; the psalm *May God have mercy on us*; the chapter reading *And let them come upon us*; and the collect for sins *Hear, we beseech you, Lord, the prayers of your suppliants*.

After this, let the priest bless the ashes, wearing only the stole. Having sprinkled holy water over them, let him place the ashes upon the heads of the brothers, saying: “Remember that you are ash, and to ash you shall return.” Meanwhile let the antiphon *Let us change our ways* be sung [Col. 0453C], with one or more verses of the psalm *May God have mercy on us*, as needed.

This done, let them go out in procession, singing the antiphons *Hear us, Lord* and *Beside the vestibule*. These two antiphons, namely *Hear us* and *Beside the vestibule*, are to be sung in the same order at all the processions of Lent held on Wednesday and Friday. When the antiphons have been completed, let two boys begin the litany.

Let the procession be conducted in this order on the Friday following the beginning of the fast, and on Wednesday and Friday throughout Lent, until the Wednesday before the Paschal feast, unless a feast of twelve lessons falls on one of those weekdays. It should be noted that if a feast of twelve lessons falls on the day beginning the fast, it is not celebrated on that day but is deferred to the following day [Col. 0453D].

On the first Sunday of Lent, at the invitatory, two shall be in white. After Compline, let a curtain be hung between the choir and the altar.

On Monday before Terce, the cross, crowns, reliquaries, and Gospel books bearing images on their exterior are to be covered. Before the 259 brothers enter the chapter house, the keeper of the books must have the books assembled in the chapter house upon a spread carpet, except those which were given out for reading in the previous year; those, when entering the chapter house, they must each carry in his own hand. The aforesaid keeper of the books must warn them of this on the preceding day in the chapter house. Let the passage from the Rule of Saint Benedict concerning the observance of Lent be read [Col. 0454A].

When this sermon has been delivered, let the aforesaid keeper of the books read the Brief concerning how the brothers possessed the books in the previous year. When each man hears his name pronounced, let him return the book that had been entrusted to him for reading in the previous year. Whoever realizes that he has not read through the book he received shall prostrate himself, confess his fault, and ask pardon.

Then let the aforesaid keeper of the books give each brother another book to read. After the books have been distributed in order, let the said keeper of the books enter in the same chapter house a brief record of the names of the books and of those who received them.

If a feast of twelve lessons occurs on this day, let two lessons be read in the chapter house, one from the Gospel and the other concerning the observance of Lent. Let one be read immediately after the other. After the second lesson has been read, only then let the reader say, “But you, Lord” [Col. 0454B].

On that day let the prayers begin: let us pray for every order of the Church; the penitential psalms while prostrate, namely the seven penitential psalms and the first seven Gradual Psalms, two at each Hour—one from this side and one from the other—until Vespers. At Vespers, let four be added, with chapters and collects for sins, ending with: “and for the benefits that you have deigned to renew in us, grant that we may come rejoicing to remember them.”

On this day let them begin to carry the hidden object only for the second lesson.

For three days, namely Monday, Wednesday, and Friday until Easter, let the board not be struck after the chapter house, nor let them speak in the cloister. On Wednesday and Friday after Sext, before they leave the choir, let them say *God, with our ears*.

On these two weekdays [Col. 0454C], after None, let them sit in the cloister. After a short interval, let the sacristan ring one of the medium-sized bells. Then let all remove their shoes and wash their hands, come to the choir, and, after the prayer has been made, let the boy begin the antiphon *Rise up, Lord, help us*. Let two bells be rung. Let the priest say *Show us, Lord*; let *Kyrie eleison* and *Our Father* follow. The psalm on Wednesday is *May God have mercy on us*; on Friday, *God, come to my assistance*. Then the priest shall say *And let it come upon us*, followed by the prayer for sins.

Afterward let the cantor begin the antiphon and sing for the procession. The litany is as above. For this procession no one is to go shod except the priest and deacon. If anyone, because of illness, cannot go barefoot, let him remain behind from the procession. When they return from the procession, no one may presume to put on shoes without permission. When Mass has been completed and the prayer at Vespers has been made, let them wash their feet and hands and say Vespers [Col. 0454D].

If a feast happens to be celebrated during Lent, on the preceding day, while the *Agnus Dei* is being sung at the principal Mass, let the curtain be drawn together and let the choir stalls that are customarily removed for twelve lessons be taken away. When Mass has ended, let the evening prayer be conducted as on Saturday. After the collect of the feast, let the antiphon of the weekday be said, with *Glory to the Father*; the psalms while prostrate are not to be said.

After Vespers of All Saints, let Vespers of the Dead be sung; the Vigil of the Dead is not to be performed. On the day of the feast, after Matins of All Saints, let Matins of the Dead be said. Then let them return to their beds [Col. 0455A].

After Prime, when the customary familiar psalms have been said, with their chapters and collects, let the seven psalms with the litany be said. At each Hour until Vespers, beginning with Prime, let them say the psalm *Incline, Lord*, instead of the psalms they would otherwise have said while prostrate. After the chapter reading, let them sit silently in the cloister until the signal is rung for Terce. The boys also, after their chapter reading, coming down from the dormitory, shall sit and read in their school during this interval.

Let them conduct the entire day solemnly; both Masses are to be celebrated at the principal altar. At the Mass of the fast, neither let the litany precede, nor let them bow over the choir stalls at the Canon.

At Vespers, unless the following day is a feast of twelve lessons, between the ringing of the bells let them say *God, with our ears*. After the collect of the feast, let the collect of the weekday be said, with *Glory to the Father*. After Vespers of All Saints, let Vespers for the Dead be sung. The Vigil of the Dead is not to be performed on that day. After Compline, let the curtain be extended and let the choir stalls be brought back into the choir [Col. 0455B].

## SECTION IV.—During the Passion of the Lord

On Saturday at Vespers before the Passion of the Lord, let the prayer concerning the cross be discontinued. Neither at the responsories, nor at the invitatories, nor at Masses is *Glory* to be said until Easter, unless the Mass is a familiar Mass within the convent or outside the convent, or unless a feast of a saint happens to be celebrated during this period. If one does occur, let *Glory to the Father* be said both at the responsories and at Mass, as at other times. During this period let Jeremiah be read until Easter [Col. 0455C].

On Palm Sunday, at the invitatory, two shall be in white. Let the Gospel be proclaimed: *When he had drawn near*. Let both the lesson and the sermon in the chapter house concern it. In that chapter house, let the abbot or prior arrange the procession, what each person is to carry, and how the brothers are to go and return in orderly fashion.

At private Masses, let the priests say only one collect. Let the Gospel *When he had drawn near* be read. No one is to read the Passion except the brothers who sing in the choir stalls. The morning Mass is to have one collect.

After the morning Mass, let water be blessed, with everyone clothed in white. Let a procession be made through the cloister, as is customary on every Sunday. When they enter the church, let the bells be rung; when the responsory has ended, and the things customarily said on Sundays have been said [Col. 0455D], let Terce be sung.

After Terce has been sung, let the Gospel *The great crowd* be read. Then let the abbot or priest approach and bless the palms, flowers, and branches placed before the principal altar upon a carpet; let him sprinkle them with holy water and incense them. The sacristans who approach shall distribute them: palms to the abbot, priors, and more honored persons; flowers and branches to the others.

Meanwhile, with the cantor beginning, let the antiphon *The children of the Hebrews* be sung, and the other one, *The children of the Hebrews*. When these things have been completed, let the procession set out, the cantor beginning what ought to be sung for this procession. When it leaves the choir, let all the bells be rung.

Let servants go first with banners; let a conversus [i.e., novice] follow, carrying a bucket with holy water; two others carrying two crosses; likewise two with two candelabra bearing candles lit above; and two others carrying two thuribles filled with fire and incense [Col. 0456A].

The incense is to be placed in the thurible either by the abbot, if he is in the choir, with the thuribles turned toward him and the small box [Note: Small box; now they call it a boat.] containing the incense being carried; or by the cantor himself if the abbot is absent. For he distributes the things that are to be carried and arranges the procession.

These are to be followed by two subdeacons carrying two Gospel books. After them, the lay monks; then the boys with their teachers. After these, the remaining brothers, preceding the abbot, who proceeds last, two by two, according to their rank as priors.

These are the things to be sung for this procession, either all of them or as many as the space through which they will travel permits: *Six days before*; *When he had drawn near* [Col. 0456B]; *Now on the first day of Unleavened Bread*; *The Lord Jesus*; *They took counsel*; *When the people had heard*. Let all praise together.

When they have reached the appointed place, let the entire convent make a station. When the cantor begins the antiphon *The crowds come to meet him*, let two priests dressed in white come out. They are to carry a bier which those same priests must have brought there shortly before dawn, and in which the body of Christ is to be enclosed.

Immediately before that bier let those carrying the banners and crosses, and the others mentioned above, proceed. While those carrying the bier stand, they too shall stand to its right and left, in orderly fashion as they came. The boys, approaching, shall stand with their faces turned toward the others, with their teachers and certain cantors who can assist them. The older members shall face one another, in the manner in which they customarily stand in the choir [Col. 0456C].

The station is to be arranged so that there is a small interval between the boys and the larger convent. When the antiphon *The crowds come to meet him* has ended, let the boys and those with them begin the antiphon *Hosanna to the Son of David*, bending their knees both at the beginning and at the end of the antiphon, because *Hosanna* is said in both places. Let the choir repeat that antiphon and likewise bend its knees.

Then let the boys sing the antiphon *With the angels*, bending their knees only at the end of the antiphon. Let the convent repeat this antiphon and likewise make a reverence.

When these things have been completed, with the abbot or cantor beginning the antiphon *Hail, our King*, let the bearers of the bier pass through the middle of the station [Col. 0456D]. Those carrying the banners and the other bearers mentioned above shall go before it, and all shall maintain the order on the return journey that they had on the outward journey. As they pass, they shall bend their knees—not all together, but individually, on either side, as the bier passes before them.

When this antiphon has been completed, let them sing others as well if the space requires more. When they have come to the city gates, let them make a station, separating from one another as the place allows on both sides. Let the bier be placed before the entrance to the gates upon a table covered with a cloth, so that the bearers standing on either side have their faces turned toward the bier placed between them. The place above the entrance to the gates should be honorably prepared with curtains [hangings or carpets] and back-cloths [Col. 0457A].

When the station has been arranged in this way, let the boys, from a suitable place, and those who are with them at the cantor’s command, sing *Glory and praise*, and let the choir respond likewise.

The boys: *You are Israel’s King*; and the choir: *To whom belongs the honor of childhood*.

Again the boys: *The Hebrew people are for you*; and the choir: *To whom belongs the honor of childhood*.

Again the boys: *The assembly in the heights*; and the choir: *Glory and praise*.

When these have been said, let the cantor begin the responsory *As the Lord entered*. As the procession enters the city, let the two greater bells be rung until the other bells are rung for Mass when the procession enters the choir.

When the procession has been arranged in this way, and has come to the entrance of the monastery, let it make a station, with the boys maintaining their order between the two choirs. Let the bier again be placed upon a table covered with a cloth [Col. 0457B].

The cantor should have begun the responsory *The rulers have gathered* in such a way that it will then be nearly completed. When it has been sung, let three or four brothers, dressed in copes that the sacristan has prepared there, sing the verse *But one of them*, standing between the choir and the relics.

When this has ended, let them enter the church on the return journey, the cantor beginning the antiphon *The rulers* and another, *He was drawing near*. After entering the church, let them make a station entirely similar, before the Crucifix, which has previously been uncovered. There, let three or four brothers in copes sing the responsory *They surrounded me*.

When it has been sung, let the abbot begin the responsory *The synagogue*, and let them enter the choir while the bells are rung for Mass [Col. 0457C]. Let them celebrate Mass holding palms and branches in their hands; after the offering of bread and wine, when the deacon begins, let all offer them in order.

Let the refectory tables be covered. After the midday meal, let them rest in their beds. As the ninth hour approaches, let the sacristan ring the small bell moderately. Then let all rise, wash their hands and faces, comb themselves, proceed to the church, and sit in the choir.

When the boys have washed and have begun to go to the towels, let the sacristan ring the greater bell. Then let all rise from their seats. When the boys have entered the choir, let them first make a prayer and afterward sing None. When it has been sung, let the prior sound the cymbal, and let all go to the refectory.

Let this order concerning the midday rest be observed throughout the summer, except on fast days, until the Kalends of October [Col. 0457D].

On Tuesday the brothers are to be shaved together in the cloister. On the following day the baths are to be prepared. The order in which this is to be done, how the brothers are to go there, and how they are to conduct themselves there has been stated above, where the preparation of the baths before the Nativity of Christ was discussed.

On Wednesday let no procession be held; let everything else be done in the customary manner until Vespers. Before Vespers, let the psalm *God, with our ears* not be said. Let the bells be rung as on feast days. Let the responsory *They surrounded me* be sung.

Let the weekly cantor sing the prayers *I said, Lord*; at the prayers, only the psalm *Have mercy on me, God*. Let the psalms while prostrate not be said.

After Vespers of All Saints, let Vespers for the Dead be said. The Office of the Dead, which is customarily said after the meal, is not to be said. The hymn at Compline is *You, before the ending of the light*, which is likewise to be said every day until the Kalends of November. After Compline, let the curtain be lowered [Col. 0458A].

On Thursday, let as many candles be lit before *Laetare* as there are antiphons and responsories to be sung. After the three prayers have ended, let each person, seated, recite silently fifteen psalms, without *Glory to the Father*, with the customary chapters and collects. At *Our Father*, let them prostrate themselves over the choir stalls; when the abbot gives the sign, let them rise.

During the psalmody and before the nocturn, let the bells be rung as at twelve lessons. When all the bells have been rung, let the weekly cantor begin the antiphon *Zeal for your house*. When they begin the psalm, let them ask pardon over the choir stalls, and likewise at Matins.

At each antiphon and each responsory, let one candle be extinguished. Let the lessons be read without *Give your blessing, lord*, or *But you, Lord*. The first three are to be from the Lamentations of Jeremiah, without chant, with the prescribed alphabet headings. In the second nocturn, let them be from the exposition of the psalm *Hear my prayer, O God, while I plead*; in the third, from Paul’s Epistle *When you come together*. Let all the antiphons and verses be sung without their concluding melody.

At the morning praises, when they begin the psalm *Praise the Lord from the heavens*, let the teachers go among the boys and face the senior brethren, as the boys do. The young men who are under guardianship are to be interspersed among the ranks of the elders.

Let the candles be extinguished throughout the monastery except one burning in the choir. That one too is to be extinguished when the cantor begins the antiphon *But the traitor* [Col. 0458B].

When the antiphon has ended, let them bend over the choir stalls in silence, saying *Kyrie eleison*, *Our Father*, the prayers *I said, Lord*, the psalm *Have mercy on me, God* alone, without *Glory to the Father*, and the collect *Look upon us, we beseech you, Lord*.

When the abbot or prior gives the sign, let them rise and bow, as usual, before and behind, and let each remain in his place until the master of the boys brings lit lanterns into the choir and distributes them to the boys. The sacristan also shall light a lamp before the altar, from which the young men may light their lanterns. When these things have been completed, let all return to their beds.

When daylight has appeared sufficiently for the boys and young men to leave without lanterns, let the sacristan ring the small bell gently. The brothers shall immediately rise, put on their night shoes, and come to the choir. Let them bend over the choir stalls in their order until the boys arrive [Col. 0458D].

When the boys have come, after the prayer has been completed and the abbot has given the sign, let them rise and immediately begin the hymn *When the light of dawn has risen*, without the verse *Glory be to God the Father*. When the antiphon has begun, let the regular psalms be said, and also *Whoever wishes*, without *Glory to the Father*.

When the antiphon has ended, let them bend over the choir stalls. Each person shall say silently to himself *Kyrie eleison*, *Our Father*, *I believe in God*, the prayers up to the confession. When the abbot gives the sign, let the confession be said.

Then let them say silently the following: *Turn us back*, and the rest; *Have mercy on me, God*, without *Glory*; the collect *Lord God, who at the beginning* [Col. 0459A]. After this, let the seven psalms be said aloud without *Glory*, with the customary litany. Then let them sit in the cloister until Terce.

When the time for Terce has come, let the sacristan ring the smallest bell, as on other days. Then let the brothers go to put on their shoes, and let everything else be done as on other days. When the signal for Terce has been rung, let the three customary prayers be made.

When another signal has been rung, let the boy immediately begin the hymn *By the faith in which we live*. But let the final verse, *Glory to you, Trinity*, not be said. After the antiphon has been proclaimed, let the regular psalms instituted by blessed Benedict be said without *Glory*. When the psalms have been said and the antiphon completed, let them bend over the choir stalls and say silently *Kyrie eleison* and the rest that follows. The collect is *Look upon us, we beseech you, Lord*.

After this, let the customary signal for the chapter house be rung. Let the lesson be read without *Give your blessing, lord*; let the verse be said in silence; let the passage from the Rule of Saint Benedict be read without *But you, Lord*. When the sermon on it has been delivered, and what ought to be corrected has been corrected, let the customs to be observed from that chapter house until the next chapter house be stated. Then let the matters to be arranged for the service of the entire day be organized.

When these things have been arranged, let them rise, singing aloud *My words*, if they have a deceased brother, or the *Brief for the deceased*. In silence let them say *Our Father*, *From the gate of the underworld*, *Deliver, Lord*. When the board has been struck, let them speak in the cloister [Col. 0459B].

When the time has come, let the signal for Sext be rung. After the prayer has been made and another signal rung, let the boy begin the hymn and the rest as they did at Terce. Then, when the signal has been rung, let them speak again in the cloister.

At that point let the sacristan ring the very small bell briefly, as at twelve lessons before the morning Mass. Then let the weekly priest celebrate the lesser Mass for the poor who must attend the Mandatum, the almoner brother leading them, with the other brothers assigned to assist. When Mass has ended, let the priest communicate those poor people from the unconsecrated offerings, making only the sign of the holy cross over them in the name of the Lord. Then let them be led to eat [Col. 0459C].

After these things, when the signal for None has been rung, and after the prayer and another signal, let None be sung as at Terce and Sext. When it has been sung, let the boys and those who are to celebrate Mass be vested: the priest or abbot honorably; the deacon in a dalmatic; the subdeacon in a tunicle; two for the responsory; three conversi [Note: That is, novices, or monk-beginners, who are converted from the lay order, as is clear below, chapter 20.] for the candelabra and thurible.

Meanwhile, let the choir stalls that are customarily removed be taken away. Let the bells be rung as on feast days. Let the weekly cantor hold the choir in a cope. Let Mass be celebrated festively. Let *Glory to God in the highest* not be said, unless a bishop celebrates Mass and makes the chrism; at this time also *The Mass is ended* is said at the end of Mass.

Let as many hosts be placed for consecration as may suffice for that day and for communicating on the following day. During these four days, let no one abstain from Communion unless there is a reasonable cause for abstaining [Col. 0460A].

[Note: Note that on Wednesday, Thursday, Friday, and Saturday they received the Eucharist.]

When Mass has nearly been completed, let the choir stalls be brought back into the choir. Let the board be struck for Vespers. When Mass has ended, let the evening prayer be made over the choir stalls.

Meanwhile, when the priest, with the procession preceding him, has come to the altar, let him go to the appointed place, most suitably prepared, and there let him place the Lord’s body, having incensed the place both before and after the reposition. Before that place let a lamp burn continually.

When this has been completed, let them go to the refectory to receive the mixed dish. After entering the refectory, let them make a bow before and behind their seats, and, sitting down, let them take the mixed dish consisting only of bread and drink, which they find placed by the refectory servants in cups upon their portions.

While these things are being done, let the cellarer, the almoner, and the others who have been assigned bring the poor into the cloister and have them sit in orderly fashion, one beside another. Before entering the cloister, the poor are to wash their feet with warm water supplied by the chamberlains.

Everything necessary for the service must be prepared in suitable places: warm water supplied by the chamberlains and prepared in proper vessels; other vessels and foot towels; hand towels; cups and drink from the cellarer; and anything else of this kind. Let the servants of the chamberlains and of the other ministers who are suitable for this service be ready to assist. Beforehand, they must be carefully instructed by those ordered to do so concerning how they ought to serve them [Col. 0460B].

When these things have been arranged, and when the abbot judges the time right, let him rise. Let the other brothers also rise and bow before and behind.

When they have left the refectory, let the boys withdraw with their teachers to their school, and there let them stand with their teachers before their own poor. Let the other brothers also rise and come before their own poor, standing in orderly fashion before them, according to their rank, each before his assigned person. The abbot shall have two.

Then, at the abbot’s command, let the prior strike the board three times. Let them bend down, kneel upon the ground, and adore Christ in the poor.

Let the abbot or cantor begin the antiphon *The Lord Jesus* and the others that are appropriate. Each person shall wash the feet of one poor person, dry them, and kiss them with his mouth and eyes.

When the feet of all the poor have been washed, let two of the brothers assigned to do so serve the abbot, one with water and the other with a towel. Let servants serve the remaining brothers. Afterward, the abbot, taking basins and a towel from the brothers who served him, and the other brothers taking them from the servants, shall themselves serve the poor. The brothers who follow them shall receive from them and serve the abbot; and the others shall provide the brothers with cups containing drink [Col. 0460D].

Then let the prior strike the board three times. Let everyone say in a moderate voice, *Bless*. After the blessing has been given, let them give drink to the poor, kissing their hands. When they have received the cups, let each give two pennies to one poor person, or as many as the abbot has ordered, again kissing their hands [Col. 0461A].

The cellarer or chamberlain is to give the pennies, according to what the abbot judges appropriate. The brothers who died during that year are to have their own poor for this service; likewise the household members for whom the abbot has decreed that one person is to be assigned among the poor at this service.

The brothers who have been assigned are to serve these poor in the manner stated above; no other person may presume to do so.

As long as they sing for this service—that is, while the feet and hands of the poor are being washed—those who wish may sit, but in the manner in which one sits in the choir: one seated between two standing. While the drink is being distributed, everyone who wishes may sit, one beside another, without observing that order of standing or sitting.

Meanwhile the sacristan must observe the appropriate intervals at which he is to strike the board for Vespers: once when the feet have been washed, and once when the hands have been washed and drink has been given to everyone. When each person has returned to his place, let the prior strike the board three times [Col. 0461B].

Then let the abbot or priest say in a moderate voice the chapter reading *Show us, Lord, your mercy*. Let all the brothers respond, kneeling upon the ground, *And grant us your salvation*. Then, bent only upon their knees, let them say *Kyrie eleison*, *Our Father*. Let the abbot or priest say in a moderate voice, *And do not lead us*. *We have received, O God, your mercy. In the midst of your temple. You commanded that your commandments be kept exceedingly. Lord, hear my prayer. And let my cry come to you. The Lord be with you. Let us pray.*

“Be present, Lord Jesus Christ, at the service of our ministry; and because you deigned to wash the feet of your disciples, do not despise the work of your hands, which you commanded us to observe. But just as these outward bodily impurities are washed away, so may all our inward sins be washed away by you. May you deign to grant this, who with the Father, and so forth.”

At its end, let all respond *Amen*, bow before and behind, and go to the church, singing the psalm *Have mercy on me, God* in a moderate voice. Meanwhile, let the sacristan and certain brothers with him strike the boards gradually, in the manner and order in which the bells are customarily rung on feast days [Col. 0461C].

When the psalm has been said and the brothers are standing in their order in the choir, let the boy immediately begin the antiphon *I will take the cup of salvation*. At its beginning, let everyone ask pardon over the choir stalls. Let the psalm *My soul magnifies the Lord* be said, and let the antiphon be repeated without its concluding melody. Bent over the choir stalls, let them say silently *Kyrie eleison*, *Our Father*, the prayers *I said, Lord*, the psalm *Have mercy on me, God*, and the collect *Look upon us, we beseech you* [Col. 0461D].

If anyone comes from outside and asks for a blessing, let him receive it at every Hour on the day he comes.

During these three days, let the refectory tables be covered. Let boards with small hammers be placed by the cymbal and above the abbot’s table. Let the verses and blessings in the refectory, and *Have mercy on me, God* after the meal, be said in a subdued voice. Let the reader read without requesting a blessing and conclude without *But you, Lord*.

Meanwhile, while the brothers are in the refectory, let the sacristans uncover all the altars and prepare two lecterns: one that is in the chapter house, and another in the monastery, which is to be carried into the refectory before the collation [Col. 0462A].

After the brothers have risen from the table and returned from the monastery and dormitory in the customary manner, let them wash their feet as is done on Saturday. Let everything necessary for the service be prepared. When the servants have eaten and the feet have been washed, let the board be struck, and let them go to the refectory to drink.

After this, when the brothers have gone out of the refectory, let the prior of the cloister, at the abbot’s command, strike the board for the service. When the brothers have entered the chapter house, and the prior of the cloister is sitting in the abbot’s place, let the abbot and prior gird themselves with linen cloths [Col. 0462B].

When the prior of the cloister begins the antiphon *The Lord Jesus*, let them come into the chapter house, the abbot on the right and the prior on the left, followed by the brothers assigned to serve them in the chapter house that day. Both shall kneel and wash the brothers’ feet, dry them, and kiss them.

The chamberlains must be ready to provide fresh towels whenever the others have become wet. When the feet of all who are in the chapter house have been washed, let the prior and the aforesaid servants serving with him sit outside before the chapter house. The abbot, girded with a towel, shall kneel and wash their feet, dry them, and kiss them, with the brothers assigned to this service assisting him.

After this, let the abbot return to his seat. Then let the prior, girded with a towel, come with the brothers assigned to him, wash the abbot’s feet, dry them, and kiss them. After washing his hands, let him immediately bring him water to wash his hands, while one of those who served him holds the towel.

Then, when the prior of the cloister has returned to the abbot’s place, let the abbot go out. He and the prior shall take basins with water and towels. Two brothers who serve in the kitchen that week, and who are to be appointed among the other assistants for the service, shall serve everyone in washing their hands, just as they served in washing their feet [Col. 0462C].

When this has been completed, let the abbot, the prior, and their servants go out. Before the chapter house, let the abbot provide them with water for washing their hands, while one of the brothers assigned to this service holds the towel.

When this has been done, let the abbot go first and the others follow him into the chapter house. Let them make the bows before and behind, as is done on Saturday by those who have performed the service. Then let the abbot go to his seat; let the convent rise until he sits down, and let the others likewise go to their places.

When the singing has ceased and the sacristan has struck the board for the collation—he having gone to strike it with permission—at the appropriate hour let the deacon enter the chapter house. He had gone to prepare himself after washing his hands; he is to be clothed in an alb, stole, and dalmatic, carrying the Gospel book. Three conversi precede him, carrying candelabra and a thurible filled with fire and incense. The deacon himself must put the incense into the thurible before he leaves the monastery [Col. 0462D].

When they enter the chapter house, the entire convent shall rise and remain standing until one verse of the Gospel has been read.

When he sees that the time has come, the abbot shall signal to the prior to go and strike the board. And when the prior has heard the deacon say, “Rise, let us go from here,” he shall strike the board, as the cymbal is customarily struck. As this is done, all shall rise, and, with the deacon carrying the Gospel book and the conversi carrying the candlesticks and thurible going before, the community shall follow into the refectory, as is done on Holy Saturday for the charitable drink.

There the secretary shall have a lectern prepared from the church; when the Gospel book has been placed upon it, the deacon shall again put incense into the thurible and incense the lectern and the book. When the senior prior is seated in the abbot’s place, the deacon shall begin the reading at his nod, from the place where he had stopped.

When the refectorer strikes his board once, the abbot and the brothers who had served as his assistants in washing the feet shall go to the place where the charitable drink has been prepared, carrying glass flasks or the brothers’ cups in their hands. Having received wine in the aforesaid vessels, while the reader remains silent, they shall proceed to the step, as is customary.

The refectorer, from the time when they begin to go gradually after receiving the drink, shall strike his board until they reach the step; when they have arrived there, he shall strike it three or four times more rapidly and then stop. Then, while all say in a subdued voice, “Bless,” the hebdomadary priest shall rise and give the blessing in the same voice.

After the blessing has been given, the abbot shall offer the drink to the prior and to the others according to their order, kissing their hands, while the brothers who brought the drink with him to the step minister to him. After the drink has been served to the seniors and to the children, the abbot shall approach the deacon who is reading the collation and, having waited for the end of the verse begun, offer him the drink; then he shall offer it to the three who serve with the candlesticks and thurible, while the abbot’s servants meanwhile hold the candlesticks and thurible.

These men, receiving the cups from the deacon and from the others, shall carry them to the abbot’s table and place them upon it. When this has been done, the abbot’s aforesaid servants who brought the drink with him to the step shall come together before that step, perform the customary obeisance before and behind, and then go to sit down. The abbot shall likewise bring them the drink, kissing their hands, while those brothers who had ministered to him in washing the feet of the prior and of these servants serve him.

When this has been done, the abbot shall go to his seat and perform the obeisance before it, while the community rises for him until he sits down. The prior, rising, shall offer him the drink, kissing his hand. When as much of the sermon has been read as the abbot wishes, the deacon, at his signal, shall finish the reading without “But you, Lord.” Having closed the book, he shall perform the obeisance before and behind, and then place the dalmatic, stole, and maniple 265 upon the lectern.

The conversi shall carry the candlesticks and thurible to the abbot’s table and perform the obeisance before that table. After this, the deacon and the conversi shall sit at the table and drink: the deacon beside the abbot, and the conversi beside the deacon, according to their order.
