After the sermon has been read, the abbot shall immediately strike the board once, and thereafter as many times as it is customary to strike the skilla on Saturday for the charitable drink after the washing of the feet. Meanwhile, two secretaries shall rise and carry the lectern and the dalmatic, together with the Gospel book, stole, and maniple, to the monastery.

After this, the abbot shall rise and say in a subdued voice, “Our help is in the name of the Lord,” and the community shall answer in the same voice, “Who made heaven and earth.” Then, with the deacon going before and the conversi carrying the candlesticks and thurible, the community shall follow to the monastery, while the secretary strikes the board for Compline. After the confession has been made, they shall say Compline, in pairs or groups of three, in silence.

After Compline they shall make the three prayers in the customary manner. The prior shall strike the board three times after the prayers for the children, as he customarily strikes the skilla. It should be noted concerning the service of this day that, if the abbot is able, he alone ought on this day to wash the feet of all the brothers; for, as blessed Benedict testifies, he exercises Christ’s role in the monastery, and especially in this ministry.

[Col. 0464B] On Friday, before the night office, the board shall be struck in the cloister, before the cellar, and before the infirmary, to awaken those sleeping. After the customary prayers, as on Thursday, fifteen psalms shall be said; the candles shall be extinguished, and the readings in the first and second nocturns shall be read from where they were read on Thursday. In the third nocturn, from the Letter to the Hebrews: “Brothers, let us hasten to enter,” and everything else until Prime shall be as on Thursday.

At Prime, when the board has been struck, they shall rise and go barefoot to the monastery, and all shall remain so until the office of the day has been completed, unless, by the abbot’s order, they put on shoes because of extreme cold. If this occurs, they shall take part in the office barefoot only.

They shall say Prime and all the hours of the day, except Vespers, until Vespers on Saturday as on Thursday, except that on Thursday the hymns are sung aloud, the psalms are intoned, and the antiphons are sung, whereas on these two days all these things are said in silence and directly. After Prime has been said, the seven psalms and the litany shall be said aloud.

Afterward all shall sit in the cloister and, beginning with the abbot, shall recite the entire psalter. When it has been completed, those who wish shall go to confession until the hour of the office.

As the hour of Terce approaches, after the board has been struck as usual, they shall go to the dormitory. Then, washed and combed, they shall go to the monastery after the board has been struck, and, having made the customary prayers, shall say Terce.

After Terce, when the board has been struck, they shall go to the chapter house. There the verse shall be said in silence, and a passage from the Rule shall be read, with its interpretation, as on Thursday. After the sermon, the matters that must be done until the next day’s chapter shall be announced and arranged. Leaving the chapter house, they shall sit in the cloister without speaking, but singing or reading.

After None has been said, the priest and the levite, and the others who are to serve at the office, shall vest. The priest and levite alone shall proceed to the altar: the priest in a chasuble, the deacon in a stole. Without any preceding supplication, the priest shall say, “Let us pray,” and the deacon, “Let us bend our knees”; and likewise at the other collect.

The altar shall be covered above with only one cloth. Two men in albs shall sing each of the tracts. The Passion shall be read without “The Lord be with you.” When the reading reaches the place where it says, “They divided my garments among themselves,” two of those who are vested shall stand beside the altar, one on either side, drawing toward themselves the two cloths that had been placed on the altar before the office, while the linen remains underneath the missal. When the Passion has been read, the solemn prayers shall be said as they are contained in the missal. Kneeling shall be done for all the orders, except for the Jews.

When these things have been completed, the priest and levite, having removed the chasuble and stoles, shall return to the choir in albs. Then two priests whom the cantor has ordered, vested in albs, shall approach the cross, which must have been prepared and covered at the morning altar. Taking it, they shall carry it forward gradually while singing the verses “My people.” Two levites in albs, standing before the steps before the great altar, shall answer, “Agios ho Theos” (“Holy God”).

The choir shall say, “Holy God”; the priests, “For I brought you out”; the levites, “Agios”; the choir, “Holy”; the priests, “What more”; the levites, “Agios”; the choir, “Holy.”

Then the priests carrying the cross shall come before the altar. When they have finished “Holy,” they shall immediately uncover it and both begin the antiphon “Behold the wood”; only then shall all kneel. The antiphon shall be repeated with verses from the psalm “Blessed are the undefiled,” for as long as the cantor judges appropriate. Thereafter other chants pertaining to this service shall be sung as much as necessary.

Carpets shall be spread 266 before the altar. First the abbot and those who are vested shall prostrate themselves upon them; meanwhile, others shall successively take the place of those holding the cross. Then the rest shall do likewise, according to their order. They shall not adore at excessive length, but shall pray briefly and sincerely. Afterward each person shall kiss the feet of the crucified one and then return to the choir.

If any clerics or laypeople should come wishing to adore the cross, it shall be carried to another place where they can adore it more suitably. If it passes through the choir, the brothers shall adore it with their knees bent to the ground, not all together, but as it is carried before them. When all have adored the cross, its bearers, lifting it, shall begin the antiphon “Above all the cedar trees,” and shall go to the place where it is to be set. Then all shall ask forgiveness with their knees bent to the ground.

[Col. 0465D] When these things have been done, the priest, having resumed the chasuble and stole, and the deacon in a stole, with the conversi carrying the candlesticks and thurible going before, shall go to the place where the Lord’s body was deposited on Thursday. Having placed incense in the thurible, the priest shall incense it and then hand it to the deacon to carry back.

On the way there and back the deacon shall follow the conversi, and the priest shall come last. When they approach the altar, all the brothers shall adore the Lord’s body with bent knees. After Christ’s body has been placed upon the altar, wine and water having been mixed in the chalice, and the priest having made confession with the deacon, the priest shall make a humble prayer at the altar. He shall incense Christ’s body and the chalice; then, in a moderate voice, he shall say, “Let us pray. Instructed by saving commandments,” and everything up to “And lead us not” [Col. 0466A] “into temptation.” The choir shall answer, “But deliver us from evil.”

Then, in silence, the priest shall say, “Deliver us, we beseech you, Lord,” and everything up to “In the unity of the Holy Spirit, God.” After this, in a moderate voice: “For ever and ever.” When the choir answers, “Amen,” he shall say nothing more. Having placed the customary particle of the Lord’s body into the chalice, he shall communicate himself and all the brothers, without the kiss of peace.

When all have communicated, the board shall be struck and the evening prayer shall be made. When it has been completed, they shall go out into the cloister, wash their feet with warm water, and put on their daytime shoes. Then, after the boards have been struck, they shall return to the choir and say Vespers in silence, with the same psalms, antiphons, prayers, and collects as on Thursday, except that in place of the psalm “With my voice,” which was said on Thursday, on this day the psalm “Blessed be the Lord my God” shall be said.

After Vespers has been said and the board struck, they shall go to the refectory, where they shall be refreshed with bread only, water, and raw herbs. The brothers’ food shall be cooked in the kitchen as on other days and carried from there to the alms distribution. The customary drink shall also be given to the poor.

While the community is being refreshed, the secretaries, joined by as many priests as are necessary and as have been ordered, shall remain in the church to wash all the altars, which must first be washed with water and then with wine.

After the servants have been refreshed, when they have returned from the monastery and dormitory to the cloister, and the board has been struck, the brothers shall go to the refectory to preserve the order, as though to drink; those who wish may drink water, but absolutely no other drink. When they have left the refectory and are sitting in the cloister, after a suitable interval the board shall be struck, and all shall go to the collation. At the abbot’s command, after the prior has struck the board, they shall rise from it and go to the refectory to drink the charitable drink.

On Holy Saturday the board shall be struck before the night office as on Friday, and everything else shall likewise be done until Prime. In the third nocturn let there be read from the Letter of the apostle Paul: “Christ assisting as high priest of the things to come.”

At Prime they shall rise in their night clothing. Prime, the seven psalms, the litany, and the other hours until Vespers shall be said as on Friday. In the chapter house a passage from the Rule of Saint Benedict shall be read, [Col. 0466D] and the matters to be done until the Easter chapter shall be arranged.

Before and after chapter, the secretaries must decorate the monastery and all the altars, place candles wherever they ought to be, and set the candle to be blessed in its place. Upon it the cantor must write which year it is from the Lord’s Incarnation, and a cross must be marked by inserting five grains of incense in five places.

After None, those who are to celebrate the office, those assigned especially to serve at it, and all the children shall vest. The priest shall wear an alb and stole; the others, albs. They shall return to the choir and then proceed to bless the fire, singing the fiftieth psalm.

First of all shall go the secretary carrying the staff on which he is to carry back the blessed fire; then the bearer of the blessed water; after them those carrying the cross and thurible; then the priest who is to bless the fire; after him the children; then the other vested men; and after them the remaining brothers, as they process on Sundays.

After the fire has been blessed, the priest shall sprinkle blessed water over it. Then the thurible shall be filled with coals from that fire; when it has been filled, the priest shall place incense in it and incense the fire. Then the candle shall be lit, which the secretary must carry on the staff. A candle shall also be lit in a lantern, so that, if the candle should happen to go out on the way, it may be relit from it. One of the children’s teachers must carry this lantern.

For this procession the candlesticks are not carried. On the return they shall preserve the same order that they had on the way out. As they return, they shall say these psalms: “O God, in your name”; “Have mercy on me, O God, have mercy on me”; “May God have mercy on us”; “O God, come to my assistance.”

At the bishop’s seat two boys shall sing the hymn “Creator of the glowing light” (Inventor rutili). The sanctified fire that remained in the cloister shall be gathered by the cellarer’s servants, and from this fire all the hearths in every workshop, having first been extinguished, shall be lit again.

Many monastic communities make this procession for sanctifying the fire on Thursday and Friday as well: on Thursday the secretary carries the candle before him on a staff or rod; on Friday, the prior; on Saturday, the abbot.

When the procession has returned to the choir without the candlesticks and thurible, the priest, vested in a chasuble, shall proceed to the [Col. 0467C] altar. The deacon, vested in a stole and dalmatic, shall come before the abbot and ask his blessing. Then he shall go to the candle and bless it, performing the obeisance neither before nor after the blessing.

When the time comes, as indicated by the cantor, one of the conversi shall bring the abbot a thurible full of burning coals. After incense has been placed in it, he shall approach the deacon and stand beside him, so that, when the time comes, the deacon may receive the thurible from him and incense the candle. The secretary shall be ready so that, when “The shining fire gives light” has been said, he may immediately light the candle.

When the blessing has been completed, the deacon, having removed the dalmatic and stole, shall return to his place in the choir. The candle shall not be extinguished until the following day [Col. 0467D] after Vespers. The readings shall immediately begin.

The priest shall say the prayers at the altar without singing, in their proper order. After the final prayer has been said, the cantor and another brother whom he chooses, vested in copes, shall begin in the choir the threefold litany, in this manner: the cantors say, “Kyrie eleison”; the right choir likewise answers, “Kyrie eleison”; then the left choir, and so on in the same manner until the end of the litany. They shall say three saints from each order. At each individual name of a saint both choirs shall bow; the cantors shall bow at none.

When the litany has begun, the brothers shall approach the choir stalls, as at the twelve readings. At the third, the priest shall return to the sacristy, and, having removed the chasuble and stole, return to the choir. When the cantors have said, “All holy ones, pray for us,” the priest, levite, subdeacon, and three conversi shall leave the choir, [Col. 0468A] and the priest shall vest in a chasuble, the levite in a dalmatic, and the subdeacon in a tunic.

When the litany is finished, the cantors shall pronounce three times in a loud voice, “Light them.” Then, for the first time, the candlesticks and the other lights before and around the altar shall be lit, and the cantors shall begin the festive “Kyrie eleison.” The priest shall proceed to the altar in the customary procession, and then the bells shall begin to be struck; they shall not cease until the end of the “Kyrie eleison.”

Only then shall the cantor give copes to those who are to sing the Alleluia and the tract. When the “Kyrie eleison” is finished, the priest shall begin, “Glory to God in the highest.” When the Gospel is read, the candlesticks shall not be held, but only the thurible.

Nearly all the principal monastic churches that in our time possess greater authority agree in this custom, as also in the fact that the offertory, the “Lamb of God,” and the Communion are not said at this Mass, although the rest is celebrated festively. In certain monasteries of no discreditable authority, moreover, the candlesticks are not carried on this day even before the priest proceeds to the altar.

When Mass is nearly finished, as the priest begins “Through our Lord,” two skillas shall begin to be struck for Vespers, as is customary on the greatest festivals. After the response “Thanks be to God” to “Go, the dismissal is made,” the evening prayer shall be made. When it has been completed, the children shall go to the refectory, if any are so small that they cannot wait until after Vespers.

Meanwhile the two greater bells shall be struck two at a time, and finally, after all the bells have been struck, Vespers shall be sung solemnly, as is fitting. The hebdomadary cantor shall begin “Alleluia” from whichever antiphon the cantor has prescribed.

The psalms shall be “Let them confess”; the chapter, “If you have risen”; the responsory, “The angel of the Lord spoke”; the hymn, “To the supper of the prudent Lamb”; the verse, “The Lord has risen.” At the Magnificat: “But on the evening of the Sabbath.” The collect: “O God, who made this most holy night.” After Vespers they shall proceed to the crucifix.

## SECTION V.—The Holy Season of Easter

On Easter Day, before the morning vigils, all the bells shall be struck; then two at a time, as is customary. For the invitatory, four men in copes. The psalms instituted by blessed Benedict shall be sung, namely, “O Lord, in your strength,” 268 and the others.

During the readings, thuribles shall be carried around, as was established for the day of the Lord’s Nativity. Finally, the entire office shall be conducted according to monastic custom. The procession to the crucifix shall go after the morning praises and after Vespers throughout the entire week.

The morning Mass on this day shall have one collect, with the procession in copes. At Vespers the regular psalms shall be said, namely, “The Lord said,” and the others customarily said on Sundays. Over the psalms shall be sung the antiphons that were said at the morning praises.

On the three following days, before the vigils, the bells shall be struck two at a time. For the invitatory, three men in copes. The ferial psalms shall be said, six under one antiphon and six under another. Two and two shall sing the first and second responsories; three, the third. The praises shall be under one antiphon.

For the thuribles, two priests vested in copes shall serve at Lauds and Vespers. The morning Mass shall have one collect. At the great Mass all shall be vested in copes. At Vespers throughout the week, the psalms that were said at Vespers on Easter Day shall be said under one antiphon.

On the three following days, two men in frocks shall serve at the invitatory; at the nocturns the ferial psalms shall be said; three readings shall be taken from the proclaimed Gospel; the great Mass and everything else shall be as at the twelve readings. During this week they shall not speak in the cloister.

The morning Mass shall be “I have risen.” All the hours shall be sung with antiphons. On Saturday alone, psalms with “Alleluia” shall be said at Vespers.

On the eighth day, three men in copes shall serve at the invitatory. At the readings, Easter sermons shall be read. In the third nocturn the Gospel shall be proclaimed: “When it was evening.” The morning Mass shall be “Like newborn infants.” The procession shall be in albs. The great Mass shall be “I have risen,” at which all shall be vested in copes.

On Monday, the book of the Acts of the Apostles shall be appointed for reading until the following Sunday. At both nocturns and at all the hours, “Alleluia” shall be said until the Lord’s Ascension.

After chapter, when the board has been struck, they shall speak in the cloister. After None, when they have left the refectory, they shall go to the chapter house and make supplication before and behind. The prior shall strike the board three times and say three times, “O God, come to my assistance; O Lord, make haste to help me.” The community shall answer three times, adding, “Glory to the Father,” “Kyrie eleison,” “Christ, have mercy,” “Kyrie eleison,” “Our Father.” The prior shall say, “And lead us not”; “Our help is in the name of the Lord.” The community shall answer, “Who made heaven and earth.” After the prior has said, “Bless,” they shall speak in the cloister.

This order of speaking shall be observed until the Ides of September on ordinary days, unless there is a fast.

On the first Sunday after the Easter octave, the Apocalypse shall be read, and the historia “Worthy are you, Lord” shall be sung for two weeks. From the third Sunday until the Lord’s Ascension, the seven Catholic Epistles shall be read, and the historia “If I forget” shall be sung.

On the Rogation Days, after Matins for the dead has been said, the brothers shall return to their beds, and those who wish may sleep longer than usual. On these days they do not sleep during the midday hours, nor are they awakened in the morning by any sound as on other days. Rather, when a suitable time seems to have come, their teachers must awaken the children as quietly as possible; while the latter are reading in the cloister, those who are still resting in bed shall rise without delay.

After Prime and the familiar psalms of Prime, the seven psalms and the litany shall be said. A fast-day Mass shall be celebrated at the great altar. After its first prayer, the other prayers that are customarily said at the great Mass on weekdays shall be said, with another added at the end, namely, “Through the intercessions of your saints.”

All shall offer at the kiss of peace; only the prior, or the one acting in the prior’s place, shall go. A passage from the Rule shall be read in chapter, and the procession shall be arranged.

After Terce, the children and the sick who cannot fast shall receive a mixed meal. When Sexta has been sung, they shall go to the dormitory as at other times, when they customarily rest in bed during the midday hours. After the briefest interval, the skilla shall be struck; then they shall descend from the dormitory barefoot, wash their hands, go to the church, and pray.

When this has been done, a child shall begin the antiphon “Arise, O Lord.” Meanwhile two bells shall be struck. When the antiphon has been sung, the priest shall say, “Show us, O Lord, your mercy.” This shall be followed by “Kyrie eleison,” “Our Father,” and the psalm “May God have mercy on us.” On the following day: “O God, come to my assistance.” Then the priest: “And may [your mercy] come upon us,” and the collect for sins.

Afterward, when the bells sound, they shall go out in procession, singing, with the cantor beginning the chants pertaining to the procession. Servants carrying banners shall go before. A conversus carrying water shall follow, and after him another carrying the cross. Then the subdeacon carrying the Gospel book; after him the lay brothers; then the children with their teachers; after them the cantors, with the priors at the rear and the younger brothers in front, according to their order.

At the monastery’s exit, the chamber servants shall be present, carrying staffs prepared there to distribute to the brothers for support.

When they have reached the church to which they are going, the cantor shall begin an antiphon or responsory of the saint in whose honor that church was founded. As they enter, the brothers shall return the staffs to the aforesaid servants, from whom they shall receive them again when leaving.

When the chant begun has ended, the priest shall immediately say the chapter concerning that saint and the collect, with “The Lord be with you,” in a loud and solemn voice. The child shall say, “Let us bless the Lord.” After this has been said, they shall bow and pray.

When the signal has been given, they shall rise and bow before and behind. While this is taking place, the priest, levite, and the others who are to serve around the altar must prepare themselves to celebrate Mass. The secretary shall also suitably prepare the altar with a pall and decent cloths; for all that is necessary for this service must previously have been brought there by the secretary.

When everything is ready, a fast-day Mass shall again be celebrated. After the first prayer, the prayer of the saint to whom the church belongs shall be said, and no other.

When Mass is nearly finished, the two brothers vested in copes who are to say the “Lamb of God” shall bow before and behind at the monastery gates and go out, taking with them some of the servants who have been ordered to do so, and saying among themselves the litany that the community will sing on its return.

When Mass has been completed, the brothers who have been ordered to do so shall immediately approach and, standing in the middle, proclaim the litany. Meanwhile the priest and those who served at Mass shall finish their preparations and return thus to the choir.

After “Saint John” and “All the choir of prophets,” they shall proclaim twice the name of the saint in whose honor the church has been dedicated. Then all shall bow before and behind and return in the order in which they came.

The cantors of the litany shall lengthen or shorten it according to the distance of the journey. On the return they must go after the children and before the rest of the congregation of singers.

[Col. 0471A] When the returning procession has come before the entrance of the monastery, they shall halt and finish the litany. When it has ended, its cantors shall return to their proper order. The aforesaid two cantors who had gone before, vested in copes and standing barefoot before the monastery gates, shall say:

“Lamb of God, who take away the sins of the world, have mercy on us.”

The choir shall answer likewise.

The cantors: “Receive our supplication, you who sit at the right hand of the Father.”

The choir: “Lamb of God,” as above.

The cantors: “Glory to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit, as it was in the beginning, and now and always, and for ages of ages. Amen.”

Meanwhile, with those carrying the banner and the other things mentioned above going before, the cantors and the rest of the community shall follow. When the “Glory” has been said, the community shall answer, “Lamb of God,” as above.

As the community enters the monastery, the bells shall be struck. The cantors shall say, “Hear us, O God”; the community, “The prayer of your people.”

When all the brothers have entered the choir, and the cross and the other things carried have been placed in their proper locations, the aforesaid two cantors, standing in the middle of the choir, shall proclaim the litany: “Holy God of holy ones, have mercy on us.” The priors shall stand on the altar side, and the others behind them, according to their order.

When the litany is completed, the bell shall be struck for None. After the prayer of None has been made, they shall go into the cloister to wash their feet. When their feet have been washed, they shall return to the choir; after another bell has been struck, they shall sing None.

At Vespers on Monday and Tuesday, the bells shall be struck as on ordinary days. Between the bell signals the psalm “O God, we have heard with our ears” shall be said. After Vespers of All Saints, Vespers of the Dead shall be said. The Vigil of the Dead shall not be held on these days if the procession has gone outside the cloister; otherwise it shall be held as usual.

On these three days, the nocturns, chapters, and collects shall be of the Resurrection, as shall Vespers on Monday and Tuesday. At the morning praises, Terce, Sext, and None, the chapter and collects shall be for the fasts.

If a feast of twelve readings occurs on these three days, the entire service of night and day shall be celebrated for that feast. After Terce has been said and all the bells struck, the Mass of that feast shall be celebrated solemnly, as at other times. The procession shall go as on other days, except that they shall go shod and without staffs. The fast-day Mass shall be celebrated at the monastery to which they have processed.

If a feast of three readings occurs, only a commemoration of it shall be made at Vespers, at the morning praises, and at the first Mass of the fast.

## SECTION VI.—The Season of Pentecost

On Saturday, the vigil of Pentecost, rising from the midday rest, washed and combed, they shall come to the church. After prayer has been made, those who are to celebrate the office and those who are to serve at it shall vest. The office shall be conducted festively as on Holy Saturday.

The cantor and another brother whom he chooses, vested in copes, shall proclaim the threefold litany as at the Easter vigil. When “Light them” has been proclaimed, the blessed candle and the remaining lights shall be lit. Only one candle ought to be burning before that hour, before the altar.

When they begin “Kyrie eleison,” all the bells shall be struck. “Glory to God in the highest” shall follow. At the Gospel the candlesticks and thurible shall be held.

After Mass, when the two greater bells have been struck, they shall pray. At None also there shall be two cantors in copes. On the following day and throughout the entire octave, everything shall be done as at the Easter solemnity and its octave, except that on the eighth day of this feast both Masses shall be “The Spirit of the Lord.”

On Monday, if there is no feast, the Mass “Lord, in your mercy” shall be said. During this week the fasts prescribed by the Rule are to begin, on Wednesday and Friday, until the Ides of September, unless a reasonable cause exists for the abbot or prior to grant permission for two meals.

After chapter, on these fast days, they shall sit in the cloister and speak. The secretary, however, shall not strike the smallest bell, as is customary after chapter, for the preparation of Mass.

After Terce, the children, those weakened by bloodletting, and the sick who have been granted permission shall go to receive a mixed meal. After Sext, the midday rest shall be taken. Rising from it, they shall come barefoot into the cloister, bringing their shoes.

After this, washed and combed, they shall come into the church. Having prayed and after two bells have been struck, a child shall begin “Arise, O Lord,” and the rest, as was stated much earlier. This order shall be observed on Wednesday and Friday until the feast of All Saints, unless there is a vigil whose Mass is celebrated solemnly; in that case the procession is omitted entirely.

On the first Sunday after the octave of Pentecost, the hymns “Rising by night” and “Behold, now the night,” which are to be sung on Sundays, shall be sung at the nocturns and morning praises until the first Sunday of October. The books of Kings and Chronicles shall be appointed for reading until the first Sunday of August. The historia shall be “God of all.”

On the first Sunday of August, Solomon shall be appointed for reading until the first Sunday of September. The responsories shall be “In the beginning.”

On the first Sunday of September, Job, Tobit, Judith, Esther, and Ezra shall be appointed for reading until the first Sunday of October.

From the Ides of September, the fasts prescribed by the Rule shall be observed continuously on ordinary days. Beginning on the Ides themselves, they shall fast as blessed Benedict instituted. They shall speak only once in the cloister until the Kalends of October, namely, after chapter until Terce.

After Sext they shall go to the dormitory. After the briefest interval, when the smallest bell has been struck, they shall descend, wash, go to the monastery, pray, and say the litany; then they shall celebrate Mass. When Mass is nearly finished, the bell shall be struck for None.

After Mass, having prayed, they shall go to receive the mixed meal. When they return, another bell shall be struck and None shall be sung.

## SECTION VII.—The Five Principal Feasts

There are five principal feasts: the Nativity of the Lord, his Resurrection, Pentecost, the Assumption of holy Mary, Mother of God, and the feast of the place.

Observing everything that has been said concerning Holy Saturday, on the vigils of these feasts the entire monastery and all the altars shall be decorated, according to the resources of the place, as honorably as possible.

The workshops and cloister shall be cleaned. The seats of the refectory, chapter house, and cloister shall be covered; the benches shall be spread with rushes.

For the fast-day Mass, those who are to celebrate it shall be suitably vested, the priest honorably: the deacon in a dalmatic, the subdeacon in a tunic; three conversi; the hebdomadary cantor in a cope; and two brothers for the responsories.

Before Mass the bells shall be struck as on feast days. The litany shall not be said. The festive “Kyrie eleison” shall be sung, and only one collect shall be said. If a feast occurs on this day, the morning Mass shall be sung for it.

At None the two greater bells shall be struck. At Vespers, two small bells, then two and two gradually, and finally all of them. Between the bell signals all the lights of the monastery shall be lit. Before each altar outside the presbytery, a single light shall burn.

The antiphons over the psalms prescribed by the cantor shall be begun. Four men in copes shall sing the responsory. The antiphon at the Magnificat shall be said three times.

The abbot and prior, vested in copes, shall incense both altars of the presbytery: before them and above them together, each one on his respective side. Two other hebdomadary priests shall be ready, namely, the priest of the great Mass and the priest of the lesser Mass. They shall receive the thuribles from their hands and carry them around the altars outside, one on each side.

When they return to the choir, they shall bring the thuribles first to the abbot and afterward to the prior, then to those who sang the responsory—not both at once, but one from one side and the other from the other—then to the two conversi in albs, and finally to the other brothers.

The one who received the thurible from the abbot’s hand shall serve the abbot from the book.

271 At these vigils the refectory tables ought to be covered.

On the following day, before the nocturnal vigils, all the bells shall be rung to awaken the brothers; then two and two progressively, and finally all together. For the invitatory, four shall sing in copes. In the three nocturns, let them sing three responsories, two and two; the fourth, four; the eighth, five; and the twelfth, six. In the three nocturns [Col. 0473D], while the third lesson is being read, two priests vested in copes shall incense the greater and lesser altars; then they shall carry the incense to the abbot, the prior, and the other brothers in order. The eighth and twelfth responsories shall be repeated from the beginning after the Gloria. When the Gospel has been announced, the altar shall be uncovered and all the lights kindled. At *Te Deum laudamus* two greater bells shall be rung. When the Gospel has been read and the collect said, all the bells having been rung, the priest shall begin the morning praises.

Then he shall again go to the vesting room, remove the chasuble and stole, and return to the choir in an alb with the maniple. When the hymn has begun, he shall go out, remove the maniple, put on a cope, and, with another brother likewise vested in a cope, go around the altars with thuribles, as at the preceding evening’s vespers, accompanied by two conversi vested with them in albs [Col. 0474A]. If the abbot has read the Gospel, he shall return to the choir after the Gospel, vested in a cope. The antiphon at the *Benedictus* shall be said three times.

At Prime, two greater bells shall be rung. Three candles shall be lit before the altar, likewise at Terce, Sext, and None; the chapter shall be conducted briefly.

The morning Mass shall be said with one collect and a preface. While the priest is in the Canon, the children, with their teachers, shall remain in the choir; they must be vested before Mass, while the others shall go to vest. Receiving their garments from the sacristan, they shall vest outside the sacristy. If the place is too small, some shall go out into the cloister or chapterhouse and vest there. The better albs shall be given to the priors and to the more honorable persons. As soon as each one has been vested [Col. 0474B], he shall return to the choir. When Mass has been completed, if it is not Sunday, and the greater bell has ceased—the bell which began to be rung at the beginning of the final collect of the Mass—the prayer of Terce shall be made. After the prayer, another bell having been rung, Terce shall be sung.

But if it is Sunday, when the morning Mass has been completed, and before the bell for Terce has yet been rung, holy water shall be prepared, as is customary on other Sundays. While *Asperges me* is being sung, the greater bell shall be rung for Terce. After the holy water has been sprinkled, the priest shall go through the offices with the bearers of the water and the cross. When the bell ceases, the prayer of Terce shall be made. When it has been completed, another bell having been rung, Terce shall be sung. Meanwhile, the priest who went through the offices, returning before the entrance of the monastery, shall say the customary prayer; then, entering before one of the altars, [Col. 0474C] *Via sanctorum*.

When Terce has been said, the copes having been distributed and those who are to carry the objects having been positioned in the choir by the cantor [probably read *debet*, “ought”], all shall go out in the following order. First shall come a conversus carrying a bucket of holy water; then two carrying two crosses; after them two with two candelabra, with candles burning above; two others carrying two thuribles filled with fire and incense; these shall be followed by two subdeacons vested in tunics, carrying two Gospel books; after them, the children with their teachers; last, the abbot and the priors, preceded by the other brothers two by two, according to their order.

When the procession begins to leave the choir, two greater bells shall be rung and shall not cease until the procession has returned to the choir [Col. 0474D]; the other bells shall cease. Proceeding through the monastery’s larger doors, they shall enter and make a station before the crucifix. When this has been done, and the chant they had begun has been completed, the abbot or cantor—whichever of them is responsible for it—shall begin the appropriate chant. Thus, with all the bells sounding, they shall enter the choir, and when the bells cease they shall begin Mass.

Before the entrance of the Mass, one or two carpets shall be spread across the choir, where the cantor and the others whom he summons to direct the choir are to stand. All the candles in the crowns, and all the other lights in the choir, sanctuary, and before the crucifix, shall be lit. The cantor shall arrange how many and which persons are to sing the individual items appointed to be sung. At the sequence, two greater bells shall be rung [Col. 0475A]. If necessary, the Communion shall be repeated with its verse and the *Gloria Patri*. When Mass has been completed, all the bells shall be rung. Each person shall take his vestment and cope, both properly folded, to the sacristan for storage in the chest.

Festal cloths shall be spread over the refectory tables, hanging down at the front. Daily cloths shall also be spread, though washed, on which the brothers shall eat. White and decent hand towels shall likewise be spread over the ordinary towels; the chamberlains are to spread these hand towels after chapter. No brother, however, is to wipe his hands there except at the first meal and in the evening at supper.

At None, two greater bells shall be rung. At Vespers, let the bells and candles be dealt with as was done at the vespers of the preceding day [272]. After supper, when the servants have eaten [Col. 0475B], the refectory attendants shall collect the festal cloths and return them, properly folded, to the cellarer for safekeeping. The chamberlain shall take and guard the more decent towels.

## SECTION VIII — Principal Feasts of the Second Class

There are other feasts which are celebrated magnificently, though not on an equal footing with the preceding ones. They are these: Epiphany; the Purification of Saint Mary; the feast of Saint Gregory; the Annunciation of Christ; the eighth day of the Paschal solemnity; the feast of Saint Alfege, martyr; the Ascension of Christ; the feast of Saint Augustine, archbishop of the English; the eighth day of Pentecost; the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist; the Passion of the apostles Peter and Paul; the Translation of Saint Benedict; the Nativity of Saint Mary; the feast of Saint Michael; [Col. 0475C] the feast of All Saints; the feast of Saint Andrew; and the Dedication of the Church.

On the days preceding all these feasts, the altars, sanctuary, choir, and the monastery’s other parts on both sides of the choir shall be decorated. The bells shall be rung as at the principal feasts. Two sections of the candle crown in the sanctuary shall be lit, as well as all the lights around the greater altar and the candle before the crucifix. If proper antiphons are available, those appointed by the cantor shall be placed over the psalms; otherwise, the psalms shall be sung with one antiphon from the feast itself. Two shall sing the responsory in copes. The antiphon at the *Magnificat* shall be said twice. Two priests vested in copes shall handle the thuribles, as was stated above concerning the principal feasts.

[Col. 0475D] The Masses of the vigils of the Ascension of Christ, Saint John the Baptist, the apostles Peter and Paul, and All Saints shall be celebrated festively. If any of these vigils, or any other vigil that is celebrated festively, falls on a Sunday, the entire night office and the morning Mass shall be of Sunday. The greater Mass, however, shall be said with the Alleluia after the responsory of the vigil—except for the vigil of the Nativity of the Lord, in which case, if this occurs, the vigil itself shall be sung and read in the third nocturn. On the following day, before the nocturnal vigils, the bells shall be rung two and two, then all together. For the invitatory, three shall sing in copes. In the three nocturns, they shall sing three responsories, two and two; the fourth, three; the eighth, four; and the twelfth, five, repeating it from the beginning after the Gloria [Col. 0476A]. When the Gospel has been announced, the altar shall be uncovered and the lights lit as at the preceding evening’s vespers. The antiphon at the *Benedictus* shall be said twice, and the thuribles shall likewise be carried around. At Prime, two bells shall be rung and three candles lit; likewise at Terce, Sext, and None. The seats shall be decorated, and cloths and towels spread, as stated above.

The morning Mass shall be of the solemnity itself, with one collect—unless it is the feast of a saint, in which case there shall be a commemoration. If that occurs, the morning Mass shall be of the saint, with the first collect of the saint and the second of the solemnity, and no more. Priests celebrating private Masses shall likewise have one collect. When the morning Mass has been said, Terce shall be sung, and Mass shall be celebrated in copes [Col. 0476B], except for the Purification of Saint Mary, when everyone shall be vested in albs for the candles, apart from the cantor and those who are with him, who must also be vested in copes.

The feasts of blessed Gregory and of the Annunciation of the Lord are likewise excepted when they are celebrated during Lent. On these occasions all shall similarly be vested in albs, apart from those mentioned above and those who sing the responsory and tract. At the cantor’s direction, these latter shall come forward and put on copes in the choir for singing; when they have finished singing, they shall go to the vesting room and remove them there. The cantor shall summon to himself as many persons as he wishes and whomever he wishes. The number of those singing the responsory, the Alleluia, and the other items to be sung shall be left to the cantor’s judgment. When Mass has been celebrated, all the bells shall be rung.

If any of these feasts falls on a Sunday [Col. 0476C], after the morning Mass has been said, holy water shall be prepared and a procession made through the cloister, as is customary on Sundays; all, however, shall be vested in albs [OCR uncertain: *albis in uti*]. At None, two bells shall be rung, and Vespers shall be conducted as on the preceding day. We count the feast of blessed Gregory among the higher feasts because he is the apostle of our people—that is, of the English nation.

If the feast of the Annunciation of the Lord falls on a Sunday during Lent, it shall be postponed until the following day; otherwise the Sunday office could not be restored. Vespers shall be conducted from the beginning up to the chapter of Sunday; the chapter shall be said from the feast. After the first collect, a commemoration of Sunday shall be made. If it falls on Saturday, the entire office of the day shall be of the solemnity itself [Col. 0476D]. After the first collect of Vespers, the collect of Sunday shall be said, except on the Saturday before Palm Sunday; if the feast falls then, the office shall be of the feast itself up to the evening chapter [273]. On that day two brothers in frocks shall sing the responsory, and one priest vested in a cope shall incense the altars. After the first collect, a commemoration of the feast shall be made.

But if it falls on the Tuesday after Palm Sunday, the feast shall indeed be celebrated as stated, but the brothers shall be shaved on the following day, and then, after chapter and after Sext, they shall speak in the cloister. But those who [need it: a word such as *indigent* (“need”) or something similar seems to be missing] shall bathe on that day. [Note: [Col. 0475D] A word such as *indigent* (“need”) or something similar seems to be missing.] If it falls on Thursday, Friday, or the Saturday before Easter [Col. 0477A], or during the Paschal solemnity, or during the three following days, it shall be postponed until the Thursday after the Paschal solemnity.

This feast shall then be conducted as solemnly as the Paschal solemnity, except that, instead of the *skilla*, before the nocturnal vigils, the *classicum* shall not be rung to awaken the brothers, nor shall a procession be made. The antiphons and responsories which would be sung for this feast during Lent shall also be sung at this time, with Alleluias added; all the verses likewise shall be said with a final Alleluia. The invitatory: “Alleluia, alleluia,” according to the melody of the invitatory; *Ave Maria*; and the canticles from Advent of the Lord.

[Col. 0477B] On the day of the Ascension of Christ, a procession shall be made in albs, either outside the cloister around the monastery court, preceded by banners and relics, with the other things that ordinarily precede a festal procession, or through the cloister without banners. As soon as the procession begins to leave, two bells shall be rung, as stated above for the day of the Nativity of Saint Mary. At Vespers, the psalms shall be *Dixit Dominus*, *Laetatus sum in his*, *Nisi Dominus*, and *Memento, Domine*, with the antiphon *De fructu ventris tui*. This psalm with this antiphon is said fourth at all the feasts of Saint Mary.

At the feast of Saint Michael, the psalms at Vespers shall be *Dixit Dominus*, *Confitebor*, *Beatus vir*, and another *Confitebor*, with the antiphon *In conspectu Angelorum*.

[Col. 0477C] At the vigil of All Saints, at Vespers the psalms shall be accompanied by antiphons from those psalms which are customarily said daily in their memory; the prayers, *Post partum virgo*, and the rest. When *Adducentur regi virgines post eam* has been said, the following shall be added: “For our absent brothers; send them, Lord; Lord, hear my prayer; Lord, Lord of hosts; the Lord be with you.” After the collect, the only commemoration shall be of the holy cross. On the following day, at Lauds likewise the prayers *Post partum virgo*; at Vespers, the psalms and antiphons over the psalms shall be as on the preceding day.

When Vespers has been said, all the bells shall be rung, and Vespers for the Dead shall be sung longer than usual, unless the following day is Sunday or any feast of twelve lessons. There shall be one collect, *Fidelium Deus*. On the following night, at the Vigil of the Dead, all the bells shall likewise be rung. On that day all the priests shall celebrate Masses for all the faithful departed [Col. 0477D]. Those who are not priests shall be assigned psalms in chapter for the Masses. The morning Mass shall be celebrated festively. All the bells shall be rung; a cope shall be in the choir; the deacon and subdeacon shall be vested in chasubles; two children in albs shall sing the responsory; two senior brothers, likewise in albs, the tract; and three conversi shall serve with thurible and candelabra. For seven days the offices shall be complete; up to thirty days, *Voce mea* and *Verba mea* shall be said.

At the feast of the Dedication of the Church, the candles lit at First Vespers on all the altars consecrated on that day shall not be extinguished until after Compline on the following day. The canticles shall be *Laetare Jerusalem*, *Urbs fortitudinis*, and *Non vocaberis ultra*. On that day Mass shall be celebrated at each altar, if there are enough priests [Col. 0478A]. When Terce has been said, a festal procession shall be made in albs, either around the monastery, if the place is suitable, or through the cloister, preceded by the things that ordinarily precede a festal procession. They shall enter the monastery through the larger doors and make a station before the crucifix. At Vespers, the psalms shall be those customarily said at the feast of virgins. This feast has an octave.

## SECTION IX — Feasts of the Third Class

There are other feasts of the third rank, which are not celebrated with so much ceremony. These are: the feasts of Saint Vincent; the Conversion of Saint Paul; Philip and James; the Invention of the holy cross; the apostle James; Saint Peter on the Kalends of August; Lawrence the martyr; the eighth day of the Assumption of Saint Mary [Col. 0478B]; the apostle Bartholomew; Augustine the teacher; the Beheading of Saint John the Baptist; the Exaltation of the holy cross; Matthew the apostle; Simon and Jude; blessed Martin; Thomas the apostle; and any other feasts which may be appointed to be celebrated in this manner.

On the preceding day, the two sanctuary altars, the sanctuary, and the choir shall be prepared. At None and Vespers the bells shall be rung as for private feasts of twelve lessons, except that the greater bells must be rung. Three candelabra before the altar and the other surrounding lights shall be lit. Vespers shall be sung with one antiphon from the feast itself, unless a feast precedes it from which the antiphon is taken [274]. Vespers shall continue up to the chapter. [Col. 0478C] If there is a proper history, two brothers shall sing the responsory in their frocks; if there is no proper history, as at the feasts of certain apostles, or if it has already been sung, as on the eighth day of the Assumption of Saint Mary, two boys shall sing a short responsory. A priest vested in a cope shall incense the altars, and a conversus shall be in an alb.

On the following day, two shall sing the invitatory in copes. In the three nocturns, three responsories shall be sung, one by each person; the fourth responsory by two, the eighth by three, and the twelfth by four, the latter being repeated after the Gloria. When the Gospel has been announced, the altar shall be uncovered and the lights lit as at Vespers on the preceding day. At *Te Deum laudamus* two medium-sized bells shall be rung. After the Gospel has been read, the priest shall return to the choir in an alb. At Lauds two boys shall sing a short responsory, whether or not there is a proper history [Col. 0478D]. The same shall be done at Vespers. At Prime one of the greater bells shall be rung; two candles shall be lit before the altar and kept burning through all the hours until Vespers.

At Mass, everyone in the choir shall be in albs except the cantor and those who are with him, who, vested in copes, must direct the choir. At None the bell shall be rung as at Prime. At Vespers, the antiphons over the psalms shall be assigned by the cantor to the young men whom he directs. The rest shall be conducted as at the preceding day’s Vespers.

At First Vespers of the Invention of the holy cross, the hymn shall be *Vexilla regis*. On the following day, the invitatory and two nocturns shall be from the martyrs; the third from the holy cross. The canticle *Domine, audivi* shall be divided into three Glorias: the first Gloria before the verse *Pro iniquitate*; the second before the verse *Egressus es* [Col. 0479A]. The hymn at Lauds shall be *Lustris sex*. The morning Mass shall be of the martyrs; the greater Mass of the holy cross. The psalms at Vespers shall be *Dixit Dominus*, *Confitebor*, *Beatus vir*, and *Laudate pueri*; the hymn shall be *Vexilla regis*.

At the Exaltation of the holy cross, the office is similar to that of the Invention of the same cross, except that at this feast the holy cross is adored, whereas at the other it is not. Accordingly, at this solemnity, after Terce has been said, the sanctuary shall be spread with carpets up to the greater altar. Then two brothers in albs, whom the cantor has appointed, shall come out from the side of the morning altar carrying a covered cross, until they reach the step nearest the altar. There the cross shall be uncovered by its bearers, and by them the antiphon *Ecce lignum crucis* shall be begun. Everyone shall bend the knee, then prostrate himself full-length upon the carpets, adore it, and kiss the feet of the Crucified One, as the senior brethren do [Col. 0479B]. When the aforesaid antiphon has been sung, the cantor shall begin the antiphon *Crucem tuam adoramus*, which they shall repeat at each verse of the psalm *Deus misereatur nostri*. Then let other suitable things be done, if necessary. After the cross has been adored, the two aforementioned brothers who hold it shall begin together, in a loud voice, the antiphon *Super omnia*. While everyone bends the knee and the cross is fixed in its place, the bells having been rung, Mass shall be celebrated. At the Introit, *In nomine Domini omne genu flectatur*; the Gospel, *Nunc judicium est mundi*.

## SECTION X — The Five Principal Sundays

There are five Sundays which have certain practices in common, distinct from those of the other Sundays [Col. 0479C]: namely, the First Sunday of Advent of the Lord; the First Sunday of Septuagesima; the First Sunday of Lent; Mid-Lent Sunday; and Palm Sunday. On these occasions two shall sing the invitatory in albs. After reading the Gospel, the priest shall remove the chasuble and stole in the vesting room and return to the choir in an alb with the maniple. He shall go out once the hymn has begun and, when the antiphon at the *Benedictus* has begun, shall likewise enter in an alb and carry incense around the altars. The choir must have been prepared from the preceding day, and rushes must be strewn throughout it.

At both Vespers and at Lauds, two brothers in frocks shall sing the responsory. The refectory tables shall be covered, and decent hand towels spread over the towels, as at all feasts in which the invitatory is sung in copes [Col. 0479D]. These shall be spread and collected as stated above.

## SECTION XI — Feasts of Twelve Lessons

On all feasts of twelve lessons, whatever they may be; on all days within octaves during which the monks do not speak in the cloister, even if those days have three lessons; on all vigils at which Masses are celebrated festively with all the bells rung; and on all Ember Saturdays, when the cantor has begun the *Gloria Patri* at the office, the priest shall enter at the altar carrying the missal in his hands. Three conversi carrying candelabra and a thurible shall precede him; the subdeacon with the Gospel book shall follow them, and the deacon shall follow the subdeacon. Having placed the missal on the altar, the priest shall pray, bowing reverently [Col. 0480A]. The deacon shall likewise pray behind him. After the prayer, the priest shall cross himself and kiss the Gospel book, which the subdeacon must have placed on the altar. The deacon, likewise crossing himself, shall do so before and behind the priest, then come to the priest’s left and kiss the corner of the altar. Afterward they shall make the confession together.

When this has been done, the priest shall place incense in the thurible, and the deacon shall hand the thurible to the priest. The priest shall incense the altar in front and above it, then return it to the deacon. The deacon shall incense both sides of the altar and the morning altar, and then return it to the conversus, who, carrying it to the choir, shall first offer it to the cantor and those with him; then to everyone in the right choir [Col. 0480B] in order, and likewise in the left; afterward to the sick who are outside the choir. The two conversi holding the candelabra before the altar shall not relinquish them until the *Kyrie eleison* has begun. Once it has begun, they shall set down the candelabra and return to the choir.

During the Gospel, when the offertory or the offertory verses are being sung, a conversus shall bring the thurible with the incense box to the cantor, whoever he may be who is directing the choir, if it is a feast of twelve lessons or one of the festive three-lesson days within the octaves described above.

When the cantor sees that the time has come, he shall place incense in the thurible and send it to the deacon at the altar; the deacon shall give it to the priest. But if the abbot or a bishop is in the choir or is celebrating Mass, then the thurible with the incense box shall be brought to him at the Introit [Col. 0480C] and before the Gospel by the deacon and conversus; after the offertory, by the cantor and conversus.

Near the end of Mass, when they have reached the prior’s collect, *Per Dominum nostrum*, the two conversi shall set down the candelabra before the altar and return with the one holding the thurible to the vesting room. When Mass has been completed, the priest shall follow the deacon carrying the missal.

If a three-lesson feast falls on a Sunday, or on another feast of a saint that has a proper history, or, if it has no proper history, is celebrated in albs or copes, a commemoration of the three-lesson feast alone shall be made at First Vespers and at Lauds [Col. 0480D], and the morning Mass shall be sung from it. But if its history has already been sung on another Sunday, or if that other feast of twelve lessons has no proper history and is celebrated neither in albs nor in copes, the antiphon of the feast from which the three lessons would have been taken shall be announced at the canticles, and thereafter the entire office shall be conducted from it until the end of the final collect. After *Benedicamus Domino*, a commemoration shall be made of the feast from which the eight lessons were taken. All the hours shall also be said from that feast, as well as the sermon in chapter and the greater Mass; the morning Mass, however, shall be from the feast from which Lauds was taken.

If the feast of a saint for which twelve lessons are read falls on a Sunday whose history has already been sung, or on the following Sunday [Col. 0481A], the entire night office and the day office shall be conducted from the saint; only the morning Mass shall be said from Sunday. For there will never be a third nocturn of Sunday unless the preceding two are celebrated from it.

On all Sundays; on the first day of the Nativity of the Lord, but only at the greater Mass; on the day of the Circumcision of the Lord; on Epiphany; on the first day of the Paschal solemnity; on the day of the Ascension; on the first day of Pentecost; at the feast of All Saints; at the Dedication of the church; at all feasts of blessed Mary; on the day of the Passion of the apostles Peter and Paul; and at the other feasts of the apostles, *Credo in unum Deum* shall be said at the greater Mass. For at the morning Mass in the convent it is never said [Col. 0481B].

## SECTION XII — The Reception of a Distinguished Person

Whenever it is arranged that a person is to be received with a festal procession, one of the greater bells shall be struck three times briefly, so that all the brothers may assemble in the church to vest. When all have put on copes—if there are enough copes, or chasubles and dalmatics if copes are lacking—and the boys have put on tunics, they shall wait seated in the choir until they proceed. Meanwhile, the sacristan shall spread one carpet and, over it, a hanging before the greater altar on the first step; he shall do likewise before the crucifix in the middle of the church. When these things have been done and it has been announced that the person is already near, two greater bells shall be rung.

Then some of the senior brothers shall take holy water [Col. 0481C] and the other things customarily carried in a festal procession. The abbot and the others shall follow them according to their rank. The boys with their teachers shall come last and stand in their proper order between the two choirs when the station for receiving the person has been made. When the person is received, the abbot shall give him the aspergillum with water in his hand; if he is a bishop, he shall sprinkle another person himself. Then incense shall be offered to him, likewise by the abbot, and the Gospel book by the prior. While these things are being done, all the bells shall be rung. The cantor shall begin a chant appropriate to the person. Then the procession shall return: the boys with their teachers shall enter the church first, followed by the others in the order in which they stood at the station; last shall come the abbot with the person received [Col. 0481D], preceded by the bearers mentioned above.

After entering the monastery, they shall make a station before the crucifix. The boys shall likewise stand between the two choirs. The aforementioned bearers shall advance gradually through their midst and stand before the crucifix, facing it. Meanwhile the person received shall pray. When the chant has ended and the person has risen from prayer, the cantor shall begin an antiphon or responsory of the saint in whose honor the church was founded. Then the aforementioned bearers shall go ahead and, as soon as they reach the altar, put down in their places the things they are carrying. The children shall follow them, then the others in the order stated above. Having entered the choir, they shall stand on either side of the altar, as the priors do. The person received shall pray again [Col. 0482A]. When the chant has ended, he shall rise; and if the person received is a bishop, after giving the blessing he shall kiss all the brothers in order. Since they are vested, the brothers shall not bend the knee before him, as they customarily do when kissing a bishop, abbot, or prince of the realm; instead, humbly bowing, they shall proceed to kiss him.

If he is a spiritual person and the abbot judges it expedient, the brothers having removed their vestments shall sit in chapter as usual; the person mentioned above shall be led there. After he has requested a blessing, a reading from Scripture shall be read before him. When it has ended with *Tu autem, Domine*, he may give a sermon on it if he wishes.

If the person received is an abbot, as the brothers leave the chapterhouse they shall kiss him. But if he does not enter the chapterhouse [Col. 0482B], at the proper hour they shall kiss him in the cloister.

## CHAPTER II — The Abbot

When an abbot is elected, all the brothers, or the greater and better part of them, must consent to his election. If the elected man is consecrated outside the monastery, when he returns he shall be received with a festal procession. He himself shall lie prostrate at both stations. When the chant of the second station has ended, the bishop, if present, or his legate, shall install him in the place and station of the abbot. Once he has been installed, if the bishop is absent, the prior shall begin *Te Deum laudamus*. While it is being sung, all the brothers shall approach, according to their rank, to kiss him, bending the knee twice—once before the kiss and once after it [Col. 0482C]. From that day onward he shall be honored everywhere with particular reverence.

At the first chapter in which he sits, all those who hold obediences within the monastery and safeguard the monastery’s property shall place the keys of their obediences at his feet. He shall entrust those obediences to them, unless he has decided that they should be arranged otherwise. The entire convent must bow when he bows after the antiphon has begun; when he is named on the chapter board, if he is present there; and when he makes a mistake in a psalm or anything else in the choir, for which he asks pardon.

When he goes to read or returns from reading, the entire convent shall rise for him. As he passes through the cloister or any other place, all before whom he passes shall rise until he has gone by [Col. 0482D]. When he enters the chapterhouse, if the brothers are already seated there, everyone shall descend from all the steps until he has likewise sat down. Wherever he may be, order and discipline must be maintained. Therefore, wherever he is, whether in the cloister or outside it, if he rebukes a brother for acting or speaking disorderly, that brother shall immediately humbly ask pardon before him, as in chapter, and shall stand before him until he orders him to sit. If he sees the brother becoming angry, the brother shall continue to make satisfaction before him by asking pardon until he has made him calm. The abbot must, however, take care not to do this in the presence of secular people.

Wherever he sits, no one shall presume to sit beside him [Col. 0483A] unless he orders it. When ordered to sit, the brother shall bend his knee before him and kiss him, then sit humbly beside him. Whoever gives him anything into his hand, or receives anything from his hand, shall kiss his hand. When he enters the refectory, two brothers shall serve him with water and a towel. As long as he is in the choir, no one shall dare discipline the boys unless he orders it.

As long as he is sleeping in his bed in the morning, no one shall dare make a sound. If the master of the boys sees that the time has passed when the prior customarily makes a sound, he shall rise and awaken the boys as quietly as possible, merely touching the cloths with which they are covered. When this has been done, they shall leave the dormitory, wash and comb themselves, say the customary prayers, return to their school [Col. 0483B], and sit in silence until the abbot rises from bed.

When he is staying somewhere outside the monastery and sends greetings or prayers to the convent, all who are in chapter shall bow, kneeling with their knees down to the footstool. The same shall be done for a greeting from the pope or king. For greetings from other persons, they shall merely bow humbly. When he sends such a greeting to any brother, wherever that greeting is delivered to him, the brother shall immediately bow humbly, kneeling with his knees to the ground.

Any brother who comes to him outside the cloister shall first say *Benedicite*, then state the reason for his coming. He shall not dare sit before him or depart from him without his permission. Having received permission to depart, he shall first say *Benedicite*, then depart. The entire ordering of the monastery shall depend upon his judgment. If, in his absence, something new is arranged in the monastery because necessity compels it or reason recommends it, it shall be reported to him when he returns, and afterward it shall be done as he orders. If he has left the monastery and spent even one night away, as soon as he returns any brother who has been assigned abstinence in chapter shall be released from it.

When he has departed from this life, an abbot or bishop from nearby shall immediately be invited to bury him. In addition to everything customarily done for other deceased brothers, the following shall be added: he shall be clothed in priestly vestments, and a pastoral staff shall be placed on his right arm; *Verba mea* shall be said for him throughout the cycle of one year [Col. 0483D], and throughout that entire year his customary allowance (*justitia*) shall be set daily on the abbot’s table, with three dishes, for distribution to the poor. Every year the anniversary of his death shall be celebrated festively.

## CHAPTER III — The Prior

With due reverence for the abbot preserved in all things, the prior, who is also called the provost in the Rule, is more honorable than the other ministers of the house of God. Alone among the other ministers, he has the first place in his section of the choir, in chapter, and in the refectory. After the abbot, he alone is served by the priest with the thurible at Vespers and Lauds whenever the thurible is carried around the choir at those hours. Matters outside the cloister are also arranged according to his judgment when the abbot is absent [Col. 0484A]. If the abbot is far from the monastery, he may remove those whom he understands to be managing the affairs entrusted to them not for the benefit of the Church. Whenever circumstances require, he holds, or orders to be held, a chapter concerning all the servants who live within the monastery’s offices; and, at his command, punishments are inflicted according to the merits of the offenders.

When he enters the chapterhouse, everyone shall rise for him, standing on the footstools until he sits down. But if he delays and the cloister prior has already taken the higher place, he must not enter. If there is a matter that cannot or should not be postponed, then, when he enters, the cloister prior shall sit on the other side of him, and the prior shall sit above everyone. When he passes through the cloister or choir [Col. 0484B], no one shall rise for him. If he wishes to sit in the cloister where the other brothers are sitting, only those beside whom he wishes to sit shall rise for him. Wherever he finds brothers sitting outside the cloister, they shall all rise for him. The cloister prior, wherever the greater prior goes, must always be present if this can be done in or around the cloister, and must preserve the order of the cloister with every diligence.

When the abbot and greater prior are absent, if any brother happens to be suffering from illness, the prior may order him to go to the infirmary, and, if the illness is severe enough, to eat meat. It especially belongs to him to visit the sick brothers, learn what they are doing and what they want, and advise them in everything necessary either for their bodies or their souls. In the absence of the greater prior, he must hold chapter for the servants [Col. 0484C] and impose punishments according to their faults; but it is not his right to add or remove anyone.

It is also his duty every day after Compline, having received holy water from the hebdomadary priest who gives it to the brothers, to remain until everyone has passed through, in some suitable place from which he can observe well who are not walking reverently, and who, at the church’s exit, do not, as is customary, cover their heads with their cowls, and many things of this kind. After the entire community has gone out, taking a lantern, if it is night he goes through the crypt and the other parts of the monastery where there might be cause for suspicion, through the cloister, chapter house, and the other workshops, carefully observing lest any brother who ought not to have remained there should still be present. When this has been completed [Col. 0484D], he goes to the infirmary [278] to consider in the same way whether all have already been placed in their beds and are keeping themselves silent and in every respect according to the rule, as is customary. On returning to the dormitory, he should observe the same things there as well.

In winter, during the interval between Matins and the morning praises, if the major prior is absent, he makes the same circuit which, as was stated above in the treatment of November, the major prior ought to make when that interval was discussed. He also makes another circuit when, because Vespers is late, the servants dine at night in the refectory and the brothers who attended the principal meal await them in the chapter house with the lamps lit. For he then goes around the places mentioned above [Col. 0485A], observing lest any who ought to be sitting with the others in the chapter house should occupy themselves with idle words or some vanity. When this occurs, if the darkness of night is so great, lamps should be lit in the monastery, the cloister, and the dormitory, so that those leaving either meal may see where they are going.

The servants, rising from the meal, should then go to the monastery before the chapter house. As they pass before the chapter house, they should go bent over until they have passed by. Before entering the chapter house, however, they should straighten themselves and, as usual, turn toward the east and bow humbly. The brothers sitting in the chapter house should likewise rise from their seats and humbly bow to them as they pass.

Whatever the major prior can grant or prohibit while he is in the monastery [Col. 0485B], and whatever he can punish or pardon, the claustral prior may also do in his absence, except in major matters, which he must reserve for the judgment either of the major prior himself or of the abbot. It was stated above that, wherever the major prior is present—whether in the refectory, the chapter house, the cloister, or outside the cloister—people must rise for him; in the absence of the major prior, people must similarly rise for the claustral prior.

## CHAPTER IV. On the Circuits.

The circuit-makers of the monastery, whom they also call *Circae* by another name, must, according to the command of Saint Benedict (Rule, chapter 48), make their rounds of the monastery’s workshops at specified hours, observing the carelessness and negligence of the brothers and violations of the established order.

[Col. 0485C] They should be chosen from the best and wisest men of the whole monastery, who never maliciously raise a complaint against anyone out of private hatred, nor conceal anyone’s negligence out of private friendship. Their number should correspond to the resources of the place and the need of the matter. They should walk religiously and orderly, especially while making their circuits, and display an example of religious conduct to those who see them. While making their rounds, they should give no one a sign and speak to no one for any reason; they should diligently inspect only negligences and offenses, and, passing by silently, later make complaints about them in the chapter house.

When they find some brothers speaking outside the cloister [Col. 0485D], the brothers who are speaking should rise together before them, and one of them should say to them, if that is the case, that they are speaking there with permission. The circuit-makers, however, should answer him neither by word nor by sign, but should pass by modestly, listening attentively to determine whether the words themselves are useless and ought not to be spoken. When they find a brother speaking with a servant or with any other layman, it is not customary for that brother to rise before either of them or to say anything to them. When they make their rounds, they must never go together, but one in this direction and the other in that, according to how they have divided the assigned duty between them and as the abbot or prior has ordered them. They should never enter the monastery’s workshops for this duty, but should look through their doors, in case some brothers are wandering through the courtyard, standing, or sitting and chatting.

[Col. 0486A] These are the hours at which, by custom, they ought to make their rounds, although they may also do so at other hours if the abbot or prior judges it appropriate. After the three prayers which the community makes before the psalms customarily said before Matins have been completed, one of them should then make the rounds of all the beds in the dormitory with a lantern, carefully inspecting all the seats in the necessaries, lest some sleeping brother should have remained there. He should then return to the monastery and make the circuit of all the altars in the crypts and those beneath both sides of the choir, as well as the other parts of the monastery where there might be cause for suspicion, carefully observing lest any brother be sleeping, lying down, or sitting disorderly there. Those who have been bled, and the sick and weak, should not be called out in the chapter house if they are found there at that hour [Col. 0486B], but should be allowed to rest sitting rather than lying down. When he finds the others sleeping, he should not touch them in any way, but should make only a sound, moderately and orderly, by which they may be awakened.

Around the middle of the second nocturn, and during the praises shortly before *Laudate Dominum de caelis*, one of them should make the circuit of the aforesaid places of the monastery with a lantern, observing everything stated above. During the day they should make their rounds after the offertory of the lesser and the principal Mass, and after the evening meal, when the brothers eat twice, and after the midday meal, when they eat once. They should go at the end of the Vigil of the Dead. They should also often rise from the midday or evening meal—not all of them, but some—when they suspect that they will find some negligence. This should not be done far from the refectory, so that, if necessary [Col. 0486C], they may immediately join the others for the verse said when the midday or evening meal has ended. These men should be heard attentively and reverently in the chapter house. After those who voluntarily ask for pardon have been heard, it is the duty of these men to make the first complaints.

## CHAPTER V. On the Cantor.

As long as the abbot is in the monastery and follows the community, the cantor should not be entered on the roster for a reading or a responsory, so that, if it should happen that the abbot is not able or willing to read or sing, the cantor may be found ready to do it for him without delay. When the abbot is outside the monastery, or is inside it but cannot follow the community, the cantor should be entered in his place on the roster for the reading and the responsory.

[Col. 0486D] Whoever is going to read or sing anything in the monastery, if he needs it, must first listen to the cantor before beginning.

It is his duty at every hour to take careful precautions lest negligence occur in any service performed in the monastery.

If someone who is forgetful does not begin when he ought to begin a responsory, an antiphon, or anything of this kind, or if, after it has already been begun properly, he deviates from it in some way, the cantor must be prepared and ready so that, without delay, he may begin what ought to have been begun, or bring back onto the right path the one who has gone astray through error. At his discretion a chant is begun, raised [Col. 0487A], or lowered. No one may raise the chant unless he himself has first begun it. It is his duty to enter all the brothers on the roster for every office, without considering the order of their conversion or their own wishes, but according to what seems to him appropriate, vigilantly considering in this matter what is honorable and edifying.
