At festivals celebrated in copes, the sacristan should select whatever is needed from the best of the copes available in the choir that day, and before the beginning of Mass place them above the choir’s right-hand form. The cantor should distribute them to those brothers whom he wishes to have with him in the choir. For the distribution of the copes is their appointment to assist him in directing the choir, and none of them may leave the choir before the end of Mass without his permission.

[Col. 0487B] The cantor, whatever his rank or age, should be in the middle of them in the choir. Whenever the Gospel book or the thurible is brought to them, both should first be offered to the cantor, unless a bishop, abbot, major prior, or the person who holds the office in question is among them. The cantor should always be in the right-hand choir. While he is directing the choir, whatever he begins—whether the *Kyrie eleison* or anything of this kind—the right-hand choir should first take up what he has begun and follow him.

All who are in the choir should sing *Sanctus, sanctus, sanctus* while bowed, unless verses are inserted; they should sing *Dominus Deus sabaoth* and what follows while standing upright. The cantor and those who are with him should sing the whole of it standing upright. At all collects, when the priest says *Orate fratres* [Col. 0487C], and throughout the whole *Pater noster*, they should bow; but at the end of the *Pater noster*, when *Sed libera nos a malo* has been answered, they should stand upright, which is not permitted to the others.

The same is done when, on feasts in white vestments, he alone or with others directs the choir. This is not permitted to the person who has served as hebdomadary cantor on Sundays and similar feasts.

At all the principal solemnities, when they occur on Sundays, he should be entered on the roster for the Mass office, together with two whom he himself chooses. What is to be done concerning the thurible after the offertory has been stated above.

When manual work is being done, it is his duty either to read or to show the master of the boys at what place the boy [Col. 0487D] should begin his reading.

On Sundays and similar feasts, once the offertory has begun, the person directing the choir should approach the cantor and give him a sign to begin the verse of the offertory. For it is his duty to begin them even when the subcantor is directing the choir. When the cantor sees the sign, he should bow to him, and the hebdomadary cantor should likewise bow to the cantor. At the beginning of each verse, the cantor should make the sign before and behind him, and all the boys should bow.

It is his duty to notify the abbot of all the chants that he himself sings or begins. The care of the Briefs that are customarily sent out for deceased brothers, and the care of counting the thirty-day and seven-day observances, belong to him. He should take charge of all the monastery’s books and keep them in his custody, if he possesses the diligence and knowledge [280] [Col. 0488A] such that their custody ought to be entrusted to him.

## CHAPTER VI. On the Secretary, or Sacristan.

It belongs to the sacristan’s office to guard all the monastery’s ornaments, all its instruments, and all its furniture belonging to the monastery; to provide for the hours [reading: *proaedere*; perhaps *providere* or *praevidere*]; at the twelve readings, after the Gospel has been announced in the third nocturn, and at the festive octaves, to uncover the altar; at that time to carry the Gospel book into the vestry, so that the priest may carry it when, dressed in a cope, he processes to the altar each day; to provide the priest, when he returns from the altar to the lectern, with a lantern and candle; and, when the collect has ended, to receive the same lantern and afterward place the Gospel book on the altar.

[Col. 0488B] It is his duty to ring the signals, or to indicate to others how they are to be rung. He asks no one’s permission for any hour that is to be sounded, except for Prime and Collation, with the exception of Terce and Vespers, when the abbot is sitting in the cloister with the brothers who are speaking. He distributes candles through the workshops according to what is needed and what the abbot or prior has ordered. He takes charge of burials, both of monks and of laymen, ensuring that they take place and determining where they take place.

It is his duty to wash the chalices twice a week, or more often if necessary, and also to wash the corporals before Easter and whenever appropriate during the rest of the year. He should do both if he is a deacon or priest. If he is not, he should inform the prior or abbot and, with his permission [Col. 0488C], entrust this duty to someone of that order. The corporals should be washed with as much care as possible. Bronze vessels, assigned to no other uses, should be kept for this work. The water in which they are washed, like that used for the chalices, should be poured into the sacrarium. Once they have been washed, every precaution should be taken while they are drying so that no dirt adheres to them.

The responsibility for making the hosts belongs to him. He must strive with the greatest care to have them made as cleanly and properly as possible. First, if it can be done, the grain should be selected grain by grain with great care; once selected, it should be placed in a clean sack made of good cloth and used only for this purpose, and a diligent servant should carry it to the mill. After it has been delivered, the servant should first have some other grain ground at that same mill, so that the grain from which the hosts are to be made may afterward be ground without any contamination.

When the flour has been brought back [Col. 0488D], the sacristan should prepare a vessel and the place where the flour is to be sifted, enclosing it around with a curtain. He himself, dressed in an alb and with his head covered by the amice, should perform this work.

On the day when the hosts are to be made, the sacristan and the brothers who are to help him should wash their hands and faces before beginning, dress in albs, and cover their heads with amices, except the one who is to hold the irons and serve from them. One of them should sprinkle the flour with water on a very clean board, and knead and work it vigorously with his hands. The brother who holds the irons in which they are baked should have his hands wrapped in gloves. Meanwhile, while the hosts are being made and baked, these same brothers should say the psalms [Col. 0489A] proper to the hours and the canonical hours, or, if they prefer, an equivalent sequence from the Psalter. They must observe complete silence in speaking. Nevertheless, the one who holds the irons may, if necessary, briefly indicate what he wants to the servant who tends the fire and carries the wood; the wood must be very dry and deliberately prepared many days in advance.

It is his duty to wash the wine and water cruets twice a week, namely on Wednesday and Saturday; every day to carry the wine and water for the celebration of Masses; to provide hosts to those making the offering at both Masses; and to light the candles for the readings and at the morning praises, and for the first collect. If these morning praises are delayed beyond measure and indecorously, the sacristan to whom responsibility for this matter has then been entrusted should prostrate himself before the step of satisfaction [Col. 0489B] until that collect has been completed through *Benedicamus Domino*. Once this has begun, he should leave without awaiting permission and should not make the sign before or behind him. He should make this satisfaction on whatever day such negligence occurs and afterward should not ask for another pardon in the chapter house.

And because the care of this ministry, both in the matters written above and in many others that are not written, is manifold and very complicated, it should be entrusted not to one person alone but to many and divided among them. One of them should be master of the others, and the rest should act according to his direction, while major matters remain subject to the judgment of the abbot or prior.

## 281 CHAPTER VII. On the Chamberlain.

[Col. 0489C]

It is the chamberlain’s duty to provide all clothing, footwear, beds, and bedding that the brothers need and are permitted to have according to the rule; also razors and scissors, towels for shaving, towels hanging in the cloister, towels and hand towels for the mandatum, and all their vessels. He makes and repairs the dormitory windows when necessary. He provides the irons for shoeing the horses of the abbot and prior, and the horses of all guests for whom the abbot or prior has ordered shoes to be provided. He also provides brothers who are setting out on a journey with copes, bandages, and spurs. Once a year he has the hay renewed in all the brothers’ beds and at that time also has the dormitory cleaned.

## CHAPTER VIII.

### SECTION I.—On the Cellarer.

[Col. 0489D]

It belongs to the cellarer’s ministry to procure, according to the resources of the place, everything necessary for the brothers in bread and drink and in the various kinds of food; to provide all the vessels of the cellar and kitchen, the cups, measures, and other vessels of the refectory, and all the necessary equipment of these three places. He should be the father of the entire congregation, taking care of the healthy brothers and especially the sick. Apart from the advice of the abbot or prior, he should do nothing in major matters.

The cantor should be asked by him to warn him several days in advance and announce the day on which his statement concerning the Rule is to be read in the chapter house, so that [Col. 0490A] on that day he may provide the brothers with an honorable and festive service in the refectory. The refectory tables, however, should not be covered. Once the statement has been read and explained in the chapter house, when the prior has said, “Let us speak about our order,” he should immediately prostrate himself in the customary place and say:

“I treat this obedience which has been enjoined upon me carelessly, lukewarmly, and in many respects quite otherwise than I ought, through my fault; and in it I offend God and our superiors in many things, through my fault. For this I ask your absolution and that of the superiors.”

After he has said this, the person presiding over the chapter should absolve him from the offenses he has enumerated there and from all the others that are in him. At the conclusion of this absolution, after all have answered *Amen* with complete devotion, as is customary [Col. 0490B], he should go to the presider’s feet and then be ordered to go and sit down.

When the chapter house meeting has ended, and *Verba mea* has been said, if it is to be said that day, the brothers should say Psalm 50 for him in the same chapter house. When it has been completed with the *Gloria Patri* and *Pater noster*, the hebdomadary should say: “And lead us not into temptation. Save your servant. The Lord be with you. Almighty and everlasting God, have mercy on your servant,” and the rest.

If, after receiving a Brief for a deceased person, they are to go into the monastery that same day while singing *Verba mea*, they should say the aforesaid psalm with its chapters and collect before going. If it happens that the aforesaid statement is read on a day when a meal cannot honorably be provided, as on the vigils of the Ember Days and similar days, the cellarer should ask the prior and chapter [Col. 0490C] for permission to postpone the meal to another day on which it can be provided more honorably and fully.

### SECTION II.—On the Brother Responsible for Guests.

The brother appointed to receive guests should have the following prepared in the guesthouse itself: beds, seats, tables, hand towels, tablecloths, cups, bowls, spoons, basins, and anything of this kind; also wood. He receives bread, drink, and the other foods for the guests in the cellar from the servants assigned to him.

Whoever wishes to speak with the abbot, prior, or anyone from the cloister must entrust his message to this brother. He, without revealing it to anyone in any way [Col. 0490D], should convey the guest’s request to the abbot or prior, and afterward whatever the latter has decided should be done. If permission has been granted for a brother who is in the cloister to speak with a guest, whether a relative or a stranger, it is this brother’s duty to lead the brother from the cloister to the guest. If the abbot or prior does not wish them to speak together, he must give the brother no word, sign, or gesture by which he could perceive anything about the matter in any way.

It is his duty above all to observe carefully, concerning the brothers who are in obediences, when they return to the monastery, whether they have suitable servants and a regular cell, and how they conduct themselves in the courtyard, so that, if they have done anything out of order [282], he may make a complaint against them in the chapter house.

[Col. 0491A] If secular clerics say that they wish to eat in the refectory, it is his duty to inform the abbot or prior of their wish. If the abbot or prior grants their request, he should instruct them properly concerning how they must conduct themselves in the refectory and, once instructed, bring them to the locutorium after the cymbal has been struck. There the abbot—or, if the abbot is absent, the prior—should give them water for their hands, and afterward the aforesaid brother should lead them to the abbot’s table. When the midday meal has ended and the community is leaving the refectory, the brother who led them should remain alone with them after the abbot or prior and follow the procession with them until he has come out through the refectory door. He should then lead them outside the cloister, singing *Miserere mei, Deus* and what follows with them in a moderate voice.

[Col. 0491B] It is his duty to lead an unfamiliar monk who is ignorant of the place through the cloister into the monastery for prayer. Briefs for the dead should be given through his hands to the master of the boys or carried into the chapter house. It belongs to him to bring secular persons who are to enter into association with the brothers into the chapter house. It is his duty, for those who wish to see the workshops, to show them the workshops, taking care that the community is not then sitting in the cloister. He must not introduce into the cloister for any reason anyone wearing boots or spurs, anyone who is barefoot, or anyone wearing only breeches. Moreover, it is his duty to bring novices who come from the world into the chapter house and teach them to make their first petition to the prior.

### SECTION III.—On the Almoner.

[Col. 0491C] The almoner should either search out for himself, if that is convenient, or have the matter investigated with great care through truthful and faithful people, to discover where the sick and weak lie who have no means by which they can support themselves.

If he himself goes to search them out and visit them, he should take two servants with him. Before entering the house to which he is going, he should have any women who are in it leave. Once inside, he should comfort the sick person kindly and offer him whatever he has that is best and understands to be necessary for him. If the sick person requests something else, he should also seek it out if he can obtain it in any way. He should never enter houses in which sick or weak women are lying; instead, he should send through one of his servants whatever he can obtain and whatever is necessary for them. Before doing anything mentioned above [Col. 0491D], however, he should inform the abbot or prior, and distribute the monastery’s alms to them according to their direction.

## CHAPTER IX. On the Infirmarian.

The brother entrusted with the care of the infirmary and appointed to serve the sick brothers should have his own cook and a separate kitchen, if the site and resources of the place are such that what must be prepared for the sick can be prepared at the proper time. He himself should serve the sick all the dishes that are to be set before them. Every day after Compline he should sprinkle holy water over all their beds. After the three prayers said before Matins have been completed [Col. 0492A], he should make the rounds of all the sick brothers’ beds with a lantern, carefully observing lest anyone who was able to rise should have remained in bed. It is his particular duty to reveal and complain in the chapter house of all negligences committed by those living in the aforesaid house.

When he perceives that a sick man is already near his end, it is his duty to order his servants to heat water for washing him. Responsibility for guarding and administering the bier, when necessary, belongs to him and his servants, as does responsibility for administering the board which the prior customarily strikes once the washing of the deceased has been completed. When a brother has died and been carried into the monastery, he should have the place where he lay cleaned [Col. 0492B] and the hay or rushes renewed.

The abbot or prior should take every possible care that nothing necessary for this ministry should ever be lacking in that house.

## CHAPTER X. On Negligence Concerning the Body of the Lord.

When, through some mishap, such great negligence concerning the body or blood of the Lord occurs [283] that it falls downward, or into another place where it cannot be fully ascertained where it has fallen or whether any of it has reached the ground, the matter should be reported as quickly as possible to the abbot or prior. He should come hastily to the place where this occurred, accompanied by some brothers. If the body has fallen or the blood has been poured onto stone [Col. 0492C], earth, wood, a mat, a carpet, or anything of this kind, dust from the earth should be collected; the relevant part of the stone should be scraped; and the relevant part of the wood, mat, carpet, or whatever else it may be should be cut off and thrown into the sacrarium.

If the place where it fell cannot be clearly discovered, but it is nevertheless certain that it fell downward, then in the place and around the place where they believe it most likely fell, the material should likewise be collected, scraped, or cut away and placed in the sacrarium. Those through whose negligence this happened should humbly confess their fault in the next chapter meeting, submit to judgment stripped, and be assigned a penance, whether fasting, disciplines, psalms, or something of this kind. When they have returned to their places from the judgment, all the priests who are then present should rise and offer themselves with complete devotion to undergo the judgment. Then the person presiding over the chapter should retain only seven of those whom he wishes to undergo the judgments and order the others to go and sit down. When the chapter meeting has ended, all should prostrate themselves together and say the seven psalms in the monastery, beginning to sing them as they leave the chapter house. These should be followed by the *Pater noster*, with the following chapters and collect: “And let your mercy, O Lord, be upon us”; “Do not remember our ancient iniquities”; “The Lord be with you”; “Let us pray: Hear, O Lord, our prayers, and spare the sins of those who confess to you, so that those whom the guilt of conscience accuses may be absolved by your merciful forgiveness”; through [Christ our Lord]. Or they may use that collect: “O God, whose proper nature is always to have mercy,” or another for sins.

[Col. 0493A] If the blood has fallen onto a corporal or some other honorable cloth, and it is certain where it fell, that part of the cloth should be washed in a chalice. The first washing should be consumed by the brothers, and the other two should be poured into the sacrarium. At the first chapter meeting, however, only those through whose negligence this happened should undergo the discipline described above. All the brothers should say the seven psalms with their chapters and collect in the monastery, as stated above [Col. 0493B]. If a Brief for the dead has been read in the chapter house that day, they should first sing *Verba mea* as they proceed to the church; afterward they should say the seven psalms as stated above.

If a lesser negligence concerning this sacrament occurs in some other way, the brother through whose fault it happened should be punished with a milder penalty, according to the judgment of the abbot or prior.

## CHAPTER XI. On Shaving the Brothers.

On the day when the brothers are to be shaved, the signal for Prime—or for Terce, if Terce is to be said before the chapter meeting that day—should be struck earlier than usual. They should not remain long in the chapter house. Once the necessary matters have been completed, they should rise, and after the board has been struck and *Benedicite* has been said, leave for the cloister. The boys should not hold chapter that day, but should leave immediately after the others and go to their school. Once everyone is seated and ready to be shaved, the abbot or prior should begin the five psalms, namely *Verba mea* for the dead. The priest hebdomadary, sitting, should say the collects. Another hebdomadary [Col. 0493C] should sit beside him and hold the psalms with him. After the five psalms, they should say all the canonical hours. At the end of these, until Vespers, the priest should say neither *Dominus vobiscum* nor *Benedicamus Domino*, but, after *Per omnia saecula saeculorum*, should immediately begin *Adjutorium meum*. After Vespers, once *Benedicamus Domino* has been said, Vespers of the Dead should be sung, followed by Compline as for the canons, and afterward the customary psalms of the hours.

No one should be shaved in a cowl. He should first remove the cowl, put on a frock, fold the cowl and place it beside him, and then be shaved. The person shaving should be undressed from his frock.

The young men who are under custodianship should shave their custodians, and the custodians [Col. 0493D] should shave the young men. If a custodian is unable or does not know how to shave, he should ask a mature brother to shave him; nevertheless, the custodian should sit beside him while watching him. Young men, whether raised in the monastery or coming from the world, who are not under such custodianship must not presume to shave one another. Rather, the seniors should be shaved by them, and they by the seniors. The masters should shave the boys, and should themselves be shaved by the boys, provided that the boys possess this skill.

In winter, when the boys, those who have been bled, and the sick receive a mixed meal after the chapter meeting, the refectory servants should shave themselves first and, after the psalms, prepare the refectory so promptly that those who are to receive the mixed meal find everything ready.

As long as the psalms are being said, no one may have his hair cut [284] [Col. 0494A], wash his head, or cut his nails, nor may anyone presume to go outside the cloister without permission. When the psalms have ended, the abbot or prior should say *Benedicite*, and after *Dominus* has been answered, they may speak. Then the [*lesciva*—a term uncertain in the supplied text] should be brought into the cloister, and whoever wishes may wash his head, each for himself and no one for another, except the masters of the boys, who must wash the heads of the small boys who cannot do so.

If the signal for an hour sounds while a brother is being shaved, he should put his cowl over his frock and go to the choir, provided that he has either shaved his beard completely or still has it entirely untouched; otherwise he should remain outside the choir. On the day when the brothers shave themselves, the tablecloths in the refectory must be changed. On other days, when the brothers are speaking in the cloister, anyone who needs to be shaved [Col. 0494B] may be shaved in the cloister, but only with the permission of the abbot or prior.

## CHAPTER XII. On Bloodletting.

Permission to be bled should always be requested immediately after the chapter meeting, and the time of bloodletting should be announced to the cellarer: in winter, after the Gospel of the principal Mass; in summer, after None and before Vespers; in Lent, after Vespers. When those who are to be bled have come in their night shoes to the place assigned to this work, they should turn toward the east and bow before and behind them. Then, with their prior beginning the verse *Deus, in adjutorium meum intende*, they should say it three times, and the rest, as in summer after None in the chapter house, when the brothers speak in the cloister [Col. 0494C]. If there is only one, he should do this alone. Afterward they should remove their frocks and prepare for bloodletting.

They must observe complete silence there, unless necessity compels them to speak and the matter can neither be postponed nor ought to be postponed. If this occurs, it should be done briefly, modestly, and in the most humble voice.

They must not be compelled to enter the choir until the next day after the prayer of Prime or Terce, at which time Terce is said before the chapter meeting. If they need more time, they should ask permission to remain outside the choir longer.

On the following day they should put on their night shoes and receive a mixed meal for two days. When the time for that meal arrives, if it is a time when the brothers eat once, all should say the verse together, both before and after the mixed meal [Col. 0494D], with the psalm *Miserere mei, Deus* and the others, in the manner in which the community says them when all the brothers eat twice. The blessing should be given by the priest prior, and the reading should be recited from memory by someone. Everything should be done in the refectory.

On the day after the bloodletting, one of those who have been bled should be called out and offer himself to ask pardon. Someone among those who know about the bloodletting should tell the prior that this brother has been bled. The prior should order him to speak standing, especially if he was bled from a vein in the arm. If the fault is light, it should be pardoned; if it is of such a kind that it ought not to be dismissed without corporal discipline, the matter should be postponed to another time.

These are the times [Col. 0495A] when the brothers should not be bled unless necessity compels it: if the following day is a feast of twelve readings, except for the Saturdays of Lent up to the Passion of the Lord; if the following day is a feast of three readings on which Mass is celebrated in copes, such as the three days after Easter and the three after Pentecost; during the fourteen days before Easter; if a canonical fast that cannot be broken occurs that day or the following day; and on the feast of All Saints, because on the following day all the priests must celebrate Masses for the Dead and the rest must say the psalms appointed for those Masses.

## CHAPTER XIII. On the Hebdomadary of the Principal Mass.

If something happens to the priest who is hebdomadary of the principal Mass while he is asleep, so that he ought not to celebrate Mass that day [Col. 0495B], then, if it is an ordinary day, he should omit nothing of his office except the Mass, the blessing in the refectory, and Compline, because sprinkling the brothers with holy water after Compline belongs to the person who said Compline and celebrated Mass.

If there are twelve readings, he should also omit Vespers and the morning praises if the priest must vest for them. Once the principal prayer has ended, when the vested priest who is performing the office in his place has left the choir, the hebdomadary priest, wherever he may be in the choir, should complete all the remaining items without waiting for any signal.

When the hebdomadary himself, vested, sings Vespers or the morning praises, and, after the principal prayer has been completed, leaves the choir to undress, he should then give a sign to someone in his choir whom he chooses to perform the commemoration of the Saints in his place [285]. Once this has been completed [Col. 0495C], the hebdomadary should return to the choir and complete what follows.

## CHAPTER XIV. On Brothers Traveling.

A brother setting out on some journey and not intending to return on the following day shall receive the blessing for going out. If, however, it happens that he returns the next day, he shall not receive the blessing for returning. But if, when setting out, he expects to return the following day, he shall not receive the blessing for going. If it happens that he remains away for more than two days, then, upon returning, he shall receive the blessing for returning. But if a brother who has received the blessing for departing [Col. 0495D] remains away for more than two days, and on the very day on which he returns proceeds to some place outside the monastery, where he spends one night, then, returning the next day, he shall receive all the blessings for returning, because from the time he first departed he has not spent the night in the monastery. If, however, he goes out without a blessing, expecting to return the following day, and this does occur, but on the very day on which he returns he proceeds to some place outside the monastery, where he spends one night, then, when he returns, he shall receive all the blessings for returning on that same day. This is done because he has spent two successive nights outside the monastery. When going out, he shall receive no blessing unless he expects to remain away for more than two days.

If any brother coming from outside receives both [Col. 0496A] blessings—that is, the blessing for coming and the blessing for going out—but it is not convenient for him to leave immediately, or even throughout that entire day, then, for however many hours he remains in the monastery, he shall receive the blessings for coming, but not those for going out—unless it happens that he remains in the monastery that night. In that case, if he wishes to leave the following day, he shall receive the latter blessing.

At Vespers or Compline the blessing for going out must never be given. If a brother who has received the blessing hears the signal for the regular hour before he has left the cloister, he shall go with the others to the choir and, when that hour has been said, proceed on his way. But if he is outside the cloister and, before he has gone out through the gate of the courtyard, the signal for the regular hour is sounded, he shall return to the church, say the regular hour [Col. 0496B] outside the choir, and afterward continue on his way.

A brother wearing a bandage, or girded, or wearing a cape, shall never enter the cloister. Brothers who have been sent on a journey, when they say the regular hour or pray, or say “O God, come to my assistance” with the “Glory be to the Father”—if it is such a day as in the monastery—shall kneel; but they shall nowhere make prostrations before or behind themselves, nor, when they make a mistake, ask pardon, unless they are in a church. On days when, praying before the forms, they are to say some hour, if they are riding horses they shall dismount; once the hour has begun and pardon has been requested, they shall remove gloves from their hands and caps from their heads, and, having remounted, shall finish the hour.

If the need to speak arises while they are chanting, then, when the conversation has ended, they shall begin the hour [Col. 0496C] again from the beginning. While an hour is being sung at their lodging, or while they are eating, they shall be dressed either in frocks or only in cowls. While riding along the road, they shall say all the psalmody which it is not convenient for them to say at night, except that which they customarily say by day to complete the order. To avoid curiosity, buffoonery, and idleness, before going to sleep they shall say Compline. After it has been said, if a serious necessity to speak arises—one that ought not to be avoided—they shall speak after the verse, as briefly as possible. If this occurs before Matins, they shall say Compline again and afterward keep silence. Wherever a monk may be, a light shall burn before him throughout the night.

Regarding monks sent on a journey, those monasteries which in our time possess greater authority within our order observe this custom [Col. 0496D]. Blessed Benedict, however, does not determine a number of days; rather, he commands absolutely that a monk returning from a journey receive the blessing at every canonical hour.

# CHAPTER XV. On Regular Silence

When a regular hour other than Compline is sung in the monastery, none of the brothers shall speak within the workshops of the entire monastery, nor anywhere within the whole courtyard, nor even in the infirmary, except those whom such serious illness afflicts that it does not allow them meanwhile to keep silence. While Compline is being sung, however, the prior and those who, by permission, remain away from Compline may speak about useful and necessary matters.

[Col. 0497A] Likewise, while the brothers are saying the regular hour in the church, no one shall eat in the refectory, except at Compline. Then those who, hindered by some useful duty, cannot finish their business before that hour, and brothers who come from outside, may eat in the refectory. If those who begin eating before the collation cannot conveniently finish their meal toward the end of Compline, they may rise from the table, go into the monastery for the blessing, and afterward return to the refectory to complete their meal.

286

# CHAPTER XVI. On Faults and Satisfactions

A brother assigned to satisfaction for a lesser fault shall be separated from the common table and shall use the same food and drink as the other brothers, unless these have been expressly forbidden to him. He shall eat at the ninth hour if the brothers eat at the sixth, or at Vespers if the brothers eat at the ninth hour [Col. 0497B].

In the monastery and in the chapter house, he shall be either the last of all or between the two groups, according to the nature of his fault and the abbot’s command.

In church he shall not celebrate Mass, read the Epistle or a lesson, read the Gospel, sing a responsory, impose an antiphon upon the psalms, or perform anything of this kind, unless he does it with the others. He shall not vest himself for the candlestick or the thurible, nor approach for the offering or the kiss of peace.

Near the end of the regularly appointed Work of God, both at night and by day, when they begin “Kyrie eleison,” he shall prostrate himself before the step where the blessings [Col. 0497C] are received, and there shall lie prostrate until “Who lives and reigns with you” is said. If a feast with twelve lessons occurs, he shall cease this satisfaction until ordinary days return. While the brothers are eating in the refectory, he shall be in the church.

When the abbot wishes to release him from this satisfaction, if he is in the monastery among the community, the abbot shall send to him, while he is prostrate, one of the priors who are near him. The prior shall give the prostrate brother a sign on the abbot’s behalf to rise. He shall rise immediately, bow humbly to the abbot, and go to his place. But if the abbot is seated in the chapter house, at the brothers’ request he shall say to him: “This satisfaction for a lesser fault is remitted to you,” or something similar. The brother shall immediately rise, go to the abbot’s feet, and afterward [Col. 0497D] return to his place.

If the abbot is on a journey, the prior—or, in the prior’s absence, the brother who holds the order—may do all this.

If any brother, God forbid, commits a serious fault, and that fault, once disclosed, cannot suitably be corrected in secret, he shall be examined in the chapter house before the abbot and the assembled brothers. By common judgment that brother shall suffer severe corporal discipline and shall be ordered to undertake the satisfaction for a serious fault. After receiving the discipline, dressed and girded, he shall lay down his knife there, cover his head with his hood, and proceed in complete silence to the place appointed for this purpose, preceded by the brother who keeps the key to that place. The abbot shall then appoint [Col. 0498A] one of the senior brothers to whom he can safely entrust the offender’s custody. That senior shall take him to the hours and, after the hours, return him to his place. After chapter, the senior shall privately inquire of the abbot in what manner the brother is to live, and what he is to eat and at what hour. That brother shall speak with him and with those others whom the abbot has ordered; no one else shall associate or converse with him.

When the signal for an hour is sounded, with his keeper leading him and his head covered, he shall come before the monastery door. If the community has not yet entered the monastery, he shall lie prostrate there until all have entered; but if they have already entered, he shall stand there, bow, and kneel as the brothers in the choir do while the hour is being sung. If any brothers pass near him, [Col. 0498B] he shall bow humbly to them. If the abbot passes, he shall ask pardon while prostrate, provided that the brother knows that the abbot is passing near him. When the regular hours are finished, he shall prostrate himself at the feet of those leaving the church, with his head covered, until all have passed. Those leaving shall say to him quietly, “May God have mercy on you.” When all have gone out, he shall return to the place from which he came, with his head covered and his keeper preceding him.

On the days appointed by the abbot, he shall come into the chapter house, led by the aforesaid keeper, and shall humbly and patiently endure corporal judgment. Suitable mercy shall be shown him regarding food and drink, lest, oppressed by excessive hardships, he be swallowed up by immoderate sorrow. He shall be treated in this way until, through humility, patience, and a promise of amendment, joined [Col. 0498C] with the prayers of the brothers, he obtains mercy.

On the day when the abbot, at the brothers’ prayers, decides to show him mercy, he shall come into the chapter house in the manner described above, prostrate himself, confess his fault, promise amendment, and ask for mercy. When ordered to rise, he shall repeatedly prostrate himself and say the same or similar words, continuing until the abbot says to him, “Enough.” He shall then be ordered to remove his clothing and undergo corporal discipline. When this has been done, the abbot shall say to him:

“Moved by the prayers of our brothers, by your patience and humility, and by your promise of amendment, I grant you this mercy: from now on you shall be with the brothers in the refectory and eat in the place we shall designate [Col. 0498D] for you; you shall no longer receive corporal discipline for this fault. In other respects, in order still to demonstrate your humility and patience, conduct yourself as a brother who is ordered to remain in penance for a lesser fault, except that, when ‘Kyrie eleison’ begins, you shall not prostrate yourself at the step; rather, when the regular hour is completed, in the place where you stand, with your knees bent to the ground, you shall make humble satisfaction, as one who makes a mistake in a psalm, according to the command of blessed Benedict.”

Having heard this, the brother shall go to the abbot’s feet. Returning to the place where he stood, he shall make three genuflections with complete devotion—forward, to the right, and to the left—giving thanks to the brothers because they have prayed for him and humbly asking them to continue to pray for him. [Col. 0499A] The abbot shall then designate the place where he is to be, and, at the abbot’s command, he shall go to sit.

This fault properly belongs to the abbot to correct. If, however, the abbot is away from the country and is not expected to return soon, the prior may correct it with the consent of the entire congregation.

If a sinning brother wishes to defend his sin rather than acknowledge and amend it, and, when formally accused before the abbot or prior, dares to answer defiantly, and, after being admonished to come to his senses, resolves to remain in his obstinacy, then the brothers designated for this purpose shall rise, seize him forcibly, and drag or carry him to the prison assigned to such arrogant men. Once deposited there, he shall be afflicted with measured discretion until he lays aside his pride [Col. 0499B], acknowledges his fault, and humbly promises amendment. If, by God’s inspiration, this comes to pass, the matter shall first be presented in chapter; afterward he shall be brought into chapter by the brother entrusted with such care. He shall enter either naked, like a fugitive monk, or clothed, as the circumstances require, with due consideration of the character and seriousness either of the preceding fault or of the subsequent arrogance. He shall afterward be treated as stated above—that is, severely if he has been assigned to the satisfaction for a serious fault, or lightly if to that for a lesser fault.

But if, filled with a diabolical spirit, he chooses to grow more arrogant rather than promise amendment, the prayers of the entire community shall be offered for him. If the abbot then sees that even his own diligence [Col. 0499C] cannot prevail, he shall prudently deliberate with the counsel of all the brothers whether it is expedient either to detain him longer or to expel him from the monastery.

If the abbot judges that a monk who has fled from the monastery should be received back into the monastery, he shall be received in the following manner. He shall first remain for some days in the guesthouse. Unless ordered otherwise, he shall not approach the cloister, the workshops of the cloister, or the monastery, so that meanwhile he may show some evidence of his repentance, humility, and patience. No brother shall associate with him or join him in any companionship or conversation unless ordered to do so by the abbot, the prior, or the one who holds the order.

On the day when he is to enter the chapter house, he shall remove his clothing [Col. 0499D] in the parlor; if he has not abandoned the habit, he shall put on a shirt and gird himself with a belt, place the folded cowl over his left arm, and take rods in his right hand. Thus, barefoot and naked above the waist, led by the brother appointed for this duty, he shall come into the chapter house. Upon entering, he shall immediately prostrate himself in the place where it is customary to prostrate. When questioned in the customary manner, he shall state his fault. Then, seated, he shall receive corporal discipline at the abbot’s command. After receiving it, wearing only the cowl there, as he came but without carrying the rods, he shall return to the parlor. There he shall put on his shoes and dress according to the rule. Returning to chapter, he shall prostrate himself until the abbot says to him, “Enough.” He shall be assigned the satisfaction for a serious fault, and in that satisfaction he shall conduct himself as stated above when the serious fault was discussed.

If a monk returns to the monastery after casting off his monastic clothing [Col. 0500A] and wearing secular dress, the other provisions stated above being observed, he shall enter the chapter house girded with the secular clothing in which he returned, as was said above concerning the shirt, and without carrying a cowl. After receiving the discipline, he shall receive the cowl, which the chamberlain shall place before him, and shall immediately put it on there.

# CHAPTER XVII. On Receiving Novices

When someone comes from the world to seek conversion, he shall first be received in the guesthouse, like the other guests. Once his intention is known 288, the brother who is in charge of the guest quarters [Col. 0500B] shall report the matter to the abbot, or, in the abbot’s absence, to the one who holds the order. The abbot, the prior, or some spiritual brother appointed for this purpose shall speak with him. If he recognizes that the petitioner’s desire is from God, the matter shall be presented to the brothers in chapter. After their counsel has been heard, if the abbot decides that the man should be received, then, on the appointed day, led by the aforesaid keeper of the guests and instructed by him how he should make his petition, he shall come into chapter and prostrate himself in the place where it is customary to prostrate. When asked what he seeks, he shall make his petition as humbly as he can, in these or similar words:

“I ask for the mercy of God, your fellowship, and the brotherhood of this place. I desire to become a monk in this monastery and to serve God.”

The abbot, or the one who presides over the order in the abbot’s place, shall answer him:

“May almighty God grant you the fellowship and association [Col. 0500C] of his elect.”

When the entire community has answered, “Amen,” he shall be ordered to rise and shall rise. The hard and difficult things endured in this order by those who wish to live piously and according to the rule shall be declared to him, as well as still harder and more difficult things that might happen to him if he behaves without discipline. If, after hearing these things, he nevertheless persists in his purpose and promises that he is prepared to endure harder and more difficult things, the one presiding over chapter shall answer him:

“May the Lord Jesus Christ so perfect in you what you promise for his love that you may obtain his grace and eternal life.”

When all have answered, “Amen,” he shall add:

“And we grant you, for his love, [Col. 0500D] what you so humbly and steadfastly request.”

Having heard this, the novice shall go and humbly kiss the feet of the one presiding. Then, at his command, the master of novices shall lead him into the church. There, seated before each altar outside the choir, he shall wait until chapter has ended.

When it has ended, the aforesaid master shall lead him to the chamberlain’s cell or to another house where what must be done can more conveniently take place. First, his tonsure shall be blessed if he is a layman, with the antiphons, psalms, and collects appointed for this office; or the rite may take place in the church before the entrance to Mass, at the step where the brothers receive the blessings; or in the infirmary chapel or the abbot’s chapel, according to the abbot’s [Col. 0501A] pleasure. Thus led to the appointed place, whether layman or cleric, the novice shall be tonsured and shaved according to the custom of monks. He shall then be stripped of his secular clothing and dressed in the regular clothing of the monastery, except for the cowl, with a sewn hood attached to his tunic. While these things are being done by the brothers appointed for them, the seven penitential psalms shall be said consecutively. Thus prepared, he shall be led into the assembly of the brothers. In the choir, if he is a cleric, he shall be last in the order of clerics; if a layman, last among the laymen. Likewise, in procession, chapter, and refectory, he shall be placed according to the order of his conversion.

He shall sleep in the novices’ cell, or in the dormitory if the monastery has no such cell. He shall not read in the assembly, sing alone, offer at Mass, or receive the kiss of peace [Col. 0501B]. In the cloister he shall sit apart with his master in the place assigned to novices. No one shall speak to him or give him a sign without his master’s permission. His master shall be a man able, by the example of his life and by instruction in words, to admonish him concerning his soul and teach him the order.

If, while the brothers are speaking in the cloister, someone wishes, out of love for God and zeal for justice, to come to him and rebuke or admonish him, he may come. After receiving permission from the master, he shall say what he wishes to say. When a cry has been made, the novice shall immediately rise before his master and, like the brothers in chapter, ask pardon. He shall not sit until the same master orders him to do so after he has promised amendment. Lesser faults shall be treated in this way. For more serious faults, he shall either be corrected in chapter according to the seriousness of the fault or, if the novices’ cell is located there, be rebuked and beaten in it [Col. 0501C] as in chapter. After the address, he shall leave chapter each day and meanwhile remain in the monastery, unless, as stated, he is to remain there to be punished for a more serious fault. For the faults he committed in the world and those that have occurred or occur to him in this order, he shall make frequent confessions to the abbot, the prior, and the spiritual brothers entrusted with this care.

After many days have passed, if his life pleases the brothers and the brothers’ way of life pleases him, his master shall advise him to ask the prior and some senior brothers to intercede for him with the abbot, so that the blessing may be given and his profession received. But if it pleases the abbot to bless him, then, on the appointed [Col. 0501D] day, after the address in chapter, he shall prostrate himself in the customary place and, while prostrate, make a petition to obtain the blessing. When ordered to rise, the hard and serious matters instituted by the holy Fathers in our order shall be recounted to him. If he replies that he is prepared to endure all these things, and still more serious ones if necessary, humbly and patiently, the abbot shall ask the seated brothers what they think and whether they grant that his requests should be accepted. When they reply that they 289 willingly grant this, he shall add: “And we grant it in the name of the Lord.” After these words, the novice shall go to the feet of the abbot, or, in the abbot’s absence, of the one who presides over the order. Returning to the place where he stood, with his knees bent to the ground, he shall bow humbly forward, to the right, and to the left, giving thanks to the brothers for the mercy bestowed upon him through their prayers. The abbot shall then command him to leave with his master. When chapter has ended, if he knows how to write, he shall write his profession; if he does not know how to write, he shall ask another to write it for him. He himself shall nevertheless make the sign of the cross at the end of the profession. Then, with the hood removed from his tunic until the hour [Col. 0502A] of his blessing, he shall remain outside the choir.

The cantor must provide him with parchment, ink, and a scribe if he does not know how to write. The time of the blessing is at the abbot’s discretion: either before the entrance to Mass, if he is not celebrating Mass, or after the Gospel, whether he is celebrating Mass or not. At the consecration of a monk, however, if it is convenient for him, he ought to celebrate Mass, as the canons command.

[Col. 0502B] After the Gospel has been read, when the novice enters the choir, preceded by his master, the community shall begin the psalm “Have mercy on me, O God,” with the right choir beginning. The novice shall come before the altar and prostrate himself upon the step. When the psalm has been said, he shall rise, read his profession, and place it upon the altar. If he is ignorant of letters, his master must read it for him, and the novice himself shall place it upon the altar. Having done this, he shall kneel before the altar, ask pardon, and then return to the place where he prostrated himself. There he shall say three times the verse “Receive me, O Lord,” and while saying it shall kneel three times. The community shall repeat the verse three times and add at the end: “Glory be to the Father,” “Kyrie eleison, Christe eleison, Kyrie eleison,” and “Our Father.” When the community begins the “Glory be to the Father,” the novice, bowing, shall turn himself around [Col. 0502C] in a circle and immediately prostrate himself. After the abbot has said “And lead us not into temptation,” and the response “But deliver us from evil” has been given, he shall begin the psalm “Out of the depths.” When it has been completed by the community, with the “Glory be to the Father,” he shall add:

“Save your servant,”  
“O Lord, send him help from the holy place,”  
“May the enemy have no success against him,”  
“Be for him, O Lord, a tower of strength,”  
“O Lord, hear my prayer,”  
“The Lord be with you.”

Then he shall say the collect “God, Father of mercies”; another, “God, who through the coeternal [Son]”; and another, “Lord Jesus Christ, who are the way.” After these three collects have been said, each with the complete conclusion “Through our Lord,” the abbot shall begin the hymn “Come, Creator Spirit.” When the community has devoutly and solemnly sung it, he shall say the collect “Holy Spirit, who [is addressed as] God and Lord” [the surviving Latin is an incomplete and uncertain incipit].

When this has been said, the novice shall rise, and the abbot shall sprinkle him with holy water. While he is standing, the cowl shall be blessed and sprinkled with holy water. After it has been blessed, the novice shall approach the abbot and stand before him on his knees. The abbot shall remove his tunic and say:

“May the Lord strip you of the old man with his deeds.”

As he clothes him in the cowl, he shall add:

“May the Lord clothe you with the new man, who was created according to God in righteousness and the holiness of truth.”

For both statements the listening brothers shall answer, “Amen.” The prayer “Merciful God, gracious God” [Col. 0502D] shall follow over him as he kneels and bows. When it has been said, the abbot shall kiss him and cover his head with the hood. He shall then be led through the choir to kiss all the brothers and shall be placed last.

[Col. 0503A] For three days he shall receive Communion of the body and blood of Christ. On the third day, at the kiss of peace at Mass, the abbot—or the person appointed by the abbot, if the abbot himself cannot conveniently do so—shall remove the hood from his head. Before this hour, from the time he was blessed, he shall keep complete silence. After the address, he shall leave chapter; he shall not go in procession; dressed in the cowl, he shall sleep with his head covered by the hood. In the first chapter at which he is permitted to speak, his master must mention him before the abbot, saying:

“Lord, if it should please you to command it, this brother could from this day forward read and sing in the community like the other brothers.”

The abbot shall answer:

“Let him do so with God’s blessing.”

The novice shall bow to the abbot from the place where he is sitting.

[Col. 0503B] From that day, whatever his order, he shall have permission to perform everything belonging to his order. If he is a priest, however, he may not celebrate Mass during the first year of his conversion unless he was of proven chastity in the world and the abbot has given him special permission for this matter.

A boy to be offered, after first having received his tonsure, shall be presented by his parents to the priest celebrating Mass after the Gospel, carrying in his hands the host and the chalice with wine, as is customary. After the priest has received this offering, the parents mentioned above shall wrap the boy’s hands in the altar cloth, which covers the altar and hangs down in front; then the abbot shall receive him. After this, the aforesaid parents shall immediately promise before God and his saints that the boy shall never abandon the order he has received, either personally or through someone placed in their position, and that they will knowingly give him nothing by which the boy—290 God forbid!—could perish. Having first written this promise before witnesses, they shall pronounce it there in words and afterward place it upon the altar.

When these things have been completed, the abbot shall bless the cowl. Stripping the boy of his cloak, skins, or some similar garment, he shall say: “May the Lord strip you of the old man,” as above; and, clothing him in the cowl, he shall add: “May the Lord clothe you with the new man,” and so forth. He shall then be led to be shaved and clothed according to the custom of our order. When, at a mature age, he is to make his profession, the other rites described above as necessary for one already converted shall be performed for him. What has now been done [Col. 0503D] need not be repeated.

# CHAPTER XVIII. On the Regular Chapter

Every day, as soon as the sound of the smallest signal begins, indicating chapter, all the brothers who are sitting in the choir shall immediately rise and, turned toward the east, stand meanwhile. The brothers who are elsewhere in the monastery shall also enter the choir. None of them shall hold a book; none shall read or look at anything in a book; no one shall sit in the cloister for any reason at that time. When the sound of the aforesaid signal ceases, the others shall follow the prior who precedes them, according to the order of their conversion.

When the brothers are seated in chapter, at the command of the one who holds [Col. 0504A] the order, after the blessing has been requested and the things customarily read and considered have been read and announced, and after the address, when “Let us speak of our order” has been said, if someone is called who shares a common name with one or more others, unless the caller distinguishes and identifies him so precisely that no doubt can exist, all those who bear the same name as the one being called must immediately rise and present themselves for pardon. They shall do so until the caller clearly indicates whom he means. This identification should, if possible, be made by order or office, in the following manner: “Dom Edward, priest”; “deacon”; “subdeacon”; “secretary”; “master of the children”; “master of the youths”; or something similar—not “archdeacon,” not “of London,” and not any surname derived from the world.

[Col. 0504B] The caller shall not pronounce judgment in that same chapter on the person against whom he makes the accusation [read: “clamorem” (accusation), not “clamatorem” (accuser)]. When questioned in the customary manner, the one who prostrates himself shall say “My fault” at every venia (request for pardon), except when he asks for fellowship, or release from obedience, or when a brother asks for the smallest mercy on behalf of a relative who has recently died after entering the order—namely, a father, mother, brother, or sister—or when one or more ask mercy for someone placed in the satisfaction for a serious fault, or when a brother is setting out on a long journey, or when something great and difficult, beyond his strength, is imposed upon a brother. In these and similar cases the response is made in this manner: “I ask for the mercy of God and for yours, and I beg it,” and so forth, according to what the reason for the request requires.

One receiving judgment shall either be beaten with only the thicker rod [Col. 0504C] upon his shirt and lie prostrate, or, naked, be seated and beaten with several thinner rods—both options being at the discretion of the one presiding over the order, with consideration of the nature and seriousness of the fault. While corporal discipline is being administered, all the brothers must remain with bowed heads and feel compassion for him with pious and fraternal affection. Meanwhile no one in chapter shall speak or look at him, except the senior persons who are permitted to intercede for him. The one who has been accused may not make an accusation in that same chapter against the person by whom he was accused. Whoever he may be to whom the abbot or prior assigns it shall administer the corporal discipline, with this provision observed: it must not be assigned to be done by children, youths, or novices [Col. 0504D]. No one there shall speak privately with one or more persons; whatever anyone says must be heard by the ruler of the order and by the entire community.

The discussion shall concern only useful matters and those pertaining to the order. When one person is speaking, the others shall be silent. No one shall interrupt the speaker except the ruler of the order, who may command the speaker to be silent if the speech seems to him perhaps excessive and useless. When the ruler of the order begins to speak, even if someone else has been speaking, that person shall be silent, and complete silence shall be observed by all.

# CHAPTER XIX. If a Brother Is Given a Higher Rank

If the abbot wishes to honor a brother for his merits and, having considered his good character, establish him in a higher place, then, after that brother has heard the abbot [Col. 0505A], seated in chapter, say, “Go and sit higher beside that brother,” he shall immediately rise, go to the abbot’s feet, and afterward proceed to the place where he has been ordered to sit. From that day he shall hold that place in the monastery, in procession, and in the refectory. Blessed Benedict does not prescribe that a converted layman be promoted in this way. If, however, the abbot wishes to promote him, he shall hold in the refectory the place he receives in chapter; in the monastery and in procession he shall be ordered to rank above those converted brothers over whom the brother beside whom he has been ordered to sit is known to have precedence.

It can happen, when such a promotion is arranged, that some honorable brothers distinguished by good works are absent, and that the brother beside whom the promoted brother is ordered to sit has precedence over them. Therefore it must be explicitly stated [Col. 0505B] to him in chapter whether he is also to rank above those absent brothers when they return. When entering chapter, a brother shall say “Bless,” if the others are speaking. When leaving, if he is going to return, he shall neither make a bow before and behind himself nor say “Bless.” If he is not going to return, he shall do both.

# CHAPTER XX. On Fellowship

A monk who is going to ask that the fellowship and benefit of the monastery be granted to him shall be brought into chapter and say “Bless.” Then, prostrate at the step where it is customary, when asked what he seeks, he shall answer with a humble and devoted heart in these words:

“I ask, through the mercy of God and of you and of all these senior brothers, for the fellowship and benefit of this monastery.”

When he has said this [Col. 0505C], the abbot shall answer:

“May the almighty Lord grant you what you seek, and may he himself grant you fellowship with his elect.”

Then, ordered to rise, he shall approach the abbot and receive from him the fellowship of the monastery through the book of the Rule. Having received it and received his kiss, he shall bow to the abbot’s feet and then go around kissing all the brothers. Afterward he shall return to the place where he prostrated himself and there make three genuflections in the customary manner. The brothers shall bow to him. Then, at the abbot’s command, he shall go to sit, after a place where he is to sit has first been designated.

But if the abbot is the one seeking fellowship, when he enters chapter the entire community shall rise for him and shall stand until he makes his petition [Col. 0505D] prostrate on the ground, as described above. When he has risen, he shall receive fellowship with his monks. Having received it, he shall sit beside the abbot; the monks, having received his fellowship, shall return to the place where they prostrated themselves and make three genuflections, as stated above. As the brothers leave chapter, they shall kiss the abbot and his monks.

If the congregation is large, the kiss may be omitted, as is already customary in many monasteries. If the person is secular, he shall stand before or beside the abbot. If he is an honorable person, he shall sit. After his petition has been presented to the brothers, he shall receive fellowship through the text of the Gospel. Then he shall go around to kiss the brothers, unless he is a woman.

# CHAPTER XXI. On the Discipline of Boys

[Col. 0506A]

At such an hour in the morning the prior must make a sound to awaken the brothers that the boys, after performing the customary prayers, may be able to read in the cloister. When they begin to read aloud, they shall sit separated from one another for as long as they read, so that neither can touch the other with hands or clothing. A child shall not give another child a sign or say anything by word unless the master sees and hears it; nor shall he rise from the place where he is sitting without an order or permission.

Wherever the boys go, one master shall be among every two boys. As they pass before the brothers, they shall bow to the brothers, and the seated brothers shall bow only to them. One lantern shall suffice for two; if there are three, the third shall carry another [Col. 0506B]. If there are more, they shall be arranged in this order. They shall give nothing into anyone’s hand and receive nothing from anyone’s hand except that of the abbot, the prior, or their master—and even this not everywhere, but only in suitable places where it cannot or should not be otherwise. The cantor, when he is in their school, may also give them and receive from them the book in which they are to sing or read. If they serve at the altar, they shall likewise give and receive there as their orders require. In their own chapter they shall be beaten, as the older brothers are in the greater chapter.

Those who are going to confess shall go to the abbot, the prior, or those whom the abbot has specifically designated in chapter. While one is confessing, the other shall sit on the footstool, with their master sitting nearby outside chapter.

[Col. 0506C] If they enter the refectory after the verse said before food, or enter the choir after the “Glory” of the first psalm at the hours, they shall go to their places and bow in the customary manner. Their master, however, shall go to the places established for those who are late.

292. No abstinence from food or drink is to be imposed on the boy who serves at the abbot’s table without the abbot’s command. If such abstinence is imposed at his command, either let him be excused from it or remove him meanwhile from the abbot’s table. In choir, when the abbot is present, unless he commands it, no one is to strike them, and no one is to make them undress. In his absence, the cantor is to correct them in matters belonging to his office; the prior, however, is to correct them in other matters in which they conduct themselves carelessly. Wherever they may be, apart from the persons designated above [Col. 0506D], no one is to signal to them, and no one is to smile at them.

No one is to enter their school, and no one is to speak with them anywhere unless permission to enter or speak has been granted by the abbot or prior.

At midday they are never to read in their beds, nor do anything else there, but are to rest fully covered. One mature and discreet master is to be master over the other masters, and, after hearing their cries, is to know how either to punish or to pardon the faults of the offenders with measured discretion. Once they have been placed in their beds, the masters are to remain with them while they are covered, during the night with lighted candles.

Young men, both those brought up within the monastery and those coming from the secular world who are entrusted to the masters for custody, are to be guarded in many respects [Col. 0507A] as the boys described above are. They are to sit apart from one another as prescribed above; outside the place of their custody they are never to go without a custodian; two by two they are to carry lanterns; they are to make their confessions to the abbot or prior, and to no one else, unless someone has been specially designated. At midday they are not to read in their beds, write, or do any kind of work, but are to rest fully covered; they are to have their beds before or between those of the masters. If they need to rise, they are first to wake the masters and then, after lighting a lantern, if it is night, they are to walk with the masters to attend to their needs.

Apart from the abbot, prior, and their masters, no one is to be free to sit in the place assigned for their custody, nor to make anything known to them by word or sign [Col. 0507B], unless permission has been received from the abbot or prior. When such permission is granted, the master must sit between the young man and the person speaking with him. A young man is not to speak with another young man unless the master hears and understands what is said by both sides. The masters are to sit among them or before them, so that they can observe them whenever they wish.

When they go to sleep, the masters are to stand before them until the young men are lying in their beds, covered. If it is night, they are to remain with them with lighted candles. In the monastery, chapter house, refectory, and processions they are to be mixed with the seniors, without observing, when necessary, the order of their conversion. If they read at table or serve from the kitchen, they are to go with the brothers to the monastery when the brothers rise from table; after the verse *Et ne* [Col. 0507C], they are to return with the custodians to the refectory. Two, or more if possible, of the community are to remain with them. But if the small number of seniors and the larger number of young men compel a different arrangement, sufficient custodians are to be appointed for them.

Moreover, if the method of guarding young men followed in some monasteries is preferred—namely, that they sit in different and separated places throughout the cloister, each having one custodian, or more if there are enough—each is to carry one lantern at night. A custodian is not to leave a young man unless he has commended him to a brother in whom, and concerning whom, he has good confidence. In short, every form of custody described above is to be applied to him.

## CHAPTER XXII. On the mercy granted to the weak

[Col. 0507D]

If a brother is afflicted by some bodily infirmity and cannot follow the community, he is first humbly to ask pardon in chapter. Ordered to rise, he is to stand and acknowledge that he cannot attend the community because of his illness. The abbot, or the person presiding over the order in the abbot’s place, is to answer him:

“May the almighty Lord grant you useful health, as he knows to be expedient for you. From now on, treat yourself according to your infirmity, and remain away from the community as seems best to you.”

If the illness has become so severe that he cannot remain with the community, the abbot is to order the brother entrusted with this care to lead the sick man to the infirmary [Col. 0508A]. In that house he is to be served, according to the resources of the place, both with the ordinary foods and with meat, so that, if possible, he may suffer no lack of anything. From the time he begins to eat meat, wherever he goes he must walk with his head covered by a hood and supporting himself with a staff.

On whatever day, having recovered his health, he wishes to return to the community, if he has eaten meat, he is first to be shaved and is to enter the choir at the hour sung before chapter; and if Mass is celebrated in the community after that hour, he is not to offer himself at it. After entering chapter, when the matter of speaking according to order has been announced, he is first to rise and, in the place where it is customary, prostrate himself and ask pardon. After being questioned and responding as usual, and ordered to rise, he is to say these or similar words [Col. 0508B]:

“Lord, burdened by my illness, I remained for a long time in the infirmary. In food, drink, and many other things I offended, and I acted against our order; for this I ask your absolution.”

After this the abbot is to absolve him, saying:

“May the almighty Lord absolve you from these and all your other offenses.”

When the community has answered, “Amen,” that brother is to offer himself at the abbot’s feet. Then, returning to the place where he prostrated himself and giving thanks to the abbot and the whole community because the things necessary for his infirmity were supplied to him, he is to make three genuflections in the customary manner. On that day, and thereafter for as long as necessary, he is to be ordered to receive the mixed portion.

But if he has not eaten meat, it is to be left to the abbot to determine at what hour he may return to the community after asking permission [Col. 0508C], and how he is to conduct himself thereafter.

## CHAPTER XXIII. On the sick who are near death

If a sick man appears to be moving more toward death than recovery, and asks to be anointed, the brother in charge of the infirmary is to report the matter to the brothers in chapter. Then, at the command of the abbot, or of the person sitting in the abbot’s place in chapter, the weekly priest, the sacristan, and four lay brothers are to go out and prepare what is required for such an undertaking.

When these things have been prepared, and the matters that the order requires to be dealt with in chapter have been completed, those leaving the monastery are to pass before the chapter house in the following order: first, one of the lay brothers with a vessel of blessed water; then another [Col. 0508D] with the cross; after these, two with candlesticks; last, the sacristan with the oil, and the priest, dressed in an alb and stole, wearing a maniple, and carrying a book.

As these pass by, the community is to rise; and, if it is a day on which the board is struck, those leaving chapter are to join them. Singing the seven psalms, they are to come to the sick man and stand around him in an orderly fashion, as the place where he lies permits. First the blessed water is to be sprinkled. Then, when the psalms have been completed, the *Kyrie eleison* (“Lord, have mercy”), the chapters, and the appointed collects are to follow up to the confession. After the confession has been made, he is to be absolved from everything, and he is himself to absolve everyone. Then he is to be kissed by all. Meanwhile, other collects are to be said up to the anointing. After the anointing, the priest is to wash his hands, and the water is to be thrown into the fire or carried to the sacrarium. [Col. 0509A] After this, when the following collects have been said, the priest is to go, preceded by two lay brothers carrying candlesticks; [Note: [Col. 0509D] Missing: “to the church for the venerable sacrament,” or something similar.] a third is to carry the thurible. When they return, all are to adore on bended knees the body of the Lord brought by the priest. Once it has been brought, after his mouth has first been cleansed, the sick man is to receive Communion, unless he has already received Communion that day.

If, on that day after chapter, the brothers are going to the monastery singing *Verba mea* (“My words”), then, after the psalms in choir and the collect have been completed, they are to prepare before the high altar the things described above, go out, and follow the order indicated earlier. The same is to be observed after any of the hours from Prime through Compline has ended, if necessity makes it urgent not to wait for chapter. But if even the hour at which this ought to be done cannot be awaited [Col. 0509B], the abbot or prior is to arrange matters as best he can, for necessity is not bound by law. When these things have been completed, the community is to return to the cloister. But the boys are not to enter in order to hold their own chapter. From this day onward, unless the sick man improves, he is not to eat meat.

Every day this service is to be performed for him: at the morning Mass, the collect *Almighty and everlasting God, eternal salvation of believers*, together with the other two; occasionally, if it is a free day, the morning Mass itself is to be sung for him. At the principal Mass, after the *Sanctus*, each person is silently to say the first psalm, *Lord, do not rebuke me in your anger*, followed by *Kyrie eleison*, *Our Father*, *Save your servant*, *Send him, Lord, help from the holy place*, and *Almighty and everlasting [Col. 0509C] God, eternal salvation of believers*. This is to continue until he appears to be returning to health.

But if he is clearly not returning to health and is instead drawing nearer to death, from the time definite signs of death begin to appear he is not to be left without two brothers. As long as he retains understanding, they are to read before him the Passion of the Lord and the Gospels day and night; when he has lost understanding, they are to continue singing the Psalter in order for as long as he lives. Arrangements are to be made so that when two depart, two others take their place. They are also to say the regular hours there.

When the sick man is in agony and, if it seems so, is about to die, the servant appointed for this purpose is to spread out a haircloth and, upon it, within the length and breadth of the haircloth [Col. 0509D], make the sign of the cross from ashes, and place the dying brother upon it. Afterwards, sitting constantly beside him, he is to watch carefully at what hour he must announce his departure to the community.

When he sees that the man is already struggling to depart, he is to carry the board in his hand, run to the door of the cloister, and strike it there sharply and repeatedly until he knows that it has been heard in the community. When the sound has been heard, if it is the time of the principal or lesser Mass, or of a regular hour, while the boys remain in choir with their masters, together with certain brothers who have been ordered to remain, all the others are to run to the sick man [Col. 0510A], coming to him while singing *I believe in one God* in a moderate voice. The brothers who remained are, after completing what they had begun, likewise to run and hasten to the dying man while singing.

Wherever else they may be, or whatever other business may occupy them, if the aforesaid sound finds them, they are all, without any excuse or delay, likewise to run and come to the sick man singing *I believe in one God*. When they arrive and have completed *I believe in one God* together, they are to sing the seven penitential psalms without the *Gloria Patri*. When these have been completed, the priest is to add the chapter:

“Spare, Lord, spare your servant, whom you have deigned to redeem with your precious blood; do not be angry with him forever.”

The priest is to say this three times, and the whole community is to repeat it each time [Col. 0510B]. Then the customary litany is to follow; it is to be lengthened or shortened according to what the condition of the brother’s departure appears to require. But if, as sometimes happens, he has not yet died when the litany is finished, the community is to depart, leaving there certain brothers who have been ordered to remain; they are to begin singing the Psalter in order. When the time comes for them to be summoned again, they are to be summoned and come in the manner described above.
