When the soul has departed from the body, the bells are to be struck three times, with short intervals between the strokes. The cantor is to begin the responsory *Come to his aid, saints of God*. When this has been completed with its verse and repetition, the priest is to add, *Go forth, Christian soul*. After this has been said, they are to begin the Commendation of the Soul. When the first collect, *To you, Lord, we commend*, has been said, with the priest and community continuing the remainder [Col. 0510C], the body is to be carried to be washed by members of the order to which the deceased belonged: a priest by priests, a deacon by deacons, and similarly in the other orders; a lay brother by lay brothers. A boy, however, is not to be washed by boys but by lay brothers.

The following are not to wash the body of the deceased: the weekly priest and the other ministers who serve at the altar and handle the sacred vessels; the weekly kitchen servants, cellarers, and refectory servants. While the body is being washed, the chamberlain is to be present, possessing suitable clothing, thread and needles for sewing, and the other things belonging to his office and necessary for his work. During the washing, the body is to be girded with the woolen garment in which he had previously been dressed, around the private parts of his body [Col. 0510D].

When washed, he is to be clothed in a new or newly washed woolen garment and a cowl. A headcloth made of woolen cloth, in the form of a hood, is to be placed on his head; the hood of the cowl is to be drawn over it and attached with thread in three places. He is to be shod with leggings made of the aforesaid cloth, reaching to the knees, and with night shoes. His hands are to be covered by the cowl. The cowl is to be sewn on both sides, and likewise around the legs; the night shoes are to be connected to each other with thread. Thus prepared, the body is to be placed on the bier and covered with a pall.

When this has been completed, and the things that had begun to be said in the community have also been completed, the prior is to strike the board once. When this has been heard [Col. 0511A], the bowed brothers are to say *Our Father*. The priest is to sprinkle blessed water around the body and cense it. Then he is to say *And lead us not*, *From the gate of hell*, and afterward the collect.

When these things have been done, the bells are to be struck, and the cantor is to begin the responsory *Come to his aid, saints of God*. Preceded by those carrying the vessel with water, the cross, the candlesticks, and the thurible, followed by the boys and the rest of the community, and with those who washed and carry the body at the rear, they are to come into the church. Once the body has been placed in the customary location, the bells are to cease. The cross is to be fixed at its head, and two candlesticks placed, one at the head and the other at the feet, with candles burning upon them; these are to continue burning there until the body is carried to burial.

When the singing is finished, the bowed brothers are to say *Our Father*; the priest is to say *And lead us not*, *From the gate of hell* [Col. 0511B], and the collect, as stated above. After these things have been done, if the sound of the refectory board had brought the brothers, they are to wash their hands, return to the refectory, and finish what had remained unfinished. Certain brothers, as many and of such persons as have been ordered, are to remain with the body and sing psalms there meanwhile. For the body must never be without psalmody, except when some common office is being celebrated in choir.

During the day the community must always be around the body, except when they are singing the hours or Masses, or making a procession around the cloister or outside the cloister, if that happens, or when they are in chapter, the refectory, or the dormitory at midday. At those times only, certain brothers are to be appointed to remain there [Col. 0511C] and sing the Psalter in order, perform the Commendation of the Soul, and say Vespers, Vigils with Lauds, *Verba mea*, and the same offices frequently.

At night, after Compline, the right choir is to keep the first vigil and the left choir the second, each performing the services mentioned above insofar as the number of nights permits. Care is to be taken that both priors are not assigned to one vigil. Near the end of the first vigil, the prior is to go out carrying a hidden light, proceed to the dormitory, and awaken the brothers who are to keep the second vigil.

After the morning Lauds, when the things required by the order have been said in choir, the boys with their masters are to spend whatever night remains singing. Those sick men who habitually remain in the infirmary and appear able to do so are also to attend [Col. 0511D]. The other brothers are to rest in their beds until morning. Then, rising, they are to put on their shoes, wash, comb their hair, say their prayers, and join the body.

After they have joined it, the boys are to proceed to put on their shoes, wash, comb their hair, and say their customary prayers; afterward they too are to come and join the others. This is to be done if it is a day on which, after morning Lauds, the brothers are permitted to return to their beds. In winter, when intervals are observed, if some of the night remains after the litany, the other brothers mentioned above may rest in their beds until daybreak; but they are to rest dressed and shod.

The boys, as stated above, are to keep their vigil around the body with their masters and the sick. [Col. 0512A] At that hour, however, all are to put on their shoes, wash, comb their hair, and say the customary prayers required by the order of that time. They are to sing the psalms seated, except at the *Magnificat* and the *Benedictus*; then they must stand. At the *Our Father* and the collects said by the priest, they are to bow upon their knees.

If a brother dies before the nocturnal vigils, and so much of the night has already passed that it is not convenient to keep two vigils, once the body has been placed in the church all the brothers are to remain there awake and singing psalms; the boys, with their masters, are to return to the dormitory to sleep.

As long as the body remains above ground, no one is to speak in the cloister. Nevertheless, if it is a day on which the board is struck, it is to be struck in chapter, and *Benedicite* (“Bless [us]”) is to be said as on other days. If, however, the brother is to be buried after chapter that day [Col. 0512B], no one may leave the monastery cloister before the burial unless the place is so near that he can return in time to bury the brother.

All who are able are to celebrate Mass for him on that day. The morning Mass is to be celebrated festively for him, even if it is a day of a principal feast. At that Mass, whenever the deacon incenses the altar, he must also approach the body with the thurible and incense it.

After a sermon has been given in chapter, the abbot, or the person presiding over the order, is to absolve him. Then he is to order thirty Masses to be celebrated for him over thirty days—that is, one Mass each day, in addition to those that are to be celebrated for the community—so that no day passes on which a Mass is not celebrated for him, except Good Friday or [Col. 0512C] Holy Saturday. Whoever begins is not to begin on the day on which he is buried, but on the following day. After each person has celebrated the Masses assigned to him, he is to report this in chapter that same day, so that the abbot or prior may assign the same duty there to the next person who is to follow. On that day the boys are not to hold their own chapter.

At whatever hour throughout the day, after the sound that the prior customarily makes in the morning to awaken the brothers, a brother dies, his burial is to be postponed until after chapter on the following day, unless a reasonable cause exists that recommends burying him either after the principal Mass or after None, especially if he happens to die before the hour that is said before chapter in summer or winter. When this occurs, in addition to the service that the brothers customarily perform for a dead brother [Col. 0512D], each brother is to be assigned an entire Psalter, together with the complete psalmody for the dead, on his behalf.

If he dies before the nocturnal vigils, he is likewise to be buried on the following day after chapter. If he departs this world during the vigils themselves, or afterward but before the aforesaid sound, he is to be committed to burial after the principal Mass. If that day is a feast of twelve or three lessons, on which the brothers are not to speak in the cloister, the morning Mass for him is to be celebrated after chapter in festive fashion, as stated above.

Then, after Terce has been said and the principal Mass celebrated, they are to proceed to bury the brother. Whether they leave chapter or choir, they are to approach the body singing *Verba mea*. Meanwhile one of the larger bells is to be struck three times, so that any who may be absent may gather without delay at the sound.

[Col. 0513A]

The sacristan is to distribute candles to the abbot, the prior, and the priest who is to perform the service, and tapers to the other brothers; the master is to distribute them to the boys. The priest is to be dressed in an alb, stole, and maniple, and two of those who previously washed the dead man are to wear albs. The albs are to be specially assigned for this service.

296. Those who carry the vessel of blessed water, the cross, the candlesticks, and the thurible are to stand on either side at the head of the deceased; the rest of the community are to stand to the right and left according to their order [Col. 0513B]. When the priest arrives, he is first to sprinkle the body with blessed water. Then, approaching the head of the deceased, he is to stand so that the bearers mentioned above are to his right and left.

Two cantors are to approach and, standing between the altar located there and the body, say “Lord, have mercy; Christ, have mercy; Lord, have mercy.” The community is to repeat the first two and say the final “Lord, have mercy” with them. Then, while all bow humbly, the priest is to say the collect:

“Let us pray. Do not enter into judgment.”

After this has been said, the aforesaid cantors are to begin, and the responsory with the verse *Who raised Lazarus* is to be sung. While it is being sung, the priest is to incense the altar there and the body. This is to be done a second and a third time, except that other collects and other responsories are to be said, as contained in the books in which the performance of this office [Col. 0513C] is prescribed.

When the verses of the third responsory have been finished, the responsory is to be repeated from the beginning, as the cantor directs. When it has been sung through, the priest is to ask that prayers be offered for him, saying:

“Our Father. And lead us not. Do not enter into judgment. From the gate of hell. The Lord be with you. Let us pray. Incline, Lord, your ear,” and the rest.

When these things have been completed, with the cantor beginning the antiphon *Into paradise*, they are to go out singing the psalm *When Israel went out*. The aforesaid bearers of the water, cross, candlesticks, and thurible are to lead. The priest and the cantor are to follow; the cantor’s particular responsibility is to take every precaution so that no negligence occurs in this service. After them the boys with their masters are to proceed, then the other brothers [Col. 0513D], with the priors at the rear and the younger brothers preceding them, according to the order of their conversion.

After everyone else, those carrying the body are to come. If conveniently possible, these are to be the men who washed it, with the assistance, if necessary, of other brothers whom the abbot or prior has ordered to help. When they begin to go out, the bells are to be struck until the body has been placed in the grave.

When they have reached the burial place, they are to stand in orderly fashion on either side, as they customarily stand in choir. The priest is to stand between the two choirs, not far from the grave. To his right and left are to stand those carrying the water and cross and the other things mentioned above. After the collect *With the affection of devout remembrance* has been said, the priest is to approach and sprinkle the grave with blessed water [Col. 0514A]. Having placed incense on the thurible, he is to give it to one of those who came down there dressed in albs, and the grave is to be incensed.

Then, after the collect *We beseech your mercy* has been said, two of the brothers who are outside are to spread the pall above. Two others, taking the body from the bier, are to hand it to those who have gone down into the tomb. They are carefully to arrange it in the grave, place the written absolution, read by the brothers, upon its breast, and cover it. Then they are immediately to come out and return to the monastery, remove their albs, put on their own clothing, and return to the community. Once the body has been placed in the grave, the candles are immediately to be extinguished and the bells to cease.

When the remaining things have been completed, as they are found in the book in which this office is prescribed, they are to return singing [Col. 0514B] the seven penitential psalms. When the priest reaches the monastery, preceding the boys, he is to turn aside into the vestry, remove the alb and maniple, put on his own clothing, return to the choir, and, prostrated with the other prostrate men, say what remains of the psalms.

When these have been said, they are to add:

“Grant them eternal rest, Lord. Our Father. And lead us not. From the gate of hell. The Lord be with you.”

Then the collect:

“May it satisfy you, Lord our God.”

After this they are to return to the cloister. When the boy has said *Benedicite*, they may speak in the cloister if it is a suitable day and hour. In the community they are to perform seven full offices for him; for thirty days they are to say *Verba mea* (“My words”), and at all the hours *Voce mea* (“My voice”), on his behalf. Individually, each person is to perform for his soul as much as the abbot has commanded. For thirty days, or more if the abbot orders it, the almoner is also to receive one loaf with drink and the regular foods.

## CHAPTER XXIV. On those who die outside the monastery

If a brother dies outside the monastery, and no brothers are with him to wash him and perform the other things described above, he is to be brought to the monastery in a bier, which is to be sent ahead for him, and is to enter through the court gates covered with a pall. With the assistance of the brother entrusted with care of the sick, he is to be placed in the infirmary. Once this has been done, the servant is to come, as usual, to the door of the cloister and strike the board; the community is to arrive, and the other rites are to be performed as though he had died in that same infirmary [Col. 0514D], except that *Go forth, Christian soul* is not said.

But if one or more brothers were with him, and the things required in such a case have been done, the community is to go out to meet him through the monastery’s principal gates, singing the following psalms: *Have mercy on me, O God*, a second time; *O God, in your name*; *Have mercy on me, O God*; *Have mercy on me*; *To the Lord, when I was in distress*; and those that follow, until they reach the body.

When they arrive, they are to make a station, facing one another. The priest, dressed in an alb and stole, is to approach, sprinkle the body with blessed water, and incense it. Then he is to exhort them to pray for him, saying:

“Our Father. And lead us not. Do not enter into judgment. Grant eternal rest. [Col. 0515A] From the gate of hell. The Lord be with you. Let us pray.”

The collect *Receive, Lord, the soul of your servant* is to follow, and another:

“Receive, Lord, your servant.”

From there they are to return, with the cantor beginning the responsory *Come to his aid, saints of God*. As they enter the church, all the bells are to be struck, and the body is to be placed where the other brothers are customarily placed. The other rites are to be performed as they would be if he had died in the infirmary and had been brought from that house to the church.

At whatever hour, from the time when the boys begin to read in the morning until the collation, a reliable messenger or letter arrives at the monastery concerning a monk of the community who has died and been buried elsewhere, or is about to be buried, if the brothers are not in chapter, the refectory, or the dormitory at midday, and if they are not engaged, inside or outside the monastery [Col. 0515B], in some service that it would not be convenient to abandon and leave unfinished, the prior is immediately to strike the board.

When the brothers are seated in chapter, he is to announce the brother’s death and add:

“Let us go and do for him what is just and what the custom of our order requires.”

They are to rise and come to the choir singing *Verba mea* while the bells sound. [Col. 0516A] After completing the psalms they had begun, with the collect, they are to say Vespers of the Dead and the office with nine lessons and Lauds, with two lights burning before the altar. The morning Mass is to be said for him festively, unless it is Sunday or a great solemnity. If that is the case, it is to be postponed to another day. After this, he is to be absolved at the first chapter.

If the succession of thirty Masses is not performed in the place where he died, it is to be assigned for him, and the other things customarily done for a brother of the community who dies within the community are to be performed.

### For the cellarer

“Our Father. And lead us not. Save your servant. Send him, Lord, help from the holy place. The Lord be with you. [Col. 0516B] Let us pray.

“Almighty and everlasting God, have mercy on your servant N., and direct him according to your mercy on the way of eternal salvation, so that, by your gift, he may desire what pleases you and accomplish it with all his strength. Through our Lord Jesus Christ.”

End of the statutes of Lord Lanfranc.

[Col. 0515]

# BOOK OF THE LETTERS OF THE BLESSED LANFRANC, ARCHBISHOP OF CANTERBURY

[Note: [Col. 0551B]

330–331. It is the established opinion of all, both ancient and modern, that Blessed Lanfranc wrote letters. Among the earlier authorities, William of Malmesbury, a monk, will serve as representative of them all. In Book I of his *Deeds of the Bishops of the English*, folio 121, section 2, no. 10, of the London edition, speaking of Letter 2, addressed to Pope Alexander, he says:

“This truth of such a discourse was confirmed by a letter sent to England at the beginning of his pontificate, which is found among Lanfranc’s letters.”

Likewise, folio 122, section 2, no. 30:

“Lanfranc himself left behind a few memorials of his genius: decretal letters, and especially the one against Berengar.”

The modern authors who discuss the letters of that archbishop are indicated in the annotations to the *Life*, page 41, letter e.]

298–299. FIRST LETTER. TO ALEXANDER II, ROMAN PONTIFF.

[Note: [Col. 0551B]

## On Letter I

[Col. 0551C] To Pope Alexander. William of Poitiers, in the *Deeds of William the Duke and King of the English*, among the writers of the *History of the Normans* edited by André Duchesne, page 197, greatly praises the holy pontiff Alexander, the second of that name, in the following terms:

“That bishop of Lucca, although he in no way sought a higher rank, was placed, by the violent agreement of very many whose authority at that time prevailed among the Romans, with the assent of a great council, in that primacy in which he would be the head and teacher of the bishops of the whole world. This election he adorned with holiness and learning. Through these qualities he shone from sunrise to sunset. The sun does not follow its course more steadfastly by nature than he directed his life along the straight path of truth: correcting whatever injustice he could find throughout the world, and yielding to no one.”

## On the community of Bec

He had long before enrolled himself in this community and had led the monastic life in it for many years. He had “devoted every effort,” to use the words of his biographer Milo, “to the peace and silence of his heart, cultivating the newly broken ground of the sacred word through constant reading and watering it with the sweet compunction of tears that he often obtained.”

Bec, or the monastery of Bec [Col. 0552B], situated in Normandy, took its name from the little river flowing between it. Gilbert Crispin, in the *Life of Blessed Herluin*, founder of that same monastery, and the *Chronicle of Bec*, page 1, says so. “But more truly,” says Papirius Masson in his description of the rivers of Gaul, in the section on the Loire, “Bec is said, in the language of the ancient Gauls or Danes, to mean the course of a waterway entering another river”; for two small rivers are found in this place, one of which flows into the other.

The following is a brief account of the foundation of this celebrated monastery:

“Let it be known to all worshipers of the Christian religion that I, Abbot Herluin, son of Ansgot, with my brothers Odo and Roger standing by and giving approval, at the command of Count Gilbert, and with Albert and Ranulf consenting, and with Count Robert and Archbishop Robert present, gave to Saint Mary a third part of the land of Burneville, and what belongs to it, and Taville, and Surcey, and what belongs to them, and the land of Sarnay, and what belongs to it, which my father Ansgot possessed during his lifetime; and also my mother’s dowry, given to me in full at my father’s command, before the witnesses Fulbert the priest, Vitalis, Rainald, and many others.”

Everything concerning the affairs of the monastery of Bec will be explained by the *Chronicle* appended to the works of Blessed Lanfranc. It has seemed appropriate merely to add certain immunities granted and confirmed by William and Hugh, archbishops of Rouen, and also by Pope Celestine III.

[Col. 0552D] 332. Charter of exemption for the monastery and parish of Bec, granted by Lord Anselm, archbishop of Rouen.

It is the custom of prudent men, and especially of those who make rational arrangements concerning the condition of the holy Church, to ensure by the authority of an inscription that what has been established should not at some time fall from its proper firmness through ignorance or forgetfulness. It is, moreover, the duty of episcopal care diligently to ensure that the monasteries [Col. 0553A] of God’s servants remain firmly established in peace and tranquility, lest minds devoted to divine services be hindered from their purpose by any circumstance.

Therefore, in accordance with this judgment of reason, I too, William, by the grace of God archbishop of Rouen, have decided to commit to writing—namely, in the time of Robert, count and son of William, king of the English—that, out of reverence for that place and for the most religious life of its brothers, and also for the salvation of my soul and those of my predecessors and successors, I grant to the Church of Bec and to Lord Anselm, its abbot, that the Church itself, together with the parish of that place and its resident parishioners, shall perpetually be free from every episcopal exaction, except those matters that cannot be administered without episcopal office: ordaining monks or clerics, reconciling churches, imposing public penance and reconciling such penitents; or determining that hidden penance which cannot be imposed without the bishop’s counsel; also conferring chrism and oil. To sum up everything briefly: [the bishop shall] exercise, as is fitting, every pastoral care over the monastery and abbot, without receiving money.

But if a case should arise in that parish which must be settled by an ordeal of iron, then, at the abbot’s discretion, the case shall either be concluded at the mother church and the ordeal undergone, or the archbishop shall send the iron for the ordeal to that place through his ministers, and the ordeal shall there be undergone in the presence of the archbishop’s ministers. If any monetary payment ensues, wherever the ordeal is undergone, it shall belong to the abbot.

In the other parishes [Col. 0553C] belonging to the same abbey and lying within our diocese, we have granted him only this: that he may keep his lay dependents in peace, but only those who possess neither land nor houses in any way. If, however, any of those whom we have granted to be free should act against Christianity, and the abbot should prove slow to correct him, the archbishop shall admonish him to correct the offender; and if afterward the abbot should refuse to correct him, the archbishop shall make the correction.

For what we have granted, therefore, the abbot shall render such honor and service to our metropolitan church that, if he is invited by the archbishop and has no legitimate excuse, he shall come to the feast of the dedication of that church, with the archbishop bearing his expenses, so that, while the archbishop celebrates Mass, he may hold the choir; or, if the archbishop should refuse or be unable to celebrate Mass for any reason, that same abbot shall celebrate the festal Mass in his place.

We have done these things after consultation with our clergy. But the abbot, after consulting his monks, withdrew and renounced certain complaints and accusations which he had made against some of the aforesaid churches, and granted that the archbishop should possess all episcopal customary rights both in those churches which the Church of Bec then possessed within our diocese outside the parish of Bec and, in addition, in all those which it was thereafter to acquire within our diocese.

[Col. 0554A] This same privilege, in the same form and in almost the same words, was confirmed in the year 1141 by Hugh, archbishop of Rouen and William’s successor.

Confirmation of the same title by Pope Alexander III.

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons Roger, abbot, and the brothers of the monastery of Bec, greeting and apostolic blessing.

From a rescript of certain letters of William of blessed memory, formerly archbishop of Rouen, it has become known to us, etc. See the text under Alexander III in the volumes of the Patrologia that are soon to be published.

### 333. The privilege of Pope Celestine III

COELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons Walter, abbot, and the community of Bec, greeting and apostolic blessing.

The most holy Roman Church, etc. See the text under Celestine III.

### 334. “You have become the cause of calamities”

The biographer of Saint Lanfranc reports how he strove with all his heart and all his strength, and with the greatest diligence he could muster, to prevent the episcopal burden from being imposed upon his shoulders. The prelates urged him in vain, the leading men of Normandy earnestly demanded it, the queen entreated him—unless Blessed Herluin had ordered it, since everything depended upon his will—or unless the king had commanded it, or the supreme head of the Church, Alexander, had prescribed it.

But when he had yielded to their wishes and had learned by experience how arduous and calamitous the episcopal office was, he implored Alexander and pressed him to release him from this office. For, as a true examiner of himself and a diligent disciple of the Master Saint Benedict in humility, he knew how burdensome it was “to undertake the difficult and arduous task of governing souls” (as the same master teaches in chapter 2 of the Rule) “and of serving the dispositions of many.” He knew that “the government of souls is an art of arts,” as Gregory the Great testifies, *Pastoral Care*, book I, chapter 1. He knew that the burden of priests is all the heavier—these are the words of Pope Gelasius I to the Emperor Anastasius—because they will render an account before the divine tribunal even for the kings themselves. He knew this because he knew himself intimately.

But, you will say: “Whoever desires the episcopate desires a good work” (1 Tim. 3:1). He desires a good work, I answer, “if anyone seeks it for this reason,” says Saint Chrysostom on the same chapter, “not through the arrogance of rank or domination, but through the care of governance and the exercise of charity; I do not condemn him, for he desires a good work.” Provided that he is first irreproachable.

“This means,” says Theophylact on these words, “that he must be conspicuous in every virtue, so that neither others may reproach him nor he reproach himself. For the one who presides over others ought to be like a star, illuminating and directing all who look upon him.”

Enough on this subject.

### By William, prince of the Normans

William, commonly called the Bastard, because he was born of a concubine whom his father Robert afterward took lawfully as his wife. He was called the Conqueror because he acquired the kingdom of England by force of arms. William of Malmesbury, book III of *The Deeds of the English Kings*, under William I, and others in various places.

[Col. 0555A] “When I presided over the monastery of Caen,” etc.

Experience had taught the great Lanfranc that he was eminent in wisdom, illustrious in the splendor of his life, in his mastery of the sciences, and in his knowledge of worldly affairs. For this reason William, duke of the Normans, had appointed him his chief counselor in administering the affairs of the whole country, as Milo Crispin relates.

Indeed, neither the duke of the Normans nor the king of the English raised men to ecclesiastical dignities unless they were distinguished by religion, piety, learning, and prudence, as William of Poitiers, archdeacon of Lisieux, asserts, pp. 195 and 208. Speaking of Lanfranc’s election as archbishop of Canterbury, he says:

“In the metropolitan see [Canterbury], William was seeking a man holy in life, distinguished in reputation, powerful in the eloquence of the divine word, who would know how to provide a suitable example to the suffragan bishops, preside over the Lord’s sheepfold, and desire to benefit all through vigilant zeal. He was also already considering the ordering of the churches,” etc.

Matthew Paris, under the year 1067.

The reason for constructing the monastery of Saint Stephen is given in the *Deeds of Blessed Lanfranc*, chapter 3, p. 5; William of Malmesbury, book III of the *Deeds of the Kings*, p. 6162, no. 10; Orderic Vitalis, book III of his *History*, p. 459; William of Jumièges, book VII of the *History of the Normans*, chapters 21 and 26. But here alone William of Poitiers, an eyewitness, is pleasing to quote, in *The Deeds of William*, p. 211:

“The basilica at Caen, admirable in design and appearance, was built from its foundations at his expense in honor of Saint Stephen the Protomartyr. He then brought to it various gifts of the most precious materials and workmanship, gifts capable of remaining honorable until the end of the age. To designate each one by description or name would be a lengthy task,” etc.

Further on he shows with what intention Duke William carried this out, in these words:

“Some powerful men unjustly lavish gifts upon the saints, often increasing their own praise in this world and their sins before God through those same donations: they despoil churches and enrich others with the very spoils.”

Let certain princes, prelates, commendatory abbots, and even preachers take note of this—men who, inflamed by divine piety so that they may appear before human beings, undertake the construction of new religious houses and distribute alms, while meanwhile, placing the divine praises of day and night second, they miserably abandon churches and monasteries [Col. 0555D] that are collapsing—whose very rich revenues they receive every year—destroyed and leveled to the ground.

But alas! Far worse than these are those utterly corrupt squanderers of Christ’s patrimony who consume everything in the gullets of their banquets, swallow it up, dissipate it in games, and make offerings to Venus.

It was with good reason that the most devout English king Edgar once attacked such men in that most elegant speech which he delivered to the fathers of a synod around the year 970:

“Thus, thus,” he said, “are the patrimonies of kings, the alms of the poor, and—even more grievous—the price of that precious blood squandered? Was it for this that our fathers emptied their treasures? Was it for this that the royal treasury, after many revenues had been alienated, was reduced? Was it for this that royal munificence bestowed fields and possessions upon the churches of Christ—that the prostitutes of clerics might be adorned with luxuries, extravagant banquets prepared, and dogs, birds, and such amusements purchased? The soldiers cry out, the common people murmur beneath their breath, the entertainers sing and dance—and you neglect it, you spare yourselves, you pretend not to see? Where is the sword of Levi and the zeal of Simeon?” etc.

Let such men at last return to their senses and listen to Saint Prosper, who in book II of *The Contemplative Life*, while briefly describing the deeds of the holy bishops Paulinus and Hilary of Arles, says:

“Such and so great men, who, wishing to be disciples of Christ, renounced everything they possessed, held the resources of the Church not as owners but as stewards. And because they knew that the possessions of the Church are nothing other than the vows of the faithful, the price of sins, and the patrimony of the poor, they did not claim them for their own use as private property, but distributed them to the poor as possessions entrusted to them.”

Enough on this subject.

### Having become king of the English

After Harold had been defeated and slain, and the whole island had been subjected to him, he was proclaimed king by everyone and at last consecrated by Aldred, archbishop of York, since Stigand, who should have performed that office, was occupying the see of Canterbury through simony; the crown was placed upon him by the legates of Pope Alexander II.

So William of Poitiers, p. 196; the monk of Malmesbury, *Deeds of the English*, pp. 56–57; Henry of Huntingdon, under the year 1066; Roger of Howden, in the first part, under William the Elder; William of Jumièges, book VII of the *History*, chapter 34 and following; Orderic Vitalis, book III, p. 492.

The aforesaid authors disclose for what reason and by what right he undertook to acquire the kingdom of England [Col. 0556C], but especially the contemporary author Hugh, abbot of Flavigny, in his manuscript *History*:

“In the year 1065,” he says, “Edward, king of the English, died. Since he had no sons, he appointed his kinsman William, count of the Normans, king after him. But Harold invaded the kingdom contrary to the oath which he had sworn to William. In that same year King William crossed the sea, and when battle was joined on the eleventh day before the Ides of October, Harold fell. On Christmas Day William was raised up and crowned king at London.”

Robert, the monk of Mont-Saint-Michel, adds other reasons in his manuscript *Chronicle*, under the year 1063:

“First, because Godwin and his sons dishonored and killed Alfred, his kinsman—that is, the duke William’s kinsman; second, because Godwin and his sons, by their schemes, had exiled Robert the bishop, Odo their kinsman, and all the French from England,” etc.

Certainly Eadmer, *History of Recent Events*, book I, p. 5, edition of London, 1623, declares that the victory should be attributed not to William’s strength or skill but solely to God.

### Hermenfred, bishop of Sion

Whether called Armenfred or Hermenfred, he served splendidly in various embassies by order of Pope Alexander II.

Florence of Worcester, a contemporary writer, under the year 1062:

“It happened at that time that, among the legates of the Apostolic See who attended his [Wulfstan’s] election, there was Armenfred, bishop of Sion, and another who had been sent by Lord Pope Alexander to King Edward of England on ecclesiastical business and, by royal command, remained at Worcester for nearly the whole of Lent,” etc.

Roger of Howden, under the year 1070:

“The aforesaid bishop of Sion held a synod in which Angelric was degraded uncanonically,” etc.

Orderic, book IV, p. 516, supports this.

Now “Sion—which Julius Caesar mentions in *The Gallic War*, book III, chapter 1—is the principal town of the Seduni, in which they establish a bishop who rules the region as both prince and ecclesiastical prelate, over free men rather than slaves; for he does nothing publicly without the consent of all the citizens.” Thus Henry Glareanus comments on the same chapter of Caesar.

Raymond Marlianus says in his *Description of the Ancient Places of Gaul*:

“The people called Sedusii or Seduni are counted among the Helvetians and partly among the Celts, or at least are their neighbors, and the river Rhône waters them. It is an episcopal city, retaining in Latin the name Tarentasia.”

But Marlianus is mistaken in these last words, for Tarentasia is an archbishopric, also called the Monastery, in the vernacular Moustier, beneath which lies the bishopric of Sion. Sion is now called Sion in the French or Savoyard language.

### Hubert, cardinal of the Holy Roman Church

Saint Lanfranc calls him a subdeacon in letter 9. He subscribed the decree establishing the primacy of the Church of Canterbury over that of York. See the *Life of Blessed Lanfranc*, chapter 11, p. 13, and William of Malmesbury, *On the Bishops of England*, book I.

The same Hubert served as Gregory VII’s legate in lesser Britain; see book V, letter 22, of Gregory’s letters. He was also sent to William, king of England, who was preventing bishops from going to Rome; the supreme pontiff wished him to admonish the king through Hubert. See book VII, letter 1. That the king submitted to the pontiff is confirmed by letter 25 of the same book, addressed to the king.

### Bishops, abbots, etc.

Concerning this assembly, consult the aforesaid *Life* at the cited place, p. 12.

### By authority of the Apostolic See

As Eadmer, Lanfranc’s contemporary, reports in *History of Recent Events*, book I, p. 6:

“In the fifth year of William’s reign, Lanfranc, abbot of the monastery of Caen, an energetic man endowed with outstanding knowledge of divine and human matters, came to England at the command of Lord Pope Alexander and the aforesaid king; and shortly afterward he undertook the governance of the archbishopric of Canterbury.”

### And so great a calamity of the holy Church

Thus, although he was steadfast and unshaken in other matters, he was oppressed by the crimes committed against God and the Church, so that there was absolutely nothing that could alleviate his grief or temper his zeal for God.

The continuator of Saint Bede vividly describes the abominable crimes in which the English of those times were entangled, book II, chapter 12:

“Nevertheless, the studies of letters and religion gradually became obsolete during the years before the arrival of the Normans. The clerics, content with makeshift learning, could scarcely stammer out the words of the sacraments; anyone who knew grammar was a source of amazement and wonder to the others. The monks [Col. 0558A] mocked the rule with elegant clothing and an indiscriminate variety of foods. The nobles, devoted to gluttony and lust, did not attend church in the customary manner, but in their bedchambers and amid the embraces of their wives they merely tasted with their ears the offices of matins and the Masses hurriedly celebrated by a priest. The common people, placed between these groups, were prey for the more powerful, who amassed heaps of treasure either by exhausting their possessions or by selling even their bodies into distant lands. The following was contrary to nature: many men, after impregnating their maidservants and satisfying their lust, sold them either to a public brothel or into foreign service,” etc.

Yet in the dense darkness and thick gloom of so foul a night, our archbishop shone like a most brilliant star, by which the whole English kingdom might be illuminated and the darkness of ignorance and vice dispersed.

### “And the monastic life, which I love above all”

It is not surprising that the great Lanfranc was so greatly delighted by the monastic life, which the foremost teachers of the Catholic Church cultivated so religiously and to which they devoted themselves entirely: Basil the Great, Gregory the Theologian, Jerome, Augustine, Gregory the Great, Augustine the apostle of England; and, after them, the Venerable Bede, Rabanus Maurus, Anselm, Bernard, and nearly countless others.

Hence Chrysostom, *Homily 70 on Matthew 22*:

“The retreats of the monks should not be considered inferior to heaven; angels, indeed even the Lord of angels himself, frequently turn aside to visit them,” etc.

And in *Homily 59 to the People of Antioch*:

“Monks are like torches, sitting in the harbor for those coming from the open sea, drawing all toward their own tranquility and not allowing those who look to them to suffer shipwreck; looking toward them in the darkness, they do not permit people to remain wandering.”

### “To say nothing of many things”

Perhaps this is what Milo Crispin reports in the *Life*, chapter 11, p. 11: that Alexander himself, namely Saint Lanfranc’s Alexander, had been his auditor when Lanfranc still held the schools at Bec.

After recounting that Alexander had risen in honor of Lanfranc while Lanfranc was residing at Rome, he gives the reason for such honor in these words:

“First, because of his great religion and eminent learning; and also because, when he was in Normandy, he received the ministers of the Church who came to him and diligently instructed certain kinsmen of the pope. It is also said that the pope declared: ‘I did not rise to him because he is an archbishop, but because I was a student at his school at Bec and sat with the other auditors at his feet.’”

But let us hear the authoritative witness Eadmer, *History*, book I, p. 6:

“On the appointed day,” he says, “Father Lanfranc was presented to Alexander, pontiff of the Apostolic See. This may perhaps seem strange to those familiar with Roman custom: the pope himself rose as he entered and gently urged him to set his foot inside. Then, continuing, he said: ‘We have shown honor not to your archiepiscopate, but to the master to whom we owe the honor due to him, by whose teaching we have been imbued with what we know. Hence, for your part, it is fitting that, out of reverence for Blessed Peter, you should carry out what pertains to you.’”

This is Eadmer’s account, to which William of Malmesbury, *Deeds of the English*, book III, p. 66, no. 20; Thomas Walsingham, *Ypodigma Neustriae*, under the year 1070; and others do not object.

### “And I would come to you with you in the palace,” etc.

Everyone gladly listened to Lanfranc, who was at once most wise and most learned. Prelates, abbots, princes, and the powerful of this world tried by words and letters to attract him to themselves so that they might enjoy his company at every opportunity.

His biographer Milo asserts this above, chapter 5, p. 6, and chapter 6, p. 7. Alexander himself also makes the point wonderfully clear in the aforementioned letter to William the Conqueror. After admonishing him to devote all his efforts to the duties of Christian piety and to defend the churches [Col. 0559B] and their persons, he speaks thus of the blessed archbishop of Canterbury:

“To accomplish these things and to attain growth in the other virtues, we exhort Your Glory to heed the admonitions and counsels of our brother Lanfranc, archbishop of Canterbury. We regret that this most beloved member and one of the foremost sons of the Roman Church is not continually at our side. Yet from the fruit which he bestows upon the Church in your kingdom, we draw consolation for his absence.”

### “After his death, neither peace nor anything good”

The holy man foretells the evils which, after the death of William the Conqueror and during the reign of his son Rufus, began again to sprout—or, rather, began to spread more swiftly—throughout England and Normandy.

The librarian of Malmesbury touches upon these matters graphically, in his customary manner:

“Under this William [the Second], the sacred dignities of the churches were put up for sale after their pastors had died. For as soon as the death of any bishop or abbot was heard, a royal clerk was immediately admitted, who recorded in writing everything that was found and thereafter brought all the revenues into the royal treasury. Meanwhile, someone suitable to be substituted in the deceased man’s place was sought, not by testing his character but his money. At last the dignity was granted, so to speak, stripped bare, though purchased at a great price.

“These things seemed all the more disgraceful because in the time of his father, after the death of a bishop or abbot, all the revenues were carefully preserved so that they could be handed over intact to the pastor who was to be appointed, and men were chosen who were praiseworthy for their religious merit.

“No one was rich unless he was a moneychanger; no cleric unless he was a litigant; no priest unless—if I may use a scarcely Latin word—a rent-holder. A little man of any condition, guilty of any crime, was immediately heard if he appealed to the king’s profit; the noose was loosened from the very throats of robbers if they promised royal advantage.

“Then came flowing hair, luxury of clothing, and the use of shoes fitted with pointed spikes. To compete with women in softness of body, to break one’s stride, and to walk with relaxed gestures and one side bare was regarded as the mark of young men. Nerve-less and softened, they remained unwilling to be what they had been born to be—conquerors of others’ chastity and prodigal of their own,” etc.

Thus far Malmesbury, *Deeds of the English*, book IV, chapter 1; Eadmer, *History*, book I, p. 14, and book IV, p. 77; the Continuator of the Venerable Bede, book III, chapter 29; and Orderic Vitalis, book VIII, pp. 682–683.

After Blessed Lanfranc had been taken from the living, Lord Anselm, having attempted in vain to remedy such calamities, voluntarily departed from England, yielding to the wickedness of the times, as Robert of Mont-Saint-Michel reports in his manuscript *Chronicle*, under the year 1098:

“Anselm, however, the archbishop, departed from England because the wicked king [William] allowed nothing right to be done in his kingdom,” etc.

*Chronicle of Bec*, at the end of the works of Saint Lanfranc, under the year 1098.

[Col. 0515C]

He asks that the episcopal burden, which he had undertaken chiefly because of the command of that same man, be ordered to be removed from his shoulders; and he excuses himself for not having come to Rome at the appointed time.

To the supreme pastor of the holy Church, Pope Alexander, Lanfranc, an unworthy bishop, offers canonical obedience.

“I do not know to whom I could more appropriately explain my misfortunes than to you, Father,” etc.

We have already given this at the end of the letters of Alexander II, *Patrologia*, vol. CXLVI.

### 300. LETTER II. TO THE SAME

[Note: [Col. 0560A]]

### On Letter II

Herman, bishop of Winchester, was of Flemish origin and served the most holy King Edward as his chaplain; he was appointed in place of Brithwold.

At length, moved by personal ambition, he asked Edward to grant him the monastery of Méldun so that he might establish his see there. But when he despaired of obtaining this, he resigned the episcopate and devoted himself to the monastic life.

Roger, *Annals*, first part, under the year 1055; Harpsfeld, century XI; and William of Malmesbury, *Deeds of the Bishops*, book I, portray Herman as follows:

“He had scarcely been fully initiated when he was expelled; overwhelmed by shame, he left England indignantly. Not long afterward, prompted at once by illness and by the fact that his secular affairs had prospered little, he grew angry with Fortune and renounced the world, becoming a monk at Saint-Bertin. But, as usually happens in such cases, when that sudden impulse toward religion had cooled, he began day by day to contemplate a return to England.

“A second rumor had reached his ears: Bishop Ælfwold of Sherborne had died. Moreover, Godwin, whom he greatly feared, had departed, and his son had come over to the king’s will, both in this matter and in others. Herman therefore received the entire bishopric of Sherborne, together with three districts, from King Edward; and, outliving the years of the giver, he remained in office into the time of William. Under William he transferred his seat from Sherborne to Salisbury,” etc.

The mind is certainly perplexed, and I do not know where to place my foot. Should we give credence to Lanfranc, an eyewitness who knew Herman intimately and thoroughly—as is clear from that letter—or instead to Malmesbury and certain other writers, to whose ears Herman’s deeds came only through popular rumor and report? Let the judgment rest with the reader.

But, to say what I think, there is truly no reason for anyone to assert that the bishop acted with the evil motives alleged. Could Herman not have withdrawn out of love for the monastic life and contempt for worldly affairs? Perhaps, oppressed by poverty and wishing to distribute alms, as is fitting for a prelate, and also wishing to lead the clergy back to the canonical form of life, he considered transferring his episcopal see to the abbey of Méldun.

Do we not read everywhere in authors—and does it not often happen in practice—that many men renowned for learning and holiness have long endured the sponges of censors and the attacks of slanderers?

Indeed, Herman, “while he flourished in manly strength,” to use the words of Blessed Lanfranc, “and in the vigor of youth, endowed with knowledge of divine and secular letters, proved a sufficiently useful person for pastoral office.”

Yet when I see nearly all earlier and later writers brought to one and the same opinion, I would not undertake the bishop’s entire defense or absolve him from every fault.

Nevertheless, if we wish to reconcile the opinions of the authors with the judgment of Blessed Lanfranc, we must assert that Herman sought the ascetic life twice. This seems plainly evident from the words of the holy archbishop himself:

“He sought the monastic life; now he is seeking to do the same thing again by every means.”

The first time was when he assumed the monastic habit in the monastery of Saint-Bertin at Saint-Omer, as Malmesbury reports above. Later, after returning to England from the monastery of Saint-Bertin, furnished with the finest instruction, piety, and virtues, and after administering the episcopate excellently for many years, he was at last worn down by illness and old age. Attracted by the sweetness of the solitary life, which he had formerly tasted, and now close to death, he greatly desired to reach the secure harbor of the regular life, so that, safe in his cell, he might fly upward to heaven—to use Saint Bernard’s words.

Nor should the example of Marbod, bishop of Rennes, be disregarded. After laying down the burden of the episcopate, he withdrew to the monastery of Saint-Albin at Angers and, clothed in the monastic habit, met death there in a holy manner. This may be learned from an ancient formula written on parchment for announcing the death of a deceased monk to the other monasteries of the same community, borrowed from the monastery of Saint-Albin.

“To all the sons of the one holy Church, the humble community of Blessed Albin, bishop of Angers, wishes full victory over the enemy and a crown from that victory.

“Apostolic authority instructs us that we should pray for one another and bear one another’s burdens, and thus fulfill the law of Christ. Therefore, servants of Christ, striving with devout concern to fulfill the law of Christ, we announce to you the death of Lord Marbod, the venerable bishop, ever worthy of honorable remembrance: eloquent of speech, eminent in religion, distinguished for uprightness of character, most learned in literary studies, whose speech was always seasoned with salt and from whose mouth every utterance flowed sweeter than honey.

“Although at that time all Gaul resounded with various pursuits, he nevertheless held a special place as the king of orators and the citadel of Gallic eloquence. On the third day before the Ides of September, weakened in body but stronger in spirit, he departed from the world, living in Christ. By his absence he left us bereaved, and he afflicted us with unbearable grief, wounded as we were by the dart of his love.

“After long exercises in liberal studies, which flourished far and wide and in which he had achieved the greatest distinction in the city of Angers, where he had become a famous and renowned teacher, he was elected by the most reverend Pope Urban at the Council of Tours and, with the Lord’s consent, ordained bishop of the holy see of the Church of Rennes.

“Girded with the sword of the Holy Spirit, he faithfully and wisely governed that dignity—or rather that burden—for twenty-eight years, although he lived among barbarians armed with a certain natural savagery. By reproving, entreating, and rebuking, he subdued the necks of the proud with the judgment of justice and reconciled disputes. At last, worn out by old age and full of days, he rested in the Lord in holy confession, as has been stated above.

“About to enter upon the way of all flesh and sensing that death was near, he laid down the pontifical burden and assumed the habit and humility of the most holy Benedict. Professing himself a monk, he gave himself to Blessed Albin; thus relieved of his burden, he followed poor Christ, himself poor.

“Previously, like Martha, he was anxious and occupied with many things; now, like another Mary, recognizing that one thing is necessary, he chose the better part, which shall not be taken away from him.

“We also commend him to your prayers,” etc.

[Col. 0562B] ### “Of venerable memory, Leo”

That is, Leo IX, a man altogether distinguished in faith and merits, who, while leading an angelic life, was frequently deemed worthy of the companionship of angels.

Leo of Ostia, book II, chapter 82 of the *Cassinese Chronicle*. He condemned the heresy of Berengar in the Councils of Vercelli and Tours; so says Guitmund, *On the Body and Blood of Christ*, book I.

Otto of Freising describes Leo’s profound humility in his *Chronicle*, book VI, chapter 33:

“He was born of a noble family of the Franks and had been sent to the see of Blessed Peter by the authority of royal excellence. While traveling through Gaul after assuming the papal purple, it happened that he came to Cluny, where Hildebrand was then, as is said, administering the obedience of the priory. Filled with zeal for God, Hildebrand approached Leo and firmly reproved him for what he had begun, saying that it was unlawful for the supreme pontiff to enter violently upon the government of the whole Church through a layman’s agency.

“But if Leo were willing to trust his counsels, Hildebrand promised to bring about both that imperial majesty should not be offended in him and that the liberty of the Church should be renewed through a canonical election. Yielding to his advice, Leo laid aside the purple and, assuming the dress of a pilgrim, set out on his journey with Hildebrand.

“When he had reached the city, Bruno was elected supreme pontiff by the clergy and people on Hildebrand’s advice, and thus, in some fashion, the Roman Church was instructed to conduct the election.”

Wibert, a contemporary author, wrote an account of Saint Leo’s deeds, which the learned Sirmond also published.

### The bishop of Lichfield, or Lichfield in England

If conjecture may be indulged, that bishop was called Peter. For during the reign of William I he transferred the see from Lichfield to Chester.

Or perhaps someone may say that his predecessor, to whom the great Lanfranc addressed this letter, was Leofwin. Yet concerning both men, and concerning the heinous crime which the blessed archbishop mentions here, there is complete silence among the historians.

Almost all writers make fun of Peter’s successor Robert, asserting that he was infected with the vice of avarice, squandered the resources of the churches, and exhausted their revenues.

But chronology conflicts with this. I see no agreement with reason or with the time in supposing that Blessed Lanfranc intended to write to Robert. Robert was never bishop of Lichfield, but of Chester—or rather of Coventry, since, after Peter’s death, he transferred the see from Chester to Coventry.

It is clear, moreover, that Robert was consecrated in the year 1088, whereas Pope Alexander was taken from this life in the year of Christ 1072—or, as others prefer, 1073. Therefore Saint Lanfranc is speaking in that letter either of Peter or of Leofwin.

It is further established from the foregoing that the aforesaid bishopric bore three names: first, Lichfield or Licfield; second, Chester; and finally, Coventry.

I did not presume to appoint anyone in his place. He does not dare to pronounce sentence against the bishop of Lichfield (even though he is a metropolitan), nor to appoint and consecrate another in his place; [Col. 0563B] for metropolitans, their comprovincial bishops, and primates may indeed hear, examine, and investigate the cases of bishops summoned to court by accusations and depositions; but they cannot in any way define them or settle them by a final judgment without the prior authority of the supreme pontiff. This is confirmed by a letter of Pope Julius to the Eastern bishops:

> “Just as the blessed apostle Peter was the first of all the Apostles, so this Church, consecrated in his name, is, by the Lord’s institution, first and the head of the others; and to it, as to a mother and summit, all the greater causes of the Churches and judgments concerning bishops should have recourse, and according to its judgment receive their conclusion,” etc.

Pope Eleutherius, Letter to the Provinces of Gaul, chapter 2, canon *Quamvis* 3, question 6:

> “Although it is permitted among comprovincial bishops, metropolitans, and primates to investigate accusations and charges against bishops, it is nevertheless not permitted to decide them without the authority of this holy see, as has already been established by the apostles and their successors with the agreement of many bishops; nor may others be appointed in their churches before their affairs have been justly settled here.” [Col. 0563C]

This was not unknown to the blessed Cyprian, who throughout his letters consults the supreme hierarch of the whole world about his affairs, especially in Book III, Letter 13, which is Letter 67. See it, if you please.

Concerning Bishop Herman: since, worn down by old age and prolonged illness, he already seems unequal to the burden; and [Col. 0515D] concerning the bishop of Lichfield, who abdicated his episcopate: whether he who has been substituted in his place ought to be permitted to receive consecration.

To ALEXANDER, supreme ruler of the whole Church of Christ, the unworthy archbishop of the English, LANFRANCUS: to bring a good ending to a good beginning.

“Since urgent necessity compels us to wait,” etc. The remainder may be found in the section on Alexander II cited above.

## 301. LETTER III. TO THE SAME

### Note on Letter III [Col. 0563C]

“In the presence of Your Highness,” etc. What the archbishop touches upon incidentally here is supplied at length by the Canterbury monk in Book I of the *History of Recent Affairs*:

> “He accused Thomas, together with Remigius, before the pope, alleging that neither of them had been lawfully promoted to the episcopate. He accused the first on the ground that the sacred canons exclude from promotion to sacred orders the sons of priests whom the religious profession does not ennoble; the second [p. 340], however, because, after an agreement had been made, he had bought his office from William after he had become king—namely, the office by which he had served him with manifold exertion and great expense while William was hastening toward the destruction of England. Since they had no plausible defense by which they could excuse themselves, they returned their pastoral staffs and rings, together with their episcopal office, and turned to seek mercy. Lanfranc, interposing himself on behalf of their requests, since he was a man endowed with piety and wisdom, showed by his eloquence that they were supported by knowledge of many things, very necessary to the new king in the new arrangements of the kingdom, and useful in many ways. When the supreme pontiff had heard this, he turned to him and said: ‘You see to it. You are the father of that country, and therefore let your prudence consider what is expedient. Here are the pastoral staffs which they returned; take them and distribute them as you judge will be most useful to the Christianity of that region.’ Then, having received them in the pope’s presence, he restored the aforesaid men to their offices, each to his own.” [Col. 0563D–0564A]

Eadmer is joined by William of Malmesbury, Book I *On the Bishops*, folio 121, and Harpsfield, *The Eleventh Century*, p. 271. A decree of Pope Alexander II is extant stating that an elected son of a priest should not be rejected, provided that he is distinguished by virtue.

York—or Eboracum—the city which Camden graphically describes in his *Description of Britain*, under the heading “Brigantes”:

> “It is the second city of all England,” he says, “the most beautiful city of this region—that is, Yorkshire—and is a singular defense and ornament to the entire northern part. Pleasant, spacious, fortified, adorned with both private and public buildings, filled with wealth and citizens, and distinguished by an archiepiscopal see,” etc.

William of Malmesbury, in the preface to Book III *On the Bishops*. The blessed Alcuin, quoted by the same Malmesbury in the same place, in the section on the archbishops of York, shortly after the middle, addresses Charlemagne concerning that famous York library:

> “Give me,” he says, “the more select little books of scholastic learning, such as I possessed in my homeland through the good and devoted diligence of my master, Archbishop Egbert. And, if it pleases Your Excellence, I will send back some of your boys, who may gather whatever is necessary from there and bring the flowers of Britain back to France.” [Col. 0564B–0564C]

Moreover, the blessed Gregory established the Church of York as a metropolitan church. The Venerable Bede, Book I, chapter 29, records him writing thus to the blessed Augustine, apostle of the English:

> “And because the new Church of the English has been brought, by the generosity of almighty God and through your labor, to the grace of that same Lord, we grant you the use of it only for celebrating the solemnities of Mass, so that you may ordain twelve bishops in the several places who shall be subject to your authority.” [Col. 0564D]
>
> And shortly afterward:
>
> “But we wish you to send as bishop to the city of York one whom you yourself shall judge should be ordained, provided only that, if that city and the neighboring places receive the word of God, he too may ordain twelve bishops and enjoy metropolitan honor; yet we wish him to remain subject to the disposition of your fraternity,” etc.

Read the same Bede, Book II, chapter 17, and the *Life of St Augustine*, after the *Lives of the Abbots of Bec*, p. 62.

I would strive to obtain primacy. I have not thought it worthwhile to bring forward here the dispute between Thomas, archbishop of York, and Lanfranc, archbishop of Canterbury, since so many different authors, both ancient and modern, have written about it that the material would grow almost without limit; and by forcing upon the reader what has already been repeated so often, I might seem rather to provoke the learned reader’s stomach to nausea than to strike his mind with a desire to read. In the *Life* cited immediately above, on the same page, one may read about the primacy of the Church of Canterbury over York, as well as in the *Deeds of the Blessed Lanfranc*, chapters 10 and 11, p. 11. The same controversy is also recalled by William of Malmesbury, Book III *On the Deeds of the English*, folio 65, and most fully in Book I *On the Bishops*, folio 118 and following; Orderic Vitalis, *History*, Book III, p. 548, under the year 1075; Harpsfield, *The Eleventh Century*; Caesar Baronius, *Annals*, vol. II, under A.D. 1071 and 1072; and many others. We too shall say a very few words below, chiefly from St Bede, so that we do not leave the reader’s mind entirely empty. [Col. 0565A]

The assembly of the English land. Concerning this assembly, see the *Life of the Blessed Lanfranc*, chapter 11, p. 12.

At the city of Venta. Camden, in the place cited above, under “Belgae,” says:

> “Venta of the Belgae is called, commonly, Winchester, a royal and most pleasant city distinguished by an episcopal see.”

See more there, as well as Malmesbury, Book II *On the Bishops*, in the section on the bishops of Winchester. [Col. 0565B]

The *Ecclesiastical History of the English People*. As is well known, this is found in volume III of the works of the Venerable St Bede. There, in Book I from chapter 23 to the end, and throughout the following books, the primacy of the metropolitan see of Dorobernia, or Canterbury, is discussed: a primacy granted by the blessed Gregory to St Augustine, the first archbishop of that city, and confirmed by later pontiffs of the Roman Church. The privileges of those pontiffs—that is, their letters bearing seals, as they are called, and also their decretals—promulgated by the pontiffs themselves in favor of the primacy of Canterbury and preserved down to his own times, the often-mentioned Malmesbury recorded word for word in Book III of *The Deeds of the English*, at the final chapter, and in Book I *On the Bishops*. [Col. 0565C]

### 341. Bede, Teacher of the English

He was surnamed “the Venerable,” a man of truly admirable holiness, a most religious observer of the Benedictine Rule, and easily the foremost of all the learned men of his age. But it will not be unpleasant to hear what he himself transmitted concerning himself to posterity—at the end, namely, of his *Ecclesiastical History of the English People*:

> “Bede, servant of God and priest of the monastery of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, which is at Wearmouth and Jarrow: [Col. 0565D] I was born in the territory of that same monastery, and when I was seven years old I was entrusted, for education, to the care of the reverend abbot Benedict—also called Biscop—and afterward to Ceolfrid. From that time I have spent the whole period of my life dwelling in that same monastery, devoting all my effort to the study of the Scriptures. In the midst of the observance of the regular discipline and the daily duty of singing in the Church, I have always found it a delight either to learn, to teach, or to write. In the nineteenth year of my life I received the diaconate, and in the thirtieth the priesthood, both through the ministry of the most reverend John, at the command of Abbot Ceolfrid. From the time when I received the priesthood until the fifty-ninth year of my age, I have made it my care to make brief notes, for the needs of myself and my own, from the works of the venerable Fathers on Holy Scripture, or even to add something in accordance with their sense and interpretation,” etc.

He then adds a catalogue of his works. More is reported about him by the Continuator of that history, Book I, chapters 5, 6, and 7, and at length by Malmesbury, Book I, chapter 3. Yet Malmesbury and that Continuator report precisely the same things—or rather, the very words occur in both—so that one may conjecture that one borrowed from the other what he relates.

Before that most holy teacher departed this life, what he did was described by one of his disciples in Surius, volume III, on 10 May. He reports that on Ascension Day, lying in bed with a hair shirt beneath him, with his understanding unimpaired and his face cheerful, Bede uttered this prayer or antiphon: “O King of glory, Lord of hosts,” etc.; and after it had been completed, breathed out his soul.

Concerning St Bede, see the Roman Martyrology on 27 May; Baronius in his notes on that day and in the *Annals*, volume [year 731]; Arnold Wion, *The Tree of Life*, Book III, 27 May, and Book V, chapter 111. Most fully of all, Edward Malhes, *Table of Trophies*, table 1.

Arnold Wion, in the last place cited, gives reasons why Bede should more properly be called “Venerable” than “Saint,” of which this is the chief:

> “For while he was alive,” he says, “it was not permissible to call him by another name, although he shone with holiness.”

But I, to state what I think, believe that he was distinguished by this title for the following reasons. First, because in ancient times, especially in Bede’s age, it was customary to call priests “venerable.” Second, the man’s exceptional holiness and singular piety, together with an equal mastery of learning and the sciences, caused his homilies to be read publicly in the churches while he was still alive; hence he acquired the name “Venerable.” Yet he is nowhere found adorned with such a title among contemporary writers, as Baronius carefully discusses in the *Ecclesiastical Annals* at the place cited above. [Col. 0566A–0566C]

Of Augustine, the first bishop of Dorobernia. “Concerning St Augustine,” observes the learned Hugo Menard, “the apostle of the English, I have judged that I should not omit here the notable passage of Aimoin of Fleury in the *Life of St Abbo*, chapter 4, where he testifies that the preachers sent into England by St Gregory were devoted to the Rule of St Benedict. ‘That nation,’ he says, speaking of the English, ‘came especially to love our father Benedict for two reasons. One was that St Pope Gregory, when he sent preachers of the faith to convert it, particularly urged them to observe the Rule of that beloved lord Benedict.’”

Thus Menard in his notes on the Benedictine Martyrology, at the seventh day before the Kalends of June.

It will not be out of place to examine more closely and broadly a matter of no small importance, to investigate it, and to dispel as far as possible from some minds the shadows of doubt. But since everyone is thought to claim too much in his own cause, I judged it suitable and appropriate to produce an English authority—one, that is, who has no personal interest in the matter. I mean Selden, who in his notes on Eadmer’s history proves quite successfully, if I judge correctly, that this same Augustine belonged beyond doubt to the Benedictine family.

First, from William of Malmesbury, in a manuscript codex *On the Antiquities of the Church of Glastonbury*:

> “From this point,” says William, “after Augustine’s arrival, episcopal sees were established in various places, and monasteries were built, serving God according to the Rule of the blessed Father Benedict, so that afterward no monks were found among the English who had not professed the Rule of the blessed Benedict. From that time the same Rule first began to be practiced in the monastery of Glastonbury, whereas previously it had followed the custom of the monasteries of Egypt.” [Col. 0566D–0567A]

“On this matter, if you please, consult Henry Vandenzyppius, Part III *On the Monastic Order of St Gregory*, chapter 5; he discusses it more fully in Part II of the same book, chapter 4, concerning the family of our Augustine. That it was no other than the one in which St Gregory had been consecrated is, I think, acknowledged by everyone. Gregory himself sufficiently testifies to this in Book VII, Letter 114, to Syagrius, bishop of Autun, where he calls Augustine ‘formerly the provost of my monastery.’

“But Baronius maintains that Gregory’s family was Equitian, not Benedictine. If I am not mistaken, he was the first to maintain this and dared at last to oppose the opinion of a most widely received antiquity, being led by conjectures neither contemptible nor, in truth, of great weight. See the *Annals*, volume VIII, under the year 1096, and what Vandenzyppius wrote against him in the places already mentioned.

“I admit that among the ancient compilers of our history it is nowhere, as I remember, taught in very explicit words that Augustine belonged to the Benedictine fellowship, although he is often simply called a monk. We read in Bede that Augustine, and many others with him, were monks, and most writers follow him. Likewise, in an old Saxon manuscript Chronicle, under the year 1096:

> ‘In this year Pope Gregory sent Augustine the monk into Britain, together with very many monks, to preach the word of God to the English people.’

“Nor do I find him mentioned otherwise in the ancient authorities in connection with this matter. Yet meanwhile, the term *monachus*—‘monk’—with the Greek article τό, when no indication of a particular family is added, always means, unless my memory deceives me, a Benedictine when used of those whom our ancestors mention by that name, just as among the Greeks it generally means a Basilian.

“Furthermore, the inhabitants of the monastery of St Saviour at Canterbury have always, from its very beginnings, been regarded among us as belonging to the Benedictine family. At least, nothing occurs in the ancient monuments that could support the opposite view—nothing that ever suggests or even hints that they assumed or abandoned the name of any other family.

“Especially relevant here is the statement of Boniface, Roman pontiff, in his letter to Ethelbert:

> ‘Glorious son,’ he says, ‘what your kindness requested from the apostolic see through our fellow bishop Mellitus, we willingly grant: namely, that your benevolence may lawfully establish in the monastery founded in the city of Dorobernia, which your holy teacher Augustine, of blessed memory, the disciple of Gregory, consecrated in the name of the holy Saviour, and which our dearest brother Laurence is now known to govern, a dwelling for monks living according to a rule. By apostolic authority we decree that your preachers, the monks, associate with themselves a company of monks and adorn their life with holy conduct. If any of your successors, whether kings, bishops, clergy, or laymen, should attempt to invalidate these decrees of ours, let him be subject to the designation [bond, *vinculo*] of anathema from the prince of the apostles Peter and all his successors, until he repents of what he has rashly done, with a satisfaction pleasing to the Lord, and makes true correction for this disturbance.’” [Col. 0567D–0568A]

“Therefore, either from the beginning, under Augustine as its founder, the fellowship of this monastery was Equitian or Benedictine. For Baronius does not doubt that both Augustine and Gregory were Equitian, if they were not Benedictine. If it had first been Equitian, it would plainly have been necessary for some later innovation to occur that transformed it into Benedictine. Yet not only is nothing of this kind found, but at its very beginnings Boniface confirms that the monks established there by Augustine were to associate with themselves a company of monks and adorn their life with holy conduct; and, lest anyone oppose that decree at all, the most serious threat is imposed. It is as though he had commanded all of them to preserve there perpetually both the name and the customs of the same family and fellowship in which they had first been instituted.

“Nor is there any trace of such an innovation, or of a change of name or rule, unless one is to put faith in mere fictions. I therefore carefully consulted the records of the monastery just mentioned, where I found many very ancient papal instruments by which it is fortified; but I found neither the slightest indication nor any trace of such a transformation. See also Orderic Vitalis, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book IV, pp. 516–517.

“But if that monastery had been Benedictine from the beginning, the very same line of reasoning which Baronius used in his conjectures concerning Gregory would demonstrate that Augustine belonged to the Benedictine family. For he himself does not doubt that Augustine was of the same kind as the monks whom the bishop had taken as companions. But let those concerned examine the matter further.”

Thus far Selden’s observations, which I have thought worth reproducing here in full—apart from the arguments given above—because scarcely any other material appears.

But I shall introduce two older witnesses among others, by which Augustine may be shown most clearly to have been Benedictine. The first will be the Englishman St Aldhelm, commended by the Venerable Bede in Book V of his *History of the English*, chapter 19, in a sermon on St Benedict by Aimoin of Fleury, toward the middle:

> “In blessed times Benedict shone forth,
>
> whom the merciful God had granted to Ausonia.
>
> “Then, after other lines, he adds:
>
> “He was the first to establish the contests of our life,
>
> how monasteries might hold the desired rule,
>
> and by what direct path the holy worshipper,
>
> ascending to the heights of heaven,
>
> might reach the summits above.
>
> “The joyful ranks of his disciples are gathered,
>
> citizens whom fertile Britain bears in her bosom;
>
> from him the grace of baptism has already flowed to us,
>
> and a venerable company of teachers has come forth.”

The second witness who illuminates St Aldhelm is John the Deacon, born in Italy, who describes the life of the great Gregory, Book IV, chapter 82, at the beginning:

> “That the monks sent by Gregory were bound to the Rule of St Benedict is also shown, among other things, by this: scarcely any of his disciples can be found who did not observe the Rule of Benedict, both in profession and in habit,” etc. [Col. 0568D–0569B]

To this may be added that the Venerable Bede—whom no one doubts to have been bound by the Benedictine laws—received the monastic tonsure under the discipline of Benedict, surnamed Biscop, around A.D. 678 and in the seventh year of his age. That same Benedict, having prolonged his life to extreme old age, died when the holy Bede was fourteen, as Bede himself teaches at the end of his *History of the English People*. It therefore seems necessary to conclude that Biscop was of the same kind as the disciples of the blessed Augustine, who died in A.D. 604, according to Bede in the place cited above, Book II, chapter 3. Consequently, it is reasonable to believe that Bede professed the same Rule as Benedict himself, and that Benedict professed the same Rule as the monks—namely, St Augustine and the other disciples who at that time introduced monastic institutions into England.

Whom shall I call as an authority for this assertion? A contemporary, certainly, and, as some hold, a disciple of St Bede: Alcuin, writing to the monks of Wearmouth, or Viremud, where that venerable teacher lived the monastic life, in Letter 49, or 23:
