> “Guard with the greatest care,” he says, “the observance of the regular life which the most holy Fathers Benedict—that is, Biscop—and Ceolfrid established for you.”

And below:

> “Let the Rule of St Benedict be expounded in the brothers’ assembly in their own language, so that it may be understood by everyone; and let each person correct his life according to its instruction, so that what you vowed before the altar may be preserved by you inviolate.”

What, I ask, could be clearer than these words? Nothing at all; and therefore they need no explanation. [Col. 0569C]

Moreover, that Gregory the Great was a monk of the Benedictine family is proved by John the Deacon in the places cited, by Matthew Lauretus, and by Arnold Wion, *The Tree of Life*, Book II, chapter 1, where, from a privilege granted by Gregory himself to St Bonitus, abbot of the Lateran, he quotes:

> “Therefore, according to your request, because of the special and singular love which we bear toward our common Father and teacher Benedict and toward his disciples,” etc.

But more fully and clearly than the others, in my opinion, Antonius de Yepes, vol. I of the *Chronicle of the Order of St Benedict*, under A.D. 576, chapter 2 and following. You will find the *Life of St Augustine* after the *Lives of the Abbots of Bec*, from a very old and highly reputable manuscript of that monastery.

Over the whole Church of York and the entire island. As the Venerable Bede cited above teaches in Book I of the *History of the English People*, chapter 19, and in the *Life of the Blessed Augustine*, p. 62, where the letter of the great Gregory to St Augustine, archbishop of Canterbury, is reported:

> “Your fraternity,” says St Gregory, “shall have subject to God, our Lord Jesus Christ, and by his authority, not only the bishops whom you have ordained, nor only those who have been ordained through the bishop of York, but also all the priests of Britain. Thus, from the life and speech of your holiness, they may receive a rule both for right belief and for good living, and, carrying out their office in faith and conduct, may reach the heavenly kingdom when the Lord wills.” [Col. 0569D–0570A]

If anyone should doubt in what city or church the blessed Augustine established his see, let him consult the same *Life*, p. 61.

Moreover, Pope Urban II once honored St Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury, with the title “pope of the other world,” as Gervase of Canterbury records in a manuscript declamation against Robert, abbot of St Augustine’s:

> “Anselm,” he says, “consecrated in the city of Canterbury, received the pallium from Pope Urban, and enjoyed such favor with him that he called him the pope of the other world.”

Selden, in his notes on Eadmer’s *History*, p. 205, note 30. Edinerus inserted Urban’s very words into Book II of the *Life of St Anselm*:

> “We judge Anselm worthy to be venerated as our equal, as the apostolic and patriarchal figure of another world.”

In ancient times it was called Dorobernia by the inhabitants of the land itself. Camden presents Dorobernia, or Canterbury, in his description of Britain, under “Kent,” as follows:

> “With the channel of the Stour divided, the river rapidly washes Durovernum, the chief city of this province—that is, Kent—and gave it its name. For *Durwhern* denotes a swift river to the Britons. In Ptolemy it is called Darvernum instead of Durovernum; in Bede and others, Dorobernia; among the Saxons, Cantwarabyrig, that is, ‘the city of the people of Kent’; among us, Canterbury; and in Latin, Cantuaria—a very ancient city, undoubtedly distinguished in the Roman age.”

Thus Camden. Malmesbury, at the beginning of the preface to Book I of the *Deeds of the Bishops*, says:

> “It is neither so great”—Malmesbury is speaking—“nor so insignificantly small that, being favorably situated on the land and endowed with the greatest fertility of soil and an unbroken circuit of walls, it does not sustain its citizens,” etc.

And shortly afterward:

> “There is the first see of the archbishop, who is primate and patriarch of all England,” etc. [Col. 0570B–0570D]

Of your predecessors, Gregory, surnamed the Great, whom we mentioned above. The Venerable Bede treats these decrees more fully in the places cited; so too does William of Malmesbury in Book I *On the Deeds of the Bishops*, where he explicitly describes the privileges granted by the supreme pontiffs to the Church of Canterbury. Consult him, if you please.

Of Boniface. “This is Boniface IV, bishop of the city of Rome,” says St Bede, Book II of the *History of the English*, chapter 4.

Of Honorius. The first of that name; Bede discusses him in the same place, chapters 17 and 18.

Of Vitalian. His letters and decrees are extant among the general councils.

Of Sergius. Namely, the first of that name.

Of Gregory. The fourth, unless my memory deceives me, under whom the council of London was held in A.D. 833.

Of Leo. We pursued Leo briefly with praise in the note on Letter 3, section b.

In that burning and destruction. Eadmer, the Canterbury monk, recorded the conflagration that he witnessed in Book I of his *History*, p. 9. He shows how much care, labor, and effort the great Lanfranc expended in that dispute with Thomas of York:

> “He labored all the more in these matters,” he says, “because almost all the privileges of that Church had perished in the conflagration which consumed the same church three years before his arrival.” [Col. 0571A]

That letter, etc. It is extant in Bede, in the place cited above, Book I, chapter 29. After the blessed Gregory prescribed to St Augustine what was to be done concerning the bishop of York, he speaks thus:

> “After your death, however, let him preside over the bishops whom he shall ordain—namely, the bishop of York—in such a way that he shall in no respect be subject to the authority of the bishop of London. Let there be such a distinction of honor between the bishops of London and York that the one who was ordained first shall be regarded as senior.”

The bishop of York was plainly drawing a futile argument, wholly irrelevant to the matter, from this passage, as the most eloquent Lanfranc demonstrates with the clarity of midday. Malmesbury recorded Lanfranc’s learned speech—or rather, fragment—in the midst of the council, in Book I *On the Bishops*, folio 121, note 20. [Col. 0571B]

A certain document. I suppose that “document” here means the profession which Thomas “presented by hand into Lanfranc’s hand before the king and his court,” to use the words of the Malmesbury librarian in the passage just cited. It is extant in the *Life*, chapter 11, p. 12. In the same librarian it begins:

> “It is fitting that every Christian,” etc.

It was a constant custom among the Scots, Irish, and English bishops to render obedience to the archbishop of Canterbury as primate of all Britain. James Ussher, in his notes on the ancient Irish letters, presents several formulas—called professions—preserved in ancient manuscripts. From these we shall insert here only one, insofar as it serves our purpose: that of Donatus, bishop of Dublin. [Col. 0571C]

> “I, Donatus, bishop of the Church of Dublin, which is situated in Ireland, promise canonical obedience to you and to your successors, O Lanfranc, holy archbishop of the Church of Dorobernia.”

Ussher likewise attests that such a profession was made in A.D. 1085.

The letter which he sent to Berengarius, etc. We have not counted it among the letters, since nearly all writers gave it a separate title: “A Booklet on the Body and Blood of Christ, or, A Book on the Sacrament of the Eucharist against Berengarius.”

Against the false accuser Berengarius, many illustrious men, endowed with both piety and singular learning, came forth from the caves of Benedictine monasteries like lion cubs of that one from the tribe of Judah: namely, Guitmund, archbishop of Aversa; Alger of Cluny; Durand, abbot of Troarn; Guibert of Nogent; Peter the Venerable; and others. By their roar, the Sacramentarian heresy was at last silenced until the times of the wicked Luther and Calvin, after its adherents, together with their leader, had been terrified and indeed overthrown. But above all, the great Lanfranc, as their champion, so refuted and convicted that arch-heresiarch by the force of his arguments that he compelled him not only to sing a recantation but also to consign his writings to the flames, and thus carried away the palm of a glorious triumph. So says Lanfranc’s biographer, pp. 4–5, and Lanfranc’s own booklet, chapter 1.

Robert of Torigni likewise records it in a manuscript *Chronicle* under the year 1051. His remarkable passage deserves particular notice:

> “Hence many disputed against him”—he is speaking of Berengarius—“both in words and in writings. Among them, Dom Witmund, a monk of the Cross of St Leufred, composed against him an elegant book on the body and blood of Christ. Lanfranc too, first a monk of Bec and afterward archbishop of Canterbury, composed against him a book on this matter, more splendidly and wonderfully than all the others. [p. 345] In it he answered commendably each of his questions and objections, refuting and convicting his erroneous statements and interpretations by the testimonies of the divine Scriptures.” [Col. 0571D–0572B]

He sets forth the controversy of the Church of York against Canterbury, explaining how it was treated and concluded in the assembly at Winchester. He sends a copy of the agreement made there and asks that he be granted an apostolic privilege; then, after recalling the pontiff’s benefits toward him, he sends his letter to Berengarius, which he had requested.

To the lord Alexander, supreme guardian of the whole Christian religion, pope: Lanfrancus, bishop of the holy Church of Dorobernia, offers due obedience with complete submission.

“Your excellency, humbly eminent and eminently humble, ought to remember,” etc. See the place cited above.

## 302–303. LETTER IV. OF POPE ALEXANDER II TO LANFRANC

### Note on Letter IV [Col. 0572]

“We have received from certain persons.” Eadmer gives a full and lucid account of the history of this letter in Book I of his *History*, p. 10. Although it may perhaps seem lengthy, I think it should be reported, both because it elucidates Alexander’s letter and because it displays what the blessed Lanfranc accomplished in this matter:

> “Nearly all,” says Eadmer, “who had been established as bishops in England by King William from the clerical order attempted to expel from certain English bishoprics the monks who had lived there from ancient times. They also brought the king himself to agree with them in this. They were certain that they would achieve their purpose, as Bishop Walchelin had nearly forty clerics assembled, tonsured and clothed in the manner of canons, whom he intended, after expelling the monks, immediately to introduce into the Church of Winchester over which he presided. The only delay in carrying this out was that permission had not yet been requested from Archbishop Lanfranc. He had no doubt in his mind that he would obtain it quickly; but the outcome was different from what he had expected. For when he heard what the bishop was attempting, he immediately recoiled from the deed and declared that, so long as he lived, he would never consent to obtain the fulfillment of such a wish by any means.” [Col. 0572C–0572D]

And shortly afterward:

> “For the bishops, with the same purpose, similar designation, common agreement, and united mind, though the religious order had not bound them to itself, began to strive at least to eradicate the monks from the primacy of Canterbury, intending that, once this had been done, they would very easily expel the others from elsewhere. They were supported in undertaking this by what seemed to them the stronger reasons: partly by the dignity of the primatial see, which must supervise the arrangement and correction of the Churches throughout England through its own representatives; partly by many other causes whose execution, as they imagined it, concerned the office of clerics more than that of monks.

“The king and the other princes of the realm were drawn into this opinion, while Lanfranc, as was his custom, resisted with all his strength and manfully opposed the efforts and hostility of them all. Yet, lest after his death something should be done which, while he lived, he knew could never be accomplished with God’s help—and since he did not know the day or hour of his death—he acted with the sagacity and skill in which he excelled, so that by the authority of the Roman and apostolic see the monks’ residence in that same Church might be confirmed and established permanently, secure and unshaken for as long as the world should last. The supreme bishop of the apostolic see, Alexander, strengthened this by his written privilege.” [Col. 0573A–0573B]

He then adds Alexander’s letter. See also Malmesbury, *On the Bishops*, Book I, folio 122.

And to appoint clerics there. King Edgar, the illustrious restorer and builder of monasteries—who lived a century before Alexander—had long since removed the clerics from the Church of Winchester. The reason that impelled him to do this is explained in these words at the council held in A.D. 966:

> “Therefore, fearing that I might incur eternal misery if, having obtained power, I failed to do what He Himself—who works all things in heaven and on earth and has shown Himself by His examples to be a just examiner—would do, I, the vicar of Christ, expelled the bands of vicious canons from the various monasteries of our realm. They could help me by no intercessions, but rather, as blessed Gregory says, would provoke the vengeance of the just. Polluted by various blemishes of vice, they did not do what God wished by His command; instead, as rebels, they did everything He did not wish. As an eager investigator, I observed the bands of monks pleasing to the Lord, who would proceed without hesitation on our behalf, and I gladly and devotedly placed them in the monasteries under our jurisdiction.” [Col. 0573C]

And because that excellent king had perhaps foreseen that the monks would one day be driven from the aforesaid Church by clerics, he struck with anathemas those who might attempt anything similar, in these words:

> “But if, on any occasion, at the instigation of the devil, it should happen that the fallen canons, puffed up with the pride of arrogance, seek by treachery to cast out the flock of monks whom I, with reverence, established together with their shepherd in God’s possession, let what happened to the arrogant angels and to the first-created man seduced by the devil’s fraud happen to them and to all who, blinded by any gift, have offered them assistance: let them be expelled from the lofty boundaries of paradise and the heavenly kingdom, and, together with those who, scorning the service of the Lord, have despised it, let them be thrust into the fires of the abyss and be tormented forever by unending misery,” etc.

And below he grants heavenly rewards to those who have benefited the monks:

> “Whoever,” he says, “wishes to enrich and make the monks prosperous with any good things, may the Creator, who possesses all things, mercifully enrich them and their offspring with the full abundance of prosperity, both in this present age and in the age to come,” etc.

Selden took these passages from a manuscript codex written most beautifully in gold letters at the king’s command and incorporated them, with his own notes, into Eadmer’s *History*, p. 155. [Col. 0574A]

### 346. “For that wicked undertaking”

Let those meanwhile take note who raise so many cries and commotions against monks and so often thrust forward the arguments alleged by the clerics of Winchester (see the passages cited above from Eadmer). In undertaking and devising this wicked work—as I may phrase it with Alexander—let them place before their eyes the illustrious monks who, by holy conduct as well as by words and writings, inserted, restored, propagated, and illuminated the Christian and Catholic faith in many places. I mean Cassiodorus; Gregory the Great; the apostles Augustine of Canterbury for England, Boniface of Mainz for Germany, Benedict for Poland, and Gerard for the Hungarians; [Col. 0574B] Bede the Venerable, Ildefonsus, Rabanus Maurus, Strabo of Fulda, Peter Damian, Rupert, Lanfranc, Anselm, Bernard, and countless others. On this subject see Arnoldus Wion, *Lignum Vitae*, books II and V.

Moreover, monks not only administered episcopal churches; according to an ancient custom, very many bishops in England who had professed the monastic life also presided over them. Indeed, if anyone, with the king’s approval, was raised to episcopal dignity from the clerical order or from among the laity, he was necessarily required, before consecration, to take the monastic tonsure and habit and to make profession of the Benedictine rule.

Among others, this is reported by Malmesbury, *On the Bishops*, book I, where, in discussing the archbishops of Canterbury, he speaks of Odo, bishop of Winchester, later elected archbishop of Canterbury:

> “He, who had not yet ceased to be a monk, resisted more steadfastly, lest he should appear to disturb the custom of his ancestors through ambition; for up to that time no archbishop had existed who was not clothed in the monastic habit.”

And afterward:

> “Therefore, having crossed the sea, he received the monastic habit at Fleury,” etc.

Nicholas Harpsfield says the same in the second century, where he describes the election of Saint Edmund as bishop of Durham:

> “Since, therefore, he saw that no room remained for any excuse, he was first enrolled in the monastic order—for this had been customary for all the bishops of Durham since the time of Cuthbert—and he summoned Egelric, a monk from the monastery of Bury, to instruct him in monastic precepts and rules,” etc.

Indeed, you have an excellent proof that the bishops themselves were subject to monastic laws, like abbots, in those regulations for monks—among Selden’s notes on Eadmer’s history—issued by King Edgar in Saxon and Latin around A.D. 900. Near the middle they read:

> “The election of bishops, as of abbots, wherever regular monks dwell in an episcopal see, shall take place if, by the grace of the Lord, a monk of such advancement can be found there. Let it be done in the same manner; and, so long as they are of the same way of life, let no one presume to proceed in any other way,” etc.

And shortly afterward:

> “The bishop who has been ordained shall diligently and with the greatest care continually observe in all things the same regular custom with his monks which the regular abbot maintains. Nor, because of the episcopate, shall he rashly neglect the precepts of the rule, whether through fearfulness—or perhaps arrogance—or forgetfulness, but let him show by his conduct how greatly it excels,” etc.] [Col. 0575A]

He confirms the decrees of his predecessors, so that monks may be permitted to hold cathedral churches, against those who were attempting at Canterbury and elsewhere to drive out monks and introduce clerics.

### Alexander, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his most reverend brother in Christ, Lanfranc, venerable archbishop of Canterbury, greetings and apostolic blessing

“We have received from certain men coming from your parts,” etc. See this among the letters of Alexander II, *Patrologia*, vol. CXLVI.

## 304. Letter V. Lanfranc to Hildebrand, archdeacon of the Roman Church

### Note on Letter V

**“To Hildebrand, archdeacon of the Roman Church.”** He was afterward called Gregory VII; concerning him, see Otto of Freising on Letter 3, section b. But let us now hear Hugh of Flavigny, a contemporary and eyewitness author, who praises him fully in his as-yet-unpublished *Chronicle* under the year 1078:

> “He was born in the city of Rome to Roman citizen parents and, what is most important, to religious parents—one who was to be enrolled as a citizen of the heavenly court. From early childhood he was devoted to ecclesiastical duties, and his boyhood was marked by clear signs that he would one day become illustrious. Accompanied by religious persons, he cultivated his adolescence, adopting a resolve to pursue holiness among those who despised the world, not without great indications of perfection. He then mastered his youth, which was devoted to the Christian militia, strengthened not only by age but also by sound doctrine and the foundation of truth. Under illustrious guardians and prelates of the entire Christian name, he devoted it publicly to the interests of the holy Church.

> “Because of the singular excellence of his outstanding intellect, Pope Nicholas promoted him to the archdeaconate of the mother Church. Through his vigorous and praiseworthy administration of this office, he soon became known throughout the world and beloved by religious people. When Pope Alexander died, he was summoned and elected to the summit of Christian government. As the divine will, by exalting its chosen one, stirred the common devotion of His servants to bear a yoke they abhorred—a yoke which he had always avoided in spirit and sometimes in body—the gentle animal submitted his neck to its Lord.

> “Consecrated, therefore, in justice and holiness, he kept watch in a wondrous manner, with constant prayers, for himself and for the flock entrusted to him. Compelled by the needs of pastoral office, he strove with all his strength to correct the distorted hearts of the wicked into the line of righteousness, and he made God’s truth known to all without partiality. He gained the love of all good people because of the fervor of his zeal for God and the execution of justice.

> “But because light has no fellowship with darkness, he incurred the hatred and slander—indeed, the fiercest persecution—of depraved men. Nevertheless, undaunted and unmoved, he proceeded firmly along the royal road he had once entered, through the weapons of justice, on both the right and the left. First, strengthened by apostolic authority and by the truthful judgments of the holy Fathers, he burned with zeal, as his entrusted office required, to eradicate the Simoniacal heresy and to command clerical chastity.

> “The author continues to describe the deeds of Saint Gregory up to the year 1085 and then records his blessed death in these terms:

> “‘Knowing, therefore, that the day of his summons was approaching, he summoned the cardinals, bishops, and his other fellow captives long beforehand and foretold the day of his death. Having completed all the duties of ecclesiastical institution, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of June, he bound the aforesaid brothers, under threat of strict judgment and by the command of holy obedience, never to presume to remain silent if they discovered anything in him that needed correction. When they had praised both his manner of life, the discipline of his holy teaching, the formation of his character, and the fervor of his holy zeal according to knowledge, he compelled them by apostolic authority, one by one, to give him their right hands, promising that they would never receive that heretical usurper of the holy and apostolic Church unless, having canonically repented, he offered a pure confession to the cardinal bishops, stripped of every dignity of ecclesiastical order.

> “‘He declared and affirmed that all who had dared to communicate with Henry, that arch-pirate and usurper of the empire, would be condemned forever, unless, after laying aside the dignity of the kingdom, he performed worthy penance according to the command of those cardinals and of the other religious men dwelling in the German kingdom.

> “‘Then he confirmed to all his vicars, whom he had established throughout the world, his own office and the power of binding and loosing, so that they might absolve, after suitable satisfaction, those whom he himself had bound, but according to the norm of the apostolic faith—not as some, deceiving themselves, erring, and leading others into error, fabricate: that he would indiscriminately absolve all excommunicated persons and, if he could, restore life to those who do not live.

> “‘Afterward, by divine inspiration, he recognized and foretold that this vanity would be scattered through many kingdoms. Finally, he absolved from all their sins all who persevered in this faith, which had become known through him, unto the end. Thus, surrendering his spirit to the Creator, he died in the year 1085 from the Lord’s Incarnation, a martyr and confessor.’”

Thus far Hugh of Flavigny, who treated the affairs of Gregory VII accurately and very fully. The manuscript history attributed to William of Nangis likewise says, under the year 1085:

> “Pope Hildebrand, also called Gregory VII, died in exile at Salerno and became famous after his death through many miracles.”]

[Col. 0517A]

Having first spoken of his goodwill toward him, he explains that the dispute with York had been settled and that a report of what had occurred had been sent to the Apostolic See, which he wishes him to read.

### To Hildebrand, archdeacon of the holy Roman Church, Lanfranc, his own, joins a holy end to holy beginnings

“My mind cannot express in writing how greatly it is joined to your sincerity by love,” etc. See this at the end of the letters of Gregory VII, *Patrologia*, vol. CXLVIII.

## Letter VI. Hildebrand to Lanfranc

### Note on Letter VI

**“For the privilege of your absent person.”** By “privilege” Hildebrand unquestionably means the pallium here. Since it was not ordinarily sent to an absent archbishop, and since the sacred canons and decrees of the Roman pontiffs forbade this, he declares that Lanfranc’s journey to Rome was necessary. How Blessed Lanfranc received the pallium from the hands of Pope Alexander is explained in his *Life*, chapter 11, p. 11. Nevertheless, in that same *Life*, chapter 5, p. 7, it is recorded that Pope Alexander granted the pallium to John, archbishop of Rouen, while he was absent, and that Lanfranc himself, who had gone to Rome for this purpose, brought it to him.]

[Col. 0517B]

He says that the pallium requested by Lanfranc’s legates had not been sent because it was not customary to send it to absent persons. Therefore, it was necessary for Lanfranc to come to Rome.

### To Lanfranc, venerable archbishop of Canterbury, Hildebrand, archdeacon of the holy Roman Church, greetings in the Lord

“The words of your legates,” etc. This exists among the letters of Saint Gregory VII, cited above.

## Letter VII. William the Conqueror to Pope Gregory

### Note on Letter VII

**“I did not wish to render fealty.”** I am surprised that King William denied obedience or fealty to the supreme shepherd of the Church—although otherwise he was highly observant toward the Apostolic See—when he himself did not hesitate voluntarily to pay the tribute, or what is called “Saint Peter’s penny.” For, unless I am mistaken, the ancient kings understood by that penny, which they were required to pay annually, nothing other than consecrating their kingdom, by a free and Christian will, to Saint Peter and his successors as tributary or feudal lord; one thing follows from the other: from tribute paid, fealty necessarily follows.

Polydore Vergil supports this truth, *History of England*, book IV, p. 89. But let us examine the matter more closely and draw something from the sources. The law of King Cnut of the English reads:

> “Return the money owed to Rome by the feast of Saint Peter. Whoever does not pay it then shall give that penny and thirty additional pennies to the bishop, and two hundred pennies and twenty shillings to the king on that account.” [Col. 0577A]

Saint Edward states it more explicitly in law 10:

> “Everyone who has thirty pennies’ worth of living money in his house, of his own property, shall, according to English law, give Saint Peter a penny; according to Danish law, half a mark. This penny is to be set aside on the solemnity of the apostles Peter and Paul and collected for the feast called ‘at the Chains,’” etc.

It was customary not only for the kings of England to pay such a census, but also for all—or nearly all—the kings and supreme princes of the various kingdoms of the Christian world. See Dithmar, book VI, and Baronius under the years 1059, 1062, 1076, and 1081.

**“When it is appropriate, it will be sent.”** Authors commonly note King William’s vice of avarice and criticize him for applying himself more than was proper to accumulating money not owed to him. But at last, yielding to the admonitions of Blessed Lanfranc, he returned to better conduct; this we shall show below in Letter 50, section 6.]

The king was advised by the legate to render fealty to the pontiff and to send money to Rome. He agreed concerning the money; concerning fealty, he refused because it was unprecedented.

### To the most excellent shepherd of the holy Church, Gregory, the glorious king of the English by the grace of God and duke of the Normans, William, greetings with friendship

“Your legate Hubert,” etc. This exists at the end of the letters of Gregory.

## 305. Letter VIII. Lanfranc to Gregory VII

### Note on Letter VIII

**“To Gregory.”** Elsewhere called Hildebrand; we briefly touched on his deeds in Letter 5, section a.

**“You have endeavored to rebuke me with paternal sweetness.”** He is responding to two letters sent to him by Gregory, preserved in book VI, letter 30, and book IX, letter 20. The first rebukes Lanfranc in these words:

> “We have often invited your fraternity, through an apostolic legation, to come to Rome, even for the confirmation of the faith and Christian religion. Yet until now, as it appears, you have delayed, either proudly or negligently abusing our patience, without even offering a canonical excuse,” etc. [Col. 0577D]

In the second letter Gregory complains that Lanfranc had fallen away from his former affection:

> “From the time,” he says, “when we, though unworthy, assumed upon our neck the priestly yoke of the supreme see, your fraternity has taken little care to come to us. How much less, then, could we hope for your affection?” etc.

**“To bring accusation against your words.”** That is, against the words by which the supreme shepherd, in the earlier letter cited above, rebukes, blames, and accuses Archbishop Lanfranc because he had acted too remissly and sluggishly in defending and advancing ecclesiastical liberty:

> “Unless apostolic gentleness,” the letter says, “and also the ancient pledge of affection had held us back until now, we would long ago have resolved to bear this very heavily. But either fear of the king—William I, whom above all others of that dignity we have always especially loved—or chiefly your own fault has denied us your arrival,” etc. [Col. 0578A]

Blessed Lanfranc therefore attempts to dispel the charges imposed upon him and to show that the pontiff complains of him unjustly. What King William refused is made clear in his own letter to Pope Gregory. Why, finally, Gregory urges Lanfranc to travel to Rome, he reveals in these words:

> “So that, with God’s favor, we may come together in person concerning these and other matters, and that the usefulness of the Church may receive increase through our conversation.”]

He clears himself of what the pontiff had alleged: that, after becoming bishop, he loved Gregory and the Roman Church less than he had formerly done. In return, he says that the pontiff’s love toward him appears to have grown less. He says that he advised the king concerning what Gregory had suggested through the legate, but did not persuade him.

### To the reverend supreme shepherd of the holy universal Church, Gregory, Lanfranc, sinful and unworthy bishop, service with due submission

“Your Excellency’s letters,” etc. See the passage cited above.

## Letter IX. To Thomas, archbishop of York

### Note on Letter IX

**“To Thomas, archbishop of York.”** “Thomas, a canon of Bayeux,” says William of Malmesbury, *On the Bishops*, book I, in the section on the bishops of Whithorn, “was appointed archbishop of York by King William. He remained in that dignity for thirty years, upright throughout his life, and there is nothing in either his deeds or his words that should be blamed, except that at the beginning of his archbishopric he contended in the matter of the primacy of Canterbury more through error than through obstinacy,” etc.

Orderic attests that Thomas wrote a funeral lament for William the Conqueror after his death, *History*, book VIII, and he himself gives it verbatim. Roger of Hoveden records that Thomas was restored to health through the merits of Blessed Cuthbert, under the year 1083, in his account of William the Elder. For Thomas’s sake, William himself granted the bishop of Durham permission to remove the canons from that church and replace them with monks. [Col. 0578C]

**Robert of Sées.** Orderic Vitalis, *History*, book IV, p. 520:

> “After Ivo, bishop of Sées, died, Robert, son of Hubert of Ryes, succeeded him. He presided over the bishopric for nearly twelve years, and, being himself fervent in the worship of God, greatly loved religious people.”

On p. 527 Robert’s participation in the council of Rouen, convened by Archbishop John in A.D. 1072, is mentioned. His learning is also indicated in book IX, p. 833.

**Mount Saint Michael.** Here Blessed Lanfranc unquestionably speaks of the famous monastery in Normandy, consecrated to the most holy archangel Michael, not of Mount Gargano.

> “This place is called the Tomb by the inhabitants,” says the manuscript history of the monastery, “because, rising from the sands like a burial mound, it extends upward for a distance of two hundred cubits. Surrounded on every side by the ocean, the place offers the narrow space of a marvelous island. It lies six miles from the city of Avranches, faces west, and separates the district of Avranches from Brittany,” etc.

Sigibert briefly touches upon its foundation in his *Chronicle* under the year 709, when Childebert II held the Frankish monarchy. He says that Saint Aubert of Avranches was its founder and that he placed clerics in the church. But when those clerics treated divine worship with utter contempt, entirely relaxed ecclesiastical discipline, and, indulging in gluttony and lust, seemed wholly immersed in vices, showing reverence neither to God nor to men, Richard I, duke of the Normans, expelled them and substituted Benedictine monks. Robert of Torigny describes this at length in the manuscript history of the same monastery. Until one of our number publishes it, as well as the cartulary, we shall not hesitate to transcribe beforehand the charter of Richard II, duke of the Normans, which is in effect a second foundation. The famous catalogue of the abbots of that monastery will follow shortly.

### Charter of Richard II, count of the Normans, in which he confirms the donations made by his father Richard to the abbey of Saint Michael

See the privileges of the same monastery.

> In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Amen.
>
> “It has been decreed and established by the institutions of our predecessors that, if anyone, inflamed by love of the life to come, wishes to give some part of his possessions to a holy place for perpetual possession, he should thereafter make a testament supported by the solemn attestation of many suitable persons, so that the gift may remain secure.
>
> “For I have learned from the reports of very many teachers of God’s holy Church that it is divinely ordained that our treasures should be stored where all fear of thieves and all destruction by moths will be absent, and that almsgiving is a kind of purgatory for sins. God demands those who are generous in giving and prepares Himself to be supremely generous. Let what is given to God be not our own but His. For what else do we think we possess except what we have received from Him? Let a cup of cold water be given, so that an eternal reward may be received. We have heard that the kingdom of God is worth as much as we possess. A farthing was enough for the widow; the distribution of half his goods benefited Zacchaeus. Finally, what comparison is there between what comes to an end and what does not end? It is, of course, to merit heavenly things in exchange for earthly, and eternal things in exchange for perishable ones.
>
> “Moved by these and other exhortations of divine authority, I, Richard, by the grace of God duke and prince of the Normans, wishing to escape the punishments of hell and desiring to possess the joys of paradise after death, give to the place of the holy archangel Michael situated on the mount called the Tomb, and to the brothers serving God there in the monastic manner, the abbey of Saint Paternus, situated in the county of Coutances, with cultivated and uncultivated lands, churches and mills, meadows and woods; bounded on the east by the public road leading to Coutances, on the north by a stream called the Venleio, on the south by a little river called the Tarn, on the west by the Ocean Sea; together with the island called Chausey.
>
> “I also give the village called Chanteleu, with its church and mill, woods and all its appurtenances; also the land of Grombaldi, situated in Briqueville, Flamenville, and Lengronne, and half of Erengerville; also the land of Durand, which lies within the boundaries of the village called Verlei; and the land of Peter the monk, which is in Batula-Gerfoy.
>
> “I further give Colombe, situated in the same county named above, with its church and mill and woods; also the land of Bernard, father of Lord Abbot Hildebert, situated in the territory of the village called Rotsoloi, with its mill and meadows. [Col. 0580A]
>
> “I also give by perpetual donation a certain village situated in the county of Bayeux, called Versum, with all the land belonging to it, cultivated and uncultivated, with all its churches, mills, and small woods, and half of the village of Mondreville, which adjoins this land.
>
> “I further confirm the donation of my mother concerning Bretteville, which she offered from her dower to the place mentioned above, for the salvation of our father, herself, me, and my brothers.
>
> “I also restore the villages that my grandfather William gave to Saint Michael in the county of Avranches, but which Count Robert later took away by force. They are called by these names: Maldre, Carcei, Marrinei, Curei, Forges, Solinei, Dummanei, Macei, Scallei, Peleton, half of Gomeray, Vergoncey, Manney, and again Saint John, a village situated near the seashore, with its church, vineyards, mill, and meadows; also the village in the valley of the castle of Mortain called Maisnilranger. I give as well the toll of the entire abbey, and the toll from merchants coming and passing through.
>
> “I also grant the monastery of Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, situated on the side of this same mountain, on the condition that the abbot or the monks there establish whatever clerics they wish for the salvation of me and my sons. If they see any of them treating the holy affairs of God’s Church in a filthy or negligent manner, they shall have the power to forbid him the divine office; and, if he does not correct himself, to depose him and appoint another in his place.
>
> “Finally, I grant all the customs of that village belonging both to me and to the bishop of Avranches, as my father Richard of blessed memory established before the Roman pope, to be possessed forever. The condition is that in every succeeding generation the abbot or monks of that mountain shall possess, without the accusation of any of our successors or of the aforesaid bishops, all the laws and all the penalties for offenses of the clerics and laypeople, men and women, of the same borough, and shall correct whatever needs correction.
>
> “But if they should deviate in any respect—which God forbid—from the path of righteousness, or neglect the care of the souls of the inhabitants of the place, the bishop of the aforesaid see, or God-fearing neighbors, shall take care to bring the matter to the notice of the prince who is then duke of the Normans. It shall thereafter belong to him to correct these matters with the advice of the archbishop of Rouen and the other leading men of the province.
>
> “Furthermore, concerning the appointment of the abbots, monks, or clerics of the place, we decree that, according to what was established by my aforesaid father with the general consent of the Roman council, the monks of the aforementioned monastery shall choose for their ordination whomever they wish, and shall have him ordained by any bishop of their vicinity, either in the bishop’s see or in their monastery.
>
> “All these things written above it has pleased me to give to God and to the holy archangel Michael, in the monastery of the aforesaid mountain, for the redemption of my soul and for the salvation of my father, mother, wife, and sons Richard and the others. I do this with their will and consent, under the testimony of Christ and of the whole Church, on this condition and under this law: that without accusation from any of our successors, whether relatives or anyone else, the aforesaid place and those dwelling in it shall have, hold, and possess these things.
>
> “If anyone, struck by the dart of diabolical wickedness, should presume in any way to inflict the force of accusation upon these gifts, let him, and all who consent to him, be entangled forever in the everlasting bonds of every execration and curse, together with the traitor Judas and Dathan and Abiram.
>
> “But so that the authority of this donation may be more truly believed, more carefully observed in every respect, and held more firmly in future times, I have taken care to confirm it below with my own hand and have ordered the names of my faithful men, with whose consent I acted, to be subscribed.”

> “The sign of Richard II, son of the great Richard, who is also called the Old; the sign of Richard, his son; the sign of Robert, his son.
>
> “I, Maugisius, bishop of the holy Church of Avranches, voluntarily confirm this charter of donation with my own hand.
>
> “Robert, archbishop of Rouen; Hugh, bishop of Bayeux; Robert, bishop of Coutances; Hugh, bishop of Évreux; Herbert, bishop of Lisieux; Niellus, viscount; Tursten, viscount; Alverel, viscount; Walter, viscount; Richard, viscount; Guimund, viscount; Hubert; Osbern, brother of the countess; Humphrey, his brother; Bocelinus; Norman Silver; Bernard, his son; Osbern, son of Arsast; Ralph, his brother; Hugh the cleric,” and many others.

[Col. 0581C]

A pact made in A.D. 1236 between the bishop of Avranches and the abbot and monks of Mount Saint Michael, however, diminishes these immunities in several respects.

## Catalogue of the abbots of Saint Michael of the Mount of the Tomb

1. Maynard I, appointed after the canons were expelled by Richard I, duke of the Normans, in A.D. 966; governed the monastery for twenty-five years; died in 991.

2. Maynard II, A.D. 991; died in 1009.

3. Hildebert I, A.D. 1009; died in 1017.

4. Hildebert II, A.D. 1017; died in 1023.

5. Almodus, A.D. 1023; resigned the abbacy in 1032.

6. Theodoric succeeded Almodus in the same year; died in 1033.

7. Suppo, A.D. 1033; fifteen years are assigned to him in the prelacy, but, compelled by the duke of the Normans, he left the abbacy in 1048.

8. Ralph of Beaumont succeeded Suppo in 1048; died in 1058.

9. Ralph, after the see had been vacant for two years, was elected in 1060; died in 1084.

10. Roger I, in the same year. Exiled to England, he died there in 1112. [Col. 0582A]

11. Roger II, while Roger I was still alive, was elected in 1106; expelled from the monastery in 1123.

12. Richard of Mere was appointed in Roger II’s place in 1123; died in 1131.

13. Bernard, formerly a monk of Bec, died in 1149 after entering the abbacy in 1131. See the *Chronicle of Bec* under the year 1149.

14. Geoffrey I, A.D. 1149; died in 1150.

15. Robert of Torigni, commonly called Robert of Mount. Previously a monk and prior of the monastery of Bec, whose *Chronicle* calls him Robert of Tougeyo under the year 1154. With the common consent of the monks of Saint Michael, he was appointed abbot in 1154. He was outstanding in every branch of learning. The manuscript *History of Saint Michael*, written by hand, reports that he produced one hundred and forty volumes and that a tower collapsed and rotted beneath the rainwater; A.D. 1169. At the command of Pope Alexander III, he attended the Council of Tours. He was sent as an envoy to receive Geoffrey, duke of Brittany, with public ceremony. Around A.D. 1176, Stephen, bishop of Rennes, celebrated Robert’s praises in verse. His *Chronicle*, or continuation of Sigebert, still exists, as does another unpublished *Chronicle*, together with a *History of Mount Saint Michael* and a commentary on the Epistles of Blessed Paul. He died in 1186.

16. Martin I, A.D. 1187; died in 1191.

17. Jordan, A.D. 1191; died in 1212.

18. Ralph des Îles, A.D. 1212; died in 1218.

19. Thomas des Chambres, A.D. 1218; died in 1225.

20. Renatus of Villedieu, A.D. 1225; died in 1236.

21. Richard of Tustin, in 1236 received the pontifical insignia from the supreme pontiff; died in 1264.

22. Nicholas Alexander, A.D. 1264; died in 1271.

23. Nicholas II, surnamed Famigot, A.D. 1271; died in 1279.

24. John le Fae, A.D. 1279; lived until 1298.

25. William du Château, A.D. 1299; died in 1314.

26. John de la Porte, the second of that name, A.D. 1314. In this year garrison soldiers were stationed at Mount Saint Michael by royal authority. Their administrator was John the abbot, who died in 1334.

27. Nicholas le Vitrier III, A.D. 1334; died in 1362.

28. Geoffrey of Servon II, A.D. 1363; died in 1386.

29. Peter Regius (le Roi), formerly abbot of Saint Taurinus of Évreux, became abbot of Saint Michael in 1386. He was a man endowed with no less uprightness of character than learning. He publicly expounded the sacred canons at Paris. As head of that monastery, he restored learning to its former splendor and made the monastery a celebrated school of every branch of knowledge. [Col. 0583A]

After serving on various embassies in the name of Charles VI, king of France, in Aragon, Hungary, and England, he went to Pisa. There—or, as others prefer, at Constance—he so won over the minds and wills of the cardinals by an eloquent and forceful speech that, by common agreement, they all proclaimed Otto, later called Martin III, commonly Martin V, supreme pontiff. On his return, he died at Bologna in Tuscany in 1410.

30. Robert Jolivet II, A.D. 1410; died in 1444.

31. William d’Estouteville II, cardinal of the title of Saint Martin, A.D. 1444; he conferred the greatest benefits upon the monastery. They say that he built the buildings of marvelous design that still exist today. He was a legate *a latere*. They also say that he himself established the procedures followed in the election of the rector of the University of Paris. He died at Paris in 1430.

32. Andrew Laure, A.D. 1482; died in 1499.

33. William de Lamps III, A.D. 1499; died in 1510.

34. Guerin Laure, A.D. 1510; died in 1513.

35. John de Lamps II, A.D. 1513; died in 1523.

36. John le Veneur III, bishop of Lisieux and cardinal of the Roman Church. Commendatory abbot. He also held the abbacy of Bec. He died in 1539. Thereafter the abbots were commendatory abbots.

37. James d’Anebaut, cardinal, A.D. 1539; died in 1558.

38. Francis le Roux, apostolic protonotary, A.D. 1558; died in 1570.

39. Arthur de Cossé, bishop of Coutances, A.D. 1570; died in 1582.

40. Francis de Joyeuse, cardinal, A.D. 1588; died in 1615.

41. Henry of Lorraine, duke of Guise, A.D. 1615; after twenty-six years he resigned the abbacy. [Col. 0583D] Under the auspices of this most illustrious abbot, monks of the Congregation of Saint Maur were introduced into this monastery in 1622 and restored monastic discipline.

42. James de Souvré, A.D. 1643; he rendered the greatest service to the Benedictine order and was its monastery’s most vigorous defender of its immunities.

[Col. 0583D]

One of my associates extracted this list of abbots and the charters set out above from the ancient monuments of Saint Michael and sent it to me.]

[Col. 0517D]

Concerning a penitent guilty of three murders and the admonitory letter of his bishop.

LANFRANCUS, unworthy bishop, to THOMAS, the beloved archbishop of York: greetings, with prayers.

Bishop Robert of Sées sent this penitent to me and reported that this most wretched man had attacked and killed three men who were going to Mount Saint Michael on the third day of Pentecost. As was customary, he imposed penance upon him and gave him a letter of admonition, so that if any bishop, moved by compassion, wished to show him mercy, he would have the authority to forgive him as much as he wished. I therefore send him to you as a witness to this matter, so that you may know that it is true and, according to what seems best to you, provide for the welfare of his soul.

## LETTER X. THOMAS TO THE SAME

### On Letter X

“So that it may clearly appear in the sight of God and human beings.” He brings this forward because of that contentious question, so often debated, concerning the primacy of the Church of Canterbury over that of York, about which we have frequently spoken above. Saint Lanfranc here supplies excellent evidence, although in abbreviated form. For if we do not love our neighbor in God, we are shown not to love God at all: “If anyone says,” the Apostle John declares in the Second Epistle, chapter 4, “‘I love God,’ and hates his brother, he is a liar; for whoever does not love his brother, whom he sees, how can he love God, whom he does not see?” Reflecting carefully upon this, Blessed Augustine says in Book VIII of *On the Trinity*, chapter 8:

> “It is clear that he [Saint John] placed the perfection of righteousness in love of one’s brother. For whoever is without scandal is plainly perfect. And yet he appears to have been silent about love of God; he would not have done this unless he wished God to be understood in that very fraternal love.”

“Very many authorities of the holy Fathers.” These are found throughout the book of the decretals and in the councils, especially canon 48 of the Apostles; the First Council of Arles under Sylvester I, chapter 10; the Council of Fréjus under Adrian I, chapter 10; and Letter 3 of Innocent I to Exuperius, chapter 6. On this subject one should read Saint Augustine, chapter 7 of *On the Good of Marriage*, and Book II of *On Adulterous Marriages*, chapters 4 and 5.

## On what should be thought concerning those who wish to leave their wives on account of fornication and take other women, and what should be done with a man who denies that he has betrothed the woman believed to be his wife

To his most beloved brother and friend, Thomas, archbishop of the Church of York, brother Lanfranc sends perpetual greetings, with prayers.

Those who love one another only physically, and for the sake of earthly gain, are separated from mutual love all the more intensely the greater the distances between them become. But those whom the sincere charity of the Christian religion joins together are in no way separated by bodily absence or by any other local distance. Let us therefore strive to advance in brotherly love toward one another, to pray for one another, and to regard the other’s need as our own, so that it may clearly appear in the sight of God and human beings that the carnal jealousy by which souls are consumed has no power to exact vengeance among us.

But concerning those who wish to leave their betrothed wives on account of fornication and take other women—for your prudence asked me about this—our Lord Jesus Christ says most plainly in the Gospel according to Mark what should be thought:

> “Whoever divorces his wife and marries another commits adultery against her; and if a wife divorces her husband and marries another, she commits adultery” (Mark 10:11–12).

Likewise, according to Luke:

> “Everyone who divorces his wife and marries another commits adultery” (Luke 16:18).

There are also very many authorities of the holy Fathers on this subject; but where the sun is shining, a candle need not be brought forward to provide light. In these dominical words it is clearer than daylight that, while the husband or wife is alive, neither is permitted to seek an extraneous union.

As for the man who denies that he has betrothed the woman believed to be his wife, either demonstrate by evident testimony or by any clear indications that he is lying, or, for the present, omit his case until the matter becomes clearer.

## LETTER XI. THOMAS, ARCHBISHOP OF YORK, TO LANFRANC

### On Letter XI

“Behold, most holy Father.” In this letter one may observe how far Thomas has departed from his former position. Previously he had denied obedience to Lanfranc, archbishop of Canterbury, so stubbornly and obstinately—as is clear from what was said above—but now he voluntarily submits himself to him and earnestly asks him to send two bishops, as was customary, for the purpose of consecrating bishops. Concerning this letter and the one that follows, see the *Life of Blessed Lanfranc*, chapter 13, page 14.

“Count Paul of Orkney.” “Although he was subject by hereditary right to the king of the Norwegians, he held the friendship of King Henry [I] in such high regard that he frequently sent him gifts,” and so forth. William of Malmesbury, Book V on Henry I, folio 91; and Florence of Worcester, under the year 1066.

“From the regions of Orkney.” A geographical description of the Orkney Islands may be read in William Camden’s *British Islands*:

> “Opposite the region of Cath in Scotland, which they now call Caithness on account of the promontory of Cath,” and so forth.

A little later:

> “Of these islands, Pomona, distinguished by its episcopal see, is the chief,” and so forth.

“To have granted it to the same cleric.” “Namely, to Ralph”—these are Selden’s words concerning this letter, in his notes on Book I of Eadmer’s *History of Recent Events*—“whose name, since it does not at all occur in the letter just mentioned, we learn from Thomas Stubbs, an old but as yet unpublished writer of the lives of the archbishops of York.”

“Let him send two bishops.” The custom that a bishop should be consecrated by at least three bishops continued in the Church. The Council of Nicaea, chapter 4, says:

> “It is especially fitting that a bishop should be ordained by all the bishops in the province. But if this is difficult, either because of pressing necessity or because of the length of the journey, nevertheless, when three have gathered together for this purpose and the absent bishops have likewise made their decision and given their consent in writing, then the ordination shall take place.”

Consult Menard on his observations on the *Sacramentary* of Pope Gregory.

“Remigius.” We saw that, in Letter IV, he went to Rome together with Thomas of York. “In his early years he formed excellent plans at Dorchester and began to accomplish some things; finally he transferred all his care and his see to the city of Lincoln.” And below:

> “This was all the more pleasing because, although he himself, on account of the smallness of his body, seemed almost a monstrosity of a human being, his spirit struggled to excel and stand out in the world; and virtue coming from a small body was all the more welcome” (Virgil, *Aeneid* 5.344).

Thus far William of Malmesbury, Book IV of *On the Bishops*, in the section on the bishop of Lincoln; and Henry of Huntingdon, near the end of Book VII of his *History*.

He asks him to send the bishop of Worcester and the bishop of Dorchester to York for the consecration of the bishop of Orkney, promising that he would claim no right over them on that account.

To the most pious and holy archbishop of Canterbury, supreme shepherd of all Britain also, Lanfranc, Thomas, his faithful servant—and, if it does not seem presumptuous to his holiness, archbishop of the Church of York—sends greeting: to open and close the gates of heaven, by Peter’s authority [or: in Peter’s place], justly to the just and unjust.

Behold, most holy Father, your son cries out to you—or rather, your daughter, namely the Church of York, turns to the Church over which you preside by divine ordinance as to a mother’s bosom. In piety she asks that, from the abundance of maternal delights, the poverty of her children who have abandoned her may be repaired—indeed, of her powers [or: mothers] situated far away and among barbarian nations.

For a certain cleric has come to us whom Count Paul sent with sealed letters from the regions of Orkney. In them he states that he has granted the bishopric of his land to this cleric. But the cleric, observing the order of his predecessors, asks us to consecrate him bishop; and we cannot unjustly deny him what he rightly requests.

Your paternity therefore is asked to send us two bishops, supported by whose prayers and assistance we may canonically complete the sacrament of so great a matter. Let that suspicion be kept far away which our brother and fellow bishop Remigius recently insinuated to us: namely, that I would subsequently seek the submission of the bishop of Dorchester or the bishop of Worcester on this account. For I say before God that I shall never do this.

If it pleases your holiness to grant our request [or: your request] and to do this for us, we have unalterably fixed and announce to you the place—York—and the time—the fifth day before the Nones of March. Therefore may you live, be well, and advance continually in spiritual growth.

## LETTER XII. LANFRANC TO WULFSTAN OF WORCESTER AND PETER, BISHOP OF CHESTER

### On Letter XII

“Wulfstan of Worcester.” How brilliantly Saint Wulfstan shone in holiness is attested by Roger of Hoveden in his account of William the Elder, under the years 1070 and 1073; by William of Malmesbury, Book III of *The Deeds of the English*, and more fully in Book IV of *On the Bishops*, in the section on the bishops of Worcester. But above all by Florence of Worcester, who for a long time lived familiarly with Blessed Wulfstan in the same monastery, under the year 1062. For the present, take these few words from him:

> “After Aldred had been elected to the archbishopric of the Church of York, there was unanimous agreement both among the clergy and among the whole people of Worcester concerning the election of Wulfstan. But when he obstinately refused, proclaiming himself unworthy and affirming under oath that he would much rather submit to decapitation than to so high an ordination, at last he was rebuked by the man of God Wulfsige the Recluse and terrified also by a divine oracle; compelled by the greatest anguish of heart, he consented,” and so forth.

Wulfstan’s outstanding saying, when he saw the old church built by Saint Oswald being uncovered and demolished, was that he could not hold back his tears. When some of his companions gently reproved him because he ought rather to rejoice, he replied:

> “I understand quite differently the fact that we wretched men destroy the works of the saints in order to win praise for ourselves. The age of those blessed men did not know how to build splendid buildings; under any sort of roof they offered themselves to God and drew their subjects to imitate them. We, by contrast, strive to pile up stones while neglecting the care of souls.”

So he speaks in the passage cited above from Malmesbury. I ask those who are possessed by an excessive itch, so to speak, to destroy ancient monuments to weigh these words.

That they should proceed to York to Thomas the archbishop for the consecration of the bishop of Orkney; and, so that they may be secure, he sends them a letter in which he assures them that neither he nor his successors will acquire any right over their Churches.

LANFRANC, by the grace of God archbishop of the holy Church of Canterbury, sends greetings to his venerable brothers Wulfstan [or: Wulfstan] of Worcester and Peter, bishop of Chester.

Our venerable brother Thomas, archbishop of York, has informed us that a certain cleric has come to him from the Orkney Islands. He testifies that, at the command and announcement of Count Paul, the cleric has been elected to the bishopric of that land. Since, according to ancient custom, it belongs to Thomas’s jurisdiction to consecrate the bishops of those islands, he asked me to send him two of our suffragan bishops who could celebrate with him the sacrament of so great a matter.

We therefore command by asking, and ask by commanding, that, setting aside every excuse, you go there and, at our command, complete what is just in the mystery of so great an affair. For it is not fitting that one who has come to this land to be consecrated and humbly asks to be consecrated should depart from so great a kingdom unconsecrated because of a lack of assistants.

The bearer of this letter will inform you of the time appointed for the consecration. And lest you perhaps be anxious, thinking that either he or his successors may on this occasion someday attempt to seize a right of precedence over your Churches, I have taken care to send to your fraternity the letters that he himself sent to me, being concerned about the future. I also command that these letters, together with those which I send you, be preserved in the archives of your Churches for the memory of future generations.

## LETTER XIII. TO JOHN, ARCHBISHOP OF THE NORTHMEN

### On Letter XIII

“To John, archbishop of the Northmen.” He calls the archbishop of Rouen “of the Northmen” because all the bishops of Normandy are subject to his jurisdiction. He uses the same manner of speaking in Letter 34, when writing to Domnald, metropolitan of all Ireland, calling him “bishop of Ireland.”

William of Jumièges followed John’s deeds in his own style in *History*, Book VII, chapter 38, and Book VIII, chapter 3; Robert of Torigni in his manuscript chronicle, under the years 1067 and 1074. But above all, Orderic Vitalis, *History*, Book IV, page 507:

> “John, from the see of Avranches, which he had governed for seven years and four months, was made metropolitan of Rouen. In words and deeds he burned in many ways with the ardor of virtues, and with excessive zeal he raged against vices like Phinehas,” and so forth.

See more in the same author, Book IV, page 527, and Book V, page 551; and in the *Chronicle of Saint Stephen of Caen*, under the year 1061 and following years.

While he was still bishop of Avranches, John published a little book *On Ecclesiastical Offices*. It was first published and furnished with notes by the most learned John le Prevôt, canon of the Church of Rouen. Concerning John of Rouen, see the *Life of Blessed Lanfranc*, chapter 5, page 7, and the notes on that work, page marked d, below again.

“He put on a chasuble.” Here *chasuble* means a sacred vestment. See Alcuin, *On the Divine Offices*; Amalarius, Book II, chapter 19; and Rabanus, Book I of *On the Instruction of Clerics*, chapter 21.

“Clad in copes.” On the ecclesiastical use of copes or pluvial vestments, see Isidore, Book XV of the *Etymologies*, chapter 12; and Helgaud in the *Life of Robert, King of the Franks*, where he speaks of the chapel. Moreover, the rite of carrying copes during the dedication of churches is still observed, as is well known from the *Pontifical*.

“Leo of the Roman see, etc.” We mentioned him above in the note on Letter 3b. That he performed the consecration of several churches, including that of Romaric, while visiting Gaul in the first year of his pontificate, is attested by the ecclesiastical annals of Caesar Baronius, volume I, under the year 1049.

“The Church of Romaric.” Mount Romaric, or Romaricum, is a place not far from the bank of the Moselle in the Vosges Mountains. Saint Romaric built a monastery for women there; hence the place was called Mount Romaric and, in the vernacular, by a corrupted form, Remiremont, as if Romaricmont. It is also called the Holy Mountain. Hugh Menard gives much information about Saint Romaric and his monastery, as well as about the Holy Mountain, in his observations on the Benedictine martyrology under December 8.

“The maniple is a common ornament.” According to Alcuin and Rabanus, the maniple is common to the other orders, like the amice and alb, since it is understood as a small cloth fitted to the left arm for wiping away fluids running from the nose and eyes. Those authors call it a *mappula*, *phanon*, or *mantle*: the former in *On the Divine Offices*, the latter in Book I, chapter 18 of *On the Instruction of Clerics*. Concerning the maniple or *mappula*, see the aforementioned Menard, in his explanation of the *Harmony of the Rules*, page 894; and Gavanti, in the *Rubrics of the Missal*, part II, title 1.

“They customarily carry a maniple.” This custom was later abolished. The Second Council of Poitiers, under Paschal II, chapter 5, says:

> “Henceforth let no monk use a maniple unless he has been ordained subdeacon.”

“And concerning the ordination of a subdeacon.” What must be done in the ordination of a subdeacon is explained with great learning, both from the councils and from the ancient Fathers, by the same Menard cited above, in his work on the *Sacramentary* of Pope Gregory, page 280.

“With the water vessel.” On the meaning of the *aquamanile*, the small pitcher, and the hand towel, see the same author in the cited place, page 281.

[Column 0520A]

He takes the occasion of the archbishop’s letter to discuss certain rites relating to the dedication of churches and the ordination of subdeacons.

To John, archbishop of the Northmen, distinguished by merited holiness and worthy of honor, Lanfranc, unworthy to be called a bishop, sends greetings, joining better things to good beginnings.

I give thanks to your revered kindness because you not only loved me, when present with you, with unfailing love for God’s sake, but also, when absent, clearly showed by wholesome admonition that you exercised a father’s care for me in my absence.

May this error be far from me, and may divine mercy turn it far from my thoughts: that it should trouble me if someone, out of concern for my salvation and contemplation of eternal life, shows solicitude for my soul; if, moved by piety, he does not delay in pointing out those things in my conduct that displease him; or, if he cannot correct me in another way, does not neglect to rebuke me in words when present or to admonish me in letters when absent. Rather, I shall consider as a friend the just man who rebukes and reproves me in mercy; but the sinner who, with the oil of wicked flattery, anoints or attempts to anoint my head, I shall regard as an enemy.

Whatever your holiness wrote concerning the stole greatly pleased me, and has never displeased me. But when you added that a bishop proceeding to dedicate a church ought, by the institution of the episcopal order, to be clothed in sacred vestments, and, in explaining those sacred vestments, mentioned the chasuble, I was greatly astonished. I could not remember ever having seen such a thing.

I have often seen bishops from different provinces dedicate churches, and I have paid as much attention as I could to everything they did. Although they acted differently in certain respects, they all, clothed in copes, performed the required services up to the celebration of Mass without a chasuble. Finally, Saint Leo, supreme bishop of the Roman see, dedicated the Church of Romaric in my presence and completed everything that the order required to be done before Mass without a chasuble.

As for your statement that, in the conferral of orders, the maniple is given only to a subdeacon, I ask you to inform me by letter where you learned this. I hear that some people do this, but I cannot remember whether the sacred authorities prescribe it.

Most people think that the maniple is a common ornament of everyone, just as are the alb and amice. In monks’ monasteries even laymen are clothed in albs, and, according to the ancient institution of the Fathers, they customarily carry the maniple.

In the books of the episcopal order that we have from many different regions, the section on the ordination of a subdeacon contains, among other things, the following:

> “Afterward let him receive from the archdeacon a small pitcher with a water vessel and a hand towel.”

In some copies it reads:

> “with an *aquamanile*.”

In others:

> “with an *aquaemanile*.”

What the small pitcher is is perfectly clear: it is the upper vessel from which water is poured for washing the hands. The Italians call the *aquamanile*, or *aquaemanile*, one part; in their language it is the lower vessel into which the water poured over the hands flows.

But if you perhaps think the passage should be divided as “the small pitcher with water, and afterward the *manile* and the hand towel,” so that you understand *manile* to mean the maniple, I ask your holy fatherhood to take care, with appropriate diligence, to indicate to me where you find the maniple called by this name in either secular or divine writing [or: where you will have found it].

Why should the maniple be placed between the small pitcher and the hand towel? And why, when the other ornaments are given by bishops, should the maniple be ordered to be given by the archdeacon? I ask you to explain this to me.

The Fourth Council of Carthage removes all ambiguity concerning this matter. It reads:

> “When a subdeacon is ordained, since he does not receive the laying on of hands, let him receive from the hand of the bishop an empty paten and an empty chalice; from the hand of the archdeacon let him receive a small pitcher with water, and an *aquamanile* and hand towel.”

Likewise Isidore, in his letter on sacred orders, says:

> “It belongs to the subdeacon to carry the chalice and paten to the altar of Christ, to hand them to the levites, and to minister to them; also to hold the small pitcher, the *aquamanile*, and the hand towel, and to provide water to the bishop, priests, and levites for washing their hands before the altar.”

May Almighty God protect your life inwardly and outwardly. May he increase in you, and preserve once increased, the love with which you formerly used to love me, so that, concerning me, insofar as this pertains to you [or: indeed pertains], you may believe what ought to be believed, and may you always repel far from your ears, with pastoral authority, the tongues of detractors.

## LETTER XIV. TO JOHN, ARCHBISHOP OF ROUEN

### On Letter XIV

“Reckless and arrogant recklessness, etc.” Here he seems to allude to what happened to John during the solemn celebration of Mass in the Church of Saint-Ouen, as I infer from the words of the following letter: “the most ruined congregation.” We shall note this there.

A contemporary author, recounting the deeds of the bishops of Rouen, described the matter in particular. Although his words run on at greater length, it will not be beside the point to hear them. They are as follows:

### On the tumult at Saint-Ouen on a feast day and in the abbey, caused by the archbishop during the time of William, duke of the Northmen

The cause was an unusual occurrence in a most noble place, free by the privilege of Charlemagne from every matter or custom belonging to the archbishop of that city—a privilege by which its members claim that they owe no justice even in great offenses. The occasion was that William, count of the Northmen and glorious king of the English, was staying at Le Mans with his expedition.

Among the other nobles present with him was John, archbishop of this see, a man of excellent intelligence and no ordinary judgment. Nicholas, the revered abbot of the monastery mentioned above, was also there.

The most celebrated birthday feast of Saint Ouen was approaching, a feast to be welcomed with every expression of devotion. Since it was customary for the archbishop to celebrate the solemnity of Mass there on that day—not because of any exchange involving even his breakfast, but almost as compensation for his consecration, which he could receive only in the aforesaid church, whose see was the one in question—he had requested leave from the king and returned quickly, while the aforementioned abbot remained behind to attend to more pressing matters.

What more is there to say? The revered day arrived. The clerics of the greater church gathered there as usual. Since the archbishop had sent word beforehand that he would come, the solemn Mass was delayed for a while. After some time, however, by common agreement, so that nothing might be taken away from so great a day while they awaited him, it was begun.

It was performed with such delay and such devotion that it is no wonder that the enemy of the human race burned with the desire to disturb this joy. He believed that he would gain greatly by poisoning with his wickedness the time that he regretted was meanwhile being lost to him.

After the *Kyrie eleison* had been completed with two sequences, the *Gloria in excelsis Deo*, which the choir had begun under Abbot Richard of Sées and performed with great solemnity and praise, was being sung. Everything was being done in expectation of the archbishop.

Behold, he rushed in like a storm, confounding all the grace of the celebration. Conceiving in his mind the full force of his indignation because he had not been awaited in every respect, with grim eyes and a furious face he cursed everyone. Then, turning toward the monks themselves, he excommunicated them by the authority of God and of himself, forbidding the present service and causing it to cease.

He tore the abbot away from the altar and prevented the ministry of the divine service. He prepared himself to complete the service and ordered his own clerics to carry it out from the place where it had been interrupted.

We have thought that nothing should be suppressed here, lest, by seeming to favor one side through silence, we appear to attribute everything to the other by disparagement. The truth needs no support from falsehood.

The brothers, although grieved that the dignity of so great a celebration had been snatched from them, nevertheless yielded to pontifical authority. They stripped off their festive vestments and left the church amid considerable tumult.

Some went here, others there; they followed one another and, ashamed of what had happened, complained to their own people. Suddenly one man, unable to bear the grief—whether he was one of them or one of their servants is uncertain—gathering more fury than judgment in his mind, hurried to the tower and struck the larger church bell.

At once he rushed outside and loudly proclaimed that the archbishop wished to carry a clod of earth of Saint Ouen to the greater church. Everyone sprang from the houses. Some seized swords, others axes, and others whatever first came to hand. They burst furiously into the church.

Some, driven by curiosity, climbed onto the roofs of the monastery. The archbishop, fearing that the furious crowds surrounding him would attack him, and fearing even more those threatening him from above, fled from the altar toward the monastery doors.

He scarcely escaped within the enclosure, entering after the doors had first been closed. He ordered seats and benches to be piled around him on every side.

Some men from his party, however, seized candlesticks, candles, and poles and attacked the monks in fury; the monks did not receive them passively. It is shameful to say by what disgraceful example the matter ought to have been settled that day.

The merit of the saint was plainly present for all on that day. By restraining the hands of the enraged on one side and rescuing the archbishop and his men from danger on the other, Saint Ouen was able, through a great miracle for everyone, to avert so great a sacrilege.

For suddenly such a dense darkness of cloud filled that part of the sanctuary where the tombs of the saints were located that it could scarcely be penetrated even by the sight of the eyes.

The miracle corresponded to the event. Since Holy Scripture represents in various places both the blindness of sinners and the protection of the Lord, this was rightly displayed in the cloud itself. On one side, the cloud of the senselessly enraged, rising like smoke, disturbed the serenity of divine grace. On the other, Saint Ouen, by his merits, restrained the hand of the Lord, provoked by their guilt to strike.

Nothing has been inserted here that contradicts the account. The entire course of the matter itself supports it. It would have been possible to estimate whose patience the Most High repays, had he not, persisting in his obstinacy, withdrawn his mind from rational consideration. But the obstinacy of his anger did not cease until, rushing against himself, he fell upon himself.

When the city’s viscount saw that the archbishop had been surrounded in this way, he feared that something might be done against him without due consideration and that he himself might later be blamed. He therefore gathered a military force, proclaimed the king’s ban to everyone, and hastened to provide assistance. He rescued the archbishop from danger, who by then was offering no resistance and had completely lost hope.

On the following day the brothers chose some of their number to inform their abbot of what had happened and to approach the king about it. But the archbishop’s messenger had arrived first and had turned all the odium against the monks.

The matter therefore returned in a corrupted state. Although the king, moved by the archbishop and certain courtiers, was angry with the monks, he nevertheless weighed the affair impartially. With a just balance he judged on one side the archbishop’s immoderate arrogance and on the other the monks’ ill-considered tumult.

He therefore ordered the archbishop immediately to reconcile the church. When the archbishop refused this with a sufficiently angry and resistant spirit, the king entrusted Michael, bishop of Avranches, with the reconciliation of the place. He concealed his own shame, intending to exact vengeance in the future.

He therefore handed over four monks of the place, whom he had heard were the leaders of the faction, to as many abbots of other monasteries, so that the archbishop might be satisfied and so that the monks might expiate during their pilgrimage the offense they had committed through insufficient deliberation.

Not long afterward, however, moved both by rational consideration and by the request of their abbot, he recalled them into his presence and restored them reconciled to the Church.

Throughout all these events he was always careful that the archbishop should not arrogantly claim anything for himself in the affairs of this church, as though under ecclesiastical authority.

Indeed, after he had satisfied the archbishop by the double exile of those brothers, he submitted the matter to deliberation and summoned a council. Because the archbishop had entered the abbey with an angry and tumultuous spirit, because he had been the cause and source of the disturbance, and because he had refused to reconcile the place, the king, with the judgment of his chief men, exacted three hundred pounds from him.

This vengeance would have sufficiently atoned for the offense if he had sincerely repented of what he had done and had judged that the patience of the Lord should not be disregarded. But his resentment—and he had not first acquired it against the monks of Saint-Ouen—could in this way be increased rather than softened.
