Three years had passed, and he continually gnawed within himself at the grief of his rejection. The example was entirely fitting: he was suspended like the fruit of that evangelical fig tree which, after being awaited for three years, bore no fruit.

When that feast returned after the intervening time, he came to the solemnity. A few months earlier he had been struck by paralysis, but he was already recovering from the illness. Since he could not celebrate Mass himself, he entrusted his place to Waselbert, bishop of Évreux. He himself stood among the singers in the guise of a precentor.

At last, pressed by royal authority—or rather, by the advice of everyone—he yielded the bishopric and, on the feast of Saint Philibert, withdrew to one of the villages belonging to his patrimony. There he survived for a short time.

In the twelfth year of his episcopate, he entered upon the way of all flesh and put off the human body. Nevertheless, his body was brought back to his own see and honorably buried in that very church.

Thus far the anonymous author from the manuscript chronology of the abbey of Saint-Ouen. We owe this account in part to the learning and piety of the distinguished John le Prevôt, whose indication and generosity made it available to us; the complete account is also found among the ancient papers prepared for the history of our order.

You will find the foregoing history described more briefly in the *Chronicle of Saint Stephen of Caen*, at the end of the manuscript of the old *History of the Northmen*, under the year 1073, as well as in Matthew Paris and the *Florilegium* under that year.

Moreover, although John—otherwise distinguished in religion and learning—acted in this matter thoughtlessly and imprudently, and even under the impulse of anger, it is nevertheless forbidden to Christian men, much less to religious men, for the sake of defending privileges, to lay violent hands upon the Lord’s anointed, the bishops, contrary to the Psalmist’s command:

> “Do not touch my anointed ones” (Psalm 104:15).

They are called by the Apostle, by a figure of speech, “ministers of Christ and stewards of the mysteries of God” (1 Corinthians 4:1)—that is, of preaching, priesthood, and the other sacred orders, as Blessed Lanfranc’s gloss explains. They are successors of the apostles, leaders of the Church, angels, and gods.

“Because they hated you, reproached you, and expelled you.” Although I said above that Lanfranc’s letter touches the monks of Saint-Ouen, nevertheless the priests who attacked the archbishop John with stones may be understood here. Orderic reports this in Book IV, page 507:

> “John labored greatly against immoral priests to remove their concubines. When, in a synod, he forbade them under threat of anathema to keep concubines, he was struck by stones and fled; as he fled from the church, he cried out forcefully, ‘O God, the nations have entered your inheritance!’” (Psalm 78:1).

He consoles him concerning the contempt shown him by some of his own people, suggests what sort of vengeance he ought to pursue, and promises that he will take care to write to the king about the matter in the manner required.

To John, archbishop of the holy Church of Rouen, brother Lanfranc, unworthy bishop, sends faithful service, with prayers.

Having read your letters, in which you took care to report the reckless and arrogant recklessness perpetrated by wretched men against the Lord and against pontifical dignity, I grieved as I ought to grieve; yet, even in that grief, I could not help rejoicing.

I grieved because something had happened to your eminence that no bishop is recorded to have suffered since pagan times. But I rejoiced because their filthy life, which has already spread the stench of its disgrace through many regions, had been publicly exposed on this occasion, and it had become clearly known what sort of people they are before God—those who, having cast aside divine and human fear, plotted so great a sacrilege in the sight of human beings.

And now let your holiness cast all resentment from your heart. Do not grieve over this beyond what is right and good; direct all your attention to how this wickedness may be punished for the honor of God and of the holy Church.

Indeed, insofar as they are concerned, you ought to grieve because they were your sons—if they were willing to be sons. But insofar as you are concerned, you ought rather to rejoice and exult, since you await the blessedness promised by the apostles:

> “Because they hated you, reproached you, and expelled you as evil for the sake of the Son of Man”—

whom you love and honor, and to whose love and honor you wished to draw them.

I intend to send a letter to our [or: your] lord the king, in the form that is required and that I ought to send. And I trust, with God’s mercy, that just as his times have been darkened by the enormity of so great a wickedness, so they will shine through the severity of an appropriate punishment.

May Almighty God guard your life and, with his right hand protecting you, defend you against all your rivals, beloved Father, worthy of every praise.

## LETTER XV. TO THE SAME

### On Letter XV
## [Note to Epistle XV]

**“Of the utterly depraved congregation.”** By “congregation,” he seems here to indicate the monks of Saint-Ouen; that they had then become lax in their way of life through the relaxation of monastic discipline is demonstrated by the subsequent reform of the monastery under Helgot, prior of Caen and successor to Nicholas. Robert of Monte records this in his manuscript Chronicle, after the appendix to Sigebert, while listing the abbots of the aforementioned monastery: “He [Helgot] corrected the order” [Col. 0590C].

**“Of Bishop Walchelin, or Walchelm.”** The librarian of Malmesbury, in *The Deeds of the Bishops of Winchester*, Book II, writes: “After Stigand was deposed, Walchelm succeeded him, appointed by King William. His good works, surpassing his reputation, will drive old age away from him for as long as the episcopal seat shall remain there. At first, indeed, as a newcomer, he had hated the monks; but, readily corrected, he often lamented that shadowy hatred, thereafter cherishing them as sons, loving them as brothers, and honoring them as lords. There is one very serious matter in which he sinned: taking three hundred librates of land away from the monks, he diverted it to the use of himself and his successors.”

**“To obey in everything, even if he himself—God forbid!—acts otherwise”** [Col. 0590D]. The disciple of Blessed Lanfranc, Anselm, aptly elucidates this passage in Book III, Letter 39, to the monks of Bec: “It is necessary that, joined together in holy unanimity, you obey your superior both in heart and will; you must not judge his deeds and words, but, without any reconsideration, preserve them with a reverent and benevolent mind as though divinely inspired. For whenever subjects become judges of their superior, they openly detract from and contradict God’s ordinance; and God both withdraws from them the help of his governance and permits them to be thrown headlong into the counsel of their own error. But whenever the superior is received with reverence, as Christ, then the whole household of Christ is governed by counsel, protected, and sustained by assistance,” and so forth.

[Col. 0522B]

He praises his patience in the injury he has suffered. He says that he has asked the king by letter to avenge the authors of the crime. He also approves what John had directed concerning the vision of a certain monk and another monk forbidden common burial.

To the distinguished Archbishop John of the holy Church of Rouen, outstanding in zeal for God and love of justice, Lanfranc, unworthy bishop, sends service and prayers.

**309** When I sent Robert, a monk of the Church [or monastery] of Bec, to you with letters, I had not yet received any letter from your fatherhood. After his departure, Hugh’s chaplain brought me one; another was brought by a certain layman who, when I asked him who he was, replied that he was in the service of the queen. [Col. 0522C] The substance of both letters was the same. In both, you clearly displayed the duty proper to your order: patience toward your adversaries and your own innocence in the face of the horrible and punishable insolence of the utterly depraved congregation [or: the utterly depraved congregation’s insolence]. In both cases God is to be praised and blessed: you, by his grace, did what you ought to have done in view of your episcopal dignity; while they, handed over by his just judgment to a reprobate mind, did what they ought not to have done under any impulse or provocation, furnishing those who did not know them with a most certain indication of their wickedness, so that it might become clearer than daylight to all what everyone ought to think them to be in the sight of God. [Col. 0522D] I am sending our lord the king a letter about this matter, and, as is fitting, I urge and admonish him as far as I can to avenge so great a crime. I would have sent it long ago, but I could not find a messenger; nor could I obtain the assistance of the man of Bishop Walchelin, who on another occasion brought you a letter, so that he might await it.

Concerning Robert, his dreamer [or “one who reports dreams”], and the monk forbidden burial in the common cemetery, I approve everything you ordered; and whatever you think about these matters, I too think with you in every respect. For one must not believe that vision to have come from God which forbids monks to remain in the monastery to whose service to God they have devoted themselves, and in which they made their profession concerning obedience, the conversion of their conduct, and their stability, since the Prophet says: “Vow, and pay” (Psalm 75:12). And when the Lord speaks of wicked shepherds, he does not say, “Flee from them; withdraw from the places over which they preside,” but rather: “The scribes and Pharisees have sat on Moses’ seat: whatever they tell you, do; but do not do what they do” (Matthew 23:2–3). And blessed Benedict says in the *Rule for Monks* (chapter 4, instruction 60): “Obey the commands of the abbot in everything, even if he himself—God forbid!—acts otherwise.”

Concerning the monk killed by lightning, a wise man resolves every knot of uncertainty with the clearest statement, saying: “Whatever death overtakes the righteous, his soul will be in refreshment” (Wisdom 4:7). Finally, the Church of Christ does not exclude other dead persons from participation in her communion, except those alone with whom, while they were alive, she refused to communicate by canonical censure. May the almighty Lord preserve your life, for it is greatly useful, among other things, for refuting the absurdities of chatterers.

## EPISTLE XVI. TO JOHN, ARCHBISHOP OF THE NORTHMEN.

He excuses his prolonged silence and wishes that mutual and inviolable concord may exist between them.

To John, archbishop of the Northmen, eminently worthy of honor because of your holiness, Brother Lanfranc sends faithful service and eternal salvation with prayers.

Although, with God as my witness, I love your fatherhood with great affection and receive you with profound reverence, I have delayed visiting you by letter for a long interval of time. I ask—indeed, I earnestly ask—that you not interpret this as having been done by me with an improper intention, nor suppose that it was caused or signified by any resentment or hatred. Rather, infer in this matter what the truth of the situation is, and what your own experience can recognize through the many who report it: my miserable condition has been shaken by the knowledge that I am continually subjected, by some hidden judgment of God, to so many and such great obstacles of this world. I endure without interruption so many resentments of mind, arising both from my own affairs and from those of others; I foresee so many calamities to come in the future from consideration of present circumstances; that very rarely am I given the opportunity to dictate or write. And when the opportunity is given, either there is no one to deliver the letter, or the persons available are not sufficiently suitable for me not to think it improper to send letters through them.

Yet I desire to learn what happens to you, together with the promise of my service and assistance, and I humbly ask that you learn what happens to me. I also ask this: that the harmonious love and dear concord which have until now endured between us may remain inviolate throughout all the days of our lives, and that no tongue of detractors may in any way prevail either to weaken or to drive them away. This cannot be securely established unless those who love discord are either converted by your exhortations to love concord, or, if they persist in their folly, are entirely excluded from conversation with us.

**310** Concerning the young man whose fate has been proclaimed to your ears by widespread report, the bearer of this letter, who saw what happened and was present, will truthfully tell you how it occurred.

## EPISTLE XVII. TO JOHN, ARCHBISHOP OF ROUEN.

He shows that it is false that he was said to criticize John’s actions; and he explains that he received Robert Pultrell, who had departed without John’s permission, with honor because Robert had brought a letter of recommendation from him. He explains his answer concerning the faith demanded from the archdeacons and his conversation with the king.

To John, venerable archbishop of the holy Church of Rouen, Lanfranc, unworthy bishop, sends service with prayers.

The letter which your fatherhood, worthy of the love of all who cherish Christian law, sent to me could not receive an appropriate reply from me at the time it was delivered, for it found me occupied; and even if I had been free, no messenger could have been found at that time to carry it. Now that an opportunity has been given me, I ought not to delay any longer.

You reported that many people had told you that I criticized certain actions of yours, and especially that I reproved you for having misunderstood the institutions of the holy Fathers concerning the preservation of clerical chastity, adding that I affirmed that you did not properly maintain the safeguards of ecclesiastical discipline. Your blessedness ought to remember that, both in person by word and in absence by letter, we have often warned one another that there are many people filled with detestable envy who always wish us to disagree with one another, so that on this occasion they may practice their wickedness more freely. Their business is always to invent new and unheard-of reports, to present things said lightly and injuriously [or carelessly] in a worse light, and, as far as they can, to twist words spoken well and prudently into the opposite meaning.

Yet, with my conscience as witness, I am aware of none of these things. Nor do I remember having said anything about your praiseworthy life, or having assented to anyone who said such a thing, which, if circumstances required it, could not be spoken in your presence with the security of your peace. Indeed, moved by your example and that of the venerable Fathers, throughout the whole of England, by pastoral authority, I have forbidden anyone of any order who is a canon to take a wife; nor [lacuna] may anyone who is a priest or deacon thereafter have one unless he is willing to lose his prebend. [Col. 0524D]

Concerning Robert, whom you called Pultrell and whom you said had crossed the sea without your permission, know this with complete certainty: he brought a letter sealed with your seal, which is well known to me. In it, if the letter was genuine, you earnestly asked me to receive him honorably, to assist him as far as I could with Abbot Baldwin because of his bodily weakness, and to provide him with help from my own resources as I found appropriate. I carried out all these instructions. For love of you, I received him honorably; I kept him with me for three weeks; and I commended him to Abbot Baldwin with requests and promises. When he returned, I supplied him, with dutiful charity, with money by which he could make the journey back. I am therefore very surprised that, if he produced a false letter, he could have obtained the seal of so great a man in order to lend credibility to his falsehood.

Concerning the faith demanded and given by the archdeacons, when the bishops of Bayeux and Coutances questioned me, I answered only that I had neither read nor seen anything of the sort. Nevertheless, I said that you were a prudent man and knew energetically what you were doing and omitting, and what you judged should or should not be done.

Concerning your affairs with our lord the king, I have recently spoken with him as was fitting and necessary. And I think, by the mercy of God, that his Excellency will no longer readily lend his ears to those who bite at your life. May the almighty Lord preserve your life undefiled, for the honor of his holy Church.

## EPISTLE XVIII. TO BISHOP OSBERN.

[Note: [Col. 0591A]]

### [Note to Epistle XVIII]

**To Osbern, a worthy bishop.** We do not hesitate to assign the name Osbern to that bishop and to identify him as the bishop of Exeter. This can be established beyond doubt both from the context of the letter, in which he is admitted, together with Blessed Lanfranc—to whom, in the king’s absence, supreme authority over the kingdom had been entrusted—to decide a case, and from what Malmesbury says about Osbern in Book II of *The Deeds of the Bishops*: “Leofric was succeeded,” he says, “in the time of King William, by Osbern, a Norman by birth and brother of the distinguished Count William, who had lived generously and familiarly in England under King Edward, since he was closely related to the royal family,” and so forth.

**“To the monastery of Saint Edmund.”** Very many writers mention it: William of Malmesbury, *The Deeds of the English*, Book II, chapter 11, and Book II of *The Deeds of the Bishops*, in the section on the bishops of the East Angles; and Harpsfield, second century, chapter 17, at the end, where he discusses the privilege of the monastery of Saint Edmund in these words: “King Edmund, the father of Edgar, freed the monastery from all public taxes and from every jurisdiction of the bishops.” And later: “In ancient times kings used to send their diadem there and afterward redeem it at a great price.”

**“I am keeping Abbot Baldwin with me.”** This man was highly skilled in the medical art. At the command of Saint Edward the king, he crossed over into England to treat Leofstan, archimandrite of Saint Edmund, whose fingers on both hands had become twisted after, moved by curiosity, he had presumed to touch the saint’s body. “He [the king] arranged for Baldwin, a monk of Saint-Denis skilled in that art—medicine—to be sent. Although he made good progress in other matters, he accomplished nothing in treating the fingers, and the man began to wonder. But once those who knew the matter had informed him of the cause of the illness, he remained there, embracing love for the martyr with all his heart. The abbot succeeded Leofstan—or rather joined him—when the latter was removed [or, according to another reading, with his consent], at the king’s command. Under him and through him, Pope Alexander granted freedom to the monastery, so that the place would be subject to no bishop in any matter, looking only to the archbishop’s authority in lawful matters” [Col. 0591C]. Thus writes Malmesbury in the passage just cited; Florence of Worcester, under the year 1097. There is also a letter addressed to Baldwin by Saint Anselm, Book II, Letter 4.

[Col. 0525B]

He explains that he is keeping Abbot Baldwin with him and that, for this reason, Baldwin cannot attend Richard’s court hearing; he therefore asks that Baldwin be excused and that the case be postponed.

Lanfranc, unworthy bishop, to Osbern, a worthy bishop, sends greetings with prayers.

**311** I have come to our village of Fracena, which is near the monastery of Saint Edmund, where, at the king’s command and because of the urgency of my bodily illness, I have decided to receive some medical treatment. For this reason I am keeping Abbot Baldwin with me, since the king himself instructed him to attend to this illness. Baldwin has received a court summons to this assembly against Richard concerning certain complaints. But, once the abbot has been excused before you and before him for making this journey, I ask and desire that the case itself be postponed until we meet together [or: until we meet together at another time], and that we then settle the matter with equal zeal and jointly, without favor toward either party. May the almighty Lord bless you and stand by you as a ready helper in all your affairs.

## EPISTLE XIX. TO HERFAST, FELLOW BISHOP.

[Note: [Col. 0591D]]

### [Note to Epistle XIX]

**To Bishop Herfast.** Godwin, in his *Book on the Bishops of England*, makes a disgraceful mistake when he asserts that this man was first a monk of Bec and learned letters there. All the writers are silent about this, and the Chronicle of Bec, as well as the *Life of Blessed Lanfranc*, makes it clearer than daylight that no one had opened schools or taught there before the archbishop himself. This is the Herfast who attended the Council of London in 1075. “And so that he might not appear to have done nothing”—these are the words of William of Malmesbury, Book II of *The Deeds of the Bishops—“as the Normans are extremely eager for future fame, he transferred the bishopric from Halmagama to Thetford. He was a man of scant intelligence, as they say, though in some measure educated in letters” [Col. 0591D].

**“A complaint concerning the clerics of Abbot Baldwin.”** In this letter Blessed Lanfranc commands Herfast not to infringe any further the rights and privileges granted to the monastery of Saint Edmund by the supreme pontiffs. For Herfast, distressed by such immunities, tried to usurp them whenever an opportunity arose. He seemed, however, to be trying to weigh the wind: Baldwin vigorously opposed him, and the metropolitan Lanfranc, and even Pope Gregory VII, thwarted his efforts without reluctance, as is clear from Gregory’s following letter [Col. 0592A].

He asks him to absolve the clerics of Abbot Baldwin from excommunication until, after hearing both sides, he himself settles the dispute.

Lanfranc, archbishop, to Herfast, brother and fellow bishop, sends greetings.

Your charity ought to remember that, while the king was with you, he ordered that the complaint concerning Abbot Baldwin’s clerics—which had arisen between you and that abbot—should remain suspended until he himself heard the case, or ordered it to be heard by me if the opportunity of time suggested this. But since he crossed the sea before that happened, I wish and ask you to absolve the aforementioned clerics, whom I have learned were excommunicated by you, and for the present to leave them undisturbed by every accusation and demand. For we shall be coming to your region after a few days, and we shall carefully hear the assertions of both parties and, insofar as it can be done without compromising the king’s allegiance, bring this lengthy complaint to a lawful conclusion.

## EPISTLE XX OF POPE GREGORY VII TO LANFRANC.

[Col. 0526A]

He directs Lanfranc to restrain Bishop Herfast so that he will not trouble Abbot Baldwin, and to ask the king not to permit it; if the latter disregards this, Lanfranc is to come with the abbot to the Apostolic See so that the disputes may be settled.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Lanfranc, archbishop of the Church of Canterbury, greetings and apostolic blessing.

“We consider it worthy of no small astonishment,” and so forth. It survives among the letters of Gregory in volume 148 of the *Patrologia*.

## 312 EPISTLE XXI. OF LANFRANC TO HERFAST, FELLOW BISHOP.

[Note: [Col. 0592A]]

### [Note to Epistle XXI]

**“Since he belonged to no order.”** This was a very well-established custom in the Church: no one was advanced to the higher orders except from the lower ones. Pope Caius to Bishop Felix: “We establish and command you and everyone to observe this: those who deserve to be ordained are to ascend through the ecclesiastical orders in the Church in this way: if someone is judged worthy to be a bishop, he should first be a doorkeeper, then a lector, afterward an exorcist; then let him be ordained an acolyte, finally a subdeacon, then a deacon, and afterward a priest; and from there, if he is worthy, let him be ordained a bishop” [Col. 0592B].

**“Take the diaconate away from him.”** That is, as regards its exercise, not its status. The Fathers commonly speak in this way in the Decretals, distinction 50: “Approaching Gorgonius,” and in the gloss on the same chapter. Estius learnedly solves this difficult point in *Sentences* IV, distinction 25, § 6.

Concerning those who are promoted to higher orders while lower orders have been omitted, distinction 52 says: “Your loving concern has sought to determine whether the bearer of these letters is fit to perform the office of deacon and priest, since it is recognized that he advanced in an improper sequence, omitting the order of subdeacon, through negligence rather than pride. Therefore, after consulting your charity, we command you to prohibit him from every priestly office until, at the next fast of the Four Seasons, you properly impose upon him the ministry of subdeacon; thereafter you may allow him to return to the higher offices.”

What punishment is imposed on those who fall into sexual sin is taught, among others, by Apostolic Canon 25: “If any bishop, priest, or deacon, after receiving the rank of deacon, commits fornication or adultery, let him be deposed; and, expelled from the Church, let him perform penance among the laity” [Col. 0592C–D].

Saint Gregory to Januarius, bishop of Cagliari, Book III, Letter 26: “He who, after receiving sacred orders, falls into the sin of the flesh shall be deprived of sacred orders in such a way that he may not thereafter approach the ministry of the altar.” Distinction 50, chapter 16: “If from now on any bishop, priest, or deacon takes a woman or retains one whom he has taken, let him fall from his own rank until he comes to make satisfaction.”

**“Or in a synod.”** The Council of Toledo IV, under Honorius I, chapter 28, prescribes that not only those deposed for a crime but also those unjustly deposed are to be restored—bishops, priests, deacons, and subdeacons—through a synod and in this manner: “If a bishop, priest, deacon, or subdeacon has been unjustly expelled from his rank and is found innocent in a second synod, he cannot be what he was unless he receives the lost rank before the altar from the hand of the bishop: an *orarium* [stole], ring, and staff in the case of a bishop; an *orarium* and chasuble in the case of a priest; an *orarium* and alb in the case of a deacon; and a paten and chalice in the case of a subdeacon” [Col. 0592D–0593A].

It should be noted, however, that in later centuries, and even now, only the pope restores those who have been deposed: *Decretum*, Part II, cause 2, question 6, chapter *Ideo*; and the gloss on chapter *Episcopus*, question 3 [Col. 0593A].

He explains how he should deal with the man whom he himself had promoted to the diaconate, although he had not yet been initiated into any order and was married.

Lanfranc, by the grace of God and not by his own merits archbishop, to Herfast, brother and fellow bishop, sends greetings.

This cleric recently came to me and told me the cause of his misfortune. He asserted that what had been said was true, on the testimony of your letters, and testified that he had been ordained irregularly: namely, that although he belonged to no order, he had been made a deacon by your fraternity. When I asked him whether he had a wife, he replied that he did have one and did not wish to leave her.

Therefore, supported by divine authority, I decide that he should be advised in the following manner: take the diaconate away from him and promote him at appropriate times to the other minor orders. He must never again receive the order of deacon unless he lives chastely and promises by canonical testimony that thereafter he will live chastely. But if he leads a celibate life and is willing to promise that he will continue to do so at all times, you are not to ordain him to the diaconate again; instead, you shall restore the office to him through the text of the holy Gospel, either in a synod or in an assembly of many clerics.

## EPISTLE XXII. TO THE SAME.

Concerning the penance of a cleric who had irregularly assumed the priestly order.

To his most beloved brother and fellow bishop Herfast, Lanfranc, unworthy bishop, sends greetings and friendship with prayers.

Concerning the cleric whom you sent to us, we hold this opinion on the testimony of the holy Scriptures, and determine that this must be observed: impose upon him, at your discretion and in proportion to his strength, penance lasting a considerable time. Take away from him the priestly order, which he assumed irregularly, and command him to refrain from the other orders, because it is written in the sacred canons: “He who invades what belongs to another will not escape unpunished.”

And Pope Leo to Marcian: “He loses what is his own who desires what he has no right to possess.”

Silverius to the transgressor Virgilius: “The faith of the holy Fathers ought to be preserved in the Catholic Church in such a way that he who has assumed, with reprehensible presumption, what he did not receive should lose what he had.”

But if, during the period of penance, he preserves purity of the flesh worthily and proves himself a diligent guardian of other good actions, then, by the mercy of God, whose mercies are without number, your experience will be able to grant him indulgence, so that, as blessed Gregory and the aforementioned Leo agree in their decrees, if his penance has been worthy, it may also be fruitful.

## EPISTLE XXIII. TO BISHOP HEREBERT.

[Note: [Col. 0593A]]

### [Note to Epistle XXIII]

**To Bishop Herebert.** We have given this letter the name Herebert in its title, since both the date and the circumstances agree. It is known from Eadmer’s *History*, Book III, that at this time Herebert was bishop of Norwich and wished to infringe the rights or privileges of the monastery of Saint Edmund, which belonged to the diocese of Norwich [Col. 0593B]. William of Malmesbury, in Book II of *The Deeds of the Bishops*, in the section on the bishops of the East Angles, says that Herebert had indulged too much in pleasures and had been stained by the blemish of the Simoniac heresy, but that, after the heat of youth had cooled, he was led into a more reformed life.

It is plainly a grievous matter to see certain bishops who, neglecting care for their own souls and dioceses, turn their attention to abolishing the liberties of monasteries granted by holy prelates of the Church for pious and just reasons, spending—or, more truly, wasting—all their energy and effort on this, like that Herebert and Richard, bishop of Durham, whose pitiable end may be seen in Matthew Paris, *History*, page 215, no. 1, and page 229, no. 1, of the latest edition.

**“Read the divine writings,” and so forth.** Firmly and devoutly adhering to the footsteps of the holy Fathers, the blessed archbishop admonishes Herebert in accordance with the Third Council of Toledo, chapter 24: “Ignorance, the mother of all errors, must especially be avoided by the priests of God, who have undertaken the duty of teaching among the people.” And shortly afterward: “Therefore, let priests know the sacred Scriptures and meditate upon the canons, so that all their work may consist in divine preaching and teaching, and that they may build everyone up both through knowledge of the faith and through discipline of conduct. For a shepherd”—as Saint Antiochus said, *Homily* 111—“must be entirely mind and eye, so that not even one of the sheep entrusted to him may become ridiculous or unworthy to be received by the Lord,” and so forth.

See also the letter of Hormisdas, Letter 4, chapter 1, to the bishops of Spain; the Third Council of Tours, chapter 4; the Second Council of Nicaea, chapter 2; and Saint Gregory, Book VII, Letter 110.

Only Salvianus, presbyter of Marseilles, is brought forward among these authorities, addressing bishops in this way in Book II of *To the Catholic Church*, near the end: “Whatever has been said about all others applies, without doubt, more especially to those who ought to be examples to everyone, and whom it is fitting to surpass all others in devotion to the same degree that they surpass all others in dignity. For nothing is more disgraceful than for someone to be eminent in rank and contemptible in character. For what else is authority without the sublimity of merits than a title of honor without a man? Or what is dignity in an unworthy person except an ornament in the mud?” and so forth [Col. 0593C–D].

**“It is read in the decrees.”** As the matter itself shows, “the decrees” means both the decretal letters of the supreme pontiffs and the synodal decrees of the councils, which are contained in the *Corpus of Canons*, mentioned by Nicholas I in distinction 19, chapter *Si Romanorum*.

**“In other authentic books of the orthodox Fathers.”** Among others, Hincmar, archbishop of Reims, discusses at length the right of primates and archbishops in tract 44, *To the Bishops on the Right of Metropolitans*, page 719 of volume II [Col. 0594A].

He asks him to stop quarreling with the cleric Berard; and, since he had despised Lanfranc’s letters, to read the sacred canons, from which he may learn what reverence is owed to metropolitans. Finally, he orders him to remove the unruly monk entirely from his company.

Lanfranc, by divine mercy and not by his own merits archbishop of the Church of Canterbury, to Bishop Herebert: may he learn humility and understand with sobriety.

[Col. 0527B]

Berard, a cleric and servant of Abbot Baldwin, brought you my letters concerning his case. As he afterward testified to me, you insolently mocked them; you uttered, before many listeners, words about me that were contemptible and wholly unworthy; and you repeatedly declared that you would do nothing on my behalf in this matter. There will be another time and place to speak about these things.

For the present, however, I command you not to claim anything belonging to Saint Edmund in these matters unless you can demonstrate by reliable documents that your predecessors had claimed it. Release the aforementioned Berard in peace and leave him undisturbed until the case comes before our hearing and receives an appropriate conclusion through canonical authority and the decision of our judgment.

Having set aside dice—and, to say nothing of greater matters, the secular games to which you are said to devote the whole day—read the divine Scriptures and devote your principal attention to the decrees of the Roman pontiffs and to the sacred canons. There you will find what you do not know; and, when you have read them, you will call frivolous that by which you trust that you can evade ecclesiastical discipline.

In the decrees—Pope Boniface, Letter 111—it is written: “In every province, he must always await the direction of his metropolitan in all matters.”

In the First Council of Nicaea, chapter 4: “The confirmation of everything that is done in each province is to be granted to the metropolitan bishop.”

In the First Council of Antioch, chapter 4: “In each province the bishops ought to know that the metropolitan bishop has responsibility for the whole province. For this reason all those from everywhere who appear to have business should hasten to the metropolitan see; and therefore it has pleased us that he should excel in honor.”

And in the Councils of Toledo: “For it is just that each person should receive the rules of discipline from the place from which he received the honor of consecration, so that, in accordance with the decrees of our predecessors, the see which is the mother of each person’s sacerdotal dignity may be the teacher of ecclesiastical order.” And shortly afterward: “Whoever proves to be a violator of these decrees shall be deprived of communion for six months and shall remain under the discipline of penance with the metropolitan, to be corrected.”

There are many other passages concerning the excellence and authority of primates and archbishops, both in the writings mentioned above and in other authentic books of the orthodox Fathers. If you were to read them with greater diligence and commit what you read to memory, you would not hold any improper opinion against your Mother Church; you would not have said what you are said to have said; indeed, with salutary rebuke, you would criticize as having been said by others.

Nor would any sober person think that it is rashly presuming something in another’s parish when, by the mercy of God, this whole land which they call the island of Britain is established as one parish belonging to our one Church.

Remove the monk Herman, whose life is said to be subject to many reproaches, entirely from your company and from your household. For I wish him either to live regularly in a regular monastery or, if he refuses this, to depart from the kingdom of the English.

## EPISTLE XXIV. TO MAURICE, BISHOP OF LONDON.

[Note: [Col. 0594A]]

### [Note to Epistle XXIV]

**“Greetings to Maurice.”** Around the year 1089, under William Rufus, Maurice was elected bishop of London. “Maurice succeeded Hugh,” says Malmesbury in Book II of *The Deeds of the Bishops*, “the king’s chancellor, a man of praiseworthy effectiveness in certain respects and of considerable reputation; certainly the basilica of Blessed Paul, which he began at London, is evidence of his magnanimity. Its magnificence of beauty is so great that it is rightly counted among distinguished buildings” [Col. 0594B]. He sat in council in the church of Saint Peter near London in the year 1102, with Blessed Anselm presiding. Eadmer, *History of Recent Events*, Book III, page 67.

**“Or letters in prescribed form.”** You will find the formula for this kind of letter after the First Council of Chalcedon, and also many examples in the appendix to volume II of the Councils of Gaul, first published through the work of Jacques Sirmond. They are called canonical, ecclesiastical, commendatory, recommendation, or dismissal letters.

In ancient times bishops used letters in prescribed form to preserve the unity of the Church, as Optatus of Milevis states in his discussion of the Roman pontiffs against Parmenianus, Book II: “With him [Siricius], the whole world agrees with us through the exchange of letters in prescribed form, in one fellowship of communion,” and so forth.

Saint Augustine, reporting the dispute he had held with Fortunatus in Letter 163, shortly after the beginning, says: “I was asking whether he could give the letters of communion, which we call letters in prescribed form, to whomever I wished, and I was asserting what was evident to everyone,” and so forth.

**“As the canons command.”** Apostolic Canon 32:

“Let no one receive any foreign bishop, presbyter, or deacon without letters of recommendation; and when they bring such letters, let them be carefully examined. If they are heralds of piety, let them be received; but if not, after supplying them with what is necessary for their sustenance, do not receive them into communion, for many things are done by stealth.”

The Council of Chalcedon, canon 13, commands the same. The Sixth Synod in Trullo, canon 17, likewise states:

“We decree that no cleric whatsoever, whatever rank he may happen to hold, shall have authority to be enrolled in another Church without the written letter of dismissal of his own bishop. Whoever does not observe this shall be deposed, as shall the person who irrationally receives him.”

See Theodore Balsamon’s commentary on the canons of these same councils [Col. 0594C–0595A].

**“Chichester.”** Stigand transferred the episcopal seat there from Selsey, with the approval of William I and by the authority of the Council of London in 1075, as stated in the *Life of Blessed Lanfranc*, chapter 12, page 13 [Col. 0595A].

[Col. 0528B]

He appoints a day for the elected bishop on which he will confer upon him the rank of priest; at the same time he answers his questions concerning a man who died in captivity, his conversation with the king, and a cleric who had come into his bishopric without the required letters.

Lanfranc, archbishop by divine mercy, to his beloved brother Maurice, elected bishop of the Church of London, sends greetings.

First, I give thanks that you say you desire my welfare as you desire your own, and that you trust you will make progress in living honorably through whatever teaching I may offer. Such things ordinarily proceed from no slight affection.

I send brief answers to your questions. Concerning the man whom you wrote had been captured and found dead among his captors, I cannot at present give you an absolute answer until I have more carefully heard the circumstances that preceded his death and, by the mercy of God, determined by canonical authority what ought to be done. In the meantime, impose some penance upon them until we meet and, through mutual discussion, decide what should be done afterward.

I have not yet spoken to my lord the king about your lands, because I have not had the opportunity to speak about my own affairs in the way I wished.

The cleric Geoffrey, who is accused of apostasy, must not depart from your bishopric [or: must depart from your bishopric]; alternatively, he must produce letters in prescribed form from his bishop, as the canons command. You will come to Chichester, as I have indicated to your fraternity, and there, on the Saturday before *Laetare Jerusalem*, with the assistance of the Holy Spirit, you will receive the rank of priest.

## 314 EPISTLE XXV. TO WALCHER, FELLOW BISHOP.

[Note: [Col. 0595A]]

### [Note to Epistle XXV]

## To Bishop Walcher, His Co-Bishop

Walcher, bishop of Durham, whose deeds and most bitter death have been recounted at length by many writers who were Walcher’s contemporaries: Florence of Worcester under the year 1080; and William of Malmesbury, Book III of *The Deeds of the Bishops*, from whom I have taken the following:

“He was placed over the still-living Egelric,” he says, “Walcher, who was at once duke of the province and bishop, so that he might restrain the rebellion of the people by the sword and reform their morals by his eloquence. While he was diligently carrying this out, he was disgracefully killed, giving the king an occasion to exterminate completely the remnants of that province, which had begun to recover somewhat.”

Robert of Torigni, in his manuscript *Chronicle*, under the year 1085, asserts that Walcher was killed during the solemn celebration of Mass and compares him with Pope St. Stephen. William, formerly abbot of Saint-Calais, succeeded him; he placed monks at Durham.

### [Note: “As the king instructed us”]

For evidently St. Lanfranc governed, administered, and directed the entire English world during the king’s absence in such a way that the supreme authority of the whole island—and even of Scotland and Ireland—seemed to reside in him alone, as Milo Crispinus relates in his *Life*, p. 15, chap. 15; and Robert of Torigni, cited above, under the year 1089. Nor is this contrary to his sanctity. For once the governance of souls has been entrusted to someone, it is neither unreasonable nor contrary to piety that he should also undertake the care of the bodies and temporal possessions of his subjects, protecting them and ensuring that no adversity befall them, just as the histories report that many men renowned for holiness did.

One most holy witness will suffice: Anselm, Book III, letter 35. Writing to Walter, cardinal and legate of England, and asserting that he could not meet him except not far from Canterbury, he says:

“Because we daily expect enemies from overseas to invade England through those ports that are near Canterbury. For this reason my lord the king himself ordered and commanded me, and sent me letters sealed with his own seal, that I should guard Canterbury and always be ready, whenever I received news of them, to order horsemen and foot soldiers to be summoned from wherever they might be, so that, when they hastened there, they might resist the violence of the enemies,” etc.

The Britons having been driven out, everything is peaceful. The Danes are certainly coming; therefore he should remain watchful and ensure that his castle is fortified with men and weapons.

**LANFRANC, a sinner and unworthy bishop, to his venerable brother and co-bishop WALCHER, greetings.**

I rejoiced at what was reported to me by you; from your letters we have learned that you possess peace, although we had been frightened by many reports from many people [variant: accounts] into believing that it was far from you. We, however, after the Britons had been expelled and all wars had been quieted, live in such great tranquility that, after the king crossed the sea, we do not remember ever having lived more peacefully.

Know with complete certainty that the affairs of our lord the king are in the highest prosperity and that he is presently crossing over to you [variant: to us]. The Danes, as the king has informed you, are truly coming. Therefore see to it with vigilant care that your castle is fortified with men, weapons, and provisions. May the almighty Lord defend you from every evil.

## Letter XXVI. To the Same

### [Note: To Letter XXVI]

To Walcher, bishop of Durham. Concerning him in the preceding letter.

### [Note: “A memorandum”]

Also called *commonitory letters*: letters by which envoys were instructed about what they ought to do in each particular matter. Pope Gelasius sent a memorandum to Faustus, the master of the embassy serving at Constantinople, in Letter 4, instructing him what answer to give to the objections of his opponents.

### [Note: “Concerning that priest,” etc.]

It is clear from chapter 60 of the Benedictine Rule that priests, deacons, and clerics of every kind, whenever they desired a stricter life of perfection or penance, often voluntarily subjected their necks in monasteries to the gentle yoke of obedience—a practice that is still observed. Hence canon 49 of the Council of Toledo:

“Clerics who seek the profession of monks because they desire to follow a better life ought to be freely granted entrance into a monastery by the bishop.”

The same is established in the Council of Augsburg, A.D. 952, canon 7. Thus it also came about that certain clerics who loved the world were forbidden under the gravest penalties to wear monastic habits outside the monastery—for they put them on in order more easily to win popular favor. This is clear from the capitulary of Charlemagne at Aachen, chapter 77:

“Those clerics who pretend by their habit or name to be monks, although they are not, must by every means be corrected, so that they may either be monks or canons.”

The Council of Aachen, in the third year of the reign of Louis the Pious, chapter 125, says:

“A practice has arisen among many canons that is blameworthy and deserving of ecclesiastical correction: contrary to ecclesiastical custom, they put on cowls, which are to be used only by monks, although they ought not in any way to usurp the habit of those from whose profession they are in some sense separated,” etc.

### [Note: “Whoever wears the religious habit for several days,” etc.]

This rests upon decree 48 of the Fourth Council of Toledo:

“Either devotion to his parents or his own profession makes a man a monk; whichever of these it may be, it will hold him bound.”

So too the Council of Tribur, chapter 6. But, for the present purpose, the same Council of Toledo, canon 55, says:

“Whoever among the seculars, having received penance, has had his hair cut off and then, transgressing again, has become a layman, is to be apprehended by his bishop and recalled to the penance from which he withdrew.”

And shortly afterward:

“Likewise those who were tonsured by their parents, or who, after losing their parents, voluntarily devoted themselves to religion, and afterward assumed secular dress, are to be apprehended by the priest and recalled to religion after having first performed penance,” etc.

See the Sixth Council of Toledo, chapter 7, toward the middle; the Council of Barcelona, A.D. 599, canon 4; and Burchard, Book VIII, chapter 34. But this ancient practice became obsolete in later centuries because of contrary conciliar decrees, especially the obligation arising from parental offering. On this subject Antonius Yepes writes learnedly, extensively, and clearly in volume II of the *Chronicle of the Order of St. Benedict*, under the year 678; Hugo Menard in chapter 66 of the *Concordance of the Rules of Benedict*; and Haestenus, Book IV, treatise 1, inquiry 5.

He excuses himself for not having sent the memorandum and replies concerning a priest who had been raised in the monks’ cloister without a blessing: he cannot return to the world.

**LANFRANC, an unworthy bishop, to his venerable brother WALCHER, bishop of Durham, greetings.**

Your letters found me both far from the city and entangled in many affairs of this world. For that reason I was unable to fulfill your requests in every respect; and even if it had been possible, the memorandum you wished to have on the feast of Saint Martin could not have been prepared, for your messenger came to me on the seventh day after the solemnity of that saint.

As for the priest about whom you wrote, saying that he had been raised in the monks’ cloister without a blessing, I cannot remember having sent you any instruction. Nevertheless, the canons and decrees of the holy Fathers do not allow those who wear the religious habit for several days in the sight of men to return afterward to the world in any manner. If he is willing to obey you [perhaps: unwilling], make use of evangelical authority, which says: “Compel them to enter” (Luke 14:23).

## Letter XXVII. To Stigand, Bishop of Chichester

### [Note: To Letter XXVII]

Eadmer mentions this letter in Book I of his *History of Recent Events*:

“With what confident freedom and free confidence the aforesaid Father Lanfranc sought to possess whatever pertained to the rights of the Church of Canterbury will be sufficiently clear to anyone who wishes to know, both from the matters we have described and from the letter that we shall now set down,” etc.

### [Note: “To Stigand of Chichester”]

“Not that Stigand,” says the Malmesbury writer at the end of Book II of *The Deeds of the Bishops*, “who afterward became bishop of Winchester and archbishop of Canterbury. This Stigand, made bishop there by King William, moved the see to Chichester, the city of his diocese near the sea, where in ancient times there had been both a monastery of St. Peter and a community of nuns,” etc. Concerning Stigand, see note d to Letter 25.

### [Note: “Archdeacons”]

Hincmar teaches what they ought to do and what they ought to avoid in volume I, p. 738, in the chapters given to presbyter-archdeacons; especially in chapter 5, where he forbids them to demand money from priests. Likewise, in order to protect the monks of St. Peter in that city from the harassment of archdeacons and to secure their future peace, Ivo, bishop of Chartres, wrote to Pope Paschal as follows:

**To Paschal, supreme pontiff, Ivo, humble minister of the Church of Chartres, with due obedience, whatever the human mind may desire and hope for in earthly and heavenly things.**

Having been admonished and strengthened by apostolic authority, we ought to devote ourselves to ecclesiastical peace and monastic tranquility. When our own efforts are insufficient for accomplishing this, we are compelled to consult the Apostolic See, so that we may experience it as our helper, just as we have acknowledged it as our commander; thus we may appropriately say to apostolic excellence: “Give what you command, and command what you will.”

We have prefaced this to Your Eminence because we wish it to be known to your solicitude that in the suburb of Chartres there is a monastery in honor of Blessed Peter, founded by my predecessors and enlarged, insofar as its resources permitted, from the goods of the Church of Chartres. In it religious observance was at times vigorous and at times lukewarm; for, as is customary, when the integrity of superiors failed, the well-being of their subjects could not follow.

But because, with God going before us and with some assistance from our own efforts, the vigor of religious life has blossomed again in the aforesaid monastery, we wish to provide that monastery with the necessary peace of monasteries and to free it entirely from the exactions and burdens that the archdeacons, seeking their own interests, endeavor to impose there. Some of our predecessors thought that they had done this, but that liberty did not possess its full strength because it had not been fortified by apostolic authority.

Therefore the entire community of the aforesaid monastery requests that, through the modest mediation of our office, the monastery with its dependencies be received under the protection of the Holy Roman Church, and that the liberty which our predecessors granted to the monastery and its possessions, without prejudice to the rights of the bishop of Chartres, be strengthened by apostolic authority. For what the principal key has locked by itself, the lesser key will not be able to open; and what it has opened, it will not be able to lock.

We have therefore sent a certain brother of the aforesaid monastery, bearer of this letter, who may specify more fully and particularly, by name, the matters that ought to be liberated and defended by apostolic authority, and may bring back to us instruments confirming the liberty.

Thus far Ivo’s letter, from the archives of Saint Mary of Évron, a monastery of our congregation in the diocese of Le Mans.

### [Note: “Those things that were anciently,” etc.]

How manfully—and indeed at the proper time—St. Lanfranc provided for the Church of Canterbury! Before his arrival in England its possessions were being taken away by everyone, especially by the nobles, and its liberties or immunities had for many years been treated as matters of complete indifference. Eadmer recorded that Lanfranc underwent immense labors and exertions to investigate these matters and restore them to use, in the place cited, p. 9, where the great Lanfranc summoned Odo, the king’s brother, bishop of Bayeux and earl of Kent, before the leading men of the kingdom to discuss the affairs of the Church of Canterbury, by order of the king:

“At last, supported by a strong argument and with the common affirmation and judgment of all, he recovered everything that was shown to have belonged from ancient times to the rights of the Church of Christ at Canterbury, both in lands and in various customs,” etc.

As for the privileges of the Church of Canterbury, the archbishop used to exercise episcopal rights as if in his own diocese wherever villages and churches belonging to that church existed in any diocese. Among many other authorities, St. Anselm teaches this in Book III, Letter 19:

“The archbishop of Canterbury has always possessed this power and custom: if the Church of Canterbury had within the diocese of any bishop a village or church that belonged by proper right to that same archbishop, then whatever pertained to the episcopal office in that village or church also belonged to him. There are still countless men alive who saw my predecessor, Lanfranc of venerable memory, dedicate churches in his villages situated within the dioceses of other bishops, with the knowledge of those bishops and without objection. St. Dunstan also …”

He orders that the money exacted by his archdeacons be restored to the clerics of the villages of the Church of Canterbury situated in his diocese. Henceforth they are neither to attend the synod of any bishop nor answer to him or pay him anything except what has been established for chrism.

**LANFRANC, archbishop by the grace of God, to his dearest brother STIGAND, bishop of Chichester, greetings.**

The clerics of our villages who are situated in your diocese have complained to us that your archdeacons, when they find opportunities, demand money from them, and have already received it from some. Your Fraternity ought to remember that, contrary to the custom of our predecessors and yours, we granted and commanded that they should attend your synods and hear from you, without interruption or any investigation, whatever might be useful to the knowledge of the Christian religion.

If any faults were found in them, punishment was meanwhile to be suspended and the matter reserved for our examination; they were to remain subject to us, whether for mercy or for punishment, as has always been the custom. Therefore we command you to order that what was wrongly taken be returned without delay, and, in the interest of preserving charity, to instruct your ministers not to presume to do such a thing again.

As for our priests who are established outside Kent, we absolutely command that they no longer attend your synod or that of any other bishop, nor answer to you or any of your ministers for any offense. For when we come to your villages [variant: our villages], we must investigate by pastoral authority what sort of men they are, both in character and in knowledge of their own order.

Let them receive chrism only [variant: however] from you, and let them pay what was established from ancient times upon receiving chrism. For just as we carefully desire to preserve unimpaired whatever our predecessors possessed from ancient times down to our own day, so we do not wish—God forbid—to deny others what is owed to them by any usurpation.

## Letter XXVIII. To the Same

### [Note: To Letter XXVIII]

Stigand. Concerning him, see the preceding letter.

He orders him to allow a woman, whose case the pope had commanded Lanfranc to hear, to remain peacefully with her husband until they meet and settle the case.

**LANFRANC, archbishop by the grace of God, to his dearest brother STIGAND, greetings.**

The pope sent me a letter in which he ordered me carefully to hear the case of this woman, which you have brought against her, and meanwhile to command that she remain undisturbed and free. Therefore I instruct you, with your consent, to let her remain with her husband until we meet together, discuss the case among ourselves with the advice of the bishops, and, with the help of divine grace, settle it with a salutary conclusion.

## Letter XXIX. To Robert, Bishop of Chester

### [Note: To Letter XXIX]

### [Note: “To Robert of Chester”]

I have thought it necessary to restore the name in the title of this letter, since the prefixed letter *P*, written through the ignorance of a copyist, can easily be detected in all the writers who have dealt with it. None of them attributes even a word of what was written here by Blessed Lanfranc to Peter, whom the *P* seems to indicate, but rather to Robert, his successor; this will be demonstrated below:

“That city of Chester,” says the Malmesbury writer in Book IV of *The Deeds of the Bishops*, “is called *Castra*, the camp of the legions, because retired legionaries settled there,” etc.

### [Note: “The monastery of Coventry”]

Or *Conventria*, whose origin the same author explains in the same place:

“In the diocese of Chester there was a monastery at Coventry, built by the most magnificent earl Leofric and his wife Godiva, with such a display of gold and silver that the very walls of the churches seemed too narrow for the reception of their treasures—a marvel to the eyes of those who saw it.”

### [Note: “You broke open their chests,” etc.]

Malmesbury, in the passage cited above, reproaches Robert with having squandered the resources of the monastery at Coventry:

“From a single beam,” he says, “which supported the chests, he scraped together five hundred marks of silver. After spending several years there, he displayed no virtue at all; so completely did he squander the sacred wealth of the place that he incurred the crime of embezzlement, and the bishop would have been liable to prosecution for extortion if an accuser had been ready. Feeding the monks on a pitiful allowance, he did not even take care to kindle in them love of the regular order; nor did he allow them to aspire to anything beyond popular learning, lest the rigor of the Rule and the vigor of knowledge should make them rise up against him,” etc.

### [Note: “While consuming the monks’ goods with your household”]

For this reason the Council of Lérida, under Bishop John I, A.D. 524, decreed:

“Those things that are offered from property belonging to a monastery are not to be touched by bishops under any diocesan law.”

The Council of Herford, presided over by Theodore of Canterbury, instructs in chapter 3, as recorded in the *History*, chapter 5:

“Let no bishop be permitted in any way to disturb monasteries consecrated to God, nor violently to take away anything from their possessions.”

St. Bede, Book IV of the *History*, chapter 5, says:

“Let those who bark at the privileges of monks and mock the judgments of the Fathers in this matter learn from the example of that bishop whether the supreme pontiffs unjustly exempt monasteries again and again. Indeed, privileges”—as Nicholas I once addressed the Gallican bishops, Letter 32 to the bishops of the Council of Senlis, toward the end—“are, so to speak, the coverings of the Apostolic See and of the entire Catholic Church; the privileges of this Church are, I say, its defenses against every attack of wickedness.”

Peter of Blois, explaining the privileges of monks, likewise says in Letter 68:

“We know indeed that Roman pontiffs have for the most part granted these exemptions for the sake of the peace of monasteries and because of the tyranny of bishops.”

Nor should the notable passage from the Fourth Council of Toledo, canon 51, be omitted, since it seems to illuminate this entire letter:

“It has been reported to the present council that monks are being assigned to servile labor by episcopal command, and that the rights of monasteries are being usurped by unlawful presumption, contrary to the regulations of the canons, so that almost a possession is made out of the monastery and the illustrious portion of Christ is reduced to disgraceful servitude. Therefore we warn those who preside over churches not to presume to do such things in the future,” etc.

In his own name and that of the king, he orders him to restore without delay what he has violently taken from the monastery at Coventry, recounting one by one the unworthy ways in which he has afflicted them.

**LANFRANC, archbishop by the grace of God, to ROBERT, bishop of Chester, greetings.**

A few days ago I sent you a letter, and, scarcely having received it, you disdained to read it and, as I have been told, threw it with great indignation onto a certain seat. Now I send another, ordering and commanding, on behalf of the king and myself, that you withdraw entirely from every burden that you are said to have imposed upon the monastery of Coventry; and whatever you have violently taken from that monastery or from its lands, restore without delay.

For both the abbot and his monks have complained to me that you entered their dormitory by force, broke open their chests, and seized the horses and all the property they possessed. Moreover, you destroyed their houses and ordered their materials to be carried away to your own villages. In the monastery itself, consuming the monks’ goods with your household, you stayed for eight days.

Recognize that these things belong neither to your office nor to your authority. Rather, it would have been more fitting for you to care for their souls with pastoral discretion and to offer, in word and deed, salutary examples of good morals and holy actions.

## Letter XXX. To Manasses, Archbishop of Reims

### [Note: To Letter XXX]

### [Note: “To Manasses, archbishop of Reims”]

He was the first of that name. Alberic of Cîteaux briefly mentions him in his unpublished *Chronicle*, under the year 1070:

“Manasses became bishop of Reims and held the see for sixteen years. He was the son of Manasses, called Bald-Headed Donkey, by Beatrice of Roucy. In the year 1031, the brothers of this Manasses’ father were Hilduin of Ramerupt and William, count of Soissons, who fathered Reginald, John, and Manasses, who became bishop of Soissons,” etc.

Hugh of Flavigny, a reliable witness in his manuscript *History*, repeatedly says that Manasses, rebuked in especially forceful language for his depraved conduct—above all by St. Bruno, founder of the Carthusians, whose conduct also gave Bruno the occasion to bid his final farewell to the world—was suspended and eventually deposed:

“He says that Manasses, the simoniacal invader of the Church of Reims, was accused by the clerics of Reims in that same council, the Council of Lyons, and suspended from office. Summoned to the council to purge himself, he did not come. After preparing many ambushes for the canons of the Church of Reims, his accusers, when they were returning from the council, he finally broke into their houses, sold their prebends, and plundered their goods. Then, after receiving letters from Rome ordering him to purge himself at a council with six bishops, he went to Rome.”

After much more, speaking of the council that was assembled under Hugh, bishop of Die, he says:

“Manasses was deposed by synodal judgment because he refused to purge himself, and also because he evaded the hearings of the bishops of Autun, Poitiers, and Lyons themselves.”

### [Note: “The king’s man and ours,” etc.]

Blessed Anselm, then abbot of Bec, appears—unless I am mistaken—to reveal this theft in Book I, Letter 46, in these words:

“So cruel and unrestrained is the savagery of malicious men raging in France that I dare not expose either myself, or any monk, or any knight to such great danger. In truth, when Lord Rodulf returned after bringing you back, he was seized in the archbishopric of Reims together with his servants, after all his horses had been taken away, even though he protested that he was traveling under the protection of the archbishop of Reims. After being detained for some time, they were at last released, scarcely retaining a single horse.”

### [Note: “Rosnay”]

Rosnay, a village, as I suppose, two miles from Reims.

He advises the archbishop of Reims, by order of the supreme pontiff, to arrange for the bearer of the letter to have restored the property unjustly taken from him at Rosnay.

**To the lord MANASSES, archbishop of Reims, most highly honored among the pillars of the Church, LANFRANC, a sinner and unworthy bishop, greetings, with service and prayers.**

The bearer of this letter, a man of the king and of ourselves, asserts that he has suffered great injury to his property at Rosnay, and for this reason has brought a tearful complaint to the ears of the supreme pontiff. The supreme pontiff has solemnly excommunicated his robbers [variant: them], unless they return everything belonging to him, and has sent you letters from the Apostolic See so that you may administer justice to him concerning those robbers.

Although Your Excellence has no need of an admonisher in such matters, I nevertheless ask—and ask earnestly—that your kindness assist him in such a way that he may recover, without diminution, his property that was unjustly taken from him.

## Letter XXXI. To Bishop Maurice

### [Note: To Letter XXXI]

Maurice, bishop. Concerning him, see the note to Letter 25, which is addressed to him.

He orders him to go to Berting and settle the dispute between the abbess and the prioress.

**LANFRANC, archbishop, to his beloved friend MAURICE, bishop, greetings.**

As in my other letters, so also in this one, I ask and admonish you, and command by pastoral authority, that, if it is convenient for you, you go to Bertingen and, after hearing the complaints of both sides, order that the abbess be abbess and the prioress be prioress. Let each remain in her own order, as is fitting; and, as the Rule of blessed Benedict commands (chapter 7, grades 2 and 3; and chapter 63), let the greater command and the lesser obey.

If, however, she commands things that are appropriate for sound reasons and that the sacred authorities by no means contradict, let both of them, preserving the dignity of their respective orders, conduct the affairs of God and the affairs of the world by common counsel. Let the nuns, clerics, and laypeople, both inside and outside, serve and obey them.

Whichever of them transgresses this constitution of ours is to be corrected through your diligent intervention and, lest she fulfill the presumption she has conceived, compelled with appropriate severity. But if discord arms the parties to such an extent that their judgment cannot be brought into one agreement, let the matter be reported to us, so that the guilty party may be subjected to regular discipline.

## Letter XXXII. To Goisfrid, Bishop

### [Note: To Letter XXXII]

Goisfrid, or Goffrid, bishop of Coutances in Normandy. He was present, among the other prelates of England, at the Council of London in A.D. 1075. Milo, in chapter 12, p. 13, of his *Life of Blessed Lanfranc*, commends him. Our Orderic speaks of Goffrid as follows in Book IV of his *History*, p. 523:

“Geoffrey, bishop of Coutances, born of a noble family of Normans, who took part in the battle of Senlac as an energetic supporter and comforter, and in other conflicts,” etc.

Likewise in Book III, p. 493:

“At that time Normandy was flourishing gloriously with learned prelates of the churches and noblemen. For the holy Maurilius, formerly a monk and now metropolitan, presided over the see of Rouen, etc.; Goisfrid over Coutances,” etc.

And finally in Book IV, p. 514.

### [Note: “Although they have not yet made profession”]

It was an ancient and carefully observed custom that, whether a man or woman was of whatever rank or condition, as soon as he or she had put on the monastic habit or had stood before the altar to be offered to the supreme Lord of all, it was thereafter in no way lawful to cast off the yoke. This is also observed by the authority of the councils, as noted in the commentary on Letter 26, note d; for whatever is said there about men must plainly be understood also of women.

This is clear from the Sixth Council of Toledo, chapter 6:

“Whoever among men or women has once voluntarily put on the religious habit, or if a man has been devoted to the choir of the church, or a woman has been assigned to a monastery of maidens, the transgressor of either sex must be compelled against his or her will to return to the profession, so that the man may be tonsured and the girl restored to the monastery,” etc.

So too chapter 4 of the Council of Barcelona, under Pope Gregory the Great, and the Fifth Council of Orléans, canon 19.

### [Note: “They were nevertheless offered at the altar”]

The offering of this kind was discussed in the notes to Letter 26, note d, and to this letter, note b. If I insert here the formulas of offering, I hope the reader will not find it tedious; they contribute considerably to clarifying ancient monastic practices. They are as follows, drawn from the most ancient parchments of our monastery of Saint-Remi at Reims.

### [Note: “In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 868, on 24 April, Saturday.”]

“Since it has been legally established and anciently prescribed that parents should offer their children in the temple of the Lord, so that they may serve there faithfully, without doubt a salutary example is provided by doing this with our own children. For I judge it right to return fruit from you [variant: from us] to our Creator.

Therefore I, Hildegrim, hand over this nephew of mine, named Rifuinus, together with an offering and petition in hand, the offering wrapped in an altar-cloth by my own hand, to Saint Remigius and of the saints whose relics are also contained here, and to the abbot presently in office, before witnesses, to remain there. From this day forward, let it not be permitted him to withdraw his neck from beneath the yoke of the Rule; rather, let him faithfully acknowledge and observe the institutions of that Rule and serve the Lord with a grateful heart.

And so that this offering of mine may remain unshaken, I promise by oath before God and his angels that never through myself, never through a suspect person, and in no way through the resources of my possessions will I ever provide him an opportunity to leave the monastery. And so that this offering of mine may remain firm and inviolate, I have confirmed it below with my own hand.

+ Hildegrim, who requested that this document be made and confirmed.

+ Bovo, his brother.

+ Walbert.”

### Another form made in the name of the father alone

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 880, on 17 September, Sunday.

“Since it has been legally established,” etc., as above.

“Therefore I, Count Achadeus, offer and hand over this son of mine, named Hilduin, together with the offering, etc., to Rofrid, provost of the same place, presently acting in the office of abbot, before the witnesses, monks of the aforesaid place: Teutbold, priest; Hardrad, priest; Guntarius and Bernarius, deacons; Stephen and Sigloard, subdeacons,” etc., as above.

“Sign of Count Achadeus, who requested that this charter be made and confirmed. Sign of Becton,” etc.

### Another form, in the name of the father and mother

“Since it has been legally established,” etc.

“Therefore I, Leudo, offer this son of mine, named Conimbertus, etc. Sign of Leudo, etc.; sign of Rothildis, his mother; likewise the sign of Leudo,” etc.

### A form for the offering of children much later than these

Namely, from the time of Philip I, king of the Franks, expressed in nearly the same words, from the monastery of Bellilocus.

“Since it has been legally established,” etc.

“Therefore I, N., and my wife, N., offer this son of ours, together with the counsel of his parents, our N., with the offering, etc. Sign of N., N. Done while Philip, king of the Franks, was reigning.”

All these formulas were made according to the prescriptions of the Benedictine Rule, chapters 58 and 59.

### [Note: “To preserve the Rule”]

Thus formerly councils and Fathers, by antonomasia, when speaking of the Rule of Saint Benedict, customarily called it “the Rule,” “the holy Rule,” or “the holy Order.” The Council of Soissons, A.D. 744, chapter 3, in volume I of the Councils of Gaul, prescribes:

“Let the order of monks or handmaids of God remain stable according to the holy Rule.”

The Council held at the palace of Verneuil, A.D. 755, canon 5, says:

“Let monasteries both of men and of women live according to the order and in a regular manner.”

And below:

“If an abbot contradicts such a decree, let him be summoned to the council, and let one be appointed in his place who will govern according to the holy order.”

But lest anyone’s mind be troubled by doubt as to whether the Benedictine Rule is understood in those decrees, chapter 11 of the Council of Mainz, under Pope Leo III, must be cited:

“And afterward we decreed, as the holy Rule says, that a monastery should, wherever possible, be organized through deans, because provosts often fall into pride,” etc.

This decree was taken from chapter 65 of the Rule of Saint Benedict, whose words are as follows:

“It often happens that serious scandals arise in monasteries through the appointment of a provost, when certain men are exalted by a spirit of pride,” etc.

And shortly afterward:

“If it can be done, let every useful arrangement of the monastery be organized through deans, as we established earlier,” etc.

### [Note: Concerning the universal observance of the Benedictine Rule in Gaul]

Since we have entered upon a discussion of the Benedictine Rule, and since a few years ago we heard that a man otherwise most learned had expressed doubt whether the Rule of Saint Benedict was formerly observed universally throughout Gaul—especially before the time of Louis the Pious—I could surely satisfy him with this single question from the emperor Charlemagne to the bishops of Gaul, in chapter 12 of the *Capitularies of Questions*, volume II of the Councils of Gaul:

“Concerning the way of life of monks,” he says, “and whether there could be any monks other than those who observe the Rule of Saint Benedict. It must also be investigated whether there had been monks in Gaul before the tradition of the Rule of Saint Benedict reached these parishes.”

And in the same work, in a brief section, chapter 12:

“By what rule did monks live in Gaul before the Rule of Saint Benedict had been handed down there, when we read that Saint Martin was both a monk and had monks under him, although he lived long before Saint Benedict?”

What, I ask, could be more explicit than these words? Does not that emperor, endowed with extensive learning, teach that at that time only the Benedictine Rule existed, and that everyone held this position? That is, at that period only Benedictines practiced the ascetic life, since he both asks whether there could be any monks other than those who observe the Rule of Saint Benedict and mentions no monks except the followers of Martin, who preceded Saint Benedict by two centuries.

However, so that nothing may remain untouched—and we have, if I may use the Apostle’s words, “a cloud of witnesses imposed upon us” (Heb. 12:1)—by which it may most clearly appear that this rule was adopted by monks throughout Gaul nearly three centuries before Louis the Pious (I shall deliberately say nothing of Saint Maurus, who first brought it there, since he is better known than to require much to be said about him), I wish to go back farther and extend the discussion, and therefore to consult the sources themselves.

The Council of Tours, held in A.D. 813, canon 25:

> “As regards monasteries of monks in which the rule of blessed Father Benedict was being observed, but which now, perhaps through some encroaching negligence, is being kept more laxly and more carelessly, or certainly is being neglected in complete forgetfulness, it seems good that they should return to their former condition,” etc.

These words require no explanation. For the expressions “Formerly the rule of Saint Benedict was being observed” and “Let it return to its former condition” signify nothing other than that, long before the time when this decree was enacted, the use and practice of the Benedictine Rule had existed among monks.

The Second Council of Chalon-sur-Saône likewise confirms this, having been held by the bishops of the province of Lyon in the thirteenth year of the empire of Charlemagne, canon 22:

> “Concerning abbots and monks we write little here for this reason: nearly all the regular monasteries established in these regions profess that they live according to the rule of Saint Benedict. Let inquiry therefore be made carefully as to where life is lived according to that order and where there has been a departure from that order, so that they may strive to live according to the institution of the same blessed man,” etc.
