Nor should anyone be troubled by the words “nearly all the regular monasteries,” since, besides the monasteries of monks, there were also canonical residences of clerics—that is, of those living under a rule, whence they were called canons—which were likewise called monasteries. This was especially so where Codegrandus, bishop of Metz, issued a rule for canons (preserved in manuscript by the very learned men Jacques Sirmond and Jean le Prévôt), although another rule, or form of institution, for canons is also extant in volume II of the *Councils of Gaul*, p. 329.

And, to return to the subject, here are arguments far older than those just cited. From the very ancient manuscript *Life of Blessed Junianus*, under Clotaire I, king of the Franks, around the year 564:

> “After a long conversation, the most glorious king asked him [Junianus] what work he performed, what his way of life was, and of what religion he was. He replied in the sweetest manner that he was living under the monastic order, that he had been placed over monks, that the institutions of the most blessed Benedict were observed, and that his regular life was observed in all respects, except that, because of the narrowness of the place, he could not fully keep it with his companions; nor did he have a place where the work prescribed according to the rule of the aforementioned Father Benedict could be carried out,” etc.

The very same words are found in André du Chesne, volume I of *Historiæ Francorum Scriptores*, p. 543 C, from a fragment of the *Life of Saint Junianus*.

In the testament of Leodebodus, abbot of Saint-Aignan at Orléans, or in the foundation charter of the monastery of Fleury, drawn up by the abbot himself in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 623, these words are stated concerning the Benedictine Rule:

> “In which monastery the monks are to remain according to the rule of the most holy Benedict and of lord Columbanus; and I resolve to confer upon Christ the ruler, from the resources of my own property in particular,” etc.

From these words it can be understood that the same rule had been received in the monastery of Saint-Aignan before that time.

Nor should anyone take issue with the fact that the rule of Saint Columbanus is mentioned here. At that time the monks in certain monasteries of Gaul observed it together with the Benedictine Rule, as, among others, Orderic Vitalis reveals in book VIII of his *History*, near the end. For the rule—or rather the rules, since it is found in three forms—seems to be nothing other than constitutions, or, as they are called, declarations concerning the rule of Saint Benedict. Two of them merely provide exhortatory precepts; the other prescribes, more specifically than Dom Benedict, the manner of inflicting punishment according to the gravity of the offense, as Stengelius shows from an old manuscript preface to the Rule of Columbanus in *Corona lucida*, p. 128. Indeed, this will by no means be obscure, in my judgment, to anyone examining these rules.

Closely related to this is the following passage from the *Life of Saint Mommolus*, first abbot of the monastery of Fleury and disciple of blessed Leobodus, from an old codex of the monastery of Sainte-Croix at Bordeaux:

> “Mommolus desired the pattern of the regular life, wishing to cling to divine contemplation; he sought the religion of the excellent Father Benedict, desiring to serve the one King of all with his inmost heart; and under Father Leobodus he deserved to serve Christ.”

Judicael, king of Brittany, later become a monk in the monastery he founded at Saint-Jean de Gaël, now Saint-Méen, commonly called Saint Meen. The manuscript foundation charter contains these words:

> “Honor and glory to almighty God and to his servant Benedict, father of monks, now dead on earth but living eternally in heaven.”

Then, after other material:

> “We permanently grant these revenues to this monastery of Saint-Jean de Gaël for the support of twenty-eight monks serving God under the rule of Saint Benedict,” etc.

These events appear to have taken place around the year 630.

The decree of Clotaire III, king of the Franks, concerning the foundation of the monastery of Corbie, in volume I of the *Councils of Gaul*, p. 500, begins:

> “Therefore, when we and our exalted mother, the lady Queen Balthild, ordered a monastery to be built in honor of the holy apostles Peter and Paul and of Saint Stephen the Protomartyr, beside the river Somme, in the place called Corbie, where the venerable man Theofridus is abbot, for the sake of the eternal Godhead, so that the monks there should live under the holy rule”—namely, the Benedictine Rule, as has been proved above.

And in the privilege granted to the same monastery by Bertefridus, bishop of Amiens, later in the same volume:

> “So that the monks themselves, living in peace under the holy rule, should serve that monastery.”

But you object: further below one finds this:

> “It was also decided to add that the monks themselves should conduct themselves and live under the rule of Saint Benedict or of Columbanus.”

What then? By these words Bertefridus supposedly indicates that the rule of Saint Benedict is one thing and that of Saint Columbanus another, since he speaks disjunctively here. Is that really so? Is the particle *vel* always disjunctive, and is it not sometimes used in place of *et*, or for fuller explanation? Let us prove the point by examples.

Terence, *Eunuchus* 2.3.23:

> “Both virtue and learning make me especially your friend.”

Cicero, *On Famous Orators* 131:

> “To serve both the honor and the danger of many.”

Grammarians know that in both passages *vel* is to be taken as *et*, “and.”

But to the point: Saint Benedict says in the Prologue to the Rule:

> “Therefore, with the loins of our faith or observance of good works girded,” etc.

The very learned Petrus Boerius, abbot of Saint-Aignan and later a bishop, explains this in his manuscript commentary on the Rule of Saint Benedict:

> “Explain this *vel* as *et*, because if good works are absent from faith, you have no merit, as James testifies: faith without works is dead.”

The same commentator, in chapter 46 of the same Rule, explaining the words “before the abbot or the congregation,” says:

> “Explain *vel* as *et*, because such betrayals customarily take place in the chapter,” etc.

And Hugo Menardus, commenting on the words in chapter 3 of the *Concordia regularum*, “under a rule or an abbot,” p. 102, says:

> “These words are to be taken conjunctively, so that the particle *vel* is put in place of the copulative. Saint Eulogius speaks in the same way in book II, chapter 4 of the *Memorial of the Saints*: ‘Those who had previously devoted themselves under a rule or an abbot.’ And Saint Benedict speaks in this way throughout, as do the authors cited in this *Concordia*. Monks are not subjected separately to a rule or to an abbot, but simultaneously to a rule and an abbot.”

The same author again, concerning the title of chapter 46, “Concerning the old or the young,” says:

> “In this title the particle *vel* is used copulatively, not disjunctively, because the chapter deals with both.”

As for why, in the foundations of monasteries and in the acts of the saints, the rule of Saints Benedict and Columbanus is so often proposed and prescribed for observance, let the following few points suffice.

The reason is that both are mentioned because, as we recalled above, blessed Columbanus had established certain laws and institutions so that the monks might adhere to the Benedictine Rule more carefully and strictly. Moreover, the teaching, piety, and holiness of Columbanus and his disciples had so illuminated all Gaul that everyone called the rule of Saint Benedict by the name of Columbanus, since Columbanus was regarded as its exceptionally devoted observer. Thus, although it was one and the same rule, it acquired a double name. The same thing repeatedly occurs even today when one reads of the Cluniac Rule, the Cistercian Rule, the Rule of the Celestines, the Camaldolese, and so forth.

Likewise, the Cluniac, Cistercian, Bec, Celestine, and Sylvestrine Orders, although they profess no rule other than the Benedictine, are adorned with differing constitutions and institutions by which they are distinguished from other followers of that same Rule.

This truth is supported by the privilege or confirmation of the foundation of the nuns of Blessed Mary of Soissons, issued by Drausius, bishop of that city, in the fourth year of the reign of Clotaire III. At the end we read:

> “So that within the monastery the virgins and chaste women may serve the Lord, according to the vow of the aforementioned God-fearing men who constructed the rule of Saint Benedict; so that, after they have entered that monastery to serve the Lord, they may have no permission to leave it; and, following the manner of the monastery of Luxeuil, which blessed Columbanus governed—that is, following the aforementioned Rule—they may strive in all things to observe it for the advancement of their souls.”

Notice, reader, the words “following the manner of the monastery of Luxeuil.” By these words that privilege plainly teaches and urges them to fulfill the precepts of the Rule of Saint Benedict according to the manner of the monastery of Luxeuil—that is, as it was observed there—together with the statutes drawn up by blessed Columbanus.

Finally, as though to provide strength and confirmation for what we have brought forward concerning the Benedictine and Columbanian Rules, let us produce some passages from the foundation charter of the monastery of Solignac—which charter asserts that its founder was Saint Eligius, bishop of Noyon—and which are relevant to our subject and worthy of being received with every veneration by Benedictines.

For the charter proclaims that Eligius himself was a member of the Benedictine family—as, with Christ’s favor, we shall demonstrate more clearly than daylight when we publish the Lives of the saints of our Order—as well as blessed Columbanus and the monks of his monastery at Luxeuil.

In this foundation charter, after the beginning, blessed Eligius addresses the abbot and his monks as follows:

> “On this condition, however, that you and your successors follow the path of the religious life of the most holy men of the monastery of Luxeuil, and firmly keep the rule of the most blessed Fathers Benedict and Columbanus.”

And after much intervening material:

> “In the same manner I ask you, most blessed Father Remaclus, abbot, and your successors or subjects; I beseech you by the majesty of the undivided Trinity to keep with all vigilance the rule of the aforementioned Fathers, which they observe in the often-mentioned monastery of Luxeuil.”

These statements are too clear for us to spend time explaining them. Let it therefore stand, on the basis of what has been said, that the rule of Saint Benedict is the rule of Saint Columbanus—especially since the authors always speak of one rule, not of rules, as will also become clear below.

Let us now proceed to other arguments—or rather to arguments always proving the same point.

The author of the life of Saint Tillo, disciple of blessed Remaclus, abbot of Solignac, while recounting that holy man’s novitiate, says:

> “When Tillo had therefore arrived at that monastery [Solignac] and had been received by the abbot with the greatest joy, marked by the novitiate of Christ and desiring Jesus alone with the most ardent love, he began to live among the brothers under the rule of the holy Fathers Columbanus and Benedict.”

So reads the manuscript book of that same monastery.

From the manuscript *Life of Desiderius*, bishop of Cahors, who flourished around the year 639:

> “At that time no monastic institution or habit of religion, or rule of a monastery, had entered the city of Cahors. The institutions of Benedict were not far away; in the time of Desiderius this sect”—that of Benedict—“entered Cahors. Under him this religious observance began to grow; for in his time the monastery of Moissac was completed by the praiseworthy men Ansbertus and Leothadius, and in the same town a monastery was begun in those days by holy men. Many other monasteries planted under his rule grew.”

From the *Life of Saint Agilus*, first abbot of the monastery of Rebais, a contemporary of Saint Columbanus, written in an ancient and excellent hand:

> “Agnoaldus, the father of Saint Agilus, had Columbanus stay for a time at his estate called Honorifiacus; he wished his son Agilus, then seven years old, to be blessed by him. But Columbanus persuaded the parents to offer the boy to God. On the appointed day, therefore, Agilus’s father brought his dear child to the sacred altars and offered him in the aforesaid monastery, granting by a testamentary instrument an estate and household.”

What is to be gathered from this? Clearly, that the formula for offering children to God at the altar was taken from chapter 59 of the Rule of Saint Benedict, where we read:

> “If someone from the nobility should offer his son to God in the monastery, and if the boy is still of minor age, his parents shall make the petition mentioned above. They shall wrap that petition, together with the offering, and the boy’s hand in the altar cloth, and thus offer him.”

And below:

> “If the parents wish to give anything as alms to the monastery for their reward, let them make a donation from the things they wish to give,” etc.

The *Life of Saint Rigomer*, from a manuscript of the monastery of Fleury, supplies the following. At the same time—that is, during the reign of Childebert, king of the Franks—

> “Saint Avitus and Saint Carilefus, in the solitude of a vast wilderness, magnificently built two cells for God under the holy rule”—namely, the Benedictine Rule—“supported also by the assistance of Saint Innocent of the city of Le Mans,” etc.

The manuscript *Life of Saint Ansbert*, monk of the monastery of Fontenelle—now Saint-Wandrille—and later archbishop of Rouen, repeatedly makes it clear that both Wandregisilus and Ansbert professed the Benedictine institution. Consequently, it must be acknowledged that the monks in that monastery observed the norm of Saint Benedict at that time, namely during the reigns of Lothair and Dagobert, kings of the Franks. But let us hear the biographer:

> “After Saint Ansbert became archbishop, by the authority of his privilege he decreed that, throughout succeeding times, according to the rule of Saint Father Benedict—and as the authority of the privileges of the preceding kings, namely Clovis and Clotaire, and likewise Childeric and Theoderic, demonstrates—the monks of Fontenelle should choose for themselves an abbot in perpetuity from among themselves. By this expression of rightful obligation he also binds those present and future who were to serve there, so that, just as under his governance, so thereafter both they and their descendants should faithfully serve Christ according to the rule of Saint Benedict,” etc.

These passages are also found among the Gallican councils, as well as among the general councils in the latest edition from the Royal Press.

In the *Life of Blessed Aichadrius*, in Surius under 15 October, it is reported that Saint Philibert, abbot of the monastery of Jumièges, after avoiding the persecution of Ebroin and taking refuge with Ansoaldus, bishop of Poitiers, was asked by that bishop to undertake the governance of the monastery he had recently built. Saint Philibert agreed on the condition that blessed Aichadrius, who at that time presided over the monastery of Quinçay, would not refuse to be placed over the monastery of Jumièges.

> “For this reason,” says Fulbert, the author of the Life, “blessed Aichadrius saw them in a dream: the bishop was offering a pastoral staff, while blessed Philibert was offering the rule of Saint Benedict. Both, as though with one voice, said: ‘Rise, brother, and obediently undertake the office imposed upon you by God. Receive the staff, by which you may correct the errors of your subjects and restore them to the right path of discipline; receive also the book, so that you may first keep what is written in it yourself and never cease instructing your subjects in these matters.’”

From this one may observe the ancient custom of presenting the rule and the pastoral staff at an abbot’s blessing, a custom that has continued to the present day; see the *Roman Pontifical* in the rite for blessing an abbot. It also follows that in these monasteries—namely Quinçay, founded by Ansoaldus on the island of Herio, and Jumièges—the holy Rule was already in force at that time.

Canon 15 of Saint Leodegarius, bishop of Autun, in A.D. 670, must by no means be passed over in silence:

> “Concerning abbots and monks, it is fitting to observe that whatever the canonical order or the rule of Saint Benedict teaches, they must fulfill and preserve in all things. For if everything has been legitimately preserved among the abbots and monasteries, then, by God’s favor, the number of monks will increase, and the whole world will be freed from harmful contagions through their continual prayers.”

Here “the canonical order” refers to abbots, since at that time those who presided over canons were also accustomed to be called abbots; the rule of Saint Benedict, however, refers to monks.

To this may be added the observation of the very learned Menardus in his preface to the *Concordia of the Rules of Saint Benedict, Abbot of Aniane*, addressed to all abbots and monks. Explaining these words, he says:

> “There comes to mind what tepid and sluggish monks are accustomed to say: ‘What do the other rules contribute to this one [the Benedictine Rule]? What does it concern me to read rules that I have not promised to observe?’” etc.

He continues:

> “Since this author is speaking to all the monks of the Western Church, and certain more sluggish men object that they have vowed only to the rule of Saint Benedict and are ignorant of the others contained in this work, it is clear that, in the time of the author of this *Concordia*—that is, in the time of Charlemagne and Louis the Pious—the monks of the Western Church observed only the rule of Saint Benedict. Otherwise the author’s dedication of the letter and his objection would be pointless.”

But, lest some scruple trouble us again, it is worth hearing the minor objection of certain people who assert that the rule of blessed Benedict was published universally throughout Gaul only in the year 743. They try, quite unsuccessfully, to prove this from canon 1 of the Synod of Liptina, in volume I of the *Councils of Gaul*:

> “The abbots and monks received the rule of Saint Benedict in order to restore the norm of the regular life.”

As though the word *recipio*, formed from *re* and *capio*, did not signify to take up again, take back, resume, or recover something that had once been deposited or handed over. Cicero, *On the Orator* II:

> “To recover a lost citadel.”

And Livy, book IX:

> “Let them recover the arms which they surrendered by agreement.”

That synod therefore declares that the abbots and monks who had gathered at Liptina wished to restore to their former rigor the observances of the Benedictine Rule, which had been treated with indifference, willingly submitting themselves to its sanctions.

Otherwise, if the synod had not intended this, it would with greater right have been necessary to admit that the clergy, bishops, and others had then first accepted the ecclesiastical laws—which it would be utterly absurd even to imagine, much less affirm. The aforementioned canon reads as follows:

> “And all the clergy of the ecclesiastical order, priests and deacons together with the other clerics, receiving the canons of the ancient Fathers, promised that they would recover ecclesiastical rights in conduct, teaching, and ministry.”

Finally, the council likewise held at Liptina, but in the preceding year—that is, convened in 742—clarifies and confirms what we reported above, in its final canon:

> “Let the monks and the monasterial handmaids of God strive to organize and govern their monasteries or hospices according to the rule of Saint Benedict, and let them not neglect to lead their own life according to the ordinance of the aforementioned Father.”

By this canon, are not all the shadows of doubt—if the word “received” has introduced any—completely dispelled? For here it presupposes that the monks had formerly enrolled themselves in the Benedictine fellowship, since the council exhorts them not to neglect to order their lives according to the rule of Dom Benedict and the ordinance of that same Father. For someone is said to neglect something when he omits or despises a command to which he was previously bound, or an office or vow entrusted or committed to him.

It follows with absolute certainty from all the foregoing that, before Louis the Pious became emperor—and no one denies that very many monasteries were then built for Benedictine monks—the rule of Saint Benedict existed at least in these bishoprics: Angers, Poitiers, Orléans, Cahors, Paris, Le Mans, Soissons, Besançon, Rouen, Meaux, Mainz, Tours, Cambrai, Limoges, Amiens, Autun, and Rennes. But enough about this.

**“But through fear of the Franks.”** What blessed Lanfrancus touches upon briefly here is narrated at length, if I am not mistaken, by Eadmer in book III of his *History of Recent Events*, p. 57. After proving that Matilda, wife of Henry I, king of the English, had not been bound in the midst of a council to the monastic life, since she had not willingly taken the veil in a monastery at the age of seven but had done so to safeguard her chastity, he asks the opinion of the bishops who were present at that council. They, bringing forward the great Lanfrancus, address blessed Anselm as follows:

> “Although we could prove this by a slight argument, we shall nevertheless, since there is no need, refrain from doing so, holding as stronger than our own arguments the equivalent judgment on this matter pronounced for a similar reason by your predecessor of venerable memory, our father and teacher Lanfrancus.”

And after other material:

> “He himself [Lanfrancus] resolved the question by the advice of the general council in such a way that he judged that the woman ought to be shown the reverence due for the chastity which she had testified that she loved by so clear an indication, rather than that any continence of religious observance should be forcibly imposed upon her unless she sought it of her own will.”

[Note: [Col. 0610B]]

## On professed nuns or those offered at the altar, and on those who were neither professed nor offered, or who did not take refuge in the monastery out of love for the religious life

LANFRANCUS, archbishop, to COISFRIDUS, venerable bishop: greetings and service.

Concerning the nuns about whom your most affectionate fatherhood wrote to me, I reply as follows. Those nuns who have made a profession to observe the Rule, or who, although not yet professed, have nevertheless been offered at the altar, are to be admonished, rebuked, and compelled to observe the Rule according to their conduct and way of life. Those, however, who are neither professed nor offered are for the present to be left alone, until their intentions regarding the observance of the order have been investigated more carefully. But those who took refuge in the monastery not out of love for the religious life but, as you say, through fear of the Franks—if they can prove this by the firm testimony of better nuns—are to be granted the freedom to leave. This is the counsel of the king and of us. May almighty God preserve your life according to his good pleasure.

## LETTER XXXIII. TO DOMNALD, BISHOP OF IRELAND

[Note: [Col. 0610B]]

### To Letter XXXIII

**To Domnald, or Dofnald, bishop of Ireland.** By this man he understands, I think, the bishop of Armagh or of Dublin, as metropolitan of the whole island of Ireland, just as above, when writing to John, archbishop of Rouen, in Letter 14, he calls him the archbishop of the Northmen. Nevertheless, that this metropolitan was subject to the jurisdiction of the archbishop of Canterbury is attested by the Venerable Bede, book II of *The Ecclesiastical History of the English People*. See what was said concerning Letter 4 above.

Bede describes the ancient condition of the Irish Church in the following way, in the cited passage, book III, chapter 4:

> “The island itself is accustomed always to have as its ruler an abbot who is a presbyter, to whose jurisdiction the whole province, and even the bishops themselves, are subject in an unusual order, following the example of its first teacher [Columbanus], who was not a bishop but a presbyter and a monk,” etc.

**“To hold this opinion concerning infants.”** From the words that follow, it seems clear that he is speaking of the communion of the body of Christ, which was customarily given to infants before the use of reason, immediately after they had received baptism.

For it was an ancient custom in the Church to confer the sacrament of the Eucharist upon baptized children, as is clear from blessed Dionysius, chapter 7 of *The Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*:

> Μεταδίδωσι δὲ τῷ παιδὶ τῶν ἱερῶν συμβόλων ὁ ἱεράρχης, ὅπως ἐν αὐτοῖς ἀνατραφείη.

That is:

> “Moreover, the hierarch makes the child a participant in the sacred mysteries, so that the child may be brought up in them,” etc.

Also from the *Book of Sacraments* of Dom Gregory, published by Hugo Menardus, in the section “Concerning the baptism of Holy Saturday,” where it speaks of the baptism of infants:

> “They are not even forbidden to nurse before Holy Communion, if necessity requires it.”

And from a letter of Jesse, bishop of Amiens, to priests concerning baptism, in the middle of the work—printed after the letters of Hincmar edited by Jean Cordesius:

> “Finally, the infant is confirmed by the body and blood of Christ, so that he may be a member of him who suffered and rose again for him,” etc.

This is taken from Saint Augustine’s Letter 102 to Vitalis the Pelagian. See p. 369, if you wish, as well as the aforementioned Menardus’s notes on the cited *Book of Sacraments*, p. 106.

Blessed Lanfrancus proves in this letter that for infants who have not yet attained the use of reason, receiving the Eucharist is not necessary for salvation. The Council of Trent also declared this, session 21, chapter 4 and canon 4. It gives the reason in these words:

> “Since, having been regenerated through the washing of baptism and incorporated into Christ, they cannot lose at that age the grace they have already obtained as children. Nor is antiquity to be condemned for having at some time preserved this custom in certain places,” etc.

Infants received the Holy Eucharist not only at the very reception of baptism; afterward also, as a practice of antiquity, they received the remnants of the sacrifice on Wednesdays and Fridays—mixed with wine and with a fast imposed upon them. See the Second Council of Mâcon, canon 6; the Third Council of Tours, canon 19; and Evagrius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book IV, chapter 35.

**“To be baptized by a faithful layman if a priest is absent,” etc.** This opinion is so clear, both from the many decrees of councils and from various enactments of the Fathers—and it is also nearly a daily occurrence in practice—that it requires no proof. Everyone admits that, in the absence of a cleric, a layman, and indeed even a woman, may in an urgent necessity baptize a small child with water in the Christian rite.

**“Yet they do not exclude him,” etc., “from the fellowship of the faithful.”** Because of the reasons given above by the Council of Trent.

**“We have decided that they must renounce.”** There is such an enormous lacuna in this letter that we had nothing besides the opening and one or another line at the end. But, thanks to Jean le Prévôt, we now publish the complete letter; he himself took the trouble to copy it from the *Book of Irish Letters* published by Usserius and to send it to me.

Nevertheless, the fact that the letter is not entirely complete in every respect is suggested by the last line of the copy borrowed from Jacques Sirmond. It reads as follows:

> “If he should presume, with polluted hands, to sanctify the body and blood of Christ. May almighty God bless you and grant you, from your pastor, the joy you desire.”

These words do not occur in the Usserian edition. It would therefore not be far from the truth to assert that this is not the conclusion of this letter, but rather the conclusion of a reply to Letter 37 of the Dubliners, or to some other letter of that kind.]

[Col. 0532B]

He teaches that for infants, before the use of reason, receiving the Eucharist is by no means necessary for salvation; but he declines to resolve questions concerning secular literature, as unworthy of a bishop.

LANFRANCUS, unworthy bishop of the holy Church of Canterbury, to DOMNALD, venerable bishop of Ireland, and to those who sent him their letter: greetings and blessing.

We were on a journey, far removed from the city in which our episcopal see is located, when we received your letter, delivered by your messenger. We asked him to remain with us at least for a few days, so that, after consulting the books, he could bring you an answer suited to our ability to your questions. He refused to comply with our request, claiming at length that he could not remain longer. Therefore, in fatherly charity we admonish your most affectionate fraternity not to take offense that we reply so briefly concerning so great a matter.

Indeed, with every ambiguity removed, know that neither the churches overseas nor we English hold the opinion concerning infants that you suppose. For we believe generally that it is greatly beneficial for all people of every age, both living and dying, to fortify themselves by receiving the body and blood of the Lord. Nevertheless, if baptized persons happen to depart this world immediately before receiving the body and blood of Christ, we do not at all believe that they perish eternally on this account—God forbid! Otherwise the truth would not be truthful, since it says: “Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved” (Mark 16:16). And through the prophet:

> “I will pour clean water over you, and you shall be cleansed from all your impurities” (Ezek. 36:25).

All expositors of this view unanimously affirm that this was said concerning baptism. The apostle Peter likewise says:

> “Baptism, corresponding to this, now saves you” (1 Pet. 3:21).

And the apostle Paul:

> “All of you who were baptized into Christ have put on Christ” (Gal. 3:27).

For to put on Christ is to have God dwelling within oneself through the remission of sins.

For that saying which the Lord speaks in the Gospel—

> “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in yourselves” (John 6:54)—

cannot, insofar as it concerns eating with the mouth, have been spoken universally of everyone. Many of the holy martyrs departed from the body after undergoing various tortures even before baptism; nevertheless, the Church counts them among the martyrs and believes them saved on the basis of that testimony of the Lord in which he says:

> “Whoever acknowledges me before men, I also will acknowledge before my Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 10:32).

The canons also prescribe that an unbaptized infant, if death is imminent, may be baptized by a faithful layman if a priest is absent. Yet, if the child dies immediately, they do not exclude him from the fellowship of the faithful.

The Lord’s saying must therefore be understood in this way: every believer who is capable, through understanding, of receiving the divine mystery eats and drinks the flesh and blood of Christ not only with the mouth of the body but also with the love and sweetness of the heart—namely, by loving and cherishing with a pure conscience the fact that Christ assumed flesh for our salvation, hung upon the cross, rose again, and ascended; and by imitating his footsteps and sharing in his sufferings insofar as human weakness permits and divine grace grants. For this is truly and beneficially to eat the flesh of Christ and drink his blood.

Explaining this opinion in the book *On Christian Doctrine*, blessed Augustine says as follows, book III, chapter 10:

> “He seems to command a crime or a disgraceful act; but it is a figurative expression, commanding us to share in the Lord’s passion and to store up in our memory, with sweetness and benefit, the fact that his flesh was wounded and crucified for us.”

He calls it a figure, that is, figurative speech. He does not deny the reality of Christ’s flesh and blood—as many schismatics have thought, and as they still do not cease to think.

And the Lord says in the Gospel:

> “Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him” (John 6:57).

Explaining this, blessed Augustine says in *Tractate 26 on the Gospel of John*:

> “For this is to eat the flesh of Christ and drink his blood beneficially: to remain in Christ and to have Christ remaining in oneself. Judas too, who betrayed the Lord, received him with his mouth together with the other apostles; but because he did not eat with his heart, he received judgment of eternal condemnation for himself.”

You sent us questions concerning secular literature to resolve; but it is not fitting for an episcopal vocation to devote itself to studies of this kind. Formerly, indeed, we spent our youth upon them, but when we approached pastoral responsibility, we decided that they must be renounced.

## LETTER XXXIV. TO WILLIAM, KING OF THE ENGLISH

[Note: [Col. 0611D]]

### To Letter XXXIV
To William, king of the English—first, or the Conqueror, whose antitheses Robert of Monte inserted into his supplement to Sigibert under the year 1087:

“William,” he says, “was stronger than all the nobles of Normandy, more powerful than all the kings of the English, and more worthy of praise than all his predecessors. He was wise, but crafty; wealthy, but greedy; glorious, but devoted to fame. He was humble toward those serving God, harsh toward those resisting him,” and so forth. He concludes in this way: “He had been so great a promoter of peace that a girl laden with gold could pass through the kingdom of England unharmed.”

What happened to so powerful and fortunate a king as soon as he departed this life, Orderic Vitalis presents in Book VII of his *History*: “Behold the most powerful hero, whom recently more than a hundred thousand soldiers eagerly served, and whom many peoples feared with trembling: now he has been shamefully stripped by his own men in a house not his own, and from the first until the third he was left upon the bare ground,” and so forth. It will moreover be clear from the notes below that when Blessed Lanfranc wrote this and the following letter to the king, William was staying in Normandy.

“Like an angel of God.” He alludes, I think, to the wise woman of Tekoa, who reproached David for Absalom’s return: “For my lord the king is like an angel of God, so that he is not moved either by blessing or by cursing” (2 Samuel 14:17); or perhaps to Esther 15:16. Or one might say that he called the king an angel because, just as it belongs to angels to drive away fear and provide everything prosperous and beneficial to salvation, so it is fitting for a king to calm the spirits of his subjects, repel trouble and enemies far away, and, sparing no labor, promote peace throughout the whole kingdom above all else.

“Count Ralph.” Concerning him, see Letter 40, which, like the following Letters 41 and 42, is addressed to him.

He dissuades the king from crossing the sea. He reports that Count Ralph and his army have been put to flight and that the king’s soldiers are pursuing them.

To his lord, William, king of the English, his faithful Lanfranc: faithful service and faithful prayers.

We would gladly see you like an angel of God, but at this time we do not wish you to cross the sea, because you would bring us great disgrace if you came to us to defeat such perjurers and robbers. Count Ralph—or rather, Ralph the traitor—and his entire army have been put to flight; and our men, with an innumerable multitude of Frenchmen and Englishmen, are pursuing them. A few days ago, as our princes instructed me, either those perjurers will flee from your land by sea, or our men will have them alive or dead. I am sending you the rest through this monk, whom you may safely trust, since he has pledged loyalty to me. May the almighty Lord bless you.

## Letter 35. To the same

Geoffrey, Bishop of Coutances in Normandy, whom we mentioned above in connection with Letter 33.

William de Warenne. Count of Surrey, or Southrey, in England. William of Jumièges, *History*, Book VII, chapter 22, and Book VIII, chapter 38, says that he founded the monastery of Saint Pancras in England, as Orderic Vitalis testifies in Book VIII of his *History*, under the year 1089. The testament of William, king of the English, records a donation to the church of Saint Pancras in the *Cluniac Library*, p. 531.

Robert Malet. The Malet family was very distinguished among the Caletes; hence the French proverb:

> The Malets and the Marteaus  
> Are the noblest of Caux.

Among the surnames of those who entered England with William the Conqueror, Malet is listed near the middle of the *History of Normandy* printed by André du Chesne, and also at the end of the following catalogue, headed “The surviving magnates, etc. Robert Malet, surviving.” Robert Malet is likewise found again in each of the next two catalogues, and in Orderic Vitalis, *History*, Book IX, pp. 804–805.

He congratulates the king that Norwich Castle has been recovered after the Britons were expelled and that peace has been restored throughout England.

To his most glorious lord, William, king of the English, his faithful Lanfranc: faithful service with prayers.

Glory to God in the highest, by whose mercy your kingdom has been cleansed of the Britons’ filth, Norwich Castle has been restored, and the Britons who were in it and held lands in England, their lives and limbs having been spared, have sworn that within forty days they would leave your kingdom and would not enter it again without your permission.

Those who served the traitor Ralph and his associates without land, for wages, obtained—after many entreaties—a period of one month in which to do this.

Bishop Geoffrey, William de Warenne, Robert Malet, and three hundred mailed soldiers remained in the castle, together with crossbowmen and many craftsmen skilled in siege engines. By God’s mercy, all the tumult of war has fallen silent in the land of England. May the almighty Lord bless you.

## Letter 36. From the clergy and people of the church of Dublin to Lanfranc

“Therefore we have chosen a priest,” etc. It was an ancient custom, especially in the primitive Church, for bishops to be created through the votes of the clergy and people. In the East, although it later became customary not to seek the people’s votes at episcopal elections—namely, after the Council of Nicaea, which in canon 3 commands that bishops be elected and ordained by bishops, without mentioning the clergy or people—and although the Council of Laodicea, in canon 13, forbids the election of priests to be entrusted to crowds or peoples, this right of voting in the appointment of bishops nevertheless remained with the people in the Western Churches and continued for a long time. It lasted until, after the Romans had been expelled, kings arose who considered it their prerogative that bishops should be elected only at their discretion and by their will. The very learned Sirmond proves this with many examples in his preface to the ancient formulas of episcopal promotions, at the end of Volume II of the *Councils of Gaul*.

“We have learned with complete certainty,” etc. Several formulas of this kind may be seen in the place cited immediately above, formula 7 and following.

They ask that Patrick, the priest whom they have chosen, be ordained bishop of the church of Dublin.

To the venerable metropolitan of the holy church of Canterbury, Lanfranc: the clergy and people of the church of Dublin offer due submission.

It is known to your fatherhood that the church of Dublin, which is the metropolitan church of the island of Ireland, has been deprived of its shepherd and left without a ruler. Therefore we have chosen a priest named Patrick, whom we know very well: noble by birth and character, instructed in apostolic and ecclesiastical discipline, Catholic in faith, prudent in understanding the Scriptures, and well trained in ecclesiastical doctrine. We ask that he be ordained bishop for us as soon as possible, so that, with God as author, he may regularly preside over us and benefit us, and so that we may serve safely under his governance. For the integrity of rulers is the salvation of their subjects; and where obedience is sound, there the form of doctrine is sound.

## Letter 37. Lanfranc to Gothric, king of Ireland

Gothric, king of Ireland. A petty king of Dublin, according to James Ussher in his *Collection of Irish Letters*, in the note to Blessed Lanfranc’s letter to Terdelvacus and to this letter: “This Gothric,” he says, “seems to have been none other than Godred, surnamed Crouan. He is mentioned in the *Chronicle of the Kings of Man* under the year 1066. Godred subjected Dublin and a large part of Leinster to himself. He so completely subdued the Scots that no one who built a ship or boat dared insert more than three nails. He reigned for sixteen years and died on an island called Ile.”

“Patrick, whom he sent to us to be consecrated,” etc. I suspect that Patrick was the bearer of the letters from the clergy and people of Dublin, as seems clear both from those letters themselves and also from this letter to Gothric. Moreover, following the custom of his predecessors, after his ordination he made a profession of obedience in the following form.

### Profession of Patrick, bishop of Dublin

“Whoever presides over others, if he himself is also subject to others, ought not to disdain this; rather, for God’s sake, he should strive humbly to show his superiors in every respect the obedience that he wishes to receive from his own subjects. Therefore I, Patrick, elected bishop to govern Dublin, the metropolitan see of Ireland, offer to you, reverend Father Lanfranc, primate of the Britons and archbishop of the holy church of Canterbury, the charter of my profession, and I promise that I shall obey you and your successors in everything pertaining to the Christian religion.”

“To leave those lawfully joined to them at their own discretion and will.” Blessed Pope Gregory VII had warned Blessed Lanfranc against this serpent-like disease in Letter 1 of the appendix, in these words: “Although your brotherhood does not need an admonisher, nevertheless, urged by our concern, we warn you to strive everywhere to cut away the more serious vices; and among all things, above all, to prohibit by every means the crime that we have heard of concerning the Scots—namely, that many of them not only abandon their own wives but even sell them,” and so forth. Blessed Anselm’s Letters 142 and 147, Book III, demonstrate that this pestilence was still spreading in his time. Earlier authors report that this vice was innate not only among Scots and Irish but also among the English, long before the time of Saint Lanfranc. Gildas, in *The Ruin of Britain*, shortly after the beginning, says: “Britain has kings, but tyrants.” A little later: “They have very many wives, but they fornicate and commit adultery.” Saint Boniface, archbishop of Mainz, brings that shameful charge against Ethelbert, king of the English, in William of Malmesbury, Book I, *Deeds of the English*. That such lust was almost hereditary among the Scots is shown by Saint Jerome, Book II, *Against Jovinian*, near the middle.

He indicates that he has consecrated Patrick as bishop and exhorts the king to correct the abuses said to be practiced concerning marriage and to make good use of Patrick’s counsels.

Lanfranc, archbishop not by his own merits but by the grace of God, sends greetings with prayers to the glorious king of Ireland, Gothric.

We honorably received our venerable brother and fellow bishop Patrick, whom, dearest son, your excellence sent to us for consecration; and, with the grace of the Spirit cooperating, we consecrated him with the rites required by canonical institution. After consecrating him, we sent him back to his own see, according to the custom of our predecessors, with letters bearing our testimony.

Although he reported many good things about your glory, and many things worthy of praise, we nevertheless believe it is not inappropriate to spur your commendable efforts by our exhortation. Just as fire shines more brightly and grows greater when fanned by the wind, so true virtue shines more beautifully through true praise and is increased for the better. We therefore ask you, as one should ask a precious son of the holy Roman Church, to preserve inviolate, with complete sincerity of mind, the true faith handed down by God himself, by his holy apostles, and by the orthodox Fathers; to display works corresponding to the faith insofar as your strength permits; and to show your majesty severe toward the proud and gentle toward the humble.

It is reported that in your kingdom men take wives either from their own kindred or from the family of deceased wives; that others abandon wives lawfully joined to them at their own discretion and will; and that some give their own wives to others and receive the wives of others in an abominable exchange. For God’s sake and for the sake of your soul, command that these things, and any other crimes that may exist, be corrected in the land under your authority. With divine assistance, show yourself to your subjects in such a way that lovers of good may love good things more ardently and those who desire evil may not dare to practice wicked deeds. If you do this, you will reign longer on earth amid the prosperity of temporal affairs, and afterward, destined to reign without end, you will pass from your earthly kingdom to the heavenly kingdoms.

I would have written more to you and at greater length, but you have with you the bishop mentioned above, your own bishop, nourished from childhood in monastic disciplines, most diligently trained in knowledge of the divine Scriptures, and, insofar as we have been able to know him, most fittingly adorned with the virtues of good works. If you listen to him attentively when he speaks to you frequently about your soul; if, having listened, you obey him as a spiritual father in matters pertaining to God; and if, having obeyed, you store in the treasury of your heart what he says to you, we hope, through the mercy of God, that neither will you go perniciously astray, nor will you allow your subjects to persist long in obstinate private [variant: wicked] deeds. May the almighty Lord defend your excellence against the enemies of mind and body by the belt [variant: arm] of his power, and, after a long life in this age, lead you happily to the life that has no end.

## Letter 38. To Terdelvacus, king of Ireland

Terdelvacus, king of Ireland. Since nothing else is available concerning Terdelvacus, it seemed appropriate to insert here James Ussher’s conjecture. In his notes to the *Irish Letters*, he asserts that Terdelvacus was by no means Gothric’s successor, but that at the same time Gothric acted as petty king of Dublin and Terdelvacus as high king of Ireland.

“Against the prohibition of the holy canons,” etc. I consider these familiar matters not to require repetition here. Concerning adulterous marriages, enough has been said in the preceding letter. The requirement that a bishop be ordained not by one bishop but by three was noted somewhat in connection with Letter 12. Ancient canons and the decrees of the Fathers repeatedly forbid establishing several bishops in one city: Pope Hilary, Letter 2, no. 4; the First Council of Lyons, canon 5; the Council of Chalon, A.D. 650, canon 4. Likewise, that money should not be demanded for ordinations is stated in the Second Council of Tours, canon 27, and the Second Council of Nicaea, canon 19. Concerning the anointing with chrism to be conferred in baptism, see our Menardus, drawing extensively both on the judgments of the Fathers and on various conciliar canons, in his *Book on the Sacramentary of Saint Gregory*, pp. 108 and following.

He praises the king for what he had learned from Patrick and urges him to order a gathering of bishops and others, and to attend it himself, for the eradication of certain wicked customs.

Lanfranc, sinner and unworthy archbishop of the holy church of Canterbury, sends blessing with service and prayers to the magnificent king of Ireland, Terdelvacus.

God has bestowed no greater mercy upon the earth than when he raises lovers of peace and justice to govern souls or bodies, and especially when he entrusts the kingdoms of this world to good kings. From this arise peace, discord is put to sleep, and, to embrace everything briefly, the observance of the Christian religion is established. A prudent observer understands that this was then divinely granted to the people of Ireland when almighty God gave your excellence the right of royal power over that land. For our brother and fellow bishop Patrick has related so many and such great good qualities concerning your pious humility toward the good, your strict severity toward the wicked, and your most discerning equity toward the whole human race that, although we have never seen you, we love you as though we had seen you and wish to offer you wholesome counsel and serve you with complete sincerity as though we had seen and known you well.

Yet among the many things that please us, certain things have been reported that displease us: namely, that in your kingdom each person abandons at his own discretion a wife lawfully joined to him, without any canonical cause intervening, and rashly joins himself, by a marital or fornication-based union deserving punishment, either to another woman related by blood to himself or to the wife he abandoned, or to one whom another man has abandoned through a similar wickedness; that bishops are consecrated by one bishop; that several bishops are ordained in villages or cities; that infants are baptized without consecrated chrism; and that holy orders are conferred by bishops in exchange for money.

No one who has even moderately read the sacred writings is unaware that all these things, and any similar practices, are contrary to evangelical and apostolic authority, contrary to the prohibition of the holy canons, and contrary to the institution of all the orthodox Fathers who preceded us. The more horrifying these practices are in the sight of God and his saints, the more diligently they must be prohibited throughout your realm by your commands without any delay; and unless they are corrected once prohibited, they must be punished with the strictest severity of your terror. For you can offer God no gift either greater or more pleasing than to strive to govern divine and human affairs according to their proper laws.

Remembering, therefore, the divine judgment, by which you will render an account to God for the kingdom entrusted to you, command all the bishops and religious men to assemble. Present yourself, together with your nobles, at their sacred gathering. Strive to eradicate from your kingdom these wicked customs and all others disapproved by the sacred laws, so that the King of kings and Lord of lords, when he sees your royal majesty subject in all things to his commands, gentle toward his servants and faithful people through fear and love of him, and hostile to the enemies of divine religion through divine zeal, may himself, appeased, hear you and your faithful people when you call upon him, crush your enemies, and grant you lasting peace in this age and eternal life in the age to come.

## Letter 39. To Count Roger

To Count Roger, perhaps the son of Count William, son of Osbern, if it is permissible to insert a conjecture. Concerning him, see William of Jumièges, *History*, Book VII, chapter 25, and William of Malmesbury, Book III, *Deeds of the English*, under William I: “Roger,” he says, “a young man of detestable treachery, whom the king bound in chains, spent—or rather inhabited—prison throughout his life, and did not resemble his father in character,” and so forth.

“Your glorious father.” William. See below, in the note to Letter 42.

“Placita.” Among learned Latin authors, this word is repeatedly used for decrees, because what has been decreed appears to have pleased the senate or the elders. Pliny, Book XXIX, chapter 1: “The same age, under the principate of Nero, passed over to Testus, who erased all the decrees of the elders,” and so forth. Here, however, *placita* signifies juridical or legal assemblies. The capitulary of Charles the Bald, chapter 20, or chapter 2 of the Council of Quierzy, says: “Let all bishops hold assemblies in their dioceses, the royal envoys in their assigned districts, and the counts in their counties,” and so forth. Likewise, in the announcement of the same Charles and of his nephew Lothair at Saint-Quentin, near the middle: “Throughout our kingdom, let the bishops, our envoys, and the counts hold assemblies; and let every man who ought to attend an assembly attend it without exception or excuse.” The Sixth Council of Arles, chapter 22, commands “that public and secular assemblies be held neither in the courtyards of basilicas nor in the basilicas themselves.” *Placitum* also means a lawsuit, whence the French words *plaids* and *placitare*—that is, to litigate or contend in court, or to act according to the pleas of laws and judgments, in French *plaider*.

He entrusts him with guarding the castles in the king’s name, proposes his father’s example of faithful service, and reports the king’s prohibition against the sheriffs holding assemblies until the king returns.

Lanfranc, archbishop by the grace of God, sends greetings and blessing to his dearest son and friend, Count Roger.

Our lord, the king of the English, sends greetings to you and to all of us as his faithful men, in whom he has great confidence, and commands us to take as much care as we can of his castles, lest—God forbid—they be handed over to his enemies. Therefore I ask you, as I ought to ask a dearest son whom, God as my witness, I love with all my heart and wish to serve, and whose father I loved as my own soul, to take such care of this matter and of every duty owed to our lord the king that you may receive praise from God, from him, and from all good men.

Always keep in your memory how your glorious father lived, how faithfully he served his lord, with what courage he acquired many things, and with what great honor he retained what he had acquired.

The king has also ordered that his sheriffs hold no assemblies in your lands until he crosses the sea and personally hears your cases between you and those sheriffs.

I would gladly speak with you. If you wish this, let me know at what place we may meet and confer about your affairs and those of our lord the king. I am ready to come to meet you wherever you command.

I ask you to do justice for the bearer of these letters, a man named Beringer, concerning those men against whom he brings a complaint over his horse, which he says was stolen from him. May the almighty Lord bless you and order your life in all goodness.

## Letter 40. To the same

William, Count Roger’s father, whose prudence, etc. “This legitimate and generous man,” says William of Jumièges, Book VII, chapter 25, “took Adeliza, daughter of Roger Toenite, as his wife, and by her fathered two sons, William and Roger the rebellious. He founded two monasteries of monks dedicated to Saint Mary, Queen of Heaven: one at Lire and the other at Cormeilles.” A little later: “He obtained the county of Hereford, together with a large part of the kingdom, by his judgment and strength,” and so forth. William of Malmesbury, *Deeds of the English*, under William I, near the middle, says: “William, son of the prince Osbern, was comparable to the best, and I do not know whether he should even be preferred to them. By his counsel King William was first encouraged to invade England, and soon, aided by his valor, to hold it by force. He possessed a courage of mind commended by an almost prodigal generosity,” and so forth.

“Concerning perjury or fraud,” etc. What Blessed Lanfranc appears to have intended by these words is reported by Florence of Worcester under the year 1074: “Roger, earl of Hereford, son of William, count of that same district, gave his sister in marriage to Ralph, count of the East Angles, contrary to the command of King William. They celebrated a splendid wedding with a very large gathering of nobles in the county of Cambridge, at a place called Ixninga, and there, with many consenting, formed a great conspiracy against King William. As soon as he could, Roger went to Lanfranc, archbishop of Canterbury, and received from him—although unwillingly—penance under oath for the deed. On Lanfranc’s advice he then sought King William, who was staying in Normandy, revealed the affair to him in its proper order, and voluntarily surrendered himself to his mercy,” and so forth. These final words clearly establish that King William was in Normandy while Blessed Lanfranc was sending him Letters 35 and 36.

He urges him to abstain from perjury and fraud and to imitate his father’s loyalty toward the king and others.

Lanfranc, archbishop by the grace of God, sends greetings and blessing to his dearest son and friend, Count Roger.

I have heard things about you that I would not wish to hear, and I grieve beyond what I can say. It would not be fitting for the son of Count William—whose prudence, goodness, and fidelity toward his lord and all his friends were known throughout many lands—to be called unfaithful and to suffer disgrace on account of perjury or fraud. Rather, it would be fitting for the son of so great a man to imitate his father and offer others an example of every goodness and fidelity. Therefore I ask you, sweetest son and dearest friend, for God’s sake and for your honor, that, if you are guilty in such a matter, you repent; but if you are not guilty, show by the clearest evidence that you are not. Whatever the truth may be, I ask you to come to me, secure in the knowledge that neither on your journey here nor on your return will you suffer any hindrance from us or from the king’s men. May the almighty Lord bless you.

## Letter 41. To the same

He says that he cannot be released from the excommunication with which he had bound him unless he seeks the king’s mercy, and promises his assistance in obtaining it.

Lanfranc, archbishop by the grace of God, sends to his once-dearest son and friend, Count Roger, the wish that he may understand rightly and take wholesome care of his soul.

I grieve for you beyond what can be said, because, God as my witness, I loved you; and I desired with all my heart to love you and serve you. But because, at the devil’s prompting and on the advice of wicked men, you undertook things that you ought never to have undertaken, I was compelled to change my mind and turn my affection, not into hatred, but into resentment of mind and righteous severity. Nevertheless, through messengers and letters, once and again I invited you to come to me, so that you might receive from me, as from a spiritual father and sincere friend, counsel for your soul and abandon, through better advice, the foolish plan you had conceived. You refused to do this.

Therefore, by canonical authority, I have cursed and excommunicated you and all your accomplices, separated you from the thresholds of the holy Church and from the fellowship of the faithful, and commanded by pastoral authority that the same be done throughout the whole of England. I cannot absolve you from this bond of anathema unless you seek the mercy of my lord the king and do justice to him and to the others whose property you unjustly plundered.

You sent word that you still wished to come. I would gladly have this happen if I did not fear incurring the king’s anger on this account. Nevertheless, through a messenger and by letter, I shall inform him of your repentance, humility, and prayers, and, without compromising his loyalty, I shall help you as best I can. In the meantime, I ask and advise you to remain quiet and not attempt anything by which you might incur his greater anger.

## Letter 42. To Abbot B……

He asks him to grant pardon, for his sake, to the bearer of the letter.

Lanfranc, archbishop by divine favor and not by his own merits, sends greetings with prayers to Abbot B……

The bearer of these letters says that he incurred your anger and therefore abandoned his homeland, where he was born and had lived, as well as his parents and friends. Because he thought that you ought to do much for my sake, he asked to be assisted by my letters to your fatherhood. Therefore, moved by our prayers, may your kindness pardon him, so that he may know that he himself has sought pardon for his offense from our friend.

## Letter 43. To Father Anselm

Anselm. This is the great Anselm, first prior, then abbot, and finally successor of Blessed Lanfranc as archbishop of Canterbury. Eadmer, whom Anselm held most dear as his secretary, wrote his remarkable life. The same author, in the book entitled *The History of Recent Events*, recounts at length the great labors and exertions that this most holy man endured until death for ecclesiastical liberty, with incomparable piety, learning, and steadfastness. Concerning Saint Anselm, see the *Chronicle of Bec*, pp. 2, 5, and 6; the *Life of the Venerable William III, Abbot of Bec*, pp. 41–42, in the appendix; and almost innumerable other authors.

“While setting out for Rome.” Namely, in the year 1071, both to receive the pallium and to settle the dispute between himself and Thomas of York. Concerning this, see above, in Letter 4a, and in the *Life of Saint Lanfranc*, chapter 11, pp. 11–12. Saint Lanfranc seems to have gone to Rome five times: first, because of Berengar; second, on account of the marriage of Duke William; third, to attend the Roman council; fourth, to obtain confirmation of John of Avranches, elected archbishop of Rouen; and finally, with the archbishop of York, as was noted immediately above.

“The dearest son of my brother to me.” Concerning him, see below in Letters 47 and 49.

“That he should read the lesson.” He derived this instruction from chapter 38 of the Rule of Saint Benedict: “Let the brothers not read in order, but let the one read who edifies those listening.” This custom was carefully observed by the ancient monks, so that beginners in the ascetic life might be trained and instructed for some time in monastic matters. They were also devoted to learning the psalms by heart and the rites of the Church before appearing in public. Lanfranc himself did the same: although he had been versed in every branch of learning, when he first entered the monastery at Bec he voluntarily did so with the greatest humility of spirit. Menardus proves this more fully in chapter 65 of the *Concordance of the Rules*, pp. 936 and following.

He rejoices that his brother’s son was received by them with greater freedom and gives thanks, while also indicating what he wishes to be observed concerning him.

To the lord, father, brother, and friend Anselm: Lanfranc, sinner, wishes perpetual salvation from God.

Your blessedness knows very well what is beneficial for me. When I came to the land of the English, or when I set out for Rome, I disclosed to your holiness everything that I then judged should be disclosed for my needs. Therefore pray in this way, and ask your friends and household to pray in this way: that almighty God may either lead me to better fruit or bring my soul out of the prison of this flesh in confession of his holy name. For this land in which we live is shaken daily by so many and such great tribulations and stained by so many adulteries and other impurities that scarcely any class of people exists that either takes care of its own soul or even desires to hear wholesome teaching for progress toward God.

I happily received the letters that you sent through Lord Robert, and I read them even more happily. I cannot express in writing with what joy I still recall them by rereading them, and reread them in recalling them—namely, because, as it was written in them, you received with immense joy the dearest son of my brother, whom I love as my own soul; because on this occasion you conceived a greater confidence in my love for you; and, above all, because you said that the burden of the priorship, which previously seemed unbearable, had been lightened for you by his arrival. Concerning this I give you a brief and truthful judgment: even if he lived among pagans, I would love him more than the other pagans, and he would benefit if I possessed anything in this world. For these matters I give as much thanks as I can to God, to the lord abbot, and to all of you, because I continually find you toward me and toward all who are loved by me to be just as I could wish [variant: as I wish].

But because a person who approaches the service of the Lord—and especially one of that age—is inwardly torn by many and varied temptations through the suggestions of tempting spirits and is tormented inwardly and outwardly by many different ticklings of the flesh, it is very necessary that you frequently make him a participant in your conversation and command all those whose instruction may be beneficial to him to converse with him whenever appropriate.

When he was leaving me, I earnestly begged and commanded him not to read a lesson this year either in the refectory, in the chapter house, or in the monastery, until he had acquired some knowledge of the psalms and some experience in his order. He completely disregarded my wish and, through the excess of his entreaties, prevailed upon you to let him read. For this reason I intended to send him a very bitter letter; but after seeing another letter of yours, I abandoned the resentment that I had conceived against his rashness of mind.

## Letter 44. From Brother Anselm to Lanfranc

He replies to Lanfranc’s recent letter and in turn commends Maurice, who is suffering from a headache.

To the reverend lord and father, truly loving and beloved, Archbishop Lanfranc, to be embraced as a Catholic mother: his brother Anselm, wholly yours, offers what he can that is most worthy.

Whenever it pleases you that something should please me, it certainly pleases me too; and what previously pleased me becomes more pleasing. You indicated that you were among the joyful because I, to say nothing of other matters, received our dearest one, your nephew, with great rejoicing. I have therefore been made joyful by this joy of yours, and the joy I had felt over our dear one, although it always remains vigorous, has been renewed and increased, in proportion as I learned that what I do not blush to admit—namely, that I had intended in large part to receive him in this way—had succeeded according to my desire. I refer to Maurice, my lord by merit, brother in faith, and son in solicitude, whom you have separated from the one by whom he was loved more than by anyone else and whom he loved more than anyone else. Judge for yourselves what you owe him. For however lowly the one who so loves and is so loved may be, surely you owe him this: that he love no less and be loved no less. Since I know the uprightness of your justice and you know our mutual affection, we refrain from every further commendation of him. Concerning his headache, I especially ask your compassion, insofar as I can influence you, that, for God’s sake and for the reward of eternal salvation, it be investigated and treated as far as possible by our dear friend Lord Albert the physician, at your urging.

## Letter 45. To Gondulf

[Editorial note: This note refers to Letter 45, but Migne printed “To Letter 46” instead of “To Letter 45.”]

### To Letter 46
## Letter to Gondulf

[Col. 0616C]

Since only the letter G had been prefixed to this letter, I supplied “Gondulf,” guided by the following conjecture: Blessed Anselm, in Book I, Letter 4, addresses a greeting to Gondulf from Lanfranc, his nephew: “Greet,” he says, “the young Lord Lanfranc, nephew of our lord, reverend and father, Archbishop Lanfranc,” etc. And in Letter 7 to the same man: “Greet the reverend and beloved lord and father of us all, Archbishop Lanfranc, and his nephew,” etc.

From these passages, therefore, and from the words of Blessed Lanfranc, it seems necessary to affirm that this letter was addressed to Gondulf, to whom Lanfranc, his nephew, had been entrusted for instruction. Or, certainly, one must say that he had several nephews in different places—for Paul, who later became abbot of St Albans, as was shown above [Col. 0616D], was his nephew—one of whom remained at Bec, and another with Gondulf at Caen. Or perhaps, more probably, that this same nephew had assumed the monastic habit at Bec and had devoted himself to study elsewhere, either before becoming a monk or afterward. Indeed, this appears clear from Blessed Anselm, Book I, Letters 19, 24, and 36, where he congratulates Saint Lanfranc and reports that he received with gratitude the fact that Lanfranc had sent his nephew to Bec rather than elsewhere to assume the monastic habit. But in a doubtful matter of little importance, let the judgment rest with the reader. Concerning Gondulf, see above, in the Life, p. 40.

He especially commends his brother’s son to Gondulf for instruction, and sends a cross with relics.

### To his dearest Gondulf, his dearest Lanfranc sends wishes for the happy perseverance of the affection begun between them.

I have learned from the report of certain people that the brothers whom, dearest brother, I especially sent to you to be instructed by your letters and formed in good conduct are being treated honorably and according to my wishes. For this I give thanks to your kindness, and, if you need admonition, I wish to urge you to persevere in what you have begun.

I commend to your affection my dearest brother’s son—your brother, that is—asking you, as I ought to ask you concerning a most delightful son and brother of mine, to love him with great joy of heart and not to cease, insofar as you are able, to form him for a praiseworthy life. I called him your brother because I want him truly to be so and earnestly ask this of you [variant: “because”]; for, as I have been told, your venerable mother is also graciously pleased to call him her son, although she is of an eminent family and he was born in a humble station. Without doubt she will receive her reward from him who said: “Whoever humbles himself will be exalted” (Luke 14:11).

I send you a cross containing relics, to be seen by the eyes of your fraternity while you celebrate Mass. I wish it to be a memorial of perpetual friendship between you and him.

You have filled me with great joy, because you wrote that, by divine mercy, you were still preserving in youth the promise made in childhood. If you carry it unharmed to its end, you will surely behold, with great security, the terrible Judge who is terrible to others.

May almighty God deign, through the inspiration of his Holy Spirit, to implant in your heart that you may love me throughout every age of your life as you once used to love me in your childhood and adolescence. May he himself bless you and, having been reconciled toward you, absolve you from all sins.

## Letter XLVI. To the Same

[Note: [Col. 0616D]]

### To Letter XLVI

“Diaprasium.” An electuary made from the herb horehound—commonly called *marrube*, Greek πράσιον (*prásion*). This medicine is highly beneficial to consumptives. Paulus Aegineta, *On the Art of Medicine*, Book VII, chapter 11; Pliny, Book XX, chapter 22; and Jacobus Dalechamps, *History of Plants*, vol. I, Book VIII, chapter 36, discuss at length the properties and various species of horehound.

He consoles a sick man and sends him a medicine to use.

### To his dearest brother Gondulf, brother Lanfranc sends blessing from God and perpetual salvation.

After reading your fraternity’s letter, I learned that you were suffering from a serious illness. For this reason I urge you not to grieve but rather to rejoice, and to offer unceasing thanks to your Creator, who cares for you, knowing that it is written: “I will gladly glory in my infirmities” (2 Corinthians 12:15). And elsewhere: “The Lord chastises every son whom he receives” (Hebrews 12:6).

For he would not wear you down in this world with such great scourges unless he had determined that after this world you would be without scourging. Therefore remember yourself; remember your final things; confess your sins. By doing this, you will either obtain bodily health from God, or you will await without fear a death feared by others—which will be the end of evils for you and the beginning of good things.

I am sending you a large quantity of *diaprasium*, which physicians declare to be very useful for this illness. You shall take from it, every third day, an amount the size of a wild nut. May almighty the Lord always be your guardian and, reconciled toward you, absolve you from all sins.

## Letter XLVII. To Brothers Lanfranc and Guido

[Note: [Col. 0617A]]

### To Letter XLVII

“To Lanfranc and Guido.” This Guido was the companion of Lanfranc’s nephew; at that time both of them were undergoing their monastic novitiate at Bec. Blessed Anselm commends both of them in this way in Book I, Letter 31, to Archbishop Lanfranc:

“Concerning my sweetest and dearest beloved, your nephew, whose manner of life I know you wish to know about as one present with you, I report to you what my conscience bears witness to. He takes such care to avoid those things which must be avoided that he appears rightly blameworthy to none of us. He devotes himself so to humble kindness and kindly humility, to quiet and silence, and to prayer, that he is deservedly lovable to all. Yet there is something which, although I truly believe that divine providence deals mercifully with him in it, I cannot see without the distress of charitable compassion. For many months now, God’s fatherly chastisement has afflicted him with such a headache that at times his cheerful participation is separated from the common assembly, and his attention is altogether prevented from reading or from any diligent meditation,” etc.

He mentions the same Lanfranc, and Guido as well, in the same book, Letter 63. But in Book II, Letter 42, he rebukes that same Lanfranc most severely—Lanfranc who, secretly and without the knowledge of Blessed Anselm his abbot, and even against his resistance, had given his consent to being appointed abbot of Saint-Wandrille—and he warns and commands him to reject the election made concerning him. The letter addressed to Walter, prior of Saint-Wandrille, should be read there.

In the end, however, Lanfranc was elected abbot, but he held the abbacy for less than a full year. For, in the year 1091, says the manuscript *Short Chronicle of Saint-Wandrille*: “Lanfranc, abbot of the monastery of Fontenelle, died; Girard the abbot succeeded him.”

As for Guido, Blessed Anselm speaks of him in the letter previously cited: “Lord Guido, whom we assigned to the instruction of boys, is so commended by pleasing obedience and humility in vigor that we may rightly boast together—both you, through whom he is ours, and we, who have him as such.”

“with a Theonine tooth.” Thus it is read in both copies, the Caen copy and that of Jacques Sirmond. But Horace, Book I of the *Epistles*, Letter 18, to Lollius, speaks of Theoninus, a fictitious name derived from the poet Theon, notorious for the most shameless abuse:

> He who is gnawed all around  
> by a Theonine tooth—do you not sense  
> what dangers will soon come upon you?

### 324. He gives salutary admonitions to his nephew and to the latter’s former friend, now his brother in the monastery. He privately forgives his nephew for not observing what he had commanded.

### To his dearest brothers Lanfranc and Guido, brother Lanfranc sends perpetual blessing from the Lord.

Because, as I believe, you loved one another in the world by divine providence, I ask you to pray God that, with his cooperation, you may love one another in the holy purpose you have undertaken. Let each be a consolation to the other in tribulation; let each take from the other an example of holy conduct.

Show humility to everyone. Restrain your tongues from every disparagement by wholesome [variant: fraternal] correction. If anyone, after being corrected by you, neglects to amend his life and continues to gnaw at the life of any brother with a Theonine tooth, let him be excluded from your conversation.

Whatever others may say about you, perhaps praising and magnifying you because you have rejected for God’s sake your parents, possessions, and carnal pleasures, always return inwardly to your consciences. Recognize that you are always sinners, and ask God through continual prayers to be propitious toward your sins.

Against you, dearest nephew, I conceived a great resentment in my mind, because you transgressed the command that I first imposed upon you concerning this matter. But, through the intervention of the venerable Father Lord Anselm, whom I desire to obey as God, I forgive you that fault with a sincere heart. I warn you not to do anything of the kind again, because the more intensely I love a friend, the greater anger I conceive against him even for a small fault.

May almighty the Lord protect you by his grace and mercifully absolve you from all sins.

## Letter XLVIII. To Father William

[Note: [Col. 0617D]]

### To Letter XLVIII

“To William.” He was, I think, first a monk of Bec and afterward of the monastery of Cormery, and finally its abbot, as Blessed Lanfranc seems to indicate in this title: “To his dearest Father William, once my sweetest,” etc. For they had formerly lived the cenobitic life together at Bec. Milo Crispin also proves that they were joined by spiritual kinship in his *Life*, p. 10, where Lanfranc reveals to William alone what had happened to him when he was contemplating flight. The same *Life* states that William was appointed abbot of Cormery, chapter 2, p. 4.

“Appoint Lord Ernustus as prior.” This concerns the monastery of Cormery, in my conjecture, although perhaps he was at that time staying at Bec. For among monks and canons—especially those who cared deeply about the rigor and observance of ecclesiastical and monastic discipline—it was customary, while they possessed the right of election, to choose, seek out, and even compel men of blameless life, approved prudence, and exceptional learning from different churches and monasteries, indiscriminately—I speak of the practice—to serve as bishops, abbots, and priors.

“Ernustus.” This is the man whom we saw Archbishop Lanfranc place over the Church of Rochester in the repeatedly cited *Life*, chapter 7, p. 9, and chapter 13, p. 15. Robert of Torigni repeats the same account in his manuscript chronicle under the year 1089.

He designates Ernustus as prior; if anything prevents this, he suggests other courses that may be followed.
