### To his dearest Father William, once my sweetest—and would that I were at least now still dear to you!—Lanfranc sends whatever is more honorable and better in this world and the next.

In the letter that you recently sent, you especially set forth and requested, among other things, that, once the man who now presides had been removed, I should advise you concerning the appointment of a prior for your church and write my advice to you without delay. I showed the matter to the brothers who are with me and earnestly asked them also to advise me, since I wished to give advice myself.

The common opinion of all was that, if you can bring it about in any way consistent with God’s will, you should appoint Lord Ernustus as the chief prior of your church. If he should refuse, or perhaps if the lord abbot should not consent to this arrangement, appoint whom the unanimous election of the brothers decides should be appointed.

If this advice displeases you, accept the counsel that cannot displease anyone of sound judgment: namely, that you do what you learn from the mouth of Lord Abbot Herluin and Lord Anselm ought to be done. For I, as a sinful man, am ignorant of divine counsel, whereas both of them, as we believe, are filled with the Spirit of God and have with them those who are able to help them with God in the affairs of this world.

May divine majesty, venerable Father and joyful brother, bless you and entirely absolve you from all sins.

## Letter XLIX. To Abbot Adelin

[Note: [Col. 0618B]]

### To Letter XLIX

“And receive them in their former places,” etc. This instruction is taken from chapter 29 of the Rule of Saint Benedict, which teaches that a monk who has left the monastery because of a crime, if he returns, is to be cast down to the lowest place: “And so,” it says, “let him be received in the last rank, so that his humility may thereby be tested.” And chapter 44, concerning those who are excommunicated: “Then, if the abbot orders it, let him be received in the choir or in the rank that the abbot has determined.”

He intercedes for monks who had withdrawn from the monastery and, having acknowledged their fault, wished to return.

### Lanfranc, archbishop, sends greetings and blessing to his dearest son and friend, Adelin [f., Adelhelm], abbot.

These brothers came to me accusing themselves and saying that they had grievously sinned against you and, through their own fault, had withdrawn from the monastery. I, for my part, greatly increased their folly in their hearing, and rebuked them, as was fitting, with sufficiently harsh and bitter words. [Col. 0543B] Later, when I asked them whether they wished thereafter to amend, they replied that they did and that they greatly regretted what they had done. They begged me to intercede for them with you and, through my intercession, to reconcile them to the monastery from which they had departed.

Therefore I ask your fraternity, if my prayers have any place with you, that, for the love of God and of us, you sincerely forgive whatever they have done against you and against the order; receive them in the places they occupied before their fault; and thereafter show them fatherly affection, so that God may be merciful to you.

## Letter L. To Reginald, Sentunus, and Henry

[Note: [Col. 0618C]]

### To Letter L

“To Rainald, abbot of the city of Poitiers.” This means the monastery of Saint Cyprian beside the city of Poitiers. The ancient parchments of that monastery state:

“Rainald, formerly a monk of La Chaise-Dieu, became abbot of Saint Cyprian. The Cluniac monks, wishing to subject him to themselves, harassed him in many ways, but, because he resisted courageously and wisely, they did not prevail. He also resisted them in three councils, with the support of Amatus the legate and Isambert, bishop of Poitiers, and the monks of Marmoutier,” etc.

You may learn how he helped the supreme pontiffs—especially Urban II, when he had been reduced to the greatest distress—from a letter of that same Urban to the bishops and prelates of Aquitaine, Gascony, etc., not yet published, so far as I know:

“Our dearest and familiar son Rainald, abbot of the monastery of Saint Cyprian, having dwelt with us for some time and having carefully observed the oppression suffered by the Holy Roman Church and the consolation she hopes for in Christ: through him, therefore, we admonish the solicitude of your charity to be zealous with due vigor on behalf of the mother of you all, the Holy Roman Church, to come to the aid of her present labors, and not to delay sending through the faithful bearer of the present letter what, with God’s help, it has resolved. Let each person, however, report to our knowledge whatever he contributes, with his name written beside it.”

Urban again wrote to Rainald:

“Trusting in your religious devotion and prudence, we impose upon you obedience to the Apostle Paul: just as Paul urged the Gentiles, whom through God’s grace he had converted, concerning the ministry being performed for the saints who lived in Jerusalem, so you too must persist, faithfully and devoutly, in urging the bishops, nobles, and other Catholics of your land to remember the poor of the Roman Church and not neglect to supply their need from their abundance. To carry this out, we have appointed our dearest son G——, abbot of Saint Sabinus, as your companion in this labor, so that together you may more promptly assist the distress of our pressures,” etc.

Thus far from the cartulary of the monastery of Saint Cyprian of the Congregation of Saint Maur. Moreover, Blessed Anselm sent Rainald the short work entitled *Menologium*, Book I, Letter 74.

“Berengar, I mean.” Berengar has been discussed at greater length above, in Letter 1, section a, and Letter 4, section u. William of Malmesbury describes his words when he was near death in this way, in Book III of *The Deeds of the English*:

“Although Berengar plainly corrected his opinion, he nevertheless could not convert all those whom he had corrupted throughout the whole world.”

And below:

“For he himself, dying on Epiphany and recalling with a prolonged groan how many wretched people, when he was a young man in the first heat of life, he had infected with his sect, said: ‘Today, on the day of his manifestation, my Lord Jesus Christ will appear to me, as I hope, for glory because of my repentance—or, as I fear, for punishment because of the others.’”

“Calling him the Lucifer of the Romans.” He seems to have reported this more from memory than in the very words of Saint Jerome, embellishing Saint Hilary with such praises. For, unless my memory deceives me, these words cannot at all be found among that doctor’s works. Jerome’s wording in Book III, Letter 141, to Marcella, is as follows:

“I do not dare to criticize so great a man, Hilary, the most eloquent of his time, who, because of the merit of his confession, the excellence of his life, and the splendor of his eloquence, is praised wherever the Roman name is known.”

Likewise, in the preface to Book VIII of his *Commentary on Isaiah*:

“If they desire a river of eloquence and polished declamations, let them read Cicero, Quintilian, and others; and, to come to our own writers, Tertullian, Cyprian, Hilary,” etc.

“Lord Jesus Christ in the same person,” etc. These words, and what follows, are very far from the charge of Trinitarian heresy that a certain cleric of Compiègne, named Roscelin, dared, after the death of Saint Lanfranc, to lay upon him—no one knows with what presumption. Indeed, so that he might more effectively hiss forth and spread his poison, he whispered, asserted, and proclaimed that the same bishop and Blessed Anselm, most holy men who had served the Catholic Church with the greatest distinction, were accomplices in or teachers of his pestilential sect.

This may be read in Anselm, Book II, Letter 41, to the bishop of Beauvais:

“I hear that the cleric Roscelin says that there are three persons in God, three separate things, just as there are three angels, yet in such a way that there is one will and power; or that the Father and the Holy Spirit became incarnate, and that three gods could truly be spoken of, if usage allowed it. In this opinion he asserts that Archbishop Lanfranc, of venerable memory, was, and that I am,” etc.

Then Anselm asks the bishop of Beauvais to undertake the defense of both his outstanding teacher and himself at the Council of Reims:

“As for Archbishop Lanfranc,” he adds, “his life is known to many religious and wise men, because nothing of this kind was ever heard from him; this sufficiently excuses him from the charge, while his absence and death reject any new accusation against him. As for me,” etc.

The words of Blessed Lanfranc, moreover, refute Roscelin more than sufficiently, restrain his audacity, and dissolve the calumny. What, I ask, does Lanfranc profess except that Christ, in the same person, is true man and true God, and that he alone assumed human nature? Since he also asserts that, in that same person, Christ truly possesses divinity and is in every respect equal to the Father and the Holy Spirit, he clearly teaches that three gods cannot be spoken of, in accordance with the creed attributed to Saint Athanasius: “As is the Father, so is the Son, so is the Holy Spirit.”

Finally, by that statement—“The only-begotten Son of the Father came into the world in such a way that he nevertheless never departed from the Father’s bosom”—he plainly demonstrates that the eternal union of the divine nature can nowhere be separated or made separable. Would not the man be judged out of his mind who asserted that something which can never be separated had been separated?

Let us hear him speaking further in chapter 1 of his commentary on Romans, p. 9, no. 20, on the word “Justice”:

“Another reason why he is not ashamed is that in it is revealed how he makes righteous those who believe, progressing from the faith of the Old Testament, in which one God was believed, to faith in the New Testament, in which the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are believed to be one and threefold God.”

In chapter 3 of his commentary on Galatians, on the words “But God is one”:

“Because he called Christ the Mediator, namely of God and of human beings, and Christ is God, there seemed to be two gods; but far be it from us! For there is one God: the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.”

There are almost innumerable other passages of this kind scattered throughout his commentary on the Epistles of Saint Paul. Finally, that some people detracted from the exceptional learning of the great Lanfranc, he himself seems briefly to suggest in his commentary on 1 Corinthians 2:13, at the end, on the words “not in learned words,” etc.:

“I would explain these things one by one, were it not that I feared the grumbling of unlearned men against such doctrines.”

“Nor will a man dwelling on earth then be able to be in heaven.” This is to be understood as referring to the powers of human nature alone. Otherwise, it is universally acknowledged among the holy Fathers and doctors of the Catholic Church, when they discuss the truth of Christ’s body in the sacrament, that this can occur only in a supernatural manner and by divine power, as Lanfranc himself proves in his short work *On the Sacrament of the Eucharist*.

### [Col. 0543C]

He defends Saint Hilary against Berengar’s accusations and teaches that the words Berengar was twisting into a pernicious meaning were spoken and must be interpreted in an orthodox sense.

### Lanfranc, bishop, sends greetings to his dearest brothers Reginald, abbot of the city of Poitiers, Sentunus [variant: Sewinus], monk, and Henry, canon.

After reading the letter sent to me by your fraternity through this man, I understood your wish to come to me, if the opportunity were given. I do not think this can conveniently be done, for the journey is long and involves many dangers, by land and sea; and I am so entangled in the many and great affairs of this world that at this time I cannot devote myself to such studies. If divine power should one day wish me to be free, my mind will always be ready both to learn and to teach.

As for what that schismatic—that is, Berengar—steadfastly asserts, as your letter testifies: namely, that blessed Hilary, once bishop of your city and your people, held perverse opinions in his treatise *On the Faith*, and expressed implausible opinions about the Lord Jesus Christ in his book *On the Divine Trinity*: your blessedness should not wonder if a man who, according to the most truthful reports, is infamous for believing and teaching so many abominable things about the head itself is, by divine judgment, permitted to speak such pernicious things about a member of that head.

Indeed, whoever brands Hilary with the mark of any heresy involves many orthodox leaders who raised him to the skies with great praise in the stain of that same error. Pope Gelasius, in his decretals (Distinction 15, canon 13), numbers all his books among the Catholic Scriptures. His authority is most appropriately recalled, accepted, and praised in the sacred canons.

Saint Augustine, in Book VI, chapter 11, of *On the Trinity*, exalts him with extraordinary praise and explains more clearly certain things Hilary had said obscurely about the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Blessed Jerome’s praises of him and all his books in some of his writings are too extensive to be contained within the brevity of a letter. He calls him “the Lucifer of the Romans,” “the lamp of the churches,” and “a precious stone to which mortals scarcely rise,” speaking of everything in beautiful and golden language. The other teachers of sacred religion, whoever spoke of him, did not in this respect depart at all from their judgment.

It is therefore safer for a reader, when faced with the most difficult opinions of the holy Fathers—opinions which the weakness of his intellect cannot grasp—to say, when asked what he does not know, that he does not know it, than, through stubborn arrogance and arrogant stubbornness, to define things contrary to the faith, to his own ruin and that of others; especially if he is a person who appears to carry the weight of authority either through literary knowledge, moral probity, or, better still, both.

I found in your letters the following words of the aforementioned doctor, which the aforementioned distorter attempts to twist into his calumny (*On the Trinity*, Book X, near the middle):

“The Son of God took a true man according to the likeness of our man, without ceasing to be God in himself. In him, although a blow might fall or a face might be torn [variant: a wound might tear him; variant: might descend], these things would indeed bring the force of suffering, but they would not inflict the pain of suffering, like some weapon piercing water, pricking fire, or wounding air.”

And shortly afterward:

“The strength of the body, without experiencing pain, received into itself the force of the punishment raging against it.”

Without prejudice to a better interpretation, we explain these words in a manner that, as we believe, accords with the testimony of the holy Fathers.

The Lord Jesus Christ, true man and true God in the same person, according to his humanity hungered, thirsted, became weary, and wept. As the hour of death approached, he began to be afraid and distressed; hence he also prayed, saying: “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me” (Matthew 26:39). As a man like us, he felt and suffered the blows of rods and the tearing of wounds; and, by assuming the other weaknesses of human nature, he assumed humanity in all things except sin.

According to his divinity, however, by which he is in every respect equal to the Father and the Holy Spirit, he endured none of these things. This has always been and remains the opinion of all the faithful, and sacred Scripture is almost everywhere filled with teachings of this kind. Yet, because of the unity of the person in which God and man were joined together, things proper to man are often assigned to God, and things belonging only to God are said to belong to man. Thus the Apostle says: “For if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Corinthians 2:8).

The Lord of glory was not truly crucified insofar as this concerns him, if God is said to have endured what belonged to man because of the man he assumed. The Lord himself says in the Gospel: “No one has ascended into heaven except he who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven” (Luke 3:13).

Again, what belonged to God was assigned to man. For a man dwelling on earth could not at that time be in heaven. But because the only-begotten Son of the Father came into the world in such a way that he nevertheless never departed from the Father’s bosom, while speaking on earth he attributed to the man he had assumed, because of the unity of the person, what belonged solely to divinity.

In this manner of expression it was said above that, in the man assumed by the Son of God, blows and wounds would bring the force of suffering but would not bring the pain of suffering. This is explained by the comparisons that follow—as though he were saying: The man who was assumed felt the force of suffering and the power of pain; the God who assumed him did not feel them. He explains this shortly afterward by saying:

“The strength of the body”—that is, the divinity assuming the body—“without experiencing pain,” insofar as this concerns divinity, “received into itself the force of the punishment raging against it,” that is, against the assumed flesh.

But if “the strength of the body,” or rather the body’s own vigor, is to be understood here, the same meaning remains in the rest, so that the sense is:

“The strength of the body, without experiencing the pain of the punishment raging against it, received it into itself”—insofar as this concerns the assumed humanity.

And in truth, without violating the faith of the Christian religion, it can be said in this manner of expression that Christ—or Christ’s body, or Christ’s flesh—suffered and did not suffer on the cross, felt pain and did not feel pain, died and did not die. There are many statements of this kind, beyond numbering.

Otherwise, if the aforementioned doctor had wished Christ’s flesh to be understood as insensible and incapable of pain, contrary to the Church’s most customary faith, contrary to evangelical authority, and contrary to the definition of all the holy Fathers, he would not have referred in the aforementioned sentence to the man assumed by the Son of God as a man like us. For what likeness is there between the sensible and the insensible, between one who feels pain and one who has no experience of pain? He did refer to him; therefore he did not intend him to be understood in that way.

I beg you, be vigilant in every way, because schismatics and their supporters are around you and among you. Set against them the shield of the fear of the Lord, attacking them with the arrows of the divine utterances. Support us, remembering us in your prayers. May almighty the Lord grant you to act well and to reach happily the destination toward which you are journeying. Amen.

## Letter LI. To Abbot T——

[Note: [Col. 0620D]]

### To Letter LI

“The case of Godwin.” This may perhaps be the man whose daughter Saint Edward, king of the English, had married, and who, having acquired the greatest authority, conducted himself most wickedly and finally met a most miserable death. See William of Poitiers, *Deeds of William*, p. 178, and below, as well as many others. But since nothing concerning an adulteress appears, I do not dare to assert that this is the same Godwin.

He orders an excommunicated adulteress to be expelled from the cemetery until satisfaction has been made to the bishop.

### Lanfranc, archbishop, sends greetings to his dearest friend, Abbot T—— [perhaps Turstin, to whom Letter 53 is addressed].

I know the case of Godwin and his adulteress Lifgina very well. Indeed, I ordered it to be investigated at London in my presence; and after hearing the assertions of both parties, we pronounced sentence against the adulterers and unanimously decreed that they had been justly excommunicated.

Therefore nothing remains except that your fraternity order the adulteress to be expelled from the cemetery until either her seducer or someone acting on her behalf does what is just for the bishop. I would gladly do what I understood might please you, and I am deeply sorry that I cannot fulfill your wish in the present matter.

## Letter LII. To Abbot G——

### 327. He commends Orricius, who was being detained by that man at the king’s command.

### Lanfranc, an unworthy bishop, sends greetings and blessing to the venerable Abbot G——.

I give your fatherhood as much thanks as I can because, whether present or absent, you speak good things to us and about us, wish us better things, and confirm both by words and by letters. And indeed, know that I have the same disposition toward you and show sincere affection in every respect toward you and yours.

What you wrote concerning Lord Orricius [Orricius] I receive gratefully. But, against the king’s command, I dare neither ask nor order anything. I do, however, ask—and ask earnestly—that, for God’s sake, for love of me, and because he is worthy, you love him, treat him honorably, and show him fatherly affection, as your prudence judges appropriate. For he is suffering persecution for justice’s sake, and when the will from above has so determined, this will be changed for him into joy and gladness. Yet the Lord has shown him mercy in willing him to be among you; and those who thought they were harming him, as the Lord willed, have greatly benefited him.

## Letter LIII. To Abbot Turstin

[Note: [Col. 0621A]]

### To Letter LIII

“To Abbot Turstin.” A manuscript history circulating under the name of William of Nangis states:

“In England Turstin, abbot of Glastonbury, committed a shameful and most abominable crime. For he had three of his monks placed upon the altar and killed, and ordered eighteen to be severely wounded. Thus their blood ran from the altar over the steps, and from the steps over the floor.”

The cause of such hatred toward the monks is given by William of Malmesbury, *On the Bishops of England*, Book II, fol. 145, where he speaks of the abbey of Glastonbury:

“Turstin, made abbot of that monastery by a gift of King William the father, consumed its lands and money in the abuses of his *lectatores* [read: followers]. He severely demanded observance of the rule from the monks, but meanwhile treated them miserably in food and provisions. From this arose verbal disputes and discord of spirit. After quarrels, matters came to arms, and the monks, driven by soldiers into the church, lamented their misfortunes before the holy altar. But when the soldiers burst in, two of them were killed there, fourteen wounded, and the rest driven back,” etc.

See also Florence of Worcester, under A.D. 1083, and Henry of Huntingdon, Book VII of the *History*, in the fifteenth year of William I.

He consoles his friend and urges him to try to move the king through himself and his friends, and not to grieve if the king rejects him.

### Lanfranc, an unworthy bishop, sends greetings to Abbot Turstin.

You asked me to communicate my advice briefly, and I have taken care to communicate it to you in a few words. Ask God to remember you and have mercy on you; do this earnestly, both through yourself and through your friends. We, for our part, are doing what we can.

Through friends and faithful intermediaries, offer our lord the king what is right. If he rejects it, do not be very sad or anxious about it. For God will visit his people when he has determined that it is expedient. May the mercy of God be with you.

## Letter LIV. To His Dear and Faithful G——

He states that he has no lordship in the counties entrusted to him, but that all the lands of his church belong to the monks’ livelihood.

### Lanfranc, an unworthy bishop, sends greetings and blessing to his dear and faithful friend G——.

[Col. 0547A] I give thanks for your kind solicitude and your solicitous kindness, because from the beginning of our mutual acquaintance you promised me your friendship. In practice, whenever the opportunity arose, you have always tried to demonstrate it. Now I ask—and earnestly ask you, although you do not need so much urging—that in the present matter you may be able to help your affairs as much as the power granted to you from above permits.

You should know, however, that in those counties whose administration has been entrusted to you, I possess no lordship, but that all the lands of your Church in those regions belong in every respect to the livelihood of the monks. Your brother, who is bringing you this letter, has reported many things worthy of praise about you; the number of these and the brevity of a letter do not now permit me to enumerate them. But may almighty God, from whose memory nothing escapes, repay you manifold, as He knows, and may He continually defend you from every evil work, as an ever-ready [variant: pious] helper.

## LETTER LV. TO ABBOT R. . . .

Concerning the monk about whom he had asked that he be received into the monastery: he now leaves the matter entirely to him, intending to approve whatever he decides.

**LANFRANC**, archbishop, to Abbot R. . . ., greetings.

When I sent you, with my letters, the brother about whom your fraternity had written to me, asking that he be received into the monastery, I did so, as my conscience bears witness, out of zeal for God and love of our order; for I do not wish either to request or command anything, under the pretext of avoiding scandal, that might in any way develop into a greater or worse scandal. Speak, therefore, with the bishop, if he happens to be present, and with his prior, Lord Godefrid; and whatever you shall consult together about this matter, and decide after consultation to carry out in practice, know that it pleases me also in every respect. For I do not wish to nourish pride, which I desire to be far removed from every class of people, and especially from our order.

## LETTER LVI. TO WILLIAM, ABBOT

[Note: [Col. 0621B]

### ON LETTER LVI

[Col. 0621C] At Gloucester. Malmesbury, in the passage cited above, Book IV, *On the Bishops of Worcester*, praises it in the most lavish terms. Henry VIII, however, after expelling the monks, established the episcopal see of Gloucester there, as Godwin relates in *On the Bishops of England*, p. 590.

With Abbot Serlo. The same Malmesbury, in the cited place, describing the monasteries, begins: “There is therefore in the city of Gloucester itself the monastery of St Peter, which I have more than once said was begun there by Archbishop Aldred. Abbot Serlo found there few monks, no more than three, having obtained from King William the Elder a scanty gift; but who could set forth in fitting eloquence how greatly the grace of God, working together with his diligence, raised up that place? The moderation of Gloucester’s religious life is well known: a weak man can undertake it, yet a strong man cannot despise it. Serlo, their standard-bearer, brought them this principle: ‘Nothing in excess.’”]

That the monk Rainald may request the monastery at Gloucester and remain there with Abbot Serlo for the space of one year.

**LANFRANC**, archbishop, to his dearest friend, Abbot **WILLIAM**, greetings.

I ask you, as much as I can and ought to ask, to grant this brother Rainald permission to remain at Gloucester with Abbot Serlo for the space of one year; for it is beneficial to his soul that this should happen. I take this above all as an indication of his character: he seeks a regular house, although he in no way disparages your monastery, in which he was brought up. He explains, however, a reasonable cause for wishing to do this. I ask again that you not take it amiss that he has come to me and, because of his need, has sought me out as your friend.

## LETTER LVII. TO ABBOT O. . . .

[Col. 0548A]

He reproves him for having granted his monk permission to wander; he orders him, after compelling the monk to return, to receive him honorably and to show him paternal affection as a son.

**LANFRANC**, archbishop, to Abbot O. . . ., greetings.

We forbade your monk, Brother Gregory, to cross the sea; we ordered him to return to his monastery, and by our command compelled him to do so. You did not act rightly in granting him permission to wander outside his homeland. This clearly shows what sort of shepherd you are and with what diligence you know how to govern the souls entrusted to you.

[Col. 0548B] We therefore command and order—and by ordering, ask—that you receive him honorably and henceforth show him paternal affection as your son. For, by the mercy of God, we believe that, if you are willing to be concerned for your order, you will be able through him to obtain counsel and assistance both in spiritual and in secular matters. It greatly rejoiced me that he testified that you possess the fear of God and are a good man; nevertheless, in his simplicity he could not deny that you are negligent toward our order.

## LETTER LVIII. TO REMIGIUS, HIS DEAR FRIEND

Many people speak ill of him before the king, but the king does not believe them. It would be advantageous for him to come to Lanfranc, so that he might hear more from his own mouth.

[Col. 0548C] **LANFRANC**, by the grace of God archbishop, to his dear brother and friend **REMIGIUS**, greetings.

Although many people say many wicked things about you, and very few, by their innate generosity [variant: freedom], oppose the words of your detractors, you should nevertheless know that our lord the king accepts the words of none of those who defame you; rather, by his royal authority, he defends you against all slanderers. Therefore, if you are nearby and have permission, it is advantageous for you to come to me, so that you may hear face to face those things which, because of their length, cannot be briefly written.

## LETTER LIX. TO HUGH . . .

[Note: [Col. 0621D]

### ON LETTER LIX

You criticize Pope Gregory. On St Gregory I have appended much in praise above to Letters 3 and 6. The schism touched on here by the holy archbishop is mentioned by the contemporary author Marianus Scotus, Book III of the *Chronicle*, under the year 1081; by Otto of Freising in the *Chronicle*, Book VI, chapter 36, and Book VII, chapter 1; and at length in Caesar Baronius’s *Sacred Annals*, vol. I. We judged worthy of publication the following eyewitness letter of St Gebehard, as yet, I think, unpublished, to Hermann, bishop of Metz, in which he briefly characterizes Guibert the antipope:

[Col. 0622A] **GEBEHARD**, bishop of Salzburg, to **HERMANN**, bishop of Metz, greetings.

Wibert, formerly archbishop of Ravenna, having neglected the obedience which he had promised the apostolic see by oath, and having even striven in every way to exalt himself against it, was irrecoverably deposed and anathematized in the Roman synod by the apostolic see and the bishops of the whole Church; nor did this happen once in one synod, but in every synod held at Rome during these seven years. This man, therefore, so hardened in perjuries and on their account irrecoverably deposed and anathematized, invaded the see of the Roman pontiff—to which he had sworn obedience—through the hands of those who had anathematized him, men like himself, while its lawful shepherd still presided over that see.

[Col. 0622B] None of those excommunicated persons presumed to consecrate him—or rather to execrate him—except the bishops of Modena and Arezzo, both of whom had already for three years been deprived of office and communion for their crimes. Yet even if they possessed office and communion and the Roman see were vacant of a shepherd, they could not appoint a pontiff for that see; for the privilege of this ordination was granted by the holy Fathers to the cardinals alone, the bishops of Albano, Ostia, and Porto. Therefore the former bishops of Modena and Arezzo, according to the testimony of the most holy Pope Innocent, could impose upon their Ravennate not the blessing but the condemnation which they possessed; and they advanced him not to be Roman patriarch but to be a most lost heresiarch.

[Col. 0622C] Let every Christian therefore beware of bowing his head to Antichrist, of worshipping the statue which Nebuchadnezzar set up, and thus binding himself in the most ruinous anathema of that heresiarch. For whoever obeys him who said, “I will set my throne in the north, and I will be like the Most High” (Isa. XIV, 14), will most certainly go with him into eternal damnation. Amen.

Thus the letter of Gebehard, from the manuscript *Chronicle* of Hugh of Flavigny, most willingly supplied to me by the Reverend Father Jacques Sirmond.]

He does not approve of Hugh’s criticizing Pope Gregory and extolling Clement with praise. Although he believes that the emperor did not lack reasons for his action, he advises Hugh not to come to England without the king’s permission.

[Col. 0548D]

**LANFRANC**, to Hugh . . . [perhaps, to Hugh].

I have received and read your letter, which you sent to me through the bearer of my letters, and certain things I found in it displeased me. I do not approve that you criticize Pope Gregory, that you call him Hildebrand, that you call his legates “thorny,” or that you exalt Clement so hastily [variant: improperly] with so many and such great praises. For it is written that no one should be praised during his lifetime (Ecclus. XI, 30), nor should one slander his neighbor (James IV, 11). It is still unknown to the human race what these men now are and what they will be in the sight of God. Nevertheless, I believe that the emperor did not undertake so great an enterprise without a compelling reason, nor could he have completed so great a victory without great divine assistance.

I do not approve of your coming into English territory unless you first obtain permission to come from the king of the English. Our island has not yet rejected the former claimant, nor has it pronounced whether it ought to obey this one. If that should happen, after the arguments on both sides have been heard, it will be possible to determine more intelligently what ought to be done.

## LETTER LX. TO RODULPH, ABBOT

[Note: [Col. 0622C]

### ON LETTER LX

Hugh of Flavigny recounts the history of this letter in the passage cited, under the year 1085. Abbot Rodulph, of whom more follows, because he most vigorously defended the cause of the holy Pope Gregory VII against Guibert, the antipope under the name Clement, suffered such persecution from Theodoric, bishop of Verdun and Guibert’s most ardent supporter, that at last, reduced to extreme misery, he left his monastery and sought the monastery of St Benignus at Dijon. When he had gone there with several monks, among whom Hugh held a leading place, and had been received with open arms by the archimandrite and the other monks of that place, Rodulph and his companions provided an example of virtue in their life and invited emulation of greater spiritual gifts; they were urged to establish stability in the monastery at Dijon. But because they had long before made profession in the monastery of St Vitonus at Verdun, they thought it unlawful to repeat it.

[Col. 0623A] “Abbot Rodulph had sought counsel in this matter,” Hugh says, “from very many persons; and Lanfranc, archbishop of Canterbury, gave him the following reply, writing to him in these words:” He then transcribes this Letter 60.

To Abbot Rodulph. Hugh, in the place cited, recounts his deeds at great length and in detail. From it I have copied the following, so that this great man may to some extent come to light: “In the year of the Lord 1075, Grimold resigned the abbacy on the feast day of St Nicholas. Rodulph succeeded him; his ordination was on the feast of St Urban.”

And under the year 1046: “The Father Rodulph of blessed memory, third successor after him [St Richard] in the governance of the Church and, as we believe, possessor of inherited holiness, now blessed in his happy departure, when he undertook to govern that place and heard from reporters many things about him worthy of recounting, and also saw the unanimous devotion of all toward his memorial cult, embraced indeed what he saw and heard universally from all; yet he burned within himself to know whether that man was of such holiness as was reported, and, as it were, sought with anxious and alert watchfulness of thought what merit he had before God. He himself also used very frequently to pray at the place of his tomb, because he had experienced there ready answers to prayer, and often to spend the night there.”

[Col. 0623B] He then describes more fully how an angel revealed to Rodulph the holiness of Abbot Richard, and adds these final words of the angel: “Therefore, now that you have learned these things about the blessed man, do not abandon the way you have begun: devote yourself to mortification of the flesh, humility, lowliness, and chastity; labor to win souls, so that with these and with others you may be endowed with the blessedness of eternal joy.”

And after other matters: “In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1090, Theodoric of Verdun died on the fourth day before the Nones of May. During his sickness he repented of communion with Wibert and of expelling the brethren, confessed his fault, and was absolved, by command of Abbot Rodulph, by a certain Brother Gerard by name, formerly a canon and archdeacon of the Church of Verdun, but then a monk of St Vitonus. Rodulph had sent him there with pious concern for this purpose, having obtained from the apostolic see power to absolve those who returned from excommunication.

[Col. 0624B] From that time Abbot Rodulph, with the brethren and the monastery entrusted to him, was recalled, after ravening wolves had entered it during his absence—sparing neither place nor reverencing God or man—and had so thrown everything into confusion and destroyed it that the memory of that confusion and devastation cannot be erased even today.”

And below: “Lord Abbot Rodulph returned to his monastery with his brethren in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1092, when Richer was already bishop of the Church of Verdun, having resigned the office of dean in the church of St Stephen at Metz.”

Finally, under the year 1099: “Lord Rodulph died on the fifth day before the Kalends of April.”

Honor and glory to God alone.

]

It is possible for a monk who has promised stability in one monastery, for just reasons, to move to another.

**LANFRANC**, archbishop of Canterbury, to Abbot **RODULPH**, greetings.

[Col. 0549B] It has been reported to me that you wish to leave your monastery and are troubled about the stability you promised, fearing that you may abandon the very place through which you strive [variant: ought] to please God. On this matter I offer the following explanation, and in offering it I give myself as an example. If I, Lanfranc, had sworn with my own hand that I would not leave some monastery, but then saw that I could not save my soul there, I would leave; nor would I incur the crime of perjury.

For whoever is bound to God for God’s sake is not released from Him unless he is released against Him. But he is in no way released from God against God who, for love of Him and in order to please Him well, moves from sons of discord, pride, and distrust—or, to put it more plainly, from sons of the devil—to sons of peace, humility, and hope, indeed to sons of God. For when someone makes such a move, does he not plainly flee from the seat of the devil to the seat of God? Who could judge that person condemned by God who flees to Him as to a father, lord, and friend?

Therefore, one who makes such a move does not pass from one Church to another; for there are not many Churches, but one Church spread throughout the whole world, and “everywhere service is rendered to one God, and service is given in war to one King.” Finally, blessed Benedict, in prescribing that stability be made firm, orders that a monk who comes from one monastery to another be received; and, if he has lived a good life, that he be urged to make his stability firm there (*Rule*, chap. 61, near the middle).

**[Col. 0549] End of the letters of blessed Lanfranc.**

The following letters were published by Dr J.-A. Gilles, *Works of Blessed Lanfranc*, Oxford, 1844, vol. [the source ends incomplete].

## LETTER LXI. TO MARGARET, QUEEN OF THE SCOTS

[Col. 0549B]

**LANFRANC**, unworthy bishop of the holy Church of Canterbury, to the glorious **MARGARET**, queen of the Scots, greetings and blessing.

The brevity of a letter cannot explain how greatly you have drenched my heart with joy through the polished letter which you, O queen beloved of God, sent me. Oh, with what delight the words flow forth that proceed inspired by the divine Spirit! For I believe that what you wrote was spoken not by you but for you. Truly, through your mouth He spoke who said to His disciples: “Learn from me, because I am meek and humble of heart.”

From this discipline of Christ came your decision that, although born of royal stock, royally educated, and nobly joined to a noble king, you should choose me—a foreign, worthless, ignoble man, entangled in sins—as your father, and ask that you might spiritually be held as my daughter. I am not what you think me to be, but may I become so because you think me so. So that you may not remain deceived, pray for me, that I may be worthy to pray to God and be heard on your behalf. Let there be between us a mutual exchange of prayers and good works. I give little, but I trust that I shall receive much greater things in return.

From now on, then, let me be your father, and be my daughter. At your request I am sending to your glorious husband and to you our dearest brother, Lord Goldewin, together with two other brothers, because he alone could not by himself complete all that ought to be done for the service of God and of you. I ask, and ask earnestly, that you strive to complete promptly and effectively what you have begun for God and for the sake of your souls. If you could or wished to complete your work through others, we would very much desire that these brothers of ours return to us, because they were extremely necessary to our church in their duties. Nevertheless, let your will be done, because in every respect we desire to obey you. May almighty God bless you and mercifully absolve you from all sins.

## LXII. TO THE ARCHDEACONS OF BAYEUX

[Col. 0550C]

**LANFRANC**, unworthy bishop, to the archdeacons of the holy Church of Bayeux, greetings.

The bishop of Coutances has informed me by letter that a certain priest of his town, situated in your diocese, committed homicide with his own hands while defending himself and his father against a man who was about to die. He added that you wished to have my advice on this matter: whether, and after how much time, the homicide might be permitted to celebrate Mass.

My brothers, it is dangerous for me to answer you on this matter, since I am completely ignorant both of the accused man and of the man’s life. If I knew that life either through my own experience or through trustworthy reports, I could answer your fraternity much more safely on so serious a matter. You, therefore, whose office requires this, investigate his life: how he has lived, how he lives, whether he repents humbly, whether he is sorrowful and mournful, and especially whether he promises that he will preserve chastity until the end of his life. If you discover these and similar signs of repentance in him, you may, after his penance has been completed, give him permission to celebrate Mass. Otherwise, it will be dangerous for you and destructive to him if he should presume, with polluted hands, to consecrate the body and blood of Christ. May almighty God bless you and grant you the desired joy from your shepherd.

## LXIII. CHARTER GRANTED TO THE CANONS OF GRAVENNA

[Col. 0551A]

**LANFRANC**, by the grace of God archbishop of Canterbury, to Walter the archdeacon and to the entire chapter of Lenham, greetings.

We grant, and by the page of this present charter confirm, the church of All Saints at Gravene to the regular canons of Saint Mary of Southwark, as an alms, together with everything belonging to that same church, whether in lands, tithes, or any other benefits.

Witnesses: Roger of Ponte, bishop; Walaric of Wroteham; Alan of Wells; John of Canterbury; Thomas of London, clerics; Richard of Gravenel; Hugh Passoriere; John the lay brother.

## PASSAGE FROM THE SPEECH WHICH BLESSED LANFRANC GAVE AT THE COUNCIL HELD IN A.D. 1072, CONCERNING THE PRIMACY OF THE CHURCH OF CANTERBURY, AGAINST THOMAS OF YORK

From William of Malmesbury, Book I, *On the Deeds of the Bishops of the English*.

[Col. 0623C] Your opinion is poor in truth, when you strive to have it said that only Augustine was granted authority over all the bishops of Britain, including even those who were ordained by the bishop of York. It would be a paltry and altogether narrow gift that an apostolic man would grant to his old familiar, the new Englishman, especially since, while Augustine was alive, no bishop of York ordained those whom Augustine would have as subjects; indeed, there was no bishop there at all. For blessed Paulinus, the first bishop of that city, was sent there not in Augustine’s time but in the time of Justus, who was the fourth bishop of Canterbury.

The *Deeds of the English* will teach one who is ignorant what I say. Understanding this, the prelates of the most holy apostolic see confirmed the subjection of all the bishops of England to Augustine’s successors, as the privileges that have been recited testify. Adorning, as they say, the Gregorian constitution with the fullest language, and supporting it with munificent liberty, the arbiters of that same see and advocates of that same judgment deem it just that all the Churches of the English should borrow their rule of life from the place from which they received the flame of faith. For who does not know that the belief in Christ spread from Kent to York and to the other Churches of England?

Furthermore, what you say—that blessed Gregory could, if he had wished, have confirmed to Augustine’s successors by an explicit statement what he had granted to Augustine—is entirely true, and cannot be disputed. But what prejudice, I ask, does this cause the see of Canterbury? I shall propose the matter by analogy. When our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ said to blessed Peter, “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church, and I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. XVI, 18), He could have added, if He had wished: “I grant this same power to your successors.” Yet the omission of that statement diminished nothing of the reverence due to Peter’s successors.

[Col. 0624D] Will you oppose these words? Will you bring forward an adverse argument? Indeed, it is implanted in the consciences of all Christians that they tremble no less before Peter’s successors than before blessed Peter, and that they gladly applaud their serene dignity when they show indulgence. The administration of all ecclesiastical affairs is valid only when it has been approved by the judgment of blessed Peter’s successors. What does this accomplish except that the force of divine generosity has been spread through the Lord Jesus from blessed Peter to his vicars? Therefore, if you know dialectic, you will pronounce the same judgment concerning similar cases.

Moreover, what holds true of the whole holds true of the part; what holds true of the greater holds true of the lesser. The Roman Church is, as it were, the whole of all the Churches; the other Churches are, as it were, its parts. Just as, in one respect, a human being is the genus of his individual members, yet in each individual there resides the complete property of the whole human being, so, in one respect, the Roman see is the genus and whole of all the Churches, yet in every Church the full integrity of the entire Christian faith reigns.

It is the greatest of all the Churches; and what is valid in it ought also to be valid in the lesser Churches, so that the authority of the first head of any Church may pass down to his successors, unless something is personally and explicitly excepted. Therefore, just as Christ said to all the Roman bishops what He said to blessed Peter, so Gregory said to all Augustine’s successors, in Augustine, what he had said to Augustine. From this it follows that, just as Kent is subject to Rome because it received the faith from Rome, so York is subject to Kent, which sent preachers there.

Now, what you allege—that Gregory wished Augustine to reside in London—is plainly uncertain. For how can it be established that Augustine, resisting the will of his master, would go against the decrees? I refuse to discredit a report confirmed by the agreement of so many people. Suppose, however, that Augustine was to move elsewhere: what does that have to do with me, who am not bishop of London? It concerns me only insofar as the usage of antiquity does not permit you to share the honor of primacy with the bishop of London. If you wish this matter to be debated with litigation set aside and peace prevailing, I shall not fail, in accordance with the duty of my jurisdiction, to give a just judgment.

[Col. 0625]

## A SHORT TREATISE OF BLESSED LANFRANC, ARCHBISHOP OF CANTERBURY, ON THE CONCEALED CONFESSION

From two manuscript codices of Saint Victor in Paris and from the codex of C. V. Alexander Petaus.

### ARGUMENT

This treatise appears to ask, when a penitent’s own priest has disclosed his confession, to whom the penitent ought to confess.

**I.** After establishing the virginity and unity of the Church, the author shows how many evils have been caused by the violator of the seal of confession.

**II.** In this situation—namely, when the penitent suffers such a shortage of priests that none can at all be found—he may confess to clerics, and even to morally pure laypeople, that is, to the faithful. This is not because that confession (to state the theologians’ view on the matter) confers grace *ex opere operato*—for it is not sacramental—but *ex opere operantis*, namely through the contrition and humility which the penitent makes manifest by revealing his sin, in order to bring upon himself a greater degree of shame; thus, in a certain sense, God supplies the priest’s office.

**III.** Where neither a priest nor a cleric nor a layperson can be found, one must not despair of salvation, but must confess to God alone; this he proves from various authorities of the holy Fathers.

[Col. 0625C] Asked about the virginity of Mother Church—how she is a virgin when she consists not only of virgins but also of married women, and of women both corrupted and uncorrupted in the flesh—I ought not, out of charity, to refuse to give testimony concerning her virginity.

For she is a virgin, truly a virgin. If we look into the mirror of purity and truth, and see that she truly possesses the image of virginity—which is the blessed Virgin Mary in the flesh—we recognize that the Church is the mother in conscience. We can direct our discussion more quickly toward this point if we carefully examine the four ecclesiastical sacraments: faith, baptism, the consecration of the Lord’s body and blood, and the remission of sins.

By faith the Church is the mother of what blessed Mary was in the flesh, because what Mary conceived through the Holy Spirit, the Church believes through the Holy Spirit. The Church is not divided in the sacraments of baptism, of the Lord’s body and blood, and of the confession of sins. Because she is truly one, she is truly a virgin; for every virgin, by the very fact that she is a virgin, cannot be divided into two. Indeed, flesh that is virgin is perfectly virgin.

Therefore blessed Mother Church is one and the same in her sacraments and in her faith, since she suffers nothing corrupted in her conscience, just as the Virgin Mother of God suffers nothing corrupted. As Mary is a virgin in body, so the Church too is a virgin in understanding.

In the mirror of this virginity, however, some people are dim-sighted when they contemplate the face of truth in the sacrament of confession—and, what is more serious, some who appear to bear the image of religion. Let us look at these matters more carefully, so that everything that is not one in the holy Church may disappear from the eye of truth.

### There are three sacraments of confession

[Note: [Col. 0631D] **Three sacraments.** It is clear that *sacramentum* is used here, as also above, for a sacred, sublime, hidden, and secret matter; the Greeks call it *mystērion* (μυστήριον). The same meaning should be understood in Wisdom II, 22: “They did not know the sacraments of God”; Ephesians I, 9: “Making known to us the sacrament of his will”; and in the Collect for the feast of the Lord’s Transfiguration: “O God, who strengthened the sacraments of the faith through the testimony of the Fathers in the transfiguration of your Only-Begotten Son,” and so forth.]

The Lord declared in His own person three sacraments of confession: the figure of baptism, one conscience made from two, and God and man meeting in the same judgment.

[Note: [Col. 0631D] **In the figure of baptism**, that is, in John’s baptism, which was the shadow and figure of the baptism of the new law. For John’s baptism was one of repentance and preparation for grace. Hence the text continues: “He who renounces through repentance and believes through faith.” Those who were initiated by John’s baptism confessed their sins and renounced them, and believed in Christ who was to come. *De consecratione*, distinction 4, canon 135; Durandus of Saint-Pourçain, *Sentences* IV, distinction 3, question 3; Soto, *Sentences* IV, distinction 2, question 2, article 2.]

The one who confesses renounces through repentance and believes through faith, just as the one who is baptized renounces and believes.

[Note: [Col. 0632D] **Just as the one who is baptized**, namely, with Christ’s baptism, which pardons sins and confers grace and the theological virtues, so that those washed with Christian water renounce Satan, the world, and his pomp. This is the common teaching of the theologians.]

Hence, at the Transfiguration, the Lord also received from the Father the same testimony that He had received at His baptism, with the addition: “Hear him” (Matt. XVII, 6). Concerning the one about whom John had heard, “This is he who baptizes” (John I, 33), the disciples heard: “Hear him,” because the one who baptizes in baptism is himself heard in the repentance he grants.

[Note: [Col. 0632D–0633A] **Because the one who baptizes is himself heard in the repentance he grants.** Christ the Lord is indicated here, since He Himself, as the principal cause, both baptizes and absolves from sins through the ministry of the priest.]

Two consciences pass into one: that of the one confessing into that of the one to whom he confesses, and that of the judge into that of the one who is judged. The Son of God implores this unity from the Father: “That they also may be one in us,” He says, “as you, Father, are in me, and I in you” (John XVII, 21). God and man meet in the same judgment, because whoever judges himself is already acting together with God (Augustine, *Tractate* 12 on John, near the end). Thus the thief on the cross, when he said, “We are receiving what our deeds deserve” (Luke XXIII, 41), because he judged himself together with the Lord, was together with the Lord in paradise.

In these sacraments, those who knowingly cause some suspicion concerning anyone who has confessed to them to arise publicly in any manner, or who defame those who have confessed, are blind. Those who betray into a confession someone who shared their crime also sin; and those who investigate matters revealed in the confession of others likewise sin.

For since confession bears the figure of baptism,

[Note: [Col. 0633A] **Since confession bears the figure of baptism.** For confession is like a second baptism, and “a second plank after shipwreck, when you have sinned, is to feel shame,” as blessed Jerome says in Book V, near the end of his commentary on Ezekiel XVI. Just as original and actual sin are washed away in baptism, so all actual sins are absolved in the sacrament of penance. Yet penance does not display the figure of baptism in every respect, as Saint Thomas proves in *Sentences* IV, distinction 17, article 3, response to the second objection of Dominic; Soto, *Sentences* IV, distinction 18, question 4, article 1; and others passim.]

we know that we are baptized in the renunciation of sin, not in the denunciation of another.

They are also regarded as sharing in the part of Judas, the Lord’s betrayer. Although the person who is defamed does not, by the fact that he sinned, signify the person of the Lord, nevertheless, by the fact that he is betrayed, he can signify Him. For the Lord, although He did not sin, was betrayed. Judas said of Him: “Whomever I kiss, he is the one; seize him” (Mark XIV, 44). And the priest who, under the appearance of familiarity, either gives or has given the penitent something like a kiss, asks that the person be seized because of a crime in confession.

[Note: [Col. 0633A–B] **Asks that the person be seized because of a crime in confession.** That is, as I think, he wishes the person who has confessed to be held afterward on account of the same sins—that is, to be regarded as impious and brought into the greatest peril of life. For just as Judas, by the sign of a kiss, caused the Jews to lay hands on Christ and thus deliver Him to death, so the priest offers the penitent something like a kiss when, with an evil intention, he professes toward him in confession a fatherly affection and goodwill, claiming to burn with an exceptional desire for his salvation, so that he may draw from the penitent a fuller knowledge of his sins and afterward make public those things that ought to have been covered by eternal oblivion. In this way he intends that the penitent be accused by others of wickedness, subjected to disgrace, and finally judged worthy of death.]

And the Apostle John says: “Everyone who commits sin is born of the devil, because the devil sins from the beginning” (1 John III, 8). We understand this sin as a violation of charity, because “from the beginning the devil sins” [variant: “lost”]. It is indeed exceedingly dreadful when one who ought, through pure confession, to be reborn from the Holy Spirit is reborn from the devil through a violation of charity in the denunciation of another.

And Scripture says: “The righteous person is first an accuser of himself” (Prov. XVIII, 17)—of himself, not of another. And again: “Confess your sins to one another” (James V, 16)—your sins, not those of another.

Here we should recall that Judas hanged himself by the neck alone. For the person who makes a denunciation in confession harms only himself, because the person who is defamed cannot, without violating the sacraments of confession, be made public or brought in any way into suspicion.

Therefore, in the sacred canons and in ecclesiastical cases, we speak openly and testify only concerning those matters that we have heard in legal proceedings and see being dealt with in their effects. In the Old Testament, too, an ox that was accustomed to gore was commanded to be confined (Exod. XXI, 29). If, while not confined in the field of public disclosure, it killed someone—that is, if it brought someone under suspicion of a mortal crime—its owner, namely the person to whom the penitent entrusted himself in confession, because he had not confined it, is commanded to die. This applies when he brings into a public case, by any means, either something said in confession or someone simply named by the one who makes the denunciation.

The revealer of confession is guilty of a mortal crime. He lies against faith; he does not observe the sacraments of confession; he sins against the unity of the Father and the Son; he blasphemes against the Holy Spirit, who is true remission; and with the Jews he says to the Lord: “Are we not right in saying that you are a Samaritan and have a demon?” (John VIII, 48).

He lies against faith when he does not preserve what has been entrusted to the faith of his Christianity. Concerning this blessed Augustine says in Homily 10 on the First Epistle of John: “Those who do not believe—that is, those who do not have faith—are worse than demons, and slower to believe.”

He violates the sacraments of confession, because he does not believe that the penitent is baptized in confession; and, so far as lies in him, he destroys that person by a second baptism—that is, by confession. He neither preserves the unity of conscience nor fears that God has concurred with him in his judgments. He sins against the unity of Father and Son when, by any disclosure whatever, he divides the unity between God the Father and the Son, represented to him in the person confessing. For when the Son says to the Father, [Col. 0628C] “That they too may be one in us, as you, Father, are in me and I in you” (John XVII, 21), he denies either that God is one, or that he is in the One who is one, or that the Almighty can effect unity in him. But since God is one and Christ’s members come together as one, it is plainly evident that, when through the violation of so great a sacrament he cuts himself off from the unity of the Church, which is Christ’s body, he is neither in God, nor from God, nor with God.

He blasphemes the Holy Spirit when he reveals what has been entrusted to him through faith and the advocacy of him who is the forgiveness of sins, showing that with him the Holy Spirit is not an advocate. Solomon likewise calls him deceitful who reveals secrets, and faithful him who conceals what has been entrusted to his heart (Prov. [Col. 0628D] XI, 13). And in Ecclesiasticus: “He who lays bare a friend’s secrets loses faith” (Ecclus. XXVII, 17), which is the source and foundation of all virtues; and he incurs despair, which is blasphemy against the Spirit and the last and greatest of all crimes. With the Jews he says to the Lord: “Do we not rightly say that you are a Samaritan and have a demon?” (John VIII, 48). By “demon” sin may be understood, as the Evangelist testifies when he says that seven demons were cast out of Mary Magdalene; and the Lord is said to be a Samaritan and to have a demon when a confessed fault is brought back against him, because he who is a Samaritan—that is, a guardian through confession—is reproached with having a demon, through participation in sin, in the person whom he guards.

But if the person who confesses persists in sin, even if the person to whom the confession was made is [Col. 0629A] anathema, he must endure Judas with the Lord until the end; nor should he ever exact any vengeance, either himself or through another, upon those denounced to him for a crime, whether through the malice or the simplicity of the confessants, lest the sacraments of confession be violated. For there are some who think that they cannot obtain pardon unless they disclose the names of their associates.

There are also others who, in confessions made to them, most zealously inquire into other persons’ sins. This seems to us most blameworthy, because, according to Pope Gregory (*On Job*, book V, chapter 3, verse 40), curiosity is a great vice. As for those who either betray others in confession, or in any way bring what has been confessed into a public proceeding, or inquire of confessants into the crimes of their associates [Col. 0629B], we rarely even hear—and do not shudder, as the rigor of the Scriptures requires—how horrible they are.

Nevertheless, having said this much, let us see to whom one should then confess.

[Note: [Col. 0633C] “Let us see to whom one should then confess.” I would not have it said here that one must determine who, in that case—namely, when one’s own priest violates the seal of confession—has the power to absolve, but only to whom one should then confess. It is thus understood that to the persons subsequently mentioned sins are to be disclosed only by humble confession, so that God may bestow mercy more abundantly upon penitents who are thereby more contrite, and that inward helps, strength, and counsel by which they may afterwards return to better fruit may be supplied by an ecclesiastical man, or even by an upright layman.]

Those first of all of whom we have spoken must be avoided.

[Note: [Col. 0633C] “Those first of all of whom we have spoken must be avoided.” Since Blessed Lanfranc in what follows enumerates all the orders, it seems necessarily to follow that he had spoken above of an unfaithful proper priest—that is, one who makes public the sins of the souls subject to him. He therefore advises that one seeking counsel should not open his conscience to such a betrayer, who seeks to divide and defame God’s Church, which is one and chaste. [Col. 0633D]]

For, if the First Epistle of Blessed John is consulted (chapter II, 2), they are Antichrists in their conduct regarding all the sacraments. Setting these aside: in the Old Testament leprosy is shown to the priests (Lev. XIII, 49); the Levites carry, set up, and take down the tabernacle of the covenant. They set a boundary between the people’s tents and the tabernacle of the covenant, lest they approach the tabernacle indiscriminately and die (Num. I, 50, 53). The tabernacle of the covenant is the body of the Mediator between God and men, from [Col. 0629C] whom the Levites set a boundary for the people when they teach for what sins they ought to abstain from the Lord’s table.

Of subdeacons it is said: “Be clean, you who bear the vessels of the Lord” (Isa. LII, 11). The vessels signify hearts; hence in the Gospel: “The prudent took oil in their vessels with their lamps” (Matt. XXV, 4). Thus subdeacons wash the Lord’s vessels when they cleanse consciences; acolytes kindle the Church’s lights. It is the office of exorcists to drive demons from possessed bodies; of readers, to proclaim God’s word; of doorkeepers, to open the church. If all these things are carefully considered, they are visibly done so that by those who do them they may be done invisibly through the cleansing of consciences.

Hence Blessed Augustine, in the sixth tractate on the Epistle of Saint John the Apostle, says of [Col. 0629D] baptism: “The water of the sacrament is visible; the water of the Spirit invisible. The former washes the body and signifies what takes place [variant: what is] in the soul.” For visible sacraments both effect and signify [variant: mark] invisible things. In this we recognize that we ought to confess hidden sins to every ecclesiastical rank.

[Note: [Col. 0633D]

“In this we recognize that we ought to confess hidden sins to every ecclesiastical rank.” This word “ought” does not always impose necessity or command, but sometimes suggests counsel, as Soto teaches among others in *4 Sentences*, distinction 18, question 4, article 1, at the end, when dealing with confession made to a layman: “The word ‘ought,’” he says, “does not signify a command, as some writers of summae think, but propriety, which in Saint Thomas’s time was more frequent in [Col. 0634A] use.”

This statement and the one following can be understood in four ways.

1. First, Lanfranc says that hidden matters should be confessed to every ecclesiastical man, or even to a faithful layman, so that the person confessing may be instructed how grave the sins he has committed are, which bar him from participation in the divine sacraments, and how thereafter he ought to refrain from his offenses. This accords with the mind of the holy Fathers.

Saint Benedict, *Rule*, chapter 7, on humility: “The fifth degree of humility is when one does not conceal from one’s abbot, by humble confession, all the evil thoughts that come into one’s heart, or evil deeds secretly committed by oneself.” The most blessed Father certainly wishes these to be disclosed for the sake of guidance; for in sacramental confession not only hidden sins, but open ones too, [Col. 0634B] must be revealed.

Saint Basil also teaches this, *Rule*, question 229; *Harmony of Rules*, chapter 15: “The rationale of confessing sins is that of a bodily wound or a condition which must be shown to medicine. Therefore, just as one does not reveal one’s bodily defects or wounds to everyone, nor to just anyone, but only to those who possess testimony of the highest skill and the discipline of care and healing, so confession of sins must be made only to those who can effectively heal and correct them,” etc.

Saint Isidore, *Rule*, chapter 13: “He who is defiled by a nocturnal illusion should not delay to make it known to the Father of the monastery; he should attribute it to the deserts of his own fault and do penance secretly,” etc.

Saint Fructuosus, *Rule*, chapter 13: “It is always necessary that a monk disclose to the Father all his actions and the contingencies of occasions, and learn from that man’s discernment or judgment what he must observe. Let no one conceal from his elder his own thoughts, revelations, illusions, and negligences; but such faults must always be truthfully disclosed, with tears, compunction of heart, and humility, to the abbot, prior, or senior prelates, and corrected by consolation, prayer, chastisement, or the exercise of suitable work.”

From the Rule of a certain author, chapter 7, in chapter 15 of the *Harmony of Rules*: “The abbot, prior, or any senior brother to whom the abbot has entrusted the receiving of confessions must by no means reveal greater or lesser crimes, except to the just Judge alone, who [Col. 0634D] washes the crimes of all who confess.”

The mystical interpretation above of the orders, from examples adduced from the Old Testament, plainly enough shows that this doctrine expresses the author’s meaning.

2. By hidden sins venial sins may be understood, and by open sins—that is, sins openly evil—mortal sins. I so interpret the passage of Saint Bede on chapter 5 of the Epistle of Blessed James, on the words “Confess your sins to one another.” He says:

“In this statement the following distinction ought to be observed: that we confess daily and light sins to one another, to our equals, and believe that we are saved by their daily prayer. But the uncleanness of more serious leprosy we should disclose to the priest in accordance with the law, and take care to be purified according to his judgment, in whatever way and for whatever time he directs.”

A comparable author, Radulphus Ardens, adds weight to the judgment of the Venerable Bede and Blessed Lanfranc. In his sermon for the greater litany, after the beginning, he says:

“To whom should confession be made? Confession of grave sins ought to be made to a priest, and specifically to one who alone has the power of binding and loosing, just as judgment of leprosy was committed in the law to priests alone. But confession of venial sins may be made to one another and to anyone, even an inferior, because on account of venial sins a man is not separated from God except through negligence, just as in the law no one was separated from the camp because of scabies or ringworm.

“This confession is made not because he can absolve from sins, but because through our own humiliation and accusation of our sins we are cleansed from sins. Therefore we do not say, ‘I forgive you [Col. 0635B] your sins’; but we say in prayer, ‘May almighty God have mercy on you,’” etc.

Thus far Radulphus, who wonderfully illustrates this proposition concerning hidden and open offenses.

3. By the words “hidden” and “open,” some understand confession in general and in particular. For when we say generally, “I, a most grievous sinner, have offended divine goodness in many crimes,” when we recite “I confess to almighty God,” etc., we conceal sins, since we do not declare them by name. But a person is known to disclose his crimes particularly when, for example, he admits that he has fallen so many times into blasphemy, fornication, and the like.

In this latter manner sins must be confessed to a priest alone, who has the power to bind and loose. Thus Alexander of Hales, *4 Sentences*, question 78, article 1.

4. The theologians give this reason why confession before a layman was formerly received in practice: such confession is directed to the confusion and shame which form part of [Col. 0635C] satisfaction. For those who disclose their crimes to a layman, or a non-priest equal to themselves, must do so from contrition; and therefore God is presumed, through the virtue of humility, to supply the priest’s part and grant them grace—not, certainly, sacramental grace, since the confession was by no means sacramental.

Thus Blessed Lanfranc advises only that hidden sins be disclosed to every ecclesiastical man, since from the betrayal of sins of this sort there arises shame and self-abasement; hence the person confessing becomes worthy of divine mercy and complete forgiveness of sins. Not so in the case of open or public sins. For how is a man ashamed and humbled when he confesses things known to all and done before everyone?

If, for instance, he kills a man in the marketplace, is condemned to death for blasphemy, keeps a public brothel in his own house, and so forth, he gains no humility or shame by revealing these things to a companion, nor will he merit any forgiveness of offenses through the virtue of confession, since the person to whom he has disclosed them lacks the power of binding and loosing sins, which belongs to a priest alone.

This latter interpretation of Blessed Lanfranc’s statement pleases me more; but it must be [Col. 0636A] supported and confirmed by theological authorities.

The book *On True and False Doctrine*—cited by most under the name of Blessed Augustine—chapter 10, in the appendix to volume IV of Augustine’s works, supplies the following:

“Shame is a great punishment; he who is ashamed for Christ is worthy of pardon.”

And shortly afterwards:

“So great, therefore, is the power of confession that, if a priest is lacking, one should confess to one’s neighbor. For it often happens that the penitent cannot confess before a priest, because neither place nor time is available to one who desires it. And if the person to whom he confesses has no power to loose, he nevertheless becomes worthy of pardon through his desire for a priest, when he confesses the shamefulness of his crime to a companion. For the lepers were cleansed while going to show their faces to the priests, before they reached them (Luke XVII, 14). Hence it is clear that the Lord [Col. 0636B] looks upon the heart when access to priests is prevented by necessity.”

Peter Lombard, book IV of the *Sentences*, distinction 17: “If a priest is lacking, confession must be made to one’s neighbor or companion.” Again, below: “A wise and discreet priest should be sought, who together with authority possesses judgment; if he should happen to be lacking, one ought to confess to a companion.”

Then, after much intervening matter, he quotes the following from Saint Chrysostom:

“He who fears God’s judgment is not ashamed to confess sin. Perfect fear dispels all shame; confession of sin entails shame, and that very shame is a severe punishment. Therefore we are commanded to confess sins in order that we may undergo shame as punishment.”

Saint Thomas, in *4 Sentences*, distinction 17, question 3, article 3, reply to 1, discussing confession made to a layman when a priest is unavailable, says: [Col. 0636C]

“When necessity presses, the penitent ought to do what lies on his part, namely, be contrite and confess to whomever he can. Although that person cannot complete the sacrament by doing what lies on the priest’s part—namely, absolution—the supreme Priest supplies the priest’s defect. Nevertheless, confession made to a layman from desire for a priest is in a certain way sacramental, although it is not a complete sacrament, because it lacks what belongs to the priest’s part.”

And a little later:

“Although he who confessed to a layman in a case of necessity has obtained pardon from God because, as far as he could, he fulfilled the intention of confessing according to God’s command which he had formed, he is not yet reconciled to the Church so as to be admitted to the Church’s sacraments, unless he is first [Col. 0636D] absolved by a priest.”

Saint Bonaventure gives the reason why confession may be made to a companion, in *4 Sentences*, distinction 17, part III, doubt 1:

“It is not made to a companion in order that he may fill the priest’s place, or that confession may thereby have the character of a sacrament, but that the will of the person confessing may be proved and made known, so that he may do all that lies in his power,” etc.

Durandus of Saint-Pourçain, book IV of the *Sentences*, distinction 17, question 11, records the following as the opinion of some:

“When access to a priest is lacking and necessity presses, the penitent should do what lies in his power—namely, be contrite and confess to whomever he can, a cleric who is not a priest or a layman. But this does not seem necessary, because when the principal ceases, the accessory ceases; confession is principally for absolution; therefore, if an absolving priest is unavailable—he alone can absolve in the forum of penance—the penitent is released from the obligation of confession.

“For this reason one may say otherwise: it is never necessary to confess to a non-priest; nevertheless, it is lawful if done from humility alone, to obtain counsel or to be ashamed for God’s sake, since shame is part of satisfaction, provided that the person confessing does not submit sacramentally to the non-priest as a minister,” etc.

Dominicus Soto, in *4 Sentences*, distinction 18, question 4, article 1, about the middle, says among other things:

“The shame of confessing and humility will increase his merit, and he will be able to receive counsel from that friend and a remedy for his diseases needing cure.”

And shortly afterwards he replies to Scolo, who asserts that such confession is harmful to salvation:

“More moderately, however,” he says, “we may say that it is no longer in use and ought not to be recommended,” etc.

See also Alexander of Hales, *4 Sentences*, question 78, member I, article 1; Gabriel, distinction 17, question 1, doubt 7; Sylvester, V, *Confessor* 1, question 1; Navarre’s *Manual*, chapter 21, no. 41; Guillaume Estius on *4 Sentences*, distinction 17, §1.]

With regard to manifest sins, however, it belongs to priests alone, through whom the Church—which knows them publicly—both looses and binds.

But if you find no one among the ecclesiastical orders to whom you can confess, seek out a pure man, wherever he may be, as is prescribed in the Old Testament:

“This is the law concerning a man who dies in a tent. All who enter that tent, and all the vessels that are there, shall be unclean for seven days. Any vessel that has no covering or cord fastened over it shall be unclean. If anyone in the open field touches the corpse of a man who has been slain, or who has died of natural causes, or touches his bone or his grave, he shall be unclean for seven days. They shall take some of the ashes of the burnt sin-offering and pour living water over them in a vessel. Then a clean man shall dip hyssop in it and sprinkle the tent, all its furnishings, and the persons contaminated in this way.
