Thus the clean man shall purify the unclean on the third and seventh days” (Num. XIX, 14–19).

It would take too long to run through the mysteries of the allegories one by one. But we must carefully consider what it means that, without any determination of rank, a pure man is said to cleanse the unclean; and we read of certain holy Fathers who governed souls, although we do not know their ecclesiastical orders.

[Note: “We read of certain holy Fathers who governed souls, although we do not know their orders.” This is clearly established in the cases of Saints Anthony, Hilarion, Pambo, Macarius, Francis of Paola, and very many others, in whose case you will find not even a word concerning their orders in reputable writers. Confessions were made before them in the manner stated above in the earlier explanation concerning hidden and manifest sins—namely, for the sake of guidance.]

And if no one is found to whom you can confess, do not despair,

[Note: “If no one is found to whom you can confess, do not despair.” Here the author plainly teaches that he had previously been speaking of confession to be made in extreme necessity; and, with precisely the same intention, he appended the authorities of the holy Fathers that follow. By “necessity” he understands the situation in which one can find nowhere one’s own priest, or another priest, or any of those whom he listed above, to whom one may safely deposit one’s offenses without fear of their being made public.]

because in this the opinions of the Fathers agree: that you should confess to the Lord.

[Note: “Because in this the opinions of the Fathers agree.” The Master of the Sentences, in the passage cited above, and Cardinal Bellarmine, in chapters 15 and 20 of book III of *On Penance*, interpret these opinions of the Fathers as referring to public confession. Consult them, if you wish. Nevertheless, Blessed Lanfranc seems to maintain that these same opinions are to be understood of the revelation or violation of the seal of confession—namely, when no one is available to whom one may safely entrust one’s sins—as he himself expressly suggests: “If no one is found to whom you can confess, do not despair, because in this the opinions of the Fathers agree: that you should confess to the Lord.”]

Thus Blessed John Chrysostom, in his homily on Psalm 50 (homily 2, on the verse “And my sin is always before me,” before the middle), says:

“If you are ashamed to tell someone what you have done wrong, say it every day within your own soul. I do not say that you should confess to your fellow servant, so that he may reproach you; but confess to God, who can heal these things.”

The same writer, in his homily on the Epistle to the Hebrews (homily 31 on chapter 12, after the middle), says:

“I do not tell you to expose yourself publicly, or to accuse yourself before others; but I want you to obey the Prophet who says, ‘Commit your way to the Lord’ (Ps. XXXVI, 5), and then hope that you can obtain mercy.”

John Cassian, in his twentieth Conference, chapter 8, says:

“If shame holds you back and you are embarrassed to reveal your sins before men, do not cease to confess them through continual supplication to him from whom they cannot be hidden—him who is accustomed to heal them without any public exposure producing shame, and to forgive sins without reproach.”

Maximus says in his Easter sermon:

[Note: “Maximus in his Easter sermon.” Or rather, Blessed Ambrose, book X on Luke, chapter 96. Bellarmine explains this statement, and the one that follows from Saint Leo, in two ways in the place cited, chapter 20, near the end:

“First, sacramental confession had not yet been instituted at that time, and therefore it is not surprising that Peter’s confession is not recorded. Secondly, Saint Ambrose is speaking of tears, which contain a kind of confession. Thus Saint Peter, knowing that Christ already knew his crime, confessed not with his voice but with tears; and this is entirely sufficient in confession made to God, who knows all things,” etc.

[Col. 0637] TO GOD ALONE HONOR AND GLORY.]

“I find that Peter wept; I do not find what he said. I read his tears, but I do not read of his satisfaction.”

[Note: Saint Ambrose says the same thing in his commentary on Luke, book X, at the end of the commentary on chapter 22, concerning Peter’s denial.]

And Leo, the tongue of the Holy Spirit, says:

“Sin is washed away by tears when shame prevents it from being confessed aloud. For the merciful Lord, even without any confession, looked upon Peter and forgave him the offense of his threefold denial.”

But priests of lesser rank, and especially prelates, must be extremely careful not to punish publicly, under the name of another person’s fault, a fault that was mentioned privately. Thus, in the line of truth—that is, under the evangelical seal—when the Son of God had said, “That they too may be one in us, as you, Father, are in me and I in you” (John XVII, 21), he did not, without profound sacramental significance, mention the name of the Holy Spirit, although the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one. The unity of the person confessing must not be brought into a third party, nor may this purity be defamed under the name of another’s fault; rather, it must be entrusted privately to the Holy Spirit.

I omit discussion of merely speaking about what has been confessed, since the Gospel, concerning matters that we see and suffer, says: “If your brother sins against you, rebuke him between you and him alone” (Matt. XVIII, 15).

Concerning this saying, Blessed Augustine writes in the words of the Gospel (*Sermon* 16 on the Words of the Lord, chapter 4, vol. X):

“Rebuke your brother between you and him alone, looking to [variant: attending to] his correction and sparing his shame; for perhaps, through shame, he will begin to defend his fault or his sin, and you, who wish to make the correction [variant: the person whom you wish to make better], will make him worse. Rebuke him, therefore, between you and him alone.”

The same writer says in the same place:

“You know that he has sinned, because he sinned against you in secret; seek secrecy when you correct what he has done. For if you alone know that he has sinned against you, and you wish to correct him before everyone, you are not a corrector but a betrayer.”

Again, in the same place:

“The sins committed before men should be corrected before men; those committed more secretly should be corrected more secretly. Assign the appropriate times, and Scripture is in harmony. Thus we act [variant: Let us act], and it must be done in this way—not only when someone sins against us, but also when someone sins in such a way that another person does not know it.”

And again:

“We must rebuke in secret and admonish in secret, lest, while wishing to admonish publicly, we betray the person. We wish to rebuke and correct; but what if an enemy seeks to hear what he may punish?” The bishop knows some murderer, and no one else knows him. I wish to rebuke publicly, but you seek to bring a charge: certainly I neither betray nor neglect him. I rebuke in secret, place God’s judgment before his eyes, terrify his bloodstained conscience, and persuade him to repent. We must be endowed with this charity.

“Sometimes people criticize us because they think that we do not rebuke, or they suppose that we know what we do not know, or that we keep silent about what we know. Perhaps what you say [variant: know], I too know; but I do not rebuke him before you, because I wish to heal, not accuse.

“There are adulterers in their homes who sin in secret. Sometimes their wives disclose them to us—often out of jealousy, sometimes while seeking their husbands’ salvation. We do not expose them publicly, but admonish them in secret; where the evil occurs, there let the evil die. Yet we do not neglect that wound; above all, we show the person who is involved in such a sin and bears a wounded conscience that the wound is fatal.”

Blessed Jerome says the following in his commentary on Matthew (on chapter 18, in the middle, concerning the words “If he sins against you,” and so forth):

“A brother must be rebuked privately, lest, if he once loses his shame and modesty, he remain in sin.”

From all this it is sufficiently clear that, if we see or suffer things which, in accordance with the Lord’s command, we can keep secret only between ourselves and our brothers who have sinned, then, if we wish to correct them, we expose everything that was confessed and are regarded as Antichrists and betrayers, as the Holy Spirit testifies. Concerning such men Pope Felix says (*Felix I*, letter 1, in the middle, vol. I of the Royal Edition of the Councils):

“Let neither the voice nor the accusation of betrayers be heard.”

That faults which have been confessed must not be punished under the name of another person’s fault, nor secretly revealed after having been seen, Pope Innocent says as follows:

“Hidden sins must not be punished, and when proof is lacking, the basis for punishment must cease.”

In all these matters it is clear that the Church, together with her Bridegroom, is one mother, and that she gives birth to her members not for division but for unity, world without end. Amen.

*[SERMON.]*

[Col. 0637]

## NOTICE CONCERNING THE FOLLOWING OPUSCULUM

(*Literary History of France*, VIII, 293.)

The later editors of the *Bibliothèque des Pères* added to the writings of Lanfranc published by Dom d’Achery another short work entitled *Sermon or Sentences of Archbishop Lanfranc*. Since Dom d’Achery had discovered it only more than twelve years after producing his edition, he had already published it in his *Spicilegium*, vol. IV, pp. 227–228, when it was incorporated into the other collection. It is a short but excellent ascetic treatise, in which one readily recognizes the pen and piety of the man whose name it bears. Lanfranc gives an admirable account of all the principal practices necessary for an ascetic and a monk to uphold worthily the profession they have embraced. At the end he touches upon what he had already established, or later established, in one of his letters (letter 33) concerning the Eucharist: that it is beneficial to give it to children, but that it is not absolutely necessary for their salvation before the age of reason.

[Col. 0637]

## SERMON OR SENTENCES OF BLESSED LANFRANC

[Col. 0637C]

There are eight matters which, if religious persons observe them carefully, will easily lead those of sound judgment to conclude that, through observing them, they are not negligent guardians of their order.

First, they must remain in their cloister, and must not leave it in any way without permission; nor, even then, unless they have a reasonable cause.

Second, they must strictly maintain their silence and must not readily break it for any reason whatsoever, unless a reasonable and unavoidable occasion arises.

Third, they must possess nothing as private property; nor, even with permission, should they seek to have more than necessity requires.

Fourth, they must obey their superiors in all things—unless, God forbid, they should command something contrary to God’s will. In that matter they must not obey them in any way, because, as Blessed Gregory says, evil must never be done for the sake of obedience, whereas good may sometimes be left undone.

Fifth, they must not dare to murmur or speak detractively for any reason, even if the reason seems just to them, lest they lose, through this wickedness, whatever good they may appear to be doing.

Sixth, they must love one another according to God, and whatever good each wishes others to provide for him, he must himself provide cheerfully and gladly for others.

Seventh, if they are able to do so, they must not neglect the service appointed according to the custom of their Church; and, while performing it, they must remain attentive and not wandering, lest by wandering they offend the gaze of the divine Majesty, before whose presence they appear to stand.

Eighth, they must make a pure confession of all their sins. Yet they must not make this confession indiscriminately to everyone, as each person may choose, but only to their superiors or to those to whom their superiors have granted authority to receive confessions.

To seek the kingdom of God and his righteousness is to desire the goods of the heavenly homeland and continually to inquire by what merits of righteousness one must attain them.

We must teach the ignorant and not revile them, just as we do not revile the blind but lead them by the hand.

The more heavily we are oppressed by the tumult of carnal thoughts, the more ardently we must devote ourselves to prayer.

Praise becomes pleasing to our God if we do not contradict in our works what we sing with our mouths.

When you recite a psalm, recognize whose words you are speaking, and take greater delight in the compunction of your soul than in the sweetness of a trembling voice; for God approves the tears of the psalmist more than his chattering.

Let your mind not be idle amid various disturbances. If they settle in your breast, they will dominate you and lead you into the greatest sin.

He says [lacuna]: the soul of the believer is the true temple of Christ.

Act cautiously even in the smallest matters; for it is not a small matter for a person to neglect small things in life.

To an idle mind evil spirits insert perverse thoughts, so that, if it rests from work, it does not rest from delight in evil works.

Reject everything that draws the soul by flattery or secret intention.

Eat short of satiety and drink short of drunkenness. Do not cling to present pleasures, nor desire those that are absent.

Let your food be easy for you, and approach it for nourishment, not for pleasure. Redeem your desires with little, because you need concern yourself only with making them cease.

A more serious appetite often arises from excessive indignation, and the pain of an injury received usually inflames it.

No believer should in any way be prevented from being a participant in the Lord’s body and blood when, in baptism, he becomes a member of Christ’s body. Nor should he be deprived of fellowship in that bread and cup if, before eating that bread and drinking the cup, he departs from this world while established in the unity of Christ’s body. He is not deprived of participation in and benefit from that sacrament, since he is found to possess within himself what that sacrament signifies.

## APPENDIX FOR THE ILLUSTRATION OF THE WORKS OF BLESSED LANFRANC

[Col. 0639]

## CHRONICLE OF THE ABBEY OF BEC

From its foundation to the year 1467, taken from an old manuscript codex of the same monastery.

[Note: There are variant readings and additions to this *Chronicle* in a separate document at column 763.]

[Col. 0639D]

### 1

In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1034, the fourth year of King Henry of France, while Robert, son of the second Richard and brother of the third Richard, was governing Normandy, Herluin, a man of revered holiness and the first abbot of the Church of Bec, inspired by our Lord Jesus Christ, the author of every good thing, set aside the earthly nobility in which he was sufficiently distinguished, abandoned the worldly splendor in which he had previously flourished to no small degree beyond due measure, and, leaving behind earthly pride, laid down the military belt in that year and devoted himself with complete dedication to Christ’s poverty. In order to be more freely available to God alone, and moved solely by the love of God, he joyfully took up the monastic habit.

His father descended from the Danes, who were the first to possess Normandy; his mother, however, was closely related by blood to the dukes of Flanders. His father was named Ansgot, and his mother Heloise. Count Gilbert of Brionne, the grandson of Richard I, first duke of the Normans, through his son Count Geoffrey, received Herluin, raised him in his own household, and held him in the highest esteem among all the leading men of his court.

Herluin was highly capable in arms and bore them with no less courage. The leading men of all Normandy counted him among their chosen companions. They elevated him for his skill in arms, his experience in every military matter, and the bearing of his person. At home and in the army he was preeminent among his comrades. For these reasons he had gained not only the exceptional favor of his lord, but also great renown and easy access with Robert, duke of all Normandy, and with the lords of foreign regions.

Such a great and distinguished man, together with his estates and resources, desired to enter the monastic state. On his own property, called Burneville, not far from Brionne, he wished to build a monastery. He constructed a church there in honor of Saint Mary, and received the religious habit from Herbert, bishop of Lisieux, a man of the greatest holiness, when he was forty years of age. He wore it devoutly. Not long afterward, he was ordained priest by the same bishop and appointed abbot, because, owing to the poverty of that place, no one else was willing to assume its governance.

It should therefore be known that in Gaul there was once a certain province [Col. 0641B] called Neustria; later, after the Northmen who came from the region of Norway, it was called Normandy. In it there is a certain place called Bec, so named from the stream flowing there, which still flows in the present day beside the walls of the meadow where Herluin, who was of Danish descent, built a second church, hence called the church of Bec.

For three reasons it is said to have grown in so short a time, not only in wealth but also in religion: within, through devotion to the work of God and the fervor of religious observance; without, through devotion to charity, in which, by the grace of God, from the beginning until now many virtues have been performed and displayed.

This monastery of which we are speaking, at the beginning of its foundation, existed for some time in the greatest destitution [Col. 0641C] and want, so that the Lord might test them by chastising them, and so that, through the testing, the saying of the wise man might be fulfilled in them: “Whatever is brought upon you, my son, accept, and endure in suffering, and have patience in your humility, for gold and silver are tested in the fire; but acceptable persons in the furnace of humiliation” (Ecclesiasticus II, 4–5). And so that it might be shown that this foundation was not from man, but from him and of him of whom the Apostle says, “No one can lay another foundation than that which has been laid, which is Jesus Christ” (I Corinthians III, 11), he did not wish the foundation itself to be carried forward through kings and princes, but through himself and through one who was humble and feared his words, as he himself testifies through Isaiah, saying: “Upon whom shall I look, if not upon the poor and contrite in spirit, and upon him who trembles at my words?” [Col. 0641D] (Isaiah LXVI, 2).

[Note:] Bonnevilla was the hereditary property of Lord Herluin; there he built the first church in honor of Saint Mary, and there he received the religious habit.

But because the place was flat and without water, he was warned in sleep by blessed Mary, Mother of God, and withdrew, with God’s help, into the valley beside the stream called Bec. There he began to build a noble monastery in honor of that same Mother of the Lord, Mary; God brought it to completion for the glory of his name and for the comfort and salvation of many people. God brought to his aid and counsel, according to the desire of his heart, Lanfranc, a man exceedingly skilled in the liberal arts [Col. 0642A] from every point of view, and afterward Anselm, a man approved in all things, eminent in character, affable in counsel, merciful, chaste, sober, and wonderfully learned in every clerical office. Both of them, with God’s help, were afterward consecrated archbishops of Canterbury.

Thereafter so many men of such distinction, both clerics and laymen born of noble families, gathered at that same place of Bec that it could suitably be said to holy Herluin the abbot: “From the abundance of your house you have inebriated the face of the earth, and from the torrent of their wisdom you have filled the whole world.”

Among them was a certain nobleman named William who, coming there to become a monk, gave the monastery of Bec the estate where the monastery of Saint Ébrulf had formerly stood [Col. 0642B] at Utica. To inhabit and administer that place, the venerable Herluin sent the aforesaid Lanfranc with three monks of Bec. Later that same William and his nephews Robert and Hugh of Grentimenti restored the aforesaid monastery of Saint Ébrulf and gave to the church of Bec the village of Russerie in exchange for the aforesaid site of Saint Ébrulf at Utica. How greatly that place of Bec still shines in our own times through the roots of charity, we leave to those who have experienced it to explain.

Hearing of the fame of the region of Normandy, formerly called Neustria, where William held the duchy by hereditary right—the William who afterward subjected all England to himself by arms—and learning from reliable report that the study of literature had greatly declined there among that barbarous people [Col. 0642C], he understood through a most provident inspiration that he could gain greater glory and considerable profit there. He therefore went there with a few companions.

But before he had become known to many, the one who called Paul from heaven drew him to himself in the following manner. One day, while traveling alone with a single student, he fell among robbers. They took away everything he had and let him depart, leaving him only an old cloak, while keeping everything else for themselves.

Then he remembered the deed of another holy man who, when he had been seized by the Lombards—as blessed Gregory relates (Dialogues, Book I, chapter 2)—and they had taken away his horse, afterward, crying out, offered them the whip with which he had been accustomed to threaten the horse, saying: “Take it, so that you may have something with which you can threaten this beast.” After saying this, he immediately devoted himself to prayer.

But they, traveling rapidly, came to a river called the Volturno, which they were entirely unable to cross. Since they could not cross it in any way, they understood that they were suffering this loss because of the wrong they had done to the servant of God. They immediately turned back and not only returned what they had taken, but also lifted Libertinus, against his will, onto the horse from which they had removed him. Then they departed at once and continued their journey freely.

“Thus,” said Lanfranc, “I shall do likewise: I shall return and offer them what they left behind, and when I have done this, they will return everything of mine to me.” But when he had done so, it profited him nothing; rather, it turned out worse for him. As he himself used to relate, Libertinus acted with one intention, whereas I acted with another: Libertinus acted with a pure mind, so that they might have and possess it, but I acted with cunning and deceit, so that they might return it to me, not so that they might have it.

When he had offered them the cloak they had left him, they became enraged, beat him, and tied him naked for a long time to a bare tree; they tied his student to another tree not far away, and then departed. Seeing himself deprived of all human help, he began to reflect and consider within himself how fragile and fleeting is the glory of this world, and how all that people labor for upon earth is vanity.

He promised God that he would wholly renounce the fleeting honors of this world and submit himself entirely beneath that yoke which is light and gentle for those who love him, if God would deign to rescue him from this captivity. As soon as he promised this vow to God from his heart and lips, all the bonds by which he was tied were loosened, as if in a single moment. Set free, he gave thanks to God, approached his cleric, released him, and fulfilled his vow at Bec.

In the year of the Lord 1042, Lanfranc, born of the noble family of the senators of Pavia and wonderfully learned in the seven liberal arts, by the disposition of God, the author of all good things, received the monastic habit at the monastery of Bec, which at that time was poorly furnished with resources, in accordance with the desire of Saint Herluin, who was abbot there. How miraculously he came there, how greatly he benefited the place, how he became the first abbot of Caen, and how laudably he flourished for a long time as archbishop of Canterbury may be found in his Life.

[Col. 0643C] In the year of the Lord 1051, the Church of France was disturbed by Berengar of Tours, who asserted that the Eucharist which we receive at the altar is not truly the body and blood of Christ. Much was therefore argued against him, both orally and in writing, by many people. Among them, Lord Wimund, a monk of the monastery of the Holy Cross of Leufred, published against him an elegant book concerning the body and blood of Christ.

Lanfranc of Pavia too—first a monk of Bec, then archbishop of Canterbury—composed a book on this subject more lucidly and remarkably than all the others. In it he responded commendably to each of Berengar’s questions and explanations, refuting and convicting his erroneous statements and interpretations of the testimonies of Scripture by means of the divine testimonies themselves.

[Col. 0643D] In the year of the Lord 1053, Hunfred of Vitullis, father of Roger of Beaumont, and his wife Albereda built two monasteries on the estate of Pratelli, one for men and the other for women.

In the year of the Lord 1060, Saint Anselm, born in the noble city of Aosta, which borders Burgundy [footnote 3] and Lombardy, although born of a noble parental lineage, was, by God’s gift, brought in a short time to equality with learned masters through the studies of eloquent teachers. Finally, through a divine vision, he was carried away in spirit to the heavenly seats, and immediately heard secret words concerning his salvation, which he fulfilled not long afterward.

When he heard, therefore, that the fame of Master Lanfranc—already a monk of Bec and holding and directing schools there—surpassed the names of almost all teachers, he despised, for the sake of God’s name, the manifold inheritance of his father and mother and came to him with several clerics who were members of his household. Remaining diligently for some time in Lanfranc’s schools and benefiting both himself and others greatly, he finally, at Lanfranc’s encouragement and on the advice of Maurilius, archbishop of Rouen, by the providential mercy of God, received the monastic habit in the church of Bec with complete devotion in this year, at the age of twenty-seven.

How great were the heights of sanctity and dignity to which he afterward rose, the diligent reader will find in what follows. Among his other heights of dignity, when in the year of the Lord 1062 the aforesaid Lanfranc, prior of the church of Bec, had assumed the governance of Saint Stephen of Caen, the aforesaid Anselm became prior of Bec [Col. 0644B], having himself been without office for three years.

Likewise, while the place of Bec still lacked many things and remained in accepted poverty, among other deficiencies a lamp did not always burn day and night in the church, as was customary, because of their want. When the hour of the nocturnal office approached, the sacristan would rise from his bed and go to the bakery or the kitchen, bringing back a light from there.

On the night following the day of the dedication, that is, on the sixth day before the Kalends of March, when the hour of Matins was approaching, the sacristan, named Gothbert, awoke from sleep and saw the entire church illuminated with such heavenly light that a needle could have been found on the floor. Rising in fear, he heard certain voices in the choir, as if people were singing psalms in silence.

He then proceeded slowly to the choir door on the altar side [Col. 0644C], looked into the choir, and saw the most blessed and most glorious Mother of the Lord, Mary, standing in the place where the venerable abbot Herluin usually stood. Before her stood the most blessed apostles Peter and Paul, and a third person whose face he did not recognize, singing Matins to her.

After he had watched this for a long time, he thought of going to the door on the other side of the choir, beside the abbot’s place, so that he might see those most glorious persons better and more closely and hear what they were saying and singing. As he did this gently and very slowly, before he reached the door the light was withdrawn and the voices of the singers fell silent. Nevertheless, so great a sweetness of wondrous fragrance was spread there that, when the brothers rose for the vigils, they were astonished and questioned one another by nods and signs about what this might mean [Col. 0644D]. The aforesaid sacristan recounted all these things as he had seen them.

Again, King William became angry with Lanfranc and removed him from his court, where he had been his counselor, because Lanfranc opposed the marriage of the daughter of the count of Flanders, whom the duke himself had married, since they were joined by carnal proximity and consanguinity. Therefore, by the authority of the Roman pontiff, all Neustria was placed under interdict.

For this reason Lanfranc went to Rome, although he was also going on account of the heretic Berengar. At that time Leo VIII was presiding, and Lanfranc also went to act on behalf of the duke of Normandy and his wife. He therefore spoke [Col. 0645A] with Pope Nicholas and showed him that his sentence—namely, the interdict—was burdening them alone. The duke had neither contracted the marriage nor could he separate them, for the duke was unwilling by any means to dismiss the girl whom he had taken.

When the supreme pontiff heard this and recognized it to be true, he granted the marriage by dispensation, but on the condition that the duke and his wife build two monasteries, in which they would gather communities of men and women, respectively, who would serve God there day and night according to the rule of holy religion and pray for their salvation.

The duke obeyed the apostolic dispensation, and they built two monasteries on the estate that had anciently been called Caen: the duke built one for monks [Col. 0645B] in honor of Saint Stephen, and his wife built the other for nuns in honor of the Holy Trinity.

After three years had been completed, while the basilica alone was still unfinished, Lanfranc, the initiator of the work, was appointed abbot of the monastery of Caen, which the duke had built at the pope’s urging, through the petition of both the duke of Normandy and the leading men. He took several men from Bec with him; shortly afterward they were promoted to positions of dignity.

In the year of the Lord 1063, during the time of Herluin, the first shepherd and founder of the monastery of Bec, the most powerful William, duke of Normandy, who afterward conquered England, began to build a church beside the village of Ermentrude, near Rouen, with the Seine flowing between the two places, on the land and hereditary property of the monastery of Bec, in the fields between Cheville and the village of Ermentrude. Both parishes belong to the patrimony of that same monastery.

This church was called the Church of Blessed Mary of the Meadow [variant: of Bononuntio], and monks from the monastery of Bec were installed there to perform the service of God.

Then, after approximately sixty-two years, in 1135, Henry I, king of the English and son of the aforesaid William, died—namely, in the year 1135—at Saint-Denis in the Forest of Lions (Forêt de Lions, or de Forge). His body was carried to Rouen and opened in the Church of Blessed Mary; his heart, tongue, and entrails were buried and interred in the Church of Blessed Mary [Col. 0645D] of the Meadow before the high altar, while his body, preserved with salt, was carried to Caen, until the wind should be favorable for carrying it to England.

[Footnote 4] In the year of the Lord 1070, the aforesaid Lanfranc, previously a monk of Bec and afterward abbot of Caen, was appointed archbishop of Canterbury, where he lived laudably and gloriously, as an example to all good people, for eighteen years.

In the year of the Lord 1073, on the vigil of the feast of All Saints, the monks of Bec left the first old church in solemn procession and with great joy of devotion [Col. 0646A] and came to the new church which the blessed Herluin, glorious abbot of that place, and Lanfranc and Anselm, men of great authority, had built.

In the year of the Lord 1077, on the tenth day before the Kalends of November, the church of Bec, in honor of Saint Mary, Mother of the Lord, was dedicated by Lanfranc, archbishop of Canterbury. He himself began this great work and, after Abbot Herluin, laid the first stone. The work was completed in fifteen years.

The bishops Odo of Bayeux, Gilbert of Lisieux, Gilbert of Évreux, Robert of Sées, and Ernald of Le Mans [variant: Arnald of Le Mans] were present at this dedication. It seems superfluous to speak of the joy of that day and its manifold gladness. No one could sufficiently describe the arrival of illustrious men and noble women from France, Normandy, and England, accompanied by a great outpouring of gifts, or the abundant provision [variant: banquet] prepared for everyone.

In the following year, that is, in 1078, the blessed Herluin, first abbot of the aforesaid place of Bec and a glorious soldier of Christ, was received by the angels among the choirs of the righteous. He left his precious body to the earth and joined his soul to heaven. He was buried and interred in the middle of the chapter house which he had built. His death was sorrow to his own people and joy to the angels.

The Lord also revealed to him the hearts of men, and he heard the souls of people leaving their bodies, seized by the demon, lamenting; and by their lamenting he recognized them [Col. 0646C]. If we wished to speak of his virtues, life, and character, the day would not suffice. We therefore refer the prudent reader to his Life, where he will find abundant material by which he may be instructed.

[Note:] The venerable man Herluin, not without the direction and providence of God, who prepares better things for all who hope in him, moved the church with all its buildings to a third site, not far from the aforesaid place now called the Chapel of Blessed Herluin, which was the first church founded on this stream of Bec. He built the church of which we are now speaking much larger, together with very extensive buildings. When this construction had been completed, Lanfranc, archbishop of the Church of Canterbury, dedicated it after sixteen years, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1077 [Col. 0646D], in October, on the second day of the last week of that month.

A certain man named Goselin, from the village called Malavilla in the district of Rouen, suffered agonizing pain and innumerable torments because both his feet were burning. After he had endured this for one full month, from the Kalends of November until the Kalends of December, and no remedy had come to him, but misery had overwhelmed him on every side—for he could take neither food nor drink nor sleep, and had no rest—his wife, friends, and neighbors advised him to go to Saint Leobinus at Chartres and have himself carried there on a litter.

He replied [Col. 0647A] that he would go no farther than the church of Bec, which was nearby, not more than one mile away. He declared that he had faith that he could recover health there through the prayers of blessed Mary, Mother of the Lord, in whose honor that church had been consecrated, and through the merits of the other saints. And as he said, so he did; and as he believed, so it happened.

Coming to the holy church on the first Sunday of Advent, which fell on the third day before the Nones of December, he remained in the church porch that day and the next. On the third day he began to rest somewhat. It happened that the fourth day was the feast of Saint Nicholas.

On that day, when dawn was already breaking, the doorkeeper of the church of Bec, named John, opened the doors. Remembering the sick man, he turned aside to where he was lying and found him awake [Col. 0647B]. Before he had asked him anything, the sick man anticipated him and said that he was entirely extinguished and well.

The doorkeeper asked when and how this had happened. He replied:

“I have been well throughout this entire night. At midnight I fell asleep; afterward, when I awoke, I found myself completely cured and cooled, and now by the grace of God I am well, through the merits of the most blessed Virgin, in whose honor this church has been consecrated.”

This happened in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1111, in December, which is the tenth month among the Hebrews and the twelfth among us.

After Father Herluin had died on the seventh day before the Kalends of September, in the eighty-fourth year of his age and the forty-fourth of his monastic profession, and after a few days had passed [Col. 0647C], Anselm, who had been prior for fifteen years, was elected abbot of the same place. In the following year, on the feast of Saint Peter called the Chair of Saint Peter, he was blessed as abbot in the church of Bec by Gislebert, bishop of Évreux.

In the year of the Lord 1082, the monks of Bec who were living at Conflans were transferred from the old church, called the Chapel, to the new church, together with the body of Saint Honorina. Count Ivo of Beaumont-sur-Oise and his wife Adelidis, wishing monks to serve God in the Church of Blessed Honorina of Conflans, gave that church and everything belonging to it to the monastery of Bec, under the free authority and administration of the abbots of the aforesaid monastery.

The revered bishop of Paris, Godfrey, in whose diocese the benefice lay [footnote 5], consented to this donation with the canons of the Church of Saint Mary of Paris, as is always customary for good men to favor good deeds. He reserved for his church the following provision: if, for any reason requiring it, the bishop of Paris should publicly prohibit the celebration of divine worship throughout the diocese of Paris, or only in the aforesaid castle, the monks serving in the said church, after receiving an order from the bishop or his messenger, would observe it.

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1089, Lanfranc, of pious memory, previously [Col. 0648A] a monk of Bec, then abbot of Caen, and finally archbishop of Canterbury for nineteen years, died.

During the time of Saint Anselm, abbot of Bec, three noble matrons placed themselves under the authority of Bec: Basilia, wife of Hugh of Garnay; Amfrida, Basilia’s niece; and Eva, wife of William Crispin.

These three lived together at Bec and, as if by agreement, determined that they would depart from this world one after another, choosing three Sundays on which they would end their lives.

The first, namely Amfrida, Basilia’s niece, who was younger in age and a virgin in body, consecrated to God, fell ill and reached her appointed end on the Sunday falling on the fourth day before the Nones of January. After she had been buried, Lady Basilia began to fall ill. After she had been troubled for several days by severe bodily illness, she was veiled by William, archbishop of Rouen, and then died on another Sunday, the seventeenth day before the Kalends of February. She was buried as was fitting for such a person.

The third, Eva, did not survive long afterward. Weakened by age and fasting, she suddenly began to be deprived of bodily strength. After the death of her husband William Crispin, she devoted herself entirely to continence and persevered in the service of God at Bec until the end of her life. Several years earlier she had received the sacred veil from the aforesaid William, archbishop of Rouen.

As her weakness increased day by day and she went daily to the church, on the feast of Saint Vincent she had herself carried into the church in the morning. There, after being visited by the whole community and anointed before the altar of the Crucified One, she received the other rites customarily administered to dying Christians [Col. 0648C].

When the community was departing, she raised her hand and blessed them, saying: “I commend you to God, my sons.” For she loved us so tenderly, as though she had given birth to all of us.

Then she was carried back home. While she was sitting by the fire, she passed away the following night. As she approached death, the brothers were present to assist her with psalms and prayers. Among them was a certain brother named Ralph, who asked her that, if it were possible, she should appear to him after death and tell him what she had found.

She replied that she would do so if God granted it to her. Thus she died on the third Sunday, the tenth day before the Kalends of February. A few days after her death, she appeared to the brother while he was sleeping [Col. 0648D].

When he saw her, he said: “What is it, my lady? How are you?”

She replied that she had received sixty years of penance. When he was astonished, he asked the reason.

She said: “Because I loved little dogs and various other such things that people regard as worthless, and I took excessive delight in them; therefore I received such a penance.”

Thus you see that these three ladies departed from the world on three Sundays: the first during part of the night; the second at midnight, while Matins was being sung; the third in the morning, while Prime was being sung.

[Note:] As the History of Blessed Anselm reports, through the man who was present with him [Note: [Col. 0649D] He is speaking of Eadmer, who reports these things in the Life of that saint and in the History of Recent Events], who says as follows:

“I attest that I have often heard him declare, under the testimony of truth, that he would more willingly remain in a community of monks, in the place of a boy among boys, trembling beneath the master’s rod, than, placed over all Britain through pastoral care, preside over a pontifical chair amid assemblies of peoples.”

When the venerable Father Lanfranc, as we have said, had been taken from this life, King William of the English oppressed the churches and monasteries of all England with exceedingly severe oppression [Note: [Col. 0650D] William of Malmesbury; Eadmer, History of Recent Events; Harpsfield, twelfth century]. In the fourth year of this oppression, that is, in the year 1093 from the Lord’s Incarnation, Anselm, abbot of the Church of Bec, a man of great sanctity and learning, was invited—indeed, adjured by an urgent appeal—by Hugh, count of Chester, and many other princes of the kingdom of the English, who had chosen him as physician and advocate of their souls. Moreover, compelled by the plea and command of his own Church for the common good, he entered England [Col. 0649B].

As he came, the nobles eagerly went out to meet him. The king himself sprang from his throne and joyfully met the man.

Meanwhile King William was seized by a grave illness and brought almost to the point of death. Among other counsels, the princes advised him to think of the mother of the entire kingdom, namely, the Church of Canterbury, and to relieve her from her former widowhood and distress by appointing a bishop.

He accepted the advice and designated Anselm for this most worthy task. Anselm resisted and opposed it, protesting in every way and calling upon everyone as witnesses. Nevertheless, he was seized and carried—more forcibly borne than led—to a nearby church with hymn and praise [Col. 0649C].

These things took place in that year, on the day before the Nones of March, the first Sunday of Lent.

In the following year, 1094, on the day before the Nones of December, he was consecrated at Canterbury with due honor by all the bishops of England, to the praise and glory of the Lord’s name.

At his consecration, that Gospel saying was found to apply to him: “He invited many and sent his servant at supper time to say to those who had been invited that they should come, because everything was now ready” (Luke XIV, 16).

What sort of merit he possessed may be found in his Life. This most holy man Anselm governed the Church of Canterbury successfully for fifteen years. He had been a cloistered monk of Bec for three years, prior for fifteen years after the venerable Lanfranc, and abbot for fifteen years after Saint Herluin, the first abbot of that monastery.

He was succeeded in the same Church of Bec by its third abbot, a man of great sanctity [Col. 0649D] and learning, William, who traced his origin to a noble Norman family. He was born of distinguished parents in the old castle on the Risle called Montfort. His father was named Turstin and his mother Albereda. She was the niece, through his wife, of Roger of Beaumont, father of Robert, count of Meulan. William was blessed at Rouen in the following year, on the feast of Saint Lawrence, by Archbishop William.

[Col. 0650A] In the year 1098, Archbishop Anselm departed from England because King William, son of William the Conqueror of England, allowed nothing right to be done in his kingdom, but intolerably harassed the provinces with taxes which never ceased, being spent on the work of the wall around the Tower of London and on the construction of the royal hall at Westminster.

That same King William was in Normandy this year, always devoted to hostile expeditions, disturbances, and the concerns of war. Meanwhile, through the worst tributes and exactions, he was not merely scraping the English people, but flaying them.

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1109, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of May, the fifth day of the week, on Maundy Thursday, the venerable Lord Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury, of pious memory, died [Col. 0650B]. In that same year his final Easter was on the seventh day before the Kalends of May.

That same revered man wrote several works worthy of remembrance, which we have taken care to append below.

While he was still prior in the monastery of Bec, he wrote three treatises: the first, *On Truth*; the second, *On the Freedom of Choice*; the third, *On the Fall of the Devil*; and a fourth, which he entitled *The Grammarian*. In it he responds to a student whom he introduces as disputing with him, and he proposes and resolves many dialectical questions.

He also produced a fifth little book, which he called the *Monologion*. In it he speaks only with himself and, setting aside all authority from divine Scripture, investigates and discovers by reason alone that God exists; and he demonstrates and establishes by invincible reasoning that what true faith believes concerning God is so and cannot be otherwise.

He also composed a sixth book, small indeed, but great in the weight of its sweet and most subtle contemplation, which he called the *Proslogion*. In that work too he addresses either himself or God.

He wrote a seventh book of letters to various people, responding to their various affairs or instructing them to attend to matters that concerned him.

He also produced an eighth work, *On the Incarnation of the Word*. Written in the style of a letter, he dedicated this work to Urban, supreme pontiff of the holy Roman Church.

He published a ninth book, which he called *Why God Became Man*.

The tenth was *On the Virginal Conception*.

The eleventh concerned contemplative prayers, which many call the *Meditations*. In them it is readily apparent to readers how great a sweetness of heavenly things had filled his mind.

The twelfth, which is the last treatise, was *On the Procession of the Holy Spirit*. For he had refuted the Greeks at the Council of Bari, who denied that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son. Taking this subject as his material, at the request of Hildebert, bishop of Le Mans, he composed this book.

His nation, life, and character have been discussed.

In the year of the Lord 1113, the church of Saint Neot was founded.

In the year of the Lord 1124, Lord William, the third abbot of the Church of Bec, of pious memory, a religious man and of honorable life, died on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of May. He was buried in the chapter house [Col. 0651A], beside the tomb of the venerable Herluin, on the right-hand side. In the same year the monks of Bec were transferred from the Castle of Clara to Scotres; Richard, son of Gislebert, carried this out.

[Note:] In the time of this William, the church of Philibert received the following privilege, with the consent of John, bishop of Lisieux, and the entire chapter.

First, the aforesaid bishop and chapter granted the said church to be held in perpetuity, with this liberty: it should never cease from divine worship on account of the offense of any person [Note: [Col. 0651D] Something is missing].

Therefore, the text continues corruptly: when the monks dwelling there are in a rebellion in which they have been [against] the bishop of Lisieux, on their own behalf or on behalf of their men living in the same parish, or have sung when not interdicted, neither those same men of the monks [Col. 0651B] dwelling in the parish shall lose divine worship on account of the offense of any person, except for their own offense.

If the church or cemetery should be violated, the monks shall have blessed water with them from the Church of Lisieux, and, by themselves and through the priest of that same church, they shall reconcile the church or cemetery without any further requisition, except in the case of assault and homicide. For these two matters the bishop must be consulted.

Because of this reconciliation, the Church of Lisieux shall not lose its dues from those who violated it, except in the case of *manu pastu*, that is, the servants of the monks; for in their case the monks had the due, namely for theft or for breaking into the church or cemetery itself. But for incest, adultery, or other matters belonging to the bishop, the bishop himself shall have the dues.

The Church of Saint Philibert itself owes the bishop by custom only two shillings per year, and nothing more for the synod or the visitation. The priest of that church shall come to the synod like the others; and if he commits an offense in his clerical order, he shall make satisfaction to the bishop.

But for a presentation before the archdeacon or dean, he shall not bring his books or vestments, nor shall he provide food for the archdeacon or dean.

In exchange for this grant of liberty, we granted to the bishop and all his successors that, at his death, only the service due for one of the monks should be performed for him, and that the canons of that church should perform the service of one deceased person when his death was heard of.

You will find the ancient original in the chest in which the charters of the aforesaid church are kept in the cartulary.

Boso, the first, succeeded him. He was highly learned in the New and Old Testament, a man of extraordinary knowledge [Col. 0652A] and incomparable learning. Divine virtue had moreover bestowed such grace upon him that no one, however sad or in need of counsel, approached him without immediately departing joyful and having received counsel from him.

Loved by God and men, he was very familiar with Henry, king of the English, because the king found in him true religion, admirable holiness, and incomparable counsel. Although Boso was continually burdened by illness, nevertheless he himself, or rather—as we believe—God through him, supplied everything necessary abundantly to his community and to those who came to it, as the need required.

In the year of the Lord 1136, Lord Boso, the fourth abbot of the monastery of Bec, of pious memory, a man of great authority and renowned throughout the world, eminent in wisdom, prudence, and especially in the spirit of counsel, died.

In the year of the Lord 1137, Theobald, elected to the Church of Bec, a man of great goodness and learning, was blessed as abbot of that church with the willing consent of the entire community, at Rouen by Lord Hugh, archbishop of Rouen.

In this year, during Advent, Abricus [variant: Albericus], legate of the Roman Church and bishop of Ostia, held a council at London. There, with King Stephen and the queen consenting, Theobald, abbot of the Church of Bec, a most venerable man, was made archbishop of Canterbury, two and a half years having passed since he had been appointed abbot. On his advice, the abbey of Bec remained without an abbot, under Richard de Belfou, the prior, from the Nativity of the Lord—or slightly before it—until Pentecost, when the aforesaid archbishop returned from Rome.

In the year of the Lord 1139, Letardus, born in the town of Bec, a man of great holiness and learning, highly educated in both Testaments, strong in counsel, affable in conversation, restrained in speech, discerning in discipline, slow to rejoice in earthly things but always rejoicing in eternal things, loving the good and correcting the wicked, was unanimously elected and instituted abbot of Bec. He governed the flock entrusted to him most excellently according to the circumstances of the time, although during his tenure the country was continually troubled by storms.

In the year of the Lord 1141, the chapter-house of Bec was begun, both through the counsel and with the assistance of Robert de Novoburgo; and in the following year the church of Beaumont was given to the Church of Bec. In the same year, the body of Saint Neot was transferred from the old church to the new church.

Note that the church, like the priory of Beaumont, was given by Roger, count of Beaumont, and founded in honor of the holy and undivided Trinity. It was confirmed by Henry, king of the English and duke of the Normans; and in the confirmation he called Waleran, count of Meulan and founder of the church of Saint Nicaise, as witness and advocate of the Church of Bec. And so that this church might conform to the other churches subject to the Church of Bec, which customarily render something annually to that church as a sign of subjection, he decreed that the prior of the Holy Trinity of Beaumont should, in acknowledgment of his subjection, render at least one ounce of gold to the Church of Bec.

In the year of the Lord 1146, the chapter of the monastery of the Church of Bec was begun on the day before the Kalends of August, in the presence of the lord Letardus, of pious memory, abbot of that place.

In this year, the dispute that existed between the monks of Bec and the canons of Exeter concerning the church of Beaumont was settled at Paris in the presence of the lord Pope Eugenius. Thus the aforesaid monks of Bec remained in possession of that church.

In connection with this matter, a miracle occurred, wrought by God through the merits of blessed Faith, virgin and martyr, in the person of Lord Turoldus, formerly bishop of Bayeux and at that time a monk of Bec, the brother of Hugh of Eu. From Hugh’s patrimony the priory of Saint Lawrence of Eu was founded; it depended upon the monastery of Bec-Herluin. This former bishop and then monk was afflicted by a certain illness commonly called “rupture”; from that illness he was miraculously healed through the merits of the aforesaid blessed virgin and martyr Faith, as is more fully evident in the book of the passion of that virgin.

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1149, Lord Letardus, of holy memory, the sixth abbot of the Church of Bec, died.

This holy man was succeeded by Lord Roger, the first of that name, highly educated in both Testaments and also suitably adorned with clerical and scholarly learning. He was elected unanimously by the entire congregation during the octave itself, namely, of the apostles Peter and Paul. He was blessed at Saint-Wandrille on the feast of Saint James the Apostle by the venerable Hugh, archbishop of Rouen. From that time onward, he watched over the flock entrusted to him, as best he could, by day and by night.

In this year Lord Bernard, abbot of Mont-Saint-Michel and a monk of Bec, also died. He had greatly reformed that monastery, both within and without.

In the year 1152, a monk of Bec named Michael became abbot of Prato, on the feast of Saint Thomas the Apostle. In the same year John the Roman, who had been a monk of Saint Sabas from childhood, and afterward abbot of Saint Mary in the Roman Capitol, and who, having left that abbey, had become a monk of Bec, went to Rome. On his return he brought with him the head of blessed Felix the martyr, companion of Adauctus, and gave it as a free gift to the Church of Bec.

In the year 1153, Gilbert de Clare, son of Richard de Clare, died and was buried at Clare in the cell that Gilbert de Clare, his grandfather, had given to the monks of Bec; it is called Stort. His son Roger succeeded him.

In the year of the Lord 1154, on the sixth day before the Kalends of June, a Thursday, during the octave of Pentecost, the monastery of Saint Michael of Peril of the Sea, after suffering almost continuous tribulation for about five years, by God’s mercy gained some respite when Robert of Tougeyo, claustral prior of the monastery of Bec, was unanimously elected by the entire community.

[Col. 0654A] In the year of the Lord 1159, on the Kalends of August, Robert de Novoburgo, vicedominus of all Normandy, a man of great prudence and goodness, weakened by illness, became a monk of the Church of Bec. First he generously distributed all his considerable possessions to the poor. He died on the third day before the Kalends of September, having been a monk for nearly five weeks. In that brief time, through God’s power, he was enriched with abstinence, admirable religious devotion, and every virtue. By his example he left all the great men of the Church an example of virtuous living: formerly rich, he now followed Christ as an exceedingly poor man.

### His Epitaph

Looking upon the august tomb cut from the cliff:

Here in the grave lies Robert of Noviburg.

May he who contains the sea, the sky, and all the ages

Cause this man truly to behold the realms of paradise. Amen.

In the year of the Lord 1161, Lord Theobald, archbishop of Canterbury, of venerable memory, died. He had governed the abbey of Bec for two and a half years, but the archbishopric for twenty-two years, an equal number of days, and three months.

In the same year the monks of Bec began the new work on the church, on the vigil of the Assumption of blessed Mary, in the presence of Rotrodus, bishop of Évreux, who afterward became archbishop of Rouen.

In the year of the Lord 1162, Thomas Becket, archdeacon of the Church of Canterbury and chancellor of King Henry, was ordained and consecrated archbishop of Canterbury on the third day before the Nones of June.

In the year of the Lord 1163, Pope Alexander held a council in the city of Tours. At it Archbishop Thomas sat on the right and Roger [variant: Rotrodus] of Évreux on the left. At the same council King Henry requested that the customs which he called ancestral be confirmed by the lord pope, but he did not obtain this, because Thomas, archbishop of Canterbury, resisted.

In the year of the Lord 1164, at Clarendon, the bishops were compelled to observe the customs of the kingdom of England. The king said that clerics deprived of office because of disgraceful conduct were to be handed over to the court and immediately punished; the archbishop opposed this. The archbishop then boarded a ship without the king’s knowledge and thereby incurred the king’s displeasure.

Note that in the year of the death of the most noble Empress Matilda, three signs were seen in the sky. In March, a comet appeared in Gaul; in July, a heavenly circle shone around the sun; and afterward, in September, at midnight, the entire moon was seen for a long time as blood-red by the kings of England and France, who were at odds with one another after the following Easter.

The emperor of Germany, together with the duke of Saxony, his nephew, sent messengers to the king of England—described in the text as the duke of Saxony’s *generum* (“son-in-law”; printed reading *genero*), an internally inconsistent designation—because he had given his daughter in marriage to that duke. He instructed him to make peace with the king of France and said that his assistance would be ready for him. He sent these messengers, together with the duke, to Rouen. The king followed them shortly afterward, made his counsel known to them, and gave them gold and silver vessels of splendid weight. Thus, having entrusted his advice to them for delivery to the emperor, he sent them back joyfully. The lord king also gave the aforesaid duke two leopards.

Note also that she became ill from the birth of her son Geoffrey and died.

In the year of the Lord 1166, Peter, abbot of Jumièges, died. Roger, a monk of Bec, succeeded him—a man dear to God, to kings, and to many others—and in his days many benefits came to the Church of Jumièges.

In the year of the Lord 1166, Archbishop Thomas came to Vézelay on Ascension Day and solemnly excommunicated the observers of the customs which in England they call ancestral.

In this year Queen Eleanor of England gave birth to a son whom she named John Lackland. Also in this year William of Pavia and John of Naples were sent to hear the case of the king of England and Archbishop Thomas, but they returned without accomplishing the matter. While the archbishop remained in France, King Louis of France provided for his expenses for four years.

In the year of the Lord 1167, at Rouen, in the meadow, the most noble lady Matilda, empress of the Romans, daughter of Henry I, the first king of the English, and formerly wife of the Roman emperor Henry IV, died on the fourth day before the Ides of September. Her body was brought to Bec and honorably buried in that church before the altar of blessed Mary, Mother of God. She had also been countess of Anjou, queen of England, and mother of Henry II, king of the English.

During her life this most noble lady was as generous in hand as she was devout. She distributed her treasures to orphans, widows, and other poor people, and especially to churches and monasteries. She adorned the monastery of Bec with a more abundant blessing of gold, silver, precious stones, and varied ecclesiastical ornament than the other monasteries. Through many humble petitions she obtained from her father that she should be buried there after her death.

In the year of the Lord 1171, notwithstanding the aforesaid interdict, Henry, son of Henry, king of the English, was anointed king at London on the Sunday after the octave of Pentecost by the hand of the aforesaid Roger, archbishop of York, in the presence of his father Henry.

A few days later Thomas, archbishop of Canterbury, returned to England from France, where he had been in exile for six years and more. He was received in the Church of Canterbury with great joy by everyone, especially by the monks, all of whom cried out: “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord” (John 12:13).

Afterward, as he was traveling toward Wdescoalh to see the new king and was staying at Suthowid, he heard messengers sent by the king instructing him not to travel through the kingdom of England in the exercise of his office, but to return as quickly as possible and take up residence in the Church of Canterbury. After he had resided there for almost one month, on the day of the Nativity of the Lord he excommunicated Nigel de Sachevilla and Robert de Brooch. Then, on the day after the feast of the Holy Innocents, he was killed by four knights in the mother church of Canterbury, before the altar of Saint Benedict. The preciousness of his death in the sight of the Lord is proclaimed by wondrous signs of miracles.

Afterward, messengers were sent by the king of England to the lord pope to excuse him for Thomas’s death and to assert his innocence. Not long afterward the aforesaid archbishop became renowned for many miracles and was called Saint Thomas. In the year 1178 the same precious martyr was canonized.

## King Henry of England’s Purgation concerning the Death of Saint Thomas

[Note: [Col. 0655] Henry is absolved of the killing of Saint Thomas. Baron, *Annals*, under the year 1172.]

> To Henry, king of England, Albert, by divine grace cardinal priest of the title of Saint Lawrence, and Theodinus, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Vitalis, legates of the Apostolic See, send greetings in him who gives salvation to kings.
>
> So that events may not fall into doubt, both custom and the common consideration of what is useful require that they be recorded in writing. For this reason we have decided to reduce this mandate to writing: you fear that those evildoers who killed Thomas, formerly archbishop of Canterbury and of holy memory, proceeded to that crime because of the agitation and disturbance which they witnessed. Concerning this deed, however, you voluntarily made a purgation in our presence: namely, that you neither ordered nor wished him to be killed, and that when the news reached you, you grieved greatly.
>
> From the coming Pentecost until one year has passed, you shall provide such a sum of money that, at the discretion of the brothers of the Temple, two hundred knights may be maintained for the defense of the land of Jerusalem for the space of one year. Beginning with the following Nativity of the Lord and continuing for three years, you shall take the cross. In the following summer you shall, God willing, set out there in person, unless you are detained by the lord pope or his Catholic successor.
>
> If, however, you go against the Saracens in Spain because of urgent necessity, you may extend the aforesaid period for the expedition to Jerusalem by as much time as passes from the moment you undertake the journey.
>
> You shall not obstruct appeals, nor allow them to be obstructed, so that they may freely be made in ecclesiastical cases to the Roman Church [variant: the Roman pontiff], in good faith and without fraud or malicious intent, so that the cases may be handled by the Roman pontiff and achieve their proper effect. This shall be subject to the condition that, if any persons seem suspect to you, they provide security that they do not seek harm to you or to your kingdom.
>
> You shall abandon the customs introduced against the Churches during your time. If any possessions of the Church of Canterbury have been taken away, you shall restore them as they were one year before the archbishop left England. Moreover, you shall restore your peace, favor, and possessions to clerics and laypeople of both sexes who, on account of the aforesaid archbishop, were deprived of them.
>
> By the authority of the lord pope, we enjoin this upon you for the remission of your sins, and command you to observe it in good faith, without fraud or malicious intent. The king swore to this; he also swore concerning the abandonment of the customs, and so did his son. Both swore that they would not depart from us and our successors so long as they had them as Christian and Catholic kings.

In the year of the Lord 1178, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of April, the Sunday on which “Rejoice, Jerusalem” is sung, the Church of Saint Mary of Bec was dedicated in the presence of Henry, king of the English; Henry, his son, the younger king; Rotrodus, bishop of Rouen; Henry of Saint-Brieuc; Richard of Avranches; and Giles of Évreux.

At the dedication of the high altar, King Henry the father offered through his chapel an annual income of one hundred pounds. Henry the younger king confirmed this gift of his father by standing there and offering his ring.

The archbishop, the other bishops who dedicated the church, and Abbot Roger also decreed that the anniversary of the dedication should never be celebrated during Lent, but always on the Tuesday after the octave of Easter. A certain archbishop granted forty days of indulgence to all truly penitent and confessed persons who visited the aforesaid church on the anniversary of its dedication, as is plainly evident from the letters of that lord archbishop.

In the year of the Lord 1179, Lord Roger, of pious memory, the seventh abbot of Bec, died. He had vigorously and religiously governed the same abbey for thirty years less three months and ten days. He was buried in the chapter-house of the same church near the feet of Lord Herluin, the first abbot of that place.

This venerable man was succeeded in the government of the same Church by Lord Osbern, a venerable and exceedingly religious man, prior of Beaumont-le-Roger.

In the year of the Lord 1187, Lord Osbern, of pious memory, the eighth abbot of the monastery of Bec, died. He was a man of the highest prudence and of religious and honorable life. He governed the same monastery for seven years, eleven months less one day, and was buried in the chapter-house near the feet of Herluin’s tomb, the founder of that place.

He was succeeded in the government of that monastery by Lord Roger, a venerable and discerning man, then claustral prior of the Church of Bec.

In the year of the Lord 1194, Lord Roger, the second of that name and the ninth abbot of Bec, died. He had vigorously governed the Church of Bec for seven years, two months, and four days, and was buried in the chapter-house of that place near the feet of the tomb of Lord Herluin the abbot.

He was succeeded in the government of the same monastery by Lord Walter, a man of revered discernment and the tenth abbot of that place.

In the year of the Lord 1196, the liberties of Saint Nicaise of Meulan were confirmed by Philip, king of the French, in the seventeenth year of his reign. In that year the bodies of Saints Nicaise, Quirinus, and Bientia, and of blessed Gratian the martyr, were transferred to the church of Saint Nicaise of Meulan on the eighth day before the Kalends of June.

In the year 1197, Walter, abbot of Bec, resigned the governance of the monastery of Bec. Hugh, prior of Prato, succeeded him in the same abbey. He governed the aforesaid monastery as its eleventh abbot for one and a half years, together with three months and three weeks. He departed this world at Prato in the year 1198, on the sixteenth day of May, that is, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of June, and was buried in the chapter-house of Bec beside the feet of the tomb of Lord Herluin.

William, the second of that name, a monk of the same place, succeeded him as the twelfth abbot of the monastery of Bec.

In the year of the Lord 1199, Matthew, count of Beaumont-sur-Oise, and Eleanor, his wife, founded the church of Saint Mary of Laye.

In the year of the Lord 1208, on the third day before the Nones of July, William, the twelfth abbot of Bec, went to Laye at the request of Matthew, count of Beaumont-sur-Oise, who had built a church there. There the aforesaid abbot, with all holiness and spiritual reverence, established a community of monks of Bec whom he had brought with him, both from the congregation of Bec and from Conflans. The aforesaid count died in the same year and was buried there.

In the year of the Lord 1211, at midnight on Sunday, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of October, Lord William, the twelfth abbot of Bec, of pious memory, died. He had governed the same monastery for thirteen years, two months, and two weeks less one day. He was buried in the chapter-house beside the tomb of the first William, the third abbot of that place, on the right side of the aforesaid Herluin, founder of that place. May the souls of all of them rest in peace.

Hence the verse:

> Here lies the second William, the twelfth abbot.

Lord Richard of Saint-Léger succeeded him in the abbacy. He was then infirmarian of the aforesaid place. He was elected by the entire congregation on the sixth day before the Kalends of October; on the fourth day before the Kalends of that month he was presented to Philip, king of France, who received him graciously; and on the Kalends of the aforesaid month, namely, the feast of Saint Remigius, he was blessed by the archbishop of Rouen in the church of Rouen.

In the year of the Lord 1214, the fourth year after the aforesaid Richard of Saint-Léger had assumed responsibility for governing the abbey of Bec, Richard began to renew and rebuild the church of that place, which had largely collapsed during the time of Walter, abbot of that place.

After the foundations had been raised high, he himself placed the first stone upon the foundation with his own hands, while his community stood around him, on the first Monday of Lent. Ingelram, master of the work of Saint Mary of Rouen, directed and assisted the project; Richard had entrusted himself to Ingelram’s counsel for beginning and managing the work.

Acting vigorously, Ingelram built the work begun during the first year with great force. He constructed the façade of the church and extended the nave lengthwise, adorning it wondrously with two very large towers. But after a year and a half had been completed, he withdrew somewhat, delaying the work and not completing it as he had promised.

When the abbot had seen and understood this, after one year and eight months had elapsed, he removed Ingelram and entrusted the project for completion to Master Walter of Meulan; the printed text’s accompanying phrase is *foro sancto* (Gilles’s edition: *facto*), a materially uncertain reading. In the third year Walter brought the aforesaid work to such a height that the new work equaled the old, together with the towers and their canopies. He entirely renewed the roof of the presbytery and the tower of Saint Nicholas with lead. Over the body of the church he placed a new roof, both over the old and over the new work, and covered it with leaden tiles.

At Vernon he renewed and enlarged the chamber (*chambre*) above the cellar and the chapel of Saint Nicholas, and founded from their foundations other buildings that had not previously existed there. He had everything covered with tiles and enclosed the courtyard with a stone wall.

At Murelos he built from the foundations a very large house and covered it with tiles. In that house he established two winepresses. He also renewed the three other winepresses belonging to the house of Bec near Meulan and had those that were uncovered roofed. He likewise renewed the houses of Bec situated on the island of Saint Cosmas, placing a new roof over them and covering them with tiles.

The same Abbot Richard completed these and many other very necessary works within three years, both in France and in Normandy, without anyone’s assistance.

In the year of the Lord 1220, on the Nones of July, the glorious martyr Thomas, formerly archbishop of Canterbury, was translated, in the fiftieth year after his passion.

In the year of the Lord 1223, Lord Richard, abbot of Bec, was elected bishop of Évreux on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of August and consecrated on the sixth day before the Kalends of September. Lord Henry of Saint-Léger, prior of that place, a man of venerable life and noble lineage, succeeded him in the abbacy of Bec. He was blessed by Theobald, archbishop of Rouen, on the fifth day before the Kalends of August.

During his tenure Henry lived laudably and religiously. He loved his community, as is believed, more than others did. From the goods which many noble and common people bestowed upon the Church of Bec generously and most abundantly in his time, he liberally established distributions for their needs.

He had a new dormitory built, because previously the monks of Bec slept in a certain old dormitory, confusedly arranged in three rows of beds. He also had a watercourse brought to the latrines, both for the infirmary and for the community, to ensure the greatest cleanliness of the house, because previously, as is said, the monks could scarcely remain long in the cloister because of the stench.

In the year of the Lord 1238, the church of Saint Neot in the diocese of Lincoln in England was dedicated.

In the year of the Lord 1243, on the day before the Ides of April, a Tuesday, between Prime and Terce, before the morning Mass, the church of Prato, together with all its buildings except the infirmary, was burned by a fire from Ermentonville.

In the year of the Lord 1247, Lord Henry, the fourteenth abbot of Bec, of pious memory, died on the vigil of the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist. He was buried in the chapter-house of that place near the feet of Lord Herluin. All the priors of the Order of Bec, both from this side of the sea and from overseas, were present for this purpose, having assembled there to attend the general chapter being celebrated on that same day.

The aforesaid priors, together with the entire congregation, elected by unanimous consent in that same chapter Lord Robert of Clare-Bec, then vintner of Bec in France, a prudent man in spiritual and temporal matters, on the feast of blessed Mary Magdalene.

He was received by Hugh of Pise, then dean of Rouen, and by the chapter of Rouen, the see being vacant at that time because of the death of Odo, archbishop of Rouen and formerly abbot of Saint-Denis. He was blessed at Rouen by the bishop of Évreux on the Nativity of the glorious Virgin Mary.

In the year of the Lord 1250, on the Sunday before the feast of Saint Michael, at Conflans, the body of Saint Honorina was transferred from an old coffin into another silver coffin, during the time of Robert, abbot of Bec, and William de Braetot, prior of Conflans. The archbishop of Rouen and the bishop of Paris were present, together with the aforesaid Abbot Robert and Prior William, by permission of Lord Innocent IV, pope, who was then at Lyons; while the most illustrious Louis was reigning as king of the French and was then on pilgrimage in the Holy Land, and Blanche, his mother, was governing the kingdom of France vigorously.

In the year of the Lord 1256, the aforesaid Louis, king of France, was at Bec-Herluin on the feast of the Annunciation of the Lord. On that day he ate in the refectory with his knights and barons, with Lord Odo Rigaud, archbishop of Rouen, seated on his left and Lord Robert, abbot of Bec, on his right, while many other prelates sat with them. From there, proceeding to Pont-Audemer, he confirmed many liberties of the Church of Bec.

In the year of the Lord 1264, on the Ides of May, the Tuesday before Pentecost, the Church of Bec was burned after Compline, together with all its buildings and houses, by a fire from the village. The fire began in the priest’s house and miserably consumed the village and the village church, and afterward the abbey. Abbot Robert was then at Lisieux attending the general chapter of abbots.

In the same year, not long afterward, the stone tower of Bec, which stood beside the cellar, collapsed and shattered the cellar and part of the church.

In the year of the Lord 1265, the most glorious Robert, fifteenth abbot of Bec, of pious memory and laudable life, died on the night of Saint Clement. Before its burning he had governed the abbey of that place for sixteen years, nine months, three weeks, and three days; after the burning, for two and a half years and eight days. Taken together, these periods amount to nineteen years, four months, and four days.

He was buried in the chapter-house near the feet of Lord Herluin, on the left side.

### His Epitaph

Monastery of Bec, mourn your fifteenth Robert,

Your abbot; he enclosed you with walls and restored you,
