Consumed by flames, and enriched you with possessions and fields.

Note that when the Church of Bec was burned, the supreme pontiffs, especially Urban and Clement, moved by our prayers, ordered that, for the rebuilding and repair of our church—which had been so consumed by the conflagration of the fire and by a disastrous accident—the revenues and income of one year from all churches and benefices in which we or the priors of our priories possess the right of patronage, located in the kingdoms of France and England, should be assigned to us whenever they happened to fall vacant during a period of up to ten years.

In the first year after they fell vacant and remained vacant, this was to apply specifically in those dioceses in which, by custom, such revenues and income were not owed to the diocesan bishops that year. In those dioceses, however, in which they were owed to the bishops in that year commonly called *le déport*, we were permitted to receive them in the year immediately following that year of *le déport*, to be converted to the rebuilding of the said monastery.

They also ordered that in the priories of our Order a fixed tribute should be received, according to the ability of the benefices. To all other faithful penitents who should give from their goods a pious alms to the Lord, he granted two hundred days of indulgence.

[Col. 0662A] This venerable man was succeeded, with the common consent of the entire congregation of that place, by the venerable John, then prior of Bec, who was blessed at Rouen on the feast of Saint John the Evangelist.

After he had been confirmed and received, they soon afterward elected as prior of that place, with the brothers’ consent in agreement, John de Plesseis, prior of Goldelina. But, being overtaken by death, he was succeeded in the priory by William de Bourgeanville, prior of Prato.

In the year of the Lord 1269, during the time of the aforesaid John, sixteenth abbot of Bec, the parish of Saint Nicaise of Meulan was transferred from the monks’ monastery to the chapel of Saint James of that same parish. That chapel was made a parish and baptismal church with the consent of the bishop of Chartres, the abbot and community of Bec, and the prior and community of Saint Nicaise of Meulan aforesaid, as well as Ivo, rector of that church. The parishioners objected, resisted, and protested, but did not prevail.

After the aforesaid John, abbot of Bec, had vigorously governed the same abbey for nearly seven years, he died on the feast of Saint Nicaise and his companions, in the year of the Lord 1272. He was buried in the chapter-house of that place near the head of Lord Herluin, the first founder of that place. In the same year the Church of Bec was joined to the confraternity of the Church of Fécamp.

The most distinguished man, Peter of Caniba, from near Bec, then prior of Eu, succeeded him in the abbacy. He was blessed by Odo, archbishop of Rouen.

In the first year of his governance, the following misfortune befell him. In the aforesaid year, on the day after Ash Wednesday, the fifteenth day before the Kalends of March—that is, in the year 1273 from the Lord’s Incarnation—the great tower of Bec collapsed, almost destroying and shattering the church. The damage caused by this destruction was greater than the damage caused by the fire, because the entire presbytery around it had to be torn out from its roots down to the foundations.

The aforesaid abbot began to enlarge the church. He began the transept and choir, and set four enormous pillars in a square at the crossing of the church in order to build another tower above them.

Concerning this collapse, the following proverb of France was composed:

> In the year of grace twelve hundred  
> Seventy-three, people saw  
> The great tower of Bec descend,  
> The day after Ash Wednesday.  
>
> Around Prime came the ruin;  
> The work beneath was not yet finished.  
> Therefore the tower came down,  
> Crushed and split the whole choir,  
> And a large part of the nave;  
> It shattered the abbey tower.  
>
> But God be thanked, dear king,  
> No one ever perished there.  
> This happened in the time of Abbot Peter;  
> Because Peter had an abundance of stone,  
> He founded it upon firm stone.

In the same year, at the general chapter, the aforesaid Abbot Peter ordered, with the consent and will of the entire chapter, that the chamberlain, who performs the duties of the office, should receive every year on the Ascension of the Lord, through the cellarer then in office, thirty Tours pounds as compensation for the *cavarum maneriorum* of the said granary officer’s manors (the precise technical sense is uncertain), which the chamberlain had previously been accustomed to receive.

This work was begun in the year of the Lord 1275. Peter, abbot of Bec, laid the first stone; the abbot of Saint Catherine near Rouen laid the second; William, the prior, laid the third; and Amalric of Meulan, who was prior, died on the tenth day before the Kalends of October in that same year. Robert of Le Lion, prior of Scotris, succeeded him. The aforesaid abbot devoted himself most diligently to this work for as long as he lived.

In the year 1286, the aforesaid Abbot Peter crossed over to England. Richard of Flamville, procurator of Oleron, having died, he appointed Brother Robert of Le Lion as his procurator there.

In the year of the Lord 1279, on the Monday after the feast of Saint John the Baptist, at the assize of Pont-Audemer, a hearing was held concerning the fine for Bec’s coinage [French: *Amende*. Marculf and Spelman, in their Glossary], which the king wished to exact from the town. We opposed this by means of our charters granted by the king of England and confirmed by his successors.

After these documents had been examined and read and recorded in the king’s parliaments, the said fine was restored to us and declared before the bailiff and many knights who were present there.

Note that, as regards the presentations of benefices—which is why the priors do not have the right of presentation in their own benefices—the reason is that whenever a question concerning the right of patronage arose, it was agreed that such a question should be pursued at the monastery’s expense. Because of the excessive costs and fear of litigation, all the monastery’s priors wished presentation to belong to the abbot, who would bear the burdens of lawsuits arising concerning the right of patronage, except, however, the prior of Cancico, who did not appear. [Col. 0663D]

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1281, on Sunday around vespers, on All Souls’ Day, the venerable lord Peter of Caniba, seventeenth abbot of Bec, a native of the region near Bec, died. He had governed the monastery of Bec most vigorously for nine years and six days. On the Nones of November, namely on Monday, he was committed to burial in the chapter house of Bec, near the feet of the tomb of lord Herluin, the first abbot, in the presence of the bishop of Avranches and the abbot of Bernay. After permission to elect had been requested and obtained, and Wednesday, the day after the feast of Saint Catherine the Virgin, had been appointed, the brothers, concordant and unanimous in their vote, [Col. 0664A] elected a suitable man in temporal matters, very circumspect in spiritual matters, and worthy of every commendation: lord Ymerius of Saint-Ymer, then prior of that place.

This elected man was confirmed at Pontoise on Tuesday after the feast of Saint Andrew the Apostle, in our priory of Saint Peter in that town, by William, by the grace of God archbishop of Rouen. On the following Wednesday he was received at Paris by the most illustrious king of France, Philip. Then, on the following Sunday, the second of Advent—namely, the seventh day before the Ides of December—he was blessed at the archbishop’s estate of Fraxinos by the same William, archbishop of Rouen; and on Monday at Rouen, in the cathedral church, he made the customary profession. On the following Wednesday [Col. 0664B] he was received at Bec with solemnity.

Note the oath that Abbot Ymerius made at his reception:

> “I, Brother Ymerius, by divine permission abbot of the monastery of Blessed Mary of Bec, swear, according to the good, ancient, and approved custom of this monastery, by God and his saints and by this most holy Gospel, that I, both personally and through suitable persons of this monastery, shall, to the honor of God and the benefit of the said monastery, with all my power, procure, preserve, guard, and defend the monastery of Bec and all its members, with all their appurtenances, both spiritual and temporal, and all the rights, jurisdictions, liberties, charters, privileges, and ancient and approved customs of the said monastery, faithfully and in their entirety. So may God help me.”

And you will find the form of the reception in the cartulary, in the bundle marked y.

In the same year the aforesaid Abbot Ymerius crossed to England to arrange the affairs and business of his church.

In the year of the Lord 1281, the liberty of the prior of Prato was declared in the full Easter Exchequer [Note: [Col. 0663D] The royal treasury, or fiscal tribunal.], before the masters of that Exchequer at Rouen. The matter concerned a certain horse that had killed a woman at the fair of Ermentruilla. The said horse was adjudged by the presiding masters of that Exchequer to the prior of Prato, and a letter of the bailiwick of Rouen was drawn up concerning this.

[Col. 0664D] In the year of the Lord 1282, on the tenth day before the Kalends of May, Abbot Ymerius, having arranged his affairs in England, departed from there and crossed to the regions of France. He was received at Bec by his entire convent on the eighth day before the Kalends of the same month.

In the same year, after so great a fire and destruction, an inquiry was held at Bec into the place where the body of the pious lady Matilda the empress had lain; it was found in front of the high altar, enclosed in a certain cowhide.

In the year of the Lord 1285, on the day after All Saints’ Day, four [Col. 0665A] foresters who guarded the woods of lord Reginald of Trie, knight, made a terrible assault at Lay, wounding the clerk of that priory and two monks—namely, John of Leone, the superior, and Brother Thomas of Tonilla—so severely that John died within five days and Thomas within fifteen days. In this year Robert of Leone, prior of Bec, also died, and Brother William of Saint-Elwald, then prior of Saint Peter of Pontisara, succeeded him.

In the same year Ymerius, abbot of Bec, in the general chapter celebrated on the vigil of Saint John the Baptist, with the assent of the entire congregation, permitted the cloistered monks to have capes whenever it was necessary for them to go outside for some business or other necessity; and he abolished shoes fastened with thongs. He decreed that the monks of Bec who were sent in obedience to reside in certain priories in England or elsewhere should, after they had remained there for six years and had conducted themselves honorably, be recalled to the cloister of the monastery of Bec, after the report and testimony of the priors under whom they had resided had been heard.

In the same chapter he excommunicated all conspirators and devisers of evils, all disobedient persons, and all who brought false accusations against their associates; all who arranged through secular persons to be transferred from one place to another against obedience; all who arranged through secular persons to obtain a priory or any office; and all who arranged, either personally or through others, that they could not or should not be removed from a priory or office. [Col. 0665C]

The aforesaid Ymerius is recorded as having attended the general chapter every year, more than any of his predecessors, and as having instituted many salutary constitutions there. In particular, by his letters patent he ordered and enjoined all the priors of the same order that every year, on the vigil of Saint John the Baptist, at the general chapter at Bec, they should submit in writing, before everyone assembled in that chapter, a report on the condition of their house or priory.

In his time he devoted himself with zeal, diligence, and prudence to the work and construction of the new church, which had been begun after its destruction in the time of his predecessor, Abbot Peter [Col. 0665D]. He assigned the aforesaid work to a certain master mason named Robert of Fonte, to construct it as far as the roofing, as is evident from the mason’s own letters. In his time he also vigorously managed the affairs of the church, preserving, defending, and pursuing the rights, liberties, immunities, and privileges of the Church of Bec in France and Normandy, and in the kingdoms of England and Wales.

He also ordained that the succentor, who bears many of the church’s labors day and night, should receive every year, in addition to the cantor’s office, fifty Tours pounds; and that the justiciar should pay the keeper of the charters sixty Tours pounds every year.

In the year of the Lord 1304, on the fifteenth day of November, after the aforesaid Ymerius had governed the monastery vigorously and laudably for nearly twenty-three years, he closed his final day. May God show mercy to his soul. He was buried in the chapter house, beside the head of lord Herluin, its first shepherd. [Col. 0666A]

In the year of the Lord 1304, on the Thursday after the feast of Saint Lucy the Virgin, after the death of the aforesaid Ymerius, while Brother William of Saint Paternus, prior, was presiding in the chapter house of Bec, with the entire convent of that monastery present, together with the priors of the priories dependent upon it, a venerable and discreet man, Brother Gilbert of Saint Stephen, then granary officer of the place, having been duly summoned for this purpose, was elected by the method of compromise as abbot and [Col. 0666B] father of that monastery. He was subsequently confirmed and blessed. He governed the aforesaid monastery wisely and religiously for twenty-two years and eight months, or approximately that length of time.

In his time he completed the new work of the church. That work had already been begun in the time of lord Peter of Caniba, the seventeenth abbot, his predecessor. The aforesaid Gilbert gave the convent, for the salvation of his soul and for the celebration of his anniversary, an annual income of twenty Tours pounds, to be received and collected by the office of the pitancer from and upon the provostship of Bec.

He died in the year of the Lord 1327, on the feast of Saint Bartholomew the Apostle, the ninth day before the Kalends of September, and was buried in the new [Col. 0666C] chapel of the Blessed Virgin Mary, behind the choir, before the altar of that Virgin Mary.

**Verses over his tomb**

> O you who pass by, remember death, I beg you;  
> What I am, you will be; please pray for me.

This venerable man was succeeded in the governance of that church by a prudent man, lord Gaufridus, called Fare [elsewhere, Fae], then prior of Prato. He was elected by the method of compromise on Saturday, the feast of the Beheading of Saint John the Baptist, in the year of the Lord 1327, and afterward confirmed and blessed as the twentieth abbot.

After he had governed that monastery laudably and vigorously for nearly seven [Col. 0666D] years, he was elected to the bishopric of Évreux in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1334, in recognition of his known merits. Because of his dignity, however, he did not abandon the regular habit of the Church of Bec; rather, everywhere he continued to wear white garments, especially the white cowl, which is the distinctive habit of that church.

In his time he enlarged and expanded the fabric of the church of Évreux, especially the choir. It is clear to those who look upon it that, from the time when he was transferred from the abbacy to the bishopric of Évreux, the following proverb was made:

> Take the head of a mackerel,  
> Of a dog, a conger eel, and a carp;  
> Of six victuals and four measures,  
> And you will find, without other titles,  
> [Col. 0667A]  
> When Geoffrey Fare resigned  
> The abbacy of Bec and took Évreux.  
>   
> On the first day of April, without doubt,  
> May God guard the household and the whole order.

Note that in 1334, in the time of lord William, the supreme pontiff was Clement. Moved by filial devotion, not compelled but acting of our own free will, under the pretext of the affairs of the Holy Land and the exaltation of the Catholic faith, we gave the said supreme pontiff fifteen thousand small florins of Florence to support those needs. Ten thousand of these were delivered immediately; the other five thousand afterward, as is shown in the cartulary by a letter drawn up concerning this matter. The letter is duplicated in the archive of election documents.

It was a general tithe levied [commonly called [Col. 0667B] *une levée*] throughout the kingdom of France by dioceses. On account of that tithe, because our lands were dispersed through the aforesaid dioceses, we paid, excluding the goods of our priories, three thousand six hundred and thirteen pounds, two sous, and six deniers, as is shown by the letters of quittance.

In the year of the Lord 1337, it was ordained in chapter that the bull of lord Pope Benedict concerning the provision for scholars should be observed. It was established that each prior should pay the said scholars, for every franc of income of his priory, three sous and three deniers, paying the entire amount into the hands of the pitancer. Thus the master lecturing in theology was to receive forty francs, the theology student the same amount, and the doctor of decretals, who lectured on canon law, [Col. 0667C] fifty; while the scholar studying law and the bachelor in the same subject were to receive thirty-six pounds, as is shown in the cartulary, in the bundle marked X.

In the year of the Lord 1318, the Apostolic See granted Philip, king of the French and of Navarre, for certain reasons, the right to levy a tithe in the province of Rouen. We were assessed, for our share and portion, the sum of 1,670 pounds, which we paid at Bec, in the king’s presence, on the fourteenth day of August of the aforesaid year, as is shown by the quittance contained in the cartulary, in the bundle of . . . [lacuna].

In the year 1346 [Note: [Col. 0667D] The years are recorded confusedly.], another levy was collected in the kingdom of France and imposed by the aforesaid Philip, who waged war against the king of England. For this we paid, on behalf of ourselves and our priories, the sum of 120 pounds.

In the year 1424, another tithe granted to the lord king was levied; for this the prior of Beaumont paid, for his share, five hundred francs.

In the year 1435, Abbot Thomas was absolved [16] because of failure to pay the tithe granted by Pope Martin V to the duke of Bedford on the revenues situated in the duchy of Normandy. It had been imposed and levied in the time of lord Robert, his predecessor, who was governing at Paris, and by the bull students at Paris were exempted [lacuna].

In the year of the Lord 1312, while lord Clement V was presiding over the Church, we gave, freely and generously, ten thousand florins for the support of the Apostolic See and also for the resolution of our affairs. If the procurator, or Master John of the abbot, had not intervened, we would have given fifteen thousand, as is shown in the cartulary.

In the year of the Lord 1369, the pope wished to levy a tithe for the repair of the church or monastery of Monte Cassino, from which our father Benedict was abbot. The collection in the province of Rouen was entrusted to the abbot of Saint-Ouen, who declared the poverty of the churches. Nevertheless, the tithe was paid, and we paid forty-nine florins for our share and portion, as is shown in bundle 1.

Note that in the years 1307 and 1345, venerable men—Master Nicholas of Oak, rector of the church of Saint Sylvinus of Glos, gave us certain decretals with the ordinary gloss, together with the fifth book of the decretals with its gloss, and the Decree with the ordinary gloss. Master John of Boesseyo, rector of the church of Saint George of Tilia, who had been raised from youth in our house and provided with a benefice, gave us all his books, to be received after his death. If he should happen, through illness or necessity, to sell them [Col. 0668C], his executors would be bound to pay us two hundred pounds. He himself was a doctor of medicine and an outstanding professor of that discipline.

In the year of the Lord 1335, on Thursday before the feast of Saint John the Baptist, on the twenty-third day of June, after Gaufridus Fare had spontaneously resigned in order to transfer to the aforesaid bishopric, while Brother John of Saint-Mellon, prior of Bec, was present and presiding in the chapter house of Bec, together with the priors of the entire order, Brother John of Granges, then justiciar of Bec, was elected shepherd of that monastery.

While governing the church laudably, among the other good works that he accomplished there, he had the new church, newly completed, solemnly dedicated, as will be shown below.

In the year of the Lord 1340, on the fifteenth day of April, the pious lord Gaufridus Fae, twentieth abbot of Bec and afterward bishop of Évreux, died. He did not forget the Church of Bec; he was brought back to it and buried there, on the left side of the choir, as his tomb makes clear. May his soul rest in peace.

In the year of the Lord 1342, on the fifteenth day of September, the seventeenth day before the Kalends of October, in the first year of the pontificate of the most holy Father in Christ, lord Clement VI, by divine clemency pope, while Philip was king of the French, lord John, his firstborn son, duke of Normandy, and lord John of Granges was the twenty-first abbot of Bec, the church of Bec was dedicated by the reverend Father in Christ, lord John, bishop of Avranches, in honor of the holy Virgin Mary and all the saints.

The high altar and likewise the lesser altar were consecrated by that bishop of Avranches in honor of Saint Mary, in the presence of the Fathers in Christ, lords the bishop of Lisieux and John, bishop of Pavia, and the venerable Fathers and lords, the abbots of Fécamp, Saint-Ouen, Caen, Saint-Evroult, Jumièges, Saint-Wandrille, Saint-Georges, Blanquerville, Bernay, Cormeilles, Prato, Grestain, Saint Catherine [Col. 0669B] near Rouen, Saint-Victor, and Corneville; the priors of Saint Barbara, of Blessed Mary of the Park near Harcourt, and of Friardel; and the noble men, lords John Malet, Robert of Neubourg, John of Ferrières, G . . . . . of Friardel, and R . . . . . of Tournebu, knights, together with many other knights and ecclesiastical and secular men, rejoicing on that day.

On the same day the altar in the prior’s chapel was consecrated in honor of Saint Benedict. In the chapel said to belong to the sacrist, an altar was consecrated in honor of the holy apostles Peter and Paul by the bishop of Lisieux; and on the same day, in the chapel called that of Ferrières, an altar was consecrated in honor of Saint John the Baptist. Likewise, in the next chapel, an altar was consecrated in honor of Saint Maurus; and in the following chapel, said to belong to the subcellarer, one in honor of Saint Martin. In the chapel said to belong to the chamberlain, the bishop of Pavia consecrated an altar in honor of Saint Stephen the Protomartyr.

On the following Monday, two altars in the vestment room were consecrated by the aforesaid bishop of Pavia: one in honor of Saint Nicholas and Saint Brendan, and the other in honor of Saint John the Evangelist and Saint Anianus the bishop. Likewise, the altar of Blessed Mary Magdalene and Blessed Honorina the Virgin, in the chapel said to belong to the almoner, was consecrated by the same bishop of Pavia, to the glory of God and the rejoicing of the people.

At that dedication, it is said that wine flowed for three days from the conduit called Angelus, in the cloister near the chapter house, for the sustenance of all the servants.

[Col. 0669D] 17 In the time of this John, a certain honorable religious man named William of Mara, also called Loeson, granary officer of the monastery, with the permission of the aforesaid John, who was presiding over the general chapter, and with the assent of the entire chapter, in the year 1340, on the vigil of Saint John the Baptist, gave the cloistered religious an annual income of ten Tours pounds from and upon the office of granary officer of that place. It was to be received on the feast of the Assumption of Blessed Mary through the hands of the granary officer in office at the time and distributed to them through the hands of the prior, so that, for the praise and glory of Blessed Mary, the antiphon called *Salve Regina, Mater*, and so forth, might be said and sung by the brothers present there after Compline had ended.

[Col. 0670A] In the same year, lord John of Ferrières, knight, gave the aforesaid religious, for the office of pitances, a certain portion of the tithe that he had in the parish of Grandchamp, subject to the payment of ten pounds of income owed on this account to the prior of Malpassu.

In the time of the aforesaid abbot, in the year 1345, lady Maria of Spain, countess of Alençon, of Étampes, gave the aforesaid religious five hundred Tours pounds to purchase forty pounds of income, to be distributed to the cloistered religious through the hands of the pitancer, so that every day Mass might be celebrated by those religious in the newly founded chapel of Blessed Mary.

This sum was delivered to the prior of Prato, so that he might pay the aforesaid income to the religious in four installments, at the feasts of Saint John the Baptist, Saint Michael, the Nativity of the Lord, and Easter; ten pounds at each installment.

At this time the Mass that is celebrated daily for the congregation, in honor of the Blessed Virgin in the morning, began. At this Mass twenty-four candles are lit every day: the abbot is to pay for four, and the other ten officers are each to pay for two. To rouse the people and the brothers, one of the larger bells is rung.

At that time wars and disagreements also began to arise and spread among the kings of France, England, and Navarre, concerning the crown of the kingdom of France, which the English king Edward claimed for himself and said belonged to him by hereditary right.

[Col. 0670C] In the year of the Lord 1350, on the nineteenth day of February, the lord John mentioned above, of blessed memory, the twenty-first abbot, died. He had governed the church religiously for fifteen years and eight months and was buried in the chapel of Blessed Mary, behind the choir, beside the tomb of lord Gilbert, the nineteenth abbot, before the altar of the Virgin Mary.

**Verses**

> May the gracious Mother place this man, born for blessedness, among the saints;  
> May he who was faithful in the world be placed in heaven.

This venerable Father was succeeded in the governance of the Church of Bec by a man of great learning, Brother Robert of Rotis, also called Couroye, doctor of decretals, elected by scrutiny, as the form of his election testifies. He governed that church for approximately eleven years.

In the year of the Lord 1356, in the time of the aforesaid Robert, after the battle of Poitiers, in which King John of France was captured by the English, while the aforesaid wars were raging in Normandy and increasing from day to day, and while the English held very many places, villages, castles, and towns, lord Louis of Harcourt, then captain and general governor of Normandy in the name of the king of France, by royal authority ordered that the church of Bec—which had recently been built large, spacious, indeed beautiful, and had recently been completed and dedicated, as stated above—should be demolished [Col. 0671A] down to its foundations and fortified with towers, for the security of the country and so that it would not be captured by the English or other enemies then active in the region.

Therefore, with the advice and assistance of the barons, knights, nobles, and neighbors, and with the chapter consenting to it, it was thought appropriate to fortify it; to block with stones the chapels around the choir and the other openings; to surround the church itself and the belfry, together with the church towers and chapter house, with defensive works; and to surround them with ditches.

For this reason it was necessary to demolish one part of the dormitory adjoining the chapter house, three sides of the cloister beside the church, and also a certain part of the cellar, the houses, and the hall called Neubourg, beside the church towers, causing the church enormous damage.

[Col. 0671B] It was also necessary for the religious to leave the dormitory and for some of them to sleep inside the church, above the vestment room; while the other officers and elders lay in the chapels surrounding the choir. Other parts of the church were occupied for the preservation of the church’s goods.

Thus nothing remained level except the circuit of the choir and the path around it, because processions could not be held in the cloister after its demolition. The church was compelled to spend its revenues and income on the pay of armed men for guarding and [18] preserving the said fortification. For that reason it was necessary to mortgage manors, lands, and tithes to support the aforesaid burdens, causing the church the greatest damage.

And the Mass of Blessed Mary, which had recently been ordered to be sung behind the choir, was, under the pressure of necessity, sung at the high altar.

In the year of the Lord 1361, on the first day of September, the aforesaid Father Robert, twenty-second abbot of Bec, departed this life. He had governed that church for nearly eleven years and five months. He was buried in the chapel of Blessed Mary behind the choir, on the left side, beside the tomb of lord Gilbert the abbot. There is neither tomb nor epitaph.

After his death, in the year 1361, Brother William of Benseville, called Popeline, a man of great religious devotion, was elected by the entire congregation as shepherd of that monastery [Col. 0671D] and was subsequently blessed. He was modest and gentle toward the brothers, and governed the monastery vigorously and laudably for twenty-seven years, while wars raged both in Normandy and in France and Aquitaine. Although the monastery was in the greatest need, by his kindness and patience he preserved it from many adversities, losses, and dangers.

In the year 1388, on the second day of May, he departed this life and was buried in the vestment room, before the altar of Saints Nicholas and Catherine, where the chapter was then being held, because the chapter house was occupied by the mill, the oven, and the granary on account of the wars.

This Father also, in his time, furnished and endowed the church with noble religious men whom he clothed. Among these, the following later flourished: Gaufridus called Harenc, abbot of Jumièges; Vincent of Rouen, called of Lieno, abbot of Prétaux; Robert of Rouen, also called le Telier, abbot of Saint-Evroult; and John of Bouleya, abbot of Cerisy.

**His epitaph**

> Here lies in the tomb Ginatus [Guillelmus] of Benseville,  
> Abbot of Bec, who held office twenty years and seven;  
> After he had clothed many, soon three  
> Became abbots; and among them one, Gaufridus of Paris,  
> And with John [John] of Hors, of Jumièges,  
> He allowed himself finally to become shepherd at Bec,  
> Twice elected, now ordered to be made, and this figure  
> Having been conquered by William’s zeal, by the weapon of his voice; in the year  
> In the year *Bisseptingento* (that is, 1388); but subtract twice six from this.  
> On the second light of May, to whom, Christ, grant heaven.

In the year of the Lord 1388, after the death of lord William, the twenty-third abbot, Brother Gaufridus of Paris, called Harenc, then prior of Conflans, a man of very keen intelligence and bachelor in decretals, was elected by the entire congregation as abbot and shepherd of that monastery.

But the election did not achieve its effect, because a certain Estodus, named of Estouteville, [Col. 0672C] formerly a monk of Fécamp and then abbot of the monastery of Cerisy, by the authority of the Roman pontiff, through the force of all the prelates, and through the power of his friends and relatives, obtained control of the aforesaid monastery.

He was the first foreigner to obtain the governance of the Church of Bec, since he was not a member of that church’s own community from the time of its foundation. He governed the monastery for two years and eight months.

The monastery, which had recently begun to recover when the wars ceased, was in the greatest need because of those wars and was bound by many debts to many people. Its houses, manors, mills, and all its workshops were in the greatest ruin and decline. At his arrival everything deteriorated, both collectively and individually, because his concern was the accumulation of money. He appropriated the office of treasurer for himself and appointed a secular receiver, something never before seen.

Daily expenses became incalculable, both because of his excessive state and because of his brothers, some of whom were bishops, others knights, and others archdeacons. At the expense of the Church of Bec, shining with singular ambition, he obtained from the Apostolic See the privilege of using the mitre, rings, and pontifical insignia for life alone.

When he was called to govern the Church of Fécamp, where he had previously been a monk, he took with him so many goods of the Church of Bec—both books and precious objects, gold and silver—that there is no memory, since its foundation, of the church having suffered such ruin.

[Col. 0673A] His brother, the bishop of Lisieux, and Estoldus founded the College of Lisieux at Paris, near Saint Geneviève. Estoldus distributed to that college the books and everything else that he had taken from the Church of Bec. May the Lord forgive him for so great an offense.

19 After Estoldus’s departure, Gaufridus of Paris, called of Harenc, who had been removed by the violence of Estoldus’s friends with the pope’s consent, was again elected by the entire congregation as abbot and shepherd of the Church of Bec. On the fourteenth day of March—that is, on the Tuesday before Palm Sunday—in the year of the Lord 1390, he was received with great joy, everyone shouting: “Noel! Noel!”

In the first year after his arrival, he had forty [Col. 0673B] chambers made in the old dormitory, and had the religious sleep there, since they had previously slept above the vestment room. In the same year he clothed sixteen monks in the religious habit. He also had all the workshops cleaned; had the stones and the materials with which the chapels had been blocked removed; had them glazed anew, especially the chapel of Blessed Mary, in the middle of which there had been a massive wall that he ordered to be demolished. The Mass that had been said every morning before the high altar began again to be celebrated in that chapel.

He also had the chapter house cleaned, which had been occupied by a mill, an oven, a granary, and large vats for storing cider. He had the chapter house and refectory painted and renovated, removed everything from the chapter house [Col. 0673C], and repaired everything that had been constructed during the war.

He also repaired the church and the workshops of the monastery by providing them with roofing, since everywhere it had rained at the time of his arrival. He carefully repaired all the manors and mills that he found in great decline and ruin. He freed the church from the many debts with which it had been burdened in the time of Estoldus, his predecessor, and of his other predecessors.

He also relieved the church of an annual life income of one hundred pounds that a certain Peter le Veulles, also called Pontrel, held for his lifetime upon our tithes and lands of Calais.

He also restored the manor, land, and revenues of Quevilly, which had been mortgaged to Gervais of Saux and his wife for their lifetimes. He paid eight hundred pounds from the goods of his father and mother, which he had recently received upon their deaths.

He also worked vigorously to protect our liberty concerning the sale of fish, against the merchants who refused to bring their fish for sale to the monastery’s kitchen before displaying them for sale, as was customary. He obtained from the Roman pontiff that he and his successors, the abbots of Bec, might henceforth use the mitre and the other pontifical insignia perpetually.

He began the enclosure of the monastery with walls and towers, so that in future the church would not be oppressed and occupied during wartime as it had been before.

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1398, on the thirteenth day of July, he set out on a pilgrimage overseas, accompanied by many noble men of France and Normandy, to visit the Holy Land of Jerusalem, the Lord’s Holy Sepulchre, and the other holy places, as well as Saint Catherine on Mount Sinai.

On the return journey he fell into a certain pit, in which he remained for three days without being found. During that pilgrimage, while he was returning with his companions through the deserts, he fell ill to such a degree that he could proceed neither on foot nor on horseback. He had to be carried with great difficulty in a litter by his companions. They came in this way as far as Italy, to a certain city called Padua, where, amid the great grief of his companions, he closed his final day on the fifteenth day [Col. 0674B] of July, in the year of the Lord 1399. He was buried there in a certain church. Some of the religious of Bec were sent there, and at the church’s expense they arranged a service and burial in his memory.

Note the privilege granted to the abbots of Bec through the favor of Gaufridus Harenc, then abbot.

“Clement, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons Gauffridus, abbot, and the convent of the monastery of Bec-Hellouin, of the Order of Saint Benedict, in the diocese of Rouen: greeting and apostolic blessing.

The sincerity of your devotion demands, and the excellence of your religious life merits, that we raise to worthy honors both you, whom we embrace with special affection of devotion, and your monastery. Some time ago, therefore, we decided to grant to a certain Estoldus, abbot of the said monastery, and to you, sons of the convent, that Estoldus, abbot, and his successors, the abbots of the said monastery who should hold office in their time, might freely use the mitre, ring, and other pontifical insignia; and likewise that in the said monastery, in the priories subject to it, and in the parish and other churches belonging jointly and commonly, or separately, to the said abbot and to you, sons, although these were not fully subject to him and to you, they might bestow the solemn blessing upon the people after the solemn celebrations of Mass, Vespers, and Matins—provided that, during such blessing, no bishop or legate of the Apostolic See were present. [Col. 0674D]

We therefore, wishing to raise you by a more ample prerogative of honor, and inclined in this matter to your petitions, grant you and your successors, the abbots of the same monastery who shall hold office in their time, by apostolic authority and as a special favor, permission freely and lawfully to use the mitre, ring, and such insignia even in synods and places of the province of Rouen, and in the presence of any persons whatsoever, even if they should shine with pontifical or royal dignity, provided that at the said synods and places the archbishop of Rouen then in office, or a legate or nuncio of the said See, is not present; and likewise to bless the corporals, chalices, and other ornaments necessary for divine worship in the monastery, the priories, and the aforesaid churches, and in the twenty places and other establishments dependent upon the same monastery; and also freely and lawfully to confer the clerical tonsure upon the monks of the said monastery. These concessions are made notwithstanding the constitution of Alexander IV, our predecessor of happy memory, beginning ‘Abbates,’ and any other apostolic constitutions issued to the contrary. Let no human being therefore be permitted to contravene this,” and so forth.

For precedence in taking a seat at the synod of the archbishop of Rouen, a dispute arose between the abbot of Bec and the abbot of Jumièges during the time of this Gauffridus Harenc. The latter claimed that the second place belonged to him, while the other asserted the contrary.

During the time of this Gauffridus Harenc, the priests customarily received ten francs annually as their stipends, and the young men who were not priests received eight. This was reduced, on account of the fortification being constructed—*fortericia* (a stronghold, in French *forteresse*)—so that the priests received only eight francs and the young men six. This continued until the time of Lord William de Valle, the twenty-seventh abbot.

Afterward, in the year of the Lord 1399, on 17 July, following the death of the aforesaid Gauffridus Harenc, abbot of Bec and twenty-fifth in succession, with the consent of the entire congregation and of all the priors, who had been duly summoned to the election, and by the way of the Holy Spirit, with everyone in agreement, the religious and honorable man William of Annullaribus, called de Valle, then claustral prior of Bec, was elected by divine dispensation. [Col. 0675C] Later he was blessed by the reverend Father in Christ, Lord William of Vienne, archbishop of Rouen, on the feast of the Translation of Saint Stephen. Then, on the following feast of Saint Bartholomew, he was joyfully received at Bec as pastor: gentle and affable to all, adorned with uprightness of character. He ruled and governed the aforesaid monastery vigorously for eighteen years and five months.

During his tenure he acquired the fief of Fengerito and the fief of Bouleyo, situated at Saint-Martin-de-Parc; likewise, the entire fief of Calvomont, at Pont-Antoine and at Russerie; the fief of Mellin of Joscelin; at Servaville, the Grandin fief; and the fief of Bosco at Pomeriaux, the fief of Henry of Grongi. He also redeemed twenty pounds of annual rent that the demoiselle Joanna Labeneste received from our fief of Muys at Marbodium. [Col. 0675D]

He also acquired our house in Paris, in the great street of Saint James, and freed and discharged the church from one hundred pounds of rent owed to the Carthusians of Paris and to the college of Dormans, by means of an agreement made between us and them. He returned two hundred gold écus to John de Vadis, who had lent them to the aforesaid Gauffridus Harenc; and to the master of the Knights of Rhodes he returned four hundred gold écus, which that man had lent to the aforesaid Gauffridus Harenc during his pilgrimage, together with many inheritances, as may be seen from the agreements.

He also devoted himself to the work of the fortification begun by the aforesaid Harenc, and brought that work to such perfection that, to those who looked upon it, the castle appeared impregnable.

At this time, while Pope Alexander governed the universal Church, a certain cardinal, commonly called Ludovicus de Flisco, cardinal of the title of Saint Adrian, obtained the priories of Bellomonte and Saint-Ymer. Through the bishop of Piacenza he procured a decree that the said priories belonged and pertained to him, and he ordered each of the abbots and convents, under the penalties contained and pronounced in the proceedings, to allow the said cardinal, or his procurator on his behalf, to acquire and take possession of the aforesaid priories. At that time Brother William de Fiscano, a religious of Bec, and Brother Richard de Malavilla, professed members of Bec, were in possession of the priory of Bellomonte. This noble Father William lodged an appeal, and it took effect.

He acquired the fief of Feugueray from Lord William, knight, for the sum of 2,250 Tours pounds. From Lord John de Boulay, knight, he acquired another adjoining fief, called Boulay, for the sum of 900 pounds.

It should be noted that Gauffridus Harenc had the walls of the fortification built to an extraordinary thickness: fifteen feet, or approximately that, at the base, and ten feet at the top; they were taller than the walls of the city of Avignon. Within those walls he began fifteen great towers. This William received an order from the king to continue the work. One tower was taller and wider than any tower in Marseille. He completed the work within five years, spending 5,000 Tours pounds each year on the fortification.

This William acquired the fief of Meslin-Jocelin in the year of the Lord 1415 from Lord Dobeaux, and paid 1,500 pounds, as is shown by the receipt.

It should also be noted that during his time a certain man named John de la Lande de Tillia, because of the legal proceedings brought between us and him, joined twelve men to himself. These men went about the abbey and our priories armed every day, so that if they could find one of our men—whether a religious or a servant—they might mutilate or kill him. They sent the aforesaid abbot a letter signed with their marks, saying that they would kill him if he happened to go outside; and if he did not come out, they would burn the whole house. In fact, they mutilated several religious men who were going about their business; at Saint-Philibert they killed one and cut off his foot, and mutilated another. Convicted of all the aforesaid crimes, and also of stealing from our woods, whose custody had formerly been entrusted to him, he was banished from Paris, as is shown by his proceedings, which are in the cartulary.

After he had been in the Church for five years, in the year 1404, after obedience had been rendered to Peter de Luna, called Benedict, which had previously been withdrawn from him on account of the schism then existing in the Church, a certain Louis called de Chantemelle, abbot of Troarn, sought to have himself appointed by the aforesaid pope to the monastery of Bec. The abbot of Bec had not yet sent to the curia or paid the vacancy charge, because of the aforesaid withdrawal. For that reason he set out for Marseille, where the aforesaid Benedict was then residing. When Benedict saw him, considered his grave steadfastness, and examined his election, he himself confirmed it. Having received permission from the Apostolic See, the abbot returned to the monastery. This controversy placed a heavy burden upon the Church, both because of the expenses and because of the vacancy payment that had to be made.

It should be noted that in the year of the Lord 1405, during the reign of King Charles of the French, in the twenty-fourth year of his reign, obedience was restored to the lord pope. Before this, benefices had been conferred at the disposition of the ordinaries, and elections were celebrated according to the order of law. After obedience had been restored into the pope’s hands, the pope wished to collect the vacancy payments of benefices, both regular and secular, that had fallen vacant before the restoration of obedience. He could not accomplish this because the king objected. He declared his intention and had it preached in the church of Our Lady in Paris; but he could not accomplish it because the king objected.

In the year of the Lord 1415, in the month of August, on the vigil of Saint Lawrence, in the sixteenth year of the rule of the aforesaid William, Henry V, king of the English, landed in Normandy with a large army and a great number of ships. He besieged and quickly captured the town of Harfleur, fortified it with his own men, and expelled the citizens. He then set out toward Calais, through the district of Calais and the county of Pont-Audemer. When he reached the district of Tervan, at a place called Agincourt (Azincourt), he fought a battle with the French army on the feast of Saints Crispin and Crispinian.

There was a great slaughter of the French in that battle. Many fell there—dukes, counts, barons, and many other nobles—and many of them were captured and taken to England in chains. Others fled from the French army. Afterward the aforesaid king crossed back to England with the great booty taken in the battle.

During this period the monastery of Bec suffered great ruin. The entire region was troubled by the French, who were attacking the king of England, and it was necessary to maintain a garrison in the monastery’s fortification at the church’s expense, because of the raids and invasions of the English, to the injury and destruction of the church itself.

In the year of the Lord 1417, on the first day of August, the aforesaid Henry, king of the English, landed again in Normandy at Touques. Within six months he obtained all Lower Normandy as far as the River Risle, except for Mont Saint-Michel. He also obtained the county of Maine, together with the adjoining region.

At that time nearly all the people living and staying around Bec, both nobles and inhabitants, withdrew with their goods into the fortification of the said monastery, in such numbers that it was necessary to supply the fortification with men and provisions at the church’s expense. It was also necessary, on the advice of certain persons, to destroy and demolish all the buildings of the monastery situated outside the enclosure of the fortification: namely, the hall called La Malmaison, the houses in front of the almonry, the smiths’ house, the guesthouses, the chapel of Saint Herluin, and many other houses and workshops nearby.

It was also necessary to ration grain in the refectory and hay in the chapter house, amid the greatest affliction and grief of all the household. After these great hardships, the reverend Father William, the abbot, anxious and saddened by such troubles, fell ill for almost four months. As his illness worsened, he died on 3 January of the aforesaid year 1417. He was buried in the middle of the choir, before the step where the blessing is customarily received. May his soul rest in peace.

It should be noted that, for the construction of the fortification of Bec, the men holding land from the church of Bec were compelled to contribute, paying half a gold florin for every acre of land they held from it. We were again granted permission by the duke of Normandy to raise, by way of a subsidy, twelve deniers from each of our men for every month, for the same purpose of the fortification, as is shown in the new inventory, under the heading “Fortification.”

It should be noted that John de Chambray made the tomb of Lord William, the abbot, and forty écus were paid, as is shown in the cartulary by a receipt in the bundle marked … . It should also be noted that he was bound to the Apostolic Camera for 1,000 florins annually, as is shown by the receipts in the chest of receipts.

## Epitaph

Here lies an example of goodness, a rule of morals,  
A temple of justice, a vessel of faith, a light of monks:  
William, formerly called Brother de Valle,  
Father of the monastery of Bec, born  
[Col. 0678D] Of Annullaribus, in the diocese of Lisieux.  

The twenty-sixth abbot, whom the grievous sword  
Of death exhausted and stripped of life and its threads.  
For, trusting in Christ, he departed from this world  
In the year one thousand four hundred and seventeen,  
When the third lamp was already shining.  

May he live among the companions of the saints above the stars of heaven.  
Amen.

In the year of the Lord 1417, on the Monday mentioned above, before the holy ashes, on 6 February, after the death of the venerable William, the twenty-sixth abbot, the lord Robert de Becco, called Vallée, a man of venerable judgment and outstanding learning, an excellent doctor of decrees, born in the town of Bec and then prior of Prato near Rouen, was elected abbot and pastor of that monastery in the chapter of Bec, with the unanimous consent of the brothers, by the way of the Holy Spirit. [Col. 0679A] He was subsequently blessed by order of the archbishop.

Because of the dangers of war and the frequent incursions and invasions of the English, he did not wish to come to Bec, but withdrew to the regions of France, to Paris and Pontoise. He remained there until the following year, when the city of Rouen, with the surrounding country, was surrendered to the aforesaid king of England.

While he was staying there, namely during the octave of Easter in the year 1418, Thomas, duke of Clarence, brother of the aforesaid king of England and his constable, obtained the castle of Harcourt. He then came with his army to Bec and besieged the fortification of that place. For almost a month he attacked it continuously, day and night, with various and very frequent assaults. Upon his arrival, the greater part of the town, as far as the church of Saint Andrew, was burned by those inside the fortification, to the great loss of the church and its inhabitants.

When assistance failed those in the fortification, who had hoped to be relieved by the king of France, they were compelled to surrender it into the hands of the aforesaid Duke of Clarence. It was handed over to him on the vigil of the following Ascension. When he entered, all the goods stored there—both those belonging to the monastery and those belonging to others—were plundered and carried away; nearly all the goods of the surrounding region had also been stored there. The people gathered there were expelled, and when they departed they were not permitted to take anything except the poor garments they were wearing.

It should be noted that in the year of the Lord 1412, a tenth was levied in the kingdom of France by authority of the Roman pontiff, to support the king and kingdom under almost unbearable burdens; a deadline was set for collecting this tenth. Nevertheless, the king of France instructed the abbot of Bec by a personal letter to provide him immediately with 300 pounds. This sum was paid in Paris by Lord Gauffridus de Fiscano, prior of Bellomonte. The assessment of the tenth, for our share and portion in various dioceses, amounted to 300 pounds, as is shown by the order and the receipt attached to it in the cartulary.

A few days after the fortification itself had been stripped, the aforesaid King Henry came to Bec and stationed there twenty men-at-arms and forty archers at the church’s expense. They consumed all the monastery’s provisions—grain, wine, cider, oxen, and the other goods stored there—leaving nothing for the religious or their household with which to sustain themselves. They lived only from the milling proceeds of their mills, receiving nothing from their rents, because the monastery’s temporalities had been seized by the said king on account of the abbot’s absence: he had not yet come to the obedience of that king. Nevertheless, the wages of the soldiers stationed in the fortification continued to be paid. For that reason we were compelled to sell all the grain stored in our granges, while the religious were everywhere in such tribulation, especially until the following March.

During this period the aforesaid King Henry obtained the city of Rouen, Vernon, Roche-Guyon, Mantes, and the entire district of Calais.

Afterward, in the year of the Lord 1418, on the First Sunday of Septuagesima, the aforesaid Robert, abbot, who had never sworn fealty concerning the abbacy, came to Rouen. On that Sunday he presented himself to the aforesaid King Henry, begging him to pardon his delay in coming to his obedience and, if it pleased him, to deign to receive it. The king received this graciously.

After this fealty had been rendered and the temporalities of his church, which had been obstructed because of his absence, had been released, he came to Bec on the day after Ash Wednesday. His convent received him with great joy, and he was installed in his seat according to custom.

The soldiers who were then in the fortification withdrew, and in their place troops of the Duke of Clarence were stationed there, fewer in number and at lower expense.

This abbot diligently governed the monastery for twelve years, usefully procuring, as far as possible and according to the circumstances of the time, the rights and liberties of his monastery, and treating his brothers charitably.

During his tenure he acquired a lodging situated in the middle of the city of Rouen, called l’Hôtel des Fontaines, near the Jews’ street. It was burdened, however, with forty pounds of rent until it could be redeemed. This lodging was very useful during the wars.

During his time he suffered much on account of the wars raging in Normandy and because of the fortification, and the entire house suffered greatly—especially because, in the year of the Lord 1421, on 13 July, the fortification itself was treacherously captured by the French through the miller of that place, without the abbot or the religious knowing anything about it. They seized all the workshops of the entire house except the great tower of Our Lady, into which all the English had withdrawn for refuge.

After making a hole in the aforesaid tower, they sent some of their men through it to notify the English who were at Bernay, Harcourt, and scattered elsewhere.

When the French entered, on the day when the English sent their men to notify the English, as has been said, toward evening, they made a great slaughter of men on both sides through the same opening by which the English had departed. The English were driven from the aforesaid tower and entered the church. Maddened with fury, they drew their swords and killed two highly devout monks, [Col. 0681A] honorable men, and wounded others, profaning the holy mother Church.

Moreover, the said English plundered the monastery and all its workshops, carrying off whatever they could find. They stripped the church of all its ornaments, chalices, and the chest in which the most holy Body of the Lord was kept upon the altar; they also stripped the corporals and denuded the tomb of the empress Matilda, which stands in the middle of the choir, leaving nothing valuable behind.

As their wickedness increased, they bound and held Lord Abbot Robert as a prisoner, raising swords over him and wishing to behead and kill him. Thus bound, together with the keeper of the said place, they led him to Rouen, while all the brothers were expelled from the monastery. Only the prior and another man, who was the monastery’s justice officer, remained.

After being expelled, some went to Saint-Philibert and others to Bellomonte, until the feast of All Saints, to the immeasurable loss of the church itself.

The Count of Salisbury, or according to another reading, the Count of Sées, who had arrived there and had brought the aforesaid abbot with him to Rouen, placed him in strict custody until he had provided sureties for his loyalty, affirming that neither he nor his monks had been guilty in any way of betraying the fortification.

This was proved in due course, because the traitors were captured and beheaded at Rouen. They completely cleared the aforesaid abbot, the monks, and all the members of the household. After their confessions had been heard, both the abbot and the keeper, who had been detained in that affair, were released after almost five months. On the following feast of All Saints, the church itself, which had been polluted, was reconciled; and on that same day all the monks, who had been dispersed among the priories because of the wars, entered the church of Bec with great joy.

The king, recognizing that both the abbot and the monks were free from the betrayal, issued letters patent ordering that the detained temporal property be restored and that the movable goods scattered everywhere could be recovered. Most of these goods, especially books and ornaments, were recovered. The king also ordered, and expressly commanded, that the fortification itself be demolished and destroyed at the church’s expense. This was done. Not only was the fortification destroyed, but all the surrounding houses had to be torn down to their foundations.

After the reconciliation of the church and the demolition of the fortification, the reverend Father Robert returned to the monastery. He began to rebuild some of the destroyed houses and to recover the monastery’s possessions, together with its revenues and rents, most of whose charters and books remained at Rouen.

After governing the monastery for twelve years and three months, oppressed by many tribulations and anxieties, he departed this world at Rouen, in the house he had acquired, in the year of the Lord 1430. His body was carried to Bec and honorably buried inside the choir, on the left side, beside the tomb of his predecessor and uncle, Lord William. May God have mercy on his soul. Amen.

## Epitaph

Here lies in this little tomb a venerable and eloquent  
Abbot, whose name was Robert, Vallée by name.  
He was a doctor of decrees and a guide in morals.  
With God’s help the brothers unanimously  
Chose him, placing in him the refuge of their minds.  
Born where he was, here at Bec he lies buried.  

In the year one thousand four hundred and thirty,  
On the fourth day of May, death struck with its sword.  
Let everyone pray Christ to place him in heaven,  
That there he may feel the consolation of the saints. Amen.

After the death of the most learned man, Lord Robert, abbot, the venerable and discreet man of great religious devotion, Lord Thomas de Becco, called Frique, then claustral prior of the said monastery of Bec, was unanimously elected by the brothers, by the way of the Holy Spirit, as pastor of that monastery, on Thursday within the octave of Pentecost and on 9 June.

This election, while the wars were raging, was celebrated at Rouen in our house of La Fontaine, acquired by his predecessor Lord Robert, since no one dared remain in the countryside except in a castle or fortification. The brothers who were not personally present at the election appointed procurators to act in the matter.

After his election he was blessed in the church of Rouen. He remained in the city of Rouen because the wars were raging so fiercely in the countryside that he could not have remained at the church of Bec without great danger. While he was absent at Rouen, the church of Bec was repeatedly plundered.

If anyone appeared to possess something from which profit could be obtained—whether abbot, prior, cleric, woman, or any other person—he was captured and tormented until he paid his ransom. Through numerous incursions of the enemy, the church was stripped of all its goods, and the church’s revenues were reduced almost to nothing, since no one remained or resided in his possession or cultivated his lands without first reaching an agreement with the enemy.

But almighty God, who helps and consoles those who trust in him, gave our good pastor such courage that he acquired for the church a small fief called Bosco, situated in the parish of Saint-Taurin. He also returned our Rouen house free of the forty pounds owed to John le Bar on account of the acquisition of that house, and he obtained its amortization from the king, as the letters drawn up concerning this matter demonstrate.

He also acquired from William le Grand, esquire, a noble fief situated near the church of Saint Mary. He made very costly repairs in the Rouen house. Although toward the end of his life he left the church burdened with many debts, may the Lord deign to forgive him.

After governing the aforesaid monastery for sixteen years and more, conducting himself vigorously and religiously toward his brothers and toward everyone, he gave up his spirit to the Lord on 5 July in the year of the Lord 1446. Everyone mourned his death, and he was buried in the choir beside Lord William de Annullaribus, whose chaplain he had been. May his soul rest in peace. Amen.

It should be noted that this Thomas had two bells cast for the church of Bec: the bell called *le timbre*, and the second bell, which is rung at Vespers and Matins. After expenses for the bell itself, its clapper, and the materials had been deducted, seven francs were paid, as is shown by the receipt in the cartulary.

It should also be noted that in the year of the Lord 1433, John Sandrin, a painter residing at Rouen, received from the aforesaid Lord Thomas, abbot of Bec, the sum of ninety-six Tours pounds for materials, paintings, and sixteen large stone images standing in the choir of our church of Bec, as is shown by his receipt in the cartulary cabinet of the election documents.

## Epitaph

This place holds a body filled with virtue,  
Thomas, whom the earth of Bec produced, and Frique by name.  
He lived flourishing beneath the rule of the cloister,  
Withdrew from evil and subjected his neck to Christ.  
Here, elected prior, he covered the sins of the wicked.  

Made abbot, he worthily ruled the monasteries;  
He himself became the twentieth Father of Bec—add eight, brother—after he died,  
In the year one thousand four hundred and forty-six,  
On the fifth of July.  

[…] May God spare him. Amen.

It should be noted that here the good deeds of our Father, Lord John de Mota, the twenty-ninth abbot of this monastery, ought to be written. But since I was not present during his time and found nothing written, I have left the matter to those who know.

After the death of the venerable Father Lord John de Lota, also called of Rouen, an outstanding doctor of decrees, who died at the house of Bec in Rouen, his body was carried to Bec. While all the brothers mourned his death, he received burial there beside his predecessor, Brother Thomas de Becco.

He was succeeded by the venerable pastor and Father, Lord Gauffridus of Spain, also called Benedict, then prior of Prato near Rouen. When his election was canonically celebrated, all the brothers considered his merits, unanimously consented to him by the way of the Holy Spirit, and accepted him as pastor in the year of the Incarnation of the Lord 1452.

When he was prior of Prato, while the wars were raging in Normandy, he suffered much. The revenues of the church of Prato were so small and weak that consideration was being given to placing it in the hands of the office of the lord of Rouen. He bore all these things patiently and encouraged everyone who visited the church he governed to love him and his church.

When he was elected, he found the church of Bec burdened with great debts and disfigured inside and out by buildings falling into ruin. He brought it to such a condition that it could no longer be reproached either for debts or for repairs … . He magnificently adorned the church of Bec far and wide, inside and outside.

The part of the church called the nave, previously despised because of holes in the earth below and cobwebs above, he adorned with a stone pavement and with the necessary glass windows around the nave. He arranged and installed three images in the chapel of Saint Apollina; and, to include everything, he left nothing of the church nave in a mean condition when he had it painted.

He established crosses around the church, inside and outside, as a sign of dedication. He placed his own tomb and that of his predecessor in the choir. In the choir of the said church he provided four pillars, formerly empty, with images of the four Doctors of the Church.

He established a bookstand in the form and shape of an eagle in the middle of the choir, to hold the choir books. He also arranged a bronze figure of Moses, carrying the legal commandments in his hand, for the chanting of the Epistle. He commissioned a magnificent bronze figure representing the four Evangelists beside the altar, for the singing of the Gospels throughout the year, as well as four extremely costly bronze candlesticks made of the same material.

He strengthened the church, which had been stripped of many vestments and was in need, with numerous honorable and costly furnishings, and with many jewels and relics. In particular, the relic containing part of the head of Saint Blaise, which had previously been kept in England at the priory of Conisborough, was transferred to Bec through the intervention and advice of our Father and placed in a most costly reliquary.

He built the house for the sick, called the infirmary, for the support of the brothers and the comfort of the needy—not only materially, but, which is better and greater, spiritually. For he obtained from the supreme pontiff that all who died in the aforesaid house should be absolved from punishment and guilt, as is more clearly contained in the bull.

From the vicars of the Lord in Christ, Father Lord William d’Estouteville, archbishop of Rouen and cardinal of the title of Ostia, he obtained that all religious who celebrated in the said infirmary, and persons of every status who devoutly heard the solemn Masses there on all Sundays and solemn feast days, might merit a relaxation of thirty days from the penances imposed upon them, as the letter drawn up on this matter declares. You will find the letter in the cartulary, under the heading of the archbishops of Rouen.

Nor should the lamp, which stands in the middle of the choir beside the candlestick, be omitted. Lord Richard le Grand, curate of Bosco-Robert and formerly an extremely devoted and familiar servant of the abbot, gave it. He also gave the convent a magnificent silver and gilded cup.

He himself, mindful of the saying that it is a holy and wholesome thought to pray for the dead, that they may be freed from sins (2 Maccabees 12:46), and that the souls of the dead need the prayers of the living for the remission of punishments, established that his anniversary should be celebrated during Lent, on the feast of Saint Benedict the abbot. He assigned ten Tours pounds, charged upon the revenue of Benseville, to those assisting at the service, to be distributed by the hand of his chaplain when he was present; and if he was absent, the matter was to be left to the prior’s arrangement.

He labored with exceptional care on the fountains and water conduits, especially before the abbot’s chamber, in the garden called La Vigne. There he transformed the conduit of the fountains adjoining the enclosure, which had been wooden, into stone, as is clear to anyone who looks at it.

He maintained three scholars for study at Paris, and sometimes four, at great expense. Some studied theology and others decrees. He honored them with the degrees of their faculties at considerable expense, and with a generous hand, out of favor toward his scholars, distributed the church’s goods especially among the doctors of the faculties of Paris. For this reason the said scholars were held in the highest esteem, above all the other students at that university.

When the noble lord Charles of most victorious memory and piety died—the Charles who expelled the English from Normandy in the year of the Lord 1449 and brought about its recovery—he left two sons: namely Louis, his elder son and Dauphin, who succeeded to the crown; and Charles, Duke of Berry. These were little in agreement until the year of the Lord 1465. This Charles, Duke of Berry, demanded from his brother Louis, the king, the duchy of Normandy, which he claimed was owed to him by hereditary right and had been left to him by their father’s testament, while the king opposed him.

When the aforesaid Charles saw that he could not reach an agreement with his brother the king, he allied himself by treaty with the lords, the dukes of Burgundy and Brittany. Carrying the said Charles’s grievance by force of arms and defending the duchy of Normandy against the king who occupied it, they launched an attack. They compelled him to flee as far as Paris with his entire army. There he sent word to the nobles of Normandy, so that they might resist more effectively; and they fought so valiantly for the king that the Burgundians, terrified by their army, fled.

Afterward, the king, having consulted the wise men of his realm for the good of the kingdom and its inhabitants, in order to settle and quiet the disputes and wars and to establish friendship among the princes, agreed that his brother should possess the duchy of Normandy, over which the dispute and controversy between the said king and his brother Charles had arisen. By his open letters he confirmed this and swore that he would never act contrary to it, but would always keep his promise firm.

The dukes, satisfied because of this promise and its magnificent confirmation, returned to their own land, the lord Duke of Burgundy with his men, while the lord Duke of Brittany remained with our Duke of Normandy, who had not yet been received at Rouen. The Duke of Brittany brought him to the abbey of Saint Catherine near Rouen. While the citizens and, in general, the whole noble estate of Normandy were waiting for him and he did not come, they all agreed to send Monsieur John, son of Harcourt, to learn why his entry was being delayed so long. He spoke with the said Duke Charles and brought him by night, with torches and splendid illumination, to Rouen. There he was received with great solemnity and the greatest joy, in the presence of the bishops of the duchy, abbots, barons, and all the nobles. A gold ring having been placed on his hand, he espoused Normandy, before all who were present, in the church of Notre Dame of Rouen; and he swore that, as a bridegroom, he would rule and govern her as his bride.

When this had been done, with only the Duke of Brittany remaining in Normandy with the said Charles, the king of France revoked everything that he had done. He said that, concerning what is written about betrothals, consent has no force where fear or coercion intervenes, and that he had given his consent under compulsion. As a sign of this, he had his men-at-arms wear two letters, A and P, over their armor, as if to say: “Hear the other side.”

When the said Duke Charles heard that, on this account, the king intended to renew the war against him—and in fact did renew it, because he wanted the towns and castles in the said duchy, of which Duke Charles had taken possession, to be restored to him—this was a great disgrace to the king, since he violated his promise against his own brother.

Recognizing that he could not resist the king’s power, the said duke left Normandy and went to Brittany. His advisers, namely the bishop and patriarch of Bayeux, the bishop of Lisieux, and many others, abandoning their homeland and their own benefices, followed the duke with his permission and on his advice. Many nobles of Normandy remained captive with the king, while others perished altogether.

While this wretched war continued, our lord and venerable Father, through his kindness and mercy, united many nobles in friendship with the Church. A few days later, by order of the king, acting through the royal court and the Exchequer, he incorporated three noble fiefs into the church of Bec as mortmain: namely the fief of Caumont, that of Feuguerolles, and that of Boullay. At great and generous expense, he had them made mortmain, in the year of the Lord 1466, as appears more clearly in the letters drawn up and written concerning this matter.

**Note:** Amortization is nothing other than making land that is subject to a lord’s dues exempt from them.

He had the panels in the hall called the Misericorde renewed, together with the directory, and likewise those in the refectory, which had previously been consumed by worms.

In the same year, many of Lord Charles’s men withdrew to the town called Le Pont-de-l’Arche and held it there for many days. The king, moved by this because they were unwilling to surrender the town at his command, came there in person, established his headquarters, and prepared to capture it by assault, unless an agreement intervened. When a pact had been concluded, he entered with his men. During the siege, he had the houses around the castle and the gate leading toward Locoveris utterly destroyed, and had the ditches of the town strengthened.

In the same year, 1466, on the feast of Saints Cosmas and Damian, in the morning, the day was so misty and gloomy that scarcely anyone could have seen a person three feet away. The Bourbons entered through the castle into the city of Rouen, without the captain or citizens knowing. This caused great unrest among the people. At last, however, through the mediation of the wise men who remained in the city, the king was appeased and recovered it within a short time. He stayed there in person for many days and strengthened the aforesaid castle with a substantial wall on its side facing toward the town, near the castle’s spring.

**27.** In the year 1467, the aforesaid lord Gaufridus Benedicti had a magnificent cross made in the church of Bec. It was gilded and everywhere adorned with precious stones, and it contained thorns from the glorious crown of our Redeemer Jesus Christ.

In the same year he began a certain belfry, on the site where one had stood in former times but had been destroyed by fire. In the opinion of experienced masons, it had to be renewed down to its foundations, in order to suspend the church bells there, because the massive towers were too heavily burdened and were further strained by the movement of the bells.

Moved by charity and devotion, he increased and enlarged the allowance of the religious—both priests and young men—at Easter: twenty sous for the priests and fifteen for the young men, who had previously received nothing. This was a great assistance to the cloistered religious.

During his time there also lived in the Church a reverend and most religious man, a man of peace and love, the lord Robert of Rouen, otherwise called le Moine, claustral prior of the church of Bec. He had previously been prior in the churches of Ida-Conflans, Bellosalt, and Évreux. Later he was called by election to be prior of the church of Bec, and in that office he proved most worthy and deeply beloved by all. He worked manfully on his house, called the prior’s house, situated above the gate called Robert Bellot, both within and without, decorating it—as is clear to anyone who looks—with paintings, coverings, and other fittings suitable for a chamber.

He chose for himself the chapel in the church called the Chapel of Blessed Mary Magdalene and assigned it to the prior. Nevertheless, the ancient registers of the Church record that the Chapel of Saint Benedict had been assigned to the prior. He enclosed the Chapel of Blessed Mary Magdalene with costly [reading uncertain: *victrinis*] work. On the altar of that chapel he devoutly erected five images of holy virgins, namely Mary Magdalene, Honorina, Margaret, and Catherine [the text appears to enumerate four names]. He also had a panel painted on which, at the sides, the images of Saints Martha and Agnes were depicted.

He installed benches around the chapel, with chests for storing its ornaments. He had all these things made at his own expense and with his own money: namely, a gilded chalice, a highly devotional silver peace-tablet, corporals, and, generally, everything visible in the chapel, for the greatest honor and adornment of the church. He also had two small silver vessels made for storing water and wine when Mass was to be celebrated. Later, in the year 1468, he had the chapel lavishly painted and provided with scenes in honor of the virgins.
