In the year of the Lord 1467, while the period was in progress during which Lord Charles, the brother of King Louis, was in Brittany, the Bretons came to Caen and the surrounding regions. In order to obtain easier access to Normandy, to support and defend the grievance of the aforesaid Charles, they made an agreement with the Duke of Alençon and arranged that he should surrender the town and castle of Alençon to the Bretons, who were acting as petitioners on behalf of the aforesaid Charles. This was done, and they came and occupied it with a very large force of their men-at-arms.

When King Louis heard this, he ordered all the nobles of Normandy, together with the free archers [in the vernacular, *Francs-arbalétriers*], to be summoned to resist the aforesaid Bretons. As they went to and fro, they harassed the population so severely that no one could preserve for himself and his household even a chicken, a goose, or anything edible. If they found ecclesiastical persons, they subjected them to taxation [Note: [Col. 0687D] *Taliare*, in the vernacular, “mettre à la taille,” to place under the taille]; and if they found anyone riding, they either exchanged his horse for a worse one or detained it altogether. While these most wicked acts were being committed, and the aforesaid Duke of Alençon remained in Brittany, a plan was devised that his wife should go to the king to moderate his anger. After she had spoken with him, she obtained by her prayers that truces should be observed between them until she had visited her husband, the Duke of Alençon, and learned his intentions. This was done.

During the intervening period, free archers—nearly forty thousand—were scattered throughout the regions surrounding the duchy. They plundered the country, especially around the diocese of Sées, so thoroughly that, owing to a lack of provisions, they were compelled to leave the province.

When the noble lady of Alençon considered the destruction of the country with her son, they went to the king of France and surrendered the town of Alençon to him. The Bretons withdrew from it, and the French entered under a peace treaty, while the Duke of Alençon continued to remain in Brittany. Nevertheless, the Bretons did not cease to carry forward the grievance of the aforesaid lord Charles. Much later they occupied towns in the lower parts of Normandy, namely Caen, Bayeux, Coutances, and Avranches, while French forces were scattered everywhere among them, especially at Saint-Lô and at the abbey of Troarn [also, Troardo], until the year 1468, when the king reconquered those regions.

In the same year, 1468, on 8 August, the noble lady Margaret, queen of England and wife of King Henry—who at that time was being held in prison by Edward of March, who had seized the kingdom of England—and also the daughter of the king of Sicily, together with her son Edward, Lord Prince of Wales, came **28** to Bec. They were received there that same day as evening was falling, with torches and immense illumination. They remained in this abbey for five days, with the greatest honor and with expressions of thanks on both sides. Then she proceeded to Notre Dame of Montfort, and afterward to Harfleur, in order to take ship.

In the same year, the prior of Bellosalt, namely Lord John de Cambrevier, who was then subprior and cantor of Bec, arranged for costly benches and seats to be made in the refectory, for the honor and great adornment of the place. May God deign to repay the grace of this benefaction in his soul.

In the year of the Lord 1468, on 16 October, after the king had subdued Lower Normandy to his rule, and after those who had supported the king had returned, the Bretons, recognizing that they could not resist the power of so great a king, while the prelates and nobles of the country and the entire population were crying out against the prince—namely, the Duke of Brittany—and demonstrating to him the devastation of the country, the confusion of the people, and the destruction of nations, they negotiated a pact and agreement among themselves.

As the men-at-arms and noble archers who had been there to fight for the king returned, they plundered the whole of this country of Normandy. Whatever ecclesiastical property could be found, they regarded as their own. They flocked from every direction into houses dedicated to God, such as abbeys and priests’ houses, slandering the ecclesiastical estate and its members. The whole population of Normandy endured such suffering until the middle of November of the aforesaid year.

In the same year, 1468, the aforesaid lord Gaufridus had the vault [*vouta*] continued and joined to the old one, namely for the protection of the road by which one travels from Bec to Brionne, as far as the garden of John Louvet. Thus the royal road was established there, where it had formerly passed through the cultivated land of our fief of Feuguerolles, adjoining the said water conduits.

Lord John Boucart, doctor and bishop of Avranches, succeeded this venerable lord Gaufridus as abbot. At that time he was confessor to Louis, king of France. This bishop was elected—or rather postulated—through the admonition and command of that same king, as pastor and abbot of Bec. He had the belfry completed and finished. He had a bell made, called the clock, and suspended in the place where it now stands, at the summit of the same belfry.

This bishop had a certain Master John le Marchand as his vicar in the said abbey. Le Marchand was dean of the church of Avranches, a man of great intelligence and shrewdness, who governed and directed the whole Church of Bec under that bishop.

At the end, the bishop resigned the abbey and placed it in the hands of the religious. Specifically, he resigned it in favor of the religious lord John of Aptot [perhaps Hautot], who at that time was claustral prior of Bec. The resignation, however, did not take effect, because the same bishop died before the resignation had been confirmed by the pope. Consequently, the same claustral prior lost the money he had sent to Rome to secure his confirmation and to pay the fees for the vacancy. An election was therefore held.

In that election, Lord Robert of Rouen, otherwise of Évreux, prior of Bellomonte, was elected. He was a religious man of honorable conduct and succeeded the Bishop of Avranches in the abbacy. After his election, and when he had become abbot, he had a new gate made at the entrance of the abbey, the one now beside the almonry gate, together with a stone wall toward that almonry. He had work carried out laudably and honorably above the ancient gate of the entrance, with steps ascending to the chambers that he had built above that same old gate. He also had work done on the watercourse before the church gate, with a stone wall enclosing the channel from the prior’s chamber to the granary, together with many other benefactions that he carried out within and outside the church.

Afterward he resigned the said abbey in favor of the venerable religious lord William of Rouen, otherwise Guerin, retaining a large pension together with the right of presentation to benefices. After this resignation had been made and confirmed by the Supreme Pontiff, Lord Robert of Évreux did not survive long. Thus Lord William Guerin, who had previously been prior of Saint Philibert and chaplain to the said Évreux, became, without opposition, abbot of the monastery of Bec.

[Col. 0691]

## ADDITION TO THE CHRONICLE OF BEC, 29

From the history of the same abbey, by Francis Carreo, a monk of Bec.

[Col. 0691A] William, later the thirty-third in succession among the abbots, was consecrated at Rouen and admitted to his seat with more solemn pomp. There, diligently unfolding the treasury of divine law, he shone among the others like a brilliant star.

In the second month of his tenure, John of Aptot, the claustral prior, who, in the hope of attaining the abbacy, had had a chasuble, tunic, and dalmatic made at Rouen of the purest gold for the adornment of the church, died at Bec and was buried in the chapter house.

Robert, who had yielded to Guerin, after completing seven years in office, rested at a good old age in the choir of Bec, beneath a bronze tomb, after a celebrated funeral. William, an emulator of the piety of the ancients, adorned the front of the high altar with a gilded panel rich in various scenes from the Passion of Christ, and with a silver chest containing the relics of many saints. He attached four angelic columns, decorated with remarkably wondrous sculpture and cast in Cypriot bronze, to the four corners of the same altar.

In addition, he offered to the church, in devotion, a golden reliquary weighing three gold marks, wondrously fashioned by ingenious workmanship and famous for its scattered gems. On the holy solemnity, the sacred body of our Lord Jesus Christ is carried about in it, with immense spiritual benefit.

He gave the community six silver basins. He also gave a magnificent silver lamp weighing fifteen marks, made with delicate craftsmen’s work and suspended by an iron chain in the middle of the chapel of the Virgin Mother.

There is no need for me to recount the various buildings he either erected or repaired, since his insignia, frequently affixed here and there, scarcely fail to testify that Guerin lived there.

Charles, however, after the Neapolitan expedition, died at Amboise of a sudden illness, leaving no free heir; Louis XII, called Aurelius, succeeded him, and he was buried at Saint-Denis.

Later John Morcenchius, who held the archpriorate of Bec, was buried in the chapter house after a wound in his shin had dried up. James Faber, prior of Saint Peter at Pontoise, succeeded him by the brothers’ election, with Guerin’s assent, but was carried off by a brief quartan fever. In his place Peter Baleolus was appointed.

At that time two winters followed, unusually severe and more dreadful because of their snows. Later, at the beginning of spring, the rivers spread over the plains and repeatedly drowned crops, livestock, and houses. This calamity of the season was followed by bubonic plague, which miserably depopulated the territory of Bec, although the monastery was preserved through the intervention of the Virgin.

Meanwhile, the aged William, foreseeing an uncertain succession of affairs, tried to cede all his rights to John Ribaldus, his nephew through his sister. Louis, however, opposed him, wishing John Aurelius of Toulouse, archbishop, to succeed the same Guerin.

In addition, after Anna had died—Anna, whom Louis had married from the Breton line in his first marriage—he joined to himself, already an old man, Mary, daughter of Henry, king of the English, who was not yet twenty years old, in a second marriage and under the terms of peace. Soon afterward he died, and he lies at Saint-Denis with Anna, the wife of his first marriage [perhaps: with his former wife Anna], leaving no male children of his own.

Therefore the royal right passed to Francis of Valois, Duke of Angoulême, who had previously married Claude, daughter of Louis. The first of this name thus reigns as the fifty-seventh king. Under him, after Guerin’s resignation had been issued by Leo X, John Ribaldus, the thirty-fourth, willingly ascended the chair. He was consecrated at Rouen by the archbishop Toussan.

Immediately afterward Guerin, an excellent man, was struck down by apoplexy and left the people of Bec a dark eclipse to be endured for many years. His pious ashes were placed in the middle of the choir with mournful ceremony on the day before the Nones of April. Each year, on that day, the memory of his death is recalled by an annual supplication.

Under Ribaldus as pastor, the beautiful porch of the church was skillfully completed, the construction of which Guerin had commissioned while he was alive. Ribaldus, however, was younger in character than the present business required. Through Adrian, cardinal Brysius and bishop of Coutances, he was expelled—by what right I do not know—and, a pension having been created, he surrendered the chair.

Nevertheless, as far as conjecture permits one to infer, and as rumor may have spread among us, the archprior Baleolus either envied his fortunate auspices or feared that he would prove harmful to the monastery, and informed King Francis by letter. The matter did not rest for long.

Adrian, having been admitted by Francis into the abbey in commendam through apostolic authority, sent men-at-arms to Bec in advance and expelled a good part of the brothers from their priories—for there were not lacking those who supported Ribaldus’s side—while exhausting others inside with chains.

Meanwhile Ribaldus, returning to his native city of Rouen, departed by night after removing a large quantity of gold, silver, tapestries, and engraved vessels, not even refraining from sacred vessels. He did this, indeed, with sounder judgment, fearing to bring the king’s fury upon himself by contending with such a man. Moreover, he knew himself to be hated by his fellow monks, since, being younger in character, he had given rise to so great a conflict.

He then obtained the administration of the monastery of Vallimont in the Pays de Caux and made the place distinguished by restoring it with the spoils of Bec. Attempting to introduce there a new and stricter rigor of life, and meeting with the displeasure of his own people, he litigated unsuccessfully in the Parliament of Rouen.

Adrian, however, after two years, abandoned Bec and took his seat at Fécamp, having attached to the cloister an image of the Virgin Mary nursing Christ.

John Dunesius, Cardinal of Orléans, whom we mentioned above, succeeded him at Bec. He was a gentle man and, by his natural disposition, highly skilled in ecclesiastical administration. He was the thirty-sixth in the succession of abbots and adorned the church of Bec with ornaments.

In the sixth year of his tenure, accompanied by six young men of the same age, I professed the prescribed rule of the blessed patriarch Benedict, with Christ as my patron. May Christ, through the prayers of the Virgin Mother, turn this to my salvation.

After the fourteenth year of this purple-robed abbot, he was summoned by Clement VII to the conference at Nice. He died in Italy, while still in the flower of his age, amid the great mourning of all, and was succeeded by John Venator, cardinal-priest and bishop of Lisieux, the thirty-seventh abbot.

This man, wise through much experience of affairs, was first dear to Charles VIII, then most closely attached to his successor Louis, and afterward served Francis I as a member of his council and as almoner.

When Francis was visiting Normandy, he entered Bec, where John Venator was introduced by the brothers into the abbatial chair under a royal agreement. There Francis celebrated the feast of Saint George with royal magnificence.

Five weeks later, setting out for Vatteville, he left Eleanor, his wife and sister of Charles V, the Roman emperor, ill at Bec.

Two years later, on the day when the memory of the relics of Bec is solemnly celebrated, deep in the night, thieves boldly committed sacrilege and plundered the beautiful lamp of fifteen marks of silver that Guerin had suspended by an iron chain in the chapel of the Virgin Mother, together with both silver basins hanging in the choir. The perpetrators received at Rouen the punishment they deserved on the wheel.

While Magdalen, daughter of Francis, was joined in marriage to James, king of the Scots, that same Francis captured by arms the castle of Hesdin near Thérouanne. Soon afterward, when a truce for ten years had been concluded with Charles Augustus, Charles traveled through central France to Ghent in Flanders, having experienced French generosity.

Soon afterward, in July, Francis returned to Normandy. He was attracted by the timely convenience of the fountains flowing in the cloister at Bec, so much so that he immediately ordered dinner to be prepared for him there, while Queen Eleanor dined opposite, in the chapter house, at the tomb of Herluin.

While royal achievements were flourishing, John, now seventy years old, died of fever at the expedition of Marolles near Merla. His successor James Annibald had his body brought to Bec. There, after being honored for three weeks with daily prayers and vigils, it rests in the church of the Virgin Mother.

His heart was buried in a leaden case in the choir beside the high altar. His body rests at Lisieux in the apostolic church, placed beside his fellow bishops, at incredible expense.

When Annibald, brother of Claudius, admiral of France, obtained these worthy ecclesiastical offices together with the monastery of Bec through royal favor, Francis’s firstborn son, Henry, Dauphin of France, was born.

James Annibald received at Bec three insignia of ecclesiastical office from the bishops of Hippo, Anianus, and Castor, with the permission of the Roman Pontiff.

He became a priest on the fifth day before the Nones of May and was consecrated bishop. From the legates of Paul III he received a purple-colored amice. On that day three monks, together with seven laymen, were tonsured at Bec by the bishop of Hippo.

In the following year Henry was consecrated at Rheims on the seventh day before the Kalends of August. Meanwhile, while the cardinals of France were traveling to Rome to see Paul III, James Annibald, under the pretext of repairing the buildings of Bec and having cunningly spread a rumor of royal consent, put a large part of the Forest of Bec—which the common people call the Park—up for sale to public purchasers for twenty-five thousand pounds. It was as though the annual income of that amount were not sufficient for a single pastor. It is established, however, that this grove, together with the monastery itself, is enclosed by a stone wall and contains four hundred and fifty acres.

In the following August, George of Amboise, a man of celebrated memory and archbishop of Rouen, died at Rouen in the church of the Virgin on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of October, with Charles of Bourbon as his successor, and was buried in a rich mausoleum. The printed phrase “at the castle of Vigny” has an uncertain syntactic attachment. With that lofty pyramid which he built during his lifetime in the middle of the church, one might easily count it among the wonders of the world.

On the Kalends of the same October, Henry was received at Rouen with unbelievable expense and rejoicing throughout the country. There, in a certain sense, the extravagant generosity of the citizens delighted in measuring not their own resources but the outstanding merits and clemency of their prince.

A certain Chappius has beautifully and elegantly commemorated this memorable expense and extraordinary rejoicing, representing them in a recent volume through twenty-nine splendid panels with lifelike images.

On the Ides of January, while the brothers were assisting at the nocturnal vigils in the choir near midnight, frequent flashes of lightning accompanied earthquakes and enormous gusts of wind. Amid these disturbances, it was impossible to distinguish with certainty either the frequent crashing in the air or the blasts of wind.

At the two pyramids of the lower church there was a small turret containing a spiral stairway, raised on two columns and formed with six corners, with stone flooring extending to the very top of the spire. It had been brought to completion more by divine prompting than by human skill. Collapsing in this same storm, it caused great destruction to the church by its fall.

And—as the sport of fortune often is, adding danger to danger—at the suggestion of Haymon Courserius, a monk of Bec who served as Annibald’s adviser and deputy, the two larger bells of the highest tower, broken up on the ground, were publicly sold off piece by piece.

Thus he did not blush to profane a precious object, purchased at great cost and dedicated to sacred uses, bringing disgrace upon his homeland together with private dishonor, like a kind of audacity worthy of Antiochus. In his desire for a small profit from it, and with shame disregarded, he despised the greatest mark of infamy both for himself and for his associates, for whose benefit this was done—a work indeed worthy of a courtier-monk.

After this, Claudius Annibald, a man of the highest distinction from the equestrian order and admiral of France, brother of James, the commendatory abbot of Bec, was staying with his men near the town of Ferra. By the mere fame of his own name he eluded the fierce army of Ruthi. Struck by a severe fever, he left holy admonitions to his only son and died steadfastly amid the sacred rites on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of February.

He was buried at great expense with a royal funeral in the church of Annibald, which was called Appeville.

A new ram now struck the king of Bec with a new blow. The estate of Planes, whose noble chief fief, celebrated for its immense privileges, lies above Appeville and is about six miles from Bec, was requested by Marquis Annibald Hwaldeus, nephew through his brother Claudius of James, the commendatory abbot of Bec. He made the request in the chapter of Bec through a certain James Perdrier, to whom the matter had been entrusted, offering in exchange Guargueslala in Alençon.

He perhaps attempted this with greater hope because of his uncle’s present favor, and the convenience of the neighboring property was being pursued more diligently for the accumulation of family wealth.

Meanwhile, three of our number were appointed to examine carefully both the land requested and the land offered, so that the matter could be handled on the basis of their report.

A massive structure was erected at Appeville between the castle and the [text uncertain], and the marquis’s hope was strengthened by the transfer of the house and towers of the Planes estate, together with its boundaries and lordship.

The people of Bec might perhaps have been satisfied, if equality and the condition of affairs had required it, had not rights opposed by the most obstinate clauses stood in the way (Cause 12, Question 2, chapters 37, 52, and 56).

Since the nephew’s affairs had therefore come to nothing, the purple-robed uncle’s anger burned against the three monk delegates, though he prudently concealed his resentment. He deprived them of their offices and expelled them to distant foreign cells—namely, the second prior, the cantor, and the sacristan.

I was the second among them, more contemptibly cast out; but such exile for the Church is sweet to us.

At that time, in the principal church of Lisieux, one of the two towers at the doors of the church collapsed with a tremendous crash and destroyed a good part of the structure. The aforementioned James Annibald held the bishopric there.

On the seventh day before the Ides of the following June, James, Cardinal Annibald, in the fifteenth year of his tenure at Bec, died at Rouen under the roof of Bec and was placed beside his brother Claudius at Appeville.

Louis of Lorraine, Cardinal of Guise, succeeded him—the man of whom we spoke shortly before—born under an unconquered star for military affairs.

Later, in the month of August, while Lord Parrisius, bishop, was carrying out at the chapter of Bec the duties of visitation on behalf of the archbishop of Rouen, and was making provision for the circumstances of the time with the small number of monks then present, he graciously relaxed something of the cloister discipline, so that the younger men might advance more conveniently in the very beginnings of learning.

They were therefore permitted to sing in the choir with open books, whereas previously this had been done from memory, with great expenditure of time.

Amid the violent plundering of monasteries, there would be enough here to make miserable Bec speak out. When the venerable community of Fathers had been driven out, while the French admiral was ravaging Normandy, the exercise of divine worship fell silent, and two monks were killed during their premature flight: Gabriel Botteus and James Nocius.

> “The last two abbots were Claudius of Lorraine, a knight of Aumale, who died a violent death at Saint-Denis in France on 3 January 1591.”

> “Dominic de Viq, archbishop of Auch.”

[Col. 0695]

## [LIFE OF SAINT HERLUIN]

**32. PREFACE TO THE LIFE OF SAINT HERLUIN**  
[Note: [Col. 0695] The author of this preface was, I think, Millo Crispinus.]

[Col. 0695C] It was customary among the ancients to erect images of their ancestors and to entrust their distinguished deeds to memory by writing, for the instruction of posterity—that is, as an example of virtue and an incentive to uprightness.

They took care to do this for the purpose of making the memory of those who did not know another life, and of those whose lives they undertook to write, as enduring as possible for themselves and for others, and, as they believed, of earning everlasting praise.

Ecclesiastical writers, by contrast, endeavored to write the passions and lives of the saints who, through their labors, left a level path for those following justice and glorified God in life and in death. They followed the same method, but not the same intention.

For they likewise wished to make known to successors the lives and conduct of the departed Fathers—not to win the favor of the crowd, but so that, recognizing their religious way of life, people might raise them to the glory of God by their praises and follow the example of right living set before them in their deeds, in order to merit eternal reward.

Hence a certain wise man exhorts us, saying: “Let us praise religious men and our fathers in their generation” (Ecclesiasticus 44:1). The Apostle likewise says: “Remember your leaders, who spoke the word of God to you; considering the outcome of their way of life, imitate their faith” (Hebrews 13:9, 7).

For this reason the vigorous deeds and marvelous virtues of the saints are written or read: so that God, from whose grace they come, may be praised in them; and so that those who are less advanced, looking upon the footsteps of their elders which they ought to follow, may run without stumbling along the road of salvation by works of goodness, toward the glory and prize of God’s heavenly calling.

The ancients did this, and many people of the present age still do it, unwilling to pass over in silence those whom they have thought to be of some importance.

Among these were the men of Bec, who, because they were the first builders and founders of that place, and because they were known to God and dear to human beings, as their deeds themselves made clear, left in writing for those who would come after them a pious memory of them. These were the blessed Father Herluin, the noble William, and the most wise Boso.

As for the life of Saint Anselm, who was the second abbot of that place, a certain man of Canterbury published it. He had attached himself to Anselm and served him until his death in the archbishopric, to which, by God’s will, he had been transferred; and he left in writing whatever he had been able to see or hear concerning him.

## LIFE OF SAINT HERLUIN, FIRST PASTOR AND FOUNDER OF THE MONASTERY OF BEC

By Gilbert Crispin, abbot of Westminster.

[Col. 0697]

[Col. 0697A] Since whatever a person reads in military history that is worthy of remembrance is published in writing for the encouragement of posterity and raised up with praise, according to the writer’s talent and eloquence, it ought not to be passed over in silence—both for the glory of divine virtue and as an example of great faith in God—which, in our memory, the venerable Herluinus, abbot of Bec, displayed splendidly in Christ’s service. His virtue should therefore be written out under a suitable heading, since at an age when others more vehemently thrust themselves upon the world, he entirely rejected it, though it was smiling upon him most delightfully and according to his desire; and at a time when, in that country, it was considered monstrous for an able-bodied man to abandon arms and become a monk.

His father derived his origin from the Danes who first occupied Normandy; his mother was closely related by blood to the dukes of Flanders. The father’s name was Ansgotus, the mother’s Heloise. Gislebert, count of Brionne, grandson through his son of Godfrey, count of Richard I, the first duke of Normandy, kept Herluinus, who had been brought up in his household, most favorably among all the leading men of his court. He was exceedingly skilled in arms and bore them with no less courage. All the leading families throughout Normandy counted him among their chosen men; they esteemed him highly in arms, in every military practice, and in the care of his person. He turned his mind away from dishonorable things and devoted all his energy to the honorable pursuits valued by the court. At home and in war he was pre-eminent among his comrades. Through these qualities he had won not only his lord’s exceptional favor, but also a very considerable reputation and familiar access with Robert, duke of the whole country, [Col. 0697C] 33 and with the rulers of foreign regions. Let us pass over the many other things he did to win renown in the world; let us not be silent about this, which reveals the strength of his spirit, the constancy of his faith, and his confidence in arms.

Once, having indignantly suffered an injury inflicted upon him by his lord, who had taken away from him the advantage of his service, he departed, displeasing to his lord, to a distant place. At that time Count Gislebert himself, provoked by injuries from certain very powerful men of Normandy, gathered a large force of soldiers, wishing to have his injuries avenged. He was a man of fierce spirit, great power, and supreme eagerness for renown, being related to so many dukes. To display his power, through messengers he announced to them several days in advance not only that he would make war upon them, but also when he would cross over. Thus, at the appointed time, both sides prepared for battle—a battle that could not be carried out without great slaughter on either side and could no longer be avoided without compromising their dignity.

When the spirited man whom we have undertaken to describe learned of this, he immediately forgot his injuries. Taking with him twenty picked soldiers, he proceeded to the day of battle, not with his lord but separately and far from that army. For, by exposing himself and his men to danger, he maintained the pledge of his loyalty and risked death, seeking no advantage or recompense from his lord in return. Enough has been said, and here it can plainly be recognized what kind of man he was. By this example we address those deserters from battle whom fear releases to the harm of others, if greed leads them to the death of their lords and the destruction of their country; and we offer this example not so much to obtain military glory as to preserve fidelity.

As the duke was leading his army down the side of a high mountain, he saw twenty armed men following at a distance across the plain behind him. Fearing that they might be hostile, he immediately ordered men to go and find out who they were. They approached, recognized their own men and the reason for their presence, approved their great courage, and reported back to the duke. Astonished that such service had been rendered to him in return for his injuries, he immediately restored them to his favor, returning everything that had been theirs with still greater goodwill.

The war that was to begin at sunrise the next day was brought to an end by messengers of the aforementioned Robert, duke of the province, who arrived during the preceding night. They appealed to justice and sacred faith, urging both sides to withdraw from arms and await the judgment of the duke’s court. Thus each side departed from the slaughter of battle without either having gained superiority over the other. Divine providence was preserving that timber, making it useful for every good work. The supreme Craftsman did not wish it to be twisted any further by the violence of worldly winds or moistened by fruitless ambitions.

He had already passed thirty-seven years in the most delightful condition of worldly life when at last his mind began to be kindled by the fear of God and love, and to grow lukewarm toward love of the world, gradually becoming colder day by day. Turning the eye of his heart away from external things toward himself, he went more frequently to church, prayed devoutly, and often burst into tears, abandoning every amusement. He was now less frequently present at court; the only thing that kept him there was his effort to win his estates for God along with himself. He achieved this by wresting them from his lord through persistent service.

Often he spent the night in prayer in churches until daybreak, and in the morning he was the first to appear at court before the lord’s table. [Col. 0698D] Because he wished to practice frugality among his companions, he devised many excuses for being absent. Often he passed the entire day fasting. His diminished attention to arms and to the care of his body clearly indicated the struggle of his spirit, which he still concealed under serious pretence.

His mind was distressed and divided among many deliberations. His chief desire was to abandon military service and every other worldly concern. Yet he did not know where to go or what manner of life to adopt. At that time there were few guides or accessible paths of righteousness in Normandy. Priests and even high prelates were married, free, and carried weapons like laymen; following the ancient custom of the Danes, they all still lived in this way. But just as “the Spirit blows where he wills” (John 3:8), so “his anointing teaches him about everything” (1 John 2:27).

Therefore, renouncing military service, dressed in a shabby covering, with beard and hair uncut, he continued for a long time among courtiers with the intention we have described, about to leave Egypt as that true Hebrew, passing over the things that pass away and exerting all his strength toward those that are eternal. From those who remained behind he tried to borrow and carry away for God’s work whatever precious thing he could. Now, while he gladly sat at his lord’s table amid many kinds of dishes and banqueters, he ate coarser bread and drank water. Everyone laughed at him, and whatever he did was considered madness. Neither threats, promises, insults, nor official duties from his lord and all the court retainers could turn him from his purpose.

The man, once so welcome to everyone, was repeatedly sent to courts, riding a donkey. Wherever he arrived he was an object of sorrow and laughter among different people, because of the favor he had enjoyed in service. Fearing to become entangled in the world, he no longer wished to ride a horse; serving his lord by riding a donkey, he did not wish to depart without his lord’s permission. [Col. 0699C] And because he was not at all ashamed to be despised for God, God was not ashamed of him either, but restored to him on earth an exceedingly great recompense.

When Count Gislebert was pursuing the case of a certain fellow countryman whose loss was leading to that man’s ruin, he brought an accusation concerning him before Robert, prince of Normandy, whose interests were involved in whatever was being done in the matter. But the aforementioned man wholly refused to carry out schemes that would bring harm to anyone. His lord persisted in his decision, urging and threatening him to report the matter to his lord by carrying his counsel. The soldier was thus compelled to show whether he preferred to serve a heavenly or an earthly lord. But as soon as the cause of the heavenly Lord required it, he immediately broke the cord by which he was held in the service of his earthly lord.

He completely renounced the embassy and departed from the court. Nevertheless, Count Gislebert, refusing to believe that he would not go, went to the court after a few days, wishing to learn what the duke would answer. But when he learned that the message had not been delivered to him, he became enraged at the man to whom he had entrusted it and ordered that everything belonging to him and his men be carried away. At once all his property was seized, and he did not care about his own loss. His poor dependents were also ravaged, and this caused him no small anxiety.

Therefore, moved by the complaints and tears of the poor, after a short interval he returned to his lord. Caring nothing for himself, he humbly pleaded the cause of the innocent. The whole court was summoned, and the case was brought forward with extreme severity. Charges were laid against him, but he removed them all by answering humbly and sufficiently. The Spirit of God was responding in him. The judge, however, was angered by his silence and brought forward certain other alleged offenses, knowing what lay beneath the matter.

“Let everything that belongs to me,” he said, “be taken from here and sold, provided that what belongs to the poor—who have deserved your anger through no crime of theirs—is restored to them.”

His lord, moved to pity—although worldly exaltation possessed him greatly—took the man aside and asked about the great change in his spirit and the end he intended. With few words and many tears he replied:

“By loving the world and serving you, I have until now neglected God and myself too greatly. I have devoted myself entirely to the care of the body and have received no instruction for my soul. Therefore, I beg you: if I have ever deserved anything good from you, let me spend what remains of my life in a monastery. Continue to love me, and give to God with me what I have possessed.”

This brought an end to the long deliberation. His heart stirred to tears, the lord could not endure hearing him speak any further and withdrew hastily to his chamber. There was much human affection in him for that soldier of his, and much devotion in the soldier toward the Lord. The man could scarcely bring himself to ask for release, but “love is strong as death” (Song of Songs 8:6) prevailed.

At last he granted his beloved dependent the release he desired, giving him control over himself and over all his possessions. The man whom he had previously loved as one who served him well, he now began to love as a lord, and for several days willingly obeyed him, keeping him with great honor and treating him with the honor due to him. He handed over to his authority and service whatever paternal rights his brothers possessed—brothers born to the same dignity and equal to him in rank—because he had become more worthy and nobler in true nobility than his brothers. It was therefore right that they should submit to him, and this was considered neither dishonorable nor unjust.

Immediately, in the village called Burneville, he undertook a substantial work for the service of God, and completed it in a short time. He not only supervised the work but performed it himself: digging the earth, carrying out the trench, transporting stones, sand, and lime on his shoulders, and personally setting them into the wall. During the hours when others were resting, he gathered whatever the work required, excluding idleness from every part of the day. As much as he had once been delicate through proud vanity, so much more patient was he now, through true humility, in enduring every kind of labor for God.

Except on the days when it was forbidden, he took food only once a day, and then neither delicately nor in great quantity, after completing his work for the day. Since he could not study during daylight, he devoted almost the whole night to learning the Psalter by heart. The new soldier of Christ was engaged in these exercises with great joy.

He learned the first elements of letters when he was already nearly forty years old. With divine assistance he progressed so far that, even among those especially learned, he was rightly regarded as remarkable in grammar and in explaining and understanding the meanings of the divine Scriptures. Since he devoted only the nighttime to this study—for the sake of reading he never interrupted the execution of his daytime labor—this achievement was believed to have been accomplished through the efficacy of divine grace alone.

He desired not only to confess the Lord on the lyre but also to sing praise on the ten-stringed psaltery (Psalm 32:2), distributing his time appropriately: now attentive to good action, now devoted to reading and prayer.

The ancient enemy devised new attacks against him, and through these circumstances he nearly dissuaded him from the highest goal he had conceived in human life, namely, the summit of the monastic order. He visited a certain monastery to inquire about the life of the monks. After praying, he approached the cloister door with every reverence and great fear, as though it were the gate of paradise, most eager to learn what the monks’ habit and customs were, and what kind of religious discipline was practiced in the cloister.

He saw that everyone’s conduct was far removed from the gravity that the monastic order demands. He was disturbed and became entirely uncertain what manner of life he should approve. Then the guardian of the monastery, seeing him enter in this way, suspected that he was a thief and struck him on the neck with his fist, pushing him out by the hair as far as the door with all the force he could muster. But the exceedingly patient man, though a layman, did not answer the monk with a single impatient word for the injury inflicted upon him.

He was greatly afraid to approach such men. Yet a branch grafted from the one who is the true Vine cannot wither under any heat of adversity, rooted deeply in his love “which bears all things” (1 Corinthians 13:7).

[Col. 0701C] Relating this episode as a consoling example, he visited another monastery of greater reputation on the following Sunday near the Nativity. When the brothers had gone out in festive procession on the day of the solemnity, he saw monks smiling indiscriminately at laymen with an indecorous friendliness, rejoicing with them by displaying their more elaborate ornaments, and struggling noisily to reach the entrance first.

Moreover, when one monk was pressing too insistently upon another, a monk struck him back with his fist, drove him away, and knocked him flat onto the ground. For, as has been said, the conduct of everyone throughout Normandy was still barbarous.

Lest this outrageous conduct make him condemn the good beginning he had made, as he observed such levity of action and depravity of morals in those to whose standard he wished to conform his life, the hand of God came to the aid of the man who was wavering. On the following night, after the office of Matins had been completed and the others had been dismissed, he remained hidden in a corner of the oratory to pray before daylight. Soon a monk, not seeing him, stood nearby to pray. Sometimes prostrate with his whole body, sometimes kneeling, he continued to pray with tears until broad daylight. By this example, therefore, he was completely restored.

We relate miracles, but far fewer than those commonly recounted by the crowd, although such miracles were not lacking. For what is more glorious than that the enemy, everywhere overcome by him, should fall because God was victorious? The enemy had tried until then to break the strength of his constancy with the hard blows of adversity, but [al., now] all his efforts were frustrated. He now attempted to undermine him through the evil examples of the wicked.

But as we read in the Song of Songs, “Each man’s sword is upon his thigh because of the terrors of the night” (Song of Songs 3:8). Whether he approached by daytime assault or stealthily at night, through the suggestion of some argument, he found him keeping watch upon the battlements. He carried in his hand a sword that penetrated all the enemy’s joints and marrow, discerning and destroying every thought and intention suggested by him. To receive the blows, he was protected by the strong shield of long-suffering and patience. Placed beneath the wall of divine protection, he was kept alert against all the enemy’s attempts by the warning of his watchfulness—he “will neither slumber nor sleep, who keeps Israel” (Psalm 120:4).

Therefore, since he had not found, as he desired, the camp of the Lord that he sought, he returned to strengthen what he was building against spiritual assaults. He immediately uprooted his paternal houses, from which he constructed dwellings for God’s servants.

When the church he had built had been consecrated by Herbert, bishop of Lisieux, he cut his hair and, laying aside secular clothing, received from that same bishop the habit of sacred religion. He was a strong soldier of Christ, already tested through so many dangers. Two of his own men took the yoke of the same order with him.

Afterward, having been ordained priest by the aforementioned bishop, he was placed as abbot over the brothers who had by then joined his leadership in considerable numbers. He was set before the others as a safe example to imitate. For three years he endured with the utmost patience the humiliation of the spiritual life before worldly people, alienated from the spectacles by which he had been nourished and which he saw others daily enjoying. He did not relax the rigor of abstinence amid the most lavish tables of lords; in short, he subjected his body to every form of humiliation at court.

Those whom he had received to govern he ruled with the greatest strictness, but in the manner of pious Fathers [al., earlier Fathers]. One might see the abbot, after the office had been completed in church, carrying seed around his neck, or holding a rake or hoe in his hand, leading all the monks to agricultural work. Throughout the day they devoted themselves to the work of the fields: some cleared the land of briars and thorns; others carried manure on their shoulders and spread it; some hoed, others carried. No one ate bread in idleness. At the appointed hour for the office, they all gathered in church for each canonical hour.

Their daily food was rye bread and herbs with salt and water. The water was muddy, since there was no spring anywhere nearer than two miles. “It is a heavenly benefit,” they would say, “when better bread and cheese, or some other food, can be obtained from anywhere.” The example and efforts of the master excluded every opportunity for murmuring. The abbot was first to the work and last to leave it, constantly working himself.

His noble mother likewise devoted herself there to such service for God. Having given to God the estates she possessed, she performed the work of a servant, washing the clothes of those who served God and carrying out with the greatest care whatever menial task was assigned to her.

One day, while she was roasting grain for the servants of God, the house caught fire on every side, I do not know by what accident. Someone ran up lamenting and announced to the abbot that the buildings had burned and that his mother had been burned there as well. Though he was covered with tears, he raised his hands to God:

“Thanks be to you, God,” he said, “that fire has taken my mother while she was serving you.”

What a strong constancy in the love of God, which could not be shaken by so many battering rams of the devil! The enemy brought forward hammers and fires, not knowing that the patient man would not be destroyed by them but purified and formed for the crown of glory. Yet the aforementioned lady suffered no harm at all in that conflagration.

After some time, he was divinely warned through a vision to leave the rural solitude, which lacked every suitable convenience, and transfer his dwelling to a place under his jurisdiction called Bec, after the stream that flowed there, in a valley one mile from the fortress called Brionne. This place lies in the forest, in the lowest part of the valley of Brionne, enclosed on every side by wooded mountains. It was suitable for human use in every way because of its thick vegetation and the refreshing stream. There was a great abundance of wild animals there. Only three houses belonging to three mills stood there, and there was very little habitable land.

What, then, was he to do? He had no share in one of the mills; in the other two, his share was one-third. Even so, he did not possess alone as much land as the capacity of the houses required. Count Gislebert possessed nothing anywhere in that forest more valuable than this place.

What more need be said? With his hope fixed in God, he began to work, and God very clearly worked with him. For the partners and neighbors who had shares there gave him all their portions, either by sale or by free donation. [Col. 0703C] In a short time he obtained the entire forest of Brionne that surrounded the site.

After the church had been consecrated, though it had been built in only a few years, he constructed a cloister with wooden columns and established the brothers there to remain permanently, according to the custom of the country. The following night, while he was intent upon prayer in his bed, the devil, seeing the beginnings of the future growth of good works there, bore it with the utmost impatience and climbed onto the roof of the dormitory with great force. Gathering himself, as it were, for an assault, he leapt upon the covering of the new walls and cast the whole structure down to the ground.

But this was not seed that had sprung up among rocks and withered because it lacked moisture. Rather, having fallen upon rich soil, it brought forth fruit through patience. In the morning he told the brothers that the enemy had done this, and, restoring their courage, he began to rebuild the fallen cloister in stone.

A neighbor named Radulfus, surnamed Pincellus, lived nearby. He was a man greatly devoted to worldly desires. Whenever the abbot repeatedly urged him to live well, he despised and mocked him. When he was tired of arms and satiated with worldly pleasure, he would reply that he would become a monk.

One Sunday, therefore, because of certain disputes arising from quarrels, the aforementioned abbot visited him, and remained with him until evening. As night came on, Radulfus was admonished and entreated in the usual manner; he returned home mocking. Around midnight of that same night, overtaken by sudden death, he departed this life.

At that very hour the abbot learned that his soul had been snatched away by demons. He heard him lamenting with pitiable wailing and being carried away over a long distance of time and place. He immediately sent someone to inquire what had happened to him. The messenger hastened there, broke through the doors when they were struck, reached the bedroom, and found him already cold and rigid in every limb, lying beside his unsuspecting wife. The abbot had one of the brothers as a witness to this miracle, for the brother had heard the same wailing with him.

One day, around evening, while he was sitting outside at work, he saw a demon in the guise of a cleric passing near the site and entering the workshop of the dormitory, where a brother had withdrawn to attend to his bodily needs. Suspecting that he was truly a cleric and that he wished to go to the oratory, he had several people call out that the way he was taking was not the way to the oratory. When the figure did not respond at all, he sent someone to call him back. But after the figure had slipped away, the messenger found no trace whatsoever.

At last he understood the enemy’s deception and awaited the outcome. The following night, a certain monk fled from the monastery and departed through the same places, thereby exposing what had happened. When the abbot learned of it in the morning, he said that from evening the unclean one had been awaiting the unclean man: the lord who had striven to carry him away was justly to carry off his attendant through unclean things.

He therefore began to grieve and become greatly anxious over the various quarrels that frequently arose within. There was no one in the cloister to preside over their settlement, and the necessity of gathering funds compelled him to remain outside. Since he had often entreated the Lord about this matter, divine mercy supplied him with suitable help, sufficient support for everything that needed to be done.

There was a certain man born in Italy whom all Latin scholarship recognizes as having restored Latinity through him to its ancient state of learning, acknowledging him as its supreme master with due love and honor. His name was Lanfrancus, etc. [Note: [Col. 0703D] The remainder appears in his Life.]

The abbot was skilled in settling disputes in secular cases, prudent in matters concerning external affairs, and, in building and procuring whatever was necessary, no one could have been more prudent or effective without compromising religious observance. When his bodily presence remained outside amid worldly concerns, his mind was chiefly intent upon caring for himself and loving God. He took no thought for secular pomp and desired in all his actions to please God alone.

He was most humble, endowed with supreme patience, and in carrying out the desires of the flesh he was exceedingly restrained by moderate rigor. He always rose first for prayer, and no great fatigue from the day’s labor kept him in bed after the others. With what justice and tranquility he governed those subject to him! He was thoroughly acquainted with the laws of the country and served as a protection for his people against unjust exactors. Whenever a dispute arose among them, he immediately settled it with the greatest fairness.

Whatever he spoke and to whomever he spoke, his speech bore the greatest dignity and was listened to. Yet that outstanding teacher devoted every effort in the cloister to quiet and to the silence of his heart, cultivating the new growth of the sacred word and watering it through continual reading with the sweet compunction of tears that he often experienced.

Thus he lived for three years in solitude amid crowds of people, rejoicing that he was unknown there except to the very few with whom he occasionally spoke. When rumor exposed what he had done and spread it far and wide, the man’s illustrious reputation raised Bec and Abbot Herluinus throughout the world in a short time.

Clerics came running, sons of famous dukes, masters of Latin schools, and laymen powerful through high nobility. Many men, out of love for him, donated extensive lands to that church. The place of Bec was immediately enriched with ornaments, possessions, and noble and honorable persons. Within, religious observance and learning greatly increased; without, the supply of every necessary thing began to abound fully.

The vision seen in that monastery a few days before so great a man entered the monastic order was fulfilled. A fountain seemed to rise in the valley of the monastery, and its water, swelling up to the mountain peaks, flowed out on every side and spread across the breadth of the plain. The abbot was the fountain, rising in the valley—that is, arising from humility. The overflowing waters, flowing out very widely in every direction, were the monks who received from him an increase of divine religion, namely, instruction in learning, by which many people afterward were improved far and wide from that place.

This abundance of fruits most pleasing to God, whose fragrance filled the house of God throughout the world, and which the abbot himself had joyfully sensed even while absent, he experienced all the more joyfully when he later sensed its growth at close hand, after traveling to England. On this journey, many signs of divine grace became known through evident miracles performed around him.

When he reached Boulogne and wished to depart for the harbor, which lies no more than six leagues from the city, the company traveling with him tried to dissuade him. The countess, wife of Count Eustace, [Col. 0705C] 37 also made every effort to persuade him to remain in the city, since there was no ship in the harbor and for nearly forty days there had been no wind at all to carry them across the sea.

But with complete confidence in God he said: “We shall go to the harbor and will have ships immediately. The brothers who remained at home will pray for us and without delay will have ships ready for us.”

He spoke, and at once the wind changed. They hastened to the harbor, where the wind brought sixteen ships before they arrived. It was then the beginning of night. Before midnight, when the wind again blew to carry them across, all the ships were drawn back into the waves around the rising of dawn.

After boarding one of the ships, while the others were attending to the various tasks required by such a turbulent undertaking, the abbot recited the litany with the monks not far away. Suddenly a certain man appeared beside them—no one knew from where—an elderly man of very dignified cheerfulness.

The brother who was leading the litany saw him and thought that everyone could see him. He assumed that the man was a poor person waiting to ask for something when the litany had ended. [Col. 0706A] But when they boarded, he saw that the same man was already seated in a prominent place on the ship. Suspecting that he might possess some great merit, the brother—who had taken him for a poor man—kept close beside him, watching him attentively.

When the ship had been carried out into the open sea, the sailors became frightened by certain monstrous creatures they saw in the water. While the others were looking about in the confusion, the old man smiled with a certain grave dignity and reproached them for their fear.

Then, as they said, they saw him for the first time. The sailors immediately demanded to know who he was, who had brought him aboard, and at what price he had hired a place on the ship. He possessed considerable authority but answered nothing at all. The brother who had seen him for a long time said:

“From the time we recited the litany, he has remained with us in the harbor. And, as I believe, the ship needs him more than he needs the ship.”

They therefore began to wonder, and in their wonder all gazed at him. The abbot had seen someone who closely resembled him, and he asked him by name whether he was that man. The old man’s face brightened slightly, and he answered only this:

“I am not.”

This was the only word he spoke during the entire voyage.

When the ship reached the harbor of Dover with an extremely favorable crossing, the old man was sought out repeatedly by the people who had been on the ships, but the companion of their voyage could nowhere be found, nor could anyone be found who had seen him leave. On the fifth day the abbot reached the archbishop safely in every respect.

What a pious contest there was then between them, each seeking to submit to the other! The supreme prelate, who exercised apostolic authority in the churches overseas, submitted himself to his former abbot as any other monk would have done, etc. [Col. 0706C]

Again, through a marvelous succession of events, everything yielded to the aforementioned abbot according to his desire as soon as he decided to return. On the day he wished to depart, around the sixth hour, those whom the archbishop had sent ahead to the sea arrived and reported that the wind was completely contrary and the sea was stormy. Yet, with his accustomed confidence in God, he set out for the sea despite everyone’s opposition. When night had already come on and much of the night had passed, he arrived and found the wind he wanted—the wind most favorable for crossing—already waiting at that very hour.

Meanwhile, while he slept as the ships were being driven out to sea, he boarded the ship at the rising of the first light. He and all his companions were immediately carried across with the most favorable outcome in every respect.

We do not embellish what happened. We record it in a simple narrative and leave it to others to consider and raise up with worthy amplification.

As he had seen in his sleep, the roots of that great tree had remained in his garden. Later, the praiseworthy man saw certain shoots sprouting from them and growing into great trees: these signified the many people who, through his instruction, came to great growth in good works. For whatever good fruit ever existed in the monastery of Bec or came from it was the seed of that man.

A tree excellent in fruit was the venerable Anselm, a cleric of the Church of Aosta. He followed that outstanding teacher into the monastic order and afterward entered the priory of the same monastery of Bec. After the death of the aforementioned Abbot Herluinus, of blessed memory, he succeeded him; and at last, after Lanfrancus, he became archbishop of Canterbury. He was a man remarkable in intellect, not inferior in eloquence, and—so far as human judgment can determine—distinguished in every virtue of conduct. The whole neighborhood bears witness to the integrity of his actions, Normandy bears witness to it far and wide, and Gaul gives the fullest testimony.

A tree especially pleasing for the sweetness of its fruit was Willelmus, abbot of the Church of Cormeilles, excellently nourished and instructed.

A tall and fruitful tree was Henry, dean of the Church of Canterbury, who afterward became abbot of Battle, a man thoroughly trained in every ecclesiastical discipline.

Trees heavily laden with the fertility of good works in the house of the Lord were the venerable Hernotus, bishop of Rochester, and the man who succeeded him in that same office there, Bishop Gundulfus, a man greatly revered for the holiness of his conduct. The aged Father saw these sons of his Church made fathers of other churches.

These are the sons of whom it is said in the Psalm (127:3): “Your sons are like olive shoots.” Having been weakened below and strengthened above, filled with the richness and fatness of God’s love, they refresh and strengthen the souls of others by their words and good examples; by strengthening them, they sustain them, and by sustaining them, they lead them to the highest growth in virtue.

He had also raised a large offspring in the surest hope of spiritual posterity in the Lord. A number already reaching one hundred young men—noble and excellent, both clerics and laymen, gathered there from many parts of the world—had reached the total of a hundred.

He saw his children’s children: namely, brothers taken from the holy monastery of Caen for the same work, who in distant nations fathered many children in the Lord.

His bodily strength was now failing him—strength greatly worn down by so many years of strenuous labor, vigils, and continual fasting. His sight was especially failing, and from the evening hours onward he needed a guide. Therefore he was no longer able to sleep in the dormitory with the brothers or join the choir in chanting; yet he was always the first to rise for the nocturnal office, and no exhaustion from the day’s labor kept him in bed after the others. The same moderation in food and drink that he had observed in youth was maintained in old age, except that, compelled by the whole brotherhood, he ate twice a day, apart from the days of the prescribed fasts. He had granted this not so much out of concern to restore his weary body as so that, taking food when those whom he directed at their work took it, he might remain at their task: he continued working until evening and very often even into the night. Leisure or pleasure found no place for itself in him. Neither his age, already exceeding the number of years of which it is said in the psalm, “and more than this is labor and sorrow” (Psalm 89:10), nor the severe illness by which he was often greatly tormented inwardly, held him back from necessary activities.

With paternal affection he was wholly attentive to his monks; he governed them by strict discipline and loved them with the most devoted affection. If he found any brother sluggish, any negligent in his calling or in the study of letters, or any sleepy in church, he regarded him as altogether hateful. “What good is a man,” he would always say, “who knows neither letters nor God’s commandments?” If he observed someone more watchful, more studious, and more ready for the practice of virtue, he became toward that man not an abbot but a servant. His favor incited many more strongly to study than love of knowledge itself. For he diligently sought to discover which of all those being educated had the sharper intellect, which the stronger memory, which applied himself more energetically, who applied himself more energetically, whose zeal he could more effectively foster; finally, which of them devoted himself more earnestly to each individual virtue and to the love of God. Whatever he saw in each person that deserved love, he strove to cherish and nourish no less than he loved it in himself.

Whenever a learned man wishing to become a monk came to him, with what joy he was received, with what kindness and reverence he was welcomed! With what persistence he urged laymen to apply themselves to learning the psalms! In what ways he pressed them to retain through love what they had begun! Making himself all things to all, he loved them all as sons, and they loved him as a father.

The new church had not yet been consecrated. He was awaiting its consecration from the very man whose counsel had begun it and whose assistance [or: “counsel and assistance”] had brought it to completion, earnestly entreating this from God. God, who had shown himself gracious to him in all other matters, granted his petition and fulfilled his desire in every respect concerning this matter. For the church was consecrated with an honor far greater than he could have presumed, and by the one from whom he had desired it. For the apostle of the transmarine nations, mentioned above, often came to the court of the most eminent King of the English, William, who was then staying in his own land of the Northmen, on various secular and ecclesiastical affairs, and so forth.

[Col. 0708D] Thus the day, long and fervently desired by many for many years, was announced far and wide. It was gladly received when it was foretold that men of consular rank, persons of the highest ecclesiastical orders, and an innumerable multitude of people would come from distant regions. The greatest expenses were amassed to receive every kind of person. When it was fulfilled, “God shall separate a willing rain for his inheritance” (Psalm 67:10).

With nothing exacted from anyone and nothing demanded, sufficient in himself, he completed what he had begun. God, who raises the poor from the dungheap and is accustomed to set him among the exalted (Psalm 112:7), supported the work by the sole assistance of his hand. In bringing this work to completion, his hand was so generous that the undertaking, though carried out at enormous expense, was sufficient and satisfactory for everyone, incurred no want for the future, and provided such joy for so great a solemnity.

For eight days previously, a most severe illness had held the father of the monastery, threatening that death was near. But, by God’s mercy, he recovered fully in time for that day, so that no cloud of sorrow might darken its brightness.

Accordingly, on the tenth day before the Kalends of November, in the year 1077 from the Lord’s Incarnation, the reverend supreme pontiff of the transmarine nations, Lanfranc, arrived to complete by consecration the church which, inspired by God, he had begun, and in whose foundations he himself had laid the second stone with his own hand.

All the bishops of Normandy assembled, together with abbots and other religious men; the nobles of the kingdom were present. The king could not attend, being detained by other affairs. Queen Matilda would gladly have been present had she not been occupied with royal duties; nevertheless, she was present through a fitting generosity of her beneficence.

The heavenly King did not wish an earthly king to place the finishing touch upon the work of his grace, reserving entirely to himself the joy of the completed work. Within sixteen years he had finished the monastery solely at the expense of the poor, together with all its workshops and buildings, a beautiful and very great undertaking.

The most distinguished nobles of the kingdom of France were also present, along with many other leading men of that kingdom; clerics and monks from all the neighboring provinces streamed together, and an innumerable multitude of people gathered. The dedication was celebrated with the greatest joy and the most solemn exhilaration. The very air, exceptionally pure, and the brightest day smiled upon the people’s delight. Because of the tumult of the crowds moving about, the choirs of singers could scarcely be heard.

Amid such a gathering, no one suffered the inconvenience of any injury, and no disorder occurred in the proceedings. When the procession had been completed, the bishops could scarcely enter without jostling. The crowd that followed burst in after tearing away all the doors, though everyone remained unharmed, as far as the spaciousness of the church could contain them.

The altars to be consecrated were distributed among the bishops; the principal altar remained to be consecrated by the archbishop. Throughout the church there was the highest celebration, and within that sacred celebration a kind of devout rivalry. Because of the multitude shouting, each singer could scarcely hear himself. Many were jubilant without knowing what was being said [or: “without knowing what they were saying”] or paying any attention to what they were singing with.

The distinguished persons of that monastery, few in number because of the excessive multitude of others, completed the solemnity through tears alone and devotion of heart. In some there resounded a voice of joy and gladness; in these, their whole affection of mind, intent upon the Lord alone, sang to him with tears.

What more is there to say? The solemnity ended with greater joy than that with which it had begun. They went to the meal, and no one lacked Paschal banquets. From morning until deep night, successive groups of brothers who had come to the feast were served, as many as the refectory tables could accommodate—all, both known and unknown—not only in the surrounding houses but also in distant villages. Whatever they requested for their necessary uses, the Church, betrothed to God the King, willingly supplied with bridal abundance, serving the greatest among them so agreeably and sufficiently that those who received it said that the proper measure had been exceeded. Nor was this done only on that day: for several days beforehand, while preparations were being made, they were served in the same way.

The venerable abbot repeatedly asked the servants, who were constantly going and returning and could not remain in one place even for a moment, to tell him what he should do and whether the expenditure was still proving insufficient. Instead, he heard from them that everything was abundant. How often on that day he said, “What shall I render to the Lord for all that he has rendered to me?” (Psalm 115:12). In saying this, he rendered to the Lord only tears, giving thanks for so many benefits granted to him—and rightly so, because, every scarcity having been excluded, all necessities were being supplied by God.

On the third day, the oft-mentioned archbishop of Canterbury, memorable throughout the ages, and so forth, asked all the brothers for permission to depart.

Who could look upon such a man, one of such great kindness toward them, as he departed, with dry eyes? All burst into tears; the younger ones could not be consoled. He deliberately hastened his departure, so that they might restrain themselves from weeping, at least after he had gone.

Abbot Herluin, who loved him more than all mortals and was loved by him, followed his departing friend for two miles, believing that he would never again return alive to his own people in this life. What bitterness of heart, what weeping there was, however much they suppressed it at that final farewell and last separation from one another!

After he had returned, he sat alone in his chamber with the one who among all was most familiar to him. Giving free rein to his tears, he raised his hands to heaven and said:

> “Now, Lord, you dismiss your servant in peace, because my eyes have seen” (Luke 2:29). “I desired above all to see this before I died, and I prayed to you for it without ceasing. You have fulfilled what I wished; now your servant will go joyfully to you, at whatever hour it pleases you.”

Thus he restrained his words, but he could not restrain the flood of his tears, until the brother who was speaking with him, unable to endure it any longer, introduced another subject.

From that time he began to be completely deprived of the use of his limbs, and long before the day itself he obtained the fulfillment of what he had prayed for concerning the turning of his soul [or, probably: “concerning the turning-point of his life; his soul obtained what it had prayed for”].

For, in the following month of August, on the third day before the Kalends of September, a Sunday, he took entirely to his bed. The aged Father perceived by certain signs that death was now at hand. When this became known to the congregation that loved him most dearly, a kind of death overwhelmed them all; anguish, and a certain stupor born of anguish, seized the minds of everyone. No food could be taken; sleep departed from their eyes. On the third day he asked that he be absolved and that the other services customarily provided for the dying be performed for him.

His sons came to bid farewell to their most beloved Father, being about to be deprived of him first. With tears and sobs interrupting the psalms and the other prayers, they at last came to the act of confession. He began to confess, but overcome by the devotion of his remaining sons and himself breaking into tears, he could say nothing. Nevertheless, having scarcely struggled his way into speech, he absolved his sons and, giving blessing and peace to all, both present and absent, commended them all to the immortal Father. As they departed, he asked them to pray for him, since he could do no more.

Sorrow, tears, and prayers followed, for they could scarcely continue the psalm. Whenever one looked upon another, as though he already saw his brother deprived of their Father, he burst into tears. They did not dare to weep before him, because, rejoicing in good hope, he wished to see them all not weeping but joyful. Whenever he sensed the sob of anyone stirred to tears, he immediately restrained it with his customary gravity.

A deep part of the night had passed—the night that dawned into Saturday, on the evening of which he died. The most reverend man Anselm, prior of that church, being not merely suspicious but certain that his end was near, placed himself at some distance from him, secretly and without letting him know, because the latter disliked anyone being around him.

But as soon as the signal for matins sounded, he immediately woke Lord Abbot Roger, who was lying beside his head, and said: “Wake the prior, so that he may say matins with us.”

Roger was greatly astonished at how he had discovered this, since he had neither come before him nor had anyone told him that the prior had lain down afterward. Early in the morning he asked that all the hours of the day be recited before him.

Finally, sensing that the hour of death was already approaching, he urgently requested to receive communion and to have his soul commended. Abbot Roger hurried away, but found no host in the Eucharist. All the brothers were thrown into confusion: death was imminent, and there was no saving sacrament of the Lord’s Body for him to receive.

[Note: [Col. 0711] He calls the Eucharist the pyx or ciborium—that is, the vessel in which the Body of the Lord is kept.]

Yet what had always been present around the living through the grace of divine mercy was not absent around the dying. At that moment, perhaps, a certain priest celebrating Mass for him was still holding the Lord’s Body in his hands, ready to be received. The abbot mentioned above therefore took one portion of that offering, which had been offered to God for commending the man’s passing, and carried it to him as viaticum.

As they were about to commend his passing, all the brothers immediately rushed in. Since he could not endure their weeping even then, after receiving communion in the Christian manner, he indicated by whatever gesture and word he could manage that they should return to the cloister, assisting him all the more earnestly as they saw that he was drawing nearer to his end.

Only the hour of his departure was now awaited, fortified by the weapons of prayers and tears. Whenever the door of the chamber in which he lay was opened, each person, fearing that the announcement might already be made that he had departed, sprang forward in astonishment and waited to hear what he feared.

He passed the day in this way until evening. Often, as though returning from somewhere else, he said to Abbot Roger, who stood nearby: “What are our lords doing? Why are they delaying? What do you suppose is the reason they do not come?”

Although Roger thought that he was speaking of other persons, he answered as though he were speaking of the monastery’s brothers:

“What do you command? They are in the cloister praying for you; they will come as soon as you wish.”

He was silent, and after a short interval repeated the same words more urgently. Roger struggled to make out whose delay he was complaining about and whose arrival he awaited, but heard nothing more from him.

After the brothers had completed the evening synaxis, together with the conclusion of the day and of the daytime office, he brought the course of human life to its end by a fortunate journey, during the night that was already approaching and that dawned into Sunday, on the seventh day before the Kalends of September.

Everyone rushed in—not only the monks, but also the servants of the household and those who had come from the villages. They tried to break through the doors and barriers, but Abbot Roger, who had been most devoted in attending the holy man during his final illness, held them back with prudent encouragement until the body, most fittingly prepared for burial, had been carried in solemn procession into the church.

Once he had been laid before the community, all were permitted publicly to mourn their common desolation. Though desolation had always attended those living with him, glory accompanied him even in death, as they rendered the final service to the brother [variant: “Father”] who, because of his exceptional holiness, had been held by everyone in the greatest love and reverence.

Many abbots and numerous venerable persons came willingly. The Bishop of Évreux, Gislebertus, a venerable man of honorable life and great literary learning, arrived and most solemnly performed the entire funeral office.

In the chapter house, a monument to his good deeds was made for him, and an eternal monument for his sons. In accordance with the custom by which those who are about to speak of spiritual studies assemble, the memory was presented of the man who, from a tyrant became religious, from being very worldly became wholly supernatural, and who was the first founder and abbot of that place and order.
