I refrain from recounting the greatest laments of the sons deprived of their most loving Father, lest I inflict sorrow on the reader or move the reader to tears by inflicting it. After he had been buried with fitting honor, the poor who had gathered from outside the neighborhood were refreshed at the most generous expense.

May God, who lives and reigns through all ages of ages, grant eternal refreshment to his soul, if anything is needed for our prayers. Amen.

[Col. 0711] Here ends the Life of Saint Herluin, first abbot and founder of the monastery of Bec.

## Epitaph

[Col. 0711D]

This stone covers the first founder and abbot  
of this monastery, a monk from a layman.

Three times eleven, plus three and four years,  
he had not known letters; afterward he died learned.

Forty-four years he passed in the monastic life,  
rightly dividing his days in half.

[Col. 0712D]

When Phoebus brought forth a new rising beneath the Virgin,  
by departing he closed the day and the week.

He was Herluin, if anyone asks his name;  
may God grant him, with the saints, whatever he is to them.

## Another Epitaph

Looking upon this tomb, recognize from the inscription who lies buried here:

To know who he himself was is the way of virtue.

When he had reached four times ten years of age,  
he despised what belonged to the world through love of God.

Thus changing his role from a soldier of the world,  
he became a soldier of Christ, suddenly a monk from a layman.

Here, joining communities of brothers in the manner of the Fathers,  
he governed and nourished them with the care that was fitting.

Whatever buildings you see here, and however great they are,  
he first founded—not so much by wealth as by the merits of faith.

The Scriptures that as a boy he had not learned, he later knew,  
so learned that a learned man could scarcely follow him, unlearned though he was.

Death’s cruelty carried him away from us as we wept,  
on the twenty-fifth day of August.

Father Herluin, thus you joyfully ascend to the heavenly realms;  
for, in view of your merits, we may believe this of you.

[Col. 0713]

# THE LIFE OF WILLIAM OF BEC

## Preface to the Lives of the Abbots of Bec, William and Boso, by Milo Crispinus, Cantor of Bec

[Col. 0713B] 41

Whenever the deeds of great men, committed to writing, are recited, the minds of listeners are instructed toward good action to the praise of God, from whose gift such men exist; the hope of the faithful is raised; and in those whose fervor for divine love sometimes grows sluggish, it is rekindled when they see others doing what they themselves are urged to do.

Therefore, wishing to offer in the tabernacle of God something from the life of our fathers, who brought us up in holy religion, we have taken care to write for the knowledge of posterity a few things, as we saw or heard them, though in an unpolished style. In their time there were men of great renown who were deeply religious and adorned with many gifts of God; by these gifts they showed their subjects the straight path by which life is to be pursued.

The men of whom we speak are the venerable William, third abbot of Bec, and Boso, a wise and good man, who succeeded him in governing the same monastery. For the first two who preceded these men in that place—namely, the most blessed Herluin, first founder and shepherd of the monastery of Bec, and the most holy Anselm, second abbot of the same place—we already possess splendid and substantial volumes composed in truthful style.

Of the two mentioned above, William and Boso, we wish to say what the Lord grants us to say, for the honor of God and the benefit of readers, so that those who come after us may know who they were, where they came from, how they lived, and how they ended their present life.

## Life of the Venerable William, Third Abbot of Bec

[Col. 0713]

[Col. 0713C] The venerable William, abbot of Bec, descended from a noble Northman lineage and was born in the old castle above the Risle called Montfort, of illustrious parents. His father was named Turstin, and his mother Albereda, the niece through her sister of Roger of Beaumont, father of Count Robert.

While he was still lying in his cradle, the child was struck by a serious affliction and almost lost his sight. His terrified mother, mourning for her son, ran to a church of Saint Germanus situated in the same castle. She placed him upon the altar of that church and vowed to God, to the most blessed Mother of God Mary, and to Saint Germanus that, if the boy escaped that affliction of the eyes through their help, she would raise him for God’s service and hand him over to be instructed in letters. At the same time she asked God that, if he did not wish to heal the boy in any other way, he would transfer that illness to herself—that is, to the mother.

What more is there to say? The grace of our Savior, together with the piety of his most holy Mother and of the most blessed confessor Germanus, assented to the good mother’s petition and vow. The child was restored to perfect health, but the illness seized the mother and soon afterward killed her.

The boy grew, and when he had reached a suitable age, he was handed over to be instructed in literary studies. He began to show a good disposition, to burn with love of God, to devote himself to honorable things, and to withdraw his mind from dishonorable ones.

[Col. 0714C] He was already spurning the world’s luxury; already in speech, conduct, and dress he displayed himself as such that even then everyone regarded him as a monk. Insofar as concerned the formation of his life and character, whenever relatives or friends sent him money for school, he avoided accepting it as though it were an evil thing. As his fellow students used to report, he detested greed.

When he was twenty-five years old, desiring to fulfill the Lord’s word, “Whoever does not renounce all that he possesses cannot be my disciple” (Luke 14:13), and, “If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me” (Matthew 16:14), he renounced the world and became a monk at Bec under the most holy abbot Anselm, who at that time was gloriously carrying out the office of abbot in the monastery of Bec.

Having entered the monastery, he devoted himself most earnestly to the monastic life. Constant in reading and silence, he worked very diligently to preserve his life honorably. Thus, desiring to please God and dear to human beings, following the standards of his Lord God of Sabaoth in the camp of the Lord, he served for fifteen years in the office of a vigorous soldier. Under the blessed Anselm as his commander, he fought in this service so energetically that everyone loved him and no one complained about him. The fame of his goodness carried the good fragrance of Christ from him throughout the surrounding region.

After the blessed abbot Anselm had been transferred to England and made archbishop, William, who had previously revered the height of that office, later deserved to receive it himself. For during the reign of King William, son of William who conquered England, Anselm, abbot of Bec, dear to God and esteemed by human beings, was compelled by certain circumstances, and especially by the counsel and obedience of his chapter, to cross over to England.

Because the see of Canterbury was vacant after the death of the venerable Lanfranc, he had long held back from traveling to England, lest he appear to desire the archbishopric. He had tried with all the effort of his mind to avoid accepting it when it was offered, since many who knew his praiseworthy goodness were proclaiming that he would be archbishop, because they wished it so.

Nevertheless, as has been said, overcome by the pleas of his friends, he crossed the sea. While he remained there, it happened that the king himself fell seriously ill. After Lanfranc’s death, this king had retained the archbishopric in his own hand for several years and had worn it down with many burdens.

While he was suffering from the illness mentioned above and had almost despaired of life, his bishops and princes admonished him to seek some good man for his recovery and appoint him archbishop of Canterbury. He replied, “Whom?”

“Anselm, abbot of Bec,” they answered.

The king was pleased by this reply and immediately ordered him to be summoned. Thus, by the election of the king and his princes and by the acclamation of clergy and people, according to God’s disposition, he was chosen as primate of all Britain, although he strongly resisted and protested.

For he said that he was the abbot of another kingdom, under the care of a bishop, and that without that bishop’s command or permission, or the consent of his community, he could not assume the care of others in a foreign land. But those who heard this made little of it and nevertheless did not cease completing what they had begun.

When the news had flown across the sea and reached Bec, the men of Bec were greatly troubled and saddened. Such tribulation arose among them that no one in the monastery of Bec had ever before witnessed the like. The whole province was stirred. The community of Bec, the bishops and abbots, all the religious, and at the same time the nobles and the lesser men of the land, mourned together that they were losing their chief teacher and supreme patron.

The Father himself in England tried by every means available to withdraw from so great a burden. The men of Bec and many others labored with words and deeds, as far as they were able, to recall him, but they could not, because, as later became clear, this was being done according to God’s disposition.

At last Anselm, overcome either by reason or by authority, yielded to God’s disposition. The men of Bec, realizing that they were laboring in vain, many of them granted what they had previously insisted they would never grant. Thus, by the command and permission of William, archbishop of Rouen, with the assent also of Robert, duke of the Northmen, and with the consent of the chapter of Bec, that election was confirmed.

After this Anselm sent letters to Prior Baldric, an honorable man, and at the same time to the community of Bec. In them he commended them to God and urged them to provide themselves with an abbot, since from that time onward they would no longer have him as abbot, but, if they wished, as a friend and faithful counselor.

A certain monk of Bec named Girard brought these letters. He came to Bec for the feast of Saint Mary in mid-August and, on the day of the feast, reported in the chapter house the greetings and words of Father Anselm and delivered the letters. They were immediately read in the same chapter.

When the brothers heard of this separation from them and of the loss of so great and most beloved a Father, who had cherished them like a nurse cherishing her children in the embrace of affection, they were disturbed beyond what can be expressed. All, struck by great sorrow of heart because of their love for their most beloved Father, from whom they were as though being orphaned, broke into tears. The brother who was reading the letter could scarcely say anything, as sobs interrupted his voice.

At last the letter was read to the end, and many other things relating to the same matter were said and done.

After this they celebrated the solemnity of that great day in a dignified and festive manner after Mass. Prior Baldric then summoned the whole community to the chapter house and said that Girard still had something to say on Father Anselm’s behalf, which they ought to hear.

Ordered to speak, Girard said that he had letters concerning the election of an abbot. He had also brought the pastoral staff from England, but first he wished to hear whether everyone would follow Anselm’s counsel concerning the election of an abbot; then he would display the letters, because he had been commanded to act in that way.

“No,” said the prior, “we shall not do that. First let us hear the letters, and afterward we shall take counsel about what we ought to do or answer.”

Girard maintained that he had not been instructed in that way, while the prior declared that he would do nothing else. At last Girard, overcome either by reason or by the authority of the chapter, yielded, produced the letters, and handed them for reading to the brother named Maurice, who had read the earlier letters.

Their meaning was as follows.

[Note: [Col. 0715D] It is found in Book III, Letter 8 of the Letters of Lord Anselm.]

> “Since, by the mercy of God, the permission of the reverend William, archbishop of Rouen, the assent of Lord Robert, duke of the Northmen, and finally your own consent, I have at last been freed from the care of you, if God grants you the favor of our lord the duke of the Northmen so that you may choose an abbot from your church, and if you wish to hear my advice concerning this, I think no one is more suitable for this work than Lord William, who was formerly prior at Préaux.
>
> “And to you, William, I command under holy obedience that you do not refuse this burden, but accept it in the hope of God’s assistance. And to you, Baldric, I likewise command that you do not abandon your office until I speak with you.”

Then Prior Baldric replied that he was willing to undertake the election, and the others likewise agreed. Thus that assembly was consoled. Anselm also asked the prince of Normandy by letter to give his assent to the election mentioned above.

Many days then passed, and at that time nothing further was done concerning the election itself. The elected man behaved as though he had heard nothing about it.

In October a certain abbot named Roger arrived, a monk of Bec, a good and deeply religious man. Anselm, as Roger said, had ordered him by letter to come to Bec and assist the men of Bec as much as he could in choosing an abbot.

Abbot Roger, Prior Baldric, and certain other brothers with them then approached the Count of the Northmen. They informed him of Anselm’s instructions and of the chapter’s election at Bec, asking him to complete with his assent what they had begun. The duke received all this graciously and ordered that the elected man be presented to him.

They quickly returned home, gathered the brothers together, and reported what they had done with the prince and what they had heard from him. Each man was questioned about what he thought of the election mentioned above and whether he consented. Almost all gave their assent.

Meanwhile, the elected man had been ordered to wait outside the community. Afterward he was summoned, entered, and sat in his proper place.

Then the prior told him that they were electing him to govern the Church of Bec and, on behalf of God and Saint Mary and all the saints, as well as on behalf of the most reverend Father Anselm, commanded him to undertake the office of abbot and the care of their souls.

But he threw himself prostrate on the ground and said:

> “I beg you, my lords, either release me altogether from what you command, or teach me how I can fulfill it.”

The prior answered:

> “There is no need to work for your release. Accept this care in the name of the Lord, and we shall obey you wholeheartedly.”

That very day Abbot Roger, the prior, and certain other brothers with them hastened to the court with their elected man and presented him to Robert, duke of the Northmen. The duke received him eagerly and with great honor and gave him the abbey according to the custom of his predecessors.

At that time Count Robert of Meulan was present with the prince, as was Robert son of Anchittillus [variant: Anschitillus], a cousin of that same William, the elected abbot of Bec. They greatly rejoiced in his promotion.

Then Count Robert of Meulan ordered Robert son of Anchittillus to escort the new elect of Bec to the monastery, and commanded all his officials that no one should dare cause any annoyance to the abbot of Bec or to his men in any matter.

At that time Count Robert of Meulan also granted that the goods purchased for the brothers’ food should henceforth be free from every customary impost. Until then, on goods intended for the monks’ food, wherever they were purchased—even in the kitchen at Bec—the officials of Brionne castle had exacted such a levy.

As time went on, the same Count Robert of Meulan granted throughout his entire land, wherever it lay within his power to exact or remit such charges, that all the lord’s goods belonging to the monks of Bec and intended for their food or clothing, wherever they were purchased for their use, whether inside the cloister or outside it in the business of the monastery, should be free from every impost called by the name of toll, passage duty, or any other name.

He did this for the love of God and of William, abbot of Bec, his kinsman. He also conferred many other benefits upon the monastery of Bec during his lifetime, for the sake of that same abbot.

Therefore, the newly elected man, having received from Duke Robert the gift of the abbacy, as has been said, and from William, archbishop of Rouen, the care of souls, returned from the court with his companions by the prince’s favor. He came to Bec late, after Compline, on the day before the feast of the Dedication. This feast of the Dedication falls on the tenth day before the Kalends of November, and in that year it occurred on a Sunday. Rising for Matins, the elected man came into the choir and stood in the place beside the abbot’s seat; and he duly completed the entire nocturnal and diurnal office of the feast as abbot. This took place in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1093.

On that very day, William the elected man sat for the first time as abbot in the chapter, from that day arranging all the monastery’s affairs, within and without, suitably, while everyone rejoiced that God had given them such a successor to Anselm and such a pastor. Yet before his benediction he neither entered the abbot’s seat [Col. 0718B] nor carried the pastoral staff; rather, he seemed to take no concern over hastening the benediction. That benediction was delayed until the month of August in the following year.

But Anselm, not forgetting what he had begun, asked William, archbishop of Rouen, about the benediction of the abbot of Bec, and informed Prior Baldwin and the convent of this by letter. As the month of August began, Prior Baldwin and certain other brothers with him went to Rouen to speak with the archbishop about the benediction of their abbot. The archbishop appointed the day of the benediction for the approaching feast of Saint Lawrence. When the prior returned, he told the convent what he had received from the archbishop.

And because the aforesaid Abbot Roger had recently died, they sent to William, abbot of Cormelles, a noble and good man, highly learned in letters and himself a monk of Bec, asking him to come to the benediction of the abbot of Bec; and he willingly complied.

On the day of the feast of Saint Lawrence, while the archbishop stood at the altar wearing the mitre, and the elected abbot of Bec was clothed in sacred vestments, and the hour was approaching when he was to be presented for benediction, he heard from those who reported it that the archbishop would not bless him unless he made a profession. But he replied that he would in no way do so.

Then Prior Baldwin of Bec, accompanied by several monks, hurried to Robert, count of Normandy, informing him that the archbishop was demanding from the abbot of Bec a profession that his predecessors had not made. At once the duke sent William of Britolio and William [Col. 0718D] son of Richard of Barduville, together with his chancellor Ernulf, ordering and commanding William the archbishop to bless the abbot of Bec without delay and to demand nothing from him except what it was established that his predecessors, the abbots of Bec, had done.

When the archbishop heard this, he was extremely angry; nevertheless, he completed what had been begun and blessed the abbot without a profession, because the prince’s command compelled him to do so. Afterwards the abbot spoke with the archbishop, and the prelate received him into such favor that he had no abbot in Normandy dearer to him or more intimate. The next day he returned to the monastery.

The archbishop, however, ordered Abbot William of Cormelles to go with him [Col. 0719A] and, in his place, install him in the abbatial seat. He came with the greatest humility he could show, barefoot, and was received by the brothers with great honor and joy and led into the church. Then the abbot of Cormelles, as he had been ordered, seated him in the abbatial seat; and, beginning the *Te Deum laudamus*, he kissed the entire convent.

Thus, by God’s arrangement, William became the successor of the venerable Anselm, assumed the governance of the monastery of Bec after him, and held it honorably for many years. During his tenure, that same monastery of Bec was enlarged externally, by God’s mercy and the generosity of princes and other faithful people, with many great estates and revenues; internally, it was adorned with religion, noble and learned men, precious ornaments, and buildings. For he who had said to Joshua, the servant of Moses, “As I was with Moses, so I will be with you” (Josh. 1:5), himself remained with the successor William just as he had been with his predecessor Anselm; through Him, William was a man who acted prosperously in many things.

At that time there were in the Church of Bec many noble and religious men, both learned and unlearned, who had come there from various provinces to serve God. Some of them had remained from the time of the blessed Father Herluin; some, under the holy leader Anselm, had begun to serve God after abandoning the world; many, under that same William, renouncing the age, rejoiced to submit their necks to Christ’s easy yoke. Later we saw many of these become honorable rulers of Churches.

Among them was Boso, who deserves to be named with honor [Col. 0719C]. He came to the order in the time of the holy Anselm; but under the same Abbot William he became prior after the often-mentioned Baldwin, and after William himself was appointed abbot, adorned with wisdom and an upright life.

Also in William’s time a certain young monk of good character, nobly born and endowed with knowledge of letters, entered the monastery. His name was Theobald. After living religiously in the monastery for a long time, he became prior after Boso; and when Boso died, he was appointed abbot, and not long afterwards was raised to the archbishopric of Canterbury.

A certain monk came to Abbot William, asking to be received into the monastery because he wished to establish his stability in that place. When the abbot had initially delayed doing this, since he neither wished to retain him nor wholly reject him, and was now considering receiving him, he saw in a dream a certain deceased kinsman and acquaintance who reproached him for wishing to join a certain madman to the brothers. Certainly, as we suppose, that dead man had never seen the brother in question. Not long afterwards that brother, having received permission, departed; and thereafter he was nowhere seen in the whole province, nor was it heard where he had gone.

The same abbot showed the greatest love and honor to his predecessors, namely the blessed Herluin and the holy Anselm. When he spoke of them in common conversation, he named them with great reverence; he recalled their statutes to the memory of others, diligently observed them himself, and ordered them to be observed. For it evidently seems just that one who wishes his own commands to be guarded should himself first strive to observe the commands of his predecessors.

Whenever he was going somewhere after praying in the church, he went to the tomb of the blessed Father Herluin in the chapter house and commended himself to his prayers; and he did the same when returning.

The same Abbot William told me that one night the holy Father Herluin appeared to him and, taking him, led him through the monastery’s workshops and around the park, as it seemed to him, and to the church at Burneville, which that holy man had built with his own hands. Then he returned to the monastery, and, coming into the cloister, found no one there except a single monk. At this Abbot William felt somewhat ashamed, and the vision disappeared. Throughout the entire vision, the holy man had the abbot at his right hand [f., “the holy one”], but said nothing to him. What this vision signified is unknown, except that Abbot William himself said that perhaps there was something in the monastery that the Father wished to have corrected.

A monk named Robert was asking permission to go to England in order to see the holy Archbishop Anselm and speak with him, as he claimed, about the salvation of his soul. When Abbot William refused to grant this, he asked him in the chapter before everyone to grant what he was requesting. But when even then the abbot was unwilling to consent, the brother said: “If you grant it, I will go; and if you do not grant it, I will go.” The abbot did not like this statement. Nevertheless, afterwards, released to his own will, he departed, crossed the sea, and came to England; and not long afterwards he died.

A certain elderly cleric named William, leading a solitary life, came to the monastery wishing to become a monk; and because he was of good reputation, he was gladly received. After he had lived religiously in the community for several years, one day, while Abbot William was sitting in chapter with the brothers, he came before him and asked permission to return to the solitary life, so that there he might work with his hands for his livelihood, as he had done before his conversion. He said that fear tormented him because, living in idleness, he was being supported by the alms of others.

When the abbot heard this, he said to those sitting around him: “This brother is dying, and the ancient enemy, seeing him near death, is attempting to lead him away from the monastery so that he may cause some impediment to his soul.” Then, turning to him [Col. 0720D], he urged him to abandon this intention and to spend the rest of his life in peace with the brothers. He was already old and weak and could no longer work. He should not fear living from the benefactions of the faithful, since many others lived in the same way; rather, he should persevere in prayer, pray to the Lord especially for those whose alms sustained him, await the end of his life, which was already approaching, and prepare himself for his coming death.

The brother obeyed the abbot’s admonition. A few days later he was seized by a bodily illness and died within a short time, repenting that he had wished to leave the monastery. He gave thanks to the abbot and the brothers because they had not allowed him to depart after Satan, who had wished to overthrow him.

This good man of whom we speak—Abbot William, a man of great wisdom, adorned with good morals, related to great men, and well regarded by the king and the leading men of the kingdom—conducted himself so modestly, humbly, and gently that at times he seemed to some almost ignorant and nearly a fool. Yet if you approached him more closely and, as though examining his understanding, questioned him about difficult matters, you would find deep prudence, profound counsel, and above all an exemplary standard of uprightness.

He was devoted to God, submissive to his superiors, kind to his subjects, gentle toward the good, severe toward the undisciplined. He usurped nothing beyond his measure; he demanded every reverence for divine things; he feared God; and he hated sin as though it were deadly poison and avoided it.

If anyone asked him for a blessing, he blessed with words rather than with his hand, saying that it was not his office to bless with the hand, but that of bishops. There was no abbot who showed greater concern for his convent. Those who adhered to him more closely know what he was like: a man so fashioned by God that he would not utter foul speech, abhorred every kind of buffoonery, and, like a virgin, knew no impurity of mind or body from his mother’s womb.

Moderate in food and drink, honorably modest, and adorned by a religious character, he had a sound understanding, pleased by gentle speech, and was useful through instruction and example. He was constant in conduct, truthful in speech, cautious in promises, faithful in what was entrusted to him, devoted to the virtues, a lover of the poor, generous in almsgiving [Col. 0721C], cheerful in receiving guests, and a protector of widows and orphans. Living in this manner, he guided the course of his life well and brought it to a good end in death. God preserved his understanding, speech, and sight for him until he gave up his final breath.

We have spoken briefly about his life; now we shall explain how he departed from the world. In the twenty-ninth year of his abbacy, in the month of September, he fell ill, and from that illness he died. The illness gradually increased and afflicted him for a year and a half, until, in the thirty-first year after he had received the gift of the abbacy, he took completely to his bed around the end of March.

Abbot Richard of Pratelles, a religious man endowed with knowledge of letters, came to visit him and remained there until his passing. When he seemed already close to death, the brothers visited him according to Christian custom, and everything due to the dying was performed around him. After the office had been completed, when the convent ought already to have departed, the venerable Prior Boso asked him, as the fathers had done, to bless them as he departed this life and commend to the supreme Shepherd the sons he was leaving behind.

He raised his hand, blessed them, and said: “Love the cloistered life, for it is the restoration of our order; and do not seek to hold obediences in the world, because many lose their souls in them. But choose an abbot as quickly as possible, for it is not good to delay such a work.”

He earnestly asked them to pray to the Lord for him. For it was his custom that, whenever he spoke with someone whom he considered a person of consequence, he commended himself to that person’s prayers.

At that time the region around Bec was disturbed by the presumption of certain men who had rebelled against King Henry and held certain castles from which to plunder the country. Therefore the king often led an army against them, to suppress their hostile attack and defend the land.

Thus, after the octave of Easter, the king came to Bec and lodged in the monastery’s buildings. Then certain monks of Bec approached the king, asking him to make a certain monk who was a personal friend of theirs abbot after the dying man. When Abbot William heard this, he forbade that the man whom they were seeking to substitute in this way should succeed him in the governance of the Church of Bec [Col. 0722B].

Another brother once said jokingly to the same abbot: “Make me abbot, and I will serve you extremely well for as long as you live.” But he replied: “Because you have said this, you will never again be abbot of this place.”

When the king heard that Abbot William, whom he loved greatly, was dying, he came with a few companions to visit him and humbly sat on the ground before the bed of the man who lay there, his friend. Among other things, the abbot asked him to provide the Church of Bec as quickly as possible with an abbot suitable in age, life, and conduct—neither an old man nor a young man—because delay in such matters would do great harm.

The king replied: “Whom do you order?”

The abbot answered: “That is not mine to say, because the sacred canons forbid anyone to name his own successor.” For he was extremely careful regarding his speech and life and was a guardian of the whole religious discipline, even at the very point of death.

Then the king took the abbot’s right hand, brought it to his own eyes and mouth, and kissed it affectionately. He then placed it again beneath the covering and said to the monks standing around: “Pray for him, because at his death you are suffering a great loss.”

During the following night, when those who were guarding him had sung Matins, he asked them to allow him to rest and began to doze, until he fully fell asleep in death. Those around him saw that he was already approaching his end, so they carried him from his chamber to the infirmary, where the brothers died [46]. Surrounded by a crowd of his sons singing the seven psalms with the litany, he gave up his spirit shortly before dawn.

His body was washed and suitably clothed in cloths according to custom, and over these he was decently reclothed, as for Mass, in sacred vestments. Afterwards he was carried into the church and placed in the choir before the high altar, where day and night he was attended by the sorrowful service of his grieving sons.

The monks mourned their devoted father; the servants and people of the place lamented that they had lost a good lord. No one complained that he had suffered an injury at his hands; all together grieved that they had lost a great patron.

In the morning the king came to the church. Seeing the body already decently adorned, he was pleased, praised what had been done, and said: “Would that my soul were where his soul is!”

A great multitude of people of both orders and every condition had come to Bec, partly because the king was staying there and partly because they had heard of the imminent death of the abbot of Bec. Among them were nine abbots, many monks, and many of his clerics and friends, who attended his funeral.

John, bishop of Lisieux, a wise and venerable man, also came. He devoutly completed the entire funeral office and fittingly rendered the final Christian service. A considerable crowd of poor people had also gathered because they hoped that almsgiving would be performed at his passing. It was carried out for two days, and no one returned empty-handed.

He was buried in the chapter house beside the holy Father Herluin, founder and first abbot of that place, on his right. He who had governed that same monastery second after Herluin was thus joined in burial to the man whom he had loved greatly during his life.

He was twenty-five years old when he entered the monastery; he was a cloistered monk for fifteen years; he spent thirty years and a half in the abbacy; and he departed this life at the age of seventy, in the year of the Lord 1124, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of May, in the week after the octave of Easter, during the festive season and Easter joy.

In this Easter joy, we ask you, Author of all things, to defend your servant from the enemy’s attack. O our Passover, Lord Jesus Christ, turn his mourning into joy and into glorious celebrations, so that his passage may be from death to life, from labor to rest, from calamity to glory, from darkness to light. There, Lord, you have established the brightest dwellings; there the souls of the saints rest; there, joined to blessed spirits and destined to enjoy eternal rest, may the spirit of your servant see you face to face, you whom the angels desire, the unfailing fountain of life, reigning eternally and without end as one with the Father and the Holy Spirit. Amen!

[Col. 0723] Here ends the *Life of the Venerable William, Third Abbot of the Monastery of Bec*.

## EPITAPH

[Col. 0723B]

Abbot William, born of a distinguished lineage,  
In his early years became a lover of religion.  
When five lustrums of his age had been duly completed,  
With sighs he began to despise the world and seek God.  
He laid aside earthly things and clung wholly to Christ.  
So that the servant might follow the Lord naked and stripped,  
At once he took upon himself at Bec Christ’s gentle yoke,  
Which he steadfastly bore for fifteen years.

After Anselm had become prelate of the English,  
This man received the care of the place and the governance of the brothers.  
The gravity of his conduct, his life, and the honor of his ancestry  
Made him illustrious and venerable beyond many others.  
He was learned, and his gentle speech pleased his hearers;  
By deeds and words he instructed those subject to him.  
From childhood he had been a follower of an honorable life,  
Preserving purity of heart and perpetual chastity.  
For thirty years he increased and advanced Bec.  
A gentle ruler to the submissive, a harsh one to the proud,  
A man so great, enriched with the finest merits of conduct—  
He was nevertheless unable to escape the bonds of death.  
On the sixteenth day of April, as it dawned,  
He completed the course and deeds of his present life,  
Commending his soul to heaven and his body to the tomb.  
He awaits the time when Christ will judge all things.

[Col. 0723D] Behold, beneath this tomb lie buried dust and limbs.  
Let us ask that the Lord grant him pardon and life. Amen.

## ANOTHER EPITAPH

Take back your fields for yourself now, O world—fields harsh beyond measure;  
Alas, they held me for so long a delay!  
Henceforth I shall cultivate them no more: the way out from you lies open,  
And I am released from a far-long exile.  
I return to my own homeland; the Lord calls me back;  
He commands me to return from the place where I had formerly been.  
[The reading is uncertain:] with tears he knows him whom I often entreated,  
That by forgiveness he might wash away all my wrongdoing.  
At last, taking pity on my bitter sufferings,  
May he lift me from the valley of the earth to the heights of heaven.  
Thus far, these things; I go, and it is no longer my place to remain here.  
I leave you my bones; if you wish, bury them.

## ANOTHER EPITAPH

A grain of wheat remains sound in the ground  
And cannot grow until it has decayed.  
So unless our flesh is touched by the bitterness of death,  
It does not receive the prize after running the course.  
Therefore it is granted to know that one ought not to grieve  
If he who was a stranger seeks his homeland.

[Col. 0723]

## 47. LIFE OF THE VENERABLE BOSO, CALLED “THE WISE,” FOURTH ABBOT OF BEC

[Col. 0723D]

In the days of King William, who subdued the English by arms, three men were born in the district of Rouen, on the estate of the monastery of Villars, to honorable parents—namely Haimeric and Lezelina. Their names were Gislebert, Boso, and Rainald. From childhood they were handed over to be instructed in letters, so that they might serve God in the holy Church throughout their lives; and this they did.

For after they had long led honorable lives among their own people, inflamed by the love of God, they sought Bec under Abbot Anselm, as though seeking a harbor after the dangers of the sea. They disclosed their desire to that abbot and, with God’s assent, devoutly received the religious habit there and held it even more devoutly to the end.

Indeed, the first and the last—Gislebert and Rainald—remaining honorably for a long time in their holy vocation, rested in peace. Boso, the middle brother, about whom we are speaking, was well instructed in letters. While still living in the world, he began to excel in good conduct, burn with the love of God, and devote his mind to religion. He was of extremely keen intellect, and what he understood subtly he expressed in lucid speech.

Consequently, perplexing questions had entangled his mind, and he could neither unravel them by himself nor free himself from them. Therefore he came to Bec and approached Anselm, whom he had heard was practiced in such matters. He disclosed to him the agitations of his mind by which he was troubled, and immediately recognized that he had received a satisfactory answer to everything.

Boso admired his wisdom, manner of life, and formation of character. Not long afterwards he changed his clothing and, under the same abbot, took up the Lord’s easy yoke there. Having become a monk, he loved with his whole mind the religion he had undertaken and strove constantly to advance in it.

When the abbot saw that the new soldier of Christ was truly seeking God, zealous for the work of God, obedient, and attentive to the other matters to which a novice ought to devote himself, he rejoiced in heart. He instructed him in the Lord’s service and continually kindled his mind to love of virtue.

Boso humbly received his teacher’s instruction with a receptive mind and stored it away for safekeeping in the treasury of his heart, so that later he might bring it forth sweetly at the proper time. Following Anselm’s conduct and formation of life, he exercised himself in piety. He was devoted to fasts, vigils, prayers, and other good works; he meditated diligently on the law of the Lord; he correctly understood what he read and explained it suitably; and he willingly accepted instruction.

Meanwhile, the devil, seeing Boso advancing daily from virtue to virtue and becoming better in his holy vocation, sent him, through a spirit of blasphemy, an extremely serious temptation. Through successive disturbances of various thoughts, it tormented him so greatly that he scarcely remained master of his own mind. Several days passed in this condition, and the temptation continually became more severe.

Therefore, troubled and confused in mind, he approached Anselm and disclosed what he was suffering. When the holy man understood each detail, he said to the brother only this, with pious concern: “May God provide for you.” Then he immediately dismissed him.

Anselm himself at once prostrated himself before a certain altar and poured out a tearful prayer to the Lord for him. Immediately such tranquility of mind followed that, as Boso himself later said, he was suddenly changed beyond what can be believed from the state in which he had been. Thus the entire temptation vanished so completely that he never again felt anything of the kind within himself.

After this, when Anselm, abbot of Bec, had been consecrated archbishop of Canterbury by God’s arrangement and by the election of the king of the English and the people, he sent for his beloved Boso, wishing to have him with him. Thus Boso crossed the sea and remained for some time with Anselm in England.

At that time Anselm heard that Pope Urban had summoned a general council at Clermont in the province of Auvergne. Since Anselm himself could not go, he sent the aforesaid Boso to that council. Because of the length and hardship of the journey, Boso became so ill that, after the council, when he wished to return to Normandy, he remained sick on the road at Saint-Walters.

After he recovered, he returned to Bec and then went back to England. But when Saint Anselm, expelled from England—first by King William, who had made him archbishop, and then by William’s brother Henry, who recalled him from exile after his brother’s death—was living in the regions of Burgundy and Italy, Boso returned to Bec.

When Anselm, after his second exile, was preparing to return to England, he asked William the abbot and the convent of Bec in chapter for permission to take Boso with him, saying that he would rather live with him in solitude than without him amid great riches. The abbot and the brothers, because they could not oppose the archbishop, granted permission.

This is the Boso with whom Anselm composed, through disputation, the book called *Why God Became Man*. He therefore remained with the archbishop until the end of the latter’s life. After Anselm’s passing, Boso returned to Bec and lived in common with the brothers. He loved them all, and he was loved by them all.

Meanwhile, when Prior Baldwin died, William the abbot ordered Boso to succeed him in the priorate. He was a man of honorable life and great prudence, distinguished by humility, endowed with the spirit of counsel, and firm in courage [48]. He consoled the desolate, became all things to all people, and helped each person as far as he could. He was kind in exhortation, restrained in correction, generous to the poor, gracious to guests, firm in faith, confident in hope in God, and abundant in charity.

When he had nothing to give to a needy person, he urged him to place his hope in God and declared that God’s help would soon arrive, since the end of the world had not yet come. He said such things jokingly, but in his heart he earnestly entreated God; and God very often helped him according to his faith.

When his wisdom, counsel, and goodness of spirit became known not only to his subjects but also to the princes of the earth, bishops, and abbots, as well as to many religious and secular people, they admired him as a precious treasure and as though he were a divine oracle. Such was the grace of God within him, and so strongly did the spirit of counsel flourish in him, that he answered those who came to him for advice subtly and sufficiently on the matters they asked about.

At that time King Henry instructed Abbot William to give Boso, prior of Bec, to his nephew Count Theobald, so that he might make him abbot in his own land. Whether the king requested this out of affection, resentment of heart, or at someone’s instigation, so that Boso might thereby be driven from the region, we do not know. Hearing this, the abbot was deeply saddened. He sent word to the king, earnestly begging him to spare both the Church and himself, to withdraw this order, and not to take his prior away. For the abbot was already worn out by old age and illness and deprived of bodily strength. The king, appeased by his entreaty, released the prior.

When Abbot William, weakened by a long illness, seemed already close to death, two monks of Bec approached King Henry, who at that time was staying at Bec and in the surrounding area because of the incursions of certain men who had rebelled against him. They said that, if Boso succeeded Abbot William, as the community desired, he would in no way render the king homage or the oath of fealty according to the custom of the land. Therefore, they said, the king ought to substitute in his place another man whom they named and recommended. They did this because they did not want to have the prior as abbot. Why they were hostile to him, however, we do not know; nor do we know that he had inflicted any injury on either of them.

When he heard this, the king was extremely angered in spirit, although at that time he concealed his anger. Acting craftily, and without the community’s knowledge, they wished to impose a master upon it, contrary to the Rule of Saint Benedict (chapter 64; question 2, canon 18), without its consent. Yet this is plainly contrary to the decrees of the Fathers, who declared that no one should be ordained against his will, but that the community of a church ought to choose its pastor according to the fear of God. Nevertheless, although this cunning of the malicious disturbed the community somewhat, it could not accomplish what it had contrived.

After Abbot William had died and been honorably buried, the entire community elected Boso. All the bishops and abbots, the clergy and people, neighbors and those from farther away who knew him, praised this election and declared him worthy of the highest honor. Accordingly, the community earnestly begged him to consent to their wishes. He opposed many reasons arising from his bodily weakness; they prostrated themselves on the ground and pleaded with him; he resisted with all his might, refusing.

The matter was brought before the king. Remembering what he had heard from the two monks about homage, as we related above—for he was exceedingly angry about it—he refused to grant his consent. Meanwhile, Gauffridus, archbishop of Rouen, a prudent and honorable man, and John, bishop of Lisieux, who had come to the king’s court while he was besieging Brionne Castle, which the men of the count of Meulan held against him, came to Bec and spoke with the brothers about choosing an abbot.

Then all of them, prostrate on the ground—for they were sitting in the chapter house—begged the prior to consent to the election mentioned above, and asked the archbishop to compel him by command. The archbishop, astonished by the brothers’ unanimity, praised their religious purpose and their great love for their prior. Then, turning to him, he admonished him, entreated him, and finally commanded him under obedience to yield to the brothers’ will.

He, on the other hand, declared that he could not do this because of the great weakness of his body, and he put forward certain other serious matters, almost sins, by which he claimed to be unworthy of it. The archbishop said to him: “Are you a monk?” He replied: “I would that I were.”

Then the archbishop said: “Truly, if you had killed twenty men, I would not release you, since I see such great and such extraordinary affection for you in the community.”

“Never,” he replied, “have I killed a man.”

Then he was compelled to reveal what he had kept hidden. Taking the archbishop and the bishop aside, he said that the pope had forbidden him ever to render homage to a lay person. For that reason he did not dare accept this obedience, lest he be forced either to become a transgressor of the apostolic prohibition or to offend the king.

When the archbishop heard this, he received the explanation wisely. The bishop of Lisieux, however, took it badly that the prior of Bec disdained to do what he and all the prelates of Normandy did according to the ancient custom of the land.

Returning to the chapter house, the archbishop and the bishop said that he had put forward a certain reason which, with God’s help, would make it unnecessary to annul this election. Afterward, several members of the community went to Rouen to see the king. Those who remained at home earnestly prayed to God, in whose hand are the hearts of kings, that he might incline the king to approve this election. But God did not yet choose to do what they asked. For the king sent the brothers who had come to him away empty-handed, ordering them to elect another, since they would not have this man.

The archbishop, however, helped the men of Bec with the king as much as he could, speaking on their behalf, with them, and without them. One day, while he was discussing this matter with the king, the king said to him: “He will render me no homage, nor will he make profession to you.”

The archbishop replied: “My lord, do what belongs to you; as for what belongs to me, we shall come to a satisfactory agreement between us.”

Then a certain honorable person sent word to the community at Bec that they should not abandon what they had begun: they had not yet prayed to God sufficiently; they should continue knocking at the divine ears with their prayers. The brothers gratefully accepted this counsel and devoted themselves more earnestly to fasts and prayers, entreating the Lord Jesus and his gracious mother Mary to look upon their church and bring to completion what had been begun.

Meanwhile, William, son of Ascelin, and Ralph the almoner, two monks of Bec, were traveling on business for the monastery. On the very road along which they were traveling, they met King Henry, who was coming toward them. When he saw them, he summoned them to him and spoke kindly with them. For by divine regard the fury that he had conceived because the prior had refused him homage had already subsided.

As they traveled together and conversed, they said to the king in the course of their conversation that they had something to say to him, if he would listen patiently. He ordered them to speak confidently about whatever they wished. Then they began again to discuss the election mentioned above, earnestly begging the king to confirm it by his assent. They added that they would render fealty to the king on behalf of their chosen man, if he wished, and that for this purpose they had intended to go to Count Theobald, so that he might petition the king by his letters.

But the king, smiling, said: “You would have labored in vain.” And with an oath he told them that, if their chosen candidate had not first mentioned the matter of homage, he himself would never have spoken of it. But now, he said, they should pray to the Lord to grant both him and them suitable counsel in this matter.

They returned home and reported what they had done with the king. After taking counsel, several more members of the community again went to the king, who received them cheerfully and willingly granted what they asked. He ordered them to bring the prior on the Sunday after Rogation Sunday, for these events had taken place before Rogation Sunday.

When this was announced to the community, they rejoiced greatly and gave immense thanks to God. The prior, however, said to them all: “Know that, from the moment I saw your unanimous love for me, even if I had known with absolute certainty that death awaited me because of it, I would not have failed to obey your will most readily—unless that reason had stood in the way, because I feared offending God.”

He therefore went with the brothers to Rouen. There the king, by a mere word, bestowed the abbacy upon him, and told him to preserve the religious life within, while the king himself would take care of external affairs. Thus it came about that the king, who had previously opposed him, now loved him greatly, willingly did many things he requested, bestowed numerous benefits upon the church, and often followed his counsel.

He also pleaded for the two monks whom we have said were opposed to his election, asking that their opposition not harm them. It was not a burdensome labor for him to forgive anyone who had offended him.

The archbishop, seeing that the king had so freely done what had been requested, as he had promised, wished honorably to perform what belonged to him in this matter. He therefore came for the approaching feast of Pentecost. On the feast day, at terce, when the cantor began “Come, Creator Spirit,” the archbishop entered the choir and honorably placed him in the abbot’s seat. Then, during the octave of Pentecost, he was ordered to go for the blessing.

Before Mass, however, he spoke with the archbishop and begged him not to compel him to make profession, which he absolutely did not wish to do, because, if he did so, he would create a great scandal in the monastery. The archbishop replied: “Let it be; all will be well.”

When the time of Mass arrived, he was brought forward to receive the blessing. The archbishop, standing at the sacred altars, questioned him according to custom, and he answered the questions as usual, until they came to the words: “Do you wish to be obedient to this Church, to me, and to my lawful successors?”

He replied: “I do.”

Then some of the clerics standing nearby began pressing him to say: “I profess.” But he again said: “I do.” When they continued insisting that he answer “I profess,” he said a third time: “I do, and I do so from the heart.”

Then John, legate of the Holy Roman Church, who happened to be present, said: “Do you not hear what he is saying? What more do you want?” And so the archbishop blessed him.

The following day the abbot returned to Bec. The community, wearing sacred vestments and arranged in procession, went out to meet him. He, too, humbly went toward the procession with bare feet, infirm though they were, and was received with great joy, as was customary in that church.

Once appointed, he remained most steadfastly what he had been. Pride and arrogance had no place in him. He was humble in heart, cheerful in speech, joyful in countenance, modest in dress, sparing in food, prudent in action, cheerful in receiving guests, and generous in offering service.

Who ever came to him desolate and departed sorrowful? Great men, both secular and religious, from near and far, came to him in large numbers for counsel about uncertain matters. He answered each person’s thoughts and questions so suitably that what each heard was sufficient for him.

He possessed remarkable patience toward every annoyance. Teaching patience, gentleness, and purity of heart, he urged people to avoid occasions of scandal, or not to concern themselves with matters that cannot be absent from this world. He said that, from the beginning of his conversion, he had so condemned occasions of scandal that no tribulation, prosperity, or adversity, no sorrow or joy, and no bodily affliction could break into his heart; he remained constant with the same countenance and the same disposition.

Sometimes, when he was told that his orders had not been carried out, he would say: “We both neglect God’s commandments and He endures it. How much more ought we to endure when our commands are despised?”

In everything to which he applied his mind, he was so capable that, whether the matter concerned God or the world, he quickly and most wisely resolved and arranged everything. He took the greatest care of the souls entrusted to him, lest any of them should perish through his negligence.

His life was holy, sober, honorable, and most chaste. His speech was rarely without usefulness; even in his jokes, anyone who considered them carefully would sometimes find great edification. His conduct, modestly religious, pleased all good people; to the weak he showed a father’s care and a pious mother’s affection.

Those who lived with him and his neighbors attest that what we say about him is true; so do people from his own region and those who knew him while living far away.

Throughout this period he was continually tormented by such severe pains in his feet, head, and internal organs that he could scarcely support himself. Sometimes he was tortured so fiercely that he seemed almost to breathe out his soul. For, when he was returning from the Council of Clermont, as we said above, a grave illness seized him. It weakened him so greatly that he never afterward recovered fully during his life. And, so that his patience might be tested more thoroughly and the righteous might become still more righteous, the Lord also inflicted upon him the wound of blindness.

But he rejoiced, gave thanks to God, and was always cheerful and always gentle. He knew that “power is made perfect in weakness” (2 Corinthians 12:9). The more he was afflicted outwardly, the more grace increased within him. Later, however, through God’s mercy, he recovered his sight by means of a certain medicine.

At last, overcome by paralysis, he was laid upon a bed. For a long time he was afflicted by such disabling weakness of his limbs that he could neither rise from his bed nor stand nor walk, and could not even lie down. He sat on the bed, resting his head on cushions arranged for this purpose on his right and left, and he called such a life a prison. Indeed, it was so: just as a person bound in prison cannot go anywhere, so the man of God, fettered by the bonds of this illness, could not leave his bed.

Yet he always kept his heart turned toward God. He retained an unimpaired mind, together with speech, wisdom, and understanding, and he asked God to preserve his patience, lest he murmur against God’s scourges.

He possessed this patience to the very end, so that amid such great and numerous hardships of bodily illness, and amid the various concerns of the Church that were brought to him for counsel, he was never disturbed. With a tranquil mind he gave fitting answers and wisely arranged everything.

Often, when he heard from the ministers that the Church was burdened by poverty, he would say: “God, help us; God, advise us.” And truly he proved in many ways that God’s help and counsel were not lacking to him. For during his time many people contributed many things to that place, from which [f., quibus] the brothers’ want was very often relieved.

A pain arising in the large toe of his left foot spread throughout his body and tormented him with such bitter anguish that it nearly tore out his soul. Swarming worms were extracted from that toe. But the pain did not cease on that account.

To those who came to him and spoke with him about the severity of his illness, he would say: “Great is the illness I suffer, exceedingly grievous beyond what can be said. If God willed it, it would be enough for me, and I would gladly finish my life in this sickness; but He does not yet will it. He still sees something in me that must be scourged and corrected by the scourge. Let His will be done. Pray, I beg you, that He preserve my patience, lest I think or say anything against His disposition.”

One day a certain brother came to see how he was. The abbot said to him: “I am in such great tribulation that I cannot possibly describe what I suffer.” He was silent for a little while, and then added: “But by the grace of God my soul is in great tranquility.”

When he saw that death was already near, he asked that the brothers visit him and that the duties owed to the dying be carried out around him. The brothers came, and he was absolved and anointed; the other rites customary among Christians were carefully performed around him.

Then he asked the brothers to pray for him and to forgive him if he had offended them in any way: “Although,” he said, “I do not remember having wronged any of you, I was your monk, your prior, and your abbot; I never harmed anyone. To use the Apostle’s words (1 Corinthians 4:4), since I came into this order, I am not conscious of having done anything to anyone that I would not have thought right to do.”

He endured this severe bodily affliction for two and a half years. Every day he heard Mass, and because of the disability of his limbs he did not fail to have himself carried by hand to the chapel for Mass—even on the very day before the night on which he died.

His bodily strength was already failing, and his voice was weaker than usual, so that he could scarcely be understood; yet he still retained his full understanding. When the brothers asked him to pray for them, he said that he intended to do so, if God granted it to him.

As night was approaching, he was carried to the common dwelling of the sick brothers, so that he might die among them; he was pleased that this had been done. Around midnight, while Matins was being sung, the brothers were summoned by the striking of the board and gathered. As they sang the seven penitential psalms with the litany, he breathed out his spirit.

His body was washed and suitably clothed according to custom, then carried into the church. There it was watched over by the brothers for the whole day and the following night. On the next day he was buried in the chapter house, to the left of the holy Father Herluin, with honor and with the great grief of his sons. The honorable Richard, abbot of Préaux, properly completed the final service of burial.

He died on the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist. That solemnity ought to have been celebrated with great joy and exultation, since many were foretold to rejoice at his birth (Luke 1:14); yet the brothers could not help grieving over the loss of one from whom they had suffered an irreparable loss. Then what the prophet said was fulfilled: “Our feast days will be turned into lamentation and mourning” (Tobit 2:6).

The years of his life are reckoned as follows: he was twenty-three years old when he became a monk; he spent twenty-six years without office; he was prior for nine years; and he governed the abbacy of Bec honorably for twelve years and twenty-two days. During his governance, the Church of Bec endured severe and considerable poverty.

He died in the seventy-first year of his life, on the eighth day before the Kalends of July, in the year of the Lord 1136.

These three brothers, about whom we have said a little, preserved the order of their birth even in death by God’s providence. Gislebert, who was the eldest by birth, died first; Lord Abbot Boso followed him both in birth and in death; and Rainald, the youngest, kept the order both of birth and of dying. May our gracious Savior, the Lord Jesus Christ, who lives eternally as God with the Father and the Holy Spirit, grant them the rest of eternal blessedness and life without end. Amen.

[Col. 0731] Here ends the Life of the Venerable Boso, Abbot of Bec.

## EPITAPH

[Col. 0731D]

Adorned in character, this shepherd lies buried here;  
Renowned for genius, sober and devout.

He was also gentle, prudent, and steadfast in sorrow;  
For as long as he lived, he endured many scourges.

Powerful in counsel, he was a relief to many,  
A consolation to the wretched and a support to the devout.

For twelve years this fourth abbot presided  
Over the monastery of Bec, the form and glory of his flock.

Despising the world, loving true virtue,  
He rendered devoted service to Christ.

This Father had already passed seventy years  
When he suffered death and became the ashes now lying here.

While the sun stretches toward its rising for the eighth time beneath Cancer,  
Our final lot snatched him away from us in sorrow.

The Baptist’s birth is celebrated while this man departs.  
He was called Boso; O God, be gracious to him. Amen.

## ANOTHER

The pious abbot of Bec whom this stone covers,  
Boso, was a great man in our time.

Surpassing many in the gravity of his character,  
He instructed and strengthened those whom he was about to admonish.

Approved in doctrine, understanding, words, and deeds,  
He flourished here, ever-watchful in sound devotion.

He endured many bodily scourges with a tranquil mind;  
Frequent holy reading restored him.

No murmur followed him for such a scourging,  
But he gave thanks to Him who had allotted him so much.

And so, after completing nine five-year periods in religious life,  
He brought his studies, strength, and commands to their appointed end.

If anyone asks where his end came to pass,  
Let him know that it was on the forerunner’s feast, the Nativity of John.

O pious Baptist, our devout Israelite,  
May he be joined with you, where Christ dwells in light.

## ANOTHER

[Col. 0734A]

The abbot of Bec, whose speech was a sword,  
Scraping away vice, through which destruction is brought.

Boso, the great Father, a lion to the proud, a lamb to the gentle,  
And sweet to the people, becomes ashes in this tomb.

He becomes ashes in this grave who, while he could live,  
Was both serpent and dove through his goodness.

Therefore, you who see these verses, lest he be plunged in black Styx,  
Pour out a prayer to the King, who is the death of death.

We believe that he ascends to the heavens, to which every faithful person ascends.  
May God, who is there, be gracious to him. Amen.

[Col. 0733]

# SUMMARY OF THE LIFE OF THE VENERABLE THEOBALD, FIFTH ABBOT OF BEC, LATER ARCHBISHOP OF CANTERBURY

[Col. 0733B]

When the venerable and wise man Boso, abbot, had died, Theobald assumed responsibility for the monastery of Bec. He was distinguished by birth, adorned in character, honorable in life, and well educated in letters. During the time of Lord Abbot William he entered the religious order, and, after receiving the habit, lived religiously in the cloister for many years, well regarded by all. He then became prior of that place for ten years; and when Abbot Boso died, he was appointed abbot by the election of the entire community.

Not long afterward, by God’s dispensation, at the summons of King Stephen and Queen Matilda, with the consent of the clergy and the acclamation of the people, he was transferred to England and received with great joy. Soon afterward, at Canterbury, he was consecrated archbishop of all Britain by Baldwin, legate of the Roman See.

During this period he endured many adversities at the hands of men of both orders. First, when he was elected abbot, Hugh, archbishop of Rouen, wished to invalidate his election because it had been made without consulting him. But when the venerable Odo, venerable bishop of Évreux, intervened, he gave his consent to the election mentioned above.

Nevertheless, he delayed giving him the abbatial blessing for fourteen months because of the profession that Theobald did not wish to make, since his predecessors had never made it. But through the entreaty and counsel of Peter, abbot of Cluny, who happened at that time to be in Normandy, the archbishop accepted his profession without a written document, by a mere word, and so blessed him; afterward he loved him greatly.

When he held the episcopate, he endured many things, almost to the point of death. For after Eustace, the king’s son, had grown up and become a knight, the king and queen, Bishop Henry of Winchester, the king’s brother, and many of the nobles—especially the household knights who loved the young man—wanted the archbishop to anoint him king.

Because the archbishop refused to do this—for Henry, son of the Empress Matilda, daughter of King Henry, was threatening England and invading his hereditary kingdom by force of arms—the king’s anger against him grew so fierce that, in the hearing of everyone, he said that this same archbishop could place no trust in him, that he would never lay his own hand upon him, but that if any of his men inflicted any injury on him, he would not care.

When the archbishop heard this, he immediately departed from the court, to which he had then gone. He boarded a ship and was crossing the Thames when, behold, nearly twelve knights followed him with swords, intending to kill him or cripple his limbs. But the One who knows how to guard His own whenever He wills preserved him unharmed.

These events occurred around the octave of Easter. They also spread many insults about him among the people in order to dishonor his life and reputation. But God, who arranges all things and, when He wills, rescues His own from distress, finally brought an end to these evils after all their plots had been nullified.

For one week before Rogation Sunday, the queen came to the end of her life and reign. Her son Eustace, the cause of many evils and also of the disturbance mentioned above, departed this life not long afterward. King Stephen followed them and brought an end to such great calamities; when he died, he left peace to the people and the kingdom.

At last Henry, now duke of all Normandy, entered England and obtained the kingdom owed to him by hereditary right. Once he had been established at the summit of royal power, Henry, brother of King Stephen and bishop of Winchester, withdrew from the kingdom and secretly crossed the sea.

Thus the just Judge, looking down from on high, rescued Archbishop Theobald from the greatest dangers and reduced all his enemies to nothing. Afterward he lived happily for several years. He departed from this life in the year of the incarnate Word 1149, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of May, on the Tuesday of Easter week.

He governed the abbacy of Bec for two and a half years, and the archbishopric for twenty years, three months, and the same number of days.

[Col. 0735]

# SUMMARY OF THE LIFE OF LETARD, SIXTH ABBOT OF BEC

[Col. 0735A]

When the venerable Theobald, abbot of Bec and archbishop of Canterbury, had been appointed, Lord Letard succeeded him in governing the monastery by the election of the entire community.

He had parents who lived in the same place and was a native of that place. In the place where he was born, he rose to great honor, for under the venerable Abbot William he received the religious habit and, from his earliest years, grew day by day in the love of God and the fervor of religion amid the sacred disciplines of that monastery. He preserved his life in purity of mind and body, with every moral excellence and honorable conduct, striving tirelessly to please the inward Examiner through fasts, vigils, and prayers.

He was altogether cautious and attentive concerning those entrusted to him, a diligent keeper of the Rule’s precepts and of the traditions of his elders, sharply reproving transgressors, and a man of excellent understanding. In conversation he was gentle and familiar, especially when someone spoke with him about the salvation of his soul. He cultivated friends with great affection—those, namely, whom honorable conduct commended. But if he noticed in them anything inconsistent with honor, he thereafter regarded their intimacy as of little value.

Such was he in himself and such toward others, both before and after becoming abbot. At first he was prior at Pontoise for many years, and afterward at Préaux. From there he was appointed to the abbacy. Then, in accordance with what is written, “that the righteous may become more righteous” (Revelation 22:11), God permitted him to suffer blindness of his bodily eyes, so that He might reveal the merits of his patience and virtues and turn his inward eyes toward the contemplation of the true light.

Struck by this affliction, he could never be seen to grow sad because of it, nor did he abandon the brothers’ way of life, except that he did not sleep with them in the dormitory or sit with them in the cloister. In the choir, however, in the chapter house, and in the refectory, he lived continually like anyone else, right up to the final end of his life.

When he contracted the illness from which he died, and after he was seen to be approaching the goal of his course, he was carried to the house of the sick, where the brothers die. There, with the brothers gathered around him and singing psalms for him, he breathed out his spirit.

The venerable Rotrocus, bishop of Évreux, together with certain abbots, carefully and honorably buried his body and performed the final office according to custom.

He died in the year of the incarnate Word 1161, on the sixth day before the Nones of July, on the Saturday within the octave of the Apostles Peter and Paul, around the tenth hour of the day, at approximately sixty-five years of age and in the fiftieth year of his monastic life. He was the sixth abbot after Saint Herluin, the first abbot and founder of Bec, and he governed the abbacy for ten years and twenty-three days.

[Col. 0735]

# MIRACLE IN WHICH BLESSED MARY CAME TO THE AID OF WILLIAM CRISPIN THE ELDER—CONCERNING THE NOBLE FAMILY OF THE CRISPINS

[Col. 0735C]

The blessed Mother of the Lord and perpetual Virgin Mary, the unique protection of Christians, through whom the salvation of the world appeared, is recognized as having found greater grace with God than all others. For this reason she is invoked by human beings more frequently, and with greater confidence and familiarity, in their necessities; and she herself is accustomed to bestow the benefit of her mercy swiftly upon many.

Accordingly, some examples of her assistance are found written down, while countless others are continually experienced in their effects but, because of their number, have not been committed to memory. Among these we wish to relate one that seems worthy of remembrance and that, because of its magnitude, could not remain hidden from the people of that region. In this event the most blessed Mother of God showed how kindly she feels toward the wretched who flee to her.

For when a certain noble and devoted man named William, surnamed Crispin, implored her mercy in great distress, she came to his aid and mercifully rescued him from imminent danger of death. But before we reveal the course of this miracle, it seems worthwhile briefly to indicate who this William was and how the surname Crispin came to him and to his family.

Before the Normans under Duke William conquered England, there was in Neustria, which is now called Normandy, an eminent man named Gislebert, distinguished by lineage and nobility. He is said to have been the first to receive the surname Crispin from the nature of his hair. In his earliest youth he had curly and stiff hair, standing upright and, so to speak, bristling upward like the branches of a pine tree, which always reach upward. For this reason he was surnamed Crispin, as if “curly pine.” We still see this same upward bristling of the hair in those who descend from Gislebert’s family. Hence they too are distinguished from the other Norman families by that surname.

This Gislebert, who, as we have said, was the first to acquire the surname Crispin, married Gonnor, sister of Lord Fulk of Alnou. By her he had three sons—Gislebert Crispin, concerning whom we have undertaken to write as follows, and Robert [the name of the third son is absent or corrupt in the supplied text]—and two daughters, Emma, mother of Peter of Condé, and Esilia, mother of William Malet. William Malet was a vigorous knight who, when he grew old, became a monk of Bec and, after spending several years honorably in monastic observance, as befitted such a man, rested in a good end.

Robert Crispin, the younger brother, left Normandy and traveled through many regions until he reached Constantinople. Received with honor by the emperor and becoming a man of great renown among all, he is said to have died there by the poison of the Greeks.

Gislebert Crispin, the elder of the three brothers, received from the duke of the Normans the castle of Tillières to hold as an inheritance; his heirs possess it to the present day.

The aforementioned William Crispin, the middle brother, was considered among the foremost of the Normans, most famous for the nobility of his lineage, the excellence of his character, and his military prowess. As we have said, he was the finest son of Gislebert, the first father of the Crispins, and emerged under fortunate auspices for the glory of his entire family. Just as the Fabii, Anicii, and Manlii were once held in distinction among the Romans, so the Crispins were regarded with special honor among the Normans and Franks.

This William, however, is said to have been the most renowned of them all. In his own time, through his military achievements, he shone forth as distinguished above almost all the men of that generation. Consequently, his outstanding excellence won him many envious persons and made them his most savage enemies.

At that time the Franks, under the leadership of Walter the Old, count of Pontoise, who claimed that all the land between the Itte, the Andelle, and the Seine ought to belong to him, were making frequent incursions beyond the River Itte and carrying off booty from the Vexin. Therefore William, duke of the Normans, who afterward became king of the English, stationed the aforementioned William Crispin in the castle of Neaufles against the incursions of the Franks, to restrain their presumption. He granted him the castle itself and the viscounty of the Vexin to hold by hereditary right, and his son after him, as we still see today.

William established his residence there and placed his household and knights in the region to resist the incursions of the Franks. Because of this, the Franks became intensely angry with him and conceived such hatred against him that they sought his death with all their eagerness.

Having given this preliminary account of the origin of the Crispin surname, let us now come to the matter itself. As we received it from truthful narrators, we shall relate it simply. It is a matter worthy of remembrance and fitting for the blessed Mother of the Lord, who after God is uniquely beloved by the human race and worthy of praise throughout all ages.

At the prompting of the Lord our God Jesus Christ, author of every good thing, a certain knight, Herluin, vigorous and wealthy, set aside earthly nobility and rejected the pomp of the world, by which previously, according to his station, he had flourished not a little. Laying down also the belt of knighthood, he devoted himself with complete dedication to Christ’s poverty, so that in monastic conduct he might serve God alone more freely. Thus, renouncing the world, which had smiled upon him according to his desire, he wished to build a monastery on an estate belonging to him, called Burneville.
