He built there a church in honor of Saint Mary; there he received the religious habit when he was forty years old, and not long afterward was ordained priest and appointed abbot.

Because the place is flat and without water, he was warned in his sleep by the blessed Lady Mary, Mother of the Lord, and withdrew into the valley by the stream called Bec. There he began to build a noble monastery in honor of that same holy Mary, Mother of the Lord—a monastery which God brought to completion for the glory of his name and the salvation and consolation of many people. God brought to him, for the help and counsel he desired, Lanfranc, a man exceedingly skilled in the liberal arts; receiving him with great joy, Herluin gave him the religious habit.

Then many learned secular men and others hastened eagerly to the aforesaid place, humbly inclining their necks beneath the Lord’s easy yoke and in obedience to the regular life. Some entrusted their children to Lanfranc to be instructed in the philosophy of the liberal arts and to Herluin to be formed in regular discipline; others diligently sought to enrich the place with their possessions to the greatest extent. Among them, the distinguished man Willelmus Crispinus offered his son, Gislebert by name, while still a child, to the aforesaid Fathers to be raised for God under regular discipline, and supplied, together with the boy, much support from his temporal resources.

Instructed by their teaching and by the examples of their holy conduct, Gislebert advanced with divine assistance in sacred and philosophical studies, so that he learned to perfection all the arts called liberal and, himself perfected in religion, poured out their streams for many others to drink. His perfection in the active and contemplative life was so great that when God placed Lanfranc over the Church of Canterbury in the highest pontificate, Lanfranc, at God’s call, appointed him to govern Westminster. He pleased God and men, as we believe, by such a grace of holiness that he displayed humility before all the prelates of his time and especially proclaimed it in a loftier manner.

For thirty-two years he benefited the place more than he ruled it. In a good old age, full of days and holiness, he was gathered to his fathers and brought this life to its close.

In the father of this Father—namely, Willelmus Crispinus, already often mentioned above—there occurred an event of remarkable excellence, wondrous to relate, and fitting for the Lady Mary, ever-Virgin, whom the whole world ceaselessly praises for her great and numerous benefits.

This nobleman, as we have already said, had been appointed by Willelmus, duke of the Northmen, as margrave in the castle of Melfia against the Franks, who, crossing the river Itta, were devastating Vilcasino by sudden raids. There he had stationed his household for the defense of the castle. Nevertheless, at certain times he inspected the land he possessed in Normandy, in the county of Lisieux, and, having arranged his affairs, returned to Melfia. As he went or returned, he never passed through Bec without seeing the venerable Father Herluin and speaking with him.

It happened that, returning as usual from his own land, by the Lord’s providence this devout man visited the church of Bec on a certain Sunday and spoke rather freely with the abbot about his affairs. After they had discussed familiarly what the needs of the matter required, he asked permission to depart and, with thanks, hurried away. When he had gone some distance, however, he stopped and immediately returned to the abbot.

The man of God was astonished at his return. After greeting him again, he asked why he had come back.

“Father dear,” Crispinus said, “I have returned for this purpose: that you may bless me and commend me to the prayers of yourself and your brothers, so that you may earnestly commend me to God and to his merciful Mother.”

At once the Lord’s man Herluin, moved in the depths of his compassion by an extraordinary affection of charity toward the man’s fervent devotion, said:

“We commend you to God and to his most holy Mother. May their protection guard you and powerfully defend you from every adversity.”

Trusting in this blessing, Crispinus kissed the abbot and the brothers and hurried with his companions to the place toward which he had begun to travel, namely, the castle entrusted to his custody.

The Franks, however, who lived opposite, beyond the Itta, heard that Willelmus Crispinus had crossed the Seine and descended into Normandy. Gathering together, they carefully watched for his return. By chance, on the very day when he was returning, they lay hidden in ambush in a neighboring forest, waiting to seize or slaughter him as he came.

Crispinus hurried toward the place, and when he was already not far from the castle, he passed beside the forest in which the Franks were hiding, prepared to kill him. As soon as they saw the man they were seeking, they rose from their ambush and boldly attacked him. His companions all abandoned him and fled. He wished to attempt escape by flight, but the density of the forest hindered him. Thus intercepted, since he could neither flee nor resist, he leapt from his horse and, compelled by necessity, sat upon the root of a felled tree that stood nearby. According to some, he hung the reins by which he guided the horse on the branches of a neighboring tree; according to others, for the greater glory of the miracle, he held them in his hand.

Hemmed in by these difficulties, Willelmus Crispinus raised his heart to God and with great devotion of mind called upon the Mother of Mercy:

“Lord Jesus Christ,” he said, “have mercy on me, and through the merits of Father Herluin and his brothers, to whom today I humbly commended myself, free me from this impending danger of death.

“O noble Virgin, undefiled Mother of the Lord, receive the unworthy prayers of your sinner [read: petitioner], and may the sacrifice of my afflicted heart rise before God and before you as an odor of sweetness.

“Virgin of virgins, Lady of angels, if you have any care for your Herluin of Bec, I humbly beseech you to deign to free me from this present destruction. Enemies press upon me from every side, already triumphing with insults over my death or capture. A hostile hand threatens me, and I cannot escape it. Intercepted at the very threshold of death, I am forced to despair of life.

“What shall this little servant of yours do, O undefiled Mother of God, sanctuary of the Holy Spirit? What shall he do whom a hostile band pursues with lances and swords?

“Come to my aid, therefore, most merciful Lady, through the power by which you are glorious among the heavenly beings, commanding among earthly creatures, and fearsome among those below; everywhere gracious, everywhere exalted, everywhere preeminent in authority and royal majesty. Renew in me the benefits of your ancient assistance, for no path of escape is open.

“Mother of Mercy, through the prayers of your servants at Bec—Herluin and the brothers of that place, to whose prayers I commended myself this morning—free me from this present image of death.”

Having uttered such a prayer before the Lord and his glorious Mother Mary with complete devotion of mind and great contrition of heart, though without the sound of his voice, he was distressed in spirit almost to the sweat of death. Suddenly, on his left, a splendid woman stood beside him for the consolation of life: pleasant in countenance, beautiful in royal dress, and clothed in a fine, white linen garment. She spread her right sleeve over him, and this covering concealed almost his entire body, for the garment descended as far as the middle of his shins and could reach no farther.

He was wearing red hose, however, and therefore drew himself together and contracted his body. Curved completely into himself, he struggled to hide his shins and feet beneath the royal maiden’s sleeve, but could not do so.

The enemies approached and hastened to search for the man with lances and the points of their swords. Prodding beneath the leaves, shrubs, and branches, they attacked from every side as far as his feet and body, but in no way touched him. Through the protection of the blessed Mother of God, he had become invisible to his enemies.

They wondered and said:

“Where did he go? What happened to him? Surely the earth has swallowed him alive? He came here; he was here. Where did he flee and disappear? Look, his horse is hanging there, the one we are pursuing. Since we have not found him, let whoever wishes seize it to his loss.”

But those among them who had sounder judgment replied that they had not come to steal a horse, but to kill the hostile enemy, if they could.

After they had labored for a long time searching for him in vain, and the day was already growing dark, they returned home in confusion.

Then that most merciful Lady said:

“Do you know, man, in the anguish of death, from where the means of life came to you? Do you know my name, who supplied you with the comfort of breathing again in the anguish of death? I am the good Mother of God, to whom Abbot Herluin commended you with all his heart when your intention devoutly asked this of him.”

After saying this, the Virgin departed.

Thus the Queen of Heaven scatters the fragrance of life among those who hope in her; thus, through abundant charity, she draws innumerable people to herself and leaves no one without glory who devoutly implores her help.

The companions of Crispinus, who had fled from him out of fear of the enemy, returned home and filled the town with sad news that their lord had either been captured or killed. Great grief and incomparable mourning filled the entire castle. Suddenly they saw Willelmus Crispinus approaching on horseback, and they ran to meet him, receiving him joyfully with great gladness.

This hero, who had previously loved the Church of Bec very much, thereafter loved it above all others for this reason and bestowed many of his possessions upon those serving God there. He left this love to his descendants as though it were hereditary, so that the children born from his lineage seem naturally to love the Church of Bec, as though they had drunk the sweetness of its love with their mother’s milk. They also invoke and entreat the Mother of the Lord, who is venerated throughout the world, as though she were worshiped uniquely at Bec, calling her “Saint Mary of Bec”; and they have often experienced her help in their needs.

Of these descendants it is said that they received the Church of Bec at its very beginning, as though it were newly born in a cradle, raised it, brought it to mature age, and supported and advanced it with their resources as far as they were able.

This distinguished man, the often-mentioned Willelmus Crispinus, when he came at last to the end of his life, sent for and asked the holy Father Herluin to come to him and give him the religious habit. While the abbot delayed, Crispinus saw demons come to him and build two exceedingly high walls around him. He was so hemmed in by them that he thought he could not escape, when suddenly he saw Saint Benedict approaching, carrying in his hands the sign of the Lord’s cross. At his arrival the entire demonic illusion vanished.

Before long it was announced that the venerable Abbot Herluin of Bec had arrived, accompanied by a monk named Willelmus, who later became abbot of Cormeilles and from whom, it is said, this account was heard.

Crispinus therefore told the abbot about the demons’ deceptions and the help of God granted to him through Saint Benedict. Then he became a monk, and a few days later departed this life. He was buried beside the church where the cloister was to be built, trusting that through Saint Mary, Mother of the Lord and his deliverer, and through blessed Benedict, he would obtain the grace and mercy of Christ.

## Epitaph of the elder Willelmus Crispinus

Nobly born, this knight lies buried here,  
Prudent and brave, upright in character.

Lest the world should drown him with itself,  
He entered this harbor; here, as a monk, he died.

After the Nones of January, and three and four hours,  
When he had already completed [the reading is uncertain], and the fifth was already beginning.

Bec was small, and its name matched its circumstances;  
With his own resources he raised it as he was able.

He was called Crispinus by a familiar surname,  
Willelmus by name; O God, be gracious to him.

This Willelmus Crispinus had a wife named Eva, fitting to him in birth and character. By her he fathered Gislebert, the aforesaid abbot of Westminster, and several other children. Eva, born of the Frankish people and of distinguished lineage, after marrying the aforesaid Willelmus adapted herself to his character and began to love the Church of Bec above all others. She embraced the abbot and monks with all her heart, as though they had been born from her own body, and venerated them with great devotion. The clothes and whatever precious objects she possessed for adornment she spent for the use of the church and the brothers; and she loved the Mother of the Lord and her Church of Bec with all her heart.

After her husband Willelmus died, she devoted herself entirely to God’s service. Living in holy widowhood, she devoted herself to fasts, vigils, and prayers as far as her sex and age permitted. She tasted neither meat nor blood until the end of her life and gave many alms to the needy. After some years she was veiled by Willelmus, archbishop of Rouen, and remained subject to the monastery of Bec until her death. When she died, she was buried beside her husband.

Their grandson through their son Willelmus, the third Willelmus Crispinus, inherited his original love for the Church of Bec and venerated it with extraordinary affection.

This Willelmus was related by blood to the count of Anjou and was therefore his familiar companion. Once, when he had gone to him as to a friend, the count was waging war against certain of his men who were rebelling against him in his territory, and Willelmus fought for him as best he could.

One day, finding the enemy, he boldly rushed upon them. They turned their backs, either out of fear, so that they might flee, or deliberately, so that they might lure him farther away and seize him. Pursuing them for some distance, he became separated from his own men. Seeing that he was pursuing them alone, one of the enemies turned, struck the horse on which he was riding, and pierced it through the flanks.

Knowing that his horse had been mortally wounded, Willelmus immediately turned the reins and, turning backward, urged the horse with his spurs. He tried to return to his own men by swift flight, calling upon the blessed Mother of the Lord in a loud voice:

“Saint Mary of Bec, help me! Saint Mary of Bec, help me!”

Crying out in this way, he reached a certain ditch, crossed it with a single great leap, and, as though he had already gained safety, fell down as if dead.

This same Willelmus Crispinus used to relate this as a great miracle, to the honor of God and his holy Mother: the horse, almost dead and pouring out blood abundantly from both flanks, carried him nearly two miles to a safe place. Indeed, as he said, the horse itself was vigorous with extraordinary speed, but he had never found it so swift.

Later, this same Willelmus was captured and kept for a long time in prison, bound with chains. Compelled by fear and anguish, he vowed that if God freed him from this tribulation, he would go to Jerusalem. Not long afterward he left the prison as a free man and took the cross, that is, the sign of his intention to go to Jerusalem.

At once he was so changed in word and deed that he suddenly appeared entirely transformed, to the astonishment of all who saw it. He fixed the time of his departure for the first feast of Saint Michael. He earnestly asked God and his holy Mother that, if he was destined to die on the journey, he might die before beginning it, so that his body could be carried to Bec and he might lie buried among his predecessors.

God granted this to him according to his goodness, just as he had asked. For, seized by illness, he put off the human person on the vigil of Saint Michael, on the fourth day before the Kalends of October, exactly as he had desired and as he had ordered when dying: on the day on which he had said he would depart.

His body was carried to his Lady, Saint Mary of Bec, and buried beside his fathers.

Through such benefits the blessed Mother of God has drawn the family of the Crispini, and many others of every rank and lineage, into her familiarity, so that with firmer faith and more ardent love they dare to implore her help in their needs and, through her intercession, may recover the grace of her Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit, God, forever and ever. Amen.

[Col. 0743]

## 57. Life of Saint Augustine, Benedictine Monk, First Archbishop of Canterbury and Apostle of the English

From an old manuscript of the Abbey of Bec.

## Prologue to the Life

What the history of the venerable Bede draws from the life and miracles of Augustine, the first instructor of the English [Note: History of the English People, Book I, from chapter 23 to the end, and Book II, chapters 1–3], and what we have found omitted by him in other ancient books, we reproduce most faithfully with our little hammer. Whatever we have read declared and written after his triumphal ascent to the stars, we add with credible faith. Those things which, visibly before the people and through the testimony of the eyes of highly approved persons, shine more brightly than daylight, illuminate believers with their own rays and dazzle the hesitant.

We could also recount many places and names of those who witnessed and investigated these matters, were it not forbidden by disgust. Above all, the testimonies of blessed Gregory are decisive [Note: Saint Bede reports this in the place cited above.], for he declares in his writings that Augustine performed very many signs.

These things, therefore, which we have learned by reading or seeing, we have explained more fully in another book [Note: The author composed a longer Life of Saint Augustine.], so that we might satisfy the sons of paternal affection, whose hunger cannot be sated. But we have shortened this little book somewhat, so that amid the solemnities of the divine and human banquet we might oblige kindly and fraternal guests [Note: He was a monk.].

At the same time, may the other sister Churches of the brethren, spread throughout this ocean, wherever these events may reach, rejoice with their native affection, like the daughters of their first parent.

Nevertheless, beyond this intention of brevity, I see that my vessel is overflowing as the oil of Elisha increases. We therefore ask all the most learned and kindly teachers and disciples of the Lord’s school: since these things have been proved with such clarity, may they not merely refuse to believe them, but receive them with the full kindness of paternal affection and, with constant faith, strive to celebrate them against the wicked.

## Here begins the Life

The armed strong man, whose court was the world, whose stronghold was the kingdoms of the earth, and whose spoil was the human race—our armed champion, encountering him in our very weakness yet mightily far stronger, pierced him with the cross prepared in himself, inflicting a wound that could never be healed. He turned back upon him all the missiles and darts of reproach cast against himself. He stripped him of all his weapons, condemned him irrevocably to eternal imprisonment and punishments, and distributed all his spoils, won by right of triumph, among his apostolic leaders. He appointed chosen princes over peoples, nations, and kingdoms (Luke 11).

There remained the level expanse of the British Ocean, cut off from the universal world. The most powerful King reserved this region for Augustine, his faithful steward, who was one day to come, turn night into day, and pour out a new and true perpetual light after darkness.

Already Pope Gregory, the immense splendor of the human race, was powerful enough to set Augustine apart by divine inspiration for the Lord’s work, just as formerly Peter set apart Barnabas and Saul (Acts 13:2). Gregory himself had intended to seize this palm, but the Lord replied that this privilege belonged to Augustine.

For, when Gregory heard that the boys recently seen in Rome, shining white as snow, were called Angles, that their province was Deira, and that the king of their land was named Alle, he said:

“The Angles ought to be associated with angels, the Deirans to be freed from the wrath of God, and the praise of God ought to be sung on earth as ‘alleluia.’”

Having therefore made preparations, Gregory sent Augustine, flourishing in divine knowledge and every virtue, with forty of the choicest companions, whom he knew to be religious and ready in divine doctrine. They hastened eagerly along the saving road and had advanced some distance for several days.

But behold, a windy rumor, spread from the mouth of the people by the evil adversary, terrified the athletes of the Lord. It said that the people they were seeking were fiercer than all mortals, thirsted for human blood, could not endure Christians living among them, and could in no way be recalled from their idols or converted to Christ.

Thus once, when the Lord’s disciples were sailing the sea, a contrary wind opposed them until the Lord rebuked their little faith and, by his command, stilled the waves upon which he himself had walked.

They therefore sent Augustine humbly to blessed Gregory, asking that he allow them to return home and not undergo such great danger in vain. But Gregory, watchful in accordance with his name, sent a letter stating that greater glory follows great labor and ordering them to obey Augustine in all things, whom he had already appointed abbot over them. Gregory also carried apostolic letters to Etherius [Note: A letter sent by blessed Gregory to Etherius, archbishop of Arles, is found in Book IX, Letter 63.], the archbishop of Arles, so that he might provide these envoys of God with assistance in their needs.

Thus they were strengthened, so that with greater joy they completed the labor which previously they had greatly feared.

Meanwhile, Augustine was divinely granted many signs, by which they were greatly comforted. By way of example, we insert one here—or rather, three in one—always the most celebrated among all the people of the place where it occurred, and also attested in written accounts.

That choir of saints, then, continuing its journey through the province of Anjou, entered a village called Sai [Note: Perhaps Caesar’s bridge, French Pont de Cé.]. A wild crowd of country people, treating them as unknown foreigners, despised them because of their humble clothing and their walking on foot and assaulted them with laughter and abuse.

The men seemed unharmed by the women’s madness. But the women, as though conspiring together, attacked the innocent newcomers with every kind of insult. After driving them from the countryside, they pursued them like rabid dogs with howling, snarling, and roaring.

The weary travelers sought to rest beneath a nearby elm, but from there too they were driven away by the women’s mocking assault. When one woman was rudely clutching the tracks of the holy leader, and he wished to repel her as a wild creature with the staff he held out, the staff was suddenly hurled from his hand like an arrow from a bow. Flying nearly three stades, it struck into the ground.

The leader followed with his devout choir, as though the Lord were calling him there. Augustine pulled out the staff, and with the staff he drew forth an everlasting spring of water. Relieved together from their severe thirst, they offered eternal thanks to the divine goodness.

There they pleasantly refreshed their weary limbs and spent the entire night in the praises of God. Although they had been driven from lodging and were resting beneath the open sky, the highest Goodness, ever merciful, covered them with glory in place of a roof: a radiance poured down from above, surpassing the sun in a new brilliance, so that the siege of darkness would not increase around those clothed in the armor of light.

Beautifully also, a column of light, which once led the children of Israel to the promised land, shone over these men who, having drawn so many peoples out of misguided Egypt—dark according to the interpretation of its name—were bringing them, with the light of faith going before them, to believe in Christ and enter the eternal kingdom of glory.

The leader of the embassy wrote his name and the reason for his journey with the staff in the earth beside the spring, in these words:

“Here Augustine, servant of the servants of God, stayed as a guest; blessed Pope Gregory sent him to convert the English.”

As dawn was already approaching, they hastened to continue their journey toward the Lord’s gains. Perhaps divine judgment was at work, so that those who had rejected the grace of blessing freely offered to them in the Lord’s guests would not obtain it when they wished.

When daylight had come, the whole neighborhood hurried there, for many saw the sun’s radiance shining from the heavenly vault down to the earth upon the citizens of heaven, still pilgrims on earth.

There they also saw the wonders of God shining forth in his saints from the earth, just as during the night they had seen the radiant column extending from the heavenly citadel. They were astonished to see a new spring pouring forth a perpetual and sweet stream, and that the guests of incomparable goodness had returned these benefits to them for their evil deeds.

Learning from the inscription both the name of the renowned teacher and the saving purpose of his journey, they lamented their guilt in the cloud of their confusion, because they had so wickedly resisted Christ’s embassy and the salvation of the nations.

“Woe to us madmen!” they said. “We were not worthy to be sheltered by the blessing of such angels or drenched with their sweetness!”

They therefore founded a church on the same spot by unanimous devotion and dedicated it to Christ in honor and under the name of Saint Augustine. They erected an altar where they had read his inscription, so that although they had not deserved to rejoice in his bodily presence, they might have him perpetually present in their church.

There too the compassionate Father displays many benefits to those who ask him and performs many miracles of healing. Nevertheless, every kind of woman is permanently excluded from this church, so that it may always stand as an example to all who insult the saints.

A certain wealthy matron came here carrying a candle and sought to enter. Although everyone threatened her, she persisted in her purpose, saying that she had not sinned against the saint but wished to honor him. Hardly had she reached the forbidden boundary when suddenly her intestines burst and she died. Her corpse was carried outside, and she taught everyone to believe what no one had believed; she who had thought to overcome everyone by her presumption publicly forbade all others ever to attempt such a thing.

Nevertheless, women have their own shelters and shrines there, where they may pray, give thanks to God, fulfill their vows, hear the divine mysteries, and receive the sacraments of salvation. They also have Augustine as a kindly listener in all their needs and as a prompt executor of their just prayers and desires, apart from the inviolable condition of his church.

Visitors from Anjou and others who know of this custom are accustomed to marvel greatly when, near the bodily resting place of Augustine, they see women approach even to kiss his tomb, while none of those women can ever reach the threshold of his church or drink from its spring.

They are answered that the women who received him enter it lawfully, whereas those who rejected him are rightly driven away.

It is fitting to add to this ancient account the miracle recently performed there, although we are lingering somewhat while hastening to follow that light-bringer on his journey to the English Ocean.

The most reverend Goiffridus, bishop of Anjou, had previously come to Canterbury, rejoicing to revisit Augustine, the ancient guest of his homeland. When he heard the monks recounting the miracles described above, he recognized them perfectly and confirmed them by faithful testimony. An excellent narrator of the recent event, both for himself and for that Church, he related it as follows:

“Indeed, in our presence I recently dedicated this church to the Lord in the honor and name of Augustine, after the people who loved so great a patron had rebuilt it more solemnly, just as it had originally come into being.

“Fields all around, far and wide, were flourishing, and the crops and sown grain were already ripening into ears and stalks. When the crowds poured in for the dedication, as though the river Loire itself were overflowing, the grain of those fields was trampled, crushed, and broken, so that the stalks were not merely struck or bent but everywhere appeared exhausted, as though the threshing floors had been swept bare.

“So completely did no one at this desirable gathering for Augustine’s solemnity consider sparing either his own crops or those of others that the hope and fruit of that year seemed to have perished forever, until another August.

“They hoped in Augustine’s generosity, but in a blessing other than the one that had then passed away. Yet from this despair arose a greater joy of wonder and faith, when this land, so utterly ruined and condemned, surpassed all the lands of the province in the harvest, both in the height and abundance of its crops.

“From this there grew around Augustine, their great advocate, such veneration and devoted faith among all that they believe him to be present wherever in the world he is invoked, and able to obtain from the Lord whatever he asks and to give it.

“Having suitably explained these matters, old and new, let us now follow the Lord’s envoy as he takes possession of the Ocean.”

When the main terrestrial circuit of the nations had been completed by the road over land, Augustine sailed across the watery world of Britain. Together with the aforementioned number of companions—forty—he was received on the rich and very large island of Kent, called Thanet.

This land rightly triumphs in blessing as the first to receive Christ in his envoys: a fortunate land in its fertility, but most fortunate in the first hospitality it offered to so many god-bearing citizens of heaven.

Thus, I say, with the Spirit of the Lord directing his way, he landed near the very gate of the royal capital, where he would have a permanent seat and, beside it, an everlasting resting place.

Behold, blessed first parent of the regeneration of the English race: leaving Rome, your august mother, you received England as a daughter, whom you would nourish as a beautiful bride for the starry King.

After traversing the great terrestrial world, you entered this other sphere of the vast Ocean, beautiful with a serene face, exceedingly fertile in fields, meadows, pastures, rivers, and straits; delightful with mountains, plains, and forests; most splendid with populous cities and the commerce of merchants from overseas; distinguished by a fair-skinned people and illuminated by the wealth of its resources.

This immense and splendid Elysium the Maker of all things long ago ordained for you, his chosen servant. He who, in the beginning, completed the world with every adornment and beauty and presented it to humanity for possession.

This people, beautiful in appearance but darkened by the soot of idolatry, will ascend completely whitened, like the Ethiopian woman of Moses, washed in part in the Jordan.

Now, for the greater glory of God and of your crown, that column of new light which led the ancient people out in faith—raised in the cross of the risen Christ—you will lead the people of the nations out of the Egyptian darkness of unbelief and the shadow of death. After Jesus son of Nun, you will introduce them into the promised land, the land of milk and honey.

For to you, evangelical leader, grace has granted the Gospel, which was denied to Moses, the lawgiver, and which he could not attain under the Law; in the true one, you have deserved to fulfill what he could not.

Now, from the spoils of the bound tyrant and from the kingdom of the captive robber, you will make a kingdom for our God (Revelation 5:10) and a people of possession (1 Peter 2:9).

After the heavenly kingdom and the rewards of your labors, this will be your perpetual possession, acquired for the Lord through you. Though you fled temporal advantages, you will now possess hereditary gains.

Placed here upon the outer wall, you will keep watch from a towered lookout, from which you will continually guard the whole homeland dedicated to you.

Edelbrithus presided over Dorobernia [Note: Canterbury. Edelbrithus, king of the Cantuarii. Malmesbury, Book I of the Kings of England, chapter 1.], third among the kings of the English, but destined to be the first citizen among the angels.

He had a most Christian wife named Bertha, a royal maiden born of royal parents among the Frankish kings. She was joined to him by such a covenant that no treachery could trouble her observance of Christianity. For the newcomers of Christ she was an open door to the king.

Therefore prudent Augustine sent word to the king through suitable messengers that he and his companions had been sent from Rome by the Roman bishop for the sake of the salvation of the king and his people—if only they would deign to heed the blessed message they brought.

The king ordered such distinguished visitors to await his timely arrival on the very island where they had been received and commanded that the necessities of life be supplied to them fully.

After delaying for a long time, he came to Thanet and sat beneath the open sky. For, through the vain suspicion of an ancient error, he imagined that he might be seduced inside a house by some spell, whereas outside, beneath the sky, this could not happen in his presence.

Outside, he granted the saints an audience with him. Absurdly, indeed, the night feared being darkened by God’s light-bearers and the sons of day.

Augustine, breathed upon by the Holy Spirit, bringing peace and salvation to the king, to all his people, and to the kingdom, reports that he and his companions have been sent to him and have come of their own willing benevolence, so that they might announce joy, glory, and an eternal kingdom, where those who obey their words will live and rejoice forever. He declares that God Almighty, the Creator of all, loved human beings whom he had made so greatly that, while always remaining God, he deigned to become man and the Son of Man, so that by his death he might make human beings, redeemed, children of God. At whose birth a new star shone; whose feet the sea served as a passable road; at the outrage of whose Passion the sun hid its rays; at whose burial and Resurrection the whole earth trembled and was restored to peace. “He is,” he says, “the Lord Jesus Christ, proclaimed from the beginning of the world by all the patriarchs and prophets as the Son of God, conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of a Virgin, and everywhere declared God and man by countless signs; and now believed in, known, and received by all nations as the Savior of all.

“Therefore, urged on by that love of his which impelled him to lay down his life for us, and by which we desire with all our heart to have you as companions in his eternal kingdom—just as we have all been begotten from one man—we announce to you this Creator and Savior of all, so that, believing in him, you may be saved. For, without any uncertainty, the promised rewards come to those who believe, and endless punishments to those who despise them.”

While the Lord’s envoy was speaking these and many other things, confirming their truth with innumerable testimonies to divine power, he also displayed an image of the holy Redeemer, beautifully painted in gold on a panel, so that even foreigners might learn to offer him thanks.

The king, amazed, praised and blessed such great promises, and at the same time gave thanks to the goodwill of the holy men who had come from so far away to care for his salvation. But because of his native blindness, his eyes were bleary and unable to endure the splendor of so great a light. He replied that he could not cast off the ancient rites of his fathers, which all England had hitherto revered, and grow young again through new and uncertain ceremonies. Nevertheless, because of their good intentions, he wished to receive them in his city of Dorobernia with friendly hospitality, to support them adequately with the necessities of life, and furthermore he readily assented to their converting as many as they could to their sect.

[Col. 0749D] Thus, with God’s providence enlightening the king’s heart, Augustine came with the Lord’s little flock—those whom it had pleased the Father of graces to give the kingdom—to Dorobernia with melodious litanies of joy. He gratefully began this antiphon and sang it sweetly with everyone:

> “We beseech you, Lord, in all your mercy, that your fury and your anger be taken away from this city and from your holy house, for we have sinned.”

By such a confession they rightly presented themselves as sinners, though they had come to reconcile and absolve them before God. As the first teachers and first fathers in the faith of Christ entered England’s metropolis with the triumphant banner of the cross, the citizens who believed were to imagine the guardian angels saying:

> “Open the gates, and let the righteous nation enter, the nation that keeps faith with its mission.” (Isaiah XXVI, 2–3)

The old error of idolatry had departed, so that henceforth the peace of Christ and of the Church might be preserved here. Here the walls of Jericho seemed already to be falling, while the walls of Jerusalem were being built. It was not walls of stone that fell, but the fortifications of demons and their stone divinities, dissolved by terror of the saints—divinities that had condemned their worshipers to eternal captivity and siege.

Here the Bridegroom of glory was already constructing for himself a new Jerusalem, through Augustine, its chief architect, and his fellow craftsmen. Its foundations and walls were of pure gold and every precious stone; its designers were the patriarchs; its surveyors, the prophets; its builders, the apostolic Fathers; its illuminators and polishers, the jewelers—that is, the martyrs; its most fully equipped scribes, the confessors; its beauty, in its ivory houses, the virgins; its ornaments, everything beautiful to behold and delightful to contemplative eyes. Upon the summit and around the circuit of its walls stood the unbroken and ever-watchful guard of angels.

Augustine was chosen as the first founder of this city so beautiful, as the paranymph of the Bridegroom, more beautiful than the sons of men, and the friend of the Bride, crowned with glory and honor. At this time he was to fight on behalf of the Lord’s camp and, after the rebellious peoples had been subdued, make a triumphal entry into the city. This chief consul and angel of the Lord’s covenant would inherit an everlasting throne and, for all his successors until the Prince of Shepherds should come, would hold the foremost place as the father of his children.

But when he had exchanged earthly labors for a heavenly crown, he would then reign more powerfully, as he does now shine, in the citadel of Zion—his splendid citadel—which rises above the city, lifting its turreted summit into the air. As the chief treasury and the grace of so many princes’ co-treasurers, it would shine wholly golden in the heights, from which, until the day of the regeneration of all things, he might protect his Jerusalem and the whole country by his power and perpetual prayer.

The Lord’s new soldiers therefore remained in the city being founded for Christ until they should be clothed with power from on high and receive timely assistance. But who could describe these cloud-born men—men like flying clouds, living angels, flowers of the desert, Antonys and Macariuses—who displayed in the city all the world’s beautiful and pleasant delights as if they were a deadly vapor, fleeing them not only themselves but also impelling all their hearers, through a laboring and inwardly travailing charity, toward the endless ages of eternal joys? They sought none of the wealth of mortals except the salvation of souls; they desired only divine and heavenly things, insatiably.

The basilica of the confessor of Christ, Martin, shines in the eastern quarter, situated almost half a stadium from the church of the Lord Savior. It was once founded by Roman Christians and is still furnished with sacred rites. For approximately four hundred years, until the emperor Maximus, the Romans had inhabited these regions; Maximus triumphed in civil war over Gratian and Valentinian, the Augusti, and by withdrawing the soldiers drained Britain of Roman strength.

In this church [Col. 0751A] the most holy pontiff Letardus regularly celebrated sacred Masses and the Lord’s offices for the most Christian queen Bertha [Note: [Col. 0751] The pontiff Letardus provided Christian religious services for Queen Bertha. Malmesbury, at the place cited above]. He had been given to her by the royal court of France as her companion and was a most proven guardian in every holy observance, lest any frenzy of demonic deception obscure the brilliant jewels of Christ’s faith in her.

And, to compare lesser things with greater, he had preceded the pronouncements of the apostolic Augustine as the morning star precedes the dawn, and the dawn the sun—namely, that Sun whom Augustine raised more brightly from the Ocean, like a bridegroom coming forth from his chamber (Psalm XVIII, 6). As forerunner and doorkeeper, he too freely opened the way for the envoys bearing Christ.

With this blessed bishop Letardus, God’s servant Augustine and his companions, adding great joy of salvation, were one in all the Lord’s mysteries: one Church and one fellowship, one spirit in their one Lord. These newcomers, following their predecessors as their own forerunners, adorned them by their arrival, like gold laid over silver. Saint Augustine and all his followers, endowed with great grace for signs, healed everyone who was brought before them or whom they visited, whether weak or sick.

The peoples were astonished, terrified by so great a thunderbolt of divine power, uncertain what they ought to admire more: whether earthly beings passing into heavenly ones; or mortals, by the certainty of their life and preaching, affirming the immortality of souls and bodies; or the love that is strong as death (Song of Songs VIII, 6), by which they burned to draw everyone with them into heavenly fellowship, offering themselves even for the salvation of their enemies, as though for that of brothers; or, finally, that the saints’ very promises had been made exceedingly credible by such evident flashes and testimonies of miracles.

Some said that human beings had been changed into gods; others, that gods were living among human beings in human form. This naïve opinion of the common people was wholly mistaken, since the Lord says of his adopted children: “I have said: You are gods, and all of you are sons of the Most High” (Psalm LXXXI, 6). Thus many, overcome by their hardness through wonder at so great a novelty, believed in Christ.

The king himself, stunned by the splendor of such events and by divine delight, was persuaded by Augustine’s continual insistence, while the Church prayed, the queen—educated in the sacred writings—softened him, and the holy Fathers offered their encouragement opportunely or inopportunely. Freely renouncing the savage divinities of hell, he became in Christ a son of divine adoption.

Now, while all the powers of heaven were sublimely rejoicing and crowds of peoples were gathering for so great a solemnity, a new Silvester baptized a new Constantine. The evangelical David was anointed with the oil of gladness and enthroned upon the gentle throne of mercy. The ecclesiastical Solomon was crowned with a peaceful crown, in equity and wisdom. He presented himself as a servant under the rule of God’s servants; the prince of commanders was converted into an evangelical little child; and the ruler of peoples professed himself the companion of the poor.

Augustine and the Church rejoiced to have in him an ally whom they had previously feared as a persecutor. He also won for Christ the kings and nobles subject to him, together with their peoples, and preferred that his former empire should be enlarged and extended as the kingdom of Christ.

Augustine, therefore, being more ready for the salvation of all than for his own elevation, sent him to Aetherius, archbishop of Arles, to be consecrated apostle to himself and his people, just as God had willed and blessed Pope Gregory had ordained through the Spirit of God. Having crossed the sea, received his apostolate from the Lord, and brought back to the English people, as the chief of all nations, a patriarchate and patriarchal protection, he was received by the God-beloved king with triumphant joy as an angel of God’s covenant.

Like little Zacchaeus receiving the Lord, the king appointed Augustine ecclesiastical head of his metropolis, where he had first received him as a guest; and he presented him not merely as guardian of the city but as a watchful guardian of his entire realm. Augustine reformed and dedicated the royal seat of government as a pontifical chair and royal hall, and transformed it into the royal church of Christ.

To the east, on a suburban hill, he raised the royal and apostolic monastery of Peter and Paul, as a defense and fortification of the city. He elevated it as the citadel and watchtower of the kingdom, a prize that already stores the most precious treasures of heaven: namely, the splendid bodies of Augustine himself, of his holy successors the bishops, and of the kings, which will rise in glory at the revelation of the glory of great Christ.

You too, episcopal Rochester, renowned under the title of your apostle Andrew and the right-hand suffragan of the Church of Dorobernia; and you, pontifical London, crowned with the glory of great Paul—you owe in the Lord eternal proclamations of blessing to our king Edelbert, blessed in memory and founder, and to Augustine, its institutor.

But the new priest of the Lord, burning to announce such joys to the most attentive Gregory, sent to Rome, on his return journey, men of outstanding holiness: Laurence, then a priest and later the first successor to his sacred primacy, and Peter the abbot, the first of his suburban monastery.

These men, admitted by the holy pope with winged eagerness and devotion, reported that the English people, together with their king, had passed into the people and kingdom of Christ; that Augustine had been consecrated bishop for them; but that, for so great a harvest of believers, the few hands of the laborers were insufficient. They also presented the various questions of the new preacher Augustine, by which the unformed people might be more certainly instructed.

Then the most excellent apostolic bishop, indescribably gladdened, poured out infinite sacrifices of thanksgiving to God and prayed the Lord of the harvest to send laborers into his harvest. He emptied his monasteries and churches and, with the whole devotion of his heart, strove to delegate to the one Augustine and the one beloved people whatever learned and religious men he could call upon for the work of the Gospel.

Four ecclesiastical leaders, or four evangelists, stood out in this holy fellowship: Mellitus, Justus, Paulinus, and Rufianus. Mellitus, the honey-flowing abbot, then shone before Gregory’s splendid choir.

He also sent the apostolic pallium to Augustine, a great sacrament of Christ and the Church, as the garment of all virtues, which is the bond of the love of God and of the brethren. Thus, as Christ’s vicar, Augustine might be the mediator reconciling God and human beings, and, girded with the belt of paternal justice, might unite angels and human beings, earth and heaven.

He added sacred gifts: life-giving pledges of the apostles and martyrs [pignera/pignora], and various ornaments suitable for churches, priests, altars, and ministers of the Lord. He also supplied a rich banquet of books and unfailing provisions for the journey to the homeland of life.

He sent as well the questions of the aforementioned inquiries, disentangled and explained, which the reader will find in Bede’s History [Col. 0753B] [Note: They are found in Bede, Book I, chapter 28, and Book XII, Letter 31 of St. Gregory]. Of these, one point seems worth commenting on here: the differing practices of the Churches should by no means create separation among sound minds, provided that faith and Catholic observance remain intact. Rather, just as one body has different members and functions, so the queen, the Bride of the Lord, clothed in variety, triumphs in glory in forms both manifold and diverse. Thus one crown is woven from multicolored flowers; one golden necklace is illuminated by the varied brilliance of gems; and through different distinctions of voice we produce one harmony.

He also wrote to Augustine concerning his jurisdiction, beginning as follows (D. Gregory, Letter to Blessed Augustine, Book XII, Letter 15):

[Col. 0753C]

> “To the most reverend and holy brother Augustine, Gregory, servant of the servants of God. Since it is certain that ineffable rewards of the eternal kingdom are reserved for those who labor for Almighty God, it is nevertheless necessary for us to grant them the benefits of honors, so that, in their devotion to spiritual works, they may labor more abundantly through the prospect of reward. And because the new Church of the English has been brought, by the gift of the same Lord Almighty and through your labor, to his grace, we grant you the use of the pallium in that Church solely for the celebration of Masses, so that in the several places you may ordain twelve bishops subject to your authority.
>
> “Your Fraternity shall have subject to you, by the authority of God and our Lord Jesus Christ, not only the bishops whom you ordain, nor only those who shall have been ordained through the bishop of York, but also all the priests of Britain, so that from the language and life of your holiness they may receive a pattern of right belief and good living. Given on the tenth day before the Kalends of July, in the nineteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Maurice Augustus.”

After the bearers of the aforementioned sacred letters had gone farther, another letter of Gregory follows them. Through Abbot Mellitus he instructs Augustine that:

> “The temples that have been well constructed should, once the idols have been destroyed, be converted and consecrated into churches and places of worship of the true God, so that the people themselves, worshiping the Lord Christ in those same temples, may more familiarly gather in their accustomed places. The animals that they used to sacrifice to demons should no longer be killed for the worship of the devil but for their own use, in praise of God, and they should give thanks to the Giver for their nourishment. Thus, in Egypt, the Lord commanded the Israelite people to sacrifice animals in his worship, so that they might sacrifice them to God and not to idols. Given on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of August, in the nineteenth year of the reign of Maurice.”

In a third letter sent to Augustine (D. Gregory, Book IX, Letter 58), the same pope, rejoicing greatly at the conversion of the people through him, exclaims in praise of the Lord, beginning as follows:

[Col. 0754B]

> “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke II, 14); for the grain of wheat, falling into the earth, died, and by its death we live, by its weakness we are strengthened, and by its love we seek in Britain brothers whom we did not know. By its gift, we have found those whom we sought without knowing them. Who could adequately describe how great a joy arose here in the heart of every believer? The English people, through the working of the grace of Almighty God and the labor of your Fraternity, have been freed from the darkness of error and filled with the light of holy faith; they now trample with wholly pure minds upon the idols to which they had previously been subject through insane fear; they prostrate themselves before Almighty God with a pure heart.”

Then, after a little, he continues:

> “I know, dearest brother, that Almighty God has wished, through your love, to display great miracles among the people whom he has chosen.”

By saying this he inspired joy and fear in the bearer of God’s sign: joy that the English were being converted to Christ through miracles, but fear lest human weakness should begin to falter amid the progress of others. He set before him the example of Moses, the great friend of God:

> “Fasting for forty days and nights, he received the tablets of the Law, while the people trembled amid flashing thunder; alone, too, he was worthy to be nourished by familiar converse with God. From heaven he supplied manna, and likewise meat in excessive abundance. At the Lord’s command, though doubting, he brought forth abundant streams from the rock. Thereafter, for thirty-eight years, he shone with countless signs. In every doubt he consulted the Lord, and, when God spoke, he was instructed. The earth swallowed those who resisted him, and he crushed his enemies in victory.
>
> “Yet this executor of such great graces was finally taken from that promised land by death through the just judgment of God, because of one fault of doubt: he had failed at the waters of contradiction before the prescribed thirty-eight years, and throughout that long period, amid such numerous, such great, and such gracious and friendly conversations with the Lord, he had neglected to acknowledge him.”

By such admonitions, Gregory, ever watchful, sought to strengthen God’s servant—already long established in every holiness—even more deeply in fear and faith. Finally, he declares him chosen, one who also strives to bring joy in heaven over the conversion of many. And therefore, in the joy of heaven and the angels, he repeats the foregoing words as he ends the letter:

[Col. 0755A]

> “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will.”

He likewise exhorts King Ethelbert [or Aldibert] after an opening full of praise, in this smoothly worded letter (D. Gregory, exhortatory letter to King Ethelbert, 60, Book IX):

> “My glorious son, carefully preserve the grace that you have received from God. Hasten to extend the Christian faith among the peoples subject to you; multiply your zeal for righteousness in their conversion; attack the worship of idols; overthrow the buildings of the temples; and build up the character of your subjects in great purity of life by exhorting, frightening, correcting, and displaying examples of good works. Thus you may find in heaven that Rewarder whose name and knowledge you have spread on earth.
>
> “For he makes the name of your glory more glorious even to posterity—the name of him whose honor you seek and preserve among the nations. Thus once the most pious emperor Constantine, recalling the Roman state from the perverse worship of idols, subjected it with himself to Almighty God, our Lord Jesus Christ, and with the peoples subject to him turned his whole mind toward him. As a result, he surpassed the name of the ancient rulers by his praises, and exceeded his predecessors in reputation as much as he surpassed them in good works.
>
> “Therefore let your glory hasten to pour the knowledge of the one God, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit into the kings and peoples subject to you, so that you may surpass the ancient kings of your nation in praise and merit, and, by wiping away the sins of others among your subjects, become that much more secure concerning your own sins before the terrible judgment of Almighty God.
>
> “Our most reverend brother Augustine, trained in the rule of the monastery, filled with knowledge of sacred Scripture, and endowed, by God’s authorship, with good works: willingly hear whatever he admonishes you to do, carry it out devoutly, and preserve it diligently in your memory. For if you listen to him when he speaks on behalf of Almighty God, that same Almighty God will more quickly hear him when he intercedes for you.
>
> “I have sent small gifts, which will not be small to you when you have received them with the blessing of blessed Peter the apostle. May Almighty God perfect in you the grace that he has begun, extend your life here through many years, and, after a long time, receive you into the assembly of the heavenly homeland.”

He also wrote to the glorious queen Bertha [elsewhere Aldibrega] [Note: A letter of D. Gregory to Queen Bertha, in which he thanks her and exhorts her to better things (Book IX, Letter 59)]. From it we have excerpted the following:

[Col. 0755D]

> “Our most beloved son Laurence the priest and Peter the monk, on their return, reported how your Glory has behaved toward our most reverend brother and fellow bishop Augustine, and how much support and what kind of love you have shown him. We have blessed Almighty God, who in his mercy has deigned to reserve the conversion of the English people as a reward for you.
>
> “For just as through Helena, the mother of the most pious emperor Constantine, whose memory is worthy of remembrance, he kindled the hearts of the Romans toward the Christian faith, so through the devotion of your Glory we trust that he is working his mercy among the English people. And since your Glory is fortified by the good judgment that truly belongs to a Christian and to right faith, is educated in letters, and now, by God’s will, has an opportune time, act so that, with divine grace cooperating, you may restore with increase what has been neglected.
>
> “Therefore strengthen the mind of your glorious husband in love of the Christian faith by continual exhortation. Let your solicitude pour into him an increase of love for God, and kindle his spirit so fully for the complete conversion of the people subject to him that you may offer a great sacrifice to Almighty God from the devotion of your service, and that what has been reported about you may both increase and be proved true in every respect. For your good works have already caused the Romans to pray more fervently for your life, and have reached through various places even to the most serene emperor at Constantinople.
>
> “Therefore we ask that, just as we have rejoiced in the support your Christianity has given us, so the angels in heaven may rejoice in your perfect accomplishment. Devoutly and with all your strength present yourselves as helpers of our aforementioned most reverend brother and fellow bishop, and of the servants of God whom we have sent there for the conversion of your people. Thus may you reign happily here with your glorious son, your husband, and, after many years, receive with the fruit of eternal reward the joys of the future life, which know no end. Given on the tenth day before the Kalends of July, in the nineteenth year of the reign of Maurice Tiberius.”

From the letters that the same honey-flowing pope wrote to the bishops of the Franks, we have excerpted these few words:

[Col. 0756C]

> “Just as fire becomes greater when the breeze blows, so the endeavors of a good mind advance through commendation. Since, therefore, through the cooperation of the grace of our Redeemer, so great a multitude of the English people is being converted to the grace of the Christian faith that our most reverend brother and fellow bishop Augustine declares that those who are with him cannot suffice to carry out this work, we have determined to send him a number of monks, together with our beloved and common sons, Laurence the priest and Mellitus the abbot. Therefore let your Fraternity show the charity that is fitting.
>
> “Moreover, what he has recommended in his letters to Lothar, king of the Franks, concerning the reception of the saints, and to Brunhild concerning the miracles spread everywhere through them, is clearly apparent in his letters.”

These writings of apostolic commendation filled the king and queen of Britain, together with their supreme bishop, not only with divine joy but also kindled them more ardently to desire the heavenly kingdoms.

Meanwhile Augustine invited the British bishops, who differed from the ecclesiastical rite, with the king’s support, to adopt the common observance of all the other Churches, using humble prayer and admonition. They not only resisted him as if in battle formation, but also declared, on the authority of the holy Pope Eleutherius, that their own practices were superior to all others.

At last the sign-bearing Augustine prepared an argument for the truth by healing someone weak. A blind Englishman was brought forward, evidently offered by God’s will so that the Britons could not claim the sign for themselves if one of their own people were healed. The blind man was presented to Augustine’s opponents. When they refused, Augustine bent his knee, poured out a prayer, and marked the blind eyes with the Lord’s cross:

> “In the name of the Lord, let this blind man be enlightened, just as our assertion is shown to be sounder.”

Immediately, a clear illumination of the eyes answered with unmistakable testimony. The splendor of so great a sign gave the rejoicing people certain proof of the truth of Augustine’s assertion. The Britons themselves approved what they could not deny. Nevertheless, they asked for a delay in order to consult their elders, setting a day on which they would return for a council.

Seven bishops therefore came, instructed by a certain Justus, a man of their party, in such a way that, if Augustine were found gentle and humble of heart, this would be recognized if he rose when the bishops arrived; then they would obey him as a messenger of the Lord and bearer of the Lord’s yoke. But if he did not rise for the bishops, who were the more numerous, he would be regarded as arrogant, and they would despise him as a contemptuous man.

Girded with such a sword, by which they themselves would perish, they were furiously indignant when Augustine did not rise for them. They rejected him and all his words, and rebelled all the more fiercely the more humbly and lovingly he entreated them to follow the harmonious rule of the Churches.

By this most gentle charity and charitable gentleness it was made even clearer that he was a disciple of Christ and servant, rather than if, by rising before the proud men, he had seemed to honor their obstinacy and, by honoring it, to approve it. Yet these perversely proud men accused the humble servant of the Lord of being seated in arrogance, although the Lord himself says, “Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble of heart” (Matthew XI, 29). Sitting, he taught that the poor in spirit are blessed—something they could not be because of the form of their pride.

But while their father in his heart, still most eager for their salvation, continued to pray that they might at least be joined to the universal Church in these three matters—that is, in baptizing, celebrating the Lord’s Pascha, and evangelizing Christ together with the English—they rejected everything outright and even banished his entire authority from themselves.

Rebuking them with a prophetic sword, he said:

> “You will perish by those enemies whom you shrink from having as brothers in the kingdom of God, and you will lose your life through those to whom you begrudge the grace of Christ poured out upon all.”

After this prophet’s triumphant assumption to the Lord, the exceedingly warlike king of the English, Edelfridus, almost exterminated the Britons in a most savage slaughter. He captured the city of the Legions, which the English call Legacæstir and the Britons call Karlegion. An immeasurable multitude of priests and monks had rushed there to pray against the enemy. More than two thousand monks had also gathered from the monastery of Bangor, all of whom were sustained by the labor of their hands.

As these men fought the enemy through prayer and three-day fasts, the hostile sword cut them down, though they were formidable opponents. Of them, twelve hundred were killed after the rest had been routed. The number of common people slain cannot be counted. Thus the despisers of Augustine found the prophet truthful whom they had rejected as a suppliant but whom they had experienced as a threat.

The confessor of the Lord, traveling with the holy choir of his companions from the rebels mentioned above toward the city of York, saw a man lying beside the road, thrice pitiable through paralysis, blindness, and poverty. He heard him asking passers-by the reason for the crowd and, recognizing the famous name of Augustine, loudly invoking the help and alms of so great a Father.

Approaching him, the imitator of the Lord’s Key-bearer said:

> “Silver and gold I have none; but what I have, this I give you: in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, rise” (Acts III, 6), “and receive your sight. Endowed with health and light, go forward; you will no longer need a bearer or a guide.”

This word of Christ’s name, as though spoken from Christ’s own mouth, immediately raised the paralytic, gave sight to the blind man, and, when his eyes of the heart were opened as well, he received baptism and at the same time gained progress in his soul together with the service restored to his body.

O man filled with the Spirit of God, for whom, whenever divine necessity required it, signs for saving were as ready as words for teaching! For who could recount how often he shone everywhere with flashes of miracles? How many crowds of believers he won for God, both on that journey and in the territory of York and in every place toward which he turned! How much more did he accomplish on other days and occasions, when on one day of the Lord’s Nativity—which the entire glory of the angels perpetually celebrates with him—he regenerated through life-giving baptism more than ten thousand men, apart from an uncountable multitude of women and children.

What abundance of priests or other sacred orders would have sufficed to wash such a people? After the river called Sualvus in English had been blessed, the supreme pontiff ordered through heralds and teachers that all should confidently enter two by two and be baptized alternately, one by the other, in the threefold name of the Godhead.

Thus, all reborn, they were transported to the opposite bank by a miracle no less than that by which once the people of Israel crossed the divided sea and the Jordan turned backward. In such a deep current, amid so great and varied a multitude of sexes and ages, no one perished and no one was injured. This was a great miracle.

But this great miracle was surpassed by one of greater eminence: every weakness and infirmity was laid down in that stream; every sick and deformed person emerged healthy and restored.

O festive spectacle of angels and human beings, when so many thousands of the white-robed people came forth from the bed of a single river, as though from the womb of one mother, and from one pool so great an offspring was born into the heavenly commonwealth!

Therefore the most serene Pope Gregory, bursting into joy with all the fellowships of heaven, could not keep this silent from the holy patriarch Eulogius of Alexandria. He wrote to him, knowing that he would rejoice greatly with him, about the great multitude baptized on that one day of the Lord’s Nativity. A church founded and dedicated beside the aforementioned river in the perpetual memory and name of this baptizer Augustine, granting the requests of believers, confirms the testimony of the aforementioned pope.

When the Gospel of the Lord had returned from York, a man entirely ulcerated with dreadful leprosy prayed to the beneficent Father for the help of salvation. When the blessing of the apostolic right hand had been infused, together with the sign of the saving cross and the name of God’s majesty, he immediately felt every pain flee from him as darkness flees from light. As though he had stripped off the old man of filthy disfigurement, he solemnly clothed himself with a new man of health and beauty.

For when the confessor of the supreme Trinity himself said, “In the name of Christ, be cleansed,” the sick man was restored to complete health by this threefold medicine of the blessing, the cross, and the Lord’s name. His swollen hands and fingers subsided; his face and all his limbs were restored to their proper beauty and function. His tongue, now loudly eloquent, cast off *taratara* [elsewhere *taratantara*], the interpreter of a voice that had until then been suppressed [Note: *Taratantara*. Servius says in his commentary on Book IX of the *Aeneid* that Ennius invented this word to express the sound of a trumpet].

Amid the glory of such signs, Christians burst forth in praise of Christ, and pagans advanced toward the faith.

From there the leader of the word of God turned aside and eventually came to a certain profane little village in the province called Dorset. There a demoniac populace dishonored the saints of God with every insult and mockery, to such an extent that—as it is even offensive to recount—they thrust forward fish-tails.

Therefore the Spirit of the Lord, angered at the perpetrators of this crime and at their entire progeny, pronounced their own disgrace perpetually through the mouth of the prophet Augustine, and poured back upon the wicked their proper dishonor, but upon the saints everlasting glory.

There was also another people in the eastern region of England, so inflamed in the sacrifices of demons by the fire of Gehenna that they not only shrank from hearing the messengers of Christ who promised the heavenly kingdoms, but also, in the complete madness of their minds, burned to punish or exterminate them.

Nothing—neither prayers nor entreaties—availed; they mocked the terrors of the heavenly judgment and of hell, and snuffed out prodigies and signs [Col. 0759D]. Faith and kindness did not allow Augustine to abandon such desperate and ruined people to destruction. Resisting the wrath from above, he prayed to the Father of mercies that he might correct the ungrateful toward mercy by means of correction. Thus, burning with the heat of their profanity, they all burned with invisible fire and sulfurous heat—a punishment such as this land had never before, nor would ever afterward, experienced. No one escaped, since no one proved innocent. Everywhere there arose a fearful chorus of wailing and the cries of old men, young people, and suckling infants burning together, so that parents too were tortured through their children.

All those who had rejected Christ’s commands flew to the footsteps of Christ’s servant, already instructed by just punishment, so that through Augustine they might be freed from their punishment in Christ’s baptism [Col. 0760A]. Thus that death-dealing fire, devouring their foul flesh—a fire that no waters could extinguish and no medicines drive away—was extinguished and expelled from all the baptized by the Lord’s fountain through Augustine’s intervention, and was forever driven from the whole territory of Augustine.

But from those whom we have mentioned above, condemned by their own disgrace, Augustine and his blessed companions had advanced five miles and wandered through deserted and waterless places. Heat, thirst, and weariness oppressed them, any one of which could have weighed heavily upon travelers. Yet he who sat at noon beside the fountain, wearied from the journey, moved by the labor of his servants and by their prayer, did not disdain visibly to bend down to his dear and faithful steward and to console him with his sweet address [Col. 0760B].

“Be steadfast,” he said, “and act confidently, my servant who has pleased me, for I am with you, a ready helper in every necessity and in accordance with your good will. Ask for whatever you wish, knowing that I always favor your kindly love. For the door of my kingdom is open to you, where you may enter into the joy of your Lord.”

After saying this, the Lord was received into heaven.

Having been abundantly refreshed by so sweet a fountain springing up into eternal life, Augustine no longer knew thirst for the fountain from which he might thirst again, nor did he labor for food that perishes, but for that which remains unto eternal life [Col. 0760C]. His sole desire was to follow with tears so desirable a vision as it departed, so that, once his eyes had been cleansed, he might reach the light of the angels. Immediately, bending his knees, he adored the place where the Lord’s feet had stood and, as though kissing the very footprints of the Lord, he watered them with Magdalene’s tears and perfumed them with eternal love.

Considering also that this land was filled with heavenly blessing through the abundant outpouring where the fountain of life had sprung forth, he pressed his staff into that very place, and with it at once drew out a boiling spring of pure water. Thus, after giving thanks to God, he refreshed them all to satiety. Once the water had spread into streams and rivulets, it made these formerly solitary places exceedingly populous.

There the confessor and theologian of the Lord, from seeing God—whom he had seen there—gave the place the name Cernhel [Col. 0760D] [Note: Cernhel gave this place its name. A monastery was built there and called Cernelium; it was said to belong to Saint Peter. See Malmesbury, *De Pontificibus*, book II, *De Monasteriis Shirburnensibus*, etc., fol. 142.]. The name is formed by joining Latin and Hebrew into one. For the first syllable, *cern*, means “vision” or “sight,” while the second, *hel*, signifies “God.” There too he constructed an oratory, in perpetual memory of the Lord’s vision, in the name of the Lord the Savior. From this the monastery, dedicated in honor of the princes of the apostles, was also called Cernelium; it is known to have been adorned by a choir of monks. That fountain, consecrated in Augustine’s name and believed by the faithful to be most health-giving, is shown here by one miracle recently made known, with the province as witness [Col. 0761A].

### 66

A parish priest under the abbot of Cernel is well known; he was accustomed to celebrate the sacred mysteries for the people. Worn down by illness, he was already carefully observed as one who was about to die. Night and sickness brought sleep to the exhausted man. He saw the most merciful Augustine standing beside him, wearing episcopal fillets and holding a radiant, festive staff. Caressing the trembling man with gentle speech, Augustine ordered the sick man to rise, go to Augustine’s fountain, and there, with faithful lips, recite the fiftieth psalm three times in succession; while chanting, he was to immerse his body three times, and in this way he would be restored to life and health.

“And lest you doubt,” he said, “know that Augustine himself is saying these things to you—the Augustine to whose fountain you are being directed” [Col. 0761B].

Wonderful to relate! Immediately awakening half-dead, he rose as though he were well; leaning on a staff, he made his way to the appointed bath. The custodians thought that, because death was imminent, he had become delirious. They followed his footsteps, not to resist him but rather to discover where and for what purpose he was going. The sick man was immersed three times in the fountain’s bath and three times chanted the psalm that had been prescribed. And—O swift physician!—the sick man, as though raised from death, returned home in good health.

What Elisha required of the leper through a sevenfold washing, by the sacrament of the sevenfold Spirit of the Lord, Augustine accomplished more briefly in the sick man—namely, through the threefold testimony of the life-giving Trinity. Who could now adequately describe the great and joyful amazement of everyone when, in the morning, the abbot and brothers, together with a large crowd, heard that the very priest whose death they had all been expecting was singing the Mass and the appointed Hours before the assembled multitude [Col. 0761C]? By publicly explaining in due order that Augustine had been the author of his recovery in Christ, he aroused everyone to an even greater praise of God and veneration of his saint.

After traversing a large part of Britain with frequent miracles, Augustine returned to his perpetual dwelling at Dorobernia. The household people came out from everywhere to meet him, as though he were the angel of their peace and as though the sun had been brought back to its rising place; all welcomed him with triumphant rejoicing [Col. 0761D].

Then, as a crowd of the infirm gathered before so great a marvel of healing, a young man appeared, thrice deserving of pity and bound by a threefold chain of calamity. With his feet bent inward, he walked on his knees instead of his feet; with his mouth obstructed and his ears closed, he could neither speak nor hear those who spoke. He was deaf and mute. He gave a groan in place of prayers. He pleaded by signs; he was questioned by signs; by signs a response was given to him when he asked. Augustine heard one who did not speak, addressed one who did not hear, and directed one who did not walk. Thus, I say, in the name of the Triune Deity, he granted threefold healing to one who was threefold miserable.

Restoring his steps, he raised the lame man; he made the mute man speak and poured hearing into the deaf man. From threefold distress there arose threefold joy in the man who had been healed. He ran without stumbling, spoke clearly, and heard distinctly. But the man’s vain mind, forgetful of his former misery and impatient of the health restored to him, so lapsed into every kind of frivolity that by his chatter and restlessness he disturbed the church and the people even during the sacred offices [Col. 0762A]. Everyone complained that the health granted to him had become more harmful to him than his former punishment. Therefore, when the Lord’s correcting mercy was angered through Augustine, his dancing feet, insolent tongue, and ears friendly to buffoonery were bound more tightly than before by their former fetters, until, once the Lord had been appeased by satisfaction, they were loosened through Augustine. Thus he was again restored to threefold bodily health and was also granted the greater security of a sound mind.

We read that the life and passion of the precious bishop and martyr Livinus were most faithfully set forth by his holy companions Folianus, Elias, and Kylianus, his own writer. From that account we insert here a few matters pertaining to the glory of blessed Augustine [Col. 0762B].
