It is related there that Augustine, beneficial to all [*profecturum*, perhaps “who was to benefit all”], came to Colomannus, the devout king of Scotland; that he baptized the boy Livinus there together with Saint Menalchius, archbishop; that the king and queen acted as sponsors during the baptism; that a golden right hand flashed with a radiance poured down upon it; and that, after Livinus had been baptized with the divine cross, he marked him three times with it while saying:

“Beloved by God and by human beings, whose memory is in blessing” (Ecclesiasticus 45:1).

When the boy grew older and eagerly desired to break the bonds of worldly glory, an angel of the Lord openly greeted him by name, saying, “Hail, brother Livinus,” and urged him to go and receive every instruction in holiness from Augustine, bishop of England and presiding at Dorobernia. As Livinus hurried toward the sea, the angel received him and, with serene beauty and honeyed exhortation, led him with the three companions already named, going before them across long stretches of sea [Col. 0762C]. They traveled with such delight that they thought they were treading not straits but solid and flower-filled meadows. They rejoiced as though they were walking upon the most splendid mountain of the Lord’s Transfiguration, where Peter wished to remain with the disciples (Matthew 17:4). By this flowery and pleasant sweetness they were taught to desire that teacher, from whose heart and mouth they would draw the nectar of paternal love and the honey of eternal sweetness; from whose garden, flowing with spikenard, they would pluck the spices of life; and under whose guidance they would run through all the flower gardens of heavenly philosophy and the richest fields of contemplative doctrine.

When the saints had reached the shores of Kent, the angelic guide, together with the splendid light, returned to heaven, leaving the companions to continue [Col. 0762D]. Thus blessed Livinus reached the Augustine he most desired. Under his instruction he advanced for five years, so that this great father’s little son, although still young in age but old in spirit, received priestly vestments from him and assumed the priesthood. Thus, from being a disciple, he became the teacher of his people, attaining the highest pontificate and the prize of martyrdom.

There follows the testimony of a certain very old man who, still surviving to this day, asserts that his grandfather saw blessed Augustine and that this same grandfather rose from Augustine’s baptistery as a modest Christian, delivered from the slippery and most mist-filled condition of paganism. He further asserts that the saint performed innumerable miracles while surrounded by a continuous crowd [Col. 0763A] [Note: [Col. 0763] [[Col. 0764] This note appears at the foot of column 763, but the callout number (91) has not been printed in the text.].

From these facts it may be inferred that the author lived about the year 1000.

The same contemporary survivor reported that his grandfather and father had handed down a description of the saint’s appearance: he had the bearing of a patrician and a tall stature, and, as he traversed his homeland barefoot, he developed calluses on the soles of his feet. He affirmed that this same grandfather, through the blessing of Augustine the baptizer, lived for well over a hundred years [Note: [Col. 0763] [[Col. 0763] This note is absent from Migne’s printed edition.]], and that this blessing of longevity descended upon his father, while he himself far surpassed the hundred-year lifespans of his ancestors.

Now wholly wounded by eternal loves, Augustine, already absorbed from earthly tumult into the Lord’s rest, pressed violently upon heaven by frequent blows of prayers, sighs, and tears. At last, understanding from the response of the Holy Spirit that his desire had been heard, he solemnly appointed as his successor the most sacred Laurence, distinguished by apostolic virtues and foremost among his holy companions, with the king and the assembled people rejoicing immensely [Col. 0763B]. He did this, as once the prince of the apostles Peter appointed Clement, because of the need for the instruction of the newly converted. Earlier he had consecrated Mellitus bishop of London and Justus bishop of Rochester [*Rofi al.*, *Roffae*] as his suffragan; Mellitus, the third, and Justus, the fourth, succeeded him in the archiepiscopate.

After exhorting the king, the Church, and the people to persevere in faith and in the love of Christ, and leaving everyone pledges of perpetual affection, in the presence of the king himself and of Bishop Laurence, amid the tears of all, while a most joyful heavenly choir surrounded him, he passed to the eternal solemnities of Christ [Col. 0764A]. Let us, his lowly praisers, follow him not with equal laments but with these triumphant songs:

“You reign, Augustine, greater than Augustus in the name and dignity of the age; you increased the commonwealth of Christ and added Britain to the Roman Church, more effectively than Caesar Augustus added Alexandria to Roman power. Kings, princes, and the senate of the English, together with a multitude of peoples, accompany you into heaven. Angels and archangels, thrones and dominions, receive you; the King of kings crowns you.”

In the monastery he founded, dedicated by Saint Laurence, by King Ethelbert himself, and by the people of the land who gathered there, his most precious body was buried with festive rejoicing [Col. 0764B]. There the Romans and his other successors are gathered together, united in one spirit as in one chamber.

How beautifully, then, Rome, the mother of the Churches, produced such pledges, destined to stand forth as the fathers and founders of the whole British Ocean! With what fragrance of sweetness and splendor of glory one love and one chamber simultaneously cherish and bind them together! If they were distributed among the various nations of the world, each patron would shine like the sun before his own people.

[Col. 0763] **Here ends the Life of Saint Augustine, apostle of the English.**

[Col. 0763]

# VARIOUS READINGS AND ADDITIONS TO THE CHRONICLE OF BEC

(Edited by Martène, *Amplissima Collectio*, vol. VI, col. 105, from manuscript no. 1303 of the library of the Most Serene Queen of Sweden.)

[Col. 0763C] Col. 653, last line: “To whom his son Roger succeeded.” Manuscript: “to whom his brother Roger succeeded.” “Robert of Touques, cloistral prior.” Manuscript: “Robert of Torigni, cloistral prior of the monastery of Bec.” In the same month Duke Henry, returning from Aquitaine, at Rouen on the feast-day of St John the Baptist, graciously gave his assent to the aforesaid election, which Hugh, archbishop of Rouen, a man of the highest piety and energy, together with the empress, the duke’s mother, had previously most willingly confirmed while present. In the following month, on the feast of Mary Magdalene, the aforesaid elect was blessed as abbot at St Philibert of Montfort by Hebert, bishop of Avranches, and Gerard, bishop of Séez, in the presence of the abbots Roger of Bec, Michael of Préaux, and Hugh of St Sauveur of Coutances.

Col. 654, line 15: “Looking upon the august tomb hewn from the rock.” Manuscript: “you behold the narrow grave hewn from the rock.”

Col. 655, line 32: “Matilda,” etc. Manuscript: “Massuldis,” etc. “Her body was brought to Bec and honourably buried before the altar of the Blessed Mary, Mother of God, in that same church. In the year 1178 this precious martyr was canonized.” Manuscript: “in the year 1173,” etc. [Col. 0764C]

Col. 657, line 23: “And by Rotrou of Rouen.” Manuscript: “by Rotrou of Rouen.” Line 24: “And Henry of Saint-Brieuc.” Manuscript: “Henry of Bayeux.” The manuscript adds: “In the year 1179 Louis, king of the French, entered England in order to fulfil vows to St Thomas and to pray, and remained at Canterbury for three days.”

Col. 658, last line: “Lord Richard of Saint-Léger, then infirmarer of the aforesaid place.” Manuscript: “Lord Richard of Saint-Léger, then justiciar of the aforesaid place.”

Col. 659, line 27: “After Ingelram had been removed, the holy market,” etc. Manuscript: “after Ingelram had been removed, the market having been held” [Col. 0764D].

Col. 662, last line: “It was in the time of Abbot Peter, because in stone,” etc. Manuscript: “It was in the time of Abbot Peter, to whom many stones fell, because in stone,” etc.

[Col. 0765A] Col. 668, line 44: “He had the new church, newly completed, dedicated, as will later appear.” Manuscript: “newly completed and finished; this dedication was carried out with the greatest celebrity and solemnity, as will appear in what follows.”

Col. 671, line 43: “William of Bensseville, called Popeline,” etc. Manuscript: “G. of Beuseville, called Popeline, [was chosen] abbot and pastor of that monastery and afterwards blessed; he was indeed a man of great prudence and probity, modest, cheerful, gentle, and beloved by all, patient, merciful, generous, and munificent, who governed vigorously and praiseworthily,” etc.

[Col. 0765B] Col. 672, line 19: “Christ, grant [him drink].” The manuscript adds: “This venerable man during his time clothed and received into the aforesaid monastery very many religious and discerning monks, among whom afterwards flourished Geoffrey, called Harenc, abbot of Jumièges; Vincent of Rouen, called *le Lieur*, abbot of Préaux; Robert of Rouen, otherwise called *le Tellier*, abbot of St Evroul; and John of Boulay, abbot of Cerisy. In the year of the Lord 1388, after his death,” etc.

Col. 678, line 18: “The reverend Father William, abbot,” etc., down to the words “where the blessing is customarily received,” as in the manuscript. The manuscript then continues: “This venerable man governed the aforesaid monastery, beloved by all his own, for eighteen and a half years or thereabouts; may God be gracious to his soul. Amen.”

Col. 683, line 30: “He brought their necks beneath Christ.” Manuscript: “their necks beneath Christ,” etc. Line 35: “In the thousandth year, the hundredth, and likewise the fourth.” The manuscript adds: “The fifth of July, the fourteenth and also the sixth; may God spare him. Amen” [Col. 0765C].

Thereupon the manuscript continues:

“When the venerable Thomas, twenty-eighth abbot of the monastery of Blessed Mary of Bec of Herluin, had been released from the prison of the flesh, the honourable John of Rouen, otherwise called de Motha, a priest and monk expressly professed in the said monastery, succeeded him, elected by the unanimous consent of the brethren. This venerable man, the tenth child of the noble Simon de Motha, citizen of Rouen, after passing through the stages of childhood and diligently receiving the rudiments of grammar, was entrusted by his parents at Paris to discerning masters in the distinguished Faculty of Arts for instruction. But since God had foreseen that he would be a burning lamp in His house, He did not wish the light of so great a splendour to remain longer hidden beneath the cloud of worldly darkness; rather, He wished to set it upon the candlestick of the contemplative life, that it might thereafter shine upon all who are in God’s house.

[Col. 0765D] “Therefore, complying with the wishes of his parents, this worthy son entered the said monastery, offered in order to test the monastic life, and was kindly received by the abbot and convent of that place for his probation. He became a new recruit of Christ, though formerly a philosopher. At once he took up the mighty arms of obedience and diligently experienced, tested, and approved the sweetness of the Lord and the lightness of His burden; he tested and approved the monastic life. His praiseworthy manner of life was tested, not rejected; for by the merit of his life, this young man of good disposition showed himself worthy of imitation by all.

[Col. 0766A] “When the year and day of probation had elapsed and the probation had thus been made on both sides, he made his formal profession according to custom. When it had been made and received by the said abbot, he was admitted among the convent of brethren with the kiss, and thereafter began to advance from virtue to virtue, to incline each of his brethren to good by his example, and, as a true cloistered monk, to devote himself to every humility. For that humble monk knew that no one can ascend to the summit of exaltation except by the steps of humility. When he was of suitable age, he was promoted to sacred orders and at last deserved to ascend to the rank of priesthood. Shortly afterwards he was entrusted with the administration of the priory of Beaulieu of Rouen, then that of St Peter of Cochiacus in the diocese of Amiens, afterwards that of Blessed Mary of Laye in the diocese of Beauvais, and then that of St Peter of Pontoise in the diocese of Rouen.

[Col. 0766B] “He studied at Paris until he attained the degree of bachelor in decrees, and proceeded toward the degree at Paris by lecturing for several years in the said faculty of decrees, according to the practice hitherto observed in studies of decrees. But afterwards, recalled to the cloister, what kind and how great a man he was is made clear by the outcome of events. He was elected cloistral prior of that monastery; subsequently he was sent to Paris to pursue a case brought by a certain cardinal concerning the priory of Beaumont in the diocese of Évreux. Meanwhile, namely in the year of the Lord 1434, he attained the degree of licentiate in the said faculty of decrees. Afterwards he was entrusted with the government and administration of the priory of Conflans in the diocese of Paris, was made doctor, and was an active regent at Paris in the said faculty of decrees. There he presided for a long time and, as doctor, obtained through the University of Paris from the lord abbot and convent of Marmoutier near Tours, of the Order of St Benedict, the priory of Oye, in French *en Terasse*, in the diocese of Thérouanne, together with a commendam.

[Col. 0766C] “In the year of the Lord 1446, when the said monastery of Blessed Mary of Bec of Herluin was vacant through the death of the aforesaid Thomas, the twenty-eighth abbot, and when a truce had been made and proclaimed between the kings of France and England, the Pragmatic Sanction having no force in Normandy, the religious of that monastery decreed that an election of a pastor should be celebrated in the chapter of that place. Assembled there on an appointed day, after the ceremonies necessary for this purpose had duly been observed, they unanimously elected the said John of Rouen by way of the Holy Spirit. At great expense they obtained confirmation of his election from the Apostolic See, and the conferral upon him by Lord Ralph, archbishop of Rouen, in the chapel of his palace at Rouen, of the rite of blessing with the fitting solemnity.

[Col. 0766D] “Once these matters had been canonically performed, the same lord abbot, notwithstanding the time of war and the desolation of the country, governed the said monastery praiseworthily, maintaining strictness in spiritual matters. For, imposing the discipline of communal life upon the harsh and perverse, he was gentle as a lamb toward the meek and devout. He showed little concern for his own person; for he showed himself kindly and approachable to all, like a lamb, was with the brethren as one of them, and displayed in himself the model of a flock rather than of a shepherd. Nevertheless, as far as he could, he retained the gravity of his prelacy.

[Col. 0767A] “In all his actions, although sufficiently expeditious, he was nevertheless well advised. Moreover, after entering upon pastoral care, he always bore sadness on his face. Indeed, I have heard from trustworthy persons that after entering the prelacy he was never cheerful as he had formerly been. Perhaps, with Blessed Gregory, he reflected what he had lost; he also reflected what he endured, saw that he had to serve the dispositions of many, reform the manners of each for the better, and finally render an account of each to the most just Judge. He also made much progress in keeping the temporal possessions of the monastery in good condition, both within and without, repairing what was desolate, and paying the very great debts of his predecessor, incurred because of the war that had prevailed in his time. When the king of France was to recover the duchy of Normandy, he was appointed envoy to that king with several other men and noblemen of rank, and the city of Rouen. Afterwards he appeared with other prelates, by the king’s command, at the convention of Bourges for the dispatch of the said Pragmatic Sanction; there he contracted the beginnings of his illness. Finally, he was summoned to the Exchequer of Normandy at the town of the see of Rouen.

[Col. 0767C] “In the year of the Lord 1452, on the seventeenth day of November, after receiving the sacraments, he departed this light and was buried in the middle of the choir, at the head of William, twenty-sixth abbot of that monastery. May Jesus Christ, Son of the Virgin Mary, be gracious to his soul. Amen.

“His epitaph follows:

> Renowned Rouen rejoices to have begotten John,  
> And Bec grieves to lack so great a father.  
> For a time he held the Parisian chair of law;  
> He guided the brethren toward better conduct.  
> Whom Rouen commends by birth, sacred law,  
> And prelacy, lies beneath the ashes.  
> The year one thousand four hundred and fifty-two,  
> And the seventeenth day of the eleventh month mark his funeral.”

[Col. 0767D] “When the venerable Father and Lord in Christ, JOHN, twenty-ninth abbot of the monastery of Bec, had been called by God, the reverend Father and Lord in Christ Geoffrey of Spain, surnamed Benedict, then prior of Le Pré, succeeded him in the government of the aforesaid monastery. On Ember Wednesday in December of the year of the Lord 1452, after all and each whose interest it was had been summoned and the customary solemnities duly performed, he was elected abbot by way of the Holy Spirit, no one opposing or contradicting the election. He was afterwards confirmed and blessed by the vicars of the archbishop of Rouen during the vacancy of the see, according to the Pragmatic Sanction, and finally swore fealty to the royal majesty. He immediately endeavoured in his charge to follow the Apostle’s teaching: ‘Feed the flock of God which is among you, overseeing it not under compulsion but willingly according to God; not for shameful gain, but voluntarily; nor as lording it over the clergy, but by becoming from the heart an example to the flock.’

[Col. 0768A] “Although he was shepherd and prelate of the flock committed to his direction, he was common to all. Thus, without prejudice to justice and pastoral gravity, he accommodated himself to the ears of each. In the ceremonies of choir, cloister, chapter, and refectory he conducted himself so religiously and reverently that he drew all his people to devotion. As ardently as he loved God’s house, so greatly did he adorn it. Hence he could deservedly say: ‘Lord, I have loved the beauty of Thy house, and the place where Thy glory dwells.’ He paved and had whitened the whole nave and the left side of the choir from the Chapel of the Virgins to the cross, because they had been blackened by the smoke issuing from a fire made there by the people. In it he caused two altars to be erected, which were not dedicated in his lifetime; above them he placed images of Saints Clarus and Apollonia. He again caused crosses to be painted inside and outside as a sign of dedication, and enclosed the vestry.

[Col. 0768B] “In the choir he placed images of the four Doctors of the Church—Gregory, Ambrose, Augustine, and Jerome—and beside the altar on the left he placed a lectern bearing four images of angels and as many prophets, among whom are four figures of the Evangelists, upon which the Gospels, one of each, are read, with four great candlesticks. Before the footpace he set an image of Moses, upon which the Epistles and lessons of the Old Testament are read; and in the middle of the choir an eagle, upon which the choirmaster places the gradual. All these things were made of copper at Paris. He also had a silver cross made from the chalices of deceased religious, of a weight of about thirty marks, adorned with relics and gems; in it are four thorns of the crown of our Lord Jesus Christ the Saviour, a portion of the True Cross, and other relics of saints.

[Col. 0768C] “At that time he had the head of St Blaise placed in a reliquary [lacuna]. He had all these relics, brought from England during his time by our fellow-monks expelled from there, authenticated. He also had made two silver ewers for carrying holy water and as many sprinklers, weighing [lacuna] marks or thereabouts. He caused two sets of silk vestments to be made, furnished with chasubles, tunics, dalmatics, white copes, amices, and prepared altar-cloths: one red, the other white. He also completed the chapel of the Caroli, which had previously been begun by his predecessors.

“Lest he and his convent be accused of ingratitude and the memory of the church’s benefactors fade, he had restored in gilded silver, weighing twelve marks and filled with raised figures, a cup encased all around with silver. The lady Matilda, Empress of famous memory, had formerly given it to the monastery; it had been worn away with time, then wholly remade in silver by the late Robert of Spain, while he was living and at his death prior of the priory of Blessed Mary of Le Pré near Rouen, uncle of that deceased abbot; and it had afterwards been put up for sale because of the church’s needs.

[Col. 0769A] “It was ordained that on every day on which either the whole choir or four [*f.*, *chorus*] sang the *Venite*, and on the anniversaries of Lord Herluin, the empress herself, and that deceased man himself, wine should be served from this cup in turn to every monk of the convent. Having tasted it, each should say: ‘May they rest in peace. Amen.’ To procure the said wine he assigned four acres of land acquired in the parish of Neuville. He built stone gutters around the Chapel of Blessed Mary, rebuilt all its timberwork, and covered it with lead as it had formerly been. He built a handsome and spacious infirmary, adorned with a chapel and several cells very suitable for bodily health.

[Col. 0769B] “Because the conduits of the springs often ceased to run owing to thick tree-roots nourished inside by the moisture of the water and obstructing the channels, he had broad underground passages, a man’s height deep and roofed with vaulting, constructed to inspect them and remove obstructions: from the field of Boulay to the mill of Feugeret, from the port of Vigne to the Prior’s ford, and from that ford to the small tower near the abbot’s cell. He also built the small tower and, in the street through whose middle the waters flow, continued the works as far as the stone vat of the cellar; and he rebuilt Martel’s hall in timber and roofing upon the old walls. He built the gate of Le Pré and endeavoured to repair most of the park walls. He newly constructed the manor and barn of Marbeuf and many other things. He rebuilt from the ground up the mills of Les Méjans. In his time the share which the lord of Mesnil had in those mills was acquired for the benefit of the convent of brethren, to increase the revenues for pittances.

[Col. 0769C] “He therefore ordained that the brethren of the convent should receive twenty shillings in pittances every year at Easter, which had been withheld from them because of the wars and the fortress in Abbot Robert’s time [Col. 0770A]. He began and built the tower for suspending the church bells to a height of 160 steps and to the beginning of the windows, but, forestalled by death, could not finish it. He vigorously defended our privileges concerning the assignment of religious to vacant priories of the monastery against those obtaining apostolic provisions and all others. Moreover, mindful of his salvation, he founded an anniversary for himself, his parents and friends, and the benefactors of the monastery. For its celebration he assigned ten livres tournois, to be distributed yearly in the manner and form contained in letters kept in the monastery treasury.

[Col. 0770B] “Finally, during an illness which he endured while praising God for almost seven years, he had many formidable opponents of his vocation—men aspiring to the abbatial dignity, procuring commendatory letters from princes and magnates of the realm, and sending great envoys, noble prudent men, and the greatest rhetoricians to persuade him to resign the dignity, offering to give him a large pension. But he always remained steadfast and cautious in his answers, for neither threats, blandishments, nor any promises could shake or turn him. He governed the said monastery continuously from the day of his election until 14 May 1476; on that day, fortified by the sacraments of the Church, he laid aside the burden of flesh. May his soul rest in peace. Amen. He was buried in the choir of that monastery beneath the tomb which, while alive, he had caused to be made together with that of his predecessor.

[Col. 0770C] “His epitaph follows:

> Geoffrey the Spaniard, bearing the surname Benedict,  
> Elected abbot of Bec by brethren of one voice,  
> Endeavoured in his time to preserve the right rule  
> Of conduct and of blessed life.  
> He completed his course; the use of life is shut from him;  
> His spirit seeks the heights; the earth holds his body.

[Col. 0769]

# CATALOGUE OF THE BOOKS OF THE ABBEY OF BEC ABOUT THE TWELFTH CENTURY

(D. Ravaisson, *Report to the Minister of Public Instruction on the Libraries of the Departments of the West*, Paris, 1841, octavo, p. 376, from a manuscript codex in the library of Avranches.)

## NOTICE

The catalogue of the books of the abbey of Bec in the twelfth century will add to the knowledge we possess concerning the extent of literary learning in that period. The abbey of Bec, where Lanfranc and Saint Anselm taught, was one of the most famous and learned schools of the time. It will be seen that, together with part of Cicero’s works, it possessed the *Hortensius*, which we no longer have; Trogus Pompeius, if indeed this designation does not refer to Justin’s abridgment; a treatise *De causis* under Quintilian’s name, probably *De causis corruptae eloquentiae*; all the works of Aristotle for which we have Boethius’s translation, and none of the others; the translation of Nemesius’s *Anthropology*, which is found again in one of the manuscripts of the library of Avranches; Plato’s *Timaeus*; Hermes Trismegistus; Caesar; Ovid; Velleius; Suetonius; Claudian; and others.

In the lists of the works of the Fathers, especially of Saint Augustine, several titles will be noted whose very names had not previously come down to us. In addition, there was Rabanus Maurus’s treatise *De naturis rerum*, still unpublished, although it exists in manuscript in certain libraries, and so forth.

# In the Year of the Lord 1089: Bonizo, First Bishop of Sutri, Later of Piacenza

[Col. 0781]

# Prolegomena: The Life, Deeds, and Writings of Bonizo

*(Oefele, Monumenta Boica, II, 780, Augsburg, 1763, fol.)*

[Col. 0781D] Many authors have collected much concerning the life, deeds, and writings of Bonizo, first bishop of Sutri and later of Piacenza. [Note: [Col. 0781D] The authors vary astonishingly in his name. One might think that sparks flash in darkness: Martin of Troppau calls him Bonisius; the anonymous writer of Melk, Ponizus; Ptolemy of Lucca, Bonzo; Berthold of Constance, Bonizo; and others Bonitho, Bonizus, Benizus, Bobinus, and so forth. Lambecius, no poor judge of etymologies, acknowledges from Berthold of Constance that Bonizo was his true and genuine name and says that it is a diminutive of the proper name Bonus, just as Domnizo comes from Domnus, Gunzo from Guntherus, Erizo from Ericus, and others of that kind.] Foremost among all is Berthold of Constance, who, almost alone among the historians—and himself a German—mentioned in his *Chronicle* a man who was highly celebrated in his own age for the events in which he was involved, for his published writings, for his adversities, and even for his bloody death. But when what had seemed to be the lost monuments of his intellect gradually began, through the investigations of learned men, to emerge from the book-chests of libraries, interest in investigating the author himself more carefully was aroused at the same time.

Among the first, the diligence of Ferdinando Ughelli, the outstanding compiler of the ecclesiastical antiquities of Italy, shone forth. Ughelli was followed by the bibliographer Peter Lambecius, of tireless and extensive learning. When Lambecius wrote about Bonizo on the occasion of discovering a codex in Ambras Castle, he proceeded into that province—as Cicero puts it—“so abundantly that he left absolutely nothing at home.”

[Col. 0783B] Bonizo therefore lived a troubled life during that great schism which, between Pope Gregory VII and the Emperor Henry IV, threw the rights of the keys and the sword into dreadful confusion. In Lambecius’s praise, at any rate, he stood out as a man of outstanding piety, learning, and constancy. Having embraced the clerical life, and striving to defend the obligations of celibate life not only in his writings but also with his blood, he first fell away from evangelical gentleness; and with the sword which, like a trumpet, he attempted through his writings and declamations to persuade people to draw against his adversaries in those wretched and mutually shameful times, he finally perished miserably and barbarously.

While still a private man, and before he was advanced to the higher dignities of the Church, he set down in a volume—still extant—the Augustinian epitome [Col. 0783C] (of which more fully below), addressed to John Gualbert, abbot of Vallombrosa in Etruria, an eminent teacher of Christian charity and gentleness—if only he had also been his own! [Note: [Col. 0783D] Baronius and Surius, as Lambeccius observes, incorrectly call him Gualbertus; through their authority this error has today become prevalent, attributing Gualbertus, the father’s name, to John the son.] “He composed this Augustinian epitome” (we give Lambeccius’s words) “before the beginning of Gregory VII’s pontificate, that is, before the year of Christ 1073, as is clear from the dedicatory letter addressed to John the abbot [Note: [Col. 0784D] *Commentary on the Augustan Caesarean Library of Vienna*, book II, chapter 8, p. 787. In the recension of the manuscript codex brought from Ambras Castle to the Caesarean Library, Cod. LXXXV].” The acts of John’s death assign it to 12 July of that same year; these acts were first interpolated by Surius (volume IV), but after Lambeccius’s death were published genuinely and without corruption.

Lambeccius therefore thought that this Augustinian epitome had been written chiefly at the urging of this John, abbot of Vallombrosa, because the dedicatory letter expressly says that “this work had been labored over for him”; that is, as Lambeccius interprets it, “that it had been collected and prepared from all the writings of Saint Augustine, according to his wishes and for his use, not without labor.”

Bonizo was, as I should mention once and for all, a man not superficially learned for his age, and in his life—so far as purity of morals and discipline are concerned—blameless and upright; but he was hot-tempered and wrathful, embittered by adversities, and, under the pretext of asserting the truth, fierce even to the shedding of Christian blood. This lack of self-control brought upon him not only adversities, enmities, and countless calamities, but finally death itself, and a most cruel death at that. The strongest evidence of this is the work itself, which we are here publishing for the first time from ancient parchment manuscripts: *On the Persecution of the Church, to a Friend*. In it the author directs all the force of his learning and eloquence toward persuading members of his own faction, by adapting to his cause the opinions of Sacred Scripture, the Fathers, the canons, and historians, that a Christian might freely assert the truth of religion by arms and the sword. [Col. 0784B] How truthfully and pertinently he accomplished this, let him judge for himself, and let others decide. We have no other purpose here than to shed further light upon the darkness of that calamitous schism, with this new torch—although it too is pitch-black and smoky, snatched from the funeral pyre of Christian piety, which was almost wholly consumed in those days.

Since Bonizo was thus turbulent and bitter in temperament, while still a private man he had already stirred up the hatred of many against himself. Against these he implores the prayers of Abbot John, asking him to protect him with the shield of his prayer from the barking of his rivals, whose teeth—by which he was to be torn apart—he ought rather to have guarded against by a gentle and prudent policy. By the name “rivals,” according to Lambeccius’s interpretation, priests who were certainly Simoniacs [Col. 0784C] and schismatics are meant; with them, as with Saint John the abbot himself, so also with his friends and disciples, and especially with Bonizo, there had been a continuous and most serious conflict.

Moreover, that distinguished man correctly concludes that, since this preface contains nothing indicating Bonizo to have been either a bishop or an exile, he composed the work before he had been elected bishop of Sutri.

Whether Bonizo was at that time in charge of the abbey of Saint Peter of Campo at Perugia, and whether the matters reported by the illustrious Muratori from an agreement made in 1072 between an abbot of this name and Mauro concerning some estate, in the presence of Duchess Beatrice and Matilda [Note: [Col. 0784D] *Antiquities of Medieval Italy*, vol. II, fol. 955, dissertation 131], relate to him, we leave for discussion to those who work closer to the places in question and to their monuments.

The monuments of that Church, as yet excavated with little success, do not adequately establish when Bonizo attained the bishopric of Sutri. Ughellus [Note: [Col. 0784D] *Sacred Italy*, vol. I, second edition] reports that he flourished in that see in 1078; Colettus, however, in his additions to the same work, moves the date earlier and prefers the year 1075. Ughellus’s words are these (that is, no. XVI): “Bonizo, a man by far the most learned, flourished in the year 1078.”

Ughellus likewise records, in his account of the bishops of Cremona, that on 13 May of that same year the church of Saint Thomas at Cremona was consecrated by Bonizo, bishop of Sutri and papal legate (vol. IV, fol. 596).

But Bonizo could not hold that see peacefully, because of the savage hostilities between Gregory VII, whose party he clung to tenaciously, and the Emperor Henry IV—hostilities that were no longer merely smoldering but were breaking out into open conflagration throughout Italy and Germany. For after the emperor had once again marched against Rome with an army in the early spring of 1082, and could not seize it because Gregory defended both the city and himself with every force and stratagem, he ravaged the surrounding territory, [Col. 0785B] driving away or capturing all who were more devoted to Gregory’s party [Note: [Col. 0785D] *Chronicle of Farfa*, in Muratori, vol. II, part II of *Italian Historical Matters*]. Bonizo, certainly, because his burning hatred made him less inclined to timid counsels, remained at Sutri and was taken captive by Henry, who had moved his army from the monastery of Farfa; this expedition is described more fully for that year by the distinguished star of Italian history, who shines still more brightly after his setting, Ludovico Antonio Muratori [Note: [Col. 0785D] *Annals of Italy*, vol. VII, p. 274; and the German translation, p. 441].

How long the captive bishop remained in Henry’s custody has not, so far as I know, been recorded by anyone. Nor is it believable that Bonizo was free to attend the council convened on 20 November 1083 to settle the disputes between the priesthood and the empire; Henry had excluded from it almost all the bishops who were more vigorously supporting Gregory’s party, among them Hugh of Lyons, Anselm of Lucca, and Rainald of Como. Nor does the proximity of the monastery of Farfa, where the emperor was generally accustomed to take refuge, allow us to believe that Bonizo, whether released or escaped, was able to return safely to his flock. Added to this is the fact that, after Henry had been driven from the city by Robert in 1084, he remained at Sutri, as is established by a charter delivered to the Church of Pisa on 23 May, which Ughellus reports [Note: [Col. 0786D] Vol. III, in the archbishops of Pisa, no. 39, col. 420]. An accurate author of notes in the German translation of the same work by Muratori observes, correctly from the remaining chronological indications of documents from the same period, that the year 1095 had slipped in for 1084 without Ughellus and Colettus noticing it [Note: [Col. 0786D] p. 452, vol. VI, note d].

It is not unlike the truth that our Bonizo returned to his former see after Henry had been driven back beyond the Alps, although the precise year of his return is not established, since affairs at Sutri are still obscured by a dense fog. He appears to have occupied his see again at the time of Anselm of Lucca’s death, which occurred on 18 May 1086, as is clear from a passage by Hubaldus, who is commonly said to have committed the Life of Saint Anselm of Lucca to writing. We too shall reproduce that passage from the same collection or compendium of ancient monuments composed long ago for Gregory VII and certain other Roman pontiffs against the schismatics—among whom our Paul of Bernried holds no insignificant place—from which both Ughellus and Oudinus quoted it, following Sebastian Tengnagel’s collection. From it it is clear that Bonizo again presided over the Church of Sutri in 1086, since he attended the funeral of blessed Anselm of Lucca, who, as we have said, was taken from human affairs in that same year:

“Saint Anselm, while he lived, requested that he be commended for burial in the chapter of the monastery of Saint Benedict, which stands on the bank of the river Eridanus under the obedience of the sacred monastery of Cluny, from which he himself had been a brother and monk. And when, with the bishop, Countess Matilda, and all the others consenting, his body was already being carried to the monastery, suddenly the bishop of Sutri named Bonizo arrived, whom the Holy Spirit had also stirred up to proclaim that it was fitting for a bishop to be buried in the episcopal church. ‘Such a lamp,’ he said, ‘ought not to be hidden; he humbled himself while still alive as though unworthy, but we ought to exalt as truly worthy the man whom we know to have been most holy.’ Immediately all applauded the same view, and the body was snatched from the monks’ attendants, carried to the episcopal church, and buried there with reverence.”

Thus writes the biographer of Anselm of Lucca, whom Ughellus declares to have been Hubaldus, bishop of Mantua. Baronius too, the father of ecclesiastical annals, did indeed report the same passage [Note: [Col. 0786D] Vol. XI of the *Annals*, under the year 1086, p. 58], but corrupted it in two places [Col. 0786C]; others had already observed this before Oudinus: for, in place of Bonizo, he named Domnizo and, instead of calling him bishop of Sutri, called him bishop of Sabina, undoubtedly misled by the better-known name of Domnizo, who wrote for Matilda herself a metrical work on the deeds of Matilda, edited by Leibniz. Since both men had enjoyed favor at the court of that celebrated woman, it was easy for matters belonging to one or the other to be combined into one.

Concerning this fictitious bishop of Sabina, whom Ughellus and Ciaconius, relying on Baronius’s authority, inserted into their catalogue of the cardinal bishops of Sabina under the year 1076, see Oudinus, who removes this error on the basis of the passage from Hubaldus just mentioned, and the Bollandists under 16 September, in the Life of Blessed Victor, [Col. 0786D] chapter 10. Their words deserve to be read here in full:

“According to Ciaconius, in the account of Gregory VII, there was a Domnizo, who, he says, was also called Regizo, and was bishop of Sabina, since he says that he attended the funeral of Saint Anselm of Lucca, who died in the following year, 1086. But Domnizo must not be confused with Regizo, nor, as I believe, was either of them bishop of Sabina, although in the latest edition of Ughellus both are found in the catalogue of the bishops of Sabina. Baronius provided the occasion for the error in his *Annals* under the year 1086, no. 10. For when the Life of Saint Anselm [Col. 0787A] reads ‘the bishop of Sutri, named Bonizo,’ Baronius’s version reads ‘the bishop of Sabina, Lord Domnizo.’ Hence Ciaconius and Ughellus alike fell into error.”

Ughellus assigns to the same year, 1086, that honorable mention of this bishop of Sutri which, he says, occurs in a privilege of Countess Matilda: “by whom,” in the words of our author [Note: [Col. 0787D] *Loc. cit.*, in the bishops of Sutri, addition XX, col. 1275], “he was held in great honor on account of his outstanding qualities of mind.”

Whether, therefore, Bonizo came of his own accord to the funeral of so great a man, or whether he had already remained with that beneficent patroness and nourisher of exiled bishops, Countess Matilda, having escaped or been released from Henry’s chains, we leave undecided until more certain evidence of the dispute comes to light. [Col. 0787B]

It is certainly easy to believe that during that intervening period, until he was transferred to the Church of Piacenza, he lived a wandering and exiled life and from time to time stayed with the generous Guelf hostess Matilda [Note: [Col. 0787D] In her, nothing displeased him except the name of her husband.] [Note: [Col. 0787D] Ughellus, in the passage cited shortly before: “He was driven from the see of Sutri for the defense of the Roman Church, and afterward, after VARIOUS AND HARSH EXILES, etc.”]. For Berthold of Constance, who, although a German, almost alone preserved the memory of this Italian bishop, expressly states, when he discusses Bonizo’s transfer to the Church of Piacenza, that he had long before been expelled from the see of Sutri for his loyalty to Saint Peter. He records this under the year 1089, which was the last year of Bonizo’s life and the most disastrous of all for him.

The words of Berthold, on which the authors of great renown build all their knowledge of Bonizo’s bloody death, read as follows:

“Bonizo, bishop of Sutri, long since expelled for his loyalty to Saint Peter, after many imprisonments—for he says ‘many,’ and therefore he was repeatedly put in chains—tribulations, and exiles, is finally received by the Catholics of Piacenza as bishop; but by the schismatics of the same place, after his eyes had been gouged out and almost all his limbs cut off, he is crowned with martyrdom.”

Ughellus, in his account of the bishops of Piacenza, expanded Berthold’s passage somewhat more fully, perhaps from other monuments, in the following manner:

“Saint Bonitius [Note: Concerning the title ‘saint,’ see below], whom Berthold in his *Chronicle* calls Bonizo. When he was vigorously defending ecclesiastical liberty against Henry and the false pontiff Cadalus, [Col. 0787D] he was driven from the see of Sutri, from which, he said, he first proclaimed divine law, at the command of the impious emperor. Then, after changing several grievous places of exile and reaching Piacenza, he was proclaimed bishop there by the Catholics of that city. While fighting against impiety and the factious schismatics, he was first worn down in prison; afterward, with his limbs cut off and his eyes gouged out, he was nobly crowned with martyrdom near Saint Domninus [Note: Having first been expelled from the city, he was finally killed nearby. The village of Saint Domninus, situated between Parma and Piacenza on the Via Aemilia, took its name from Saint Domninus, who, while Maximilian was raging, won the palm of martyrdom there, as Ughellus explains at greater length, *Sacred Italy*, vol. II, p. 62], in the sixth month after he had begun to administer the Church of Piacenza, in the year 1089, on 14 July. His sacred body was carried to Cremona and there placed in a tomb at Saint Lawrence, where the following verses are engraved:

GLORIOUS PIACENZA BORE FOR YOU A NOBLE DEPOSIT:

BISHOP BONIZO, A MARTYR FOR THE NAME OF CHRIST;

THE FOURTEENTH DAY OF JULY GATHERED HIM INTO THIS TOMB.”

Most people attribute the cause of the murder to the faction of Henry IV, which opposed Gregory VII; but the nearer causes of the hatred must be derived from those internecine movements in which priests on one side fought not merely with writings and words but with sword and fire, some for marriage and, under that pretext, often for concubinage, others for celibacy.

Bonizo himself calls this entire conflict among the clergy the *PATAREA* [Col. 0788B], and expressly asserts—although the meaning of this name later changed and it was transferred to the defeated party—that those who supported Gregory VII in favor of celibacy against married, concubinary, and Simoniacal clergy were called Paterines. Bonizo himself was among them; and since he had taken upon himself not so much the duties of a soldier as those of a commander, he ultimately brought ruin and the most cruel death upon himself amid the fury of that raging populace, after the Paterines had been driven from the city by the opposing faction.

The public order of the city could not but be thrown into confusion when so many women and children were violently deprived—these of the public honor of their birth, those of the recognized respectability of lawful marriage—with the utmost disgrace to their families. Once this conflagration had been kindled, those who were in truth concubinary and Simoniacal, and who recoiled equally from lawful marriage and from celibate life, under the pretext of public morality and of avenging the broken bonds of civil society, and whose number, given the corruption characteristic of that age, was by far the greatest, fanned the flame of sedition still more fiercely and relentlessly in order to protect their own dissolution. The result was that, when no place remained in so disturbed a commonwealth for any good man or any priest most devoted to Christian piety and peace, those who equally abhorred the impure and unrestrained conduct of one side and the savage, violently excessive conduct of the other, beyond all Christian gentleness, withdrew themselves from these waves into safer and more peaceful waters and preferred, under the rule of Saint Augustine, a common fellowship of life and discipline to these shameful and bloody disputes. [Col. 0788D]

In the course of time, once married priests had finally been suppressed, the factious name “Paterines” adhered to the defeated party, as though obscene and stained by much slaughter and blood; for, as commonly happens, the victors transferred to the vanquished whatever had been disgraceful in the victory. Pagius [Note: [Col. 0789D] *Critical Notes on Baronius*, vol. IV, under the year 1057, sections IX and following] clearly demonstrates and precisely examines this matter, both from the passage of Bonizo excerpted by Lambeccius and from the *Chronicle* of Hugh of Flavigny under the year 1084—the critical winnowing-fan of Baronius’s harvest. The passage of Galvaneus Flamma, who wrote a history of the Milanese from the founding of Rome to approximately the year 1336, should also be consulted on this matter in Muratori [Note: [Col. 0789D] Vol. XI of *Italian Historical Matters*, chapter 150, *The Handful of Flowers*], who published his *Handful of Flowers*—the title he gave the work—from a parchment manuscript in Milan and another in the Ambrosian Library.

As for Bonizo’s murder, although they mention that Piacenza’s sedition, the older writers on Piacenzan affairs are almost unanimously silent. John de Mussis, a citizen of Piacenza, who described the affairs of his native land in a brilliant style from the year 222 to 1402, and whom Muratori, after publishing him, commends at length, is nevertheless more silent about Bonizo than a fish. We observe the same thing in other writers of that Church, even earlier ones, who in turn drew from still older sources and whom the often-praised Muratori commends for their reliability and wealth of material (*Italian Historical Matters*, vol. XVI, p. 443). Yet these writers, so abundant, so rich, and so lucid, mention not even Bonizo’s name, much less his deeds or his cruel murder.

We shall bring forward one of them, a meager annalist whom Muratori published from an Este manuscript and whose discovery he thinks deserves thanks, to support what we have asserted:

“In the year of Christ 1089 there was discord between the knights and the common people of Piacenza; and the knights left the city, occupying castles and villages and preventing the people of the bishopric from coming to the market of Piacenza. Then the common people [Col. 0789C], leaving the city against the knights, attacked the castles as far as Trabantianum. Then the knights, gathering by another route, entered the city, excluding the common people from the city. The common people, unable to enter the city, remained near Saint Lazarus, and finally, on the feast of Saint Michael, they made peace with one another” (*loc. cit.*, col. 251).

Here one finds nothing that reflects the face of those times, when the smoldering fires and conflagrations of Arialdus and Herlembaldus were raging more savagely than ever before.

As for what Petrus Maria Campius, the most recent historian of the ecclesiastical history of Piacenza—and not an careless writer, but one well known through the praise of the greatest men—assembled concerning Bonizo, we understand that it was taken from the same sources from which we drew our material; nor did he have the opportunity to examine and work through Bonizo’s life. We can say the same, and say it emphatically, about what John Liron of Chartres, a monk of the Congregation of Saint Maur and a man distinguished for varied learning, collected concerning Ponizo in volume I of his *Miscellanies* [Note: [Col. 0789D] *Literary Singularities*, vol. I, no. XIII, pp. 310–313], though with a somewhat desultory brevity, from Lambeccius and others.

These, then, are the facts about Bonizo’s life and deeds and about his bloody death that have so far reached posterity. Some of them, and not merely from ecclesiastical literature but from the whole abundance of polished and serious learning alike, were kindly communicated to me, after I had consulted them by letter, by men raised above my praise: Franciscus Toepselius, provost of Polling, and Eusebius Amort, whose very name has already begun to serve as a eulogy, dean of that same most ancient canonry under the rule of Saint Augustine.

Concerning the title “saint” and “blessed,” bestowed by some upon this man, who was imprudently inflamed by the fever of his age and faction, we report the judgment of the Antwerp hagiographers all the more willingly because it has always seemed to us fairer than the generosity of certain recent writers, which rests neither on authority nor on judgment. Thus write the collectors and perpetual keepers of the archives and records of the Christian city [Note: [Col. 0790D] In the note on omissions under 14 July; there, because of the printer’s error that put June in place of July, the distinguished Amortus warned me, and through me warned others]:

“Ferrarius had not dared to number Bonizo of Sutri, and afterward of Piacenza—bishop, as they wish (indeed, whether they wish it or not)—among the saints of Italy in his earlier catalogue; but in another general catalogue he spoke somewhat more freely: ‘At Piacenza, the blessed Bonizo, bishop and martyr,’ of whom, as a saint and blessed man, no one has hitherto made mention. In his notes he confusedly cites I know not what *Annals of the City of Piacenza* and Baronius under the year 1089.

“I therefore first consulted Baronius, in whom I found absolutely nothing about Bonizo except the very words of Berthold of Constance, in Hermann’s appendix under the year 1089.”

Cuperus, the most accurate scholar, then reports the passage of Berthold—and he is the author of these notes—and continues:

“Baronius added nothing of weight or authority from himself, not even the title ‘blessed.’ I have seen no other *Annals of Piacenza* than those published in Italian by Petrus Maria Campius, which we examined elsewhere. In the index of his work he incorrectly asserts that Bonizo was canonized, and he is no more accurate on p. 358 when he says that Baronius called him ‘Saint Bonizo,’ unless he substituted for the text of the annals, foolishly, an index compiled, I know not by whom. Bucelinus adds no greater strength; he incorrectly assigns the date to 3 June.

“I acknowledge and revere Bonizo’s distinguished labors and all the very grievous wounds inflicted upon him by the schismatics; but that he was ever declared a martyr by legitimate authority, or that he was venerated as such at Sutri, Piacenza, or Verona, is not proved by the records of those Churches. Nor does Ughellus’s eulogy, vol. I, col. [Col. 0790D] 190, where Bonizzus is named, say anything about any cult. Nor am I permitted to anticipate the judgment of the Apostolic See.”

He adds the epitaph at Cremona, in which Bonizo is indeed called a martyr; but since it is more recent, it proves nothing, antiquity protesting against it. Sandius observes in his notes and comments on Vossius’s work *On Latin Historians*, now refined by the additions and critical revision of most learned men (p. 353, Amsterdam edition, 1677, in twelves), that Bonizo, or Bonithus, was called by some “ONYTHON,” because the first letter B was thought to signify “blessed.” Anyone who uses a sharper nose can detect this more recent and dull-witted invention.

No one will be greatly surprised, with Casimirus Oudinus, that Bonizo is not mentioned among the more distinguished bibliographers—Sigebert of Gembloux, Henry of Ghent, John Trithemius, Cardinal Bellarmine, William Eisengrein, Aubertus Miraeus, Antonio Possevino, Conrad Gesner and his epitomizers, or Gerard John Vossius, whose concern with historical writers brought him more nearly into contact with the matter—if they have closely considered how carelessly most of them treated that vast and inexhaustible subject, which their very abundance sometimes made them poor in. For their number was so great and so immense—the number of those whose writings were then widely available—that the works and reputations of those whose fame and writings were buried beneath deep darkness and neglect were easily forgotten.

Yet the memory of Bonizo and his works had not entirely faded, so that no trace remained at all. An anonymous writer of Melk, contemporary with our Bonizo and brought to light by Bernard Pez, mentions him [Note: [Col. 0791D] Chapter 112, p. 489, at the end of the same *Benedictine-Maurist Library*] in these words: “Ponizo, priest of Sutri, writes excerpts from the canons in the time of the Seventh.” And in Muratori’s *Italian Historical Matters*, vol. III, which contains the *Deeds and Lives of the Roman Pontiffs* written by Nicolaus, cardinal of the Holy Roman Church of Aragon, it plainly appears in the Life of Leo IX that Nicolaus had Bonizo’s histories before his eyes: he appropriates not only his subject matter but also his words (p. 277). Nor was it only in the deeds of Leo, but also in those of Stephen IX, Nicholas II, and Alexander II, that Nicolaus plowed energetically in Bonizo’s field, even though he did not meanwhile mention him by name. To establish this in greater detail, now that the works of both men can be compared with one another, does not seem to belong to this place. Let it suffice to note by way of example that in the Life of Alexander II Nicolaus mentions a statute made by the Lombard bishops, at the instigation of Guibert of Parma, providing that they should not receive a pope unless he came from the paradise of Italy; these very words are found in our author.

Ricobaldus of Ferrara, canon of Ravenna, in his *History of the Roman-German Emperors*, continued from Charlemagne to the year 1298 and published in the work of the much-praised Muratori (*Italian Historical Matters*, vol. IX)—who had it reprinted more accurately and more fully with the aid of an Este manuscript after it had previously been edited by the distinguished Giovanni Giorgio Eccardo—quotes certain material from Bonizo in his account of Emperor Henry II (col. 121), and stumbles only over the name, calling him Deonitus:

“In the book of Deonitus,” he says, “which he sent to Countess Matilda, it is said that when the aforesaid priest (the discussion concerns the man who bought the papacy, Gratianus), led by simplicity, had acquired the pontificate for himself with money, in order to oppose the schism he soon recognized his error and, on the emperor’s advice, renounced the office.”

These words, however, are found not in Domnizo—whom one might think he meant by his “Deonitus,” whose books to Matilda were revised by the illustrious Leibniz—but in our Bonizo, and in a fuller form. Muratori himself, with his great integrity in editing monuments, points out that in the manuscript “Bonici” was written between the lines in place of Deonitus. Thus the otherwise keen scholar came very close to the truth, but the better-known name of Domnizo drew him away from it: he knew that Domnizo had dedicated a book to Matilda, and therefore restored the reading, “or perhaps Donizi, that is, Domnizo?”

Under Henry IV, Ricobaldus recounts the history of Hildebrand [*loc. cit.*, col. 222], later Pope Gregory VII and formerly a Cluniac, who convicted the archbishop of Ebron of simony by an extraordinary argument and forced him to abdicate, in almost the same words that we now read in Bonizo’s extant work. In this passage Ricobaldus reports his author’s name not truncated or deformed, but truly and correctly, calling him Bonizo. Muratori, however, suspects so little genuine material that here too he thinks Donizo should be restored.

Finally, Martin of Troppau also mentions Bonizo in his *Chronicle*, although not in all manuscripts and not in the same form. It is useful to hear Lambeccius himself on this matter, for he compared eight manuscripts, all of which are held by that most richly endowed and truly Augustan library over which he presided. He writes:

“These, then, are those chronicles of Bonizo—or, as the same man is elsewhere corruptly called, Bonisius—*On the Deeds of the Roman Pontiffs*. Martin of Troppau mentions them in the preface to his *Chronicle* in these words:

‘Now I have compiled this little work from the writings of Livy, from the chronicles of Orosius, from the chronicles of Pope Damasus *On the Deeds of the Pontiffs*, from the chronicles of Bonisius, bishop of Sutri, *On the Deeds of the Pontiffs*, from the chronicles of Paul the Deacon,’ and so forth.

“This passage must genuinely be read in this way, not as it is incorrectly and corruptly printed in the Basel edition of John Oporinus, 1559, in folio, and in the Antwerp Plantinian edition of Sufridus Petrus, 1574, in octavo: ‘On the Deeds of Bonisius, bishop of Sutri, on the deeds of the pontiffs.’ For this reason John Fabricius, surnamed Caesar, deserves censure: in his edition of the same chronicle, printed at Cologne by Gerard Grevenbruch in 1616 in folio, he omitted entirely the words of Martin of Troppau’s preface that mention the chronicles of Bonisius, or Bonizo, *On the Deeds of the Roman Pontiffs*—for no other reason, evidently, than that this Bonisius or Bonizo was wholly unknown to him [Note: [Col. 0791D] In the dissertation on the Ambras manuscript Cod. LXXXV].”

Thus far Lambeccius. In the same book II, chapter 8 [Note: [Col. 0792D] In the recension of Cod. CCLIV, in large quarto, which contains Martin of Troppau’s *Chronicle*, pp. 872 and following], he indicates the variant readings of the manuscripts mentioned above in these words:

“I think it necessary to add here, as a sort of corollary, how the same passage appears in the eight manuscript codices mentioned above in the Augustan Caesarean Library. In the first and second of those codices it reads as follows:

‘Likewise, from the chronicles of Bonitus, bishop of Sutri, *On the Deeds of the Pontiffs and Emperors*.’

“In the third it reads: ‘Likewise, from the chronicles of Bobinus,’ and so forth.

“In the fourth it reads: ‘Likewise, *On the Deeds of Bonisius, bishop of Sutri, On the Deeds of the Pontiffs*.’

“In the fifth, sixth, seventh, and eighth it reads: ‘Likewise, from the chronicles of Bobinus, bishop of Sutri, *On the Deeds of Both*.’”

These, then, are the things I have been able to gather about Bonizo, given the abundance—or rather, perhaps, the poverty—of the evidence and learning available. Of him we may truly assert what Cicero says of the nobility of Servius Sulpicius in *Pro Murena*: “that it is better known to men of letters and historians, but obscure to the people and the voters.” What remains concerns the monuments of his mind, which must now be reviewed individually and in order. [Col. 0793B]

## Catalogue of Works

### Epitome of All the Works and Sayings of Saint Augustine, Entitled *The Augustinian Paradise* and Divided into Eight Books

The first person to extract information about this work was that voracious devourer of books—whom Cato used to call such—Petrus Lambeccius, by far the most worthy director of the Augustan Caesarean Library at Vienna. Together with other ancient codices, he had transferred it by imperial command in the sixty-fifth year of the previous century from Ambras Castle to the Caesarean Library. He carefully and accurately described it in the second book of his *Commentaries*, which he left to posterity as a very rich work on that library, though he did not bring it to completion.

The work survives in Cod. LXXXV, a paper manuscript in folio, written in the year 1439. Bonizo had dedicated it to John the abbot, whom learned men have long recognized as that celebrated John Gualbert, founder of Vallombrosa, renowned for knowledge, piety, and Christian gentleness. Lambeccius inserts almost the whole letter, enriched with notes of hidden learning, into his *Commentaries*, because in it the plan and subject of the work are explained plainly and clearly. The learned reader will not find it untimely or burdensome if we reproduce it here, as though in its proper place, where Bonizo’s affairs are being treated systematically [Col. 0793D] [Note: [Col. 0793D] Oudinus reported it before us, vol. II of the *Commentaries on Ecclesiastical Writers*, col. 739 and following].

Bonizo, the least among the household of God, sends greetings to the most reverend John, abbot.

“By the voice of the Lord, the man is accused who preferred to cover the talent entrusted to him with earth rather than put it out at interest with the money-changers. Wishing diligently to avoid the guilt of that offense, I have resolved, with God’s grace helping me, that as long as the breath of life shall invigorate my limbs, whatever I can perceive through the hearing of heart and body, distinguish by understanding, and chew over with the palate of my heart, I shall gladly share with brothers in need. Receive, therefore, venerable Father, the *Excerpt of the Sayings of the Miraculous Doctor Augustine*, labored over for you and scarcely brought to completion over the course of a year. Divided into eight volumes, I have adorned it with the name *Paradise*, and not without justification,” and so forth.

Lambeccius subsequently reports what Bonizo mentions concerning the subject of each book toward the end of the same letter:

> “Therefore gird yourself, dear Father, and examine the sentences of the most admirable Doctor, and consider by subtle inquiry what God is and what God is not, what the Trinity is and what unity is; consider the diversity of the Persons, the proper attribute of each Person, the mission of the Son, and the procession of the Holy Spirit; how one is three and how three are one. In the first book, read and investigate divine providence with determination.
>
> “In the second volume, inquire concerning rational creation: how the angelic creature was created and how the human creature was created; why God created the devil, whom He had foreseen would sin; why He created man; and inquire diligently concerning free will and grace, and you will find the answers.
>
> “In the third, examine courageously the origin of Adam, Easter, the sacrament of baptism, the Eucharist of the Lord’s body and blood, and charity.
>
> “In the fourth, inquire why God should be worshiped, since He knows what is necessary for us; concerning the seven petitions; concerning love of God; concerning the natural law; concerning the fact that it is better for a person to be conquered by another person than by vice; concerning the acquisition of virtues and the avoidance of vices; concerning fleeing from falsehood and its eight kinds; concerning the taking of nourishment; and against the mathematicians and against the Origenists. If you seek these matters diligently, you will find them clearly explained.
>
> “In the fifth, you will find discussion of Christian doctrine; of the fact that, among all signs, words hold the chief place; of ambiguous signs and figurative expressions; of how Holy Scripture is to be understood; of avoiding the vices of barbarism; of knowledge of the arts; of eloquence; of Tyconius’s seven rules; and of the fiftieth and fortieth.

[Col. 0793D–0794D] On this Tyconius, an African by nationality, Lambeccius refers the reader to Gennadius, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, ch. 18, and to the authors cited there in Aubert Miraeus’s scholium. On the work of this Donatist itself, now often published, the distinguished Schoetgenius has much to say in book XIX of Fabricius’s *Library of Middle and Lower Latin*, p. 764.
>
> “In the sixth, concerning the authority of the Seventy Interpreters and who they were; and from the very beginning of Genesis through the times of Solomon, you will find multiple difficult questions solved by Blessed Augustine.
>
> “In the eighth, you will find written what hell is; whether only the wicked or also the good will remain in hell; whether bodies can exist in perpetual burning; for whom sacrifice is beneficial after death; how the dead appear in dreams to the living; concerning offerings and almsgiving for the dead; that Adam was freed from hell by the Lord’s death; concerning the two resurrections; that, when judgment has been completed, there will be a conflagration of fire; whether the bodies of all the dead will rise in the likeness of the Lord’s body; concerning the newness of the spiritual body and the possession of eternal blessedness; concerning the nature of the vision by which God will be seen in the future; and concerning the happiness of the eternal city of God.

> “Feed upon such fruits of delight; nourish yourself on these delicacies. Thus, fattened on the sweetness of the tree of life, you will keep Christ’s words and will never taste death. Taking pity on my weakness also, and not forgetting my labor, protect me from the barking of my rivals with the shield of your prayer.”

He subsequently reports the beginning of the first book in these words:

> “Everything that exists is one thing, that by which it is constituted another; that by which it is distinguished another; that by which it is fitted together another. Therefore the entire creation …”

In commendation of the work itself, that indefatigable librarian adds the following:

> “This work is certainly most worthy of being made public through the aid of the printing press, both because it elucidates the teaching of Saint Augustine and also on account of Bonizo himself, whose affairs he pursues here at length and with great labor from Berthold of Constance, Ughelli, Baronius, and Ferrarius.”

## II. On Ecclesiastical Sacraments

John Mabillon, by far the greatest ornament of the republic of letters, was the first to bring this little work to its attention. He found and examined it—brief as it is—in the Ambrosian Library at Milan when, in 1685, he was traversing Italy, that richest marketplace of literary commerce, with tireless steps. He writes as follows in the *Italian Journey* prefixed to volume I of the *Musei Italici* [Col. 0795D; Paris, 1724, quarto, p. 13; under April 1685, in the description of the Ambrosian Library at Milan]:

> “In another codex there is a book by Bonizo, bishop of Sutri, concerning the sacraments, addressed to Gualterus, abbot of the monastery of Leon. In this book the author mentions another little work of his against Hugo the schismatic.”

This is how Mabillon mentions it there, almost in passing. The distinguished Muratori stopped to examine it more closely and published the work itself, copied from the same Ambrosian codex that Mabillon had seen, in his celebrated work *Italian Antiquities of the Middle Ages*, dissertation XXXVII.

[Col. 0795D] *Volume III, p. 599 ff., dissertation XXXVII, “On Hospitals for Pilgrims, the Sick, Exposed Infants, etc.”*

For, while dealing incidentally with ancient charters drawn up at Leno, in the diocese of Brescia, he brings to light various monuments of the monastery of Leon, or “ad Leones,” as it was called in later times. But it is preferable to hear Muratori himself explaining the occasion on which he published the little work:

> “But when, in the place mentioned, we came upon the monastery of Leon, I promise myself the readers’ pardon—pardon? Rather, their gratitude—if I do not leave it before adding to these monuments of the ancient centuries a little work hitherto deprived of the light of day. Its author is Bonizo …”

After making Bonizo better known from Berthold, Ughelli, Lambeccius, Cave, and Oudinus, he further notes that before him not only Mabillon but also Pietro Maria Campi, author of the then unpublished history of Piacenza, had mentioned this little work as one he had himself seen at Rome, under the title *On Ecclesiastical Sacraments*:

> “This little work, then,” Muratori continues, “which I formerly drew from a manuscript codex of the Ambrosian Library, I wish to add to this dissertation. It is addressed to Gualterus of the monastery of Leon—not to the abbot, as Mabillon hastily read, but to the prior.”

We deliberately leave this to others for examination and revision, although it is worthy in many respects of the meditation and study of learned men, since it requires deeper investigation and has already been made public.

In it Bonizo mentions another book written by him against Hugo the schismatic, concerning which we shall speak in its proper place.

## III. The Decretal, or Syntagma of Ecclesiastical Decrees Proven from Sacred Scripture and Approved Councils, as well as from the Records of the Roman Pontiffs, the Holy Fathers, and Other Orthodox Authors, Collected and Divided According to Commonplaces into Seven Books

Lambeccius describes this distinguished work from a parchment codex at Vienna, and we may properly hear him narrate the matter in his own words.

[Col. 0795D–0796D] A much fuller manuscript copy, hidden among the manuscripts of the Church of Brescia, will shortly be indicated. The Viennese copy is a parchment small folio, or large quarto, written, as Lambeccius says, not long after Bonizo’s death. Speaking of Bonizo’s labors, partly theological and partly historical, he says:

> “Among the Latin historical manuscript codices of the Imperial and Royal Library at Vienna, which have not yet been assigned definite numbers, I found one especially memorable. The volume containing it is parchment, in small folio, or large quarto; and, as far as can be judged from the script and other circumstances, it was written not long after Bonizo’s death. The former possessor of this exceedingly rare and perhaps unique manuscript codex was, as he himself testifies in his own hand on its first leaf, Johannes Albertus Widmestadius, counsellor of the Emperor Ferdinand I and chancellor of the eastern provinces of Austria.”

After praising this most learned man, the polyhistor and Polyphemus of his age, and even after the learned and erudite commentaries on his literary merits by the distinguished Schoellornius and Maschius, Lambeccius continues:

> “The previously mentioned codex contains Bonizo’s hitherto unpublished decretal, or syntagma of ecclesiastical decrees, collected from Sacred Scripture and approved councils, as well as from the records of the Roman pontiffs, the holy Fathers, and other orthodox authors, and divided according to commonplaces into seven books. Prefixed to it, in place of a preface, is an epitome of the history of the Roman pontiffs, from Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, to Pope Urban II, who was elected on 12 March 1088. The title of the aforementioned epitome is: *Chronicle of the Roman Pontiffs, Published by Bonitho, Bishop of Sutri, a Man Most Learned in Every Respect*.”

He subsequently reports the beginning of the work. Since it is missing from the acephalous Brescian codex, we present it as he copied it from the Viennese codex:

> “Since I am about to write concerning the excellence of the Roman Church, the privileges belonging to the bishop of that Church, and its constitutions, I ask the diligent reader not to break at once into mockery of me when he sees that, in so extensive a work, I have said little about great matters. For if Moses, learned in all the knowledge of Egypt, who was the gentlest of all the people dwelling on earth, whom the Lord knew face to face [the OCR reads *ex homine*], says that he is uncircumcised of lips lest he be sent to Egypt; and if Jeremiah calls himself a child, excusing himself from being sent to uproot and plant, to build and destroy kingdoms—what will I, most wretched and conscious of no goodness or knowledge in myself, judge myself to be other than unworthy of so great a work?
>
> “But because God spoke in the thornbush, and, whenever He wished, loosed the tongue of a braying creature into acceptable speech, I shall take confidence from Him, from whom every good gift and every perfect gift comes, and shall beseech Him in prayer—if only He would not disdain to visit my thornbushes.
>
> “As for me, who make and ponder many vows, nothing better occurs to me than this: that this most holy Church was founded not by synodical constitutions but by the voice of the Lord Himself, who said to blessed Peter: ‘You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church.’ To it was added the fellowship of blessed Paul, teacher of the nations, so that she who had been chosen as the head of the nations might be the seat of the prince of the apostles and the teacher of the nations.
>
> “For she is the summit and foundation of all the Churches, as the Lord says to blessed Peter: ‘I have prayed for you, Peter, that your faith may not fail; and you, once converted, strengthen your brothers.’ What shall I say, since the whole Christian religion …”

Thus far Lambeccius, from the Viennese codex.

A fuller knowledge of this work is supplied by the Brescian codex, which Johannes Hieronymus Gradonicus, a regular canon of Brescia and the highly praised author of *Sacred Brescia*, reviews from the archive of that cathedral church. He was a man distinguished not only by the nobility derived from blood but also by that true nobility produced by letters.

He had decided to append to the complete series of the Brescian pontiffs [Brescia, 1755, from the press of Giovanni Battista Bossini, quarto] an index of the manuscript codices kept in that church’s archive. But later changing his plan, and sadly excluding learned readers from their expectation, he stopped with the description of a single codex, which contains Bonizo’s decretal. But let us rather hear the account of the man who had that codex before his eyes and on his knees [in the appendix on the manuscript codex, p. 443]:

> “The learned men of Brescia are pleased to leave this field for someone else to adorn, and to linger for a while over the description of a single codex. It was written in the eleventh century. At the top of the second page it bears the following title: *Of Bonizo, Bishop, Concerning the Authentic Canons of the Holy Fathers, to the Presbyter Gregory*.”

After a brief account of Bonizo and his labors and books, the most learned man continues:

> “But among these none surpasses the one whose description we now give from the Brescian archive, whether one considers the matters it contains or the rarity and excellence of the codex. For mention is made of only one other in the records of the Viennese Library, which Oudinus, in the place cited (*vol.* II, p. 737), calls exceedingly rare and perhaps even unique. Moreover, that one is defective, since it contains only seven books, whereas the Brescian codex contains ten. Since its first leaf is missing, the beginning of the first book is also absent; the beginnings of the remaining books are as follows:

> “The second book begins: ‘What must be taught to everyone before he is baptized; what baptism is; in what ways it is performed; and from whom it took its origin.’

> “The third book begins: ‘Clement to Bishop James. In these cities the prince of the apostles established primates, where formerly the chief flamens …’

> “The fourth book begins: ‘Since I am about to write concerning the excellence of the Roman Church and the privileges belonging to the bishops of that Church, etc.’

> “The fifth book begins: ‘In the preceding three little books, what sort of man ought to be chosen as bishop … it remains now to explain concerning priests and deacons of the second order and the other orders, insofar as God grants, and first let us begin with ordination, etc.’

> “The sixth book begins: ‘We have learned from blessed Benedict that there are four kinds of monks, etc.’

> “The seventh book begins: ‘It seemed worthwhile to write concerning the Scriptures about kings and judges, and about those who are established in the lay order, etc.’

> “The eighth book begins: ‘Since in the preceding book we dealt with prelates and those placed in the lay order … it remains now, in the further book, to investigate briefly how subjects ought to order their lives.’

> “The ninth book begins: ‘This book is entitled medicinal, because it contains various medicines for the souls of the sick.’

> “The tenth book begins: ‘I remember saying in the preceding book … it seemed worthwhile to me to collect briefly the authorities and examples of the holy Fathers and to insert in this little book their judgments concerning crimes and how they judged them.’”

From all this the distinguished man rightly concludes that this Brescian codex is far superior to the Viennese one.

[Col. 0799A] The anonymous writer of Melk, whom we cited above, appears to have been the first to mention this work; he seems to have known Bonizo from a single work. After Lambeccius’s account, Gradenigo continues:
