> “The knowledge of the Brescian codex was first published in the supplements to Labbe’s edition of the councils by Dominicus Mansi (*vol.* II, preface to the appendix, p. 3), whom we had informed of the discovery of the precious codex. The learned abbot Trombellius, whom we praised, having seen that codex with us several years ago in the archive mentioned, undertook to bring it to light, having obtained permission from the most illustrious and reverend canons to copy it for that purpose.”

It is certainly to be hoped that the most reverend John Chrysostom Trombellius, now general abbot of the Congregation of Saint Saviour and distinguished by so many monuments of exceptional talent and learning, will not drive us from that hope on account of the exceedingly corrupt and acephalous Brescian codex, which others had praised far too obligingly after only a passing inspection. Especially since hope has not yet been severed of repairing, correcting, and restoring what is gaping or missing in the Viennese codex.

In the catalogue of the Brescian codices, according to Gradenigo, it is listed as follows:

> “Of Bonizo, bishop, etc., etc. It is a collection of canons completed in the year 1100 scarcely past”—indeed, Bonizo had already died a decade or more before that date—“and is an unpublished work. The first page is missing, as are several others in several places.”

## IV. Epitome of the History of the Roman Pontiffs

[Col. 0799C]

The same Viennese codex mentioned above, which contains Bonizo’s decretal, presents this work:

> “Prefixed to it in place of a preface”—these are Lambeccius’s words [the cited place, p. 797]—“is [an epitome] from Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, to Pope Urban II, who was elected on 12 March 1138. The title of the aforementioned epitome is: *Chronicle of the Roman Pontiffs, Published by Bonitho, Bishop of Sutri, a Man Most Learned in Every Respect*.”

The distinguished Muratori, who overlooked nothing that could in any way illuminate the affairs of Italy, moved every stone to make this monument public when he read this account of Lambeccius. He testifies to this in the following words [*Italian Antiquities of the Middle Ages*, dissertation XXXVII, vol. III, col. 599]:

> “Since I was exceedingly eager for the final book of this work—the epitome of the history of the Roman pontiffs—I eventually learned that nothing else was presented there except a mere brief catalogue of the Roman pontiffs, of which we have many; and for that reason I refrained from pursuing it further.”

The final words of this epitome are:

> “Thus far, beginning with blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, we have arranged in summary the deeds of the Roman pontiffs down to our own times. It remains now for us to discuss, with God’s help, not at length but concisely, the privileges belonging to the Roman pontiff and the prerogative of that see.”

After this he proceeds, as it were by a transition, to his decretal, which we discussed above.

Casimir Oudinus, who was the first after Lambeccius, and chiefly on his authority, to include Bonizo among the writers of ecclesiastical history, mentions another manuscript copy of this epitome from Thomas Smith’s catalogue of the Cottonian manuscripts [vol. II, pp. 744–45; the catalogue was published at Oxford in folio in 1696, p. 2]:

> “Another manuscript copy of this work exists in the Cotton Library of England, under the effigy of Julius, letter A, codex VII, no. II, with these words: *Chronicle of the Roman Pontiffs, published by Bonitho, Bishop of Sutri, a most learned man, down to Urban II*, as the title has it. Of this Roman pontiff’s deeds, the author says that he wrote intimately:”

That is what he says there. Yet the most learned man is mistaken when he supposes that Martin of Poland, when citing Bonizo’s *Deeds of the Pontiffs*, had this epitome before his eyes. It is clear that he intended to designate the book addressed to Amicus, which truly bears the title *Deeds*.

## V. A Little Book Against Hugo the Schismatic

This book, which covered the beginnings of Urban II, we are today compelled either to await as something still hidden or to lament as lost. Bonizo himself mentions it in two places. He mentions it once in the little work *On the Sacraments of the Church*, which Muratori brought to light, in these words:

> “If anyone wishes to know how Saint Clement was first by Peter’s election and third in rank, let him read the book that I wrote against Hugo the schismatic; there he will find the matter fully clarified.”

[Col. 0800D] *In the little book On the Sacraments, in Muratori, vol. I, p. 602.*

He mentions it again, and more fully, in the conclusion of the epitome of the pontifical history discussed above, as follows, in Lambeccius:

> “If anyone wishes to know the deeds of Pope Urban and concerning his victory, let him read the book that I wrote against Hugo the schismatic; there he will find the matter fully elucidated.”

The writers of those times, each according to his partisan inclination, report much concerning Hugo Candidus, cardinal, who stirred up disturbances against Alexander II at the side of our august Agnes, the mother of Henry IV, and later opposed Gregory VII most vigorously in favor of Henry, his son. Bonizo himself makes extensive mention of the affairs of Alexander II, but undoubtedly he had treated them much more fully in the writing that we now lack—a work that may perhaps emerge successfully together with the nearly already lamented writings of our author.

Antoine Pagi, in *Historical-Critical Chronology of Baronius’s Annals*, volume IV, under the year 1044, p. 166b—of whom Longuery, a prodigy of learning, further fashioned a critical nose—writes as follows concerning Hugo on the occasion of this very little work:

> “It was entitled *Against Hugo the Schismatic*, that is, against Hugo surnamed Candidus, cardinal priest of the titular church of Saint Clement, who in 1061, after the death of Pope Nicholas, was the leader and standard-bearer of those who maintained that a new Roman pontiff ought to be created only after consultation with and consent of the emperor Henry IV.”

## VI. The Book Addressed to Amicus

Bonizo himself identifies it in this way at the end of the epitome of the pontifical history, prefixed in the Viennese codex to the collection of canons undertaken by him. This is the distinguished work—the very work that we are now bringing to light from Bavarian parchment manuscripts containing nine books.

Bonizo briefly outlined its subject as follows:

> “Furthermore, if anyone wishes to know about Theophylact of Tusculum: how he sold the papacy to the priest John; how, at one and the same time, Theophylact, Gregory, and Sylvester did not rule but devastated the Roman pontificate; and how King Henry, son of Conrad, freed the Roman Church from such shepherds, let him read the book that I composed, entitled *To Amicus*. There he will find these matters arranged in orderly fashion.
>
> “There also he will find how Pope Clement was elected and how King Henry was appointed emperor by him; how many days Damasus, his successor, spent in the papacy; what the distinguished Leo did in the papacy and how he ended his life; what Victor, his successor, did and what new event occurred in his time; concerning Stephen, brother of the Duke Godefrid; how, in his time, the Pataria arose at Milan; concerning Pope Nicholas and the dispute he had with Benedict the intruder, and what he did in the papacy; concerning Pope Alexander, the dispute he had with Cadolus of Parma, his victory, what he did in the papacy, and his death; concerning Gregory VII, his election, his life and character, how he was captured at the altar of the Lord at the Nativity by Cencio, a cruel man, and freed that same day by the grace of God; concerning the war he endured from the Emperor Henry; concerning the controversy he had with Wibert; concerning the hardships he suffered; concerning the siege of the city and of himself; how he was freed by Robert, duke of the Romans; and how he came to rest in a blessed end—all of these matters are most appropriately explained.”

These are Bonizo’s words, which Pagi, the distinguished commentator on Baronius’s celebrated work, repeats exactly and illustrates with notes in his customary manner. We refer the reader to those notes. How highly he himself valued this monument of ecclesiastical history can readily be inferred from the words with which he laments its loss:

> “It is certainly most deeply to be regretted that a work has perished which would have shed the greatest light upon the ecclesiastical annals. Nevertheless, these excerpts are sufficient to show how well informed he was concerning the events that took place at Rome in that period.”

[Col. 0802A] The work itself will provide a fuller account. Withdrawn from the eyes of scholars and removed from their memory by long oblivion, it came close to suffering shipwreck almost within sight of the harbor. From the Bavarian Library, where the unknown codex lay concealed and unnoticed, it was transferred to the library of a private man—a superfluous piece of the luxury and power of his household. After his death it awaited, in some corner, a convenient time to be divided among the heirs and then sent to the makers of gold leaf, until the Reverend John Edelweck, then provost of the clerics regular of Saint Cajetan residing among us, came upon it by the guidance of Minerva. He was thoroughly equipped, in keeping with the dignity of his birth and institution, with both the more serious and the more agreeable branches of learning, and restored the fugitive or abducted book to its family.

[Col. 0802B] The codex itself is parchment, in the format called quarto, and in the smaller, genuinely square form. It passed from the Schedelian collection into the Bavarian one, so often mentioned by us. No trace of its earlier owner remains there. On the back board, however, on an attached slip, one reads in the character called monastic:

> “The little book of *Boni Thonis*,”

and then:

> “A chronicle from Constantine onward, etc.”

On the outer front, however, is written:

> “The history of Bonitho, bishop of Sutri, concerning the persecution of the Church.”

Added to this is an old note of the State Library: VII, no. LIV A. This arrangement, after the library had been transferred from Taufkirchen Castle to Munich by Albert, remained unchanged, and the mark is still affixed to the codices. Today the manuscript is designated among the Latin manuscripts as no. DCXVIII.

The codex reproduces the script of the twelfth century so vividly that it could serve beginners in diplomatics as a model of the subject. The capital letters are now red, but traces of the silver with which they had been coated are still clearly visible.

There is nothing concerning the work itself that I need add to what has already been said. I present a new witness to those times—and whether it is also a witness to the truth, let those decide who compare the praises of the ancients with recently discovered testimonies. I have added no notes, and this deliberately, lest I make cooks more hostile to me than diners; and, as the chief point of my policy was concerned, I did not wish to lose the fish on account of the broth. I have served it fresh; let others season it.

If there are people who will carp at my inserting Bonizo among the writers on Bavarian affairs, I do not consider them worthy opponents against whom I should defend myself with the example of the greatest men, insofar as I can. To me, at least, an author hitherto lamented as lost, who would illuminate not only German affairs but also Bavarian affairs in very many places, seemed entirely worthy of publication whenever an opportunity was presented—not merely an opportunity offered but one seized—especially since he contains what, “for anyone who reads it, leaves little desire for a connected history of those times; for everything concerning the interests of rulers, the vices of leaders, and changes in the commonwealth is written out in such a way that nothing in them remains unseen” (Nepos, *On Cicero’s Letters to Atticus*).

[Col. 0803]

# The Book of Bonizo of Sutri, Later Bishop of Piacenza, Addressed to Amicus, or Nine Books Concerning the Persecution of the Church

Now for the first time transcribed and published from the sole parchment codex formerly belonging to the Schedelian Library, now to the Bavarian Library, by Andreas Felix Oefelius.

## Here Begins the Book of Bonizo, Bishop of Sutri, Entitled *To Amicus*

[Col. 0803D] *These words are in silver letters.*

## Here Begins the First Book

[Col. 0803A]

You ask me, the only refuge from the tribulation that has surrounded me, why it is that in these troubled times Mother Church, placed upon earth, groaning cries out to the Lord but is not heard according to her desire; is oppressed but not delivered; and the sons of obedience and peace lie prostrate, while the sons of Belial rejoice with their king—especially since He who orders all things is Himself the one who judges with equity.

There is another matter concerning which you ask me for authority from the examples of the ancient holy Fathers: whether, as it was permitted in the past, so it is permitted for a Christian to contend with arms for the faith. If you lend a sound-hearted ear to these wavering thoughts of your mind, an easy answer will be given, both because the answer is readily available to us and because at this time it has seemed very necessary for me to write about it. Therefore, trusting in God’s mercy, who makes the tongues of infants eloquent, let us begin our discourse.

Mother Church, who is above and is not enslaved with her children, is especially liberated when she is oppressed; she grows most when she is diminished. For no one will be deemed a fellow citizen of Abel in the heavenly kingdom unless, in the present life, he has been worn down to purity by Cain’s wickedness [the OCR reads *ad puerum*].

Thus Enoch, having been found approved, “was taken away, lest wickedness should change his heart” (Wisdom 4:11). Thus Noah, the restorer of the human race, after suffering for nearly six hundred years many afflictions from those who had stained themselves by illicit intercourse [the OCR reads *commutatione*], escaped safely with his household while the world perished in the water that purged it.

And if the children of Jerusalem are at times held captive, they are nevertheless not enslaved. Although they sit and weep beside the rivers and do not delight in the watered places, they hang their instruments upon the willows and do not sing a song in a foreign land, but sigh for Jerusalem. Therefore blessed are those who dash the little ones against the rock, but wretched is the daughter of Babylon (Psalm 136).

Thus that Hebrew, Abraham, did not remain in Ur of the Chaldeans [the OCR reads *Hur*] or serve Babylonian arrogance; rather, he made his way toward Jerusalem, namely to Melchizedek, and, blessed by him, was called by the Almighty “father of many nations” (Genesis 17:4).

As it is written that he had “two sons, one by a slave woman and one by a free woman: the one by the slave woman according to the flesh, but the one by the free woman through the promise” (Galatians 4:22–23), these are the two peoples: one of Catholics, the other of heretics. Just as then “the one according to the flesh persecuted the one according to the spirit” (ibid., 29), so it is now.

Thus Scripture says: “Cast out the slave woman and her son. For the son of the slave woman will not be heir with the son of the free woman” (ibid., 30). And so, when Sarah cried out to Abraham, with the Angel interceding, Ishmael was disinherited because of persecution, while Isaac was endowed with the inheritance (Genesis 21).

Here is another persecution, which Isaac patiently endures. He digs the wells that his father had dug earlier and finds water, on account of which the Philistines quarreled (Genesis 26:19–20). He did not resist but endured patiently until he found abundance and, through abundance, reached Beersheba (ibid., 32–33), which is interpreted as “the seventh well” and “rest.” This demonstrates more clearly than daylight that when persecution is inflicted upon us by those outside, it is to be overcome by endurance; but when it comes from those within, it must first be cut down by the evangelical sickle and afterward defeated with every strength and weapon.

We shall demonstrate this better through examples. But what have we to do with allegory? Let us now come to evangelical truth. Let us come to the light “which enlightens every person coming into this world” (John 1:9). Let us come to the words more enduring than heaven and earth, and we shall find that we have nothing friendly or in common with the world.

Therefore we should not grieve when we perish, but rather rejoice. For the Savior says:

> “Do not be surprised if the world hates you; know that it hated me before you” (John 15:18).

And again:

> “I give you my peace; I leave you my peace. I do not give to you as this world gives” (John 14:27).

O what dignity it is to have the world regard us as enemies together with the Son of God, so that we may have the Father who is in heaven as our one friend!

Later, inviting us to suffer, He says:

> “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul” (Matthew 10:28).

And shortly afterward:

> “If anyone comes after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me” (Matthew 15:24).

Since we are members of the supreme Head, we ought, by imitating Him and clinging to Him, to strive toward the place where we know with certainty that He arrived [perhaps insert “through” or “after”]. Through reproaches, scourges, mockery, and the most shameful death of the cross, He reached the glory of the resurrection; having been perfected, He was crowned with glory and honor and sits at the right hand of God the almighty Father.

So, if we are children of the supreme Father, we ought to die to worldly possessions with Him, so that, rising together with Him, we may also reign together. The first founders of our mother, who has neither stain nor wrinkle (Ephesians 5:27), taught this by their instructions and demonstrated it by their examples.

For the prince of the sheepfold, the chosen vessel, the sons of Boanerges [thus the codex], the brothers of the Lord, and the other rams of the Lord’s flock respond differently and taught us this: that, abandoning the world with its pomp, we should set our minds on the things above, not on the things upon the earth (Colossians 3:2).

They demonstrated this by their example when they went away rejoicing from the presence of the council because they had been deemed worthy to suffer disgrace for the name of Jesus (Acts 5:41). Therefore, after their sound had gone out into all the earth (Psalm 18:5), having been made perfect, they were established as princes over the whole earth (Psalm 44:17).

A white-robed army of martyrs followed them. By encountering death through various kinds of punishment, they gained eternal life. Some were hung upon stakes; some were killed by various tortures; some were beheaded; some were flayed alive; some were burned in flames; some were drowned in rivers; some were pierced with bars; some were buried alive; some were deprived of their eyes; some were weakened in their other limbs; some were cut to pieces; some were stoned; some endured chains and scourging; and, in addition, they went about in prisons, in sheepskins and goatskins (Hebrews 11:37).

The pontifical dignity led them to such splendid glory. Although it had by then been spread through nearly the whole world, it displayed by examples what it proclaimed in words.

In particular, the Roman and Christian senate, which, taking its beginning from the blessed prince of the apostles, fought against the ancient enemy for nearly two hundred years, until the time of the devout Constantine, by continual campaigns, day and night, and triumphed over that poisonous serpent thirty-three times, did not cease to contend through endurance, subjecting principalities and powers to itself (1 Peter 3:22), because it subjected the ruler of the Roman Empire himself to the Christian religion.

## The First Book Ends

## Here Begins the Second Book
Therefore, when Constantine had been baptized by Sylvester, bishop of the holy Roman Church, and had been elevated by that same bishop with the imperial diadem, the temples were closed, [Col. 0806B] the churches were opened, images of the Savior began to be painted on the walls, and the image of Jupiter was publicly cast down; altars began to be erected and idols cast down. Peace was restored to the churches throughout the world, although it was not destined to last long. For in the time of that same pious prince there arose Arius, the Church’s greatest devastator, from whom the Arian heresy arose, and from him a thousand innovations of heresy—against which every Christian must fight as a matter of duty, no one who considers the matter having any doubt. For the aged and decrepit man, grieving that the imperial vessels by which he had persecuted the Christian religion had been taken from him, gathered himself entirely into anger; and through certain men of his craft, intoxicated with false justice, he did not cease—and does not cease, nor will he cease until the time of him “who exalts himself above everyone who is called or worshiped as God (II Thess. II, 4)”—to stain the purity of the Church. [Col. 0806C]

But since we have begun with Constantine, let us pursue Constantine’s praises. This is the Constantine who established a law consonant with evangelical teaching: that all bishops should have the bishop of Rome as their head, just as all judges have the king. This is the discoverer of the Lord’s Cross, the greatest propagator of the Christian name, the founder of gracious new Rome, and the chief builder of basilicas. This is he who assembled for us the holy Council of Nicaea, at which he himself arranged the seats of all the bishops; and he himself, sitting on a low footstool, judged it unworthy that the imperial seat should be mingled with the thrones of those whose seats are seats of judgment over the twelve tribes of Israel (Matt. XIX, 28). When one day the bishops presented him with written accusations, he is said to have replied: “Far be it from me to judge gods! For it was said concerning you: ‘I said: You are gods (Ps. LXXXI, 6).’” Nor is it right that a greater should be judged by a lesser.

This is the man of whom it is recorded that he said that, if he found someone wrapped in religious clothing committing an obscene act, he would cover him with his own cloak, lest the dignity of so great a name be disgraced.

He left sons, heirs indeed of the kingdom, but not of religion. For his son Constantius, who, after the death of his brothers, assumed the sole rule of the empire, devastated the Church with astonishing zeal for the Arian heresy. He banished bishops into exile and, indeed, cut some down with the sword. When, through the prefect Hermogenes, he attempted to expel Paul, bishop of Constantinople, [Col. 0807A] the Catholic people, armed with zeal for the divine law, fought for the truth so vigorously that they burned the prefect himself, together with his entire household and family. This deed was not condemned by the wise, but rather praised.

Why should I speak of the Alexandrians—how much they endured for the holy bishop Athanasius, and how many praiseworthy battles they waged against the Arians out of zeal for the orthodox faith? What of the Milanese, how they resisted Constantius by arms when he wished to seize the bishops who were hiding in the Church, and forcibly snatched them from his bloody hands?

But since the aforesaid Constantius persecuted the bishops—not equaling his father, but almost in the manner of pagans, although with zeal for God yet not according to knowledge—the state was greatly troubled in his time. For the Persians crossed the Roman frontiers, and the powerful nation of the Franks invaded the banks of the Rhine; it remains subject to Christian, though not Roman, rule to this day.

When Constantius died, Julian succeeded him in the kingdom, an apostate man hateful to God. During the three years in which he did not govern but rather devastated the Roman Empire, it is not easy to say how many massacres of priests he caused, or how many Christians he afflicted with various punishments.

Yet at that same time there were men not only of the priestly order but also of the military order who openly resisted his madness, such as Jovian, who succeeded him in the empire. Although he had been a commander of a thousand, he renounced the military belt before he renounced the doctrine. Nor will I pass over Valentinian’s fervor of divine love.

One day, as he was proceeding in the line of duty—for he was commander of a legionary cohort—a king was about to enter the temple of Fortuna, and a priest, as was customary, sprinkled him with water as he entered. It happened that this most Christian man saw a drop of water on his cloak. Immediately, inflamed with zeal for the Christian name, at the very entrance of the temple and in the presence of the savage emperor, he struck the priest with his fist and knocked him down, crying out that, because of this sprinkling, he, as a most Christian man, had been defiled rather than cleansed. God was so pleased with this deed that, before the year had run its course, he entrusted Valentinian with the government of the whole Roman Empire.

For when Julian ended his life disgracefully among the Persians and Jovian succeeded him in the empire, Jovian was buried in peace before the year had run its course. When he died, Valentinian succeeded him in the kingdom, [Col. 0807D] a courteous and most Christian man. At the beginning of his reign he made his brother Valens his colleague in the empire—alas! entrusting him with authority over the entire East—while he himself governed the western regions.

He chose Milan as the seat of empire. After the death of the heretic Auxentius and the peaceful burial of Saint Dionysius, it happened that the bishops of Italy assembled there in order jointly to elect a bishop for themselves. The king’s presence was eagerly awaited for this purpose. When he heard of it, however, he absolutely forbade it, establishing a law consonant with evangelical truth: that no lay prince or powerful man should dare to interfere in the election of a patriarch, metropolitan, or bishop; and if this were done, such an election would be irregular. He added: “Choose one according to the decrees of the canons who can heal our wounds.” God, looking down from on high upon the very pious humility of the prince, heard him and gave Ambrose as bishop both to him and to the Church. As long as he lived, he governed the Roman Empire in peace, most devoted to the priest of God.

From the time of the pious Constantine until the cruel reigns of the Lombards, five rulers of the Roman Empire existed who were obedient according to the fear of God, the counsel of the bishops, and especially under the Roman bishop: honoring the churches, loving the clergy, and respecting the priests. While they lived, they governed the state in profound peace and exchanged death for eternal life. Those who were disobedient, however, perished by an evil end.

Such was Valens, the brother of Valentinian. After he succeeded Valentinian upon his death, Valentinian’s son, together with his heretical mother Justina, seized the tyranny; wholly Arian, he devastated the eastern churches and banished the bishops into exile. In his time the Goths and Massagetae also crossed the Danube, occupied Illyricum, and invaded Epirus. At last, coming to Chalcedon, they killed that wicked man himself and besieged Constantinople. But—marvelous to say—

his widow, left behind, accomplished what the man had been unable to do and liberated the city from the barbarians.

There were also other pestilent rulers, such as Zeno, Constantine, and Anastasius, who, after speaking insolently about the pope, was struck down by a divine thunderbolt; and Valentinian, who was expelled from his kingdom together with his mother Justina, but recovered it through the pious prince Theodosius. There were also Basil, Leo, and Maurice, who was condemned to death together with his wife and children by Phocas; and many others who, dishonoring the priest of God and attempting to remove the privileges of the Roman Church, neither found rest in the present life nor escaped eternal perdition.

In their times, the army of the Persians invaded Mesopotamia, and the most wicked nation of the Saracens wrested from Roman rule all Africa, Marmarica, Libya, Egypt, Arabia, Judaea, and Phoenicia. From the north, the ferocity of the Huns, the Gothic storm, and the Vandal tempest devastated the whole West, until the tenth horn of the beast—that is, Lombard madness, drawn from the sheath of the Lord’s fury—invaded the regions of Italy. Of that persecution it is better to remain silent than to say little.

[Col. 0808D] There were also exceedingly religious emperors, such as Theodosius, Honorius, that same Theodosius, the pious pair Marcian and Valentinian, Constantine, Irene, Leo, Justinian, and certain others who, as we mentioned above, governed the state in profound peace and exchanged death for eternal life.

While Theodosius the First was emperor, Ambrose, Augustine, and Jerome were living their earthly lives; they left us many salutary precepts for living. When Ambrose was threatened with expulsion from the Church by order of Valentinian and Justina, he was defended by the armed populace. The priest of God did not condemn the people’s divine fervor, but rather praised it.

At the same time, the venerable Augustine urged the prince Boniface to plunder and devastate the Donatists and Circumcellions. [Col. 0809A]

But since mention has been made above of religious princes, I have judged it necessary to insert into this little work something about their lives and the laws promulgated by them. Let us now begin with Theodosius himself. Having assumed the governance of the kingdom, he wonderfully defeated and subdued the barbarians, expelled the Arians from the churches and restored the churches to the orthodox, forced the Persians to remain within their own borders, and expelled the tyrant Maximus from the kingdom.

Meanwhile, after bringing peace to the kingdom, he came to Thessalonica and, by royal authority, rashly ordered the people to be killed. When he came to Milan, he was barred by Saint Ambrose from the threshold of the church. Thus, recognizing his sin, he wept publicly outside the church until [Col. 0809B] he obtained forgiveness—the manuscript reads *donec* (“until”) here—and a law was enacted that sentences pronounced by the princes under threat of punishment should not have binding force for forty days.

How much reverence his sons Arcadius and Honorius showed toward the priest of God is testified by the laws they promulgated, as follows:

“The emperors Arcadius and Honorius, Augusti, to Theodorus, prefect and governor. If anyone should fall into this kind of sacrilege, namely, by invading a Catholic church and inflicting any injury upon the priests and ministers, or upon the worship itself and the place, let the provincial governors take notice of what has been done; and let the governor of the province know that injury to the priests and ministers of the Catholic Church, to the place itself, and to divine worship must be punished by a capital sentence imposed upon those convicted or confessing.” [Col. 0809C]

And a little later:

“Let it be considered praiseworthy by all to prosecute atrocious injuries inflicted upon priests as a public crime and to earn vengeance for such deeds,” and so forth.

Let us also hear what the pious pair Marcian and Valentinian wrote to the blessed Pope Leo:

“And we believe that your Holiness, possessing primacy in the episcopate of the faith, should justly be addressed first in sacred letters. We invite and entreat you that, for the stability of our empire and the security of the state, your Holiness pray to the eternal Divinity.”

Now observe how Constantine—not the first, but another, surnamed Pius—the emperor, wrote to the lord pope:

“By God Almighty, there is with us no favor toward either party; rather, we shall observe equality toward both parties. We shall in no way impose any necessity upon those who are loved by you, in whatever matter they may be involved; we shall consider them worthy of every appropriate honor, generosity, and reception. If they should agree with one another, well and good; but if they do not agree at all, we shall send them back to you with every courtesy.”

And a little later:

“We can invite and entreat them toward every correction and the unity of all Christians, but we absolutely do not wish to impose compulsion.”

Now attend to what the emperors Constantine and Irene wrote to Pope Hadrian:

“We ask your paternal Blessedness—indeed, the Lord God asks, ‘who wishes all to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth (I Tim. II, 4)’—to give himself and make no delay, and to come here.” [Col. 0810A]

Hear also what Justinian wrote to the holy Pope John in laws that he promulgated:

“We ask your paternal affection to make it clear to us, by letters sent from you to us, that your Holiness receives those who rightly confess the aforesaid doctrines, and condemns those who, in Jewish fashion, have dared to deny the true faith.”

But after, as we related above, Lombard madness invaded the regions of Italy, it is not easy to say how many kinds of punishment and how many bitter and most cruel deaths they inflicted upon Christians during the three years in which they remained pagan. After they received baptism in the Arian heresy, the suffering was somewhat less; [Col. 0810B] but for 140 years, during which they did not govern Italy but ravaged it, they exercised such a cruel tyranny that anyone wishing to know about these calamities should read the book of the *Dialogues* and the *Pontifical Deeds of the Saints*; there he will find calamities of calamities and miseries of miseries.

The second book ends.

## The Third Book Begins

In the time of Hadrian, the supreme pontiff, when the aforesaid pope saw himself oppressed by many miseries, he sent his apostolic letters by sea to Charles, the most excellent king of the Franks, entreating him, just as his father of holy memory, Pippin, had done, to come to the aid of the holy Church of God against the insolence [Col. 0810C] and tyranny of Desiderius, king of the Lombards.

Then Charles, protected by the Lord, gathered the entire multitude of his army and besieged that same Desiderius in the city of Pavia for six months. When the feast of Easter arrived, he hastened with great eagerness to the threshold of the apostles. The pontiff sent venerable crosses—that is, standards—to meet him, together with all the military schools and boys carrying branches of olive or palm.

When the most excellent king saw those most holy crosses and standards, he immediately dismounted from his horse and proceeded on foot with his men to blessed Peter. The venerable pontiff awaited him on Holy Saturday of Easter, on the steps of the apostolic hall itself, with the clergy and Roman people. When Charles arrived, having kissed all the steps of blessed Peter, he reached the aforementioned pontiff.

After they had embraced one another, the most Christian king took the pontiff’s hand and hastened with all his men to the confession of blessed Peter. There he prostrated himself on the ground and paid his vows to God and his holy apostle.

Then the king earnestly begged the pontiff to grant him permission to enter Rome so that he might pray in the various churches. Together they descended to the body of blessed Peter with the Roman and Frankish judges, and, having mutually strengthened themselves by oaths, immediately entered Rome. After the celebration of Easter, on Wednesday he offered great gifts to blessed Peter and returned [Col. 0811A] to the siege of Pavia. With God and that same apostle assisting him, he carried away Desiderius, king of the Lombards, together with his wife, and subjected his entire kingdom to himself.

When Charles died, his son Louis succeeded him, a very gentle man and the first of all the Frankish kings to be elevated to imperial dignity. He offered many gifts to blessed Peter and restored privileges established in ancient times. He enacted the following law for the future:

“In the election of the Roman pontiffs, let neither slave nor free man presume to come forward in order to place any obstacle before those Romans whom the ancient custom, established by the constitution of the holy Fathers, has admitted to this election. And if anyone should presume to act against this constitution of ours, let him be handed over to exile. Moreover, we prohibit any one of our agents from daring to devise any pretext for interference in the aforesaid election.” [Col. 0811B]

After his death, through the many cycles of succeeding times and down to the pestilential age of Lothair, those who descended from him governed the empire most worthily. If any diligent person wishes to know them, let him read the laws promulgated by them, observe the tombs of the martyrs decorated with gold and gems, and their basilicas adorned with wonderful beauty; let him also consider the religious monasteries of both sexes established by them, and the communities of clergy living according to rule that they first organized, as well as the relics that remain into our own times. From these things he will readily perceive how Christian and how beloved by God they were.

The laws promulgated by them are as follows:

“From the capitularies [the manuscript reads *ex victis*] of the emperors Charles and Louis: Since we are not ignorant of the sacred canons, and so that, in the name of God, the holy Church may enjoy its honor more freely, we give our assent to the ecclesiastical order: namely, that through the election of clergy and people, according to the provisions of the canons, persons should be chosen from their own diocese, without regard to the acceptance of persons or gifts, on account of the merit of their life and the gift of wisdom, so that by example and word they may everywhere be able to benefit those subject to them.”

Also, a constitution of the emperor Charles:

“We wish and command that all who, with the Lord’s help, are subject to our rule—Romans as well as Franks, Alamanni, Bavarians, Saxons, Lotharingians, Ripuarians, Gauls, [Col. 0811D] Burgundians, Britons, Lombards, Gascons, Beneventans, Goths, Spaniards, and all the rest who are subject to us, whether bound to us by any bond of law or connected with us by customary practice—should all observe this judgment as a perpetual law.

This judgment, which we sent in response to the questions addressed to Duke Ablavius from the sixteenth book of the Emperor Theodosius, namely chapter eleven, and which, with the advice of all our faithful men, we placed among our capitularies to be held as law, shall be observed by all as an everlasting law:

Whoever has a lawsuit or is a petitioner, whether at the beginning of the lawsuit or after the passage of time, whether when the case is being initiated or when judgment has already begun to be pronounced, if he chooses the judgment of the bishop, the antistes of the sacred law, he shall immediately, without any doubt—even if one party objects—be directed, together with the litigants’ statement, to the judgment of the bishops. For the authority of the sacred religion investigates and brings forth many matters that the constraints of extensive legal prescription do not permit to be brought forth in court.

Therefore, all cases, whether handled under praetorian or civil law, once concluded by the judgments of bishops, shall be confirmed by the law of perpetual stability; nor shall it be permitted for the case decided by the judgments of bishops to be litigated further. Let the testimony even of a single bishop be accepted without hesitation by all judges, and let no other testimony be heard when the testimony of a bishop has been offered by either party. For we confirm by this salutary edict, and decree that it be held by perpetual law, that which has been established by the authority of truth, that which the conscience of an undefiled mind has delivered through a most holy man.”

[Col. 0812B] These are laws worthy of Christian emperors, who governed the kingdom not, as is customary among Greek emperors, through the cunning of eunuchs, but through the prudence of priests. Therefore they are blessed: because, as long as they lived in the present world, they rested in profound peace, and in the future they will reign with Christ without end.

But when the aforesaid Lothair had often been admonished by Pope Nicholas to dismiss his concubine Waldrada, and refused to comply, he deserved the sentence of excommunication. Unhappy man that he was, he did not repent but added sin to sin; he dared to slander the gift of the elder pope of Rome. Therefore he was not only excommunicated but also deposed from imperial dignity and from all Frankish power.

[Col. 0812C] How many calamities he inflicted upon the Romans, how he injured the pope’s gift, despised him when he demanded an accounting from him, seized the church of Saint Peter by military force, and perished by a most shameful death—these things are testified both by the histories of the Franks and by the kingdom of the Franks, which remains divided to this day.

Meanwhile, after the Frankish kingdom had been destroyed through pride, the Italian kingdom suffered various calamities. At one time it was not governed but rather devastated by the tyranny of the Lombards; at another, by the violence of the Burgundians; and most often, by the arrogance of the Salian Franks.

At the same time the Roman Church was subjected to dangerous disasters. For, since the emperors were unable to bring aid to the Romans because of the very frequent incursions of the senators, and since the Franks, as we said above, were divided and separated from the Church, the captains of the city of Rome, arrogating to themselves the empty name of patriciate, devastated the Roman Church with great violence.

That name was empty because it is found nowhere in the Roman records, either in pagan or in Christian times. If it were some genuine dignity, either its holders would be found designated in the records, or laws promulgated, or tablets marked with it. Yet nothing of this sort is found anywhere in Roman laws. But let it be granted that it was some dignity perhaps suitable for establishing an emperor; it was in no way appropriate for the ordination of the supreme pontiff.

How this institution began I shall explain briefly, if I can. When Rome was being oppressed by the Gothic storm, the Vandal sword, and Lombard madness, the Romans, unable to withstand the attacks of the barbarians, implored military protection from the emperors. The emperors willingly provided it insofar as circumstances allowed. For, sending from their side eunuchs who were highly approved men, such as Narses and Belisarius and many others, they appointed them commanders of the army. When these men came to Italy, they often put the barbarians to flight; at other times they merely defended the walls of the city.

The simple Roman populace called them “fathers of the city,” or patricians, following the custom by which the leading men of the Roman city are still called protectors today.

But let us continue with the sequence of events. The captains of the city whom we mentioned above, once they had seized tyranny, did everything as they pleased. For [Col. 0813B] they not only disgraced the cardinalates, abbeys, and bishoprics through the most shameful buying and selling, but also bestowed the very pontificate of the Roman Church—without regard for any dignity of character or for any prerogative of so great a Church—solely at their pleasure, upon whomever they wished or whoever filled their hands most generously, and not only upon clergy but also upon laymen. Thus, often on one and the same day, a man was both layman and pontiff.

As the head grew weak, the other members also became infirm, to such an extent that not only the ministers of the altar of the secondary order—priests and Levites—but even the pontiffs themselves were commonly regarded as living in concubinage. The practice had by then grown so widespread that it seemed to erase the infamy, and the custom of the most shameful buying and selling somehow appeared to lessen the offense. These things were done not only in the regions of Rome but throughout the lands of the entire West. For while the shepherd was silent—or rather, while he fled, indeed while he himself had become a wolf as guardian—who would stand in defense of the sheep? [Col. 0813C]

While these things were happening, the most contemptible nation of the Saracens ravaged the coastal regions of Italy; thereafter it invaded part of Calabria and all Sicily. From the north, the powerful nation of the Hungarians crossed the Danube, devastating all the regions adjoining it, and moreover plundering all Germany and Gaul as far as the British Sea. Finally, coming through the kingdoms of the Burgundians into Italy, it so devastated the country that, with the country people nearly all led away captive, it was reduced almost to a wilderness.

The third book ends.

## The Fourth Book Begins

[Col. 0813D]

While Hungarian savagery was raging, a certain king of the Saxons and Franks named Otto arose. He defeated them in war twice and, in the third war, almost annihilated them, forcing them to dwell within their own borders.

But since mention has been made of so great a king, I think it worthwhile to write from what ancestors he was descended and how he reached the heights of the Roman kingdom. He was a Saxon by race, the son of Henry, the great king of the Saxons and Franks. Henry was first duke of the Saxons, but after King Conrad had died, he received the insignia of the kingdom through Hemurard, Conrad’s brother.

Having assumed the royal insignia, Henry very quickly pacified Francia and, by engaging in war, liberated Saxony from Hungarian servitude. Then, after expelling King Arnulf, he subjected Bavaria to his rule and afterward handed it over as a duchy to his son Henry. He received Burchard, duke of the Swabians, into submission. Thereafter, through his son-in-law Cunibert, he joined western Francia to the Saxon empire. He also gave his daughter Uta in marriage to Louis, king of the Latins and Franks. Thus, after settling all affairs, he designated his son Otto as king in his place and, as a great builder of God’s churches and propagator of the Christian religion, rested in a blessed end.

His son Otto succeeded him, a magnificent and wholly Christian man. First, as we said above, he defeated the Hungarians; and he liberated not only his entire kingdom but also the whole of the West from their servitude. He restored his kinsman Louis to the paternal throne and kingdom, from which Hugh’s tyranny had expelled him. For Otto entered Francia with a military force, besieged and captured the city of Reims, and entered Paris. He pursued Hugh, the author of the tyranny, as far as the British Sea.

From there, coming to Aachen, he ordered the eagle, the Roman standard that for many years had stood with outstretched wings against the Germans, to be displayed before the Franks to this day. [Col. 0814B]

From there he came to Mainz and deprived Rudolf, king of the Burgundians, who was waging war against him, of life and kingdom. Rudolf’s lance—the distinctive emblem of the empire—is carried before our imperial rulers to this day.

When these matters had been completed, and so great a king had been deprived of his first wife, he heard the report of the most noble and prudent Adelaide [written between the lines: Adelhaida], formerly the wife of Lothair, king of the Lombards. The tyrant Berengar had besieged her together with Count Otto at Canossa for many years. Pitying the sufferings of so great a queen and admiring the loyalty of so great a count, Otto resolved to bring aid.

He very quickly gathered the multitude of his army. After Berengar had been killed and his sons expelled from the kingdom, Otto peacefully took possession of the kingdom on the advice of the count, and took Adelaide as his wife.

Thereafter, wishing to see Rome on the advice of that same Otto, he gave Pope John of the city of Rome a bodily oath in the following form:

“To you, my lord Pope John, I, King Otto, promise and swear by the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, and by the wood of the wondrous Cross, and by these relics of the saints, that, if God permits me to come to Rome, I shall exalt the holy Roman Church and you, its ruler, to the best of my ability. I shall never, by my will, consent, counsel, or exhortation, cause you to lose either your life or your limbs or the very honor that you possess. In Rome I shall make no agreement or appointment concerning anything that pertains to you or to the Romans without your counsel. Whatever land of Saint Peter comes into our power, I shall return to you. Whoever I entrust with the Italian kingdom, I shall make him swear that he will be your helper, according to his ability, in defending the land of Saint Peter.”

Then, proceeding toward Rome, he was honorably received by the Romans and elevated by the lord pope with the imperial blessing. [Col. 0815A] He was the first of all the German kings to be called emperor.

After pacifying Italy, he returned with his wife to Saxony. By her he had a son, to whom, both in succession of name and of kingdom, he gave a wife of Roman blood—namely, the daughter of the emperor of Constantinople.

After Otto had built a church of marvelous beauty at Mainz [*Mainburc*; Hartmann Schedel, whose the codex once was, wrote in the margin: “Magdeburg”] and had recalled many peoples of the gentiles to the way of truth, he was seized by illness and reached the end of his life. His body was buried with fitting honor in the aforesaid church.

When his son had assumed the empire, he equaled his father in every respect and became most zealous in the worship of the churches and most devoted to the Christian religion. After arranging the affairs of the kingdom well, he hastened to Rome [Col. 0815B] and received the imperial blessing.

Thereafter, advancing into Apulia, he waged war against the emperor of Constantinople and, having been defeated twice on the same day, appeared victorious on the third occasion. Returning to Rome, he was seized by the violence of a fever and died at the threshold of the apostles. There he lies buried in peace, truly blessed, and thrice and four times blessed, since, out of so great a number of emperors and kings, he alone deserved to share a burial among the pontiffs with the prince of the apostles.

He left a son, indeed as heir of the kingdom and name—if only also of his piety! When the boy had begun to reign and had already reached adulthood, at his mother’s urging he sent a certain John, bishop of Piacenza, Greek by birth, across the sea [Col. 0815C] to obtain for him a wife of Roman blood.

At that time a certain Crescentius, captain of the city of Rome, who had arrogated to himself the empty name of patriciate, seized the tyranny and expelled from the pontificate the lord pope who had crowned Otto, the father of this young man. Fearing the king’s proximity—for the king had already crossed the Alps—and greatly alarmed by the fact that the pope was already awaiting his arrival at Ravenna, Crescentius considered within himself that he might appease the fury of the king and queen in this way: by ordaining as pontiff the bishop John whom we mentioned above, the king’s closest friend and the queen’s foster-brother.

But “there is neither wisdom nor counsel against the Lord (Prov. XXI, 30).” For when the aforesaid king came to Rome, he captured Crescentius, who had been besieged for a long time, and cut off his head. The invader of the supreme pontificate [rather, “the pontificate”], inflamed with zeal for justice—but more than justice required—he deprived of his sight and dishonored in his other limbs.

This deed so displeased God and blessed Peter, the prince of the apostles, that before he attained the imperial blessing, and before the moon had completed its course three times, he ended his life, hateful to the Lord, without the viaticum. Although he died in a suburb less than thirty miles from the city, all the Romans, by common agreement, scorned to give him burial.

His body, cut with knives and preserved by the art of physicians, was carried to Saxony [the manuscript reads: “was transferred”]. When he had died and been buried in hell, the entire power of the Saxons, Franks, Bavarians, and Swabians assembled together and chose as their king Henry, a man of the same blood, most Christian and suitably adorned with virtuous character.

Meanwhile, the Lombards, finding that they had an opportune moment, assembled at Pavia and chose Arduino as king, a man vigorous in arms but imprudent in counsel. Tedald, however, duke and margrave, withdrew from that conspiracy and transferred himself and his possessions to the German king. With his counsel and aid, after many varied disasters of war, King Henry gained possession of Italy and, coming to Rome, was elevated to imperial dignity by Pope Benedict.

What more is there to say? He possessed the principality of Apulia in peace, granted many privileges to the Roman Church, and gave it the most generous gifts. Then, coming to Pavia, he captured it—since at that time it did not resist him—more by deceit than by arms, and gave it to the flames. He crossed the mountains and, having no sons, established the bishopric of Bamberg from his own property; through a charter of donation he handed it over to blessed Peter. There he built and magnificently adorned a church of the blessed princes of the apostles. In his time Stephen, king of the Hungarians, received the sacrament of baptism, and through him the entire people subject to him did likewise. [Col. 0816B]

The aforesaid Henry, since he had no son, chose the apostles as his heirs. As he reached the end of his life, he rested in a blessed death. His body was buried with fitting honor in the church of the blessed apostles, which he himself had dedicated.

The fourth book ends.

## The Fifth Book Begins

[Col. 0816D] [The heading is written in the margin, but by the same hand, in silver letters.]

Conrad, by surname, succeeded him in the kingdom, a most warlike man. After the death of the emperor Henry, he defeated the Bohemians, who were carrying the royal standards, and brought back their standards. He very quickly pacified Francia, which was in turmoil. He expelled from the duchy and stripped of his patrimony a certain Canon [I think Cunon is intended], duke of the Bavarians, who claimed some share of the royal dignity for himself, and forced him to flee to Hungary.

Then he entered Saxony. After all the affairs of the kingdom had been properly settled, he attacked the Luticians and carried on the war, forcing them to flee as far as Belgrade.

[Col. 0816D] After these events, he sent his honorable envoys, as was fitting, to the lord pope, entreating him to send a banner from the side of blessed Peter, so that, strengthened by it, he might subject the kingdom of Hungary to his rule.

When the pope heard this, he gladly granted the request and, sending noble men from his own side—namely, the bishop of Porto and Belinzo, a most noble Roman of the Marmorata—gave them these instructions: if the king did not object, they themselves were to carry the banners in the first battle line; but if the king objected, they were to tell him:

“Behold the victory that we promised you; see that you do not ascribe it to yourself, but to the apostles.”

And so it happened. For [Col. 0817A] when battle was joined, the Hungarians fled, and even the lance of the Hungarian king was captured. It was brought to Rome by those same envoys, and to this day it is displayed before the confession of blessed Peter the apostle as a sign of victory.

Meanwhile, having won the Hungarian victory, Conrad entered Italy. He captured Aribert, archbishop of Milan, but Aribert escaped by flight. Then Conrad came to Rome and deserved to receive the imperial blessing.

Afterward, returning to Milan, he ravaged certain suburbs and was driven back from the city. Thus, with his undertaking unfinished, he crossed the Alps, was seized by the violence of a fever, and died. His body was buried at Speyer with fitting honor.

His son Henry succeeded him, a most wise and wholly Christian man. At the beginning of his reign he defeated the Hungarians when they were in turmoil and very quickly brought them to submission. [Col. 0817B] When he had duly pacified all the affairs of the kingdom and was planning to set out for Italy, messengers coming from the city of Rome and delaying him made him remarkably anxious. For, as we mentioned above, the captains of the city of Rome, and especially the Tusculans, were devastating the Roman Church under the empty title of the patriciate, so that they seemed to possess the pontificate for themselves by a kind of hereditary right. Indeed, after John, the brother of Pope Benedict, had died—the man who on one and the same day had been both prefect and pope [Note: [Col. 0817D] These words had been erased, but were substituted in the codex by the same hand]—Theophylact succeeded him. Gregory, his brother, claimed for himself the name and dignity of patrician. On this occasion Theophylact, fearing neither God nor man, was called, by way of antiphrasis, Benedict [Note: [Col. 0817D] Benedict IX]. After he had perpetrated many shameful adulteries and murders with his own hands, he finally wished to take his cousin as his wife, namely the daughter of Girard of Saxony. When Girard said that he would in no way give her to him unless he renounced the pontificate, Theophylact withdrew to a certain priest named John, who at that time was considered a man of great merit, and, on his advice, condemned himself and renounced the pontificate. This counsel would have been highly praiseworthy had not a most shameful sin followed afterward. For that same priest, of whom we have spoken above, taking advantage of this opportunity and seduced by wicked ambition, through the most shameful sale and by the payment of enormous sums of money compelled the entire Roman people to swear allegiance to him; and thus he ascended to the pontifical dignity, and, changing his name, they called him Gregory [Note: [Col. 0818D] Gregory VI].

When these things had happened, Girard of [Col. 0817D] Saxony, together with the other captains, chose as pontiff a certain bishop of the Sabines, whom, changing his name, they called Sylvester [Note: [Col. 0818D] Sylvester III]. When Gregory the patrician and Peter, Theophylact’s brother, heard this, they again raised Theophylact—deceived by the hope of marriage—to the heights of the pontificate. But where could there be any place of remedy for us amid such calamities, except for that evangelical voice which strengthens the apostle, saying: “I have prayed for you, Peter, that your faith may not fail” (Luke XXII, 32)? Yet certainly Peter’s faith did not fail, nor will the faith of the Roman Church fail for ever.

For amid so great and violent a storm the Lord stirred up the spirit of a certain Roman archdeacon, Peter, [Col. 0818A] who summoned bishops, cardinals [Note: [Col. 0818D] He adds “bishops”], clergy, and monks, men and women whom the fear of the Lord had touched to some degree. Withdrawing himself from communion with the aforesaid usurpers and moved by zeal for God, just as that Omas, the Hebrew priest, once did, Peter crossed the Alps and approached the king—not to accuse anyone, but for the common welfare of the Church. Falling at his feet, he tearfully begged him to come to the aid of his desolated mother as quickly as possible. The king then summoned the bishops who were present and ordered them to travel to Rome with him and convene a synod. This was done without delay.

That abusive Gregory, however, who seemed to govern the chair of the Roman Church, was asked by the king to come to meet him. Since, as the subsequent outcome showed, he was conscious of no evil in himself, he came as far as Piacenza [Col. 0818B] and found the king there, who, as was fitting, was honorably received by him at Pavia. For the bishops who were then present did not think that it would be religious to condemn anyone without judgment, least of all one who seemed to be the pontiff of so great a see. Thus they proceeded together and came to Sutri. When they had arrived there, the aforesaid king asked the man who at that time seemed to be the pontiff that a synod be convened. He granted this and confirmed it by decree. For he was an unlearned man and of remarkable simplicity.

Accordingly, when the synod had assembled, the man who held the place of the Roman pontiff took his seat, and at his command the patriarchs, metropolitans, and bishops sat in their appointed places. Among them there happened to be Poppo, patriarch of Aquileia, a most eloquent man; Bruno, bishop of Augsburg; Rembaldus, archbishop of Arles; [Col. 0818C] and many others. When the question concerning Sylvester the usurper arose, all judged that he should be stripped of his episcopal and priestly office and handed over to a monastery for the rest of his life. Concerning Theophylact, they judged that the matter should be left aside, especially since he himself, as Roman pontiff, had judged that he ought to be deposed.

But concerning the third man, what could they do, and where could they turn, when no permission was given to accuse or testify against the judge? When the bishops begged him to disclose the grounds for his election, he, being unlearned, revealed the whole purity of his election. He said that by the mercy of God he had been a priest of good testimony and reputation and had always lived from childhood with a chaste body. At that time this seemed among the Romans not merely praiseworthy but almost angelic.

For this reason, he said, he had acquired much money, which he kept so that he might restore the church’s roof and walls or accomplish some great new work in the city of Rome. And when he often considered the tyranny of the patricians and how they appointed pontiffs without any election by clergy or people, he thought that nothing could be better than to restore, with this money, the election which tyranny had unjustly taken away from clergy and people.

When religious men heard this, they began with the greatest reverence to point out to him the deceits of the ancient enemy, saying that nothing which was bought and sold could be holy. [Col. 0819A] Persuaded by these and other admonitions, he began already to conceive the Holy Spirit in his mind. Recognizing that he had possessed zeal for God, but not according to knowledge, he addressed the bishops in these words:

“I call God to witness concerning my soul, brothers: I believed that by this I would obtain remission of sins and merit God’s grace. But now I truly recognize the cunning of the ancient enemy; advise me publicly what I ought to do.”

They replied to him:

“Take your case into your own bosom; judge yourself with your own mouth. It is better for you to live here poor with blessed Peter, for whose love you did these things, so that you may be rich for eternity, than, with Simon Magus, who deceived you, to shine with riches in the present and perish for eternity.”

When he heard this, he pronounced sentence upon himself in these words: [Col. 0819B]

“I, Gregory, bishop and servant of the servants of God, on account of the most shameful sale of the Simoniac heresy, which through the cunning of the ancient enemy entered into my election, judge that I must be removed from the Roman episcopate.”

And he added: “Does this please you [Note: [Col. 0819D] This Synod of Sutri and the record of Gregory VII’s voluntary abdication are greatly illuminated by this writer of ours amid the very great disagreement of the authorities; and he also preserved with the greatest accuracy what had been done at Sutri, which for some time afterward benefited that see]?” They answered: “What pleases you, we also confirm.”

When the synod had been duly celebrated, the king and the bishops came in great agitation, both because they had no pontiff who could bestow imperial power upon the king and because, in choosing another, the clergy had the right of election but did not at all have the subsequent acclaim of the people. For the aforesaid John had bound them by an oath never, while he lived, to acclaim another pontiff.

Meanwhile, since they had no one from their own diocese—for, as we mentioned above, when the head was languishing, the other members were so feeble that in so great a Church scarcely one person could be found who was not either unlearned, or Simoniac, or living with a concubine—in this necessity they chose for themselves Sicherius, a Bavarian bishop. The canons forbade anyone to ascend to the Roman pontificate who had not been ordained priest and deacon in that same Church. In his favor a few laymen, but those who had not sworn to John, gave their consent.

He was the first after the blessed prince of the apostles, in so long a succession of Roman pontiffs, who, though consecrated elsewhere, was called Roman pontiff. But according to the decrees of blessed Pope Innocent, what necessity discovers as a remedy must necessarily cease when the necessity ceases. The same pressure also prevailed [thus in the codex, perhaps “urgebat”], because one order is legitimate, while another is a usurpation which present circumstances compel to occur.

But let us now return to the matters at hand. After the king had been endowed with imperial dignity, he, sympathizing with the calamities of the state, freed the city from the tyranny of the patricians. This would have been very praiseworthy had a subsequent act not stained what he had done. For, enticed by popular rumors—whereas it is a most serious maxim that such rumors ought not to be believed—he seized the tyranny of the patriciate, as though some dignity had been established in the lay order that possessed more privilege than imperial majesty. But what could be more bitter or cruel in this calamity than for one who shortly before had punished the Tusculans for tyranny to wish to become like those very men whom he had condemned?

What, indeed, drew the mind of so great a man into so great an offense, except that he believed that through the order of the patriciate he could appoint a Roman pontiff? But alas! Where was the prudence of so many bishops, where the learning of so many experts in law, that they should believe what had not been permitted to lords was permitted to servants? It had not been permitted for any emperor, even one holding supreme power, to intrude himself into the election of a Roman pontiff; would it be permitted to a man placed under authority?

But they will say: “We read that Charlemagne too was designated by the name of patrician.” If they read this, [Col. 0820B] why did they not understand it? In the time of Charlemagne, Constantine and Irene governed the Roman Empire. Therefore, what could the apostolic see confer upon the most excellent king of the Franks at that time except to call him the father and protector of the city of Rome? For this is how he is read: “Charles, king of the Franks and Lombards, and patrician of the Romans.” We never read that he was endowed with imperial power [Note: [Col. 0820D] He had said this above as well, and I am not sure with how much good faith]. But after his death, his son Louis was the first of all kings foreign to Roman blood to merit the imperial benediction from the Roman see; and because he had the highest things, he did not seek the lowest.

But let us return to the narrative.

Accordingly, after he had properly settled affairs in Italy, Emperor Henry returned to his homeland, taking with him the venerable John whom we mentioned above. The God-beloved Hildebrand followed him, wishing to show reverence toward his lord. For he had formerly been his chaplain. Not long afterward, when the aforesaid John had reached the banks of the Rhine, he was struck by illness and died.

After his death and burial in peace, the venerable Hildebrand set out for Cluny, where he became a monk and pursued philosophy with distinction among religious men.

Meanwhile, when Clement, the Roman pontiff, had died, the Romans made their way to the emperor and asked that a pontiff be given to them, and he consented. For, by the tyrannical power of the patriciate, he gave them from his own side a certain bishop, a man full of every kind of arrogance, and ordered the renowned Duke Boniface to lead him to Rome and enthrone him on his behalf. This was done; and they also called him by another name, Damasus. After he had seized the pontifical see, before twenty days had passed he died in body and soul. When the bishops from beyond the Alps heard of his very rapid death, they thereafter feared to come there.

Meanwhile, the Romans, terrified by the pontiff’s sudden death, nevertheless, since they could not remain long without a pontiff, traveled northward, crossed the Alps, and went to Saxony. There they found the king and asked that a pontiff be given to them. But because this could not easily be done at that moment—for the bishops were unwilling to travel to Rome—he decided to visit the land of the Franks along the Rhine, believing that he could find in the kingdom of Lothair a bishop whom he could give to the Romans as pontiff.

This was done. For only after many prayers and the Romans’ entreaties was Bruno, a most noble man, decently adorned in character, namely bishop of Toul, barely persuaded. When he came to Besançon, the venerable abbot of Cluny went out to meet him, taking with him in his company the venerable Hildebrand, whom we mentioned above.

When Hildebrand heard from someone recounting the reason for the journey, he began to ask his father not to proceed there, saying that the man was not apostolic but apostatic [Note: [Col. 0821D] These words are found in almost the same form in the Life of Leo IX by Nicholas, cardinal of the Roman Church of Aragon, who unquestionably copied them from Bonizo. But Wibert, archdeacon of Toul and contemporary of Leo, whom the distinguished Muratori appended to Nicholas, completely disproves the story of Hildebrand’s taking on the clothing of a pilgrim at Cluny at Hildebrand’s urging. Whatever may be true of this story—or, as Muratori thinks there, of this fiction—he is certainly mistaken in considering Otto of Freising its first architect, since Bonizo had reported it long before], who, at the emperor’s command, was attempting to seize the Roman [Col. 0821B] pontificate.

When the venerable father heard this, he indeed kept silent, but came to Besançon. Taking the opportunity, he promptly disclosed these matters to the venerable bishop, adding at the same time praise of his character and the integrity of his way of life.

Why say more? The pontiff asked to obtain an interview with him. This was done, and when the three had gathered in the name of the Lord, according to the evangelical saying, “where God was in the midst of them” (Matthew XVIII, 20), Bruno, yielding to Hildebrand’s advice, laid aside the papal insignia that he was wearing, took up a pilgrim’s wallet, and hastened to the threshold of the apostles. When he came into the church of the prince of the apostles, he addressed the Roman clergy and people as follows:

“Brothers, I have heard your embassy, and I ought not to have refused you. I have descended here to you, first from a desire for prayer, and then wishing to obey your commands.”

When the bishops and cardinals replied to him in these words: “This was the reason for calling you: so that we might elect you as our pontiff,” and the archdeacon, as customary, cried out, “Saint Peter has chosen the Lord Leo as pontiff,” while the people following repeated this with their voices, the cardinals and bishops, according to custom, enthroned him in the chair of the blessed prince of the apostles.

After he had attained the papal dignity, he promoted the venerable Hildebrand, the donor of such salutary advice, whom he had scarcely obtained from the abbot after many prayers, to the honor of the subdiaconate, and appointed him steward of the holy Roman Church. [Col. 0821D] On his advice he soon convened a synod, to which bishops from various regions assembled. In it, under penalty of anathema, it was forbidden for any bishop to sell archdeaconates, provostships, abbeys, or benefices of the churches, or prebends, or commendations of churches or altars.

It was also forbidden for priests, Levites, and subdeacons to have intercourse with their wives. This aroused the ancient serpent to great anger. When the bishops heard this, at first they kept silent, unable to resist the truth; afterward, persuaded by the enemy of the human race, they concealed their disobedience.

Meanwhile, in Rome, bishops, cardinals, and abbots ordained through the Simoniac heresy were deposed, and others were ordained there from various provinces: from Gaul of Lyon, Ubertus, bishop of Silva Candida; from the Burgundian people, Stephen, abbot and cardinal; from Mount Romericus, Hugh Candidus, who afterward became an apostate; Frederick, the brother of Duke Gotefrid; and, from Compendio, a certain Azolinus, bishop of Sutri; from the territory of Ravenna, Peter Damiani, a most eloquent man; and many others.

Then the strong man armed, who had guarded his courtyard in profound peace (Luke XI, 21), recognized that he had been bound. [Col. 0822B] In the following year the aforesaid pontiff convened a synod, in which all, clergy and laity alike, were commanded by the authority of Saint Peter and the Roman Church to abstain from communion with fornicator priests and Levites.

This synod plunged the sword into the enemy’s entrails. For not only in Rome were incontinent priests and Levites forbidden the ministry of the altar, but also throughout the neighboring regions all around and throughout Tuscany, with the assistance of monks, religious men who labored zealously in the word of preaching.

This blessed pontiff also sent his legates to Constantinople, since he had disputes with the Greek bishops concerning certain matters. Among their number was the aforesaid Frederick, the brother of the great Duke Gotefrid. When they came to Constantinople, they were honorably received by the emperor Monomachus.

After the business of the bishops, on account of which they had come, had been settled very quickly, they were presented with magnificent gifts. Carrying very great offerings to blessed Peter, they returned to their own country.

Meanwhile, the most powerful people of the Normans, who had withdrawn Apulia and Calabria from the dominion of the Greek kingdom, invaded the Beneventans. At that time the Beneventans, compelled by necessity, went to Rome and, handing over Benevento to blessed Peter by a charter of donation, implored aid from the lord pope.

When this had been done, he was moved not only by the lands of the holy Roman Church that had been invaded, but also by the bitterest punishments which they inflicted upon Christians. At first he struck them with the sword of excommunication, and soon judged that they should be struck with the material sword as well.

But since the counsels of God are a great abyss (Psalm XXXV, 7), when battle was joined, by God’s ineffable providence the Normans emerged victorious. They captured the pope, but treated him honorably, as was fitting, and led him through the midst of the slaughtered dead as far as Benevento.

But why say more? Those who had been struck down in battle while fighting for justice, God showed by signs [Col. 0823A] and miracles to have been very pleasing to him, giving future generations great confidence to fight for justice, since he deigned to number them among the saints.

When these things had happened, the most blessed pope returned to Rome. When he had reached the church of the prince of the apostles, he was overcome by illness and carried before the confession of that same apostle. There, before all the clergy and the Roman people, he entrusted the care of that Church to the God-beloved Hildebrand and gave up his spirit to heaven. His body was buried in the same church with great honor. The sick come to his tomb and are healed, and those afflicted by various illnesses are continually freed from them.

But when the venerable Hildebrand perceived that the Roman clergy and people had agreed upon his election, only with many tears and supplications could he obtain that they follow his counsel in the election of a pontiff. Then, crossing the Alps with religious men, he approached the emperor and became so closely joined to him in friendship that in frequent conversations he showed him how great a sin he had committed in the appointment of a pontiff.

Yielding to his salutary advice, the emperor laid aside the tyranny of the patriciate and granted the Roman clergy and people the election of the supreme pontiff according to the ancient privileges. He then brought with him unwillingly to Rome, against the will of that same emperor, a certain bishop of Asti [the text intends to say “of Aist”], the aforesaid emperor’s steward. When the clergy had elected him in Saint Peter’s Church according to ancient custom and the people had acclaimed him, the cardinals immediately enthroned him, as is customary, and called him by another name, Victor. [Col. 0823C]

During the time of this pontiff, the renowned duke and margrave Boniface died, leaving behind young heirs. Not long afterward, Duke Gotefrid, a magnificent man and most capable in military affairs, came to Italy and took his widow as his wife.

When the emperor heard this, he came to Italy but did not find him in the Lombard kingdom. Thus, when the aforesaid king came to Lombardy, he first took Otto’s daughter, Adelheid, still a little girl, as a wife for his own son. After settling all the affairs of the Lombard kingdom, he was invited by the pope to Florence, where he held a synod.

At that synod, through the counsel of the venerable Hildebrand, [Col. 0823D] the Simoniac heresy and the most shameful fornication of priests were struck by the divine sword. For at that synod many bishops were deposed on account of Simony, and very many on account of the crime of fornication. Among them the bishop of that city was also deposed.

Why delay over many details? After the council had been duly celebrated, the emperor, enriched by pontifical blessing, returned to Lombardy. When he had arrived there, he took Beatrice, together with Boniface’s only daughter, named Matilda—for shortly before her son and elder daughter had died through the evil act of someone unknown—and carried them deceitfully with him beyond the mountains, seeking to acquire Boniface’s inheritance and not knowing that his final day was soon to be prepared for him.

For, struck down by the violence of a fever, as soon as he entered the land of the Franks along the Rhine, he summoned the magnificent Duke Gotefrid to him.
