After returning his wife to him, together with Boniface’s daughter and all the possessions belonging to her, he earnestly begged him to show loyalty to his son, already designated as king. A few days later he died, and his body was honorably buried at Speyer with his father. His son, together with his mother, assumed the government of the kingdom.

A few days later the pope also died [Note: [Col. 0823D] Christophorus Sandius, a distinguished man, author of notes and observations on the three books of Gerardus Johannes Vossius on the history of Latin literature, who was chosen not from the common people but from the senate, promised himself some remarkable information from Bonizo concerning Victor’s death—if Bonizo should ever be brought to light—in the cited place, p. 196; but here he is treading as though on eggs and ears of grain], [Col. 0824B] after whose death the clergy of the Roman Church assembled together and, with the acclaim of the people, elected for themselves Frederick, abbot of the monastery of Cassino, whom we mentioned above. They called him by another name, Stephen, and, according to ancient custom, consecrated him Roman pontiff at the altar of blessed Peter. He promoted the venerable Hildebrand to the order of the diaconate and ordained him archdeacon of the holy Roman Church.

**The fifth book ends.**

**THE SIXTH BOOK BEGINS.**

At the same time, the Church of Milan, which for almost two hundred years had withdrawn itself from the dominion of the Roman Church through the arrogance of pride [Note: [Col. 0823D] Nicholas, cardinal of Aragon, again transcribed this almost word for word from our author in his Life of Stephen IX [Col. 0824D]. The distinguished Muratori severely chastises him for this, unaware that he had received it from a contemporary writer; he also accuses Papebrochius of credulity for detecting something of a schism there. Yet our Bonizo, holding a torch openly before obscure matters, makes clear that the story was not so groundless, and it plainly appears that the ecclesiastical history brought to light from this writer received a great addition], first recognized itself as subject among the other Churches. Since I believe it will be necessary for posterity to know when this happened, I have decided to insert it into this little work.

The city of Milan, therefore, the metropolis of all Lombardy, was in the time of the Roman emperors the seat of the imperial government. Many religious bishops flourished there, among them blessed Ambrose, the jewel of priests, whose flowers of eloquence still give off their fragrance in the Church.

He, following the Easterners, first established the singing of the antiphon in the Church, and, long afterward, blessed Gregory granted the Westerners the office of singing. Recognizing that the kingdom of God consists not merely in unity of song, but in obedience and peace, he allowed the Milanese Church, united in all the sacraments with the holy Roman Church, to sing according to the ancient custom out of reverence for blessed Ambrose the teacher, whom he followed in this matter, intermingling Ambrose’s antiphons with his own chants. [Col. 0824D]

After a long time, when the aforesaid Church was wholly serving the Simoniac heresy [thus in the codex], the bishops, fearing Roman judgment, spread this saying among the people: “Let the Ambrosian Church remain in its own status.” In doing so, they accused Ambrose of falsehood, repeatedly thundering in his writings that anyone who withdrew in any respect from the dominion of the Roman Church was a heretic.

In the time of the aforesaid Roman pontiff, however, Guido was ravaging the Milanese Church: an unlearned man, living with a concubine, and, without any shame, a Simoniac. In Guido’s time there were two clerics in that city. One, named Landulf, came from a noble ancestral line and was a cultivated and most eloquent man. The other was called Ariald and traced his origin to an equestrian family. He was highly educated in the liberal arts and was later crowned with martyrdom.

Since they often devoted themselves to the sacred books, and especially to those of blessed Ambrose, they discovered how great a crime it is to hide the talent entrusted to one. For this reason, entrusting themselves to God and to the blessed prince of the apostles, one day, with divine grace helping them, they preached the word to the people.

In that preaching they disclosed to the people the frauds of Simoniac commerce, demonstrated as clearly as daylight how shameful it was for priests and Levites living with concubines to celebrate the sacred mysteries, and declared, with blessed Ambrose as witness, how heretical it was not to obey the Roman Church.

Those who were predestined to life received this willingly, especially the poor, whom God chose to confound the strong (1 Corinthians I, 27). But the multitude of clerics, which in that Church was as innumerable as the sand of the sea, incited the captains, the varvassors, the sellers of churches, their relatives, and the kinsmen of their concubines. When sedition arose, they tried to impose silence upon the two men, but they were frustrated in their hope.

For as the number of the faithful grew each day, the wonderful athletes of God labored more ardently in the word of preaching. Once their wickedness had been exposed, the enemies of God were daily struck down and diminished, to such an extent that one day they drove the very man who was called the pontiff of that Church out of the church.

When the Simoniacs saw this, although they were still unable to resist the truth and so great a multitude, they were confounded. They reproached the two men with poverty and called them Paterines, that is, “ragged men.” Those who said “racha” to their brother, indeed, were liable to judgment (Matthew V, 22). For *rachos* in Greek means *pannus* (“rag”) in Latin. These blessed men were worthy to suffer insults for the name of Jesus (Acts V, 41).

Why say more? The glorious race of the Paterines grew daily, until they resolved to send honorable men to Rome to ask blessed Pope Stephen to send religious bishops with them who might rebuild their church from its foundations.

For in so great and innumerable a crowd of clerics scarcely five out of a thousand could be found who were not entangled in the stains of the Simoniac heresy. When the pope heard this, he rejoiced, and immediately sent from his side bishops together with the God-beloved Hildebrand, the archdeacon.

When they came to Milan, they did not find the archbishop there. Conscience accusing him, he had fled from their presence. But the people received them most honorably, as was fitting. For several days they strengthened the people and devoted themselves to the work of preaching.

When these things had happened, the God-beloved Hildebrand reached as far as Lyon in Gaul. There, after a great council had been celebrated, he pursued the Simoniac heresy and the detestable fornication of the clergy as far as the Pyrenees and the British Sea.

At that council God displayed through the aforesaid archdeacon a sufficiently great and manifest miracle. A certain archbishop of Hebron happened to be present at the synod, a very eloquent man. When some accused him of Simoniac heresy, he made all his accusers his friends with money on the following night. When morning came, he taunted the judge, saying: “Where are those who accused me? No one has condemned me.”

When the aforesaid archdeacon heard this, he said to the bishop: “Do you believe, bishop, that the Holy Spirit is of one substance and divinity with the Father and the Son?”

When he answered, “I believe,” Hildebrand said: “Say, ‘Glory to the Father and to the Son and to the Holy Spirit.’”

When the bishop confidently began the verse, he said, “Glory to the Father and to the Son,” but he was unable to name the Holy Spirit. When he had begun this repeatedly and made no progress, he fell at Hildebrand’s feet and confessed that he was a Simoniac.

As soon as he had been deposed from the episcopate, he confessed in a clear voice: “Glory to the Father and to the Son and to the Holy Spirit.” This event struck the Simoniacs with great terror, so much so that on that same day eighteen bishops confessed that they were Simoniacs and renounced their episcopal sees.

When such a holy synod had been celebrated and ecclesiastical affairs had been duly settled, they returned very quickly to Rome, to the supreme pontiff.

The aforesaid blessed Pope Stephen is said to have possessed the spirit of prophecy. For a few days before he died, he summoned the bishops, cardinals, and Levites and addressed them in these words:

“I know, brothers, that after my death men will arise from among you, loving themselves, who will seize this see not by the decrees of the holy Fathers but through lay persons.”

When they heard this, they all denied it together and, having given an oath into the pope’s hand, bound themselves mutually never to ascend to the pontifical see, or consent to those ascending it, except as the decrees of the holy Fathers require.

A few days later, while he was coming through the region of Tuscany, he was overcome by illness and gave up his spirit to heaven. After his death, the captains of Rome, and especially Gregory of Tusculum, who had once claimed for himself the empty dignity of the patriciate, assumed tyrannical power. Contrary to the oath he himself had shortly before sworn into the pope’s hand, they raised a certain bishop of Velletri, a cardinal, to the papal dignity, and, changing his name, called him Benedict.

While these things were happening, the wife of Emperor Henry, together with her young son, held the government of the kingdom, as we related above. With much feminine audacity she was doing many things contrary to law.

At the beginning of her reign she entrusted all the affairs of that Italian kingdom to a certain Guibert, born of a noble Parmese family, and appointed him chancellor. Meanwhile, the God-beloved Hildebrand, together with the cardinal bishops, Levites, and priests, assembled at Siena and chose for themselves Gerard, bishop of the city of Florence, whom they called by another name, Nicholas [Note: [Col. 0827D] Nicholas II].

He invited that same Guibert, chancellor of the Italian kingdom, to a synod on behalf of blessed Peter and in true obedience. He also invited the magnificent man Gotefrid, and not only the bishops of Tuscany but also those of Lombardy, so that they might come to Sutri and deliberate concerning the perjurer and usurper.

When the aforesaid Benedict heard that they were approaching Sutri, his conscience accusing him, he abandoned the see that he had invaded and withdrew to his own home. When this was reported at Sutri, the venerable Nicholas entered Rome victoriously without any opposition. He was honorably received by all the clergy and people and enthroned by the cardinals in the seat of blessed Peter. [Col. 0827B]

Not long afterward the aforesaid Benedict, who was also called Mincius, came and threw himself at the pope’s knees, claiming that he had suffered violence, although he did not deny his perjury and the crime of invasion. On the basis of his own confession he was deposed from the episcopal and priestly orders.

When this had been done, the magnificent Duke Gotefrid returned home together with the chancellor and the bishops. But the venerable pontiff, protected by God, set out for Apulia and absolved the Normans from the bond of excommunication. By investiture he handed over to them all Apulia and Calabria and the lands of blessed Peter that they had formerly invaded, except Benevento. They accepted all the territories from him, swore allegiance to him, and through them he very quickly freed the city of Rome [Col. 0827C] from the tyranny of the captains.

For they not only trampled upon the pride of the Tusculans, Praenestines, and Nomentans, but also, passing through Rome, devastated Galeria and all the castles of Count Gerard as far as Sutri. This act freed the city of Rome from the dominion of the captains.

When these things had taken place and the Northmen had returned to Apulia, envoys from Milan petitioned the pope to take pity on their Church, which had been utterly desolated. For this reason the venerable pontiff immediately sent Peter Damian, bishop of Ostia, a man endowed with every kind of learning, to visit the aforesaid Milanese Church. When he arrived there, he rebuilt, with great discernment, what he found destroyed. For he took priests and levites whom he could find who were the more religious, of chaste life and good reputation, and who had not received ordination through venality; although they had been ordained by a Simoniac, he reconciled them and entrusted the Church to their governance. Many of their number remained religious men down to our own times. What seemed blameworthy to some was highly praiseworthy to the wise. For what more praiseworthy course could have been found at that time than that such a Church should not perish for lack of priesthood?

Not long afterward the aforesaid pontiff convened a synod. At it Guido, bishop of Milan, is known to have taken his seat, willingly or unwillingly, compelled by the Patarines. He brought with him the stiff-necked bulls, the Lombard bishops: Cunibert, bishop of Turin; Giselin, bishop of Asti; Benzon, bishop of Alba; Gregory, bishop of Vercelli; Otto, bishop of Novara; Opizo, bishop of Lodi; and Aldemann, bishop of Brescia. All of them were ordered in that same synod to exclude concubinary priests and levites from service at the altar. Concerning the Simoniacs, they decreed that no mercy was to be shown. By the common counsel of all the bishops, this law concerning the election of a pontiff was defined in the synod, and 113 bishops subscribed to the law.

> “If anyone has been enthroned in the apostolic see without the agreement and canonical election of the cardinals [Note: [Col. 0827D] This word was erased by a somewhat later hand and replaced by another [Col. 0828D] in the codex.] and of the other religious clerics who follow them, let him be regarded not as an apostolic bishop but as an apostate; and let it be lawful for the cardinals, together with the other God-fearing clerics and laymen, to anathematize the invader, drive him from the apostolic see by human assistance and effort, and restore the one whom they have chosen. But if they are unable to accomplish this within the city, let them, by apostolic authority, assemble outside the city at a place they choose and conduct the election, with authority granted to the elected man to govern and administer affairs for the benefit of the holy Roman Church according to the circumstances of the time, as though he had already been enthroned.”

When the council had thus been duly celebrated, the Lombard bishops returned home. After receiving large sums of money from concubinary priests and levites, they observed the decrees of the Fathers—except for one, namely the bishop of Brescia. When he came to Brescia and publicly recited the pope’s decrees, he was beaten by the clerics and nearly killed. This deed gave no small increase to the Pataria. For not only at Brixen but also at Cremona and Piacenza, and throughout all the other provinces, many people abstained from communion with concubinary priests.

At this same pontiff’s time, Hugh the White, a Roman cardinal whom we previously reported to have been ordained by Pope Leo of blessed memory, withdrew from communion with the Roman Church. Concerning the perversity of his morals, it is better to remain silent than to say little; but, to summarize everything briefly, as he was in appearance, so he was in his deeds. For just as he had twisted eyes, so his actions were twisted.

Meanwhile the number of the faithful was increasing not only throughout Italy but also throughout all Gaul; day by day Simoniac priests were being exposed. The venerable Pope Nicholas, however, after having lived only a few years in the papacy, rested in a blessed death. After his death, in accordance with the decrees of the ancestors, the Roman clergy and people chose for themselves Anselm, bishop of Lucca, a Milanese by birth, a man sprung from noble lineage and accomplished in both branches of learning; they called him Alexander by another name [Note: [Col. 0828D] Alexander II].

Meanwhile the Lombard bishops, believing that they had found a suitable opportunity, came together at the instigation of Guibert, whom we previously called chancellor, and held a council of evil men. At it they deliberated that they could obtain a pope from nowhere other than the paradise of Italy, and one who would know how to sympathize with their weaknesses. Then they crossed the mountains and, appealing to the empress’s womanly nature, won her over by composing certain fabrications that seemed almost true. For they said that their lord, just as he was heir to the kingdom, would also be heir to the patriciate, and that the blessed Nicholas had confirmed by decree that henceforth no one was to be counted among the pontiffs unless he were elected with the king’s consent.

Deceived by these and similar machinations, the empress, with womanly license, gave her assent to a wicked undertaking such as had not existed since the day the nations began to be: that, where no Roman cleric or layman had taken part in the election of a pontiff, a pontiff should there be elected by fornicator- and Simoniac-like men, and that he, receiving the cross and papal insignia from the hands of the king and queen, should come to Rome from the north. Thus, according to Jeremiah, evil would break forth against all the inhabitants of the earth.

What more need be said? They chose for themselves Cadolus of Parma, a man rich in wealth but poor in virtues. Surrounded by many soldiers, he entered Lombardy, accompanied by the stiff-necked bishops of Lombardy, who did not know how to bear the Lord’s gentle yoke. Then the Simoniacs rejoiced, and the concubinary priests exulted with immense delight. But what more need be said? According to the Gospel saying, all their exultation was cast down to the ground by the contradiction of one woman, and the whole power of the proud vanished like smoke when Beatrice alone forbade it.

Not long afterward the aforesaid Cadolus secretly came to Bologna, where he awaited his soldiers. After receiving them, he set out for Rome, carrying with him enormous weights of gold and silver. But at that time there were in Rome pestilential men who loved themselves, avaricious and greedy men, who joined themselves to him; among them were the Roman captains, who wished to oppress the Roman city and reduce it once more under their own power, as in ancient times.

Meanwhile that man hated by God pitched his camp in Nero’s meadow and, when battle was secretly joined by God’s judgment, appeared to be victorious. But, O ineffable providence of God, O wondrous mercy of God! Although he had been victorious, before a month had passed, when Duke Gotefrid came to Rome, Cadolus obtained—only with difficulty, through many prayers and magnificent gifts bestowed upon that duke—to depart as one defeated.

He came to Parma, the workshop of the world’s iniquity, gathered money, and, after a year had passed, secretly came into Romagna like a thief. There, after giving a large sum of money, he gathered a company of cavalry with the help of the captains and certain pestilential Romans. By night he entered the Leonine City and attacked the Church of Saint Peter. At daybreak such terror from heaven seized the soldiers who had come with him that, leaving him alone in the church, they all fled without anyone compelling them.

On the advice of a certain pestilential Roman named Cencius, he entered the fortress of Saint Angel and protected himself there. He was besieged in that fortress for two years and endured many and various calamities. He was not allowed to leave until he bought his release from that same Cencius for three hundred pounds of silver. Content with a single attendant and assisted by one beast of burden, he barely reached Berceto among the *oratores* [“intercessors” or “petitioners”; reading uncertain] [Col. 0830A].

While these things were taking place, canonical cohabitation first arose at Milan (so the codex), a development that aroused great envy among its enemies. A few days after these events, Landulf, the Milanese cleric whom we mentioned above, died and was buried in peace.

Meanwhile the archbishops and bishops, abbots, dukes, and counts of the Germans established a court for themselves. There they deliberated, judging it unworthy that the empress should henceforth live in private garb and that the kingdom should be ruled by a woman’s will: first, because she was a nun and it was not fitting for her to serve secular cares; and second, because their lord appeared already to have reached maturity. By common counsel they decreed that the venerable Anno, archbishop of Cologne, should hold the reins of government for the king and queen. They deposed Guibert and appointed Gregory, bishop of Vercelli, chancellor of the Italian kingdom.

The aforesaid Anno, thinking of nothing better than that the kingdom should be united with the priesthood, came into Italy and proceeded to Rome. He met the pope and asked how he had dared to receive the Roman pontificate without the king’s command. When the beloved-of-God Hildebrand told him that, according to the decrees of the holy Fathers, nothing had been granted to kings in the election of Roman pontiffs, and when he replied that this was permitted to him by virtue of the dignity of the patriciate, the venerable archdeacon immediately brought forward the following synodal statements, from the synod of Symmachus, at which 150 bishops were present:

Laurentius, bishop of Milan, said: “It has not seemed right that a layman should be established as having any power in the Church, for he must remain under an obligation to obey, not possess authority to command.”

Eulalius, bishop of the Church of Syracuse, said: “Although laymen may be religious, it is nowhere recorded that any authority to dispose of ecclesiastical matters has ever been assigned to them.”

When he brought forward the decrees of Pope Nicholas, he was very quickly answered by the decree of that same Pope Nicholas, to which 114 bishops had subscribed. The aforesaid archbishop then asked the lord pope to deign to convene a synod and give an account of himself. When he heard this, although such a thing was foreign to the dignity of the Roman pontiffs, nevertheless, because necessity compelled him, he promised to do so.

Soon afterward they summoned a synod at Mantua, where Cadolus could meet with the Lombard bishops. All the Lombard bishops, together with their metropolitan, came there except Cadolus, who, accused by his conscience, was afraid to come. The venerable pope came to Mantua and gave an account of himself; he immediately made all his enemies into friends. For all the Lombard bishops at once fell at his feet, confessed that they were guilty, asked forgiveness, and obtained it. Thus, with kingdom and priesthood united, the pope returned honorably to Rome, while the bishops hastened gladly to their own places. The duke Gotefrid and Otto the Saxon, duke of the Bavarians, took part in this great council.

When these matters had been completed, the king took as his wife Berta, beloved of God, daughter of Otto and Adaleta [above the line: Adalheida]. Her father had given her to him when she was still a little girl and he himself was still a boy. After the marriage had been duly celebrated, he began to hold the reins of the kingdom personally. Soon afterward, at the request of Guido, archbishop of Milan, he gave the bishopric of Cremona to his nephew Arnulf. I omit narrating how Arnulf had sworn an oath to the people of Cremona before he was elected, and how at the beginning he appeared light-minded in character, since I believe these matters are widely known.

But when the Milanese captains and varvassors, the sellers of churches, saw that they were being stripped of their money, they were grieved. Taking the opportunity afforded by a certain sermon that the venerable Ariald had preached to the people—saying that it was not lawful to fast on the days of Pentecost—they stirred up a sedition among the people, as though this were contrary to the litanies of Saint Ambrose. They plundered the house of the clerics who lived together, and a few days later expelled Ariald himself from the city.

As he was departing into exile, a certain priest in name only joined himself to him and handed him over to the archbishop’s relatives. They took him, crippled all his limbs, and finally drowned him in a lake [the word *necaverunt* (“drowned”) was erased and replaced by another word in the codex]. After his body had lain beneath the water for ten months, it was revealed. When Herlimbald, the full brother (*germanus*) of the aforesaid Landulf, heard this, he gathered the entire multitude of the Patarines and besieged the fortress of the archbishop’s relatives until they returned to him the body of the venerable Ariald. It was brought to Milan and buried with the greatest honor in the Church of Saint Celsus, where, through his merits, various illnesses are healed down to the present day.

Meanwhile the word of God was growing wondrously at Cremona. How twelve men, moved by zeal for God, swore an oath at the counsel of Lord Christopher the abbot; how the whole people of Cremona imitated them; how they expelled all concubinary priests and levites; how they beat the bishop himself when, on the very day of the Lord’s Passion, he tried to arrest a priest of the Patarines; and how, after Holy Easter, they sent honorable men as envoys to the pope—I shall not trouble to relate.

I have decided to insert into this little work the shield that the venerable pope sent to the people of Cremona through those same envoys:

> **ALEXANDER, servant of the servants of God, to the religious clerics and faithful laymen of the Church of Cremona, greeting and apostolic blessing.**
>
> We give abundant thanks to God, the inspirer of all good things and the author of good will, who has armed you against the enemy of the human race with the weapons of his virtues and has inflamed you zealously to destroy the Simoniac heresy and the filth of clerical fornications.
>
> For, as we have learned from your letters, you have risen against the cunning of the ancient serpent; and he who, like a two-headed snake, was spewing the poisons of his wickedness over you through the pipes of his twofold throat sighs that he has been pierced and cut down by the zeal of your holy zeal and by the dagger of your virtue. Clearly, he who long ago imposed upon the serpent in paradise the sentence of eternal condemnation has himself stirred you unanimously against the craft of the hidden dragon in our own time.
>
> Therefore, let the strength of your holy efforts and of this holy apostolic see be added to your endeavors. We decree that you are to observe in every respect among yourselves what we do not doubt was instituted by our holy predecessors and by nearly all the founders of the sacred canons: namely, that subdeacons and deacons, and above all priests, who mingle carnally with women and are polluted by Simoniac filth, are to be deprived both of ecclesiastical benefices and of the office of the dignity they have received. For it is unworthy that one who has been deprived of the honor of the order he received, either through bodily incontinence or through the commerce of sacrilegious venality, should thereafter enjoy ecclesiastical property.
>
> As for the other clerics, namely those who hold lower offices, if they are bound to lawful wives, we command that they remain in their grades, and we do not deny them the benefits appropriate to ecclesiastical support.
>
> But since, beyond these matters, you consult us about several things that are very necessary for you, so that an answer may be given to you by our authority, we urge you not to hesitate to send prudent men from among yourselves to the synodal council which, God willing, we shall celebrate after the coming Easter. They should explain to us clearly, not through the evidence of letters but by the service of the living voice, whatever must be demanded and whatever must be provided for your interests.
>
> For in this war, which you have undertaken with the zeal of divine fervor—not sluggishly but with every exertion of virtue—the Roman see hastens to your aid, extends its arm, sets before you the shield of defense, and kindles you so that you may rise more and more vigorously against the members of the devil [the codex reads *non enerviter*, “not feebly”].
>
> Therefore, each of you, girded with the sword of divine virtue, should say: “Whoever is for the Lord, let him join me” (Exodus 32:26). Thus, with Moses, as though from gate to gate of the camp (ibid., 27), let him rush like a fiery warrior upon the sacrilegious, so that he may close with slaughtered corpses the gates of Simoniac venality and clerical adultery, through which the devil had entered your Church.
>
> May the Almighty, beloved sons, bless you with his right hand and, through the ministry of his blessed apostle Peter, open to you the gate of the heavenly kingdom.

Enflamed by these saving admonitions, the people of Cremona immediately began the work pleasing to God and expelled Simoniacs and fornicators from their Church. The people of Piacenza imitated them, immediately subjected themselves to the obedience of Rome, expelled Dionysius, their bishop, who had been excommunicated by the blessed pope, and confirmed the entire Pataria by oaths.

At the same time Hugh the White, whom we mentioned above, after enduring many and various miseries under Cadolus, finally came to the venerable pope, asked forgiveness, and obtained it. When he was sent to Spain in the office of legate, whatever he built up he again destroyed. For at first he vigorously persecuted the Simoniacs, but afterward, having accepted money, he reconciled them. When this became known at Rome, they immediately recalled him from Spain and ordered him to live at Rome. They showed him this clemency chiefly out of reverence for his ordainer, namely the blessed Pope Leo.

Meanwhile the aforesaid Guido, archbishop of Milan, came to Milan, moved by repentance. After laying aside his pontifical insignia, he lived in private garb. When the sellers of churches, whom we mentioned above, saw this, they quickly turned his fickle mind toward the worse. They gave him the deadly advice to sell the bishopric to a certain Gotefrid, a cleric born of noble lineage, sufficiently eloquent, and inclined to every wickedness, and to transfer himself to the fortress. This was done without delay.

The aforesaid Gotefrid, on the advice of the Simoniacs, the Milanese captains, and the Lombard bishops, crossed the Alps and approached the king. He very easily won over the king, who was still a young man. For he promised that he would destroy the Pataria and capture Herlimbald alive and send him beyond the mountains if the king would grant him the bishopric of Milan by investiture. For this reason, and after a small amount of money had also been given, he received the investiture he sought, but did not obtain the bishopric.

For Herlimbald, protected by God, as soon as he heard of his attempt, gathered a multitude of God’s army and withdrew from Gotefrid’s control all the fortresses belonging by right to the bishop. Then he besieged him for many days at Castellione, his hereditary fortress. While he was being besieged and seemed almost capable of being captured, the Simoniac and concubinary clerics set fire by night to the middle of the city of Milan, at the instigation of a certain cleric whose name I leave for the diligent reader to investigate. I know for certain and affirm without doubt that the perpetrator of so great a crime was unworthy of the priesthood.

What more need be said? As the fire seized the buildings and devastated the glorious basilicas of the blessed martyrs, it finally consumed half the city in triumph. When this was reported to the Milanese who happened to be present at the siege, the greatest terror seized them. They abandoned Herlimbald, together with the few who feared God, and immediately returned home.

But the strongest soldier of the Lord, like Judas Maccabaeus (2 Maccabees 12:42), stood undaunted. After strengthening the siege, he celebrated Holy Easter there. When the Easter festival had passed, the aforesaid Godefrid, bringing with him a multitude of cavalry and infantry, fought with Herlimbald and fled. Thus, by God’s mercy, the soldier of God, possessing a bloodless victory, returned to Milan.

At the same time the Northmen invaded Campania. Seeing this, the beloved-of-God Hildebrand immediately summoned the magnificent duke Gotefrid to the aid of Saint Peter. As it happened, the aforesaid duke had come to Italy in those days, bringing with him the most excellent countess Matilda, daughter of the renowned Duke Boniface. Gathering the whole multitude of his army, he came to Rome with his wife and the most noble Matilda, expelled the Northmen from Campania without a battle, and restored it to Roman rule.

This was the first service that the most excellent daughter of Boniface offered to the blessed prince of the apostles; not long afterward, through many services pleasing to God, she deserved to be called a daughter of Saint Peter.

While these things were taking place, Herlimbald, protected by God and wishing to free the Milanese Church from Simoniac servitude, resolved, with the counsel of the pope and of the beloved-of-God Hildebrand, on the holy day of Epiphany, with the assistance of religious clerics not only from Milan but also from Cremona and Piacenza, to obtain a bishop through the election of the clergy according to the decrees of the holy Fathers. He chose Otto, a cleric of that Church, noble by birth but nobler in character, elected by the religious clergy and acclaimed by the Catholic people.

The old serpent did not look upon this with favorable eyes. He found certain men skilled in his craft, and through them stirred up sedition among the people. They surrounded Herlimbald, protected by God, who was residing in the palace with the newly elected man; they attacked the palace and plundered everything. They wounded the elected man, dragged him as far as the altar of Saint Mary, and compelled him to swear that he would never again involve himself in that bishopric. Then they handed him over to a cleric of that same Church to be guarded until morning.

When morning came, Herlimbald, protected by God, came fearlessly to the church. When the sellers of churches and the relatives of fornicator-priests saw this, they began to shout and joined battle. By God’s mercy, the soldier of God quickly won the palm. For they drove all the enemies of God far from the city, and, after everything belonging to the Church that had been taken by the enemies of God had been restored twofold, he secured the church and palace. On that same day the Lord’s elected man could have been enthroned without any opposition, had the bond of his oath not stood in the way.

For this reason religious men were sent to Rome to report these events to the pope. When the venerable Alexander heard them, he declared that an oath made contrary to ecclesiastical law was not binding. By the common decree of the cardinal bishops, priests, and levites, he judged the Milanese elected man to have the right. He immediately sent his letters to the king, admonishing him as a son to cast away from himself the hatred of the servants of God that he had conceived in his heart and to permit the Milanese Church, according to God’s will, to have its bishop.

When the king heard this, he immediately sent his secretaries from his side. They came to Lombardy, established a court for themselves at Novara, and, having given an oath before the multitude of bishops gathered there, affirmed that it was the royal will that Gotefrid should be consecrated.

When the Lombard bishops heard this, although they had been excommunicated from the Church, they did not willingly consecrate him; rather, they cursed him. Perhaps certain clerics from the Milanese Church took part in this cursing. Among them was Tedald, who, while Gotefrid was still alive, invaded the same bishopric.

When the venerable Otto, the elected bishop of Milan, heard this, he betook himself to the Roman see, where all ecclesiastical cases are brought to an end.

Hugh the White, whom we mentioned above, obtained from the lord pope a legation to Gaul, where he committed many acts contrary to law and right; these will later be narrated in their proper order. At the same time Cadolus, bishop of Parma, died in body and soul, and not long afterward the bishop of Ravenna died.

Meanwhile Guibert of Parma, whom we mentioned above, was wonderfully eager to obtain the bishopric of Parma. He approached the king with many prayers and gifts, striving to have the bishopric given to him. When he could not obtain it, and when all his relatives and outsiders alike, both great and small, clerics and laymen, were entirely opposed, he went to the empress. As it happened, she was there in those days, and through her intervention he received the bishopric of Ravenna. The bishopric of Parma, however, was given to a certain Everard, a cleric of Cologne.

The aforesaid Guibert came to Lombardy and entered Ravenna with a large retinue and great power, as was his custom. Not many days later, during Lent, he came to Rome for his consecration. A synod had already been held, at which Hugh the White was publicly accused of simony by Cluniac monks and certain religious bishops. At that synod, at the urging of the empress, the lord pope publicly excommunicated certain counselors of the king who wished to separate him from the unity of the Church [Note: the word *hortatu* (“at the urging”) was erased and replaced by another in the codex].

But let us return to the narrative. The aforesaid Guibert came to Rome bringing with him Dionysius, bishop of Piacenza, who had been deposed by that same pope many years before. Clothed in feigned sheep-like simplicity, he deceived many, especially the beloved-of-God Hildebrand. When he had repeatedly asked the pope to lay his hand upon him, and the pope refused to consent, he is said, being full of the spirit of prophecy, to have said:

> “I am already being offered up, and the time of my release is near; but you will experience its bitterness.”

The outcome later revealed the truth of this saying.

After the consecration had been duly celebrated, Guibert bound himself by an oath to be faithful to Pope Alexander and to his successors who should be elected by the better cardinals. He made no mention whatsoever of emperor, king, or patrician, and he faithfully kept this oath. For after the death of the venerable Alexander and the election of the venerable Hildebrand by the better cardinals, the religious archbishop showed him such due submission that, when summoned to a synod, he came; at that synod, by virtue of his Church’s privilege, he sat at the pope’s right hand; and, not under compulsion to confess but spontaneously, he professed him pope in every respect.

But let us now continue the order of events. After the celebration of Easter, Guibert had received permission from the blessed pope and the venerable archdeacon to return to Ravenna. Before he entered that city, however, the pope’s death was announced to him, for on the feast of Saint George the blessed Alexander gave up his spirit to heaven.

**The sixth book ends.**

**The seventh book begins.**

On that same day, after the body of the aforesaid pontiff had been buried in the Church of Saint Savior, while the venerable Hildebrand was occupied with his burial, a sudden gathering of clerics, men, and women took place, shouting: “Hildebrand, bishop!” When the venerable archdeacon heard this, he was terrified and, wishing quickly to calm the people, ran to the pulpit. But Hugh the White forestalled him and addressed the people as follows:

> “Men and brothers! You know that since the days of the lord Pope Leo, this is Hildebrand, who exalted the holy Roman Church and liberated this city. Therefore, since we can have neither a better man nor one such as may be elected to the Roman pontificate, we elect this man, ordained in our Church, known to you and to us, and approved in every respect.”

When the cardinal bishops, priests, levites, and clerics of the succeeding order had shouted together, as is customary, “Gregory, pope; Saint Peter has elected him” [so the codex], he was immediately dragged and carried away by the people and, against his will, enthroned at the chains of blessed Peter, not at Brixianorium.

The following day, reflecting inwardly on the danger into which he had fallen, he began to be distressed and troubled. Nevertheless, gathering the strength of faith and hope, he found no better course than to notify the king of his election and, through him if possible, to avoid the papal burden that had been imposed upon him.

Accordingly, he immediately sent letters to the king, notifying him of the pope’s death and announcing his own election. He warned him that, if he gave his assent to the election, he would never patiently tolerate the king’s wickedness.

But things turned out very differently from what he had hoped. The king immediately sent Gregory, bishop of Vercelli and chancellor of the Italian kingdom, to confirm his election and attend his consecration. This was done. He was ordained a priest during the fast of Pentecost, and on the feast of the apostles he was consecrated bishop by the cardinals at their altar, according to ancient custom.

The empress attended his consecration together with the most excellent duchess Beatrice, then a widow. For a few days earlier the magnificent duke Gotefrid had died.

As soon as the venerable pontiff assumed care of the holy Roman Church, he judged that nothing was better than, at the beginning of his pontificate, to admonish the king not to sell bishoprics and to acknowledge that he was subject to the holy Roman Church.

He immediately made the glorious empress, the king’s mother, the minister of this holy embassy. She had with her in her retinue the venerable bishops Gerard of Ostia [Note: [Col. 0835] This famous Gerard of that age, eventually raised to the cardinalate, was a citizen of Regensburg’s son, a singular ornament of the Bavarians], Hubert of Praeneste, and Rainald of Como. Crossing the Alps, she found her son in Bavaria.

What more need be said? The Roman envoys were honorably received by the king. After hearing from them every day for many days a discourse of correction, he finally prohibited from his conversation the familiar associates whom the blessed Alexander had previously excommunicated.

Then, when he was asked to mediate a synod, he assembled the bishops outwardly but inwardly evaded the matter, intending that no council should at all be held in his kingdom. The subsequent outcome proved this. For through Lemar, bishop of Bremen, a most eloquent man and highly learned in the liberal studies, the council was interrupted.

He maintained that, by ancient privileges, the bishop of Mainz had been granted the right to act in the regions of Germany in place of the Roman pontiff, and therefore that Roman envoys were not permitted to celebrate a synod within his legation. He failed to consider carefully the passage of the first Leo sent to the bishop of Thessalonica, which reads:

> “For the pope entrusts his own functions to all archbishops in such a way that they are called to share in the care, not in the fullness of power.”

For this reason Lemar, the archbishop, was suspended by the Roman envoys from priestly office.

After the council had been interrupted by this maneuver, the king promised that he would willingly do everything the Roman envoys demanded. They were given magnificent gifts and returned honorably to Rome, carrying with them the aforesaid king’s letters, in which he promised the venerable Pope Gregory due submission in every respect.

A few days later a certain Hermann, bishop of Babenberg, came to Rome to receive the pallium. The king’s letters preceded him; they informed the pope that the king, deceived by the fraud of certain evil men, had given Hermann the bishopric in exchange for money. When the matter was investigated and found to be so, the aforesaid Hermann was deposed from the bishopric, and another was enthroned in his place by order of the lord pope. That man was later granted the dignity of the pallium by the same pope. The same was likewise done in the case of the bishop of Constance.

While these things were taking place, the Milanese captains, the sellers of churches whom we mentioned above, held a conference with the king and turned his mind toward the worse. For they promised him that they would destroy the Pataria and kill Herlimbald. The king gladly heard this and willingly promised whatever they asked.

Meanwhile the venerable Gregory, suspecting no evil from the king, convened a synod. Guibert, bishop of Ravenna, took his seat there, together with an innumerable multitude of bishops gathered from various provinces. While the affair of the people of Piacenza and Cremona was being discussed, the aforesaid Guibert gravely defamed the Cremonese. Through Dodo, a young man of excellent character and a citizen of Cremona, it became perfectly clear that he had lied. For in the middle of the synod Dodo both absolved the Cremonese from the infamy and branded Guibert himself with infamy.

What more need be said? When these and other cases had been settled, Robert and the Northmen were excommunicated in the same synod. The most excellent countess M. [Matilda], Azo the margrave, and Gisulf, prince of Salerno, were present at the synod. When the council had been duly celebrated and the bishops returned to their own places, Guibert remained at Rome with the pontiff.

He promised the pope that he would undertake a great expedition against the Northmen and that after Easter he would pitch camp with the same pope against Balneo, a count of the king. By these and similar crafty machinations he deceived the pope, who suspected nothing evil.

But his own mind, carrying anger like a wild beast, was thinking of nothing other than what the outcome of events later revealed. For throughout almost all the days of Lent that he remained there, he went around Rome under the pretext of prayer, making friends with all the pestilential men he could find, and with those who hated the pope because of his justice. By giving money, he bound them by oath, among them Cencius, son of the prefect Stephen, whom we mentioned earlier as having been with Cadolus during the time of Pope Alexander.

When his father had died, during the time of Alexander, he wished to obtain the prefecture, but all the Romans rejected him because of the ferocity of his character. By common [Col. 0838B] agreement, the prefecture was entrusted to another Cencius, the son of a certain John, the prefect. Although they had the same name, they were very different in character: in the one was the appearance of every evil, in the other of every good. This man killed his godfather without any cause and utterly destroyed his house; likewise, he was an associate of robbers and an accomplice of plunderers. Through the many and various adulteries that he committed, or whose perpetrators he protected, he made Rome, which had been free, into a slave. For, building a tower of extraordinary size on the bridge of Saint Peter, he made all who crossed it tributaries. The aforementioned Guibert joined such a man, so pestilential, to himself and armed himself through him against the saintly one.

Moreover, there were many pestilent men in Rome who hated justice, such as the sons and relatives of priests living with concubines. But the venerable pontiff, at the beginning of his ordination, gave all the Roman clerics the option either of living canonically, possessing nothing of their own and following the rule of the saints, or, after abandoning the property of the Church, of remaining separately in their own homes. Many of them had previously chosen to live as private persons rather than bear the Lord’s gentle yoke; they were remarkably hostile to the pope, and not they alone, but also their relatives.

There was also in Rome an ancient and very evil custom, which the blessed pope entirely uprooted from that Church in his own time. For in the church of the blessed prince of the apostles there were more than sixty lay mansionarii, married and for the most part living with concubines. They guarded that church in shifts, by day and by night, and by their authority all the altars except the principal one belonged to them; they sold them daily for prayers. All of them, their beards shaved and wearing mitres on their heads, claimed to be priests and cardinals, and in this way deceived those who came to pray, especially the rustic multitude of the Lombards. Believing them to be priests, these people commended themselves to their prayers. In the silence of the deep night, under the pretext of keeping watch, they practiced various robberies and shameful acts of sexual violence. The blessed pope, with great difficulty, expelled such men from the church of the prince of the apostles and entrusted it to religious priests for its custody.

The aforementioned Guibert made such men his friends. The venerable Gregory, however, ordered the church of Saint Peter to be closed to worshippers until the morning hour; previously, during the watches before the vigils, many murders had taken place there, and on that account many thefts and adulteries as well. There was also in that same church another very evil custom, which the same venerable pope entirely uprooted.

Every day before daylight, and generally before dawn had begun its course, the cardinals, motivated by avaricious profit, celebrated Masses upon the altar of the prince of the apostles. By the authority of blessed Peter and his own, he forbade them all to do this, so that thereafter they were not permitted to celebrate Mass at the altar of blessed Peter before the third hour of the day. This brought great hostility upon him. What more need be said? The aforementioned Guibert, like another Catiline, made all the criminals he could find his friends.

Then, as the Paschal feast approached, he asked the venerable pope for permission to return to Ravenna and obtained it, [Col. 0839B] promising that after Easter he would lead an army against the counts at the king’s bath.

Meanwhile, the venerable Gregory was preparing an expedition against the Northmen. Going out to meet Duchess Beatrice as far as the castle of Saint Fabian, he invited her and her daughter to join the expedition. They were willing, in a pious spirit, to obey the pope’s command, but a tumult of Lombard valvassors prevented them. For, when a sudden uprising arose, they broke up the expedition, and thus, with the undertaking unfinished, the pope returned to Rome; Beatrice and her daughter returned to their own lands.

Not long afterward, the pope was suddenly seized by bodily illness in the outskirts of Rome. Cencius, whom we mentioned above, believing that he was already destined for death, suddenly spewed forth the hatred he had conceived in his heart. For in those days he had been the trustee of a certain Cencius, namely, the son of Count Gerard, who had bequeathed a certain estate by testament to the blessed princes of the apostles. But that hateful man, believing that the pope was already dead or near death, committed the crime of both sacrilege and perjury by falsifying the testament and appropriating the estate for his own use, giving only two hundred pounds to the princes of the apostles.

Meanwhile, as the pope recovered, the matter began to be pursued. What more need be said? He was proved to have acted most wickedly, and, after giving hostages, he returned the estate to the princes of the apostles according to the deceased man’s wishes. But his fury did not abate. For, at the counsel of that same pestilent man, Hugh the White, whom we mentioned above, turned a second time toward apostasy. Going into Apulia, he stirred up Robert and the Northmen, who had long before been excommunicated by the pope, in a remarkable fashion against the holy Roman Church. For he said that they had been falsely excommunicated and that the pope was not a pontiff according to the decrees of the holy Fathers, but an invader of the holy Roman Church. He added that he and his supporters would give Robert the imperial crown if Robert expelled the pope from the Church by military force.

When he repeated this openly and secretly every day in the court of the aforementioned duke, he received the following reply from that most prudent duke:

“If you need it, and if it pleases you, accept from me a gift in gold, silver, or any other money, or assistance in horses and mules; but you will not be able to persuade me to arm myself against the Roman pontiff. For it is impious to believe that, because of your hostility or anyone else’s, the pope can be deposed—he who, when the papal chair was vacant, was enthroned at the altar of Saint Peter by the election of the clergy and the acclaim of the Roman people, and consecrated by the cardinal bishops.”

Thus shamefully rejected, he withdrew to Guibert, the supporter of his wickedness.

While these things were taking place, the Milanese captains and the sellers of the churches’ offices, returning to Milan from a conference with the king, stirred up great seditions by devising various schemes. In this way they attracted even the simple, who knew nothing of the uprising, saying that they wished to swear to the integrity of blessed Ambrose.

But Herlimbald, protected by God, whom we mentioned above, saw the devil’s schemes gradually increasing. He burned with zeal and could find no better course than to defend himself and the people of God who wished to fight for justice, like the strongest Judas, with weapons (II Maccabees XIII, 14). What more need be said? The number of the unfaithful increased daily, and from day to day the number of the Paterines diminished. At the same time the entire city of Milan was consumed by fire. Many remarkable churches, and especially the mother church, were destroyed to the ground. This gave the enemy of the human race weapons for the struggle, for all, whether friends or enemies, cried out with one voice, as it were, that this was the sin of the Paterines.

After Easter, an army and a multitude of their confederates suddenly gathered and attacked Herlimbald, who suspected no evil. When he attempted to fight, they killed him in the middle of the street. They pursued and plundered others, and, disgracefully stripping him naked, heedless of his lineage and dignity, they left him unburied throughout the entire day, to the shame of all Christendom. At night he was buried with honor by religious men at Saint Dionysius.

At his tomb God continues to perform great miracles to this day. On the following day they mutilated the ears and nose of a certain priest named Liprand. [Note: The author himself died a few years later by the same kind of death as Herlimbald.] But all who had not consented to the conspiracy were either killed or stripped of their possessions. Many of them came to Cremona and were received most honorably by the brothers. When the death of Herlimbald was heard of, not only in Rome but as far as the British Sea, all Catholics were saddened, and, weeping, they said: “How the mighty has fallen, he who fought the battle of the Lord” (I Maccabees IX, 21).

Meanwhile, during Lent, Pope Gregory convened a synod. Guibert was summoned but refused to come; therefore, on account of the crime of perjury, he was suspended from episcopal office. Hugh the White, in accordance with the Apostle’s command—“Avoid a heretical man after the first and second admonition” (Titus III, 10)—was permanently separated from the Church.

At that time, perhaps, that hateful Cencius whom we mentioned above was being held captive by the prefect of the city of Rome. According to Roman law, he received a capital sentence. But through the prayers of the glorious Matilda, who was present there in those days, and through the entreaties of many Roman citizens, his life was scarcely spared. He gave hostages into the pope’s hands, as well as the tower by which he had tried to ascend to heaven; that tower was utterly destroyed.

Meanwhile Guibert was cunningly arming himself at Ravenna against his lord, the pope. In letters addressed to the stubborn Lombard bishops, and especially to Tetald, archbishop of Milan, he remarkably incited them against the pope. Since mention has been made of this Tetald, I shall briefly explain, if I can, how he came to the bishopric of Milan.

When the death of the glorious Erlinbald, martyred for the name of Jesus, had been reported to the king, the king remembered his promise, which he had previously made to the Milanese captains. He immediately sent into Italy Count Everard, his counselor, whom Pope Alexander had previously excommunicated. When Everard came to Lombardy, he promptly convened a royal assembly at Roncaglia. There he thanked the Milanese for the death of Erlinbald and invited them across the mountains, promising to give them whichever lord-bishop they wished.

Then he proclaimed all the public Paterines enemies of the king. He immediately attacked the people of Piacenza, who were nearby, and, finding most of them unprepared because of their lack of courage, drove many from the city and captured others into submission. They were freed through the counsel of the most blessed Beatrice.

The Cremonese, however, whom he heard to be full of faith and fortified by virtues, he left unharmed—not through fear of God, but because he could not do otherwise. What more need be said? At the king’s command, after a very evil consultation, the Milanese captains who sold the churches chose Tetald, a cleric of the Milanese Church. He had previously sworn fidelity to Gotefridus. He was indeed born of noble stock and sufficiently stout in body, but slender in virtues.

They brought this man with them to the king. The king, forgetting the investiture that he had previously given to Gotefridus and disregarding the oath that Rapot had sworn on his behalf at Novara to the bishops—that it was the royal will that Gotefridus should be consecrated—invested Tetald while the other was still alive. This was contrary not only to divine laws and the custom of Christian kings, but even to the practice of tyrants.

Such a man ravaged the Milanese Church. Guibert sent Hugh the White to him, so that, on Hugh’s advice, Tetald might approach the king and incline the king’s mind toward the worse course. And so it happened.

At that time a grave and unheard-of outrage was committed at Rome. For the hateful Cencius, after forming a conspiracy, seized the pope on the very night of the Nativity of Christ while he was celebrating the sacred rites, taking him from the altar of Saint Mary, the holy Mother of God, which is called “at the Manger.” He carried him by force, wounded, all the way to the tower of extraordinary strength that he possessed at Rome. [Note: A little earlier, the author had said that this tower was destroyed.]

What more need be said? The Romans immediately besieged the tower and, when morning came, captured it by force. They would have killed the criminal himself had the most blessed Gregory, disciple of the good Master, not freed him from death through prayers and supplications. Afterward, when the pope had returned to the Lateran, the Romans expelled from the city the perpetrator of so great an outrage and all his accomplices, and destroyed their towers to the ground.

While these things were taking place, the Saxons rebelled. We have avoided writing the cause of their rebellion because of its length; we know only that, because of the grave and unusual burden of servitude that certain men were striving to impose upon them, they came to such bitter hostility. But let us now follow the sequence of events.

When the Saxons had rebelled, the king entered Saxony with a strong force and a great multitude. With him were the excellent duke Rudolf, Duke Guelf, the illustrious Duke Gotefridus, husband of the most noble Matilda, Duke Theoderic, and an innumerable multitude of marquises and counts. They suddenly attacked the Saxons while they were unprepared, and, although the victory was most bloody, they were victorious. For it is reported that fifteen thousand men fell on the king’s side in that battle.

Thus victorious, though the undertaking remained unfinished, he returned to Francia. He then summoned a multitude of bishops, but did not seek God as the author of his victory, nor give him thanks for the victory granted to him. Instead, his heart was exalted and his eyes were lifted up; he set his mouth against heaven. Following the counsel of Hugh the White, whom we mentioned above, he repudiated in writing the lord pope, who had governed the universal Church in peace for three years, after the example of the pestilent Lothair, whom we mentioned above. He compelled his bishops to subscribe.

Alas! He did not consider that venerable chapter of Leo III, which reads:

“If anyone separates himself from the fellowship of the Roman Church, he will be able neither to enter through the gate of heaven nor to be freed from the bonds of sins.”

Meanwhile, letters severing the unity of the Church were carried to Rome by legates, for the king’s command pressed them. When they came to Piacenza, they gathered all the Lombard bishops there. On behalf of the king, they were ordered to confirm the king’s action.

But the outcome was very different from what they had hoped. For, with Dionysius, bishop of Piacenza, leading them, they all publicly swore with their own mouths that they would never again render obedience to the pope.

Then, from the workshop of iniquity—that is, from the city of Parma—they made a certain Roland, a cleric, the minister of this embassy. When he came to Rome, he happened to find the pope sitting in synod. Filled with the spirit of the devil, he forbade him, in the middle of the synod, to exercise pontifical office on behalf of the king, a layman, and ordered him to descend from his seat. This would have been culpable even if said to a presbyter of the second order without a judgment by the bishops themselves. Then he ordered the cardinals to travel beyond the mountains and choose a pontiff there for themselves.

The venerable Gregory, following the example of the good Master, first rescued his insulter from death. Then, once the tumult had scarcely been calmed, he celebrated the synod with alacrity.

On the following day letters from the bishops beyond the mountains were brought to the pope. In them they confessed that they had sinned and erred and sought pardon, promising that thereafter they would offer obedience as to a Father. But when the time approached for the synod to be dissolved, the venerable Gregory, who was ready to die for his sheep, did not allow the dishonor inflicted upon the holy Roman Church to go unpunished. With the counsel of all the bishops—numbering six hundred—he excommunicated the king, who did not recognize himself as one of Christ’s sheep, and judged him alien from the kingdom of God.

This was neither new nor blameworthy. It was not blameworthy because it had been done according to the rules of the holy Fathers. For in the Council of Chalcedon, in which six hundred bishops were present, the following is read concerning Dioscorus of Alexandria:

“How the second transgression greatly surpasses the first in wickedness. For he presumed to pronounce excommunication against the most holy Pope Leo.”

Anatolius, bishop of Constantinople, said:

“Dioscorus was not condemned because of the faith, but because he excommunicated the lord Archbishop Leo.”

Does it say there that an inquiry was made as to whether Dioscorus had pronounced that excommunication justly or unjustly? Certainly not. Rather, without any controversy, they were punished for this: although inferior, he attempted to assail a superior with every kind of insult.

Consider also what the holy Fathers defined on this matter at the Eighth Synod:

“We believe and define that the Lord’s saying, which Christ spoke to the holy apostles and his disciples—‘Whoever receives you receives me’ (Matthew X, 40), and ‘Whoever despises you despises me’ (Luke X, 16)—was spoken also of those who, after them and in their place, became the supreme pontiffs and chief shepherds in the Catholic Church.

“Therefore we define that no worldly power-holder may dishonor any of those who preside over patriarchal sees, or attempt to remove any of them from his own throne. Rather, they are to be judged worthy of all honor and reverence, especially the most holy pope of elder Rome; then the patriarchs of Alexandria, Antioch, and Jerusalem; and thereafter the patriarch of Constantinople.

“Nor may anyone weave or compose accusations against the most holy pope of elder Rome under the pretext of certain alleged crimes, as Photius recently and Dioscorus much earlier did. Whoever uses such boastfulness or audacity as to bring, in writing or without writing, any insults against the see of Peter, prince of the apostles, in the manner of Photius and Dioscorus, shall receive the same and equal condemnation as they did.

“But if anyone, relying on some power from God and trusting in his strength, should attempt to drive out the aforementioned pope of the apostolic chair, or any of the other patriarchs, let him be anathema.

“Moreover, if a universal synod has been convened and any ambiguity or controversy arises concerning the holy Roman Church, the proposed question must be examined with reverence and suitable respect, and a solution received, or advancement and completion achieved; but no one may boldly pronounce a sentence against the supreme pontiff of elder Rome.”

Behold how you have heard that the imitators of Photius and Dioscorus are to be condemned for the mere defamation of the Roman pontiff, and that powerful men attempting to drive the pope of elder Rome from his seat are to be anathematized. Therefore it is not blameworthy for a king attempting to drive the pope from his seat without judgment to be excommunicated; this is supported by the rules of the holy Fathers.

It is not unprecedented, for we read that many Roman pontiffs, for lesser causes, not only excommunicated men but also deposed them from their kingdoms. This will be clearer by an example.

Pope Innocent excommunicated the emperor Arcadius, son of the great Theodosius, because he had taken part in the deposition of John Chrysostom, whom Theophilus of Alexandria, together with the other eastern patriarchs and with the agreement of the other bishops, had pronounced excommunicated without the consent of the Roman pontiff; Innocent annulled their deposition. When the most reverend emperor learned what had happened, he did not rebel; rather, he humbly sought and obtained pardon.

Pope Constantine excommunicated the emperor Justin, son of Justinian, because he had failed to receive his legates with due honor. Later, in the street of Constantinople, Justin prostrated himself at Constantine’s feet, together with his kingdom, and sought pardon until he obtained it.

Pope Anastasius also excommunicated the emperor Athanasius. Speaking insolently about the pope, Athanasius was struck by lightning and died in the very palace.

Pope Gregory III not only excommunicated the emperor Leo but also deprived him of his kingdom. Pope Stephen deposed Charles, the brother of King Pippin, from the kingdom and appointed Pippin in his place. Pope Gregory, the Roman teacher, deprived every person of all dignity who violated the page of his privilege.

For he is found to have subscribed in one of his privileges as follows:

“GREGORY, to Senator, priest, and abbot of the Frankish hospice, among other things:

“Therefore, all these things that the page of this command and decree of ours contains, we decree that they are to be observed perpetually both by you and by all who shall succeed you in the order and place that you hold, as well as by those whom it may concern.

“But if any king, priest, judge, or secular person, knowing this page of our constitution, should attempt to act against it, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honor, and let him recognize himself as guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity committed.”

And what shall I say of Nicholas, who excommunicated two emperors at one and the same time: the eastern emperor, Michael, because he had driven Ignatius, bishop of Constantinople, from his see without a judgment of the pope; and the western emperor, Lothair, because of his relationship with his concubine Gualdrada?

What shall I say of the Roman pontiffs, when Ambrose, bishop of Milan, the lily of the Church, excommunicated the tyrant Maximus and excommunicated the emperor Theodosius after he had been expelled from the Church?

But who, unless deprived of reason, does not know that royal power is subject to the pontiffs? Who would believe himself free from subjection to the Roman pontiff except one who, because his sins demanded it, did not deserve to be numbered among the sheep of Jesus?

But now let us continue the sequence of events.

## The Seventh Book Ends

## The Eighth Book Begins

Meanwhile, after news of the king’s ban had resounded in the ears of the populace, our entire Roman world trembled, and Italians and people beyond the mountains reached differing decisions concerning these matters. For after Easter the Italians held at Pavia a council of malignants, in which all the Lombard bishops and abbots alike, with Guibert as their author and following the example of Photius and Dioscorus, excommunicated [Col. 0845B] the lord pope of elder Rome. Nothing like this had been heard since the beginning of the world: that the enemy of the human race had armed so many bishops, driven mad in mind, against the holy Roman Church at one time.

While these things were being done in Italy at the devil’s prompting, the princes beyond the mountains assembled together. In a salutary council they set the opposing parties before them as though in judgment, so that it might become clear to them whether the pope could excommunicate the king or not, and whether the king had been justly excommunicated or not.

They did not wish to destroy their own law, for it had been written that if anyone was not released from excommunication within a year and a day, he would lose every honor of dignity. Therefore, the most prudent bishops, abbots, and clerics of that kingdom, after deliberation, decreed according to the decrees of the holy Fathers and the examples of their predecessors that the king could be excommunicated by the pope, but that, following the example of Photius and Dioscorus, he had been justly excommunicated.

What more need be said? Finding nothing better suited to the circumstances, they confirmed the decision by an oath, together with the dukes who followed them, Rudolf, Guelf, and Theoderic. For Gotefridus, husband of the most excellent Matilda, had died a few days earlier. Together with the other pontiffs of that kingdom, they swore that, if their king wished to follow their counsel, they would bring him beyond the mountains before the year had passed, so that he might be absolved from the bond of excommunication without evil intent. They compelled the king, after he had sworn an oath, to swear with his own mouth that he would await the pope’s judgment as a private man.

When this had been done, they all again swore unanimously that, if the king wished to observe the oath he had given, they would undertake an expedition with him into Italy, attack the Northmen after he had been elevated to imperial dignity, and free Apulia and Calabria from their domination. But if, because his sins demanded it, he made the oath he had given void, they would never again receive him either as their lord or as their king.

Meanwhile they sent the bishop of Trier to Rome, so that he might bring the pope beyond the mountains to Augsburg. But how he was captured through the king’s cunning at Piacenza, and was not released until a letter from Spira, bishop of Piacenza, arrived ordering that he be set free, I omit to relate because of the length of the history.

Meanwhile, for the sake of peace, the venerable Gregory was traveling toward Augsburg with the greatest difficulty [Col. 0846A] because of the journey. For an extremely severe winter was then setting in. But the king suddenly entered Italy, thinking little of his oath. There are those who say that he wished to capture the pope unawares; this appears sufficiently probable. For Gregory, bishop of Vercelli and the king’s chancellor, to whom the princes had commanded that he bring the pope beyond the mountains, heard, after he had crossed the Apennine pass, that the king had secretly entered the city of Vercelli. When he reported this to the pope, the pope immediately entered Canossa, the extremely secure castle of the most excellent Matilda.

Meanwhile, when the king saw that his schemes had been exposed, he appeared to have laid aside all his ferocity. Clothed in dove-like simplicity, he went to Canossa and, for several days, remaining barefoot upon snow and ice, deceived all who were less discerning. From the venerable Gregory, although the pope was not ignorant of his deceits, he obtained the absolution he requested, with the Lord’s sacrament as mediator, during the celebration of the Mass, in the following manner.

With bishops, abbots, religious persons, clerics, and laymen standing around the divine table, the pope made him a participant in the sacrament on this condition: if he had humbled himself in mind as well as in body, and if he truly believed the pontiff to be pope, and believed himself to be justly excommunicated according to the example of Photius and Dioscorus, and thereby believed that he could be absolved, then the sacrament would become salvation for him thereafter. But if the matter were otherwise, then, through the morsel, Satan would enter into him as he entered Judas.

What more need be said? After the celebration of the Mass, they shared a common meal. Then he and all who had been released from excommunication were commanded to avoid the company of the excommunicated.

There are some who say that he swore to the pope to preserve his life, his limb, and his honor. I affirm nothing at all concerning what is unknown to me.

Meanwhile, after the king had been absolved from the ban, he appeared outwardly sufficiently devout and obedient to the pope. For he kept himself apart from the company of all the bishops, considering them excommunicated, while at night he submitted entirely to their wicked counsels. He was considering what later became clear through the outcome of events, and he acted in this way throughout the entire period during which he remained at Piacenza, especially fearing the presence of his most religious mother, the empress, who happened to be there.

At that time the hateful Cencius, whom we mentioned above, came to him. By day the king refused him, as an excommunicated man; by night he gave himself entirely to Cencius’s pestilential counsels. When Cencius saw that the pope could in no way be drawn from the castle of Canossa, he went toward Pavia. There the hateful Cencius died a bitter death, and Guibert, together with the other excommunicated men, celebrated his funeral with remarkable pomp.

While these things were taking place in Italy, the princes beyond the mountains assembled at Forken and established Duke Rudolf as their king, a man of great counsel and most vigorous in arms. This event brought great calamity upon the Roman world.

Meanwhile, while the king was staying at Pavia, when he heard of Rudolf’s election he was extraordinarily agitated. But because he was a man of great counsel and remarkably shrewd, he pretended humility and asked the pope through messengers to excommunicate Rudolf. The pope immediately promised to do so if Rudolf, when summoned, could not give an account of this action. For it did not appear canonical to excommunicate him before he had been defeated.

But the king, unrestrained in mind, quickly crossed the mountains and energetically regained Bavaria and Francia. But what more need be said? Rudolf, no less active, invaded Francia, and a most serious battle was fought. Many thousands of men fell on both sides. Some say that Henry was victorious in this battle, while many attribute the palm of the contest to King Rudolf. Whoever won, however, possessed a victory that was nevertheless most bloody.

Meanwhile a grave and irreparable disaster suddenly arose at Rome. For Cencius the prefect, a most Christian man, was killed by the treachery of Stephen, the brother of Cencius, the hateful man whom we mentioned above. When his body had been brought to Saint Peter’s in Rome, God performed many miracles through him.

The Romans, after deliberation, captured by force the castle into which that criminal had withdrawn. They cut his corpse into pieces, severing the head and hands, and committed it to the flames. They hung his head and hands in the curtain of blessed Peter. Of the remaining accomplices in so great a crime, they killed some and expelled others from their homeland.

A few days after these things had taken place, Gregory, the venerable pontiff, returned honorably to Rome and immediately convened a synod. Messengers of both kings were present. By the authority of blessed Peter, they were ordered not to fight but to choose a place where the bishops of both parties could meet safely and render an account before the legates of the holy Church.

But this salutary counsel was interrupted at the devil’s instigation, and battle was again joined. Many thousands of men fell on both sides, especially Bohemians. When this was reported to the pope during the following Lent—for this most serious battle had been fought on the feast of Saint Agatha—he convened a synod. Messengers of both kings were present, and they swore with their own mouths that the council had not been interrupted through any fault of their lords. But since it is not sufficiently apparent which of them had perjured himself, I omit to say.

What more need be said? The venerable pontiff resolved to send religious bishops beyond the mountains to forbid the kings to fight and to summon the bishops to a council: namely, Peter, bishop of Albano, a most religious man, who, before becoming a bishop, during the time of Pope Alexander, had passed unharmed through the midst of flames against the Simoniacs at the command of his abbot [Note: Hence he was called Peter Igneus, “Peter of Fire”]; and Oudalric, bishop of Padua, a very eloquent man and sufficiently faithful to King Henry; and the patriarch of Aquileia.

Crossing the Alps, they found the king in Bavaria. But neither by supplications, prayers, nor any other stratagem could they persuade King Henry to allow a synod to be held in his kingdom unless they were willing to excommunicate Rudolf without a summons. When they refused to do this, since the canons forbade it, they returned to Rome with the matter unfinished.

Battle was again fought, and many thousands of men fell on both sides.
