## The Eighth Book Ends

## The Ninth Book Begins

Meanwhile King Henry, after deliberate consideration, sent legates to Rome: namely, Lemar, archbishop of Bremen, whom we mentioned above; the bishop of Pabebaria; and several others bearing an arrogant and unheard-of embassy. Their message was that, if the pope wished to excommunicate Rudolf without judgment, the king would offer him the obedience due to him; otherwise, the king would acquire for himself a pope who would act according to his will.

The venerable pontiff, who was ready to die for the truth, not only did not condemn the man who offered a reason for his position, but also excommunicated the king himself, who spoke arrogantly. This action caused great uncertainty among the Roman people.

Meanwhile, when the aforementioned king’s legates came into Tuscany, they attempted in every way to turn the people away from obedience to the most excellent countess Matilda. Because the populace is always eager for novelty and faithless toward its former lords, and because this same populace is naturally unreliable, they were able to do very easily what they wished.

Then, coming into Lombardy, they left Margrave Albert and Count Boson in the region of Tuscany, invited all the Lombard princes to an assembly at Brixianorium, divided the kingdom and the priesthood, and returned to the king.

Meanwhile, after Pentecost, the venerable pontiff held a meeting with Robert, duke of the Northmen, on this side of Aquino [understand: “held a conference,” and so forth]. He absolved him from excommunication, and Robert, becoming the pope’s own knight, received from him the entire principate of Apulia and Calabria.

While these things were taking place, the Lombard bishops and princes assembled at Brixianorium. The king likewise came there with his bishops and the princes beyond the mountains. After a very evil deliberation, Guibert was chosen as Roman pontiff by men like himself. No Roman cleric or layman was present there, while the venerable Pope Gregory occupied the Roman see and had already governed the universal Church in peace for five years.

This diabolical deed had not been heard of from the day when peoples began to exist until that day. And because sin is often the punishment of sin: from the root of pride he came to perjury, through perjury to disobedience, through disobedience Guibert fell into excommunication, and through excommunication he came to idolatry.

The king, Henry, chose such a man as pontiff for himself, as we described above, with no Roman clerics or laymen present or consenting there except Hugh the White, who, because his sins demanded it, had long since been separated from the Church. At the urging of Dionysius, bishop of Piacenza, the king swore with his own mouth that he would receive the imperial crown from Guibert.

What more need be said? They were all so blinded in mind that they did not look upon the face of the earth. And because they had pitched their camps far from the city of Rome, alas, all who were there bowed down and worshiped the false prophet; and all who worshiped him fell far from the bosom of Mother Church.

Therefore, having celebrated the feast of the chiefs of the apostles in this manner, the king, strengthened by the blessing of so great a pontiff, returned to his own territories; but Guibert, carrying papal vestments with him together with his accomplices, entered Italy. But because the counsels of the Lord are a great abyss (Ps. 35:7), by the ineffable providence of God Heinricus did not suffer the Lord’s scourges according to what he deserved; rather, he experienced [Col. 0849B] success that astonishingly increased the arrogance of his wickedness. For not long afterward he entered Saxony with great power and a strong force. Rudolfus came against him, and when a fierce battle had been joined, Heinricus shamefully turned his back; in that battle the victorious Rudolfus fell.

Rudolfus did not die as cowards usually die. He was not killed while fleeing or seeking hiding places, but was found struck down by his own men amid the heaps of enemies and upon the corpses of the dead. His death was announced to Heinricus eight days later, while he was hiding in a certain fortress and considering flight. He immediately lifted his horn on high and spoke iniquities against the Lord (Ps. 74:6); failing to recognize Satan’s deceit, he believed that his sin had pleased God. A few days after [Col. 0849C] these events, his son fought against the army of the most distinguished Mathilda and won the victory.

Elated by these successes, he suddenly entered Italy, and after Easter, taking the beast with him, headed for Rome. On the vigil of Pentecost he pitched his camp in Nero’s Meadow. But, O God, who could fail to marvel at the madness of so many prudent men? Even if they had lost the eyes of their minds, they had not lost their bodily eyes. Did they not see whom they were escorting and how honorably he was received by the Romans? For one could see lances in place of candles, armed men in place of the choirs of clerics, insults in place of praises, and howls in place of acclamations.

What more need be said? After the devastation of the fields and many varied murders, after the different disasters and miseries that the Romans endured because they refused to receive the false pope [Col. 0849D], the king returned to Lombardy with him, his undertaking unsuccessful.

The following winter, taking the pestilent man with him, he entered Romania again. He ravaged the cities, overthrew the fortifications, and finally besieged Rome throughout the whole Lenten season. After Easter, when his army had been spread throughout the cities and neighboring fortifications on every side, he left Guibert at the Tiber and himself returned to Lombardy.

Guibert, however, “as Alcimus” [thus the manuscript], was doing enough for his priesthood: throughout the entire festive season he carried out great plunderings and various mutilations of Roman citizens; thereafter, ravaging the crops and fields with fire, he was wickedly considering the deprivation or starvation [Col. 0850A] of children.

The following winter the king returned to Rome once again. After it had been secured by oaths that all religious persons wishing to visit Rome from whatever kingdom would come safely, he captured the bishop of Ostia and other religious monks and clerics. Seeing that the abbot of Cluny and all the bishops, both clerics and monks, regarded him as excommunicated, he immediately resorted to crafty arguments. To win popular favor, he said that he wished to receive the imperial crown from the venerable Gregory. When the Roman people heard this, not only the laymen but also the religious persons who were present—bishops, clerics, abbots, and monks—began to pray tearfully and most earnestly that he might have pity on a homeland that was almost lost.

But the venerable [Col. 0850B] pontiff, who was prepared to die for the truth, absolutely refused to do this unless the king first made public satisfaction for his excommunication. Since the king, accused by his conscience, refused to do so, and since the Romans begged the venerable pontiff for many days to receive the king, while he remained unmoved by all their entreaties, the king mentioned above gradually began to acquire the favor of the populace. After gaining almost all the Romans for himself by money, terror, and force, and despairing of the strength of the venerable Gregory, he resolved, to the disgrace and infamy of the whole Church, to ordain Guibert in the seat of Saint Peter.

He had no cardinal bishops, priests of the holy Roman Church, levites, or neighboring bishops, whose custom it is to enthrone the pope. No one from so great a number [Col. 0850C] had been with him except those who had exiled themselves from the faith. Previously they had preferred to be deprived of their own sees, and, if necessary, to be weakened in all their members, rather than to become participants in such pollution.

He was enthroned in the seat of blessed Peter by the bishop of Modena, the bishop of Bologna, and the bishop of Aevenia [sic]. Such a phantom has never been heard of in the world. Thereafter, at Easter, he received the imperial blessing from such a man; thus he entered the city, taking with him the threefold chimera, and proceeded as far as the Lateran palace.

When the venerable Gregory learned of the people’s agitation, he had already for some time established himself in the fortress of Saint Angelo. The king armed all the Romans to besiege it. Pretending not to know of the arrival of the most powerful duke Robert, he destroyed the Capitoline palace, [Col. 0850D] came with Guibert to the church of Saint Peter, and utterly destroyed the city of Saint Peter, which Pope Leo IV had built. Then, bidding farewell to the Romans, he withdrew together with Guibert.

But before he had reached Siena, the most powerful duke Ruodpert attacked Rome. Unlike Heinricus, who took three years, Ruodpert captured the treacherous city by force of arms on the very day after his arrival, freed the pope from the siege, and, victorious, took possession of almost all the districts of the Roman city by sword and fire.

Afterward, while spending many days at the Lateran palace, he sold many thousands of Romans as though they were Jews; some he led away captive as far as Calabria. They deserved to be punished with such a penalty, for, following the example of the Jews, they had betrayed their shepherd.

What more need be said? [Col. 0851A] The venerable pope, together with Ruobert, reached Salerno. Remaining there for several days, he offered the people very salutary admonitions. But not long afterward, overcome by bodily illness, he returned his spirit to heaven. At his tomb God continues to perform many thousands of miracles to this day. Truly, three and four times blessed is he who was deemed worthy to suffer insults for the name of Jesus.

He indeed reigns with Peter in the heavenly places [in the manuscript: “with Peter”]; but this man, hated by everyone, is regarded by no living person as apostolic, although some say that he is so through the king’s favor. Yet there are people who, through the king’s favor, fabricate certain schemes in order to defame Lord Gregory, but they cannot do so.

Some say that he was not lawfully apostolic [Col. 0851B] because of certain decrees of Nicholas the Younger, by which they claim that an anathema was pronounced forbidding anyone to aspire to the Roman pontificate except with the consent of the king and his son. This will be shown in every way to be utterly false; yet even if it were true, it would still be of no consequence. For although Roman pontiffs may temper the rigor of the canons according to the necessities of the times, they may not utterly destroy them.

What else would that be except completely to destroy Christian law, to violate the decrees of the holy Roman pontiffs who founded the Church with their blood, and to invalidate the four sacred councils, which human beings ought to venerate as they do the Gospels?

But let us free Nicholas, of blessed memory, from this accusation, and demonstrate by suitable witnesses that he did not issue such decrees. Let Guibert come forward, a suitable witness from whom the Caesar received the imperial crown, and let him convict those men of speaking falsely.

For if, according to the decrees of Nicholas [Col. 0851C], it is true that no one should be regarded as apostolic who was not elected Roman pontiff with the king’s consent [thus the manuscript], and that Alexander was enthroned in the Roman see without his will, it follows that the same man was not apostolic but excommunicated. And if he was excommunicated and separated from the Church of God, what did he confer upon Guibert when he consecrated him as bishop? He could not give the blessing that he did not possess; therefore he gave the curse that he possessed. If, then, he was accursed, how was he pope?

But this is false. Guibert lawfully received an episcopal blessing, and Alexander, who obtained the Roman pontificate against the king’s will, was legally ordained as apostolic, with Guibert as witness.

The same must be thought concerning [Col. 0851D] the Caesar. For if this were true, how could a man of such great counsel and skill have given obedience to Pope Alexander for so many years, and how could he have received the imperial crown from Guibert, his bishop?

Let a third witness come forward, Hugo Candidus, a Roman cardinal, and prove that they were *incitos* [Note: Thus the manuscript; I confess that I am uncertain about this word.]. For how could he have chosen Gregory on the very day of the burial of the aforementioned pope? If the decrees are true, then he is excommunicated. And if he is excommunicated and infamous, how could Hugo alone have chosen Guibert as pope at Brixianorium [Col. 0852A], against the will of the Roman citizens?

These claims, however, are false and like children’s games. No one doubts that the venerable Gregory had the king’s consent at his ordination. For the bishop of Vercelli, sent by the king to Gregory, was present at his consecration.

If the king had anything against him, he ought to have said so at the beginning, before he had honorably received his envoys; before he had publicly received absolution from them for his excommunication [Note: The word *publicly* appears to have been added in the margin, marked by the same hand at Col. 0852D, though in different ink.]; before he had sent to him in Rome Bishop Herimannus of Bamberg to be deposed; and before, at his command, he had appointed another in his see.

If he says that, when he was young, he was deceived [Col. 0852B] by the scheming of his counselors, what shall we say of Lemarus, archbishop of Bremen, a most wise man and highly skilled in every art? After he had been suspended from office by the envoys of that same pope, did he not abstain from the priesthood until he came from Saxony to Rome, taking with him the philosophers of that kingdom: Giticlinus of Cologne, and Guczolo the provost, who later devastated the Church of Mainz, and Mainardus of Bamberg? With these men he threw himself at the pope’s feet and tearfully begged forgiveness until he obtained it and received back his priestly office.

I would indeed say: if the pope was not pope, why did Lemarus receive absolution from excommunication from him at Canossa—unless there are those who say that an extorted confession is not a confession?

Those who say this badly understand [Col. 0852C] the decrees of blessed Alexander, fifth Roman pontiff after blessed Peter. For they do not call a confession “extorted” except when someone is compelled by punishments or threats either to deny the truth or to sin in idolatry, or when the truth is brought forth unwillingly [thus the manuscript]. This belongs to the guilty. Such a confession is not an extorted confession but an unwilling one: when someone is compelled to confess what the truth reveals, although with a wicked mind he had decided to deny it.

There are also others who say that the venerable Pope Gregory was legitimate, but that he pronounced a sentence of condemnation against himself. For on the Monday after Easter, at Saint Peter’s, when he had excommunicated the king, he added:

“Let it be known to all of you that, if Heinricus does not repent by the feast of Saint Peter, he will be dead or deposed; and if this does not happen, you must no longer believe me.”

[Col. 0852D] Misunderstanding these words, they eagerly seized upon them, and some twisted them toward the worse according to their own wishes. But he did not pronounce a sentence against himself. For it is one thing to say, “You ought not believe me,” and another to say, “I judge him to be deposed.” Nor can a sentence be called a sentence when it is issued before the matter has been examined.

Moreover, a sentence pronounced without consideration possesses no firmness. Although popular ignorance may have understood the words otherwise than it should have, everyone of sound judgment nevertheless does not doubt that he spoke truly.

For since it is written in the Law [Col. 0853A], “If anyone prophesies in the name of the Lord and what he predicts does not come to pass, let him be crushed with stones, because he has made the name of the Lord void” (Deut. 18:22), what are we to say about Jonah? He prophesied the destruction of Nineveh, yet when Nineveh was not destroyed, he is recorded neither as having died nor as having been rejected. This is because a particular kind of destruction was understood there.

Thus it is said: “Overturn the wicked, and they shall be no more” (Prov. 12:7). Likewise, by the Lord’s voice it was said to the first-formed man: “On whatever day you eat of it, you shall die by death” (Gen. 2:17), although he is shown to have lived more than nine hundred years after tasting what had been forbidden. The meaning is that he was threatened with punitive death, not natural death, by which the soul is released from the bond of the body.

For Scripture teaches us of three deaths. One is spiritual death, by which the soul dies to vices and lives to the Lord; concerning this it is written: “Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord” (Rev. 14:13). Another is natural death, by which the soul is released from the bond of the body. The third is punitive death, concerning which it is written: “The soul that sins, it shall die” (Ezek. 18:4).

No one doubts that the man [Col. 0853B] who prostrated himself and worshiped the beast at Brixianorium died by this death. But they say that on that day he was not deposed from the kingdom, failing to understand either that the conjunction is disjunctive rather than affirmative, or that, although perhaps not before human eyes, he was nevertheless deposed before the divine eyes.

For who could deny that Saul, after Samuel had said to him, “God will tear your kingdom from you today and give it to one better than you” (1 Sam. 15:28), and after the anointing had been given, reigned before human eyes, filled with a devilish spirit, until the exceedingly bitter battle of Gilboa, to his own destruction?

How much better it would have been [Col. 0853C] had he, on the day when he was rejected by the Lord, been deprived of royal power, rather than later, swollen with desire for kingship, kill the priest of the Lord through Doeg the Edomite and order the death of eighty-five men girded with linen ephods; and had he been rejected on that same day, as I said above, he would not have worshiped the devil in Samuel or heard him say: “Tomorrow you and your sons shall be with me” (1 Sam. 28:19).

What more need be said? It is sufficiently clear that he died and was deposed on the day when he prostrated himself and worshiped the beast.

Again, there are some who say that the venerable Gregory [Col. 0853D] truly was Roman pontiff, but that he excommunicated the king without cause, according to the decrees of Pope and martyr Felix, in which we read:

“No one who has been stripped of his possessions or driven from his see may be excommunicated or judged before everything has been restored to him,” and so forth.

Although this chapter appears to pertain specifically to bishops, it will nevertheless be demonstrated most clearly that it does nothing to help them prevent the proof that the king was justly excommunicated.

If there had been some dispute concerning the kingdom [Col. 0854A]—whether he held the reins of the kingdom justly or unjustly—I concede that he ought first to have been restored to his position before being excommunicated and judged. But the controversy between the pope and the king arose for no other reason than that, following Photius and Dioscorus, “having set his mouth in heaven,” he attempted without judgment to drive the lord pope of Old Rome from his see [thus the manuscript].

The second excommunication was imposed for this reason: the lord pope had admonished him once, twice, and three times not to fight and to give way so that a council might be held in his kingdom, but he refused. Therefore, imitating the Teacher of the Gentiles, who declared himself ready to avenge every disobedience, the pope took care to restrain the rebellion of the proud son by excommunicating him—not wishing to kill him, but to call him to repentance.

But since you had previously asked me, dearest friend [Col. 0854B], whether it is permissible for a Christian to fight with weapons for the truth, you were asking for a history, which I have now composed. Although it is well known to many, it will benefit those who come after, so that you may know this: if a Christian was ever permitted to fight for any cause, it is permitted in every way to fight against the Guibertists.

For if blessed Gregory commanded all to fight against the Simoniac and Neophyte heresy, out of consideration for his office, there can be no doubt that one must fight all the more against this heresy, which is the mother of all heresies.

Nor shall we judge soldiers to be alien to the kingdom of God. The Lord’s Baptist not only did not abhor them [Note: It should rather be read “did not abhor,” as the sense requires.], but rather commanded them to be content with their pay and to serve as soldiers (Luke 3:14).

Did our Lord Jesus Christ not place the faith of the centurion before that of the children of Israel? And did he not disdain to heal his servant? After his glorious ascension into heaven, the first fruits of the nations [Col. 0854C] who believed were soldiers. Their almsgiving and prayers were so acceptable that, when Simon Peter entered Cornelius’s house, before he laid hands upon Cornelius and those who were with him, and before he cleansed them with the water of baptism, they received the gifts of the Holy Spirit (Acts 10:44).

And although there are certain offices from which, after baptism, a person ought not to return, they served under pagan commanders [Note: The words “it was not permitted” should undoubtedly be inserted, although the manuscript does not contain them.].

Therefore, if it was permitted for an earthly king, shall it not be permitted for a heavenly one? If it was permitted for the commonwealth, shall it not be permitted for justice? If it was permitted against barbarians, shall it not be permitted against heretics?

Did not Saint Hilary, as we read in the history, arm Clovis, king of the Franks, against the Arian heretics? Blessed Augustine, that distinguished teacher, also urged Boniface to hang and pursue the Circumcellions and Donatists, and wrote to him as follows:

[Col. 0854D] “To Boniface, a distinguished man, A. sends greetings. You complain gravely about the war; do not doubt that I shall give useful counsel to you and yours. Take up weapons in your hands; let prayer strike the ears of the Author. For when battle is joined, God looks on with open eyes and grants the palm and victory to the side he sees to be just. Do not think that it is impossible to please God through weapons of war.

“Saint David was among those who bore them, and the Lord gave him this great testimony: ‘From the fruit of your womb, t. p. s. s. t.’ (Ps. 131:11). The centurion was among them, concerning whom the Lord says: ‘Amen, I say to you, I have not found such great [Col. 0855A] faith in Israel’ (Matt. 8:10). Cornelius was among them, whose almsgiving was accepted before God (Acts 10:14). What more shall I say? Necessity, not the will, should destroy an enemy who is fighting.

“The same is found in the Lord’s sermon delivered on the mountain. When he was speaking of the beatitudes and came to ‘Blessed are those who suffer persecution for justice’ (Matt. 5:10), he likewise said that those who inflict persecution for justice are blessed, just as those who suffer persecution for justice.”

Jerome, in his *Treatise on the Pentateuch*, likewise says:

“If the Hebrew was commanded not to spare father, mother, or wife who sleeps in his bosom, if she wished to turn him away from the truth, how much more should you, O Christian, understand that you must not spare a heretic who tears apart the garment of the Lord Jesus.”

The same author says [Col. 0855B] to the rustic of Narbonne: “Cruelty for God is not impiety.”

The aforesaid holy Jerome, in his *Treatise on Jeremiah*, writes to Eusebius of Cremona, among other things:

“To destroy murderers, adulterers, and wicked persons guilty of death is not murder, but observance of the laws.”

The venerable Ambrose, that jewel among priests, boasts in one of his letters that he was defended by the arms of the people against the fury of the empress Justina.

The most holy Gregory, that golden star, is reproved by the emperor Maurice because he was providing the soldiers who guarded the walls of the Roman city with a greater abundance of food and arms than they were accustomed to receive from the emperor. Let us hear what he writes to Velox, master of soldiers:

“Nor did it seem useful that a few soldiers should be sent there” [Note: Rather, “nor did it seem useless” should be read; but the manuscript, exceedingly corrupt, reads as printed.]; “[Col. 0855C] your Glory should take care to admonish and encourage them to be ready for labor. When the opportunity arises, speak with our most glorious sons Marcio and Vitalio, and whatever they decide with God’s help for the benefit of the commonwealth; and if you learn that Aiulphus is still making excursions into the territory of the Ravennates, work against him from the rear, as befits brave men.”

To Marcio and Vitalio, among other things:

“Glorious sons, be vigilant, because, as I have learned, the enemy has gathered a multitude and is said to be stationed under arms. If, with God angry at him, he should wish to make an advance here, ravage his positions as far as God enables you.”

The same author says in the *Moralia* [Col. 0855D]: “To kill the cruel is not cruelty.”

You have heard [Col. 0856A] the teachings of the holy Fathers; consider also the examples of those who fought for the truth. We read that Hermogenes, the prefect who, out of zeal for the Arian heresy, persecuted Paul, bishop of Constantinople, was burned with his entire household by the orthodox. We know that this was not condemned but praised by everyone.

What shall I say about the Alexandrians? Are they not praised throughout the world for the various battles and different struggles that they waged against the Arians? Are not the Milanese raised up with worthy glory by the Catholics, because they rescued orthodox bishops who were fleeing into a church from the hands of Constantius? Did not Cyril, bishop of Alexandria, whose praise is proclaimed at the Council of Ephesus, place among the martyrs Ammonius, a monk who, driven by zeal for God, struck the prefect Orestes with a stone, although he did so without perfect knowledge, and who had been stoned by Orestes’s officers for that reason?

Let us now come to our own times [Col. 0856B] and see what the Almighty bestowed upon those who fought against the Northmen under Pope Leo. For he crowned them with glory and honor (Heb. 2:7), and demonstrated by signs and wonders that they had pleased him.

What should I say about Herlinbald, a religious man, and Decentius, the Roman prefect, a most Christian man, at whose tombs God performs many miracles?

Therefore let the most glorious soldiers of God fight for the truth; let them contend for justice; let them fight courageously against the heresy that exalts itself against everything that is called and everything that is worshiped (2 Thess. 2:4).

Let them emulate for good the most distinguished countess [Col. 0856C] Mathilda, daughter of blessed Peter. With a manly spirit, she has set aside all worldly things and is prepared to die rather than violate God’s law, and to attack in every way, as far as her strength permits, the heresy that now rages in the Church. We believe that Sisera will be delivered into her hand and scattered like Jabin in the torrent of Kishon (Ps. 82:10–11), because he has destroyed the Lord’s vineyard and grazes upon it as a solitary creature (Ps. 79:14), having become like dung upon the earth.

But let us, according to the duty of our office, pray that, having been burned with fire and undermined [thus the manuscript], he may perish most swiftly at the rebuke of your face (ibid., 17).

[Col. 0856D] Here ends.

[ON THE SACRAMENTS.]

[Col. 0855]

## Prefatory Notice to the Following Little Work

(Muratori, *Antiquitates Italicae*, III, 599.)

The author of this little work was first Bonizo of Sutri, then, according to Berthold, the historian of Constance, the bishop of Piacenza, who in the year of Christ 1089, because he opposed the schismatic enemies of the Roman Church and its other foes with manly courage, was cut down by them and met death in a glorious struggle. The Anonymous of Melk, edited by the most distinguished P. Pezio, long ago included him among ecclesiastical writers. Then Ughelli discussed him in the first volume of *Italia Sacra*, among the bishops of Sutri, and in volume II, among those of Piacenza; afterward Peter Lambecius treated him in his *Commentaries on the Imperial Library*, and William Cave in his *Ecclesiastical History of Literature*; and most recently of all, and at greatest length, Casimir Oudinus in his *Commentaries on Ecclesiastical Writers*.

His works lie hidden among the shelves of the Imperial Library of Vienna: namely, a *Collection of Decrees* gathered from Sacred Scripture, councils, and the Fathers; and an *Epitome of the History of the Roman Pontiffs*. Since I was exceedingly eager for the latter book, I eventually learned that it contained nothing except a mere brief catalogue of the Roman pontiffs, of the sort of which we have many; for that reason I stopped trying to obtain it further. Other little works composed by him are also believed to have perished; concerning them, the aforementioned Oudinus should be consulted.

As for the present work, Mabillon had already written the following in his *Italian Itinerary*, page 13, when discussing the Ambrosian Library of Milan:

“In another manuscript there is a book by Bonizo, bishop of Sutri, on the sacraments, addressed to Walter, abbot of the monastery of Le Mans; in this book the author mentions another little work of his against the schismatic Hugh.”

But even before Mabillon, Peter Maria Campi, in his *Ecclesiastical History of Piacenza*, under the years 1044 and 1087, supplied much information about the aforementioned Bonizo. Among other things, he noted that he had seen in Rome Bonizo’s book *On Ecclesiastical Sacraments*.

Therefore, I wish to append here this little work, which I formerly copied from a manuscript of the Ambrosian Library. It was written to Walter, not the abbot but the prior of the monastery of Le Mans.

[Col. 0857]

## Here Begins the Little Book on the Sacraments, Published by Bonizo and Sent to Walter, Monk and Prior of the Monastery of Le Mans

[Col. 0857A]

Holy and universal Mother Church, joined to Christ as to one man, because she does not walk in shadow but already enjoys with certainty the reality of God’s grace, does not receive many sacraments. Nevertheless, she possesses a few: two handed down by the Lord himself, while certain others were instituted by the apostles.

For the command to baptize, and the manner in which baptism ought to be given to those being baptized—the baptism by which a person is reborn as a new human being and without which, according to the testimony of the Truth, no one will enter the kingdom of heaven—we read that the Lord gave this command to the apostles after the resurrection in the Gospel according to Matthew, in these words:

“Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28:19).

Thus teaching is to precede baptism: that is, the person who is to be baptized must first be taught to believe before being baptized. For just as faith without works is dead (Jas. 2:17), so works, if they do not proceed from faith, are of no benefit.

This is not observed in the case of infants, because they are believed to be saved through the faith of their parents and of those by whom they are received in holy baptism. Nevertheless, when they reach the age of understanding, they must be taught not only what they ought to believe in their hearts, but also what they ought to observe in their conduct.

Although we read that the disciples baptized before the Lord’s Passion, since the Lamb who had come to take away the sins of the world had not yet been sacrificed, such baptism did not open the entrance to paradise for those who received it. Nor could they rise as new human beings, since they had not been buried with Christ through baptism into death (Rom. 6:4).

Nevertheless, although the gate of the heavenly kingdom was not opened to such persons through this baptism, it was not entirely superfluous. For that baptism benefited them as much as exorcism and catechetical instruction benefit those who are to be baptized.

Nor should anyone be troubled that such baptism is called Christ’s baptism in the Gospel. The faith with which catechumens are instructed is also called Christ’s faith, and it is. Yet without receiving baptism it does not save catechumens.

Indeed, although we read that after the resurrection the apostles received from the Lord both the command to baptize and the manner of baptism, we do not read that they baptized until after the coming of the Holy Spirit, the Paraclete.

On the holy day of Pentecost, when the apostles were speaking in the languages of all nations, while the Jews loudly declared that they were full of new wine (Acts 2:1), Peter demonstrated by the prophecy of Joel that the faithless had spoken falsely. Evangelizing them with David’s testimony that Jesus had risen after the pains of death had been loosed, he baptized, in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, those who had been pierced in heart—three thousand in number that very day.

For this reason the Roman pontiffs have determined that, just as help must be given at all times to the sick, to those in danger of death, to those under siege, to those in shipwreck, and to those in other dangers, so that they may not perish without the grace of baptism, assistance is to be given to the healthy and unharmed only on the holy Saturday of Easter and on the Saturday of Pentecost.

Moreover, if at any time, through the madness of heretics or the ignorance of foolish priests, one of the three persons has been left unnamed in baptism, the baptism will not be valid, nor can it be called repeated baptism, since it is clear that the first baptism was not correctly performed.

We read that Paul did this in the Acts of the Apostles with those who had been baptized with John’s baptism. Since they did not yet know whether the Holy Spirit existed, they were baptized again—or rather, they received true baptism.

For those who are to be sons by adoption must be reborn in the Spirit by whom the Lord’s humanity was conceived in the Virgin’s womb. By God’s grace we are reborn. And because the divinity of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is one, their will is one, and without doubt their operation is one.

Let what I have now said briefly concerning the sacrament of baptism suffice. Now let us pass to the sacrament of the Eucharist.

## On the Sacrament of the Eucharist
Finally, after the Lord had celebrated the Passover with the apostles, concerning which, according to Luke, you have the Lord saying: “With desire I have desired to eat this Passover with you before I suffer. For I say to you, I shall not eat it from now on until it is fulfilled in the kingdom of God. And, having taken the cup, he gave thanks and said: ‘Take this and divide it among yourselves. For I say to you that from now on I shall not drink of the fruit of the vine until the kingdom of God comes’” (Luke 22:15). Therefore, the sacrament of the old law having been abolished, and the carnal ceremonies of the Jewish people having been rejected—those which are designated here by the name “old”—he immediately entrusted to the apostles the sacrament of the New Testament and the rite of its celebration, taking bread and saying: “This is my body, which will be given over for you. Do this in remembrance of me.” Likewise, after he had supped, he took the cup, saying: “This is the cup of the new testament in my blood, which will be poured out for you” (Matthew 26:26).

But after the Lord’s resurrection, while Christ repeatedly ate, drank, and conversed with the apostles, it was not fitting for the apostles, filled with the joy of the resurrection, to celebrate the sacrament in remembrance of the Lord’s Passion. For what did the roasted fish eaten by Christ after the resurrection and handed to the disciples signify, if not the suffering Christ? At the same time they ate the bread and the fish placed upon the coals, and in the sacrament they ate that same thing as bread, fish, and honeycomb.

After the coming of the Holy Spirit, the Paraclete, upon the disciples, when the multitude of believers was of one heart and one soul (Acts 4:32), we read in the Acts of the Apostles that the apostles broke bread in the houses and around the houses in remembrance of the Lord’s Passion, and that the believing peoples shared in communion. They were not greatly concerned whether the bread was unleavened or leavened.

Later, as the Christian religion began to flourish, with the disciples dispersed throughout the world, and especially when the Chosen Vessel, having preached the Gospel, had sown it from Jerusalem as far as Illyricum, and as far as Spain and the intervening islands, the churches began to assemble on the first day of the week to hear the word of God, wherever they could. After the preaching—or rather, the instruction—bread and only plain wine were placed upon a table, whether wooden or constructed of stone. After the priest had duly recited over the Eucharist supplications, prayers, and petitions, including those which the Church still chants on Holy Friday, and after the Lord’s Prayer had been chanted in a low voice, so that it could scarcely be heard by those standing nearby, the people communicated in remembrance of the Lord’s Passion according to the Lord’s tradition. In most churches this was done by those who were fasting; in some, following the example of the Lord’s Supper, it was done by those who had eaten.

We know from the teaching of blessed Augustine, in the letter which he wrote to Januarius the bishop concerning the Lord’s Supper, that this continued even into the time of blessed Augustine himself. Blessed Paul the apostle, teacher of the nations, while instructing Timothy for episcopal governance, says among other things: “I exhort, first of all, that supplications, prayers, petitions, and thanksgivings be made for kings and for all who are placed in high positions, so that we may lead a quiet life” (1 Timothy 2:1), and so forth.

That this rite of the sacraments was celebrated by the apostles and handed down to the churches, blessed Celestine, Roman bishop, teaches us in his decretal letter sent to the African bishops. While discussing the grace of God, he says among other things:

> Let us also receive the supplication of the priestly sacraments, which, handed down by the apostles, is celebrated uniformly throughout the whole world and in every Catholic church, so that the law of praying may establish the law of believing. For when the priests of the holy peoples perform the embassy entrusted to them, they plead the cause of the human race before the divine clemency; and, with the whole Church groaning together with them, they ask and pray that faith be granted to unbelievers; that idolaters be freed from the errors of their impiety; that, when the veil of their hearts has been removed, the light of truth may appear to the Jews; that heretics may come to their senses through receiving the Catholic faith; that schismatics may receive the spirit of renewed charity; that remedies of repentance may be granted to the fallen; and that, when catechumens have been led to the sacraments of regeneration, the hall of heavenly mercy may be opened to them.

We are instructed that these things were thus celebrated by the apostles and handed down to the churches through the tradition of blessed Paul the apostle, and we are taught the same by the letter of blessed Celestine, Roman pontiff.

It remains for me now to write how this institution, which is celebrated in our parts of the western world in the Mass, ought to be celebrated, and from which authorities it took its beginning. But do not delay in praying for us, so that the Lord, having taken a coal from the altar with tongs, may deign to cleanse my lips by his grace. For who am I, that I should be able to unfold such great mysteries? Yet the Lord also spoke among thorns. And would that you, O good Jesus, who take away the sins of the world, would not shrink from my brambles!

[Col. 0860B] After the renowned martyrdom of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, who received it on the same day as blessed Paul, teacher of the nations, under Nero Caesar, thereby making the Roman Church glorious, Clement, a Roman by nationality, assumed the Roman pontificate. If anyone wishes to know how he was first after Peter by election and third in rank, let him read the Book which I wrote against the schismatic Hugh; there he will find the matter fully explained.

This man, filled with the Spirit of God, observing that the solemn prayers mentioned above might become commonplace if they were too frequently recited in the ears of the people—and, what is more, lest they perhaps be committed to memory by pagans and recited at crossroads and in public squares, in theaters and in the shrines of idols—decreed, out of reverence for the apostles, that they should be celebrated on one day, namely Holy Friday, according to the former custom.

He himself established the Canon, to be recited secretly over the Eucharist throughout the whole year, so that the people might receive it all the more secretly, eagerly, and reverently. He likewise instituted that on Sundays the believing people should be summoned to a suitable place wherever one could be found; that after the collection had been given—which blessed Augustine calls a supplication—and after the Gospel had been read by the people, bread should be placed upon the table after the preaching, and only plain wine should be used.

After the priest had secretly chanted the supplications over the offering, he instituted that he should greet the people in this manner: “The Lord be with you.” When the people responded, “And with your spirit,” he again admonished them to have their hearts above, so that they might think about the things above, not those on earth. When they responded that they had them with the Lord, he immediately invited the people to give thanks to God. When they responded that it was worthy and just to give thanks to God, he at once began as follows:

> It is truly worthy and just, right and beneficial for us always and everywhere to give you thanks, holy Lord, almighty Father, eternal God, through Christ our Lord; through whom angels praise your majesty, dominions adore it, powers tremble before it; the heavens and the virtues of the heavens, together with the blessed seraphim, celebrate it with shared rejoicing. With them, we beseech you to admit our voices also, as we say in humble confession:

And when the whole Church had chanted:

> Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of Hosts. Heaven and earth are full of your glory. Hosanna in the highest. Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord. Hosanna in the highest.

he immediately instituted that the Canon—which blessed Augustine calls a prayer—should be recited secretly over the Eucharist in this manner:

> Therefore, most merciful God, etc.

[Note: [Col. 0861D] The Canon of the Apostles follows. There is mention up to and including Saint Thaddeus; no others are mentioned.]

> Therefore, we beseech you, O Lord, graciously to accept this offering of our service and of your whole family, through Christ our Lord. Deign, O God, we beseech you, to make this offering blessed, enrolled, ratified, reasonable, and acceptable in every respect, so that it may become for us the body and blood of your most beloved Son, our Lord Jesus Christ. Upon which things, with a favorable and serene countenance, etc.

[Note: [Col. 0862D] The words of consecration are not present.]

> Through him, O Lord, you always create all these good things, sanctify them, give them life, bless them, and grant them to us; through him, and with him, and in him, etc.

After these things had been read, and after the Lord’s Prayer had been secretly completed, he invited the people to the blessing and instituted that blessings—what blessed Augustine calls petitions—should be given over the people. Those who wished communicated with a particle of bread placed inside the cup. And thus the Mass was finished.

In this manner Anacletus, who succeeded Clement in the pontificate, and Evaristus, Anacletus’s successor, celebrated Masses. Blessed Alexander, Evaristus’s successor, added to the Canon the remembrance of Christ’s Passion, beginning at the place where it says, “Who the day before he suffered,” and continuing to “Upon which things, with a favorable and serene countenance.”

He also instituted that only unleavened bread should be offered, for previously both leavened and unleavened bread had been offered indiscriminately. He likewise ordered that water be mixed with wine in the sacrifice. This was done only in the solemn Masses mentioned above, and in all respects he followed the institutions of blessed Clement. His successor Sixtus imitated him in every respect.

Telesphorus, Sixtus’s successor, added the angelic hymn to be chanted at solemn Masses. Telesphorus, Hyginus and Pius, Agnitius and Soter, Eleutherius and Victor, Zephyrinus and Calixtus, Urban and Pontian, Anterus and Fabian, Cornelius and Lucius, Stephen and Dionysius celebrated Masses without adding anything to the Canon, offering unleavened bread and mixing water with the sacrificial wine according to the institution of Pope Alexander.

Felix, Dionysius’s successor, instituted that the names of the martyrs, like those of the apostles, should be recited in the Canon. He also added to the Canon, beginning at the place where it says, “To us also, sinners,” and continuing to “Through whom, O Lord, you always create all these good things.”

He also ordered that Masses be celebrated over the tombs of the martyrs and over relics. Blessed Augustine praises this as rightly done in his treatise on John, so that the memory of the martyrs’ passion might be mingled with Christ’s Passion.

After him, Mark and Eutychian, Gaius and Marcellinus and Eusebius, Melchiades and Sylvester, Mark and Julius, Liberius and Felix, Damasus and Siricius and Anastasius celebrated Masses according to the rite of their predecessors, adding nothing to the service of the Mass.

Innocent, Anastasius’s successor, instituted that, after the Lord’s Prayer had been completed but before the particle of bread was placed in the cup, peace should be announced to the people in a loud voice and given during the solemn Masses, the people having already been blessed by the bishop or priest before the Lord’s Prayer. Zosimus and Celestine, Sixtus and Leo the First celebrated Masses according to this rite.

Leo the First instituted that, after the Gospel, the Creed should be chanted by the entire people. Hilary, Leo’s successor, and Simplicius, Felix and Gelasius, who composed the Book of Collects, which blessed Gregory later corrected, Anastasius and Symmachus, Hormisdas and John, Felix, Boniface, Agapitus and Silverius, Vigilius and Pelagius, John and Benedict, and Pelagius, blessed Gregory’s predecessor, celebrated Masses according to the earlier tradition, adding nothing.

Blessed Gregory the First instituted in the Roman Church that the antiphon called the Introit should be chanted to soothe the minds of those listening; he obtained this from the Church of Milan. He then instituted that the Kyrie eleison should be chanted nine times by the clergy, and that after the Epistle the Gradual and Alleluia should be sung, except from Septuagesima to Easter; during that period he established that Tracts should be sung.

After the Gospel had been read, while the offerings were being presented, he instituted that the Offertory should be chanted. He also added to the Canon:

> Arrange our days in your peace, and rescue us from eternal condemnation, and command that we be counted among your chosen flock, through Christ our Lord.

He also added:

> Instructed by saving commands and formed by divine institution, we dare to say: Our Father, etc.

He established that this, together with the Lord’s Prayer, should be chanted aloud by the priest over the Eucharist, so that the following prayer, which begins, “Deliver us, Lord, from all evils,” and which had previously been chanted aloud, should be said secretly.

After the breaking of the Eucharist, once the people had communicated, he instituted that the antiphon which he calls the Communion should be chanted. After the Eucharist had been received and thanksgiving had been offered to God, he instituted that the petitions which had been given over the people from the time of blessed Clement until his own time should be given over the people after the Communions had been completed and before “The peace of the Lord” was said. Previously, after obtaining the priestly blessing, he would depart from the people as though secure, and did not remain to render thanksgiving to God.

Sergius, Roman bishop, who was the twentieth after blessed Jerome [Note: [Col. 0862D] Read “Gregory”], instituted that the Agnus Dei should be chanted during the solemn Masses, as is done today.

## On Salt and Its Power

I shall now come to the sacraments instituted by the apostles. First, with God’s help, I shall begin to speak about the sacrament of salt.

In the Old Testament every sacrifice was sprinkled with salt. Salt signifies discernment, which is the teacher of the virtues; without it, even what appears to be virtue is vice. By salt the stench of diseased flesh is removed, and entrails preserved in salt are kept for a very long time.

In the Gospel you have the Lord saying to the apostles: “Have salt in yourselves” (Mark 9:49). And elsewhere he says to the same apostles: “You are the salt of the earth” (Matthew 5:13).

But it has been defined uniformly throughout the whole Church. When someone comes to be catechized, he asks for the priest’s exsufflation, by which the unclean spirit is driven out; he receives salt from the priest’s hand, the same priest saying: “Receive the salt of wisdom, which will benefit you unto eternal life.” This does not mean that eternal life is given to catechumens, but that salt is the sacrament of faith, which works through love and leads the baptized to eternal life.

In most churches salt is given to catechumens once; in some, at every scrutiny.

## On the Threefold Oil and Its Powers

We must now pass to the sacrament of oil, which is divided in three ways. There is chrismal oil, by whose signing the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit is given. There is also exorcized oil, with which catechumens are anointed to drive away the enemy. And there is the oil of the sick, prepared for the healing of body and soul.

Oil also has this particular property: when mixed with other liquids, it floats above all liquids and does not mix with them. It signifies the truth, which tends upward and is from above, and does not mix with falsehood. It is also suitable for giving light. Not only does it give light when kindled; even when poured upon the sea during the darkness of night, it illuminates the waters.

Oil also has this particular property: it illuminates, nourishes, heals wounds, reduces swellings, extinguishes fevers, and repels heat.

We also read that, toward evening, the dove returned to Noah carrying an olive branch in its beak; from this he learned that peace had been restored on earth to the progenitor of the human race. The man, filled with the Holy Spirit, understood that, through a bird without gall—which signifies the Holy Spirit—the human race was to be reconciled to God the Father through the sacrament of the olive, as the world was growing old. Although Christ was anointed not visibly but invisibly, above his companions, nevertheless “Christ” is interpreted as “Anointed.”

We are called Christians from Christ, “a people of possession, a holy nation” (1 Peter 2:9), and, as Cephas says in his epistle, “a royal priesthood” (ibid.). In ancient times only kings, priests, and prophets were anointed with chrismal oil. In the New Testament, however, all who have been reborn through baptism are sanctified with invisible oil and anointed with visible oil, although we do not read that this was given in the primitive Church which flourished in Judea after the Lord’s Ascension.

Moreover, in the primitive Church which began in Judea, believers were not called Christians but Nazarenes. The Chosen Vessel makes this sufficiently clear in the Acts of the Apostles when he says to the governor Felix: “But concerning the sect of the Nazarenes, against which I am accused, I serve my God in this way, so as not to oppose the traditions of my fathers.” In Antioch, however, to avoid the mockery of the Jews, the name “Christians” first arose.

Through this sacrament, instituted by the apostles before they separated, the Spirit began to grant the baptized, reborn in Christ through the apostles and their successors, the bishops, the gift of grace through prayer, so that they might have the Paraclete as their protector, through the laying on of hands and the marking with chrismal oil.

That the oil of the sick was instituted by the apostles is testified by the apostle James, who says: “Is anyone among you sick? Let him bring in the presbyters of the Church, so that they may pray over him, anointing him with sanctified oil. And the prayer of faith will save the sick person; and if he is in sins, they will be forgiven him” (James 5:14).

This used to be consecrated at all times during the solemn Masses by presbyters at the place where it says: “Through whom you create all these good things.” Now, however, it is consecrated there only by bishops at the Mass of the Lord’s Supper.

Chrismal oil receives an admixture of fragrant balsam. The oil of mercy, truth, and light thus spreads its fragrance far and wide, so that, through good works, our Father who is in heaven may be honored by those who see them, and those who do not consent to the truth may have no grounds for attacking religion.

Blessed Anacletus, Clement’s successor, says in his decretal letter: “A bishop cannot be consecrated by fewer than three.” He confirms this by the example of James, bishop of Jerusalem, who was ordained by Peter, John, and James, and this on Sundays.

He also says that the bishop’s head ought to be anointed with chrism, so that our principal faculty, the mind, anointed with the Holy Spirit, may live, understand, and be conformed according to the image of God. His hands also, by which works are signified, should be anointed with chrism, so that he may hear from the one consecrating him: “Whatever you bless shall be blessed, and whatever you consecrate shall be consecrated.”

These are the hands that prepare the chrism; through its anointing, at the bishop’s invocation, the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit is poured out upon the baptized. The same chrism anoints the hands of priests and grants them the power to baptize and preach and to celebrate Masses for both the living and the dead.

We read in ecclesiastical histories that the consecrations of churches and altars took their beginning from blessed Sylvester. Previously, although there were oratories in which God’s people assembled, they did not dare to have altars or churches publicly consecrated while the pagan storm raged. Instead, they secretly celebrated Masses in crypts, cemeteries, and houses.

After Constantine submitted himself to the Christian religion, he built in his Lateran palace a church in honor of the Savior. He established that an image of the Savior should be publicly painted on the walls, that the image of Jupiter should be thrown down from above, that the temples should be closed, and that churches should be built publicly.

From that time, stone altar tables began to be anointed with chrism in imitation of the stone which Jacob erected as a memorial, which signified Christ, who is the cornerstone (Ephesians 2:20), “who made both one” (ibid., 2:14).

There are also other sacraments which the Church now uses according to the Lord’s example, although not by an explicitly transmitted command: exsufflation in exorcisms, the opening of the ears of catechumens, and the laying on of hands, by which the Holy Spirit is given through the signing of the baptized; by which sinners are reconciled to Mother Church; and by which the power of ministry is transmitted to bishops, priests, and deacons.

*Here ends the little book on the sacraments, issued by Bonizo, bishop of Sutri, and sent to Gualterus, monk and prior of the monastery of Le Mans.*

## [Fragment of Pontifical History]

## Notice on the Following Fragment

(Mai, *Spicilegium Romanum* VI, 273.)

There exists in a miscellaneous Vatican manuscript a certain historical epitome of the Roman pontiffs, which Bishop Bonizo of Sutri placed at the beginning of the fourth book of his still unpublished canonical Collection. It is extremely brief, and, up to Siricius, it also inserts here and there excerpts taken from the Pseudo-Isidorian materials. It is therefore sufficient for me to present here only part of this epitome, after Siricius.

Indeed, when Adrian I is reached, I shall no longer draw Bonizo’s text from the aforesaid manuscript, but from the unpublished Collectanea of the scholar Albinus, who, in the final part of his work, copies from Bonizo’s unknown book *On the Christian Life* the account of the remaining pontiffs up to Urban II, at whom Bonizo in fact stopped. Elsewhere I shall publish further material from the aforesaid Albinus.

## Fragment of Pontifical History from Bonizo of Sutri

[Col. 0865B] I would indeed speak of Anastasius, and of Innocent, who ordered that a fast be kept on Saturday and that peace be given during the solemn Masses. And of Zosimus, a Greek by nationality, who ordered that a candle be blessed on Holy Saturday in all the titular churches. And of Boniface, who forbade nuns and deaconesses to touch the sacred vessels or altar cloths. And of Celestine, who decreed that the 101 psalms of David should be sung antiphonally before the Canon, for previously only the Gospel and Epistles were read. And of Sixtus, who built the church called “at the Crèche,” today called the Major Church, on Mount Livy [Note: [Col. 0865] Namely, near Livia’s market on the Esquiline, as is clear.]. And of the great Leo, and of Hilary, a Sardinian by nationality, and of Simplicius of Tibur, and of the bishop Felix.

And of Gelasius, a scholastic and wondrous teacher, who composed the Gelasian book, and made hymns and tracts like blessed Ambrose; who declared which books ought to be received in the Church and which rejected, and at what time the ordinations of priests and of the other orders ought to take place. And of Anastasius, his successor, and of Symmachus the Sardinian, who decreed that on all Sundays and on the birthdays of the apostles the angelic hymn should be chanted. And of Hormisdas, a man of great life and merit, and of John, his successor, and of Felix, and of Boniface, who established that the election of a Roman pontiff should not take place until the third day after his deposition.

And of John, his successor, and of Agapitus, and of Silverius, who was the first after the time of blessed Sylvester to be ordained bishop by the hand of the Goths without imperial assent. And of Vigilius, and of Bishop Pelagius, who ordered that schismatic bishops should be suppressed by secular powers. And of John, his successor, and of Benedict, and of Pelagius, Gregory’s predecessor, who handed down nine prefaces to the Church to be chanted before the Canon. If it were my task, I would set forth the Roman pontiffs in sequence.

I do not think I should be silent about blessed Gregory, from whom were issued the Book of the Sacraments, the Antiphoner, both for day and night, the treatise on Ezekiel, eleven Homilies on the Gospels, and the work on Job, arranged morally, allegorically, and briefly according to its historical sense; also the book of Dialogues, the Pastoral Care addressed to John of Ravenna, and the Register, sufficiently useful for governing the Church.

He instituted that the antiphon called the Introit should be sung to soothe the minds of those listening; then that the Kyrie eleison should be chanted nine times by the clergy; and after the extensive Gradual and the Alleluia—except during the seventy days in which he instituted that Tracts should be sung—that after the Gospel, while the offerings were being presented, the Offertory should be chanted; and that after the breaking of the Eucharist, once the people had communicated, the Communion should be sung.

He also added to the Canon: “Arrange our days in your peace.” He likewise established that the Lord’s Prayer should be chanted aloud by the priest over the Eucharist.

He instituted that from Septuagesima until Easter the Alleluia should not be sung; that at the festive morning assembly only eight responsories should be sung, followed by the Ambrosian hymn, and that at the daily assembly only two should be sung. He also ordered that the priest should say, “O God, come to my aid,” which is Psalm 118.

How honorable this prayer is, and how useful for our salvation, a holy angel taught a certain monk. The angel said that he had once been the guardian of that exceedingly strong Samson and that he had then been assigned to guard the same monk. Among many other exhortations to salvation, he carefully admonished him of this also: that we ought diligently and frequently to recite this psalm, which has been especially commended. We shall sing it as follows: “O God, come to my aid.”

This same Gregory instituted the Greater Litany, joined the English nation to the Church of Christ, and, having been admitted among the choirs of angels, gave his spirit back to heaven. He was buried in the basilica of Saint Peter before the sacristy.

What shall I say of Sabinianus, his successor, who added lights in the church of blessed Peter? And of Boniface, who received from Caesar Phocas the privilege that the Roman Church should be placed above Constantinople? And what of the other Boniface, who obtained from Caesar Phocas that a temple in Rome, which the ancients called the Pantheon, should be given to the Catholic Church of God? That Caesar gave it to the bishop, who established a law in the Church, under threat of excommunication, that no woman should take her son from the font, and likewise in confirmations.

And of Boniface the third after Gregory, and of Honorius, his successor. And of Severinus, in whose time there was the most Christian emperor Heraclius, who, after extinguishing Chosroes, brought the Lord’s cross back to Jerusalem. And of John, his successor, and of Pope Theodore, who composed a penitential book [Note: [Col. 0867D] Recall what is said on p. 133, n. 1. Indeed, the same thing is explicitly affirmed about Pope Theodore in another pontifical chronicle preserved in the Vatican manuscript of Cinthius the chamberlain, p. 109.].

And of the thrice-blessed Pope Martin the martyr, who, while celebrating the solemn Mass at the altar of the Virgin Mary, Mother of God, which is called “at the Crèche,” was protected by divine kindness when the spatharius of Duke Olympius, sent to kill him, was struck with blindness and could not see him at all. For these are the rams of the Lord’s flock, the pontiffs of the Roman Church, who consecrated the Church of God by their own blood and by their constitutions.

If I did not fear that the length of my discourse would produce weariness in the minds of readers, I would write fully about Eugene, who succeeded blessed Martin. And about Vitalian, who composed the chant used by the Romans. And about Adeodatus, in whose time a most splendid star appeared, one never seen before. And about Agatho, and Leo [Cod. Folcone], and Benedict, and John, his successor, who composed the book *On the Dignity of the Pallium*.

And about Conon, and Sergius the Younger [Note: [Col. 0868D] Perhaps the elder?], who restored the Lateran basilica, instituted that the Agnus Dei should be chanted during the solemn Masses, caused the church of blessed Silverius within the walls of the city of Rome to be built, and dedicated the altar of that church with his own hands. And about John the Fifth and the Sixth, and Sisinnius, and Constantine, and Gregory the Second, and Gregory the Third, who was elected at the bier of his predecessor. And about Zacharias, a man of great merit and holiness, who ordered that the sons of godfathers and godmothers should not marry one another.

And since the little page is now approaching its end, I must not be silent about Adrian, Zacharias’s successor, and so forth.

## Then from the Collectanea of Albinus, as We Have Said

### Bishop Bonizo in His Book *On the Christian Life*

I judged it worthy to write about Adrian, Zacharias’s successor, at whose request King Charles entered Italy with great power and a strong hand, defeated Desiderius, king of the Lombards, and drove him from the Po, then besieged him in Pavia.

Afterward, coming to Rome, he hastened on foot from the mount called the Mount of Joy to the church of Saint Peter. The most blessed pope awaited him on the steps of Saint Peter and, as he approached, led him decently as far as the confession of Saint Peter, with the hymns, praises, and psalms of the clergy, and with the praises of the Roman judges, as is customary.

That most powerful king, offering many gifts to blessed Peter and promising faith and due reverence to his vicar, was elevated by the Romans to the honor of the patriciate. Returning to Pavia, he captured the city and led King Desiderius, together with his wife, beyond the mountains. From that time he deserved to be called king of the Franks and Lombards and patrician of the Romans.

And about Leo the Third, who was called the Sermonizer. And about Stephen, his successor. And about Paschal, who built in Rome a church in honor of blessed Mary, called Dominica, and clothed it with marble stones. And about Eugene, who composed a penitential book and sent it to France. And about Valentine, who consecrated Louis, the son of Charles, as emperor. And about his successor Gregory. And about Sergius, in whose time the Saracens devastated Italy.

And about another Leo, who crowned Charles, the son of Louis, emperor and who also built the city called the Portico, which he named Leonine after himself. He made a silver ciborium over the altar of Saint Peter, and before that altar a golden panel, as well as silver tiles for the confession. He also built in Rome the church now called Saint Mary the New and the church of the Four Crowned Ones.

This same man, maliciously accused concerning certain crimes, convened a synod and demonstrated by oath that he was innocent. But although envy can be overcome, it cannot remain at rest. A few days later, the malicious men who had accused him out of envy, stirring up sedition among the people, insulted him and dragged him from the palace to the Roman Forum. There, by diabolical prompting and popular violence, they blinded him.

When King Charles heard this, he came to Rome and slaughtered many of the people; the actual instigators of the sedition he hanged from a tree. Although deprived of his sight, Leo governed the Roman Church for as long as he lived.

And about Benedict, his successor. And about Nicholas, who reconciled Sophronius, the deposed bishop of Piacenza, through another synod, and who at one and the same time excommunicated two emperors: the Eastern emperor, Michael by name, because of the unjust deposition of the patriarch Ignatius; and the Western emperor, Lothair by name, because of his association with Waldrada, his concubine.

And about Adrian the Second, who made Louis, the son of Charles, emperor. And about John the Eighth, who disputed with Queen Angelberga concerning the city of Ravenna and who also ordained Charles, his son, emperor. And about Martin, his successor, in whose time there were two glorious bishops in Lombardy: one of Piacenza, named Paul, the empress’s nephew, who rebuilt from the foundations the church of Piacenza, which through Sophronius’s negligence had been utterly destroyed; the other of Parma, named Gundolfus, who established the canonical church of Parma and was himself the emperor’s nephew.

And about Adrian, who succeeded him in the pontificate. And about Stephen and Formosus, in whose times, when the Lombards rebelled, the Franks lost the empire. And about a certain Stephen, in whose time the Saracens seized Sicily. And about John of Tusculum, in whose time the Roman captains claimed the patriciate for themselves by tyranny.

And about a certain Sylvester, a man highly skilled in every art, who was first abbot of Bobbio, then archbishop of Ravenna, and afterward became Roman pope. And about John X of Tusculum, the brother of Alberic the Elder, who fought with the Saracens and drove them from Italy into Sicily. He built a basilica in the Lateran palace.

And about Sylvester of Tusculum by birth. And about a certain Pope Benedict the Roman, who on one and the same day was both a layman and a pontiff. And about John of Tusculum by birth, who crowned Otto, king of the Saxons, emperor.

And about a certain Silverius of Tibur, who, after Alberic of Tusculum had died—Alberic having claimed the title of patrician for himself—was ordained pope by Crescentius of Nomentum, who was called patrician. Silverius also ordained Otto the Second emperor. Later, however, he was expelled from the papacy with great disgrace by that same Crescentius.

Then a certain John, bishop of Piacenza, Greek by birth, who had served as legate of Otto the Younger, returned from Constantinople and, while coming to Rome for the sake of prayer, was captured and detained by the aforementioned Crescentius and the Romans. Although unwilling, he was nevertheless ordained the unhappy Roman pope.

When the king, unrestrained in mind, heard this, he came to Rome, captured Crescentius after a long siege, and beheaded him. But the pontiff himself, after being deprived of his eyes and weakened in his other limbs, the king ordered to be dragged through the streets of the Leonine City, as a disgrace and humiliation to the priestly order.

Before thirty days had been completed, however, the king himself died in body and soul.

And concerning Benedict of Tusculum, who made Henry, grandson of Otto the Great, king of the Teutons and emperor. And concerning his brother John, who on one and the same day was both a layman and a pontiff. I did not think I ought to remain silent about these men.

Furthermore, if anyone wishes to know about Theophylact of Tusculum—how he sold the papacy to the priest John, and how, at one and the same time, Theophylact, Gregory, and Sylvester did not govern the Roman pontificate but ravaged it; and how King Henry, son of Conrad, freed the Roman Church from such plagues—let him read the book I dictated, entitled *To a Friend*, and there he will find these matters set out in orderly fashion. [Note: [Col. 0869D] Up to this point the account is found in Albinus the scholar, from Bonizo; what follows likewise belongs to Bonizo, but is taken from the manuscript of the canonical collection, or *Decree*, written by him.]

There he will also find how Pope Clement was elected and how King Henry was ordained emperor; and concerning his successor Damasus, how many days he spent in the papacy; and concerning the distinguished Leo, what he did during his pontificate and how he ended his life; and concerning his successor Victor, what he did and what new event occurred in his time; and concerning Stephen, brother of Duke Godfrey, and how, in his time, the Pataria arose at Milan. [Note: [Col. 0869D] Concerning the Pataria—that is, the heresy of the Patarines, which arose at Milan at that time—see Pagius in Baronius under the year 1058, no. 3. See the same Pagius again under the year 1044, nos. 7–9, where he notes that Bonizo wrote three times about the Roman pontiffs and reports this final portion of Bonizo from Lambecius.]

And concerning Pope Nicholas, and the dispute he had with Benedict the usurper, and what he did during his pontificate; and concerning Pope Alexander II, and the dispute he had with Cadalus of Parma, and his victories, and what he did during his pontificate, and his end; and concerning Gregory VII, his election, life, and character, and how, on the Nativity of the Lord, he was captured at the altar of Saint Mary by Cencio, a cruel man, and was liberated on that same day by the grace of God.

The account also explains most clearly the war he endured with the Emperor Henry, the controversy he had with Guibert, the hardships he suffered, and the siege of the city and of himself; how he was freed by Robert, duke of the Normans; and how he came to rest in a blessed end.

But if anyone wishes to know the deeds of Pope Urban and his victory, let him read the book I wrote *To Hugh the Schismatic*, and there he will find fully elucidated whatever he wishes to know.

[Col. 0869]

# BONIZO’S DECRETAL

See the Ballerini brothers’ investigation of the ancient canonical collections and their compilers, part IV, chapter 15, in *Patrologia*, volume LVI, column 338. Cf. what Oefelius stated above in the Prolegomena to Bonizo.

## IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 1090. WILLIAM, ABBOT OF SAINT ARNULF OF METZ

[Col. 0871]

# HISTORICAL NOTICE

(*Literary History of France*, VIII, 305.)

[Col. 0871A] William succeeded Warin in the dignity of abbot; Warin died on 20 August 1050. He found regular discipline in almost all its vigor and was very careful to maintain it. The wise and peaceful manner in which he governed his house made him famous throughout the world: *known, scattered throughout the regions of the world*. Study was one of his principal occupations, and he willingly devoted to it all the time left him by his other indispensable duties. He was especially fond of reading Saint Jerome, and took care to have some of his works copied; he also had a singular veneration for Saint Augustine.

After the death of Herimar, abbot of Saint-Remi of Reims, in 1071, that monastery remained without an abbot for nearly three years and was thereby more exposed than before to the vexations of Archbishop Manassé. Pope Gregory VII, having learned of this, wrote forcefully to the prelate (Register I, letter 13) and ordered him to arrange as soon as possible for the election of an abbot possessing the skill, learning, and virtue necessary to govern it well in spiritual and temporal matters. The letter dates from the end of June 1073; and as soon as Manassé received it, he had William, already abbot of Saint-Arnulf, elected there. This election greatly pleased the pope, as he testifies in another letter (letter 52).

But when the new abbot found the monastery in a state of great desolation, and moreover saw himself insulted and harassed in many ways by the archbishop—against whom he opposed nothing but gentleness, patience, and prayer—he despaired of accomplishing any good there and regretted having accepted the additional dignity. Hugh, abbot of Cluny, expressed his surprise at this, since he knew the archbishop’s scandalous conduct.

William thought he had no other course than to abdicate. When he had occasion to write to the pope concerning his elevation, he earnestly begged him to help release him from so heavy a burden. Not receiving a favorable reply as quickly as he wished, he went to Rome himself to explain to the pope his reasons for leaving the monastery of Saint-Remi. He declared that he would rather live in poverty at Metz than in abundance at Reims.

This journey did credit to our abbot. He was already favorably known at Rome, where Manassé—his own persecutor—had represented him as a man who loved peace, valued humility, was always occupied with reading, and had thereby acquired an honorable reputation. William appeared so to the Romans, who in fact recognized in him good morals, learning, virtue, and the character of a wise and judicious man. The pope strongly urged him to continue governing the monastery of Saint-Remi without ceasing to care for Saint-Arnulf. But our abbot continually refused, regarding this as a task beyond his strength.

[Col. 0872A] Seeing his extreme reluctance to undertake it, Gregory wrote two letters on the matter, one to Manassé and the other to Herimann, bishop of Metz. In the first (letter 52), he ordered the archbishop, if the abbot of Saint-Remi persisted in abdicating, to arrange, together with William, for another to be canonically elected there. In the second (letter 53), the pope asked Herimann to receive this abbot favorably and even to give him, out of consideration for him, new signs of his goodwill, so that he might understand that it had been beneficial for him to have made the journey to Rome—*because he came to us*: these are Gregory’s words, which clearly presuppose the journey, although none of the historians of our abbot mentions it.

He made the journey at the end of 1073 or the beginning of the following year, as appears from the date of the two letters. Both are dated on the second day before the Ides of March, in the eleventh indiction—that is, 14 March 1074—and Abbot William was probably their bearer.

Manassé paid no attention to the pope’s letter. Far from urging William to resume governance of the monastery of Saint-Remi, he demanded back from him, rudely, with threats and violence, the pastoral staff, which was the sign of his dignity, and installed Henry, already abbot of Homblières, in his place. William appears to have had no part in this choice, although the pope had ordered that it should not be made without his advice. He was then confined to his abbey of Saint-Arnulf, where he lived in good harmony with Bishop Herimann. This prelate even made several gifts to his monastery, out of consideration for William and for the venerable recluse Hodierna, who lived near the house.

[Col. 0873A] Yet, despite his attachment to Bishop Herimann, whom Henry IV, recently crowned emperor, expelled from his see in 1085, William had the unfortunate weakness of allowing himself to be ordained bishop of Metz in his place. Shortly afterward, the new bishop exercised episcopal functions with regard to Luipon, whom he confirmed in the dignity of abbot of Saint-Trond, which Luipon had usurped.

Seeing, however, as early as the following year, that he could not maintain himself in the see of Metz, William went to Herimann. After gathering around him the leading members of the clergy, he solemnly renounced the episcopate in their presence. As proof of the sincerity of his repentance, he withdrew to the abbey of Gorze to expiate his ambitious intrusion there. He was appointed master of the children being educated there; and after some time Bishop Herimann, moved by his penitence, restored the abbey of Saint-Arnulf to him.
