William thus returned to his first dignity, to which he had been elevated nearly forty [Col. 0873B] years earlier. This suggests that he held it for only a very short time after being reinstated. Accordingly, it is hardly likely that he lived beyond the year 1089.

His death is assigned to two widely different dates: the eleventh day before the Kalends of March in the necrology of Saint-Arnulf—that is, 19 February, if the copyists are not at fault—and the eleventh day before the Kalends of January in his epitaph—that is, 22 December. The latter date deserves preference, since it is confirmed in the same epitaph by expressions admitting no ambiguity: they state that it occurred three days before Christmas. Here is the epitaph, which is no better than so many others from the same century.

## EPITAPH

When William, ruler and abbot of the monks, departed from life,

Known throughout the regions of the world,

Is borne amid mournful funeral rites to the sacred church,

[Col. 0873C] Here rests Father Arnulf, holy in body,

Outside the royal walls of Metz, near the city,

Where the South Wind breathes its fragrant odors,

And where, worthy of the place, he presents the ornament of the church’s summit,

The lofty house consecrates twice six companies to the altars,

When January, as customary, reaches the eleventh day before the Kalends,

With the sun setting, or when evening withdraws from heaven,

And three days later the joys of God’s newborn Son are celebrated.

The poet (*Analecta*, pp. 430–431) added thirteen further verses to serve as a general epitaph for his already-deceased confrères, specifically for the monk Rainard. This addition is a kind of circular letter in which the author urges those to whom it is sent to pray for the dead and not to forget the living.

Before Dom Mabillon brought William’s writings out of the dust, he was not only unknown as a writer, but it was not even known that he had been abbot of Saint-Arnulf and Saint-Remi. Nevertheless, [Col. 0873D] the Chronicle of Hugh of Flavigny and several letters of Pope Gregory VII mention him unmistakably.

His writings consist of:

1. A collection of letters to various persons. The first is written to Pope Gregory VII to congratulate him on his elevation. The author therefore wrote it in 1073, when he was already abbot of Saint-Remi of Reims. After briefly mentioning the advantage the Church enjoyed in having a pope so well instructed in its rules and so careful to enforce them, he praises him because his election had taken place with perfect unanimity. He speaks of the bishop of Vercelli, who had disturbed the pontificate of Alexander II, his predecessor, and was still stirring up trouble in Gregory’s pontificate. Returning then to Gregory, he urges him to employ the sword with which he was armed to subdue all the enemies of the Church.

William ends his letter with a sad description of his condition at Saint-Remi, both because of the fruitlessness of his labors [Col. 0874A] and because of the violence of Archbishop Manassé, whom he indicates without naming. He implores Gregory to help him leave a dignity into which he had entered too easily on the advice of people who had deceived him. The Continuators of Bollandus judged this letter so honorable to the memory of the pontiff that they reprinted it at the beginning of his acts.

William addresses the next two letters to Manassé. In the first, he politely thanks him for relieving him of the dignity of abbot of Saint-Remi and thereby procuring for him the rest he had desired. Since the prelate had pressed our abbot to give it up, employing grave threats and demanding back the pastoral staff, the symbol of that dignity, the author takes the opportunity to give an agreeable but sad portrayal of this staff, showing that it had been incomparably more burdensome to him than gracious.

To Manassé’s threats he replies that, in order to carry them out canonically, the archbishop must first live according to the canons himself; and that in such a case there is nothing to fear from a prelate who despises all rules and lives scandalously. He adds that, if Manassé continues to tear him apart with slanderous speeches, he will make him feel the sharp points of his pen, and that he knows he can speak all the more freely because the archbishop is less able to retaliate. Nevertheless, he assures him that, in renouncing his pastoral staff and prelacy, he is very far from renouncing the charity he owes him, because he knows that we are obliged to love even those whom we cannot move to return our love.

This somewhat lively letter is only a prelude to the next, in which the author keeps the promise he had made Manassé not to spare him if he continued to defame him. William devotes the whole letter to detailing what he had suffered from the archbishop during the short time [Col. 0874C] he had been at Saint-Remi. A little more respect for the episcopal character and greater moderation in his reproaches would make this a fairly fine composition.

The author uses here the old Gallic word *follis*, which passed into our language and from which we derived the word *fou* (“fool”). The end of the letter suggests that he wrote it particularly to justify his departure from the monastery of Saint-Remi. Indeed, he concludes from everything he has said that he had not done so out of frivolity, and that everyone who knew Manassé would applaud the course he had taken.

William addresses his fourth letter to a person whom he calls his lord and father, but whose name is indicated only by an H. This gives strong grounds for believing that it was Saint Hugh, abbot of Cluny. It is a reply to that abbot, who had expressed surprise that William had accepted the abbey of Saint-Remi, especially because of Manassé’s disorders. The author explains how the matter had come about and gives him a vivid portrait of the archbishop’s appearance.

The fifth letter is an exhortation to a monk, urging him never to lose sight of the one thing necessary, to which everything must be directed. The author adds excellent advice for avoiding relaxation through the example of bad monks, of whom he gives a brief but accurate portrait. At the end he touches on the reasons he had for leaving Saint-Remi; from this it appears that the letter was not written earlier than 1074.

The sixth is addressed to the same person. William had learned that the man had not benefited from the first advice he had given him concerning the wicked with whom one is obliged to live. Here he reproves him for casting aside the shield of patience and gently criticizes his weakness. He then shows him that the company of the wicked—who will always be mixed with the good in this life until the separation that will take place on the last day—contributes to sanctifying the good, and he lays down excellent rules on this subject.

In particular, he tells him that they must be endured without presuming to judge them, and that one should separate oneself from them only in the feelings of the mind and heart. The letter is very fine and shows that its author was thoroughly instructed in the teaching of Saint Augustine.

The seventh and final letter—which should have been the first if chronological order had been followed—is the best written in the entire collection, although the others also possess their beauties. It is a reply to Adelmann, or Alestan, formerly William’s teacher, who, upon learning that William had renounced the world, wrote to express his profound grief.

William proves to him that, far from grieving over it, he ought to rejoice. The arguments he uses are, on the one hand, the motives that had led him to take this course and, on the other, the peace, sweetness, and delights he enjoyed in the bosom of true philosophy, which he invites his teacher to come and share with him. The author’s descriptions of the spiritual miseries of this life and of the benefits of the cloister, when regular discipline is exactly observed there, are vivid and animated and, though brief, well sustained. The letter contains not only fine passages of eloquence but even a certain elegance.

[Col. 0876A] 2. Besides these seven letters, we also possess a very fine prayer by Abbot William, in which he left great signs of a lively faith, an enlightened as well as solid piety, and profound humility. It is in honor of Saint Augustine and was composed to be recited before ascending to the altar to offer the divine mysteries; from this we learn that the author had received priestly ordination.

It is a continual outpouring of the heart, composed partly of very moving passages from Scripture and partly of passages from the collects of the liturgy. Although, by invoking Saint Augustine in particular, the author shows that he had special confidence in the saint’s intercession, he displays no less attachment to the doctrine of this holy teacher.

Dom Mabillon, having unearthed these brief works in a manuscript of the abbey of Saint-Arnulf at Metz that appeared to have been produced in the author’s own time, published them in the first volume of his *Analecta*, where he accompanied them with learned observations. As may be seen from the observations we ourselves have made while discussing these same writings, the author knew the liberal arts well and possessed the ability to write effectively for his age, but he did not sufficiently restrain the liveliness of his style, which on certain occasions became impetuous.

[Col. 0875]

# LETTERS OF WILLIAM

(*Mabillon, new edition of the Analecta*, p. 456.)

## FIRST LETTER. TO POPE GREGORY VII

*(Year 1073.) He congratulates him on his election.*

[Note: [Col. 0883D]

### ON THE FIRST LETTER

In this first letter William congratulates Pope Gregory VII on his election, which took place in 1073. He then indicates that he had been asked to govern the abbey of Saint-Remi at Reims, which had been without a pastor since the death of Herimar in 1071, but that he refused to undertake this burden.

The following letters of Pope Gregory VII relate to this matter: namely, the thirteenth letter of Book I, addressed to Manassé, bishop of Reims, in which he warns him not to harass the monks of Saint-Remi any longer and to ensure, in accordance with canonical sanctions, that an abbot be appointed there. He commends the same matter in the following letter to Hugh, abbot of Cluny. Both letters were issued in the eleventh indiction, that is, in the year 1073.

The letters of the same book numbered 52 and 53 concern our William more directly. They were written in the twelfth indiction. The first is addressed to Manassé, whom Gregory praises for placing over the monastery of Saint-Remi a man honorable in character and learned in letters—namely our William—of whom he adds:

“The abbot is very pleasing to us; and if he were able to bear the burden of governing both abbeys, namely the Metz and Reims abbeys, I would have praised him for it, because he is a religious and wise man.”

But because William attempts in this letter to remove this burden from himself, Gregory adds:

“Otherwise, if the burden of governing both is beyond his strength, as he himself admits, lest he succumb beneath excessive weight, we ask your prudence—or rather, by apostolic authority we order you—to appoint there, with his advice and consent, through the election of the community and according to the Rule of Saint Benedict, a suitable superior, God permitting.”

Finally, Gregory writes Letter 53 to Herimann, bishop of Metz, on the same matter: namely, that William, abbot of Saint-Arnulf—not Abbot Arnulf, as is incorrectly stated in the heading of the commonly circulated letter—wishes to resign the abbey of Saint-Remi and be content with the one at Metz.

That “devil of Vercelli,” namely Gregory, bishop of Vercelli, was first excommunicated by Pope Leo for adultery and other crimes and later absolved. Having become chancellor of Emperor Henry IV in Italy, he always adhered so closely to Henry’s faction that, at his instigation, he created Cadalus, bishop of Parma, as an antipope after the death of Nicholas II, with the bishop of Piacenza conspiring with him. The same Gregory was sent to Rome by that emperor to confirm the election of Gregory VII, which he had initially opposed. Finally, after a synod had been convened against him, he died miserably.

At the end of the letter William does not hold a very favorable opinion of the monks of Saint-Remi; but at the end of the fifth letter he moderates his judgment, declaring that there were some very honorable men in that community, through whose most benevolent charity the others ought to be judged tolerable.]

[Col. 0875C]

To the venerable and universal Lord Pope G., W., a sinner: the affection of devoted prayer and the fulfillment of humble service.

Although the wisdom of God governs all things made through it by marvelous arrangement and unshaken order, etc. See *Patrologia*, volume CXLVIII, column 14.

## SECOND LETTER. TO MANASSÉ, ARCHBISHOP OF REIMS

*He resigns the prelacy of the monastery of Saint-Remi.*

[Note: [Col. 0885C]

### ON THE SECOND LETTER

In this and the two following letters William attacks Manassé perhaps more bitterly and harshly than was fitting. Nevertheless, anyone who has observed Manassé’s character will more readily pardon William. On this subject one should read both Hugh of Flavigny, Manassé’s contemporary, in his *Chronicle*, and Guibert, abbot of Nogent, in Book I, chapter 11 of *On His Own Life*, where he attributes Saint Bruno’s withdrawal from the city of Reims to Manassé’s disgraceful life.

“After the death of the most famous Archbishop Gervasius,” Guibert says, “Manassé intruded himself simoniacally into the government of that city: a noble man, indeed, but possessing none of the serenity that ought first to adorn nobility . . . . . Since he was exceedingly fond of soldiers and neglected the clergy, he is reported once to have said: ‘The archbishopric of Reims would be a good thing if one were not obliged to have Masses sung there,’ etc.”

Manassé’s disgraceful life proceeded so far that he was reduced to the lay order in 1080 at the Council of Lyon. From this one may understand that William did not burn against him without cause, although this author seems to have possessed a temperament somewhat too fiery and biting.

*Luscius Lavinius.* He was an exceedingly abusive poet, whom Terence mentions in the prologues to the *Andria* and the *Heautontimorumenos*, where he calls him, without naming him, a malicious poet.]

To Lord M., archbishop of Reims, Brother W.: prayer and service.

We offer you very numerous and great thanks, both for your goodwill, by which you wished us in Christ the condition of the rest we desired, and because you released us sooner from the yoke of your lordship, beneath which we were miserably oppressed. This will add no small strength toward attaining that undisturbed rest for which our longing sighs.

For just as this visible brightness is a delight to healthy eyes but a torment to inflamed ones, so that intelligible and delightful light deigns to reveal itself only to the mind that strives to clear its vision of every earthly darkness. It is therefore sufficiently clear how great a benefit you have conferred upon us, since you have enabled us to approach more frequently and familiarly that highest good, highest joy, highest gladness, and light of holy minds. Thanks, therefore, to you—thanks to you!

But as for your staff, which you order to be returned to you with excessive threats, know that we do not possess it. We consider it wholly unworthy to carry away with us a staff that we never found agreeable to carry at all. For what, I ask, is this staff of yours, except that staff of reed about which the prophet proclaims that it is unfit to support anyone? Whoever leans upon it can more easily be wounded than supported.

Good Jesus, how bitterly we have experienced that staff! How many insults and terrors we have suffered from it! Indeed, we scarcely believe that we are still alive. May the Lord turn such a staff away from his servant and hand it over to his enemy. We have said this not to accuse your severity but to display our pain.

We therefore renounce your staff; we also renounce the abbey—but, if it pleases you, not friendship. We renounce your prelacy, but in no way our affection. For, with the Lord’s inspiration, we know that we must love even those whose minds we cannot move to love.

But as for your threat that you will canonically exercise the power of subjection over us, you yourself must first live canonically, so that you may pursue the matter canonically. No one can lawfully exercise canonical discipline who, by despising the divine canons, leads an impure life; [Col. 0877A] nor can one be competent to judge the affairs of others who, by indulging in the unlawful affairs of others, is found to be errant in his own conduct.

For the present we have written these few words to you, earnestly begging you to restrain your most insolent tongue with the bridle of moderation. Otherwise, if you show yourself to us as Luscius Lavinius, we may be compelled to sink our sharpest tooth into you. You know that we can now write more freely, since you have no means by which you can proscribe us.

## THIRD LETTER. TO THE SAME

*On the same subject.*

[Note: [Col. 0886A]

### ON THE THIRD LETTER

Here William compares Gervasius, archbishop of Reims, with Manassé, his successor, giving Gervasius a much higher place. He praises him both for his study of the liberal arts, in which he excelled, and for the churches he built and the temples he adorned—namely, the churches of Saint Nicasius and Saint Dionysius, which he restored—and finally for his honor toward religious men. He was the first to introduce monks of the Order of Saint Benedict into Saint Nicasius and regular canons into the monastery of Saint Dionysius.

Why William calls him a tyrant I do not know, unless it is because the ancients reported that the soul of the deceased man was rescued from the power of demons through the holy martyrs Dionysius and Nicasius.

By the word *follis*, which the author uses here, the ancient Gauls meant “madman” and “fool,” as John the Deacon testifies in Book IV, chapter 96 of *The Life of Saint Gregory*. “But he,” John says, “rebuking the holy old man in the Gallic manner as a fool,” etc.]

To Manassé, oppressor of the Church of Reims, W., a sinner.

What sweetness and love I always felt toward you after some unknown fortune subjected me to your yoke is clearly shown by this: although I very frequently suffered insults and terrors from you, I so restrained the impulse of justified indignation that I never broke out into words of disparagement or bitterness.

Indeed, even your associates marveled at this and praised me highly for remaining, amid your most turbulent threats and dreadful storms of spirit, with a tranquil mind and undisturbed heart. And truly I was sitting in a most secure harbor, with the anchor of my heart fixed to that rock from which the Israelite people once drank and from which Peter derived his name. I despised all your turbulences and assaults, and the storms of your threats and blows, as though they were vanishing smoke and foam on a whirlpool.

But because whoever is moved by true love cannot fail to grieve over the errors of any neighbor, I confess that I lamented your frenzies more than my own injuries. I often repeated to myself the verse, “Deliver my soul from the sword, O God, and my only one from the hand of the dog”; and at times I poured forth fiery prayers to the Lord for you as well, with tears.

For I did not desire to be freed from the hands of this dog in such a way that you would remain doglike in your conduct, but so that, if it were possible, after laying aside the savagery of your mind and the bestiality of your behavior, you too might rejoice with me in the sweetest charity and the dearest sweetness.

O how often I applied to you the medicines of Scripture! How often, as though with certain charms, I tried to soothe your fury with heavenly words! How often, with the Thracian and Davidic lyre, I tried either to drive out or to calm the demon by which you are afflicted!

But you, most savage of men, possessing more aloe than honey, never accepted gentle admonitions and never allowed divine seeds to grow in the soil of your heart, where the plant of most impious greed and most greedy impiety had grown strong.

Once, certainly, among certain philosophers there was a widespread belief in the transmigration of souls. In your case it is not without reason confirmed, since people of our time think that, just as Euphorbus passed into Pythagoras, so Gervasius has passed into you. Yet I would not grant you that he passed wholly into you, since that former tyrant possessed traces of the liberal arts, in which he excelled and of which you are entirely devoid.

He built churches; you destroy them. He adorned the temples of the Lord; you strip them. He honored religious men in no ordinary way; you persecute them. Nothing good of his has therefore migrated into you; only his vices have done so.

Ah, it is shameful to recall the miseries I suffered under your servile and barbarous domination! It is shameful to remember how many evils you returned to me for good, and how many darts of insult and wounds of abuse you brought against me in return for my love!

I pass over your threats. I pass over the fact that, on the very feast of blessed Remigius, you called me *follis*—“fool”—in rustic speech. And indeed not unjustly. For if I had not been a fool, I would not have come to you, such a harsh, savage, violent, monstrous beast.

Yet it was certainly astonishing that I, who became a fool by coming to you, did not become even more foolish by remaining under your tyranny.

I pass over how shamelessly you tried to extort from me the money I had set aside for my journey to Rome; by what methods and tricks you surrounded me through your Sarabaites and circumcellions.

I pass over the letters you wrote about me to my lord, the bishop of Metz. I pass over those you sent to the cleric Gipuino. I shall touch briefly on those your messengers brought to the apostolic lord, in which your madness and wickedness of mind appeared so clearly that you became an object of mockery and horror both to the venerable pope and to the sacred senate.

For in those letters you asserted:

“I am a peaceful, humble, and quiet man, always devoted to reading, and for that reason I do not fit the customs of the Franks and of your people. Moved by a certain fragrance of my reputation—which peace, not virtue, had nevertheless produced in me—you entrusted me with the abbey of Saint-Remi.”

O monster whose vices no virtue redeems! Do you think it shows less virtue to live peacefully with temperance, moderation, and sobriety than to fight fiercely and bravely in war, when peace is accustomed to weaken even strong spirits, while battle strengthens the weak and idle?

Hence that distinguished orator did not unreasonably persuade men that arms should yield to the toga, plainly considering that fewer people are able to live continently in peace than can patiently endure the labors and dangers of war.

Yet I would confidently say that one whom a long peace could not corrupt cannot be overcome by war; and a vessel placed in water that does not soften does not know how to split apart in fire.

The apostolic lord therefore laughed at those letters of yours. What you sent to injure me brought me praise and glory. That same venerable pope accordingly granted me free authority either to retain or to leave the abbey of Saint-Remi, and by the authority of his letters commanded you to do nothing concerning that abbey except what my will and counsel prescribed.

On my return, after long and careful deliberation with myself, and after weighing my character against yours, I considered it the greatest sacrilege if my sight were ever again polluted even by seeing you. It should therefore not be attributed to frivolity or inconstancy that I fled from your abbey and your companionship; anyone who recognizes you readily forgives me.

## FOURTH LETTER. TO A CERTAIN ABBOT

*On the same subject as the two preceding letters.*

To the desirably venerable and venerably desirable lord and father H., W., a sinner: prayer and service.

[Cols. 0879B–0880B]

I received your letter—a letter of pure goodwill, a letter glowing with the fire of the most sincere love and shining with the ineffable splendor of deepest affection. In this letter of yours you declared that you were not a little astonished that I could have been so deceived and misled as to allow myself to be shut up so rashly and easily in the land of the Franks, as though in a lions’ den—especially since the savagery of that bloodiest beast ought to have recalled me from this deadly deed, even if everything else had been sufficiently peaceful and secure. I confess that this is so, and, when you truthfully rebuke my rashness and my folly, I admit that I have no excuse or defense to offer. Yet you ought to remember human weakness, and that no one, while living in this body of death, can be so perfect as not to be subject to the uncertainty of change. For what wonder is it that I yielded to the counsels of others and staggered somewhat from the firmness of my own stability, when David, the wisest of the prophets, believed the false accusation of the servant against his lord Mephibosheth; and when that most holy king Josiah, distinguished by unique devotion to the Lord, rose up against Neco, king of Egypt, on behalf of the king of Assyria and provoked the Lord’s anger? Yet, lest the merit of so great a man should perish, this was settled by a transitory punishment and a temporal death. It is therefore not surprising if we also, who are enveloped in the darkness of sins, slip on a slippery road and grow dim in our counsels, since such great men could be obscured by the cloud of ignorance, men in whose life and conduct the light of justice—and even the brightness of the sun—shone forth.

I too was deceived by a certain appearance of virtue; and, so that the savagery of that worst beast and horrible monster might be less clearly perceived and, once perceived, guarded against, my intention of coming to their aid became the cause of misery to the monks and the afflicted place. For that boar from the forest repeatedly promised, with many exceedingly frightening oaths, that he would never again ravage the Lord’s vineyard, nor take anything from it except what the spontaneous generosity of my hands might bestow upon him. I believed his promises, I confess, thinking that it would not be a matter of slight merit or insignificant reward if, through me, his ferocity could be restrained. But that most rapacious wolf, craftily flattering and making false promises, was striving by every means to sink his teeth into our little abbey, which, according to its modest means, seemed sufficiently orderly and well arranged, and to seize whatever he could as something alien, stuffing it somehow into the belly of his wickedness—things which his pestilence had trampled down. When he saw that he was striving in vain and that his schemes were making little progress, he burst into open madness and his customary fury. He did not know how to frighten me with threats or overthrow me by treachery, poor man, unaware that under the shadow of that Head I was indefatigably contending, of whom the prophetic trumpet proclaims that the lion and the dragon are trampled underfoot. Thus, just as he was not lacking in poisonous plots, so, God being favorable, I was not lacking in devices and craft with which to repel them. Although I had imprudently subjected myself to his yoke for a short time, I nevertheless endured patiently and escaped wisely.

Yet I am overwhelmed with no small shame that I believed another’s words more than my own eyes; and when signs of every kind of wickedness appeared to me in him, I am miserably ashamed that I consented to remain with him or under him even for a moment. Certainly I saw in him a stiff and uplifted neck, eyes full of furies darting here and there, nostrils breathing contempt, speech changeable and unlike itself, consistent in neither sequence nor reason, shoulders prone to tossing about, unsteady feet, an uneven, disordered, and unbecoming gait, and hands rapacious and violent, ready for slaughter and injury to those nearby. Since I perceived in him these signs of a poisoned mind, it was the extremity of misery that I could become so absent to myself as ever to allow myself to be defiled either by his companionship or by conversation with him. I hope, however, that henceforth I shall be more watchful, more cleansed, and more cautious, provided that you do not refuse to help me and to act through your most powerful prayers so that this lapse, contracted through a certain sheepishness of mind, may be forgiven me. Farewell.

## LETTER V. TO A CERTAIN MONK

He exhorts him to seek the one God.

[Cols. 0880C–0882B]

To his dearest brother A., W., a sinner, sends the affection of deepest love.

All human beings who glory in the gift of holy faith and divine knowledge ought to live in a holy and praiseworthy manner. Yet a greater burden of this duty rests upon those who, voluntarily subjecting their souls to a more excellent calling and, through the marvelous fervor of their spirit, surpassing the summits of all the commandments, shine forth in the body of Christ like certain exceedingly bright lights. For although marriages are praised by the apostolic voice, and those who distribute a portion of their possessions to the poor attain the seats of the blessed and the Elysian fields, these men, nevertheless, out of love for a more perfect life, despised all visible things and preferred at once to seize the Monad itself rather than construct from temporal things the steps by which one ascends to it. Scripture clearly shows that everything is referred to the Monad and that it holds primacy over all things made through it, when, speaking of Wisdom, it says: “Though she is one, she can do all things.” The Psalmist also testifies that he asks one thing from the Lord. And the ark constructed by Noah, for which the measurements are given from heaven, is described as having below a length of three hundred cubits and a width of fifty; yet, rising toward the higher parts, it is forced to narrow, so that its summit ends within the space of a single cubit.

You see, then, how everything is reduced to the Monad. Whoever can obtain it in the present life assuredly already attains in this mortality that to which, in the common resurrection, every rational creature strives to become holy and pure. Then, as the divine writings promise, God will be all in all, when the Son has handed over the kingdom to God the Father—that is, when he has brought the faithful, in whom he now reigns through faith, happily and desirably to the contemplation of God the Father. Moses, that great lawgiver and ardent lover of divinity, desired to apply a free gaze to this most excellent vision. When he spoke with the Lord, he prayed with the deepest devotion that the Lord might deign to show himself also to him. For that extraordinary man knew that the highest blessedness consisted in contemplating the principle of all things and embracing in the mind that Monad from which everything takes its origin and in which everything finds its end.

It is therefore clear how great in virtue and excellence it is, after rejecting every secular hope and the happiness of the world, to desire that one good toward which the aspiration of such great men yearned. Therefore, at the regeneration, when the Son of Man sits upon the throne of his majesty, those who have left everything out of regard for his love will rightly receive judicial authority from the Lord. Anyone of sound judgment understands that this accords with equity: those who were truly humble in their pilgrimage should be glorious in their homeland.

I am therefore compelled by certain reasoning to believe that you will obtain the most eminent place among such heroes. For when you descended to such great humility, it was not, as with some, the recollection of sins that invited you, but a life commendably conducted and the desire for the heavenly homeland. Always, then, be watchful; always be prudent; strive with every effort and the whole intention of your heart so that, passing continually from good things to better, you may make the end correspond with the beginning, and so that what began in integrity may not be violated by any fraud of the ancient enemy. I beg you, do not let the sluggishness of others cool your fervor, nor let the examples of those who display outwardly in their habit what they pursue in their conduct make you more negligent. For many such men—as I do not think is hidden from you—lie concealed under an angelic habit. Their way of life is so wretched and their conduct so perverse that they often instill repentance for the holy calling even into good minds, and by contact with a worse life they never cease to obscure the radiance of the holy and heavenly warfare—which in itself is always splendid, always luminous, always excellent.

But a well-founded mind is not disturbed by this, nor can the depravity of any wickedness separate it from the highest love. It knows that in the Lord’s threshing floor the grain groans amid the chaff, and that it ought not to be thoroughly cleansed by the winnowing fan of divine judgment before the end of the age. It knows that in the present fishing, the net of the word encloses both good and bad fish, and that they cannot be separated except upon the shore. Thus we must govern our minds and temper the poison of impatience with the antidote of long-suffering, so that we may patiently endure the wickedness of the bad and never abandon the good on account of the worst.

Here you may perhaps accuse me of having left the abbey of Saint Remigius so quickly and easily, since it cannot be doubted that some most honorable men were found in that community, whose exceedingly benevolent charity ought to have made the others tolerable. I confess that this rebuke of yours would be partly justified, unless that pestilential fig-tree trunk, that useless wood, had occupied that land miserably. Under its shadow no good seed can spring up; and if any had sprung up, it would be killed. For that poisonous and most bitter tree is so dark and dense that wherever it extends its twisted arms and deadly branches, no sun of justice or light of truth can gain access. To flee from such a monster and such a portent must therefore be attributed not to the fault of impatience or inconstancy, but to the highest virtue and the highest prudence.

## LETTER VI. TO THE SAME

He explains the hidden judgments of God to one failing in the fervor of his vocation.

[Cols. 0882C–0883C]

To brother A., W., a sinner, sends the greeting: “clothed with the sun and having the moon under his feet.”

Since anyone who is stirred by the impulse of true love rejoices no less in the progress of his neighbors than in his own, I remember recently sending you a congratulatory letter, hoping that the beginning of your conversion would be matched by the course and conclusion of your whole life and purpose. But, as I have been informed, the matter is far otherwise: you have been overcome by the wickedness of the bad and have thrown away the shield of patience. If your brotherhood wished to arm itself with this shield, a considerable gain in virtue would accrue to you both from the improvement of some and from the endurance of the worst.

For it is brought about by an ineffable order and a marvelous arrangement that all the wickedness of the reprobate should always serve the benefit of the elect; and the more deeply the Egyptians are plunged into their darkness and gloom, the more purely the true Israelites enjoy heavenly and divine light. I am wrong if sacred history does not testify to this: in that plague upon Memphis, it records that palpable darkness was found among the Egyptians, but the clearest light among the people of the faithful. Thus these two peoples are distinguished: although they are in one province and dwell in the same house, one is nevertheless always surrounded by light and the other by darkness. Nor is this surprising. The power of that delightful light and divine radiance is so great that whatever hearts it touches, it immediately illuminates and kindles; but those whom it judges unworthy of its contact remain in their own dark and cold gloom. Why the whole human race emerged from one mass of perdition, why all are held liable to original sin before they are reborn, why the grace of conversion is granted to some through divine inspiration while others remain in their own obscurity—this is not to be weighed by the examination of human reason or on the scales of mortal understanding.

Yet from this very depth of divine judgment we are profitably warned not to abandon too readily and rashly the companionship of weak brothers, because our understanding is not capable of grasping what that most secret Judge disposes concerning them in hidden places. It often happens that those who seem to be oppressed by the weight of sins and to dwell in the northern regions are suddenly pierced by divine inspiration, shake off the filth of their faults, and build homes for themselves in the southern land through works of virtue.

Since this is so, it is utterly monstrous and intolerably proud to wish to anticipate the sentence of the hidden and eternal Judge, and to attempt in the present life to exercise discrimination among the fish enclosed in the nets of the same mysteries, before they reach the shores of the sea. Certainly the divine writings teach this, and the whole well-considered sequence of Scripture answers accordingly: for the time being, the good must be separated from the bad in heart, not in body—not by distance of place, but by the quality of their affections. That day will certainly come—indeed, it will come—on which that shepherd who cannot be deceived will judge between the lean and the fat livestock, between the flocks of rams and goats. Then the hidden things of darkness will be brought entirely into the light, and wolfish hearts will no longer conceal themselves beneath sheep’s fleeces. For through the power and might of that most blessed resurrection it will come about that, as each person was here in character, so each will appear there in the very body. Finally, that luminous city is compared to pure glass because, like the clearest glass, whatever is within it will be visible outwardly, and the very thoughts of souls will wonderfully lie open to the sight of the eyes. Therefore, dearest brother, let us prepare ourselves by holy conduct for that ineffable purity. Let us ourselves be good, and let us endure with the greatest patience those whom we cannot draw toward better things. Farewell.

## LETTER VII. TO A. . . . HIS TEACHER

He exhorts him to despise the world.

### Note: Concerning Letter VII

[Cols. 0886B–D]

We do not know who William’s teacher was, to whom his seventh letter is addressed, because the truncated name of this teacher is indicated only by the first letter A. Nevertheless, I conjecture that he was Alestan, a disciple of Fulbert, bishop of Chartres, whom Adelmann praises in rhythmic verses:

> We would scarcely lament Alestan’s loss while Odulf survived,  
>
> Such was his greatness in ancient learning,  
>
> As those whom he taught, who today possess sufficient strength.

In any case, we understand how solidly our William was imbued with piety especially from the three final letters. A most religious man, Dom Joseph Homassel, then subprior of the monastery of Saint Arnulf at Metz and a member of the congregation of Saint Vanne, copied them, together with four others, from a manuscript codex of that monastery and sent them to me.

Here I have thought it appropriate to append a prayer of William the abbot, to be recited on the feast of Saint Augustine. This William was abbot of Fécamp and Dijon and restored the discipline of monastic religion, both in several other places and especially in the monastery of Saint Arnulf at Metz. I am moved by the following conjectures to attribute the appended prayer to this later William rather than to the other William whose letters I have so far presented. First, the Metz codex at the monastery of Saint Arnulf was written while that William was abbot. Second, the prayer is entitled “Of Dom William the Abbot,” without any other honorific qualification, whereas the earlier William was already then called the blessed abbot of holy memory. Thus Warinus, in the letter edited above, calls this man “the lord abbot William of holy memory.” Moreover, the younger William was especially devoted to the teaching of Saint Augustine, as is clear above all from the preceding sixth letter.

To his teacher A., W., a sinner: “to flee from the face of the bow.”

[Cols. 0883D–0884D]

When I consider the pursuits and desires of mortals, such great astonishment and stupor overwhelm me that, with the satirist, I am compelled to exclaim:

> O the cares of men! O how much emptiness there is in human affairs!

For who would not be exceedingly astonished that wretched human beings are carried away by so great a desire that neither reason, nor will, nor finally fear of the Lord places any limit upon their greed? For it happens, in a remarkable way, that the more they accumulate, the more they burn with the torches of desire, and the love of money increases as money itself increases. Hence the divine justice must be proclaimed beyond expression: it has decreed that sinful man should die in such a way that death would threaten him daily because of uncertain accidents, yet, because of life’s brevity, could never be far away. The supreme Divinity evidently provided that man might resist his desires and restrain illicit pleasures if fear of punishment were always before his eyes. For who, placed under the fear of death, can take even the slightest pleasure in temporal things, which, whether he wishes it or not, he himself will have to leave behind?

It is therefore now very easy to see through how many rivers of tears those must be mourned who, having despised the Lord’s medicinal severity, have once surrendered themselves to the abyss of wickedness so completely that they can neither will nor are able any longer to retrace their steps and emerge into the air above. To avoid more easily their astonishing—or rather pitiable—blindness and the punishment of that blindness, I withdrew into the bosom and embrace of true philosophy. For it heals souls, removes empty anxieties, frees them from desires, and drives away fears. Its delight is so great, and its beauty so beyond measure, that one day lived well and according to its precepts is most rightly preferred to a sinner’s immortality.

You see, then, if you love me, how greatly you should rejoice with exultation, since I have chosen such a bride for myself, one whose beauty and sweetness surpass all things. Dry your tears, then; restrain your weeping; drive away all sorrow. Know for certain that I have chosen the better part. Believe me, believe me: sublimity will follow humility, laughter tears, and riches poverty. Great are the things that she promises to her lovers. Indeed, who could be sufficient to imagine how great wealth Wisdom will bestow upon those who love her, when poverty itself, embraced for love of her, becomes a delight? It is therefore good for me to cling to her, and no day will ever come that tears me away from her embraces and love.

But if you wish to know by what rule we serve in her camp, I shall describe it briefly to you. Everything is common among us; we have one heart, one soul, one and the same purpose. The virtue of obedience, however, so prevails that, although our zeal for reading is extraordinary, no one dares to prefer reading to obedience. What should I say about voluntary poverty, when everything touched by bodily sense is held in utter contempt by us, and, turning the mind away from the body, we accustom ourselves to die? Who denies that this is arduous and difficult? Yet, with philosophy as our guide, we believe that we shall accomplish it. This is the praiseworthy life that we lead; this is the true philosophy to which, my friend, we invite you. If I cannot bring you to it, you will never draw me away from it. Farewell, and have pity on your soul.

## PRAYER OF DOM WILLIAM

To be said in commemoration of Saint Augustine before the consecration of the Mass.

*(Mabillon, Analecta, p. 460.)*

[Cols. 0887A–0890A]

Remember, Lord, the soul of your servant Patrick and of your servant Monica. And if, concerning the soul of their son, my lord Augustine, your most beloved confessor, it is permitted to me, a wretched sinner, to desire anything even with the deepest affection of my heart, would that my will itself might not speak to you altogether in vain. I know, Lord, and recognize with certainty that I am a sinner, most wretched, liable to every crime, and stained by immense offenses; but I know that he was holy, just, and pious in this present life, and marvelously adorned with every virtue. Now, exalted magnificently in your sight with every honor and glory, may he be glorified and magnified more and more: this I desire and pray for, insofar as I dare presume to do so.

As for what I ask through him in my great need, though with however little faith, you, most gracious knower of hidden things, God who searches hearts and reins, look upon it favorably, so that through his merits and intercession, and those of all your saints, you may absolve me and all our brothers from every bond of sins, and again deal with us and with all for whom we implore your mercy according to the multitude of your mercies.

I also beg that, through his intercessions and merits, you grant me what I certainly do not deserve to obtain through my own: namely, that concerning the divinity and humanity of your beloved Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, I may be worthy to feel what he felt, to know what he knew, to understand what he understood, to believe what he believed, to love what he loved, and also to be able to preach what he taught.

I pray, Lord, that, with the help and assistance of your goodness and the supplication of all your saints, I may breathe forth my final spirit with sincere faith, secure hope, and unfeigned charity. I also ask, Lord, that you not permit me to dread that day and hour—the departure, namely, of my soul from the body—with a destructive fear, but rather make me live in such a way that it may be fitting, profitable, and useful for me to desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ. For to be dissolved and to be with Christ is certainly nothing better, nothing more glorious, nothing happier, nothing more joyful, nothing more delightful, nothing sweeter, nothing more pleasing, nothing more lovable, nothing more desirable, nothing more longed for.

Yet if it is necessary to remain still in the flesh for whatever persons, what shall I say? Certainly, although conscience torments me because it is keenly conscious of its own evil, I shall say, “Father, I shall say: Let your will be done!” For you alone, who know even how to make good use of evils, know why you have done this. You have power to make from the same lump of clay one vessel for honor and another for dishonor, with no one resisting your power, no one preventing it, no one contradicting it. And what can a creature say in contradiction to its Creator, a work to its Maker? Does the molded thing say to the one who molded it, “Why have you molded me so?” Indeed, he has mercy on whom he wills, and whom he wills he hardens.

Therefore mortal man does not know whether he is worthy of hatred or of love; everything is reserved uncertain for the future. One thing, however, is certain, firm, stable, and unchangeable in everlasting eternity: that you are God, that you are omnipotent, that you are good. Therefore, in us and concerning us, most merciful Father, let whatever is good in your sight be done—let it be done! Everything is placed under your dominion, and there is no one who can resist your will. If you decide to save us, we shall immediately be freed. Do not let the multitude and magnitude of my sins make me an exile from, and unworthy of, that grace of liberation. Command, Lord, that my most wretched soul be consoled by the truth that you have mercy on all and hate nothing that you have made, overlooking human sins for the sake of repentance.

Therefore make me, Lord, produce fruit worthy of repentance. Most merciful one, grant that, before I fall into the abyss of despair, before death seizes me, before the final day closes the way for me, your servant may find his heart ready to make satisfaction to you for such great, horrible, and unspeakable crimes, to which I confess myself liable before your majesty—and most gravely so, alas, alas, most damnably! But you, most merciful and most loving God, turning your face away from these evils, do not judge me according to my deeds. Rather, mercifully accepting my satisfaction, hear me, so that, even now, near the end of my life, when I shall no longer have to labor for long, I may not neglect or delay occupying all my inward faculties in your holy service.

Illuminate my mind, I beg you, Lord, to investigate, seek out, and search the path of your commandments, so that no iniquity may now rule over me, nor any masters apart from you possess me. Rather, I beg you: may you possess me; may you rule over me. I ask you, most gracious one, teach me to do your will, because you are the Lord my God, and I am your servant and the son of your handmaid.

Let it therefore come to pass for me now, Lord, through your grace, that, having renounced every domination of the vices, neither pride, nor avarice, nor lust, nor that most wicked of all the wicked, that worst of all the depraved—the spirit of blasphemy, intolerable in its most ungodly cruelty and most cruel offensiveness—nor any plague of the vices may be able in any way to tear my mind away or turn it from confidence in your immeasurable goodness.

Strengthened, however, by faithful confidence in the immensity of your mercies, I ask that I may dare to say more securely concerning you: “I am yours,” so that you may recognize me as a member of that holy body of yours, which you delight to address: “Hear, Jacob, my servant, and Israel, whom I have chosen, making and forming you from the womb, your helper, because I am he who blots out your iniquities for my own sake, and I will remember your sins no more.”

Remember my sins no longer, but, for your own sake, I beg you, blot out my iniquities. For your own sake grant me your grace, so that, as I approach the mystery of so great a sacrament, you may forgive what conscience fears and add what prayer does not presume to ask.

## IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 1091: SAINT WILLIAM, ABBOT OF HIRSAU

## HISTORICAL NOTICE ON SAINT WILLIAM

[Col. 0889]

*(Fabricius, Bibliotheca Latina of the Middle and Lower Ages, III, 150.)*

William, abbot of Hirsau in the diocese of Speyer from the year 1068, died in the year 1091, on the third day before the Nones of July. Concerning him, see Trithemius, chapter 352 of *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, and *On German Writers*, chapter 57; book II of *Illustrious Benedictines*, chapter 102; and the *Chronicle of Hirsau*, page 62 and following; and the Anonymous of Melk, chapter 108.

His writings are:

- *Constitutions, or Customs, of the Monks of Hirsau*, in two books. They were published in the Benedictines’ distinguished collection of ancient monuments from the congregation of Saint Blaise at St. Blasien, entitled *Ancient Monastic Discipline*, Paris, 1726, quarto, pp. 37–132. Mabillon published the prologue in volume IV of the *Analecta*, p. 465 (new edition, p. 134 and following).
- *Three Books of Philosophical and Astronomical Instruction*, published at Basel in 1531 by Heinrich Petri.
- *On Music and the Tones*.
- *On the Correction of the Psalter, or Errors Detected in the Chants*.
- *Questions on Computation*.
- *On the Clock*.
- *Letters to Various Persons*, and to Anselm of Canterbury, some letters of whom to this William also survive.

## LIFE OF BLESSED WILLIAM, ABBOT OF HIRSAU

By Heymo, a monk of Hirsau, his contemporary and a disciple of blessed William.

*(Mabillon, Acts of the Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict, sixth century, part II, p. 717, from Charles Stengelius, monk of Saint Ulrich of Augsburg.)*

## PRELIMINARY OBSERVATIONS

[Cols. 0889B–0891D]

1. Although the monastery of Hirsau had already been restored for several years before William was placed over it, and nearly all the buildings of the entire monastery had been completed; the monks had inhabited the monastery for about eight years, the condition of the monastery was not yet secure, both because of the disputes of Abbot Frederick with the monks and because of the fickleness of Count Adalbert. He had not so completely withdrawn from the monastery’s goods, which he had possessed unjustly for so long, that he did not consider claiming them for himself at some future time if a suitable opportunity arose. Our William, however, soon brought a remedy to both diseases. In him, the highest prudence in conducting affairs, courage of spirit in overcoming adversities, and piety and devotion in restoring and maintaining monastic discipline shone forth so brilliantly that he rightly and deservedly belongs among the more illustrious men of the eleventh century.

Heymo, his disciple, wrote the life of this blessed man. After the death of blessed William, Gebhard was made abbot and appointed Heymo prior of the monastery. Concerning this Heymo, Trithemius speaks as follows in the *Chronicle of Hirsau* under the year 1091:

“He was certainly a most diligent man, excellently learned in both the divine Scriptures and secular literature, subtle in intellect and very well adorned in speech. He left behind distinguished monuments of his learning. Among other small works of his intellect, he wrote the life and miracles of the blessed William, the abbot mentioned above; but afterward another brother, wishing to enlarge it, made it shorter. He also wrote several sermons and homilies, which, mostly through error, are attributed to another man of the same name, Heymo, formerly a monk and later bishop of Halberstadt, a man equally learned.”

In the Saint Gall edition Trithemius likewise observes that this author’s true name was Haymo. He says that some, wishing to supply a fifth letter, called him Heymo, using the custom of the Saxons in place of the first letter. He then praises his great care and diligence in collecting and transcribing the works of the holy Fathers. Although he was most devoted to every branch of learning, he induced his brothers by word and example to do the same, and in a short time established a very well-stocked library in the monastery of Hirsau.

Concerning his writings he says:

“He was [lacuna] practiced no less in verse than in prose, and in conduct also orderly, mature, and most religious. He surpassed his brothers in every purity of regular observance [lacuna] Among other small works he wrote [lacuna] the life, conduct, and miracles of the most holy abbot William in two volumes, which a certain brother later abridged. He also wrote a short and useful little book *On Music*, as well as several homilies for the brothers, which are often found, through error, attributed to Heymo, bishop of Halberstadt [lacuna] He also compiled certain other collections.”

Two conclusions may be drawn from this. First, some of the small works of our Heymo were attributed to Haymo of Halberstadt; and, as Trithemius continues, the writings of the one and the other are usually so confusedly mixed together that, unless the reader knows how to distinguish them through careful discernment, he cannot easily judge to whom they should be attributed, since he does not perceive the difference in their phrasing. Second, from the words of Trithemius quoted above we gather that the *Life of Blessed William*, which we now possess in a single book, was originally divided into two volumes.

However that may be, it is always the work of Heymo. Since he was blessed William’s disciple, he committed to writing what he had seen and heard in person, as he himself explicitly testifies more than once. In section 24, indeed, he recalls that he was present at the pious Father’s death. What Trithemius says about this same William in both editions of the *Chronicle of Hirsau* has been drawn principally from this Life. We shall present it here from Charles Stengelius, a monk of Saint Ulrich, who published it with observations and notes in a separate booklet, printed at Augsburg in 1611. Before presenting it, however, several preliminary matters should be noted, as is our custom; these we shall borrow chiefly from Trithemius, while relegating the rest to notes on the text of the Life itself.

2. Nothing concerning William’s parents or his education in the monastery of Saint Emmeram requires observation beyond what is contained in his Life. Nor is it my intention to treat here at greater length everything that he [did] either in the monastery of Hirsau or in other monasteries founded or restored by him. I shall present only a few matters to illuminate the deeds of the blessed abbot that are lacking in the Life and could not easily have been confined within the limits of marginal notes.

William was therefore chosen abbot by the monks of Hirsau after Frederick’s deposition, with the consent of his own abbot, and came to Hirsau on 28 May 1069. He took possession of the abbey on the following 2 June. “But he was unaware,” says Trithemius, “of the injuries inflicted upon Frederick.” When he learned of them, he began to urge Count Adalbert to restore the innocent man to his dignity, since no one was permitted to occupy his place while he was alive. For this reason the holy man was already preparing to return, lest he make himself a participant in such a crime.

Nevertheless, afterward compelled to yield to the prayers of all the brothers, he remained in such a way that, while Frederick lived, he never received the blessing from the bishop and refused to occupy the abbatial position. This was the condition of Hirsau until the following year, when, after Frederick’s death, William was solemnly blessed as abbot by Henry, bishop of Speyer. Trithemius writes that this took place on the fourth day before the Nones of May, on the feast of the Ascension of the Lord; but these chronological indications do not agree with one another. For from the year 1050 to the end of this century, the Ascension of the Lord fell on 4 May only once, namely in the year 1060, which cannot have been the year of William’s appointment, since Frederick was certainly not yet abbot then.

The author of the Life writes that the blessed man was installed in the abbatial see on the very day of the Ascension, on the fourth day before the Nones of June. This can have occurred only in the year 1071.

### 3

When Wilhelmus was consecrated abbot, he found the monastery’s resources so meager that they scarcely sufficed to support fifteen monks. These monks, moreover, were so subject to the will of Count Adelbert of Calw that they scarcely dared undertake anything in the monastery without his permission [Col. 0892A]. The most devout abbot could not tolerate this. Therefore, after overcoming many difficulties, he finally obtained the liberty of his monastery from the count, and took care to have it secured by a charter of imperial authority and by confirmation from the Supreme Pontiff. Trithemius reports the letters of both—the Pope and the Emperor—in the old and new editions of the *Chronicle of Hirsau*; whether they are the same documents praised by the author of the *Life*, others may judge.

Berthold praises Wilhelmus because he wonderfully exalted the monastery of Hirsau both in its buildings and in its regular discipline, and permanently liberated it under Pope Gregory by a privilege of the Apostolic See. Thereafter, once Wilhelmus and his monks had been freed in this manner from an alien yoke, he devoted himself entirely to feeding his flock and restoring the monastery’s buildings.

In 1071 the church which Adelbert had begun ten years earlier was completed and consecrated by the Bishop of Speyer. The count himself promoted the work; he had now been changed from a disturber of the monastery into its defender and benefactor. The monastery’s resources also greatly increased as the number of monks grew. For, as Trithemius writes, Wilhelmus had obtained from the Lord a singular grace for winning souls, and through his work he converted many—indeed, almost numberless people—to the service of Christ in the monastery . . . . He also greatly increased the temporal substance of its household from the offerings of the faithful in a short time.

From that period onward, there were always one hundred and fifty monks in the monastery of Hirsau under Wilhelmus’s discipline. Although many were frequently sent from there to reform other monasteries, the number was immediately restored from those who newly entered the monastic life. It is worthwhile to set forth, in Trithemius’s own words, what their exercises were under so great a Father. In the new edition of the *Chronicle* of that same monastery, near the end of the year 1070, he writes:

### 4

“These men were always devoted to divine praises and prayer, and were continually intent upon meditation and the reading of the Holy Scriptures [Col. 0892C]. Those who seemed less suited to contemplation of heavenly things were assigned to necessary manual labors, so that no time passed idly among them.

“But the holy Father, wisely instructed by experience and knowing that the necessary nourishment of the mind is the reading of the divine Scriptures, trained twelve of his monks as excellent scribes and entrusted them with the task of copying books of divine authority and the treatises of the holy Fathers. Besides these there were other scribes, without a fixed number, who with equal diligence devoted themselves to writing volumes. Over all of them was placed one monk, highly learned in every branch of knowledge, who assigned each man some good work to copy and corrected the mistakes of those who wrote carelessly.

“The brothers copied many volumes over the course of time,” Trithemius adds, “yet only a very small part of them remained in this monastery of Hirsau. For the holy Father, who always placed the profit and benefit of souls above all the things of the world [Col. 0892D], whenever he sent brothers to other monasteries for their reform, freely and willingly gave them books and whatever else seemed necessary to them, and so forth.”

O man admirable in every respect, who placed souls redeemed by Christ’s blood above the advantages of passing gain, and who, consulting the welfare of others, did not seek the perishable riches of the world! Truly, it is a virtue found in few abbots to strip their own monasteries of either ornaments or books in order to relieve the poverty of others.

### 5

Besides the one hundred and fifty monks whom we have said lived in the monastery of Hirsau under the discipline of blessed Wilhelmus, there were other brothers called *barbati*, or conversi. Devoting themselves chiefly to manual labor, they provided what was necessary for the support of the monks dedicated to contemplation.

“Among these,” says Trithemius, “were workers highly skilled in every mechanical art, who completed all the structures of the entire monastery with their own hands and with the greatest diligence [Col. 0893A] . . . and who built the whole monastery and church in a beautiful arrangement, as can still be seen in the sculpture of the towers. The clothing-makers, tanners, shoemakers, and all those engaged in whatever craft is required for the use of the cloister were not secular persons, hired laborers, or paid servants, but were all conversi, or bearded monks.

“The holy abbot Wilhelmus himself was the first in Germany to establish this order of conversi. Assisted by their labors, he founded so many monasteries and commendably supplied all the needs of the monks. The man of God gave them statutes conforming to the holy Rule; through continual instruction in these, he inflamed their minds with contempt for the world and love of heavenly things.”

Trithemius adds the laws of those conversi, which are given below in no. 23 of the *Life*.

There were also others, called oblati, distinct from the conversi. As Trithemius continues, the blessed abbot had established them in his monastery after the example of the Cluniacs. He permitted them to remain in their former condition—that is, dressed in the manner of secular people—by a sacred constitution. Matters requiring attention outside the monastery were assigned to them. They had a monk as their master for their instruction, and a place for meals was assigned to them, separate from the monks and conversi, so that they would not disturb them [Col. 0893B].

### 6

The holy man omitted absolutely nothing that could provide suitable institutions for the disciples of all these orders. Hence he was extremely diligent in investigating the devout customs of celebrated monasteries, adopting from them whatever seemed more useful to himself and his own monks.

He speaks of this matter himself in the prologue to the *Customs of Hirsau*:

“I resolved within myself,” he says, “that wherever I perceived by sight or hearing—or certainly by reading the sacred books—anything useful for forming the conduct of the brothers, I would contribute the whole of it, as though it were living stones, to the construction of the spiritual building.”

Bernard, abbot of Marseille and at that time the Roman Pontiff’s legate in Germany, greatly assisted the holy abbot in this matter [Col. 0893C]. Because peace between the priesthood and the empire had been disturbed, Bernard was forced to spend almost an entire year in the monastery of Hirsau.

When he noticed that the brothers of that place were burning with the most ardent zeal to live justly and holily, he advised Abbot Wilhelmus that, if he wished to know perfectly the institutions of monastic life, he needed to borrow them from the monastery of Cluny. At that time Cluny stood out among the other monasteries of Cisalpine Gaul both for the number of its most holy monks and for its careful observance of regular discipline.

Wilhelmus thereafter omitted nothing that might enable him to understand the Cluniac manner of life. Therefore, when the Cluniac monk Udalricus, long bound to Wilhelmus by friendship, was later sent to Alemannia and turned aside to Hirsau, the devout abbot obtained from him a careful written account of the customs of the monastery of Cluny. Udalricus subsequently carried this out in practice, as we shall say below in his *Life* under the year 1093 [Col. 0893D].

Difficulties nevertheless arose that could scarcely be resolved in writing. Wilhelmus therefore decided to send two monks to Cluny to see matters for themselves. Shortly afterward he sent two others, and then two more. These men examined all the Cluniac institutions so thoroughly, he says in the prologue mentioned above, that their own teachers declared that they had never had disciples of that spiritual school comprehend the art of their instruction either more completely or more faithfully.

Thereafter, at the command of Hugh, abbot of Cluny, to whom Bernard had greatly commended the abbot and monks of Hirsau when he returned to Gaul, Wilhelmus assembled a council of the elders. From the customs he selected those practices that best suited the usages of the homeland, the climate, and the situation of the places. He recommended that his disciples observe them both at Hirsau and in other German monasteries of the same institute. On this subject he wrote two books, which he entitled *On the Customs of Hirsau*.

These customs, as Trithemius notes [Col. 0894A], flourished in most German monasteries until the Bursfeld reform, whose constitutions almost entirely abolished the institutions of Hirsau.

### 7

Wilhelmus’s concern was not confined within the walls of a single monastery of Hirsau. Trithemius should be heard concerning his efforts to procure the reform of other monasteries. In the old edition of his *Chronicle*, after recounting several of Wilhelmus’s miracles, he concludes as follows:

“But I shall scarcely dwell on the narration of these miracles, since the greatest of all miracles is his restoration of the monastic order and regular discipline, of which I have not yet spoken. For he was the one who strove to reform our order, miserably collapsed in almost every province of the German kingdom, and who wonderfully reformed it in many monasteries.

“He recalled whatever monks he could, by word and example, to the observance of regular discipline, inflamed by the most fervent ardor of the Holy Spirit. With extraordinary zeal he desired to restore to the monks of his own time that former fervor of spirit with which our holy Fathers Benedict, Maurus, Placidus, Columbanus, Gallus, Giles, Gregory, Boniface, Lullus, and almost countless others once burned toward God [Col. 0894B].”

He then lists seven monasteries newly erected by the blessed abbot or by his disciples, which are likewise praised by the author of the *Life*. He later enumerates, in both editions of the *Chronicle*, all those places that belonged to the Hirsau congregation, and gives the names of the abbots who established the Hirsau customs in each place.

Finally, he lists other monasteries that maintained an association with the Hirsau communities. But it is not part of our purpose to pursue these matters at greater length. Let it suffice to say a little about those places built, or at least restored, by blessed Wilhelmus himself.

### 8

Among those monasteries, Trithemius gives first place to the new monastery of Hirsau, chief of the others [Col. 0894C]. Wilhelmus built it entirely from its foundations in honor of the holy apostles Peter and Paul beside the river Nagold, while the earlier monastery of Saint Aurelius remained on the opposite bank of the same river, where its buildings were more confined.

Wilhelmus began this work in 1082. As we have already said, its principal craftsmen were the monks and bearded brothers of the place. The expenses were supplied by neighboring noble and wealthy men, attracted by the reputation for holiness of blessed Wilhelmus and his disciples.

Among these benefactors, special praise is given to the wife of Margrave Hermann, after her husband, touched by divine love, had withdrawn to Cluny. There, unknown, he became a swineherd and remained until the end of his life under the discipline of blessed Hugh.

After nine years, when the buildings of the new monastery had been completed, its church was solemnly dedicated by John, Bishop of Speyer, on the octave of Easter in 1091, shortly before the death of the blessed abbot, which occurred in that same year on 4 July, as we shall say in its proper place below.

### 9

In 1083, the fourteenth year of Wilhelmus’s abbacy, a monastery was built at Reichenbach [Col. 0894D]. The documents of its foundation, issued by Wilhelmus himself, are preserved by Trithemius in the following form:

“In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. I, Wilhelmus, not by any merits of my own but solely by the mercy of God abbot of the monastery of Hirsau, desire it to be known to all, present and future, that a certain free man, an elder named Bern, gave his small estate situated in the Black Forest—at a place called Reichenbach, from the stream that flows into the Murg—in the presence of suitable witnesses, to Saint Aurelius of Hirsau as an everlasting inheritance. His sole request was that I should take care to build a monastery there.

“Having therefore obtained the common and unanimous counsel of our elders, we sent three of our brother monks and five lay brothers to that same small estate, which was thickly overgrown with a very dense forest [the reading *bispidum* is uncertain], so that, after clearing the forest and cleaning the site, they might build a monastery to blessed Gregory.

“In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1082, in the fifth indiction, around the Ides of May [Col. 0895A], when these brothers had arrived at the aforesaid place, they used a bare fir tree as a hut for quite a few days. One of them was named Ernestus, an upright and courteous man, who had long before given himself and all that he possessed to our obedience. We granted him, together with all his possessions, to that place for its assistance.

“Thus Ernestus became provider for the place and for the brothers, almost a second father. For clearing the forest, cleaning the site, building the monastery, and constructing the workshops, he himself supplied the greatest part of the expenses and acquired what was suitable from every direction. I therefore judged it worthy that the memory of him and his parents, as well as of myself and my own parents, should be solemnly kept there, and I confirmed this in writing. These things were done in the year prescribed above.”

Trithemius notes that, besides this one, many other priories were founded by Wilhelmus. Some of them later became abbeys, while others gradually withdrew from the obedience of the Hirsaugians. He says that in his own time this monastery, together with Schönrain in the diocese of Würzburg and the provostship of Roth in the diocese of Augsburg, still remained under the immediate jurisdiction of the abbot of Hirsau [Col. 0895B]. We shall speak of Reichenbach again when discussing the monastery of Hasungen.

### 10

The second monastery newly built by blessed Wilhelmus is called Saint George’s, in the diocese of Constance, situated in the Black Forest. Hezilo, a noble and wealthy man, granted the estate. At the urging of Hesso, he promised to provide the expenses, together with his property, for the construction of the monastery.

Wilhelmus undertook the work. Once the buildings necessary for regular discipline had been completed, he placed Henry in charge of the new monastery and sent him there with some of his other disciples. When Henry died, Wilhelmus appointed another in his place. Since this man proved less suitable to govern the monastery, Wilhelmus recalled him to Hirsau. For the holy man did not release from his own subjection those to whom he entrusted the care of such places.

Gebhard, Bishop of Constance, nevertheless took this badly. He had solemnly blessed this abbot, just as he had blessed his predecessor [Col. 0895C]. Therefore he refused to appoint a third unless Wilhelmus first made him free from his obedience. This third abbot was Saint Theogerus, likewise taken from the monastery of Hirsau. After twenty-eight years of governance—Trithemius gives thirty in another place—he was ordained Bishop of Metz.

Theogerus greatly adorned the monastery of Saint George and built other monasteries of monks and nuns, so that he is said to have had charge of seven hundred souls, both men and women. With God’s help, we shall speak of him in the following century.

The monastery of Saint George was invaded not long ago by the Lutheran Duke of Württemberg. The monks, together with their abbot, were forced to move elsewhere and withdrew to Villingen, where they have remained to the present.

### 11

The third monastery said by the author of the *Life* and by Trithemius to have been built by blessed Wilhelmus was situated in Bavaria. It was founded under the patronage of blessed Martin of Tours. Those authors provide no further information about it, except that the holy man sent there an abbot and several monks highly approved in regular discipline [Col. 0895D].

### 12

The fourth place is occupied by the monastery of Saint Peter of Erfurt in Thuringia. Wilhelmus entrusted its care to Giselbert, who at that time was already abbot of the neighboring monastery of Reinardsbronn, as we shall say below.

After the death of the blessed abbot, however, his successor Gebhard, in the eleventh year of his administration, sent twelve monks there with Burchard, whom he appointed abbot over them.

Trithemius proves by many arguments that this monastery was not older than Wilhelmus, although in his own time some people maintained that it had been founded by King Dagobert.

### 13

The fifth monastery, under the patronage of blessed Mary, was situated at “Double Water,” called *Zwifalten* in the German language, in Swabia, in the diocese of Constance near the Danube, as Berthold notes.

It certainly had an older origin, but at that time it lay so utterly destroyed that nothing at all remained of the ancient monastery [Col. 0896A]. At the request of Duke Berthold, Wilhelmus entirely rebuilt it from its foundations. He placed monks there and appointed Notger as their abbot. As Trithemius repeatedly testifies, Notger nourished the flock entrusted to him by word and example in true innocence.

Notger’s memory is commemorated in Bucelinus’s Benedictine *Menology* on 6 March, where he is said to have died in 1095. The same author commemorates on 18 August Luitolf, a monk of Zwiefalten who had formerly been Count of Achalm, and says that he died there in 1098. On the same day he celebrates Luitold, Count of Achalm, who died in 1096; but this is the same person as Luitolf. Berthold praises Luitolf, formerly a count and later a monk, as having died on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of September in his *Chronicle*.

### 14

The sixth monastery blessed Wilhelmus built was in a village called Wilheim. It underwent various changes of fortune.

From Trithemius under the year 1083 we learn that it was first built there under the title of a priory. It was later transferred to Mount Saint Peter and raised to the dignity of an abbey. As time passed, however, it lost the title of abbey, was reduced to its former status, and was finally transformed into a parish residence.

Trithemius gives the following account of this cell under the year 1085:

“It is now a parish residence at Gilheim, entirely incorporated into the monastery of Hirsau and subject to its abbot.”

The first person appointed by blessed Wilhelmus over this monastery is called Adalbert by the same Trithemius. He was, as the author also testifies, exceptionally devoted to the observance of the Rule.

### 15

Finally, the seventh monastery said to have been erected from its foundations by blessed Wilhelmus was situated in the duchy of Carinthia, at a place called Laven.

The blessed Father sent twelve monks there and placed over them Wezilo, a man of approved virtue, born in eastern Francia. Trithemius writes that Wezilo was venerable for the merits of his life and distinguished by many virtues, and that he restored and reformed many monasteries in those provinces that had almost collapsed [Col. 0896C].

Among the monks who had arrived in Carinthia with Wezilo, two—Sigewin and Gaudentius—were elected abbots. The former, says Trithemius, became abbot of the monastery of Rosac near Aquileia in Slavonia; the latter became abbot of another monastery whose name he does not give.

They had presumed to do this without the permission of the abbot of Hirsau. Therefore, by a common decree of the Hirsau monks, it was established that their names should be erased from the holy college of the brothers and that they should never be regarded among the Hirsaugians as abbots.
