Stricken by this matter, Sigewin returned to Hirsau. He resigned the title of abbot into the hands of Gebhard, who had already succeeded blessed Wilhelmus, asked forgiveness, and, at Gebhard’s command, took his seat last of all in the congregation.

The same abbot later not only relaxed the penance of the repentant man but also restored him to the dignity of abbot and permitted him to return to Rosac.

This concludes the account of the monasteries built by blessed Wilhelmus.

### 16

Besides these, the author of the *Life* mentions three others that the same saint restored when they were almost destroyed: Schaffhausen, Petershausen, and Kempten [Col. 0896D].

We have said more about Schaffhausen, for which he appointed Digefrid as abbot at the request of the monks of the place, under the year 1075, on the occasion of Eberhard, a former count who became a monk there.

Petershausen, or rather Peterburg, that is, “Peter’s house,” was founded in the tenth century by Gebhard, Bishop of Constance, as we said in his eulogy in the preceding century under the year 995. More information about the foundation of that monastery is given there, but it is not useful to repeat it here.

Wilhelmus appointed Dietrich, or Theoderic, formerly prior of Hirsau, as abbot of this place. The monastery is situated in Swabia opposite the city of Constance, beyond the bridge of the Rhine, on the right bank of the river as it emerges from Lake Constance. Scengelius recounts its various disasters in his *Monasteriology*. It continues to exist and is still famous under our order.

Finally, construction of the monastery of Kempten began in 1079 under Count Burchard of Rothenburg [Col. 0897A]. Nine years later, when the monastery buildings had been completed, he obtained from blessed Wilhelmus twelve monks from the monastery of Hirsau, together with their abbot Gouther.

Gouther was, says Trithemius, “a holy and deeply religious man who, diligently carrying out the pastoral office entrusted to him, gathered in a short time at that place a great multitude of monks serving God.”

The Hirsau monks arrived there in 1088, the nineteenth year of Abbot Wilhelmus and the eleventh indiction. In that year, on 21 December, the church of Kempten, together with its chapels and fourteen altars, was dedicated in honor of Saint Nicholas by Saint Adelbero, Bishop of Würzburg, in whose diocese it was situated.

Besides Burchard, it had other distinguished benefactors, especially his brother Henry, later duke, who is said to have given the monastery four towns and several villages.

That place remained famous under the Benedictine order until the time of Trithemius. But eventually, he says, “in these last days of ours, the monks of Kempten followed the devil persuading them inwardly, withdrew from the holy order which they had professed, and, desiring to live without a Rule, became, in name and manner of life, secular canons” [Col. 0897B].

### 17

To these monasteries praised by the author of the *Life*, Trithemius adds others that were reformed by blessed Wilhelmus.

Among them was the monastery of Altdorf in the diocese of Strasbourg, over which he appointed Welicho as abbot. Trithemius praises Welicho because he stirred not only the monks entrusted to him but also the neighboring peoples to the love of God. More about this monastery may be found above in the observations on the *Life of Saint Leo IX*, under the year 1054.

In the monastery of Isny, in the diocese of Constance, Wilhelmus likewise appointed Erchinbold as abbot, a man distinguished for learning and holiness of life.

For Ottenbeuren in the diocese of Augsburg he appointed Wilhelmus; for Buren in the same diocese, or Benedictbeuern, he appointed Azelin as abbot.

In the monastery of Hugshofen, in the diocese of Strasbourg, he appointed Conrad as abbot and sent him there from Hirsau with ten monks. He sent another eight to the monastery of Beinwil in the diocese of Besançon, situated on the borders of Alsace, together with Abbot Esso, who had long served as cellarer in the monastery of Hirsau [Col. 0897C].

Esso died on the sixth day before the Kalends of January, shining with miracles, as Trithemius testifies, but the author does not state the year of his death.

The same author reports that monks were first placed in the church of Gundelfingen around this same time, but that they were later transferred to Hirsau, for reasons unknown to me, and that canons were substituted for them by Count Adelbert, the founder of the place.

At the request of the brothers living there and of the archbishop of the city, Abbot Hildebold was appointed over the monastery of Saint John of Magdeburg. Trithemius says that Hildebold spread monastic discipline throughout Saxony according to the model and constitutions of his holy teacher Wilhelmus.

### 18

The foundation of the monastery of Hasungen in Thuringia was also famous in the time of Abbot Wilhelmus [Col. 0897D].

It was founded by Siegfried, Archbishop of Mainz, who had withdrawn from his see because of the dispute between the Roman Pontiff and Emperor Henry. Siegfried chose this place because it was already famous for the frequent miracles occurring at the tomb of Saint Heimerad the priest, who had been buried there in 1019.

After the monastery had been completed and endowed, Siegfried obtained from blessed Wilhelmus thirteen monks from the Hirsau community. From among them he appointed Giselbert, a learned, prudent, and deeply religious man, as abbot.

For some time the monastery of Hasungen flourished under his rule. No fewer than seventy monks or conversi lived there, whom the devout abbot formed in regular discipline by word and example.

When disturbances grew stronger, however, Giselbert feared that his disciples might deviate from the right path through contact with the schismatics. He therefore returned with all of them to Hirsau. They were all kindly received by Wilhelmus and the other brothers and spent some time at Hirsau [Col. 0898A].

Later, the cell of Saint Gregory at Reichenbach was given to them for habitation; we have made further observations about it above, in no. 9.

Finally, blessed Wilhelmus appointed Giselbert abbot of the monastery of Reinhardsbrunn, or the Fountain of Reinhard, situated in the Thuringian forest. He also entrusted him with the care of the monastery of Erfurt, as we said above, until it was suitable for the monks to inhabit.

This concludes the account of the various colonies of monks led from the monastery of Hirsau under Abbot Wilhelmus into different regions of Germany. We must now speak of his more celebrated disciples, who brought distinction to the Church and to our order.

### 19

“The fame,” says Trithemius, “of the most holy man Wilhelmus, abbot, spread far and wide throughout the world. Many who were noble and wealthy in the secular life began to flock to him. Having despised all the possessions and pomps of the world, they undertook under his obedience to bear the Lord’s gentle yoke” [Col. 0898B].

Indeed, as Berthold says—a contemporary of Wilhelmus—in his *Chronicle* under the year 1083, speaking of the three monasteries of Saint Blaise in the Black Forest, Hirsau, and Schaffhausen, margraves and counts, as well as other noblemen admitted among the Hirsau brothers, considered it a delight to feed pigs and perform other such lowly tasks [the printed text reads *ministriis*, “services” or “tasks”] under Wilhelmus’s obedience.

Trithemius lists some of these men who were later elevated to ecclesiastical dignities.

First among them stands Saint Thiemo, formerly a monk of Hirsau, who was made Archbishop of Salzburg and eventually suffered martyrdom on a journey to Jerusalem, as we shall see in his *Life* in the following century.

Trithemius adds two men named Gebhard. The first, the brother of Duke Berthold, was elevated to the see of the city of Constance. He consecrated the new church of Hirsau and, having become a legate of the Apostolic See, endured many labors in defense of the Church.

The other, formerly prior of Hirsau, became abbot after the death of blessed Wilhelmus and was eventually ordained Bishop of Speyer [Col. 0898C].

Theogerus must also be counted among them. He was the father of many monasteries and later became Bishop of Metz; after his death he deserved a place among the saints. With God’s permission, we shall give his *Life* in the following century.

### 20

We have praised most of the abbots chosen from among Wilhelmus’s disciples when discussing the monasteries founded by him.

To them must be added Gotfrid, who succeeded Notger, the deceased abbot of Zwiefalten, after the death of blessed Wilhelmus. Trithemius says that Gotfrid departed this life “not without a reputation for holiness.”

The same author praises Erminold, a disciple of Wilhelmus and abbot of Lorsch. After resigning his dignity and returning to Hirsau, he eventually became the first abbot of Prüfening. Distinguished by many virtues, he earned the title of saint after his death. We shall also give his *Life* in its proper place in the following century.

### 21

Nor should the priors of Hirsau who flourished under Abbot Wilhelmus be omitted.

The first encountered in Trithemius is Adalbert, a man who, says Trithemius, was adorned with the ornament of every virtue, a listener to the paternal tradition in the holiness of his life, and its most devoted guardian and imitator [Col. 0898D]. Although weak in body, he advanced in mind and spiritual fervor stronger than many of the strongest . . . . Whoever did not become holier after seeing his manner of life was certainly never holy.

After his blessed departure from this life [the printed text reads *vi a*; evidently *vita*], the blessed abbot appointed Theoderic in his place. Theoderic was distinguished by wisdom and knowledge of the Scriptures, and was no less holy in the merit of his life than learned through his devotion to study.

When, as we were just saying, Theoderic had been made abbot of Petershausen, Wilhelmus appointed Otto, formerly cellarer, as prior. He was a man mature in age. Gebhard succeeded him; as we have already said, after the death of blessed Wilhelmus Gebhard was ordained abbot of Hirsau in his place.

Adalbert the count must also be counted among Wilhelmus’s more distinguished disciples. Moved by the holy manner of life of the blessed abbot and his disciples and led to a better way of living, he finally professed the monastic life and died a holy death.

We learn this not only from Trithemius but also from Berthold, the continuator of Hermann, who was writing in those regions at precisely this time. He writes as follows under the year 1099:

“Adalbert, count of pious memory, long devoted to the fidelity of Saint Peter against the schismatics, finally became a monk from a count and happily ended his life on the tenth day before the Kalends of October. He was honorably buried in the monastery which he had built from his own resources, in which he had received the monastic habit—namely, at Hirsau, while Lord Gebhard was presiding as abbot.”

### 22

Finally, Trithemius writes that in these times many illustrious and distinguished monks flourished in the monastery of Hirsau under the instruction of the most blessed Father Wilhelmus. Some were highly learned in every kind of writing; others were renowned for the merit of their holiness; and still others were perfected before God and human beings both in knowledge of the Scriptures and in the merit of their lives.

The earthly-detached manner of life of Wilhelmus’s disciples was so pronounced, says Udalricus in the preface to the *Cluniac Customs* [Col. 0899B], that they expected no other life than that which is heavenly and everlasting.

Saint Anselm himself admired this way of life when he saw it. For, if Trithemius is to be believed, Anselm came to Hirsau and spent fourteen days there, living among the brothers as one of them, conversing with them about the Holy Scriptures, the formation of regular conduct, and the love of God and the salvation of souls, and answering all the brothers’ questions.

Certainly, we learn from Anselm himself that he had long desired this. He concludes a letter written to blessed Wilhelmus as follows:

“If I were present before you and before your holy congregation, about which I hear many good things from many people in agreement, I would prostrate my whole body with a suppliant mind and ask you to grant me, in fraternal charity, a perpetual share in the good things that God works in your monastery.

“But since I cannot do this, I presume—not on my own merits but on your holiness—to ask that you seek this for me from those same sons of yours, not with a humbled body but with a gracious mind, and grant it together with them.

“Farewell.”

This letter is numbered 56 among the other letters of Anselm in Book I. Trithemius presents it in full, and indeed in an interpolated form, in both editions of the *Chronicle of Hirsau*. In those editions he inserts several details about Saint Anselm’s journey to Hirsau that are not found in other editions.

The same author is also mistaken when he writes that this letter was composed by Saint Anselm after he had become Archbishop of Canterbury, having known Wilhelmus at Rome. The falsity of this is established by the single fact that Anselm was not raised to the see of Canterbury until after Wilhelmus’s death.

23. It is not possible to report all the testimonies of authors written in praise of Wilhelm. That he was most closely attached to Saint Hugh, abbot of Cluny, will be clear from the Life below. Blessed Udalric praises both his humility and his charity, especially in [Col. 0899D] the preface to Book III of the *Customs of Cluny*, where he calls him the foremost lover of the whole religious life. His charity shone forth above all in receiving exiles who, during the vehement dispute between Pope Gregory and the Emperor Henry, were compelled to leave their own homes and fled to the monastery of Hirsau as to a safe harbor.

“Trithemius says that many good men fearing God—counts, barons, knights, nobles and commoners, clerics and laymen, rich and of moderate means—who wished to keep their souls undefiled by communion with the schismatics, abandoned their castles, houses, and churches and came to the monastery of Hirsau as to a certain city of refuge. Many of them, changing their clothing, became monks, while many others, remaining in their former dress, served God and the monks of the holy congregation until death.”

It is astonishing that, at the time when the other abbots and bishops were being driven out by the schismatics, no one ever dared to expel Wilhelm from the monastery [Col. 0900A], although not only did he himself and his followers remain obedient to the Apostolic See, but he also strengthened those who were wavering, recalled those who were straying, and finally received and nourished them all in his monastery. Such was the reputation of his holiness.

“For,” says Trithemius, “this holy Wilhelm, servant of God, could never be induced to consent even in the slightest degree to, or communicate with, the schismatics who were disturbing the Church of God. . . . This, finally, is Wilhelm, most holy abbot and servant of Christ, who in his own time labored to restore and reform in Germany the order of our holy father Benedict, which had almost collapsed and been disfigured by the arrogance of monks; and he brought more than a hundred monasteries, both through himself and through his followers, back to the former observance of regular discipline. . . . Finally, this Wilhelm, the thrice and four times most holy abbot of Hirsau, founded eight monasteries of our order in different provinces.”

Berthold’s continuator of Hermann also praises him at length [Col. 0900B] and lists several monasteries built or restored by him.

“Wilhelm,” he says, “abbot of Hirsau, of pious memory, most fervent in the cause of Saint Peter and most devoted to monastic religion, as the father of many monasteries, migrated to the Lord on the third day before the Nones of July [July 5]. He first raised the monastery of Hirsau wondrously, both in its buildings and in its regular disciplines, and secured its perpetual freedom by a privilege of the Apostolic See under Pope Gregory. He also built many other monasteries entirely from the foundations: two in the Black Forest, one of Saint George and the other of Saint Gregory; . . . another at Duplicem-Aquam [Double Water] near the Danube; another in the diocese of Würzburg, at a place called Camberg. He also established the monastery of Schaffhausen and that of Petershausen on the bank of the Rhine, which had long before been built, in regular disciplines. He likewise founded many other monasteries in various regions, both personally and through those subject to him, and instituted in regular disciplines those already built. And later:

“Above all, the study of monastic strictness prevailed in him; in it he burned so intensely that he seemed never to have had any other object of study. He was a man of wondrous holiness, holy simplicity, and most fervent charity—alive to God and crucified to the world. The Lord called him in a good old age to the eternal homeland, after he had served Him from his youth with unwearied labor in this pilgrimage.”

24. Wilhelm’s outward appearance most excellently represented the greatness of his inner spirit. Trithemius, as he says he had learned from ancient records, describes it in these words in both editions of the *Chronicle*:

“He was in every respect a man worthy of honor, whose bodily bearing itself demanded from those who looked upon him a certain reverence. He was tall in stature, bald on the front of his head, and had sparse hair elsewhere; his face was handsome and somewhat elongated, with a color mingling blue and white. The fingers of his hands were slender and of beautiful length, and his entire body [Col. 0900D] had been arranged in due proportion for virtue. His voice was deep and manly, of the kind which, with a certain natural adornment of words, ordinarily makes the best of orators. Hence he was highly effective in exhortation, so that, outstanding in the sweetness of his voice and in a certain authority of speech exercised with the greatest moderation, he seemed to hold the minds of his listeners in his power; whatever he wished to say, he could persuade his hearers of with astonishing ease and beauty. Skill in speaking commended nature in him, so that by easy persuasion he could attract whomever he wished through the sweetness of his speech,” and so forth.

25. Wilhelm produced several short works that earned him a place among ecclesiastical writers. Trithemius lists them in the older edition of the *Chronicle of Hirsau* as follows:

“He wrote on music, on the construction of the monochord, on the astrolabe and its construction, also on the construction of a clock, on the correction of the Psalter, and on the method of ecclesiastical computation.”

He repeats nearly the same list [Col. 0901A] in the other edition of the same *Chronicle* and in the *Catalogue of Illustrious Men*, adding in both places one book of letters and two books *On the Customs of Hirsau*, besides several other short works that had not come into his hands.

Peter Wagner, a monk of Saint Ulrich, as Charles Stengelius reports in his notes to the Life of Blessed Wilhelm, praises, in addition to all these works, a certain dictionary attributed to our Blessed Wilhelm in his compilation of illustrious men. In it, many things are collected concerning individual words; for that reason it was customarily called a book, or *Wilhelm on the Universe*.

It is not permissible, however, to omit what Berthold, a serious author and Wilhelm’s contemporary, says about the same blessed man’s short works. He writes of our Wilhelm:

“He left us many memorials of his natural ingenuity. For he devised a natural clock modeled on the celestial hemisphere. He showed by certain experiments how to determine the natural solstices or equinoxes and the state of the world. [Col. 0901B] One of his associates also took care to commit all these things to writing. He likewise resolved many questions concerning Computus by thoroughly tested arguments. He was highly skilled in music and elucidated many subtle points of that art unknown to the ancient teachers. He also corrected, with sufficient rational method, many errors detected in chants according to the rules of the art. In the quadrivium he seemed to surpass nearly all the ancients.”

Of all the works of the blessed abbot, scarcely anything survives except his books *On the Customs of Hirsau*, which are still found here and there in various libraries of monasteries of our order in Germany. Their prologue, edited from the Weingarten manuscript, is found in volume IV of the *Analecta of Antiquity*, p. 465. His book *On Music* is said once to have existed in the library of Saint Ulrich at Augsburg. Stengelius admits, however, that he searched for it in vain for a long time. It survives in the Villing manuscript together with other writers on the same subject.

26. The author of his Life himself testifies that Wilhelm died in the very year in which the basilica of his new monastery was dedicated [Col. 0901C]. Trithemius agrees with him, assigning both events to the year 1091.

Concerning the dedication [Col. 0902A] he writes:

“In the same year, 1091, on April 20, which was the eighth Sunday of the feast of the Lord’s Resurrection, the new church of the principal monastery mentioned above was solemnly consecrated, at the request of the most blessed abbot Wilhelm, by John, bishop of Speyer, in honor of our Lord Jesus Christ and his most blessed apostles Peter and Paul.”

That year Easter fell on April 13, and consequently its octave fell on April 20.

Concerning his death:

“Wilhelm happily rested in the Lord on the fourth day before the Nones of July [July 4], in the year 1091 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the fourteenth indiction, under the Emperor Henry IV and Pope Urban II, in the twenty-third year of his reign and the sixty-fifth year of Wilhelm’s age.”

These chronological markers agree very well with one another. In the new edition, Trithemius gives the thirty-fourth year of the Emperor Henry.

Berthold, the continuator of Hermann the Lame, treats our Wilhelm at length under this very year, 1091, likewise recording his death, but on the third day before the Nones of July [July 5]. Perhaps Wilhelm died during the night between July 4 and 5. Certainly the author of the Life himself, whom we judge preferable to any other authority, [Col. 0902B] writes that the blessed abbot died on the afternoon of the fourth day before the Nones of July [July 4].

Nevertheless, his memory is celebrated on July 5, the third day before the Nones of July, in the Benedictine calendars by Dorgain, Arnold Wion, and Hugh Menard in the *Benedictine Martyrology*, and by Gabriel Bucelinus in the *Menologium*. Ferrarius follows them in his *General Catalogue of the Saints Who Are Not in the Roman Martyrology*.

It is astonishing that a distinguished man, so devoted to the Apostolic See and so renowned for miracles before and after his death, has not yet been granted public sacred worship by official authority. German and Benedictine historians frequently discuss him. In his notes to Wilhelm’s Life, Stengelius presents an old hymn in Wilhelm’s honor, transcribed from a manuscript of the Viennese monastery of the Blessed Virgin at the Scots. It seemed appropriate to publish it after the Life, together with the blessed man’s epitaph, since that hymn appears to suggest that a feast of Blessed Wilhelm was at some time publicly [Col. 0902C] celebrated.

# The Life Begins

[Col. 0901]

[Col. 0901C] **1.** The most reverend abbot Wilhelm, sprung from the lineage of the Bavarians and born of devout parents, grew in the holy disposition of his mind under the inspiration of Christ’s grace, and this made him beloved by all. While still a boy, he was offered to God by those honorable parents in the monastery of Saint Emmeram the Martyr [Note: [Col. 0901D] Trithemius adds that at that time Saint Rambold was abbot of the monastery of Saint Emmeram. But he is mistaken, for Rambold died in the first year of this century, as we saw in his Life.]. Like a prudent bee, he gathered the flowers of virtue from the divine Scriptures and from the examples of spiritual elders and stored them in the hive of his heart.

Although the vigor of monastic religion had grown somewhat lukewarm in that monastery, he nevertheless continually advanced in the same religious life through the grace of God. Therefore he was greatly feared by the careless and negligent, but was dearly loved by the good and devout because of the sincerity and purity of his life [Col. 0901D].

Finally, with divine mercy accompanying him, he possessed such excellence of intellect that, together with the distinction of honorable conduct, he also excelled in the study of various arts, concerning which he left us many memorials of his natural ingenuity. For he devised a natural clock modeled on the celestial hemisphere; he showed by certain experiments how to determine the natural solstices or equinoxes and the state of the world; and he also took care to commit all these things to writing. He likewise resolved many questions concerning Computus by thoroughly tested arguments. He was highly skilled in music and elucidated many subtle points of that art unknown to the ancient teachers. He also corrected, with sufficient rational method, many errors detected in chants according to the rules of the art. In the quadrivium [Note: [Col. 0902D] The writers of his age called the four later arts among those called liberal arts the *quadrivium*; the three earlier ones they called the *trivium*. Berthold reproduces this entire passage concerning Wilhelm’s works in his *Chronicle*.], he seemed to surpass nearly all the ancients [Col. 0902C].

**2.** Desiring only to please God, and having undertaken to crucify his flesh with its vices and desires (Gal. 5:24), he disciplined his body with fasts, vigils, and even the harshness of a hair shirt [Col. 0902D]. Thus, established in faith, strengthened by hope, rooted and grounded in charity, and adorned with every moral excellence, [Col. 0903A] by the providence of almighty God he was appointed as administrator of the monastery of Hirsau for the consolation of many.

At length, when the brothers serving God in that monastery had been left without a superior, delighted by the sweetness of his reputation, they sent respectable envoys to summon him. But after learning the circumstances, he did not become elated with pride. Rather, devoting himself to fasts and prayers and joining spiritual men to himself, he resolved that the Lord’s will should be sought in this matter.

At last, permission having been obtained, although all good men congratulated him on his elevation to the position of honor, they nevertheless grieved that they would be deprived of the exceedingly sweet consolation of his companionship and conversation. He, however, seeking not his own interests but [Col. 0903B] those of the Lord (Phil. 2:21), declared that he would not agree to the election in any way unless the monastery itself were first restored to complete freedom.

Because Count Adelbert, the advocate of the place, had reduced this monastery to his own jurisdiction together with his relatives [Note: [Col. 0903D] We discussed the restoration of the monastery of Hirsau and Count Adelbert in the Eulogy of Frederick V, above, under the year 1070.] and had almost destroyed it, when he learned of the man of God’s steadfastness and greatness of spirit, he pretended that he would obey him in everything. For he went with the blessed man to the royal court and, with secular cunning, deceitfully drew up a charter [*chirographum*], while Wilhelm, in his dove-like simplicity, suspected nothing sinister. Adelbert obtained the charter’s confirmation with the royal seal.

When the feast of the Lord’s Ascension arrived, which that year fell on the fourth day before the Nones of June [June 2] (see *Observations*, no. 2), a multitude of clergy and laity was convened. By the common vote of all, this venerable elected man was praised and, amid an immense outpouring of tears, installed in the abbatial seat [Col. 0903C].

Having assumed this dignity, he began to burn ever more intensely with the fervor of heavenly study, in proportion as he recognized that he had been placed before the others as an example. He directed his keen attention above all toward the observance of monastic religion. He was energetic in exhorting and severe in correcting. Envious of no one, he was rich in charity and generous in liberality. His affability was sweet yet dignified, and through it he gently entered human hearts. He regarded each person’s business as though it were his own, cherished strangers and the poor with paternal affection, and very often, after removing his own shirt and other garments, covered the limbs of the unfortunate [Col. 0903D].

**3.** Amid these exercises of virtue, he was tested rather than assaulted by a certain temptation; the trial proved beneficial to him as a crown and to the monastery of Hirsau as a source of stability and defense.

For he learned, through the secret disclosure of the aforementioned count’s wife, that the charter of freedom had been deceitfully drawn up and that, under the pretext of the said freedom, nothing had been reduced from the former violence and unjust subjection of the Hirsau cloister; rather, these had been increased and strengthened.

Disturbed to some extent by this situation because of the state of the place, [Col. 0904A] he appealed to the Lord with constant prayers and tears, asking that He free from the yoke of earthly power the place which Wilhelm had undertaken to govern for His love.

And so the merciful Lord, who, according to the Psalmist’s words, is near to all who call upon Him in truth (Ps. 144:18), suddenly surrounded that same count with such adversity that he almost despaired of being able to find any means of escape. Thus constrained, he sought with complete devotion the counsel and help of spiritual men.

They told him that he would not escape such dangers in any other way unless he restored in complete faith to freedom the place of Hirsau, which he had unjustly possessed. Accepting their counsel, he renounced in complete faith every right of ownership over that place and had a charter drawn up with the greatest care, according to the advice of those who feared God [Col. 0904B], while the earlier charter was entirely erased and cast aside.

After the venerable Father Wilhelm had composed the new charter with the utmost diligence through his own labor and effort, he himself presented it to King Henry to be confirmed with the royal seal.

**4.** When this had been completed according to his desire, he also decided to visit the Apostolic See and obtain for the monastery of Hirsau a privilege according to the provisions of the canons. He then set out and reached Rome on a prosperous journey.

There, Lord Gregory of blessed memory, the Apostolic Lord, received him kindly. After learning the reasons for which he had come, Gregory most willingly granted what was appropriate. For he gave him a privilege fully endowed with apostolic authority and, for the protection of the monastery of Hirsau, placed in the shrine of Saint Peter one charter received from him [Col. 0904C].

After remaining there for some time, Wilhelm was struck by a very serious illness. He was oppressed by a horrible swelling of the abdomen, so severely that he could move neither foot. When he had suffered from this illness for a long time and even the most skilled physicians despaired of his recovery, one day he ordered himself to be carried to the altar of Saint Mary Ever-Virgin. Leaning his afflicted abdomen against the altar, he earnestly begged in his inmost prayers for a remedy from the most merciful Mother of God.

By the grace of God, through the love of His sweetest Mother, he obtained such hope and faith that, suddenly and contrary to everyone’s expectation, he began to recover, to take nourishment, and, after not much time had passed, returned to his own place amid everyone’s rejoicing.

**5.** At that time the Catholic Church was being torn apart by a pitiable and detestable schism [Note: [Col. 0904D] A letter of Gregory VII concerning this matter to A., bishop of Padua, and to our Wilhelm is extant; it is the second letter of Book IX.], by enemies of Christian unity.

But because this man, truly worthy of God, had been wholly inflamed by the fire of divine love and burned with zeal for souls, he also encouraged everyone by salutary counsel to hold fast to and preserve the unity of the Church. And because he pursued this matter with a simple and pure eye, whatever he did pleased the minds of all religious people; whatever he said delighted the hearts of all good men with the deepest affection of love.

With dove-like simplicity, there flourished in him so much serpent-like prudence that he seemed, in the judgment of the prudent of this world, to surpass everyone in wisdom, while the wise according to God honored him greatly for the innocence of his pure mind [Col. 0905A].

**6.** He overflowed with such a benign abundance of charity that he despised no one who earnestly desired to devote himself completely to divine service on account of his poverty, and rejected no one because of lack of learning.

He urged nobles and commoners, rich and poor, men and women, to despise the world, and by word and example kindled each person to love the heavenly life. He distributed much to guests and much to the poor; yet he did not neglect the care of those entrusted to him, but with paternal solicitude and great charitable affection provided everyone with what was necessary.

If any shortage of household resources arose, he made it not only bearable but welcome to himself and his people by gentle yet manly admonition, asserting that this was a testing of Christ’s beloved and that, if patience accompanied by thanksgiving and frequent prayer were present, [Col. 0905B] manifest consolation from God would undoubtedly soon come.

This was often made clear by evident signs, since in every difficulty the Lord deigned to open the door of His mercy to him when he knocked with faith and prayers.

When reports of his praiseworthy actions spread everywhere, the faithful flocked to him as to the good fragrance of Christ: some wishing to make use of his most salutary counsels, others commending themselves to his prayers, and many choosing his instruction after casting off the burden of the secular life.

**7.** [Col. 0905C] Out of humility, he did not wish to be clothed for the ministry of the divine office in vestments decorated with gold embroidery or woven with any precious metal. He also detested the kissing of the abbot’s hands and knees and would have abolished such a custom entirely if the elders had not scarcely compelled him to accept this reverence from them.

Wherever he followed the community of brothers going before him, he watched them carefully, groaning and weeping, and lifting his eyes and heart to heaven, prayed for them with the greatest attention.

If more carefully prepared food was offered to him at table, he signaled to the server that it should be set before everyone alike. If the server agreed, he tasted a little of it; otherwise, he immediately distributed it to the weaker brothers.

He despised the variety of delicacies and banquets that serve as fuel for luxury and was content with small and ordinary fare. Whenever necessity required him to go somewhere, he took no pleasure in a proud horse but rode a mare or the back of a worthless donkey [Col. 0905D].

He loathed bright clothing and costly wool, especially sleeves or cowls, which he even cut off under threat of excommunication. He forbade, with the harshest condemnation, utensils and other objects to be decorated with excessive and pompous ornament.

Whenever an obedientiary or anyone else who was tempted or weighed down by sadness came to him, he did not despise or reject the afflicted person. Rather, by soothing and flattering words of consolation, he softened the person’s grief and sent him away joyful and glad.

For he was a burning and shining lamp (John 5:35), hidden not under a bushel but set upon a lampstand (Matt. 5:15), and therefore he strove to become for everyone an example of good living [Col. 0906A].

**8.** Amid these and his other virtues, no speech can fully explain how powerful he was in sincere and perfect faith. Clothed in this virtue as in a breastplate, he overcame every adversity with a manly spirit. More than once he undertook things difficult and nearly impossible for many and, with the Lord’s help, brought them to a successful conclusion.

To mention briefly one of many examples: one day, while the holy Father was discussing household affairs with the brothers who managed external matters, they announced among other things that, because of a certain unavoidable necessity, five pounds of silver were required.

Since he had neither that amount immediately at hand nor any means by which they could acquire it even through an approved loan, and since the pressing necessity required the money to be paid without delay [Col. 0906B], they were so distressed that they did not know how to manage the matter.

But the pious Father, trusting in the Lord, sought to encourage their faintheartedness with words of consolation, saying that one must in no way distrust God’s mercy. They, however, receiving his consolation rather coolly because of their anxiety and insisting that they were distressed not for themselves but because of the common loss, he rose from the gathering.

While they awaited his return, he went outside and implored the Lord’s help. Immediately the kindly Lord came to the aid of His faithful servant. Suddenly an unknown man arrived and gave him the entire amount of money.

He soon returned, brought out five pounds of silver from his hand, and, charitably reproving the brothers, said: “Here is the money over which you became fainthearted. Learn, then, never again to despair of the manifold goodness of almighty God” [Col. 0906C].

**9.** Again, one day at dawn the Father beloved of God set out from the monastery and soon encountered a poor man with his wife and eleven small children, earnestly begging for his alms.

The brothers accompanying him had brought from the storeroom only a few loaves, [Col. 0906D] scarcely sufficient for a few people’s single meal, since they were going to dine in a certain meadow.

The man of God therefore invited the poor man, his wife, and his children to dinner. When they had all sat down, a considerable crowd of horsemen, common people, and poor persons suddenly arrived.

The companions of the blessed man were disconcerted and at the same time covered with embarrassment because of the small amount of food. But the man full of God said to them with a cheerful face:

“The five loaves with which the Lord fed five thousand people, as long as they remained whole, were neither multiplied nor did anyone eat from them. But when they were broken by the Lord, then they were multiplied, and more people were fed from them” (Luke 9:16–17).

As he said this, he distributed the small amount of food to the crowd with ready spirit and generous hand. Through his faith and merits, God wondrously multiplied it sufficiently for everyone. Although many marveled at his faith and generosity, all were abundantly fed from the little food.

When everyone had returned home joyfully, the man dear to God kept the aforementioned poor man with his wife and children and, providing them for a long time with what was necessary for their sustenance, supported them until the harvest of the new crops [Col. 0907A].

**10.** On another occasion, while crossing a bridge over the river called the Nagold, he encountered a poor man who had lain for many years in the almonry and could not move his feet except by supporting himself beneath the arms with two staffs.

When the venerable Father met this same poor man in the middle of the bridge, he forcibly took away one of his staffs and, proceeding a little farther with it, stood firm and commanded the needy man to come to him.

The man replied that he could not walk without the support of the other staff. The elder answered: “Certainly, I shall not leave this place until you come to me.”

The poor man obeyed his command and, dragging himself forward step by step with whatever effort he could manage, came to him. Then, abandoning all support, he walked with firm feet, sound and unharmed in his entire body [Col. 0907B].

**11.** Nor do we consider this worthy of being concealed in silence, for we saw and observed it with our own eyes.

A canon of the Church of Strasbourg [Note: [Col. 0907D] This was Gebhard, if Trithemius is to be believed; he later succeeded Blessed Wilhelm and eventually became bishop of Speyer, concerning whom Trithemius gives further information.], born of very noble parents, came to the monastery of the man of God. He was devoutly received and lived there even more devoutly.

Soon, at the beginning of his conversion, he was paralyzed throughout his body, so that, apart from his tongue, no limb remained joined to its proper function. This man possessed a remarkably keen and steadfast intellect, together with distinction in knowledge and eloquence. It was therefore necessary that he be restrained by the Lord’s kindly scourge, [Col. 0907C] lest, since the human mind is always inclined to evil, he should be lifted up by some wind of arrogance and then fall into an immense precipice.

He suffered from this illness for more than a year, so that he could not bring his hand to his mouth or turn from one side to the other without the assistance of others; as stated above, he was deprived of the use of all his limbs.

The time for showing him mercy had now come. The Lord was already looking down from on high, and behold, his bodily strength began to return. He was able to sit for eating and reading and to move about by crawling, but the use of his hands was entirely denied him, because this was being reserved for the greater glory of the Lord.

One day Lord Wilhelm entered his cell to visit him and encouraged him to obtain through prayer from the Lord the use of his right hand [Col. 0907D]. The man refused with the greatest horror, declaring that he considered bodily health altogether unimportant.

But the pious Father, filled entirely with compassion and mercy, took hold of his hand, blessed it, and kissed it. He then entered the chapel of Saint Mary, Mother of God and Ever-Virgin. There he prostrated himself for a little while in prayer, visited the sick man again, and found that his right hand had been restored [Col. 0908A].

A few days later, the wife of his brother came to the monastery to visit both it and him. He was carried to her in a sedan chair. During their conversation, which combined spiritual edification and friendly familiarity, mention was made of his healed right hand.

With feminine affection she kissed it, but immediately it returned to its former rigidity. As soon as he felt this, he bade her farewell, concealed his misfortune, and withdrew to his cell, grieving somewhat over what had happened.

The man of God immediately followed him and, taught by the Lord’s spirit what had occurred, asked the cause of his sadness. The man revealed it with a sufficiently simple and humble confession.

The man full of God spoke words of consolation to him, blessed the hand he had taken, and restored it to its former health.

**12.** At another time, he visited the cell of certain brothers in the lower hermitage who, with his permission, lived there in something like the manner of hermits. He had announced his arrival to them on the previous day.

They were therefore [Col. 0908B] delighted beyond what can be believed, as being judged worthy of a visit from their most loving Father, almost like a visit from an angel of God. They prepared everything necessary for so great a Father and everything suitable for those accompanying him.

The place was well suited to catching fish, and a somewhat younger man living among them was practiced in this kind of work. The brothers earnestly begged him to serve both them and the Father and to devote all his skill to catching fish.

He praised their request and did what he could, but the undertaking made no progress. For although he labored throughout the night and accomplished absolutely nothing according to his wish, overcome at once by his promise and by shame, he presumed to steal a fish from his companions. In the morning he brought the brothers a trout of unusual size and, leaving them in no small amazement, departed [Col. 0908C].

Among the brothers there was one of superior and more perceptive intellect. Wondering at the fish’s extraordinary size, he began to investigate it more carefully. At first, as people of this sort commonly do, the fisherman denied and abhorred the theft with the greatest indignation. But when he was proved guilty by gentle words, by reason, and by the facts themselves, he simply confessed his fault.

Then one would have seen those brothers deeply saddened and placed in a quandary, because the theft had made the fish abominable and no other dish was readily available to be set before the Father when he arrived.

Then, with charity covering the matter, they decided by common agreement to serve the fish to the Father and resolved privately to wipe out that offense among themselves through fasts and prayers. They transgressed the boundary of justice because they had not maintained due measure in their affection [Col. 0908D].

The day was already growing late when the desired Father arrived. They went out to meet him, received him, and led him to prayer. Then the beloved Father disclosed to his dearest sons that he was suffering from an unusual hunger and urged them to set before him quickly whatever cooked food they had.

They reclined at table, and that fish was served. They watched with the greatest attention to see what the man full of God would do.

The man was instructed inwardly by God, his host. Although, as stated above, he was suffering from no small hunger, he nevertheless rejected with astonishing loathing the dish placed before him and, tasting nothing at all, seemed carried beyond himself [Col. 0909A].

None of the disciples, visitors, or residents dared ask about the man’s sudden change. The visitors were utterly astonished, while the inhabitants were filled with the greatest fear.

The next day, with the greatest devotion and contrition of heart, they confessed their fault. The most merciful Father received them kindly and warned them, under a strict threat, never again to presume to do anything of this kind.

**13.** At the same time, the man of God sent from the monastery one brother named Benno, together with certain peasants hired for wages, to bring eleven wagonloads of wine by cart. A citizen of Mainz named Wignandus had sent this wine to the people of Hirsau as an act of charity.

While they were traveling with the wine, robbers [Col. 0909B] attacked them at night and used force against them to take their goods. But, with God protecting them, they escaped unharmed with their possessions, except that the right arm of the aforementioned brother was so badly weakened by the blows of his attackers that he had to bind it to his neck with bandages and despaired of ever regaining its use.

After this, another misfortune befell them. One of the barrels full of wine, which had been specially designated for almsgiving, fell into a ditch when the wagon tilted, and nearly all the wine flowed out into the ditch.

After the peasants had drained it and the empty barrel had been lifted back onto the wagon, those who had suffered the loss continued the journey in great sadness.

The aforementioned brother, however, left his companions and hurried ahead to the monastery. He tearfully reported to the man of God the injury to his arm and the loss of the wine [Col. 0909C].

He answered him cheerfully and steadfastly in the words of blessed Job: “The Lord gave, the Lord has taken away; as it has pleased the Lord, so it has happened. Blessed be the name of the Lord” (Job 1:24).

Then, sealing his arm with a blessing, he restored it to its former health.

Afterward he ordered him to inspect carefully, with the lids removed, all the barrels of wine that had been brought and to give entirely to the poor whichever one he found fuller than the others.

When the brother quickly fulfilled the order, all who were present saw it and were astonished and rejoiced together: the barrel that had previously been empty was, as we believe, so overflowing with wine through the merits of the man of God that none of the others could be found so full.

When the aforementioned brother joyfully and exultantly reported this to the man of God, he immediately received the command to reveal it to no one. Nevertheless, it was spread everywhere by the others who had been present.

As for the peasants, who had first been willing voluntarily to pay one pound of silver for the wine they had lost through their negligence, Wilhelm ordered that one solidus be added to the agreed wage for their labor. He had them generously supplied with food and drink and sent them joyfully back home [Col. 0909D].

### 14.

[Col. 0910A]

While the holy man was staying at a village called Wilc, the aforementioned brother Benno, who was administrator of the monastery’s affairs there, offered him a few little fish at mealtime, saying that, on account of his arrival, he had labored long and hard at fishing, but had been able to catch nothing more than these. The holy man immediately ordered him to return to the pool for the sake of fishing and not to distrust God’s mercy. When Benno hastened to carry this out, he cast his net into the water and, at the word of the man of God, immediately caught eight very large pike. With them still wrapped in the linen of the net, he returned to the man of God. Then the most kindly Father ordered all the poor who could be found in that village to be invited to dinner, and the fish to be prepared and set before them for their meal.

### 15.

Again, one day, when the man of God was ordering the almoner to prepare provisions for the poor more generously than usual, he heard from him that very little grain remained for making bread. He ordered him to inspect more carefully how much grain was left. The almoner opened the chest, examined it carefully with another brother, measured it, and found scarcely one modius; he reported the truth to the man of God. But when morning came and the almoner opened the same chest in order to carry out the Father’s instructions, he found it filled to the top with grain, by a manifest act of divine power proclaiming the faith and merits of His faithful servant. The chest was so large that it normally held twenty modii. Since the holy man was always diligent and intent on fulfilling God’s will in all things and on providing for his neighbors what was [more] beneficial than what was beneficial for himself, the merciful and just Lord therefore came graciously and effectively to the aid of his devout petition in every need and difficulty.  
[Col. 0910B–C]

### 16.

Having recalled some of the matters concerning the holy man that pertain to miracles, we must now, as evidence of such great faith and holiness, relate other things about him—not so much marvelous as pleasant and useful to hear, and possible for human weakness to imitate. For we are not commanded to imitate the signs and wonders of God’s saints, but the practice of good works. As Scripture of sacred authority testifies: “Mercy, compassion for the wretched, and zeal for souls please God more than sacrifices, and knowledge of God more than holocausts” (Hosea 6:6).

Thus this friend of God, continually devoted to works of mercy, as has often been said, one day received from the monastery called Hasunga more than seventy brothers who had fled to him and were seeking his salutary counsel and trustworthy consolation. For the bishop of Mainz, elected and ordained by the schismatics—since that monastery was subject by right of ownership to the Church of Mainz—was trying by threats, persuasion, and blandishments to bring those same brothers under his authority and contaminate them through participation in illicit communion. They, on the contrary, steadfastly preserving their faith in the unity of the Church, spurned the flatterer as though they were deaf to him and, according to the counsel and command of the devout Father William, abandoned everything and betook themselves to him.

This happened around the month of August, before the harvest of the new crops. Although in that year and the following one grain was purchased for money for the most part and supplied for the brothers’ daily sustenance, William, nevertheless placing great confidence in God and glorifying the Lord for their arrival, ordered the customary quantity of bread to be increased as though all the storehouses were full of grain, saying: “Since the Lord has increased the number of His servants, we too must increase their allowance.” After keeping those brothers with him for some time and showing them every kindness, he later granted them the cell of Saint Gregory, with everything belonging to it, for as long as they wished.  
[Col. 0910C–0911B]

[Note: Concerning this monastery and the others mentioned here and below in no. 22, we have said more in the preliminary observations.]

[Note: Here the bishop seems to have been Wetzilo, successor of Siegfried, who, together with the legates of the pseudo-pope Clement, presided over the council held at Mainz in 1085 against Gregory VII. William had been summoned to that council but refused to attend.]

### 17.

At another time he was traveling toward a certain cell which he had built beside the Danube at the request of a certain count. He had already begun to approach it when, behold, he caught sight of a little hut on the edge of the forests. Taking one of his companions with him while the others continued along the road, he did not delay in making his way there.

When he came to the little house, he found a very poor woman. He entered, forgot his dignity and his customary severity, sat beside the fire, and ordered her to sit down. Then, amid words of sacred instruction, he looked around and asked her how she and her husband lived, since they possessed nothing in the house from which they could obtain the necessities of temporal life. She confessed that nothing remained to her except a wretched existence: they lived on bread and water, and could scarcely obtain even this through the daily labor of their hands.

Meanwhile her husband returned from the field. William asked them whether they knew the Catholic faith, without which no one can attain eternal life. They frankly confessed that they had no idea at all what faith was. Then he sighed more deeply and, from the depths of his heart, sympathized with their twofold poverty:

“What wonder,” he said, “if you appear poor in outward things, when inwardly—for it is pitiful to say so—you are empty of God, who abundantly provides all things for us to enjoy?”

After this he briefly explained the faith to them, as far as they were able to understand it, and, having instructed them for the moment, ordered them to follow him to the same cell. They came the next day, and he received them kindly, kept them with kindness for some time, and greatly relieved their necessities. Thus it came about that he both filled the poverty of their minds with the word of sacred instruction and generously alleviated their bodily want.  
[Col. 0911B–D]

### 18.

When he was traveling through the territory of Bavaria in winter, he encountered two poor men who asked him for clothing as protection against the harshness of the cold. Immediately remembering Saint Martin, who gave half of his cloak to a shivering poor man, William withdrew with one servant from the other travelers. He divided in two the cloak that was customarily spread beneath him both when he was riding and when he slept, and gave one half to each of the poor men so that they might protect themselves from the cold.  
[Col. 0911D–0912A]

### 19.

I shall relate something about the blessed man that bears upon the proof and admiration of the purity and simplicity of his spirit, and upon the detestation and condemnation of the vanity of many who bore his name.

A certain abbot was devoted to costly clothing, beyond what was fitting for such a person and so lofty a vocation. The man of God loved him for the many other good qualities granted him by God, but in this matter, out of zeal for the Lord, he often rebuked him sharply, though with little effect.

On one occasion, as though it were a blessing, this same abbot offered William a costly bed covering and asked him to accept it as a memorial of their mutual affection. The man filled with God accepted it with great simplicity and paid no attention to the duplicity of the giver. The giver intended by this somewhat to conceal his own vanity in his devotion to expensive clothing: namely, if a man so praiseworthy and so perfect in every monastic profession used such a thing, his own similar practice would not be noticed so much. For that abbot had formerly professed under the man of God and had been advanced by him to such an honor.

The man of God used the bed covering for only one night. The next day, a certain brother more devoted than the others to serving him secretly approached him and warned him that he had been deceived. On hearing this, incredible though it may seem, William was terrified and horrified at what he had done, and immediately divided the ill-received bed covering among ten poor people as assistance.

Among his other virtues, this beloved servant of the Lord possessed a quality worthy of every praise: whatever good advice he heard from anyone in the way of correction, he received with complete devotion as though it had been sent from heaven. I am compelled to mourn the lofty arrogance and singular pride of many who bore his name. This man, a mirror of virtues and of every form of goodness, chose correction from every person and honored the truth from whomever he heard it.  
[Col. 0912A–C]

### 20.

He possessed compassion so naturally and intensely that he showed it not only toward human beings but also toward brute animals. Thus, one winter, when an unusually severe cold descended because of an abundance of snow, the same Father, moved by the bowels of piety, summoned the provost and said to him in a plaintive voice:

“The birds are perishing from cold and hunger. Take bundles of oats and thrust them around the hedges, so that they may find something on which to feed.”

The other replied: “Lord, we have run out of bundles of oats.”

“Do you have,” he asked, “bundles of rye or wheat?”

“I do,” he replied.

Then the devout Father said: “Very well. Sell those and buy bundles of oats.”

The other obeyed the order and instructed his assistant to go out to the farm in the morning and carry out the assigned task. That very night, when he was to go on the following morning, the Lord’s grace rewarding the kindness of His servant, the severity of the frost was softened by a mild temperature.

William humbly visited the poor in the almonry, and peasants lying ill in the villages; he comforted them with devout consolations and, finally, committed the dead to burial with careful attention. He did not disdain to receive any of those who suffered from insanity of mind. Either he recited psalms and blessings over them with the entire community of the brothers, or, with certain brothers, he performed what was appropriate to such a matter. With the Lord’s mercy following, they returned home rejoicing in soundness of mind and body.  
[Col. 0912C–0913A]

### 21.

The monastic life, which had almost grown cold in the German provinces among those who merely professed the religious habit, began through the zeal of this blessed Father to grow warm again and be restored. Not only did the monastic order prosper through his emulation, but each rank of the ecclesiastical order was instructed by his example.

He instructed monks in humility, charity, fervor, and religion; he advanced bishops, priests, and clergy of every kind through teaching and authority; he taught laypeople conversion and submission; he formed virgins, widows, and women in purity and chastity; and by word and deed he dissuaded Christ’s poor and pilgrims from being content with little, from holding the world beneath their feet, and from all its glory. All the faithful of Christ fled to him as to a mother’s breast, and through him made great progress in God.  
[Col. 0913A–B]

### 22.

At last I shall come to relate what among all his works was preeminent and would benefit many souls to be saved through the coenobitic life until the end of the age. For he was exceedingly diligent in founding new monasteries and restoring old ones.

In the end he built seven monasteries from their foundations, both personally and through his disciples, in various places. The first was the cell of Saint Gregory, which properly belongs to Hirsau. The second was that of Saint George the Martyr; both were in the Black Forest. The third was in Bavaria, in honor of Saint Martin. The fourth was in Thuringia, called Erphefurch [Erphord]. The fifth was at Duplicis Aqua, in honor of Saint Mary. The sixth was in the village of Wilheim, later transferred to Mount Saint Peter. The seventh was in the province of the Charentines.

He also restored three others, namely Schaffhausen, Petershausen, and the monastery of Camberg, which were almost entirely destroyed.

In governing these, he faced this considerable difficulty amid his daily concerns: finding within the community of brothers persons who were useful and suitable for winning souls. For, according to the Lord’s saying, “The harvest indeed is plentiful, but the laborers are few,” while those who are to preside over others must be proved both in deed and in word and must be instructed no less in secular than in spiritual knowledge.

But because very few are found who excel in both, there are nevertheless many who possess one without the other: either a good life without knowledge or eloquence in teaching, or the word of teaching without a religious way of life. That wise architect took pains to advance them, wherever they appeared, as squared stones in the spiritual building—those whom he knew to live commendably with polished manners, even if they lacked some of the other necessities. In this he followed the memorable deed of Pope Gregory VII.

The clergy and people of a certain church presented two elected men for the episcopate and asked that either one of the two be ordained as their bishop. But the pope hesitated over which of the two he should prefer, knowing that one was a good teacher but not religious, while the other was religious but lacked the necessary learning. Through the prayers of a certain servant of God he obtained a divine revelation of the matter in this way.

That spiritual man, when the pope had vigilantly entrusted this matter to him and he had earnestly pleaded that God’s will be revealed to him through the intercession of Saint Mary, God’s Mother, saw the blessed Virgin Mary appear to him in a vision. She showed him two rings, one of which seemed to be pure gold and the other a translucent gem. When he asked her which of the two he should choose, she replied: “The gem.”

When he awoke, he related his vision to the pope, still uncertain what the gold or the gem signified in the case under discussion. Immediately the pope, who possessed a discerning intellect, said:

“There is no doubt that, as sacred speech testifies, wisdom is signified by gold, while by the gem is signified the simple and pure life of a human being. Therefore, by the judgment of the most chaste Mother of God and ever-virgin Mary, the man who lives chastely, justly, and devoutly, even if he lacks the gold of wisdom or eloquence, deserves to preside over the people as an example of good living; for although his tongue is silent, his life teaches. In such an election the decrees of the canons must be observed with the utmost care, and for the governance of souls not just any popular persons, but only regular persons, must always be advanced.”  
[Col. 0913B–0914B]

### 23.

Instructed, therefore, by this example, the faithful and prudent servant of the Lord appointed religious monks together with lay conversi in some of the aforesaid monasteries, setting abbots over some and priors over others.

Indeed, the gracious Father, burning with zeal for souls, was the first to institute that monks should employ the faithful ministry of lay conversi in administering external affairs, and conversely that these laymen should receive from the monks what pertained to the care of souls and, as far as they were able, imitate their cloistered discipline outside the cloister in correcting their conduct. It is worthwhile to recall something about their way of life, which the aforementioned Father organized by God’s inspiration, since we are certain that many can benefit from it both in the present and in the future.

At the nocturnal vigils all assemble in the church, although, because of the labor of the work assigned to them during the day, Matins is sung briefly. Afterwards those who wish return to their beds; the others remain in the church until the monks have finished the nocturnal office.

At first light they hear Mass; then they assemble in the chapter house. There they ask pardon for various offenses and receive appropriate discipline from the Master. When this has been completed, and, for those who need it, confession of sins has followed, each one turns to the work assigned to him.

For each of them has been assigned particular duties to be carried out within or outside the cell, which they handle and administer as faithfully, honestly, and diligently as though they had been entrusted with them by God. They possess nothing as their own; rather, as it is written in the Acts of the Apostles, “All things are held in common, and distributed to each according as he has need” (Acts 4:32).

In conducting business they avoid not only quarrels and disputes but also idle speech. They obey their superiors, and without their permission they do not even travel any considerable distance outside the cell. They receive Communion every Sunday, so that half of them reverently receive the body and blood of the Lord on one Sunday, and the other half on the next; on the principal feasts, however, they all receive together.

Anyone who is going to travel receives Communion that same day, provided he does not expect to return before the following Sunday. On returning from a journey, they ask pardon for offenses committed on the way.

In serving in the kitchen and preparing food both for themselves and for the monks and guests, they carry out their weeks in turn. They eat together, serving food to one another.

They do not come to the church for the daytime hours except those who are free to do so. At Compline, as at the nocturnal office, all, or almost all, are present. Afterwards they return silently to their beds.

For the observance of this spiritual life, the holy Father William built a suitable dwelling at the same place, Hirsau: namely, a new monastery in honor of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul and of Saint Aurelius the Confessor, on the southern side, through the hands of those serving under his obedience. It was completed within nine years and dedicated in the tenth.

[Note: This new church was dedicated by John, bishop of Speyer, in the year 1091, on April 20, that is, on the octave of the Lord’s Resurrection. On the following day the same bishop consecrated the chapel of Blessed Mary behind the chapter house.]

Finally, before the church itself was dedicated, he filled it all around with poor people, from the upper part down to the doors; after the doors had been closed, he himself ministered to them. At that time and thereafter, until his death, he distributed provisions to the needy more generously than usual.  
[Col. 0914C–0915C]

### 24.

After the aforesaid dedication he lived for nine weeks. When the feast of the apostles Peter and Paul was already approaching, illness seized him. Although weak, he attended the nocturnal vigils and the daytime ministry, and on the following day celebrated a private Mass at the principal altar.

During the next night, when he was unable to rise because of his bodily suffering, he received consolation from God through a vision. He was told that Saints Peter and Paul were present and ready to help him.

At dawn, when he could scarcely move his feet, he ordered himself to be carried to the oratory and prepared for the celebration of Mass. Supported between the hands of attendants on either side, he offered the sacrifice of the living victim upon the altar of the apostles Peter and Paul. As though he were about to depart to the Lord, he sang on their feast the words of Saint Paul that he was already uttering as his dissolution approached and that also fitted his own situation perfectly:

“I know whom I have believed, and I am certain that the just Judge is able to guard my deposit until that day” (2 Timothy 1:12).

This was his last celebration of Mass.  
[Col. 0915C–0916A]

On the fourth day he came to the chapter house to see and admonish the brothers. Whatever he had previously taught them, he began to repeat point by point, exhorting them to advance from day to day toward what was better. Above all he urged them to continual love of God, fervor in the monastic life, observance of mutual love, the practice of hospitality and its exercise with every care, and the love and voluntary distribution of alms, together with many similar matters.

Afterwards he added in a plaintive voice:

“There is one thing that greatly embittered and burdened me, which I shall disclose with lamentation to God and to you.”

When we were all struck with astonishment, he said:

“Certain brothers lived among you according to the wisdom of the flesh rather than according to spiritual simplicity. By their words or counsels they often disturbed me and opposed the simplicity that had been established. But almighty God separated them from us individually and removed them from the cloister.”

After saying this, he immediately added:

“From now on, beloved, I shall hold no chapter with you. Therefore, my little sons, hear the Father’s final judgment and retain in memory what you have seen and heard.”

When the chapter was over, he withdrew to his humble dwelling and, as usual, made himself available to all who wished to visit him.

Then, on the third day, he ordered himself to be carried to the oratory of Saint Mary. There, while the community of brothers celebrated Mass for him, he fortified his departure with the anointing of the oil of the sick and with the reception of the body and blood of the Lord. He asked pardon from everyone and granted pardon to everyone himself, kissing and embracing each one with fatherly affection. He said his final farewell to those present and entrusted his intimate affection to those absent. At the same time he earnestly implored and charged them all to remain inviolably, until death, in the unity of the Church and in submission to the Apostolic See, as he had handed this down to them.

Finally, raising his hands before everyone, he concluded in a brief speech:

“I call God to witness that until now I have always acted faithfully and kindly toward you.”

When he had been carried back from the oratory, each one came to him individually with groans and sighs. To them he spoke a memorable word:

“The death of a just man should not be called death, but rather a change, because he is changed from mortality to immortality, from earthly things to heavenly.”

The next day, after he had been carried to the infirmary and the community of brothers had assembled there before noon, while everyone wept and mourned pitiably, he completed his blessed course on the fourth day before the Nones of July and returned to God a soul filled with blessed merits. Freed from the Egypt of this world, he went to dwell eternally in the land of the living.

Two bishops and five abbots assembled.

[Note: According to Trithemius, these were John of Speyer and Gebhard of Constance, bishops; the abbots were Theoger of Saint George in the Black Forest, Notker of Zwiefalten, and three others whose names have been lost.]

Clergy also came in considerable numbers, together with a multitude of both sexes. After the funeral rites had been celebrated for five days, he was buried with due veneration in the middle of the Church of the Apostles.

[Note: The same Trithemius writes that the funeral rites of the blessed abbot were celebrated for five consecutive days.]  
[Col. 0916A–0917A]

### 25.

Not long after his death, as though after the night of sorrow that had oppressed everyone, a day of consolation dawned upon us with the arrival of Lord Gebehard, then prior and later the deceased Father’s successor in governing the monastery. He brought relics of the holy apostle Peter—namely, some of his hairs—which had been sent by the most reverend Hugh, abbot of Cluny; before his death, Father William had sent Gebehard to obtain them.

The people of Hirsau ought to embrace and venerate these hairs with heartfelt devotion above all gold and precious stones, because we have learned that they truly came from the hair of the chief of the apostles, Peter.

In ancient times, before the bodies of the apostles Peter and Paul were separated from each other and placed in the secure places where they are now buried together, there was a religious man named Oddo who served as their custodian on behalf of the church.

[Note: His life was published in the preceding volume.]

Oddo renounced the world, sought admission to the monastery of Cluny, and was later made its abbot. Among other relics of the saints, he brought with him some hairs of Saint Peter. The aforementioned abbot of Cluny, an ardent lover of our community because we had received from him the plan for building a monastery and living according to the Rule, testified with the most certain assurance before venerable elders that the hairs he sent us had been taken from those.

We considered it necessary to record this here so that no one might be disturbed by any scruple of doubt concerning these same hairs, since it is established that the truth has been confirmed by so many and such authoritative witnesses.

Those who brought the aforesaid relics, before they reached Hirsau, prudently entrusted them for safekeeping to a certain religious priest living in a nearby village, until the feast called Saint Peter in Chains. On that very day, after abbots and other religious men had assembled, the relics were received in the monastery of Hirsau amid the greatest rejoicing of the monks and the people. They were first placed upon the tomb of the blessed Father William, to whom they had been specially sent, as though being presented to him by the loving devotion of his sons.

Finally, amid joyful praises of God, they were kissed with humble veneration by everyone present and placed in a little silver reliquary, where they are preserved to this day.  
[Col. 0917A–D]

### 26.

It is read concerning Saint Gregory and Saint Gall [Note: The Life of Saint Gregory was published in Century I; that of Saint Gall in the following Century.] that, long after their departure from this life, they became renowned through many signs because the monasteries they had built in God’s honor were defended by their patronage against many adversities.

We have also learned from known and trustworthy persons of certain events of this kind that occurred in our own times concerning this holy man of God. We have taken care to record them in writing as a commendation of his holiness.

There was a certain abbess in the province of Noricum, devoted to pious works, at whose counsel the aforementioned man of God had once been placed in charge at Hirsau, because she loved him greatly for the merits of his life. After his departure, she learned by report that many men of the evil party had conspired in this undertaking: to destroy the monastery of Hirsau utterly.

Therefore, afflicted by continual sorrow, she repeatedly appealed to the merciful God in prayer, asking Him to avert so great a crime by the aid of His protection and to bring the new planting of His faithful servant to growth.

While her heart was distressed by such pious anxiety and she was earnestly beseeching the Lord because of the impending danger, the man of God appeared to her one night as she slept. He looked upon her sadness with a cheerful face and gladdened her, saying:

“There were indeed many who eagerly desired to perpetrate so great a crime, but it has been entirely forbidden that it should happen.”

Then, when she anxiously asked who had forbidden this to be done, he replied:

“A good angel of the Lord.”

Immediately the vision of the speaker vanished.

For truly, as the Psalmist says, “The angel of the Lord encamps around those who fear Him and delivers them” (Psalm 33:8).

Although, as the same Psalmist testifies, every just person dwells under the Lord’s protection, those who attempted to exterminate the people of Hirsau at the command of King Henry, the fourth of that name, experienced God’s vengeance even more evidently and severely. They did so because the Hirsaugians refused to consent to his heresy against the Roman Church or to contaminate themselves in any way by communion with him. For he was a most wicked man and the most criminal of all whom the earth had sustained.

At his instigation, a certain bishop of Strasbourg named Werner attacked Hirsau with military force in order to devastate it.

[Note: Bruschius, in his Catalogue of the Bishops of Strasbourg, says that a lengthy account of this bishop’s death is given in the Hirsau Chronicle. But the authority of the author of this life is of great weight, since he was certainly present at the events.]

On the very day when he mounted his armored horse in order to commit so great a crime, he was overtaken by sudden death and expired before he could remove his armor. Alive, he descended into hell.

I say “alive,” as it is written (Numbers 16), because he labored knowingly and deliberately to act wickedly and desired to destroy the innocent servants of God. Even the soldiers who were being forced against their will to assist him considered this so abominable that they dissuaded him and refused to aid such a crime.

This occurred long before the death of the man of God; but thereafter it instilled universal fear of presuming to undertake anything of the kind against the holy place and its inhabitants.  
[Col. 0917D–0918D]

### 27.

It is worthwhile to append here something else not very different from this, which also serves to terrify and restrain invaders of Hirsau’s property.

A certain man named Wintheir, from a village called Allmendingen, renounced the world and assumed the habit of holy conduct under Abbot William. From his own possessions he legally donated to the use of the brothers of Hirsau an estate situated in the aforesaid village.
