After both men had departed this life—that is, Abbot William and the aforementioned man—a certain young man usurped the estate with reckless audacity, as though it had passed to him by hereditary right.

One day, while he was violently carrying away from the same property two wagonloads of wine and other things of this kind, one foot of the oxen that were dragging the plunder was broken on the road. The young man himself also fell headlong from the horse on which he was riding, as though suffering from lethargy (*lethargum*), became insane, and even lost the use of speech. He had to be carried in the hands of others.

As time passed, however, his mental and bodily strength gradually returned. He began to consider that he had not endured such a scourging—one he had never before experienced—without a just judgment of God. After deliberating with himself, he had himself carried to the monastery of Hirsau. There he changed his habit together with his worldly mind, devoted himself faithfully to God, and, after a few years, happily ended his present life in holy conduct.

When we hear these things and consider so terrible and fearful a judgment of God upon these two men—one of whom was suddenly hurled into death, while the other was mercifully preserved for a better life—we may appropriately wonder with the Psalmist and say:

“Come and see the works of the Lord, how terrible He is in His counsels concerning the sons of men” (Psalm 65:5).

From the same consideration we are compelled to exclaim with the Apostle:

“O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How incomprehensible are His judgments and unsearchable His ways! For who has known the mind of the Lord? Or why does He have mercy on whom He wills, and why does He harden another, so that he may not be saved?” (Romans 11:33–34).

Therefore, since according to Solomon’s saying, “No one knows whether he is worthy of hatred or love, but all things are reserved for the future” (Ecclesiastes 9:1), let us fear the hidden judgments of God and venerate them, and while venerating them let us fear them. As long as we are in this body, let us serve the Lord in fear, according to the Psalmist, and rejoice in Him with trembling (Psalm 2:11).  
[Col. 0918D–0919C]

[Col. 0919D] **28.** How great a care, as we have said, the holy Father Wilhelm, now reigning with God, exercised over his monastery was also shown quite clearly by another vision. Since we learned of it from the report of an elderly man, an innocent and simple person to whom the same vision was granted from heaven, we have judged it necessary to transmit it in writing to posterity, because through it the monks of Hirsau—both those yet to come and those now living—are admonished diligently to observe the statutes of the aforesaid Father, especially in the distribution of aid to the poor and guests, and in the observance of cloistered discipline.

He himself had established, with the common counsel of the elders, that some of the lay brothers who came for conversion should serve in the house of the poor in lay clothing, yet should be supported, not from alms, but from the common food and clothing of the brothers. His successor altered this custom so that the aforementioned brothers obtained all the necessities of the body from the alms they administered. As a result, a very grievous thing occurred: the customary mercy was withdrawn from pilgrims and other poor people, to such an extent that the needy, excluded during the freezing nights of winter, would cry out miserably in the street from hunger and cold, often disturbing the brothers who were sleeping at night.

The abbot was frequently admonished by the brothers about this trouble, but he neglected to correct it and many other things of the same kind. One night, when the Lord’s Ascension was being celebrated, an elder of that monastery, approved in life and conduct, saw in a nocturnal vision that he was lifted up and placed, as it were, above an immeasurably lofty mountain. Everything there was filled with the splendor of immense light, the wondrous fragrance of an extraordinary scent, and the sweetest harmony of the blessed inhabitants. He was exceedingly delighted and constantly desired to remain there. Among the other things he saw, he recognized Abbot Wilhelm, formerly most familiar to him, radiant in appearance and clothing like snow, together with two men adorned in pontifical vestments but unknown to him.

He asked who they were and heard that one was Saint Udalric, bishop of Augsburg [Note: [Col. 0919D] The Life of Saint Udalric is found in the preceding century. Saint Conrad died, according to Bruschius, in the year 976.]; the other, Conrad of Constance, likewise a holy man and formerly a bishop.

When Abbot Wilhelm had answered his questions about the other things he had seen there, he finally charged him to make the following known to the people of Hirsau:

> “On behalf of the supreme majesty of God, I command you to tell the abbot and prior, and the other brothers at Hirsau, that they must serve the needy and guests with every affection of charity, according to what they received from us. Let them order their conduct and life according to the Rule of Saint Benedict; above all, let them cast away with every form of malice anger and indignation, hatred and detraction, by which they continually offend God, and let them preserve sincere and continual love for one another. If they do not observe this, let them know without doubt that they will experience divine vengeance.”

After saying this, he left the man to whom he had spoken these words and, with the others who were present, penetrated into the higher secrets of heaven.

[Col. 0920D] The elder to whom these things had been revealed, not daring to disclose them to the abbot himself, made everything known through another elder. The abbot then ordered that the former arrangement of Abbot Wilhelm concerning alms should indeed be observed, but left uncorrected the other matters by which he had disturbed the monastery. Therefore, in accordance with the aforesaid threat of the blessed Father Wilhelm, scarcely anything prosperous happened to him.

For shortly afterward he was deprived of the governance of the monastery and invested with the episcopal mitre at Speyer. By foolish conduct he aroused the hatred of everyone against himself, but natural death intervened and removed him from their midst.

[Note: [Col. 0920D] Trithemius gives a fuller account of this under the year 1105, when Gebhard was ordained bishop of Speyer by Ruthard, bishop of Mainz, in the presence of a great assembly of nobles [Col. 0921C]. The same Trithemius assigns him only one year and several months of government; others assign him more. After his death he was carried back to the monastery at Hirsau and buried before the high altar of the principal church.]

[Col. 0921A] **29.** We must not pass over negligently, but must carefully consider, how worthy of veneration the most holy Father Wilhelm is on earth, since according to the aforesaid vision he enjoys in heaven the company of such great bishops, whose glorious memory the faithful people of Holy Church solemnly celebrates each year with devotion.

If anyone, doubting because of his unbelief, should say that a vision of this kind ought not to be heeded but counted among empty dreams, let such a person know without question that it has never been written in the hagiographers, nor ever heard, that any human being has at any time been warned, openly or secretly, by the suggestion of demons to turn away from evil and do good—as happened here through the most kindly Father Wilhelm.

It is also well known that the distinguished and foremost teachers of the Church, the blessed Gregory and Augustine, inserted in their works certain visions even of secular persons for the edification of the faithful; yet the testimony they offer for them is nothing other than that they expressly attest that particular people saw these things in a dream.

Finally, to seal with the mark of the purest truth all that we have set forth concerning the holy man, we shall produce one further testimony. Through it we prove that he was divinely appointed to the work of the ministry in which, as a faithful and prudent servant, he labored in the house of the Lord, and that he is truly to be called holy according to his vocation, since all things worked together for good for him who loved God diligently.

**30.** When the holy Father was afflicted by a serious illness—the illness, namely, in which he is known to have paid the debt of Adam—he was visited by many distinguished persons from the surrounding region. Thus they might both fulfill to a good conclusion their devotion, by which they had always honored the man of God wonderfully, and entrust their souls to the soul of one so holy as he was departing.

Among the first to arrive was the distinguished and most devout visitor, the bishop of Worms, [Note: [Col. 0922C] Stengelius thinks that this was Eppo, who succeeded Dithmar, who died in 1085. But Bruschius places Dithmar’s death in 1109, after two years of rule; consequently the Worms bishop mentioned here must be Adelbert, Dithmar’s predecessor.] who had always been particularly close to that simple soul, and to whom the beloved of the Lord, compelled by the bishop’s excessive intimacy, often disclosed his secrets.

To this person of such excellence and proven standing in the Church, Wilhelm revealed the following among their other familiar conversations, and confirmed it under oath by the divine name:

> “While I was still at Regensburg in the monastery of Saint Emmeram, one night a man of mature age appeared to me, of beauty wonderful beyond human measure. With a cheerful countenance he addressed me, carrying in his hand the most beautiful grapes, which he also offered to me, saying: ‘Receive them, my beloved.’
>
> “Struck by the novelty of the gift and by the graciousness of so great a man, I confess that I remained for a long time astonished, wondering within myself. Then he said: ‘I have undertaken to establish a school, and before all ages I predestined you to preside over it. If you govern it according to my will, you will be rewarded eternally with a good recompense. Do not doubt, my friend: the same one who rewards is also your fellow worker.’
>
> “Awakening at these words, I considered many things within myself and repeatedly reconsidered them. When my mind had been stretched by many meditations, at last I fled to the safest harbor of the great mercy of God and entrusted everything of mine to the Lord my God as intimately as I could.
>
> “And behold, on that very day our brothers from this monastery arrived, bringing letters with many entreaties. By a very powerful force they tore me away from monastic quiet and compelled my insignificance to preside over them; invoking the divine name, they forced me not to refuse their requests. I confess that I accepted the yoke of the Lord unwillingly, overcome by such unanimous entreaty.
>
> “If in this office I have done anything pleasing to God, let praise, honor, and every kind of thanksgiving for this and all his mercies and benefits belong to him, without whom nothing is strong and nothing holy, to him, I say, from whom all good things proceed, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.”

## Epitaph of Saint Wilhelm, Abbot of the Monastery of Hirsau, Hung over His Tomb

[Col. 0921]

[Col. 0921D]

In this inscription, Father Wilhelm, your life  
shines forth as a mirror to all of the life of the good,  
so that every learned person may correct his own deeds from it,  
discerning what must be avoided and what must be done.

Like a mirror, the holy life  
of Father Wilhelm, bright with the light of virtues, shines forth.

Let such a mother rejoice, Bavaria, in her offspring;  
let Swabia rejoice that she possesses so great a patron.  
Noricum bore him as a son,  
and Hirsau received him as a father,  
happy in such a spiritual shepherd,  
the father of many begotten through instruction.

Distinguished in conduct and rich in virtues,  
he consecrated to the Lord a perfected people and dwelling.  
For you, Aurelius, Peter, and Paul, venerable fathers,  
he founded a cell, and for you, Gregory and George;  
and arranging many other holy places,  
he built and instructed them,  
because he led them along the straight path,  
restoring the monks’ life, long since fallen into ruin.

He surpassed the ancient teachers of the quadrivium in their art;  
through song he corrected various errors according to the rules of music.

[Col. 0923A] Examining the boundaries of the earth and the hours of time,  
and the numbers of the abacus, he perceived them with such an intelligent mind  
that scarcely anyone could be compared with him in these arts.

What he taught in words he proved by the power of his deeds.  
For the poor, widows, lame, blind, pilgrims,  
the sick, the healthy, and all afflicted by whatever suffering,  
he provided prosperity and removed every adversity.  
Simple and upright, he became all things to all people.

Alive for you, Christ, and truly crucified to the world,  
after he had endured many struggles for you,  
in the year one thousand and ninety [Note: [Col. 0923] One year has been omitted because it would have fitted the difficult meter less well, although no regular meter is maintained in the other verses thereafter.],  
on the fourth day before the Nones of July,  
here seeking the excavated tomb,  
he died and now lives happily with you forever—  
that venerable Father and man worthy of every praise.

Illustrious Wilhelm, Father adorned with virtues,  
by your holy prayer now bring it about that we may be freed  
from the bitter death of body and soul,  
we who devoutly serve God here,  
walking around the tomb prepared for you, Father, whom we honor.

May good things be given there,  
where our minds may be purified,  
where you await Christ with us in sweet sleep,  
the Supreme One who will come  
and give the goods of life to the just.

May the life of Abbot Wilhelm—ah!—join us to the blessed,  
and grant me, after [an uncertain corrupt reading], to behold your brightness alone,  
the choir with its company above the heavenly stars,  
praising God in the customary manner and exulting in sweet song,  
rolling forth joyful hymns through the meadows of paradise,  
to the King of kings, the Lord who sits there upon a lofty throne.

May the voice of praise endure forever,  
as those who remain there forever prosper. Amen.

## Hymn in Honor of Blessed Wilhelm

[Col. 0923]

[Col. 0923B]

Hear, O God, the prayers  
of your hymn-singing servants,  
who in supplication  
celebrate the solemn feast of your holy confessor.

Here he shone through kindly and wondrous deeds  
and through virtues,  
a shining lamp for all  
who dwell in the house of God.

Founding in Christ  
very many monasteries of monks,  
he raised walls from heaven,  
using living stones.

[Col. 0924B] Here he was a living sacrifice  
through every span of life;  
he slew vices within himself  
by bearing the marks of the cross.

O Christ, you have now become  
the victory and glory of this man;  
through his intercessions  
grant us the joys of life.

We praise you, God the Father,  
and your only Son together,  
and the Spirit, the Paraclete,  
now and throughout every age. Amen.

[Col. 0923]

# The Hirsau or Gengenbach Constitutions of Saint Wilhelm

*(Ancient Monastic Discipline, or Collection of Authors of the Order of Saint Benedict, for the most part unpublished, who nearly six hundred years ago treated of monastic discipline in Italy, Gaul, and Germany, edited and prepared by *** priests and Benedictine monks of the Congregation of Saint Blaise in the Black Forest. Paris, printed by Osmont, 1726, quarto.)*

## Notice

Saint Wilhelm, a monk in the monastery of Saint Emmeram at Regensburg, was appointed abbot of the monastery of Saint Aurelius by the monks of Hirsau after the middle of the eleventh century, because of his reputation for holiness and learning. Out of his exceptional zeal for restoring monastic discipline, he asked Udalric—or Wldaric—a monk of the church of Cluny, not to consider it burdensome to share with him the constitutions that the elders possessed at Cluny.

Udalric agreed and sent him three books of Cluniac custom written by himself—though Wilhelm mentions only two. In the first book he dealt with psalmody and the solemn celebrations of Mass, as well as the various festivals of the year; in the second, with regular discipline; in the third, with governance and officials. All three books were published in print by Dom Dachery in volume IV of the old edition of the *Spicilegium* and volume I of the new edition (*Patrologia*, volume CXLIX, [Col. 0925] column 633).

But when the holy man had acquired a more expert knowledge of these customs, he obtained permission through Bernard of Marseille from Hugh, abbot of Cluny, and shortly afterward sent six of his monks from Hirsau to Cluny. Their purpose was to observe and learn the rites, practices, and ceremonies directly, and to record as diligently as possible every detail belonging to monastic discipline.

Thus, when Wilhelm had become thoroughly acquainted with the entire institution of the Cluniacs in this way, he took counsel with his monks to select from Udalric’s books only those things suited to the customs of their country, the situation of the place, and the character of the climate. Accordingly, in those same books he changed some things, omitted a few, and added many more, especially those which Wilhelm had learned as a boy in the monastery of Saint Emmeram.

In this manner the laws and constitutions for that celebrated congregation of Hirsau were first made. The author himself explains this at greater length in his prologue.

Wilhelm presided for twenty-two years, one month, and one day. He died on the last day of the year 1019 after Christ. His eulogy is found in the *Chronicle of Hirsau*, as follows:

> “This is Wilhelm, most holy abbot and servant of Christ, who in his time strove to restore and reform the order of our holy Father Benedict, which had almost collapsed and been disfigured in Germany by the insolence of monks; and through himself and his disciples he restored more than a hundred monasteries to their former observance of regular discipline.
>
> “Apart from the reform and congregation of the Cluniacs, which surpasses the others in the number of its monasteries, no reform has yet existed in our order that could be compared in the number either of monasteries or of notable persons with the restoration accomplished by the people of Hirsau.”

There, page 225.

Among the first monasteries into which the Hirsau constitutions were introduced is the monastery at Gengenbach, in the diocese of Strasbourg, founded by Saint Pirminius, bishop of Meaux, in the time of Theuderic, king of the Franks. For in this monastery, as the aforesaid *Chronicle of Hirsau*, page 176, states:

> “Marquard, abbot, was sent with twelve monks from Hirsau by Gebhard, the venerable Father who succeeded Saint Wilhelm in the abbacy of Hirsau. This most reverend Abbot Marquard, reforming the monastery of Gengenbach entrusted to him in both its conditions, wisely recovered its lost temporal resources and quickly increased the number of its monks considerably.”

We have included these details so that it might be entirely clear that the Gengenbach constitutions recorded in the Einsiedeln manuscript, which we used, are wholly the same as the Hirsau constitutions that Lucas Dachery intended to publish in volume I of the new edition of the *Spicilegium*, page 639, and that Jean Mabillon intended to include in volume IV of the old *Analecta*.

As for the other monasteries into which these same constitutions were introduced, Trithemius reports them in the *Chronicle of Hirsau*, beginning on page 274. It is useful to quote his words here, so that the spread of these constitutions may be more fully understood:

> “We have resolved to list in order the names of the monasteries of our order that, from Hirsau, were either newly established by Blessed Wilhelm, Abbot, and his disciples after him, or reformed after desolation, so that we may show that there were more than a hundred.
>
> “First of all, the head and principal monastery is this greater Hirsau, which he built anew from its foundations.”

### New Monasteries

[Col. 0925A]

Zwilfalta. Saint George the Martyr in the Hercynian Forest. Saint Peter at Erfurt. Saint Martin in Carinthia. At Bruweningen. The priory at Weilheim. The priory at Reichenbach. The provostships at Rothe. At Camberg. The priory at Schonrain. At Braitenawe. Odenheim. Hasungen. Pauline cells. Petershausen. Leoben in Carinthia. [Col. 0925B] At Passau. Hugeshofen. Saint Walburga. Niiwilen. Vraugium. At Lorch.

### Reformed Monasteries

At Schaffhausen. Lorsch. At Reinharzbronn. At Altdorf. Saint Alban at Mainz. At Bildenstat. Saint James at Mainz. Bruwilen near Cologne. The monastery at Mediolacum in Lorraine. [Col. 0926A] Saint Disibod, bishop, in the county of Sponheim, now inhabited by Cistercians. At Limburg. At Hornbach. At Tholey. At Sels. Maurimünster, which they call Morsmünster. At Gengenbach. At Schutter. Ettenheim. Schwarzach near Strasbourg. Schwarzach in East Francia. Saint Stephen at Würzburg. At Amorbach. Neustadt near the Kinzig. Theris beside the Main. Mount of the Monks at Bamberg. [Col. 0926B] At Münchurach. Steinach. Saalfeld. Magdeburg in Saxony. Rheinau. Admont in Austria. Saint Ulrich at Augsburg. At Isny. Rozaz near Aquileia. At Elchingen. Reichenau Major. At Weingarten. At Besselbronn. At Bregenz. The Hermits. Kempten. [Col. 0927A] At Altha. At Deckingen. Ottenbeuren. At Albersbach. Benediktbeuern. At Glauburg. At Neckarsheim. Schuttern. At Ochsenhausen. Saint Blaise. Muchart. Mure. Nauen. Tersau. [Col. 0928A] Salzburg. At Heidenheim. Saints Peter and Paul in the Black Forest. At Wiblingen. Saint Trudpert. At Trube. At Ellwangen. At Thierhaupten. Saint John in the Thurtal. Faurndau. At Andechs. At Fischingen. At Blankenstetten.

We found these names of monasteries of our order recorded. Either from the beginning of their foundations, monks of the monastery of Hirsau first planted regular discipline in them, or, when they had been founded in antiquity and disfigured by excessive age or neglected institution, they reformed them according to the path of regular observance. Thus far the *Chronicle of Hirsau*.

We further inform the reader that we have compared the Hirsau constitutions with Udalric’s books, and have marked in the text with the letters **UD** each and every item taken from those books. We have distinguished with an asterisk the matters added by Saint Wilhelm; we have designated variants with the letters **VAR.** In this way it is immediately apparent what the people of Hirsau adopted from the customs of Cluny and what Saint Wilhelm had learned as a boy in the monastery of Saint Emmeram, before the institution of the Cluniacs.

From this the learned reader will also easily gather how the monastic discipline that flourished in Gaul differed from that received by custom in Germany. Anyone who wishes to form a sound judgment on this matter should also compare Bernard’s *Customary of Cluny* with these constitutions. For certain chapters of these constitutions, omitted by Udalric, are contained in that work; yet, so that we might not make the work incomplete and mutilated, we have taken care to print them here in full as well.

# The Hirsau or Gengenbach Constitutions

*[From the Einsiedeln manuscripts.]*

[Col. 0927]

## Book One

### Prologue

[Col. 0927B]

After [Note: [Col. 0927C] This prologue is lacking in the Einsiedeln manuscript; I supplied it from the Weingarten manuscript, which I afterward found published in volume IV of the old *Analecta*.] I, Brother Wilhelm, by God’s ordinance and the election of the brothers of Hirsau, had been appointed administrator of that place, I first introduced among them the customs of regular life that I had learned as a boy in the monastery of Saint Emmeram.

But because many things in them seemed gradually, through the advance of negligence, to have degenerated from monastic rigor and from the nobility of that manner of life, I immediately resolved that, wherever I might perceive anything useful for forming the conduct of the brothers—whether by sight, hearing, or certainly by reading the sacred books—I would contribute the whole of it, as though it were living stones, to the construction of the spiritual building.

While I commended this intention of mine through diligent prayers to the one who fills the desire of his faithful with good things, God, arranging everything wonderfully and mercifully, brought to us the venerable man Bernard, worthy of the memory of every good thing, abbot of Marseille and legate of the Apostolic See. Prevented by the difficulty of completing the journey he had undertaken, he spent almost an entire year with us.

When he had carefully examined the conduct of the brothers and the condition of our monastery, he addressed me one day, among other conversations, as follows:

> “As I see it, dearest brother, this place is exceedingly well suited to monastic life, and the brothers themselves seem to burn with the most ardent zeal for living justly and holily. But I should like to know who you chiefly have as teachers of your institution and from which monastery in particular you derive the customs you observe.”

I replied:

> “It is our endeavor, as far as we can, to imitate all religious men who pursue this way of life. But if you deign to restore us to the way whenever we deviate in anything, without doubt we shall follow most willingly wherever you lead us by the hand of wise counsel.”

To this he replied:

> “Your way of life, so far as the acuity of our small intellect can perceive, appears acceptable to God and truly admired by all wise people. But even if it were still more glorious and shone forth, so to speak, adorned with apostolic signs and virtues, it will nevertheless not be so pleasing and acceptable to those who sincerely pursue monastic perfection unless it has been made similar to other monasteries regularly instituted—in habit, tonsure, and the remaining customs.
>
> “But among all the monasteries of Cisalpine Gaul, if you seek my opinion, I especially advise you to choose the monastery of Cluny. There, through the authority of the most perfect monks and the antiquity of time, the monastic religion has grown so strong and glorious that, if any traces of holiness still appear in other monasteries, there is no doubt that each stream has flowed from this one as from a living and inexhaustible fountain.”

When this man, as the saying goes, had added spurs to those already running through such arguments and motives, he returned after completing the legation for which he had come. On his return journey, passing through Cluny, he commended us earnestly to the Father of that monastery and made him quite favorably disposed toward us, should we ask anything of him.

About the same time, an elder Udalric, a Cluniac, was sent by God’s will to Alemannia on business concerning a monastery and remained with us for some time. Since he had formerly been very familiar to us and had already been trained by long experience in the Cluniac disciplines, we asked him to write out his customs for us.

He agreed and promised, and, as he had promised, wrote two small books for us concerning the aforesaid customs.

Afterward, considering that many things were lacking in those books for acquiring a complete knowledge of the same customs, we sent first two of our brothers, then another two, and finally two more to Cluny. They investigated all the secrets of that Order with such diligent examination that their own teachers, in whose hearing they recited the written customs, declared that they had never had disciples of that spiritual school comprehend the art of their institution either more fully or more accurately.

When those brothers finally returned and joyfully brought back the sheaves of so fruitful a work, they conveyed to us a message from the Lord Hugh, venerable abbot of Cluny: relying on his authority, and having assembled our council of elders, we were to remove from these customs whatever proved superfluous according to reason, the custom of our country, the situation of the place, and the character of the climate; to change whatever needed changing; and to add whatever needed adding.

Applying ourselves to this with intelligent zeal, changing a few things and cutting away far fewer, we arranged all those customs in two books, divided according to their chapters and propositions.

We undertook so costly a work with this intention and in hope of this recompense: that you, dearest brothers, revered Fathers and lords, and all in whom there is love and zeal to be formed according to you, may by observing these things be able to merit eternal life; and that, while you rejoice that our labor helps you to live well, you may also assist us by your prayers to live forever in blessedness with Christ.

Therefore receive with cheerful spirit and, as the saying goes, open hands, these small gifts of our Father, produced with much labor and sweat. Embrace them in perpetual memory of the old man who will shortly die; preserve and observe them, and store them in the inmost recesses of your hearts, so that succeeding generations may know from their observance how sincerely you loved him while he lived.

Now, applying our hand to the work undertaken, we judge it appropriate to begin with the reception of novices and their instruction, and thus to make them the starting point of everything that must be said.

## Chapter I: The Different Kinds of Novices

**UD.** There is therefore some diversity among these novices. For they come not only without the habit, as laymen and clerics do, but also with the habit, already made monks. Such persons differ in three ways.

Some come from distant and foreign monasteries, intending to profess again and thereafter remain with us.

Some come from our own cells and, either because of illness or because of the remoteness of the place, have already received a blessing from the lord abbot, with their profession deferred and reserved until they reach our house.

Otherwise, when a novice has been received in one of these cells, he is not to be clothed there in monastic dress except by permission. Instead, he is brought to us with the garments he is to put on in order to receive the habit; all the other things he offered to the Lord remain there, in the place where he was received.

But after he has been instructed in our order and received the blessing [Note: [Col. 0929D] Here *blessing* is used for monastic profession.], he will return to the place where he was first received, if this seems good to the lord abbot.

The lord abbot is nevertheless accustomed to permit those priors who live in very remote places not only to clothe the novices they have received there in the monastic garment, but also, if so serious an illness threatens danger of death, to consecrate them as monks.

This blessing, which is thus performed as an aid [Note: [Col. 0930D] *Blessing as an aid* is monastic profession made when danger of death is imminent.], is granted by him to priors both near and far, provided that such a serious illness has been announced to them and either some circumstance prevents them from going to the sick person or it is not expected that they will be able to arrive there in time.

**UD.** Some do not come from such a monastery of ours, but have an abbot of their own without the lord abbot. Even if they receive the blessing and make profession, they are nevertheless regarded by us in every respect, both in life and after death, as though they had made profession among us, except that the thirty Masses are not sung.

There are also other monasteries associated with us which, although governed not by abbots but by priors, possess sufficient resources for the regular order to be observed in them. Therefore these men, who are governed by priors, after making profession among us, and those who, as was said, have an abbot of their own, **UD.** whenever they come to us, whether out of charity or for some business, enter confidently and without delay. According to the time at which they were received into the aforesaid monastery, they will likewise not be deprived of their proper rank.

*There are still other monasteries* [Note: [Col. 0931D] The Congregation of Hirsau, discussed in the preface.], which have no further relationship with us except that they are governed through the abbot of our congregation and according to the constitution of the lord abbot.

When the monks of these monasteries come to us, they associate with us in the choir and everywhere in the cloister, except in the chapter. They do not enter there unless either they or their abbot obtains permission. The manner in which this is to be done should be sought in the chapter of the same abbot (Book II, chapter 2).

All the others who come for conversion are not permitted to enter unless, first, according to the word of Saint Benedict, they spend one night outside the cloister. **UD.** Those on foot stay in the almonry, unless they are monks or more distinguished clerics; those on horseback stay in the monastery.

At the hour of their reception, whether they are staying in the almonry or in the guesthouse, they are led from there into the chapter by the porter.

If, when they arrive, they have brought any possessions to the monastery, they are to make a gift of them according to the Rule of Saint Benedict (Book II, chapter 36). Once this has been done, the offerings themselves are taken by those to whose obedience they belong. Who has charge of them is found in the chapter concerning the chamberlain.

*(UD–Var.)* Before entering the guest hall, they are to be instructed by the same porter how to make their petition. First, they must know how to ask permission according to our custom, so that, prostrated and asked by the presiding officer what they want, each one says: “We wish willingly to have God’s mercy and yours, and your fellowship”; or, if there is only one, he says: “I wish.”

After the presiding officer has answered, “May God grant you the fellowship of his faithful,” they rise and come to his feet—unless they are monks, or have been consecrated by the lord abbot, either because of illness or because of the remoteness of the place, as stated above. Such men are to show this reverence only to the abbot, if he is present.

Then they step back a little, bow respectfully, and withdraw to the lectern. [Col. 0931D] This law of bowing, in the form stated here, is to be observed by all who come to the feet of another for whatever reason.

*(UD–Var.)* If someone is, as I said above, from one of our cells, he is invited to appear before the brothers seated in chapter. After making the petition as stated, he is ordered to sit last among the brothers who have not yet made profession.

If there are any novices in the monastery who have not been consecrated [Note: [Col. 0931D] Novices were said to be *consecrated* and *blessed* in monasteries when, after completing the year of novitiate, they made their vows.], [Col. 0932A] he is superior to them at the *mandatum* and in the refectory [Note: [Col. 0931D] The *mandatum* is the washing of the feet, during which the words from the Gospel are sung: “I give you a new commandment,” etc.], and also in the choir, if he is literate [Note: [Col. 0932D] A distinction is made between monks who possessed learning and aspired to holy orders and monks who did not know letters, who are often also called *illiterate* or *idiots*]; but if he is not literate, he is superior to those among the novices who are illiterate.

## Chapter II: The Monk Who Comes from Another Monastery

*Anyone who comes to be received from another monastery, after making the petition in the same manner, is to be asked whether he wishes to be content with the custom of our order and promises to obey in all things until death, as God grants him strength.*

Then, after permission has been granted him to live with the brothers, he is to sit where he is ordered, according to what the lord abbot wishes and judges appropriate for the person.

Care must be taken that he be ordered to sit in a sufficiently modest place, so that after he has made his profession he may be recalled from the last place to the first—a customary procedure—and, when it pleases the lord abbot, may still be promoted higher if the dignity of his merits requires it.

If the lord abbot is not in the monastery, the prior must not receive this man into the cloister without his permission, unless the abbot is so far away that he cannot be reached by messenger within three days.

In that case, unless the prior knows that the abbot will come sooner, he may receive such a person and associate him with the community in every place. He will have no access to the chapter without the lord abbot’s permission, nor will he even enter it to make his petition. Instead, he is brought into the church at some suitable hour and there associated with the community by the officer responsible for the order.

Afterward, if necessary, he is shaved and clothed according to our custom.

[Col. 0932C] If his clothing is not made according to our custom and is so poor and scanty that he cannot conduct himself suitably among the brothers in it, regular clothing sufficient for his needs is given to him. If afterward he does not wish to persevere, he is not forbidden to depart before profession.

As long as he has no place in the chapter, he remains meanwhile in the novices’ cell until the chapter is over. For the first few days after his oblation, he goes there after the prior’s Mass, with permission, for instruction, and returns from there only with the other novices. Once he has received some instruction, he comes to the same school only after that Mass has ended. When the lord abbot has returned home and has learned from the prior what has been done concerning this brother, at the first chapter which he himself attends, after calling the brother to him and making the customary petition, he grants this permission—unless he has already granted it to him through a messenger. It can also sometimes happen that a novice must be received while the lord abbot remains in the monastery but is unable to come to chapter. Then the prior receives him by the abbot’s command and, if he is a monk, at once assigns him a place. Whether it is this man or that one to whom the lord abbot, being present, has granted entry to chapter, he enters only with permission, though with the warning of the master by whom the novice is instructed, [suppl. “he shall enter”]. For it belongs to that master to report to the lord abbot or the prior whatever must be made known concerning any novice.

His profession is prolonged beyond that of the other novices; and after he has been introduced into our custom, nothing in which he errs is overlooked through leniency, but he is corrected in everything, so that it may be proved whether he truly seeks the Lord. Thus, if any part of our customary order pleases him, he asks the lord abbot of his own accord to grant him permission to make profession—either in chapter with leave, or elsewhere without leave. Any novice does the same outside chapter for the reception of the holy order, if his heart fervently urges him to it. Nevertheless, according to custom and according to the Rule of Benedict, this confession and reception into the holy order is to be granted to no one before a full year, except on account of illness.

Meanwhile he is assigned to any offices, whether in church or outside the church, just like the other brothers, unless he is a literate man. Neither before nor after the day of profession does he presume to undertake the office of Mass, Epistle, or Gospel without the permission of the lord abbot. He is not admitted to the reading at table or to the office of weekly cantor until the armarius has tested whether he is suitable for these duties.

[Note: The armarius is the prefect of the library; an entire chapter describing his office is found in Book II.]

For it belongs to the armarius’ judgment to assign all these duties to him, just as it belongs to the prior to appoint him assistant in any obedience carried on within the cloister. Although the prior may receive a novice in any manner while the lord abbot is absent, nevertheless, if the novice does not wish to remain, the prior cannot dismiss him without the abbot’s command. Nor may he punish him for such instability of mind with harsh words or lashes. The abbot himself must likewise avoid this, since what Saint Benedict prescribes (chapter 58, section 11) ought rather to be observed in his case: that, just as he came freely, so he should also depart freely.

If anyone comes as an apostate from another monastery, having cast off the monastic habit and come to us in clerical dress for the sake of conversion, he is not received. Instead, he is persuaded to return and to repent worthily. If, after he has returned and promised suitable satisfaction, entry there is denied him, then, if he asks, he is received here. Before he enters the cloister, however, he is dressed in a cuculla and frock.

[Note: Cuculla: a familiar garment, namely one with which the head was covered.]

Afterward he is shaved according to our custom and clothed in the other garments required by the order, but his profession is postponed longer than that of any other novice.

*(UD. Var.)* A cleric or layman who has not yet had sufficient experience of our life must be carefully instructed, as the Rule states, how hard and harsh the things are which he must necessarily endure if he comes under our subjection. This subjection compels him to have no power over his own will, but to depend entirely on another’s direction. When, as stated above, they have answered, received the declaration of acceptance, and come a second time to the feet, the master leads them into the church to a suitable place, where they are to sit until they are clothed.

If one of them is literate, a book is given to him meanwhile for occupation, until, when chapter has ended and as soon as it can be done, he is led out to be shaved and to change his habit. If for any reason their shaving must be delayed for a short while, the aforesaid master leads them to the novices’ cell. There, after keeping them for some time in spiritual conversation, either leaving them there or leading them back into the church, he makes them wait for the hour of shaving.

If the community is to be shaved after two or three days, the cleric’s shaving may meanwhile be postponed, if this seems appropriate. The laymen, however, are awaited unshaven before the principal Mass. Before the bell is rung, he is to be led into the choir, where a chair has been placed before the steps outside the high altar.

*(UD. Var.)* Chairs for this ministry are always kept in the sacristy. Ordered to sit, he is crowned after his hair has been cut off, and, with his beard shaved, he is assigned to the training of Christ.

This tonsure is carried out in the following order. The armarius attends the priest who is about to celebrate Mass, carrying a book; the master of novices attends with scissors and a cloth, which the chamberlain has supplied and which are continually kept in the sacristy for this work. Holding the cloth in his hand, the same master receives into it the hair cut off by the priest’s hand.

First, after *Dominus vobiscum* has been said, the prayer *Praesta, quaesumus* is recited. Then he sprinkles them with holy water and shaves them. Immediately afterward, a young man begins the antiphon *Tu es, Domine* without vocal modulation [Note: That is, without modulation of the voice.], and the community completes it, with the verse *Conserva* added, together with the *Gloria*. The same antiphon is then sung again.

After the tonsure the priest says, “Let us pray. *Praesta, quaesumus*.” When this has been done, *Dominus vobiscum* is said for the shaving of the beard, followed by *Deus cujus specie*. After this prayer he does not sprinkle them, but immediately begins to shave. If there are ten or more, then, after the priest has assigned crowns to two or three of them, the master calls some of the older brothers to help him shave. After each of these assistants has cut some hair from the head and beard of one of them, they wait in the same place until both the priest and each assistant kiss the person whom he has shaved.

The aforesaid master sees to it that the cloth, scissors, and chairs are returned to the sacristy, so that he may always have them ready for such a ministry. According to custom, no layman is received into the cloister for conversion unless he has advanced to an age at which he has at least enough beard for the rite of this tonsure to be completed, and unless he is not thereafter to be placed under custody—except if he should begin to become so heedless that this exception is necessary.

Thus, after the novices have been assigned in the choir as described, they follow the same master to the warming house, because there they are to be shaved by the person appointed to the barber’s work, with other brothers whom the master has taken along to assist him. For it belongs to the master to ensure that the novices are shaved according to the rule.

When the shaving is finished, the chamberlain does not fail to be present and leads them to the wardrobe. They are all clothed there by the chamberlain’s servants. The garments which they then remove are stored until the day of their profession.

**UD.** Their clothing must be entirely like ours, except that, as long as they are without the blessing, they lack only the cuculla. Later, a cap is sewn onto their frock, so that, while living among us, they may not appear conspicuous through their difference.

*(Var.)* Whether they are few or many, even though they do not come to our chapter and sleep separately—in the novices’ cell with the master, since they never enter our dormitory unless they have been blessed—they are nevertheless not separated from us in the refectory or in the other places.

As soon as they are clothed, the master receives them and leads them to the aforesaid cell. There he instructs them in the few things presently necessary, then goes with them to the choir and places them in a suitable spot. Afterward all the things which they ought to have for their beds are brought by the chamberlain to the same cell, with the master’s knowledge and with suitable arrangements for each person; cucullas are brought as well, if this can be done. They are kept there until the day of their profession.

The names of each one, written by the novices themselves on as many small slips [Note: *Schedulis*, “slips” or “small sheets.”], are meanwhile sewn by them onto the outside backs of their respective cucullas. At the hour of consecration, each one puts on the cuculla assigned to him. The other things which they need at the beginning of their reception are requested by their master from the chamberlain.

After three or four days from their arrival, books for reading are given by the armarius to those among them who are literate, at the master’s request. They are not, however, entered against them as they are for the other brothers, who were registered for their books at the beginning of Lent.

## CHAPTER III. How They Are to Conduct Themselves in the Novices’ Cell and How They Are to Be Instructed There

Novices, whether few or many, are instructed in the aforesaid cell. Every day all who are to be taught assemble there, namely on feasts of the Twelve Lessons and on the octaves of the Nativity of the Lord, Easter, and Pentecost, after Prime.

On ordinary days they come after the prior’s Mass. Some monks who are still inexperienced in the order also come with them, with permission; but they return when they hear the signal for chapter—except those who have come from elsewhere and have not yet received this instruction by permission of the lord abbot.

Furthermore, whenever any of the novices wish to ask or learn something, they come of their own accord to him in the same cell whenever an interval occurs during the day—for example, after Mass, after the cymbal has been struck, or in winter after dinner. Indeed, at these times they are often found coming to receive his instruction there.

After supper, or during Lent after dinner, they never go there for this purpose, because no one is instructed there then except a novice within the first three days after his reception. In the brothers’ auditorium, none of them otherwise speaks for the purpose of instruction.

When they assemble at the hour mentioned above, even if chapter is held with them, they do not openly recite *Pretiosa*. Their master alone says, “Bless.” Anyone who knew that verse did not delay in reciting it until that hour; whoever did not know it recited the Lord’s Prayer three times in its place.

If it is the feast of the Twelve Lessons, they are first admonished in the Gospel sermon, which is also delivered in chapter that day. When it concludes with *Per omnia saecula saeculorum*, all answer, “Amen.” On ordinary days they are sometimes encouraged with a brief admonition suited to them, so that they may progress toward better things. Sometimes also certain passages from the Rule which are useful to them are preached. afterward they are instructed concerning the order.

If anyone commits an offense for which he is called to account either by the same master or by another of his fellow students, he asks forgiveness but does not undergo his judgment. No one asks forgiveness there for any fault unless he has been called to account by another.

If anyone among them is found negligent in learning the order, or lukewarm in some such matter, and is thus discovered to be blameworthy, the master first admonishes him several times on this account. If he does not correct himself, he is rebuked before the others harshly and severely, as Saint Benedict prescribes (chapter 2, section 22). Not only is he corrected by the master at that moment, but harsher penalties are proposed to him—namely prison, the *Bogae* [Note: *Bogae*, or *Bojae*, are a type of fetter, both iron and wooden shackles.], excommunication, and lashes—which he will certainly suffer among the brothers at some time if he is not fervent to the best of his ability in holy conduct.

If, however, the master sees that someone is attentive to what he hears and diligent in all matters pertaining to this purpose, he does not exhort him on this occasion but, at some suitable time, takes him aside from the others and encourages him to struggle bravely against the enemy’s temptations and to progress daily toward better things.

Thus, as stated, when he has instructed them according to what seems appropriate to him at the time, he goes to chapter, even though it is partly over.

A novice, whether in the community or elsewhere, may at some time commit a fault such that, for it, he is called to account in chapter either by one of the brothers or by the master himself. If, after being admonished several times, he neglects to correct it, he is led to chapter and undergoes the rod at the master’s hand, the claustral prior or his assistant having been sent there during that same chapter.

A young novice may perhaps sometimes commit a fault for whose correction he is not admonished many times, but is corrected immediately after he has been called to account, before chapter has ended, in the manner stated above. For example, if he says something to another young man placed in custody, or laughs, or makes some sign, provided that he knew he ought to have guarded against such things.

After the master of novices has returned to the community, as stated above, when their chapter has ended, they review there what they have learned. Those among them who are more advanced in the discipline of the order instruct separately those who are still weaker. Instruction in this work is fervent among them; they frequently ask forgiveness; they learn the customary inclination and the other practices ordinarily exercised in such a school.

If the lord abbot or the prior has imposed a flogging (*Hagellum*) upon one of them as penance, he receives it at that time from a priest, if the master can find among them someone suitable for this purpose, in the place assigned to such business. If no such priest is available there, he must bring a priest from the community to the same place at the appropriate time.

During that period, if two or three of them speak separately about the order, they are not rebuked for it. If one of them wishes to mend some part of his clothing or make his bed, he may do so at that time.

On the Vigils of the Nativity of the Lord and on the Annunciation, they attend the brothers’ chapter to ask forgiveness, and, after the prior has said, “Speak concerning the order,” they return.

If guests of high standing are sometimes brought there for admission into the brotherhood, the novices are summoned for their sake at the end of chapter. After the guests—whether clerics or laymen—have been led away, the novices leave with the community when the psalmody beginning *Verba mea* has begun.

This does not happen when, after chapter, they hear the wooden board [Note: A wooden board struck with a small hammer, by which the monks were awakened. The same board was struck when an office was about to be performed.], or when they hear the signal for the office for the dead or for the psalm *Verba mea*, which is sometimes done for a deceased person; for then they all immediately come into the community.

If it is Lent, on those ordinary days when silence is observed in the cloister, they join the community after chapter has ended and the community has sat down for reading. If it is a feast of the Twelve Lessons, when after chapter the community goes to the greater church with the psalm *Verba mea* and thirty psalms are then to be sung, the novices join the community before those psalms begin. If a novice is present who has come for conversion within the preceding three days, his master may lead him away for instruction after ten psalms have been completed.

If the day of silence mentioned above is then occurring, such a novice, at the master’s command, waits for him in the cell while the others depart. At every time when the community is permitted to speak, they are present, except when their hoods have been removed. They speak dispersed among the brothers. A brother is not forbidden to speak with a novice.

On the Twelve Lessons, after chapter, they wait again for their master or assistant to teach them: on lesser feasts, until they hear the signal for Terce; on Sunday, when they are not to be clothed in white, until the sprinkling with holy water; and, when they are to be clothed, until after the Gospel of the prior’s Mass.

If, after chapter, *Verba mea* or the office for the dead follows with the striking of the signal, they return for instruction after it has been completed. If it is a feast [Note: I think the text should be restored: “on which four antiphons are usually sung at Matins after *Venite*.”], on which four antiphons are customarily sung at Matins after *Venite*, they ought to go to the church immediately after chapter has been held, except when the master wishes to teach something to some of the newly arrived novices.

If, after chapter, the striking of the bells is then to follow for the office for the dead or for *Verba mea*, none of them remains there. A novice who has come for conversion is entrusted to someone well trained, who is to care for him wherever possible and pray beside him in church.

Throughout the entire time they remain in the same cell, except on the day before their profession, they go about without *capitia* [*caputia*].

[Note: “*Capitia*” should be read; they are head coverings sewn onto cowls. *Capitium*, or *capicium*, commonly meant a part of a sacred building, the presbytery.]

Those among them who seem suitable for this are appointed by the prior as assistants to the church custodian or the refectorer. Nevertheless, they may assist priests in celebrating Masses without the prior’s permission. They are registered by the armarius, along with the others, for work in the kitchen and for carrying the light in the church; for their names had previously been written out and presented to him by the aforesaid master. The master himself afterward instructs them in each office to which they were assigned in chapter.

Whenever the brothers wash one another’s feet before the Mandatum in the western part of the cloister, the novices do this separately. In summer, after None, when the wooden board is to be struck, the novices and the monks not yet united with the chapter pass through the chapter house and go into the church. There they sit near the entrance with books, if they find any there, until, after the board has been struck, they go out into the community.

If one of them is skilled in writing or bookbinding, the master may assign this work to him in the novices’ cell, provided that the armarius has asked him to do so.

A literate novice who is still young is entrusted by the lord abbot to the custody of another novice, at the master’s warning, and is assigned to be kept by him. If the latter is absent and cannot conveniently be reached even through the prior’s messenger, both the young novice and any other person of that age are assigned by the prior to custody.

If a novice who is to be received comes from the cell wearing a frock, his hood must be removed outside the cloister if he is to be blessed on the day on which he is received, or if some novices are then staying in the novices’ cell with their hoods removed.

It must be known that none of the novices ever receives Communion before he has been consecrated, except on the five chief feasts and on the three days before Easter, unless an illness has come upon him which makes it necessary for him to communicate. A novice who is a monk, however, does not observe this rule, even if he has not yet made his confession to the lord abbot or the prior.

None of them presumes to come at night from the church to the cell unless he has taken at least one companion and has a light. For he finds several *Absconsae* [Note: An *Absconsa* is a covered lantern, which the monks generally used when going through the dormitories.] near the altar and close to the church door, and he may take one of them.

If illness makes it necessary for him to sit before the choir, to go at night to the infirmary to quench his thirst, or to wear night shoes during the day merely because of pain in his feet, he may obtain permission for this from the master. He comes to the infirmary for the reason stated above with the master himself leading him; but on the following day he does not leave there unless the infirmarian obtains permission for him from the prior.

If he needs to bathe at Christmas or Easter, he does so with the knowledge rather than the permission of the same master. At other times he does so only after receiving permission from the prior.

As long as he is without the blessing, it is not customary to prepare cooked remedies or any other such medicine for him, except for bloodletting, unless perhaps the necessity is so great that, given its magnitude, it would seem impious not to break the custom.

Meanwhile, while he is not blessed, if he flees from the monastery, he is not to be pursued, because he is not yet a monk or professed. If he returns voluntarily, he is not readily to be received, but deliberately treated with contempt. If he bears this patiently and repents from his heart, he is not to be presented naked in chapter, because he has neither cuculla nor hood. He is simply brought into the cloister by the abbot’s command and joined to the community.

When lying ill, he does not eat meat, even if he is very weak in the infirmary, unless he cannot be restored by another food. If he recovers, he does not ask forgiveness for this.

If a monk is instructed among the novices, he does not abandon this instruction until it seems to the master that the time has come. During their time of probation the novices are instructed in the matters that follow.

## CHAPTER IV. Concerning the Inclination

*(UD. var.)* Although someone might regard this as a small matter, unworthy of mention, every novice must nevertheless be instructed with no little diligence to know how to incline according to the rule—not with his back raised, as is familiar to certain negligent persons, but so that his back is lower than his loins and his head higher than his back.

We call this inclination, by customary usage, *ante et retro* [Note: The expressions *ante* and *retro* occur frequently in this Ordinary, but always signify an inclination of the body which begins toward the East and ends toward the West. We discussed this in the *Ordinarium Cluniacense*.]. It begins toward the East and ends toward the West.

We perform it first before Nocturns, after the three prayers, and after Compline has ended, and again after the following three prayers. Thereafter, whenever we assemble in the church, or conduct business in chapter or in the refectory, we perform it both on entering and on leaving.

In church, the Lord’s Prayer is first said, except when Compline is begun and when we go into the church after dinner or supper; then we incline only on leaving, whether a regular hour follows or not. Likewise, at an office, if it is sung during the day, we do not incline except at the end, and we incline whenever we come to the church of Saint Mary.

Whenever a procession is made there before Mass, there is no inclination at the end. After the anniversary psalms [or *annuales*], when we return to chapter, we incline only once on that occasion, namely before the striking of the wooden board.

In the choir, whenever we change stations, we incline toward either Mass. At Masses the senior brothers stand first, nearest the principal altar. At the regular hours they stand last, at the far end of the choir, except at Terce on the Twelve Lessons, when, because the morning Mass usually precedes that hour and the principal Mass follows immediately, I think the station is not changed.

The aforesaid student of Christ is instructed in this not so much by hearing as by seeing.

## CHAPTER V. Concerning Silence and in Which Workplaces It Is to Be Observed

*(UD.)* He must also diligently learn the signs by which, while silent, he may in a certain manner speak, because before he has been united with the community he is permitted to speak only very rarely.

There are workplaces in the cloister in which our Fathers have established and prescribed that perpetual silence be maintained: namely, the church, dormitory, refectory, and regular kitchen. In each of these, both by day and by night, if he speaks even one word where anyone can hear him, he voluntarily asks forgiveness. If he incurs this negligence several times, however, he does not always escape judgment.

Elsewhere, if he says anything, he does not ask forgiveness unless he has been called to account; but then he rarely escapes judgment.

*(UD.)* If he names even one antiphon, responsory, or anything similar without a book, and does not see it in the book at the same time as he utters the word, this is judged nothing other than a clear breach of silence.

In the auditorium he is not permitted to speak while seated except with the lord abbot, the prior, or the claustral prior who is exercising full authority over the order. Nor does he ever speak there or elsewhere in the cloister on the Twelve Lessons, or on ordinary days in summer before the litany has ended, or in winter before Terce.

The same rule is observed in the novices’ cell, except that the lord abbot, the prior, or the master of novices may at the customary time hear the confession of a novice there.

## CHAPTER VI. Concerning the Signs for Speaking

Concerning these signs, to give some examples—for instance [Note: See chapter 17, part I, of the *Ordinarium Cluniacense*]—first those which concern food.

*(UD., var.)* For the general sign for “signs,” join the fingers of both hands and move one hand around the other.

For the sign for bread, make one circle with both thumbs and the two fingers next to them, because bread ought also to be round.

For the sign for bread cooked in water, which is usually better than ordinary bread, after making the general sign add this: place the inside of one hand upon the outside of the other, and move the upper hand around as though rubbing and moistening it.

For the sign for twice-baked bread, after making the general sign, blow slightly against the upright index finger; then raise the following finger, holding both separated from each other.

For the sign for a *tortula*, which is given in addition to the customary pound on the principal feasts [Note: *Tortula*, a diminutive of *torta*, a kind of cake. See the *Glossarium mediae et infimae Latinitatis* under *torta*.], place the two fingers next to the thumb, slightly separated, upon the two corresponding fingers of the other hand, likewise slightly separated.

For the sign for a large host [Note: The name “large host” was given to the very thin bread made from flour and water and baked over a fire in iron presses, which the priest uses for the sacrifice, to distinguish it from the smaller hosts which the priest distributes to others.], after making the general sign, encircle the thumb and the finger next to it around the eye.

For the sign for unleavened bread, after making the general sign, press the right hand obliquely upon the left and the left conversely upon the right.

For the sign for wheat bread, again after making the general sign, add this: make a cross through the middle of the palm, because this kind of bread is customarily divided into four parts.

## CHAPTER VII. Concerning the Signs for Legumes

*(UD.)* For the sign for beans, place the tip of the finger next to the thumb beneath the first joint of the thumb, and make the thumb project in this way.

For the sign for peas, conversely, place the tip of the thumb beneath the uppermost joint of the index finger.

For the sign for lentils, place the tip of the aforesaid thumb beneath the uppermost joint of the little finger in the same way.

## CHAPTER VIII. Concerning the Signs for Fish

*(UD. var.)* For the general sign for fish, imitate with the hand the movement of a fish’s tail in water.

For the sign for sturgeon [Note: *Sturio*. See Du Cange under *sturgio*. The French call it *esturgeon*; in Italian, *sturione*.], after making the general sign add this: place the tip of the thumb beneath the chin.

For the sign for salmon, after making the general sign add this: place two fingers around the eye.

For the sign for *lasso*, make the same sign as for salmon, adding the sign for likeness.

[Col. 0941D] For the sign for lamprey [or *muraena*], imitate three or four punctures in the jaw with a finger.

For the sign for cuttlefish, separate all the fingers from one another and move them in this way.

For the sign for pike, after making the general sign add this: place the right hand over the nose, with the fingertips projecting upward.

For the sign for the fish commonly called carp [Note: *Carpe*, *Cyprinus*; French *carpe*, German *Karpffen*.], after making the general sign add the signs for pig.

For the sign for trout [Note: *Truita*, also *Tructa*, *truta*; French *truite*.], after making the general sign add this: draw a finger from one eyebrow to the other. This is also said to be the sign for “woman,” because of the bindings women wear in that place.

For the sign for eel, close both hands as though holding and squeezing an eel.

For the sign for the fish called barbel [Note: *Barbo*, *barbus*; French *barbeau*.], after making the general sign add this: with two fingers imitate someone arranging his *grenones* [Note: *Grenones*, *grenniones*, means the hairs of the head divided by a parting, or rather that part of the beard beneath the nose, that is, the moustache.].

For the sign for the fish called *hasco* [Note: *Hasco* appears to be the same as the Saxon *hacod*. *Mullus*; French *mulet*.], after making the general sign add this: make the tip of the index finger spring across the thumbnail into the hand, as though imitating someone removing its scales; for it is more abundant in scales than the others.

For the sign for herring, after making the general sign add the sign for salt.

For the sign for *prasima*, after making the general sign add this: extend the hand, imitating its breadth.

For the sign for *rupa* [Note: *Rupa*, a white fish somewhat larger than the *gordione*, which the Belgians call *roche*.], after making the general sign add the sign for rock.

For the sign for *munua* [Note: *Munua*, perhaps the same as the river *capito*, or mullet; French *munier*.], after making the general sign pass the extended right hand across the middle of the thumb and index finger of the other hand, imitating the drawing of iron. This is also the sign for anything that we commonly use.

For the sign for small fish, after making the general sign add the sign for a small thing.

For the sign for roasted fish, blow slightly against the projecting index finger; afterward, with that finger and the one next to it, imitate someone digging or tearing, holding them separated and turned downward.

For the sign for crab, after making the general sign add the sign for pincers.

## CHAPTER IX. Concerning Various Kinds of Food

*(UD. var. \*)* For the sign for cheese, join both hands obliquely, as though pressing cheese.

For the general sign for *gara* [Note: *Gara*: I do not know what food this is, whether a food made from cheese or something used with cheese. Perhaps it is the same as *flato*, which was made from cheese and bread; certainly its sign immediately follows the sign for cheese in the manuscript *Ordo* of Saint Victor, Paris, chapter 25.], after making the sign for cheese add this: imitate sowing with three fingers.

For the sign for eggs, with one finger against the other, imitate cracking or pricking an eggshell.

For the sign for eggs cooked in fat, blow against the index finger as described above, adding the sign for fat. If you wish them to be roasted in the fire, extend both inner hands, holding the left part downward and the right upward, and moving the lower one slightly through the air.

Do the same if you wish apples to be roasted.

For the sign for milk, place all the fingers of the right hand around the little finger of the other hand and draw them through the air, imitating the milking of an animal.

For the sign for a cake, after making the general sign for bread and cheese, bend all the fingers of one hand and place the hollow hand upon the inner surface of the other hand.

For the sign for *crispellae* or *frigdolae* [Note: *Crispella*: among the peasants in Normandy, a *crêpe*, a few eggs mixed with flour and fried in a pan.], grasp the hair with the fist, as though wishing to make it curly in that way.

For the sign for *raseolae* [Note: *Raseolae*, also *rufeolae* and *rufellae*. They do not seem very different from hosts or wafers—French *oublies*, *gaufres*, German *Hippen*—if they are larger.], after making the general sign for bread, imitate with two fingers the small folds made in them on the side where they are folded and almost round.

For the sign for bread cooked in a frying pan, blow against the finger in the prescribed manner and add the sign for fat.

For the sign for a dish made with vegetables, imitate cutting those same vegetables with the right index finger at the top of the left fist.

For the sign for a little broth, that is, food made from herbs and vegetables, make a circular movement with the right index finger against the extended left hand, because it too is stirred around in a pot.

For the sign for millet, after making this same sign add this: make the thumb project slightly at the tip of the little finger.

For the sign for eating, bring the two uppermost fingers, joined together, once to the mouth, with the other fingers folded into a fist.

For the sign for meat, touch the outer surface of the other hand with two fingers of the right hand, adding the sign for eating.

For the sign for fat, extend the left hand and gently draw the three middle fingers of the other hand across its inner surface, imitating someone rubbing it with ointment.

For the sign for natural oil, which is usually made from nuts, after making the sign for nut add the sign for fat.

For the sign for honey, make the tongue appear slightly and apply the fingers as though you wished to lick.

## CHAPTER X. Concerning the Signs for Fruits
For the sign of an apple, enclose the thumb with the other fingers. For the sign of a pear, after making the general sign, extend the index finger. For the sign of a quince [Note: [Col. 0944D] *Cotanum*, a quince; German *Kitten*; French *coing*. *Cotana* is found in F. Laurentius in *Amal.*], after making the general sign, add the sign for a stone. For the sign of a peach, after making the general sign, add the sign for a skin or hide. For the sign of a medlar [Col. 0943D], after making the general sign, add the sign for a king. For the sign of a large nut, place the tip of the index finger at the edge of the mouth. For a small nut, do the same, adding the raising of the little finger, which always signifies a small thing.

For the sign of a cluster of grapes, join all the fingers of the left hand evenly, and, with all the fingers of the other hand placed around them, draw them gently toward the end of the left hand, pretending to gather grapes. For the sign of a large plum, after making the general sign, place the index finger over the right eye and the middle finger over the left eye [Col. 0944A]. For a small plum, do the same, adding the raising of the little finger. For the sign of cherries, after making the general sign, place a finger on the cheek, since this always expresses the color red. For the sign of strawberries, join the tips of the three largest fingers, likewise bringing together the other two, and, applying the three fingers of the right hand, pretend to pluck mulberries. It should be understood that strawberries of both black and red color have one and the same sign, except that you should distinguish the black ones by the sign for a tunic, and the others by the sign for the color red.

## CHAPTER XI. On the signs for foreign fruits

* For the sign of a citron, after making the general sign, add this: place the inner side of the thumb beneath the chin. [Col. 0944B] For the sign of a fig, after making the general sign, interlace the fingers of both hands; then, with the hands joined together, separate them again above, like someone dividing something. For the sign of a chestnut, place one hand upon the other and rotate it around two or three times.

## CHAPTER XII. On the signs for vegetables

* The general sign for vegetables is to extend the index finger downward, that is, toward the ground, but in such a way that its tip is placed against the middle joint of the thumb. Although this first applies to all vegetables, it signifies the leek in particular and properly.

For the sign of an onion, after making the general sign, join all the fingers of the left hand together and draw the right index finger across their tips, pretending to be cutting something with a knife [Col. 0944C]. For the sign of a melon, join the fingers in the manner described above, and draw the index finger downward along their joints, as though you wished to depict the lines that are usually found on it. For the sign of rue, after making the general sign, add this: pretend to pluck it with the whole hand. For the sign of fennel, add the sign by which the brightness of the eye is indicated. For the sign of Rhine panacea [Note: [Col. 0944D] *Panoceta*, a species of *panax*, called Rhine panacea because it grows more easily around the Rhine], after making the general sign, place the extended hand against the chest, adding the sign for goodness, because it is a sufficiently useful thing for the sick.

For the sign of dill, after making the general sign, bring the thumb together with the adjacent index finger to the nostrils, adding the aforesaid sign for each thing. For the sign of celery, after making the general sign, add the sign for bloodletting. For the sign of sage, after making the general sign, add the sign for salt. For the sign of piglet, after making the general sign, add the sign for a pig [Col. 0944D]. For the sign of lettuce, after making the general sign, press together all the fingers of the right hand and immediately separate them, as though pretending to indicate its softness and breadth. For the sign of chervil, add the sign for wax to the general sign. For the sign of a cabbage, after making the general sign, press the closed hand slightly toward the ground, like someone planting something. For the sign of parsley, after making the general sign, add the sign for a stone.

For the sign of watercress, which is commonly called *cresso* [Note: [Col. 0944D] *Cresso*, *Cardamine*, watercress. French *cresson*], after making the general sign, make the tongue appear and, applying the index finger, pretend to lick it. [Col. 0945A] For the sign of a poppy, after making the general sign, raise the fist upward. For the sign of a lily, after making the general sign, add the sign for straw-colored. For the sign of a rose, after making the general sign, add the sign for the color red. For the sign of hyssop, after making the general sign, add this: hold the inner surfaces of the spread hands turned downward near the ground, because it is a lowly herb and always signifies humility.

For the sign of southernwood [Note: [Col. 0945D] *Abrotanum*, for *abrotonum*. French *aurone*], which is also called *stabiwurtz*, after making the general sign, add the sign for wood. For the sign of wormwood, after making the general sign, separate two fingers—the index and middle—from the others, and move those two while also keeping them separated from each other. For the sign of garlic, after making the general sign, extend a finger toward the slightly open mouth [Col. 0945B]. For the sign of the elongated radish [Note: [Col. 0945D] *Rafa* and *rapa* differ in that the former is oblong, while the latter is round and white. German *Retich*, *Ruben*], after making the general sign, extend the index finger of the left hand and draw the index finger of the other hand along it toward yourself, pretending to scrape something. For the sign of the turnip, after making the general sign, draw the aforesaid index finger over the other in a ring.

## CHAPTER XIII. On the signs for spices

For the sign of ginger, after likewise making the general sign for herbs, pretend with the right fist, at the top of the other hand, to be turning a mill; again pretend to turn a mill; then make the tongue appear and, applying the index finger, pretend to lick it. For the sign of incense, make the sign for a bean first, and afterward bring the thumb together with the adjacent finger to the nostrils [Col. 0945C].

## CHAPTER XIV. On the signs for various liquids

* For the sign of water, join all the fingers of the right hand and move them obliquely. For the sign of holy water, after making the general sign with the extended hand, add the sign of the cross.
