For the sign of beer, after making the sign for drinking, blow a little toward the right hand, which is extended lengthwise.

For the sign of mead [Note: [Col. 0945D] *Medo*, *Meda*, honey-water, a drink mixed with honey], after making the sign for drinking, apply the hand to the mouth and pretend to lick it, which is also the sign for honey. For the sign of a man, bend the index finger and join it to the lips. In the same way you will also make the sign for drinking. For the sign of spiced drink, which is called *claret* [Note: [Col. 0945D] See the note in chapter 13, part II, of Bernard in the *Ordo Cluniacensis*], or, as many call it, *liittranch*, close both hands and pretend to turn a mill, adding the sign for wine [Col. 0945D].

For the sign of a drink made with honey and wormwood, first make the sign for wormwood and likewise add the sign for wine. For the sign of mustard, rotate the right fist on top of the other, as though pretending to grind; then make the little finger protrude at its outermost joint. For the sign of vinegar [Col. 0946A], draw the index finger downward just once on the right side of the throat. For the sign of red wine, draw the index finger across the cheek. For the sign of clear wine, place two fingers around the eye.

## CHAPTER XV. On the signs for vessels

(UD. For the sign of a bowl, raise the hand and bend the fingers slightly without joining them, because the bowl itself is concave. For the sign of a deep bowl [Note: [Col. 0945D] *Cavata*, a deeper basin], place the tip of the thumb against the middle of the left hand, letting the four following fingers hang while rotating them slightly. For the sign of a spoon, join only the fingertips, and in this way pretend to lift a little sip with the spoon itself.

For the sign of a cup, which we call a *justitia* [Note: [Col. 0945D] *Justitia*, a wine cup containing as much drink as is sufficient for each person; for some, a *justa*, for others, a *justella*], incline the hand downward and hold it hollow in this way, with the fingers slightly bent [Col. 0946B]. For the sign of a drinking bowl, bend three fingers slightly and hold them upward in this way. For the sign of a *cicothus* [Note: [Col. 0946D] *Cicothus*, a type of drinking bowl among our monks], after making the same sign, add this: rotate one finger around another.

For the sign of a glass phial, after making the sign for a drinking bowl, add this: place two fingers around the eye, so that the brightness of the eye signifies the brightness of the glass. For the sign of a small vessel in which salt is kept, after likewise making the sign for a drinking bowl, add the sign for salt. For the sign of a basket, after making the sign for any kind of wood, bend an upward-pointing finger, and then make the sign for bread.

For the sign of any kind of wood, with the right hand extended into the joint between the other hand and arm, pretend to be a craftsman cutting with an adze. For the sign of a vessel ordinarily used to carry vinegar [Col. 0946C], after making the preceding sign, add the sign for vinegar. For the sign of a vessel commonly called a *cannata* [Note: [Col. 0946D] *Cannata*, a larger wine cup, or wine vessel. German *Canne*, *Canten*], after making the general sign, add this: bend the finger as described above, together with the sign for wine.

In the same way make the sign for a mustard vessel, adding the sign for mustard. For the wine vessel commonly called by the common people a *zuber* [Note: [Col. 0946D] *Zuber* here signifies a wooden wine vessel; two somewhat larger vessels of this kind, filled with wine, are carried by a strong man with both hands. The word is known to the Germans; elsewhere, *Biitschen*, *Golten*], after making the general sign, bend both index fingers again in the manner described above. This is common to the signs for all vessels that seem to have two handles; finally add the sign for wine.

Thus, for vessels in which bread is usually carried, the sign for bread must likewise always be added. For the sign of a pole by which wine or something similar is customarily carried, after making the general sign for wood, join the fists one above the other, bring them to the shoulder, and pretend to be the carrier carrying it.

For the sign of a bowl in which crumbs are customarily gathered, after making the sign for a bowl, pretend with the right hand inside the other to gather the crumbs with a little broom [Note: [Col. 0946D] *Flabellum* is a familiar word, but here *flagellum*, that is, a small broom, seems to be intended, since it is made from several rods joined together. If it is made from feathers or the wings of birds, it may correctly be called a *flabellum*.] suited to this purpose. For the sign of the aforesaid broom, after making the sign for wood, which was mentioned last, add it. For the sign of a bellows, place the right fist over the left and move both as someone using a bellows does [Col. 0947A]. For the sign of a wine cup, after making the sign for wood, join both hands, slightly bent, to each other and rotate them as far as possible, finally adding the sign for wine.

## CHAPTER XVI. On the signs relating to clothing

For the sign of a woolen garment [Note: [Col. 0947D] *Stamineum*. See Du Cange], hold its sleeve with three fingers, namely, the little finger and the two next to it. For the sign of breeches, after making the general sign for linen cloth, draw the hand downward along the thigh, as someone putting on breeches. For the sign of a *froccus*, hold its sleeve in the same way as the sleeve of the *stamineum* is to be held.

For the sign of a fur garment, spread all the fingers of one hand and, placing them on the chest, draw them together as someone tightening wool [Col. 0947B]. For the sign of a *gunella* [Note: [Col. 0947D] *Gunella*, a diminutive of *guna*, signifying a fur garment], after making the sign for a *froccus*, add the sign for the *subtile* [Note: [Col. 0947D] The *subtile* is the subdeacons’ garment, also called a close-fitting tunic], but omit the sign of the cross.

For the sign of shoes, rotate one finger around another, as someone tying shoes with a lace, adding the sign for day. For the sign of night shoes, add this: place the hand against the cheek as a sleeping person does. For the sign of socks, make the same sign as for shoes, and add this: hold the sleeve of a *froccus* with the fingers.

For the sign of woolly socks, commonly called *Cucinga*, make the same sign previously given for daytime shoes, adding the sign for a fur garment. For the sign of felt shoes [Note: [Col. 0948D] Felt shoes], likewise make the sign for shoes, adding this: touch the left hand with two fingers where it is thicker.

For the sign of bandages, after making the established sign for shoes [Col. 0947C], add this: rotate both index fingers around the shin. For the sign of coverings [Note: [Col. 0948D] Read *coopertorium* for *coopertorum*; this is how it is read in the manuscript of Saint Victor], make the same sign as for a fur garment, and add this: draw the hand downward again along the arm, as someone covering himself with a covering.

For the sign of a quilt [Note: [Col. 0948D] *Cottum*, *cotus*, a mattress], draw the hand along the arm in the same way as above, and add this: hold the sleeve of a *froccus* with the fingers; place the outer side of the hand beneath the chin; move the index finger and the one next to it slightly downward, which is the sign for a goat; then add the sign for spreading out.

For the sign of a bedcover [Note: [Col. 0948D] *Stragula*, here a coarse woolen cloth spread over a mattress, still used by reformed monks], which is placed beneath one and is called a *Lena* by Saint Benedict (*Rule*, chapter 55, section 17), first make the sign for a *froccus*, then that for sleeping, and finally spread the hand by moving it; this is the sign for spreading out something wrapped up.

For the sign of a pillow [Col. 0947D], commonly called a *Cussinum*, raise the hand and move the bent fingertips as though flying; afterward place the hand against the cheek, as a sleeping person does. For the sign of a mattress, do the same, adding the sign for spreading out.

For the sign of a belt, or a strap for the *stamineum*, rotate one finger around another, and bring together the fingers of both hands from either side, as someone girding himself with a strap. For the sign of a belt for breeches, make the same sign, and add this: draw the hand downward along the thigh, because this belt must be inserted into the breeches and leggings [Col. 0948A].

For the sign of a needle, strike fist against fist, which signifies metal; then pretend to hold thread in one hand and a needle in the other, and to be about to pass the thread through the eye of the needle. For the sign of a knife, draw the hand across the middle of the other palm, as someone cutting something with a knife. For the sign of its sheath, thrust the edge of the right hand along the length of the other hand, as someone putting a knife into its sheath.

For the sign of a comb, draw three fingers through the hair, as someone combing himself. For the sign of tablets on which people customarily write, after making the general sign for wood, spread out the left hand [Col. 0948B] and pretend to write upon it. For the sign of a tablet, after making the general sign for wood, interlace both hands and then pretend to unfold what has been interlaced. For the sign of a stylus, strike fist against fist and pretend to write with three fingers.

For the sign of *scalae* [ladders; Note: [Col. 0948D] *Scala* perhaps for *scilla*, or *skilla*, a small bell], after making the sign for metal, add this: close the end of the foot with two fingers, namely the middle and index fingers. For the sign of gloves, draw the right hand over the other and pretend, with extension, to put them on. For the sign of a stone, place the four bent fingers of the right hand against the temples, as though you wished to strike something with a stone.

## CHAPTER XVII. On the signs for ecclesiastical persons and objects

* For the sign of any other altar, first make the sign for any stone [Col. 0948C], and add the sign of the holy cross. For the special sign of the principal altar, after making the general sign, add this: raise all the fingers, separated and bent upward; this sometimes signifies something great.

For the sign of the altar of any virgin, after making the general sign, draw the index finger across the forehead from one eyebrow to the other; this is the sign for a virgin or woman. In the same way make the sign for the altar of Saint Mary, adding the signs for a king and for the cross.

For the sign of the altar of Saint Michael, after making the general sign, raise the hand and move the bent fingertips as though flying; this is the sign for angels, since they are believed to fly. For the sign of the altar of Saint John the Baptist, after making the general sign, place the hand on the neck because of his beheading; this is common to all who were martyrs only and not also bishops [Col. 0948D].

For the sign of the altar of Saint Peter, or of all the apostles, after making the general sign, draw the right hand downward from the right shoulder to the bottom of the chest, and in the same way from left to right, because of the likeness to the pallium worn by bishops; add this: with the hollow of the hand, pretend to make a crown on the head.

For the sign of bishops and confessors, after making the general sign, add the sign for the aforesaid pallium and, in addition, that for a pastoral staff [Col. 0949A]. For the sign of confessors who were not bishops, after making the general sign, add the sign for the pallium.

For the sign of the altar of Saint Paul the Apostle, after making the general sign, add this: make the index finger protrude slightly below the front hair, because he is reported to have been bald. For the sign of the altar of Saint Lawrence, after making the general sign, add the signs for heat and for a grating. For the sign of the altar of Saint Benedict, or of others who were abbots, after making the general sign, grasp with two fingers—the index and middle fingers—the hair hanging over the ear; this is also the sign for any abbot.

For the sign of the altar of the Holy Cross, place one index finger over the other and pretend to make the cross. For the sign of a reliquary, join the tips of all the fingers of both hands alternately, except the thumbs; then make the sign for martyrs and finally add the sign for a sheath [Col. 0949B].

For the sign of a chalice, make the sign for a drinking bowl with the left hand, and with the right hand above it express the sign of the cross. For the sign of a paten, place the tip of the index finger before the joint of the thumb, as though wishing to indicate its roundness. For the sign of an offering, the only difference is that you place the same index finger behind the aforesaid joint.

For the sign of a tube, or reed, from which we customarily receive the Lord’s blood, after making the sign for metal, apply the tip of the index finger to the mouth, as though you wished to drink from it. For the sign of a corporal, after making the general sign for linen cloth—that is, placing the fingers of both hands one over the other and drawing them back once and then a second time—add this: reverently bring the joined tips of the thumb and index finger to the mouth, with the other three fingers extended. This application of the fingers to the mouth is also the sign for receiving Communion.

For the sign of a cloth suited for offering, after making the general sign for cloth, add the kissing of the hand. With the same kiss, you will also make the sign for offering. For the sign of a thurible, after making the sign for metal, add this: pretend to move it slightly with three fingers.

For the sign of a candlestick, likewise after making the general sign for metal, add this: with three fingers separated from one another and turned downward, pretend to indicate feet. For the sign of an incense-box, bend the hands slightly and join them; then pretend to count denarii, which is the sign for silver; afterward touch the tip of the nose with two fingers [Col. 0949D], finally adding the sign . . . . .

For the sign of basins [Note: [Col. 0949D] *Bacinus*. Italian *bacino*, French *bacin*, from *bacca*, which signifies a vessel or pitcher], after making the general sign for metal, add the sign for a bowl.

## CHAPTER XVIII. On the signs for Masses and the Hours

* For the sign of Mass, make the sign of the cross with the extended hand. For the sign of a high Mass, add the sign for something great. Likewise, for the morning office, add the sign for a small thing. For the sign of a Mass for the dead, add this: draw the index finger obliquely across the throat [Col. 0950A], which is also the sign for the dead.

For the sign of the nocturnal Matins, make the sign of the cross, then the sign for sleeping, and finally that for something great. For the sign of the morning Lauds, likewise make these first two signs, and afterward add the sign for a small thing. For the sign of Prime, after making the sign of the cross, add this: join the tips of the thumb and index finger.

For the sign of Terce, after making the sign of the cross, add this: with the left hand extended, draw two fingers—the middle finger and the one next to it—along the length of the index finger. For the sign of Sext, make the sign at the nearest joint. For the sign of None, do the same at the next joint.

For the sign of Vespers, after making the signs of the cross and of something great, blow against a finger, which signifies not only heat but also day [Col. 0950B]. Then quickly unfold the slightly bent hand, which signifies something done or finished; for this reason it is added to this Hour, to show that the day has already ended.

For the sign of the collation, after making the sign for reading, join all the fingers together, signifying that all the brothers have gathered into one. For the sign of Compline, after making the sign of the cross, add the sign for sleeping.

## CHAPTER XIX. On the signs for priestly vestments

* For the sign of a cope, pretend with both hands to be holding it, and move them as though putting it on. For the sign of a chasuble, the only difference is that you add the sign of the cross to the aforesaid sign.

For the sign of an amice, after making the sign for linen cloth, add this: draw downward the hands placed on either side of the head [Col. 0950C]. For the sign of an alb, grasp the garment on the chest with three fingers and draw it downward slightly.

For the sign of a *fano*, or small cloth [Note: [Col. 0949D] Although *fano* denotes a cloth, here it is used for the maniple, since in ancient times sacred ministers carried a small linen cloth in the left hand. Otherwise *to fano*, *sindon*, *mappa*, from the German *Fahnen* or *Fanen*, a word still used for cloths hanging from poles [Col. 0950D]], draw the left sleeve, grasped beneath the arm, slightly downward.

For the sign of a dalmatic, make the aforesaid sign for the *fano*, adding the sign of the cross on the forehead. For the sign of a *subtile* [Note: [Col. 0950D] The *subtile* is the subdeacon’s garment. See above], tighten the left sleeve stretched around the arm, adding the sign of the cross on the chest.

For the sign of a pallium, after making the sign for cloth, add the sign for a good thing. For the sign of a curtain, first make the sign for cloth; then place the outer surfaces of the right hand over the inner surfaces of the other, immediately separate them evenly, and, as you separate them, raise them slightly, as though indicating something hanging [Col. 0950D].

For the sign of a hanging wall-cloth [Note: [Col. 0950D] *Dorsale*, a pallium or tapestry hung on walls, so called because it is hung behind the back of someone sitting], which is made of a pallium, first make the sign for a pallium and then, holding the hands in the manner described above, separate them as for a curtain. If it is made of wool, first make the sign for a *froccus*.

For the sign of tapestries, likewise hold the sleeve of a *froccus*, and after making the sign for a fur garment, draw the extended hand slowly away from the chest. Do the same for the sign of bench coverings [Note: [Col. 0950D] *Bancalis*, a covering for a bench or seat, a carpet spread over a stool or bench], but omit the sign for a fur garment.

For the sign of a festival, first make the sign for reading, and afterward extend all the fingers of both hands; then extend the index and middle fingers, with the others bent. For the sign of a mat [Note: [Col. 0951D] *Matta*, a mat or covering; the monks slept on mats], after making the general sign for herbs, hold the sleeve and add the sign for spreading out.

## CHAPTER XX. On the signs relating to divine service

* For the sign of reading, press the index finger against the hand and chest, and, after drawing it back slightly, make it spring forward, as someone turning over a page of a book. For the sign of a responsory, place the thumb beneath the joint of the index finger and make it spring forward. For the sign of a verse, place the thumb beneath the joint of the little finger and add to it the aforesaid motion of springing forward.

For the sign of an antiphon, join the tips of the thumb and little finger and draw the thumb slightly downward. For the sign of the Introit, extend the thumb and the finger next to it with their tips joined, apply the hand to the mouth, and finally add the sign for Mass [Col. 0951B].

For the sign of the Gloria, bend all the fingers of the right hand and apply that hand to the mouth, signifying singing. For the sign of the Alleluia, raise the hand and move the bent fingertips as though flying, because it is believed to be sung by the angels in heaven.

For the sign of the Prose [Note: [Col. 0951D] The ritual books of the Church call the prayer sung at Mass before the Gospel on major feasts a *prose*, or sequence], which some call the Sequence, raise the inclined hand, and, moving it away from the chest, turn it over so that what was previously uppermost becomes lowermost.

For the sign of a responsory, draw the hand downward across the belly, signifying that it is always performed in a drawn-out manner, and apply the hand to the mouth in the aforesaid way. For the sign of the Offertory, after making the general sign for the song of offering, add the sign [Col. 0951C]. For the sign of Communion, likewise after making the general sign for singing, add the sign for receiving Communion.

## CHAPTER XXI. On the signs for books

* The general sign for books is to extend the hand and move it as a book’s page is accustomed to move. For the sign of the Missal, after making the general sign, add this: draw the extended right hand through the space between the thumb and index finger of the other hand, as though filing iron. This also applies to anything that we have in abundance.

For the sign of the Epistolary, add this to the general sign: make the sign of the cross on the chest. For the sign of the Gospel book, after making the general sign, add this: make the sign of the cross on the forehead.

For the sign of the book from which one reads at Nocturns [Col. 0951D], after making the general signs for a book and for reading, add this: place the hand against the cheek. For the sign of an antiphonary, after making the general sign for a book, bend all the fingers of the right hand because of the neumes [Note: [Col. 0951D] *Neuma*, a jubilus, an extension of the chant on the final letter of an antiphon]; afterward make the thumb spring forward from the middle joint of the index finger.

For the sign of a Gradual, bend all the fingers in the same way as was described above [Col. 0952A]. For the sign of the Rule, after making the general sign, add this: grasp with two fingers the hair hanging over the ear [Note: [Col. 0951D] From this passage you may infer that the monks’ hair was not shaved completely. Add to this the fact that combs were allowed for their use, as will be evident from what follows [Col. 0952D]], because of the two names by which an abbot is called, namely *abbot* and *lord*; Saint Benedict was both the author of this Rule and the holder of this office.

For the sign of a hymnary, after making the general sign, add this: extend the thumb and index finger of the right hand and join their tips, signifying the present time or what comes first. This sign was devised for the hymnary solely because of the word *primo*—“first”—found in it: “First of the days.”

For the sign of a Psalter, after making the general sign, add this: place the fingertips of the right hand, held hollow, on the head, because of the likeness to the crown customarily worn by a king, since David, the author of the psalms, was a king [Col. 0952B].

For the sign of the book of the prophets, after making the general sign, add this: draw the straight hand through the hair toward the right ear, signifying old age. For the sign of a library, after making the general sign, add this: extend all the fingers of both hands. For the sign of Paul’s letters, after making the general sign, add the sign for baldness.

For the sign of the books of Job, after making the general sign, hold the chin with the right hand; then place the same right hand, spread out, upon the chest, which is the sign for illness. For the sign of a Glossary, after making the general sign, add the sign for reading; then join all the fingers of the right hand together, signifying that all the brothers have gathered.

For the sign of a book of sequences, after making the general sign, add the sign for a martyr. For the sign of a Breviary, after making the general sign, draw the index finger obliquely across the nose, pretending to cut off something [Col. 0952C]. For the sign of a book of customs, after making the general sign, press the garment against the chest.

For the sign of parchment, after making the general sign for books, add this: with the fingers of both hands joined, rotate one hand around the other; this is also the sign for signs. For the sign of a roll [Note: [Col. 0952D] *Rotula*, a roll, sheet, or document rolled up in the form of a little wheel or disk], rotate one finger around another and then pretend to write.

For the sign of a brief [Note: [Col. 0952D] *Brevis*, an inventory or document containing an index, and so forth], bend the first joints of the four fingers, and likewise pretend to write. For the sign of a Martyrology, quickly draw the tip of the thumb across the tips of the other fingers of the right hand as though counting, beginning with the little finger.

For the sign of a secular book, composed by some pagan, after making the general sign for a book, add this: touch the ear with a finger, as a dog does when it scratches an itch with its paw. Not without reason is an unbeliever compared with such an animal; this is also the sign for a dog.

For the sign of a lectern [Note: [Col. 0952D] *Analogium*, a pulpit or ambo], after making the sign for wood, join the hands together, simultaneously bent, and hold their inner surfaces facing the face. For the sign of a wooden object made for holding a light, extend the left hand with its inner surface turned upward, and raise the other hand above it at the joint of the hand and arm, as you see the instrument itself constructed; add the sign for light [Col. 0953A].

For the sign of a formula, after making the sign for wood, extend the empty hand and make the sign for prostrating oneself on the ground; this is also the sign for pardon.

## CHAPTER XXII. On the signs for persons

* For the sign of the lord abbot, make the same sign previously given for the Rule. For the sign of a monk, hold the hair of the cowl with the hand. For the sign of a recluse, add the sign for a window, that is, the sign for brightness.

For the sign of a monk who was brought up in the monastery, after making the general sign, bring the little finger to the lips, because an infant sucks in this way. For the sign of a prior, pretend with two fingers to hold a small bell [Col. 0953B], and make it sound in this way. For the sign of the Major, add the sign for something great.

For the sign of the cloister prior, after making the general sign, turn the index finger downward and rotate it as though turning around. For the sign of his assistant, likewise after making the general sign, extend the little finger, because it always signifies a small thing.

For the sign of the armarius and precentor, after making the general sign, add the signs for singing and striking, because during the twelve lessons, at the High Mass whose office is his, he begins by striking the first small bell. For the sign of the circuitor [Note: [Col. 0953] The *circatores* were those responsible for going around the monastery; their office will be explained more fully in book II], after making the general sign for a monk, extend the index finger in the manner described above.

For the sign of the church custodian, after making the general sign, pretend with the hand to sound a bell. For the sign of the chamberlain [Col. 0953C], after making the general sign, pretend to count coins. For the sign of the cellarer, after making the general sign, pretend to hold a key in the hand and insert it into a lock.

For the sign of the granary keeper, who receives and stores grain, pretend with both hands to be putting grain into a vessel for measuring. For the sign of the gardener, after making the general sign, bend and draw the index finger as someone pulling a rake across the ground.

For the sign of the guest-master, where wealthier guests are received, after making the general sign, pretend to draw a sword from the hand. For the sign of the almoner, who receives the poor, draw the hand from the left shoulder to the right side, as a beggar’s bag strap is customarily worn.

For the sign of the infirmarian, who attends to the sick, after making the general sign, add the sign for illness [Col. 0953D]. For the sign of the refectorer, after making the general sign, make the sign for refreshment.

For the sign of the guardians of the young, after making the general sign, bring the little finger near, which is the sign for a youth, and place the index finger at the eye, which is the sign for seeing. For the sign of the novice-master, draw the hand obliquely through the hair toward the forehead, which is the sign for a novice and for something new, and add the sign for seeing.

For the sign of someone well educated, or also for the sign of knowing, rub the chest slightly with the tip of the index finger. For the sign of the provost, after making the general sign, make the index finger protrude at the forehead, which is the sign for an ox, because he is the provider for such persons [Col. 0954A].

For the sign of the master of the masons, after making the general sign, place one fist upon the other in turn, as though pretending to build a wall. For the sign of an old man, draw the straight hand over the hair toward the right ear.

For the sign of the marshal, hold the front hair with two fingers, because of the manes horses have. This is also the sign for a horse. For the sign of the keeper of asses, place the tip of the thumb at the ear and move the other fingers extended, as an ass moves its ear, adding the sign for seeing.

For the sign of a fellow countryman or relative, hold the hand before the face, placing the middle finger on the nose, because blood sometimes flows from there. For the sign of a father, after making the same sign, add the sign for an old man. For the sign of a brother, likewise after making the sign for kinship, add the sign for a small thing.

For the sign of a mother [Col. 0954B], do the same, adding the sign for a woman. For the sign of a sister, do the same as for a mother, adding the sign for a small thing. For the sign of a cleric, rotate a finger around the ear, as though turning it, because of the likeness to the crown that a cleric wears on his head.

For the sign of a layman, hold the chin with the right hand as though pulling a beard. For the sign of a man who speaks another language, touch the lips with a finger, because of speech. For the sign of a shoemaker, after making the sign for a layman, place the right index finger over the left index finger in the shape of a cross, and, moving them as someone making a hole with an awl, pretend to sew.

## CHAPTER XXIII. On the signs for various things
* For the sign for **everything**, grasp the hair at the forehead. For the sign for **speaking**, hold the right hand before the mouth and move it in that manner; this is also the sign for **reading**. For the sign for **hearing**, hold the index finger toward the ear. For the sign for **not knowing**, touch the lips with the raised index finger. For the sign for **forgetting**, move the index finger from the right ear to the left. For the sign for **lying**, draw the index finger placed over the lips. For the sign for **kissing**, place the index finger on the lips. For the sign for **a discarded custom**, or another forbidden thing, or something that has already ceased, let the right index finger pass before the tip of the left, as though pretending to cut something off with a knife. For the sign for **putting on clothing**, especially the alb, draw the hand downward across the chest. For the sign for **taking off the garment** that you are wearing, draw it away from the chest with thumb and index finger. For the sign for **removing footwear**, first make the sign for the strap, then add the sign for taking off clothing. For the sign for **washing the feet**, press the inner surfaces of both hands together and rub them slightly, pretending to wash. For the sign for **good**, whatever you have said is good and beautiful, place the thumb against the cheek and the next two fingers against the other cheek, and gently bring them together at the point of the chin. For the sign for **evil**, with the fingers spread and placed against the face, pretend to draw back a fingernail as a bird tearing at something. For the sign for **indicating**, or **bringing something**, move the four fingers toward the face in the customary manner. For the sign for **negation**, place the tip of the middle finger against the thumb and make it spring forward. For the sign for **speed**, extend the right hand and place it over the left in the manner of a bolt, moving it quickly as though drawing a bolt. For the sign for **handing over**, draw the hand gradually from the navel across the belly. For the sign for **being angry**, pretend to scratch with four fingers. For the sign for **committing a fault**, with the fingers of the right hand held evenly together, strike the chest as though being pierced with penitence, adding this: touch the chest again with the index finger, as though accusing yourself. But if you wish to accuse someone else, after striking your own chest, turn the index finger toward him, as though showing that he has sinned. For the sign of **anything that has been done**, hold the right hand slightly bent toward the chest, with its inner surface turned upward, and quickly roll it upward. For the sign for **doing something willingly**, grasp the dangling flesh beneath the chin with two fingers. For the sign for **likeness**, draw the outer side of the right hand downward along the right cheek, then do the same with the inner side along the left. For the sign for **dividing**, draw two fingers—that is, the index and middle fingers—through the middle of the left hand. This is also the sign for **chants**. For the sign for **anointing the sick**, after making the sign for sickness, make the sign of the cross with the thumb in the middle of the palm. For the sign for **weeping**, draw the index finger downward twice beneath the eye. For the sign for **someone’s name**, if you ask, “What are you called?”, touch the head on the right side with the tip of the index finger, then move the hand, extended toward the person whom you are questioning, a little; this is always the sign for asking. For the sign for **extinguishing a light**, after making the sign for light, add the sign for the dead: draw the index finger diagonally across the throat. For the sign for **a cemetery**, draw the bent index finger toward yourself, and likewise add the sign for the dead.

## CHAPTER XXIV. Signs for buildings

* For the sign for **any building**, join and raise the fingertips together, then separate the hands below, as though wishing to represent the shape of a roof. For the sign for a **church**, after making the general sign, add the sign of the cross. For the sign for a **chapter house** [*Capitolium* is used for *Capitulum*, or the place where the monks gathered to conduct matters of monastic discipline], after making the general sign, add the sign that you make for asking pardon. For the sign for an **auditorium**, after making the general sign, place the index finger against the ear; this is the sign for conversing or hearing. For the sign for a **dormitory**, after making the general sign, add the sign for sleeping. For the sign for a **refectory**, after making the general sign, add the sign for eating. For the sign for a **latrine** [*necessarium*], after making the general sign, draw the index finger downward after placing it against the belly. For the sign for a **warming room**, add the sign for heat. For the sign for a **chamber**, after making the general sign, add the sign for counting. For the sign for an **infirmary**, add the sign for being ill. For the sign for a **kitchen**, after making the general sign, add the signs for heat and eating, to distinguish it from the warming room. For the sign for a **library** [*armarium* is used for a library; hence *armarius*, the librarian or prefect of the library, about whom Book II deals here], add the sign for a book. For the sign for a **cloister**, after making the general sign, turn the index finger downward and around; this is the sign for going around. For the sign for the **novices’ cell**, after making the general sign, add the sign for something new. For the sign for a **procession**, place the index finger over the index finger in the form of a cross, adding the sign for going around. For the sign for **wax**, with the hands held level with each other, pretend to make candles. For the sign for a **candle**, do the same, adding the sign for heat. For the sign for a **large candle**, first make the sign for wax, then clasp the left arm with the right hand. For the sign for a **candle twisted into a circle**, after making the general sign, circle the index finger around the left hand, adding the sign for heat. For the sign for a **lantern**, after making the general sign for justice, add the sign for brightness. For the sign for a **hidden lamp**, make the sign for justice and heat, then add the sign for heat.

* For the sign for a **writing room**, after making the general sign for wood, place the extended hands evenly upon both knees, adding the sign for writing. For the sign for **ink** [*holocaustum* is used for *encaustum*, ink], after making the general sign for water, add the sign for writing. For the sign for **red ink**, make the sign for the color red, and likewise add the sign for writing. For the sign for **pumice**, make the general sign for stone, then with the right fist against the inner part of the extended left hand, pretend to clean parchment. For the sign for a **pen**, after making the sign for flying, add the sign for writing again. For the sign for a **compass**, place the right index finger in the middle of the left hand and move the middle finger around it.

## CHAPTER XXV. Signs for tools

* For the sign for an **iron tool made for preparing altar-breads**, after making the general sign for metal, join the outer sides of both hands together and then separate them again. For the sign for **tongs**, make the general sign for metal, then join the index and middle fingers, which were first separated. For the sign for a **razor**, or **shaving knife**, after making the sign for a knife, place the right index finger over the left in the form of a cross, pretending to sharpen it against the latter. For the sign for an **axe**, **adze**, **billhook**, **auger**, or **plane**, after making the sign for metal, pretend as suitably as possible to be working with the tool in question. For the sign for an **awl**, after making the sign for metal, place the right index finger over the left in the form of a cross and move it, pretending to pierce with an awl. For the sign for **gold**, after making the sign for metal, add the sign for red. For the sign for **silver**, after making the general sign, pretend to count pennies. For the sign for **bronze**, after making the sign for gold, add the sign for measuring. For the sign for **tin**, after making the sign for silver, add, as above, the sign for measuring. For the sign for **lead**, after making the general sign, add the sign for thick. For the sign for a **bit**, after making the general sign for metal, extend the middle finger toward the open mouth, with the other fingers folded. For the sign for a **saddle**, strike the left shoulder twice with the right hand, adding the sign for a horse. For the sign for a **staff**, after making the sign for wood, bring forward the right hand closed into a fist, as though holding the staff itself. For the sign for a **seal**, after making the sign for short, close the right fist within the left hand, as one who impresses a seal in wax. For the sign for a **cauldron**, after making the sign for metal, hold both hands curved upward toward one another. For the sign for the **iron from which a cauldron is suspended**, join both index fingers together in the manner of a chain. For the sign for a **frying pan**, after making the sign, draw the right hand upward from the joint of the left hand along the arm. For the sign for a **metal pot**, after making the general sign for metal, add the sign for justice; but if it is made of clay, after making the general sign for justice, draw the bent index finger toward yourself, which is the sign for earth. For the sign for a **fork**, after making the general sign for metal, with the index finger and the finger next to it bent, pretend to draw meat with it. For the sign for **tongs**, place the index finger over the inverted index finger and move both in the manner of that tool. For the sign for a **snuffer**, extend the index and middle fingers apart, after making the general sign, and add the sign for light. For the sign for a **cymbal**, after making the general sign, pretend to strike it with a hammer. For the sign for a **talking board**, which is struck in order to speak, after making the sign for wood, pretend to strike it. For the sign for **laughing**, extend the index and middle fingers apart toward the mouth. For the sign for **blood flowing from the nose**, after making the sign for kinship, rub beneath the nose with the bent index finger, as blood ordinarily flows. For the sign for **vomiting**, place the inverted right hand beneath the chin and move it rapidly through the air. For the sign for a **horse**, grasp the forelock with two fingers. For the sign for a **donkey**, place the tip of the thumb against the ear and move the other fingers extended, like a donkey’s ear. For the sign for a **mule**, after making the sign for a horse, add the sign for a donkey. For the sign for a **sheep**, with two fingers pretend to shear sheep with a pair of shears. For the sign for a **ram**, add this: hold the bent index finger beside the right ear. For the sign for a **goat**, place the outer sides of the hands beneath the chin and move the adjoining fingers slightly downward toward each other. For the sign for a **pig**, press the fist against the forehead. For the sign for a **cat**, pretend with the fingers to arrange the *grenones* [the beard beneath the nose, that is, the moustache; this has already been explained above]. For the sign for a **stag**, make all the fingers of both hands protrude like horns. For the sign for a **hare**, extend the index finger and the finger next to it backward beside the ear, and move them like a hare’s ears.

And, to bring such matters to a conclusion, whatever you wish to indicate, always first make the general sign and then add what follows. With these instructions for the education of novices set out, the discipline that must continually be observed by one who wishes to live in community with us must now be given in order.

## CHAPTER XXVI. How a brother should rise for nocturns, and how he should pray

(UD. var.) First, then, when he hears the signal for nocturns, he hastens to rise immediately. Before throwing off the bedcover, while sitting on the bed he puts on the cuculla and covers his legs with it before getting up from the bed. After he has risen, he may, if he wishes, put on another fur garment over the cuculla while standing, but secretly. He does not leave the bed carelessly either (UD.), but arranges it properly by spreading the bedcover over it. He hides the entire pillow beneath it, then puts on the froccus; and, if necessary, he does not neglect to wake with a sound the two brothers sleeping nearest to him. For if they are not awakened by him and do not take part in the common prayer of the brothers, when they ask pardon in the chapter house the following day in the customary manner, he too asks pardon. If he is asked, “Who slept nearby?”, he must do the same. He must act likewise when the brothers take their midday rest [that is, sleep after midday; hence they said *facere Meridianam*, “to sleep at midday”].

(UD.) In summer he does not enter the latrine unless he covers his head with a cap. In the dormitory, however, neither by day nor by night does he observe this rule, except after compline, if he wishes.

He must always remember not to spit on the dormitory steps. He must not place any of his clothing in the cloister before the three prayers have been completed. He must not look at the board or antiphonary. He usually comes into the church before the boys—or, if they are not there, before the young man who follows the brothers last with the lantern—having first washed his hands if necessary, or if he must dress for the invitatory. While the bell is being rung, he lies prostrate; or, if it is a day on which one bows, he prays for whatever he wishes. Each person receives his place in this order according to the time of his conversion.

If he is a novice, whether he is a monk or is not yet consecrated, he has his place among his peers at the steps [*comparēs* should be read, not *compatres*, as the manuscript erroneously has]. A space is left beside them near the steps, through which one may go to the other side of the choir. The steps . . . those who are to occupy the rear of the choir usually enter through the lesser choir.

If he is a young man, he places himself with his custodian between the choir stalls [*forma*: a seat, bench, or singers’ stall in the choir], behind the novices, with other brothers also interspersed according to their rank. Each of those who usually pray between the stalls, not only at this time but also at any other, must, whenever possible, take care to pray in that part of the choir to which he has been assigned. The order of the young men with their custodians in every place is more fully found in the chapter concerning both groups written in the following book (Book II, chapter 22).

[Col. 0958D] But if he is one of those of higher rank, he has a place in one of the seats along the walls. If he is one of the seniors, he occupies either of the western enclosures. When prayer is made prostrate, he is supported upon the bench placed before his feet. If he has a place at the right-hand wall, he lies somewhat crosswise upon the seat. If at the left, he places his forearms upon the bench, likewise turned toward the right side. At neither wall, however, whether prayer is made standing or prostrate, does he ever have another person beside him.

Whenever prayer is made standing, a brother, if he is somewhat weak, is not forbidden to use a support, but only until the bell is dismissed. If he is weaker and is literate, he may sit within the same space in the lesser choir, but in a more secluded part. Nevertheless, after the signal for the three prayers has been given, he must attend the choir if he is able despite the crowd, whether then in his own place or wherever he can stand. If he is illiterate, he sits outside the choir for the time being, but away from the sight of those entering.

If a weaker young man begins to stand in the choir for prayer, he remains until after the three prayers, and then, having received permission by the sign for sickness, he enters the lesser choir without his custodian. But if his custodian perceives that he is suffering from such severe weakness that he cannot possibly endure this interval in the choir, as soon as he has entered the church he leads him through the greater choir into the lesser choir. They remain there until the bells are dismissed: the young man sits, while the custodian beside him bows for prayer. After they have made the three prayers standing, the young man, having received permission as stated above, remains there, while the custodian withdraws to his own station.

The young man who follows the community from the dormitory, and at whose entrance the bell is dismissed, extinguishes the light he has brought, places the lantern on the step, and, if he does not see a place among the other young men for prayer, stations himself with his custodian in the middle of the space previously said to have been left beside the novices, for the three prayers, so that if anyone enters after him he may be able to find a place for prayer.

When praying prostrate, he draws the froccus behind him over his elbows and knees, so that it does not hang down over his feet to the ground. The manner of this prayer is ordinarily such that each brother can sing the prayers slowly on each occasion. If this is carefully observed, whenever three prayers are performed by the brothers together or individually, except at compline, when each is completed more quickly, then, after each person has prayed standing or prostrate during the ringing of the bell, he makes the first prayer in his place; for the second he withdraws slightly to the left; for the third he returns again to his previous place—provided that the place is one where this alternation of withdrawals can be observed, such as between the walls and the stalls.

Where they are so crowded that no one can turn aside to either side, they are exempt from this rule. Thus, at the first two occurrences of this prayer, when the signal has been made by the one before him, each person rises, and standing in the same place makes the sign of the holy cross and bows. At the third occurrence, after rising and blessing himself, wherever he is standing, if he has room, he moves a little to the left, makes the movement forward and backward, and observes this for all prayers that he performs either alone or together with the assembled community.

## CHAPTER XXVII. That he must attend the same prayers that are made before nocturns

He must be careful to attend these three prayers, which, as has been said, are made after the signal has been dismissed. For if he has not attended them, or at least the last of them, he asks pardon in the chapter house. But if he was not present in the choir for the first prayer, he may attend the remaining two, provided that he does not then cross to the other choir; nevertheless, he must not make a practice of this. He does not enter for the third, but makes it before the choir beforehand, and will be free from asking pardon. However, if he makes a practice even of this, he is called to account.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. Concerning the brother who, after the three prayers have ended, goes through the beds in the dormitory and visits the brothers outside the choir

* When these three prayers have ended, the brother appointed for this task—who sleeps above the dormitory near the doorway, closing and opening it at the proper times—lights the hidden lamp that he brought with him from the dormitory. Returning there in place of the cloisterer prior, he carefully inspects the brothers’ beds, and if he finds anyone uncovered or carelessly covered, he leaves him in that disorder and will publicly report this negligence in the chapter house. If he finds anyone asleep there or in the latrine, which he also inspects at that time, he wakes him with a sound.

Then he goes by the direct route through the lesser choir to the sacristy, to the beds of the church custodians, and does the same there. Returning by the same way, he first inspects those who are in the lesser choir and all those who are staying anywhere outside the choir. If he sees any of them asleep after having been bled [*phlebotomi minuti*, those who have been bled, or have had blood removed; such persons are mentioned several times in these Constitutions], he wakes them from sleep by drawing the hidden lamp noisily upward from their shoulder against the wall.

If he sees a literate brother among the conversi, he indicates to him that he should enter the lesser choir and join the other literate brothers. If he does not promptly obey him, or does not indicate an illness preventing him from doing so, he will call him to account in the chapter house.

If he finds a stronger conversus separated from his peers among the weaker brothers, hidden away in some more remote place, he makes him go to the other conversi [lay monks, devoted to lay work and to the service of the monks, are called *conversi*], who are on the outer side of the wall to the right of the choir—provided that he can find a place among them. For there too the arrangement of the seats is as it is below in the choir.

And whatever stronger conversi are habitually unable, because of their number, to be in the choir remain outside according to the same discipline as within, whether standing or sitting, but only in the row along that same wall. If any still remain, let them choose a station for themselves wherever they please; they are not constrained, for they are not forbidden to sit together. Whoever is conscious of possessing such strength joins himself to the wall of his own accord. But whoever distrusts his strength for this does not fail to let the others stand there.

Whatever any one of them does contrary to the order of his group must be reported to the others, and especially to the circator mentioned above, so that it may be brought to the chapter house. He, as stated, after inspecting with the hidden lamp whatever is outside the choir, places it on the altar beside the church door, where it remains until he again makes his circuit with it at the two final psalms of the second nocturn and at the last psalm of matins. Then he first goes to those in the lesser choir, passes through it toward the left to those altars, and, returning by the same way, goes to those who are everywhere outside the choir.

This hidden lamp is not the one with which the choir is inspected between the lessons, but the one that the cloisterer prior placed after compline beside the light illuminating the dormitory and the passage leading to the latrine.

## CHAPTER XXIX. How a brother should conduct himself during the psalms recited after the prayers mentioned above

After the three prayers mentioned above, fifteen Gradual Psalms, or thirty psalms, are recited, if it is a day on which they must not pray prostrate. At the divisions of those same fifteen Gradual Psalms [*incisiones*: cuts, sections, chapters], those who sit on the stalls usually raise themselves gently by extending a hand and turning slightly backward for this purpose, and lower themselves in the same manner to avoid making a noise. Each of them must observe this whenever he sits, either alone or with others.

Those who sit on the benches placed below the stalls do not then support themselves backward, nor do they ever do so; rather, while sitting, they lean forward as far as they can. Whenever anyone has a misericord [*misericordiae*: small seats attached to the raised choir stalls, on which the elderly or infirm are permitted to sit as an act of mercy while the others stand], he supports himself there, as at the *Gloria Patri*. At that time the others stand bowed without support.

When all must remain bowed for a longer time, as at the prayers and intercessions, these men sit on the benches as stated above, likewise leaning forward. When those on the stalls bow, those standing before the stalls lie upon the stools placed before them. As many of those who are senior as go up to the line that has been designated and prostrate themselves upon the transverse stalls facing the altar, the others who remain prostrate themselves upon the seats along that same line. If any of those who have fixed stations still remain, they sit at the step and prostrate themselves.

At nocturns, if they cannot suitably be in the choir, they withdraw outside. For it is always avoided that they stand behind the stalls before those who have places along the walls. It should be noted that no one performs those three prayers made prostrate after compline outside the stalls or walls, except the prior alone with his two assistants.

A similar order must be observed by everyone at both Masses within the Canon, at the verse that follows after dinner, and also at the prayer performed on Wednesday and Friday before the procession. This too must be observed: whenever those standing at the enclosures and walls prostrate themselves upon the stalls, the outermost among them withdraw sufficiently to prostrate themselves, so that those senior to them can lie upon the stalls.

Whether it is a time for praying standing or prostrate, while the psalms mentioned above are being sung, a brother who has to go to the dormitory—and who, if he wishes, may inspect the board and antiphonary while passing—may do so. Nevertheless, if he fears being called to account, he takes the greatest care to do this rarely.

But none of those placed under supervision [those placed under the authority or discipline of a veteran monk] is permitted to go out at that time, unless some unavoidable necessity suddenly overtakes him that absolutely cannot be postponed until the end of the same psalmody. Whenever this occurs, he does not leave the choir before the entire community has sat down.

No one may leave merely to inspect the board or book, except the librarian, and those who sometimes leave the choir at the beginning of the psalm *De profundis* to dress for the invitatory. They themselves, however, bring the antiphonary into the vesting room, so that they may ascertain beforehand what they must sing at that time.

Moreover, since no one assigned to any office is permitted to neglect looking beforehand on the preceding day to see what he must do at nocturns, if anyone is found, through his own negligence, not to have arranged this but to have postponed it until nighttime, and to make a practice of this, he will undoubtedly be subject to public rebuke.

However, if someone had prudently taken care of this beforehand but perhaps consigned it to forgetfulness during the course of the night, or if he wishes to perform an office for another brother who asked him at this nocturnal hour to do so—although no one ought to have been interrupted about this unless necessity compelled it—he may briefly look at what he wants either during the fifteen Gradual Psalms, in the order stated above, or afterward, whenever it is convenient. But he also takes care not to do this frequently, if he is concerned to avoid being called to account.

Everyone must know this: he must not obtain a substitute for a lesson unless it is someone who has not been marked down for either of these two duties. For according to custom no one is assigned to perform both offices in a single night. If, however, there is an adequate supply of such persons for the reader and the cantor . . . .

Since the book and the board mentioned above are placed in each location, divided between the two—the board before the church, the book inside—no more than two brothers ever stand at either of them at once, nor do those two stand so close together that they can inspect the same thing simultaneously. When one withdraws, another takes his place in order to look.

He does not preview at this time the lesson that he must read at nocturns. Meanwhile, when two or more signals are sounded for nocturns after the aforementioned psalms, those who have fixed positions remain there. Those who had first been sitting at the steps stand there in their proper order, if it is a day on which they prostrate themselves, until they prostrate themselves there together; then all or some of them, if they cannot remain standing inside, leave the choir. But if it is not a day for prostration, as soon as those same psalms have ended they take their places inside, if they can; otherwise they withdraw.

## CHAPTER XXX. Concerning one who enters the choir at the *Gloria*, or after the *Gloria*

* Whoever comes to the beginning of the Work of God so late that at the *Gloria* of the first verse he can be not in his own place but only at the very entrance of the choir does not prostrate himself or bow there with the others, unless he has a place at that extreme end. But when the nocturnal office, or any other Hour, begins with bowing, he must come to his own place, if he can, before it begins as it did.

If, however, he comes to his station after the psalm has begun—or, if it is a hymn, after it has begun—he bows deeply upon reaching his station. If the same office begins with prostration and he has a place near the wall at the aforementioned entrance, while those beside him are lying prostrate he does not go behind them to his own seat; instead, he waits beside the end. As soon as they rise from the stall, he prostrates himself upon that same stall, as near as possible to his own seat, taking care to place himself together with them in his proper place.

If his station is at the wall of the other choir, or somewhere among the stalls, he prostrates himself with the others at the step; or, if they are so numerous, he may prostrate himself behind them. If he has a place at the western enclosures, he can indeed reach his seat there behind those who are prostrate, since the way is short.

If he cannot reach the end of the choir during the same interval in which pardon is sought, he does not prostrate himself among those outside the choir. Instead, while passing through, as was stated concerning one who bows, he asks pardon before bowing.

But if he enters the church near the end of the first psalm, as at nocturns, vespers, and compline, or at the other Hours near the end of the hymn, he observes this manner of entering the choir: after first asking pardon, he begins to bow with the others at the *Gloria Patri*—or, if it is a hymn, at its final verse—or, if he has neglected this, he at least takes care, after asking pardon, to bow with them before they rise.

To return to the nocturnal office: after he has once entered the choir, he does not withdraw merely for the purpose of sitting. The beginning of this church office is observed with such reverence that, once the signals begin to be sounded, no one who is in the lesser choir sits until the nocturnal psalms begin, except one burdened by serious illness. Nor does anyone sit in that part of the church which lies to the right of the choir. If one of those who are in that part is unable to stand at that time because of illness, he withdraws from the sight of those passing by.

## CHAPTER XXXI. Concerning one who does not enter for nocturns because of illness

* Whoever is taken ill during the night and cannot enter the choir, as soon as he comes from the dormitory chooses for himself a suitable place in the church where he may rest afterward. But whoever, after entering the choir, feels his illness increasing so that he does not expect to be able to remain inside withdraws outside without permission. For this reason he does not make the movement forward and backward, nor does he signal to the person standing beside him to ascend into his place.

If within five or six psalms he recovers sufficiently to hope that he can remain in the choir thereafter, he returns. But if he remains outside longer, even if he recovers, he enters the choir neither for matins nor, if prime follows immediately, for prime. After his station has appeared vacant once as many psalms have ended as were mentioned above, his neighbor, despairing of the brother’s return, occupies it. For no one who intends to return will remain outside the choir longer than this number of psalms, except when blood is flowing.

Any such sick person who is literate, and hopes that he can be of some assistance to the others in singing, chooses a seat for himself in the lesser choir in such a place that he can sit continuously, except at the *Benedictus* and *Magnificat*. If he is an assigned literate brother for a lesson, responsory, or antiphon, he performs that office himself if he can; otherwise he appoints a substitute. He does not sing the responsory that follows the *Gloria Patri*, even if he is strong enough for this. If it is to be sung by one person, he asks another to sing it in his place; but if he must sing it with another and is able to do so, he comes into the choir to his own place to sing it, and then returns.

But if he does not hope to be of any assistance to the others, then, so as not to become a burden to them in any way, he places himself outside in a suitable location. For this purpose he does not put on the cap, but he may nevertheless bow toward the ground.

On that night, if the brother carrying the hidden lamp either knows of his illness himself or has learned of it from someone else, he does not present the lamp to him. But if, unaware that he is ill, he has placed it beside the sleeping man, the sick brother himself, or the person sitting beside him, must carry it around voluntarily or at his request; otherwise he will be called to account.

After that night, for as long as he sits before the choir, the hidden lamp is placed beside him whenever he is found sleeping. Whether he is the one who entered the choir because of illness, or the one who left it, he asks pardon the following day: the former by saying, “At night I was outside the choir because of my illness”; the latter, “I did not enter because of my illness.”

When the prior asks him whether he is feeling better, if he answers, “Yes, my lord,” he is ordered to go and sit; but if he says, “No,” he is ordered to remain outside the choir for a while. And if he is one who, because of illness, was unable to be nourished from the common food of the brothers, the cellarer is instructed for the present to care for him in the refectory.

Afterward he will sit in the place suitable to his illness, whether in the lesser choir or outside. If his illness is one that he can overcome through the rest granted to him, as soon as he has recovered his strength more fully within the week, he will enter the choir either at terce or at prime, which precedes the chapter house, or at the preceding evening’s twelve-lesson office.

But if within the time mentioned his illness worsens, then the prior—whether the sick man indicates the increase of his illness in the chapter house by asking pardon or in some other way, or whether he does so voluntarily or after being admonished by another brother—orders that the same sick man be taken to the infirmary by another brother.

## CHAPTER XXXII. Concerning one who comes to any Hour after the *Gloria* of the first psalm
*If it should happen in any way that someone—whether one of those accustomed to remain outside the choir or one of those accustomed to remain inside—is present neither at the beginning of the Nocturns nor afterward, before the Gloria of the psalm* Venite, *and, whether he is in the choir at his own stall, outside at some vacant place where he can suitably bow with the others, or comes from the sacristy where the church custodians sleep, arrives within the smaller choir: on entering the choir and coming to the step, he courteously and slowly asks pardon by prostrating himself briefly upon his hands and knees, holding his hands on the upper part of his froccus; then, rising, he bows more deeply toward the altar. He does the same at Matins if he has come after the Gloria or after* Deus misereatur. *Then one of the brothers standing near him takes care that the time of his bow toward the congregation coincides with the end of the hymn or psalm. Such a person indicates the appropriate moment to him while he is standing; when permission has been given by a slight inclination of the head, as is customary, he returns to help the brother complete his act. The latter inclines slightly toward him with his hand, in the manner of one signaling permission, and, having made the bow before and behind, returns to his station, if he is one who can and ought then to stand in the choir. There he again asks pardon as before, but will not ask it a third time, even if it is a day for prostration; when the congregation bows, he likewise bows.

If, however, on some occasion the procedure described above has not been anticipated for this intermediary, or if the brother who is then presiding, seeing him at the step, immediately orders him through a messenger to leave of his own accord—although he may sometimes pretend not to notice certain men who make a practice of this fault—then that brother, after asking pardon, bows toward the congregation, and the congregation bows toward him. If his station is outside the choir, as he proceeds from the step toward his own choir, he gives way to the man standing there last in line or in formation until he has made his request for pardon and his bow as described above. Afterward he withdraws outside; or, if he is one who may likewise stand inside as described above, he remains.

The same procedure is followed at the daytime Hours for anyone who is not present in the places mentioned before the Gloria of the first psalm, except that, if someone has incurred this fault more often through negligence than through necessity, he will not receive permission from the one then presiding to leave the step. Instead, after asking pardon there as described above, he does not move from the spot until the regular Hour has ended. Then, bowing only toward the altar, he goes to his place, whether his station is inside or outside. During the Hour, while the others are bowing, he bows only toward the altar; at the prayers, whether they prostrate themselves or remain bowing, he imitates them there. Such a person, whenever he comes during the psalms, comes to the steps. If he comes after the psalms, he remains outside the choir and therefore asks pardon in the chapter house.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. Concerning one from whose nose, or from a ruptured vein, blood flows

*If flowing blood from someone’s nose or from a ruptured vein prevents him from arriving at the Hour on time, whenever he enters before the psalms have ended, he does not go to the step for this reason; but when the others urge him to do so, he indicates the cause by a sign. If he is literate, he does not neglect to sing this Hour with them; if he is illiterate, he hears no other than what is sung publicly. He may hear it while standing at the washroom, and, if he knows the psalms of that Hour, he may recite them; otherwise, in the meantime, he may recite the* Pater noster *several times with himself.*

It also sometimes happens that, at the Nocturns after the Gloria of the psalm* Venite, *or at the other Hours after the Gloria of the first psalm, someone who had not previously been in the choir but only before the choir, and who was present at the beginning of that Hour, enters. He nevertheless does not come to the step, and this is done as follows. Whenever some of the lay brothers cannot attend the choir because of the crowd, those stationed outside carefully observe whether one of those attending the choir leaves in the same manner in which he will return, so that any one of them who chooses to enter at that moment may gain a place inside through the opportunity created by the one who leaves.*

Thus, at the Nocturns after the Gloria of the psalm* Venite, *whoever is given an opportunity to enter in this way enters through the smaller choir during the first psalms, lest, if he entered then through the general entrance of the choir, he be thought to be entering the church for the first time and therefore be driven to the step. For anyone who satisfies the rule for a late arrival by going to the step, as stated above, never enters through the smaller choir on that occasion. Whenever the opportunity to enter is given after the verses of the psalm, he enters through the upper entrance of the choir, because there will then be no suspicion that he has come late.*

The same procedure is followed at Matins. At the daytime Hours, however, after the Gloria of the first psalm, anyone of them who wishes to enter of his own accord likewise enters through the smaller choir. But if the one presiding over the order then instructs him—or, if no prior is present at that moment, which ought never to happen, if a circuit-brother ordered to enter separately instructs him—then, since there will likewise be no suspicion against him, he enters through the upper entrance; otherwise, if he entered then, willingly or unwillingly, he would go to the step.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. How a brother should conduct himself during the Hours

(UD, variant.) At the Gloria of each psalm sung at the regular Hours, both by night and by day, no one keeps his hands inside his bosom; rather, he puts them into his sleeves and gathers the sleeves tightly, so that they do not reach the ground when he bows. That bow should be very low. This is not done for the other psalmody, for there the bow is made much less deeply, so moderately that the hands are not put into the sleeves and gathered for it. *At the longer Gloria of the psalms mentioned above, each person carefully observes that he rises together with the others at the end of the word* Sancto.

(UD.) If he wishes to sit during the psalmody, he takes care not to sit beside another person who is sitting, but in such a way that one stands while the other sits; and they should take turns providing each other the opportunity to sit. *At the Nocturns, this is done over the space of two psalms; at Matins, by dividing the five psalms equally, and likewise at the other offices and Hours, according as the alternation of sitting then seems appropriate.*

It must be understood, however, that at Matins, during the psalm* Deus misereatur, *no one sits either in the smaller choir, or outside beside its wall, or along the western line of the smaller choir before the following psalm has begun; nor does anyone leave the church at all. This interrupted sitting of the brothers is to be begun by the seniors immediately at the very beginning of the Nocturns.

No one descends from the wall to the formation, even for a brief moment, in order to stand between others. Instead, for that purpose someone standing by the wall withdraws to the fourth stall. Conversely, from the formation to the wall, whether literate or illiterate, one may withdraw for this reason from either the upper or lower places, except anyone assigned to the greater custody. That person alone may assist those beside him in this matter, provided neither of them is assigned to that same custody, just as at Mass and at Saint Mary’s. He customarily does this with the one standing by the wall, for then he is his associate, if he still holds an equally high position in the order.

At the other offices he does not go there, even if part of the wall is vacant. None of those standing in the formations or outside them, whether literate or not, ever goes to a vacant seat by the wall in order to rest. Anyone who is accustomed, during the nocturnal office, to go out once to the dormitory at an appropriate time is not reproved for this, nor is one who goes there twice or three times, provided his illness is known.

These, however, are the occasions when going there is inappropriate, and therefore care must be taken that it not happen except in great necessity: during the hymn and the lesson, during* Te Deum laudamus, *and afterward during* Benedictus *and the prayers. Anyone who has left the choir before any of these offices hastens to return in time if he can, as also for the procession sometimes performed after Matins with a responsory. If he has not attended the procession held on private nights twice in a week—provided the absences were not consecutive—he is not marked down for it.

If someone comes from the dormitory during one of these occasions, he joins his place in the order if he can do so suitably; otherwise he does not approach until the order of the seniors has passed by. He takes care that, at that time, the brothers do not wait for his entrance while standing in everyone’s view beside the entrance to the chapter house; rather, he regulates his approach so that, as soon as he arrives, he can enter appropriately.

It should also be understood that if, after the congregation has entered Saint Mary’s, someone arrives during Matins for All Saints, he must ask pardon if it is a time for prostration, up to the end of the psalm* Laudate Dominum, *but not afterward.

To return to the Nocturns: whoever goes to the dormitory during the psalms, if he is literate, does not neglect to recite those same psalms while he is there; if he is illiterate, in the meantime he recites as many* Pater noster *prayers as the congregation sings psalms in his absence.

## CHAPTER XXXV. How a brother should sit

[Col. 0968B]

(UD, variant.) Wherever a brother sits, he must never allow his sleeves to hang negligently down to the ground. If his hands are inside his bosom, the sleeves outside the bosom must be gathered crosswise. If for some other reason he has to go so far from the choir that he would be absent from the congregation, or if he arrives after the Hour has begun or for another office, he bows toward the altar before turning aside to his place.

When he reaches it, if the others are neither turned toward the altar nor sitting as low as they were just before, he bows toward the altar with his face; all likewise bow, with their hands inside their sleeves, though they do not bow as deeply as he does. He never bows toward the high altar except with his hands inside his sleeves and with his head lowered as far as is appropriate, as he does toward the cross. Toward the other altars and toward the crucifix in the chapter house, he bows more moderately.

He reverently bows to the reader, going from the step where he makes the bow before and behind to the reading, and returning to sit. *Everyone will learn the remaining bows by sight rather than by hearing.*

If he knows the psalms and makes a mistake in any verse, immediately, before the verse ends, and each time he makes the mistake, he asks pardon before himself in the same way that I stated above that pardon is to be asked at the step for a late arrival. If he makes a mistake in the *neuma*—that is, the prolongation of the chant on the final letter of an antiphon—or in the psalms, or neglects to announce an antiphon or responsory, he asks pardon for it. He asks pardon not only at the regular Hours but also at every divine office celebrated in the oratory if he makes a mistake in a word.

## CHAPTER XXXVI. How he should carry the wooden lantern at the Nocturns

(UD, variant.) If, during the lessons, the person carrying the wooden lantern, customarily called the *Absconsa*, comes to someone and, thinking that he is asleep, holds the light toward his face, and he is awake, he bows reverently again. But if he was asleep and the lantern is placed before him, after being awakened by the person sitting beside him, he first illuminates with it the right-hand choir, beginning with the seniors. He then illuminates those standing above the step on the right side of the choir, returning through the middle—namely, among those seated opposite one another in the formation and along the line of that choir—in a single passage, showing the *Absconsa* now to these, now to those. Proceeding in this way into the smaller choir, and beginning in the middle of the western line, he illuminates its right side, then those beside its entrance, then the left side, and finally returns to the left-hand choir, following in every respect the same order as before in the right-hand choir. Meanwhile no one presumes to awaken anyone who may be sleeping beside him.

(UD.) If he sees someone asleep, he holds the light toward his eyes three times. If he does not awaken on the third occasion, he places the lantern before him, so that, after being awakened by it, he too may carry it in the same way. If he wakes in such a way as to bow toward him, then, before he turns away, the one who placed it there must take it from him.

If so many are found sleeping that the carrying of the lantern is prolonged until the Gloria of the responsory, which is the last item in that Nocturn, then it continues until that point.
