If someone who is currently supposed to read or sing is found asleep with the lantern before him, when he wakes he indicates the reason for his duty to the carrier, if the latter is still close enough, so that he may take away the *Absconsa*. But if he has already gone farther, he assigns the same task to the brother beside him, and that man performs this brother’s turn by carrying it around.

No one is handed the lantern again on the return journey, even if he is found asleep by the person passing by, unless he is near the exit of the choir. If it has been placed before someone assigned to the greater custody, he alone illuminates the greater choir with it in the manner described; and, if he finds no one asleep there, he places it beside the lectern standing in the middle of the step. There it is taken by a lay brother and carried around the choir.

## CHAPTER XXXVII. Who should carry the *Absconsa* in the interval

It is first carried by the lay brothers who are outside the choir, not in order, but by whoever can do it best, each one getting ahead of another. If they neglect to carry it, all of them are called to account for this.

At the twelve lessons, it is brought into the choir immediately at the beginning of the third, seventh, and eleventh lessons. If there are nine lessons, as before Easter, it is brought in at the second, fifth, and eighth. If there are three long lessons, it is brought in at each one. If the lessons are short, it is brought in at the second.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. The rule of the smaller choir

[Col. 0969D]

*Because the smaller choir is joined below the larger choir in such a way that it provides passage for those entering the larger choir, the seniors and the others who have their stations by the walls in the lower part of the larger choir enter through the smaller choir not only at the Nocturns but whenever the brothers come into the church, except after the meal and the chapter. They also always leave through it, except when they withdraw in order with the others from the choir.*

When the congregation returns from the refectory, no one turns aside from the procession before the choir, except one who has been bled; instead, all enter there together. Immediately afterward, those who customarily stand nearby go out through the smaller choir, as though meeting the congregation.

Conversely, when coming to the larger church after chapter, all remain outside the choir, where they also have their place for chapter and after Compline. Beginning with the seniors, all those outside the choir leave it in order when the signal is rung for chapter. After Compline, as soon as the bow is made before and behind, they enter the larger choir through the smaller choir and leave it from there in their proper order, except that after Compline any persons who have been bled, if there happen to be any, precede the congregation from the church.

To make clear who are permitted to remain in this choir: among the literate, those who are not strong enough either to stand or to sing so that they can assist the others in the larger choir, yet are able to remain with the congregation in other places, are assigned to the smaller choir out of mercy.

There are also others exhausted by excessive labor in God’s service. They too are permitted to rest in this choir for as long as necessary, or to attend Saint Mary’s at both the daytime and nighttime Hours, and after Matins to go to sleep, until they recover their former strength.

There may still be others who are weaker because of some more serious illness, such as gout, or so lame that they cannot do without a staff, yet otherwise attend the congregation in good health. Since they cannot customarily remain in the choir mentioned above, they are permitted to sleep in the infirmary or in the novices’ cell and to attend the Hours at Saint Mary’s by day and by night, except the Hour that the sick customarily sing immediately before their meal; for this Hour they hear in the larger church.

Thus, illiterate men do not intrude among those who are continually granted a place in the smaller choir, unless they see a vacant place, and then especially if they are able to assist the others in some way by singing. The church porter, however, has a place there beside the door facing outward, whether he is literate or not.

As stated above, all the stronger literate men stand by the wall of that choir and observe the same discipline by which those in the larger choir conduct themselves. They have this relief, however: whenever they need it, they may have lay brothers stationed nearby stand in for them, or have others readily available, and they themselves may again rest on the seats if they see any vacant there.

There are also other seats in that choir where the weaker brothers sit continually, to avoid taking turns standing. Among these is a formation placed for the same purpose, but turned so that those sitting on it face toward the smaller choir. At the time of prostration they also lie there, unless some of them then yield their place out of reverence to their superiors, while the others who stand by the wall prostrate themselves meanwhile on the seats and on the ground.

All who are able to sit in the seats mentioned above are permitted, by the mercy granted them, to rest there continuously without having to rise. Sometimes, too, someone who suddenly falls ill during the day enters there for Mass or for some Hour without permission—except young men assigned to the greater custody—and yet he neither asks pardon nor is called to account by anyone; immediately one of them gives him a place to sit.

## CHAPTER XXXIX. How one with gout or lameness should conduct himself in the congregation

*To return to the man who suffers from gout, as stated above: he is permitted to sit on a stool at chapter, even if he belongs to a higher rank, because the customary order of sitting is that those of higher rank sit near the feet of the lord abbot or prior; then they sit in the middle or at the front according to their order. At the refectory he sits in his proper order; in the cloister, at the reading, he sits suitably wherever he can.*

But one who is so lame that he cannot do without support does not attend any procession. In the chapter house and in the refectory he sits at the end; when returning from there, he follows last all the way to the monastery.

One who sits continually in the smaller choir and, because his illness is worsening, withdraws outside for Matins does not ask pardon for this. Nor does the lay brother standing before the choir do so when sudden illness overtakes him, if on account of his illness he withdraws to a more remote place.

When everyone, except the lay brothers, puts on white garments or cowls, all the literate men who had previously been staying in the smaller choir then enter the larger one. Those who are infirm, whatever their rank, stand by the wall after the seniors and continue sitting. Whoever among them is weaker, if the feast is of such a kind, indicates his infirmity to the sacristan distributing the cowls and humbly refuses to receive a cowl.

If everyone puts on white garments, they sometimes give their places to the seniors who stand before them in the formation, while they temporarily fill the seniors’ stations in the formations. They do not do this, however, if those in the formations wear cowls while those by the walls wear white garments.

No one who is wearing a cowl ever stands by the wall during Mass. In any such office, when there is no procession, the stronger lay brothers, and those who happen to know how to sing something, enter the smaller choir without being vested again; nor does anyone wearing a white garment remain there during Mass, except when a reader is among them.

If a procession is to be held on such a feast, they too, dressed only in white garments, occupy that same choir as stated above; they are never commonly vested in cowls. But if anyone among all of them is so weak that he cannot remain vested through Mass, after receiving permission to remove the garment he sits outside those who are in the smaller choir.

They do not bow to the reader when he comes to the lectern at the Nocturns, nor does he bow to them. But if the congregation bows to a brother entering the larger choir, they too bow. Conversely, when they bow to someone entering among them, the congregation does not bow.

## CHAPTER XL. How a brother who has returned to bed after Matins should lie down, and what he should do during the winter interval

(UD, variant.) Returning to bed after Matins, he lies down again with the same discipline as after Compline, unless he sees that the time for the signal is already near. Then he puts on his daytime shoes and lies down in bed dressed in them. *He must not lie down at all if the day is so bright that he can read.*

But during the winter season, when the interval is observed, unless he needs to go to the dormitory, he returns to the church. After sitting down, he covers his head and waits in his Matins seat. The exception is an illiterate man who is the custodian of a young man. He then leaves the seat where he stood during the Nocturns and goes to the young man where he sits in the formation or along the line, the brother who had previously stood beside him to allow him to stand giving way.

If he is literate and has a place by the wall, whether he is praying or engaged in sacred meditation, he nevertheless does not approach the altars for a special prayer unless he is one of the more important persons. Before rising from his seat, he uncovers his head.

## CHAPTER XLI. How he should rise in the morning and what he should do immediately

(UD.) At the signal made at dawn in the dormitory to awaken the brothers, he rises as quickly as at the signal for the Nocturns. On that occasion he puts on no shoes other than those made for daytime, unless he has been bled. He takes care not to forget to carry his knife with him.

He washes his hands and, if he wishes, his face. When four towels hang together in the cloister, he does not dry himself with one other than the one assigned to his group: two are assigned separately to priests and deacons, the third to subdeacons and illiterates—*that is, those who have not been taught letters and are not distinguished by sacred orders*—and the fourth to those whose hands are not healthy.

He combs his head—*[this passage makes still clearer the note given above, namely that the monks’ heads were not shaved completely]*—and sprinkles himself with holy water. If he is illiterate and has not been promoted to any sacred order, he receives the same sprinkling from anyone he finds sprinkling himself there, just as a literate man receives it from anyone in a sacred order equal or superior to his own.

If, while sprinkling himself, someone sees a person of higher sacred order approach very near, or even incline his head to be sprinkled, he offers him the sponge; if it is not accepted, he goes away. A young man sprinkles his custodian if the custodian is not literate, and no one else.

(UD, variant.) On entering the choir he makes three prayers, especially if he can be in the place appropriate to his rank, as at the Nocturns. *Otherwise he does so wherever the opportunity is given him, whether outside or within the formations, except beside the screens, where only the seniors pray.* He takes care not to pray outside the formations when sufficient space between the formations appears available.

If meanwhile the signal for Prime is rung, he does not remain any longer at prayer; immediately, after making the bow before and behind, he withdraws to his place.

## CHAPTER XLII. How he should sit for the reading

(UD.) When sitting for the reading, he sits so that there is one cubit between himself and the person sitting beside him. He always draws the front of his froccus into his lap so that his feet can be clearly seen. He also gathers his *girones* on both sides so that they do not lie scattered on the ground. [Note: Col. 0973. *Giro, gyro, garo*: fringes—that is, the part of a garment or gown by which it becomes looser or spreads out below into a broader shape.]

*When he finds someone sitting before him, he bows, and those immediately beside him do likewise, even if one or both of them have been separated by a somewhat greater space. He observes this not only when he first sits there but whenever he returns after leaving. He does the same at chapter and at the conference whenever he arrives afterward without entering in his proper order.*

## CHAPTER XLIII. When, to whom, and how he should come to confession, and what should be imposed on him as penance

(UD, variant.)

*He should know that on ordinary days in winter the time for confession is before Terce, as at other times it is before Prime, and always after chapter, for as long as the psalm* Verba mea *is being said for a brother’s anniversary. No one is permitted to remain there at that time unless he immediately finds a priest to whom he can make confession.*

But after going out with the congregation, if he wishes to return, he is not forbidden to make confession before the congregation leaves the church. On solemn days, confession is permitted until the Gospel of the morning Mass, and no later. In Lent, it is permitted on the three days during which silence is kept in the cloister until Sext. If a feast is being celebrated, it is permitted until Terce.

It must be understood that after the signal for Prime has begun to be rung, no one may make confession unless he can briefly complete a confession that he began earlier, or at least entered the chapter house for this purpose. Similarly, before Terce, after hearing the signal for washing, the person who has already begun must complete it quickly.

During these Hours, therefore, whatever he committed in secular life against the salvation of his soul, he first confesses to the lord abbot or prior. Later, whenever he needs to come to confession for some offense, he comes to whichever priest he prefers among those assigned this duty.

Standing before him, he draws his right hand from his sleeve and places it on his chest, which is the sign of confession. When the priest rises and proceeds to the chapter house, he follows him. First he asks pardon before him, prostrating himself with his whole body. Then, when the priest extends his hand toward him both to raise him and to question him, saying, “What do you say?” he answers, “My fault.”

Ordered to rise, he sits down. When the priest says, “Bless,” he answers, “Lord,” and then says what he has to say. If he himself is also a priest, whether celebrating Mass or not, as soon as he has risen from asking pardon, the other priest bends to the same act of pardon. Although supported by this man, he does not rise from it before he has answered “My fault” to him as he questions him.

Finally, after he has imposed penance on him for what he has confessed, he too, accusing himself of his own offenses, receives something from him as penance. In this mutual confession, however, the following distinction is observed: if that priest has been counted by the lord abbot among the confessors, the penitent reveals his more secret matters to him as he then thinks appropriate, provided he had previously decided to make confession to that priest. But if the same priest has not been assigned to this office, the penitent briefly and summarily accuses himself before the Lord of having sinned in many ways, and asks him to give him something as penance; this may customarily also be done by a deacon.

After briefly encompassing the whole of his sins, he may also commend himself to the prayers of any person, but he receives nothing as penance.

Both men must take care not to sit so close together that their garments touch one another in any way. They must also lower their voices as much as possible when speaking, and must not come together for confession before the other brothers are able to read their books aloud.

After he has told the priest everything he wishes—but without unduly prolonging the account—he receives penance for these matters according to the priest’s judgment. The offense may be such that he is ordered to recite the Lord’s Prayer several times, or a psalm, or both together, or even several psalms. The lapse may be so serious that he is assigned sixty or one hundred psalms, or the entire Psalter, or even the same thing repeated several times; or, if he is of such a rank, several Masses may be imposed.

Flagellations or fasts are granted by the abbot, or, if he is absent and for as long as he is absent, by the prior. The flagellations are received from the priests at the intervals between the Hours and during the first Mass. By custom, however, they are not performed from Easter to Pentecost or during the Octave.

A person fulfilling a fast must remain during the meal at Saint Mary’s or in the regular kitchen, with permission, and afterward eat with the servers if there is one meal, or at supper with the congregation if there are two meals.

Moreover, the lord abbot has this privilege above others: if he judges it appropriate, he may impose penance on a brother until the end of his life. Genuflection is not ordinarily imposed as penance except on one who is continually stationed with the congregation, because it cannot be performed regularly and frequently.

The abbot should choose as his deputies for this business men who will faithfully admonish faint-hearted brothers and those who dangerously conceal their offenses, so that they do not presume to conceal anything from the abbot himself. It is entirely just that he should know both their evil deeds and their good deeds, since after the Lord he ought to be their chief governor.

If something happens to him at night which we discreetly call “frailty”—*that is, a nocturnal pollution*—before confession he recites the seven penitential psalms; or, if he does not know the psalms, the Lord’s Prayer seven times. After he has confessed, he recites whatever the priest has ordered him.

*On that day he neither kisses the Gospel book nor comes forward for the kiss of peace, nor approaches for the offering, nor goes to the altar, nor serves in the presbytery, nor touches anything sacred, whether in vessels or among the other utensils, that has been blessed. The exception is that at the Purification of Saint Mary and on Palm Sunday, he does not omit to offer a blessed candle or branches for that purpose.*

In the refectory he does not distribute the *oblatae*—*bread, or hosts offered for Mass but not consecrated, which were distributed in the refectory by priests who had not received the Lord’s body that day*—nor give the blessing, except to the servers if necessary.

He does not assist in dressing or undressing a priest for the celebration of Mass, nor does he himself put on a consecrated alb. Apart from those assigned for the celebration of Mass, the other albs, according to our custom, are not blessed; therefore, whenever circumstances require it, he may wear them.

He must know that he should never ask permission to do anything from which he has been prohibited, even if some special solemnity is approaching. Nevertheless, on Easter Day and on the three preceding days, according to custom, no one withdraws from communion either for this reason or for any other necessity, except for a criminal sin.

If this happens to you at midday, you will not, for this reason, abstain on the following day from the matters prescribed, provided confession preceded it. But if a shaving or some other matter prevents him from confessing, he postpones the confession to another time; meanwhile, however, he does not undertake any of the activities mentioned above.

(UD.) We have a private washroom with a water conduit. There he washes his undergarments to the extent that they have been soiled by the incident, whenever an opportunity is given him during the day, except when the midday sleep is being taken—*sleep after the meal, or at midday*. If he is under custody, his custodian leads him there and waits for him outside the door. The door is always open except when someone is carrying out this private act inside.

It should be understood that it is not our custom for a monk to hear the confession of a woman or of any secular person, unless he is so approved that the abbot has assigned this to him; and even then, not without the permission of the bishop to whom the care of such persons belongs.

## CHAPTER XLIV. How and when he should put on his clothing

(UD.) If he has his change of clothing ready, he changes out of what he is wearing. He does not presume to approach the matters mentioned above before changing, unless both of the things just described are unavailable to him.* For this reason, priests and deacons performing their office customarily have three pairs of undergarments.

(UD.) No one changes while wearing only the cowl unless he is also wearing a fur garment and a froccus, or a tunic, lest any part of his nakedness be seen by someone.

*If it is an Hour at which, after dressing, he should not lie down to sleep, he sits on the covered bed—at other times it is not permitted to sit on the cover—with his feet placed on a stool.*

(UD.) At the same time he immediately folds the garments he has removed, wraps the undergarments in *stamineum* (a woven cloth), and ties both together with their sleeves in the cupboard appointed for this purpose in the cloister beside the ascent to the dormitory, or in another suitable place, whether they are to be put away that day or another day. They must be found there on Tuesday after the Gospel of the first Mass, ready to be taken away for washing; they must nevertheless be carried in such a way that they do not come before the congregation. For this reason they should be kept beneath the stool in front of the bed until they can suitably be carried to the cupboard.

At the same time he also carries the pillowcase there, if it needs to be washed; but he must place it on the wall of the dormitory ascent or separately.

If a custodian wishes to change clothes with his junior, he must meanwhile entrust the latter to someone else, and he himself must change in some vacant bed. The time for changing is determined as follows: except on private days, from the Kalends of October to the Kalends of November, and during those three days before Easter, it is always after Matins, when the brothers are resting in their beds. Then, I say, whether before settling himself back in place or afterward, waking before the sound, anyone who wishes may change—unless he is a junior. If, before hearing the sound, he has removed one boot, or at least inserted a *brachile* (a ligature or bracelet-like band) into his breeches, he does not desist from completing the task; and thus, if perhaps he has neglected the three prayers to be made in the morning, this will not be counted against him.

But if he hears the sound before the time just mentioned and wishes to return to dress himself, he quickly washes, combs his hair, and, wearing his night shoes [Note: *Nocturnales*, shoes used during the night], after making these three prayers, returns so that, having changed his clothes, he may come to Prime at the proper time. If Prime is sung together with Matins, he may change before Terce. But if Prime is completed at some time before daylight or afterward in such a way that he cannot read in the cloister, then, in the same manner described above, he will sit in the Choir during the interval until he hears the sound made at the proper time in the circle of the dormitory door.

## CHAPTER XLV. At what hour the cook is to attend to his cooking

(UD.) If he is a cook, as they commonly say, and does not inspect his cooking at the customary time, he must neither inspect it nor taste it before Prime; or, if Prime has been joined to Matins, as I mentioned above, before Terce; and, if these intervals have been so short that this cannot be done then, after the Gospel of the morning Mass; and also after supper—or, if there is only one meal, after Vespers—provided that he does not thereby break silence.

* Freshly washed cloths must be readily available, so that he has no need to say anything. This is to be done in the infirmary by the servant appointed for it; and in matters belonging to this task, one person may be assisted by another. When this has been done, he is to wash there at the infirmary washbasin and dry himself with the towel assigned to him. He may attend to his cooking after dinner, whenever he has a suitable opportunity, but he must first obtain permission and request from the chamberlain whatever is necessary for it.

## CHAPTER XLVI. At what hours and times he is to wash his clothes, or if he wishes to do anything else with his belongings

(UD.) If he wishes to wash any of his clothes, which he may customarily do in the regular kitchen, he finds there a cauldron solely for this purpose, in which water may be heated and lye prepared. In the cloister, however, there is a very large trough hollowed out with many separate compartments, so that the stamineum may be washed in one and the breeches in another. He puts them into warm water before Chapter, so that they may soften; after the striking of the board he washes them, and no longer than the permission to speak lasts. Meanwhile, while the priest and the other ministers are dressing, he is not forbidden to wash—except on a fast day—after Terce.

If it is Lent and a private day, he washes after Chapter and after Sext, even if we are not speaking in the cloister. Whatever he washes, however it has been washed, he removes after the washing hour and dries it, so that it does not lie dirty and sodden before the eyes of the brothers leaving the refectory.

## CHAPTER XLVII. How one is not to leave at the regular hour except for unavoidable necessity

(UD.) When he hears the signal rung for Prime, he returns to the armarium both any book he sees lying beside him and the one he has in his hands.

If this is neglected, both of those between whom the book has remained lying must be called to account. Although this is observed also at the other hours, it is not observed at those hours after which the convent is immediately to return to the cloister for reading; nor at the Office for the Dead, nor when the bell is struck for drinking. At such times everyone leaves his book where he has been sitting, so that he may find it there upon his immediate return. No one else may then take it, except perhaps the person who received it for reading during Lent and needed it during that year. Nor should he request this book, or any other book, from any brother.

As for the books brought back for Collation, the armarius or his assistant sees to it that they are properly replaced in the armarium.

At the first ringing, therefore, after the books have been returned to the armarium, those who have heard Matins at Saint Mary’s customarily hear the other hours there as well—except for obedientiaries and any others who are able to attend the Choir—and immediately withdraw there from the convent. At the ringing for the other hours, all those among them who attend with the convent enter together and, with it, say before the Choir the prayers that precede those hours. If there is only one person, any latecomer may say them there in a more secluded place, provided that the hour has not yet begun.

When he hears the signal for any hour, if someone going up to the dormitory has set his foot on the first step, he may continue; otherwise, unless there is a greater necessity, he must immediately return to the church.

(UD.) But when the ringing of the signal for Prime is properly prolonged until the seven psalms can be sung, someone may occasionally, if he wishes, leave for a bodily necessity after the convent has passed through. On returning he washes his hands, so that, when the time comes for the offering, he will not have to leave again. If he has gone out so frequently, he will find that this has been proclaimed in Chapter.

No one may ever leave while any of the regular hours of the day is being sung, except for unavoidable necessity—for example, if blood is flowing from his nose. To make this even less doubtful, not even the abbot may cross the Choir or summon anyone from it after an hour has begun.

At Compline, custom permits leaving before the *Gloria* of the first psalm. During that hour one may speak only to the abbot himself and to the prior, in the customary places and offices of the cloister.

In the Choir at Prime, while *Quicumque vult* is being sung, no one sits. At this hour and at Compline, or whenever the brothers confess to one another, they must observe the following rule: whoever precedes another in the sacred order must himself make the confession first, even if he is inferior to the person to whom he is confessing.

When, after the seven penitential psalms, the Litany is sung by the prostrate brothers, the seniors arrange themselves at the steps for the final psalm, and the others likewise arrange themselves so that, when the time comes, they do not delay one another in prostrating themselves. A conversus must not lie among the literate brothers unless he is the custodian of a junior; the conversus is then to go to him wherever he may be lying. A junior must not neglect to come to his literate custodian.

In this Litany the name of no saint is repeated, except that of the saint regarded as the particular patron of that place. At the verse *Per passionem et crucem* (“Through the Passion and Cross”), as each person distinctly says it, he also makes the sign of the cross with his right hand over his face, through his sleeve. Immediately, at the verse *Per gloriosam Resurrectionem tuam*, the priest and the other ministers of the morning Mass must leave, so that, as soon as the Litany has ended, they may enter prepared for the altar. Therefore, although they remain in their proper order, they will lie in such a way that, as they leave, they do not disturb the others.

No one approaches for the offering earlier or later than his proper order, provided that he is present. But if someone has neglected this, the person then nearest to him, even if inferior in order, must not delay in offering.

## CHAPTER XLVIII. How one is to prepare himself for Chapter, or what he is to do if he is conscious of some offense

(UD. var.) When the bell is rung for Chapter, he ceases the work he is then doing and prepares himself for Chapter. He pulls his stamineum down all around and arranges it decently; and he lays down any keys he may have, whatever obedientiary office he may hold, so that he is ready if he happens to be ordered to undergo judgment.

* He also takes care to be present for the verse to be said there; if he has made a habit of neglecting this, he is called to account. He attends to whether his name is mentioned among those marked on the tablet, so that he may bow at that point; and whether he is named as hebdomadary, whether his office or his own name is heard; and when any feast to be celebrated in Cappae is announced there. He likewise bows when the lord abbot bows; and when the same lord abbot—or the prior presiding in due order—says *Benedicite*, he bows.

After this has been said, anyone leaving or entering for any reason, unless he is entering with the lord abbot or a naked person has entered, says *Benedicite*, so that those sitting near the entrance of the Chapter house, hearing it, answer *Dominus*. If he has brought someone in, he says it somewhat more distinctly, and then the convent responds. If two or more enter, only the one who leads says *Benedicite*.

## CHAPTER XLIX. That the conversus should not be absent from the sermon

* The conversus takes the greatest care not to be absent from the sermon, since it is held especially for such persons. If he sleeps during it, he is called to account.

After the person presiding has said, “Speak about the order,” and the business of Chapter has begun, it is first determined whether any sick brother is present who must ask mercy for having taken the food necessary for bodily restoration, and whether the circatores, who make the first proclamations, have anything to say.

(UD. var.) Next, if he has committed some offense in any way for which he ought to ask mercy without being called to account, he asks mercy before being called, so that he will not be called to account—whether someone saw it or not—and confesses his fault. However much he confesses, he does not ask mercy more than once beyond what he has already asked, unless he is called to account.

It should be understood that several persons are not forbidden to ask mercy simultaneously for different reasons, and that there is no day, except the solemn first day of Easter, out of reverence for which mercy is not to be sought and a proclamation entirely avoided. Nevertheless, on the principal feasts this is done more sparingly than on other days.

## CHAPTER L. For what reasons he is voluntarily to ask mercy

* There are certain regulations which, if he neglects them, he is voluntarily to ask mercy. That is, if, while remaining within the circuit of the wall or nearby outside it, he has been absent from any regular hour, or from the three prayers said before Nocturns—or in winter before Terce—unless perhaps he is a priest celebrating Mass in the meantime, or his assistant, or the custodian of the church with his assistants is preparing the hosts, or someone is bathing for an hour because of illness.

If he has missed Chapter, Collation, the procession held before Mass, manual work, or a general command—even if he arrived after the washing of the feet—or the general meal; if the reader at table or the hebdomadary of the kitchen, marked for Saturday, has neglected the blessing; if he has not been present for the common shaving of the brothers; if, coming from a journey, he has not received the blessing at the end of some hour on that day, or has left the monastery without it and not returned within two days.

Not only for the matters mentioned above, but also for certain other negligences mercy must be sought. For example, if he has not reread within the year the book given to him on the Thursday of Lent; for this he asks mercy when the year has passed, on that same day. If a corporal, an offertory cloth, or a linen cloth fitted for carrying the chalices or wrapping the paten has fallen to the ground through his negligence; if he has entirely neglected his reading or responsory; if he has made such a noise at night in the dormitory that he has disturbed the brothers; if, having been permitted to sleep in the infirmary or in the novices’ cell for the sake of mercy, he has drunk before Nocturns, even though he did not leave there in the morning without permission; if he has found his change of clothing in Chapter on Sunday, whether or not he was in the monastery on the preceding day.

If he has broken, lost, or spilled something such as a large candle; if he has damaged any article of his clothing; if he has cut a razor strap so that it is no longer fit for its proper use; if, through his negligence, the book from which the reading is to be given in the refectory has been absent there at the proper time— for all these matters, I say, he is to ask mercy without being called to account, and a prayer for pardon is to be imposed upon him, unless the fault is so frequent and so serious that, in the prior’s judgment, it should not be remitted in this way.

Nevertheless, three matters remain for whose neglect he is likewise to ask mercy voluntarily, but will by no means escape judgment. First, if, secretly or openly, he has incurred in the Body or Blood of the Lord one of the negligences dealt with in the abbot’s Chapter. Second, if twice in the year, that is, when the Nativity of the Lord and the Annunciation of the Lord are announced in Chapter, he is not present at the proper time to make mercy with the convent. This is especially serious because the ringing that precedes those Chapters is longer than the ringing for the other Chapters.

This rule, however, is established only for those who, having remained in the monastery on the preceding night or having come from nearby, were absent from those Chapters through their own negligence. Third, if, when he has been assigned to the service of the three poor, neither he nor anyone else at his request has performed it.

But if, on either of the aforementioned feasts, someone is in one of the cells or obediences situated far away, or if someone sent on a three-day journey has begun his return in good time but on the journey has suffered some impediment involving his animal, his companion, or himself, so that he cannot arrive before Chapter, he asks mercy, explains the cause of his necessity, and is released.

For the negligences that a brother may thereby incur—if he has been absent from the nocturnal prayer, a regular hour, the Litany after Prime, or the other such services mentioned above—nothing excuses him from asking mercy, except a ruptured vein or a flow of blood from the nose, even if he happens to be occupied within the monastery or outside it nearby.

When he was not obliged to attend one of these observances, then, in addition to the cases already mentioned, he must seek mercy for the assignment to serve the three poor; for neglecting the two occasions for mercy, namely the vigil of the Nativity of the Lord and his Annunciation; for neglecting *Benedicite* after returning from some hour; for not receiving it when leaving; and for not returning from a journey within two days.

It should be understood that, if he has ever neglected None by sleeping during the summer, he asks mercy immediately when the board is struck and does not wait until the next day’s Chapter.

## CHAPTER LI. For what reasons he is not to ask mercy unless called to account

* If someone makes a complaint against him, then whenever he hears someone complain against him, or hears the prior say something of the sort that marks his fault, he immediately asks mercy.

When he has risen, if he knows himself to be guilty, he confesses his fault with all humility and with a promise of correction, making no defense—unless there is a reasonable cause or great necessity by which he incurred the offense. In that case he makes his promise simply and humbly, without many words, and patiently accepts the judgment of his superior for such a fault, knowing that the fault of impatience must be corrected by more severe discipline.

But if he is not conscious of the fault for which he has been called to account, he should neither confess nor deny it importunately, but should honorably state the truth of the matter. If, while seated and hearing a complaint against him, he answers before asking mercy, he is thereby called to account and, while still in his froccus, receives one stroke with the rod. After receiving it, when he has answered, “My fault,” he is ordered to rise. He then undergoes whatever the superior determines for the matter of which he was accused.

Therefore, if someone hears himself called to account while seated, or is warned by another who heard it, he immediately rises and asks mercy, even if he has not understood what was alleged against him. No one may presume to excuse him before he has asked mercy, even if he knows him to be innocent.

The person making the accusation must take care not to make him ask mercy twice for one matter. He must first state the matter openly and by name. If he says that the man acted against the order, but does not immediately add what he did, the man does not delay in asking mercy, intending to ask for another after the matter has been stated.

If he has called him to account in a manner contrary to what is proper, this must indeed be tolerated until the man comes forward and sits; then he is to be called to account. It must also be understood that no one except the person presiding over the order may speak there about another in a speech directly addressed to him—for example, saying, “You did this or that.” Nor should anyone call another to account unless he is certain of the matter, so that, if the accused denies the alleged fault, he can clearly state how he knows it.

Nevertheless, the prior has authority to determine how such a fault is to remain. Although lesser matters are generally handled more mildly, if the matter is serious it will not remain unexamined. Nor, if the brother who saw it cannot make the complaint at the next, third, or fourth Chapter, will he therefore keep silent; rather, he will retain it in memory until he has an opportunity to make the complaint.

Although it is not customary for anyone to proclaim the entire convent, whoever presides over Chapter sometimes takes the opportunity to order universally that those who do not have their day shoes and knives present ask mercy. Sometimes he orders those who were absent from the three prayers made in the morning after the sound, and sometimes those who were absent from the procession or station held at the cross or at Saint Mary’s.

According to the institution of blessed Utilo [Note: Odilo, abbot of Cluny], this must be avoided with the greatest care, lest an improper complaint be heard in Chapter. But if someone, through ignorance, happens to begin uttering such a complaint, the prior, or anyone else who hears it, reverently takes care that it does not come to the hearing of the convent. Nor does the person who knowingly presumed to utter such a thing there escape judgment.

No mention of eating or drinking is to be made there, unless it is honorably said of some weaker brother who has taken too little food that he is unworthy of the grace, or an admonition is made concerning bread or some other food negligently prepared.

But if a brother does something that cannot be publicly complained of, and, when admonished, refuses to correct it, the person who has learned of the matter must inform the prior, so that the offending brother may be privately rebuked by him with a sharp rebuke. If he still refuses to correct himself, the prior, when he has been called to account in Chapter for some other fault, recalls to him that he has committed something that may not be complained of there, so that the convent may know of it and he may be corrected more severely without offending the brothers.

In making judgments, the person presiding over the order must exercise no small discretion. For a fault alleged against anyone, according to the nature of the matter, either leniency, flogging, or a milder sentence follows. Silence or fasting is imposed on no one. Only the abbot binds someone by a sentence for a serious fault.

I shall not speak on this occasion about the matters that appear to belong to a more serious fault. Moreover, no one is beaten after being stripped of his *stamineum*—a woolen under-tunic or shirt used by monks in place of a hairshirt; Innocent III forbade Benedictines linen shirts—unless he appears to be rebellious.

A person is judged rebellious if he rashly contradicts the prior in Chapter, or if, although he does not contradict in words what is enjoined upon him, he nevertheless disdains to do it; and, to pass over greater matters, even if he refuses to correct the smallest negligences alleged against him.

I. Rebellion properly means disobedience, when the abbot or prior enjoins something upon someone and that person openly declares by defiant speech that he will not do it.

II. Rebellion exists when someone is rebuked by a superior and not only fails to endure the rebuke humbly, but also dares to answer against it proudly and defiantly.

III. Rebellion exists when someone, having often been rebuked for any matter, scorns to correct himself.

IV. Rebellion is also said to exist when something is enjoined upon a brother and, although he does not dare to contradict it in words, he nevertheless disdains to do it.

These four causes are regarded as rebellion and are customarily punished by stripping off the stamineum.

The person ordered to undergo such a judgment sits with his cuculla and froccus removed and placed at his feet. The chamberlain approaches with a knife and, having cut open the stamineum, pulls it slightly downward from both shoulders. The brother in question does not neglect to mend it as soon as he has an opportunity, so that it will not be received for washing in that condition.

The brother who administers the judgment performs this while standing behind him. No one receives two judgments in a single Chapter, except for contradiction. But if, after such a flogging, another matter is alleged against him which seems not rightly to be left unpunished, he is ordered to ask mercy for it at the next day’s Chapter.

If, after receiving judgment, anyone presumes to show by words or even by his clothing some sign of disdain, he should know that he will not leave until, either spontaneously or at least compelled by a sharp rebuke, he has promised with all humility a satisfaction appropriate to the best of his ability.

## CHAPTER LII. On the discretion of those who administer judgment

* Those who are so discerning that they know how each fault ought to be corrected are ordered to administer such judgments. They must carefully attend to what is alleged against each person, examining together both the fault and the diligence or negligence of the accused, and not merely satisfying their own will.

It often happens that one of the more diligent brothers falls into a serious fault which is not corrected in him in the same way as it would be in some negligent person.

A man ordered to receive judgment does not prepare himself until he has been called to account. Before being stripped, he neither asks mercy nor says anything. Once stripped, he places his clothes so that, lying stretched out, he can scarcely reach them with his head. If necessary, the person who is to administer judgment first arranges his stamineum.

Since rods of various sizes, supplied by the Granatarius, are always available there—larger ones for correcting the less cautious, smaller ones for the more diligent—he must choose for administering the judgment whichever size he sees the matter itself to require.

After the first stroke, neither the one being struck awaits the hand of the striker nor does the striker await the other’s voice saying, “My fault.” Rather, without maintaining equality in this matter, the one immediately continues striking while the other says, “My fault,” until the prior orders the striker to stop. Nevertheless, both must avoid excessive haste.

Although only more serious faults are corrected with brooms, as has been said, this kind of correction is nevertheless begun moderately; but, if it seems right to the superior, it is gradually increased at his command. Fraternal compassion must everywhere be preserved in judgment, whether it is administered with the rod or with brooms, so that “the strictness of discipline may terrify the proud, and the application of mercy may cherish the subject.” Yet remedies of kindness are sometimes also applied to the less cautious, so that those whom the rigor of strictness has not conquered may be conquered by the love of compassion.

Although it is not customary for the person receiving judgment to say anything other than “My fault,” nevertheless, when the matter is dealt with using brooms, if he happens to say that he will correct himself, he is not only not censured, but the priors gladly accept this. The intercession that ordinarily comes spontaneously from them for the more diligent brothers even in lesser judgments is applied to the less cautious in greater judgments, elicited by their promise of correction, as has been said.

If several people are to be corrected, each, after judgment has been carried out against him, is ordered by the prior to go and sit down, giving place to the person administering judgment among them. If someone has more to say about him, he does not do so at that moment, but after all the others have come to sit down, since it is not customary for anyone to speak there while another is prostrate for judgment, unless the superior wishes to say something briefly.

Therefore, care must be taken that, when the prior orders someone to be stripped, he temporarily defer it unless someone has indicated that he wishes to speak about that person, until the one who has something to say has brought it forward. If he neglected to do so at that time, however, he will not remain silent merely because judgment has been carried out.

A word of defense concerning a fault already corrected is now prohibited, lest the person who ordered judgment to be administered appear to be at fault.

## CHAPTER LIII. What both the accuser and the accused must guard against

* The person called to account must take care not to murmur about his accusation to anyone, either outside Chapter or within it. No one may speak outside Chapter about matters of this kind conducted in Chapter, unless it can be done in such a way that it produces not scandal but rather the edification of those who hear.

Care must also be taken that, when someone sees a brother placed in anxiety because of some serious offense, he does not, as though then finding an opportunity for the first time, exaggerate the brother’s fault by mentioning things previously kept silent voluntarily or by recalling any of his former actions.

Likewise, every accused person must take care not to look toward anyone except the person presiding over the order—and not even toward him unless he is speaking to the accused—and must not call to account the person who has accused him in that Chapter. The same precaution applies at the next, or even the third or fourth, Chapter, if the other has made a serious accusation against him.

Nor, in that Chapter, is anyone ordered to administer judgment against the person who first accused him. This must be wholly foreign to conversi as well. For a priest administers judgment against a priest, and each person against one who is either of his own order or inferior order; sometimes one of those standing in judgment is ordered to administer it.

## CHAPTER LIV. That there is to be no respect of persons in accusations

* In accusations there is no respect of persons: seniors are called to account by juniors, and juniors by seniors. If a senior is found in the same fault as a junior, attention is paid not to whose age but to whose diligence is at issue; nor is anyone exempted from judicial sentence unless he is exempted together with the junior, although the sentence is usually moderated for the diligent.

Sometimes a novice is exempted if he is still so ignorant of the order. However many people have been called to account, all ask mercy. Therefore the lord abbot himself takes care not to say anything by which he would have the convent called to account all at once.

It is not without reason that the convent is held in such honor by the lord abbot, to whom the highest reverence is shown everywhere, as is fitting. Thus, whenever he walks anywhere according to monastic custom, no one presumes to go out to meet him.

But if it is alleged that, through negligence, one, two, or more verses have been omitted from some psalm of an hour, only those who recognize themselves as more specifically guilty in this matter ask mercy. After the psalms, all the prostrate brothers sing *Verba mea*, or a psalm, even if it is a day on which they do not prostrate themselves at the hours.

For the first psalm omitted, the seven penitential psalms are sung, together with any prayer for sins. For a neglected prayer or antiphon at the suffrages of the saints, whatever seems right to the person presiding is done. If it is noticed before the end of the psalm that a verse has been omitted, the psalm must be repeated from the beginning.

In other negligences of this kind, where nearly the entire convent, or certainly a large part of it, is at fault, if the matter is nevertheless a lesser one, an admonition for correction rather than an accusation should be made.

Whenever some brothers are occupied in an obedience, each negligent person must first be admonished by the others; but if he refuses to correct himself, he is also to be accused.

Since, however, it is impossible to write down every individual thing that may be done against our custom and order, there are also certain matters that cannot be accused in Chapter because of the scandal they would cause. Anyone who does not know whether a matter belongs among those requiring accusation must first ask about it.

## CHAPTER LV. That a request for mercy follows confession of fault, when the fault is to be stated and mercy sought together

* It must not now be passed over that a request for mercy follows confession of fault. Whenever someone must confess a fault and at the same time ask mercy—for example, if he has heard of the death of his father, mother, or sister; or if the anniversary of either parent will be the next day; or if it is the day on which he received the blessing of monastic life, and he must also ask mercy for some offense—the fault is dealt with first. Then, in asking mercy, he asks only once, even if it happens that he is going to ask mercy both for himself and for his parents.

In that case he first accuses himself of negligence in the life he has already lived, and then announces the death of his parent, but asks only once, so that the prior may respond to both by wishing indulgence, and so that he himself may come to the prior’s feet as many times as required.

When departing, he observes the rule of bowing written in the first chapter of the book and given to all who come to the feet. Even before coming to the feet, he bows to the reverence of the convent when it bows, and he remains as submissive as possible for every absolution given there.

Custom has established this rule: before the first blessing is to be said, the convent bows at every absolution, while the person who is then standing before it for whatever reason remains submissive.

## CHAPTER LVI. Concerning one who has seen a deceased brother suffering punishment

It is also customary that, if someone has received a revelation in a vision that a deceased brother is suffering punishment, he privately informs the abbot or prior. If ordered, he asks mercy for him in Chapter with permission, reporting what he saw about him in sleep. After the absolution has been requested for the deceased brother, he also prostrates himself at the prior’s feet.

The prior then enjoins the brothers to do something for the deceased brother, either collectively or individually. It should be understood that someone asking mercy may, if he lacks permission, be called to account at that moment.

If the lord abbot sends someone into Chapter to announce the death or anniversary of one of his relatives, that person asks mercy for this matter only if ordered by the abbot himself. If he is to ask mercy either for himself or for one of his relatives, he does so with the same request.

Those who intend to ask mercy voluntarily because they have lost something within the cloister should know that they must first inquire in Chapter about the lost item—unless it is so small as a needle, or something similar—and then, if it has not been found, ask mercy at the following Chapter.

Those coming from a journey because they have lost items outside ask mercy at the next Chapter. If they arrive while Chapter is in session, after the cloister door has already been closed, they may knock; the doorkeeper in Chapter, having received permission by hand, comes out to open it for them.

Once admitted, they say a prayer in the monastery and immediately come to Chapter. After they have sat down, if they have a message to deliver while standing, the one to whom it has been entrusted first performs this duty in his place. Then, if any of them must voluntarily ask mercy for some offense, or if one of them has anything to accuse against another—including matters done on the journey contrary to custom, especially matters which the person, after being admonished, refused to correct—he does not neglect to do so.

Certain messages, however, are minor and are not spoken standing [Col. 0986D], but seated, whenever the speaker considers it appropriate; for some dignities require greater reverence and others less. To bishops and abbots, to communities both of canonical and monastic institution, and also to certain secular authorities such as dukes, the following reverence is to be shown: only their greetings are to be spoken by those standing, while everything else is to be spoken by those seated. Only to our lord abbot, to the apostolic lord, and to our king is this added: that pardon be sought by the convent for their messages; and the same is observed by the person to whom the lord abbot gives any such command individually, wherever he gives it to him. To all others who command the offering of their prayer or service, only the reverence of an inclination is owed.

Apart from these persons, no one may speak standing in chapter unless he is asking pardon. Hence obedientiaries, and anyone who is going to leave in such a way that he will not return to chapter, must ask permission while seated and speaking: obedientiaries for their obediences, naming those of their own rank or other brothers whom they need to accompany them on their departure. Concerning anyone leaving in such a way that he will not return, if someone has anything to say because permission has been granted to them, he by no means omits it. All others who are leaving in such a way that they will return ask permission to leave with their hand while standing where the prior can see them; and the prior, seeing them, does not fail to nod assent with his head slightly inclined. But it may happen that he is otherwise occupied and does not look toward them; therefore, whether or not he then sees them, they leave freely.

If someone calls another out of chapter at the command of the lord abbot, he sits at the very entrance of chapter, if he was already present; otherwise, in his own place. But he too will not leave without permission. For the one who is summoned to the lord abbot likewise does not depart from there without permission, just as he does not leave the monastery without permission if he is vested in an alb and knows that he is going to speak; nor does he leave the refectory without permission if he will not return.

If someone has left chapter with permission in such a way that he will not return, but is then recalled for some reason or returns voluntarily, he does not perform the bowing forward and backward again. If he again needs to leave before chapter has ended, he obtains permission and nevertheless performs the bowing forward and backward as before.

## CHAPTER LVII. On the lesser fault.

[Col. 0987C]

(UD.) A person assigned to the lesser fault is treated as the Rule itself prescribes (chapter 24). * No one is assigned to it unless he has committed something for which he would also deserve to undergo severe discipline, and especially if, because of old age or bodily weakness, he cannot endure severe beating. At None he eats and sits in his own place; and in summer he does not come to the table before the convent has withdrawn from it after drinking. (UD. var.) During the night prayers and all the canonical hours he lies prostrate. He does not offer, kiss the Gospel book, approach for the kiss of peace, or go to Mass with the others. If a feast day with twelve lessons or an appointed office occurs, he is released for the time being [Col. 0987D]. When an ordinary day arrives, he enters again into the place in which he had previously been, until he is absolved.

He is absolved especially when he is lying prostrate at the step during the prayers, by a brother sent to him by the prior, who indicates to him that he has been absolved. * He then performs the bowing forward and backward and departs. If the prior has perhaps neglected this, he absolves him after being reminded by the claustral prior or by one of the elders—provided that it still seems appropriate to him.

UD. Absolution is also customarily carried out in this way if, after someone has been assigned to this penance for the same offense, it later happens that he is accused again of some fault and beaten. If this has not occurred, he is not absolved until his satisfaction, while lying at the step or for one hour, has first been seen by the convent. * The prior may subject someone to the yoke of this sentence even when he knows that the lord abbot is present in the monastery, but he may not absolve him without the abbot’s assent. If such a sentence is imposed on someone while the abbot is away, and the abbot should meanwhile arrive, that person is absolved from it not by the prior but rather by the abbot himself. If the abbot departs before absolving him, the prior then does not absolve him without the abbot’s permission.

The same arrangement applies between the greater prior and the lesser prior, except that if the greater prior departs somewhere, the lesser prior is not sent after him for the brother’s absolution, as one is sent after the lord abbot; instead, the claustral prior absolves him. It should also be noted that if someone is told, “Remain today in the lesser fault,” he will be entirely free of it on the following day, because “today” alone was said.

## CHAPTER LVIII. How one should stand wherever one may be standing.

[Col. 0988B]

UD. When standing before the lord abbot, or wherever he may be standing—where this can be observed—he must also take care to keep his feet evenly placed, and never spread apart while standing. * He also observes this: he never steps over a footstool or any somewhat larger piece of wood unless he places a foot upon it, or goes around it because of the shortness of the route.

## CHAPTER LIX. Concerning things that may not be done except during the time for speaking.

(UD. var.) On leaving chapter, if it is a day on which speaking is permitted in the cloister, he must first say no word. If he knows letters, he takes a book and sits down. Converts who do not know letters are not required to have books. Nevertheless, while standing he speaks. But if he was perhaps absent when, after the striking of the board, the prior said *Benedicite*, and later, on meeting someone, he says *Benedicite* to him, neither he nor the one who meets him and replies *Dominus* is to be entered for this. And the first person whom he addresses in the convent he precedes with *Benedicite*.

(UD. var.) Whoever speaks speaks in a low voice. His conversation and hearing are to concern only spiritual matters or those things without which this temporal life cannot exist. * He also takes care not to speak to another brother sitting or standing opposite him or farther away.

UD. If he needs to ask the chamberlain for something, he asks at this time in particular. If he needs to cut his nails, he must tell the brother sitting beside him that he needs his nails cut; the latter must assent, saying: “With God’s blessing,” and, after the former has said *Benedicite* and the other has replied *Dominus*, cuts the nails of the brother mentioned. If he needs to wash his own bowl and cup, UD., he washes them then, observing silence there. He does not put the washed vessels in the cloister to dry, * but immediately carries them back to the refectory.

UD. If he needs to sharpen his knife, he sharpens it on the whetstone that hangs in the cloister on a chain for this purpose; * or, if he prefers, on the other one hanging similarly beside the washbasin. If something in his garment has come apart and he wishes to mend it, he does this during the time for speaking, or before Prime in summer, but in winter before Terce; and, if there is one meal, after dinner, sitting on his bed in his cowl and fur garment, if necessary. For he has two, and if one needs mending, he sits in the other.

UD. If he needs to spread something from his clothing in the sun, he does so, and remembers carefully to take it away before collation, or, if there are twelve lessons on the following night, before Vespers.

## CHAPTER LX. Concerning one who wishes to visit a sick brother.

* If he wishes to visit a sick brother, he obtains permission to visit at this time in particular. On going there he must recite the psalm *Domine, ne in furore tuo arguas me*, etc., adding the Lord’s Prayer and one collect for the sick man, *Omnipotens sempiterne Deus*, etc. With sick brothers he may speak until the next hour is announced. But if the hour is announced sooner, so that he cannot complete what he has begun, he does not return afterward without permission. Not only at this time, but also at other suitable hours, permission is granted to certain more important persons to visit sick brothers.

(UD.) He calls nothing his own, but says “our” for everything except father, mother, and fault; concerning these he may properly say “my” and “mine.” Even when speaking of himself, he says “I,” not “we.” If he addresses a brother, he never addresses him by his bare name unless he adds *domnus*; instead, he calls young brothers “brothers.” Likewise, when saying a proper name, he precedes it with “brother.” At this or any other suitable time, for example between the two Masses [Col. 0989C], he may meet a secular friend with permission, and not without a witness if the friend is known to be somewhat imprudent. He kisses no woman at all—not even his own mother.

## CHAPTER LXI. Concerning those wishing to have blood let, or to undergo phlebotomy.

(UD. var.) If he wishes to have blood let during the Twelve Lessons, or on any other day on which silence must be kept, at the very hour when people leave chapter he asks permission from the person in charge, with a sign. * On ordinary days, when speaking is permitted in the cloister, if he can sit beside the prior, he asks permission verbally; otherwise, by a sign. If the lord abbot or the prior has held chapter and, immediately after chapter has ended, has gone away somewhere, so that the person who is to be bled cannot come without permission [Col. 0989D], he asks permission from the person currently governing the community.

The weekly priest, the weekly deacon and subdeacon, the weekly cantor, the reader at table, and the weekly kitchen servants must take care never to presume to have blood let unless they have first asked pardon in chapter and received permission. (UD. var.) To continue in the order in which this is done: after receiving permission, he arranges to inform the cellarer himself, so that he may ensure that the servant assigned to this business is ready after the Gospel of the principal Mass. At that moment he leaves the church and puts on his night garments, which he will wear until the third day, except when some procession is to be conducted in white garments, as often happens at the reception of some important person.

Therefore, at the same time that he puts on the night garments, taking his band from his bed, he goes to the place for letting blood. Before everything else he performs the bowing forward and backward and says three times the short verse: “O God, come to my assistance.” “Lord, have mercy.” V. “Our help.” Then, after performing the bowing forward and backward, the letting of blood begins.

## CHAPTER LXII. In which places one who has been bled is to perform the bowing forward and backward.

* It should be known that he is to perform the bowing forward and backward nowhere except in the church or before a cross, except for manual work, bloodletting, and in the regular kitchen. UD. He keeps silence unless he says something brief about the work he has in hand. * The cellarer arranges to send his assistant there, so that he may see how many have been bled.

UD. Rising from there, he comes to the refectory to eat and drink a little of his allowance, as also on the two following days after the Gospel of the principal Mass; on the fourth day, however, he eats with the servers. * At such a meal the customary refectory verse is not said, even if it is the regular fast on which he will dine after Terce and will not lack his allowance.

When the common meal of the brothers has ended, if necessary he may leave after the verse among the first. At the next hour after the bloodletting he withdraws before the altar where the sick usually lie during the morning Mass; and, lying there in whatever manner accords with his health, no one blames him. If he trusts his strength, he sits there in the customary manner until the following hour, and thereafter remains outside the lesser choir at the other hours wherever he wishes.

When, after Vespers, the morning procession is conducted to Saint Mary, he follows the priors and remains in chapter, unless he is a young brother. He must not prostrate himself at any canonical hour; nor, for those three prayers which the convent customarily performs after the sound in the choir while standing or prostrate, does he perform more than one, and that one seated before the choir. At the end of each hour, going out with the others, he performs the bowing forward and backward; and before the beginning he performs it with the others. At the litany, if he wishes to prostrate himself, let him prostrate himself; if he wishes to sit, let him sit, and no one is to rebuke him.

(UD.) At dinner, when the others have their allowance, he receives the general allowance for two days, and at supper three eggs. But if it is wintertime—that is, from the Kalends of October until Lent—and if the brothers generally eat only once, then on the first day only, after Vespers, as *Placebo* begins, he performs the bowing forward and backward; after washing his hands he goes to the refectory, * and, without the customary verse, sits at the left end of the table and eats, with the cellarer providing what he needs.

If he returns from supper before the convent comes to drink, as can often happen in Septuagesima, he does not fail to return again with the convent to the refectory and, if he wishes, drink. But if the convent finds him eating supper, when they leave he stands more upright and inclines himself [Col. 0991A] until all those who are not inclining have passed by.

(UD. var.) On the second and third days, coming to the refectory after chapter, he says the morning verse and takes three cooked dishes; on the fourth day, when he is to dine with the servers, he receives a quarter of cheese, or its equivalent in value. * On the third day, having put on his day garments, he returns to the choir at Prime if there are twelve lessons; if it is an ordinary day, at Terce. If he does not trust his strength, he informs the prior.

Meanwhile, if he has fallen asleep at Nocturns, no one disturbs him with the hidden object. But even if he has rested in bed for a while, he leaves dressed as he was for this purpose from chapter, when *Deus auribus* begins, or, if that is not sung at the time, when *Exsultabunt* begins. He is not permitted meanwhile to ask pardon in chapter, UD., if something has been complained of against him; instead, ordered to stand, he inclines himself for pardon. * This must nevertheless be avoided if he can know that he has been bled.

If, however, in the refectory during these two days in which he is being bled, he makes a sound or does anything else deserving pardon, either he or one of the two brothers beside him asks pardon. If he commits such a thing at another time, however, that it should not be kept silent in chapter, it is to be deferred until the third day.

He must take care not to have blood let between Easter and the Wednesday after Pentecost, unless he is an obedientiary who regularly stays outside, having obtained permission from the prior. If someone else, on the aforesaid days or whenever it is equally unsuitable, cannot wait for an appropriate time because of illness, UD., he must obtain permission in chapter with pardon. [Col. 0991C]

Each person must also take care not to have blood let on a day whose following night has twelve lessons, except in Lent. Then he always has blood let on Saturday after Vespers, after *Benedicamus Domino* has been said, because he does not fast on Sunday, when by custom he must have his summer meal after the Gospel, and on the third day he hears Vespers with the sick.

If he anticipates the brothers’ established meal so that he will not eat afterward, he remains at Saint Mary during the common meal of the brothers. * On Sunday, when he is to conduct a procession outside the cloister, he puts on his day garments; but he may avoid the other processions that are conducted barefoot, after obtaining permission.

UD. After Compline, of the three prayers he performs only one, and that one seated, and immediately leaves. Those to whom permission has been granted out of mercy to hear the canonical hours at Saint Mary remain there meanwhile while they are under the rule for those who have been bled. It is sometimes also granted to certain others who have been bled that, after the morning offices there have ended, they may return to their beds and remain there until they appear in the choir on the third day at Prime, or in winter at Terce.

It must not be overlooked that no one is permitted to come to the infirmary solely because of bloodletting, unless he wishes to have blood let from a vein in the foot, or unless he is one of the elders whose weakness is so great that he cannot observe this order in the convent at all. Even this is entirely avoided if a feast with twelve lessons is approaching on the following night, unless, as stated, permission has been obtained beforehand.

If, in summer, he wishes to have blood let in some other manner than from a vein during the Twelve Lessons, he informs the chamberlain of his wish after obtaining permission, so that he may provide what is necessary for this purpose. He nevertheless waits until None has been sung, and then immediately goes to the place for letting blood; after the verse has been said, while silence is observed except where necessary, the bloodletting begins.

From the Kalends of October until Lent, immediately after chapter, he eats with those who have been bled; and after the Gospel of the principal Mass, or after dinner at the suitable time, he too has blood let. After the bloodletting he does not enter the choir, but rests outside where the other persons bled are, whether it is winter or summer, neither prostrating himself nor performing the bowing for pardon [Col. 0992B]. If he puts on his hood, no one rebukes him. At supper he receives an allowance from the cellarer; or, if supper does not follow, when the brothers are drinking together, he is given the better drink. On the second day he enters the choir at the hour at which anyone bled from a vein enters on the third day; and on that day, after chapter—or, if it is another season, after the Gospel—he does not miss the meal of those who have been bled.

## CHAPTER LXIII. How, if he hears the signal for a canonical hour while speaking, he is to hasten to prayer.

(UD.) But to return to the place from which I digressed briefly: while speaking, if he hears the signal for a canonical hour, he does not finish in the cloister the very word he has in his mouth [Col. 0992C], but immediately becomes silent and hastens to prayer. When it is finished, he sits in the choir and attends to the reading until the priest is vested to sing Mass. But as soon as he hears the second signal, he immediately ceases and rises, as also at the two signals rung for Vespers, or whenever all the signals are rung. He carefully observes the pardon he seeks, so that he never seeks it later or earlier than the others. He inclines himself when the others incline themselves; he rises when the others rise, at pardons, prayers, and orisons.

When the others are not reading and are attending to nothing except the divine office, he too never opens a book for reading, especially in the choir, unless sometimes he opens the gradual for the principal Mass because of a chant that is currently being sung, or, if he is illiterate, (var.) the book of hymns at Vespers because of a hymn to be sung on that occasion.

* Likewise, for the chant and hymn of the morning office he may look into a book, but he must not leave his own place, nor meanwhile use any other light except the light that shines for the community. (UD. var.) If he is the weekly priest, he may look ahead in the collectary to what he needs, namely, the chapter for the present hour.

He does not like frequently to make the hand-signs used for speaking, especially when the convent is watching; and whenever he makes them, he makes them reverently and out of necessity. Just as he restrains his other limbs, so he restrains his eyes from wandering. When Mass has ended, he sits in the deepest silence at the reading until the servers and boys, if they are present, return from the *mixtum*.

[Note: [Col. 0993D] *Mixtum*: bread and wine granted to the reader at table for the servers in the Rule of Saint Benedict.]

## CHAPTER LXIV. What discipline is to be observed in the refectory, whether one comes after the others or leaves before the others, and how permission is to be obtained.

(UD.) At the hour of dinner or supper, if he has not gone up to the dormitory, he comes immediately to the refectory after washing his hands. * After performing the bowing forward and backward, he may go a little way toward the regular kitchen, or, if he is not young, before the cellarer, so that, if he needs something he could not previously ask for verbally, he may address the cellarer about it with signs.

UD. Returning from there, he reverently waits standing for the lord abbot, or, if he cannot stand, seated. * If he is young, he sits on the lower seat; if he is older, he sits on the upper seat. When the lord abbot enters, he inclines toward him and immediately straightens himself, standing upright until the abbot, passing by, reaches his place for striking the small bell.

(UD.) After he has struck it, and the verse, prayer, and blessing have been given, he sits in his own place and draws the tablecloth toward him, but eats nothing at all before the reading begins and before he receives from the priest’s hand the *oblata*, provided that it is an ordinary day and he has not communicated on that day.

[Note: [Col. 0993D] *Oblata*: bread offered at Mass but not consecrated; concerning it, see below.]

If he wishes to leave the refectory after the verse has been said in order to bring water or for some similar reason, * he does not leave before the reading itself begins.

UD. He tastes nothing of the general food before it has been blessed. A brother never brings anything to himself except salt and water, unless he comes while serving to his own place. If something is brought to him by another, he reverently extends his hand toward it and inclines slightly. He inclines similarly toward everything that is then given or placed before him, or received from him.

If something is sent to him by the person sitting at the small bell, he rises completely and inclines more deeply toward him, even if he is sitting in line; and however strongly he may wish to abstain, he does not fail to taste this. He also brings his dish to the brother sitting above him beside him, so that he may eat with him. If that brother refuses, he brings it to the one below; and if the latter also refuses, however much remains of what he did not wish to or could not eat, he does not send it farther to any brother for any private favor.
