Nevertheless, he does not fail to indicate to one or the other of his neighbors that it should be brought to the brother sitting above or below.

If something is sent to two brothers and one of them happens to be absent in the meantime, the one who returns does not fail to incline. * If he has made a sound loud enough to be heard throughout the refectory, he asks pardon; at another time, when there is drinking but no reading, he does not do so.

If, while he is going there, *Tu autem* is said, he does not therefore return before he has asked pardon. If he spills so much drink or liquid food that a morsel of bread cannot cover it, whether the reading is taking place or not, he asks pardon.

If he breaks a spoon into pieces, he picks up the fragments and places them at the step, and asks pardon. Rising from there, he takes them back and replaces them at the end where the spoons and other refectory utensils are kept. If it is not divided but is nevertheless so broken that it is unfit for eating, he observes the same manner of satisfaction.

If he breaks a knife, he does the same, except that, after taking it back from the step, he carries it with him to the table, puts it in its sheath, and returns it to the cellarer at a suitable time in order to receive the same knife repaired or another one. In the same way anyone satisfies for himself who, while eating or drinking in the refectory, or before the refectory in the cellarer’s room or before the cellarer’s room, or in the regular kitchen, commits any of the aforesaid offenses [Col. 0994B]. The exception is that he asks pardon for a sound only when he has made it in the refectory or in the regular kitchen in the manner prescribed.

If he spills a sextary of wine or beer, or half a sextary, he makes satisfaction for this both in the refectory and on the following day in chapter. He puts nothing on the cup of justice, nor dips bread into it, unless he has first placed it on the table before him.

[Note: [Col. 0994D] The “cup of justice” is the same as the wine vessel called *justitia*, or “the just measure.”]

He must not dip bread in the same cup together with another brother. He uses nothing at all—not even the fan with which flies are driven away in summer—while *Benedicite* is being said over the food and drink.

If he is forced to leave while eating because of some necessity, he does not speak on that account if he hopes to return, unless he is the porter receiving guests. But if, immediately after he has eaten a little, nausea or a flow of blood comes upon him so that he cannot return to the same meal, afterward he eats with the servers without permission.

(UD.) He takes the utmost care concerning crumbs, so that nothing, however tiny, falls and is wasted. With his knife he removes them from the tablecloth, so that at the end they may be gathered with the small brush made for this purpose into a dish and carried to alms.

(var.) As long as he has not been separated from the convent to be with the sick, he does not taste even a single grain of pepper, nor receive any food or drink except in the refectory. He never drinks except while holding the cup with both hands—except when he has been bled—and never except while seated.

* If, after the small bell has been dismissed, he has remained outside the door, he by no means then presumes to enter, but waits outside until he hears the reader having read the verse. If he has not yet arrived, or if he enters later, after the reading has begun, and sees someone standing at the step who has received permission to eat, he stands somewhere beside the table and watches for the other person to leave and give him room to approach; and even then, if the place is very narrow, he must remain standing there.

If he sees the server about to strike the general bell, he stands there during the blessing and humbly inclines himself. The same is observed by anyone who happens to be walking about while carrying out some service in the refectory; if he is carrying anything in his hands, he takes care to place it on the table.

When approaching anyone whom he meets, he humbly inclines himself as the other does, unless he is carrying something in his hands that prevents him from making this inclination. If he happens to make a sound or do anything else deserving pardon while approaching, he asks pardon before the verse, just as he does after the verse.

If he commits anything of this kind while leaving the step, and then comes to the step, he asks the person sitting at the small bell for permission to eat by joining the first two fingers of his hand and directing them once toward his mouth. UD. When that person assents, he acts and speaks by himself as though he had done and said these things with the others: first the bowing forward and backward, then the verse—if it is dinner, *Oculi omnium*; if supper, *Edent pauperes*, etc. Inclining, he says *Gloria Patri* and the Lord’s Prayer; * standing upright, he blesses with hand and mouth, saying, “Let us pray: Bless, O Lord,” etc.; and, inclining, returns to sit down.

If his place is near the end of the table, below one brother, that brother rises and gives him room to approach, just as later, if he rises, he gives him the opportunity to leave. Once seated, if he does not find food of any kind already placed before him for the brothers, and the servers are unaware of this, one or the other of his neighbors indicates to one of them that it should be offered; or, if this cannot be done, he himself rises and brings it to him.

Furthermore, if two or more who arrive late at the table enter together to receive permission to eat, as many as can enter together go first, and the others follow in order. The one who holds precedence among them in sacred order is also placed in the middle of those going first, whether he is literate or not, and whether or not he performs the office of that order; he, I say, is given precedence in receiving the blessing.

But if all are of the same order, the one who is senior goes first, unless he is a convert; the others are literate. After the blessing has been given, those coming later wait, withdrawing a little, so that those who preceded them in approaching may also precede them in leaving.

If one of those who went first does something deserving pardon while approaching, he asks pardon before the verse while the others wait; but if they are following, he postpones it until after the verse. Care must be taken that, once the small bell has been struck for the general signal, no one receives permission to eat, nor permission to leave after he knows that the crumbs have been removed.

If he should at some time need to rise from the table before the others—which, unless he is an obedientiary, he must take care not to do—or if some task has been assigned to him that must nevertheless be completed quickly, he arranges the bread and the cup of justice as they should be arranged if he were rising with the others.

Again, if he does something deserving pardon while rising or approaching, he asks pardon before seeking permission to leave. But he postpones this pardon until after the verse if, among several others, he approached following them because of the narrowness of the place. For if he committed the fault together with them, and they saw or knew it, they wait for him to ask pardon first.

(UD. var.) Rising from there, he comes to the step and, drawing his extended hand slowly from his chest, asks permission to leave with this sign. After receiving it, he inclines to the ground and says the verse. If it is dinner: *Confiteantur*. Inclining: *Gloria Patri*. Standing upright: *Agimus tibi gratias*. If it is supper: *Memoriam fecit*, and *Benedictus Dominus*, etc. Amen.

After performing the bowing forward and backward, he proceeds slowly, singing the fiftieth psalm, as far as the refectory door. There, inclining toward the principal table, he says everything that is said in the church by the priest or the convent, namely: *Dispersit*. *Benedicam Dominum*. *In Domino*. *Magnificate Dominum*. *Sit nomen Domini*. *Retribuere*. *Benedicamus Domino*. Amen.

Finally, after performing the bowing backward and forward, if he committed anything of this kind during the verse, he asks pardon as he withdraws from the step, and thus leaves. If the brothers eat only once that day, he says no other verses than those pertaining to supper, together with *Agimus gratias*. But he never does both on one occasion, namely, arrive later than the others and rise earlier than the others.

## CHAPTER LXV. Concerning the meal of the servers.

* When the general meal has ended, the servers and the others who are going to eat immediately assemble. Although they are few, they are served with the same order and reverence as the convent. By custom there are no more than the person sitting at the small bell and the reader at table, together with the servers, unless it happens that the greater or claustral prior, his assistant, or someone arriving from a journey eats with them.

It sometimes also happens that an obedientiary, prevented by some serious labor, is absent from the principal table with the prior’s permission. He is therefore not forbidden to eat with the servers. Likewise, although permission to do so is granted to no one except out of great necessity, after receiving permission he may leave before their meal has ended.

On the principal feast days, however, the porter and those administering the other major offices may, if necessary, eat after the Gospel of the principal Mass with the prior’s permission, in such an arrangement that afterward they may not repeat that meal either with the priors or with the servers.

When the servers leave the refectory, only those brothers through whom they pass incline and rise; or, if the brothers are sitting in chapter, they all incline and rise. It is customary for one of them, if it is night, to carry a lighted candle before the others as far as the church.

## CHAPTER LXVI. Concerning one’s conduct after dinner and after supper.

(UD.) After the meal, silence is enjoined upon him with greater strictness at this hour than at any other. In accordance with the time and the order of the day, he is to sit in the cloister reading or singing; or, if he goes to sleep and wishes to read, he reads lying down, arranged as though he wished to fall asleep immediately.

* At the hour when he goes to sleep, he does not take a book with him, but first—though he must not leave it openly—he places it by the bed, just as afterward he must not return it openly to the book chest. If a convert has his psalter at his bed, then, when he rises afterward, he need not return it if he wishes.

[Col. 0997A] Understand this concerning everyone, even if there were such an abundance of books that, while some lay continually at the beds, others could be available to those sitting in the cloister.

UD. When lying in bed, he avoids not only the signs made with the hand but also directs his eyes toward no brother’s bed, not even for a moment, in order to look there.

After None, whether or not he is thirsty, he nevertheless does not fail to go with the others to the refectory to drink, unless he is an obedientiary * and is excessively occupied outside at that hour.

UD. Whenever supper is eaten after Vespers, after supper he goes up to the dormitory, * places his knife at his head, puts on his night shoes, and comes to sit in the cloister. There, for as long as he sits at that hour, he applies himself so diligently to silence that, if someone skilled in writing happens to write something, he makes no sound at all either with the parchment or with the pen itself; or, if he comes down from the dormitory later than the others, he places his foot so gently that, even if his walking is seen by others, it cannot at all be heard by him.

Such silence need not be observed so carefully at other times. * Care must be taken, both after dinner and after supper, that no one presumes to wash his hands, except scribes and any priest who needs to look ahead in something in the missal. At that time he is to carry the missal nowhere unless it is wrapped in a cloth. The sacristan is to ensure that such cloths are never lacking there.

## CHAPTER LXVII. Concerning the lighting of the cloister at its proper time.

[Col. 0997C]

Care must also be taken that in winter, if Vespers ends late, a light is immediately lit throughout the cloister, because the convent, dressed in night garments, and the young brothers as well, sitting with lighted lanterns but without books, wait until the bell is struck for drinking.

Then the prior immediately shakes it, and the weekly sacristan, performing the bowing forward and backward before the drinking has ended, strikes the signal for collation only when ordered, so that collation may follow as the convent leaves the refectory.

At this same drinking, any obedientiary who leaves before the others without permission because of an urgent need connected with his obedience is not accused, unless he repeats this too often.

## CHAPTER LXVIII. Concerning the reader of the collation.

[Col. 0997D]

* Since it is not our custom for the reader at the collation to be noted on the tablet, the armarius must take particular care to make timely provision, lest negligence in reading at the collation occur. Therefore, on Sunday he gives the book to the reader for the week and shows him where he is to begin. For the reader of the preceding week shows the armarius where he finished reading. The armarius must beware never to assign the reading at the collation to someone who is too poorly instructed, but to a person sufficiently suitable and intelligent to read in such a way that those listening may be edified. On the principal festivals, when the *Venite* is sung by four, or even when they are in copes, if they have a proper sermon, the reading for the collation is taken from there, provided that no other reading has immediately preceded it or is to follow. If it can be read through in two nights, it is read for as long as necessary, until it is finished.

The reader must also know that he should never begin the reading unless he has first made the sign to himself, except at the command on Saturday: then, as soon as the armarius finishes the chant, he must not delay in reading. Whoever comes to the collation at such an hour that, while sitting, he hears even half a verse of the reading does not for that reason ask pardon at the chapter on the following day. When the reading has ended, the reader makes the forward and backward bows there beside the lectern and immediately leaves, unless he is on watch; then, turning aside for a short while, he waits for his fellow custodian. All who remain from chapter, when the collation has ended, leave the chapterhouse and turn to the left, until the whole convent has gone out and they receive permission to depart from the abbot or prior. Then, if any of the brothers are thirsty, they make the sign and receive permission to drink. Such permission must by no means be requested later, nor thereafter except rarely—unless someone is seized by a violent thirst that is utterly intolerable. No rule has been established for such violence: whenever such intolerable thirst afflicts anyone, even in the middle of matins, he shall ask permission to drink. Once it has been granted, he shall go to the infirmary at the prior’s command, accompanied by someone, and afterward he shall not return to the convent except at the time when any sick person does so, and not without permission. It should also be known that those who remain from compline, when they make the aforesaid sign to leave, may also ask for permission to drink again during that night, if they intend to drink. Others who are sometimes absent from the collation by permission because they are occupied with their offices—for example, the guest-master, the almoner, and others of this kind—ask the cellarer for this permission, if they happen not to be able to obtain it from the cloister prior while he is making his rounds after compline.

## CHAPTER LXIX. On the brother who sprinkles the dormitory

* After compline, the brother appointed to sprinkle the dormitory—who may also be a conversus—immediately withdraws before the choir when compline has ended and, beside the altar where the sick sit, makes only the first prayer. After doing this, he sprinkles himself with holy water and then goes up to the dormitory to sprinkle it. He never omits this, unless it is Sunday. When compline has ended, as stated, and they again make the three prayers, he occupies the last place for these, while the priors occupy the front. When these prayers have been completed, he is the last to leave the choir and reverently bows to the altars there. The brother who has been sprinkled with holy water nevertheless observes this same practice when he has been sprinkled by the priest.

(UD.) When he comes to the church door, he covers his head with his cap and does not uncover it again until he has settled himself in bed.

## CHAPTER LXX. How he is to settle himself

(UD.) Therefore, when he comes to his bed, if he is wearing the froccus and cuculla, he folds the froccus and places it on the board, or, if necessary, beneath the pillow. Then, having thrown the coverlet toward the lower part of the bed, he climbs onto the bench and, having entered, prepares himself so that he may sit properly on the bed; then, drawing his hands out to the sides, not toward his feet, he removes his shoes, taking care not to place one leg over the other. After lifting both feet equally and placing them on the bed, he does not remove the cuculla before drawing the coverlet up beneath his elbows. Then, having removed it, whether it is worn with the pellicium or not, he folds it and places it at his head; or, if he feels such cold, he spreads it over himself, with its hood turned toward his head. A novice who has not yet been consecrated does the same with the froccus. He may place the pellicium over the other coverings if he wishes, but not turned inside out. Whenever he wishes, provided he does so moderately, he may arm himself with the sign of the holy cross; he may do the same when he rises.

However much warmth he may sometimes feel, he must never uncover more of his body than his feet, arms, and chest. When appropriate, he may fasten a moderately sized board at the head, facing the front of the bed, either to support the pillow or to keep out the light of the lamp. Likewise, he is not forbidden suitably to fit a board between the bed and the wall, to place frocci or something of that kind upon it. However he may lie down—on his back, on his side, or with his knees drawn up—no one reproves him.

He may never go to the privy in the cuculla and pellicium until after the convent has settled in its beds; then he does not spread the coverlet over the bed. In the cuculla alone, however, he may go there whenever he wishes. If blood flows from his nose, he leans outside the bed toward the wall; but if he does not sleep beside the wall, he turns toward the front of the bed. If he feels nausea growing upon him, he goes toward the corner of the privy and covers the excrement with hay.

If he hears a brother lying beside him rousing another brother in his sleep in any way, he immediately wakes that brother—not by making a sound, but by pulling at some of his coverings or bedding. He may sleep in socks and, if necessary, with his cap, but never in the pellicium. Whether in bed or outside it, he must never look upon another’s face with his eyes in the dormitory. Whenever he passes by the Crucifix there, he bows to it.

## CHAPTER LXXI. On him who becomes extremely thirsty

[Col. 0999D]

(UD.) If he suffers from such severe thirst that he has no hope of enduring patiently until the signal for nocturns, he discreetly awakens the prior and indicates to him by a sign what he wants. The prior immediately leads him to the infirmary and tells the infirmarian the reason for his coming; then, leaving that brother there, he returns to bed. The brother, settling himself in the bed that the infirmarian shows him, comes to nocturns with the sick. At dawn, after obtaining permission from the prior through the infirmarian to leave, and after the daily garments have been brought from the dormitory, he returns from the infirmary to the convent at the time when any sick person does so.

And, to return to the nocturnal period when a brother begins to thirst: if he can endure until the convent rises for nocturns, he joins those who pray in the lesser choir and waits for the arrival of the prior, who is to enter there into the greater choir, until the three prayers have been completed. Then, having received permission from the prior, and having drunk in the infirmary as stated, he remains there for the rest of the night until morning. But if he can refrain from drinking until after nocturns, then, with permission and once the heat of thirst has been quenched, he must sing matins through with those who at that hour sing it for the sick lying in bed; or, if there are no such sick persons, he must sing it through if he is able. If he is illiterate, he asks no one to sing it for him.

Anyone who wishes to be a man of this discipline and manner of life must, as far as he can, take the greatest care to prevent such a necessity from ever becoming a burden to him.

(UD.) These few things have been said, as they came to mind, from among many by which novices, if possible, should be instructed before they join our community.

## CHAPTER LXXII. By what rule novices are to conduct themselves before their consecration

* When it pleases the lord abbot to advance the novices to the monastic order, he first receives notice from their master and mentions it in chapter. If the brothers are to receive the blessing on that same day, the master, being ordered to bring them, removes their caps. After they have entered and asked pardon, they repeat the same petition that they made at the beginning of their reception.

The same procedure is followed if, after their caps have been removed, they have spent some time in their cell and thereafter remain separated from the convent there for fifteen days or fewer, if the abbot so decides; except that they attend the divine service in the lesser choir. During these days they not only sleep in the aforesaid cell, but also devote themselves there to reading and eat there. During these same days they do not approach for the kiss of peace or for communion, nor do they offer. Each day, after hearing the morning Mass, they come to the brothers’ chapter and sit there on the bench and stool on the right near the door, with no one mixing among them except their master. They sit there until the sentence of the Rule has been read and explained, or, as is customary on feast days, until the Gospel reading has been given.

When, after the sermon, the lord abbot says, “Speak about the order,” they immediately make the forward and backward bows and follow their master, who goes before them, to his cell, so that the customary chapter may be held among them there. If they have committed any such offense, they are not exempt from judicial sentence; for this reason their master has with him there a brother of more advanced age who may pass judgment upon them, unless he entrusts this to one of the novices.

When the convent makes a procession to Saint Mary after matins and vespers, they follow last and do not enter the church, but wait outside in the chapterhouse for the convent to come out. Then, approaching more closely, they stand in order, bowed, with their master, until everyone has passed by.

When they are going to eat, they leave the church before the convent and, after washing their hands at their own lavatory, go to the kitchen so that each may bring his own beans. For bringing the common dish and pottage as well, as many rise as are needed, according to the wishes of the person who serves them as cellarer. They must also observe this: they are to make the ringing of their bell coincide with that of the brothers in common, so that they do not begin earlier, though they finish sooner.

Before the meal, one of them takes a book and reads until their presiding master orders him to stop at the ringing of the bell. When he eats with the others near the end of the meal, he rises again and reads a little, finishing the reading with “But you, O Lord.” In these and other ways, as far as they can, they imitate the discipline that we observe in the refectory.

They must also know that after the refectory, there in their cell, they are to finish the verse without the psalm, in such a way that they reach the place of bowing before the convent passes from the refectory. The person who has spoken before the refectory has indicated this: after each meal they are to stand bowed there, arranged from the door of the refectory to the step of the dormitory as the convent leaves the refectory and passes by them with a similar bow. They themselves then follow it, all singing the psalm that they had previously omitted.

Wherever they are to go together, their master must precede them and bow everywhere together with those who are bowing. If one of them wishes to go from the church to their cell, he must not presume to do so unless he takes at least one companion with him; and, if it is night, he must not go without a light.

They come to the brothers’ collation. When the convent rises, they stand bowed in the same place where they had been sitting, until everyone has passed by. When the others drink at the mandatum or during the collation, they turn aside to their cell and do the same.

Just as they are to enter the church last, so after the sprinkling of holy water they are also to leave last. For as long as they are without their caps, the *absconsa* is not placed before them, just as it is not during those two nights after nocturns following the reception of the novices’ blessing. After nocturns, or from chapter, they may never leave without a light if there is need; but the one who appears to be senior among them goes before the others with a lantern.

On Sundays, while the others go out for the procession, they stand in ordered ranks, bowed, at the exit of the church inside the church itself, until the brothers pass by. Meanwhile, while they are without their caps, they may freely wear albs and copes, and they may also attend any procession that does not take place outside the monastery; but they come last, preceded by their master. At the station that is to be held in the vestibule, they must stand behind the elders, forming something like a line.

## CHAPTER LXXIII. On the repeated petition of the novices

* When the aforesaid days have ended and they are now about to receive the blessing of monastic life, after the first Mass they do not come to the brothers’ chapter, but meet with their master in their cell. There they wait until their master returns to the convent and, after the chapter has been prolonged for a short time, the lord abbot orders them to be presented to him in that same chapter.

(UD.) When they come and ask pardon, they are again questioned about what they want. Lying prostrate, they answer as they did at the beginning of their reception. After they have risen, the lord abbot again, as before, sets forth some things about the austerity of regular discipline, and among other matters does not conceal that it is better for them to return to the world without the blessing than, having received the blessing, not to persevere.

* If there are any among them—God forbid—who do not wish to persevere, their master removes their habits from them in their cell and, restoring their former garments, lets them depart unharmed. They immediately come to his feet two by two; and if three remain, those three come together to his feet. As they leave the chapterhouse, they are carefully instructed about what they must do in the very reception of the blessing. On the day on which they are ordained, the psalm *Levavi* is sung for them at each hour, if the lord abbot gives the order at the time; and for this reason they prostrate themselves at his feet.

## CHAPTER LXXIV. On the blessing of the novices

(UD.) Immediately after the Gospel of the principal Mass, the blessing is to be duly performed, and it is to begin in this manner. Each has written out how he is to make his profession, as follows:

“I, brother N., promise stability, conversion of my manner of life, and obedience according to the Rule of Saint Benedict before God and his saints in this monastery, which has been built in honor of blessed Mary ever-Virgin, in the presence of the lord abbot.”

(Var.) As soon as each has read this through at the step from his booklet, he immediately places the booklet upon the altar, where it is to be kept permanently. If he does not know his letters, the master reads it for him; he nevertheless writes the sign of the cross with his own hand at the end of the same little document. An educated novice does not do this. When it has been read, the novice himself receives it from the master’s hand and places it upon the altar. After placing it there and kissing the altar, he withdraws a little, asks pardon on his knees, and immediately returns to his place before the step.

(UD.) When they have stood in order before the step, they ask pardon three times, upon their hands and knees, also saying this verse three times:

“Receive me, O Lord, according to your word, and I shall live.”

The whole convent responds to them in the same way each time. At the third response, with “Glory be to the Father” added, they make a circuit on bent knees and afterward prostrate themselves for prayer.

Whether or not he celebrates that Mass, the lord abbot intones:

“Lord, have mercy. Our Father.”

Then, after *Miserere*, and after these verses have been said:

“Save your servants,” etc.  
“Send them help, O Lord,” etc.  
“Let nothing prevail,” etc.  
“Be for them, O Lord, a tower of strength.”

These collects follow:

“God, Father of forgiveness.”  
“O God, who through your co-eternal Son,” etc.  
“Lord Jesus Christ, who are,” etc.  
“Come, Holy Spirit, who are God and Lord,” etc.

He blesses the cucullas with:

“Lord Jesus Christ, who are a covering,” etc.

When the novices, after the blessing has been completed, rise from prayer, and if there are many of them, they are sprinkled with holy water while standing in the same place. If there are few, they come into the sanctuary to be sprinkled there by the abbot. They remove their frocci and put on their cucullas. While each is being undressed, the lord abbot says to him:

“May the Lord strip you of the old man with his deeds.”

While he is being clothed, he says:

“May the Lord clothe you,” etc.

Then the brothers who are in the sanctuary around them, beginning with the lord abbot himself, kiss them. Afterward they go around through the choir, preceded by their master, and all the brothers who can do so kiss them until the time for the offering, beginning with those who occupy the choir, or, if they are absent, with the elders at the choir-stalls. For they alone offer on that day, provided there are twelve lessons. They do not return later for kissing, even if they did not give everyone the kiss earlier. They approach for the kiss of peace last, and for communion first. There may be so many of them that during these three days, even if they are *privati*, no one except the novices themselves offers at the principal Mass or approaches for the kiss of peace and communion.

It should be noted, however, that a monk who comes from another monastery and must read the booklet of his profession on that very day reads first of all. If he previously held a higher place in the convent, he must nevertheless immediately go of his own accord—whatever sort of person he may be—to the last place of the literate brothers in the choir, if he himself is literate. In chapter and in the refectory he will be last even among the conversi.

## CHAPTER LXXV. On the conduct of the novices during the three days after the blessing

[Col. 1003C]

During these three days they do not uncover their heads, keeping them continually covered with their caps; they sleep in their cucullas, though they remove their frocci. They also put aside their shoes and knives and cover themselves with coverlets. If they wish, they remove the pellicia from their cucullas. They speak absolutely nothing. For this reason, when the speech in chapter ends, they leave and go to the church, remaining there throughout the entire time allotted for speaking.

They attend the service of God in the lesser choir, and there make the three prayers before prime. During these same days they attend no procession except the one made to Saint Mary. Each day, offering, they approach for the kiss of peace and communion; they do not omit this even if something else happens to them while sleeping. If they make a noise or anything of that kind in the refectory, they ask pardon while wearing their cucullas.

(UD.) Finally, on the third day, at the principal Mass—or, if the lord abbot so decides, at the Mass sung for the sick at Saint Mary—when the priest has kissed them, he removes the caps from their heads. Thereafter they may speak and remove their cucullas as the other brothers do.

If a sick man receives, as they say, the blessing *Ad succurrendum*, and because of his illness cannot keep silence, he makes his profession at the step before the others. While the others who are being blessed cover their heads, he covers his as well. He observes everything that they do during those three days, and whatever had previously been omitted is supplied. A man assisted by this blessing, however, has no chapter standing if the lord abbot has not consecrated him; and although he is last in rank, he will nevertheless be superior to all the novices. After they too have been consecrated, he descends to his former place in the order.

## CHAPTER LXXVI. On a layman who, coming to the point of death, asks to become a monk

* If at any time a layman who has reached the point of death asks to be assisted by consecration in the monastic habit, he is clothed and consecrated in the monastic habit by the lord abbot—or, if the abbot is absent or prevented by some necessity from coming to him, by the prior in his place—just as any novice received into the cloister is ordained *Ad succurrendum* if he has been so weakened by illness.

For he makes his profession in words only, as he is able, and the customary prayers are said over him. But if his death is seen to be so near that it is believed he cannot live long enough to receive the blessing in this manner, he is to be clothed only in a blessed cuculla and, immediately, if he can endure it, brought to the monastery. If he pays the debt of death in that same place, he is nevertheless received into the cloister and buried among the brothers.

But if he is brought to the monastery and recovers from his illness, after prime—or at another time after terce—he is led by the infirmarian from the novices’ cell to chapter, to make his petition, with the master. Although he has been assisted by the monastic blessing, he will nevertheless have no chapter standing, even if he has been consecrated by the lord abbot, unless the abbot himself, or, in his absence, the prior by his command, has granted this—until he makes his profession with the others who are to be blessed and performs the other things that custom requires during the three days.

(UD.) From the third day, however, when the cucullas have been removed from their heads by the priest, as stated, they are no longer separated from chapter. The abbot then orders them, according to the grace given to each, to serve in the church thereafter—that is, to read and sing, if they know how.

## CHAPTER LXXVII. That novice priests and deacons must be carefully examined before they are permitted to perform their office

[Col. 1004D]

(UD.) Those who are either priests or deacons must nevertheless be carefully examined concerning how they were ordained and what their conscience is like, and their conduct must be tested for some time before they are permitted to exercise this ministry. In particular, one who was a priest before he came is entirely prohibited from this office until, by observing repeatedly, he learns with what manifold care we handle such a sacrament.

* When the lord abbot grants this permission to the novices, either personally or through a messenger, after their master has admonished them, they do not come to his feet—as they do not come to the feet of the prior sitting in his place—but merely bow from their seats. They do the same when they are ordered to stand before him. To novice priests, brothers skilled in this office are immediately assigned, one to each, to instruct them diligently in the great care with which these sacraments are handled among us. No novice, however skilled, may celebrate the principal Mass among us within the space of half a year without grave necessity.

(UD.) To mention here both those who are being examined and those who, having already been examined in some fashion, are ordered to serve: each of them, while sitting in chapter, must pay careful attention so as to notice whether he has been assigned to any service that is to be performed either in the church or outside it.

## CHAPTER LXXVIII. On the weekly cantor

(UD.) If he is designated for the invitatory, before beginning it he stands at the step with his colleague and, whether before beginning or when he finishes, makes the forward and backward bows on both occasions. * Before beginning the invitatory, after he has begun it, and also before beginning it again after the *Gloria*, he observes one form of bowing: that is, he bows only forward. After the final verse of the psalm *Venite*, however, he remains bowed for a while while the convent sings the invitatory. Whether two or four prechant the *Venite*, they observe this rule of bowing.

(UD.) If, among two men who are to sing the invitatory, the first is designated, he will also be the weekly cantor and throughout the whole week will sing the *Venite* both at the office of three lessons and at that of twelve lessons. He does not do so thereafter unless he is designated for it on the Saturday of the preceding week, except when a festival occurs on which it is to be sung by four. Then that first man is again designated on the tablet. In the office of twelve lessons, however, it is not the cantor of the completed week who sings the *Venite* with him, but rather the one whom the armarius appoints for it each time.

Whenever four are to sing the invitatory, those four leave the choir at the third incision of the fifteen steps, and, after first washing their hands, enter the sacristy, put on albs and copes, and, after the verse “Salvation belongs to the Lord” has been assigned, enter the choir. They do so in such a way that those higher in sacred order stand in the middle, while those lower stand last at the step, each, if possible, on his own side of the choir. Even if all are from one choir, they must observe this order when entering.

Then, after completing the customary bowing as described above, they begin the invitatory moderately. Those standing on the right sing the first verse through together; thereafter they sing the whole psalm antiphonally, one verse according to one group and the next according to the other, until *Sicut erat*, where all must sing together. Before the verse “Today, if you hear his voice,” the armarius is to raise the pitch of the invitatory, if necessary.

But, to return to the weekly cantor: throughout the week he intones the office of the principal Mass, except for the offertory verse, concerning the intoning of which he gives the armarius a sign. If at any time a morning Mass is to be sung festively during the following week, it is also his responsibility to intone the office for that Mass, even if it is for the dead; at that Mass he will also be the last of those offering.

(UD.) On Sunday, or on any comparable day, when all the signals for the principal Mass are to be rung, it is his responsibility to begin ringing the bell first and to lead the choir. He puts on the cope, which he has brought for himself during the ringing or the psalms.

* If he is a priest, after the offering has been placed following the Gospel, he may receive permission to sing the Mass or for some other such necessity; then, after handing his cope to one of the oblates, he makes the forward and backward bows and leaves.

[Note: [Col. 1005D] This is relevant here: Trithemius, *Chronicon Hirsaugiense*, p. 229, says the following about Saint William: “The man of God William also instituted, following the example of the Cluniacs, the custom of oblates, whom he permitted by sacred constitution to remain in their former habit. He was accustomed reasonably to make use of their service in many matters, especially in those tasks that seemed necessary to be carried out among secular people, where it was not permitted to send bearded men (*Barbatos*, that is, conversi) or monks. Consult the passage cited.”]

(UD.) He also places in the thurible the incense brought to him, with which the body of the Lord is to be incensed before the consecration; he does the same on the principal feast of the Virgins.

* Whenever he has the time and opportunity, he may sit. When the others bow during the singing, he too bows, except when the *Sanctus* is sung; then he stands upright. When the Lord’s Prayer has ended, he immediately straightens himself. At the first and last collects and at the secrets he remains bowed throughout. When the Mass has ended, he does not leave his place before the reader at table has received the blessing.

(UD. var.) At the office of twelve lessons, at nocturns and matins, he intones the antiphons for which he is designated. On the other nights he intones whatever antiphons are to be intoned in his choir, both in the following week and in the present one. Nevertheless, at all the canonical hours he intones the antiphons, except at vespers. He does not intone at vespers on a festival at which each responsory is sung by two people; then he intones only the first, and the armarius assigns the others to whomever he sees fit.

* If a festival occurs on which one antiphon is to be sung over the ferial psalms at first vespers, this too is intoned by the weekly cantor. Likewise, he sings every first responsory, whether short or long, that is to be sung at matins or vespers; nor does he withdraw when two or more are to sing it.

The litany preceding the Mass, which is sung for the procession, is not prechanted by the cantor of the preceding week, but rather by those to whom the armarius hands the book. A little before the prayer “O God, by whose mercy,” has ended, they proceed to the step and bow only toward the altar; immediately when the prayer has ended, they begin the litany.

The aforesaid weekly cantor, every day at the principal Mass, even if he is from the left choir, is assisted by the right choir when he begins, wearing the cope. But when we are all clothed in albs, the office of the principal Mass belongs not to him but to the armarius.

## CHAPTER LXXIX. On him who is designated for the first antiphon

[Col. 1007A]

(UD.) If he is not the weekly cantor but is designated for one of the nocturns’ antiphons, when he has intoned it, after the first verse of the psalm has ended he makes the forward and backward bows, unless he is facing the altar. For all those who stand on that side where the seat of the lord abbot is located bow only forward at that time.

If he has completely neglected to intone it, so that someone else begins it, he does not for that reason ask pardon either there or later in chapter, unless he has been called to account. But if he makes a mistake while beginning it, he immediately asks pardon before bowing, provided that he has made a mistake in a word. No one asks pardon for *neumes* [Note: [Col. 1007D] See what we said above concerning neumes], because Saint Benedict did not prescribe this either.

## CHAPTER LXXX. On him who is designated for a reading

[Col. 1007B]

If he is designated for a reading, before reading he comes to the step and makes the forward and backward bows. From there he approaches and withdraws from the lectern with a deep bow, except on those occasions when the convent has not yet sat down—provided that the lectern is placed so that the reader must pass through the convent.

(UD.) After he has finished reading, he again makes the forward and backward bows at the step and also first asks pardon upon his hands and knees.

(Var.) It should also be noted that this is our custom: when the prophets are read in the church, a reading that begins prophetically but ends historically is concluded with “But you, O Lord”; one that begins historically but ends prophetically is concluded with “Thus says the Lord.” “But you, O Lord” is also said at the end of each completed book of the prophets.

## CHAPTER LXXXI. On him who is designated for a responsory

(UD.) If he is designated for a responsory, he bows moderately. Before intoning it and afterward, when the verse or *Gloria Patri* has ended—if the latter is to be added—he makes the forward and backward bows there, and after the verse lowers himself in another brief bow. If he is to sing with another, he sings at the step.

## CHAPTER LXXXII. On the weekly priest
(UD.) If he is appointed to exercise the priesthood and has sung the principal Mass during the present week, he shall also sing one at the following Matins, whether it is to be sung in the monastery or at Saint Mary’s. At this entrance, the deacon and subdeacon unfold the altar cloth, and likewise fold it up when the Mass is finished.

UD. Of the things the priest is to say, he ought to know not a few by heart: first, the three collects for singing the fifteen gradual psalms before the nocturns; or, if the psalmody continues to the end of the Psalter, the collects for the suffrages of the saints; the collects for the office for the faithful departed; the collects for the psalms for members of the household; the collects for the psalmody “God, give ear”; and the cursus for tonsure. * He ought also to know our usages in many respects, especially in saying and arranging the collects, UD. so that he may never say anything in choir that in any way differs from the customary practice.

He ought to know that if something follows immediately after the psalms for relatives—* for example, the office or Mass of the dead, a procession, or a litany—“Let us bless the Lord” is not said. If anyone is unable, because of old age or dullness of understanding, to learn the prescribed material by heart, he is in no way permitted to do any of these things contrary to order in choir. (UD.) But to whomever, when circumstances require it, this is permitted, however much he may think himself knowledgeable about everything, he ought nevertheless not to disdain frequently asking the armarius, like all the others appointed beforehand for some divine office, about matters of which they are uncertain.

* If there is room for it, at the form or at the end of the wall, during the week in which he is appointed to sing Mass, a place somewhat higher against the wall is to be granted him [Col. 1008B] out of reverence for the office entrusted to him and so that he may be properly heard by the community. He must also observe that he begin no Hour before the signal is given.

Whenever twelve readings are held, whether during the singing or beforehand, he ought, if he wishes, to wash his hands at the lavatorium. Therefore, after the nocturns he does not leave the choir before, by the alternation of the singers, they have reached the verse “The heavens are full”; but then, leaving, he immediately enters the sacristy, puts on the alb, stole, and chasuble, and, after reading through the Gospel, with the armarius listening if necessary, * places incense there, and thus proceeds from the vestry with the procession, so that he may enter the sanctuary when the verse “Each day” has been imposed.

UD. He places the Gospel book, which he reverently carries between his arms, against his breast and lays it in the middle of the altar; he also censes it in the form of a cross, and there, before the altar, bows for the Lord’s Prayer.

(var.) When they have reached the verse “In you, O Lord, I have hoped,” he stands upright, makes the sign of the cross over himself, and, after kissing the altar, takes up the book and again arranges it properly between his arms as before, so that, when the community sees the same Gospel book, it may bow; * and thus he proceeds toward the lectern. But the conversus carrying the thurible, going ahead of that priest, censes the lectern in the form of a cross, and, withdrawing, does not bow.

After the Gospel has been read, and the other things that holy Benedict commands to be done at that time have been properly completed, the same priest does not move from his place before beginning Matins, UD. until he has said with the others, “Glory to the Father,” bowing slightly. When the others stand upright, he withdraws. But he always hastens so as to have returned to the choir before the first psalm of Matins is finished; * and if “Come” is sung in albs, he returns to the choir wearing the alb.

If he sees five candelabra before the principal altar, he ought, wearing the cope, to cense; then he leaves during the hymn in order to put on that same cope. Then, even if he has left the lord abbot in the choir, and if he hears him impose the antiphon, when the canticle “Benedictus” begins he approaches him with the incense boat, the conversus carrying the thurible following; and, after kissing his hand, he offers him incense to be placed in the thurible.

But if the lord abbot is not then in the choir, he himself, after placing incense in the sacristy, takes the thurible and enters the sanctuary at the beginning of the aforesaid canticle, so that he may cense the altar.

## CHAPTER LXXXIII. How he ought to cense the altars

(var.) The manner of censing is as follows. First he censes the face of the altar three times; then, three times, its surface; likewise, the middle of the altar; then each horn three times on the surface and once across it; afterward each side, just as he censed the face; finally, wherever the relics and plenaria ordinarily stand behind it [Note: [Col. 1009] *Plenaria*: perhaps reliquary chests or ornaments], he directs his hand with incense three times on each side.

Afterward he censes the smaller altars nearest the choir and the altar of the Holy Cross, making over each one a single sign of the cross with the incense. * If relics of a saint are in the chapel of Saint Mary, whose feast it is, he goes there also and censes only the altar on which the relics are located in the same manner as the other smaller altars.

Then, if the lord abbot, or a bishop, or another such person is in the choir, he enters with the thurible and, after first making a humble bow, offers incense to him, and then to the prior. But if none of these persons is present, the priest ought to offer incense to the prior alone, out of reverence.

If, however, seven candelabra have been placed before the principal altar, censing is to be done by two men; for this reason the sacristan signals another priest, who censes together with the hebdomadary priest. Although lower in rank, the hebdomadary customarily censes the right horn of the altar and afterward, on returning, stands in his choir.

These two, if the lord abbot or any of the persons mentioned above is in the choir, ought to enter together with their thuribles and likewise offer incense together to him and to the prior. If the hebdomadary asks another to read the Gospel in his place, the latter, after reading, must know that he is to perform all these prescribed actions.

But if the person asked for this returns to the choir wearing the alb, when he goes out to remove the alb, the hebdomadary says the suffrages of the saints and the other things that follow at that time. If he returns without the alb, he performs the suffrages of the saints and the other rites up to the procession; and if he is going to celebrate the principal Mass, although the other Hours do not belong to him, he shall nevertheless complete the Hour that immediately precedes the Mass, and None, which immediately follows dinner, as well as Compline, just as he does Vespers if he is to cense.

(UD.) On ordinary days, whenever we eat twice, before the signal for Terce is rung he washes his hands according to custom, so that after making the prayer he may immediately put on the priestly vestments and impose Terce. Then, when that verse of the Litany, “All,” etc., has been sung while seated, he leaves the choir to put on the chasuble and come to the altar with the procession. He observes the same order of departure after the prayer has been made, whether the Litany precedes the Mass.

* If it is a day on which we eat only once, he vests himself while the Litany is being sung; and if a procession is to be held, as on Thursday in Lent, he does not vest until that too has been completed. * Then [Col. 1010A] he departs through the lesser choir to wash his feet, and hastens so as to impose incense in the vesting room at the proper time. UD. Thus approaching the altar, he himself carries the missal in his left arm.

* If a bishop or abbot is to sing Mass, his deacons ought to carry the same missal.

(UD. var.) After setting it down at the right horn of the altar, he bows toward the middle of the altar for the Lord’s Prayer in particular. When this is completed, fortifying himself with the sign of the cross, he kisses the altar and the closed Gospel book—if it is decorated externally with some workmanship; otherwise, the open book.

* Then he gives the deacon a place so that he can stand near the right horn of the altar. He himself stands near the left, and, bowing toward the deacon and subdeacon, they likewise say the confession while bowing.

[Col. 1010B] UD. Its prescribed form is such that neither at Mass nor at the Hours at which it is to be said is it to be expressed in more words than these:

“I confess to the Lord and to all his saints, and to you, Father, that I have sinned in thought, speech, and deed, through my fault. I ask you: pray for me.”

“May almighty God have mercy on you and forgive you all your sins; may he deliver you from every evil, preserve and strengthen you in every good work, and bring you to eternal life. Amen.”

With the addition: “Pardon, remission, and assistance.”

After saying the collects, he gives the missal to the deacon to place at the left horn, unless he prefers to carry it with him in case he wishes to look ahead at something.

(UD.) At the Epistle he sits until they come to the Gospel. To the deacon who is about to read he gives the blessing in this form: “May God have mercy on us and bless us.” On this occasion he stands near the right horn of the altar, and the deacon near the left.

* When the deacon withdraws from the altar to the lectern, the priest turns himself after him and stands in this manner until the Gospel has been completed. Not only does he, but the whole community reverently turns in that direction wherever the Gospel is read.

## CHAPTER LXXXIV [Note: [Col. 1009] See chapter 35 of Bernard’s *Ordinarium Cluniacense*, part I]. With what care the consecration and communion of the Lord’s Body are celebrated

(UD. var.) It seems worthy and necessary to insert here with what care and diligence service is rendered for the consecration of the Lord’s Body and Blood.

First, for this very purpose, a small cupboard was made before the face of the principal altar, very well joined together and lined on every side inside with cloth. Nothing else is stored in it except those utensils necessary for the solemn celebration of Masses—specifically, those celebrated by the community as a whole. These are chiefly two chalices with patens of different sizes, and two corporals: one double-sized, as all corporals ordinarily are for private Masses, and the other single-sized.

The smaller chalice with the double corporal is for the Mass at Matins; the larger, with the single corporal, for the principal Mass. For one single corporal is always kept at the left horn of the altar in a small chest neatly adorned with silk, as I learned from our predecessors, so that it may be at hand against the danger of fire, should such a thing occur; for it is very effective when brought.

There is also a medium-sized silver paten and a bowl of the same metal, with a lid joined to it by metalwork. There are ampullae there for supplying wine and water; for wine is also customarily offered in an ampulla before the consecration. There is a silver ewer with its appendage for washing the hands. There are several small linens, without which the individual sacred vessels are neither washed nor carried anywhere.

The cupboard itself also has a shelf in the middle, so that the more sacred objects may be above and the others below. At the beginning of Mass it is to be brought by the chief custodian of the church or by his assistant, who is then hebdomadary. It is covered above with the same cloth, and he places the paten there together with the corporal. Holding the chalice with its linen cloth stretched lengthwise over it, and covering it above, he carries it to the water jar, which is always made of tin and kept in the church in a suitable place, so that all the chalices used for private Masses may be washed there.

There too the hebdomadary carefully washes the chalice that has been brought, pouring water into it twice. If he is not a priest or levite, he asks a substitute of another order for this purpose, so that on Wednesday and Saturday the inside of the chalice may be thoroughly rubbed by hand down to the bottom, lest it perhaps acquire an odor because of the frequent pouring in of wine. Thus washed, it is brought back and placed on the cupboard.

The subdeacon washes his hands in advance so that he may be ready for the service of the chalice. Meanwhile, while the Gospel is being read, he takes the chalice together with the paten and corporal and tests whether any water has remained in it during the washing; he pours it into a hollow made for this purpose near the altar, just as another has been made there somewhat farther away, over which the same subdeacon and the other ministers wash their hands.

He stands beside the priest until the Gospel is finished. He places the corporal on the middle of the altar, approaching from the front, while still holding the chalice and paten. He accompanies the priest as he proceeds a little toward the brothers, so that the offering may be made by each of them.

* After the Gospel has been read, the minister receives the Gospel book from the deacon and brings it to the priest to be kissed, and then to the first offerer. This is always observed except on Good Friday, because then, after the Passion has been read, no one except the deacon kisses the Gospel book.

It should be known that on the days when the Creed of the faith is sung, the minister—who at that time, as also at all festive occasions with twelve readings, holds it in front—waits until the same Creed is nearly finished. Then, taking the chalice from the subdeacon as described above, he pours into the same hollow any water that remained and places the corporal on the altar.

UD. The deacon brings water and a towel and presents them reverently. After washing his hands, he approaches the altar. And, to speak precisely here of the principal Mass, he takes both corporals—either the one that always lies on the altar or the one brought by the subdeacon or minister—and spreads them, placing beneath them the one that always lies there.

* When the offering has been completed, the priest also washes his hands and dries them with the cleanest linen, UD. which is assigned for this purpose to him alone, taking care afterward not to touch anything else with the fingers with which the Lord’s Body is to be touched.

The subdeacon carries the hosts to the deacon standing beside the altar and covering himself, so that from all of them he may choose three that he wishes to consecrate. The wine that has been offered is poured by the subdeacon himself into the other chalice, and he leaves only as much as is sufficient for the consecration. He himself, however, does not mix water with it, because he is permitted to pour in neither wine nor water; instead, he gives the ampulla of water that has been brought, together with the chalice, to the deacon so that he may mix it.

He also gives him a cloth with which the outside of the chalice is carefully dried, lest any wine or water remain on the exterior.

(var.) After the hosts have thus been arranged on the altar, the subdeacon, returning with the paten and ampulla, places the paten on the cupboard and the ampulla in the place where it is customarily kept. He takes another silver paten stored beneath a golden bowl, wipes it carefully with an exceedingly white cloth that hangs continually near the cupboard for this very purpose, and afterward wraps it decorously and reverently in a linen cloth.

* Meanwhile the deacon gives incense to the priest to place in the thurible. If it is an ordinary day, as on feast days, the conversus brings it to the ruler of the choir. After it has been placed in the thurible, the priest censes the altar and the sacrifice in this manner: first he censes the face of the altar three times; then he makes three crosses with the same incense over the sacrifice; afterward he censes each horn of the altar three times, as far as he can extend his hand.

(UD.) [Note: [Col. 1011] This passage differs here because entire paragraphs found in William, who has them in Udalric’s manuscript, have been omitted.] When he has said before the preface, “World without end,” the deacon comes to stand behind the priest; the subdeacon bows before the step, at the approach itself, facing the altar, as the minister will also do at the twelve readings, and stands there holding the paten up, covered as described above.

They stand upright until they reach the point at which “Holy, holy, holy” is sung. Afterward they must remain bowed and intent upon prayer until the Lord’s Prayer has been completed by the priest.

In every procession the subdeacon and minister must take the utmost care not to come behind the priest before the deacon, wherever he has censed, has returned. The deacon also notes when the priest bows during the canon, so that afterward he may rise with him, uncover the chalice with him, raise it with him when he raises it, and cover it again when it has been set down. First, however, at the approach itself, he kisses the altar and then the priest’s arm slightly below the shoulder.

After the Lord’s Prayer, he takes the paten from the subdeacon, giving it to the priest with a kiss of his hand, just as the subdeacon has done to him. The priest places it at the foot of the chalice. After breaking the host, he puts one portion—as is the general custom—into the chalice, and two on the paten, and covers both with the corporal. First, however, he carefully shakes his fingers over the chalice, lest anything from the Lord’s Body should have adhered to them while he was breaking it.

Keeping those fingers still closed with every care and applying them to his breast [Note: [Col. 1013] Bernard, *Ordinarium Cluniacense*, part I, chapter 35, has: “and applying his hands to his breast in the form of a cross”], with his right arm placed over his left, he first gives the kiss of peace to the deacon and subdeacon, and then to the minister; and if anything of the Lord’s Body remains, he himself receives it.

Afterward he descends to the brothers for the same peace, while the deacon remains near the altar and takes care that no negligence occur with respect to the Lord’s Body or Blood. The subdeacon, carrying back the paten belonging to the chalice, which he had placed on the cupboard, puts it on the altar together with the linen cloth and afterward stands bowed in supplication at the right horn of the altar until the priest returns.

When he returns, he receives a portion of the Lord’s Body and then places the paten on which the Lord’s Body is to be divided into the bowl that the altar minister has brought from the cupboard and holds over the reclinatorium. Then, standing on the right side of the altar—for this purpose a place has chiefly been made there between two ciborium columns—he immediately gives the Lord’s Body to the deacon and then himself receives the Blood, giving the chalice to the deacon. With it the deacon immediately withdraws to a suitable place so that he, and any of the brothers who have received the Lord’s Body, may communicate from the same Blood of the Lord.

Then the subdeacon receives the Lord’s Body, and after him all who wish, and finally the minister holding the bowl, if anything remains. First, however, they ask permission; and those who are in albs or copes merely prostrate themselves upon their hands. Afterward they avoid asking permission or even bowing at all, even if the lord abbot should meet them, until they have drunk the wine.

Each person must draw so close to the bowl that if, while receiving, the Lord’s Body should happen to fall either from the mouth of the communicant or from the hand of the one administering it, it can fall only into the bowl.

If someone wishes to communicate from another choir than the one in which the offering is made, he approaches for the peace and communion in his own order after obtaining permission. If someone from his own choir is ordered to go to another choir for Mass, he does not approach with that choir for the peace and communion without permission, unless he is required to remain. But if this is being done in his own choir on that day, he ought to receive the peace and, if he wishes, may communicate.

It should be noted that on every ordinary day, by custom no more than five people come forward to communicate, since the hosts are divided into only three portions. After the subdeacon has received the Lord’s Body, he immediately comes to the deacon with the reed and ampulla, from which he pours wine into the chalice when he sees that the Blood has been diminished by those drinking.

Then, as soon as he has finished with that and sees that the last person is communicating at the altar, he takes another chalice from the cupboard and brings it to the priest, together with the ampulla of wine, so that the priest may wash his fingers in it. First he pours a little wine over the priest’s four fingers with which he had broken the Lord’s Body. After the priest has drunk this, he drinks a second time what is poured in, so that that chalice too may be washed to some degree.

After all who had received the Lord’s Body have communicated in the Lord’s Blood, it is finally brought to the minister, so that he too may drink from the same Blood of the Lord, provided that he had received the Lord’s Body. For by custom he does not communicate unless some portion of the Lord’s Body remains.

Meanwhile the deacon folds the corporals, and, taking up the paten that the subdeacon had placed on the altar, gives it to him together with the corporal. At the same moment the minister takes the bowl containing the silver paten, and both he and the one holding the chalice withdraw and stand behind the priest: the one with the chalice opposite the right horn of the altar, and the one with the bowl opposite the left.

As these two withdraw there, the whole community, out of reverence for the Lord’s Body and Blood, asks permission. The one carrying the candelabrum, after the priest has returned from the peace, holds it raised up and does not lower it before the first collect after communion has begun to come to an end.

The paten together with the chalice is immediately returned to the cupboard. There, however bright the day may be, the subdeacon and another servant inspect both objects most carefully by candlelight to see whether anything, however minute, remains of the Lord’s Body.

If the minister sees that a larger portion remains, he does not touch it with his hand but lifts and consumes it only with his tongue—provided that he himself has already communicated. If he has not, the subdeacon consumes it.

Whether something remains or nothing does, this is nevertheless not neglected: the paten on which the Lord’s Body was divided is washed twice with wine, which, having been received in the bowl placed beneath the chalice, is drunk with no less reverence than if it were the consecrated Blood itself.

When the priest withdraws from the altar, he gives the missal to the deacon to carry back. He himself folds the stole, unless it is, as on the principal feast days, embroidered with gold; then the sacristan folds it.

It should be known that when None immediately follows Mass, or Vespers, as in Lent, after the priest and the other altar ministers remove their vestments, they say in a secluded place the prayer belonging to that Hour.

On ordinary days the unconsecrated hosts are carried to the refectory, so that they may be distributed to those who did not communicate that day by the hands of the hebdomadary priest and the hebdomadary prior. This is customarily done in the following order: first some of the hosts are given to the lord abbot; then distribution begins on both sides, to his right and left, and continues to the end of both walls, just as afterward it is done in a line, and each recipient kisses the hands of those distributing.

When giving the blessing, he makes three crosses: toward the principal table, toward those seated opposite, and toward those below him; for the drink, only one. If he was absent from the refectory for the first blessing and arrives afterward, he says the remaining things himself.

After Compline, before the third prayer is finished, he leaves the choir for the holy water, so that with it he may sprinkle each person.

## CHAPTER LXXXV. On the blessing of new crops, to be performed by the same hebdomadary

[Col. 1015B] * There are still certain varieties of blessings which, since they are to be said by the priest, ought not to be passed over here. Among them is the blessing of grapes, which is also found in many missals, especially under the name of Saint Sixtus.

If the grapes are not yet ripe, the dean of the village takes care that, when they first ripen, he brings them to the church’s custodian, so that the latter may offer them to the priest at the appointed time and during the canon for blessing.

[Note: [Col. 1015D] The consecration of the first fruits to God derives from the institution of Pope Eutychian, as in the pontifical of Damasus: “He instituted that fruits, beans, and grapes be blessed on the altar,” as also in the martyrologies of Rabanus and Notker. [Col. 1016D] See Hugh Menard, *Book of Saint Gregory*, p. 173.]

The armarius must also be present there, for he shows the priest the prayers to be said over these things. Afterward the blessed grapes are distributed in the refectory by the priest and the hebdomadary of the preceding week, in the place of the hosts; this is not omitted even if it is Sunday.

[Col. 1015C] There are also three other kinds that are customarily blessed in the refectory: namely, new beans, new bread, and must. The procedure is as follows. The reading at table is begun first; after its first verse, the priest stands in the middle of the refectory before the principal table, and, after the greeting, blesses each item without a stole.

For the beans: “Bless, O Lord, these fruits.”

For the bread: “Bless, O Lord, this creation of bread.”

For the must: “Almighty Lord Jesus Christ, who from five loaves …,” and the rest.

## CHAPTER LXXXVI. How a private Mass is to be sung—that is, read

(UD.) If the priest wishes to sing a private Mass, he signals to the conversus with the sign of the cross, which is the signal for singing Mass. The conversus immediately follows him to the place where the utensils for the solemn celebration of Masses are stored, lights a candle, and places the priestly garment on his left arm, arranging it so that, with the lower edge of the alb turned underneath, the missal may be placed on top.

Although the priest, like the conversus, has previously washed his hands at the lavatorium in the cloister, he nevertheless does not omit to wash them more carefully from the vessel in the church assigned for this purpose. He also takes the chalice, already prepared for the sacrifice with wine and water mixed together, and likewise the paten with the host and corporal placed upon it. In addition he takes two ampullae, one of wine and the other of water, lifting both with his left hand, while carrying the chalice in his right and holding the paten with the corporal above it with his thumb. Thus, followed by the conversus, he proceeds to the altar where he is to sing.

(UD.) Provision has also been made for the vestment, neither unexpectedly nor inadequately: at each altar there is a board on which a projecting piece of wood, fixed into the wall, is placed, and on this the ampullae are set. A small towel also hangs ready at hand, with which the priest, after vesting, dries the tips of his fingers after washing them, since these must necessarily touch the sacred objects.

When the conversus has placed the vestment and light in their proper place, and the priest has likewise set the ampullae down, the priest holding the chalice on the right and the conversus on the left, they approach the altar. After the conversus has genuflected, they unfold the folded altar cloth, place the chalice in the middle of the altar and the missal on the right, and the priest, removing his tunic before the altar, genuflects.

Meanwhile the assistant takes the loosened shoulder garment, spreads it, and applies it to him; then he holds the alb, spread out below but folded on the side of the head-opening, toward him. After the priest has put it on, he gives him the cincture, then the fanon [Note: [Col. 1016D] *Fanon*: *sindon*, *mappa*. See above and in our index of terms], and then the stole.

Before the priest has placed the stole around his neck, (var.) if the signal is rung for the regular Hour, he sends his assistant to the prior and, after receiving permission, sings Mass. If the signal is rung before Terce, earlier than usual, for washing, or if, impeded by some necessity, he has at least washed his hands before that same signal, he does not desist from what he has begun; he sprinkles himself and his assistant with holy water. He likewise does not omit this if he wishes to sing immediately after the litany.

While holding the stole, he says the confession, with the conversus responding to him with the verse “May [God] have mercy,” and immediately adding the confession. While the priest responds to him, he places the stole around himself, kissing it, and adds “Pardon” together with the verse “Our help,” etc. * The conversus receives this pardon with a genuflection. He also adjusts the chasuble on the priest after he has put it on and arranges the humeral at the top of the chasuble according to custom.

Then, after washing and drying his fingers, the priest makes a brief prayer while bowed. When it is finished, he stands upright and fortifies himself with the sign of the cross. After kissing the altar, he looks in the missal for what is to be said.

[Col. 1016D] (UD.) From there, beginning Mass, he reads all the singing that belongs to him—* in accordance with the ordinance of our Fathers—more as a recitation than as something he dares to sing. At “Glory to the Father” he bows; at “The Lord be with you” he turns completely around, with his hands raised and head bowed.

He says the collect without tone at the right of the altar, repeating “Through the Lord” only in the first and last collects. When he is about to read the Epistle, he places the book on the left, and there says the rest up to after Communion. While he says the first, middle, and last collects, his assistant sits bowed.

At the Canon, on feast days and during octaves, [Col. 1017A] he stands or sits; but on ordinary days he prostrates himself on his knees. When he is about to read the Gospel, he receives a blessing from the lord abbot, if he is present; then he kisses the altar, and while saying “The continuation of the holy Gospel,” makes individual crosses with his thumb on his forehead, mouth, and breast.

Then, after the conversus responds, “Glory to you, O Lord,” and signs his face with the sign of the cross, the priest kisses the Gospel. He does the same after reading it, and immediately offers it to the conversus and to the others who wish to communicate, for kissing.

After saying “The Lord be with you” following the Gospel, he immediately takes from the altar the linen cloth that continually lies there for the offering, folded, and hands it to his assistant; then he gives him the chalice with the paten for the offering. Someone other than his assistant may make the offering if the assistant does not wish to communicate.

While saying the offertory, he spreads the corporal in the middle of the altar. Meanwhile the conversus stands bowed with the chalice, the paten placed upon it, until the priest has finished preparing himself to receive them.

When the priest has received them one by one—first the paten with the host, then the chalice, both offered with a kiss of the hands—he places the chalice covered above with the corporal, and the paten covered beneath it. Before taking the chalice, he receives the folded linen cloth from the conversus, not without a kiss of the hands, and replaces it on the altar.

Then he washes and joins together the first two fingers of each hand with which the Lord’s Body is to be handled. He does not separate them again before washing them after Communion, except when they must be separated to make the crosses. Thus at last he bows for the prayer “Receive, O holy Trinity,” etc., and always says this prayer in the same manner at the Mass for the living and for the dead.

After saying it, he turns to the people standing on the right and says with a humble inclination of the head, “Pray for me, a sinner.” Then, turning again to the right, he goes to the left horn of the altar and says the secret collects in the same order as the first collects. But before the first he says only “Let us pray,” and he ends each with “Through Christ our Lord,” except the last; for at that one he says “Through our Lord” secretly up to “World without end,” which is to be pronounced more loudly.

While saying “Lift up your hearts,” he reverently raises both hands to the shoulders, with the four fingers joined together as described. It should also be known that from this point he must not change the posture in which he then is before completing the consecration of the sacrifice, except when he is bowed or occupied with making a cross or handling the sacrifice.

For the rest, after saying the preface, he bows at “Holy,” and, remaining bowed, signs his face at “Blessed is he who comes.” The conversus must do both likewise. But when the priest begins “Therefore, most merciful Father,” he rises, though remaining bowed; and when he has said “Humbly we ask you” and “We beg you,” then, with a kiss of the altar, he rises fully for the first time.

While saying “These + gifts, these + offerings, these holy + and unblemished sacrifices,” he makes three common crosses over both offerings.
