He does likewise when he says “Blessed +, approved +, ratified +”; but at the words “the Body + and Blood +” he makes two crosses separately, one over the hosts and one over the chalice.

When he says “He took bread,” he takes the host with the first four fingers and raises it slightly; he does not set it down before saying “This is my body.” When he says “He blessed it,” he holds this same host with two fingers of his left hand and makes a cross over it with his right.

Likewise, when he says “Taking also this glorious chalice,” he takes the chalice, covered with the corporal, and raises it slightly. After saying “Giving you thanks,” he sets it down while still holding it with his left hand, and at “He blessed it +” he blesses it.

At “Take this,” he raises it again and holds it until he says “This is the chalice of my blood.”

Likewise, when he says “A pure + host, a holy + host, an unblemished + host,” he makes three common crosses over both together, and one over the Lord’s Body when he says “the holy Bread [Col. 1018B] of eternal life,” and another over the chalice when he says “and the Chalice of everlasting salvation.”

For he ought to have placed the Lord’s Body between himself and the chalice on the corporal in such a way that, whenever the order requires, he can make both individual and common crosses over them.

At “Humbly we ask you,” he bows. When he says “From participation in the altar,” he rises after kissing the altar; and while saying “the most sacred Body and Blood,” he makes no cross whatsoever. But when he says “that we may be filled with every heavenly blessing and grace,” he signs himself on the face with a cross.

Likewise, at “You sanctify +, enliven +, bless +,” he makes three common crosses over both together.

At “You grant us,” having taken up the Lord’s Body, he covers the chalice with the paten. While saying “Through him +, and with him +, and in him +,” holding the chalice in his left hand and the Body in his right, he makes three crosses with it over the middle of the chalice; then he makes three more before himself, outside the chalice, on the side of the chalice, when he says “All honor and glory are yours, God the Father + almighty, in the unity + of the Holy Spirit.”

While saying “World without end,” he holds the Lord’s Body between himself and the chalice with the first four fingers and supports it together with the chalice, raising both slightly from the corporal with both hands.

At “Saving precepts,” having set down the chalice, he places the Lord’s Body nearer than before, so that, after immediately flicking his fingers between the chalice and the Body lest anything of the Lord’s Body have adhered to them, he may cover the Lord’s Body together with the chalice. After the Lord’s Prayer has been said, the response is “But deliver us from evil”; he himself silently responds, “Amen.” [Col. 1018D] He likewise immediately begins “Deliver us, we beseech you, O Lord,” and, having said it, secure from every disturbance, he then takes the Lord’s Body, covering the chalice with the paten. While saying “through our Lord,” he cuts the right-hand portion of the Lord’s Body with his finger; he does not completely separate it, but when he says “who lives and reigns with you,” he entirely divides the left-hand portion and joins it to the middle. And when he says “through all ages of ages,” he takes the right-hand portion, with which, at “The peace of the Lord,” he makes three crosses above the middle of the chalice with such haste that he completes them during those five little phrases; at the end of them he puts that portion into the Blood, and holds the other two over the chalice with two fingers of his left hand, where he has made this fraction of the Lord’s Body, [Col. 1019A] until he himself then sings the “Lamb of God” completely, and, bowing, receives them over the chalice in communion.

If he sings a Mass for the dead, no one communicates except he himself. But if it is a Mass for the living, while holding the Body in this manner he gives the Peace to the Convert, and the latter gives it to any bystanders who wish to communicate. Nevertheless, at a private Mass no more than two are permitted; the assistant receives the Peace from the priest and then gives him a sign to communicate, adding the sign for two, so that he understands that two wish to communicate. Once he has received one portion, he divides the other in two and gives it to both, after they have first asked pardon on their knees and kissed his hand. [Col. 1019B]

To their mouths, as they communicate, he applies the Lord’s Body with great care, holding it in his right hand together with the chalice, which he supports with his left, so that, while the Lord’s Body is given to the communicant, the hand of the giver is in no way separated farther from the chalice. Then, after receiving the Blood himself, he gives the communicants from that same chalice; the one who communicated first receives the chalice from him with the cloth by which it was offered. And when both have taken from the same part of the chalice from which the priest took the Blood, the priest receives the chalice. Then his assistant—whether he himself has communicated or not—gives him wine for washing.

[Note: [Col. 1019D] Thus the cited manuscript: “The remaining servant also comes forward with another chalice from outside the reclinatorium, so that the priest may wash over it, with wine, the fingers with which he handled the Lord’s Body, just as the deacon does as soon as he has communicated and before he folds the corporals, so that the priest may again drink this wine, which the second servant pours, so that that chalice may be washed on both sides.”] [Col. 1020D]

Then he pours it in such a way that, for the second washing, he washes over the chalice the four fingers with which he handled the Lord’s Body; he must also insert them into the upper part of the chalice, at the place where he took the Blood. Each time, he himself must consume the wine poured in, although the communicants too must soon drink wine from that same chalice. They should know that only then, with the kissing of his hand, is the chalice to be returned to the priest. [Col. 1019C] But immediately after the washing of the chalice he does not delay in folding the corporal; and, after placing the Missal to the right, he will complete the Mass once the Missal Communion has been said.

It must be known that on the greatest feasts everyone must communicate, and at the principal Mass they must not receive the Peace, so that the others may communicate more quickly. Therefore, when at the end he says “The Lord be with you,” turning toward those standing there, he turns back toward the altar in the same order as before; and, having kissed the altar, he bows slightly toward it and silently says that prayer of the altar, “May the Holy Trinity be pleasing to you.” [Col. 1019D] Thus, having closed the book, he withdraws from the altar.

Then the Convert takes the chasuble, holding his hands beneath it, receives it by the top of the hood, and folds it after removing it. Meanwhile the priest [lacuna], and the Convert, turning downward, fold the stole together with the fanon and the humeral veil, taking care that none of these things falls to the ground. Then the Convert gathers the chasuble and the other folded vestments together in the alb. Afterwards, having asked pardon before the altar, the priest, dressed in his tunic, washes the tips of his fingers, especially because of the chalice [Col. 1020A] and the corporal. These, together with the cruets, book, and vestments, are to be carried back and put away in the place from which they were brought, in the order in which they were brought there by the priest and the Convert.

(UD.) The priest singing a private Mass must also know this: if, while the Hour is beginning, he has finished Mass in such a way that he can come to the Choir before the “Gloria” of the first psalm, he leaves the Convert with the vestments unfolded and himself goes to the Hour. But if he cannot come before the “Gloria” of the first psalm, he does not move from the place, nor does the Convert, until the Hour has ended; rather, he sings it there.

These, then, are the times when priests may sing such Masses without permission: every day before Prime, provided that Prime is not joined to Matins, as often happens in winter; and after the chapter [Col. 1020B] up to Terce. But during Lent, on the days of the twelve readings, when according to custom thirty psalms are sung, they must attend that psalmody until the end of the first ten psalms; or, if the chapter is after Terce, until Sext; nor [may they do so] earlier than after Sext, provided that the brothers have not then gone to sleep. Sometimes, however, after the Gospel of the principal Mass, one of the priests may obtain permission; nevertheless, this is censured if it is done frequently.

*It must also be known that no priest should sing two Masses in one day, unless great necessity compels it and unless the lord abbot or the prior grants him permission. He must sing these Masses together, and at the earlier one he must defer washing both his fingers and the chalice. But a deacon or subdeacon must not read at two Masses, except in the case of fairly serious necessity.* [Col. 1020C]

## CHAPTER LXXXVII. On the Subdeacons

(UD.) The subdeacon who is to read the Epistle, proceeding with the priest to the altar, carries the Gospel book and places it in the middle of the altar. He does not carry the cushion except at the twelve readings. After setting it down and saying the Confession, if it is a day of the twelve readings, he stands in the presbytery facing north until the priest begins the collect. Once it has begun, he turns toward the east and stands bowed until he proceeds to read.

On ordinary days, whether he is under custody or not, he stands in the right choir by the wall. There too, when the first prayer begins, he bows down with the other brothers over the misericord until the final prayer is said, “Through our Lord.” [Note: [Col. 1021D] A bench or seat. See above.] If a prophetic reading is to be recited, he who is to read it, even if he belongs to the right choir, occupies the corresponding place in the left choir; no one else performing any duty may do this without the prior’s command.

(UD.) Before beginning and after finishing the reading, in both instances he makes the prescribed gestures there, in front and behind. *When the reading is finished, he replaces the book in the small cupboard which is in the presbytery.* [Col. 1021A] And if it is a day of the twelve readings, he sits near the deacon without permission. It is the duty of the weekly sacristan to provide him with a chair; when he rises, or later whenever it seems appropriate, the sacristan carries it away.

At every solemnly celebrated Mass, this man must carry the Gospel book, with a cushion beneath it, around the choir and outside it, even when the Mass is for the dead. If it is then carried without a cushion, he first goes to the one who presides over the choir, then to those standing at the forms in the right and left choirs. All who wish to do so approach these, and those outside them follow. Then he returns to those standing in line on that side and does the same in the left choir. He must know, however, that he is never to bow wherever he goes while carrying the Gospel book.

Every day at the earlier Mass he presents the book to the priest, and to the one who first offers, alone, for kissing. The exception is a festive celebration, when at the principal Mass the minister does this on ordinary days. If the same book is ornamented, both the deacon and the priest kiss it while it is closed. Those who kiss it bow not before but after the kiss. On ordinary days the subdeacon holds the paten during the Canon; at the twelve readings, however, the minister does so. [Col. 1021B]

## CHAPTER LXXXVIII. On the Singers of the Graduals, Responsories, Alleluia, and Kyrie

(UD. var.) Those who sing the responsories, graduals, responses, Alleluia, and “Kyrie eleison” also make the prescribed gestures in front and behind at the step; before beginning, they bow reverently; and on ordinary days these are to be sung only collectively by the convent. [Col. 1021C]

*If a feast falls further into the week, the chants are to be sung again by those who previously sang them on Sunday. In the following week they themselves are to sing the same chants at the earlier Masses, provided that those Masses are celebrated solemnly—except when a Mass for the dead is to be celebrated with the greatest rite. Then they sing the responsories assigned by the armarius (librarian). The senior brothers, or the weekly officials themselves if they are such, hold the scilla (bell).*

When these men sing the verses for the souls, they bow forward only when they begin; at the end they make the gestures in front and behind. None of them, nor any other attendants there, removes his vestments before the offering has been completed. [Col. 1021D] UD. If all are wearing copes or albs, the sacristan indicates whomsoever he wishes to sing them in their place.

## CHAPTER LXXXIX. When There Is Not to Be Loud Singing in the Cloister

*This too should be noted: no one sings in the cloister on feasts of the twelve readings that are kept for the Apostles, except those brothers who are designated for the Gradual or the Alleluia. Before Prime these men may rehearse the aforementioned chant with one another, but in a subdued voice. If Prime is hastened so much that the short interval does not permit this, they will prepare the same chant in the vestry while putting on their albs, with the armarius (librarian) listening.* [Col. 1022A]

## CHAPTER XC. On the Deacon

(UD.) The deacon customarily precedes the priest to the altar. When the priest bows for the prayer, he too bows. When the priest rises, he signs himself and makes the gestures in front and behind. Approaching the left corner of the altar, he kisses it. He goes to stand opposite the priest, so that he may confess together with him; and if it is a feast day, the priest gives him incense, with the kissing of his hand.

(var.) Afterwards, receiving it, he censes the sides of the altar and the rear corners; then the altars behind that are nearest the choir—first the middle one, then beginning with the outermost altar on the left side and proceeding through the others. Above each he makes the sign of the cross once with the incense and returns to the presbytery. [Col. 1022B]

If relics of the current feast are kept in the monastery or in the chapel of Saint Mary, wherever he knows them to be stored in an altar, he takes care to cense that altar alone as well. But if a solemnity of such magnitude is being commemorated that four men sang the invitatory that night, he censes all the altars at Saint Mary’s, together with the one by the cross; moreover, at the Invention and Exaltation of the Holy Cross he censes that one altar.

When he returns to the choir, if he finds the lord abbot or another such person there, he offers incense to him also. Immediately returning to his place with the thurible, he stands behind the priest, moving slightly to his right. When the priest turns to give the greeting, [Col. 1022C] the deacon does not turn with him, except only at “Go, the Mass is ended.”

When the prayer has been completed, the deacon takes the Missal and places it at the left corner of the altar. When the priest sits, the deacon lifts his chasuble at the back and arranges his stole. The deacon himself also lifts his dalmatic, and the subdeacon his tunicle, if they sit. If it is a day on which the deacon himself is clothed in a chasuble, as during Lent, he immediately wraps it around himself folded, according to the general custom, and then sits—but only after the priest has first indicated this.

(UD.) If he wishes to examine the Gospel more carefully in advance, he takes the book from the altar, inspects it sufficiently, and replaces it. [Col. 1022D] *Then, as stated above, he gives incense to the priest, so that he may cense the Gospel book.* Once it has been censed and he has received back the thurible, he receives the blessing.

If the lord abbot or another such person is present, the Convert brings him the incense-boat, which he has received before the altar; the deacon asks him for incense to place in the thurible and receives back the blessing he requested. The priest nevertheless censes it, making over it the full sign of the cross. The deacon, receiving it, kisses the altar on its right side, while the subdeacon carries the cushion before him. When the Gospel is finished, he gives the book to the subdeacon; then, once the Mass is finished, he again makes the gestures in front and behind.

If the “Credo in unum” is sung, when they reach “who has spoken,” and so forth, he washes his hands. If it is not sung, he does so immediately after the Gospel has ended. [Col. 1023A]

It must be known that at the time of the offering the censing is to be done only in the manner stated above, except if he finds a priest celebrating Mass at another altar. If this occurs during the Gospel or the Canon, he must not approach him at all, unless he perceives that he is almost finished. If he arrives at another time, he gives the thurible to the priest, who censes in the manner stated above.

## CHAPTER XCI. How Incense Is to Be Used on the Feast of Saint Michael

*There is also a special manner of censing at the dedication of Saint Michael the Archangel. After the offertory verse has ended and the repetition “And the smoke went up” has been made, two deacons approach the principal altar and cense both its sides, having placed a large quantity of incense on it. Having done this, they approach the rear corners and, with their faces turned toward each other, continuously cense the upper part of the altar without stopping until the repetition of the offertory has ended.* [Col. 1023B]

It must first be arranged that the priest completes his censing over the chalice precisely at the end of the offertory verse. One of the deacons is the one serving that day; the other is provided by the sacristan and is dressed in a cope. From there they proceed to the altar of Saint Benedict and observe there the same procedure as at the principal altar whenever it is censed by two priests. Then, separating from one another, they cense all the altars of the monastery and of Saint Mary’s, making a cross above each.

(UD.) It should also be known that at other times, when two men cense, the same procedure is to be followed. But the deacon serving that day censes at the cross. [Col. 1023C]

*At the end of Mass he never says “Go, the Mass is ended” unless “Glory in the highest” has also been sung. Throughout the entire week, both at Matins and at Mass, he reads according to custom; and because of his frailty he will refrain only at Mass.*

## CHAPTER XCII. On the Servants of the Church

The servants, because of the duty by which they carry the thurible and candlesticks, carefully ensure that they are never absent from the service of the priest, levite, or subdeacon. Whenever they remove those vestments for any divine office, or need water and a towel in order to wash their hands, they also kiss the arms of the priest and levite. One of these same servants continually attends him. [Col. 1023D]

*They perform their service in the following order. First, they attend those who are going to sing the invitatory, if the occasion then requires that they put on albs or copes, and afterwards, without their assistance, fold the garments they have removed. Then, during the chant, they leave the choir, as does the priest, and wash their hands at the lavatory. When the eleventh reading is being read, whether they are in the choir or outside it, they come without delay to the vestry, where they put on their albs as usual.*

It must also be observed that the one who is senior among them should also be the older in age; he is assigned the duty of carrying the thurible and the cross. During the blessing of the salt and water in the house, and during the procession, he stands and walks to the priest’s left. [Col. 1024A] In the proper place he also lights the coals kept in reserve in a pouch assigned for this purpose. The other two are appointed to carry the candlesticks.

When the procession proceeds, the one who was from the left choir will also stand on that side. If both are from one choir, the junior in rank withdraws to the left choir. They do the same at Mass.

When the verse “In you, O Lord, I have hoped” begins, the one holding the thurible makes the sign of the cross over the lectern and, withdrawing, does not bow. After everyone has returned to the sacristy, if it is a day on which the altar is to be censed by one man, the one who is to carry the thurible remains outside the choir wearing his vestments while the others remove theirs. If it is a feast on which the altar is to be censed by two, one of the candle-bearers remains with him—namely, the senior in rank, if possible. [Col. 1024B]

Then the priests take their individual thuribles in the vestry, unless the lord abbot is present, put incense in them there, and proceed to cense the altar; the servants follow with lighted candles. But if the lord abbot is present for this purpose, and either wishes to cense with the priest himself or has placed incense in the thuribles of two others entering through the greater choir, they do not light the candles immediately when they approach him, because at that time they are carrying the thuribles. They light them only after they have freed their hands by placing the incense in the thuribles.

The priests proceed to the altar, and then they light the candles. While the priests, after censing the Lord’s altar, go to the five altars placed behind it, cense the middle one in the manner of the principal altar, and return, the servants proceed only then. [Col. 1024C]

When the priests return to the choir, one of these servants censes the right choir and another the left: first by the wall, then in the smaller choir each his own side; afterwards those standing in line; finally those at the forms. If the censing is done by one man, he first censes those standing by the right wall, then those standing by the left; next, in the smaller choir, the right side and then the left; afterwards the forms in both choirs; then those outside the choir, bowing briefly to each. Afterwards he censes those altars which the priest did not cense, provided that anything remains in the same thurible, extending it three times toward the face of each. [Col. 1024D]

If the lord abbot alone wishes to cense, the sacristan brings him the incense-boat and one of the servants brings the thurible, whether the abbot is in the choir or in the vestry. The same procedure is followed at Vespers. But then, before the hymn, the minister of incense goes out to prepare the coals; and if he is to be vested, he does so before the priest follows him. Nevertheless, they do not wash their hands then, because they did this before Vespers as well.

For the procession on Sunday, one of the candle-bearers, carrying consecrated salt in two small dishes, precedes the brothers; the other carries blessed water. On entering the infirmary, he sprinkles each of those sitting there in the beds—for all must sit there at that time—though the priest does not wait for him after the prayer has ended. In all the other workshops, however, the sprinkling is in no way prolonged beyond the end of the prayer. [Col. 1025A]

The one carrying salt places one dish on the table nearest the door at the entrance to the refectory, so that it may be available there for the brothers’ needs at the hour of the meal; he carries the other to the church.

Once Mass has begun, they arrange themselves properly in the sacristy, so that when the cantor begins “Glory to the Father,” they may proceed to the altar without delay. After the Confession has ended, the servant offers incense to the deacon, kissing his hand. After receiving it back from him when he has returned from censing the altars, he censes first the deacon, then the ministers of the altar, and afterwards the convent in the order recalled above for Matins. The only variation is that he likewise offers incense both to those standing at the forms and to those standing behind them by the wall; and, after censing the smaller choir, he first attends to those standing by the sacristy. But then he brings the incense-boat with the thurible to the one who presides over the choir for the placing of incense. [Col. 1025B]

If the lord abbot or another such person is present, the same cantor brings him the incense-boat, and the Convert brings him the thurible. On ordinary days he censes only once, namely after the offertory, in the manner stated above.

It should be noted that at the principal Mass on the twelve-reading days incense is to be administered to these brothers, as also when Masses for the dead are celebrated festively. When “Kyrie eleison” begins, the candle-bearers place the candlesticks among the other larger ones. Since on the Saturday of Pentecost the Mass begins with “Kyrie eleison,” they place them as soon as they enter, and they do not lift them before the Gospel is read. After it has been read, they place them again; but they do not lift them before the priest has returned from the Peace. Then, holding them aloft, with the bearer of the thurible standing between them with the thurible and incense—which he places there—they remain until the first collect after Communion has ended with “Through our Lord”; he does not withdraw before then. [Col. 1025C]

During the week, when it is not a feast of the twelve readings, they take turns so that each carries the candlestick and thurible on his assigned day. In the following week, at the earlier Mass, they perform the ministry of carrying lights and incense if the celebration is festive; if it is not festive, one of them carries the light. He also does not remove his vestments, but while communicating he holds the candlestick and does not set it down until the first collect after Communion has ended—unless Mass is sung at Saint Mary’s or at the altar of the Holy Cross. Then he waits for the priest and the other ministers.

Whether there is one servant or three, once they have administered the water to the deacon, they do not delay in offering it. Afterwards two of them remove their albs, intending to return to minister water to the priest; but the third, who must carry the incense around, delays removing his vestments in the meantime. The weekly sacristan replaces the candlesticks, with their candles, in their proper place after the first collect following Communion has ended. [Col. 1025D]

However this Mass is celebrated, they assist the ministers of the altar as much as they can when putting on or removing their vestments. [Col. 1026A]

## CHAPTER XCIII. On the Ministers of the Altar

*What seemed necessary to say above about those whom we call ministers of the altar has already been set forth. In summer, when the heat begins to increase, one of them must fan the priest every day at the principal Mass—sometimes standing near the right corner of the altar, sometimes behind the priest—lest flies come and disturb him.*

(UD. var.) The position of these men, and of the priest, deacon, subdeacon, and candle-bearers, on ordinary days is as follows: as at the Hour before Mass, at which they attend wearing albs. Each stands in his own choir. No one passes from one choir to the other unless ordered to do so. [Col. 1026B]

## CHAPTER XCIV. On Those Ordered to Change Choirs

*If someone wearing an alb is ordered to change choirs in this manner, he returns at the following Hour. Otherwise, without an order he does not return, unless he is one of the uneducated.*

The priest stands at the grating above the seniors; or, if an abbot is in that choir, below him. The deacon and subdeacon, if both are free of custody and of mature age, and the ministers of the altar if they are literate, stand outside custody at the grating. But if they are assigned to custody or are younger, they stand at the top of the line. The same ministers, if they are Converts, are placed at the top of the wall opposite the altar, even if they are acolytes, subdeacons, or candle-bearers. Care must be taken that no more than two of all these are in custody. [Col. 1026C]

## CHAPTER XCV. On the Reader at Table

If the reader at table is not under custody, he devotes himself entirely in the smaller choir, during both Masses, to what he is going to read. If he is under custody, he sits in the larger choir at the western end of the form. If he has doubts about anything, he is permitted to ask the sacristan or any other experienced brother.

When the earlier Mass is celebrated at Saint Mary’s, if he is under custody, he remains there; otherwise he sits in the vestry. When the brothers put on albs or copes together, he too sits in an alb, not in a cope, to secure the reading. [Col. 1026D]

(UD.) If the sequence is sung on that day, once it has begun he enters the choir and returns after the Gospel has ended. When the solemnities of the principal Mass are finished—or if that Mass is sometimes sung outside the monastery, at the end of the earlier Mass—he comes to the step, makes the gestures in front and behind, and then, with the convent responding, says this verse: “O Lord, open my lips,” and so forth. The priest continues with this blessing:

“Save your servant. Send to him, O Lord. The Lord guard you. May the Lord guard your entrance and your exit, and take from you the spirit of pride.”

Or this one:

“Turn away, we beseech you, O Lord, from this servant of yours the spirit of pride and ignorance, so that, reading humbly, he may grasp the meaning and understanding of the reading. Through our Lord.”

When the blessing is finished, the reader bows in front and behind. If, however, because of some intervening circumstance he is absent for this verse, another says it in his place and asks pardon for the blessing that was omitted. [Col. 1027A]

*Before the general meal he tastes bread, in accordance with the precept of Saint Benedict (chapter 38). He must also take care not to presume to go there before the end of Mass, or sometimes of the prayer of the following Mass, since he must not leave from there without the weekly kitchen servants.*

When the meal has begun, if he hears the board struck for the office of the dead, he immediately rises and goes to the church; after three readings have ended, he returns, and the others do likewise. But if it is struck for a brother who is dying, those who run there do not return at all.

Coming into the refectory and standing in his place, he does not make the gestures in front and behind while the others bow toward him; he stands upright. If he can come for the blessing without his clothing touching the brothers’ heads, he does not change his place. Otherwise, when the verse begins, he moves to a place from which he can reach the step without hindering the brothers. [Col. 1027B]

(UD.) Since none of the brothers will taste anything before the reading has begun, as soon as the lord abbot or the prior has sat down, the reader asks for the blessing. But at the Lord’s Supper and on Good Friday he does this silently and begins the reading without delay.

*If the book is ever unavailable through negligence, he reads whatever appropriate passage he can then recall from memory. The person through whose negligence this has occurred asks pardon for it in chapter the next day.*

If he is to read a homily that was read at Matins on the preceding night, he gives only the Evangelist’s words beforehand—for example, “When you hear of wars,” without adding “and the rest,” and without mentioning anything about the expositor. But if it is one that was not previously read at Matins, he likewise gives the Gospel words beforehand and, adding the expositor’s name, begins the homily. [Col. 1027C]

Whenever it happens that an Epistle, Passion, or life of a saint is to be read, he never silently passes over their preceding and following words. He must also be certain that this is to be done at the beginnings and endings of the Prophets and of the other books; but in sermons only their preceding words are to be given.

If he has begun the life or Passion of a saint, and a Sunday or another feast occurs before its end, he reads what is appropriate to the occasion. Once these things have been completed, he resumes whatever remained of the life or Passion. If the time meanwhile arrives for some history or prophecy that can appropriately be read at a later time, he does not omit what he began on account of it.

When beginning the reading, if he reads in a subdued voice, he receives from the arriving armarius (librarian) a sign to read more loudly. If he reads incorrectly, the prior makes this known to him, either by a sign or by correcting the word itself.

The same reader also observes that, when the scilla is to be struck, he must not hinder the one who is to strike it by prolonging the reading. After he sees that man approaching the table with the dish, he should either keep silent, if he can do so appropriately, or read more quickly than usual. He may also take breath more frequently if necessary, but moderately. [Col. 1028A] If at times he reads more loudly than is appropriate, he may suitably alter his voice if he wishes.

At the Lord’s Supper and on Good Friday, once the reading is finished, he pays close attention to the lord abbot and, when he sees his sign, stops reading. If the abbot signals him at the end of a verse, he repeats some words of that verse so that the reading may end more suitably.

When the reading is finished, he comes to the step, makes the gestures in front and behind, and, if he is not under custody, withdraws to the dormitory or the regular kitchen. If he is under custody, he goes to his place of justice and waits there standing upright until the verse ends. When it has ended, without making the gestures in front and behind, he joins his custodian; then, likewise without making the gestures in front and behind as in the refectory, he summons his custodian and goes to eat, making the gestures in front and behind only then, when he reaches his place.

There too his custodian commends him to one of the brothers, who nevertheless does not later walk beside him with the psalm, since he was sitting by the scilla. If he needs to drink before supper, he may do so with permission, while the convent has not yet entered. During the week, if for some necessity he asks another brother to read in his place on two days, he is not censured; but if more than this . . . (UD. var.) unless because of illness, and, on that account, asking pardon, he has shown it in chapter. [Col. 1028B]

## CHAPTER XCVI. On the Reader for the Ministers

(UD. var.) The one who reads carries the book in which the reading is to be given to the refectory and brings it back to the servants; the reader at table assists him if necessary. As soon as he has put it down, the reader at table finds what is to be read. [Col. 1028C]

*This man too is permitted to prepare what he is going to read whenever, except during the times of Mass, he has the book and leisure. For reading, he will not delay leaving as soon as he knows that after the meal the convent has entered the choir completely with the psalm. If he is under custody, he leaves the church in the same order as described above, and he too is entrusted to someone in the refectory.*

But if he is not under custody, when leaving the choir he makes the gestures in front and behind; when the meal has ended and the ministers have made the customary inclination at the step, he may receive permission in that same place to drink. But there again, before drinking, he must make the gestures in front and behind if None follows, because he is then going back to the church to sing it with those same ministers. [Col. 1028D]

Whenever he has no duty to perform this, he does not customarily wait for them. Whether he is under custody or not, when leaving the lectern he carries the book with him and places it on the table in line until he has made the gestures in front and behind.

## CHAPTER XCVII. On the Weekly Kitchen Servants

*There are ordinarily as many weekly kitchen servants as are sufficient. The senior among them, whether he is the obedientiary or another, is in no way forbidden briefly to indicate verbally before the storeroom to the cellarer if something is urgently necessary and cannot be explained by signs. The same is permitted to the infirmarer and the refectorer.*

(UD. var.) They first do this after Vespers for All Saints has been sung on the twelve-reading days, up to “Kyrie eleison”; [Col. 1029A] on ordinary days they go to the kitchen to receive the beans; after receiving them, they wash them carefully in the water already poured, and in that same water they let them remain overnight in a well-covered cauldron.

After Sunday Matins has ended, when those who served during the preceding week come to the step and give thanks to God for the completion of their service, saying this verse three times with the response of the entire convent, “Blessed are you, Lord God, who have helped me and comforted me,” these men, who are likewise about to undertake the service, ask for God’s help by saying, “O God, come to my assistance,” and so forth.

*If one of them is not present there, the one who is then standing nearest receives the blessing in place of the absent man; nevertheless, that man asks pardon the next day for this omission.*

UD. For those going out, the priest is to say the following versicles: “Save your servants”; “Turn back, O Lord, how long?”; and that collect, “O God, to whom the humble always…”; “Merciful and most loving God, who everywhere [your servants].”

For those entering: “Save your servants”; “Send to them, O Lord.” Prayer. [Col. 1029B]

Before the community leaves the church of Saint Mary, so that they may put on their shoes and meanwhile go down while the community is at the latrines, they wash their hands and faces and comb their hair; they say the three prayers, as is customary in the church, if they are able to enter it, or otherwise near the church doors. * From the Kalends of October until Easter, after Prime has ended, they go to the dormitory and put on their day-shoes; they wash their hands and faces and comb their hair, and, if possible, light a fire, [Col. 1029C] so that when the litany has ended—for they are never absent from it—the same fire may be ready for putting the beans on to cook.

Udalric. On entering the kitchen they wash the beans in three waters and then place them over the fire. When the water in the cauldron is boiling and the foam is bubbling up, they briskly drive it away with the crosswise spoon, lest the beans floating together with the foam should accidentally be thrown out. They also stir them repeatedly from the bottom with the same spoon, lest, when they are to be eaten, they taste of smoke. When the skins of the beans begin to split, they no longer leave them over the fire. They cool them again with cold water and stir them back and forth once more with the spoon. They put them into a single cup having a well-fitted cover. The cauldron in which they were cooked is also washed inside until it is clean. [Col. 1029D]

A board is also leaned against the wall, and when the beans have been washed they are placed upon it; water is poured over the entire board and it is scrubbed with brooms. First, however, after making the customary inclination, they say three times again the verse that they said in the choir, adding here, each time, *Gloria Patri*, the Lord’s Prayer, and the verse *Adjutorium nostrum*, etc. After making the customary movement forward and backward, they finally lean the board against the wall. They sing all the regular hours according to canonical custom. They insert Vespers for the faithful departed in its proper place, and finally *Verba mea*. When the water has been poured off, they wash the bowls and pour it into them to be heated; with this water the vegetables are to be cooked. [Col. 1030A]

If Matins happens to end late, especially on principal feasts and during the summer, while the signal for Prime must be rung earlier, then, before doing anything else, they lean the board against the wall and begin the hours. If anything remains that they have not sung before Prime, it is not customary to sing it publicly after Prime. When Prime has ended—or, on ordinary days, after the Gospel of the morning Mass—they put the vegetables into the cauldron, and after the chapter they put the beans into the other cauldron again.

They take bacon [Note: [Col. 1029] Hence *oleum lardinum*, or bacon fat, which was granted to monks because of the lack of olive oil]. When it has been cooked a little, they squeeze it together with the vegetables and pour the rendered fat over the beans. Nevertheless, not everyone withdraws from the High Mass for this purpose, but only two, especially if some of them are illiterate, who must not be granted by their fellow servants permission to hear a private Mass. As stated above, these men pour in the fat, and through them the beans are heated again. If, because the cooking is taking too long, they see that more water should be poured over the vegetables, they first heat as much as they wish to add in a frying pan, because vegetables have the property of acquiring a worse taste from cold water. Care is also taken, when they are put into the cauldron, that they are washed with no water except hot water. The beans are not seasoned or sprinkled with fat until they have been thoroughly cooked, lest the salt perhaps lose its force through too long a delay. If one of the cooks wishes, he is not forbidden to taste a little of the bean-water, to test whether they have been properly seasoned.

[Col. 1030C] For the mixed portion they receive only what Saint Benedict prescribes: a quarter of a loaf, without its pound, and wine. Nevertheless, on the day when one of the brothers is buried after High Mass, they have no mixed portion. When the hour has ended and the brothers are about to eat, they go out quickly to serve the beans, either at the beginning of the psalm *Miserere*—on the day when heads are shaved—or, if the psalm is not sung, at the prayers. The senior of them, provided that he knows the task well and possesses the requisite skill, puts the beans into the bowls with a spoon made for this purpose; the others carry them to the tables, beginning with the principal table. Vegetables, on the other hand, are customarily served in the reverse order, beginning with the last table.

When the bowl containing the vegetables has been placed before the lord abbot [Col. 1030D] or prior, the one who placed it asks the presiding officer with a moderate sign for permission to order the little bell to sound. * When he has assented, the server inclines slightly, goes to the bell, and rings it until the youth begins to say *Benedicite*. (Udalric.) Meanwhile, while the priest completes the blessing, the aforementioned server stands bowed before the high table, and then makes the movement forward and backward. The intermediate dish served between beans and vegetables is customarily a *pietantia* three days a week, namely Monday, Wednesday, and Friday; on the other days it is a *generale* . . . We call that a *generale* which is given to each person in his own bowl. A *pietantia* is that which is given, for example, in one bowl to two persons. Sometimes, instead of a *pietantia*, one piece of uncooked cheese or four eggs is given without a bowl. [Col. 1031A]

The cheese is served in such a way that it is placed in the bowl of the person sitting by the bell; to the others, at each table, bowls filled with pieces of cheese are handed out, so that each may take as much as he wishes. If eggs are served, eight are placed together in the first bowl for two persons. A *pietantia* given jointly to two persons is not divided in half for the person sitting by the bell or for the prior in his place. For a *generale*, five eggs are given to each person, and cheese is never given except cooked.

Whatever is a *generale* is served beginning with the last table, and the bell is rung for it as for the vegetables. A *pietantia*, however, is begun by the prior, and the weekly kitchen servants do not involve themselves in its serving at all, except that at the end of the meal they collect its fragments. The cellarer, with those whom he has indicated for the task, serves it. Whatever is a *generale* is placed before the brothers, unless it consists of fish; the cellarer himself places the fish before each person who indicates that he wants it, while his assistant does the same on the other side. When these have been served, the cellarer himself rings the bell. If there is another kind of *generale*, the senior of those serving it rings the bell. * If it is served later than usual, the prior does not delay ringing the bell before himself. Raw fruit or herbs are never given to anyone in the refectory at dinner when the brothers eat twice a day. (Udalric.)

They collect only those bowls in which beans and vegetables have been served. For this reason one man always remains in the kitchen and promptly washes them while they are still thus smeared with oil [Note: [Col. 1031D] That is, smeared with oil], using the same water with which they were washed at dawn, lest, if the remains of food have hardened, the difficulty of washing them should become greater. They show the same diligence with the cauldrons, so that these too are washed, if not earlier, at least before the servants’ meal has ended. The hearth is also carefully covered, so that it may be found alive the next day.

After Vespers, once the beans have again been washed, they say the aforesaid verse as a thanksgiving: *Benedictus es, Domine, qui adjuvisti me*—“Blessed are you, Lord, who have helped me”—in the same way as they said the other verse at Matins. If they wish, however, they may be excused from washing the bowls on two days, namely Monday and Wednesday; on those days the cellarer, according to custom, cannot object if the bowls, carried to the cellar at dawn, are entrusted to his servants to be washed with greater care. (Udalric.)

On Saturday, after None or after Vespers, they sweep the kitchen and pile outside the door all the dirt produced through the use of ashes or wood, so that it may be carried away by the cellarer’s servants. They heat water for the Mandatum, and on that day postpone the verse *Benedictus es, Domine* until the Mandatum has been completed and the reading of the Collation in the refectory has also ended. On the following Saturday, since our watercourse has muddy water, whatever the feast may be, they sweep both washing places, both the one used for the church and the one used for the hands.

They also sweep the latrines and gather against the wall throughout the week the remains of hay consumed there. [Col. 1032A] If it is summer, throughout that week they serve water in the refectory after None. * This serving of water, like the midday rest, begins on Palm Sunday and continues until the Kalends of October. It must be understood that on any day of Lent when the brothers eat once, the cleaning of the washing place described above is to be carried out after dinner. When they eat twice, however, it is postponed until after None; during Lent it is carried out immediately after Sext, always with clean brooms supplied by the almoner and used only for this task.

It must also be understood that the aforementioned servants are expected by the community during Lent and at other times whenever the Office of the Dead is to be performed after supper, except when it is performed with the greatest solemnity, or when a brief service for some deceased person arrives, for which all the signals are rung together, or when it is too late. In such cases these same servants may ask the other brothers to serve in their place twice or three times a week.

## CHAPTER XCVIII. On the utensils of the kitchen

(Udalric.) These are the utensils that must never be lacking in the kitchen. First, three cauldrons: one for beans, another for vegetables, and a third together with an iron tripod, so that, if someone wishes to wash his clothes, he may make lye. Four cups: one reserved for holding the beans when they have been partly cooked; another into which the watercourse flows and in which the vegetables are first washed before being put into the cauldron; a third in which the bowls are washed; and a fourth solely for receiving hot water for the Mandatum and the shaving, with which the brothers wash themselves while being shaved. This last cup must also be heated by those who served during the preceding week.

Likewise, four spoons: one for the beans, another for the vegetables, a third, not very large but of medium size, for squeezing out the fat, and a fourth, made of iron, for covering the hearth with ashes. For arranging or disturbing the fire there must also be iron tongs of the same kind. Likewise, four pairs of sleeves, so that the sleeves of the brothers’ woolen garments are not soiled by the familiar blackness of the kitchen.

There are also two pairs of *palmariae* [Note: [Col. 1032D] A type of glove covering the palm of the hand, as we have already noted in the Cluniac customaries], as they are called in the vernacular. They protect the hands from the heat of the cauldron when something that has just been taken from the fire must be moved or tilted. Three small hand towels, which are changed every Thursday; the brothers’ ordinary towels, which hang in the cloister, are never used for drying the hands. One knife for cutting bacon, together with a whetstone for sharpening it. One pan for heating water, if necessary, and for melting fat. Another, very small and perforated with tiny holes in its bottom, so that the fat itself may be strained through it. One box in which salt is stored, and one chest in which various small things are kept. One jar for drawing water, and two brooms for sweeping the cauldrons after cooking. Two pieces of netting, to be used for washing the bowls and the cauldrons.

[Col. 1033A] Two boards for the bowls: one on which they are placed after the meal, once they have been washed in some fashion; the other on which they are placed at dawn, when they must have been washed thoroughly. Two stools, commonly called benches; one low, four-legged seat on which the cup containing the vegetables is placed when they are about to be put into the cauldron. One stone, larger even than a millstone, on which the cauldron is again placed, whether beans or vegetables are being served; another stone on which another cup is placed, from which the bowls are washed during the meal. One bellows for blowing the fire. One wicker fan for fanning it. One pole for carrying the cauldrons; another for moving the fire. One trough in which lye is always kept, for washing the hands more frequently. There are also two *tigrones*, each made from three pieces of wood, even if their angles are unequal; they can be swung back and forth like doors. Chains hang from them, by which the cauldrons are suspended. Once suspended, the cauldrons are filled with water near the watercourse and then drawn without effort directly over the fire.

It must also be understood that, for no necessity, is anything else cooked in the regular kitchen besides beans and vegetables; nor is any other kind of legume cooked. * If beans are lacking, nevertheless they do not omit singing the aforementioned course and psalmody there, because various other duties do not allow them to be idle: the fire must be tended, water for washing the cauldrons and bowls must be heated, bacon must be cooked with the vegetables, and afterward the fat must be squeezed out, together with other similar tasks which necessity itself teaches must not be neglected. [Col. 1033C]

(Udalric.) Beans, moreover, when they are still so young that they are seasoned with pepper as a delicacy, are cooked not by the brothers but by the servants. In the regular kitchen itself only the scribe is not forbidden to mix ink, if he wishes [Note: [Col. 1033] *Incaustum*, *encaustum*, Italian *inchiostro*, Latin *atramentum*, “ink”]. If someone wishes to grease his shoes, he must choose a suitable time: in summer before Prime, in winter before Terce, and, if the midday office is not being held, after None—provided that the servers have no further serving to do. The boys too make whatever candles they need in the same kitchen, together with their masters.

## CHAPTER XCIX. When the brothers anticipate the Mandatum on Thursday, and how they wash their feet beforehand

[Col. 1033D]

* Whenever a feast occurs on a Saturday or Sunday on which the psalm *Venite* must be sung four times, the Mandatum is to be anticipated on the preceding Thursday. The brothers then also wash their feet beforehand. If someone is so weakened in his feet by gout or another illness that he cannot suitably wash them with the others in the cloister, he may, with permission, wash them in the infirmary, and the infirmary servant will provide him with water; afterward, however, those feet are not washed again at the Mandatum.

This must be understood: this washing of the feet is performed immediately after Vespers, once the day-shoes have been changed, provided that there is no supper. It must be performed beforehand and followed by the Office, even if at that very hour a brief service should occur for which all the signals must be rung together. The day-shoes, once changed, must nevertheless be returned to the cloister. No one except someone who has recently been bled is to omit washing them at least a little, whether there is a practical need or not, because this custom, derived from the ancient institution of the fathers, is to be observed more for humility than for necessity.

For some members of our order are so humble that they never allow their woolen garments or other clothing to be washed by anyone but themselves. Nevertheless, only the officials who must afterward go out for some necessity do not put away their day-shoes; instead, with the straps arranged beneath them, they attend the Mandatum wearing them. It is customary, when the shoes are carried in the hands, to hold them only by their straps with the arm extended, so that between the hand of the bearer and the hanging shoes there is a distance of approximately one cubit.

After the feet have been washed and the day-shoes have been rinsed briefly, if anyone wishes to cut his toenails, he must do so in the same place, since at that time he is permitted to carry a knife solely for this purpose. He is also permitted to shake out his socks there. When these things have been completed, they do not delay carrying their shoes and knives to the bed. Returning immediately to the cloister, they wash their hands and, if the Office of the Dead is not to be performed, they sit on their beds and await in the deepest silence the striking of the board for the Mandatum, or of the bell for drinking if they have not supped. [Col. 1034C]

If, as sometimes happens in winter, the community cannot meanwhile have a reading because the servants are dining and night is pressing on, they await the striking of the board with the lights burning in the chapterhouse. After the servants’ supper, or after the common drinking, the prior asks the lord abbot whether he wishes to attend the Mandatum. Whether he wishes to attend or not, the prior nevertheless does not omit striking the board.

## CHAPTER C. On the Mandatum of the brothers

* When the board has been struck, the weekly kitchen servants who served during the present week for washing, and those who are to serve during the following week for drying the feet, prepare themselves. The community enters the chapterhouse; after making the movement forward and backward, they sit and await the entry of the abbot or prior. For the prior, they rise upright upon the stools; for the abbot, they rise when he enters, but do not bow.

When the lord abbot imposes the antiphon—or, if he is absent, the precentor—the men who will wash the brothers’ feet go ahead; those who will dry them, girded with towels, follow. Thus they enter the chapterhouse. If there are four, the first and third in order wash on the right side, the second and fourth on the left, taking care immediately to place the shoe beneath the foot they have washed. Those who wash and dry the feet of the lord abbot, and of those brothers alone who sit on a stool [Col. 1035A] or on the rush mat, observe the same order, washing and drying the brothers’ feet on their knees upon the ground. Those who finish washing their own side first help those washing on the other side, so that they may complete the task more quickly.

When the washing of the feet and the towels has been completed, outside the chapterhouse, where the water had been supplied to those washing by the conversus appointed to this duty, they provide one another with water for washing their hands in the same place, but do not dry them. Then, when the men carrying basins for washing the hands enter, no one rises in the prior’s absence, even if the abbot is absent; each remains seated and awaits the water-server. If, however, a bishop or an abbot is sitting there in the place of the lord abbot, everyone rises when he rises. If he is standing on a stool, the conversus does not descend to the ground either, but waits standing on the stool until the other sits down. [Col. 1035B]

When the washing of the hands has been performed in the same order as the washing of the feet, if someone who is not a weekly servant is serving at the request of one of the weekly servants in his place, then, after setting down his basin outside the chapterhouse, he returns to his place, makes the movement forward and backward there, and sits. The man in whose place he had been requested to serve then goes out, joins the others in his order before the chapterhouse, and, with those who washed the feet leading, all make the movement forward and backward together before the seat of the lord abbot. The conversus who supplied the water while they were washing then follows them, comes to his place, and makes the movement forward and backward there himself.

The reader for the Collation, rising as soon as the sacristan, having received permission, has gone out to ring the bell, asks for the blessing and begins the reading as soon as he hears the singing end. After one or two verses have been read, the man who is then sitting in the principal place as keeper of order signals to the one next to him in maintaining the order. The latter makes the movement forward and backward and goes out with a gentle step to strike the bell, provided that he has heard the verse being read; the refectorer follows him with the same measured step.

When the bell has been heard, the brothers proceed orderly into the refectory. Those who are on the right as they go bow to the man striking the bell; he too, remaining bowed, does not rise fully until all have passed. The reader, as he goes into the refectory, is neither first nor, even if he is of higher rank, does he retain his usual place; instead, he keeps the order that happens to meet him among the first until he reaches the refectory. There he must also read the verse while standing.

The entire community likewise waits until the keeper of order observes each person whom he has passed making a bow; that person immediately signals to him to read. As soon as the refectorer hears the reader’s voice, he causes the little bell to sound once by hand, so that, when they hear it, the conversi and the youths whose special duty this is rise to serve the drink. The refectorer fills their cups without regard to their order, in whatever order they approach. They in turn stand, as they withdraw from him before the step, either on both sides of the table dividing the refectory lengthwise or one behind another. When the person at the end has begun to move forward, he awaits the next person’s reading, and then rings the little bell until a youth—or one of the boys, if any are present—begins *Benedicite*.

Then, after the priest has given the blessing, the first of them standing at the step opposite the prior hands the cup to him, and he pours into his own bowl. The others pour for the others, beginning with the priors on both sides of the refectory and ending with those seated in the middle. When each has poured into his own bowl as much as he wishes, he hands it to the person sitting beside him.

If the lord abbot is present, he alone receives the vessel in which his drink has been served, whether it is a phial or his own bowl; after drinking, he places it before himself. The same is permitted to any abbot or prior sitting beside him, or to anyone himself maintaining the order. The cupbearers pour into the bowls of those who are serving the drink. When they have completed their duty, they do not form up as before but join together in whatever numbers can appropriately stand together. The ones who preceded them, followed by the others in the same order, make the movement forward and backward at the step on both sides of the central table, and then return to their places to drink. [Col. 1036B]

If one of the brothers arrives while the reading is not yet finished, he receives permission to drink. If anything remains in the cups of those drinking, they pour it into their own vessels and place the bowls upside down. When the reading has ended, the reader places the book at the upper end of the row of tables nearest his seat; after making the movement forward and backward, he takes the book, comes to his place, and sets it before him. Then, sitting, he drinks.

Afterward, when the prior thinks the time has come to rise, he strikes the little bell. Standing in the same place and facing the community, he says the verse *Adjutorium nostrum in nomine Domini*—“Our help is in the name of the Lord.” Then, after making the movement forward and backward, they return from there to the church. It must nevertheless be understood that in this procession alone the brothers may change places with one another, because of officials who are leaving and who may then depart from there with permission. Such a change is not permitted in any other procession except at the end.

## CHAPTER CI. When the brothers drink during the Collation

* Whenever the brothers drink during the Collation, they shall observe the following prescribed order. Since the occasion has brought the matter up, the times when this is done should not be passed over in silence. On all feasts celebrated with the greatest solemnity, they drink during the Collation on the feast day itself, whether the feast has a vigil or not. If it has a vigil, the brothers drink during the Collation on the day preceding the vigil. They also drink whenever, during the summer, they are to fast on the following day, and whenever the prior judges it appropriate, either because of excessive heat or for some other reasonable cause, and this practice continues until the Ides of September.

## CHAPTER CII. On the washing of the poor men’s feet

(Udalric.) The roster (*brevis*) is closed in the chapterhouse with these three men who are appointed for the daily Mandatum. It begins at the beginning of the fast and continues until the Kalends of November. Every day, whether the community eats once or twice, it is performed after supper.

When the community enters the church after supper with a psalm, those who are to perform this service pass through the lesser choir and gather together near the door. * Immediately after the verse has ended, the board is struck, and they go out first or among the first, beginning the psalm *Laudate*. The priest walks in the middle, while the others walk beside him on either side, singing the same psalm.

When they have reached the door, the youngest of the three goes slightly ahead, opens the door, and goes out first; then the other follows him, with the priest following, and so they proceed to the place appointed for this work. Udalric: there they find three poor men already with their feet uncovered and prewashed by the almoner’s servant. * Before them, in the same order in which they arrived there, they ask pardon, whatever the day may be. [Col. 1037B]

Udalric: When the psalm has ended, the senior gives place to the priest, withdrawing himself to the middle. After imposing the antiphon *Mandatum novum*—“A new commandment”—they wash the poor men’s feet. * After washing them, they dry them first with a towel and then wipe them a little with their hair; they kiss them and touch them with their eyes as well. The last in the order takes the same towel from the servant and places it in the priest’s hand; then the priest passes it to the middle man, and the middle man to the last.

(Udalric.) After first washing their own hands, they also offer water and a towel to the hands of the poor. When the priest has struck the little bell once, they stop singing. Finally the bell is rung; when it has ceased, *Benedicite* is said over the food and drink, if there is any, [Col. 1038A] and it is served to the poor. Bread is placed in their right hands and drink in their left, and both hands are kissed.

Then they change places, stand, and bow according to the following order: *Ostende nobis, Deus*, etc.—“Show us, O God”; *Kyrie, Christe, Kyrie*; *Pater noster*—“Our Father”; *Et ne nos*—“And lead us not”; *Suscepimus, Domine*, etc.—“We have received, O Lord”; *Tu mandasti mandata tua*, etc.—“You have commanded your commandments”; prayer: *Dominus vobiscum. Oremus. Adesto, Domine*, etc.—“The Lord be with you. Let us pray. Be present, O Lord”; after making the movement forward and backward and imposing the aforesaid psalm, they withdraw.

When they come to the brothers sitting in the cloister, they walk bowed, and the brothers likewise rise slightly, bowing as they pass. Reaching the step in the choir with the same psalm, they again say the Lord’s Prayer, the verse *Et veniat super nos misericordia*—“And may mercy come upon us,” the collect *Actiones nostras*—“Our actions,” *Dominus vobiscum*—“The Lord be with you,” and *Benedicamus*—“Let us bless.” [Col. 1038B] * They again make the movement forward and backward.

## CHAPTER CIII. Who may be admitted to this daily Mandatum

It must be understood that the weekly priest is never appointed for this Mandatum. A priest who has been suspended from his office, as well as a deacon, may perform this Mandatum in the priest’s place, because that same priest, even if he is not exercising the priestly office, says *Dominus vobiscum* everywhere. A conversus who is to perform this Mandatum with a priest or deacon and another literate brother must be appointed in the second place, if his rank requires it.

Here our discourse must now be closed. Amen.

# BOOK TWO

[Col. 1037]

## PREFACE OF SAINT WILLIAM

[Col. 1037C]

Since in the description of the preceding book we first laid down a rule concerning the discipline of novices and then concerning the other institutions of our custom, especially those to be carried out daily within the limits of the cloister, we now divide into a second book what remains concerning the individual duties necessary for each office, whether outside or inside. And because we believe the abbot—placed in the stead of Christ—to be the head and teacher of our entire obedience, at the beginning of this volume we place him first, intending to speak of the care due to his election and of the reverence to be shown to the man elected.

## CHAPTER I. On the special election and installation of the lord abbot

The election of the lord abbot has this as its lawful and perpetual character: no mortal customarily takes part in it except those alone who are professed members of our church. Therefore, first of all, the matter itself is most diligently commended to God through the earnest prayers of all the brothers. Then, once the council of the seniors has been assembled, the election itself is discussed, and with complete attention they inquire how it may be conducted according to the Lord.

When they have reached the prayer of the election, the entire community first prostrates itself in the chapterhouse and chants the first seven of the fifteen psalms of the Gradual, followed by the Lord’s Prayer. The prior himself then rises while the others remain prostrate and, after first saying the verse *Ostende nobis, Domine, misericordiam tuam*—“Show us, O Lord, your mercy,” says this prayer [Note: [Col. 1037] This prayer was composed by Saint Hugh, abbot of Cluny, as is inferred from Udalric’s codex]:

“We are present, Lord Holy Spirit—we are indeed held fast by the enormity of sin, but specially gathered together in your name. Come to us, be with us, and deign to enter our hearts. Teach us what we should do, where we should walk, and show us what we must accomplish, so that, with your help, we may be able to please you in all things. Be the salvation, the counsellor, and the accomplisher of our judgments; you alone possess, with God the Father and his Son, the glorious name. Do not allow us, who love the highest equity, to be disturbers of justice, so that ignorance may not draw us to the left, favor may not bend us, and the acceptance of a gift or love of a person may not corrupt us. Rather, join us truly to yourself by the gift of your grace alone and of your glory, so that we may be one in you and deviate from the truth in nothing. Thus, gathered together in your name, may we uphold justice in all things with a moderation informed by compassion, so that here our judgment may disagree with yours in nothing, and in the future we may receive eternal rewards from you for our good deeds.” [Col. 1038D]

All respond only, “Amen.” The prior then addresses them again with confidence, urging them not to doubt in any way the presence of divine grace. He also says several things appropriate to the matter and the occasion.

* In the meantime, whether it is the prior himself or another senior whose soul is possessed by the fear of the Lord, the other superiors admonish and ask him to state first what he thinks should be done concerning the election. If some portion of the brothers disagrees concerning the man whom he first names, the matter is deferred until the following day, or, if necessary, until the third day, and meanwhile God’s mercy is invoked more insistently through fasts, prayers, and almsgiving.

Finally, once an abbot has been elected according to the Rule of Saint Benedict (chapter 64), the prior imposes the antiphon *Confirma hoc, Deus*—“Strengthen this, O God”—in the chapterhouse. The psalm *Exsurgat Deus*—“Let God arise”—is sung in the proper tone, and thus the elected abbot is led into the church. There he lies prostrate at the step until the psalm and antiphon have ended, together with the Lord’s Prayer and the verse *Et veniat super nos*, followed by the prayer *Actiones nostras*, etc. He then rises, is installed in the place of the lord abbot, the hymn *Te Deum laudamus* is imposed, and immediately afterward the custodian begins to ring the great bell.

At the same hour, at the second verse of the aforementioned hymn, the individual brothers begin to kiss him, asking his pardon. When this has been done, all return with him to the chapterhouse, and all the officials of the monastery place their keys at his feet. He orders them to take them back. Later, at the first suitable opportunity, the bishop is invited to bless him, and the bishop himself, not another, gives him the pastoral staff.

[Col. 1039C] Having briefly prefaced these matters concerning the election of the lord abbot, let it be said that this applies generally, without respect of persons, to our order and to anyone who has held the office of abbot.

## CHAPTER II. On the general office of the lord abbot

(Udalric.) The lord abbot is accorded singular reverence in every place, as is fitting. * First, in the church, while the little bell is being rung before Matins, he rests, if necessary, on the misericord of his stall [Note: [Col. 1039] That is, he sits on the seat for the sake of comfort while the others bow their heads], while the brothers meanwhile bow as usual. If prayer is made prostrate, he himself lies on the platform within the space mentioned above and says the three prayers there.

No one stands in the choir beside him in the nearest stall except another abbot. Nevertheless, he alternately gives a place for sitting to anyone standing near him. Whenever an antiphon is imposed, he bows, and everyone bows with him, even when he asks pardon because he has made a mistake in some word. If he should ever doze while the blessing is being given to the reader, the one sitting nearest him courteously wakes him.

(Udalric, variant.) As long as he is with the community, he is always appointed for the eighth responsory, or, if this is a brief service, for the seventh responsory, and for the twelfth lesson. When he proceeds to it, everyone rises and does not sit until he has passed. So that they may not have to rise again for him when he returns from the lectern after the lesson has ended, he is appointed again [Col. 1040A] until they rise for the *Gloria Patri* sung by the cantor of the responsory. Then, returning before his seat, he makes the movement forward and backward as before. During the three nights before Easter, however, he is appointed for the sixth responsory and the ninth lesson.

(Udalric.) Whenever all or some of the responsories are sung at the steps, he sings the one assigned to him from his own seat with his fellow singers beside him, if possible; otherwise they stand behind him. When it has ended with them, he steps forward slightly from his seat and makes the movement forward and backward.

The cantor also first comes to him, announcing whether there is an antiphon that he must impose or a responsory that he must sing. * If he does not wish to sing or impose the antiphon, or if he is not present, the same cantor acts in his place for this purpose. The cantor also approaches him to give a reminder if he notices that he has not come for the lesson.

To his care properly belongs the hymn *Te Deum laudamus*: either to begin it himself or to instruct another standing beside him to begin it. (UD.) If he neglects this, the prior begins. It also belongs to him to read the Gospel whenever it is to be read after Matins, * and then to sit in the choir wearing the alb, if it is such a feast that he ought to incense the altars. Then, I say, dressed only in the alb, he incenses alone, if it is such a feast that he should likewise be incensed by another priest. (UD.) Then too, at his own seat, he begins the antiphon over the Gospel canticle, and afterward puts incense there. But if it is such a feast that the cope must be worn, during the hymn he comes to the vestry to put it on; and [Col. 1040C] if he does not wish to begin the antiphon, he puts incense there. If, however, he is going to begin the antiphon, he returns again to his seat and, after beginning the antiphon, puts incense there. Here it should be noted that whenever he incenses alone—whether he is in the choir or in the vestry—the sacristan brings him the incense box and the servant the censer. Over the Gospel canticle he puts on an antiphon only at the Twelve Lessons.

(UD.) A priest who is about to offer incense first brings it to him, if he is in the choir, so that it may be placed in the censer by his hand; likewise the deacon before the Gospel. The one who presides over the choir does the same when offering it, even if the lord abbot is celebrating Mass at that time.

At the beginning of the fast, if he is present, by custom he imposes ashes on the brothers; afterward he himself receives them from the prior, [Col. 1040D] as does a priest if the lord abbot is absent. Anyone among his professed monks, unless he is an abbot, kisses him and asks pardon both before and afterward, except at the solemn celebration of Mass. His bed is in the middle of the dormitory, near the crucifix.

(UD. var.) He himself makes the sound by which the brothers are roused to rise at dawn. If he occasionally sleeps longer than usual, the prior makes the sound in his place. If he is present when the bell ought to be rung for chapter, he rings it himself if he wishes. * If he is not present, however, it must not be rung unless he has first been informed—since he may wish to attend from the beginning. If one of the greatest solemnities is imminent, his chaplain, before the bell is released, turns into the lesser choir and remains there until the community proceeds. Then he takes the pastoral staff, which is kept constantly beside the entrance to the choir, enters chapter before the reader, and places it at the lord abbot’s right. When chapter is finished, he returns it to the place where he had first taken it.

Whenever, in his presence, the brothers hear his name recited in the brief, they all bow each time he bows. When the sermon is finished, if such an offense happens to him in the sacraments— * when he has celebrated Mass, namely, if he has consecrated wine without water, or water without wine, as the Lord’s blood; or if something from those same sacraments has fallen; or if he has received the Lord’s body twice—he begins to act as follows. First, sitting, he accuses himself with all humility and asks to be helped in this matter by the brothers. When they hear this, the ministers who were serving where the same offense occurred rise and, having asked pardon, receive judgment in the *stamineum*. When they have returned to their seats, all the priests who celebrated the office of Mass ask pardon. Of these he selects a seventh, if he thinks fit, and an eighth in his place, and makes them, like the ministers, undergo judgment. When chapter is finished, after the psalms, the brothers prostrate themselves and sing the seven penitential psalms, unless it is Easter; and these prayers are said: “Grant us, your servants,” and “Ineffable One,” or “Hear us, we beseech you, O Lord,” with the following verses: “After childbirth.” Verse: “Help us, O God.” But since the aforesaid offenses can happen not only to the abbot but also to other brothers in different ways, it must not be left unsaid how they are likewise to be corrected.

## CHAPTER III. What is to be done if some negligence should happen concerning the body or blood of the Lord

* If some of the Lord’s blood falls upon the corporal, the corporal is to be put away and preserved as a relic. If it falls upon the altar pall, that particular piece is to be cut out and preserved as a relic. The same is done if it falls upon the chasuble. But if it falls upon the ground, the place—whether stone or earth—is to be licked, wiped, and scraped, and the dust itself is to be stored in the sacristy or in the piscina. The one to whom such negligence has happened first tears open his *stamineum* before his chapter in such a way that, if the abbot wishes, he is ready to receive judgment naked. Although this preparation is not customary, no one reproves him for it. After this, what was prescribed concerning the ministers, the priests, and the seven psalms is carried out. If something from the Lord’s body falls upon the altar pall, that portion is not cut out but is washed only with wine.
