The one to whom this negligence has happened, while asking pardon in chapter, receives an appropriate judgment upon the *stamineum* together with the one through whose carelessness such a thing occurred. But if the Lord’s body falls upon the ground, everything is to be done in the same way as was stated above concerning the Lord’s blood. If a fly, spider, or something of that kind falls into the Lord’s blood, since such a thing cannot be swallowed without danger, it must, when necessary, be burned in the fire. The satisfaction for such an occurrence is left to the discretion of the superior: he may order the one to whom it happened either to receive judgment, or to recite psalms, or even to give alms publicly, or to sing psalms in the community, as he sees fit.

It must be understood that whenever any of these negligences happens to a brother after chapter, correction is in no way postponed. If the abbot is in the cloister, he is informed—for such matters are never handled without him—and immediately the board is struck to summon the brothers. Whenever the lord abbot comes to chapter, no one asks pardon there and no one is called to account [Col. 1042B] until he has finished whatever he has to say on that occasion. If he had been about to depart somewhere and meanwhile one of our brothers had died, after his return the sacristan is to remind him at the first chapter that he should seek pardon.

## CHAPTER IV. Concerning an imprisoned brother

* If he finds a brother imprisoned whom a fitting penance, according to the testimony of the prior and of the seniors whom the prior himself had sent to him, requires to be released from prison, he asks pardon for him from those same seniors and orders him to be released and brought to chapter. When, by asking pardon, he shows a penitent heart, he orders him to sit in the last place—or even, if it seems appropriate, frees him entirely from the same offense. If he comes to chapter during the sermon, he does not enter before it has ended. If, on entering, he finds a brother standing under judgment, or even stripped, the prior immediately makes him sit down; and if the negligence is such that it ought not to be lightly dismissed, he then says to him: “Go and sit down, and afterward return.” When he returns, he bows deeply. This is observed by anyone who is ordered to go and return in this manner. At his entrance the brothers rise, and, standing upright before their stools, remain there until he has passed.

If there is doubt about some custom, whatever he determines there in common counsel with the seniors is thereafter held as law. For the seniors must, as far as they are able, take care that no custom is ever changed through him except for the better. [Col. 1042D] If he changes some custom without the brothers’ consent in such a way that it cannot afterward endure, he is to be humbly admonished about it; and whatever the community commonly decrees on the matter, he does not delay to accept, in accordance with the tradition of the elders. It belongs to him alone not only to appoint the chief obedientiaries but also to appoint certain assistants for them—for example, an assistant to the church custodian, the chamberlain, the cellarer, the master of novices, the infirmarian, and the sacristan. The obedientiaries themselves, however, as well as the prior of any cell, may be suspended from their obediences by the prior only in a case of necessity, if the lord abbot happens to remain elsewhere for so long, or is so far away, that a message cannot be sent to him. Such necessity compels him to suspend any of them from his obedience if he has committed something that he cannot correct by himself without the lord abbot. The aforementioned assistants he may change in the abbot’s absence for a similar or even lesser necessity. To the abbot alone it is also reserved to send any brother into the more serious fault. And this is the procedure for it.

## CHAPTER V. Concerning the more serious fault

* A brother who has been stubborn, disobedient, or in any way contrary to the holy Rule is also to be dealt with according to the Rule. But if he has incurred some such crime as theft or sacrilege, and realizes that it has become so public that he cannot escape being accused of so great a crime, while the lord abbot is presiding over chapter he voluntarily asks pardon; then he lamentably declares in what crime he has fallen. (UD. var.) When he hears him say, “Go out, strip yourselves, and remove your shoes, and return as is customary,” he goes out, with the chamberlain preceding him to the audience chamber. There, with the chamberlain’s assistance, he first bares his feet and loosens the hood of his *stamineum* by a cut on the right and left, so that he can draw his arms through it and tie the *stamineum* with its sleeves around his thighs. The knife and belt, however, are not taken from him. He takes in his right hand a bundle of rods that always lies there, * tied together at that moment by the chamberlain, and in his left a cowl hanging in a suitably folded arrangement. With the chamberlain preceding him, he thus comes into the presence of the lord abbot. Having placed the rods and cowl before him, he asks pardon. Ordered to rise, he sits on the ground and places the cowl upon his knees. * He is beaten as much as seems appropriate to the lord abbot. Then, ordered to dress himself, he puts the cowl on his naked body while still seated and rises. After this he is ordered to go out to dress. The same man who accompanied him above accompanies him again. Returning barefoot, he prostrates himself once more. When he hears the lord abbot say, “Brother, remain in the more serious fault,” he immediately bows his head and puts on his cap. He does not remove it afterward for as long as he remains under that sentence, except when he prostrates himself before the church door; then he lowers it slightly. Afterward he proceeds to the place designated for such men, accompanied by the brother whom the lord abbot then assigns to him.

In the western corner of the aforementioned audience chamber [Col. 1043D] there is a small cell for receiving such brothers, of a size sufficient for one man. It is kept constantly locked by the chamberlain, except when someone is being held in the more serious fault; then it is locked at night only by his custodian, if there is suspicion that he might flee. Before this brother enters the little building, he remains seated near his custodian until, once chapter has ended, it is swept by the almoner if necessary and strewn with rushes. He remains there continually, barefoot and without a guard. There he sleeps and eats upon the rushes. No one speaks to him except the brother mentioned above. For that brother must warn him in advance of everything that is to be done and, at the time of his meal, provide whatever is necessary. At the hour and in the quantity prescribed by the lord abbot, he brings him rye bread, his allowance with water, and his cup—unless the aforesaid Father gives him something additional out of mercy. Whatever his meal may be, he is not forbidden to wash his hands before it; but he is not allowed to have either a tablecloth or a table. His food is not blessed. The remains of his food and drink, if the drink is not water, are given separately to some poor person, without the brothers’ scraps. For bodily necessity he may go to the infirmary. At all the hours he takes care to come before the church before the hour has begun; then, asking pardon, he stands near the door—or, if he is ill, sits—until the community begins the *Kyrie eleison*. (UD. var.) Then, prostrating himself full length and rising after the collect, he puts his cap back on. He does not raise it again after the psalm until the brothers are to leave and all have gone out. He remains in the corner of the chapterhouse for both Masses.

* The lord abbot deliberately orders certain seniors to come to him and exhort him to accept gratefully whatever temporal correction has been inflicted upon him, so that he may be reconciled to divine mercy. When it seems right to the lord abbot, he also agrees with those same seniors that they should ask pardon in chapter for the guilty man—(UD. var.) especially if they have well tested him and can testify that, because of his guilt, he has a contrite spirit and a broken and humbled heart. When they have heard this, they report it to the brother. At the next chapter, when they ask pardon for him and publicly announce his penance, the community’s prayers are added. The abbot agrees that he should show mercy to him and sends for him. Such a brother may be one who is not left under this sentence for more than one night. For how he is to be treated must be inferred by the abbot from his previous manner of life and his present penance. When the prior and chamberlain have been sent for him, he strips in the same way as above; he comes back and is beaten again, if it seems appropriate to the lord abbot. Then, wearing his cowl, he prostrates himself at the feet of the abbot and all the brothers—first at the feet of those sitting above on the lord abbot’s left, then on his right; afterward, returning to those sitting on the bench, he observes the same order. Having done this, he asks pardon again. [Col. 1044D] He is ordered to go out and dress himself; only the chamberlain accompanies him. Dressed and shod, he returns and asks pardon again.

* He is ordered to sit in the last place. From then on he is last of all everywhere: whether literate or not, he is always last against the wall in the choir, on the bench in chapter, and at the middle table in the refectory.

Meanwhile he does not receive Communion, just as no one who is last because of any fault does. He does not come forward for the kiss of peace and does not kiss the Gospel book. In church he is not assigned either to a reading or to singing. He serves only in the kitchen and at the service of the brothers and of three poor people, though not in the priest’s place. For the rest, no obedience is assigned to him during this period.

[Col. 1045A] After each hour he asks pardon on his knees, but he does not therefore turn toward the altar. He never wears an alb unless a procession is to be conducted in albs. When he is in the choir without an alb, he is temporarily moved from his place at the wall, behind no one wearing an alb or cope.

(UD.) Each of these rules is to be observed for anyone placed last for any reason, except that, as we stated above, the asking of pardon after the hours is specifically assigned to the man under discussion. As time passes, he humbly asks some of the seniors to intercede for him, but without asking pardon. No one ever seeks such intercession with pardon in the community or in chapter itself. Those same seniors, as soon as they can, do not delay to plead for his complete release, provided that they have perceived his inward penance. For a brother who habitually commits such offenses is not so quickly recommended to the lord abbot for release. In response to their petition, the aforesaid Father usually replies as he knows the penitent’s condition requires. He may be a man whom he restores to his former place at the next chapter, or one whom he judges it is not yet beneficial to restore.

This intercession is usually made in four ways. Sometimes the seniors who previously interceded for him remind the lord abbot, so that he does not forget him in chapter. Sometimes it happens that the aforesaid brother is accused of some small negligence; thus, on that occasion, both the same seniors and the other brothers petition for him. Sometimes, in the abbot’s presence, he voluntarily asks pardon, so that the brothers may more opportunely intercede for him. Sometimes the lord abbot himself calls him, telling him to rise and come into the midst, without anyone’s prompting. When he asks pardon, the abbot speaks words suited both to the case and to the person and restores to him his former place—or, if he wishes, a lower one. He falls at his feet, as does anyone, both in church and in chapter, whenever the abbot promotes him to a higher place. If the abbot himself is prevented and entrusts this matter to the prior, and the prior reports it in the brothers’ chapter, the promoted man immediately prostrates himself at the prior’s feet. Although from then on he suffers no separation from the others, [Col. 1045D] if he had been the brothers’ confessor or had been promoted to sacred orders, he does not perform these offices at all unless the lord abbot later grants this to him for the merits of a good life. If he was publicly accused of some crime among secular people, he is never again sent outside the cloister unless he has lived so holy and just a life that he can thereafter be trusted. If he committed such a thing in another place rather than among us, he will never return there again, whatever testimony he may have received and however old he may be. If there has been some evil suspicion concerning a brother, he will carry the lantern under guard until he has deserved to be released from it through the utmost humility and a holy way of life. Thus far concerning one who, while the lord abbot was residing at home, fell into a capital crime.

[Col. 1046A] But if someone has been publicly accused among the brothers of such a fault while the abbot is far away, the prior suspends him, if he is a priest, from his office, from whatever obedience he then holds, from the Lord’s body, and from other things of this kind; the rest he postpones until the abbot’s presence. The prior observes the same procedure for any cell if such a thing happens there, and in addition brings the brother himself to the principal place, either personally or through another, just as he does the one who returns from flight; for he does not admit the latter into the cloister there. If one of our professed brothers, assigned to an abbot from among us who is in charge of another monastery, commits such a thing, that abbot corrects him according to custom. Nevertheless, if he has returned from flight, when he first comes to us he is not received into the cloister without the customary satisfaction, even if the lord abbot was present at that earlier satisfaction—unless the abbot himself should have decided that he be received clothed in the hearing of the brothers. When the man I have mentioned, who committed a capital crime elsewhere, is brought to us to receive the customary blessing, he immediately enters the cloister, whether the lord abbot is at home or not. If the abbot is not at home, this brother does not come into his presence before his return; meanwhile he remains in the infirmary until, at the abbot’s command, he is stripped by the prior and chamberlain and presented naked in the audience chamber before chapter. If the lord abbot is in the monastery when he arrives, although he may meanwhile be in the community, he does not come before him until he has been summoned by him to chapter. After asking pardon, [Col. 1046C] he undergoes in every respect the discipline prescribed for the more serious fault.

This law of correction, which we have described, is always to be observed in such lapses, unless the matter has been secretly brought to the lord abbot and he himself wishes to handle it secretly, since the treatment of such a case depends solely upon his discretion. If someone accused of a serious fault denies it, so that the matter becomes doubtful, and customary judgment meanwhile establishes what is proved, the matter is deferred by the chapter and, once proved secretly, is brought back there; the sole exception is the crime of fornication. In that case, because of the scandal, the matter is usually not brought forward publicly but is secretly reported to the lord abbot—or, in his absence, to the prior. If someone makes an indiscreet accusation, the matter likewise must be deferred by the chapter for an opportunity of investigation. But once it has been proved, it is never to be brought back there, for this reason: if someone is found guilty, he should experience this through secret strictness; in the public disgrace, consideration is shown not to him but to the others. The prior also conducts this investigation when the lord abbot is no farther away than a two-day journey.

## CHAPTER VI. Concerning other kinds of correction

(UD.) There are among us still other kinds of correction, which not only the lord abbot carries out but also, if necessary, the prior in his absence. No monastic church is so greatly dishonored by something committed by a brother as it is by the fact that something wickedly done is negligently left without worthy correction. Therefore, if someone is reported among the people for having committed some disgraceful act outside the cloister, he is usually corrected in the presence of the people, so that those who learned of his offense may also learn of his correction. With everyone who wishes to see watching—and especially in the middle of the square of the place where it was committed—he is stripped, bound, and beaten. Although this is the strictest kind of correction and disgrace, afterward he is nevertheless subjected to the more serious fault in the principal place.

But if his fault is not among the more serious evils, but perhaps he has behaved dishonorably in a dispute with someone in the hearing of the people, then, when Sunday or another feast day on which work ceases arrives, as the people gather in a large public assembly at the beginning of the morning Mass, he stands at the church near the doors, barefoot, and holds a fairly large book in his hand. He does not put on his cap, so that he may be recognized by everyone. He speaks to no one entering or leaving. A servant is always beside him to tell those who ask why such a penance has been imposed upon him. He does not leave that place until Mass is finished.

## CHAPTER VII. How a rebel is to be treated

(UD.) If someone is disobedient and rebellious in some way in chapter, the brothers do not, according to custom, wait to be ordered to seize him. Instead, they immediately rush upon him of their own accord, seize him, and strip him against his will. If the prior thinks fit, even if he has already been beaten, he orders him to be harshly beaten with rods; moreover, he may order him to be put in the Bogas or in prison, a practice which custom does not forbid even if the lord abbot is in the monastery. But if he shows some rebellion while being taken to prison, they frighten him only with threats. When they put him in prison, they first remove his belt and knife. While he lies there, he tastes nothing of food or drink except what the lord abbot—or, in his absence, the prior—orders. The prison is one into which one descends by a ladder; it has neither a door nor a window.

## CHAPTER VIII. Concerning the Bogas

[Col. 1047D] (UD.) Concerning the Bogas: there are some lighter forms, in which the enclosed man sleeps in the dormitory, does not miss the procession, and moreover carries the lantern at night. There are others that are more severe, so that the enclosed man cannot go up to the dormitory but sleeps in the infirmary under guard.

[Note: [Col. 1047D] Another manuscript has *Boijas* instead of *Bogas*, that is, fetters or bonds. The prison was so harsh that it moved Stephen, archbishop of Toulouse, to pity, and in the year 1350, on January 27, by order of the king, the punishment of offenders was made milder throughout the kingdom of France. On this matter see the notes of Stephen Baluze on the chapter, p. 1088.]

## CHAPTER IX. Concerning one who is disobedient outside chapter

(UD.) If he has shown his disobedience in some way outside chapter, the board is immediately struck at the lord abbot’s command; this is the signal for assembling, [Col. 1048A] for the purpose of beating him again. He may also have spoken something so presumptuous in the presence of the lord abbot or even of the prior that for this reason too the board is struck, likewise at the lord abbot’s command. In such a man—a monk not in reality but in name alone—neither the established order nor the abbot’s compassion nor the seniors’ sympathy is to be applied; rather, bodily strictness is to be increased until he begins willingly to do what his previously presumptuous hardness had prevented him from doing. If a brother has disturbed the prior even slightly, he immediately makes satisfaction with pardon. A brother’s offense against another brother may be such that he merely shows him, by signs, his repentance. But if he does something of this kind in the community, knowing that it causes scandal to the others, he voluntarily asks pardon for it in chapter; otherwise, if accused, he will undergo a harsher sentence.

## CHAPTER X. Concerning a brother who voluntarily leaves the monastery or is expelled

(UD.) With regard to the brother concerning whom Saint Benedict commands the abbot to use the iron of amputation (Rule, 28.7): he is led by the chamberlain to the vestry, stripped of his monastic habit, dressed in the clothing he himself brought or in similar clothing, and expelled. One who has been expelled or has left the monastery through his own fault is to be received three times. Once received, if he lacks the monastic habit, he is kept in the almonry; if he has it, in the guesthouse, until the day on which he is to be associated with the community. If, persuaded again by the devil, he wishes to leave before he is received into the cloister, he is to be dismissed if he is wicked and incorrigible. If, however, he has been tested and is useful, he is to be sent on his way, for such a man, even if he flees, must be pursued and captured.

On the day when he is to be brought in, the porter and the chamberlain are sent for him by chapter. These two strip him in the guesthouse audience chamber, as is customary, and lead him into chapter with the rods that the porter has brought with him from chapter. The chamberlain brings him a cowl, if he lacks one, passing through the western part of the cloister; he carries the clothing that he has then removed back by the same route into the audience chamber located in the cloister, because while the brothers are holding chapter no one except this man is permitted to pass there. When the abbot’s sentence concerning him has been completed, he is ordered to sit in the last place. In the abbot’s absence, the prior does not receive him unless the abbot is away on a three-day journey. The prior then receives him, but naked, telling him that, according to custom, judgment for so great an offense is reserved for the lord abbot. For this reason, however, he does not come to the abbot’s feet. When the aforementioned prior returns, the man remains constantly in the infirmary, taking the utmost care not to appear before him unless summoned. When he is ordered to come to chapter, his *stamineum* is torn open in the audience chamber by the prior and chamberlain who are to bring him; it is suitably wrapped around his loins, and he is dressed in another garment, so that, if he is ordered to receive the reserved judgment, he may obey without delay.

## CHAPTER XI. Concerning the promotion of brothers in rank

* According to the judgment of Saint Benedict (Rule, chapter 63), it belongs properly to the lord abbot to promote brothers in rank. The promotion is as follows. If he promotes a lay brother in rank for some reasonable cause, that brother observes that rank everywhere, except that in church he does not stand among the literate brothers. He grants no place among the literate brothers to any lay brother unless he is of such good conduct and such advanced age, and has learned singing so well, that he knows how properly to sing psalms, hymns, and responsories and to read a lesson. If he seems suitable, he permits such a man to stand in the same rank in the choir, in chapter, and in the refectory. When someone is promoted—while, I say, the man whose rank had previously been there is present—the latter does not lose his own place when he returns, unless the lord abbot says, “Sit beside him,” and adds, “in every place.” But if the man who previously held the rank there is present and at that time sits in another part of chapter, he will afterward be lower than the newly promoted man.

## CHAPTER XII. Further concerning the lord abbot

(UD.) Wherever it happens that the lord abbot and one of the brothers are speaking together, if the brother perceives that the abbot is becoming angry with him, he immediately prostrates himself at length and asks pardon, * except in the presence of secular men. The abbot must see what and how much is permissible to him, so that he does not overstep the bounds of this holy Father of ours, Benedict. UD. No one passes before him, wherever he may be, without bowing deeply to him, * except in the dormitory and in the church, or when going for wine after Communion, or when the subdeacon is carrying the Gospel book. Whoever meets him stands bowed deeply until he has passed. UD. In church, the priest himself stands below him wearing an alb and stole, or even a cope. In the Sunday procession he walks before those wearing albs and carries the pastoral staff; he observes the same practice in every procession of the Twelve Lessons in which he takes part. For this procession, which is conducted in albs, he himself uses a cope, which he removes once the procession is over. If he wishes to celebrate the principal Mass, he puts on the stole with the fanon brought to him by the sacristan, and himself begins Terce; when it is finished, he puts on the chasuble in the sacristy. For the procession of this Mass, the deacon carries the missal to the altar. His chair is placed beside the right corner of that altar, with his face turned toward the choir. But if he himself wishes to sing the Mass, one of the copes belonging to the sacristy is brought to him by the sacristan, so that the choir may be directed by him.

If he walks somewhere at night with a bishop or abbot, only his lantern precedes them both. If he hears Mass at Saint Mary’s, or arrives while it is being sung there, the book is brought to him after the Gospel to be kissed, and the kiss of peace is given. There, or wherever he hears Mass, the priest or deacon who is to read the Gospel turns toward him for the blessing, unless he is far away.

It lies within his power, when necessary, to depose any abbot of such a place that is wholly subject by right of ownership to the principal place; for on the occasion of such promotion the profession of obedience is not annulled and the yoke of subjection is not cast off. The procedure for such a deposition is as follows. If he has lived irreligiously and not according to our order, and, after being warned about this with all humility twice or three times by his seniors, has proved incorrigible, the matter belongs to the lord abbot. Thus, as soon as possible, either he comes to them, or they are invited to come to him, so that such obstinacy may be proclaimed before him and the matter itself may be discussed and settled jointly, as reason demands. The abbot must first admonish him discreetly and paternally twice or three times, and also correct him with severity. If he is not corrected even then, only afterward is he deposed, brought back to the principal place, placed last, and treated according to the measure of his fault. There is also another cause for which he must be deposed without any preceding warning and without resistance: if he has become notorious for some criminal sin and, when the matter has been examined in the principal place, has been unable to clear himself, he must be completely deposed, even if he has otherwise lived well. But if he committed such a crime known only to a few, and, pierced to the heart, penitent and confessing, has promised amendment, he is not deposed, provided that he has otherwise led an honorable and religious life.

(UD. var.) In the community, if the lord abbot wears a cope, he takes his meal with clerics and visiting monks who go on foot with us and are about to dine in the refectory. He himself gives them water for their hands, and for this reason the refectorer always keeps a basin and towel ready, which are also used to serve the abbot himself when necessary. Such men always sit at the principal table, and they are served freely, as the lord abbot is, except that certain things are given to him separately and more frequently than to them.

* Whenever he attends the brothers’ common meal, he finds two pounds of bread before him. He sends one of these, together with a bowl full of some dish—which the brother serving him first gathers before the brothers—along with a drink, regularly to some poor person. If he is so weak that he does not make the customary movements before and behind the table, he has the prior or another brother strike the bell for him, and he sits until it is time to say “Benedicite”; nevertheless, on that occasion he begins it first. If, while the reading is in progress, he makes a sound that deserves pardon, he rises and bows toward the community, and the community bows toward him. If the brother serving him spills something of this kind, he asks pardon. That brother must also be so well versed in signs that whatever the lord abbot wishes to give someone out of charity, he can do through this brother by signs alone. The brother assigned to this office must be advanced in age and character. If the abbot sends something to the infirmary, the same brother immediately gives it to the infirmarian, so that he may carry it there. He also sometimes sends a charitable gift to the reader and the other ministers through this brother. The brother places it at the end of the principal table and later distributes it to them when they are eating, indicating by a sign who is the author of that charity. They immediately turn toward the principal seat and bow with equal reverence, as though the lord abbot were present. Like anyone sitting at that table, he also strikes the bell hanging before him if he notices that the common meal is being served later than usual.

[Col. 1051B] When the meal is finished and the community is leaving, one of the chaplains waits, lest the abbot turn aside alone on the way to the church for some necessity. As long as he rests in the infirmary, he takes part in no procession and rides nowhere on anyone’s business. He also sometimes sends his charity from the novices’ cell to the refectory; the brother who receives it bows reverently before him.

(UD.) After night has fallen, a lantern is carried before him, both within and outside the convent, all the way to his bed. The person who carries it serves him both when he lies down and when he rises. He never eats without a reading; therefore, since in the refectory a reading ought to be heard only at the common meal or at the ministers’ meal, if it is neither of these, he never eats there. When he is traveling, the brothers accompanying him continually watch him on the road, so that they are present whenever he sings any regular Hour; for if one of them should happen not to be present, he does not sing it afterward without his permission.

*They carefully note one another’s negligences while traveling, just as in the cloister; and in the chapter which the lord abbot may hold with them anywhere, as circumstances require, they make their complaints openly. No one in his company may be in military arms. As long as he is traveling, he imitates, as far as he can, the mandatum performed on Saturday, namely by washing his feet and drinking the portion of charity. He does the same if, while staying in the monastery, he has not attended the brothers’ mandatum—which, nevertheless, he never omits except because of unavoidable necessity.

(UD.) If he has gone to Rome or has stayed somewhere for half a year, when he returns he is received in procession, with the brothers generally clothed in albs or capes. For such a reception he must arrive before dinner, since he ought that day to attend the brothers’ common meal; and because of his arrival the portion of charity there ought to be longer than usual. If it can suitably be done that same day, after some regular Hour has ended, he anticipates all those who will be coming out of the church and stands or sits near its door, with the brothers who were traveling with him standing beside him, and the brothers who were traveling with him kiss each person individually as he comes out. But if this cannot be done that day, it is done on the following day after chapter.

## CHAPTER XIII. What order the lord abbot is to observe when he eats in the novices’ cell

[Col. 1052A]

* Whenever the lord abbot eats in the novices’ cell, the cellarer or his assistant customarily serves him. The reading he has while eating is read by the chaplains, but in a different manner: since none of them eats there without his command, it is begun by one of those who has been ordered to eat there, but it is finished by one of his companions who has come by permission from the brothers’ meal. If, however, after eating, he returns before the lord abbot’s meal, that same man both begins and finishes it. Meanwhile the Father may insert some word of edification, if he wishes.

The chaplains therefore eat with him rarely, and only when ordered, because very often weaker brothers are summoned by him to attend his meal. Their portions are brought there from the refectory by the refectorian, at his direction, together with the tableware, by the infirmarian; but they are not taken back before those same brothers are known to be going to eat in the refectory. For if they are to drink after None, other portions are set before them in the refectory—provided that they sing that None in the monastery or at Saint Mary’s; for they do not presume to sing any Hour in the aforesaid cell unless ordered to do so by the lord abbot. If this is ordered for them, on that occasion they may properly drink there after None.

Anyone who is summoned there for only one meal returns as soon as it is finished and does not return there again for this reason unless ordered. After the collation no one may drink there, unless perhaps someone is then dining with the lord abbot. Great care must nevertheless be taken that he does not happen to dine so late, unless compelled by pressing necessity, that he may sometimes forgo the colla[lacuna]nam [term interrupted by the lacuna]. For no healthy brother [lacuna] eats in the cloister after the ministers’ supper for any reason.

At the aforesaid time, the chaplains who were not dining with the lord abbot may, with permission, drink in the refectory. It must also be known that no one speaks in the Twelve Readings during summer, or during the octaves, before chapter or before Terce—which are preceded by three prayers—or during a regular Hour, except for the novices’ confession mentioned above. Nor do the obedientiaries ever speak there about their obediences or any other matter without the permission of the lord abbot or, in his absence, the prior.

No secular person ever enters it, except servants who are occasionally ordered to enter at suitable times to carry out some business there, and guests whom the guest-master sometimes introduces between one Mass and the other for the purpose of viewing it. No one speaks with these persons except the abbot himself, and likewise no one speaks with the servants mentioned above except the person who brings them. Everyone who remains there for any reason with permission observes this rule: no one speaks to another, or even says anything during the time allotted for speaking; but as soon as the brothers’ board is struck, they join the brothers’ conversation. The chaplains are excepted: even during the time of silence they may remain there, though the lord abbot is absent, if they have been assigned something such as making booklets that must be completed without delay. If, for this purpose, they briefly say things to one another that they cannot express by signs, they are not reproved for it.

The chaplains themselves must note that they have no more permission to leave the cloister or enter any workshop than do the other brothers who continually remain in the convent, except for that same cell. If one of them approaches the door seeking the abbot, he does not presume to enter unless he truly knows that the abbot is inside.

Any one of them who can be freed from his service to offer at Mass, attend chapter, attend the procession, attend the office for the dead—which is celebrated with the greatest solemnity until at least three readings have been completed—and attend the mandatum and the brothers’ common meal will not be absent if he wishes to escape being called to account. If they abandon the lord abbot anywhere alone, all of them are to be called to account together.

No obedientiary is to hear the abbot’s Mass in the same novices’ cell, just as nowhere else in the monastery, except at the time when the other priests customarily sing. It must also be known that the frequently mentioned cell is not always locked when some people are sleeping there; rather, even when the lord abbot is present, it is secretly inspected by the cloister prior. To conclude briefly: such discipline is observed there in every respect that no item of clothing belonging to anyone sleeping there is hung up in the cloister of that cell.

## CHAPTER XIV. When, and for which offices, he is to be listed

* But to return to the cloister: twice a year, if the abbot is present and in good health, he is listed for the principal Mass, namely on Easter Sunday and Pentecost. On these occasions, however, another priest, at the direction of the armarius, is to sing the regular Hours, except Vespers and Matins, and to give the blessing in the refectory. On those same days, at the Gospel canticle, he is to wear a cape no poorer than the one worn by the abbot himself; he is to incense the altars together with him and hold the service book for his use.

At Christmas he is listed only for the principal Mass, and the priest prescribed for Saturday—or, if Christmas falls on Sunday, the one appointed by the armarius—performs the remaining duties. Although he is not listed more often, whenever he wishes throughout the year he sings the principal or lesser Mass, Vespers, and Matins.

It must be known, however, that it is an ancient custom of the Cluniacs for the lord abbot and the cellarer, together with the deans, to perform the kitchen service at Christmas. We have not wished to leave this unmentioned, so that you may observe how holy that place was at its beginning, although this is no longer the practice and the same example of humility and religious devotion could not now be carried out without great inconvenience. So many brothers and so many guests [Col. 1054A] come for this most holy solemnity, and the abbot has to answer each of them concerning such different matters, that it would be wholly unsuitable for him then to occupy himself with shelling beans; at another suitable time, however, neither he nor the brothers excuse themselves from it.

On this occasion, as also at Easter and Pentecost, the stewards of the estates, who are called deans, are briefly listed for this service; their customary number is not reduced when the abbot is listed with them. In the refectory he no longer takes part in this task, except that he first places on the tables certain bowls brought to him by the brothers. He begins this service with the other kitchen servants when the cymbal has been struck, orders the prior or another person to strike the small bell, and, when the time comes, he himself first gives the blessing, *Benedicite*, and after the verse has been said goes to sit down.

Every Sunday he also performs the mandatum for a poor man with the boys, if they are present: he washes the man’s feet, gives him two denarii, and gives each boy one, so that they may distribute them to the poor. If the mandatum is neglected by him, it is then provided for by the boys and their master, or, if they are absent, by the armarius. If he is to hear the confession of those same boys, the aforesaid master brings them to the entrance of the chapterhouse and waits there for them to return.

## CHAPTER XV. On choosing an abbot for another place, and on the reverence to be shown him

[Col. 1054C]

* If the lord abbot is asked by someone to appoint one of his brothers abbot of another monastery, he chooses, with the advice of the seniors, someone who seems worthy of such an office. If the person chosen has good sense, he refuses as far as he can to undertake such a burden; nevertheless, he preserves obedience if he sees that the Father persists in his decision. After obedience has been imposed upon him, he bows and, at the Father’s command, sits to the lord abbot’s left.

When he has come to the place over which he is to preside, and has been designated abbot to those brothers by the lord abbot or by his messenger, the remaining rites pertaining to his promotion are performed in the manner described above for the election of the lord abbot. After this promotion, when he first comes to us, he is received in procession. His pastoral staff—or, if he has not brought his own, one of the lord abbot’s staffs—is placed by the sacristan, both then and afterward whenever he returns to us, beside the altar nearest the door through which one passes from the cloister into the church, so that the brothers may be reminded to show him the reverence due to him.

If he lacks a chaplain, the prior assigns a suitable one to him. As long as he remains with us, the brothers bow to him, even in the presence of the lord abbot. In the abbot’s absence he gives the blessing everywhere and imposes the antiphon over the Gospel canticle at the Twelve Readings, which the armarius announces to him. When he bows with the abbot, or, if he makes a mistake, asks pardon, the convent bows with him.

After the inclination he places incense, if another priest is to perform the censing; that priest presents the incense boat to him with a kiss of the hand. He sings the eighth responsory at the step with the others, or alone in his own seat. In the absence of the Father of the monastery he reads the twelfth lesson; when the Father is present, he reads the eighth, and he sings the twelfth responsory in the same order as the eighth.

When he proceeds from his seat to the step to read a lesson in the absence of the aforesaid Father, the brothers rise upright; when the Father is present, they rise slightly from their seats and bow, and do the same when he returns. When he must cense by himself, he places the incense outside the choir; after censing the altars, he offers incense to the lord abbot and the prior. Even if no abbot is present, he carries it back into the choir on account of the prior alone.

The lord abbot, receiving the thurible from a lay brother, in turn incenses this abbot. When censing with another priest, or with another abbot of whom he himself is prior, he is to offer incense to no one except in the choir, and then only to the lord abbot. When he censes with a priest and no abbot is present, he himself administers the incense to the prior, while the priest administers it to him.

At a procession and in the choir, even if he is not dressed in an alb, he nevertheless ranks above those dressed in albs. When he wishes to celebrate Mass, the sacristan supplies him with vestments better than usual. He does not come to chapter except with the lord abbot; with him also he sits at the principal table in the refectory, or alone in the abbot’s absence. After the ministers’ meal, when eating at one of the upper tables, he sits with his companions somewhat apart from him.

By custom he sleeps in the dormitory; if necessary, however, the prior may arrange for him to sleep in the novices’ cell or in the infirmary.

If he wishes to acquire fellowship with his brothers and our chapter, he must ask pardon in chapter before the lord abbot. When asked what he says, he replies, “I seek mercy,” and, rising, declares his wish. The lord abbot rises with the convent, grants him fellowship and a place in the chapter, and is likewise received by him.

Before fellowship has been confirmed by them in this manner, none of us coming to them, or of them coming to us, is permitted to attend chapter unless he earns this privilege by asking pardon. If he does something by which he realizes that the brothers of our house have taken offense against him, as soon as he arrives he humbly makes satisfaction for it to the convent, so that what could provide an occasion of ruin may become an example of edification.

If he has perhaps been expelled from his place because of some persecution, but hopes to return and must nevertheless remain with us for a longer time, he does not observe the order described above. Instead, according to custom, he humbly asks the lord abbot not to have the brothers’ inclinations or a chaplain with a lantern provided for him. If he speaks with a brother without permission at a suitable place and time, this is then overlooked in his case; but the brother is certainly called to account. If afterward he transgresses the order in such matters, he is charitably admonished so that he may amend.

If he thereafter despairs of returning to his own monastery, he will remain content with his former order, unless the lord abbot promotes him.

## CHAPTER XVI. On appointing the prior

[Note: [Col. 1055D] See chapter 2, part I of the *Cluniac Customary*.]

(UD.) When a prior is to be appointed, the lord abbot first consults the seniors and places the election in their discretion. He then reports their decision in chapter, and everyone praises the person on whom they have agreed. If the person chosen has good sense, he asks pardon, excusing himself as unfit for such an office. Finally, if obedience is imposed upon him, he does nothing else but bow. He sits to the lord abbot’s left.

When they rise from chapter, they go with the customary psalmody to the principal church. There [Col. 1056B] the new prior immediately takes the seat of his predecessor. When the psalms have ended, he comes to the step and makes the gesture before and behind, saying three times the verse: “O God, make haste to help me.” The convent likewise responds.

The lord abbot himself gives him this blessing:

> We humbly beseech your omnipotence, most merciful Father, that you would deign to pour upon this servant of yours, whom we commit to the service of you and your servants, the spirit of wisdom, understanding, and discernment. Grant him to act in this your house and to administer the office entrusted to him in such a way that he may please you and, with your help, fulfill most perfectly the welfare of your servants, for which he may receive from you, the most gracious giver, the reward of his labors in the fellowship of your saints, both in this world and in the age to come.

> Through [you], etc.

And so that his absolution here also may not be delayed, he should remember, when he is to be absolved, to say with him the verse: “Blessed are you, Lord God, who have helped me and consoled me.” He is absolved with this blessing:

> Lord Jesus Christ, who are a generous rewarder and merciful giver to those who faithfully serve you, respond with your customary kindness to the labors of this servant of yours, who until now has faithfully labored in this your house and, by obeying you and your servants, has administered the office entrusted to him with your help. Show yourself a merciful remunerator, and grant that he may remain continually in this your house and receive from you the reward of his labors, both here and in the recompense of the just; and may he have no doubt that you are the most abundant giver of all good things.

* It is customary, if circumstances require, that while the Father is being released from this obedience, another person should be considered, if possible, to be substituted immediately in his place, so that at the same hour when the former receives the blessing for departing, the latter also receives the blessing for departing. If the former is removed from the priorate because of some crime, he is immediately placed last and afterward dealt with according to the matter; otherwise he returns to his former order.

The same is to be done, as stated, with any prior of one of our cells who, after being summoned to us, is removed from his priorate for a similar reason. He retains none of what he brought with him, except his clothing; everything else, together with the horse he rides, is sent back, and afterward assigned to his successor.

(UD.) From the hour of his appointment, the newly elected prior takes charge, after the lord abbot, of all matters and cases belonging to the monastery, except the church treasury and the library [Note: [Col. 1057] *Armaria*: library, hence *armarius*, librarian.], which remain in the abbot’s power.

* He stands foremost in the left choir. Likewise, in the refectory he sits foremost at the table to the lord abbot’s right; and if the abbot is absent, he sits in his seat in the refectory. He may send to whomever he wishes; outside the refectory, however, no mortal is permitted to send anything to him.

* All who hold any obedience look to him, UD.; and if they are about to do anything important, it is by no means done without his advice and consent.

(Var.) If he goes to the obediences or elsewhere, he takes with him one brother who sings the regular office with him, together with priestly vestments and a chalice. On returning, however, he immediately gives these back to the church custodian. If, while traveling, he returns to the cloister that same day, he must not eat on the road without permission. He himself can grant this permission to no one while the lord abbot is in the monastery, nor even in his absence except in a serious necessity.

He has no money privately. UD. For when he returns from outside, he gives everything he brings to the chamberlain and receives from him whatever he needs. Our Fathers took this precaution so that that evil plague of private property, especially dangerous to monks, might in no way creep in.

* Nevertheless, whatever is brought to him inside or outside by anyone as a portion of charity, he may lawfully accept; but he spends this also for the common benefit of the brothers, unless the lord abbot orders something else to be done with it. He does not read or sing at Matins unless the armarius lists him for it. Although he has no chaplain, he never leaves the cloister alone unless he takes one of the brothers with him out of reverence.

## CHAPTER XVII. What reverence is to be shown to the prior, and what he may and may not do

* Whenever he holds the choir with the armarius, he kisses the Gospel book before the armarius does, but he does not place the incense. He himself, dressed in a cape, or another person at his nod, offers at that same time. He removes his cape without the precentor’s permission if he happens to leave before the end of Mass. It belongs to him to give permission for the celebration of Mass, or for the abbot or others to remove their capes, after the lord abbot has approached the altar at the celebration of Mass after the offertory; anyone governing the order may likewise do this.

When the prior himself is going to celebrate Mass, after he has first approached the altar he gives no one permission to do anything; rather, the person who is governing the order at that moment does so.

At chapter, and after Compline, when the bell rope is struck, someone lowers it out of reverence and replaces it when the ringing is finished. After he has left the choir, no one presumes to go to meet him.

At chapter, everyone shows him every appropriate reverence; nevertheless, he takes care not to interfere in matters which he knows belong to the abbot’s judgment, being concerned there and everywhere to handle what pertains to him with piety and discretion. After the abbot’s return, he does not release anyone whom he himself has subjected to a lesser fault without the abbot’s command.

With obedientiaries or other brothers, outside chapter, he does not speak harshly or severely, lest because of his inopportuneness anyone be compelled to ask pardon irregularly—unless, in the absence of the lord abbot, some matter of the kind mentioned above must be dealt with on the advice of the seniors and is not to be made public in chapter. Whoever is caught in such an offense asks pardon every time he is called to account by anyone.

He places no one last except someone who has returned from flight after the abbot’s removal. He sends no one into the sentence of a grave fault. Everything else pertaining to the strictness of regular discipline is in his power.

When the brothers speak louder than usual in the convent, or are heard less distinctly in church during prayers or the litany, he admonishes them by a sound made before him for this purpose. If he has attended the regular Hour preceding the meal, except Vespers, and leaves without intending to return after *Benedicamus Domino*, he himself, or another elderly person at his nod, strikes the cymbal, beginning with “Through the Lord.” The ringing continues until half the convent has left the church; it then ends with five strokes, two drawn out slightly and three joined together.

After this he seeks the lord abbot in the sacristy, the infirmary, the novices’ cell, and before the cellarer’s quarters. If he learns that the abbot will not come, he goes and strikes the bell, continuing until he knows that the brothers have arrived from the dormitory, though with due solemnity.

The cloister prior does the same, striking the cymbal; and when either of them has been found—whether the lord abbot or the prior—he does not afterward report it to the other unless the one found has ordered him to do so. If the person striking the cymbal knows that the prior hears it, he reports it to neither of them; rather, the prior announces it to the abbot.

As with anyone sitting at the small bell, no one places anything before him in the presence of the convent except a whole loaf. If, while seated there, he makes a sound or spills or breaks something, he makes the same satisfaction as the lord abbot. He names no brother there to dispense a portion of charity. Whenever a general allowance is given to the brothers, he alone, whether sitting at the small bell or in his own place, receives a complete portion.

He must know that the reading is to be prolonged because of the abbot’s crumbs. If he has been bled, he does not hesitate to enter the choir with the convent. After each meal, when the psalm has ended, he must stand before the vestiarian until he sees that the brothers have gone out. Whenever the brothers go to the refectory to drink, he must not leave the small bell before he sees that everyone has entered.

With his permission, any brother may be absent because of illness from the procession held on weekdays and from manual labor. He may also sometimes, because of extreme cold or another necessity, release him entirely from that procession or, if necessary, give permission to put on his shoes after it has been completed.

While seated before the choir, whether he has been bled or is suffering from another illness, he gives no one permission to do anything in the choir, because that is then the office of the person governing the order. On Sundays, when the brothers proceed from the vestibule into the choir, he—or whoever is governing the order at that time—walks last after those dressed in albs.

On Saturday he is customarily listed for the principal Mass and for kitchen service, but less often than the others because he is occupied with many matters. When listed for Mass, he performs everything as another priest does, except that, in the abbot’s absence, he neither says the verse in chapter nor in the refectory; nevertheless, care is taken that the deputy is not absent for this purpose.

He also orders each person to enter the infirmary to rest whenever he perceives that the person is so ill. Nevertheless, afterward, if it is needed to restore his strength, he cannot grant him a meal of meat while the lord abbot remains in the monastery, except by the abbot’s command.

In the memorial book [Note: [Col. 1059D] The memorial book, otherwise called the necrology, in which the names of benefactors and friends were recorded. In the manuscript in which the rule of the holy Father Benedict was written, only the more illustrious benefactors and those bound to the monks by an exceptional bond were recorded [Col. 1060D].], he has anyone recorded whom he wishes, but not in the register without the lord abbot’s permission. If he orders a psalm to be sung for some tribulation after the abbot’s departure, and this is continued until the abbot returns, it is immediately discontinued when he returns.

If he sings the regular Hour preceding dinner at Saint Mary’s because of some necessity, he is not listed for it. There he precedes Prime and Compline with a confession, and gives the blessings at the nocturnal readings, even if he is under the infirmary rule; the cloister prior, however, does not do this even when he is well.

On the day when he returns from the infirmary after recovering, he does not leave the cloister before chapter. If he has something to say to someone, he may make it known briefly at that time in the brothers’ auditorium, provided it is a weekday. If the lord abbot attends chapter first, he asks the customary pardon for eating meat; he does not do this if he arrives afterward.

It must be known, however, that as long as he remains in the infirmary, no one presumes to come to him without the permission of the person then governing the order. Although, while remaining there in every respect, he does not make himself unlike another sick person, if he wishes to send something to anyone, he is not listed for it.

When he comes to cells wholly subject to us, as long as he remains in any one of them he observes in every respect the same order that he observes in the principal house. If he takes with him a brother who is prior to the prior of that cell, that brother takes precedence over the local prior in rank. This does not apply if such a person comes there with the lord abbot without the prior: in that case the prior of the cell observes there in every respect both the rank and the duties of his obedience.

The deans and priors who preside over places where the regular order is observed in such a way that the small bell hangs at the refectory table rise from the table and go to meet not only the principal prior but also the cloister prior if they arrive while the meal is in progress.

All these matters and similar ones are reported against the prior if, while remaining within the circuit of the wall or so near it that he can promptly run to the regular Hour when he hears the signal, he sings it anywhere other than in the principal church or at Saint Mary’s; if he leaves it before it has ended in the choir except because of unavoidable necessity; if he speaks during any Hour except during Compline, and even then only if it is absolutely necessary; if he hears anyone’s confession anywhere other than in chapter, except for novices; if he prolongs a sermon on the Gospel or the Rule beyond the customary length; if he makes the brothers wait at the refectory longer than usual after the first course has been served to him; if he uses clothing other than that commonly assigned to the brothers; if he distributes anything given there as a portion of charity anywhere except for the common benefit of the brothers; if he leaves the cloister alone; if—God forbid—he speaks alone with a woman; if he frequently goes to bed later than the others; or if he presumes in any way either to act against the order or to permit others to do so.

## CHAPTER XVIII. On the prior’s assistants, whom we call deans; the order in which they and other persons departing receive the blessing; and how they are to conduct themselves on the road

(UD.) The prior’s assistants in external matters are the stewards of the estates, whom we call deans. Like none of the brothers, they may ride out from a cell anywhere without permission, even if they are to return that same day.

* Like anyone else who is departing, after the Hour has ended they ask permission to leave by raising their hand and making the sign of the cross toward the lord abbot or prior. If it should happen that the lord abbot, or the major prior—the prior who is then governing the order in the choir—enters to receive the blessing, those who are then following him, and any who are then departing with him in that very choir (except those who are to accompany him), even if they are dressed in albs, ask permission from him as he approaches the step, before he makes the gesture before and behind.

When he gives assent, and they bow at the step as is customary, UD. (or, if it is such a day, prostrate themselves), the priest continues with these verses:

> Save your servants.
>
> Send them help, O Lord.

Collect: “Be present, O Lord, to those who entreat you.”

When this is finished, if those dressed in albs wish to leave immediately, they ask the same person who gave them permission to depart for permission to remove their albs; but they do not make the gesture before and behind in their own place. If they neglect this, they seek the same permission from the person who is presently governing the order, and then make the gesture before and behind in their own place.

If prevented for some reason from departing that day, they nevertheless receive the same blessing on the following day when they depart. If they are to receive it on Sunday after Matins, the blessing of the kitchen servants must come first.

They must know this: from the Kalends of October until Easter they may never, except during the octaves, during the Twelve Readings, or whenever chapter follows Terce, take a meal immediately after receiving the blessing and after Terce, provided it is not a general fast. If it is a regular fast and chapter has followed Terce, they eat after it has ended and do not eat again afterward except by permission.

But if a universal fast is impending and they fear that they will not have the means to eat outside, they take the necessities for their meal with them when they leave. They observe the same rule in Lent; therefore, they do not anticipate the brothers’ dinner for this reason. If, after receiving the blessing following None, they await the common meal, afterward they may lawfully proceed, whether far or near. At another time, however, no one may do this after Vespers except the person who must acquire fish, either by buying or by fishing.

Before leaving the cloister, they take care not to make it necessary to return. For whatever the reason, if they have returned, they do not presume to leave the cloister again without permission. If someone has prepared himself to mount his horse immediately, but happens to hear the signal for any regular Hour while he is still within the walls, he returns to the Hour after laying down his traveling equipment and does not presume to leave again without permission.

When the board is struck because of a departing brother, if he is outside the gate he does not return; nor does he return for the signal given for the Brief if he has already left the cloister. If he wishes to leave around the time of None, and meanwhile the signal is struck that wakes the brothers to rise, or, in winter, the signal before Terce to put on their shoes, he does not omit his departure for this reason.

After leaving the gate of the cell, he covers his head with his hood until he has left the village. He observes the same rule when passing through any village. UD. When he is about to mount his horse, he puts on his cape before fastening his belt, and does not remove it before first unfastening his belt. However muddy the road may be, if he is not wearing a cape over his frock, he rides unbelted; but in a cuculla without a frock he never rides unless a cape is worn over it.

He greets monks, clerics, and everyone in the habit of conversion whom he meets, saying to them, “Bless.” He addresses secular people in the ordinary manner. If he wishes, he may kiss a secular friend whom he meets while remaining seated on his horse; but he never kisses a monk unless he first dismounts.

(Var.) Wherever he mounts, he seeks a higher place and mounts with due solemnity. For this reason a mounting block has been placed before the monastery gate. On the road he must take care that no one can observe anything irreligious in him or contrary to our order: his clothing must not trail behind him (except that he may sometimes wear his cape because of rain), but must lie neatly below the saddle; neither the front nor the rear saddle strap, nor anything similar, must be missing; and he must not look back while turning on the horse.

He must not ride without stirrup straps, if he wishes to go more than one mile from the cell.

* If he cannot have a second spur, he must be content with one, unless he is an obedientiary or wishes to go farther. He must not disdain to carry a saddlebag with him on the horse if necessary.

(Var.) On a journey longer than two miles he will never have a pedestrian as a companion; nevertheless, when he comes to a river, he may, if necessary, transport another person across on the horse, which is nowhere else permitted.

UD. He must take the greatest care never to loosen his horse’s reins so that it may run. He himself never runs except because of a funeral or a fire.

While he is on the road, if it is a day on which permission must be sought at the Hours, whenever he wishes to sing any Hour he too dismounts, removes his cap from his head and his gloves from his hands, and, asking permission, says the Lord’s Prayer. Then, rising and making the sign of the cross, he again asks permission; when the Hour has been announced and he has mounted his horse, he continues on his way. Nevertheless, if the road is so muddy, or he himself so weak, that dismounting is difficult, he remains seated on the horse and first recites the psalm *Miserere mei, Deus* (“Have mercy on me, O God”), and then, after saying the Lord’s Prayer, sings the Hour. At the Twelve Lessons, however, and whenever permission need not be sought, he neither sings the psalm nor dismounts. Therefore, before leaving the cloister, he must have made provision for the occasions when the Twelve Lessons are read in his absence. He must also, as is customary, sing the Office of Saint Mary. If he is illiterate, something is assigned to him to sing in place of the Regular Hours—that is, the Lord’s Prayer, and whatever similar prayer he knows.

[Col. 1062C] He may lawfully eat on the road without Mass, even on the greater feasts, because he presumes neither to hear Mass except in familiar places or from a priest known to him, nor, if he is himself a priest, to sing it on his own. If frailty should befall him, he abstains from celebrating Mass for one day only; he does not avoid doing so for longer, even if he cannot obtain another change of clothing or make confession. He observes the regular fast outside, unless, when leaving, he has received permission to eat. He may eat in a meadow if necessary. The person who supplies him with food or drink never does so while wearing only a shirt or only breeches, unless it happens that someone other than his companion must serve him. While eating, if he says anything briefly, he does so only about what he needs at that moment …; from longer conversation, however, he refrains. Before eating, after saying the verse, he reads something from Holy Scripture, and does the same at the end. On the road, if he is thirsty and, having no vessel, drinks from his hands at a spring, he does not deserve to be censured for this. No one who is beardless, or who shaves his beard, is to be in his company. Nor does he presume to dismiss his companion and ride alone. Wherever he wishes to lodge, if a church is sufficiently near, he does not omit singing Vespers there. He does not sing Compline and Matins there, but in bed or in a suitable place beside the bed, unless the lodging is attached to the church.

[Col. 1062D] He is especially careful not to enter any church wearing spurs and a cape, or to accept anything from a woman’s hand, sit at table with her, or say anything to her without a witness sitting near them. Before nightfall, unless prevented by some great necessity, he never postpones Compline until the last moment.

There are also matters that he observes both outside and at home: if he has taken off his cowl, whether by day or by night, he utters no word. He also takes care not to place it anywhere farther from him than one cubit. (var.) He may sit or walk in the cowl without its fur lining. * If he comes to a monastery belonging to our order, or to one where we have a chapter, he observes there the same discipline that he ordinarily observes at home. If he had not previously been there, then, when he enters the choir or chapter—if a chapter is in session—and no one leads him in, he seeks the last place; nevertheless, in that choir he occupies the station that is his at home. But if he comes to an entirely foreign monastery, he does not enter the cloister unless ordered to do so; he acts there as he is shown. In any monastery to which he comes, he does not leave the cloister without permission, nor does he say anything to his companion. It should also be known that whenever he is about to enter a monastery of our order in which he has not been for half a year, or which he has never entered, he kneels before the door through which he first enters and asks permission; and at the places established for those returning from the road to pray, he prostrates himself—unless it is Easter Day.

[Col. 1063B] If two brothers come together to a monastery, one of whom has never been there while the other was there recently, the younger is to imitate whatever the elder considers proper concerning asking permission at the threshold of the door and making the prayer. These matters, stated specifically of one man, are to be observed generally by all monks of our order.

Some matters, however, are specially to be observed by the dean: namely, that after eating he is not to beat any of his household; nor, if it can be arranged otherwise, is he ever to lack the testimony of another brother who continually stays with him. Likewise, if his obedience lies within half a day’s journey, he must return to the monastery every Saturday. For he presumes neither to put on washed clothes nor to shave himself except there. He acquires nothing by cunning; he diligently cultivates the fields and vineyards and tends livestock and beasts of burden. He has nothing hidden away or entrusted to an outsider’s house—something that our predecessors have altogether anathematized.

[Col. 1063C] When the grain and wine have been entirely gathered, the prior must, according to custom, inspect everything in the granary and everything in the cellar. He leaves, in whatever quantity seems appropriate, supplies for the same dean and for arriving guests, and for agricultural work; whatever remains he orders to be brought to the monastery. He does the same at that time in our cells where only six or ten brothers live, if there is such an abundance of goods that more people could be supported: he leaves those brothers sufficient food and clothing, and what is necessary for guests, and orders whatever remains to be brought to the monastery.

[Col. 1063D]

## CHAPTER XIX. The common order for those returning from the road

[Col. 1064A]

* Having set out the order for those travelling, the common order for those returning from the road must not now be omitted. Brothers who come from the road kiss no one within the enclosure of the walls before they have prayed. If, however, they briefly say something necessary outside the cloister, they are not censured for this. If they arrive at midday after the ministers’ meal, they do not enter after the brothers rise. For this reason the entrance is not closed during the ministers’ meal, so that anyone arriving then may be able to enter. Those who return at the time appointed for conversation say only “Bless” at the very entrance of the cloister to those who are sitting there.

[Col. 1064B] On the day on which they return, therefore, they do not receive the Lord’s Body unless they have made confession, since human weakness cannot avoid sinning many times through use, hearing, or even speech. On that same day, after each of the Hours, they make the customary prostrations before and behind, and one of the following collects is said:

“Almighty and eternal God, of our …”

“We beseech you, almighty God …”

“Almighty and eternal God …”

Before these verses, “Save your servants,” which is always first, is said; the second is either “Turn again, O God,” or “Behold, how good,” or “Blessed are those who dwell …” If the collect is said three times or more in their place, it is not to be said for them at Compline, except after the two verses mentioned above and without the salutation:

“Have mercy.”

“Almighty and eternal God.”

* This, however, is not to be said to the lord abbot, nor to a bishop, nor to any abbot or to our prior; rather, the collect is said in the same way as at the other Hours.

No one neglects the blessing on account of the midday meal if he eats with the ministers at the time when None is sung. For, having finished eating, he receives it and then returns to the meal. It should be known, however, that if one of the brothers stationed outside wishes to attend the solemnity of Easter, he must have arrived on Wednesday. If he has happened to neglect this, whoever he may be, when he comes during those three days he does not lack the aforesaid blessing after each completed Hour; but no one offers him a kiss during those same days. If he is one of our professed monks, he must also take care not to leave before the third day during the three feasts—namely, the Nativity of the Lord, Easter, and Pentecost—unless compelled by great necessity; and even then he waits until the chapter has ended.

[Col. 1064C] This too should be known: if some arrive while the convent is not in the choir, and the monastery’s main gate is then closed, they are sprinkled with holy water, first at the cross, then in the choir, and afterward they prostrate themselves lengthwise before Saint Mary, between the choir stalls, if it is such a day; otherwise they must pray by bowing. If they arrive during Chapter, they make the third prayer at the altar situated on the right side of the choir. If they arrive during a Regular Hour, so that they can enter the choir before the *Gloria* of the first psalm, they enter the choir only after being sprinkled; when the Hour is finished, after receiving the blessing, they pray at the cross, if the gate is closed at that time, as stated above, and then at Saint Mary.

If they enter the church after the *Gloria* of the first psalm, [Col. 1065A] for they do not presume to wait outside, they do not ask permission upon reaching the step. After the sprinkling, they make one prayer at the aforesaid altar and must wait there for the blessing; for even those who arrive in this way may not leave the Regular Hour except for bodily necessity. But if they arrive during Compline, they do not pray at the cross. Instead, after making the same prayer at the aforesaid altar, they wait there; after Compline, having received the blessing, they pray at Saint Mary.

Those who arrive in such a way that they can take neither part in the servants’ supper nor eat afterward before the collation must attend the collation; after Compline, having received the blessing, they may then eat. If they cannot arrive during Compline, they do not presume to enter their cell afterward; rather, on the following day they enter in such a way that they receive the prescribed blessing after each Hour.

Those who remain outside for only one night receive no blessing either when they leave or when they return, unless it happens that someone who comes from the road and is going to receive the blessing for those returning leaves again that same day and returns the next day. In that case, the blessing that he would have had on the previous day had he remained is not withheld from him. But if someone is to receive at the same Hour both the blessing for returning and the blessing for departing, when he approaches the steps he asks the superior of the order, by the sign of the cross, for permission to leave; after making the customary prostration or bowing before and behind, he may receive first the blessing for returning and then the blessing for departing. If the priest does not know that he has returned from the road, one of those standing nearby who does know informs him.

[Col. 1065B] Those returning from the road must attend Matins in the choir, unless someone is coming from far away and is burdened by such illness that he is permitted to attend those same Matins outside the choir or at Saint Mary.

## CHAPTER XX. The claustral prior and his assistant

(UD.) The claustral prior is in every respect the vicar of the greater prior. Therefore he sends not only weaker brothers to nearby places for rest, but also stronger brothers to very remote cells, to assist the brothers living there while the lord abbot or prior is far away. Nevertheless, on ordinary days and at the Twelve Lessons, he never approaches to offer or to give the kiss of peace after someone wearing an alb, unless it is his turn in the order. On feasts celebrated in albs, however, when the prior is absent, he is also the first to proceed on each such occasion, except when the lord abbot or prior is singing Mass in the convent: * then he does not in any way allow himself to be first in these matters, unless he is first of all the priors in rank.

Whenever he himself is presiding in the order in such a way that he does not expect either the lord abbot or the prior to arrive in the meantime, he walks last in the procession held on ordinary days. When he comes to Saint Mary, he stands in the left choir, even if his station is in the right. If someone needs to go to the infirmary to rest while the prior is absent, he grants permission; and during the meal of those brothers, just as anyone presiding over the order at that time does, he does not neglect to come there. He speaks briefly and charitably with each, as the time permits. When eating with the ministers, he sits beside the bell.

He is the one who remains continually in the cloister, wherever the lord abbot or prior may go, and who chiefly bears the burden of the entire order. This does not, however, give him a higher rank among the brothers.

[Col. 1065C] To make him more available for this office, the armarius never assigns him anything during the meal or collation. This, however, he does without fail every day: after Compline, immediately after being sprinkled with holy water—unless he himself performed the sprinkling—he withdraws to stand near the church door, so that he may observe each person and see how they bow before the altars and before the priest by whom they are sprinkled.

After everyone has gone out, whether he performed the sprinkling or not, he takes the covered lamp lit by the hebdomadary and, wearing his cap, inspects the whole cloister.
