First he sees whether the door of the guests’ hearing-room is closed; then the almonry; whether anyone is still in front of the cellar, and for what reason; whether the regular kitchen is locked; the refectory; then the novices’ cell and the infirmary, seeing whether the sick have already lain down and how they are, and whether any of them has remained in the church of Saint Mary. (var.) He goes up to the dormitory, carrying with him anything he may happen to find neglected in the cloister. He also examines all the seats of the necessaries.

[Col. 1065D] In winter, when the brothers wait in chapter after supper for the collation, he makes one circuit through all the workshops and offices of the cloister, watching lest anyone who ought then to be sitting in chapter be occupied in idleness. He also makes another circuit during the interval customarily lying between Matins and Lauds. On it he goes around all the beds in the dormitory and in the novices’ cell; from there he proceeds to the door of the refectory, the regular kitchen, the cellar, and the almonry; then to the door of the cloister. From there he goes through the chapterhouse to the infirmary, returns through the hearing-room into the greater church, goes around all the altars and the corners of the church and sacristy, then returns through the choir. Thus, with the lamp turned only toward the young men, he passes through and puts the covered lamp back in its place. If during all these inspections he discovers any negligence, he will report it the following day.

(UD.) He also regularly makes these circuits while fully fulfilling his office. If he has been bled or is burdened by some illness, he assigns this duty to another.

To conclude briefly concerning his office: if the lord abbot is absent, and so is the prior, not only all the obedientiaries who are in the cloister obey his command, but even the deans do whatever may be necessary. It is therefore very necessary that one be appointed who is considered capable of managing so many and such great matters.

* Whether he is presiding over the order or not, as soon as he hears the signal for the collation he must enter chapter, lest, by entering later, he make the convent labor by having to rise. In other respects, although he may lawfully do all the things mentioned above, while the prior remains in the convent he gives no one permission to do or say anything. He is not censured, however, if at that time he speaks, whether on his own initiative or at someone’s request, in the novices’ cell or in other claustral offices about what is necessary.

[Col. 1066A] He himself also has one assistant, who takes his place in each immediate task when he is absent and assists him in every respect when he is present, whenever the prior goes away or remains in the infirmary because of illness. He also has assistants, guardians of the young men, and circatores.

(UD.) When the claustral prior is released from the same obedience, he asks permission for indulgence; the other assistants of obediences, however, ought not to do this according to custom.

## CHAPTER XXI. The circatores

[Note: [Col. 1067D] See *Ordinatio Cluniacensis*, part I, chapter 4.]

[Col. 1067B]

(UD.) It is the duty of the circatores to note every negligence that can in any way occur against the order and to report it in chapter. Therefore they go around the entire cloister not once but many times a day, so that there is neither place nor hour in which any brother who has committed such a thing can feel secure that it will not be detected and made public. They investigate especially when the brothers are occupied with reading, lest someone perhaps not be attentive to it.

* Thus, every day one of them goes around all the altars before Prime, or at another time before Terce; and if he sees more than two obedientiaries with their assistant at any other altar—except on the highest feasts—or if he sees any negligence, he does not fail to report it. They ordinarily make their other circuits immediately after each Hour has ended, except after None, when the brothers are going to drink; after the offering at the conventual Mass; after the Gospel of the greater Mass; at the Office of the Dead; after the three lessons; and also whenever the condition of any place requires it.

These circuits must therefore include the almonry; the area before and within the cellar, up to the threshold of its outer door; up to the threshold of the outer kitchen door; the regular kitchen; the refectory; the novices’ cell; the chamber; the infirmary; the place where people are cooking and where blood is let; the chapel of Saint Mary; the cemetery; the workshop; the scribes; the sacristy; and every place where such work is being carried out.

Whatever worthy of report is seen by these same circatores is reverently disregarded on the spot; but when “Speak in chapter about the order” has been said, it is reported without delay. In these reports, as in all matters, all partiality toward persons must be avoided.

[Col. 1067C] Every day, after the bell has been struck for the meal, one of them also stands before the refectory door until the convent has entered, carefully observing how the brothers conduct themselves at the washing place, whether anyone negligently turns aside anywhere in an unsuitable manner, or comes disorderly in haste at the sound of the bell. Near the end of the meal he likewise goes to the regular kitchen, the cellar, and the novices’ cell, so that, if anyone has gone there without reasonable cause, it may not escape him.

Before “But you …” is said, he returns, noting whether the brothers whom he passes sit with their feet together and conduct themselves regularly in every respect, just as he did when leaving. He makes no sign to anyone there; but if he sees anything contrary to the order, it remains in his memory until the time for reporting it. He does not, however, avoid doing this in the cloister: as he goes around there, he discreetly signals anyone whom he sees sitting with his clothing hanging down to arrange it.

[Col. 1067D] He must know that the offenses of the young men are especially to be noted and called out, since those who offend less are corrected more sharply than the others. At midday he goes around the cloister and checks whether the almonry is locked; from there he proceeds to the novices’ cell and the infirmary, and at that hour he ascends to the dormitory as quickly as he can. No one enters the infirmary while the sick are eating; rather, from the doorway he investigates, as far as possible, how they are. Likewise, standing inside the offices adjoining the cloister, he can look outside to see whether anything blameworthy is being done there by any brother.

On every feast celebrated in copes or albs, one of them, after the Gospel, lays aside his fanon for the moment in the place of his station, leaves his cope in the vestiar­y, and makes the customary circuit. When it is finished, he puts it on again and returns to the choir.

Although they must note every negligence with the utmost care, they must not enlarge upon it in words but report it simply—unless some careless person wishes to defend himself carelessly; such a person is not spared in the report until the truth itself has been examined. They must always take care, when they see brothers conversing at an unsuitable hour, not to eavesdrop on whether they are speaking secretly, nor to disturb them by any sign. If the brothers have received permission to converse, they immediately indicate this to the circator by words and signs.

[Col. 1068A] The obedientiaries who cannot avoid occasionally speaking about their obediences while others are silent, though at a suitable time and place—namely, before the cellar—do not become silent merely because they see one of the circatores approaching, nor do they tell him what their conversation is about, since in such a place they ought to be speaking about nothing other than their obediences. It is also their duty to call the superior of the order to the refectory if they see him lingering too long after the first course has been served.

On the Monday of the first week of Lent, after the distribution of the books, they all ask permission, accusing themselves of not having fulfilled the office of circation as they ought. If one of them is prevented for some reason from fulfilling that same obedience, he is released from it, and another is temporarily substituted in his place.

## CHAPTER XXII. The young men and their guardians

* A brother who is of such an age that he still needs guardianship, even if he has voluntarily renounced the world and is of the best reputation, will nevertheless by no means be without guardianship. (UD. var.) For this reason, a layman is not received into the cloister unless he is of such advanced age that he can be without a guardian; nor is a schoolboy received. If circumstances require that entry cannot in any way be denied him, he is sent to some cell until he reaches an age capable of understanding.

The same applies especially to those who have been brought up in the monastery: if they do not wish to be men in their conduct, their manly age will not benefit them by releasing them from guardianship. For one who has been placed under guardianship, his bed in the dormitory is first situated near the bed of his guardian. Without the guardian he never approaches or leaves it.

[Col. 1068B] At night, wherever he may go, and also before Compline if he is later than usual, or after the sound of the bell if it is very early, and also when summoned, if he needs it—as often happens in winter—he carries a lantern before him. The guardian sees to it that he always has a candle. In the refectory he extinguishes it and places it on the footstool beneath his feet. The young men must always be seated interspersed in such a way that between two young men two other brothers sit, so that, if one should happen to leave, the other remains.

If the guardian leads him to the necessaries, after the guardian himself has risen he keeps continual but discreet watch over him, even though the lantern is standing before him. If he needs to rise during the night, he wakes his guardian by touching his pillow or some part of his covering. He himself lights the lantern and goes to the necessaries; it is not extinguished by the guardian until he has lain down again.

At other times the young man himself always lights and extinguishes it, except after Compline and after Matins. Then it is to be lit by the guardian and, when the young man lies down again to sleep, extinguished once more. If the guardian leads him to the church or the refectory, he does not leave him until he is in the presence of the convent. If he has been assigned to the kitchen, he does not come there before the sound of the bell.

[Col. 1068C] He must carry out this duty with no one other than his guardian. The guardian must carefully guard him there and everywhere, and continually report his negligences; for whatever he does wrong in the guardian’s presence is entirely attributed to the guardian if he does not call him to account for it. At the three prayers properly made before Matins, at those made before Prime or before Terce, and at those made after Compline, and also at the litany after Prime, they are never separated from one another. During the litany, the one under guardianship lies to the guardian’s left.

If the young man stands in one choir and the guardian in the other, the young man must keep watch at the guardian’s vigil when we have a dead person.

When they proceed to the holy water, Communion, or a procession, if they have different ranks, the one under guardianship moves up or down, while the guardian does not change his own order, unless this is on account of someone who has been placed last because of some offense. If someone is caught in such an offense, even though in every respect he has the same rank as the person described above as being last, he is nevertheless never bound by the penalty of a more serious fault. Instead, as soon as he has committed such a thing, he is corrected with harsh and excessive beatings. Therefore he must never voluntarily take the scourging secretly upon himself.

[Col. 1069A] In every procession held around or outside the cloister, if his guardian is a lay brother, the young man is lent to someone literate, especially for the singing, just as the man who has one of his guardians from the superiors and who himself is of lower rank is to be commended. If a deacon or subdeacon is placed under guardianship and something occurs that prevents him from reading at Mass, he does not address anyone like himself by word or sign so that the person may read in his place. Instead, he makes the matter known to his guardian, with the testimony of his guardian, so that the guardian may speak to a brother of the same order about taking his turn at reading. But if he does not wish to do this at that time, he informs the armarius early enough for the latter to arrange in good time whom to assign the task of reading.

The one who is to read is led by his guardian to the vestiar­y and clothed with the assistance of the servants. The guardian also entrusts him to one of those serving there until, after completing his duty, he removes his clothing again.

Each such young man, if—as the saying goes—he wishes to take care for his own back, must take the greatest care everywhere that they do not stand or sit together without an intermediary, paint one another (*pingant*), or touch one another’s clothing in any way. Neither is one ever to presume to make any sign to another young man, whether under guardianship or not, even with a glance of the eyes, or to smile at him, or to pretend any familiarity with him, or even to sit in such a way that one can look at the other with their faces turned toward each other. For these and similar things, each person reports the other according to custom.

[Col. 1069B] He also reports anyone who shows him any familiarity or speaks with him while his guardian is not listening. He reports his guardian only for this: if the guardian leaves him without guardianship, or if he exercises toward him a severity where he ought to show humanity.

Each must take care that, in the cloister, while carrying tablets granted to him for writing, he cannot be found by a passing circator, who examines those tablets, to have written anything of such a sort that he deserves to be reported. It should also be known that none of them is to eat meat, unless he is so ill that it is permitted; nor is he to bathe or have blood let.

If bloodletting is granted to someone because of illness, at the next Hour, after receiving permission to have blood let by the sign, he withdraws to the smaller choir and remains there until the third day. Nevertheless, by custom he does not fail to attend the three prayers after Compline and the nighttime interval in the greater choir. At Saint Mary he sits in his place without wearing a cap, and, as far as he can, merely keeps his eyes away from the light.

If at another time he becomes so ill that he cannot remain for Matins, he likewise seeks permission by himself and goes to the aforesaid choir; nevertheless, on the following day he does not ask permission for this reason. If he has been assigned a responsory that night, he sings it in the greater choir and immediately returns; nevertheless, he never sings the fourth or eighth responsory unless they are short. If illness overtakes him so severely that he cannot attend the convent, he is then ordered to go to the infirmary, where he is guarded no less diligently than if he were in the convent, and there too he carries a lantern.

There are also some young men who have been released from stricter guardianship, and others who have never been placed under guardianship but are nevertheless subjected, on suspicion arising from youth—which sometimes deserves little credence—to lesser guardianship. Their condition is that they never presume to go outside the convent without a guardian, nor dare to ascend to the dormitory before Matins without lanterns.

[Col. 1070A] For this sole purpose, as many lanterns are to be placed before the altar near the church door by the chamberlain, and candles by the sacristan, as may suffice for this need. Such young men do not have permanent guardians; but whenever one of them has to leave the convent, he signals someone suitable and available for the purpose, and that person does not refuse to follow him immediately.

It should be known that no young man, whether under guardianship or not, is permitted to go alone to or return alone from any cell without another brother of more advanced age, since it would be highly conspicuous if he alone received the blessing. He must also know that, if he is still sent out from guardianship or from the choir stalls, he is not released from guardianship upon his return, even if he has remained somewhere for ten years; rather, he returns again either to guardianship or to the choir stalls.

Whoever is sent to either kind of guardianship because of some offense returns immediately, once released from it, to the wall, if he previously had a station there. The young man through whom the prior distributes his charitable portion in the refectory carries to the table and brings back his bread and his allotted portion with a spoon. If he wishes to come to confession, his guardian permits him to go to the confessor; after confession, the confessor leads him back to the guardian, who is waiting for him near the entrance of the chapterhouse.

If, God forbid, the workshops of the cloister catch fire, the young men do not run with the others to extinguish it. Meanwhile, with their guardians, they prostrate themselves in the choir to sing the litany.

It should be noted that none of them enters a seat situated beyond the seat of the lord abbot, except at the time when the priors stand facing the altar. Even then, none of them may stand in a seat at the altar unless he is wearing an alb.

At Vespers and Matins, or at the Office of All Saints, they impose the antiphons upon the psalms and the hymns; at the Office of the Dead they impose the antiphons and sing the short responsories.

Meanwhile, while crowns are being assigned to the novices in the choir, the young man appointed for the week imposes the antiphon “You are God who …” and leads the litany before Mass. The verses are pronounced entirely by these young men if there are enough of them; otherwise they are said both by other young men and by these. They also begin the antiphons for the suffrages of the saints; then, whenever an antiphon has been imposed, they must stand until the priest says “Let us pray.” Moreover, whenever the antiphons at Matins are to be imposed by the seniors, if one of them happens to omit an antiphon, one of these young men immediately imposes it.

[Col. 1071A]

## CHAPTER XXIII. The armarius

(UD.) The precentor, who is also the armarius, has obtained the name *armarius* because the library, which is also called the *armarium*, is customarily in his charge. * This is an obedience that, by custom, no one deserves unless he has been brought up for it, or unless he is otherwise suitable for this office. Conversely, those obediences that I mentioned above and still intend to mention are not deserved except by men already of mature age, or by clerics, and by those who, having come from another monastery and professed again among us, have for some time lived among us with sufficiently exemplary conduct.

[Col. 1071B] (UD.) This official, of whom we are speaking, properly has one assistant, who also sings for the boys, if they are present, and performs the brief offices of the litany, the responsory, and the other services. No one other than he assigns the brothers’ names, unless he himself should wish his second to do so and that second possesses the skill and judgment for this work.

To touch briefly on his continual occupation: the entire ordering of divine service in the church depends on no one so much as on him. In this matter he has no other master than the one he has outside the church, and everyone must always obey him in such matters. If, however, he presumes against custom or neglects something, this is entirely disregarded for the moment, until it is reported in chapter.

[Col. 1071C] (var.) He imposes the antiphon at the singing of the Gospel, at Vespers, and at Matins, except that, in his absence, the lord abbot imposes it at the Twelve Lessons. * If he has imposed them incorrectly, or not quite properly—that is, if he has sung them incorrectly—either of the brothers standing beside him may admonish him in a low voice in order to correct him. (var.) If he makes a mistake in taking up a psalm, any knowledgeable person standing in the same choir assists him. If there is an error in a tone, no one’s skill takes precedence over his, since everyone is paying attention chiefly to him and following him.

(UD.) As long as the lord abbot is in the convent, the armarius does not assign himself to any lesson or responsory, so that, if the abbot should happen not to read, the armarius may read in his place. * When the lord abbot is absent, he may assign himself to a lesson or responsory. He is never assigned to any other service, except the kitchen duty and the service of the three poor men; at the collation he may also read, if he wishes.

(UD.) He alone is not censured if he names an antiphon or responsory without a book, assigning some brother to sing it. * He also imposes all the verses of the offering at the greater Mass. At the imposition of each of them, at the Twelve Lessons he makes the customary prostration before and behind, unless he is facing east; then he merely bows, as on ordinary days, wherever in the choir his station may be.

He alone also imposes only the *Alleluia* at Mass on ordinary days during Eastertide. He never imposes a hymn except at the Twelve Lessons, and then only if the hebdomadary is standing in the same choir.

[Col. 1072A] However quietly someone may be singing, no one else dares to raise his voice above it. * He must never fail, when something is being sung too quietly, or too quickly or too slowly, wherever or whenever this occurs, immediately to indicate by hand to the brothers whatever must be corrected in the singing. Although this may lawfully be done, he must never do it except with great reverence, nor presume to do so from one choir to the other; rather, if necessary, he should approach more closely.

(UD.) He should also know that no divine office is celebrated, either inside or outside the church, at which he or his deputy is not present. Every day, at the appropriate hour, he hears the reading of the boy or young man who is to read it in Chapter on the following day, [Col. 1073B]—(var.) and also the readings to be read at Matins during Lent after Sext, but in summer after None; or, if there is only one meal, after dinner. * If on some occasion the shortness of time does not allow him to hear it after None or after dinner, he hears it in the vestiar y while Vespers is being rung, provided that God is not being sung to the ears at that moment. After Vespers, however, he never does so, unless perhaps necessity requires it on account of someone less learned. (UD.) He must also hear the reading which the lord abbot is to read; but where and when this is done is left to the abbot’s discretion.

When the principal morning Mass is to be sung, after the priest has vested with the other ministers, the armarius is never absent by custom: first, so that he may see [Col. 1073C] whether all those who are to serve are present, and indicate anything that needs to be indicated. (var.) He does likewise whenever, after Matins, the Gospel is to be sung, or whenever those who are to sing the invitatory are vested in albs or copes. He is the chief organizer of the whole matter.

If a sick brother is to be anointed with the oil of the sick, or if he has died and is to be carried out for burial, or if someone brought from outside is to be received, it is his responsibility to determine which priest is to vest, how the anointing is to be performed, how the Lord’s body is to be brought, how Communion is to be administered, and which collects the prior is to say over the deceased; also what is to be done while the body is washed and vested and before it is brought into the church, what is to be sung, how the tomb is to be blessed within the canon of the morning Mass, and how the burial is to be carried out. In all these matters he is to be the principal guide.

He himself receives from the prior the arriving brief notices concerning our deceased brothers, writes their names in the martyrology, and distributes the other written notices among brothers travelling through the various provinces. Nor does he forget the Masses for any brother who dies, since, according to the proper arrangement, they are entrusted to six brothers, thirty Masses in all. He must also lend the morning-service books to the doorkeeper and the almoner, and after the death of guests and pilgrims—for those who fall ill among us are attended not by him but by the secular priest—he is to ensure that they receive Communion.

At all processions nothing whatever is sung except what he himself has appointed. On the three Rogation days he informs the brothers suitable for assigning the antiphons, and distributes to them the books in which those same antiphons are written. (var.) Finally, whenever anything of this kind, as though new, arises to be done, he must be especially mindful and diligent: when new beans, new bread, or must is to be blessed in the refectory; when such a person arrives that a reading must first be recited before and after he is received; when manual work has been completed; or when the crown or beard of some novice is to be shaved. In each of these matters and similar ones, he must take care that there is no negligence either concerning the person or concerning what the person is to say.

## CHAPTER XXIV. When, as they say, the choir is to be directed by him himself

* On all feasts celebrated in albs, and also on Holy Saturday, Easter, Pentecost, and Palm Sunday, the armarius is customarily to direct the choir, but on feasts in albs he does so alone, except on the Purification of Saint Mary. On the days of those two Saturdays, however, he joins to himself the brother who sings the litany with him. In the psalms he has as many assistants as he needs, assigning each of them a cope himself.

At the Nativity of the Lord, for the first two Masses, two brothers who are to preside over the choir are to be designated according to his wishes; he voluntarily joins himself to them in the middle. UD. At the Nativity itself, and at Easter and Pentecost, for the office of the principal Mass and for directing the choir, he is accompanied by two of the better singers who appear suitable for this purpose. Yet they do not presume to come forward on their own unless he has given them copes with his own hand. * These copes are always prepared at the head of the forma by the chief sacristan, from among the better ones, before Terce—or, if a procession is held, after it. He does not distribute them beforehand, however, until Benedicamus Domino has been said for the approaching hour; and after receiving them they do not put them on until they reach the station.

When the armarius has entrusted the bell which he rings to another to ring, he puts on his own cope and joins them. If any one of them wishes to leave, for another reason, after the appointed chant has been sung with the signal for Mass, he seeks permission to leave with the signal for departure from the person then directing the order. He then returns to his former place and, having indicated his departure to the armarius by the signal, leaves from that place after bowing forward and backward. If he is wearing one of the better copes, he removes it there and places it on the chancel rail; but if it is one of the ordinary copes, he leaves still wearing it, removes it in the vest iary, and folds it.

(var.) If necessary, he may change the brothers at his sides from right to left or from left to right. The thurible is first brought to him by a conversus, unless the prior or some other superior person is present. In all other respects, whatever his rank, the aforesaid armarius does not lose his precedence.

If he wishes to receive Communion, he is last at the kiss of peace but first after the subdeacon at Communion. As for his deputies, if one wishes to communicate, he approaches in his proper order merely at the armarius’s nod, provided that he knows that the choir is to communicate that day. If not, after seeking permission from the prior, he likewise approaches only at the armarius’s nod, while the others who remain sing Agnus Dei and the Communion during the distribution of the peace; verses from the Psalms may be added if necessary.

None of those designated for the Gradual or the Alleluia enters among them, except those to whom the armarius gives the signal by handing them booklets. The number of singers on each side must also vary according to the solemnity of the feast: on a feast, two sing the Graduals and three the Alleluias; in copes, three Graduals and four Alleluias; but on the principal feasts the armarius appoints as many as he wishes on each side, though he orders more Alleluias than Graduals to be sung.

UD. He informs the lord abbot and every priest with what tone he is to begin Gloria in excelsis, and, if necessary, the deacon with the tone for Ite, missa est. (var.) At the end of Mass he is the first to remove his cope and to bow forward and backward; he takes down the cords of the signals, and when Deo gratias has been said he rings the bell, as he did before Mass, after Deo gratias, when the familiar psalms have been completed.

[Note: [Col. 1075D] The familiar psalms are those which accompany the Hours in all twelve lessons. Their burdensome—and, indeed, to many people, tiresome—multiplicity was gradually brought about for many reasons; because it weighed upon many, it was altered in this respect at the petition of many and of almost the entire community. These are the words of Peter, abbot of Cluny, in the Statutes of Cluny, chapter 21.]

But if it is Sunday, he waits until the reader at table has almost received the blessing. During the Mass at which he directs the choir, whether alone or with several others, he observes the same manner of bowing and rising as the hebdomadary cantor.

* Now that the order which he must observe in the office of Mass on feasts has been set out, it must also be explained how, amid differing degrees of solemnity, he is to designate the brothers on the board for the vigils of Matins.

## CHAPTER XXV. How he is to designate the brothers for each feast

* Thus, on feasts in albs, he designates one brother for each responsory; for the fourth and eighth, two, with the lord abbot added at the eighth if he is present; for the twelfth, three. In copes likewise he designates one brother for each responsory, but for the fourth and eighth three with the lord abbot, for the eighth four if he is present, and for the twelfth four.

On the principal feasts, however, he designates two brothers for each responsory; for the fourth, four; for the seventh, three; for the eighth, five; for the eleventh, three; and for the twelfth, six or more. He must also designate priests in such a way that no one suitable for this office excuses himself from the week of the principal Mass on account of some obedience, except the cellarer, the infirmarian, and the chaplain of Saint Mary. For no one, whatever dignity he possessed before his conversion, is entirely released from any office to be performed in the church or outside the church if he is able to perform it, unless he has earned such release by previously obtaining leave in Chapter.

Even the armarius is not permitted to release anyone on his own from any office announced in Chapter for Saturday, except from the readings of the servants, from the Graduals, or from the responsories. Sometimes, however, in the aforementioned brief designation [Note: [Col. 1076D] Breviatio, inbreviatio, is a brief notation, or sheet, on which the ministers of the altar were designated; see an example in Guido, book 2.] he observes not the order of persons but rather that of the time and the character of the feasts. When such a designation is to be made, it is not made on the daily board but on another, larger board specifically assigned to feasts.

UD. We also customarily make another useful and not unhelpful designation. Since the armarius is otherwise so occupied, he entrusts his assistant with recording in order all those who have served in the kitchen, so that through forgetfulness no one is burdened with that duty more frequently than another.

* Since the order in which the brothers are to be designated for the nocturnal office has been written down, it is also necessary to know who are to sing the responsories of each feast at Vespers and Matins. On feasts in albs, two, one of them being the hebdomadary; in copes, two together with the hebdomadary, making three. On the principal feasts, at First Vespers four, but at Matins or Second Vespers three.

Each of these also says Benedicamus Domino at each feast. They must first be provided for by the armarius at the appropriate hour and warned beforehand what they are to sing. It must be his responsibility that, just as the feasts differ in excellence according to their solemnity, so he designates different brothers for singing and reading according to the suitability of each person’s age and learning. He must observe this not only on the feasts mentioned above but also in the other twelve lessons: thus, for the fourth lesson he should designate an older brother, even if he holds a lower place in the order, and for the eighth an older man standing in a higher place.

Likewise, he must not neglect to ensure that, when two or three of them sing some responsories together, at least one of them is more advanced in age; and when there are four or more, several older men are interspersed among them.

If twelve lessons fall on the Monday of the first week of Lent, he arranges that first the Gospel reading and then the reading from the Rule be recited in Chapter, with Tu autem pronounced at the end of each. Two sermons are also given then, the first on the feast and the following one on Lent.

Whether this occurs on a feast day or another day, after the person then directing the order has said, “Speak according to the order,” he, seated in his place, recites the names of the brothers and the books distributed to them in the previous year for reading through. Having brought these books with them to Chapter, they all place them, at the voice of the reciter, on the carpet spread out for the purpose. The armarius then distributes the books to be read through in the coming year, first to the person directing the order, whom he chooses, and then to the others on his right; his assistant distributes them on the other side to each person who comes from his place to receive one. They take care, however, not to give anyone a psalter, hymnal, or other book with neumes.

After this distribution has been made, the two sit again on their respective sides and write down briefly the names of the brothers against the individual books. Meanwhile, the brothers who did not read through their books in the preceding year ask pardon for this. Anyone who was absent while the books were being distributed is to be entered later against the book he receives from the armarius. Anyone who wishes may exchange his book with another person’s. If he reads through that book, after the year has passed he does not ask pardon, because he did not read through the book he received from the armarius.

He may lend books outside without permission, but not without security.

[Note: [Col. 1077] Vadimonium, vadium, wadium: pledge, security, surety.]

Whenever a leap year occurs, he divides the reading from the martyrology so that half is read on one day and half on the other. On Maundy Thursday he alone has only the hosts consecrated; on the following day he alone draws new fire from the crystal. On Good Friday, when he sees that the cross has almost been venerated, he hastens to arrange the procession in the vest iary, so that the Lord’s body may be carried from the altar where it was placed the previous day back to the principal altar.

This is done as follows. First two priests vested in albs and fanons proceed with candlesticks, while a third proceeds with the thurible—for no conversus admits himself to this office. Two other priests vested in chasubles follow them, with the hebdomadary priest following. One of the latter carries a chalice with water and unconsecrated wine; the other carries nothing, but as soon as they arrive there, he covers the Lord’s body with a disk and, after it has been incensed by the hebdomadary, carries it in the dish in which it is stored to the principal altar.

That altar, having shortly beforehand been folded (?) by the sacristan, is immediately covered by him; after the corporal has been spread over it by the priest, and the paten with the Lord’s body placed on top, the chalice is also placed there, as is customary. The deacon and priest do not take part in this office, because the priests mentioned above perform their role in every respect. Those who hold the candlesticks and thurible, standing before the altar, do not leave until they know that everyone has received Communion.

In everything, therefore, that the aforesaid armarius does or arranges, he takes the greatest care not to presume anything contrary to custom. To state some points explicitly: he is no more permitted than the others to go beyond the cloister precincts for any reason, nor may he ever speak during the time of silence except with permission. He does not allow anyone to enter the room where the books are kept, except to bring in or take back something for a reasonable purpose, or to do there some other necessary task belonging to that person’s obedience. He writes nothing there, reads nothing, and sings nothing. He does not confer a single word there with anyone except for an unavoidable reason that cannot be communicated by signs. His deputy must not come there at all unless instructed by him, and then only when he is carrying out the absent armarius’s duties in every respect.

Between the two Masses, if he can be absent without detriment to the choir, and after the cymbal has been struck at the hour of the meal, provided that he reaches the table in good time, he may write in the cloister or perform some similarly necessary task. Some others too are permitted to sit there after the cymbal has been struck if they have written something or done some other necessary and useful task. They are not, however, permitted to sit there during any regular Hour; as soon as they hear the signal, they hasten with the others to the work of the Lord.

## CHAPTER XXVI. On the scribes

There are also other scribes who are instructed to sit continually in the chapels for writing and to sing the regular Hours there, except on feasts that are observed as holidays, and at First Vespers, Terce, and the Mass of those feasts which are celebrated without a feria. They do not neglect to come to Chapter and Collation, nor to the office for the dead, which is celebrated with great solemnity.

If, whether present or absent, they hear the sound of the board being struck for something that must immediately be done . . . . they attend until the end of the three lessons, and on ordinary days they attend the procession and the following Mass until after the Gospel. In winter, after the litany has ended, they do not change for Matins until they hear the signal by which the brothers are summoned to wash. After changing then, and completing the other things that follow, they return to their usual work until, after three prayers have been said, the signal is sounded for Terce; then they too, after the appointed prayer, do not delay to sing that Hour.

If one of them wishes to sing privately after the Gospel of the principal Mass, he must obtain permission in the choir from the director of the order. If any of them has undergone bloodletting, he must, by custom, attend the choir on the third day at Prime, or at Terce if it is another time.

## CHAPTER XXVII. On the church custodian

[Col. 1078C] (UD.) The apocrisiarius, who guards the church treasury and in whose hands is everything offered by the people at the altars, must be a priest. So that he may be able to fulfill his office worthily, the assistance of several brothers is assigned to him.

* Among them there is one more prominent brother who acts in his place when he is absent. The apocrisiarius may therefore speak during the time of silence about what is necessary for his obedience with any of these brothers, although he is by no means permitted at that time to speak communally with everyone, except on Saturday—unless the shortness of the time or some other necessity prevents this. For every Saturday he must assemble them together and instruct them in the uses of the church, and especially entrust the following week to one of them.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. On the church doorkeeper

* The church door is specially entrusted to one man, who always closes and opens it at the proper time. A man is chosen for this with care who is serious in character and not quick to laughter, lest those entering or leaving detect any frivolity in him at that place.

UD. He is strictly forbidden, whenever he closes or opens the door, to extend even a foot beyond it for any reason. Hence, if it should ever happen * that a guest remains in the church during Chapter, or if it is a feast on which reliquaries are hung around the altar, he remains there; meanwhile he is not forbidden to read.

[Col. 1079A] [Note: [Col. 1079D] Philacteria: little chests or cases in which the holy relics are kept.]

His bed is placed before the sacristy, beside the door through which one enters the lower part of the church on the left side of the apse.

[Note: [Col. 1079D] ἀψίς, apsis: a vault or arch.]

UD. He alone, apart from the others, is charged every Saturday to scrape clean the basins and the dishes of the candlesticks in which the candles burn, so that nothing remains from the dripping wax. With similar care he first cleans the entire pavement around the principal altar after pouring water over it, and sweeps the pavement of the other altars clean with a broom.

(var.) He also closes and opens the church doors in various ways at different times. Before Matins, after the fifteen or thirty psalms have been completed, he always opens them, both in winter and in summer. In winter, however, after the two nocturns have ended and before the office for the dead, which is sung at night, he always closes them; they remain closed until the bell is rung before Terce. After the morning Mass has ended he closes them, and they remain closed until after Sext; then they are opened, and after Mass has ended they are closed until Vespers. After regular Vespers they are closed and remain so until Matins.

In summer, therefore, when they are closed immediately after regular Matins, they are opened at Prime and remain open until the morning Mass has ended. They are then closed and opened for Mass; afterward they are shut until Vespers. When Vespers has ended, they are completely closed until Matins.

During Lent, on ordinary days, they are closed after the morning Mass until Vespers has ended. At the twelve lessons, both in winter and summer, they are opened at the bell that sounds after Compline. He nevertheless acts diligently so that, if anyone strikes them from early morning until after Compline, he is ready to open them, whether he himself hears it or learns of it from someone else.

* He also slams them shut against each other with such force that the community, if it is in the choir, can hear it. To be better suited to this office, while the community remains in the church he too remains in the lesser choir.

## CHAPTER XXIX. On the church hebdomadary

(UD.) The others take their weekly turns, beginning Matins on each Sunday night in rotation, in the manner prescribed for them by the sacristan; and each must carefully attend to what he is to do during the week.

* First, as I said, for Matins, after the clock has struck and the aforesaid sacristan has begun to ring the bell, he takes it from his hand and rings it until he sees the boy or young man assigned for this purpose enter the choir with a lantern. Meanwhile, while another rings the bell in his place, he may, if necessary, go up to the dormitory and, on returning, wash his hands at the lavatory. He must always do this at the twelve lessons as well.

[Col. 1080A] UD. After three prayers have been said, he rings one of the larger bells until the psalm Laetatus sum. (var.) Second, he rings the smaller signal for a short while at Requiem aeternam, until the Lord’s Prayer with the collect has ended. Third, from Kyrie eleison until the Lord’s Prayer with the collect has likewise ended. Fourth, after the collect, all the bells are rung at Per Dominum; but if it is an ordinary day, two are rung at Kyrie eleison.

(var.) At the final division of the Songs of Ascents, before the end of the psalm Memento—or, if thirty are recited, at Laudate Dominum de caelis—he lights the two candles fixed to candlesticks before the altar and a third behind the altar.

* If at times on ordinary days he does not return in good time to ring after lighting the candles, one of his associates rings it. Three candles hang behind the principal altar; the middle one—the one mentioned above—is lit every day for Matins and Vespers, and at the twelve lessons for Mass. On feasts in albs, two are lit for Matins and three for the Gospel; all are lit together for Mass and for both Vespers. On any more eminent feasts they are likewise to be lit for both Vespers and Matins, but extinguished at the Gloria of the eighth responsory. At that point twenty-four candles placed around the upper circuit of the altar are lit.

For Mass those three are to be lit, but five of these are around the altar on the eastern side. Likewise, for the readings he ensures that the light with which the reading is to be done is always brought at the last psalm of Matins, at the time when the reader goes to the step, bowing forward and backward at the Gloria of that psalm, and goes to the lectern, so that he himself does not encounter the reader while departing.

(UD.) Thus, at the ninth lesson, which is from the Gospel, in the place where the homilist is named, he also lights a third candle before the altar. When the priest is about to say the collect, he provides and brings him a light as well, at the twelve lessons, at the octaves, and in similar prayers, when they are almost finished. * On those days when psalms follow the prayers, he does this during the psalm Inclina; in Advent and Lent, before the prayers.

The service book lies continually beneath the form before the priest, placed there by the aforesaid brother, so that he may have it close at hand, unless someone takes it away to the tomb. He takes care, however, that the question book is not missing at its proper time; otherwise he will not escape a reprimand.

But if that priest, either because of a feast does not stand in his place at Matins and Vespers, or asks another to perform his duty, the hebdomadary brings and returns the same book with a light to whichever priest is serving in those turns.

Immediately after Benedicamus Domino, if no antiphon of a feast follows and no blessing is received from anyone, after extinguishing all the candles around the altar, he relights the one that had previously been burning in the basin, so that it may burn by day and night, unless it is extinguished because of other candles that have been lit. He also lights the one fixed to the candlestick and places it above the step, so that it may be carried in the procession customarily made to Saint Mary or the Holy Cross.

[Col. 1080D] [Note: [Col. 1080D] A concha is a concave candlestick, usually suspended by a rope or small chains. See the index of foreign terms.]

It must nevertheless be understood that the two candlesticks are never to be brought there unless the forms are covered with carpets. They are always to be placed before the altar of Saint Mary.

* For the Holy Cross he goes ahead of the community, so that he may fasten to the columns of the basilica as many burning candles as suffice; (UD. var.) they are to continue burning until the community has departed.

For Saint Mary, whenever a procession is made there, he lights as many lights as are necessary, including one of the three that hang in the Chapter—the one nearest the doors of that church. He also lights, on feasts celebrated in copes, three candles before the principal altar in the greater church at each Hour, except Compline.

When dawn appears, the priests begin to sing private Masses. For these the same hebdomadary, immediately after Benedicamus Domino, first lighting the aforesaid lights at Saint Mary or the Cross, * then, after combing his head and washing his hands, provides wine and water, so that they are not lacking for the brother assigned to prepare the sacrifice after he too has combed his head and washed his hands at the same time.

The same brother, who must be a priest or deacon each day except on Good Friday and Holy Saturday after Matins, or in winter during the litany before Chapter, and before the Gospel of the principal Mass, briefly washes all the chalices belonging to the private Masses. He prepares them for the sacrifice by placing hosts upon them and pouring in wine and water, so that when the priests first approach they find everything ready.

This same man carefully washes them every Wednesday and Saturday, whatever the day may be—in the case of feasts after Matins, and on ordinary days after the Gospel of the first Mass—with his fingers inserted inside them. Every day before the hour of dinner, when no further Mass is to be sung, he examines them and carefully checks whether anything of the Lord’s body adheres to them. If anything is found, he himself or another at his nod immediately consumes it.

He also examines the missal books, the priestly vestments belonging to those chalices, and the wine with the water; he pours the contents of the aforementioned cruets back into the larger vessels.

Before undertaking this office, however, the aforesaid hebdomadary unlocks the armarium, which has three compartments. In the upper compartment the aforementioned chalices are stored, with the corporals placed above them; UD. in the middle are the hosts and candles, without which no Mass is to be sung; in the lower compartment are the larger and smaller cruets—the larger for wine, the smaller for water—and the amphora in which wine brought from the cellar is kept.

* There is also another small cabinet in which the missal books belonging to the aforesaid chalices are kept together with the priestly vestments. Outside, two further cruets are to be filled; from them as much water as must be mixed into the sacrifice is poured. The amphora from which hands are washed is kept separately.

[Col. 1082A] The other is placed in a recess near the armarium in which the chalices and the other aforesaid utensils are kept. At dawn the smaller cruets, filled with water by the aforesaid brother, are placed in the same recess and left there until the private Masses have been completely celebrated. They are not carried out except as much as is needed for the Masses; afterward they are returned to the wine cruets.

(UD. var.) The wine from which the sacrifice is to be taken is kept in the cellar in a sealed cup. Whenever the hebdomadary approaches it, he carefully washes not only his hands but also the little spout and the bottom of the vessel around the spout before taking any of the wine. Any wine remaining in the greater church or at Saint Mary he carries back to the cellar on the following day, so that it may be mixed with vinegar for the wine steward.

If it is the time when Prime is sung with the beginning of that same day, he properly puts on his daytime shoes for the familiar psalms, washes his hands and face, and returns to the litany with the larger amphora full of water before it has completely ended. After only the names of the saints have been recited, he rises, as does the frequently mentioned brother, and hastens to bring wine and water.

On such a day he does not uncover the altar board before ringing the bell by which the signal is given to the brothers to prepare themselves; in summer, or whenever there are two meals, he does so before Prime. Conversely, for Mass, when the litany precedes it in its proper place, or, if it is the familiar psalms, whatever the day may be, he covers it. On the two Sundays in albs, he gives a signal so that they may perform their duty in this matter.

After Mass it is uncovered and left so until after Vespers. At the vigils of the principal feasts it is not uncovered for Mass. On all feasts celebrated in copes, however, after the covering of that altar has been removed, the sacristan places a pall over it for Mass, and it is left there until after Compline.

## CHAPTER XXX. How he is to ring the bells for each Hour and what other duties he performs

(UD.) He is diligent to ring the signals for each Hour at the proper time, but he presumes nothing unless ordered by a superior and according to what has been established by custom.

When the brothers wash their hands before Terce or before None, he stands or sits below near the church door. When he sees that the boy or young man, at whose entrance the bell is customarily released for Matins, has washed, he does not delay to ring the signal.

After three prayers have been said—or, if it is before None, one—he rings the larger bell. At Sext, as soon as he knows that those who have undergone bloodletting have eaten, he rings; if they are absent, he does not presume to ring unless ordered. He observes the same rule afterward, although that interval must be very short. It will last no longer than the time needed for the priest and the others who are to serve at the principal Mass to wash themselves, so that they may be ready to vest.

But if the principal Mass follows Sext, he does not undertake the ringing until he sees that the kitchen servants, having already received the mixed drink, have returned; and he prolongs that ringing until he knows that almost everyone has arrived. He observes the same practice concerning None: he sits below in the church near the door, unless it is a universal fast. If it is, after the ministers remove their vestments, he rings after a short interval.

He also observes that from the feast of Saint Luke the Evangelist until the Purification of Saint Mary, whenever there are two meals, he rings None immediately after dinner, when the verse has ended, because then we do not wait for the servants with it, nor return to the refectory before Vespers to drink.

On ordinary days, every day after Chapter, shortly before Terce—if, that is, Terce immediately follows—he rings the bell by which he warns the priest and the other ministers to prepare themselves for vesting.

Whenever a barefoot procession is to be held, after the signal has been given at Per Dominum, the brothers are informed to rise in summer and, at other times, to remove their footwear. He places the cross upon the altar and the water upon the step, so that, when the collect said by the priest while prostrate is almost finished, the bearers may take them up there.

In summer also, whenever the brothers eat only once, they are to be awakened at midday by the larger signal.

For both Masses he provides whatever is needed, and first washes the chalice with which the priest is to offer, after the Introit.

UD. There are two chalices: the smaller for the morning Mass and the larger for the public Mass. At the twelve lessons, since an offering is made at Mass by only one choir, he brings for this purpose only one paten and one cruet with wine. After the Gospel has been read, he gives them into the hands of the first person approaching, so that he may offer.

At the principal Mass, however, the prior signals to one man—namely, the cloister prior—to offer on his behalf. If the feast is celebrated in copes or albs, no one offers except the armarius himself, if he is able.

For those who wish to communicate, five hosts are sent on Sunday, and on other days only three, except on the greatest feasts. The armarius also sees that enough are sent for everyone to be able to communicate.

On ordinary days, at the first Mass, since everyone offers, the same hebdomadary takes care to have ready as many medium-sized chalices made for this purpose, with wine, as are sufficient for the offerings, together with matching patens containing hosts.

(var.) At the time of the offering he distributes these to the brothers with the offertories, beginning with the prior. After this he takes his place in the left choir at the end of the forma, holding in his hand a dish filled with hosts, which he distributes with a silver spoon to those offering. Beside him is the hebdomadary of the completed week, who likewise, holding a cruet of wine, serves those offering; they themselves offer last.

At the principal Mass there is no offering except by one choir, because fewer chalices are prepared, and the hebdomadary alone stands there to hand the hosts to those offering.

[Col. 1084A] When the priest and the other ministers gather in the vest iary, and either the principal or the lesser Mass is sung, the church hebdomadary always brings the candlesticks with candles from the altar, the Gospel book, and the lectionary from the small cabinet. For the missal book always lies beside the priest’s preparation.

[Note: [Col. 1083D] There is no doubt that this was added by William, since in the preface he himself admits that he added certain things according to the character of the place and the temper of the air.]

* If it is winter, either he or his companion brings the priest glowing coals from the regular kitchen.

After the Mass has ended and “Thanks be to God” has been said, he rings for None, if it is such a day, or, if it is Lent, for Vespers. Whenever the sign for None follows the Mass, the same sign is rung somewhat longer after the prayer has been said. On ordinary days, except on the vigils of the five principal feasts, the Saturdays of the Ember seasons, the three Rogation Days, and when grape blessings are given, he carries to the refectory two small dishes containing the hosts offered at the earlier Mass and places them on the principal table. From these, as was said above, each of those who did not wish, or were unable, to communicate may receive. When the meal is over, he takes the same dishes from the table; the procurator of the completed week receives the larger of them from him at the step, and thus the first men leave.

After they have come into the church, he entrusts the dish to his companion, so that he may be free to ring the bell. For it belongs to him always to ring it after the meal and at the collation, and for this reason he comes into the choir first. But for the mandate and for the collation, if these take place so late—for at that time he carries the light before the prior—his companion enters the church before the others in order to ring the bell. On the day when the brothers eat only once and twelve lessons are read on the following day, he must not fold up the choir stalls [Note: [Col. 1084D] *Formae*: benches or seats in the choir; see above.] before he knows that the ministers have come from the refectory, so that, if a brief commemoration of a deceased person should occur, the brothers may prostrate themselves upon the stalls during the collects of the office. Nevertheless, the vigils of the principal feasts are excepted; on them the brothers prostrate themselves neither at the solemn Mass nor afterward.

When he rings for Vespers, he observes the following order in ringing. If “Deus, in auribus” is not sung—as is the case from the Kalends of November until Septuagesima, for during this period it is sung at night after the prayer—he draws out the bell somewhat longer than the sign for None when Mass follows. But if it is sung after the prayer has been said, he continues ringing it until that same psalm has ended. Having dismissed it, he withdraws before the choir and says the same prayer as that which precedes None when there is only one meal. After the next two psalms have been sung through, he rings the second sign; he does not stop it before he knows that the first three psalms of the fifteen-step psalms [Note: That is, the psalms called the Gradual Psalms; see also above.] have been completed. He begins the third sign at the next Gloria before the psalm *Saepe expugnaverunt*. Having likewise dismissed it, he waits after the three psalms have ended until the conclusion of the prayers, and then, with another person assisting him, rings until it is sufficient. When they cease ringing, the priest, omitting “Let us bless the Lord,” begins Vespers.

The same order of ringing is observed in this psalmody if all the signs are rung, except that in that case the senior sacristan begins to ring the bell. In Lent, on the day when the procession takes place, as soon as some of the brothers have washed the feet, “Deus, in auribus” is begun. For Vespers he lights the candles while the bell is being rung continuously. When this is finished, as soon as the brothers have left the choir, he takes his companion and withdraws into the minor choir, or elsewhere where he cannot be seen by the community; after covering the altar panel, he goes to Saint Mary’s behind the community.

In winter, while the bell is being rung for the collation, if it is so late, he lights three lamps in the chapterhouse. Sometimes, if it happens that the ministers dine so late, he does not neglect to light them before the collation. At this sight the brothers follow, even if the mandate is to be performed, and so they wait; for neither the mandate nor the collation is ever begun until the ministers have returned from the refectory. Carrying one of these same lights before the head of the order into the refectory, he fixes it in the candlestick that he finds placed on the principal table. On returning, he precedes the same superior to the choir in the order described above. But if the superior withdraws before the choir for some necessity, he nevertheless precedes him into the choir with the light, so that, when the light is seen, there may be no delay in carrying out the appointed order. He acts similarly whenever a light is needed for the collation. The aforesaid order for carrying the light is also observed when the brothers go into the refectory during the collect in order to drink. But if it should happen that a light is needed not during the collect but in the refectory, then the refectorer places a candle on the table, which the aforesaid weekly officer will carry before the prior into the church.

In summer he never omits the same order for carrying the light at the mandate. After Compline, in his proper order, he precedes the sprinkling of water, and then turns into the minor choir and remains there until the community has passed through, so that he may hand the light, concealed from view, to the claustral prior. Having done this, he gathers in orderly fashion onto one prong the rings of all the signals customarily collected on a single iron four-pronged implement—namely, those to be rung at Matins—so that at Matins he may not err by taking one for another.

On Wednesday and Saturday he prepares the chalices belonging to the public Mass and to the Matins Mass after their entrances—provided that he himself is the priest or deacon; if not, he obtains a substitute for this purpose. He carefully washes the chalices with which the offering is made, inserting his hand after the offering at either Mass. He carries all the larger and smaller cruets, if there are twelve lessons, after Matins; otherwise, after the Gospel of the earlier Mass, to the water conduit and washes them most carefully, using a tool of iron or wood provided for this purpose, with which he can scrub them well at the bottom. A lay brother may also take part in this washing of the cruets; for a lay brother may likewise wash the chalices in which the offering is customarily made, since they have not been consecrated. It also belongs to him on the three Rogation Days to provide the priest and deacon at the morning Mass with the vestments for the solemn Mass, and the thurible with its incense-box for the candle-bearer; he also lights two candles before the altar and, as on all feasts celebrated in albs, spreads the bench-coverings [Note: *Bancale*: a covering or carpet of a bench or seat, with which a stool or bench is covered.] in the chapterhouse.

## CHAPTER XXXI. Likewise concerning the apocrisiarius

[Col. 1086B]

(UD) Now, to say a little about the apocrisiarius himself: from what is offered by the lay people, he gives the tithe of money and whole loaves to the almoner; eggs, cheeses, and other edible products to the cellarer, * although he may retain a little of such products for the uses of the church. UD. For the rest, whatever comes into his hands he expends chiefly on repairing the roofs of the church, lest they ever fall into disrepair, and on lights, and on the other things that are necessary and useful in the church. He gives candles to the refectory; to the infirmary; to the chamberlain; to the guest-master; and to the lord abbot and any prior who may go anywhere, for they never sleep without a light. * Moreover, he provides one light in the brothers’ dormitory. Besides these things, whatever is necessary for the mandate, which is performed each week, he supplies from his own administration. UD. To ensure that he never lacks the means for all these things, he has one sufficiently good estate with tithes, vineyards, and fields.

## CHAPTER XXXII. Concerning the making of hosts

[Note: See the *Ordinarium Cluniacense*, Part I, chapter 53.]

(UD.) Since what concerns the Eucharist and the body of the Lord ought to be carried out with the greatest reverence and care, it is fitting that the manner of carrying it out should not be passed over in silence. (var.) First, therefore, the grain from which the hosts are to be made, however naturally good and pure it may be, is nevertheless selected grain by grain [Col. 1086D], and by no persons other than the brothers themselves, namely the assistants of the apocrisiarius, * and sometimes in the chapterhouse by novices not yet consecrated. When it has been selected in this way, it is carefully washed and dried in the sun on a clean cloth spread out for the purpose. It is gathered into a sack preserved solely for this purpose and made of good cloth. UD. Once gathered in it, it is entrusted to a servant mature both in character and in age and diligent in his work. (var.) Carrying it to the mill, he cleans the millstone and covers it completely with curtains above and below; he dresses himself in an alb and, over his humeral, binds about his head [Note: A linen cloth that covers the head and shoulders.] a cloth, so that nothing of his face except his eyes can be seen. Thus he grinds, and thus he sifts the flour [Col. 1087A]; he also first washes the sieve carefully. Since no fixed time has been established for the number of times in the year when the hosts are to be formed, the church custodian provides for their making whenever it is necessary.

* On that day the makers of the hosts do not attend the chapterhouse or the regular Hours, and yet they do not ask pardon on the following day. If he himself is not a priest or deacon, UD. he seeks a substitute for this work, and two others who belong to those orders; a fourth may be a lay brother, if that seems appropriate. These four, if it is winter, after the Night Office—or, if it is summer, after Matins—(var.) put on their shoes, wash their faces and hands, comb their heads, and withdraw to some secluded altar. There they sing whatever is to be sung until the hour of dinner. For afterward [Col. 1087B] they take no part in this work at all. Therefore, after washing their hands, the three who are priests or deacons put on albs and humerals in the place where they are to make the hosts, as was stated above concerning the man who grinds the flour. One of them sprinkles the flour with water and kneads it very vigorously on an exceedingly clean board having a rim around it, slightly higher than the rest of its surface, so that the water cannot run off. He sprinkles it with cold water, because they say that hosts made in this way are whiter. The other two form the hosts.

The lay brother holds the implement in which they are to be baked and covers his hands with gloves. Accordingly, a board is placed between the lay brother and the makers of the hosts; two stakes are fixed into it, and a crosspiece is placed across the stakes [Col. 1087C]. Upon this he places the implement for putting in the hosts. When they have been baked, they are scraped with a knife and fall downward into a dish placed on the board and continually covered with a cloth, except when the hosts are being scraped. They maintain complete silence and take the utmost care that not only their saliva but even their breath may in no way reach the hosts. If anything is needed, the lay brother alone makes it known in a few words to the servant who tends the fire; nothing is sent to it except dry wood specially prepared for this purpose.

* After the brother who kneaded the flour has finished, he devotes himself to selecting the hosts, setting aside those that are entirely intact for the celebration of Mass [Col. 1087D], and reserving those that are slightly cracked for offering. If any are found broken, either there or elsewhere after having fallen to the ground, they are carefully collected and, at the time the weekly sacristan considers appropriate, carried to the refectory and put into some basket for fragments. (UD.) On that day the workers who made the hosts do not eat with the community but with the servants; (var.) and for so much labor they receive a portion from the cellarer.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. Concerning the washing of corporals and other things of this kind

(var.) When the corporals [Note: A *corporale* is the linen cloth which supports the host and chalice on the altar while Mass is celebrated. See Bernard, *Ordo Cluniacensis*, Part I, chapter 54.] are to be washed, they are washed with no less care, and a fixed time is appointed for this as well, namely before Easter. Vessels of bronze are assigned for the purpose, as large as basins, in which they are washed and which are used for no other purposes. After Vespers, in the church beside the pit over which the chalices are customarily washed, they are dipped twice in cold water and rubbed by hand. Water is poured in a third time, so that they remain in it throughout the night; in the morning they are wrung out there and the water is poured, as before, into the same pit. It should be noted that the water in which they are dipped must be brought in the same vessel in which it is also offered for mixing with the sacrificial wine. They are then carried to the workshop of the secretary, where they are to be washed. There the servant has already prepared the clearest lye and strained it most carefully; nevertheless, it is not poured over the corporals until they have first been [Col. 1088B] wrapped on every side in cloth. * After they have been thoroughly washed and somewhat dried, they are dipped by a brother dressed in an alb into a clear, liquid flour-water mixture made from the finest flour, and are thus dried completely. UD. Meanwhile they are by no means left without a diligent guardian, especially one who will drive away the flies. He does not remove his alb at all, nor does he withdraw from the place. * If he should happen to neglect an Hour on account of this, he does not ask pardon.

UD. He does not neglect first to wash the cord on which they are hung; this cord is continually kept in one pouch solely for this purpose. When they are smoothed [Note: *Levigare*: to polish; *leviga*: an instrument for smoothing, also called a *complanatorium* (‘levelling tool’). John of Genoa, *Germ. Beglen*.], one cloth is substituted for another, and they are never placed on bare wood. * At the same time, and whenever necessary, the same brothers wipe the offertory cloths [Col. 1088C] and the small linens with which the chalices are carried. The apocrisiarius carries out all this together with his other younger assistants and sees that it is always done before dinner. In addition, he has under him certain servants whose entire concern and labor are, when necessary, to make candles from wax received for the purpose, to shape tapers properly, to prepare oil, to sew, mend, and wash vestments, to sweep the oratory with brooms as often as necessary up to the cross, to hang curtains, and, after the celebration is completed, to take them down, fold them, and put them away; and also to provide certain other church utensils, as the sacristan sees fit. The interior assistants of the sacristan do not admit themselves to such tasks unless there is something they cannot complete without their help. At the aforesaid time when the corporals are washed, these same servants also wash the linen altar coverings with the albs, if any happen to require washing that year, except those belonging to the solemn Mass, private Masses, and the morning office; these must always have been washed by the first Sunday of Advent and of Lent, and whenever they need to be washed thereafter. Hand towels and other things of this kind are washed by the same servants not only at this time but whenever necessity requires.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. Likewise concerning the apocrisiarius

[Col. 1089A]

* What belongs solely to the apocrisiarius—or, if he is absent, to his substitute—is first to regulate and arrange the clock. Since it may sometimes be wrong, he marks it in wax and observes the course of the stars, or even of the moon, so that he may cause the brothers to rise at the proper hour.

Therefore no one else begins to ring the bell for Matins except him. He nevertheless does not do so before lighting two lights, one before the church doors and the other before the dormitory. If he realizes that he has rung too late for the twelve lessons, during Matins or at the Kyrie eleison he prostrates himself before the step; and, unless the prior has previously ordered otherwise, when the prayers are finished he leaves without making the customary movement backward and forward. But if this happens on an ordinary day, he asks pardon in the chapterhouse. When the time comes to ring for Prime, he does so.

This ringing, however, is not carried out in a uniform manner. On Easter Day and on the other principal feasts, one of the largest bells is rung; on the remaining feasts, one of the smaller bells, according to the dignity of each feast. On Palm Sunday, and whenever a procession is held to some church outside the cloister, two of the largest bells are rung until the procession arrives there, and the same is observed on the return. On ordinary days, the ringing for Terce, and also every day the ringing for Vespers, is left to his discretion, except in Lent and when the lord abbot is at the assembly; then permission to ring is requested from him. Whenever the weekly officer begins to ring during the time of speaking, no one, by custom, will forbid him.

If the sacristan needs to keep watch in the church during the general meal, or to perform something that cannot be postponed, he may absent himself from that meal without permission and receive a mixed portion that day with the kitchen servants. The ringing for the collation is not at his discretion but at the prior’s. Whenever the mandate is performed, after it has been completed he comes before the prior and asks permission to ring. After dismissing the sign, he returns to his place and goes with the others into the refectory to drink; he will return before the others in order to gather up and store the basins and hand towels used at the mandate.

[Col. 1089D]

After Compline, he sees to it that the porter, with several guardians of the church, searches the entire church, lest a thief should find an opportunity to hide there. He never fails to fasten at night the church door that faces the cloister and is near his bed, so that it cannot be opened without a key; and the key itself never leaves his side. He also provides on the principal feasts that, from the brothers’ entrance for Matins until the end of the solemn Mass, two candles burn continuously on the high altar; on the other feasts celebrated in copes, this is observed only during Mass.

It is customary on the octave of Pentecost, on the feast of All Saints, at the dedication of the church, and on the highest feasts, that at the third lesson of Matins, and at the sixth and ninth, a priest dressed in a cope incense the principal altar and carry incense to all the brothers within and outside the choir. The same apocrisiarius invites whichever priest he sees for this purpose, giving him a signal concerning the incense. Likewise, at Matins on the principal feasts, when three hangings of different colors are placed upon the high altar, he himself, if he cannot otherwise do so, removes them one by one with his assistant: namely, at the Gloria of the third and eighth responsories. At that same point, even at the twelve lessons, he also uncovers the altar panel, which until then has been covered with a cloth. He takes the Gospel book from the altar and carries it to the sacristy; there, after lighting a lamp, he follows the priest proceeding to the altar as far as the presbytery. There he stands on the left beside the candle-bearer until the priest has reached the lectern from the altar and opened the book; then he hands him the light, with a kiss of the hand. His assistant, the weekly officer, receives it from him after the prayer has ended, without a kiss. After the Gospel has been read, the sacristan lowers the cords of the signals, and when the collect has ended, at *Per Dominum*, he rings the bell.

When the priest returns from the lectern after the morning lesson has been imposed, he receives the Gospel book from his hand and replaces it on the altar. On ordinary nights, when the morning office immediately follows Matins and the customary psalms are not added, after the collect has ended and “Thanks be to God” has been said, he rings for the morning lesson. But if those psalms are added, he begins ringing at *Per Dominum* of the following collect.

He must regulate the winter interval so that the claustral prior can go around the entire cloister with the concealed light. He must also use such caution with the morning signal that, after the morning lesson, the first light of day can clearly be seen. If this is ever not observed, Prime nevertheless is not delayed, together with the things belonging to it.

At a feast on which incense is to be offered with two thuribles, if the lord abbot has not sung Vespers and Matins but the weekly priest has, and if that priest then incenses with him, the apocrisiarius, as I have said, invites another priest, but from the other choir.
