He does not do this, however, if the lord abbot has sung Vespers and Matins, because then, by custom, the weekly priest will incense with him.

He must remember that on the vigils of the principal feasts, after Matins, and on the vigils of feasts such as Saint John the Baptist’s, while the brothers are in the refectory—or, if there are two meals, after None—the back-hangings are to be suspended and the altars prepared. If such a vigil falls on a Sunday or on another day with twelve lessons, they are to be suspended before the vigil. If a feast with twelve lessons follows that vigil on the same day, the back-hangings are not to be taken down, just as they are not taken down during the week of the Nativity, Easter, or Pentecost. He must also see that during the three days of those feasts immediately following, and on the commemoration of Saint Paul, nothing is removed from the church’s equipment.

He must also remember the proper arrangement for every kind of feast: on which the entire church is to be adorned with hangings [Col. 1091A], and on which only the presbytery; on which seven candles are to be lit before the principal altar at Vespers and Matins, and on which only five; which celebrations are to be conducted in albs and which in copes. The copes are distributed in one choir by him, and in the other by his assistant. If both are lay brothers, they distribute them to each brother dressed in an alb. Near the end of Mass the brothers may remove them without permission, so that they may be ready to receive the copes and other vestments together with their amices and then depart.

If the feast is one celebrated in copes and a procession is to take place, but Terce precedes it, the amices, distributed together with the albs, are not collected before the processional chant has ended. But if Terce follows, they are immediately taken back after the psalms have ended. If there is no procession, they do not use the amices at all. On every feast celebrated in albs, whether or not there is a procession, they are not collected until *Per omnia saecula* has been said. Nevertheless, although, as stated, copes or amices are distributed and collected in this order on individual feasts, on Palm Sunday and the Purification of Saint Mary they are given to no one, just as relics are not carried on those days.

The aforesaid sacristan should also know with what ornaments the procession is to be conducted on the principal feasts. Within the space of the choir, he is to arrange everything belonging to this through his assistants. In that procession, therefore, holy water, crosses, and the Gospel books are carried first. They are borne by the subdeacon who is to read the Epistle and by the ministers of the altar, dressed in tunics; incense is carried before both of them, while the candlesticks are carried at their sides. Then come the small crosses, boxes, and other lesser ornaments. Finally, the relics of the saints are carried by certain senior brothers who are less able to sing. After them come the priors from the nearby houses, as is customary on Sundays, as far as the vestibule of the secretary’s office; having made a station there, they enter the choir last.

If it should ever happen that the morning Mass is to be sung at the high altar, as on the Nativity of Saint Mary, it is celebrated in every respect in the manner in which the solemn Mass is customarily celebrated on ordinary days, except that the prior alone offers three hosts—or, if it is Sunday, five. Although he alone makes the offering, the other choir nevertheless approaches for the peace, and whoever wishes receives the body of the Lord. After three copes have been distributed according to custom, with all the bells ringing and the chant begun, the procession takes place.

The ashes that are placed on the heads of the brothers at the beginning of the fast are made through his diligence from the charred remains of vine-shoots, and are carefully cleaned and sifted.

On the first Sunday of Lent, after Compline, a veil is suspended through his provision between the high altar and the choir; it is likewise removed on the Wednesday before Easter. [Note: See Bernard of Cluny, Part I, chapter 63.] It should be understood concerning these things that no one except the guardians or ministers of the sanctuary dares to pass through without reasonable cause. On the following day, after the litany, all the ornaments are removed.

Those things that cannot be removed are veiled. It also belongs to him on the vigils of the saints whose feasts are celebrated in Lent, and on the Saturdays of the same season after Sext, to adorn the high altar and the altar on which the relics of the approaching feast are placed with a hanging. On all feasts celebrated either in copes or in albs, he likewise sees to it that all the altars are adorned with hangings.

(UD. var.) On Palm Sunday he must choose certain more diligent lay brothers who know how to carry the chests and cases of the holy relics on their shoulders in the procession. In this procession holy water is carried first, then crosses, two Gospel books, four candle-bearers, and two thuribles; next come all the lay brothers, and finally the seniors, as in every procession held outside the cloister. But before the aforesaid procession the servants carry the banners, as they also do on the three Rogation Days. He keeps the crystal stone from which the fire is to be drawn on Maundy Thursday. On that day and on the two following days he presents it to the armarius so that fire may be brought forth from it; the sacristan’s servants, however, must kindle and tend it. On the same day, when the community goes out to dinner, the sacristan remains with his assistants so that he may strip all the altars of their coverings.

[Col. 1092C]

On Good Friday, after Terce, he has the crosses and the other things that had been covered during Lent uncovered; only the greater cross remains veiled until the antiphon *Ecce lignum* is imposed. At the same time he prepares the cross for veneration, as is customary. Through his agency the high altar is also covered with the whitest linen, and a corporal is placed upon it—but shortly before the body of the Lord is brought back there. He also sees to it that on that day, during the brothers’ meal, all the altars are washed with water and wine by the more honorable priests whom he himself summons, while they are still barefoot. Whatever liquid has been poured upon the high altar is gathered with sponges, wrung out, and poured into the sacrarium.

On Holy Saturday he has curtains hung in the principal church [Col. 1092D] and in the chapel of Saint Mary, to protect the back-hangings; they are not removed before Advent, except while the monastery is being swept on the principal feasts. Likewise, on that Saturday and at Pentecost, it belongs to him to ring the bell for Mass, because the sacristan then keeps the choir.

On the three Rogation Days he and his assistant distribute *phylacteria* to the brothers. Those, however, abstain from them who happen to be barred from the peace and communion. He provides whatever is necessary for Mass to be carried to the church toward which the procession proceeds. There also he stands by the altar while the brothers lay down their *phylacteria*, and he receives as many as he can and places them on the altar. Likewise, when they receive them, he stands by and returns to each person what he had previously carried; or, if someone does not recognize his own, they take them themselves or point out to him which is to be returned. They should know this: after laying them down and before receiving them, they ask pardon in both places. During those days no one is permitted to wash his clothes or perform any similar work in the cloister. Brothers assigned to these tasks may write, sew, or mend garments in other suitable places. On the principal feasts he sees to it that the *phylacteria* are hung around the altar and taken down. On both occasions, the one who hands them over and the one who receives them are dressed in albs.

Also on those feasts, two priests summoned by him bring the offering: one, the hosts and wine [Col. 1093B]; the other, a golden or silver strainer and a cruet of water with which the wine is to be mixed. A deacon is also sent there from the sacristy. Having received the strainer from the hand of that priest—just as the priest received it from the subdeacon, who carried it suspended in his hand during the Mass or in the procession—he pours the water through it into the chalice when the wine and hosts have been offered by the prior. On feasts of copes he calls one of the literate brothers to bring the hosts and wine.

On the feast of All Saints he sees to it that there is no altar in the principal church or at Saint Mary’s before which a candle does not burn from Vespers until Vespers, indeed until after Compline. When the dedication of either church is commemorated, all the altars of that church alone, whose dedication is then being celebrated, are likewise illuminated. If the dedication of some monastery should fall during Lent, all the altars are merely adorned and incensed by two men in albs. The Introit is repeated three times; the responsory is sung by four, and the Kyrie eleison, Sanctus, and Agnus Dei are sung from the greater chants. Above all, the aforesaid sacristan carefully observes that the corporals, altar cloths, veils, and curtains of the church, and other things of this kind consecrated to divine service, when they have grown old, are committed to the fire, and that their ashes are placed in the piscina or baptistery.

## CHAPTER XXXV. What is to be done when a storm arises

[Col. 1093D]

* When a storm arises, the sacristan must place a cross in the cloister turned toward that storm, together with relics and holy water. Immediately two of the largest bells are rung until the danger appears to have passed. But if he sees the danger increasing so greatly that the brothers must be summoned, then without delay he rings the two largest bells signifying hail. Whenever they are rung in this manner, the brothers, hearing them and recognizing that hail is imminent, are to assemble in the church wherever they may be, at any hour by night or day—not running, but walking more quickly than usual—and, unless they have already begun to sing Mass or a regular Hour, they are immediately to begin the litany. When it has ended, they are to add the seven psalms, if necessary. Meanwhile all the bells continue to be rung without interruption.

This custom is observed with such care that, even if the brothers are in the refectory when hail begins to fall, they start the litany there. They do the same when they recognize that the danger of fire is imminent. Although people run there in haste, no one speaks until the prior says *Benedicite*, if he sees that the fire is prevailing to such an extent.

## CHAPTER XXXVI. Concerning the chamberlain

(UD.) The chamberlain himself goes to our estates and receives, at the proper time, as much money as we can obtain from them. (var.) From those estates situated so far away that neither the wine nor the grain grown there can reach us [Col. 1094B], the produce is sold there and the price is brought to the chamberlain. Finally, whatever gold or silver is given to us anywhere out of charity, he himself receives in full, except for what I am about to state. If someone gives ten solidi or less, or that amount in gold or silver, these gifts are always assigned to the cellarer for this purpose only: that he may show some charity in the refectory to the weaker and more delicate brothers, in addition to what is generally given to everyone. * But if they exceed the aforesaid number by even one denarius, the chamberlain receives them. Sometimes the lord abbot orders a portion of such an offering to be given immediately to the cellarer, so that he may show some charity to the weaker brothers, as was said. Nevertheless, nothing that is offered in gold or silver, clothing, or any similar form of charity is ever spent for any use before it has been presented in the chapterhouse.

It is also customary that, if someone personally presents an offering in the chapterhouse, he himself places his gift at the prior’s feet and hears the prior wish him an eternal reward. If the donor is standing, the prior rises and gives him the brotherly greeting; if he is kneeling, the prior, while seated, gives it. If the lord abbot gives it, however, he will not instruct the donor to kneel, but will give it while remaining seated. If there are two or more donors, they are introduced together and make their offerings together, because their offerings are assigned as one.

Money sent to us for charity may also be delivered on one day and presented at the next chapter, provided that it exceeds the sum of ten solidi mentioned above; in accordance with custom, the same chamberlain receives it. The offerings of novices, and those offered for deceased lay persons, after being presented or reported to the lord abbot—or, in his absence, to the prior—are all assigned to the chamberlain, except for the following: hangings, golden and silver vessels, and everything of this kind belonging to the use and adornment of the church. The sacristan receives the missal books; the armarius, the other books and parchment; the cellarer, cows, sheep, and goats for the use of the brothers; the dean of the estate, oxen for plowing. From the same offerings the chamberlain gives the guest-master as much as is necessary for a mattress, sheets, and anything similar. For the rest, as was stated above, everything comes into the hands of the chamberlain—and not without reason, since it frequently happens that we have little from all the things produced annually to support our temporal life, apart from what must be purchased with money. When this occurs from time to time with food, everything belonging to clothing must be purchased not occasionally but continually, and almost entirely.

## CHAPTER XXXVII. What is to be given to each brother every year in clothing
(UD. var.) Each brother must always have one frock, and, if possible, two cowls. To prepare these, the chamberlain requires from each brother the old garments, so that he may measure the new ones according to them.

[Col. 1095B] A new fur garment, if possible, is given to each brother every year, and on the feast of Saint Michael—or in the meantime, while the community is at dinner—it is placed on his bed. The distribution of these fur garments lies solely within the chamberlain’s discretion. Those to whom they are given must mark them with their names themselves, or have others do so at their request. Again, on the feast of Saint Martin, new footcloths are placed on the beds. On Maundy Thursday, if possible, shoes are given in the following manner. Before the brothers leave the church, three poles suspended by the chamberlain’s servants are brought into the chapter house, and the poles themselves are laid upon four stakes fixed in the ground. After the sentence of the Rule has been expounded, at the command of the abbot, the chamberlain and his assistant rise, and through them the shoes are distributed, the armarius and his assistant choosing them and supplying them to hand.

[Col. 1095C] The names of the individual brothers are written and sewn onto small labels attached to the individual pairs, except in the case of those who have recently arrived, whose names cannot yet be written. Therefore the shoes intended for them are hung separately. (UD.) Those receiving new garments return the old ones, thoroughly washed, at the same time—provided that they have more than one pair for daily use—so that the old ones may be given to the poor.

Concerning woollen undergarments (*staminea*) and breeches, or anything similar, no other provision has been made than this: when they have become old and no longer useful, they are to be washed and returned by the brothers themselves to the chamberlain, and other garments are to be given in their place.

And, to state here once and for all what each brother may regularly and customarily possess for clothing in general: first, two cowls and one frock; two woollen undergarments (*staminea*) and two pairs of breeches; two pairs of shoes, one pair with straps for night use; two pairs of leggings; two fur garments; a cap made of sheepskin or cat-skin; and five pairs of footcloths. For the bed: a pillow, a bedcover covered with woollen cloth, a blanket, a brachiolineum [Note: [Col. 1095D] See the index of exotic words.] with which the breeches are fastened, a deerskin strap, with which the woollen undergarment is girded and from which a knife with its sheath hangs, and a needle with thread and a needle-case.

A priest and a deacon, when performing their office, customarily have three pairs of breeches, so that, if anything happens to them during the night, they have others ready to put on. If the chamberlain wishes, out of compassion, to add a third fur garment to someone who has two, or to provide bandages because his shins are weak, the recipient must obtain permission from the prior. But if the chamberlain gives someone one pair of leggings made of sheepskin even without permission, neither the giver nor the recipient deserves to be reproved for it.

* A brother may lend any garment of his to another brother, but he must not give it without the prior’s permission. Each brother must be given garments suited both to his size and to their quality. If the chamberlain neglects this, the recipient may admonish him about it. Beyond the garments specified above, anyone who wishes to possess more of this kind is judged to have it neither as a matter of justice [Col. 1096B] nor of compassion, but as a grave excess.

All fur garments are made of sheep’s wool or goat’s hair; bedcovers, however, are made either of sheep’s wool, cat-skin, hare-skin, or polecat-skin, and never of any more highly valued material. The frock and cowl are made of such cloth as is found in this province, provided that it is not lamb’s wool or another material of precious quality.

UD. If the chamberlain at any time buys or sells anything of this kind, then, after completing his business in its entirety, he voluntarily returns to the merchant with whom he has dealt a certain number of additional pennies, according to the nature of the transaction and the person involved, because of Saint Benedict’s command (Rule, chapter 57) that our goods should always be sold more cheaply than those of other people.

[Col. 1096C] Whenever we speak in the cloister, the chamberlain himself or his assistant, who carries the key to the chamber, is always present. He is then to hear from each person what this one or that one needs. If he neglects this on several occasions, he is called to account. On such occasions, however, one of the two stands before the chamber, distributing what is to be distributed, so that the brothers do not have to speak during the time of silence.

* Sometimes it may happen that someone, prevented by lack of time or by some other necessity, cannot ask for what he needs. Anyone who is entirely unable to make his request known by signs is nevertheless not forbidden, with the chamberlain’s permission and at a suitable time, to enter the chamber and speak briefly of what is strictly necessary—provided that the pressing need cannot be postponed until the next permitted time for speaking.

A brother whose fur garment, woollen undergarment, or breeches are so torn that they can still be mended places them at dawn in the place assigned for this purpose, so that the chamberlain’s assistant, when he comes, may carry them outside to the tailors. After vespers, when he brings them back, he replaces them in the same place, so that the person to whom they belong may collect them.

* It should be understood that, both on the days of the twelve readings and on ordinary days, everything placed there must be collected before the collation, even if it has not been mended. If it should happen that someone neglects this, he may collect it after compline while passing through, provided that he causes no delay for what follows.

Anyone who washes one of his own garments and hangs it on a cord in the cloister must remember to take it down before the collation—or, if the following day has the twelve readings, before vespers. A frock, cowl, woollen undergarment, breeches, and leggings may be hung there, but only after they have been washed. A bedcover may not be hung there.

Socks are to be washed there and placed to dry on the cloister grass. Nothing at all, however, is to be left there during the twelve readings or when a procession is taking place. It should also be understood that in the dormitory only sheep-wool bedcovers, turned inside out, are to be hung.

It should further be understood that the chamberlain’s assistant takes his place in every respect when the chamberlain is absent, whether inside or outside the cell; when the chamberlain is present, he acts in this way only within the enclosure [Col. 1097B] of the cell. For he does not dare to go outside unless his superior orders him.

When the brothers are about to leave, or when they return from a journey and receive a blessing, this same assistant must carefully observe which brothers, and how many, receive the blessing, so that he may know how to arrange the beds. He also sees to it that in the dormitory, in a more respectable place, one or two beds are always prepared for guests. No one may move from one bed to another or turn the head of a bed in another direction without his permission; only he may make such changes in the dormitory. Even if he is hindered, he will not be absent from the place where each person who is about to leave arranges his garments, taking care that no one carries away more of the same garments than use and necessity require.

[Col. 1097C] The chamberlain must know that a brother who has stayed here in the monastery or in some cell for half a year or less is not, according to custom, sent from here to there or from there to here around the feast of Saint Michael, whether for wintering or for remaining thereafter, unless he too is clothed with the garments commonly distributed to the brothers at that time. If the prior of a cell neglects this and sends one of the brothers here around the appointed time dressed in old and worn clothing, he is to be sent back to be clothed by the abbot, or by the prior of the place from which he came, as has been stated; and, if it seems appropriate, he is ordered to return again.

The aforementioned chamberlain must also give the doorkeeper, for the use of traveling brothers, cloaks and leg-wrappings, spurs, gloves, and belts; and, for the use of clerical guests who sometimes eat in the refectory, as many surplices as are necessary. No literate person may eat in the refectory unless he is dressed in clerical clothing.

He also gives the almoner the brothers’ old garments that are unsuitable for their use—if any remain after being passed on to the outside brothers—for distribution to the poor; to the armarius, skins, knives, dyes, and everything necessary for making books; to the refectorer, for the use of the abbot and the guests eating in the refectory, two basins with a hand towel; and, in addition, two other basins to the infirmarer for the use of the sick lying in their beds.

At the Nativity of Saints John and Paul, he receives hay [Col. 1098A] from the village dean and has it spread on the brothers’ beds. He and his assistant also provide hot water in winter for washing the brothers’ feet after the procession and before the washing of feet. Among other duties, he is responsible for the fullers who wash the brothers’ cloth, and for ensuring that tablecloths and hand towels are washed separately from the other cloths. Every Tuesday after the Gospel of the morning Mass, his assistant leads these men into the cloister, so that they may collect the brothers’ cloths for washing from the chest in which the brothers always gather them. He also has considerable responsibility for all the tools needed in the cloister, for the brothers’ razors, and for the scissors and linen cloths used in shaving.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. The Brother Who Keeps the Razors

[Col. 1098B]

* One brother is specially assigned to guard the razors. He keeps them in a small chest, secured with a lock (UD. var.), which is placed high beside the entrance to the dormitory. He also keeps the linen cloths, which likewise hang there continuously. Three or four days before the shaving, he carries the chest into the cloister and sits in one part outside the community, facing the cellarer’s door, sharpening and preparing the razors for this work, apart from the other times when the community sits in the cloister for the morning Mass. He must not, however, be absent for the offertory; like anyone else who is in the cloister, he may attend to the office for the dead after the three readings. An assistant is also given to him if necessary.

## CHAPTER XXXIX. The Shaving of the Brothers

[Col. 1098C]

(UD.) When the time has come for the general shaving, the board is struck in the chapter house and permission to speak about the shaving is given. The brothers leave the chapter house and form almost two lines for sitting, namely by the cloister grating and near the wall, each in the same order as in the chapter house.

* They must take care that no one gives another the signal to be shaved before he has sat down. (UD.) In one line the aforementioned brother, and in the other his assistant, give each brother one razor. Newly washed bowls are distributed by the almoner, one to each pair of brothers. They do not move from their places but wait in disciplined fashion until the person who carries the bowls or [Col. 1098D] razors comes to them.

The keeper of the razors sees to it that the linen cloths are distributed in the meantime. But before each person, while sitting and bending forward, receives what has been given to him, the lye-water is brought. Before the board was struck for chapter, it had been placed in suitable locations—not, however, before the church doors—through the arrangements of the chamberlain’s assistant. Each person prepares himself for shaving.

No one moistens his head before the psalmody begins. No one sits for shaving before the church door or before the chapter house if space is available elsewhere.

(UD.) Whoever shaves another removes his frock and shaves in his cowl; the person being shaved is shaved in his frock, with his cowl removed and placed beside him. If he happens to have offered to bring lye-water [al. hot water], he carries his neatly folded cowl on his arm.

[Col. 1099A] During the shaving, the psalmody “My words” is sung, followed by the psalm “Praise.” If that day has the psalm to be sung for the cellarer, or the three psalms customarily sung for some tribulation, and anything else of this kind that is to be sung after chapter, these are also sung. The canonical cursus follows in the same order in which it is sung during manual labor. At the end, the psalms for the familiar dead are added, except those belonging to vespers. The psalms customarily recited by those prostrate, as in Lent, are then added, except the vespertine psalms.

The weekly priest, who recites the collects in the midst of the brothers, must sit so that he can be heard by everyone. When the canonical cursus is finished, before the remaining psalmody is completed, he assigns the turn of his office to another brother who has been relieved, so that he too may be shaved.

One or two literate circatores go around while the psalmody is being sung, to remind the brothers to sing. They cease this duty only when the psalmody has been completed, and only then do they stop shaving. If anyone, when admonished by them, refuses to correct any neglected matter or takes the admonition badly, he rarely escapes being called to account. Whatever is necessary for the shaving may be requested from one another by signs.

(UD. var.) Moreover, until the psalmody has been completed, there is absolute silence, except that the person shaving first says, “Bless,” and the person being shaved replies, “The Lord.” The person being shaved says nothing unless he is wearing his cowl.

No one dares to cut hair with scissors before the psalmody has ended. When it has ended and the prior has said “Bless,” those who need it cut their hair with scissors in their frocks—* however hot the summer may be—with their cowls put back on, near the cellarer’s quarters and nowhere else. Similarly, only then may those who wish wash their heads in their frocks without a cowl, if they have been shaved completely; otherwise they are not to wash until they have been shaved.

The other shaved brothers sit in such a way that no one among them shaves, and without books. It should be understood that a junior brother does not shave his keeper before he himself has been shaved by that keeper. Afterwards he may shave anyone else; with the keeper’s permission, however, he may not shave a junior. Although he himself is never to be shaved with a linen cloth, he may nevertheless use one when his hair is being cut with scissors. Linen cloths are also granted to the other younger brothers for shaving, if any remain after the seniors have used them.

The razors that each person has used last are dried and returned to the chest after the next hour by the brother who keeps the razors, to be collected again in the usual place—unless some are left with the brothers still to be shaved in the warming room, where the linen cloths have also been hung by him to dry, together with the scissors.

Nor should this be left unsaid: if someone does not wish to learn to shave when he is able to do so, he is not given his portion of drink on the day of the shaving itself.

If a bell is rung for any hour, those who have not yet begun shaving come into the choir, but do not proceed to the kiss of peace. Any half-shaved brother puts on his frock and goes to the church, but he does not enter the choir; rather, he stands apart in some secluded place. When the hour is finished, if he is to receive the blessing, he enters the choir with his head uncovered but with his cap drawn down below it, as far as suitably possible, so that the half-shaved condition is less visible.

[Col. 1100A] Otherwise, he leaves immediately at the end of the hour and is completely shaved in the warming room during Mass; no one else may do this without permission.

But if the time allows, and after sext the brothers return from the church and sit in the cloister, or before the hour, while the priest and the other ministers of the altar are being vested for Mass, then, after prayer, both those who wish to have their hair cut with scissors and the half-shaved may lawfully do this in the cloister, in the same place as before.

At the intervals—that is, after Mass and after the cymbal has been struck—anyone may cut his hair with scissors in the warming room that day without permission. But if someone who was in the cloister while the others were shaved remained unshaved, or if he came from the road after the hour of shaving, he is shaved only with permission, and then only in the warming room. At that time, however, there must be silence whenever anyone is shaving or cutting hair with scissors.

Anyone arriving after the day of the shaving, even if it is a day with the twelve readings and not a working day, shaves after chapter with permission. He never does so on Sunday or on another feast involving a procession, even if he is not required to take part in it; instead, he shaves on the following day after the morning Mass, at suitable intervals.

If a monk of our congregation who is staying outside has decided to come to a cell on the day of the shaving or during the following three days, he must not presume to arrive shaved, even if he comes on a day other than the actual day of shaving. Similarly, anyone who is to leave that day, however far he must travel, must neither be shaved before the appointed time nor leave unshaved, unless he is ordered to do so because of great necessity, with the expectation that he will return before supper.

The keeper of the razors shaves none of these men or any others—not even the prior—except the novices, by virtue of his authority over them. He supplies what is necessary for those who are to be shaved from the items in his keeping. The bowls supplied by the almoner are to remain continually in the warming room for the needs of any unshaved brothers who arrive.

## CHAPTER XL. The Times for Shaving Throughout the Year

(UD.) The times for shaving throughout the year are as follows. First, before the Vigil of the Lord. Between that time and Septuagesima, since the weeks do not always fall in the same way and there may be neither more nor fewer of them, no fixed limit is set at all; the prior alone considers how the shaving may most suitably be carried out according to the season.

* When Septuagesima arrives, three weeks are always left between one shaving and the next, until Easter. Before Easter, it is done on Holy Saturday, but without the canonical cursus.

At the beginning of the shaving the board is struck once by the prior, and silence is then observed until, near the end of the shaving, the prior says “Bless” (UD.). After that, at Easter, it is done on the Sunday “The mercy of the Lord.”

Before the Rogation days, it is done on that Thursday, provided that no intervening feast prevents it. Before Pentecost, it is done on Thursday. From that day, because the number of weeks again varies until the feast of Saints Peter and Paul, shaving is again left to the prior’s discretion.

Afterwards there is no uncertainty about any of the times, because it has been customarily arranged that we always shave on the Translation of Saint Benedict, the Chains of Saint Peter, the Assumption of Saint Mary, Saint Othmar’s feast, and the Advent of the Lord.

It should be understood that on the vigils of the principal feasts, and on Friday, shaving is never performed, unless one of those feast vigils happens to fall on a Saturday. In that case, because the brothers would otherwise be shaved when the twelve readings are being held on Thursday, they are shaved on Friday, necessity requiring it.

## CHAPTER XLI. The Brothers’ Baths

(UD. var.) It is customary for people, after shaving, to bathe immediately as well. But there is not much to say about our baths. Only twice a year, and then without permission, may anyone who wishes bathe: before the Nativity of the Lord and before Easter.

* At any other time, anyone may bathe because of illness, with permission. No one may put on there a linen undergarment other than the one in which he arrived, speak there, or return to the community with a wet head.

If the prior’s signal sounds after someone has already entered the bath, or has even begun to undress, and for that reason he sometimes omits one canonical hour, this is not held against him (UD. var.), unless the signal is repeated by the prior.

## CHAPTER XLII. When and How the Brothers Are to Receive Their Newly Washed Clothing

[Col. 1101C]

* Every Saturday after None, and during Lent after supper, the brothers’ newly washed clothing is placed in the cloister on the bench near the cellarer’s quarters. The master of novices is always present there, to ensure that no one through carelessness or ignorance takes clothing other than that on which his own name is written.

It is an ordinance of our fathers that no one omit having his name written in ink [that is, with ink] on the inside of the front edge of his linen undergarment. On the bedcover, pillow, and breeches, the name is likewise to be sewn with thread at the front, but on the outside.

Anyone may make this inscription before Prime, or at another time before Terce, during the intervals between the hours, and before either of the two meals in the community, although he must not bring the clothing there openly into the midst of the community.

[Col. 1101D] Once they have taken the clothing, they immediately place it on their beds. If they wish, they insert their belts into the loosened breeches and hang them up. Anyone who wishes, except the junior brothers, may out of charity collect another person’s clothing and place it on his bed, if he sleeps nearby.

If any of this clothing remains in the cloister before the ringing of all the bells—or, during Lent, until the striking of the board for the washing of feet—the aforementioned master collects it and places it on the chapter-house grating. Those who were not there earlier, or who were unable because of some serious occupation to collect their clothing, or who could not find it even though they searched, may pass by and collect it there after vespers until the sound of the board.

Those who had previously neglected to collect their clothing without necessity must then collect it, but the keeper of the clothing records them; if they do this frequently, they are called to account in chapter.

After compline, if anyone sees clothing left there, he takes it while going to the dormitory and carries it to his own bed. On the following day he places it in the chapter house. No one may take his own clothing from there unless he has first sought pardon, provided that he has established by inspection that it is his own. If he has not, he is subject to penance; their names are written on the garments themselves. The chamberlain then, at the prior’s command, keeps the clothing that has been removed, so that he may later return it to those who come looking for it.

## CHAPTER XLIII. The Cellarer

[Col. 1102B]

(UD.) The cellarer is appointed and released from office with the same blessing as the prior. Once appointed, he must know how varied the service to the brothers in the refectory must be.

(var.) In the week there are three days—namely Wednesday and Friday—on which we have the pietantia; on the other four days we have the general fare. He must know also that on Sunday and Thursday the fare consists of fish, if fish can be obtained; if there are no vegetables, the general fare is continued.

Whenever there are twelve readings, we have the general fare. Whenever something else is served, the cellarer must have some other food prepared with it, so that he may substitute it for the general fare for brothers who cannot eat the general dish.

* He must also see to it that when the pietantia is served, several bowls are prepared in such a way that, if one is to be given to a single person, that person does not have to wait while the pietantia is offered to him. The pietantia is divided among the other dishes only in the case of fruits and vegetables.

(UD.) On feasts such as the Translation of Saint Benedict, we have both the general fare and the pietantia, if possible, and better bread than usual.

(var.) There are also many anniversary days which, if they fall on a day when the pietantia is customarily served, cause the fare to be changed along with the general dish. The cellarer keeps a shortened list of these days [Note: [Col. 1101D] That is, written in a catalogue.] But he must not be unaware of those on which we abstain from fat: namely, during the Advent of the Lord, except whenever the twelve readings take place, and from Septuagesima until Easter; then it is buried with the Alleluia.

* Therefore, every Saturday he holds a consultation with the prior, the chamberlain, and the others required for this purpose concerning each day of the coming week, so that whatever is to be given on this day or that may be provided in good time.

(UD.) He must also note in a brief the total number of pigs and rams owed from the obediences, so that he may immediately raise the matter if, through negligence, anything is lacking from the total owed by any obedientiarius.

Several small villages situated near the water depend upon the cellarer’s obedience. (var.) He feeds his horses there; he stays there to purchase fish or to construct devices with which fish are caught.

If one of the brothers is so ill that he cannot rise from bed, the cellarer comes to him every day at first light together with the infirmarer. There, before his bed, after they have said the verse “Precious,” he asks about everything that the sick brother has or can obtain, and whether there is anything he thinks should be prepared for him.

* He also does not fail to come there at another time, so that the other sick brothers may ask him for anything they need.

(UD.) Whenever the general fish dish is served immediately after Sext—or, if the fast lasts that long, after None—the whole meal must be arranged and set out in bowls on the table in the vestibule of the cellarer’s quarters. Thus the prior, or even the abbot, when he comes, can see before sitting down at the table what is in each bowl, whether it is equal, and whether it has been divided in such a way that the better portions do not go to the priors. In this matter great care is taken to avoid favoritism based on rank.

[Col. 1103B] * The same cellarer must also take care never to sit down to eat with the brothers at their common lunch or supper, unless he has been bled or is burdened by another illness.

If, while dining with the servants at the main table, he spills or breaks anything, he seeks pardon in chapter; if he makes a noise, he merely bows.

(UD.) On the day when the sentence of the Rule concerning him is read (chapter 31), the brothers show him charity in chapter.

* If this occurs on Monday, Wednesday, or Friday during Lent, it is postponed until the following day, because on those days only two cooked dishes are customarily served. While it is being read, he must always be present.

(UD.) On the following day he again seeks pardon in chapter and confesses himself guilty of many negligences occasioned by his obedience.

* If he is not present because of illness or some unavoidable necessity, his assistant does the same on behalf of himself and of the cellarer. The prior likewise asks indulgence for both of them.

Whether the cellarer or his assistant makes this confession, he names individually any faults that he has newly committed. Having then been absolved by the prior, he comes to the prior’s feet.

(UD.) The prior orders that the first psalm, together with the collect “Almighty and everlasting God,” be sung for them all by everyone after the psalm “My words” (var.). The brothers then stand facing one another; if it is such a day, they prostrate themselves in order; otherwise they bow down over the benches.

If on that day “My words” is to be recited for a deceased person, after all the bells have first been rung, this is done first; then the aforementioned psalm is sung; finally, three psalms for tribulation are sung, and the rite is closed with “Let us bless the Lord.”

(UD.) It is customary that, if the cellarer can foresee that bread or another food then required cannot be prepared in time, he should warn the sacristan by signs or words (var.) to postpone, by ringing, the hour following Mass until the cellarer lets him know that it is time for the signal to be rung.

If he should neglect this, he himself must remove the mallet, so that the prior does not strike the cymbal at its appointed time. Nevertheless, the cellarer himself immediately strikes it when he sees that the aforementioned food has been prepared, while the brothers meanwhile are occupied with reading in the choir.

These are the assistants whom the cellarer has. The first is the one who acts in every respect in his absence and answers for everything for which the cellarer himself usually answers.

## CHAPTER XLIV. The Granary Keeper

(UD.) The second is the person who receives the grain, whom we also call the granary keeper. When the harvest has been completely gathered, the prior informs him how many measures are to come from this obedience and that one. What he hears once, he keeps in his reckoning until it has been delivered.

The bakers are under his authority. When they have received the grain, they are to return two kinds of bread, so that, whatever bread may be obtained from another source, the bread given to the brothers may nevertheless be of the best quality.

Thus, from a measure of grain, eighty pounds of white bread and eighty pounds of dark bread are produced. He carefully distributes these to everyone according to what the constitution—or the circumstances of each case and the cellarer’s judgment—requires.

* He also distributes the grain ration for the beasts, and likewise gives it to the doorkeeper for the use of guests whenever necessity demands. It is especially his responsibility to ensure that the brothers lying in bed are never without somewhat better bread.

(UD.) If the bakers commit any negligence, either by failing to produce the customary number of loaves or by making the bread less good than it ought to be, he reports this to the prior and the cellarer, so that they may correct them according to the measure of their fault.

For this reason he always sleeps in the dormitory, although sometimes, because of his work, he sleeps elsewhere, since it often happens that necessity requires him to retire later than the others.

## CHAPTER XLV. The Keeper of the Wine

(UD. var.) The third assistant of the cellarer is the person who receives and keeps the wine and beer. When the vintage has been completed, the prior informs him, just as he informs the granary keeper concerning the grain, how many cartloads of wine [Note: [Col. 1103] *Carrada*, a vehicle, wagon: French *charrette*, *chariot.] he should expect from this place and that.

He gives vinegar and mustard to the refectorer whenever he knows that they are to be poured into the food.

* He sleeps in the cellar with the cellarer, but never without a light. (UD.)

## CHAPTER XLVI. The Village Dean

* The fourth is the provider for the cell’s external needs, whom we call the village dean. He arranges for the cell, gardens, vineyards, and meadows adjoining the cell to be enclosed with hedges; for firewood to be supplied; and for whatever similar things are necessary within or outside the cloister.

He also provides the hay to be spread annually on the brothers’ beds, as well as coffins for their burial and wooden boards with small pegs.

He is also in charge of the woodcutters. Although their labor is commonly used for many purposes in the monastery, he takes the greatest care to have them repair the cloister’s fallen roofs. Whatever he himself, or someone else who has warned him, knows will be useful to the brothers in the cloister through his obedience, he eagerly and without delay provides, putting external matters second.

For carrying out all these duties he receives whatever he needs from the cellarer.

Like the other obedientiaries, whenever necessary he may leave the cloister in the morning. In winter, as soon as the daily litany has ended, he may put on his daily shoes, wash and comb himself, and go out to his obedience. Afterwards, however, he must return early enough to be sprinkled with holy water together with the community and to attend the three prayers.

## CHAPTER XLVII. The Gardener

[Col. 1105B]

(UD.) The gardener must also be subject to the cellarer, so that, if there is anything in the garden that the cellarer wishes for the service of the brothers, the gardener may obediently obtain it from him.

If a brother asks him for any such produce from the garden because of an illness, he must not provide it except with the cellarer’s permission.

* He is in no way permitted ever to omit the midday canonical hour, unless on some day he has a great necessity for remaining behind. In that case he asks permission from the prior.

* When he sees that the fruit is ripe and that useless weeds have grown up in the garden, he must inform the prior. The cellarer must do likewise if necessary, removing fresh beans from their pods, so that, whether the weeds are to be pulled up or the apples gathered, at the prior’s command the first signal may be rung earlier on the following day and the psalmody postponed for that purpose.

Nevertheless, no such work is ever undertaken by the entire community unless it has been regularly arranged.

Whenever such work must be done, some of the lay brothers, at the cellarer’s request, are ordered to go from the morning Mass or from chapter to the guest hall, or to another place of this kind adjoining the cloister. While engaged in such work, however, they are not permitted to speak at all, except when the board is struck to permit speaking.

## CHAPTER XLVIII. How Manual Labor Is to Be Performed According to the Rule

* To explain how manual labor is regularly performed, on the day appointed for it, as soon as the brothers have risen and said their prayers, the signal is immediately rung for Prime at the prior’s sign. Prime is followed, with the psalms omitted, only by the litany and the morning Mass.

Chapter is also made shorter than on other days. As soon as the board has been struck and the abbot has first said, “Bless,” the abbot announces, “Let us go to manual labor.” The psalmody that was omitted after Prime is begun.

They proceed in procession, with the juniors first and the seniors last. When they have reached the place where they are to work, they all stand in order facing east. At the end of one psalm they perform the customary movement forward and backward, and when the abbot has pronounced the verse, “O God, come to my aid,” the following is said: “Lord, have mercy. Our Father. Our help.”

After bowing again, they begin to work.

[Col. 1106A] This is the psalmody that is sung while they are working. First, that which remained after Prime and after the chapter. Thereafter, all the regular Hours according to the custom of the canons. During their prayers the psalm “My words” (*Verba mea*) is also added, and the seven psalms are divided among the other Hours; the three that remain are said together during the prayers of Compline. Compline itself precedes Vespers for the faithful departed. The psalms that are customarily said for the familiar dead after Terce and after the two following Hours are added. If it seems good to the lord abbot that they work longer, the psalmody is extended from the psalm “When I was troubled, I cried to the Lord” (*Ad Dominum cum tribularer*) to the end of the Psalter; then also, from the beginning of the Psalter, “Glory be to the Father” (*Gloria Patri*) is always inserted after every three psalms. When these psalms for the familiar dead have been completed, the lord abbot, whenever he first wishes, [Col. 1106B] signals the brothers to cease from work and draw nearer to him. He orders something to be read there, but it must be finished quickly, because he himself—or another at his command—is going to give a sermon on it. This is chiefly to concern the life or conferences of the Fathers, so as to edify those listening. When it has ended, psalmody is again begun, and they return without performing the forward-and-back gestures (*ante et retro*). The boys too, if they are present in the place, or the young men, as soon as they reach the threshold of the cloister, raise their voices, and do not fall silent before the community has taken its place before the chapter. When the lord abbot pronounces the verse “Our help” (*Adjutorium nostrum*), all perform the forward-and-back gestures; then, after “Bless [us]” (*Benedicite*) has again been said, they receive permission to speak. But first, after washing their hands, they take up their books before saying anything [Col. 1106C].

Thus None is also hastened more than on other days. When the time for speaking has arrived, they are compelled to return to manual work. This is the psalmody with which they then begin: after “O God, we have heard with our ears” (*Deus auribus*), the psalms for the familiar dead that are customarily said at Vespers, namely “Lord, hear my prayer” (*Domine exaudi orationem*), “Thou hast been gracious” (*Benedixisti*) with the rest, without the appendage, and Vespers for the faithful departed. When the Office for the dead is performed without Matins, these are always reserved for the night, together with *Verba mea*, if they have the thirty-day commemoration; afterward the psalmody is begun where it was left off the previous time. When they have returned and sat down, after *Benedicite* has first been said, a sermon is delivered in the cloister, the little bell having been struck before the chapter. Rising from there and then performing the forward-and-back gestures, with the lord abbot pronouncing the whole formula, they say the verse “Blessed art thou, O Lord” (*Benedictus es Domine*); then follow “Lord, have mercy” (*Kyrie eleison*) with the customary appendages, “Our help” (*Adjutorium nostrum*). After performing the forward-and-back gestures, they say *Benedicite*, and thus permission to speak is granted.

And because it is customary for them to drink after the work is done, after the signal for Vespers has been given, they perform the order under a brother whom the prior has appointed for this; when the cymbal has been struck, they go to the refectory to drink. It must be understood that whenever this occurs, they do not afterward drink during the conference, as they otherwise do. If they work only once, the place for the sermon is in the cloister, and it is not postponed until *Benedictus es*; rather, it is said briefly, with the customary inclination made beforehand and afterward [Col. 1107A]. And if twelve lessons are to be read on the following night, they do not work twice.

## CHAPTER XLIX. On the refectorer

[Note: [Col. 1107D] The person responsible for the refectory, that is, the place where the monks eat.]

There are two keys to the refectory. The cellarer always keeps one of them, so that, if some brother should for any reason need to drink before Compline has been sung and the prior has taken his place, he may, with the cellarer’s permission, drink if necessary. But that anyone should eat after Compline, or even after the meal of the servants, is never permitted to any healthy brother for any reason, except to those arriving from a journey.

* If anyone needs to drink during the meal of the servants [Col. 1107B], he asks permission from the brother directing the order at that time, unless he knows that the abbot or prior is seated at the little bell; from him alone he receives it at the step. Having received permission, and after performing the forward-and-back gestures, he goes to his place. After first saying *Benedicite* in silence, he gives the blessing over the drink with the sign of the cross and drinks. Rising, he performs the forward-and-back gestures and leaves. If the same need to drink arises for anyone after the servants’ supper has ended, then, if he is in the community, he secretly seeks permission by a sign. If he cannot do this, he leads the prior aside for this very purpose; coming before him, he makes the customary inclination at the proper place, and, when he is going to drink, carries out the rest as prescribed above.

After the conference, whoever has need to drink, as the community leaves, turns aside with the others a little before the chapter or its doorway [Col. 1107C]. There, after receiving permission, he asks the cellarer—or any one of those who turn aside—to come with him. Sitting at the very entrance at the end of the table, he says *Benedicite*, openly pronouncing the blessing with the sign of the cross, and drinks. Anyone else who drinks after the conference does the same. Thus, on returning from the refectory or from anywhere else—unless he is coming from a journey—if he arrives so late that he cannot say his confession outside the choir with someone before the *Gloria* of the first psalm, he enters according to custom and, standing in his place with the brother next to him standing above him, says the confession standing.

(UD.) But, to return to what was said above: the refectorer has several brothers under his direction who, with him, every day after chapter, lay out the tablecloths again at the end of each table [Col. 1107D]. When this has been done, they return to the chapter, since they are never absent when the signal is struck for speaking.

(Var.) When the signal has been struck, they return to the work they had begun. First, they carefully wipe the spoons with a clean cloth and put them down; they are not to be removed so long as a bowl remains visible before the prior. They also put down the loaves. If any are somewhat burnt, they have knives for this purpose with which they scrape them. They also have small cloths, which they first hang around their necks, so that while scraping the loaves they may properly lean them against their chests. They themselves must also serve bread, drink, and the other things belonging to them to those who have been bled and to the others who eat at this hour. After the Gospel of the principal Mass has been read, they distribute the drink according to the allotted portions.

Whatever they do of this kind, they always take care that no layman appears in the refectory at their invitation. If there are two meals, after *Benedicamus Domino*, as they leave for Vespers, they inspect all the tables to see whether anyone needs bread or drink. If someone has eaten his entire pound and drunk his allotted portion, half a pound is then added, and nothing is deducted from his portion; this must always be given on that occasion and, if necessary, increased. For even if they do not eat again at some time, they never omit drinking again.

* If anyone has a small amount left over from his pound, it is reserved for him who is going to supper [Col. 1108B], and is increased to the quantity of half a pound; nothing is deducted from anyone else, however much he may appear to have taken from it. If the refectorer and his assistants are insufficient for carrying out what has been written, other brothers, when asked by the refectorer, do not refuse to come to their aid. He must always have candlesticks and candles supplied by the sacristan, so that whenever necessary he can set them down lit, whether for those eating supper or those drinking.

Whenever a charitable drink is served, he and one of his assistants pour it into small vessels (*mediolis*) [Note: [Col. 1108D] Victorius, cited above, p. 156 n.]. Two of them also season with mustard or vinegar whatever dish is suitable for it. It belongs to him alone to strike the little bell, which hangs for this sole purpose at the end of the refectory.

(UD. Var.) Immediately after the general blessing he strikes it once, so that, warned by this, the brothers may rise to serve the drink. This little bell is struck for the blessing of the drink on every feast celebrated in copes or albs and on the three days of the Rogations; likewise on every major anniversary. It is not, however, observed in this way if such a drink is served for the lord abbot, or for a prior returning from a journey or from the infirmary, or by order of the cellarer, or if some other familiar offers us a charitable drink, unless it is a feast of twelve lessons. But the refectorer, standing, raises his arm with his hand extended as though holding a cup, thus giving the signal for serving the drink. At this, without waiting for the bell to be struck, the brothers bring drink in their own bowls.

When the brothers work after None, however, the procedure is different. After the community has entered the choir at the sound of the signal for Vespers, and after the prayer has been made and the cymbal struck, the refectorer goes ahead and prepares the customary vessels filled with drink. At his request, or even of their own accord, the brothers withdraw at the entrance, take them, and carry out the rest in the customary order. He must know that whenever the signal is struck for drink at the brothers’ preceding midday meal, a similar signal is nevertheless given at the following meal of the servants. He himself, or his assistant, when the brothers take their midday rest after the meal, does not fail to return to the refectory; after quickly completing the things belonging to him, he does not linger but goes to sleep.

When the community does not take its midday rest, whether it eats once or twice, he and his assistants return there, if necessary, to attend to the things belonging to them. They remove the spoons and wash them at the fountain, as well as those things that they removed after the meal. If there is only one meal, they also remove, as after supper, the tablecloths that they see to be empty. For the sake of removing them, however, no one should pass from table to table and join himself to another. After supper, he first puts on the nocturnal garments with the others; but in winter, coming to the refectory after *Benedicite* at Vespers, he first provides the brothers’ drink, and when Vespers has ended, he too puts on the nocturnal garments with the others. After supper he ensures that the tables are completely swept.

[Col. 1109B] It is his responsibility to keep the lord abbot’s knife and to bring him a bowl, as also a spoon. He alone, and no other, brings him bread with a hand towel; out of paternal reverence, the bread customarily requested by him should be better than the common bread. He must always have rye bread ready, so that, whenever someone gives a sign for it, or of his own accord for brothers whom he knows to enjoy eating it, he can immediately give it to them. For no kind of bread is eaten in the refectory that is not customarily brought by him; yet he brings it with a hand towel to no one except the lord abbot.

He himself customarily removes the leftover bread, both after the servants’ meal and after the brothers’ meal, using baskets, except when the leftovers belong to almsgiving. If it is very late, he may also remove the servants’ supper with the crumbs, so that they need not remain longer on this account. If someone happens to eat before the conference, the refectorer must provide him with bread and drink. Whoever eats afterward will receive what is necessary from the cellarer. At the Mandatum, he immediately follows the brother who goes out to strike the cymbal.

On Good Friday he washes the cymbal and the little bells, and ensures that wooden mallets, which he receives from the village dean, are kept in the same place. When guests arrive, he arranges for them to have a place in the choir according to what he sees being given to them; he himself also gives them a place to sit in the refectory. He returns their allotted portions newly washed, if they need to be washed. For this reason, whenever someone is either leaving or returning from a journey and receives a blessing, he or his assistant carefully observes who and how many brothers receive the blessing at that time [Col. 1109D], so that he may know which portions to set out, taking care never to place a brother at another brother’s table or below him without knowing his order.

It also belongs to him to change every Sunday and Thursday after chapter those hand towels that hang in the cloister for wiping hands. He must also know on which days the tables are to be completely covered with tablecloths. This is whenever all the brothers wear albs for either Mass on the feasts of saints that occur in Lent, on the vigils of the five principal feasts, and on five Sundays: the First Sunday of Advent, Septuagesima, Lent, Mid-Lent, and Palm Sunday. On other days, only half the tables are covered, apart from the principal table, and in such a way that neither bowls nor allotted portions are placed upon the tablecloths.

## CHAPTER L. On receiving persons

If any person is received with a procession, all the brothers put on albs. Unless the lord abbot commands it, no one is ever received in copes except a king, the pope, and the father of the monastery himself. The porter must take care that whoever is to be received is not too far away at the hour of reception.

When all have put on their vestments and gathered in the choir, those who serve in the procession stand in due order before the step, with their faces turned toward the community. The priest or deacon who carries the Gospel book stands in the middle; on either side of him stand those carrying the candlesticks, turned toward him. Those carrying the water and thurible stand at the outer ends, on either side. All these must be in copes, as must the lord abbot or, in his absence, the prior. As the person to be received approaches, all the bells begin to be rung. Then, as they go out, those carrying the water and thurible go first; they are followed by those carrying the candlesticks, with the Gospel book between the candlesticks, the lord abbot accompanying them. After them the priors proceed in the same order in which they ordinarily proceed to the cross [Col. 1110C]. While the others remain inside the church, the lord abbot, with the aforementioned procession, goes out to meet the person as far as the church doors.

If the person received is the pope, the king, or the father of the monastery, the entire community proceeds as far as the Gate of Paradise.

[Note: [Col. 1109D] The Gate of Paradise: Paradise was a four-sided portico in front of the Vatican basilica, built by Constantine the Great and restored by the Roman pontiffs Simplicius and Symmachus. Panvinus and Severanus discuss it in *The Seven Churches of the City*, and Paulus de Angelis in his notes on the Roman Canon. Furthermore, as is stated in no. 8 of the ancient prayer-book of the Basilica of Saint Peter [Col. 1110D], it was a four-sided portico-oratory of the basilica, called Paradise, from which the clergy proceeded in procession through Paradise from that oratory. Even today, among us, the four-sided atrium of the principal church is called by this same name, commonly *Paradeis Haeflin*.]

If the person is the pope or a bishop, a fan is given to him so that he may sprinkle himself. Otherwise, the person who sprinkles those receiving him offers the incense that has been placed there himself, regardless of the recipient’s rank. Then, after the Gospel book has been kissed and a chant has been begun, the procession returns. The lord abbot leads the person received by the hand as far as the carpet spread before the altar of the Holy Cross over the rushes. There he releases him, and the man prostrates himself for prayer. The abbot waits there until he has finished praying. Those serving in the procession stand here before the altar in the same order as above at the step. When the chant has ended, the bell-ringing stops, and one of the following little verses appropriate to the person received is added: “Our protector, look upon us, O God” (*Protector noster, aspice Deus*); “Let thy hand be upon us” (*Fiat manus tua super nos*); “May the Lord guard thy coming in and thy going out” (*Dominus custodiat introitum tuum et exitum*); “May thy priests be clothed with righteousness” (*Sacerdotes tui induant justitiam*).

All return silently to the choir, each to his own place, with the priors nearest [Col. 1111A] the principal altar. When the lord abbot and the person received, together with those serving in the procession, enter the choir last, a chant is begun again if the person received is the father of the monastery, a king, or an apostolic dignitary. If he is a bishop or abbot, the first psalm is sung. Meanwhile the lord abbot removes his vestments and, returning without delay after the first psalm and the Lord’s Prayer, adds, in the case of a bishop, one of the five verses mentioned above, provided that he has not previously said it. For an abbot, the verse *Salvum fac servum. Mitte ei Domine* is added, with the order appropriate to him. If a bishop and an abbot are received together, these verses are said: *Sacerdotes tui. Mitte eis*.

If the abbot or bishop belongs to our order, they lead him to whatever place he chooses. If he is the pope, a king, or a bishop of the clerical order, they lead him to a place previously and suitably prepared for this purpose with carpets and curtains. There, after the blessing has been given, he has something from divine law read before him. After three or four words have been read, the lord abbot signals the reader to finish the reading. After *Benedicite* has been said, he kisses the person received, and the other brothers who are with him likewise kiss him at his feet, once, first asking pardon, if he is a bishop or abbot; if he is a king or apostolic dignitary, they ask pardon both before and afterward. Then he speaks with him about whatever seems appropriate. Finally, he has him led to the guesthouse and ensures that he and all his companions are treated charitably and honorably.

It must be understood that no one who is making profession in Lent is received with chant or in albs; only those serving in the procession are clothed in albs and copes. Nor do we ever receive anyone with a procession after we have put on the nocturnal garments.

## CHAPTER LI. On the porter, that is, the guardian of the guesthouse

(UD. Var.) The guardian of the guesthouse, who by custom is a priest, receives with every kindness guests who arrive on horseback, monks and more honorable clerics who arrive on foot, the wives of the stewards, and all bearers of brief letters. He asks the cellarer for whatever is needed; and if the cellarer is absent, he asks the chamberlain, so that, if the place permits it, the item may be provided without any excuse. If the cellarer is absent and something needed immediately for the guests’ use is locked away, he does not hesitate, in such necessity, to break open the vessel in which he expects it to be kept, acting with pious force so that the integrity of charity may be preserved in every respect in showing hospitality to the guests.

It is also customary, if the cellarer has nothing to set before them, for the porter to come into the refectory before the abbot or prior and give a sign there. The presiding officer immediately signals him to take what has been placed before him. Yet he takes diligent care never to permit an outside monk to enter the cloister until he has carefully learned from him why he has come: whether he has arrived as a messenger, whether he intends to stay, or whether, while making a journey, he merely wishes to lodge.

(UD.) If he seeks only this last thing, the porter leads him into the cloister without delay and without permission [Col. 1112A]. If he does not know our order, the porter first humbly explains our custom to him: namely, that, if he wishes, when entering the church he should ask pardon at the threshold and prostrate himself in prayer, if it is a feast day. He remains continually beside him and shows him in which places he should pray: first at the Holy Cross, then in the choir at the principal altar, if the community is not there and the church is not closed; if the church is open and some laypeople are inside, only at the altar on the right side of the choir; and at Saint Mary’s in the middle of that chapel.

If he arrives for this reason while the brothers are taking their midday rest, he is introduced after None. If his arrival for the same reason is recognized as occurring after Compline, he leaves the cloister that night and remains outside. On the following day, before Prime—or at another time before Terce—he is introduced to pray in the same manner and to receive a verse after each Hour.

If such a guest wishes to remain in the monastery for some time for whatever reason, he may be of such a status that entry is not readily granted even if he is an abbot. He remains outside for as long as seems good to the lord abbot and is introduced afterward. Because of the long interval between his arrival and introduction, he does not observe the prescribed order of prayers. Even if he has his own chaplain, the prior provides another for the abbot, who carries before him at night the lamp received from the chamberlain; through this attendant’s diligence in other matters pertaining to the order, the guest’s ignorance is also assisted.

[Col. 1112C] When the time for the meal arrives, the prior and abbot enter the refectory together, and he proceeds with the prior at an equal pace to the table. When the prior sits at the little bell, the guest sits on his left and gives the blessing to the reader. If two chaplains have come with him, they sit together, as do the other guests, although in the choir and at the conference they may, according to the prior’s judgment, be separated from one another. If there are more than the number stated, they are not all seated together.

If he arrives at the hour when the servants have already sat down to eat, the prior meanwhile detains him in spiritual conversation. After the servants have eaten, the guest eats as well, sitting at the head of either of the upper tables, with his companions seated beside him. If he arrives so late that he cannot eat before the conference, he waits until after Compline. Having received the blessing, he eats sitting in the place mentioned above, though no other brother may sit there eating at that time; rather, the other brother sits at the end of the outermost table. If he arrives during the servants’ meal so late that they cannot fully serve him a meal, when they rise he remains at the presiding officer’s signal and stands bowed until they have passed by; having eaten, he finishes the verse with its psalm before the same table.

If the abbot mentioned above seeks our society, after the matter of the order has been discussed in chapter, the prior, as he sees fit, sends for him. When he comes into chapter, both he and his companions—those inferior to him prostrating themselves—ask pardon [Col. 1113A] for entering that society. After pardon has been requested and the desired admission granted, they rise. The prior, as would the lord abbot if he were present, and the entire community must rise and stand until he and his companions have received brotherhood. After they have received it, as is customary, he is asked, with the book, to sit, and he is not permitted to ask pardon again. His companions, however, withdrawing to the lectern, ask pardon three times, on their hands and knees, facing the prior, to his right and left, while the brothers opposite rise slightly and incline. Even if the chapter must be ended quickly, a place to sit is nevertheless assigned to them.

In the church, the abbot is given a place to stand beside the lord abbot’s seat, on the right, whether the latter is present or absent, so that he may impose the antiphon, give the blessing to the readers [Col. 1113B], and place incense in the thurible. The keeper of the book cupboard must take care not to admit him to a reading, responsory, Gospel, principal Mass, or early Mass without the prior’s consent; he may, however, impose this duty upon an abbot of our congregation himself. In every procession he proceeds with a pastoral staff and the same vestments and insignia as the lord abbot, whether the latter is present or absent.

A monastic guest who remains with us for some time reads lessons, sings responsories and private Masses at the direction of the keeper of the book cupboard, and, if he wishes, joins him in directing the choir. If he is found doing anything contrary to the Rule or the order, he is admonished several times in words so that he may correct it; if he does not correct it, he is dealt with according to the Rule [Col. 1113C].

(UD. Var.) A guest who is going to eat in the refectory, if he is a cleric, also puts on clerical dress, namely a surplice and a cope over it. Brought to the door of the cloister, he waits until he is invited, so that the lord abbot—or, in his absence, the prior—may offer him water for his hands. The prior also goes ahead to strike the little bell. When it is heard, the guardian of the guesthouse brings in the guest. If he is not a bishop or abbot, they stand until the verse has ended beside the entrance to the refectory: the guest upright, the guardian inclined, as is the community. When the verse has ended, he leads him to sit at the principal table.

* When this has been done, he goes to his own place and, after sitting, performs the forward-and-back gestures. If he is a bishop, he gives the blessing to the reader. Whatever the brothers’ food may be, the guest is to be served generously together with the prior. When the brothers rise from the table, the guardian of the guesthouse leaves last, walking slowly with him [Col. 1113D] and singing the psalm *Laudate*, which he finishes in the guest auditorium in the manner in which the community finishes it with the verse, without an inclination. The same is done for pilgrim monks and clerics, except that they are brought in with their bags and without surplices. No secular layman is permitted to eat in our refectory.

Whenever a guest is going to eat there, the prior or porter must notify the refectorer. If fellowship is granted to lay clerics in chapter, they do not ask pardon.

(UD.) If they eagerly wish to see the cloister’s workshops, after permission has been requested, the guardian of the guesthouse leads them, at one of the two Masses, first into the almonry, then into the cellar, kitchen, refectory, novices’ cell, dormitory, and infirmary. Where the brothers do not speak, he too says not a word. He takes every care not to introduce anyone into the cloister wearing spurs or only breeches. When bishops, dukes, counts, and other persons of high standing arrive, two candles burn continually before them until they have been placed in bed. Another candle, which is to burn there throughout the night, must also be provided. The guardian of the guesthouse obtains these candles from the sacristan and administers them. If he does not find them readily available, he takes them wherever they are found, without incurring blame. The sacristan also gives them a light that burns throughout the night whenever some brothers sleep in the guesthouse, as often happens when novices or other brothers come to our cells to make their profession.

Before guests depart, he supplies new horseshoes for all who have unshod animals. He must close the cloister door every night after Compline, as well as the door of the church vestibule; his servant likewise closes the outer gate of the walls. The cloister is never opened before the sound of the bell or, at another time, before the litany has ended. He secures the outer door of the guest auditorium before chapter. While the brothers are in chapter, if anyone knocks, it is his duty to rise, and, after permission to leave has been requested by a sign, to open the door for him. The same applies at midday: [Col. 1114C] he secures the cloister door, but not before the servants’ meal has ended.

## CHAPTER LII. On the almoner

(UD.) Just as all who travel on horseback are received by the guardian of the guesthouse, so all who travel on foot are to be received by the almoner, who is a priest, except the wives of stewards and bearers of brief letters. All monks and more honorable clerics, however, are gathered by the guardian of the guesthouse, as stated above, even if they arrive on foot. If some of them happen to have horses or donkeys in their company, the guardian of the guesthouse receives and cares for the horses with an equal number of men [Col. 1114D], while the almoner cares for the donkeys—unless something is perhaps contributed with them for charity to the monastery; in that case, the guardian of the guesthouse receives and cares for them with an equal number of men.
