So that the almoner may have the means to provide what is necessary for these people and for the others who belong to his charge, it has been established that, apart from the tithes assigned by the canonical statutes to individual churches within whose boundaries our properties are situated, tithes of all goods brought to the monastery and for our use from whatever source are to be given to the almoner: namely, of grain, wine, oil, legumes, fruit, vegetables, fish, animals, vessels, clothing, money, gold and silver, iron or any other metal, and hay [Col. 1115A] that grows in the cellarer’s obedience, or an equal amount from the meadows. The cellarer must also give each year, on the Nativity of Saint Mary, one cartload as the tithe of hay, or one solidus . . .

Finally, everything that grows, is raised, or is produced by manual labor within the cell is tithed; everything brought from outside or from our properties; and everything that novices bring when coming for conversion. From these goods, however, the chamberlain is to exempt from the tithe the amount needed to clothe them: thirty solidi if the person is to become a monk, and the value of one talent if he is to become one of the outside brothers. The only things not tithed are those purchased with money or other goods that have already been tithed; everything obtained from animals already tithed—food or drink, milk, cheeses, eggs, wool [Col. 1115B], honey, wax, and other similar products; and everything made into food or drink from grain that has already been tithed.

Also exempt are vessels, cloaks, clothing, wax, incense, money specifically paid from the census to the church, and anything else assigned to the church’s service. If anything from these or from other ecclesiastical goods is sold for the brothers’ use, the money itself is tithed. Whatever is offered at the altars, if it pertains to food or drink, is handed over to the cellarer, except for loaves that are not whole, which, as stated above, are given to the almoner.

(UD. Var.) In addition to all this, from the food remains left over by brothers eating lunch or supper in the refectory or infirmary—except for meat served to the sick for restoration—the almoner is given daily half of the cooked dishes [Var.], which are nevertheless removed after being tasted, and whatever bread, less than a quarter, remains for each person who has eaten.

Also, on every Friday of Advent and of Lent, and on the vigils of the five feasts—namely the Ascension of the Lord, Pentecost, the Apostles Peter and Paul, the Assumption of Saint Mary, and All Saints—the bread leftovers are given in their entirety on Good Friday and on the day when one of our brothers, provided he is a monk, is buried among us, together with whatever bread and cooked food and whatever drink remains toward evening. If such a burial happens to occur on one of the days mentioned above [Col. 1115D], what was to have been given for the fast is supplied on another day.

A full daily portion is also given for thirty days, whether the deceased was a monk or one of the outside brothers.

[Note: [Col. 1115] *Praebenda*: a daily portion of food and drink provided to a monk.]

The same is done on the anniversary, but only for monks.

Thirty portions are also given each year to the almoner for familiar dead: in Lent, after the Nativity of the Apostles Peter and Paul, and after the feast of All Saints. The service of three poor persons, even if it is not performed by the brothers throughout the whole year, nevertheless never ceases as almsgiving. For although the almoner’s servant does not wash their feet from the vigil of All Saints until the beginning of Lent, he nevertheless gives them a pound and an allotted portion with some food, as throughout the year, and a pound of such bread as the brothers have in the refectory.

When bread leftovers are given as alms in the refectory, the almoner himself comes on the following day to the infirmary during the early Mass with his servant and takes, for the use of the poor, whatever bread and drink remained for the sick the previous day.

Every day, if he is literate, he asks the reader or the keeper of the book cupboard how many names of deceased brothers were pronounced in chapter that day, so that, to avoid the negligence of error and forgetfulness, he too may write the same number of portions on a tablet that hangs permanently for this purpose before the cellar [Col. 1116B]. If the cellarer cannot give them all in full on that day, he erases those already received and leaves standing the remainder that he will receive on another occasion.

The almoner administers these matters as part of his obedience. He has all underground water conduits and the drainage channel cleaned whenever necessary; he has the dirt beneath the washing place removed; he has sand placed beneath the small mortar into which liquid foods are poured in the refectory, to prevent foul smells; and he has stones and similar useless objects removed from the cloister. He must also see to it that running water for the brothers’ privies never fails. Therefore, in summer, when the water diminishes because of dryness, he frequently has the channels closed, so that, after being held back for a while, the water may come with greater force.

He must also provide the same privies with soft hay cut a second time from the meadow, and in no small quantity; he also has the herbs that grow in the cloister. If he cannot obtain hay, the brothers bring wooden shavings. He provides vessels for receiving the blood of those who are bled and, when anyone has been bled, has that blood poured the following day during the early Mass into a pit made solely for this purpose.

He must provide rushes both for the church and for the cloister. Seven times a year he has the church, the chapel of Saint Mary with the other chapels, the cloister, the novices’ cell, the infirmary, and the refectory swept and their floors completely covered with newly acquired rushes: namely, at Christmas, Easter, Pentecost, the Nativity of Saint John, the Assumption of Saint Mary, and All Saints [Col. 1116D]. Moreover, on all feasts at which we sing two responsories in succession, he sprinkles rushes throughout the entire church, the chapel of Saint Mary, and the whole cloister. On feasts celebrated in copes or albs, and on all the Sundays of Sexagesima, he does not neglect to spread rushes through the churches, from the door of the principal church to the entrance of the chapter, in its middle, and wherever necessary. Whether there is one meal or two, he must do this during the midday meal; but he says absolutely nothing in the cloister unless, while the others are silent, he is administering rushes or something else belonging to his obedience.

Nor does he neglect to have mats spread in the church, in the cloister, [Col. 1117A] in the chapter house and refectory as well, over the seats, on the vigil of All Saints; or to provide brooms with which the drains, latrines, regular kitchen, and lavatory may be cleaned. He also provides baskets in the refectory for receiving leftover bread. He supplies small leafy branches for driving away flies in summer, small dishes and fans for brushing away crumbs, and whenever necessary has cobwebs removed from the cloister, dormitory, and novices’ quarters.

On the holy day of Pentecost, during the hymn “Come, Creator” (*Veni, Creator*), he must refresh with bread, meat, and wine, if available, as many poor people as he knows there are brothers in the monastery at that time. He also provides for lights to be prepared in the dormitory, infirmary, cellar, and the [Col. 1117B] novices’ quarters; his servant must carry their lamps from each place whenever necessary, with him going ahead, during the earlier Mass, and return them filled with tallow received from the chamberlain and prepared for lighting.

Under his supervision the graves of all those to be buried in the designated place—both brothers and outsiders—are dug. But for the burial only of the poor, pilgrims, and others who die in the almonry, he himself provides the wood; for everyone else the village dean does so. He also never fails to make a circuit of the whole village once a week, looking to see whether some poor person is lying sick somewhere; and if it is a man, he enters to visit him; if a woman, he stands at the door and sends his servant to her with bread [Col. 1117C] and wine, and with such other provisions as he has been able to find of the best quality.

## CHAPTER LIII. Concerning those who hear the regular office at Saint Mary’s

Those who are permitted to hear the regular office at Saint Mary’s have different reasons for going there, and accordingly observe the rule there in different ways with respect to the order of service. For, apart from the sick, who remain separated from the community for as long as they are ill, the others who receive this permission are divided into three groups. Nevertheless, in all other respects they attend the community: namely, the cellarer, chamberlain, granary-master, village dean, porter, infirmarian, and the man in charge of the masons’ work; also those who, exhausted by excessive labor in divine service, can offer no assistance to the choir in singing; and those who, because of some weakness, habitually cannot remain seated or standing within or outside the choir.

Thus, when the bell is rung for nocturns, all these come together in the church of Saint Mary and withdraw to that section of the building in which they are assigned a place in the choir. Each chooses, according to his rank, a place for prayer, whether he is to sit or prostrate himself, in the following manner.

If it is a feast of twelve lessons, those who are stronger sit on the misericords of the seats [Note: [Col. 1117D] See the note to chapter 29 of Book I]; but the weaker, having lowered the seats, lie upon them during prayer. If some still remain, [Col. 1118A] they fall to their knees and elbows in the middle, on the floor. All therefore maintain this posture of prayer in the same place, moving in succession to the left and right by turns, until they hear the sound of the second ringing. Then they all rise together, sign themselves, and, without moving to either side, make the prescribed movements forward and backward. None of them who has failed to take part in these prayers seeks pardon for this in the chapter house.

When the psalms preceding nocturns have been sung while seated, they rise at the ringing of the two bells and, from the beginning of nocturns to the end of the hymn that follows the psalm “Come” (*Venite*), they honor the office in this standing posture—except those who are so burdened by weakness of their limbs [Col. 1118B] that they cannot stand. Each also observes this standing posture of reverence at the chapter of these nocturns, and likewise at the beginning, chapter, and hymn of matins and of each of the hours, especially at “We praise you, O God” (*Te Deum laudamus*), “Whoever wishes” (*Quicumque vult*), “Blessed” (*Benedictus*), and “Magnifies” (*Magnificat*), unless he is weighed down by such weakness, as has been said.

During the singing, until the end of nocturns and matins, and after the completion of the other hours, anyone suffering some physical difficulty is not censured for relieving himself in whatever seated manner he can—for example, by leaning while seated on the floor against the stalls, a bench, or some other support, or by stretching out or drawing up his legs. [Col. 1118C]

When nocturns and matins and the other offices that must be sung have been completed, whether it is summer or winter, after the sick have settled themselves, the brothers exhausted by excessive labor in divine service, and likewise the officials mentioned above, resettle themselves with permission. The chamberlain sees to it that they have beds for this purpose in the infirmary or in the novices’ quarters. Yet they are not permitted, on account of any illness, to sleep upon a mattress, nor is anyone who is able to attend the community permitted to do so.

The others, however, who do not require this indulgence but have nevertheless been assigned there for the reason stated above, whether at their own request or through the abbot’s or prior’s spontaneous compassion, although temporarily separated from the community, must imitate it in this way: if, according to custom, that sick person ought to resettle himself, they must on no account presume to anticipate him without permission, nor may they sleep at all in their beds after matins if the order of the community forbids returning to sleep.

Meanwhile, seated in the church of Saint Mary, they withdraw to the infirmary—either to the dormitory or to the cloister—when the community arrives in procession, making way for it. When the community leaves, if the time is suitable, they return there and spend the intervening period and the remainder of the night. They also hear all the daytime hours there, except the officials and those who are such that they can attend in the choir, unless they anticipate the sick person’s meal. At each of these hours, except the first ringing of Prime, they always participate with the community, with which they are then present, saying before the choir the prayer that precedes the hour.

Sometimes, however, it happens that while Mass is being sung for the sick, the bell is rung for Prime—or, at another time, for Terce. Then, once the signal has been given, everyone except the sick and the others hearing that Mass makes the prescribed movements forward and backward and signs himself with the cross; nevertheless, they postpone singing the hour that is due until the Mass has ended. When it is over, both the sick and the others who have heard that Mass, making the movements forward and backward and signing themselves, all sing the same hour together.

Accordingly, once the hours have been sung, no one, except for great necessity, presumes to leave the church before the hour then being sung in the choir has ended, unless he is going to receive a blessing. If one of them arrives there after the *Gloria* of the first psalm, he takes care, if he is literate, to be able to enter the lesser choir; if illiterate, to come before the choir before that same *Gloria*. If he cannot even do this, he comes to the step. Then, withdrawing according to custom, he departs outside after performing what follows in the manner stated more fully elsewhere.

But if one of the officials has been working so far from his cell that he cannot arrive for the regular hour, he sings it where he is working. All the others, on hearing the signal, immediately come to the church to which they are assigned. Any travelers who arrive after the hour has ended may, according to custom, sing or hear that same hour at Saint [Col. 1119C] Mary’s church. They must hear the earlier and the principal Mass, as well as the hour that the sick sing before dinner, either before the choir or in the lesser choir; and they must also hear Vespers on the days of Lent, with the sole exception of the cellarer.

If it should sometimes happen that one of the officials is ordered by the lord abbot or prior to attend the company, he may hear the aforesaid hour with him, provided that the lord abbot or prior gives the instruction. But if any of those mentioned above are found to possess such strength that they can offer the others some assistance in hearing the chant, they are not only permitted to enter either choir for both Masses; even if they do not enter, they are reprimanded accordingly.

[Col. 1119D] Any one of the officials may, if he wishes, hear the Mass sung for the sick in the morning; some of them hear it elsewhere, where it is sung privately. On feasts of twelve lessons, these same officials and the other persons mentioned above who are able and willing come to the major church. If they are literate, they may enter either choir; if not, they may remain before the choir for both Vespers, as well as for matins and the other hours.

Moreover, if these feasts [Col. 1120A] are celebrated with albs and a procession, all whom illness does not prevent put on albs. When no procession takes place, this is not required of those among them who are illiterate. In the procession in which those wearing albs join the others—provided, however, that they hope to have places within the choir—they enter; in the procession conducted without albs, they turn aside before the choir.

Whenever any who are not illiterate officials hear the regular office at Saint Mary’s, they never dare omit wearing albs whenever the brothers generally put them on. Wearing albs, they attend with the others the office that occurs immediately before Terce, unless an illness then afflicts them so severely that it prevents them altogether from attending it; even then they do not dare omit it without permission.

No priest who regularly attends the hours at the aforesaid chapel may sing either the principal or the earlier Mass, except occasionally on feasts of twelve lessons; on those occasions the earlier Mass is sung immediately after chapter, with no hour preceding it. [Col. 1120B] If someone who hears the hours there by a granted privilege is ordered, because of illness, to rest for some time in the infirmary, he will retain the same Mass with his former permission when he returns, if the lord abbot granted him permission and if he has not yet recovered. No one except the lord abbot can grant this permission permanently.

## CHAPTER LIV. Concerning the chaplain of Saint Mary’s

The chaplain of Saint Mary’s always stands by the wall beside the left choir, on the western side, though not in the highest place—unless he surpasses the other men standing there in rank. The sick stand in that choir, as do the others, in which the station is located in the major church. The youths placed in custody stand before the stall [Col. 1120C], so that they can be seen by everyone. If he considers it necessary, the same chaplain will be able to see both the sick and the others who are there in both choirs.

He sings matins and the other regular hours aloud, but does not begin them until he knows that they have begun in the choir, except from Septuagesima to Easter. Then, after the bell has been dismissed, he immediately completes the prayer before nocturns and begins the psalmody; afterward he adds nocturns without delay. When these are finished, he inserts, with the familiar psalms, matins for All Saints, for Saint Mary, and for the dead, as he does throughout the whole winter. Then, after saying the prayer, he imposes the regular matins.

He arranges the rest in such a way that the familiar psalms belonging to Prime are sung before Prime, together with the seven penitential psalms and the litany. He hands the book from which the matins lessons are to be read to someone whom he knows to be suitable for this task. The responsories are to be sung by whichever brother is more knowledgeable in this matter. He ought to know that he must anticipate the proper time for singing by rising early. But when the responsory is finished, or even the invitatory, he does not make the prescribed movements forward and backward. The youth, if one is present, reads and sings standing the verses and short responsories, as well as the lessons concerning Saint Mary and those for the office of the dead with its responsories.

Thus, in winter, after the chaplain has finished the matins of the sick and the other appended services that follow, he adds Prime, even though very often a considerable part of the night still remains. Since he never returns to bed after matins to rest without permission, unless the community has done so, he remains in the same church until the procession is conducted there. Then he goes out in front of the chapel toward the cloister of the sick, or into the infirmary itself, and waits there until the community goes up to the dormitory. If it is not a time when the community ought to sleep after matins, he himself waits in the same chapel as long as the others do.

It is also his responsibility to sing Mass for the sick every day at first light; on feasts of twelve lessons and vigils, on the fasts of the four Ember seasons, and in Lent, always the Mass of the day; on other days, the Mass for the dead or whichever Mass he wishes. If a feast of twelve lessons occurs on a fast day, he sings there a Mass of that fast. At each Mass he does not merely read the chant, as at other private Masses, but sings it. He always has all the things necessary for Mass stored there; wine and water must also never be lacking there at night, so that, should anyone need to communicate a sick person, [lacuna], they may be readily available.

If it should ever happen that Prime is to be rung earlier than usual—or indeed whenever he wishes—he rises before the sound, wherever he is sleeping, and, immediately after washing his hands at the brothers’ lavatory and saying the prayer, puts on his alb and stole before Prime is rung. For if he has not put on the stole before the ringing of Prime, he will not sing without permission; instead, he sends his assistant to request permission.

He must also not fail to sing the other hours at their proper times, except when, because of some feast, he is wearing an alb or cope and has attended the community. Then they themselves will sing Terce and also Sext, as they do when he has been prevented by some accident from arriving there in time.

The chaplain must also be present every day at both Masses in one or the other choir, except when he must sing Sext for the sick during the principal Mass, or Vespers in Lent. He must nevertheless afterward be present in the choir or before the choir, unless some necessity intervenes.

He must also know that on the day of the Nativity of the Lord, during its octave, and on the feast of All Saints, the daily office of Saint Mary is to be recited, and that it is always to be sung in one and the same manner—except in Advent and during the Nativity season. Then the chant appropriate to that season is sung concerning her. He must also know that at matins of this office on feasts of twelve lessons the hymn “We praise you, O God” (*Te Deum laudamus*) is not to be omitted, and that after *Verba mea* the annual prayer is to be said daily by him, as in the community.

Likewise, whenever, on account of tribulation, the three psalms—namely, “O Lord, how they have multiplied” (*Domine, quid multiplicati*), “God is our refuge” (*Deus noster refugium*), and “To you I have lifted up” (*Ad te levavi*)—are to be sung [Col. 1122A] after chapter, these are not to be neglected by the sick. Instead, after the regular hour preceding chapter, they too are to sing them prostrate, if it is such a day. Nevertheless, whenever “My words” (*Verba mea*) is to be sung after chapter for a deceased person whose memorial notice is presented in that chapter, the sick do not sing the hours, nor the psalter on Good Friday.

Furthermore, whenever the regular fast is observed, and from the Ides of September to the Kalends of November, and also from Septuagesima to Lent, after the sick persons’ Vespers have ended, he does not delay performing the office of the dead before they go out to dine. He must also sing “I shall please the Lord” (*Placebo Domino*) at second Vespers of a feast of twelve lessons when, on the following day, the commemoration of a deceased person is to be observed with the greatest solemnity.

If any verse or psalm is omitted in the regular hours at Saint Mary’s, the chaplain himself and the others who come to chapter, if they recognize that they have been at fault in this matter, seek pardon.

## CHAPTER LV. Concerning the infirmarians, or the sick

[Col. 1122B]

**(UD. var.)** The infirmarian, who must be a priest, has a cook and kitchen assigned separately for the service of the sick. He himself also asks the chamberlain every day for whatever he may need, so that what is to be prepared for the sick’s refreshment may be prepared in good time.

The sick, although they hear Mass every day that the aforesaid chaplain sings for them, nevertheless always remain at matins until the first prayer after Communion has been completed. When they enter the church for this Mass, the senior among them—if he is literate—sprinkles them with holy water, even if they were sprinkled at dawn in the chapel. After all have taken their seats, it is left to their discretion whether they sit there with their heads covered or uncovered, and likewise at Saint Mary’s. There too, if someone is so weak that he must rest, he may lie upon the rushes, which are constantly prepared there for such persons in the manner of a bed-covering by the storekeeper or his assistant, with a fur garment placed over his head.

It must nevertheless be understood that on the day when they are to be shaved, or when shaving is to take place, they do not come to the morning Mass but are shaved in the meantime. They are shaved, as stated above, on the day before the community, unless some feast or deceased person happens to prevent this. For this purpose the infirmarian keeps razors and towels separately; the servant sharpens them and distributes them to the barbers at the time of shaving.

On the day when the brothers are commonly shaved in the cloister, the sick also speak from the striking of the board until the psalmody begins. But whenever the community has eaten twice, or has completed a general fast, those who are not lying in bed do not fail to attend the principal Mass until the Gospel has been read; then they withdraw to Saint Mary’s to sing Sext and do not delay any longer before dining, except on Good Friday. [Col. 1122D] Then they remain there until the end of the office, and barefoot.

**(UD.)** If the community has fasted until None, they sing Sext after chapter—or, if chapter is being held, before Terce—and, from the Ides of September to the Kalends of October, after Terce, standing, with the prayer said beforehand and again at the same prayer. Likewise, at any hour, if it is a time for prostration, those who are not so ill prostrate themselves over the stalls and make the prescribed movements forward and backward. Those who are so sick that they cannot do this merely sign themselves with the sign of the cross while seated; when the hour is finished, they refresh themselves.

On every feast of twelve lessons, as soon as they hear the sound, they rise and, after sprinkling themselves with holy water, come to Saint Mary’s. They perform only one prayer standing—or, if they are so weak, seated, or on ordinary days when the signal is given, prostrate. **(UD.)** They never take their midday rest longer than the community does.

At dinner they have three courses, and at supper one. At supper in the monastery, after Vespers, when *Benedicamus Domino* has been said, they hasten to come at all times so that there is never any need to omit the reading at collation. For as soon as they have finished singing Vespers, the infirmarian, taking the servants and, if necessary, his assistant, hurries to the kitchen, so that he may bring in good time whatever they need for food.

If a mandate is to be carried out—namely, after Vespers and the other appended services, to wash their feet—they do not delay going; in Lent, however, they do this after dinner. Every day during the aforesaid period, those who wish anticipate their cooking or go to the latrines, so that when he returns they do not delay being refreshed.

**(UD.)** Those who remain in the infirmary without eating meat and are not healthy enough to eat with the others in the refectory are refreshed at the same times as the others. In Lent all the sick [Col. 1123C] sing Vespers immediately after the Gospel and go to the table without delay. For after None they sing the psalm “O God, our ears have heard” (*Deus auribus nostris*). Outside Lent, if a general fast occurs, as during the Ember seasons, they likewise sing None after the Gospel of the principal Mass and then refresh themselves. **(var.)**

Some sick persons are such that they no longer leave the infirmary. If they recover, they are nevertheless permitted to sit in the community in the morning, to offer in their proper order at the morning Mass, and to come to chapter; yet they eat and are shaved with the other sick, do not put on daytime shoes, and do not carry knives with them.

These persons always receive the Lord’s Body at Saint Mary’s, except on Good Friday. [Col. 1123D] Then, in the major church, they receive Communion according to the customary practice, like the others. Those who remain there either for a time of rest or to regain strength by eating meat are deprived both of Communion and of confession, unless one of the five greatest feasts occurs. Then each confesses in the infirmary before his own bed to the infirmarian or to the chaplain of Saint Mary’s. For this reason, on Sundays as well as on the aforesaid feasts, two or as many consecrated offerings as the matter requires are consecrated there.

**(UD.)** If someone’s illness is plainly so severe, yet does not greatly impair the strength required for fasting—as in the loss or blindness of an eye—he is not forbidden to eat once when the community eats once. Meanwhile, while the other sick are being refreshed, he remains in the church of Saint Mary’s; when the Gospel of the principal Mass has ended, he is refreshed. If he is to eat twice, after receiving permission for this from the prior through the infirmarian, he thereafter refreshes himself with the others whenever he wishes.

**(UD.)** But to return to the infirmarian: after saying the prayers at nocturns, he takes the *absconsa* and goes around the beds of all the sick to see whether any of them has not yet risen and for what reason he has remained behind. Returning from there to the chapel, he looks over both the sick and those who are well there; if he finds anyone asleep, he awakens him by dragging the *absconsa* along the wall or over the stall. The same round is made again when the second nocturn is nearly finished and during the matins praises, at the last psalm. It is also his responsibility, if someone cannot rise from bed, to come at first light with the cellarer—as I have already said elsewhere—so that they may agree on what is to be prepared for that person’s refreshment.

## CHAPTER LVI. The order in which the office is sung for a sick person lying in bed

For such a sick person the prior will designate one or two of those who are permitted to hear the regular office at Saint Mary’s, to sing the hours for him for as long as seems appropriate to them. One of them must be a priest or deacon, on account of what is to be read there on feasts of twelve lessons.

If no such persons are found there, two somewhat more advanced brothers are to be appointed by the prior every Saturday, after the infirmarian has reminded him of this matter, to sing the regular hours for the sick person throughout the entire week. These brothers must carefully observe the times appointed for this purpose: on ordinary nights, in both winter and summer, they must not delay coming there after the second nocturn with its collect has ended; on feasts of twelve lessons, after the hymn *Te decet laus* has been said, together with the following collect. They make the prescribed movements forward and backward and, after singing the regular office *in directum* [reading uncertain], must join the community at Saint Mary’s, if this can be done.

For the remaining hours they do not leave the choir until after *Benedicamus Domino*. Compline is excepted, however, because the infirmarian sees to it that it is sung there by one of the sick. Whoever sings it, whatever his rank may be, also adds the blessing.

The aforesaid brothers also sing Terce together with Prime for that sick person on feasts of twelve lessons throughout the summer and during octaves, in order to anticipate dinner. In winter, whenever there is an interval, they add Prime to matins; each day, when there is only one meal, they add None to Sext, except when the brothers take their midday rest.

If there is a sick person who is not lying in bed but nevertheless cannot fast, he sings Terce by himself if he is literate. If not, he listens to it from one of the sick—a practice that is also permitted to any of them who arrives late at the chapel—and he does not delay dining any longer, provided that he has received permission from the infirmarian. But if it is necessary for him to take something as a remedy for some illness, he will not wait for Terce on this account, if that seems appropriate.

## CHAPTER LVII. Further concerning the infirmarian, or the sick

**(UD.)** At the proper hour the infirmarian goes to the kitchen assigned to his office, to make the fire and prepare what must be prepared. At the hour of refreshment the sick immediately turn aside to the lavatory in their cloister; those who wish sharpen their knives on the whetstone that continually hangs there on a chain, and thus each approaches his own table.

Those who eat meat are ordered to sit separately from the others. For, so that they may not burden one another on account of their different illnesses, they remain separated in different houses joined together under one building. One house is specially assigned for the servants who attend the sick: they sleep and eat there, wash the dishes, heat the water in which the dead are washed, and do the brothers’ cooking. There is a certain open place in the middle, covered on every side, where the brothers customarily let blood, inspect their cooking, and wash and anoint with cold water the legs of those who need it.

**(UD.) (var.)** The infirmarian, with his assistants, brings and sets before the sick the courses that are to be served, both to those who receive meat and to those who do not. The servants likewise bring them, but do not set them before the sick. When this serving begins, either the sick themselves or the infirmarian pronounces “Bless” (*Benedicite*), and a blessing is said over the food. Whoever began the reading before the meal finishes it after the meal. At every feast of twelve lessons something from the feast is read there.

If someone happens to be absent during the blessing and arrives afterward, he completes, with the help of someone else, what he would have said with the others, but more quietly.

None of them presumes to sit down to eat wearing only his cuculla and fur garment, nor to speak in bed, except someone so weighed down by illness that he is compelled on account of it to eat while sitting in bed. None of them is permitted to give any food or drink to a servant. During the meal, if a general dish or pottage is served, he is not deprived of the blessing. If those who usually refresh themselves with meat abstain from meat on some occasion, they observe the same manner of blessing.

Whenever the brothers generally receive a *pietantia*, the sick also receive one. If, while they are sitting at table, a memorial notice for a deceased person is brought and the board is struck to summon the brothers, they do not rise; afterward, however, they perform the same office with three lessons. None of them should rise from the table except for the greatest necessity, nor fold his napkin while anyone at all, even the least important person, is still eating there.

When the meal is finished, if they are not too ill, they rise and begin the verse; **(UD.)** after the psalm has ended, however, they finish it while seated at the *Gloria*, and do not make the prescribed movements forward and backward.

Whatever remains from the food, if it is of a quantity worth keeping, the infirmarian stores away. He has a small cupboard in which he stores such things, as well as candles and apples. Pepper, cinnamon, ginger, and other healthful roots are rarely or never absent from it, so that something that may perhaps benefit a sick person is always ready at hand—whether to give to someone suddenly struck by an attack, as may happen, or to prepare a medicinal mixture for him if that is useful. The chamberlain willingly provides the infirmarian with the means for this.

He also has a cellar in which leftover drink, tableware, and other such things are to be kept. He gives the servants who attend the sick a *pietantia* from the food left over. As for the remainder, he returns the bread and meat to the cellarer; but on those days when bread is given to the almoner in the refectory, he gives it to the almoner. If there is any meat that can decently be returned as such, it is kept for them.

**UD. (var.)** If the lord abbot or prior is in the infirmary and omits the common meal on their account, this is not counted against him. After Compline he sees to it that holy water is sprinkled over all the beds of the sick, either by himself or by some brother sleeping there, except on Sundays. When the time has come for everyone to have settled down, he or his assistant carefully makes the rounds of the necessary places with the *absconsa*.

It is unnecessary to say that each of them may drink during the day, whenever necessary, and after collation, with permission, since no such rule has been imposed on the sick. For this reason, after Compline the infirmarian arranges for several measures of drink to be placed ready, so that anyone suffering thirst may quench it even during the night. He must know, however, that at that time he should bless the drink only by himself.

The infirmarian must also observe that he does not speak with any sick person during the time of silence, except concerning what cannot be communicated by signs by both of them in turn; the exception is someone burdened by such an illness that, because of his sickness itself, he cannot observe this rule. He does not place a mattress beneath anyone who is very ill without permission; nevertheless, he permits anyone unable to fast to anticipate the others by dining earlier.

The sick are likewise absolutely forbidden to speak to one another during the time of silence, especially while eating. At that time, however, they are not forbidden to speak with the infirmarian about what is necessary, according to the procedure stated above, without permission. On the first day of the fast they too receive ashes, not barefoot. On the Purification of Saint Mary they are last to offer candles, and on Palm Sunday they are last to offer palm branches. If anyone lacks the strength to fast, he does not receive ashes. If anyone can be refreshed during Lent by another food, he uses milk or some similar food.

On every day of the regular fast, after hearing the second signal, they say the prayer at None before beginning. They hang their garments that are to be suspended in their own cloister; those who sleep there by a granted indulgence, however, do not do so. They are also especially warned never to speak there without permission on the pretext of the indulgence granted to them.

None of them washes his hands at the sickroom lavatory except from some necessity, such as a flow of blood. Likewise, those who attend to their cooking wash there. The sick may always put on their woolen garments after their own matins.

## CHAPTER LVIII. Concerning the servants who attend the sick

According to custom, there are as many servants belonging to the sickhouse as are sufficient for the service of the sick. **(UD.)** If they wish, they hear Mass daily at Saint Mary’s and receive the kiss of peace; and whenever it seems appropriate, they may receive the Lord’s Body.

Every day, unless there is a general fast, they taste a little food and drink during the morning Mass, so that they may more easily await the general dinner. What service they render to the sick must not be passed over in silence.

Accordingly, at nocturns, when they hear the signal, one of them sees to it that a light is kindled in the necessary places and, when necessary, also in their cloister. After nocturns have ended, the infirmarian does this. At that time, unless it is winter, the aforesaid servant does not neglect to prepare a fire for them.

None of them presumes to remain in the infirmary during chapter, unless some sick person is close to death. Then one of them remains, and one of the infirmarian’s assistants remains with him, so that he cannot steal away to chapter and listen to something that it would not be proper for him to hear. After part of the chapter has been completed, the infirmarian returns to him, so that he too may be present at the same chapter.

When chapter is finished, they spread the tablecloths over the boards and set out the bread and spoons. They postpone filling the measures with drink and placing them on the tables until the very hour of dinner, because only then do they first bring that drink from the cellar.

They are also disciplined in this way: as long as the sick are eating, they never sit or stand before them; when one of them has finished the task for which he was summoned, he immediately goes out again. During the meal they set before the sick no food except salt, vinegar, and mustard, if needed; yet they themselves remove the bowls and anything similar. The measures remain on the tables until after supper, so that those who wish may drink. Only then are they removed and emptied together.

If a general mandate is to be carried out at that time, before the sick begin supper, whether in summer or winter, these same servants wash each person’s feet with water and dry them with a linen cloth.

After the community has entered the refectory once the mandate has been completed, the servants take in the cellar, at the infirmarian’s request, the wine that they are to drink as their charitable portion. Having brought it, they pour it into bowls and offer it to the sick. The sick do not bless this drink before everyone has taken it in his hands, and they do this publicly, just as they do whenever they drink together or individually.

Whatever remains for those drinking, the same cupbearers, sitting in the house where they usually eat, drink as their charitable portion. None of them, however, tastes any food or drink there unless he also sleeps there.

**(UD.)** One of them is assigned especially to wash the cloths necessary for the brothers’ cooking, to make the fire, and to heat the water in which the dishes are to be washed. He is strictly forbidden to presume to touch any of the food or drink belonging to the sick.

# CHAPTER LIX. Concerning a brother whom illness overtakes at night or during the day

*If a brother is seized in the dormitory at night by such an illness that he cannot remain there until Matins without disturbing the brothers, the brothers sleeping near him, after obtaining permission from the prior, immediately lead him to the infirmary. But if he suffers from an illness so moderate that he can await Matins, as soon as he knows that the three prayers have been completed, he informs the prior of his illness and, immediately at the prior’s command, is led to the infirmary by one of the brothers. The same is done with a young brother entrusted to custody if he falls ill in this way, after the custodian has obtained permission. A brother who begins to fall so ill that he cannot remain with the community discloses his illness to the prior—or, if he prefers, asks pardon in chapter and shows that he is ill. If his illness is visibly of such a kind, the prior, either on his own initiative or after being warned by another, immediately orders him to go to the infirmary. Otherwise, he may remain outside the choir, so that he may sit according to his wish.*

[Col. 1128C] *(UD. variant.) The cellarer takes care that he not be left in the refectory without an extra allowance. When two or three days have passed, if he has not improved, he again asks pardon for the same reason and is ordered to go to the infirmary. But if his illness should increase so greatly even on that same day, he enters, at the prior’s command, the infirmary where those who lack meat in their meals live together, accompanied by someone who goes with him and shows him the way. *For at whatever hour it seems expedient to anyone then fully governing the order, he causes any sick brother to go to the infirmary.*

A similar procedure is observed for one who leaves the choir during Matins because of illness, or who, compelled by the same necessity, does not enter the choir. For this reason he asks pardon in chapter on the following day, and when the prior asks him whether he is better, if he answers, “Yes, lord,” he is ordered to go and sit; but if he says no, he is ordered to remain outside the choir for a while.

[Col. 1128D] It must be understood, however, that if someone is ordered to go to the infirmary during chapter, he does not return to his place until that chapter has ended, unless he hears from the prior that he ought to go there at once. Then, after making a reverence toward his place, both before and behind him, he departs without anyone leading him—unless he is a young brother placed in custody, in which case the infirmary attendant follows him. If necessary, he settles himself temporarily in a bed, provided he finds no one lying there; for no one may settle in another’s bed, even for a moment, unless that person permits it. Or, if he wishes, he goes to the chapel. But if he did not leave chapter, when the community enters the chapel he proceeds to the infirmary through the auditorium. The infirmary attendant has his bedding brought from the dormitory and his portion with a spoon from the refectory; he will later carry these back with the same spoon as soon as the sick brother has recovered and returned to the community.

He does not eat meat unless, as Saint Benedict says, he is altogether weak and sick. If that is the case, the prior, after being reminded by the infirmary attendant at the hour of dinner, visits him and leads him to a place suitable for such a sick man. He also has meat brought and orders him to eat it, presenting it to him with his own hands. *(UD.)* If the prior is occupied elsewhere and cannot come, he may entrust his place in this matter to the infirmary attendant. From that time onward, he goes nowhere without the staff that the servant places near him while he is eating, even if circumstances require him to abstain from meat for three days or more; he covers his head only with a cap. He places the staff in the bed at night and at midday, and during the remaining hours keeps it beside him. *He must not go anywhere without his frock, except to the necessaries—unless he is so weak that he needs to be supported by another.*

It is the responsibility of the infirmary attendant to examine carefully the need of each person requiring such nourishment and, as far as he can, to report the truth of the matter to the prior. *(UD.)* He comes to the church for both Masses, that is, the major and the morning Mass, although, as has been said, he does not attend the major Mass himself until after the Gospel. Even if he does not enter chapter, he listens to what is read there, namely, the sentence from the Rule or from the Gospel, and again to what is read at the collation. But when the proceedings reach the point at which the brothers’ negligences are discussed, he should not be inquisitive about hearing this: he immediately withdraws from the doorway, where he had been listening while reclining. If he has a bed, he lies down; otherwise he may rest either in the chapel or in the cloister beside it. According to custom he remains silent until, after chapter, the board is struck as a signal for speaking. If he needs any such medical treatment, he may obtain it through the infirmary attendant without the prior’s permission. But if he needs a preparation to be cooked or bloodletting performed, he obtains permission from the prior through the infirmary attendant.

The following procedure is to be observed by any sick brother for this letting of blood. When the regular fast is being kept, it is to begin only after the regular Hour has ended—the Hour sung by the sick brothers before their dinner; but in Lent it begins after Vespers has been said for them and “Benedicamus Domino” has been spoken. When there are two meals, it begins at the start of the major Mass. While eating, a sick brother may lawfully share some of his food and drink with another sitting beside him. *(UD.)* After dinner he is not permitted to give himself to talkativeness; instead, he immediately lies down in his little bed or waits at Saint Mary’s until the brothers return from the refectory, if he is judged to be of such grave condition. *Likewise, at night, after the sick brothers’ Matins has been sung, he may remain there until the community proceeds there in procession.* Neither of these permissions is granted to the younger brothers.

Or, if it is a time when the brothers do not take their midday rest—[Note: [Col. 1129D] That is, they sleep during the midday period.]—he likewise goes to the chapel if he prefers; *(UD.)* this is also forbidden to none of the sick. *But none of them may look at any book there, even for a moment, unless he is able to read a lesson at Matins or sing a responsory. If he wishes to read, he is immediately told to return to the community. Again, after supper he sits or lies there when the brothers are sitting in the cloister for the reading.*

# CHAPTER LX. Under what rule obedientiaries who fall ill are to remain in the infirmary

*When the prior, chamberlain, cellarer, sacristan, or the other brothers, occupied with obediences within or outside the monastery, enter the infirmary because they have fallen ill, they immediately withdraw from the execution and administration of all their obediences. The only exception is that the brothers placed under them may sometimes, when necessary, make use of their advice in matters requiring action. Nothing is assigned to them concerning their obediences at their command; rather, if he thinks fit, the prior orders their assistants to bring whatever and however much he wishes—not only for them but also for the other sick brothers in common. If anything directed to those same obedientiaries by us is sent to them, it is not presented to them but received by the cellarer and distributed in common; afterward, if it seems appropriate, the matter is briefly reported to them.*

*(UD.)* The visitors frequently inspect the infirmary and carefully investigate how the sick brothers are faring. If the infirmary attendant sees any negligence on their part—for example, if on Sunday they do not sit up in bed for the sprinkling of holy water, or if they frequently come late to the table, especially because of talking—and if, after being admonished once, twice, or three times, they refuse to listen to him, he must bring the matter forward in chapter. As soon as they have been accused, the prior sends the cloister prior and the visitors to them; after calling everyone together, chapter is held with them. If any of them is found to have transgressed the admonition, he will at times experience the rod. If he should again presume to repeat the same offense, he is summoned to chapter and will certainly undergo judgment. If he is one who receives meat as nourishment, he leaves his staff in the auditorium when going there. *But one whose illness is such that he cannot do without a staff carries it with him into chapter.* The elders who continually remain there and commit some such offense are not to be corrected there but in chapter, since by acting badly they have scandalized those to whom they ought to have been examples of good conduct.

# CHAPTER LXI. When the sick are to come to chapter of their own accord or when summoned

*It must be understood concerning the sick that, although they never take part in any procession, they are nevertheless summoned to chapter on account of certain highly esteemed guests, and also on the vigils of the Nativity of the Lord and of his Annunciation. Then none of them is to be absent when pardon is to be sought there from everyone in common, unless he is unable to come because of illness. After the sermon has ended, however, they do not remain there longer,* but, at the infirmary attendant’s warning, are immediately ordered to return.

Meanwhile, while a brother is being nourished with meat, he is not forbidden to kiss visiting brothers, just as the others do. *(UD.)* When he has recovered sufficiently to return to the community, he asks the prior for permission to return through the infirmary attendant. *For it lies within the prior’s discretion that no one leave there before the proper time seems appropriate to him.* His day shoes are then greased, and on the following day he puts them on in order to return. When the signal is first struck for Prime—or, if it is the time when Terce is sung, before chapter—he stands near the door at Saint Mary’s. When he sees that all the brothers have passed, he follows them into the church.

*If he is one of the obedientiaries, he must not presume either to speak or in any way to concern himself in chapter with his obedience, nor may he mount a horse that day—unless something occurs which would cause serious damage to the monastery if he did not go, such as planting or a similar matter. For so great a necessity he may even leave the infirmary and go into the garden, but under no circumstances to a place where it would be necessary for him to ride. Even then he does not leave through the cloister; instead, he is led by one of the few who know about it through some hidden place, by which, once the business is completed, he returns again to the infirmary.*

*(UD.)* When he comes to chapter and, after the reading, the prior orders the brothers to speak about the order, he immediately rises, provided he has been receiving meat, and, asking pardon, continues as follows:

“I was in the infirmary and did not observe our order as I ought.”

But if there are two or more, the one who is senior among them answers in the same words for all, saying, “We were in the infirmary,” and so forth. The prior replies:

“May God forgive you whatever you committed there.”

Then they bow more deeply toward the prior, toward the right, and toward the left, and each of them receives a similar bow from the individual brothers. The prior then assigns them, as a penitence, to sing seven psalms, or, for those who do not know the psalms, the Lord’s Prayer seven times.

*It must also be understood that any brother who has been receiving meat may communicate on the day he returns from the infirmary, provided nothing of this kind happened to him while he was sleeping during the night; but he must first make confession. Or, if he is a priest, he may sing a private Mass.*

If someone is so ill that he lies in bed and cannot be nourished by any other food, he is permitted to eat meat during Advent or Septuagesima. *Whenever he recovers, even if it is the middle of Lent or Palm Sunday, he asks pardon in chapter, as is customary for eating meat.* All the others do not remain there longer but join the community. Whether this is done on Sunday or on Monday is left to their discretion. But after pardon has been sought, if the infirmary attendant warns that one of them seems unable to remain with the community, he is immediately ordered to return.

It must be understood that on the day he returns from the infirmary, if he has eaten meat, neither does he accuse another nor is he accused by another; otherwise, both he and another brother are accused by one another. He may have committed such an excess that on the following day he voluntarily or when summoned asks pardon. It should also be noted that if a sick brother is to be sent to some cell for the sake of recuperation, he must first ask pardon in chapter and afterward receive the blessing for his departure.

# CHAPTER LXII. Concerning the anointing of a sick brother

*(UD.)* When a brother feels that, as his illness grows worse, he is soon to depart from this world, he confesses his entire conscience to the lord abbot or the prior and asks to be anointed with the oil of the sick. If he is so weak that he needs support, two brothers first bring him into chapter between them. Asking pardon, he confesses himself guilty of many negligences against the Lord and against them. The prior grants him absolution, with everyone answering, “Amen,” and he likewise answers them. He is brought back and placed in a bed of such a kind, and so low, that the brothers can stand around him on every side.

*(Variant.)* After chapter, once the psalms *Verba mea* have been recited and the board has been struck, the weekly priest, or another priest to whom the armarius assigns this duty, puts on an alb, stole, and maniple. He is accompanied by the water, preceded by a cross and followed by two candles carried at his sides, while the armarius follows carrying the book and the oil of the sick.

[Col. 1132C] *After him comes the community, if there is only a small number of brothers in the place. But if the crowd does not permit this, as many brothers as are sufficient for the office, both younger and older, are to be selected by the armarius.* They go there through the church of Saint Mary and return through the auditorium. Psalm 50 is sung. When it is finished, *Deus in nomine tuo*, and so forth, is sung, followed by: “Have mercy on me, O God, have mercy, you who said through your blessed apostle James: ‘Is anyone among you sick?’” and the rest.

*(UD. variant.)* Seven psalms are imposed with these antiphons:

“Heal me, O God.”

Psalm: “O Lord, rebuke me not in your anger.”

1. Antiphon: “There was a certain royal official.”

Psalm: “Blessed are those.”

Antiphon: “Lord, my servant.”

Psalm: “O Lord, rebuke me not in your anger.”

2. Antiphon: “A contrite heart.”

Psalm: “Have mercy on me, O God.”

Antiphon: “Lord, descend.”

Psalm: “O Lord, hear.”

1. Antiphon: “Lord, I am not worthy.”

For the dead, antiphon: “When the sun had set.”

Psalm: “O Lord, hear.”

Meanwhile the priest performs the anointing in this manner. He applies oil to his thumb and with that thumb makes the sign of the cross over each eye, saying:

“Through this anointing and his most merciful compassion, may the Lord forgive you whatever you have sinned through sight.”

Likewise over both ears, because of hearing; over both lips, because of taste; lengthwise over the nose, because of smell; over the hands, because of touch; and externally over the feet, because of walking, and over both sides of the loins, because of the heat of lust. He washes his hands, first rubbing his fingers with ash and with the water that is customarily poured into the fire.

*(Variant.)* If the sick brother has received Communion on the same day, the same priest first says these verses:

“Save your servant.”

“Send him help, O Lord.”

“May the enemy gain nothing against him.”

“Be for him, O Lord, a tower of strength.”

He then adds these collects:

“O God, who [to] your servant Hezekiah…”

“Look upon us.”

“Good God, who are the maker of your creation.”

“Gracious God, who [to] the human race…”

“God of the heavenly powers.”

“Holy Lord Father, almighty and eternal God.”

“O God, hear our prayers.”

“May [it] go before this servant…”

“Lord our God, who [concerning] offense…”

“Be present, O Lord, to our supplications and to me, who…”

“Grant, we ask, O God, to this servant of yours.”

“Kind God of the human race.”

[Col. 1133B] But if circumstances require that he receive the Lord’s Body, then, at the armarius’s direction, another priest continues these same collects. Meanwhile the weekly priest, leaving the cross and holy water behind, returns to the church with the two candlesticks in order to bring the Lord’s Body. *There he washes his hands again, pours wine and water into the chalice, and before receiving it merely bows. After placing on the altar the pyx in which the reserved Lord’s Body is kept, he makes the sign of the cross over it with incense, which the sacristan has meanwhile prepared for this purpose. He breaks the Lord’s Body over the chalice and holds over the chalice the portion he is to carry away. Both the priest’s hands *(UD.)* and the chalice itself are covered by the armarius with a very white cloth. Then, as before, he returns after the psalm *Laudate* has been begun.

[Col. 1133C] *If necessary, the psalms *Deus in nomine tuo* and *Miserere mei, Deus* are added for him.* All whom he passes, and all who meet him, ask pardon. Care is also taken meanwhile to wash the sick man’s mouth.

*The one who is to receive the Lord’s Body makes confession, with the priest and the others responding, “May he have mercy on you.” After this has been said, the priest adds, “Absolution,” and so forth. *(UD.)* He receives the sacrament dipped in wine [Note: [Col. 1133] The Lord’s Body was dipped in wine so that the sick man might receive it more easily.] Then, after drinking that same wine, he also drinks the chalice’s ablution, and secondly the ablution of the priest’s fingers, and a third time the chalice’s ablution. The cross is brought to him so that he may kiss it. As though bidding a final farewell, he also kisses first the priest, then all the brothers, and the boys themselves, if they are in that place. The community returns in the same order and with the same equipment with which it came. *If the same brother escapes death, he may be anointed again after three years.*

# CHAPTER LXIII. Concerning the anointing of the lord abbot

*If the lord abbot falls ill, he is brought into chapter in the same manner as the brother mentioned above. Sitting in his place, he repeatedly confesses that he has sinned against both God and the brothers, and humbly prays that he may obtain pardon from the Lord. But the prior immediately rises, moved by the common affection of the brothers, and with all due reverence and submission, as is fitting, expresses the wish that the abbot receive the pardon he requests; the abbot does likewise for them. This done, he is brought back. When chapter has ended, the prior himself, dressed in an alb and stole, proceeds with the community to anoint him with the oil of the sick; the bearers of the holy water, cross, and candlesticks are also dressed in albs.*

# CHAPTER LXIV. Concerning a brother approaching death and the vigils to be held around him

*(UD.)* When a brother has come to such an illness, one servant is assigned to him who has no other duty except to serve the sick man. At night all the servants keep watch carefully, but in turn, so that his death may not occur unexpectedly.

*A wooden cross made expressly for this purpose and kept continually at Saint Mary’s is brought by the infirmary attendant and fixed before his face, if his death appears to be very near. The light of a candle is not lacking until broad daylight, for as long as he has not improved. If there is a brother who, out of special affection, wishes also to remain keeping watch with the sick man, the prior willingly grants his request.*

When the servants who are greatly practiced and experienced in such matters see that the end is now approaching, they sprinkle in the form of a cross the ashes left from the beginning of the fast, which the infirmary attendant has kept for this purpose until now. *(Variant.)* They spread a hair shirt over them *and lift the sick man from the bed and place him upon the hair shirt.* The infirmary attendant immediately reports this to the prior. If the sick man still has understanding, the prior has someone read the Passion before him; otherwise he orders two or four brothers to sing psalms there without interruption until it is clear that the soul is about to depart swiftly from the body.

When the servants see this, lights are kindled throughout the infirmary cloister and, if it is night, in the auditorium. One of them strikes the board against the door of the dormitory or church—or wherever he knows the community to be—with frequent and continuous blows and with such force *that anyone dwelling within the walls, inside or outside the cloister, can hear it.* Since this is the signal of one about to die, as soon as it is heard everyone hurries there, singing and resinging the greater Creed. *(UD.)* Although it is entirely forbidden to a man of our order ever to walk hurriedly for any reason, it is nevertheless commanded that he run to a dying brother and to a fire.

If this striking of the board occurs while either Mass or a regular Hour is being sung, all who are standing outside the greater choir hurry there. Those in the choir do not, except those to whom the prior gives a sign, together with the armarius and the other obedientiaries who have something to perform at the funeral rites.

*But if the board is struck during the washing of the feet on Maundy Thursday, during any washing of the brothers’ feet, on Holy Saturday during the office celebrated before the bell for Mass or during the office afterward, or during any procession after the cross has already been carried into the vestibule, no one runs except those to whom the prior gives a sign, together with the obedientiaries mentioned above.* *(UD.)* If they are still sitting in the refectory or at the collation, they leap up from there as well.

Nevertheless, after the body has been washed and carried into the church, *if the reading with the verse “We give you thanks” has not yet ended, everyone returns to the refectory.* If they were still going to eat and drink when they heard the blow of the board, they afterward eat and drink, even if it is Lent. *(UD.)* But if, at the sound of the board, they had all already stopped eating and the reading with the verse had ended, then, after the body has been washed and carried to the church of Saint Mary, they finish in the major church with the psalm *Miserere mei, Deus.* *They return to the collation in the same way if they have not yet finished the reading.*

At night, too, if the board is struck, everyone must run with such haste that, if they are in the dormitory, they do not even cover their beds on that occasion. Yet it is not permitted to run wearing only a cowl and fur garment, nor to the young brothers unless they have lit lanterns. On the feast of the White Garments, those brothers partly dressed in white who had not yet entered the choir must also run. They run without delay from the shaving and from chapter, even though these may be finished afterward, and from the litany sung after Prime or before Mass. Those leaving the litany resume it at the place where it was dismissed.

At night, after Matins has ended—or, if there are twelve lessons, after the Gospel and prayer have been read at the lectern—if the brother has not yet died, everyone runs. Once the body has been brought into the church, they immediately begin the reading of Matins, but first they say the appointed familiar psalms, if they are to be said. If this interruption occurs during the familiar psalms, or even during some such psalmody—for example, the psalm sung from the refectory—then, after returning, the partially sung psalm is begun again from the beginning.

The sick brothers do the same, except that, when they hear the board, they leave a regular Hour to be recited from the beginning afterward, whereas if Nocturns or Matins has not yet ended, they complete it from the place where it was interrupted. To state the matter briefly: whatever order is interrupted for this reason, apart from the exceptions mentioned, is resumed after the body has been washed and, as stated, brought into the church, so that the same order may be observed.

The infirmary attendant must take care, if possible, that the board is never struck before the order then in progress has been completed, unless the brother’s death is so near that it cannot be delayed any longer. If it is struck during Mass or a regular Hour, then, once that Mass has ended—or, if it is Sunday, once the blessing has been given to the reader at table—or once the Hour has ended, and likewise once the blessing has been received, if someone returning from the road is to receive it; or, if it is at Vespers or Matins, once the commemoration of a saint has been made, if one is required, and, if it is Sunday, once the blessing has been given to the kitchen servants—then, if he has not yet died, everyone runs as though the board had been struck, singing the Creed as stated above.

But if he has died, they burn incense moderately, singing *Placebo Domino*, and, when they arrive there, join the psalmody of those whom they find there. Whether the entire community runs or only part of it, those standing around the brother sing *Credo in unum* twice or three times if he has not yet died. *(UD.)* Then the litany is to be said, with the lord abbot or prior leading it, and “pray for him” is to be added after each name of the saints. It is to be lengthened or shortened according to the time available and according to what can be perceived or judged concerning the condition of the one about to depart: it is lengthened by repeating the names of the saints or adding others, and shortened by omitting certain portions. When the names of the saints have been completed, the following is immediately added: “Be merciful, spare him, O Lord,” with the rest.

[Col. 1136B] When the litany has ended, if he has not yet died, *Credo in unum* is sung by everyone twice, three times, or as often as the situation itself indicates. If he has not yet given up his spirit, the community withdraws at the prior’s signal, leaving behind some who sing psalms or read the Passions, if the sick man’s awareness has returned.

*(Variant.)* If they again perceive that the moment of death is approaching, the board is nevertheless struck, and everyone runs there in the same order as before. The Creed is sung together with the litany, and this recalling of the brothers and repetition of the litany are carried out as often as seems necessary.

When they no longer doubt that he has died, the lord abbot or prior says these collects:

“Moved by an affection of pious remembrance.”

“O God, to whom all are alive.”

“Receive, O Lord, the soul of your servant.”

[Col. 1136C] *After these verses have been said: “Do not enter into judgment.” “From the gate of hell.” “The Lord be with you.”* As the community leaves to sit, it sings Vespers for the dead before the chapel of Saint Mary, with no collect other than the one that always follows it:

“Almighty and eternal God, to whom…”

It is customary that, as long as the sick man lies upon the hair shirt, the secretary who regulates the clock goes there after Compline with a covered lantern, both before he dies there and before he rings the small bell for Matins, and also during the day. According to what he is able to observe there, he regulates the time and takes care that no negligence in the service of God arise on account of the brother’s death.

# CHAPTER LXV. Concerning the same brother after he has died

[Col. 1136D] *As soon as he has died, his head is immediately covered with a cap, and at the last the conversi hurry to strike all the bells and to ring them at length, and to bring another cross and holy water, *(variant)* candlesticks and a thurible. As soon as this cross has been brought, the wooden cross is carried back.* When these things have been brought, the dead man is sprinkled with holy water and incensed. *After a short time he is carried out together with the hair shirt and the things that have been brought, into the small building between the chapel of Saint Mary and the infirmary, made solely for the purpose of washing him.* It has a somewhat larger window in which the woolen garment and the other things with which the dead man is presently to be dressed are meanwhile placed. *(UD.)* But no brothers other than those who are his equals in the sacred order, or outside the order, carry him, wash him, or place him in the grave.

*The priest of the current week must take care not to involve himself in this business. It is the infirmary attendant’s responsibility to provide hot water; the chamberlain provides the garments in which he is to be dressed. The chamberlain must also have ready a square woolen cloth into which several needles with threads have been fixed.*

*(UD.)* He is placed on a board intended solely for this purpose. His stockings, breeches, and woolen garment are removed, and he is washed from the crown of his head to the sole of his foot. Only his private parts are covered with that same woolen garment. Incense is supplied there abundantly. *He is dressed in a freshly washed woolen garment, a cowl, night stockings, and a cloth in which a cross of linen fabric has been sewn.* The cloth is made of the same material as the woolen garment, as are the stockings; neither has an open edge, but is sewn closed. The cowl’s hood is sewn together on both sides over the face, toward the chest, over which his hands are also folded outside the cowl. The cowl itself is sewn tightly throughout at the places requiring stitching, so that it is loose nowhere. The night stockings are likewise sewn together.

While he is being washed, the washers sing the Office of the Dead. *(Variant.)* The prior and the armarius are also present there, and the prior says this collect:

“Almighty and eternal God.”

The sick brothers, seated apart from the community, also sing the same office with the nine lessons. *(UD.)* After he has been dressed, the prior places incense—of which there has meanwhile been a continual supply—upon the bier and at the same time sprinkles it with holy water.

[Col. 1137C] Then, after the dead man has been placed in it, sprinkled, and incensed, the cover is put over him. Before putting on their frocks, the washers wash their hands at the infirmary washbasin with the water they used in washing the dead man, but they do not dry them. He is lifted and carried as far as the door facing the community. When the community has sung the office through to the end, the prior watches and strikes the board only once. Then, with everyone bowing, the Lord’s Prayer is said. The prior says, “And lead us not.” “From the gate of hell.” “The Lord be with you.” The prayers are said: “God, giver of life”; “God, who [of] human beings…” The responsory *Subvenite* is imposed. *(UD.)* Likewise *Heu mihi, Domine*. Likewise, if necessary, *Ne recorderis*.

In the procession, the boys, if they are present in the place, follow the cross; then the priors; afterward the conversi; and the bearers of the dead man come last. Once the ringing of all the bells has begun, he is carried into the church of Saint Mary, where he is supported before her altar until the collect *Deus veniae largitor* is said for him, preceded by the verse “From the gate of hell” and “The Lord be with you,” with the brothers turned toward the altar.

*Then he is placed in the lower part of the same church, facing north, beside the bench, in such a way that he does not obstruct those passing by. A cross with candlesticks assigned solely for this purpose and kept there continually is fixed at his head. Only then does the ringing cease, and the community returns to complete the order, if it happened to have left any part unfinished. The sick brothers complete whatever was left unfinished by singing *Exsultabunt**.

The infirmary is not blessed, nor is holy water sprinkled there. [Col. 1138A] Only the house in which the brother died is swept and strewn with rushes. *(UD.)* From that hour until he is carried to the grave, there is no cessation from psalmody except while the regular Hour is being sung in that same church. When the first signal is struck for it, the psalmody ceases, except for Nocturns alone; then it continues until the small bell is dismissed.

If the brother’s death occurs before the sound has been made in the dormitory, or—as happens in winter—before the litany has ended, or even after it has ended, he is buried that same day, unless the day is so bright that reading can be done in the cloister, or unless on the day of shaving the Hour ends at a time when he could have a morning Mass. The same is done if an intolerable stench or something similar intervenes. For an intolerable stench he is buried without Mass as well, if he died at such an hour.

For the psalmody and vigils to be performed for him at night, a Mass or a psalmody is assigned to each person, in addition to what all owe him in common or individually. *(UD.)* If it is a winter night—from the Kalends of November until the Lord’s Supper—it is divided into three vigils only on the nights of the twelve lessons and of the octaves. The right choir, with the armarius, conducts the first; the left choir the second; and the final one is conducted after Matins, when the community has gone to sleep, by the secretaries and the young brothers with the custodians, together with an equal number of novices and other brothers, so that the psalmody may be completed and the entire Psalter said at each vigil.

Then, in the evening, the Office and the Matins praises for the dead are added, always with *Verba mea*, without the following psalm *Voce mea*, and with the collect *Absolve, Domine*.

The armarius goes up into the dormitory as soon as the first vigil is almost completed, to awaken the brothers. During Matins the sick and the others who hear the regular Hours at Saint Mary’s do not leave there until the community comes there in procession.

It must be understood that when we celebrate a brother’s funeral at night, a bright lamp illuminates our cloister. On ordinary nights of that season—that is, from the Kalends of November until the Lord’s Supper—the night is divided into two vigils, which, as has been said, are conducted in turn by each choir. But the entire community is present there during the interval. *(Variant.)* Afterward those who sleep in the infirmary and in the novices’ cell by an act of permitted mercy remain there until daybreak.

But if it is a summer night, it is divided into three vigils. At each of the two held before Nocturns, one hundred psalms are said, together with the other things that follow.

At the third, after Matins, the psalmody is to be prolonged by the secretaries and the other brothers mentioned above until the sound of the signal. On the nights of the twelve lessons the only variation is that at each vigil, before Nocturns, fifty psalms are said with their appendices, provided that the first vigil begins near nightfall or during the night itself. If it begins earlier, the Psalter is sung through, divided equally between the two vigils mentioned above.

When the community is in the refectory, or when it is the time at which the brothers ordinarily sleep at midday, some of the novices and other, stronger brothers remain. At the appointed time the customary three little prayers are not neglected. If anyone wishes to change his clothing, he changes it either before or afterward.

It must be understood that as soon as the morning Mass ends, the entire community, except the novices and the others who do not have chapter, returns to the choir. There they devote themselves to reading until the signal is struck for chapter. But those same novices are ordered to remain there for chapter together with the sick. Likewise, during the foot-washing, some of them are ordered to remain.

As soon as some of the brethren have drunk the drink of charity in the refectory, they are directed there from the armarium, so that those who have been sent may come and, having received permission to approach, drink the same drink of charity [Col. 1139B].
