At whatever hour the brother’s death occurs, whether in winter or summer, the psalter is not to be begun unless it has first been completed in its entirety [lacuna] after he has died; and in the evening, for the dead man, the office, the matins, *Verba mea*, and also the matutinal Mass are sung for him, even if he is not buried that day. Then, on the following day, all must be present in order to make the offerings. After the Offertory, the priests who wish may sing Masses for him without permission, provided that it is a day with twelve lessons. After the deacon has incensed the altars, he also incenses the deceased, making the sign of the cross over him. When the grave has been made, these collects are to be said over it: *Deus, qui simplicibus*; *Deus, qui hominem*; *Domine Jesu Christe*. When this has been completed [Col. 1139C], it is sprinkled with holy water, and this collect follows: *Ineffabilis*. This is done within the canon of the matutinal Mass.

## CHAPTER LXVI. How and when burial is to take place

*When the chapter has ended, and if it is such a day, after the board has been struck, the prior lightly touches one of the larger bells three times. The brethren assemble, and candles are distributed by the church custodians to each person, including the sick who are standing either before or outside the chapel. The priest who sang the first Mass, the burial priest of the deceased, is dressed in an alb reserved for this purpose and in a stole. The armarius, having summoned another brother, begins: “Kyrie eleison. Christe eleison. Kyrie eleison.” When all have likewise responded, they bow down for the Lord’s Prayer, and the priest, without a salutation, says these collects: *Ne intres*; *Fac, quaesumus, Domine*; *Inclina, Deus*. Before each one he says: “Let us pray.” The following responsories are imposed: 1. *Induta est*. 2. *Scio, Domine*. 3. *Libera me, Domine*. The verse is sung by the armarius with another brother, as above at “Kyrie eleison.”

Each time he incenses the principal altar, he likewise incenses the body of the deceased, making a cross over it. An antiphon with Psalm 80 is imposed. In this procession, holy water, incense, and the cross with two other candlesticks, newly brought from the church, are carried first; the priest and the armarius follow them; after these come the novices and lay brothers, then the priors and [Col. 1140A] Dom Abbot, and finally the deceased. The sick, who meanwhile had been standing outside the church of Saint Mary, enter it as soon as the convent has gone out, and there celebrate the office which the convent also sings.

When the convent reaches the cemetery, it spreads out in the form of a crown. During the burial, under the prescribed psalmody, the following antiphons are sung:

- Antiphon: *Aperite*. Psalm: *Confitemini Domino*.
- Antiphon: *Ingrediar*. Psalm: *Quemadmodum*.
- Antiphon: *Haec requies*. Psalm: *Memento, Domine*.
- Antiphon: *Dextra*. Psalm: *Domine, probasti*.
- Antiphon: *Ne intres*. Psalm: *Domine, exaudi*.
- 2. Antiphon: *Omnis spiritus*. Psalm: *Laudate Dominum de terra*.
- Antiphon: *Absolve, Domine*. Psalm: *Benedictus Dominus Deus*.

As soon as the priest reaches the grave, he says these collects: *Obsecramus*; *Deus omnipotens, qui* [Col. 1140B]. The grave, both before and after it has received the body, is sprinkled with holy water and incensed—not three times, but only once—with the verse *Redemptor*. A wooden cover is placed over the deceased himself, and the first priest, if Dom Abbot is not present, takes a shovel and casts earth over him three times, adding these collects: “Let us pray. Dearly beloved brothers, who [are concerned] with the just”; *Debitum humani*; *Temeritatis*.

When these have been completed, they withdraw from the grave together with the cross and proceed before the chapel in the middle of the cemetery. There, after the Lord’s Prayer has first been said in silence, the following is added: “And lead us not [into temptation].” Verse: *Ne intres*. “The Lord be with you.” *Tibi, Domine, commendamus*. After the candles have been extinguished, Psalm *Laudate* follows again, with the Lord’s Prayer. Verse: *A porta*. Collect: *Deus, cujus* [Col. 1140C] *misericordia*. After the customary bow has been made and the seven psalms have been imposed, they return. On this occasion the priors are also to be in front, and, when they reach the choir in the same order, they prostrate themselves with those psalms. The priest, having removed his alb and stole, concludes them with this collect: *Absolve, Domine, animam*, wherever he may then be lying prostrate.

The sick also begin these psalms when the convent begins, and sing them prostrate. The signals that began to be sounded immediately when the deceased was carried out are not stopped before the bier has been placed over the grave. Immediately after the burial, the bier is carried back by the infirmary servants to the aforesaid little building, so that it may always be found there whenever needed.

### Variant

On the day on which the deceased is buried, if there are two meals, whatever bread or drink remains from supper [Col. 1140D] is given as alms for him; if there is only one meal, it is given at dinner. Each priest sings three Masses as soon as he can. Each person who knows the psalms sings sixty psalms for him; the illiterate sing the Lord’s Prayer that many times.

On the following day his seven-day and thirty-day observances begin. The seven-day observance is conducted so that for seven days the office and Mass are sung for him generally by the convent. The thirty-day observance is conducted so that for thirty days his provision is given fully as alms, and Psalm *Voce mea*—which is customarily said for him at all the hours—is then said, together with *Verba mea*. The prior, at the armarius’s reminder, assigns six priests to sing thirty Masses for him. Other deceased brothers are not included in this thirty-day observance unless they died on the same day [Col. 1141A]. When each priest has completed the fifth, he announces that same day in chapter that another is to begin on the following day.

(UD.) This is never interrupted for any feast, except for six days during the year: *the Nativity of the Lord, the Resurrection of the Lord, and the three days preceding the Sunday of the Resurrection, and the holy day of Pentecost.* If any one of them should happen to neglect one of these observances, he is ordered, after asking forgiveness, to complete it; moreover, the penance that seems appropriate to the prior is imposed on him. After these Masses have been completed, the prior prays absolution for him, just as he had likewise done in chapter before he was buried. On the feasts mentioned above and on the other principal feasts, the Office of the Dead is not performed unless the body is actually present.

### Variant

[Col. 1141B] His clothing is kept by the chamberlain, so that it may be given to any brother who needs it. Whenever his anniversary occurs, or that of any one of our professed brothers, his provision is again given as alms. The Mass that is likewise to be sung for him is sometimes prevented by some necessity; but at the next suitable opportunity it is restored.

## CHAPTER LXVII. Concerning one who dies in one of our cells

(UD.) A brother who, having been sent to one of our cells for whatever reason, dies there, shall also have thirty Masses there, provided that there are priests in that place so that this can be done, together with the other things I mentioned above. (Variant: otherwise this is not done there.) When the notice of his deposition arrives, the office [Col. 1141C] and Mass are performed for him with all the bells sounded. In all other respects, both there and among us, the seven-day observance is to be conducted in the same way, with the provision added, together with Psalm *Verba mea* for thirty days. *His anniversary is also entered in the rule among those of our other brothers.*

## CHAPTER LXVIII. What is to be done for one who dies among us, in our cells, or elsewhere

(UD.) I cannot easily say what is to be done in our cells for any brother who dies among us or elsewhere, except that, when his notice arrives there, the office is performed, and whichever priest is present sings three Masses for him; anyone who is not a priest sings one hundred and fifty psalms, or the Lord’s Prayer that many times. (UD.) Nevertheless [Col. 1141D] those places in which a provision is not given for him are rare. *For in some it is given for seven days, in some also for thirty days, and always on his anniversary; the other things mentioned above are also to be done for him, and he is to be entered in the martyrology.* (UD.) All this was arranged and ordered by Dom Abbot, according to what he recognized as the possibility and capacity of each place.

## CHAPTER LXIX. Concerning one who, God forbid, dies a sudden death outside the cloister

*If a brother is struck by sudden death—God forbid!—or dies outside the cloister through some kind of neglect, he is carried to the infirmary, and immediately [Col. 1142A] the board is struck in the manner in which it is customarily struck for one who is dying, provided that the brethren are not at that moment occupied with one of the aforesaid observances. The convent runs there with as much haste as it hastens to a dying man, singing, namely, the Creed.

But if his death is first announced in chapter, the board is not struck after chapter. Instead, the convent proceeds slowly, singing Vespers for the dead. In all other respects everything is to be done for him as for the deceased mentioned above.

## CHAPTER LXX. Concerning two or perhaps three persons to be buried

*If it should ever happen that two or three brothers are to be buried at the same time, as many thuribles, crosses with candlesticks, and priests are to be provided as there are deceased persons [Col. 1142B]. Of these priests, however, the weekly priest says the collects that are to be said in the chapel of Saint Mary, and he must incense the altar and the deceased themselves. They too are to be carried to the burial according to the time of their deaths, in this order: the one who died first is last in the procession, followed by the weekly priest, who performs for him the duties belonging to his office; the other two precede in similar order and do everything in the same way.

When the collect *Temeritatis* has been completed, and the weekly priest has turned away from the grave with the cross and has stopped before the chapel in the middle of the cemetery, the other two priests join him as colleagues, one at his right and the other at his left. They remain standing in this way until that priest says collectively for the same deceased the collect *Tibi, Domine* [Col. 1142C] and so forth; he also concludes with *Deus, cujus miserationis* for all who are buried there.

## CHAPTER LXXI. Concerning an abbot departing from this life

(UD.) In addition to all the foregoing, the following is to be done for Dom Abbot when he departs this life: he shall remain unburied until the brothers of our congregation can assemble from all the monasteries and cells. His tomb is to be prepared in the place required by his merits—though more ornately than those of others. (Variant.) For burial in it he is clothed in all the priestly vestments. Four brothers who sing the verses of the three responsories are dressed in copes, and four who carry him to the tomb are dressed in albs. *The pastoral staff is placed only at his right side; a chalice is not put into his hand.*

For an entire year his provision is given as alms, (UD.) not only among us but also in all our monasteries and cells; it is always placed upon the principal table, and thirty Masses are sung there for him, provided that there are priests able to fulfill this.

(Variant.) His anniversary is also celebrated in this manner, even if it falls in winter after the twelve lessons. First, all the bells are sounded for a longer time at Vespers for the Dead, which are also sung in the choir on that occasion before the procession proceeds to Saint Mary. *This is not to be done in summer; for then, if such an anniversary occurs after the feast of the twelve lessons [Col. 1143A], it is to be deferred to the following day.* (UD.) Likewise, the office and Mass are celebrated festively, and sung without omitting the *tractus*, while all the bells are nevertheless sounded.

*Each priest sings a Mass for him; the others sing the seven psalms, or, if they do not know the psalms, the Lord’s Prayer that many times.* (UD., variant.) On that day the brothers have a charitable meal in the refectory, except when it falls during Lent on Monday, Wednesday, or Friday; in that case this provision is deferred until the following day. *Twelve poor people are also fed in the hospital, not only with bread and wine but also with meat; otherwise provision is made for them of equal value.* (UD.) This refreshment of the poor is provided only on the anniversary of one of our abbots, unless [Col. 1143B] it is perhaps supplied by common decree for some great benefactor of ours.

(UD.) Whenever the anniversary of someone who has made a gift to the monastery is to be celebrated with the greatest rite, the gift is brought out with the beginning of the *Placebo* for him. Whether it is a pallium or another such ornament, it is placed on the altar to be seen in his memory, and is not removed until the following day, when the Mass of the Dead sung for him has also been completed.

## CHAPTER LXXII. Concerning a brother who dies during Lent and is to be buried on a day with twelve lessons

(UD.) If one of the brothers dies during Lent and is to be buried on a day that is solemn with twelve lessons, a Mass of the Dead is sung for him after Prime [Col. 1143C], with only three collects: namely, *Omnipotens sempiterne Deus*; *Deus veniae largitor*; *Fidelium Deus*. This does not mean, however, that the Mass of the feast after Terce or the Mass of the fast after None is omitted. But if the burial occurs on Sunday, a fourth collect is added: *Sanctorum tuorum*, which would not otherwise be omitted on that day.

## CHAPTER LXXIII. Concerning one who is to be buried on the days before Easter

(UD.) Likewise, if someone is to be buried before None on any of the three days immediately preceding Easter, *he is buried without lights and incense; and if it is Good Friday, he is buried by brothers walking barefoot. There is no Mass of the Dead, although it is later sung on Holy Thursday of Easter Week, and no otherwise than if the body of the deceased were actually present.* From the hour at which the new fire is blessed until the following morning, neither in the church nor at the burial is there any lack of light.

## CHAPTER LXXIV. Concerning one who is to be buried during the Rogation days

* (Variant.) Likewise, if someone is to be buried during the Rogation days, a Mass of the Dead is sung for him after Prime, and the Mass of the Rogations after Terce. No offering is made at the latter, nor is the peace received except by one person, and after chapter he is buried.

## CHAPTER LXXV. Concerning one who is to be buried when we ought to shave

[Col. 1144A]

(UD.) Likewise, one who is to be buried on a day when we cannot properly change the shaving is buried immediately after chapter, once the board has been struck. For as long as he remains unburied, it is not permitted in the cloister either to speak or to do anything else, except to devote oneself to the psalms for the funeral rites.

Only the armarius writes the deceased brother’s name in the memorial book and the notices that are to be sent without delay through the cells. *After writing them, the same armarius presents them to the cellarer who is to send them before the cellar; and if he is not immediately available, he places them there in the spot assigned for this purpose.* Since, according to the ancient institution of the Fathers, these notices are sent without any delay, they are carried about by servants appointed solely for this purpose [Col. 1144B]. The chamberlain clothes these servants so that they may always be ready, while the cellarer must provide their daily food.

## CHAPTER LXXVI. When the notices are to be sent

*The order in which such notices are to be sent must not be passed over in silence. Therefore, through all our cells, whether far or near, provided that they are not very far apart from one another, one notice is sufficient to announce a brother’s death. After it has been brought to the nearest of those cells, it is to be sent from place to place by the priors residing there. But if those cells are known to lie farther apart in different regions, it is necessary for individual notices to be sent from the principal monastery through the cells of each province [Col. 1144C].*

This transmission of notices is carried out in the same way if the death of a brother occurs in some cell and his notice reaches us, except that one is to be sent from the place where he died to another cell situated in the same region.

## CHAPTER LXXVII. That the Office of the Dead is to be performed without delay when a notice arrives concerning one of our brothers

If such a notice is brought before chapter by the guest-master, who receives all notices, it is presented at the next chapter to Dom Abbot or the prior. As soon as he has read it privately and announces the place from which the notice came, together with the brother’s death and name [Col. 1144D], he immediately requests the customary absolution without interruption, and chapter is shortened more than usual so that it may end with the psalm *Verba mea* and the office may be performed for the repose of his soul. If the office is not performed immediately after chapter has ended, it is not to be performed later unless the board is first struck.

It should also be known that if several notices from different places—that is, concerning our professed brothers and brothers from elsewhere—are presented together in chapter, they are all joined in the Masses of the seven-day observance and in the other rites that are performed, except for the thirty-day observance.

If the notice is brought at any hour thereafter, up to Collation, or, when there is only one meal, before the brothers drink, the board is struck slowly and loudly to summon the brothers without delay, provided that the convent is not at that moment occupied with some observance. According to the ancient institution of the Fathers, the board must be struck for the performance of this office with such care and urgency that, once the cymbal has been struck and some beans have been distributed, the brothers, setting everything else aside, assemble for the performance of that office.

Thus, whoever assembles stands there without observing any fixed order of station, but according to the suitability of each person’s place, forming a front and rear outside the chapter house. When the prior ceases striking the board and has made the front and rear, announcing *Benedicite*, the convent responds in the customary manner. He then reads the same brief notice privately in chapter and announces that the brother has died, adding: “Let us go and perform the office, so that almighty God may grant him everlasting rest” [Col. 1145B]. Afterward he does not pray absolution for him in chapter. When the convent responds “Amen,” they depart without forming the front and rear.

When the three lessons have been completed, the officials and certain others who have business of this kind may leave, as the reader at table and the weekly kitchen servants do. If it should ever happen that, as soon as they have sat down, they hear the board being struck, they taste no food.

For this office no more than three prayers are said, namely: *Omnipotens sempiterne Deus*; *Deus veniae largitor*; *Fidelium*. But if it is performed after None, the customary prayers are added, since nothing else follows later that day. The prior may nevertheless defer this same office until the following day on such feasts as impose an especially heavy burden of God’s service upon the brothers [Col. 1145C].

## CHAPTER LXXVIII. Concerning our living and deceased associates, and what is done for them

(UD.) There are certain communities, not only of monks but also of clerics, that have a partnership and brotherhood with us, so that when a notice concerning one of their deceased arrives, or ours arrives among them, the office and Mass are performed, and afterward the seven-day observance with offices and Masses. *For no deceased abbot do we do more than for one of his brothers.*

There are also certain communities for which we do no more than this: when a notice concerning one of their deceased arrives, after chapter, with all the bells sounded, we recite six psalms—that is, *Verba mea*—with this prayer: *Absolve, Domine*.

(UD.) Likewise, many faithful Christians, both poor and rich, who, having been brought to our chapter, ask that they too may deserve to have our brotherhood. Their request is granted, and a book is given to them, so that they may have a share and communion in all the good works performed in any manner, whether in prayers or in alms, not only among us but also in all places that appear to belong to our jurisdiction.

For all these people, as long as they are alive, Psalm *Deus in adjutorium* is sung specially at each hour, together with the collect *Praetende, Domine*; and whenever it is added to the greater or matutinal Mass, it is added for them. After they have died, Psalm *Voce mea* is sung after each hour when it is not sung for the thirty-day observance of some brother, and every day after chapter, after Psalm *Verba mea*, this prayer is said: *Absolve, Domine*.

[Col. 1146B] (Variant.) Moreover, three times each year—that is, after the first Sunday of Lent, after the Nativity of the Apostles Peter and Paul, and after the feast of All Saints—we make a special commemoration of them, with office and Mass, with the seven-day observance and provision, namely in the same way as is customarily done for any absent person who dies in one of our cells, except that the priests do not sing a Mass, nor do the others sing *Laudate*. Since this has been reported sufficiently clearly above, it is unnecessary to repeat it here.

## CHAPTER LXXIX. What is done for those who are buried in this place

*When, on the Monday after the octave of Pentecost, the memory of those who are buried among us is celebrated with the greatest rite, everyone who knows the seven psalms sings them; the illiterate sing the Lord’s Prayer that many times; each priest sings one Mass; and whatever remains at supper of bread and drink is given as alms.

On the feast of All Saints, after Vespers, when all the bells have been sounded, Vespers for the Dead are also sung. At night the office together with matins and the matutinal Mass are solemnly celebrated for all the faithful departed, with only one collect, namely: *Fidelium Deus*. For them each priest is to sing a private Mass, while the others sing the seven psalms, or, if they do not know the psalms, the Lord’s Prayer that many times. Twelve poor people are to be refreshed with more abundant bread, meat, and wine; and however many other poor people arrive, mercy is to be shown to all with the customary generosity [Col. 1146D]. Moreover, on the feast of All Saints itself, whatever bread and drink remains in the refectory at supper is given as alms.

[Col. 1147]

# THE MUSIC OF SAINT WILLIAM, ABBOT OF HIRSAU

(Dom M. Gerbert, *Ecclesiastical Writers on Music, Especially Sacred Music*, vol. II, p. 154.)

## NOTICE

The music of Saint William, abbot of Hirsau, concerning whom a contemporary author, Berthold of Constance—or, as is generally held, the same person as Bernold, priest and theologian of Gebhard III, bishop of Constance, and monk of Saint Blasien—writes in his *Chronicle* in Urstisius, *German Writers*, vol. I, p. 364:

> “He was exceedingly skilled in music and elucidated many subtleties of that art unknown to the ancient teachers. He also corrected, with sufficient reason, many errors discovered in the chants according to the principles of the art. In the quadrivium he plainly surpassed almost all the ancients.”

These words are read verbatim in the *Life of Saint William*, written by his contemporary and disciple Haymo, in Mabillon, *Acta Sanctorum*, fifth century, part II, p. 726. In the anonymous author of Melk, chapter 108, the following is added immediately after these same words:

> “Nevertheless, he wrote one treatise on music, which, having been summoned by God’s call to govern the monastery of Hirsau, he did not complete.”

I first found this little work of Saint William in the sole San-Blasien manuscript, which was consumed by fire together with the monastery in the year 1768. It happened fortunately that I deposited a copy at Bologna in the very extensive library of P. Giovanni Battista Martini, containing writers on musical matters; he later shared it with me again, with the same kindness with which he had received it from me. Subsequently we found the same little work in the Vienna manuscript, and we inserted its variant readings in cursive type in their proper places in our copy.

The explanation of the twelve tropes in this little work is remarkable; it seems to have provided Glarean with a torch for the *Dodecachordon* that he published. Glarean used this very San-Blasien manuscript—then belonging to the monastery of Saint George—from which this little work was copied, in preparing his edition of the works of Boethius; as he testifies on the title page, he calls it “GOLDEN.”

# WILLIAM’S MUSIC

[Note: [Col. 1147] Addenda to the works of William may be found at the end of this volume.]

## I. The prologue to the art of music by Abbot William begins, composed under his name and that of a certain Othloh in the form of a dialogue

[Col. 1147A]

**OTHL.** Since, by God’s gift, you have satisfied my requests and questions in the discipline of astronomy, it follows that our discussion should now be transferred to music, so that, after the principles concerning the things that pertain to astronomy—things that, as the philosophers say, proceed not without harmony—you may bring forth, insofar as the Author of nature has permitted, the origin and nature of the harmonic art itself, which still lies hidden.

**WILH.** You command something sufficiently arduous, since it has hitherto remained untouched by the most experienced men. But because you hold me by the powerful hand of charity’s bridle, wherever you lead me into the mountains, I think I shall more easily slide back or fall backward [Col. 1147B] than resist. Nevertheless, lest after the end of a day’s journey we rashly undertake a new and as yet uncertain enterprise at the time of making camp, let the remaining part of the day be granted to rest and meditation, and tomorrow let us assemble in the name of Jesus. Thus, with him mediating and guiding us, let us begin the journey we have proposed.

**WILH.** I cannot discharge the debt of yesterday’s promise, which you demand of me, dearest brother, in any other way than by recalling or reviewing those matters known to you both from Boethius’ music and from the credible writings of modern authors, and by preparing a kind of introduction to what is unknown.

**OTHL.** Nothing is more delightful than that treatise in which new and old things are brought forth. Indeed, for this very purpose I would draw you, unwilling though you might be, by persistent entreaties, so that you might either place the opinions of the ancients and the moderns before your own or interweave them with it, in such a way that, if they have said too little, you may add to it; if anything is obscure, explain it; and if anything is incautious, correct it [Col. 1148A].

**WILH.** Perhaps, because at the command of charity I kneel before you with the gentleness of a camel, while you wish to carry several little gifts to these small people, one of which would have been enough, you do not consider either the difficulty of the Alpine journey or the modest strength of the animal’s spirit when loading it. Nevertheless, lest I act without confidence in the Lord, I shall attempt to take the road so heavily laden, and enter the path trodden by the earlier musicians, until a place for turning aside appears.

## II. The music of Abbot William concerning the regular structure of the monochord

[Col. 1148B]

**WILH.** The entire regular structure of the monochord consists of fifteen strings divided into two octaves. The lower of these extends from *proslambanomenos* to *mese*, while the upper extends from *mese* to *nete hyperboleon*; and each contains, as is known, seven distinctions of pitch.

Within these fifteen strings are found tetrachords very different in name, genus, and species: namely, the Hypaton, Meson, Diezeugmenon, and Hyperboleon tetrachords. There are also the tetrachords of the deep, final, upper, and highest [*gravium, finalium, superiorum, excellentium*]. This is their difference in names.

They differ in genus—or derivation—because those mentioned first are shown to be subject to measurement. From those that follow, melody appears to be extracted [Col. 1149A]. For when, dividing the entire measure in order into tetrachords, we descend from *nete hyperboleon*, saying “tone, tone, semitone,” and likewise “tone, tone, semitone,” what else are we establishing than those first tetrachords?

They also differ in species, since the former have the semitone at the end, while the latter have it in the middle. The former are joined in pairs within each octave, because we follow Guido in the placement of the letters: they will have the *synaphe* of E and e, and the nearest *diezeuxis*—the tone—above *mese*. If the latter are joined in a similar way, they designate the *synaphe* of D and d, while the nearest *diezeuxis*—the tone—lies below *mese*.

In the former’s dual joining, or singular arrangement, the tone remains between the two octaves in the lower of the former and in the upper of the latter. From the former, the first descends from a to e, the second from e to b, and there the tone remains, or causes the disjunction; the third proceeds from A to E, the fourth from E to B, and likewise a tone remains. Conversely, from the latter the first ascends from A to D, the second from D to G, where the tone bears witness; the third rises from a to d, and the fourth from d to g, with a surplus tone as well.

Those are the noteworthy ones. These I name, as they truly are, the principal ones. These are the specific differences of the tetrachords. For music is a certain relationship of the differing arrangement of tones and semitones.

**OTHL.** I see that you complained in vain about the questions imposed upon you. With the powerful stride of your teaching, which brings forth new and old matters most openly, you have taken up the road; and I do not doubt that your strength will be sufficient to reach the destination even though you are heavily laden. In the various writings of musicians, the same names of the tetrachords that you mentioned are indeed collected; but I confess that their differences and the qualities of their properties have been left almost entirely untouched by everyone and have remained unheard of until now.

And since you have now turned aside from the path of your predecessors, proceed, I ask you. Set aside the earlier tetrachords, which concern only measurement, and explain how those that pertain to melody pertain to it more than the others, and why you call them principal. Finally, even simpler people know their common names—deep, final, upper, and highest—and know that they have been so called.

## III. On the primacy of the four tetrachords

[Col. 1149D]

**WILH.** These four tetrachords are all principal, and are rightly called principal, because they contain within themselves the power, order, and nature of all species, modes, and tropes. Yet in all of them one is found from which the others receive their name, power, dignity, and very being. It is not the one that Mercury is said to have discovered, namely the Meson; nor the one that the ancient musicians called the Hypaton; nor yet the one which modern scholars affirm to be first, namely the tetrachord of the finals.

**OTHL.** Please name it quickly, lest you suspend one who is most eager even for a moment.

**WILH.** It is the one that nature—or rather the Author of nature—first wished to be expressed by quadrupling; I mean the tetrachord of the deep. From this, surely, because the others are derived from it as from a kind of fountain, they borrow the name of primacy and the wondrous effect of nature [Col. 1150A].

For the tetrachords of the finals, the upper, and the highest are nothing other than its fourfold placement, or its threefold repetition. It seems to be called principal for many reasons. First, because it is first of all; second, because it is enclosed by the first strings of the principal tetrachords; third, because the differences of the tropes proceed from it, if the harmony is restricted to the seven principal distinctions of the two tetrachords, namely the deep and the final; fourth, because in the general constitution of the tropes the *protus* is constituted from it, just as the *tetrardus* is constituted from the final; fifth, because the entire natural order and calculation of the species, and even the other three tetrachords and the whole harmony, as we said above, as well as the four elements or mutations of the tropes, are produced and derived from it as from a certain fountain of nature [Col. 1150B]. Some of these matters are explained here for the present; others are reserved for fuller explanation in their proper places.

## IV. From what causes they are called principal

First of all, it is called principal because, through a wondrous and natural kind of investigation, it shines forth at the very beginning of the measuring monochord, not only before the other tetrachords but before all intervals of the lesser sounds. For such force and power resides in the quadruple proportion that whatever is made through it is first in name, sound, and dignity.

Thus, when the monochord is initially divided into four spaces, the first space is as if empty; the second is the octave; the third is the fifth; and the fourth claims for itself the fourth. Moreover, if the measure is begun from the other side, in reverse order, the tetrachord itself will be the manifest beginning of the whole harmony.

Those who wish to know can readily see that these three intervals—namely, the fourth, the fifth, and the octave—are first among all intervals in name and dignity; that the first species of these consonances reside in these same spaces; and that the very points of each of the principal tetrachords, apart from the first point of the highest, produce the first pitches.

It is also enclosed by the first strings, because, since in the four tetrachords there are four first strings, four second, four third, and four fourth, the fourth itself is placed not only among the first but among the first of the first [Col. 1150D]. For these and still other reasons, which will be explained below, the name of primacy is rightly granted both to it and, from it, to the other tetrachords that flow from it as has been said.

But the proper order of the exposition, now with the help of heavenly illumination, urges us to observe how much force and power of nature it itself contains, and how wondrously it pours that power into the other tetrachords flowing from it.

## V. That the other tetrachords are born from the tetrachord of the deep
Therefore, returning to the beginning, wisdom is seen not in that which is folly with God, but in that which treads underfoot the necks of proud and lofty philosophers, since the entire discipline of the musical art, and the whole structure of the monochord, is produced from that tetrachord which they call the *grave*, but which I call the *principal*. This tetrachord, doubled in the lower diapason, generates from itself the tetrachord of the finals; and from these two proceed the seven principal intervals of the voices. For seven times seven different vocal intervals are found on the monochord. Repeated once more in the upper diapason, with the *phthongus nete hyperboleon* added, they complete the entire construction of the monochord.

For the tetrachord of the upper notes is itself principal, while the tetrachord of the highest notes is final; and between these there will be no difference in nature, but only in name and position, provided that the principal remains one and the same in all of them. But just as everything arises from the principal, so everything is governed, arranged, and judged by the final. Therefore the entire natural force of harmony is active in these two, so much so that the others would not be necessary at all if everyone could perceive the general power of these two more simply. For, as has been said, they contain seven vocal intervals, sufficient for every variety of the musical art, as anyone skilled in this discipline will easily discover if he investigates the matter.

Here too a most evident indication is given of the original dignity of the principal tetrachord and of its complete unity with the tetrachord of the upper notes: every melody which, under the license of wandering through the spacious range of two diapasons, begins in the upper register, if it is restrained below by the same seven intervals through a natural reversion, takes its beginning in the graves—that is, in the same principal tetrachord. For example, all the different forms of the melody belonging to the first, fourth, and sixth tones which begin on the high *a* have their natural beginning on the grave *A*, as is clear from the rule of the *diaphonia*.

And now you have heard, concerning the principal tetrachord so often mentioned and so often to be mentioned, everything—at least in part—about why I have called it the principal, the source and origin of the other tetrachords, or the sum of the whole monochord; and you have also heard what force and power of nature I have declared it to possess in itself. You may still hear more fully about the power that originally springs forth within it and about its diffusion into the other tetrachords. You will see this more easily if you first consider from what things the nature of the musical art is chiefly apprehended, and how these same things are found in the tetrachords.

## VI. From what the nature of the musical art is chiefly known

The nature of the musical art is chiefly discerned, after the nine intervals of the sounds, through knowledge of the following four things:

1. the measured and rationally ordered constitution of the three species of consonances: the diatessaron, diapente, and diapason;
2. the most careful and naturally made arrangement of the modes;
3. the vigilant examination of the difference of the modes—or, more accurately, the recognition or proper character of the modes;
4. the highly necessary operation of the principal notes.

These four things—the constitution of the species, the arrangement of the modes, the difference or recognition or proper character of the modes, and the operation of the principal notes—are present in the principal tetrachords by a certain natural and inseparable property. If you seek them in the matters that belong to measurement, however, you will find them in no suitable order, as will become clear below.

It also seems appropriate to say what I remember having postponed above until this point: namely, that these same tetrachords are divided into four first, four second, four third, and four fourth tetrachords.

The first of the graves is *A*; the second, third, and fourth are *B, C,* and *D*. Likewise, the first of the finals is *D*; the second, third, and fourth are *E, F,* and *G*. The first of the upper notes is *a*; the second, third, and fourth are *b, c,* and *d*. Likewise, the first of the highest notes is *d*; the second, third, and fourth are *e, f,* and *g*.

Thus the first notes of the principal tetrachords are *A, D, a,* and *d*; the second are *B, E, b,* and *e*; the third are *C, F, c,* and *f*; and the fourth are *D, G, d,* and *g*. I have not hesitated to designate them both individually and collectively because the texture of what follows frequently requires their supporting thread.

And do not be surprised that, with *nete hyperboleon* omitted, the other fourteen notes are divided into sixteen: for four times four makes sixteen. You should know that two of those fourteen—namely *D* and *d*—are two-formed and must be counted twice. How they are two-formed in the arrangement of the modes will become clearer below. For among the tetrachords mentioned there are some which, when compared, produce the species of the diatessaron; others, when set against one another, produce the species of the diapente.

## VII. In which notes the species of the diatessaron, diapente, and diapason naturally reside

Let us therefore see what these are, and how they proceed from them by a credible method, without confusion of order, along a level road and without stumbling.

From the natural joining of the principal and final tetrachords all the species of the diatessaron arise. The first of the graves and the first of the finals produce the first; the second of the graves and the second of the finals produce the second; likewise the third of the graves and the third of the finals produce the third; and the fourth of the graves and the fourth of the finals once again represent the first, or, more accurately, retain the fourth in the form of the first.

Although this may appear to be the first species, when the nature of the harmony is examined more carefully it is shown to be the fourth in three ways: first, because it is contained among the fourths; second, because in the general arrangement of the modes, as we said above, it belongs to the tetrardus; third, because it is contrary to the first, since just as the melody rises from the first, so from the fourth it always descends, as the following examples in this same final tetrachord testify:

- Protus: “Make with me.”
- Antiphon: “From two years of age.”
- Tetrardus: “I will give in Zion.”
- “Judaea.”

Likewise, when the middle tetrachords—that is, the finals and the upper notes—are compared, all the species of the diapente arise with the same natural beauty and order. The first of the finals and the first of the upper notes contain the first; the seconds of the two tetrachords contain the second; the thirds contain the third; and the fourths conclude the fourth.

The two remaining tetrachords, namely those of the upper and highest notes, likewise produce the species of the diatessaron, just as the first pair did, because, as has been said, they are identical in nature. The first of the upper notes and the first of the highest notes display the first; the seconds, the second; the thirds, the third; and the fourths once again contain the fourth in the form of the first.

If, therefore, you seek species of the diatessaron among those belonging to the diapente, or species of the diapente among those belonging to the diatessaron, you will encounter an obstacle, because you will not be able to find their established order. To make what we are saying more evident: if you find the same species anywhere other than in the places explained above, you should know that they are less regular, because they are contained within one fewer number.

Do you see, dearest brother, how in this constitution of our species the natural order of the species and of the notes, both in name and in dignity, is preserved, as has been said? And do you see how the same order proceeds along a level road and without stumbling, where the first species both begins and ends on the first notes, the second on the second, the third on the third, and the fourth on the fourth?

Do you not clearly understand that the species themselves are naturally called first, second, third, or fourth from the notes that constitute them? Do you not also observe more clearly their internal arrangements—how the first species of the diatessaron has the semitone in the middle, the second at the beginning (I speak of ascending motion), and the third at the end? And how the first species of the diapente has the semitone after the tone and then the ditone; the second has it at the beginning; the third at the end; and the fourth after the ditone and then the tone?

Do you not clearly perceive how this order of the species can be proved natural above all by the fact that it assigns the first species its place within the principal tetrachord, which lies between the first of the first notes—namely, *A* and *D*—as I previously explained to you, though you did not yet understand it?

Consider carefully, I beg you, and also consider how, in the natural progression of the first species themselves, the final tetrachord too has been produced by a certain hidden order and law of nature. What, then, is the beginning of these species if not the principal tetrachord? And what is their completion if not the final tetrachord, generated and produced from the principal?

In the same way, in the constitution of the species of the diapente, the tetrachord of the upper notes proceeds from the final tetrachord, and, from the succeeding species, the tetrachord of the highest notes proceeds from that of the upper notes. Thus, in each of the tetrachords that pertain to the institution of the modes, the first species arise from the first of the principal tetrachord, the seconds from its second, the thirds from its third, and the fourths from its fourth, as from four elements of different natures—or they are derived from the tones as from their source.

**OTHL.** Everything you say is highly pleasing. I not only consider these matters carefully, but through their explanation I now see quite clearly certain other things that were previously obscure—things I would have asked about earlier, had I not, captivated by the sweetness of these new matters and astonished by their wonder, been unwilling to interrupt the most delightful sequence of your words.

I see, I say, that one of the modern writers made a considerable error. In establishing the species of the diatessaron and diapente, he takes the first species of the diatessaron as beginning from the *lychanos meson*, that is, from *G*, and ending at the *lychanos hypaton*, that is, at *D*. But because *D*, as you have already said, is two-formed, it is counted both among the first and among the fourth notes; whereas *G* belongs simply to the fourths. Thus, looking only at the appearance of this species and at the quality of the semitone placed in its middle, he failed to perceive the inner force and proper character of nature.

Similarly, he begins the second at *A*, which is a first note, and ends it at *E*, which is a second. To summarize all the individual points of this error briefly and together: in arranging the species of the diapente in his customary manner, he inserts no species of the diatessaron—neither the first, second, nor third—in its natural place, except the one he places fourth, which lies between *A* and *D*, both of them first notes.

Let us now pass briefly over the crooked paths of those who err and hasten back to the straight roads of nature. But one question still remains, and it should not be passed over: why are the species arranged by some musicians in descending order, when you have established the whole order of those same species by ascending?

## VIII. Why some arrange the species in descending order

**WILH.** Whenever you find this done, you should know that it has been arranged according to descent—the manner in which the species are more clearly revealed in singing—not according to ascent, although ascent is everywhere prior to descent. This is so with a bow, with an arrow directed upward, and with rain: all these things first rise or are directed upward before they descend to the place from which they proceeded.

Finally, if the individual species, having been raised from tetrachord to tetrachord in the order described above, are made to descend, beginning from the furthest points where we established their limits, they all return by the same route by which they came to the principal tetrachord, as to the source and front of their origin. Nevertheless, every melody that has departed from the principal is governed, as we said above, by the final; it is regulated and judged by it.

**OTHL.** Since, therefore, dearest one, you have also satisfied me on this question, after the most beautiful production of the species of the diatessaron and diapente from their natural chamber, after the progression of the tetrachords, and after the subtle derivation of the first, second, third, and fourth notes from the principal tetrachord—and thereby, as you promised, of the whole harmony—please make the species of the diapason proceed with the same beauty as the lesser consonances.

## IX. On the species of the diapason

**WILH.** What more do you wish to know about the species of the diapason than what all musicians assert: namely, that there are seven, corresponding to the seven intervals of the voices? And since these same intervals are doubled on the monochord, the first rises from the first interval to the first—that is, from *A* to *a*; the second from the second to the second—that is, from *B* to *b*—and so it ascends by semitones or tones through the order of the letters, until the seventh ends at *g* in the highest register.

**OTHL.** If you, whom I would readily prefer to many investigators of nature’s more hidden Nile-like source, prove this constitution of the species of the diapason by the method you promised—that is, by showing that it proceeds with the unhindered step of natural order from the principal tetrachords—then I shall have no reason to labor further inquiring about them.

**WILH.** The ancient and modern authors of the musical art have written many plausible things, many useful things, and many that are highly necessary. Indeed, they discovered the first veins of this art and, with the pickaxe of Peripatetic reasoning, partly uncovered the clearest spring itself—that is, the principal tetrachord—although some, because ignorance somewhat disturbed one or another of the four matters in which the essence of this art consists, have offered us draughts that were not clear.

Therefore we ought to rise reverently before them in all things; and if they drank anything turbid, we must examine it more carefully and humbly purify what we have understood. This will be ready at hand if, with the Father of lights granting it, I bring forth, as I have begun to do, not only the lucid sequence of the species of the diapason that you request, but also the entire series of the four memorable matters, all inseparably joined to one another, from the purest and truest fountain of nature.

For just as, immediately after hearing the natural constitution of the species of the diatessaron and diapente, you judged that one of the moderns had gone astray, so, when the purity of the other matters has been examined, you will either discern for yourself with power what the ignorance of earlier musicians has disturbed in them, or you will quickly understand me when I discern it.

Nature makes it clear that there are eight species of the diapason, according to the number of the modes divided into authentic and plagal. Yet they must not be counted according to the order of natural number in such a way that you say first, second, third, fourth, fifth, sixth, and so reach the eighth. Rather, after the first four, another four must be counted and established, beginning again not from the fifth but from the first.

Therefore, if you place the principal and upper tetrachords opposite one another and join them, with the final tetrachord interposed as a kind of middle link and bond, four species of the diapason—the ones you desire—will proceed from them with the beauty of natural origin and order.

The first species of the diapason is contained by the first of the graves, *A*, and the first of the upper notes, *a*, and is distinguished by the middle of the first of the finals, *D*. The second is enclosed by the seconds of the two tetrachords, *B* and *b*, and is joined by the second of the finals, *E*. The third is formed by the thirds, *C* and *c*, and is joined by the third of the finals, *F*. The fourth is enclosed by the fourths, *D* and *d*, and is linked to the fourth of the finals, *G*, in its proper, almost hereditary and native seat.

You must repeatedly reflect upon the fact that these two notes, *D* and *d*, are two-formed and double, until you commit it to your tenacious memory, because the greatest error is avoided through knowledge of this, just as it is incurred through ignorance.

Likewise, if you compare the principal and highest tetrachords with one another across the upper tetrachord, the other four species of the diapason will appear with a similar adornment of nature.

The first species of the diapason is contained by the first of the finals, *D*, and the first of the highest notes, *d*—since they are double in number, as is the fourth—and is joined by another middle bond, namely the middle of the first of the upper notes, *a*. The second is bounded by the seconds of the two tetrachords, *E* and *e*, and is united by the second of the upper notes. The third is enclosed by the thirds, *F* and *f*, but is distinguished by the third of the upper notes, *c*. The fourth is contained by the fourths, *G* and *g*, and is joined by the fourth of the upper notes, *d*.

Must not those be called, and truly be, the first species of the diapason which are contained by the first notes and by the extremities, distinguished by the middle, and constituted from the first species of the lesser consonances? And are those which are formed in the same way from the second, third, or fourth notes not rightly called the second, third, or fourth?

**OTHL.** You have proved what you promised by a powerful and irresistible argument. But please continue quickly, so that, with the Lord’s help, you may bring the work to its completion.

**WILH.** Thus, once the eight species have been naturally constituted, the natural arrangement of the eight modes—improperly called “tones”—arises, so that the first four pass into the four plagal modes and the following four into the four authentic modes.

For if the four modes which exist by nature are distributed into eight in order to distinguish the variety of song, that which is the first of the first four species of the diapason is converted into the plagal protus, the second into the plagal deuterus, and the remaining two likewise into the other two plagal modes. Similarly, that which is first among the following four species, the one contained between *D* and *d*, is transferred into the authentic protus; the second into the authentic deuterus; and the remaining two into the two authentic modes left over.

If, however, they are arranged so that each authentic mode together with its corresponding plagal mode is regarded as one undifferentiated mode, then the two species of the diapason—one from each group of four—which the authentic and its plagal mode claim and from which they are constituted must be joined and combined.

For example, in the undifferentiated protus, the first species of the two groups—one extending from *A* to *a*, the other from *D* to *d*—come together. In the deuterus, to be composed without distinction, the second species of both groups meet: one extending from *B* to *b*, the other from *E* to *e*. In the tritus, the third species of both orders unite: one extending from *C* to *c*, the other from *F* to *f*. In the tetrardus, similarly to be joined, the fourth species from both groups come together: one extending from *D* to *d*, the other from *G* to *g*.

## X. The whole force and recognition of the modes lie in the operation of the principal notes

But whether this arrangement of the modes is spread into eight or confined to four, its entire natural power, as well as the innermost, most acute, and most careful investigation or recognition of that power, lies in the operation of the principal notes.

Not only this, but also the entire constitution of the species already described, the difference of the modes still to be discussed, all the principal divisions of the melodies, and their other properties—in short, whatever material is drawn and, so to speak, massed from the vein of the principal tetrachord—is formed by the same principal notes of each mode, as though by hammers.

Although, according to the division of a genus into species, I have placed the other three matters on an equal footing with this one—that is, with the operation of the principal notes—the latter nevertheless surpasses them by a marvelous effect of nature. For just as charity is subordinated to virtue, together with its other parts, according to the rule of division, while everything of which virtue is predicated is accomplished through charity itself, so the operation of the principal notes, although it belongs under the genus that is the discipline of music and shares its rank with the other matters, nevertheless in a certain way performs, arranges, and governs them all.

**OTHL.** I would now have believed the constitution of all the species and the arrangement of the modes to be so perfectly complete that anything further added would be superfluous rather than necessary. For it has placed the first species among the first notes, the seconds among the seconds, the thirds among the thirds, and the fourths among the fourths; and it has arranged the modes so naturally that the protus, together with its plagal mode, consists of the two first species of the diapason, the deuterus of the second species, the tritus of the third, and the tetrardus of the fourth.

**WILH.** There can be no progress in these matters, nor in those still to be presented, without the operation of the principal notes. You will eventually understand this operation more easily—whether it is complete or incomplete—in the things already constituted or arranged, after I have explained, as the Lord grants, which notes are the principal ones, how they receive different names according to different effects, and how they operate more strongly in the greater consonances and less strongly in the lesser.

## XI. Which are the principal notes, and what their operations are

The same notes which are called first in the constitution of the species because they contain the first species, and which are called second because they contain the second, third because they contain the third, or fourth because they determine the fourth, are called principal in the arrangement of the modes.

This is because, although, as I stated above, they generally possess the greatest power in all things, in this particular matter they preside with a marvelous and ineffable dignity; and in it, since its range is greater, they accomplish far more than they do in the constitution of the species of the diatessaron or diapente.

For the diatessaron or diapente, each of which is individually a tetrachord or pentachord, need only begin and end on first, second, third, or fourth notes. The diapason, however, from which the modes are arranged, and each of which consists of both the diatessaron and the diapente, is an octachord. Therefore, as though greater in extent, the diapasons are not only begun and ended on those same principal notes, but are also divided within themselves in various ways.

The four species of the diapason which establish the four plagal modes as their middles require divisions of this kind: they must have the diapente above and the diatessaron below. Those which pass into the authentic modes, however, must be divided so that the diatessaron is above and the diapente below.

And now, rather than speaking further of the species of the diapason, let us speak of the modes which are constituted from them, and of how the species themselves are transferred into the modes; let our comparison likewise pass from the species to the modes.

## XII. The natural arrangement of the modes: separately in eight, jointly in four

Each of the eight modes has only one middle division when considered separately; when joined and naturally arranged, they have two. To explain this more precisely, let them all be set out together here, both separately in eight and jointly in four, so that through their beginnings, endings, and middle divisions the full dignity and distinctive government of the principal notes may be expressed.

The authentic protus, which extends from *D* to *d*, has its middle division on *a*. Its plagal counterpart, which extends from *A* to *a*, places its middle division on *D*. If the two are joined so that they form the undifferentiated protus, it rises from *A* to *d*, containing two middle divisions, namely *D* and *a*.

The authentic deuterus, which extends from *E* to *e*, receives its middle division on *b*. Its plagal counterpart, which extends from *B* to *b*, places its middle division on *E*. If the two are united so that they form the continuous deuterus, it rises from *B* to *e*, containing two middle divisions, namely *E* and *b*.

The authentic tritus, which extends from *F* to *f*, draws out its middle division on *c*. Its plagal counterpart, which extends from *C* to *c*, marks its middle division on *F*. If they are joined so that they form the uniform tritus, it rises from *C* to *f*, containing two middle divisions, namely *F* and *c*.

The authentic tetrardus, which extends from *G* to *g*, takes its middle division on *d*. Its plagal counterpart, which extends from *D* to *d*, marks its middle division on *G*. If they are joined so that the tetrardus is naturally one mode, it reaches from *D* to *g*, determining two middle divisions, namely *G* and *d*.

Although, as I believe, this arrangement of the modes has now been completed distinctly and fully, lest its very fullness blunt the edge of the understanding with some cloud of confusion while one attempts to penetrate each detail, let the clarity of this figure be set before both the bodily and the inward eye more plainly still. See Figure A below, in Aribo and Cotton.

## XIII.

In this figure you will marvel to see the whole abyss of the subject we have undertaken—which has already been spread, through the course of our discussion, over the broad plain of the constitution of all the species and the arrangement of the modes—gathered and collected, by a certain natural movement, as though beneath the rim of a very small pool.

It has four paths, corresponding to the four natural modes—that is, to the modes united with their plagal counterparts. Each path, standing for the mode whose place it occupies, has the four principal notes inscribed upon it after the established intervals of the diatessaron and diapente, or of the diapason. These paths are shown to contain the briefest, yet fullest and clearest, recapitulation of the entire discussion traversed above.

For such great force and efficacy reside in the principal notes, as I have already mentioned, that this brief connection of them contains nearly the whole of what has already been touched upon or remains to be touched upon.

In the last path, which is entitled “protus,” when all the first elements have been gathered together and proportionally separated from one another, as on the monochord, it is clearly seen that *A* and *D*, as was said in the constitution of the species, conclude the first species of the diatessaron; *D* and *a*, the first species of the diapente; *a* and *d*, again the first species of the diatessaron; and *A* and *a*, the first species of the diapason. Likewise, *D* and *d* conclude the first species of the diapason.

It is also seen how the authentic protus consists of that first species of the diapason which extends from *D* to *d*, making its middle division on *a*, with a diatessaron above that *a* and a diapente below it; and how its plagal counterpart consists of that first species of the diapason which extends from *A* to *a*, establishing its middle division on *D*, with a diapente above that *D* and a diatessaron below it.

It is further seen how these two species of the diapason together constitute the undifferentiated protus, expanded by two middle divisions; and how, by an entirely wondrous regulation of nature, the operation of all the first notes alone constitutes the protus.

Likewise, in the second path, marked “deuterus,” all the second notes are arranged in the same proportion of intervals; in the third, marked “tritus,” all the third notes; and in the fourth, marked “tetrardus,” all the fourth notes. The matter is recognized not through a slow riddle that dulls the mind, but by the instantaneous and perceptible survey of the eye, as though face to face: each series of principal notes has in the mode to which it is assigned the same power of governing and operating specifically that the first notes have in the protus.

Whatever *A* and *D* constitute in the protus, the same do *B* and *E* in the deuterus, *C* and *F* in the tritus, and *D* and *G* in the tetrardus. The same holds for the others.

And so that you may see this also with bodily vision, let us release each path of our figure—which we confined by a brief description of the principal notes, placing them in the place of the four natural modes—into the full extent permitted by the rule, as follows. See Figure B below.

## XIV. The figure of the monochord and its explanation

It must be noted universally here that all the authentic modes, beginning from the finals, ascend to the highest notes and are divided in the upper register. All the plagal modes, however, beginning from the graves, end in the upper register and have their middle divisions in the finals.

Thus the finals and the upper notes are common to both groups; the graves belong to the plagal modes, while the highest notes belong to the authentic modes. The natural, or undifferentiated, four modes begin from the graves and extend all the way to the highest notes, receiving their middle divisions both in the finals and in the upper notes.

This happens in such a way, however, that the beginnings, endings, and middle divisions of all the modes are unequally distant from one another, yet equality governs everything: each mode both begins and ends and is divided by its own principal notes, as we mentioned above, and consists and is governed entirely by them. Thus the protus consists of all the first notes, the deuterus of all the second, the tritus of all the third, and the tetrardus of all the fourth.

It also seems sufficiently noteworthy that here the authority of nature clearly grants Ptolemy the point he makes when he proves, by the truest reasoning, the consonance of the diapason with the diatessaron—although the ancient philosophers rejected it because it is constituted from a *superpartient* proportion. For although each of the four natural modes is composed from these diapasons according to the aforementioned joining of the species, nevertheless, according to the plain form of this description and the simple number of the notes, each of them exists as a consonance consisting of that diapason together with only the diatessaron.

Thus, when the eight modes are kept distinct, each has three principal notes; when they are rejoined in four, each has four. Consequently, two modes separated from one another and considered individually contain six principal notes, whereas, when joined and reduced to one mode, they have only four.

This is also almost the most memorable point of all, and one that surpasses nearly everything else here: this distribution of the principal notes through the beginnings, endings, and middle divisions of the eight modes clearly demonstrates what we mentioned above and said must be repeatedly reconsidered and pondered—namely, how *D* and *d* become two-formed and double.

Three modes of their two-formed and double character are plainly shown here.

## XV. Why *D* and *d* are two-formed and double

First, in the order or number of the principal notes of the tetrachords, they are the last of the graves and upper notes, and the first of the finals and highest notes.

Second, in the arrangement of the modes, they occupy one and the same interval in both the authentic protus and the plagal tetrardus.

Third, in the difference of the modes—that is, in the recognition of the modes—they establish both the first mode and the fourth.

This third mode of their doubleness will meanwhile be more obscure to you than the other two, until we begin to discuss the modes of the voices.

For these three reasons we owe the supreme giver all the greater thanks, since these matters have remained unknown and hidden from all ancient and modern writers until now, and, while hidden, have been for them the greatest cause of error. For although, as was said above, they have deviated in various places through ignorance of the four matters in which the essence of the musical art consists, in this particular matter—that is, in recognizing the two-formed character of *D* and *d*—they were struck by a special blindness and, as though driven back by a unanimous stumbling, were all led into error.

Therefore, as we contemplate more deeply the wondrous nature of *D* and *d*, considering that in each mode of their two-formed and double character both together make one, we have not inappropriately called them “cornerstones.” But considering the fact that all musicians have seriously stumbled over them, we rightly call them “stones of offense” and “rocks of stumbling.”

To prove this beyond doubt, let us recall how greatly the foremost of the ancients, Boethius, and the most eminent of the moderns, Otto and Guido, stumbled over these notes.

## XVI. How Boethius and the other musicians went astray concerning *D* and *d*, and why the double *A* must necessarily be assumed
Boethius, in the disposition of the eight modes represented diagrammatically, where he calls the modes by their original names—authentic protus, Dorian; deuterus, Phrygian; tritus, Lydian; tetrardus, Mixolydian; and the plagals hypodorian, [Col. 1161C] hypophrygian, hypolydian, and hypomixolydian—went so far astray that, although the plagals are so called because they are subordinated, subjected, or placed beneath the authentics, he placed the plagal of tetrardus, which we call the eighth, above its authentic Mixolydian, and consequently called it “hypermixolydian.” Here, to say not merely how incongruous but how entirely impossible the place of a plagal would be, the authority of nature itself teaches us that each mode has been assigned, as we have sufficiently explained, such a position that it receives its beginning, ending, and medial distinction on its principal strings, and that the arrangement of the modes forbids it to exceed the limit of the four principal tetrachords, which lies at high g. Hence, establishing D and d as double and two-formed both in the number and in the function [Col. 1161D] of their strings, he completes the entire arrangement of the modes within fourteen strings—that is, with seven intervals set down twice—and thus allows high a to remain as though superfluous, on which, according to Boethius, that plagal ends.

Why should we say “according to Boethius,” and not “according to Ptolemy,” or “according to all the most ancient musicians”? Boethius himself recalls in his *Music* that this same diagram of the arrangement of the modes was derived in his time from the ancient musicians, and that Ptolemy, their most distinguished representative, added the same plagal at the top. After completing the arrangement of the modes, he says:

> “So that the reasoning may be grasped not only by the understanding, but that its form may also be recognized by the eyes, the diagram handed down by the ancient musicians must be set below.”

And after inserting some intervening material:

> “And this,” he says, “is the eighth mode, which Ptolemy appended above.”

He also explained the reason for this addition: namely, that since the ancients received only seven modes, just as there are seven species of the octave according to the seven intervals of the voices, their arrangement of the modes began from the *proslambanomenos*, which is A, and was led step by step by the customary intensification of tones and semitones to the *paranete hyperboleon*, which is g, where it ended. Since this arrangement of the modes consists of only fourteen simple strings, and the highest string of the double octave, the *nete hyperboleon*, which is a, was still lacking, so that the entire double octave might be contained in this order [Col. 1162B], Ptolemy added an eighth mode and placed it between a and high a.

By this statement the ancients seem to have thought that the modes should be increased for the purpose of ensuring that nothing would remain over from the total number of strings in their arrangement. We, however, truly think that additional strings must rather be placed so that nothing is lacking—not only from the natural arrangement, but also from the regular extension and freedom of the modes, in which the whole force of harmony resides. For we say—and prove this by the most certain examples of Gregorian chant—that all modes sometimes extend above and below the limits of their natural octave to a neighboring note, and sometimes to the third. High a is therefore entirely necessary so that this freedom may be assigned equally to all.

For this reason also high a cannot in any way be lost from the total number of strings, since the quadruple, which is the beginning of measuring the monochord, first terminates its space there. Anyone who understands even the simplest matters knows how completely indispensable it is for this further reason: in the general structure of the monochord, nothing proportional can be found in its regular order without it. For these three reasons, therefore, the *nete hyperboleon* is firmly established; and it is not abolished merely because it may appear superfluous in the natural arrangement of the modes. Indeed, it should already be clear, I think, that without it the double octave would have to exist wholly within the space of fourteen strings—that is, from sixteen strings reduced to fourteen.

## XVII. How the modern musicians went astray regarding these same strings

[Col. 1162D]

So much concerning the place of error according to the ancients. Let us now consider it according to those moderns whom we have proposed to discuss, and do so all the more strictly because we have treated the scandal of the ancients at greater length for the sake of clear understanding.

Otto makes it sufficiently clear in his *Enchiriadis* that, through the elevation of his natural intelligence, he alone detected this common place of error. But while he was excessively cautious and seemed in this matter more circumspect than the others, he stumbled more seriously than they did. For he alone understood D and d as two-formed and double; and while he tried to present this distinctly and openly for everyone to understand, he exceeded the proper measure in distinguishing them.

Since D is one and the same final string of the graves and first string of the finals, and since it is likewise both the first and the fourth, he, in his description—where he speaks with an extremely subtle and sufficiently truthlike method about the modes and the principal strings of each mode—did not wish, as I believe in order to avoid confusion, to call it both first and fourth in one and the same place. Instead, in order to designate more clearly that it was double, he calls it fourth in its proper place and order, but, with a tone interposed, declares it first in the fifth place. Thus, from one natural D, in which the two together make one, he makes two in a certain sense contrary to nature. The same should be understood concerning d.

To compare his error with the scandal of the ancients: what nature doubles, they make simple, so that we may coin a word according to the character of the matter; and conversely, what nature makes simple by joining and uniting, he doubles by separating and dividing.

They, concentrating only on the seven distinctions of the voices and believing all the strings of the monochord to be simple, established only seven modes from them. They did not see the eighth, which lay concealed among them through the aforesaid doubleness of D and d, since they understood less fully that these same strings are both first and fourth. For since the principal tetrachords are naturally distinguished in such a way that each contains one of the four orders of principal strings constitutive of the modes—namely, the first from the first, the first from the second, the first from the third, and the first from the fourth—and since the tetrachords of the graves and finals converge at D, so that the same string is both fourth of the graves and first [Col. 1163C] of the finals; and in the same way the tetrachords of the superiors and high strings terminate at d, so that the same string is both fourth of the superiors and first of the high strings: they, ignorant of this twofold nature, as we have often said, call both strings first and remain silent about their being fourth. Thus, depriving the tetrachords of the graves and superiors of their fourth, they in a certain sense empty and mutilate their natural perfection in their principal strings.

He, on the contrary, penetrating more sharply than anyone else with the edge of his understanding both the twofold or double nature of D and d and the natural perfection of the tetrachords—that is, their fourfold solidity in the arrangement of the principal strings—and wishing, as we have said, to make this clear to everyone, wanted to assign fully and distinctly to each tetrachord its own first, second, third, and fourth, as well as its own beginning and end, in each set of strings. With this intention, however, he severed the natural joining and conjunction of the first and fourth at D and d by the ill-advised and insufficiently cautious interposition of a tone, and thus, [Col. 1164A] by disturbing the regular order of the entire structure of the monochord, destroyed it. He thereby confounded the whole contemplation of harmony, both that which is according to the ancients and moderns and that which is according to the authority of nature herself.

As is evident to those who investigate the matter there, in his description there is no arrangement of species, either customary or natural; no disposition of the modes; no complete operation of the principal strings; and no coherent order in the recognition of the modes. For none of the strings in his description is found to be the same at the octave, although this is proved both by the unanimous assertion of all and by the invincible truth of nature to be necessary.

Let this suffice concerning the error of the venerable Otto. If we have lingered longer than promised over it, we think this pardonable because of the difficulty of its knot, scarcely capable of being loosened or escaped.

**OTHL.** You cannot be accused of having said anything here except what is useful and necessary.
