For although you repeated certain things said above, they are so entirely relevant to this subject that without their elucidation the cloud of obscurity could in no way have been dispelled; therefore the repetition is neither superfluous nor absurd. What is so necessary to know is not repeated without reason, since, if it is once unknown, the very useful knowledge of many matters proceeding from it is lost. Thus, being more confident of pardon than if you had failed to say some of what has just been stated, please continue and explain how Guido also fell into this place of error.

## XVIII. How Lord Guido, recognizing the error of the ancients, did not correct it

[Col. 1164C]

**WILH.** Guido, stumbling seriously in that same place, first followed the deviations of the ancients. But in the course of his treatment, as though touched by a certain bright illumination of intelligence, he partly recognized that those whom he was following had been led astray. Thus he stopped, so that he neither wandered farther after them nor corrected their errors by retracing his path.

For in his *Music*, asserting that the eight modes are more truly four in nature, and that each one of the four contains two—that is, protus contains the first and second, deuterus the third and fourth, tritus the fifth and sixth, and tetrardus the seventh and eighth—and wishing to express this diagrammatically, he places all the principal strings in a single order and assigns to each its proper mode together with its plagal: to each first, the first with the second; to each second, the third with the fourth; to each third, the fifth with the sixth; and to each fourth, the seventh with the eighth. He describes it in this way.

[Col. 1163] **[Note:** Here and elsewhere among the ancients, B *durum*, or square B, is understood; later writers express it by H, as in the scale above.]

[Col. 1165A]

In this description, therefore, insofar as he deprived the tetrachords of the graves and superiors of their fourth, he did not understand the twofold nature of D and d. For if he had understood it, he would likewise have marked first together with second, and seventh together with eighth, on both sides, in this manner:

And insofar as he assigns four principal strings to all the other undifferentiated modes, but grants only two to tetrardus, he followed the deviations of the ancients.

As regards the fact that in the same description he did not concentrate on the seven distinctions of the voices according to the most ancient authorities to such an extent that he rejected the eighth mode, and that, while accepting it, he does not place it between A and a, above its authentic according to Ptolemy, he perceived in some fashion that those whom he had followed were misled and stopped; yet he did not wander through and gather all the traces of their seduction.

Again, insofar as he gives the same eighth mode a seat between G and g—that is, within the range of its authentic—and not rather between D and d, he is recognized as having failed to correct the errors. He also fell twice elsewhere into the same common scandal, as is apparent from the fact that he did so while speaking about the modes of the voices, or the recognition of the modes. After what the Lord may grant us to say about this, the matter will be discussed more coherently and more easily understood.

**OTHL.** Although I seem to perceive everything you have said, both from the exceptionally clear order of your exposition and from the unmistakable judgment of your diagram, I am uncertain about one thing: whether all the strings of the entire monochordal description are principal, or only some; and, if all are principal, whether they become principal simultaneously or alternately.

## XIX. How all the strings, although principal, are mutually above and below one another

**WILH.** If the universal structure of the monochord is divided into tetrachords according to the method of measurement, as we discussed at the beginning of this conversation, scarcely any string can be principal. But if it is naturally divided into principal tetrachords, all will be principal except Γ and high a, which exceed the limits of the principal tetrachords. All the others, I say, are principal, though not simultaneously, but by mutual succession.

For if the melody of any mode is taken up, for as long as it is being sung, its principal strings, claiming for themselves authority, rule, and leadership throughout the entire monochord, unanimously preside, while all the others are subjected to them as though to a kindly servitude. We shall explain this more clearly when treating the modes of the voices.

**OTHL.** The more matters have been deferred to this treatise, the less do I wish you to insert anything into it. Begin at once in what seems to me a suitable order.

**WILH.** You have observed the proper order: after explaining three of the four matters on whose knowledge the summit of the musical art depends, we should append the fourth, namely the modes of the voices. In this matter, as in all others, because I wish to comply with your good will, let us first explain what the modes of the voices are and why they are more properly called recognitions of the modes, so that whatever we say about them may be understood more easily.

## XX. On the four modes of the voices

The modes of the voices are the properties of the species of chant, that is, of the modes. For the four modes themselves, which we call natural and undifferentiated, are four species of chant, differing from one another by such diversity of neumes that, as the venerable Guido testifies, none of them grants the other a place in its own domain, and either never receives the other’s neume or transforms it once received.

Each of the four modes, which we improperly call tones, therefore possesses its own qualities of neumes. From these qualities musicians recognize, immediately at the beginning or even in the middle of each chant, to which mode the chant belongs. These different qualities of neumes are called “modes of the voices” by the memorable Guido, who alone speaks about them. We think that, for the reason already given, they should more properly be called “recognitions of the modes.” But, out of due reverence for the Fathers who preceded us, retaining the customary name, let us treat the modes of the voices—when the Spirit, breathing where it wills, inspires us—with such a discussion as we can, of the kind you requested at the beginning of this dialogue: namely, that if the venerable Guido has said too little about them, something should be added; if anything is obscure, it should be explained; and if anything has been stated without sufficient caution, it should be humbly corrected, not in rash display but in obedience to charity.

Accordingly, there are four modes of the voices, corresponding to the number of the four natural modes. From each of them one of those modes is recognized, as has been said. Lord Guido explains them as follows:

The first mode of the voices occurs when a voice descends by a tone and rises by a tone, a semitone, and two tones, as between A and D.

The second mode occurs when a voice descends by two tones and rises by a semitone and two tones, as between B and E.

The third mode is that which descends by a semitone and two tones but rises by two tones, as between C and F.

The fourth descends by a tone but rises by two tones and a semitone, as between D and G.

After this he adds:

> “And note that they follow one another in order: the first on A, the second on B, the third on C; likewise the first on D, the second on E, the third on F, and the fourth on G.”

Those who first discovered the musical art, or who used strings discovered in various ways after their construction, established the beginning of the monochord at the *hypate hypaton*, which is consequently interpreted as “the principal of the principals.” In producing chants they had only fourteen strings. Later, Ptolemy, king of Egypt, placed at the beginning the voice called *proslambanomenos*, A—that is, “the acquired,” or rather *prosmelodos*, “suitable for melody.” These are the fifteen regular strings of the monochord. I have passed over their names and interpretations for the present, since I have found many people who have written about them. The moderns have also added at the beginning one low sound, the *synemmenon* B, for certain advantages that we shall discuss later.

The four principal tetrachords made according to the method of melody, or according to the institution of the modes, differ from the four made according to the method of measurement in this respect: the former have the semitone in the middle, whereas the latter have it at the end; the former are joined at low D and high d, whereas the latter are joined at e and E; in the former, a tone remains above in each octave, whereas in the latter it remains below.

The beginnings of the modes are recognized wherever their differentiae—that is, their *saeculorum amen*—begin. Each authentic mode begins above its final on the fifth degree, that is, in its proper species of diapente, except deuterus alone. Because of the imperfection of the semitone—or rather because of the boundary and seat of the modes—it transfers itself from its second principal string to C, where protus naturally begins. Deuterus therefore begins on C by transposition, as has been said; tritus begins by nature there, while tetrardus begins on d.

A plagal, however, does not begin above its final on the diapente, as the masters say, but has its beginning somewhat below it, wherever this suits them. Thus the plagal of protus begins on F; the plagals of deuterus and tritus begin together on the middle note; and the plagal of tetrardus begins on c.

Thus the first, fourth, or sixth tone begins on the middle note; the second alone on F; the third, fifth, and eighth on C; the seventh alone on d. Each mode ends together with its plagal on its proper final string: protus on D, deuterus on E, tritus on F, and tetrardus on G. Hence this is also called the tetrachord of the finals.

Differences among the modes occur in two ways. First, they differ naturally from one another in structure, consonances, species, principal strings, distinctions, modes of the voices, beginnings, and endings; and one does not grant the other a place in its own domain, while one either transforms the other’s neume or never receives it, along with many other matters of this kind.

Second, the chants of the individual modes do not always have one and the same beginning. A chant that begins on the final string of any mode occupies the place of the first differentia. One that begins below the final, on a neighboring or third sound, bears the name of the second or third differentia. A chant beginning above the final on the third, fourth, or fifth sound will be recognized as having the fourth, fifth, or sixth differentia.

## XXI. How many intervals of the voices there are

Lord Guido testifies that there are only six intervals of the voices by which every chant is arranged: the semitone, tone, ditone, diatessaron, and diapente, together with the unison at the beginning; at the end, however, he cuts off the diapente with a semitone and the diapente with a tone, saying that these should not be recorded with the others because they can never properly be approved in regular chant.

We, however, find not only these nine intervals but also the diapente with a semitone—that is, twice a diatessaron—and sometimes even the diapason itself in Gregorian chant. Therefore, if we ought to reject any of these intervals, we do not know which one.

Since Lord Berno has elucidated nine consonances with examples, we shall explain those he omitted. Unison occurs when the voice does not change, but many neumes continue through repeated iterations on one sound, as is shown at the beginning of this antiphon:

> **Antiphon:** “Behold, the Desired One will come.”

The same is especially clear in this antiphon:

> “Turn back to me with all your heart.”

The diapente with a semitone occurs when the voice rises or descends through four tones and two semitones, as in the verse:

> “Give me understanding.”

Anyone who begins it correctly after the end of the preceding chant by this interval can prove the point. In the verse:

> “Lord God, you have known,”

at the descent of the final neume, “my justice,” and at the ascent of the first, “I have not concealed,” the interval is recognized as a diapason.

These consonances must therefore be known correctly to the mind and ears. For this art and knowledge are collected in vain unless they become thoroughly familiar through use and practice.

## XXII. On the consonances

There are six consonances, three simple and three compound.

The simple consonances are the diatessaron, diapente, and diapason.

The compound consonances are the diapason with the diatessaron, the diapason with the diapente, and twice the diapason.

## XXIII. What intervals consist of

[Col. 1168C]

The diatessaron consists of two tones and a semitone; the diapente of three tones and a semitone; and the diapason of five tones and two semitones.

## XXIV. How many species these consonances have

The diatessaron has three species, the diapente four, and the diapason seven.

The first species of diatessaron has the semitone in the middle, as from A to D.

The second has it first, as from B to E.

The third has it in the last place, as from C to F.

The first species of diapente has the semitone after a tone, followed by a ditone, as from D to a.

The second has the semitone first, followed by a tritone, as from E to [the source is incomplete here].

The third has the semitone last, after the tritone, as from F to c.

The fourth has the semitone after the ditone, followed thereafter by a whole tone, as from G to d.

[Col. 1168D]

The order of the species of the diapason according to the position of the letters in the monochord is as follows: the first species from A to a, the second from B to b, the third from C to c, and so on.

Examples of the intervals or consonances will be clear in the verses of the most illustrious Hermann:

> Three times three joined intervals of sounds there are.

That is: the kinds of neume sounded by the semitone, tone, semiditone, ditone, diatessaron, diapente, diapente with a semitone, and diapente with a tone.

## XXV. What proportions the intervals consist of

The diatessaron consists of the sesquitertian proportion; the diapente of the sesquialteran; the diapason of the duple; the tone [Col. 1169A] of the sesquioctave. The parts of the semitone are called *apotomes*.

## XXVI. How many strings each mode ascends or descends

Each authentic mode may ascend from its final to the tenth string, and no farther, except tetrardus, which ascends only to the ninth sound. Below its final, each authentic descends to a neighboring or third sound, never to a fourth, unless it is a common chant, which is an undifferentiated mode.

The plagals, however, rise from their final beyond the diapente to the sixth sound, and rarely to the seventh; below their final they often take a tone in addition to the diatessaron.

## XXVII. To which mode each string belongs

[Col. 1169B]

The first principal strings of the individual tetrachords belong to protus and its plagal: A, D, a, d; the second belong to deuterus: B, E, e; the third to tritus: C, F, c, f; and the fourth to tetrardus: D, G, d, g. Thus each of these modes has one string among the graves, one among the finals, one among the superiors, and one among the high strings.

First, because each mode, according to the property of its nature, is equally intensified and relaxed on its principal strings. Thus in protus all the first strings—A, D, a, d—are lowered by a tone and raised by the first species of diapente.

Similarly, deuterus is lowered by a ditone on all its principal strings, namely the second strings B, E, e, and is raised by the second species of diatessaron.

Tritus is raised by a ditone on all the third strings, C, F, c, f, [Col. 1169C] and lowered by the third species of diatessaron.

Tetrardus is raised by a tone on all the fourth strings, D, G, d, g, and lowered by the fourth species of diapente.

Second, on the first principal string of each mode occurs the deepest descent; on the second, the melodic ending; on the third, the beginning of the differentiae; and on the fourth, the highest ascent.

Third, the neumes of the modes are distinguished and extended on these same strings.

Fourth, the second and fourth principal strings conclude the authentics, while the first and third conclude the plagals.

## XXVIII. On the seats of the modes

The seats or boundaries of the modes are eight, but their legitimate seats are recognized in only four places: C, [Col. 1169D] G, a, and c.

Let us therefore see how many boundaries, or intervals of boundaries, can be made in the monochord, and why they are said to be more legitimate in the places mentioned than in others, as was stated above.

According to the method of melody or the institution of the modes, four tetrachords are established in the monochord: the graves, A, B, C, D; the finals, D, E, F, G; the superiors, a, b, c, d; and the high strings, d, e, f, g.

If you add a tone to either side of any one of these tetrachords, some boundary of the modes arises. Thus, from the graves, the first boundary is from Γ to E; from the finals, the second is from C to a; from the superiors, the third is from G to e; from the high strings, the fourth is from c to high a; and through the *synemmenon* a fifth may arise from F to d.

The first boundary, from Γ to E, because it begins with a regular tone and ends less perfectly in a semitone, supplies no seat for a mode and is therefore not legitimate.

The second begins with a regular tone and ends in a regular tone, that is, on the middle note; it is therefore most noble and perfect. At its beginning and end the modes rest, as it were, in certain seats.

The third begins with a regular tone, namely on G, but ends less perfectly in a semitone, namely on e. It is therefore legitimate at its beginning, but its end is not accepted.

The fourth begins with a regular tone, namely on c, and is therefore not perfect because it ends on high a. But since the *synemmenon* cannot be a seat of the modes in the monochord, the fifth, which is placed in the middle, is entirely rejected because the *synemmenon* is less regular.

You see, therefore, that the legitimate seats of the modes are in the places that have been mentioned.

## XXIX. In which tetrachords the principal strings of each mode are found

The first principal string in every mode is in the tetrachord of the finals, the second in that of the superiors, the third in that of the high strings, and the fourth in that of the graves. Thus, for protus: D, d. The last is therefore the gravest, because the authentic must first be constructed through these strings before its plagal; just as the authentic is constructed upward, so the plagal must be constructed downward.

Let us separate authentic protus from its plagal. The authentic begins on D and ends on d, and has these three principal strings above it: D, a, d. The plagal, however, beginning on A and ending on a, likewise has these three below it: a, B, A. Joined together, these make six.

Do the same with the others.

## XXX. That the strings are common to authentics and plagals, and which are proper to each

The authentics have two principal strings in common with their plagals, in the tetrachords of the finals and superiors, and one proper string in the tetrachord of the high strings.

The plagals have one proper string in the graves and likewise two in common with their authentics, namely in the finals and superiors.

Thus authentic protus, ascending from D to d, has its first and middle strings in common with its plagal, while its third is proper to it. The plagal, extending from A to a, has its first string, A, as its proper string, while its second and third, D and a, are common with the authentic.

Hence what was said above: strings that are simple receive a simple mode and mode of the voices; those that are double receive a double one. The two middle strings jointly conclude the authentic and the plagal; the first, A, determines the simple plagal, and the fourth, a, determines the simple authentic.

## XXXI. Which strings enclose the authentics and which the plagals

The second and fourth of the principal strings conclude the authentic, while the third is its middle string. The first and third conclude the plagal, while the second is its middle string.

Thus, in protus, D and d enclose the authentic, whose middle distinction is a; A and a enclose its plagal, whose middle string is D.

## XXXII. On the eight modes

[Col. 1171A]

The eight modes of the tropes consist in this: that it is shown separately what kind of symphony the proper neumes of each of the eight tropes produce.

## XXXIII. On the circles of the modes

The circles of the modes occur when the chant of each mode, led along its regular course and brought back to its final, repeatedly returns to it.

## XXXIV. How the modes are similar

They are almost alike in this respect: authentic tetrardus and its plagal compose their melody through the same species of diatessaron.

But they are very unlike in this respect: in the natural modes of their voices they make greatly different distinctions.

For if you add a tone above the first species of diatessaron, the first species of diapente arises, which belongs to protus; or, conversely, if you add a tone below that same first species of diatessaron, the fourth [the source reads “third” in one place] species of diapente arises, which belongs to tetrardus.

Thus, wonderfully, in the contrary ordering of their natural voices, if you add a tone on either side of the first species of diatessaron, the lower tone, being relaxed, causes the first mode of the voices, that of protus, to be intensified through its proper species of diapente and causes it to be relaxed by a tone; but the upper tone, being intensified, causes the fourth mode of the voices, that of tetrardus, to rise by a tone and to be lowered through its proper species, namely the fourth diapente.

Whatever species of diatessaron you add a tone to, above or below, produces for you a species of protus or tetrardus. Whatever species of diapente belonging to protus or tetrardus can be made there—for deuterus and tritus possess some species in the diatessaron in their modes of the voices—protus and tetrardus possess in the diapente. The former have these in intensification, the latter in relaxation.

## XXXV. On the refraction of the modes

The refraction of deuterus and tritus appears first in the modes of the voices, because what protus and tetrardus have in the diapente, these have in the diatessaron.

Second, they cannot be constituted in the diapason in two ways, through the diapente and diatessaron, as the others can: deuterus in the plagal and tritus in the authentic.

Third, the principal string of deuterus is very rarely reached because of the seats of the modes above and below.

## XXXVI. How the three plagals have the species of diapente below the final

The fact that the three plagals seek their proper species of diapente within the final more by force than by the power of nature arises from the fact that the lower *synemmenon*, invented by the moderns, is less regular and therefore less natural.

The first plagal descends through D, C, B, A by its proper species of diapente.

The second is lowered through E, D, C, B, A by its diapente.

The third is lowered through F, E, D, C, B by its proper species of diapente.

The fourth plagal, which does not touch the *synemmenon*, has a natural diapente below the final from G to C. It seems to some musicians that it is not needed in a regularly composed higher chant, because they give the least consideration to how necessary its advantages are even in the lower range—not merely for the adornment of sweet chant, but also for the natural and unavoidable arrangements of all the plagals. These seek below their final not only the diapente but also their proper species of diapente more by force than by the power of nature, except the fourth plagal.

## XXXVII. That the modes are constructed in various ways by ascent and descent

The diapason of protus is constructed in two ways: from D to a by a diapente and from a to d by a diatessaron; conversely, from d to G by a diapente and from G to D by a diatessaron.

You can do the same with the diapason of its plagal and with the diapason of authentic deuterus.

The diapason of the plagal of deuterus, however, cannot be constructed a second time from B to b through a diapente and diatessaron, because there are only two semitones between B and F, below which there is no tritone; for the diapente consists of one semitone and three tones.

Similarly, authentic tritus is not constructed in two ways within its diapason through a diapente and diatessaron, because below the two semitones the tritone is lacking. If you say once that from F to c is a diapente and from c to f a diatessaron, you have no way to do this conversely a second time.

Its plagal and authentic tetrardus with its plagal are constructed once by intensification and a second time by relaxation, just as protus and its plagal are constructed in two ways.

The four principal strings of protus—A, D, a, d—because all are equally lowered by a tone and raised by the first species of diapente, produce the quality of the first mode.

The principal strings of deuterus—B, E, [e], e—lowered by a ditone and raised by the second species of diatessaron, reveal the difference of the second mode.

The principal strings of tritus—C, F, c, f—lowered by the third species of diatessaron and equally raised by a ditone, disclose the quality of the third mode.

The principal strings of tetrardus—D, G, d, g—all raised by a tone and lowered by the fourth species of diapente, reveal the difference of the fourth mode.

Behold: the four principal strings of the modes manifest with the greatest clarity the different qualities of the four modes.

These differences are said to occur in seven intervals because, in the monochord, the seven voices in the high range—that is, from the middle note to the end—are not different from those in the low range, but are the same. Thus each mode has in the high range the same principal strings that it has in the graves. Protus, for example, has A and D as its principal strings in the graves, and likewise a and d in the high range. The same applies to the others.

## XXXVIII. On the modes of the voices
The first mode of the voices arises wherever a voice can be lowered by a tone and raised by the first species of the diapente, as may be recognized in the principal strings of the protus, A, D, a, d. [Col. 1173A] This mode is therefore assigned indifferently to the protus, as this authentic antiphon proves: “The prophets have proclaimed.” The second mode displays a voice lowered by a ditone and raised by the second species of the diatessaron. It occurs in the principal strings of the deuterus, B, E, e, and the same mode is assigned to it; this plagal antiphon displays it: “This is the glory.” The third mode is lowered by the third species of the diatessaron and raised by a ditone, as the principal strings of the tritus, C, F, c, f, declare; it too belongs to this mode. An indication of this kind is found in this plagal antiphon: “A little while, and you will not see me.” The fourth mode we attach to the tetrachord: it is raised by a tone and lowered by the fourth species of the diapente, because its principal strings, D, G, d, g, constitute it. This mode possesses the following special feature among the others: [Col. 1173B] it can be recognized not only in this authentic antiphon, “If indeed, brothers,” but also in this plagal antiphon, “Many are coming.” First, because, although all the strings within the established limit repeat their octave fifteen strings later, the soft b also repeats its B; second, because no mode can have its proper species of the diapente below its final without the lower synemmenon, except the tetrardus.

### XXXIX. The proportions by which the four consonances are constituted

The diatessaron consists of the sesquitertian proportion, as four is to three. Here the greater number contains the lesser number in full and, in addition, its third part—that is, one unit—which, joined to the former, makes seven. Thus, by measuring the monochord according to seven, you will have in the middle, on either side, the most certain consonance of the diatessaron.

The diapente consists of the sesquialteral proportion, as three is to two. Here the greater number contains the lesser and its half; joining them together, you will have five. For by measuring the monochord according to five, you will find the consonance of the diapente.

The diapason consists of the duple proportion, as four is to two. If you join these, they make six; therefore you must measure the consonance of the diapason according to six.

The diapason with the diatessaron consists of the double-superpartient proportion, as eight is to three. For eight contains three twice, and for this reason it is called “double,” together with two thirds; these joined together make [Col. 1173D] eleven. Therefore you must measure that consonance according to eleven.

The diapason with the diapente consists of the triple proportion, as three is to one; joined together, these make four. Therefore you must measure the same consonance according to four.

The bisdiapason consists of the quadruple proportion, as four is to one. These, then, joined together, make five; therefore you must measure that consonance according to five.

### XL. The measurement of the monochord

Whoever wishes to construct our figure—the “theorem of the tropes” [text uncertain: *vecribrum*] of the monochord, as we think it may not improperly be called—quickly and continuously should first leave a space, appropriately marked by letters, according to the height of the monochord, and divide the remainder into four equal intervals. Let each of these be assigned to one of the tropes and inscribed with its proper name. The lowest interval, adjacent to you, shall be called protus; the one next to it, deuterus; the penultimate, tritus; and the highest, tetrardus. It contains not only the tetrardus but also the arrangement of the regular monochord.

The names to be written on the individual intervals should be the first syllables of the four tropes: PR, DE, TR, TE. You must commit these monograms so firmly to memory that, whenever you name something, you immediately understand to which trope that interval belongs.

Having therefore established, as we said, five intervals distinguished by the drawing of lines, place points on the last line at either end, according to Guido’s measurement, opposite one another. To find these more quickly, it is useful to employ the more rapid measurement of the lord Guido; I have not hesitated to set it down here also, so that whoever has not previously used it may have it ready at hand.

When you divide the distance from Γ to the end into nine steps—that is, into nine parts—the first step ends at A, the second is empty, the third at D, the fourth is empty, the fifth at a, the sixth at d, the seventh at aa; the remaining steps are empty.

Likewise, when you divide the distance from A to the end into nine parts, the first step ends at B, the second is empty, the third at E, the fourth is empty, the fifth at [text missing in source], the sixth at e, the seventh at [text missing in source]; the remaining steps are empty.

Likewise, when you divide the distance from Γ to the end into four parts, the first step ends at C, the second at G, the third at d, and the fourth reaches the end.

When, similarly, you make four steps from C to the end, the first ends at F, the second at c, the third at cc, and the fourth reaches the end.

From F, with four steps, the first ends at the round b, that is, the synemmenon; the second at f; the remaining steps are empty.

From the round b to the end, with two steps, the first ends at bb and the second reaches the end.

From d to the end, with two steps, the first ends at dd and the second reaches the end.

According to this measurement, with points impressed on the terminal lines and letters attached to each point, you will arrange the whole structure with the greatest ease. But since some difficulty and confusion arise from the fact that each trope’s measurement has the synemmenon in its own fixed places, we distinguish the synemmena themselves and the semitones next to them by the two syllables SY and SE, as follows. We mark with the monograms to which SY has been added the synemmena; with those to which SE has been added, the neighboring places of the semitones.

Thus, on dd and on the point directly opposite it, the summit of the protus is marked by a straight rule; on cc, the boundary of the deuterus together with the protus; on [the unlettered point in the source], the extremity of the tritus; on the round bb, DE and PR; on aa, the end of TE, TR, and PR.

At g all the tropes meet together at their highest points: TE, TR, DE, PR. At f: TE, DE, PR. At e: TE, TR, SE, PR. At d, all the higher ones sound together: TE, TR, SE, DE, PR. At c: TE, SY, TR, DE, PR. At n: SE, TE, TR. At the round b: SY, TE, DE, PR. At a: TE, TR, PR.

Likewise, at G all the final notes sound together; at F: TE, DE, PR; at E: TE, TR, PR. [Col. 1175A] At D all the lower notes are gathered together; at C: TE, DE, together with the beginning of the protus; at B: SE, TE, TR, the lower synemmenon between B and A, together with the beginning of the deuterus; at A: TE, together with the beginning of the tritus; at Γ: TE, together with the entire beginning of the structure.

The semitones of the tritus and deuterus, together with the synemmenon of the protus and deuterus, still remain.

To find the semitones of the tritus, divide the distance from the penultimate point of the line separating the deuterus and tritus in the middle—that is, from the A of the tritus—to the end of the right-hand *magada* into nine parts. The first ends at a semitone, the second is empty, the third ends at a semitone, the fourth is empty, the fifth ends at a semitone, the sixth ends at a semitone, and the remaining parts are empty.

To find the semitones of the deuterus, divide the distance from the same point to the *magada* into ten steps. The first is empty; the second ends at a semitone; the third is empty; the fourth ends at a semitone; the fifth is empty; the sixth ends at a semitone and at the synemmenon of the protus; the seventh ends at a semitone; the remaining steps are empty.

You will be able to find the synemmenon of the deuterus, which alone remains, more easily by the sesquialteral proportion. And so that the entire structure may be made still clearer, lines of a dark color should be drawn through those four principal places—D, G, d, and g—at which all the tropes converge alike, because all the principal strings also meet there: namely, the lower, final, upper, and highest strings. The same names should be written on each of these individually: the lower strings at D, the finals at G, and the others in order.

When the structure has thus been completed, the double-lettered *nete* notes should be erased, so that the figure may stand complete in itself.

But since this is highly useful for arousing [the voice or attention], the places of the differences themselves should also be indicated. In the order of the authentic protus and tritus, the differences are placed at the fifth place; those of their plagals at the third place from the final. In the order of the deuterus and tetrardus, the differences of the authentic deuterus are placed at the sixth place, those of the tetrardus at the fifth; their plagals are placed at the fourth place from the final.

Here you have the metric and prose measurement. You should know, however, that the metric version was composed for the more acute, and the prose version for those less skilled, like ourselves.

[Note: Here the Blasian codex ends; what follows is added by the Vienna manuscript, namely the metric measurement mentioned here.]

### XLI. The measurement of the theorem of the tropes according to the metric art

[Col. 1175]

Whoever wishes to measure the new theorem of the tropes,

First divide the ends of the *magada* across their breadth;

Namely, leave A, B, and C empty above,

And divide the remainder into four equal spaces.

Thus the four tropes, ruling over an equal number of spaces,

Let each seize its own and mark it with its proper sign.

Grant the adjacent place of A and B to the tetrardus;

From here let the tritus, from here the deuterus,

And let the protus hold the last place.

Then place, according to Guido’s measurement, between the *magadae*

As many points as he himself wishes. Nor should the highest *nete* be absent.

Add to this highest *nete* the synemmenon and the lower A.

Thus twice eleven points will be set out in order.

Let the final boundary likewise be marked with points at either end.

Here is the base of the protus, and there the highest point of the tetrardus.

And let the measurement immediately be carried out continuously.

Its completion will be easy if you remember

That the tropes are titled by their first syllables, PR, DE, TR, TE,

And keep this monogrammatic figure in mind:

It consists of as many spaces as there are points of Guido,

As we said, and extends from dd to the lowest gamma,

Retaining in these spaces the monogram of the tropes

Which the line touches when the rule passes through the points.

We clearly mark the synemmena by the monograms

To which SY has been added; but the *lemmata* by those

To which SE has been added.

Keep each of the neighboring ones in mind.

[Col. 1177] You will seek the *lemmata* in this way:

For the deuterus or tritus, which lies beneath one line

And overhangs another, by which they are separated in the middle,

First divide the distance from the point that has the penultimate point

Into ten steps, and from there into nine.

From the ten, these leap to the *lemmata* of the deuterus:

The seventh and sixth, the fourth together with the second.

Opposite the sixth, the synemmenon of the protus must be placed.

But this order marks all those belonging to the tritus from the nine:

The third and first, the fifth, and after these the sixth.

When these have been arranged, you will not yet have

The synemmenon of the deuterus in its proper relation,

Which you will also add without difficulty.

[Col. 1177] The music of the blessed Father William, abbot of the monastery of Hirsau, ends here.

## In the year of the Lord 1090. Herimann, bishop of Metz

[Col. 1177]

## Historical notice concerning Herimann

*(Gallia Christiana nova, vol. XIII, p. 732.)*

[Col. 1177A] Herimann, born of illustrious parents in Saxony, a disciple of Hanno, archbishop of Cologne, provost of Liège, was appointed and consecrated bishop in 1073 by the unanimous agreement of clergy and people. Deeply distressed that he had accepted investitures from the emperor, he soon sought pardon from the supreme pontiff. Not long afterward he took part, together with several prelates and nobles, in the assembly held at Gerstungen to pacify the disturbances in Germany.

He kindly received Walon, abbot of Saint Arnulf, as Walon was returning to Metz; Manasses, archbishop of Reims, had likewise placed him over the monastery of Saint Remigius, at the recommendation of Pope Gregory VII. Herimann restored him to favor. In his honor he also restored the fairs held perpetually on the feast of the dedication. Later, however, he did not lack occasion to reproach Walon—and indeed out of affection for him—as we shall relate below.

He journeyed to Rome with Theodoric, abbot of Saint-Hubert, in 1074. He celebrated the Paschal feast at Pisa; continuing his journey, he reached Rome and visited Pope Gregory VII, pouring out prayers at the tombs of the holy apostles. From the pope he received not only tokens of personal affection but also marks of benevolence for the bishops of Liège and Bamberg, Theodwin and Herimann, who had been accused of violating the sacred canons.

Around the year 1076 a disastrous and long-lasting schism arose. Its principal author was Henry VI, king of Germany, who was disturbing the kingdom by wicked acts. After repeatedly admonishing him kindly but without result, Gregory VII again ordered him through legates, at the end of the preceding year, to appear during the second week of Lent at the council summoned in Rome and to give an account of the crimes of which he was accused. If he neglected to do so, he was to know for certain that he would be separated from communion with the Church.

Deeply offended by this message, the king drove the legates from his presence and convened an assembly at Worms on Septuagesima. At that assembly Gregory was deposed from the pontificate, contrary to the judgment of many bishops and especially of Herimann, who openly declared that canon law prohibited condemning an absent bishop. Nevertheless, he had to yield to the larger number.

The pope, persuaded that many bishops had given their assent only under force and fear, sent letters to Udo, archbishop of Trier, Theodoric, bishop of Verdun, and Herimann, exhorting them to remain faithful to the Holy See and to wipe away their fault by suitable satisfaction. Herimann, for his part, did not persist long in his error: he obtained absolution from Jaranto, abbot of Saint-Bénigne at Dijon, on Christmas Eve of that same year, 1076.

In August of the same year he received a letter from the same pontiff, in which the pope stated that all who communicated with the king had incurred censures and that he himself possessed the right to excommunicate. In the following year, at the command of the same pontiff, Herimann settled a dispute that had arisen between the bishop of Liège and Wulphad, abbot of Saint Lawrence, who had been expelled from his monastery without a formal case being brought against him.

Nevertheless, because of his exceptional devotion to the Holy See, Herimann incurred the emperor’s displeasure and was denounced at the assembly of Mainz as an enemy of the empire. To avoid persecution, therefore, he went to Theodoric, bishop of Verdun, who, having been recommended by the pope, received him with the greatest kindness. Afterward, having pledged some estates of his church, he fled to Liège, where he lived at the expense of the monastery of Saint Trond.

Because he held direct jurisdiction over that monastery, he appointed Lanzo, abbot of Saint Vincent of Metz, to govern it together with Henry, bishop of Liège, in 1083. For this reason the Chronicle of the monastery of Saint Trond accuses him of converting the monastery’s revenues to his own use and violating the privileges of the abbey.

Besides the emperor’s harassment, he was almost continuously troubled by wars waged by Theodoric, duke of Lorraine, who plundered the castles of Épinal and Danubry and several churches and monasteries.

Meanwhile, a general council was held at Rome in 1080, on the Nones of March. There Pope Gregory pronounced anathema against the emperor, who continued to embroil Germany in war and arms and persisted in obstinacy, and he confirmed Rudolf in the royal dignity. He declared that he had proceeded to these extremes unwillingly and only after other remedies had been tried in vain.

Enraged still further by this action, Henry summoned at Brixen, a city of Noricum, an assembly of thirty partisan bishops. He renounced the legitimate pope and opposed to him Guibert, archbishop of Ravenna, as antipope under the name Clement. Herimann, however, remained firmly on the pope’s side.

The emperor, angered by this, drove him from his see and intruded the aforementioned Walon, abbot of Saint Arnulf, in his place. Walon occupied the see in 1085 and the following year. But when he saw that he was accomplishing nothing, and was then moved by remorse for the see he had usurped, he went to Herimann, asked pardon for the crime he had committed, and withdrew to the monastery of Gorze as a penance, where he became keeper of the boys.

At last, compelled by the example of such great modesty and penitence to feel compassion, Herimann restored him to his former dignity. Not long afterward the same prelate was again driven from his see, and a certain Bruno, son of Albert, count of Calw and a monk of Saint Trond, was intruded into it. The people of Metz could not endure his insolence; they stabbed him with swords and lances and killed him inside the nunnery of Saint Peter.

Herimann, meanwhile, had gone to Italy. During these days the schismatics recognized him as an exceedingly fierce defender of the Roman See. He was carried captive into Tuscany and worn down by prolonged imprisonment. He did not return before 1088, when the pope honored him with the dignity and office of the pallium and of an apostolic legate or vicar.

When he returned to Metz, he was received by his flock with the greatest honor and affection amid every danger. As soon as he had reentered the city, a young man of innocent life named Hugh was divinely shown that he should visit Herimann, warn him to transfer the body of Saint Clement, and tell him of his impending death, which would follow on the third day after the translation.

The young man reported this vision to the abbot of Saint Felix, where Saint Clement rested. The abbot too had been divinely admonished to change his way of life and become a monk. He disclosed one matter to the bishop but concealed the other, which concerned the bishop’s death.

Herimann did not immediately believe the visions. At length, however, after being struck by illness, he carried out the undertaking in the year 1090, on the sixth day before the Nones of May, despite his extreme weakness. Hugh, abbot of Flavigny, recounted the history of this translation at greater length in his Chronicle, and from that time the monastery of Saint Felix was distinguished by the name of Saint Clement.

There survives a charter of Herimann concerning this matter, reporting everything in detail. It states that, through many visions and revelations granted to many persons, it had become known that the body of the holy bishop should be raised from the place where it had been deposited by Bishop Deoderic of blessed memory, who had once tried to transfer it to its proper see but had been unable to do so because divine power prevented him.

Herimann, however, had delayed the matter because he did not believe the visions; but at last, chastised and struck blind from heaven, he proceeded. Thus, on the sixth day before the Nones of May, amid a great gathering of clergy, monks, and faithful, he reverently arranged the most holy body in a gold and silver shrine and transferred it to the cathedral church of Saint Stephen, where it rested during the following night.

From there he returned it to the place called the basilica, from which it had been taken the previous day—that is, to the monastery of Saint Felix—and bestowed many gifts upon it for the support of the monks who would serve God at Saint Clement’s.

To ensure that the day of the translation would be observed with greater solemnity, Herimann established a fair there for eight days. If laymen wished, as was then customary, to exercise themselves in horse-racing, he ordered that half the prize should be assigned to the victor and the remainder to the church of Saint Clement.

It is clear from his letters preserved in the monastery of Saint Clement that he gave to Abbot Hugh the almost deserted church of Saint Peter at Arenas, where the brothers were to perform pastoral duties.

On the third day after the translation of Saint Clement, already afflicted by a serious illness, Herimann summoned the clergy and his household, bestowed his blessing, armed himself with the sign of the cross, invoked the Holy Trinity, the Blessed Mother of God, and all the saints, and departed most devoutly on 4 May 1090, as had been revealed to the young man Hugh.

Abbot Hugh arranged his funeral and buried him in the church of Saint Peter at Arenas. In his tomb, on 13 October 1712, a lead plate was found bearing this inscription:

“Herimann, bishop of Metz, legate of the Apostolic See, honored by Gregory VII with the dignity of the mitre and pallium, died in the Lord in the year of the Lord 1090.”

[Col. 1181]

## Concerning the translation of Saint Clement, or Charter for the abbey of Saint Clement, issued on the day of the translation of his body, in the year 1090, on the third day of May

*(Meurisse, History of the Bishops of Metz, p. 377.)*

[Col. 1181A] In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, I, Herimann, humble minister of the Church of Metz, to all present and future: everlasting salvation in Christ.

Because the whole corrupted posterity of the human race, through the loss resulting from the first stain of the earth-born [Adam], cannot long endure, and because it is also darkened by the gloom of forgetfulness with regard to the inward vision of man [the text is uncertain: *interioris intuitu hominis*], we have judged it worthwhile to commend to the memory of posterity the events that have occurred in our own time, lest, if deeds so great and so exceptional were condemned to the silence of oblivion, this should afterward be attributed to our stupidity and negligence.

In the year 1090 of the Incarnation of the Word, in the thirteenth indiction, [Col. 1181B] while our Lord Jesus Christ reigned, while Henry III, the most noble Caesar of the Romans, held the imperial power, and while Duke Theodoric, Count Folmar, and Judge Burchard held authority in the realm, when kingdom and priesthood were at variance with one another and consequently both worldly and ecclesiastical affairs were miserably tossed about, heavenly goodness refreshed us sinners and afflicted people through the pious consolation of Blessed Clement, our first shepherd.

For when the merciful God, in his provident ordering, had determined to have pity on the city and people of Metz, as is clearer than daylight, the aforesaid eminent bishop, the angel of great counsel going before him, made himself known to us through many visions and revelations granted to many people. He piously admonished us, by repeated entreaty, that he should be raised from the place where our predecessor Deoderic of blessed memory had once deposited him when attempting to transfer him to his proper see but had been unable to do so because divine power prevented it, so that through the most worthy intercession of the pious father the visitation from on high of the rising sun might come forth for the people walking in darkness and the shadow of death.

We doubted that what was being announced to us was frivolous, mindful of Solomon’s saying, “Dreams have led many astray,” and we foolishly delayed in unbelieving minds. But because of the hardness of our heart, we were suddenly struck by the divine sword by which we were already being removed from their midst. Thus, with the final lot compelling us to bring the delays of our tardiness to an end, on that very day—namely, the sixth day before the Nones of May—while innumerable crowds of clergy, monks, nobles, and laymen surrounded us, acclaiming hymns and praises to God, we raised the most holy body from the sarcophagus, where it lay upon gold and precious topaz, [Col. 1181D] placed it in a shrine suitably adorned with gold and silver, [Col. 1182A] and honorably transferred it to the church of Saint Stephen, which holds the episcopal cathedra of that blessed man.

On the following night, vigils and praises having been solemnly celebrated there before the relics of the holy body, on the next day I, Herimann, before the altar of Saint Stephen, upon which the body of blessed Clement lay, with the counsel and assent of the entire Church of Metz, both clergy and people, hoping through such a benefit to have a share with him in the resurrection, gave to him and to those who would serve him perpetually Cuminam, which is at Chamberes beyond the Moselle, together with the house situated there, and the vineyard called Bertold’s, which is at Mont, together with the adjoining field, and the *bannus* and hundred, and the meadow at Prunvet, which the peasants of Nominey cultivate, together with the *bannus* and hundred.

I also gave the entire *bannus* and hundred of the five parishes situated in the village called “at the basilicas,” namely, those of Saint John the Baptist, Saint Genesius, Saint Mary among the Martyrs, Saint Lawrence, and Saint Amantius. They were to be free from every advocate and from every jurisdiction of the city, but subject solely to the care and authority of the abbot, just as I had held them in my own hand.

I also gave a certain woman from Pierreius, named Thyebot, together with her sons and daughters, and Hamezon and Richard, under the law by which they had been held.

Therefore, by unanimous decision, all the clergy and people present resolved that henceforth they would keep this day universally as a feast, in order to renew each year their pious devotion toward their patron.

Accordingly, because the sacred place of his burial deserves to be honored both on account of the venerable presence of the body itself and on account of the swift remission of sins, as is believed, for those who piously flee to him, we established, with the eager approval of all, that a solemn fair should be held there for eight consecutive days. We proclaimed that firm peace should be maintained under threat of anathema for all who hastened there.

We exclude, however, the crime of homicide, unless someone reaches the threshold of the saint after being driven there by force of arms by an enemy.

Moreover, lest this charter slip from memory or anyone usurp anything other than what is contained here, we judged it worthy to insert that Abbot Hagano of that place, in my presence and with the approval of Burchard the advocate, granted the meadow of Prunoet in fee to him and his successors, both for the defense of this benefit granted by me [Col. 1182D] and for the protection of the whole Church, [Col. 1183A] on the condition that none of his heirs should claim this fief unless he held the advocacy of the city.

And so that the memory of this translation might be kept more pleasantly and ceremonially by those who gathered at the fair, the advocate himself shall present there a horse worth fifteen solidi. If, as is customary, certain laymen who take pleasure in horse-racing wish to exercise themselves particularly with horses, half the assessed prize shall remain with the victor and the remainder shall be assigned to the Church.

But if this feast should not take place on the same day, the horse shall be released to the Church without dispute at vespers. If he does not present it as stated, the abbot of the place shall demand it from him; he shall have no right whatsoever to refuse.

And because we judge these to be fairs under the *bannus*, the same advocate shall carefully provide, either in person or through the city’s *castaldi*, that nothing be taken away from the appointed time and that none of the merchants—especially the Buccharians—withdraw. He should know that the legal dues exacted from all of them in this market are an addition to his fief. Nevertheless, whatever injuries may occur within the *bannus* of the aforesaid churches to the Church granted by me, whether then or at any future time, shall belong to the justice of the abbot of the place and his officers alone.

This solemn grant having been given and received, and confirmed by the common oath of all, on that same day, namely the fifth day before the Nones of May, the most holy body was carried back, with a great crowd of people accompanying it, to the place called the basilica, from which it had been taken the day before and which the saint himself had chosen during his lifetime as the place of his rest. [Col. 1183C] There, honorably established, the pious and merciful saint, a powerful hearer of those who devoutly invoke him, shines forth through innumerable miracles, to the praise and glory of the name of Christ.

Therefore, by the authority of almighty God, of blessed Clement, and of ourselves, we confirm that this grant and these gifts shall remain valid and unshaken for all time. We strengthen them also by the impression of our seal and by the subscriptions of trustworthy persons, charging all our successors faithfully to preserve them forever under the scrutiny of strict judgment.

If any ecclesiastical or secular person should presume to violate any part of these provisions, let that person, unless he repents, be separated from the most sacred body and blood of the Lord and be anathema on the day of Christ and of God.

We have judged it worthy to record below the suitable witnesses, observers, and hearers of all these matters. Their names are as follows:

Hagano, abbot of the place; Henry, abbot of Gorze; Lanzo, abbot of Saint Vincent; Durandus, abbot of Saint Symphorian; Adalbero, archdeacon; Ruocelinus, archdeacon; Gervoldus, archdeacon; Matfridus, archdeacon.

Canons: Ermerannus; Arnulfus; Lietardus; Bertulfus, cantor; Folmarus, cantor; Folmarus again; John; Anselm; and others.

Monks of the same place: Richerius, prior; Odilo; and others.

Names of the laymen: Theodoric, duke; Folmar, count; Burchard, judge; Wypald, *scabinio*; Gerard; and others.

[Col. 1183]

## Charter of Herimann by which he confirms to Walon, abbot of Saint Arnulf of Metz, the right to the annual market, “wrongfully taken away through the conspiracy of certain persons”

*(Meurisse, History of the Bishops of Metz, p. 369.)*

[Col. 1183C] In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, Herimann, by the grace of God bishop of the holy Church of Metz, to all faithful people, present and future: may they sing the mercies of the Lord forever.

Since the blessedness of the saints consists both in the gift of grace and in the reward of justice, every faithful person must strive with the utmost care to attain, through hope and action, the joys of eternal life. And since all things work together for good for those who love God, one must act well in every way, according to what is written: “Whatever your hand is able to do, do it earnestly.”

We therefore approve these and similar teachings, wisely and beneficially stated in the judgments of the holy Fathers, and, weighing them with the clearest reasoning founded upon the firm entirety of truth, after God the author had raised us to the pontificate of this holy see of Metz, we began to recall the salvation of our soul more earnestly, both through the inward examination of our mind and through the pious conversation of religious men.

When the Lord’s saying came to mind as something greatly beneficial to this purpose—“Give alms, and all things are clean for you”—there came to us the venerable Walo, abbot of the monastery of Saint Arnulf, formerly to be remembered and forever to be venerated, of the city of the Mediomatrici. If we may speak of his human nobility, the emperor and Roman patrician Charlemagne was his great-great-grandfather in the line of descent.

As often happens, when conversation arose between us and the aforesaid abbot concerning many matters, he complained that the aforesaid place was suffering many losses at the hands of wicked men. He added that the annual market, which had been held for four years during the dedication of that church in the time of our predecessor, Adelbero of holy memory, had now been wrongfully taken away by the conspiracy of certain persons who consider it their profit if they inflict loss upon others. [Col. 1185A]

Therefore, wishing to extend the work of mercy for the salvation of our soul and for the benefit of the Church, at the request of that abbot, of the most religious virgin consecrated to God and enclosed there, the lady named Hodierna, and of all the brothers’ pious supplication, and with the unanimous consent of our faithful, we restored and returned the market, to be held perpetually on the solemnity of the dedication.

Thus, in order that we, as executors of a pious work, might deserve to become participants in the heavenly kingdom, whatever right we discovered that we possessed in that market, retaining nothing for ourselves, we bestowed in its entirety upon the brothers serving God there. Ten solidi were assigned among the *primicerius*, the treasurer, the canons of Saint Stephen, and the city’s advocate. Of these, five are given in restitution for the money paid to them from the private markets of eight days.

The other five are likewise given so that they may not sharpen the tooth of envy against us because of the brothers’ good revenues, but may rejoice with those who rejoice, so that what is written may be fulfilled: “Whatever you wish people to do to you, do the same to them.”

Moreover, the aforesaid advocate separately received ten solidi; and the three *deans* and the *scabinius* received three solidi each, individually as payment for their office, so that they should neither inflict injustice or injury upon anyone nor allow anyone to suffer it.

Beyond these thirty-two solidi, let no one whatsoever presume unjustly either to demand or retain anything. If any injustice or injury should occur, as commonly happens in such matters, the abbot shall receive without resistance the amount of the penalty that the law exacts in retribution for the offense.

Finally, we beseech all bishops who shall come after us, by all the mercies of the Lord and by the authority of the twelve apostles, especially of Saint John, the Lord’s most beloved disciple, whose tooth is preserved and venerated in the aforesaid monastery, as has been confirmed there by the authority of blessed Pope Leo IX, and by the love of all the saints. We also adjure them by the power that we have received from God neither to annul this work of mercy themselves nor to allow anyone else to annul it. We confirm it by this present writing, by the authority of our hand, and by the names of our faithful.

[Col. 1186B] I, Herimann, bishop of the Church of Metz, have signed.

Sign of Primicerius Adalbero.

Sign of Richerius, archdeacon.

Sign of Gernoldus, archdeacon.

Sign of Udelricus, archdeacon.

Sign of John the treasurer.

Sign of Count Folmar.

Sign of Count Conrad.

Sign of Count Herimann.

Sign of Count Udo.

Sign of Rothfridus of Prisneio.

Sign of Cuono of Tincher.

Sign of Burchard, advocate.

Sign of John, first *scabion*.

[Col. 1186C] Sign of Altericus.

Sign of Abbot Walon.

[Col. 1185]

## Concerning the death of Herimann

*(Hugh of Flavigny, Chronicle, under the year 1090)*
[Col. 1185C] As the appointed day for transferring the venerable relics of Saint Clement drew near, he regained some strength, by the Lord’s assent; and on the Kalends of May, while transferring blessed Clement, he fulfilled his desire by divine grace, with the utmost devotion of clergy and people. The entire city—indeed, the entire region—stood ready to hear his preaching, while dew from heavenly sweetness dripped from his mouth. When all had been absolved, and all had sought absolution from everyone as though from God himself, at last he expressed his desire in the hearing of all, saying:

“It is enough for me. Would that God would look upon me, bring my labors to an end, and receive my spirit in peace through the intercession of Saint Clement, whose most sacred body, by a magnificent gift bestowed upon us from heaven, we have been granted to see, touch, and transfer today!”

At these words the people groaned and, grieving with him as he broke down and implored an end to his labors, shared his sorrow. Two days later, as though foreseeing his imminent passing, he ordered letters to be written to the faithful of the Church, praying and adjuring them by him who lives for ever and ever [Col. 1186C] to conduct the affairs of the Church without deceit or pretense, in simple and unadorned truth. He bade everyone a final farewell, with marvelous emotion in his words and countenance.

On the third day, around the ninth hour, [Col. 1186D] realizing that his passing was near, he ordered the brothers to be summoned, and restrained his sons, who stood near him, from grieving, both by voice and by gesture. When they asked him to whom he was leaving them in their desolation and what he commanded them, he said:

“I commend you to God. Stand firm in the faith and teaching of blessed Peter, just as you have seen and heard from his successors.”

After this he blessed them all, armed himself with the sign of the cross, invoked the Holy Trinity, commended himself to holy Mary, and implored the common protection of the saints. With eyes and hands raised toward heaven, without any sound of voice or movement of body, as though falling asleep, he gave up his spirit.

The following night he appeared to a beloved man whom he had adopted as a son. Because he had fallen asleep from grief while the psalms were being sung, he said to him: “Do not be sad; I am safe.” He appeared again to a venerable man and said: “They say that I am dead, but I live.” This became known through the testimony of abbots and other persons of no slight standing.

IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 1090. THEODORIC, MONK OF SAINT OUEN.

[Col. 1187]

HISTORICAL AND LITERARY NOTICE.

(*Literary History of France*, VIII, 364.)

[Col. 1187B] Thierri, whom we are undertaking to discuss, has nearly lost, in the judgment of posterity, the principal glory of his literary labors. Indeed, a writer of great renown attempted to transfer to a foreigner the authorship of one of his works, by which it is recognized that he composed others as well. This was the celebrated Henschenius, who attributed to Fridegode, an English author, the verse *Life of Saint Ouen*, bishop of Rouen; from that work is drawn what is most certain concerning the history and writings of Thierry.

But the learned successors of that hagiographer made it their duty to restore the work to its true author, as several scholars had already done.

One should not expect the life of a man of letters hidden in the obscurity of a cloister, where he appears to have lived without office or dignity, as Thierri did, to furnish many highly memorable events. All that is known of his person is that he had embraced the monastic profession at the abbey of Saint-Ouen of Rouen, and that he flourished under Nicholas of Normandy, who was its abbot for fifty years, from 1042 until February 1092. Good studies were then held in honor in that house, and Thierri found himself associated there with several fellow monks who competed eagerly in cultivating letters, especially sacred poetry and history.

Besides a Fulbert, who left several works of his pen, as will be said in his particular notice, there was also a Maurice, quite different from another monk of that name, the disciple of Saint Anselm. Nothing remains of this Maurice except the epitaph of Abbot Nicholas in leonine verse, which is found in various collections (MAB., *Annales*, I, LXVIII, no. 35). But by this he showed that he was capable of doing something else; and perhaps he did so, although we have not been informed of it.

Nor are we told whether it was Thierri, or one of the other two learned fellow monks just named, [Col. 1187D] who at that time directed the schools of Saint-Ouen. It is known, however, that pupils of merit were then formed there, who through their works acquired the title of writers of some reputation (POMMERAIE, *History of Saint-Ouen*, p. 339). One such was Ambrose, who employed his pen to celebrate in prose and verse the illustrious Saint Agnes, virgin and martyr. Another was John, who from the age of twenty began producing works, part of which has come down to us. This pupil of Saint-Ouen became especially famous because he was chosen at the Council of Reims in 1119, under Pope Calixtus II, to hold the pen and perform the duties of secretary (Council, vol. X, p. 872).

We lack sufficient information to say whether Thierri, who undoubtedly contributed, at least by his example, to the progress of studies in his monastery, survived Abbot Nicholas. But since no date is better known for his history than the death of that abbot, to whom he dedicated his principal work, we have thought it necessary to choose it as the point at which to place his notice.

Among Thierri’s literary productions, some are in verse and others in prose. But not all scholars agree about which works belong to him in either genre; and this is what we are now going to undertake to examine.

1. No one today disputes that the verse *Life of Saint Ouen*, bishop of Rouen after the middle of the seventh century, is the product of our writer’s labor, and that those who wished to honor Fridegode, an English author of the tenth century, with it confused this holy prelate with Saint Owin, a monk of Lichfield in England, of whom it is not even known that a Life was ever written.

Thierri drew the entire substance of his work from another *Life of Saint Ouen*, which Surius published under the false name of Fridegode, [Col. 1188C] after distorting its original style on the pretext of polishing it, but which the continuators of Bollandus have since given us in its purity. Our poet merely put this prose Life into verse, adhering slavishly to its wording. Since he chose leonine verse for the undertaking, this form of writing, which entails an additional constraint because of rhyme, introduced into his versification an additional flatness and obscurity.

This poem of Thierri is preserved at Saint-Ouen in a manuscript that Abbot Nicholas considered so precious and so important to his monastery that he himself wrote at the bottom—or had written in his name—the most terrible curses against anyone who might remove it in any way or tear out even the smallest leaf. There is every appearance that this is the original of the poem and that the copy possessed by the Bollandists came from it. [Col. 1188D] These hagiographers did not think it appropriate to publish the work of our poet, because it contains nothing that is not found even better in the prose work on which it is based. They wisely limited themselves to printing only the first eight verses of the preface, or dedicatory epistle to Abbot Nicholas, so that the piece might be judged from this sample.

Father du Moustier showed greater honor to the epistle, giving it in full in his *Neustria pia*, where he also inserted fairly long fragments from the body of the work. He had even copied the entire poem by hand from the Saint-Ouen manuscript, together with the prose Life, intending to publish both in another collection that was to bear the title *Neustria Sancta*. But it appears that this projected plan remained merely an idea. Here this writer [Col. 1189A] shows that he believed the prose work—which he nevertheless sometimes cites under the false name of Fridegode—to be Thierri’s, just as the versification is. This, however, cannot be maintained, since the prose Life was composed before the ravages of the Normans and consequently more than two hundred years before Thierri.

[Col. 1189]

FRAGMENTS OF THE METRICAL LIFE OF SAINT OUEN WRITTEN BY THEODORIC.

(From P. du Moustier, *Neustria pia*, pp. 23, 24, 72, 73, 346, and 347.)

I. Prologue to Nicholas, abbot of Saint-Ouen.

[Col. 1189B]

To the sincere father, serene in tranquil peace,

To the illustrious father, blessed with the flower of virtues,

THEODORICUS to the holy Abbot NICHOLAS: the care of the flock entrusted to you is signified by the rod,

With which you draw the weak and drive the rebellious far away.

Here are the things you entrusted to me, and the things you asked to have written:

Concerning the holy life and merits of blessed

Bishop OUEN; I have carried them out as far as I could.

For earlier I wished to recount a senseless refusal,

And—even if worthy of a wrinkle in my verse—

The wrinkle envy draws from a marked, crooked nose,

Rather than fail to fulfill your command or that of the brothers.

Therefore I humbly ask you, for the common good,

[Col. 1189C] to hold fast what I have transcribed or briefly noted,

Although my Muse does not dare approach greater matters:

With you defending them, may they be retained; at your command,

May they be authorized, preserved, and given their titles [Note: [Col. 1189D] In answer to his pious wishes, Abbot Nicholas left the following words of imprecation in the present manuscript against thieves or those who tear it apart:

“I, Nicholas, abbot, and the entire congregation entrusted to me, eternally excommunicate and anathematize anyone who removes this book from this monastery of Saint Peter the Apostle and Saint Ouen, archbishop, by any means whatsoever, whether by deceit, theft, or robbery. And whoever erases these words or cuts out a leaf shall be subject to eternal malediction. Amen. So be it.”].

May the life I have written while still alive be my praise and reward;

May it be my profit to have obeyed your commands, Father,

So that the starry seat of paradise may receive you.

Furthermore, I ask your nobility above all:

May you first decide that whatever can be condemned or rightly criticized

Should be corrected before anyone reads it,

For I have scarcely been able to compose so slight a written work,

Being occupied with the many things that the activity of the world stirs up.

Therefore, because I did not carefully preserve every detail,

I have used inept words of my own after removing the original ones.

Yet whoever reads this life and asks lasting life for its author

deserves to attain the heavenly homeland and to see God, joined to him for ever:

In which, together with the heavenly saints, you praise, illustrious Father,

Ouen, God who governs sea, lands, and stars.

II. Blessed Ouen transfers the relics of Saint Marculf.

It happened, then, that at a certain time he also

Was traveling to the domains of the district of Constantine,

Offering to all examples of eternal salvation.

The highly revered Abbot Bernuinus

[Col. 1190B] came cheerfully to meet him and received him,

Rejoicing with him and offering what was worthy of a bishop,

Saying: “Hail, bishop, illustrious through the gift of your merits.

We ask one thing of you, which we trust you are prepared to grant,

Nor is it fitting that you refuse or reject it with a mere word;

But deign to yield to the pious wishes of all:

Command that the relics of our father and our patron,

Marculf, be moved from here.”

After this the holy man followed the wishes of all

And caused the sacred relics to be carried elsewhere,

First undertaking the greater labor himself:

For he lifts them from the ground and, bending his neck,

Carries them to a reliquary polished with gems and gold.

When he had placed them in it, he immediately said to the abbot:

“May we be permitted to carry away relics from the body

Of him whose honored memory we celebrate?”

The abbot, in turn, promptly replied:

“I do not deny it, worthy Father; indeed, I willingly grant it,

And whatever your devotion seeks, you shall be permitted to carry away.”

As he was considering how he might carry the head himself,

He was granted from heaven a written sheet,

On which the writing, and even the rare erasure of the writing,

Gave these commands, marked in sacred words:

“Do not touch the head, nor remove it from the neck.”

Thus, taking whatever you seek, you may have it.

III. On the foundation of the monastery of the Cross of Saint Leufred.

But when sacred Ouen, worn down by great old age and by time,

Worthy of perpetual honor,

Was touring villas, villages, districts, and towns,

[Col. 1190D] he was not riding a horse but sitting high

In a carriage, no longer daring to ride on his own:

They fixed their course, fixed by divine power,

And the mules, fixed in place, could not pull the carriage away.

Though the driver pressed them with goads and struck them with the whip,

They beat, tore, spurred, and constrained them excessively;

They drove them forward, accomplishing absolutely nothing.

But the servant of the Lord, compelled by the strangeness of the event,

Turned his gaze upward to the spectacles of heaven,

[Col. 1191A] where he was granted to recognize the life-giving sign of the cross.

There he understood why the animals stood fixed in place,

And what such a fixation meant or required.

Then, looking around and pondering many things in his mind,

He summoned a farmer whom he saw plowing nearby.

From the farmer’s goad, marked with the sign of the cross,

He took the sign, set it in the ground, and withdrew.

That sacred place is called the Cross of Ouen;

There miracles are marveled at and performed,

Especially the first miracle, by which it happened to be consecrated.

Not long after night had clothed the world with its twin wings,

Many suddenly saw a fire-emitting column,

[Col. 1192A] whose brightness surpassed the lights of Phoebus.

O mercy of the Lord, O wondrous power of the Lord!

How well he exalts what he exalts and enriches what he arranges!

For the place, formerly uncultivated, is now visited,

Frequented, cultivated, and consecrated to the Lord.

There healing is restored to lepers, light to the blind,

And gifts of salvation to the deaf and mute.

Then, under the honor of the saving cross and of God,

And of Father Ouen, revered for the merits of his life,

The church of Leutfred was founded and enriched with possessions.

There the order of holy men is established,

And they now and forever serve the King of kings.

IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 1090. GUIDO, ABBOT OF FARFA.

[Col. 1191]

HISTORICAL NOTICE.

(FABRICIUS, *Library of Medieval and Late Latin*, III, 130.)

Around the year 1093 there lived Guido, a monk and subsequently, after Hugh, abbot of the Farfa monastery of the Blessed Virgin in the territory of Acutianum in the Sabine country, in the Duchy of Spoleto, of the Benedictine order. Two books by him, *On the Use and Order for Adorning the Catholic Church and for Preserving the Norm of the Regular Way of Life in the Farfa Monastery*, were published from two manuscripts, one Vatican and the other from the monastery of Saint Paul in Rome, in the distinguished collection of ancient monuments by Benedictines of the Congregation of Saint Blaise in the Black Forest, entitled *Ancient Monastic Discipline*, Paris, 1726, quarto, pp. 37–132.

[Col. 1191]

GUIDO’S DISCIPLINE OF FARFA AND OF THE MONASTERY OF SAINT PAUL IN ROME.

NOTICE.

The Farfa monastery in the Sabine country, in the Duchy of Spoleto, named from Mount Acutianum, adopted the customs of Cluny under Abbot Hugh toward the end of the tenth century. The account of this matter is recorded in the *Benedictine Annals*, vol. IV, pp. 120 and 206. Although these customs agree in some respects with the published books of Udalricus in Dacherius’s *Spicilegium*, vol. I of the new edition, they nevertheless contain much that is lacking in that same author and that deserves particular attention.

In the first book the divine offices are arranged; in the second, regular discipline is explained. In them mention is made of the *Concord of the Rules* and of Hildemar’s tradition. This is because the customs of Cluny were taken from the *Capitula* of Saint Benedict of Aniane, who compiled that *Concord*.
