The structure of the Farfa monastery is described; the measure of garments, monastic profession, the abbot’s blessing, the offering of children, and many other matters most worthy of knowing are discussed. These same customs were afterward brought by Odo of Cluny into the monastery of Saint Paul in Rome and, after him, were confirmed there by monks of Gorze at the command of Pope Agapitus.

These customs are still preserved in an old codex of the monastery of Saint Paul in the City and in another manuscript formerly belonging to Farfa, now in the Vatican, under this title: “Here begins the complete use or order for adorning the Catholic Church and for preserving the norm of the regular way of life in the monastery of the Blessed Mary ever-virgin in the territory of Acutianum, arranged.” From these two manuscripts Jean Mabillon had a copy made, which the very courteous Dom Vincent Thuillier granted me from the same collection.

Although these customs were taken from the Cluniacs, they nevertheless existed before those customs were written down, since the latter were not committed to writing until the eleventh century by Bernard and Udalricus, of whom we shall speak somewhat below. The manner in which the rites were received from the monastery of Cluny, and by whom, is explained by the prologue, which was written by Guido the monk, perhaps the same man who succeeded Abbot Hugh at Farfa.

DISCIPLINE OF FARFA AND OF THE MONASTERY OF SAINT PAUL IN ROME

From Vatican manuscript no. 6808 and the old codex of Saint Paul in the City

[Col. 1193]

PROLOGUE.

[Col. 1193A] When throughout all Italy the precepts of Christ were being annulled and held, as it were, in contempt, diabolical suggestions began to increase and to be put into practice, so that even those established in sacred orders took wives, as laymen do, and freely practiced the Simoniac heresy.

Then, with heavenly clemency favoring the King who once redeemed the world with his precious blood, a certain monk splendid in monastic beauty arose, named Romuald. He renewed the rule of ancient righteousness in both sexes and orders.

Following his example, the venerable Abbot Hugh renewed the ancient practices of the holy Fathers and of the distinguished and illustrious Father Benedict in the monastery of the Blessed Mary ever-Virgin, in the place called Acutianum, where the entire order and arrangement of the monks had been almost completely destroyed. He placed upon their shoulders the custom of the monastery of Cluny, built in Gaul and at that time flourishing throughout the whole world, beyond all other monasteries, in the regular way of life.

For when the fame of the aforesaid monastery and also of the aforementioned Fathers—namely Romuald and Lord Hugh, the most kind abbot—rang far and wide, these Fathers, burning with immense zeal and agreeing with one another, shone forth. Lord Romuald was distinguished in the contemplative life [Col. 1194A] and also in the founding of many monasteries. Father Hugh, becoming his follower in the royal monastery, went so far as to bring to the studies of the venerable monasteries of Gaul, of Cluny, where the venerable Father Odilo still shines like a radiant lamp, many things from their custom for the benefit of the brothers entrusted to him and gathered into Christ’s sheepfold, for the salvation of souls.

Among these, one greatly inspired and inflamed with monastic fervor, a disciple of Lord Romuald named John [Note: [Col. 1193B] He is said to have lived under the most religious Abbot Joseph, in an unspecified monastery. Mabillon also reports, *Annals*, vol. IV, p. 207, that this same John [Col. 1194B] wrote a second prologue, which nevertheless did not come into my hands.], hurried with one companion to that same monastery of Cluny to observe and record its customs. He wrote them down on small pages as he saw them with his own eyes, fixed them in books, and handed them on to posterity to read.

Lord Father Hugh, becoming in every respect their imitator, brought these and many other things into his royal and ancient monastery, so that it might differ in nothing from their practice, desiring to fulfill what is read in the Acts of the Apostles: “The multitude of believers was of one heart and one soul” (Acts 4). Whoever fulfills this custom will be exalted in the present life and afterward rejoice within an everlasting pasture, and so forth.

TABLE OF CHAPTERS OF BOOK I.

[Col. 1193]

Here begins the beautiful practice of the monastic rule: how one should act during the eight days before the Nativity of the Lord. When the Lord arrives, remember to observe these things. Stephen seeks to observe this venerable rite. The noble John also surveys these customs from his lofty place. Brothers, join this rite to the praises of the infants. What should be done if Sunday occurs during these solemnities. Also, concerning the celebration itself that takes place on weekdays. Brothers, run through the octave of Saint Stephen in this manner. Let us observe the octave of the Theophany in the order of life. Thus the Theophany is completed during its octave. The converted Paul requires such practices for himself. Sing these laments on the shores of Chobar. Observe these practices for forty days. How one should act on Saturday with twelve readings. Thus may the Passion of Christ admonish you. It is fitting for brothers to celebrate every year in the psalms. Thus celebrate the Paschal customs with rejoicing. Concerning the preceding Easter. Christ ascending into heaven requires these practices. These things must be done at the coming of the gracious Spirit. Saint John the Baptist requires these practices. Thus let observance honor the apostolic feast. Come with me, all, and celebrate the Assumption of the Virgin in this way. Let the crowd of her servants celebrate the birth of the Mother of God in this way. Let these begin for you on the Ides of September. Thus let all the heavenly host complete their joys. Observe these customs on the Kalends of November. How one should act on the anniversary of the consecration of a basilica. Odilo, leader and abbot of our monks, established these annual rites for the feast days. Let the brothers observe these things on the Kalends of November.

BOOK ONE.

[Col. 1195]

CHAPTER ONE [Note: [Col. 1195B] The divisions of the chapters have been added by us for the reader’s convenience. Some material is missing at the beginning.]. On Palm Sunday.

[Col. 1195A]

[lacuna] From this point the following proceed: the little boys, two by two, with their teachers. The other older boys, beginning with the first two, proceed in order, two by two, with antiphons, all joining in those they can and know how to sing. Finally comes Lord Abbot, followed by all the ranks of the laity.

As they go out, all the bells are to be rung. The two larger bells are to be prolonged in ringing until the procession returns to the Galilee [Note: [Col. 1195B] *Galilaea*, *Gallaria*, gallery, portico; likewise Greek ναῦς (*naus*), the nave of a church.]. If the whole group has become too large, the servants of the place should go beside the elders, protecting the children so that the work of God is not hindered.

Here there is no need for us to insert anything that every practitioner of God’s service ought to know by heart, namely, how far it is fitting for him to observe and preserve the rule [supplied: or discipline] of his order in the best manner.

When they come to the church outside the monastery, they are to enter and say this antiphon: “Savior of the world, save us,” and all the bells are to be rung. “Let us pray. Grant, we ask, and so forth.” When it is completed, let them offer the prayer and incense the altar. Then let them return with praises in the same manner in which they came. When the antiphons are insufficient, let antiphons from the vespers [alternative: responsories] of that day be sung.

As they approach the monastery, six of them, chosen by the armarius, are to go and put on copes in order to sing “Gloria, laus.” Let the procession stand in order just as it came. Let the banners [Note: [Col. 1195B] *Fanones*, veils, banners, from German *Fanen*.] stand on either side, face to face. Let the elders stand as they customarily stand in the choir. Let the children with their teachers have the ornaments first [supplied: perhaps “carry them”], as in the Sunday procession.

When those wearing copes have completed the verse, “Gloria, laus,” let the paraphonist begin: “As the Lord entered.” Let all the bells be rung. When everyone has reached his place, let Mass begin. Three are to perform the office in copes. The other brothers who must sing the responsory or tract are to remain in albs; the deacon and subdeacon are to wear the chasuble. At the Passion let him say: “The Lord be with you”; “Glory to you, O Lord.” Let them respond. Let them say: “I believe in one God.” At the offertory let all return the palms to the priest, kissing his hands. At the end of the sacred [chanting], let the deacon say, “Let us bless the Lord.”

In the refectory let the tables be covered. At midday on that day, let the rest prescribed by Saint Benedict begin. When the time of None arrives, let the custodian ring the small bell [Note: [Col. 1196B] *Squilla*, *skella*, *scilla*, a little bell or handbell.] gently, or one of the medium-sized bells, until he himself can finish “Have mercy on me, O God,” so that they may rise and wash their hands and faces.

Those who arrive first at the church are to sit in the choir reading until the children come; they too are to come into the choir for prayer. When they arrive, let the larger bell be rung for None until they rise for prayer. After it has been said, let them come to the refectory at the sound of the cymbal. The brothers who had performed kitchen duty during the preceding week are to bring water to everyone.

When the service has been completed, those coming to the step are to bow before and behind [Note: [Col. 1196B] “Before and behind” refers to a bowing posture, which will be discussed below.]. Whoever is in charge, whether the prior or, if he is present, the abbot, is to strike the small bell once; at this signal, each person is granted permission to drink the wine that is before him. Finally, let him strike the bell three times; rising, let them return to the cloister.

This order is to be observed throughout the summer, except on days of fasting, until the Kalends of October. Throughout the entire week, proper antiphons are always to be appointed at Lauds. On Tuesday, let the deacons read the Passion according to Mark at Mass, with the salutation but without “Glory to you, O Lord.”

On Wednesday after Palm Sunday no procession is to be held. At the sacred office: “In the name of the Lord.” Prayer: “Grant, we ask, almighty God, that we who . . .” Reading: “Tell the daughter of Zion.” Responsory: “Do not turn your face away.” Reading: “Isaiah said, ‘Lord, who has believed?’” [Col. 1197B] Let two tracts be sung in albs. Let the Passion be read with the salutation and without “Glory to you, O Lord.”

At vespers: Responsory, “They surrounded me.” Hymn: “The royal banners.” Prayers: “I said, ‘Lord, have mercy on me.’” The Office of the Dead is not sung; rather, after Compline the curtain is to be removed.

If a feast of the saints occurs, let it be postponed from this point until the Thursday of Easter Week, and celebrated afterward.

CHAPTER II. How the Lord’s Supper is to be celebrated.

On Holy Thursday, before Matins, let fifteen candles be lit on a wooden stand before the high altar, as many candles as there are psalms to be appointed. When thirty psalms remain, before the nocturns let them say fifteen in silence after the three prayers have been made. Let the sacristan ring the bells as usual.

When these have been said and the bells are sounding, before they are dismissed let the weekly server begin the antiphon, “Zeal for your house.” Immediately one candle here and another there are to be extinguished, and this is to be done as all the psalms begin [alternative: are begun].

For the matutinal office itself, whether at the hours of the day, the antiphons they say at the end are not to be given a tone as they customarily are. Let the children recite the psalms. Let the readings begin without a blessing and end in meter or melody.

Let the first three readings be taken from the Lamentations of Jeremiah: “And it came to pass after Israel had been led into captivity.” Among us they are to be read without chant, like the other readings. Then three more are to be taken from Saint Augustine’s sermon on the psalm “Hear, O God, my prayer.” Afterward, from the Epistle to the Corinthians: “First of all, when you come together.”

When the psalm “Praise the Lord from the heavens” is appointed, let all the candles except one be extinguished, and let the teachers come among the children to guard them. One of the teachers is to light the candles and the lantern. When the cantor begins the antiphon “But the betrayer,” let the one candle that remained be extinguished.

When the canticle and antiphon are finished, let them prostrate themselves and say the prayer, the petitions, the psalm, and the collect in silence. When the prior gives the signal, let the brothers rise and return to the dormitory.

When dawn begins to appear, let the small bell be rung gently. Let them sing Prime, hymns, and psalms together with the antiphon; but let the petitions be said separately in silence. Let the seven psalms also be recited generally with the litany, as at nocturnal and matutinal Lauds, without the verse “O God, come to my assistance.” Thus all the other regular Hours are also to be recited after the hymn without the Gloria.

Perhaps you have not understood well? Let us say it again, so that you may understand better. At the Hours, let them perform the hymn as they did previously during Lent, and appoint the regular psalms. Let “Glory to you, Trinity,” “Glory be to the Father,” and so forth, and “O God, come to my assistance,” be omitted on these three days.

[Col. 1198B] When the Hour is finished, if a brother has come from a journey, let him receive a blessing as usual. When the bell is rung for Terce, let preparations be made in the customary manner. Meanwhile, while Terce is being said, let the shoes that are to be given to the brothers in chapter be hung in order in the middle, on four poles supported by an equal number of attached columns. Immediately after Terce, let them come into chapter.

Likewise, as in church, without a requested blessing, after the reading and verse have been recited and the customary prayer has been said in silence, and after the reading from the Rule, let the boy announce the short [reading] and name the kitchen servers; and let them be more numerous than at other times [Note: [Col. 1197D] Supply: “in chapter.”].

After the sermon has been given, let one chamberlain rise on one side and another on the other, and let the shoes be distributed to the brothers as they have been written down. Once the other necessary matters have been arranged, the abbot ought—and may command—those who are assigned that week to name six brothers who are to wash his feet, followed by the elders.

When the weekly servers leave chapter, let them say aloud the five psalms according to custom, if it is an anniversary; let the Lord’s Prayer and the petitions be said in silence.

If any need night garments [Note: [Col. 1197D] *Nocturnales*, garments in which the monks dressed at night; by contrast, they called *diurnales* those worn during the day.], let them receive them from the chamberlains, returning the old ones, since they already received their day garments together above in the place mentioned.

After chapter, when a short interval has passed, let the bell be rung for the matutinal Mass, for the gathering of the poor. The priest who had sung the principal Mass during the preceding week is to say the Mass of the pilgrims and distribute the offerings. Let the doorkeepers of the church serve these priests when the bell has been rung, as prescribed above. Other priests who wish to celebrate Mass are to do so without fire until the principal secret has begun. Afterward, those who have not said it may have fire once they have received permission.

At the proper hour let None be celebrated. Then let those who are to complete the services of the Mass, the singers, the three servers, and all the children put on their vestments. When they come into the choir, let the abbot begin the psalm “Have mercy on me, O God,” and then let them proceed in order to bless the fire: first the holy water, then incense, and finally the cross.

[Col. 1199A] The priest and the sacristan, who is to carry the pole that day, then the children, and afterward Lord Abbot and the others in their order. The priors and lay brothers place them in the last positions, two by two.

When they arrive, let the priest say, “The Lord be with you,” bless the new fire, sprinkle it with holy water, and then light the candle on the pole from another candle that the child is to carry in a lantern.

Then let them come singing three psalms: “O God, save me by your name”; “Have mercy on me, O God, have mercy on me”; “May God have mercy on us.” “O God, come to my assistance,” as they enter through the door of the larger church. Let the psalmody continue until they come into the choir.

The procession is celebrated in the same way on these three days. Then let the benches [Note: [Col. 1199D] *Formutae*, *formae*, benches or seats.] be turned, and let all the bells likewise be rung. Afterward, neither in the church nor in the cloister is any metal instrument to sound; whatever the brothers must do is to be announced by the sound of the wooden board until Mass on Holy Saturday.

Then let Mass be celebrated festively. Let the cantor in the choir be vested in a cope, the deacon in a dalmatic, and the subdeacon in a tunic. At the Introit of the Mass let them say, “Glory be to the Father.” At the Epistle, “When you come together,” let two brothers sing the responsory, “Christ became obedient.” The Gospel is “Before the feast of Passover.” The Offertory is “The right hand of the Lord.”

Let only as many hosts be placed for consecration as will suffice for Communion both on that day and on the following day. All must also come to the kiss of peace, and everyone, including the children, must receive Communion.

After Mass, when the board has been sounded, let a brief prayer be made, as is customary on other days before vespers.

[Col. 1199C] After those who have administered the holy rites have removed their vestments, let everyone come together into the refectory to receive the mixed drink. Meanwhile, let the cloister dean and the more senior outside dean, together with the chamberlain—and also taking any other brothers they wish—lead the poor to the appointed place, namely, in the cloister beside the church, so that they may sit.

When the brothers leave the refectory, the prior shall strike the board; all shall assemble in the cloister and stand beside the pantry, standing there in their established order, as is customary for the procession. The boys shall go to the school, with the master standing among them beside their assigned places, and the poor in front. When the cantors begin the antiphon, “The Lord Jesus,” all shall bend their knees to the ground toward the west, so that Christ may be adored in them. The masters shall do the same before the pilgrims with the children, and shall begin the washing after the psalm, “God, have mercy.”

After they have completed each verse together with the antiphon “The Lord Jesus,” the psalm “Blessed are the undefiled” shall be begun; and at each division it shall again begin, “The Lord Jesus,” up to “a lamp to my feet.” Then let the other antiphons be sung until each brother has washed, wiped, and kissed the feet of one poor person. The one who washes shall wipe and kiss their feet; another, taking the towel and basin first, shall go to the place where the brother is standing with water and a towel, wash his hands, and return to his place. The others shall do likewise. When all have been washed, they shall begin to give water to the poor persons’ hands, with a brother holding the towel for them in turn; each shall always do this in the same way. When he has done so, he shall return again to his place.

As soon as everything has been completed, the prior shall strike the board only once. Then the cellarers shall have wine prepared, and the chamberlains, one on one side and another on the other, shall pour wine for the brothers. They shall also have coins prepared, so that, while the brothers receive the cup, they may give them to the poor. When the poor give back the vessel, the brothers shall kiss their hands and again give two or three coins with a kiss.

When this has been done, the abbot, if present, shall say: “Show us, O Lord, your mercy.” “Lord, have mercy. Christ, have mercy. Lord, have mercy.” “Our Father,” and “And lead us not.” After this prayer they shall say aloud: “We have received your mercy, O God. You have commanded your commandments, O Lord. You have washed the feet of your disciples.” Then the prayer: “Be present, O Lord, to the service of us your servants.” The psalm “Have mercy on me, O God” shall be said silently. Thus, while the boards are being sounded, they shall go into the choir for Vespers. When each has reached his place, a boy shall begin the antiphon, “The cup of salvation.” Psalm: “I believed.” Antiphon: “With those who.” Psalm: “To the Lord, when I was troubled.” Antiphon: “Guard me.” Psalm: “O Lord, I have cried.” Antiphon: “I was considering.” Psalm: “With my voice.”

As the elders go to the refectory, the sacristans shall uncover the altars. In the refectory the tables shall be covered, and they shall perform the charitable meal. On that day the almoner must receive neither bread nor wine, nor, on Holy Saturday, whatever remains in the refectory. When the brothers have gone out, they shall say the verses and everything else silently; then they shall wash their feet and prepare themselves for the brothers’ foot-washing ceremony.

When they have first assembled for the foot-washing, the weekly servers who are to leave the kitchen on the following Sunday shall wash everyone’s feet. Afterwards, the lord abbot, if present, shall wash the feet on one side and the prior on the other; they shall wipe and kiss them. When this has been completed, the lord abbot shall come to his place, and two brothers shall wash his feet. The attendants shall wash the feet outside the chapterhouse.

When their hands have been washed, the deacon and three attendants shall come and vest in the church: the deacon shall wear the stole; two shall take candlesticks with candles and the thurible with incense; and the sacristan, with permission, shall strike the board. Another shall carry the lectern, and the deacon the Gospel book. When they enter the chapterhouse in this order, all shall rise before the Gospel, and, when the abbot has announced it, the deacon shall begin to read.

When he comes to the passage where it says, “Rise, let us go from here,” the board shall be sounded, and they shall proceed in this order to the refectory: first the lectern and the thurible with incense; then the two with the candlesticks, with the deacon between them; then the others, two by two. The children shall come last, before the abbot.

When they have reached the refectory, the brothers appointed to serve the lord abbot and the prior shall, as they serve them, kiss their hands; the children shall do likewise. When the reading has ended, the deacon, having removed his stole, together with the others who are in albs, shall sit at the lord abbot’s table; they too shall receive and drink the beverage. When they return from there to the church, each shall stand in his place facing east; the young men shall stand at the stalls and sing Compline silently, each by himself.

## CHAPTER III. How the rites are to be conducted on Good Friday

On Good Friday, as many candles shall be lit at the nocturns as there are psalms to be appointed. After the threefold prayer, the boards shall be sounded throughout the cloister in place of bells. The reading at the entrance shall be “And Jerusalem remembered,” from Jeremiah. At the second nocturn: “But considering,” from the treatise of blessed Augustine. At the third nocturn let “Let us hasten to enter,” from the Epistle to the Hebrews, be read; the rest as above.

On this day and on Saturday they shall say the Hours silently, according to the rule, with their faces turned toward the altar. The young men shall stand at the stalls. “The Lord be with you” shall nowhere be said on this day. At Prime they shall come barefoot and say it silently. The antiphon shall be taken from that day’s Gospel. As they had used their own antiphons at the Hours on that day, so on Holy Saturday they shall continue with the proper antiphons. After Prime they shall say the seven psalms together and the litany.

The brothers shall leave together and say the entire Psalter in the cloister, from “Praise the Lord from the heavens” onward. The children shall do the same with their masters. The crowns and all the crosses shall be uncovered before Terce. On these two days the interval shall be longer than they usually make it.

After None, those who are to perform the service of the church shall vest in albs, and all the children likewise. When they return from the blessed fire, the prior shall carry the light. As soon as they have arrived—so the manuscripts read—in the choir, the subdeacon shall read Jeremiah’s lesson: “Thus says the Lord God: In their tribulation they will rise early to me.”

When they return from the blessed fire, the priests shall come silently from the sacristy to the altar in their sacred vestments, singing nothing, and asking that prayer be offered for them. When the confession has been made, the levite shall say, “Let us pray”; the deacon shall announce, “Let us bend the knees,” and after a short while shall say, “Rise.”  

[Note: The same deacon said both “Let us bend the knees” and “Rise,” while the subdeacon remained silent.]

The priest shall pronounce this prayer: “O God, from whom Judas …” The prophecy: “Thus says the Lord.” The tract: “Lord, I have heard.” Then the priest shall go before the altar and say, “Let us pray.” The levite shall announce, “Let us bend the knees.” The prayer: “O God, who [—] the ancient sin …” The reading from Exodus: “The Lord said to Moses.” The tract: “Deliver me, O Lord.” In the same way they shall recapitulate the rite for each verse. The Passion shall be read without a salutation.

When the reader says the verse, “They divided my garments among themselves,” one shall come to the altar from one side and another from the other, and they shall divide the linen cloths among themselves. When this has been done, the priest shall come to the altar and say the solemn prayers found in the Book of the Sacraments. “Let us bend the knees” shall not be said for the Jews.

When these things have been completed, carpets shall be arranged before the altar. The priest shall remove his chasuble and stole, and the deacon his stole, since at this hour he must be without a chasuble. Then two priests or deacons, dressed in albs, shall come out carrying the cross, which must be veiled; behind the altar they shall sing the verse, “My people.”

These things shall be done together before the altar. Two or three others, likewise dressed in albs, shall respond in Greek: “ἅγιος ὁ Θεὸς” (“Holy God”). Then the clergy shall continue in Latin: “Holy God, holy and mighty.” Next, the two carrying the cross shall move forward a little, singing again the verse, “Who led you out.” The two shall respond, “ἅγιος ὁ Θεὸς,” and then the clergy shall continue: “Holy God.” Again, as the two carrying the cross approach near the altar, they shall sing, “What more could have been done?” The two shall respond, “ἅγιος ὁ Θεὸς,” and then the clergy: “Holy God.”

Then the two holding the cross shall come before the altar, uncover the cross, and begin the antiphon, “Behold the wood of the cross.” When the antiphon is finished, the choir shall say, “Come, let us exult,” or “Blessed are the undefiled.” Then all shall throw themselves upon the ground and adore the holy cross. While it is being adored, the two shall hold it until the others come to adore it themselves. The choir shall sing the antiphon, “Your cross.” After the antiphons these verses shall be sung: “Faithful cross,” and the others as they are written.

When the cross is removed from the place where it was adored and set up in the appointed place, the antiphon “Above all the cedars’ trees” shall be appointed. When this has been done, two presbyters and the deacon who is to handle the Lord’s body shall wash their hands and put on chasubles or copes. They shall come to the altar prepared for this purpose with candlesticks and incense, arrange there a chalice with wine and water poured into it, and prepare the Lord’s body.

As soon as they have completed this and begun to proceed to the main altar, where they have prepared the linen cloth and corporal, all shall immediately prostrate themselves. The priest shall likewise take the thurible, incense the chalice, and say aloud, “Let us pray: At the command of the Savior …” “Our Father.” Then, silently, “Deliver us, we beseech you, O Lord …” This shall be followed aloud by “World without end,” and he shall place the Lord’s body in the wine. “The peace of the Lord” shall be omitted.

Then all shall come in order to receive communion, including the children. When they have communicated, the board shall be sounded. After prayer has been made, they shall wash their feet, put on their shoes, return to the church, and, while all the boards are being struck, say Vespers silently, each by himself.

Antiphon: “With those who.” Psalm: “To the Lord.”  
Antiphon: “From wicked men.” Psalm: “Deliver me, O Lord.”  
Antiphon: “Guard me from the snare.” Psalm: “O Lord, I have cried.”  
Antiphon: “I was considering.” Psalm: “With my voice.”  
Antiphon: “From the hand of the sons.” Psalm: “Blessed.”

Nothing else shall be appointed except the antiphon, and they shall say the Magnificat secretly to themselves. Then: “Lord, have mercy,” and so forth; “Our Father”; the prayers; “I said, Lord”; adding the psalm “Have mercy on me, O God.” “Let us pray,” and the rite ends.

The sacristans shall prepare themselves and wash the altars, first with water and afterwards with wine. For the two preceding days the attendants shall have kept the church swept and have strewn something made of rushes; likewise in the cloister and chapterhouse. When the elders go to the refectory, they shall receive only bread and water, and herbs if they wish. Whatever has been prepared shall be received by the almoner.

Again, according to custom, when the board has been struck they shall come to drink. If they wish, the almoner shall also receive all the wine intended for them while they drink water. But when they assemble for the collation, after the board has been struck for the charitable meal, wine shall be brought for everyone to drink.

## CHAPTER IV. How the rites are to be conducted on Holy Saturday

The morning vigils and everything else shall be celebrated as we have already set forth. In the first nocturn, readings shall be taken from Jeremiah’s Lamentations. In the second nocturn, the exposition “O God, my praise.” In the third nocturn, “Christ, serving as high priest.”

Very early the entire church shall be adorned with linen and woolen curtains and hangings all around the walls. Carpets shall surround the choir stalls; benches shall surround the choir. They shall decorate the principal arch with large ornaments suitable for the occasion and arrange the other ornaments as on the day of the Lord’s Nativity.

On the Paschal candle, the armarius shall write the years of the Lord and the epact, showing how it is observed in that year, before he begins the blessing. After None, all who have anything sacred to read, sing, or perform shall vest. Then the children and all the brothers shall come into the church and go to bless the fire in the cloister. The abbot shall carry the light.

When they return, the deacon shall put on his stole and dalmatic and immediately begin to sanctify the candle. Once it has been blessed, it must always continue burning, as blessed Gregory says in its blessing, until the following day, when Mass has been completed. Eight men wearing copes shall stand around it; they are to sing the Alleluia or the tract at Mass.

On this day the morning Mass ought not to be celebrated unless the readings have been completed or begun. If someone wishes to celebrate Mass before them—which should rarely be permitted—but has obtained the lord abbot’s permission, he must have three or four ministers to assist him. Nevertheless, he shall perform it without fire at this hour, unless perhaps the lord abbot has provided him with a sufficiently remote place where he can bless the fire.

Whether this man or those who celebrate Mass after the reading, they shall perform the litany before beginning Mass. Those who celebrate the sacred rite before the candle has been blessed shall have a light. The senior brothers shall read the lessons first, and then the younger ones.

The reading from Genesis—neither for this Mass nor for any other—shall be recited in full; only the beginning of the reading, whatever it may be, shall be begun.

The same shall be done on the Saturday of Pentecost. First reading: “In the beginning.” When it ends, the priest shall come to the altar and say this prayer: “O God, who wondrously created humankind …”

Second reading: “It came to pass at the morning watch.”  
Tract: “Let us sing to the Lord,” sung by two men dressed in albs.  
Prayer: “O God, who [—] ancient miracles …”

Reading: “Seven women shall seize one man.”  
Tract: “A vineyard was planted.”  
Prayer: “O God, who [—] us to celebrate …”

Reading: “This is the inheritance.”  
Canticle: “Give ear, O heavens.”  
Prayer: “O God, who [—] your Church …”

Without a reading, the canticle from the psalm “As the deer longs” shall be sung.  
Prayer: “Grant, we beseech you, almighty God, that those who celebrate the feast …”  
Another prayer, from the same forty-first psalm: “Almighty and eternal God, look upon us graciously …”

Then two brothers wearing copes shall come into the choir and begin the litany, in every respect as the boys customarily say it on weekdays before Mass. First the two themselves; then the abbot’s choir; afterwards, from the other side, “Be propitious.”

When they have said “Lamb of God,” the priest shall proceed to the sacristy with the other ministers, and the subdeacon shall then put on the tunic. As soon as these things have been completed, they shall begin: “Kindle,” “Lord, have mercy,” “Lord, have mercy,” “Lord, have mercy,” saying them as is customary at Mass.

Then all the bells shall be sounded and candles lit before the altar; one candle shall burn at each altar until the end.

On this day no light shall be carried from the sacristy before the Gospel, but incense alone. Nevertheless, from the beginning of the Gospel until the end of Mass, the candlesticks shall be held as usual, and they shall come to the altar, where the priest and levite shall pray.

When the bells have ceased, the priest shall say, “Glory to God in the highest.”  
Prayer: “O God, who has made this night holy …”  
Epistle: “As you have risen.”  
Alleluia: “Give thanks to the Lord.”  
Tract: “Praise the Lord.”  
Offertory and Communion.

The “Lamb of God” shall not be said, because he himself has truly been sacrificed as the Lamb for the sin of the world. As soon as communion has been received, the prayer after communion shall be said, followed by “Go, the Mass is ended.” Two small bells shall be sounded together.

At Vespers the prayers shall be made. At the end all the bells shall be rung together.

[Note: *Classicum*, from *conclassare*, means the ringing of all the bells.]

Alleluia at Vespers. Psalm: “Let them confess,” with the others.  
Reading: “As you have risen.”  
Responsory: “Mary Magdalene.”  
Hymn: “To the supper of the Lamb.”  
Verse: “He has risen.”

The abbot and priest shall put on copes to incense the altars.  
Antiphon: “But on the evening of the Sabbath.”  
Prayer: “O God, who has made this holy night …”

When the suffrages for the saints have been completed, they shall go to the holy Cross while singing this responsory: “When he had crossed over.”  
Verse: “Declare among the nations.”  
Prayer: “O God, who has brought us to eternal life through the resurrection of Christ …”

When Vespers itself has been said, they shall go to take refreshment. On that day the tables in the refectory shall be covered and the charitable meal shall be given; they shall have better fare than they had been accustomed to on other days. They shall not perform the foot-washing ceremony on that day, because it was performed on Thursday, with God’s help.

## CHAPTER V. Observe the Paschal customs in this joyful manner

On the most holy day of the Lord’s Pascha, before the nocturnal office, all the crowns shall be lit,

[Note: *Corona*: a candlestick in the form of a crown or circle.]

and the phari,

[Note: *Pharus*, *pharum*, *farus*: a circular lamp or lantern containing a fixed number of lamps or candles.]

as well as three candlesticks before the altar and one behind it. For the canticles, ten shall be added in front, nine behind, and fifteen above.

The invitatory shall be sung by four men wearing copes.

At the first nocturn: antiphon, “I am who I am.” Psalm, “O Lord, in your strength.”  
At the second nocturn: “I asked my Father.” Psalm, “The Lord is my light.”  
At the canticle: “I slept.” Canticle, “Who is this?”

Eight readings from the Gospel: “But on the evening of the Sabbath.” Exposition by blessed Jerome. After three readings the priest shall be dressed in a cope; he shall incense only the principal altar and then the brothers in the choir. The responsories shall be said by pairs.

At the third nocturn, the homily of blessed Pope Gregory, “Mary Magdalene.”

At the morning praises: antiphon, “But the angel of the Lord.” When the antiphon ends, they shall repeat the Alleluia from it, and do the same in the choirs.

At the station: responsory, “Mary Magdalene.”  
Verse: “Declare among.”  
Prayer: “O God, who through the resurrection …”

Before they begin Prime, three golden chalices, together with the smaller ones, and the same number of books, as well as the altars and two candlesticks that are to burn continually through the perpetual day, shall be placed on the altar above. At each Hour three candlesticks shall be lit. At the end of the hymns they shall say: “We beseech you, author of all things …”

Gloria shall be sung at the morning Mass. They shall say one prayer and omit the preface. The abbot shall order one of the brothers to sing another Mass for the laity who are to receive communion.

While “Holy, holy, Lord” is being said at this Mass, all shall vest in albs, from the greatest to the least. As soon as the water has been blessed, they shall appoint the antiphon, “I saw water.” Then two of the young men or children, whom the armarius has indicated, shall come and put on tunics to carry the Gospel books and the other books.

Then the lord abbot shall appoint the antiphon, “When the King of glory.” As they go out into the atrium before the monastery door, they shall stand in order as they came, with the elders in the middle, as is customary for standing in the choir. Then the armarius shall signal to whichever cantors he wishes, so that they may assemble in the middle behind the children; they shall appoint the antiphon, “Crucified in the flesh,” with its repetition, “Do not be afraid.”

As they enter the church, the paraphonista shall begin the antiphon “Christ, rising,” or the responsory “Christ has risen.” When all the bells have been struck, they shall say the prayer and celebrate Terce.

The sacristans shall cover the altar with two hangings,

[Note: *Palleis*, *palleum*, *pallium*, *palla*: a white linen covering for the altar. See Du Cange, *Glossarium latinitatis*, under *palla*.]

and an additional white one. Then they shall give out the copes, which are to be in the choir by the armarium. The sacristan himself shall then distribute to each of the others—[the manuscripts read, “albs”]—including the lay brothers, and tunics to the children.

When all the bells have been sounded, they shall maintain the office of the twelve. Four responsories, six Alleluias; twelve candles before the altar and ten behind. At the sequence two bells shall be sounded; when Mass has ended, the other bells shall be sounded.

In the refectory they shall have the following general arrangements. For the first course, the cellarer shall prepare small fish and the weekly server shall carry them in. Second, whatever the cook has prepared shall be brought in and the cellarer shall serve it. When this has been done, the bell shall be sounded with the abbot’s approval; immediately the refectorer shall rise and strike the small bells once.

Then all the lay brothers shall rise to pour the drink. Meanwhile the cellarer and his officials shall carry the portion to the table, first to the lord abbot and then to the others. Immediately the refectory steward shall rise, do as before, and all the deacons shall assemble carrying the charitable portion. Then the kitchen servers shall give their dish.

As soon as the small bell has sounded again, the refectory steward shall go and act as customary. Then the priests shall assemble and pour the wine. As many times as they pour it, so many strokes of the small bell must be made.

What we have set forth is not merely for satisfying gluttony or drunkenness, but for maintaining charity and fulfilling the love of Christ. This threefold pouring signifies the Trinity, because whatever we do we ought to begin and complete in the name of the undivided Trinity. In this matter, without doubt, anyone who searches will be able to find it in the Harmony of the Rules.

[Note: The author of this *Harmony of the Rules* was Saint Benedict of Aniane. Hugh Menard published it.]

And in Hildemar’s exposition of the Rule.

[Note: We shall include in our chain of commentaries and anecdotes Hildemar’s ninth-century exposition of the Rule of Saint Benedict.]

After rising from the meal, they shall rest in their little beds. As the hour of None approaches, the bell shall be sounded moderately; they shall rise and wash their hands and faces. When the sign is sounded again, the boys shall go to their place in the choir; they shall maintain the signal until they rise from prayer.

At Vespers all the candles shall be lit before the altar.

Antiphon: “When the Sabbath had passed.”  
Psalm: “The Lord said to my Lord.”  
Responsory: “Christ has risen.”

For the commemoration of the saints, every day they shall say the antiphon concerning the cross from the feast itself. At the station: an antiphon concerning Saint Mary for the nations.

They shall celebrate three days in copes with the utmost devotion, as follows. From the beginning of the nocturnal office two bells shall be sounded; three candlesticks shall stand before the altar and one behind. Two boys shall say the invitatory: “The Lord has truly risen. Alleluia.”

On the first and second nocturns, or at Vespers, the boys shall say the Alleluia. During the Hours of the day the weekly servers shall say the antiphon. The Gospel shall be proclaimed throughout the entire week. Responsory: “The angel of the Lord.”

At the praises, fifteen candles shall be lit before the altar and seven behind. Then all the bells shall be sounded, and they shall begin the antiphon “But the angel of the Lord” and the others that follow, singing only one each day, begun by the weekly server. The priest shall be in a cope, and he shall incense the altars.

At the Hours: three candles. At the morning Mass: one collect. The offertory and everything else shall be said throughout the week as they were said on Sunday, except for the preface, which is not to be sung except on these three days.

At the main Mass all the priests and levites shall be in copes. The altar shall be surrounded by three corporals. The candles before and behind shall be lit. Six shall hold the offertory. At the completion of Mass all the bells shall be sounded.

In the refectory they shall perform the charitable meal every day, and likewise the collation. Throughout the week they shall say at Vespers the psalms as on Sunday, with the Alleluia in whatever manner is desired. The lighting shall be as at Mass.

On the other three days, moderately: for the nocturnal office there shall be three candlesticks before the altar and one behind. At the morning praises all the bells shall be sounded. One candle shall be added and the board uncovered. The boys shall not complete the responsory or “Let us bless the Lord” beforehand, but it shall be done in its proper place. The priest shall wear an alb for incensing.

The reliquary chests shall be covered with an outer stole,

[Note: That is, cases in which the holy relics are kept, adorned with a stole or pallium.]

and the carpets shall be removed from the choir stalls. At the morning Mass all the collects shall be said as usual. At the main Mass they shall proceed as is customary in the Twelve Readings, and likewise with the candlesticks. The preface shall be omitted.

### Saturday in White

Invitatory: “Alleluia, alleluia.” At the praises or at Vespers, let them have whatever short Paschal responsories they wish. Let them sing the Alleluia on each day both at the nocturns and at the Hours; likewise the verses that are noted for that day.

At Vespers there shall be five candlesticks before the altar and three behind. Let them appoint the psalms “Let them confess.” Antiphon: “When it was evening.” Prayer: “Grant, we beseech you, almighty God …”

## CHAPTER VI. The octave of the Lord’s resurrection

Let it be celebrated with the greatest care. As soon as the canticle of the Gradual Psalms has been completed, three candles shall be lit before the altar and one behind; for the canticle, two shall be added in front, one behind, and fifteen above.

Two men in copes shall say the invitatory: “Alleluia.” Reading from the holy Fathers or from the Acts of the Apostles: “The former account.” Responsory: “The angel of the Lord.” The fourth, eighth, and twelfth shall be sung by two men. The twelfth shall be recapitulated from the beginning after the Gloria Patri.

In the Gospel, antiphon: “After eight days.” At the morning Mass: one collect and the Paschal preface.

For the procession, when they have come before the monastery door and been arranged in the customary order, four shall go ahead in the middle and say, “Crucified in the flesh.” All the priests and levites must then be in copes.

At the main Mass there shall be seven candlesticks before the altar and three behind; the preface shall be sung. At the explanation of the sacred rite all the bells shall be sounded. At the Hours there shall be three candlesticks.

At Vespers they shall carry out the Alleluia in the manner in which they have customarily appointed it day by day,

[Note: That is, on each individual day.]

and recite the psalms of that Sunday.

## CHAPTER VII. The Pascha of the preceding year

[Note: The annual day on which Pascha was celebrated, or the anniversary of Easter Day.]

If the holy Pascha that we celebrated in the preceding year falls during Lent, it is not celebrated at all. But if it is found to fall after Pascha, everything shall be completed as it is to be sung at the Lord’s resurrection, except for the Gospel that is read: “There was a man of the Pharisees.” When it falls among the Twelve Readings, the morning Mass shall be celebrated from it; and if it occurs on ordinary days, they shall celebrate the main Mass from it.

When the octave of Pascha has been celebrated, they shall proceed in this manner on ordinary days. As soon as they have completed the nocturnal office, the signal shall be sounded and the morning praises begun.

Before we insert anything else at this point, we think it very worthwhile to say a few words. Perhaps there will be some who ask why an interval is not made, as the Rule prescribes. I reply: there are some brothers who suffer from different illnesses, and our predecessors wisely foresaw that this discretion should be exercised: as soon as “Come, let us exult in the Lord” has been said at the nocturnal office, and “God, have mercy on us” at the praises, those who need to leave may go out and return as they are able. For any other matter [or reason—we supply the missing word], we give no approval whatsoever; indeed, we correct those who do this frequently.

Moreover, the psalms that, with the Lord’s help, we ought diligently to sing must be begun without delay because of the shortness of the nights. In the Gospel, the antiphons that were used on the day of the resurrection may be said together with the others appointed for Sunday, up to the day of the Lord’s Ascension.

When the suffrages for the saints have been completed, they shall go singing an antiphon concerning Saint Mary and perform the morning office of all the saints, as well as the morning office for our deceased brothers, and five psalms for the brothers recently deceased.

Before Prime, the church hangings and the other ornaments that are customarily removed shall be taken down. At Prime: “Have mercy on me, O God,” the seven psalms, the litanies, and a Mass for the dead.

When they assemble in the chapterhouse, they shall say three times, “O God, come to my assistance,” without kneeling. When they rise from this, the child who is first among the others must always prepare the board for the prior, or for the one who holds the office if the prior is absent; it must be struck six times.

They shall omit the psalms of the familiar Hours that they used to say. If it should happen that some psalm must be appointed, or they have already begun one, or are observing one for the dead, it seems appropriate to sing it for this purpose.

When the hour of Terce is signaled, all shall assemble in the church. When the prayer has been completed, the priest shall go with the ministers, and they shall put on albs.

[Note: *Albis se induant*: “let them put on albs.”]

Returning to the choir, they shall sound the signal again and celebrate the Hour. The boy shall begin the litany. They shall go to the offertory as is customary.

On Friday they must celebrate a Mass of the holy Cross.

After None, when they leave the refectory, they shall assemble in the chapterhouse. The lord abbot shall say three times, “O God, come to my assistance; O Lord, hasten to help me.” At no time shall the knees be bent three times during this prayer.

First a reverence shall be made and the board sounded. “Let us pray.” “Our Father.” “And lead us not.” “Our help is in the name of the Lord.” “Bless.”

If anyone is absent at the hour of None through negligence of sleep, he shall make satisfaction in the chapterhouse while all stand. The other matters, after the sacred rite has been performed, shall be concluded. When they leave there, they shall bow forward and backward, and each shall proceed to whatever has been assigned to him.

At Vespers, when the attendants leave the refectory, the signal shall be sounded; all shall assemble together, and the Office of the Dead shall be performed.

## CHAPTER VIII. The first Sunday after the octave of Pascha

On Saturday at Vespers: responsory, “I am like a vine.” Invitatory: “Alleluia.” At the first nocturn: “Alleluia, I am.” Reading from the Apocalypse of the apostle John. Responsory: “Worthy are you, O Lord,” for two weeks.

### The Second Sunday

As on the first. The school shall say the short responsory with the Gloria Patri.

At the first: “The Lord has risen from the tomb.”  
At the second: “The Lord has truly risen.”  
At the third: “The disciples rejoiced.”

These proper chants pertaining to the day shall continue to be said until the Kalends of September, except when a narrative is appointed; in that case the senior brothers shall bring it forth from the narrative itself.

At the Lord’s resurrection, the attendants, leaving the refectory, shall go through the school to the oratory of Saint Mary, singing softly, “Have mercy on me, O God.” They shall do this throughout the entire summer when they are to eat twice. In the evening they shall not turn back from there, but shall go through the upper cloister beside the pantry.

### The Third Sunday after the octave of Pascha

On Saturday at Vespers: responsory, “The waters saw you, O God.” On the following day, readings shall be taken from the seven canonical epistles. Responsory: “If I forget you.” This continues until the Ascension of the Lord.

### The Feast of the Apostles Philip and James

At Vespers: five candlesticks before the altar. Reading: “The righteous shall stand.” Responsory: [lacuna] “Alleluia, I am the vine,” to be said by two men in copes. Readings from their Passion. Responsory: “With great power.” The fourth, eighth, and twelfth shall be sung there.

At the third nocturn, a reading of the exposition of that day’s Gospel.

At the morning praises: antiphon, “I am the way,” together with four other responsories; the boys shall sing “Let us bless the Lord” before the altar, and celebrate the morning Mass from it.

At the main Mass all the priests and levites shall be in copes. Seven candles shall stand before the altar; four brothers shall carry out the office.

Epistle: “I am confident about you in the Lord.”  
Alleluia: “The righteous shall stand.”  
Another Alleluia: “They shall confess.”

At Vespers: one Alleluia from that day’s antiphons only, and the psalms of the apostles.

### The Finding of the Holy Cross

At Vespers: responsory, “Above all.”  
Antiphon: “Crucified in the flesh, alleluia, alleluia.”  
Psalms from the weekday of that day.  
Chapter: “But as for me, far be it.”  
Responsory: “Above all.”  
Hymn: “The banners.”  
Verse: “This sign of the cross.”  
Antiphon: “O cross.”  
Prayer of that day; then they shall repeat the antiphon concerning the saints.

The station shall be held at the holy Cross; the responsory and prayer shall concern that Cross. Two men in copes shall say “Come.” Alleluia shall be said as is customary on Sundays; hymn: “Eternal Christ.” Eight readings from the saints. Responsory: “Precious.” The fourth, eighth, and twelfth shall be sung by two brothers.

At the canticle: antiphon, “Alleluia, sweet wood,” or “Because of the wood.” Canticle: “O Lord, I have heard,” divided between two pairs: namely, “Glory: Is it not in the rivers?” and “Glory: You went forth for salvation.”

Homily from the Gospel “There was a man,” with its exposition.

At the praises, the antiphons that are brought forth, and the shortened responsories without “Let us bless the Lord,” shall be proclaimed by the boys before the steps, both at this Hour and at Vespers.

They shall celebrate the morning Mass from the feast of Saints Eventius and Theodulus. Before beginning the main Mass, all the priests and levites shall be clothed in copes. Seven candlesticks shall be arranged before the altar, together with those carried by the converts. Four shall carry out the office: “But we …”

Epistle: “I am confident about you in the Lord.”  
Alleluia: “Sweet wood.”  
Another: “Alleluia, alleluia, Christ rising.”  
Gospel: “There was a man.”

At the Hours, the antiphons of the week shall be said.

At Vespers: antiphon, “Alleluia, crucified.” Psalms: “The Lord said,” “I will confess,” “Blessed,” “Praise.” Hymn: “The banners.” Prayer. The cantors shall repeat the antiphon concerning the saints with the Gloria.

### The First Sunday before the Rogation Days

The psalm “To the Lord, when I was troubled,” shall not be said, nor “Out of the depths” for the dead, because on those three days they shall be celebrated festively.

## On the Days of the Rogations

For the nocturnal service they are to read the canonical epistles accurately; they are to come into another choir and sing there the matins of All Saints and of the dead, without antiphons. They are likewise to do this at vespers. [Col. 1210D] After completing these matins, they are to go to the dormitory and rest.

After Prime, however, let the psalm “Have mercy on me, O God” be sung; and if another psalm has been appointed, let it be said before that one. Then let this psalmody follow: “O God, we have heard with our ears,” with fifteen psalms for all tribulations, with prayers or commemorations for benefactors, and also for the repose of the dead: five psalms, therefore, for the dead, then seven psalms, and the litany.

Let them celebrate the morning Mass of that day and the collect, in every respect as on other days; and if a saint’s feast should happen to fall on that day, let the prayer for that saint be said at this sacred service, adding “of your saints” [Col. 1211A], and let them celebrate the morning Mass at the high altar. Let everyone make the offering; one person is to receive the peace.

At Chapter, the verse “O God, come to my assistance” is not to be said, as on other ordinary days, nor is anyone to speak in the cloister during these three days. At the Hours, let the readings and prayers be from the Lord’s Resurrection.

After Sext they are to go to the dormitory and rest a little; or those who wish may read in their beds until they hear the signal. When they hear it, they are to come barefoot and wash their hands and faces. On coming into the church, after prayer, let the boys say the antiphon “Arise, O Lord.” Then the sacristan or keeper of the books is to distribute phylacteries containing relics to each person, except the boys and those who have contracted some contagion during sleep.

After the antiphon [Col. 1211B], let prayer again be made, and let the psalm “May God have mercy on us” be said, followed by the Lord’s Prayer and Chapter: “And let it come upon us.” The collect is “Remember your family.”

They are to proceed in an orderly manner, as though forming a procession. The servants are to go first carrying banners. One brother from the conversi is to carry the cross, another the holy water, and the subdeacon the Gospel book. On one side the candlesticks are to go, and on the other the censer. When they begin to leave, let all the bells sound, and let them say the antiphon “The relics go out from Jerusalem.”

After the Gospel book, those who do not know how to sing are to leave; then the schola with its masters, followed by the singers, walking two by two in order. Everyone is to join together and continue singing the antiphon until they reach the oratory where they are to celebrate Mass.

As they leave, the servants [Col. 1211C] are to stand before the door of the atrium, one on each side, with prepared rods. They are to distribute these to everyone, including the children, both on the way out and on the return. When they enter the church, those who distributed them are to collect and keep them.

Finally, when they arrive in order, as described above, before the doors of the church where they are to perform the sacred rites, the moment they arrive there the singers are to begin the responsory concerning the relics of the saints. There the consecration is performed while the bells are sounding.

When the responsory has been completed, the priest is to say the verse and the prayer of those same saints, followed by “The Lord be with you.” After the verse, the elders are to place the phylacteries [Note: [Col. 1211D] *Phylacteries*: relics of the saints, as we noted above, col. 1207] on the altar, one on each side, just as they stand in the choir, bending their knees. As soon as they have placed them [Col. 1211D], they are all to pray together and celebrate None. The priest and ministers are to put on the sacred vestments.

Before the brothers assemble there, the sacristans are to have everything prepared: the pallium laid over the altar and the rush mat spread on the chapel floor. As soon as the appointed Hour has arrived, the precentor is to begin the office. First the priest is to say the collect proper to that day, and another for the saints whose relics have been dedicated there.

After the Gospel reading, the person appointed to sing the “Lamb of God” is to receive permission, as are the kitchen servers and the managers of the refectory. One person is to perform the offering and the peace. When each person receives the phylactery containing the relics [Col. 1212A], let him bend his knees as before.

Then let two people begin the reading, at the signal of the keeper of the books, one of the elders. As they say “Lord, have mercy,” let them continue until they reach the monastery; then let them say the name of the saint to whom that church belongs twice. Afterward they are to make a reverence.

The same persons are to begin again as above: “Holy Mary,” and the other saints who follow, saying each name twice. They must return in order, just as they came. When they reach the doors of the church, the litany is to have been concluded. Then the two men, clad in cappas, one on one side and the other on the other, are to begin the “Lamb of God.” As they say “Glory to the Father,” everyone is to enter the church.

Meanwhile the servants are to sound the bells. The brothers are to place the phylacteries on the altar table, bending their knees [Col. 1212B]. Once they have placed them, and the bells have ceased, the two men wearing cappas are to begin “Hear us, O God.” The clergy are to respond.

Then those same men are to say for the second time, “Hear us, O Christ,” and the clergy are to follow with “Have mercy on us.” Again the two together are to say, “Hear us,” and the clergy, “Be favorable.” Meanwhile the two men are to say for the third time, “Holy God of holy ones.” Finally, the other saints are to be proclaimed once each by two other men. The clergy are to respond together, and thus the litany is to be concluded.

They are not to bow except at the names of the saints whose relics have been consecrated [or: placed] in that very place. As soon as the three names from the company of holy women have been said, let them proclaim twice: “All you saints, intercede for us.” Then let them say “Hear us, O God,” as they said it at the beginning, three times, adding: “Lord, have mercy; Lord, have mercy; Lord, have mercy” [Col. 1212C].

Note that, when this has been said, they are to bow forward and backward, and then proceed to the dormitories, where they are to take their leggings and wash their feet. When the cymbal has been struck, they are to go to the refectory to eat bread. They are then to receive the general meal, as is customary on Thursday, adding vegetables in place of the *pitantia*.

During these three days they must not eat fat [*sagimen*]. They are to give the charity portion, and the almoner is to receive whatever bread and wine remains during these three days. They are to omit the Office of the Dead, which they ordinarily say after supper on ordinary days.

## CHAPTER IX. The Vigil of the Ascension of the Lord

[Col. 1212D]

On the Vigil of the Ascension of the Lord, at Prime after the litany, let them celebrate the morning Mass at the high altar, concerning the three-day fast; and if a saint’s feast falls on that day, let that saint’s collects be added.

Let them celebrate the principal Mass in the church to which they will proceed in procession, concerning the Ascension of the Lord, adding only the collect of the saints in whose honor the basilica has been consecrated, and another for the people dwelling there: “Your ineffable mercy.”

After they have returned and the litanies have been completed in the choir, they are to leave, wash their feet, and put on their shoes. When the cymbal sounds, they are to assemble in the refectory to eat. The sacristans are to adorn the church and do everything according to custom.

At [Col. 1213A] vespers, twelve lights are to be placed before the altar and two groups of three behind it. The antiphon is “Alleluia, thus he will come.” The psalm is from the weekday office: “Praise the name of the Lord.” The reading is “The first account.” The responsory is “All beauty.” The hymn is “Let us sing a hymn.” Two priests are to put on cappas and carry incense around the altar.

The antiphon is “Father, I have manifested,” followed by the prayer “Grant, we ask, almighty Father.” Let the station be made at the holy cross. The antiphon is “O King of glory, Lord of hosts,” or the responsory “The time has come.” The prayer is “O God, whose Son…”

At Compline let them appoint the two verses “We beseech you, author of all things” and “Glory to you, O Lord, who ascend.” Let these be sung every day at all the Hours. Let the other hymns end with whatever form of “Glory” has been prescribed, as the teachers have ordered.

## CHAPTER X. Christ Ascending into Heaven: These Are the Required Practices

[Col. 1213B]

On the feast of the glorious exaltation of the Lord, as soon as the gradual psalm has been completed, three candlesticks are to be lit before the altar and one behind it. Four men in cappas are to sing the invitatory: “Alleluia, Christ the ascending Lord.” The hymn is “Jesus, our redemption.”

During the readings, incense is not to be put on the altars. Finally, the readings are to be taken from the homilies of blessed Augustine: “Glorified by the Father,” for the first and second Nocturns; in the third, a homily of blessed Pope Gregory.

The responsories are to be sung two and two. At the canticle, the candlesticks are to be increased to nine before the altar, five behind it, and fifteen on the pole. At the station, the responsory is “You make the cloud,” with its prayer.

Before Prime the sacristans are to bring out the furnishings for the seats [Col. 1213C] and decorate the chapter room. At the morning Mass there is to be only one collect, and the preface proper to the day is to be sung.

Everyone must be dressed in white before Terce. Let a procession be arranged in proper order. When they arrive in the atrium before the monastery door, let them begin the responsory “Men of Galilee,” and let them enter while all the bells sound. The church keeper is to receive and distribute cappas to each person, including the conversi; the children are to receive tunics.

When the bells have ceased, eight singers are to perform the office. Twelve candles are to be placed before the altar. Four alleluias are to be sung; then six alleluias. “I believe in one God” is to be sung. Two persons are to receive the offerings; after the sacred service all the bells are to be rung.

At vespers, let there be as many candles as there were at the sacred service [Col. 1213D]. The antiphon is “Alleluia, thus he will come.” The psalm is “The Lord said,” with the other psalms. The antiphon at the Gospel is “O King of glory,” repeated three times.

Throughout the week the invitatory is “Christ ascending on high.” The reading at the Nocturn is from the Acts of the Apostles: “The first account.” A versicle and [supplement: readings] from sermons of the holy Fathers appropriate to the day are also to be given. The responsory is from the feast itself.

At Prime, let the psalmody be as on other days; also let there be the litany and the Mass for the dead. After Terce, let them celebrate Mass from the Ascension of the Lord, saying a short litany beforehand.

## The First Sunday after the Ascension

The invitatory is “Alleluia, Christ going before in the Ascension.” Let the morning sacred service [Col. 1214A] be from the Lord’s exaltation; let the principal Mass be that of Sunday every day. If a saint’s feast occurs within the octave, let three readings be taken from it.

Let the invitatory be sung by two persons, “Alleluia.” Let them read a lesson from the Acts of the Apostles. Let the responsories be from the saint of that day, adding the other customary items at Mass.

On the following Wednesday, let the Sunday office be said, adding a collect from the day of the Ascension and the other customary collects. The epistle and Gospel are to be from the weekday office.

### The Octave of the Ascension of the Lord

Let there be two invitatories. The brothers are to sing in white. Let the antiphons be sung in order at the Nocturns; but at Lauds let them continue as they sang them on the feast itself, together with the accompanying responsories.

Let the eight readings be from a sermon of Saint Augustine, “Our Savior, beloved brothers” [Col. 1214B]. The fourth, eighth, and twelfth responsories are to be sung by the boys.

The short responsories are:

- “Christ ascending on high.”
- “God ascended amid jubilation.”
- “I am ascending to the Father.”

The homily is from the Gospel “I will send my Father’s promise upon you,” with the exposition of the priest Bede. Let them celebrate Mass as on the feast.

Let vespers be sung under “Alleluia” with these psalms: “The Lord said”; “I will confess”; “Blessed”; “Praise.”

During the two days remaining after the octave, the invitatory is “Christ ascending,” and everything else is to be taken from the feast itself. If a saint’s feast occurs, let three readings be made from it, and let everything be done as we have prescribed above for the days within the octave.

## CHAPTER XI. What Must Be Done at the Coming of the Life-Giving Spirit

[Col. 1214C]

On the Vigil of Pentecost, before Prime, let them adorn the monastery and do everything as on Holy Saturday. In particular, at Prime let them celebrate the litany and the Mass for the dead.

After Chapter, let everyone assemble together for shaving. After Sext, let everyone go to sleep. When the signal has sounded, let them rise, wash their hands and faces, and go into the church without any sound of bells; there let them pray together. The boys are also to go before the altar.

Then those who are to read or sing are to vest—their names having been written beforehand in the list—as are all the children. Let the readings first be read as the preceding ones are. When the priest has reached the presbytery, let them go and sit in the appointed place.

The reader is to proceed to the lectern and begin the reading “God tested Abraham.” The prayer is “O God, who in Abraham…” The reading is “Moses wrote.” The canticle is “Give ear, O heaven.” The prayer is “You who gave us a prophet.”

The reading is “Seven women will take hold.” The canticle is “Let us sing to the Lord.” The prayer is “O God, who has brought us to celebrate…”

The reading is “Hear, O Israel.” The canticle is “A vineyard was planted.” The prayer is “O God, unchanging strength…”

The canticle is “As the servant.” The prayer is “Grant, we ask, almighty God, that those who by the solemnity…”

When these rites have been properly completed, two men are to put on cappas in order to say the litany in the choir; they are to say it in every respect as on Holy Saturday. These two are then to remain in the choir until the Mass has ended, while the choir repeats it from both sides.

As soon as they have said it, the priest and ministers are to go out into the [Col. 1215A] sacristy. The deacon is to put on silver stoles and a gilded dalmatic; the subdeacon a tunic bordered with gold. Eight or five singers are to put on cappas, six or three of them to sing.

Let one group sing “Alleluia, Give thanks to the Lord,” and two others the tract “Praise the Lord, all nations.” Two conversi are to carry candlesticks [supplement: let them carry them], and a third the censer. The two who sing the litanies are to say at the end, “Light them. Lord, have mercy.”

Let the bell be rung and seven candlesticks lit before the altar. Then the priest is to come and make confession. When the bells have ceased, let him sing “Glory to God in the highest.” The prayer is “Grant, we ask.”

The epistle is “While Apollos was…” The Gospel is “If you love me.” The offertory is “Send forth your Spirit.” Let the “Lamb of God” be said, followed by the communion “On the last day of the feast”; the Gospel books [Col. 1215B] are to be carried through the whole assembly.

Five hosts are to be sent. Let everyone receive the peace. When these things have been completed, let the bell be rung and let them pray. The servers are to go and receive the mixed drink; afterward let them sing None, and then go to eat.

On this day they are not to eat fat. They are to distribute the charity portion, and the almoner is to receive the bread and wine, as on all vigils of feasts except Easter.

At vespers two bells are to be rung together; twelve candles are to be placed before the altar and ten behind it. Let them begin the “Alleluia” from the antiphon “They were all filled.” The psalms are those of the day. The reading is “When the day of Pentecost had been fulfilled.” The responsory is “They appeared to the apostles.” The hymn is “Come, Creator Spirit.”

Two priests are to put on cappas and carry incense around the altars [Col. 1215C]; the precentor is then to repeat the antiphon with the others. The prayer is “Grant, we ask, almighty God, that of glory…”

At Compline let them appoint verses, and also at all the Hours: “Here, Christ, now the Paraclete” and “Glory to you, O Lord.”

## CHAPTER XII. What Must Be Done at the Coming of the Life-Giving Spirit

On the most holy day of Pentecost, let the coming of the Holy Spirit be celebrated with the greatest reverence and devotion. During the nocturnal services they must light all the lamps of the coronae and arrange everything with the utmost care; the ringing of the bells is to be moderated, and finally they are to resound loudly when they are rung together, continuing until the children come into the church.

For the invitatory, four men are to put on cappas [Col. 1215D]. Before the altar, three candlesticks are to be placed for the first and second Nocturns. For each Nocturn let there be one antiphon.

Let eight readings be said from the Gospel read at the Vigil, together with a sermon of Saint Augustine. Four other readings are to be from a homily of Pope Gregory, from the Gospel of that day. At the third reading of each Nocturn, the priest is to incense the high altar, and the brothers likewise.

Let the responsories be sung two together. At the canticle, fifteen additional candles are to be placed on the pole. Let five antiphons be sung in white. The boys are to perform the short responsory: “The Holy Spirit proceeding.”

Before Prime let the altar be adorned. At the morning Mass let one collect be said, as is customary. Then let everyone put on white [Col. 1216A].

After the Mass has been completed, the priest is to bless water. As soon as it has been blessed, let him begin the antiphon “I saw water.” When this and the prayer have been said, let them proceed in order, singing.

The antiphon is “Today, beloved brothers.” Then the masters with the children, and the abbot behind them; the other elders are to follow two by two, as the preceding group did.

When they begin to leave, the abbot is to begin the antiphon “As they passed.” As soon as they reach the monastery gates, six or eight of the singers selected by the keeper of the books are to come forward in the middle and sing the antiphon “Crucified in the flesh.”

As they enter, let them begin the responsory “The Holy Spirit filled,” while the bells sound. After Terce let them celebrate Mass with all diligence, as [supplement: on the day of] the Lord’s Resurrection.

Let two persons hold the offerings, one offering bread and wine, the other water [supplement: let him offer it]. In the refectory let them distribute the charity portion, as at the feast mentioned above.

At vespers the antiphon is “Alleluia, they were speaking.” The psalm is “The Lord said.” The responsory is “They were all filled.”

### During the Octave

Let two men [supplement: sing] the invitatory “They were all filled with the Holy Spirit, alleluia,” in the same tone as “The Lord has truly risen.”

Then the lighting of the lamps, the proclamation of the Gospels, the ringing of the bells, the morning sacred service, the revesting in cappas, the ringing of the bells after the celebration of Mass, and the evening psalms are all to be done completely as in Easter Week.

At Lauds or the Hours, let them sing in an “alleluia-like” manner [Note: [Col. 1215] To sing *alleluiatice*: with modulation of the voice] concerning the Resurrection [Col. 1216C], the Ascension, and also the celebration that has now taken place.

At Mass the arrangement is as follows.

On Monday: the office “He will feed.” The prayer is “O God, who [gave] to the apostles.” The epistle is “Peter, opening his mouth.” The first Alleluia is “Send forth”; the second is “They were speaking.” The Gospel is “For God so loved the world.” The offertory is “It resounded.” The communion is “The Holy Spirit.”

On Tuesday: the office “Receive gladness,” and everything else as it is found.

On the remaining four days, let them celebrate Mass as on Pentecost. The epistle and Gospel are to be as throughout the year on a weekday; let them be proclaimed as they are arranged in the sacramentary.

On Saturday at vespers, five candlesticks are to be lit before the altar. The antiphon is “They were all filled.” The priest is to be in cappas. The antiphon at the Magnificat is “I will not leave you” [Col. 1216D]. The prayer is “O God, who on this day…”

If the fasts of the fourth month occur during this week, let them proceed as follows. Before Terce, let them celebrate the Mass of the feast, everything in order as we have already stated. The fast is to continue until None. There is to be no procession, nor is the litany to be sung.

After Sext, when they hear the signal, let them rise from the dormitory, wash their hands and faces, come to the oratory without the sound of any bell, and pray. The priest is to vest with the ministers.

When they are vested, the precentor is to begin the office: “O God, when you went forth.” The prayer is “Grant, almighty God, that our minds…” The reading is “Solomon said.” The responsory is “Be favorable.” The prayer is “Grant, we ask, almighty and merciful…”

The reading is “Hear, Jacob.” The responsory is “The earth was shaken” [Col. 1217A]. The Gospel is “The disciples approached Jesus.” One person is to receive the offering and the peace. The offertory is “I will meditate.” The communion is “My peace.”

On Friday the antiphon is “Let my mouth be filled.” The collect is “Give, we ask, to the Church.” The reading is “Rejoice, sons of Zion.” The responsory is “Be to me.” The Gospel is “A man came to Jesus.” The office, Lauds, and communion are “The Spirit breathes where it wills.”

On Saturday let the already established order be preserved. After prayer, let the priest come with the ministers into the sacristy and put on the sacred vestments. Let all the boys dress in white. Let the cantor be in the choir with a cappa. The chant is “The charity of God.”

Only one conversus is to be present, carrying the candlestick. At first the younger children are to read the lesson; then the others, as the preceding group did. They are to sing the responsories in turn, one by one.

When the priest comes to the altar, he is to make confession with the levite and say the prayer “For our minds,” or “I will pour out from my spirit.” The responsory is “Protector.” The prayer is “With that fire,” or “The Lord has spoken.” The responsory is “Be favorable.”
