Prayer, “Your Church, O God” (*Ecclesiam tuam*), or from Wisdom, “I desired, and understanding was given to me” (*Optavi et datus est mihi sensus*) [Col. 1237D]. Responsory, “The just man shall flourish like a palm” (*Justus ut palma*). Alleluia, “The mouth of the just man” (*Os justi*). Gospel, “A certain man went abroad” (*Homo quidam peregre*). Offertory, “The just man shall flourish like a palm” (*Justus ut palma*). Communion, “Blessed is that man” (*Beatus ille*). Let Vespers be performed from the Office of a confessor.

## CHAPTER XXXVI. The First Sunday of October

On Saturday at Vespers: responsory, “Yours is the power” (*Tua est potentia*). Antiphon at the *Magnificat*: “Give peace, O Lord, in our days” (*Da pacem, Domine, in diebus nostris*).

At the nocturn let the hymn “First of the days” (*Primo dierum*) be said. Let the history of the Maccabees be read. Responsory, “May the Lord open” (*Adaperiat Dominus*). At Lauds: hymn, “Eternal maker of things” (*Aeterne rerum conditor*).

On that day, finally, let the midday rest during which the brothers usually sleep in summer be suspended [Col. 1238A]. As soon as they leave the meal, let them immediately come into the cloister and meditate on the lessons until the servers come from the refectory. As soon as they have reached the church, let the custodian sound the greater signal for as long as necessary, until the children come and proceed before the altar to pray. When this has been done, let the signal be sounded again and let the Hour be performed.

When it is completed, let them come to the refectory at the sound of the little bell. From then on, water shall not be served until Palm Sunday. Likewise, as soon as either the prior, or the abbot if he is present, is there, let him strike the little bell, and let each person drink whatever wine he has before him. Let them place their mouths to their proper measure [Note: [Col. 1237D] “Proper measure,” a measure of wine], and then let the little bell be struck three times. Rising, let them return to the cloister. On feast days let them proceed in the same way until the feast of Saint Martin [Col. 1238B].

On ordinary days of that October, after Matins, let the brothers return to their beds. When daylight begins to appear, let the church custodian sound the lesser signal moderately. Without delay, let the brothers come to the church, sing Prime, and after the seven psalms say the litany. Then let them come and sit silently at their lessons. First let the children read aloud, then more softly, or sing; the brothers, however, ought to read or sing decorously.

The weekly kitchen servants, cellarers, and deans, or those to whom some obedience outside has been assigned, are to put on only their footwear. When the time of the regular Hour arrives, let the custodian sound the lesser signal moderately. Going to the dormitory, let them put on their shoes and then wash their hands and faces [Col. 1238C].

When the children come to the church, let the greater signal be sounded, and let everyone together in the choir make a threefold prayer. When these have been completed, let them bow before and behind. Let the lesser signal be struck again. Let them sing Terce, and afterwards Mass.

When Mass has been completed, let the prior, with the abbot’s command if he is present, sound the signal for the chapter. Let the brothers come there in order, as they are to sit or deliberate [variant: “sit”]. When this has been completed, let them say five psalms for those whose names have been pronounced there. Then let the prior sound the board with the abbot’s consent, and let the abbot himself order each person to go to his office. Let the children come to chapter, and afterwards to the refectory.

If on another day or on the third day there are brothers weakened by loss of blood [Col. 1238D], they must go to the refectory as soon as they leave chapter, and the cellarer is to give them three dishes. At that hour of eating, the custodian should not wait for anyone except the abbot or prior, since he foresees that the sixth synaxis has arrived that day. After Sext no one is to speak in the cloister until the children leave the church.

If any of the brothers wishes to have blood let, then it is time to request permission and tell the cellarer to have everything necessary prepared as soon as the Gospel has been read, in the appointed place. Likewise, the brother who wishes to have blood let after the meal must do so then; and after Vespers he must go to the refectory and also have some charitable provision.

On the following day let them walk during the nocturnal Office. During these two days let them have three dishes, as stated above. On the fourth day let a quarter of a cheese be given to each person after Mass.

On Wednesday and Friday after Sext, following a short interval, let the sacristan moderately sound the signal, and let everyone remove his shoes. Then let them wash their hands and go into the church to pray together [variant: “praying,” or supply “say prayers”]. Rising, let them begin the antiphons and make a procession as is customary.

On the other days, after Sext, after some delay, let the master have the hands of those children who are to serve at Mass washed. Then, when the church custodian sees that the time has come, let him sound the signal for Mass. Let everyone proceed into the basilica and offer prayers. When they rise, let one of the children say the litany; then let those who are to minister at Mass vest themselves [Col. 1239B].

When it is finished, let the signal for None be sounded. After prayer has been made, let the kitchen servers, cellarer, and lector go to the refectory to receive the mixed wine. Let the other brothers sit in the choir until the lesser signal is sounded; when everyone has assembled, let them say None. After None, let them come to table. When the meal has been completed, let them sit in the cloister.

## CHAPTER XXXVII. The Vigil of the Holy Apostles Simon and Jude

At the vigil of the holy apostles Simon and Jude, at Mass: Office, “Let it enter into your sight” (*Intret in conspectu*). Prayer, “Grant, we beseech you, almighty God, that just as the apostles . . .” (*Concede, quaesumus, omnipotens Deus, ut sicut apostolorum*); and the other customary prayer, “The souls of the just” (*Justorum animae*) [Col. 1239C]. Responsory, “Avenge, O Lord” (*Vindica, Domine*). Gospel, “I am the vine” (*Ego sum vitis*). Offertory, “The saints shall rejoice” (*Exsultabunt sancti*). Communion, “The souls of the just” (*Justorum animae*).

On that day let them eat no fat; whatever remains in the refectory is to be received by the poor. Before Vespers is sounded, let the church custodian adorn the altars with silks and place carpets on the benches.

At the Vespers synaxis, let five lamps be lit before the altar. Chapter, “You are no longer strangers” (*Jam non estis hospites*). Prayer, “Grant” (*Concede*). Invitatory: two in copes. Let eight lessons be read from the homily of Saint Augustine, “Remember my word” (*Mementote sermonis mei*). Let there be three candles before the altar and one behind.

At the entrance, the homily of Pope Saint Gregory, “The Lord designated” (*Designavit Dominus*); let two lights be added before the altar. Let them sing the antiphon and tract concerning the apostles, and let two candlestands be added before the altar. Let two say the fourth, eighth, and twelfth responsories, and let them repeat the twelfth from the beginning after the *Gloria*.

At Mass let all the priests and levites be dressed in copes, and let eight lights be lit. Office, “They cried out” (*Exclamaverunt*). “Let us pray,” “O God, who [gave] your apostles” (*Deus qui apostolis tuis*). Epistle, “The just will stand” (*Stabunt justi*). Responsory, “Greatly honored” (*Nimis honorati*). Alleluia, “Come to me, all” (*Venite ad me omnes*). Gospel, “The Lord designated” (*Designavit Dominus*). Offertory, “Into all the earth” (*In omnem terram*). Collect, “You who followed me” (*Vos qui secuti estis me*).

In the refectory let the tables be covered, and let them have an excellent meal. At Vespers let five lamps be lit. Let the antiphons and psalms be said as is customary in the Office of the apostles, namely: “The rod of your power” (*Virgam virtutis*), “Let him place” (*Collocet*), “Going, they went” (*Euntes ibant*), “He was strengthened” (*Confortatus est*), and others similar to these [Col. 1239D].

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. The Vigil of All Saints

[Col. 1240A]

Before the second Hour is performed, let the whole monastery be decorated with hangings. Let benches be extended around the choir, carpets placed on the benches, and the altars decorated. Let Gospel books be placed in the greater church. Let the altar of Saint Mary be adorned with hangings and silks; in the chapterhouse let the benches be arranged. Likewise, let the refectory stewards receive cloths and benches to decorate the building.

If a saint’s feast falls on that day for which three lessons are to be read, let them say the morning Mass for that saint, adding a collect for the dead, and let everyone offer. If the vigil falls on Wednesday or Friday, let a procession be made; if it falls on another weekday, let the signal be sounded [Col. 1240B].

After Sext, let them go and pray, and then say the litany. Let the bells not be rung, and let there be no cope in the choir, but only the deacon dressed in an alb and stole, and the subdeacon likewise in an alb.

Offertory, “Fear the Lord” (*Timete Dominum*). Collect, “O Lord our God” (*Domine Deus noster*). Then the other collects. Epistle, “Behold, I, John, saw in the midst of the throne” (*Ecce ego Joannes vidi in medio throni*). Responsory, “The saints shall rejoice” (*Exsultabunt Sancti*). The Alleluia is not to be sung. Gospel, “Jesus, coming down from the mountain” (*Descendens Jesus de monte*). Let half perform the offering, and likewise the peace. Offertory, “Rejoice” (*Laetamini*). Communion, “Amen, amen, I say to you” (*Amen, amen dico vobis*).

Let no fat be eaten on that day. Let the almoner receive the bread and wine that remain in the refectory.

At Vespers, first let no bell be sounded except the little bell alone. Let twenty-four lights be burning before the high altar, and one behind each of the other altars [Col. 1240C]. Antiphon, “In the council of the just” (*In consilio justorum*), and the other antiphons that follow. Chapter, “Behold, I, John” (*Ecce ego Joannes*). Responsory, “Give praise” (*Laudem dicite*). Hymn, “Christ, redeemer of all the saints” (*Christe, sanctorum redemptor omnium*). Let two brothers dressed in copes carry the incense. Verse, “Rejoice in the Lord” (*Laetamini in Domino*). Antiphon at the *Magnificat*: “Savior of the world, save us” (*Salvator mundi, salva nos*). Alleluia, “O how glorious is the kingdom” (*O quam gloriosum est regnum*). Let them repeat it three times.

Chapter, “After giving birth, the Virgin” (*Post partum virgo*), and the other chapters customarily said concerning all the saints. “Let us pray,” “Almighty and everlasting God” (*Omnipotens sempiterne Deus*). Then let them repeat the antiphon concerning the saints with the *Gloria*. Prayer concerning that blessed saint, and afterwards concerning the holy Cross without the *Gloria*, together with its prayer.

After this, if a psalm has been appointed for the living or the dead, let them say and complete it.

Before the little bell is sounded for the nocturns [Col. 1240D], let all the lamps be lit, and let there be one behind each altar. As soon as the Gradual Canticle has been completed, let them place three candles before the high altar. For the invitatory, four brothers in copes. Hymn, “Jesus, author” (*Jesus auctor*). Let eight lessons be read from the sermon of Pope Saint Boniface, “We read in ecclesiastical histories” (*Legimus in ecclesiasticis historiis*). Let two and two pronounce the responsories.

At each nocturn, let a priest in a cope cense only the high altar, with the brothers in the choir. At the canticle: antiphon, “They rejoice in heaven” (*Gaudent in coelis*). Psalm, “You saints of the Lord” (*Vos sancti Domini*). Verse, “The saints shall rejoice” (*Exsultabunt sancti*). Let nine candles be added before the altar. Let the Gospel be proclaimed: “Jesus, seeing the crowds” (*Videns turbas Jesus*). Homily of Pope Saint Leo, “When our most beloved” (*Praedicante dilectissimi*). Let the twelfth responsory be begun from the beginning after the *Gloria* [Col. 1241A].

At the morning Office: antiphon, “I saw a great crowd” (*Vidi turbam magnam*). Four alleluias. Lesson . . . Responsory, “But the just will live forever” (*Justi autem in perpetuum vivent*). Verse, “and with the Lord” (*et apud Dominum*). Hymn, “Christ, redeemer of all” (*Christe redemptor omnium*). Verse, “Rejoice” (*Laetamini*). Antiphon for the Gospel, “You, glorious one of the Apostles” (*Te gloriosus Apostolorum*); let them repeat it three times. “Let us pray,” “Almighty and everlasting God” (*Omnipotens sempiterne Deus*).

Antiphons concerning the Cross: “We adore you, O Christ” (*Adoramus te, Christe*); “Save us, O Christ” (*Salva nos, Christe*); “We have become servants” (*Servi facti sumus*). Its prayer. After this let them say five psalms for the dead.

Before Prime, let them place golden chalices and the other customary ornaments on the altar.

At the Hours let the candles be lit. Let them say the antiphon from the Gospel mentioned above [supplement: “said above”]. Let them celebrate the morning Mass for Saint Caesarius.

Before Terce let everyone be in albs. As soon as the Hour has been said, let everyone, including the lay brothers, put on copes, and the children tunics. Let them place two pallia on the altar, with an alb over them. Let there be twelve candles before the altar and ten behind it. Let eight brothers arrange the Office, “Let us rejoice” (*Gaudeamus*).

Epistle, “Behold, I, John, saw another angel” (*Ecce ego Joannes vidi alterum angelum*). Let four brothers chant the responsory, “Fear the Lord” (*Timete Dominum*). Six alleluias, “The voice of rejoicing” (*Vox exsultationis*). Gospel, “Jesus, seeing the crowds” (*Videns turbas Jesus*). Offertory, “God is wondrous among his saints” (*Mirabilis Deus in sanctis suis*). Let them take two offertories. Communion, “Rejoice, just ones, in the Lord” (*Gaudete, justi, in Domino*), or “These are holy men” (*Isti sunt viri sancti*).

When Mass has been completed, let all the bells be sounded. In the refectory let them proceed as on the chief feasts, except that the wine is mixed only once.

At Vespers let twelve candles be lit before the altar and ten behind it. Antiphon, “In the council of the just” (*In consilio justorum*) [Col. 1241C]. Alleluia. Responsory, “Rejoice in the Lord” (*Laetamini in Domino*). Hymn, “Christ, redeemer” (*Christe redemptor*). Let them repeat the antiphon three times. “Let us pray,” “Almighty and everlasting God” (*Omnipotens sempiterne Deus*). Let them say the antiphon concerning the saint with the *Gloria*, or the antiphon concerning the Cross without the *Gloria*: “Because of the wood we have become servants” (*Propter lignum servi facti sumus*). Its prayer. Afterwards, psalms for the dead; then let all the bells be sounded.

Let Vespers for the dead be said with antiphons. For on this day of the feast also, after the chapter, let the dean and cellarer provide a meal for all the poor who come, as is customary to do at the Lord’s Supper. Whatever remains that day after the Vespers synaxis from the brothers’ supper, let the almoner receive.

It was established, with the consent and at the request [Col. 1241D] of all the monks of Cluny [Note: [Col. 1241D] Under Saint Odilo, abbot of Cluny], that, just as throughout the churches of God built far and wide across the world the feast of All Saints is celebrated on the day of the Kalends of November, so among us the commemoration of the faithful departed should be celebrated in festive fashion as follows:

On the following day, even if it is Sunday or the feast of some saint for which twelve lessons have been read, as soon as the suffrages of the saints have been completed, let all the bells be sounded, and let them perform the Office and Matins of the dead. Let twelve candles be lit before the altar. When these have been completed [Col. 1242A], let them go to the other choir and say Matins of All Saints, and six psalms for the dead.

At the morning Mass let twelve candles be lit before the altar. Let one child be in the choir with a cope, another in a chasuble to bring forward the epistle, and two others in albs, from whom the responsory is to be sung. Let two brothers, likewise in albs, chant the tract, “Out of the depths” (*De profundis*). Let three lay brothers also be dressed in albs, two of whom are to carry the candlestands and the third the censer. Then let all the bells be sounded.

Let everyone perform the offerings, and let the priest say these prayers: “God of all the faithful” (*Fidelium Deus omnium*), adding, for the anniversary, “Grant, we beseech you, O Lord” (*Praesta quaesumus, Domine*). Finally, let all the priests celebrate private Masses on that day for the repose of all the souls of the faithful, using only the collects for the dead mentioned above [Col. 1242B].

Likewise, let these collects be said at Vespers without Matins, and let abundant meals be prepared for twelve poor people on that day. If this ordinance falls on a weekday, let them perform the vigil of the dead after the nocturnal Office.

And so that this decree may retain perpetual force, we will, request, and command that it be observed both in this place and in all places belonging to it. If anyone takes an example from this faithfully devised observance of ours, let him become a sharer in all good vows [Note: [Col. 1241D] From this it is further evident that the propagation of the commemoration of the faithful departed, instituted by Odilo, was accomplished; we shall speak of him a little below] [Col. 1242D].

## CHAPTER XXXIX. The Kalends of November. “Observe these November practices on the Kalends”

[Col. 1242C]

If the Kalends of November fall on Sunday, the feast of All Saints is celebrated. On the other weekdays, thirty psalms are to be said before the nocturns. Long lessons from the prophecy of Ezekiel are to be read. First, the responsory “I saw the Lord seated” (*Vidi Dominum sedentem*), then Daniel [Note: [Col. 1242D] These matters are taken from the tradition of Hildemar].

At the end of the lesson let them say, “But you, O Lord” (*Tu autem Domine*). When the twelve prophecies are read, let them say, “Thus says the Lord” (*Haec dicit Dominus*). If the prophecy itself ends in the reading, in whichever of their books it may be, let the reader complete it with “But you, O Lord.”

Let them perform the Office of the Dead together with Matins. Then, with the antiphon, let them go to the other choir, where they are to say Matins of All Saints, and the psalms “O God, with our ears” (*Deus auribus nostris*). If they have a deceased person, let them say “My words” (*Verba mea*).

Afterwards let the children go to the dormitory under supervision [Col. 1242D]. Returning from there, as the Rule prescribes, let them learn in the chapterhouse, while seated, the chant as much as necessary. Let the brothers sit in the choir, attentive to psalmody and prayers. If anyone wishes to pray more privately, let him pray outside the choir, and immediately return and sit in the choir.

If the Kalends fall on Monday, Tuesday, or Wednesday, let them begin the responsory from the prophets on the preceding Sunday, and likewise the lessons from the prophet. But let them begin the three long lessons and the intervals only after the Kalends.

If the Kalends fall on Thursday or Friday [Col. 1243A], with an ordinary day occurring after the Kalends, let them complete the psalmody, lessons, and intervals—or everything—as it is customary to retain throughout the winter; and on the following Sunday let them appoint the lessons and responsories according to order.

The church custodian must be carefully instructed to see that he begins Matins in such a way that Matins, Prime, and the litany are completed together with the daylight. If he is deceived by some uncertainty and some darkness remains after the litany, let the brothers act as was stated above concerning the interval: namely, while passing through the hours of the night in this way, no one except the weak and sick is to return to bed.

At first light, let everyone assemble in the cloister for lessons, sitting with the discipline specified earlier [Col. 1243B]. From then on, let the processions that are customarily made on Wednesday and Friday be suspended, as well as the washing of feet customarily performed for the poor until the beginning of the fast. Let them also suspend the two psalms for the dead until Septuagesima.

At Compline let the hymn “Christ, you who are the light” (*Christe qui lux es*) be said without the twelve lessons and the octaves, until Easter.

On the fourth day before the Nones of November, let a full Office be performed for seven days for all our household members, as is customary to do for brothers who have recently died; and let one proper measure be given for thirty days. A full Office must be performed for seven days, and on the first day alone all the bells are to be rung, both for the vigils and for Mass.

Let the collects be said as they are customarily said. On that day alone let twelve poor people be fed [Col. 1243C], and let the almoner receive whatever remains in the refectory. For thirty days, let the following be said at the Hours: “With my voice” (*Voce mea*) and “O God, with our ears” (*Deus auribus nostris*). Let them sing five psalms for them.

## CHAPTER XL. The Vigil of Saint Martin.

They shall adorn the entire monastery as on the Vigil of All Saints. No other fast is observed except the one customary on ordinary days. At Vespers, twelve candles shall be placed before the altar and ten behind it; the Lauds antiphon shall be *Behold the great priest*. The responsory shall be *Lord, if still for your people*. The hymn shall be *King Christ of Martin*. Two priests shall be vested in copes to incense the altars, and two conversi in white garments shall carry [an object not specified in the text] to the brothers. The antiphon at the *Magnificat*, *Martin, [son] of Abraham*, shall be repeated three times by all, with the *Gloria*. When Vespers is finished, each brother ought to find two foot-cloths prepared at his bed by the chamberlain. Before the nocturnal office, before the bells sound, they shall light the crowns. For the invitatory, four shall be vested in copes. The hymn shall be *King Christ*. The lessons shall be read in full from his life. Let the responsories be sung two and two. At the canticle, fifteen candles shall be lit before the altar and nine behind it; the Gospel shall not be announced. After the *Gloria*, they shall begin the twelfth responsory again from the beginning.

At the Matins Lauds, the hymn shall be *A warrior in arms*. At the morning Mass only one collect shall be said. At the principal Mass all the brothers shall be in copes, and twelve candles shall be before the altar. Let eight [brothers] take the Office, four the responsories, and six the alleluias. After Mass all the bells shall sound. At the Hours three candles shall be lit, and after each Hour they shall say this verse, *Martin, equal to the apostles*, through the end of the hymn.

After dinner, when they have left the refectory, the children shall come to their place in the choir. As soon as the priest has said, *And lead us not*, the children who are to read in the refectory shall leave; immediately the custos shall sound the signal, and they shall begin None, while the servers remain behind. They too, after taking their food, shall say None. Afterward they shall not return to drink in the refectory until the feast of Saint Mary. At Vespers twelve candles shall be lit before the altar; they shall say the antiphons that were used at the morning office.

[Col. 1244B] During the Octave of the same illustrious saint, the invitatory shall be *King of confessors*. The hymn shall be *King Christ of Martin*. They shall say an antiphon from the same feast, namely, so that at the nocturnal office the antiphons are sung one to each group of six psalms. The lessons, however, shall be of moderate length and read from the prophets. They shall sing the responsories about the blessed saint. They shall not kneel upon the forms. The familiar psalms shall not be sung; rather, as soon as they have completed the nocturnal office, the Office of the Dead shall be performed, followed by their Matins. Then the signal shall sound, and they shall begin Matins Lauds. On each day they shall say one antiphon in order, as they are inserted in the authentic book, and sing five psalms of the feast after the suffrages of the saints.

[Col. 1244C] When this is completed, they shall come to the other choir and say the Matins of the saints, together with *God, with our ears*. Also five psalms for the dead. When this is finished, the brothers may return to their beds if it is not daytime. At Prime: seven psalms and the Litany. Then a Mass for the dead. From Chapter until Terce they may speak in the cloister. Before Mass they shall say the Litany. At the Hours they shall bring out the antiphons that belonged to Lauds. At Vespers, under one antiphon that is used at the nocturnal office, they shall say the four psalms that occur daily, from the feria.

If a Sunday should fall within the Octave, they shall say the invitatory, antiphons, responsories, and lessons of Saint Martin according to this arrangement, and one … antiphon likewise, and canticles … If the feast should occur within the Octave [Col. 1244D] [that is, during the Octave], so that three lessons are performed, as much is added from the Octave as is taken from the feria at other times.

### The Octave of Saint Martin

For the invitatory, two brothers shall be vested in white garments. The antiphon shall be *We adore Christ the King*. Eight lessons shall be read from his life; at the corresponding time, they shall bring forth the responsories from the proper of the saint: *This is Martin*. At the third nocturn, let them read the homily from the Gospel, *Let your loins be girded*. Let them celebrate Mass solemnly, as we stated above, and sing the sequence on that same day. At Vespers, the antiphon shall be *Martin still*; and three alleluias. The chapter and responsory shall be from a confessor; the hymn and prayer shall be of the blessed saint himself.

## CHAPTER XLI. The Vigil of Saint Andrew

[Col. 1245A]

Let them celebrate the morning Mass of Saint Saturninus. The chant, and everything else, shall be performed as is customary for a single martyr, adding a collect for the dead. When the ninth hour arrives, let them celebrate the Mass of the apostle, as it is contained for his Vigil in the sacramentary books, adding prayers for the living as on other days. No fat shall be eaten on that day. After None they shall proceed to eat and drink well. The almoner shall take whatever remains from the brothers. While the elders are at the meal, the church-keeper shall adorn the presbytery and choir.

At Vespers five candlesticks shall be lit before the altar. The lesson shall be *The blessing of the Lord is upon …* [the text ends incompletely]. The responsory shall be *As soon as he heard the voice of the Lord*. The priest shall put on a cope in order to carry the thurible around the altars. The antiphon shall be *Not triumphantly*. For the invitatory, two brothers shall be surrounded by copes. All the priests must read the eight lessons. Two shall sing the fourth, eighth, and twelfth responsories before the altar.

Let them celebrate the morning Mass of the saint himself, and let all the collects that are customary be brought forth. At the morning Mass all the priests and deacons shall adorn themselves with copes, as shall the conversi who are able to sing. Upon the greater altar they shall place two pallia and a white cloth. Seven candles shall burn before the altar, together with those carried by the conversi, and three behind it. Let them provide six chants. The Epistle shall be the one appropriate to the day. Three shall sing the responsory, four the alleluia, and they shall receive two offertories. When the Mass is completed [Col. 1245C], all the bells shall sound. At the Hours they shall say the versicles that were used for the nocturnal office, and at each Hour three candles shall be lit.

At Vespers they shall take the antiphons that were used for the nocturnal office, *The Lord saw Peter*, and the others. Psalms of the apostles shall be sung; five candles shall be lit before the altar and three behind it. On that day the tables of the refectory shall be covered at the appointed hour.

If the feast of Saint Andrew should fall on a Saturday before Advent, the entire Vespers shall be said of Saint Andrew. Afterward let the office of the Advent of the Lord be brought forth with the *Gloria Patri*: *Behold the name of the Lord*.

During the Octave of the same apostle nothing is performed from it [Col. 1245D], but everything is done as on a feria. On the Octave of Saint Andrew, two shall be in white garments for the invitatory. Eight lessons shall be read from the saint himself: *So great and such is the sublimity of divine Scripture*. Let them sing the responsories in the same order in which they were sung from the authentic book at his feast, and likewise celebrate the Mass as it appears in the sacramentary. At Vespers, the antiphons and psalms shall be as given above.

If this feast of the Octave should fall on a Saturday of Advent, let them perform Vespers of the apostle. They shall say the chapter, responsory, hymn, and prayer from Advent; then they shall repeat the antiphon in honor of the apostle, with the *Gloria*.

## CHAPTER XLII. How the anniversary of the dedication of the basilica is to be observed

[Col. 1246A]

On the dedication of the basilica, before Vespers, all the altars shall be fully adorned, and a single candle shall be fitted to each one. At the greater altar there shall be five in front and three behind, and the Gospel book shall be placed upon the altar itself. The chapter shall be *I saw the holy city*. The responsories shall be two from among the brothers, *It has been founded*. The hymn shall be *Blessed words*. Two priests shall adorn themselves with copes in order to perfume the altars, both at this Hour and at the Matins and Vespers that follow. The collect shall be *O God, who through each …* At the station, the responsory shall be *My house*. Then: *The Lord be with you*. The prayers shall pertain to that day.

[Col. 1246B] Before the nocturnal office there shall be one candle at each altar. When the Canticle of Degrees has been completed, three [candles] shall be added before the greater altar, and individual rear [lights shall be lit] for it. For the invitatory four brothers shall be surrounded by copes: *Holiness befits the house of God*. The hymn shall be *Blessed city*. The lessons and responsories shall be appropriate to that day. The fourth shall be sung by three, the eighth by four, and the twelfth by four. At the canticle, the antiphon shall be *Today to this house*. The canticles from the psalms shall be *I rejoiced*, *Unless the Lord*, and *Praise the Lord, Jerusalem*. Then two lights shall be added to the greater altar in front and likewise behind, and fifteen on the beam.

At Lauds, the boys shall sing the short responsory at the steps. The hymn shall be *The cornerstone foundation*. [Col. 1246C] At the station, the responsory shall be *Holiness befits your house*. Then the prayer of that day. Three candles shall be lit at the Hours.

Let them celebrate the morning Mass in the oratory of Saint Mary. At the greater altar all the priests and deacons must be vested in copes. There shall be five candlesticks before the altar and three behind it. All the children shall be dressed in tunics. The chant shall be *Terrible is this place*. The prayer shall be *O God, who each year …* The Epistle shall be *I saw the holy city*. The responsory shall be *This place was made by God*. The alleluia shall be *I shall adore*. The Gospel shall be *There was a man named …* In the refectory the tables shall be covered.

At Vespers, the antiphon shall be *The Lord will be my portion*. The psalm shall be *The Lord said*. The antiphon shall be *When he awoke*. The psalm shall be *I rejoiced*. The antiphon shall be *Jacob saw*. The psalm shall be *Praise the Lord, Jerusalem*. The hymn shall be *Blessed city*. The prayer shall be *O God, who each year …*

Likewise, when this feast occurs in Septuagesima or Sexagesima, let everything be done as prescribed above. They shall add the following to the Mass: the deacon and subdeacon shall put on chasubles; *Glory to God in the highest* shall not be sung; the responsory shall be *This place was made by God*; the Tract shall be *Those who trust*; and *Go, the Mass is ended* shall not be added. But if it occurs during Lent or at the end of Advent, it shall be celebrated in the same way as those feasts that are celebrated in white vestments.

## CHAPTER XLIII. Observe this annual rite on feast days

The custom for the annual feasts was decreed by the abbot Lord Odilo [Col. 1247A], together with the brothers, to be observed as follows: namely, that the Nativity of our Lord, the feasts of the chief apostles Peter and Paul, and the Assumption of Saint Mary shall be celebrated according to one custom. The entire monastery shall be adorned. The brothers shall pronounce all the responsories two and two. Two thuribles shall be carried for the Vesper and Matins offices, and one for the nocturnal office. Before the nocturnal office all the bells shall be rung twice. The invitatory shall be sung by four brothers. Three cups shall likewise be served to each of the brothers, apart from the daily portion of wine.

Likewise, the day of the Lord’s manifestation, *ύπαπάντι* [Greek: “Meeting,” traditionally the Presentation of the Lord], the Ascension, and the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist shall be celebrated in one manner. All the responsories shall be pronounced by two cantors, and the invitatory by four. For the Vespers and Matins offices, two thuribles shall be carried at the Gospel canticle. Half of the church shall also be adorned with decorations.

Moreover, the feasts of All Saints and of Saint Martin shall be celebrated in every respect like the feast of the apostles Peter and Paul, except that the bells customarily rung twice before the nocturnal office shall here be struck once, and that the brothers shall be given one mixture [of drink] in the refectory.

## CHAPTER XLIV. Odilo, teacher and abbot of our monks

It was also decreed by the aforesaid Father, Lord Odilo, with the consent of all the Cluniac brothers, that just as throughout the churches of God constructed far and wide across the world the feast of All Saints is celebrated on the Kalends of November, so among us the Commemoration of the Faithful Departed shall be celebrated as a feast [Col. 1247C]:

[Note: [Col. 1247D] Sigebert states that Odilo instituted the Commemoration of All the Departed in the year of Christ 998, on the second day of November, in his monastery, and that this institution spread to other churches on his example. Odilo’s decree concerning this matter was published in the *Bibliotheca Cluniacensis* and in volume I of the sixth Benedictine century.]

In this manner: on that day, after Chapter, the dean and cellarer shall provide food for all the poor who come, as is customary at the Lord’s Supper, and whatever remains from the refectory on that day the almoner shall receive. On that same day, after the Vesper assembly, when all the bells have been rung, let them sing Vespers for the dead. Likewise, on the following day, when the bells have again been rung, let the Office for the Dead be performed. A solemn morning Mass shall also be celebrated for the dead. Two brothers shall sing the Tract. All shall make private offerings, and publicly celebrate Masses for the repose of all the souls of the faithful [Col. 1247D]. Twelve poor people shall be fed.

And so that this decree may possess perpetual force, we wish, ask, and command that it be observed both in this place and in all places belonging to this place. If anyone should take an example from this faithful intention of ours [variant: “invention”], let him become a sharer in all the good of the vows.

## CHAPTER XLV. When there is manual labor, follow this procedure

When the brothers are about to go out to manual labor, immediately after Prime, with the customary psalms and the seven psalms omitted, the priest shall begin the reading. When it has been read, just as at Matins, and the Mass has been completed, they shall all leave together after Chapter. When they have arrived at the place where the work is to be done, the prior shall begin the verse, *O God, come to my assistance*. When the others have responded, after the third repetition they shall say, *Our help is in the name of the Lord*, and thereafter those who are to work shall begin.

When they have said the familiar psalms with the canticle in course—as they are accustomed to do when shaving—the reading from the book that is read in the refectory shall be read there, if it is one that concerns building or construction. The brother who read it to the servers during that week must carry the book there, just as to the refectory. The prior, or the person to whom he has assigned it, shall give a sermon on the reading while the brothers rest. Then they shall begin work again and sing the psalmody that the prior indicates through the armarius; only those to whom it is permitted may speak there, and they shall continue until the time for returning arrives.

When they have returned to the cloister, after the verse has been said, they shall immediately speak. In the same manner, when they are about to undertake manual labor after None, they shall proceed.

[Col. 1248C] When they leave after None, they shall first sing the familiar psalms of Vespers, likewise those of All Saints and Vespers of the Dead with the office, together with *God, with our ears*, and they shall perform them before and behind. Afterward: *Our help*. Only then shall they bow. When they have returned from the collation, they shall read a lesson; after a brief sermon has also been given, they shall speak after the verse has been said.

But when they go out to manual labor only once during the day, when they have returned to the cloister they shall read a lesson from the Collations or from the Life of the Fathers; after a sermon has also been given, they shall converse after the verse has been said.

If they go to the bakery, they do not therefore omit the psalmody of Prime. Nor is a reading given to those returning; instead, after the verse has been said and their hands have been washed, they shall prepare themselves for the ecclesiastical work [Col. 1248D].

[Note: [Col. 1248D] This is to be understood of the hosts, or breads, to be offered at Mass, since the monks themselves, with particular diligence, prepared flour and so forth in the bakery for this work, as we have seen in the *Constitutions of Hirsau*, book II.]

[Col. 1247] End of the first book.

# BOOK TWO

[Col. 1249]

## WHAT IS TO BE PROVIDED ON ORDINARY DAYS ACCORDING TO THE RULE OF SAINT BENEDICT

[Col. 1249A]

First, set forth in verse.

Whoever wishes to ascend to the eternal kingdom

Must in mind enter the starry heaven,

Seek through holy religion the path of life,

By which he may swiftly climb to the golden realms.

For monks the life of Benedict, the Father,

Is a life perfected on a level and gentle path;

But harsh and difficult for boys and novices,

Whom a life of milk long nourished in its bosom.

From our fathers, in sacred song, you learn:

This is life for the good, and also the rule of salvation.

It disciplines its children well with maternal love,

Reproves them while teaching, and remains without bitterness.

[Col. 1249B] It weighs, balances, and threatens while exercising moderation;

It reproves, entreats, rebukes, and willingly corrects.

Nor ought he hereafter to suffer anything requiring washing,

And the royal way should lead him through the midst.

The duties of sacred law encourage him.

Then whoever loves to gather the shining fruits of the saints

Will be able to climb the blessed realms of heaven.

Let him be associated with them on every night.

Born of good character and adorned with a chaste body,

Let him live, and he will always be loved by the Lord.

Let him be silent, humble, most gentle, and kind;

Let him be patient, temperate, prudent, and devout.

Of good disposition and teachable, wise and humble in mind,

Let him go forth contrite, peaceful, and very cautious.

Meanwhile contrition of heart causes a spring to rise,

[Col. 1249C] Which may wash away the filth and uncleanness of the soul

By the outpouring of chrism: the flowing of the fountain of tears.

It makes stains equal and wipes them away, as it wipes the black ones;

It wipes them away and makes those cleansed into proper inhabitants

Of paradise, so that he may now possess citizens without end,

Who can continually offer thanks of praise,

Live always with the Lord, and belong to him.

## CHAPTER I. On the arrangement or measurement of the buildings

[Note: [Col. 1249D] This chapter is absent from two manuscripts. It must be understood as concerning the monastery of Farfa, as is found in the *Benedictine Annals*, volume IV, under the year 1009.]

The church: 140 feet in length, 43 in height, with 160 glazed windows. The chapter house: 45 feet in length and 34 in width; four windows toward the east, three toward the north, and twelve balconies toward the west, with two columns attached to each of them. The audience chamber: 30 feet in length. The chamber: 90 feet in length.

The dormitory: 160 feet in length and 34 in width. All the glazed windows in it number 97, and all have, in height, the stature of a man stretching himself as far as he can reach to the tips of his fingers; their width is two and a half feet. The walls are 23 feet high.

The latrine: 70 feet in length and 23 in width. Forty-five seats are arranged in that building, and beside each seat a small window is fitted into the wall, two feet high and half a foot wide. Above the seats that have been set out there is a stack of wood; above that wooden structure are 17 windows, three feet high and one and a half feet wide.

The warming house: 25 feet wide and the same in length. From the church door to the entrance of the warming house: 75 feet.

The refectory: 90 feet in length, 25 in width, and with walls 23 feet high. The glazed windows in it, eight on each side, are all five feet high and three feet wide.

The regular kitchen: 30 feet long and 25 feet wide. The kitchen of the lay brothers has the same measurements. The cellar: 70 feet long and 60 feet wide.

The alms-cellar is ten feet wide and 60 feet long, corresponding to the width of the cellar. The Galilee [Note: [Col. 1249D] That is, porticoes. In Italian, *galleria*. Mabillon interprets it as the nave of the church.] is 65 feet long, with two towers of the Galilee standing at its front. Beneath them is a courtyard where the lay people stand, so that they do not obstruct the procession.

From the southern gate to the northern gate: 280 feet. The sacristy: 58 feet long, together with the tower situated at its head. The oratory of Saint Mary: 45 feet long, 20 feet wide, with walls 23 feet high.

The first infirmary is 27 feet wide and 25 feet long, with eight beds and an equal number of small rooms in the portico outside, beside the wall of that cell; the cloister of the aforesaid cell is twelve feet wide. The second cell is fitted out in every respect in the same way. The third likewise. The fourth likewise.

The fifth shall be smaller, where the sick may gather to wash their feet on Saturdays, or those brothers who have undressed [Note: [Col. 1250D] This should be read, not *exusti* (“burned”), as another codex has it. See the *Benedictine Annals*, volume II, p. 570, where you will find a drawing of the ancient building of the monastery of Saint Gall.] to change their clothing. The sixth cell shall be prepared where the servants attending them may wash bowls and all utensils.

Beside the Galilee there ought to be constructed a palace 155 feet long and 30 feet wide, to receive all visitors who arrive at the monastery with horses. On one side of this house there are prepared 40 beds and an equal number of woolen blankets, where only men may rest, with 40 latrines. On the other side [Col. 1251A] there are arranged 30 small beds where countesses or other respectable women may rest, with 30 latrines where they alone may attend to their needs. In the middle of the palace let tables be fixed, like the refectory tables, where both men and women may eat.

On great feasts let this house be adorned with curtains, hangings, and bench-coverings [variant: *bancalia*] on their seats. At its front there shall be another house, 45 feet long and 30 feet wide. Its length shall extend as far as the sacristy, and there all the tailors and shoemakers shall sit, sewing what the chamberlain orders them to sew. A table 30 feet long shall be prepared there, and another table shall be attached to it; the width of both tables together shall be seven feet.

Between this dwelling and the sacristy, the church, and the Galilee there shall be a cemetery where the lay people are to be buried.

From the southern gate to the northern gate, toward the west, there shall be constructed a house 280 feet long and 25 feet wide. There shall be built in it horse stalls divided into small compartments, and above them a loft where the servants may eat and sleep. Tables shall be arranged there, 80 feet long and four feet wide. All visitors who cannot be fed in the dwelling mentioned above shall be fed in this one.

At the head of this dwelling there shall be a suitable place where all those people who arrive without horses may gather and receive from the almoner brother charity in food and drink, insofar as is appropriate there.

Outside the brothers’ refectory, which is sixty feet long, at the head of the latrine there shall be twelve crypts [text: *crytae*, perhaps *criptae*], and an equal number of vats prepared, where baths may be prepared for the brothers at the appointed times.

After this arrangement, the novices’ cells shall be constructed. It shall be divided into four corners: the first for meditation, the second for eating, the third for sleeping, and the fourth, at the side, for the latrine. Beside it another cell shall be arranged, where goldsmiths, engravers, or glassworkers may gather to practice their art.

Between the crypts and the cells of the novices and goldsmiths they shall have a house 125 feet long and 25 feet wide, whose length shall reach as far as the bakery. The bakery itself, in length together with the tower constructed at its head, is 70 feet, and 20 feet wide.

## CHAPTER II. How novices are to be treated

As soon as they have left the novices’ cell, or previously been in the cloister, they are not to be brought into Chapter except when the abbot commands it. As soon as he has finished his sermon in Chapter, they shall come and inquire into the will of each one. Nevertheless, before this, they must have all their offenses disclosed.

Then, with their caps removed from their tunics, they shall sit in the church until they have reached the consecration. For example, if the brothers eat at the sixth hour, as soon as Terce has been said, let him do so. But if they eat at None, as soon as the litanies have been said, let the novices come before the altar and stand in order [Col. 1252A] as they arrived, and let each one read his profession. If he does not know how, another shall be substituted to do it in his place. The novice himself, however, shall make the sign and place it upon the altar. Thereafter he shall not have permission to remove it.

From then on let them say this verse alternately: *Receive me, Lord*, and always kneel. Adding the *Gloria Patri*, on the third repetition they shall turn themselves around upon their knees, and then all shall prostrate themselves in order.

Then the abbot shall have a stole and stand at the right side of the altar, and say: *Kyrie eleison*, and so forth; *Our Father*; *And lead us not*; and the psalm *Have mercy on me, O God*. This is to be said by all to the end. Then the chapters and prayers shall be said as they are found in the book.

As soon as these have been completed, the novices shall rise, and the abbot shall bless the cucullae [monastic cowls] and sprinkle blessed water upon them. From there he shall come to them and begin to say this verse: *May the Lord strip you of the old man*. Then they shall be clothed in the cuculla, and he shall say: *May the Lord clothe you*. The abbot shall kiss them, and all the brothers in order. They shall remain veiled until the third day.

At the offertory all, still veiled, shall proceed, receive the kiss of peace, and go to communion. They shall stand last in the choir and in the refectory. At Chapter, as soon as something from our custom has been said—*Remember*—the brother who is responsible for them shall seize them, lead them outside Chapter, and place them in the church. He shall do this until the third day, on which the abbot shall celebrate Mass; after the peace, he shall remove the veil with the assistants and give them communion.

[Col. 1252C] Afterward, in Chapter and in all places, they shall be associated with the brothers. During their first year the novices shall not speak with anyone without their guardian, nor with those brothers who are cloistered, except with someone to whom permission has been given. The guardian himself shall sit between the novice and the person who wishes to speak with him. In Chapter he shall not presume to speak unless questioned about some matter, until a year—or five years—has passed.

## CHAPTER III. On appointing an abbot

First, he is elected by the entire congregation in the presence of the bishop of that diocese and of the senior to whom the abbey belongs, without any gift or acceptance of a person [variant: “partiality toward a person”], because cursed is the one who gives and cursed is the one who receives.

Then, after the bishop has received from him the donation and the election has been confirmed by all, the bishop begins the antiphon *Confirm this, O God*, and so forth. The entire choir of singers follows him, singing aloud the psalm *Let God arise*. Thus, with such triumph, the bishop holding the man to be ordained by the hand leads him into the sacristy, while the others remain in the choir and continue singing.

When *Let God arise* has been sung, the prayer is said: *Let us pray: Direct our actions*. Then the bishop and the elected man vest themselves, and both come before the altar. The election is read again from the ambo, so that it may be heard and confirmed by the monks, the clergy, and all persons of both sexes.

Then, with carpets spread before the altar [Col. 1253A], the bishop and the man who is to be blessed as abbot prostrate themselves together. Those standing in the choir begin the seven penitential psalms, adding a short Litany, not a lengthy one. When these have been completed, after they have said the final *Kyrie eleison* and completed the Lord’s Prayer, only the bishop rises, while the man who is to be blessed remains prostrate, and he says:

*And lead us not into temptation.*

*Chapter: Save your servant.*

*Send him.*

Here he shall receive the blessing.

*Lord, hear.*

*The Lord be with you.*

Then the blessing follows:

*Grant, we beseech you, almighty God, that your servant …*

*God, author of all things …*

*Almighty and eternal God, [grant] an abundant spirit …*

*May he receive today, by your generosity, O Lord …*

*O God, to whom belongs all power and dignity …*

*O God, source of all good things and of the righteous …*

[Col. 1253B] When this solemnity has been completed, the bishop, or one of the abbots who are present, begins in a loud voice: *We praise you, O God*. They establish him in the station or place assigned to the abbot in the choir.

When they have reached the second verse, where it says, *You, the eternal Father, the whole earth venerates*, all the brothers of the congregation begin to kiss him in order, reverently asking his forgiveness.

In this ordination the bishop and abbot must be vested in white garments, stoles, and copes. The bishop shall hold his staff in his hand; the same staff that he is to give to the abbot shall lie beside the abbot on the carpet while he lies prostrate to be consecrated.

Once consecrated, he shall receive it from the bishop’s hand, the bishop saying:

*Receive the staff of pastoral office, so that you may be fierce in correcting vices; and when you have become angry, you shall remember mercy.*

## CHAPTER IV. On the measurements of the garments

Saint Benedict entrusted the garments of the brothers to the abbot’s prudence, so that they might be measured. What that measurement should be, according to the definition of the Fathers, we investigate as far as we can.

The cuculla, which is especially proper to our order and was anciently called a *colobium*, that is, a tunic without sleeves, ought to have enough width to fit both elbows suitably. Its length in front should reach as far as the ankle of the foot, and it should fit the body so that it is round on every side.

The hood, apart from its complete border [Col. 1253D], must contain on every side the square measure of a man’s foot. The upper opening shall measure one cubit up to the top of the thumb; the lower opening, one full cubit and three fingers. In front, the width of the cuculla with its hood shall be visible.

Likewise, beneath, around the feet, the tunic must be measured in a rounded form [Note: [Col. 1253D] In clothing, *sagitta* denotes the part drawn together into folds, because it forms the shape of an arrow. Udalricus, book II of the *Cluniac Customs*, chapter 11.]. It shall have arrows or gores [Note: [Col. 1253D] *Girones* means the same as *sagitta* in the same Udalricus. The word seems to derive from the Germanic *Geron* or *Giron*, German *Geren*, “fold.”] in such measure that they do not hinder the wearer as he walks, either by excess or by insufficiency. Its sleeves must extend on both sides as far as the second joints of the fingers.

[Col. 1254A] The *staminia* [Note: [Col. 1254D] *Staminia*, *stamineum*: a woolen undergarment or shirt, commonly *étamine*.] must have such a measurement that, when girded, it can reach the ankle of the foot. Likewise, as with the cuculla, its lower opening shall end at one cubit.

Its hood shall have a full foot, and the wider part of the sleeve likewise. Toward the hand, where it normally narrows, it shall extend from the base of the thumb to the end of the index finger. The strap by which the *staminia* is girded, when fully extended, shall be one thumb-width.

A knife, between the blade and the handle, shall have a length of half a foot, with a width of three fingers added.

The breeches that Saint Benedict allowed for those traveling—because nowadays it is uncertain who is sent outside or at what time, they are allowed to all—shall be measured in such a way [Col. 1254B] that they fit the body suitably in length. In width, each side, as is customary, being doubled, shall have one cubit up to the thumb once sewn.

The leggings shall have a full foot sewn onto their upper part. They shall also be made long enough that, according to the man’s stature—as must be provided for with all garments—they fit the legs suitably. From the top down to the foot they shall be tightened in such a way that, while above they have a full foot, below they have half a foot.

The strap [Note: [Col. 1254D] *Cesta*, *cestus*: a belt.] of the leggings, once sewn, ought to be long enough to be tightened within the fist.

The shoes, in height, apart from the border that is sewn on, shall have half a foot; in the front, their width shall reach the joints of the fingers. The foot-cloths shall likewise be measured so that they may fit the feet sufficiently.

## CHAPTER V. On the prior of the monastery

When a prior has been elected by all the brothers, after Chapter they shall all rise and go to the church. Then the man who is leaving the office [of prior] shall say three times, with everyone repeating, this verse before the altar: *Blessed is the Lord God*. Having received the blessing that is said when someone is released from an office, he shall depart.

Then the man who is about to enter office shall approach and say three times, with all listening, this verse: *O God, come to my assistance*. Having received the blessing that is said when brothers are appointed to an office, he shall administer that office.

In accordance with custom, he shall stand in the church on the left side of the choir; in Chapter on the southern side; and in the refectory on the northern side.

## CHAPTER VI. How brothers sent on a journey are to be treated

If a brother is going abroad on a journey and will not return for two or three days, he shall receive a blessing. If necessity requires him to return on the following day, and he must go out again, he shall not receive the blessing for going and returning.

Likewise, if a brother returns from a journey, he shall receive a blessing. If he must leave again immediately, he shall receive the blessing for departing. If afterward he remains for one or two Hours, he shall receive the blessing for returning.

Likewise, if a brother comes from a journey, he shall receive the blessing for returning. If he immediately goes somewhere else and sleeps one night, on the following day he shall not receive the blessing for returning.

On a journey, if two conversi and one priest are traveling, and the priest is the younger of them, wherever they sit the priest must sit between them. But when one of them travels with the priest, the priest must always sit above him [possibly “in the superior place”]. It is not fitting for him even to speak without the priest’s permission.

When returning, if they have been on the road for three Hours, at Compline *May he have mercy on you* shall be said over them. It shall never be said to the lord abbot.

## CHAPTER VII. Likewise, how the same brothers, when assigned to journeys, are to perform the Hours
Brothers sent out on a journey, when they see that it is time for an Hour, if there is a suitable place where they are standing or walking, should kneel, dismounting from their horses. If they kneel on benches in the monasteries, they should do the same wherever they are staying. When it is completed, they should impress the sign of the holy cross on their foreheads, and should not turn around, but only ask pardon; then they should begin the Hour, mounting their horses, proceeding and chanting the Hour. They should remove their gloves (*wantos*) from their hands until they have finished the divine office. [Note: [Col. 1255D] *Wantos*, *quantos*, Italian *quanti*: “gloves.”] If some necessity arises requiring them to say something during the sequence of psalms of that Hour, [Col. 1255C] they should begin again from the beginning. When returning, each may put his gloves back on his own bed. In the basilica, when they have returned, they should make the prescribed order, prostrate; even if it is the Twelve Lessons.

## CHAPTER VIII. On manual labor

When the brothers are going to manual labor, as soon as Prime has ended, they should begin the litany. After the Chapter, immediately when they have risen and the board has sounded, they should begin at once. First, the familiar psalms from Prime, and all should go together singing, so that no one—including the cellarer—is excused, as far as the place of work.

When they have arrived there, the boys should stand in ordered ranks in front, and bow forward and backward. Then the prior should begin: “O God, come to my assistance” (*Deus, in adjutorium meum intende*); thirdly [Col. 1255D], “Glory be to the Father” (*Gloria Patri*). Then: “Lord, have mercy” (*Kyrie eleison*); “Our Father” (*Pater noster*); “And lead us not” (*Et ne nos*); “Our help” (*Adjutorium nostrum*). Then they should begin their work, and resume the psalms where they had left them, together with the seven special psalms and five for the dead. Afterward, the canonical course with the familiar psalms of the Hours.

The weekly server of the Mass should say the collects. If they go twice, a reading from the book read at dinner should be given there, if it is of such a kind as to edify the hearers. The brother who reads for the server must carry the book, and the prior, or someone whom he orders, should explain it while all sit in silence. Again, if it seems good to the prior that they should work longer, let them do so.

When the work has been dismissed, on the return they should go [Col. 1256A] singing psalms as far as the cloister: “Blessed is the man” (*Beatus vir*), or whatever the abbot has begun. When they are before the Chapter, the prior should say: “Our help” (*Adjutorium nostrum*), “Bless” (*Benedicite*); and each should go to his own duties. From this Hour onward, the secretary should sound the small bell.

## CHAPTER IX. Also, if they are to return after None

After None, if they are to return again, as soon as they have come out of the refectory they should make absolution in Chapter, as on other days. After “Bless” (*Benedicite*) has been said, they should bow forward and backward, and immediately the prior should begin the familiar evening psalms: “Lord, hear my prayer; listen with your ears” (*Domine, exaudi orationem meam, auribus percipe*), first of all, and so forth.

Then follow Vespers of All Saints, Vespers of the Dead and their office, and “O God, with our ears” (*Deus, auribus*), together with five psalms for the dead. Thus they should return singing the psalm “To the Lord, when I was troubled” (*Ad Dominum cum tribularer*).

In the cloister, the boys who go ahead to the entrance of the Chapter should sing until everyone has assembled. Then, when they are seated there, a boy should ask for a blessing and read a lesson from the book read at Collation; at the prior’s command he should finish it, and then give a sermon. Afterward everyone should rise and make a reverence. The prior himself should say this verse: “Blessed are you, Lord, my God” (*Benedictus es, Domine Deus meus*). They should do this whenever they go twice.

## CHAPTER X. Also, when they go to work only once

When they go to work only once, they should do everything throughout the days as in the morning, except that the reading is given in the cloister and the verse is said: “Blessed are you.” The familiar psalms should be said at the morning praises. Matins of All Saints or of the Dead should not be said except in church.

## CHAPTER XI. Also, when they go to the bakehouse

When they go to the bakehouse, they should not omit the psalms of Prime. After Chapter they should wash their hands and begin the five psalms for the dead and those of the canonical Hours, namely, “O God, in your name” (*Deus, in nomine tuo*).

On returning, they should not read a lesson; only the verse “Blessed are you, Lord God” (*Benedictus es, Domine Deus*) should be said. Before Chapter, the children should stand with their masters, and the older brothers in the cloister beside the church.

## CHAPTER XII. On the prior of the monastery, or the deans, or those who carry out their duties in their absence, and on how they should carry the covered lamp at the appointed times

[Col. 1256D]

After Compline, the cloister prior or dean, taking the covered lamp, should go around the cloister in the following order: first the calefactory; afterward the refectory; then the kitchen. He should see whether everything has been properly done there. From there he should go to the cellar and see whether everything is in order. Next, on the side of the almonry, he should inspect all the doors to see whether they have been properly secured. Afterward, coming to the infirmary, he should see whether everything is being properly conducted.

If he finds anything neglected in the cloister, he should reserve it for the next day and bring it to Chapter. [Col. 1257A] At night, after the three prayers, the brother who is responsible for the sick should go and see that none of them, overcome by sleep, remains in his bed. The dean mentioned above, or another brother to whom the care named above has been assigned, should go to the dormitory, lest any brother have remained negligently in his bed, held fast by deep sleep. He should extinguish two lamps; he should leave the third, which is in the dormitory and is necessary, burning continuously until morning.

He should return to the church and go around the crypts and each section, seeing whether anyone is lying or sitting there apart from the sick or those undergoing phlebotomy. If he finds anyone of this kind asleep, he should wake him. If he does not accept this with thanksgiving, the matter should be complained of in Chapter. He should do the same at the second nocturn and at Lauds. [Col. 1257B]

At the times when an interval occurs, he should go around the dormitory, cloister, and everything else, as we have prescribed above. At the Twelve Lessons, a convert should carry the lantern during the third lesson, inspecting everyone. On ordinary days, he should look around at every lesson.

Anyone who does not wish to bow toward him should place the lantern before him. He should do the same if anyone is found dozing. As soon as the man has been awakened, he should take the lantern and go, bow in the middle of the choir toward the altar, then come to the choir of the Lord Abbot and humble himself again before him. He should go around everyone and return by the other side, inspecting the same things. Afterward he should go around those who are outside; when he has examined each one, he should place the lantern in its appointed place.

If it has been given to a young brother, he should go around only the choir and restore it at the steps. Never give it to the children.

## CHAPTER XIII. On those who arrive late at the oratory

If a brother comes after the Glory of the first psalm, he should go before the altar to the steps and kneel there. He should immediately rise and remain standing until the prior has absolved him. After being absolved, he should turn forward and backward, come into the choir to his place, and ask pardon again. When he rises, all the brothers should bow.

If he has remained outside because of some slight illness and has not arrived by the Glory of the first psalm, he should enter the choir as stated above. After being absolved, however, he should go outside and ask pardon on his knees, doing what his illness permits.

Likewise, if a brother comes to the Hour after the Glory of the first psalm, or arrives at any later time, up to the *Kyrie eleison*, he should enter in this manner so that he does not lose the whole Hour, and should go to the appointed place until he is absolved. If he remains for the entire Hour, and the brothers kneel on the benches, he should do so on the steps. When the Hour is completed, he should leave without an order.

## CHAPTER XIV. How one under a light penance should be bound by the order imposed

Brothers who, because of a light fault, are separated from the table according to the Rule should make satisfaction in the oratory as follows. When, after the psalmody, the others bow or kneel for the prayers, they should come before the altar and prostrate themselves at the steps until the prayers and the oration are finished. Then, rising and bowing forward and backward, they should do this at all the Hours.

If a feast occurs before they have been absolved, from Vespers until the following Vespers they should join the brothers in all communion; those who are priests may also celebrate Mass and perform everything belonging to divine service.

No prior should impose such a judgment on a brother while the Lord Abbot is in the monastery. If the abbot arrives afterward, the prior may meanwhile absolve them himself, before the matter comes to the Lord Abbot’s knowledge. But if he does not do so, and the brother has asked pardon once in the abbot’s presence, the prior can no longer absolve them.

A child who has stood before the abbot should not be placed under the judgment of fasting by his master or anyone else while the abbot himself is inside. [Col. 1258B]

Whenever the master has sent boys to judgment, the prior may absolve them without the master’s permission. No one else may prescribe anything to them—not a sign or any other action. Nevertheless, the person who holds the order, if it seems to him that they should be absolved, should make a sign to the master so that they may be absolved.

If the Lord Abbot sends a brother to judgment and goes somewhere, forgetting to absolve him, the prior cannot absolve him. [Note: [Col. 1257] The material that follows, enclosed between brackets, has been taken from the Farfa manuscript.]

[If the prior has sent someone to judgment, the dean cannot absolve him except by the prior’s permission. If a young brother is sent to judgment for a light fault, and goes everywhere under supervision, when the brothers are eating he should be in the kitchen. The older brothers, however, should remain in the church [Col. 1258C] or in the oratory of Saint Mary.

If a brother has been sent into the lesser penance for several days, and the Twelve Lessons occur during those days, he shall be absolved at the vigil when the small bell sounds for Vespers. After Vespers, if it is mealtime and the brothers have gone, he too should go with them and eat and drink whatever is served to them, even if drink or some food has been forbidden him.

On a feast day he should celebrate Mass and do everything as the others do. If he is the kitchen worker, he should perform that duty. He may help sing the Mass, but he shall not receive the kiss of peace. If he has been assigned to carry the candlestick, he should carry it. If he has been assigned to the responsory, he should not impose it himself but appoint another who will perform that office. When the feast is over, he should return to his penance.]

## CHAPTER XV. But a grave fault requires this entire monastic procedure

[Col. 1258D]

When a brother commits a grave fault, he should not come into the presence of the Lord Abbot until he has been summoned to him. If the abbot himself arrives without the brother’s knowledge, the brother should ask pardon before him until the abbot has driven him away. He should then wait until the Lord Abbot sends him to penance.

Then, barefoot and naked, he should come into the assembly. After receiving the judgment, he should go to the customary place—namely, the auditorium—put on his shoes and clothes, and return to Chapter. He should ask pardon before the Lord Abbot. At the abbot’s command, he should enter into penance. Immediately after leaving Chapter, he should cover his head, and, as the Rule prescribes (chapter 25 and following), no brother should join him without the Lord Abbot’s permission.

As long as he is in penance, he should not come to Chapter except twice: when entering and when leaving. Whenever the signal is struck for an Hour, after all the brothers have come into the church, he should come to the church door with his head covered and stand upright there until, when the *Kyrie eleison* is said in the choir at the prayers, the brothers bow. Then he should uncover his head and lie prostrate facing the door, or at the feet of all the brothers, until the whole assembly of brothers has gone out.

Then, with his head covered again, he should go to a solitary place and do this until he is summoned into the assembly for reconciliation.

When he is to leave that penance, he should again come into Chapter naked and barefoot, as he came previously. After receiving the judgment, he should rise, put on his cuculla and tunic, and prostrate himself at the abbot’s feet. At the abbot’s command, he should go outside to the auditorium, put on his shoes and clothes, and return to Chapter. He should ask pardon before the abbot, and at the abbot’s command go and sit in the last place. From then on he should do everything as written in the Rule (in the same place).]

## CHAPTER XVI. On various determinations and regulations that must be observed by those living in monasteries

If, in summer, after None or after the evening bell, the brothers wish to drink wormwood mixed with honey, after “Our Father” has been said, the prior should sound the cymbal and they should go. Everything should be done as is customary at the charitable drink (*charitas*) of Collation, except for the reading. Whenever this kind of charitable drink is held, no other such drink is to be held that night. The cymbal shall never be sounded twice in one day for the charitable drink.

If something made from new crops is set on the table for blessing, one verse from the reading should first be recited, and then the blessing should be said.

If a brother is engaged in general writing with the Lord Abbot’s permission, at the abbot’s command he may omit the familiar psalms, the morning and principal Mass. These three, however, may not be omitted: the litany, the offertory, and the vigil of the dead.

A brother wearing leg-bindings—*fasciolatus* [Note: *Fasciolatus*: this is to be understood of bindings around the legs, so that a brother does not enter the monastery with his feet wrapped in bandages. The same is prescribed in the Cluniac Customs, chapter 62: “After removing his spurs and bindings at the monastery entrance, let him ask pardon.” Hoeften confuses this kind of binding with *pedules*, as the distinguished V. C. du Cange observes, *Glossarium mediae et infimae Latinitatis*.]—shall in no way enter the cloister.

Boys who are unable to carry the charitable drink—that is, flasks—to the table [Col. 1259D] should not wipe their hands on the towel (*zalla*) [Note: *Zalla*, perhaps from Old Germanic *zwalla*, German *zwelen*, “towel.”] in Chapter on Saturdays.

A boy may shave his master if he is able. If the master is present, he should not send into judgment a boy who has eaten before the abbot.

The boys should have books in the school, razors with bowls, and pots for washing their heads. What more? [Col. 1260A] They should also have there, on their own, everything necessary for them. When it is time to speak, they may speak there; outside the school they should never speak.

On days when the brothers speak in the cloister, after Sext has ended they should nowhere speak until the boys leave, and one of them—the younger—should say “Bless” (*Benedicite*) in a loud voice. Those who sit in Chapter during the time of speaking should not say anything inside.

No brother should wash another’s head; each should wash his own. The boys should do the same in their school. On Wednesday and Saturday they may have themselves tonsured in the school. At the mixed drink, in their place at the board, they should bow forward and backward; they should do the same after the mixed drink.

[Col. 1260B] If the brothers shave on Wednesday or Friday, they do not for that reason omit the customary procession, nor do they omit it when they go out to receive or bury a body.

If someone from outside is buried where the brothers proceed, the fast-day observance should not be suspended for that procession.

At the Twelve Lessons, the priest who carries the censer around the altars should carry it first to the Lord Abbot. If the abbot is absent, he should carry it to the prior; if the prior is absent, he should hand it to the convert. The convert should give it first to the priest, then to the right choir and the left. Next he should cense the young brothers standing at the benches on the right, then the boys among them, and then the others on the left, young brothers and boys.

On ordinary days, at the principal Mass, if the Lord Abbot is present, the offertory should first be brought to him for the offering. If he is absent, it should be brought to the prior. If the prior is absent, it should be given to the cloister dean.

On feast days, a boy should carry the Gospel book through the choir to all the brothers. When it has been brought, a prepared convert dressed in an alb should receive it and carry it to all the brothers standing outside.

A brother leaving the infirmary, after making satisfaction in Chapter, may sing Mass that same day if he wishes, because while he was in the infirmary cell we do not permit him to sing Mass there.

While the brothers are in Chapter, the novices should be in the kitchen. From Pentecost until Advent, if the Twelve Lessons occur on a Saturday and the history is to be changed on the following day, the entire Vespers of the saint should be said on Saturday.

[Col. 1260D] A brother singing his responsory should bow to the others when he has finished the verse. The brothers arranged farther away should bow forward and backward. The boys, however, should bow individually in their seats.

When they themselves are about to say the responsory, they should always turn after the verse has been said. When going from the reading and returning, the boys should always bow, as should all the brothers, especially those who sit on the benches. At the Lord Abbot, everyone should rise from his seats while going and returning.

When the abbot reads the Gospel at the morning praises, the sacristan, according to custom, should go and prepare the Gospel, the prayer, and the signals for him. When the abbot begins the *Te Deum*, if the weekly server has read it, the sacristan should not go according to custom. But on the preceding day that brother should listen with the sacristan to whatever is needed.

If two brothers are vested to carry censers around the altars, the one who is the weekly server should go in front.

Brothers leaving the kitchen should, during the following week, wash the font where the brothers clean their hands and faces. When the brothers cut their hair or shave, they should heat the water and carry it.

[Col. 1261B] When the sacristan listens to the boys’ readings or responsories, all of them should always stand upright before him until they finish, from the youngest to the oldest.

[[Note: [Col. 1261D] This material has been supplied from the Farfa manuscript.] When the brothers go to the stations at the altars, they should say the prayer plainly and not loudly, unless perhaps a feast of a saint whose altar is there happens to occur. As they proceed there, they should say the verse of the saint and “The Lord be with you. Let us pray” (*Dominus vobiscum. Oremus*) in a loud tone.]

The brother who is to read at table, while the brothers say the verse before the meal and pray, should stand upright in his own place or in a higher one.

The brothers who are in the infirmary should, whenever the brothers shave, do so one day beforehand, unless they are going out with the others. No one should drink in the refectory while sitting on the footstools beneath the seats [Note: *Suppedaneum*, a footstool. See Du Cange.] or on the boys’ stools, but they should sit at the table where they dine. No one should eat or drink without a table, except those who are in the infirmary.
