No one should eat before Terce unless the first signal has sounded.

Tablecloths in the refectory should be changed every fifteen days. Hand towels should be put out every Sunday at daybreak, before the boys rise.

A brother who has been somewhere else, when coming to Chapter, should not enter until the boy has read the martyrology with the saints. While the child is saying, “And many other saints” (*Et aliorum plurimorum sanctorum*), he may go in. He may enter for the Gospel reading or when a short reading is being given.

If anyone wishes to use a hot drink at the charitable drink of Collation, he may do so in his place; the boys may do so as well, including when they shave on Friday.

[Col. 1261D] Bowls containing food should not be placed on the tablecloths unless the boards have been covered. When someone announces the prayers of the faithful on behalf of the Lord Abbot, the others should descend from their footstools and ask pardon. The announcer himself should neither descend nor ask pardon, but should say them supplicantly.

As a matter of ordinary practice no one descends from the footstools for any announcement, except when the Nativity of Our Lord Jesus Christ is announced and at the Annunciation of the Lord, when they should ask pardon on their knees. At the Twelve Lessons, if anyone wishes to sing the Mass after Chapter, he need not ask permission.

On Sundays Saint Benedict commands (Rule, chapter 48) that everyone should read; this should not be neglected but done eagerly. Nevertheless, for the sake of the work of God, if anyone has a responsory or Alleluia for Mass, he should sing it before Prime, quietly enough not to disturb the others. The others should read at the Hours. They should do the same on the greatest feasts, provided the sacristan has directed the inexperienced brother to do so.

On Sunday the brothers should see that everyone is present for the procession. The same should be done on Wednesday or Friday, so that both the abbot and everyone else are barefoot, except those who cannot fulfill this because of illness—and then only with permission.

Boys who were not present for the verse said before the meal, when they arrive should go to their places and bow forward and backward there. The master should come forward and make a sign that the prior should order him to eat. After receiving permission, he should say the verse and go.

If a boy is overcome by sleep during the work of God, he should not be beaten for this one Hour [alternative manuscript: “for this at every Hour”]. But when the master sees that he is often overcome by sleep, he should place some little book in his arms for him to hold until he rouses him from that sluggishness.

If anyone wishes to wash or sharpen his own *justitia*, cup, or knife during the time when there is speaking in the cloister, he should do so. If he does it between Sext and the meal, or between None and supper, whoever sees it may bring a complaint the next day. [Note: [Col. 1261D] The words enclosed in parentheses were written by a much later hand; they are not found in the other manuscripts.] [“But he will say: What is that to me?”]

[Col. 1262C] The Lord’s Body must in no way be carried anywhere without light and incense.

In summer, a boy who recites the short reading from memory at Nocturns, after “But you, Lord” (*Tu autem, Domine*), should bow forward and backward. Another who is beside him should say the responsory.

Young brothers who leave the school after removing their albs should not presume to read or sing unless commanded by the abbot.

A brother may change his clothes while wearing his cuculla, or another garment worn over the cuculla; likewise, he may change them while wearing the cuculla and a fur garment (*pellicula*) [Note: *Pellicula* is the same as *pellitia* or *pellicea*, a garment made from skins.] He should not do this while wearing only the cuculla.

When a young brother reads at table, after finishing the reading he should go to the cellar and remain there in silence. If he is one of the older brothers, he may be in the kitchen or, if he wishes, in the storeroom.

After finishing his reading and making a reverence, a boy should remain before the table, at the step, until the others rise, and go with them into the church. When the prayer is finished, he should go with the other boys and the master to eat.

The weekly kitchen server may serve wearing a sleeveless fur garment, or one with sleeves if he wears an arm covering over it [Note: *Bracile* here means the same as *brachiale*, an ornament or covering for the arms.].

When the boys leave Chapter, if the brothers are speaking in the cloister, the younger one should say loudly: “Bless” (*Benedicite*). They should do the same after None in summer, and likewise at those times when the mixed drink is taken after Terce, if the brothers are speaking in the cloister.

Finally, they should first leave for Chapter after None or Collation.

At the Twelve Lessons, when the people do not celebrate, the brothers may bring clothes and footwear into the cloister on Saturday to repair them; but on that same day they should remove them before Vespers. On ordinary days they should do the same.

On the feasts mentioned above, the scribes may write, even if the feast has been celebrated in copes. On the greatest feasts and on Sundays, however, they should not write, nor should the brothers put out clothes.

After Compline no one should read in his bed, nor should anyone presume to leave the dormitory for the cloister. The same applies at midday, before the small bell sounds. During the midday interval, however, any of the older brothers who wishes may read. The younger brothers and boys should never presume to do so.

At these times, anyone who wishes to cover himself with his fur garment or cuculla may do so, but he should take care not to lie down with his shoes on. The young brothers and boys should make themselves fully ready, just as at night.

The young brothers should not leave the dormitory before the boys rise. After the boys have left, they too should go under their supervision. Without supervision they should not presume to go anywhere, even into the church when they wish to receive the Eucharist.

In the cloister each should sit beside his supervisor. In the dormitory they should have their beds beside or before the master.

When the young brother himself is the weekly server, he may leave the dormitory with his master before the boys and begin his obedience after the three prayers. But if he is with the other brothers, he should not leave at all until his supervisor wakes him. He should rise together with him, wash his hands and face, and say the three prayers. From there they should return to the kitchen, and the master should leave him there under the supervision of whichever of them he considers appropriate.

On the principal feasts, if the abbot is absent, it is not proper for anyone except the weekly server to sing Mass. Nevertheless, the sacristan should take care not to assign to the brief the person next in order, but someone who knows how to perform this divine office usefully.

When there are two censers on these feasts, the abbot is vested for one and the weekly brother for the other. If the abbot is the weekly server, one of the brothers whom the secretary appoints should also vest.

[Col. 1263D] When the abbot is vested for the Gospel canticle and the weekly server is on the other side—the sacristan must find the collect and place the sign—the weekly brother who is vested should hold the book of collects [Note: *Collectaneus*, an ecclesiastical book containing collects or prayers.] before the abbot, if the abbot permits him. If not, one of the young brothers standing at the bench should hold it for him. If the abbot is vested alone, one of the young brothers should do so.

If the brothers celebrate the Twelve Lessons, the boys should not wash their heads or footwear on Wednesday.

On feasts when the entire monastery, or half of it, is decorated, three candles should burn before the altar at the regular Hours. For the principal Mass, all the bells should be rung.

[Col. 1264A] On the greatest feasts, twelve candlesticks should stand before the high altar at the morning praises, Mass, and Vespers; at the other Hours, as above.

When each responsory is sung by two brothers at Matins, only one collect should be said at the morning Mass. On those days, “To the Lord, when I was troubled” (*Ad Dominum cum tribularer*) should not be sung for the dead at the Hours.

If the master sends boys to judgment, the matter should belong to no one except the person who holds the order. If it seems good that they should be absolved, he should make a sign to the master so that they may be absolved.

A priest should not ask pardon at a deacon’s confession. The abbot and priests should always make satisfaction among themselves when they do this.

At every time when there is an interval for reading, the signal should be held at Prime until everyone has assembled, so that they can chant the seven psalms while bowing. After the abbot has made the signal, they should be dismissed and the Hour begun.

At Terce, Sext, or None, the secretary should hold the second signal until the abbot comes into the choir. If the abbot is absent, there is no need to wait. At Sext the second signal should be held until “O God, have mercy” (*Deus misereatur*) has been said. At None, during the midday period, he should hold the small bell only until “Have mercy on me, O God” (*Miserere mei, Deus*) has been finished. At Vespers, at each signal, when it is rung, it should continue long enough for “O God, come to my assistance” (*Deus, in adjutorium meum*) to be brought forth.

The secretary is not responsible for the Mass of guests. The doorkeeper should take care of it and tell the person who holds the order to appoint someone who can carry it out diligently.

The boys should not go to the morning Mass sung at the Holy Cross to serve the priest there. The secretaries should provide him, together with the deacon, with whatever is appropriate.

The master should not discipline the boys in the choir if the Lord Abbot or the prior is present, nor should he discipline those from the choir in which the person holding the order is standing. If the Lord Abbot and the prior are absent, the master should administer the discipline from his own choir, unless he does not preside in the choir from which the person holding the order comes—unless that person himself has ordered it.

If at some time a convert is negligent concerning a candlestick, a boy may carry and hold it until he has said the *Kyrie eleison*. The next day his master should lodge a complaint against him.

If the Lord Abbot has acquired a book from another monastery and must return it at a fixed time, or if some other necessity arises, and the Lord Abbot gives orders or sends instructions to the monastery, that brother may omit the familiar psalms, Mass, or the midday office because of this writing.

## CHAPTER XVII. How boys are to be offered

When parents wish to give their children to God in the monastery, they should first deal with whatever property they possess in every respect as the Rule says (chapter 58 and following). Then, when the Gospel has been read at Mass and the offertory begins, the abbot should first make his offering. The boy should then come before the altar or to the steps, and the offertory with the host and a flask of wine should be placed in his hands. One of the brothers whom the abbot commands should read this document:

“I, Brother So-and-so, offer this boy, named So-and-so, together with the offering in my hand and the petition, his hand wrapped in the altar cloth, in the name of the saints whose relics are contained here and of the present Lord Abbot. I hand him over before witnesses, to remain according to the Rule, so that from this day it is not permitted him to shake his neck free from beneath the yoke of the Rule. Rather, let him faithfully recognize that he must observe the institutions of that same Rule and serve the Lord with the others with a grateful heart.”

After it has been read, the document itself should be placed in the boy’s hands, and he should offer it together with the offering. Then the abbot should take it for safekeeping. If laypeople are present, they should be summoned to see and hear, so that they may be witnesses.

Then the abbot should bless the cuculla and clothe the boy. Immediately they should begin the offertory of the Mass, and the child should be placed with the others.

When the time of consecration appropriate to his age arrives, the abbot should not remove his cuculla. Instead, he should read the profession with the others, and, after giving the blessing, place the cap on his head and kiss him. In all else he should proceed as the other brothers do.

## CHAPTER XVIII. On the weekly cellarer and how he should serve the brothers in the refectory

At the Twelve Lessons and on Tuesday, Thursday, and Saturday, the senior brothers should be served first. The cellarer, with the weekly servers, should provide the second serving, beginning with the last. The kitchen brothers should provide the third, likewise beginning with the younger.

If the cellarer prepares some extra dish (*pietantia*) [Note: *Pietantia*, *pitantia*: a dish or food granted in addition to the regular fare.], it should afterward begin at the Lord Abbot’s table.

On Monday, Wednesday, and Friday, the weekly servers should first come to the small bell. The cellarer, with what we call his extra dish, should begin with the senior brothers, without the sound of the small bell. The weekly brothers should give their serving beginning with the last, and afterward ring the signal for Vespers with permission.

When fruits or vegetables are served, after the table has been blessed and all the brothers have sat down, the cellarer and his companion should first carry them to the senior brothers, always in small bowls. When the fruits are small, he should carry them in a basket, and each person should take according to what he sees fit. To the boys he should afterward carry them in a bowl and give each one as he thinks appropriate.

Finally, the cellarer himself should carry the extra dish of small fish with his companion. If it consists of fruit, he should do so with the refectorian; when it consists of vegetables, the gardener should do so with him. If he performs a *neuma* [Note: To perform a *neuma* with a brother means to sing with another brother.], he should do so with the brother appointed over the granary. Whenever the cellarer wishes, he may summon whichever brother he chooses and work with him.

When his own chapter has been announced, on that day he should receive his general portion from his side and prepare something else as well, as best he can. They should hold a charitable drink of spiced beverages without the sound of the small bell. If it has been read on Monday, Wednesday, or Friday, he should give, between two brothers, a bowl of fish more generously than they are accustomed to receive on other days, and a portion should be set before all the brothers without the sound of the small bell.

On another day he should make satisfaction in Chapter, and the Lord Abbot should absolve him. If the abbot is absent, the person holding the order should do so. After Chapter they should sing five psalms for the dead, then, for the brother who has been absolved, the psalm “Have mercy” (*Miserere*); “Lord, have mercy” (*Kyrie eleison*); “Our Father” (*Pater noster*); “And lead us not” (*Et ne nos*); Chapter; “Save your servant” (*Salvum fac servum*); “Send him, Lord” (*Mitte ei, Domine*); “The Lord be with you” (*Dominus vobiscum*); “Almighty and eternal God, have mercy on your servant” (*Omnipotens sempiterne Deus, miserere famulo tuo*).

On that day the brothers should receive a more generous portion in the refectory.

## CHAPTER XIX. What the refectorian or the boys should do when they are servers
If the servers are boys, they themselves must wash the spoons [Col. 1266B] and sweep; the refectorer, however, is to receive the bread. If the boys are absent, one of the servers must wash the spoons and gather up the crumbs from the tables. Nevertheless, the refectorer must exercise oversight in everything, so that there is no negligence; for if there is, it will fall upon him.

At the Twelve Lessons, as soon as the customary signal has sounded, the servers are to bring the second course: the refectorer is to come and strike the bell. If a boy is present who has come with another to read, he is to take the flask and serve the drink. In the first place, when the refectorer sounds the bell, if the boy is absent, he himself—or whichever of the servers he signals—is to do it. At midday he himself is to mix the water; at None, with the weekly servers who belonged to the preceding week. Every day he is to wash the abbot’s *justitia* [Col. 1266C], and after the cymbal has sounded, or he himself has sat down at the table, he is to carry everything away. He himself must wash the *justitia* of the brothers returning from a journey. He is to keep under his custody the abbot’s *zalla* [Note: [Col. 1266D] *Zalla*, a hand towel, as we noted above.] and basins [Note: [Col. 1266D] *Bacile*, the Italian word *bacino*, a basin.], or the one assigned for the poor or for visiting brothers. He is to clean the loaves by the pound [or: the loaf] of every trace of dirt. He must always have a linen cloth assigned for this work around his neck, until he has inspected everyone.

## CHAPTER XX. How it is to be done when they assemble for shaving

One or two brothers are to be assigned the duty of sharpening the razors and gathering them at the chest where they are stored. He must also provide the shears assigned for this work and to be kept in the dormitory [Col. 1266D], and likewise the razors.

On the day appointed for shaving, as soon as they assemble in chapter and have spoken about the salvation of souls, at the abbot’s command—or, if the abbot is absent, at the command of the one who holds the order—the brothers who served in the kitchen during the preceding week are to rise and go prepare water at the appointed place. When they rise from chapter, the signal is to be sounded, and each is to come and receive a razor from the hand of the person responsible for them. Then the almoner is to have vessels arranged beforehand in the place where the seniors will assemble. When they have received them, each is to carry water for himself. The boys are to carry their benches.

The abbot or prior is to begin five psalms: first, for the dead who were announced in chapter, and the canonical course of the Hours, as is customary to chant in the kitchen. Afterwards, the psalms proper to the regular Hours are to be said. While the psalmody lasts, no one may do anything else except shave; nor may anyone wash or cut his head, except while saying the psalms, nor cut his fingernails. The refectorers are not to go to the refectory until the psalms have been completed.

No one may speak. Nor may any brother shave another while wearing a fur garment with wide sleeves, unless he is wearing one with narrow sleeves, or a tunic. When the psalmody has been completed, the abbot is to say, “Bless.” Each is to return to the assigned duties [Col. 1267B]. At this hour the secretary is to strike the bell, if they are to eat there.

If any of the boys has not been shaved, they are to proceed to the school and do it there. If something happens to one of the brothers—namely, that he has begun to shave when the signal sounds—he is to abandon the work, rise, put on his cowl, go to the church, and remain outside the choir. When the Hour has been completed, he is to return and shave himself.

After that day has passed, no one may anywhere perform this task without permission. The boys, however, may cut their hair in the school on Wednesday and Saturday without their cowls and without a tunic. No brother is to cut his own hair, and each is to have his hair cut in a circle to the middle of the ears. Whoever wishes to wash his head may do so on that day without permission; on another day it is not permitted. Whenever he does so, he must be wearing a tunic with wide sleeves.

## CHAPTER XXI. What the monks must always observe in the kitchens

In the kitchen, the brother who arrives first at dawn may do nothing else while he is alone except light the place. After another or both others have arrived, they are to say the entire psalmody from beginning to end, as in shaving, except for the psalms proper to the regular Hours, which each may say in church with the others or by himself at that time.

In the psalmody that they say in the kitchen, while shaving, or during another manual task, at the first set of five psalms—that is, “My words”—“The Lord be with you” is said. After the prayer: “May they rest in peace.” Afterwards, “The Lord be with you” and “Let us bless the Lord” are not to be said except at Vespers. Likewise at Vespers let them say: “The Lord be with you. May they rest in peace.” At Compline let them say: “The Lord be with you,” and the blessing. With the final psalms proper to the Hours: “The Lord be with you. Let us bless the Lord. Bless.”

## CHAPTER XXII. How the priest who wishes to celebrate his Mass privately is to act

As soon as they have left the services of Matins, if it is daytime, he is to signal to whichever one of the converts he wishes, and they are to go, wash their hands and faces, and proceed to the church. They are to make three prayers, if the time is appropriate. Or, if the Twelve Lessons have been completed, he is then to go, take the book and the alb, and place them at one of the altars; for no one is permitted to remove them elsewhere once he has taken them.

He is then to return to the sacristy and take the host and chalice. He is to rinse the chalice with water in the vessel, and wipe it with a small cloth before he has put wine and water into it. The convert who is to assist him is to take and light a candle, and proceed to the place where he is to celebrate the sacred rite.

Then the priest is to remove his tunic, kneel, and put on the priestly vestments. While wearing the stole, he is to make confession with the brother. Then he is to perform the order of service at the altar, make the sign of the holy cross on his forehead, and begin to offer sacrifice to God. The convert is to bow during the collects and the secrets, kneel at the Canon, or pray standing.

If the signal for the Hour sounds while the priest has not yet put on the stole—even if he is already wearing the alb—he is to remove it in this manner and go to the Hour. When the bell is sounded before Terce, if he has only the chalice prepared, he may celebrate Mass in this way without reproach.

If the brothers enter for the Hour during his Mass, after his Mass he is to kneel while he is still undressed and say the Hours. Until the seniors are standing at the Hour, he must not presume to enter to carry things back. Once the Hour has been completed, however, he may proceed to the psalms proper to the Hours. The convert is to carry the alb and book; the priest, the chalice and cruet, to the appointed place.

## CHAPTER XXIII. How the priest and ministers are to act at the general Mass

[Col. 1268C]

When the priest says, “Pray, brothers,” the boys are to bow for the duration of the Lord’s Prayer, and immediately rise, turning their faces toward the east. The elders, however, are to remain bowed until the priest says, “For ever and ever.” At the end, when he has said, “For ever and ever, etc. Let us pray. At the command: Our Father,” all, boys and elders alike, are to be bowed, saying, “But deliver us from evil.” The children are to rise; the brothers are to remain bowed until he says again, “For ever and ever.”

At the Twelve Lessons, the priest is to put incense in the thurible in the sacristy at the entrance of the Mass. When the one responsible for the service begins “Glory to the Father,” proceeding before the first altar, he is first to make a prayer. Then he and the levite are to make confession [Col. 1268D]. When it is completed, the priest is to take the thurible and incense the altar. The levite, taking it again, is to carry it around the altars and to the lord abbot, and the convert is to carry it throughout the choir, first to the one serving in the liturgy.

At the Gospel, the lord abbot is to put incense into the thurible, with the levite carrying the incense vessels to him. If the abbot is absent, the priest is to put it in. When this has been done, the priest is first to kiss the Gospel, then the levite the Gospel book, and then the altar. The subdeacon is to take the book and carry it to the priest, to the lord abbot, and to all the brothers, first to the one occupied with the service.

After the offertory, the convert is to carry the incense vessels to the cantor, and the cantor is to carry them to the lord abbot; if he is absent, the cantor is to perform the task himself. When the priest says, “For ever and ever” [Col. 1269A], the levite is to come, and after him the subdeacon below. The levite and acolyte are to carry the covered paten with the offertory and stand below the deacon.

As the deacon comes forward to uncover the chalice, he is first to kiss the altar, then the priest’s arm or hand, and withdraw humbly and bow. When the priest has finished the Lord’s Prayer, the acolyte is to hand the paten with the offertory to the levite, kissing his hand, and the levite is to return the offertory to the boy.

On feast days and at all solemn Masses at which the boy wears a tunic or a chasuble, he himself is to carry the Gospel book, and another boy the chalice. On ordinary days, the convert who carries the candelabrum to the Mass is to carry it from the choir in which that Mass is being celebrated, from that side; incense must always be present for that Mass [Col. 1269B].

The boy who reads the Epistle is himself to carry the chalice, if he is able and knows how to do it properly. Three hosts are to be offered each day. Whoever wishes to receive Communion may do so if he belongs to the choir from which the brothers offer; if he belongs to another choir, he is not to do so unless the prior orders it. On Sundays five hosts are to be offered; on other feast days three, except at the greater solemnities.

## CHAPTER XXIV. On Sundays, feast days, and ordinary days: how many lights the secretaries are to light in the churches

On Sundays and all feast days on which the Twelve Lessons are said, at every season except when Mass is celebrated in copes, let them proceed as follows.

At the first watch, before the signal sounds, five lights are to be lit in the appointed places, namely [Col. 1269C]:

1. one before the high altar, which is to burn day and night;
2. another in the choir near the abbot, before the lectern;
3. a third before the altar or outside the choir;
4. a fourth in the northern arm, in the sacristy, before the altar of Saint Benedict;
5. a fifth on the southern side outside the choir, at the entrance of the church.

When the Song of Degrees has been completed, two are to be added before the high altar. In the third nocturn, when the deacon has announced the Gospel and says, “And the rest,” two secretaries are immediately to uncover the board, they are to light the third candelabrum, and the lectern is to be carried in. At Lauds, when “Let us bless the Lord” has been said, they are to be extinguished.

At Mass, two are to be added to the three; the converts are to carry them, making five. At Vespers there are to be three before the altar.

On weekdays they are likewise to proceed in the appointed places, except for those lights added in the third nocturn [Col. 1269D]. Two candles are to be lit before the principal altar. When the Song of Degrees has been completed, there is to be a third, which is always to remain burning there.

When the two nocturns have been completed, the two candles are to be extinguished until “The vigil of the dead” and their Matins are said. At Lauds they are to be lit again before the signal is sounded. At Mass there are to be three before the altar; at Vespers, two.

On all Saturdays, there are always to be three lamps lit before the altar at Vespers. The same is to be done on all vigils of male or female saints when the Twelve Lessons are to be said on the following day.

## CHAPTER XXV. On the verses of the offertories

[Col. 1270A]

As soon as the offertory has been said, the brother responsible for the service is to come before the abbot and signal who is to begin the verses. When the abbot begins, all are to bow. If he does not impose the verses, he is to signal others whom he considers suitable; as soon as the verse has been begun, the person is to make a reverent bow, while all the boys on either side bow.

If the abbot is absent, the prior is to do this. If the prior is entirely absent, he is to signal the dean. When the dean is absent, the librarian is to impose the verses; if all those named are absent, the service-brother himself is to complete the task.

When the verses are nearly finished, the convert is to come with the thurible to the cantor, who is then to carry it to the abbot. If the abbot is absent, the cantor is to do it himself [Col. 1270B].

Throughout Lent, all are to chant every day; likewise thereafter during the days of Easter and on feasts that are celebrated once a year. On Sundays, when they arrive, they are to chant only one throughout the entire week. Of the feasts of the saints that they celebrate, one or two are to be brought forth.

## CHAPTER XXVI. How the kitchen boys are to act with their masters

The boys who serve in the kitchen are to do in the kitchen everything that must be done by the weekly servers. On Saturday they are also to wash and dry the brothers’ feet, together with such seniors as supervise them, not with young men.

They are not, however, to serve at dinner or wait at table; rather, other brothers whom the master requests are to do so [Col. 1270C]. When the kitchen brothers see that the bowls need to be boiled because of grease, they are to give them to the cellarer on Wednesday or another day. He is to have them washed and they are then to return them to the kitchen boys.

On Saturday the kitchen is to be cleaned and swept. They are to leave fresh, very soft water for those entering. They are to heat water for washing the brothers’ feet. One of those going out and another of those entering are to carry it before chapter. Those entering are to bring linen cloths from the storeroom; the secretary is to bring basins and towels. The abbot is to dry feet at only one of these basins.

Two boys are not to wash at the same time. The master and one boy are to wash while another boy sits on his own stool. When they assemble to wash the linen cloths, the weekly boy is to rise from his stool and go outside the chapter house with another boy, and they are to wash the linen cloths.

When this has been completed, they are to wash their hands and bring water for washing the hands of all the brothers. One of these boys, the younger, is to go to his stool and remain there until everyone, including the boys, has washed his hands. Then the boy is again to rise from his stool and come outside with the other child.

When they have put down the utensils with which they served the brothers in the appointed place, they are to come forward into the middle of the chapter house in an orderly fashion, make a reverence, and go to their stools. When the boys have washed their hands, the secretary is to give the signal for striking the bell. Having received permission, he is to go, and the reader is to come into the middle before the lectern. When the secretary gives the signal—with the abbot’s assent—he is to receive the blessing and begin the reading [Col. 1271A].

After he has read two verses, or something more, the one whom the abbot signals is to rise at the abbot’s command and strike the cymbal. From then on all are to rise, make the reverence before and behind, and go until the drink has been blessed.

The kitchen weekly servers are to go, cover the fire, and return together. There they are to make the reverence before and behind, imposing this verse three times: “Blessed are you, Lord my God.” “Kyrie eleison. Our Father. And lead us not. Our help,” etc. Then they are to withdraw.

If the abbot is absent, they are to do the same in the place of the one who holds the order. On ordinary days they are to do this when the cymbal sounds. On days when the cymbal is not struck, once they have completed everything that must be done there, they are to say this and withdraw.

On Sunday, after chapter, they are to return the clean and sound vessels to the cellarer by number, and they are to be given to those entering [Col. 1271B].

## CHAPTER XXVII. On the confession of the boys

When the children are led to confession, if the lord abbot is present, the master is to lead them to him. When the abbot rises, the master is to sit before the entrance of the chapter house. In the place customarily assigned to the children, they are to hold chapter and make confession there.

The first boy is to approach first and make his confession standing; the other is to sit to the south on one of their seats. After confession, the master is again to receive them.

When they wish to confess to the prior or to the dean of the cloister, the master is to lead them to him and immediately withdraw. The prior is to lead them into chapter and, after confession, return them to the school [Col. 1271C].

When some of the children are to leave the school for the children’s chapter, the lord abbot is to come and have the other children leave. He himself and the master are to remain with those who are to leave, and he is to hear their confession. After confession, the master is to return them and the others.

He himself is to supervise them until they come to the consecration; afterwards, let the others do what they are ordered to do.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. How the librarian or cantor is to act on Saturdays and feast days, and what duties he must perform

On Saturdays there are to be four who prepare the brief schedule: the boy, who writes the incipits of the responsories; the cantor, who announces the names of the brothers who are to sing [Col. 1271D]; and the librarian, who records the names of those who are to read.

Likewise, the weekly cantor is to specify the service: “Let such a one sing the responsory with such a one; let such and such sound the Alleluia”; and he is to assign the reader to the servers. The librarian is to indicate who is to have the Mass, which boy is to read the Epistle, which the Gospel, and who is to read the lesson at table. The cellarer is to specify which brothers are to serve in the kitchen.

At the Twelve Lessons there are to be three: the librarian, the cantor, and the boy. The librarian himself must make arrangements for those feasts celebrated in copes. If the weekly server for the service is not suitable, he is to order other brothers to sing the Invitatory and afterwards to serve with him who is responsible for the service at Mass.

At table and at the collation, whatever book he has placed is to be read by the reader [Col. 1272A]; no brother is to presume to assign another book. He must listen to the readings, responsories, and everything that the brothers sing or read inside or outside.

He himself must bind, cover, or correct all the books, either personally or through other learned brothers. As for the general books that the brothers are to copy, he must make every effort to prepare and bring them to completion; and whichever brother he orders to assist him must obey him. If any of them refuses, he is to be accused on the following day.

If the abbot is absent, he is to impose the antiphons that are taken from the Gospel. He must take care to correct the Mass, the service, the Gospel, and all the other matters belonging to the church if anything has been neglected. Every day he is to take out and bring back the books with the cantor [Col. 1272B]. He must also have many other matters under his care, which we have already written down in various places and which there is no need to insert here.

## CHAPTER XXIX. On processions

Whenever the brothers make a procession on Wednesday and Friday, as soon as one of the processional antiphons has been said, two boys are immediately to say the litany, both along the route and in the church when they return to the choir.

No one may leave before the litany has been completed, even if he has permission, unless a necessity arises that he absolutely cannot postpone. Once it is completed, if anyone urgently needs to do something, let him ask permission from the lord abbot or, if the abbot is absent, from the one who holds the order, and let him go. Nevertheless, he must first make a reverence, wash his feet, and attend to what must be attended to.

No one is to do anything anywhere without permission until Mass has ended. The same applies during the Rogations or other processions.

Furthermore, at those times when they go outside the monastery, they are to go saying responsories and antiphons for sins, and whatever they wish from the [supplementary office] of blessed Mary the Virgin. When they are approaching the place, they are to begin a responsory from among the relics of the saints whose names are there consecrated [or: written; *consecrata* / *conscripta*] [Col. 1272C].

As soon as it has been completed, the priest is to say, “Let us pray,” and the prayer of those saints. Then all are to prostrate themselves and make the prayers. The priest is not to say “Our Father” aloud at this place, nor “And lead us not” [Col. 1272D]. Instead, he is immediately to bring forth the psalm for the dead who rest there: “Praise, my soul, the Lord.” Chapter: “From the gate of hell.” “The Lord be with you.” Prayer: “O God, by whose mercy…”

Then two boys are to begin the litany, “Kyrie,” before the altar and proceed to those saints, saying it there up to the name of blessed John. Then they are to say it three times, followed by the names that come next. They are to make the reverence before and behind and proceed in the same manner as they came.

## CHAPTER XXX. How the relics of the saints are to be carried processionally to the place where they must be taken, and how they are to be received with praise

When relics are to be carried somewhere, they are to proceed as follows. With the librarian signaling—or speaking, if it is a time when speech is permitted—or with the one who holds the order giving the signal, all are to put on copes, and the boys albs.

The relics are to be suitably arranged. The church secretaries are to strike the bells. Two candelabra are to be carried by converts, together with holy water, the cross, and incense. The *phonones* [Note: [Col. 1273D] *Phonones*, *phanones*, *fanones*: veils or banners.] are to be carried by the servants, and one bell is to be sent with them.

The cantor is to begin the responsory “Saint Marcellus,” or another according to the kind of relics. They are to be incensed, and all are to go together outside the monastery gates, by which the monastery is enclosed.

Then the other brothers who are to receive the relics of the saints are to be present. They are to tell the servants to carry them wherever necessary, and the brothers are to begin the psalms: “To the Lord, when I was in distress.” They are then to return to the choir, remove their vestments, and go each to his own duty.

At the time when they are to return, they must first arrange for word to be sent to the monastery, so that all the brothers may be in copes and the children in albs. The prior is to begin the psalms: “Have mercy on me, O God”; “O God, in your name”; “God, have mercy”; and they are to go out to meet the holy relics.

The secretaries or servants are to sound the bells until everything has been completed. Then they are to begin the responsory “This saint.” The priest is to say the verse, “Great is his glory,” or another according to the kind of relics, together with the appropriate collects and prayers. Then they are to be incensed.

Again they are to begin another responsory suitable for the holy relics. When this has been completed, they are to go into the monastery, and the relics are to be placed where they are to be kept. They are to be incensed again, and each is to return to his work.

## CHAPTER XXXI. Further concerning the same matter

[Col. 1273C]

When the sacred body is to be carried outside, they are to be dressed in albs and sing either a responsory or an antiphon of the saint whose relics are being carried until the prior gives the signal to return. On the return journey they are to say psalms.

When the relics are being brought back, the brothers are to come out to meet them dressed in copes. When they leave the choir, the prior is to begin: “Have mercy on me, O God”; “O God, in your name”; “Have mercy on me, O God, have mercy on me”; “May God have mercy,” etc., until they reach the relics.

After incense has been offered, the prayer of that saint is to be said. Then the librarian is to begin a chant of that saint, and they are to proceed in this manner to the monastery.

## CHAPTER XXXII. For escorting the king

[Col. 1273D]

When the king’s arrival at the monastery has been heard, the abbot or prior is to signal—and, if it is not a time when speech is permitted in the cloister, the brothers are to be informed by a sign—so that all assemble in the church. All, including the converts, are to put on copes, and the children are to put on tunics.

The secretaries are to prepare the procession. Then two larger bells are to be sounded, and they are to begin proceeding in the order shown by these symbols:

> Cross, Thurible, Candelabrum, Candle, Candle, Water, Cross, Gospel Book, Gospel Book, Gospel Book, Cross, Thurible, Candelabrum, Candle, Candle.

The converts are to be in pairs, then the children with their masters [Col. 1274A], then the lord abbot, and then the other brothers two by two, according to their rank above. Nevertheless, they are to go in silence.

When they reach him, they are to give him holy water; he is to kiss the Gospel book and be incensed. Then the responsory “Behold, I send my angel” is to be begun, and the servants are to sound all the bells.

In the church two carpets are to be laid out, one before the altar of the holy cross and the other before the high altar. Then the abbot is to begin whatever antiphon or responsory he wishes, provided that it is suitable.

When it has been completed, he is to say the chapter and these prayers:

> Almighty and eternal God, who govern heavenly and earthly things together. Alleluia. Almighty and eternal God, have mercy on your servant.

Then they are to return to the cloister.

The same is to be done for the queen. However, as they enter the church, they are to chant this antiphon: “When the Son of Man shall sit…”

## CHAPTER XXXIII. For escorting the bishop

[Col. 1274B]

As soon as the bishop’s arrival has been announced in the monastery, the prior or the one who holds the order is to signal the brothers—if they do not speak in the cloister—so that all assemble in the church. All are to put on copes, and the children albs.

Then the converts are to take holy water, the cross, two candelabra, and the Gospel book, and proceed in silence. They are to give him holy water; he is to kiss the Gospel book and be incensed. Then they are to begin the responsory “Behold, truly an Israelite,” or “Hear, O Israel.” All the bells are to be sounded, and they are to proceed into the church.

Two carpets are to be laid out, one before the principal altar and the other before the altar of the holy cross. Then they are to return to the cloister.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. Further concerning escorting an abbot

[Col. 1274C]

For an abbot, the bells are not sounded, nor do all put on vestments; only those who carry the procession do so, and they are nowhere to sing, either on the way out or on the return.

If, however, he is a person of such dignity, all the brothers may be in copes and the boys in albs.

## CHAPTER XXXV. For asking for clear weather

When it has rained heavily, they are to assemble in chapter and unanimously determine that this psalm be said in the litany: “You have blessed, O Lord, your land.”

On Wednesday and Friday, at the procession, the antiphon “The waters have overflowed”; and from it the morning Mass. Office: “All that you have done for us.” Collect: “To you, O Lord, we cry.” Other prayers are to be said according to custom for the dead, and the reading from the prophet Jeremiah:

> Thus says the Lord: “Have you utterly rejected Judah?”

Responsory: “Our protector, look upon us, O God.” Alleluia: “Show us, O Lord.” Gospel according to Luke:

> At that time Jesus said to his disciples: “I have compassion on the crowd, because they have now been with me for three days.”

Offertory: “As a burnt offering.” Communion: “Incline your ear,” or “When I called upon you.”

At the principal Mass, after the offertory, when the priest has begun to arrange the chalice with the deacon upon the altar, the cantor [is to begin] in the choir the responsory “O God who are seated: To you the poor man is abandoned” [Col. 1275A].

All are to prostrate themselves on the ground. When they rise, they are to stand facing the altar until the priest says, “Pray for us.”

## CHAPTER XXXVI. The office for asking for rain

“Salvation of the people.” Collect: “O God, in whom we live.” Reading: Jeremiah the Prophet.

> Jeremiah spoke, saying: “Rise, praise in the night.”

Responsory: “Be merciful.” Alleluia: “Show us.” Gospel according to Luke:

> It happened on one of those days that Jesus went up into a boat.

Offertory: “As a burnt offering.” Communion: “Incline your ear.”

## CHAPTER XXXVII. For making various prayers

This is the manner in which an ecclesiastical appeal to the Lord is to be made [Col. 1275B].

At the principal Mass, after the Lord’s Prayer has been said, the ministers of the church are to cover the pavement before the altar with sackcloth. Upon it they are to place a crucifix, the Gospel book, and the bodies of the saints. All the clergy are to lie prostrate on the pavement, singing the psalm “Why, O God, have you rejected us forever?” in silence.

Meanwhile the church custodians are to strike two bells. The priest alone, before the newly consecrated body and blood of the Lord and before the aforementioned relics of the saints, is to begin this appeal in a loud voice:

> Show us. Be our help, Lord. Remember us, Lord. Remember the congregation. Rise, Lord. Lord, hear our prayer.

> In a spirit of humility and with a contrite heart, before your holy altar and your most sacred body and blood, Lord Jesus, Redeemer of the world, we approach. We acknowledge ourselves guilty before you because of our sins, for which we are justly afflicted.

> To you, Lord Jesus, we come; to you, prostrate, we cry out, because wicked and proud men, trusting in their own strength, rise up against us from every side. They invade and plunder the lands of this sanctuary of yours and of the other churches subject to it, and lay them waste. They force your poor worshipers who serve there to live in sorrow, hunger, and nakedness; they even kill them with tortures and swords. They also seize our possessions, from which we must live in your holy service and which devout souls have left to this place for their salvation; they take them from us by violence.

> This church of yours, Lord, which in ancient times you founded and exalted in honor of the blessed and ever-virgin Mary [Col. 1275D], sits in sorrow. There is no one to console and free her except you, our God.

> Rise, therefore, Lord Jesus, to our help. Strengthen us and assist us. Overcome those who attack us, and break the pride of those who afflict your place and us. You know, Lord, who they are and what their names are; their bodies and hearts were known to you before they were born.

> Therefore, O God, as you know what is just in your power, make them recognize their evil deeds, and free us in your mercy. Do not despise us, O God, as we cry to you in affliction. For the glory of your name and because of the mercy by which you founded this place and exalted it in honor of your mother, visit us in peace [Col. 1276A] and rescue us from our present distress. Amen.

When this appeal has been made, the relics are to be carried back to their places, and the priest is to say silently the collect, “Deliver us, we beseech you, O Lord.”

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. Further concerning the same matter, in another formulation

When they rise from chapter on Sunday, the bell is to be sounded and they are to make the prayer. Then the priest is to go out with the children and prepare for Mass. The larger bell is then to be sounded twice, as the principal announcement.

At the completion of the Gospel, “I believe in one God” is to be said. When it has been completed, the librarian is to ascend the pulpit and announce to the people the wickedness of the persecutors.

Then another brother is to come forward and read the anathemas or curses from both the New and Old [Col. 1276B] Testaments, according to the usefulness and command received from the Apostolic See, together with the confirmation of neighboring bishops: the curse upon those who do not correct themselves, and the blessing upon those who prepare themselves for correction.

After it has been read, the candle is to be extinguished and all the bells sounded. After the dismissal, all are to prostrate themselves on the ground and chant these psalms: “Lord, how they have increased.” “O God, come to my assistance.” Or, adding these two: “You have blessed”; “The foundations.” Or whatever others they have appointed.

Chapter: “Show us.” “Be our help.” “Rise, O Lord.”

Prayers: “Grant us, your servants, we beseech you, O Lord”; “Almighty and eternal God of the sorrowful.” Or, as we have said, according to the decrees they have established.

They are to rise, sing the offertory, and complete the Mass [Col. 1276C]. On other ordinary days they are to proceed in this way: as soon as they have risen from chapter, they are first to come and say five psalms for the dead. Then the bells are to be sounded, they are to throw themselves upon the ground, and say the prayers as above.

## CHAPTER XXXIX. How they are to act if they are to process to Saint Mary

When they go to the basilica of Saint Mary, as soon as they have risen they are to begin the psalms for the dead. Afterwards, prostrate for the tribulations, without the sound of *tonnitorum* [Note: [Col. 1275] *Tonnitorum sonitus*: I think this means the sounds or notes of musical tones, as though he were saying: let them say the psalms for the tribulations while prostrate and without melody.], they are to say the psalms as we stated above.

Sometimes, if they wish to add the psalm “Incline, O Lord” and “You have blessed,” they are to say these chapters: “After childbirth”; “Show us”; “Be our help.” Collects: “Grant”; “O ineffable God”; “Who receives the contrite,” or “The offering of our…” [Col. 1276D].

When these have been completed, they are to go out. The prior is to sound the board if it is a time when speech is permitted in the cloister, and each is to proceed to his own duty.

## CHAPTER XL. On brothers leaving the monastery

When a brother who has fled from the monastery wishes to return, he is to come naked and barefoot into chapter, carrying his cowl on his arm and a staff in his hand. After receiving judgment, he is to go outside to some place, dress himself, and put on shoes. Returning to chapter, he is to ask pardon before the abbot, and at the abbot’s command sit down as the Rule prescribes (chapter 29).

If the lord abbot is absent, judgment is to be reserved for him [Col. 1277A]. When he has returned, the brother himself is to withdraw from the abbot’s sight until he comes to a suitable place where he may ask pardon by making satisfaction, and he is to do what the abbot commands him.

He is to lie one night in the guesthouse before he is received. If he has fled from a cell and returned there, he is to be received as stated above; and when he comes to the head of the monastery, he is likewise to do this.

If he has fled from a cell, has not returned there, and comes to the head of the monastery, he is to be received as noted above until the prior of that cell is summoned and the complaints of both parties are heard. Wherever fault is found, it is to be corrected. Afterwards, if the prior thinks fit, the brother himself is to return to that cell.

## CHAPTER XLI. On bloodletting

[Col. 1277B]

## CHAPTER XLI. On Those Who Are Bled

If any brother wishes to have blood let, let him arrange to inform the abbot, or the prior if the abbot is absent. Having obtained permission, let him go and inform the cellarer, so that he may arrange to have an *arcedo* [Note: *Arcedo*: a band by which blood is constricted, derived from *arcere*, “to restrain,” although the elders also called this band by another name, *benda*. Bernard, *Ordo Cluniacensis*, part I.] or, if it is winter, arrange for a fire to be lit in the warming room. Then let him proceed to the door of the Almonry and receive a vessel. As soon as the Gospel has been recited, let him go in silence and perform the customary rite; then let him say three times, “O God, come to my assistance,” adding, “Glory be to the Father.” “Lord, have mercy.” “Our Father.” “And lead us not.” “Our help.” “Say the blessing.” When this has been done, let him proceed through the refectory.

If he wishes to visit after dinner, let him have everything prepared as we stated above. When he has been bled, let him go immediately to the refectory and make pieces of bread. If the servers are seated at table, let him ask permission from the one who is seated at the bell. If the lord abbot has been bled, let them receive the mixed drink on the following day; and if anyone is absent from the bloodletting, when he arrives, let him ask permission, say the verse, and approach the table. Let him do the same if the prior has been bled.

An ill man who receives the mixed drink because of his illness is not to ask permission or say the verse. The lord abbot ought to receive the mixed drink at the bell. The prior, however, if the lord abbot is in the monastery, is to receive it in his stall; and if the abbot is absent, he is to sit at the bell. The dean is to do likewise if the prior is absent.

When those who have been bled come together with the boys, then let them say the verse together. The child is to recite the lesson from memory; afterward let them eat. Let them have three cooked dishes prepared by the cellarer, but the boys are to have one. As they rise, let them say the verse together.

If eating takes place there, whoever wishes to take the mixed drink is to eat from his own portion and measure after Mass, without the verse. At Vespers, let the cellarer give him something to eat.

## CHAPTER XLII. How Letters of Recommendation Are to Be Given to Monks

“I, that humble abbot, send greetings. Let your affection know that this brother, So-and-so, has requested us to give him permission to live with you. Since we know that you maintain regular order, we have given our consent for him to live with you. Now I commend him to you, so that you may treat him as I do, and render an account to the Lord for him as I do.” [Note: This formula of the letter has been taken from the tradition of Hildemar.]

## CHAPTER XLIII. On the Monastery’s Porters

The porter brother ought never to ride, unless perhaps raiders have appeared within the monastery’s boundaries; for this purpose he may go out. When mounted travelers arrive at his cell, he and the servants and attendants are to receive them honorably, at the prior’s command and according to the rank of their persons.

The aforesaid brother is to bring bread and wine there daily for those under his charge [Note: *Subjectanei*: subordinates, subjects, those entrusted to his care]. When guests are not staying there, they are to go to the kitchen to eat, since, when free, they ought to make the brothers’ hoods. He is to procure horseshoes or bands.

The servants who care for the riders eat there; the porter’s servant-pupils are to serve them, and afterward they themselves are to eat with the cooks. This brother, together with all those who arrive, is to spread the beds; they are to sleep there. On the following day, whoever wishes to come to the church early is to light his lantern and escort him in, if he is such a person; but if he does not wish to occupy himself with this, let him instruct the household to do it.

The door between the gallery [*galilea*] and the cloister is to be opened every morning by the aforesaid brother and closed in the evening before the reading conference. [Note: *Galilea*: Galilee, gallery, or passageway. See the remarks above.]

## CHAPTER XLIV. How the Constable Brother Is to Act

[Note: *Constabulus*: the count of the stable, who was responsible for the stable and the horses.]

The constable brother is to have under his custody the horses, all the bedding and bridles for the riding animals, and the fodder or straw in the appointed places. He himself, together with his household servants, is to care for outsiders who arrive or depart.

They are therefore to do nothing except what the aforesaid brother orders them to do. Without reproach, he may give them something to eat, though he must request it from the cellarer. He is by no means to carry anything away from the refectory, neither he nor any other brother, unless someone has been ordered to do so.

## CHAPTER XLV. How Guests Are to Be Received

Let one or two brothers, together with their servants, take the greatest care over this: when guests arrive at the lodging assigned for such persons, let them all be led in and received with every courtesy. After supper, let the servants wash their feet and prepare bedding for them. If they wish, let them remain for three days without objection; and when they wish to depart, let a denarius be given to each.

If one of them arrives ill, let him, until he becomes better, remain inside and not go out, if he wishes. This, however, is to be provided only for the poor and pilgrims.

The brother responsible for that place is to receive daily from the storeroom seventeen loaves, and three pounds of that bread which the elders have in the refectory. For each person pronounced dead on any given day, he is to receive as many rations, both of bread and of other foods, as would have been given to them had they been alive. Similarly, for those whose anniversary is observed with the full office, he is to receive as many portions or measures as have been established in that place.

The cooked dishes are to be supplied by the weekly servers or the cellarers, as though they ought to have been placed on the table from everything prepared there for the brothers’ use; they are to put them into a small basket [Note: *Situla*: a sack or little basket in which bread and food are carried], which the responsible brother is to keep prepared there. Similarly, let two small baskets be prepared in the refectory.

The superiors of those places, wherever they may have returned from, are to strive to fulfill this duty. If they are absent, the cellarer is to do it, so that the servants’ rations may be gathered together. During all the fasts of the Four Seasons throughout the year, whatever remains from the refectory is to be assigned to this purpose; and the same is to be done with what remains from the house of the sick. Likewise, this is to be done for all the vigils that they celebrate.

From the Lord’s Advent until his Nativity this decree is in force; and from the beginning of the fast until the Paschal solemnity, everything is likewise to be given as alms daily, except on Sundays.

This brother, together with his assistants, is also to fulfill the following duty: he is to arrange for grass to be cut, choosing the better of what he sees, and he is to take responsibility for having it carried to the brothers’ latrine. He is to provide the lighting in the dormitory and the sick-house, in due order and with his assistants. He is to keep the vessels assigned to him for bloodletting, so that no negligence may occur.

He is to see that the church oratories, the cloister, the sick-house, the refectory, and the chapterhouse are cleaned, and that rushes are spread everywhere. He is to keep under his care the basins assigned to the brothers for shaving, distribute them at the proper times, and afterward put them away clean and neat. He is not to enter the cell into which he is not permitted to enter. The washing of the feet of the poor is to be carried out there.

He is to keep the orchard under his custody together with the cellarer, for planting and guarding it. [Note: *Pomerium*: a place where apples grow or are stored; or, for *pomarium*, a garden.]

## CHAPTER XLVI. How the Washing of the Feet of the Poor, Which Is Performed Daily, Is to Be Carried Out

The brother who has undertaken this duty is to have, with his assistant, everything necessary prepared there: namely, a cauldron in which to heat water; a basin for washing their feet; and three linen cloths. One of these is to be assigned for the elders who are going to perform this service. As soon as they have washed their feet, they are to wipe their hands on it. The second is for the feet of the poor; the third for washing their hands.

A basin and a bell are also to be kept there for carrying out this duty. Therefore, before the elders rise from dinner, when they have eaten together, or when they are going to dine at the sixth hour and in the evening, the servant is to have everything prepared that is required there, so that the brothers, coming together without delay, may devote themselves to washing the feet of three poor persons.

On Sunday, the lord abbot is to go with two boys and their master to supervise them. If the abbot is absent, the prior is to act in his place. Then the others are to proceed as they are listed below for the weekdays. On Saturday only, the masters are to perform the service with the boys.

As soon as they have risen from supper and the prayer in the church has been completed, the servant is to strike the board before the church doors. The three who are going to perform the service are to come out. The first of them is to come in the middle, while the other two go on either side, beginning the psalm “Have mercy on me, O God.” When they have come before the poor, they are to stand in the order in which they are senior, and kneel before them. Then let them begin the antiphon “A new commandment,” and the other appropriate prayers, and begin washing their feet.

As soon as he has washed the first person, he is immediately to give another a linen cloth, so that he may wash, dry, kiss, and cleanse the poor person with the hair of his head. He himself is to go to the place where the servant stands ready with water and a cloth, and wash his hands. The others are to do the same.

Then the first of them is to take the water, and another the cloth, and he is to pour water three times over the poor man’s hands. Each is to do likewise, kissing the hands meanwhile.

Then let the bell sound, and let him bless the food and drink that are to be given to them. First, let each one take in his hands a measure of wine and a pound of bread, and with thanksgiving give these to them, kissing their hands.

Then one of them is to take the little book, which must always be present there. The chapters and prayers written in it are to be said. Then let them bow before the poor, and let one of them say the verse:

“Show us, O Lord, your mercy.”

“Lord, have mercy.”

“Our Father.”

“And lead us not.”

“We have received, O God.”

“You commanded.”

“The Lord be with you.”

Prayer: “Be present, O Lord, to the service of our bondage.”

Then let them leave reverently, chanting the psalm “Have mercy on me, O God.”

As they pass through the church, let them kneel at the steps while “Lord, have mercy” is sung, and offer these prayers to God:

“Our Father.”

“Show us,” or, “May it come upon us.”

“The Lord be with you.”

Collect: “Direct our actions,” or, “Almighty and everlasting God, direct our deeds.”

Then let them leave and do as the others have done.

## CHAPTER XLVII. On the Brothers Who Have Been Received into Our Community

The chamberlain is to have these verses written on the bed frame [Note: *Fustis lectorum*: the wooden framework of a bed] or on their mattresses [Note: *Plumatae*: a cushion or pillow, the upper part of a bed] in the brothers’ dormitory:

“Behold, the little bed of the arriving brothers is seen here:

The flowering bedclothes of the brothers are seen.”

The chamberlain himself, together with another brother, is to purchase, obtain, and distribute all the brothers’ clothing, to each one as is fitting and as has been established in that place. Specifically, he is to give every brother annually two woolen garments, and likewise breeches; two cowls and two tunics with wide sleeves; two little fur garments with tight sleeves and a third with wide sleeves; and he is to distribute leggings, for night and day.

He is to give each four pairs of foot-coverings to ward off the cold, two pairs for the night and two for the day; and to each one a sheath with a knife, except that scribes are to have two, together with a belt for fastening around the waist. He is to provide boards, needles, a comb [Note: Read *pectines* for *pectene*] with stuffing [Note: Read *indumento* for *dumento*, or perhaps *tumento*, that is, a mattress], and a cap for the head, which is also called a head-covering.

For each bed there is to be assigned a *lena* furnished with a little fur covering, a woolen cloak, and a pillow.

When clothing or footwear is torn or needs sewing, each brother is first to wash it, then bring it before the door of the auditorium. The chamberlain is to receive it and carry it to the tailors to be repaired. No brother is to go to them or make any alteration to his clothing according to his own desire, except what is customary in the monastery and what the chamberlain has ordered.

Whoever does otherwise is to be strictly judged by all the brothers, so that the others may fear. The brother himself is always to be attentive wherever he sees a garment belonging to one of the brothers that has anything blameworthy about it, so that it may be repaired or removed, since responsibility rests on him if he is negligent.

He is frequently to inspect the beds with the prior, lest anything befall anyone. Together with the tailors, he is to arrange for straw or hay to be placed in each bed eight days before the feast of the prince of the apostles. When he distributes new garments, he is to receive the old ones in return.

He is to provide suitable linen cloths for the hands and feet, and likewise tablecloths for the refectory. He is to see that he always observes the abbot’s commands, and likewise those of the prior, the dean, or whoever holds the authority when the abbot is absent.

Neither he nor the secretaries or cellarers is to keep anything hidden under his care that is not known beforehand to the prior or dean, and the same applies to all offices. For if the matter comes to judgment and something is found among any of these brothers, it will be assigned as personal property and he will be plunged into punishment, as happened in the monastery of blessed Pope Gregory to the monk Justus. [Note: He was a proprietor, and therefore was severely punished by Gregory the Great, who was then abbot of the monastery of Saint Andrew in Rome, specifically in the year 589. His dead body was not buried in the common burial place of the brothers but was thrown into a dung heap.]

In the regular or household kitchen, he is to prepare all utensils and pots, except benches and small dishes, which are to be supplied by the cellarer and the superintendent.

## CHAPTER XLVIII. On the Brother Appointed over the Granaries

The brother appointed over the granaries, as an aid to the cellarer, is to perform the following duties daily. He is to have the grain for distribution and collection under his authority, keep the key to the granary, and take care to procure everything belonging to the baker’s craft.

In the storeroom he is to have an appointed place where he gathers the loaves under lock and key, to be carried to the refectory by himself or by a delegated person at the prescribed hours, according to the number of brothers. Everything remaining from the meal is to be managed under his supervision, except during those periods when the almoner is to receive it.

He is to receive the cooked dishes left over by the servers, except for beans on weekdays, which belong to him at the appointed times. He is to distribute bread alone, by himself, to the household members of all who arrive or remain in those places.

He is to care for the harness and trappings of the animals by which provisions are gathered, so that it is not neglected by the servants.

When the third day arrives, he is to have two bags for the brothers’ change of clothing—while the elders are standing at the morning Mass—and he is to come with the servants’ laundry vessel [Note: *Ablutatorium*, derived from *abluere*, “to wash”: a vessel in which dirty clothes are collected] to collect the garments which all the brothers remove, before the signal for the first or third hour, at the appropriate times while they are free from lessons, so that when the signal sounds they will have placed them in the appointed place.

The boys are likewise to deal with their clothing: when they remove their night garments before Prime, they are to carry them away and put them into the chest. When the bell sounds for Terce, they are to go together and put on their leggings, and only then carry their garments to the steps. Then they are to go to the privy, and on returning take up the garments and empty them into the chests established for this purpose.

If any brother, forgetful or negligent, delays putting his clothing there at the appointed time, it will in no way be washed later; and unless he first informs the granary keeper, he cannot have the task completed.

If anyone wishes to wash his own clothing, let him do so without reproach in the following manner. On a weekday, as soon as he has made the offering at the morning Mass, let him go and carry it to the appointed place in the cloister and arrange it there. Then let him go to the kitchen and draw … from the capital and heat it. As soon as he has risen from chapter, let him go and perform whatever work is necessary.

This is therefore to be observed: at the hours when the brothers are occupied with lessons, or when it is not the time for speaking in the cloister, he is not to presume to do this work. Each brother is to wash his own foot-coverings. A cowl and tunic are to be washed less often, but each brother is nevertheless to attend to them himself.

Whoever is so weak that he cannot perform this duty is to inform the aforesaid brother, so that he may have it done for him; for it is fitting that each person should fulfill his obligation in this matter.

The water with which everyone is to wash is not to run short at any time; the brother to whom the granary has been entrusted is to keep it under his care. He is also always to receive the kitchen linens and return them himself.

He is to receive from the refectory the dining cloths and towels, as well as the linens with which the elders wipe their hands, have them washed, and return them to the same brother.

The brother entrusted with this service is to take towels and cloths from the sick-house and return them to the aforesaid official for washing, so that they may all be restored to him together.

When Saturday arrives, if they have eaten once, as soon as they have left the refectory the aforesaid brother is to come and receive them from the servant by number. Then the elders are to go first, and each is to receive his own. If they have eaten twice, let them do in the evening as above.

The master of the boys is to obtain their clothing and return it to them at school, or carry it to their beds with some of them.

If necessary, the cellarer may take up the small striker from the cymbal, provided that they have prepared something better than usual. The brother appointed over the granaries is to arrange for the signals that are to be given throughout the offices, so abundantly that they do not need to be reminded. He is to distribute them to each person, except for the sick-house, where the servants assigned to that service are to procure what is sufficient for them.

## CHAPTER XLIX. On the Secretaries

### Verses to Be Written on the Chalice and Paten

The secretaries are to wash the chalices every Wednesday, and very thoroughly on Saturdays, and at all times, every day, rinse them one hour before Mass. These verses are to be written on them, two for each vessel, with a cross:

**V.** “From here the mystical sacraments of the Lord are taken.”

**V.** “O sons, embrace what you receive: me.” +

**V.** “From here the Lord’s blood is taken, poured from the body.”

**V.** “You who drink this draught, drink it with great trembling.” +

**V.** “The abbot named Vodilo made these vessels.”

**V.** “He presented them to the altars as a gift of King Henry.” +

### On the Tablets to Be Made for Each Altar, Dedicated by Their Names on the Walls

**V.** “With the doctrines of the word girded about by an outstanding voice,”

**V.** “In the wondrous sequence of Bartholomew who dwells here,”

**V.** “And likewise of the pontiff Martin, rightly worthy of reverence,”

**V.** “The altar shines, adorned with exceedingly bright splendor.”

**V.** “And for you, radiant nobles, this altar is consecrated,”

**V.** “To the supreme priest of the Lord, John, James, and Thomas,”

**V.** “And under the sacred name of Gregory and Augustine,”

**V.** “And also of Taurinus, the venerable confessor.”

**V.** “This altar shines, dedicated by the mercy of the Lord.”

**V.** “O blessed Father, pillar and leader of monks,”

**V.** “Columban, shining star, sweet Filibert [or Iberia],”

**V.** “By our honey-flowing name this house gleams.”

### The Following Is to Be Written on the Back of the Cross

The cross is the guardian of children.  
The cross is the head of men.  
The cross is the end of the old.  
The cross is the light of those sitting in darkness.  
The cross is the magnificence of kings.  
The cross is the perpetual shield.  
The cross is the wisdom of fools.  
The cross is the freedom of servants.  
The cross is the philosophy of emperors.  
The cross is the destruction of temples.  
The cross is the law of the impious.  
The cross is the rejection of idols.  
The cross is the proclamation of prophets.  
The cross is a stumbling block to the Jews.  
The cross is the gathering of the apostles.  
The cross is the destruction of the impious.  
The cross is the glory of martyrs.  
The cross is the strength of the lame.  
The cross is the abstinence of monks.  
The cross is the physician of the sick.  
The cross is the chastity of virgins.  
The cross is the cleansing of lepers.  
The cross is the joy of priests.  
The cross is the rest of paralytics.  
The cross is the foundation of the Church.  
The cross is the safeguard of the earth’s globe.

## CHAPTER L. On the Relics of the Saints

The image of Saint Peter contains these relics: a portion of the Lord’s cross; a portion of the garment of holy Mary, the mother of the Lord; a portion of the actual body of Saint Peter the apostle; and a portion of the flesh of Saint James the apostle. It also contains relics of Saint Stephen the first martyr; bones of Saint Sebastian and Saint Cecilia; and of other holy martyrs; and of Saint Gregory and Saint Innocent.

It contains portions from the bodies of Dionysius and his companions, and from their garments; a portion of the stone of the Lord’s tomb; a portion of the stone on which the Lord stood when he ascended into heaven; a portion of the Lord’s manger; a portion of the tomb of Saint Lazarus, whom the Lord raised; and a portion of Moses’ staff.

A bone of Bishop Saturninus. Relics of Saint Marcellus, martyr of Chalon; and the bones of the holy confessors Silurus and Agricola, bishops of the city of Chalon; and of many other saints.

In a silver chest are contained the body of Saint Marcellus the pope; relics from the actual body of Pope Gregory; and a portion of the hair of Saint Majolus in a glass vessel.

## CHAPTER LII. On Sick Brothers and How They or Those Serving Them Are to Act

When sick brothers have been sent to the sick-house because of their illness, they are to rise for the nocturnal office as soon as the signal sounds, and come to the oratory of Saint Mary. Let them pray as the Lord grants them strength, and then sit in their appointed place.

When the signal is sounded again, let them arm themselves with the sign of the holy cross and begin the Gradual Canticle. Those brothers who are unable to rise are to have the servants who attend them come and carry them into the church, supporting them with their arms, and place them there as well as they can.

No one ought to regard this as burdensome, since we have often seen a brother depart from this life on that very day and pass to Christ, even breathing out his spirit in the church itself. Who could doubt that such persons immediately enter the heavenly kingdoms?

Divine works are sweet to those who desire them, but appear bitter to those who do not. They are to perform the Work of God in every respect as do the healthy brothers in the monastery, except that they are to say it gently and rapidly. They are not to make pauses; they are to omit the “God” addressed to the ears; and, when the Work of God is completed, they are to return to the dormitory.

Those who are so overwhelmed by the severity of their illness that they cannot rise in any way are, as soon as the nocturnal office has been celebrated in the monastery, to receive the permission of the brother who holds the order for two brothers to sing the divine office for them.

When they rise from their beds as above, once daylight has appeared or the sun has already risen, they are to wash their hands and faces and assemble in the oratory of Saint Mary. They are to hear Mass from those priests who gather there early in the morning. If no priests are present, the brother responsible for them in the cloister is to come and give permission to whichever brother he chooses. They are to go out, and he is to say Mass; whoever wishes to receive Communion may do so.

At no time are the sick themselves to be allowed to pass a day without hearing the sacred office. None of them may read or sing Mass while they remain there, except that they may recite the psalms from memory or use the Psalter if they wish.

Before Terce, their custodian, together with his servants, is to have everything prepared: for each person, a little table three feet long and one and a half feet wide. On each table he is to place a small linen cloth, a measure of wine, and a pound of bread.

When the signal for Terce is sounded in the monastery, they are to assemble in the basilica of the glorious Virgin Mary and perform the appointed service.
