On leaving, whoever wishes to eat something in place of the mixed drink is to do so. If they wish and are able, they may celebrate Sext together and eat before the signal is sounded. When they are waiting for Sext, as soon as the signal sounds they too are to approach for the hour.

On leaving, they are to come and wash their hands, and go to eat. They are to say the verse at table, as in the refectory, at each serving; whenever something is given to them, they are always to bless it.

Whenever their procurator enters the door with small dishes, he is always to say “Say the blessing,” and the others are to respond, “The Lord,” with every expression of gratitude and affection. They are to say the verse after the food there.

They are to sing all the hours in the church. Whatever remains is to be returned to the cellarer, except for what is to be given from the meats or cooked dishes to the servants serving them, by the brother in charge of this duty. The sick brothers are not responsible for giving them anything.

On the days when the almoner receives bread and wine from the refectory, he is likewise to receive them from this lodging.

Whatever the sick request is to be given to them, even if it must be purchased. The Rule commands, after all, that care and solicitude for the sick be applied before and above everything else (chapter 36).

The responsible brother is to have in their cells everything they may need: utensils, hand basins, wine and water vessels, cauldrons, and kindling [Note: *Cremium*, from *cremare*, “to burn”: dry wood] for minor tasks. There are to be small dishes, their measures, and their cups.

When the brothers shave, the sick are to shave one day beforehand. If one of them is to go out on the following day with the elders, let him do so. On Saturdays, after Vespers, the servants are to have warm water so that they may wash the sick brothers’ feet.

All the brothers who are to go out [Note: Read *exituri*, as we have restored it, not *exusti*, as it is incorrectly read in the manuscripts] are to perform their bodily needs there.

The servants of that place are to prepare leaves, with great care and in one corner. When they are going to prepare the bathing treatment [Note: *Calefactoria facere*: a particular kind of bath in which herbs were boiled in water], the cellarer’s servants are to have the prepared leaves ready.

Whenever the lord abbot returns, he is to come there and inquire of each person concerning the condition of his soul and body, and whether he suffers any want or negligence from the servers or cellarers.

He is also to see whether anyone has recovered sufficiently for him to grant permission to return to the cloister, since no one may leave or enter without an order. The prior, or whoever holds the order, is to do the same.

The brother who returns to the cloister is to act as follows. As soon as the signal for the first or second hour sounds, the boys are to pass first; then he is to come after them in the choir to his own place and do everything as the others do.

In chapter, as soon as the words “Remember from our order” have been said, he is to rise, make satisfaction, and accuse himself of his negligences. Then the lord abbot is to absolve him and order him to chant seven psalms, or only “Have mercy on me, O God,” in place of a penance. He is to fall at the abbot’s feet, then come to the place where he previously stood and bow again to the abbot.

From that point onward he is to bow here and there toward the elders, first toward the abbot’s choir, and they are likewise to do the same. At the abbot’s command, he is to go and sit in his place.

When the boys have been brought into that house, one of the elders who are there is to take charge of them—one who knows how to provide for his own affairs and not neglect those of others. At the proper hours, when it is customary for the others to proceed with a lantern, they are likewise to do so. They are to sleep near the lights, not beside one another.

Afterward, when they go out for this purpose, they are not to make satisfaction either in the greater chapter or in their own chapter. The older brothers who do not eat meat there are not to carry a staff in their hands; satisfaction in chapter is not granted to them.

The responsible brother is to rest in the dormitory with the servants. During the hours when the elders sit in the cloister, those assigned to this service are by no means permitted to pass through without a monk to accompany them.

They are not to walk barefoot at any hour. Those who continually tend the light are to sleep on the ground before the lamps. After Compline, the sick are to receive holy water daily as they go out, which they are to find prepared there before the door.

Their custodians are to sprinkle holy water over each bed while carrying a lantern with them. After everyone has gone to rest, they are to inspect how each person is behaving.

A candle is therefore to burn in each of their cells until morning; or the cells nearest one another are to be arranged so that, when the lights are placed in the little wall windows, both are illuminated. If they have no other source from which light may be kindled, or if none can be found, a candle is to burn in each cell.

## CHAPTER LIII. How Companions Are to Visit Sick Brothers

We have omitted many matters above that we now consider worthy of inserting.

If any brother from the cloister wishes to visit a sick person, he is to request permission from the prior; without it he is by no means to enter. Once he has permission, he is to begin the psalm “O Lord, rebuke me not in your anger” on the way, and recite it during the journey. After the psalm, let him say:

“Our Father.”

“Save your servant.”

“Send him, O Lord.”

Prayer: “Almighty and everlasting God, eternal salvation.”

When he reaches the sick man, let him say, “Say the blessing.” Then let him ask him how he is suffering from his illness, and what patience he possesses, and let him offer him good encouragement. He is not to ask about bodily matters.

If the sick brother complains about some necessity, let the visitor come to the prior and say: “With your permission, I went to that sick brother, but I heard a complaint about such matters.” It belongs to the prior, if it seems appropriate, to provide for such matters.

### Likewise

The brother, however, who because of his illness is sent to the infirmary and sleeps and eats there, though he does not eat meat, may pass through the brothers’ community if he wishes to go to church, provided that it is a time when speaking is permitted in the cloister. Nevertheless, as he comes in, he is to say “Benedicite” and then leave. He is not permitted to sit or converse, nor to enter the chapter or the conference. Meanwhile, the brother who remains there until the day of his departure is to fulfill whatever he can according to the Rule. If it seems suitable for him to sit in the cloister, he may do so, and he may also come to chapter and conference; but he is not to be required to attend by custom if he is absent. Yet he himself should observe everywhere that we shall render an account to God for all the good things we can accomplish but do not accomplish, even for our thoughts—how much more for our deeds. The lame and the old, who burden the community or are infirm, are to remain, sleep, eat, and hear the Work of God in those very cells, and there carry out whatever they need to do. The brother responsible for those cells, together with his servants, is to exercise every care over them and provide whatever they need, so that they lack nothing.

### CHAPTER LIV. How the community is to proceed when it enters to visit a sick brother

Before chapter, the prior is to inspect the sick man and ask whether he wishes to receive the Lord’s Body or to be anointed with holy oil. The sick man is then to make his will known and make confession to the abbot or prior. When the chapter has arrived, after the sermon has been delivered, the prior should make known to the community the sick man’s desire and say: “It seems right to us that we should go together for the purpose of visiting him.” The community, therefore, should answer with genuine affection and love: “Since this is your will, we willingly receive these orders from you with thanksgiving, out of love for our brother and in obedience to your command.”

Rising from chapter, they are to go to the oratory of Saint Mary while singing five psalms for the dead. When they leave, the prior is to strike the wooden signal—if it is a time when speaking in the cloister is permitted, without prolonged conversation—and continue doing so until they return from there. When they arrive in the choir, the priest is to put on an alb and place a stole beneath it. Then there are to be four lay brothers: one is to carry holy water, another the cross, the third the thurible, and the fourth the sacred oil. The abbot is to intone the psalm “Have mercy on me, O God,” and they are to proceed in order: first the holy water and the cross, followed by the incense and the vessel containing the oil. The priest is to follow them, then the boys, and then the lord abbot; the others are to come two by two, according to their seniority.

When they have arrived, the priest is first to say: “Peace to this house.” The others are to respond: “Amen.” “The Lord be with you.” “And with your spirit.” He is then to make an incensation and sprinkle the holy water.

**Prayer:** “Almighty and everlasting God, who through your blessed apostle said…”

After this prayer, the whole community is to sing the following psalms: namely, seven appointed psalms, with the succeeding antiphons for each one, just as they are included in the collectary. They are to say everything they are to say in a measured manner, so that the priest can calmly complete all that he must do, while the others stand in order as they do in the choir. The boys, with their teachers, are to remain as is customary when they stand in procession for the king.

The priest is first to anoint the sick man’s sight and the other bodily senses, and, repeating the formula for each one, say: “Through this anointing and through his most merciful compassion, may the Lord forgive you whatever you have sinned through sight.” When the sick man has been anointed, the priest is to wash his hands. The infirmary’s steward is then to receive the water used for washing and throw it into the fire. Afterward he is to take the vessel, wash the sick man’s mouth, and put the water into the church’s drain or into the fire.

While these things are being done, the priest, with the four lay brothers, is to go to the church and take from there the Lord’s Body and a chalice covered above with a small cloth. Two lay brothers are to take the candlesticks, the third the thurible, and the fourth a flask containing wine. They are then to return while singing these psalms: “Have mercy on me, O God”; “O God, by your name”; “May God have mercy”; “O God, come to my assistance.”

When they begin to enter the house, all are to bend their knees toward the Lord’s Body, including the sick man himself, insofar as he is able to raise himself. The priest is then to give him communion and dip his finger into the wine. When the psalms have been completed, they are to say: “Lord, have mercy”; “Our Father.” **Versicles:** “Show us”; “Send him,” and so forth. After this, the same sick man is to kiss the cross, and all the brothers, including the boys. When these things have been completed, the abbot is to intone the psalm “Have mercy on me, O God,” and all are to withdraw in silence.

### CHAPTER LV. Another order for anointing the sick

If a brother is so afflicted by illness that it is necessary for him to be anointed with holy oil, the infirmary’s custodian is to report this to the abbot, or to the prior if the abbot is absent. If the prior sees that it is necessary, he is to announce it in the brothers’ community.

If the sick brother has sufficient strength to walk, he is to come to chapter, supported by one or, if necessary, two brothers. Prostrate before the abbot and all the brothers, he is to ask forgiveness for all the negligences and sins he has committed. After absolution has been given, the abbot and all the brothers are to prostrate themselves before that brother and ask forgiveness if they have committed any offense against him, so that the brother may likewise grant them absolution. After absolution has been given, the brother is to return to his bed. The brothers, however, when they have left chapter, are all to go together to the greater church—if it is not a time when speaking in the cloister is permitted—singing the psalms that are to be said after chapter. They are to enter the choir with the psalms, and the weekly priest is to put on an alb with a stole around his neck. The sacristan is to prepare a vessel with blessed water, the cross, two candlesticks, and a flask with holy oil. They are all to proceed together to visit or anoint the sick man, singing the psalm “Have mercy on me, O God.” When it has been completed, he is to say: “Lord, have mercy,” and so forth.

### CHAPTER LVI. How one is to proceed at the hour of death

As soon as the soul appears to be approaching its departure, the man himself is to receive communion of the Lord’s Body and Blood, even if he has eaten that very day, because that communion is given to him as assistance against the devil and his snares. If anything of life remains, the Passions are to be read, a litany is to be said by all for that soul, psalms are to be sung, and prayers are to be celebrated attentively. The servants are to guard him day and night, and he is to be watched without interruption both by them and by the brother who is their overseer.

When they see that he is already near death, they are to lift him from the bed on which he lies. They are to have prepared beforehand a bed on the ground, with a haircloth spread upon it and ashes placed on top. They are then to take the sick man and place him there as best they can, because a Christian’s son ought to depart only upon ashes and in haircloth, as we have already learned from many examples of the saints.

When the soul is now entering upon the way of all flesh and the wooden signal has sounded at the final moment, as is customary, wherever the brothers hear it they are immediately to begin “I believe in one God” and come there with all speed, whether they are in the dormitory or in the refectory. If the regular hour is already being sung in church, those whom the lord abbot—or whoever is in charge of the order—has instructed to go there are to come; the others are to remain with the boys in the choir until that ministry has been completed. If they are all in the refectory, they are all to come together.

When all have arrived there, they are to sing faithfully together the faith of the Nicene Synod, namely, “I believe in one God.” Once they are assembled there, if the dying man is still alive, they are to begin the psalter and continue until the soul has been separated from the body. Then all the bells are to be rung together and the Office of the Dead is to be performed. After the office, they are to say Vespers and five psalms.

When everything necessary for washing the body has been prepared, the brothers are to separate to one side with the boys, except for those who are to wash the body and place it in the bier. Once it has been washed, they are to dress it in a woolen garment, then a shroud and a cowl; they are to put shoes on its feet, but no trousers. Its arms are to be placed across its chest. They are then to spread a linen cloth and place a pall beneath it.

A priest wearing a stole but no alb is to be present, together with two candlesticks, a crucifix, a thurible, and holy water. Both those who perform this office and those who wash the body are to say the Office of the Dead and the prayers there, including “Incline, O Lord.” At Vespers only this prayer is to be said: “Grant, O Lord”; also “Hear my words,” and five psalms, followed by the collect “Absolve, O Lord.” If they remain longer, they are to intone the following psalms: “O God, with our ears”; “O God, the nations have entered”; “O God of vengeance,” and the others that follow; or the psalter is to be begun.

When everything has been completed, the wooden signal is to be struck, and the abbot or the weekly priest is to say: “Our Father,” and so forth, as contained in the collectary. With all the brothers preceding them with the cross, blessed water, the thurible, or the candlesticks, and with the response “Come to his aid” being intoned, they are to go first to the church of Saint Mary, place the bier there, and incense the altar. When the responsory has ended, the prayers “From the gate of hell” and “The Lord be with you” are to be said, followed individually for him by the prayer “God, giver of forgiveness.” Then they are to intone another responsory, “Alas! for me, O Lord,” and the body is to be carried into the monastery while the bells are rung, until it is placed in the appointed location. A crucifix is to be placed at its head, and candlesticks on either side, until the body remains there.

If those who had been recalled from the refectory for this purpose had not completed that order, they are to begin it wherever they left it, until the reading is finished; after the verse has been said, they are to return to the church.

As long as it is daylight, all are to sit beside the body and say psalms, except those occupied with duties that they absolutely cannot abandon. The armarius is to put on the tablet the names of the brothers who are to keep the first and second vigils, and so divide them according to the length of the night, or arrange that at each vigil they say the psalter with the Office of the Dead and its matins, and Vespers and five psalms after the office.

After the morning praises, if the brothers whom the prior has ordered to leave have gone out, they are to remain there and sing the same psalmody there that the others say in the chapel. Afterward, the teachers with the boys are to keep vigil for whatever part of the night remains, until the other brothers can come. Whoever can say Mass is to do so and return again to the body.

The morning Mass is to be solemnly celebrated in the choir for that soul. The bells are to be rung. Four boys are to be vested: one in the choir wearing a cope, another at the reading wearing a chasuble. The reading is to be delivered without a chasuble; two others in albs are to sing the responsory. The deacon is to recite the Gospel in a chasuble. Two lay brothers are to carry the candlesticks, and the third the thurible. The priest is to say only one collect: “Almighty and everlasting, who are never without hope.” All are to come to the offertory; afterward psalmody is again to be said. After the greater Mass, the body is to be buried, unless circumstances arise in which it cannot be kept that long.

When the greater Mass has been completed, the prior is to sound the signal three times so that all may assemble, receive candles from the sacristan, perform the service for the dead, and all stand around the bier. Those brothers who are in the infirmary and are able to rise from their beds are to stand there until the elders return; their overseer is to come, receive candles from the sacristan, and distribute them to them in the oratory of Saint Mary. The boys, on one side with their teachers, are to turn their faces toward the east, as they do in procession.

Two brothers—the armarius and one of the others—are to come and stand beside the dead man, crying out: “Lord, have mercy.” The weekly priest is to be vested in an alb with a stole and say the prayer: “Do not enter into judgment.” Afterward he is to take the thurible and incense only the greater altar and the body. The two brothers mentioned above are to begin the responsory “Alas! for me,” followed by “Lord, have mercy.” After saying the prayer “We beseech you,” the priest is again to incense the altar and the dead man; the two brothers are to say another responsory. The priest is to say the prayer “Incline” and incense the altar and bier.

The body is then to be carried out of the church and the bells rung. With the antiphon “Into Paradise,” all are to proceed in order.

When they have come to the burial place, the brothers are to stand around it as they do in the choir, with the boys placed in the middle, as is customary when they stand in procession in the church. The priest, with incense and blessed water—or the entire procession—is to stand over the grave. While the brothers sing the psalms, he is to say the collects. After the antiphon following the canticle “Benedictus” has been said, the priest is to pronounce, for all to hear: “Our Father.” When this prayer has ended, he is to say the customary prayers for the dead and the prayer “To you, O Lord, we commend him.” The bells are then to be dismissed and the candles extinguished. The prior is to begin “Have mercy on me, O God,” for the souls resting there. The priest is again to say “Our Father,” followed by the prayer “O God, by whose compassion…”

With the prior beginning again, they are to say the seven psalms, prostrate in the choir. If a brother dies before dawn, he is to be buried that same day, with all the observances described above. All the deans and other brothers who are within one or two leagues are to come with every expression of charity to assist at the vigils or burial. No one in the monastery, refectory, or infirmary—except the boys or those detained by a serious illness—is to take food or go outside before the body has been buried.

If he was a priest, priests are to wash the body and provide the entire funeral, carry it to the church, and place it in the ground. If he was a levite, levites are to do so. If he was a layman, laymen. If one of the monastery’s boys should die, everything is to be done for him as for the senior brothers. The boys themselves are to wash him, place him in the bier, carry him to the church, and afterward, at the appointed time, carry him to the grave or place him in the ground.

After chapter, once the wooden signal has been struck, no one is to speak in the cloister. All are to go to the body except those occupied with various duties. As long as the body of the dead brother remains above ground, no one is to speak in the cloister. On that day the boys are not to hold chapter, and the almoner is to receive whatever remains from the refectory, bread and wine.

If he departed before dawn or before chapter, the lord abbot is to absolve him after the sermon has been delivered; if he died later, this is to be done the next day. The armarius is to write the names of six brothers on the tablet, each of whom is to offer sacred hosts to God daily, without interruption, until the thirtieth day, for that soul. When each has completed his five offerings, he is always to make it known in chapter, so that another may take his place.

“By my voice” is to be sung by the brothers after the Hours; “Hear my words” after the matins of All Saints; and “O God, with our ears.” Until the thirtieth day, the almoner is to receive daily the due portion of bread and wine and of the entire allowance.

The armarius is to prepare brief notices for that soul, and the cellarer is to have them announced through the priors and deans, so that they in turn may transmit them through their dependent houses and to the abbots or monasteries entrusted to our prayers.

His clothing is to be sent to the servants to be washed. The washer is to receive one denarius for it. Once the clothing has been cleaned, it is to be returned to the chamberlain, who is to bring to chapter everything that was on the bed. There is no need to count each item individually; but to reach the smallest object, even a needle is to be brought—how much more the other things? If he has books, they are to be placed in the library, and each person is to act according to what he receives from that property and what is commanded him, making this offering **[supplement: prayers for the soul of the deceased]**.

If a brother dies after the greater Mass and it is entirely impossible to keep the body until the next day, he is to be buried that same day, since necessity permits it. On the following day, however, they are to celebrate the morning Mass solemnly for him, as is customary in the complete office.

If the deceased should appear to anyone in a dream the next day, that person is to make the matter known with appropriate satisfaction, because Saint Augustine says concerning this: “His angel does not abandon him as long as he is able to help him.” Those who were known to him, or his relatives, are to offer to God on his behalf, through intercession and a most salutary Mass, the sacrificial host, or an offering of alms; for these things the Lord will undoubtedly be propitiated toward him—unless the guilt committed was so grave that one ought not to pray for him. Thus blessed John says that one should not pray for impious dead persons; may it never happen that this applies to anyone from our order!

The lord abbot—or, if the abbot is absent, the person in charge of the order at that time—is then to absolve him and command all the priests to celebrate Mass for him. The other brothers, who are unable to do so, are to provide assistance through psalmody, as they have been instructed.

### CHAPTER LVII. The observance concerning a deceased brother who is seen outside the place

When a brother of our congregation dies in another place, as soon as the messenger arrives the prior is to strike the wooden signal, if it is an hour at which they can assemble. If the messenger arrives after Prime has begun, Prime and the morning Mass are to be said, and then, when all have come to chapter, the news is to be announced there. When they rise from chapter, they are immediately to perform the office for the dead while the bells are rung.

If they are going to the refectory and the prior receives the written notice before the small bell is sounded, they are to perform the office before eating, after the wooden signal has been struck. If the notice arrives after the meal and the midday Hours are not to be said by the brothers, the office is to be performed immediately, and permission is to be given to the servants to remain. If they are to say the midday Hours, and the wooden signal is struck after None, the office is to be performed after the verse has been said. Whoever customarily performs the office after Vespers that day is to remain, unless another messenger arrives. But if the office has been performed before None for this reason, he is not to remain.

### CHAPTER LVIII. Such observance is to be celebrated for the repose of the brothers

If one of the monks who are subject to our houses dies, and they are so far away that he cannot be brought to the monastery at all, the brothers who are stationed in that place are to do everything as is customary in the principal monastery for those who have recently died. When the messenger has arrived at the monastery, they are to perform the full office for him for seven days. The bells are not to be rung except for the one who is first celebrated; the due portion is to be given for thirty days, and “By my voice” and five psalms are to be sung for him. His name is also to be written in the Rule and in the Book of Life.

**Note:** [Col. 1293] The same book that was elsewhere called the Necrology, or the book in which the names of the dead were recorded.

They are to act similarly in all the places subject to us. If the place where the deceased brother died does not have enough priests to fulfill the thirty days of Masses for him, the monastery’s brothers are to do so.

Likewise concerning those monks who have made profession in the very place where they live: none of the brothers is to go to him to confess his sins, nor to that layman or cleric. He is to exchange his cowl, and on whatever day he is summoned from the prison of the flesh, one office is to be performed for him, unless the abbot sees fit, out of mercy, to order more.

Similarly, concerning monks who come from another monastery on some mission or personal business: although they may share our fellowship, no one is to disclose his sins to them, because it often happens that great disorder is caused in that very place. They are not to go to chapter either, unless the abbot orders it, or the prior if the abbot is absent. In the cloister, the young men under supervision and the novice brothers are to have no conversation with him.

Concerning those monks who have been received into our associations: when the messenger arrives at the monastery, he is to be delayed until the matter has been announced in chapter the following day. Then the lord abbot is to absolve him from every bond of sin, or the prior if there is no abbot. When they rise in chapter, they are to go to the church as soon as the psalms for the dead have been said. All the bells are to be rung, five psalms are to be said for him, and they are to finish. For an abbot, however, they are to perform the entire full office.

On an anniversary, if a cope is present in the choir and three candlesticks before the altar, and the deacon and subdeacon have chasubles, then, whatever sort of brother he was, they are to have the general office, and the small bell is to be rung at the meal.

A sick man who receives the habit outside the monastery, and dies there, is not to have anything done for him by the brothers except that his body is to be buried in the brothers’ cemetery or placed in such a place as is appointed for such a deceased person. Under no circumstances is he to be placed in a public cemetery. But if he is brought to the infirmary and dies there, everything is to be done for him as for another brother, and “By my voice” is also to be sung for him.

Likewise, when a messenger arrives concerning any professed brother who has died, the wooden signal is immediately to be struck, and they are to go to the church. All the bells are to be rung and the Office of the Dead performed. At that hour three candles are to be placed before the altar for the first Mass that they will sing for him, and one boy is to be in the choir wearing a cope. After the familiar psalms and “Let us bless the Lord” have been said, all the bells are immediately to be rung. Two other boys, dressed in albs, are to say the responsory before the altar. The deacon and subdeacon are to wear chasubles, and there are to be three lay brothers, two carrying candlesticks and the third the thurible.

When one of the parents of a monk of that place dies—his father, mother, or sister—and the news has been announced to him, he is to perform satisfaction the following day. When asked, “What do you request?” he is to answer: “I ask for the Lord’s mercy and your reward.” He is then to rise, and the prior is to absolve the deceased; the brother is to fall at his feet. The abbot, or the prior if there is no abbot, is to command all to say fifty psalms. Anyone who does not know the psalms may fulfill this with only “Have mercy on me, O God”; and anyone so ignorant that he cannot do that is to do so with the “Our Father.”

On their anniversary, the brother whose parents they are is to ask the priests privately, whenever he finds them, to pray for them.

### CHAPTER LIX. How the full office is to be performed when it is to be celebrated

At the vigils, after all the bells have been rung, three candlesticks are to be placed before the altar and for the Mass. For the morning Mass, all the bells are again to be rung. Four boys are to be vested: one in the choir with a cope, another to read the Epistle in a chasuble. At “Lord, have mercy” he is to remove it; after the Epistle has been read, he is to put it on again and remain in his place in the choir until the Mass has ended.

Two others in albs are to sing the responsory. Three lay brothers are to serve, two at the candlesticks and the third carrying the thurible through the choir, first to the boy standing in the choir for the office, and then to all the brothers. The deacon, in a chasuble, is to read the Gospel. When it has been read, the boy is to carry it past all those standing in the choir.

The priest is first to say the collect for the person for whom the office is being said, and then the other customary prayers. On that day the brothers are to have three cooked dishes in the refectory, whatever kind of day it may be, and drink is to be served to all the brothers with the sound of the small bell.

### CHAPTER LX. For the abbot of that place

At Vespers, after the commemoration of the saints, all the bells are to be rung, and Vespers for the dead sung. Five candlesticks are to be before the altar at that hour and likewise at the vigils and Mass. The office is to be as on whatever weekday occurs.

**Responsory:** “If I walk,” sung by two boys dressed in albs.  
**Tract:** “Out of the depths,” sung by two brothers in albs.  
All the other parts are to be celebrated as set out above.

For the anniversary office of emperors:

**Office:** “Do not deliver us to the beasts.”  
**Responsory:** “If I walk in the midst.”  
**Tract:** “You have moved.”  
**Offertory:** “Deliver, O Lord.”  
**Communion:** “I am the resurrection.”

If the brothers encounter the body of a dead person while traveling, they are to sing these psalms: “Have mercy”; “O God, by your name”; “Have mercy on me, O God, have mercy on me,” and so forth, to the end of the psalter, if they remain there that long. They are to proceed in order, the younger brothers first and the senior brothers afterward.

When they have reached the body, it is to be incensed and sprinkled with blessed water, and the prior is to pronounce: “Our Father.” **Versicle:** “From the gate of hell.” **Prayer:** “Absolve.” When this has been completed, they are to intone the responsory “Come to his aid, saints of God,” and thus carry the body to the church. When the responsory has ended, they are to go to the cloister to carry it out for burial. While the priest says the prayer “Do not enter into judgment,” all are to bow.

### CHAPTER LXI. How the offices for the dead are to be determined

**Note:** [Col. 1295] Under this heading the following verse appears:

“John was a man of law when he wrote these things.” In the same hand.

From the Kalends of November until Septuagesima, if the anniversary of the abbot of that place occurs, then at Vespers, after the suffrages for the saints have been completed, all the bells are to be rung, followed by Vespers for the dead. They are then to go in procession with Vespers of All Saints. On the following day, after the nocturnal service, the bells are again to be rung and the Office of the Dead performed. The same is to be done at Mass.

No tracts are sung among us for anyone else except for the persons whose names we now set out: for the abbot of that place; for the king and queen; for the bishop on the very day he is taken from the flesh; for the founder of that place; and for the four full offices that we have already designated.

For the aforesaid abbot, whatever weekday it occurs on, the brothers are to have the customary general meal and a pittance in the refectory, as well as drink with the sound of the small bell. The tables are not to be covered.

From Septuagesima until the Kalends of November, if this occurs, the bells are not to be rung except for the Office of the Dead, which is performed in the evening, and for the Mass on the following day.

On the anniversary of the dead, Mass is not to be celebrated before the office, if we intend to grant him the manner that he wishes to obtain—namely, from the feast of All Saints until Septuagesima, when the vigil of the dead is held at night. For example, if twelve lessons are read today, the vigil of the dead may be held on the following day after the nocturnal service. Finally, they celebrate the morning Mass for the anniversary itself.

During the season of Septuagesima until the feast of All Saints, when the vigil is held after the evening synaxis—for example, if twelve lessons are read today—we cannot celebrate the Mass of the anniversary itself on the following day according to the rite, unless the next day has arrived. In this way we are able to accomplish everything we desire. Likewise, the matins of the dead may either be said or … and thus they can be celebrated for them on another day with antiphons.

Some people customarily ask whether it is permissible to pray every day or offer sacrifice to God for the dead. They are answered as follows: many do not offer sacrifice for the dead on Sundays because of the special reverence owed to the Lord’s Resurrection—namely, because he alone among the dead was free. Therefore it is highly fitting that his unique Resurrection be celebrated reverently by all, without the inclusion of any deceased person.

### CHAPTER LXII. How deceased bishops are to be received in the monastery

When a bishop dies and is to be brought to the monastery, all the brothers are to be vested in copes, and the boys in albs. The prior is to begin “Have mercy on me, O God,” and so forth, and they are to go outside the gate with banners, servants carrying the body, two crosses, four candlesticks, two thuribles, and holy water.

When they have come to the appointed place, they are to stand in order as in a procession and sing these psalms: “To the Lord, when I was in distress,” through “Praise the Lord from the heavens,” if they remain there that long. But as soon as the body of the deceased arrives, they are to stop the psalms, and the priest is to say: “Our Father.” “And lead us not…” **Versicle:** “Do not enter into judgment,” and so forth. After the body has been set down, it is to be incensed, and the responsory “Come to his aid” begun.

While all the bells are rung until the bier has been placed in the church, seven candlesticks are to be placed both at the head and at the feet. It is then to be incensed again. A Mass with the full office is to be celebrated for him, with all offering. When the Mass has ended, the largest bell is to be sounded three times, and candles distributed to all. Two brothers are to begin: “Lord, have mercy.” The lord abbot is to say: “Let us pray. Do not enter into judgment.” He is then to incense the altar three times and likewise the body of the deceased.

When this has been done, all the bells are to be rung. Then the antiphon “Into Paradise” is to be sung. The entire procession is to be as described above, except for the banner; all the remaining things that must be done are to be performed according to the custom for a deceased monk.

### CHAPTER LXIII. How the offices for deceased laymen are to be performed

When a layman dies and is brought to the monastery, all the brothers are to meet him in the church. The lay brothers are to take the candlesticks, holy water, incense, and the cross. The prior is to begin in the choir the psalm “Have mercy on me, O God,” and the others, and they are to sing toward the deceased as they go to meet him.

The prior is to say “Our Father,” and so forth, as above. The bells are then to be rung and they are to enter the church. The priest is to be vested in an alb with a stole. Two brothers are to begin “Lord, have mercy.” The priest is to say the prayer. He is then to incense the altar of the Holy Cross and the body of the deceased three times.

When this has been done, he is to begin the antiphon “Into Paradise,” and they are to go to the cemetery in the following order: holy water first, then the cross, followed by incense with two candlesticks; the boys and lay brothers; the others are to proceed according to their seniority; and the bier is to follow everyone.

When the psalms and the Gospel antiphon “Absolve” have been completed, the priest is to pronounce: “Our Father. And lead us not…” **Versicle:** “From the gate of hell,” and so forth. As all return, seven psalms are to be sung until they are in the church, and each person is to go to his duties.

They are not to speak in the cloister until the boys have left and said “Benedicite,” if it is a time when speaking is permitted. If one of the middle-ranking brothers dies, as many as the prior orders are to go. The boys are to perform nothing at this hour. As many lay brothers as are necessary are to go in order to carry everything appropriate for this service. In all other respects, they are to act as described above.

### CHAPTER LXIV. The full offices to be performed three times a year for the parents of monks or for our familiars

At the beginning of Lent, or on the day before the Nones of July, or on the third day after the feast of the apostles Peter and Paul, or on the third day after All Saints, the following is to be written at the head of the page in the Martyrology:

“On the second day before the Nones of July, a full office is to be performed for seven days for all our familiars, as is customary for brothers who have recently died; and one due portion is to be given for thirty days.”

For an emperor who is worthy of it, it is to be written thus:

“On the third day before the Ides of July, the deposition of the lord Emperor Henry Augustus, dearest to our association and fraternity; a full office is to be performed, twelve poor people are to be fed, and the due portion is to be given for seven days.”

For the abbot of that place it is to be written thus:

“On the deposition of the lord N., abbot, a full office is to be performed, and twelve poor people are to be fed.”

Likewise for some friend:

“A full office is to be performed, and the due portion is to be given.”

Monks or friends are to be written in the Martyrology in this manner:

“They died: Adalgarius; Gerbertus, a monk of our congregation; and the deposition of the lord Conrad, king, and Henry, duke, our friends. Ihdimus, a monk of our congregation,” and so with the others.

In chapter, the boy is to pronounce it as follows:

“The deposition of the lord Conrad, king; Ihdimus; Fulcher, a monk of our congregation; and the other familiars of ours,” and so forth.

When they are abbots:

“The deposition of, or the death of, Hugh, abbot of our congregation, and Wido, our friend. A full office is to be performed for both, and twelve poor people are to be fed.”

The full office is not to be announced in chapter; rather, the names are to be written at the front of this book for remembrance.

For bishops, archbishops, or abbots who are monks and have made profession, it is to be written in the Martyrology:

“The deposition of, or the death of, Lord N., bishop or archbishop, a monk of our congregation.”

For those who have not made a vow of stability but have merely been received into our prayers, it is to be written thus:

“N., archbishop, died; the deposition of N., bishop or abbot.”

If it is a woman:

“N., a holy woman or abbess, died.”

Nothing else is to be written for servants except at the end, where it says: “And our other familiars.” If something concerning one of them is included, only the name is to be entered.

These are the people for whom we customarily give the full office annually.

**+ The cross-shaped mark reveals the name, as the order indicates.**

For deceased brothers, a brief notice:

“N., a monk of our congregation, died.”

At the end, his byname and the province from which he originated are to be written, so that he may be recognized.

For boys:

“N., a boy of our congregation, died.”

Another form, with a supplication, for monks:

“N., a monk of our congregation and cantor, died; for him we humbly ask all the faithful living under holy profession to intercede with the Lord.”

## APPENDIX TO GUIDO

[Col. 1299]

### PREFACES OF GREGORY THE MONK TO THE FARFA CHARTULARY

Partly first edited, and partly revised from published material, by the late Dom Ozanam, in the book entitled *Documents pour servir à l’histoire littéraire de l’Italie* [Documents for the Literary History of Italy], etc.

[Col. 1299C] In the name of Christ, almighty God, begins the prologue of Lord John the Grammarian concerning the books of this work.

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, to the honor and praise of the holy Mother of God, the ever-virgin Mary, our most glorious Lady.

While Lord Henry IV, patrician and emperor of the Romans, was reigning;

From the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ, in the year 1092, the fifteenth indiction, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of May;

By divine grace inspiring him, Lord Berard, most reverend abbot of this church of Farfa, descended from the noblest family of the city of Florence, decided to gather into a single volume all the privileges and charters of this sacred monastery, [Col. 1299D] as well as its tomes and legal documents, already almost entirely consumed by excessive age, and to leave them most carefully explained for the memory of posterity and transcribed with the greatest fidelity. This was done on the wisest counsel, lest—what we know has very often already happened—through either the negligence of custodians or the excessive ravages of age, the aforesaid charters, tomes, [Col. 1300C] documents, and privileges should be consigned to oblivion. In laboriously verifying them, we added, removed, or altered absolutely nothing. Rather, after correcting the corrupted passages rhetorically, we transferred them legally, in the form in which they had been written, through the hands of our confrater Gregory, a man of great discernment, born in the county of Sabina, descended from very noble parents in the fortress of Catinum, and nourished from almost infancy on the milk of our church.

Gregory, holy servant and attendant of Mary,

Desiring to attain the life of the everlasting kingdom,

Ever renewed the writings of that Blessed Lady,

Burning to leave behind, after death, a famous offering.

His father offered him, and Donadeus likewise offered him as a gift,

Restoring one hundred and ninety pounds,

So that, in the temple of the Theotokos [Greek: Θεοτόκος, “God-bearer”; genitive Θεοτοκοῦ], kindly,

[Col. 1300D] The brothers might receive the rewards of Farfa’s sacred rule.

Thus the first shepherd, Berard, made both of them monks.

A little later he migrated to heaven in a higher rank,

In the year 1068 after Christ.

At last, the younger brother Gregory, having been advanced,

And thereafter exceeding thirty years, more or less—

For after he had received the habit under the rule,

When twice ten years and twice four had been completed,

[Col. 1301A] After our first kindly shepherd had departed,

Berard, who was then abbot for the second time,

Ordered these carefully arranged sheets of the charters of the gracious Virgin

To be written, for he wrote freely, since he sought the rewards of life.

From these verses you will recognize Gregory of Catinum,

If you read again the letters that form the beginning of the statement:

“May Christ grant the writer to ascend to heaven.”

These are the beginnings of the book of Peter the priest:

For he himself offered ten solidi for the charters.

In the name of the highest God begins the prologue of Gregory, the writer of this book.

The industry of prudent men has above all been vigorous for this purpose: that they should record the deeds of the holy ancient fathers who came before them through the true succession of times, so that for those who followed them their victories might become impressed footprints, and their blessed memory might be recalled more worthily and held more dearly forever. The Apostle says, moreover, that “whatever was written was written for our instruction, so that through the patience and consolation of the Scriptures we might have hope.” For this reason, therefore, the times of the just have especially been recorded, so that, while we live, we may pass our own times in a more cautious and comparable felicity, without offense. For it is written that the examples of those just men who preceded us make us more cautious; if we follow their path, we do not stumble on the way. Finally, the wise man changes his conduct with the times without guilt.

But God, who is neither local nor temporal, but is present everywhere and remains everlasting, nevertheless chooses certain places devoted to his worship for the salvation of his faithful. These places are increased by the merits of the saints who dwell there and grow through him, who brings many good things to perfection. Every place is either increased by the blessed merits of its inhabitants or destroyed by the sins of wrongdoers. Truly, a place is very often built up through a human being, but a human being is only rarely built up through a place. God is also wondrous in his saints, worthy of praise and fear in every place without exception, because when he exalts the dwelling places of the saints on earth, there is no doubt that he prepares for them eternal and radiant dwellings in heaven. For as often as the places of the saints are increased through divine worship, so often do the reward and crown of those who built them increase in the regions of the heavenly homeland. Woe in every respect, moreover, to those through whose industry the decline of a divine place or the occasion of its desolation has come about. [Col. 1301D]

But let us, brothers, take every possible care lest in our own times we be found negligent in increasing the things that belong to God. Rather, let us strive to increase the places of the saints, so that we may be aided by their patronage and made equal to their merits—those who strove to work all things for the good and remained continually in the true faith. The merciful and compassionate Lord is rightly proclaimed wondrous in his holy and faithful servants, in whom he has worked innumerable wonders in individual places and times. With him cooperating, they performed marvelous and astonishing deeds, and left us straight paths on which to walk; in these they are always worthy of imitation and in every respect most fittingly [Col. 1302A] worthy of praise.

Among these, especially worthy of being raised up in praise are those who, following the example of the most blessed patriarch Abraham, departed from their own dwellings and left behind all that was theirs, hastening to foreign peoples so that, like transplanted trees, they might more readily produce the fruit of life and leave to posterity a worthy example of true living.

Thus acted our present father, the most holy man Laurence, who came to Italy from the regions of Syria and proved exceedingly acceptable to God and to human beings. For while he flourished in the greatest virtues in this region of Sabina and was honored with worthy distinctions by the entire people, he abandoned all the favors of the world and, desiring to devote himself solely to the praises of God the Creator, chose the habit of a more secluded and peaceful life. He assumed the monastic clothing and [Col. 1302B] built this holy monastery of Farfa, not from public resources.

At what time he did this cannot be known with complete certainty, because of the great distance of time and the desolation of that place which later came upon it through the barbarians. This, however, we know without doubt: as is stated, if I am not mistaken, in the privilege of Lord John, Pope VI, the venerable monastery of the holy Mother of God, the ever-virgin Mary, “which Laurence, formerly a bishop of venerable memory, coming from abroad, established in the estate called Acutianus in the territory of Sabina,” acquired there, because of his religious way of life and his assiduity in divine service, certain places both by purchase and through the offerings of the faithful, together with those who lived there with him. It is enough, therefore, to know that this holy cenobium was built by that most holy man, and not from public resources.

Since we do not know the time of its foundation, we have therefore preferred to remain silent about it rather than say something false or frivolous. We are not permitted to listen to a lie; how much less is it in any way fitting for us to utter one!

Nevertheless, in the authentic preface to its foundation we read that, “in the times of the Romans, before Italy was handed over to be ravaged by the sword of the pagans, three men came from Syria, namely Isaac, Julian, and Laurence, together with their sister Susanna.” Concerning the first of these two men, the blessed Pope Gregory—who was the sixty-sixth after blessed Peter and was elevated to the pontificate after the year 603 of the Lord’s Incarnation, ten months and twenty days later, in the second indiction, on the third day before the Nones of October, while Tiberius Augustus was reigning—thus makes mention in Book III, chapter 14, of the Dialogues:

“In the earlier times of the Goths there was near the city of Spoleto a man of venerable life named Isaac, who lived until the final times of the Goths. Many of our people knew him, especially the holy virgin Gregoria, who now lives in this city of Rome beside the church of blessed Mary, ever-virgin.”

And shortly afterward:

“I learned many things about this same man from the venerable father Eleutherius, who had also known him intimately and whose life gave credibility to his words.”

This venerable Isaac, then, was not born in Italy; rather, he first came from the regions of Syria to the city of Spoleto.

Prudent reader, consider what those “earlier times of the Goths” were, and what the times of the Romans were, before Italy was handed over to be ravaged by the sword of the pagans. It is therefore established that this monastery was founded a considerable time before the aforesaid most glorious pontiff, since the venerable Gregory of blessed memory described that blessed Isaac, companion of Laurence, the most holy abbot of this monastery, as one whom he had not seen and who had not existed in his own times, but declared truthfully that Isaac had lived in the earlier times of the Goths.

For the earlier times of the Goths, as may more reliably be believed, were those found in the written histories of the priest Orosius, when the emperor Arcadius was reigning, at the time when Ambrose shone at Milan, Martin—whose glorious death occurred 412 years after the Passion of the Lord, at the age of eighty-one and in the twenty-sixth year of his episcopate—shone in Gaul at Tours, and Jerome shone at Bethlehem; Jerome migrated to Christ after completing ninety-one years of life, and all shone like stars.

Radagaisus, king of the Goths, barbarian by character and nature and a Scythian, having with him 290,000 men, first devastated Italy. Later, while Arcadius’s brother Honorius was reigning, Alaric, king of the Goths, invaded Rome and burned part of it with fire on the eighth day before the Kalends of September, in the 1164th year from its foundation. On the sixth day after he had entered it, he departed from the plundered city, while the year 413 from the Lord’s Incarnation was being observed.

At that time, too, the most brilliant master of the whole Church, Augustine, was flourishing at Hippo. In the third month of the siege of that city, in the seventy-sixth year of his life, he rested in Christ. Then, while Leo was presiding over the Roman Church, Rome was captured by Genseric, after Alaric had first invaded it for the second time, forty-four years having elapsed from that event, in the 1208th year from its foundation and the 457th from the Incarnation of Christ.

After this, in the time of Pope Agapitus, in the year 529 of the Lord’s Incarnation, the Goths possessed the city and consumed everything around it through plundering and fires; Witigis was then reigning. At that time Justinian was emperor in the East.

Finally, after Witigis had been defeated, the Goths appointed Hildebrand king, who was killed in that same year. Eraric then received the kingship, but before a year had been completed he was slain. They then set Baduila, also called Totila, over themselves as king. Having gathered an army from every direction, [Col. 1303D] they again invaded all Italy, and entered the besieged city after thirteen [or, according to another reading, 101] days, in the time of Pope Vigilius and the emperor Justinian, namely 540 years after the Lord’s Incarnation, in the thirteenth indiction.

From King Arcadius, therefore, to Justin the Younger, under whom Narses, patrician of the Romans, fought against Totila, the last king of the Goths, defeated him, and drove him away, there are approximately 188 years.

We have related this at such length so that, prompted by the account of blessed Laurence, abbot of this monastery and companion of the holy Isaac, whom the most holy Pope Gregory mentioned and whom we have introduced here, we might explain as best we could what the earlier times of the Goths were. But lest we weary the reader [Col. 1304A] with a lengthy narrative, let us now be silent about it.

At what time this monastery was first destroyed, just as we do not know clearly or distinctly when it was founded, except for what is read in the same book of its foundation: after the death of the blessed and most holy man Laurence, the inhabitants had been driven away by the Longobards, who had been scattered throughout the surrounding region, and the place itself had been desolated and reduced to solitude. It remained without an inhabitant through many cycles of years, until a man of venerable life, Thomas the priest, came from the province of Maurienne in Gaul and stayed at the Lord’s sepulchre. There he was admonished by Mary, the ever-virgin and Mother of God, to return to Italy, and he found this holy monastery already desolate.

As for the fortunate and glorious period of this aforesaid abbot Thomas, by carefully and clearly assembling the years of the pontiffs, the times of the kings, the successions of the abbots, and also the indictions of the charters written below, we found it to have been around the year 680 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the eighth indiction, in the fourth year of the supreme pontificate of Lord Adeodatus, and during the reigns of Constantine, Justinian, and Tiberius Augustus—the Tiberius who captured the emperor Leo, who had overthrown Justinian Augustus, and thereafter held him in custody and seized his kingdom. Later Justinian Augustus had them put to death and recovered the principate.

## The Preface Begins

In the Old Law it is commanded that no one should be found sterile or without leaving offspring in Israel, lest he be punished with the penalty of a curse. In the New Grace the same thing is taught spiritually: that an unfruitful tree should not be found, and that the talent entrusted by the Lord to his servant should not be hidden away from him in the present, but should be left for the future to advance through an increase pleasing to God and through useful teaching.

Blessed, therefore, is the person who has passed through his days not sluggishly or vainly, but carefully, and who has left to posterity in the holy Church instruction of worthy usefulness, the fruit of good works, and the seed of a true inheritance. In them God, the Creator of all, is continually praised together, and the reward of the worker of good is increased in heaven!

By the grace of this God, with divine inspiration and the administration of his mercy, I, the least of monks and a sinner, Gregory, suggested to Lord Berard, the succeeding abbot, and to the principal elders that I undertake this exceedingly useful work [Col. 1304D] (sic). Since we must carry out everything excellent at the command of our spiritual father, and must hold most firmly to what we are bound to observe, and since we most truly believe that God almighty has divinely inspired within us the understanding he has given us, “to obey is better than to sacrifice.” From the teaching of the prophet Samuel we have learned that one who does not obey his spiritual father “sacrifices incense to false gods,” which is also to apostatize from God and is the sin of divination.

Therefore, desiring in every way to avoid this impious and detestable crime, and wishing in some manner to share in the holy work and truly earn the merit of obedience, I afterward most willingly accepted the burden of this work at the command of the aforesaid father and the other elders [Col. 1305A].

Although it seems impossible to me, nevertheless, since we believe that God can do all things—he who once commanded a dumb animal to speak human words—may he himself, for the sake of his most pure Mother, mercifully grant me the ability to complete this work most usefully for the restoration of her house.

I feel no strength of my own; rather, trusting in God’s charity and his assistance, through the intercession of our most glorious Lady, I have striven attentively to complete this work with greater fidelity and truth, as a highly devoted and exceedingly profitable undertaking.

This is not because I am sufficiently capable of correcting corrupted passages of rhetoric. Rather, according to the smallness of my knowledge, I have tried to correct what seemed excessively confused, though not so completely that simple people might think the original form of the charters had been confused, in which they had first been issued [Col. 1305B].

Especially, I did not sit secretly and alone, removed from the crowds, so that I could devote myself more attentively to quiet leisure. Instead, I was placed in public and could scarcely remain quiet even for a little while, as the solitude appropriate to this work would require. Nor do I see myself as sufficiently suited to this task, since I was not educated in the schools of poets, nor trained in the profundity of grammarians, but was nourished from almost the cradle in the schools of the divine services of this holy cenobium. I was fed faithfully on the wisdom of the Mother of God’s milk.

Therefore, just as I was ordered by the aforesaid abbot and the other religious elders, I removed nothing from what I saw in the charters, and added nothing in transferring the matters contained in them. Rather, I tried to rewrite what I perceived with my eyes as I wrote, and what I could grasp with truthful attention [Col. 1305C], except for the lengthy and useless repetitions of words and certain discharged obligations. I did this lest, being wearied for a long time by the many corruptions of the passages and lingering too long in writing, I should produce a volume that was slow to complete, tedious, unsuitable for examination, and immense.

Content, therefore, solely with the truth of the matters and the usefulness of their causes, with diligent and subtle discernment I strove, with Christ’s favor, to complete this most truthful work without any fraud, aided by the perpetual intercession of his Mother, the ever-virgin, whose assistance was also the cause of the undertaking.

We also took care to insert in each sheet of the charters the names of the witnesses, just as we found them written in the originals. But those which we saw had been consumed by extreme antiquity, gnawed by worms, and made exceedingly difficult to decipher, we omitted untouched according to an equitable judgment. We did not wish to insert into this most meritorious little work anything except what we could distinguish clearly with our eyes or grasp with truthful understanding [Col. 1305D].

Thus, just as I have obtained and transferred a most truthful and faithful rendering of the matters, so may I deserve, through the intercession of our Lady, to receive from almighty God the most certain remission of my sins, and to acquire everlasting reward for my parents.

Furthermore, we have given this book the name *gemniagraphum*, that is, “a record of the description of lands,” because in it we have inserted the lands of this cenobium, acquired by anyone and anywhere, and have gathered them together in a single volume for perpetual remembrance. We also decided that it should be called *cleronomiale*, that is, “the inheritance of the church of Farfa” (sic), since from the beginning it clearly displays its own freehold possessions.

We have prefixed the names of all the places, adding to each its own numbered chapter, and have most carefully noted in what documents one may find them. First, however, we arranged all the charters and privileges in sequence, as follows:

The venerable man, therefore, lord of this cenobium, the most holy abbot, devoted himself with great discernment to the increase of his monastery in both human affairs and divine rule. For when Faroald, duke [Col. 1306B] of Spoleto, learned of him through the blessed Mother of God Mary, he asked him to come to him at Spoleto and strove to commend himself to his prayers; through his own charter he also granted a considerable donation to this monastery.

Although many charters issued by him for this ancient monastery have been consumed by age and consigned to oblivion through the destruction that befell the monastery, one small copy of a letter is nevertheless still found. It was addressed to Lord John VI, the pope, so that by his pontifical authority he might confirm all the charters of this monastery, formerly issued by him to this monastery and to the venerable father Thomas. Its beginning is certainly believed to have been as follows.

## The Letter of Lord Faroald the Duke Begins

[Col. 1306C] To the holy and thrice-blessed lord, worthy of proclamation throughout the whole world, and to our father in Christ, Lord John, pope: Faroald, your son.

We believe that it is not hidden from your holy fatherhood how, for the love of God and out of reverence for holy Mary, the ever-virgin Mother of our Lord Jesus Christ, we restored, through certain donations of ours in the form of lands, servants, or tenant farmers, a monastery situated in our territory of Sabina, by means of Thomas the abbot, our commendatory administrator, and how, through the firmness of our charter, we established that venerable place there.

Therefore we have judged it useful to send this present letter of ours to your presence through the same Thomas. Thus we ask you, and as though you were present we entreat you, [Col. 1306D] to order that for future times your blessedness, for the sake of perpetual security, have a privilege made in writing for that place. Let this be done on the following terms: after examining the very charters by which, with the greatest devotion, we have granted things to the monastery of holy Mary, whether for the consolation of pilgrims or for the benefit of those serving there, may your holy fatherhood order them to be confirmed by such a privilege that no one at any future time may presume to commit any insolence or extortion, or to take away those properties from that holy place or from the donation of those servants of God. Whoever should presume to do this, may your holiness order him to be bound under the bond of anathema [Col. 1307A].

We greet you and commend ourselves to your holiness, and ask that you deign to pray for us.

[Col. 1308A] After the letter has been reread, we ask that it be returned to their monastery [Note: [Col. 1307] This passage arouses in me some suspicion that the letter was fabricated at a later time. For why should they ask that the Roman pontiff return this letter to the people of Farfa, when they could have obtained it more briefly from Faroald the duke himself? [Col. 1307A] Later times can furnish an example of this matter. I do not know whether those centuries, too, can show anything similar.] for perpetual security.

## In the Year of the Lord 1090: Aribo the Schoolmaster

[Col. 1307]

# The Music of Aribo

(Dom Gerbert, *Ecclesiastical Writers on Music*, II, 197.)

## Notice

We now publish for the first time Aribo the schoolmaster’s *Music*, addressed to Ellenhard, bishop of Freising, whose death in 1078 is demonstrated by Father Charles Meichelbeck in his *History of Freising*, from the twelfth-century Admont manuscript. We found certain fragments of this work in the manuscript of St. Emmeram, and have compared them in their proper places with the Admont manuscript.

The anonymous writer of Melk mentions Aribo: “Cirinus the musician wrote a *Music*, which, because of the speed of its measurement, he called a *caprea* [“doe”]; for, he says, it ran more swiftly while I was hunting it, because it was God’s will that what I wanted should quickly meet me”—as Aribo’s words below have it.

What that anonymous writer further relates about Saint William—namely, that a new measurement of the pipes was invented by him and transmitted to Aribo—is absent from the material concerning William himself. This should be thought to have happened because writers commonly say that William’s music was incomplete.

[Col. 1307B] To his lord Ellenhard, most worthy of bishops and distinguished in every excellence of character: Aribo sends what God has prepared for those who love him.

Father and venerable lord, I ask that the dignity of your presence be presented with my letters until you receive through the ears of mercy what my ragged pen has sent as a message. Although it does not enter wearing a wedding garment, I beg you again and again not to reject it before it has delivered its message.

Since you possess the greatest capacity in the rules of music and the monochord, as the diligent observance of your songs bears abundant testimony, I have presumed to choose you as a Palaemonian judge for the apprehension of a certain theorem—that is, a subject of contemplation [Col. 1307C]. After laborious application to serious matters, may you sometimes find in these things a relaxation, almost like a game, that gives pleasure.

## On the Fourfold Figure of the Moderns

There is a certain fourfold figure held in such high esteem by modern musicians that very few monochords exist without it. It is constructed in such a way that one series contains together the measurement of the first and second tones, the second that of the third and fourth, the third that of the fifth and sixth, and the fourth that of the seventh and eighth.

Its arrangement serves a convenience that is by no means negligible. For just as, after the indiscriminate and general series of the alphabet, vowels, semivowels, and mutes had to be brought together in particular groups, so, after the natural commingling of the monochord, the modes with their subordinate modes had to be distinguished more specifically. In the same way, the elements became more clearly distinct when they had left behind the bosom of their primitive confusion.

When the modes have been arranged separately, we perceive more clearly how the protus with its subordinate mode consists of the first of the graves, in A, and the first of the finals, in D. We also see more distinctly how the deuterus with its plagal mode is constructed as the second of the graves, the second of the finals, the second of the superiors, and the second of the excellents, in B, E, e. We see how the tritus with its plagal mode is constituted by all the thirds, in C, F, c, f. And how the tetrardus, with its plagal mode joined to it, is arranged from all the fourths, the fourth of the graves being in D, which is of a double nature: for just as it is the fourth of the graves, so it is the first of the finals.

All these matters will become clear in what follows, when we discuss more fully the nature of the principal notes of the modes and tetrachords [Col. 1308C], since the present treatise is principally to be entitled “On the Fourfold Figure.”

## On the Defect of the Fourfold Figure

There is nevertheless something in this same figure which, speaking as one of lesser wisdom, does not seem to me to be entirely clear down to the bottom.

### He Makes the Bishop Attentive

Here, father, turn both ears more kindly toward me.

As you ponder these trifles, be wholly attentive to them.

### On People Who Degenerate

People are accustomed to reproach someone severely when they see him degenerate from the virtue of his parents. We know, however, that this figure, and every musical figure, took the beginning of its origin from the primitive regular arrangement of the monochord. But when we see here what is dispersed there gathered together, and what is gathered there dispersed here, does not this figure degenerate from its mother, namely, the measurement of the monochord?

## On the Perverse Gathering of the Tetrachords

In this figure all the graves have been gathered into one place, all the finals into one place, and likewise all the superiors into one place, and all the excellents as well. The nature of the monochord does not permit this at all, since it assigns to each of the four tetrachords a different place.

## On the Perverse *Diezeugis*, That Is, Disjunction

In this figure the fourth of the graves, the first of the finals, the fourth of the superiors, and the first of the excellents have been separated. In the natural structure of the monochord they occupy one and the same place, namely, one and the same note.

## On the Unnatural Acuteness of the Protus and the Incompetent Gravity of the Tetrardus

In this same fourfold figure the protus is the highest and the tetrardus the lowest. Anyone even moderately instructed in these matters can easily observe how contrary this is to the nature of the monochord.

## On the Dictator’s Wonder

As I turned these matters over with myself in prolonged astonishment and investigated whether anything more natural might present itself, I discovered the doe, very like its mother. It has in one place the fourth of the graves, the first of the finals, the fourth of the superiors, and the first of the excellents. It has, in four different places, the graves, the finals, and the superiors. It has the protus as the lowest and the tetrardus as the highest, so that they do not lose in the little chambers of the daughter the nature they possess in the principal womb of their mother.

## On the Vermilion Lines of the Tetrachords

Four oblique lines, drawn in vermilion over the four tetrachords of the graves, finals, superiors, and excellents, penetrate the breadth of our fourfold theoretical system in such a way that they demonstrate not only each grave, final, superior, and excellent within the interval of its own mode, but also in its true and natural place, according to the condition of its first maker, which is found in the monochord.

## What the Fourfold Figure Explains Well and What It Explains Badly

The fourfold figure of the moderns correctly expresses each of the principal notes or strings assigned to its own mode. But it errs in this: it establishes the divisions of the modes in a place other than that which the monochord requires. It constructs the law of gravity and acuteness less well than it should, and what is greater, it distributes it without due caution.

But thanks and praise be to the Father of lights, from whom every good gift and every perfect gift comes—so that, with the psalmist, we may say, “Not to us, Lord, not to us, but to your name give glory”—for he both establishes the divisions of the modes correctly and clearly sets forth, according to the natural monochord, the difference between their gravity and acuteness.

## On the Natural Truth of the Doe and the Great Ease of Its Measurement

[Col. 1310A]

Since this has such great natural truth according to the most ancient origin of the monochord, it can be commended still more by the fact that the simple measurement of the monochord proceeds only slightly more quickly by this method.

Every tone, every semitone, every *synemmenon*, and finally the measurement of all four modes, is most evenly set in opposition to itself. But in the measurement of that which was the cause of this present work there is such difficulty and such inextricable confusion that its structure is exceedingly hard.

## Why It Is Called the Doe, and What Is Offered to the Bishop

Because of the speed of its measurement I have called the novelty of our theory a *caprea*, a doe. Since it came more quickly to meet me while I was hunting it—for it was God’s will that what I wanted should quickly meet me—I offer this same doe to you, venerable father, for tasting with the palate of your heart. If anything in it tastes good to you, may your soul bless me.

## What Convenience There Is in the Doe

In it you have an easy method of measurement, and a truth in accordance with nature that cannot be refuted; it represents everything proper to the monochord, as it should. For to construct a derived figure from the primitive monochord in any other way than the monochord requires is like making a left shoe according to the right foot.

How this has been avoided in our theorem is left entirely to your judgment.

## What Causes the Contrariety Between the Monochord and the Fourfold Figure of the Moderns

[Col. 1310C]

I believe, or rather I know, that the cause of the contrariety between the figure favored by the moderns and the monochord is that the arrangements of the modes begin in such varying ways: the first is preceded by the second by a tone, the second by the third by a tone, and the third by the fourth by a semitone.

They ought rather to have arranged matters so that the grave of the first arrangement, namely A, would precede the grave of the second arrangement, B, by a tone; that the grave of the second arrangement, namely B, would precede the grave of the third arrangement, C, by a semitone; and that the grave of the third arrangement, namely C, would again precede the grave of the fourth arrangement, D, by a tone.

This would be very easy if they began the complete measurements from a single starting point, or, beginning with the graves, observed the aforesaid diversity of beginnings.

But enough about the doe for now. Leaving it to the scrutiny of your favor, we proceed to other matters.

## On the Fact That the Monochord Is Divided Neither in Disjunction nor in Conjunction

It is believed that there are three reasons why the monochord is not confined to a single octave.

The first is that it would seem too short to simpler minds, who, with an unmodulated voice, do not know how to return to the lower register of the organ. Just as an untrained horse with a stiff neck cannot be turned within a narrow circular shield.

The second is that a higher voice charms the ears more pleasantly, just as a slender body delights the eyes more agreeably.

The third is that the natural capacity of the string and voice itself spontaneously seeks further boundaries [Col. 1311A], just as at times we proceed willingly, rather than out of necessity, into pleasant places.

## Why There Are Not Three Octaves in the Monochord

The sound of the highest string, extremely thin and consonant with none of those below it, does not permit the monochord to be stretched across three octaves. For just as boys produce melodies in the moderate height of their tender voices so discordantly that a man cannot understand them, like the trumpeting of an elephant and the chirping of a cicada, so there is a measure in things and, finally, there are fixed limits beyond and short of which the true cannot remain.

## Why It Is Divided into Tetrachords

The reason the monochord is divided into tetrachords rather than into dichords, trichords, or pentachords is that, after the octave, no arrangement possesses as much similarity as the tetrachords.

If the division had been made into dichords, dissimilarity would have appeared first, because after the tone from A to B comes a semitone.

If it had been made into trichords, diversity would likewise block the path. For after the semiditone from A to C there would follow the ditone from C to E.
