But if the division had been made into pentachords, the same troublesome dissimilarity would present itself, since from A to E there is a fifth, and there a semitone follows, producing dissimilarity.

## Some Tetrachords Belong to the First and Some to the Second Kind of Similarity

Some tetrachords, therefore, belong to the first kind of similarity, and some to the second.

The tetrachords of the graves, finals, superiors, and excellents belong to the first kind, because they are both raised and lowered according to a complete similarity: tone, semitone, tone.

The hyperboleon, diezeugmenon, meson, and hypaton belong to the second kind of similarity. Although, when compared with one another, they do not differ in their raising and lowering, since each is raised by a semitone and a ditone, and lowered by a ditone and a semitone, the raising and lowering themselves are dissimilar. In the former tetrachords they are most similar, because just as they are raised by tone, semitone, tone, so they are also lowered by tone, semitone, tone.

## On the Similarity of Neumes

The similarity of the tetrachords serves the similarity of the neumes. For the same neume that is raised from A to D is raised from D to G; and the one that is lowered from G to D is likewise lowered from D to A. The same is true in the other cases, as anyone can very easily observe.

## On the Fact That the Monochord Is Divided Neither in Disjunction nor in Conjunction

[Col. 1311D]

The reason why the monochord was not divided into tetrachords that were either entirely conjoined or entirely disjoined is that the aforesaid similarity would then cease.

If the tetrachord of the superiors began at G, where that of the finals ends, similarity would fail, because the tetrachord of the superiors would be raised by a ditone and a semitone, whereas the preceding tetrachords are raised by tone, semitone, tone.

Likewise, diversity would arise if the tetrachords were entirely disjoined. Since all this is sufficiently clear, there is no need to explain it more fully.

## On the Diezeugmenon and Synemmenon

[Col. 1312A]

The foregoing reasoning makes clear that the tetrachords *diezeugmenon* and *synemmenon* are necessary. For if the conjunction or disjunction of the tetrachords were complete, both their similarity would perish and frequent failure would occur in song.

### Why each higher and lower string should have a fourth and a fifth

Because of the *diatessaron* and *diapente*, which exercise great authority in song, every string or letter desires to have a fourth and a fifth above or below it. Hence F and f greatly need the *synemmenon*, so that the lower one may have a fourth above it, and the higher one a fifth below it, sounding back to it by the *diapente*.

### The common relation of the tetrachords

[Col. 1312B]

The same ascent and descent belong to all those tetrachords that ascend, namely, the tetrachords of the lower, final, higher, and highest notes. All those that descend—namely, the *hyperboleon*, *diezeugmenon*, *meson*, and *hypaton*—have the same ascent and likewise the same descent, although their upward and downward progressions are dissimilar, because their ascent is by semitone, whole tone and whole tone, and their descent by whole tone, whole tone and semitone.

### The difference between ascending and descending tetrachords

If you have the leisure and are willing to admit a reasonable explanation, I shall also explain how these tetrachords differ. They differ in name, which is obvious; they differ in quality, which requires explanation, because they are designated more by Latin names [Col. 1312C] than by Greek ones as the constituents of the three species of symphony—*diatessaron*, *diapente*, and *diapason*. They differ in species because one has the semitone in the middle, while the other has it at the extremity.

### Of which letters and strings each tetrachord consists

According to Guido, the tetrachord of the lower notes consists of A, B, C, D. According to Boethius, this is the *proslambanomenos*, *hypate hypaton*, *parhypate hypaton*, and *lichanos hypaton*.

The tetrachord of the finals is, in Guido’s notation, D, E, F, G. In Boethius it is the *lichanos hypaton*, *hypate meson*, *parhypate meson*, and *lichanos meson*.

The tetrachord of the higher notes, according to the moderns, is a, c, d. In Boethius it is the *mese*, *paramese*, *trite diezeugmenon*, and *paranete diezeugmenon*.

The tetrachord of the highest notes, according to Guido, is d, e, f, g; according to Boethius, it is the *paranete diezeugmenon*, *nete diezeugmenon*, *trite hyperboleon*, and *paranete hyperboleon*.

### How the tetrachords produce the species

Let us not dispute how these tetrachords produce the constitution of the species of the *diatessaron* and *diapente*. When the tetrachord of the lower notes is compared with the tetrachord of the finals, it completes all four species of the *diatessaron* in the following way.

The first [string] of the lower notes, joined to the first of the finals, gives birth to the first species of the *diatessaron*. In the same way, they stand in the place of parents:

[Note: [Col. 1311] An addition seems necessary: “the second of the lower notes and the second of the finals [produce] the second species of the *diatessaron*.”]

the third of the lower notes with the third [Col. 1313A] of the finals, and the fourth of the lower notes with the fourth of the finals, produce the third and fourth species of the *diatessaron*.

The same birth of the species of the *diatessaron* occurs in the conjunction of the higher and highest notes, and in the same natural order: the first species proceeds from the firsts, the second from the seconds, and the third and fourth from the thirds and fourths. This is necessary because the comparison of the higher and highest notes is nothing other than a repetition of the comparison of the lower notes and the finals. Thus whatever occurs between the lower notes and the finals must occur between the higher and highest notes, because the higher notes correspond to the lower notes, and the highest notes correspond to the finals.

### That the *diatessaron* and *diapente* consist between different tetrachords

All four species of the *diapente*, therefore, are found between the finals and the higher notes in the same way as all the species of the *diatessaron* are found either between the lower and final notes or between the higher and highest notes; and they are arranged by the same ordering of nature, so that the first species consists of the firsts, and each species consists of the strings and letters bearing its own number.

### That the *diapente* is not found in the places of the *diatessaron*, nor the *diatessaron* in the seats of the *diapente*

That the generation of the species is natural between the lower notes and the finals, and between the higher and highest notes, while the generation of the species of the *diapente* is natural between the finals and the higher notes, may be understood from this: the species of the *diapente* do not naturally proceed between the lower and final notes, or between the higher and highest notes, where the *diatessaron* has its natural seats; nor are natural seats of the *diatessaron* found between the finals and the higher notes, where the species of the *diapente* naturally proceed. By “natural species” I mean, as I said earlier, those consisting of the letters bearing their own names: the first from the firsts, and so forth.

### On formal species

It is timely to speak of formal species. Those species are called formal that possess form but not nature. For example, the interval from D to G has the form of the first species of the *diatessaron*, having the semitone in the middle. But since it does not consist between two firsts, but between the first and the fourth, it should be called the first formal species, not the first natural species.

The natural first species, however, is the one that not only has the semitone in the middle but also consists between two firsts, such as the species between A and D, one of which is the first of the lower notes and the other the first of the finals.

Thus the first species of the *diapente* between A and E is formal rather than natural. Although, like the first natural species, it proceeds by whole tone, semitone, whole tone, and whole tone, it does not consist between two firsts, but between the first and the second, like the species between final D and the higher note.

### That the principal strings are those constituting the modes

The principal strings are those that assume the chief place in the arrangement of the modes. Thus, in the authentic first mode, these are principal: the first of the finals, the first of the higher notes, and the first of the highest notes.

The final is rightly principal among the firsts. For if we begin a song according to the agreement that it first teaches us, and cannot proceed to the end, it shows that the song is either defective or must be governed according to another mode.

Some people sing the antiphon *Alliga, Domine, in vinculis*—“Bind, O Lord, in bonds”—beginning it on G according to the agreement of the final. But because a deficiency of strings occurs, so that it cannot be sung, let us consider whether it should be jubilated according to another mode or whether it is entirely corrupt. We ought not, however, first declare it false before testing it by beginning according to the agreement of all the finals, to see whether we find it faultless in any of the modes. For if we begin it on F according to the agreement of the first final, we can sing it through without difficulty.

The final must also be called principal because the beginning and opening of a song sometimes proceeds from it, as in:

*Ecce nomen Domini* — “Behold, the name of the Lord.”

*Ecce in nubibus caeli* — “Behold, in the clouds of heaven.”

*Ecce veniet Deus et homo* — “Behold, God and man will come.”

*Leva, Jerusalem* — “Lift up [your eyes], Jerusalem.”

There are countless other examples, which are very easy to find.

It is principal because the beginnings of distinctions sometimes rest upon it, sometimes their endings, or because they stand at some musical proportion from it—either a whole tone, semitone, semiditone, whole ditone, *diatessaron*, or *diapente*. It is rightly principal, since the end and repose of every song are in its dwelling.

The higher strings are honored with the name of principal because they join the principal parts of the authentic modes—namely, the *diapente* and *diatessaron*—by the bond of their middle point. Principal neumes, that is, the beginnings and endings of distinctions, sometimes reach them, as do the differences of the tones.

The highest strings are rightly principal because they rule the authentic modes so completely that their ascent ends in them.

### Which strings are principal in the plagal songs

[Col. 1314C]

In the plagal modes also, by the same reasoning, the lower, final, and higher strings are called principal. It is therefore not difficult to transfer the same analogy from there to here.

### That the principal status of the strings must be distinguished

The principal status of the strings must be understood discriminately: it is not to be considered everywhere, but within its own species.

Thus the first of the lower notes, the first of the finals, and the first of the higher notes are principal in the first species of the plagal songs, that is, in the second tone, whose constituents they principally are. I say “principally” because other strings cooperate, while these, as stated above, rule—just as columns are the principal parts in the construction of a hall.

They are likewise principal in the second species of the plagal modes, that is, in the fourth tone: the second of the lower notes, the second of the finals, and the second of the higher notes principally constitute it.

In the same way, the third and fourth of the lower, final, and higher notes are constitutive of the third and fourth species of the plagal modes, that is, of the sixth and eighth tones.

### On the authentic first modes

The first of the finals, the first of the higher notes, and the first of the highest notes are principal in the first species of the authentic songs, that is, in the first tone, which they principally constitute.

The second of the finals, the second of the higher notes, and the second of the highest notes are principal in the second authentic species of the *diapason*, that is, in the third tone, whose principal constituents they are.

Similarly, the third authentic *diapason* is constituted from the thirds, and the fourth from the fourths.

### That the beginning of similarity is found in them

[Col. 1315A]

The strings are also called principal because they are the beginning of the same relationship. By “relationship” I mean the similarity of ascent or descent, or of both, as when the ascent from A to D is like the ascent from D to G, and the descent from G to D is like the descent from D to A. For such agreement exists not only in fourths but also in fifths above and below, so that the middle point of one takes the elevation of the other and the lowering of the other.

When it is compared with a fourth above, its ascent corresponds to a fifth above; conversely, with a fourth below by descent, it agrees with a fifth by ascent. The exception is the lower deuteros and the higher [deuteros], which does not find a *diatessaron* below itself and lacks a *diapente* above itself, although there are five strings.

This also warns us to define the symphonies carefully. If someone asks me, “What is a *diatessaron* or a *diapente*?” and I answer, “Four strings” or “Five strings,” I shall not have spoken cautiously. For there are four strings—A, b, c—and yet they contain only a semiditone. There are five strings—B, C, D, E, F—and yet they contain only a *diatessaron* and a semitone.

Therefore let us say: a *diatessaron* is a semitone with two whole tones that share no interval. A *diapente* is a semitone with three whole tones that share no interval.

I say this because the tone from a to [uncertain letter] shares with the tone from b to c the interval that lies from b to [uncertain letter], which is the greater space of the tone [Note: [Col. 1315D] F.: “Of the greater semitone.”], called the *apotome*. Otherwise it could be proved that a tone and a semitone constitute a *diatessaron*, and that a *diatessaron* constitutes a *diapente*.

[Note: [Col. 1315D] Better: “a tone and a semitone.”]

### The resemblance of the rich and poor to the two kinds of mode

The authentic and plagal modes agree and disagree like the rich and the poor. Although the former dwell in a high place and the latter in a low one; although these [Note: [Col. 1316D] San-Emer.: “walk”] are represented as moving about in tragedy while those murmur in comedy, they nevertheless await one and the same death and end. Thus, although the authentic and plagal modes ascend and descend differently, they nevertheless receive the same finals.

### The resemblance of the male and female chorus to the authentic and plagal modes

The authentic modes agree and disagree with the plagal modes as if four modest brides, together with their bridegrooms, were to proceed from four bridal chambers and join two circles of dancers, so that the bridal chambers themselves were the centers of the female chorus—that is, the middle points terminating the male choruses—and so that in this too the books of the Evangelists might be represented.

Of these the prophetic Ezekiel declares: “The spirit was like a wheel within a wheel.” For just as the works of the Evangelists agree and disagree, so do the authentic modes with the plagal modes.

They have five strings in common, but three individually, so that the two circles are intertwined in such a way that the extremity of each cuts through the center—that is, the midpoint—of the other. They have a common middle space, while on either side there is a space situated without participation.

### The difference between the authentic and plagal modes according to Horace Flaccus

The authentic and plagal modes also differ in the manner expressed by a saying of Horace:

> “On feast days commanded to move, the matron  
> Will take part, somewhat bashful, among wanton satyrs.”

For it is not proper to a matronly gait to imitate dancing satyrs, as Alphesiboeus does, just as the plagal song does. It directs these beginnings and these endings of distinctions toward the fifth, while it rarely sends them toward the fourth. See fig. A.

### Another difference between the tetrachords

[Col. 1316B]

There is also a certain difference between the tetrachords, because the tetrachords of the lower and higher notes are the keys of the plagal modes, while the tetrachords of the finals and highest notes are the keys of the authentic modes.

The finals and higher notes occupy the place of the midpoint: the finals of the plagal modes and the higher notes of the authentic modes establish the *diatessaron* and *diapente*, and from these compose the *diapason*.

### How the tetrachord of the lower notes mystically pertains to Matthew and to Christ’s humanity

The tetrachord of the lower notes typologically corresponds to the humanity of the Savior described by Matthew. In it Christ endured every hardship: hungering beneath the fruitless fig tree, thirsting and growing weary beside the well, poorer than the foxes and the birds that have their holes and nests, since he had nowhere to lay his head.

### How the tetrachord of the finals corresponds to the Savior’s passion and death

[Col. 1316C]

The tetrachord of the finals signifies Christ’s life-giving death. For not only did he himself end his life for a time, but the veil of the Temple, the solidity of the rocks, the brightness of the sun, and the stability of the earth were also brought to their end.

### How the tetrachord of the higher notes signifies Christ’s resurrection

The tetrachord of the higher notes represents Christ’s glorious resurrection, in which he returned to the higher things of this life and entrusted to us the inheritance of the life above.

### How the tetrachord of the highest notes signifies the Ascension of Christ

[Col. 1316D]

The tetrachord of the highest notes typologically celebrates the excellence of Christ’s Ascension, in which “God ascended with jubilation, and the Lord with the sound of the trumpet,” showing himself to be supremely excellent.

### That two tetrachords pertain to Christ’s humility and two to his exaltation

Of these tetrachords, two—the tetrachords of the lower notes and the finals—are low, and therefore signify the humility of Christ, which was manifested in his humanity and Passion. Two are exalted—the tetrachords of the higher and highest notes—and they declare the Savior’s exaltation, which became manifest in the Resurrection and Ascension.

### On the disagreement of the tetrachords, and on the fact that some begin species while others end them

[Col. 1317A]

The tetrachords disagree because one is the beginning but not the ending of the species of the *diatessaron* and *diapente*, as is the tetrachord of the lower notes, while another is their ending but not their beginning, as is the tetrachord of the highest notes.

Some are both initiatory and determinative, namely, the tetrachords of the finals and the higher notes. For the finals determine the species of the *diatessaron* and begin the species of the *diapente*; the higher notes end the species of the *diapente* and begin the species of the *diatessaron*.

This occurs in such a natural order that, whether a species begins, ends, or does both, the first species is between the firsts, the second between the seconds, the third between the thirds, and the fourth between the fourths, whether it be a species of the *diatessaron* or of the *diapente*.

### How the lower notes begin the species of the *diatessaron* bearing their own names

[Col. 1317B]

The first of the lower notes begins the first species of the *diatessaron*, the second begins the second, the third begins the third, and the fourth of the lower notes—that is, D, which is two-formed—begins the fourth species of the *diatessaron*. It also ends the first species, insofar as the first final is likewise D.

### How the finals end and begin the species

The first final, namely D, ends the first *diatessaron*, but begins the first species of the *diapente*.

E, the second of the finals, both ends and begins the second species of the *diatessaron* and *diapente*.

F, the third of the finals, both ends and begins the third species of each.

G, the fourth of the finals, ends and begins the fourth.

### That, contrary to the rule of the finals, the higher notes end and begin the species

[Col. 1317C]

Conversely, the first of the higher notes, namely A, ends the first species of the *diapente* and begins the first species of the *diatessaron*, which the first of the highest notes ends.

### The opposition of the tetrachords

The tetrachords of the finals and highest notes are opposed to the tetrachords of the lower and higher notes. The latter begin all the species of the *diatessaron*, while the former end them.

The middle tetrachords are also opposed, namely, those of the finals and the higher notes, because the finals begin all the species of the *diapente*, while the higher notes end them.

The outer tetrachords are likewise opposed, as are the middle tetrachords. The tetrachord of the lower notes alone begins all the species of the *diatessaron*, while the tetrachord of the highest notes alone ends them. The finals begin all the species of the *diapente*, while the higher notes end them. The finals end all the species of the *diatessaron*, while the higher notes begin them.

### That three are alike in beginning, three in determining, and two in both

[Col. 1317D]

Three are alike in beginning: the tetrachords of the lower notes, finals, and higher notes.

Three are alike in determining: the finals, higher notes, and highest notes.

Two do both: the finals and higher notes individually. Only the lower notes begin, and only the highest notes end.

### That there is also opposition among the species of the *diatessaron* and *diapente*

The final and middle species of the *diatessaron* and *diapente* are also opposed to one another. For the ascent of the first is the descent of the fourth, and the ascent of the second is the descent of the third.

The first species of the *diatessaron* ascends from A to D by whole tone, semitone, whole tone. The fourth descends from G to D in the same manner. The second ascends from B to E by semitone, whole tone, whole tone; the third descends from F to C by semitone, whole tone, whole tone.

### On the opposed species of the *diapente*

The first species of the *diapente* ascends from the final D to the higher A by whole tone, semitone, and ditone. The fourth descends from the higher D to the final G by whole tone, semitone, and ditone.

The second rises from the final E to the higher b by semitone and tritone. The third descends from the higher e to the final F by semitone and tritone.

### That the opposition of the species resembles that of metrical feet

[Col. 1318B]

The first species of the *diatessaron* is constituted like an *amphimacer*, from a long, a short, and a long—that is, from whole tone, semitone, whole tone.

The second, in ascent, is like a *bacchius*, from a short and two longs. In descent it is like an *antibacchius*, from two longs and a short.

The third species of the *diatessaron* is, in ascent, like the second and, with respect to descent, like an *antibacchius*; in descent it is like the second and, with respect to ascent, like a *bacchius*.

The fourth is again like an *insulanus*.

### How the species of the *diapente* correspond to metrical feet

The first species of the *diapente*, in ascent, consists of a trochee and a spondee, as in *liberant*—“they set free.” In descent it consists of a spondee and an iamb, as in *convenerant*—“they had assembled.”

The second, in ascent, consists of a first epitrite, as in *Sacerdotes!*—“Priests!” In descent it consists of a spondee and a trochee, as in *Sacramenta*—“Sacraments.”

The third, in ascent, is like the second in descent, consisting of a spondee and a trochee. In descent it is like the ascending second, consisting of a first epitrite.

The fourth, in ascent, consists of a spondee and an iamb, as the first descends; in descent it is like the first in ascent, consisting of a trochee and a spondee.

### On the species of the *diapason*

The first species of the *diapason* consists of the first species of the *diatessaron* and the first species of the *diapente*; the second consists of the seconds, the third of the thirds, and the fourth of the fourths.

In these species of the *diatessaron*, *diapente*, and *diapason*, we rightly marvel at the natural order, because all end at the same point at which those species bearing their own names also end.

[Note: [Col. 1317] Perhaps read: “at which those too end (namely, the species of the *diatessaron* and *diapente*) that bear their own names.”]

### On the four species of the *diatessaron*

The first species of the *diatessaron* begins at the first of the lower notes, A, [Col. 1318D] and ends at the first of the finals, D.

The second species begins at the second of the lower notes, B, and ends at the second of the finals, E.

The third begins at the third of the lower notes, C, and ends at the third of the finals, F.

The fourth species begins at and ends at the fourth: D to G.

### That all the species of the *diapente* likewise begin and end

In the same way, the species of the *diapente* begin and end. The first begins at the first of the finals and ends at the first of the higher notes, D to A; the second begins and ends with the seconds; the third consists of the thirds; and the fourth of the fourths: E, c, G, d, as printed.

### That all the species of the *diapason* begin and end in the same manner

[Col. 1319A]

The first species of the *diapason* consists of the first of the lower notes, the first of the finals, and the first of the higher notes. Thus the lower and higher notes are the proper keys of its ascent and descent, while the final is the middle bond of that *diapason*, in which D is the junction of the *diatessaron* and *diapente*.

In the same way, the second species of the *diapason* is enclosed by the second of the lower notes and the second of the higher notes, and is bound together by the second final, E.

The third is formed from the thirds, and the fourth from the fourths; they are enclosed and divided in the middle by C, F, c, D, G, d.

### That the authentic species likewise consist from the other species, just as the subordinate species consist from those already described

Just as these four species of the *diapason*—that is, the four plagal species—consist of the lower and higher notes, while they are divided in the middle by the finals, the first by the firsts, the second by the seconds, the third by the thirds, and the fourth by the fourths, so the four following species belonging to the authentic modes are enclosed by the finals and highest notes, while they are divided or bound together by the higher notes: the first by the firsts, the second by the seconds, the third by the thirds, and the fourth by the fourths.

Thus the natural order, most perfectly preserved, may praise by God’s will the nature of things, illuminating every human being, since it has permitted discerning minds to investigate what lay hidden in nature.

### Whether there are seven or eight distinctions of the voice, since the *synemmenon* seems to be an eighth

The *synemmenon* does not make an eighth distinction of the voice, because the soft and square b never come together in one neume. Since every distinction of the voice is made either by a whole tone, a semitone, or consonances composed from these, and there is no consonance between b and [the other b], it is plainly evident that these two letters count as one distinction.

The neumes of these letters never come together as one, just as the Balance and the Ram are never seen together. The rising Ram lifts up the Balance, and the Balance plunges its fleece downward.

### That the division of the monochord is made either according to quantity or according to quality

The division of the monochord is twofold. When I say that the whole monochord is divided into two *diapasons*, or that a *diapason* is made by two steps, a *diapente* by three, a *diatessaron* by four, and a tone by nine, this concerns quantity and number, which belong to the measurement of the monochord.

But when I say that certain tetrachords ascend by whole tone, semitone, whole tone, while others descend by ditone and semitone, I indicate quality, which belongs to melody—as if I were saying: when the tetrachord of the lower notes, the finals, the higher notes, and the highest notes ascends and descends by whole tone, semitone, whole tone, you can make any neume resound upward or downward; and understand the same concerning those tetrachords that descend.

### Whether the mode called Dorian should be called hypomixolydian because D–d is two-formed

In ancient times there were only four natural modes.

Why I call four modes natural is worthy of examination. Since each authentic mode, together with its subordinate plagal mode, consists of the first of the lower notes, the first of the finals, the first of the higher notes, and the first of the highest notes, what prevents there from being one mode, since, so to speak, it is made from one set of strings, namely, all the firsts?

But by convention four became eight, though reason compelled this. Since any song could legitimately wander through eleven strings, and that course was assigned to each authentic mode together with its associated plagal mode, it often happened, because of the length of a song, that a verse or short psalm attached to it did not agree with it, since it could not complete its entire ascent or descent.

At last it was devised that each of the four modes [Col. 1320B] should be divided into two, each of which would be restricted to one complete *diapason*, so that each might match the course of its subordinate, just as, sometimes because of the weaker horse of one’s companion, we seek lodging nearer at hand.

### That the four-part figure and the doe imitate the ancient modes

The natural antiquity of the four modes is evident in the four-part figure of the moderns and in our doe. Their division is represented by our circular figure, which we constructed from male and female choruses.

### That the four modes are divided into eight

Our predecessors, observing that each mode, while still undivided, consisted of four principal strings in such a way that the strings compared on either side could produce two species of the *diapason*, divided them into authentic and plagal modes. They called the authentic modes authoritative and more worthy, and the plagal modes lateral and subordinate.

The name of subordination is also confirmed by their Greek names. The first tone is called *Dorius* in Greek; the second is called *hypodorius*, that is, the subordinate of the Dorian. Likewise the fourth and sixth are called *hypophrygius* and *hypolydius*.

They divided the *protus* by joining the first of the finals with the first of the highest notes placed on the other side, and established the first authentic mode, namely, the first tone. They compared the first of the lower notes with the first of the higher notes situated on the other side and composed the first plagal mode, namely, the second tone.

In the *deuteros*, they joined the second of the finals with the second of the highest notes placed on the other side and composed the second authentic mode, namely, the third tone. They joined the second of the lower notes with the second of the higher notes and established the second subordinate mode, namely, the fourth tone.

In the *tritos*, they joined the third of the finals with the third of the highest notes placed on the other side and formed the third authentic mode, namely, the fifth tone. Similarly, they joined the third of the lower notes with the third of the higher notes written on the other side and established the third plagal mode, namely, the sixth tone.

In the same way, in the *tetrardos*, they compared the fourth of the finals, namely G, with the fourth of the highest notes established on the other side and composed the fourth authentic mode, namely, the seventh tone. They joined the fourth of the lower notes, namely D, [Col. 1321A] with the fourth of the higher notes marked on the other side, namely d, and wished to establish the fourth subordinate mode, namely, the eighth tone.

But because they had earlier made the same mode, in the *protus*, an authentic species of the *diapason*, namely, the first tone, they refused either to possess or to call it plagal in the *tetrardos*. They failed to see that D–d are two-formed letters, naturally capable of constituting both a plagal and an authentic species.

Therefore, because of the [authority of the ancients; the text perhaps requires the word “authority” here: Note: [Col. 1321D] “Perhaps ‘authority’ should be supplied”], that two-formed mode did not acquire the name owed to its subordinate nature, so as to be called *hypomixolydian*, that is, the subordinate of the Mixolydian, namely, the seventh tone.

### How younger theorists understood the twofold power and nature of the same mode

[Col. 1321B]

The younger theorists, more carefully observing the nature and efficacy of the mode just mentioned, assigned it plagal formulas or differentiae:

*Octo sunt beatitudines* — “There are eight beatitudes.”

*Seculorum amen* — “World without end. Amen.”

*In illa die et cetera* — “On that day, and so forth.”

*Seculorum amen* — “World without end. Amen.”

*Dum medium silentium* — “While deep silence prevailed.”

### That Saint Gregory perceived the twofold operation of the same mode

It is entirely clear that blessed Gregory, author of nearly the whole of ecclesiastical song, recognized its twofold operation. In the authentic mode he loves not only authentic melodies but also plagal ones. Since his own testimony and that of Saint Ambrose prove it to be plagal, what reason have we to doubt that we should call it, as it is, not only Dorian but also hypomixolydian?

### That the same mode has the material of a plagal mode

[Col. 1321C]

Since the same mode has the material of a plagal mode, let us compose a plagal form from it. Or, if we can naturally deny that D is not the fourth of the lower notes and that d is not the fourth of the higher notes, let us grant that they are.

If we deny this, we shall be compelled by the following argument of our opponent. Every string that is the *synemmesis*, that is, the conjunction, of two tetrachords is the end of one and the beginning of the other. But D is the *synemmesis* of the tetrachord of the lower notes and the tetrachord of the finals. If it is the end of a tetrachord, it is the fourth string; but it is the end, therefore it is the fourth, since every final of a tetrachord is its fourth. This is an argument from the genus.

The major proposition is that what holds in all cases holds also in one case. [The following text is corrupt or incomplete.] From the preceding argument, the iambic [element], placed opposite, could ascend by a ditone, by which the two species compose a *diapente*.

According to the judgment of the ear, the preceding element, placed opposite, could rise by a ditone through a *diatessaron*. But the beginning of the preceding [element] and the end of the following are joined by no proportion.

Conversely, the preceding element, placed opposite, could ascend by a ditone through a semiditone proportionally, since both are enclosed within the *diapente*; but this would not produce a complete euphony.

### On the interposed interval

The interposed interval must necessarily be both ascending and descending: in the *diatessaron*, by a whole tone or semitone; in the *diapente*, by ditone, semitone, whole tone, and semitone. For the *diatessaron* has either a whole tone or a semitone in the middle. The *diapente*, however, has either a ditone, a semiditone, a whole tone, or a semitone.

### On the proper movement called mixed

Mixed movement is more venerable than all the others. It can be joined above and below to two *diapentes* or *diatessara*, and to a ditone and semitone; but in such a way that the iambic semitone ascends rather than descends, unless two semitones are joined together. For then each semitone, both trochaic and iambic, will ascend and descend more appropriately.

### On the distinctions of songs, and why the finals and higher notes are so called

Although the beginnings are to be considered, the endings of distinctions are especially important. They ought chiefly to repeat the finals, as lord Guido teaches when he says:

“Likewise, almost all distinctions should run to the principal voice, that is, the final; nevertheless, this is found less often than it is frequent.”

It is found in this antiphon:

*Nativitas tua, Dei genitrix Virgo* — “Your birth, Virgin Mother of God.”

*Gaudium annuntiavit universo mundo* — “Announced joy to the whole world.”

*Ex te enim ortus est sol iustitiae, Christus Deus noster* — “For from you has arisen the sun of justice, Christ our God.”

*Et confundens mortem, donavit nobis vitam sempiternam* — “And, overthrowing death, he gave us eternal life.”

The final voices seem to be so called for three reasons: because they end the legitimate ascent of the authentic modes; because they determine every song; and because distinctions sometimes reach their ends in them.

I say “sometimes” because they do not always reach them, but sometimes reach the higher notes and the beginnings and endings of distinctions; and, in authentic songs, they may reach the first of the notes below the finals, while in the plagal songs they may reach still lower.

The higher notes are so called either because they are the upper keys of the plagal song, or because they are situated above the finals as the mediators of the authentic *diatessaron* and *diapente*, from which they compose the authentic *diapason*, or because the higher notes are farther above the finals than the finals are above the lower notes, or the highest notes above the higher notes.

### On the useful species of the *diapente* and *diatessaron* in the authentic *protus*, which devise melody

Having set forth the benefits for modulation that we share with lord Guido—for we have not only explained his words but also proposed more useful species of movement, which he entirely passed over—let us proceed to the particular gifts of jubilating divinely granted to us.

Let us take only the authentic *protus* as our example, so that we may not despair of finding in the other modes the convenience of modulation that we experience in the species of this one.

The authentic *protus*, that is, the first tone, contains five species of the *diatessaron*: one first formal species, one second formal species, one third natural species, one third formal species, and one first natural species.

Each of these five has three changes: the continuous or dense saltatrix, and the ternary.

The saltatrix touches the last two strings; the continuous touches all of them; the ternary touches three. The saltatrix and the dense form are each twofold, in ascent and descent. The ternary is fourfold—twofold in ascent and twofold in descent—because there are five species of the *diatessaron*, each of which has two saltatrices and two continuous forms.

Five times four, or four times five, gives twenty. Since the ternary is fourfold, let us multiply four by five: this again gives twenty, which, added to the preceding twenty, makes forty.

In the same *protus* there are also four species of the *diapente*. Since each has two saltatrices, two dense forms, three quaternaries, and three ternaries, multiplication by four produces forty. Added to the same number previously obtained, these complete eighty changes, apart from those that can be made in the same mode by ditone, semiditone, whole tone, and semitone.

Once the number of the principal changes in the *protus* is known, it must first be considered that the neumes arising from the changes mentioned above are not all of the same rank. Some belong to the first dignity, some to the second, and some to the third.

The more distinguished among them should be admitted to the swanlike dances of the Muses; the rest should be left not to Orpheus but to outsiders.

All the saltatrices are praiseworthy, but they nevertheless seem to us more distinguished than to the Lombards. For they take pleasure in denser song, while we prefer rarer song.

The first, second, and fourth dense species of the *diatessaron*, both ascending and descending, sound well, but the third sounds more harshly.

Among the same kind of density, the fourth formal species of the *diapente*, and the first and fourth natural species, are sufficiently euphonious both in ascent and descent. The second and third, because of the hoarseness of the unnamed tritone, should be assigned to the *melibei* and the howlers, [Col. 1323C] except for the saltatrix, which is the same in all cases, apart from the difference of low and high pitch.

The ternary form of the *diapente* is threefold and has some degree of sonority. The ternary form of the *diatessaron* is twofold and less sonorous.

The second and third species of the *diapente* are rejected, except for the saltatrix. Let us gather the useful forms so that we may know their number.

From the second and third species of the *diapente* we shall reject four dense forms, six quaternaries, and eight ternaries. From the five species of the *diatessaron* we shall reject ten ternaries—two from each species. Thus, having rejected twenty-eight from eighty, fifty-two remain, suitable and useful for those devising songs.

## On the Various Opposition of Neumes

At times a *saltatrix* is to be set against a *saltatrix*, a *spissa* against a [Col. 1323D] *spissa*, a *quaternaria* against a *quaternaria*, and the other equivalent forms against one another; at other times they are to be varied, so that a *spissa* is opposed to a *saltatrix*, or to a *quaternaria* or *ternaria*, or a *spissa diapente* to a *diatessaron*, so that an admirable similarity or dissimilarity may commend itself to those who know how to discern it. Such people should seek not only this but also the proportion of the neumes, so that there may be a threefold sweetness: first, that of the chant, which is approved by the ears; second, that of the proportional relation of the voices and of the neumes to the divisions, which is the delight of reason; third, that of the beautiful similarity and dissimilarity of the six consonances.

## On the Nobility and Baseness of the Consonances

Of the six consonances, three are noble and three base. [Col. 1324A] The noble ones are the *diapente*, *diatessaron*, and tone, because they can declare their origin and parentage: the *diapente* is of sesquialter proportion, the *diatessaron* of sesquitertian proportion, and the tone of sesquioctave proportion. For this reason also we believe them to be less sweet-sounding.

## On the Consideration of the Constitutive Parts of the *Diatessaron* and *Diapente*

At some times we should consider the constitutive parts in the *diatessaron* and *diapente*, at other times their species, and sometimes also the insertion of the lesser consonances. The constitutive parts of the *diatessaron* are tone and semiditone, or ditone and semitone.

Sometimes we place the parts first, sometimes afterward; and if on one occasion we place or postpone these, on another occasion we place or postpone those. At times, too, we surround the *diatessaron* with its parts, with the *diatessaron* itself placed in the middle as their mistress. [Col. 1324B]

The constitutive parts are placed first, and the *diatessaron* itself follows, in this manner: “Behold, I send you as.” The intensified tone is placed first: “Behold”; the intensified and relaxed semiditone is placed first: “I”; the *diatessaron* follows, *spissa* through relaxation and *saltatrix* through intensification: “send you as.”

Both parts of the *diatessaron* are placed first—the tone, semiditone, semitone, and ditone—and the *diatessaron* follows, as in: “I ask you, therefore, Father, that.”

Sometimes the whole is placed first, to be divided into its parts, as in: “They arose.” This consideration is not to be despised, since in it quality shines forth dialectically. For the composition of the parts makes the whole, while the resolution of the whole reveals the parts.

The same observance should apply to the [Col. 1324C] *diapente*. Its parts are the tone, *diatessaron*, semiditone, and ditone. When these have been set before it, it follows in their footsteps, as in “the Lord’s laden beasts are expected.”

We say this not because it is always found in that form, but because it ought naturally to occur in that form: since without the parts the whole cannot exist, nor can it be absent when the parts have been placed.

## On the Fellowship of the *Diatessaron* and *Diapente*

At times the *diatessaron* and *diapente* serve together, so that if one *saltatrix* is intensified, the other *spissa* is relaxed; or if this *quaternaria* is relaxed, that *ternaria* is intensified.

Then one *diapente* may be compared with another, so that if this one rises as a *spissa*, the other descends as a *saltatrix*, *quaternaria*, or *ternaria*. Sometimes they are linked with one another through the mixed motion that we discussed above.

The same applies to the *diatessaron*: other consonances too [Col. 1324D] may either be lowered together twice, intensified together, or joined in a mixed sequence. And because of their pleasantness, these twin species, the *diatessaron* and *diapente*, display their fellowship very clearly in certain chants.

## On the Consideration of Proportions in These Species

In all these matters, then, let us observe the consideration of proportion. If the *diapente* is *saltatrix* in one neume, let there be in the other either a tone or another *saltatrix*, whether it occurs in a *diapente*, *diatessaron*, ditone, or semiditone, so that the response may be equal.

Alternatively, let us set against a *saltatrix* either a *spissa diatessaron* or a *quaternaria diapente*, so that the proportion may be double. Or let us set against a *saltatrix* a *ternaria diatessaron* [Col. 1325A] or *diapente*, or a *spissa ditone* or semiditone, so that the response may be sesquialter.

Thus nothing should be done rashly or ignorantly among us without subtle consideration of comparison. We ought to be altogether unlike those stage-performers who sing sweetly in jubilation while being completely ignorant of the true nature and proportion of singing.

All *saltatrices* in all consonances are compared in equal proportion, and likewise tones and semitones with them. *Spissae diapentes* are compared with one another in equal relation, or against a *saltatrix* together with a *ternaria*; or against a *saltatrix* together with a *spissum ditone* or semiditone; or against a tone or semitone together with a ditone or semiditone; or against a *quaternaria* and a simple neume; or against one simple neume and four repeated notes; [Col. 1325B] or against a tone or semitone and three repeated notes.

It is easy to weigh which consonances are joined in equal proportion. Let us therefore return to the comparison of the others. A *quaternaria* in relation to a *ternaria*, ditone, or semiditone is sesquitertian; in relation to a tone or semitone, however, it is double. A *ternaria*, ditone, or semiditone makes a sesquialter proportion in relation to a tone or semitone.

## On the Multiplicity of the Species

The *saltatrix* and *spissa* are twofold, since they have one kind of intensification and one of relaxation.

There is no *quaternaria* in the *diatessaron*, because it has only four strings, which produce the *spissa*. The *ternaria* in the *diatessaron* is eightfold: fourfold in intensification and fourfold in relaxation.

The *quaternaria* in the *diapente* is tenfold [Col. 1325C], because it is intensified in five ways and relaxed in five ways.

We have now discharged what we believed might be of some use to the authors of chants. See Figure B.

## Repeated Commendation of the *Caprea*

I commend to your favor, lord, the *caprea* that I presented to you, so that its very nature may commend it to your experience. It displays an evident division of the modes and has earned praise among modern musicians because of its fourfold arrangement.

But if the quadripartite arrangement is pleasing because it does this unnaturally, let the *caprea*, which accomplishes the same thing naturally, not be hated. If the quadripartite arrangement is praised for bringing all the graves into one line against the nature of the monochord, let our *caprea*, which gathers them into one line according to the constitution of the monochord, not be blamed.

The quadripartite arrangement separated the fourth of the graves from the first of the finals—something which the primitive arrangement rejects—whereas our *caprea* brought them together. If that perverse division is commended, let this natural collection not be condemned.

If the quadripartite arrangement, making the *protus* extremely acute and the *tetrardus* extremely grave, is celebrated by everyone, let it not completely obscure the *caprea*, which has in fact given natural gravity and acuity.

Let no one criticize the fact that the same letters are placed opposite one another in our *caprea*. Rather, let him criticize the claim that this could be done otherwise according to nature, since grave A is the grave of the *protus*, which according to the monochord differs by a tone from the grave B of the *deuterus*. [Col. 1326A] If A were not opposite A in the descent of the *deuterus*, which is in the arrangement of the *protus*, there would result either a perverse conjunction or a perverse separation.

If B were set against A, there would be a perverse conjunction, which I criticize in the quadripartite arrangement, where the graves of two modes meet in one place. But if the gamma of the *deuterus* were set against the A of the *protus*, there would be a perverse separation: the grave A of the *protus* and the grave B of the *deuterus* would be divided by a ditone, something which the nature of the monochord entirely rejects.

Why should we go further? I do not know in what respect the quadripartite arrangement surpasses our *caprea*, except in the difficulty of measurement. If difficulty is rightly considered more praiseworthy than ease, I know that this will produce admiration in many.

Nature has never said one thing and my *caprea* another.

## Useful Explanation of Guido’s Obscure Statements

[Note: [Col. 1325D] *Em.*: “flat.”]

[Col. 1326B]

“And let some voices have a pause twice as long as, twice as short as, or trembling in relation to other voices. Shortly afterward, let such a distribution of the neumes be guarded against with the utmost care that, whether the neumes are made by repeated notes of the same sound or by the connection of two or more, they should always correspond and answer one another either in the number of voices or in the proportion of the neume durations.”

It seems to me that these words designate three kinds of comparison in a chant. He wants the relation to be proportional, either in the interval between two voices—what he indicates by saying, “Let some voices have a pause twice as long as, or twice as short as, or trembling in relation to other voices”—or in our proportional consideration of the number of voices, which he intimates by the words “in the number of voices”; or there should be a comparison [Col. 1326C] in the proportion of the duration of the voice itself.

For these three matters to be understood more clearly, examples must be supplied.

A pause is twice as long or twice as short when the silence between two voices is double in relation to another silence between two voices. In the same way, a pause is twice as short when the silence between two voices is single in relation to another silence between two voices.

When he says “or let them have a trembling,” I think this should be understood as follows. A *tremula* is the neume that we call a *gradatus* or *quilisma*. It indicates the duration of which he speaks—twice as long—when accompanied by the following stroke; without the stroke it indicates the shortness suggested by his saying “or twice as short.” [Note: [Col. 1326D] *Microl. GUIDONIS Aret.* ch. 16.]

The second part of the proportion, described by the words “or in the number [Col. 1326D] of voices,” has, I think, this meaning. The number of voices itself must be compared reciprocally, so that neumes may answer equal numbers to equal numbers, double or triple numbers to single numbers, and at other times in sesquialter or sesquitertian comparison.

Equal numbers answer equal numbers, as in “The seed fell into good soil.” There are five voices in the first two words, “the seed fell,” and just as many in the following three, “into good soil.”

At times double numbers answer single numbers, as in “And he brought forth fruit.” “And he brought forth”: there are four voices, two in “fruit”; the comparison is therefore double.

At times triple numbers answer single numbers, as in *aliud*. The word *a* has one voice, while *liud* has three, because in the neume already mentioned we can count two voices in *li* and one in *ud*. [Col. 1327A] Three against one makes a triple relation.

At other times the relation is sesquialter, as in “a hundredth half,” the word *centum*: it has two voices, while *medietas* has three—one in *si* and two in *mum*—which produces a descending, that is, an inclinatory, result.

Three in relation to two makes a sesquialter comparison, and four in relation to three a sesquitertian comparison, as in “Come, O blessed.” “Come” has three voices, while “blessed” has four.

The third part of the proportion is described by the words “or in the proportion of the durations of the neumes, so that they correspond and answer one another.” Duration is the prolongation of the final voice, which is compared reciprocally so that both the number of voices and their intervals are sometimes equal to equal, sometimes double or triple to single, and at other times sesquialter or sesquitertian, and so correspond and answer one another. [Col. 1327B]

Concerning this duration or prolongation, lord Guido says:

“Duration—that is, the pause of the final voice—is somewhat longer in a syllable, however short it may be, but very long in a division.”

For example: “The Lord said to the Canaanite woman.” There is one division in “said,” and a phrase in “said to the Lord”; the division is “The Lord said to the Canaanite woman.” Let us consider the syllable.

In *dixit*, the final *-xit* should be prolonged a little. In *dixit Dominus*, the final *-nus* should be prolonged more. In *dixit Dominus mulieri Cananeae*, the final syllable should be prolonged for the greatest duration.

Let the musician determine according to which of these divisions he should make the chant proceed, [Note: [Col. 1327D] “Or . . .”: the divisions are absent in *Em.*] or what those divisions are.

Just as there are many divisions of meters—some Asclepiadic, some Sapphic, some Alcaic, and likewise [Col. 1327C] Hipponactean, with some also Glyconic—so the neumes of melodies have many divisions. One division consists of equal units answering equal units; another and a third of double and triple units answering single units; a fourth or fifth of sesquialter and sesquitertian divisions, with divisions equal to divisions, as appears in well-ordered chants, for example in the responsory:

“Behold, now is the acceptable time”—one division.

“Behold, now are the days of salvation”—another.

“Let us commend ourselves”—third.

“In great patience”—fourth.

“In many fasts”—fifth.

“By the weapons of justice”—sixth.

“Of God’s power”—seventh.

Nearly all these are commensurable, [Note: [Col. 1327D] *Emer.*: “Sometimes, as in the manner of a running horse, and more rarely the voices . . .”] so that the voices approach the place of breathing like a running horse.

[Note: [Col. 1327D] *Emer.*: “Very often, or rarely.”]

The notes, when composed densely or sparsely as appropriate, can provide an indication of this matter. [Col. 1327D] A horse, while running, strikes the ground more frequently with its hooves; when it is preparing to stop, it places its footprints farther apart. In the same way, near the end of the divisions, the chant should be arranged so that rarer—that is, slower—voices follow.

[Note: [Col. 1327D] “What . . . provide” is absent in *Emer.*]

But when he says, “The composed notes, densely or sparsely as appropriate, can provide an indication of this matter,” [Note: [Col. 1328D] *Em.*: “The distinction in writing and neuming is to be made more closely.”] the distinction in writing and neuming should be made more closely until the end is approached.

Near the end, however, the writing should be dispersed together with the neumes, so that it may provide the singer with an indication of the aforementioned slowness, in this manner: “Have mercy on me, O . . .” [Note: [Col. 1328D] Here *San-Emeram* ends, and what follows here is not connected with what precedes.]

For if the end is on the tetrachord’s fourth string, its beginning is on the first string; but this is the case here. Therefore D, according to this reasoning, is both the fourth of the graves and the first of the finals.

By this same argument it is proved that *d* is the fourth of the superiors and the first of the excellents.

## That This Proof Concerns the Matter of the Authentic and Plagal Modes

We have already proved that the often-mentioned mode established between D and *d* is as much the material of the fourth plagal mode—that is, the eighth tone—as of the first authentic mode, namely the first tone, and that it may truly be called both *hypomixolydian* and *Dorian*.

Since it consists of the fourth of the graves, the fourth of the superiors, the first of the finals, and the first of the excellents, it must be proved that the fourth of the graves and the fourth of the superiors are material to the plagal mode.

Alternatively, let us remove, if we can do so naturally, from the three graves A, B, C and the three superiors *a*, *b*, *c* the claim that they are constitutive and material to the three plagal modes, namely the second, fourth, and sixth tones. Or let us concede that they are material keys of the fourth plagal mode, ultimately the eighth tone.

But it is impossible to remove from the constitution of the three plagal modes the three graves and superiors set before them. Therefore it is possible, and entirely true, to concede that the fourth of the graves and the fourth of the superiors are essential to the fourth plagal mode, that is, the eighth tone.

## On the Characteristic Properties of the *Proti*, *Deuteri*, *Triti*, and *Tetrardi*

[Col. 1328C] The characteristic property of the *proti* is that they correspond in elevation through the *diapente* and in descent through the tone.

The characteristic property of the *deuteri* is that they correspond in elevation through a complete *diatessaron* and in descent through a ditone.

The characteristic property of the *triti* is that they correspond in intensification through a ditone and in relaxation through a *diatessaron*.

The characteristic property of the *tetrardi* is that they are opposed to the *proti*, so that the elevation of the former is the relaxation of the latter.

## That No Argument Is Stronger Than Characteristic Property

Although it has been sufficiently proved that the material of the plagal mode—namely, the fourth of the graves, the fourth of the superiors, the fourth plagal species, that is, the eighth tone—can be conformed in this way, for we cannot truly deny that a stylus of gold can be made from gold, nevertheless [Col. 1328D] we still wish to do violence to the sufficiency of the matter by supplying an abundance of arguments that are not necessary.

We cannot find a more effective argument than the characteristic property itself. Nor did we rashly decide to place the properties of the modes beforehand. Let us see whether D and *d* can possess the properties both of the *tetrardus* and of the *protus*.

The property of the *tetrardi* is that the intensification of the *proti* is their relaxation. But D is relaxed through tone, [Col. 1329A] semitone, tone, just as A, the *protus*, is intensified through tone, semitone, tone.

## That Species and Their Proper Characteristics Are Predicated Equally of One Another

Every human being is capable of laughter, and everything capable of laughter is human. Every *tetrardus* is capable of being relaxed through tone, semitone, tone, and every relaxation through tone, semitone, tone is a *tetrardus*.

But D and *d* are relaxed through tone, semitone, tone; therefore they are *tetrardi*. If they are *tetrardi*, then they are either authentic or plagal. They must be plagal, because no authentic mode consists of graves and superiors.

Having completed these incontrovertible arguments and brought to an end our lengthy examination of its nature, let us baptize this same mode, calling it *hypomixolydian*, so that it may be binominal, just as we know it to be two-formed. [Col. 1329B]

## Why They Are Called Modes

They are called modes from returning, because wherever the chant may ascend or descend, it ultimately returns to its final dwelling place.

## Whether the *Trite Synemmenon* Should Be Placed Below or Above the Transductive Line, and Whether the Flat, Rounded *B* Is More or Less Necessary Than the Square One

The cause is older than the effect, just as fire precedes combustion. Since the gap of the *diezeuxis*—that is, the disjunction of the tetrachords—had presented our forebears with many obstacles to singing, the final *tritus* F lacked a fifth above it, and the excellent *tritus f* lacked a fifth below it. They inserted the *trite synemmenon* [Col. 1329C] to remedy the defect of the jubilation.

There the cause is the *diezeuxis*, while the insertion of the *synemmenon* is the effect; therefore the latter is subsequent. What is later in invention should also be later in position, like a newcomer in another’s house.

Once received, however, just as the iamb received the stable spondees into its paternal rights—conveniently and patiently—not so that it would yield its second place or take a fourth place in fellowship, so the *synemmenon* should be placed below, not above.

We can assess which of these strings is more useful if we distinguish which one is more frequently used.

## That the *Tritus* Especially Needs the *Synemmenon*, Since It Supplies the Place of the Superior *Tritus*

The chants of the fifth and sixth tones especially need the *synemmenon*, since it acts as the substitute of the superior *tritus*. [Col. 1329D] It also sings along with the *protus*, but very rarely, as in “Behold the name of the Lord” (*v. d. l.*).

The square *B*, however, occurs constantly not only in the *deuterus*, which is its domestic mode, but also in the *protus*, the *tetrardus*, and even in the *tritus* itself. Although it is not joined to the familiar *tritus* by proximity, since it is separated from neither the final F nor the excellent *f* by any consonance, it is nevertheless possible to judge from this that the flat *b* is useful, while the other sign is much more useful, and therefore much more convenient in conjunction and disjunction.

For this reason, from their more frequent and rarer usefulness, we may conclude that the sign below *b* and above the other sign should be marked in this way.

## That the Fifth, Sixth, Seventh, and Eighth Species of the *Diapason* Should Not Be So Called, Although There Are Eight

[Col. 1330A]

Although there are eight species of the *diapason*, the truth of nature does not permit the fifth, sixth, seventh, and eighth to be so called.

Since every whole is rightly named from its parts, we must consider the same matter in the whole *diapason* and in its parts, namely the *diatessaron* and *diapente*. We know that there are no more than four species of the *diatessaron* and *diapente*. But since the species of the *diapason* are constituted from the species of the *diapente* and *diatessaron*, there cannot be more species than there are species of the parts.

There are four species of the *diapason* in which the *diatessaron* precedes and the *diapente* follows; these are the plagal species. There are four others in which the *diapente* precedes and the *diatessaron* follows; these are the authentic species. It is therefore plainly evident that there are eight species, but that none of them can truly be called the fifth, since there is neither a fifth species of the *diatessaron* nor of the *diapente*.

Who would say that a wooden hall was constructed from parts that were not wood? Likewise, who would say that the fifth species of the *diapason* was composed of fifth parts, when there is no fifth *diapente* and no fifth *diatessaron*, which are the constitutive parts of the *diapason*?

Nevertheless, there are eight species of the *diapason*, although there is no fifth, because the number eight is correctly possessed and counted where the number four is doubled. There are four authentic species of the *diapason* and four plagal species, which complete the number eight; nevertheless, as we have said, none can truly be called the fifth.

## On the Resemblance of a Creature That Bears Twins Four Times

[Col. 1330C]

Let us imagine some creature so fertile that it bears twins on four occasions. We may call some of them first-born siblings, or, so to speak, second-born, third-born, and fourth-born; but we cannot call any fifth-born, since none of them was born on a fifth occasion, although we do not doubt that there are eight of them.

## That Some May Say There Is One Muse, or Two, Three, Four, Five, Six, Seven, Eight, or Nine, According to Various Proportions

We can assert that there is one muse: the universal monochord of the human voice, which, from the single pipe of the throat, most effectively sings in jubilation every kind of melody. No hydraulic instrument and no other pipe can be compared with it.

Since this one performs the office of all the others, we may conjecture that there are two muses in the duality of authentic and plagal modes, or in the duality of striking and blowing. One serves cymbals and strings, the other pipes and flutes. Or there are two in the divided nature of arsis and thesis, that is, elevation and descent, without which no musical sound occurs.

What is music? Movement of voices. Every movement of a voice occurs either through arsis or through thesis.

We understand three muses, not unreasonably, as the three genera of music: diatonic, chromatic, and enharmonic. Or there are three muses in the mixture of the human voice with striking and blowing, resounding like a siren among marine rocks.

It receives its name from Greek. *Syrin* (συρειν) in Greek means “to draw together,” from which *syrtes* are named, places where sands are drawn together. Hence also the comic poet is called a *Syrus*, because by his cleverness he had drawn fugitive money to himself. [Col. 1331A]

There are few things in stories that are not derived from some source of truth. They say that sirens are singing women of the sea who kill unwary sailors, lured toward them by sweeter melodies. Certain hollow rocks rise from the sea, and in them the clash of storms imitates a sweet-sounding melody. By its sweetness it draws passing sailors toward itself and sometimes sinks them in a pitiable shipwreck.

So too the sirens of this world—namely, its enticements—flatter us and, like those sailors, sink us in the most perilous shipwreck of our souls.

We do not rashly suppose that there are four muses, whether the four continuous [Col. 1331B] modes of the ancients that we mentioned above, or the four tetrachords G, F, S, E, which possess the whole melody; or the four Pythagorean hammers, through which he discovered the proportions of the four symphonies—tone, *diatessaron*, *diapente*, and *diapason*; or the quadripartite division of the monochord, which, in ascending, establishes the *diatessaron* at the first constitutive step, the *diapente* at the second, and the *diapason* at the third, while in descending it establishes, conversely, the *diapason* at the first constitutive step, the *diapente* at the second, and the *diatessaron* at the third.

We believe there are five muses in the five greater symphonies: sesquitertian, sesquialter, double, triple, and quadruple; or in the five vowels, without which articulated sounds cannot be formed; or we may refer all letters, divided in five ways, to the five muses: some [Col. 1331C] are vowels, some [I] semivowels, some [II] mutes, others liquids, and [III] [IV] some doubles. Or [V] we may understand five muses as the five harmful windows of the senses, through which the soul drinks temporal pleasures and muses.

Let us consider six muses as the six lesser consonances: semitone, tone, semiditone, ditone, *diatessaron*, and *diapente*, by which every regular neume is formed. These six alone lord Guido loved.

Let us take seven muses as the seven distinctions of voices, since the remaining ones are not additions but repetitions of the same ones; or as the seven planets.

Let us understand eight muses as the eight tones, by whose guidance [Col. 1331D] we arrange and govern the whole body of the chant.

All antiquity agreed that there are nine muses, an imitation of the cosmic music contained in nine circles. The two circles of heaven and earth, joined to the seven planets, complete the number nine. In imitation of this, they counted nine muses in our earthly music, namely nine consonances: unison voices, semitone, tone, semiditone, ditone, *diatessaron*, *diapason*, *diapente* with semitone, and *diapente* with tone.

Examples of unison voices are: “Help us, O God” (*s. n.*). An example of a semitone is: “Gabriel was sent to Mary” (*G. a. ad M.*). But it is childish to use examples of such obvious matters.

Let us give examples only of the last two, [Col. 1332A] namely the *diapente* with semitone and the *diapente* with tone, since these are both less proportional and less common. The *diapente* with semitone sounds at the beginning of the hymn “Sea, fountain, gate”; the *diapente* with tone occurs in “To you I have lifted my soul, O my God (*m. d. m.*), in you,” and in “Now you are no longer guests (*h.*) and strangers, but citizens with the saints (*s.*) and members of the household.”

## On the Simple Measurement of Cymbals in Sesquitertian and Sesquialter Proportion, Intensified and Relaxed, and Why the Measurement of the Monochord and Cymbals Is Similar

I think the measurement of the monochord and of cymbals is alike for this reason: in both cases striking produces the sound, and the ringing of the string and of the cymbal strikes the free air, enclosed by no surrounding structures.

The measurement of pipes differs from theirs, perhaps [Col. 1332B] because the air within them is constricted. Since it does not have the freedom to expand, being confined by the structure of the pipe, it requires an addition not only of length but also of thickness. Therefore, when finding the tone, we take not only an eighth part of the preceding pipe’s length but also an eighth part of its thickness, that is, its diameter, as will be clear below.

But let us return to the cymbals.

Because of the slowness of the tone, I have established that their measurement should be intensified and relaxed according to sesquitertian and sesquialter proportion. Eight cymbals are to be measured by weight, using wax. From the amount of wax that you spend on the first cymbal, carefully provide two portions: divide one into two parts and the other into three.

Using half of the portion you divided into two, and adding to the other portion a third of itself, form two cymbals [Col. 1332C], corresponding to the first through the *diatessaron* and the *diapente*.

Then take the wax-weight of the portion that you divided into two; divide it into four, remove one quarter, and use the remaining three parts to construct the second cymbal.

Take the wax-weight of this second cymbal, place half of it upon itself, and form the sixth cymbal.

Divide the wax-weight of the sixth into four parts, remove one quarter, and use the remaining three to form the third cymbal. Divide this in half, add an equal amount to the half, and designate the seventh cymbal.

Divide its wax-weight into four, remove one quarter, and make the *synemmenon* from the remaining three.

## The Measurement of the Monochord Established According to the Same Proportions

[Col. 1332D]

Divide the whole monochord from gamma into four steps, and place C at the end of the first, G at the end of the second, and *g* at the end of the third.

After gamma, ascend three steps, and establish D at the end of the first and *d* at the end of the second. Then descend a *diatessaron* to D in three steps, placing A at the fourth position; ascend from A by three steps, intensifying a *diapente*. Place E at the end of the first and *e* at the end of the second.

Then descend three steps of a *diatessaron* to E, placing B at the fourth position. Intensify a *diatessaron* from C and write F at the end of the first and *c* at the end of the second.

Intensify a *diatessaron* from F, so that you find the *synemmenon* first and *f* second. The remaining letters A, *a*, and [a] are to be found from their homonyms in double proportion. [Col. 1333A] Descend the same *diapente* in two steps to F, and at the third position below write the *synemmenon*.

## Epigram on the Same Measurement

Divide the whole at the outset into four steps.

Placing gamma, divide after three equal intervals C, C, *g*.

Write D and *d*; after these, return three steps to D.

Let grave A be written; after three, suspend E and then *e*.

Place B at the fourth position, descending three steps to E.

Coming twice two steps from C, write F, and afterward *c*.

Thus make the *synemmenon* and *f* at the same number of steps from F.

Whatever still remains should now provide a double proportion.

A, then again *a*, and [a] are to be established with their homonyms.

For B, seek the rule of *b* according to the same method.

## Another Measurement of the Monochord, Beginning from the High Notes

[Col. 1333B]

The first step from *a* descends through a *diatessaron* to E; the second is empty; the third ends at A; the fourth is empty; the fifth ends at E; the sixth at D; the seventh and eighth are empty; the ninth ends at A.

Descend from *a* through a *diapente* to D; from D descend through a *diatessaron* to G. From G, the first step through a *diapente* ends at *c*, the second at G; the third is empty; the fourth ends at C; the fifth is empty; the sixth ends at gamma.

Let it be arranged that we ascend from *f* to *c* twice two equal steps. From *f* descend through a *diapente*: the first step ends at the *synemmenon*, the second proceeds to F, the third is empty, and the fourth ends at the lower *synemmenon*.

From *e* descend a *diatessaron*: the first ends at the other sign, the second is empty, the third at the previously discovered E, and the fourth is empty at B.

## The Ancient Measurement of Pipes, Which Is Intensified

[Col. 1333C]

It will be sufficient here to describe the measurement of two rows, that is, sixteen pipes; according to this method anyone may add as many other rows as he wishes.

Choose the first pipe with such length and width as moderation and judgment prescribe. Its length is measured upward from the mouthpiece; its width is the capacity of its hollow, where it opens at the top in the form of a circle.

This circle is called the diameter not according to its circumference but because it is divided through the middle into two semicircles. Measure the length of this diameter with a compass, and immediately after constructing the first pipe draw it at the top of that same first pipe with two equal lines.

Divide one of these into eight parts, the other into two and three parts, and then into four equal parts. After this, the entire measurement will be very easy for you.

To obtain the second pipe from the first, remove an eighth of the diameter of the first pipe from its length. Divide the remaining space down to the mouthpiece into eight parts; discard the ninth at the top, and you will have the second pipe.

To find the third, remove an eighth of the diameter from the length of the second pipe. Divide the remaining space down to the mouthpiece into nine parts, and, omitting the ninth part at the top, you have found the third.

To find the fourth, remove a third of the diameter from the length of the first pipe. [Col. 1334A] Divide the remaining space down to the mouthpiece into four parts; by removing the fourth part, you have added a fourth pipe together with a complete *diatessaron*.

To find the fifth, separate half the diameter of the first pipe. Divide the remaining space down to the mouthpiece into three parts; by separating the third part at the top, you have joined the fifth pipe together with the *diapente*.

To add the sixth, likewise cut off half the diameter from the length of the second pipe. Divide the remaining space into three parts; leaving one third, you have added the sixth.

To display the *synemmenon*, cut off a third of the diameter from the fourth pipe. Divide the remaining space down to the mouthpiece into four parts; by omitting one quarter, you have designated the *synemmenon*.

You will find the seventh if you cut off half the diameter from the third pipe, divide the remainder into three, and, rejecting the third at the top, establish the seventh final pipe.

Once these have been arranged [Col. 1334B], you can most easily organize the eighth from the first, the ninth from the second, the tenth from the third, the eleventh from the fourth, the twelfth from the fifth, the thirteenth from the sixth, the lower *synemmenon* from the upper *synemmenon*, and the fourteenth from the sixth, in this manner:

For each of the upper pipes, deduct a complete diameter, divide the remaining space down to the mouthpiece into two parts, and, with the upper part set aside, take the lower part—the one adjacent to the mouthpiece—as the octave.

## The New Measurement of Pipes, Which Is Relaxed

The venerable lord Willehelmus, formerly a monk of Emmeram at Regensburg and now abbot elsewhere [Note: [Col. 1333] namely at Hirsau, whose music we gave above; nevertheless, in the two [uncertain reading] there is nothing concerning this measurement of pipes], sought out a new measurement of pipes by converting the former intensification into relaxation, and shared it with me.

For he loved my smallness beyond the dignity of smallness: he who is the first musician, namely the modern Orpheus and Pythagoras. This is his arrangement.

[Col. 1334C]

The length of the first pipe, as lord Willehelmus determined it, extends to the mouthpiece as follows. The thickness, which is equal in all the pipes, is represented by this circle.
