[Col. 1334D]

Let the quantity of the first pipe be divided into eight, and let an eighth part of it together with an eighth of the diameter be added to it; this will be the second pipe.

Likewise, let the length of the second be divided into eight; when an eighth together with an eighth of the diameter has been added, it will be the third.

Let the first likewise be divided into three; when a third together with a third of the diameter has been added, you will have the *diatessaron* completed in the fourth pipe.

Here the complete smaller and earlier order begins. [Col. 1335] [Col. 1337] [Col. 1339A] Let the third pipe likewise be divided into eight; when an eighth together with an eighth of the diameter has been added, the *synemmenon* is found.

Likewise, let the first be divided into two; when half together with half of the diameter has been added, the fifth is completed.

Likewise, let the length of the second be divided into two; when half together with half of the diameter has been added, the sixth is completed.

Similarly, let the third be divided into two equal parts; when one part together with the corresponding part of the diameter has been added, the seventh is produced.

Let the eighth be found from the first in this way: double the first and add an entire diameter; the eighth is found.

Just as the eighth was found through the first, so you will be able to find all the succeeding pipes very easily, provided that you add an entire diameter to each one.

## Aribuncula’s Measurement of Pipes, Neither Entirely Relaxed nor Entirely Intensified, in Sesquitertian and Sesquialter Proportion

[Note: [Col. 1339D] That is, of Aribo himself.]

[Col. 1339B]

But as we proceed in both directions, sometimes lengthening and shortening this one, sometimes relaxing and adding to that one, we incline toward neither, because we do not wish to discover the tone through eight or nine divisions. This is not without reason: for the more rapid the measurement, the more accurate it is. It is almost obvious to everyone that a fourth, a third, a half, or an eighth or ninth part of some interval can be sought more certainly and quickly. Therefore we have arranged that the sesquitertian and sesquialter proportions should extend both upward and downward. A third part of the first pipe, with a third of its diameter added to it, forms the fourth. Likewise, half of the first, joined to half of its diameter, produces the fifth. A fourth part of the fifth, removed together with a third of the diameter, gives the length of the second. [Col. 1339C] Half of the second, together with half of its diameter, gives the sixth measurement. A fourth of the sixth, together with a third of its diameter, being rejected, constitutes the third. Half of the third, with half of its diameter superimposed upon it, is the source of the seventh. A fourth of this, with a third of the diameter cut away, leaves the length of the pipe retaining the *synemmenon*. Let us lay aside the veils of anxiety, since we have now reached the haven of safety. The first, doubled and combined with the whole diameter, gives the eighth; the second, the ninth; the third, the tenth; the fourth, the eleventh; one *synemmenon*, another *synemmenon*; the fifth, the twelfth; the sixth, the thirteenth; and the seventh, the fourteenth. For Lord William’s experience approved the use of just as many pipes; to two rows, namely fourteen pipes, he added three, [Col. 1339D] so that he might lay out the tetrachord, with suitable sharpness answering in the smallest pipes and appropriate gravity in the largest.

## The measurement of the arrangement of the pipes

From A, suspend the first fourth at D. From A again, lead the inverted fifth to E. Lower it and, from E, step down a fourth to B. Again, at F, remembering B, raise the fifth. From F, lower the form of the fourth to C. From C, raise the touching fifth to G. From D, the fourth must be suspended at *Sy*.

## How the pipes themselves should be made suitably

Just as the pipes are of the same thickness, so the sheets from which they are made are of the same width. First, following Lord William, we drew a circle according to the required thickness. We must carefully consider from what width it can be produced. Macrobius says in *The Dream of Scipio*: “Every diameter of any circle, tripled and supplemented by a seventh part of itself, gives the measurement of the circumference.” These are Macrobius’s words. Therefore, following his authority, let us triple the diameter of the aforesaid circle and add to it a seventh of the diameter at the same time; the width of all the sheets used as material for the pipes should then be made equal to the length of the line that proceeds from this calculation.

These sheets are thinned at their lateral edges. In particular, the edges should meet when the sheets are bent by the smith’s hand; they should not overlap one another, but should touch only with a very close-fitting seam. [Col. 1340B] To cover the joint of this seam, prepare small sheets having the thinness and width of a straw. These should be joined to one another with very strong solder, or with some other binding material that will endure more slowly and for a longer time.

After the length of each pipe has been determined on the still-open sheet by points fixed on either side, let a line run transversely from one point to the other. That terminating line should mark the opening and mouth of the pipe. The mouth should be cut along that line so that it opens to half the width of the pipe. The reed should also be glued very tightly onto that line. From this reed the lower lip of the mouth should be separated by the width of an ordinary straw.

## On natural and artificial music

[Col. 1340C]

Although, as one of the wise has asserted, art discovers nothing first that nature does not discover at last, nevertheless what proceeds uncultivated and rough from the womb of mother nature is made more polished through art. For art is said to derive its name from the strict rules by which things must be constrained and shaped.

We can especially judge that music is closely related and natural to us from the fact that all sorts of performers, entirely untrained in the art of music, sing any kind of lay song faultlessly, offending against none of the various arrangements of tones and semitones and returning properly to the final chord. Thus, although not truly, yet plausibly, Plato discusses the generation of the soul, saying that it was composed according to musical proportions. When the double, sesquitertian, sesquialter, and sesquioctave proportions sound pleasantly in our minds, the pagans may reasonably believe that souls consist of these same proportions, since likeness is friendly and unlikeness hateful. For good people also love the good, while the reprobate love the perverse.

But performers and other such musicians are natural, not artificial, musicians. The artificial musician is one who subtly understands the natural constitution of all the species of the fourth, fifth, and octave; who rationally recognizes the arrangement of the modes as nature’s attendant; who effectively grasps the operation of the principal chords; and who memorizes the properties of the modes, which consist in the six chords. [Col. 1341A] He should also, through the capacity of art, know very well how to approve what is legitimate, correct every defect, and devise irreproachable melodies by himself.

## On the moral character of the musical art

Anyone can perceive that music is ethical—that is, moral—from the fact, mentioned above, that it confers its benefits without the apprehension of art. Hence, once possessed through art, its use is all the more stable and enduring for us because it is more natural to us, just as gold adheres longer to silver than to copper.

Its thoroughly moral character is shown when every sex and every age takes delight in it. It communicates its pleasure not only to human nature but also to the nature of wild animals. We have learned that hunters, singing authentic melodies while accompanied by leaves, have lured roe deer and other wild animals to themselves. It is also clear that the story of Orpheus soothing Pluto with his lyre is not entirely fabulous, since we read that David, by playing the cithara, softened Saul’s demonic savagery.

Did not the musician Arion escape the danger of death by throwing himself upon one of the dolphins that gathered around his melody? Plato likewise demonstrates the moral character of music when he says: “We likewise established the tranquillity of souls in the soothing and affability of music.” Plato rightly says that the tranquillity of souls lies in music, since no restlessness dwells together with the constant enjoyment of music.

Yet, as we read, there was someone experienced who judged it established in this matter that nothing is wholly fortunate. He perceived certain modes as weaker and others as healthier: the Phrygian led someone into a certain chamber, while the Hypophrygian brought him back repentant.

We too know that certain species of the fourth and fifth are more beautiful than others, just as the first and fourth surpass the consonance of the second and third. The first and fourth have a semitone in the middle and therefore sound better. The second and third have a semitone—this one at the beginning, that one at the end—and therefore sound more harshly.

But among the species of the fourth the difference is tolerable: in the second, a ditone follows the semitone; in the third, it precedes the semitone. In the fifth, however, the second and third species are intolerably disturbed by the tritone. Because of the discordance of melodies, we may call it another Corydon; [Col. 1341D] nevertheless, it is sometimes necessary for the service of song, just as the rustic Corydon is necessary for the expenses of his masters.

## On the appropriateness of melodic composition

There is a twofold sweetness in singing if the divisions and distinctions of the neumes are proportionally arranged in the same way as the voices of the monochord themselves are arranged, as Lord Guido teaches. [Note: [Col. 1341D] See *Patrologia*, vol. CXLI.] He was indeed the latest in time among musicians, but first in usefulness. By his merit we compare the other teachers of this art with him, as one compares mute things with vocal ones. His words are as follows:

> “Above all, care must be taken that the distribution of the neumes be such that, whether neumes are made by the repetition of the same sound or by the connection of two or more, they should always correspond and answer one another either in the number of voices or in the proportion of tones: now equal to equal, now double or triple to simple, and elsewhere in a sesquialter or sesquitertian comparison. Likewise, so that, after the manner of verses, the distinctions may be equal, and sometimes repeated identically or varied by some small alteration; and, when they have been very attractively doubled, that they should have parts which are not excessively different, and which sometimes are transformed in the modes as identical, or are found similarly intensified and relaxed. Likewise, so that a returning neume should return by the same route by which it came and retrace the same footsteps. Likewise, so that the form or line that one makes by leaping from the high notes may be answered oppositely by another, inclined in the other direction, responding from the low notes. Likewise, so that sometimes one syllable may have one or several neumes, and sometimes one neume may be divided among several syllables.” [Col. 1342A–B]

Since Lord Guido left these precepts without examples, believing them to be self-evident, we shall explain them in very simple terms, according to our understanding.

Neumes of one sound are made by repetition when they are simple—that is, either one upright stroke or one lying down—or when they are double or triple through the repetition of the same sound; then they are made by the connection of two or more. All neumes are made by the connection of two or more sounds, except those mentioned above. Two with three . . . three with three . . . and others involving larger numbers we pass over for the moment.

Nevertheless, they should always correspond to one another either in the number of voices or in the proportion of tones, now equal to equal. Equal things correspond to equal when simple things are opposed to simple, doubles to doubles, and triples to triples. This may be either in the number of voices—for example, among equals, two correspond to two and three to three; among doubles, two to one and four to two; among triples, three to one—or in the proportion of tones.

“Duration” means the holding of a voice. It is equal when two are compared with four voices, and the smaller the number of the two is, the greater their duration should be. Thus, in the older antiphonaries, we very often find the letters C, T, and M, which indicate speed, slowness, and moderation.

In antiquity there was great care not only among the inventors of songs but also among the singers themselves, so that everyone might compose and sing proportionally. This consideration has long since died—indeed, it has been buried. Now it is enough merely to invent something sweet-sounding, without considering the sweeter joy of proportionate correspondence.

Likewise, the distinctions should be equal after the manner of verses. We find this in well-arranged songs, which we may call metrical, such as:

> “I will not leave you orphans. [II.] Alleluia. I am going and I will come  
> to you, alleluia, and your [III.] heart will rejoice, alleluia.”

Such consideration resembles the rhetorical figure called *compar*, which consists almost entirely of an equal number of syllables. “This will not arise from our grumbling,” says Tullius, “for that is childish, but use alone will bring it about.”

“Sometimes repeated identically or varied by a small alteration” shows the diversity of neumes, because likeness is the mother of association, as Tullius says. Let this be an example. [Note: [Col. 1343D] These are accompanied by ancient notation; what follows consists of the beginnings of antiphons:] “In Jerusalem . . . .”

> “Repeated identically or varied by a small alteration.”  
> “The Father raises up” [m.m.c.d.].  
> “Fluxum S. c. and satisfied five thousand with loaves.”  
> “And when they have been very attractively doubled”—this is virtually an interpretation and exposition of the preceding words, as though he were saying: Let them be repeated identically, but only when they have been made very attractive.  
> “And which are sometimes transformed in the same way through the modes”—as in “Festum”: now [c.] the semitone is on either side, but the modes differ and the quality of the raised and lowered notes is similar, as in “qui cogitaverunt.”  
> “Likewise, so that a returning neume should return by the same route by which it came”—as in “stars, seas, enclosing fields.”  
> “Likewise, so that the form or line that one makes by leaping from the high notes may be answered oppositely by another inclined in the other direction, responding from the low notes”—as in “O admirable.”  
> “Likewise, so that sometimes one syllable may have one or several neumes”—as in “praises to God.”  
> “Sometimes one neume may be divided among several syllables”—as in “the battle of Christ.”

Lord Guido also says: [Note: [Col. 1343D] See above.]

> “A movement will be placed before another movement—that is, positioned above it; or placed beside it—that is, when the end of one is the beginning of the other on the same note; or placed between it—that is, when one mode is positioned below another and is both less grave and less acute; or mixed—that is, partly placed between and partly placed beneath.”

We shall provide examples of these as we did of the preceding cases, so that the simplicity of some people may not be troubled:

> “A movement will be placed before another movement,” as in “Clear glory”;  
> placed beside it, as in “Behold, I . . .”;  
> placed between it, as in “He will be born for us and will be called”;  
> mixed, as in “At the right hand of the Father, who . . .”

## On the appropriateness of the movement called “placed before,” and on the extent of its ascent

The movement placed before will be more appropriate if the first rises by a tone and, with a semitone intervening, the movement placed before it rises again by a tone, because in this way both remain within the fifth, as in “Clear glory.” Or, if the movement placed before proceeds by a ditone, it should return by a fifth to the beginning of the preceding movement, since we must consider proportion—that is, correspondence—in these matters.

Therefore, a movement placed before should not be formed through a fourth and a fifth. But if the first rises by a semitone, with a tone intervening, the movement placed before should ascend by a tone, so that its beginning and end return to the beginning of the preceding movement by a fourth and a fifth, and to its end by a tone and a ditone. In other ways it will be less suitable, since the convenience and consonance of proportion are not considered. [Col. 1344A] This same movement is made only by ascending.

## On the suitability of the movement placed beside another, and on its occurrence in both ascent and descent

The movement placed beside another is subject both to ascent and to descent, as in “Behold, I . . .” and “And they will say: Glory to you, Lord.” Likewise, when intensified: “Bless the Lord.” This movement will be more decorous if the intensification is made in the first mode as follows: if the preceding movement rises by a tone, the movement placed beside it should ascend either by a tone or by a trochaic semitone—that is, one in which the long interval of the tone precedes the short semitone. For the semitone is a kind of trochee, consisting of a long and a short; another is iambic, consisting of a short, as in D–E–F–G.

A uniform ditone is only spondaic, or it proceeds through a fourth or fifth. But the movement placed beside it ascends better by a fourth, because its beginning and end correspond proportionally to the beginning and end of the preceding movement: its end to the preceding movement’s beginning and end by a fourth and a fifth, and its beginning to its end by a tone.

But the movement placed beside it in the manner of a fifth responds only at the end to the end of the preceding movement through a fifth. Or, if the preceding movement rises by a trochee, it has a semitone . . . [Note: [Col. 1344D] Everything that follows is abrupt and does not cohere with what precedes.]

But these matters will present themselves more clearly in conversation to those who are present than in writing to those who are absent. The detestable interruption of places deprives us of this convenience. We have left this discussion only in its final part so that we might render the melody suitable to its tetrard.

You ought to remember, my most beloved lord, that the venerable Guido said: “Let us take these five vowels.” Perhaps they contribute as much to agreement in words as they will provide consonance in neumes. Let them therefore be placed beneath the letters of the monochord; and because there are only five of them, let them be repeated until each sound has its own vowel written beneath it, and let them direct themselves in the following manner:

> Γ A B C D E F G  
> a b c d e f g  
> a [a] b [b] [] c [c] d [d.]  
> o [a] u [e] a [i] e [o] i [u.]  
> o [a] u [e] a [i] e [o] i [u.]  
> o [a] u [e] a [i] e [o] i [u.]  
> o [a] u [e] a [i] e [o] i [u.]  
> o [a] u [e] a [i] e [o]

After inserting certain intervening material, he adds:

> “But so that no burdensome necessity may be imposed upon you—for voices corresponding to the five vowels scarcely occur in this way in every symphony, and it is often impossible to pass beyond them at will—let a verse of the vowels also be added, so that you may wander somewhat more freely elsewhere. But let it be different in such a way that it begins from the third place of the preceding one, as follows: ‘Behold how he dies.’”

All the syllables are placed against their corresponding vowels except *hau*, which occurs in *hauriat*, namely in the final part of this verse. For the letters of the syllable *hau* are *h*, *u*, and *e*, and the musician gives the reason why he changed it in this way: *hau* sounds more suitably on F than on G, which ought to be the final of the fourth mode. [Note: [Col. 1344D] See the table in Guido.]

## Aribo’s opinion

[Col. 1345A]

Although two tones are always contained in one letter or voice, nevertheless the formulas of the second, fourth, sixth, and eighth tones correspond much better and more frequently to individual neumes and sounds. The formulas of the first, third, fifth, and seventh do not correspond unless the song descends from a high point and reaches a grave ending.

## Another opinion usefully explained

Although a song is authentic, more of its neumes and sounds move within the five chords common to authentic and plagal modes than within those chords assigned separately to the authentic modes. Therefore, the formulas of the plagal modes more often and more suitably fit the neumes of authentic songs, in which they more frequently remain.

In the antiphon “Behold the name of the Lord,” although it is authentic, more of its neumes may nevertheless be regarded as plagal than authentic. For example, *Behold*, *and the name*, *and of the Lord*, *and from afar*, *and the brightness*, *and of it*, *and it fills*, *and the orb*, and *of the earth* are plagal, since they proceed within the range of the plagal modes. Only *comes* is authentic; yet all its neumes must be called plagal, because it does not rise beyond the fifth chord from the final. The same principle must be applied in many other cases, which need not be discussed individually here.

But when melodies rise a fifth above the final chord and touch the sixth, seventh, and eighth, then they correspond to the formulas of the authentic modes, which extend upward. This is what he means by “unless the song descends from a high point,” and by “in G, D, and F.”

[Col. 1345] Here ends Aribo’s *Music*.

**In the year of the Lord 1092, Henry, cleric of Pomposa**

[Col. 1345]

# Notice concerning the following little work

*(Montfaucon, Italian Diary, p. 80)*

We saw the monastery of Pomposa, once very extensive and renowned for the fame of its holiness, now deserted. In the eleventh century it began to be especially frequented through the work of Guido, its abbot, and first father of that revered place. Later it was greatly ennobled by the arrival of princes and nobles, who, under Guido as their teacher, undertook there the beginnings of the ascetic life.

Guido is mentioned in the preface of the distinguished Mabillon to the first part of the sixth century of the Benedictine order. His death falls in the year 1046. He is said to have been among the first to introduce voluntary self-flagellation, and his Life is read in the same work, p. 509.

After this, still in the same century, under the care of Abbot Jerome, the monastery was furnished with very many books, so that Henry the cleric testifies that the Pomposan library surpassed the other libraries of Italy, not excepting even the Roman one. Henry makes this statement in a letter to a certain Stephen, together with the attached catalogue of that library. My intention is to append it here, so that the reader may understand how great an undertaking it then was to assemble extensive libraries, since this library, which surpassed the others, cannot now be compared even with mediocre libraries of our own age.

The letter and catalogue came from the library of the Most Serene Duke at Modena. They were presented to me in Rome by my very dear friend Giulio Fontanini, cardinal and imperial librarian, although they had not yet been made public.

From what Henry notes concerning Livy in column 1353, he indicates that many Decades of that great author had already been lost and lamented in his own age, although he does not accurately grasp the matter. No one, of course, is unaware that, of Livy’s fourteen Decades—that is, 140 books, or, according to others, 142—only thirty-five survive, and therefore 107 have been entirely lost.

When he discusses Trogus Pompeius, take care not to suppose that the complete Trogus existed in this library, since he had already perished many centuries earlier. Rather, understand him to mean Justin, the author of the epitome. In composing his epitome, Justin struck down and removed from view Trogus, a most distinguished writer, just as Livy perished for the greater part when Florus and the author of the *Arguments* brought about his destruction. For once abridgements had been published, the original authors were dismissed and gradually, through neglect, either perished entirely or were mutilated in a large part of their contents.

[Col. 1345]

# Letter of Henry the cleric to Stephen

[Col. 1345B]

To Stephen, suitably steeped in the fountain of philosophy, Henry the cleric sends the illumination of heavenly wisdom.

Having heard the reputation of the venerable Jerome, abbot of Pomposa, you confess that you greatly desire that whatever can suitably be found anywhere in the enlightened world in the sacred page should be copied without ceasing into your little book, and to know the number of the books which, by God’s inspiration, he has amassed in his own time, and what he studied in them so diligently that he almost neglected everything else.

As far as I can, dearest of men, I shall faithfully disclose this to your affection in the following letter, however imperfect it may be, insofar as I learned it from his own mouth or through my own experience. But in order to approach the matter more clearly and make it evident through transparent reasoning, I must begin somewhat farther back.

The basilica of Pomposa, as I have learned, began to be wonderfully honored and enlarged from the time of Guido, a man of remarkable holiness and the first father of that revered place. His holiness inspired and gladdened the people, and very many persons from everywhere hastened eagerly to this venerable and secure refuge, desiring to be instructed in the disciplines of so holy a teacher and to correct their lives under the monastic rule.

Among them were also sons of certain marquises, counts, and nobles. Abandoning luxuries and setting aside worldly pomp, they gathered there, and through God’s action they have not ceased to do so down to the present day. [Col. 1347B] At that time my lord Jerome, the subject of our discussion, was brought there as a boy and sufficiently learned the monastic rule. He then studied the foundations of grammar, and at some point also tasted the subtleties of dialectic. Under God as his teacher, he made great progress in a short time.

He was then gratefully appointed abbot by the brothers, having previously been a monk. Since he was quick in intellect, gentle in spirit, a lover of the brothers, highly polished in the uprightness of his conduct, and prudent in mind, he saw that so great a community could not bear fruit in divine worship without the plough and hoe. He therefore immediately and diligently began to seek everywhere the volumes of various teachers, so that they might leave instruction for those then living and for posterity. Thus, just as the members of the community differed in birth and study, so each person might observe in these books what he ought to imitate and what he ought to reject.

It seems difficult to me for anyone to distinguish virtues and vices freely while ignorant of the riddles and teachings of Scripture. For who knows how to give an antidote to the sick unless he has learned? And who, ignorant of navigation, would dare entrust a fragile vessel to the savage sea?

But since the goads of the envious often sharply spur good men, certain people of unsound mind began to quarrel, dissent, and reproach the excellent abbot on this account. Some insistently claimed that he was uselessly dissipating the monastery’s goods on trifles; others asserted that he was doing this so that, at some point, he might flee with all the books and acquire a bishopric for himself. My mind was far removed from such opinions, and it always believed that what was good and just lay behind this undertaking.

At the abbot’s command, a monk named Bonus, formerly a hermit, directed this work. He was learned and highly skilled in every doctrine. Even though he was eager to collect as many copies of books as possible, he did not care about distinct and elegant letters, but accepted letters formed in any manner. For the aforesaid abbot had decided to have the books recopied and gathered into a single body for the library. Hence I have opponents among the brothers because of the excessive use of titles, since they are unable to read the books written by me.

No church, city, or province—and finally not even Rome itself, the head of the world—could compete in praise with fortunate Pomposa’s abundance of holy books. Who, then, is so hard, so savage, so bestial, [Col. 1348A] and so witless that he would not wish to rest in the Pomposan cloister from the uproar of worldly corruption, where he may continually understand words of edification and salvation?

For just as corrupt conversations corrupt good conduct, so, conversely, good conversations destroy evil conduct and introduce good conduct.

But lest what I have said about the books seem insufficient to you, I would also like to write down the title of each individual book, so that what you do not believe on the basis of mere words you may at least believe when it is placed faithfully before your eyes. Nor have we undertaken this in vain, since it may happen that through error one of these books is secretly removed and consigned to oblivion. Once this page has been read, however, the faithful guardian of the books may diligently inquire whether a brother or visitor has taken it and immediately return it to the cupboard. [Col. 1348B]

Note, prudent reader, that you may recognize each individual book more quickly, since several works are contained in one volume: wherever a figure shaped like the letter Γ appears, all the titles contained between Τ and Γ belong together in a single volume.

What concerns the life of the holy man Jerome, the abbot, the number of the brothers, the pleasantness of the wilderness, and the buildings of the whole place, you may find in the little book that I wrote specifically on that subject. The matter was recorded in the book of bishops in the year 1093 from the Incarnation.

This book, after the letter later added at its beginning, begins: “It moved certain people, and the question is asked …” One book, Exposition of the Letter of James to the Twelve Tribes; this book begins: “To those who are in the dispersion, greetings.” Two books On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins and On the Baptism of Infants, to Marcellinus; this work begins: “Although amid the central and great storms of cares …” One book On the One Baptism, against Petilianus, to Constantinus; this book begins: “To answer those who think otherwise.” One book On the Maximianists and Donatists; this book begins: “We have already said many things, we have already written many things.” One book On the Grace of the New Testament, to Honoratus; this work begins: “You proposed five questions to me for examination.” One book On the Spirit and the Letter, to Marcellinus; this book begins: “Having read the little works which I recently prepared for you, my son.” One book On Faith and Works; this book begins: “It seems to some people …” Three books, A Brief Summary of the Conference with the Donatists; this work begins: “When the Catholic bishops and those of the Party of Donatus …” One book After the Conferences against the Donatists; this book begins: “Why are you still being deceived, Donatists?” One book On Seeing God; this book begins: “Mindful of my obligation, I asked that matter in this way, and now I remind you.” One book On Nature and Grace; this book begins: “The book which you sent …” Twenty-two books On the City of God; this work begins: “The most glorious city of God.”

One book To Orosius the Presbyter, against the Priscillianists and Origenists; this book begins: “He answered the questioner, dearest son.” Two books by Orosius to Jerome the Presbyter: one On the Origin of the Soul, and the other On the Sentence of James. This work begins: “Our God, who called us …” One book To Emeritus, Bishop of the Donatists, after the Conference; this book begins: “If now, my son Emeritus …” A book On the Proceedings of the Pelagians; this book begins: “After it had come into our hands …” One book On the Correction of the Donatists; this book begins: “I praise, congratulate, and marvel.” One book On the Presence of God, to Dardanus; this book begins: “Brother, dearest brother Dardanus.”

Two books Against Pelagius and Coelestius, On the Grace of Christ and On Original Sin, to Albinus, Pinianus, and Melania. This work begins: “How greatly we rejoice in your bodily, and especially your spiritual, salvation.” One book, Proceedings with Emeritus the Donatist; this book begins: “To the most glorious Augustus Honorius, in his twelfth consulship, and to Constantius.” One book Against the Sermon of the Arians; this book begins: “I answer their preceding disputation with this disputation.” Two books On Marriage and Concupiscence, to Valerius. The first begins: “The new heretics, dearest son Valerius”; the second begins: “This is a concern of your military service.” Seven books of Expressions; this work begins: “Since the holy Scriptures, which they call canonical …”

Two books On the Soul and Its Origin. This work begins—in the book to Renatus—“Your sincerity toward us”; the second, to Peter, begins: “To the most beloved brother and fellow presbyter Peter.” The final two books, to Vincentius and Victor: the first begins, “What I thought ought to be written to you …”

Two books To Pullentius [sic], On Adulterous Marriages. The first begins: “The first question, dearest brother Pullentius, is …”; the second begins: “Regarding the matters about which you had written to me.” Two books Against an Adversary of the Law and the Prophets; this work begins: “The book which you sent, dearest brothers.” Two books Against Gaudentius, Bishop of the Donatists; this work begins: “Gaudentius, bishop of Thamugadensis among the Donatists” [sic; in the printed editions, *Thamugadensis*]. One book Against Lying; this book begins: “You sent me many things to read.” Four books Against Two Letters of the Pelagians; this work begins: “I knew you, indeed, as most famous report proclaimed.” Six books Against Julianus; this work begins: “Your insults and abusive words, Julianus.”

One book To Laurentius, On Faith, Hope, and Charity; this book begins: “It cannot be said, dearest son Laurentius, how much I delight in your learning.” One book On the Care to Be Taken for the Dead, to Paulinus, bishop; this book begins: “For a long time, venerable fellow bishop Paulinus, to your holiness …”

One book On the Eight Questions of Dulcitius; this book begins: “As far as I can see, dearest son Dulcitius …” One book To Valentinus and the Monks Who Are with Him, On Grace and Free Will; this book begins: “Because of those who [assert] the free will of man.” One book To Them, On Correction and Grace; this book begins: “Having read your letter, dearest brother Valentinus …”

Τ Ten books of the *Recognitions* of Clement, bishop of the city of Rome, apart from the letter and prologue joined to the beginning. The first begins: “I, Clement, born in the city of Rome, from my earliest age devoted myself to chastity.” The second begins: “When the day appointed for discussion in speech …” The third begins: “Meanwhile Peter, rising at the crowing of the roosters …” The fourth begins: “Having departed from Caesarea so that we might go to Tripoli.” The fifth begins: “On the following day, somewhat earlier than usual.” The sixth begins: “When the darkness had begun to disperse.” The seventh begins: “At last, having departed from Tripoli, the first city of Phoenicia.” The eighth begins: “On the following day Peter …” The ninth begins: “On the following day Peter, together with us …” The tenth begins: “When morning had dawned, Clement …”

An Exposition of the Apocalypse of the Apostle John by Saint Ambrose, bishop, contained in eighteen books. The first begins: “In the reading of the revelation of the Apostle John, dearest brothers.” The second begins: “Dearest brothers, in the lampstand, concerning which you heard when the Apocalypse was read …” The third begins: “Just now, dearest brothers, we hear blessed John.” The fourth begins: “And I saw upon the right hand of him who sat on the throne a book.” The fifth begins: “As you have just heard when the divine reading was being read.” The sixth begins: “And I saw another angel ascending from the rising of the sun.” The seventh begins: “Just now, dearest brothers, when the Apocalypse was being read, we heard …” The eighth begins: “The voice from heaven is the command of God, who touches the heart.” The ninth begins: “What we heard, dearest brothers, in the reading that was recited …” The tenth begins: “Just now we heard, dearest brothers …” The eleventh begins: “In the reading that has just been recited, dearest brothers …” The twelfth begins: “In the reading of the Lord that was recited, dearest brothers, Saint John said …” The thirteenth begins: “Saint John, dearest brothers, while speaking of the seven angels’ bowls and plagues …” The fourteenth begins: “Just now, when the divine reading was being read, dearest brothers, we heard blessed John …” The fifteenth begins: “In the reading that was recited, dearest brothers, [concerning] those kings …” The sixteenth begins: “Whenever I have mentioned Babylon, you have heard, dearest brothers: do not understand it as a city made of stones.” The seventeenth begins: “In the reading that was recited, blessed John the evangelist says …” The eighteenth begins: “As we have just heard, dearest brothers, the angel of the Lord spoke to blessed John, saying …”

Γ Here begins the Commentary of Saint Jerome on the Apocalypse of the Apostle John; this book begins: “John, whose name is interpreted as ‘grace of God,’ bore the figure of Christ.”

Γ Here begins Bede, servant of Christ, Exposition on the Apocalypse of the Apostle John, in three books, apart from the prologue joined to the beginning. The first begins: “The Apocalypse of John, disciple of Christ, which God gave him to reveal openly to his servants, the Church having been founded through the apostles.” The second begins: “And I saw seven angels standing in the presence of God.” The third begins: “And I saw another great and wondrous sign in heaven.”

Here begins the treatise of Ambrose of Milan, bishop, On Psalm 118, whose prologue begins: “Although the mystical [meaning] also rebukes, as though with the sound of a trumpet.” The book itself begins: “‘Blessed are the undefiled,’ he says, etc. ‘Blessed are those who search,’ etc.—what a beautiful order, how full of instruction!”

Here begins the treatise of Saint Ambrose of Milan, bishop, On the Song of Songs, in five books, apart from the prologue joined to the beginning. The first begins: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth, for your breasts are better …” The second begins: “The voice of my cousin—behold, he has come.” The third begins: “Behold, the bed of Solomon is surrounded by mighty men of luxury.” The fourth begins: “Rise, north wind, and come, south wind.” The fifth begins: “You are beautiful, my beloved, sweet and lovely.”

Here begins the treatise of Saint Ambrose On Psalm 61, in which he severely rebukes the faithlessness and impiety of Maximus the tyrant, who dared to kill his lord, the emperor Gratian, by fraud and deceit. He says that this emperor dwells in the Lord’s tabernacle and rests upon his mountain. This book begins: “It is the unquestioned custom of us all …”

Bishop Ambrose of Milan to his sister Marcellina, On the Staff, one book; this book begins: “Your anxious holiness …”

The embassy of the Council of Aquileia to the emperors Gratian, Valentinian, and Theodosius; this book begins: “To the most merciful and most Christian emperors.” Likewise, a letter of Ambrose to the same: “To the most merciful emperors and Christian rulers.” Likewise, another letter of the same council: “To the most merciful emperors.” Likewise, another to the same: “And this, most merciful prince, [is] for your glory.”

The embassy of Bishop Ambrose to the Emperor Valentinian: “Ambrose to the Emperor Valentinian.” Likewise, another to the same, On Rejecting the Worship of Images: “Since all human beings who are governed under Roman rule …” Likewise, to the same emperor, the report of Symmachus, prefect of the City, requesting that the altar and images be restored. It begins: “When the most distinguished senate first …” Likewise, Ambrose to the Emperor Valentinian and Symmachus, prefect of the City: “To the most blessed ruler and most Christian emperor Valentinian Augustus, Ambrose, bishop.”

A letter of Ambrose and the other bishops of Italy to the Emperor Theodosius: “To the most blessed emperor and most merciful ruler, Ambrose, etc.” Likewise, another from the same bishops to the same emperor: “To the most blessed emperor and most merciful ruler Theodosius, Ambrose and the other bishops of Italy.”

On the Humanity and Religion of the Younger Valentinian. Ambrose to the Emperor Theodosius: “My silence was broken.” Here he excuses himself for having rightly avoided the presence of the tyrant Maximus. Ambrose to the Emperor Theodosius. Likewise, a letter of Bishop Ambrose to Theodosius: “Ambrose to the Emperor Theodosius.”

A letter of Ambrose to the Emperor Eugenius: “To the most merciful emperor Eugenius, Ambrose, bishop.”

Here begins the book of Saint Ambrose On the Death of the Emperor Theodosius: “This grave disturbance for us …”

Here begins Saint Ambrose, bishop, On the Departure of His Brother, two books. The first begins: “We have brought forward, dearest brothers, my sacrifice.” The second, on the same subject, begins: “On the eighth day, in the preceding little book, we indulged somewhat in our longing.”

Ambrose, bishop, to the clergy: “Very often something has stolen into human minds …” Ambrose, bishop, to Irenaeus: “You ask me why the Lord God rained down manna.”

Τ Six books of Augustine, Catholic bishop, against the books of Julianus, the heretic of the Pelagian heresy, apart from the letter joined to the beginning. This work begins: “Your insults and abusive words, Julianus.”

Γ Three books of Augustine Against the Books of Parmenianus the Donatist; this work begins: “There are indeed many other things against the Donatists.” Likewise, Augustine, On the Good of Marriage; this book begins: “In the marital bond, indeed …”—this is from the Book of Revisions.

The prologue of Saint Augustine, On the Spirit and the Letter, to Marcellinus, to whom he had written three books. The book of Saint Augustine to Marcellinus, On the Spirit and the Letter; this book begins: “Having read the little works which I recently prepared …”

A sermon of Saint Augustine, On the Presence of God, to Dardanus; this sermon begins: “I confess to you, son Dardanus …” Likewise, a sermon of Saint Augustine, On Virginity; this book begins: “How great a blessedness in the heavens holy virginity possesses.”

Here begins Augustine’s book On True Religion; this book begins: “Since the way of every good and blessed life …”

Γ Three books of Saint Augustine On the Word of the Lord concerning the Three Evangelists, namely Matthew, Luke, and John. We have this work written in two volumes. I do not mean that a single book was divided into two volumes, but that we have the same work written twice. We had indeed written it earlier, but not as fully as afterward. The first begins: “We heard the evangelist, and in him the Lord rebuking them.”

Γ Four books On the Agreement of the Evangelists; this work begins: “Among all the divine authorities contained in the sacred writings …”

[Col. 1357D] Τ The Book of Etymologies of Isidore, bishop of Seville [sic].

Γ Ten books of Livy [sic] From the Founding of the City, but forty chapters are still missing from Abbot Pomposius, who eagerly longs to find them.

Γ The Book of Prefaces, On the Books of the New and Old Testament. Likewise, the book of Saint Isidore On the Life, Origin, and Death of the Holy Fathers Who Are Praised in Scripture; this book begins: “Here begin the names … [lacuna] …” The Holy Fathers of the Old Testament mystically expounded by Saint Isidore, bishop of Seville. This book begins: “Adam bore the figure of Christ.” Likewise, the names of the saints of the New Testament; this work begins: “Four …”

The Chronicle of Saint Isidore, bishop of Seville, describing a brief history from the beginning of the world to the time of Heraclius, one book.

The Book of Differences of Isidore, bishop of Seville; this book begins: [lacuna]. Likewise, On the Distinctions of the Four Vices; this book begins: “Against these four kinds of virtues …” Likewise, the second book, On the Differences of Words; this book begins: “Isidore to the reader, greetings. Many of the ancients strove to distinguish the differences among expressions.”

A sermon of Isidore Against the Arians; it begins: “Come, Lord Jesus Christ, our redeemer.”

A sermon of Saint John Chrysostom, On Psalm 50 and David’s Repentance; it begins: “We summon you to the remnants of the meal.” A letter of the same to those who ask, “Why was the devil not removed from the midst?” This book begins: “Again we offer you the table which I promised earlier.”

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, here begin the acts of Saint Methodius, bishop of Patara, On the Kingdoms of the Gentile Kings and a Certain Christian Demonstration Concerning the Last Times.

Two books of Augustine On Genesis against the Manichaeans; this work begins: “If the Manichaeans were to choose those whom they might deceive.” Likewise, two books of Saint Augustine to Simplicianus; this work begins: “The highly gracious and truly delightful dignity of your questions …” Likewise, Augustine to Dulcitius, On Eight Questions; this work begins: “As far as I can see, dearest son Dulcitius …”

Here begins the Exposition on the Song of Songs by Apponius; this book begins: “As they marvel at the voice of the Holy Spirit …”

Τ Decrees of the pontiffs, [lacuna], of Pope Clement to Damasus.

Τ Likewise, Augustine’s fifteen books On the City of God: ten in one volume and five in another.

Τ Forty-four books of the ancient histories of Trogus Pompeius.

Τ An Exposition of the Gospel of Matthew, issued by an author whom I do not know, with a prologue joined to the beginning. This book begins: “When, with diligent study and careful attention to the various testimonies of the prophets, we wish to establish the number of the evangelists …” This work extends to the Gospel passage that says, “Then little children were brought to him, so that he might lay his hands upon them and pray”; and the exposition of the book is divided into seventy-six chapters.

Remember, prudent reader, that through the diligent care of the most energetic abbot Hieronymus mentioned above, he has already had almost all the books listed above copied for himself by painstaking effort. I say “almost” because certain works which Saint Augustine mentions in his Book of Revisions his eager hand has not yet been able to reach. Thus his sagacious mind never rests, but diligently asks and investigates where suitable books of the saints may lie hidden, so that he may reach them, discover them, and add them to his library, in order that the Pomposian Church may shine wonderfully among the churches of Italy.

May all things be attributed to God’s mercy toward his own, which makes faith burn so strongly that, like one who is hungry, it eats and is not satisfied, and, like one who is thirsty, drinks and thirsts still more. Indeed, his desire finds no limit in its searching, but he strives eagerly and laboriously so that, while he lives, he may enrich his own church with an exceptional abundance of books.

But because envy and the contagion of wicked tongues often gnaw at happy, secure, and well-accomplished works, [Note: Col. 1359A: I think *linguae* (“tongues”) should be read thus; only one word is missing.] we know that there will be certain superstitious and malicious persons who, in order to disparage the holy place and bring accusations against the excellent abbot, will investigate with impudent zeal why that venerable abbot Hieronymus wished to insert the books of the pagans, the tales of error, and the histories of ancient tyrants into divine truth and the pages of the books of the saints. To them one must reply in the apostolic words: “For in a great house there are not only vessels of gold and silver, but also of wood and earthenware” [2 Tim. 2:20].

[Lacuna] He did this so that, according to his inclination and merit, each person might have something in which to take pleasure and exercise his own intellect. Hence Truth itself says: “In my Father’s house are many dwelling places” [John 14:2]. I believe that the holier someone is here, the more blessed he will be there.

The same pagan literary inventions, if understood with a pure intention, are useful [Note: I think this should be supplied in this way]. For what else do they signify than that worldly pomp is nothing? Hence the Apostle says: “We know that all things work together for good for those who love God” [Rom. 8:28]. Let them therefore be silent; but may the resourceful abbot persevere in his holy work, so that the one who has begun well may persevere to the end, and books useful to posterity may be written and likewise recorded for remembrance in future times.

**In the year of the Lord 1092, Robert of Tumbalena, abbot of Saint Vigor.**

[Col. 1359]

## Historical and Literary Notice

(Oudin, *Script. eccles.*, II, 769.)

[Col. 1359A] Robert of Tumbalena, a monk of Saint Michael “in peril of the sea,” as Orderic Vitalis writes in Book VIII of his *History* under the year 1094, later became abbot of the monastery of Saint Vigor outside the walls of the city of Bayeux in Normandy. He went to Rome, where Pope Gregory VII honorably retained him; until his death he faithfully served the Roman Church, as the same Orderic writes under the year 1087 in the cited book. Among other monuments of his learning, he left to the Church a brief, lucid, and profound exposition of the *Song of Songs*, as the same witness attests.

This Commentary on the *Song of Songs*, whose prologue John Mabillon published in vol. I of the *Analecta*, p. 125, from a manuscript of the Cistercian abbey of Balerne in the duchy of Burgundy, is identical with that which has hitherto been ascribed to Saint Gregory the Great. Peter de Gussanville, in the latest edition of the Works of Saint Gregory the Great, judges that it cannot in any way belong to him. A manuscript, moreover, exists in the notable library of Saint Victor at Paris, not anonymous as is usual there, but with a preface absent from other manuscripts and with the author’s first, or initial, letter R inscribed in the codex [Col. 1360A] RR. 12, fol. 187. The same work, either anonymous or simply under Gregory’s name, exists in manuscript in many libraries of France, as the cited Peter de Gussanville states where, in his edition of the Works of Saint Gregory the Great, he discusses the manuscripts with which he collated it. I add that other manuscripts of this work exist in the libraries of Clairvaux and Orval, codex 92, of the same Cistercian order, and widely in the larger libraries of that order. That this commentary is one and the same as that called Gregorian will be apparent to anyone who compares the beginnings of both with what follows. No one will contradict so evident a fact unless he has abandoned sound judgment.

Nor should one object, from vol. I of the *Analecta*, p. 128, that Robert, abbot of Saint Vigor, left his Commentary in two books, whereas the anonymous author in vol. III of the Works of Saint Gregory the Great, p. 461, made an uninterrupted exposition of the same *Song*. For this was done later by holy writers, in order to comply with the abbot’s instruction: he had wished it and enjoined it upon copyists at the end of his preface, vol. I, p. 128, of the *Analecta*. Nor should one insist that the prologue of the said Commentaries in the Works of Saint Gregory differs from that in the *Analecta*. For the prologue in the Works of Gregory, according to Peter de Gussanville, p. 458, is absent from many manuscripts; in others it differs, and in others it is read shorter or longer, according to the understanding of any given scribe. The actual prologue of this work and its author is found in the cited *Analecta*, from the Balerne manuscript, with the author’s name, and in another manuscript of Saint Victor at Paris, from which Jacques Hommey drew it, as discussed below.

Two other manuscripts likewise occur among the manuscripts of the cathedral churches of England and other notable libraries: in manuscript 9, no. 2, of the manuscripts of the cathedral and metropolitan church of Saint Peter at York: “Brother Robert on the *Song of Songs*. Beginning: ‘To Ansfrid, servant of God.’” And in manuscript 8666, in manuscript 944 of the Jacobean Library: “Robert’s Commentary on the *Song of Songs*, printed among the Works of Gregory the Great.” Thus the catalogue of the manuscripts of those libraries. Finally, I add that the prologue printed in the edition of Gregory’s Works was fabricated by some copyist who chose to do so, and excerpted from the prologue of Richard of Saint Victor on the same *Song*, p. 489 of Richard’s Works; some anonymous person partly altered it and partly, at will, abridged it. Finally, Jacques Hommey, an Augustinian hermit, very recently published this Commentary under the name of Saint Radulf, abbot of Fontenelle, p. 276 of a work which he undeservedly entitled *Supplement of the Fathers*, [Col. 1362A] published at Paris in octavo in 1684. Misled solely by the initial letter R of the name, which he found in a manuscript of the Library of Navarre at Paris, as he admits on p. 273, he assigned this anonymous Commentary, on conjectural grounds, to Saint Radulf, abbot of Fontenelle, with an altogether fanciful ascription of sanctity and authorship. Yet the complete prologue in vol. I of John Mabillon’s *Analecta*, p. 125, expressly attributes it to Robert, abbot of Saint Vigor at Bayeux, after Orderic Vitalis, a contemporary and eyewitness, a native of the same region, time, and order. Nothing of force can be advanced by anyone against such great authority.

Ansfrid, to whom Robert dedicates his work, seems to be Ansfrid, abbot of Préaux, called Aufridus by others, whose epitaph Orderic relates in the cited passage; or at least Ansfrid, third abbot of the monastery of Saint-Sauveur of Coutances. For further material on Ansfrid of Préaux, see the chronicle of Robert of Torigni in Arthur du Monstier’s *Neustria Pia*, and the brothers de Sainte-Marthe, vol. IV of *Gallia Christiana*, in the Catalogue of the Abbots of Préaux. But who that Anastasius is, at whose request Robert undertook this work, I have not yet ascertained, together with Mabillon, *Analecta*, vol. I, p. 132. Robert, therefore, abbot of Saint Vigor, flourished from about the middle of the eleventh century until its end, or thereabouts. On him see my own *Supplement to Bellarmine on Ecclesiastical Writers*, p. 348; and John Mabillon, vol. I of the cited *Analecta*, p. 125 ff.

[Col. 1361]

## Two Books of Robert of Tumbalena, Abbot of Saint Vigor, of Commentaries on the Song of Songs

(Oudin, *Script. eccles.*, II, 773.)

### Letter, or Preface, of the Author to Abbot Ansfrid

[Col. 1361B]

To his dearest enclosed servant of God, Ansfridus, formerly his son and friend, now—by the favor of the divine grace, to whomsoever it wills—a father and lord, Brother Robert, least of men, sends life, joy, and glory, which is true glory.

[Note: Robert. Thus the full name appears in the Balerna manuscript, whereas the manuscript codex of Saint Victor in Paris has only the initial letter R. This gave James Hommey, an Augustinian hermit, occasion to err: in his *Supplement to the Fathers*, p. 276, he ascribed this work to the imaginary writer Radulf of Fontenelle, a saint of the new calendar, without guide or authority.]

For some time now, through many messages, your zeal for the Lord has been urging my sluggishness to send you the book that I wrote some time ago on the *Song of Songs*. I scarcely send it even now, although I would wish it to remain hidden from everyone if I could. For an inexperienced and unpolished craftsman fears to have others see the ring he has made; he has little confidence in himself and does not trust another’s judgment. He fears that what does not please him perfectly before being examined will displease many when it is examined. So, from one who displays it and trembles in this way, accept the little work of your friend. Judge what pleases you, [Col. 1363A] and write back what you have judged.

I may perhaps seem to many—as I fear I seem also to you—to have begun this work presumptuously and completed it presumptuously; if indeed it should be called complete, since it still requires examination, and certainly correction, by more learned and better men. For I confess that it seems to me a matter for great indignation that I, so crude in study, so dull in understanding, so sullied by sin, should have burst into so ancient, learned, and polished a work in order to explain the words of Solomon, though I possess nothing of Solomon except, perhaps, what I read concerning him that is abhorrent—namely, that when he grew old, he ceased to be wise.

Yet believe your friend that I began this little book, which I send you, at another’s request and completed it after being urged many times. The lord Anastasius, my dearest brother and lord, requested it of me; and many others, together with him, urged me—not so much considering my inborn folly as desiring that they themselves might acquire some understanding of words so secret. Although certain others, and especially the lord Bede, have labored at this same work, revealed its secrets, and left a most useful reading for posterity.

Therefore, servant of God, read humbly what you find; and if it pleases you, transcribe what you have read.

I ask you to divide this work into two beginnings, because, since its style changes from one part to another, it would be disgraceful to enclose the whole under a single beginning. While I was explaining the *Song of Songs* in a solitary cell, it happened that some friends of mine arrived and found me engaged in the exposition. When they read in sections what I had already explained, they praised the work, but said that one defect was present: I had not inserted examples from the canonical books by which my statements might be proved.

From that time onward I appended whatever examples came to mind that suited the subject, although they had not seemed necessary to me. For I had chiefly devoted myself to compunction in the exposition, and had stated things not as matters requiring proof, but as truths inserted inwardly. Later, however, when gathering examples and striving for brevity, I explained things more tersely, and they appear less agreeable to the reader.

The variation in style caused by the insertion of examples is marked at the point where it says: “I will go to the mountain of myrrh and to the hill of frankincense” (*Song of Songs* IV, 6). When this has been said and explained, let the first book end, and let the second begin as follows: “You are wholly beautiful, my beloved, and there is no blemish in you” (*Song of Songs* IV, 7). If you lack parchment, I will send you as much as will suffice.

Read, therefore, dearest brother, the words of the wisest Solomon: the *Song of Songs*, which, because of the reverence due to its most sacred meaning, the excellence of nuptial love, and the most sweet union of the Bridegroom and Bride, is called not merely a song but the *Song of Songs*. In its exposition, if anything displeases you, pray for my ignorance; if anything pleases you, pray for my sins, since I speak well but act badly. If you wish to copy this book for yourself, do not write it in the margins as it appears here, but continuously on the pages, as other expositions are customarily written. I want this letter placed at the beginning.

## Author’s Prologue

Solomon was called by three names: Solomon, that is, “peaceful”; Jedidiah, that is, “beloved”; and Ecclesiastes, which is *Qoheleth*, that is, “preacher,” because he gathers assemblies. Corresponding to the number of his names, he published three books: Proverbs, that is, *Mashalot*; Ecclesiastes; and the *Song of Songs*.

In Proverbs he teaches a little child, instructing him, as it were, concerning present duties. In Ecclesiastes he instructs a man mature in age, so that he may not think anything in worldly affairs perpetual, but may recognize that everything we see is fleeting and brief. Finally, having become a mature man and being prepared after trampling upon the world, he joins him to the embraces of the Bridegroom in the *Song of Songs*. For unless we first abandon vices and renounce the pomp of the world, we cannot say: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth.”

In this order the followers of the philosophers are also educated: first they teach ethics, then physics; and once they have seen that someone has progressed in these, they lead him through theory all the way to theology. This should be noted. For in Proverbs the title reads: “The Proverbs of Solomon, son of David, king of Israel.” In Ecclesiastes: “The words of Ecclesiastes, son of David, king of Jerusalem.” But in the *Song of Songs* neither “son of David” nor “king of Israel” or “of Jerusalem” is prefixed. For beginners, a father’s dignity and the proper name of the kingdom are sufficient; he is an equal teacher and does not know himself to be a king.

Christ is the peaceful one of God the Father and our Ecclesiastes. Having destroyed the dividing wall and abolished enmity in his flesh, he made both one (Ephesians II, 14): “I give you my peace” (John XIV, 27). Concerning him the Father said to the disciples: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; listen to him” (Matthew III, 17), because he is the head of the Church.

## Chapter One

*(The kiss of the mouth: the Bridegroom’s inspiration.)*

### 1. Verse 1. “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth.”

The mouth of the Bridegroom is the inspiration of Christ. The kiss of the mouth is the sweet love of inspiration.

Thus the Bride, burning with desire and inflamed for the embrace of her Bridegroom, says: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth.” As though she were saying: Let him come whom I love above all things—or rather, whom alone I love—let him touch me with the sweetness of his inspiration; for when I feel his kiss, I immediately abandon myself through a sudden transformation and, liquefied into his likeness, am at once changed into him.

For the holy mind is disgusted by everything it perceives through the body, and longs to be wholly transformed into those spiritual things. While these bodily things clamor around it, it flees toward those spiritual realities and desires to hide itself there, so that it may not perceive these things. Therefore the Bridegroom’s kiss must come first: if he does not draw her by the bond of the most welcome love, she cannot at all discover how to turn toward him, held as she is by the force of her most burdensome heaviness.

But the compassionate Bridegroom, perceiving her anxiety, loving her affection, and hearing her desire, offers her a kiss. Lest she grow weary through longing, he soothes her with a taste of his sweetness; and while he presents his presence to her, he kindles her toward a greater kiss of love. Hence, feeling him, she turns toward him; and having him present, she soon rejoices and, with her voice changed, addresses him and says:

*(The breasts of the Bridegroom: love of God and neighbor.)*

### 2. “For your breasts are better than wine, fragrant with the finest perfumes.”

The breasts of the Bridegroom are love of God and neighbor. From these breasts he nourishes his Bride with the milk of compassion; amid the storms of temptations he cherishes her with them and renews her so that she may persevere.

But what is expressed by wine except temporal care? Every worldly mind is intoxicated by it, so that it becomes wholly or almost wholly insensible to the knowledge of invisible things. Yet the breasts of the Bridegroom are better than wine, because wine kills, whereas they nourish; wine clouds the eyes of the mind, whereas they sharpen them; wine makes the wise apostatize (Ecclesiasticus XIX, 2), whereas these make even the ignorant exceedingly wise. As often as the Bride sucks from them with an abundance of love, so many sayings of wisdom does she draw into the womb of her memory.

For charity makes the heart peaceful, strengthens the mind in temptations, and, so that the soul of the righteous may be the seat of wisdom, grants it rest and prepares a place for it. These breasts, therefore, are fragrant with the finest perfumes, because they carry with them the scent of sweetness through words of wisdom and examples of holiness. Whoever refreshes himself with the holy love of God experiences both the fragrance and the sweetness of spiritual gifts. By the abundance of these good things he draws his neighbors with him to taste inward realities, and nourishes them with these breasts so that they may grow strong in divine love.

*(The name of Christ is poured-out oil.)*

### 3. Verse 2. “Your name is poured-out oil.”

The name of the Bridegroom is Christ. But the name of the Bridegroom is poured out like oil, because all who are truly counted by the Christian name overflow with holy charity. By it they are softened, and by the same charity they are continually drenched so that they may emit the flames of good example. Through this charity they are kindled more intensely toward love of Christ himself, and from him they receive that by which they may cling to him more fully—the very thing with which they are suffused.

Hence what follows:

*(The young women: holy souls.)*

### 4. “Therefore the young women loved you.”

What are signified by the young women except holy souls, who are regenerated through the water of baptism by the Holy Spirit and transformed into new life through the New Testament? They love Christ because of the pouring out of oil, since, called to grace, they find in him the sweetness of perpetual life. For love of this sweetness they reject all the vanities and riches of the world.

There are some who love God in such a way that they despise themselves; they are drawn into the interior in order to find God. Since God does not lie on the surface, they labor in meditation, examine their thoughts with the greatest subtlety, devote themselves to reading, and do not cease by every means to seek how God may be found. These truly perceive the fragrance of perfumes and anoint themselves with the pouring out of oil, because, while they cast away every corruption of vices, they find flowers for themselves. Through their composition they make fragrant perfumes and prepare them for God.

The person who is such burns with desire and, as though possessing nothing, always longs for greater things. Since he lacks sufficient strength in himself, he gazes toward God and asks to be drawn after him, saying:

*(The fragrance of perfumes: divine grace, which we follow.)*

### 5. Verse 3. “Draw me after you; we will run in the fragrance of your perfumes.”

No one runs who is not drawn, because one whom divine grace does not assist is weighed down by the burden of his corruption. Divine grace goes before us: showing us the sweetness of inward things, it pierces us with remorse concerning outward things. Then, as the mind passes into those realities, it despises temporal things because of its love for them.

The one who is drawn therefore runs, because, willingly following the bond of love and strengthened by the love of grace, he passes through all obstacles without heaviness. Nor is this surprising, since he follows the fragrance of perfumes. When the sweetness of spiritual gifts is felt, what is there in this temporal existence whose desire could hold back Christ’s holy Bride and prevent her from hastening toward that place? There she rejoices in the gentleness of perfumes, and while she breathes through the nostrils of discernment, charity smells sweet to her.

Hence he passes from the singular number to the plural, because in the love of God he also finds the commandment that urges us to love our neighbor. Instructed by this commandment, she gives forth to us what she has tasted sweetly within, saying:

*(The inner chambers: the mysteries of holy contemplation.)*

### 6. “The king brought me into his inner chambers.”

What should we understand by the inner chambers of this Bridegroom, who is king, except the secrets of Holy Scripture, which we investigate, and the mysteries of holy contemplation? If we are refreshed by their delights, we immediately grow strong.

Whoever is brought into them undoubtedly despises all temporal things at once, because he is enriched with eternal things. Therefore it follows:

*(Exultation in the breasts of the Church.)*

### 7. “We will exult and rejoice in you, remembering your breasts more than wine.”

The holy soul, Bride of Christ, exults in the delights of her Bridegroom when she rejects bodily things and hides herself in spiritual realities. She makes that same Bridegroom her delight, and in consideration of him cares nothing for all worldly things.

But she does this in remembrance of the breasts, because, when she recalls how greatly Christ loved her—he who, dying on the cross, redeemed her with his blood, and who daily nourishes her in the bosom of the Church, his mother, with the milk of that same blood—she undoubtedly intensifies her love for him more and more.

This milk is rightly said to be sweeter than wine, because through Christ’s blood we are mercifully nourished, whereas previously we were harshly constrained by the letter of the Law. Through this love what is said is fulfilled:

*(The upright: Christians.)*

### 8. “The upright love you.”

Only the upright truly love Christ, because whoever still runs after the crooked paths of vices, continually stumbling against the line of uprightness, cannot love Christ, the author of justice, at all.

A person walks along the way of truth when he both performs works of virtue and always acknowledges his sins. Therefore he also says:

*(The Bride’s blackness and beauty through mortification.)*

### 9. Verse 4. “I am black but beautiful, daughters of Jerusalem, like the tents of Kedar, like Solomon’s curtains.”

The holy soul rightly says that she is both black and beautiful, because she continually sees the ugliness of her sins, yet carefully displays outwardly the form of that justice which she sees in her inmost self.

She is rightly called black like the tents of Kedar and beautiful like Solomon’s curtains, because, insofar as she bears the darkness of mortality, she is stained by the blackness of corruption. For Kedar is interpreted as “darkness”; Solomon, who signifies Christ, is called “peaceful.”

She therefore says that she is beautiful like Solomon’s curtains because, while she does not neglect to imitate the saints who mortify themselves in imitation of Christ, she is joined by likeness to their beauty. But lest her neighbors, concentrating on her blackness, love her good examples less for imitation, she satisfies them by showing the cause of her ugliness. She turns the daughters of Jerusalem away from admiring her, saying:

*(Every holy soul is dark in comparison with Christ.)*

### 10. Verse 5. “Do not look at me because I am dark, because the sun has discolored me.”

The sun signifies Christ. The sun therefore discolored her because, however brightly the soul may shine, in comparison with Christ it loses its radiance.

There are some who in this night of the world shine like stars for human beings and appear as lights to their neighbors. But as soon as they compare themselves with Christ’s justice, they are almost without light—although previously they shone incomparably for human beings.

How she came to shine even to a small degree, she shows when she adds:

*(The Bride’s mother: the holy Church, whose sons are the apostles.)*

### 11. “The sons of my mother fought against me; they appointed me guardian of the vineyards.”

The Bride’s mother is the holy Church; the sons of her mother were the holy apostles. Before the preaching of the apostles, almost the entire world was rebellious; almost every soul had defiled itself with the worship of idols and accumulated criminal desires.

When the preaching of the apostles arrived, it fought against all these things by the word. In many places it overthrew the kingdom of demons and enlarged the kingdom of Christ, that is, the holy Church.

Therefore the apostles appointed the congregation bound to Christ and sanctified by him as guardian of the vineyards. They scattered the first believers throughout the world into churches, so that they might gather and guard them. She reveals the reason for this dispersion when she says:

*(The vineyard: Judea.)*

### 12. “I did not guard my vineyard.”

What is signified by the vineyard in the singular except Judea? It expelled the faithful from itself because it scorned being guarded.

After the soul has been overcome by preaching and made the Bride of Christ, she burns with love and, seeking the one whom she loves, exercises herself in the interior, saying:

*(She makes Christ rest at midday.)*

### 13. Verse 6. “Tell me, you whom my soul loves, where you pasture, where you lie at midday, lest I begin to wander after the flocks of your companions.”

Christ pastures and lies at midday under the shade when, in the cooling of the Holy Spirit, he prepares for himself a kind of rest and nourishment. By midday the heat of vices is expressed; by shade the breeze of spiritual grace is signified.

At the burning of midday, therefore, Christ rests in the shade, because while the heat of vices blazes in the reprobate, he grants refreshment to his Bride and makes in her a pleasant place of rest for himself.

But the Bride asks that this be disclosed to her, although it is never revealed to anyone except one who receives the same gift of sanctifying grace. Why she burns to receive these things is made clear when it says:

*(Lest she wander after the flocks of passions.)*

### 14. “Lest I begin to wander after the flocks of your companions.”

Truly, anyone in whom Christ does not lie wanders, because the mind that is not filled by the sweet and weighty Spirit of Christ is scattered and carried about by many thoughts.

But who are Christ’s companions, after whose flocks the Bride fears she may wander, except the false Christians? They are called brothers of Christ either because of the name alone or also because they share in the sacraments; by dwelling together in the Church, they associate with the elect whom Christ himself called brothers.

Their multitudes are rightly called flocks as a reproach, because, living like irrational animals without order, they are handed over to deceptive spirits for devouring. Whoever, expelled from his inward desire, imitates the folly of the reprobate in very similar desires wanders after such flocks.

The elect endure these people with distress; yet, tested by their persecutions, they are brought purer to eternal goods. Hence the Bride is admonished when she is reproved:

*(We must fight against temptations.)*

### 15. Verse 7. “If you do not know yourself, O beautiful among women, go out and follow the tracks of the flocks.”

If the Bride does not know herself, let her go out and depart. For whoever does not know that he has been placed here in order to overcome temptations through endurance withdraws from intimacy with Christ. Placed in battle, he refuses to fight alongside his Lord.

Everyone must know that when we are in temptation, we are commanded to fight against the powers of the air, because we cannot be crowned without victory. Even if the adversary were absent and there were no one for us to defeat, the crown would nevertheless be lacking, since we receive it only by conquering.

Whoever does not know this is in battle yet rejoices as though at peace, and is wounded all the more frequently because he is more secure: he does not know what he should beware of. Rightly, therefore, he is separated from the fighters and made to follow the tracks of the flocks, because, neglecting to imitate the prudent, he necessarily follows the reprobate, whom folly has made like brute animals.

*(Goats: impure thoughts; the shepherds’ tents: gatherings of heretics.)*

### 16. “And pasture your goats beside the shepherds’ tents.”

By goats, impure thoughts are signified; by the shepherds’ tents, the conventicles of heretics are represented.

Whoever, therefore, does not know how to fight pastures goats beside the shepherds’ tents. For anyone who does not manfully resist temptation with the swords placed before him nourishes impure thoughts in his heart like wanton goats, and becomes like one who has also departed from the faith.

But Christ teaches the soul that longs to become the Bride of Christ how it should conduct itself when he immediately says to her by comparison:

*(The Israelite cavalry, tested by many temptations.)*

### 17. Verse 8. “I have compared you, my beloved, to my cavalry in Pharaoh’s chariots.”

We know that the Israelite cavalry, fleeing Pharaoh’s chariots, left them submerged in the sea. Yet it did not immediately enter the promised land. First it endured many temptations in the wilderness for forty years, overcame many kings through many labors, and finally reached the blessed land in which it would rejoice with the Bridegroom.

To it is fittingly said what follows:

*(The Bride’s cheeks.)*

### 18. Verse 9. “Your cheeks are beautiful, like those of a turtledove.”

After a turtledove has once lost its mate, it never joins itself to another, but always lives alone and perseveres in mourning, because, unable to find the one it loved, it seeks him.

So every holy soul, while absent from her Bridegroom, does not withdraw from his love, but always yearns and sighs for him. Since she does not find the one whom she loves greatly, she withdraws from every alien love and, as though in the modesty of her cheeks, displays the chastity of her heart through her very outward bearing and conduct.

It follows:

*(The Bride’s neck: preachers.)*

### 19. “Your neck is like necklaces.”

By the Bride’s neck, the preachers of the holy Church are signified. Preachers are compared with necklaces either because they are the ornament of the Church or because they protect the Church, as a necklace protects the breast—or because of their roundness, that is, their perfection.
