In necklaces, jewels are set in gold. By gold, wisdom is expressed; by stones, adornments are represented. The Bride’s neck is therefore like necklaces because every upright preacher of the Church clothes himself inwardly with wisdom and outwardly performs the works he has seen in wisdom.

To her it is also said:

*(Golden chains: Holy Scripture.)*

### 20. Verse 10. “We will make golden chains for you, studded with silver.”

The moray is a fish which, when caught, coils itself into a circle. In imitation of it an earring is made, called a *murenula*, and by it preaching is signified, since preaching clings to the ears and penetrates them.

Necklaces are fastened to the neck by chains, because both wisdom and religion are attached to preachers from the Holy Scriptures. By the chains, Holy Scripture is understood.

They are rightly called golden and studded with silver, because Holy Scripture shines with wisdom and is heard throughout the whole world through resonant preaching. For just as wisdom is represented by gold, so holy preaching is represented by silver.

The Bride responds to these words of the Bridegroom and, through bodily images of things, reveals the love with which she burns spiritually within, saying:

*(The Bride’s nard: good example.)*

### 21. Verse 11. “While the king was on his couch, my nard gave forth its fragrance.”

Nard is a low-growing herb which, when tasted, drives away cold and warms the limb.

The king entered his couch when our Lord Jesus Christ bodily penetrated the inner regions of heaven. While he rested there, the Bride’s nard gave forth its fragrance, because the virtue of the holy Church spread the sweet fame of goodness far and wide.

For the Lord ascended to heaven and sent his Holy Spirit upon the disciples. Filled with him, they preached words of salvation to the world and spread everywhere the fame of good odor through holy works.

Every faithful soul receives him in baptism so that through him it may compound perfumes for itself from the mixture of virtues and refresh its neighbors by displaying its example, as though by the fragrance of perfume.

It follows:

*(A bundle of myrrh: mortification.)*

### 22. Verse 12. “My beloved is a bundle of myrrh to me; he will dwell between my breasts.”

The bodies of the dead are customarily embalmed with myrrh so that they may not decay. Myrrh, then, [lacuna]. The remainder, to the end of the Commentary, is found word for word in the exposition published under the name of Saint Gregory the Great among his works. See *Patrologia*, vol. LXXIX, col. 471.

## Letter of Robert of Tumbalena, Prior of Saint Vigor, to the Monks of Saint Michael of the Mount

*Concerning a certain epileptic monk converted from frivolity.*

*(Mabillon, Benedictine Annals, vol. V, Appendix, p. 659, from a manuscript formerly in the library of Saint Stephen at Caen, now Ottoboniana.)*

To the brothers dwelling on the Mount of Blessed Michael: Brother Robert and the other brothers serving blessed Vigor at Mont-Chrismat.

Blessed is God the Father, and blessed is the Son of God, and holy is the Spirit of both: the triune God, one in the substance of the same majesty. He hates nothing that he has made (Wisdom XI, 25), because he wills all human beings to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth (Titus I, 1). He does not despise even us, who are despisers; rather, he converts those who oppose him, loves those who have been converted, and raises those whom he loves to the most joyful and blessed vision of his countenance, through the marvels of his singular power.

This is our God, alone to be feared, alone to be loved. He does not regard a man [read: men], but destroys what exists in order to instruct what does not exist. Among us also, his lowest servants, he has revealed his fear and love, striking the proud and healing the humble.

I shall tell you of a matter worthy of remembrance, unheard-of in our time. Although its extraordinary character can astonish everyone’s ears, it especially strikes and troubles you, brothers of the mountain, because it concerns you and is being sent to you.

A certain brother named Hugh lived among us. He was the nephew of the abbot of Lonay, whom you know very well, since he was raised as a boy in your schools. The man of whom I speak suffered an event which it is necessary for you to know.

One day in the choir, on a Tuesday, while our brothers were celebrating the morning Mass, he himself was there with the others, as it seemed to us, healthy and cheerful. Feeling a slight pain in his head, he went to bed to lie down and rest. While he lay there, without any of us knowing, he was suddenly seized by the disorder which physicians call *epilepsy*, using a Greek word, or the sacred disease, because it attacks the sacred parts of a human being, such as the head and mind. We commonly call it the falling sickness, because it causes a person to fall.

He was seized by it, immediately lost consciousness, and closed his eyes, which he also squeezed shut with his hands. He bent his knees, kicking and rolling about on the bed.

I happened by chance to be sitting in the cloister writing when a distressed brother ran up and said that Hugh was dying. At these words I rose trembling and ran after him. By then the Mass had ended, and all the brothers were running, carrying a cross and holy water.

When we arrived, we found him lying without consciousness, squeezing his eyes with his hands and kicking with his knees. We therefore began the seven penitential psalms. Seeing that his hands were pressing upon his eyes more than seemed appropriate, I pulled them away and gave them to the brothers to hold, although he struggled violently, despite feeling nothing.

After we had stood there for a short while, praying psalms over him and signing him with the cross, I ordered that he be carried into the oratory. The obedient brothers could scarcely carry him, grasping him from every side; for the disease threw him about in our hands, and all his limbs were twisted and dislocated with a wonderful and pitiable contortion.

They laid him prostrate before the altar of blessed Nicholas. They too prostrated themselves and prayed with profound contrition. When I was present there, I suffered such extraordinary grief, shaken by tears and sighs, that I could neither speak nor recite the psalms; I remained fixed to the ground, doing nothing but weep mournfully.

After the seven psalms and the litany had been said, thirty psalms were then recited, which it is customary for monks to celebrate before the nocturnal synaxis. Then he rose, uttering pitiable cries and shaking us, who had surrounded him, with immense and unbearable grief.

I then rose from the ground and went to him where he had lain in the brothers’ hands. He had risen enough to sit. Looking at him—he could scarcely recognize me—I asked him, drenched in tears, to tell us how he was. At length, speaking very [lacuna] and quietly, he said that he had been miserably tortured and broken.

I therefore ordered that he be placed on a bed that was there, so that he might rest. When this had been done, I asked the brothers to go to the chapter house as usual, because I could not withdraw from the brother, since grief was tormenting me completely. I sat before him, mourning and weeping.

When I spoke with him, he said: “Just now a certain terrifying voice addressed me, saying: ‘Why have you left your monastery?’”

While this voice was rebuking and frightening me, another voice, which I heard, immediately replied, quite peacefully and sweetly: “What is that to you?”

When I asked whether he had seen anything, he said that he had only heard something and had seen nothing.

At last, when the chapter meeting had ended and certain brothers had been summoned, I ordered that he be carried to the infirmary. After he had been carried there and lay down, I followed him, since so new and sorrowful an event did not allow me to leave him in any way, and I remained constantly with him.

Up to the same hour on the following day, the same attack seized him seven times in our presence and before our eyes. On the other days he suffered the same thing almost every day, once or twice.

Accordingly, two very learned physicians who happened to be present in the city were summoned. They did everything they could for him. But God, who had cast him down by his own hand and had determined to heal him by his own action alone, did not make him suitable to be raised up by the efforts of human hands.

While these things were happening, one day I entered the house where the brother was kept apart, as was appropriate for such a condition. I found him laughing, sitting, and joking with the servants who, at my command, diligently attended to his needs.

For he was as frivolous as you know. When he had lived with me in the cloister before this illness, no threats, blows, blandishments, or admonitions could bring him back to himself or make him recognize himself. He was utterly unrestrained in frivolity, jokes, and youthful wantonness; he followed buffoonery in every way, utterly despising restraint and never curbing himself by any other means.

But why do I speak of human effort, when at that time he was being tortured by divine judgment and tormented by uncertain and horrifying sufferings? Even then his hardness was not broken, so that he became in any degree less wanton; rather, he became increasingly loosened in his conduct. The attack did not continue without interruption, but came at uncertain intervals: he was tortured, held, and released.

When released, after an hour or half an hour, having recovered his strength, he would rise and feed upon his former frivolity. Tortured by the disease, he indulged the madness of youth all the worse the more pleasurably he was tortured.

As I had begun to say, when I entered the house, I was greatly displeased by his excessively importunate laughter, but I kept silent and sat with him. I spared him and said nothing; I even pretended not to be displeased by what he was doing. I feared that if I spoke to him somewhat harshly, he might be disturbed by my words and fall into his customary attack. Thus, often even while concealing my feelings, I joked with him, wholly rejoicing in his health and tranquility.

While I was sitting with him, he said: “Last night, while I was sleeping, I seemed to myself to be brought before the divine judgment. When I stood there, with my conscience tormenting me, I was accused. Many evil deeds that I had committed were brought before me; I blushed at them painfully, more than I can now comprehend in thought.”

When I heard this, and saw in him no fear or seriousness, I grieved silently. With my eyes lowered, I considered how hard-hearted a man he was—one who was not terrified or frightened even by the divine judgment.

At last, after twenty-seven days had passed in this alternation of the affliction’s coming and going, on the twenty-eighth day I—who kept him constantly in mind—entered the brothers’ refectory after supper and sat beside the curtain that hung stretched before the brother’s bed. After I had sat there for a long while, while he lay in bed, I wondered that he was not speaking. Opening the curtain, I looked in, and behold, he was lying on his back, his eyes closed, as though asleep. While I hesitated, wondering whether he was held by sleep or illness—for he was not moving at all, as he had formerly done when the affliction approached—I went nearer, shook his head, and called him by his proper name. When he did not answer or open his eyes, I realized that the affliction had come upon him, and I waited until it withdrew. When it had withdrawn, he opened his eyes, [Col. 1373C] and, stretching out his legs, uttered a plaintive cry, saying that he had suffered greatly and was exhausted by the assault of his limbs. Thus, while he spoke with me, the affliction came and went three times within that same hour.

Seeing my brother and son—whose sake I would have laid down my life, if I could—suffering in such distress, and being unable to help him, I groaned inwardly. Then he said to me: “Father, Father, what a dreadful night I must endure—the night that lies before us!” When I asked him to say what he feared and how he knew it, he added: “I heard a voice terrifying me greatly, saying: ‘Ask your prior Robert and your other brothers to pray for you, because unless divine mercy comes to your aid, you are going to suffer this most dreadful night. Therefore, Fathers, help me now and pray for me, because I am very much afraid, considering the words that were spoken to me.’”

At my command, four brothers whom I designated by name were immediately summoned. The most sacred body of Christ our Lord was brought with a cross and candlesticks. After I had exhorted him and confession had first been made, he received communion of the sacred body. Then, made more secure, he lay there while we all sat before him and together awaited either the grace or the judgment of God, because he can do whatever he wills.

And behold, night had now fallen and the brothers were sleeping, except for those who were with me. When the affliction came upon him, he withdrew from us as usual, closing his eyes and lying motionless. While we were singing psalms and he was repeatedly going and returning, I ordered the brothers who were sleeping to be awakened and come. As soon as they entered, we all sang psalms with the same intention, praying that divine mercy would come to the aid of our brother, who was as we were.

Then suddenly, while we were all watching, he closed his eyes in his customary manner and withdrew. After lying there for a short while, he returned, opened his eyes, and looked at me—I had always been standing beside his face. He said: “Tell those lords to go and rest, because by God’s grace I am free and released from this affliction; I shall suffer nothing until the third day.” When I asked him how he knew this, he replied: “I heard a voice saying to me: ‘Tell the servants of God who are around you to go and rest, because until the third day you will suffer nothing from this illness.’” Thus, having become certain, I ordered those who had come to withdraw, and they went away.

After these words and deeds, the brother became well, remaining so throughout that day, the following night, and the following day, until the ninth or tenth hour of the third day. Yet he remained extremely fearful, and his former lightness was greatly restrained. With heavy sorrow, he awaited what God intended to happen to him.

I approached him and addressed him, asking him to return to his senses, recognize what had happened, confess all his sins, and especially those by which his conscience had tormented him as though with instruments of torture in the divine judgment, just as it had appeared to him in his dream. Hearing this and assenting, he immediately confessed and explained to me his entire past life, as far as he could remember. With whatever lamentation he could muster, he accepted from me the counsel I found best.

On the third day, the day of the threats, following my counsel and admonition, he went in the morning to the oratory, and I went with him. While the brothers celebrated Prime, the subsequent psalms, and the morning Mass—which they also celebrated by our order for his sins—he remained seated outside the choir, persevering in meditation and tears. When we had finished what needed to be finished, we entered the chapter house at that hour and sat down. After other conversations that seemed necessary, I introduced a discussion of him. With everyone’s assent, he was summoned to the chapter house. He had requested this of me, and, after consulting and admonishing him first, he followed me; for he had already been so thoroughly subdued that in every matter he could, he entirely followed my will.

When he entered, he threw himself face down before us, filled with such abundant tears and broken by such grief that he shook me to the depths of my heart. His sorrow was so great that I could scarcely speak in response to his words, being agitated by mingled joy. I rejoiced greatly because I saw one who had been so proud, so wanton, and so obstinate in every vanity of youth now prostrate, so humble and restrained, and converted to the full seriousness of penitence.

At my command he rose, and, still persevering in the same grief, so that he could scarcely speak, he asked us to prescribe what we wished concerning him and his sins. He acknowledged that he had committed very many sins and was burdened by them beyond what he had expected. I therefore answered for everyone as best I could; for the groans of my heart and the tears flowing down prevented me from expressing fully what I wished.

He then accepted from the brother appointed for this purpose the judgment of the rods, stripped of his woolen tunic, with such humility—as he later told me privately—that it seemed little to him that he was being beaten.

I therefore ordered the brothers, who were obedient in everything, to fast that day and abstain entirely from eating cooked dishes. “As for your meal,” I said, “I myself shall have your customary food prepared in full, but let the poor in this same refectory dine one hour before you, so that in every way we can—in fasting, prayers, and almsgiving—we may come to the aid of our brother placed in such great need.”

When all this had been granted, and the brother who stood before us weeping profusely and sighing heavily had asked for prayers, and when we who were seated had first interrupted our speech with scarcely restrained weeping, we rose and went to the oratory, singing the seven penitential psalms. There we lay prostrate until they had been completed.

After all this I ordered one of the brothers immediately to celebrate Mass for his sins, which he himself was to hear and at which he was to receive the sacraments of Christ’s body and blood. When everything prescribed had been done, and the poor had been fed and given one denarius each, I also had a poor man who had been found sitting there eat in the presence of the brother for whom all these things had been done, dining together with him.

I wanted Christ, in the form of a poor man, to be refreshed not only for him but also with him. We were all beseeching Christ to become our helper in the necessity that was so near at hand. Two denarii were also given to this man; I had handed them to the brother for that purpose.

When we had all eaten and the feared hour was drawing near, I entered the house and found the brother sitting there, frightened. He immediately gave me his hand, and, when I took it, rose from the place where he was sitting. He went with me and threw himself onto the bed. After I had sat before him for a while, he sighed and said: “Alas, Father, how badly my head hurts now! Now my knees hurt me; now my legs; now my arms; and behold, pain is repeated and increasing throughout my whole body.”

While he was saying this and suffering intensely, a layman arrived, with whom I needed to speak. I went out, but was immediately called back by the boy who was attending the sick man. Entering the house, I found him lying there, seized by his former affliction. He did not, however, kick or roll about as before, but lay motionless with his eyes closed, as though asleep.

After a short time, when I returned, he opened his eyes and looked at me standing beside him; then he was seized again in the same manner. When this happened repeatedly and he foamed at the mouth, I, seeing how greatly he suffered, groaned from the depths of my heart and sent for the community of brothers, asking them to be present. While they were there and we were singing psalms, the illness seized the sick man before everyone.

While he was still held by it, with his eyes and fists closed and sensing nothing of what we were doing, he suddenly opened his right hand, raised it to his head, and made the sign of the cross over himself three times, while we watched and wondered.

We therefore sang psalms as much as we could, waiting for him to return to his senses so that we might learn from him why he had done this. And behold, he returned, shaken by lamentation, saying: “God, God, how tightly I am bound!” While the others were singing psalms, I asked him to explain what was happening to him. He replied: “Evil beasts are attacking me.” When I asked whether they were now present or had withdrawn, he said: “They have withdrawn.”

I immediately ordered all the brothers to go and perform the evening prayers and praises. After they had gone out, I remained alone with the brother lying there and questioned him carefully, so that I might hear from him the truth about the sign of the cross he had made three times and the beasts he had mentioned.

When he saw me concerned about this, he said: “Just now I seemed to see a man enter through that little door, black and more horrible than I can say, with fiery eyes, casting fire from his mouth and breathing it over me. He was dragging two horrible dogs by the hand, just as horrible as he was. When he stirred them up against me and drove them on, and I was greatly terrified by their attack, I struck one of them—the one who was leading—with my fist and drove it away. When the other approached, though it did not come as near as the first, I struck it with my fist as well and drove it away after the first. Freed from them, I went to the man who had remained fixed in place and, striking him similarly with my fist, drove him away after the dogs. Thus, by the Lord’s mercy, I was freed from these three enemies by three blows. I understood, therefore, that those three blows were the three signs of the cross which I had seen being made while we were singing psalms.”

Meanwhile, one of the brothers who had gone away was called back, and we completed the appointed evening prayers and praises with the sick man, who also sang psalms with us. Afterward I ordered another to be summoned, so that there would be three of us with the brother lying there. All the others, after completing the offices of the day, went to bed earlier than they were accustomed to, by our order.

I was reasoning in my heart that, if some great necessity—death or some other calamity, for we were uncertain what would happen—were imminent, all ought to be present. It would be good if they had been somewhat refreshed by sleep and could act more soberly in whatever needed to be done.

Thus there were three of us with the fourth, who was suffering, speaking with him and comforting him as far as we were able. His body was so weak and exhausted that, when he wanted to arrange himself in the bed in which he lay, in any way that might make even a slight relief from such great distress by changing his position, he could not do so at all. We who were present, wishing to adjust him according to the need we saw in him, could scarcely move him even with great effort.

When he wanted to attend to the needs of nature, he could neither rise nor move from his place. He offered himself to be raised and carried by two brothers with their arms extended. They carried him, with great difficulty and without any helpful movement on his part—except that he dragged one foot along the ground more than he controlled it—and placed him back on the bed before me as best they could.

Although he was weighed down by such a burden of sickness, he nevertheless said that it seemed to him that he was suffering nothing in his body, because of the fear by which his spirit was tormented. When I asked what he feared, he said: “I fear that I shall return into the hands of those whom I saw, or into the hands of worse ones.”

We were speaking in this way to one another when, as night was now approaching, he was seized again and foamed at the mouth. Raising his hand as before, he signed himself entirely.

When we were singing psalms and he returned, we asked whether he had seen anything. “I saw,” he said, “three men entering this house, carrying three fiery spears that stank as though they were made of sulfur. When they wanted to pierce me with them, I defended myself with the sign of the cross that seemed to be held by me”—for we were holding a cross in his hand—“and drove them away.”

Thus he lay suffering and lamenting bitterly, yet, having received consolation, he said that he hoped he would escape very well.

While I was saying something to the brothers who were present, in order to strengthen his consolation, about the Scriptures and the faith of the Trinity, and a large part of the night had already passed, he suddenly, while listening attentively, closed his eyes and lost consciousness.

While he was in this same ecstasy—for I must now call it an ecstasy, not an illness or affliction—he joined his hands and raised them toward heaven as though praying. We were reciting the psalm of faith, “Whoever wishes to be saved” (*Quicunque vult salvus esse*), and repeating it antiphonally. He opened his eyes, kept his hands raised as he had joined them, and said: “Glory to you, God.”

When we hastened to complete the psalm, and he repeatedly said, “Glory to you, God,” we greatly desired to know where he had received such a joyful and lovely voice, which he repeated so many times, and we questioned him. Looking at me somewhat sternly, he said: “Let all the monks of Mont Saint-Michel who reside in this monastery be summoned to me, for I have been sent as a messenger.”

This displeased me greatly. I feared that it might be some deceptive apparition, and I was also afraid of tiring the brothers, who would have to rise for the nocturnal prayers, by waking them. I resisted this with many words. But he firmly opposed me, saying that it was entirely necessary for this to be done.

At last I did not wish to resist further, fearing on the other hand that, if this were a divine command, I would make the brother disobedient to God, and that both he and I would consequently be held guilty. We asked him what he thought would happen to him, and he replied that he still did not know.

Those whom he wished were therefore summoned, and they arrived very quickly. When they were present, and I asked him to speak, he said: “In the name of God, Saint Michael, and Saint Vigor, the excellent patron, I say to all of you: never again return to or enter Mont Saint-Michel in order to remain there, as long as the man who is now abbot there is alive. If you go and remain there, you will be destroyed by an evil end and a most dreadful death.”

When they bowed at these words, weeping for joy, he added: “I shall tell you signs that these words are true, but I have not yet heard them; I await the signs that are to be heard.”

When he had said this, I said to those mountain brothers—there were five of them: “Come now, my lords, you have heard what has been commanded you by God. Go away now, so that you may again rest in your beds.”

Although I had carefully attended to everything else, I had understood nothing about the signs that were to be announced. But he later made clear to me, with everyone who had been present as witness, that he had told me precisely what he said.

At my command the brothers were therefore obeying more quickly and had already begun to rise, when the man lying before us was seized again. Seeing this, I detained the brothers who had already risen, so that we might sing psalms together while awaiting the outcome.

We therefore recited the entire psalm “Whoever wishes to be saved” and added the “Glory to the Father.” When it was finished, he returned and sat up in bed, saying: “Blessed be God, blessed be God.” Joining his hands and adoring, he looked at us with bright eyes and said: “Here are the signs I shall tell you, if you are willing to hear them.”

When we all replied that we were entirely willing, we who had recited Compline spoke, while those brothers who had recited it with us signaled their assent. He said: “If at any time henceforth, throughout all my life and yours, you see me suffering any sign or affliction of this illness because of which I lie here, know that what I have said was in no way true. And behold, I have now been made completely well and strong, able to rise, walk, and do whatever a healthy man ought to do.”

When, astonished with joy and at the evidence of the event—for we saw on his face some indescribable divine sign of health—we marveled, one of the brothers and I began in a restrained, quiet voice to say, “We praise you, God” (*Te Deum laudamus*). The brothers who, because of Compline, had no license to speak went to their beds at my command.

But he immediately rose, while we remained before him and those of us who had not gone away rose with him. Taking my hand, he stood up healthy, cheerful, and vigorous like us.

He stood rejoicing, while we looked at him with wonder and rejoiced with him. We had just seen a man lying on a bed, battered and crushed by a long and distressing illness, almost disintegrated in every limb, so that he could not even move to sit up, and for whom the very softness of the bed had been an immense torment. Yet at that very hour we now saw him rise vigorously, stand healthy and joyful with us.

We therefore blessed God, who strikes and heals, puts to death and gives life, leads down to the underworld and brings back (Tob. 13:2). He is therefore today in the cloister, blessing God with us—God who truly struck and healed him, as a loving father strikes and heals his son. For, being healed in body, he received a better and greater healing in the faith of his soul. Having been rebuked and corrected, he completely changed his conduct and subjected his very life to almighty God, giving testimony that he had truly felt the hand of the Almighty, to whom be honor, glory, and power forever and ever. Amen.

## In the Year of Our Lord 1092: Gerard II, Bishop of Cambrai

[Col. 1379]

### Historical Notice on Gerard II

*(Gallia Christiana III, 21.)*

[Col. 1379A] Gerard, born in the territory of Aalst, monk and provost at Saint-Vaast under Abbot Adolph, being a nephew of Saint Lietbert, was elected as his successor in 1076. He received investiture from King Henry; for this reason Pope Gregory VII doubted the legality of his ordination and instructed Hugh, bishop of Die and his legate, to convene a synod and ascertain whether Gerard had accepted the investiture in ignorance, or in full knowledge, of the prohibition of the Apostolic See against receiving investiture from a lay hand. [Note: [Col. 1379D] Gregory’s letter directing that, upon oath, Gerard should affirm before a gathering of bishops that he had been unaware of the pope’s decree forbidding lay investitures, is dated 12 May, indiction XV, that is, 1077; from this the time of Gerard’s election may be conjectured.]

After the defects apparent in his promotion had been remedied, he freely exercised the episcopal office under the legate Hugh. In 1079, indeed, the fourth year of his episcopate, he ordained Alard I abbot of the monastery of Anchin; he supported by letters issued in that year the foundation of that abbey near Douai, as recorded by Miraeus, chapter 40 of the *Belgian Diplomatic Records*. [Note: [Col. 1379D] In the cartulary of the Holy Sepulchre it is recorded that, in 1079, the second year of his episcopate, he gave Walter, abbot of the Holy Sepulchre, the altar of Lewes; here the first year of his episcopate seems to be reckoned not from his election, but from the time when Hugh, legate of Pope Gregory VII, rendered judgment concerning him.]

In the same year he subscribed to the letters of Philip, king of the Franks, for the monastery of Saint-Quentin of Beauvais, published by Antoine Loisel in the *Monuments of the Church of Beauvais*. About 1081 he ordained John abbot of Sithiu. At that time the care of the Church of Thérouanne had been entrusted to this bishop because of the internal dissensions of the people of Thérouanne with their bishop; these had continually grown worse from the death of Bishop Drogo during the time of three bishops—namely Hucbert, Lambert, imposed by Robert the Frisian, and Gerard—as is evident from the letters of Gregory VII and the chronicle of Iperius. In 1082 he subscribed the letters by which Baldwin, count of Flanders, and his mother Richildis subjected the monastery of Saint Dionysius at Brocqueroy to La Sauve-Majeure, according to Mabillon. He consented to the foundation of the monastery of Affligem about 1083, as is reported in the history of that monastery, book I, chapter 4, where Gerard is praised. He approved the letters of Anselm of Ribemont for the establishment of a monastery there, and likewise King Philip’s diploma of that same year, 1083. In the following year, on the advice of Baldwin, count of Hainaut, he gave the church of Saint Peter of Mons to the monastery of Saint Dionysius near Mons in Hainaut. He dedicated the church of Blessed Mary at Valenciennes, founded through the pious liberality of the same Baldwin and his mother Richildis. In 1085 he attended the Council of Compiègne, according to volume II, p. 599 of the *Spicilegium*. He mediated between the canons of Saint-Géry and the monks of the Holy Sepulchre concerning fishing in the River Scheldt.

In 1089, the fourteenth year of his episcopate, he ceded several freeholds from his own property to the Church of Cambrai. Having sent many such pious works before him to heaven, he departed for heaven on 11 August 1092 [Note: [Col. 1380D] On the day before the Kalends of August, according to Baluz’s manuscript notes to *Gallia Christiana*, 3 July, from Raissius.], and was buried in the greater church of Blessed Mary. During his tenure at Cambrai occurred the event of which Gregory VII writes to Godfrey, bishop of Paris, in book IV, epistle 20: “We have likewise been told that the people of Cambrai consigned a certain man to the flames because he had dared to say that simoniacs and fornicating priests ought not to celebrate Masses, and that their ministry ought by no means to be received. Since this seems to us a matter of great horror and, if true, one to be punished with every rigor of canonical severity, we admonish your fraternity diligently to investigate the truth of it. If you discover that they have stretched forth their impious hands to such cruelty, do not delay to exclude alike the instigators and accomplices from entry into and every communion of the Church, and endeavor to report to us the certainty of the matter.” In March 1077 this bishop issued certain statutes for the monks of Saint-Ghislain.

[Col. 1381]

### Charter of Gerard II, Bishop, on the Foundation of Anchin

*(Gallia Christiana III, 87.)*

Gerard the Second, by the grace of God bishop of Cambrai, to all Christ’s faithful: eternal blessedness.

Two knights of our diocese, distinguished by birth and wealth, namely Walter and Sicher, laying aside the belt of worldly knighthood and despising every possession of this world, promised to pursue the contemplative life; giving themselves and all that they possessed to God, they promised to serve him alone for ever. They chose the place called Anchin, wishing to restore the church there, which they had heard had once been built by Saint Gerdan, who led an eremitical life in that place. Walter and Sicher disclosed this settled plan to Anselm—Walter through his mother, Sicher through his wife. Anselm, moreover, surrendered into my hand the island of Anchin, the reed-bed belonging to it, and the adjoining estate called Vedret, which he held from us as a benefice; and I granted them in perpetual right to the church of Anchin.

Sign of Wido, archdeacon. Sign of Widricus, arch. Sign of Anselm. Sign of Vilard, John, Fulk, Ingebrand, Hubert, Wlfer, Alard. Sign of Walter, castellan of Douai. Sign of Clarebald.

Done in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1079, indiction XI, the twenty-sixth year of King Henry, and the fourth year of the episcopate of Lord Gerard II, bishop of Cambrai.

## In the Year of Our Lord 1093: Rainald I, Archbishop of Reims

[Col. 1381]

### Historical Notice on Rainald I

*(Gallia Christiana III, 21.)*

[Col. 1379A] “After many kinds of dissensions,” says the Chronicle of Nicaise, “after various oppressions of the rich and the humble, after innumerable dispersals of church ornaments, which were carried out within and outside the city by a certain Manasses, who unjustly sought the episcopal name and resisted God and all people with all his strength, suddenly a new light arose,” and so forth.

The reference is to Rainald, treasurer of Saint Martin of Tours, descended from the distinguished family of the Berleii, son of Berleius of Monasteriolum and of Graecia, or Grisia, who later married Geoffrey Martel, count of Anjou. Rainald—whom some call Rainold or Raginold—having attained the height of episcopal honor in 1083, devoted all his efforts to repairing what his predecessor had most disastrously done. For he found not only the city but the whole surrounding region devastated and trampled down as though by barbarians. Yet, skillful and ever watchful, he gathered what had been scattered and restored what had been emptied to its former dignity, [Col. 1382A] so that he seemed to have been born for the good of the Church and the welfare of the commonwealth.

In that same year, 1083, he subscribed to the foundation of the abbey of Ribemont. The following year he held a council at Soissons and wrote to Gerard, bishop of Cambrai, ordering him under obedience to cease harassing Christ’s poor—that is, the monks of Affligem—and not presume to trouble them further.

In the same year he confirmed the donation of the altar of Ventelay to Marmoutier, made by Count Theobald the Palatine in the time of King Henry and Guido, archbishop of Reims. In 1085 he convened a synod at Compiègne, at which the liberty of the church of Saint-Corneille of Compiègne was confirmed against Hilgot of Soissons. In the same year he sent monks from the abbey of Saint-Thierry to the village of Peteghen, then in the diocese of Tournai and now in that of Ghent.

In 1086 he gave seven altars to the monks of Saint-Basle and the church of Saint-Hilaire of Maroeuil to Abbess Agnes of Avesnes; [Col. 1383A] and he vigorously defended the monks of Affligem against Gerard of Cambrai. In the same year, when he was preparing to visit the thresholds of the apostles, he granted certain altars to the monks of Andain, and to the monks of Saint-Remi the altar situated in the village of Saint-Remi. He confirmed this latter donation in 1089.

In 1088 he granted the church of Buzancy, near the town of Tours on the Marne, to the church of Tours, so that his anniversary might be celebrated there. In 1089 he received a privilege from Urban II, supreme pontiff, by which the archbishops of Reims were to use the pallium, be called primates of Second Belgium, and consecrate the most Christian kings.

Returning from Italy through Auvergne in 1090, he stayed at La Chaise-Dieu. There, when he discovered that the monastic order was flourishing under stricter statutes through the care of Saint Robert’s disciples, he conceived the idea of bringing some of them with him to Reims, so that they might completely restore the monastery of Nicaise, which had utterly collapsed immediately after the death of Archbishop Gervais. Abbot Seguin consented to his most devout wishes.

In the same year he granted the altar of Vallis Monasteriolum to the nuns of Saint Peter of Reims. In 1091 he confirmed the gift of the church of Tours on the Marne, given in 1083 to the Cluniacs by Hugh, son of Manasses. In 1092 he held a council at Reims, by whose authority Robert, count of Flanders, ceased seizing the property of clerics who died. In the following year he gave the altar of Hermundeville to the monks of Saint-Thierry.

This archbishop is frequently mentioned in the history of the restoration of the proper bishopric of Arras, which occurred in 1092 and 1093 and which we formerly treated in the third volume of this *Gallia Christiana*. In the same year, 1093, he summoned a council at Soissons against the heretic Roscelin.

Meanwhile, when the king’s divorce was stirring up the greatest disturbances in the kingdom, Ivo of Chartres wrote to Rainald about it in the following terms (Epistle 13):

“Recently,” he says, “when I had been invited by the lord king to a conference, so that I might assist him in celebrating the marriage that he was preparing to contract with Bertrada, the wife of the count of Anjou, I replied that this ought not to be done, because the case between him and his wife had not yet been decided. He asserted that it had been fully decided by apostolic authority and yours, and by the commendation of you and your fellow bishops.

“On hearing this, I replied that I did not know of it and that I did not wish to attend such a marriage unless you were its consecrator and author, and your fellow bishops its defenders and collaborators, since this belongs by apostolic authority and ancient custom to the right of your church.

“Because, therefore, I have confidence in your religious character, I am certain that you will do or say nothing concerning a matter so dangerous to your reputation and so destructive to the honor of the entire kingdom unless it rests upon authority or reason. I most earnestly and devotedly beseech your charity to disclose to me, as I waver, the truth of this matter, which you know, and to give me sound counsel about it, even if that counsel is difficult and severe.”

Pope Urban also sharply rebuked Rainald and his suffragan bishops because they had not vigorously opposed so great a crime.

In 1094 a council was convened at Reims concerning this same matter. “King Philip,” says the Chronicle of Saint Peter of Vivi, “assembled the archbishops and bishops of his kingdom in the city of Reims and obtained from Archbishop Richer, by repeated entreaty, that he would not disdain to go to the council at Reims. He pointed out that Rainald, archbishop of Reims, was crippled by gout and unable to proceed from his see.” Hence that prelate was called by some Rainald the Crippled.

In the same year Rainald absolved Hugh, count of Rethel, who had been excommunicated on account of the harassment he had inflicted upon the men of Saint-Remi, after he had repented of his deed. The form of his absolution may be seen in the appendix among the documents.

In 1095 he consecrated Philip as bishop of Châlons. After giving the church of Hautmont to the monks of Saint Vincent of Laon, he attended the Council of Clermont, conscious of no involvement in the king’s adulterous marriage. Shortly beforehand he had subscribed to the council held that same year at Mont-Sainte-Marie.

Finally, while he was striving to secure the affairs of the people of Arras, which Pope Urban II had entrusted to him, omitting no effort or labor by which he might cut off at the root every future source of litigation with the people of Cambrai, he was seized by illness and died at Arras on the twelfth day before the Kalends of February in the year 1096. Some believe that he was buried there as well.

The necrology of the Church of Reims seems to contradict them, however, in these words: “The twelfth day before the Kalends of February: Rainald, our archbishop of good memory, rests within. He gave three altars to Saint Mary, so that the canons might be buried there; the remainder is distributed on his solemn anniversary among the canons present in the city.” Yet it is clear that nothing conclusive can be inferred from the word “within,” because we shall cite below a similar formula concerning Rainald II, buried among the monks of Igny.

Whatever the case, in the middle of the choir of the cathedral church there is a black tombstone bearing this epitaph:

> RAINALD THE CRIPPLED, ARCHBISHOP.

The chapter of Arras, in order to repay the labors he had expended and preserve his memory forever, decreed that an anniversary should be celebrated for him every year in the major church.

Balderic, abbot of Bourgueil, honored him with elegiac verses in which he commends Rainald’s virtue as follows:

> To the people of Reims, Christ’s grace had given Rainald  
> As a light and a steadfast pillar.  
>   
> Raised from the church of blessed Martin,  
> He greatly benefited the Church of Reims.  
>   
> Death touched him while he flourished in so great  
> A pontificate, and again left the chair vacant.  
>   
> His orphaned citizens, weeping for so great a prelate,  
> Here placed the body of their bishop.  
>   
> The people worthy of the earth’s soil bestow honors upon him;  
> May the Almighty bestow forgiveness upon his soul.  
>   
> The twelfth day before the Kalends of February  
> Removed him from the world and set him in heaven.

[Col. 1385]

## Letters of Rainald

*(Ecclesiastical Province of Reims.)*

### I. To the Clergy of Arras: On the Consecration of Lambert

*(1093)*

[Col. 1385A]

Rainald, by the grace of God archbishop of Reims, sends greeting and blessing in the Lord Jesus to Lord Gualbert and the entire congregation of the Church of Arras.

You wrote to us asking that we inform you of the date on which we wished to consecrate your elected candidate. But since, according to the sanctions of the canons, that consecration appears to belong not only to our authority but also to that of our fellow bishops, we judged that we ought by no means to send you the date of this consecration without their counsel.

Since, however, at the feast of Saint Mary in mid-August we shall have a large gathering of bishops and clergy at Reims, we shall not delay informing you of the advice we receive from them concerning this matter, as well as the date on which we ought to consecrate your elected candidate. Farewell.

### II. To Lambert, Elected Bishop of Arras: On His Election

*(1093)*

Rainald, by the grace of God archbishop of Reims, sends greeting and blessing in the Lord Jesus to his beloved brother and fellow priest, Lambert.

We have received the letter that the lord pope sent us concerning your consecration, and we have also seen a copy of the letter addressed to you. After reading it through, we forwarded it to our fellow bishop of Soissons and ordered him to forward it to the other suffragans, so that, after receiving their counsel, we might reply to your fraternity.

Therefore we order you to delegate to us one of your representatives by the octave of Saint Andrew, through whom we may write back to your affection about what we intend to do concerning everything that the lord pope has imposed upon you. Farewell.

### III. From the Clergy of Arras to Rainald: On the Election of Lambert

*(1093)*
To the beloved Father and lord, [Col. 1385D] RAYNALD, by God’s ordinance archbishop of Reims, whom we love and honor in truth, the clergy and people of the Church of Arras, together with Lambert, though an unworthy servant of his holiness, send true affection, with prayers and obedience.

We offer manifold thanks to Your Excellency’s dignity, because until now you have gladly provided us assistance like a devoted father and have promised to be kindly disposed toward us in all matters [Col. 1386A] concerning our cause. But we are greatly astonished that, at the conclusion of our affair, your fatherly concern should have grown cold, since, within the time-limit imposed by the apostolic authority for the consecration of our elect, you have neither summoned our elect to consecration by your solemn letters, as we supposed you would, nor designated a definite day within that period. Now, however, since the consecration can no longer take place within the thirty-day limit, we earnestly and peacefully beg you at least to provide us with letters of your authority, to be delivered to the apostolic lord, as he commanded, for the consecration of our elect. Farewell.

## IV. RAYNALD TO POPE URBAN II

*Concerning the election of Lambert. (Year 1093.)*

[Col. 1386B]

To the lord and most reverend pope of the holy and apostolic see, URBAN, RAYNALD, although unworthy, by the grace of God archbishop of Reims, offers in the Lord the fullest gift of health, service, and due submission.

After Your Fatherhood had first sent us letters, it pleased you, most serene Father, in your apostolic office, to send us others as well, commanding us to delay no longer than thirty days after seeing your letters before consecrating the elect of the Church of Arras as bishop. Your prudence also added that, if any reason should arise by which we feared to undertake that duty, we were to send him to you for consecration, together with a letter from us [Col. 1386C] confirming the matter.

Having therefore received the written text of this command of yours, and wishing to presume nothing without consulting our co-bishops and fellow priests—since it is certainly clear that this consecration depends both on their authority and on ours—we sent a copy of your mandate to all to whom we could send it, and asked each one’s opinion, so that they might provide us with advice on this matter which would preserve our obedience to you and would not diminish the dignity of the Church of Reims.

Accordingly, this was the single voice and judgment of all our bishops and clergy: that we should indeed withhold our hand from consecrating that elect, but should send him [Col. 1386D] to you, since your letters commanded this, and should leave to your judgment whatever your lofty prudence decided ought to be done. For they feared, and still fear, that the people of Cambrai might take this act as an occasion to sever themselves from the Church of Reims, since their city belongs to another kingdom—a kingdom whose king has long been hostile both to us and to the Roman Church.

They also added that the exchange would be extremely disadvantageous if, while the Church of Reims consented to have a bishop made at Arras, it were to lose Cambrai, which is six times more extensive and more prosperous than Arras. Therefore we beseech Your Excellency, most holy Father—and our bishops and clergy beseech you as well—that you, who preside from the citadel and watchtower over all the churches, regulate this affair in such a way that, God forbid, no one may censure the disposition of your decrees on this matter, and that the Church of Reims may suffer no loss of her dignity in your time.

Nevertheless, we, who have always resolved to comply with your decisions, shall, whatever the manner of his consecration, kindly receive him once your dignity has consecrated him [Col. 1387B], and thereafter honor him as our bishop and suffragan. For the rest, we wish Your Highness to know that we have by no means delayed this matter so long in order either to attempt to resist your commands or to detract in any way from that lord. We judge him worthy not merely of this honor, but also of the highest rank of any other promotion, which we rightly deem should be conferred upon him.

May Your Blessedness remain unharmed in the Lord.

## V. TO THE COUNT OF FLANDERS

*Concerning the confirmation of Lambert’s election. (Year 1094.)*

RAYNALD, by the grace of God archbishop of Reims, [Col. 1387C] sends an abundance of health and blessing in the Lord to the glorious prince, lord ROBERT, count of the Flemings.

We kindly received your letters and read them with pleasure. Since in them you asked us to write back and tell you what opinion we held concerning the appointment of our most beloved brother Lambert as bishop of Arras, we do not wish our dearest prudent friend to remain unaware that we kept him with us for many days, so that what ought to be done concerning him might legitimately be settled with the advice of our bishops. Finally, at the council which we held at Reims with our co-bishops and many princes on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of October, in accordance with the commands of lord Pope Urban—which it would be sacrilegious to disobey—we received his profession according to ecclesiastical custom, with the counsel and consent of our co-bishops, and, confirming his consecration, we confirmed it [Col. 1387D].

We therefore entrust him to your care, so that from now on you may receive him with due honor and due reverence, and may publicly and privately share in his labors for the love of God. Insofar as ecclesiastical order permits, obey him as your shepherd and as your bishop. Farewell.

## VI. TO LAMBERT, BISHOP OF ARRAS

*Concerning the absolution of certain clerics. (Year 1094.)*

RAYNALD, by the grace of God archbishop of Reims, [Col. 1388A] sends to his dearest son, his fellow priest and co-bishop LAMBERT, whatever is appropriate in the Lord.

Know that we have absolved this canon, namely Engelbert. As for the others who, because of our excommunication, have already come to you or are going to come, we wish and command you both to absolve them and to strive to place them under regular discipline, where they may have consolation of body and soul, until their Church comes to its senses; and then, after our absolution and permission, let that Church receive them as its own sons. Farewell.

## VII. TO THE SAME

*That he should attend the synod convened by Urban in Italy. (Year 1094.)*

[Col. 1388B]

RAYNALD, by the grace of God archbishop of Reims, sends health and blessing in the Lord Jesus to his dearest brother and fellow priest LAMBERT, bishop of the people of Arras.

We considered it worthy to inform your affection that we recently received a letter from lord Pope Urban, and that he has instructed us to urge you to take care to come into his presence, with your brotherhood summoned, around the middle of next February, at the council which he will at that time celebrate in Tuscany or Lombardy. Therefore, in response to his admonition, we likewise admonish your brotherhood to take care to present yourself at that council around the aforesaid time, together with all your abbots [Col. 1388C]. Farewell.

## VIII. TO THE SAME

*That he should attend the Council of Clermont.*

RAYNALD, by the grace of God archbishop of Reims, sends health and blessing in the Lord Jesus to his dearest brother and fellow priest LAMBERT, bishop of the people of Arras.

We do not wish your dearest brotherhood to remain unaware that we recently received a letter from lord Pope Urban, in which he warned us to come in person to the council that he will celebrate on the octave of Saint Martin—namely, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of December—at the church in Auvergne which is also called Clermont [Col. 1388D]. He also commanded us to invite all the suffragans of our metropolitan church to that council, summoning both abbots and the other leading men of the churches, as well as the more distinguished princes.

Since we do not wish to oppose the apostolic summons—for that would be wrong—we judged it right to dismiss the council that we had planned for the octave of All Saints. We therefore admonish your concern by this letter to set aside every excuse, to present yourself at the same council, and, as stated above, to admonish both the abbots and leading men of your other churches, as well as the princes of your diocese, especially Baldwin [Col. 1389A], count of Mons.

Let no one dare to use poverty or any other necessity as an excuse for failing to come, since we require only persons who are not accompanied by a great crowd of servants. Whoever, after this admonition of ours, is absent from the council should know without doubt that he will incur danger to his rank and will store up for himself, certainly not with impunity, the anger of lord Pope Urban. Farewell.

## IX. TO BALDERIC

*Concerning the chronicle of Cambrai. (Year 1094.)*

RAYNALD, archbishop of Reims, sends greetings to BALDERIC, cantor of Thérouanne.

[Col. 1389B]

My dear friend, you ask my judgment concerning your *History of the Church of Cambrai and Arras*. I am writing back to you what I learned from brother Sigibert. Like a diligent bee flying devotedly around holy places, he seems not to have passed over any place from which you did not pluck something with incredible diligence.

Thus the marvels of God and of the saints will not be in the land of forgetfulness, and you have built for posterity. Until now, therefore, sufficient acknowledgment has been given to your modesty and reserve; grant the remainder to the prayers of the devout and to the will of the pious bishop who has died, and do not take from the dead what you consecrated to the living with tireless industry and a mind attentive even to the smallest details.

Release it from your hands, so that it may circulate in churches and monasteries. My mind already foretells that this work will bring you glory, be useful to posterity [Col. 1389C], and in the present become a source of delight and ornament to both Churches.

Given at Reims, on the Ides of January, in the year 1094.

## X. TO LAMBERT, BISHOP OF ARRAS

*That he should restrain Hugh of Inchy, violator of God’s truce, with the sword of anathema. (Year 1095.)*

RAYNALD, by the grace of God archbishop of Reims, sends health and blessing in the Lord Jesus to his beloved brother and fellow priest LAMBERT, bishop of Arras.

We believe that you clearly remember all that we recently discussed at length with your brotherhood concerning Hugh of Inchy [Col. 1389D]. This Hugh recently came with an armed force to the village of Saint Gaugericus called Felcheriae, during the truce of God. Rushing about all around it, he completely burned the entire village with fire and carried away with him a very considerable amount of plunder and a multitude of people in miserable captivity.

It has also reached our ears that he boasts of possessing a letter from us by which he ought—God forbid!—to be released from all fear of the bishop of Cambrai and from the excommunication of all priests, whatever madness he may have been carried away into. Therefore, wishing you to know that all his boasting is void [Col. 1390A], we command your brotherhood to admonish even him, whom we especially love, so that, every excuse being removed, you may wield against him the sword of anathema as against a violator of holy peace. By the authority of your command, moreover, forbid divine worship to be celebrated any longer, until he comes to satisfaction, in all his places of refuge or in any place where he or his accomplices are physically present. Farewell.

## XI. TO THE SAME

*Concerning the same matter. (Year 1095.)*

RAYNALD, by the grace of God archbishop of Reims, sends health [Col. 1390B] and blessing in the Lord Jesus to his brother and co-bishop LAMBERT of Arras.

At the meeting with Count Robert, and in order to receive justice from him on the octave of Saint Mary in August, we shall be ready either to appear in person or to delegate our messengers, as we have already commanded you and our co-bishops of Noyon and Thérouanne.

As for what you have written to us concerning Hugh of Inchy, we believe it is clear to you that at the council which we held at Compiègne, in response to the complaints and outcries of Gerard, bishop of Cambrai, we wielded against him and all his accomplices and supporters the sword of anathema, by the judgment of all who presided. Yet neither he nor his son thereby ceased persecuting the Church of Cambrai. They were tormented by an equal expectation of vengeance and bound by an equal bond of malice and excess [Col. 1390C].

Therefore, since—as the Apostle says—“I have become foolish; you compelled me” (2 Corinthians 12), and again, in the Acts of the Apostles, to the Jews: “Since you judged yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the Gentiles” (Acts 13), so, because that same Hugh judged himself unworthy of conversion and reconciliation, Gerard, bishop of Cambrai, entered into an alliance with the count of Flanders to defeat Hugh’s malice.

For this reason, no equitable consideration permitted Gerard, bishop of Cambrai, to make peace with Hugh without the count of Flanders, nor did we for that reason regard Hugh as anything other than excommunicated. But if it were his will, and if we had the bishop of Cambrai ready at the appropriate time to come to Reims in our presence in order to do and receive justice from him, then we too would weigh the claims of both sides on the equal scales of judgment and mercy, and would not fail to observe moderation in every respect.

He ought not, however, to come to amendment through you alone, nor ought he to fear only the sentence of your excommunication, since he is recognized as a parishioner of the bishop of Cambrai, and Inchy, through which he exercises this wickedness, is situated in the bishopric of Cambrai. Farewell, and write back to us what you have done with the count of Flanders.

# [TREATISE OF JOHN COTTON ON MUSIC]

[Col. 1391]

## TOWARD THE END OF THE CENTURY: JOHN COTTON’S *MUSIC*

*(D. Gerbert, Writers on Music, II, 230, from the manuscript of Saint-Blaise, twelfth century, collated with the Viennese and Leipzig manuscripts.)*

## NOTICE

Among the more distinguished short works on music by writers of the Middle Ages, John’s *Music* is rightly counted. Until now I have studied in vain to discover who this John was. In the Leipzig manuscript he is surnamed Cottoneus; concerning this matter the distinguished custodian of the Imperial Vienna Library, Martinezius, who collected the variant readings from the Viennese manuscript of excellent quality, noted nothing.

In the Paris manuscript the prologue is identified as “The Letter of John Cotton to Fulgentius, bishop of the English.” In the Saint-Blaise manuscript, which was destroyed by fire in the year 1768, it was simply entitled “John’s *Music*,” as elsewhere also. This author frequently appears, on account of his excellence, as second to no one of the eleventh or twelfth century after Guido of Arezzo, whom he cites, as he also cites Berno of Reichenau.

Some have argued that he was a Roman pontiff on the basis of the formula “Servant of the servants of God,” which he uses. Yet other religious men also used this formula, such as Faustus, monk of Glanfeuil, in the *Life of Saint Maurus*.

The learned Englishmen who today devote themselves with great zeal to the study of music may perhaps bring something concerning John to light from the name of Fulgentius, the English bishop to whom he dedicates the book; nevertheless, I consulted them in vain.

## PROLOGUE

[Col. 1391A]

To his venerable lord and father, FULGENTIUS, bishop of the English—one whose name truly reflects his character, since he excels in wisdom and shines with soundness—JOHN, servant of the servants of God, offers whatever a son owes his father and a servant his lord.

When you saw me investigating many and varied fields of study, yet devoting myself especially to one art, namely music, you began to question me about that art. You urged me to take care to send forth some little spark of my scanty talent for the instruction and illumination of the less learned. When I shrank from this, doubtful and trembling, as one who seemed entirely unsuited to fulfill it, you repeatedly struck my ears with your admonitions and always instilled in me that verse of the teacher of truth and lover of charity:

“Hidden wisdom and concealed treasure—what benefit is there in either?”

When I replied to you that I was dull and weak in talent, you restrained me with this objection: “What is it that you say, my son? What is it, I ask, that you are saying? Have I not discovered that you have read Boethius’s *Music*, as well as Guido’s and, if I remember correctly, Berno’s? Have I not also learned from very many trials how great is the power of your talent, so that I know what your shoulders are able to bear—and no one knows it better or with greater certainty than I do?

“Surely you are defending yourself against me with neither a good nor an acceptable argument. If you wished to weigh everything more correctly, you would have no reason not to follow me and my admonitions. For, to say nothing of Martial, Otto, and Notker, whose books you are said to have carefully examined, since they are highly esteemed in this art, you could, if you wished, extract from the works of the aforesaid men rules sufficiently apt and useful for readers [Col. 1392A]. Therefore, so that this one excuse may entirely cease, I admonish you that, as blessed Gregory also says, charity supplies the strength which inexperience denies.”

Thus rebuffed by these words—or, more accurately, compelled by so powerful a command—I immediately and confidently undertook the work you had imposed upon me. For I preferred to be exposed to the mockery of the wiser and more perceptive rather than incur your displeasure by refusing to obey.

I acknowledge that I have used a childish style. Nevertheless, I have briefly gathered from the little books of others what seemed more useful and necessary, sometimes adding something from my own small flame. I decided to divide the little book into several chapters, so that if a reader should seek something eagerly among the other material, it might be found more quickly and easily through the preliminary headings [Col. 1392B].

I therefore offer to your mercy this work, which I began at your urging and completed with the Lord’s help, so that it may be tested by you, corrected by you, and defended by your authority from the poisonous bites of detractors.

The preface ends; the chapters begin.

## CHAPTERS

I. How one ought to prepare oneself for the discipline of music.  
II. What benefit there is in knowing music, and how the musician differs from the singer.  
III. From where music received its name, and by whom and how it was invented.  
IV. How many instruments there are of musical sound.  
V. Concerning the number of the letters and their distinctions.  
VI. How the monochord should be measured.  
VII. From where the monochord receives its name, and what it is useful for.  
VIII. How many modes there are by which melody is woven together.  
IX. What the differences of voices are, and concerning the octave.  
X. Concerning the modes which we improperly call tones.  
XI. Concerning the reciting notes of the modes and their finals.  
XII. Concerning the regular course of the modes and license.  
XIII. An exposition of the Greek names of the notes.  
XIV. What should be done with a chant which fails in its continual course.  
XV. How the ignorance of fools often corrupts a chant.  
XVI. How different people take pleasure in different modes.  
XVII. Concerning the power of music, and who first used it in the Roman Church.  
XVIII. Precepts concerning the composition of chant.  
XIX. What the best form of modulation is.  
XX. How chants can be composed through vowels.  
XXI. What usefulness the neumes invented by Guido provide.  
XXII. Concerning the rejection of improper usage and certain excessive distinctions of the modes.  
XXIII. Concerning diaphony, that is, organum.  
XXIV. Concerning the first mode and its derivative, with their differentiae.  
XXV. Concerning the third and fourth tones and their differentiae.  
XXVI. Concerning the fifth and sixth and their differentiae.  
XXVII. Concerning the seventh and eighth and their differentiae.

The chapters end.

# JOHN’S TREATISE ON MUSIC BEGINS

[Col. 1393]

## How one ought to prepare oneself for the discipline of music

[Col. 1393A]

First we impose this requirement upon anyone who desires to prepare himself for the discipline of music: he should diligently learn to establish the letters of the monochord together with the syllables written above them, and should not desist from this work before he knows them by heart. But we defer speaking of the letters for now, so that afterward we may treat them more conveniently and fully; for the present, let us say something about the syllables.

[Col. 1393C]

There are six syllables which we adopt for the work of music. They differ among different peoples, but the English, French, and Germans use these: *ut, re, mi, fa, sol, la*. The Italians, however, have others; those who wish to know them should ask them directly.

They say that the syllables we use were taken from that hymn whose beginning is:

“Ut queant laxis resonare fibris  
mira gestorum,”

that is, “So that they may resound with loosened voices the wonders of deeds.”

This is easily understood: from *UT queant laxis* we have *ut*; from *REsonare fibris*, *re*; from *Mira gestorum*, *mi*; from *FAmuli tuorum*, *fa*; from *SOLve polluti*, *sol*; from *LAbii reatum*, *la*.

Thus, through these syllables, let the person who desires to know music learn to sing certain songs until he thoroughly and clearly understands their ascents, descents, and manifold variations. Let him also diligently accustom himself to practicing through the joints of the hand, so that afterward, whenever he wishes, he may use it in place of the monochord and test, correct, and compose a chant upon it. When he has practiced these things for some time according to what we have said and has committed them to a strong memory, he will without doubt have an easier path to music [Col. 1393D].

## II. What benefit there is in knowing music, and how the musician differs from the singer

It now seems appropriate briefly to touch upon the benefit provided by knowledge of music. For the more diligently anyone applies himself to music, the more he comes to know the usefulness of the art itself.

[Col. 1394A]

Music is one of the seven arts called liberal; it is natural, as are the others. Hence we sometimes see even jugglers and stage performers, who are entirely uneducated, weave together sweet-sounding songs.

But just as grammar, dialectic, and the other arts would be uncertain and confused if they had not been written down and clarified through precepts, so it is with this art. It should be understood that this art must not be regarded as among the lowest of the arts, especially since it is [Col. 1394C] most necessary for clerics and useful and delightful to all who practice it.

Whoever continually devotes himself to it and applies himself tirelessly without interruption can obtain from it this fruit: that he will know how to judge the quality of a chant—whether it is polished or vulgar, true or false—and how to correct what is false and compose something new. Therefore the knowledge of music is no small praise, no slight benefit, and no labor to be despised: it makes the person who knows it a judge of composed chant, a corrector of false chant, and an inventor of new chant.

Nor should it be passed over that the musician and the singer differ from one another considerably. The musician always proceeds correctly through art, whereas the singer sometimes follows the right path merely through practice.

To what, then, could I better compare the singer than to a drunkard who indeed returns home but has no idea by which road he is returning? A millstone, too, sometimes produces a well-regulated screech, although it itself does not know what it is doing, since it is an inanimate thing.

Thus Guido says beautifully in his *Micrologus*:

“There is a great distance between musicians and singers:

The former speak; the latter know what music has composed;

For whoever does what he does not understand is defined as a beast,”

and so forth.

## III. From where music received its name, and by whom and how it was invented

[Col. 1395A]

Music is called *musica*, some say, from *musa*, which is a certain instrument of music that sounds with sufficient elegance and delight. But let us see by what reasoning and authority *musica* derives its name from *musa*.

As we said, *musa* is a certain instrument surpassing all instruments, since it contains within itself the power and character of them all. It is inflated by human breath like a flute, controlled by the hand like a *phiala*, and activated by a bellows like an organ. Hence it is called *musa* from the Greek word μέσα (*mesa*), that is, “middle,” because, just as different spaces meet in some middle point, so various instruments meet in the *musa*. Therefore music has not incongruously received its name from its principal part [Col. 1395B].

Some also say that music received its name from the Muses because among the ancients they were believed to be perfect in this art and their skill in modulation was sought. Hence they are thought to have been called Muses from *ἀπὸ τοῦ μύσω*—that is, “from seeking” [Note: [Col. 1395D] Or rather, *ἀπὸ τοῦ μασένειν*].

Others take *musica* as though it were *mod(us)ica*, that is, from modulation; others derive *moysica* from water, which they think was called *moys*. Others think that *musica* is as if *mundica*, named from the song of the world and of heaven.

If anyone has a better view concerning the name of music, we do not begrudge him, because, as the Apostle Paul says, “the Holy Spirit distributes to each as he wills.”

Moses reports that Tubal was the inventor of this art. Others believe that Linus of Thebes, Amphion, or Orpheus discovered it. [Col. 1395C]

But the Greeks, to whom, as Horace says, the Muse granted speech with rounded mouth, want us to think differently about this. They assert that a certain Samian philosopher named Pythagoras was the inventor of this art.

He was, they say, a man most distinguished for wisdom, unconquerable in eloquence, and exceedingly sharp in intellect. Accordingly, he is said to have discovered music through a very subtle investigation. For once, while traveling, he passed by a workshop and heard there, as commonly happens, the different sounds of hammers. When he had listened attentively for a while and was increasingly delighted by the various sounds, he recognized, in his intense eagerness, that the power of the art of music lay hidden there.

Without delay he entered the workshop and began more carefully to weigh the hammers. Little by little he skillfully investigated the distinctions of the seven notes and also their consonances, about which we shall speak more fully below [Col. 1395D]. Thus that outstanding man was the first in Greece to discover, formulate, write down, and teach music, previously shapeless and unknown. Knowledge of it was later made known to the Latins through Boethius and others trained in Greek literature.

## IV. How many instruments there are of musical sound

It should also be understood that there are two instruments of all sounds: natural and artificial. The natural is of two kinds, worldly and human. According to the philosophers, the worldly natural instrument is the consonance accompanying the revolving movement of the heavens, which is properly called harmony.

[Col. 1396A]

By the human natural instrument I mean those cavities of the throat which we call windpipes. They are naturally suited to receive and emit air, from which natural sound is produced. For this reason some people also customarily call them *commercia*, as Prudentius says in the *Psychomachia*:

“. . . and they constrain the evil soul,

compressing the broken passages of the intercepted throat.”

The artificial instrument, on the other hand, is that which is adapted to produce sound not by nature but through craftsmanship.

Natural sound is of two kinds: distinct and indistinct. Distinct sound is one that contains certain consonances; indistinct sound is one in which no consonance can be discerned, as in the cries or groans of human beings and the barking of dogs or roaring of lions.

[Col. 1396B]

In the same way, you can distinguish distinct and indistinct sound in artificial instruments. The pipe with which little birds are deceived, or even a pot covered with parchment, with which boys customarily play, produces indistinct sound. In the *sambuca*, however, in stringed instruments, cymbals, and organs, the diversity of consonances can be clearly and distinctly discerned.

Music therefore by no means admits the sound which we have called indistinct; only distinct sound belongs to music, and this is properly called *phthongus*—a tone or articulate sound. For music is nothing other than the ordered movement of voices.

We have said this especially against the ignorant, to restrain the error of those who foolishly assert that every sound is musical. It should also be added that, although there are three kinds of musical melody—enharmonic, diatonic, and chromatic—the first was rejected because of its excessive difficulty and the third because of its excessive softness; practice retained the middle one.

[Col. 1396C]

## V. Concerning the number of the letters and their distinctions

Having first set out these preliminary matters, let us now begin to discuss the signs of the monochord, and first speak of their number.

The most ancient authorities placed no more than fifteen letters on the monochord, beginning with capital A and ending with small *a*. At that time Γ had not yet been added, nor had *b*, which we call soft or round. Some call the latter by the Greek name *synemmenon*, that is, “joined” or “attached.”

But the moderns, observing everything more subtly and intelligently—for, as Priscian says, “the younger, the more perceptive”—saw that those notes were insufficient to express every melody, and that the chant of the plagal first mode sometimes failed because of the scarcity of letters. Therefore they placed Γ in the first position. Anyone who wishes can easily observe this in the antiphon:

[Col. 1396D]

“O DFE, king FD of glory FDCDD; Lord CEFFF of virtues, GFDD,”

and so forth. For the phrase “Spirit of truth,” which must begin from capital A and descend, would have nowhere to descend if Γ had not been added.

Moreover, because the round *b* sometimes seemed necessary in chant, they added it and gave it this name, calling it *b molle*, “soft b,” because of the softness and sweetness of its sound. With these two letters added, there are seventeen in number.

But lord Guido, whom after Boethius we acknowledge to have possessed the greatest authority in this art, places twenty-one notes in his *Music*, so that no deficiency can now arise in any chant [Col. 1397A].

Let us now consider their distinctions. First, the diligent reader should observe that all the notes of the monochord differ in shape. For example, Γ differs in form from capital G; capital A from small *a*; B from *b*; C from *c*; D from *d*; E from *e*; F from *f*; and G from *g*. Again, the smallest *a* differs from doubled *a*; *b* from doubled *b*; *c* from doubled *c*; and *d* from doubled *d*.

They also vary according to spaces and lines. When Γ is placed on a line, *g* will be in a space; when capital A is in a space, small *a* will be on a line, and the same applies to the others.

It should also be noted concerning the soft *b* and the square *b* that they differ both in shape and in the syllables written above them [Col. 1397B]. They occupy a single place, whether in a space or on a line, but they are distinguished in this way: wherever the soft *b* sounds in a neume, it must be written above that same neume by the scribe.

All the letters of the monochord have another distinguishing variation, namely this: from Γ through C they are called low, because of the depth of their sound; from D through G they are called finals, because the chant of all the modes ends on them; from small *a* through *d* they are called high, because of the high sound they produce; from *d* through *g* they are called super-high, because they surpass the high notes in the sharpness of their voice.

Again, from doubled *a* through doubled *d* they are called excellent, because in the delicacy of their sound they surpass even the super-high notes.

[Col. 1397C]

Some also assign them another distinction through Greek terms. Since this seemed to provide little benefit to the less learned, it has been omitted for the present.
