All these distinctions of the letters are made so that, since they have different properties, we may more easily distinguish one from another. Enough has now been said concerning the number and distinctions of the letters; let us see next how the monochord is to be measured.

## VI. How the monochord should be measured

[Col. 1397D]

There are indeed many and varied measurements of the monochord, but recounting them all would produce weariness rather than benefit for readers. Therefore, pursuing brevity, we have taken care to insert into our rules one among the many, which seemed easier and quicker.

First, place Γ wherever you wish on the left side of the monochord; from it to the end measure nine equal steps. Once these have been measured equally, observe carefully that the first step ends at A, the second is empty, the third at D, [Col. 1398A] the fourth is empty, the fifth at *a*, the sixth at *d*, the seventh at *a* [a], and the remaining positions are empty.

Likewise, from A to the end, divided equally into nine steps, the first step will end at B, the second is empty, the third at E, the fourth is empty, the fifth at the square, the sixth at *e*, the seventh at the doubled note, and the remaining positions are empty.

Likewise, when you have divided the distance from Γ to the end into four equal steps, the first step will end at C, the second at G, the third at *d*, and the fourth at the end. Similarly, when the distance from C to the end has been measured in four equal steps, the first will end at F, the second at *c*, the third at *c* [c], and the fourth at the end.

From F to the end, in four steps, the first will end at flat b, the second at *f*, and the remaining positions are empty.

[Note: [Col. 1397D] This is taken almost word for word from William of Hirsau’s *Music*, above, where he nevertheless inserts the following: “Likewise, from round B-flat to the end, in two steps, the first will end at b [b], and the second at the end. From D to the end, in two steps, the first will end at d [d], and the second at the end.” What follows here—“from f”—is absent there.]

From D to the end, after making four steps, the first will end at G, which has already been placed, the second at *d* [d], and the remaining positions are empty. From *f* also to the end, divided into four steps, the first will end at the doubled round note, and the remaining positions are empty.

By this division—namely, the one made in four steps—anyone who applies care will be able to measure the entire monochord with complete accuracy. For from any note to the end of the monochord, four equal steps are made: three of them contain the diatessaron, the diapente, and also the diapason; the last ends the measurement.

For example, when four measured steps are made from Γ to the end, the first ends at C, which is the diatessaron; the second at G, which is the diapente; the third at *g*, which is the diapason; and the fourth ends the measurement. In the same way you can find the remaining intervals.

## VII. Why the monochord is so called, and what use it has

[Col. 1398C]

Now that the measurement of the monochord is known, we must consider why it is called a monochord and what benefit it provides. The monochord received its name from the single string that alone it possesses. For *monos* (μόνος) in Greek means “one” and “alone”; hence *monk* is also so called, because he ought to be solitary and singular. Thus, just as the *decachord* is named from ten strings and the *octachord* from eight, so the *monochord* is named from one string.

This instrument is especially useful for testing upon it whether a song about which there is doubt is true or false. It should also be used for boys or youths aspiring to music, so that, guided by it, they may more easily attain through sound what they wish to learn. Moreover, it is of great value against the rebellion of certain senseless people. For there are many clerics or monks who neither know this art nor wish to know it—and, what is worse, avoid and abhor those who do know it. If, as sometimes happens, a musician reproves them concerning a song which they utter either incorrectly or disorderedly, they angrily and shamelessly shout back, refuse to yield to the truth, and pour forth their error with all their strength.

Although unwillingly, yet in order to correct their stupidity, I should not unjustly judge such men [Col. 1399A] more foolish than a blind person. A blind man, recognizing that he lacks sight, seeks outside himself—namely, the guidance of a person or a staff—and thus takes precautions against falling into a pit. But these useless men, whom the Greeks aptly call *energoumenoi* [Note: [Col. 1399D] More correctly, ἀνεργουμένους, that is, “without perception or action,” inert], neither see for themselves nor strive to walk under the guidance of those who see.

Therefore, as we have said, the monochord is brought forward to refute their obstinacy, so that those who refuse to believe the musician’s words may be convicted by the testimony of the sound itself.

## VIII. The modes from which melody is constructed

Among other things, it is useful to know that there are altogether nine modes through which every melody is constructed: unison, semitone, tone, ditone, semiditone, diatessaron, diapente, semitone with diapente, and tone with diapente.

Of these, six are called consonances—namely, those which most often sound together in song, that is, sound simultaneously—or, more precisely, those whose sounds, born from certain proportions, contain one another. These proportions are called *sesquioctava* (nine-to-eight), *sesquitertia* (four-to-three), *sesquialtera* (three-to-two), and *dupla* (two-to-one). Since treating these matters would be burdensome both to boys and to the less educated—for we are speaking to boys and to those not yet fully trained—we leave them to the subtlety of mathematicians.

[Col. 1399C]

Unison is so called as though it were “one sound,” because, although it is a single voice, it is continually struck back.

The tone is called from *tonare*, “to sound powerfully”; and a tone has a strong sound in relation to a semitone. Or, alternatively, the name is taken from the Greeks: since they say *tonos* (τόνος), we say *tonus*, changing *o* into *u*. Thus *calamus* comes from κάλαμος (*kalamos*), and *hymnus* from ὕμνος (*hymnos*).

The semitone was called *limma* by Plato, because it is not a complete tone but an imperfect one—not, as certain unlearned people explain it, half a tone. Virgil speaks of the “half-men, the Phrygians,” that is, men who are not complete, because they dress like women.

The ditone is called in Greek by that name because it contains two tones.

The semiditone is so called because it is not a complete ditone. It has two species: one consisting of a tone and a semitone, the other of a semitone and a tone.

The diatessaron is interpreted as “of four,” because, beginning from one note, it leaps to the fourth. It consists of a ditone and a semitone, as from Γ to C. The diatessaron has three forms, for example: [ut–fa], [re–sol], [mi–la].

The diapente means “of five” in Latin, because, beginning from one note, it makes a leap to the fifth. It contains a diatessaron and a tone. It has four forms: the first between [C and G], the second between [D and *a*], the third between [E and the square], and the fourth among the lower syllables, between [Γ and C].

The two remaining modes—namely, semitone with diapente and tone with diapente—are called intervals. Note that when you say “semitone with diapente,” you signify one mode; but when you say “semitone and diapente,” you express two modes. Consider the same distinction in the case of tone with diapente. These two combinations are found more rarely in song.

To make clear the rising and falling of all the modes we have discussed, the following figure should be examined.

## IX. The number of differences among the voices, and the diapason

[Col. 1400D]

Anyone wishing to know examples of all these intervals in song should learn this chant:

“Three times three are the modes from which every song is constructed,” and so forth. [Note: [Col. 1400D] You will find this in Hermann’s *Music*.]

This is so useful for recognizing all the varieties of singing that it provides even boys with an extremely easy entrance into music. Likewise also: “G a G f D G a D G G F D G.”

“Three sets of three are the intervals of conjoined sounds.” [Note: [Col. 1400D] See it in the same place.]

Earlier, when we were discussing the notes of the monochord, we left one matter unexplained—namely, why the same notes are repeated seven times. We shall now disclose the reason.

Seven notes are set down on account of the same number of differences among the voices. After seven have been set down, the same notes are repeated because, although the seven voices are dissonant from one another, the eighth agrees with the first. That outstanding investigator of the arts [Note: [Col. 1401] Virgil] observed this most correctly, for he says:

> “The distinctions of voices answer in seven measures.”

Thus, just as all time proceeds through seven days—when seven have passed, the same days are repeated—so music proceeds through only seven varieties of voices.

It should nevertheless be noted that the same notes are repeated, but are not altogether the same, because their figures are not the same. Γ has a figure different from capital G, and capital G itself a figure different from lowercase *g* [Col. 1402A]; and the same is true of the others.

Therefore, just as the eighth note is the same as the first, but not altogether the same, so the eighth voice agrees with the first in sound, but is not altogether the same, because one sound is low and the other high.

This manner of singing is found very rarely in song. In Greek it is called *diapason*, which means “through all.” It has this name either because it includes all the consonances within itself, or because, beginning from one voice, it makes a leap to the eighth and thus contains within itself all seven differences among the voices.

How beautiful and fitting a concord the diapason possesses can easily be proved if two or three sing together, in such a way that one uses a low voice, the second a high voice, and the third an exceedingly high voice, as follows:

[Col. 1401A]

> Let us sing praises to the Savior with a supplicating voice.  
> Let us sing praises to the Savior with a supplicating voice.  
> Let us sing praises to the Savior with a supplicating voice.

[Note: [Col. 1401] In the musical scale, the low and high voice are represented in our notation in this way. The exceedingly high voice is placed in the highest octave, or double diapason.]

[Col. 1401B]

Some also call the diapason a consonance, either because of its proportion, or because it produces a consonant melody between the first and the eighth, or also because it consists of consonances. For the diatessaron and diapente together constitute the diapason, especially since between the first and eighth voice there is either a diatessaron below and a diapente above, or the reverse—as between C and *c*, D and *d*, and E and *e*, as you can observe in this figure.

[Col. 1401]

## X. The modes that we improperly call tones

[Col. 1403A]

It should also be known that the modes which, as Guido asserts, we improperly call tones are eight in number, corresponding, so to speak, to the eight parts of speech. For it seems fitting that, just as everything that is said is contained in eight parts of speech, so everything that is sung should be regulated by eight modes.

Yet although there are now eight, formerly there were only four, perhaps in imitation of the four seasons. For just as the ages of the world are changed by four seasons, so every song is distinguished by four intervals. The Psalmist seems to indicate these four modes when he says: “Sing praises to our God, sing praises; sing praises to our King, sing praises.”

But why there are now eight, whereas formerly there were only four, may be passed over for a little; we must explain why they are called modes or tropes.

The modes are named from *moderare* or *modulari*, “to regulate” or “to modulate,” because through them a song is regulated, directed, modulated, or composed. Anyone possessing knowledge of music who undertakes to compose a regular song first decides within himself to which tone he will make it belong.

We said “someone possessing knowledge of music” because a person without training, even if he does correctly what he does, is nevertheless undervalued because he does it unknowingly—especially since actors and leaders of dances often sing sweetly, not because art provides it to them, but because nature does.

They are called *tropes* from a suitable turning or conversion. For however the song varies in the middle, it always turns suitably through tropes or tones toward its final. What we call modes or tropes, the Greeks call *phthongoi*.

It should be known that Guido considers it inappropriate and abusive to call them tones. But if we examine the matter more carefully, the term will not seem entirely abusive. Latin speakers, lacking expressive resources, often lack proper designations; when necessity compels them, they sometimes adopt and appropriate foreign terms. The Greeks call this *catachresis* (κατάχρησις) [Note: [Col. 1403D] That is, the use of a name belonging to another thing. Festus: “Catachresis is a trope; we call it abuse, when we use foreign terms as though they were proper terms, because proper terms are lacking.”]

When the ancient Latins called a certain consonance in music a tone, grammarians likewise began, by an appropriated use of the name, to call the accents or distinctions of speech tones. Later, Latin singers, observing that there was considerable similarity between song and the accents and modes of prose speech, decreed that this name should be common to both.

For just as tones or accents are divided into three species—low, circumflex, and high—so three varieties are distinguished in song. Sometimes a song moves among low notes, as in the offertory *In omnem terram* (“Into all the earth”); sometimes it revolves around the finals, as though with a circumflex, as in the antiphon *Benedicat nos* (“May he bless us”); sometimes it moves among high notes as though leaping, as in the antiphon *Veterem hominem* (“The old man”).

Alternatively, they are called tones in imitation of the tones which Donatus calls distinctions. For just as three distinctions are considered in speech, which may also be called pauses—namely, the colon, or member; the comma, or incision; and the period, or closure or circuit—so it is in song.

In prose, when something is read with suspense, it is called a colon. When a sentence is divided by a proper point, it is a comma. When the sentence is brought to its conclusion, it is a period.

For example: “In the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar”—this, at all its points, is a colon. Then, where it continues, “under the chief priests Annas and Caiaphas,” there is a comma. At the end of the sentence, “the son of Zechariah in the wilderness,” there is a period.

Similarly, when a song pauses by suspension on the fourth note above the final, it is a colon; when in the middle it returns to the final, it is a comma; when at the end it reaches the final, it is a period. Thus in the antiphon *Petrus autem* (“But Peter”) is a colon; “was kept in prison” is a comma, “and prayer was made” is a colon, “for him without ceasing” is a comma, and “by the church to God” is a period.

From this it can be observed that the intervals are not entirely abusively called tones, nor is it inappropriate that they receive the names of distinctions or accents, whose varieties they imitate.

What grammarians call colon, comma, and period in prose, certain musicians call *diastema*, *systema*, and *teleusis* in song. *Diastema* signifies a distinct ornament, produced when a song pauses becomingly not on the final but on another note. *Systema* indicates a joined ornament, whenever there is a becoming pause of the melody on the final. *Teleusis* is the end of the song.

It is certainly necessary to form an opinion about the fact that there are now eight modes, although formerly there were only four.

Those who first wrote about music, having carefully considered the nature of voices, distinguished every variety of modulation into four modes, insofar as the power of their intellect at that time allowed. Hence there are only four finals.

But modern musicians, examining the discoveries of their predecessors more subtly, observed that the harmony of the modes was confused and dissonant. They saw that a song of the same interval sometimes began among the low notes and moved about there, while at other times it began among the high notes and remained chiefly there.

Wishing therefore to remove this dissonance, they divided each mode into two, so that the mode of singing which moved among the high notes would be called *authentic*, that is, authoritative or principal, while the one which remained more among the low notes would be called *plagal* or *plagalic*, that is, collateral or subordinate.

They are distinguished as follows:

- Authentic protus is called the first tone by Latin singers; plagal protus, the second.
- Authentic deuterus is the third; plagal deuterus, the fourth.
- Authentic tritus, that is, the fifth; plagal tritus, the sixth.
- Authentic tetrardus, that is, the seventh; plagal tetrardus, the eighth.

*Protus* means “first,” *deuterus* “second,” *tritus* “third,” and *tetrardus* “fourth.”

*Authentus* means “authoritative” in Greek—ἀυθέντης (*authentēs*); for they call authority itself ἀυθεντία (*authentia*). *Plagius* may be explained as “partial” or “collateral” [Note: [Col. 1404D] Πλάγιος, as though “oblique,” or joined from the side.]. We say, “in that flank,” meaning “on that side” or “in that part.”

The Greeks express the *phthongoi*, that is, the tones, by the following names:

Dorian [I], hypodorian [II]; Phrygian [III], hypophrygian [IV]; Lydian [V], hypolydian [VI]; Mixolydian [VII], hypomixolydian [VIII].

## XI. The tenors of the modes and their finals

Just as there are eight tones, so there are eight tenors belonging to them. *Tenor* comes from *teneo*, “I hold,” just as *nitor* comes from *niteo*, “I shine,” and *splendor* from *splendeo*. In music we call tenors the places where the first syllable of the *saeculorum amen* of each tone begins. For they seem to hold the keys of the melody and give us access to recognizing the song.

Guido also calls the lingering of the final voice a tenor.

It should be noted that, just as the endings of the eight tones are arranged on four notes—which are therefore also called finals—so four notes have been assigned to the eight tenors, that is, to the tonal patterns, but in a different arrangement. The endings of two tropes always refer to one note, and those of two others to another, and so on.

The arrangement of the tenors is different. Sometimes one tenor is assigned to one note, while three are assigned to another. The tenor of the second tone is on F; the first, fourth, and sixth are on high *a*. The third, fifth, and eighth are on C; the seventh is on *d*.

It is not inappropriate that the tenor of the second and that of the seventh have claimed solitary positions for themselves: the second descends especially far, to the fourth, while the seventh ascends higher than all the others.

As we said above, the proper finals of the four tones are D, E, F, and G. D is the final of the first and second; E of the third and fourth; F of the fifth and sixth; [Col. 1406A] G of the seventh and eighth.

We said “properly” because songs sometimes claim other finals for themselves. How and why this occurs we shall sufficiently demonstrate in the following section, God willing.

It should be known that the entire force of a song refers to its finals. Wherever a song begins and however it varies, it must always be assigned to the mode in whose final it comes to rest.

Thus the responsory *Praeparate corda vestra* (“Prepare your hearts”), although it appears to have the course of protus and ends only on the final E, is legitimately assigned to deuterus.

Likewise the responsory *Factum est silentium* (“There was silence”), although its beginning resembles the responsories of the seventh tone, such as *Missus est Gabriel* (“Gabriel was sent”), *Lapides torrentis* (“The stones of the torrent”), and *Ductus est Jesus* (“Jesus was led”), is nevertheless disqualified from being first by its ending.

This seemed not inappropriately to have been provided by the musicians’ wisdom: they assigned the consideration of the modes to the ending, since in practical affairs it is consideration of the end alone that distinguishes the wise from the heedless. Boethius bears witness to this when he says: “Providence measures things by their outcomes.”

Therefore, just as the action of things looks toward the end, so the melody of songs fittingly tends toward the end. Hence the common proverb still used today: “All praise is sung at the end.”

Since something has now been said about the tenors and finals of the intervals, it will not be amiss also to inform the reader where the *gloria* of each tone begins.

The *gloria* of the second tone begins on low C; that of the fourth on final E; those of the first, fifth, and sixth on F; those of the third and eighth on G; and that of the seventh on high *c*.

Now let us give examples of the tenors, finals, and *gloria* of the tones, beginning by illustrating the *gloria* and, in every case, the *saeculorum amen*.

For the finals, we have thought it worthwhile, in order to demonstrate more fully the understanding of the tropes, to append here certain little songs, which we may also call the patterns or formulas of the modes. [Note: [Col. 1405] These examples, taken from Berno’s *Tonary*, are marked with ancient notation in the manuscript.]

### Finals

“Seek first the kingdom of God” | D |

“And the second is like it” | D |

“Today is the third day since these things happened.” | E |

“At the fourth watch he came to them.” | E |

“Five wise virgins entered the wedding feast.” | F |

[Col. 1407A]

“At the sixth hour he sat beside the well.” | F |

“There are seven spirits before the throne of God.” | G |

“There are eight beatitudes.” | G |

It should also be understood that among certain people the *phthongoi*, that is, the tones, are designated by vowels, while the differences of the tones—which some improperly call “definitions”—are designated by consonants, as follows.

The first tone is marked by *a*, the second by *e*, the third by *i*, the fourth by *o*, the fifth by *u*, the sixth by Greek H, the seventh by *y*, and the eighth by ω. The first difference of each tone is indicated by *b*, the second by *c*, the third by *d*, the fourth by *g*, and the remaining differences by the mute letters in order.

Having arranged these matters usefully, it is now time to give rules concerning the regular or permitted course of all the modes.

## XII. The regular course and the permitted range of the modes

[Col. 1407B]

Since we are about to speak of the course of the modes, we must first examine what we call their course. By the course of the modes or tones we mean the law by which they are constrained under a fixed rule—namely, how far each should ascend or descend, and how far it should be raised or lowered.

Since, when a song is raised or lowered, this may be called ascent and descent, and since in the course of the intervals we likewise call these ascent and descent, as well as raising and lowering, it is necessary to distinguish the terms, so that no opportunity for uncertainty may be given to the inexperienced reader.

Accordingly, we call the ascent and descent of the tones the definite rule governing their rising and falling—that is, how far they ascend or descend from their finals.

We call the raising and lowering of the tones the determination of the intervals by which each must have its beginning from its own final.

With these necessary preliminaries, let us discuss the course of the modes as we proposed.

All authentic tones regularly ascend from their final to the octave, which is the diapason; by permission, they may ascend to the ninth or tenth. We have separated the permitted range from the rule so that it may be understood that the notes allowed by permission should occur very rarely.

What someone possesses by rule, he possesses as though by right, and therefore may use it more freely. But what is possessed by permission is possessed as though by grace and must be handled more humbly and cautiously.

They descend from the final to the nearest note; I have found that some permission for them to descend farther has been granted by experienced musicians.

The authentic tritus, however, which is simply called the fifth tone, is excepted. No descent below its final is assigned to it, for no other reason than that the imperfection of the semitone does not permit a suitable descent.

All plagal tones ascend from the final to the fifth, which is the diapente, and by permission they take the sixth. It is not surprising that the plagals have less permission to ascend than the authentics, because the plagals must always remain in the lower region and should very rarely ascend from the final to the fifth.

Indeed, the most experienced authority in this art, and Guido at the end of his treatise, confirm that a song which, ascending from the final, strikes the fifth three or four times belongs to an authentic tone.

[Col. 1408A]

Hence the antiphon *Ecce tu pulchra* (“Behold, you are beautiful”), although it falls within the course of the second tone, is assigned to the first because above it repeatedly echoes the fifth from the final.

Likewise *Rex Dominus omnium* (“The King, the Lord of all”), because it more frequently moves in the upper range and descends in the *unctio* to capital A, is nevertheless assigned to the first tone. This is done so that honor may be preserved for rulers. For a lord or master has authority not only over what belongs properly to him, but also over what belongs to his subjects. A subject ought to be content if he is permitted humbly to use what his master has granted him, rather than rashly rushing into what belongs to his superior.

Therefore, if the plagals should very rarely reach the fifth in ascent, how much more rarely should they reach the sixth?

All the subordinate, or plagal, tones descend from the final to the fourth, which is the diatessaron, and also, regularly, to the fifth. I have nowhere read that permission to descend farther has been granted either to the authentics or to the plagals.

It should nevertheless be known that certain musicians, not without reason, measure the regular course of the eight modes through eight diapasons. According to their assertion, nearly all the modes take one note below the final by permission, whereas previously we assigned it to them regularly.

Since the eight tones proceed through eight diapasons, two tones are joined together like master and disciple, and their diapasons are likewise connected, so that it can easily be observed in them which notes properly belong to the plagal, which to the authentic, and which are common to both. The figure of the eight wheels that we have appended demonstrates this most clearly to anyone who examines it carefully. [Note: [Col. 1407] The figures are missing; perhaps they are the same as those found above in Aribo’s *Music*.]

[Col. 1408C]

It also seems necessary to explain how we should understand the statement that the authentics ascend to octaves and the plagals to fifths. As we testified above, in this little work we are marking out a path for boys.

When tones are said to ascend to octaves or fifths, this should be understood to mean that they ascend high enough to possess the capacity for such an ascent. For not every song of the authentics reaches the octave, nor does every melody of the plagals reach the fifth, as is clear in this antiphon of the first tone, *In tuo adventu* (“At your coming”), and in this antiphon of the second, *Consolamini, consolamini* (“Be comforted, be comforted”).

The raising and lowering of the modes should be understood as follows. All the authentics are permitted to raise each beginning from its final to the fifth and to lower it to the note immediately below the final. If it is permitted to reach the fifth, how much more is it permitted to reach the fourth or third?

Only authentic deuterus, that is, the third tone, transgresses this rule: it usually raises its beginning to the sixth, as in the antiphon *Tertia dies est* (“It is the third day”).

The subordinate tones are permitted to raise their beginnings, or even their *hemitonia*, to the fourth, and sometimes to lower them to the fifth.

We use *hemitonia* equivocally in the same sense in which we use “tones”: we call the beginnings of voices produced by a pause in the middle of a song *hemitonia*; properly speaking, *hemitonia* means semitones.

It should further be observed that, although the foregoing law and fixed rule has been established for the courses of the tones, many recent composers, attending only to the desire to please the ears, very often confuse it and make a common song by assigning the course of two tones to a single melody. This is clear in the song *Ter terni sunt modi* (“Three times three are the intervals”).

In songs of this sort, composed so loosely and confusedly, it is left to the singer’s judgment to adapt the song to whichever tone its beginning answers more suitably.

## XIII. An explanation of the Greek names of the notes

Since it is tedious, in a continuous treatment of the modes, to place the actual notes themselves, we shall interpret their names, which they receive from the Greeks, so that whenever necessary we may introduce those names in place of the notes.

We gave the names of these terms in the treatment of the fourth chapter. But we postponed discussing them then, lest we overwhelm the inexperienced and untrained mind of the new reader with sudden obscurity.

To make what follows easier to understand, we must insert something about the tetrachords of the ancient musicians.

The ancient musicians arranged four tetrachords on the monochord. The first extended from A to D, and they called it the tetrachord of the principals, because those notes were placed at the beginning.

The second extended from E to *a*, and they called it the tetrachord of the middle notes, because through these middle notes—that is, intermediary notes—the song proceeded and returned from the low notes to the high.

The third extended from the square to *e*, and they called it the tetrachord of the disjunct notes, because they regarded these as disjoined from, that is, different from, the preceding notes both in figure and in the raising of the sound.

The fourth extended from the *e* mentioned above to the doubled note, and they called it the tetrachord of the highest notes, because they saw these notes as surpassing all the others in the slenderness or high pitch of their sound.

According to those musicians—who admitted neither Γ nor the three notes that we place after the doubled note—the following names, which we are about to interpret, were imposed upon the musical notes.

The first, A, is called by Greek musicians *proslambanomenos*, “acquired” or “assumed,” because it was taken from grammar, for which it had first been devised, and assumed for the work of music. Or it is called “acquired” because the oldest musicians did not originally place it there.

The second, B, was arranged so that the disposition of the voices would begin from the smallest interval, or semitone, which lies between B and C. Hence B itself is called *hypate hypaton*, “principal of the principals,” because among the most ancient musicians it was the first of the principals, that is, of the low notes.

This is the opinion of some. But a shrewd listener may object that the reason we inferred from the semitone is not compelling. If the oldest musicians wanted the arrangement of the voices to begin from a semitone, they could just as well have placed it between A and B as between B and C.

Therefore it is better, following the earlier opinion, to say that A was placed first on the monochord. But then it may again be objected why B is called “principal of the principals,” since A ought rather to be called this, because it is the first of the low notes.

To this we reply that B is not called “principal of the principals” because it is first in the order of those notes, but because it is the first among the principal notes to produce a divided sound. For A, being placed at the beginning of the monochord, produces no difference of sound.

C is called *parhypate hypaton*, “beside the principal of the principals,” because it lies beside B.

D is called *lichanos hypaton*, “finger-note of the principals.” It is called a finger-note, as though it were a distinguishing note, because it distinguishes—that is, separates—the principal notes from the middle notes.

E is called *hypate meson*, “beside the principal of the middle notes.”

G is called *lichanos meson*, “finger-note of the middle notes.” It bears this name because, as one of the middle notes, it distinguishes the capital notes from the minuscule notes.

Next comes *a*, which is called *mese*, “middle,” namely, between capital A and doubled *a*. For among the older musicians no note is repeated three times except this one.

The square is called *paramese*, “beside the middle,” namely, beside *a*.

Next comes *c*, which is called *trite diezeugmenon*, “third of the disjunct notes.” It receives this name from the reversed order of counting. Since *d* follows *c*, and *e* follows *d*, if you call *e* the first and *d* the second, *c* will be the third. What we call “third of the disjunct notes” means as much as if we said “one of the three called disjunct.”

After this comes *d*, which is called *paranete diezeugmenon*, “beside the last of the disjunct notes,” because it lies beside *e*, which is called *nete diezeugmenon*. *Nete* means “last,” and *diezeugmenon* means “of the disjunct notes.”

Next comes *f*, *trite hyperboleon*, “third of the highest notes.” The same interpretation should be applied to this name as to that of *c*.

After *f* is placed *g*, which is called *paranete hyperboleon*, “beside the last of the highest notes,” because it lies beside doubled *a*, which is called *nete hyperboleon*, “last of the highest notes.”

To make what we have said clearer, we have appended below the tetrachords of the ancient musicians together with the names written above.

## XIV. What should be done with a song that fails in its continuous course

[Col. 1411]

[Col. 1411A] Having thus explained the names of the notes, we must now speak of chants which, failing to complete their proper course, take other finals for themselves. This irregularity in chants occurs in some cases permissibly, but in others not at all. Sometimes it arises from the fault of the singers, but more often from an antiquity that cannot be gainsaid. The chants in which this disturbance occurs tolerably are these three modes: the protus, deuterus, and tritus. Musicians pardon their transgression of the rules for this reason: they have related notes. We call those notes related which agree in descent and ascent. For example, the final D of the protus agrees with the acute a: both descend by a tone and ascend by a tone and a semitone.

[Col. 1411B] Likewise, the final E of the deuterus has an affinity with b quadratum (square b), since they are similarly lowered and raised. In the same way, the final F agrees with the acute c in descent and ascent. There is no true affinity in descent unless both movements, or at least the ascent, are doubled. But since the final of this tetrachord has no such affinity, it is consequently denied pardon for its fault. For whoever cannot have a substitute must himself properly perform his own office. Therefore, if some deviation occurs in a chant of the tetrachord, we say that it proceeds from the singers’ ignorance and must be corrected by the skill of musicians. In the chants of the aforesaid modes—the protus, deuterus, and tritus—related notes are not improperly substituted for the finals whenever necessary.

[Col. 1411C] To make what we are saying clearer, we add examples. *Gaudendum est nobis*, although it belongs to the protus, cannot be sung in its proper place, because in certain passages it requires C, the low note beneath the *parhypate hypaton*, which is not present there. But if it begins on the *mese*, that is, on a, it will be brought without error to the same A at the end. The same is true of this antiphon, *Magnum haereditatis*. Some people, wishing to avoid this difficulty, place A and the Greek B, which they also call *synemmenon*, that is, “joined,” so that they may have a tone beneath C. Nevertheless, they cannot confirm this by any authority. For Guido, who devoted himself solely to ensuring that there should be no defect in the monochord, would certainly have inserted this note had he considered it necessary.

There is also another argument that disproves their assertion: namely, that the chant often requires not only the note beneath the *parhypate hypaton*, but also the whole range beneath the *parhypate meson*. We are therefore compelled to have recourse to the higher notes, as in this communion, *Aufer a me*, and in this antiphon, *Germinavit*. Likewise, the chant fails to complete its proper course in this antiphon, *Tu Domine universorum*. The chants of the tritus also sometimes cannot be sung in their proper place, as in this communion, *De fructu*. Whoever sings all these on notes related to the finals will reach the end without error.

XV. How the ignorance of fools often corrupts a chant

[Col. 1412A] Whether the fact that these and similar chants cannot be sung in their proper course has arisen from the fault of the singers, or whether they were first uttered in this manner by the composer, we do not know. But this we know with absolute certainty: through the ignorance of certain people, chants are very often corrupted—indeed, we now have more corrupted chants than we could enumerate. The authority of the composers did not originally produce them in the form in which they are now sung in churches. Rather, the perverse voices of men, following the impulses of their own minds, distorted compositions that had been correctly arranged, and brought the distorted versions into an incorrigible usage, so that the worst custom is now held in place of authority.

For ignorant singers, sometimes weighed down by weariness of singing, lowered what ought to have been raised; and often, led on by wantonness, they raised above the rule what ought to have been sung lower. This is evident in the gradual *Qui sedes Domine*. For *super Cherubim*, which ought to begin on the *paranete diezeugmenon*, they customarily begin on the *mese*. Consequently, the chant proceeds unlawfully to the *lichanos hypaton*.

[Col. 1412B] Likewise, in this communion, *Principes persecuti sunt me*, many make a serious error. For *Concupivit*, which ought to begin on the *trite diezeugmenon*, they begin on the soft b, thereby producing an unusual interval between E and soft b and depriving the chant of its lawful course.

Similarly, some raise the gradual *Probasti Domine* improperly. Its verse, *Igne me examin.*, which ought to begin on the *trite diezeugmenon*, they begin on the *parypate meson*, and thus completely disrupt the legitimate order of the chant.

But just as in this chant people sin by lowering what ought to be raised, in certain others some err by trying to raise what ought to be lowered. Thus, in this responsory, *Ductus est Jesus in desertum*, although *Dic ut lapides* ought to begin on the *trite diezeugmenon*, they begin it on the *trite hyperboleon*.

In this responsory also, *Terribilis*, many commit an error at the place where it says *et porta coeli*: they suddenly raise it, leaping to the acute notes, although it ought rather to be sung around the final D.

[Col. 1412C] Unlearned singers are also very often mistaken in judging tones and chants with similar beginnings. For example, many assign this antiphon, *Iste puer*, to the plagal deuterus because at its beginning it agrees with the antiphon *In odorem*. But *Iste puer* belongs to the authentic protus, whereas *In odorem* belongs to the plagal deuterus.

Likewise, some incorrectly assign these antiphons, *Ipse praeibit* and *Dirupisti Domine*, to the hypophrygian, although they are mixolydian, because they appear to agree with certain hypophrygian antiphons: *Ipse praeibit* with *Rorate coeli*, and *Dirupisti* with *Da mercedem Domine*, and so forth.

Likewise, the antiphons *Malos male*, *et qui odit*, and *novit Dominus*, although they are hypomixolydian—as their intervals and systems clearly demonstrate, for this is evident from their conclusion—are assigned by some to the phrygian, because at their beginnings they agree with these antiphons: *Domine spes Sanctorum* and *Tu Bethlehem terra*.

In the same way, the antiphons *Ascendente in* and *Benedicta sit Gloriosi*, although they are hypomixolydian, are adapted by some to the phrygian. *Gloriosi*, however, seems to agree more closely with the hypolydian.

[Col. 1413A] Some are misled not only by similar beginnings; they also, of their own accord, turn certain chants away from their proper course through their faulty voices. Thus they treat these antiphons—*Quid retribuam*, *Cum inducerent*, and *Cum audisset Job*—as follows. Although they belong to the Dorian mode and ought to begin gently, they raise them to the acute notes with a harsh, sustained voice, so that they agree with these chants: *In principio*, *Qui de terra*, and *Quando natus es*.

Nor should we be surprised that they corrupt beginnings, since they also pervert the endings of chants and turn them improperly from their established course, as in the antiphon *Petrus autem*. Although it follows the course of the protus, as its intervals and systems plainly demonstrate, some cause it to end rather discordantly on the *hypate meson*.

XVI. How different people take pleasure in different modes

[Col. 1413B] Since many examples have now demonstrated how the modes vary and how they are also corrupted by incompetent singers, it seems appropriate to add this concerning their character: different people take pleasure in different modes. Just as not everyone’s palate is pleased by the same food, but one person is helped by sharper foods and another by milder fare, so certainly not everyone’s ears are delighted by the same kind of sound.

Some are pleased by the first mode’s deliberate and courtly wandering; others are captivated by the second’s hoarse gravity; others enjoy the third’s severe and almost indignant leaping; others are drawn by the flattering sound of the fourth; others are moved by the fifth’s restrained impetuosity and sudden fall to the final; others are soothed by the sixth’s tearful voice; others willingly hear the seventh’s theatrical leaps; others love the eighth’s decorous and almost solemn melody.

[Col. 1413C] Therefore, in composing chants, a careful musician ought to take such measures that he use most fittingly the manner by which he sees those whom he wishes to please most delighted. Nor should it seem surprising that we say different people take pleasure in different things, since nature itself has implanted in human beings the fact that not everyone’s senses have the same appetite. Hence it often happens that what seems exceedingly sweet to one person in a chant is judged dissonant and altogether ill-composed by another.

I myself certainly remember singing several chants before certain people, and what one person praised most highly was entirely displeasing to others.

The modes have particular properties of sound, different from one another, so that they spontaneously disclose their identity to a careful musician or even to an experienced singer. Just as someone who has investigated the customs and dress of various peoples can skillfully distinguish a person of any nation he sees—identifying one as Greek, another as German, one as Spanish, and another as Gaul—so a musician, not merely by name, immediately recognizes, upon hearing any harmony, to which tone it belongs.

[Col. 1413D] Yet this sometimes deceives even an experienced person. For at times a chant uses, not only at its beginning but also in the middle of its course, the character of one tone, although at the end it contradicts that tone. This is clear in the responsory *Gaude, Maria virg.* Although at its beginning and in its middle it serves the authentic deuterus, at the end it declares itself plagal tritus.

[Col. 1414A] Chants of this kind warn us not to judge tones rashly, but rather to await their ending with care, since the entire judgment of singing depends upon it. Otherwise, if someone announces the tone before the proper time, he will regret not having kept silent when the ending refutes his declaration.

It must also be considered that chants of certain modes sometimes agree with such similarity that a singer can scarcely, or never, discern to which tone they ought more correctly to be assigned. This commonly occurs with the authentic tritus and the authentic tetrardus, and also with their corresponding plagal modes. It may be observed in these antiphons: *Gloriosi principes* and *pro nobis Gallus*. For they agree so appropriately with the hypolydian and the hypomixolydian that it is not easy to discern to which they should rather be attributed.

[Col. 1414B] Likewise, the responsory *Genti peccatrici* seems to suit both the lydian and the mixolydian. Hence among some people it is customary to sing it in this way: *Esto placabilis*; but most sing it in this way: *Esto*.

Some assign this introit, *Dominus in loco*, to the lydian, others to the mixolydian. I judge, however, that those should be followed who assign both of these to the lydian.

The Greeks, if I am not mistaken, had noticed the consonance of the modes mentioned above when they gave them names that were so little distinct and almost identical. In the others you will find no such agreement, except that the chant of the protus sometimes pauses suitably on the *hypate meson*, which is the final of the deuterus, as in the alleluia *Juravit Dominus* and in this communion: *Principes persecuti sunt*.

Likewise, some chants agree with such similarity that, according to their different ways of being sung, they may appropriately be joined to different tones. This is the case with these antiphons: *Et respicientes* and *Lupus rapit*. The former points toward the plagal tetrardus, and the latter toward the plagal tritus, if they are sung in the following manner.

[Note: [Col. 1413D] The musical notes are missing.]

Indeed, he was exceedingly great, alleluia.

The proper sheep, alleluia.

But both will be phrygian if they are sung as follows:

Exceedingly great, alleluia.

The proper sheep, alleluia.

XVII. On the power of music, and who first used it in the Roman Church

[Col. 1414D] Nor should this be left unsaid: musical song has great power to move the minds of listeners. It soothes the ears, uplifts the mind, incites warriors to battle, recalls the fallen and despairing, strengthens travelers, disarms robbers, calms the angry, gladdens the sorrowful and anxious, reconciles those at odds, drives away vain thoughts, and moderates the frenzy of the deranged.

Thus we read of King Saul in the Book of Kings that, when he was seized by a demon, he was calmed when David played the cithara, but was again tormented when the music ceased. Likewise, a certain deranged man is said to have been freed from his madness when the physician Asclepiades played music.

It is also remembered of Pythagoras that by musical modulation he recalled a certain extravagant young man from excessive lust.

Music has different powers according to its different modes. Thus, through one kind of singing you may provoke someone to lust, and through another recall that same person as quickly to repentance. Guido reports an experiment concerning this involving a certain young man.

[Col. 1417A]

[Col. 1415]

Since music therefore has such great power to move the minds of human beings, its use has rightly been welcomed in the holy Church. The use of music in the Roman Church began first with Saint Ignatius the Martyr and also with Saint Ambrose, bishop of the Milanese. After them, the most blessed Pope Gregory, with the Holy Spirit—as is reported—present with and dictating to him, composed the chant and gave to the Roman Church the chant by which the divine office is celebrated throughout the year.

That the Lord ought to be praised by singing has considerable authority in the Old Testament. For we read in the Book of Exodus that, after Pharaoh had been drowned, Moses and the children of Israel sang a song to the Lord.

[Col. 1417B] The Psalmist, likewise not ignorant of this art, sang praises to the Lord on the ten-stringed instrument, and urges us to sing together, saying: “Sing to the Lord a new song; his praise is in the assembly of the saints.”

Nor did he wish us to use only the natural voice in praising the Lord, for he also admonishes us to praise the Lord with instruments made by human art: “Praise the Lord with the sound of the trumpet, with psaltery and harp, with timbrel and choir, with strings and organ.”

Since, then, this discipline has authority in the Old Testament, since such religious men established it in the Church, and since—as has been said—its power is effective in moving human minds, who would be reluctant to cultivate this knowledge soundly? Who would not cleave to it with wholehearted devotion?

[Col. 1417C] But since not only the sacred official chants mentioned above have been composed in the holy Church, and since there have also been other composers of chants not long before our own time, I see no reason why we too should be forbidden to weave a chant. Although new melodies are not now necessary in the Church, we may nevertheless exercise our ingenuity in setting to song the rhythms and mournful verses of poets. Since we both request and grant permission to compose melodies in turn, it seems appropriate to set forth rules for composing chant.

XVIII. Rules for composing chant

[Col. 1417D] We therefore append the first rule of composing melody: the chant should vary according to the meaning of the words. We previously explained which manner of singing suits each subject when we said that different people take pleasure in different things. For we showed that some modes are suited to courtliness, some to wantonness, and some even to sadness.

Just as a poet seeking praise must take care to make his deeds correspond to his words and not say anything discordant with the fortunes of the person he describes, so a composer who desires praise must take care to present the chant so appropriately that the chant seems to express what the words signify.

Therefore, if you wish to compose a chant at the request of young men, let it be youthful and wanton; but if it is for old men, let it be deliberate and express severity. For just as a writer of comedies would be ridiculed if he assigned the part of a young man to an old man, or that of a luxurious man to a miser—as Plautus and Dorsennus are portrayed by Horace [Note: [Col. 1417D] Horace, *Epistles*, Book II, Epistle 1, line 170]—so a composer may be criticized if he introduces a leaping mode into a sad subject or a tearful one into a joyful subject.

[Col. 1418A] The musician must therefore take care to regulate the chant so that it is lowered in adversity and raised in prosperity. We do not prescribe this so strictly that it must always be done; but when it is done, we say that it provides ornament.

We have some examples of what we have said. The antiphons for the Lord’s resurrection appear to express exultation in the very sound. But this antiphon, *Rex autem David*, seems to sound sorrow not only in its words but also in its chant. Complaints, however, are very frequently sung in the hypolydian by composers, because that mode has a mournful sound.

[Col. 1418B] Furthermore, we impose this on a composer who desires praise: he must not go astray by repeating a single neum excessively, just as a skilled poet takes great pains to avoid the fault that the Greeks call *homoioptōton* (ὁμοιώπτωτον), that is, “similar case-endings.” With equal effort, the composer of chants must avoid singing the fault that musicians call *homoiophthongon* (ὁμοιόφθογγον), that is, “similar sounds.”

Let grammarians or rhetoricians discuss the former fault [Note: [Col. 1418D] As does Quintilian, Book IX, chapter 3]. We shall give an example of the latter, which we have said musicians must avoid, in the responsory *Ecce odor*. At the place where it says, *Crescere te faciat Deus meus* (“May my God make you increase”), the repeated insistence on a single neum is faulty.

Likewise, in the responsory *Qui habitat*, the frequent repetition of a single *podatus* is faulty at the place *et refugium meum* (“and my refuge”).

[Col. 1418C] If, however, some graceful neumes are repeated once in a while, we do not condemn this, as at the end of the responsory *Qui cum audissent*, where it says *laudantes Clementiam* (“praising Clemency”), and likewise at the end of the responsory *Sint lumbi vestri*, where it says *a nuptiis* (“from the wedding”).

It should be understood, however, that in the principal modes it is praiseworthy gradually to lead the chant toward the end; in the collateral modes it is fitting to hurry the chant toward its conclusion.

XIX. What is the best form of melodic composition

[Col. 1418D] The best form of melodic composition is for the chant to receive its final pause where the meaning of the words makes its division. You can observe this in the antiphon *Cum esset desponsata*.

The person who composed the melody of those verses beginning *Homo quidam erat dives* (“There was a certain rich man”) did not properly observe this rule. For that same verse nowhere reaches its final at a correct division.

Harmony is also greatly embellished if, in the chants of the plagal modes, this is observed: they should often repeat the final and revolve around it, pausing only very rarely on the fourth and never on the fifth. If they happen to touch the fifth, they should quickly and almost fearfully pass over it and hasten back, as in the antiphon *Ait Petrus*.

[Col. 1419A] In the chants of the principal modes, care should be taken that they dwell especially on the acute notes; and after pausing twice or three times on the fifth above the final, they should seek the final and hasten back again to the higher notes. For just as the plagal modes chiefly remain among the low notes, so the authentic modes chiefly dwell among the acute notes. You have an example of this rule in the antiphon *Muneribus datis*.

The diapente should also be observed: in the melody of the plagal modes it should never leap from the final to the higher notes; the diatessaron, however, may freely be made above and below. The fourth mode nevertheless descends and rises more suitably by the diapente than by the diatessaron. Nor is this surprising, since the melody of the authentic modes is more often and more effectively raised and lowered to the sixth than to the fifth.

It should also be noted that in the chants of the authentic modes it is highly appropriate for them frequently to descend and rise from the final by a diapente. In the third mode this is less harmonious, but in the fifth it is most decorous. In the latter it is also ornamental if its chant generally rises from the final by a ditone and a semiditone, as is evident in the antiphon *Paganorum*.

[Col. 1420A] We briefly give this rule concerning both groups: the chant of the plagal modes should very rarely touch either the region below the final or the fifth above it—the former because of excessive gravity, the latter because of excessive brilliance, lest it be attributed to an authentic mode. The chant of the principal modes, unless it is the fifth, should descend to the note nearest the final. Both the fifth and the other principal modes may rise powerfully to the octave, but should very rarely touch the ninth or tenth. The following figure teaches you this clearly.

[Col. 1419B] It should further be observed that the two consonances, the diatessaron and the diapente, produce the greatest pleasure in a chant if they are suitably placed in their proper positions. They produce a beautiful sound if, after being lowered for a while, they are immediately raised on the same notes, as is clear in the antiphon *Vox exult.*

The diatessaron, however, produces a much sweeter melody, especially in the authentic deuterus, if it is sometimes repeated in varied ways three or four times, or even more. This is clearly evident to anyone who pays careful attention at the end of this antiphon, *O gloriosum lumen*, in the following manner:

[Note: [Col. 1419B] The musical notes are missing.]

Those whom you made recognize the light of truth.

[Col. 1420B] It is also beautiful if the neum descends through the same notes by which it immediately ascends, as here:

*Meruit* [a g e F ga] *divina revelatione* (“He deserved it by divine revelation”).

It is also most graceful in a chant if the diatessaron is sometimes varied so that a semiditone or ditone precedes it at one time and follows it at another, as this example makes clear:

*Hodie proces - - sit ad ortum* (“Today he proceeded to the rising”).

There are also many other excellent forms of melodic composition. We should not recount them all, lest we burden readers with weariness rather than instruction. Musicians call chants of this kind carefully composed, because care is applied to their composition. They also call them “metrical,” by analogy, because they are measured according to fixed rules in the manner of meters, as are the Ambrosian chants.

XX. How chants can be composed through vowels

[Col. 1421A] We shall now show another way of composing melody, a beautiful one indeed, but unused before Guido. First determine with yourself the tone in which you wish to compose the chant. Then set the five tones alongside the same number of vowels, in the order written above, on tablets; and, according to the vowels assigned to the individual syllables, proceed correctly in singing in the following manner:

[Col. 1422A]

Likewise, another mode by the same rule: F G A c.

[Col. 1421B] Since the rule we have given might seem rather loose, we shall explain how you can prepare a more relaxed and freer method of composition. Arrange six, eight, or even more notes in order, if you wish, and assign vowels to them in a doubled sequence, so that two vowels in succession are attributed to each note, in this manner [Note: [Col. 1421D] Nearly the same material appears above in Guido and Aribo. The ancient notes again fail in various places in the example presented [Col. 1422D].]:

*i o u a e i o u*  
*F G a b c d e f*  
*o u a e i o u a*

“[I am] the voice of one crying in the wilderness: prepare the way of the Lord;

Make straight the paths of our God.”

[Col. 1421C] Take care that the arrangement of vowels we have set out above does not lead you to think that they must always necessarily be arranged in this way. For just as painters and poets are free to begin whatever they wish, so one who composes in vowels has equal power to arrange them at the beginning according to his will. Likewise, just as painters and poets must take care to complete what they have begun, so the composer must strive to carry the order he has begun through to the end.

For example, since in the preceding chant I assigned *oi* to the *parypate meson*, you may place there *ei*, *ao*, *au*, or anything of that kind, provided that you persist in the order you have begun.

[Col. 1421D] To make this clearer, we append a melody of another kind as an example:

*e i o u a e i o*  
*C D E F G a b c*  
*i o u a e i o u*

[Col. 1422B] [Note: [Col. 1422D] Here the ancient notes are expressed in the manuscript.]

“A messenger coming from lofty Olympus promises that you will be a great godfather to one who is to be born, and promises a name and the ordered course of the life he is to live.” [The damaged verse remains somewhat uncertain.]

The vowels could also be tripled or quadrupled in this manner, except that excessive confusion would then impede the composition of the melody. Since, then, as has been shown, a chant is composed through vowels, and since it is evident that whatever is spoken consists of vowels, Guido is entirely correct in saying that everything spoken can be reduced to chant.

XXI. What usefulness the neumes invented by Guido provide

[Col. 1422C] Lest the reader be troubled by the fact that in the first chapter we instructed him to become accustomed to singing through musical neumes, but have postponed speaking about them until now, let him observe that we did not do this without reason. Unless he first knew how to sing musically, he could in no way understand the examples introduced throughout the work for various reasons.

Why such neumes were invented by Guido should not have been explained immediately, since their cause and usefulness can be adequately understood from what has already been said. For ordinary neumes cannot distinguish intervals, and the chants expressed through them cannot be entrusted to a stable memory; consequently, many falsities creep into chants. These neumes, however, clearly display all the intervals, to such a degree that they completely exclude error and, once they have been perfectly learned, do not permit forgetfulness in singing. Who would not see that they are of great usefulness?

[Col. 1422D] It is very easy to consider in the *virgulae*, *clines*, and *podati* how irregular neumes generate error rather than knowledge. All are arranged alike, and no manner of raising or lowering is expressed through them. Consequently, each person raises or lowers such neumes according to his own pleasure. Where you sing a semiditone or diatessaron, another produces a ditone or diapente; and if a third is present, he disagrees with both.

One person says, “Master Trudo taught me this”; another adds, “But I learned it in this way from Master Albinus”; a third says, “Indeed, Master Solomon sings it quite differently.” And, not to delay you with lengthy digressions, rarely do three people agree in one chant—much less a thousand—for while each person gives forth the teaching of his own master, as many divisions of singing arise as there are masters in the world.

[Col. 1423A] To see plainly that chants are often corrupted through ignorance even in regular neumes, take as an example the antiphon *Collegerunt*. Most people lower the *cline* on the first and the penultimate syllable more than is right, thereby making a diapente and beginning the following neum a tone lower. Yet it is established that from G to D, the *lichanos hypaton*, there is a diapente, and that below Γ there is no note. Moreover, no plagal mode ought to touch the sixth below its final.

Some also confuse the chant of the same antiphon in another passage: they begin *concilium* on the note by which *Pharisaei* descend, and begin the antepenultimate syllable of the word lower than they sound the first.

[Col. 1423B] Whoever wishes to submit to the truth of the rule rather than cling incorrigibly to faulty custom should sing it in this manner:

[Note: [Col. 1423D] This is again expressed with ancient notes.]

*Collegerunt pontifices et Pharisaei concilium et dicebant.*

“But the communion *Beatus servus* also contains a slight error, produced by an improperly rendered *podatus*.”

Some correct this as follows: they make *Dominus*, which descends from the *trite diezeugmenon* c to the *mese* a, and begin *Invenerit* on the *parypate meson* F, and *super omnia* on the *lichanos meson* G.

Others correct it in this way: they begin *Invenerit* according to common usage, and, beginning its penultimate syllable on the *mese* a, sing it on the *lichanos meson* by unison. This also pleases Guarino and Stephen, who are subtle in music.

[Col. 1423C] But if someone objects that semitones are lacking in certain places, we reply that semitones are not necessary where they seem to be required. For it often happens through the incompetence of singers that, among their other corruptions of chants, they produce semitones where they should not, and sometimes neglect them where they should not neglect them.

It is now clear that harsh and unformed human voices avoid semitones as much as possible, whereas those who have flexible voices take great pleasure in semitones, so much so that they sometimes produce them even where they ought not to be produced. This is evident in many antiphons of the fourth tone, such as *Custodiebant*, *Ex Aegypto*, and *Sion renovaberis*.

In a similar way, some err in the responsory *Conclusit u. m.*, sounding semitones where none exist, namely in the words *In, unicus insidiator*.

Likewise, many confuse the same responsory at the end, because they begin *animae meae*, which ought to begin on the *mese* a, on the *nete diezeugmenon* e.

But we shall discuss more fully in the following chapter chants corrupted through irregular neumes.

Some people customarily repair those neumes with certain letters, by which they seem not to teach the singer but to hinder him through a doubled error. For since there is no certainty in the neumes, the letters written above them offer no less uncertainty, especially since many words of different meanings begin with them, and it is therefore unknown what they signify.

[Col. 1424A] Even if some definite meaning is assigned to them, this does not eliminate every uncertainty, since the singer remains unsure of the manner of raising and lowering. For c is the beginning of various words, such as *cito* (“quickly”), *caute* (“carefully”), and *clamose* (“clamorously”); likewise l begins *levia* (“lightly”), *leniter* (“gently”), *lascive* (“playfully”), and *lugubriter* (“mournfully”); similarly s begins *sursum* (“upward”), *suaviter* (“sweetly”), *subito* (“suddenly”), and *sustenta* (“sustain”), and so forth.

We can briefly state this concerning musical and regular neumes: music leads the singer along such a true and easy path that, even if he wishes to, he cannot go wrong. After anyone, whether great or small, has learned four histories or an equal number of offices through these from the precentor, he will be able to learn the entire antiphoner and gradual without a teacher.

[Col. 1424B] Irregular neumes, as has been shown, produce uncertainty and errors, and are unable to confer even the slightest usefulness on a singer. After learning through them the entire gradual except for one office—or, to say more, except for one communion—from a teacher, he would not know how to sing that one remaining communion by himself.

It is therefore clear that whoever embraces these neumes is a lover of error and falsehood, whereas whoever adheres to musical neumes wishes to keep to the path of certainty and truth.

It should further be understood that musical neumes are made in three ways. The first is through notes arranged on the monochord, which the ancient musicians used. The second is through the designation of intervals, a method of forming neumes said to have been discovered by Hermann the Lame. It is made in this way [Note: [Col. 1423] See this in the music of Hermann the Lame, from which we have corrected the present text]:

E indicates equality of voices.

S marks a semitone.

T indicates a tone.

[Col. 1424D] T joined with S shows a semiditone, in this manner: TS.

A doubled T declares a ditone, thus: TT.

A capital D indicates a diatessaron.

Δ indicates a diapente. If you add S to it, it marks a semitone with a diapente, in this figure: ΔS. If, however, you add T, it indicates a tone with a diapente, as follows: ΔT. If you wish to indicate an octave, join Δ and capital D, thus: ΔD.

Each of these signs without a dot indicates raising; with a dot, lowering.

All this is taught most fully by the song said to have been composed by Hermann himself: E equalizes unisonous voices, and so forth, except that the octave does not produce a raising.

The third method of forming neumes was invented by Guido. It is made through *virgae*, *clines*, *qualismata*, points, *podati*, and other such little signs arranged in their proper order. A mark placed in the margin also makes them much easier to understand.

[Col. 1425A] Whoever wishes by this method to be introduced quickly and profitably to musical singing should know that three labors must be undertaken. The first is to consider carefully which syllables, and how many of them, are assigned to each voice. Next, he must no less carefully determine which voices are placed on a line or in a space. The third labor concerns the chant, so that the varying arrangement of the voices does not lead the singer into error. This can easily be avoided if he carefully observes that each letter is marked with red and each C with saffron.

Some people, however, when the color is absent, put a point at the beginning of the line in place of red. We therefore insist that these two things—the letter and the C—or even the colors by which they are marked, be observed with the greatest care, because the other notes are governed by them; when they are moved from their place, the others move together with them.

[Col. 1425B] But if these neumes lack their colors or letters, they are like a well without a rope.

XXII. On abandoning faulty usage and the superfluous distinctions of certain modes

[Col. 1425C] It is now pleasant to recall certain chants that have long been corrupted through irregular neumes, and to urge most strongly that faulty usage, corrupted both in these chants and in all the others, be abandoned.

Since the Lord delights in one faith, one baptism, and complete unity of conduct, who would not believe that he is offended by the discord of numerous singers, which they produce not unwillingly or unknowingly, but voluntarily?

We, therefore, who by God’s will know the correct path of singing, ought not to tolerate error. Nor was it necessary to be greatly concerned if certain foolish singers, obstinate in their faults, refuse to give place to the truth, provided that we can bring it about that some sound-minded people abandon error and correct themselves willingly.

In correcting the chants, we have used such moderation that, because of their small number, they do not burden readers with weariness, and that in their correction they do not depart very far from the customary path.

[Col. 1425D] It should certainly be understood that whatever is sung incorrectly is distorted either at the beginning, in the middle, or at the end. At the beginning, a chant is sometimes corrupted when it is begun either not on its proper note or, though begun on its own note, is excessively lowered or raised by the ill-composed voice of the singer. In the middle or at the end, it is generally corrupted by an unsuitable sound of elevation or descent. Let us give examples of each.

Various singers begin this **R. Ego pro te rogavi** at different places: some, namely, on hypate meson [E], some on lichanos meson [G], and others on mese [a]. When they see the error in the middle, they declare the chant false and attempt to correct it. Nevertheless, if it begins on paramese, it proceeds lawfully and without impediment to its final.

Likewise, an error is found in the middle of the chant, as in **R. Bethlehem civitas**, which should properly be corrected in two places: namely, so that **dominator** begins on the final syllable at parypate meson F, and **in terra** begins on paranete diezeugmenon [d].

In **terra nostra**, some err at the end of the chant, as they do in **R. Mane surgens Jacob**. Although this is most truly of the fourth tone, some unskilled singers emit it on lichanos meson [G], and yet improperly assign to it the usage of the fourth tone. Some also emit this antiphon, **Pater manifestavi**, although it is hypolydian, on lichanos hypaton [D] and assign it to the Dorian tone. Those avoid this fault lightly who sing it on parypate meson [F] in unison.

Likewise, many unlearned singers err in the antiphon **Simile est regnum coeli decem**, making it go out on parypate hypaton [C], because they are unwilling to sing high, as though it were a great sacrilege if, after Pentecost, an antiphon or other chant were sung high. The same fault rebukes those who sing the offertory **Posuisti Domine** on mese [a] and leave the high notes aside.

It should also be noted that, as we said above, the person who often corrupts a chant is the one who begins it not with a suitable voice but according to his own opinion, as is clear in this communion, **Scapulis suis**. Since some begin it on lichanos meson [G], they observe that it suffers a defect and judge that it ought to be corrected. But if it is begun on parypate meson [F], it returns without error to its final and needs no correction.

Moreover, it should be understood that, as we showed above, there are some chants that fail in their proper course but proceed without impediment in related courses: for example, this introit, **Exaudi, Domine, vocem meam**, and the rest, and the communion **Dicit Andreas**. According to those who assign it to the plagal tetrardus, it should be sung in the related courses; in its proper course it is sung well.

There are also some chants that can be sung neither in their proper course nor in related ones. Concerning these we give the following instruction: they should be corrected to their proper course. But if they are very confused and can more easily be corrected in related courses, they should be directed accordingly, as with this offertory:

**In die sollemnitatis vestrae usque et lac et mel**

**Alle—luia.**

Attention must also be given to **R. Hic qui advenit**, so that it begins on mese [a], and, in the same place, *habens* [reading uncertain] should be begun, and it should be emitted on paranete diezeugmenon [d]. The same care should be taken with **R. Viri impii**, so that it is corrected at this place:

**Sapientiam et rei facti sunt in cogitationibus.**

This **R. Domine ne in ira** also needs correction in the middle. For **Miserere**, whose proper usage begins on lichanos hypaton [D], should be begun on lichanos meson [G]. Likewise, in this **R. Egregie Dei martyr**, some corrupt the chant because they do not emit it on trite diezeugmenon [c], and they do not pronounce **Ecce** gently.

Again, in **R. Aegypte noli flere**, some err by raising **flere** above mese [a]. In this gradual, **Ad Dominum**, some err because they do not begin **dum tribularer** on parypate meson [F]. In this gradual, **Esto mihi in Deum**, some are confused because they do not begin **protectorem** on lichanos meson [G].

Consider also the offertory **Confirma hoc Deus**. **Confirma** must not be raised above mese [a], while **Deus** must begin on parypate meson [F]. The offertory **Oravi Dominum meum** also needs correction in two places, namely at the beginning and where **super** occurs.

In the communion **Cantabo Domino**, they sing perversely because they do not begin **bona** on parypate hypaton [c]. But the communion **Potum meum** is sung more correctly if **cum fletu** and **et ego** are begun on parypate hypaton [c]. Likewise, the communion **Domus mea** should be begun thus: **Domus mea domus orationis**, and so forth. [Note: [Col. 1427D] The musical notes are lacking.]

For the present, let it suffice that we have corrected these verses of the chants. After this, in the tonary also we shall correct some examples that come to mind.

Now, before we come to illustrating the modes, we must discuss their superfluous differences. Since “differences” are spoken of in many ways, it must first be explained what we call the differences of the modes.

We call them differences in the tones when certain neumes are reasonably permitted at **saeculorum amen**. It should be understood that among the differences assigned to the tones, some are suitable and necessary; some are suitable but not necessary; and some are neither suitable nor necessary, but entirely nothing.

We call suitable and necessary those differences that the usage of singers has received as established by the ancient composers. Suitable but not necessary are those that are added not out of necessity but merely as a matter of courtesy, as is clear in this antiphon: **O beatum pontificem**. Since this belongs to the second difference of the authentic protus, many, although neglecting that difference, nevertheless adapt one to it:

**Saeculorum amen. O beatum pontificem.**

Those differences are neither suitable nor necessary that are adapted not according to the correct melodic tenor but according to the singers’ preference, as in:

**Saeculorum amen. Nos qui vivimus**, and so forth.

But there are also certain differences that some insist are differences, although I do not say merely that they are not necessary: they are entirely nothing. This occurs when one **saeculorum amen**, diversified in no part in any consistent way, is attached to many chants having different beginnings.

Thus, from among these, some make two superfluous differences for **Ant. Tecum principium** and **Biduo vivens**, although both properly belong to the first tone. For if the different beginnings of chants gave number to the differences, there would be far more differences in the hypolydian, mixolydian, and hypomixolydian tones than there are now. All this will be sufficiently clear in the tonary.

We wish the reader to understand that this is what we have discussed; the others, since we regard them as superfluous, we leave aside.

Nor should it be passed over that there is much error in the ferial antiphons, in which such practice is least appropriate. Some of them are not properly emitted, some are governed by incongruous differences, and some are delivered in both illegal ways. Anyone who has even a modest knowledge of the tones sees this manifold error clearly.

Such antiphons have been corrupted by rustic and uncultivated clerics through their indiscriminate attention to common neumes, as is evident in **Ant. Facti sumus**. It is so perverse that the **saeculorum amen** usually adapted to it cannot be sung at all when either one of the two is lacking. To make this corruption more evident, we set down the antiphon just mentioned, marked with irregular neumes, together with the **saeculorum amen**:

**Saeculorum amen. Facti sumus sicut consolati** [Note: [Col. 1428D] With musical notes.]

It must certainly be emitted as authentic tritus on parypate meson [E]. Other chants corrupted in this way could also be corrected quite easily by a small alteration, if, as Berno says, vicious custom could in any way be torn from the mouths of singers.

## XXIII. On Diaphonia, that is, Organum

We now wish to discuss diaphonia briefly and concisely, so far as we can, in order to satisfy the reader’s eagerness in this matter as well.
