Diaphonia is therefore a suitable dissonance of voices, performed by at least two singers, in such a way that while one holds the correct melody, the other moves appropriately around it through different notes, and at each breath both meet on the same note or at the diapason.

[Col. 1428D] This manner of singing is commonly called organum, because the human voice, suitably dissonant, expresses the likeness of an instrument called an organ. **Diaphonia** is interpreted as “dual voice” or “dissonance.”

But before we give instructions for organizing, we wish to touch briefly on the movements of voices, consideration of which is useful for this task. Since organum is made through consonances, and their arrangements vary according to the movements of voices, no one can doubt that an account of their insertion here will be useful.

Movements of voices are made through **arsis** and **thesis**, that is, through elevation and descent. Every neume, except simple and repercussed neumes, is formed by a twofold movement of arsis and thesis. We call a simple neume a stroke or point; a repercussed neume is what Berno calls a **distropha** or **tristropha**.

Arsis and thesis are sometimes joined to one another as arsis to arsis or thesis to thesis, and sometimes one to the other, as arsis to thesis. The joining itself is partly made from similar movements and partly from dissimilar ones.

Dissimilar movements occur in the aforesaid joining when one has more or fewer notes than the other, whether more closely joined or more widely separated. In a joining made similarly or dissimilarly, one movement is sometimes found placed before another, as when it is positioned above; sometimes placed after it, that is, positioned below; sometimes placed beside it, when the note at which the preceding movement ends is the beginning of the following one; sometimes interposed, when one movement, placed below another, is both less grave and less acute; and sometimes mixed, that is, partly interposed and partly placed after, before, or beside it.

If I were to give examples of all these matters, I would burden the reader with tedious prolixity rather than benefit him, especially since anyone who is a diligent investigator of chants can observe all these things for himself.

The same neumes vary in their movements according to the different properties of the modes. We wish to provide an example of this, so that from it the person learning to organize may make progress, and the person wishing to compose a new chant may also have a formula for composing.

[Col. 1429C]

**Ancilla [DFE] Christi [FGEF] sum [D] ideo me ostendo servilem personam.**

“I am Christ’s maidservant; therefore I show myself to be a servant.”

Consider also that if you sing a chant of the protus in the course of the deuterus with a similar arrangement of voices, you will observe very little incompatibility. The same usually occurs between the tritus and the tetrardus.

Having inserted these matters so briefly, let us return to diaphonia. Different people use it differently. Its easiest use, however, is this, if the variety of movements is carefully observed: where there is an elevation in the straightforward melody, there should be a descent in the organum, and conversely.

The organizer must also take care that if the straightforward melody lingers in the grave notes, he himself meets it by singing in the acute notes at the diapason; but if the melody is in the acute notes, he should produce consonance with it in the grave notes at the diapason. When the chant makes pauses on mese [Col. 1429D] or near mese, he should answer on the same note.

It must be observed that the organum should now be woven on the same note and now alternately at the diapason, although more often and more conveniently on the same note. Although what we have said is clear to the diligent reader, we nevertheless wish, as a gesture of goodwill, to provide a small example.

**Laudate Dominum de coelis** [Note: [Col. 1429D] The musical notes are lacking.]

You should also note that although I have placed simple organum in the simple movements, it is nevertheless permissible for anyone organizing, if he wishes, to double or triple the simple movements, or to gather them together in any other suitable way.

And let it suffice that we have said this little concerning diaphonia.

## XXIV. On the Modes and Their Differences

[Note: [Col. 1429D] These four chapters, previously marked off separately, are here condensed into one because they belong to the tonary, which we omit.]

Now, since I am about to exemplify the modes in every respect, I shall raise the question some people ask concerning the order of the differences—namely, why they have the order they have.

I find no reason for this except usage, nor have I found it written by any musician. For as to what some say, that they were arranged in the antiphonary according to the arrangement of the antiphons, even an unlearned person can see that this is not so.

Nor have I neglected to mention that those seem to me to have acted more correctly who decreed that the principal **saeculorum amen** of all the modes should have a simple neume at the end than those who arranged them otherwise. The former provide the singer with some certainty; the latter never do.

And lest anyone think that I am going to discuss the etymology of the names of the offices, such as responsories and antiphons, and so forth, I expressly reject that at the outset. It is enough for me if I can fully carry out what I have undertaken. Anyone who wishes to know these matters I direct to Isidore’s book entitled [Col. 1430C] **Etymologies**, or also to Amalarius’s useful work.

I shall likewise refuse to arrange the tonary in Berno’s manner: that is, I shall not prescribe **nonannoeane** for each mode, nor insert the differences that I have above judged superfluous, nor collect into one place all the antiphons belonging to a single **saeculorum amen**—especially since prolixity is tedious, and a few examples are sufficient for the reader who has advanced this far.

Of every kind of office chant I shall give concise examples, without the little chants that I called the formulas of the modes above, since there is no need to give again what I have already set down.

With these matters prefaced, let us discuss, as planned, the principal **saeculorum amen** of all the modes and their differences.

[Col. 1430D] Here ends John’s treatise on the art of music.

Here begins his tonary.

The authentic protus consists of the first species of the diapente and, above it, the first species of the diatessaron. Its final syllable in **saeculorum amen**, and so forth. [Note: [Col. 1430D] We judge it superfluous to describe or publish the Tonary, in which the same differences as in Berno’s Tonary are marked, though in much smaller quantity; others agree almost word for word.]

# In the Year of Our Lord 1090. Fulco, Abbot of Corbie

[Col. 1431]

## Fulco’s Letter to Pope Alexander II Concerning Corbie’s Freedom, Harassed by the Bishop of Amiens

*(Mabillon, Benedictine Annals, IV, 622)*

Wido was governing the Church of Amiens, after Fulco his brother, for nearly five years. What he had been unable to accomplish through his brother, he now tried by every means to bring the monastery of Corbie under his control.

First, by a letter addressed to him, he ordered Fulco, an outstanding man, to come with the monk Baldwin to the synod on the third day before the Nones of July; if he failed to appear, he threatened that he would unquestionably be struck with anathema.

The abbot modestly excused himself from obeying the command. Without delay, Wido subjected him to anathema.

Then Fulco submitted a supplicatory petition to Pope Alexander. In it he set out the monastery’s immunity, granted first by Bertefrid, bishop of Amiens, then by the Fathers of the Council of Paris, and confirmed by the Roman pontiffs, an immunity which Corbie had enjoyed for nearly five hundred years.

He said that it had first been attacked by Bishop Fulco at the instigation of his brother Wido; but that Fulco soon abandoned his undertaking through the authority of Pope Leo, who, when consecrating the church of Saint Remigius at the synod held at Reims, saw the privileges of Fulco’s monastery and, with the synod’s assent, restrained the bishop’s unjust undertaking under penalty of anathema. He also ordered Fulco, since he was then only a deacon, to go to Rome to be ordained priest.

Then Fulco said:

[Col. 1431A] The abbot said: “I came and returned ordained, bringing this privilege with me for this matter.” But behold, the same man who is now bishop came to Rome with his co-archdeacon John, falsely marking me before the lord pope with many accusations, and, in addition, concerning the apostolic blessing I had received [that is, the priesthood].

“I was absent; therefore both of us—he and I—were ordered to appear at Vercelli, so that the matter might be dealt with synodally. I appeared on the appointed day, but there were no accusers.

“The pope sent letters to the lord archbishop, instructing him to support our privileges, and he ordered the bishop of Amiens not to do anything impious against us.

“As long as Bishop Fulco lived thereafter, the place enjoyed complete freedom. Fulco was succeeded by the present Wido, who strives with all his might to invalidate what so many apostolic acts have established with holy authority.

“This is the source of my trouble: there were many assemblies. In the midst of all this, someone instructed me to make a payment for the good of the church; and the bishop was to leave to us undisturbed those altars at which monks had formerly ministered, restore his favor toward us, and fully consent after hearing the privileges.

“I gave something worth forty pounds, and, in the presence of Count Baldwin and so many of his princes, an agreement concerning the aforesaid matter was confirmed.

“But behold, he observes it only in part. He accepted the money, but he neither gave us the altars nor consented to peace. He summoned our clerics to Amiens; if they delayed going, he excommunicated them.

“Not bearing this injury equably, we brought in Baldwin as witness to our agreement. Both of us—I mean the bishop and I—came to Courtrai, and there was also a large gathering of abbots and clerics. When the privileges had been read before so great an assembly, the bishop was unable to oppose them.

“After all this, his anger had not yet gone to sleep. Behold, he held a synod and ordered me to attend, although the privileges grant him no authority at all in this matter, and none of my predecessors had carried it out.

“I was ill. I sent my brother, even though a layman, to defend our case and to establish that I could not attend. He disregarded the excuse and delayed the excommunication no more than seven days.

“After this unjust act of binding had been announced, both of us were summoned to the archbishop’s court. He himself did not appear at the appointed time; I nevertheless appeared. Having heard the account of our case, the archbishop, recognizing that the sentence of excommunication had been unjustly issued, again admonished him to release me.

“He did not heed the admonition, but excommunicated me again.

“Behold, most distinguished father, excellent shepherd, what a mass of calamity has fallen upon us. In you is our hope; in you is our defense. When a member suffers, the head ought also to suffer with it. God has placed you over the Church, and it is just that you defend the Church entrusted to you.

“The desolate place of Saint Peter deserves your support, because he is especially the defender of Saint Peter.”

Thus far Fulco, the abbot.

Alexander replied to these complaints by sending letters concerning the matter both to Wido, bishop of Amiens, and to Gervasius, the metropolitan, by which he received the monastery of Corbie under the protection of the apostolic see.

[Col. 1431]

# In the Year of Our Lord 1090. Gilbert, Monk of Elnone

[Col. 1433]

## Historical Notice Concerning Gilbert

*(Literary History of France, VIII, 429)*

After entering the religious order, Gilbert was raised to the dignity of priest and to that of dean of the church of Saint Andrew, the third of those that made up the monastery of Elnone, or Saint-Amand, in the diocese of Tournai. This church was originally served by monks mixed with clerics, who later became its sole possessors until the beginning of the thirteenth century. At that time Pope Innocent III restored the monks there.

Disgusted with the world, Gilbert became a monk at Saint-Amand, where he shone through his intelligence, virtue, zeal, and learning *(Spicilegium*, vol. XII, p. 370; Mabillon, *Acta*, V, p. 65, n. 13; Bollandists, 6 February, p. 843, n. 128). But he was never its abbot, as Casimir Oudin asserted without offering the slightest proof *(Scriptores*, vol. II, pp. 754–755).

He had withdrawn there before February 1066, or rather 1067, when the monastery was reduced to ashes by an unforeseen fire *(Mabillon, ibid., vol. II, p. 732)*. Consequently, it was decided that the relics of Saint Amand should be carried through the towns and countryside, in order to stir the piety of the faithful to contribute to the restoration of his monastery.

This transfer was carried out in the same year, from the fourth of June to the following fourth of July. Gilbert was one of the monks who accompanied the shrine everywhere it was carried, and thus placed himself in a position to write the history of the translation, which he subsequently did.

He possessed the gift of speech and talent for the pulpit *(Bollandists, ibid.)*, qualities united in his person with great intelligence in the divine Scriptures and a life recognized as holy. By using these gifts to combat vigorously the prevailing vices of his age, he acquired among clergy and people alike the reputation of an excellent teacher and celebrated preacher.

Another writer, nearly his contemporary, adds that throughout the country he was regarded as a prophet. He enjoyed such great influence there that Radbod, the diocesan bishop, had recourse to him to persuade Master Odo, who later became his successor, to restore the monastery of Saint Martin at Tournai, a task in which the prelate himself had been unable to succeed.

Gilbert died on 7 December 1095 *(Mabillon, Annals, book LXIX, no. 17; André, *Bibliotheca Belgica*, p. 288; Vossius, *History of Latin Literature*, book II, chap. 47; Oudin, ibid., p. 755)*. He was first buried in the middle of the church of Saint Peter, with the following epitaph. His body was later transferred to the underground vault of the Martyrs.

## Epitaph

“Here Gilbert lies beneath this marble, covered,

Bearing sacred teachings and ever clinging to Christ;

He who bore the form of a shepherd among our shores,

At last taken from the earth, summoned, seeks the stars.”

Sweertius, Valère André, Vossius, Oudin, and other bibliographers *(Sweertius, *Athenaeum Belgicum*, p. 288; André, ibid.; Vossius, ibid.; Oudin, ibid.; Bollandists, ibid.)*, who include Gilbert among their writers, do not all explain clearly the writings they attribute to him. Some speak as though he had written only one work; others as though he had written three or four. This is a matter requiring the necessary clarification.

1. He wrote a history of the circuitous transfer of the relics of Saint Amand through Flanders, the Cambresis, and part of France, together with an account of the miracles performed there. Gilbert appears to have undertaken it immediately after the relics returned to their church. No one was better suited than he to carry out this work successfully. As has been said, he had accompanied the holy relics everywhere and possessed a talent for writing reasonably well.

He therefore believed himself entitled to attest his sincerity and accuracy, and clerics, monks, and laymen who knew the same events bore witness to them *(Bollandists, ibid., p. 895, n. 1)*.

The manuscripts represent this work as divided into four books; in the printed editions it was reduced to four chapters, not counting the short preface. The third and fourth books are written partly in prose and partly in verse, which is no better than the versification of other poets of the same period.

This writing was first printed among the works of Philip Harveng, abbot of Bonne-Espérance, which appeared at Douai in 1621. It is incomplete there; and some, seeing it thus joined to the works of that abbot, took the opportunity to attribute it to him. But this is plainly an error, since the text itself shows that it belongs to a contemporary author, which Abbot Philip was not.

The first successors of Bollandus, having revised that edition against two ancient manuscripts, reprinted the work in full after the acts of Saint Amand. Dom Mabillon limited himself to publishing selected excerpts *(Acts, vol. II, pp. 732–734)*.

2. Gilbert also composed a poem on the burning of his monastery, which, as noted above, occurred in February 1067 and therefore before Easter. This work cannot reasonably be confused with the preceding one, as some seem to have done. Apart from the fact that the earlier work mentions it only briefly, the passage in which it is discussed is in prose and not in verse; and this does not fulfill the idea given us of the poem by a monk of Saint-Amand himself, who says on this subject:

“Gilbert celebrates in plaintive verse

The disaster he received,

And follows it with mournful strains.”

Valère André makes it appear that he had seen this poem in the manuscripts, since he tells us that it was divided into four books and well written for its time. “He wrote,” says this bibliographer, “in elegant verse, four books on the fire at Elnone.” Nevertheless, the poem is regarded as lost *(Bollandists, ibid.)*.

3. In Sanderus’s time, a manuscript was seen in the library of Saint-Amand containing a Commentary on all the Epistles of Saint Paul under the name of Gilbert, a monk of that place *(Sanderus, *Bibliotheca Belgica*, manuscript, part I, p. 46)*.

The manuscript was numbered 165 and bore the title: **D. M. N. Gilleberti monachi S. Amandi Expositio in omnes Epistolas S. Pauli**—“The exposition of Dom Master Our [or: of our master] Gilbert, monk of Saint-Amand, on all the Epistles of Saint Paul.” The three initial letters may mean **domni magistri nostri** (“of our lord master”), and show that this inscription was written by a hand other than that of the original author.

4. Sanderus adds that the same library preserved another manuscript, numbered 188, containing sermons for every feast day throughout the year. They bore no name of Gilbert. It was merely marked that they were the work of a monk of Saint-Amand; and they displayed much illumination and solidity, together with a great store of piety and learning. All these characteristics, when compared with Gilbert’s personal qualities, make it almost impossible to doubt that this was one of his works.

The first continuators of Bollandus speak particularly of a sermon on Saint Amand that they had found separately in the manuscripts and of which they published the opening lines *(Bollandists, 6 February, p. 843, n. 131)*.

Even if this sermon did not belong to the preceding collection, it could not reasonably be denied to our author, especially since the piece is later than the monk Milo and was made to be read on the feast of Saint Amand’s birth, just as Milo’s writings were read on the day of the elevation and translation of his body.

The records of the abbey of Saint-Amand that discuss Gilbert’s writings state that he had written about the restoration of this illustrious abbey: **De reparatione ejusdem coenobii**, “On the restoration of the same monastery.” If this portion of history was not treated in the poem intended to recount the burning of the same monastery, it would be a separate work and would increase the number of Gilbert’s writings.

[Col. 1435]

# History of the Miracles of the Body of Saint Amand Carried through France, by Gilbert, Monk of Elnone

*(Acts of the Saints, Bollandists, February, vol. I, day 6, from the manuscripts of Ghent and Belfort, collated with the edition of the Works of Philip of Eleemosyna.)*

## Author’s Prologue

[Col. 1435A]

1. Although the human mind is sometimes deceived by fantastic visions, it cannot be deceived by the signs of miracles that the Lord, worker of virtues, deigns to perform in his faithful.

For by a fantastic illusion the Egyptian king of Memphis was captivated, together with all Egypt, by the Egyptian magicians, who took false and imaginary things for the truth. But after the wonders of divine power had been displayed, the magicians themselves, together with the others, although at first unbelieving, later confessed that this was the finger of God *(Exodus 8:19)*.

The heavens—that is, all the faithful—speak of the glory of God, and the sound of his mighty works goes forth into all the earth.

Therefore, according to the measure of our ability, [Col. 1435B] in an unpolished style indeed, but concerning no ignoble subject, [Col. 1436A] I shall attempt to convey certain notable matters to the knowledge of posterity: how, in our own age, the immortal King revealed upon earth his soldier, namely blessed Amandus, whom he had endowed with the glorious gift of immortality in heaven.

If anyone, with an obstinate mind, should try to rebuke our style in this matter, supposing that we wish to follow nothing but common rumors, we oppose to him the weapon once used by the shepherd and chief pillar of the Church against those who rejected the truth: “We cannot,” he said, “not speak of what we have heard and seen” *(Acts 4:20)*.

For this pen reveals nothing in the course of its writing except what the writer’s eyes clearly established [Note: [Col. 1435B] From this the writer’s period is established.], with the monks, clerics, and even laymen of that same time, venerable in memory and distinguished in reputation, bearing witness to it [Col. 1436B].

[Note: [Col. 1435B] We distinguish the history below into chapters, indicated in the margin according to our custom. They were read as follows:

1. Concerning the bells sounding as they burned, with no one ringing them.

2. Concerning the madman at Cambrai restored to his senses.

3. Concerning a sick woman restored to health.

4. The mouth and tongue of a mute are opened.

5. Concerning a weak boy healed.

6. Concerning the madman at Laon restored to his senses.

7. Concerning a contracted woman raised upright beneath the bier of Saint Amand.

8. Concerning a blind woman restored to sight.

9. Concerning a woman mute from birth speaking there.

10. Concerning a boy who, though his eyes had been opened, could not see, and was given sight through Saint Amand.

11. Concerning a blind woman at Noyon given sight.

[Col. 1437D] 12. Concerning a cripple healed.

13. Concerning a woman suddenly crippled at Douai and raised upright before the bier of Saint Amand.

14. Concerning a prisoner at Coucy freed through invocation of Saint Amand.]

## Chapter One. The Fire at Elnone; Miracles Performed at the Relics of Saint Amand at Cambrai and Coucy

[Col. 1437A]

2. Chapter 2. In the year from the Lord’s Incarnation 1066, but 406 from Amandus’s passing [Note: [Col. 1437D] He follows Milo’s chronology.], on the third day before the Ides of February, the houses in the marketplace at Elnone caught fire at about the third hour [Note: [Col. 1437D] The Amandine records state that this fire occurred on a Saturday, which that year fell on 2 February. John Buzelinus reports the same event, together with the miracles, in book IV of his *Annals of French Flanders*.].

From there the flame burst through the tiles beneath the wooden roofing into the church of the aforesaid bishop, which was roofed with lead—because, as we believe, of the envy of the ancient enemy. The church itself, together with all its cloisters, was immediately devastated by the fire, as was also the church of the chief of the apostles and that of his brother [Note: [Col. 1437D] Saint Andrew, whose dean the writer Gilbert was.].

The bells [Note: [Col. 1437D] Seventeen in number, according to the Amandine records and Ruzelinus.] were reduced to powder by melting. All the ornaments of the church were also destroyed, including, I mean, the columns of Parian stone together with the dignified structure of the lectern [Note: [Col. 1438D] **Analogium** is a higher place, or pulpit, from which sacred readings are delivered. Saint Benedict, in the Rule, chapter 9: “Let three readings be read in turn by the brothers from the book above the lectern.”].

There occurred something most worthy of report which, just as it greatly astonished those who saw and heard it, will, I think, seem like a marvel to those who read it. For as soon as the bells themselves were seized by the flame, they began all together, moved by no one except God alone, to resound as though divinely admonished to mourn the destruction of themselves and of the church, until, as has already been mentioned, they were reduced to powder.

3. For the restoration of this dwelling, the brothers, together with the abbot of the place [Note: [Col. 1438D] Lambert, also called Fulcard, appointed abbot in 1063 and deceased in 1076, after laying the foundation of the greater basilica.], at the counsel of the marquis [Note: [Col. 1438D] The marquis of Flanders, Baldwin the Pious, or Baldwin of Lille.], and of the bishops, and also at the urgent request of the Franks, carried through Gaul the bier on which the little body of the revered Father rested. Wherever they went, the Gauls received them honorably and with the greatest devotion, together with so great a treasure.

We left the monastery on the seventh day before the Ides of June and returned to it on the fourth day before the Nones of July. What took place during this interval of four weeks, through the merits of the often-mentioned bishop, before an immense multitude throughout that region, Mother Church must not leave unspoken. She rejoices that her orthodox children, and her children’s children preserving themselves everywhere in good perseverance, have been honored by the peoples.

But leaving these matters aside, let us now turn our pen, however foolish, to those things that we have resolved to record and entrust to memory.

4. (Chapter 2) As we traversed certain places, we came to the illustrious city of Cambrai, distinguished by its episcopal see. There, beside the gates, an insane man sat with his feet tightly fastened in fetters. As the inhabitants openly informed us, in the madness of his deranged mind he had wounded one of his female relatives. When we had been honorably received by Bishop Lietbert [Note: [Col. 1438D] Blessed Lietbert, bishop of Cambrai, died in 1076, on July 23] and by all the clergy of that place, and were staying there as guests, we appealed to him that the wretched man be given to Saint Amand, so that the saint, to whom he was being entrusted, might obtain from divine mercy that he be released from demonic bonds when his bodily bonds had been removed. And so it was done. For the bishop granted our petition, and that pontiff of ours, whose body was being carried, obtained from Christ, the supreme Pontiff, a free mind for the man who had hitherto been held captive, so that, proceeding from there with us, he displayed no further sign of an unsound mind.

5. (Chapter 3) Turning our steps away from that city, we proceeded with an immense company of its citizens toward a town called Coceium [Note: [Col. 1438D] Coceium, commonly Coucy, between the rivers Oise and Aisne, near the abbey of Nogent], where many injuries were being inflicted by the townsman or judge of that place upon the household of Saint Amand, which lived around the town itself. But when we had drawn near the place toward which we had arranged to travel, behold, we encountered a certain priest named Milo, of the church built in honor of Saint Remigius, together with a considerable crowd of common people of both sexes. He humbly begged us to allow the shrine of so great a pontiff to be carried into that church of Saint Remigius and to rest there for a little while.

Not far from this place is a certain village called Vernulium [Note: [Col. 1438D] Vernulium, a neighboring village in the diocese of Laon, commonly Verneuil]. In it lay a woman stretched upon a bed because of an immense weakness of her limbs; for twice five years she had been unable to leave her bed. When she heard the sounds and songs of the crowd turning toward that place, she asked the reason. When she learned that the body of Saint Amand was being carried there by faithful throngs, she immediately burst into these words:

“If only I were granted at least the ability to crawl on my hands like a quadruped to meet him, I would implore the saint to support my weakness through his holy intercession!”

But while she burned with longing that what she had desired might be fulfilled, merciful divinity anticipated her prayers through the intervention of so great a Father; for it is ready to grant mortals what they do not even dare to wish for. At once the blood, coursing around the nerves, strengthened the weak woman’s limbs: it drained away her weakness and consolidated her with strength. Thus, gently springing from the bed on which the bedridden woman had lain through prolonged illness, she began gradually to advance as far as the threshold of the house. Not content merely to walk from there, she ran at full speed—as is customary among women—seized the bier, and related, with suitable witnesses, what that outstanding worker of miracles had done for her and how great was his patronage. Then she placed a strap around her neck like a slave’s yoke, and, now free, devoted herself to the service of the saint.

Nor was this undeserved, since he had made her, who by a defect of nature had been condemned to leave her bed like a quadruped, a biped by natural use, so that she might joyfully come to meet him.

6. (Chapter 4) A certain young man, also her cousin, himself free, more than thirty years old, was brought forward. He had been mute from birth, though he fully possessed hearing and understanding. He had visited many churches of the saints in order that the use of speech might be divinely granted to him; but, as may be said without offense to them, this gift had been reserved for the merits of so great a Father.

Ancient miracles are renewed in him, and we recognize that the imagined age of another Zechariah has arisen. The relatives of that Zechariah gestured to him, asking what name he wished to give his son; the relatives of this man likewise gestured, asking under what condition he wished to subject himself to the saint’s service. The former requested by a gesture that a writing tablet be given him, so that his fingers might indicate what his tongue could not; the latter similarly indicated by a gesture that he would pay the same saint four silver coins each year as a poll tax for his head. What the former wished to set down on the tablet, once the use of his tongue had immediately been restored, he pronounced in clear speech.

Let us see how, in this joyful miracle, the latter also imitated him: standing before the bier, he placed a strap around his neck. Then the priest Milo, whom we mentioned above, in whose diocese he was also said to have been born and raised, came forward and addressed him briefly:

“What are you waiting for, brother? If you cannot speak, at least express by the sign of your fingers, before those present as witnesses, what you hold in your mind.”

“All fell silent, and held their faces intent.” (Virgil, *Aeneid* II.1.)

Then, when he tried to indicate four silver coins with four fingers, he proclaimed in a clear and first utterance what he had been attempting to express with his fingers. O what applause, and how great, you would have seen, had you been present, from the throngs streaming together from every side, praising God with hymn-filled voices along with us and, in their immense joy, wetting their cheeks with overflowing tears!

What shall I say about the very age in which he was formed in speech? Christ restored through his Passion a man dead in sins and mute in the praises of God during that same age; he opened his mouth to divine praises. Through holy intercession, blessed Amandus obtained from divine mercy that this servant of his, who in every respect was comparable to a dead man, should be given life as though through speech, and he caused him to exalt the praises of God and to form words for the thanksgiving owed to God.

7. (Chapter 5) I consider that we must also proclaim what we saw wondrously happen at the very threshold of the gates of the aforementioned castle. As soon as the litter bearing the saint’s body had been placed across the way, so that the people might submit their necks to it with the utmost humility, a certain woman came hurrying forward, carrying in her arms a feeble son who, though nearly a year old, had been unable to tread the earth. When his mother placed him beneath the bier, he began to cry out so that all could hear:

“Put me down, mother, as quickly as possible, from this conveyance in which I am being carried, because I seem now to be able to become your follower on foot. I beg you, do not oppose my healing or stand in the way of your own joy.”

But she, believing that he was saying these things in childish or even mistaken words, replied:

“Do not, my son, do not, lest you be crushed by the crowd pressing around you, since you cannot bring to completion what you are saying.”

And the boy said: “I can, mother, I can.”

After this, without waiting for his mother’s reply, he immediately tore himself from her arms and, gradually testing the way, cheerfully broke into a run. By such signs of miracles, performed around the castle, the merciful pontiff, I believe, preferred to restrain the townspeople from harassing his household by kindness rather than frighten them with threats.

But since we have measured these matters according to the capacity of our little intellect, let us now transfer our pen to what remains, which shines more clearly than daylight, invoking for their completion the patronage of him whose merits we believe such remarkable deeds to be credited.

## CHAPTER II. Miracles performed at Laon, Chauny, Noyon, and Douai

8. (Chapter 6) At last, when the following dawn had ended the night, we approached the mountain of Laon [Note: [Col. 1439D] Laon, or Lugdunum Clavatum, commonly Laon], immediately climbed it, and rested there that day after being received with great veneration by Bishop Elinand [Note: [Col. 1440D] This bishop Elinand is mentioned in the miracles of Saint Hubert, November 3] and by all the clergy of that place.

Meanwhile the sun was declining toward sunset, and behold, they brought in a certain madman bound hand and foot. Night fell upon the Ocean, while boys and unmarried girls, young men together with old men, surrounded the shrine of that most precious treasure and began devout vigils with burning torches and lamps.

Now night already held the middle of the heavens, and the falling stars were urging sleep, when the man, suddenly lying beneath the bier, burst into these words:

“Why these bonds bind my arms, or where I lie cast down, I ask you who stand around me to tell me.”

Then, struck with amazement, they thought that he was uttering wandering words as before. Nevertheless, they instructed him about what he asked:

“Because of the excessive madness of your mind, you have been brought here bound with knots of cords, to the patronage of Saint Amand, whose body you should know is resting in the present church of Saint Mary.”

“Give thanks to God with me,” he said. “The monstrous force of madness has departed. I beg that the chains now be removed.”

As soon as he had been freed from every bond, he signed himself with the sign of the holy cross. If, instigated by the devil, he had uttered any word against the purity of the faith while in his error, he beat his breast and acknowledged himself guilty. Then he surrendered himself as a servant to Saint Amand, whose prayers he continually regarded as the support of his mind.

And rightly did he submit himself to the saint’s service, since by his aid he knew himself to have been expelled from the prison of a savage torturer, having previously been powerless over his own mind.

9. (Chapter 7) Nor should those things be passed over in silence which, as we were returning from there on Sunday, were seen by everyone to have occurred upon the mountain itself. As we were leaving behind the city gates situated on the brow of the mountain, with a great company of both sexes and in the full heat of midday, behold, a woman approached with her legs twisted beneath her, crawling on her hands and with her face fixed toward the ground. When everyone opened the way, she drew near the bier.

A wondrous and most astonishing thing! When she mingled with the bearers, she rose with her nerves restored and, wonderful to say, firmly seized the carrying-frame itself. O what a roar resounded from the mouths of the people, and what a tumult arose in praise of God from monks, clerics, and laypeople! Then one could see crowds converging from every side to witness this remarkable event, pressing so heavily upon the bearers out of their desire to see the woman that scarcely any of them could move his feet.

Indeed, following a wise plan, we caused the holy body to rest for about three hours upon a certain rock in that same place, so that, having recovered our breath somewhat, we might afterward descend from the brow of the mountain.

10. (Chapter 8) I report a thing that stupefies me, and I recount a marvel, seeking a faithful hearer; yet I relate only what happened before the approving eyes of this writer, and all within scarcely an hour. For immediately a person of the female sex came forward who had completed the cycle of seven years in the sorrow of blindness. As soon as she touched the bier with her eyes, the darkness was wiped away and she recovered the loss of her vanished sight. Restored to her former light, she proceeded with us and began to proclaim the great deeds of Christ accomplished in her regard.

11. (Chapter 9) A certain girl was also brought by both parents. They declared that, from the moment her mother’s womb had delivered her, she had been without the use of her tongue up to that very day. As soon as she likewise kissed the receptacle of the venerable body, the plectrum of her tongue was loosened, and the organs of her voice were raised in praise of God.

By these and many similar miracles the people of Laon gladdened their hearts, giving thanks to the majesty of the Most High. The countless crowd of both sexes and every age prevented our eyes from witnessing some events, which were afterward reported to us by faithful men.

Not only the inhabitants of this city but also those of the other cities, who came together to witness these spectacles, gave voice to God in hymn-like songs, praising the divine power because it had happened that the saint was carried there. They believed that such things would never have proceeded from so great a patron before their eyes unless his church had been devastated by fire. For they would not even have rejoiced that he had been brought into their neighborhood.

12. (Chapter 10) From there, turning our steps away amid the immense, eager press of the crowd, we proceeded toward the walls of Noyon. The golden sun was preparing to plunge its chariot into the Ocean when we arrived at a little castle called Calneium [Note: [Col. 1441D] Thus in the manuscripts; the printed edition has *cursum*. Calneium—Calnicum according to Masson, commonly Chauny—is a town not far from the river Oise, from which a channel is led near the walls between La Fère and Noyon.]. We were cheerfully received as guests there and rested during the night.

In the morning, after the nocturnal vigils, we saw a certain matron who was warming a child in her lap. She carried a lamp without light: I mean that the little eyes in his head contained no lamp at all. She approached and began to speak, but stopped halfway through her speech, sobbing with grief as she expressed what afflicted her concerning her son, who had suffered from birth with a cataract and blindness.

“With this child,” she said, “I have spent this night awake, keeping vigil beneath the bier of Saint Amand. I gave birth to him for the world without natural light, and I brought him here so that he might be illuminated by the rays of this saint’s merits. But since I have not yet obtained what I vowed, I beg you to touch the places of his eyes with some relics of this saint, if divine mercy might in some way bend toward my supplication and enlighten him by its grace.”

Then, taking the tooth of the aforementioned Father, finely polished in gold by a craftsman, and also the staff with which he had governed his episcopate of preaching, we placed them, as the mother had requested, upon the places of the child’s eyes. After a short interval, the child’s little eyes immediately began to perform their function, growing bright through divine power with no darkness hindering them at all.

Then all who stood nearby, especially the father and mother, wishing to establish the matter by a certain test, offered him necklaces, little candles, and other objects with which a child’s mind is usually delighted. He, judging everything clearly, quickly seized them all and then, playing, immediately tossed them back to those who held them out to him in turn. They also gestured with their fingers, and he responded in the same way. Without delay the canons rushed to the bells, while we and the people burst into divine praises.

13. (Chapter 11) Thereafter we reached Noyon, toward which we had been traveling. There we encountered two shrines of Saint Eligius, once Saint Amand’s closest friend while both were alive: one accompanied by monks, the other by clerics. The suburban townspeople from various orders, clerics together with monks, came to meet us. Receiving the shrine of our patron with immense veneration and the greatest devotion, they carried it into the church of the episcopal see.

After our tent had been extended in the city square, they reverently received it—not without the bishop of that place, Baldwin [Note: [Col. 1442D] “Baldwin, bishop of Noyon, after, as Buzelin testifies in book IV of the *Annals of French Flanders*, having courageously undertaken many labors for the sake of the Christian Church”]—and carried it away, rejoicing in so great a guest.

When the customary nocturnal vigils had been completed, and the solemn offices of morning had also been performed among us, behold, a woman appeared, oppressed by an enormous pain of vertigo, so severe that she could not turn her head upward, to the right, or to the left, and was deprived of the joy of light.

Standing beside the bier, she remained there until the light of midday, and then was restored so completely that, before everyone, she rejoiced in the remedies of which the pain in her head had deprived her. Immediately crowned again with her former sight, she looked up to heaven to offer thanks to God, and, moving her eyes around, gazed here and there at those standing nearby, recounting the Lord’s marvelous virtues unfolded around her.

14. (Chapter 12) As soon as this had been spread through the mouths of the people, a certain man sitting [Note: [Col. 1443D] Perhaps “walking”] with a twisted foot was brought forward. Since he did not trust his own foot to the ground, he was supported by another’s assistance. Thus he sought the help of the most holy confessor and tested the grace of his merits.

For a long time he remained trembling before the saint’s presence, invoking the prayers of so great a bishop, which would benefit him before divine mercy. At last he found what he sought; and he who had come on another’s feet returned on his own, realizing that the saint’s patronage would not be lacking to him.

These and many similar signs of power were displayed not only in these but also in other cities of Gaul through this patron of ours, as we have already mentioned. The immense press of the people prevented our sight from attaining knowledge of them all. But because we did not wish to exceed our promises, for the present we write only of those remarkable deeds whose signs did not escape our eyes.

15. (Chapter 13) Nor do we think it appropriate to keep silent about what we saw remarkably accomplished at Douai [Note: [Col. 1443D] This city now possesses a distinguished university]. Among other women, one woman came before us in good health; but, I do not know on account of what guilt, she was not found worthy to meet the saint—perhaps because she was guilty of some blasphemy against him, for which she had not yet been punished with worthy repentance. “The judgments of the Lord are a great abyss” (Psalm 35:7).

Thus it happened that, as soon as she returned home, her feet adhered to her buttocks and her hands to her breast as though fixed there with nails, and she lay half-dead. We ourselves saw her carried to the refuge of our patron as though dead and displaying no sign of life at all. Yet not long afterward we saw her standing erect before the saint’s bier, with her feet freed and her hands reversed in position.

These are the things by which the Lord was pleased at that time to declare throughout the province of Gaul the merits of the most blessed Amandus [Note: [Col. 1443D] The manuscripts and the printed edition had *et*]. Along with them were other matters reported to us by the sick themselves after they had been restored to health, with faithful men as witnesses.

Whatever their quality and however great those other things may be, blessed be the name of the Lord in all his works forever. Amen.

## CHAPTER III. Through the help of Saint Amand, a prisoner is freed and a hanged man restored to life

[Note: [Col. 1443D] The title of this chapter had been printed in the list given above, but the verses were lacking.]

[Col. 1444A]

16. (Chapter 14) It was the custom of the ancients, and it remains so among the moderns,

for the writer’s pen to traverse varied furrows.

Thus prose and meter vary the mind of the one dictating;

therefore in meter we sing of a wondrous deed,

accomplished at Coceium after we ourselves returned.

We learned it not now through our eyes, but through the fountain of hearing.

A certain Landricus devoted himself abundantly

to the cultivation of the earth; practice had enriched him.

In the summer sunlight, together with the reapers,

at the season when summer has already cut the yellow crops,

standing, he took the joyful fruits of his own labor for his own use,

when a horseman, sent ahead, came from the castle,

urging his horse with the spurs of his hands,

hastening toward the aforementioned

Landricus, prepared to use force against him.

Landricus was trying to carry some sheaves from the field for himself;

then and there he felt that the owner of the field held authority.

In the end, each of the two engaged in a ridiculous duel:

one denying what was his, the other seeking what belonged to someone else.

Then the robber, sent to seize the crop and empowered by the right of seizure,

having failed in his own attempt, returned shamefaced.

As soon as what had happened was reported to Albricus

(the castellan was known by that name),

“Bring him,” he said, “with his arms bound behind his back.

Let Landricus, bearing a dreadful knot beneath his throat,

properly experience the depths of the prison as well.”

At his word, savage prison bonds surrounded and tormented him,

and a pit held him fast with horror.

This castle was rightly called by that name:

for its savage people thrust themselves into the deeds of that abyss,

whose streams, mingling with it, drive Cocytus [Note: [Col. 1444D] Cocytus, a river of the underworld, from Greek *κωκύειν*, “to mourn” or “to weep”]

Cocytus, mingling with its streams, draws Coceium after itself through the wickedness of its inhabitants.

17. How he was drawn from the foul cavern of the prison

we shall disclose, as trustworthy witnesses have related.

Chained and enclosed by a binding iron clasp,

he began to be dragged in different directions; then he remembered

what Amandus, distinguished by honorable titles,

had recently accomplished, giving speech to the mute and light to the blind.

Then, praying with tears and offering sighs from his heart,

he uttered these words to so great a patron:

“O Amandus, pontifical glory and excellent accomplisher of deeds,

bishop, I now ask that your triumphs be present.

You do not seek someone who uses words in vaulted phrases [Note: [Col. 1444D] That is, covered or concealed expressions. *Camera* means a vault in ancient usage, a room or upper chamber among the Belgians; hence *camerare*. Another manuscript had *cameracis].*

I speak simply: now be near me.

If what we recently discovered about you is true—

that so many things around our borders

have been completed, not by natural means—

now mercifully exact a true trophy from the enemy

who keeps me, utterly undeserving, in the cavern of the prison

and heaps upon me every kind of evil.

I beg you to help me by your prayers, lest the squalor of this prison

torment me for long and threaten me with death.”

Immediately after his words, the weights of the iron began to be loosened,

simultaneously, wonderful to say,

as though someone were lifting him from the iron with his hands.

Then, feeling his way slowly and taking the path step by step,

he went out and came to where the judge was conducting legal business,

supported at his side by a guard,

hearing vain pleas and offenders from every side.

Placed before him, Landricus came out in full view of everyone,

and afterward saw no one else rise.

Thus he whose merciful compassion had formerly heard the man crying out

now protects him as he goes.

18. (Chapter 15) We shall make known in some sort of written account, for those who wish to read it, a particular miracle performed by blessed Amandus in the region of Noyon, as we learned from the report of certain people [Note: [Col. 1445D] He was there with the relics of Saint Amand; for this reason the event is separated from the other miracles then performed].

When blessed Amandus was staying with twelve brothers in the region of Laon, at a place called Baresetum [Note: [Col. 1445D] Or Barisiacum], it happened that the Frankish king Dagobert [Note: [Col. 1445D] We have said that this place was given to Saint Amand by King Childeric, the grandson of Dagobert I. Is Dagobert, the son of Saint Sigebert, intended?] came one day to Compiègne [Note: [Col. 1445D] A handsome town at the confluence of the rivers Aisne and Oise [Col. 1446D]]. When blessed Amandus learned of his arrival, he decided to go there.

When he had reached a village called Melincotum, he turned aside for lodging at the house of a certain widow who had one only son. Meanwhile, certain raiders coming from the region of Beauvais were leading before them some plunder that they had carried away by theft.

When they saw the inhabitants of that region rapidly pursuing them at close quarters, they immediately plunged into a darker forest with their plunder. Still uncertain of their lives, they fled from their pursuers at a rapid pace. By chance, the son of the widow in whose lodging blessed Amandus had stayed was walking alone through that same wood.

Since they did not know the reason for his presence, the robbers left their plunder with him as though for safekeeping, while they themselves, wishing only to save their own lives, began to flee more quickly. The men who were hurrying to snatch the plunder from the hands of the robbers found the young man alone in the forest with the booty the robbers had abandoned.

Because they thought that he was one of the robbers, they seized him and immediately hanged him. There was no delay: a rumor arose, a cry was raised, and word was announced that the widow’s son had been hanged and was already dead. Almost all the inhabitants living in the surrounding area ran to see. The mother too, wailing with pitiful cries over the hanged man, hurried with blessed Amandus, whom she had received as her guest.

What more need be said? The holy man felt such compassion for the woman that, prostrate on the ground, he remained devoted to prayer and tears until, by God’s favor, he restored the young man alive and unharmed to his own mother, rejoicing and exulting.

For this reason, a small chapel was built at that same place, at little expense, in honor of blessed Bishop Amandus, as a worthy and venerable memorial of the paradoxical event, to the praise of our Savior God Jesus Christ, who gloriously honors his saint in heaven and on earth, and who, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, lives and reigns as God forever and ever. Amen.

## CHAPTER IV. A danger of death removed. A bedridden woman is healed

[Note: [Col. 1446D] These two chapters are contained in the Amandine manuscript, added later, either by the same Gillebertus or, more probably, by another.]

19. Let the service of the stylus unfold the miracle that follows these events,

so that what is clear to those present may become known to those who come after.

As time passed, while the church rose again

upon its foundations [Note: [Col. 1446D] Therefore after the death of Lambertus, or Fulcardus, abbot, under Bovo, or in the first years of Hugh],

and advanced vigorously,

many laborers were occupied with various tasks.

Two of them were sent to dig earth and sand,

Willebertus by name, with Albertus as his companion.

Thus paired together and agile for the work,

they diligently carried out the task assigned to them.

When, at one point during the day, they entered the worksite with a spade,

they fell into the snare of death.

When it seized them, it did not hold them fast,

but offered a loosened fold;

and those whom Satan terrified, our bishop rescued.

Those whom savagery disturbed, mercy sheltered.

For there was a hollow place beneath their feet,

and earth together with stones hung over their necks.

What more need be said? The mass collapsed and nearly crushed them.

Willebertus was held inside up to his waist;

Albertus, however, was thrust down to the very bottom of the pit.

The neighborhood rushed there and searched for dead limbs.

For who could believe that anyone would live whom so great a mass had struck down?

Yet he lived through the illustrious merit of the holy bishop.

Through him it became clear, wondrously, that he had snatched his servant from death.

When the neighbors removed the fallen earth

and the rolling masses of stones, they found scarcely the head

of the half-dead man, which they had almost crushed

by throwing stones upon it there;

they drew him out like a dead corpse.

They perceived in him no breath of life or living respiration.

For from about the third hour

until almost the seventh he had lain buried

in dreadful darkness.

Then, pulling him out pale

and almost indistinguishable from a dead man,

as they carried him away from the pit

and prepared a grave, they saw him grow red

and understood that he was alive.

He afterward lived for a long time with that companion,

healthy in body, and most certainly continued in service after him.

20. [Note: [Col. 1446D] These words were placed before the passage as a title: “Saint Amand of Bizo.”]

In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1090, one of the monks of Saint Amand had a vision during sleep, as though the heavens were opening and sending forth a flaming fiery heat. And immediately a fiery plague attacked human beings [Note: [Col. 1447C] We discussed the “sacred fire” that raged in those years and was announced from heaven in the *Life of Saint Antony*, January 17, in a special treatise following the translations, in the section on his miracles]. It proclaimed to those who despised the Creator the heat of divine punishment.

For this is the cup of just condemnation that the prophet Jeremiah gives to drink to those opposed to holy religion (Jeremiah 25:15). The Lord clearly deigned to declare this by the event itself. For people who were burning were carried to the places of the saints [Note: [Col. 1447C] Saints Piaton, Rictrude, Martin, the Virgin Mother of God, and Saint Antony, as we stated there from Buzelin and others], and were extinguished by their merits.

What else did he wish to show mortals beforehand through the event of both groups, except that the disobedient justly deserve the fire of Gehenna, while those who obey the Lord’s commands mercifully attain the refreshment of eternal rest?

Therefore, when relief was granted to certain people in the church of Saint Amand, while the monks stood there amid the rejoicing of their hearts and voices and the ringing of bells, a woman lay outside in a house, bedridden through prolonged illness. Hearing the sound of the bells, and saying that this was being done as a remedy for those who were burning, she called her daughter, whom she had at home, and a certain household servant, and asked to be supported with a staff and led by them to the oratory.

For she confessed that she faithfully believed that Saint Amandus could also obtain for her from God, through his merits, the benefit of healing. And so it happened. Reaching the church with such supports, after great labor and pain, she prostrated herself and implored the assistance of so great a Father.

Not long afterward, gradually raising herself and somewhat improved, and now confident that her healing would increase, she reached the altar, giving one hand to her daughter and holding the staff with the other. There, praying in faith, she was restored completely to her former health.

When she realized this, she rose and began to return joyfully. As her daughter offered her right hand and urged her to take up the staff to guide her on the way, the woman sprang up, ran around the altar, and proclaimed that she no longer needed the staff for support or anyone’s assistance, since divine mercy had granted her the benefit of the healing she had desired through the gifts of Saint Amand.

The rejoicing that then took place among the monks and clerics praising God, and among laypeople of both sexes who flocked there, is revealed by the excellence of so great an event.

At that time the metropolitan bishop of the church of Reims, who was attending a council [Note: [Col. 1447C] Rainoldus or Rainaldus, “the Contracted,” in French Retiré. By order of Pope Urban II he divided the bishopric of Arras from that of Cambrai; he died at Arras in 1095, on January 21, the day on which the church of Arras still celebrates his anniversary], and who heard that people were being consumed by such a grievous disease, established that a three-day fast should be observed in the manner of the Ninevites, so that the humility of the penitent might appease the judgment of God, which the obstinacy of the disobedient had offended.

The author of all things therefore bestowed so great a grace upon his people that even little children devoted themselves to this appointed observance with both faith and devotion. When he saw iniquity turned into righteousness, he mercifully removed the punishment that he had justly inflicted upon humankind: the God who lives and reigns in perfect Trinity forever and ever. Amen.

## In the Year of the Lord 1090. William, monk of the monastery of Cluse

[Col. 1447]

## HISTORICAL NOTICE

(*Literary History of France*, VIII, 452)

William, a monk of Cluse, was formed in the monastic life there under the venerable Abbot Benedict II, who began to govern that monastery in 1066. The writings he left to posterity are evidence of the progress he made in literature. His inclination led him to associate chiefly with those who cultivated it. Gerauld, the librarian of the house, who had an incomparable zeal for collecting books, became one of his closest friends.

The other events of William’s life are unknown. We can only judge from the *Life of Abbot Benedict*, his teacher, which he wrote shortly after Benedict’s death in 1091, that William was already flourishing at that time and that he undertook the work around 1097.

[Col. 1449] We know only two works by our author; moreover, the editor has published only one of them in full and the other only in part.

1. William composed the history of his monastery, from the time of its foundation, inserting certain earlier miracles, through the death of Abbot Benedict I, who governed that monastery for forty-four years and was still alive in 1031, when he attended the great Council of Limoges.

He begins it with a description of the place where the monastery was built, which he takes up again below, and ends it with an abridged life of the same abbot. He says that what he wrote was based on the report of the brothers with whom the author lived and who had learned it from the venerable Aicius, prior of the house under Benedict.

The *History* is well written for its period; but besides the fact that we do not possess it as it came from William’s pen, it is too concise. Moreover, its author fell into considerable errors. At one point he names Nicholas, and at another Sylvester, as the pope governing the Church of Rome at the time of the foundation of the abbey of Cluse in 966. It is certain that there was no pope named Nicholas in the tenth century and that Sylvester II did not become pope until February 999.

Dom Mabillon published of this history what was supplied to him on loose sheets obtained from M. Baluze. It consists of two fragments. The first, fairly short, contains the beginning of the history together with part of its continuation, which is found more fully in the following fragment. The other fragment, much more substantial, has no beginning; and the fragment preceding it does not appear, in its present form, sufficient to supply the deficiency. Perhaps what is missing could be recovered from the copy preserved among the Vatican manuscripts (MONTF., *Bib. bib.*, p. 41). There it is entitled *History of the Monastery of Cluse, by the Monk William*, although the editor gave the printed work the title *Life of Benedict I, Abbot of the Same Monastery*. The reason is that, at the end of the writing, this abbot is indeed discussed specifically.

2. Our author also composed the *Life of the Venerable Benedict*, another abbot of Cluse, whom he surnames the Younger in order to distinguish him from the preceding one, and who has been omitted from the best catalogues of the abbots of that house.

This Life is written with great order, method, and piety, and in a style much better in every respect than was then commonly found. One readily sees that its author was a man of intelligence, judgment, and learning. He has scattered through it various indications of his modesty, humility, and religion, which testify in favor of his eminent virtue. Although his writing promises only the life of an abbot of merit and piety, it nevertheless contains several matters concerning the history of Italy in general, and especially the Church of Turin. The author even makes known a cardinal of the Roman Church who escaped the investigations of Onuphrius.

At the end of the writing are found two kinds of epitaphs for the venerable Abbot Benedict, in rhymed elegiac verse, which are far inferior to those immediately following the preface. For this reason we do not believe them to be by our author. We make the same judgment, and for the same reason, concerning other long rhymed verses that come after the two epitaphs, as well as three hymns in honor of the same abbot, of which only one has been printed.

The edition of this Life is owed to Dom Mabillon, who took it from an ancient manuscript and supplied it with brief preliminary observations.

[Col. 1449]

## HISTORY OF THE MONASTERY OF CLUSE (FRAGMENTS), BY WILLIAM THE MONK

[MABILLON, *Annales Benedictini* III, 712.]

### I

[Col. 1449A] At the borders of Italy there rises a remarkable mountain, twelve thousand paces distant from the Alps, which the inhabitants call by the common name—though not through an ordinary error or accident—Pyrchiriana, that is, “the fire of the Lord,” or “the fiery city,” on account, as I think, of the angels’ future presence there. On its highest summit stands a church of the blessed archangel Michael. There was a certain Ravennese named John, surnamed Vincentius, a man adorned above all with extraordinary simplicity and spiritual understanding. In his native land he is said to have held episcopal office; but, inflamed by a passion for the solitary life, after traveling through many provinces he had withdrawn to the mountain called Caprasius, which lies opposite the aforementioned mountain on its northern side.

[Col. 1450A] From that time, therefore, the holy hermit John, using a nearby cell, began to inhabit the mountain alone. At that time Amizo was bishop of Turin. During the reign of the younger Otto Augustus, a certain nobleman named Hugh, from the county of Auvergne, with his own wife . . . .

After completing the stretches of a long journey, when he had arrived at Susa, full of good intention, together with his wife and his household, he then vowed to build a monastery to the holy archangel Michael, if he should deserve to be cured.

Therefore, rising early and mounting their vehicles, they quickly went to the estate of Margrave Ardoinus, which at that time was only thirteen thousand paces away, at the castle of Avigliana. There, by divine providence, so that they might not be wearied any longer, they found him likewise with his wife. [Col. 1451A] They explained the reasons for their arrival and repeatedly requested permission to build a monastery in the place mentioned, on the understanding that the glorious margrave would kindly accept as much gold or silver as he wished, together with the largest possible quantity of the mules and other vehicles they had brought, and would release the place from all secular authority belonging to himself and his heirs by a written legal act, so that those who would thereafter serve God there might enjoy freedom from everything imposed by the powers of the world, whether as a matter of obligation or through fear. The most generous prince readily consented.

There was present there, by the will of God, a religious man of the monastic order named Atvertus, who had previously held the office of abbot in the monastery of Lizathium, but had been expelled from it by opponents of holy religion. He had then returned from the threshold of the Apostles and had remained for several days as a guest in the same lodging. Hugh overcame this religious man Atvertus with many entreaties; leaving him, for the present, what necessities he could have as a pilgrim, he entrusted the place to him and returned joyfully to his own home, intending to come back soon.

From then on Atvertus, a man filled with God, laboring with complete devotion, began to build suitable little structures for the monks according to the character of the place, which was extremely rugged with rocks. When the appointed time came, Hugh returned as he had promised, and, providing all the necessary expenses for completing the construction of the church, went once more to the aforementioned margrave. From him, as before, after paying the price, he acquired a neighboring village called Cluse, together with adjoining lands suitable for building smaller villages. But, so that not the slightest doubt might remain concerning the freedom of the place for which he was striving, he approached the bishop of Turin, whose name was Amizo. Having offered gifts befitting so great a man, he favorably obtained from him, again, the release of the place from every obligation, with an anathema also imposed upon violators. From there he went to Rome and reported to Pope Sylvester* the terms of all the promises made both by the bishop and by the margrave, as well as the entire beginning of his undertaking. He caused the place to be confirmed in writing and by name, for the present by the authority of the prince of the Apostles, and later by the imperial majesty. But lest any doubt concerning what has been related arise in the hearts of the faithful, the son of the aforementioned Hugh, Maurice, is a witness, and the household itself is also a witness.

Accordingly, the venerable Pope Nicholas—for that name plainly signifies the victory of the Catholic people—became the approver and commander that this account be begun, so that all readers might know that the care of the aforesaid place belonged in a special way to the Apostolic See.

In the year 966 of the Lord’s Incarnation, when, as is said, the monastic buildings had happily been constructed at the same place as far as possible, and when that illustrious man Hugh, valiant in arms but toward the end more devoted in matters concerning God, had handed over to the abbot and monks alone for their possession the place which, as we related above, he had claimed as his own by purchase and fortified by apostolic authority or royal decrees, and after Saint John the hermit and Atvertus, of blessed memory, the abbot, had departed to the Lord, a man named Benedict succeeded him in the government, by the consent and election of the brothers, worthy for his simplicity and prudence.

### II

[Col. 1451]

[Col. 1451C] . . . . You are not unaware; climb without fear. And when you have found there collected everything that you feared had been stolen from you, do not hesitate to complete in that same place the work I had commanded . . . . . he remained . . . . Through an angelic revelation the very region, previously regarded as uncultivated and worthless, began to be held in honor and affection. The venerable bishop Amizo, too, as he approached the place, lodged in the castle of Avigliana. But behold, around midnight—marvelous to say!—an immense fire, like a great column, descended from heaven upon the mountain and, with its flashing flames, licked it all around in the clear air. The people, awakened from their beds by the novelty of the miracle, stretched their hands imploringly toward heaven and beat their breasts with their fists. Everyone cried out that Pyrchiriana was being utterly consumed. The shouting rose to the stars. The bishop himself, stunned by so great a disturbance, arose and, gazing at a portion of the radiant light already withdrawing, said to his companions: “How greatly this place is to be feared! This has truly been done by the Lord, and it is marvelous in our eyes. Here is the burning bush in which the Lord once appeared to Moses. Here is another Mount Sinai, about to receive the fiery law through the disposition of the angels.”

The next day, when they had arrived at the place and the venerable bishop, with his revered company, had stood humbly at the doors of the little basilica, he saw what seemed to be a stream of oil flowing down from above, and the figure of a cross appearing in thick liquid upon certain rocks projecting from the little church. Amazed at this, and struck with terror together with all the people, he entered humbly, prostrated himself on the ground, and through the mediation of the archangel earnestly begged from the Ruler of heaven and earth a perfect conclusion to so great a manifestation of power. When his prayer was finished, and he had lifted his eyes filled with tears, he saw a title of extraordinary beauty standing upright, undoubtedly fitted together by angelic hands, and sweating balsam and oil abundantly all around and above, so much so that it seemed to flow down to the ground. Seeing this, he quickly took a linen cloth and reverently wiped away the oil; then, with the title covered, he most devoutly celebrated the solemnities of Mass there. What power proceeded from the linen cloth with which the sacred altar had been wiped, it is beyond our ability to recount: for no weak person, no one possessed by a demon, no one afflicted by any illness was touched by it without being permitted by the power of the archangel, through the immediate reception of health, not to remain inexperienced in divine mercy.

Moved by so many miracles, and entreated by the hermit’s prayers and by honorable noble persons who were present, the pious bishop established, under threat of perpetual anathema, that the place should be free forever from the secular dominion or interference of himself and his successors, on the condition that anyone who in the future became a despiser of this decree should be liable to the judgment of the Apostolic See.

From that time, therefore, the holy hermit John, using the nearby cell, began to inhabit the mountain alone; and the holy archangel of the Lord did not delay in making it perfectly clear that he was the lover and protector of his place. For not much time had passed when, behold, men hastening to visit the thresholds of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, and also the shrine of that same holy archangel on Mount Garganus, saw, while they were in the valley of Susa, the church described above, situated like a watchtower on the summit of the mountain. Unaware of its history, they carefully asked who had built it and to whose name it had been dedicated.

When the old man had told them what had recently happened, one of them, who was severely afflicted with gout, became very joyful and addressed his companions as follows: “You know, comrades, how great is the pain with which my feet torment me, and how often I have offended you on this journey by my slowness. Since, therefore, I cannot reach that holy mountain of Garganus as I had intended, I beseech you by him whom we especially believe, after death, to be the guide of faithful souls: let me at least visit this holy oratory dedicated to him, and pray to him to be merciful to my soul at the hour of my departure. Either climb up with me for your reward, or wait at the foot of the mountain for my speedy return.”

But they angrily railed against him, saying: “What are you talking about, wretched man? By what effort can you climb steep and rugged places when even the level surface of the road injures you? Go wherever you wish, madman; perish whoever waits for you.”

Then, abandoning the company of his companions and taking confidence from his love of the archangel, he undertook what they thought impossible. Crawling mainly on his knees and hands, he at last, scarcely but victoriously, attained his desired goal. Entering the church, he moistened its floor with abundant tears, and amid the vows and prayers that he poured forth from the depths of his heart, he complained to the Lord and to his archangel that he had been abandoned by his companions, and made mention of his illness.

Meanwhile, as commonly happens, sleep overcame the man through weariness and sorrow. After several hours, when he awoke from his slumber, he found himself safe and sound before the altar of Saint Michael—on Mount Garganus, unmistakably. How much he then gave there while weeping, and what rivers of tears he shed from joy, if he wished to describe it in Ciceronian terms, eloquence itself, unless I am mistaken, would fail. Perhaps what we are saying may seem incredible to anyone because of its novelty and the magnitude of the miracle. But you who doubt it need only be willing to reread the ancient history of Daniel and consider how the angel of the Lord carried Habakkuk by the hair over so many stretches of land to Daniel, who was sitting hungry in the Babylonian pit. If you can understand that, believe without hesitation that this too happened. Or will you deny, unbeliever, that what was then done through an angel could now be done through the archangel himself?

After that man had offered as many thanks as he could to the author of his recovery, he returned from there joyful and exultant. He had already passed through Rome, while his faithless companions had not yet reached the City. When they saw him from a distance, returning to meet them, they wondered, and one said to the other: “O God, whom do I see? Is this our companion, whom we left behind at Cluse?” The other replied: “It is not he, but someone like him. That man was gout-ridden; this one walks firmly and in good health. But what? It certainly is he. Hail, good man.”

He answered: “Hail to you, good companions.”

“What is this?” they asked. “Who brought you here, and how did you become well?”

When he had recounted to them the sequence of the miracle described above, they were stunned by the novelty of so great an event and said to him: “Did you not report all this in due order to the holy Apostolic man? Return with us, ungrateful one, return, and tell him how much God has done for you.”

He replied: “I shall do so, although you have not deserved it.”

He returned, told the story, and kindled Rome, the mother of cities, to love this venerable place; and throughout all Italy, wherever they went, the fame of the miracle resounded.

During the same period, while the younger Otto Augustus was reigning, a certain nobleman named Hugh, from the county of Auvergne, with his own wife . . . . . was troubled by anxiety. He strove to bend Peter . . . . through tearful sighs, without openly revealing himself, to have pity on the hope of the wretched, because his tongue trembled with an evil confusion, which customarily increases sin by concealing it; and he was ashamed to confess what he had not been ashamed to commit. At last, compelled, he revealed to his wife and those standing around him by what fire he was tormented . . . . . . and, after baptism . . . . . indeed the first proves me an apostate with respect to the renunciation of the Enemy. I assent, confess, and renounce, and from the fountain of David, which lies open for the cleansing of the menstruating woman, I seek counsel through the ministry of my lord Peter.”

This complaint moved the sweet heart of Roman mercy, and the man guilty of so many crimes made a promise—at the urging both of the aforesaid pope and of the apostolic ministers—to build a monastery in which God would perpetually be served by monks. Cleansed, therefore, by such penance and confession, he was at last promised that he might enter the holy thresholds and kiss the place of the Lord’s footprints. Eager to carry out what he had promised, he began joyfully to return to his own country.

After completing the stretches of the long journey, when he had arrived at Susa, full of good intention, together with his wife and household, and had lodged in the home of an old friend familiar to him, his host, out of friendship, carefully began to ask how he had completed his journey. Hugh related everything in order and gave him the marvelous account of the whole affair that we have mentioned. The host, stunned by the wonder of so great a miracle, and lingering at length over praises of the Lord’s almighty mercy, said to him:

“O lord Hugh, if you desire to become a good man, after the grace of the prince of the Apostles it is fitting that you build a monastery for no one more than for the prince of the heavenly army, the archangel Michael. Thus, after all your sins have been forgiven, he may be the deliverer of your soul at its departure from this exile, and Peter its receiver.”

At the same time, by pointing out how near the aforementioned place was—only twelve thousand paces away—and by continuing his noble account of the miracles already mentioned, he kindled the man’s mind, long inclined toward this undertaking, with sparks of good exhortation.
