Thus at last both the words of salvation and the day on which they had arrived exhausted were brought to an end by the following night.

The archangel appeared in a vision to both sleeping spouses, and was seen and heard by them in the same form and with the same words. He urged and commanded them to fix all their resolve upon the place indicated by their host, and, without hesitation, to build a monastery there, confident that they were constructing a heavenly palace for their souls.

After the revelation, the man awoke first and then related the whole content of the vision to his wife, whose name was Insengard. When she too had reported the agreement of her own vision, she sprang more quickly than he from her bed and, asking their hosts how the matter could best be brought to completion, shrewdly sought their advice. Then the host’s wife, Eve—an Eve superior in counsel to the first Eve, with whom they had spoken late, for she herself had strongly urged these things—rejoiced that the archangel’s account of the mountain had been confirmed. Together with her husband, she began, with all the ingenuity at her disposal, to investigate every direct approach to beginning and carrying out the undertaking.

At last, while they were consulting together, sound counsel flowed from the fountain of the Father’s Wisdom, who promises his faithful in the Gospel, saying: “Where two or three are gathered in my name, there I am in the midst of them.”

Therefore Hugh and his wife, who were about to raise the burden of so great a palace, prudently examined every obstacle that might harm the undertaking and prepared with fortunate effort to block it, so that they might lay a secure foundation upon solid rock, one that would never fall.

Rising early and mounting their vehicles, they quickly went to the estate of Margrave Ardoinus, which at that time was only thirteen thousand paces away, at the castle of Avigliana. [Col. 1455D] There, by divine providence, so that they might not be wearied any longer, they found him likewise with his wife. It was announced to the prince that nobles and elegantly formed pilgrims had arrived from the regions on this side of the Alps, and he immediately went out to meet them. It is in some sense natural for nobles, when they are good, to be received honorably.

They explained the reasons for their arrival and repeatedly requested permission to build a monastery in the place mentioned, on the understanding that the glorious margrave would kindly accept as much gold or silver as he wished, together with the finest supply of mules and other vehicles they had brought, and would release the place from all secular authority belonging to himself and his heirs by a written legal act, so that those who would thereafter serve God there might enjoy freedom from everything imposed by the powers of the world, whether as a matter of obligation or through fear.

The most generous prince readily consented. At first wishing to carry out freely what was requested, he later, on more prudent consideration, graciously accepted a fair price, so that, following the Gospel example in which the field purchased with the Lord’s price was used for the burial of pilgrims, a living burial-place might be provided in the same place for monks who were to die to the world, and so that no occasion might arise in future for opposing the freedom of the monastery.

After this Hugh returned joyfully to his lodging, intending, also on the advice of his host, to seek a man to whom he could entrust the guardianship of the place. Meanwhile, since an opportunity for the journey presented itself, he was drawn with a few companions to the summit of the mountain to see the character of the place, more by the strength of his spirit than by that of his body, for the route was extremely difficult. Exhausted by heat and labor, or rather fainting from thirst by the will of God, he fell at the feet of the hermit, whose tiny cell stood beside the church, and begged him to find as quickly as possible, if not by human counsel, then through the archangel, a remedy for so great a danger.

He learned from him that there was no water nearby; but there was wine in a small flask, scarcely sufficient for the celebration of a single Mass. He himself had no remedy at all. For the archangel’s power could undoubtedly do everything.

As the danger of thirst and heat pressed upon him, the hermit was at last moved by compassion and begged the archangel, if the condition of the place pleased him, to remedy the devout man’s peril. At once—what I am about to say is marvelous—he saw the aforementioned little flask overflowing as though a spring were welling up from its depths, and the supreme archangel displaying his power visibly.

Those who had come drank as much as was necessary. After receiving the blessing, they returned, and, as we said, hurried to their lodging, wishing to find a man suitable for the guardianship of the place, since the hermit now had no concern except for heavenly matters.

The devoted man of God reported to his host what had happened, and, amid his conversation, burning with the heat of good desire no less than previously with bodily thirst, he repeatedly returned to the question of whose care the place should suitably be entrusted.

There was present there, by the will of God, a religious man of the monastic order named Atvertus, who had previously held the office of abbot in the monastery of Lisathium, but had been expelled from it by opponents of holy religion. He had then returned from the threshold of the Apostles and had remained for several days as a guest in the same lodging.

“This man,” said the host, “was, I think, provided by divine grace. He will love the little, as yet disordered place, not as a beginner but as one experienced in monastic office, with small expenses and in poverty of spirit. Through the service of his humble poverty he will gather sufficient riches for those who will thereafter serve Christ.”

On hearing this, the venerable sinner Hugh was lifted up in praise of the Redeemer. He overcame the aforementioned religious man Atvertus with many entreaties; leaving him what necessities he could have as a pilgrim for the present, he entrusted the place to him and returned joyfully to his own home, intending to come back soon.

From then on Atvertus, a man filled with God, laboring with complete devotion, began to build suitable little structures for the monks according to the character of the place, which was extremely rugged with rocks. Whatever he could gather anywhere, he spent on this alone, content with modest nourishment.

At the appointed time Hugh returned as he had promised, and, supplying all necessary expenses for completing the construction of the church, went once more to the aforementioned margrave. From him, as before, after paying the price, he acquired a village adjoining the mountain, called Cluse, together with adjoining lands suitable for building smaller villages.

But, so that not the slightest doubt might remain concerning the freedom of the place, for which he was chiefly striving, he approached the bishop of Turin, whose name was Amizo. Having offered gifts befitting so great a man, he favorably obtained from him the release of the place from every obligation, with an anathema also imposed upon violators. From there he went to Rome and reported to Pope Sylvester the terms of all the promises made both by the bishop and by the margrave, as well as the entire beginning of his undertaking. He caused the place to be confirmed in writing and by name, for the present by the authority of the prince of the Apostles, and later also by the imperial majesty.

After this, for as long as he lived, he either brought or sent to the monastery everything necessary as far as he was able. From then on, with God’s favor, the monastery grew in due course through appropriate increases, by the merits of the archangel, and, shining with various miracles, became pleasing and venerable to many peoples.

But lest any doubt concerning what has been related arise in the hearts of the faithful, the son of the aforementioned Hugh, Maurice, is a witness, and the household itself is a witness; through events involving themselves or their close relatives in recent days, the angelic power graciously made itself known by such great signs.

Accordingly, the venerable Pope Nicholas*, whose name plainly signifies the victory of the Catholic people, became the approver and commander that this account be begun, so that all readers might know that the care of the aforesaid place belonged in a special way to the Apostolic See; and whoever among the faithful desires, at the end of this fleeting and transitory life, to be carried to heaven on angelic wings should fear to undertake anything unjust against the place that Michael, prince of the angels, loved and chose. Thus, in his house, without divisions of heart, with the peace that belongs to men of good will, may the name of the Lord always be blessed—he who freely sends all his ministering spirits into the service of his Church for the sake of those who are to inherit salvation.

In the year 966 of the Lord’s Incarnation, when, as is said, the monastic buildings had happily been constructed at the same place as far as possible, and when that illustrious man Hugh, valiant in arms but toward the end more devoted in matters concerning God, had handed over to the abbot and monks alone for their possession the place which, as we related above, he had claimed as his own by purchase and fortified by apostolic authority or royal decrees, and after Saint John the hermit and Atvertus, abbot of good memory, had departed to the Lord, a man named Benedict succeeded him in the government, by the consent and election of the brothers, worthy for his simplicity and prudence, and Benedict by name.

Since he flourished with very many virtues, he is said to have been filled with such an abundance of charity and to have been so generous in hospitality that he most willingly welcomed all who came to him seeking the steep mountain and the archangel’s protection, especially peoples from Gaul, Aquitaine, and Spain traveling to Rome; and he kindly bestowed upon them whatever could properly be allotted from the resources of the brothers.

Many, admiring his grace—for he was adorned with angelic character and manners—said: “Behold the prudent man who built his house upon a rock, in whose mouth no deceit is found. Through this faithful steward the Lord’s archangel rejoices, and he extends everywhere the distinction of the fame of this place.”

Some began, especially from beyond the mountains, to gather at this place out of religious devotion and, renouncing the world, to submit themselves under that glorious old man to the discipline of the rule. For many Lombards, supported by a cunning hostile to the faith, were not easily willing to assume the monastic habit.

Many nobles and rich men, desiring to show their gratitude for his blessings and thereby to win the prince of the angels as their ally on the day of their departure, enriched the place with their possessions; others entrusted their children to the Lord to be raised there while still tender in their early years.

The place is removed from every disturbance and worldly tumult. No human being or animal makes a din there; shouting and roaring lie silent. The extended plain of Italy, cheerful with its lakes and rivers, sometimes offers sights capable of refreshing human vision. The winters are mild; summer resembles spring. The mind of those serving God, enjoying such complete quiet and admonished by the advantageous beauty of all things, cries out, often jubilating with exultation: “Great is the Lord and greatly to be praised in the city of our God, on his holy mountain.”

That venerable old man Benedict, therefore, beloved by God and men, excellently carrying out the guardianship of the flock entrusted to him, shone in his time through the grace of holiness as an outstanding shepherd. With the archangel’s favor he enlarged the monastery in its possessions, persons, and honors.

Although many guests and monks repeatedly urged him, as though offering advice, to entrust his place to the protection and governance of great monasteries and to adopt their customs, he would not agree. He said:

“Allow it, brothers, allow the Rule of our Father Benedict to suffice for our small community. If something seems to need adding, it permits the abbot to supply it according to judgment and circumstance. It is not as you say: you see that the place is difficult and steep to reach and must be regulated by another custom. For he who often enjoys the angels’ consolation, rejoices in the protection of so great a guardian, and sometimes receives a ministry that is sufficiently fearsome, has no need of any human instruction.

“In this mountain there is no place for crime, nor is it lawful, before his gaze, for criminal hiding-places to remain concealed by wickedness. Even if a crime is committed anywhere on the mountain, he hurls fire at the sacred heights, so that it terrifies many innocents. Nor does he know how to kindle a fiery tumult until what was hidden from human eyes and remained unpunished has perhaps obtained pardon through satisfaction and confession.”

Thus the illustrious Father spoke; thus, eloquent in apostolic simplicity, he understood. He urged that only the Rule of the blessed Father and outstanding leader of monks, Benedict, should be examined and observed, and that people should cry out over it. For the rest, he held that the ordering of each monastery depended upon the judgment of its abbot. This has remained a celebrated practice of the community of that place down to the present day.

I do not think I should pass over in silence a certain miracle that Aicius, the prior of holy memory, himself also venerable in his conduct, used to relate concerning the abbot just mentioned. His testimony is believed to be supported by truth because, as they say, he was a man made perfect in every detail, wholly polished and rounded in religious conduct.

Among the other virtues of the soul in which he was very strong, he possessed discretion—the mother, guardian, and regulator of all virtues, as the Fathers teach—to such a degree that, whether on a feast day or an ordinary day, no one could induce him either to add to or subtract from the customary strictness or quantity of food.

Always constant in his holy purpose, and frequently devoted to vigils, he restrained his own little body with scourges; he diligently applied himself to manual labor and reading. Chaste in mind and body, he finally, having grown old and bearing abundant fruit, yielded to nature.

When some of his disciples among the brothers opened his tomb, moved by a certain curiosity, they were filled with an extraordinary fragrance.

This prior, I say, asserted concerning that venerable Benedict that it had been his custom, night and day, to perform devoutly and solemnly before the venerable altar of the blessed Mary, Mother of our Lord and Savior—the altar distinguished by the presence of the image of that glorious and incomparable woman—the offices of praise.

Since he never interrupted this practice, one night, while he was about to read there according to custom, he himself held a lamp, which was extinguished by a gust of wind, as commonly happens. When this accident made him all the more anxious because of the delay in reading, a flame suddenly sprang from the candle burning perpetually before the altar of Saint Michael and, to the astonishment of the brothers, lit the lamp in his hand.

When the servant of God saw this, he was greatly amazed, prostrated himself on the ground, and worshiped for a long time. He forbade the brothers, for as long as he lived, to disclose the miracle to anyone.

What more? He ruled the monastery manfully for eleven years and four months, and at last, like a fruitful olive tree in the house of the Lord, rested in peace.

Such was the beginning and growth of that holy place; such were its founders; and so glorious and venerable has it been from then until now among all peoples, except the people of Turin, who, like Scyllan dogs, have always barked against it and, with envious eyes, have never ceased to look askance at the monastery’s prosperity.

Nevertheless, the archangel so powerfully crushed their teeth, and the “vines” (*vites*, an apparently corrupt or uncertain reading) of all who wickedly lay in wait against the place, that, if not in words, at least by his deeds, he seemed to cry out: “Whoever touches these touches the apple of my eye.”

No one has ever attacked the place or anything belonging to its jurisdiction and gone away unharmed. Whether called or uncalled, he is present; he graciously attends to the prayers of those who worthily serve him in his court and humbly beseech him, and he continually protects them from the mouth of the most savage dragon.

Therefore, O flock of Cluse, rely upon the protection of him whom you have specially chosen for yourself as the prince of the heavenly court. It is fitting that you venerate and glorify him above all through perpetual worship. May he, cherishing you piously beneath the shadow of his wings, defend you in battle, so that you may not be condemned without me at the dreadful judgment.

Explicit.

[Col. 1459]

## LIFE OF THE VENERABLE BENEDICT, ABBOT OF CLUSE, BY WILLIAM THE MONK, HIS DISCIPLE

(MABILLON, *Acts of the Order of Saint Benedict*, vol. IX, p. 697.)

### PRELIMINARY OBSERVATIONS

[The supplied source ends here.]

1. The monastery of Saint Michael at Clusa, formerly renowned, is situated in the diocese of Turin at the foot of Mount Pirchiriano, namely at the Clusae, or passes and narrow defiles of the Alps, which Desiderius, king of the Lombards, unsuccessfully attempted to block against Charlemagne as he advanced into Italy. In the eleventh century this place had two abbots of the same name: Benedict the elder and Benedict the younger. William, a monk of that place and the disciple and familiar associate of Benedict the younger, set down the deeds of both in writing; William himself bears witness to this in the prologue that follows. We suspect, however, that the deeds of the earlier Benedict have been lost. We infer the period in which he lived from the Council of Limoges of 1031, in whose acts “Benedict, rector of the monastery of Saint Michael at Clusa” is praised as still living. This commendation cannot apply to Benedict the younger, who died in 1091, “in the twenty-fifth year of his pastoral care”; consequently, he did not assume that dignity before 1066. The day of Benedict the younger’s death is given as “the last day of May” in the verses prefixed to his life, and as “the following day” in the same sense in his epitaph. Thus the following entry in the necrology of the abbey of Saint-Gilles at Nîmes must be understood as referring to him: “On the day before the Kalends of June, Benedict, abbot of Clusa, died.” The necrology of Saint-Bénigne at Dijon agrees. Francis Augustus omitted both Benedicts from his *Chronologia Pedemontana*.

[Col. 1461]

2. There is no single, universally accepted opinion concerning the origin and founder of the abbey of Clusa. The chronicler of Maillezais is inconsistent with himself: at one point he says that “the monastery of Saint Michael at Clusa was begun” in the year 872; at another he places the event a hundred years later, that is, at the same time when the monastery of Saint Michael on the Mount was founded. The chronicler’s words are these: “At that time another monastery of Saint Michael at Clusa was begun by Saint John, bishop and hermit; its first abbot was Arveus.” They say that this John was bishop of Ravenna.

Francis Augustus, however, holds a different opinion. He says that the founder of the monastery of Clusa was not Bishop John but Hugo Marinus, a most powerful, as he himself calls him, “Auvergnat,” and lord of Mont-Bucer, who, while returning from Rome to his ancestral home, arranged for this monastery to be built and for its church to be dedicated by Anucco, bishop of Turin, in the year 966. From chapter 3 of the following Life it is certain that this was Hugo, who entrusted the same place to the Apostolic See and endowed it with privileges; but who and what sort of man that Hugo was, William does not explain.

It is certain, however, that this was an ancient conviction of the monks of Clusa: that their founder Hugo was an Auvergnat and belonged to the family of the lords of Mont-Bucer. This is attested by a letter of the abbot of Saint Michael at Clusa, issued in the year 914 to Louis of Mont-Bucer. “Following,” says the abbot, “the footsteps of your ancestors, and especially of the lord Hugo of glorious memory, formerly lord of Mont-Bucer and our founder, from whose illustrious lineage he is known to have descended in a direct line, he donated to us eight hundred gold pieces.” Our Claude Estiennot extracted this letter from the archive of the marquis of Dienne. For the rest, see Francis Augustus.

Pontius, abbot of Vézelay and brother of Peter, abbot of Cluny, “was taken from the monastery of Clusa,” as is read in the brief Chronicle of Vézelay preserved by Labbe in volume II of the *Bibliotheca nova*. At present the abbey of Clusa is a community of very few secular canons.

## PROLOGUE

[Col. 1461A] 1. WILLIAM, least of the servants of Christ, to GERARD, the armarius.

Your brotherhood remembers well, dearest Gerard, how often very many of my brothers have invited my insignificance, through their repeated exhortations, to let my pen run at least somewhat over the life and deeds of Benedict the younger, formerly our abbot.

“Why,” they say, “do you snore night and day, while the money entrusted to you lies tied up in a handkerchief, if you waste away in idleness? Why do you allow the outstanding deeds of our Father, performed even before your own eyes, to be forgotten through the long passage of time—deeds which, if written down, would benefit many?”

To them I reply: “Do not, my brothers and lords, do not mock me in this way. I alone know what my shoulders are worth and what burdens they refuse to bear. I certainly know the powers of my little intellect, sufficiently feeble [Col. 1461B] and sluggish, which possesses little eloquence and even less wisdom. There are many of its pupils in the monastery of Clusa who surpass me in knowledge or in merit of life; I do not doubt that this work might be entrusted to their vigilant diligence.”

“And you,” they answer, “who from almost the time of childhood were nourished by the milk of his teaching and the solid food of his vigorous deeds, and have now grown into manly strength; who, thirsting like all of us, drank in his rules of discipline—you will not permit yourself to remain entirely silent about this great leader of ours, who gathered us all together, fed us like a loving mother, and cherished us in the lap of mercy. You who once took pains to commit certain deeds of the earlier Benedict, also abbot of this place, to writing—come, then, come; begin, setting every excuse aside. [Col. 1461C] For although you are unskilled in speech, you are not unskilled in knowledge.”

2. Stirred by these and similar blasts of argument, while I sail safely in the harbor of silence and quiet, [Col. 1462A] I submit my shoulder to the burden which charity commands me to undertake from the hearts of my brothers, and which it is not lawful to resist. I hope that, with obedience as its oar, the boat of our work may be steered so that it passes safely and unharmed between Scylla and Charybdis, avoiding the savage dangers of the sea and the beguiling songs of Circe and the Sirens with ears made utterly deaf.

Your diligence also, Gerard, has brought my mind to writing. For many years, like a most prudent bee, you have flown around various places and monasteries, never ceasing to gather the honeyed sayings and books of the Fathers, with which you fill our bookcases—treasures more valuable than the wealth of Croesus or the rich hoards of the Arabs. You devote yourself to increasing them and carefully guard them as though they were chambers of spices.

Among these things, at the command of Lord Ermengaud, [Col. 1462B] the abbot, may it please you to accept this little gift of our booklet, poor though it is. I have tried to offer it in the tabernacle of the Lord, who does not despise the hairs of a humble confession, like those of a goat, after my head has already been covered with flowering and gentle gray hair. But lest I now seem to be “painting a dolphin in the woods” or “a boar amid the waves,” let us gird ourselves for what we have proposed concerning this man. Although it may appear insignificant because of the unpolished nature of the language, it will nevertheless, if I am not mistaken, be welcome and dear to his disciples, in view of the well-known excellence of his deeds and their subject matter.

You were rightly given the name Benedict,

And by your character fulfilled the office of your name.

[Col. 1462C] You were a good teacher and governor

Of your flock and people;

You were the boundary of justice and piety.

The flock entrusted to you celebrated your Father’s funeral

As the final day of May passed away.

## TEXT OF HIS LIFE

[Col. 1463]

[Col. 1463A] 3. Benedict of Toulouse. He becomes a monk, comes to Clusa, and is received there.

Benedict, servant of God, was by birth a native of Toulouse, born to parents who were not undistinguished in the nobility of their rank. Yet he himself made them more illustrious by the praises of a holy way of life, just as the morning light-bearer and golden star, dispersing the shadows of night, surpasses all the stars with its radiant beams.

When he was still a little child of good character, his father, named Bernard [Note: [Col. 1463D] He died in the monastery of Clusa; see below, chapter 20.], a good and most Christian man, entrusted him to the monastery of Saint Hilary [Note: [Col. 1463D] This monastery of Saint Hilary was situated in the city of Carcassonne.] to be formed according to the rule. There he spent the years of childhood and adolescence in chastity and sobriety. Devoted to divine studies as well as to secular learning, and under his father’s supervision, he subdued and mastered the youthful desires of the body.

But when at last he observed that the same monastery [Col. 1463B] had strayed somewhat from the regular path, fearing that perhaps the dissolution of the order might gradually drag one who lingered there headlong into ruin, and at the same time inflamed by a desire for spiritual progress, he came to Italy. There he was kindly received by the abbot of the monastery of Saint Michael, which, at the very gateways of Italy, the summit of Mount Pirchiriano displays to all peoples as venerable in appearance and religion.

4. He becomes a priest.

Thus, day by day, he began to advance more and more in God through the practice of the virtues. By the gentleness and friendliness of his character he wonderfully kindled everyone’s affection for him, and eagerly drank in the streams of divine philosophy. He competed with adolescents in submission, with young men—himself still young—in courage, and with old men—himself already mature—in [Col. 1463C] gravity. Although he surpassed all in every quality of honor and usefulness, he was equally dear to everyone and gave no one occasion for envy.

Accordingly, with all the brothers consenting and the abbot commanding it, he was promoted to the priesthood. He performed the duties of that office so humbly and reverently that, always proclaiming himself unworthy in the judgment of his mind, he would approach the altar even after several days in order to offer the sacrifice. Later we learned from his preaching that, whenever he had resolved to celebrate Mass on a given day, he sometimes waited to see whether the prior would order him to do so. He firmly believed that, through the power of obedience, his offering would be commended to God; by the testimony of Scripture, this is rightly preferred to holocausts and sacrifices.

[Col. 1463D] 5. He is elected abbot.

At length, when that abbot had died and still remained unburied—for fear that the wicked plague of the bishop of Turin might, as usual, thrust itself against the holy decrees of the canons and the Rule—the entire assembly of the brothers, piously and unanimously, [Col. 1464A] in the presence of Airald [Note: [Col. 1463D] You have a similar example in *Saeculum superius*, p. 781.], abbot of Bremet, at that time a man most renowned for religion and wisdom, was gathered together to conduct the election of the Father simply, under the gaze of their archangel, their pious protector.

Then the chapter of the Rule concerning the appointment of an abbot was read, and the aforesaid abbot explained it clearly and openly. As usual, some acclaimed one man and others another. Some strongly favored Bertrannus, a certain man of Cumiliac, who was humane and kind, possessed a great zeal for religion, and zeal according to knowledge. Most, however, favored Aicius, the prior, highly learned in the monastic order and distinguished for the strictness of his discipline.

Our Benedict stood there, troubled by the death of the deceased Father and seemingly concerned with his funeral. He had been related to him by blood [Col. 1464B] and humbly considered all the brothers senior to him, thinking nothing less than of his own promotion. Suddenly, however, the votes and judgments of everyone, drawn together from every side, converged upon this one man, so that not even a single supporter dissented from him. With one voice and one judgment, although he cried out and resisted vehemently, he was seized and led to the church with praises.

I have briefly completed this account of his election, showing how it was carried out through God’s will with pure intention and proper order, so that it may plainly appear to the reader that Benedict, God’s living stone and a pillar of truth, resting upon such a foundation and base at his entrance, could rightly not be shaken or disturbed by any future storms of tribulation. Before this, in Italy, the election of scarcely any prelate had been heard of for several years that was not carried off either by a royal hand or by some destructive secular ambition.

6. The bishop of Turin opposes his election.

Yet the ancient enemy’s customary spite and envy were not absent at that time. When not only the sons of the Church but also the marquises and dukes of all Italy, together with the entire people, applauded this most just election, the sole pontiff of Turin, Chunibertus [Note: [Col. 1463D] The author seems to speak rather harshly of Clunibertus, but Chunibertus’s own conduct in other matters deserves no small degree of censure, since he permitted the clerics of his Church, whatever their order, to enter into what was virtually a legal marriage with women. Peter Damian reproaches him for this in a letter written to him; and he was excommunicated by Pope Nicholas because, at the assembly of Milan, he granted the clergy, together with certain other bishops, permission to have wives. See below, chapters 8 and 11.], who had bad outcomes after good beginnings, swelled up with the pride of office.

When the brothers requested from him the consecration of their elected abbot, he burst out in bestial fury with words full of insult and blasphemy:

“Who,” he said, “is this Benedict, and from what ancestors was he born? With what audacity or authority, and by whom, in my absence, [Col. 1464D] was he elected?”

To this the brothers replied, invoking the authority of the canons and their Rule, that such an election was not subject to his approval unless perhaps the monks had by common consent preferred a vicious and depraved person to themselves; but that the consecration alone belonged to the good man who had been elected.

Then, inflamed beyond measure by his confused bile, he grew still more heated, and, swelling with anger, said:

“Far be it—far be that detestable right by which, through you or through your Rule, as you claim, this man, especially unknown to me, should enter! The election is mine; he will be my abbot, subject to my authority alone, my familiar, domestic, and subordinate. For just as a hawk, when it presses soft doves, seizes with its claws whichever one it wishes for itself, so I, suddenly arriving among you while you wait, shall take the man who alone has found a place in my mind and who is dear to me, and shall set him over all of you.”

Does he not seem, in these few and bombastic words, to have said to you: “The abbot will enter through me, not through Christ”? [Col. 1465B] He will climb up by another way, like a thief and robber, to slaughter and destroy, not through the door.

O clever comparison, worthy of a bishop! You were insane then, Bishop Chunibertus, beside yourself; in speaking such things, you were truly insane in such a theatrical buskin. These words revealed the power of your intellect—or rather, the manner in which you puffed yourself up with it—your gross and bloated understanding. For when you represented your greed under the appearance and name of a hawk, you depicted yourself in that form as the persecutor of the simple and the robber of the innocent.

It is therefore clearer than daylight that the doorkeeper, who is the Holy Spirit, did not open to you the door of truth; and thus the swollen arrogance of your wisdom subsided, crushed. The following speech will make this clear.

7. He appeals to Rome.

When the Lord’s servant Benedict had learned of the bishop’s madness and his unreasonable [Col. 1465C] and harsh exaction, he first decided, out of humility, to avoid giving such fury an opportunity by hiding himself and declining the honor. But again and again the brothers urged him to act firmly, to climb up in opposition and stand as a wall for the house of Israel, not to yield to the attacking wolf and devil, and to have pity on himself. At last, worn out by their long and repeated appeals, and encouraged by the strength of constancy and obedience, he stood manfully and sent a certain brother named Boso to Turin to appeal to the Apostolic See.

Boso carried out his orders and escaped alive only with difficulty, amid stones and the clubs of the raging crowd. Benedict then set out for Rome with a few brothers. The bishop followed him with a force of his own, intending to pursue him [Col. 1465D] with all his strength.

8. He is blessed by Alexander II.

What more need be said? An assembly of sacred pontiffs and cardinals was convened before Lord Alexander, at that time Roman pontiff, and Gregory the archdeacon, later an apostolic pontiff. The bishop repeated the proud words quoted above, relying more upon rhetorical eloquence than supported by the cause of truth.

At his speech the holy assembly of prelates, and especially the archdeacon Gregory, expressed great astonishment and spoke as follows:

“What is this that you are saying, bishop? Where is your wisdom? Do you call him your abbot, and say that he will belong to your authority alone? By what authority, I ask, or by what reasoning do you claim him as yours? Is he your possession or your servant? Have the sacred canons so completely escaped your mind? Or [Col. 1466A] do you think we do not know that the protection of that place belongs solely to the Roman See? The founder of the monastery itself, a man named Hugo, entrusted the care of that place forever to blessed Peter the apostle and his vicars, and the place thereby deserved to be fortified by apostolic privileges.”

The pious Pope Alexander himself, having learned of the bishop’s injustice, addressed him gently:

“Be peaceful, my son Chunibertus; be kind. Restrain your mind, for your eye has been disturbed by fury. Recall your spirit from indignation, which in no way ought to reside in a priest’s breast. It certainly seems unjust and intolerable to us that this place, although it belongs to your diocese, should be so wrongly harassed when it has been entrusted solely to our protection and jurisdiction. Therefore we admonish you to show the abbot who has been canonically and regularly elected the paternal spirit and affection that befit you, and kindly to grant him consecration.”

[Col. 1466B] When the bishop stubbornly declared that he would do this in no circumstances unless it were for another whom he himself had elected, his insolence was disregarded. To keep the story short, in accordance with the decision and judgment of the entire venerable assembly present, our Benedict was blessed and consecrated by the Roman pontiff himself.

The bishop was then commanded under threat that henceforth he must not dare to inflict any annoyance upon the abbot or the monastery’s possessions, nor demand anything further from it except what was canonical and regular—unless, perhaps, he did not fear endangering his own ecclesiastical status. That cunning dissembler of his malicious mind answered kindly at the time, as though a father, while intending to inflict many misfortunes that he was turning over in his heart. [Col. 1466C] We shall set these forth in due sequence at the appropriate point, for the greater glory of Benedict’s patience.

[Col. 1466C] 9. He rejects alien customs and inculcates the Rule.

Having undertaken the governance of the flock, we shall now attempt, according to the limited measure of our knowledge, to report how vigilantly he administered it, how holily and religiously he lived by doing and teaching what was just, although it is beyond our ability to unfold it fully, as we heard and saw “in the city of our God, on his holy mountain” (Psalm 47:9).

First, when he discovered that very many brothers of the congregation took pleasure in certain novel practices and institutions contrary to the Rule, he strove to uproot this sand, which would later prove harmful, [Col. 1466D] and to clear the field of these thorns, so that he might build upon the firm Rock.

“You know, my brothers and most beloved sons,” he said, “how the divine word rebukes those who prefer human inventions to divine commands and judgments. Hence the psalmist prophet sings: ‘They provoked God by their inventions, and therefore destruction was multiplied among them’ (Psalm 105:29); and, ‘He was avenging all their inventions’ (Psalm 98:8).

“The Lord himself also says in the Gospel: ‘Woe to you, Pharisees, who have abandoned the commandments of God because of your traditions’ (Matthew 15:6); and Paul says: ‘For, abandoning the righteousness of God and seeking to establish their own, they have not submitted to the righteousness of God’ (Romans 10:3). Scripture likewise says: ‘In vain do they worship me by commandments and doctrines of men’ (Isaiah 29:13).

“Therefore I exhort your brotherhood [Col. 1467A] that, setting aside certain superstitions and human institutions which have no bearing on the matter and are alien to true religion, you turn your minds wholeheartedly to the Rule of our holy father Benedict, in which all evangelical and apostolic perfection consists.

“For I received nothing else from the Roman pontiff who consecrated me except that same Rule, which I was to preach; nor do I remember being commanded to teach or follow the various customs of monasteries. In that same Rule (Rule of Saint Benedict, chapter 64) I hear the same Father and leader thunder at me, so to speak, and continually press upon me above all that I preserve the present Rule in every respect. Elsewhere (ibid., chapter 3), almost as a threat, he declares: ‘Therefore, in all things, let them follow the Rule as their guide, and let no one rashly depart from it.’

“For if something seems lacking in the Rule or expressed too briefly, every abbot is commanded to complete and arrange it with moderation, since he says (ibid., chapter 65): ‘We have determined, for the preservation of peace and charity, that the ordering of the monastery should depend upon the abbot’s judgment.’ This can readily be observed in many chapters of the same Rule.

“It is therefore not necessary to labor greatly in writing down the customs of many monasteries while neglecting the Rule which each person has professed. What is written here may be understood of it: ‘This is the way; walk in it. Do not turn aside from it, either to the right or to the left’ (Deuteronomy 5:32).”

10. He sends opponents away to priories and forms new recruits.

[Col. 1467C] He spoke, and ordered that certain additions made to the Rule—almost superfluous additions concerning food, clothing, and beds—should be abstained from and practiced more sparingly. Since some considered this harsh and unbearable, being forced, in their old mindset, to contemplate new things, he did not reject them altogether. [Col. 1467D] He retained with himself the few who were willing to observe these practices and ordered the rest to remain in the cells. He believed that they might eventually come to their senses and, through the passage of time, grow accustomed to wholesome institutions.

But when they persisted in their harmful course and judged sacred only what they had learned previously, while trying in some way to excuse themselves when invited to the Lord’s supper, he resolved to gather rich and poor alike, and especially to raise the sons of nobles, so that, like a good commander, he might restore with new soldiers the loss of the legion that had in a sense been diminished, and, by replenishing the number of sheep with a fresh and newly formed cohort of young men, might not merely restore it but increase and multiply it.

He applied himself diligently to forming these men and advancing them toward better things: preaching, reading, praying, and assigning every kind of work, so that they would not grow sluggish through idleness. He displayed to his flock the worthy vigilance of a good shepherd. In particular, he urged each one to commit to memory the twelve steps of humility, saying that the sum of the virtues consisted in them, and that from there one could readily climb to heavenly heights. He compelled each to possess and imitate a written copy of Saint Serapion’s conference on the eight principal vices. [Col. 1468A]

11. How he behaved toward penitents, and how he expiated his own sins.

When someone confessed a crime, he descended to him with such affection and not without tears, as though he himself were a participant in the same offense; immediately, in accordance with the authority of the canons, he prescribed the law of penance. Not long afterward, if by examination he perceived that the man was contrite, humble and quiet, and trembling at the Lord’s scourges, he moderated the canonical censure and reconciled him to the sacred altars, yet in such a way that the man never ceased to mourn and weep in remembrance of his offense.

We saw a weak brother who, even after completing his penance, was unstable and prone to sin. In order to lay down his own soul for the sheep, Benedict took him with him into the church of Saint Benedict, which is more secluded. There, fasting with him for several days on bread and water, he devoutly completed the Psalter, not without tears, being scourged in turn with him at every verse. [Col. 1468B] At last he offered an oblation for the brother’s sins. Thus, by God’s grace, he obtained for the brother not only forgiveness of his past offense but also—what is better—an end to his inclination and desire to sin.

He very frequently confessed his own excesses, prostrate on the ground, to spiritual brothers or to bishops and priests well known to him who were traveling to Rome; and he expiated them according to their judgment by generous almsgiving, while he himself very often spared neither his own body nor its flesh, scourging it with hard, knotted cords until it bled.

12. His exercises.

Three Lents each year [Col. 1468C] [ms. “four Lents”] he wrapped his entire body, down to his feet, in haircloth and subdued it with fasts. At all times he slept dressed in a cowl and tunic, with a hard belt fastened around him, as though stationed in battle.

He treated the infirmities of the body more with the antidote of prayers and fasts than with any medicinal electuary, considering it unworthy to tend anyone’s body with the laxative of Galen, since it is more fitting that the body be a vessel of the sacraments. Even when bloodletting, he could not be deprived of his continual reading.

He devoted himself to private prayers so diligently that he rarely ever indulged in rest after matins, even in summer, when pleasant sleep commonly steals upon the eyes. Rather, he went around all the altars of the oratory, striving to preserve and increase [Col. 1468D] the strength and purity of mind sought through the night vigils, and singing in spirit at matins: “I will destroy all the sinners of the earth” (Psalm 101:8).

After compline he was accustomed to pray and read for a long time, saying: “If I give sleep to my eyes and slumber to my eyelids, until I find a place for the Lord” (Psalm 131:4). When I was still beardless and an adolescent, following his footsteps with a lamp, I could not endure, because of my weak age, the great labor of his prayers and vigils. Yet I heard him repeatedly uttering tireless sighs, drawn from the depths of his being.

Who among the old or young was ever so ardent and vigorous in religion that, if he took someone with him for a while, he would not in a sense leave him defeated and exhausted by his spiritual exercise?

[Col. 1469A] He had resolved to build and enlarge the monastery’s oratories and all the necessary dwellings for the brothers. To this work, very often followed by a crowd of brothers and young men, he carried stones and mortar with his back bent and not without sweat, singing psalms in silence.

No commander or soldier ever gloried so greatly in splendid weapons and powerful horses as he rejoiced in the abundance of books, those immortal treasures of the soul. He devoted himself to writing and correcting them with unexhausted and continual labor.

He did not bathe except by pouring water over himself. He did not eat meat or fat, cheese or eggs, although he allowed the eating of meat and himself prepared it with his own hands and cut it up for the weak.

[Col. 1469B] He strove to maintain this daily frugality in food without wavering at all times: satisfied with cheap, less appetizing, and tasteless foods, he avoided satiety in every way and fled strong, harsh wine as though it were poison.

He was kind and most humble toward subjects and the obedient; toward the proud and resistant he appeared terrible, like lightning.

13. The author is kindly received by him.

I certainly remember—and no day will ever remove this memory from my mind—how kindly, in the manner of a loving father, he came out to meet me when I returned as a most wretched son. He ordered that I, a fugitive and useless servant, a prodigal and hungry son, be clothed in a robe and have shoes put on my feet.

[Col. 1469C] He did not allow me to be counted among the hired servants. Although unworthy, he always admitted me to the number of the sons who had always been with him, and did not exclude me from the feasts and joys of the fattened calf.

[Col. 1469D] For this, great gratitude is rightly owed him by me. I have wished, and shall always wish, that his soul, exalted to the heavenly dwelling places, may possess the sweetness of nectar and the authority of the kingdom, where, through his holy merits, he may obtain for me to be joined with him forever.

14. How he celebrated festivals; he did not approve sleep after matins.

Who could adequately relate how swift, energetic, and cheerful with spiritual joy he showed himself in celebrating solemn feasts? On the preceding day, during their vigils, he was exceedingly sparing in food and drink, saying that one must first have compassion on the holy martyrs, with whom one would afterward always rejoice.

Then he allowed himself a little sleep and, rising from his bed earlier than the others, spent part of the night in prayer. Afterward, with the brothers, he performed the offices of praise so energetically that he seemed to be standing among the angels before the divine majesty.

You would see him rouse the others to psalmody and song with his clear and limpid voice, so that none of them would languish in sleep; he went around the stalls with a lamp. He appointed as leaders the chosen and humble singers whose voices were more harmonious for singing and who were more learned for reading, so that, in his presence, the choir needed no other leader or precentor.

With these very eyes I observed him, during processions, singing and exulting in a piercing, high-pitched voice, while tears flowed down his face—a thing which, I think, can happen to few except spiritual men.

[Col. 1470A] He observed the readings and prolonged the processions so that the divine work might continue until daybreak, lest the envious deceit of the enemy steal anything from those returning to bed after matins, something that might scorch the sweetly fragrant flowers of chastity and, by defiling the solemn joy, drive them away from holy communion.

15. What he ordained concerning Masses and communion.

In the chapter, when postponing until the following day whatever had to be said, he did not permit the brothers to waste time in excessive speech. After delivering a pure and exhortatory sermon on the Gospel and impressing it sufficiently upon the minds of his hearers, he urged them all to prostrate themselves together with him before the holy cross and earnestly to ask God, through the intercession of the holy feast being celebrated, for forgiveness.

When they had unanimously fulfilled this with tearful [Col. 1470B] sighs, he was the first to rise. He absolved them as far as he could and exhorted them to prepare themselves devoutly and humbly for celebrating Mass and to partake reverently of the most sacred Eucharist.

No priest was to withdraw from the choir to celebrate a private Mass before the common offering; rather, all were to approach at one and the same time in the sight of the Most High God, to offer a sacrifice as a fragrance of sweetness.

He also ordered the almoner to refresh all the poor and guests on that day more generously than usual. At the same time, during the solemnities of the Masses, he himself distributed gifts of money to the crowd of poor who flocked to him.

[Col. 1470C] When everything had been constructed and arranged according to his judgment, how he proceeded and stood, most reverently, at the venerated altar of Saint Michael the Archangel—an altar which, I do not think, has an equal anywhere in the world—with his chosen order of ministers: who could express this with eloquence, however great?

For my part—let me be permitted to concede what is true—I am overcome with astonishment and fail at this point. Yet lest I incur guilt by keeping entirely silent about so great a matter, I shall not express everything exactly as I saw and feel it, but shall say at least what I can.

When he performed the divine mysteries in trembling, standing according to custom with his arms extended in the form of a cross and his gaze fixed upon heaven, he seemed, drenched in tears, to contemplate the very divinity at close range. Entirely burning with love, his innermost entrails shaken from their depths, and transported in mind among the angels, if it is permissible to say so, he could no longer be considered a man but a spirit, or—to speak with reverence for the saints—somehow another angel.

[Col. 1470D] Thus the true minister of God kindled his entire self as a holocaust to God through contrition of heart: he himself was the altar, he himself the priest, and he himself the sacrifice.

He frequently recalled what blessed Gregory said about this great mystery (*Dialogues*, book IV, chapters 58–59):

“Let us consider what sort of sacrifice this is for us, which continually imitates, for our absolution, the passion of the only-begotten Son of God. For what believer could doubt that, at the very hour of the offering, at the priest’s voice the heavens are opened; that in this mystery of Jesus Christ the choirs of angels are present; that the highest and lowest things are joined, earthly things united with heavenly things, and one reality made from visible and invisible things?

[Col. 1471A] “Yet when we perform these things, we must sacrifice ourselves to God in contrition of heart; for those who celebrate the mysteries of the Lord’s passion must imitate what they perform. Then the victim will truly be offered to God for us, when it has made us ourselves into a sacrifice. And I say confidently that after death we shall not need a saving victim if before God we have ourselves been made a victim.”

When Benedict therefore gave the portion of the Lord’s body to those to whom he gave it, he looked as carefully as possible into their faces and minds. If he perceived that any were not at all contrite or were unworthy, he immediately barred them from participation in the sacrament.

Finally, what powerful man or any secular person could draw from the cloister, on a feast day, a man devoted to God and occupied with reading, unless some great and unavoidable business compelled it?

[Col. 1471B] 16. In this manner he celebrated solemn days, especially the feasts of the Lord himself and of his undefiled Mother, although on ordinary and weekday occasions he certainly did not know how to cease from celebrating Masses.

He recalled every day, with pure devotion, the Annunciation of the Lord; his Nativity; Circumcision; Epiphany; Presentation in the Temple, when he was presented by his parents in obedience; baptism; fasting; holy temptation; and angelic ministration, as well as his preaching and miracles; likewise his Transfiguration, Passion and death, Resurrection, Ascension, and Advocacy, and, according to the memory of the whole saving dispensation assumed for our sake.

Amid these observances he interwove fifty psalms, suitably divided, with fitting antiphons and collects.

[Col. 1471C] **17. He receives guests as Christ.** As for his hospitality, we have thought it unnecessary to say much about it, since by the reality and experience of the matter he became so renowned that he won a singular distinction among his contemporaries and, through it, became celebrated and most widely known to nearly all who lived throughout the Roman world. For, since “God loves a cheerful giver” (II Cor. 9:7), he displayed great cheerfulness of spirit and countenance at the arrival of guests; and he believed himself especially visited and, in a certain sense, blessed by God whenever not merely one guest but many arrived together. Since he denied this generous kindness of humanity to no people of any sort, he served especially the members of the household of faith and pilgrims, as commanded, with a particular and most humble affection, as though they were Christ himself, attending to them with every reverence. [Col. 1471D] Their numbers often streamed to him, exceedingly weary and exhausted, since the place lies on the Roman road.

To all of them—whether they were bishops or Roman cardinals, canons, abbots, or monks—after customarily meeting them with his brothers in every service of charity, he suitably assigned prepared lodgings, adequately spread with carpets, and appointed for them chosen, energetic servants who were always ready to attend them at his command. He himself, like a host with his garments tucked up, hurried here and there, and at mealtime hastened to pour water over everyone’s hands. Then he ordered dishes to be served abundantly, according to each person’s observance. So that no one might lack anything, he encouraged the servants and, going around, saw to everything, wishing, as the saying goes, to overcome the various fastidiousness of the dinner. He also took care that no offensive bedcloth, no dirty tablecloth, wrinkle anyone’s nose. The household equipment of cups, dishes, and pitchers was to shine like a hearth-fire in its cleanliness.

Finally, although previously severe and sparing toward himself, by sharing the guests’ table he kindly relaxed the spirit of the host; while the bridegroom was present, he considered it foolish and unjust to maintain his customary rigor of fasting, making up after their departure through stricter abstinence whatever had been done less rigorously than usual on their account, in accordance with what is written: “The children of the bridegroom cannot fast while the bridegroom is with them; but the days will come when the bridegroom will be taken away from them, and then they will fast” (Mark 2:19).

During the meals themselves, with every disturbance removed far away, either reading alone resounded, or, to make the guest cheerful, there was pleasant conversation about spiritual matters. What more need be said? By abundantly supplying all their needs, he believed that he was refreshing Christ, according to the prophetic saying: “This is my rest; refresh the weary” (Isa. 28:12).

**18.** Indeed, some people seem to fulfill the duty of charity by serving guests for two or three days. When Benedict kept them with him for several months or a whole year—or, to speak truthfully, for two or three years—providing for them, their horses, and their servants everything that was necessary for their use, his former goodwill toward them neither changed nor diminished. Maintaining an unwavering and identical disposition, he showed at the end the same—and a still more fervent—charitable affection that he had displayed at the beginning. And lest he seem to benefit them only with food, he clothed some in very fine garments, as though prepared for his own use; gave horses to others; and filled the purses of others with money. To some who lacked all these things, or who had been stripped of their possessions and robbed on the road, he gave everything at once. Thus they returned home joyful, blessing God anew and giving thanks to his servant.

The weak also, afflicted by prolonged illnesses on the road, struggled with all their strength to reach the monastery as quickly as possible, for they were certain that it was like an asylum and common refuge for all the wretched. The holy Father refreshed such people with even greater kindness and restored their bodies, weakened by serious illness, with more delicate foods and the use of baths, until he brought them back to their former state of health. Then he sent them away supported by provisions for their journey and by his blessing, especially those from whom he expected no recompense in the present age.

**19.** I was present when a certain brother—whose name I prudently omit—came before Father Benedict. Inflated by an evil spirit of mind against the frequent arrival of guests, because it seemed to him that they were consuming the monastery’s goods, he complained to him boldly in these words:

“What is this that you are doing? Why do you squander and scatter our abundant supplies so lavishly and for so long among unknown persons and newcomers? Does it seem fair and right to you that, while they feast excellently and splendidly, we, lacking the necessities of life, should go hungry like famished men? As we have certainly heard from truthful people, and have proved by experience ourselves, the abbots of other monasteries do not follow such practices. If a guest arrives at evening, he either departs the next day or, at most, perhaps stays for two days. But you, believing that nothing has been done for guests while anything remains to be done, never cease to lavish upon them, with excessive partiality, whatever you can scrape together from every source.”

As he vomited out such words in distrust, swollen with ignorant and fainthearted grumbling, the good man, being gentle and calm, sought to oppose each of his biting remarks with nothing other than the apostle’s authority: “Be hospitable to one another without grumbling” (I Pet. 4:9). Thus, overcome both by the authority of the holy apostle and by Benedict’s gentleness in patience, the brother never afterward burst out into such acts of distrust or impatience.

**20.** Through the works of piety and mercy described above, whose fragrance he spread everywhere like a field full of the Lord’s blessing, he became beloved by God and human beings. Thus Pope Gregory, of blessed memory—the restorer and most incorruptible guardian of the sacred canons, who endured countless assaults of persecution for the truth of God’s law from Henry, the faithless and simoniacal king, and from Guibert, the heresiarch and invader of the apostolic see—raised him up and encouraged him with such consoling words in his letters:

“The hearts of the saints have found rest through you, brother.”

Let this suffice concerning his hospitality. Let us now say a little about his care for the poor and his almsgiving. His zeal for this was so intense that, although he considered it wrong to have any of another person’s money stored in his own purse, he nevertheless always carried with him a fund for almsgiving, so that no poor person might ever return from him empty-handed. And although, like another Martin, he could not easily be drawn away from his monastery, if circumstances nevertheless caused him to descend from the mountain, almsgiving, as Scripture says, “sweated in his hand” wherever he went, so that by his continual generosity he might cleanse his daily failings—failings that often creep in through the cares of household affairs and worldly business.

When he was outside the monastery, he said that the protection and care of widows, orphans, and children without parents who belonged by right to his church particularly concerned him; and he anxiously took care that they should not be oppressed by anyone’s violence. We often saw him compelled to sit among judges while the advocates sharpened their tongues for litigation. He would quietly await the conclusion of the case, holding before him the book of which he could not be deprived, and devote himself more to reading until, at the end of the hearing, he necessarily had to decide or determine something.

What mortal would dare, in his presence, to chatter or play foolishly, behaving loosely like a scamp, breaking into uncontrolled laughter or shameful buffoonery? Such integrity and severity of spirit appeared, bursting forth in fitting signs, in his handsome and gracious countenance, and the beautiful height of his distinguished person always and everywhere stood out with such authority that it not only invited but drew the eyes of those who saw him toward reverence for honesty and the worship of God.

**21. He visits the priories.** When he went to visit the brothers who lived farther away in the monastery’s cells, and for whom he had the greatest concern, he first took particular care to bring with him such a quantity of books that it would suffice until his return as nourishment for his soul and those of his companions. Once on the road, he would devote several hours to reading with his companions before leaving the lodging. If the disturbance of secular people happened to interfere, he would choose in the orchards or vineyards of the house a place favorable to quiet, while the others waited on account of some matter of business or any other affair.

When they reached the places for whose sake he had set out, he diligently investigated the life and conduct of the brothers, “digging through the wall,” as the prophet says, and examining everything with the greatest care; then he supplied the necessary instruction and correction. He compelled them to construct cloisters and the other regular buildings. In some cases, by supplying poorer men with the expenses for this work, he wished to impoverish himself; in others, he delayed his own departure by building in person until the work was completed.

He strongly urged them not to live like Sarabaites, with only two or three—or certainly as individuals—remaining together; rather, whenever possible, they were to exceed such a number and frequently return to the monastery or to cells where stricter order was observed, carefully attending to the salvation of their souls. He adjured them by Christ not to be tainted in any way by the Simoniac heresy, and he detested with the utmost abhorrence those who, for the sake of obtaining tithes or churches, would give even the price of a single obol, as had been customary among certain monks.

**22. He is missed when absent from his own.** When circumstances occasionally arose that caused him to remain beyond the time he had promised and fixed, the community recalled him through the faithful desires and prayers of the brothers:

“O pious shepherd and greatest of Fathers, you have now been away too long. You promised a speedy return, and now your absence, so unwelcome to us, troubles hearts filled with love for you and concern for your holiness.”

He knew how to comfort them with the apostle’s words (Phil. 2):

“If there is any consolation in Christ, any comfort from love, any fellowship of the Spirit, any affection and compassion, complete my joy by being of the same mind, having the same love, united in soul and intent on one thing. Therefore, my beloved, just as you have always obeyed—not only in my presence but much more now in my absence—work out your own salvation with fear and trembling.”

When he returned, and the report of his arrival struck the brothers’ ears, the tears they shed from excessive joy testified how happily the hearts of all rejoiced.

**23. Likewise, he is missed by the poor.** I say nothing about the poor, whose numbers then filled the mountain’s ravines so densely that passage through them was scarcely possible. When they heard his name, they raised such cries to heaven with tears and applause, in great rejoicing:

“At last you have come, beloved Father; you have come! Now you restore light to your homeland, its sole sweet consolation and protection, and hope to your orphans, cripples, and widows.”

Others applauded and sang in response:

“O best of Fathers and guardian of our possessions, would that God grant you a long life, so that we may be nourished by your almsgiving for many years!”

As he climbed the mountain slopes, some emerging from their huts and humble dwellings, others—sick—lying hidden in their caves or beds, and some orphans and wards going before and following behind, all sang with triumphant voices, like another army of Christ accompanying its commander:

“Blessed is he who comes: Father Benedict.”

He, meanwhile, singing psalms and walking, sometimes barefoot like a good shepherd who wisely recognizes the face of his own flock, personally gave more generously to all the needy, taking particular care of the blind, the weak, and the crippled. Whenever he climbed the mountain, he did not neglect to perform these deeds, so that he might wash away the stains of household concerns in obedience to the Lord’s command: “Give alms, and behold, everything is clean for you” (Luke 11:41).

**24.** Perhaps someone will be angry with me and declare that this work I am weaving is worthless, barren, and of no importance because it contains no signs or miracles, not understanding that any saint should be measured and praised more by the true virtue of the spirit and by excellent conduct than by miracles, which can be common to the good and the wicked. But such a judgment would be unjust. For the things we have related about God’s servant produce holiness; the others merely speak of it. The former offer edification to readers, whereas the latter generally produce only wonder.

It is also a better and more excellent proof of great virtue for each person to drive vices and the fuel of wicked pleasure from the spirit, and thus, by carrying the cross daily, to be in a certain sense always a martyr, than to cast out crowds of unclean spirits from human beings—a deed which we know many false practitioners can also perform—and to extinguish diseases and groups of various fevers in another person’s flesh, something that can plainly also be accomplished through the powers of herbs and medicinal antidotes.

Let the seeker and lover of miracles fear what the Savior reproached his slanderers with in the Gospel: “An evil and adulterous generation seeks a sign” (Matt. 12:39). And when the disciples boasted about the effect of miracles, saying, “Lord, even the demons are subject to us in your name” (Luke 10:17), he said to them: “Do not rejoice because the demons are subject to you; but rejoice and exult because your names are written in heaven” (ibid., 20).

That the enormity of certain sinners’ offenses can sometimes cause divine miracles to cease, we infer from the fact that a certain impotence is attributed to our Lord, although he is truly omnipotent, when the Evangelist says of him: “And he could do no miracle there”—that is, in Capernaum—“because of their unbelief” (Mark 6:5–6).

And blessed Pope Gregory says in his *Dialogue*: “Many today do not perform signs, and yet they are not unlike those who perform signs.” Again, in one of his homilies:

“These signs were necessary at the beginning of the Church. For, so that the faith of believers might grow, it had to be nourished by signs and works of power. When we plant young trees, we pour water over them until we see that they have grown strong in the ground; but once they have taken root, the watering ceases.”

Therefore, fearing what the herald of truth, Paul—in whom Christ speaks—used to charge against the faithlessness of the Jews, “For the Jews seek signs, and signs are not given to the faithful but to the unbelieving” (I Cor. 14:21), let us press on toward perfection. In this servant of God, let us not seek the efficacy of signs, but admire the strength of spirit, the true love of God and neighbor—by which the whole law is fulfilled—and the dignity and steadfastness with which he was outstandingly marked. Nevertheless, we too are preparing to write several things about him that may not be entirely unworthy of admiration.

**25. Benedict suffers violence from Bishop Chunibert.** It is now worthwhile to insert the many adversities that he suffered from the Simoniacs and schismatics, and especially from Chunibert of Turin, so that, since it is written, “The furnace tests the potter’s vessels, and the trial of tribulation tests righteous people” (Ecclus. 27:6), he too, pressed by various hardships, may appear suited for the crown of the eternal King like tested gold and a precious stone, and, after suffering for a little while with the saints, shine with them in everlasting light.

From the time when, as I stated at the beginning, Chunibert received instructions from Pope Alexander that, if he wished to preserve the friendship of the Roman see, he should not molest the monastery of Clusio, formerly entrusted to the sole protection of blessed Peter, or its abbot Benedict, the envious dissembler of an evil mind left the papal court and revealed through the outcome of events the schemes he had been devising. He began to harass and provoke the abbot with many insults and abusive, unjust exactions, although at times he restrained himself from injuries lest he offend the Roman pontiff’s authority.

But after the aforesaid Pope Alexander had been taken from this life and the archdeacon Gregory had attained the summit of the apostolate, a great division arose between Gregory and King Henry, who had been excommunicated for the Simoniac heresy. Then Chunibert, along with many other bishops of Italy, finding an opportunity in the schism, followed his king and was likewise bound with him by the chain of anathema. Foolishly, he leaped away from communion with the Roman Church and, finally unrestrained, devoted all his strength to persecuting the church of Clusio and its abbot.

**26.** First he tried to corrupt the minds of the brothers through various promises and seductive flatteries, to see whether he could in some way undermine them and turn them away from obedience or submission to their abbot. When his schemes achieved nothing, he attacked them by another route. By inflicting whatever harm he could and threatening to take away their crops, he caused some of the brothers, without Father Benedict’s approval, to come to him, hoping perhaps to obtain from him the use of the current year’s harvest.

When the boastful man saw them—being extraordinarily greedy for human praise, a clanging cymbal that lacked charity himself—he immediately stirred up the entire city and summoned all the citizens and his fellow townspeople concerning the penance of those brothers, because they had communicated with Benedict as though he had been excommunicated by Chunibert himself; though they were unwilling, he harangued the people. Finally, he delivered a speech full of praise for himself and contempt for Benedict, adding in song: “Come, children, listen to me.”

Those brothers, thus deceived, returned to the monastery, not without regret that they had been so defiled by association with him. Then Chunibert, another Herod, seeing that he had been made a laughingstock by them, inflamed with a greater fire of indignation and anger, brought out his forces. With a hostile army he ravaged the monastery’s fields, burned its villages and churches, and, after carrying off much plunder—but not without great loss among his own men—returned home with his troop of soldiers badly battered.

**27.** But while Benedict watched this fearlessly, grieving and praying more over Chunibert’s madness, Chunibert nevertheless conspired with Margrave Peter to arrange that, after the aforesaid abbot had been expelled from the monastery, another might be placed there in his stead—shameful as the proposal was. Without delay, both men, accompanied by many soldiers, hurried to the holy place. The gates were broken down, and God’s servant Benedict was ordered to leave as quickly as possible.

But divine power was clearly present. Night was already approaching. While the man of God spent the night without fear in prayer and the praise of God, his enemies themselves feasted throughout the whole night and drank an excessive quantity of unmixed wine. When morning came, driven, I believe, by angelic power, they left at a rapid pace, forgetting the reason for which they had come, and dispersed without saying anything to anyone, their business unfinished.

**28. Benedict is expelled.** Not long afterward, Chunibert came to his senses—but was by no means converted by the divine miracle. He approached the margrave and, assailing him with wicked agreements, accused him of perjury because he had not expelled Benedict from the place. To him the margrave replied:

“What is this you are saying, madman? Are you in your right mind? Did I not, as I promised, hand over the place and the abbot to your power? It no longer concerns me. ‘What has been done,’ they say, ‘do not undo.’”

What more need be said? The old man, hardened by age, drove the young man to change his mind through many deceptions and, repeatedly hissing poisonous counsels into his open ears, pressed him toward the crime by which he himself was destined to die prematurely, before half his days had passed.

They therefore came to the monastery as quickly as possible. Father Benedict was expelled, while many of his own people wished to accompany him with tearful sighs. Although he could easily have resisted his enemies, since Mount Pyrchirian was sufficiently fortified by nature and art, he preferred humbly to yield to his adversary, following the Lord’s command: “If they persecute you in one city, flee to another.” At the same time, he “gave place to wrath,” imitating the footsteps of the supreme Father Benedict, the distinguished leader of all monks, who likewise abandoned his own place when driven out by the plots of a wicked priest.

He therefore remained poor and exiled for some time outside the monastery’s possession, in a village called Saint Antoninus. Nevertheless, the eyes of the entire congregation were directed toward him, and they depended upon his will and direction, although the guards and servants of that wicked and sacrilegious man, who lived on the mountain, eagerly devoted themselves to seizing the offerings of the sacred altar.

**29. He learns that Cassian is necessary for understanding the Rule.** At about the same time, when he was particularly free from worldly tumult and devoted himself to the friendly peace of quiet and the study of reading, he knocked at a friend’s door concerning certain passages of the Rule that greatly troubled him because of their difficulty. Saint Benedict, the legislator and standard-bearer of monks, appeared to him in a dream.

It seemed to him that this great Father was sitting at a table and, while Benedict stood beside him and served him, was offering him cups of wine to drink. Then, rising from the table, he said to him: “My son, follow me.”

When Benedict, ordered to do so, followed slowly in the footsteps of the one going before him, he said: “My father, would that you would deign to clarify for me certain passages placed in your Rule that I understand less clearly.”

The elder Benedict replied: “If you wish, dearest son, to be more fully instructed about what troubles you and desire to attain the perfection of the monastic order, seek for yourself the book of John Cassian, who sets forth the Institutes and Conferences of the Fathers in a more expansive style.”

Having received this vision and rejoiced greatly—more than enough—our own eyes testify how ardently he afterward devoted himself to reading that book. Some time had passed when he related the sequence of this vision to Hugh, the venerable abbot of Cluny. Hugh then said to him:

“You received the cup from our Father, for whom you were serving it, in order immediately to follow him; for it is necessary, brother, that you become a participant in the cup and passion of the saints by sharing their sufferings.”

The outcome of events proved that this had been signified just as that great interpreter said. But first it must be told how, without human assistance, our shepherd was restored to the monastery by God’s will.

**30. His adversaries pay the penalty.** One day, summoned by the brothers’ prolonged tears, he ascended the summit of the mountain with a few companions, the sun already departing in its course. As soon as that sacrilegious band, which had polluted the place by its unworthy presence and plunder, heard his famous name, it was struck with such great terror that it immediately fled and scattered.

Margrave Peter, because he had violated the holy place and, in his rashness, had grieved the man filled with God, was struck, as we believe, by angelic vengeance after a period of three months and ended his life badly. Chunibert too did not long glory in the deeds of his wickedness. He had previously seemed powerful through wisdom and episcopal dignity, but at last, entangled in the error of proud King Henry and consequently condemned by the apostolic see, the higher the position from which he fell, the more grievously was he crushed by his fall.

Moreover, since by the just demands of his deserts he had been handed over to a reprobate mind, he irreverently profaned the place that Michael, prince of the angels and most ready avenger of pride, had chosen. He was immediately deprived of life and, as one excommunicated, did not deserve burial among the tombs of his fathers—that is, in his own see.

**31.
