Benedict is hated by Emperor Henry and is seized by him.** It would take too long to relate, and the length of the reading might burden ears insufficiently purified, if I wished to explain in detail how many and how great the bitter things our good teacher endured from King Henry and his Simoniac accomplices, for his steadfastness in truth and religion. But to finish the matter briefly and truthfully: because he held Catholic truth in the highest esteem, favored blessed Pope Gregory and his followers, and—as we have already said—was pleasing through the abundance of his charity and generosity, the Simoniac dogs had gradually filled the royal court with this report and their barking: Benedict alone was responsible for causing the king’s crown to be taken from him, and frequent conspiratorial meetings were being held in the monastery of Saint Michael concerning how he might be deprived of both life and kingdom.

Therefore, when Benedict had become very hateful to the royal court, and had once been invited to Rome by lord Pope Gregory, to whom he was especially dear because of his merits, he enjoyed his conversation and then set out for Mount Cassino. When this became known to the king two days later, he ordered him pursued with such determination that he could not escape the king’s impious hands. After much exertion by soldiers and horses, he was captured before he reached his destination, dragged along, and brought back to the king, not without calumny.

O what applause and rejoicing there was then! The wicked priests who kept watch in the palace—not of a heavenly but of an earthly king—adjudged him worthy, some of crucifixion, some of being burned in avenging flames, some of having red-hot iron driven through his temples, and many of being blinded and thrust into prolonged exile, so that the kingdom might be cleansed of such filth. It was made into a truly remarkable trophy: the common enemy had been captured, a monster and great hater of the king’s welfare and that of all his people.

**32. He is rescued through Adaleida’s favor.** Assigned to this dreadful imprisonment, stripped of his possessions, and subjected to these verbal crosses and countless insults of the same kind, he had already endured everything meekly for a long time. Nothing else remained for him but the supreme dangers of death and the abuse of his body. But by God’s will and the providence of the archangel, the Margravine Adaleida came to his aid. At that time she was deeply devoted to the things of God and exceptionally steadfast in the administration of affairs; our homeland still laments her death, after which much plunder was made.

Since she possessed great influence with the king at that time, she entered boldly before him and humbly begged him, in his clemency, to return to her the servant of God, who had also come with her. She declared that he was the honor of his homeland, a pillar and almost the sun of Italy, and that she could not return unless he was restored to her.

The king therefore thought her request difficult, yet judged that it would not be right to offend her, since she held, in a certain sense, the keys of the kingdom and the entrance to Lombardy. Though unwilling and strongly resisting, he returned Father Benedict to her.

Thus rescued like a sheep from the savage jaws of wolves and returned to the monastery, he bound himself to the things of God through fasts and almsgiving to the same degree that, wandering outside his cell, he had been involved with worldly affairs and crimes. “Whoever touches pitch,” he said, “will be defiled by it”; and, “No one serving God entangles himself in worldly business.”

**33. The wicked character of Bishop Witelmus.** After Chunibert of Turin had died, as stated above, a certain Witelmus succeeded him.

[Note: [Col. 1479] Nevertheless, Franciscus Augustinus substitutes Wibertus for Chunibertus, Maynardus for Wibertus, and makes no mention of Witelmus.]

Although Witelmus was the most disgraceful in character of all whom the earth supports, he was nevertheless able, by means of a quantity of gold, to obtain from the insolent King Henry possession—not, in truth, possession but pollution—of the name of bishop. Having usurped episcopal dignity, this very scum of the earth—born to consume crops and formerly a Stoic or, as some say, a Paterine—rejoiced in his changed fortune. Rejoicing in his changed fortune, he devoted to his greedy belly whatever he could gather from any source.

But nothing was enough for him. If I remember correctly, he would demand food by bawling four times during the night and as many times during the day—enough to satisfy three bears. After he had turned the bishopric’s goods into smoke and ashes, his appetite, worthy of the rapacious harpies, boiled over in plundering our poor. For many years this pest, storm, and butcher’s abyss grievously afflicted the holy man of God and our monastery. After stuffing his belly with the sacrilegious seizure and plunder of our possessions, he finally burst, swollen in the middle like a wineskin, and thus polluted the upper and lower airs with his own filth and dirt.

**34. Likewise, the Bishop of Vercelli.** The Bishop of Vercelli also came to the monastery, himself likewise a plague and a Simoniac. His priest had already placed the chalice upon the venerable altar of Saint Michael and was about to celebrate Mass when, at Father Benedict’s command, the brothers arrived, threw the chalice to the ground, dragged the bishop and his priest away from the altar, and expelled them from the church, not without injury.

With what savage threats that powerful man then thundered, together with the margravine, to whose court he had come! What losses of property and injuries we endured from them on this account! I have said this to show with what steadfastness the man of God and his disciples always avoided the company of Simoniacs and guarded themselves against it more cautiously than against viper’s blood, although their love of truth and zeal brought them many hardships.

**35. A monk is wonderfully restored to health.** A certain brother, whom I believe is still alive today, was suffering from a very serious illness and, lying at the point of death, had lost the use of his tongue. But when the man of God Benedict arrived quickly and called him repeatedly by his name with fatherly affection, and he did not respond, Benedict said:

“I command you under obedience, my son Peter”—for that was his name—“to speak to me.”

At these words he immediately opened his eyes, made confession of his sins, and, after receiving the divine sacraments, quickly recovered through the prayers of the great Father.

**36. Another likewise.** We knew another brother who bore my name. While he was walking recklessly and incautiously upon an upper floor of astonishing height, he fell. His bones were almost all crushed by the fall, and he was carried to the infirmary. Although he was treated with many baths and fomented with medicinal poultices, he lay there in despair.

As he lay there, almost lifeless and limp, an old man distinguished by gray hair and white garments appeared to him in a dream and said: “Rise and follow me.”

Because of his weakness, of which he was conscious, the brother hesitated and delayed. Again the elder repeated:

“Rise, I say, rise; and take this staff, by which you may support your weak limbs.”

When morning came, the sick man told Father Benedict, who was sitting beside him, the sequence of this vision. It happened that a good Teutonic man offered the abbot a skillfully made staff. The Father took it and gave it to the sick man, saying:

“This is the staff that was given to you in your dream, dearest son. Take it, doubt nothing, and rise.”

Immediately—wonderful to relate—he stood upright, and thereafter his feet and all his other limbs vigorously performed their functions.

**37.** Once, warned by the common needs of the brothers, he had gone out into Lombardy. But because, even in his absence, he continued to care for the flock entrusted to him, after his customary manner he offered tearful prayers to the Lord as holocausts for his sons after Compline. Then, lying on his bed, he began to turn over in his mind the conduct and life of the brothers.

While he was thus burning with concern, as usually happened to him, sleep stole over him. He saw an angel, as though girded and prepared to undertake a journey. He asked him:

“Where are you going, blessed one, that you are so intent on proceeding?”

The angel replied:

“I am going to the monastery at the Lord’s command, to rebuke a certain unrepentant brother who has forgotten his offense.”

At the same time, he indicated to him both the brother’s name and the deed he had committed.

Not long afterward, when the man of God had returned to the mountain, he found that monk, marked out by the angelic vision, lying in bed with a severe illness. As soon as Benedict arrived—the monk had been anxiously awaiting him—the monk rejoiced and begged him to visit him. He confessed the sin for which he was being punished by the divine scourge and, through the saving remedy of the penance imposed and Benedict’s prayers, quickly obtained health not only of soul but also of body.

## 38. The Paschal Candle

A certain Lombard had come to Saint Michael for the sake of prayer, together with his own son. While he was devoutly attending to his prayer and going around all the altars of the Oratory, it happened that the boy wandered about too freely, released from his father’s supervision. Though overcome by childish desire, he secretly broke off small pieces from the paschal candle placed before the holy altar, as is customary. Although this might seem no great offense, the power of the archangel nevertheless did not leave it unpunished, so that, as I believe, it might afterward become clearly evident what he accomplished through his faithful servant Benedict.

For when, shortly afterward, that man was descending from the mountain with his son, the boy began to tremble all over, afflicted by severe pain in the hand that had been involved in the theft, and addressed his father in these words: “Run, father, run quickly! Look, I am dying unless you help me immediately.” When the man saw that the boy’s hand—and by now both arms—were swelling greatly, distraught by the excessive agony, he raised his hands to heaven and uttered these laments: “Wretched me, what shall I do? Holy angel, why did you wish to do this, that you should take from me my only son, whom I had presented to you?” [Col. 1482A]

Recovering his composure and calming his tears, he gently questioned the boy: “Dear little son, what have you done? Did you touch something in the shrines by which you might perhaps have offended the majesty of the holy archangel?” Then the boy said: “It is true: I stole for myself some pieces from his holy candle.” [Col. 1482B]

Understanding from this what had caused the illness, the father returned to the holy place and, seeking forgiveness for his son’s wrongdoing, filled the monastery with tearful cries. Summoned by these cries, the man of God came with the brothers and deeply pitied the unfortunate father. After praying, he sprinkled the boy’s painful and swollen limbs with water that he had immediately blessed, and thus restored the boy to his father, crying out that he was well and in good health.

How greatly that good man rejoiced as he descended, celebrating the praise of the archangel and of his servant Benedict! This could be understood from the song with which the entire grove resounded.

## 39. A Boy Unharmed after a Fall

Nor should that miracle be passed over in silence which many who witnessed it are accustomed to relate, struck with great amazement. A certain nobleman from this side of the Alps, when he was at some time revisiting the cells beyond the mountains, had entrusted his little son, named Guigo, to so great a Father for education in the monastic order. [Col. 1482C]

As he was taking the boy with him on a horse that was excessively spirited and ferocious, given to him by one of the brothers, one of the capable servants, Morestinus—he is a well-known man—saw that the child was suffering as he was tossed about by the instability of the impatient horse. He placed him on a mule, so that he might be more gently carried on the back of the milder animal.

They had reached the place of a certain great valley called Gumnisia, where the violent river Beza, having eaten away its banks on either side, does not permit travelers to have a road beside it. Necessity therefore compelled them to ascend along a narrow path on the side of the mountain, from which the gaping abyss below, by its depth, could alarm the eyes of those passing along the heights. [Col. 1482D]

It happened that the child, frightened by the horse going ahead and turning its hindquarters this way and that, pulled the reins too hard and fell headlong with the same mule on which he was riding. As much sand and as many stones lying on the mountain’s slope rolled down with him, he slid to the bottom.

Then his father Benedict, who was following not far behind, repeatedly made the sign of the cross over the falling child and prayed. People came running there from various directions. The boy was thrown clear of the mule and, although buried and covered by a mass of earth and rocks, was found without any sign of injury. Yet on the mule’s saddle, while the animal’s entire body had been torn apart, not even one sound piece could be found. [Col. 1483A]

Many therefore wept for joy, and the boy, entirely safe and unharmed, was returned to the abbot. When he questioned him—“My son, if you feel any pain in any part of your body, tell me; confess it, and be careful not to conceal anything from me”—the boy replied: “I am suffering no harm at all. For when I was falling, it seemed to me that you yourself, Father, were holding me by the cloth of my cloak and telling me to stand firm.”

By such words, it was made sufficiently clear by the innocent child that he had then been saved through the merits of so great a Father and by the life-giving sign of the cross. If you could see that precipitous abyss, your own eyes would convince you that this was indeed a stupendous miracle.

## 40. William the Allobrogian

A certain soldier from the Allobroges, named William, of neither ignoble character nor birth, once came to conversion. The distinguished Father gladly received him in his customary manner, remembering, of course, that saying of the Lord: “Everyone who comes to me I will not cast out” (John 6:37). He joyfully went out to meet all who desired to flee the world, and without prejudice on account of wealth or rank he opened to everyone the embrace of his mercy. [Col. 1483B]

That brother, therefore, eagerly absorbed the practices of holy discipline, and, utterly despising the vanity of the world and serving the Lord in spirit, was seized by illness and brought to his final days. He was visited by that same Father and also by Cardinal Herimannus, [Note: [Col. 1483] Onufrius did not know who this Cardinal Herimannus was.] a man of holy preaching and profound learning. After receiving the sacred anointing and the holy Eucharist, although he was a layman and completely ignorant of letters, he nevertheless began to converse with them in Latin words as though he had been educated among grammarians from his earliest years. [Col. 1483C]

In a wondrous manner, while discussing spiritual matters, he foretold that the end was approaching for many of the brothers who were to die in that same year. Declaring that he was contemplating the Holy Trinity close at hand, that blessed soul happily cast off its human garment.

At this the holy Father was exceedingly joyful and did not cease giving thanks to God, sending before him to the Lord such fruits and first offerings of souls from his labor.

## 41. The Youth Lantelmus

There was also a young man who was his disciple, named Lantelmus—it is a well-known fact—who had recently been promoted to the order of the diaconate and excelled in the virtue of simplicity and chastity. Seized likewise by a severe illness and nearing death, he had long since been deprived of the use of his tongue. Suddenly he indicated with his finger that certain brothers assigned to guard him should come to him. [Col. 1483D]

When they approached, he said: “The voice of the Lord cutting through the flame of fire.” When they pressed him to explain why he had said this, he fell completely silent.

After a few hours had passed, while they were chattering among themselves as if beside themselves—I do not know about what—he signaled to them in the same way and said: “O you priests of the Lord, you could be saved more easily if you always saw the one whom you have present before you.” Having said this, he was silent in the same manner.

As the day was already growing late, Father Benedict hurried to visit him, for it had been his custom to visit the sick brothers before all else and above all else—that is, morning and evening—while caring for them. [Col. 1484A] Addressing the young man, he said: “My son, as you are dying, why do you say nothing to me?”

Then the youth, opening his eyes already weighed down by death, said: “What do you wish me to say, Father? I am indeed dying, but it is not at all surprising, because that old man who is sitting there will follow me after three days.”

He spoke, and, closing his little eyes, was released into the sleep of a holy death.

That old man, whose end he had foretold by the spirit of prophecy, was the father in the flesh of Benedict the abbot. He was distinguished by holy conduct and marvelous simplicity. On the following day he went out unharmed with the others to the funeral and burial of that monk. But soon afterward he was seized by a severe fever and, on the third day, followed into blessed rest—as is believed—the young man who had foretold his departure. [Col. 1484B]

After a short interval, that dead boy appeared to the holy Father, clothed in a shining dalmatic, and told him that he was well. Whoever judges that the praise of disciples ought to be referred to their teacher will understand that these things were not written without reason: the merits of those brothers were deservedly attributed also to their father and teacher, Benedict.

## 42. Benedict Baptized at Three Years of Age

The same often-mentioned Father was once speaking familiarly and conversationally, as is customary, with certain brothers. One of them, more lively than the rest, said: “Lord, your head is already growing white with age.” [Col. 1484C]

Father Benedict replied: “Thanks be to God. It is therefore fitting that, by the Lord’s mercy, once the flowers have burst forth, their fruits should follow more promptly. But why should this not happen, brother? I am already nearly sixty years old.

“Yet there is one thing I remember, through which I hope to obtain God’s mercy. I was three years old when I received the grace of baptism. When I was immersed in the saving bath, it seemed to me that I did not descend lower, but that, for as long as I remained in that sacred font, I stood in a lofty state of mind, from which I could see the whole world situated below.”

He spoke these words not long before he was to depart from the world. Perhaps his spirit was in some way conjecturing from them that the end of his life was near; our pen will now briefly touch upon the nature of that end.

## 43. In His Illness He Refuses to Eat Meat

For nearly a year before his death he was afflicted by a serious and uncertain illness. Although some physicians advised one course and others another, he obeyed them while they were present. But as soon as they had withdrawn, impatient of rest because of the fervor of his spirit, and returning to his customary rigor of discipline and abstinence, he knew how to grant no indulgence to bodily necessity. Consequently, he easily suffered a recurrence of the illness. [Col. 1484D]

When he was somewhat better and had recovered, again forgetful and heedless of his weakness, he tried to climb to the nocturnal communal vigils, supported by the help of three brothers—one behind him and one on either side.

Finally, when he was more severely afflicted by the royal disease, as was evident from his jaundiced and saffron-colored complexion, he did not know how to spare his body by departing from his accustomed frugality and quality of diet, although, as they told him, that illness was called “royal” because it was said to be cured by royal foods and delicate dishes. [Col. 1485A]

When many people grew angry with him and said that he could still be relieved by eating meat, he replied: “Look, I am dying, and shall I eat meat?”

## 44. Foreseeing His Death, He Foresees the Character of His Successors

The Lord willed that his servant should waste away toward the end of his life through constant and prolonged weakness, so that, if any wounds of even a lighter fault remained unhealed in him, they might be treated and cured through a hard and bitter passage.

Blessed Gregory confirms that this can happen on the authority of the history of the Kings, where it is said that a lion killed a prophet because of the sin of disobedience, but did not taste the holy corpse. [Col. 1485B]

Concerning the end of his life, we learned that he had long beforehand received certainty through a vision. He seemed to see himself, naked, reaching the shore by swimming across the sea. There he found a few small branches of trees, rather weakly rooted, and clung to them as best he could.

He carefully interpreted this vision to me while I was keeping constant watch beside him, saying: “Through the sea of this world, as you see, brother, swimming naked and poor amid laborious illness, I am being dragged toward the end of life. The weak root of the branches on which I could scarcely rely signifies that my successors will be weak and unstable.”

We testify that this revelation did not deceive either its author or its interpreter, all of us who, alas, though still alive, witnessed his death not in good circumstances and know that the ship of our church was almost shattered by the instability and faintheartedness of those who succeeded him, as though by a storm of winds. [Col. 1485C]

## 45. How He Prepared Himself for It; He Is Anointed and Strengthened with Viaticum

Instructed by these and other revelations of this kind, he foretold that, after an interval of three weeks, the dissolution of his body would occur at the sixth hour of the day. No longer uncertain about this, he thereafter set aside entirely the needs of his flesh and devoted and bound himself wholly to spiritual exercises. [Col. 1485D]

Streams of tears flowed daily from his eyes. He confessed his sins to the bishop of Orange (bishop of Orange), who was then present by God’s will, and to the brothers. Frequent visits and Masses were offered for him, as well as daily distributions of alms. Psalms and divine readings resounded before him night and day.

Although his body was already half dead and all his strength exhausted, he himself began the psalms that were to be sung and often joined those who were singing.

Finally, after the sacred anointing had been performed and he had been strengthened with the Lord’s Eucharist, he sang three times, with abundant tears wetting his face as far as he was able, this antiphon of blessed Andrew:

“Lord Jesus Christ, good Master, receive my spirit in peace, because now it is time for me, when you come, to desire to see you.”

## 46. He Dies, Desired by All

Having exercised himself in these and similar pious works, our excellent shepherd gave his spirit to the Lord on the vigil of holy Pentecost.

For his funeral rites, properly and devoutly celebrated over three days, many bishops and abbots assembled, almost all the neighboring clergy and monks, and laypeople also flocked together in groups—bands of soldiers and peasants of both sexes. Some were drawn by the fame of his holiness; most had experienced the depths and sweetness of his charity. [Col. 1486A]

There was common weeping; above all, his disciples watered the ground with their tears. Whose heart, even if made of stone, would not have been moved to compassion by the tears of widows and the poor whom he himself had kindly been accustomed to support?

So great and so abundant was the grief of all—especially that of the nuns, who mourned inconsolably the death of their patron, the same Father having gathered them for the love of Christ—that on that day the funeral could scarcely be completed because of the multitude of the weeping crowd and those pressing upon one another.

He died in the fifty-eighth year of his life and the twenty-fifth of his pastoral care, in the year 1091 from the Incarnation of the Lord. [Col. 1486B]

## 47. Wonders at His Tomb

Truly blessed, blessed are you, community of the brothers at Clusa, which deserved to be adorned by so great a patron. Before your eyes you have one whose sincere faith and upright conduct, if you cultivate them worthily, can make you a companion of his everlasting joy.

At his tomb, those who are sick frequently experience the marks of his holiness, if with faithful minds they implore Christ for aid through his merits. Numerous witnesses exist to this fact, having obtained healing from their illnesses through him. I could certainly introduce them, if I did not wish to bring this work to its appointed end.

It is more appropriate that secure silence should fully convey the mass of so great a subject than that reckless loquacity should weaken and diminish it through a rich but feeble talent. [Col. 1486C]

### Verses over His Tomb

Whoever you are who perhaps turn toward this tomb of ours,

Know how I am now and what I once was.

I am dust; I was once made great in name,

You too will become like me, though now you are flourishing.

Such is the condition of the flesh assigned to mortals,

Because of the forbidden apple [lacuna].

Therefore pray to the Lord [lacuna]

That I may have rest [lacuna].

### Another

Behold, Benedict, you are enclosed in a beautiful [lacuna] tomb,

Joined, according to your merits, to the angelic citizens.

And the mystery of the cross arms you with the [lacuna] sword,

By which you despise all the ambushes of the demon.

Here for twice ten years he ruled many brothers;

He strengthened them by admonitions and pious deeds.

The following day of May was our Father’s last;

He foresaw it securely for himself, and on that day he died.

Happy and joyful, he rests in peace, having obtained

The solace of light. Sing, reader. Amen. [Col. 1486D]

### Verses on His Death

Upon the highest mountains a mountain shone, higher than the mountains themselves,

A mountain exceedingly upright, filled with exceedingly great goodness,

Reaching toward heaven and shining with heaven’s light;

Surpassing the mountains, sending forth springs in every direction,

To tell the truth, it bore a cedar upon its summit;

I saw this cedar piercing heaven with its crown:

It fed everyone with its fruit and filled them with its fragrance.

Alas, wretched and sorrowful, what shall I now recount concerning these things?

The mountain falls, and the cedar, Benedict, leader of the monks;

The Father of Clusa himself has fallen from the lofty mountains,

He has not fallen altogether, because his spirit has sought the heights, and so forth. [Col. 1487A]

### Hymn about the Same Man

The distinguished servant of God,

The excellent abbot of Clusa,

Was Benedict in name,

And so he was by Christ’s gift.

Keeping his faith in his works,

He bore in his heart

The seal of the renowned Rule,

Through which, Lord, may you be praised.

When you commanded him to leave

His own lands, with sacred observances,

You gave a pious shepherd from heaven

To the sheep of Clusa. [Col. 1487B]

Naked of fear of the world,

Relying on the fervor of faith,

Among deadly entanglements

He ruled the monks of Clusa.

Steadfast in the precepts of the Rule,

He instructed them in the best way,

And always subjected his neck

To the gentle yoke of the Lord.

A distinguished shepherd,

Cherishing the flock in his own embrace,

He kept watch over all of them

With every strength, anxiously concerned. [Col. 1488A]

He was stern toward the wicked,

Pursuing them with punishments they deserved,

Lest the enemy deceive by his schemes

Those whom Benedict nourished.

The highest orders praise you,

O God; we humbly beseech you

That, through his intercession,

You may spare us in this world. Amen. [Col. 1488B]

[Note: [Col. 1487] Two other hymns followed, entirely unpolished. Since they contained nothing distinctive, we deliberately omitted them.]

# In the Year of the Lord 1095: Durandus, Bishop of Clermont

[Col. 1487]

## Historical Notice

*(Literary History of France, VIII, 424)*

In 1095, Guillaume, bishop of Clermont, having been driven from his see on account of simony and intrusion, Durand was elected to occupy it. He was ordained immediately in a council held at Clermont itself, and nevertheless continued for two years to govern the abbey of La Chaise-Dieu. Baudri, abbot of Bourgueil, who had known him personally, testifies that he made the golden ages reappear in very troubled times. This gives us a highly favorable impression of his episcopate.

It was not of long duration. The pious bishop took such pains with the preparations for the great council that Pope Urban II had summoned to Clermont for the end of 1095 that he fell dangerously ill and died two or three days before the council opened. Baudri of Bourgueil composed two epitaphs in memory of our prelate, but for our purpose it is sufficient to copy one of them.

### Epitaph

In muddy times, a man of great vigor,

Durand restored the golden ages.

As bishop of the Auvergne, he did things worthy of a most worthy bishop;

As a religious man, he did things worthy of God.

You might say that his funeral resembled a triumph

And that it displayed the signs of God’s providence.

Urban was present, surrounded by a hundred bishops;

The number of abbots, however, was greater.

Durand had formed connections with Anselm, prior of Bec, and with other men. Yet there is no indication that this literary association produced any other writings from him apart from a letter to Anselm (Book I, Letter 61). It is very well written for that period, and makes one regret either that the author did not use his pen more often or, if he did, that his writings were not preserved for us.

It contains a fine eulogy of Anselm’s *Meditations*, which had reached Durand when he was still only abbot of La Chaise-Dieu. In the same letter he requested that his monastery be associated with Bec through a mutual union of prayers. Anselm replied (Letter 62), enhancing Durand’s merit as much as he diminished his own. There is also a letter from Pope Urban to Durand, urging him to settle an existing dispute between the monks of Saucillauges and the canons of Billom. [Col. 1489]

## Durand’s Letter to Anselm

*(See *Patrologia*, vol. CLVIII, col. 1132.)*

# In the Year of the Lord 1095: Hemming, Monk and Priest of Worcester

[Col. 1489]

## Historical Notice

*(From Fabricius, *Bibliotheca medii et infimae latinitatis*, III, 206)*

Hemming, an Englishman, monk and priest of Worcester around the year 1095, whose five books *On the Endowment, Privileges, and Possessions of the Church of Worcester* are preserved in manuscript in the Cotton Library. From them come the *Life of Saint Wulstan, Bishop*, and the *Acts of the Synod Held in the Year 1092*, as well as other material published by H. Wharton in volume I of *Anglia Sacra*, p. 541 and following. There is also material in the first volume of William Dugdale’s *Monasticon Anglicanum*, as was already noted by the distinguished Cave. [Col. 1489]

## Life of Saint Wulstan, Bishop of Worcester, by Hemming the Monk

*(Wharton, *Anglia Sacra*, I, 541.)*

### Notice

I did not wish to omit the brief life of Saint Wulstan, out of regard for its antiquity. Its author, Hemming, a monk of Worcester, composed in five books a work on the endowment, privileges, and possessions of the Church of Worcester. An autograph copy still exists, stolen from the Church of Worcester a hundred years ago and subsequently transferred again to the Cotton Library, Tiberius A. 13.

From it the distinguished William Dugdale published certain passages in volume I of *Monasticon Anglicanum*. The author himself disclosed his name and date in many places in the work. Thus, on folio 138b, he writes:

“This little book concerning the possessions of our monastery was composed by me, Hemming, a monk and priest, though unworthy, and a fellow servant of the servants of God dwelling in the monastery of Saint Mary, the holy Mother of God, situated in the city called in English Wigorneceaster, instructed by the reports of many ancient men and especially by the report of Lord Wulstan, our most pious father and bishop.”

And on folio 188b:

“The most pious and reverend Wulstan, bishop of this holy see, had this little book written for the benefit of his successors.”

The life of Saint Wulstan that we publish is found there on folio 186.

## Here Begins the Life

[Col. 1489A]

By the foreordaining of the lavish grace of almighty God, and, as it is right to believe, with the assistance of blessed Mary, ever virgin, together with the intercession of blessed Oswald, Archbishop Alured appointed the venerable man Wulstan, not yet elected to the episcopal dignity, as sacristan of the Church of Worcester.

For he saw chastity flourishing in him and various other virtues dwelling within him; he saw that he was endowed with praiseworthy conduct and did not live as others did; that he utterly despised worldly pomp and eagerly desired only heavenly things. [Col. 1490A]

Therefore he was honored and deeply loved not only by Archbishop Aldred himself but also by everyone—by kings, dukes, and princes. All raised him up with fitting honors and loved him above all others because of his religious devotion. He, being of dove-like simplicity, embraced them in the heart of Christ with mutual charity.

Advancing from day to day toward better things and adding virtue to virtue by God’s help, he was compelled by divine providence to assume the priorate of the Church of Worcester. Yet he accepted it more as an act of obedience than for the acquisition of glory. [Col. 1491A]

Meanwhile, the venerable Countess Godgiva, having heard of his reputation for goodness, began to love him with all her heart and to assist him in the various necessities of this world. At her request, Count Leofric, her husband, gave him two estates called Blacawella and Wulfordilea, which the Danes and other enemies of God had previously seized by force and entirely alienated from the Church of Worcester.

Aelfgar, son of the aforementioned count, also acquired from certain persons another estate, which its inhabitants call Ikacumb, and, for the remedy of his own soul, transferred it into the right of the aforesaid man of God.

When the venerable Archbishop Aldred saw this servant of God laboring at good works, caring nothing for earthly things and desiring only heavenly ones, he resolved to raise him to the bishopric of the Church of Worcester. Although Wulstan strongly resisted, he soon carried out in deed what he had resolved in his mind. [Col. 1491B]

Having therefore received the summit of so great an honor, no one will be able to say adequately how he maintained it under God’s protection and adorned it with holy works. He remained in the episcopate for thirty-two years, four months, and three weeks.

His brother Aelfstan succeeded him in the priorate of the Church of Worcester. By his own vigor he acquired three estates, namely Lenc, Dunhamstede, and Pecceslea.

The servant of God Wulstan, while still remaining in this wilderness where we dwell, became all things to all people so that he might win everyone for Christ. He was loved by King William more than the others and, because of the merit of his life, was honored above men of both greater and lesser rank. [Col. 1492A]

When he asked, King William gave him an estate of two cassates called Cullaclis, and another of fifteen cassates called Aelfestum. He also recovered for himself the estates called Mittun and Eastun, the two Lynderycgeas, Penhyl, and Grimanleah.

He entrusted all these to the venerable prior Thomas, who obtained the priorate after Aelfstan. He also gave a mill at Northwican and a quarter of an estate for the use of the brothers. He placed the monastery situated at Westbirie under the custody of that same prior Thomas. [Col. 1492B]

Blessed Oswald had first built this monastery, established monks there, and enriched it with estates and with the people who cultivated them. But after his death it was so devastated by the wicked sons of the devil, namely pirates, that only one priest remained, and he rarely performed the office of divine service.

Wulstan, worthy of remembrance, rebuilt it after receiving the episcopal dignity. He enriched it with estates, people, and vestments belonging to the service of God; gathered monks there according to the situation of the place; and subjected the monastery, with everything that was in it, to the Church of Worcester. [Col. 1491]

## Hemming’s Book on the Growth of the Church of Worcester

*(Monasticon Anglicanum, I, 134.)*

[Col. 1491C]

I, Hemming, a monk and priest, though unworthy, and a fellow servant of the servants of God dwelling in the monastery of holy Mary, the Mother of God, situated in the city called in English Wigornacealter, instructed by the report of many ancient men and strengthened by the authority of our most pious father, Bishop Wulstan, have composed this little book concerning the possessions of our monastery.

I have also inserted from my own memory certain matters in which I either took part or which were done in our own time, such as the estates invaded by the French. I speak of all these things with the greater certainty because our memory recalls that they happened.

I composed this work especially so that it might become clear to our successors what and how great were the estates belonging to the jurisdiction of this monastery, which ought to have been held solely for the sustenance of the servants of God, namely the monks, and how unjustly we have been deprived of them by force and deceit. [Col. 1491D]

What benefit may be produced by this labor of mine, God’s mercy knows better; to him I entrust everything. As far as my own intention is concerned, it is this: if, at some time by God’s grace, the king’s heart, now wasting away, should be strengthened in justice, and the law, now confused by unjust rulers, should be established with justice as its support, then let the bishop, dean, or any prelate of this monastery know, when a suitable opportunity arises, how to claim these estates and how to seek them, lest, hidden in the fogs of ignorance, they be entirely erased from memory. [Col. 1492C]

For when the causes, persons, and times are known—whether by whom or in what manner the estates or possessions were taken from the monastery’s authority—any claimant on behalf of them, and any energetic and just advocate seeking their restoration to the monastery’s right, can compose his speech more effectively and appropriately and, once composed, support his claim with greater authority by carefully and specifically stating each cause, person, and time. [Col. 1492D]

Let the diligent reader know that I began this work not through my own presumption but at the request of many, and especially at the command of our most reverend father already mentioned and often to be mentioned, namely Lord Wulstan, bishop. Supported by his prayers, I truly believe that I have brought it through to the end. [Col. 1493A]

For during the pleasant conversations of his admonitions, which he often enjoyed having with us as a pious father, he used to rebuke—not only me by name, but all the brothers whom chance happened to place before him—for sloth and laziness. He asked why, while we were sluggish in idleness, we were unwilling to commit to writing the events concerning the possessions of our church that had taken place either earlier or in our own time, when we had seen many things done with our own eyes and he, as a man of venerable age and gray hair, could recall much that was not preserved in the memory of many others.

He also said that it could bring no small benefit to our monastery in the times of our descendants if these matters were entrusted to written memory; conversely, harm would result if they were neglected, since no one would remain who could recall them from memory or relate to that later age the truth or sequence of events. [Col. 1493B]

Greatly stirred by these exhortations, and finally bound by his command and strengthened by his authority, I undertook this work, relying more on the prayers of the one who ordered it than on my own powers.

That same most reverend father, although entirely without desire for worldly affairs, was always deeply concerned for the interests of this monastery. He prudently took precautions as far as he could, lest through his negligence, like that of some of his predecessors, the church entrusted to him should suffer any loss in future times. [Col. 1493C]

Accordingly, he had the monastery chest opened in his presence and carefully examined all the ancient privileges and charters concerning the possessions of this church, lest through the negligence of its custodians they should have decayed or through the greed of unjust men been dispersed.

When he had found some of them, as he had expected, he diligently repaired those that were decaying and energetically recovered those that had been unjustly alienated. He gathered together what he recovered and arranged the collected documents in two volumes.

In one he arranged all the original charters and privileges in which it was made clear how or by whom the possessions of the estates had first been given to this monastery. [Col. 1494A]

In the other he arranged the charters by which blessed Oswald, archbishop, with the assistance of King Edgar, assigned to the church estates that had for some time been unjustly held by powerful men. By royal authority, with the consent of the senators and the testimony of the leaders of the country, he stipulated in each charter that the estates should be returned without opposition to the right of the church after the passing of two or three generations of heirs. He also made the contents of the charters known to his successors through copies placed in the chest of the holy church as testimony.

After arranging these matters, he ordered that everything be written in the same order in the library of the holy church, so that even if, as commonly happens, some negligence caused the original charters to be lost, their copies written there would not be handed over to oblivion. [Col. 1494B]

When this too had been carried out according to his will and command, he further ordered that all the privileges and charters of the estates specifically belonging to the sustenance of the monks be gathered separately from these documents and likewise united in two volumes in the same order. The diligent reader can observe that I have done this in this little book, as I said, at his command, according to the measure of my small ability.

I therefore beg that, if this labor of my insignificance is pleasing to anyone, he not refuse to pay me, a sinner, the reward of his prayer. But if anyone dislikes it or judges it superfluous, let him know that I have labored not for the fastidious and lazy but for the vigorous and diligent, and that I have dedicated this work to those who, for the benefit and advancement of holy mother Church, do not hesitate not only to strive energetically but, if necessary, to expend themselves as well. [Col. 1494C]

May almighty God grant this, and may the honor and power of holy Church continually grow and increase, to the praise of our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God forever and ever. Amen.

# In the Year of the Lord 1098: Radbod II, Bishop of Tournai and Noyon

[Col. 1493]

## Historical Notice

*(From the new edition of *Gallia christiana*, vol. IX, col. 996)*
[Col. 1493C] Ratbod was the maternal uncle of Evrard, castellan of Tournai, a man highly distinguished for learning and pious character. He was promoted to the see of Noyon in the year [Col. 1494C] 1068, and in the following year, the second of his episcopate, he gave the altar of Bethencourt to the monks of Saint Eligius. In the same year he attended the dedication of the church of Saint-Quentin [Col. 1495A] of Beauvais. Likewise, in 1070, he attended the dedication of the basilica of the monastery of Hasnon and personally dedicated the basilica of the monastery of Aldenburg. In the same year he subscribed the donation of the estate of Hertin, made to the monastery of Elnon by Anselm of Ribemont. In 1071 he subscribed the charter of Count Burchard for the abbey of Corbie. In 1072 he transferred the body of Saint Gerulf the martyr from the records of the monastery of Tronchiennes and consecrated the commemoration of the faithful departed in the church of Blandain, from the *Acta Sanctorum* of the Benedictines, vol. III, p. 59. In the following year he transferred part of the relics of Saint Bavo to the church of Nieuwkasteel.

In 1075 he was in litigation with William, bishop of Utrecht, over the estate of Bruges. In order that Ratbod might be compelled to restore it, if it could be established that it belonged by right to the church of Utrecht, Pope Gregory VII wrote to Manasses I, archbishop of Reims. In the same year Ratbod attended the Council of Paris and subscribed the privilege of King Philip I for the abbey of Tournus. In 1076 he attended the council held at Saint-Médard of Soissons [Col. 1495B] and gave the altar of the estate of Emme to the Theoderician monks. In 1077 he subscribed the royal charter confirming the donation of the church of Saint-Symphorianus of Autun, made to the monastery of Fleury. In the same year, when he had been accused of simony, he confessed his simony to Hugh, bishop of Die and papal legate, in the presence of the bishops of Laon and Langres, as Hugh himself relates in his letter to Pope Gregory VII, in Labbe, vol. X, p. 364. The matter, however, was brought before the supreme pontiff at the Council of Poitiers in the following year, ibid., p. 367. Gregory does not appear to have decided anything.

Later, when Ratbod still seemed not to have cleared himself, Urban II wrote to the clergy and people of Noyon in these words, quoted from Vassor, p. 788: “As long as Ratbod was with us, no one brought any charge against him. We therefore send him back to you with the full abundance of our favor. Nevertheless, if any complaint should arise against him, whether concerning his entry into the episcopate or for any other reason, [Col. 1495C] let it be heard more carefully before the legate at Lyon.”

Meanwhile, that prelate attended the Council of Issoudun in 1081. About the same year he ordained as priest Godefrid, a monk of Saint-Quentin on the Mount, later abbot of Nogent and finally bishop of Amiens. In 1083 he subscribed the foundation charter of the abbey of Ribemont. In 1084 he attended the Council of Soissons. About the same year he granted Aldenburg for the construction of a monastery there. In 1085 he attended the Council of Compiègne. In 1086 he gave the altar of Cappy to the monks of Saint-Martin-des-Champs and subscribed the letters of Rainald, archbishop of Reims, donating the church of Marolles to the nuns of Avenay.

[Col. 1496A] In 1087 he confirmed the foundation of the college of canons of Harelbeke. In the same year, the nineteenth of his episcopate, he granted the church of Bredenai to Gervin, abbot of Saint-Riquier, and the altar of Menin to Lotbert, abbot of Hasnon. Again in the same year, on the day before the Nones of July, the twentieth of his episcopate, he subscribed the charter of Robert, marquis of Flanders, for the church of Tronchiennes.

In 1088 he gave the Vincentian monks the priory of Saint John the Baptist, situated above the town of Fara on the river Yser, and also gave the altar of Ghydts to the chapter of Saint Peter of Lille; he likewise dedicated the basilica of Elnon. In the same year he transferred near Ostend the body of Saint Godelieve, whose life, which is found in Surius, Bishop Drogo of Thérouanne had dedicated to her. In December 1090 he confirmed the privileges of Saint Donatian of Bruges. In 1091 he subscribed the charter of Rainald, archbishop of Reims, for Cluny. In 1092 he gave Odo of Orléans and his companions the little church of Saint Martin of Tournai, which later became a most celebrated abbey of the Order of [Col. 1496B] Saint Benedict.

In 1093 he attended the Council of Soissons against the heretic Roscelin. In the same year he subscribed the letters of Helinand, bishop of Laon, by which that most munificent prelate granted three altars to the monks of Thérouanne. Again in the same year he gave the church of Saint Bertin the altar of the estate of Colmunt, under perpetual patronage. In 1094 he gave the church of Saint Mary of Bruges to nuns; the donation, however, produced no effect. In 1095 he subscribed the council held at Mount Saint Mary. In the same year he confirmed the donation of the estate of Alania, made by Robert, prince of Péronne, to the monastery of Saint-Quentin on the Mount; he subscribed King Philip’s letters confirming the foundation of the abbey of Nogent, and attended the Council of Piacenza.

In 1096, together with Hugh of Soissons and other bishops of the province of Reims, he laid hands upon Manasses II, elected archbishop of Reims. In the same year he subscribed the charter of a certain donation made to the monastery of [Col. 1496C] Auchy. He died at Bruges by a sudden fate on the Sunday within the octave of Epiphany, in the year 1097—that is, 1098—not yet fully cleared of the crime of simony of which he had been accused. He was buried at Tournai in the basilica of Saint Mary.

King Philip had granted him the castle of Carisiacum in the district of Soissons to possess in perpetuity, by letters which you may read in the *De re diplomatica*, p. 264. Herimannus describes his death in the *Restoration of the Abbey of Saint Martin of Tournai*, in the *Spicilegium*, vol. II, pp. 435–436. He wrote a great deal, most of which has perished. We possess a sermon of his on the Annunciation of the Blessed Mary and a Life of Saint Medard.

[Col. 1495]

## Literary Notice

(*Histoire littéraire de la France*, vol. VIII, p. 457.)

[Col. 1495D] Until now, hardly any bibliographer has mentioned our prelate in the catalogue of his writers. Yet he deserved, with complete justice, not to be forgotten there; and this will be apparent from the enumeration of his writings.

1. He wrote a Life of Saint Medard, bishop of Noyon and Tournai, one of his predecessors in the sixth century. Fortunatus, who lived shortly afterward, had already worked on this subject, but without succeeding. Three hundred years later, an anonymous monk of the abbey of Saint-Médard at Soissons tried to supply what was lacking in that first history, and was no more successful. Ratbod in turn undertook to write the same history. But, it must be admitted, he had scarcely better success, and his work leaves much to be desired, although he knew how to profit from what the two earlier writers had said. The substance of his work is taken principally from that of the anonymous author, which he reworked in his own manner, adding various details about the saint’s episcopate and several features of his virtues that are not found in the other two.

Ratbod’s work later suffered the same fate as that of the anonymous author. A fourth writer used it to compose a new version suited to his own genius and purpose. He merely added and removed whatever seemed good to him, without realizing that what he omitted was better than his new [Col. 1497A] additions. We have his work in the Library of Fleury, part II, pp. 113–135. The successors of Bollandus judged that this edition was sufficient and did not reproduce it in their great collection.

They treated the writing of Bishop Ratbod with greater honor, placing it after those of Fortunatus and the anonymous author of Soissons (8 June). Surius had already printed it (8 June), without altering its style, which is good for its period, but attributed it to Fortunatus. It is nevertheless clear that the piece could not belong to that writer, since it makes extensive mention of Drausius, or Drosion, and of Vérembert, successive bishops of Soissons after the middle of the seventh century, when Fortunatus had already been dead for more than sixty years. This led the first editor to suspect that the work had been revised by some author who had added material to it.

All critics—Bollandus, ibid., p. 87; Du Cange, *Glossarium*, index of authors; Baillet, 8 June; *Table critique*, no. 1; *Spicilegium*, vol. VIII, preface, pp. XI–XII—are now convinced that it is one of the productions of the pen of our prelate. Two ancient manuscripts containing the work attribute it to him without the slightest ambiguity: one belongs to the Royal Library among the manuscripts of M. de Thou, and the other to the abbey of Compiègne. The latter bears the inscription: “Life of Saint Medard, which the lord Ratbod of Noyon thus composed.” The inscription of the other is no less clear and decisive.

2. It is believed—Bollandus, 11 April—that Ratbod was also the author of the Life of Saint Godeberte, a virgin whom the church of Noyon honors with a special cult; she lived at the end of the seventh century. Although one cannot positively assert that this work belongs to him, there is nevertheless legitimate reason not to doubt it. Besides the considerable resemblance between the style of this piece and that of our prelate’s Life of Saint Medard, a manuscript of the cathedral of Noyon, which contains it together with several other [Col. 1497C] of his writings, explicitly attributes it to him.

As may be seen, a considerable period separated the author from the saint’s own time. He could not therefore succeed in writing her history without good records, and it does not appear that he possessed any. Accordingly, he tells us very few interesting events from her life. Instead of such facts, he filled his work chiefly with the miracles she had performed during her lifetime and after her death. He begins it as though it were a sermon, and there is considerable reason to think that he delivered it orally. The work does in fact retain several features of a panegyric, although its style is simple and artless.

Surius greatly abridged and reworked it in his own manner, and Mosander was the first to publish it. Later, Léon de Montigny, canon and archdeacon of the church of Noyon, having recovered it complete in the manuscript mentioned above, made a translation [Col. 1498A] into our language, accompanied by learned notes; it was printed in 1630. It was from the same manuscript that the continuators of Bollandus published it in its original purity, with their customary notes and observations. Dom Mabillon, who denied it a place in his collection of the Acts of the Saints, limits himself to saying that this Life appeared to him to have doubtful authority, without giving any reasons.

3. Ratbod frequently made use, for the instruction of his people, of the gift of speech that he possessed. There is therefore every reason to believe that he left several sermons of his own composition. Nevertheless, very few remain to us, at least so far as is known. Valère-André mentions only one (*Bibliotheca Belgica*, p. 784), namely, a sermon on the Annunciation of the Blessed Virgin, which in that bibliographer’s time was found in a manuscript of Saint Martin of Tournai. It is also found in the Lectionary of the abbey of Saint Eloi of Noyon—Du Cange, new edition, vol. II, p. 249—where it was formerly used at the night office on the day of the feast of this mystery. It is believed to have been composed and delivered in 1081.

The sermon in question is also read in a manuscript of the cathedral of Noyon, together with another by the same author on the Nativity of this Blessed Mother of God. Jacques le Vasseur doubtless took both of them from there and published them in his *Cry of the Eagle*, after translating them into our language.

Besides these two sermons, Sanderus (*Bibliotheca Belgica*, manuscript, part I, p. 124) recognizes a third, also composed by Bishop Ratbod. This one, which is on the Conception of the Blessed Virgin [Note: [Col. 1497C] There is reason to suspect that Sanderus wrote the word “Conception” here in place of some other word, since [Col. 1498C] this feast was instituted in the Church only a very long time after Bishop Ratbod.], was still found in the last century among the manuscripts of Saint Martin of Tournai and begins with these words: “We have heard, dearly beloved brothers, the shepherd…”

4. Ratbod also worked to enrich the liturgy. He did in fact compose the Office of the Annunciation of the Blessed Virgin, which was still used in [Col. 1498C] the church of Noyon on the day of that feast in Le Vasseur’s time, as he attests (*Annals of Noyon*, p. 778).

He also composed an Office, or part of an Office, for Saint Godeberte, which was formerly sung in the church of that saint—Bollandus, ibid., p. 32.

5. Finally, we possess a letter of our prelate written to Lambert, the new bishop of Arras. It is the twenty-third among the letters of the latter and those addressed to him—Bale, *Miscellanea*, vol. II. The author sets before him the vexations suffered by the abbey of Saint-Amand at the hands of a lord of his diocese named Anselm, and urges him, by pressing arguments, to remedy them, even by means of excommunication. At the same time he asks permission to pronounce excommunication himself from his own side against the guilty man, if he should not come to repentance. The extremity of the evil can easily be judged from the violence of the remedy.

[Col. 1499]

# Life of Saint Medard, Bishop of Noyon and Tournai, by Ratbod

(Bollandus, *Acta Sanctorum*, June, vol. II, 8 June, p. 87.)

## Chapter One. His Birth, Distinguished Deeds in Youth, and Priesthood

[Col. 1499A]

### 1

The most blessed Medard, a man of outstanding holiness, was born of his father Nectard and his mother Protagia at Salency, the hereditary possession of his ancestors, and was brought up there. This estate of Salency lies in the bishopric of Vermandois, but in the region of Noyon. At that time Noyon was a castle or fortified place; later, through the ordination of that same glorious pontiff Medard, it was raised to the dignity of a pontifical see, as we shall reserve for discussion below.

Thus the holy boy, carefully raised under the protection of his parents and instructed by divine providence through his studies of letters, within a short time shone more brightly than his other companions through the light of knowledge inspired in him.

### 2

At that time he had a certain companion named Eleutherius, whom he loved with great intimacy, as one like himself loves his like—a boy, namely, loving a boy, a companion his companion. Once, as they were conversing with one another, the boy himself, moved by the spirit of prophetic grace, foretold that Eleutherius would become a bishop. Not long afterward, the Holy Spirit, through whom he had prophesied, fulfilled his spiritual prediction.

For when divine grace had bestowed upon Eleutherius the gifts of age and character, he was raised, with God’s approval, to the pontifical chair in the city of Tournai. Thus Medard, like a prophet, had already demonstrated by the divine Spirit what he had foretold.

[Col. 1499C]

### 3

He had great concern for the needy, so much so that, while still a little boy, he disciplined himself with much abstinence, distributed his spending money to the poor, and willingly gave his clothing to those in need. One day, while he was holding a little cloak that his mother had made for him at considerable expense, he happened by chance to meet a blind man. Moved by compassion for the nakedness from which the man was then suffering, he most kindly handed it to him. Although he respected the displeasure of his earthly parents, he did not hesitate to present to God, his spiritual Father, what he had received from them.

### 4

At that time it happened that his father, whom we have already named, returned from a journey and entrusted his horses, which were tired because the servants were absent, to this holy boy, so that they might recover in the meadow under his care.

The boy cheerfully received the horses at his father’s command and, agreeing with his wishes, hastened to perform the duty entrusted to him with the greatest diligence. While he was intent upon watching them, he happened to see an unknown man passing by, carrying behind him a riding saddle and the other equipment appropriate for a rider.

The boy began to ask why he was traveling so heavily laden, since all those things seemed a considerable hindrance to a traveler merely making his way along the road.

“My horse,” the man replied, “has happened to be lost. Yet I thought it useless to lose the things belonging to the horse as well: it will be easier for me to acquire a horse alone than to replace both the horse and the equipment suitable for such a task.”

The boy, who was of good character, felt such compassion for the man’s exhaustion that, when he saw him sweating from excessive labor and almost collapsing, he said out of the most devout affection of his heart: “In the name of the Lord, take one of these horses that I have received into my care here.”

Since the traveler, uncertain whether this lay within the boy’s authority, hesitated for a little while, the boy said: “Take it, as I have said, and wherever it happens that you pass, you will have me without hesitation as both the author and defender of this grant.”

The rider, persuaded by the boy and extremely tired, gladly obeyed. He saddled the horse as quickly as possible and departed joyfully, giving many thanks.

### 5

After he had gone, when the meal had already been prepared at home, the boy was invited by one of the servants, sent by his parents, to attend the midday meal. But the servant who had been sent, looking from a distance, saw that the boy had withdrawn a little from the horses because of the rain that had suddenly begun to fall. Seeking a shelter from the downpour, he seemed to have left his duty.

Then, raising his eyes high, the servant saw an eagle with its wings spread and its whole body extended for this purpose, covering the boy so perfectly that, although the rain was raging all around, not a drop of the overflowing downpour could touch him.

After marveling at this for a long time, he finally approached with considerable trembling, drew near the holy boy with the greatest humility, and earnestly invited him, in obedience to his father’s command, to attend his father’s meal.

But the boy refused to go, saying: “I beg you, brother, when you return home, to have me excused before my parents in this matter.”

Perhaps he wished to delay for this reason, so that the rider mentioned above would get farther away during the delay and perhaps not be found by anyone who wished to pursue him.

The servant therefore returned and repeated the son’s excuse to his parents. With great astonishment, he described in order how the eagle had spread its shade over the boy. The parents, murmuring together with the whole household about what they had heard, rejoiced; and, in order to become more certain, they eagerly urged one another to go and see so great a miracle.

Leaving the meal, the father rushed out with the whole household; the mother, running with her maidservants, almost wore away the ground beneath her feet. They all had one desire: that, if possible, they might confirm by sight what they had learned by hearing.

When they arrived there, they examined the matter carefully and truly acknowledged, by the testimony of their own eyes, what they had learned by report. The father and mother, weeping with great intimacy over their son, commended the boy to God and, with profound devotion, reflected upon the innocence of their dearest child.

### 6

Meanwhile, the soldiers whose horses he had been guarding counted them and found one missing. As is customary among human beings in such matters, they insistently sought it from the boy. They treated him gently and lightly, repeatedly asking whether they could recover from him in any way the loss that had occurred.

There was in fact some suspicion concerning him, since they knew that he was generous toward the poor and had heard that he spent for the use of the needy whatever he could find anywhere.

When the servants reproached him for this both privately and publicly, he approached his father and related the matter in order. The father marveled at the son’s most compassionate feeling. Although he knew that some loss threatened him, he nevertheless greatly rejoiced in the benevolent compassion of the benevolent boy.

Since the Lord saw fit to manifest so greatly the service of this boy in accordance with his own will, at that very moment he suddenly displayed a great miracle. For when they carefully counted the horses again, by the operation of divine majesty they unexpectedly found the entire number intact.

Those present marveled, and the whole household rejoiced. The father and mother embraced their son with the greatest affection and tearfully urged him to rise to higher things.

“Son,” they said, “everything we possess is yours. Use our property as you wish. Use both your property and ours, as seems good to you, in the grace of God, so that you may have us as sharers with you in the reward of eternal life.”

They did not doubt that they would be saved through the prayer of one whom they already saw shining with such great virtues from God. Saying these things, they brought the boy home with them; and, with much joy, giving thanks to God for these and the other deeds of their good child, they gladly refreshed themselves.

### 7

Later, while the boy was still living at home, a considerable dispute arose among the local inhabitants over the boundaries of their fields, as frequently happens: a continuous and endless argument. They often quarreled from morning until evening and, as is customary among rustic people in such matters, had almost advanced to arms while reproaching one another.

This kind of country people, if some disagreement arises among them, do not know how to settle it without great disgrace. At last, by common agreement, they proceeded to determine the boundaries of their cultivated land. It happened that this venerable boy was present with them.

When they reached the place, and the various parties held different opinions, the boy saw a stone fixed in the ground, of the sort commonly seen marking the boundaries of fields. He set his foot upon it and said: “This is the boundary and the surest limit of this dispute.”

At his slightest touch, that stone sank down as wax melts before the face of glowing iron. The shape of his foot appeared in it, so subtly expressed in the stone that no craftsman could have carved or marked it more precisely.

Thus, with the dispute settled, they returned to their homes, glorifying the Lord who works great things through small ones. That same stone still exists among us to this day and is held in great veneration by those who know of it.

It is enough to have related these two things that we learned were done during his childhood. From now on, with God’s approval, our whole attention must be directed to the things that the Lord worked through him at a more mature age.

### 8

When his good parents observed the benevolence of their good child and noted his diligence in the service of God, they commended him to the bishop who at that time presided over the church of Vermandois. They most devoutly begged that, through the bishop’s blessing, he might be advanced to the clerical office.

The bishop kindly received the boy entrusted to him, affectionately embraced him, carefully nurtured him, and generously worked to educate him in faith and ecclesiastical teaching as though he were his only and natural son.

It is beyond our ability to state with certainty how much generosity, holiness, or chastity he displayed from childhood; with what humility or reverence he shone before both God and the bishop of the city. He was magnanimous in adversity, gentle in prosperity, preferring all others to himself through his careful obedience, surpassing them in the clarity of his character, and coming to the aid of the needy with generous compassion.

Thus, bravely trampling down the fuel of vices and climbing the narrower ladder of virtues, he avoided whatever he perceived to be contrary to God, while carrying out with every effort whatever he knew to be pleasing to him.

He was constant in prayer, devoted to fasts and vigils, and tearfully compassionate toward the tribulations of others as though they were his own. He had become all things to all people, so that he might strengthen everyone with eternal consolation.

Why say more? As many witnesses testify, he was a pilgrim in this world and was already believed, with certainty, to be a dweller in heaven. His face was cheerful, his tongue eloquent, and his mouth was always open in praise of God.

Resisting the pleasures of the flesh, he pursued the more perfect path of the spiritual life with all his strength. Through the virtue of obedience he made himself an example for all; through frugality, worthy of praise; and through every moral excellence, distinguished.

According to the Psalmist, he passed from virtue to virtue, so that he might be worthy to see the God of gods in Zion.

### 9

After passing with great propriety through the lower grades of the orders and administering them well, by the favor of divine grace and with the testimony of people of both sexes, he was promoted to the priestly office.

Once he had been promoted to so exalted a dignity, who could explain with what moderation he mortified his body? He himself, afflicting himself with much abstinence, refreshed the hungry; though thirsty himself, he refreshed the thirsty; he mercifully clothed the naked, not sparing his own nakedness; and, setting aside his own needs and those of his household, he generously gave to the poor and needy whatever he could take away from himself.

After the blessed man had attained the dignity of the priesthood, as has been said, he deserved, through the grace of divine providence, to be made publicly known by the manifestation of many miracles. For God, whom he worked manfully to obey through holy instruction, did not disdain to reveal him to the world through many distinguished signs.

## Chapter Two. His Wonderful Benevolence toward Thieves; Other Miracles; His Assumption of the Episcopate

### 10

It happened once in those days that a thief broke into the vineyard of the same saint at night and, with great greed, tore off and irreverently carried away grapes, branches, and whatever else he could seize.

He cut with a sword whatever he could not tear off with his hands, and trampled underfoot whatever escaped his hands. Saint Medard, perhaps at that very hour, was engaged in his customary prayers. As befitted such a man, he was praying to God both for his enemies and for his friends.

Whether he had prayed or not, the vigilant Guardian of Israel was neither asleep nor sleeping. When the wretched thief tried to flee with his hands full of plunder, he went around the entire vineyard throughout the night but could not find an exit. Rather, whether he wished it or not, he remained there until dawn, bound by his own theft.

What could he do? Crawling and running, he traversed the vineyard from end to end. Finding the exits closed to him, he was tormented most severely by the consciousness of his wickedness. He could not let go of the grapes he had picked; indeed, he was forced to keep them as though they were his own, for the increase of his punishment.

When dawn broke, the guards suddenly arrived. They found the vineyard trampled, the branches broken, and the vintage irreverently cut down, and immediately pursued the thief on every side.

The unfortunate robber, exceedingly terrified, hid in the vineyard. His own plunder had almost condemned him already, as though he had been judged. He held the theft in his hands; indeed, he himself was held by his own theft. No escape remained for the wretched man; rather, he himself openly carried his judgment in his hands.

Finally dragged from his hiding place, he publicly confessed the disgrace of his confusion. He confessed that he had secretly entered the vineyard in order to steal and that, although he had worked at it for most of the night, he had nowhere found an exit.

It was a sight of misery: to see that wretched man carrying within himself the sentence of his own condemnation, since he had seized the plunder and publicly confessed that he was constrained by the very plunder he had stolen.

He could not taste the fruits of his theft, and because he had unjustly attacked the holy priest, he did not escape the danger of condemnation without punishment.

He had therefore been sentenced and was already being led to punishment when the holy priest himself suddenly hurried up and became a protection for the wretched man. Remembering the Lord’s Prayer, in which we pray, “Forgive us, as we also forgive our debtors,” the servant of God scarcely managed to rescue him from the hands of his pursuers.

Then, treating him gently and kindly, he mercifully absolved him from this offense and allowed him to depart freely, laden as he was.

### 11

The holy man often showed the same patience toward others. Once, when another thief had stolen his bees by night, the bees themselves, taking vengeance on the holy man’s behalf, left their hives and pursued the evildoer as he fled in every direction, stinging him most sharply, until they forced him, whether he wished it or not, to return to the saint.

He threw himself at the saint’s feet and humbly begged forgiveness for his crime. As soon as the saint extended his hand in blessing, the bees, as though obedient, ceased pursuing him and clearly returned to their former master and owner.

### 12

Nor should we be silent about the bull that was likewise stolen from him, lest evildoers fail to know how greatly God cares about the oppression of his faithful.

A wicked man dared to drive the saint’s bull secretly into foreign parts. So that none of his pursuers might catch him, he removed the little bell hanging from its neck and stopped it up by pressing in a great quantity of grass.

When he had reached his own home without anyone pursuing him, and no longer doubted that the stolen animal had certainly become his property, sound returned to the bell he had thus disabled. It rang so loudly that, wherever it was placed, it sounded continuously and could be heard all around.

The thief repeatedly hid it in inner rooms, most often in a chest or box, but nevertheless it always and everywhere proclaimed his crime in a completely unobstructed sound. The neighbors heard it and marveled. Not yet knowing what the matter signified, they supposed that something extraordinary was being indicated.

At last the fraudulent thief, long tormented by his conscience and now fearing that, because of so great a miracle, he had been judged in the divine presence, tearfully explained this most shameful deed to his friends and relatives, since he could no longer conceal it. Following their wise advice, he humbly restored to Saint Medard what he had wickedly defrauded him of.

[Col. 1505A]

### 13

Later, King Chlothar moved his army and forcibly crossed the Somme. Wherever he could, he plundered and devastated the entire neighboring territory.

He was returning to Noyon with much booty between the Somme and the Oise. But because he had plundered the bishopric of Vermandois and the possessions of the church subject to it, he did not escape the sentence of divine vengeance, which deserved to be proclaimed with fitting praise.

The Lord spared Chlothar himself and the accomplices who had participated in this crime with him, but he fixed their horses and all their vehicles—carts and everything else in which the booty was being carried—so firmly by divine power that for three full days they were completely unable to move from that place.

When they perceived this great miracle of God, they humbly fled to the holy priest of God, Medard, who at that time was staying at Salency. With unanimous devotion they restored to him what they had plundered. After receiving absolution from him for what they had done, they were released from that divine bond and returned home happily and cheerfully.

O wonderful and ineffable mercy of God! Those whom God himself had bound for three days by the most just condemnation of his judgment, holy Confessor Medard released in a single moment through the absolution he granted.

Truly, Peter’s tongue and those who receive the keys from him are the keys of the kingdom of heaven; through them truly repentant people are permitted to be powerfully absolved from the bonds of sins.

[Note: [Col. 1505D] In the other Life the following is added: “Whenever his swineherds drove his pigs to feed on acorns, as often as the pigs were secretly led away, so often did they return to their own master. For without any guide they came back from a distant interval to the blessed man.”]

[Col. 1505C]

### 14

Later a certain man named Tosio, weighed down by an extremely severe assault of the devil, was brought to the man of God only after great exertion by his parents or friends.

The saint grieved that the image of God had been seized by the devil and poured out a most confident prayer to God. Then, after making the sign of the cross, through the most powerful virtue of the Holy Spirit he both expelled the devil and restored that man to his former health.

The whole people admired this servant of God so greatly that whatever they received from his mouth they carried out with the greatest devotion and diligence.

He was just in judgment, prudent in counsel, gentle in prosperity, strong in adversity, patient in tribulation, and generous in helping the wretched with compassion. Although he was judged superior to everyone, he nevertheless served everyone with the greatest humility as though they were superior to him. In all things he obeyed his superiors and showed himself friendly and approachable toward his subjects.

He was constant in prayer and generous in almsgiving. He regarded the misfortunes of others as his own and diligently entreated the Lord for the prosperity of everyone.

[Col. 1506A] **15.** It happened, then, at that time that the bishop of Vermand, who had governed that Church for several successive years, was summoned by God’s foreordaining mercy to divine judgment; and, her bridegroom having been taken away, that Church was left widowed for some time. When the vigils for their bishop had been completed amid much weeping, with the assent of the king and the nobles, all the people of Vermand and all those living in the neighboring parts of the province unanimously acclaimed the most holy priest Medard to be consecrated their bishop.
