Since the man of God resisted their petition for a long time, judging himself unworthy, he at last yielded, worn down by their manifold prayers according to the divine dispensation; and he accepted the care of governing the episcopate of Vermand, not without the most devout contrition of heart [Col. 1506B].

[Note: [Col. 1505D] In the same Life it is said: “The blessed Remigius, archbishop of Rheims, was the head of this consecration. He anointed the blessed Medard with the oil of sanctification and appointed him shepherd over Christ’s flock, with the Holy Spirit cooperating” [Col. 1506D]. Thus far the passage. We discussed the age and year of Saint Remigius’s death on 6 February, and demonstrated that he lived at least until the year 530; we shall proceed further to the Kalends of October, when we shall discuss him expressly.]

That people wept, fearing the holy confessor’s so hard-hearted obstinacy; and the Saint himself was moved, astonished at the sorrowful devotion of that people. At last the suppliant prayer of the beseeching people prevailed, as did the obedience imposed upon him by the holy bishops; and although unwilling, he nevertheless undertook the governance of the Church. What he had accepted unwillingly, he administered successfully and attentively. Raised to the honor of this office and confirmed by the sacrament of the most holy anointing, he meditated day and night on the law of the Lord and persevered without weariness in divine praises. Since from infancy he had diligently labored in caring for the poor, he now applied himself to this with especially greater zeal, not doubting that in them he embraced the very majesty of God [Col. 1506C]. By constant preaching he freed the souls of his subjects from diabolical deception, strengthened them by the good example of his conduct, and, by preaching, recalled from the very jaws of death to life all whom he knew to be wayward or mistaken. What more need be said? Whatever he preached with his mouth, he did not neglect to fulfill openly in his actions, lest he should become reprobate while instructing others.

## CHAPTER III. The See Transferred to Noyon. The Bishopric of Tournai Added. Illness. Death

**16.** But before the most blessed bishop had been raised to the episcopal chair, all Gaul had been devastated by frequent and intolerable incursions of the Vandals, Huns, Hungarians, and other peoples [Col. 1506D].

[Note: [Col. 1506D] The Vandals, under their leader Gunderic, ravaged Gaul in the year 407; the Huns, under Attila, in the year 451. Radbod added the Hungarians, distinguishing them from the Huns, since they did the same in succeeding centuries.]

With its cities destroyed, the Gallican Church lamented in ruins; the bodies of infants were thrown out unburied after the wombs of their mothers had been cut open; husbands had been killed and matrons remained widowed; and, through the immense devastation, nearly all the inhabitants had been brought to the point of extermination [Col. 1507A]. Thus the blessed man, grieving over the desolation that had already befallen that city of Vermand, whose governance he had undertaken, and fearing a renewed incursion of the pagans [Col. 1507D],

[Note: [Col. 1507D] Especially because of the civil wars in which the pagans often became involved.]

established the episcopal see at Noyon, which we have already described as more strongly fortified, with sound enough judgment. That region is fertile and pleasant, rich in vineyards and gardens and abundant in the cultivation of grain; it produces warlike men and persons of both sexes who serve God nobly in ecclesiastical offices. The region is also surrounded by forests and marshes and is, by its own natural advantages, no little protected against hostile raids. Noyon itself is situated between two streams: the Galliola flows around it on the east and the Margareta on the west [Col. 1507B]; a third stream, called the Versa, receives both of them; thus, flowing together, they empty not far from those walls into the Isara, a river of great renown. Orchards are green all around; the plain there is pleasant, and the exceedingly lovely meadows and green pastures delight its inhabitants greatly. The place itself is also so enclosed on the east and west by rocks and streams, and by mountains and the channels of valleys, that it can be defended most conveniently by a few against very numerous enemy incursions.

**17.** There, then, after securing the episcopal see so that they would no longer be exposed to the plundering of peoples, the holy prelate of the Lord strengthened his sheep by the persistent labor of much preaching. He earnestly preached the remission of sins promised to penitents [Col. 1507C]; he preached to all that the kingdom of God was drawing near and that God’s judgment would soon come. Through these and many other forms of preaching, he was dear to God and held in the highest affection by the people.

**18.** While he was governing with great success the church he had built at Noyon and, as we have said, strengthening all his people for eternal reward, it happened that Saint Eleutherius, bishop of the Church of Tournai—the man whom he himself, as we mentioned earlier, had foretold in his infancy would become a bishop—departed from this life; and, after the successful administration of his episcopate, he passed from earthly things to be crowned among heavenly ones [Col. 1507D].

[Note: [Col. 1507D] We stated in the Acts of Saint Eleutherius, on 20 February, that he departed this life in the year 531.]

After his mournful funeral rites, when they were discussing among themselves the election of a bishop, they completed a three-day fast and devoutly offered solemn sacrificial offerings to God. Then, suddenly inflamed by the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, they unanimously elected this holy Medard, trusting that they would be fortified by his prayers against the assaults of evil spirits. The clergy acclaimed this, and the people acclaimed it; the king himself and the palace nobles agreed, especially the bishops of the neighboring provinces. For they had read that “the voice of the people” is itself “the voice of the Lord,” and they judged that what the people had so unanimously desired ought to be done without any excuse being admitted [Col. 1508A].

**19.** The illustrious prelate of God most humbly refused what the people had so unanimously acclaimed. With stubborn resolve he resisted them courageously, declaring that he was incapable and unworthy. At last, overcome by the authority of the pontiff—namely, the metropolitan and his fellow bishops—and compelled by the assent of the king and nobles and by the people’s unceasing acclamation, he scarcely consented. By the unanimous authority of the bishops and the king, he finally made those two Churches one: the outstanding shepherd accepted both folds, with the counsel and authority of the bishops of the neighboring provinces, in the time of Pope Hormisdas [Col. 1508D], under the most holy Remigius, archbishop of Rheims, with the assent of the king and the court officials and the acclamation of both peoples [Col. 1508B]; and, so that the honor of a cathedral might always remain with each Church, he graciously granted this arrangement.

[Note: [Col. 1508D] This is a σφάλμα (*sphalma*), an error, of the author or interpolator. For Saint Hormisdas died in the year 523, on 6 August, the day on which he is commemorated. The same seems to have to be said concerning Saint Remigius.]

How many and how great insults he endured in that region, how many and how great injuries; how often he was assailed with threats by the people of Tournai; how often he was condemned to punishment for his unceasing preaching—although this is unknown to us, no one doubts that it was manifest to God alone. That people was savage and untamable, a stiff-necked and implacable nation, exceedingly subject to the wicked observances of idols and obstinately defending the worship of its gods. The holy bishop courageously threw himself among them and fearlessly preached the evangelical and apostolic teachings; he answered their false objections with great-hearted courage [Col. 1508C] and bravely overcame their imaginary opinions by the truthful prophecies of the prophets. Divine grace was always present with him: it protected him from the attacks of the unbelievers and softened the ears of those same unbelievers for the sweet instruction of spiritual teaching. Thus it happened that, in a short time, an innumerable multitude of them was converted to the Catholic faith; and, by God’s foreordination, through the immeasurable persistence of this holy bishop, the greater part of them was sanctified by the water of holy baptism.

**20.** In this holy shepherd the truthful saying of the supreme Shepherd is proved, as the sacred and evangelical history teaches us: “These signs,” he says, “will accompany those who believe in me: in my name they will cast out demons, they will speak in new tongues, they will take up serpents; and if they drink anything deadly, it will not harm them; they will lay hands on the sick, and they will be well” (Mark 16) [Col. 1508D].

The holy athlete of God cast out demons when, by preaching the remission of sins, he restored the image of the Creator from the worship of idols. We do not doubt that he spoke in a new tongue, since we know that, at his preaching—which they had never before heard—the unbelievers passed to the faith [Col. 1509A]. It is clear that he cast out serpents when, by the antidote of holy preaching, he was granted to heal the hearts of those peoples, which were sick from the poisonous assaults of the accursed serpent. He drank deadly things many times, yet they did not harm him, since, always resisting profane persuasions, he yielded neither to the devil nor to his servants. He made the sick well when he converted them from their most infirm unbelief to the health of true faith.

Thus, in imitation of the supreme Shepherd, who, as we have received from the Gospel, having other sheep “made one fold” from two (John 10), the holy bishop Medard joined that fierce people of Flanders to his Church of Noyon. For fifteen years, although they were separated by some distance, he labored unceasingly to instruct them in divine worship [Col. 1509B]. For fifteen years he occupied the chair divinely entrusted to him; during that period, not without much labor, he led the unbelieving and faithless to the Catholic faith. After rebuilding the churches, he fittingly consecrated those who were to serve God there, not without the laying on of his sacred hand; and whatever he knew to be pleasing to God, he ordered continually and with unimaginable devotion [Note: [Col. 1509D] In another Life it says that “Saint Medard imposed the veil upon Saint Radegund and initiated her into the first principles of the holy profession, teaching her both what ought to be followed and what ought to be avoided.” These matters can be examined more accurately in the Life for 13 August [Col. 1510D].]

**21.** When this period had passed, it happened that the holy bishop of God was brought low by a very serious bodily illness; and, as the disease grew stronger, his bodily senses gradually failed from day to day. He lay there, the holy body deprived of almost all its own strength [Col. 1509C]; but his spirit, because it had always desired Christ, yearned toward him with every effort. The weary body longed for its own matter, while the soul reached toward the inheritance from which it had proceeded.

From every direction those whom he had undertaken to govern flocked to visit the weeping holy shepherd; from every direction his children came, mourning that their father’s consolation was being taken from them. Yet although that grave urgency of death had seized his body and bodily senses, the eloquence of his most holy tongue was not held back from the duty of preaching. He sighed for God in his heart and confessed him with his mouth; he preached God without ceasing and, until the very moment of his death [Col. 1509D], earnestly exhorted to the Catholic faith as many as he could.

**22.** As this blessed bishop was drawing near the end of his life, it happened that King Chlothar returned from the region of the Britons after burning his son Chramnus together with his wife and daughters. When he learned of the bishop’s illness, he hurried humbly to visit him, trusting that he would be fortified against diabolical assaults by the bishop’s blessing and reconciled through his intercession with the divine majesty [Col. 1510A].

While, during this royal visit, the bishop’s burial was being discussed in his presence and that of the nobles, the Saint himself, with the assent of his sons, arranged that he should be buried at his own see. The king stubbornly opposed this decision and ordered that he be transferred to Soissons, declaring that he would suitably build a basilica over his body and establish there a monastic rule for servants of God in praise and glory of the divine majesty.

The most blessed bishop therefore yielded to the king’s disposition. After commending himself and his people unceasingly to the Lord, he completed his prayer and breathed out his spirit. O happy body, and happier soul! Immediately, according to the certain testimony of those who were present, the heavens opened and the divine lights appeared before the Saint for nearly two hours, signifying that he had certainly passed from transient darkness into perpetual light [Col. 1510B]. Animated by this great miracle of the most blessed prelate, they were inflamed with a greater desire to transfer him. When the holy body had been arranged and carried to the church, they celebrated a funeral vigil that night with great devotion.

[Note: [Col. 1510D] In the same place: “Torches overcame the darkness because of the immense brightness, and the entire basilica shone, adorned with many lamps of candles.”]

## CHAPTER IV. The Body Transferred to Soissons. Various Miracles Performed

**23.** When morning came, and the bishops who had been able to attend had celebrated the customary office for the deceased, an unanticipated multitude of nobles assembled. An immeasurable crowd hurried from castles and cities, from the surrounding fields and districts: some devoutly desiring to participate in his rites, others deeply mourning that a father was being separated from his children [Col. 1510C].

The king therefore broke through the midst of the weeping tears, together with the bishops and nobles, and lifted the most holy body upon his own shoulders, wishing to carry it to Soissons for burial, as he had foretold. At that hour, those who were able to be present were terrified by the ineffable groaning of the grieving people. They heard the mourners uttering one and the same voice not only in that church but throughout the entire city and suburb, in the streets and squares as well.

The inhabitants of that city recalled the most kindly preaching of the holy Father, by which they had hitherto been instructed; but they grieved and were deeply distressed [Col. 1510D], because, having lost their Father, they were also being deprived of his burial by the violence of the king and nobles. Those who had come to the scene sympathized with the great, contrite weeping of that people; but because royal authority pressed them on, they labored intently to transfer the most holy body. Thus, scarcely and only after much labor, having taken the father away from his sorrowing and grieving children, they set out on the journey as they had received the king’s command.

**24.** When the transfer of the most holy confessor became known, and a certain blind man did not despair of the mercy of so great an intercessor, he humbly placed himself beneath the litter amid the ranks of the bearers. Immediately, according to his faith—for he had hoped well—he received his sight through the merit of Saint Medard, by the gratuitous gift of God [Col. 1511A].

What more need be said? Those who had earlier heard in the city of the great devotion of the mourners, and who then saw in the illumination of the blind man so great a miracle of God and of the holy bishop, most willingly placed their shoulders beneath that holy burden. Each believed himself richly rewarded if he was permitted somehow even merely to touch, though not to carry, that holy bier. The bishops and nobles gladly encouraged one another to perform this service; and, finding the burden light, they crossed the river Axona by boat near the estate of Attipiacum, at the king’s command [Col. 1511B]. Afterwards, proceeding against the current of that same river, they turned their journey toward the city of Soissons, as the king had arranged.

**25.** By the grace of God and of the holy bishop, Bandaredus, bishop of Soissons, came forward reverently with the proper procession and honorably received the most holy body, as was fitting. Thus that fortunate city of Soissons solemnly received the holy confessor of God and festively embraced its patron, henceforth to possess him as its own native defender.

Among the crowds hastening forward, a certain man entered who had long been deprived of the use of his ears. As soon as he devoutly touched and kissed the cloth with which the sacred body was covered, he immediately deserved, through the intercession of the holy bishop, to recover the use of his hearing [Col. 1511C]. The king rejoiced greatly; the bishops and nobles also rejoiced; great joy arose in heaven; and all who stood by reverently worshiped God with their whole hearts and not without tears.

**26.** At the king’s command they crossed back over the aforementioned river Axona and reached the estate where the king had arranged the burial. There, by the disposition of God, who foresees and foreknows all things, it happened that the litter on which the holy body was being carried was set down, for some reason unknown to me.

And behold, repeated miracles multiplied, and the merits of the most holy prelate were glorified before the universal gaze of those standing by. When they wished to carry his most holy remains to the burial, in accordance with the duty assigned to them [Col. 1511D], they perceived by divine will that the body was so heavy that they could not move the Saint from the place where they had set him down. One group after another took its turn and labored with all its strength to lift him; some reproached others as weak and incapable. Yet although they accused the others of weakness, when they themselves prepared for the task, they were utterly frustrated in their desire.

The king and those present carefully considered the event, but since they entirely failed to understand what the matter signified, they humbly begged God alone for assistance. A considerable tumult arose among the people over this delay. Some said that this had happened deservedly and by divine judgment because he had been carried away from his see like a captive; others objected [Col. 1512A] that the king had reverently transferred the holy body out of genuine devotion.

**27.** The king, greatly astonished, approached the Saint’s bier with much devotion. After a solemn grant of half of the royal estate of Croviacum, where the Saint himself was to be buried, he confirmed by the impression of the royal seal that this half was to belong perpetually to the same Saint.

Immediately an admirable event occurred, worthy of narration. When they placed their arms beneath the most holy burden, they were able to raise one side without any difficulty; but on the other side they perceived an incredible weight, and found it completely immovable. At this the king, with a sufficiently joyful countenance, recalling the great grace of God, ordered that the remaining portion—which he had retained for himself—be resigillated and transferred as quickly as possible to the possession of the most holy confessor [Col. 1512B]. There was no delay: by God’s grace they immediately lifted the holy body, now made so light that what they had previously despaired of was carried by a few people to the tomb without any difficulty.

**28.** The holy body was therefore carried to the burial; but along that journey God did not disdain to glorify his most precious pearl. Before the holy body was placed in the earth, a certain man bound by enormous chains around his arms and legs forced his way with great difficulty through the midst of the hastening crowds. As soon as he was granted permission to touch the covering of the holy confessor, all the barriers of the chains immediately sprang apart; the bonds of his fetters broke, and he followed his benefactor in complete freedom, giving many thanks [Col. 1512C].

At last they reached the burial place that the king, not without God’s providence, had arranged for him. After first completing the rites belonging to God, the bishops and abbots most fittingly commended that most holy body to the earth.

**29.** Behold, the sacred glory of the Saint is renewed. For when his most sacred limbs were being enclosed in the tomb, the sky opened, and two doves were seen to descend like clouds; then a dove, white as snow, emerged from the Saint’s mouth.

Thus the athlete of God, Medard, summoned from the earth, rejoices with the angels. Taken away from his grieving children on earth, he is crowned in heaven with his brothers, as he had always desired [Col. 1512D], where henceforth he follows the Lamb joyfully with those same brothers wherever he goes. He follows the Lamb and dwells in immeasurable light; he rejoices that he has been transferred from earthly afflictions to heavenly prosperity; he gives thanks that he has been transferred from this transient misery of ours to perpetual well-being and taken from these darknesses into incomparable light. He also rejoices that, stripped of carnal allurements, he has been enrolled among the angelic choirs.

Let us therefore also rejoice, beloved brothers, over the most glorious reward of our most blessed shepherd Medard. Let us entreat his Rewarder, God, namely the almighty Father, that, persuaded by the prayers of this most holy bishop Medard, he may deign to enroll us with him in the inheritance of his eternal kingdom [Col. 1513A], through our Lord Jesus Christ, his Son, who with him in the unity of the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God, forever and ever. Amen.

## CHAPTER V. A Church Built for Him. Other Miracles. The Dreadful Death of Bishop Warimbert, Who Wronged the Monastery

**30.** When the funeral rites of the most blessed athlete of God had been celebrated with the greatest solemnity, King Chlothar ordered a small hut to be built temporarily over the venerable body of the Saint, until the necessary funds could be gathered to build a church there. After collecting a considerable sum of money from whatever sources he could, he hastened eagerly to begin that dwelling of God and, setting aside many other affairs, labored with the greatest exertion to complete it [Col. 1513B]. In a short time he accomplished what his benevolent mind had conceived—unless, as happens to each person, he had departed from human affairs at a most inopportune time.

For while he was hunting in the forest of Cotia, he was seized, alas, by a violent fever. After returning to the palace at Compendium, he was overtaken by death a short time later. He was subsequently buried honorably in the very church that he had already begun to build, before the altar of God’s [servant] Medard.

The expenses he had prepared for this work, just as King David had done for his son Solomon for the construction of the Lord’s temple, he left to his son, named Sigebert, to be spent on the construction of the church he had vowed to God. He repeatedly commanded him that, if any affection of due love for his father remained in him, he should set aside every other concern and devote his entire attention to the sacred building mentioned above until it had been honorably completed [Col. 1513C].

**31.** After his father had been buried and he had been established in the kingdom, Sigebert carried out with great generosity the task he had undertaken from his father. He adorned that church with an admirable construction of various kinds of stone, as he had received it from his father; he lavishly furnished it with gold and silver and with a variety of ornaments necessary for ecclesiastical service; and, as befitted royal dignity, he endowed it richly and magnificently with revenues and income.

When the church had been elegantly arranged, he ordered the most distinguished persons he could find from every source to be consecrated there, so that both his father’s vow might be most graciously fulfilled and ecclesiastical worship might perpetually be offered there to God as a duty, for the universal salvation of himself, his father, and all the faithful [Col. 1513D].

The same venerable King Sigebert, when he planned to besiege his brother Chilperic at the city of Tournai, was killed at Vitry through the trickery of Queen Fredegund. After he had first been buried at Lambres, he was later brought by that same brother of his, Chilperic, to Soissons, and was honorably buried near his father’s tomb in the church that he had most beautifully arranged [Col. 1514A].

**32.** Since, in discussing the construction of that holy church and the veneration of the Saint for whom it was built, and also the honor of the kings whom we have mentioned, we have deviated somewhat from the course of our subject, we now consider it necessary to return to our intended sequence. We shall commit to writing, although only a few of the many, the miracles God performed for his honor after the glorious confessor’s passing.

As the fame of this Saint increased everywhere [Note: [Col. 1513D] In the Life by a monk of Soissons, a lengthy paraphrase relates that the blind, deaf, crippled, lame, leprous, insane, paralyzed, and possessed were healed.], it happened that the sick, afflicted by various illnesses, came from many regions of the earth to his memorial. By the merit of his holy athlete, divine grace did not disdain to come to their aid. Let us relate first what first comes to mind, so that, in recounting each case, not merely individual but manifold thanks may be offered to God [Note: [Col. 1513D] Here, in the other Life, as it is found in our manuscript, there had been inserted a fabulous advancement of the monastery of Saint Medard’s privilege, which Boscius omitted [Col. 1514D].]

**33.** The little hut that, as we have stated, had been built over the holy body was found, by the disposition of divine grace, to possess such power that if anyone suffering from toothache touched the painful place with one of the twigs from which it had been woven, the entire ailment of his teeth immediately disappeared. This became known even in the king’s palace.

For a certain man named Carimer, who at that time was regarded as King Childebert’s *referendarius*, was suffering severely from this same illness and was taken to the same basilica of Saint Medard. When he found the doors of the church closed, and the pain in his teeth pressed upon him more and more, he confidently cut a little stick from one of the doors and, with complete confidence, applied what he had cut to the place where the illness was raging most severely. Immediately he was freed from the pain he had long endured.

We also possess his staff, by which we have found that many sick people have experienced remedies for various illnesses [Col. 1514C].

**34.** A certain man, too, bound inseparably by the straps of chains and worn down by an exceedingly grievous affliction, sought the holy aid of this Most Holy One, trusting that through his most holy intercession he could be released from that impediment. As soon as he touched the doors of the holy basilica, with a sudden crash, at one and the same moment the sky thundered and the massive bonds of his fetters broke apart and flew far away. Still unaware of the generosity granted to him, the man fell prostrate on the ground, overcome by profound astonishment [Col. 1514D].

Then, recovering his strength, when he realized that he had been set free, he began with loud cries to magnify God and Saint Medard, through whose intercession he had obtained this. Everyone marveled at the exceedingly swift operation of divine power, and with a united acclamation all praised the most powerful intervention of the holy bishop.

[Col. 1515A] **35.** A certain very old little woman, in a manner already surviving her own corpse, had a withered hand hanging from her arm like something foreign to it. Although, because of her excessive age, she had already despaired of life, she nevertheless came with the most devout mind to the memorial of the holy confessor, whose celebrated fame she had heard. With prayers of many kinds and a great outpouring of tears, she begged him to restore her withered hand, which caused her so much distress.

When she had presented herself before the presence of the most blessed bishop with much lamentation, the aid of the divine majesty suddenly came through the merit of that Saint. What had been taken from the woman by the defect of nature was immediately restored; the natural integrity of the withered hand was renewed in her; and what it had received insufficiently from its mother’s womb, it recovered through the most gracious assistance of its intercessor [Col. 1515B].

The hand came back to life with youthful vigor on the already lifeless arm of the old woman. She who had previously begged for alms from door to door, as though incapable of work, now became able to labor and began to live by the earnings of her own work. Restored to health, she rejoiced and was glad, offering many thanks to her benefactor. She worshiped and revered God.

Similarly, another little woman suffering from the same disease of the hand was restored to health before the presence of the same Saint.

[Note: [Col. 1515C] These two miracles are distinguished more fully in the same Life, so that what is said here of the first woman is divided between the two, as follows:

“Nevertheless, at another time there was a very poor woman whose withered hand hung down, entirely drained of moisture, like an old branch. For, shriveled as it was, with the structure of its sinews drying up, it had become so numb and inactive that, incapable of work, it merely clung to the arm, exhausted of the fullness of its vigor [Col. 1515D].

When she learned from the report of many that the sick frequently flocked to the Saint’s memorial, inflamed by the fires of that same love, she came breathlessly to the place venerated throughout the world. Among the mixed crowds, she spent that very night in sacred vigils, just as she had arrived, and passed the following day with many others in festive divine praises.

But while the brotherhood publicly celebrated the solemnities of the sacred Mass, behold: the sinews stretched out, and suddenly the appearance, as though lifeless, began to be animated. When the joints of her fingers had been moved, the hand immediately revived through the favor of the holy bishop; returning to bloom, it once again began a woman’s work. She therefore approached the altar and, while all looked on, presented her hand sound; there, having fulfilled her desire, she returned home in good health with immense joy.

Another woman, likewise poor in the very limited resources of her possessions, had been afflicted by the same misfortune from the cries of her earliest infancy into years unquestionably marked by old age [Col. 1516C]. For her right hand, dried up, had taken away her hope, health, help, and means; and, from the very origin of her natural birth, with her fingers twisted together in her palm, it had likewise deprived her of the ability to work.

Yet trusting that the Saint’s power could come to her aid, since it was accustomed to bring the benefits of healing to others, she humbly approached the same place with a great company of the weak, where abundant healing was available to the sick [Col. 1516D]. After keeping vigil there for several days and persisting in continual prayers of devout supplication, she obtained through the long-desired protection of the most holy confessor of Christ what she had almost lost from her mother’s womb.

For, after a long period of grievous illness, the grace of renewed youth shone forth in an instant upon her withered joints; and the skin that grew over the hand, consumed by the decay of extreme age, was itself a great part of the miracle as the sinews revived. Moreover, that same right hand appeared sound before the eyes of everyone, as though it had suffered no harm during so long a period of her life.

Then, for the first time capable of working with wool, she learned to perform women’s tasks successfully. She who had previously provided herself daily with alms from door to door afterward sustained her surviving old age with distaff, spindle, and thread. Restored to health, she raised her voice in jubilation over the benefits granted to her; and, returning home, she revealed the divine mystery to everyone she could.”]

36. After some interval of time, when the place had already come to be held in great veneration throughout the surrounding region, a certain man named Warimbert, [Col. 1515C] after the death of the venerable Autbert, received by royal command the governance of that same monastic community. After he had held it for several years, Drausius, bishop of the city of Soissons, happened to die, and that see remained vacant for some time without a pastor. After his mournful funeral, the king and the citizens, by unanimous agreement, appointed this Warimbert, whom we have mentioned, to that episcopal chair—though, as later became clear, according to his own will rather than God’s. Having obtained the episcopal office, he labored with great effort not to be deprived of his former dignity; and, although with no small difficulty, he nevertheless secured what he had wrongly sought.

Alas, how sluggish and idle is the human mind! This wretched man, burning with excessive ambition, while he never ceased enlarging the traffic of his wicked ambition, prepared destruction for his body and—what is more grievous—for his soul as well. Entirely absorbed in secular affairs and greedily intent upon his own depraved desires beyond what was proper, he began to neglect that holy place and to retain for his own evil uses whatever had been assigned there by kings and others as charitable gifts. Whatever faithful people had appointed there, by the grace of God and Saint Medard, for those serving God, he himself hid away in his own treasuries; and, setting aside concern for God’s servants, he irreverently distributed the church’s revenues among his own henchmen.

While his own men belched from excessive gluttony, that spiritual community went hungry; while his own men burned with an abundance of wine, the holy household of the holy bishop nearly perished from the excessive heat of thirst. The naked and poor servants of God grieved and lamented, while the familiars of that most wretched bishop strutted through the streets in the most costly garments. The bishop passed over the servants of God’s cries with a deaf ear. Although he had been placed over them, he regarded their complaints as nothing, with no little arrogance of heart and speech, as though no one could rebuke him, unaware of the vengeance that threatened him. He was permitted to treat the Lord’s sheep according to his pleasure—that wretched man who had unworthily assumed the name of shepherd—but he could in no way escape the hand of Him to whom they truly belonged. Let anyone, therefore, who exercises the office of ecclesiastical authority listen attentively to how terrible a judgment struck him for the outcry of God’s servants.

37. There was, in the district of Le Mans, a certain estate which King Sigebert, founder of that church, had established as the property of the community he had gathered there for the Lord. That estate was called Matvallis, a name composed from the British and Latin languages; it may be rendered in our—that is, the Roman—vernacular as “Good Valley.” Warimbert had usurped that Matvallis—that is, Good Valley—for his own destruction, because it abounded in revenues, and, entirely neglecting those brothers, as we have said, he subjected the revenues of the estate to his own uses. [Col. 1517B] The poor community of Medard groaned, because what had been assigned for their use was being wickedly squandered in the bishop’s residence, contrary to canonical institution.

One day, then, when, according to custom, wagons loaded with produce from that estate were being taken, as we have said, to the episcopal palace, those brothers, having discovered that the bishop was absent, compelled the vehicles—inasmuch as they were their rightful property—to turn toward the church of the holy bishop. In defending justice, they did not shrink from enduring bodily harm, should it in any way be inflicted upon them. After they had stored their own goods with their own in the storerooms, they tearfully commended the merits of the most holy athlete of God, praying that either, through his intercession, that furious invader might be appeased, or that through his protection they might be shielded from his madness.

They feared what soon afterward came to pass, unless divine grace should, in its merciful kindness, assist his grieving household. For when news of what had happened reached the bishop—alas, he neither reconsidered the canonical institution nor revered God’s judicial sentence—he dared to hasten to the very basilica of Saint Medard with clubs and swords, no longer as a prelate but as a bloodthirsty man, with great pomp of arrogance and accompanied by a gathering of the ignorant populace. When they irreverently shook the doors of the sanctuary and pursued with insulting reproaches those who, expecting their sudden torments, had blocked the entrance, the furious bishop himself burst through the middle of them and, with extreme presumption and great arrogance, threatened to torture the guards unless they quickly opened the doors for him.

38. In such an imminent peril of death, the trembling servants of God commended their souls to God and Saint Medard, not without a copious shedding of tears. Thus divinely strengthened, they ordered the church to be opened to those furious men. As soon as the wretched bishop entered the monastery, he noticed that the man who had opened the door for him was hiding beside it out of excessive fear. He struck him on the head so violently with the staff he was carrying that nearly the whole of the man’s clothing became soaked with the blood that poured forth. The brother, stunned and almost falling, sighed to God; and, since he dared not do otherwise, tearfully entrusted the cause of this complaint to Him in the innermost murmur of his heart.

Let tyrants hear the protests of God’s servants and show reverence; let all the faithful hear of God’s swift consolation and take courage. Immediately that most wretched Warimbert, senseless and unrepentant, as soon as he bent his knees before the memory of the most holy confessor as though to pray, was terribly struck by divine judgment. His bowels poured out through the secret places of his belly, and he miserably expired. The brothers of the church, unwilling to repay evil with evil, quieted the complaint of that brother whom we have said was struck, and honorably buried the dead man in that same church.

[Col. 1518C]

39. There, through the merit of the most blessed bishop Medard, glorious miracles often occur; there, those who pray faithfully obtain welcome remedies; there, certain pardon is not denied to the truly penitent. May He grant it also to us sinners, who nevertheless do not despair of his grace, through the intercession of that same Saint Medard—He who promised his faithful the consolation of eternal happiness, Jesus Christ, Son of God, who with God the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God, forever and ever. Amen.

[Col. 1517]

# Life of Saint Godeberta, Virgin, of Noyon in Belgica Secunda, by the author apparently Ratbod, Bishop

*(Bolland, Acta Sanctorum, April, vol. II, p. 33.)*

## Chapter One. The Pious Education and Consecration of Saint Godeberta

[Col. 1517D]

1. As we are solemnly preparing to celebrate this glorious day of the outstanding virgin Godeberta, brothers, it is most fitting that we devoutly beseech her herself, to whom this day is consecrated, so that, through her prayers, whatever we undertake in her praise may redound to the grace of God. For it must certainly be believed that all who in any way venerate God’s saints, by that very veneration of the saints honor in no small measure the majesty of God himself, by whose grace they are so greatly venerated.

For her glory, therefore, this distinguished virgin whose passing we celebrate—we shall hasten, with the support of her prayers and God’s permission, to record for your charity where she was born, how she served the Lord in this human life, what miracles God worked through her, and by what end she put off her human condition.

2. She was born, then, in the district of Amiens, [Note: [Col. 1519D] Perhaps in the land or castle of Bova, or de Bovis, or Bobarum, or even Bothua, commonly called Boves, about two Gallic leagues from Amiens. It was formerly distinguished by the title of barony and is now likewise a notable marquisate. Hence may have arisen the popular tradition that she came from the family of Boves. Certainly, if the saint was born there, we scarcely doubt that her parents were the lords of that place, who, as appears from what follows, were exceedingly noble. But whether the family of Boves, splendidly illuminated by Adrian de la Morlière after his work *On the Antiquities of Amiens*, is so ancient that it can claim this saint for itself, we leave for others to investigate.] of Christian parents. Reborn in holy baptism from water and the Spirit, she willingly and reverently received and carried out, wherever she could, the teachings of the holy faith. For, recognizing that by debt she was subject to a mortal condition, she already fortified the tenderness of her age with the sign of the holy cross; and night and day she most humbly commended herself to the pious prayers of the saints.

She avoided the wanton gatherings of young women whom she had heard to be irreverent; but those whom she knew to be occupied with what was useful and honorable she gladly joined and attentively imitated. For she had heard that good morals are corrupted by wicked conversations; she had also heard that one becomes holy with the holy, and that anyone is branded with the infamy of wickedness in the company of the perverse.

3. Thus carefully brought up by her parents, when she reached marriageable age, many noblemen, since she was nobly born of noble parents, tried to take her as their wife. But her parents, because they had received their benefice from the king’s hand, did not dare to consent to such a marriage with anyone without consulting the king. When the betrothal of this virgin was being discussed in the presence of King Lothair, and everyone’s attention depended upon the royal decision in the matter, Saint Eligius, by the Lord’s prior arrangement, entered their midst, betrothed the virgin with his golden ring, and most confidently presented her as Christ’s bride in the presence of the king and her parents.

O immeasurable grace of the Holy Spirit! At once the girl, as later became clear, already pregnant with the spiritual conception of divine love, rejected every carnal pleasure and set aside even the desirable succession of offspring; indeed, scorning the delightful allurements of a girl’s life, she steadfastly renounced the king and her parents and gladly commended herself in their presence to the most blessed bishop Eligius, to be consecrated to the Lord.

4. At that time this most holy bishop was governing the holy church of Noyon; by his example and preaching, very many people, converted from error and abandoning the worship of idols, rejoiced greatly that they had received the Catholic faith under so great a shepherd. This most kindly shepherd, therefore, eagerly gathered this little sheep of most gentle character into his fold, calling her from the active life into the contemplative through the spiritual ring of divine betrothal.

Thus the outstanding virgin, in the presence of the king and the nobles, freely rejecting her parents’ flattering appeals, followed without any delay Eligius, whom by the grace of the Holy Spirit she had received as her spiritual father. The bystanders were seized with great astonishment at this sudden inspiration of the Holy Spirit; her father, weeping, considered the matter with deep affection. King Lothair, too, greatly marveled at the magnificent power of divine grace in the sudden transformation of the marriage. Yet, so that this virgin might be commended by her happy prayer before the Lord, he himself hastened first to strengthen her devout purpose with royal generosity.

With those present consenting, he gave her, together with the oratory of Saint George, the palace he possessed at Noyon [Note: [Col. 1519D] Some think that the king’s palace was located there, where the Beguines’ house now stands; Montigny considers this claim to be advanced without any foundation.] He also ordered two estates [Note: [Col. 1520D] The same writer grants that it may be believed that these estates were at Vauchelles, about five leagues from Abbeville, since the Beguines still possess some property there. Thus he seems to acknowledge that they came to form part of the goods once assigned to the monastery of Saint Godeberta, and perhaps succeeded the nuns who had disappeared under a new institution.] and twelve women from the royal treasury to be assigned, under the governance of the holy virgin, for the support of divine worship.

5. They therefore gathered in the suburb of the city of Noyon, specifically in the oratory which they had received from the king, and labored tirelessly to serve God day and night. The virgin herself, instructed by Saint Eligius, formed those living with her not only through preaching but also through manifold examples of virtue.

Avoiding the gatherings of worldly people, she continued fasts of two or three days. She constantly ministered to the hungry with food, to the thirsty with drink, and to the naked with clothing, even though you would have seen her herself in need of all these things. She also spent the entire night in vigils and prayers, continually beseeching the Lord for the salvation of all. She persisted constantly in these and similar practices; and although she was still held bodily in the world, each day she nevertheless offered herself as an acceptable holocaust to the Lord.

Seeing such perseverance in his beloved, the Lord did not disdain to glorify her devotion openly while she still remained in fragile flesh. For God worked frequent miracles through her intercession: he restored sight to the blind, walking to the lame, and health to the paralytic; and, what we believe to be more pleasing to God, through her exhortation he frequently brought unbelievers to the faith. Therefore, so that she may become a certain example to all the faithful, setting aside the detraction of her rivals, we shall relate a few things from among the many.

## Chapter Two. The Miracles of Saint Godeberta During Her Life

6. Let us therefore recount what first comes to mind, so that the hearts of the faithful who happen to hear it may be strengthened and the foreheads of unbelievers may be crushed by the hardest stones of her miracles. In her time, as the sins of the people of Noyon demanded, a pestilential sword of mortality raged in that city. For an implacable wrath had gone forth from God and was devastating the inhabitants on every side: it ceaselessly slew parents with their children, husbands with their wives, masters with their household servants, and raged without restraint against both the powerful and the common people.

Those who could escape fled in every direction; and, since most of the inhabitants had already been taken away, many houses remained empty in the city. An even more grievous misery followed this great calamity, alas, when, with everyone terrified by fear of death, the bodies of the dead were thrown out unburied. Whoever buried a dead person was himself suddenly carried out, dead, to be buried. No one at all was without fear of the death threatening him, whenever he happened to bury or touch a dead person.

7. In the midst of this great danger of mortality, the distinguished virgin Godeberta, attentive to the universal grief of the citizens, imposed a three-day fast upon the whole Church. She taught them to persist tearfully in prayer and to appease divine indignation by fasting and almsgiving: “For,” she said, “just as water extinguishes fire, so almsgiving extinguishes sin.”

The outstanding virgin also taught them the salutary repentance of the Ninevites: how, sitting in ashes and sackcloth, through the mysteries of fasting and prayer they restrained the sentence of divine condemnation that already hung over them. She likewise recounted to them the remarkable example of King David, who, as God himself testifies, was found to be a man after God’s heart, and how readily he was received into healing through repentance for the adultery he had committed. She added Peter’s denial, the confession of the thief on the cross, and the mournful lamentation of the sinful Mary, showing how easily they obtained forgiveness for their deeds through penitential tears.

Breathing in response to these and other exhortations of the glorious virgin, they undertook that three-day fast with the greatest devotion; and immediately, through her merits and intercessions, the pious grace of God caused that pestilential sword of mortality to cease.

8. A few days later the same virgin—who had worn down her tender flesh with excessive austerity—fell into a most painful bodily illness, as often happens to those who in some way become unaccustomed to their customary foods: they waste away for a long time or suddenly become disordered. [Note: [Col. 1521] We have corrected this conjecturally; the manuscript reads: “Many times indeed it happened to those who how accustomed.”]

The virgin therefore lay exhausted in bed, yet with the whole desire of her mind she yearned toward the Lord. Though burdened in body, she remained vigorous in spirit and constantly persevered in praising God. During this illness of hers, an unexpected fire suddenly broke out around the principal church of Saint Mary. In its sudden advance, it completely consumed all the church’s ornaments. The flame swept around and seized everything; since no one could resist it, each person sought safety by fleeing before it. Everything lay exposed to this danger: some things had already been consumed, while others still remained to be devoured by the advancing fire.

As the inhabitants of the city fled in every direction, as we have said, the mother church of the holy Virgin Mary remained deserted. Since the flame had already become stronger than their powers, the deeply saddened people commended it to God alone with the most devout tears. Moved by the great sobbing of the mourners, the virgin Godeberta, though weighed down by a grave illness, nevertheless ordered herself to be carried out in a chair and confidently placed against the violence of the fire, wherever the flame might strike.

When she had been set down near the very blaze of the fiery chasm, while many were already despairing of her sight, she confidently opposed the sign of the holy cross, which she knew to be most salutary in every danger. Immediately that destructive fire was extinguished.

9. At another time, a certain blind woman named Trausirica came to the holy virgin, so that through her pious intercession she might receive the temporal light of her eyes, which she had lost in infancy. As she persisted in tearful prayers with certain hope of illumination, the outstanding virgin, after first making intercession to God, placed her hand upon the woman’s eyes. Having lightly made the sign of the holy cross, she obtained through her prayer the desired favor of divine mercy, and restored bodily light to the woman. Thus it came about that, while she recovered temporal sight, she was also enlivened by spiritual vivification of the soul and afterward served God there, beside her illuminatrix, for the whole of her life.

10. Thus Trausirica deserved to be illuminated through devotion. But Vulgudis, of whom we must now speak, was punished by the same Virgin with interminable blindness for her disobedience. This Vulgudis had devoted herself to God in the monastery of Saint Godeberta; but, being far too impatient in spirit, she behaved contentiously and irreverently toward the others. For that reason, when she was frequently corrected by the holy virgin, she quarreled arrogantly with her and spoke excessively shameful and abusive words in her presence.

The holy virgin, greatly provoked by that foolish woman’s anger, perceived that she was incorrigible and was irreverently resisting the spur of obedience. One day, while the woman was engaged in her shameful quarrel, the saint, extremely angry, spat directly in her face. Immediately that unfortunate woman lost the light of her eyes and remained blind for all the days of her life.

11. Through these and other reports of miracles, this virgin became known everywhere, and her most celebrated reputation spread far and wide. Consequently, multitudes of sick people came to her from distant regions, and through the holy intercession of the virgin God’s most merciful compassion bestowed upon them the benefit of various kinds of healing.

From these things that have come to our knowledge you can infer that this virgin performed many other miracles, which have already exceeded human report. Although they are hidden from us, her true devotion is known to God alone; he rewarded her mortal life with the immortal prize of eternal perpetuity. For the Lord, seeing the spirit of his beloved immovably fixed upon the purpose of holy religion, so that no further wickedness might alter her heart and no deception might mislead her soul, summoned her from earthly things to heavenly things, from labor to rest, and from temporal misery to perpetual happiness. Mercifully stripping her of the corruptible body of human frailty, he more mercifully adorned her soul with the incorruptible garment of angelic fellowship.

12. Thus the most holy virgin Godeberta, having happily completed the time of her earthly dwelling, was placed with the choirs of holy virgins in the beauty of the heavenly paradise. There she joyfully sings a new song to the Lord with the other saints; there she awaits with confident hope the day of the future judgment. Although the archangels themselves must tremble and quake at that day, they will nevertheless tremble in compassion for the sentence of the perdition of human beings, not of themselves.

This, then, is the end which, as we have said, the virgin, now joined to God, awaits; and in heaven she unceasingly entreats God for our sins. Thus the outstanding servant of God was buried on the third day before the Ides of April, in the oratory of Blessed George, in the church now called of the Holy Apostles. [Note: [Col. 1523D] If the author of the Life is Ratbod, should we conclude that, after the body of Saint Godeberta had been removed from that church, it first began to be called by her name? It would not be unreasonable that, as time passed and the church fell into decay, it was later restored and consecrated under Saint Godeberta’s name, although her body had long ceased to be kept there. We nevertheless admit that the contrary seems more fitting; and for that reason we have doubted whether the first translation of Saint Godeberta was not made much later, perhaps in the thirteenth century, when the canons grew weary of continually assigning four of their own body to serve in a different church.] There they also honorably buried the body of Saint Mommolen, bishop of that same city. Many benefits are bestowed there upon the sick and needy through her holy intercession, to the praise and glory of her name, whose honor and dominion endure forever and ever.

## Chapter Three. Miracles Performed at the Tomb of Saint Godeberta

[Col. 1523D]

13. But lest anyone doubt this virgin’s heavenly reward, we do not refuse to commit to writing those miracles that God performed at her burial as well. After her passing, a woman named Agildrud, blind from infancy, happened to hear of the most celebrated fame of the holy virgin. Confidently hoping for herself what she had heard about others, she came to Noyon, though not without great difficulty.

When she had entered the oratory in which the virgin lay, she asked those present to lead her to the tomb where she had heard that the body of the blessed virgin had been buried. When she reached it, she wept there for a long time on the pavement and with heavy sighs prayed that, through the prayers of the holy virgin, the sight she had long ago lost might be obtained again for her from the Lord.

There was no delay: because she prayed faithfully and did not despair in prayer of God’s grace and Saint Godeberta’s power, through the saint’s intervention she deserved to be illuminated with bodily sight. Nor do we doubt that she was illuminated not only in bodily but also in spiritual eyes, since afterward, for the whole of her life, we heard that in the same place she followed the regular discipline with the others in the service of God. Thus, by God’s permission, it came about that while she prayed for physical light, the spiritual eyes of her soul were also illuminated through the intercession of this virgin.

14. Nor does it seem right to pass over Audemia: we should relate how, brought there from the village of Raugia, she was healed at the virgin’s tomb. [Note: [Col. 1524D] So writes Louis de Montigny, whom we would consider more trustworthy than Surius, who writes *Raugiam*, in identifying the name of a place situated in the diocese of Noyon. But since our copyist’s writing is ambiguous, and he nowhere indicates in his annotations where this place is, we fear that it may have been equally unknown to him.]

From infancy this woman had been completely weakened throughout her body, as though paralytic. When she heard of the holy virgin’s celebrated reputation, she scarcely obtained from her friends—who had already grown weary of her prolonged illness—that she be carried there. At last brought to the aforementioned basilica, she ordered them to present her as near as they could before the presence of the holy virgin.

Having obtained this, she crawled as best she could across the pavement and, with the whole desire of her heart and mouth, appealed to the holy virgin, asking that through her most sacred intercession she might deserve to receive from the Lord healing from the paralysis that was bringing her to death. Suddenly she perceived that health had been restored to her limbs. Made strong, she rejoiced greatly to return on her own feet, though she had come in another’s vehicle.

15. The healing of Gislegardis also now comes to mind. Since she had been afflicted with blindness of the eyes from infancy, she received her sight through the virgin’s intervention. A white film had been dripping from her eyes and, from the time she was a baby, had spread a dark obscurity before them. In the presence of all who stood by, her face brightened, and before the virgin’s tomb she received the freely given gift of sight.

16. Nor will we be silent about the healing of a certain woman named Imperia, who was almost recalled from death itself through Saint Godeberta’s intercession. She was already half-dead and had lost nearly every bodily function: her sight, hearing, and even the power of speech had almost entirely failed her. To conclude everything briefly, she lay on her little bed like some aborted creature.

When she learned of the many miracles of this woman devoted to God, she obtained permission to be brought before the memory of the saint’s prayer. When she had been carried there and laid down beside her holy burial place, she commended her desire to the holy virgin as best she could, murmuring humbly that through her she might receive some remedy from the Lord for such great suffering.

What could she do? She sighed with her heart and wept with her eyes; but with her mouth, since she could not fully form words, she seemed amid the groans of her innermost being to howl rather than speak. Yet, though the tongue of her heart was silent, she displayed as much devotion as she could and, more through inward movement than speech, urged the holy virgin to intercede for her weakness.

Seeing such earnestness in that half-dead woman, the virgin, through her successful intercession before the Lord, obtained the removal of her illness and restored the long-desired health to that most wretched body. Immediately the woman who had long lain paralyzed received back the light of her eyes, the hearing of her ears, and also the freedom of her tongue. Giving thanks to God and to the holy virgin, she returned safely to her own dwelling.

17. Perhaps, beloved, you are weary of hearing so many and such great miracles of the holy virgin. Yet even if they are tedious to you, God will permit us not to be silent about the mighty works of God and the saints. For God himself, through whom every holy thing is sanctified, testifies in the Gospel that he is received or rejected in the reception or rejection of the saints, saying: “Whoever despises you despises me, and whoever receives you receives me.”

It is therefore necessary, brothers, both that you retain with gratitude what you have heard and that you receive with cheerful and attentive spirit what remains to be added.

18. Amid these and certain other things that God worked through her, the annual cycle happened to revolve, and the anniversary day on which the holy virgin had passed from the world was presented to the faithful people. With what and how great rejoicing they received that day, and with what and how great devotion they celebrated it, neither are we able fully to reconsider in meditation nor has our incompetence been granted to explain vividly.

For who could describe so great an assembly of people? Who could set forth the devotion and tearful joy of those who had gathered, or their spontaneous offerings? You would see crowds of both sexes, mingled together, hastening from every direction like bees to a hive; ranks of clergy, communities of monks, crowds of virgins—in short, the entire gathering of both sexes—converging upon the same joy and, with one mind and equal agreement, invoking the blessed memory of the holy virgin.

After the solemn office of Mass had been performed and many acts of thanksgiving had been offered to God and the virgin, everyone returned to his own home. The church’s custodians, after extinguishing nearly all the lights and closing the church doors, went out at the proper hour for refreshment.

After the meal, when many of them had returned to that church to give due thanks to God, the doorkeepers opened the doors and found all the lamps and candles—which they had extinguished in the presence of everyone—miraculously rekindled.

19. There was great applause from everyone over this miracle of God and the holy virgin. All gathered into the same joy; with one and the same mind, unanimous and equal in agreement, they hurried to the holy virgin’s oratory. The same devotion filled their minds, and the same universal joy was present in all because of God’s ineffable benefaction. As some entered and others returned, they all encouraged one another with a single consolation to praise God.

Some recalled the merit of the holy virgin; others marveled at the wonderful gift of divine recompense. He, plainly, who entered to his disciples when the doors were shut, entering now also through closed doors, declared through the lighting of the lamps that this virgin was without doubt one of those whom the evangelical bridegroom, according to his own testimony, brought with him to the wedding with lamps kindled.

Nor did he grant this alone to his virgin; he also miraculously permitted those same candles and lamps, without any diminution of wax or oil, to burn for the following seven days in the presence and testimony of the entire people. [Note: [Col. 1525D] Surius, who had greatly abridged the account of the miracles in this chapter, has only a few lines from this point onward and concludes the entire narrative in that way.]

20. Many miracles are frequently reported to occur in that same place. As commonly happens because of their frequency, some are known to have slipped from memory and others to have lost their importance; nevertheless, we are not reluctant to record again for your fraternity those that come to our memory.

The very celebrated fame of the blessed virgin, which had stirred many others, reached the ears of a certain paralytic named Gregory. He was so weakened and undone by the disease of paralysis that he could not move even a hand or foot; indeed, his body was already half-dead, and scarcely could the vital spirit breathe in his chest alone.

Nevertheless, trying to crawl across the ground by whatever means he could, he finally reached the desired tomb of the most holy virgin. There, shedding many streams of tears with great devotion, he implored the remedy for his illness through the merit of the virgin Saint Godeberta.

After he had persisted without fatigue in groaning and weeping, crying and lamenting until evening, he received in an instant, through the pious favor of the most sacred virgin, complete health throughout his body, as though he had never suffered any injury. Everyone wept for joy, because they saw walking, healthy and unharmed, the man whom they had almost believed to be lifeless.

Nor do we think that we should pass over what we marvel that this virgin accomplished through Harveus. [Note: [Col. 1526D] Surius likewise calls him *Harneus*; our copy reads *Haureus* both times.]

21. This Harveus, afflicted with blindness, had traveled through many holy places for this reason and had also visited the shrines of the Apostles Peter and Paul. After waiting there for several days, when he perceived that he was gaining nothing for himself, he returned sadly to his own home with his endeavor unsuccessful.

Thus sitting in darkness and almost in the shadow of death, he mourned his days. Since he lived among others who could see, he repeatedly observed their light, thereby increasing his own sorrow. After visiting, as we have said, the oratories of many saints, he reached the memory of this virgin for the same purpose. There, kindled by the fervor of faith and stretching his hands toward heaven, he sang in the hidden place of his heart the words of David: “The Lord,” he said, “is my salvation and my illumination” (Psalm 26:1).

Turning with his whole heart to the most holy virgin, he earnestly commended his devotion to her. The most devout intervention of this holy virgin was heard in this matter as well; and at her humble entreaty Harveus, because he had persevered faithfully in prayer, was not deprived of his desire.

There are also many other miracles of this virgin, beloved, which, as we have said, have not come to our knowledge. But concerning both those that are manifest and those that are unknown, we ought to praise together the most holy magnificence of God, who, through the imitable example of the weaker sex, continually invites such fragile human beings to the everlasting reward of eternal life.

## Epilogue
22. Therefore, brothers, although we use bodily eyes, we are nevertheless blind in soul; being excessively intent upon earthly things, we wickedly put heavenly things second; lusting after temporal things, we value nothing spiritual. Let us now, even if late, earnestly implore the virginity of this patroness of ours, namely the most blessed virgin Godeberta; and, so that she may deign humbly to intercede for us before the divine majesty whom she served tirelessly, let us recall this virgin’s devoted persistence in God’s service; let us marvel at the clemency of our Savior, inclined, so to speak, to answer her prayers.

We have just heard that this blind man Harveus, when he had obtained nothing from the holy apostles concerning his blindness, recovered his sight through this great virgin. Let us also believe that through her, if we seek rightly, we may be truly illumined by God from the blindness of our hearts. We have heard that the paralytic Gregory received a remedy for his paralysis through her mediation. Let us also believe that, if we repent from our hearts, we shall be healed through her—those who, deprived, alas, of all the functions of the soul, are too sluggish to walk along the way of virtue.

We read that the lamps which had been extinguished in her oratory were suddenly kindled with fire. Let us believe and hold it as certain that the spiritual darkness of our souls can, through her intervention, be divinely kindled.

Now, dearly beloved, let us raise our hearts together with our hands to the Lord in true confession, and in undisguised repentance and manifold prayers let us anticipate his face, so that, through the merits of this virgin whom he has set before us as an example, and who for the sake of her true love for him renounced the bonds of carnal marriage, he may grant that, freed from this heavy body, we may be joined bodily to his only-begotten Son, Christ our Lord, in the heavenly fellowship of the holy angels, through the same Christ our Lord. Amen.

[Col. 1527]

## RADBOD’S SERMON ON THE ANNUNCIATION OF THE BLESSED VIRGIN MARY

[Note: This sermon was formerly read in the form of lessons at Matins of the Annunciation in several churches of the diocese of Noyon.]

*(Acts of the Ecclesiastical Province of Reims, II, 100.)*

### FIRST LESSON

[Col. 1527B]

We have heard, dearly beloved brothers, of that shepherd of sheep, David—I mean the prophet, indeed the magnificent psalmist—who was divinely raised from the humble and servile keeping of sheep to the throne of a kingdom, and who earnestly invites all things to the magnificent praise of God when he says at the end of the Psalms: “Let every spirit praise the Lord.”

Earlier in the same psalm he had said: “Praise the Lord in his saints.” The psalmist David therefore urges that the Lord be praised in his saints: that is, the body in its members; the Lord in his servants; the Creator in his creation; the king in his soldiers; the teacher in his disciples; and, in things that are seen, the invisible Creator of us all. He also invites every spirit to these praises: rational creatures, that is, and irrational animals. For irrational creatures too praise God when, according to the law of their own nature and in accordance with the divine ordering, they obey the Lord their Creator.

The Lord is indeed praised in his saints when, working through them, he illumines the hearts of unbelievers, grants the power to perform miracles, sustains the weak through their benefits, and recalls to the heavenly kingdom as heirs those who were expelled from paradise because of the first transgression.

### SECOND LESSON

Since, as has been said, he urges that the Lord be praised in his saints, he teaches that he is to be honored especially in and through her from whom the culmination of the redemption of all those saints proceeded: namely, the most holy Mary, mother of our Lord Jesus Christ. To weaken the violence of death and restore to us the inheritance of the heavenly kingdom, she conceived as a virgin and gave birth while remaining a virgin; she did not lose the seal of virginity at conception, in childbirth, or even after childbirth.

By God’s wondrous and ineffable dispensation, flesh proceeded from flesh without being produced by any carnal union. What, then, brothers? Let your charity hear what the depravity of heretics rejects, what the unbelief of the Jews contradicts, and what the Catholic Church of Christians must believe from the heart.

The most holy virgin Mary, as we do not doubt you believe, descended from a royal tribe. Today she was greeted by the angel; today she conceived in her womb; today she was overshadowed by the Holy Spirit. For the angel said to her: “Hail, Mary, full of grace; the Lord is with you; blessed are you among women.”

### THIRD LESSON

He confesses her to be blessed among women—that is, among all women—since after the announcement of the divine birth she does not hesitate to profess herself a devoted and humble handmaid:

“And blessed,” he says, “is the fruit of your womb.” He foretells that the fruit of her womb is blessed; for through him, once the curse of our first parent had been erased, a blessing destined to bless the whole race of believers descended upon them. Truly she is worthy of blessing, for she gathers what was scattered, strengthens what was broken, and restores what was lost.

(Although the virgin was troubled by the vision and the angelic greeting with indescribable wonder, and, overcome for a little while by human weakness, trembled inwardly, the divine associate did not fail to perceive what she may have thought or turned over in her heart; the angelic paranymph could not remain unaware of it.)

Rather, he answered her thoughts as though they had been openly expressed. For he said: “Are you afraid, virgin? Do not fear. Are you troubled? Do not be troubled. You have found grace with the Lord, through whom the fruit of your womb is also blessed.

“For behold, you will conceive and bear a son, and you will call his name Jesus”—that is, Savior, the Savior of all his own.

At this angelic consolation the young virgin breathed again for a little while and, with lowered face, said: “How shall it happen that I give birth, when I have never experienced the condition of giving birth? I have not endured the pleasures of childbirth; I have in no way undergone the experiences of a woman; moreover, I have not known a man.”

“Why,” said the angel, “are you needlessly afraid? You will conceive the wondrous one wondrously, because ‘the Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you. Therefore the holy one who will be born from you will be called the Son of God.’”

“The Holy One,” he says, “will be born. What Holy One? The Holy of Holies. And what is the Holy of Holies? The Son of God,” he says.

O longed-for promise, immaculate conception, wondrous and saving birth!

### FOURTH LESSON

It was said to our first mother: “In sorrow you will conceive and give birth”; but to the most holy Virgin it was said: “The power of the Most High will overshadow you.” For just as rain falls upon fleece, so the power promised by God descended into the virgin’s womb.

The Son of God was incarnate from the Holy Spirit and became the Son of Man in the virgin’s womb, proceeding from it like a bridegroom from his bridal chamber.

What are you thinking about these things, Mary? What are you considering within yourself, inviolate mother?

Come, let those who believe in the Lord’s Annunciation rejoice together with the most devoted response of this holy young woman:

“Behold,” she says, “the handmaid of the Lord.”

You are a virgin, yet you are chosen as a mother without being humbled by a man; you are to be preferred to mothers, the mother of the Savior and King—and you profess yourself a handmaid. True Humility looked upon your humility. For from you will proceed that holy Humility at whose command all pride will fall, the gates of hell will fall, and it will introduce its faithful into the kingdoms of heaven.

“Behold,” Mary says, “the handmaid of the Lord.”

When she voluntarily professes herself to be in this condition, she does not deny that by right she is subject to the Lord’s dominion:

“Behold,” she says, “the handmaid of the Lord; let it be done to me according to your word.”

“Let it be done” expresses one who desires, not one who commands: “Let it be done, so that the presence of our Redeemer may, through me, his little handmaid, come to the aid of his faithful, whom until now the destruction of the devil’s lot has swallowed, the devil’s ferocity has slaughtered, and finally the insatiable voracity of evil spirits has devoured in the lower hell.”

Thus, the true Son of the true God, announced by the angel, was conceived today in the virgin’s womb; and for this reason this day’s festival was called the Annunciation of the Lord.

### FIFTH LESSON

In this holy celebration, therefore, brothers and dear friends, let us venerate the beginnings of our redemption; let us offer to God, with the greatest devotion, the most devoted sacrifices of our souls, so that through the same Christ we may safely attain the most holy joys of the promised restoration.

The solemn rites of this festival, fixed on a definite date—namely, the eighth day before the Kalends of April, as we said—were hallowed by the angelic visitation, consecrated by the overshadowing of the Holy Spirit, and confirmed by the authority of the holy Fathers to be celebrated in the same Holy Spirit.

But because it often happened to fall on the days of the Lord’s Passion or Resurrection, on which the commemoration of the saints is forbidden, we have learned from the holy Fathers that, in a certain council of the Church of Toledo, it was decreed that whenever this occurred, the feast should solemnly be transferred to the fifteenth day before the Kalends of January. Thus the Lord’s days might be celebrated as duty required, and the most devout solemnity of the holy Annunciation might not be neglected.

According to this decree, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1081, on the Thursday before Palm Sunday, the date of the festival happened to fall. Because of the council’s decree, neither did the people celebrate it, nor did the priestly order announce that it should be celebrated, as was its duty.

The people therefore went out to servile labor: some to agriculture, some to tending vineyards, some to crafts, and others to the work of building or repairing. Both sexes devoted themselves to various labors. But because this most holy virgin endured these things with indignation, she wished the matter itself to be made manifest wondrously on that very day.

The Queen of Heaven could, not unjustly, have avenged the violation of her day and the dishonor of her solemnity more severely and upon the stronger male sex; but, in pious mercy, although she was angered, she restrained her wrath. As a mistress toward a handmaid, as a queen toward a very humble person, she mercifully exposed the offense of the woman who had sinned by working, so that others might be chastened.

### SIXTH LESSON

At that time there was in Gaul, specifically in the suburb of the city of Noyon, a certain young girl named Eremburgis, born in that suburb and descended from that same people. She was poor, born of very poor parents, and therefore worked diligently at her labors.

(She earned her living by skill and manual labor, engaging in textile work according to the custom of her sex.)

On that same day, while, as is customary for women when spinning, she moistened thread with saliva, the thread adhered to her tongue and twisted both together as though bound fast.
