Her tongue was almost wound around her swollen lip. What could she do? She struggled in vain, trying to pull it away. She called out to others for help, but achieved nothing.

Already, from the extremity of the pain, coagulated saliva had disfigured her mouth into foam, and her lips, joined to her tongue, had lost the natural power of spitting. The girl wept and was tormented terribly. Those standing by also grieved, sincerely sympathizing with her.

Her mother happened by chance to be absent from this unhappy spectacle; but when the neighbors summoned her and she saw her daughter almost lifeless, she too, as though lifeless, declared that the girl was suffering such things by divine judgment, because her own father had informed her on the preceding day that the feast of holy Mary was soon to be celebrated.

The neighbors tried to bring her some medicinal remedy, but they did not know that the miracle of this cure had been reserved for the most sacred virgin whom the girl had provoked to indignation.

At last, following wiser counsel, they presented the wretched girl to the holy confessor Eligius, to obtain heavenly indulgence. While he lived, he was remarkable for doctrine and virtue; even today, by God’s arrangement, his virtues are frequently made manifest by miracles, as we ourselves have seen with our own eyes.

They vowed their vows at his tomb and offered prayers to the Lord with tears, then returned without accomplishing their purpose. Nevertheless, we believe that the saint later obtained for her, through his pious intervention, what was done.

In that great gathering of the people, therefore, the merciful one who reveals things to little ones and hides them from the wise, taking pity on the misery of the wretched, sent them in his own mission to the church of the mother of his own mother, so that the girl might be freed by the merits of the one against whom she had sinned, and absolved by the prayers of the one whom she had rashly offended.

Thus they went to the principal monastery of Saint Mary, and an innumerable crowd of citizens gathered there. Some, pouring out tears, others, with silent prayers, entreated the divine mercy to deign to remove from the poor girl the sentence of so severe a punishment.

Everywhere one might see the tools of the laborers thrown aside, the works of their hands abandoned, and all the work of the artisans utterly renounced. Those who had sinned promised to amend their fault, and they and the others vowed with all their hearts that thereafter they would celebrate the solemnity with the greatest devotion.

### SEVENTH LESSON

Meanwhile, as they hastened to the basilica of Saint Mary, a priest of not entirely sound mind happened to meet them. When they answered his questions, he took this as a pretense for profit and said:

“I will sympathize with your groans, and for the present I will be the faithful physician of this suffering young girl.”

Saying this, he violently seized the hanging thread and pulled it even more violently. But when the tongue was almost torn out by his pulling, he was terrified by the girl’s loud cry and, confessing before the people that he had sinned, withdrew in confusion from what he had begun.

Meanwhile they reached the episcopal seat of the holy Church of Noyon. The grieving mother and her daughter were placed before the altar of the most sacred ever-Virgin. The priests and the people earnestly sought the intercession of the same Mother of God, asking that, setting aside the offense, she might turn toward the girl the merciful compassion believed to be her own, so that through her liberation they might render thanks to God through her grace, and so that this solemn feast might be solemnly celebrated in that city forever and ever.

A great multitude of both sexes had indeed gathered in the church, entreating and faithfully awaiting heavenly indulgence for the poor girl’s grievous suffering. With contrite and humbled hearts, the priests blessed the Lord; indeed, all with one accord entreated the clemency of the glorious Virgin, asking that in her accustomed kindness she might pity their tears and not disdain to loosen the bonds of the young girl, who was already as good as dead.

(At last the most blessed Virgin, moved by such prayers and by the returning force of their tears,)

turned judgment into mercy before him who through her came into the world for the deliverance of the wretched. She obtained relief for the afflicted girl and, before those standing by, granted by miraculous grace the loosening of her bonds.

For when the girl, seething with extreme anguish yet asking forgiveness with whatever groan she could produce, tearfully kissed the altar of the same holy virgin Mary, divine grace came down from heaven to confirm the faith and devotion of the faithful. What neither the girl’s own strength, nor that of the aforementioned priest, nor that of her parents could accomplish, grace mercifully shook loose the bond from her little lip before those standing by. Her tongue, however, remained tortured for a little while longer under the same kind of twisting, so as to magnify the glory of Christ and his Mother.

And behold, once more the people returned thanks to God with tears of devotion for the remission already received, asking God with still deeper contrition that he who had begun kindly might himself bring the matter to a more gracious completion.

At last the kindness of our Savior received the prayers of the humble through the intercession of the glorious ever-Virgin. He sent the antidote of remission and mercifully poured a drop of the sweetest dew to cool the burning of the swollen tongue.

### EIGHTH LESSON

The thread was rejected by divine mercy, the tongue was completely loosened, and indeed the full function of speech was restored. The greatest thanksgiving was offered; tears were turned into rejoicing and groans into musical instruments.

There was great joy among the people. Praises to the Lord rang out everywhere. As the church bells resounded, the spiritual orders of the clergy devoutly sang the *Te Deum laudamus*, while men and women of both sexes praised God with whatever voice they possessed.

(Since the poor girl had no offering at hand to present at the altar of the most holy Virgin for the health she had recovered, she gratefully gave herself thereafter as her bondwoman [capitalitia], on the advice of those standing by.)

Thus, after immense thanksgiving, the people who had earlier been moved to contrition by compassion later departed, shedding tears of devotion for joy.

From this point onward, therefore, brothers, since we have discussed the conception of the Lord, let us turn our pen for a little while, by his own grace, toward the virgin from whom he was conceived, and let us dwell at least briefly upon her praises. From her undefiled womb we rejoice that we have wondrously received so great a Redeemer.

Before the Lord’s coming, all the faithful awaited this holy virgin, devoted to God, ineffable and to be preferred above all, with faithful prayers. The most holy prophets, in the Holy Spirit, foretold her wondrous conception; and although they did not know the limit of her future glorification, through her they awaited for themselves and for all future believers an endless aid in saving redemption.

The prophet Isaiah teaches us about the glorification of this virgin:

“A branch,” he says, “will come forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower will rise from his root.”

Again the same prophet says more explicitly:

“Behold, a virgin will conceive and bear a son.”

Thus the prophet speaks of the Virgin:

“Behold, a virgin will conceive.”

But the angel says to the same Virgin:

“Behold, you will conceive and bear a son,” and so forth.

Let the faithful hear that the words of the prophet and of the evangelist do not differ. Let them marvel at the virgin’s ineffable faith and at the still more ineffable conception of Christ.

Shall I call it Christ’s conception, or the virgin’s? But, to speak more accurately, I shall call it both Christ’s and the virgin’s. A woman conceived, and a man was conceived; the same woman, a virgin, conceived, and the same man, Christ, was conceived.

(Therefore, all who do not consider themselves redeemed by this conception should rejoice with the Son and the Mother in this solemnity.)

Let them venerate the Son’s mother in exultation; let them praise the mother’s Son in holy devotion. For just as the praise of a disciple is the honor of the teacher, so the veneration of the Virgin is the glory of Christ. Thus may the admonition of the prophet David be fulfilled:

“Praise the Lord in his saints.”

For is it not fitting that Christ also be praised in this holy Mother of his, since, after the many and innumerable miracles he worked through her, he so mercifully deigned to assist the young girl whose case we have recounted, for the honor of her solemnity?

But because the people of Noyon recognized that they had been heard for the strengthening of believers’ faith, and because they faithfully experienced the miracles wondrously performed publicly in honor of the holy Virgin, they learned that the present solemnity should be celebrated perpetually in that place until the day of the Lord’s Supper. In this they did not dissent from the councils of the holy Fathers, but confidently believed that, after so great a miracle had been manifested, they would serve the Lord more fully in this matter also.

Let us therefore celebrate too, brothers, with the greatest devotion, the solemnity of this holy Annunciation. Let us believe that through her the good of redemption has come to us in its fullness, and that through her the faithful will likewise receive the joys of the perpetual resurrection. May the same Son of God and of man lead us to them—he who, born from God the Father before all ages as God, and conceived in time from the Holy Spirit by his mother as man, lives and reigns with the same Father in the unity of the same Holy Spirit, forever and ever. Amen.

[Col. 1533]

## RADBOD’S LETTER TO LAMBERT, BISHOP OF ARRAS

*(See under Lambert, around the year 1115.)*

[Col. 1533]

## RADBOD’S CHARTERS

### I. Charter by which Radbod, Bishop of Noyon, grants the altar of Capi to the church of Saint Peter of Cluny

In it the bishop’s authority over monks placed in charge of churches and over abbots is declared. *(Year 1086.)*

*[Marrier, History of Saint-Martin-des-Champs, p. 340.]*

[Col. 1533D]

I, RADBOD, unworthy bishop of Noyon, wish it to be known to all the faithful that, moved by the fear of God and through the intervention of the monks, I received the altar of Capi from the hand of Rodbert of Péronne and his heirs, to whom it had fallen by benefice; and, with the clergy of Saint Mary consenting—in fact, urging me—I granted it to the church of Saint Peter of Cluny to be held perpetually, for the remission of my sins.

This was on the following condition: that the priest serving me should render an account to me of the care of souls he had undertaken and should pay to me and my ministers the customary due. If, by God’s ordering, a community should be established there, the abbot would have power to correct faults. But if the abbot or prior acted negligently, correction of the monks would then devolve upon the bishop of Noyon.

So that this charter might remain more firmly established in future times, we have written below the names of those present.

Sign of Radbod, bishop. Sign of Gerilin, dean. Sign of Baldric, archdeacon. Sign of Walcher, treasurer. Sign of Odo, provost. Sign of Guido, chancellor. Sign of Ivo, castellan. Sign of Wincmar Rodbert. Sign of Gosbert.

Done at Noyon, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1086, indiction IX, while King Philip was reigning, in the twenty-fifth year, and while Lord Radbod was bishop, in the nineteenth year.

### II. For the Restoration of the Abbey of Saint Martin of Tournai

[Note: The abbey of Saint Martin of Tournai was founded in 652 by Saint Eligius, who placed religious there under the rule of Saint Columbanus. The Norman invasion in the ninth century drove out the religious, and the abbey remained deserted until 1092. At that time Radbod established regular canons there; two years later they embraced the rule of Saint Benedict and recovered the properties that had been usurped.]

*(Year 1094.)*

*[Ecclesiastical Province of Reims, II, 119.]*

In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, I, RADBOD, bishop of the people of Noyon and Tournai, extend every good wish to those of the future as well as to those of the present.

Let your charity know, dearly beloved brothers, that the church of Saint Martin of Modicum, situated on Mount Modicum near the walls of the city of Tournai, was formerly an abbey. But when pagans invaded that city, it was destroyed and subsequently reduced to lay control, and it nearly came to nothing. Its desolation became so complete that not even the office of a single priest could be fully maintained there.

That community was scattered and departed by the hostile hand; the household of that church was slain and perished. A lay hand had held its lands as a benefice from the hand of our predecessors and from ours for a long time afterward.

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1092, however, the pious mercy of God, remembering that church, kindled from heaven with spiritual grace the minds of Brother Odo and four others. With one and the same purpose, fearing that they might become entangled in the filthy abyss of this world, they chose rather to serve God in poverty in the aforesaid church than to abound in worldly riches to the destruction of their souls.

When for this reason they had come into our presence, with the counsel and assistance of Radulf the advocate, who at that time possessed it by hereditary right, and in the presence of clergy and laity, we granted that same church to them, together only with its adjacent courtyard, on the condition that they should possess it freely as an abbey and serve God there under the rule of Saint Augustine as regular canons.

In the following year after their entry, they were inspired by God with an even greater desire, since they were already laboring to share in the fellowship of the good. They voluntarily chose what they considered stricter, namely, to serve God; devoting themselves to divine grace, they received with contrition the habit of Saint Benedict.

Having recognized their tireless perseverance, in that same year, with God’s assent, the church grew so greatly through the alms of the inhabitants that seventeen monks were established there under the authority of the aforesaid Odo, the abbot, and were organized to serve God and Saint Martin according to the Rule of Saint Benedict.

When the people living around them saw something of the brothers’ devotion, they reminded us of the lands that the abbey had held in ancient times, asking that we recollect them and return them, for the remission of our sins, to the uses of the brothers to whom they had been assigned.

Although this seemed exceedingly difficult, we willingly yielded to their favorable requests. We approached the advocate Radulf, whom we learned was then holding the lands as a benefice, and for the consolation of his soul we carefully advised him, in accordance with our office, what he ought to do in this matter.

Immediately, inflamed by the ineffable grace of the Holy Spirit, the man’s heart responded graciously to everything. He returned freely to Saint Martin the lands that he possessed in his own domain, so that we might restore them to that church; and he also freely and willingly granted to the church all the other lands belonging to the same jurisdiction which others held from him in pledge or as a benefice, in whatever manner they might come to the church—whether by redemption or through the charitable manumission of those who held them.

Let every age and sex that may hear this know, therefore, that Radulf, together with us, freely granted to the church of Saint Martin all those lands which the church had held in ancient times, whenever and however they might be freed from those who had until then possessed them, and freely returned them to be held thereafter and forever for the use of the brothers dwelling there.

But so that this acknowledgment of ours may remain unshaken forever, we have impressed our seal of humility upon this charter. If anyone knowingly violates it from now on, unless he returns to make amends, let him incur the inextricable bond of God, of all the saints, and thereafter of our excommunication.

Sign of Lord Radbod, bishop. Sign of Baldric, archdeacon. Sign of Peter, cantor. Sign of Ornulf, priest. Sign of Roscelin, priest. Sign of Maurin, priest. Sign of Segard, deacon. Sign of Gerelin, deacon. Sign of Alold, deacon. Sign of Stephen, subdeacon. Sign of Landric, acolyte. Sign of Odo, acolyte. Sign of Hagenon, acolyte. Sign of Hugh, castellan. Sign of Hugh of Calmac. Sign of Helinand, knight. Sign of Sagnato, knight. Sign of Gosbert, knight. Sign of Walter, archdeacon of Tournai. Sign of Peter, dean. Sign of Herimann, provost. Sign of Olbert, cantor. Sign of Stephen, priest. Sign of Hellin, priest. Sign of John, priest. Sign of Ledbert, deacon. Sign of Bernuin, subdeacon. Sign of Ingebrand, acolyte. Sign of Werric, acolyte. Sign of Onvard, castellan. Sign of Rodulf, advocate. Sign of Gonter, knight. Sign of Rodulf, knight. Sign of Lidbert, knight.

Done at Noyon, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1094, indiction I, while King Philip was reigning, in the thirty-sixth year, and while Lord Radbod was bishop, in the twenty-sixth year.

I, Guido, chancellor, have read and confirmed this below.

### III. Charter of the Donation of the Church of Saint Mary of Bruges, Made by Radbod, Bishop of Noyon, to Nuns

*(Year 1094.)*

*(Gallia Christiana nova, vol. V, col. 354.)*

In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, I, RADBOD, the least of the bishops of Noyon and Tournai.

I wish it to be known to all generations of the faithful, both those now living and those who will succeed them in the future, that I have granted the church of Saint Mary, which is at Bruges, the following privilege of freedom.

The cleric Bernerus and Gummarus, who had long held that altar in the capacity of its incumbent, moved to contrition by the regard of divine grace, repeatedly appealed to me with tireless insistence through Walter, then archdeacon, and the other clergy, asking that I receive that altar freely from their hands, release it freely from every secular exaction, and establish nuns to serve there from the revenues of the same altar and from the other resources that they had vowed for the remission of their sins.

Giving a favorable ear to their benevolent petition, I freely received the aforesaid altar of Saint Mary, as they had requested. I granted the nuns who were to be established there the power to elect their own abbess canonically, to whom the bishop would entrust spiritual care and the administration of temporal goods.

The abbess herself, receiving both forms of authority from the bishop, would render to the bishop, in both matters, the canonical and due obedience; and, once elected by the nuns and canonically installed by the bishop, she would have the power to distribute the prebends canonically. Each year, on the feast of the holy apostles Simon and Jude, she would pay five solidi to the bishop in recognition of the church.

Since the aforesaid church remains under the bishop’s lordship, I have, with the counsel of our confrères, added a further provision to it: namely, I have granted the church the power both to excommunicate canonically those who wronged it and to absolve them, on the condition, however, that if the excommunication were confirmed by the bishop’s ministers, compensation for the excommunication should be paid to the bishop and his ministers.

So that this privilege of our grant may not henceforth be dissolved, I ordered this charter to be confirmed under the testimony of priests and clerics by our seal:

Sign of holy Lord Radbod, bishop. Sign of Walter, archdeacon. Sign of Peter, dean. Sign of Herimar, dean of Noyon. Sign of Herimann, provost. Sign of Siger, cantor. Sign of Elbert. Sign of Tetbert. Sign of Lambert.

Done at Tournai in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1094, indiction II, while King Philip was reigning, in the thirty-fifth year, and while Lord R. was bishop, in the twenty-sixth year.

I, Wido, chancellor, have confirmed this below.

## IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 1098: AGANO, BISHOP OF THE CHURCH OF AUTUN

[Col. 1539]

## HISTORICAL NOTICE

*(From the new edition of Gallia Christiana, vol. IV, p. 381.)*

[Col. 1539A]

Agano, or Hagano—or, apparently in corrupt form, Aginus—was first abbot of the Church of Autun, that is, of one of those abbeys which had been united to the chapter and whose leading canons assumed their title. This is clear from the charter of Bishop Helmoinus, cited by Mabillon, *Annales*, vol. IV, appendix, p. 711; indeed, in another diploma of the same prelate, in the same place, p. 730, he is called abbot and provost.

He later became bishop, but in precisely what year he received the pastoral staff is unknown to us. The Sammarthani say, not implausibly, that it was in 1055, although on a false basis. For they maintain that in that very year a synod of Autun was held, concerning which Hugh, a Cluniac monk, says the following in the *Life of Hugh, his abbot*:

“The duke of Burgundy, Robert, was harassing Hagano, bishop of Autun, with excessive persecution, and Burgundy was suffering everywhere from the repeated incursions of raiders. For this reason the bishops Gaufredus of Lyon, Hugh of Besançon, Achard of Chalon, and Drogo of Mâcon assembled at Autun and asked the great father of counsel, Hugh, abbot of Cluny, to come.

“He came, and the duke also came, but in wicked arrogance he refused to take part in the assembly. Angered by this, Hugh went to him and, after severely rebuking him, brought him back with him like the gentlest of sheep, to everyone’s astonishment.

“There, before a most distinguished gathering, he spoke of peace. Immediately the author of discord appeared to leave the assembly in the form of a tall man with a savage face; and at once a brilliantly white dove was seen to settle upon the abbot’s head. This portent moved the duke to reconciliation and to pardon the killing of his son for those who had been responsible for it.”

From this it is evident that this synod was not held in 1055. At it, Robert spared those who had killed his son; yet the son was not killed in the assigned year, but in 1057, as we learn from the Chronicle of Saint Stephen of Auxerre, cited by D. Duchesne, *Proof of the Genealogy of the Dukes of Burgundy*, p. 14, in these words:

“In the year 1057 Hugh, son of Robert, duke, consigned the village of Saint Bricius to fire, and 110 men perished inside the church; and in that same year he himself was killed.”

Others record this event in the year 1073, others in 1063 or 1066. We shall examine their opinion in the cases of the bishops of Chalon and Mâcon.

In 1059 he was present at that august ceremony at which Henry, king of the Franks, arranged for his eldest son Philip to be raised to the throne and made partner in the kingdom, and to be consecrated.

He subscribed the privilege of Leodegarius, archbishop of Vienne, by which he transferred the nearly ruined abbey of Saint Julian in his city to the canons of Brioude. It is said to have been dated:

“On the third day before the Kalends of March, the seventh day of the week, in the year from the Incarnation 1066, and in the thirty-fifth year of Leodegarius’s archbishopric.”

The chronological notes do not agree among themselves: in the year 1066, the seventh day of the week, that is, Saturday, fell not on the third but on the fifth day before the Kalends of March.

“In that same year, indiction IV, while Philip, king of the Franks, was reigning in the seventh year of his reign,” he subscribed the diploma by which Robert, duke of Burgundy, acknowledged the ban of the abbey of Saint Benignus of Dijon.

According to the Sammarthani, he is named in a diploma issued in the following year—so they say—in indiction IV, in the seventh year of King Philip, with Odo of Flavigny and Herminius of Saint-Seine as abbots. But this is that same year, 1066.

In the year 1070 the Second Council of Anzy was held. Nothing survives from its acts, and we know of it only through a document of Achard, bishop of Chalon, by which he gave the ancient monastery of Saint Lawrence, almost completely reduced to nothing, to the monastery of Île-Barbe, so that it might be restored. Hugo of Besançon, Agano, bishop of Autun, and Drogo of Mâcon subscribed it.

In the twelfth year of King Philip, A.D. 1072, he gave the chapel of Saint Hilary to the monastery of Cluny. In the same year he appears in the document recording the election of Hugh as abbot of Saint-Rigaud, which is said to have been made “with the great assistance of Lord Hugh [Agano], bishop of Autun.”

He was present at the act by which King Philip confirmed the ancient privileges of the monastery of Tournus in 1075, and strengthened its charter with his subscription. In the same year, on the thirteenth indiction, on the third day before the Ides of November, there is a letter of Pope Gregory VII addressed under the name of Aginus, bishop of Autun, to the bishops of Burgundy on behalf of the monks of Pothières, harassed by the clergy of Langres.

The suburban church of Saint Symphorian at Autun had by this time been almost reduced to a desert. Therefore Pope Gregory ordered it to be restored to its former condition as a monastic institution. To carry this out, Pontius of Glana, advocate of that place, with the consent of Bishop Agano, entrusted it to the monastery of Fleury to be reformed for the better. King Philip confirmed this by his letters, to which Agano subscribed in 1077.

He is mentioned with Walter the dean, Norgaudius the precentor, and Hugh of Mont-Saint-Jean, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of October 1078, with Robert the chancellor.

In the charter of King Philip he subscribed first in the following year, when the church of Saint Martin in Paris, which at that time belonged to canons, was given to Hugh, abbot of Cluny, and his successors, to be restored for the better and converted to the monastic state: “Publicly enacted at Saint-Benoît-sur-Loire, in the year of the Incarnation of the Word 1079, in the nineteenth year of our reign.”

He was present at Walter’s election as bishop of Chalon and subscribed its document in the year 1080. In that same year Count Geoffrey took the cell of Saint Denis at Nogent (Nogent-le-Rotrou) from the monks of Saint Peter of Chartres and assigned it to the Cluniacs. The document drawn up for this purpose bears the signatures of our Agano, Hugh of Langres, Walter of Chalon, and Landric of Mâcon.

Finally, he attended the Council of Meaux.

In 1081 serious disturbances arose in the Church of Tours. Fulk Rechin, count of Anjou, at the urging of King Philip, drove Archbishop Ralph from his see. Accordingly, “A. [Agano] … bishop of Autun, R. [Rainaldus] … of Langres, G. [Walter] … of Chalon, L. [Landricus] … of Mâcon, acting as primate and administering the Church of Lyons …” wrote and announced to all the bishops, abbots, and others of the province of Tours that they had summoned Fulk the count, Geoffrey, the bishop of Anjou—who had done nothing for the afflicted archbishop—and the monks of Marmoutier to the judgment of the holy see of Lyons. When these men fled the judgment by their absence on the appointed day, they removed the bishop temporarily from his episcopal and priestly office; but they struck Fulk and the aforementioned monks with the sword of excommunication by the authority of Blessed Peter and of Lord Hugh, primate and legate of the Roman Church.

In the same year he attended the Council of Issoudun and subscribed the charter by which Richard, archbishop of Bourges, granted the church of Saint Martin of Brive to Marmoutier.

In the year 1082, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of November, as the monk Clarius says in his Senones Chronicle, Walter, bishop of Meaux, died. In the following week Hugh, bishop of Die, assembled a council in the same city and there ordained Robert, abbot of Rebais, as bishop.

Agano attended. With the other prelates he subscribed the decree of Hugh the legate concerning the evil customs by which the count of Brienne was oppressing the monastery of Der. He also subscribed the charter of Guarin, count of Rosnay, for the same monastery.

He had a very serious dispute with his brother Raginardus. The latter was oppressing the people of Beaulieu “with new and unheard-of laws, excessive payments, unjust exactions, evil customs,” and other intolerable burdens. When the bishop was informed of these matters, he showed no consideration for flesh and blood; rather, using the authority of Roclenus, bishop of Chalon, and Hugh, duke of Burgundy, he restrained his brother’s crimes and abolished all the burdens under which the wretched people were being crushed.

At first Raginardus refused to obey, but at last he came to his senses and drew up a charter, which ends as follows: “Publicly enacted at the city of Autun in the month of May, on the very feast of Pentecost, on the first feria [Monday], in the fifth indiction, under Agano the bishop, Philip the king, and Gregory the universal bishop.”

The authors disagree about the year. In my judgment, however, no year other than 1082 can be assigned, since from the beginning of Gregory’s pontificate, which was in 1073, until his death, the fifth indiction fits no other year.

King Philip confirmed several churches to Raginald, abbot of Flavigny, and to the monastery, in a charter reported by D. Duchesne (*Proofs of the Genealogical History of the Dukes of Burgundy*, pp. 27–28), which concludes: “Bishop Agano was present there; he requested that this be done and praised the deed. Enacted at Orléans in the year of the Incarnation of the Word 1085, and in the twenty-third year of King Philip.”

In the year 1094 a council was held at Autun on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of November. At it the excommunication of King Henry was renewed because, while his wife was still alive, he had taken another woman, as well as that of Guibert, the usurper of the apostolic see.

In the same year Frogerius of Murassalt gave Cluny the church of Saint Nicholas in the castle itself, with the advice and consent of Lord Agano, bishop of Autun, in whose parish the church was situated.

Agano also appears to have attended the Council of Clermont in 1095. Certainly, when Durannus, bishop of that city, had committed the monastery of Mauziac to the authority and governance of Hugh, abbot of Cluny, and his successors, and when King Philip had confirmed this by a royal charter, Agano subscribed the act among the others. Shortly afterward he received Pope Urban II at Autun. The pope, entreated by him and by the chapter of Saint Nazarius, confirmed everything that Agano himself or his predecessors had granted to the canons.

Agano also founded a college of canons in the church of Saint Germain at Planesia, as is proved by the charter printed in the appendix.

When the monastery of Flavigny had already been without a pastor for seven years, it happened that Hugh, bishop of Lyons, was then occupied with the consecration of Berard, bishop of Mâcon, assisted by Agano, bishop of Autun, and Walter, bishop of Chalon. Considering this a suitable opportunity, Agano complained of the desolation of the aforesaid church and asked that the monk Hugh, well known from the Chronicle, be placed there as abbot. With difficulty, but finally, he obtained this from Hugh of Lyons, whose letter on the matter to Agano survives in the *Chronicle of Verdun*. Soon afterward he consecrated the aforementioned monk Hugh at Flavigny on the tenth day before the Kalends of December 1097. In that same year Agano gave the church of Arnay-le-Duc to Jarenton, abbot of Saint-Bénigne.

He was taken from the living in the year 1098, on the seventh day before the Kalends of July, says Hugh. In the necrology of Saint-Bénigne, however, we read: “The sixth day before the Kalends of July: Agano, bishop.”

One of our writers says that an old catalogue appends Helneus to Agano; the four-part *Gallia Christiana* omitted him, while Saunier also reports him in his *History of the Church of Autun*. Saunier says that in his time a council was held at Autun under Gregory VII, presided over by Hugh of Die, later bishop of Lyons. But Hugh, who at that very time was living as a monk in the diocese of Autun, after reporting Agano’s death immediately adds: “After the venerable Agano, Norgaudus assumed the governance of the Church of Autun; in that same Church he had served as precentor.”

[Col. 1541]

## Judgment of Agano against Raginardus

(See *Patrologia*, vol. CXXXII, col. 476, in the appendix to Regino.)

[Col. 1541]

## Charter of Agano for the foundation of the church of Saint Germain and Saint Saturninus at Planesia

(*Gallia Christiana*, new edition, vol. IV, appendix, p. 82.)

[Col. 1541C] When we recall the deeds and sayings of the Fathers who came before us, we clearly recognize how devoutly and beneficially they admonished their successors, by example and teaching, to devote themselves to divine worship. Since, with conscience bearing witness, we all offend in many things and are in no way sufficient for our own salvation, we must necessarily implore the help of those who deserved, by living justly and piously, not only to receive the fruit of their labor but also to obtain for us the forgiveness of our sins from the divine mercy.

To secure their favor for ourselves, let us strive with complete devotion to build sacred places for God in which their memory may be worthily and laudably honored, so that, by their help, we may be led out of this valley of tears and, reaching their fellowship, may finally deserve to see their God in Zion.

Since we have learned, through the truthful testimony of Sacred Scripture and the manifest evidence of miracles, that Blessed Germanus is not the least among those who can intercede for us in this matter, I, Agano—although unworthy, yet called bishop of the Church of Autun, may it not be to my detriment—seeing that the place where the church of the aforesaid confessor has now been established by divine will was suitable for religion, being removed from all popular disturbance, and also learning from the report of certain people and from the testimony of the tombs being unearthed there that it had once been dedicated to God, approached a priest of good life named Bernard concerning the religious life.

I often admonished him to serve God and the aforesaid confessor there under the institutions of canonical life, and at last I obtained his consent to my admonitions, on the condition that, as long as I remained alive and divine mercy provided the opportunity, I would attend to the needs of that place.

Later, learning from certain priests that, as avarice increased, the resources of the aforesaid church were being obstructed, and that religious men were being harassed because of the exaction of those offerings which the people whom the priests called their parishioners had left to God and to blessed Germanus for the remedy of their souls, I determined, by the authority of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles; of blessed Nazarius, our patron; of Lord Pope Gregory; of Lord Hugh, archbishop of the Church of Lyons and legate of the apostolic see; and by our own authority, that if any layperson from any parish, whether of Autun or of another diocese, should flee for refuge to the churches, villages, or cemeteries of Blessed Germanus, and should remain there for the space of a year, whether as a resident or because of the need for lodging—namely, at the church of Saint John the Evangelist situated at Bar, at the church of Saint Saturninus of Planesia, or at the church of Saint Martin of Dronventicus—it should be lawful for the clerics of the aforesaid churches, so long as they live together and without private property, to regard such people as their own parishioners, and to receive and retain, without disturbance from anyone, the offerings that those people make for themselves either during life or at death.

But whoever has not previously joined himself to them as a parishioner, if, while dying in another parish, he wishes to leave any of his property to them or to their churches, or to have burial at any of their churches, provided that he pays his own priest whatever is fitting or renders a suitable service, we confirm by the authority stated above that this too shall not be prevented by anyone’s accusation or opposition.

Therefore, if any layperson or cleric should grant permission for his body to be buried in the cemeteries of the aforesaid churches, in order to support the poverty of Christ’s poor, and if, fortified by the viaticum of the body and blood of Jesus Christ, he has made confession of his sins, may he deserve to receive the absolution that we can and ought to impart by the authority entrusted to us.

The sign of Agano, bishop of Autun. The sign of Wido, archdeacon. The sign of Hugh, archdeacon. The sign of Sevinus, archdeacon and provost. The sign of Norgaudus, archdeacon and cantor. The sign of Ramerius, cardinal archpriest. The sign of Robert, archpriest. The sign of Durandus, chaplain.

[Col. 1543]

## Letter of Agano, bishop, and the other bishops of the province of Lyons on behalf of Ralph, archbishop of Tours

(Mabillon, *Benedictine Annals*, V, 176.)

[Col. 1543C] [Note: At that time enormous disturbances arose in the Church of Tours. Their occasion and cause arose from the fact that Archbishop Ralph favored Amatus and Hugh, bishop of Die, legates of the apostolic see, who wished to deprive King Philip of the bishoprics of his kingdom. Hence the king ordered Fulk Rechin, count of Anjou, to drive the archbishop from his see. After this had been done, the aforesaid Ralph appealed through messengers to Pope Gregory, asking that the count of Anjou and the canons of Saint Martin, who had refused to receive the pope’s legates in procession, be excommunicated together with the entire district. The monks of Marmoutier also took Fulk’s side, as we learn from the letters of Agano and the other bishops of the province of Lyons. At that time the see of Lyons was vacant following the death of Archbishop Gebuin, and the bishop of Mâcon is said to have administered it.]

A. [Agano], bishop of Autun; R. [Rainaldus], bishop of Langres; G. [Walter], bishop of Chalon; L. [Landricus], bishop of Mâcon, acting as primate and administering the Church of Lyons, together with the entire assembly of the Church of Lyons, send divine grace and their own greeting to all the bishops, abbots, clerics, and monks of the province of Tours, and to the laypeople obedient to Ralph, the venerable archbishop of Tours.

We believe that none of you is unaware with what astonishing cruelty Fulk, count of Anjou, plunged the sword of his persecution into the entrails of the mother Church of Tours, or with what arrogant presumption the monks of Marmoutier rose up against that same mother church.

Nor is it unknown to you that Geoffrey, bishop of Anjou, possessed the power to compel Fulk to make amends for so great a crime, if he had preferred to obey divine commands rather than tyrannical ones, and if any zeal for ecclesiastical discipline had been alive in him.

But he violated the purpose of his profession. He obeyed neither divine commands nor the admonitions of his archbishop. While his brothers were laboring in defense of justice, he nourished his heart in idleness and pleasures, and supported rather than attacked the wickedness of the aforementioned Fulk.

When, therefore, the outcry of the Church of Tours had reached our concern regarding all these matters, we summoned both Count Fulk and the bishop of Anjou and the monks to the judgment of the holy see of Lyons, so that they might do and receive justice.

When, on the appointed day, they fled judgment by their absence and remained in their perversity, we suspended the bishop of Anjou from his episcopal and priestly office, from which his own archbishop had also forbidden him to act. But Fulk, together with the monks of Marmoutier, we struck with the sword of excommunication by the authority of Blessed Peter and of Lord Hugh, primate and legate of the Roman Church.

We also included all their supporters, or those who communicated with them, under the same excommunication.

We entreat and exhort your fraternity to strive with all your strength to console the sorrows of your mother, as sons grieve with their father, and to obey Ralph, her archbishop, completely, as you would your father. Do not communicate with the excommunicated persons mentioned above, lest you burden your souls with the crimes of others.

Farewell.

[ODALRICUS, PROVOST]

[Col. 1545]

## Testament of Odalricus, provost of Rheims, drawn up between the years 1075 and 1100

(*Gallia Christiana*, new edition, vol. X, appendix, p. 27, from a manuscript of the library of the cathedral church.)

[Col. 1545C] In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, I, Odalricus, provost of the holy Church of Rheims, have determined during my lifetime to arrange my testament in this way and thereby to settle any lawsuits or disputes that might arise.

I wish it to be known to those living now and to those who will come after that I held the allod of Olchinies from the canons of Saint Mary for a trecens, namely six solidi. I increased it as much as I could, acquiring for its enlargement lands from the field called Limaz, together with various other properties, increasing both the rent and the wine dues, and constructing there my vicarage.

I leave this property, thus enlarged and equipped, together with the demesne vineyard, to the canons of the Church of Saint Mary of Rheims. I decree that it be entrusted to the man who will be provost of the thousand beeches, who shall pay the aforesaid trecens—six solidi—annually to the canons and shall give the vicar his wage from the rent and wine dues owed there. Whatever remains he shall preserve for maintaining the vicarage.

From the cheeses he receives during the year, he shall give the canons seventy-two each year on the first Sunday of Advent, to be divided among them. He shall also give the canons cheeses in the refectory on the second and seventh days of every week of Advent. If a feast day or a fast should occur, he shall neither give them nor make up the amount.

From everything he receives throughout the year from the vicarage, he shall pay a tithe to Saint Denis, as I did during my lifetime. Whatever remains, if anything, he shall preserve for maintaining the vicarage.

For this I ask the canons for the following return: on the day after they have received the aforesaid blessing, let them make a commemoration of my soul.

If, because of our sins, all those cows should die or be stolen—as often happens—I ask the canons, present and future, for God’s sake and for the remission of their sins, not to permit this common benefit of theirs, which I have established with pious devotion, to be annulled. Rather, whatever the administrator cannot restore from the revenues of that allod, let them permit to be supplied from the common fund.

I also wish and decree that the canons of Saint Denis hold and cultivate the allod of Mutations, which I purchased with God’s help and that of his most holy Mother. In return, they shall pay the canons of Saint Mary eighteen solidi each year on my anniversary. Over my grave they shall also distribute to the poor bread from two sextarii of flour and one modius of wine.

The allod that I redeemed from my brothers and nephews, namely Roureio and Stogia, they shall likewise hold and cultivate. In return for it, each year, on the first Monday of Lent, they shall give one hundred new bowls and ten knives in the refectory of Saint Mary, each knife being worth two denarii of Rheims currency.

I therefore humbly ask the canons that on that very day, after the verse in the refectory and after the blessing of the meal, they say for my soul, “I lift up my eyes”—that is, the psalm *Levavi oculos meos*—to the end of the psalm. When it is finished, let the dean—or the weekly officiant—say, “May he rest in peace,” with the collect.

Let them also give a prebend on that day to the cleric who presents the bowls and knives.

I have arranged this in such a way so that they may receive from Stogia and Roureio only the amount necessary for the stated payment; if anything is lacking from the income to fulfill what I have prescribed, they may at least supply it from this property. If anything remains over, they shall have it.

I also wish to add another provision to the work prescribed above, by which I may recall our little works to the memory of future generations.

It is well known that the saving star, namely Pope Leo, once visited the province of Rheims in order to illuminate all Gaul. After the dedication of the church and the elevation of the precious body of blessed Remigius, he celebrated a synod in the presence of that most holy confessor. At it he diligently restored divine religion, which had grown excessively lukewarm, and also admonished and vigorously terrified those present concerning the Simoniac heresy and ecclesiastical offices. [lacuna]

Then I, together with certain of our own people, terrified by so great a threat of judgment, returned our offices to Lord Wido, the archbishop, lest we incur the divine vengeance that the pope threatened.

But because the lord pope had found me faithful in this office, he asked Archbishop Wido to impose that same office upon me under the name of obedience. The archbishop willingly complied, and the lord pope himself imposed the same duty upon me under the strictest obedience. Since I had previously been faithful in matters belonging to the brothers, from then on I strove to be still more faithful.

But when my mind burned with untiring desire for many honorable and useful improvements in the brothers’ affairs, I repaired certain things worn down by age. Among other works, I raised from the foundations certain structures in the cloister that had not yet been begun, including the winter refectory.

I also arranged one matter concerning the canons’ prebend, which both the rule prescribed and necessity demanded. For although our rule states that each canon should have four pounds of bread, our canons had only two and a half. I therefore began to work more diligently so that in our time the fixed quantity of bread prescribed by the rule might be supplied.

To make this possible, I arranged several ploughlands in the estate and villages of Saint Mary. From their produce I eventually made it possible for the canons to receive, in addition to the bread weighing fifty solidi, another smaller bread weighing thirty solidi.

Lest this arrangement fall into nothing after our death, at my own expense, with the counsel and help of Lord Gervasius, the venerable archbishop, I built two mills at the bridge of Saint Remigius. I grant them to Blessed Mary and assign them for the production of the smaller bread, giving them for a trecens [lacuna] with asses, a winnowing basket, and the bridge, on these terms: that the holder also maintain the bridge and pay annually into Saint Mary’s granary eight modii of grain.

At the hospice he shall pay six sextarii of flour as a tithe and six sextarii of wine.

I also gave, for the production of the smaller bread, a mill that I built at my own expense at Lancia, and I gave it for a trecens of two modii of grain each year.

I also strove with the utmost care to bring this to completion: just as I had provided beds from my own resources in the dormitory, so I arranged that a mattress and pillow should be placed beneath each bed. Whenever one of our brothers dies, I decree that, by order of the dean, a mattress and pillow be carried to the hospice of Saint Mary.

Another mattress with a pillow is to be restored from the allod of the court of Salonis, which I gave to Blessed Mary. To make this possible, I arranged that the seven pounds I received from my household, together with the wine from Risseio, which I estimate to be worth four pounds, should be placed in the hands of Lord Herman, a man of great trustworthiness and usefulness.

I charged him, for God’s sake and for the remedy of his soul, to provide from this money the aforesaid beds, mattresses, and pillows. I wish the allod to be entrusted to the man who will be provost of the men of Saint Martin.

Thus, if two or three canons, or more, should die in one year, and the allod cannot provide what is needed, he shall supply it from his office; and whatever he gives there when it has come from the allod, he shall receive back.

I ask only this of the brothers: whenever they make a commemoration of the soul of a deceased canon, let them include me in that commemoration. Where they would say it in the singular, let them say it in the plural.

## In the year of the Lord 1098: Bernard, bishop of Lodève

[Col. 1549]

## Notice

This was Bernard of Provencheres, who endured immense labors in defending the rights of the churches. He attended the Council of Clermont in 1095 and, roused there by Urban II’s trumpet call, took the cross. Three years later, after the capture of the Holy City, he put off his mortal body. This charter also reveals his brother Austorgius and his kinsman William of Provencheres.

[Col. 1549]

## Donation for the church of Saint Gregory of Rodez

(Year 1095.)

[Recovered from the archives of Saint-Victor by D. Furnerius. Edited by D. Martène, *Amplissima Collectio*, I, 552.)

[Col. 1549A] In the name of God, I, Bernard, by the grace of God bishop of Lodève, wish it to be known and made clear to all people that, by my own resources, ingenuity, and labor, I redeemed the church of Saint Gregory, which is in the diocese of Rodez, in the territory of Valleol, from the hands of laymen who were my kinsmen—namely William of Provencheres, who unjustly and by seizure held a third part of that church.

For that third part I gave [lacuna] thousand Puy solidi, with the intention that I might permanently arrange, freely and properly, according to regular discipline and for the love and service of God, the aforesaid church, which had been badly and dishonorably ordered.

Desiring therefore to fulfill this intention, with the counsel and approval of my brother Austorgius, I now give and grant the aforesaid third part of the church, which, as stated above, I redeemed through my effort and resources, to the venerable Richard, abbot of Marseille. Through him I give it to Blessed Mary and to Saint Victor the martyr of Marseille, and also to the successors and monks of the aforesaid abbot, present and future, so that they may have and possess it and do with it whatever they wish for the service of God.

The aforesaid abbot and his monks must always know that they obtained this gift of the church through no one other than me and my relatives. I make this gift to them for the remedy of my sins and the souls of my parents. Therefore let them be careful always to acknowledge this gift to me and my parents and to pray to the Lord for our salvation.

But if anyone should come against this gift of ours and attempt to violate or disturb it, whatever his rank, condition, or order, may he be unable to prevail, but incur the wrath of almighty God. Moreover, may this charter of our donation remain firm and stable forever.

[Col. 1550B] This was enacted on the sixth day before the Nones of October, in the year of the Lord 1095.

The sign of Bernard, who made and confirmed this gift and asked the witnesses to confirm it.

The sign of Austorgius.

## In the year of the Lord 1098: Foulcoie, subdeacon of the Church of Meaux

[Col. 1551]

## Historical notice

(*Literary History of France*, vol. VIII, p. 113.)

1. Foulcoie [Note: In the inscription of Foulcoie’s poems, as it is read in the Beauvais manuscript, the author is called *Fulco* and *Fulconus*.], the most prolific and one of the most celebrated poets of his time, nevertheless remained obscure until near the end of the last century. Dom Mabillon then began to bring him out of obscurity; subsequently Dom Toussaint du Plessis, historian of the Church of Meaux, and the learned Abbé Le Beuf made him still better known.

He was born around the year 1020 at Beauvais, from which place his parents came, as we learn from Foulcoie himself. It is said that he was a pupil of Fulbert of Chartres, but he was still too young when that learned prelate died. It is much more likely that he studied at the school of Rheims and had as his teacher the celebrated Herman, whose epitaph he composed and whom he describes by that title.

To the qualities of a man of judgment and sound counsel he added knowledge of languages and of laws. But since his genius inclined him toward poetry, he devoted himself to it so completely that it became his principal study and almost his entire occupation.

Four leagues from Meaux lies the priory of Celle, formerly a considerable abbey. Its situation appeared so charming to Foulcoie that he took delight in it. Thus, in the agreeable description he composed of the place, he did not fail to represent it as a delightful seat of the Muses: *Musis gratissima sedes*, “a dwelling most pleasing to the Muses.”

Foulcoie began to become known as a poet at least during the reign of Henry the Black, and therefore before 1056. Soon afterward his reputation spread throughout France and flew as far as Rome. This is shown by the poems he addressed to Popes Alexander II and Gregory VII, to Hugh of Die, the papal legate, and to Gervasius, archbishop of Rheims, as well as by the replies sometimes sent to him.

It nevertheless appears that our poet’s Muse was not entirely disinterested, although she was grateful for the gifts she received. Foulcoie himself did not conceal this. “What have you received?” he asks her, addressing her concerning the works of his that had been taken to Rome: *Quid tibi divisit?*—“What has he given you?”

“They did nothing,” he replies, “but return sounds for sounds: *Carmen pro carmine misit*”—“They sent a poem for a poem.”

But the city of Rheims and Archbishop Manassé did not act in the same way. They took care to pay handsomely for his verses, something he wished his Muse never to forget:

*Mercedemque dedit, quae non a mente recedit.*

“And he gave a reward that never leaves the mind.”

If we followed Dom Mabillon’s wording (*Annals*, I, LXVI, no. 27), where he says that Foulcoie composed the epitaph of Ives I, abbot of Saint-Denis, we would have to acknowledge that our poet lived beyond January 1094, the date of that abbot’s death.

But it appears from other evidence that Foulcoie merely dedicated to him the collection of epitaphs he had composed for other people. This is confirmed by the two epitaphs of that same abbot reported by Dom Mabillon himself, who took them from writings other than those of Foulcoie.

The same critic, discussing elsewhere the precise period in which this poet lived (*Annals*, I, LXI, no. 113; *Acts*, vol. III, p. 658, no. 7), places his flourishing from 1060 until about 1080. But it has been shown above that he had begun writing verse before 1056, and his death cannot be placed before 20 October 1082. That is the date of the death of Gautier Saveyr, bishop of Meaux, whose epitaph he composed. The proof is conclusive.

Foulcoie died at Meaux. Care was taken to adorn his tomb with several elegies in which the cities of Beauvais, Meaux, Chartres, Orléans, and Paris are introduced. By vying with one another in celebrating his praises, they testify to the extreme grief they felt at his loss.

Our poet is represented there as the most skillful master that the city of Meaux had ever possessed, and could even possess thereafter—a master whom Beauvais, Rheims, and Rome itself rightly envied.

Among all these pieces, which are all epitaphs, we choose the one spoken in the name of the city of Paris, and end with it the history of this excessively praised poet.

## Epitaph

Why, man, do you presume to violate the rest of the tomb?

What so great thing will you find? A foul and empty corpse.

Even if some wicked hand should injure me,

My tongue has nevertheless won me one burial

That neither fire nor river will wash away through all the years,

Nor the hard axe strike down together with solid walls.

All the poems of Foulcoie that have come down to us are found in three manuscripts dating from the author’s own time, or at least from the beginning of the twelfth century. The manuscript preserved in the library of the cathedral of Beauvais appears to be the most complete.

It contains one hundred and seventy-two folios. At the beginning are several treatises on the Old and New Testaments, which occupy more than half the manuscript and in which the author displays great piety.

For a clear and distinct account of Foulcoie’s poems, one must consult a preface found in a manuscript of the King’s Library, numbered 1181, or 738 among the manuscripts of M. Colbert, which contains part of our poet’s works.

This preface, written by an outsider at the end of the same century, after briefly introducing Foulcoie’s person, informs us that all his writings were divided into three volumes comprising ten books. The first was entitled *Utrum*, the second *Neutrum*, and the third *Utrumque*. A contemporary poet indicated this in the mournful verses in which he makes the city of Beauvais speak of the author’s death, using these words:

“I wrote books in twice five, three volumes,

Whose names are *Utrum*, *Neutrum*, and *Utrumque*;

One ploughs, another sows, the other gathers.”

According to this poet’s conception, Foulcoie’s first volume merely prepares the soil; the second casts in the seed; and the third offers the harvest to be gathered.

The author of the preface just mentioned, attempting to explain these highly unusual titles, says that Foulcoie gave the first volume the title *Utrum* because it was intended merely to display his Muse, as though to test his powers.

The first tome or volume contains only one book, in which the poet’s letters, epitaphs, and other short pieces are collected.

Among these poems are praises of the most eminent people of his time: Popes Alexander II and Gregory VII; Gervasius and Manassé, archbishops of Rheims; Richer of Sens; Hugh of Die; the emperor Henry the Black; William the Conqueror; Blessed Lanfranc; Saint Anselm; Herman of Rheims; and many others.

Of all these minor poems, Dom Mabillon first published a dozen or so verses relating particularly to Manassés I, archbishop of Reims, followed by a description of La Celle in Brie, where the poet took pleasure in exercising his muse. Dom du Plessis also printed a considerable fragment of a letter to Saint Hugh, abbot of Cluny, written in elegiac verse. This interesting fragment concerns the discovery of the head of a false divinity, which Foulcoie recognized as that of the god Mars.

It has been said that the collection of epitaphs is addressed to Ivo I, abbot of Saint-Denis from 1075 to 1094. It contains those of King Henry I; several bishops of Meaux; Adelaide, the mother of Archbishop Manassés; the father, mother, and brothers of our poet; Esceline, his nurse; Hermane, his teacher; and several other persons. Dom du Plessis made public the epitaph of Gautier Saveyr, bishop of Meaux, which consists of ten elegiac verses, as well as only two verses from that of Saint Gilbert, one of his predecessors. In Dom Mabillon’s collection of Acts there is the epitaph of Otger and Benedict, famous monks of Saint-Faron in the time of Charlemagne. It consists of twenty verses and is in our poet’s manner. Elsewhere there is one verse from the epitaph he composed in memory of a certain Hugh, who exchanged military service for the monastic life.

Foulcoie’s second volume is entitled *Neutrum* because he did not yet dare undertake what he had proposed to himself. It is divided into two books, and the author confined himself there to exercising his poetic vein on the lives of the saints of the diocese of Meaux, who, he says, were numerous. We owe Dom du Plessis the recovery from obscurity of part of the list in which the poet enumerates them—a list that appears to form the beginning of the Life of Saint Blandin, buried at La Celle in Brie.

The Life of Saint Faron, bishop of Meaux, one of those on which Foulcoie worked, had originally been written in prose by Hildegar, one of that prelate’s successors. Our poet merely put it into verse, without obliging himself to follow the original text literally. Dom Mabillon, who had found it detached from Foulcoie’s other works, initially believed it to date from the end of the tenth century. He later recognized, however, that it was not composed until after the middle of the following century, in the time of Abbot Galfride, or Geoffrey. The manuscript of Saint-Faron in which it is found also contains the Lives of the monks Otger and Benedict, whose epitaph Foulcoie, as stated above, composed. It further contains the catalogue of the books in the library of the monastery of Saint-Faron, which was not then very extensive and was governed by the same abbot. This suggests that the manuscript belongs to that period and consequently predates the year 1062.

Besides the Life of Saint Faron, Foulcoie also composed in verse a eulogy of the same saint, at the request of Abbot Galfride and his monks. Dom Mabillon had both works in his hands, but did not think it appropriate to publish anything from them; he rightly believed that the work of Hildegar, which he had brought to light, was sufficient for the history of the holy bishop. Only Dom Hugues Menard printed four verses from our poet’s Life in his notes on the *Concord of the Rules* of Saint Benedict of Aniane.

There is also, in the second volume of Foulcoie’s collection, a Life of Saint Aile and verses on Saint Fiacre, the hermit of Brie. Dom Mabillon, however, implies that this latter piece forms part of the Life of Saint Faron and is not a separate work. Although it is the work of a poet, it may perhaps be preferable, as regards factual truth, to the poor legends of this saint, who lived in the seventh century. Some make him of royal blood and even the son of Eugenius IV, king of Hibernia, and suppose that he refused his father’s crown—an account that cannot be accepted. Others relate still more extraordinary events, which deserve no greater credence. The least unsatisfactory is the one that Surius and, following him, Dom Mabillon published; even this, however, was written nearly a century after Foulcoie and appears to have borrowed from him whatever it reports that is most plausible.

Finally, the third volume of our poet is entitled *Utrumque de nuptiis Ecclesiae* (“Both: On the Marriage of the Church”), because in it the author brings together the Old and New Testaments in Jesus Christ, the Father’s Word and the Author of grace, who has made one people out of two. To this one bridegroom he betroths the Church as an entirely pure virgin. This volume is written in the form of a dialogue between the spirit and the man and is divided into seven books. Here one finds the resolution of the verse quoted above:

> I have written ten books in a threefold volume.

For these seven books, joined to the three preceding ones, make ten, and this final work, set beside the other two, makes three volumes.

[Col. 1555] This final work of Foulcoie is found in manuscript 58 of the library of the Sorbonne. It is none other than the treatises on the Old and New Testaments with which the manuscript of Beauvais Cathedral begins and which occupy more than half of it. It is dedicated to Archbishop Manassés, the poet’s beloved Maecenas, and to the dedication he added other verses addressed to Pope Alexander II and to the archdeacon Hildebrand, later pope under the name Gregory VII. It is evident from this that the work was completed before April of the year 1073, when that archdeacon occupied the Holy See. The Abbé Le Beuf published these final verses less because they might help clarify history than in order to show how greatly quantity was then neglected in versification.

There is every appearance that the body of the work is no more correct. Yet the author of the preface found in the manuscript of the Royal Library speaks of this long poem only as an admirable work: *mirifico carmine composuit*, “he composed it in wondrous verse.” It is true that this is the judgment of a writer from the end of the eleventh century, and we know the value of his praises in matters of poetry. What is also true is that the unusual titles our poet chose to announce his threefold collection of poems are hardly calculated to predispose readers in favor of the execution of his design.

The attentive reader will doubtless have observed that the manuscript of Beauvais, which contains the three volumes of Foulcoie’s poems, does not preserve the same order that they originally had among themselves. In their original order, the collection of letters, epitaphs, and other minor poems occupied the first place, and the dialogue the last. The opposite is true in the manuscript under discussion, if we rely on Dom du Plessis. Yet the description Dom de Montfaucon gives of the same manuscript presents these three volumes in the same order and with the same titles as the preface to the manuscript of the Royal Library: that is, *Utrum* at the head of the other two and *Utrumque* last.

To the large number of poems we have just enumerated, Foulcoie promised to add a treatise on the liberal arts. But if he carried out this projected design—which would have pleased the curious—his work still lies buried in the obscurity of some library, or perhaps has been irretrievably lost. It has already been suggested that Foulcoie’s poetry has nothing superior to that of the other versifiers of his century. He was a more laborious than delicate poet, more fertile than scrupulous.

[Col. 1555]

## Letter of Fulcoius of Beauvais, subdeacon of Meaux, to Hugh, abbot of Cluny

(Dom Du Plessis, *History of the Church of Meaux*, II, 453.)

[Col. 1555A]

Meaux once had a celebrated wall, as its ruin bears witness,  
Though in former times; the name still remains:  
The ancient inhabitants called it the temple of Mars;  
And still, countryman, you call these stones the temple of Mars.  

You called it this, yet by calling it you did not preserve the thing:  
The discovery supplied the indication of the name.  

While a peasant was plowing the fields here, amid the half-ruined remains,  
He found a likeness—an effigy, as it were.  

He found a sculpted head, unlike any other,  
One that no living thing possessed and no human being represented.  

A dreadful head, yet dignified by that very horror;  
Its terrifying eye made terror itself seem fitting:  

[Col. 1556A]

With gaping mouth and savage face, beautiful in its savagery,  
A misshapen form, whose form was nevertheless appropriate.  

When the image was first brought to my attention as I entered the region,  
I tried to determine what it was, to whom it belonged, and whose it might be.  

After hearing the corrupted name of the place as pronounced  
By the language of the common people, and while I examined both the place and the neglected head—  

Though neglected, both were nevertheless fitting—  
The place, the name, and the fierce head disclosed the truth.  

This place is the temple of Mars; and this head is the profane image of Mars,  
An error that supposes it to be a god, etc.

[Col. 1555]

## Fragments in which the saints of the diocese of Meaux are enumerated

(D. Du Plessis, ibid., p. 452, from manuscript codex 120 of the church of Beauvais.)

### I. From the Life of Blessed Blandin, hermit of Brie

[Col. 1555A]

Fulcoie, walking through the paradise of Brie,  
While I revisit its springs and groves, its Thessalian Tempe,  

[Col. 1556A]

Sampling, like a bee, what there is in the tree and what there is in the grass,  
Came upon this place situated above the River Mucra.  

A small island in situation, yet a dwelling most pleasing to the Muses,  
Surpassing Helicon, the great delight of the gods,  

[Col. 1557A]

Whose name is Cella; the inhabitants called it Cellam.  
Invited by the place, captivated by the region, I settled there.  

[lacuna] the parents  
I do not know; I call the Camales spiritual parents  

And Raimericus was the father, and Syon, illustrious, the mother.  

[lacuna]

Why, I ask, is there a sore that becomes a swineherd under a father?  

[lacuna]

The saint did not disdain to lead the life of a countryman.  

[lacuna]

He makes Christ his heir, so that the father may make him his heir.  

[lacuna]

He is worthily laid in a bier; there is a place for Peter.  

[lacuna]

Meaux, fertile mother of holy men,  

[Col. 1557B]

Of the just Walbert, and likewise of the holy Canoaldus,  
Of Faron and Fara, who knew how to love Christ,  

For whose sake she makes her earthly bridegroom a stranger.  

Meaux brought forth Celinia, a goddess of celibate life,  
And Meaux bore Rigomerus, stern toward his enemies.  

[Col. 1558A]

What am I doing? The city of Meaux produces Partusius for the countryside.  
Here are three brothers, sound in deeds and doctrine,  

Who loved Christ and replaced themselves with him.  

Here are Addo and Rado, the most illustrious offspring of Dado,  

Founders of excellent places, who, dedicating their possessions and themselves,  
Established Radolium, Jotrum, and Resbascum.  

Here is Hildevertus, a shepherd true in deed and name.  

Here was the bishop accustomed to strike down the fierce;  
Swift toward his fellow servants, severe toward the proud, was Ebregisilus.  

From here shines in heaven the shepherd and faithful servant,  
Gislebertus, a man now secure through the gift of hope,  

Which God confirms by signs worthy, I pray, of such a bishop, etc.

### II. On Dudo, abbot, who flourished under the rule of Philip I

[lacuna]

[Col. 1558B]

His nobility possessed ancestral seats;  
Through fitting signs worthy of command and rank,  

He proved illustrious, unlike most men …  

Tried at length, proved through trials,  
The good abbot Dudo …  

[Col. 1557]

## Epitaph of Otger and Benedict, soldiers who, in the time of Charlemagne, received the monastic habit in the monastery of Saint-Faron, by Fulcoie

(Mabillon, *Acts of the Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict*, century IV, p. 657.)

[Col. 1557C]

How poorly he distinguishes what he loves, or what he despises,  
Who delights in the air of earth and finds the air of heaven displeasing.  

An exile in a foreign land, far from the heavenly region,  
Captive to love of the road, he does not remember his homeland.  

The conversion of the soldier Otger is worthy to be seen  
As a mirror in which you may fix your eye.  

He was a man of the law, wealthy, second only to the king;  
Noble and wise, vigorous and patient.  

Surrounded by flowers, having attained an eminent position,  
He set everything else aside and gave himself to God.  

[Col. 1558C]

He summons Benedict, the unconquered companion of worldly affairs,  
So that, his equal in military service, he may share in forgiveness.  

The cross is received together, and this place of the cross is entered together:  
The emperor’s garb is stripped away, and the emperor’s garb is put on.  

Go forth, equal souls, foremost through every host,  
Strong limbs of Caesar, strong limbs of God.  

Strong athletes, farewell through all the ages;  
The form of the cross is alike, and alike will be your rest.  

O beautiful equal pair! Equal in life and equal in the tomb;  
Equal was the burial mound, and equal will be the inscription.

## At the close of the century, Constantine the African, monk of Monte Cassino

[Col. 1559]

## Historical and literary notice

(Oudin, *Commentaries on Ecclesiastical Writers and Writings*, II, 694.)

[Col. 1559A]

Constantine the African, a monk of Monte Cassino, flourished during the time of Alfano, archbishop of Salerno. Alfano assumed responsibility for the Church of Salerno in 1057 and died in 1086, in the twenty-ninth year of his episcopate. Constantine dedicated to him his book *On the Natural and Non-natural Affections of the Stomach*. A Carthaginian by birth, an outstanding physician and philosopher, he traveled through various regions of the East and, residing especially in Babylon, cultivated his intellect in every discipline of the Chaldaeans, Arabs, Persians, and Saracens. Leaving Babylonia, he went to India, then to Ethiopia, and finally to Egypt, bringing back with him the spoils and treasures of every people. After spending nearly forty years in this way learning the studies and languages of various nations, he returned home, [Col. 1559B] where, having narrowly escaped ambushes, he withdrew to the monastery of Monte Cassino. There he assumed the monastic habit and, already advanced in years, fell asleep in the Lord. Many works were published under his name, though nearly all of them were translated from Arabic into Latin from the books of ancient physicians. These matters have little bearing on our purpose, but since he became a monk, they may in some measure belong among ecclesiastical writers, whose works we shall now review.

Various medical tracts appear under his name in the printed catalogue of the Bodleian Library, Oxford, 1674, folio, by Thomas Hyde, under the letter C, p. 171, col. 1, namely:

*Works*, Basel, 1539, C. 2, 9. Med.

[Col. 1559C]

The work called the *Breviary*, or *Viaticum*, on diseases of the human body, Lyons, 1570, octavo, A. 4, Med.

A little book *On the Use of Animals in Medicine*, Basel, 1560, octavo, C. 34. Med.

The book *On Fevers*, p. 202, Venice, 1576, F. 1, 9. Med.

*On the Principal Members of the Human Body*, p. 313, in the middle of the book, Basel, 1541, A. 2. 5. Med.

Besides the book *On the Natural and Non-natural Affections of the Stomach*, which he dedicated to Alfano, archbishop of the Church of Salerno, nearly all the others [Col. 1560A] were translated by him from Arabic into Latin, although they were boldly published under his name in a folio edition at Basel in 1536 and 1539 by Heinrich Petri, in the following order:

*Viaticum*, on the knowledge and treatment of diseases, in seven books.

*On the Knowledge of Remedies and Diseases*, book I.

*On Urines*, book I.

Constantine’s own work, *On the Natural and Non-natural Affections of the Stomach*, book I.

*On the Regimen of Various Diseases*, book I.

*On Melancholy*, two books.

*On Intercourse*, book I.

*On the Difference between Soul and Spirit*, book I.

*On Incantation and Adjuration, and on Suspension from the Neck*, a letter to his son.

[Col. 1560B]

*On the Diseases of Women*, book I.

*On Surgery*, book I.

*On the Degrees of Simple Medicines*, book I.

From the manuscript codices of the Bodleian Library and other libraries it will readily be established that nearly all these works were not composed by Constantine but translated from earlier Greek or Arabic works. For:

Among the manuscript codices of the Bodleian Library: codex 708; among the manuscripts of William Laud, letter C, codex 56, no. 2: Constantine the physician’s *Viaticum* in seven books; *On Universal and Particular Diets*, in Greek, folio.

In the same library, codex 1252; among the manuscripts of William Laud, letter G, codex 87, no. 6: *Viaticum* in seven books by Constantine the monk; *On Fevers*, five books; *On Urines*—all from Arabic. [Col. 1560C]

In the same library, codex 1507; among the manuscripts of William Laud, letter II, codex 81: *Constantine the African, monk of Monte Cassino, Breviary called Viaticum, on the Diseases of the Human Body*.

In the same library, codex 2069; among the manuscripts of Thomas Bodley, letter C, codex 1: *Constantine the African’s Viaticum*, *The Practice of Medicine*, book VII.

In the same library, codex 2444; among the manuscripts of Thomas Bodley, letter F, 8, codex 4, no. 4: Isaac’s *Dietary*, or *On Universal Diets*. No. 5: his *Book of Urines* and *Book of Fevers*, translated by Constantine the monk.

[Col. 1561A]

In the same library, codex 2753; among the manuscripts of Thomas Bodley, above no. 2, Arts, codex 11, no. 6: *Universal and Particular Diets* by Master Isaac. No. 7: his *Book of Urines*. ## [On Matters Common and Necessary for a Physician to Know]

### Prologue of Constantine the African to the book *On Matters Common and Necessary for a Physician to Know*: What the Students of Medicine Ought to Be

[Col. 1563B]

He who wishes to obtain the status of a physician must honor his teacher as a master, praise him, and serve him as he would his parents. Honor must be shown to parents because one receives one’s being from them. The teacher must be honored because from him one’s rough and unformed nature is formed. Whoever the teacher undertakes to educate must ensure that the student is worthy of him. He must afterward teach those who are worthy, and must do so without payment, without a contract, and without concern for any future profit or reward. He must strive to drive the unworthy away from this science.

He must labor to restore the sick person’s health, and must not do so out of hope for money. He must not consider the rich more than the poor, nor the noble more than the lowborn. He must neither teach a harmful potion himself nor approve those who teach such things, lest some ignorant person, hearing of his authority,

[Col. 1564B]

prepare a potion of death. Nor must he teach how to produce an abortion.

When he visits a sick person, he must not turn his heart toward the patient’s wife, or look upon her maidservant or daughter. Such things blind the human heart. He alone should be aware of the illness entrusted to him, for sometimes a sick person reveals to a physician what he is ashamed to confess to his parents.

He must avoid lust and beware the pleasures of the world together with drunkenness. These disturb the mind and strengthen bodily defects. He must love constant study in caring for bodily health and not grow weary of reading, so that, if he ever loses his books, memory may assist him. Nor should he disdain to visit any of the sick, so that he may always become more capable through experience. Let him be pious, humble, gentle, and amiable, seeking divine assistance and wishing to be helped by it.

[Col. 1563]

To the most reverend father, lord Desiderius, abbot of Monte Cassino, foremost ornament of the entire ecclesiastical order, Constantine the African wishes every blessing.

[Col. 1563C]

Many, most reverend Father, doubt whether medicine is a science or not. While they exclude it from the arts and sciences, they themselves are excluded from the most excellent of the arts, medicine. For while they waste their time uselessly on sophistical questions of no value, they never reach the true and useful contemplation of the art.

Acute minds argue that medicine is not a science, although it treats more than any other discipline of the works of nature. Yet all the works of nature are joined together in the most certain order, and their principles are more certain than those of other things.
