Nor is it easy to find an art that proceeds in such order, or in which one thing is understood through another in this way.

Let no one claim to be a complete philosopher unless he possesses this knowledge. For all other things serve this end, the end of all philosophy—except sacred philosophy. What benefit is there in knowing the combinations of the elements for one who does not proceed to learn the various temperatures

[Col. 1564C]

and constitutions of the parts, the causes of corruptions, the order and arrangement of the members, and the other matters of this kind?

Therefore, after examining all the good authorities on medicine, ancient and modern, Greek and Latin—especially the Greeks, who still surpass the Latins in this discipline, as in many others—I have compressed into a small compass all that can make a perfect physician. For some matters seemed to me to have been written by them at excessive length, others too briefly. And not everyone can buy all their books.

Even if I have achieved nothing else through these labors of mine and added nothing—for I believe that I have also discovered and added much—there were nevertheless suitable commentaries and interpreters of Hippocrates and Galen, as well as of other writers. Some repel the reader by excessive verbosity; others by an excessive obscurity of brevity. All whose judgment is sound will acknowledge that we have maintained the proper measure.

[Col. 1565A] I hope that no one will justly complain that we have written in vain after such great men. Even if I admit that what they said was well said, I wished to serve the public good, not the glory of my own name. Your fatherhood will see that I have said nothing well with a view to that glory.

For I wish to train the physician, to preserve good health for the healthy, and to restore it suitably to those who are not healthy and have lost it. For this reason I have discussed so carefully the causes of diseases, [Col. 1566A] their natures, their signs, and their accompanying conditions. Without knowledge of these things, it is impossible to correct what is contrary to nature or to treat illness.

We have transmitted nothing unless it has been proved either by ourselves or by others through experience and certainly known by reasoning, so that it is clear that the matter cannot be otherwise. We commend ourselves always to your fatherhood and always wish you good health.

## In the year of the Lord 1099, Deusdedit, cardinal priest of the Holy Roman Church, of the title of the Apostles in Eudoxia

[Col. 1565]

## Historical notice

(In Fabricius, *Bibliotheca of Medieval and Modern Latin Literature*, vol. II, p. 25.)

Deusdedit, also called Deodatus, cardinal priest and a vigorous champion of the party of Pope Gregory VII, died in 1099. He wrote four books *On Ecclesiastical Terms* for Victor III, the successor of Gregory VII in 1086; alternatively, this may refer to a manuscript *Compendium of Canons* in the Vatican Library. He also wrote a four-part book *On the Privileges and Authority of the Roman Church and of the Ecclesiastical Order*, directed against invaders of ecclesiastical property, Simoniacs and schismatics, the Guibertines—as the anonymous writer of Melk calls them in chapter 113—and the Henricians, that is, those who supported Guibert, or the antipope Clement III, and the emperor Henry IV. Hence Urspergensis joins the Wibertine and Henrician heresies, p. 247. It is surprising that these books were not given a place in Giovanni Tommaso Rocaberti’s most extensive pontifical library.

[Col. 1565]

## Dissertation on the Vatican manuscript collection of Cardinal Deusdedit, containing several documents hitherto unpublished

(See the Ballerini brothers’ *Discussion of the Ancient Collections and Collectors of Canons*, part IV, chapter 14, in *Patrologia*, volume LVI, works of Leo the Great III, col. 330.)

[Col. 1565]

## Preface of Cardinal Deusdedit to his Collection of Canons

[Col. 1565A]

To the most blessed and apostolic man, the pontiff, lord Pope Victor III, and to all the clergy of the holy Roman Church: Deusdedit, an insignificant priest of the title of the Apostles in Eudoxia.

Your Blessedness knows that the holy Roman Church is written of and believed to be the mother of all Churches because Blessed Peter, its founder, first established patriarchal sees in the East and afterward, from his own side, gave the first pastors to all the cities that are in the West. This arrangement was especially appropriate to that apostle whom Christ, the Son of God, after entrusting him with the keys of the heavenly kingdom, principally commanded to feed his sheep and ordered to strengthen his brothers in the same faith.

[Col. 1566A]

Carefully considering the splendid prerogatives and gifts of this most excellent privilege, the 318 Fathers who assembled at the Council of Nicaea decreed—as

[Col. 1567A]

Bishop Athanasius of Alexandria writes to Pope Felix—that councils ought not to be held without the judgment of the Roman pontiff, that bishops ought not to be condemned, and that all major matters ought to be referred to his judgment.

The Council of Sardica, which, according to the universal synod that is called the eighth by its authors, had 300 bishops, likewise established the same thing in chapters 3 and 4, and (Cor. VII and X), 6 and 9. Among other things it wrote as follows to Blessed Pope Julius:

> It will appear most excellent and entirely fitting if the priests of the Lord from each and every province report matters to the head—that is, to the see of Blessed Peter the Apostle.

Even before that synod, the ancient Fathers are said to have shown such great reverence toward this see that the distinguished martyr Cyprian, primate of the African province, is recorded in his letters

[Col. 1567B]

to have humbly obeyed the regulations of the Roman presbyters and deacons who governed the Roman Church after the martyrdom of Fabian, and to have rendered them an account, by letters addressed to them, of what was being done in his own province.

Indeed, that same clergy is recorded to have sent letters to Cyprian, to Sicily, and to various regions. While Cornelius was not yet presiding, they also summoned bishops to assemble a synod at Rome because of the urgent matters then at hand.

Although this is so, it seems sufficiently impious for anyone who boasts of the Christian name, in Christian times, not to heed the admonitions of the Roman Church, since, under the cruelty of persecution, pontiffs worthy of God obeyed them so devoutly—even while it lacked a [Col. 1567C] pontiff. For the Fathers, filled with the Spirit of God, judged that the blessed apostles Peter and Paul lived and presided there through their illustrious merits, and that the faith which it had received from them—the faith which, as the same blessed Paul testifies, was proclaimed and praised throughout the whole world—would never fail there throughout the ages; and that, as had been commanded to the same blessed Peter, it should strengthen everywhere the brethren established in that faith. Although this faith is sometimes oppressed by the contrary winds of the world, it is not overwhelmed, because of the merits of the chief apostles, who both live and preside in it. For although at times the gates of hell are able to prevail against it for its testing, they can never prevail, since the Lord Jesus prays that Peter’s faith may not fail.

Therefore, wishing—with the Lord’s help—to disclose to the ignorant the privilege of that authority by which it stands above the entire Christian world, I have drawn up this present little work from the authorities of various holy Fathers and Christian rulers, collecting the more important passages into one body, and dividing it into four parts. The first book contains the privilege of the authority of that same Roman Church. And because the Church cannot exist without its clergy, nor the clergy without the possessions by which they are sustained in temporal matters, I have appended a second and a third book concerning the clergy and the possessions of that same Church. Since, however, worldly power attempts to subject God’s Church to itself, its liberty, and that of its clergy and possessions, is clearly demonstrated in the third and especially in the fourth book.

I have not arranged each excerpt inserted in this work according to the order of the chapters [Col. 1568A], because nearly all of them contain either two or several matters within themselves; and if they were divided according to the number of matters with which they deal, this would impose much labor on me and bring detriment to the authority of the work. I therefore warn the copyist—so that the reader may not be seriously offended—to apply care not only in correcting the manuscript but also in keeping and most cautiously correcting both sets of numbers: namely, the number placed under each chapter and the number assigned throughout the whole manuscript to each excerpt.

Moreover, if anything inserted here—something that often also occurs in the Evangelists—should appear contrary to something else, careful discrimination will readily show that it conflicts neither with itself nor with the writings placed elsewhere. [Col. 1568B] If, however, it should plainly prove contradictory, the lesser authority must yield to the greater.

I therefore first excerpted the best material from certain universal synods: Nicaea, the First Council of Ephesus, Chalcedon, and the Sixth, Seventh, and Eighth Councils. These are known to have been universally celebrated, some by four or five patriarchs, and some by their vicars, at different times. No one but a madman doubts their authority. I also thought it not beside the point to borrow suitable material from the other Eastern councils, since I saw that the Roman pontiffs had received authority from them in their constitutions—as the inquisitive reader will also be able to discover.

In addition, I took certain material from the Carthaginian synod held under Pope Zosimus by 217 bishops, with his legates, Bishop Faustinus and the presbyters Philip and Asellus, present. In their presence African councils were confirmed and incorporated into that synod under various chapters; some of these Coelestine, Symmachus, and Hadrian appear to have inserted into their decrees.

And since an adversary, when overcome by reason, attacks authority, it must be known that all councils, whether universal or provincial, held before the Council of Chalcedon were afterward confirmed and strengthened in that council, chapter 1, which reads as follows: “We decree that the rules of the holy Fathers established up to the present in the several councils shall retain their proper force.”

For the Council of Chalcedon, held by 630 Fathers under Pope Leo [Col. 1568D], possesses such authority and firmness that whoever does not hold fast to its solidity, whatever his life and conduct may be, would, as blessed Gregory says, lie outside God’s building, even if he appeared to be a stone.

I have also collected material concerning the authority of the canons of the Apostles, which are said to have been translated from Greek into Latin by Clement, the Roman pontiff. The Seventh Universal Council of 350 Fathers, and the same Gregory in his *Register*, also appear to have used their authority. Concerning the authority of these and of any other canons, Anastasius, librarian of the Roman Church, writes in the prologue to that same Seventh Universal Council—which he translated from Greek into Latin—for Pope John VIII:

“By the decree of your predecessor, Pope Stephen, and by your apostolic authority, the Church receives not only the fifty canons of the Apostles [Col. 1569A], as the trumpets of the Holy Spirit, but also admits the rules and institutions of all approved Fathers and sacred councils—provided only that they do not oppose the true faith or good morals, nor in any substantial way contradict the decrees of the Roman See; indeed, they powerfully oppose its adversaries.”

The letters of Clement to James, against which certain people appear to chatter, are shown to be authentic by his successors Anacletus and Alexander, and by certain other pontiffs, as well as by Benedict, the father of monks, blessed by God, who inserted many statements from them into his writings.

I have also gathered here much material concerning the authority of the Apostolic See; some material from the works of blessed Jerome, whose eloquence, as Augustine says of him against Julian, shines from East to West like the sun [Col. 1569B]; and some from the works of the blessed Cyprian, Ambrose, Augustine, and other Fathers. I have taken every possible care that the material collected here should be filled with the fullest authority. For I knew that, just as there would be some to whom these things pleased, so there would not be lacking others who would begrudge them.

Furthermore, I wished to insert into this work the ancient order for the election or consecration of the Roman pontiff and his clergy. For certain people once wrote, in contempt of the sanctions of God and the holy Fathers, to display themselves and claim for themselves a vain authority which can stand under no canonical law, a new ordination of the Roman pontiff. I shudder to write how wicked and hostile to God were the provisions they made. Let whoever reads understand.

I have inserted here only a little concerning the manner of teaching subjects, since I judged it laborious and belonging to another work to excerpt sacred Scripture for this purpose. The most important sources for that task seemed to me to be the Gospel, the Epistles of the Apostles, Clement, Gregory’s *Pastoral Care*, his forty homilies on the Gospels, and his homilies numbered 8, 9, and 10 on Ezekiel.

And because, while striving for brevity, I regret passing over many useful things, I advise the inquisitive reader [Col. 1570B], when he has leisure, to study the works from which these excerpts were taken—not in order to add anything to the excerpts, but to satisfy his own desire.

I have therefore dedicated this work to Your Paternity, since I judged that it would be useful not only to the holy Apostolic See but also to the whole Church and all the clergy. I beseech the reader in the Lord to intercede with the Lord for my transgressions.

[Col. 1569]

# FRAGMENTS OF THE BOOK

*On the privileges and authority of the Roman Church and the ecclesiastical order, and against invaders of ecclesiastical possessions, Simoniacs and schismatics, the Guibertines and Henricians.*

(BARONIUS, *Annals*, under the years 1059, no. 31; 1080, no. 31; 1081, no. 32.)

## I. On the decree of Pope Nicholas the Younger

[Col. 1569C]

There are some who object that Nicholas the Younger established by synodal decree that, when the apostolic pontiff died, a successor should be elected and his election reported to the king. After the election had been made and, as stated above, reported to the king, only then was the pontiff to be consecrated.

If this is to be accepted as rationally done, we reply in order to refute it that the aforesaid king and his nobles made themselves unworthy of that constitution: first, because afterward, when the aforesaid Nicholas had rebuked the archbishop of Cologne for his offenses, they took it very badly and, so far as lay within their power, deposed him from the papacy on this account, forbidding his name to be mentioned in the canon of consecration [Col. 1569D]. Therefore his decree ought by right to be invalid, since, although he was regarded as pope by the whole world, according to their judgment he was not their pope—as though whether someone was or was not pope depended not on God’s will but solely on theirs.

For, as wise men know, the Roman pontiff not only cannot be deposed, but by Christian law cannot be judged by anyone whatsoever.

In the second place, the same decree had provided that the election of the Roman pontiff should be conducted by the Roman clergy and people and afterward reported to him. Yet, violating the aforesaid decree, they elected—though they had no right to do so—first Cadalus of Parma, afterward Guibert of Ravenna, clothing them in the apostolic insignia and calling them apostolic men, apostates, and forerunners of Antichrist [Col. 1570C].

Moreover, the aforesaid Guibert, or his supporters, in order to attach favor to his party, added certain things to the decree and altered others, making it so inconsistent with itself that few, or no, copies can be found agreeing with one another. What sort of decree is it when it appears so different from itself that one does not know what in it ought chiefly to be believed? . . . .

The excommunication, moreover, which is pronounced so terribly in the aforesaid decree, is believed to have been inserted solely by Guibert or his supporters, since it appears quite differently in the older copies of this decree. And this will indeed come upon those who inserted it there for their own advantage, and upon those who presume to say that it must be feared: upon them, that they may fall into the pit which they dug, and that the trap which they concealed may seize them, and so forth.

## II. On Guibert the antipope

After rendering to his lord, Pope Gregory VII of blessed memory, oaths of fidelity, and after displaying obedience for eight [the text reads “nine”] years, he invaded the apostolic throne with the cooperation of King Henry. By seducing Henry into the Simoniacal heresy—into which Henry had already fallen some time before—he drove him more deeply into it and turned him away from observing the oath which he had given at Canossa, a town in Tuscia, to the same lord pope, in order to restore peace and justice in the kingdom which he had disturbed with great arrogance and wickedness.

For all these reasons, after the same lord pope had repeatedly entreated him to come to his senses and had summoned him again and again to make satisfaction, he was at last compelled, first by excommunication, then, if he would not submit, by the threat of deposition from the kingdom, and afterward once more to fulfill his oath by making satisfaction.

But afterward, as has been said [Col. 1571B], he was seduced by the aforesaid Guibert, a new Simon Magus and a second Nero: namely, by the claim that he, although merely king, ought not to satisfy anyone at the judgment of the Apostolic See—as though he were not one of the sheep of blessed Peter and were exempt from the obligation concerning which God says to him: “Whatever you bind on earth will be bound also in heaven,” and so forth.

Thus, by transgressing the two aforesaid oaths at Guibert’s persuasion, he was again bound by the bonds of anathema through the synodal judgment of the Apostolic See, until he should come to his senses.

## III. On Henry the persecutor

At last the aforesaid tyrant, namely Henry, hardened like Pharaoh, left forces in Germany for resistance, gathered an army partly of his own men and partly of mercenaries or common soldiers, and for four years devastated Rome and its suburbs by plundering, burning, and slaughter as far as he was able. Finally, after his own Simon had been enthroned more by money than by force, he received the imperial crown from him.

Shortly afterward he was disgracefully routed and departed in flight before the military force of the Northmen under Duke Robert, who had hastened to the aid of the lord Pope Gregory, then staying at the Castle of Sant’Angelo. He inflicted a savage and prolonged persecution both on those who did not favor him and on those who refused communion with him and his accomplices, both in Rome and throughout his entire kingdom.

Because of this, and because nearly the whole Church throughout the kingdom was desolated [Col. 1571D], the Christian religion was almost destroyed, and ninety thousand people and more in various regions were slain with the cooperation of the false pope Guibert [Col. 1572A].

After expelling Catholic bishops and abbots, Guibert substituted in each city, hospice, or church one, and sometimes two or annual, wicked and ignorant prelates, by the damnable commercial transaction of his former prior and master, Guibert the Simon. While no one was able to resist him by force of arms, he plundered sacred places and Christians who did not favor him—and even those who did favor him—far and wide, displaying a will no less than that of his Nero, though less ability.

But thanks be to God, who, as the Apostle says, “always triumphs over us in Christ Jesus.” For that same emperor, his Nero, abandoned by his wife—whom, God as his witness, he had prostituted to many—and by his sons because of his cruelty, has at last been so weakened by an encounter not with any king, duke, or marquis [Col. 1572B], but with one woman, the glorious and God-beloved Countess Matilda, that the great Roman emperor, scarcely fifty years old, now walks with difficulty. By the just and strict judgment of God, the man who had so often sold and denied God was overcome by a woman’s triumph. He had thrown off from himself the gentle yoke of God like his father Belial, and, forgetful of the holy king Job, who says, “If I despised judgment with my servant,” he disdained to submit to the judgment of blessed Peter the Apostle in order to make satisfaction to those whom he had persecuted with the greatest hostility.

That same Guibert, who ought much more properly to have been called “Pope the Madman” than “Clement” [Note: [Col. 1571D] The same is said by Leo of Ostia, book III, chapter 69], now awaits in his little town, called Argentum, a tower built high as if for his own fortification [Col. 1572C], the Simoniacal angels with whom he may fly and fall, his legs broken, into the most shameful Stygian marshes—namely, with his affairs, by God’s mercy toward us, already almost shattered and reduced to nothing.

No one showed him apostolic reverence or obedience except his own Nero, his wicked accomplices, and those who, because of greed—which “is the service of idols”—sold themselves to him either permanently or temporarily by sworn agreement. Many of these, whose treachery had become notorious, fled so as not to be present while he celebrated his accursed sacrifices. They knew that Guibert had succeeded none of the Roman pontiffs, but that, in the manner described, he had been imposed upon Lord Pope Gregory by Henry, the perjured and invading Simon, King Henry [Col. 1572D], and so forth.

# AT THE END OF THE CENTURY: WILLIAM OF POITIERS, ARCHDEACON OF LISIEUX

[Col. 1573]

## Historical Notice on William

(FABRICIUS, *Bibliotheca Latina mediae et infimae aetatis*, III, 162)

William of Poitiers, or Pictaviensis, archdeacon of Lisieux, or Lexovium, recorded the deeds of William I the Conqueror, king of England, whose chaplain he was. The work was written after 1066 and published from the Cotton manuscript in André du Chesne’s *Normannic Histories*, Paris, 1619, folio, pp. 178, 213; but it is mutilated at the beginning and end. William of Jumièges praises it in VII, 44, as does Orderic Vitalis, book III of the *Ecclesiastical History*, p. 503.

[Col. 1573]

## Deeds of William the Conqueror, by William of Poitiers

(See *Patrologia*, volume CXLIX, column 1217, under the year 1087, in the section on William the Conqueror.)

[Col. 1573]

## William of Poitiers’ Poems against Guibert the Antipope

(USSHER, *Hibernian Letters*, letter 29, note, p. 138, from a manuscript formerly belonging to the subchantership of Thorney among the Halifax manuscripts.)

**William, the least of the canons of blessed Hilary,**

**To Guibert:**

Do not despise, Ravenna-born Guibert, seeing these verses written to you:

Do not think sound counsel will prove worthless to you.

Return quickly to your heart, enjoying reason in the morning.

If you have a pure heart, it will show you to be mad,

You who hurl an impenetrable weapon against heaven.

Your recklessness is evident, since you raise your horns on high,

Demanding for yourself Christ’s kingdom with a wretched outcome.

Established wholly as a laughingstock among the sane,

You wrongly believe yourself to be pope of the Holy See,

Which you violated with your foul body, having become a robber.

Madman, your name is deservedly and badly fixed as Clement,

O head of error, flowing with much blood:

Now your error will reveal and prove

Those whom, like silver, the testing of faith proves.

Therefore beware of persisting in your enterprises too quickly,

And, casting off pride, see what you are, you who must die.

Prostrate before the pope, declare your past crimes;

Seek pardon and confess your guilt.

He is first a pardoner, yet equally an avenger of crime.

# FROM THE YEAR 1011 . . . JOHN OF GARLAND

[Col. 1575]

## Notice

[Note: [Col. 1576] See Thomas Smith’s *Catalogue*, p. 39.]

Garlandius. In the catalogue of the manuscripts of Marquard Gude, he is less correctly called John of Gallandia [Note: [Col. 1575] p. 575, no. 356]. He flourished in the year 1040 [Note: [Col. 1575] See Bostius of Bury in the catalogue printed by John Bale, *British Writers*, century II, no. 48].

He wrote:

1. **On Accent**, book I, beginning:

> “He who wishes to know the rule of the sacred Church . . .”

An *Accentarius* survives in manuscript at Cambridge in the archives [Note: [Col. 1575] See John Pits, *On the Illustrious Writers of England*, p. 185].

2. **On the Mysteries of the Church**, book I, beginning:

> “England, where are you heading, while . . .” [Note: [Col. 1575] See Bale, cited above.]

3. **One Book of Everything**, book I, beginning:

> “While they seek advantages, neglecting . . .” [Note: [Col. 1575] See Bale, cited above.]

4. **A Satirical Work**, book I, beginning:

> “At last I am writing a new satire . . .” [Note: [Col. 1575] See Bale, cited above.]

5. **The Epithalamium of the Blessed Mary**, book I, beginning:

> “The noble woman is raised, having first been proclaimed by the world . . .” [Note: [Col. 1575] See Bale, cited above.]

A manuscript epithalamium of the Blessed Virgin Mary, in honor of the heavenly bridegroom and bride, in elegiac verse, by John of Garland, survives in Robert Cotton’s library, Claudius X, I.

6. **A Work of Synonyms**, book I, beginning: [Note: [Col. 1576] See Bale, cited above.]

> “Lest I seem to bring waters to the sea . . .”

It survives without the author’s name, though joined to other books of John of Garland, in manuscript in the ducal library at Wolfenbüttel, in that portion which formerly belonged to Marquard Gude. I am persuaded that much can be extracted from this book that contributes to the true meaning of words and is therefore useful, indeed necessary, to future lexicographers. We shall provide a specimen of a comparison made with Faber’s *Thesaurus*, edition of 1710. We shall publish the book itself in full in section II of the poems of the Middle Ages, from the manuscript mentioned above, first observing that a gloss written in the manuscript makes its author Master Matthew of Vendôme, or his pupil Ganfridus.

7. **The Book of Equivocal Words**

Perhaps this is the same work that, without the author’s name, is entitled *A Poem on Latin Names and Verbs of Equivocal Meaning with Commentary* in the catalogue of the manuscript books which Anthony à Wood bequeathed to Oxford University [Note: [Col. 1576] See *Manuscript Catalogues of England and Ireland*, II, p. 400, column 2]. It is the second part of the book *On Synonyms*, as is gathered from verse 38 of the *Book of Synonyms*. The manuscript book survives in the same Wolfenbüttel codex. I do not wish to transcribe it in full now, lest our history be overwhelmed by verses. I shall give only its first lines.

8. **The Mysteries of the Church**

I believe this book is not different from the one cited above under no. 2, and that Bale is mistaken in giving the opening of the work. The manuscript book survives in the aforesaid Wolfenbüttel codex, from which I shall extract the prologue and first chapter.

9. **A Book on Orthography**

This too survives in manuscript in the praised Wolfenbüttel codex. At the end of its copy are read the words:

> “Here ends the book on orthography, for which John of Garland was the efficient cause; and it should be noted that he extracted this book from the greater volume of Priscian.”

10. **The Horned Work, or Distichs**, book I [Note: [Col. 1576] See John Bale, *On British Writers*, century 2, no. 48].

11. A metrical book of John of Garland survives among the manuscript codices in the Jacobaean buildings, no. 777 [Note: [Col. 1576] See *Manuscript Catalogues of England and Ireland*, II, p. 246].

# Little Works of John of Garland

(POLYCARP LEYSER, *History of Medieval Poetry*, p. 311.)

[Col. 1577]

## A Work of Synonyms

[Col. 1577A]

Lest I seem to carry water to the sea,  
a spark to the fireplace, leaves to dense forests,  
or a pyre to Calabrian guests, wine to Bacchus,  
grain to Ceres, honey to bees, or thyme to meadows,  
apples to Alcinous, or soft incense to the Sabaean,  
I take care to add our concerns to those of the ancients.

But, offering a little milk to children, I set forth a few things for the little ones,  
whom only the gifts of their mother tongue enrich.

I give children the elements of the Latin language,  
whose manifold benefit, reader, you may foresee.

Whoever wishes to abound in Latin speech  
and to preserve what his slippery mind quickly pours forth,  
should here choose among many changing expressions.

This work teaches how to signify the same thing in different ways,  
joining synonyms in verse  
and in rhythmic [the text has *ricinis*; read *rhythmis*] form, so that an abundance of words may be available.

Through varied examples, the brief and the extended are taught.

Many things are placed under many words, and one thing under one word.

We assume that what usually happens always happens.

In this way we deceive others, and are ourselves deceived by them.

Therefore it is necessary to know how synonyms differ  
from equivocal and univocal words.

A univocal word signifies many things of one kind,  
as “human being” signifies particular human beings.

An equivocal word conceals several things under the same word:  
their name is the same, but the account of each beneath it is different.

What swims in the sea, shines in the sky, and barks in a house—  
these three things are signified by the word “dog” in three different senses.

[Col. 1577C]

Different things are signified by one synonymous word:

“Point,” “sword,” and “blade”: one thing is called  
by these names. The same thing is signified by these words.

But since many words belong to dactylic meter  
and evade the rule of the work, words are needed here  
whose short syllable may be lengthened and whose long syllable shortened,  
so that they can be placed in different parts of the verse.

Otherwise synonyms could not be joined together.

It seemed fitting to complete this work with two sections:

[Col. 1578A]

The first part yields to words with many names, the second to equivocal words,  
so that each item may be assigned to its proper place.

A double alphabetical order distinguishes this arrangement.

The soul has many names according to its many functions:

While it perceives, it is “sense”; while it indicates, “reason”;  
while it recalls something, it is “mind”  
[Note: [Col. 1577C] Therefore “mind” is not so called because it is the eminent part of the spirit, as Faber maintains];

while it thinks, it is “spirit” or “mind”  
[Note: [Col. 1577C] Hence *animus* is not properly the same as *anima*, as Faber asserts; I shall suppress his name in the observations that follow];

when it desires something, it is “heart”;  
when it wills, it is called “will.”

“Spirit” means soul, the departed spirits, perfection, life,  
power, entelechy, nature, capacity, inner virtue,  
or a human being; to these meanings “shadow” is added  
[Note: [Col. 1577C] Most of these meanings are omitted in the Lexicon].

“Orcus” possesses departed spirits  
[Note: [Col. 1577D] Therefore *manes* are not simply souls separated from bodies];

bodies live through souls; spirits are in heaven;  
shadows wander through the tombs  
[Note: [Col. 1578C] Therefore *manes* are not the same as shadows].

Hall, courtyards, camps, and royal palaces of kings.

Winged, winged creature, bird, flying creature, and swift-winged.

[Col. 1578B]

If it is a bird, I use *capio*; if it is bound, *garrio*.

“I take auspices,” “auspice,” and “augur” together;  
“I practice bird-catching” and “bird-catcher.”

“Augur,” “augury,” and “I augur” are likewise to be formed.

Say “boxes,” “cases,” “chests,” or “book-chests,” “caskets.”

“Small box” and “little chest” are diminutives of “chest.”

Steep, lofty, high, sublime, and tall,

highest, raised, elevated, and lifted,

and thus “raised up” is associated with the preceding terms.

Say “help,” “aid,” “support,” or “refuge,”

“protection” or “assistance,” to which add “relief.”

To these join “helping,” and likewise “aids”;

to these add “support” and “assistance”  
[Note: [Col. 1578C] This word is absent from the Lexicon].

From “favorable” comes the noun “favor.”

Torrent, river, water, stream, lake, and wave;

[Col. 1578C]

say “brook,” “water,” “wells,” “ponds,” and “marshes.”

To these add “river,” and likewise “flowing water.”

A river joined to water is called *mediarana water*  
[Note: [Col. 1578C] The Lexicon gives no meaning for this].

Gravel, gypsum, slime, clay, and bitumen.

“Glis” means an animal; “glis,” tenacious earth; “glis,” burdock.  
[Note: [Col. 1578C] Faber cites this verse in his Lexicon and attributes it to Silvaticus.]

“Ris” means the animal  
[Note: [Col. 1578D] Clearly the genitive of *glis*]; “sis,” tenacious earth; “tis,” burdock:

In this way the gender and genitive of the word are determined.

[Col. 1579A]

There is a frying pan, dish, cauldron, pot, or bronze vessel  
[Note: [Col. 1579D] The Lexicon does not know this word].

From *pateo* derive “pans”  
[Note: [Col. 1579D] The lexicographer did not observe this], and join “dishes.”

I call a vessel a “pan,” but the covering one a “lid”  
[Note: [Col. 1579D] Omitted in the Lexicon].

From Greek *sarcos* and *ago*, thus is *sarcago* named  
[Note: [Col. 1579D] Perhaps the word is actually *sartago*, meaning the same thing, and is written incorrectly, or was once written correctly but read incorrectly, since *t* and *c* scarcely differ in ancient manuscript codices]:

For Greek *sarcos* means “flesh” in Latin.

I pursue, love, desire, long for, and yearn  
[Note: [Col. 1579D] The Lexicon lacks this sense];

I wish, admire  
[Note: [Col. 1579D] You will seek it in vain in the Lexicon], long for, delight in, seize,

I go around; from this come “ambition” and “ambitious.”

A charioteer, driver, or coachman is called *vereda*.

A wagon and a little wagon should be counted among these.

I think *vereda* is derived from *veho*  
[Note: [Col. 1579D] Boxhorn, on the contrary, derives it from an Arabic word].

The charioteer derives his name from *aures* (“ears”) and *rego* (“I rule”).

The parts above the wagon are called *epyreide*  
[Note: [Col. 1580D] Perhaps *epirhedia*, which is a kind of vehicle in the Lexicon, though the form is less correct].

[Col. 1579B]

A pig, boar, and male swine are male; a sow, female pig, and breeding sow  
are female; but a young sow and piglet are diminutives.

*Sūs*, *suis*. From it the flesh should be called pork.

A *scrobs, scrobis* is a pit. This is *scobs, scobis*, from which the former is formed.

From “ditch” say “breeding sow”  
[Note: [Col. 1580D] The Lexicon is unaware of this etymology], the animal that digs the earth with its snout.

And the boar that sweeps the ground is called *verres*, from *verro*  
[Note: [Col. 1580D] Not from *verpes*, as the Lexicon has. Let this suffice as a specimen of the observations; let the inquisitive reader supply the rest].

A ram is a breeding male sheep, possessing the power of generation.

From “two-toothed” comes “two-toothed implement.” Call it a *bidental*,

a thunderbolt which fell where a victim was made with a two-toothed instrument.

But with bleating, “I bleat” represents the bleating animal.

The sacrificer celebrates; from sheep come “celebration” and “applause.”

The ram carries a worm on its head. So does the sheep.

Hence the flesh of a ram is called mutton.

He builds, affirms, and asserts: these are three.

[Col. 1579C]

“Maintains” is the fourth; all four signify one thing.

I assent, concede, and admit; I grant you.

He renounces, contradicts, denies, rejects, and disavows;

he opposes and refuses: these signify one thing.

When he gives support, helps, assists,

comes to the aid of, succors, and favors,

add “comes to the rescue.” If meter permits, “gives aid” may be added.

He withdraws, raises, removes, and snatches away;

he steals, strips, and carries away other people’s possessions,

deprives, plunders, and defrauds: these belong together.

He meets, addresses, summons together, and calls;

“calls in,” “speaks to,” and “addresses” are associated with the preceding words.

He increases, augments, exaggerates, and heaps up;

he piles up, accumulates, gathers together, collects, and adds;

[Col. 1579D]

he enlarges, amplifies, applies, and adds on;

with the preceding words, “joins,” “attaches,” and “unites.”

He keeps off, restrains, forbids, holds back, and controls;

curbs, represses, narrows, and constricts;

compels, binds, forces, tightens, and afflicts;

[Col. 1580A]

presses and compels: these have the same sense.

The indignant wild ass, unwilling to serve, is called one who resists across the fields;

but the submissive donkey is bound by the law of servitude;

the foal will be a little ass. Those are like it in character

who do not receive instruction with a hardened heart.

He is said to accuse equals and inferiors;

he is said to blame superiors and betters;

but he who excuses a crime diminishes it, while he who refuses rejects it.

What the judge gives by judgment, he adjudicates; what

the judge takes away by judgment, he abjudicates;

and, settling a dispute, he judges between the parties;

and those whom he afflicts with punishments, he judges.

“I judge you”: I condemn; “I judge for you”: I seek advantages for you.

The terms “maker” and “agent” take the name of “craftsman.”

The inventor is an *autor*; the actor acts; the *auctor* enlarges a matter.

*Autor* comes from *autentim* without *c*; the agent speaks of himself;

*actor* comes from *ago* without *v*; *auctor* comes from *augeo* with *c*.

He is greedy, desirous, avaricious, and ambitious;

the desirous person seeks riches, the ambitious one honors.

Timid, rash, and bold differ among themselves:

The bold man leaves what ought to be left undone and does what ought to be attempted;

the timid refrains both from what should be attempted and from what should be fled;

the rash dares what ought to be left undone and what ought to be done  
[Note: [Col. 1580D] An interesting distinction between the bold and the rash, which the Lexicon does not know].

He nourishes, fosters, restores, cherishes, and refreshes;

feeds and sustains: these words have one meaning.

From this come “nourishment” and “food,”

and alongside “fostering” come “sustenance” and “nourishment.”

“Whitens,” “is white,” “makes white,”

“becomes whitish,” and “makes white”: these differ among themselves.

Allow the first two to be transitive.

“Becomes white” marks a beginning; “becomes whitish” both diminishes and repeats it;

[Col. 1580C]

both of these are commonly used independently.

“Am white” and “become white” are intransitive. “Make white” is transitive.

An ointment, a poultice, spikenard, and an aromatic substance are said [to be such].

An aromatic substance reeks, producing the odor of Silenus.

What usually gives off a scent does not “smell sweet,” but simply “has an odor.”

The sediment of oil ought to be called *amurca*  
[Note: [Col. 1580D] Therefore it does not differ from *faex*, as Faber maintains].

An old woman is an aged woman, but “little old woman” diminishes the meaning.

While the old woman bends, she hisses like a cave.

Augur, diviner, fortune-teller, and haruspex;

add “soothsayer.” Hence comes “to practice divination.”

And “mathematician” and “observer of omens” are joined to these.

“Tree” and “trunk” have one meaning.

*Stips, stipis* is the maple; *stipes, stipitis* is a tree-trunk.

From “I pack” and “I pack together” come “stipends.”

[Col. 1580D]

The arbutus is a species of tree, just as *arbuta* is its fruit.

*Stips, stipis* is a small coin; the indeclinable word means a weight.

From this comes *dispondius*  
[Note: [Col. 1580D] Rather, something like a double weight or *pondo*], as a doubled unit.

Another part of the *as* is the *semis*; two-thirds is the *bisse*;

then come *cussis*, *quincussis*, *occussis*, and thence *decussis*.

[Col. 1581A]

“Assiduous” is said of one who continually devotes himself to study;

“assiduous” is also said of a rich person from the *as* he has given.

Shrewdness, cunning, caution, or craft;

to these may be joined prudence, cunning, and subtlety.

He demands, carries through, does, accomplishes, and works;

performs, acts, completes, consummates, perfects, and fulfills.

He executes, closes, concludes, and brings to an end,

sits down, and allows; he brings intermediate matters into action.

Say “storerooms,” “cellars,” or “shops.”

From the first comes “first,” the one who guards the storerooms.

A shop is a house to which all provisions are delivered.

A mortgage concerns immovable property: a house or a field.

Pledges of movable things are handed over in the hand.

Pledges of children are called *pignora*; pledges of things, *pignera*.

But because the law has taught that *pignora* may be used for “pledge,”

he names, calls, gives a surname to, and calls these things.

He cries out and judges; these are joined in the same sense.

He applies; although “applying” comes from the noun *appello*.

The doors which he unlocks he opens, spreads wide, and reopens;

add “removes the barrier” to these words of the same meaning.

Join these three: he uses, presumes, and dares.

He furrows, plows, turns the clods, cultivates, and improves the fields.

He is cold, becomes cold, freezes, and grows cold; hence

“cold” and “coldness.” “The wing of the sea” is likewise called;

“is chilled” is associated with the foregoing terms.

An altar, or altar-table, is called the Lord’s table,

and Apollo’s altar is customarily called a tripod.

Hence a *haruspex* is understood as one who inspects altars.

He puts on, covers, clothes, dresses, and conceals,

and veils: all the preceding words have the same meaning.

[Col. 1581C]

There is a globe, a heap, a pile, a mound, and an embankment.

There is a mass; from it arise “I heap,” “I make globular,” and “I collect into a mass.”

Say anchorites, recluses, and hermits.

This comes from *eremos* [Greek ἔρημος, “desert”]. But from *ana* comes the following.

Hence anchorites are so called as those who cultivate heavenly things in their hearts.

I walk, go, proceed, travel, walk about, and advance;

add to these “stroll,” “come,” and “set out.”

He says “hail” when coming, “greetings,” and “farewell” when departing.

An *amussis* is a plumb-line, indicated by a rule.

Hence *ex amussim* means “exactly” or “without deviation.”

Say that *ave* (“hail”) signifies a heavenly greeting to you.

One meaning of “to mutter” is also “to doubt.”

I make oblique, bend, curve, arch, and leave:

usage has given all these verbs the same sense.

[Col. 1581D]

Balsam is a tree; balsams are liquids.

The tree’s opobalsams flow out when its bark is cut.

Know that *folibalsama* is made from the leaves and is bitter.

Crushed or cut wood produces *colobalsams*.

Bacchus is the planter of the vine; *bacha* is said of sacred persons.

From this we call any mad person *bacchari*, “to rave like a Bacchant.”

Those who live through Bacchanalian rites live insanely.

Support, prop, base, and structure;

the foot properly provides support, and so does the column.

In Greek *basilios* means “king” in Latin.

From this I know that *basilicum* and *basiliscum* arise.

A baron is a serious and authoritative man.

The same word signifies a heavy object, and also an elephant.

For Greek *barres* means “heavy” in Latin.

Wool-bearing sheep, bleating sheep, and two-toothed sheep

we call them: these are all names for the same animal.

The verse would have been complete if “little sheep” had not been omitted.

A golden belt encircles distinguished matrons;

silken threads mixed with gold have woven it.

“Beta” and “maguderim”: call it a stalk . . .
according to,
Hence the adjective *betasius* occurs.

It signifies the same as *bilis offensa*, resentment, and anger.

But strictly speaking, *bilis* is the bitter humor of gall.

A *bilibris* is a measure of two pounds.

“Two-leaved” things are called *bifores*, because their paired leaves meet.

I sound, or resound, roar back, bellow, and cry out.

From *boo* come *buccella* (“morsel”), *bucula* (“little cow”), *bucca* (“cheek” or “mouth”), and *boatus* (“bellowing”).

From *cano* and *bucca*, together with *buccinia*, comes *bucula*, which rages.

[Col. 1582B] *Os*, *oris*, “mouth,” is *bucca*; but *buccula* diminishes the meaning.

For the cheeks of infants, say *ocella* or *oscula*.

A *buccella* is as much food as one receives in a single mouthful.

The *lituus*, trumpet, pipe, and *buccina* differ from one another.

A thin sound comes from the *lituus*, while the sound of the others is coarser.

The *buccina* derives its name from the material from which it is made.

*Bubo*, *bubastus*, *bos*, *bostar*, *bucria*, *buris*,

*Bubalus*, *bulcus*, *bucrilus*, *buglossa*, and *bubulcus*.

From *boo* there are also *bosforus* and *bootes*.

A *bostar* is a station for cattle; the curved part of a plow is

the *buris*; *bubastus* is a grape with swollen clusters;

a small ox is a *buculus*; but a *bubalus* is larger than an ox,

though similar in form to an animal of another species.

There are fish called *bulbi*; cattle are tended by *bubulci*.

It has the sound of an ox’s tongue; the plant is called *buglossa* (“ox-tongue”).

[Col. 1582C] But horned animals are called *butria* in Greek.

The road is called *bosforus* because it is traversed by cattle.

The star *bootes* stands fixed at the Arctic pole.

There are *bufo*, *rana*, *ranunculus*, and *rubeta*—all names for a frog or toad.

A *bombex* is a worm; its excretion produces silk.

The silken garment called *bombicina* bears witness to this *bombex*.

The owl is an ugly bird; the toad is an especially ugly beast.

The same thing is called *blata* and *vespertilio* (“bat”):

hence to babble with a chattering sound is *blaterare*.

The Greeks customarily call a frog *beta*,

as is found written in Isidore, the Spaniard,

and, if you count correctly, *agredula* is added to these.

Victory grants a reward for the course—*bravium*—

but everyone who neglects food is *imbrumatus*. [The precise sense of *imbrumatus* is uncertain.]

[Col. 1582D] *Bractea* and *bracteola* are said of a very thin sheet.

Rain, winter, and *bruma*: one thing is called by these three names;

but the name *bruma* is derived from the shortness of the days.

For in Greek *brachos* means “short” in Latin:

*hymera* means “day.” These two words form *bruma*.

*Brucus*, *acalaber*, and *locusta* are names for the same creature.

Thus three ages give the animal three names:

while it is small, it is a *brucus*; when it rises from the earth,

it is called an *acalaber*; after it becomes mature, a *locusta*.

With a concordant name, as though we were speaking of a long spear,

call conflict, war, engagement, and the wing of battle *duellum*.

Siege, Mars, rebellion, battles, and combat

are *acies* and *guerra*, to be associated with the foregoing.

He is fortunate, happy, favorable, and blessed;

say *beans* for “one who withdraws,” and *trabeatus* for one clothed in a *trabea*.

[Col. 1583A] The same thing is *femoralia*, *perizomata*, and *brachae*.

From *bracos* come *bracale* and *lumbare*, a garment for the loins.

A *fiber* is the same as a beaver, *biver*; from the beaver come *castoria*.

Its testicles yield *castoria*; nevertheless, we call castrated persons *castrati*.

*Boletus*, *tubera*, and *fungi* signify one thing:

the fruits of the earth produced by the coming together of rains.

Add *asparagus*; the sense of all these is the same.

*Dragma*, or *aureus*, *uma*, *besantius*, and *talentum*.

But strictly call *dragma* a kind of weight.

*Dragma* is neuter; its genitive is *dragmatis*.

You may call a question a *dramaticum* kind of expression.

*Dragma* means “melody” and “weight”; thus its genitive is *dragmatis*.

But if the genitive is *dragmae*, it denotes weight.

Beautiful, handsome, tall, or distinguished,

[Col. 1583B] recognize a tall man; take Juvenal as witness.

Splendid, excellent in form, and lovely in appearance,

illustrious, shining, handsome, and likewise graceful.

Call the body of every tall person *procerum*.

*Marsupium*, *bursa*, *forulus*, *loculus*, and *tometra*.

A dog is a *canis*, *catulus*, *leporarius*, or *molossus*,

lest, for the sake of the meter, an inappropriate odor be present in them. [Text uncertain.]

*Aether* and *aethera*, the pole, heaven, and *Olympus* are names for the sky.

A latrine is likewise called *cacabunda*, *cloaca*,

and *tristega*, as though one were reading “sad” (*triste*).

*Chorda*, *fidis*, *restis*, *funis*, and *funiculus*:

the rope by which you hang thieves is called *torquinus*.

*Antemna*, *rudens*, and *amentum* are added to these.

Say that *rudens* comes from *rudo*. *Fidicen* is formed from *fidis* and *cano*.

One who walks on a rope is therefore called a *funambulus*.

[Col. 1583C] *Cantharus*, *patera*, cups, vessels, and *crater*,

*scyphus*—among the ancients, horns—*concha*,

*cimbia*, *calathos*, and *carthesia* are joined to these.

You may believe that *spadones* are so called from *spatha*.

There are *cophinus*, *calathus*, *sporta*, *sportula*, and *corbus*,

to which *lus*, *quaxillum*, and similar terms are to be added. [Text uncertain.]

A *fiscina* or *fiscella*, in which cheese is made,

is a vessel; call a large vessel for milk *multrale*,

which plainly takes its name from *mulgere*, “to milk.”

*Balteus*, *cropheum*, *cinctoria*, *cingula*, and *zona*

are *ocreae* and *caligae*, garments worn by you.

We call *camisia* and *interula* one and the same thing;

to these are added *subuncula* and *subirara*, garments. [Text uncertain.]

Raw, cruel, harsh, wicked, atrocious,

wild and fierce, violent, bitter, and savage,

[Col. 1583D] impious, unmild, ferocious, troublesome, and rough,

inhumanly harsh, tyrannical, and insolent,

grim, untamed, and severe are joined to these.

There are *chorus*, *cohors*, assembly, public gathering, and company.

Say *consortia*, *contubernia*, and *chorea*;

add *turma*, *phalanx*, *acies*, and *cuneus* as associated terms.

A legion consists of six hundred and sixty;

to complete the number, add six thousand to this,

but call the remainder of five hundred a cohort.

Assembly, small assembly, and band are added to these;

join to them council and *constabula*. [Text uncertain.]

Add cymbals, bell, *nola*, and tinkling bells.

Field, little field, land, countryside, garden, little garden, and cultivated ground,

[Col. 1584A] which the gardener continually cultivates: *hortulanus* comes from *hortus*.

Curtains, hangings, and draperies are *anabastra*;

the border of a curtain is called *peripetasma*.

We say *aulaea* because they are stretched out in a hall.

Since *ana* means “upward,” and *bachos* means a step, *ana*—

avoid contests, quarrels, disputes, and wranglings;

there is contention, disagreement, and litigation,

when *agonia* is joined to *agoni*. [Text corrupt or incomplete.]

There are *coma*, *caesaries*, *crinis*, *pilus*, and *capillus*.

I believe *caesaries* is properly applied to men.

From combed hair comes *coma*, properly applied to women.

The front part is the chariot of the head, stripped of hair;

the front part of the head is *crinis*, a dense mass of hair.

It is called *currus* because it carries the *alauda* around it. [Text uncertain.]

The mane of a four-footed animal is *juba*; the bristles of pigs are called *seta*.

[Col. 1584B] *Caesaries* belongs to a man, and *coma* properly to a woman.

The hair of either may properly be called *capillus*.

*Laurea*, *cernane*, wreath, diadem, and crown—

add *aureola*, which is so called from *pavois*. [Text uncertain.]

And I believe that the thing which removes two [ends] is called a diadem,

just as every round thing makes its end like its beginning.

Using the general terms, say *currus* and *curriculum*;

from *veho* comes *vehiculum*, which is foreign to the verse.

Here I give the species of these, which follow below:

give *quadrigae*, *carpenta*, *esseda*, and *bigae*;

join to these *pilentum*, *fartagum*, and *libramen*.

*Testudo*, *cithara*, *chelys*, and *lyra* signify one thing.

From *cithara* come *citharizo* and *citharaedus*.

From this come the lyric song and *lyricen*; *lyra* is formed with *cano*.

[Col. 1584C] I touch the lyre with my thumb; with a plowshare I make a ridge (*lyra*).

From this we customarily regard *deliri* as fools,

and hence those who are discordant are said to *delirare*.

He is uncertain, doubts, fluctuates, hesitates, and clings,

and *musso* supplies no other sense than those stated above. [Text uncertain.]

There are house, dwelling, manger, little house, and roof;

building, little buildings, dwellings—call them stations;

join to these *pastoforium*, *magalo*, and huts,

as well as *mapale*, hut, and *ypepis*; *mansio* is joined to them.

*Lar* and dwelling-house: one is called a part of a roof.

A woman is *hera*, mistress, lady, matron, or *virago*.

Doctor, instructor, adviser, tutor, and agent,

corrector, *didascalus*, and teacher are associated with these.

I destroy, dissolve, ravage, consume, and lay waste,

[Col. 1584D] demolish, scatter, overthrow, and squander.

Call thickets, bushes, brambles, *arbusta*, and *fruceta*;

and believe that *rubetae* (toads) are so called from *rubus* (“bramble”).

Places of trees and shrubs are *arbusta* and *fruceta*.

Things that grow like shrubs seem to be *fruticare*.

Riches, wealth, revenues, money, and treasures

are abundance, possession, and private property;

property and ownership: hence *proprietarius* is formed.

Food, delicacies, feasts, nourishment, provisions, and sustenance,

pasture, banquets, livelihood, and eating are also included.

A morning meal is *jentamen* or *jentaculum*;

but *obsonia* often refers to food purchased as an accompaniment,

and at midday the proper order provides *prandia*.

There are *sonipes*, wild horse, *equiferus*, and *caballus*.

[Col. 1585A] To these add quadrupeds and the *emissarius* horse.

A *dextrarius* is a large horse suited to the right hand.

Give *vectores*; we call them *veredes*.

We call them eunuchs, castrated men, or *spadones*,

if the meter permits the word *cuintitulatus* in this place. [Text uncertain.]

Nature makes men castrated; violent wickedness makes *spadones*;

only the will makes eunuchs.

These verbal expressions have one meaning:

I conjecture, think, or infer, or suppose;

I assert, conjecture, suspect, estimate, and believe.

Ditch, cavern, pit, grotto, cave, or den.

*Scrobs* and *scrobis* mean a pit, but *scobs* and *scobis* are used for it. [Text uncertain.]

Add *traco*, winding passage, hollow place, and abyss.

[Col. 1585B] From this flow rains, the cataracts of heaven, and passages.

Slave, servant, dependent, household-born servant, minister,

administrator, boy, attendant, little household servant, and slave;

join *satrapa* and *satelles* to the foregoing.

Grating, pore, gallery, window, and opening.

I call a square opening in a wall a *cancellum*,

in which pigeons are accustomed to build their nests.

The innermost part of a temple is called a *cancellus*.

To cancel is to mark what must always be condemned:

a line drawn through the middle signifies this;

what erases badly written matter gives rise to *cancellarius*.

On the cross Christ stretches out his arms crosswise for our sake.

Ravager, predator, brigand, robber, and thief

are also *stratilites*, cattle-drivers, and *vespiliones*.

A thief takes things away at night, a brigand by day;

[Col. 1585C] *Vispilio* is so called as one who strips by force of his right. [Text uncertain.]

Those who lie hidden like robbers are called *stratiletes*, as I say, from *strata*. [Text uncertain.]

Those who drive away cattle and herds are *abigei*;

we also call sea-raiders pirates.

I congratulate, exult, rejoice, applaud, and resound;

I rejoice, celebrate, exult, and sing with jubilation;

I take pleasure and also cheer up; among these is *hilaresco*.

Sword, *rumphea*, *framea*, point, or sword;

to these is added *sica*, from which *sicarius* is formed.

There are *stilus*, *graphium*, and *calamus*, suitable for writers,

as well as *pugillaris*, so called because it is held in the fist.

A hump or goiter is properly a swollen part of the back.

From this we say *gibbosus* and *strumosus*.

I shudder, dread, fear, am afraid, and tremble,

[Col. 1585D] and I tremble when I am terrified; I am agitated, afraid, and become fearful.

Fire and little fire form *focus* and *caminus*.

Add funeral pyre, *pira*, and furnace.

Insane, violent, senseless, deranged, and witless,

foolish, demented, raging, stupid, and mad;

Tartarus, hell, Acheron, Styx, Orcus, and Avernus—

join Erebus, the abyss, and Gehenna to these.

Reed, rush, *bibilus*, papyrus, and cane;

with *canna* and *calamus* these are associated.

I fumigate, burn incense, and smoke with incense; to these I add

*incenso*, which usage has given the same meaning.

Let *suffio* be removed, as the author proves in this way,

and let *suffire* be restricted to the place where incense is taken from the censer.

He kills, destroys, murders, slays, and sacrifices.

[Col. 1586A] He kills, sacrifices, extinguishes, or cuts to pieces;

suffocates, strangles, makes a corpse, or throttles;

puts to death, cuts off, ends, or deprives of life.

Door, gate, doors, double doors, entrances, and leaves.

Call women who practice magic *veneficae* and *magicae*; also call them *lamiae* and witches.

The same thing is designated by these terms, to which are associated

*incantatrix*, *sagana*, and *praestigiatrix*.

Actor, flatterer, mime, or gesticulator,

banqueter, good-for-nothing, parasite, buffoon, and messenger;

likewise pantomime actor, comedian, or jester.

From the serpent *nepa*, add *nepotes* to these terms.

Heel, pebble, little pebble, millstone, stone, and millstone;

add *cautis*, which is often encountered by sailors,

rock, stone, boulder, flint, and little stone.

[Col. 1586B] Chorus, layer, bed, dance, and pallet;

add couch and sleeping quarters, together with bedchamber.

*Phoebe*, moon, *cyntania*, and *mena*;

the newness of the moon is therefore called *neomenia*.

Little document, document, codex, book, and little book.

If it is permitted to lengthen a short word and shorten a long one,

join *codicillus* and *volumen* to these.

Know a little book by its taste; know a little book by its appearance. [Text uncertain.]

A *subligar* is a strap that binds the sandals high;

join mud, mire, *volutabrum*, and slime to these;

hence *coenolentus* and *illimus* are formed.

Say sea, sea-water, waters, and deep;

join *pelagus*, sea, straits, and *bicaterassum* to these. [Text uncertain.]

Say *Amphitrite*, because she circles and wears away the world.

A prostitute is a harlot, *scortum*, *Thais*, she-wolf, goat, or *chimera*;

add *post nova*, *prostans*, and *novaria* to them. [Text uncertain.]

Call *gausape*, tablecloth, napkins, and hand-towels;

add *mancile*, so called because of the hands.

Soldier, horseman, recruit, young recruit, and Roman citizen;

also *Neoptolemus*, a new warrior, is among these.

Call it *materia* or *materies*, the material of houses;

from equality comes *paries*, “wall,” which is joined to these.

But walls, properly, or *moenia*, are those of a city.

It is also called a rampart, a palisade, or a structure made of wicker;

hence *invallare* means to enclose with a rampart.

A garden and field are enclosed by hedges and fences.

[Col. 1586D] An *indago* encloses forests and what lies hidden in the woods;

hence *indagare* means to investigate hidden things.

He intimates, insinuates, explains fully, and reveals;

marks, uncovers, expounds, and discloses;

doubles and opens out, gives to the age, brings forth, and publishes;

announces, sets forth, elucidates, and clarifies;

explains, exercises, declares, or makes manifest;

expresses, unlocks, divulges, indicates, and

notifies: these words have the same meaning.

He makes clear, unrolls, opens, strips bare, and reopens.

*Interit* and *occumbit* signify a violent death;

*interit*, *exspirat*, *moritur*, and *defungitur*,

as do *occumbit*, *obit*, *dissolvitur*, and *exanimatur*,

are otherwise associated with a natural death.

*Excidit* and *exhalat*—“he falls away” and “breathes out”—are added to these.

[Col. 1587A] And you can express the same thing in a fuller phrase:

“He is removed from our midst; he pays the debt owed to nature,”

“he pays the general tribute owed by us to our nature,”

“he closed the life of the present world with a final burial,”

“his spirit, released from the bodily prison, departs,”

“he died to the world, intending afterward to live for Christ,”

“he happily completed the course of the present life,”

“his spirit freed itself from its bodily prison.”

Funeral, destruction, death, demise, and ruin;

add killing, destruction, and *libitina*;

join death, demise, destruction, and fate to these,

which is called *libitina* because it concerns whatever may please. [Text uncertain.]

Associate extermination and setting with these.

There are *linter*, *lembus*, *scapha*, *prora*, *liburna*, and *faselus*;

ship, little ship, stern, raft, and keel.

[Col. 1587B] Together with fleet, *sclaria*, *mortaria*, and *chelox*,

join *cimba*, bireme, and trireme.

A ship governed by a triple arrangement is called a trireme.

Energetic, freeborn, illustrious, or noble;

distinguished, excellent, renowned, and outstanding;

add patron, highly distinguished, and noble to these.

Grove, forest, woodland, thicket, and green plantation;

let us join *arbustum*, said to come from *arbor*.

A *lucarius* is the guardian of a grove; here *luceo* is derived from *lucus*. [Text uncertain.]

I weave; *nemus*, forest, and silence; but *lucus* is derived from shining. [Text uncertain.]

I withdraw, report, weave again, review, and narrate.

He neglects, scorns, disdains, rejects,

despises, refuses, rejects, and declines;

thus he undervalues and treats as worthless.

[Col. 1587C] Coverlet, patchwork quilt, bed covering, cushion, mattress, and blanket;

there is also a featherbed; add those supported by tapestries,

together with a pillow that gives warmth to the neck.

Little moon, moon, *nychelides*, necklace, and earrings;

*flammea*, little *flammeum*, hook, band, and *peplum*;

add bracelets and a necklace to the right-hand ornaments;

also *cernale*, *spinter*, brooch, and *mitra*;

ring, gem, *lymber*, glove, and tiara;

join little cap and hat to these.

Women take care of their own hair arrangement.

Pitcher, little pitcher, jar, amphora, and vessel;

pot or water-jar; call a wine vessel a flask;

*obba*, *onophorum*, *orca*, *fidelia*, and vessel;

we associate bottles and phials with the foregoing.

[Col. 1587D] Arch, brothel, *genedea*, disgrace, and *lupinar*.

Flank, fat, grease, fatness, and nourishment;

add abdomen, *adapes*, and *popisma* to these;

join *tegedum* and *proseuta* to the foregoing. [Text uncertain.]

Bundle, small bundle, weight, pack saddle, and bundle;

the first is said to have placed a flask upon himself. [Text uncertain.]

A bundle denotes food; *fasces* denote honors;

little bundle, burden, globe, mass, and heap.

Bread, baker’s bread, pastry, cakes, and pie;

join *arthocrea* and *arthocaseus* to these,

and because material takes the place of the thing made from material,

add *simila*, *similago*, and rye.

Cloaks, little cloaks, *chlamys*, *ciclad*, and mantle;

add *abilis*, *manus*, and little cloak to these. [Text uncertain.]

Skins provide cloaks; *matrix*, properly, and *cirogallus*;

the same is supplied by rabbits through *cisimus* and *laerones*. [Text uncertain.]

[Col. 1588A] These are garments made solely from skins:

*pellicium* and *reno*, to which *endromis* is joined.

Very small, little boy, child, infant, and tiny;

hence *pusillanimes*, small-minded in spirit.

*Lethofagus*, *Cyrces*, *acroceramina*, and *syrtes*;

the Sirens, together with *ceramina*, *Scylla*, and Charybdis.

A whirlpool of a river is called Charybdis of the sea.

Skin, little skin, hide, little hide, and leather.

When it lacks flesh, *cartu* is associated with skin. [Text uncertain.]

Flesh with hide is the back; for you, *tergora* means skins.

Ancient, old, aged, and worn out;

decrepit, old, aged, veteran, and senile;

long-lived among these; likewise ancient and *metreta*. [Text uncertain.]

Slow, inactive, idle, lazy, and sluggish,

[Col. 1588B] torpid, lukewarm, inactive, numb, and lax;

one lacking the fire of spirit is called *ignavus*;

*deses* grows unaccustomed, and the inactive person slumbers at his craft;

without fire he is sluggish; I think *resides* comes from sitting back,

but the lazy are called *aegri* because their feet are weak. [Text uncertain.]

Scale, balance, steelyard, weight, burden, and balance;

also a pan and a swarm: these are among the terms for a balance.

Something weighed is *appensum*; call a balance *stater*.

Call the steelyard a balance.

*Examen apis* is a swarm of bees; *examen* is the tongue of a two-pan balance.

Dew, rains, clouds, and showers;

*roscida* comes from dew, but *hybernus* from rain.

I carry, bear, carry away, sustain, lift, and transport;

*gestio* means “I desire”; *gesto* means “I carry weights.”

[Col. 1588C] I proceed, walk, approach, go, or set out;

join *eo* and *itinero* to the foregoing verbs.

I trace, investigate, explore, seek, and search out;

I inquire, investigate, question beforehand, and ask.

Net, dragnet, snare, hunting net, little dragnet, and trap;

net and little net: *retia* is derived from *rete*;

hence *irretire* means to entangle.

Rustic, farmer, uncultivated, rural, and country-dwelling;

together with *ruricola*, join *villicus* to these.

We call keepers of sheep *opiliones*,

who are called *archimandritae* (“chief shepherds”).

A keeper of mules is called a *mulio*,

while those responsible for oxen are called *bubulci*.

*Orbiculare* and *rotundum* differ from one another.

[Col. 1588D] Call a spear smooth, but an apple round.

A sphere or egg retains the shape of an apple;

hence *sphaerica* is believed to be named from *sphaera*.

I go back, return, retrace my steps, and turn back.

I crawl back, come back, return, run back, and hurry back.

Door-bars are bolts, locks, barriers, and levers.

Call *parma*, *clypeus*, *ancile*, *aegis*, and *scutum* shields;

*pelta* is rounded; the central part of a shield is called its boss.

There are *callis*, path, track, roadway, footpath, and boundary;

little village and village; public road and street.

A *bivium* is a twofold road; a *trivium* is a threefold road;

call a safe road with four branches a *quadrivium*.

*Callis* comes from *callum*; *orbita* from *orbis* and its circuits;

*semita* comes from *transcendo*, while *iter* gives *semita* from *semis*. [Text uncertain.]

Sun, Titan, Phoebus, title, and *ephebus*. [Text uncertain.]

[Col. 1589A] Stool, footstool, benches, chair, and little stool;

join platform, seat, and seats to the foregoing.

There are crop, Ceres, fruits, sown fields, and harvests:

when it is being sown, it is a crop; when roots cling to the ground, it is sown grain;

when it bears fruit, it is produce; when it is reaped, it is harvest.

Ceres is said to derive her name from creating, because she creates all things.

That which annual use demands is called *annona*.

Mausoleum, *pollandum*, tomb, and sepulcher;

sarcophagus, funeral pyre, mound, or pyramid are one thing;

a monument is joined to these as a memorial of death.

Seed, seedbed, and sowing are the same;

let seeds be joined to the foregoing, said to derive from *sero*, “I sow”;

and *sementa* is the thing born from seeds sown.

Dish, bowl, platter, little bowl, and *perapsis*,

[Col. 1589B] likewise *bilanx* from *lanx*, and *parasitus* from *perapsis*. [Text uncertain.]

There are partner, companion, comrade, colleague, and associate.

The lot gives a partner; the road gives a companion; the table gives an associate;

a mission gives a colleague; labor produces a companion in the same way.

Standard-bearer or *signarius* signifies the same thing;

join *primiferus* and *vexillifer* to these;

among them, the *primipilus* is the one who carries the first spear.

He shines, sends rays, gleams, glitters, and flashes;

he sparkles, twinkles, glows red, shines, and shines back.

Plumes, decay, putrefaction, and pus are the same thing.

Filth, uncleanness, dregs, and foulness;

with stain, corruption, and contagion, these are sores and blemishes.

Call the filth of copper *scoria*, and the dross of metal *scoria*.

I say no more about the remaining terms concerning *tabes* and *tabum*.

[Col. 1589C] Let the bald-headed man be *glabero*; the condition occupying his head is *glaberosus*.

The scabies of the rest of the body gives the term *scabiosus*.

A pustule clings entirely to the body, and so does an ulcer.

There are serpent, water-snake, snake, *hydra*, and *celindrus*;

let *vipera*, *nepa*, and *anguis* be joined to these;

also *dracena* and *draco*; the scorpion belongs to these species.

I sacrifice, make sacred, offer sacrifice, perform a sacrifice, and immolate.

The name of the executioner derives from *mactare*, “to sacrifice.”

Those whom we call *lanistae* are said to derive their name from *lanio*, “butcher.”

Shoe: sandal, *pero*, or *sotularis*, *aluta*;

because it cleans mud, *aluta* takes its name from this. [Text uncertain.]

He is foolish, dull, mistaken, and senseless,

ignorant, brutish, simple, idiotic, and stupid;

join unlearned and lacking in taste to these,

[Col. 1589D] unadvised and *eligius*, to whom words are denied. [Text uncertain.]

[Col. 1590A] Let him be careless, imprudent, and inexperienced among these.

Temples, monasteries, shrines, and sanctuaries are so called;

we join basilica and church to these.

Shaft, spear-shaft, javelin, catapult, and arrow;

missile or weapon; nor should reed be added. [Text uncertain.]

Power, earth, ground, soil, land, or dry earth.

House, bedroom, chamber, inner room, and retreat;

add private chamber, *canapeia*, and household gods.

Scripture marks *canopeum* for us as *reticulum*. [Text uncertain.]

There are *canopeia*, tents, and pavilions,

so called, I believe, because they carry leather above them.

For incense, call the vessel an incense-burner;

*acerra*, which signifies the same thing, is joined to these.

Wines, unmixed wine, Bacchus, Bromius, Liber, and Iacchus;

[Col. 1590B] to these are joined Lenaeus and Lyaeus,

and from *temetum*, “wine,” comes *temulentus*, “drunken.”

There are hydromel, mead, nectar, beer, *cisra*,

spiced wine, new wine, honey-wine, and Falernian wine.

*Sapa* is what physicians place under the name of wine.

Whirlwind, wind, breath, breeze, and air.

Receive the kinds of winds in these verses:

Subsolanus, Vulturnus, Eurus, and Eous;

Circinus, Zephyrus from the west, and Favonius blow,

but Aquilo, Boreas, and Chorus come from the north,

while at midday Notus and Africus blow.

Garment, clothing, dress, and covering;

add cast-off garments, spoils, rags, and woven fabrics.

[Col. 1590C] What is covered is *tectus*; woven cloth drives away the cold.

A poor man’s little rag and coverings are joined to these.

To these are joined clothing and covering,

though the latter cannot be placed in the verse when lengthened. [Text uncertain.]

*Vinetum*, vineyard, and vine signify one thing;

*vinetum* properly means places where a vineyard grows.

The *pampinus* is a leaf; the *botrus* is a flower; the vineyard is the fruit;

a shoot or branch is a *palmes*, or a runner.

Call many grapes together a cluster, but the individual grapes are grains.

A wild, barren vine is called *labrusca*.

Belly, little belly, stomach, and abdomen;

to these is added the uterus, properly belonging to pregnant women.

The belly of a virgin is called *alvus*, and it is so named from *alere*, “to nourish.”

From *uterus* come the terms *germani* and *uterini*.

[Col. 1590D] Here end the synonyms.

[Col. 1589]

## Fragment from the Book on Equivocal Words

[Col. 1589D] *Augustus*, *-ti*, *-to*: take it as Caesar or as the month.

*Augustus*, *-tus*, *-ui*: it is to mean divination.

When *mobile* is made *augustus*, it signifies “noble.” [Text uncertain.]

*Augeo* supplies the first; *gustus* and *avis* supply the second. [Text uncertain.]

*Aura* may mean favor, splendor, breath, or air.

[Col. 1590D] An *abacus* is a table; *metrum* is the capital of a column.

This *acus* is a stylus, curling iron, or awl, *rome*. [Text uncertain.]

This is made from *acer*, but *acus* gives this genitive.

This *acus* is straw, just as *haec acus* and *hic acus* adorn [the phrase], and so forth. [Text uncertain.]

[Col. 1591]

## Fragment from the Book on the Mysteries of the Church

### Dedication

[Col. 1591A]

England, where he shines and where they rejoice in a distinguished bishop,

London, and Paris, where the study of wisdom flourished,

golden foundation, radiant Fulco,

stronghold of justice: receive the mysteries of the holy

Church, set forth with the learning and meter of John.

So that the mysteries may come more safely into the open

under so great a judge, though these things have been approved when recited at Paris,

they seek your subtle discernment, pious shepherd,

who institute holy men as sacred ministers and teach sacred things.

### The Mysteries of the Church

The church is the house of the Lord. The supreme craftsman

builds it in heaven from living stones, both square and round,

[Col. 1592A] and joins them according to the pattern of love,

laying the foundations. The foot and foundation is Christ the stone.

The wall surrounding it is the gentile and Hebrew people,

founded upon Christ through the four quarters of the world.

The saints are square stones, polished with a chisel.

[Note: *Celtes* is a certain instrument suitable for cutting stones. Thus reads the manuscript gloss on this passage.]

Square and stable in virtue, and prepared for heaven

by the highly trained hand of the supreme craftsman. Of these,

some are carried but do not carry: these are the simpler ones.

Others carry and are carried: these are of intermediate rank.

There are also those who carry and are not carried; nevertheless, these are

saints whom Christ carries to the stars of heaven.

[Col. 1591]

## Fragment of the Book on Orthography

[Col. 1591A] If anyone in the church ever reads a little sacred word,

so that you may avoid faults, be learned in orthography.

Examine whether I am useful; do not make me an object of envy,

as a target of envy. I do not seek a poet’s praise,

though it is rare. Let my meaning not be miserly.

[Col. 1592A] Not thus are the five talents entrusted to me held back.

In you, Christ, my hope is fixed, so that this book,

through you, may be completed, relying on your lightning,

since every letter is rightly a source of Scripture.

At the beginning, what the discussion is in itself may be treated, and so forth.

## Rufinus, Bishop

[Col. 1591]

## Two Books on the Good of Peace by Rufinus, Bishop of Uncertain See, from the Year 1056

*(R. P. Bernardi Pezii, Bibliotheca ascetica, vol. IX, Regensburg, 1726, in 12mo, p. 3.)*

### Notice

Nothing is sweeter to an ascetic, and nothing more necessary, than peace—whether inward or outward—for without it the pursuit of piety can neither be undertaken successfully nor maintained for very long. Two books concern this subject: the little books of Bishop Rufinus that you have before you. They contain almost everything that could be said by a writer of the Middle Ages concerning the good of peace.

The style is obscure and involved in some places, partly through the fault of the manuscripts and partly through that of his century, namely the eleventh after Christ was born. That Rufinus flourished at this time is certain from his dedicatory letter to Abbot Peter. Peter was appointed to the administration of the monastery of Monte Cassino in the year 1056 and soon yielded it to Frederick in the following year, as Leo of Ostia records in Book II, chapter 92 and following chapters, of the *Chronicle of Monte Cassino*.

I searched long and diligently, but in vain, for which see this Rufinus was bishop of, since no bishop of that name appears in Ughelli’s *Italia Sacra* or elsewhere who could have been contemporary with Abbot Peter of Monte Cassino.

The little work was copied from a three-hundred-year-old Tegernsee manuscript by the most gracious and learned Reverend Father Bonaventura Perghoffer, a Tegernsee ascetic. I later compared his copy with another, written in a more recent hand from a Bamberg manuscript and formerly communicated to me by the most learned Joannes Fridericus Schannat; however, the latter little book was lacking from it.

## Book One

### The Letter Begins

To the venerable abbot of Monte Cassino, concerning the little work *On the Good of Peace*, issued by Master Rufinus.

[Col. 1593A]

To his most holy father, lord, and exceedingly great benefactor, Peter, by the grace of God venerable abbot of Monte Cassino, Rufinus, as humble as he is useless, an unworthy bishop, wishes to earn the repose he desires.

A few days ago, because of a certain occupation connected with a domestic necessity, I had postponed supper until late. At last, while some brothers were reclining with me in the black darkness of night, a letter from Your Blessedness arrived. It brought the table itself the brightness of a joyful light, but it also mixed a sharper seasoning into the dishes that had already been prepared.

For prominent in it was Your Dignity’s earnest request that I compress into the body of a single little instructional book those matters which I had treated separately and publicly, *On the Good of Peace*, at the request of the venerable Bishop Soranus. Thus, after drawing breath for a while from the tumult of conflicting causes in which your prudent and pious concern often compels you to take part, you might keep the little Book of Peace before your eyes, so that, once read, it might sweep away every trace of former quarrels from the sanctuary of your heart and, once read, enliven the innermost recesses of your mind like the greenness of a meadow.

This command certainly brought me no small trouble and perplexity.
