I feared that I would either be guilty of disobedience if I disregarded the orders of so great a father, or be branded with rashness if I approached a task altogether beyond my powers—namely, that the sluggishness of my heavy intellect and the inadequacy of my unworked tongue should forge a volume on a more exalted subject, to be carved into chapters and rubricated with titles.

Yet amid these narrow confines of doubt it finally seemed better to disregard the accusation of presumption and not hesitate to undertake the work imposed upon me. I knew that I would incur the charge of ingratitude if, in any way, I proved disobedient to you, from whom I have already been worthy to receive so many, so great, and so timely consolations of piety.

Accordingly, first obeying your commands, [Col. 1594A] I composed this artificial page, *On the Good of Concord*, in the concise brevity of both work and time. I have decided shortly to offer it to the hands of Your Venerability, earnestly beseeching you, and calling upon God, the source of all goodness, that you not publish this compilation before examining it carefully, so that, if anything requiring correction should perhaps be found in it, you may either correct it yourself with merciful charity or be willing to send it back to me for correction.

The letter ends.

## Chapter I — On the Sacrament of the Name “Peace”

For those who wish to possess a complete knowledge of the good of peace, it is customary first to set forth the teaching concerning the name of the thing, and afterward that concerning the thing named.

The name of this good is therefore “Peace.” This word certainly expresses an outstanding sacrament of the eternal Trinity. For this name is declined, but does not turn into the plural, thereby suggesting that distinct unity in God. In it there is both distinction of persons and preservation of the simplicity of one and the same nature.

Just as this name consists of three letters, one letter being P, another A, and another X, which together form one word not resolved into a plural number—for we do not say *paces*—so the Godhead consists in three persons: one person the Father, another the Son, and another the Holy Spirit. These three are not several essences, but one essence and one God.

P, because it is the first letter, suggests the Father; A, which is in the middle, the Son; X, which is placed last, most properly represents the Holy Spirit.

Moreover, P signifies the person of the Father for two reasons. The first is that the name *pater*, “father,” begins with that letter. The second is that, although there are two letters that open compressed lips—P and B—when the lips are pressed more tightly to form P than B, they open with a more pronounced sound in order to release that same voice.

Thus, just as the lips open more widely in this letter so that the formed voice may be uttered, so everything that had previously lain hidden in the recesses of the divine ordering, like a sound conceived in the heart, began to be formed and, as it were, opened through the work of creation.

Scripture [Col. 1595A] customarily attributes the authority of this creation rather to the Father, whenever it recalls that all things were made by him. Hence the Apostle says to the Corinthians: “One God, the Father, from whom are all things.”

Likewise, A is believed to indicate the Son for two reasons. First, because it is a vowel—that is, it sounds by itself—and the Son was seen and known in himself. Second, because this letter is first before all the elements of the letters, and the Son is the firstborn before every creature.

But just as he is before every creature, so he is also after every creature. For he is Alpha and Omega, the first and the last; hence he is called “Firstborn” and “Only-begotten”: “Firstborn,” because no one existed before him; “Only-begotten,” because no one will exist after him.

So that the conception of this name might remain complete, the third letter, namely X, is added to the two preceding letters. This letter prefigures the person of the Holy Spirit in a twofold manner, namely through the nature of its sound and through the order of its arrangement. Through the nature of its sound, because it is a double consonant; and in this it appropriately signifies the Holy Spirit on account of the twofold harmony of charity understood in him: one by which he joins the Father to the Son, and another by which he joins creation to the Creator. For, as the most divine teacher Augustine has handed down, the Holy Spirit is love, joining the two and joining us beneath them through the order of arrangement.

It signifies him also through the order of its arrangement, because this letter is third from the end, that is, the antepenultimate letter. For only two letters, Y and Z, follow it in the alphabet. Of these three letters, therefore, X is the first; and through this is conceived that form of the mystery in which, although there are three kinds of rational spirits—namely, the uncircumscribed, the circumscribed but not enclosed, and the simultaneously circumscribed and enclosed—the Holy Spirit is the first of these three, namely the uncircumscribed spirit; the angelic spirit is circumscribed but not enclosed; and the human spirit is both circumscribed and enclosed.

Y, which begins from a single stem and then divides into two branches, is the angelic spirit, created good, certainly; but afterward shown divided through the turning away of some and the conversion of others. Z, which is written with a more winding character, signifies the human spirit. Although God created it, according to Ecclesiastes, simple and upright, it afterward attempted to entangle itself in winding and endless questions.

## CHAPTER II — On the reality signified by the name

After briefly setting forth the meaning of the name, let us now append a treatment of the reality signified by the name, proportionately more extended, since every reality is held to be more enduring than its name.

Peace, then, in the most general sense, is some kind of natural tranquility, or a harmonious relation among things differing from one another in number. The first definition assigns peace to each individual thing; the second, although not to each individual, nevertheless attributes it to a multitude and collectivity of several individuals.

So great and sweet, moreover, is the good of peace itself that no one is so depraved or savage that he does not desire to obtain this good and rejoice when it has been obtained. For although many, as Paul testifies, are “without affection” and “without a covenant,” unwilling to unite with others either in the affection of humanity or in any fellowship of concord—such, they say, were Cacus, that half-man, and Timon of Athens—nevertheless no one fails to love having peace within himself, since he is evidently horrified by his own agitation, disturbance, and restlessness. Hence even those who desire wars wish to purchase peace through wars. For those who desire the peace in which they are to be disturbed do not hate peace; rather, they prefer to have it changed according to their own will.

Not only rational creatures, but also those devoid of reason and everything that exists naturally, desire peace and love to be cherished in the embraces of peace. Indeed, according to the great Dionysius, nothing that exists will have fallen entirely away from every union of peace. For what is wholly restless, and entirely disordered and without place, is neither “a being” (*ὄν*) nor among beings.

The distinguished teacher of the Latins wrote in agreement with this judgment: “They would in no way be natures,” he says, “if they did not subsist through some kind of peace.” So that knowledge of so great a good may flow more familiarly to those eager for instruction, let us divide this rough and undigested material concerning peace into its parts.

It must therefore be understood that, according to the canon of divine Scripture, peace is divided into eight kinds:

- the peace of God with himself;
- the peace of God with human beings;
- the peace of angels with themselves;
- the peace of angels with human beings;
- the peace of the devil with himself;
- the peace of the devil with human beings;
- the peace of human beings with themselves;
- the peace of human beings with one another.

## CHAPTER III — On the peace of God with himself

The peace of God with himself is an ineffable communion of unity between the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. We infer it from these three points: identity of being, unanimity of will, and the authority of undivided action. For they do not differ in essence, disagree in will, or vary in action. As this peace is prior to all time, so it is found to surpass every understanding. Concerning it Paul says to the Philippians: “And the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your thoughts.”

This peace is an ocean of repose, an abyss of tranquility, and the source of all concord divinely bestowed upon creatures. Hence the previously mentioned philosopher of the Greeks, in the third book cited above, when he praised it in anagogical terms, wished to call it the chief or sovereign peace:

“For it,” he says, “is the unifier of all things, and the consensus and begetter and maker of natural kinship.”

Accordingly, all things desire it: it converts their divisible multitude into complete unity and unites the civil war of the universe into an equal-form fellowship through participation in divine peace. Therefore the Psalmist, looking toward this peace, says: “Seek peace and pursue it.” This supreme peace must be sought here for merit, so that there it may be found as a reward. Hence elsewhere: “Seek the Lord and be strengthened; seek his face always.”

## CHAPTER IV — On the peace of God with human beings

The peace of God with human beings—or rather, between God and human beings—is the coming together of divine command and human obedience into one, namely, when human readiness is prepared to fulfill what God commands. The Apostle recalls this peace when he declares: “Therefore, having been justified by faith, let us have peace with God.” He also wished it for all whom he greeted in his letters, saying: “Grace and peace to us from God.”

This peace was first violated by our parents when, despising the command of their Creator, they preferred to enter into alliance with the laws of the devil.

At that time an exceedingly hard wall of enmity arose between God and humanity: namely, a wall of sins, which made God not only inaccessible to us but also invisible, in accordance with what Isaiah reproaches sinners: “Your iniquities,” he says, “have divided between you and your God, and your sins have hidden his face from you.” Hence Job, lamenting and at the same time questioning on behalf of such people, says to the Lord: “Why do you hide your face and regard me as your enemy?”

O what a great evil! What intolerable dangers of war the arrogant transgressor incurs when, having broken the covenant of this peace, he rebels! For, having thus joined himself to the devil, he declared war on God, stretching out his hand against God and strengthening himself against the Almighty, according to the testimony of the holy man Job. Therefore the Lord, moved by the zeal of righteous indignation, armed all creation for vengeance against his enemies. Against the destruction of the rebellious servant he summoned not only the angelic powers but also irrational and mute elements, as auxiliary forces of armed soldiers.

Hence it is said: “The whole world will fight on his behalf against the senseless.” “For,” as another Scripture threatens through a portent, “the heavens will reveal his iniquity, and the earth will rise up against him.” We often observe and lament this taking place: besides the diseases of pestilence, the ruins caused by earthquakes, the strikes of lightning, the blows of hail, and the fury of storms—through which the elements themselves sometimes rage against us—almost everywhere the earth, called the mother of all mortals, withholds its customary abundance of maternal kindness, and the sky denies the grace of cooling rains. And this happens to us because we first renew the hatred of those who transgressed against God and, with deliberate wickedness, despise the commands of our Creator.

Moses invoked this savagery of the elements against the transgressor of the law when he said:

“May the Lord strike you with the poverty of fever and cold, with burning heat and feverishness, with corrupt air and tempest, and may he pursue you until you perish. May the sky above you be bronze, and the earth you tread iron. May the Lord give the dust of your land as rain, and may ashes descend upon you from heaven until you are crushed.”

Yet because the purpose of divine mercy was to chastise, not destroy, and to correct, not condemn, the human being whom his hand had formed and made, therefore, when the time of God’s favor arrived, the most merciful Lord, without being sought by us, himself sought from us what belongs to peace.

In this seeking of peace he did not wish to delegate an external messenger, nor even an archangel familiar to him, but sent his only Son into the world. Through his intervention he would break down the barrier of these enmities and restore peace between us and God on better terms.

Christ was therefore mediator and reconciler between God and humanity: mediator in his birth, reconciler in his death. For no one can rightly be a mediator unless he possesses a quality akin to both of the parties in disagreement. Thus Christ truly became mediator between us and God when he was born, assuming a nature that, through the fullness of its virtues, was like God and, through its assumption of human weaknesses, appeared not unlike us.

He is believed to have become reconciler in his death because it was then that he offered the sacrifice of reconciliation and effaced, with the stylus of the most blessed wood, the written bond of the former debt.

[Note: Codex Tegernseensis reads *delevit* (“erased”) instead of *interlevit* (“wiped out” or “obliterated”).]

As Paul testified to the Romans: “When we were enemies, we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son.” And again, to the Ephesians:

“He is our peace, who made both one, breaking down the middle wall of the barrier—the enmities in his flesh—nullifying the law of commandments in decrees, and through the cross killing the enmities in himself.”

The Prophet also expressed this sufficiently when he said: “The discipline of our peace was upon him, and by his bruise we were healed.”

This wall of enmity is the wall that the Prophet tacitly indicates would be brought low in Christ and therefore easily crossed: “In my God,” he says, “I will pass over a wall.” But so that you might understand that the one named “God” here is none other than the Son of God, he immediately adds, concerning the mystery of his incarnation: “My God, his way is undefiled”—by these words foreseeing and commending, long beforehand, the womb of the undefiled Virgin.

Hence, when the Lord was born in the flesh, the restoration of this peace was proclaimed to human beings through angels: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will.”

Indeed, the same Lord, coming in the flesh, spoke this peace to his people and upon his holy ones and upon those who turn to him. Afterward, when he rose from the dead, he offered it to the whole world through his disciples, saying: “Peace be with you. As the Father sent me, so I send you”—that is, just as I, sent into the world, restored peace to the world, so you, sent by me to those to whom you proclaim the gospel, are to be ministers of this peace, saying: “Into whatever house you enter, say: Peace to this house.”

Thus the world may understand that fulfilled in you which was once sung through the prophetic instrument: “How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of those who proclaim good things!”

Each person is recognized as renewing the covenant of this peace with God when, at the very beginning of conversion, he promises to renounce the devil and his pomps. Concerning the violation of this covenant the Prophet sorrowfully says: “I saw those who did not keep the covenant, and I wasted away.”

## CHAPTER V — How the peace of God with human beings was restored on better terms

We rightly said that this peace was restored on better terms. For this peace is more universal, more intimate, and more enduring than the former.

There was indeed some restoration of this peace among the fathers of earlier times—for example, in Abel, toward whom, and toward whose offerings, the Lord is read to have looked; and in Enoch and Noah, because each of them, as Scripture says, walked with the Lord. There was also such restoration in Abraham, of whom it is said: “Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness, and he was called the friend of God.”

Even among the people who sprang from this father’s loins, namely the Hebrew nation, the friendship of this peace seemed to have revived to such an extent that the Lord made that generation his special people and called it his firstborn son, according to the saying in Exodus: “Israel is my firstborn son.”

But this peace was certainly particular, not universal. The pledges of this peace were not granted to everyone, but only to certain fathers and to one particular people. Divine speech expresses this in the following manner: “Say to the house of Israel; say to the house of Judah.” At that time God was known only in Judea; in Israel alone his name was great, and there alone his dwelling was established in peace, and his habitation was in Zion alone.

The reconciliation of peace, however, which the dispensation of Christ the mediator brought about, is promised and offered to everyone without exception, according to what he says through the Prophet:

“I create the fruit of the lips: peace, peace to those who are far off and peace to those who are near.”

Peter also noted the universality of this divine peace when he said:

“In truth I have discovered that God is not a respecter of persons, but in every nation whoever fears God and practices righteousness is acceptable to him. He sent the word to the children of Israel, announcing peace through Jesus Christ. He is Lord of all.”

Through the restoration of this peace, which was accomplished through Christ, human beings also deserved to be reunited with God by a more intimate bond of friendship. For whereas previously we were merely friends of God in certain fathers, now, through Christ the mediator, who deigned to unite our flesh to his divinity, we have truly obtained the right to be called not only friends of God but also his brothers and his neighbors.

We read him proclaiming this in the Psalm and in the Gospel: “I pleased [them] as a neighbor and as our brother.” And: “Go, announce to my brothers that they should go to Galilee.”

Finally, we rightly considered this peace more enduring than the former. The covenant of that peace by which the former people appeared to have been reconciled to the Lord—the covenant that he had made with them through the patriarchs, the law, and the prophets—was annulled because of their deserving offenses, and the peace by which he had joined them to himself in fatherly favor was dissolved, as we read one of them lamenting: “The covenant has been annulled.” He cast down the cities; he did not regard human beings.

Likewise, in Jeremiah: “Do not,” he says, “console them, because I have taken my peace from this people,” says the Lord.

But the covenant of this peace, which God established with the Church through Christ, remains confirmed by everlasting laws, just as he promised in Ezekiel, saying:

“David my servant”—that is, Christ—“will be their prince forever; and through his intervention”—understand, “I will strike a covenant of peace with them”—“it will be an everlasting covenant for them.”

## CHAPTER VI — On another kind of peace between God and humanity

There is also another, more secret peace between God and humanity, marked out by the testimonies of divine Scripture: namely, when the spiritual person subjects his good merits to the majesty of divine rewards, judging that the sufferings of the present time are in no way worthy of the future glory that will be revealed in us.

The Lord’s parable concerning the form of this peace and the conflict that precedes it was woven as follows:

“What king, going to engage in war against another king, does not first sit down and calculate whether he can meet with ten thousand the one who comes against him with twenty thousand? Otherwise, while the other is still far away, he sends a delegation and asks for the terms of peace.”

A king prepares war against another king when someone considers himself destined for salvation through his own merits. But such a king will certainly not be saved by his great virtue, for, according to the Prophet, “all our righteousnesses in the sight of God are like a menstrual cloth.”

When does a person meet God with ten thousand, if he proudly boasts of the merits of his works? God comes against him, as it were, with a doubled number when he examines not only the work itself but also the thought behind the work. Therefore, while we still believe that he is far away because judgment is delayed, let us send him a delegation of prayers, asking for the terms of peace and saying: “Do not enter into judgment with your servant, Lord, for no living person will be justified in your sight.”

## CHAPTER VII — On the peace of the devil with himself

Fearing the offense of simple ears, I would say that there is no peace of the devil with himself, were I not to find it noted by the Lord:

“When a strong armed man guards his courtyard, everything he possesses is at peace.”

This peace of the devil was nothing other than the secure possession of the human race. The devil did not obtain this peace through the power of his own virtue, but through the stupidity of our cowardice. For the devil is timid; if resistance is offered to him, he is immediately put to flight, as James says: “Resist the devil, and he will flee from you.”

But before the most high King, Jesus Christ, declared war on the devil through the dispensation of his flesh, no one appeared who would resist him. All had turned toward his patronage. “There was no one who did good, not even one.” Therefore, in a certain secure peace, he acquired possession of those whom he had begun to possess by tyrannical right, until one more ferocious than he came upon him, broke his peace, and utterly plundered both his courtyard and his house.

The courtyard of the devil’s house is the carnal life; his house is hell. For just as one enters a house through a courtyard, so through carnal life one reaches hell. Therefore, so that the devil might possess his house more successfully, he stations himself as guardian in the courtyard, because he strives to recommend carnal life for this reason: that hell may be filled more abundantly with the number of the lost.

How unlike this peace of the devil is to the peace of God that we set forth first! The former is supremely good; the latter supremely evil. The former, as we said earlier, is the source of all holy concord; the latter is the source of every discord that harms humanity.

## CHAPTER VIII — On the peace of the devil with human beings

The peace of the devil with human beings is the agreement of diabolical wickedness and human will through the mediation of vices. Prophetic speech marks this peace when it speaks in the voice of the faithless:

“We have made a covenant with death”—that is, with the devil—“and with hell we have made an agreement; therefore, when the overwhelming scourge passes through, it will not come upon us.”

When you see someone allied with the devil’s service, agreeing in every way with his desires—namely, stretching out his tongue in curses and obscenities, indulging in luxury, inflaming lust, kindling greed, and enflaming anger—know that such a person has made a covenant with death, that is, with the devil. Since the devil sees that such a person in no way opposes him, he maintains what appears to be peace with him, neither attacking him with temptations nor overthrowing him with afflictions.

But if at some point he senses that the person wishes to raise his eyes upward—to desire what is eternal, hate pleasures, put on uprightness, love justice, embrace continence, and plan to flee luxury—then, as soon as the law of this kind of peace is disturbed, he pursues the one who is withdrawing with every goad of anger. He employs a thousand devices against him and a thousand arguments of cruelty, by which he may draw him back from the narrow way that leads to life to the broad way that leads to death.

This was formerly shown figuratively in the children of Israel laboring under Pharaoh’s yoke. As soon as Pharaoh was urged through Moses to release the people, he began to weary them with harsh burdens of labor.

The same thing was expressed more clearly in the Gospel, where it is said of the lunatic that, when he saw the Lord, the spirit immediately convulsed him; he was thrown to the ground and rolled about; and at the Lord’s command the spirit cried out, tore the man, and departed. For often, when after sin we wish to turn to the Lord, we are attacked by more severe tortures from the devil.

Such peace of the devil with a human being is the repose and sleep of Behemoth, who “sleeps in the shade, in the secrecy of the reed, in damp places.” Those who are preparing to seek God through the pursuit of virtues awaken him from this slumber and challenge him to battle. Hence Job, speaking of them, says: “Let those who curse the day curse him, who are ready to rouse Leviathan.”

## CHAPTER IX — On the peace of angels with themselves

The sequence of the proposed distinction requires that, after what we have said in two ways concerning the peace of God and of the devil, we discuss what is appropriate concerning the peace of angels with themselves, that is, among themselves.

The peace believed to exist among angels is a harmonious progress toward the veneration, knowledge, and love of God, together with a certain gradual descent toward what is lower. Scripture did not remain silent about this peace through the blessed man Job: “Power and terror,” he says, “are with him who makes concord in the heights,” that is, among the angels.

The first and greatest discord arose among the angels when Lucifer, who rose like the morning star, conceived the plan of invading the summit of divinity, saying: “I will set my throne in the north, and I will be like the Most High.”

Then “there was a great battle in heaven: Michael and his angels battled with the dragon, and the dragon and his angels fought, and they did not prevail, nor was their place found any longer in heaven.” For that great dragon, who is called the devil and Satan, was cast down—cast down, I say, to the earth, and his angels were sent down with him.

This battle that took place among the angels must not be thought to have been fought with material iron but with intellectual zeal—not through the clash of weapons but through opposition of affections. For insofar as the devil and his accomplices, under the figure of pride, rose up against God, Michael and those like him chose, through the devotion of humility, to submit themselves to the commands of the eternal King. Therefore, while the latter remained in heaven more exalted than they had previously been, the former were expelled and fell into the lowest regions of the earth. “For everyone who humbles himself will be exalted, and whoever exalts himself will be humbled.”

Once those who had been the cause of discord had thus been driven from the heavenly boundaries [Cod. Tegern.: *coelestibus*, “heavenly regions”], the others, always standing before the faces of the most tranquil deity, enjoy among themselves the joys of eternal peace.

The harmony of this peace was signified in the two golden cherubim whom the Lord judged should be placed in the sanctuary, their faces turned toward one another and toward the mercy seat. Through the cherubim, the entire assembly of the angelic host is shown, as it were, by a part representing the whole. They are said to look toward the mercy seat with faces turned toward one another because they are believed, with perfectly harmonious minds, to yearn for participation in that supercelestial hierarchy.

The fact that this is prefigured in two signifies that all concord is a friendly equality, which is first expressed through the number two. The same thing should be thought to be represented again in the other cherubim, which Solomon placed in the middle of the temple so that they were joined by their wings touching one another. In the wings, by which flight is made toward the heights, the power of heavenly contemplation is indicated. The cherubim, that is, the angels, therefore join their wings because they understand one and the same thing completely concerning the truth of the divine essence.

As for the gradual descent toward lower things that we included in our description of this peace, it has the following meaning: according to the most excellent Dionysius, there are three angelic hierarchies. The first contains seraphim, cherubim, and thrones; the middle contains powers, dominions, and virtues; the last contains principalities, archangels, and angels.

These are arranged according to the ordering of the highest art in such a way that the first hierarchy, as one that clings directly to the divine vision without an intermediary, draws from the very source of light the primary knowledge of how these lower things are to be administered. The middle hierarchy afterward learns from the first, and the last from the middle, what is to be done.

Hence the first hierarchy is said to purify, illuminate, and perfect; the last to be purified, illuminated, and perfected; while the middle hierarchy is proclaimed to be adorned by the condition of both.

## CHAPTER X — A question concerning this peace

Someone may ask how we can say that the angelic powers have eternal peace among themselves when we hear in Daniel that they contend against one another:

“I came,” says one angel, “because of your words; but the prince of the Persians”—that is, the angel appointed over that nation—“resisted me for twenty-one days. And behold, Michael, one of the chief princes, came to help me.”

And a little later:

“Now I will return to fight against the prince of the Persians. When I was departing, the prince of the Greeks appeared, coming.”

But Father Gregory teaches as follows:

“Then the angels come against one another when the merits of the nations subject to them contradict one another in turn. For the exalted spirits who rule over those nations do not fight on behalf of those acting unjustly; rather, they examine their deeds in a just judgment. When the guilt or righteousness of each nation is brought before the heavenly council, the rulers of that nation are said to have prevailed or not prevailed in the contest. Yet there is one victory belonging to all of them: the supreme will of their Maker over them. While they continually behold that will, they never desire what they are unable to obtain.”

## CHAPTER XI — On the peace of angels with human beings

The peace of angels with human beings—that is, between angels and human beings—is a concord shaped in the service of God by similar offices, and a written constitution under the laws of the same heavenly homeland, as though it were a city. Paul recalls this in the Letter to the Hebrews:

“You have approached Mount Zion and the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, the assembly of many thousands of angels, and the church of the firstborn who are written in heaven.”

And again elsewhere: “Our citizenship is in heaven.”

Just as Christ the mediator restored peace between God and humanity, so he himself, through the mystery of the cross, made peace between angels and human beings, as it is written to the Colossians:

“For in him”—that is, in Christ—“all fullness was pleased to dwell, and through him to reconcile all things in him, making peace through the blood of his cross between those things that are on earth and those that are in heaven.”

Hence we read that angels were worshiped by human beings in the Old Testament, whereas after the mystery of the Lord’s incarnation an angel prevented a human being who wished to worship him:

“See that you do not do this,” he said; “for I am the fellow servant of you and of your brothers.”

We rightly called this peace “a concord shaped by similar offices.” For just as the offices of the angels are differentiated, as stated above—some being superior, others inferior, and others occupying the middle position—yet all, according to the dignity of their order, serve their king with harmonious service, so among us, when some are placed over others, some are subordinate, and others are designated by professions that involve both authority and submission, all serve the supreme Lord with united minds and efforts according to the order of their rank.

This distinction between ruling and being subject, both among human beings and among angels, will be abolished when the end of the world arrives, when Christ hands the kingdom over to God the Father. Then, according to the Apostle, he will abolish every principality, authority, and power.

This peace between us and the angels will then be fully consummated, when nothing in our nature can be discordant with the nature of the angels. There, too, the body that is now animal is believed to rise as spiritual; there will be no corruption of those generated and no generation of those corrupted. “For they will neither marry nor be given in marriage there, but will be like the angels of God in heaven.”

## CHAPTER XII — Description of the threefold peace of human beings with themselves

Behold, we have treated of the peace that exists in the higher realms. Let us now turn the purpose of our discourse to what is found in the lower realms, that is, to the peace of human beings with themselves and of human beings with one another.

The peace of a human being with himself is distinguished by a threefold variety. One kind belongs to the wicked, another to the good, and a third to the blessed.

The peace of the wicked is the prosperity of the flesh and of the world, which falsely flatters them. The peace of the good is the joyful security of a good conscience. The peace of the blessed is the perfect agreement, in the enjoyment of heavenly things, between reason and sensuality.

## CHAPTER XIII — On the peace of the wicked with themselves

Concerning the peace of the wicked you may ask Asaph:

“I was jealous,” he says, “of sinners, seeing the peace of sinners, because there is no decline in their death, nor firmness in their affliction. They are not in the labors of human beings, and they will not be scourged with human beings.”

The Lord disapproved and reproached this peace among the Jews when he said: “For if you too had known, and indeed on this your day, the things that are for your peace.”

Job also describes it in the form of a lament, saying:

“Why do the wicked live, are they lifted up, and are they strengthened with riches? Their seed remains before them, a crowd of relatives and descendants in their sight. Their houses are secure and peaceful, and the rod of God is not upon them. Their ox conceives and does not miscarry; their cow gives birth and is not deprived of her offspring. Their little ones go forth like flocks, and their children exult in play; they hold the drum and the lyre and rejoice at the sound of the organ. They spend their days in prosperity, those who said to God: Depart from us; we do not desire knowledge of your ways.”

In similar words David says concerning the children of foreigners:

“Their sons,” he says, “are like young plants, firmly established from their youth; their daughters are adorned and embellished like the likeness of a temple. Their storehouses are full, overflowing from one side to the other. Their sheep are fertile and abundant in their journeys; their oxen are fat. There is no breach in the wall.”

They are granted such secure tranquility that “there is no passage” and no disturbing “cry in their streets.”

How destructive is this peace, in which the pleasure of the flesh and worldly prosperity are joined to human beings by laws that are indeed flattering but deceitful! How destructive, I say, and how deeply shadowed by illusion! For the peace of this kind that appears is not true peace: it deceives our eyes and continually grows toward its own destruction.

When sinners are seen to be unharmed, when they appear exceedingly rich, when they are observed to rule over many peoples, and no one whom they fear appears anywhere in the world, they are thought to possess peace. But this peace is always at strife with conscience; it contends inwardly, and when it has no enemy, it fights against itself.

For the wicked are, as prophetic speech puts it, like “a raging sea that cannot rest.” “There is no peace for the wicked,” says the Lord.

Such peace is not only a snare of captivity for its possessors but also an occasion of perdition for others—namely, for Christians weak in faith, who, when they see the good afflicted by adversity but the wicked favored with prosperity, either accuse God of injustice in judgment or blaspheme by claiming that he does not care about human affairs. Concerning them Proverbs says: “The turning away of the simple will kill them, and the prosperity of fools will destroy them.”

For the person who possesses this peace, the memory of death is exceedingly bitter, according to the saying attributed to the Wise Man when he cries out to death itself:

“O death,” he says, “O death, how bitter is the memory of you to a person who has peace in his possessions!”

Conversely, whoever hates this peace—that is, prosperity of the flesh—loves the coming of death. Concerning such people the righteous man speaks, describing those who endure the voluntary bitterness of the soul:

“They await death,” he says, “and it does not come; like those who dig for a treasure, they rejoice exceedingly when they find the grave.”

The kisses of this peace are the kisses of a prostitute, whose lips are a dripping honeycomb and whose throat is smoother than oil; but her end is as bitter as wormwood and sharp as a two-edged sword. Not without reason can the saying of Hezekiah be applied to this peace: “Behold,” he says, “behold, in peace my bitterness is most bitter.”

For the possessors of this kind of peace, because they do not trust their own lives, even if there should perhaps be peace around them, nevertheless quarrel continually within themselves through fearful and mutually conflicting suspicions, as it is written: “The sound of terror is always in his ears.” Even when there is peace, that person always suspects ambushes.

For, as the Book of Wisdom declares, “wickedness is always timid.” And another Scripture says: “The wicked flee when no one pursues.” Again, the Lord says of such people in Leviticus:

“I will put fear in their hearts, and the sound of a flying leaf will terrify them.”

But if some of them should happen to be so undisturbed by unrestricted prosperity that every anxious concern has been uprooted from their hearts and their inner eye has been completely blinded, so that they regard everything they desire as permissible and never imagine that they will be deprived of the joys of this peace, then, when true and eternal disturbance suddenly succeeds this fantastic and momentary peace, this peace will abandon its lovers all the more unhappily because it will do so when they are less prepared.

“For when they say,” according to the Apostle, “‘Peace and security,’ then sudden destruction will come upon them, like labor upon a pregnant woman, and they will not escape.”

## CHAPTER XIV — On the discord that the reprobate will suffer in their own nature in hell

[Col. 1606C]

This destruction is the deprivation of the present light and the ruin of the soul, which will be followed by the condemnation of both soul and body. Then those who here seemed blessed amid the successes of a vain peace will truly seek peace and not find it within themselves—that is, they will suffer within their own nature a conflict whose distress could not be imagined as more grievous or bitter. For there an irreparable quarrel between punishment and flesh, an interminable struggle of pain and body, will persist: suffering will be so opposed to nature, and nature so opposed to suffering, that neither will this mutual wrestling be brought to rest by the victory of either. There the force of pain will contend and quarrel with the very nature of the body, so that neither will ever yield to the other. Here, when such a conflict occurs, either death, when pain overcomes, removes sensation, or, when nature prevails over pain, the restoration of health removes the sickness. But there both pain remains in order to afflict, and nature endures in order to feel, because neither is consumed, lest the punishment come to an end, as it is written: “He will labor forever and live to the end.”

The Lord perhaps wished to point out the evil of this dissension, at once divided and detested, through Isaiah [Note: [Col. 1605] Everything that follows up to the words “about the cruel servant” is absent from cod. Bam.]: “And man will fight against his brother, and man against his friend, and city against city, and the spirit of Egypt will be torn apart within its very entrails.” To the mystery of this event that also contributes which John saw at the opening of the second seal: the one seated upon the red horse—that is, Christ, who willed to be clothed in human flesh—was given, as I say, the power “to take peace from the earth, so that people would kill one another,” and a great sword was given to him.

This peace of the Egyptians, which the Lord himself had earlier broken apart through the apostles, he afterward shattered by no lesser separation: “He sent forth his arrows and scattered them; he multiplied his lightning flashes and threw them into confusion,” as may be observed in one of them, namely Paul, who, as we read in the Acts of the Apostles, dissolved the concord of this wicked peace by an exceedingly skillful stratagem. Knowing that one party of those persecuting him consisted of Sadducees and the other of Pharisees, he cried out in the council: “Brothers, I am a Pharisee, the son of Pharisees. I am being judged concerning the hope and the resurrection.” And when he had said this, dissension arose among them, and the assembly was dissolved. “For the Sadducees say that there is no resurrection, nor angel, nor spirit; but the Pharisees confess both.” See how, at this utterance of Paul, the crowd of the reprobate is divided against itself and the council is dispersed; and while the multitude of the rioters is scattered into two parties, an opportunity for Paul’s escape is opened. The righteous are rescued when the wicked are divided. For this reason also, at the Red Sea, when the wave is divided into two parts, a way is opened for the chosen people toward the land of promise.

Hence the one who, fleeing, had gone far away hopes that he will finally be saved from the storm if God divides the wickedly gathered unity: “I was waiting,” he says, “for the one who would save me from faintheartedness and storm.” To bring this about: “Hurl them down, Lord, and divide their tongues,” just as, as we said, you divided the lips of the giants. And concerning the cruel servant he said that “the lord of that servant will come on a day when he does not expect him, and at an hour he does not know, and he will divide him.” For the wicked servant is then divided within himself when he is torn apart among various and contrary things; when in the underworld the most wretched man is compelled [*courgetur*, presumably *cogetur*] always to live while dying and always to die while living. This makes death intolerable to him: death itself is always without death.

## CHAPTER XV — On the peace of conscience possessed here by the good

After presenting evidence concerning the peace that the wicked have within themselves, let us now append a discussion of the peace of the good—that is, the peace believed to be possessed within himself by every just person. As we have stated above, the security of a joyful conscience bestows upon this peace its title and praise. Conscience is truly joyful when it not only defends the person most vigorously but also caresses him on account of his virtue. For the security of conscience is not joyful merely because it flees what deserves blame, unless it is also kindled by devotion to what deserves praise. As it is said, abstaining from evil avoids punishment; doing good earns the palm. He had experienced this caress of conscience who said: “Our glory is this: the testimony of our conscience.”

Speaking of this peace of conscience, the Psalmist says: “Great peace belongs to those who love your law, Lord, and there is no stumbling-block for them.” No one versed in the divine books will fail to understand that by “stumbling-block” an offense of conscience must be meant. There is great peace for those who love God’s law when they are secure from punishment not only because of the good of their innocence, but also when, on account of the merit of their virtue, they joyfully await their reward. Paul wished this peace for the Colossians when he said: “And let the peace of Christ”—that is, the peace Christ possessed and gave them to possess—“rejoice in your hearts.” The wicked do not have this peace: neither does a good conscience reconcile them to themselves, nor does tranquility of mind make them serene. For the absence of this peace the sinner, at once guilty and penitent, groans: “There is no peace,” he says, “for my bones because of my sins.” Here “bones” signifies the natural powers of the soul, which ought to have been strong against sins.

But how great is the multitude of heavenly sweetness, how ready the bowels of divine mercy! The sinner regains in a single little pang of compunction the abundance of peace that he had lost through the devil’s many snares, or, as cod. Teg. reads, “through a single sigh of a compunct heart”; he regains it through a single little tear of the eyes. To demonstrate this, the following Gospel example will suffice. What was said there to the sinful woman concerning this peace? How do you read it? What answer do you hear the Lord give her in her repentance? “Your faith,” he said—“your faith has saved you; go in peace.”

How far this peace is separated from the peace of the wicked—how great and contrary is the difference by which it is separated from the nature of that peace! That peace is tumultuous; this is quiet. That is empty; this sincere. That is sorrowful; this joyful. That is fearful; this secure. Finally, that gives birth to eternal punishment; this earns for us the glory of everlasting salvation.

I have rightly described this peace as sincere, quiet, secure, and joyful. For this peace contains nothing of emptiness and nothing of deceit mixed with it. Its sincerity is tenacious, and it is always conscious of the truth; although it may sometimes be deceived, it does not itself know how to deceive. Hence, when he who is the Truth sits as judge of all, he will accept the testimony of conscience alone, which cannot lie, as the Apostle says: “Their conscience bearing witness to them.”

This peace is quiet: it is startled by no rumors, agitated by no tumults, disturbed by no afflictions. Even if the tribulation of the flesh roars around it, even if the world’s fury rages from without, the spirit of the possessor of this peace will nevertheless always enjoy the leisure of blessed quiet. Habakkuk briefly noted this when he said: “I will rest on the day of my tribulation.” And the Lord said to the disciples: “I have spoken these things to you so that you may have peace in me,” although “in the world you will have distress.”

Micah likewise foretold the same thing in a beautiful figure: “And he himself”—namely, the Lord—“will be our peace when the Assyrian comes into our land and treads upon our houses.” *Assyrian*, which in Latin is said to mean “one who rebukes” (*arguens*), prefigures the image of the devil. For to rebuke (*arguere*) is to accuse. And who is more deserving of the name “accuser” than the one against whom the voice of the triumphant angels is uttered: “The accuser of our brothers has been cast down, who accused them before the presence of our God day and night”?

By “our land” and “houses,” in which the Assyrian treads, the dwelling-places of our flesh are signified. Therefore we have peace when the Assyrian comes into our land and treads upon our houses, because although the devil afflicts or kills the body of a holy man, he never takes away the rest of eternal peace. Hence the saying from the Proverbs of the wise man: “The just man will not be saddened by whatever happens to him.” This peace is called “the Lord,” moreover, because such peace is obtained only through his grace.

This peace is also secure. In it the mind, placed as though in a certain citadel, looks down upon the terrors of hostile domination, spits upon its threats, despises its savagery, and counts the violence of every opposing power as though it were straw. This security is understood in Solomon’s saying: “The just man will be confident like a lion, without terror.” He relied upon the security of this peace who could say: “If armies encamp against me, my heart will not fear; and if battle rises against me, in this I will hope.”

Peter also looked toward this security of peace when he said: “Who is there who will harm you if you are zealous for what is good?” The mind of the just is like the higher region of the world, nearer to heaven: it is not forced into a cloud, driven into a storm, or whirled into a tempest; thunder does not roar there, lightning does not rage, and winds do not quarrel. So too is the blessed mind, whose way of life is in heaven. It has already been raised and stands out at such a height of virtue that its firmness can never be shaken by the crash of threats, its serenity beclouded by clouds of terror [cod. Teg., “showers”], or its tranquility disturbed by floods of war.

Finally, this peace is joyful: the more it contracts itself toward prosperity and the more generously expands itself toward adversity, the more it rejoices in losses, exults in dangers, mocks punishments, and laughs at death. Hence that grateful voice resounds: “In tribulation you enlarged me.” A good man expresses this joy and security of peace together when he says: “You will not fear calamity when it comes; in famine and devastation you will laugh; you will not fear the beasts of the earth, and you will know that your tabernacle possesses peace.”

O wondrous peace, through which those who do not possess it are wretched, while those who possess it deserve to be called children of God: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they will be called children of God!”

## CHAPTER XVI — On the peace that the blessed will then have within themselves

They will then be called children of God when that third peace appears: the blessed harmony of reason and sensuality. As was shown above, this peace is attributed not to all the good but only to the blessed—that is, to those who have already departed from the world. The just man hoped finally to attain it at death when he said: “In peace, together, I will sleep and rest.” And Simeon, while blessing God, sang: “Now you dismiss your servant, Lord, according to your word, in peace.”

Among the souls of the saints this is the harmony of perfect peace: everything that is in a human being—spirit, senses, and soul—must always feel the same thing; that is, they must agree with an undivided will in the desire for the supreme good. The fullness of this peace can indeed be sought here, but it cannot be found. Here the flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh, so that we do not do whatever we wish.

Even the great Paul himself, who had been caught up into the third heaven and had tasted the first fruits of such peace, while still living in the flesh endured small struggles within himself. He perceived another law in his members opposing the law of his mind, so that he did not do what he wished but, against his will, carried out what he did not wish.

John wished to mark this beautifully in the Apocalypse when he wrote that “there was silence in heaven for about half an hour.” If heaven is the seat of God, according to the saying, “Heaven is my seat,” while the soul of the just, according to Scripture, “is the seat of wisdom”—that is, of God—what could be more fitting than to understand the soul of the just as heaven? “Silence, therefore, for about half an hour” is heard in heaven because in the soul of the holy man “half”—that is, not perfect—rest is believed to exist here.

Therefore this peace, in which there is no opposition between flesh and spirit, is promised to be granted to us in the future, as the Lord says: “I leave you peace; I give you my peace.” It must be recognized that “I give” is spoken for “I will give,” according to the same manner of expression by which, speaking above about the sheep, he added: “And I give them eternal life.” Thus Christ leaves one peace to his chosen in this age, and without doubt will give another in the future. He leaves the intermediate peace, which belongs to the good; he will give the third, which, as we have said, belongs to the blessed.

Yet he wonderfully chose to call not the peace that he leaves here but the most perfect peace that he will then give “his”: “I give you my peace.” For now we cannot possess God’s peace—that is, the peace that God has—because, as stated above, we endure a certain quarrel within ourselves. But then the Lord will give us his peace, when body, spirit, and soul are joined in a harmony entirely like the divine peace. Just as there is such great peace in the Godhead—as we briefly indicated at the beginning—that in the three there is one substance, one will, and one authority of action, so then these three will be joined to one another by such a great friendship of peace that, besides being understood to become, in a certain sense, of one nature [cod. T., “to become, in a certain sense, in name”], when the body itself passes into the nature of the spirit, as Saint Paul asserts, they will then all have exactly the same understanding and will always be occupied with the same work: namely, the sacrifice of heavenly praise.

This brief work had requested that we append in connected writing the matters that remain to be treated [cod. Bamb., “that remain”]. But the reader’s memory will be better served if the intervals of a twofold book separate what follows from what has preceded.

## The First Book on the Good of Peace Ends

# BOOK TWO

## CHAPTER I — On the three kinds of peace among human beings

After certain mysteries concerning the peace that exists within a person have been disclosed, this second book now treats the peace that exists between one person and another. The peace that exists between human beings, and that is maintained and honored among them, likewise extends into three kinds. One is the peace of Egypt, another the peace of Babylon, and the third the peace of Jerusalem.

The peace of Egypt is the conspiracy of the wicked toward a single depravity. The peace of Babylon is the secure way of life of both wicked and good people, protected from external or civil war and from private quarrel. The peace of Jerusalem is understood as the brotherhood of Christian society.

The peace of Egypt requires a communion of crimes; the peace of Babylon, a communion of possessions; the peace of Jerusalem, the common capacity for every virtue. The devil brings about the peace of Egypt, the world the peace of Babylon, and Christ the peace of Jerusalem. Pride makes the peace of Egypt, impunity nourishes it, and obstinacy strengthens it. Justice makes the peace of Babylon, humanity nourishes it, and prudence strengthens it. Charity makes the peace of Jerusalem, piety nourishes it, and humility strengthens it.

## CHAPTER II — How the devil is the conciliator of the peace of Egypt

Understand as the peace of Egypt that peace which the Lord condemned in the Gospel when he said: “Do not think that I have come to bring peace upon the earth; I have not come to bring peace but a sword”—namely, the sword of the spirit, by which the communion of this sacrilegious peace is cut apart. “For I have come with a sword to separate a son against his father, and a daughter against her mother, and a daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law; and a man’s enemies will be those of his own household.”

We rightly identified the devil as the conciliator of the peace of Egypt. He was the leader and author of the first rebellion that began. He bound the first human being to himself in the same conspiracy of impiety. From the beginning to the end of the ages, he strives to gather into his ranks as many as he can. For it is written: “He drags every person behind him, and before him are innumerable people.”

## CHAPTER III — That pride especially builds this peace

Although different evils customarily produce this peace for different reasons, the excess of the giants shows that pride principally creates this abominable peace. Departing from the East, they found a plain in the land of Shinar, settled there, and said: “Come, let us build for ourselves a city and a tower whose top may reach to heaven, and let us celebrate our name before we are scattered over all the lands.”

You will rightly regard this city as an assembly of the wicked if you consider the place where it is built. This city is not founded upon a lofty mountain, like the city of God, whose foundations are in the holy mountains, but upon a grassy plain—that is, upon the breadth and greenness of bodily pleasure. And what else does the towering height of the giants announce than the elevation of swelling pride? Of this the Psalmist also speaks: “I saw the wicked exalted above measure like the cedars of Lebanon.”

The giants, moved from the East, gather into a single plain, while the wicked, departing through the figure [variant: *typhum*] of pride from the one who is “the Dawn from on high,” are joined together in a single fellowship of carnal life. Yet pride itself, which binds together the concord of this peace, afterward violates and divides it, since, desiring the privilege of singularity, it rejects as common what it loves. Hence Solomon’s proverb testifies that among the proud there are quarrels: each individual tries to claim for himself above the others what could in no way stand out in each individual.

Nor is it surprising that pride, as though acting against itself, seeks to overthrow what it has built, since its author, Satan, is divided against himself and therefore his kingdom cannot stand. Meanwhile, this evil of eminence often produces the result that a man whom perhaps a more arrogant swelling has inflated, so that his glory may be raised more loftily, does not deem those whom he attempts to overcome worthy of acceptance as peaceful or submissive, but instead desires to conquer them as rebels. Thus, according to the elementary lessons of the schoolroom, a certain exceedingly proud and distinguished enemy of the Roman state is said to have declared in boastful speech: “It harms me when I lack enemies, and we consider it a loss of arms unless those who could be conquered rebel.”

## CHAPTER IV — How impunity nourishes this peace

You know how impunity nourishes this kind of peace among the reprobate if you consider why such people associate with one another. They come together into one body for this purpose: that the wickedness which each of them could not so easily and so safely accomplish alone, they may, by joining their forces together, exercise more freely and more fearlessly. Hence in the Proverbs comes that voice of theirs inviting another into the pact of this wicked society: “Come,” they say, “come with us; let us lie in wait for blood; let us hide snares for the innocent; let us swallow him alive, like the underworld; we will seize every precious possession; we will fill our houses with spoils. Cast your lot in with us; let there be one purse for all of us.”

They commit these shared crimes more boldly because, for the time being, there is no judge by whom they may be punished. “Because,” as Ecclesiastes says, “sentence against the wicked is not quickly pronounced, therefore the children of men perpetrate evil without any fear.”

## CHAPTER V — How this peace is strengthened by obstinacy

Finally, if you wish to know how obstinacy strengthens this worst of peaces, hear the Lord himself speaking about the body of the devil: “His body is like cast shields.” What else is signified by these cast shields than the hardness of reprobate minds? Jeremiah’s lament did not remain silent about this hardness when, remembering and condemning the stubbornness of the Jews in the Lord’s passion, it said: “You will give them the shield of your heart’s labor.”

Cast shields are strong in receiving the blows of arrows but fragile when they fall: they do not yield at all to the blows of those who strike them, but by their own fall they shatter into fragments. The body of the devil, therefore, is the collection of a wicked council, since the arrow of the divine word does not pierce those whom obstinacy has made hard toward evil, although the fragility of life breaks them every day.

The Lord marked this concord of wicked unity in Job when he declared figuratively concerning Leviathan: “The members of his flesh cleave together.” By the flesh of Leviathan we understand all the reprobate, whom we do not see rising through desire toward the solidity of spiritual life. They are “members of the flesh” who join themselves to those acting perversely and leading them toward iniquity, just as it is also said by the Apostle concerning the Lord’s body: “You are the body of Christ, and members from a member.”

To this execrable peace belongs the friendship that Herod is also read to have entered into with Pilate during the Passion. For “they became friends on that day, whereas previously they had been enemies toward one another.”

## CHAPTER VI — What is the fruit and outcome of this peace

The book of Ecclesiasticus compares this same union of sacrilegious peace to collected straw: “The congregation of sinners is straw gathered together, and their end is a flame of fire.” Behold the end toward which it extends, and the fruit that the concord of the reprobate deserves: the flame of unquenchable fire and the burning of an immense and unbearable conflagration.

The completion of straw is not compared here to the burning of sinners because of the thinness and transience of the fire, but because of the speed and totality of the punishment, just as straw is burned up completely and quickly. In this sense the prophetic word says elsewhere: “Woe to Ariel!”—Ariel is the city that David conquered—“the multitude of those who fan you will be like fine dust.” Here the army of the Romans is understood, compared to dust not because of its smallness but because of its great number [cod. *numerositati*].

Just as any combustible material produces a greater conflagration if it is burned all at once than if it is burned in separate parts, so the collected multitude of the wicked will be burned by a more severe punishment in proportion to the greater number that bound it together in sin. Hence that divine sentence of the Teacher: “Gather the weeds and bind them into bundles to be burned.”

## CHAPTER VII — That we must always be unreconciled to this peace

Behold, you see the peace of Egypt explained—the peace that you ought to pursue, not embrace. You will be at peace with God only when you remain unreconciled to this peace. This is that peace, according to the theoretical sense, which the Shechemites wished to contract with Jacob and his sons: “Let them trade,” they said, “in the land and cultivate it, because it is spacious and broad and needs inhabitants. We will take their daughters as wives, and we will give ours to them.”

But how zealously the agreements of this peace were rejected is not hidden from anyone acquainted with divine Scripture.

Nor was that alliance unrelated to this peace which Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, is described as having formed with the wicked king Ahab. “Jehoshaphat,” it says, “was very rich and illustrious, and he was joined to Ahab by an alliance; and after some years he went down to him in Samaria.” For this the Lord rebuked him through the seer: “Do you give help to the wicked, and do you join yourself in friendship to those who hate the Lord?”

There is no concord of friendship to be maintained with those who hate God; rather, hatred must be set against them, as David did when he said: “Do I not hate those who hate you, Lord, and waste away because of your enemies? With perfect hatred I hate them, and they have become enemies to me.”

Therefore, wherever you find this pernicious peace and wherever you are able, according to the duty of your rank, scatter and burn it with the sword of the word and the ardor of divine zeal, following the example of your Teacher and Lord, who, as we stated above, came to send a sword upon the earth, by which the bonds of this peace would be broken apart. His faithful witness Isaiah had long before asserted that he would do this: “Behold, the Lord will ascend upon a light cloud and enter Egypt; the idols of Egypt will be shaken before him, and the heart of Egypt will melt within it, and I will make the Egyptians fight against the Egyptians.”

## CHAPTER VIII — On the peace of Babylon, and how justice produces it

Having now excluded the peace of Egypt from our minds as well as from our words, let us turn to consider the peace of Babylon. Its testimony is expressed in Jeremiah, where he admonished the children of the exile to pray for the peace of Babylon: “Seek the peace of the city to which I caused you to be carried away, and pray to the Lord for it, because in its peace there will be peace for you.” Paul likewise remembers this peace in his letter to the Hebrews: “Pursue peace with everyone.”

Finally, since it is asked how justice produces this peace, while, as stated above, the world brings it about and justice attaches it to the virtues, the matter may be sufficiently explained as follows. Here justice should be understood not so much as divine or political justice but as natural justice, which is called by another name equity. Seeing that all human beings are born from one parent, it establishes for them, as for brothers and sisters, the common use of all things, assigning to all of them a common home: the most beautiful dwelling of this world. Of this the prophet speaks: “O Israel, how great is the house of the Lord, and how vast is the place of his possession!”

This house is unquestionably exceedingly great: it gathers and encloses within its most capacious bosom the rich and the poor alike, the noble with the ignoble, the old with the young.

How beautiful is the foundation of this house—the surface of the earth, paved with white, purple, golden, crimson, and a thousand other-colored flowers! How beautiful is its roof—the face of heaven, shining like a jeweled ceiling with choirs of stars! In this house, what storehouses of food and drink are available from the shrubs and springs! What repositories of fragrances from the flowers and herbs themselves, like vessels of myrrh! In this house the splendor of the moon serves as a lamp by night, and the sun’s heat serves by day as a hypocaust—that is, a heating chamber accustomed to be warmed in winter by breathing fires.

In this house beds are spread from the grass for couches, and the elements themselves spontaneously offer service in place of domestic attendants.

This house is common to everyone, just as entry into it and departure from it are equally provided for everyone, as the Wise Man demonstrated when he said: “I too am a mortal human being, like everyone else, descended from the earthly race of the one who was first made; in my mother’s womb I was formed as flesh. For ten months I was compacted in blood from human seed, and when I was born I drew in the common air; I fell upon the earth, formed in the same way, and I uttered my first voice, weeping like everyone else. None of the kings had any other beginning of birth. There is therefore one entrance into life and a similar departure.”

For we are all born naked, and we die naked. There is no distinction among the corpses of the rich and the poor, except perhaps that the bodies of the rich give off a more dreadful stench than those of the poor.

That natural justice made all things common to everyone may be inferred from the saying that the one who shares his goods with others will endure forever and ever: “He scattered; he gave to the poor; his justice endures forever and ever.” Likewise from a certain proverb: “A just king raises up the land; a greedy man destroys it.”

Since this natural justice therefore judged the world itself and everything in it to be common, greed afterward distributed rights of possession among individuals. From this there later arose desires for possessions, lusts for honors, disputes and quarrels, and the struggles of wars. This plague of evils can never be cleansed unless, at some time, human hearts return through this justice flashing forth again to some grace of the former common life—even if not to a complete one—so that, for example, those who were enemies toward one another, rebels, or foes, who had never possessed anything earthly in concord, may now, as the equity of natural justice begins to spring up within them, unite their minds, form friendships and alliances, although they may not yet begin to share common speech and customs.

To this great good, which natural justice brings about, we shall attach no name more fitting than peace, provided that we understand it here not as the peace of Jerusalem—which, as remains to be discussed, rejoices in greater merits—but as the peace of Babylon, the peace with which we began to deal.

It may also be said that divine justice in a certain way produces Babylonian peace, if you observe that all human beings are of one and the same kind not only according to the law of flesh but also according to the likeness of God. “For we are indeed his offspring,” says Aratus. Since, therefore, we are God’s offspring and all alike bear the noblest image of God, we who are united by so great a likeness ought never to confront one another with the dissimilarity of a quarrelsome spirit, just as birds of the same kind are friendly toward one another and know nothing of hostile hatred among themselves. “Birds,” as a proverb has made known in writing, “come together with those like themselves.”

And if you do not think that these arguments have persuaded you that justice produces this peace, let the testimonies of Scripture at least satisfy you concerning the matter. For the noblest of the prophets says: “The work of justice will be peace, and the service of justice will be quiet.” David, when he set forth praises concerning the King who was to be born from heaven, intending to speak of the peace that the world deserved to have at his coming, first mentioned justice as its cause, saying: “Justice will arise in his days.” Then follows: “And abundance of peace.” Elsewhere likewise: “Justice and peace have embraced one another.”

## CHAPTER IX — What humanity is, which nourishes this peace

Humanity, by which this peace of Babylon is nourished, is a certain mutual assistance in human necessities, through which the diverse condition of mortals is maintained either by reciprocal aid or by alternating exchanges.

This is how it works: soldiers protect the peasants with weapons, while the peasants strive to provide food for the soldiers through agricultural labor. Likewise, when one kingdom needs grain and another perfumes; when one province needs metals and another textiles; when one region needs timber and another marble; and when, through a thousand other kinds of goods, human mortality needs one another’s assistance in turn, humanity arose. Through it, in the peace of the Babylonian covenant, alternating scarcity is sustained by alternating abundance through these exchanges; without them this peace, neglected, would collapse.

It is like the joining of stones in a constructed building, in which the stones support one another by their mutual embrace: if, with the walls gaping, they cease to hold one another together, the whole structure will quickly fall.

For room to be made for this humanity, it is necessary above all to learn one another’s language. Without this, mutual assistance contributes little toward joining human beings together. How could those who cannot explain their needs to others through the meanings of words either support one another through reciprocal services or exchange useful goods?

The diversity of an unknown language is accustomed to generate not humanity but inhumanity, as is shown by the oracle of prophetic threat: “Behold, I will bring upon you a nation from afar, house of Israel, says the Lord, a strong nation, an ancient nation whose language you will not know, nor understand what it says.”

How necessary this humanity is for nourishing peace between kings and peoples, prelates and subjects, is evident: the king must provide protection to the people, and the people must render payment of civil obligations to the king. “For this reason,” says the Apostle, “you also pay taxes.” A prelate owes his subjects the solicitude of provision, while subjects owe their prelate the devotion of obedience. These mutual forms of assistance are so necessary on both sides that one cannot endure without the other.

Without the provision of kings and governors, the people are prepared for slaughter; and without the service of the people, all the dignity of kings and prelates vanishes. Therefore, when a king is instituted, a certain tacit pact is made between him and the people: the king is to rule the people humanely, and the people are to remember to honor the king through established taxes and levies. This is the covenant that the priest Jehoiada made between King Joash and the people of Judah, as the history of the Kings records.

Through this mutual exchange of humanity, therefore, the concord of Babylon—that is, of worldly peace—is nourished between kings and peoples, and between prelates and subjects. If this concord is sometimes, as often happens, held in contempt, so that either subjects deny their superior the services they owe, or superiors subject their inferiors to tyrannical laws, and the evils of oppression and rebellion rise from this, suddenly the authority of governance is dissolved together with the peace, and the kingdom too is transferred, as it is written: “A kingdom is transferred from nation to nation because of injustices, injuries, insults, and various deceits.”

## CHAPTER X — How prudence gives this peace stability
Moreover, let King Solomon serve you as an example of how this peace gains stability through prudence. Most prudent in the counsels of his wisdom, he strengthened his kingdom in the most tranquil and prosperous peace throughout the course of eighty years, as Josephus’s history relates. His son Rehoboam foolishly destroyed the good seed of this peace, dividing the kingdom into two. Concerning him the Book of Ecclesiasticus says: “Solomon came to his end among his fathers, and left behind him, from his seed, folly for the nation, and Rehoboam, diminished in prudence, who turned the people aside by his counsel.” Scripture likewise says of him: “A foolish king will destroy his people, and cities will be inhabited through the understanding of the prudent.” And in the Book of Wisdom: “If you delight in thrones and scepters, you kings of peoples, love wisdom, so that you may reign forever.” For then, as the most eloquent teacher writes, “then commonwealths are happy when either philosophers rule or rulers philosophize.” — “Learn wisdom, therefore, you who judge the earth.”

This peace will be confirmed above all by the king’s prudence if the king himself, through a skilled policy of governance, makes himself approachable and, as it were, popular toward every class of people over whom he presides, every order, sex, and age—while nevertheless preserving the privilege of discipline (for it is written: “Maintain discipline in peace, children”)—so that he may always deserve to possess the people’s favor. History has made it widely known that Octavian, called Augustus, acted in this way among the Romans; for this reason, they considered that he maintained his peaceful rule for a longer age. Let him who is placed over a people or nation prudently beware lest, while caring for one party, he neglect another. For this causes an exceedingly destructive condition among a people—namely, envy, sedition, and discord—when he who rules all chooses to provide not for everyone’s needs, but for the interests of some single group.

Likewise, the prudence of others will confirm this peace if those among whom it has been established conduct themselves toward one another with such caution and propriety that nothing at all appears, through their agency, to violate the covenants of peace. For even if, through someone’s levity, it should happen to be slightly injured, it ought to be restored by prudent remedy immediately, not after many days, while the matter is still new and has not been aggravated by greater injuries—just as limbs, when first struck by a wound, begin to be separated by a sort of opening from their continuous structure; if the physician’s skill comes to them at once, they can be rejoined to the remaining flesh without deformity. This will not happen if such a remedy is postponed for a very long time. The Apostle’s saying is not unrelated to this judgment: “Let not the sun go down upon your anger.”

## CHAPTER XI — The Difference between the Peace of Babylon and That of Egypt

[Col. 1618D]

This peace is distinguished by a great difference from the peace of Egypt, since, as has been said, the latter must always be rejected, whereas this one is often to be sought and cultivated—not only with household members and the faithful, but also with outsiders, barbarians, and pagans. If this peace ought not to be cultivated with unbelievers, why did Isaac make a covenant with Abimelech, Ochozath, and Phicol, the men of Gerar? If this peace ought not to be cultivated with unbelievers, why did the people of Israel seek a peaceful passage from the king of Edom and from Sihon, king of the Amorites? If this peace ought not to be cultivated with unbelievers, why did the Lord say through Moses in Deuteronomy: “If you go to attack a city, you shall first offer it peace. If it receives this and opens its gates to you, all the people who are in it shall be saved”?

[Col. 1619A]

This peace must be maintained with unbelievers to such an extent that we read that holy Jacob sent gifts to his brother for the sake of its good.

## CHAPTER XII — The Three Classes of People with Whom the Peace of Babylon Is Not to Be Cultivated
