We said that peace is not always, but often, to be cultivated with everyone because sometimes we must by no means keep peace with such people; rather, it will be more expedient to challenge them to war, as with the pestilent, the persecutors, and the rebels. Considering this, the distinguished teacher says: “If it is possible, so far as depends on you, live at peace with all people.” Since he knew that there were some with whom it was not lawful to bind concord, he added a condition before saying, “Live at peace with all”: “If it is possible.”

By “the pestilent,” understand those who, by means of Babylonian peace, wish to weave with us a covenant of Egyptian peace—that is, of vices. No pact at all is to be made with such people; rather, we must strive against them with all our strength unto destruction. To this pertains what Moses set before Israel in the Law:

“When the Lord your God has brought you into the land which you are entering to possess, and has destroyed before you many nations—the Hittite, Girgashite, Amorite, Canaanite, Perizzite, Hivite, and Jebusite, seven nations much greater in number than you and stronger than you—and when the Lord your God has delivered them to you, you shall strike them down unto destruction. You shall not make a covenant with them, nor pity them, nor join yourself to them in marriage. You shall not give your daughter to his son, nor take his daughter for your son, because she will seduce your son from following me, so that he may instead serve foreign gods.”

[Col. 1619C]

Such contagious people are not found only among outsiders. Even when they are citizens, household members, brothers, sons, or parents, it will be the duty of peace—or rather, of holiness—to overcome such people by the sword of vengeance when necessary. Thus we read concerning the sons of Levi:

“Taking up swords in vengeance for idolatry, they passed through the middle of the camp, and each man killed his brother, his friend, and his neighbor whom he encountered.”

For this reason they were praised as having consecrated their hands to the Lord. “You have consecrated,” he says, “your hands today, each man upon his son and brother, so that a blessing may be given to you.” So Phinehas, not sparing the sins of the citizens, struck down the Israelite who was coupling with the Moabite woman; by the fire of his own anger he extinguished the fire of the Lord’s anger.

Persecutors are those who, attempting to overthrow either the condition of common concord or the reverence due to public decency, do not fear to commit cruel crimes or blush not at perpetrating acts of the most solemn infamy. Against such people both the rights of the laws and the arms of kings have customarily opposed inexorable severity. “For he does not bear the sword without cause, but for the punishment of evildoers and the praise of the good.”

We count as rebels those who seek to shake off the yoke of legitimate rule and usurp illicit freedom for themselves, rejecting even public envoys, despising royal decrees, refusing to reckon with the treasury, and providing no tribute. Against such people the Lord says: “Render to Caesar what belongs to Caesar.” And Paul says: “Render to all what is owed: tribute to whom tribute is due, revenue to whom revenue is due.” To this is related what the outstanding poet, singing the praises of Roman imperial power with no less provident skill than polished meter, says:

> Remember, Roman, to rule the peoples with authority—  
> these shall be your arts:  
> to impose the custom of peace,  
> to spare the subjected and subdue the proud.  
> VIRGIL, *Aeneid*, Book VI, lines 854–857.

## CHAPTER XIII — Why a Kingdom Not Lawfully Acquired Should Be Considered Robbery Rather Than a Kingdom

[Col. 1620B]

We added the qualification “of legitimate rule” rather than simply “kingdom” for this reason: to wish to conquer and subjugate a people of a distant region that has never bowed its neck to your authority and has never inflicted any trouble upon you, merely from a desire to rule, is not the duty of a king but of a tyrant—indeed, of a robber and bloodstained criminal. For this reason the excellent teacher Augustine (*City of God*, Book IV, chapter 4) writes:

“Remove justice, and what are kingdoms except great robberies? For what are robberies themselves except little kingdoms? A band of men is there, ruled by the authority of a leader, bound by a pact of association, and dividing its plunder according to an agreed law. If this evil grows through the successive additions of ruined men to such an extent that it occupies places, establishes settlements, subjugates provinces, and seizes cities, it openly assumes the name of a kingdom; for what gives it that name is now plainly not the removal of desire, but the addition of impunity.”

Thus a pirate captured by Alexander the Great, when asked why he made the sea so dangerous, is recorded to have replied with bold and elegant frankness: “And why do you make the whole world dangerous? But because I do it with a small vessel, I am called a pirate; because you do it with a great fleet, you are called an emperor.”

Hence, to bring war upon neighboring peoples, to advance from there against others, and to crush peoples who have caused no trouble merely from a desire for dominion is nothing other than what must be called robbery.

## CHAPTER XIV — How It Benefits the Good of Peace Itself When Peace of Babylon Is Not Kept with the Foregoing Classes

[Col. 1620D]

See, then, why peace is not to be kept with those three classes of people, but war is rather to be declared against them. No wise person will fail to understand that this contributes to the good of peace itself. For the vigor of severity pursues these few so that peace may be preserved more fully and safely among the rest. The Lord indicated this sufficiently when speaking against the Jewish people through the prophet, saying:

“Who will make me a thorn and a briar in battle? I shall march against it; I shall burn it up together. Or rather, will it hold fast to my strength, will it make peace with me, will it make peace with me?”

Understand this as referring to the very burning with which he declares that it is to be consumed.

[Col. 1621A]

Such people must therefore be attacked so that peace may remain unharmed, either among those who have been restrained by the experience of punishment itself or at least among others who have been instructed by their example. For this reason alone public war is waged, for this reason arms are taken up, and for this reason the laws prescribe punishments: so that the good of peace may remain inviolate in every respect.

## CHAPTER XV — The Three or Four Degrees of Worldly Peace

This worldly peace proceeds through three degrees. First there is the peace of the world, then the peace of the city, and afterward the peace of the household. The first is general, the second civic, and the third domestic. Thus the peace of the world is to be maintained even with foreigners, the peace of the city with citizens, and domestic peace with relatives.

Since it was said above that the peace of Babylon requires a sharing of goods, it can therefore be understood that, at each of these degrees, peace demands a communication of goods. General peace—for example, among kingdoms and provinces—creates common markets and languages; civic peace creates the forum, the temple, laws, and certain customs; domestic peace creates the estate, the house, the common life, and, in marriage, the bedchamber, as well as tombs and monuments of ancestors.

General peace, which we have also said must be maintained with foreigners, and likewise that peace which binds citizens together—this peace, I say, although it does not include domestic habitation, nevertheless, if it is advanced among certain people with domestic affection, becomes private peace and takes for itself the sweet name of friendship. Thus a fourth degree also arises, to be joined to the three higher ones: those whom we previously counted as having the peace of the world, the city, and the household may, at the fourth degree, count the peace of friendship. Friendship is cultivated and maintained through a reciprocal exchange of care and services. Otherwise the bonds of friendship will endure in no way unless an affectionate willingness to serve is evident on both sides.

## CHAPTER XVI — The Condition of Domestic Peace

Since every household is a small part of the city, and every part is directed toward the integrity of the whole of which it is a part, domestic peace ought to be formed according to the standard of civic peace, so that, just as civic peace is preserved by public laws, domestic peace may likewise be legitimately governed by private traditions. Hence, just as the one who protects the public peace is called the father of his country, so the one who governs domestic peace deserves to be called the father of a household.

Since he is regarded as a father with respect to his family, he ought also to show paternal kindness to all his servants, who are part of the household, so that the opportunity for disturbing domestic peace may be removed. A wise man of widely recognized authority did not depart from this judgment when he taught:

“Live with one beneath you as you would wish a superior to live with you. Whenever it comes to mind how much power you have over your servant, let it come to mind how much your Lord has over you.”

And Jesus son of Sirach says: “If you have a servant, let him be to you as your own soul, and treat him as a brother.”

Yet one should exercise kindness toward one’s household in such a way as not to lose the rigor of discipline altogether. For a lax softness will empty the harmony of domestic peace no less than severe harshness, as we recognize happened in David’s case. Because he had treated his sons with excessive indulgence, the history of the kings does not hesitate to proclaim how much confusion, scandal, and danger he afterward suffered because of them.

Moreover, since domestic peace is a member of civic peace, if domestic peace must be violated by members of the household so that civic peace may not perish, then domestic peace between father and son must be broken, just as we read that those who wrote more eloquently about the condition of the commonwealth taught.

Lest you think that domestic peace receives no praise from sacred Scripture, Ecclesiasticus therefore speaks of it:

“There are three things pleasing to my spirit, which have been approved before God and human beings: harmony among brothers, love of neighbors, and a man and woman consenting with one another.”

## CHAPTER XVII — Certain Circumstances by Which Private Peace Is Disturbed, and Their Remedy

Finally, this twofold peace—domestic peace, namely, and peace joined by domestic affection (for this is friendship itself)—the closer it is, the more frequently it is accustomed to be torn by dissensions: for example, by anger, excessive talk, and especially whispering; still more by insult or reproach; and much more by pride, deceitfulness, and the exposure of secrets; and, more malign than all these, by a wicked woman. The Proverbs of the Wise have noted each of these matters.

For it is said in Proverbs: “A perverse man stirs up quarrels, and a talkative man separates rulers.” Likewise Ecclesiasticus says: “The whisperer and the double-tongued are accursed, for they have disturbed many who were living at peace.” And again: “An angry man kindles strife, and in the midst of those who live at peace he introduces enmities.” And again:

“He who throws a stone at birds will bring them down. So also he who insults his friend dissolves friendship. Even if you draw a sword against a friend, do not despair, for there is a way back. If you open your mouth against a friend in bitterness, do not be afraid, for reconciliation is possible—except in the case of insult, reproach, pride, the revelation of a secret, and a treacherous wound: in all these matters a friend will flee. If you expose his hidden things, do not pursue him afterward. As one who releases a bird from his hand, so you have abandoned your neighbor, and you will not recapture him. Reconciliation with a cursed person is impossible; to expose a friend’s secrets is despair for an unfaithful soul.”

The same passage adds concerning a woman that “a strong woman delights her husband and will fill the years of his life with peace.” But just as blessed is the one who lives with a sensible woman, so, conversely, “to dwell,” it says, “with a lion and a dragon would be preferable to living with a wicked woman,” especially one who, through continual insolence of speech, inflicts bitter distress upon a quiet and peaceful husband. Hence: “As a sandy ascent is to the feet of an old man, so is a talkative woman to a quiet man.”

Therefore, lest friendship and household peace be broken by such things, let anger be excluded by gentleness and excessive talk by restraint in speech. Let us close our ears to all whispering and shut our mouths against every insult. Let us not raise an arrogant brow against a friend, contrive no treacherous plots against him, and not expose with an itching tongue the secrets of our friends that we know. It is the judgment of tested discernment that these three things—enmity, duplicity, and treachery—are poisons of friendship. Moreover, you who administer the affairs of a private household must never consent to submit to the insolence of a woman or wife. For it is written: “A woman, if she has primacy, is contrary to her husband.”

## CHAPTER XVIII — How Great a Consequence of Good Things the Peace of Babylon Possesses

It has now been shown in what ways the peace of Babylon—that is, of the world—ought to be established and preserved. How great a consequence of temporal goods this worldly peace possesses can be demonstrated by thousands of examples.

First, therefore, consider in the whole world itself a certain natural peace by which the hand of the heavenly Artisan has gathered the elements of different natures into one body and caused things utterly unlike to aspire toward such harmony that they cannot endure unless bound together by one another’s support. For heaven, unless there were something upon which it could pour its light, would have none. Heaven gives color to the air; the air nourishes the earth with rains and grants life to all living creatures through respiration. Water irrigates by means of rivers, which themselves would not endure if the earth’s deepest foundation did not hold them. By such laws, therefore, the elements, joined in covenant, possess an ordered and perpetual peace.

But if any disagreement should arise against itself within this material, and this structure should contemplate its own dissolution through some rebellion; or if, by divine will, something should be moved from this peace—if the sea should boil, or the earth quake; if destructive rain should fall, or the sun withdraw and retreat with its light removed; if the air should blaze with heat, or the nature of fire should boil beyond its proper measure—then the world’s destruction and ruin would unquestionably be expected, since the good of peace among the elements would be overturned by this rebellion.

To pass over kingdoms and innumerable peoples, and to pass over cities, families, and households, all of which endure through peace and concord but are dissolved and perish through dissension; to say nothing even of the city itself, which, while peace flourished in it, was formerly mistress of the world but now lies almost prostrate, humbled by seditions and shaken by civil wars—to pass over all these things, look to Israel, so familiar from the divine utterances. Did they not, while they maintained peace among themselves and groaned with one accord toward the Lord, deserve to be brought out of Egypt amid triumphant signs? The sea saw them united and fled; the rivers turned backward before them, imitating the service of their kindred sea; heaven supplied food to the hungry, and the rock supplied drink to the thirsty. This was a blessed people, whose Lord was their God—abounding in population, rich in wealth, and so strong in power that one could pursue a thousand and two put ten thousand to flight.

But afterward, when it began to be oppressed by scandals and dissensions and divided into factions; after Jeroboam and Rehoboam appeared as joint rulers; after factions and seditions arose; after the younger began to offend the elder and the lowborn the honored—what it came to and what it suffered are recounted by the histories of old and by Jeremiah’s Lamentations. For everywhere the frenzy of wars and the unrestrained license of the sword raged against them. The splendid city was overthrown, the consecrated temple profaned, no one spared the aged, no one the infants; young men were slaughtered without regard, no modesty was left to matrons, and no shame to virgins. During the siege itself, before they surrendered themselves to the hands of the sword, they were tortured by such hostile famine that, in famine, the sweetest consolation of their children became a remedy for hunger. Finally, driven from the borders of their homeland, they were scattered throughout all the provinces, lamenting the misery of eternal captivity. Behold the outcomes and fruits of discord!

From the effects of its opposite, therefore, we now see more clearly how great the good of this peace is. For this peace produces the commonwealth, extends power, strengthens kingdoms, ennobles liberties, establishes laws, nourishes the arts, illuminates honors, fosters religion, fills the city, multiplies offspring, nourishes childhood, protects adolescence, gladdens youth, and adorns the gray hair of old age. You can gather all this from a single testimony of Scripture. When Genesis was recounting the quarrel between the herdsmen of Gerar and Isaac’s herdsmen, it added that Isaac called the first well, over which they had quarreled, “Calumny”; the second, “Hostilities”; and the third, over which there had been no quarrel, he named “Spaciousness” (*Latitudo*). And Solomon says in Proverbs: “Joy will follow those who devise counsels of peace.”

Add that this peace is a kind of road and ladder by which one reaches the possession of the peace of Jerusalem. Indeed, the peace of Jerusalem is included and preserved within this peace, as could be observed above from Jeremiah’s words. Paul also teaches Timothy to pray for this peace:

“I urge, therefore, first of all, that supplications, prayers, petitions, and thanksgivings be made for all people, for kings and all who are in high positions, so that we may lead a quiet and peaceful life in all piety and chastity.”

For this reason, when our Lord came to give peace to the Church, he prepared such peace for her that he would remove wars to the ends of the earth, break the bow, shatter the weapons, and burn the shields with fire.

## CHAPTER XIX — On the Peace of Jerusalem, That Is, of the Church

It is now time to attach what must be said about the peace of Jerusalem, that is, of the Church. This peace, as we remember having set out earlier, is the concord of Christian peace. Paul was its guide and teacher when he said: “The kingdom of God is not food and drink, but righteousness and peace. Therefore let us pursue the things that make for peace.” And again to Timothy: “Pursue righteousness, faith, friendship, charity, and peace with those who call upon the Lord from a pure heart.”

The Lord admonished his disciples more explicitly concerning this peace: “Have salt in yourselves, and have peace among yourselves.” You know that salt signifies the seasoning of wisdom. But what wisdom is truer than that of which it is written: “We preach Christ, the power and wisdom of God”? Therefore, when he was about to command this peace, he first warned them about salt, because no one deserves to possess this peace unless he has first chosen to receive Christ in his heart through faith. For he himself, as we said earlier, is the reconciler and author of this peace: “Father,” says the sacred word, “of the age to come, prince of peace.”

## CHAPTER XX — How This Peace Is Bound Together through Charity

That this peace is built through charity, as we intimated earlier, is testified to me by the Psalm: “Let peace be in your strength.” By “strength,” understand the queen of all virtues, charity. It is called a virtue in its proper sense because it is strong as death—for “love is strong as death.” No one resists it when it comes: it kills what we have been badly, so that we may become something else well.

Indeed, how charity makes this peace is hidden from no one who professes knowledge of the sacred books. Charity is in this peace as the vital spirit is in the body. Just as the limbs of the body live when enlivened by the spirit and retain a kind of peaceful solidity and organic continuity, but, when the spirit departs, must die and be dissolved, so charity alone consolidates the children of the Church in the unity of this peace; when it departs, this peace is torn apart. Thus, although for a time it retains, on account of the Church’s sacraments, a semblance of the body’s structure, nevertheless, through the sin of hatred—which is the death of the soul—they utterly lose the sense of life.

The Teacher of the Nations explained this with subtle reasoning in several passages of his letters, placing a very close correspondence between the members of Christ and the parts of the human body. To the Corinthians he writes:

“As the body is one and has many members, and all the members of the body, though many, are one body, so also is Christ. For in one Spirit we were all baptized into one body.”

To the Ephesians he writes:

“Let us grow in him who is the head, Christ, from whom the whole body, joined and bound together through every supporting joint, according to the working proportionate to each member, produces the growth of the body for its building up in charity.”

You will find that he wrote the same thing, in nearly the same words, to the Colossians.

Charity, therefore, is what gives life to the members of Christ and binds and harmonizes them into one body. “Therefore, diligently preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace.” This is the blessed bitumen of Noah’s ark, with which the very timbers were smeared so firmly that it did not allow the waters of the Flood to enter. This is the bond by which the upper loop is joined together, which fastens divinity to humanity; the line that the Lord laid out upon the earth and by which he raised humanity into the heavens.

This alone, therefore, unites the Church in unity. Indeed, it is itself the unity of the Church: that seamless tunic, woven from above throughout, which does not pass by division to many but comes by lot to one. If only one person receives this tunic, let no one think that he possesses charity if he does not remain in the unity of the Church. Indeed, there is no way of salvation and no place of remedy for those whom the bosom of Catholic unity does not include, as the symbolic history of the aforementioned ark of Noah indicates. For all who were found outside it perished in the chastising waters. The mystery of Passover spoke the same thing: “In one house it shall be eaten, and you shall not carry any of its flesh outside the door.” The flesh of the lamb foreshadowed the sacrifice of the Lord’s body. This sacrifice is the clearest sacrament of ecclesiastical unity.

Divine Scripture also prefigured the same thing in the house of Rahab when it said: “You shall gather your father and mother and all your kindred into your house. Whoever goes out through the door of your house, his blood shall be upon his own head.”

Because of the bond of this peace and unity, Mother Church herself is called “one dove” and is also simply called “unique”: “My dove is one, my perfect one.” And David, speaking in the person of the Lord, prays that his unique one may be delivered from dogs and lions, saying: “Deliver my unique one from the hand of the dog; my unique one from the lions.” This is the union by which, in Ezekiel, the two pieces of wood—namely, the people of the Jews and of the nations—are joined one to the other so that from the two there appears one body of wood, glued together.

## CHAPTER XXI — What the Piety Mentioned Is, and How It Nourishes the Peace of Jerusalem

By the piety through which we said that the peace of Jerusalem is nourished, we must understand works of mercy, by which, in want of temporal or spiritual goods, we assist one another in fraternal charity. Concerning these it is said: “Ask for the things that make for the peace of Jerusalem.” As though it were saying: O you who sit in judgment, ask and inquire of her what things are and what things avail for nourishing the peace of Jerusalem.

From this it is subtly suggested that those who will sit upon twelve thrones judging the twelve tribes of Israel will examine people chiefly concerning works of piety, asking whether they have performed these works for one another. This applies both to preachers and to the congregations: whether those to whom spiritual things have been sown have handed over to the cultivators—that is, to the preachers—the harvest of material things; and conversely, whether those who received stipends of material support from their congregations have striven to refresh them with the nourishment of spiritual food. For the shepherds of the Churches are merchants, contracting necessary commerce with the believing people. To them it is said: “Conduct business until I come.”

Just as merchants come from different regions into the marketplace and meet with others there, exchanging useful goods with them—giving them what they need and receiving from them what they themselves lack—so prelates are to be understood as doing with their subjects.

This marketplace is the Church, into which, as into a certain central place, people from different nations come together as one. The heralds of God come there from the mountains—that is, from the lofty summit of virtues—and the subjects ascend there from the valleys, that is, from a lower and earthly manner of life. Perhaps the Truth signified this in the Gospel when he said:

“To what shall I compare this generation? It is like children playing in the marketplace, who call out reproachfully to their companions: ‘We played music for you, and you did not dance; we lamented, and you did not mourn.’”

For when prelates in the Church preach eternal joys to reprobate hearers, they generate no joy in their hearts. Whatever is said to them about heavenly things, they regard as fiction; and when their fathers threaten them with future punishments, they are not pierced with remorse or sighs, because they suppose that hell is nothing and that there are no torments after this life.

This exchange of spiritual and material goods—or whatever alternating service of piety takes place among brothers—is, as our most noble author explains, that equality of which the Apostle was mindful when he said: “Not that there should be relief for others and affliction for us, but from equality.” This equality is itself the peace of Jerusalem: bodily works of mercy are joined to the spiritual works of preaching, and peace comes about through giving and receiving. While the psalm is taken up and the tympanum is given, a pleasing psalterium [*spalterium*] is made with the lyre. [Note: Many older writers use *spalmus* and *spalterium* for *psalmus* and *psalterium*.] “Let the one who is instructed in the word share all good things with the one who catechizes him.”

## CHAPTER XXII — How Humility Strengthens This Peace

Finally, let the modeled construction of the tabernacle of the covenant teach you how humility strengthens and reinforces the peace of Jerusalem. There the Lord commanded Moses to make, on the sides of the boards, two projections by which the boards themselves might fit together through mutual attachments. The two projections of the boards may be understood as the twofold humility of every faithful person: namely, that he should not swell with pride over temporal successes and should not exalt himself above others because of whatever grace of spiritual goods he may possess. Through the projection by which the boards are joined to one another, the ark is fastened together, because through the craft of humility the peace of the Church is guarded.

Considering this, Paul says to the Philippians:

“If there is any consolation in Christ, any comfort from charity, any fellowship of the Spirit, any affection and compassion, complete my joy by being of the same mind, having the same charity, united in soul, thinking one thing: doing nothing through rivalry or empty glory, but in humility regarding others as superior to yourselves.”

Humility, therefore, preserves the peace of Jerusalem unbroken, just as its opposite—namely, pride—alone cuts apart the unity of this peace. Who, I do not say from among the good alone, but from among the wicked whom the Church still endures, and whose separation would injure the tranquility of ecclesiastical peace—who, I say, has been destroyed by them except one who, blown about by the puffed-up arrogance of pride, is separated bodily merely because they are wicked? Hence, as the Scriptures testify, such people are worse than the harmful. They are like the lighter chaff, which, before the threshing-floor is winnowed, is snatched from the mass of grain by the sighing blasts of the wind, while those who are heavy with the weight of humility await the winnowing of the universal judgment. For this reason it is said: “In a weighty people I will praise you.”

Likewise Lot deserved to be raised up by praises that were not undeserved because he alone continued to live as a good man among the worst: “He rescued,” Peter says, “the righteous man, oppressed by the outrage and licentious conduct of the wicked. For, by sight and hearing, that righteous man was living among those who day after day tormented his righteous soul with wicked deeds.”

How great, finally, is the humility of this ecclesiastical peace, which tames the rage of the wolf, subdues the ferocity of the leopard, and knows how to lay aside the pride of the lion, so that, according to the prophetic proclamation, the wolf may now dwell with the lamb in the assembly of ecclesiastical peace, the leopard lie down with the kid, and one may see the lion and the calf dwelling together?

## CHAPTER XXIII — Several Differences by Which the Peace of Jerusalem Is Distinguished from the Peace of Babylon

This peace is distinguished from the peace of Babylon by very many differences. Although both are good, this peace is adorned with better titles. For that peace, apart from the humaneness we mentioned, is generally satisfied with doing no harm; this peace demands a willingness to benefit everyone and to do good to anyone it can. Perhaps this is what the Teacher of the Nations has in mind when he says: “Peace to everyone who does good.”

Likewise, as was entrusted to the preceding page, the peace of Babylon gives birth to joy; but the peace of Jerusalem produces blessedness from joy. Hence Tobit, speaking to Jerusalem, says: “Blessed are all who love you, and who rejoice over your peace.”

Again, in the peace of the world those who rule are masters; in the peace of the Church they remain servants. Hence one of them says: “We do not preach ourselves, but our Lord Jesus Christ, and ourselves as your servants through Jesus.” And the Lord says to his disciples: “Whoever wishes to be first among you shall be your servant.” Since, as was stated above, charity governs this peace, and love knows no rank, all who are bound by the covenant of this peace will strive to serve one another with equal devotion, according to what Paul says to the Galatians: “Through charity of the Spirit, serve one another.”

The peace of Jerusalem forgives every injury, as that daily prayer bears witness, in which we say: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.”

Again, the peace of Babylon establishes a law that injury should be met with retaliation. Likewise, as was shown above, those who cultivate Babylonian peace are hostile toward those who violate the public peace; but those who possess this peace do not cease to be peaceable even with those who hate peace. For, “with those who hated peace, I was peaceable.” Yet, when no danger to the salvation of the others is feared, it pursues them with pious severity—not striking them with the sword of evil, but with the spiritual sword, striking the rebel. For, as the Apostle says, “the weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but powerful through God.” I have called it “pious severity” because the severity of excommunication must be exercised outwardly against those who are subject to it in such a way that, inwardly, the bowels of fraternal charity toward them are not torn apart. Hence Paul says to the Thessalonians: “If anyone does not obey our word, mark him by letter, and do not associate with him, so that he may be ashamed; and do not regard him as an enemy, but correct him as a brother.” [Col. 1629B]

Again, those who cultivate Babylonian peace, judging that the goods belonging to that peace are sufficient for them, seek or desire nothing beyond them. Thus one of them is recorded as having said: “Let there be only peace and truth in my days.” But for those who love this peace, better things to be possessed after this life are reserved, as you will find written: “For there are remnants for the peaceful man.”

Again, the peace of Babylon grants immunity from persecutions; the peace of Jerusalem requires only endurance of adversities. He intended to indicate this who, while enumerating the virtues, immediately placed patience after peace: “The fruit of the Spirit is charity, joy, peace, patience.” [Col. 1629C]

Moreover, if the peace of Babylon becomes more tranquil, more abundant, and more enduring, it will soften into an excessively luxurious and effeminate pleasure, in accordance with the sharpness of that satirical reproach directed against the Romans:

> Humble Fortune once kept the Latin women chaste,  
>
> nor did labor, brief sleep, Tuscan wool,  
>
> the torment of toil, hard hands, Hannibal close to the City,  
>
> and husbands standing on the Colline tower permit  
>
> their little homes to be touched by vices.  
>
> Now we suffer the evils of a long peace;  
>
> luxury, more savage than arms, bears down upon us  
>
> and takes vengeance on the conquered world.

On the other hand, the more the peace of Jerusalem increases and endures, the more manfully it will strengthen the merits of the virtues. Therefore Peter says to the faithful: “Grace and peace be multiplied to you.” And Paul desired for the Thessalonians not a long peace, but an everlasting one: “May the Lord of peace himself give you everlasting peace in every place.” [Col. 1629D]

Finally, there is also this important difference: the fellowship of worldly peace—especially that which is established among household members and friends—is judged to be all the more bitter in its final separation, which occurs through death, the sweeter it has been. For it cannot happen that the death of one whose life was exceedingly sweet to us should not be exceedingly bitter. But the blessed fellowship of ecclesiastical peace is not torn apart by death; it is changed for the better. [Col. 1630A]

Hence the faithful, united in this fellowship, when they have carried one of their number out for burial, suffer no grief beyond what natural human obligation demands; rather, with a certain inward joy, they accompany the companion who has gone before them into the homeland, knowing that death is not a reef but a harbor, an honorable discharge for a soldier, the reward of labor, and the taking possession of an inheritance. For, “when he gives his beloved sleep, behold, the inheritance of the Lord.” [Col. 1630B]

## CHAPTER XXIV — The three articles by which the peace of the Church is maintained

This peace rests, as upon three foundations, upon three articles: unity of faith, unanimity of will, and conformity of conduct.

Of the first article it is written to the Romans: “Now may the God of hope fill you with all joy and peace in believing.” [Col. 1630C] Concerning unanimity of will, the same Paul had said above: “May the God of patience and consolation grant you to have the same understanding toward one another according to Jesus Christ, so that with one mind and one mouth you may honor God.” Concerning conformity of conduct, that same man admonished the Philippians “to think the same thing and remain in the same rule.” By the name “rule” he signifies conformity of life.

Indeed, all who belong to Christ agree upon one standard of faith. We already perceive this by visible evidence, when we see how peoples of such varied worship, faces of such dissimilar appearance, and forms of speech so different are united in harmony with him. For all who are reckoned by Christian profession are servants of one Lord, sheep of one shepherd, and soldiers of one flock. One Father has begotten us; one mother, the Church, has conceived us; we are recognized as members of one body. [Col. 1630D]

It is not immediately necessary, however, that all should come together in unanimity of will and the same likeness of conduct, except in those points of conduct and will that the decrees of evangelical and apostolic instruction have established, whether written or unwritten, according to which the condition of the entire Christian race must be marked by an undivided character of will and conduct.

Otherwise, although we read that the children of the newly founded Church were most closely conformed in conduct and spirit—“the multitude of believers was of one heart and one soul”—yet in our own times, both because of human frailty and because of the multitude of believers scattered throughout the whole world, it is far beyond the capacity of every human possibility for them all to be formed into one quality of will and conduct. [Col. 1631A] They do not all converge upon the same affection and way of life; different things please and belong to different people.

Yet there are some whom this peace has bound so closely that it grants them not only agreement of mind but also shared residence in one dwelling. Of them it is written: “God, who makes those of one manner dwell in a house.” And again: “Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together.” And in the Gospels: “Where two or three are gathered in my name, there am I in the midst of them.”

## CHAPTER XXV — The disagreement between Paul and Barnabas

Finally, if it should happen that the very harmony of minds among the just is wounded by some disagreement, one must not immediately despair, nor must one disparage those who are at variance, since we read that the evangelical fellowship of Paul and Barnabas was once separated by a cord of disagreement, as it is written: “Barnabas wanted to take with them John, who was called Mark; but Paul insisted that he who had withdrawn from them in Pamphylia and had not gone with them to the work ought not to be received. There arose a disagreement, so that they separated from one another; and Barnabas, taking Mark with him, sailed to Cyprus, while Paul, choosing Silas, departed, having been entrusted by the brothers to the grace of God.” [Col. 1631B]

Later Paul received this Mark into his affection and also took care to commend him to the Colossians, saying: “Aristarchus, my fellow prisoner, greets you, and Mark, the cousin of Barnabas, concerning whom you received instructions”—before, that is, he had departed (for these indeed [lacuna])—“if he comes to you, receive him.” [Col. 1631C]

Since, therefore, faith is the principal foundation of ecclesiastical peace, if at some time among the members of Christ there should arise, not a hostile division but a fraternal quarrel over some contention—which nevertheless does not exceed the bounds of moderation—there is no need for complete fear. Such quarrels can easily be healed, since in them neither the peace of faith nor the truth of piety collapses. This should be regarded as a loosening rather than a severing of fraternal concord: the practice of charity is relaxed, but hatred is not provoked. [Col. 1631D]

## CHAPTER XXVI — How this peace is pleasing to the angels and terrifying to the demons

This peace is exceedingly marvelous and solemnly worthy of all praise: it is pleasing to angels and terrifying to demons. For the peace of the Church resembles that heavenly and primordial harmony, or the movement of the seven planets running toward the east.

A sweet voice, full of the most pleasing sonority, is produced when the ether, cleft apart, so skillfully and evenly blends the high notes of the sounding planets with the low that a harmony is formed, so sweet that it ineffably surpasses every song of melodious sweetness. Yet our ears are unable to distinguish this movement of the spheres, which resounds with immeasurable force, just as those are found to have written who directed their household eyes into the secrets of the heavens. For, they say, because of long familiarity with that clamor which sounded from our first birth, the sense of our ears has grown dull through daily exposure to the filled ears—or rather, we are less able to hear its melody, just as hearing is battered and dulled in a metalworking shop by the constant blows of the workers. [Col. 1632A]

Perhaps, according to the historical sense, this is related to what the Lord said in Job: “Who will declare the order of the heavens, and who will make the harmony of heaven sleep?”—understand, “if not I?” The harmony of heaven is said to sleep by God’s action when that harmonious movement of the planets, composed by the art of the supreme Craftsman, has a most thunderous sound, but becomes silent to human ears as though through the quiet of sleep. [Col. 1632B]

That the concord of ecclesiastical peace ought to be compared with the concordance of musical voices is proclaimed by the final psalm: “Praise him with the timbrel and the choir; praise him with strings and organ.” Since a choir has the uniting of many voices, the unity of ecclesiastical concord is represented by the choir. The comparison is apt because, just as in a plurality of voices the harmony becomes sweeter when one song is composed not from identical but from different sounds, so in the state of ecclesiastical peace the concord is more beautiful when not everyone performs every office, but each person is recognized as serving the others in distinct and varied duties under one bond of charity. [Col. 1632C]

What sort of concord of the Church would you suppose it to be if everyone wanted to teach, each person to exhort, everyone to give alms, and likewise to perform the other duties enumerated by the Apostle? If all these things existed simultaneously in each individual, the usefulness of them all would perish, since no one would receive from another what he himself did not need. Thus the peace of the Church, which we have argued is contained in the piety of giving and receiving, would vanish.

But now, while you preach doctrine to me in my ignorance and I distribute food to you in your need; while one prays for another in the church, and another petitions for that one in the court, and so with the remaining duties of the same kind, then the pleasing concord of the many faithful is composed like the gentler harmony of many voices.

This is perhaps that music which the Wise Man forbids to be hindered: “Do not hinder music.” And who is understood to hinder it except one who is found to disturb the harmony of fraternal peace? Finally, it is not without reason that we are admonished to sing divine praises in this choir—that is, in the unity of ecclesiastical peace—for no one is believed to praise God, and no one is ever known to work well, if he wanders outside the enclosure of ecclesiastical peace. [Col. 1632D]

From these things, therefore, it is clear how the fellowship of fraternal peace is akin to the concordance of sounds. But how it is like the harmony of the planets could be known by the one who knew why the true sons of God, from whom this concord is composed, are compared with the lights of heaven. The Apostle says of such people: “That you may be blameless and simple sons of God, without reproach in the midst of a crooked and perverse nation, among whom you shine as lights in the world.” [Col. 1633A]

That harmony is produced from the seven planets, and the fellowship of our peace is harmonized through the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit. That orderly movement proceeds toward the east because every fraternity of regular unity looks toward the consummation of the end, Christ, concerning whom it is written: “Behold, the man whose name is Orient.” That heavenly harmony sleeps while, in the tranquility of our peace, spiritual men, withdrawn from the secret tumults of the world, meditate upon the depths of inner wisdom, just as the bride responds to the Bridegroom in the voice of such persons, saying: “I sleep, but my heart is awake.”

Just as that heavenly harmony is imperceptible to us but distinct and sweet to the region above, so worldly people are ignorant of the spiritual integrity of Christian fellowship—for “the animal man does not perceive the things that are of the spirit.” Yet the citizens above, that is, the angels, perceive it distinctly and listen to it with the ears of grateful acceptance, as to a kind of modulation of a sweet song, according to the saying of the Song of Songs addressed to the Church: “You who dwell in the gardens, the friends listen to you,” each saying: “Let me hear your voice.” [Col. 1633B]

By the name “friends,” understand the heavenly spirits, concerning whom mention is made in the Gospel: when the shepherd finds the sheep, “he comes home and calls together his friends and neighbors, saying: Rejoice with me, because I have found my sheep that was lost.”

Finally, just as ecclesiastical concord is pleasing to the angels, so, as we have already suggested, it is fearful to the demons. For just as the battle line of the Roman camps became terrifying to its enemies when the force that had previously fought divided among many ranks later joined its wings and launched an attack against the enemy, so it must likewise be understood to occur in the defenses of the Christian army. If, on some occasion, the divided Church attempts to fight the princes of darkness in separate parts, it is less fearsome and therefore gains victory over the opposing force more slowly. But it becomes terrifying and conquers with the greatest ease if, united in concord, it advances its spiritual armor against the enemy. [Col. 1633C]

The Wise Man, admiring and praising this, says: “Who is she that comes forth like the rising dawn, beautiful as the moon, chosen as the sun, terrifying as an army set in array?” [Col. 1633D]

## CHAPTER XXVII — The signs of both human and ecclesiastical peace

The signs by which both this peace and the peace of Babylon are sought, given, bound, and distinguished are manifold. Some are expressed in words, others in objects, and others in actions.

In words—for example, in greetings, agreements, and oaths; in objects, as with branches of laurel, olive, and palm. Hence etymologists call the palm, as it were, the nourishing one of peace (*pacis alma*). In actions, an older custom is used in the joining of right hands, the piling up of stones, and the striking of the victim that is to be sacrificed.

## CHAPTER XXVIII — The kiss of peace

Among all the signs of peace enacted through actions, however, the chief and most expressive is the kiss—not, I mean, of the foot, forehead, ear, or any other limb, but only of the mouth. Since we express the mind’s intention more clearly through the office of the mouth than through the gesture of the other limbs, we therefore mark the good pleasure of peace more suitably through a kiss of the mouth. [Col. 1634A]

The kiss of the peace of Jerusalem is given to the brothers in the Church not at any hour, but at Mass, after the immolation (sacrifice) and before the reception of the Lord’s body. This kiss is first given by the priest to the ministers, so that from them it may be extended to the others.

In the peace that the priest first gives, the peace of God toward us—namely, our reconciliation, upon which the peace of Jerusalem depends and rests—is signified. The priest offers the kiss of this peace first because the peace of reconciliation has been announced and granted to us through ecclesiastical prelates, as it is written: “Let the mountains receive peace for the people.” [Col. 1634B] Hence one of these mountains, offering this kiss of peace to the Corinthians as it were, says: “He gave us the mystery of reconciliation. Therefore we act as ambassadors for Christ, as though God were exhorting through us. We beseech you on behalf of Christ”—that is, in his place—“be reconciled to God.”

And because this peace was consummated in Christ’s death, the priest rightly offers the kiss of this peace after the immolation, which represents the remembrance of the Lord’s death. But because the kiss that is subsequently communicated to each individual signifies the concord of fraternal peace, it is given before the reception of the sacrament, so that, every hatred having been wiped away, a clean dwelling of the heart may be prepared, into which the Lord may choose to enter and dwell. [Col. 1634C]

This is the kiss that Paul established should be offered in the greetings of the Romans and Corinthians: “Greet one another,” he says, “with a holy kiss”—that is, a sincere one, not a false one, such as was the kiss of Judas, with which he betrayed the Savior, or that of Joab, who, as though caressing Amasa, struck him in the side with a kiss, spilled out his entrails, and killed him.

## CHAPTER XXIX — Those who disturb ecclesiastical and fraternal peace, their sin and punishment

The counterfeiters of this kiss are to be understood especially as schismatics and heretics. They imprint kisses not of a dove but of a raven, not of a lamb but of a wolf, polluting and corrupting the purity of ecclesiastical peace. The former do not hesitate to divide concord with their fissures; the latter tear apart catholic unity through their errors, flattering people for the purpose of seizing and killing them. [Col. 1634D]

This overthrow of peace is said to have been prefigured by the game of Ishmael with Isaac, which the Apostle called persecution: “As then he who was born according to the flesh persecuted him who was born according to the spirit, so it is now.” This persecution is more to be feared than one that advances through open assault. Caution is easier where danger is manifest. The enemy is more to be feared and guarded against when he creeps in secretly, when he advances by hidden approaches under the appearance of peace, inflicting greater wounds precisely because his malignity had been less clearly revealed beforehand. [Col. 1635A]

Seeing such divisions beginning to sprout among the Corinthians, the Apostle said: “I beseech you, brothers, by the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that you all say the same thing, and that there be no schisms among you.” We also recognize such divisions signified in the apostolic net, which Luke records was torn because of the multitude of fish.

The Lord permits such heresies and dissensions to arise so that, while he tests our minds by the discernment of truth, the integrity of approved faith may shine forth more brightly. “There must be heresies,” says the Apostle, “so that those who are approved may be made manifest.” [Col. 1635B]

For many wolves, while the Church is peaceful, are thought to be lambs and sheep; they are believed to be sons and brothers. But when the rest of the Church begins to be disturbed by schisms and heresies, they foam out into public view the wickedness of mind that had been concealed and calculated within them. They openly tear apart certain innocent people and are thought then to go out from the Church, although it is clear that they had never in any way truly belonged to the Church, according to the saying of the Apostle John: “They went out from us, but they were not of us. For if they had been of us, they would certainly have remained with us.”

Conceived in the womb of the mother Church, such people shook her entrails before they were formed, and so were expelled as abortions. “They are alienated,” the oracle of the Psalm reveals, “the sinners are alienated from the womb; they have gone astray from the belly; they have spoken falsehood.” [Col. 1635C]

Finally, this sin, by which ecclesiastical concord is defiled, is so detestable that every other fault, when weighed against the gravity of this crime, is judged light and venial. This crime is worse even than the sin of those who deny Christ. In the latter case there may have been necessity; here the will is often culpable. In other offenses the loss may perhaps affect one soul; here the danger extends to many. And although it may happen that a person sins once, a schismatic is proved to sin every day.

So great is the excess of this transgression that it cannot earn pardon even through blood, as the authoritative statement consecrated by the martyrdom of the eloquent Cyprian declares: “The guilt of discord is inexpiable and grave; it is cleansed neither by blood nor by martyrdom.” [Col. 1635D]

How severe is the punishment of those who, as was said above, disarticulate or even tear apart the concord of the Church itself, is taught us by the new and utterly astonishing death of Dathan, Abiron, and Korah. Because they attempted to create dissension among the people, the earth broke apart at its joints, opened itself into a wider cavity, and swallowed them alive, together with all that belonged to them, with its deep mouth, as the sacred history of Numbers depicts: “The earth split apart beneath their feet, and opening its mouth swallowed them with their tents and all their possessions; and they descended alive into hell, covered by the earth. Fire also went forth from the Lord and killed Korah and the two hundred and fifty men who were offering incense with him.” [Col. 1636A]

The Prophet announces a similar punishment, in the form of a curse, against those who divide the Church: “Let death come upon them, and let them descend alive into hell, for wickedness is in their dwellings, in their midst.” What wickedness? “For,” he says, “they have defiled his covenant”—that is, the speech of sacred Scripture—in such a way that, “divided from the anger of his face,” namely, from the Lord, they raised up against one another the malignities of opposing error, with the divine judgment angry against them: Arius against Sabellius, Eutyches against Nestorius, the predestinarian against Pelagius, and Manichaeus against Carpocrates.

And because they have thus been divided and “have not been pierced”—although they fight against one another with diverse doctrines, they nevertheless attack the concord of Christian unity with concentrated efforts of wickedness—the prophetic saying also applies to this event, in which it is said that Manasseh persecutes Ephraim, Ephraim Manasseh, and both together Judah. [Col. 1636B]

Furthermore, reason makes clear how culpable is the guilt incurred by those who divide not the universal Church, but even the concord of several people or of merely two, or who corrupt the peace of fraternal charity among themselves with the ferment of hatred.

Those who drain away the grace of fraternal love through hatred offer no sacrifice of any good work to God for as long as they are at variance with the charity of their brothers. Therefore it is written of Cain, who did not have peace with his brother because of the zeal of envy: “The Lord did not look upon Cain and his offerings.” And in the Gospel: “If you offer your gift at the altar, and there remember that your brother has something against you, leave your gift there before the altar, and go first to be reconciled to your brother; then come and offer your gift.” [Col. 1636C]

Who would dare to conceal how great a sin oppresses those who sow discord among brothers—namely, whisperers? Since God and the devil oppose one another with the greatest possible contradiction—for just as nothing is more precious to God than the virtue of love, so nothing is more desirable to the devil than the extinction of charity—and since, once charity has been extinguished, the chorus of the other virtues collapses, although charity is known to be the mother of them all, it follows that God abhors the whisperer, who destroys charity by spreading hatred, all the more because in this work of wickedness he serves his adversary, the devil, who is known to love this above all else. [Col. 1636D]

Again, in the Proverbs of Solomon: “There are six things that the Lord hates, and his soul detests a seventh: haughty eyes, a lying tongue, hands that shed innocent blood, a heart devising the worst thoughts, feet swift to run into evil, one who utters lies, a false witness, and one who sows discord among brothers.”

Since “apostate” is the proper name of the ancient enemy, the whisperer, as he is the devil’s heir in sowing discord, is likewise found to be his equal in the name of apostasy. Concerning the apostate angel, when weeds had been sown among the good seed, it is written: “An enemy has done this.” And concerning the whisperer, the Proverbs cry out: “An apostate man, an unworthy man, continually sows quarrels.” [Col. 1637A]

The chief remedy against this evil will be to exclude such a sower of weeds from the fellowship of the brothers as quickly as possible: “When the wood fails,” says Solomon, “the fire is extinguished, and when the whisperer is removed, quarrels cease.”

How great a punishment is being prepared for such people, the same Wise Man explained in a slight word but with a weighty sentence, when he said: “The wicked man always seeks quarrels; but a cruel angel will be sent against him.” [Col. 1637B]

## CHAPTER XXX — How the peace of the present Church is not perfect

From what has been covered in the immediately preceding chapter, it is now possible to see what things are accustomed to profane the concord both of the universal Church and of the particular fellowship in Christ. Since the tranquility of ecclesiastical peace is disturbed by so many assaults, although in comparison with the peace of Babylon it is in some way blessed, it is nevertheless not absolutely pleasing, blessed, or perfect. So many snares are stretched out against it, so many scandals placed in its way, so many ambushes, and so many barking calumnies, as is commonly said in the Proverbs: “You will walk in the midst of snares, and you will tread upon the weapons of those who suffer.” [Col. 1637C] And again, after a little: “Beware for yourself, and attend carefully to your hearing, because you walk with your overthrow.”

How great, indeed, is the fear of the mother Church in this peace! How great the sorrow over those who depart, and the fear concerning those who are about to depart!

Moreover, this adds to the accumulation of difficulties: “The life of man upon earth is warfare,” certainly for those who, instructed for various battles, wage continual war against the powers of the air. All these things make this peace not only troubled but also fruitful.

## CHAPTER XXXI — The most perfect peace of the Jerusalem above

Another peace must therefore be awaited and longed for: I mean the Jerusalem not of this world, which journeys on the way, but that which reigns in the homeland, where neither attack from outside nor sedition within is feared. [Col. 1637D]

Whatever takes place in the peace of the present Church is referred to the peace of that Jerusalem. In this peace are the merits; in that one the fruit of the merits is stored up.

The God-fearing David desired a vision of this peace when he said: “May you see your children’s children; peace upon Israel.” Peter also desired it for believers, saying: “May grace and peace be fulfilled for you.” And the psalm, singing the praises of the city above, proclaimed concerning it: “He has placed peace within your borders.” Concerning it the Wise Man also said, speaking of the martyrs: “They seemed to the eyes of fools to die, but they are in peace.” David likewise promises it to the meek, saying: “The meek shall inherit the earth, and shall delight in the abundance of peace.” [Col. 1638A]

The condition of this peace is also understood to be signified by what the Lord promises to Zion: “The uncircumcised and unclean shall no longer pass through you.” And again through Joel: “Jerusalem shall be holy, and strangers shall no longer pass through it.”

The Gospel rightly also marks this state of peace: after the Lord’s resurrection, it enclosed many large fish, and yet the net could in no way be torn. The words of blessed Job do not differ from these testimonies: “There the wicked cease from tumult, and there those weary in strength rest; and those once bound rest together without harassment and do not hear the voice of the taskmaster. Small and great are there, and the servant is free from his master.” [Col. 1638B]

How perfect and blessed, therefore, is the peace of that Jerusalem, where there is freedom without domination, fellowship without dissension, rest without anxiety, undivided unanimity, fearless security, and undisturbed tranquility! There joy, perpetual and most complete, is possessed without fear. No one will be there for whom it is necessary to grieve; no one enters concerning whom it would be appropriate to doubt or be afraid.

For immeasurable spaces lie between the elect and the reprobate, with a great chasm fixed in the middle. Just as the misery of the latter cannot be cleansed through the former, so the happiness of the former cannot be polluted through the latter.

We have arranged these reflections on the good of peace not according to the greatness of the subject, but according to the capacity of our talent. Therefore, bringing the course of the proposed treatise to a halt at these boundaries, let us now impress a seal upon the writing and silence upon the mouth. [Col. 1638C]

[Note: The following document is an addendum to the *Constitutiones* of William of Hirsau, beginning in column 1147 of this volume.]

[Col. 1639]

## Preface of Saint William, Abbot of Hirsau, to his Astronomical Work

[Note: It survives in a nearly contemporary manuscript from Emmeram, but is mutilated toward the end.]

*(Around the year 1073.)*

[Edited by the Rev. Fr. Bernard Pez, *Newest Treasury of Anecdotes*, vol. V, part I, p. 259.]

[Col. 1639A]

One day, after the sacred office had been completed, I withdrew to a more secluded place for the sake of the quiet I desired. There I could place myself before the eyes of my mind and examine, with something like judicial strictness, the excesses of my miserable life.

When I had immediately examined its condition, I discovered in myself many things deserving of reproach, many things most worthy of sorrow and mourning, and many things plainly crooked and harsh, less ordered according to the way of the Lord. Among these, one particular increase of grief [or: “reason for grief”; the reading is uncertain] came to mind, somewhat heavier than the other burdens of my passions: that, compelled by I know not what force of the violent divine will, I had devoted myself entirely to the whole quadrivium, and especially to the study of astronomy.

In the meantime, while I had proposed to labor alone in this discipline, I was disturbed by the unexpected visits of certain people, even some most learned. [Col. 1639B] And while I endeavored to obey each of them when they demanded that I introduce them to the art itself, I saw that I had been cast down not only from the height of heavenly contemplation but also from the proper daily degree of service to God.

As I anxiously turned these matters over in my mind, my dearest and very special friend O [another hand notes: “Otochus”] arrived. Seeing me with the lively affection customary to him, he immediately asked the cause of my sadness.

Fearing to confess the truth to him—because he himself had first betrayed my secrecy by bringing the public occupation with the aforementioned art upon me, and, being bound to me by the strongest intimate affection, had kindled that occupation with a powerful flame—I attempted to conceal the matter from him through a kind of circumlocution and disguise. [Col. 1639C]

But because it is difficult to hide the truth of a matter from a wise man by a fabricated likeness, suddenly devised contrary to the heart’s abundance, he immediately perceived it, accused me of deception, and began, with friendly persistence, to ask what was troubling me. In order not to delay matters with many words, the customary force of his affection finally drew the truth from me.

When he learned the matter, he immediately smiled and said:

“In this wavering of yours, dearest friend, I silently consider how the ancient serpent, always wandering about in order to infect all the gifts of heavenly grace with the poisons of envy, has crept up to violate this gift also, which has been divinely granted to us.

For a long time he had perceived that I was seeking a suitable opportunity to learn, through the most delightful exchange, those marvelous things in this art that God has revealed to you and that human subtlety has so far been unable to discover. I wished to commit them all to writing and thus make them available for the common use of students.

Against the intention of this purpose, however, he has now, through his cunning, forestalled me, who have only now come here after you, wishing under the pretext of religion to suggest to your innocence that you would rather bury the Lord’s money in the earth than hand it over to be multiplied for human advancement. [Col. 1640A]

Come, then, and pass beyond the winding track of his error with manly steadfastness; let us often undertake the course of our proposed dialogue. If you order me to do so, I will set it forth in writing by divine grace, so that it may be completed today with God between us. In this way I will both satisfy the expectation of my long-standing desire and make an unobstructed way for the theoretical study to which you are wholly devoted.

For since you have already embodied those truly marvelous inventions of yours in demonstrative instruments, if you also cause them to be expressed in writing, you will earn the greatest gratitude of students and a deservedly welcome pardon from them for the sake of holy quiet.” [Col. 1640B]

“I remember,” I replied, “dearest brother, that you previously gave me this salutary advice. But because the present age, amid countless storms of vices, suffers greatly from envy, I confess that I feared that, if such great matters—left untouched or treated and abandoned in doubt by ancient philosophers because of their difficulty, or treated and examined but concluded with insufficiently cautious proof—were brought forth under the person of my own unworthiness, they might be a source of disgust rather than study to certain people, and might rashly be judged by them more corrupt than true. [Col. 1640C]

This is especially so since they assert that we monks are permitted no liberal science beyond the Psalter.” [Col. 1641A]

Then he said:

“Why, he said, do you make any mention at all of those who hold that nothing has authority for the enemies of Christ’s cross except what they themselves determine, wishing to obscure the light of our profession, which has arisen from the radiance of the most holy Fathers, by the murky alteration of their doctrine? For if mere knowledge of the Psalms is sufficient for us, how, I ask, shall we be able to understand the Old and New Testament, the *Life of the Fathers*, the *Conferences of the Fathers*, Gregory’s *Dialogues*, and the other books which, by the command of Saint Benedict, are to be read throughout the annual cycle?

“Did not that supreme planter of the Church after the apostles, Jerome, in [Col. 1641B] repeatedly use these same disciplines in his homilies and expositions, and smelt the ore of this vein into the purest mass of divine eloquence? If that sweet-voiced trumpeter of the heavenly word, Gregory, untrained in the dialectical art, had been ignorant of the soul’s threefold power in the universal nature of things, what equally delightful exposition would he have sounded forth on that Gospel passage: ‘Go into all the world and preach the Gospel to every creature’? In explaining it, he says:

“‘There are stones, but they neither live nor feel. There are shrubs: they do live, but they do not feel. There are irrational animals: they live and feel, but they do not discern. There are angels: they live, feel, and discern. But the human being possesses something of every creature. For he shares being with stones, life with plants, sensation with animals, and understanding with angels. [Col. 1641C] If, then, the human being shares something with every creature, in a certain respect every creature is human. Therefore the Gospel is preached to every creature when it is preached to the human being alone.’

“Certainly—and rightly—it is fitting for us to investigate secular philosophy, to seek gold in the mud, to despoil Egypt, and to pluck fragrant fruits from thorns, provided that we transfer the ore excavated there to the most purified treasure of sacred eloquence, and plant the slips taken from there among the spice-bearing trees of the fertile field that the Lord has blessed, arranging them in proper order. And if the profane madness of those whom you mention goes so far that they reject the sacred authority of such great men merely because they were monks, then for a still stronger reason let us close their mouths [Col. 1641D], so that the deceitful lips which speak in pride and abuse against justice may become completely mute.”

It is plainly evident to all uneducated Catholics that, with the exception of the Son of Man, who is above all, no one in the whole human race ever was or will be holier than that first-formed man, Adam—he who, before the transgression, naturally knew the good and did not know evil. Indeed, he possessed such great holiness that, after he had undoubtedly been condemned for his fault to this exile in the present world, and the purity innate in his mind began to be corrupted by the wickedness of his descendants, the merciful Maker, grieving that his creation was being degraded from the original dignity of divine reason, summoned the human race to recover, by an inherited strength of soul, the sublimity of the heavenly breath of life and the likeness of God: first through the patriarchs, then through the Law and the prophets, and finally through his own Son [Col. 1642A], his Gospel, his signs and wonders, the words and examples of his disciples, and those of all the teachers of the Church.

Moreover, not only is it permitted us to imitate the holiness innate in him, but we must also follow, as far as we can, his intellectual acuity in natural science. Indeed, all those who live actively and have received from the Lord the talent of intelligence are not permitted to abstain from this exercise.

Let us see whether the discipline under discussion was absent from the fullness of his wisdom. In the *Book of the Conferences*, which is held in the highest authority, it is written:

“‘[Col. 1642B] Human beings fell away from that true discipline of natural philosophy which that first man, who immediately followed the constitution of all natures, was able clearly to attain and transmit to his descendants by a sure method of reasoning. For he had seen the infancy of the world itself, still tender and in a certain sense palpitating, and still crude. And into him there had been infused, by that divine breathing, not only such fullness of wisdom but also such grace of prophecy that he could discern not only the rages and poisons of beasts and serpents of every kind, but also the powers of herbs and trees and the natures of stones, and could distinguish the changes of times not yet experienced. Thus he was able effectively to say:

“‘“The Lord has given me true knowledge of the things that exist, so that I might know the arrangement of the world, the powers of the elements, [Col. 1642C] the beginning, end, and middle of times, the changes of vicissitudes and the divisions of times, the courses of years and the arrangements of the stars, the natures of animals and the ferocities of beasts, the force of spirits and the constitution of human beings, the varieties of trees and the powers of roots; and whatever things are hidden I have learned readily.”’

“Behold, from what a limpid fountain we are drawn, even against our will, by natural intelligence, as though through certain channels, toward the whole discipline of the quadrivium! Therefore, with all who speak maliciously thoroughly confounded, let us, in the name of him who numbers the multitude of the stars and calls them all by name, traverse our astronomy along the course of our proposed conversational dialogue.”

[Col. 1642D] Then I said:

“By your most powerful arguments, dearest brother, you have both encouraged me against my opponents and bound me so forcefully that I dare no longer resist your commands. But I obey on this condition: since I am still to be heavily occupied with diagrams and with the many instruments belonging to this subject, you should set down and complete our discussion in writing, as you promised, and so forth.””

## Here Begins the Work

Accordingly, the order of our discoveries begins from the solstices and equinoxes, because, while still ignorant of the natural limit of human beings, I confess that much, and so forth.
