**To be baptized for the dead:** what it means, 80, 81.

**The baptized:** are called holy by the Apostle, 163.

**Basilia:** wife of Hugh of Gournay, a. 5.

**Beatitude:** only observance of God’s commandments is necessary for it, 57. Why eternal blessedness is called a lot, 163.

**Bec**, v. 2.

**Bec:** Blessed Lanfranc foretells the destruction of its dormitory, v. 5. Larger buildings are constructed on Blessed Lanfranc’s advice, v. 6. The monks of Bec inhabit a new church, v. 9. Description of the same monastery, v. 9. Consecration of the church, v. 10. The origin and etymology of Bec, a. 1, 35 and 33. Why Bec grew so greatly, a. 1, 35. It was in extreme poverty, a. 1, 35. God was its principal founder, a. 1, 35. A church was built in honor of the Blessed Virgin, a. 1, 35. Another monastery was built, a. 1, 35. Form of its foundation, 331. Many nobles flocked there and devoted themselves to monastic life, a. 2. The monastery of Saint Ebrulf was given to Bec, a. 2. The Blessed Virgin sits in the church, and Saints Peter and Paul chant Matins, a. 3. The consecration of the same church was carried out by Blessed Lanfranc, in the presence of several bishops, a. 4, 38. Three noble matrons of Bec devoted themselves to God, a. 5. They died on three different Sundays, a. 5. The priories paid money to the same monastery as a sign of subjection, a. 7. A second dedication of the same church, a. 9. After the church had been largely destroyed, it was restored, a. 11. A new dormitory was built, a. 11. A general chapter was held at Bec, a. 11 and a. 13, 14. Saint Louis ate in the refectory at Bec and confirmed its immunities, a. 12. The abbey was burned, a. 12. Privileges of the supreme pontiffs for restoring the abbey, a. 12. A tower collapsed, and its fall inflicted enormous damage on the monastery, a. 13. The right of patronage over the priories belongs to the abbot, a. 13. Form of the abbots’ oath, a. 13. What is to be noted in the clause “By divine permission,” a. 13. When the men of Bec go outside, they are permitted to wear cloaks, while secular footwear—shoes fastened with straps—is forbidden, a. 14. After they have remained six years in the priories, they are compelled to return, a. 14. Statutes of the general chapter, a. 14. They wear white garments, a. 15. Statutes from Pope Benedict’s bull concerning students, a. 15. Monks teach various sciences, a. 15. The sum of money exacted by King Philip is paid by the men of Bec, a. 15. The church is dedicated for a third time, a. 16. The monastery is largely destroyed and fortifications are built against English incursions, a. 17. Which first abbot obtained pontifical insignia, a. 18. Bec of Herluin, a. 19. The privilege of the abbot of Bec, by which he is granted power to use pontifical insignia, bless chalices and ornaments, etc., and confer the tonsure on his monks, a. 19. A strongly fortified stronghold, a. 20. The monks suffer many calamities, a. 21 and following. The men of Bec, studying literature in Paris, surpass others in learning, a. 25. The first commendatory abbot was John Boucart, bishop, a. 28. Profession before the archbishop of Rouen, a. 14. The extreme austerity of the monks of Bec, a. 33. Many noble and learned men were monks even in the time of Abbot William, a. 44. Privileges granted by the archbishop of Rouen and confirmed by the supreme pontiffs, 332 and following.

**Bede:** teacher of the English, 301. He composed a history of the English, 301. At the age of seven he was given to the monastery of Wearmouth under the discipline of Blessed Benedict Biscop, 341. For more, see the *Life of Bede*, 341. Why he is called “Venerable,” 341. Contemporary authors did not use this title at all, 341. He was a Benedictine monk, 343. In his monastery the cenobites always professed the Benedictine Rule, 343.

**Priory of Beaumont:** given to Bec by Roger of Beaumont, a. 7. Controversy over the same priory between the clerics of Exmes and the men of Bec, a. 7. This priory was wrongly obtained by Louis of Flers, a. 20.

**To bless:** Abbot William refused to do so by hand, asserting that it belonged solely to a bishop, a. 45.

**Benedict (Saint):** appears to William Crispin and protects him from a demon, a. 55. Who truly observes his Rule, 253. It is called the Rule of monks, 309. Feast of the translation of Saint Benedict, 272. The Rule is to be read at the beginning of Lent, 259. It is shown that Blessed Augustine introduced the Rule of Saint Benedict into England, 341 and following. The Benedictines are the apostles of the English, 342, 343. The Benedictines are distinguished for holiness and learning, 346. They are apostles, 346. What in the Benedictine order may sometimes be changed and what may not, 253 and following. Several bishops in England, although they held that dignity, were bound by the laws of the Rule, 346. The Benedictine Rule was customarily called the Holy Rule, the Order, the Rule, and the Holy Order, 363. It is proved that the Rule of Saint Benedict was observed throughout Gaul before Charlemagne and Louis the Pious, 363 and following. In Charlemagne’s time the monks neglected observance of the Rule, 364. When the Rule of Saint Benedict is carefully observed by monks, the world is spared harmful contagions through their prayers, 367. See also Rule.

**Benedict (Saint) Biscop:** professed the Benedictine Rule, 343.

**Bull of Pope Benedict concerning students:** its observance is prescribed in the monastery of Bec, a. 15.

**Monastery of Saint Benedict:** see Floriacum.

**Benedict Haestenus**, 360.

**Ecclesiastical benefice:** no one should sell or buy it, v. 13.

**Vacancies of benefices:** the pope tries to obtain them, but the king opposes him, a. 21.

**Berengar:** heresiarch, v. 4. His heresy, v. 4 and v. 5, and a. 2. Condemned by Leo at the Council of Vercelli, v. 4 and 234. At the Council of Tours under Victor II he abjured the heresy, 234 and a. 107. Summoned by Pope Nicholas II to the Roman Council, he abjured the heresy before everyone and issued a confession of faith, a. 107 and 232. He returned to his vomit, 232. Blessed Lanfranc replied to his writings, 231 and 232. What Fulbert of Chartres, dying, thought of Berengar, 374. Berengar assailed Cardinal Humbert with insults, and likewise the Roman Church, 232, 242. He was a deacon of the Church of Angers, 242. His profession of faith, 242. His second profession, 233. He travelled here and there through Normandy to infect everyone with the poison of his heresy, a. 106. He was repulsed by Henry, duke of Normandy, a. 106. Summary of the history of his heresy, a. 106. An assembly was summoned at Brionne to refute Berengar, a. 106. Several Benedictines wrote against Berengar, 344. His homeland, character, studies, etc., a. 21, 68, 72, 250. His final words at the point of death, 374.

**Bernard:** abbot of Mont Saint-Michel, formerly a monk of Bec, a. 7.

**Bertha:** queen of England, descended from the kings of the Franks, a. 59. Learned in sacred letters, 61 and a. 63. Bishop Liudhard served as her chaplain, a. 61. Praised by Blessed Gregory, a. 63. She bestowed many benefits on Blessed Augustine, a. 63.

**Berthefridus:** bishop of Amiens; grants a privilege to the monastery of Corbie so that the Rule of Saints Benedict and Columbanus may be observed, 365.

**Bientia (Saint):** her body at Mellent, a. 10.

**Blasius (Saint):** part of his head is in the monastery of Bec, a. 25.

**Blasphemers:** who they are, 197.

**Blasphemy:** what it is, 148. Blasphemy against the Holy Spirit is the final and greatest of all crimes, 381.

**Temporal goods:** Christ does not prohibit providing for them, 84.

**Pope Boniface IV**, 344.

**Good and evil:** are immediate opposites in the Christian religion, 22.

**The fool’s accuser of the good**, 116.

**One who wishes to do good:** must drive out evil, 23.

**Boso:** fourth abbot of Bec, a. 6. Outstanding in learning and holiness, a. 6. His life, a. 47. Homeland and parents, a. 47. He became a monk together with two brothers, a. 47. Most learned, a. 47. Blessed Anselm drove from his mind the temptation by which he was being grievously oppressed, a. 47. He was carefully instructed by the same saint, a. 47. By order of Blessed Anselm he attended a council in his place, a. 47. He lived for some time in England with the same saint, a. 47. He loved Boso most devotedly, a. 47. He disputed with him in the book *Why God Became Man*, a. 47. He shone with every virtue, a. 47. Everyone admired his wisdom, a. 48. He was unwillingly elected abbot, a. 48. He refused to declare himself the king’s client, a. 48. His virtues are enumerated, a. 49. What he did when his commands were rejected, a. 49. He was severely afflicted by various illnesses, a. 50. Endowed with exceptional patience, a. 50. He died, a. 7 and 50.

**Brandanus (Saint):** altar, a. 16.

**Assembly of Brionne**, a. 106.

**Britons:** expelled from England, 314.

**Bruno:** bishop of Angers, accused of Berengarian heresy, a. 107.

**Bruno (Saint):** why he withdrew into the wilderness, 361.

**Burneville:** inheritance of Blessed Herluin, a. 1.

He is instructed in letters and, then endowed with the sciences, traveled through Gaul with the scholars and taught in the city of Avranches, v. 2 and a. 2. He taught the liberal arts and philosophy at Bec, a. 53. He falls among robbers, v. 2 and a. 2. He goes to Bec and becomes a monk there, v. 2 and a. 2. His observance of the Rule, v. 3. How humble he was, v. 3. He did not read the lesson in choir until he had recited it before the cantor, v. 3. His fame spreads throughout the world, v. 3. His notable obedience when he read in the refectory, v. 3. The uneducated monks envy him, v. 3. He plans to flee in order to lead an eremitical life but is prevented by divine intervention, v. 3. He is appointed chief counselor by Duke William, although he nevertheless becomes estranged from the duke’s will, v. 3 and a. 3. Why, a. 3. He is ordered to leave Normandy, and the monks of Bec are consequently afflicted with great sorrow, a. 3. He visits the duke and, after addressing him with his customary eloquence, is restored to favor, a. 3. He went to Rome on account of the duke’s unlawful marriage and the case of Berengarius, a. 3. After opening the letters that Berengarius had sent to him, he is suspected of heresy, v. 5. At the command of Pope Leo IX he clears himself at the Roman council, v. 5 and 234. He refutes and convicts Berengarius both by arguments and by writings, v. 5 and a. 2. He wrote against him more lucidly and remarkably than anyone else, 344, 345. He obtains from Pope Nicholas II a dispensation for the marriage of Duke William, 344, 345. He establishes schools at Bec and teaches publicly, v. 6. Whatever he received from the students, he gave to Blessed Herluinus, v. 6. Many nobles flock to him, etc., v. 6 and a. 53. He was tutor to the nephews of Pope Alexander, and even to the pope himself, 300. Through his work and industry the monastery of Bec is built, v. 6 and a. 53. He becomes abbot of Caen, v. 6, 7 and a. 3. Duke William used his counsel in acquiring England, a. 3. He is extolled with praises, a. 3. A most vigorous opponent of heresies, a. 3. The prelates of the Church held his wisdom and learning in the highest regard, a. 3. The Roman pontiffs and other prelates of the Church attempted to retain him, a. 3, 300, 357. He was most prudent, 337. His life was a perfectly straight rule of life, 337. He delighted in rebukes, 307.

[Col. 1661] He refuses the archbishopric of Rouen, v. 7. He went to Rome for the fourth time so that Pope Alexander might assent to John’s election as archbishop of Rouen; from Alexander he received the pallium to bring to John, v. 7. He is appointed archbishop of Canterbury, v. 7 and a. 4. How much he did to avoid that burden: at last, at the command of Blessed Herluinus and of the supreme pontiff and his legates, he yielded unwillingly, a. 4 and v. 11, and 299, 336. How highly the king regarded him, 336. He writes to Pope Alexander asking to be freed from the episcopal burden, 299. He sends Alexander the little book against Berengarius that he had published while abbot of Caen, 303. Why that little book is not counted among the letters, 344. He enriched the monastery of Bec, v. 8 and a. 36. He was an adviser to Blessed Herluinus, a. 36. He furnished the library, a. 36. Why he so strongly refused the archbishopric, a. 36. At last he gives his consent, a. 36. How many labors he endured in reforming the English Church, v. 8, 336. Papal legate, v. 9. His disciples, v. 9. His humility before consecrating the Church of Bec, v. 9. He consecrates it, v. 10. He builds the Church of Canterbury, the monks’ workshops, etc., v. 10. He enriches the aforementioned church with precious ornaments, v. 10. He restores everything, v. 10. He builds two poorhouses (ptochotrophia): one for men and the other for women, v. 10. He resists Odo, who had occupied the lands of the Church of Canterbury, v. 10 and 361. He recalls those lands to the jurisdiction of the Church, v. 10. He summons a council at which the question of the primacy of the Church of Canterbury over York is chiefly discussed, v. 11. He is honored beyond custom by Pope Alexander, who rises when Lanfranc comes to him, v. 11 and 302, 336. He is given a double pallium, 336. In the presence of the supreme pontiff, he modestly rebukes Thomas of York, who was contending over the primacy, v. 12. The pope decrees that this controversy should be debated in an English council, v. 12. He informs Pope Alexander about what was done in the synod, v. 13 and 301. He also writes letters about the same matter to Hildebrand, 301. He presides over the council held at London, 301. He supports the monks against the king and bishops so that they will not be expelled from the cathedral churches, 345. His noble saying against a certain flatterer of the king, v. 14. He restores the Church of Rochester and appoints Hernostus bishop, v. 14. He restores the abbey of St. Alban, v. 14. Blessed Dunstan assisted him in difficult matters, v. 39. He frees a deacon from demonic bondage, v. 15. In the king’s absence he is virtually viceroy in England, v. 15 and 359. This is in no way contrary to his holiness, 359. In the midst of the greatest wealth he singularly cultivated poverty, 359. At his consecration a portent was found above his head, 359. He was outstanding in distributing alms, 359. He doubts whether Blessed Ælfheah should be honored as a martyr, v. 16. Because Blessed Anselm found a ring on his bed, Blessed Lanfranc predicts that Anselm would become archbishop after him, v. 16. Restorer of the Christian religion and monastic discipline, etc., v. 16. He governed the Church of Canterbury for eighteen years, a. 4. He closed his final day, a. 4 and a. 5. Evidence of his holiness, a. 5. He refutes the crimes attributed to him by Gregory, 348. He protects the rights of his own Church but does not wish to usurp those of another, 315. St. Anselm and Peter Lombard mention his commentaries on the Epistles of Blessed Paul, 6. He restores the monastery of St. Ebrulfus, a. 2. Builder of the Church of Bec, a. 4. He consecrates that same church, a. 4. His little book against Berengarius, 232 and following. He takes part in the Council of Vercelli, 234. He prefers to be a Catholic simpleton rather than a learned and witty courtier who is a heretic, 235. He uses dialectical art unwillingly in matters concerning the faith, 236. Alexander calls him “father of his country,” 340. He wrote decretal letters, 331. The bishops of England call him their father and teacher, 368. He went to Rome for the fourth time, 372. ## The Letters of Blessed Lanfranc

Letter I: To Alexander II, Roman pontiff. He asks that the episcopal burden, which he had accepted under the compulsion of the pope’s command above all, be ordered to be removed from his shoulders; and he excuses himself for not having come to Rome at the appointed time, 515.

Letter II: To the same. Concerning Bishop Herman, who, exhausted by old age and prolonged illness, now seems unequal to the burden; and concerning the bishop of Lichfield, who resigned the episcopate—whether he ought to permit the consecration of the man who has been substituted in his place, 515.

Letter III: To the same. He sets forth the controversy of the church of York against Canterbury: how it was treated and concluded at the assembly at Winchester; and, sending a copy of the agreement that had been written down and sent to him, he asks the pope to grant an apostolic privilege. He then recalls the pontiff’s benefits toward him and sends the letter to Berengar that the pontiff had requested, 516.

Letter IV: Pope Alexander II to Lanfranc. He confirms the decrees of his predecessors, allowing monks to hold cathedral churches, against those who were attempting to drive monks out at Canterbury and elsewhere and introduce clerics, 516.

Letter V: Lanfranc to Hildebrand, archdeacon of the Roman Church. After speaking of his goodwill toward him, he explains that the York controversy has been settled and that an account of what happened has been sent to the apostolic see, which he wishes Hildebrand to read, 517.

Letter VI: Hildebrand to Lanfranc. He explains that the pallium requested by Lanfranc’s legates was not sent because it is not customary to send it to absent persons. It is therefore necessary that Lanfranc come to Rome, 517.

Letter VII: William the Conqueror to Pope Gregory. The king has been admonished by the legate concerning the oath of fidelity to the pontiff and the money to be sent to Rome. He agrees concerning the money; concerning the fidelity, he refuses because it is unprecedented, 517.

Letter VIII: Lanfranc to Gregory VII. He clears himself of the charge made by the pontiff that, after obtaining the episcopate, he loved him and the Roman Church less than he had formerly done. He says that, on the contrary, the pontiff’s love seems more remiss toward him. He states that he advised the king concerning what the pontiff had suggested through the legate, but did not persuade him, 517.

Letter IX: To Thomas, archbishop of York. Concerning a penitent guilty of three homicides, and concerning the letters of that bishop containing warnings, 517.

Letter X: Thomas to the same. Concerning what judgment should be made about those who wish to leave their wives on account of fornication and join themselves to other women, and what should be done concerning a man who denies that he betrothed the woman who is thought to be his wife, 518.

Letter XI: Thomas, archbishop of York, to Lanfranc. He asks him to send to York the bishops of Worcester and Dorchester to consecrate Orchad, promising that he will claim no right over them on that account, 518.

Letter XII: Lanfranc to Wulfstan, bishop of Worcester, and Peter, bishop of Chester. He asks them to travel to York to consecrate Orchad, the bishop, with Archbishop Thomas; and, so that they may be secure, he sends them Thomas’s letters, in which Thomas guarantees that neither he nor his successors will thereby acquire any right over their churches, 519.

Letter XIII: To John, archbishop of the Normans. Taking occasion from his letter, he discusses certain rites concerning the dedication of churches and the ordination of subdeacons, 521.

Letter XIV: To John, archbishop of Rouen. He consoles him concerning the dishonor inflicted on him by his own people; he suggests what sort of vengeance he ought to undertake and promises to make sure that he writes to the king about the matter as he ought, 521.

Letter XV: To the same. He praises his patience under the injury he has received. He has asked the king by letter, concerning the perpetrators of the crime, to take vengeance. He also approves what John had reported concerning a vision of a certain monk and concerning another man forbidden a common burial, 522.

Letter XVI: To John, archbishop of the Normans. He excuses his prolonged silence and wishes that mutual and inviolable concord may exist between them, 523.

Letter XVII: To John, archbishop of Rouen. He shows that it is false that he was said to criticize John’s actions. As for Robert Pultrell, who had departed without John’s permission, Lanfranc explains that he received him with honor because Robert had brought a letter of recommendation from John. He also discusses what answer he should give concerning the demand for an oath of fidelity from the archdeacons and concerning his conversation with the king, 524.

Letter XVIII: To Osbern, bishop. He explains that he is keeping Abbot Baldwin with him, preventing Baldwin from attending Richard’s court; he therefore asks that Baldwin be excused and that the case be postponed, 525.

Letter XIX: To Herfast, fellow bishop. He asks him to absolve the clerics of Abbot Baldwin from excommunication until Lanfranc himself, after hearing both sides, settles the dispute, 525.

Letter XX: Pope Gregory VII to Lanfranc. He asks him to restrain Bishop Arfast so that he does not trouble Abbot Baldwin, and to ask the king not to do so either. If Arfast refuses, he is to come with the abbot to the apostolic see to settle the disputes, 526.

Letter XXI: Lanfranc to Herfast, fellow bishop. Concerning how he should conduct himself toward a man whom Lanfranc himself had promoted to the diaconate although he had not yet been initiated into any orders and had a wife, 526.

Letter XXII: To the same. Concerning the penance of a cleric who had irregularly assumed the priestly order, 526.

Letter XXIII: To Bishop Herbert. He asks him to stop Berard the cleric from quarreling; and, because Berard had despised Herbert’s letters, to read the sacred canons, from which he may learn what reverence is owed to metropolitans. Finally, he asks him to remove an unruly monk entirely from his company, 527.

Letter XXIV: To Maurice, bishop of London. He designates the day on which he will confer the priestly rank upon the elected bishop; at the same time he answers his questions concerning a man who died among his captors, a conversation with the king, and a cleric who had come into his episcopate without the required observances, 528.

Letter XXV: To Walcher, fellow bishop. After the Britons have been expelled, all is peaceful. The Danes are certainly approaching; therefore he should remain vigilant and see that his castle is fortified with men and weapons, 528.

Letter XXVI: To the same. He excuses himself for not having sent a warning and answers concerning a priest who had been raised in the monks’ cloister without a blessing: he cannot return to the world, 529.

Letter XXVII: To Stigand, bishop of Chichester. He orders him to have the monies exacted by his archdeacons from the clerics of the villages of the church of Canterbury that lie in his diocese restored. Henceforth they are neither to attend the synod of any bishop nor answer to anyone nor pay anything except what has been established for chrism, 529.

Letter XXVIII: To the same. He asks him to allow the woman concerning whose case the pope had ordered Lanfranc to hear judgment to remain peacefully with her husband until they meet and settle the matter, 530.

[Col. 1676]

Letter XXIX: To Robert, bishop of Chichester. In his own name and that of the king, he orders him immediately to restore what had been violently taken from the monastery of Coventry, recounting one by one the unworthy ways in which he had afflicted them, 530.

Letter XXX: To Manasses, archbishop of Reims. At the command of the supreme pontiff, he warns the archbishop of Reims to see that the bearer of the letter receives back the property unjustly taken from him at Rosnay, 531.

Letter XXXI: To Bishop Maurice. He asks him to go to Bertinga and settle the dispute between the abbess and the prior, 531.

Letter XXXII: To Bishop Geoffrey. Concerning professed nuns or those offered to the altar, and concerning those who are neither professed nor offered, or who have fled to the monastery not out of love of religion, 531.

Letter XXXIII: To Domnald, bishop of Ireland. He teaches that for infants not yet possessing the use of reason, reception of the Eucharist is by no means necessary for salvation; but he declines, as unworthy of a bishop, to resolve questions concerning secular literature, 532.

Letter XXXIV: To William, king of the English. He advises the king not to cross the sea. He reports that Count Rodulf and his army have been put to flight and that the king’s soldiers are pursuing them, 533.

Letter XXXV: To the same. He congratulates him on the recovery of the castle of Norwich after the Britons had been expelled, and on peace being restored to all England, 534.

Letter XXXVI: The clergy and people of the church of Dublin to Lanfranc. They ask that Patrick, the priest whom they have elected, be ordained bishop of the church of Dublin, 534.

Letter XXXVII: Lanfranc to Gothric, king of Ireland. He informs the king that he has consecrated Patrick bishop and urges him to correct the practices concerning marriage that are said to be wicked, and to make willing use of Patrick’s counsel, 535.

Letter XXXVIII: To Terdelvacus, king of Ireland. He praises the king on the basis of what he had learned from Patrick and advises him, in order to eradicate certain depraved customs, to order an assembly of bishops and others and to take part in it himself, 536.

Letter XXXIX: To Count Roger. In the king’s name he commends the guarding of the castles and sets before him the example of his father, who had served faithfully. He also writes concerning the king’s suspension, until his return, of the judgments of the viscounts, 537.

Letter XL: To the same. He asks him to abstain from perjury and fraud and to imitate his father’s fidelity toward the king and others, 537.

Letter XLI: To the same. He cannot be released from the excommunication with which Lanfranc had bound him unless he implores the king’s mercy; Lanfranc promises to assist him in obtaining it, 538.

Letter XLII: To Abbot B . . . He asks him, for the sake of the bearer of the letter, to grant pardon in Lanfranc’s case, 539.

Letter XLIII: To Father Anselm. He rejoices and gives thanks that his brother’s son has been received by them with greater freedom, while also indicating what he wishes to be observed concerning him, 539.

Letter XLIV: Anselm’s brother to Lanfranc. He replies to Lanfranc’s recent letter and in turn commends Maurice, who is suffering from an illness of the head, 540.

Letter XLV: To Gondulf. He especially commends his brother’s son to him so that Gondulf may instruct him, and he sends a cross with relics, 540.

Letter XLVI: To the same. He consoles him in illness and sends a medicine for him to use, 541.

Letter XLVII: To Lanfranc and Guido, brothers. He gives salutary admonitions to his nephew and former friend, now his brother in the monastery. Privately he forgives his nephew for not having observed the things he had commanded, 542.

Letter XLVIII: To Father William. He asks him to appoint Ernust prior; if anything prevents this, he suggests other courses that may be followed, 542.

Letter XLIX: To Abbot Adelilin. He intercedes for monks who had withdrawn from the monastery and, having recognized their fault, wished to return, 543.

Letter L: To Reginald, Sentunus, and Henry. He defends Saint Hilary against the calumnies of Berengar and teaches that his words, which Berengar was twisting into a perverse meaning, had been spoken and were to be interpreted in an orthodox sense, 543.

Letter LI: To Abbot T . . . He orders him to have an excommunicated adulteress expelled from the cemetery until she makes satisfaction to the bishop, 545.

Letter LII: To Abbot G . . . He commends Orricius, who was being detained by royal command in the abbot’s custody, 546.

Letter LIII: To Abbot Turstinus. He consoles his friend and advises him to try to bend the king through himself and through friends, and not to be saddened if the king rejects him, 546.

[Col. 1677]

Letter LIV: To his beloved and faithful G . . . He explains that in the counties entrusted to him he has no lordship of his own, but that all the lands of his church belong to the sustenance of the monks, 546.

Letter LV: To Abbot R . . . Concerning the monk for whom he had asked that he be received into the monastery, he now leaves the matter entirely to him and will approve whatever he decides, 547.

Letter LVI: To Abbot William. He asks that the monk Rainald be allowed to seek the monastery of Gloucester and live there under Abbot Serlo for the space of one year, 547.

Letter LVII: To Abbot O . . . He rebukes him for having granted his monk permission to wander; he advises him to receive the monk honorably after compelling him to return, and to show him fatherly affection as though he were a son, 548.

Letter LVIII: To his beloved Remigius. Many people speak ill of him to the king, though the king does not believe them. It would be advantageous for him to come to Lanfranc, so that Lanfranc may hear more from his own mouth, 548.

Letter LIX: To Hug . . . He does not approve of that man’s disparagement of Pope Gregory and praise of Clement. Although he believes that the emperor had reasons for his action, he advises him not to come to England without the king’s permission, 548.

Letter LX: To Abbot Rodulf. A monk who has promised stability in one monastery may, for just reasons, transfer to another, 549.

Letter LXI: To Margaret, queen of the Scots, 549.

Letter LXII: To the archdeacons of Bayeux, 550.

Notes and observations of Dom Lucas d’Achery, Benedictine monk, on the letters of Blessed Lanfranc, 551.
